# Manuscript Spine

->[Exterior Binding]<-

The spine of this volume is bound in a light tan silk fabric, now showing the heavy patina of age. Large, dark reddish-purple stains—likely resulting from spilled ink or pigment during its long history in a workshop or library—mark the upper and lower sections of the binding. 

The delicate silk has frayed significantly over time, particularly along the joints. In the center-left portion of the spine, a large rectangular section of the fabric has worn away entirely, revealing the structural layers of the binding underneath. There are no visible titles, dates, or library shelf marks on this portion of the exterior.

<meta>This page continues the cataloging and description of high-value items within the National Central Library of Florence, specifically focusing on a landmark 1481 edition of Dante's work.</meta>

In Codex 18, Shelf VI of this Library, there exists a document under the entry for Landini <note>referring to Cristoforo Landino (1424–1498), a humanist scholar and commentator on Dante</note>, which demonstrates that this is the very copy presented to the Lordship <term>Signoria; the governing body of Renaissance Florence</term> of Florence by Messer Cristoforo Landini. In return, he was gifted a tower in the Castle of Borgo alla Collina, his homeland in the Casentino region, in whose church his uncorrupted body still lies.

# Dante Alighieri, The Divine Comedy with the Commentary of Cristoforo Landino
## Florence, by Niccolò di Lorenzo della Magna. 1481. On vellum.

This copy, besides being extremely precious for other reasons, may be considered the only one printed on vellum <note>fine parchment made from animal skin</note>, because the other copy existing in the main Library of Paris <note>The Bibliothèque Nationale de France</note>, in addition to missing several pages, has almost all the others flawed; some of them are printed on one side only. It can be stated with confidence that the Paris copy was assembled using the vellum sheets discarded from the present copy. The Paris copy was originally part of the Niccolini Library and was sold in Paris in 1818, where it was acquired by that Library (then the Royal Library) for 821 Francs. The Magliabechiano copy <note>referring to the core collection of the Florence National Library, founded by Antonio Magliabechi</note> is the same one presented by Landino to the Lordship of Florence. In reward, he received a house at Borgo alla Collina in Casentino, his native village, where he was also buried in the parish church. 

At the beginning of this century, his mummified and perfectly preserved body was kept in a chest in the sacristy for the convenience of showing it to the curious. However, the Parish Priest, having received word that Princess Violante of Austria <note>Violante Beatrice of Bavaria (1673–1731), Grand Princess of Tuscany, often referred to as "of Austria" due to her Habsburg-Lorraine connections</note> wished to see it, noticed that because the body was entirely naked and the genital parts were quite distinct, he sought to prevent the scandal such a sight would cause to the Princess’s modest gaze. Knowing no other effective remedy, in his opinion, he mutilated the body; thus, the poor Landino found himself turned into a eunuch three centuries after his death. 

One can admire several tempera paintings of the finest workmanship in this book. The one framing the beginning of the *Inferno* surpasses the other three in the volume in beauty and labor. In it are depicted the coats of arms of the Republic, and in the lower margin, outside the border, the coat of arms of Landino himself appears in a small black shield. In the Initial N <note>The first letter of "Nel mezzo del cammin di nostra vita," the opening line of the Inferno</note>, there is a portrait of the Poet as imagined by the painter. Dante holds his radiant Poem open and pressed to his chest. The binding is adorned with beautiful silver nielli <term>niello; a black mixture used as an inlay in engraved metal</term> representing the arms of the Republic on the four corners. In the center of the covers, there are likewise two niello medallions: in one, Hercules is depicted (the seal of the Republic), and in the other, the Lion (known as the *Marzocco*) <note>the heraldic symbol of Florence</note> holding the banner with the Lily in its right paw. The ancient cover of white and red satin, worn by time, was removed in the last century and replaced with leather of the same colors.

The 4th of April, 1871.

--- Page 7 ---
<meta>This page marks the beginning of the "Proemio" (Preface) of the landmark 1481 edition of Dante’s Divine Comedy, featuring the influential commentary by the Florentine humanist Cristoforo Landino. This edition is famous for its attempt to reclaim Dante as a purely Florentine cultural hero during the Renaissance.</meta>

. i.

# COMMENTARY BY CRISTOFORO LANDINO, FLORENTINE,
# ON THE COMEDY BY DANTE ALIGHIERI,
# FLORENTINE POET

## PREFACE

<image-desc>The left margin features a lavishly illuminated border with intricate floral and foliate motifs in blue, red, gold, and green. It includes two medallions: the top one is blue with the word "FREEDOM" <note>original: "LIBERTAS"</note> in gold; the bottom one is a red shield with a white cross. The text begins with a large decorative initial "B" containing a red cross on a white background, symbolizing the People of Florence. At the bottom of the page is a circular library or collector's stamp depicting a seated figure on a throne.</image-desc>

ALTHOUGH THERE IS NO CLASS OF LEARNED WRITERS, our most illustrious lords, to whom the human race does not owe supreme, innumerable, and immortal thanks—especially considering that they have contributed all their industry, discipline, most vigilant study, and laborious late-night work for the common good, so that they might benefit not only themselves and their contemporaries, but also bring no small utility to all men who will have lived in various centuries in the years to come—nevertheless, I have often turned over in my mind the almost infinite number of those who have left a memory of themselves in either the Greek or Latin tongues, and I find no one who can be compared or equated to this poet. Certainly, through the depth and variety of his learning, and through the elegance, richness, and sublimity of his style, he can not only show us great things pertaining to our lives and our salvation, but he also adorns them by covering them with a sober and marvelous veil. Thus, beyond the incomparable utility drawn from such vast and varied learning, the joy of the soul and the pleasure of the senses taken by a well-educated mind and refined ears from such a poem is incredible. But we shall speak a little further down regarding the praises of the poetic faculty.

In the meantime, having been persuaded by most manifest arguments since my early youth—and having also been moved by the authority of many most learned men who, in different nations and languages, have always preferred poets over other writers—I have spent no small part of my life in the study of them. Now, because I had recently interpreted and translated into Latin letters the allegorical sense of Virgil's *Aeneid* <note>Landino refers to his work "Disputationes Camaldulenses," where he interpreted Virgil’s epic as an allegory of the soul's journey</note>, I judged that it would not be useless to my fellow citizens, nor unpleasant, if I were to investigate with the greatest possible study and industry the secret, hidden, and altogether most divine meanings of the *Comedy* by the Florentine poet Dante Alighieri. And just as I had expressed the Latin poet in the Latin tongue, I would interpret the Tuscan poet in the Tuscan tongue.

This is an undertaking which, without doubt, due to the greatness and multiplicity of the subject matter and especially its novelty, could bring the highest honor to any of the most literate men. Yet for me, who am decorated with neither great learning nor eloquence, it has been most laborious and perhaps not free from temerity. But the ardent love for this kind of Muse has made the weight less heavy; and as the well-worn proverb of the wise says, "Nothing is difficult to the lover." 

However, there will perhaps be some who judge our counsel to have been in vain if I have not brought what I proposed from the beginning to its proper end. Or they may deem it superfluous, since many have commented on this poem who, having been either contemporaries or close to the poet's time, seem to have been better able to understand his mind. Furthermore, by having made a profession of theology, they might more easily interpret the deep meanings hidden within him, which he has drawn divinely from the intimate secrets of that science, not without the wonder of those who read. Two of his sons, Francesco and Pietro, commented on our poet. Benvenuto of Imola commented on him, and he did so in Latin. Jacopo of Bologna commented on him in his native tongue. Brother Riccardo, a Carmelite theologian, commented on him. Andrea—I believe of Naples—commented on him, as did Guiniforte, a jurist from Bergamo. Our Giovanni Boccaccio began to comment on him, but he did not carry the work further than halfway through the first "cantica" <note>Referring to the Inferno, the first of the three parts of the Divine Comedy</note>. All of these I commend, because they have said many things worthy of their learning and not useless to the listener. Finally, Francesco da Buti commented on him in the Pisan language. This man, after Boccaccio, strove more than the others to reveal the allegorical sense, though not in all its parts.

But it seemed right to me to repeat the mind and purpose of Dante from a higher principle, and with a steady course to investigate in him more recondite learning. When I turn this over in my mind, a terrifying wonder is suddenly born within me, and I become almost like a bat in such great light. And like those who live near the cataracts of the Nile and become deaf from the excessive sound <note>A common classical reference found in Cicero and Pliny, suggesting that one can be overwhelmed by too much of a great thing</note>, so my intellect loses all its sharpness and judgment, overcome by the material and the invention. To such invention, the mind finds itself not only unequal, but not even fertile except after a long interval. 

Nevertheless, with divine favor aiding my fervent will, I have uncovered in some part some of the barely searchable traces of so divine a poet, following him first through the descending cliffs into the deep abyss. And then, pulled by his help up to the arduous ridge of Purgatory, I have led myself along a difficult path. And finally, elevated by his wings, I have seen the end of so long a pilgrimage. Regarding how much profit and utility I have achieved in this, I will leave such judgment to those more learned than I. This alone I affirm: I have liberated our citizen from the barbarism of many foreign idioms in which he had been corrupted by commentators. At present, appearing so pure and simple, I have deemed it my duty to present him to you, our most Illustrious Lords, so that by the hands of that magistracy which is supreme in the Florentine Republic, he may be restored to his homeland after a long exile. Let him be recognized as being neither Romagnolo, nor Lombard, nor of the idioms of those who have commented on him, but purely Florentine...

<summary>In this preface, Cristoforo Landino presents his new commentary on Dante's Divine Comedy to the leaders of Florence, arguing that Dante is a supreme poet whose work requires a "purely Florentine" interpretation to rescue it from previous "barbaric" dialects.</summary>
<keywords>Cristoforo Landino, Dante Alighieri, Divine Comedy, Florence, Humanism, Renaissance, literary criticism, Virgil, Aeneid, Boccaccio, vernacular literature</keywords>

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Proemio" (Preface) by Cristoforo Landino. Having established Dante's supreme intellect in the previous section, Landino now shifts to defending the Florentine dialect and addressing the common criticism that Dante was an enemy of his own city due to the harsh political critiques found in the Divine Comedy.</meta>

...as a clear witness of how much it surpasses all other Italian idioms: for no one in whom intellect or learning appeared ever wrote in verse or prose without striving to use the Florentine idiom. But we will speak of the language a bit later. Therefore, you, our most illustrious lords, recognizing in this volume of ours the divinity of Dante’s intellect—which anyone who recounts a numerous series and continuous succession of centuries and an ancient and very primal memory of all nations could count among the very few—recognizing also a stupendous accumulation of doctrine, of which variety, so recondite and so hidden, he who has known the most has barely known a mediocre part, you will congratulate your fatherland, to which the highest God has granted such a gift. And you will frequently read your poet, the first splendor of the Florentine name, the best and rarest example of eloquence and doctrine. For by imitating him, you will adorn your speech with eloquence and dignity, your life and customs with prudence and probity, and your mind with doctrine and humanity.

## APOLOGY IN WHICH DANTE AND
## FLORENCE ARE DEFENDED FROM FALSE ACCUSERS

<image-desc>Decorative initial "R" within a square frame. The letter is gold on a blue background with floral patterns. Inside the loop of the "R" is a small portrait medallion of a man in profile, possibly a scholar or poet.</image-desc>
The order of things required that the life and customs of the poet be continued and joined to the preface. But a false opinion, long ingrained in the minds of many, forces me to postpone the life for a short space and refute this [opinion], so that at the same time both my fatherland and the poet may be liberated from a grave slander, by which both are undeservedly offended. Many people read in various places of this *Comedy* bitter invectives against the Florentines who ruled in those times, and very sharp rebukes of their various and most wicked vices. This not only appears to be a disgrace to the city, but it also seems to bring blame upon the poet for obscuring the fame of his fatherland, which he ought to praise like a dutiful son. We, therefore, will first demonstrate that it is false that Dante vilifies his fatherland. Then, running through some examples of how things were administered, we will prove that not only does our republic not deserve blame, but on the contrary, it is necessary that by all those who are free of envy and do not lack judgment, it be placed most honorably among the first republics.

But let this be the beginning. Our poet was of such a noble spirit that he would have been indignant to openly call himself a Florentine if he had judged it to be an infamous fatherland. But in many places in the work, he seems to glory in being Florentine. Therefore, he judges Florence a most noble city. But there is no need to search for conjectures about his opinion and what he feels for his fatherland, since in many places he praises it so much. For in the *Inferno*, through the mouth of the magnanimous Farinata <note>Farinata degli Uberti, a Ghibelline leader whom Dante meets in the circle of the heretics; despite being a political enemy, Dante treats him with great respect.</note>, he calls it "noble fatherland." And in the twenty-fifth canto of the *Paradiso*, he desires greatly to return to it, calling it the "beautiful sheepfold." But a sheepfold is a sanctuary for innocent and benign animals. Therefore, he praises the city, and he praises the people contained within it for both beauty and virtue. And in the fifteenth canto of the *Paradiso*, he says:
*Florence, within the ancient walls,*
*From which she still takes her Tierce and Nones,* <note>Refers to the bells of the Badia Fiorentina marking the hours of the day.</note>
*Abided in peace, sober and modest.*
And what can be greater praise in a republic than to live in peace? This cannot happen without supreme prudence and justice. And that she lives "sober and modest" are two virtues which make for perfect temperance.

But I pray you, let us read this entire canto and we will understand how wonderfully the good poet praises the ancient fatherland, especially in these verses: *To such a restful, to such a beautiful / Living of citizens. To such a faithful / Citizenry. To such a sweet hostelry.* And in the sixteenth [canto] he writes: *With these people, and with others with them / I saw Florence in such repose / That she had no reason to weep. / With these people I saw your people so glorious / and just, that the lily / Was never placed backward on the spear / Nor made red by division.* <note>The "lily" is the *giglio*, the symbol of Florence. Dante refers to a time before the city's flag was changed from a white lily on a red field to a red lily on white due to internal civil war.</note> What infamy, then, can be given—or rather, what praise can be taken away—from a people who are just? This cannot be without supreme self-control and glory, since glory cannot be born except from many, excellent, and long-lasting virtues. I leave aside many other places in which, with every kind of praise, he magnifies and extols such a city.

But perhaps someone will say: "Read the places in which he vilifies the Florentines." To which I reply that he does not vilify the Florentines—whom, as we have shown elsewhere, he calls sober and tranquil, glorious and just—for it would be a great frivolity in such a great poet to write repugnant and self-contradictory things. But he vilifies those Florentines who, through ambition and faction, had become unjust, rapacious, cruel, and greedy. In the same way, Sallust <note>Gaius Sallustius Crispus, a Roman historian who critiqued the moral decline of the Roman Republic.</note> does not vilify Rome when he vilifies the ambition, luxury, and avarice of his times, or the perfidy of Catiline, Lentulus, or the other conspirators; or when he notes Albinus, Calpurnius, Scaurus, or many others with supreme infamy. Rather, by praising the ancient Roman discipline, he demonstrates how much these men had degenerated from their ancestors.

Dante, therefore, vilifies the wicked governors—or rather, the plunderers of his people. He asserts that they, instead of being true shepherds of the "beautiful sheepfold of Saint John" <note>San Giovanni (Saint John the Baptist) is the patron saint of Florence; the city is often called his sheepfold.</note>, are wolves. This we must grant him, both because he narrates true things and because, if he hurls a tragic invective against the worst citizens—or rather, impious tyrants—like a new Archilochus <note>An ancient Greek poet famous for his biting, aggressive satire.</note> shooting iambic verses in the form of pestiferous arrows, he nevertheless in many places most honorably exalts many others worthy of true praise and adorns them with perpetual fame. Add also that, having been unjustly made an exile and a rebel by those of his fatherland, he deserves excuse if he somewhat exceeds the limit through righteous indignation. And let this suffice for the defense of the poet.

<summary>Landino defends Dante against the charge of being a "hater" of Florence, arguing that the poet's harsh critiques were directed only at corrupt leaders and not at the city itself or its virtuous citizenry.</summary>
<keywords>Dante Alighieri, Florence, Apologia, Cristoforo Landino, Florentine idiom, political exile, Farinata degli Uberti, Sallust, Archilochus, republican virtue, Ghibellines, Guelphs</keywords>

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page continues Landino’s "Apology," shifting from a general defense of Florence to a specific argument about the city's Roman character and its excellence in both the active and contemplative spheres of life. It concludes with a historical account of Florence’s resistance to the tyranny of Walter of Brienne.</meta>

<sig>. ii.</sig>

Now, in praise of our **Republic**, I dare to affirm among the first things that she has never degenerated from the form of her founders: that she has always shown herself to be a true colony of Roman citizens. Because immediately around her beginnings—even though these were humble, as happens in almost all cities—she nonetheless laid great foundations of both justice and magnanimity. And afterwards, in the following times, administered with excellent institutions and laws, she first claimed her liberty. Then, loved for her supreme justice and feared for her great boldness of spirit in avenging injuries, she added many peoples to her empire without injustice. But so that the many and most egregious virtues of our people may appear more clearly, let us remember that according to the judgment of philosophers, there are only two generations of life lived according to reason. One is for those who, elevating themselves in contemplation, are entirely given to the investigation of the most excellent disciplines and doctrines: and this is called the **contemplative life**, signified in the Mosaic doctrine by **Rachel** and in the New Testament by **Mary**. The other is for men who, knowing themselves to have been produced not only to benefit themselves alone but others as well, as far as their own strengths extend, have taken up public care and government. Loving the social and civil life, they live in company: a life which the ancient Hebrews signify through the mystery of **Leah** and the first Christians through the anxious care of **Martha**. Who, then, will be so unfair a judge and estimator who, reviewing our ancient annals, would not find that there have been innumerable excellent men in the Florentine people in both the one and the other life?

But because in every nation and in every century there have always been more civil men than contemplative ones, let us repeat, I pray you, from the first cradles and from the origin of our city: and we shall see in every age how great has been the abundance of those who, through supreme prudence and sharpness of wit, have known how—and with greatness of spirit and true liberty, have been able—and with burning charity, have willed to well-advise and administer the Republic. And because it is a **Sallustian maxim** <note>original: "Salustiana sententia"; referring to the Roman historian Sallust</note>—though born from the most righteous sanctuaries of **Platonic discipline**—that in civil administration it is necessary first to consult well, and after wise counsel, to execute what has already been determined with mature speed: I could speak of the obscurity of our annals. Because they were written by men more truthful than eloquent, they gain faith through their simplicity from those who read them, yet they are read by few because of their rough style. Nevertheless, I could bring to light from that obscurity many who, in arduous and ambiguous cases, imitated the prudence of **Numa Pompilius**, and of **Fabius Maximus**, and of the two **Catos**, of **Sertorius**, and many others. If these men had not been celebrated by writers, they would be submerged in the same darkness as our own. And certainly, I approve the opinion of those who estimate that the Athenians did great things, but that the abundance and eloquence of their writers are the reason they appear much greater. So, by contrast, I do not hesitate to affirm that in our people, the style of the writer has been more lacking than the matter of the doer.

But let our oration return to where it began. Our ancestors did not lack prudence. But so that, along with prudence, their strength may also be known: what time was there ever in which they did not show invincible spirits and supreme confidence in adverse things? The city of **Lacedaemon** <note>Sparta</note> was universally held to be of bold spirit; so was **Carthage**. But we see both of them surpassed by the Romans. And among the Romans, **Julius Caesar** had a spirit equal to such great felicity. The two **Scipios** were bold men, who, manfully opposing **Hannibal** in Spain, fell. In the same family were the two **Africans**, and in the **Aemilian house**, the two **Pauli**. Without any fear, **Marcellus** ran toward every great enterprise, as did that **Gracchus** who, with a slave army, defeated the unconquered army of Hannibal. But the Florentine people have always had not just one **Farinata** <note>Farinata degli Uberti, a famous Florentine leader mentioned in Dante's *Inferno*</note>, but many at different times. Nor does it seem to me necessary to investigate individual examples, since I can demonstrate that my entire Republic at all times has had an invincible spirit, and in every calamity has always risen more manly and more audacious.

The Florentine liberty was miserably oppressed by **Gualtieri** <note>Walter VI of Brienne (c. 1304–1356), a French nobleman who became a short-lived tyrant of Florence</note>, who, with false titles, wished to be named the **Duke of Athens**. To him, after many civil discords, an annual dictatorship was granted by the people as to a man esteemed by all to be a true friend. And certainly, that versatile and subtle prince showed no small signs of probity and justice. Therefore, it was easy to persuade the credulous people that finally, through his authority, he would settle every civil sedition and bring about true tranquility and firm peace. But, O true God, how many are the hiding places in human breasts! How hidden are the counsels? With how many simulations? With how many dissimulations are the good deceived by fox-like minds! The wicked Gualtieri, then, took up the legitimate magistracy committed to his faith with the appearance of a gentle shepherd. But inside, he was a most rapacious wolf; he converted every power given to him into tyrannical cruelty. And with the favor of nearby princes and the army granted to him—with those very arms the people had granted him for their defense—he offended them. With supreme perfidy, he occupied the tyranny.

But celestial aid is not lacking to those who are not lacking to themselves; and in generous spirits, a righteous purpose overcomes every difficulty. A universal and heavy grief for their lost liberty appeared in everyone. But since there was no one ready to act as duke and guide for everyone in such great danger, different men were chosen by different groups. At one and the same time, many conspiracies—each knowing nothing of the other—armed themselves against the tyrant. Armed with spirit, they revealed themselves in such a way that, after not a few of his men were killed, he was forced to seek his safety by fleeing. Nor, in such a magnanimous recovery of liberty, is it clear which is more worthy of admiration: the greatness of spirit in daring against one who was bolstered by a great abundance of arms and men, or the faith and silence in which all the conspirators constantly persevered.

<summary>Landino argues that Florence is a direct successor to Roman virtue, excelling in both the active and contemplative lives, before detailing the city's heroic overthrow of the tyrant Walter of Brienne.</summary>
<keywords>Florence, Roman origins, Active Life, Contemplative Life, Rachel and Leah, Mary and Martha, Walter of Brienne, Duke of Athens, tyranny, liberty, Farinata degli Uberti, Sallust, Plato</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s argument for the greatness of Florence, moving from the city's Roman origins to specific historical examples of its resilience and moral integrity in the 15th century.</meta>

But let us hear this other example. It was in the age of our fathers—either by wicked fate or by the imprudence of the hired captains <note>original: "conductitii principi," referring to mercenary leaders or *condottieri*</note> of our armies—that the defeat of Zagonara occurred, a most unhappy event. It was no less calamitous to us than the Battle of Cannae was to the Roman Empire. <note>The Battle of Zagonara (1424) was a crushing defeat for Florence against Milanese forces; Cannae was Rome's legendary defeat by Hannibal.</note> The men-at-arms were lost. The horses were lost. The baggage trains were lost, and—what exceeded every other loss—the captains, who had been hired shortly before with an innumerable amount of money, were also lost. Because of this, the enemy remained not only most ferocious due to such a great victory, but also so wealthy from the rich plunder that their forces doubled in every respect. And who would have believed in those times that either the enemy troops would not have rushed to our very gates by the shortest route, or that our Republic, stunned by the sudden wound, would not have been forced without delay to accept those extreme conditions which the victor is accustomed to impose upon the vanquished? 

But, oh, invincible souls! Oh, true Roman colonists! The Florentine people immediately understood their losses, yet they did not grow faint-hearted upon hearing them. They did not yield to fortune. They did not fall into ultimate despair. Instead, in the briefest moment of time, a sudden gathering from all parts of the city was made before the supreme magistrate. Nor was anyone found who went there merely prepared with speeches to give advice; rather, each person brought as much as his own estate could bear, loaded with money to offer help. Nor was there long-winded debate, nor were various opinions voiced in the consultation. Instead, there was one sudden voice among all: that liberty should not be lost before life itself. And who would deny that this could seem admirable even in Rome or in Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note>? 

The treasury was exhausted by the heavy and most dangerous war. Private wealth was much diminished by large and constant taxes. And nonetheless, not in a day, but in a few hours—not by public decree, but by spontaneous and voluntary contribution—so many thousands of florins were paid out to the **Ten Men** <note>The "Dieci di Balìa," the committee responsible for diplomatic and military affairs during wartime</note> in charge of the wars, that with incredible speed they gathered and hired from all over Italy whoever was serving as captains, cavalry, or infantry. And at that time when our most powerful adversary expected a suppliant embassy from us, ready to receive any unfair condition, he saw a new army already opposed to his troops. From this, an honorable peace followed. 

Therefore, if the Roman Senate gloried in having had one **Appius the Blind** <note>Appius Claudius Caecus, who famously persuaded the Senate not to make peace with King Pyrrhus</note> who made Pyrrhus see that Rome was unworthy of defeat, who will be so unfair an estimator of things—so greedy a detractor of our praises—that he does not judge it worthy to place among the rarest examples the sight of such a high spirit in a people during such low fortune?

I have perhaps been too prolific in this one thing. But how can I pass over in silence what we have not merely heard from our ancestors, but have seen in our own times? The strength of our empire was much worn down by the war unjustly made upon us by **Alfonso of Aragon**, King of Naples; who, although emboldened by the power of his seven kingdoms and very eager to propagate his empire, had assaulted us with the greatest forces both by sea and by land. Nonetheless—to speak more honorably of him than of ourselves—he was finally forced to abandon the enterprise and return to his kingdom with a shattered and mutilated army. 

Our forces were thus much worn down, and behold, a new war was rekindled: not only by the aforementioned King, but by the most excellent Venetian Empire. Although not many years before, largely through our prompt assistance, they had expanded their empire into Lombardy, nonetheless, judging the death of **Filippo Maria** <note>Filippo Maria Visconti, Duke of Milan</note> to be an optimal occasion, they greatly desired the Duchy of the Visconti. They had most flourishing armies and the most ample treasures; and the fame of **Jacopo Piccinino** as the leader of their troops was already most widespread for every military virtue. The authority of the King carried great weight throughout all Italy. And on our side, it seemed that only the marvelous and innumerable virtues of **Francesco Sforza** remained—and the glory of such a Duke, who in all times was most invincible. We were exhausted; he was placed in the most extreme penury of all things with which wars are administered; and the novelty of his rule made every enterprise most dangerous. 

Indeed, there were many of the firm opinion that the Florentine people would have to yield to fortune and prefer convenience over faith <note>loyalty to one's word</note>, especially since the adversary invited us and offered us peace and confederation, provided that we remained neutral. But I could recount innumerable other examples which most clearly demonstrate that nothing at any time has ever been more esteemed in our Republic than faith. But in such grave danger, it was to be esteemed above all. 

There came into consultation, therefore, danger on one side and faith on the other. But in short, utility was conquered by honesty <note>moral integrity</note>, especially through the counsel and authority of the great **Cosimo de' Medici**, a man of as much prudence as the rarest advisors of republics have ever had. He, with the eyes of the two-faced Janus, foresaw future events as much as many do not even recognize present ones. And not only with his work and industry—which was marvelous and of a genius more than human—but also with his money, of which he was most abundant, he came to the aid of the public. 

In this way, the allied Duke <note>Francesco Sforza</note> was helped, so that he not only remained in the lordship he had shortly before acquired, but he took such a Duchy <note>Milan</note> out of the hands of the Venetian dominion. Although the Venetian dominion is deservedly held in the highest veneration among all peoples for its excellent administration, nonetheless it seemed it was rising to be too formidable by increasing so much in power. I believe that through these examples I have demonstrated with what an invincible spirit the Florentine people have been endowed. But in these same examples, as in a clear mirror, there also appears the image of the prudence and faith conserved by them at all times. 

I could mention many other excellent advisors: from the same **Medici** family, **Vieri**, a true Florentine knight and a man always attentive to public peace; **Bartolomeo Valori**; **Rinaldo Gianfigliazzi**, men of high counsel; **Niccolò da Uzzano**; **Giovanni**, father of the great Cosimo; **Gino Capponi** and **Neri** his son. Nor do **Lorenzo Ridolfi**, a most celebrated legal consultant, **Palla Strozzi**, **Piero Guicciardini**, **Niccolò Alessandri**, **Luca degli Albizzi**, and **Andrea Minerbetti** deserve to be passed over. To...

. iii .

...Manno Salviati. And in recent times, Giovanni Canigiani, a Florentine knight <note>original: "equite," a title of social rank and military honor</note> and a man most devoted to his fatherland, possessing very mature and farsighted judgment. But because, according to the teachings of Plato and Aristotle, counselors alone are not enough for a republic, there are also needed emulators and defenders <note>original: "propugnatori," those who fight on the front lines for a cause</note> who may avenge injuries received and defend liberty. Let us see then, with the greatest brevity, what our citizens have been capable of in every quarter. Nor do I deny that in the present centuries—just as with all other Italian republics and princes—we have not conducted our wars with mercenary armies and hired leaders <note>original: "duchi conductitii," referring to the *condottieri* or professional military contractors</note>. But let us remember the men who governed it, and the times in which no one else was in our army but the citizens themselves. The order of that ancient discipline is still known, and into what parts the people were divided and formed. The names of the captains <note>original: "prefecti"</note> remain. The standards and banners remain. We see hanging in our Baptistery in our own day that *Carroccio* <note>The *Carroccio* was a large four-wheeled chariot carrying the city's banners, serving as a sacred rallying point in battle</note>, the supreme banner of the people, which rarely returned without victory. Without fail, the celestial virtues—called "secondary causes"—can do much in matters committed to fortune; and deservedly so, because that "Immovable Mover" <note>A term for God derived from Aristotelian philosophy</note> who created them willed it so. For this reason, the very origin of the Florentines, enlightened by Mars, flourished immediately in the martial arts.

Fiesole was still powerful in the days when, where we now see our walls, only scattered buildings rose. It was always their constant will—or rather, their stubborn obstinacy—to oppress our city; and they almost could, because it seemed to them they had the power. They were highly reputed for their antiquity, confident in the number of their people, and, by the natural site of the mountain and human industry, they were impregnable. 

We, oppressed in the plain, unknown to our neighbors because of our novelty, and little esteemed because of our small number—what other remedy could we oppose to our adversaries, who assaulted us every day, if not a lively and most excellent virtue? The difficulties were most laborious and the assaults most dangerous as Florence rose; but it was even greater that, once built, she defended herself against a powerful enemy placed right above her head. War lasted between these two peoples not only for many years, but for ages—sometimes hidden and feigned, sometimes open war, and because of their proximity, almost a civil war. But at last <note>original: "tamden," a variation of the Latin *tandem*</note>, these bitter contentions produced a sweet victory, in which our people were victors through industry, and with the highest clemency, they shared their republic with their neighbors. Nor did they lack justice in observing the faith they had pledged, nor prudence in making their adversaries their own citizens, doubling their strength by reducing two peoples into one. This concord was so effective that in the following times, although all of Italy was submerged by a perpetual and long-lasting flood of various barbarian nations, and Florence was nearly desolated, nonetheless, in a short time, she grew marvelously. 

It is not my intention, most illustrious lord, to recount at present how many times our army—your army, I say—not filled with mercenary soldiers but composed of your own citizens, not guided by an external captain but ordered by its own leaders, brought back the widest victories, with which it expanded our very narrow borders. The people of Volterra are witnesses to this, who, cast down from such a high rock, saw our men enter by force and occupy the land. The people of Epifani <note>Possibly a reference to a local territory or specific campaign</note> are witnesses. The people of Arezzo, of Fano, and of Lucca are witnesses, all of whom remained inferior in every enterprise in the end. And who restored their fatherland to the Guelph faction of Bologna? The Florentines. Who to those of Modena? The Florentines. Who to those of Reggio? The Florentines. It was by the work of our captain Forese Adimari that Casca—a man of great strength and giant stature—fell in the square. Who in the Kingdom of Naples performed the best deeds against Manfred and largely turned the victory toward King Charles and the papal faction? The Florentines. From this, the Guelph name acquired so much praise from the Supreme Pontiff. From this, it was distinguished with the most honorable titles. From this, it received excellent privileges granted to few others. From this, our immortal friendship with the House of France, begun in the times of Charlemagne, was renewed. Nor did Niccolò d’Este, Marquis of Ferrara, defend his principality with any other army than with fifteen hundred *barbute* <note>original: "barbute," a term for armored cavalry units named after the style of helmet they wore</note>—as they called men-at-arms in those times—all of whom were Florentine citizens and largely nobles, whom our Republic sent to aid the allied prince. 

The conflict at the Arbia <note>The Battle of Montaperti (1260), fought on the banks of the Arbia River, a famous Florentine defeat</note> was most unhappy, in which about three thousand of our men fell fighting manfully. But let the enemies not exult much over it, nor let the imperial troops and squadrons take glory for it. For those were not equal to our men; rather, it was the prudence of Farinata degli Uberti, and the most burning civil hatred of the Florentine Ghibellines who were exiles at that time, and our commoner deserters, who because of factionalism abandoned our standards all at once and turned with the exiled Ghibellines against the *Carroccio*. Thus, the Florentines were not defeated by the Sienese, but by their own Florentine rebels. And certainly, there was in Farinata a Caesarean greatness of soul; a Fabian prudence; in Guido Guerra, a Papirian speed and a hawk-like eye in foreseeing future events and providing for them. And if the military deeds of those centuries had found a wealth of good writers, certainly we too would have someone not much different from Camillus, some imitator of Africanus, some rival to Marcellus <note>References to great Roman generals: Camillus, Scipio Africanus, and Marcus Claudius Marcellus</note>; and it would be seen that these were men not much degenerated from the likes of Marius, Pompey, Fabricius, and Cincinnatus. 

But certainly, fortune prevails in all things: for even among the most excellent men, I know not by what fate the fame of many can be obscured if writers are lacking. But I will not omit this other example. Our fathers saw the sober Niccolò Acciaiuoli, who governed the Kingdom of Naples. They saw Pippo Spano <note>Filippo Scolari, known as Pippo Spano, a Florentine who became a legendary commander in Hungary</note> among the Hungarians—what an immortal man of God!—who through his admirable virtues rose through all military ranks to the supreme level. Twenty-three times he went into pitched battle against the Turks, and every time he brought back a glorious victory. Nor did he only fight against barbarian peoples, but also in Italy as a duke for the armies of Sigismund Augustus <note>Emperor Sigismund</note>, he occupied Friuli and in battle...

...already defeated Carlo Malatesta. Leonardo Bruni saw him when he was already an old man; Bruni, who wrote the Florentine histories <note>Referring to the *Historiarum Florentini populi libri XII*</note> most elegantly, and who had most diligently read the Greek and Latin [authors] of every age. This man affirmed that from Julius Caesar until his own times, one could find no one who should be judged superior to Filippo Spano <note>Filippo Scolari, known as Pippo Spano (1369–1426), a Florentine who became a legendary military commander in Hungary</note> in military discipline. We read that the wisdom of Hannibal was very profound, and among his first deeds his cunning is commended, with which he, though besieged on all sides, was able to escape the hands of Fabius Maximus. Mithridates is also much praised for a similar kind of virtue. 

But in what part was the admirable astuteness of Filippo inferior? Especially at Belgrade, when, by feigning extreme fear, he lured and led the enemies into a place where—using only vessels of stone <note>Likely referring to boulders or stone-filled containers</note> rolled down from a high place over steep and sloping cliffs—he killed as many thousands as twice the number of the gates of Florence. This was, without fail, a stupendous wit: that with a thing that might sooner move one to laughter than fear, the hostile ranks were broken in such a manner that he afterwards easily killed them all with a small number of his own men. 

But I return to more ancient times. During the reign of Honorius III, the Emperor Otto <note>Otto IV, though Landino may be conflating details of the Fifth Crusade</note> crossed the sea for the conquest of Damietta <note>A strategic port in Egypt</note>, and many peoples from Italy followed him. In our city, a robust troop was formed, filled with many commoners. But from the noble families, among the first were: Bonaguisa della Pressa (from whom the house of Bonaguisi is descended), Florio dell’Arca, Lamberto Lamberti, Masseo Ubaldini, Donato Donati, Francesco Vitella, Ormanno Foraboschi, Federigo Pigli, Verde Infangato, and Niccolò Giuochi. Furthermore, the Bostichi, the Soldanieri, and those of the Tosa family. 

Damietta was manfully defended by the Saracens, and well furnished with walls and every kind of defense. But virtue overcomes every difficulty. The Christians besieged it and fought it every day; and finally, Bonaguisa was the first commander of our people who, with his troop, scaled the walls and fixed our red and white standard <note>The traditional colors of the Florentine Republic</note> upon the battlements. And although it was not without the loss of many of his men, he was the first to enter the city. His courage was undoubtedly great in the climbing, greater in the staying, and greatest in throwing himself inside among the most crowded and thickest of the enemies. For this reason, he was ordained a "Gilded Knight" <term>aurato equite</term> <note>A high-ranking knightly title often bestowed by emperors or popes</note> by Otto, and honored in many other things. 

And since we have made mention of overseas affairs, I will add Federigo Solchi, who, to the wonder of the fleet of the Great Master of Rhodes <note>The Knights Hospitaller</note>—and supported by three brothers and eight nephews, all distinguished in the sacred militia—reported glorious victory in eighteen battles and took ample spoils from the Saracen enemies. 

Worth of every military leader was, first, the counsel and then the frank enterprise of Giovanni de' Medici in succoring the nearly lost town of Scarperia. In those times, this land was besieged by the Prince of the Milanese <note>The Visconti of Milan</note> and surrounded by his valid armies in such a way that it seemed impossible that any help could be brought to it. But what can a man not do when he does not lack wit, does not lack will, and does not lack courage? Giovanni was most swift in gathering the people. He was diligent in choosing the most useful. He was cautious in scouting the place and the time. He was of invincible spirit in assaulting the enemies and making his way with the sword. 

The recently passed age saw Nanni Strozzi, to whom the Marquis of Mantua entrusted his entire army, in which there were three thousand horses; and he was always honorably defended by him from the forces of the Duke of Milan. It saw Piero di Carlo of the same family <note>The Strozzi family</note> who, with two hundred of our lances, forcibly occupied one of the gates of Milan through the hope of a conspiracy. And on the day of our "more than prophet," the Baptist <note>St. John the Baptist, the patron saint of Florence</note>, he made the horses run for a prize <term>palio</term> placed at the walls <note>Running a horse race outside the walls of a besieged city was a supreme gesture of defiance and insult to the enemy</note>. 

It saw in the Altoviti family Meo Altoviti, a captain for the Lord of Padua, who, to succor Verona when it was besieged by the most powerful army of the Duke of Milan, assaulted the enemies with two hundred lances. And with the sword—a marvelous thing to those who saw it—he opened a way for his men through the armed enemies, and manfully rebuffing them by force, he entered the city and freed it from the siege. This deed was esteemed by all as being of no small prudence, but of such courage that he was ever after called "Meo the Fearless." 

Among the most ancient families of Florence, the Ubaldini are numbered. But there still lives one who saw Bernardino Ubaldini—named for their castle of La Carda—a most excellent leader of armies, of whom I would relate egregious deeds if a green memory of them did not still remain in gray heads <note>Meaning the deeds are so recent that they are still remembered by living elders</note>. At this point, my path is cut short, so that I must remain silent on a matter that deserves to be placed among the most excellent, and by which alone the Florentine name could be immortal, provided I were allowed to pronounce the truth. But one cannot always do what one desires. 

Nevertheless, every man knows how much the Carthaginian Hamilcar was surpassed in every kind of military virtue by his son Hannibal. To many, this will seem an obscure enigma; but I do not despair of being understood, because the world is never without an Oedipus <note>The mythical solver of riddles</note> nor without a Sphinx <note>Referring to the rumor that the great general Federico da Montefeltro was the biological son of Bernardino Ubaldini; Landino is being cautious for political reasons</note>.

->FLORENTINES EXCELLENT IN LEARNING<-

<image-desc>A large, illuminated initial 'S' in blue with white vine patterns, set within a multi-colored (red, green, and gold) square frame.</image-desc>

If I insist further on the civic life, it is because even in the contemplative life, there is no kind of learning celebrated among the ancients by which the Florentine name does not remain most adorned. Philosophy is the mother of all the good arts, and from her, as from a most overflowing fountain, every doctrine is derived. And I could name in "First Philosophy"—which even our people call by the Greek word "Theology"—nearly infinite men. But whom can we place before Luigi Marsili? Or Leonardo Dati? To whom all the schools of philosophers in their times yielded. Who before Bartolomeo Lapacci? But read, I pray, the great volumes of Antonino <note>Saint Antoninus (Antonino Pierozzi), the Archbishop of Florence and author of the *Summa Theologica*</note>, who, both for the holiness of his life and for the greatness of his learning, was placed over the Florentine church as pastor by Eugenius IV, although he much refused it...

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s survey of illustrious Florentines. Having previously discussed military leaders, he now turns to the city's great theologians, scientists, architects, and the institutions of charity and faith that define Florence’s character.</meta>

...to whom not only the Florentine but also the Roman church was entrusted. In our times, no one was more diligent in meditation; no one wrote more things, nor more useful, nor more learned. A marvelous man and a prince among the physicians and theologians of his day, Roberto of the noble Bardi family <note>Roberto de' Bardi (died 1349) was a prominent theologian and chancellor of the University of Paris</note> lived in Paris. He held the chancellorship of the University of Paris for forty years. He refuted thirty-eight theological conclusions of Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century German Dominican friar and philosopher</note> and Thomas Aquinas <note>The highly influential Italian Dominican friar and Doctor of the Church</note>; nor has there been anyone since who has refuted his refutations. He lived without a wife in a chaste and celibate life.

Not only has the doctrine of our religion been celebrated, but that religion itself has always been adorned and cultivated with every diligence in our city. The beauty and greatness of the temples are well known. In them, I confess that the most precious jewels of the Venetian Saint Mark <note>Referring to the treasures of St. Mark's Basilica in Venice</note> are stupendous things, worthy of such a dominion. But let one look at our own temples and the silver of the vessels, and the other items dedicated to divine worship. Look at the wonderful abundance of gold and silk cloths in the consecrated vestments. Look with what dignity and majesty divine worship is celebrated with pontifical ceremonies. 

But what may be truly admirable—both for their number and their adornment—are the seventy-four monasteries (called *monasterii*) within the city and in the suburbs. All of these house a community of men or women; of these, not a few are the size of castles, with wonderfully decorated buildings. Some were built by various citizens among our ancestors, and in our own age, not a few were built by the most magnificent Cosimo de' Medici <note>The de facto ruler of Florence and a great patron of the arts and architecture</note>. Furthermore, besides the monasteries, there are fifty-three parish churches. There are thirty-five hospitals, among which I dare to place Santa Maria Nuova <note>Founded in 1288, it remains one of the oldest and most significant hospitals in Europe</note> as the first among all Christians. In this place, more than three hundred sick people are continuously cared for, month after month. There are always—though it be a very difficult task—clean white beds chosen, and always someone to watch over the sick and provide for their needs at every hour. Neither the room, nor the food, nor the medicine is common to all, but rather specialized for each person according to their disease. Physicians, doctors of physics, and surgeons are always ready, and they provide orders for everyone individually. Because of this, many foreign men, both noble and very wealthy, who were overcome by some illness while traveling, have chosen this residence for their care.

But I return to the scholars. There were two lights of our homeland: Torrigiano of the Valori family <note>Torrigiano de' Torrigiani (died c. 1350), a famous physician</note> (who were formerly called the Rustichelli) and Dino del Garbo <note>A famous 14th-century Florentine physician and philosopher</note>. The volumes written by them manifest how much they were capable of in physics and medicine. Torrigiano was such a sharp theorist that in the interpretations he wrote of Avicenna <note>The Persian polymath Ibn Sina, whose medical texts were standard in Europe for centuries</note>, he is named by everyone as more than just a commentator. Dino del Garbo wrote on Galen's <term>On the Malice of Complexion</term> <note>original: *de malitia complexionis*; a medical text regarding the balance of bodily humors</note> and on the book *On the Differences of Fevers*. He also wrote very learnedly on the nature of the fetus. Taddeo <note>Taddeo Alderotti, a pioneer of medical education in the 13th century</note> wrote on Hippocrates and on the *Regimen of Acute Diseases*, and on the *Amphorisms* <note>Referring to the *Aphorisms* of Hippocrates</note>. He also wrote on Avicenna. Nor will I leave behind Niccolò Falcucci, who in eight very widely circulated sermons manifested and opened up all of physics and the practice of medicine. And today there live not a few who are either already perfect or are making such progress on the path that leads to perfection that they will achieve a great name in future centuries among those who come after us. 

We see in our times Giannozzo Manetti <note>A humanist scholar and diplomat known for his vast linguistic skills</note>, an excellent physician and metaphysician, and learned in three foreign languages <note>Latin, Greek, and Hebrew</note>. He translated from Greek; he translated not a few and very useful books from Hebrew. He wrote on moral and natural philosophy. 

But where do I leave Leon Battista Alberti <note>The quintessential "Renaissance Man"—architect, artist, and theorist</note>, or in what generation of the learned should I place him? You might say among the physicists. Certainly, I affirm him to have been born solely to investigate the secrets of nature. But what branch of mathematics was unknown to him? He was a geometer. He was an arithmetician. He was an astrologer. He was a musician. And in perspective, he was more marvelous than any man of many centuries. Nine books of architecture <note>Alberti's *De re aedificatoria*</note>, most divinely written by him, clearly demonstrate how much all these doctrines shone within him; they are filled with every kind of learning and illustrated with the highest eloquence. He wrote on painting. He wrote on sculpture (the book which is titled *The Statue*). Nor did he only write, but he created with his own hand; and there remain in our hands most highly commended works of the brush, the chisel, the burin, and of casting made by him.

But since we have entered into this kind of learning, let us remember Guido Bonatti <note>A famous 13th-century astrologer</note> of Florence; although he took such offense at his exile that, making his home in Forlì, he wished to be called not a Florentine but a man of Forlì. This man in his time was very truthful in his judgments. He wrote a most useful volume for astrologers, universal in every kind of doctrine. In his final years, he entered the Order of Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans</note> and was seen humbly begging for bread. 

Let us remember Paolo the mathematician <note>Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli (1397–1482), the mathematician and astronomer who famously sent a map to Columbus</note>, whose tomb remains most honorably placed in the Church of the Trinity. But even greater monuments are impressed in his writings, which neither the age of centuries, nor the injury of the heavens, nor iron or fire will be able to harm. And although it is my intention not to name any of the living, I will nonetheless add to this first Paolo a second one <note>Likely referring to a contemporary like Paolo di Middelburg or another scholar of the same name</note> who has already reached his final old age—a man practiced and most learned in the same doctrine, and also an excellent physicist and physician, and to us a venerable image of antiquity.

### EXCELLENT FLORENTINES IN ELOQUENCE.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'E' featuring an architectural scene or landscape within the frame of the letter.</image-desc>

**E**loquence is a most wonderful thing among men. And since two things are proper to man—and in which no other animal participates—namely Wisdom and Eloquence, nonetheless there have been many more who were wise than who were eloquent. It is certainly a stupendous marvel that, although speech is common to all men, those who become excellent in it are extremely rare. Eloquence is the queen of men, and when it is joined with probity and true virtue, it is more useful than all other things. Truly, this can inflame the sluggish toward every honorable danger, and extinguish the spirits...

<meta>This page continues Landino’s preface, moving from the religious and civic institutions of Florence to a defense of its literary supremacy. He traces the lineage of Latin and vernacular eloquence from the Roman collapse through the "resurrection" of letters led by Dante, Petrarch, and the Humanists.</meta>

...infuriated: and to return them from tumult and sedition to tranquility. But it is not the right time to recount his praises. 

I affirm only that few things exist in that art that are not common to both the poet and the orator. These two types of writers grew as the Latin Empire grew; and they reached their peak in **Virgil** <note>Publius Vergilius Maro (70–19 BCE), the greatest Roman poet</note> and in **Cicero** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), the Roman statesman and orator whose Latin style became the gold standard for Humanists</note>. Afterward, as the Empire diminished, they also declined. And finally, when Italy was submerged by various floods of barbarian nations, they perished entirely. But why do I ask this? I have set it down so that the Florentine people might obtain favor from all of Italy for two reasons. 

First, because as **Petrarch** <note>Francesco Petrarca (1304–1374), the scholar and poet often called the "Father of Humanism"</note> writes in one of his orations: the last laureate poet held in esteem in the Latin language was the Florentine **Claudian** <note>Claudius Claudianus (c. 370–404 CE). Though historically associated with Alexandria, Landino claims him for Florence to bolster the city's prestige</note>. And second, because the first person who, after the resurrection of the poetic faculty, received the laurel crown was Petrarch. This was because **Dante** <note>Dante Alighieri (1265–1321), author of the Divine Comedy</note> refused to accept such an honor unless he could receive it in the Florentine Baptistery. Our city was, therefore, the last in which such a faculty was extinguished, and the first in which it was reignited. 

The father of Claudian was a great Florentine merchant, but learned and eloquent. Seeing Italy as continuous prey due to the frequent invasions of barbarians, he sailed to Egypt; and in Canopus, a city above one of the branches of the Nile, he took a wife with whom he had previously been in love, and fathered Claudian. For this reason, many affirm him to be Egyptian. This poet flourished in the times of **Theodosius** <note>Theodosius I (reigned 379–395 CE), the last emperor to rule over both the Eastern and Western halves of the Roman Empire</note>. He was a pagan at first, but later became a Christian. Our Republic, then, deserves favor from all of Italy: since within it were born the first men who brought both forms of eloquence—not only dead, but buried for so many centuries—back to life, and recalled them from <term>Tartarean darkness</term> <note>original: "tartarce tenebre"; referencing Tartarus, the deep abyss of torment in Greek mythology, used here to represent the "Dark Ages"</note> into clear light. 

Read, I pray you, the contemporaries of **Guido Cavalcanti** <note>A major Florentine poet and friend of Dante</note>; and you will judge that there is a tasteless infancy in them, containing nothing that is not most vulgar. But in Guido, there began to appear—if not fully expressed, then at least shadowed—not a few oratory and poetic ornaments; and he could have been esteemed for his sober and learned style, had he not been overtaken by a greater light, becoming as the moon does to the sun. 

But of Dante and Petrarch, we shall speak in another place. Here, we shall refer to them only with the greatest, infinite, and immortal praises: because they rediscovered the path, lost for many years, which leads the lovers of the Muses to **Parnassus** <note>The mountain home of the Muses in Greek mythology</note> and to the **Pegasean spring** <note>The Hippocrene fountain, said to have been created by the hoof of Pegasus and a source of poetic inspiration</note>. It had been covered with thorns and briars and was thus unknown, but they cleared it in such a manner that it has since been trodden by many. 

**Giovanni Boccaccio** <note>Author of the Decameron and a key figure in the transition to Humanism</note> imitated their footsteps. **Zanobi da Strada** <note>A scholar and poet (1312–1361) who was a friend of Boccaccio</note> also imitated them, not without reward for his vigils. Indeed, through the favor of **Niccolò Acciaiuoli** <note>A powerful Florentine statesman and Grand Seneschal of the Kingdom of Naples</note>, he became known to the Supreme Pontiff, and his virtues became known to the Pope. For this reason, he was crowned one day with the laurel crown, and the Pope appointed him among the first protonotaries to promote him to a higher rank. But, overtaken by an untimely death—not without loss to that century—he ended his days in the forty-ninth year of his life. 

The public letters of **Coluccio Salutati** <note>Chancellor of Florence (1331–1406) and a central figure in early Renaissance Humanism</note> were highly esteemed everywhere. This was not only because the ornaments of the ancient orators began to shine in them once again, but also because he was well-practiced in every study of philosophy; and to universal learning, he brought a most sharp wit and very wise judgment. He was most effective in affirming and refuting; his style was grave and deliberate, filled with impregnable arguments and abundant in every wealth of thought. Hence, the Prince of the **Visconti** <note>The ruling family of Milan, who were the bitter enemies of Florence</note>, a fierce enemy to the Florentine name, used to say that the letters of Coluccio did him more harm than a thousand horsemen. Some volumes written by him are highly prized. 

**Leonardo Bruni** <note>The first modern historian and a successor to Coluccio as Chancellor</note> succeeded him; he was the first to restore to the ancient language its original ornaments. **Poggio Bracciolini** <note>A famous humanist and book-hunter who recovered many lost classical texts</note> followed. But I pass over these two in silence, because many volumes make them famous in every place where the Latin tongue resounds. 

Nor do I wish to pass over **Ambrogio**, General of the Camaldolese <note>Ambrogio Traversari (1386–1439), a monk and scholar who bridged the gap between Greek patristics and Humanism</note>. Besides being ornate, he is so easy and so sweet that just as Tyrtamus—the excellent Peripatetic—was nicknamed **Theophrastus** <note>original: "Teophrasto .i. di diuina elocutione"; from the Greek 'Theos' (god) and 'phrasis' (speech)</note> by men for his living oratory, so I believe divine providence willed that from the sweetness of his speech, which was to be in him, he was named Ambrogio <note>A play on "Ambrosia," the food of the gods</note> from childhood. 

His disciple was **Gabriello**, my paternal uncle, a writer of lyric verses, who wrote very elegant odes in honor of Augustine, Jerome, and Ambrose. Afterward, he began the Pisan War in heroic verse, where he rose with great spirit and could have pleased every learned man; but, prevented by an untimely death, he left the work imperfect. **Leonardo Dati**, nephew of Leonardo the most learned theologian, was a man of excellent style in prose; but as a noble poet, he wrote most graceful elegies and very grave tragedies. 

There comes to my mind the style of **Leon Battista Alberti** <note>The famous "Universal Man" of the Renaissance, architect, and theorist</note>, who, like a new **Chameleon**, always takes on the color of the thing about which he writes. To no one living at present was **Donato Acciaiuoli** unknown; though philosophy drew him entirely to itself, he nevertheless did not give himself to such studies before he had acquired great strength and not a few ornaments in his style. But we have narrated his eloquence and the volumes written by him at length in the funeral oration we gave at the public gathering of his obsequies. 

**Matteo Palmieri** <note>Florentine humanist and politician</note> wrote *De Temporibus* <note>original: "de temporibus" (On Times), a chronological history</note>, a clear and very useful volume, which has been mutilated by the printers with great injustice. He is of such invention in his poem written in Tuscan verses in imitation of Dante that, had he not fallen into some heresy, he could easily have lived on <note>Palmieri's poem, "La Città di Vita," was condemned for suggesting that human souls were the angels who remained neutral during Lucifer's rebellion</note>. 

Untimely death took **Lapo da Castiglionchio** <note>Lapo da Castiglionchio the Younger (1405–1438), a humanist translator</note>, who, in his work on nobility and in that on avarice, showed an ornate style and a youthful abundance that was perhaps somewhat playful. But as Cicero and Quintilian demonstrate, such a vice is a sign of great virtue in tender years. Certainly, in the things which he translated from the Greek into the Latin language with the greatest ease, the meanings are seen to be faithfully transferred; and the quality of the style is preserved with such diligence that nothing appears changed except the language. **Niccolò Niccoli** <note>A wealthy bibliophile and center of the Florentine humanist circle who famously refused to write anything himself, fearing it would not meet his own high standards</note> left no monument or vestige of eloquence, except the testimony of his contemporaries...

<summary>Landino presents a history of Latin and Italian literature, arguing that Florence resurrected the arts of poetry and oratory after their medieval decline. He catalogs the city's great Humanist scholars, from the giants Dante and Petrarch to the political chancellors and translators who restored classical elegance to the West.</summary>

...and praise his style. But certainly, no one was a more diligent investigator of antiquity: and in truth, every man of letters found in him another **Lucullus** or **Maecenas** <note>Lucius Licinius Lucullus and Gaius Maecenas were famous Roman patrons of the arts; their names became synonymous with generous support for scholars</note> insofar as his means allowed, for he showed himself to be of every kind of liberality.

Many of those still living remain; whom I do not name here to avoid inciting envy. But certainly, our republic is filled with men illustrious in every branch of letters. Nor was there ever a time where eloquence was more joined with doctrine. We have an abundance of **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of the philosophy of Aristotle, who taught while walking in the Lyceum</note>. But we can also boast of having those who have brought the **Platonic discipline** <note>A reference to the Platonic Academy in Florence, led by Marsilio Ficino and supported by the Medici</note> back to the light. Poets arise. Historians arise: who in the future shall not be defrauded of their fitting honors. 

But I truly believe I can conclude that in the adornment of speech, Florence follows in the footsteps of Greek Athens. This is fitting in its very name, if it is true what notable Greek writers report: that Athens was not named after **Athena** <note>original: 'athena .i. Minerva'</note> (that is, Minerva), but from ***anthos*** <note>original: 'anthos .i. fiore'</note> (that is, "flower"). It is fitting that just as that city surpassed all other noble dialects, so this city surpasses all other Italian ones. And eloquence is innate to this nation. Concerning this, beyond experience, I can offer many examples: for many princes use the work of Florentines in their embassies. 

But it was a marvelous thing to anyone who judges without envy: that at the creation of **Boniface VIII** <note>Pope from 1294 to 1303</note>, a time when eloquent men are always chosen to congratulate a new assumption to the papacy, twelve Florentine ambassadors were sent most honorably by twelve different princes, with all the pomp customary for such times. Thus, **Vermiglio Alfani** was the legate of the Emperor. **Musiatto Franzesi** was for the King of France. **Ugolino da Vicchio** for the King of England. **Rinieri Langru** for the King of Bohemia. **Simone de’ Rossi** for the Emperor of Constantinople. The **Great Tartar** <note>The Mongol Khan</note> also sent **Guicciardo Bastari** with a hundred Tartars. The King of Apulia sent **Manno Adimari**. **Federigo**, King of Sicily, sent **Guido Talancha**. The Grand Master of Rhodes sent **Bencivenni Folchi**, I believe the nephew of the Admiral mentioned above. Finally, there were also legates **Lapo**, son of **Farinata degli Uberti**, and **Cino di Dietisalvi**—the former for the Republic of Pisa and the latter for **Gherardo**, Lord of Camerino. 

This circumstance caused such admiration in the Supreme Pontiff that, in the senate of the first fathers, he affirmed that the Florentines were the **fifth element** <note>Traditionally, there were four elements: earth, air, fire, and water. By calling them the "fifth element," the Pope suggested Florentines were essential to the functioning of the world</note> in human affairs. And certainly, such a numerous delegation from a single city was a marvelous thing. But it is no less worthy of admiration that in this same republic, a single family had such singular men that, at one time, they were sent as ambassadors by three different powers. While matters pertaining to the common safety of Italy were being treated in the most excellent city of Venice, and legates were coming from every side, the Florentine people sent **Messer Palla**, the Marquis of Ferrara sent **Messer Nanni**, and the Marquis of Mantua sent **Messer Ruberto**—all three from the **Strozzi** family of Florence. And let this suffice regarding eloquence.

### FLORENTINES EXCELLENT IN MUSIC

<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial 'N' featuring a seated scholar or philosopher at a lectern or desk, possibly representing Landino or a classical figure.</image-desc>

Nor was music ignoble in the Florentine republic. How much power nature has placed in music is marvelously demonstrated by all the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who believed the universe was governed by musical/mathematical ratios</note> and a great part of the Platonists. Even the philosopher **Socrates**, a man of such gravity that he was judged the wisest by the Oracle of Apollo, learned music most avidly in the eightieth year of his life. Nor is the opinion of the Sicilian **Aristoxenus** <note>A Greek philosopher and theorist of music</note> entirely false—if rightly understood—that our soul is **harmony**. 

In this field, I could mention many excellent men. But the love of my lineage requires that I do not defraud of his due praise **Francesco the Blind** <note>Francesco Landino (c. 1325–1397), a famous composer and the author's great-uncle</note>, the brother of my grandfather. Nature granted him as much judgment in hearing as she took from him in sight. It is certainly a marvelous thing that, entirely deprived of sight, he was not unlearned in philosophy, nor unlearned in astrology, but in music he was most learned. He was so skilled in playing the organ that in the most noble city of Venice—by the judgment of all the musicians who had gathered there from all parts—he was crowned with the **laurel wreath** by the King of Cyprus and the Venetian Doge. 

But our own times have seen and heard in our temples **Antonio**, surnamed "**of the Organs**" <note>Antonio Squarcialupi (1416–1480), the most famous organist in 15th-century Italy</note>. Of him, I will mention only this: that just as one reads that many came to Rome from the city of Gades in furthest Spain just to see the historian **Livy**, so too from England and the extreme North, many most excellent in music crossed the sea, the Alps, and the Apennines just to hear the music of Antonio.

### FLORENTINES EXCELLENT IN PAINTING AND SCULPTURE

<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial 'R' featuring a standing figure in classical or Renaissance robes, possibly representing an artist or patron.</image-desc>

There remains painting, which among the ancients was never held in low esteem. The Egyptians write that painting was their invention and that it came from Egypt to Greece. But some Greeks say it was found in **Sicyon**, others in **Corinth**. The first paintings consisted of a single line, with which they traced a man's shadow. Afterward, they began to paint with a single color; hence such painting was called **Monochrome** <note>original: 'Monocromata .i. dun solo colore'</note>, that is, "of one color," because *monos* means "alone" and *chroma* means "color." Nor was it very ancient, because according to **Pliny**, in the times of the Trojan Wars, painters were not yet found. 

The first in Greece were **Serdice of Corinth** and **Theophane of Sicyon**. But **Parrhasius of Ephesus** raised it to great dignity. Many followed who were praised by many, among whom the first rank is held by **Apelles**, reputed by all to be insuperable even in future centuries. But after reaching perfection, this art—like many others—was almost extinguished during the "Italian servitude" <note>A term used by humanists to describe the period between the fall of Rome and the Renaissance</note>. And the paintings in those centuries were not at all lifelike, and without...
