<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s "Proemio" (Preface), moving from the literary excellence of Florence to its revolutionary achievements in the visual arts, followed by its contributions to Civil Law and its immense economic power through trade.</meta>

...without any bias of the mind. Therefore, the first was Giovanni the Florentine, surnamed **Cimabue** <note>Cenni di Pepo, known as Cimabue (c. 1240–1302), credited with moving away from the "stiff" Byzantine style toward naturalism</note>, who rediscovered natural lines and true proportion, which the Greeks call **Symmetry** <note>original: 'Symmetria'</note>. He made the figures of earlier painters, which seemed dead, appear alive and with varied gestures, and he left behind a great fame for himself. But a much greater fame would have been left had he not had such a noble successor as **Giotto** the Florentine, a contemporary of **Dante**. This man was so perfect and absolute that many who have labored since, wishing to surpass him, have found it difficult. Italy is very full of his pictures. But most admirable is the mosaic ship at **Saint Peter’s in Rome** <note>The 'Navicella,' a famous mosaic depicting Christ walking on water and saving the boat of the Apostles</note> of the twelve apostles, in which each one has lively and prompt gestures, and all are different from one another, and yet fitting and appropriate. From the school of Giotto, as if from the **Trojan horse** <note>An allusion to the great number of heroes who emerged from the horse; Landino means many great artists were trained by Giotto</note>, emerged admirable painters. Among whom the grace in **Maso** is much praised. **Stefano** is called by everyone the **"ape of nature"** <note>Stefano Fiorentino; the term "ape of nature" was a high compliment for an artist whose realism was so perfect it seemed to mimic nature itself</note> because he expressed whatever he wished so vividly. A very great art appears in **Taddeo Gaddi**. **Masaccio** was an excellent imitator of nature, skilled in great **relief** <note>term: 'Relief' (rilievo). The artistic technique of making figures appear three-dimensional and solid through the use of light and shadow</note>, a good universal composer, and pure without unnecessary ornament, because he gave himself only to the imitation of truth and the relief of figures. He was certainly good and as skilled in **perspective** <note>The mathematical system for representing three-dimensional space on a flat surface</note> as any other of those times, and of great facility in his work, being quite young when he died at the age of twenty-three. **Fra Filippo** <note>Fra Filippo Lippi</note> was gracious, ornate, and skillful beyond measure; he excelled in compositions and variety in coloring, in relief, and in ornaments of every kind, especially those imitated from truth or imagined. **Andreino** <note>Andrea del Castagno</note> was a great draftsman and master of relief, a lover of the difficulties of art and of **foreshortening** <note>term: 'Foreshortening' (scorci). The technique of depicting an object or figure in a picture in depth</note>; he was very lively, prompt, and quite easy in his execution. **Paolo Uccello** was a good and varied composer, a great master of animals and perspective; if he had been as skilled in coloring as he was in drawing and perspective, he would have been even greater. **Fra Giovanni Angelico** <note>Beato Angelico</note> was charming, devout, and very ornate with the greatest ease. **Pesello** excelled above others in animals. There followed the refined **Pesellino**, excellent in the composition of small things. **Filippo di Ser Brunelleschi**, the architect, was also very skilled in painting and sculpture. He especially understood perspective well, and some affirm that he was either the rediscoverer or the inventor of it; and in both arts, there are excellent things made by him. **Donato** <note>Donatello</note> the sculptor is to be numbered among the ancients, admirable in composition and variety, prompt and with great vitality in the arrangement or placement of his figures, all of which appear to be in motion. He was a great imitator of the ancients and understood perspective well. **Desiderio** <note>Desiderio da Settignano</note> was very great, delicate, charming, and of the highest grace; he polished his works greatly. And if a very premature death had not snatched him away in his early years, every learned man in that art hoped he would have reached the highest perfection. **Lorenzo Bartoluccio** <note>Lorenzo Ghiberti</note> is very well known for the bronze doors of our **Baptistery**. There remain perfect works by **Antonio** nicknamed **Rosso** <note>Likely Antonio del Pollaiuolo</note>, and similarly by **Bernardo** his brother, a noble architect.

### CIVIL LAW

<image-desc>Large decorative drop cap 'D' featuring classical architectural elements and foliage.</image-desc>

**I** desire to put an end now to these teachings, but I fear that the jurists might accuse me of an injustice. And certainly, as nothing is more pernicious in a republic than the interpretation of laws by venal and fraudulent men, so is that jurist a supreme protector of justice and the only refuge for innocence in whom there is true doctrine and true integrity. If, therefore, anyone asks how much we have been able to achieve in this kind of writing, we can show him that **Accursius** <note>Accursius (c. 1182–1263) was a Florentine jurist whose 'Great Gloss' became the standard commentary on Roman law for centuries</note> the Florentine alone was chosen of all commentators, whose glosses were written alongside the volumes of the civil laws. There similarly remain the works of **Francesco**, his son, who, as he himself writes, was against the Bolognese jurists—who were most greedy to extinguish the fame of Accursius—and was a true and pious defender of his father’s glosses. Nor is it difficult to show who **Dino di Mugello** was, for he is known in every school in Italy and watched over even outside of Italy. **Giovanni Andrea** is also known, not as a Bolognese but as a Florentine, although through adoption he acquired a Bolognese father.

### COMMERCE

<image-desc>Large decorative drop cap 'M' with intricate floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>

**B**ut because commerce has always been held in high esteem in every city, provided it is practiced with dignity, I cite even my adversaries here as witnesses, for I fear no one and doubt no one. Nor can there be such an unfair slanderer who does not affirm that the Florentine merchants have obtained the supreme rank in all the maritime and Mediterranean regions where commerce is practiced. For such a pile of money has been found many times among our people that it would be difficult for many to believe it. I will only report this: that from the years of salvation **1365** until the year **1406**, the Florentine people had five wars. The first was with the Pope and lasted three years, and in that, twenty-five hundreds of thousands of **florins** <note>The 'fiorino d'oro' was the gold coin of Florence, the international reserve currency of the era</note> were spent. The second and the third were due to the attacks made against us by the **Count of Virtue** <note>Giangaleazzo Visconti, the Duke of Milan, known as the Conte di Virtù</note>, in which during the whole time fifty hundreds of thousands of florins were spent. There followed the fourth in **1401** against the Duke of Milan, and it ended in **1404**, and in this, twenty-five hundreds of thousands of florins were spent. After this, the war of **Pisa** began immediately, in which in one year and a few months fifteen hundreds of thousands of florins were spent. We can therefore conclude that in less than thirty years, one hundred and fifteen hundreds of thousands of gold florins were spent solely on wars. A hundred weighs more than a pound. Therefore, forty thousand make a load of four hundred pounds. This being so, it is necessary that one hundred and fifteen hundreds of thousands be two...

--- Page 17 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Proemio" (Preface) by Cristoforo Landino, moving from the artistic achievements of Florence to its economic power, geographical advantages, and the far-reaching influence of its noble families across Europe and the Mediterranean.</meta>

...to eighty-seven sums of gold <note>original: "some doro," referring to a specific measure of weight/currency</note>: which for the most part was gathered from the taxes paid by private citizens. And certainly, just as we see the bees from a single hive spread out across the whole region and bring back honey from every side, so does this people spread throughout the entire world, and with industry, they accumulate and bring wealth home. For this reason, there is no city in Italy, after Rome, that is more well-known or more famous. In every country, she is distinguished by three titles: that she is most famous, that she is most beautiful, and that she abounds with the most subtle wits <note>original: "sottilissimi ingegni," referring to the intellectual sharpness of the Florentines</note>. We can add an exquisite refinement and cleanliness in living, which is truly civilized. We can add a supreme skill in agriculture, such that in land that is not very fertile, we equal the most fertile places in the abundance, plenty, and variety of all fruits. No region is our equal in the villas <note>country estates</note> which, to the amazement of anyone who sees them, surround the city on all sides for a great distance. 

And because all these blessings have come from human industry, let us also add, if you please, the natural gifts. Among the first is to see our city from the north and east surrounded in the shape of a semi-theater <note>an amphitheater</note> by most pleasant hills clothed in fruit-bearing trees, and from the west extending into a joyful plain. The air of Arezzo is thin and produces very sharp wits; that of Pisa is more condensed, whereby the men excel greatly in memory. But our air, located in the middle between one and the other, being tempered, produces many who are excellent both in memory and in docility <note>readiness to learn</note>. The city is protected by several branches of the Apennines against hostile attacks. It is located in the center of Italy. For this reason, it allows the Florentine to add his own industry to join and disjoin the Italian powers <note>a reference to Florence's role as the "balance of power" in Italian diplomacy</note>. 

The city has always been copious in nobility. And what is altogether admirable is that there are many cities in Italy in which there are families connected, and in good standing as kinsmen, to some of the families of Florence. In Bologna, the **Bianchini** are a family of no small nobility, kinsmen of our **Acciaiuoli**. In Ferrara and in Mantua are the **Strozzi**, and in both cities, they are much honored by the princes. From the **Ricci** are descended those who live under the same name on the coast of Amalfi. In Alessandria della Paglia <note>modern Alessandria in Piedmont</note> are the **Rotti**, a very numerous family, most decorated in arms and military discipline, and the **Order of the Golden Spur** <note>original: "aurata militia," a high order of knighthood</note>, and excellent in civil law through many legal experts; they once even subjugated a great part of Monferrato. They are the equals of the Florentine **Adimari**. The **Alberti** have kinsmen in several places in Lombardy. The **Medici** have kinsmen who are Neapolitan citizens. They have them in Parma. They have them in Crete <note>original: "Candia"</note>. And in Seville, there is a rich family decorated with many knights of the Golden Spur. They are called **Martelli** and for their coat of arms they carry the griffin, and they confess to being of the Florentine Martelli. From the **Bonciani** family was **Guasparri**, a man of such prudence and faith toward Queen Joanna of Naples <note>Joanna II of Naples (1371–1435)</note> that during her life she entrusted him with the entire care of the realm; and when she died, she willed by testament that he should be the first of the administrators until the arrival of René, her adopted son and King <note>René of Anjou</note>. This man became lord of Santa Agata di Liceto, Monte Acuto, Ascoli, and Treteveri. 

**Esau Buondelmonti** ruled in Greece and was the Despot of Arta and of Zante <note>original: "desposo dellarte et di iacintho"; Esau was Despot of Epirus</note>. He married one of his sisters to the Marquis of Crotone, and another to the Duke of Cephalonia. He left successors until the final captivity of Greece <note>the Ottoman conquest</note>. The **Acciaiuoli** were lords of Corinth, Athens, and Thebes, and of other lands in Greece until the captivity of the Empire of Constantinople. **Nerozzo Pitti** became lord of Soukamine near Negroponte <note>Euboea</note> and of Panaia near Thebes. In our times, his successors are Antonio and Piero, his sons. In England, there were three brothers, Gherardo, Thomaso, and Mauritio, of the very ancient **Gherardini** family of Florence, sent into exile because of civil dissensions. These men, in the conquest of Ireland—an island not much smaller than England—provided such prompt, bold, and faithful service to the King of England that, once the island was subjugated, they were distinguished with the lordship of all the plain part of it, where there are many peoples. Even in our own times, there remain their descendants as lords, and especially the **Earl of Kildare** <note>original: "conte di Chaldaria"</note> and the **Earl of Desmond** <note>original: "conte di Dicimone"</note>. They have neither changed their name nor the coat of arms of the ancient Gherardini. 

Not only in great matters has this republic always been excellent, but even in minor things, she has shown generosity. She wished to be called **Florentia**. In this, I certainly approve the opinion of Pliny, who writes that the city was named **Fluentia** from the beginning because it was located between two rivers, the Arno and the Mugnone. But later, as such noble geniuses flourished within her, and as she flourished with every kind of beauty, it pleased her citizens to name her no longer Fluentia, but Florentia <note>a play on words: "Fluentia" from flowing water; "Florentia" from flowering/blooming</note>. Furthermore, she chose the lily among flowers, the lion for her sign among animals, and among excellent men, the image of **Hercules** for her seal. 

I realize that by being distracted by various matters, the material makes me too wordy and I distance myself too much from my goal. But because perhaps there will be someone who, among so many virtues narrated of my people, will want to reproach them for ingratitude—seeing as they so unjustly drove into exile such a useful citizen, so adorned with every virtue <note>referring to Dante Alighieri</note>, and after he was exiled, never recalled him. To this, the answer is easy: this was a vice of the times and not the nature of the people. And if we seek the truth, it was the power of a few, in whose judgment all public administration then rested, who committed such wickedness, not without the supreme sorrow of the people. Of which I take the best conjecture: because the people, while Dante was living, could not exercise their liberty, but they used it after his death when the leaders of the opposing party were already diminished. By public decree, they commissioned the prefects of the building of the Great Temple <note>the Duomo of Florence</note> to establish for our poet, from the public funds, a marble and artfully sculpted tomb in that temple and in an honored place, with such statues and signs that he might be seen as most honored. But even this was hindered by the envy of a few powerful men. You, therefore, our most illustrious lords, both by the vigor of such a decree—which has never been revoked at any time, nor in any part diminished—and by the prayers of the Florentine people...

...no, who desires it most greatly. And through your piety toward the father of your country, let him be recalled from exile by the right of return <note>original: "iure postliminii," a Roman legal term referring to the restoration of rights and status to a person returning from exile or captivity</note>, and restored to his city, and placed in that temple which is the highest and the cathedral. Let a proper and honored seat be established for him, so that at last <note>original: "tandem"</note> he may rest where, before his long exile, he labored for the peace of your liberty. And certainly, if among the Athenians it was considered the highest honor for someone to be supported at public expense in their Prytaneum <note>the "pritaneo" was a public hall in ancient Greek cities where distinguished citizens and Olympic victors were fed</note> because of some merit, then the piety of the Florentine people and the merits of the poet demand—and demand most greatly—that a perpetual monument to him appear not only in a public place, but in a sacred and majestic one. The divine precepts will this. Human laws command it. All equity desires it. And it greatly serves the public good that the rewards and honors of the dead should kindle the living to imitate the footsteps of those who, through their immortal virtues, have become immortal from mortals. And who does not know that the fame and glory of those who, though dead, always live, is a most burning flame which always ignites human hearts toward every noble virtue and learning? Nor can that city ever be miserable in which various rewards are always set before learned men; for the sentence of Plato is most true and entirely prophetic <note>original: "sybillina," referring to the Sibyls, ancient Greek prophetesses</note>: that republics will always fare well in which those who govern are philosophers, or rather, those who govern begin to philosophize. But because I know it is entirely superfluous to light a fire for one who already burns, or to incite one who runs swiftly by his own accord, I will not weary myself with a longer oration, our most illustrious Lords, in persuading you of that toward which your benign nature always draws you. Therefore, leaving behind all exhortation, I shall proceed. But I will speak with very brief words regarding the life of the poet, which I cannot entirely omit if I do not wish to likewise omit the well-instituted and always observed custom of every interpreter of poets. Nor should I report it at great length, because it has been related perfectly and with much elegance by many other learned men, and especially by Giannozzo Manetti.

### LIFE AND CHARACTER OF THE POET

It is, therefore, a constant report, always increased by many writers of no small authority nor ignoble status, that from the noble Frangipani family—which in Rome was of the senatorial order and from which Saint Ambrose was born—was born Eliseo <note>original: "Helifeo"</note>. He, after our city was restored by Charlemagne <note>original: "Carlo magno"</note>, came to Florence and established his home in the district of San Piero near the Donati and the Pazzi families. From him, his successors, having left behind the name Frangipani, were called Elisei, and they flourished for a long time in the republic. Among these was Cacciaguida, to whom was married a Ferrarese virgin of the noble Alighieri <note>original: "aldighieri"</note> family. For this reason, one of the sons born to her was named Aldighieri. This man, because of his excellent virtues, held the highest authority and veneration in the republic. Just as Eliseo had changed the name of Frangipani, so this man changed the name of the Elisei, and from him they were called Aldighieri. But later, the letter "d" being removed, they were named not Adighieri, but Alighieri. Others say that the family did not take its name from this man, but from the wings <note>original: "ale"</note> which it is clear they had as their coat of arms. But I leave this to be investigated by those who are more curious. I only affirm that from the successors of the first Alighiero was born another of the same name. And by him was fathered Dante <note>original: "Danthe"</note> our poet, in the year of salvation 1265, and during the papacy of Clement IV.

Nor should a wonderful dream be omitted which appeared to his mother shortly before the birth of the child. It seemed to her that she was in a green and flowery meadow, and in it, near a crystalline fountain and under a tall laurel tree, she gave birth to a son. For a time, he nourished himself on the berries of the laurel and the water of the nearby fountain, and in a short time, having grown, he became a shepherd. And wishing to take some of the branches of the laurel, he fell; but immediately he rose up, no longer a man, but having become a peacock. Boccaccio interprets this dream at length. But I, reducing it to its essence, believe that by the shepherd is understood his philosophical and theological learning, with which he can excellently feed every well-disposed mind; and the most ornate feathers of the peacock presaged his adorned poem. Nor should anyone marvel at this, because many times, and in various regions and centuries, portents have occurred that have announced the excellence of some man. For one reads of Virgil <note>original: "Marone"</note> that his mother, on the night preceding the birth, dreamed she gave birth to a laurel branch, which in a short time became a great tree, filled with various fruits and flowers. And Astyages, King of the Medes, dreamed that from the genital members of his daughter a vine was born, whose branches in a short time overshadowed all of Asia; and the interpreters of dreams replied that from her was to be born a very powerful man who would overwhelm his kingdom. Nor did it happen otherwise, for from the girl was born Cyrus, who occupied Persia and transferred the kingdom of the Medes to the Persians. Nor do only dreams, but also other portents, foretell this same thing. Thus one reads that bees carried honey into the mouth of Plato when, still at an infant age, he lay in his cradle. This predicted the future sweetness of his eloquence and learning. 

But I return to the poet. Dante was, from his earliest years, of an excellent nature, and he showed most open signs of his future probity and genius. Even in his childhood years, the image of a sharp man could be seen in his face, and every gesture of his was with gravity. Nor was it a small demonstration of a noble and generous soul, full of humanity, that he was most ardently taken by the love of a young girl, the daughter of Folco Portinari, called Bice, whom he later always—

<meta>This page continues the biography of Dante Alighieri, shifting from the legends of his birth to his youthful love for Beatrice, his extensive education, military service, and the political entanglements in Florence that eventually led to his exile.</meta>

...we call her by the more worthy name of Beatrice. She was, as he shows in his verses, in her eighth year, and he had not yet finished his ninth. She was so deeply fixed in his very marrow that he loved her not only while she lived, but after she died in the twenty-fourth year of her age, he mourned her most bitterly for a long time. Although such love may differ from that fury described by Plato <note>referring to Platonic "divine madness" or eros</note> and true divine love, it is nonetheless sought here on earth through corporeal beauty as an image and likeness of that higher love. Nor, if it is preserved as chaste and modest, is it worthy of blame, but rather of praise; for through these earthly beauties, we are raised to the divine. It also happens to those with a poetic mind that the "sweet bitterness" of love often awakens and excites them to write amorous poems, sharpening their wit and granting them eloquence.

It is incredible how ardent his studies were in every branch of learning. In his early years, he made great progress in the faculty of oratory, and even greater in poetry. In these arts, his teacher was Brunetto Latini, a man who—as much as the roughness of those times allowed—was very learned. Afterward, he practiced dialectic <note>the art of logical argument</note> and all the mathematical sciences. He exercised himself in moral philosophy and physics, and took great delight in music. For this reason, he was a close friend to all the musicians of that age who had any reputation. Nor did he lack courage in his strength or in military discipline, for he often found himself in war. In the very dangerous Battle of Campaldino <note>fought in 1289 between the Guelphs of Florence and the Ghibellines of Arezzo</note>, as he himself writes in one of his letters, he fought manfully, bringing honor to himself and benefit to his fatherland.

But I return to his love, regarding which we can apply the verses of the poet Horace to this poet:

> Place me in the sluggish plains where no tree is refreshed by the summer breeze; in that part of the world urged on by clouds and a wicked Jupiter. Place me under the chariot of the too-near sun, in a land denied to houses; I will love my sweetly laughing, sweetly speaking Lalage. <note>original Latin: "Pone me pigris ubi nulla campis Arbor estiua recreatur aura... Dulce ridentem lalagen amabo Dulce loquentem." Horace, Odes 1.22</note>

The longing for the deceased Beatrice was so heavy upon him that he lived in perpetual sorrow and tears. His friends could find no form of consolation, though they labored greatly at it, which might mitigate even a small part of such grief. Neither the passage of time, nor various exercises, nor prosperous things, nor adverse ones were of any help. For this reason, his friends advised leading him to marriage, hoping that a new and living love for a legitimate wife might extinguish the old flames. Certainly, it is the opinion of wise philosophers—and repeated by him—that just as one nail is drawn out by another nail, so a new love can draw the old one from the human breast. As the elegiac poet also expressed:

> Every lover is removed by a new successor. <note>original Latin: "Successore nouo tollitur omnis amans," from Ovid's Remedia Amoris</note>

But this advice led to the opposite result. He was joined with a wife, certainly most noble, born of the ancient Donati family and named Gemma. In other habits, she was worthy of praise, but she was so moody and stubborn that she surpassed the Socratic Xanthippe <note>Xanthippe was the wife of the philosopher Socrates, traditionally depicted as a shrewish and difficult woman</note>. Therefore, the comparison of their contrary characters caused the love of Beatrice to return with even greater force. Just as Beatrice had sharpened and refined him in many liberal arts, so Gemma was a troublesome impediment to many things. In the end, although she had borne him several children, he was forced to separate from her. Never again, neither in his homeland nor in exile, did she live with him.

He was of no less wit and counsel in civil administration and government than in learning. He was such a lover of justice and public tranquility that during the most pestilential civil dissensions of those times, although he was a Guelph and a supporter of the Church, he nevertheless attempted with every industry to bring about public concord. Because of these virtues, he was so loved by the people that in the creation of magistrates—which at that time was not by lot, but arose from public votes—he obtained every dignity. Ascending through all the grades of office, in the thirty-fifth year of his age, he was created one of the Priors <note>the *Priori* were the highest executive body of the Florentine Republic</note>, which is the supreme magistracy in our republic.

But often those things subject to the temerity of Fortune bring calamity with them: from where we hope for the greatest tranquility, there arises the greatest and most turbulent distress. Dante knew this by experience. For that magistracy—which he hoped would bring him the greatest rewards because he administered it with the highest integrity—was the cause of his exile. The city was already infected by the "White" and "Black" factions, of which we narrated extensively in the first *cantica* <note>referring to the *Inferno*</note>. The Guelphs of Florence were divided into these two parts. In vain, our poet tried with all his industry to induce concord among his citizens and extinguish the discord, demonstrating that such fighting would only weaken the strength of the Guelphs and give the Ghibellines an undoubted victory.

Finally, being unable to find a remedy, his plan was to leave public administration and live a quiet and literate life. But the pleas of friends, and perhaps also some ambition, prevailed over his right purpose. The discords grew more every day. There was such temerity among the leaders of the Blacks that, seeing the Whites prevailing, they gathered in the Church of the Trinity. After long consultation, they determined to send to Boniface, the Supreme Pontiff <note>Pope Boniface VIII</note>, to beg him to send someone of royal blood and authority to settle our republic and quiet the discords.

It was offensive to Dante that public councils were being conducted by private citizens in a private place without a decree from the supreme magistracy. Therefore, he persuaded those who were his colleagues that such license should be repressed and the insolence of the great should be punished. His authority was so great that several leaders of the Black faction were sent into exile: Messer Corso Donati, Gieri Spina, Giachinozo de' Pazzi, Rosso della Tosa, and some others. Finally, members of the White faction were also pronounced exiles: Messer Gentile and Messer Torrigiano de' Cerchi, Messer Guido Cavalcanti <note>a famous poet and Dante's "first friend"</note>, Baschieri della Tosa, and Baldinaccio Adimari.

Shortly thereafter, as the discords did not cease, he was appointed legate to Boniface. He was very hesitant about this embassy, for it did not seem he could leave the city without danger, yet he saw no one to whom he could conveniently entrust such a mission. While he stood almost distracted by this deliberation, he was heard to say, not thinking he was being overheard: "If I go, who stays? And if I stay, who goes?" <note>original: "Sio uo chi sta: et se io sto chi ua"</note>. His rivals ascribed this voice to great arrogance, as if he alone...

...it was judged that public governance was restored. Finally, Messer Corso Donati <note>Leader of the "Black" Guelph faction in Florence</note> departed and then returned. He prevailed so much with his faction that Dante, along with many other distinguished citizens, was exiled and their properties were confiscated. This was the reward our poet received for the many great labors he undertook to lead his people toward peace and harmony. Therefore, after he had tried in vain many ways to appease his adversaries, he joined with the Florentine exiles. Having elected Count Alessandro of Romena as their captain, they attempted to return by force. But when this also failed, he crossed the Apennines and was kindly received by Alberto della Scala, Lord of Verona. From there, turning to prayers and humble supplications, he wrote very frequently to Florence, both to the public and to private citizens, asking for nothing else but to be recalled. When this finally did not succeed, he went to Paris; and there, although he was greatly oppressed by poverty, he turned with all his devotion to philosophy and theology. It was a marvelous thing that among such a number of highly learned men, he was inferior to no one in debates. He had completely returned to the favor of the Muses.

But as the Emperor Henry <note>original: "Arrigo"; refers to Holy Roman Emperor Henry VII</note> passed into Italy, a new hope was kindled in Dante of being able to return to his homeland. He returned to Italy and persuaded the Emperor against the Florentines, because they had refused to promise his legates reception in Florence upon his arrival. He urged him to leave the siege of Brescia, which he had surrounded, and to occupy Florence instead. Henry came through Liguria to Pisa, and from Pisa by sea to Rome; there, having defeated his adversaries, he took the crown. Incensed against King Robert of Sicily and against the Florentines, he marched toward Florence. But even this path did not succeed for Dante. For Henry came in vain and set up camp in vain at San Salvi, a mile from the city; and after a few days, having lost all hope, he took the road toward Rome, fell ill at the castle of Buonconvento near Siena, and died. Dante moved to Romagna and was kindly received in Ravenna by Guido Novello, the Lord of Ravenna. There he established his home, where after several years he finished the last day of his life in the 56th year of his age. He was buried with no ordinary funeral rites in the Church of the Friars Minor <note>The Franciscan Church in Ravenna</note>.

He was of medium and becoming stature. His face was somewhat long, his eyes rather large, and his nose aquiline. He had broad and hanging jaws. His lower lip was proportionately thicker than the upper one. His complexion was dark, and his beard and hair were black and curly. Because of this, a funny thing happened in Ravenna: as Dante passed where some women were sitting, one <unclear>of them</unclear> said, "This is the one who went to Hell and returned." Her companion replied, "I believe it; for he has become black from the darkness and smoke of Hell, and his hair is singed by the fire." His portrait still remains, painted by the hand of Giotto, his contemporary, both in Santa Croce and in the Podestà's chapel <note>in the Bargello, Florence</note>. He always dressed modestly, even before his exile and when he possessed a large inheritance. He was grave in appearance and speech, but graceful. He was of the highest moderation in food and drink, for which reason he always hated the voracious and the gluttonous. He had deep and fixed thoughts; he was so eager to read new things that when a book was brought to him at an inappropriate time—even where people were dancing and celebrating at a solemn feast with a great crowd—he read it all through without intermission. He was so fixed upon it that while reading, he neither saw nor heard anything. He was very eloquent in extemporaneous speech. Because of this, he held a most honored position in the Republic for some years and served as an ambassador for his homeland to many princes and republics.

Every man confesses that Dante first brought back to light rhetorical and poetic ornaments; and he largely restored the ancient elegance, composition, and dignity that had been completely extinct for many centuries. He wrote eclogues <note>pastoral poems</note> in Latin, which show poetic genius and possess as much of antiquity as could be desired in those rougher times. In the same language, but in prose, he wrote three books titled *Monarchia* <note>original: "Monarchia"; a treatise on secular and religious power</note>. Likewise, *On Eloquence in the Vernacular* <note>original: "De vulgari eloquētia"</note>. He wrote in the Florentine language in p<gloss>ro</gloss>se the *Convivio* <note>The Banquet</note> and the *Vita Nuova* <note>The New Life</note>. He wrote many sonnets and songs in verse, in which it is a marvelous thing that in amorous matter—in which he vented all his affection—he added a very subtle allegory drawn from intimate philosophy and theology, in which stupendous learning appears. He wrote the *Comedy* <note>The Divine Comedy</note>, which we have interpreted, divided into three canticles. He gave it a beginning before he was sent into exile and wrote the first seven chapters; the rest he composed in his exile. But the final cantos of *Paradiso* remained hidden after his death in a secret part of the house where he lived; they were long sought, not without great distress, by everyone who read the work. But the ghost of the poet appeared in the night, dressed in white, to his son Jacopo and showed him the place where they were. Whereupon the young man, having woken up, searched there immediately and found them. A little further below, we will attempt to show the divine virtues of this work.

Meanwhile, we shall give him innumerable and greatest thanks, because he was the first who greatly ennobled our native language—which until his time was rough, unpracticed, and lacking in abundance and elegance—making it cultivated and adorned. Homer found the Greek language already very abundant and cultivated by Orpheus, Musaeus, and other poets older than himself. Virgil found Latin already polished and adorned, and amplified by Ennius, Lucretius, Plautus, Terence, and other ancient poets. But before Dante, no one had found any grace in the Tuscan language, nor any learned elegance or light. Except for rhymes—though even those were inept and rough—the ancients have nothing in which one can see the slightest trace of a poet. Dante was the first who, having recognized in Latin writers the ornaments common to the orator and the poet, and having understood how sharp a wit is necessary in poetic invention, how much judgment in arrangement, and how many various colors and lights in eloquence... moreover, how many fictions the poem must be veiled in, and how much and how varied a doctrine it must be filled with... with a happy omen, he introduced all these things into our language. This was something that no one had attempted in the past centuries.

<meta>This page transitions from the historical biography of Dante's life and exile to a broader defense and celebration of the Florentine language. ...he gave it its beginning: he greatly brought it toward perfection, something that has rarely happened among mortals. He was the first to demonstrate how suitable the Florentine idiom <term>The local dialect of Florence, which became the basis for modern Italian</term> was, not only for expressing but for amplifying and adorning all matters that fall under discussion.

Dante is followed by **Francesco Petrarch**, an immortal and divine man, worthy of great admiration. In his songs and sonnets, I would not hesitate to not only equal him to the first Greek and Latin lyric and elegiac poets, but to prefer him to many. By the common consent of all, he is a supreme Pindar <note>A Greek lyric poet known for his complex and celebratory odes</note> in lyric verses—the one whom Horace rightly affirms to be inimitable. Nor was there anyone in Greece who would not contend to prefer him to Homer; and certainly, for the magnificence of his spirit, for his profound thoughts, and for his figures of speech, he excels and surpasses everyone. There was no one better at forming a compound word from several others. But this is so characteristic of the Greek language that neither Latin nor Tuscan can do it; but, by God, let this be said without envy. Consider how often Petrarch rises, and how he soars like a swan. Consider how rich he is in profound thoughts, and how they fit perfectly in every part. He is sharp in invective and in reproof, and with that same vehemence with which Alcaeus <note>A Greek lyric poet known for his political songs and attacks on tyrants</note> strikes tyrants in his verses, Petrarch pursues vices. In matters of love, he is now happy, now sad, and he expresses all these feelings so well that I do not place him behind Ovid or Propertius. But that in which he wins the palm above all in every playful matter: although he is most delightful, he nevertheless observes a joyful modesty and never becomes obscene. And none of the most eloquent men would deny finding in him many things not only expressed but "painted"—things which they previously judged impossible to say with any elegance in this language.

**Giovanni Boccaccio** followed, much inferior to him, but endowed by nature with poetic genius and very ornate in his inventions. **Fazio degli Uberti** <note>original: "Bonifatio uberti"; author of the 'Dittamondo'</note> could have been numbered among the poets if nature and practice in him had been aided by art and learning. **Leon Battista Alberti** <note>The famous Renaissance polymath and architect</note> has greatly expanded this language; in both oratory and prose, he has surpassed and conquered all those before him. The eclogues <note>Short pastoral poems</note> written by him in Tuscan verses demonstrate how learned he is in poetry and how much judgment he possesses.

But there is already one flourishing who—if my judgment is worth anything—will be among the first and rarest. Truly wonderful is his genius, so much so that (as the eminent say) he is *Eutrapelos* <note>original: "Eutrapele"; Greek for "versatile" or "well-turned," likely referring here to Lorenzo de' Medici</note>, that is, adapted to everything; for wherever he turns, it seems he was born for that thing alone. Without doubt, every species of poetry proceeds to him from a celestial influence. He is most wise in his inventions and very rich in his speech, in a way that gives majesty to great things, dignity to medium things, and in the lowest things his style is such that, although it seems common to the folk, it cannot be imitated by the learned without difficulty; because in it, art competes with nature, and each excellently defends its part. This would certainly be marvelous even in those who have spent a long time in literary leisure and study. Therefore, what shall we say of him, who has been able to do so much in his youthful years? Especially amidst such numerous, varied, and great occupations in the public government, which have distracted him day and night, not without grave dangers, and from which he could not depart for a single moment. I do not deny how much natural talent can do in this; nevertheless, if from his tender years he had not given himself with most ardent study to Latin letters and the faculty of oratory—if he had not followed my most faithful precepts with the highest industry—let no one believe that the force of nature alone would have raised him to such an exalted rank. My tongue cannot express in him what my mind feels. But whoever reads the things written by him will know me to be stingy in praise rather than lavish in flattery.

But returning to the language, I affirm that just as in ancient centuries first the Greek language and then the Latin became refined from a rough and poor state through the great abundance of writers who polished them over time, so has our own. And already now, by the virtue of the writers I have named, it has become abundant and elegant; and every day, if studies do not fail, it will become more so. But let no one believe themselves to be not only eloquent, but even a tolerable speaker in our language, if they do not first have a true and perfect knowledge of Latin letters. For no one doubts that every speech is composed of words and thoughts. Words are always inept without oratory precepts, and thoughts are frivolous without varied learning. But neither theoretical art nor any learning can be known to us without either the Greek or Latin language. Therefore, at least Latin is necessary to us. This is why many of our writers, void of Latin letters and learning—although their genius and practice sometimes sustain them—nevertheless often fall into ruin, because they proceed like the blind if the light of art is not held out. Nor can a writer ever have juice or muscle <note>meaning strength or vitality</note> in their style if they are not entirely learned, or at least somewhat introduced to philosophy.

To these two reasons, add a third. Everyone understands how the Latin language became abundant by deriving many Greek words into it; likewise, it is necessary that our own becomes most rich if every day we transfer into it new words taken from the Romans and make them common among our own people. For this reason, let the Florentine youth exercise themselves in the study of the liberal arts, and being practiced in their native language, let them make it most eloquent. For nothing is found in a free and well-instituted republic that brings more utility and ornament with it than eloquence, whether oratory or poetic—provided it is accompanied by true virtue and the highest probity. This can bring the wickedness and fraud of the wicked into the hatred of the good and lead them to punishment. This can free the innocence of the powerless from the penalty of false judgments. This can incite a people, who by themselves are slow and sluggish, to those things where public honor lies, or recall them from errors, or inflame them against pestilential citizens, or mitigate them when they are incited against the good. This was done in Athens by Demosthenes and in Rome by Cicero—although one and...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Dante’s education and preparation, transitioning from his mastery of the Florentine vernacular to a philosophical defense of poetry itself. ...the other of the lowest condition was preferred: and in every dignity, he made the most noble superior to all. Recognizing this, our poet <note>Referring to Dante Alighieri</note>, being already highly cultivated in every doctrine, judged it to be a most excellent thing to be able to adorn every weighty thought with eloquence. For this reason, by practicing for a long time in both prose and verse, he became so eloquent that finally, adorned with wisdom and eloquence, he set himself to write the Comedy which we presently have in our hands. Of its magnificence and ornaments, we shall speak in their proper place. But first, with the utmost brevity, we shall relate some things necessary for the understanding of the poet and of poetry.

# WHAT POETRY AND A POET ARE, AND CONCERNING THEIR DIVINE AND ANCIENT ORIGINS

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'S' depicting a figure seated within a landscape, framed by a blue and gold square border with delicate floral patterns.</image-desc>
If we turn over in our minds, our most illustrious lords, what a poet is, how ancient their origin, how divine it is, and how ample and varied their learning, we will certainly recognize what is approved by the consensus of all the most serious philosophers: that no generation of writers can be found who, either for the greatness of their eloquence or the divinity of their wisdom, have at any time been equal to poets. I believe this led Aristotle—a man of great genius and unique learning after Plato—to believe that in the first ages, the same men were both theologians and poets. And he esteemed this so much that he wrote two books on the poetic faculty and three on poets. He easily recognized that poetry was not one of those arts which the ancients, because of their excellence, called "liberal" <term>The Liberal Arts: The traditional curriculum of grammar, logic, rhetoric, arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy, considered essential for a free person</term>. In any of these, if someone is held to be excellent, they have always been held in great prize. 

But poetry is a certain thing much more divine than the liberal disciplines. For poetry, embracing all of those arts, bound by defined rhythms <note>original: "numeri"</note> and circumscribed by distinct poetic feet, and adorned with various lights and flowers, adorns with marvelous fictions everything that men have ever done, known, or contemplated, and translates them into other forms. It demonstrates that it tells of something much lower and more abject, or some fable to delight the ears of the idle; yet all the while, it secretly writes of exalted things drawn from the fountain of divinity. Thus the listener, recognizing his error, not only comes to the knowledge of the greatest things—which a moment before he did not perceive hidden under a divine veil—but also takes marvelous pleasure from such a fiction. Whoever considers this art to be merely human and not divine deserves to be esteemed by the learned as far less than good. 

That the origin of poetry is more excellent than the origin of human arts is manifest because the <term>divine fury</term> <note>Also known as "poetic madness" or inspiration, a concept from Plato where the poet is possessed by a higher power</note> from which poetry originates is more excellent than the human excellence from which the other arts originate. And that the poetic faculty proceeds from divine fury is effectively proven by Plato in the book he titles *Ion*, through three signs. First, because men do not learn any of the other arts except after a long time without divine fury. But true poets—as he affirms Homer, Hesiod, and Pindar to be—place in their poems certain indices of all the arts and signs that they understood them. The second sign is that while in a fury, they sing many stupendous things which, once the fury has ceased, they themselves hardly understand; as if they had not pronounced them themselves, but God through their mouths. Third, that it is not the most prudent men, nor those most learned from their tender years, who become the best poets, but those who are driven by fury, as Plato writes happened to Ion and Tynnichus of Chalcis and to Hesiod. And that great philosopher adds that the Muses sometimes inspire this divine spirit into the most inept men, because divine providence wants to show us that the aforementioned poems are not the invention of philosophers, but are gifts from God. Furthermore, he affirms in the *Phaedrus* that no one, however diligent or even most learned, becomes a poet unless he is stirred by divine fury. Whence comes that saying: <note>original: "Cum deus i nobis agitate caleſcimus illic : Impetus ille ſacre ſemina mentis habet"</note> "When God is within us, we grow warm through His movement; that impulse contains the seeds of a sacred mind." 

We can also add that only poets, contrary to the custom of other writers, invoke divine help, because they understand the poem to be divine and not human, proceeding from divine fury. This is affirmed by Democritus, Origen, and Cicero. For this reason, it is no wonder if poets are most ancient, since God willed from the beginning <note>original: "abinitio"</note> that His mysteries be described to all peoples by poets. This, as I said a little earlier, I believe led Aristotle to call poets "theologians." 

But if we investigate the nature of both with diligence, we will find no small similarity between the poet and the prophet. For this reason, the Latins wanted <term>vates</term>—said to come from the force of the mind <note>original: "ui mentis"</note>, that is, from vehemence and agitation of the mind—to be a name common to both. And the Greeks called them "poet" from the verb <gloss>piin</gloss> <note>original: "piin" — Landino refers to the Greek 'poiein', meaning to make or create</note>, which stands midway between "to create"—which is proper to God when He produces something into being from nothing—and "to make"—which belongs to men in every art when they compose from matter and form. For although the fiction of the poet is not entirely from nothing, it nevertheless departs from "making" and approaches very close to "creating." And God is the supreme poet, and the world is His poem. And just as God disposes the creature—that is, the visible and invisible world which is His work—in number, measure, and weight (whence the prophet says: <note>original: "Deus omnia facit numero menſura et pondere"</note> "God makes all things in number, measure, and weight"), so the poet, with the number of poetic feet, with the measure of short and long syllables, and with the weight of thoughts and emotions, constitutes the poem. 

I will not dwell long on this similarity. But I will add that it was not without reason that the ancients said Apollo and the nine Muses had the protection of poets. Nor do they mean anything by Apollo other than the supreme God, who is unique and without plurality, as this name Apollo denotes in Greek. And Macrobius...

He argues that poets were the original theologians, using metaphorical "veils" to hide profound spiritual truths from the unworthy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Landino’s philosophical defense of poetry, moving from the historical role of poets as the first theologians to a Platonic explanation of "Divine Frenzy." He links the mythological figures of Apollo and the Muses to Christian celestial hierarchies, setting the stage for his argument that Dante's poetry is a vehicle for divine truth.</meta>

...in his *Saturnalia* <note>A work by the 5th-century writer Macrobius</note>, wishing to demonstrate divine singularity and refute the idea of many gods, he relates all the names of various gods and all their powers back to Apollo. Thus, all things are under the protection of Apollo and the nine Muses—that is, the nine angelic choirs. God is the supreme giver and father of light; therefore he is also called Phoebus <note>A name for Apollo meaning "bright" or "radiant"</note>, the god who reflects his light into the Empyrean heaven. From this First Mover <note>In medieval cosmology, the outermost sphere that moves all others</note>, the nine spheres are set in motion: by the First Mover we understand Jove <note>Jupiter</note>, and by the spheres, the nine Muses. For this reason, Virgil learnedly said: *From Jove the beginning, Muses; all things are full of Jove.* <note>original: "A ioue principiu Muse iouis omnia plena"</note> Poets, therefore, come from God. They also come from the First Mover—that is, from Jove—and from all the nine spheres which are the Muses, because they receive divine influence from them.

### DIVINE FRENZY

<image-desc>Illuminated initial 'E' in gold on a blue ground with red and green floral decorations extending into the margin.</image-desc>

And I judged it wrong to omit what the ancient philosophers—and especially Pythagoras, Empedocles, Heraclitus, and finally the divine Plato—understood regarding divine frenzy. These men affirmed (as Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with ancient wisdom</note> had written before them) that before our souls descend into bodies, they contemplate Wisdom, Justice, Harmony, and the beauty of the divine nature within God, as if in a mirror. Afterward, stretched out within bodies—where previously they fed upon ambrosia and nectar, that is, the knowledge of God and joy—they are submerged in the river Lethe <note>The mythological river of forgetfulness</note> and fall into total oblivion. They cannot return to heaven unless they first regain such knowledge. Nor can they do this without justice and religion. By "justice," they mean all the moral virtues and the active life; by "religion," they mean the intellectual virtues and the contemplative life. These virtues Plato calls "two wings" with which we can fly to heaven. Thus, in the *Phaedrus*, he writes: only the minds of philosophers recover their wings, because through meditation they withdraw themselves from the body, and being filled with God, they rise toward God. Such abstraction they call "frenzy," and this is divided into four parts. 

We cannot remember divine things except through certain images of earthly things, which are like shadows of the divine; these we can grasp with our bodily senses. This is further confirmed by the Teacher of the Gentiles, Paul <note>Saint Paul the Apostle</note>, and Dionysius the Areopagite, saying: the invisible things of God are seen by us through those things which are made visible here. Therefore, human wisdom is an image of divine wisdom; the music of our instruments is an image of divine harmony; and similarly, the beauty of a well-proportioned body adorned with soft color represents, in some part, divine beauty to us. 

But it is not my purpose at present to speak of the other types of frenzy. Through the ears of the body, the soul receives numbers and musical consonances; by these images, it is stirred with a more vehement spirit to consider celestial harmony. This harmony, as Plato maintains, is of two species: one consists in the eternal mind of God; the other in the order and celestial motions from which a wonderful concord is born. The soul enjoyed these two before it entered the body. But afterward, imprisoned in so troublesome a jail, through the sense of hearing it perceives not the divine harmony, but this music which exists among men. And because this is an image of the celestial, the soul desires to recover the celestial so it may fly to heaven and return to divine harmony; nonetheless, it still hungers for this music it hears with its ears. This is no wonder, for whoever desires a thing also delights in having its image. 

Our soul, then, strives to imitate this; but such imitation is of two species. There are those who delight in the harmony of the voice and musical instruments; these are common and superficial musicians. Others, who possess a weightier judgment, express the innermost feelings of their minds with measured verses. These are the ones who, stirred by a divine spirit, can write the most serious and meaningful verses. This is what Plato calls "poetry," which does not merely delight the ears with the sweetness of the voice like common music, but as I said, describes high, secret, and divine meanings, feeding the mind with celestial ambrosia. This divine frenzy—as we say when treating the poetic art—they hold to proceed from the Muses. Therefore, whoever tries to become a poet without this divine frenzy labors in vain. But I return to the praise of the poetic faculty.

### THAT THE ORIGIN OF POETS IS ANCIENT

<image-desc>Illuminated initial 'P' in gold on a blue ground with red and green floral decorations extending into the margin.</image-desc>

Poets also surpass others by a great interval in their antiquity. It is likely that among the first men in whom any religion was excited and awakened, they immediately applied their genius to the praises of God and to their prayers. They used industry to craft more elegant orations, reducing words to a certain order and linking them with determined rhythms and poetic "feet." We see this in Orpheus, of whom they say for no other reason that he was able to stop rivers, move stones, and soothe wild beasts with his lyre, except because he could repress the impulse and fury of many men with the sweetness of his verses. These men, trusting in their physical strength, were beating down and trampling all others; others who were of a hardened, stupid, or almost senseless mind, he led to a rational and civil life. 

Amphion, with the sweet sound of his lyre, compelled stones to arrange themselves together and form the walls of Thebes. This demonstrates nothing else than that he brought men who were wandering and dispersed through the woods and caves into a gathering and congregation to live in common. Similarly, we shall interpret that Amphion moved stones with his lyre to join together and make the Theban walls because, through the sweetness of his verses, he brought together those men who, without laws or customs, were wandering the nearby mountains and living in solitude...

He uses the myths of Orpheus and Amphion as allegories for how poetry creates social order and leads the soul back to God.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Landino’s argument for the divine origin of poetry, moving from the philosophical concept of "Divine Frenzy" to a historical defense of the antiquity of verse. He argues that poetry predates Greek civilization, finding its roots in Hebrew scripture and early Roman civic life, while also serving as the foundation for oratory and philosophy.</meta>

...and by softening their hardness, [he] settled them into civil life. I will not labor at present to investigate what we see Plutarch diligently sought in his book *On Music*: who among the Greeks was the first inventor of verses; in which age the lyric poets, in which the heroic, and in which the elegiac were found; because it is difficult among such a variety of opinions to pronounce the truth.

And we see such art was celebrated much earlier in Syria and Egypt than in Greece. Since, for the Hebrew people—a people most ancient, as they affirm and we believe—King David wrote the Psalms in verse. Nor is it that we cannot number him among the ancient ones, for he lived in the times when Codrus <note>The last semi-mythical King of Athens</note> reigned in Athens, more than 400 years before the founding of Rome. Moreover, the works of Solomon his son, and Deuteronomy, and the Song of Isaiah are written in verse, as Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian</note> and Origen <note>An early Christian theologian</note>, most authoritative authors, affirm. 

But in even more ancient centuries lived Moses—a man marvelous in military discipline and learning—who freed the Egyptians from the Ethiopians and the Hebrews from the Egyptians. And according to Eupolemus, a Greek writer: because he was the inventor of letters, he was called Mercury Trismegistus <note>A legendary figure often conflated with Moses by Renaissance humanists seeking to link Egyptian and Judeo-Christian wisdom</note> by the Egyptians. He, as appears in his writings, was no ignoble poet; a man so ancient that when he led the people of Israel out of Egypt, Cecrops <note>The mythical first king of Athens</note> reigned in Athens. And all the excellent things done in Greece are after the times of Cecrops. But even before Moses, Job the Idumean <note>A reference to the biblical Job, whom Landino places in Edom (Idumea)</note>, who lived about three ages after Israel, wrote his consolation in elegiac verses.

But it is time now to return from such distant regions to our mother Italy, and to Latium, where—although Livius Andronicus was the first to show himself a poet and to write plays for the theater—nonetheless, Cato shows in his *Origins* that it was a most ancient custom for verses composed in praise of excellent men to be sung at banquets. And Livy, a most truthful historian, affirms that Numa Pompilius, the second king of the Romans, instituted that verses be sung during sacrifices. 

You have seen what poetry is, and how it takes its origin not from mortal wit, but from divine frenzy <note>Plato's *furor divinus*, the idea that poets are divinely inspired</note> infused into human breasts. Nor has it been hidden from you whence the word "poet" is derived. And finally, no other generation of writers in antiquity is more noble. It remains, therefore, to show you how much utility and pleasure it offers us in public and in private. 

And let our beginning be with the queen of our minds, the faculty of oratory, which is deservedly called "soul-bending" <note>original: "flexianima"</note> because it persuades us of whatever it wishes, and turns and bends us. Who does not know how much spirit, how much splendor, and how much dignity the poet brings to the orator? Who does not understand how they are magnificent and elevated in the greatest things; weighed and temperate in mediocre things; and elegant and polished in humble and low things? Note the introductions. Read the narrations. Enumerate the divisions. Consider the confirmations and refutations. And finally, do not overlook the epilogues and conclusions. You will certainly understand that there is nothing more suited to winning goodwill, nor to narrating more briefly and clearly, nor to dividing more ornately and perfectly, nor to confirming more probably and effectively, nor to refuting more vehemently and harshly than the passages written by poets. And this much regarding oratorical adornments.

But who does not understand how splendidly they have treated philosophy? Not only by subtly compressing this or that philosophical point with brevity—as we see especially in Homer, in Virgil, and in Dante—but also by describing matters entirely, diffusely, and in order: as among the Greeks with Pythagoras, [Alcaeus of] Mitylene, Xenophanes, Empedocles, Parmenides, and many others. Among the Latins, Titus Lucretius and Marcus Varro—whom the excellent teacher Jerome does not hesitate to call the most learned of all. 

I could add an ineffable pleasure and unspeakable joy, upon which the human ear and mind feed as if upon the sweetest ambrosia. But who is so alienated from all humanity? So deprived of all judgment? So an enemy of the Muses that he does not understand that no concert or well-proportioned harmony can equal the poetic sound? From this it arises, our Most Illustrious Lords, that among every nation poets have always received the greatest honor. From this it arises that Orpheus and Linus were held in such reverence that they were honored not as mortal men, but as immortal gods. 

Seven cities in Greece contended for Homer, each affirming he was its citizen; and the Smyrnaeans built him a temple as if to a god. Nor will I be long in relating the supreme honors that Archelaus, the Macedonian king, conferred upon Euripides. Alexander the Great, in the destruction of Thebes, willed that all descendants of Pindar be saved. To Hiero of Syracuse, Simonides was most welcome. Fulvius Nobilior held Ennius in such high regard that he always honored him greatly; and to gratify him, he consecrated to the Muses the money taken from the spoils—which the Latins call *manubiae* <note>original: "manubie," referring to money from the sale of war booty</note>. And Scipio Africanus willed that [Ennius] be buried among the most noble tombs of the Cornelii. 

But I find no suitable words with which I can return due thanks to you, O most illustrious Maecenas <note>Landino likely addresses his patron Lorenzo de' Medici by the name of the famous Roman patron</note>, true father and protector of the Muses. You, the supreme ornament of your centuries—which [poet] will I say was eminent, or even mediocre, that you allowed to be defrauded of his due reward? Ovid Naso proclaims you his benefactor; Propertius confesses he owes you his life; Horace, through your liberality, became rich from being poor. I am silent about Varro. I do not name Tucca. I do not recount the many others both raised up and honored by you. To the prince of poets, Virgil, you made Octavian <note>Augustus Caesar</note> such a friend that he not only recovered his own possessions, but could also cause the return to his fellow citizens of those of all the Mantunans, which had already been distributed to soldiers as a reward. 

If, therefore, poets are not human but divine; if they are unique among writers in that all disciplines are contained within their volumes; if they are the most ancient of all writers; if utility and pleasure together are expected from them; and if infinite rules and examples of both speaking well and living well are found in them, we ought with most ardent study and supreme...

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s introductory defense of Dante Alighieri. Having previously established the divine and ancient origins of poetry, Landino now shifts to a technical and aesthetic praise of Dante’s specific skills in rhetoric, imagery, and his command of all branches of human knowledge—from theology to natural physics.</meta>

...diligence will provide knowledge of these things. But we shall strive especially to investigate the mind of our citizen, Dante. Whose poem is unique in its invention, most masterful in its arrangement, and supreme in its elocution through many rhetorical colors and lights. And what is marvelous is how he doubles these "colors" in a way that one takes ornament from the other. This multiplies the pleasure for the listener, as in these verses:

> Not green leaves, but of a dark hue;
> Not smooth branches, but gnarled and warped;
> No fruit was there, but thorns with poison.
> <note>original: "Non fronda uerde..." These lines from Inferno XIII describe the Wood of the Suicides.</note>

Repetition <note>the recurrence of "Non"</note> achieves much here. Much is done by dissolution <note>the lack of conjunctions</note>, much by correction, and much by adjunction. Each of these rhetorical colors, though they please the ear greatly on their own, nonetheless—because they are placed together—create such a harmony as we often hear from the well-proportioned but distinct strings of a cithara <note>an ancient Greek instrument similar to a lyre</note>. But his similes are so new that I can give no likeness to them. Nor can his comparisons be expressed by any comparison. They are unique, and more frequent than in any other poet, and yet more fitting. They are not only most effective in expressing the writer's mind, but most perfectly suited to the location. For this reason, he does not draw comparisons in the *Inferno* from the same things as those in *Paradiso*, but places in each those that are natural to it. Furthermore, he often moves from a comparison into an opening where he either reveals a natural cause or gives the listener knowledge and doctrine of some natural thing, as when he says:

> And as one awakens at a sharp light
> through the visual spirit that runs there
> to the splendor that goes from layer to layer.
> <note>original: "Et chome allume acuto..." Paradiso XXVI. Landino notes here how Dante uses the mechanics of sight to explain spiritual awakening.</note>

Sometimes he imagines things that are not as they are, but if they were, the comparison he seeks would be born from them, as in this tercet:

> And such he became in his appearance
> as Jupiter would become if he and Mars
> were birds and exchanged their feathers.
> <note>original: "Et tal nella sembianza sua diuenne..." Paradiso XXI. A hypothetical image used to describe the changing colors of the spheres.</note>

Sometimes he makes a comparison of that which never was. Which, if it were, would make an incomparable comparison; such as the splendor of a star imagined in the sign of Cancer when the sun is in Capricorn. Nor does it seem right to me to omit one of his most masterful passages in which various ornaments are enclosed. Let us hear these:

> As the peasant who rests on the hillside
> In the season when he who brightens the world
> keeps his face least hidden from us:
> When the fly gives way to the mosquito,
> he sees fireflies down through the valley,
> perhaps there where he harvests and plows:
> with so many flames it all shone.
> <note>original: "Qualel uillano..." Inferno XXVI. Landino admires this for its layering of simple pastoral life with complex astronomical timing.</note>

And so forth. Certainly a marvelous comparison: which, beyond its proper duty of opening the place he describes, brings the highest joy to the listener, who seeks a relaxation of the mind after a long narration of sorrowful things. Furthermore, he adorns the passage with a double description of time, which the Greeks call <term>chronographia</term> <note>a description of time</note>, because it describes summer within the year, and night within the revolution of the heavens. And to this "chronographia" he adds another rhetorical color called <term>periphrasi</term> <note>periphrasis or circumlocution</note> by the Greeks and <term>circuitione</term> by the Latins. This is when one says in many words what could be expressed in one. Thus, he could have said "in the summer," but instead used many words: "When the sun keeps his face least hidden from us." Nor did he even say "sun," but in place of sun said "He who brightens the world." Likewise, through <term>circuinstriptione</term> <note>circumscription</note> he denoted the night, saying: "When the fly gives way to the mosquito." And he even joined this color with denomination, for he puts the mosquito that flies at night in place of the night itself. 

His descriptions are such that they leave nothing obscure or confused in the mind; but like pictures, they represent things to the eyes in a form so that the internal sense sees what the external eye never saw. No journey is more well-known to us, even those we have walked many times, than the descent into Hell, the laborious climb of Purgatory, and the flight to the Heavens. He guides the reader through terrifying places not without fear, and through pleasant ones not without delight. He is marvelous at moving the affections and passions of the mind. He suits his particular descriptions closely to places and times; sometimes proceeding leisurely and abundantly, as when he describes the season of the hoarfrost; other times brief and concise, as in this tercet:

> They have wide wings, and human necks and faces,
> Feet with claws, and a great feathered belly;
> They make laments upon the strange trees.
> <note>original: "Ale hanno late..." Inferno XIII, describing the Harpies.</note>

He is very prompt in metaphors, as when he says: "But let the grass be far from the beak," and shortly below: "And let them not touch the plant / If any still rises from their dung." Likewise: "Like the little sheep who do not know / they return from the pasture fed on wind." Likewise: "In this eternal spring." Likewise:

> The will in men flowers well,
> But the continuous rain turns
> the true plums into blighted fruit.
> <note>original: "Ben fiorisce ne glhuomini..." Paradiso XXVII. A metaphor for how good intentions are ruined by bad influences.</note>

I omit all the other rhetorical colors with which he distinguishes, adorns, and illustrates his poem—with the highest gravity when the subject requires it, and with the highest festivity and wit. He uses words that are proper and in common usage. Sometimes he uses ancient ones like *fovente* <note>cherishing/warming</note> and the like. He crafts new ones, such as <term>inmiare</term> <note>to enter into 'me'</note>, <term>intuare</term> <note>to enter into 'thee'</note>, and <term>inoltrare</term> <note>to go further within</note>. 

But with such eloquence, he relates not the errors of Ulysses, nor the written Trojan battles, nor the arrival of Aeneas in Italy, nor the empire of the Latins, nor the tears of Venus, nor the immortal hatred of Juno, nor the wounds of Mars—things in which we see Homer and Virgil toiled so much. But what genius, O immortal God! What depth of mind! He embraces the heavens. He embraces the earth. He embraces the Tartarean kingdom. And starting from the center, having already expressed the eternal pains of the wicked to frighten men from sins, ascending through Purgatory with eagle’s wings, he flies to the celestial seats. These things, although they hide the highest science under various veils, nevertheless depart in no place from true theology. 

And what theologian has been able to express to us mortals with more order or more manifest demonstrations that which the immortal spirits contemplate up there in the most lucid fountain of nature? What physicist ever wrote with clearer reasons of all natural motions, whether according to place or according to form, whether imperfect or perfect, whether animate or inanimate? What course of a star, what conjunction, what revolution of the sky has been omitted by him? What transformation of one element into another? What alteration in the air of hail, rain, or winds?

He argues that Dante's genius encompasses all fields of knowledge, including theology, physics, and astronomy, making him equal or superior to the ancient poets.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landini’s introductory defense of Dante Alighieri. Having discussed Dante's rhetorical skill and use of similes, Landini now moves to Dante's encyclopedic knowledge of the natural world, geography, and moral philosophy, framing him as a "new Homer." The page concludes with a celebratory letter from the philosopher Marsilio Ficino, praising Landini for "restoring" Dante to Florence.</meta>

...made or of other similar things. What composition of minerals solidified under the earth have the physicists <note>natural philosophers or scientists</note> demonstrated that this poet has not at least hinted at? The soul has four powers; it has various offices and various properties. But of all these, we have true knowledge through Dante. And who does not know with what true knowledge and grace he describes now the universal site of the earth, now some particular region within it? But what shall we say of that philosophy which Socrates first recalled from heaven to earth <note>a reference to the Roman thinker Cicero's claim that Socrates moved philosophy away from abstract physics toward human ethics</note>, and with the greatest utility to men introduced into republics, into private homes, and finally into the human breast? In which philosopher are the arguments that lead to the highest good and true happiness, or the rules and precepts pertaining to the good and blessed life, more open and manifest? With what ardor, with what sharpness does he strike down and condemn injustice, treachery, incontinence, cruelty, small-mindedness, and insolence, along with all other vices! With how much praise and how many rewards does he invite us to the virtues, and persuade us to observe justice, to practice temperance, to have a bold and constant mind, and to refuse no danger for our country, our parents, and our friends! To have true religion toward God, the highest piety toward our elders, and ardent charity toward all. 

For which reason it is most truly concluded that his entire poem contains nothing other than the praise of virtue. And as the Greeks say of Homer, it can be affirmed that he is similar to the ocean. For just as all rivers are born from the ocean and return to the ocean, so all the sciences <note>original: "scientie," referring to branches of knowledge or "liberal arts"</note> are drawn from him and overflow back into him. Add to this his knowledge of history and how diligent an investigator of antiquity he was—not only of our own affairs, but also of the Greek, the Hebrew, and all other nations. Even if he had treated these things without any decorative eloquence, we ought nonetheless to learn them diligently for the great utility acquired from such knowledge. Now, being adorned with such an incredible abundance of words, illustrated with such admirable gravity of thought, composed with such grace of style, and distinguished by such a variety of rhetorical "lights and colors," who would not grant him their nighttime vigils <note>original: "nocturne uigilie," meaning staying up late to study</note>, seeing that in such reading the highest utility is joined with the highest joy? 

We, therefore, invoking divine help, shall set ourselves to sail such a wide sea; and we shall use, insofar as our strength allows, the office of a faithful interpreter. Nor shall we only reveal the natural <term>natural sense: the literal or surface meaning of the text</term> sense, but also the allegorical, tropological <term>tropological: the moral sense, teaching us how to act</term>, and anagogical <term>anagogical: the spiritual or heavenly sense, pointing toward eternal glory</term>. These three senses, because they have much in common, we shall call collectively "allegorical." May it please Him who is pleased by all good, and from whom all good proceeds, to elevate us as much as our Platonist Marsilio Ficino demonstrates in one of his letters. His example, so that it may be a perpetual testimony of our mutual and immortal benevolence, we shall transcribe here below.
