## THE WORDS OF MARSILIO FICINO THE FLORENTINE

<image-desc>Large decorative drop cap 'F' containing a portrait of a figure in a red hood and garment (likely Dante Alighieri) against a blue background, surrounded by elaborate golden foliage and floral scrollwork.</image-desc>

Florence, for a long time mournful but at last joyful, congratulates her Dante Alighieri, now revived after nearly two centuries and restored to his homeland, and finally crowned. You once prophesied, my Dante, while in exile, that a time would come when piety, overcoming impiety, would happily return you to your fatherland and crown you with Apollinean wreaths <note>laurel wreaths sacred to Apollo, god of poetry</note> in the exalted temple of John the Baptist <note>the Florence Baptistery, where Dante wished to be crowned</note>. Not in vain did your ancestors teach you your omen. Indeed, recently your father Apollo, pitying my long weeping and your long exile, commanded Mercury to slide into the pious mind of Cristoforo Landini, the divine poet. Putting on Landini’s face, he first woke you from your sleep with his life-giving wand; then, lifting you up with the rowing of his wings, he brought you within the Florentine walls. Finally, he wreathed your temples with Phoebean laurel. Today, at last, by divine will, the command of Phoebus <note>Apollo</note>, the work of Mercury and Landini, the prophecy of Dante, and the vow of Florence have been fulfilled. 

You have come at last, with Minerva showing the way and Mercury as the guide of the path. A most brilliant troop of all the poets accompanies you. Finally, as you enter, the Graces have happily received you. The Muses and the nymphs have given you embraces and kisses. You have come at last, and your piety, long expected by your parent, has overcome the hard journey. It is granted, my son, to look upon your face, and to hear and return your familiar voice. Indeed, I was lead to believe in my mind that it would be so, counting the times; nor did my care deceive me. O, how much more beautiful and how much more blessed do I receive you now, sweet son, than when I lost you? Your former mortal face has turned into an immortal and divine one. Florence has been transformed, as night into day. For your fellow Florentines, all sorrow has turned into joy. 

Rejoice, all you most happy citizens, for whom a twin sun now rises most wonderfully in place of one—not with flames, but with doubled rays. Do you not see that today heaven itself clearly congratulates your happiness? Look up, O citizens, look up for a moment at the sky! Behold now, while our Dante is being crowned, the house of almighty Olympus opens. The flames of the Empyrean heaven <note>the highest, fiery heaven in medieval cosmology</note>, no longer seen by anyone, today flash manifest for us, congratulating the crowned Dante. Furthermore, what do you think is this great, new, and sweet sound now filling your ears? Truly, it is the sound of the prophets and the nine Muses, heard in no other ages, today publicly applauding the coronation of Dante. Hark! Hear the sweet songs of the Dominations <note>one of the orders of angels</note> from Phoebus...

Florence, for a long time grieving: but finally happy, she greatly congratulates her poet Dante, who at the end of two centuries is revived: and restored to his homeland: and now gloriously crowned. O my Dante, in the time when you were placed in unjust exile, you predicted in your sacred poem / that when mercy overcomes cruelty—which locked you out of your sheepfold <note>a reference to Dante’s description of Florence in Paradiso XXV</note>—then you would return to your homeland much more adorned than before: and in the exalted temple of the Baptist <note>the Baptistery of San Giovanni</note> you would worthily take the poetic crown. This foresight of yours was not in vain. But because you predicted this from the highest paradise / therefore you predicted it with truth. Since your father Apollo, moved to mercy by your long exile and my weeping / commissioned Mercury in these times: to fly immediately into the pious mind of the divine poet Cristoforo Landino: and transformed into the image of his face, to use the miraculous wand to restore life to you: and also to ascend to bring you back to your homeland: and beyond this, to crown you with the Apollonian laurel. 

Finally, on this day, the command of the highest Phoebus <note>another name for Apollo</note> is seen fulfilled: the pious work of Mercury transformed into a man. Your prophecy, O my divine Dante. The long desire of Florence. Today, mercy overcoming cruelty at last returns to me my most desired son. The goddess Minerva showed the way. Mercury has led you together with the most illustrious company of all the poets. Upon entering within these walls, the joyful Graces reach out their hands to you: the gracious Nymphs also kiss your brow. O most joyful and happy day: in which I now receive my second sun, through whose splendor the night becomes day for me. 

O how much more beautiful and more blessed you return to me, my poet, by the grace of mercy: than when you left by the fault of cruelty. You left me with a human face: You return truly with a divine face. Wherefore my ancient sorrow is already converted into supreme joy. Therefore, make feast and exult in joy, happy Florentine citizens: to whom wonderfully, in place of one sun, two suns already shine in doubled rays and not together. Now do you not see that today heaven makes feast for your happiness? Raise up, citizens, raise your eyes on high. Behold, while our Dante is crowned, the Empyrean heaven <note>the highest, most spiritual level of heaven in medieval cosmology</note> opens above us. And to show joy at such a coronation, it shows to our eyes its marvelous splendor never before seen in other times. Beyond this, do you not now hear this sound so new, so sweet, so great: which equally delights and fills our ears? This is without doubt the harmony of the nine spheres and Muses never heard before: which makes feast for the crowned Dante. Hear again, hear the sweet songs and hymns of the Dominations: and of the archangels: who from the sphere of the sun and of Mercury spread such a song toward us. Glory in the highest <note>original Latin: "Gloria in excelsis"</note> to the highest Phoebus. Glory to the Muses always: and to the Graces. Finally, Peace, Joy, Happiness to the Florentines, now wonderfully adorned with two suns.

## SITE, FORM, AND MEASURE OF THE INFERNO AND THE STATURE OF THE GIANTS AND OF LUCIFER

Although this poet is marvelous in every thing: nevertheless I cannot consider without the greatest wonder his new invention, never devised by any other. Homer placed the Inferno [in his work]. So did Euripides. Many other Greek poets placed it there. Furthermore, Virgil, Ovid, and Claudian: and some others among the Latins. But what figure do they imagine in it? What capacity do they give it? What site? Through which, as in a known thing and painted by an Apelles <note>the most famous painter of ancient Greece</note>, they might guide the listener as Dante guides [us]: who, through his high fantasy illustrated by a most subtle mind and by mathematical discipline, places before our eyes the form: the size: and the quality, in such a way that it can be understood with definite measurements. 

Which thing having I understood in good part, mostly through the work of our Antonio di Tuccio Manetti <note>a Florentine architect and mathematician (1423–1497) who was the first to attempt a rigorous mapping of Dante’s Hell</note>: who, investigating for a long time, has—if I am not mistaken—accurately understood the invention: and the description of this poet in general and in particular of all the Inferno / I judged it to be a most pleasing thing: and full of utility: and of joy / if I demonstrated it as clearly as possible before we come to interpret the text. Let the beginning be this then. Many excellent mathematicians—but especially Dante in his *Convivio* <note>The Banquet, a prose work by Dante</note>—place the earth’s circumference at twenty-four thousand miles. Therefore the half-diameter <term>radius (the distance from the surface to the center)</term> is three thousand two hundred forty-five and five-elevenths miles. Now, he imagining himself to have descended into the Inferno, it is certainly likely that, imitating Virgil, he places the same entrance: and this is near Lake Avernus, not much far...

The man who was born and lived without sin is Christ: who was consumed and died at Jerusalem. Here also is the river Acheron. After this is the second distance: but the *first circle*: and this is Limbo: and here are the moral souls who lived without Christian faith: and the innocent little ones who died without baptism. We shall call this second distance the first circle. The second place: and here the second species of souls who are the moral [virtuous pagans]: and the third which are the innocent little ones. The third distance is the second circle: and third place: and fourth species of souls who are the lustful. The fourth distance is the third circle: fourth place: and fifth species of souls who are the gluttonous punished in the rain. Whence he says:

<note>original: "Io sono al tertio cerchio della pioua." From Inferno VI.</note>

<note>original: "Chosi scendemo nella quarta lacca." From Inferno VII. "Lacca" is an archaic term for a ditch or cavity.</note>

Likewise, the tenth place and third ring: and the thirteenth species of sinners: who are the violent against God, nature, and art. This denotes that in that place they were on a perpendicular line below Crete where he describes the statue: and they had not yet turned through the whole circle. But to understand how much more they had to turn, we shall make on a nautical chart a straight line from Rome to Damietta in Egypt, and we will find that it crosses through the island of Crete: And in this way we will understand where Dante was under the earth. Then, crossing a straight line from Cuma where he feigns the gate of Hell to be, all the way to Jerusalem: and measuring with the compasses <term>seste|dividers or compasses used for measuring distances on maps</term> up to a thousand miles / we will understand that little remains to finish the whole circle. For this reason, it is to be estimated that he had finished it all in that place where he mounts upon the shoulders of Geryon. And being very close to the number of a thousand miles, it is to be estimated that he has circled Hell with this thousand-fold number. Hell, where he says:
> And if you were now reached the hemisphere
> Which is opposite to that which the great dry land
> Covers, and under whose peak was consumed
> The man who was born and lived without sin.
<note>original: "Et se hor sotto lhemisperio giunto / Che opposito a quel che la gran secca Copchia / et sotto el cui colmo consumpto / Fu lhuom che nacque et uixe sanza pecca." This refers to *Inferno* XXXIV, 112–115. The "man without sin" is Christ, and the peak is Jerusalem.</note>

In these verses, he describes Jerusalem, as we shall say in its proper place. Therefore, the circumference of this greatest breadth upon the surface of the earth is eleven thousand miles. It is likely that since there is a gap of one thousand miles across ten locations, it shows that in seven circles, he [Dante] passed through a tenth part of each of those. Now, because from Geryon <note>the three-bodied monster who carries Dante and Virgil down the cliff into the eighth circle</note> downward, the manner of traveling toward the center changes—having already shown how wide the mouth of Geryon's ravine is—it clearly appears that the diameter is 1,342 miles. Dante descends upon the shoulders of Geryon in a perpendicular line down to a breadth with a diameter of thirty-five miles. And here the head of **Malebolge** <term>Malebolge|literally "Evil Ditches," the name of the eighth circle of Hell</term> is joined. It remains to be seen the diameter of each ditch, from which the circumference can be calculated, in which the largest measures thirty-five miles.

And the rule he gives us is the ditch of the second-to-last, where he says that the valley winds twenty-two miles; and of the last, where he says that it winds eleven miles. But searching for the proportion they have together, we will not say that the enclosing one is always twice as much, as twenty-two is to eleven. For if it were, the third would have forty-four, the fourth eighty-eight, and proceeding thus, the tenth would have five thousand six hundred and thirty-two miles; and the greatest breadth of Hell is no more than three thousand five hundred miles. So you see that toward the center, there would be more breadth than at the surface, which is contrary to all dimension. Nor is such a distance consistent with the description he makes above of the bridges and the ditches.

But we will say that the enclosing one is always eleven miles more than the enclosed one. And thus all the ditches will equally have a distance of eleven miles, as we see when multiple moats surround a castle with equal distances: where each moat is one mile and three quarters wide, which will make the largest one thirty-five miles in diameter. And this is also quite easily understood in his narrative, where he shows no difference except for that last one, which is only half a mile in width, and the others are all a mile and three quarters. And this has some proportion to the greatest breadth of Hell, which we place at thirty-five hundred miles, with a circumference of one hundred and ten hundred [11,000] miles. And **Malebolge** has a diameter of thirty-five miles and a circumference of one hundred and ten.

Therefore, the first ditch is thirty-five miles [in circumference], in which there are the **pimps and seducers**. The second contains the **flatterers and sycophants**, and has a diameter of thirty-one and a half miles. The third, of the **simoniacs**, is twenty-eight. The fourth, of the **diviners**, is twenty-four and a half. The fifth, of the **barrators** <note>corrupt politicians who trade public office for money</note>, is twenty-one. The sixth, of the **hypocrites**, is seventeen and a half. The seventh, of the **thieves**, is fourteen miles. The eighth, of the **deceivers**, is ten and a half miles. The ninth, of the **schismatics**, is seven miles. Because of this, the circumference of such a diameter will be twenty-two miles. Whence Virgil says:

> Think if you can count them,
> For the valley winds twenty-two miles.
<note>original: "Pensa se tu annumerar gli puoi / Che migla uentidue la ualle uolge." From *Inferno* XXIX, 8-9.</note>

The tenth and last of Malebolge, where there are **falsifiers and alchemists**, is three and a half miles in diameter. Whence he says:

> Although it circles eleven miles,
> And is not less than half a mile across.
<note>original: "Con tutto che la giri undici migla / et men dun mezo di trauerso non fia." From *Inferno* XXX, 86-87.</note>

And certainly, subtracting two half-miles from its diameter (as they are taken within the circle), there remains a void diameter of two and a half miles. And this last one has a distance of half a mile from one summit of the bank to the other. Now, the circles of Malebolge could, on a flat plane, enclose one another successively with equal space between each; but the place is not on a plane, but on a slope, inclining toward the center. Whence he says in Canto XXIV:

> But because all of Malebolge slopes
> Toward the entrance of the lowest pit,
> The site of each valley carries
> That one bank rises and the other descends.
<note>original: "Ma perche malebolge inuer la porta / Del bassissimo pozzo tutto pende / Lo sito di ciaschuna ualle porta / Che luna chosta surge et laltra scende." From *Inferno* XXIV, 37–40.</note>

And elsewhere he shows the bottom and the steepness of these valleys, saying:

> There he gently set down his load,
> Gentle because of the rugged and steep rock,
> Which would be a hard passage for goats.
<note>original: "Quiui soauemente spose el carcho / Soaue per lo scoglio sconcio et erto / Che farebbe alle capre duro uarco." From *Inferno* XXIII, 139–141.</note>

Because of this, it is necessary that the valleys be wider, though only slightly if measuring them on a flat plane. Therefore, it seems to me that the half-part of the half-diameter of the widest place of such a site—which comes to be half of seventeen and a half miles—shall be the figure of the slope of this site: that is, the end of Geryon's pit is eight and three-quarter miles higher than the edge of the pit of the giants. From the end of Geryon's pit, which is the beginning of Malebolge, as I have said, until the center of the earth, it is thirty-two and a half miles. And subtracting that which Malebolge slopes—which seems to me to be eight and three-quarter miles—there remain twenty-three and three-quarter miles.

And let this suffice to have said about the site of Hell. But similarly, to understand the immense stature of the **giants**, we will investigate in the verses of the poet more measurements written by him. And first, we will note in Canto XXXI, where he writes thus of **Nimrod**:

> His face seemed to me as long and large
> As the pinecone of St. Peter's in Rome;
> And all his other bones were in proportion.
<note>original: "La faccia sua mi parea lunga et grossa / Come la pina di san Piero a Roma: / Et a sua proportion tutte laltre ossa." From *Inferno* XXXI, 58–60. The "Pigna" is a famous ancient Roman bronze pinecone, nearly 4 meters tall, now in a courtyard of the Vatican.</note>

According to these verses, the height of the head of this giant would be five and two-fifths Florentine cubits <term>braccia|a traditional unit of measurement, about 58 centimeters</term>, because we know that such is the size of the aforementioned bronze pinecone in Rome. Painters learned in symmetry say that a well-proportioned man is as long as eight of his heads. Therefore, this giant would be forty-three cubits or more. This, then, will be the height of the giants according to the poet's position.

It follows that by some principles laid down by him, we may similarly measure the size of **Lucifer**. But first we will note that after the circles and little circles and rounds of which we have spoken until now, there remain four spheres of bloody and frozen water, which have the universal center as their center. And in the one furthest from the center is founded the pit of the giants; and this is called **Caina**. Within this is enclosed the second, called **Antenora**. And in this...

the third is named **Ptolomea** <term>Ptolomea|The third zone of the ninth circle of Hell, named after Ptolemy of Jericho, who murdered his guests</term>: and within Ptolomea is enclosed the **Giudecca** <term>Giudecca|The innermost zone of Hell, named after Judas Iscariot, where the greatest traitors are frozen</term>, the smallest of them all. > Than giants do with his arms. 
<note>original: "Et piu con un gygante io mi conuegno / Che gyganti non fan colle sue braccia." This quote from *Inferno* XXXIV, 30–31, establishes the scale of the fallen angel.</note>

Dante says, therefore, that his own body has more in common with the size of giants than the bodies of giants have with the arm of Lucifer. And because Dante was of average height, we can estimate him at two <term>braccia|The Florentine "braccio" (plural braccia) was a standard unit of measurement, approximately 23 inches or 58 centimeters.</term> and seven-eighths. We concluded above, according to the measurement of the face compared to the pine cone at Saint Peter’s <note>The "Pigna," a massive bronze pine cone in Rome, used by Dante as a reference for the size of the giants' heads</note>, that the giants are forty-three braccia tall. Therefore, Dante would fit fifteen times into a giant. Consequently, a giant would fit the same number of times into the arm of Lucifer. 

This results in the arm of Lucifer being six hundred forty-five Florentine braccia. And because we see that a well-proportioned man is measured at three braccia, and the arm of such a man is one braccio and one-sixth long, it follows according to this proportion—if the arm of Lucifer is six hundred forty-five braccia—that his body is not far from two thousand braccia. Specifically, according to the measurement, it would be exactly one thousand nine hundred eighty braccia. But since he demonstrated that the giants compare poorly to his arm, we can set it at that round number. The same is true if we look at the measurement in **palmi** <note>palmi: spans or palms, another unit of length</note>, because every three palmi make a braccio; and measurements of heights are about two Florentine braccia. 

This much regarding his body. But as for the sphere of the Giudecca, in which the universal center lies, and from which Lucifer emerges from the waist up, it seems to me that its diameter is half of the aforementioned two thousand braccia—which is one thousand braccia. This is because from the middle of the chest to the top of the head is the measure of two heads; and just as much (that is, the measure of two other heads) should emerge from the side of the legs, since he has the middle of his body at the universal center, which is similarly the center of this sphere, as is noted in these verses:

> When we were there where the thigh 
> Turns exactly upon the thick of the haunches, 
> The Guide, with labor and with anguish, 
> Turned his head where he had his legs, 
> And grappled to the hair like one who climbs, 
> So that I thought we were returning to Hell. 
<note>original: "Quando noi fumo la doue la coscia / Si uolge apuncto in sul dosso dellanche / El duca con faticha et con angoscia / Volse la testa ouegli haueua le zanche : / Et aggrappossi al pel comhuom che sale / Sichininferno io credea tornare anche." From *Inferno* XXXIV, 76–81, describing the moment Virgil and Dante cross the center of gravity at Lucifer's hip.</note>

Thus, there would remain in the sphere the measure of four heads, which are half of the whole of Lucifer. Therefore, the diameter of the Giudecca will be one thousand braccia. And **Ptolomea**, which is contiguous to this, will be—I believe—the size of the whole body of Lucifer, that is, two thousand braccia. And then **Antenora**, which encloses this, will be three thousand braccia. And **Caina**, which is the largest, will be four thousand braccia. And if you ask what conjecture leads me to this opinion, I respond that this same rule is seen in the circles and the ditches of **Malebolge**. I have nothing else to contribute regarding the site of Hell and the stature of the giants and of Lucifer. Therefore, we shall hold to this opinion until someone of greater judgment comes along and shows us better the description of Dante, which we follow in this. 

His exit from Hell is quite clear, because he goes along a small stream that ends in the tomb of Lucifer, and on the surface of the earth in the other hemisphere, on the island where the **Mount of Purgatory** is located. Thus the poet writes:

> There is a place below, as far removed from Beelzebub 
> As his tomb extends, 
> Which is known not by sight but by the sound 
> Of a little stream that descends there 
> Through the hollow of a rock which it has eaten away 
> With a course that winds and slopes but little. 
<note>original: "Luogo e / laggiu da Belzabu remoto / Tanto quanto la tomba si distende / Che non per uista ma p suono e / noto / Dun ruscelletto che quiui discende / Per la bocca dun saxo che gliha roso / Col corso che glauuolge et pocho pende." From *Inferno* XXXIV, 127–132.</note>

The Guide and I, by that hidden path, 
Entered to return to the bright world; 
And without caring for any rest, 
We climbed up, he first and I second, 
Until I saw, through a round opening, 
Some of the beautiful things that Heaven bears; 
And thence we came forth to see again the stars. 
<note>original: "Leduca et io per quel camino abscoso / Entramo a ritornar nel chiaro mondo / Et sanza cura hauer dalchun riposo / Salimo su et primo et io secondo / Tanto chio uidi delle cose belle / Che porta el cielo per un pertugio tondo / Et quindi uscimmo a riueder le stelle." From *Inferno* XXXIV, 133–139.</note>

And that they exited against this stream, **Cato** <note>Cato the Younger, the guardian of the shores of Purgatory</note> demonstrates in the first canto of *Purgatorio* with these words:

> Who are you, that against the blind stream, 
> Have fled the eternal prison? 
<note>original: "Chi siete uoi che contro al cieco fiume / Fuggito hauete la prigione etherna." From *Purgatorio* I, 40–41.</note>

He said, moving those venerable plumes.

**I found myself within a dark wood**
for the direct way was lost.
And how hard a thing it is to tell
what this wood was like—wild and rugged and harsh—
that in the very thought it renews the fear!
It was so bitter that death is little more;
but to treat of the good that I found there,
I will tell of the other things I saw.
I cannot well say how I entered there,
so full of sleep was I at that point
when I abandoned the true way.
But after I had reached the foot of a hill,
there where that valley ended
which had pierced my heart with fear,
I looked on high and saw its shoulders
already draped in the rays of the planet <note>The "planet" refers to the Sun, which in the Ptolemaic system was considered a planet and here symbolizes divine light or reason.</note>
that leads others straight on every path.
Then the fear was somewhat quieted,
which had endured in the lake of my heart
through the night I passed with such anguish.

<column-break/>

We have narrated not only the life of the
poet and the title of the book and what a
poet is, but also how ancient and venerable, how
noble and varied, how useful and joyful such
doctrine is. How effective it is in moving human
minds; and how much it delights every noble spirit. Nor
did we think it right to remain silent about how much
the excellence of the genius of
our poet excelled in such divine discipline.
In which, if I have been more brief than
perhaps would be fitting, let the reader consider that
the numerous and almost infinite abundance of things
which must be treated forces me—as I do not wish
the volume to grow beyond measure—to compress
and involve rather than explain and expand
on many things, especially those which, even
if I were silent, would not leave the
exposition of the text obscure. We shall come then to that.
But because I believe there is no reader of
so low a mind, nor of so little judgment, who,
having understood both the depth and
variety of the doctrine, and the excellence and divinity
of the genius of our Tuscan and Florentine
poet, does not persuade himself that this beginning
of the first canto must, by its sublimity and greatness,
be equal to the stupendous doctrine of the things
that follow: therefore with all industry we will investigate
what allegorical sense this "midst of the journey"
brings with it, and what the "wood" might be. Regarding which,
I see no small difference has existed among
the interpreters and expositors of this canticle.
For some say that the "midst of human life"
is sleep, moved—I believe—by the opinion
of Aristotle <note>original: "aristotele"</note> saying in his *Ethics* <note>original: "ethica"</note> that there is no
difference between the happy and the miserable during half
of life, because the nights, which are half of the time,
bring sleep; and from that it arises that we can feel neither
good nor evil. Therefore, these people want
the poet to place the "midst of life" for the
night, and the night for sleep, to note that this
poem is nothing other than a vision that appeared
to him while sleeping, through which he had knowledge of
the things described by him in these three comedies.
They say, therefore, that he imitates John the Evangelist,

who, sleeping upon the breast of Christ the Redeemer, had a vision of celestial things; or
he places the night to show that he began his poem at night, in which the mind,
gathering itself into itself and absolving and liberating itself from every care, might understand better. But although such

that it does not seem worthy of the elegance of such a poet. First, because it does not follow that, although in the

such an interpretation for the day as for the night. Others say that he wanted "the midst of the journey" to mean

<meta>On the previous page, the commentator Cristoforo Landino introduced the spiritual and literal importance of Dante’s work. He began by presenting the opening lines of the poem and started a scholarly discussion on the "middle of the journey," referencing the classical and biblical definitions of the human lifespan.</meta>

It seems he approves of the opinion of certain poets who divide the human age by the <term>number seven</term> <note>This "septenary" system was a common medieval and Renaissance way of categorizing the stages of life, influenced by both astrology and theology.</note>, attributing the first seven years to infancy; the second to childhood; and the third—reaching twenty-one—to adolescence. Afterward, they designate two seven-year periods for youth, reaching thirty-five; and at this same point, Aristotle argues in his writings that one is at the perfect age to celebrate marriage. After youth follows the "virile age," which through two seven-year periods reaches the forty-ninth year. At this time, because men possess perfect judgment and have not yet lost their physical strength, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle was often referred to simply as "the Philosopher" in medieval and Renaissance texts.</note> judges that a man is most fit for the government of the republic. Finally, he places the remainder of life into three seven-year periods, setting the limit at seventy years—almost as if he were foretelling his own death, which occurred in the seventieth year of his life. He was primarily moved by this because the number seven is not only made of seven units but is also multiplied by ten, which is a perfect number. This same sentiment belongs to the Psalmist, who says: <note>original: "Anni nostri sicut aranea meditabuntur; dies annorum nostrorum in ipsis septuaginta anni. Si autem in potentatibus octuaginta anni: et amplius eorum labor et dolor."</note> "Our years will be considered like a spider’s web; the days of our years in themselves are seventy years. But if in the powerful they are eighty years, more than that is their labor and sorrow." Pythagoras of Samos set the end of life at the eightieth year, and similarly, he died at that time. Solon the Athenian also set the limit at eighty years.

The astrologers, who refer everything to the course of the stars, grant ninety-five years. These thinkers believe the Moon contributes four years; Mercury ten; Venus eight; the Sun nineteen; Mars fifteen; and Jupiter twelve. Afterward, in the remainder of the "decrepit" age, Saturn rules; in this stage there is coldness, fatigue, distress, and heaviness of both body and mind. For this reason, few reach it. There were several who—as Servius reports in the fourth book of the *Aeneid*—said there were three types of limits to our life: of nature, of fate, and of chance. They believe nature extends until the fourth cycle of Saturn; because Saturn makes its revolution every thirty years, this would be one hundred and twenty years. Fate is three cycles of Saturn; therefore, death comes in the ninetieth year. But if the benevolence of some lucky star breaks the malice of Saturn, a man can reach the fourth cycle already mentioned. Hence Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian.</note> in his *Antiquities* writes that God, after the flood of Noah, shortened the years of human life—which before the flood had in some cases passed nine hundred—and decreed that the final limit should be one hundred and twenty. For this reason, certain interpreters of Statius hold that when he writes: <note>original: "Dadraste rex Ibi tranquille medio de limite uite. Ingenium uergens populos Adrastus habebat"</note> "King Adrastus was there peacefully at the middle limit of life. Adrastus had a character leaning toward the people," he intended this to be in the sixtieth year, which is the middle of one hundred and twenty.

Nevertheless, because the common opinion of men follows Aristotle and David <note>King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note>, they understand the middle of life to be thirty-five years. But although such an explanation is not entirely far from the truth, nonetheless, for such a high poem, it seems that another principle is required. To express this better, we will briefly repeat some things from further back, which will clearly open the mind of the author to us, making it easy to interpret this beginning.

It is likely, then, that Dante proposed for himself the same goal that Homer among the Greeks and Virgil among the Latins had proposed. And just as those authors—one through Ulysses, the other through Aeneas—show how, by coming to the knowledge of vices and, once recognized, purging oneself of them, one finally arrives at the contemplation of divine things; so Dante, under this fictional pilgrimage, feigns having made a journey with Virgil. In his own person, he demonstrates that very same thing. For man is composed of soul and body. The soul is divine, simple, immortal, and incorruptible. Because it is produced by God in His image and likeness, it is divine and full of light; it is capable through contemplation of coming to the knowledge of divine things and enjoying God. In this consists our supreme good, as we will treat more fully in another place. The body, on the contrary, being composed of the matter of the four elements, is by its nature corruptible, dark, and full of shadows. The soul, then, submerged in this "dark prison," loses almost all its celestial vigor; and through the darkness of the body, it remains almost deprived of every light of reason—one could say it is buried under the corporeal mass. Hence the divine Plato wisely posits two types of death: one he calls "animal death," a thing known to everyone, which occurs when the soul is separated from the body. The other is the "death of the soul"; and this occurs when the soul—as we have already said—submerged by the weight and darkness of the body, loses so much vigor that none of its excellent powers can operate.

Because of this, we see man, not only in the first years of infancy and childhood but in a large part of adolescence and youth, living only according to the senses. And because he knows nothing else but that, he does not believe himself to be anything else, and considers nothing good except those things that delight the physical senses. Nor does he consider anything bad except what saddens them. Like one drunk and oppressed by profound sleep, he neither knows himself nor understands for what purpose he was created; nor does he know his ignorance or his misery until, having reached a mature age through the experience of many things—partly through acquired learning and through precepts received from those wiser than himself—he begins to awaken his reason. And then, finally, he recognizes himself to be in a "dark wood"—that is, he sees his soul is oppressed by ignorance and by vices through the contagion of the body. This is, therefore, the meaning of the text: **I FOUND MYSELF WITHIN A DARK WOOD**, which signifies: "I realized my soul was submerged in the body, through the contagion and darkness of which it had lost the straight and true way." **IN THE MIDST OF THE JOURNEY OF OUR LIFE**: that is, in the middle of the course of human life, at which time discretion begins to awaken in man, which until that point had been almost extinguished. Having awakened, he notices his error and takes the path of salvation—unless he allows himself to be so overcome by sensuality that, instead of proceeding forward, he returns backward into the darkness of the wood. From which misery David prays to the Lord to guard him, saying: "O Lord, do not call me back in the middle of my days." Nor is it necessary to interpret "the middle" as exactly that point which is equidistant from the extremes, as we will say there is a middle...

It transitions into an allegorical interpretation, where the "dark wood" represents the soul's imprisonment in the body and the awakening of reason in adulthood.</summary>

<meta>On the previous page, Cristoforo Landino discussed the symbolic meaning of Dante being "midway through the journey of our life," calculating the human lifespan at seventy years based on biblical and Aristotelian cycles of seven.</meta>

<header>CANTO ONE</header>

seventeen, because it has eight on each side <note>Landino is continuing a mathematical or symbolic division of ages or numbers from the previous page</note>. Therefore, the "middle" should not be interpreted so strictly: for even among philosophers, the "middle" is often said to be that which is distant from the extremes, even if it is not exactly equidistant. **OF THE JOURNEY.** Excellently said, because our life is not placed in eternity where everything is stable and in eternal rest, but in time, which is nothing other than a continuous flow and course. Furthermore, as the Apostle says, we are not in our homeland here, nor do we have a permanent city. Instead, this life is a <term>pilgrimage</term> <note>A common medieval trope of "homo viator"—man the traveler—wandering through the world toward heaven.</note> which, if we proceed along a certain path, leads us to the heavenly Jerusalem, our true homeland, where we are "citizens with the saints and members of the household of God." <note>original Latin: "ciues sanctorum et domestici dei," referencing Ephesians 2:19.</note> Nor should we overlook, for the clarification of this passage, that he said "I found myself" and not "I entered." For the soul enters the body as soon as it is created, but it does not realize its own ignorance except in the "middle of the journey," as we have said. Nor is it without reason that he uses the <term>wood</term> <note>The "dark wood" or *selva oscura*.</note> to represent the body, and consequently to represent vice. This is because both Plato and many other philosophers call corporeal matter <term>hyle</term> in Greek, which in Latin is *silva* <note>meaning "wood" or "forest"</note>. Just as the soul possesses every excellence and happiness through its indivisible, incorporeal, and incorruptible nature, so, on the contrary, it possesses every calamity and every vice through the "wood"—that is, through the body, which is corruptible. For this reason, Plato rightly calls God the cause and source of all good, and conversely calls the "wood"—that is, our earthly prison—the cause of all evils. Thus, Boethius wisely wrote: "Happy is he who could break the heavy chains of the earth." <note>original Latin: "Felix qui potuit grauis terre rumpere uincula."</note> And certainly, he is blessed who can break the bonds of the heavy earth, free the soul from the contagion of the body and from sensuality, and elevate himself to celestial things. This is why the Greeks call the body <term>demas</term>, because *dein* means "to bind," and the body, as has been said, is the bond of the soul. Indeed, just as the fly, drawn by the sweetness of honey, plunges into it until it drowns, so the soul, ensnared and entangled by earthly sweetnesses, becomes so submerged and drowned in their pleasantness from the beginning that, having become entirely drunk, it hardly wakes up, nor can it taste the nourishment of true joy, which is the contemplation of celestial things. From this it follows that although our soul is led toward this contemplation, the "wood" nevertheless makes it lose the way; for the contagion of the body robs it of the knowledge which, if it possessed it, would allow it to understand how much our nature surpasses other animals. For animals feel nothing but the pleasure of the body and direct themselves toward it with every impulse. But the human mind is nourished by learning, and through thinking, it is always investigating or truly engaged in some action. He therefore uses the "wood" to represent the contagion of the body and the darkness and ignorance, imitating his master Virgil, who said: "Woods hold all the middle parts." <note>original Latin: "tenent media omnia sylve," from the Aeneid.</note>

**STRAYED**: and not "lost," because one who has already wandered into vices, when they eventually return to virtue, had not lost the way, but only strayed from it. **AH, HOW HARD IT IS TO SAY**: what it was like is a difficult thing. Here is a rhetorical ornament called an "exclamation," used when we wish to demonstrate the greatness of a thing, or truly when we wish to express a just indignation against what seems to us most worthy of blame—as when he says, "Ah, Constantine, of how much ill were you the mother!" <note>Dante often blamed the Emperor Constantine's "Donation" for the corruption of the Church.</note> And so he uses this word "ah," which the Latins call an interjection. Therefore, "ah, how hard a thing"—that is, difficult—it was "to say"—that is, to narrate—"what"—that is, of what quality—was this "savage wood"—that is, this wood that was derelict, abandoned, and remote from all cultivation and human habitation. For vice is entirely removed from human nature, since the Platonic and Aristotelian philosophers prove with effective demonstrations that to live according to nature is to live according to virtue. Therefore, it is "savage," as if to say it is "feral" and not human; for he who is infected by vices, although he retains the human form, has nevertheless become a most cruel beast in his habits—against God, against himself, and against his neighbor. **RUGGED**: certainly the wood of vices is rugged. Just as nothing is sweeter than having a pure conscience, which keeps the soul tranquil, joyful, and without any fear, so vice continually goads us with constant fears—either of the future eternal punishments ordained for the soul of the sinner, or of the present punishments with which civil and moral laws threaten us. The flaming caverns of Etna or Mongibello do not surge or boil as much as the conscience of a sinner. **TOUGH**: because it is difficult and almost impregnable to remove a habit already contracted in vice. **WHICH RENEWS THE FEAR IN MY HEART**: And certainly, just as we remember laudable deeds with pleasure and the highest satisfaction of conscience, so on the contrary, when we have returned from vice to virtue, we remember our past and vicious life with horror and the deepest repentance. For this reason, Plato admonished his friends to remember that corporeal pleasures and delights were momentary and brief, and left nothing but repentance after them. **AND SO BITTER**: that death is little more. **BUT TO TREAT**: of the good I found there, I will tell of the other things I perceived. There is the death of the animal, as we said shortly before, and there is the death of the soul. And the death of the soul is also understood in two ways: either according to the Platonists, when the soul, entering the body, is submerged and suffocated by it and loses almost all its vigor; or truly when the soul is separated from the body and remains dead in sin. It is this second one he means at present, because it is the most horrific, since it has no redemption and such death is eternal and sensible. For the soul is "dead" not because it does not remain immortal and endure forever, but because it is placed in eternal and supreme misery. Therefore, we shall say that the wood is "bitter" because such is the vicious life of a man still living in the body. But because he has redemption and can convert to God and do good, it follows that the death mentioned just above is more bitter because it is beyond all hope. **BUT TO TREAT of the good I found there.** And certainly, it is no small good to know the darkness of the wood—that is, the vice which deprives the soul of every light—because once that is known, it becomes so abominable that we flee it and purge ourselves of it with every industry. Therefore, we find this "good" in the wood. Thus Horace wisely said: "Virtue is to flee vice, and wisdom..."

He explains the rhetorical and philosophical significance of Dante's "straying" as a temporary departure from virtue rather than a permanent loss of the soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on the opening of Canto I. Having previously discussed the "dark wood" as a symbol of the physical body and worldly vice, Landino now moves into the transition toward the "hill" of virtue and the role of human reason.</meta>

-># INFERNO <-

to have been without the first folly: and to flee from vice is virtue. And to drive folly away from oneself is the beginning of wisdom. Some say that the poet wants to show that even in Hell one finds good, because justice is found there, which is the sum of all moral virtues. Although this may be true, the first interpretation fits the text better.

**I CANNOT WELL REPEAT HOW I** entered it, so full of sleep was I; This explains what we said above regarding the <term>wood</term><note>The *selva oscura* or dark wood, symbolizing the material world and vice.</note> and the entry of the soul into the body, and subsequently all that time when reason is dormant and nothing but the senses can act within us. Therefore, a man cannot say how or in what way he enters the wood—that is, how the soul enters the body, from which it contracts many vices—because at 그 point it is "full of sleep." This means it becomes so intoxicated by the corporeal mass that reason falls asleep within it and does not wake until the "middle of the journey." And so it follows: **SO MUCH** was I full of sleep at that point; That is, the soul was so lulled by the drunkenness of the senses that reason, being thus asleep, left the <term>straight way</term><note>The path of virtue.</note>, which cannot be seen by one who walks in darkness. As every philosopher confesses, moral virtue is a middle point established between two extremes. For example, there is a virtue regarding the distribution and spending of our money, which observes a moderate middle ground between "too little" and "too much," and it is called <term>liberality</term><note>Generosity.</note>. This has two extremes: the defect called <term>avarice</term><note>Greed.</note>, because it falls short and does not reach the middle; and the excess called <term>prodigality</term><note>Wasteful spending.</note>, which does not restrain itself within the boundaries of moderation but exceeds and surpasses them. Therefore, just as if you were to draw a line always through the center of a wide and spacious field, it must be straight, and all others that bend in any direction will be crooked, even if they were innumerable; so too only virtue is "straight," because it always proceeds with equal distance from the extremes. All others are "crooked" because they twist toward one extreme or the other. And similarly, just as it is impossible to find the center line in that field in the dark and continue along it without twisting, so without the light of reason, it is impossible in human life to find the middle ground of virtue and persevere in it without slipping into some extreme where the vices are. Because walking in the dark, one does not find the middle line, which is only one—or if it is found by chance, it is not maintained. But the other paths, which are many, are easy to find without any light; and it is also easy to decline from one into another, always wandering. For this reason, the Greek poet Hesiod wisely said that vice could be taken all at once. But God did not wish for one to come to virtue without sweat. And Arcesilaus, the Academic philosopher, used to say that the road leading to Hell is easy because one goes there with eyes closed—that is, without the light of reason—because every sin proceeds from ignorance, which is nothing other than the privation of reason. For this reason, David, speaking of the works and actions of the sinner, said: *Let their ways be dark.* <note>original Latin: "Fient uie eorum tenebre," from Psalm 35:6.</note> And certainly, the ways of the sinner are darkness, because in them one does not discern the truth. I believe I have demonstrated quite clearly why the poet calls the way of virtue "straight" and why sleep makes one lose it. Therefore, let us proceed.

**BUT AFTER** I had reached the foot of a hill, there where that valley ended. Let us first understand this according to the literal sense: that walking through the woody valley, he encountered a mountain in such a way that it was necessary either to turn back the way he came to avoid the climb, or to climb the hill if he desired the path to be straight. One does not come to the virtues except by climbing the mountain. For this reason, Basil said: *The road that leads to virtue is at first rough and almost impassable, full of continuous sweat and labor. Therefore, it is not for everyone to undertake it because of its steepness, nor is it easy for the one who does to reach its summit.* <note>original Latin: "Aspera primo et pene in uia et sudoris continui et laborun piena est uia quae ad uirtutem ducit..." Landino quotes Saint Basil the Great on the difficulty of the virtuous life.</note> The mountain, then, is <term>contemplation</term>; and at the summit is the sun, which is wisdom. And just as Virgil places the golden bough, which is wisdom, at the top of a tree surrounded by valleys, so Dante places the sun at the summit of the mountain. Virgil uses doves—representing contemplation—as guides for Aeneas to the golden bough because they fly high; and elsewhere he says: *Therefore, look high with your eyes.* <note>original Latin: "Ergo alte uestiga oculis," from the Aeneid.</note> Therefore, through the tree, the doves, and this verse, he demonstrates the height that Dante demonstrates through the mountain. While he looked into the valley, he saw nothing but darkness, because in earthly things the sun—that is, wisdom—is not seen. But it is seen on the mountain—that is, in the elevation of the soul to divine things. Whence David said: *I lifted my eyes to the mountain.* <note>original Latin: "leuaui oculos meos ad montem," from Psalm 121:1.</note> Under this figure, we shall understand the same thing that Pythagoras, the philosopher from Samos, expressed through the letter **Y** which he devised. This letter has a single line at the beginning until it reaches the point of the fork. There it divides into two: one goes straight up to the right, the other twists to the left. This represents all of human life: for there is almost a single life for all men until the "years of discretion." This is because nothing done in early childhood is imputed to perfect virtue or complete vice, as ignorance is excusable there without true choice. Therefore, here the poet, by the way of the wood, meant the first part of the aforementioned letter. Then, at the end of the valley, he found that the path which had been one until then divided into two: one followed straight up the steepness of the hill, the other twisted to the left at the foot of its base. Having reached this <term>crossroads</term><note>The Pythagorean *bivium*, the point in youth where one must choose between the path of virtue or vice.</note>, just as he had gone in darkness until then, he then began to see the light of the sun, which already struck the shoulders of the mountain, and having seen it, he directed himself toward it. For when we reach the years of discretion, the light of reason begins to shine in us, showing us the mountain already resplendent and inviting us to climb it. This signifies that reason directs us to the contemplation and knowledge of divine things, in which our supreme good consists. God created us in his image and likeness—not our body, but our soul. Therefore, there is innate within the soul a supreme and seraphic love to join ourselves with Him. And through such love, reason is awakened—which until this time had been drunk and sleepy—and having fallen in love, it deserves to be enlightened by the <term>Cherubic light</term><note>An intellectual illumination associated with the Cherubim, the order of angels known for their knowledge of God.</note> with which it sees and knows God as much as its nature is capable. He therefore used the mountain to represent such contemplation. Two things are in the mountain: it is elevated, and it is closer to heaven. This admonishes us that all our inquiry and search should be for the...

<summary>Landino explains Dante's "sleep" as the dormancy of reason and discusses virtue as a middle ground between extremes. He uses the metaphor of the Pythagorean 'Y' to describe the choice between vice and the difficult climb toward divine wisdom.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on the opening of Canto I of Dante's Inferno. Having previously discussed the "dark wood" as a symbol of worldly vice, Landino now analyzes the "mountain" of contemplation, the role of reason (symbolized by the sun), and the psychological states of virtue and vice.</meta>

# CANTO FIRST
a. iiii

high and celestial things, not low and earthly ones. Furthermore, it is certain because, in truth, one does not reach such contemplation without difficulty. Not only has this poet used the mountain to represent such contemplation, but many writers of sacred scripture also use it as a similar figure; especially the poetic prophet David in the psalm where, saying: **"Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place?"** <note>original: "Quis ascendet in montem domini aut quis stabit in loco sancto eius"</note> he asks nothing other than who shall arrive at this knowledge. He climbed the mountain with the help of the sun, which showed it to him, because without the sun—that is, without **reason**, which is the true guide of human virtue and the queen of our soul—the way that leads us to contemplation is not perceived. This sun is that which leads us to safety through every path—that is, way. Because none of our actions can be perfect if reason does not show it to us and judge it to be so. Nor can a man in any way work in the <term>active life</term><note>The life of practical action and social duty.</note> or investigate in the <term>contemplative life</term><note>The life of prayer, study, and meditation.</note> in a manner that achieves the proper end, except through reason. We shall treat this more distinctly when the occasion arises. Nor is it a new thing that he uses the sun to represent reason, because even among the sacred writers it is said: **"let not the sun go down upon your anger."** <note>original: "ne occidat sol super iracundiam vestram"</note>

**THEN WAS THE FEAR A LITTLE QUIETED:** Excellent! Because when reason begins to shine within us, showing us the mountain—that is, the road that goes to the goal of salvation—fear does not cease entirely. For although we have seen the way, we are not yet upon it. Nonetheless, the mind is somewhat calmed, and the fear decreases, because hope is born in us of being able to reach the goal, seeing now the true path.

**WHICH IN THE LAKE of my heart had lasted:** The human heart has three <term>ventricles</term><note>In Renaissance anatomy, the heart was thought to have three chambers or 'ventricles' where the vital spirits were refined and the 'spirits' of life were housed.</note>. In the middle one, nourishment reaches its perfection. Of the two extremes, one is the receptacle of the blood, which is drawn from the liver; the other of the spirit, drawn from the lungs. In the heart is the principle of life. And because the spirit is that which, like a craftsman, forms the limbs, and this spirit would perish as soon as it is created if it did not have a certain seat in which it could receive the increase of its essence and generation, therefore, in the body of the animal, the heart—the seat of the spirit—is created before any other limb. And all primary heat and virtue come from the heart. Thus, according to the quality and quantity of the heart, the greatness of the soul is born, as is timidity; about which we have disputed more at length in our second dialogue *On the Soul*, written in the Latin language. And for this reason, the poet said "in the lake of the heart." And note that this fear lasted a great while from the moment he perceived himself to be off the true path until the sun gave him hope of being able to return to it.

**THE NIGHT:** That is, all the past age which, deprived of the light of reason and obscured by ignorance, is deservedly called "night."

**PITY:** <gloss>Lament</gloss>. First, it should be noted that in the Florentine language, one finds <term>pietà</term><note>pietà with a grave accent on the last syllable</note> meaning "compassion"—hence the saying: **"Here pity lives when it is well dead."** <note>A quote from Inferno XX, 28, where Virgil rebukes Dante for feeling compassion for the damned, suggesting that true justice leaves no room for pity toward those God has judged.</note> Also, one finds <term>pièta</term><note>pièta with an acute accent on the penultimate syllable</note> meaning a "lament" suited to move one to compassion; and it is in this sense that the poet uses it. Nor is it without reason that he says **THE NIGHT that I passed with such pity**, because he wants to show that when he realized he had lost the way, he grieved for it. And by this we understand that although he was in vice, nonetheless he had not yet made a firm habit of it; therefore, he could more easily extricate himself from it. He was, then, not "intemperate" but "incontinent."

So that this may be more clearly understood, let us say there is a virtue called <term>temperance</term><note>The ability to control one's desires habitually and without struggle.</note>, in which he who has formed a habit stays within bounds and abstains from every pleasure and vicious or dishonest delight, so that no difficulty hinders him, nor is it a burden to abstain. And likewise, he who has formed a habit in the vice of <term>intemperance</term> gives himself entirely to a lascivious and voluptuous life and to every lust without any impediment of shame or remorse of conscience. And for this reason, we say that the former is true virtue and the latter—that is, intemperance—is true vice, because in each there is a "habit," without which there can be neither virtue nor vice. But before a man contracts such habits of either temperance or intemperance, we have two dispositions through which we slide into the habit. One leads us to virtue and is called <term>continence</term><note>continentia: the state of doing the right thing but only after a difficult struggle against one's own desires.</note>. For the continent man wants to abstain from a lascivious life, but he does not restrain himself without great effort, because he has not yet made a habit of temperance. But by persevering in this continence through long practice, he forms a habit in it, and afterward, he restrains himself without difficulty; he is no longer "continent" but "temperate." The other leads us to vice. For the <term>incontinent</term><note>incontinentia: the state of knowing what is right but failing to resist temptation.</note> man likewise would not want to fall into vice, and he fights against lust just as the continent man fought; but he does not conquer it as the continent man does, but allows himself to be conquered. And after many times, he forms a habit in lust and no longer fights but willingly follows it, and becomes "intemperate."

Therefore, following the fiction of Virgil, **Dido** at the beginning, when she saw **Aeneas**, was temperate and willingly and without effort abstained from all lasciviousness. Whence he says: **"Then briefly Dido, her face downcast, speaks."** <note>original: "Tum breuiter Dido uultum demiſſa profatur"</note> Afterward, after the banquet, beginning already to incline toward love, from being temperate she became "continent," because as the flames grew, she inclined toward love; but still, although it was difficult for her, she nonetheless abstained from lustful acts. Therefore she was no longer temperate but had become continent, and she fought with vice but still conquered it. For which reason she says: **"If it did not sit fixed and immovable in my soul, that I should not wish to join myself to any in the bond of marriage... perhaps I could have succumbed to this one fault"** <note>original: "Si mihi non animo fixum immotumque ſederet. Ne cui me uinclo uellem ſo ciare iugali Huic uni forſan potui ſuccumbere culpe"</note> and a little below: **"I recognize the traces of the old flame."** <note>original: "Agnoſco ueteris ueſtigia flamme"</note> She is, therefore, fought by love, but still conquers it. Whence she concludes that she would rather be struck by Jove's lightning than violate her chastity. But not long after, she becomes "incontinent." Because as love continues to torment her, she finally allows herself to be conquered, though unwillingly—mostly through the persuasions of her sister. Nor did she stop falling to the bottom until she became "intemperate," because having now made a habit of lasciviousness, she willingly gave herself to it. This the poet shows by saying: **"No longer does Dido contemplate a secret love."** <note>original: "Nec iam furtiuum Dido meditatur amorem"</note> See, therefore, what Temperance, Continence, Incontinence, and Intemperance are. Therefore, returning to our purpose...

<header>INFERNO</header>

Dante was not "intemperate" because he had not made a habit of vice, but rather "incontinent," because although he fought against vice, he nonetheless allowed himself to be overcome by it. <note>In Aristotelian ethics, the "incontinent" person knows what is right but fails due to passion, while the "intemperate" person has lost the sense of what is right entirely.</note>

Through an excellent comparison and true simile, he shows that having left the woods, he looks back at them no differently than a man who, having been shipwrecked at sea and finally brought to shore, looks back at the water and considers the grave danger he faced in the shipwreck. And truly, the soul is in no less vexation and agitation when, having lost every rudder and sail of **reason**, it is carried away by the impetuous waves of the sea—that is, by the furious disturbances and passions that proceed from appetite and sensuality. These cause the soul to break upon the rocks of vice; from which, with the greatest diffi-

->So my soul, which was still fleeing,<-
->turned back to look again upon the pass<-

-culty one can be brought to shore. And certainly, while our soul, having lost its reason, is carried away by disordered appetite—whether by vain joy, heavy grief, excessive fear, or immeasurable greed—it is similar to a ship caught in a grave storm. I demonstrated this quite clearly in our *Camaldolese Disputations* <note>Landino’s own philosophical work, the *Disputationes Camaldulenses* (c. 1472).</note> in the allegory of the Virgilian storm, where Juno, with the help of Aeolus, tries to sink the Trojans. This denotes that the greed of ambition persuades the lower reason to remove Aeneas from Italy—that is, from the <term>contemplative life</term><note>A life dedicated to the study of divine truths.</note>—and push him toward Carthage—that is, toward the <term>active life</term><note>A life of political and social engagement.</note>.

**BREATH** (*LENA*): in our language means what the Latins call <term>respiration</term><note>original: "respiratione"</note>, which is a quiet and tranquil breathing that is maintained effortlessly and pleasantly within one's strength. But either too much physical fatigue or too much mental disturbance often causes such breath to labor. Therefore, if someone persists in an exercise for a long time without getting tired, we say they have "good breath."

**PERILOUS** (*PErigliosa*): that is, dangerous. **AND GAZES** (*Et GVata*): that is, gazing, he considers the past danger. **WHICH WAS STILL FLEEING** (*CHE Anchora fuggiua*): that is, he was still in fear. For just as one who has a strong and unconquered soul in the face of horrifying things is said to have "presence of mind," so on the contrary we say the soul "flees" from those who fear the horror of such things. And he demonstrates here what happens: even though the danger that made you fear has ceased, nonetheless the fear does not cease so suddenly. 

But how shall we interpret it when he says that the **pass** from which he emerged **never left any person alive**, given that he himself did not perish there? We shall say, then, that he uses that rhetorical ornament which the Greeks call **hyperbole** <note>original: "hyperbole"</note> and the Latins call **exaggeration** <note>original: "Superlatio"</note>. In this, to demonstrate the greatness of a thing, one goes beyond the literal truth. He means "never left any person alive" in the sense that, even if some pass through safely, they are so few that one can say "no one" in comparison to the infinite number who perish there. And certainly, those who escape the darkness of ignorance in such a way as to arrive at the light of true knowledge are extremely rare. 

Some understand that the way of sin kills whoever walks upon it; hence: **The soul that sins, it shall die.** <note>original: "anima que peccauerit ipsa morietur" (Ezekiel 18:20).</note> Others want "living person" to be the agent and say the pass never let any living person go; because, as we have said, no one comes into life who is not from the beginning oppressed by the ignorance from which sin is born.

**AFTER I HAD RESTED MY TIRED BODY** (*POI POsato hebbi el corpo lasso*): He wisely makes mention of the body. For notwithstanding that climbing the mountain—that is, the contemplative life—is where our highest good consists, and for this reason a man must strive to purge the soul of vices so that it becomes capable of holy doctrines (since the spirit of wisdom does not enter a malevolent soul), nonetheless the body is not to be deprived of necessary things. There is an excellent precept from the Apostle saying: **I chastise my body and bring it into subjection** <note>original: "Castiga el corpo et reducilo in seruitu" (1 Corinthians 9:27).</note>, because one should not nourish it with so many delights that the appetite rebels against reason. But he does not command that it be entirely abandoned, because it should not be deprived of necessities. For a body that is sick or too exhausted hinders the soul and does not let it act according to virtue. Therefore, the poet wisely shows that the body should not be kept in too much ease, but rested when it is tired, and rested only a little—that is, as much as necessity requires.

**ACROSS THE DESERT SLOPE** (*PER LA piaggia diserta*): That is, abandoned, because "desert" in Latin signifies "abandoned." From this we call deserted places "uninhabited." And certainly it is true that the path which leads man to knowledge is abandoned, because very few are those who give themselves to the contemplative life. Hence Petrarch said: **"Poor and naked you go, Philosophy," said the crowd intent on base gain; "You will have few companions on your way."** <note>Lines from Petrarch's *Canzoniere* (Sonnet 7), lamenting the decline of interest in wisdom during his time.</note>

And when he says that **the firm foot was always the lower**, he demonstrates the manner of climbing upwards. In such a journey, the foot that moves rises, and the one that is still remains lower. Allegorically, this shows that our cognition must proceed in order, and one foot should not be raised until the other is first firm. This means that we should not proceed forward in contemplating higher things if we are not first well-confirmed in the science of the lower ones. We can also say that the "foot" signifies the love and appetite for things. For just as the body is carried by the feet, so is the soul by appetite. Whence he said in the eighteenth chapter of *Purgatory*...

for if love is offered to us from without, and the soul does not walk with another foot, whether it goes straight or crooked is not to its merit. Therefore, the lower foot signifies the love of inferior things, and this was "firm" because it still had more power over him than the higher foot—that is, the love of celestial things—because he was not yet purged of his vices.

And without fail, the doctrine of our poet is profound. Not without reason does he propose **Virgil** as his guide and leader: for he goes on imitating him in every part, though so discreetly that few notice it. Virgil, through Aeneas, intended to demonstrate how a man might arrive at the Supreme Good. He posits three primary obstacles that prevent us from attaining our end: the first is **Lust**, meaning by lust every lewdness and every unbridled willpower and pleasure of sensuality; the

The second is **Avarice**, which he expresses through the Harpies <note>Landino refers to the "Strophades," the islands where the Harpies lived in the Aeneid.</note> and through many other things. The third is **Ambition** and the immoderate desire for honors, magistrates, and empires; he demonstrates this vice primarily through the immortal enmities of Juno against

<column-break/>

the Trojans. Therefore, the man who by his nature loves virtue and hates vice, and desires his Supreme Good and flees misery, would always proceed along the straight path if three things did not impede him. These are **Pleasure, Utility, and Honor**: and to pursue these, we often leave the direct road. Consequently, Dante signifies these same things now through the three beasts: the **Leopard** is Pleasure; the **She-wolf** is Utility <note>specifically, the greedy pursuit of material gain</note>; and the **Lion** is Honor <note>or prideful ambition</note>. He had already exited the woods and, seeing the summit of the hill illuminated by the sun, was preparing to reach it by climbing the slope, as we have explained allegorically above. And so it happens that when a man arrives at the years of discretion, and reason is awakened in him, he prepares himself to desire the Supreme Good. But this good will is impeded by the aforementioned vices. First by pleasure: for in the years of childhood and youth, the pleasures of man are most burning, and it is difficult to put a rein on them in the fervor of the blood. Wherefore infinite is the crowd of the intemperate or the incontinent; for which reason they are rare in that age who, affected by the flatteries of a lewd and voluptuous life, do not abandon the climb up the mountain.

The poet signifies this to us through the **Leopard**, which was the first beast that tried to impede his ascent. Many doubt what animal a "lonza" <note>Landino identifies the "lonza" as a member of the feline family, likely a leopard or lynx.</note> is. Certainly, we find three species of beasts to have skin marked by various spots: the *lupo ceruero* (which the Greeks call the **Lynx**), the **Pard**, and the **Panther**. Some wish the "lonza" to be understood as the lynx, because Virgil introduces Venus in the hunt dressed in the skin of such an animal. And because this beast is very forgetful, there is no vice that leads us into greater forgetfulness of excellent things than corporeal pleasure. If the "lonza" is a Pard, it will have the same significance. For this animal has the same skin and is very much ignited with lust. Not only does it mate with its own species, but as **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the Natural History.</note> posits, it mixes with lions; furthermore, it does not wish to be seen when it feeds, and in feeding, it sucks the blood. This is characteristic of lust, because more than any other thing, it empties us of blood. Wherefore Virgil says: *The female consumes their strength little by little and burns them by being seen* <note>original: "Carpit. n. uires paulatim : uritq[ue] uidendo femina"</note>. And **Juvenal** says: *Let him indeed receive the reward of his blood, and turn as pale as one who has stepped on a snake with bare heels* <note>original: "Accipiat sane mercedem sanguinis : et sic palleat : ut nudis pressit qui calcibus anguem"</note>. I believe this moved **Homer** to depict Paris—a lustful man—clothed in a leopard skin. The authority of **Giovanni Boccaccio** also applies here: he writes that the Florentine children, seeing a leopard, would cry out, "See the lonza!"

We can also very conveniently understand this as the **Panther**, which many do not distinguish from the pard except in having a whiter color; some want the panther to be the female among pards. Pliny affirms its skin is so beautiful and of such grace that every beast desires it; but they fear the ferocity shown in its head. Therefore, the panther, hiding its head and showing its back, attracts various beasts with the beauty of its spotted skin and then, with a sudden rush, seizes and devours them. This is very similar to this vice, in which beauty flatters and draws us, and then devours us, because time, money, fame, the body, and the soul are consumed therein. He places this same beast for the same vice of lust in the sixteenth chapter <note>Landino refers to Inferno Canto XVI, where Dante mentions the cord he used to try to catch the leopard.</note>. "I had a cord girt around me, and with it I thought at one time to take the leopard with the painted skin." And he said excellently: "And behold, almost..." because this word **"Behold"** <note>original: "Ecco" / Latin "ecce"</note> is never used by poets except when they show something happening suddenly and unexpectedly. And thus pleasure is so friendly to the sensitive appetite that it occupies a man before he notices it. The leopard was "light and swift" because there is great mobility in the voluptuous life. Wherefore the ancient poets depict **Love** as winged. As **Propertius** says: *Not in vain did he add wind-swept wings; he made the god fly within the human heart. For truly we are tossed on alternating waves, and our breeze stays in no one place* <note>original: "Idem non frustra uentosas addidit alas; Fecit et humano corde uolare deum. Scilicet alterna quoniam iactamur in unda: Nostraque non ullis permanet aura locis"</note>. And one can be taken by love in a moment. And certainly, it is difficult not only to say, but even to think, how great is the lightness and instability of the lover. By the "spotted skin"—that is, marked by various colors—he shows that lewd love consists in the skin, which is the surface of the body. Nor is anything else sought but extrinsic beauty and the variety of colors, sounds, and smells to satisfy sight, hearing, and smell. But
