more of the things that delight taste and touch; which two senses are more corporeal and seek more examined and vicious pleasures. **AND IT DID NOT DEPART FROM BEFORE MY FACE**: because the form of the beloved thing always stays fixed in the mind. Virgil demonstrates this in Dido: who says that she saw and heard Aeneas even though he was absent. This greatly impedes the path, because there is nothing that draws us back from speculation as much as lascivious love: it is of such a nature that it often twists even high intellects and marvelous men from the true path. And who was more elevated in the knowledge of divinity than King David and his son Solomon? And nevertheless, both were so troubled by love that King David, although he had so many wives and so many concubines, was nonetheless taken by the beauty of Bathsheba <note>original: "Bersabe"</note> and did not hesitate to send her husband Uriah <note>original: "Vria"</note> into battle in such a way that he would be killed. Therefore, so great a King and so great a prophet, of whom God said: **I have found a man after my own heart** <note>original Latin: "Inueni hominem secundum cor meum"</note>, in order to enjoy a common woman, he endured having the governor and leader of his army killed, not without the greatest public harm; and he became the perpetrator of three most grave crimes: homicide, treachery, and adultery. I could recount many philosophers; but let the prince of the Peripatetics, **Aristotle**, be enough, who, overcome by love, performed for his concubine Hermia those same sacrifices that the Athenian people performed only for the Eleusinian Ceres, the most celebrated goddess among them.

->It was the beginning of the morning,<-
->and the sun was mounting up with those stars<-
->that were with him when Divine Love<-
->first moved those beautiful things;<-
->so that the hour of the time and the sweet season<-
->were cause for me to have good hope<-
->of that beast with the gay-spotted hide.<-

<column-break/>

In this place, the poet uses **chronographia**, that is, a description of time. Note, therefore, that he began the ascent at the beginning of the day, which hour we call morning; because the Latins call it *mane*. Nor is it without reason that he chooses this hour, because the word *mane* is used, which in the Lanubian language means "good." And certainly, it is not only good, but the optimal hour: in which we begin to direct ourselves toward the way of salvation. Furthermore, it demonstrates that a good work should be started early. Therefore, there is a just complaint in **Petrarch**: *But the fault is mine: for I should have opened my eyes sooner and looked to the end: for to tell the truth, it is now too late.* <note>Landino quotes Petrarch’s Canzoniere, sonnet 364.</note> One can also add that, wanting to show that the poet had a vision of the things he writes, he set the time at dawn: because in that hour, visions and dreams are true, as he shows below, saying: *But if near the morning the truth is dreamed.* In which place we will strive to prove this same thing with philosophical reasons. Furthermore, it is the best principle to take the path of speculation at the time when the sun begins to appear—that is, when reason awakens in us, without whose light one cannot proceed in any knowledge. Whence David says: **In the morning I will stand before you and I will see: for you are a God who does not want iniquity** <note>original Latin: "Mane astabo tibi et uidebo: quonia deus nolens iniquitate tu es"; Psalm 5:5</note>; he judges, therefore, that the morning is the appropriate time to know that He is God, who does not want iniquity. **THE SUN WAS MOUNTING UP**. After the description of the hour of the day, he also describes the season of the year; and he posits that the sun was in **Aries**, that is, in the Ram: by which sign he denotes the Spring. There are four seasons of the year: Spring, which begins when the sun enters Aries; Summer, when it enters Cancer; and similarly, entering Libra makes Autumn; and in Capricorn, Winter. It was, therefore, morning at the beginning of the ascent; and at the entry of the sun into Aries. By this, according to many, he wants to demonstrate that this optimal purpose of climbing the mountain came to him on the Friday of the Passion, which was on the twenty-fifth day of March, in which even in the times of Christ, the sun was already in Aries by the correction of the year made by Caesar the Dictator. But in the present year 1480 <note>original: "M. cccc. lxxx."</note>, the sun enters Aries in March, and informs us that on the eleventh day at noon, it will be in the thirty-fourth minute of the first degree of Aries. And certainly, the Author of human salvation willed to suffer in that season of the year in which the world was created by Him. For when that first day began—which can deservedly be called the birthday of the world—the sign of the Ram was in the middle of the sky. And because the middle of the sky is almost the summit and head of that sky, therefore mathematicians place Aries as the first of the signs of the zodiac: because in that beginning of light, being in the most excellent part, it can duly be called the head of the world. But since we have made mention of the birth of the universe, I will briefly set down the site of all the heavens. It is in the eighth heaven, where the other fixed stars are, a circle called the **Zodiac**, which surrounds the whole heaven, named from the Greek word **zoon**, that is, "animal," because it is divided into twelve signs figured in the form of animals. These are Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces. Under this eighth sphere are seven other spheres, and in each of them is a planet. Of these, the highest is Saturn. Then in order are Jove, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon. This is the lowest of all and closest to the earth. They say, therefore, that in such a beginning, the Ram being, as we have said, in the middle of the sky, the sun appeared in Leo, and the moon in Cancer; Mercury in Virgo, and Venus in Libra; and similarly, Mars was in Scorpio, Jove in Sagittarius, and Saturn in Capricorn. Because of which, each of the seven already mentioned signs are called the domiciles and houses of that planet which they then received. There remain five out of the twelve; and these, removing the sun and the moon—which planets have no other domicile than those already mentioned—are distributed to the other five in such a way that Aquarius belongs to Saturn, Pisces to Jove, Scorpio to Mars, Taurus to Venus, and Gemini to Mercury. These, therefore, have two domiciles, and the sun and the moon only one: the sun has Leo, and the moon has Cancer. I have said this briefly about the seven planets and...

<header>CANTO ONE</header>

of the twelve signs of the zodiac, not only for the understanding of the present text, but because such knowledge will be useful for the interpretation of many other passages. See then that the poet shows he set out on the path of salvation and ascended to contemplation in that season of the year which was the beginning of the world, and in which He who had created us free, after we had fallen into servitude, redeemed us. **WITH THOSE** stars: understand those of Aries <note>the Ram</note>, which are eighteen. Aries signifies "ram." And the poets say that this ram, converted into such a sign, was the one that had the golden fleece and passed through the sea with Phrixus and Helle—though Helle fell into the middle of the sea, but Neptune preserved her and from her fathered Paeon. And the ram was the son of Neptune and Theophane. For Neptune, loving this girl, transformed himself into a ram in order to have her, and transformed her into a sheep. Therefore, their forms being those of a ram and a sheep, what they fathered was a ram; and the poets say the gods transformed such a ram into this first sign of the zodiac. Nigidius <note>Nigidius Figulus, a Roman scholar</note> writes that this is the ram that appeared to Bacchus when he was leading his army through the sandy Libya where there is no water; and it showed him a spring, which is the only one in that region. And for such a favor, Bacchus transformed it into this sign, and where the spring was, he established a temple to Jove, his father, which is nine days' journey from Alexandria in Egypt. This sign has one star in the head, three in the nostrils, two in the neck, one in each of the front feet, four on the back, one in the tail, three in the belly, and one in each of the hind feet. But leaving aside the fables, this sign, according to the mathematicians <note>astrologers/astronomers</note>, is named "Ram" to express the nature of the sun. For the nature of the ram is to lie on its left side in winter and on its right in summer; likewise, the sun in winter goes to the left hemisphere and in summer to the right. We shall conclude for all these reasons that, besides the hour of the day, the season of the year also gave him hope, being that in which God created man and, having created him, subjected every other created mortal thing to him, as the prophet witnesses: **You have subjected all things under his feet, all sheep and oxen, and also the beasts of the field** <note>original Latin: "Omnia subiecisti sub pedibus eius oues et boues uniuersa insup et pecora campi"</note>. As if to say: if this is the season in which God was so liberal and gracious toward man—first creating him and giving him dominion over so many things, and then, after he was spiritually dead through his own fault, recreating him anew—I can easily hope for the grace to climb the mountain. Nor would his hope have been in vain had he not been impeded by the three beasts. For without doubt, a man can hope, with divine grace, to reach true knowledge, provided he is not impeded by vices. But he who has a soul stained by the foulness of vices should not hope for it. For as Wisdom says: **Into a malevolent soul the spirit of wisdom shall not enter** <note>original Latin: "In animam maliuolam non introibit spiritus sapientie"</note>. And David, as I said above, asking: **Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord? Or who shall stand in His holy place?** <note>original Latin: "Quis ascendet in montem domini : Aut quis stabit in loco sancto eius"</note>—that is, who shall climb the mountain of the Lord, which is nothing other than elevating oneself to the knowledge of divine things—responds: **He who is innocent of hands and pure of heart** <note>original Latin: "Innocens manibus et mundo corde"</note>. By "innocent of hand" he means one who does not sin in vicious actions; and "pure of heart" is he who does not sin in thought. And for this reason, Plato—who placed the supreme good of man in the contemplation of divine things, which are known through the intellectual virtues—nevertheless wants us first to begin with the moral virtues, so that we may first purge ourselves of vices through them; because as he himself says: **It is a sacrilege for the impure to touch the pure** <note>original Latin: "Purum impuro attingere nefas est"</note>. And certainly it is a nefarious and wicked thing that he who is impure and vicious should attempt to touch divine things, which are most pure. Nor does the immense Majesty wish that **the holy be given to dogs**. **FIRST MOVED those beautiful things**: He created the heavens and the other creatures; and not without reason did he say "Moved," because every natural body has its own motion, and God alone is immobile but moves everything. Whence Boethius: **And remaining stable, You grant all things to move** <note>original Latin: "Stabilisque manens das cuncta moueri"</note>. **SO THAT the hour of the time and the sweet season gave me hope** of being able to have **the skin of the gaudy beast**—that is, to be able to kill it and, as a sign of victory, carry away its skin. **THE HOUR of the time**: because it was morning; and he who begins his journey early in the day can reach the desired end before night. This hour is praised by the prophet saying: **In the morning hours I will meditate on You because You have been my helper** <note>original Latin: "In mattutinis meditabor in te quia fuisti aiutor meus"</note>; and Horace: **Father of the morning, or Janus, if you prefer to be called so** <note>original Latin: "Matutine pater seu Iane libentius audis"</note>. And because this is the best hour, the Latins call it *mane* <note>morning</note>, which in the Lanubine <note>likely referring to the ancient Sabine or Lanuvian</note> language means "good." And the sweet season of spring in which the world had its beginning, and in which man was redeemed. Therefore, a man can hope for every happiness in that season. Some raise a doubt, saying that the sweet season of spring should rather have given him fear than hope of conquering such an animal, considering that in such a time every animal is naturally incited to lust. But this is not against the poet's word but in his favor. And the meaning is this: If I, in that time in which man is more than usual stimulated by the lust of the senses, could begin the contest—that is, overcome the difficulty found in the speculative life—it was to be hoped that in any other season I could ascend much more easily. But Dante, in this place, as a poet of excellent genius and artifice, wished (though occultly) to imitate Virgil. To make this appear more clearly: Aeneas, at that time when he was striving with all his strength to defend Troy, was persuaded by Venus to leave such an enterprise because the gods willed that that city perish and he sail to Italy. The allegory of this, as I demonstrated in the fourth book of my *Camaldolese Disputations* <note>original: "disputationi chamaldulensi"</note> written in the Latin language, is that Aeneas in his youth loved Troy greatly—that is, the voluptuous life—and for the defense of that, he was ready to put himself in every danger, until Venus—that is, the love of celestial things—showed him that the gods, and especially Pallas, were those who were undoing Troy; and she persuaded him to go to Italy, which Virgil posits as the speculative <note>contemplative</note> life. Therefore, Virgil in that place shows that Aeneas would never have abandoned Troy—that is, the voluptuous life in which tender and youthful age places the supreme good—nor would he have gone to Italy if Venus had not led him. Where he posits Venus for the love of celestial things: And certainly, the path is so arduous and difficult...

<summary>Landino explains the astronomical setting of the poem, linking the sign of Aries to the creation of the world and the resurrection of Christ. He uses both classical mythology and Christian theology to argue that the "sweet season" of spring and the "morning hour" provide the spiritual hope necessary to overcome vice.</summary>

of that virtue which, if the love of it did not draw man, no one would endure so many hardships. For this reason, it is quite manifest to anyone who diligently investigates the meaning of this passage that, just as Virgil shows that Aeneas would have perished in Troy—that is, in a life of pleasure—if Venus <note>original: "uenere," here meaning celestial love</note>, that is, the love of heavenly things, had not persuaded him to depart; so Dante would not have hoped to overcome the leopard if he had not been aided by the sweet season of Venus <note>the spring</note>, that is, of celestial love; for as the Florentine proverb says: "Love carries every great burden."

> but not so that I did not feel fear
> at the sight that appeared to me of a lion
> This seemed to be coming against me
> with its head high and with ravenous hunger
> so that it seemed the air was afraid of it.

<column-break/>

This lion is configured as the second vice, which we can call pride or, by a more common term, ambition. For just as in our youthful years, lusts and pleasures bind and ensnare our souls so that they abandon virtue, so afterward, in our mature age, there awakens in us an immeasurable appetite for honors, magistracies, empires, and lordships. These things, although they may seem to belong to an excellent and generous soul, are nevertheless the cause of many vices committed to acquire them. And those who strive to reach such ranks through fraud, betrayals, and corruption are far more numerous than those who do so through true virtue. It would be a very long task to narrate the killings and homicides committed to acquire lordships, and the wars through which not just one or two cities, but vast and most powerful kingdoms have been turned upside

<column-break/>

down. Son has killed father, and brother has killed brother. There was not just one Eteocles and Polynices <note>the warring sons of Oedipus</note>, or Atreus and Thyestes <note>legendary brothers who committed horrific acts against one another for the throne of Argos</note>, but they have been infinite. And regarding republics, what else has stripped away not only empire but leisure, peace, and finally liberty, if not the parties and factions born among citizens, each wishing to be first in honors and to have more power than the laws? Although we could easily prove this with domestic examples <note>likely referring to the internal strife of Florence</note>, I nevertheless prefer to recount foreign ones and bring to memory Marius, Sulla, Cinna, Octavian, Caesar, Pompey, and infinite others. But let us suppose that some seek dignities through virtue and justice and administer them with all honesty, desiring with their toil and sweat to benefit the republic and its citizens, and to suppress civil discords and nourish harmony with a paternal rather than tyrannical government. Nevertheless, being occupied in momentary and transitory things, they leave behind the investigation of celestial and divine matters, in which all our happiness consists. Therefore, most truly, as of all other things, so of this did the Truth itself <note>referring to Christ in the Gospel of Luke</note> say: *Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things; but Mary has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her.* <note>original Latin: "Martha Martha sollicita es: et turbaris erga plurima: Maria aute optima ptem elegit que no auferetur abea"</note> That is, Martha was occupied in various things with constant thoughts and cares and not without great perturbation, while Mary had chosen the best part which cannot be taken from her. And in the Old Testament, they place Leah, cross-eyed <note>or "tender-eyed" as per Genesis 29:17</note> but fertile in conceiving and giving birth, and Rachel her sister, with clear and healthy eyes but sterile. Most wisely, then, Dante expresses the same thing through the lion that Virgil expresses through Juno, who was always most hostile to the Trojans and to Aeneas when he wished to come to Italy. One reads that the lion does not attack one who throws himself on the ground and yields, but rather the one who goes against him. So the ambitious man seeks to be superior; he accepts the one who yields and contends with the one who does not. As Plautus says: *The proud man despises his inferiors and envies his superiors.* <note>original Latin: "Superbus minores despicit maioribus inuidet"</note> And Boethius: *The man of intemperate anger roars, so that he is believed to possess the spirit of a lion.* <note>original Latin: "Ire intempantis fremit ut leonis animum gestare credatur"</note> **THIS** seemed to be coming against me: not without reason did he say this of the lion, whereas he had not said it of the leopard, because it is an easy thing for an elevated mind moved toward contemplation to know that a life of pleasure is not the highest good. But dignities and honors have in themselves such force and such an appearance of honesty that they deceive excellent souls. Therefore, he could easily cast pleasure away from himself, but not ambition; and so he imagines that the lion came to meet him. These things all denote the elation and haughtiness which are in the ambitious man. Whence he shows that he comes with his head high, because ambition is never without pride. **AND** with ravenous hunger: because such greed is an insatiable and ravenous appetite. Whence Caesar used to say frequently the verse of Euripides, the tragic poet: *If reason and justice must be violated, they are to be violated for the sake of ruling.* Nor without reason does he add: **SO THAT** it seemed the air was afraid of it: because those who reach a high degree greatly desire to be feared, and especially by the "air"—that is, by superior and great men. This is denoted by the air, which is a superior element.

> And a she-wolf that with all cravings
> seemed laden in her leanness
> and has already made many people live in misery
> She brought such heaviness to me
> with the fear that came from the sight of her
> that I lost the hope of the heights

<column-break/>

He places the third impediment which prevents us from ascending, and by the she-wolf, he intends Avarice. Those who describe the nature of the wolf report that no animal is more greedy or voracious; it does not only harm the flocks, because the injury reaches not only the devoured beast but the man who is the master of such a beast. Nor does it only take prey by attacking openly, but also by lying in wait, or during dark nights or foggy days with ambushes and snares, it stealthily carries away the animal. And if it is not discov-

<column-break/>

ered by the shepherds or the dogs, it does not stop until it has killed the whole flock, believing it can never be filled. So the covetous man, now with fraud and deceits, now with open robberies, takes that which brings detriment to others. Nor can he accumulate so much that his desire is satisfied; but like a person with dropsy <note>a medical condition causing swelling and unquenchable thirst</note>, he does not quench his thirst by drinking.

<summary>In this passage, Landino interprets the Lion and the She-Wolf from Dante’s Inferno as allegories for Ambition/Pride and Avarice. He uses classical and biblical examples—such as Roman generals and the sisters Martha and Mary—to illustrate how these worldly pursuits distract even noble minds from the path of spiritual contemplation.</summary>

# CANTO ONE

...it grows poorly: Thus avarice grows in man just as much as his treasures grow. Horace says in his *Odes*: <note>original: "Crescit indulgens sibi dirus hydrops: Nec sitim pellit nisi causa morbi fugerit prius et aquosus albo corpore langor"</note> *The dire dropsy grows by indulging itself; nor is thirst banished until the cause of the disease has fled the veins, and the watery faintness from the pale body.* <note>Dropsy, or edema, was a common medical metaphor for greed: the more fluid the patient drinks, the thirstier they become.</note> And Virgil: <note>original: "Quid nõ mortalia pectora cogis auri sacra fames"</note> *To what do you not drive the hearts of men, O accursed hunger for gold!* Seneca: <note>original: "Auaro deest tā quod habet quam quod non habet"</note> *The miser lacks as much what he has as what he has not.* And the wolf is consecrated to Mars, the god of wars, because wars are not waged except to usurp what belongs to others. Therefore, the wolf is rightfully used to represent avarice. And this same reasoning is why prostitutes, who sell their chastity and reputation for money, are called *lupae* <note>she-wolves</note> in Latin; and the places where they publicly reside are called *lupanari* <note>brothels</note>. Therefore, just as the youthful age is hindered by pleasures, and the mature age by ambition and the desire for honors; so is old age by avarice—certainly the worst vice of all. But we shall treat this more extensively where the avaricious are punished. And the sentiment of Sallust is true: that avarice makes both the soul and the masculine body become effeminate. THIS SHE-WOLF seemed, that is, she showed herself to be, laden with all cravings: that is, with all greeds and desires, because to crave signifies to desire very passionately. IN HER leanness: He depicts the wolf as lean because the leaner any animal is, the hungrier it is. And every other vice is satisfied and filled sooner than avarice, which is compared to the dropsical man, as I said. And the miser is always thin because he does not dare to eat or drink as much as necessity requires, so as not to diminish his wealth. AND MANY people she has already made to live in sorrow: That is, grieving and discontented; for this is what this word means in the Lombard language. <note>original: "grame"</note> And certainly, avarice saddens the miser and those who are despoiled by the miser. The miser is always in distress, both to gain and to guard what is gained; and by accumulating, he never enjoys what he has acquired. He is like Tantalus, placed in the underworld by the poets, oppressed by hunger and thirst: he is in the clearest water up to his lower lip, and various apples and fruits hang above him down to his lip; but when he bends to drink, the water sinks; when he wishes to rise to eat, the fruits pull away. This happens to the miser because although he is in an abundance of every good, nonetheless avarice ensures that he removes neither his hunger nor his thirst. This same thing is denoted by the fable of Midas; nor did he who feigned that when this king touched any food or drink it immediately became gold intend anything else, except that through avarice he wished to make money out of that which should have sustained his life. And he adds that the fear which came out of her sight—that is, from her appearance—weighed him down in such a way that he lost the hope of reaching the mountain. And certainly, the greed for earthly goods so encumbers the soul and so oppresses it that it cannot rise to any high contemplation. Nor is any vice more of an enemy to virtue than avarice, as we shall demonstrate in its proper place.

> And as he who is willing to gain,
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;and the time comes that makes him lose,
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;who in all his thoughts weeps and is saddened;
> Such did the beast without peace make me,
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;which, coming against me little by little,
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;pushed me back to where the sun is silent.

<br/>

> While I was rushing down to a low place,
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;before my eyes there was offered
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;one who through long silence seemed faint.
> When I saw him in the great desert,
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;"Have mercy on me," I cried out to him,
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;"whatever you may be, whether shade or certain man."

<column-break/>

This is an excellent comparison by which he demonstrates that just as the more a man is greedy to acquire, the greater is his pain when it happens that he loses; so it was all the more troublesome for him to be pushed back down, the greater his will was to climb. The beast without peace came against him: that is, avarice, in which there is never rest. Instead, there is distress in gaining, and distress in preserving what is gained. And it brings with it an inextinguishable thirst and a blind greed which, the more it acquires, the more it grows, and it never lets a man rest. AND IT CAME little by little: because in the beginning we propose to ourselves a temperate desire; and it will seem that you ought to be content with a thousand; and then, having gained those, the will and the desire to double them grows; then to triple them. And thus, always bringing it to a greater sum, one proceeds to infinity. And through this care for momentary and transitory things, the burdened soul loses the lightness required for mounting; and it is pushed back by that care to where there is no sun: that is, where only appetite and sensuality reign, full of ignorance and darkness, and where the sun of reason does not shine.

<br/>

A marvelous invention: and marvelously adorned with profound doctrine and supreme eloquence, and wisely distinguished and divided, has this been: in which the poet demonstrates in what way the human mind, having arrived at the years of discretion, becomes aware of the forest in which it finds itself and of its own ignorance; and having seen the sun of reason at the summit of the mountain, it sets itself to climb toward contemplation to know those things which can make it blessed. Then he has made us learned that although our will may be ardent for such an undertaking and our soul may be prompt, nonetheless the infirmity of the flesh hinders our ascent: now the lusts and pleasures of the flesh, now the glory and the pomps of the world. Now avarice is such an obstacle that by ourselves, if some help is not given to us, we cannot arrive at the desired end. Nor should it move anyone that, although there are so many and such varied vices which are obstacles to a virtuous life, the poet sets down only three. For these three contain all the others; since he who is not corrupted by pleasures (which is the leopard), or by the greed for having (which is the she-wolf), or by the desire for honors, positions, and lordships (the lion), can be conquered by no other vice. This, then, is what he has treated up to this point. In what follows, he sets down the help received. Therefore he adds:

<header>INFERNO</header>

As he was falling back down, unable to resist the she-wolf, Virgil appeared to him in the desert; Dante commended himself to him and begged for his help. We said above that although our happiness is located at the height of the mountain—that is, in the contemplation of divine things—nevertheless, the human mind cannot make itself fit or suitable for such an ascent and climb unless it first purges itself of every vice, as we have shown above. Nor can one be purged of vices if one does not first recognize them. From this it follows that Dante could not reach heaven—that is, the knowledge of celestial things—if he did not first go through Hell and Purgatory; that is, if he did not first recognize his vices and, having recognized them, purge himself of them. And because our human frailty makes it either impossible or very difficult to undertake this journey without a leader and guide, the poet shows that he has taken Virgil as his guide. First, because in truth he most learnedly imitated Virgil in this work of his. Second, allegorically, he takes Virgil to represent moral philosophy and all the teachings of the pagans <note>Landino refers to "Gentiles" or non-Christians of antiquity whose philosophy prepared the way for Christian truth.</note>. This is because such teaching is sufficient to achieve the first two parts—namely, recognizing vice and, once recognized, purging oneself of it. But it is not sufficient to give us true knowledge of divine things, which can be drawn from no other source but that of the sacred theology of Christians. Therefore, he establishes that Virgil guides him only through Hell and Purgatory, because for Paradise, as we shall see in its proper place, he will need a more learned guide <note>This refers to Beatrice, who represents Divine Revelation or Theology.</note>. But so that in the progress of the poem this name does not lead into any error or difficulty in understanding the allegorical sense, let it be noted here at the beginning that the name "Virgil" will be used not in a single sense, but equivocally. Sometimes it will mean nothing other than the poet himself. At other times, it will signify simple human reason, while Dante will represent sensuality <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "sensuality" refers to the lower, physical part of the soul driven by instincts and desires.</note>. At other times, we shall interpret him as the intellect enlightened by various and many teachings. At still other times, we shall express through him "superior reason," and then Dante will signify not sensuality alone, but also "inferior reason." Returning then to the text, it follows: **WHILE** I was rushing down to the low place: That is, while the she-wolf was preventing me from ascending to contemplation and making me fall back into the low desires of earthly things. Whereupon I despaired of being able to conquer such a cruel beast by myself: Virgil appeared before me. And in this part, he demonstrates what usually happens to circumspect men who, seeing for themselves that they cannot reach where they desire, seek out who might be a more useful guide. Thus, Dante searching within his mind, Virgil offered himself, who "seemed faint through long silence." Because Virgil signifies the doctrine and the rational part of man, he seemed faint through long silence for good reason, because sensuality awakens in man long before reason does. Sensuality governs and commands man, ruling him with its bestial government, while reason remains almost asleep and silent. Not until one is midway through the journey of life does reason awaken or speak. And even then, it speaks faintly because, although reason begins to rouse itself, it is nevertheless still submerged in sensuality and cannot speak clearly at first. Therefore, in the early years, reason is entirely silent. Then it begins to speak, but it speaks faintly because it is still confused and does not discern well. Then finally, it speaks clearly. We can also say that Virgil seemed faint from long silence because, until Dante's time, the Latin language had been poorly understood for many centuries and kept almost in silence—especially Virgil. Dante was the first who investigated the deep meanings of Virgil. Because it would be too lengthy to recount them here, I expressed and declared them according to my ability in the third and fourth books of our *Camaldolese Disputations* <note>original: "disputationi chamadulesi". This is Landino's own famous philosophical dialogue written in Latin.</note>, a volume which our disciple Andrea Cambini translated into the Florentine language. **WHEN** I saw him in the great desert: He sees Virgil in the desert, but he does not yet know who he is. That is, in the uncultivated forest of the infinite movements of sensuality, he sees reason which already begins to appear, though faintly. <note>The word "fiocba" is likely a printer's error for "fioca" (faint/hoarse).</note> But he does not recognize it. Yet, because he already understands his own misery, he asks it for help. There is a time when we are in ignorance and do not realize it; then comes a time when we begin to realize it, but not very clearly because reason is still confused. But still, we seek a remedy, because reason pushes us so that, having recognized our evil, we ask for help against it. **HAVE MERCY** on me, I cried to him: Because when sensuality sees itself perishing, it asks reason for help. **I CRIED** because, being near the wolf and seeing himself in manifest danger, he wanted to show that he needed immediate and undelayed help. By this, he admonishes us that when we realize we are being persecuted by vices, we should not delay in asking for help; because by delaying, such a habit can be formed that we are later too late. The rest of the following verses are simple history and do not require allegory. He asks if he is a shade or a certain man, because in desert places shades or phantasms often appear. Allegorically, in the "desert"—that is, in the sensitive part of the soul—there often appear not "men" (that is, true reasons), but "shades" (that is, vain and false reasons), which show something to be good when it is not. But he who goes wandering through the forest—that is, he who is still entangled in vices—asks for help from the shade as if from a certain man; that is, he allows himself to be persuaded by false reason just as by the true. Thus, he remains deceived.

> He answered me: "Not a man; a man I once was,
> and my parents were Lombards,
> and Mantuans by homeland, both of them.
> I was born under Julius, though it was late,
> and I lived in Rome under the good Augustus
> in the time of the false and lying gods."

<column-break/>

Virgil therefore responds that he is not a man, but was one. For neither the soul alone nor the body alone is called "man," but these two joined together according to the Aristotelians. Wherefore man is defined as a "rational, mortal animal." "Animal" signifies an animated body. Therefore, there is no "animal" where soul and body are not together. Nor is man "mortal" except on the part of the body, because the soul is immortal. Nothing of...

# CANTO ONE

> I was a poet and I sang of that just
> son of Anchises who came from Troy
> after proud Ilium was burned.
> But you, why do you return to such distress?
> why do you not climb the delightful mountain
> which is the beginning and cause of all joy?

> Now, are you that Virgil and that fountain
> that pours forth so wide a river of speech?
> I answered him with a bashful brow.
> Oh, honor and light of the other poets,
> may my long study and great love avail me,
> which have made me search your volume.

<column-break/>

...at least the Platonists, when they say "man," mean only the soul: and they want the body to be like a vessel where the soul is contained. <note>Landino refers to the Dualist view that the true "self" is the spirit, while the body is merely a container.</note> But we will discuss this more extensively in a more convenient place. Furthermore, we can say that there is also an allegory here when Virgil says "I was a man and at present I am not," as if he were saying: "in the time of the heathens I was a man"—that is, I possessed the doctrine that then seemed sufficient for man. But now, in the time of Christians, "I am not a man"—that is, the doctrine of the heathens is not enough for man. PARENTS: that is, the father and the mother, because in the Latin language this word *parens* <note>original: "parĕs"</note> carries this meaning. LOMBARDS: because Mantua, his homeland, is in Lombardy. *Ambo dui* is a Lombard term meaning "both"; he adapts the word to the person, who was a Lombard. Publius Virgilius Maro was born on the thirteenth of October in the year that Pompey the Great and Marcus Crassus were consuls, in the year of the world five thousand one hundred thirty-one, and in the second year of the hundred and seventy-seventh <term>Olympiad</term> <note>A four-year period used in ancient Greek chronology.</note>, and sixty-eight years before the birth of Christ. There are, therefore, 1,522 years in this year of salvation 1480. <note>Landino’s calculation of the time elapsed since Virgil’s birth.</note> He was born in the territory of Mantua in a village called Andes. His father was named Maro, and his mother Magia. His mother dreamed on the night before his birth that she gave birth to a laurel branch, and once planted, it grew quickly and, having become large, produced various fruits and berries. He studied at Cremona and Milan; he took the <term>toga virile</term> <note>The "toga of manhood" assumed by Roman boys around age 14-16.</note> on the same day that the poet Lucretius died. He also studied at Naples and became most excellent in medicine and in all the mathematical sciences. Then, having come to Rome, he became a very close friend to Maecenas, and through his intercession, he entered the friendship of Caesar Augustus. He held such authority with Augustus that he obtained the restoration of the possessions of all the Mantuans, which the Emperor had previously seized and divided among his soldiers. It would be very tedious to recount the various doctrines and the supreme eloquence of this poet. Nor can the pen keep pace with the will, nor does the place require it, and the matter is manifest to every learned person. But I conclude that for many very obvious reasons, he does not yield to Homer, who was the first poet among the Greeks. I WAS BORN UNDER JULIUS: We will speak of Julius Caesar and Augustus below. He calls Augustus "good" because, in truth, among the twelve Caesars, he ruled more justly than many others. THE FALSE and lying gods: These are the idols which in those times were worshiped by the Romans. THE JUST SON OF ANCHISES: He means Aeneas, who was of royal lineage in this form: Dardanus, the first king of Troy, fathered Erichthonius, and from Erichthonius was born Tros, and from Tros was born Ilus, successor to the kingdom, and from Ilus, Laomedon, and from Laomedon, Priam. Furthermore, from the said Tros was also born Assaracus, and from Assaracus, Capys, and from him Anchises, father of Aeneas. The poet, therefore, calls Aeneas "just," because Virgil always presents him so in his book which he titles the *Aeneid*, because in it he describes the virtues of Aeneas: "Aeneas was our king, than whom none was more just in piety, nor greater in war and arms." <note>original: "Rex erat Eneas nobis quo iustior alter Nec pietate fuit nec bello maior et armis."</note> PROUD <note>original: "SVperbo"</note> in this place means noble, and in prompting Virgil to speak, Dante adapts Virgil's own words to him, as Virgil said: "and proud Ilium fell." <note>original: "ceciditque superbum Ilion."</note> And understand that Ilium is the city of the Trojans, so named from King Ilus mentioned just above. And thus the whole region and the country of the Trojans is called Troy from the aforementioned Tros, just as one might say "Tuscany," while the city itself is Ilium, just as one might say "Florence." BURNED: *combusto*, because *comburere* in Latin means to burn. BUT YOU, why do you return to such distress? Such as that of the darkness of the woods, and of ignorance, and of the vices from which you had emerged shortly before. He introduces Virgil—that is, the rational part of the soul and the doctrine—which rebukes the sensuality that allows itself to be conquered by vices and falls from its good purpose. And the poet shows in this part the progress of the man who, although he begins to see his errors, is nonetheless not temperate at the start. For the temperate man has already despised worldly pleasures and has conquered them in such a way that they no longer fight him. He is not, therefore, temperate, but "continent." For the continent man fights with vice and overcomes it, but with difficulty abstains from it; and he often wavers in such a way that if his appetite were not continually restrained by reason, the she-wolf and the other beasts would push us back into the woods. WHY DO YOU NOT CLIMB the delightful mountain: Understand "delightful to the soul," which feeds and nourishes itself on contemplation, and in that finds peace and delight. WHICH IS THE BEGINNING and cause of all joy: that is, of all good. God alone is the whole and supreme good, and good in such a way that no other thing is good except insofar as it participates in the divine goodness. Therefore, the mountain clothed in sun—that is, the contemplation of the soul illuminated by the sun of the intellect—is the beginning and cause by which we know God; and knowing Him, we love Him; and loving Him, we enjoy Him, wherein consists all joy—that is, our entire and perfect good and happiness.

Dante responds to the words of Virgil, who, when asked who he was, had not pronounced his own name, but had made himself known through a circumlocution of words. Stupefied, therefore, that Virgil had appeared to him in such a place, Dante says: NOW ARE YOU THAT VIRGIL. And he rightly calls him a "fountain," because just as the fountain is the origin of the river, so this poet was the origin from which perfect and polished Latin poetry was born. The first poet in the Latin language was Livius Andronicus, and after him many...

-># INFERNO<-

> You are my master and my author,
> you alone are the one from whom I took
> the beautiful style that has done me honor.
> See the beast for which I turned back;
> help me from her, famous and wise one,
> for she makes my veins and pulses tremble.

<column-break/>

...others; and among the first were Ennius, Plautus, Terence, and Lucretius. <note>These are early Roman poets and playwrights who preceded Virgil.</note> But before Virgil, the Latins did not have perfected poetry. He compares eloquence to a river because both Greek and Latin writers do so. Therefore, there must first have been some spring from which the river was born, but none so wide nor so abundant as Virgil. And certainly, Virgil—that is, the rational part of man—is the source and principle from which every river of doctrine, wisdom, and the true knowledge of divine things is born within us. WITH A BASHFUL BROW:

This arose from the reverence he felt for him. Shame is the fear of doing wrong. And this especially assails us when we are in the presence of someone we highly esteem. For then we are anxious that not only our deeds and words, but even our gestures, should be approved. He could also be ashamed for not having recognized him at the first meeting. This pertains to the literal sense of the text. But allegorically, Dante—that is, sensuality—is ashamed for not having sooner recognized Reason. This is an excellent sign, because whoever feels shame for a fault shows that they intend to correct themselves. He calls him the "honor of the other poets" because he holds the primacy among them, and from him proceeds the splendor of glory which poetry possesses. Or truly, let us say he is the "honor and light" of others because by imitating him they acquire honor and the splendor of fame, and are illuminated by his doctrine.

But allegorically, Virgil is the honor and light of other poets because all the other powers of the soul, and especially the internal senses, are excellent at perceiving (like the "common sense"), composing and dividing (like the "imagination"), and judging what is to be sought or fled (like the "thinking power"), and finally retaining what is judged (like the "memory"), or moving the soul to pursue what is judged (like the "appetite"). <note>Landino is describing the medieval map of the human mind, where different "senses" or faculties process information before Reason makes a final decision.</note> Nevertheless, if such senses are not illuminated by Reason, they can neither move from the particular to the universal, nor distinguish particulars any differently than brute animals do. Therefore, Virgil is the honor and light of poets because Reason illuminates the senses and makes them more excellent in man than in brutes. 

But because this speech which Dante makes to Virgil is highly adorned and suited to the person, the place, the time, and the matter, it will be useful and pleasant for the listener to briefly demonstrate its craftsmanship. And first, since there are three genres of rhetoric—demonstrative, deliberative, and judicial—this falls under the deliberative genre. Its purpose is either to persuade someone that a thing is useful and honorable, or to dissuade them because it is useless and dishonorable. The poet wants to persuade Virgil to defend him from the she-wolf. He begins with a "proem" <note>An introductory speech intended to prepare the audience.</note>. Every writer strives in the proem to make the listener attentive, docile, or benevolent. We will not speak at present of attentiveness or docility, because in such a great multitude of things it is necessary to omit many, unless we wish the volume to grow to infinity. 

We acquire benevolence from the listener in many ways, but especially when we praise him for some excellent virtue, and by that show that we esteem him greatly. And in this part, we will always praise that virtue which is useful to us, which he might show in granting our petition. For example, it was useful to Cicero, if he wished to win his case, that Caesar use mercy toward Quintus Ligarius, whom he desired to be pardoned. Therefore, he praises Caesar's mildness and mercy above all his other virtues. Thus, Dante, having need of Virgil’s doctrine and eloquence, praises him for that. OH, HONOR AND LIGHT OF THE OTHER POETS: He has until now sought benevolence from Virgil by praising him. 

But because in the deliberative genre, where we ask for something, it is necessary to show that the thing is easy, useful, and honorable—and if possible, necessary—it is understood that his petition asks Virgil to defend him from the she-wolf. This contains nothing else but that Virgil should offer him so much light from his doctrine that he is not conquered by avarice. <note>Landino identifies the "she-wolf" in Dante's poem as the sin of Avarice (greed).</note> He shows this is easy for Virgil: for if his doctrine has brought honor and light to other poets, it can do the same for him. Then his petition was just, saying: MAY MY LONG STUDY AND GREAT LOVE AVAIL ME. For justice highly requires that we favor and help those who are students of our work and who love us greatly. And finally, having gained benevolence and shown the ease and honor of the task, he comes to the petition. Let this suffice to show the craftsmanship of the speech. 

MAY MY LONG STUDY AVAIL ME: This at once seeks benevolence as he has already done, and shows the petition to be honorable, as we have said. But it also teaches the method to anyone who wishes to become learned. For one must not only study, but study for a long time. Because great and many things cannot be understood in a few months or years, but require a long and lasting space of time. Thus Hippocrates laments in the beginning of his *Aphorisms* that "art is long, and life is short, and experience is deceptive." <note>original: "ars longa, vita brevis"</note> And Theophrastus, the disciple of Aristotle, complained that nature had granted a long lifespan to crows, but a short life was attributed to man, who through his intellect could learn many things. And Petrarch says: "But time is short, and our desire is long." 

We see, therefore, that study is necessary for anyone who wants to know. And understand that study is nothing other than a fervent and assiduous application of the mind to the thing we desire to know. Therefore, to study is to keep the mind always occupied and intent on that thing we seek to recognize. And because this cannot be done without great effort, sweat, and sleepless nights—where it is necessary to leave behind many delights and pleasures, and even many useful things—men would not endure these labors if they were not ignited by a most ardent love for the doctrine they seek. For the proverb is true: "Love carries the burden." <note>An old Italian proverb: *l’amore porta il fascio*.</note> Therefore, Dante, understanding all these things, did not say only "May my study avail me," but added...

The long. And because the hardships of long study are not endured unless there is no mediocre love, he added **THE GREAT** love that has made me search your volume: because only love has made him constant and patient in enduring hunger, thirst, sleep, heat, and cold, and in leaving behind many pleasures. These things he would not have endured without love. **YOUR volume:** Although Virgil wrote many other minor works in his youth, there are nonetheless three principal ones: the *Bucolics*, the *Georgics*, and the *Aeneid*. From the first two he drew some things, but he imitated the *Aeneid* in everything. **SEE The beast for which I turned:** These words can move the listener to great compassion. *See the beast*: as if to say, "You yourself can consider its ferocity, and you see that since it is present, it is necessary that I perish if your help is not quick." Therefore, it is an honest request. **DEFEND ME** from her, famous and wise: He makes him benevolent by calling him famous and wise. And in part, it shows that he can easily offer doctrine, being famous and wise. And in this way, he makes his petition easy. **FOR SHE makes my veins and pulses tremble.** Veins are those where the blood is. But some have much blood and less spirit. Some have less blood and more spirit: and these in Latin are called *arteriae* <note>original: "arterie"</note> or rather pulsing veins; and we call them pulses because *pulsant*, <note>original: "pulsant," meaning "they beat" in Latin</note> that is, they beat. And every time we have fear, the pulses tremble, that is, they beat more often. Therefore, "she makes my veins and pulses tremble," that is, the pulsing veins; namely, she makes me terrified.

> "To you it behoves to take another road,"
> he replied, after he saw me weeping,
> "if you wish to escape this savage place.
> 
> For this beast, because of which you cry out,
> lets no one pass along her way,
> but so much hinders them that she kills them;
>

It is an easy thing to obtain just things from the just. Moved therefore by just prayers, Virgil determines to help him and demonstrates that it is impossible for him to flee the forest by the way of the wolf, because we cannot exit the ignorance and blindness of worldly things through the way of avarice. We want to go from the forest—that is, from ignorance—to the mountain—that is, to contemplation—by the way of the wolf—that is, of avarice. But this is impossible because she hinders our path and holds us back in the desires for riches, so much so that she kills us before we can arrive at the end. And truly, he who is held back by the wolf—which is nothing other than making a habit of avarice—that habit kills him, because vice kills the soul and extinguishes in it the light of reason. And if someone were to say, "I know that avarice hinders the journey; nonetheless, a person can give himself so much to seeking treasures that he becomes very rich; and just as a hungry man, once he is filled with food, is free from hunger, so this man, having become rich, will no longer be greedy, but free from avarice will be able to climb the mountain," to this Virgil responds that the nature of avarice is never to be satisfied. But it is so wicked and guilty that it never fills the "greedy," that is, the longing and covetous will. But after the meal—that is, after the riches are acquired—it has more hunger and thirst for treasure than before. Therefore, let a greedy man never hope to extinguish or satisfy his will, and having satisfied it, give himself to the contemplative life, because he never satisfies it. But the more he acquires, the more he desires; wherefore there never remains time for him to give himself to contemplation. And what is even worse, from avarice proceed many other vices, which entirely remove him from every virtue by which he could give himself to the knowledge of celestial things. Wherefore follows:

Some are those who push. **MANY are the animals to which she weds:** that is, many are the men to whom the wolf—that is, avarice—"weds," that is, joins herself inseparably, just as a wife by the bond of marriage cannot be separated from her husband. And certainly, when we have made a habit of avarice, it is almost impossible to separate oneself from it. And he most excellently said "animals," as if they were men in whom reason is buried; for by reason alone are we men and different from brutes. And he did not call them men to show that in such ones reason does not reign. One can also give another interpretation to this text. Since he has shown us avarice under the name of the wolf, a savage animal, he wishes to stay within the metaphor <term>translatione<gloss>The Latin term for metaphor or trope.</gloss></term> and uses "animals" to represent vices. And having already shown that avarice is not only a great vice, but also of a quality that always grows and never diminishes, he now adds that besides this, it accompanies many other vices. For avarice induces falsehood, fraud, perjury, theft, robbery, killings, assassinations, and other innumerable pests to human life. These vices proceed from avarice, and every day more will proceed from it until someone comes who destroys it. And to stay within the metaphor which he has made from the vice to the beast, he calls this one who will kill it a "Greyhound" <note>original: "veltro"</note>. For beasts are killed by hunting with dogs. And we call "Greyhounds" those who with velocity overcome the beasts in the...

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on the first Canto of Dante's Inferno. Having introduced the She-wolf as a symbol of Avarice, the text now focuses on the prophecy of the "Veltro" (the Greyhound), the mysterious figure destined to drive the wolf back to Hell.</meta>

<header>INFERNO</header>

chased and, having reached them, they seize and kill them. Therefore, it is manifest that he uses the Greyhound <note>original: "ueltro"</note> to represent the one who will kill Avarice. But who this person may be is very ambiguous. Nevertheless, a great part of the expositors understand it as Christ when He shall come to judge. And they wish the sense to be this: many are the animals, that is, beastly men, to whom Avarice is "wived," <note>original: "fammoglia," meaning joined as a spouse</note> that is, inseparably joined; and they will always multiply until the day of the last judgment, when Christ shall come to judge the living and the dead, and then Avarice shall cease. 

And neither earth nor "pewter" <note>original: "peltro," a metal alloy of tin and lead</note>—that is, neither earthly fruits nor any kind of metal—shall feed this one. That is to say, Avarice shall not reign, which consists in wanting to possess many possessions or in accumulating treasures which are gold and silver and other metals. And because pewter is not a simple metal but composed of several, he used this kind of metal to represent all the others. **BUT WISDOM,** love, and virtue: his food shall not be the temporal goods that Christ will provide, but wisdom, love, and virtue. Because man—having fallen into vice through ignorance and disobedience, which proceeds from not loving his superior—Christ, to restore him to his original dignity, will offer him wisdom against ignorance, love against contempt and disobedience, and moral virtue against vices. 

We can also interpret love, wisdom, and virtue as three principal things through which we can attain beatitude. For no one will acquire this beatitude if they do not first know where it consists, which wisdom gives us. Nor is it enough to know it if we do not love and desire to have it, and for this, love is necessary. Nor, after it is known and loved, can we possess it if we are not purged of all vices, which we do through moral virtue. **AND HIS nation:** They do not understand this as the birth of Christ when, incarnate, He came from the womb of the Virgin Mary, but they interpret it as the appearance He will make when He comes to judge the world; because everything that appears anew can be said to be "born." **IT SHALL BE between felt and felt:** <note>original: "tra feltro et feltro"</note> that is, between heaven and heaven, because He will appear in the air. This is because felt is composed of hairs pressed together and not woven with threads like cloth; and hairs are less corporeal than threads, and the heavens are less corporeal than the elements. 

Many, therefore, as we have said, wish the poet to use the Greyhound for Christ coming to judge the world at its consummation, which he rightly estimated should not be far off, because he wrote his work in the sixth age of the world, which sacred writers say is the senescence and old age of the world. I believe that the poet, as an excellent mathematician, had seen through astrology that in the future there would be certain revolutions of the heavens through the benevolence of which Avarice would entirely cease. These would certainly be Golden Ages in which this would occur, provided it comes soon. Therefore, the Greyhound will be such an influence that shall be born "between heaven and heaven"—or rather, that prince who shall be produced by such an influence. 

Wherefore he will say below: "I see clearly and therefore I narrate it." And certainly in the year 1484, on the twenty-fifth day of November at 13 hours and 41 minutes of that day, there will be the conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter in Scorpio in the ascendant of the fifth degree of Libra, which demonstrates a change of religion. And because Jupiter prevails over Saturn, it signifies that such a change will be for the better. Because there can be no religion truer than ours, I have firm hope that the Christian republic will be restored to the best life and government, in such a form that we may truly say: *Now the Virgin returns, the Saturnian kingdoms return.* <note>original: "Iam redit et uirgo redeunt saturnia regna," a quote from Virgil's Fourth Eclogue</note> 

Nor does a third opinion of learned men displease me, who say that Dante, being a great lover of the doctrine of Virgil, wished in this place to be ambiguous and obscure in imitation of that passage of the *Bucolics* where he says: *Now the Virgin returns, the Saturnian kingdoms return; now a new progeny is sent down from high heaven.* <note>original: "Iam redit et uirgo redeunt saturnia regna : Iam noua progenies celo demittitur alto"</note> These verses have such obscurity and are so ambiguous that some interpret them as the advent of Christ according to the verses of the Sibyl; others understand it as Octavian; others as the son of Pollio; and others as others. Therefore, let the reader take from these expositions the one he judges fits the text best. Or if he finds a more convenient one, let him set these aside and with his own industry illuminate those who walk through the darkness.

**OF THAT** humble Italy she shall be the salvation: By "Italy," understand every country where one lives under the Christian religion. And he put Italy for the whole as the most principal part, and for many other very well-known reasons, especially because the Apostolic See and head of Christians is in Rome, in Italy. He said "humble," perhaps in imitation of Virgil, in whom he had read: *Humble Italy which we see.* <note>original: "Humilem que uidemus Italiam"</note> Or rather, he said "humble" not because it was humble then, but because it will be humble and devout when Avarice ceases. 

But so that we may understand the force of this word "humble," *humus* <note>original: "hamus," though the context clearly refers to "humus"</note> in Latin means earth. Whence "humble" signifies not high nor elevated, but low and depressed and almost touching the earth, which among the four elements is the lowest. And afterward, by metaphor, we call a man "humble" who lowers himself and makes himself more inferior and of less esteem than his genius, or merits, or state, or condition requires. And this sometimes proceeds from pusillanimity and meanness of soul, which makes us grow cowardly in magnanimous enterprises and not take that daring and frankness that befits an excellent soul. And this is a vice condemned by all true doctrine. In this significance, the ancient Latins used it, saying "humble," that is, base and cowardly; and it signifies "humble," that is, low and ignoble of lineage. Wherefore Petrarch says: "And many others who were of humble nation." Therefore, he calls it a "humble nation," meaning ignoble. 

Sometimes theologians take "humility" not for meanness of soul, which is a vice, but for a virtue which they wish to be a species of innocence. Justice has several parts within itself, among which is innocence. And innocence is justice through which you do not inflict injury, nor violence, nor villainy upon anyone. Innocence has two parts within itself: humility and meekness. And humility is that through which, not out of meanness but out of humanity, we of our own will submit ourselves and depart from our glory and excellence and draw back.

**FOR WHICH** died the virgin Camilla: As if to say, from the part of Italy where Rome is, which through the greed of the Popes is more oppressed by this vice than other parts. Because the death of these four names...

<header>CANTO ONE</header>

born in the text proceeds to obtain the empire of Latin origin and the beginning of the Roman Empire. Therefore, that Italy which Euryalus and Nisus died to obtain: and which Camilla and Turnus perished to defend. Euryalus and Nisus were distinguished youths in the army of Aeneas: of whom Virgil makes mention in the fifth book <note>The *Aeneid*</note> when he describes the games: and later in the ninth book, sent by Ascanius to meet Aeneas, they encountered a body of soldiers which King Latinus was sending to Turnus. By these men, Euryalus was killed first, and then Nisus, as a most loyal friend, avenged him and, fighting boldly, was finally killed. Camilla was the daughter of Metabus, king of the Volscians <note>An ancient Italic tribe</note> where Privernum is, a city in our times called Piperno. They say that Metabus, driven from his kingdom and fleeing enemies who pursued him, arrived with Camilla in his arms—who was still breastfeeding—at the river Amasenus; and despairing of being able to cross it, he wrapped her in cork bark, tied her to the spear he had in his hand, and threw it to the other bank. Having fixed the iron tip in the ground, he preserved Camilla so that she did not perish. Later, while hiding in the forests, he nourished her with the milk of wild beasts. And because in throwing her he had vowed her to Diana <note>The Roman goddess of the hunt</note>, he willed that as she grew, according to the custom of Diana, she should practice hunting and use the bow and the spear. Hence she became so strong that, having returned to her kingdom after her father's death and there being war between the Latins and the Trojans, she came to the aid of the Latins; and while fighting, she took the lives of many. But finally, she was killed by Arruns the Trojan, who had placed himself in a treacherous ambush. Turnus was the son of Daunus—whence Apulia is sometimes called Daunia by poets—and was king of the Rutulians. Before Aeneas came to Italy, he had been betrothed to Lavinia, daughter of King Latinus. Later, because Latinus, encouraged by oracles and various omens, gave her to Aeneas who had already arrived in Italy, Turnus, enraged and with the help of his mother-in-law named Amata, turned Latinus against them and led him to make war on Aeneas, in which war Turnus was the captain of the Latins. With both wisdom and the sword, he did marvelous things and killed Pallas, the son of Evander and a soldier of Aeneas. But in the end, Aeneas killed him. Wherefore Petrarch elegantly said: *I saw him who wept under Antandros / The death of Creusa and took his love / From him who took his son from Evander.* <note>Petrarch refers to Aeneas, who wept for his wife Creusa in Antandros but later killed Turnus, who had killed Evander's son, Pallas.</note> Evander was the king of Pallanteum, which city was located where Rome was later built. Giovanni Boccaccio reports in his book *On the Genealogies* <note>The *Genealogia Deorum Gentilium*</note> that in the time of Emperor Henry III, the body of Pallas was unearthed not far from Rome; it was still whole and so large that, standing upright, it surpassed the Roman walls. **THESE** <note>Referring to the Greyhound</note> will hunt her <note>Avarice</note> through every town: as if to say that just as in vicious centuries Justice, driven from the earth, returned to heaven from whence she had descended; so in this happiness of times, Avarice, driven from the earth, shall be sent back to hell. From whence the envy that the devil bears toward man had brought her. Although man is in his free will and in his hand is placed death and life, nonetheless the devil, who was envious of human happiness—seeing that man was to succeed to his place in the glory of heaven from which he had been cast out—so tempted the first man that he made him a transgressor of God's commandments, from which proceeded avarice and all other sins. Therefore it is true that envy moved avarice from hell. We can also say that avarice proceeds from hell because riches, from the greed for which avarice proceeds, are in hell—that is, in the lowest part of the world which is the earth—because they consist either in the possessions of the earth or in the metals and stones that are under the earth. Whence the ancients willed that Pluto, the god of hell, should also be the god of riches: and the rich man in Latin is called *dives* from this name *Dis*, which signifies Pluto. Avarice came, therefore, from hell, that is, from the greed for lowly things: and he shall drive it back into hell because then avarice is extinguished when we despise riches and leave them in the depths as a lowly thing. And we can also say that the greed for riches is born from envy: for man would be content with little if he did not see others having more than he. But seeing the high palaces, the jewels, the cloths, the horses, and other similar things, he is moved by envy to seek the same for himself. Wherefore Jerome rightly said: *It is through the eyes that we cannot bear poverty* <note>original: "Oculi sunt per quos paupertatem ferre non possumus"</note>. Nor is envy anything other than a sadness and pain of the soul which we take from the prosperous things of others, even though they do not harm us.

<margin>o</margin> **O** The first conclusion of the proposal. For if it was necessary for Dante to exit the forest; and if the way by which he had already set out was forbidden to him by the beast; and if by himself he knew no other way, it was necessary that he have a leader and guide to conduct him to safety. This Virgil promises him, and not without excellent allegory does the poet proceed: which, so that it may be better understood, we must remember that in man there is reason—or rather, mind—and appetite. And the former, like a queen, must hold the dominion over all of life and rule and command; and the latter, like a servant, is bound to obey the precepts of reason. Appetite is of two kinds: for one is placed in reason and always obeys it, and is called the "will"; the other is in the senses and is a friend to them, and is defiant, rebellious, and disobedient to reason. And this, among modern philosophers and theologians, has no other name than "appetite." But the ancient Latins called it *libido*, that is, unbridled concupiscence <note>Unregulated desire</note>, alien and rebellious to all reason. Similarly, the reason...

<header>INFERNO</header>

<column>
> In all parts He rules and there He reigns;
> there is His city and His high throne;
> oh, happy is he whom He chooses to be there.
</column>

<column-break/>

<column>
[Rea]son is divided into two parts. One is 
called "superior" and concerns itself with universals <note>General principles or truths</note>: as, for example <note>original: "verbi gratia"</note>, if it is the
proper duty of kings to tame the proud and those who 
do not remain patient under reason: and to defend the innocent
from a tyrannical life. The other is called "inferior," which 
</column>

operates concerning particulars. For example, if it is a fitting thing for the Florentine Republic to offer aid in these times to Pope Sixtus against the Turk <note>A reference to Pope Sixtus IV and the Ottoman invasion of Otranto in 1480, contemporary to the commentator Landino</note>. The superior part is found in the contemplative life; and the inferior in the active life. I leave behind many sub-divisions of the mind and the appetite. But I will not omit that only the appetite is that which moves the soul either to desire what is (or appears to be) good, or to flee what is (or appears to be) evil. Therefore, the divine Plato, wishing to express the essence and the powers of our soul, said that it was similar to a chariot whose yoke was winged and was pulled by two horses: one white, beautiful, and well-made; and one black, ugly, and poorly made. And upon the chariot he places the charioteer, that is, the ruler of the horses. The chariot, then, is the essence of the soul. The horses that pull it are the appetite; by the white horse he means the rational appetite, and by the black the irrational. This was not unknown to the divine genius of Petrarch, who, wishing to demonstrate how the appetite in himself was disobedient to reason, describes it in the likeness of the black horse, saying:

> So strayed is my mad desire
> In following her who has turned in flight
> And from the snares of love, graceful and loose,
> She flies before my slow running.
> For the more I lose myself in following her,
> The less she listens to me along the safe road.
> Nor does it help me to spur it or turn it,
> For Love by its nature makes it stubborn.
> But then, as it gathers the bit to itself by force,
> I remain under its lordship,
> Which, against my will, carries me to death.

The Platonic poet <note>Petrarch</note> demonstrates, then, that the black horse carries us to death because the irrational appetite leads us to vice, which is the death of the soul. The chariot is therefore our soul. The horses are the appetite. And the charioteer or ruler is the mind and reason, which rules and governs the soul. The reader should therefore commit this division to memory, not only for the explanation of this text, but because it will be necessary many times in the course of the work. But to return to our purpose: Dante, who desires to leave the forest and climb the mountain but cannot because he is hindered by the aforementioned beasts, signifies the rational appetite obedient to the "inferior reason"—that is, the active life. The active life cannot, by itself, come to the state of bliss <term>beatitudine</term> <note>Supreme happiness or blessedness</note>, which consists in the doctrine and knowledge of celestial things. This is because the active life contains "beasts" within it—that is, various perturbations of the soul. Since man is restless because of these, he cannot have a soul as tranquil as is necessary for one who wishes to be fit and suitable for contemplation. This was wonderfully expressed by Him who speaks the truth—rather, who is Truth itself—in the Gospel of Matthew <note>Landino likely means the Gospel of Luke 10:38–42, where the story of Martha and Mary occurs</note>. There, setting Mary as the symbol for the contemplative life and Martha for the active life, He said that Martha was full of cares and anxieties and was troubled by many things, while Mary had chosen the best part, which never abandons the soul. This is because the active life and civil operations—signified by Martha—last only as long as we live in this present mortal life. But the contemplation of divine things is never taken from us and follows us into the other life, which is eternal. Dante, then, desires but cannot climb the mountain. Wherefore Virgil—who signifies "superior reason" and the science and contemplative life—looking upon Dante's good will, is moved to compassion. Sent by the Graces (of whom we shall speak below), he promises his help. But it should be noted that Virgil signifies only the "doctrine of the gentiles" <note>Pagan/Classical philosophy</note>, through which we can recognize vices and, having recognized them, purge ourselves of them. But this is not enough without Christian theology to give us that knowledge of celestial things wherein our bliss consists. Therefore, Virgil will be able to guide him through Hell and Purgatory—that is, to show him the nature of vice and how one may be purged of it—but he will not be able to lead him to Paradise. Let this be said briefly for the exposition of this passage. Now, returning to the text, it follows: **WHEREFORE I** for your sake think and discern. "Wherefore," that is, because of which thing, and it is the conclusion of all the words already spoken. "I think and discern": these are different acts. For we "think" when, searching for the best in a thing, we go about examining and weighing all the parts to understand which of them all is the most important. Afterwards, having examined them all, we "discern"—that is, we pick the best one and choose it. Here it should be noted that every decision a man makes should be prudently considered. And "prudence" <term>prudentia</term>, according to Plato and Aristotle, is a certain reason with which we rightly administer all things in the active and civil life. To this, Aristotle attributes "good consultation," "skill," "sagacity," and "judgment" in the text of his *Ethics*. Two things, as the same Aristotle posits in his book on the Republic <note>The *Politics*</note>, are those in which all praise for right operation and government consists. One is that the end <note>The goal or purpose</note> we propose for ourselves be true and right. The second is that we find the things which lead us to the end already proposed. Therefore, for Prudence—whose goal is to arrange all human operations rightly and with the best method and order—all the virtues that lead us to the end and those that operate toward the end are necessary. And first is "consultation." This is nothing other than a diligent inquiry into those things that lead us to the end. Counsel has three duties: first, it seeks if any way can be found to lead us to the end. Then, if they are found, it asks what they are. And having found one or more, in the third place it seeks in what way we can use them. All this is within deliberation and consultation, after which follows "judgment." Its duty, after we have found the aforementioned ways, is to dispute and weigh which of them is most suitable, most honest, or most useful. Once this judgment is given, "election" follows, which is nothing other than taking that which we have already judged to be the best. And philosophers define "election" as a consulted appe...
