<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante Alighieri's Divine Comedy, specifically focusing on the end of Canto I of the Inferno. The commentator (likely Cristoforo Landino) is explaining the allegorical roles of Virgil and Dante, and the transition from the dark wood toward the journey through the afterlife.</meta>

# CANTO ONE

...petition and desire for those things which lead us to the end. Counsel is made right and straight by good consultation and <term>shrewdness</term><note>original: "folertia" - a Latinate term for practical ingenuity or quick-wittedness</note>. To counsel well is nothing other than to lead comfortably to a good end through honest ways and means. And shrewdness is a prompt and alert investigation of the aforementioned ways and means. Judgment becomes clear through <term>sagacity</term>, which is right and most prompt judgment. Likewise through <term>sentence</term><note>In the legal/philosophical sense of a formal decision or opinion</note>: and the definition of "sentence" is to be a judgment of goodness and equity. Virgil, therefore, wishing to persuade Dante to follow him, wanted to show that he had taken such a course with optimal prudence. And when he said **I THINK**, he placed counsel investigated with good consultation and shrewdness. And when he said **I DISCERN**, he placed judgment aided by sagacity and choice. For which reason, Dante ought to consent to the course taken with all the parts of prudence.

But let the reader understand that our order and purpose is this: that whenever, for the interpretation of the text, it happens that we must arrange some point of philosophy or another science, I will strive with brevity to show it entirely; so that if in the course of the work it is touched upon again in some part by the poet, the reader can return to the same place where the whole is found. Because in this way, the reader will have gathered the whole together, and we will not have to repeat the same thing many times.

Up to here we have seen that if Dante—that is, the **lower reason** with the **rational appetite**—wishes to arrive at knowledge, it is necessary to follow Virgil: that is, the **higher reason** and **speculative science**. And he promises to lead him out of this low place of sensitive and material things, guiding him first through the knowledge of vices; and he calls it the **eternal place**, either because Hell—that is, the pains of the damned—has no end. Whence he says below: *Before me were no things created, except eternal ones, and I endure eternally.* <note>original: "Dinanzi a me non fur cose create: se non etherne: et io etherno duro." - quoting the inscription on the Gates of Hell</note>. Or truly because Virgil—that is, Science—is not of particulars, which are corruptible, but of universals, which are eternal and incorruptible.

**DESPERATE cries**: because they are without hope. This desperation increases the pain of the damned as much as the hope of one day being free lightens the burden for those who are in Purgatory. And then of these he says they are **content in the fire**, because they hope to come to beatitude after their purgation, whether it be long or short. And he says the damned cry out—that is, crying they beg for the **second death**. Where some believe that the second death is the second damnation by the final sentence given by Christ on the Day of Judgment, when souls are reunited with their bodies and both together will be damned. And they say they do this moved by envy, meaning that then they will have more companions. But it pleases me more that by the **first death** we understand the separation of the soul from the body; and by the **second** we understand that they desire that even the soul, already separated, should become mortal and annihilated: because the pain is so great that they would rather be nothing than be in such distress.

**TO WHICH then if you wish to climb**: to those blessed people, that is, to Paradise. **A SOUL shall be more worthy of this than I**: and here he means **Beatrice**, whom he sets as **Christian Theology**, which alone can lead to Paradise. And not I, Virgil, who because I was rebellious to the law of that Emperor who reigns up there—that is, the Supreme God—because the Evangelical law says: *Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.* <note>original: "Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua et spiritu sancto non intrabit in regnum celorum." - John 3:5</note>. Virgil, that is the poet himself, was rebellious to God because he was not a Christian. And Virgil, standing also for the **science of the gentiles** <note>Pagan/Classical knowledge</note>, was rebellious to God because such science, not having true knowledge of God, does not lead to Paradise—that is, to the knowledge of divine things.

**IN ALL parts He commands and there He reigns.** Everything is subject to God. Whence the Apostle says: *In the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, and those on earth, and those under the earth.* <note>original: "In nomine iesu omne genus flectatur celestium terrestrium et infernorum." - Philippians 2:10</note>. But His royal seat is in heaven, in the manner that we will demonstrate in the first canto of the *Paradiso*. Whence: *The Lord's throne is in heaven.* <note>original: "dominus in cielo sedes eius." - Psalm 11:4</note>. Likewise: *The heaven of heavens is the Lord's.* <note>original: "celum celi domino." - Psalm 115:16</note>. Likewise: *He who dwells in the heavens shall laugh at them.* <note>original: "qui habitat in celis irridebit eos." - Psalm 2:4</note>. And the same sentiment is in the eleventh of *Purgatorio*: *Not circumscribed, but through greater love.* And in *Paradiso*: *In the heaven that takes most of His light.*

**O HAPPY is he whom He chooses there.** Whence Christ, the supreme good, said: *You who have followed me shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life.* <note>original: "Vos qui sequuti estis me centuplum accipietis et vitam ethernam possidebitis." - Matthew 19:29</note>. And the poet uses here a rhetorical color called **exclamation**, which poets and orators use when, narrating something, they wish to move the listener to indignation, commiseration, or admiration. Therefore, Virgil in this place uses exclamation not only to demonstrate the wonder of such beatitude, but also out of commiseration for himself, being deprived of it. And certainly, it is a heavy pain to the damned to know the good of which they are deprived. Whence Persius, the satirist poet, desires no other punishment for the vicious man except that he should know how much good consists in virtue, so that he may grieve more bitterly for having abandoned it; he asks God to punish them thus: *That they may see virtue and waste away for having left it.* <note>original: "Virtutem ut videant intabescantque relicta." - Persius, Satires 3.38</note>.

---

> And I to him: "Poet, I beseech thee
> by that God whom thou didst not know,
> so that I may flee this evil and worse,
> That thou lead me there where thou just saidst,
> so that I may see the gate of Saint Peter
> and those whom thou makest so sorrowful."
> Then he moved on, and I kept behind him.

Dante responds and prays that he do what he has said. This denotes that when the appetite and the **lower reason** begin to be illuminated by the **higher**, they turn entirely to it and desire to follow what it shows. And morally it admonishes that when true doctrine is offered to a person, even a learned one, he ought to make every demonstration of desiring it, and supremely pray for it. He prays then to Virgil, saying to him: **by that God whom thou didst not know**: that is, as the true God, though as a philosopher you knew Him in life. Virgil knew God as a Gentile philosopher—as the **Prime Mover** and **First Cause**—but not distinctly the Trinity and the Incarnation of the Word and the Redemption...

# CANTO SECOND
## .b.ii.

and sincere praise which, though not sought for itself, follows virtue as the shadow follows the body; it is the reward of pious virtue and should not, nor can it, be given except to the good. But in place of these three <note>referring to the three theological virtues or perhaps the types of true glory mentioned previously</note> follow the pleasure of the body, the possession of fleeting and earthly goods (which is avarice), and finally the vain glory of the world, which is ambition. Therefore, the human mind cannot reach the sun <note>the light of God or Truth</note> with only the lower reason and in the civil life, where the disturbances that father all vices are very powerful. But nevertheless, being desirous of it, the mind deserves to be aided by Virgil—that is, by superior reason and by learning. This shows him that wishing to go to Paradise—that is, to happiness—it is first necessary to pass through Hell and Purgatory; that is, to descend into the knowledge of vices and, having known them, to purge oneself of them. Once the mind remains purged of these, it can easily come to the knowledge of divine things, wherein beatitude consists. And Virgil rightly promises to lead Dante safely through Hell and Purgatory, but confesses he cannot lead him to Paradise because, as we have said, philosophical science can give us the knowledge of vices and instruct us in how we may be purged of them, but it cannot lead us to Paradise—that is, to the knowledge of divine things. Because this is the proper science of the sacred theology of Christians. Wherefore it can truly be said that the first canto stood in the place of a prologue. In this second chapter <note>Canto</note> he places the invocation, which we showed above to be the second principal part of the entire work. And afterward, he moves a doubt to Virgil, distrusting that he is sufficient to make such a journey, since he is neither Aeneas nor Paul the Apostle. After which doubt, Virgil comforts him to follow, and gives him firm hope by showing him that he does not come by his own power—which perhaps would not be sufficient—but that one has come from Heaven who sends him. He begins, then: THE DAY was departing; and he performs a <term>chronography</term> <note>a description of time</note>. He shows the author having descended into Hell in the nighttime. This he feigns truly because one goes into Hell by night—that is, through the darkness of ignorance—because every sin comes from ignorance when disordered appetite extinguishes in us the light of reason. For this reason, some ancient philosophers said that it was easy to go to Hell because one went there with eyes closed. And Virgil said: ->They went obscured under the lonely night through the shadows.<- <note>original Latin: "Ibant obscuri sola sub nocte per umbras"</note> Or truly, by the night he wishes to demonstrate the nightly vigils which are necessary to those who wish to make progress in the contemplation of great things; and the mind is much more sharpened in nightly studies because it is free from every noise and tumult of the day. He shows, then, that in that hour in which—because the night comes and spreads darkness through all our hemisphere—all animals give themselves to sleep and rest, he alone prepared himself to sustain the war. This passage is drawn from the fourth book of Virgil where he induces Dido to stay awake through pain and anxieties in that hour in which all animals rest. AND THE brown AIR: The air is a <term>diaphanous</term> body <note>transparent or translucent</note>, that is, penetrable and transparent, but by its nature dark if it is not illuminated by the sun or another light. Therefore, when the sun descends to the other hemisphere, the shadow of the earth spreads through ours and makes night. Because night is nothing other than the shadow of the earth. TOOK the animals that are on earth from their labors: Because the night, being useless for doing any work due to its darkness, invites animals to sleep, which is a great recreation to the body. Allegorically, he shows that he alone—that is, the man given to speculation, who is "alone" because it is necessary that he live in solitude and separated from every crowd and frequency and tumult that hinders thought—consumes in speculating the night which other men and animals, who seek the comforts of the body, consume in sleeping. Therefore "I alone"—that is, I placed in solitude. Or truly "I alone" demonstrating that the contemplative are alone and very few. Whence Petrarch says: ->Philosophy, you go poor and naked,<- <margin>The crowd, intent on base gain, says: You will have few companions on your way.</margin> And certainly, because man, considered as this composite of soul and body, always seeks company, one does not find anyone who lives solitary unless it is either one who, through a melancholic humor, has corrupted his fantasy and become almost a beast, or one who, through height of genius, despising human things, transcends with speculation to divine things. Whence Aristotle rightly said in the *Politics*: that he who leaves the sociable and civil life has become either a beast or more than a man. PREPARED to sustain the war, both of the journey and of the pity. The literal sense is that going through dark places was fatiguing, and the pains of the damned moved him to pity. But allegorically he shows that one cannot go into Hell—that is, have true knowledge of vices—without war and combat, because in this the soul often fights with itself; since the sensitive part tires in contemplation and flees such labor, and the mind and intellect seek to understand because the spirit is willing and the flesh is weak. Furthermore, it is war because the appetite judges a thing one way and reason another. For example: in defrauding the family of owed nourishment, the appetite of the miser falsely judges that it is a virtue called parsimony, and reason truly judges that it is a vice called avarice. He was, therefore, prepared to sustain this war. Likewise, the war of pity: because we cannot know vices without also knowing that they proceed from the infirmity and imbecility of human nature, which proceeds from the corporeal mass that weighs down the soul. And this duly moves to compassion any wise man who comes into such speculation. Whence: ->God saw our frailty and had mercy on us.<- <note>original Latin: "Vidit deus figmentum nostrum et misertus est nostri"</note> And for this same reason, Heraclitus of Ephesus, seeing continually infinite errors in human life, assiduously wept, moved to compassion for its misery. WHICH—that is, which journey and which pity—my mind shall retrace, as if it will describe and commit to letters. Because it was not the hand of the poet, which is an instrument, but the mind in which he has such knowledge that wrote. THE MIND SHALL RETRACE, which does not err: Gaining attention and goodwill. Because we become well-disposed and listen attentively to that writer who promises us...

# INFERNO

to write things that are true and without error. And he most excellently said *The mind that does not err*. For the lower reason, which with prudence administers the practical and civil life, consists of particulars where one can err: But the mind, that is, the intellect and the higher reason, because it exercises itself in universals—of which there is true science—cannot err. But so that we may better understand what the mind is: I say that although our soul is one, simple, incorrupt, and indivisible, nonetheless, according to various powers and various virtues, it has various and diverse names. Therefore, insofar as it vivifies the body, it is called *anima* <note>soul</note>. Insofar as it feels, *Senso* <note>sense</note>. Insofar as it possesses wisdom, it is called *animo* <note>spirit/intellect</note>. Insofar as it understands, they call it *mente* <note>mind</note>. Furthermore, when it discerns, it is called reason. When it remembers, memory. The rational and intellectual light with which we make any discourse and understand is called *mind* by the philosophers. This form is made in the image and likeness of God, formed by Him without the interposition of any other nature. It is called *mind* because it is a very eminent, that is, excellent part of the soul. And in short, the mind is the eye of our soul. The gaze of this mind is reason: and its seeing is the intellect. It is therefore necessary for every rational soul to have this eye of its own healthy, and to look with it so that it may see. This eye is healthy when it is purged and removed from all the desires for mortal things. And it looks when it fixes its eyes on the light of God. And finally, it sees when in that contemplation it knows: how much joy, how much gladness, how much serenity, and how much delight there is. And repeating this, we shall say that health makes this eye serene; the gaze makes it straight; and seeing makes it blessed. The mind, therefore, that is, this light of the soul, will *draw* <note>original: "ritrarra"</note>, that is, express and demonstrate that upon which the eye was fixed, and by fixing it, saw and knew. And he most excellently used the word *draw*, that is, openly demonstrate. For we say "to draw" when either the painter or the sculptor represents something in its own likeness in such a form that in his work it is recognized as it is in itself. And in this way we say that Apelles drew Alexander the Great. And Giotto drew Dante. Because he formed him in such a way that whoever saw the painting saw Dante. And so the mind of the poet will paint with words what he has achieved in contemplation.

O MUSES: Hesiod writes in his *Theogony* that the Muses are daughters of Jove and Mnemosyne, that is, of Memory. And he adds that Jove joined with her on Mount Pieria for nine nights, whence nine Muses were born, the names of which are Clio, Euterpe, Thalia, Melpomene, Terpsichore, Erato, Polymnia, Urania, and Calliope, who is the most excellent above all the others. Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman provincial writer</note> maintains that there are nine to demonstrate, by the first eight, the song of the eight spheres, and by the ninth, the harmony and consonance that is born from them. This was perhaps the reason why Hesiod said that Calliope, who is the ninth, is the most beautiful. Anaximander of Lampsacus and Xenophanes of Heracleopolis demonstrated that by the nine Muses are signified nine things which generate the voice, which are these: first, four teeth struck by the tongue, without which there is born a hiss rather than a voice; then the two lips; the tongue; the concavity of the palate; and the arteries that produce the breath from the lungs. And finally, because Apollo is placed with the Muses, they add the lungs for Apollo. Clio signifies fame, because the Muses acquire fame for those who exercise them and for those who are praised by poets. Euterpe signifies delight, which is great to those who write verses and to those who hear them. Thalia is so called because in Greek *Thalin* signifies to turn green again and to flourish, whence we say *thallo* <note>to bloom</note>, and the memory of poets always turns green again. Melpomene, song, because song is proper to poets. Terpsichore, joy, which they give supremely to poets. Erato, love, without which one cannot support the great labor that is in writing any poem. Polymnia, memory of many things, without which there can be no perfect poetry. Urania, celestial, because as we narrated above, poetry is a celestial thing. Calliope, good song, because no music delights as much as a well-composed poem.

O HIGH GENIUS, now help me: The Latins call *genius* <note>original: "ingegno"</note> that force of the soul by which we are capable of learning doctrines. And this has two parts: one is that sharpness with which we sharpen ourselves to investigate and learn, and this the ancient Latins call docility, and modern philosophers call the apprehensive power. The second is that virtue by which we retain what we have already understood, and this is called memory. Therefore, "O high genius," that is, O power of the soul apt to achieve the knowledge of great things. For this reason Augustine said that genius is that power of the soul with which the soul sharpens and exercises itself to know what it did not yet know. Whence it is defined: *That genius is the extension of the intellect to the knowledge of unknown things* <note>original Latin: "Quod ingenium sit extensio intellectus ad incognitorum cognitionem."</note>. Therefore, genius investigates and reason judges the things investigated by genius, and memory stores them once judged.

O MIND THAT WROTE: We showed above which power in the soul is called mind. But often writers use "mind" for "memory"; thus Virgil: *The judgment of Paris remains stored deep in her mind* <note>original Latin: "Manet alta mente repostum iudicium Paridis."</note>. And so here the poet turns to his memory, saying, "O memory which wrote," that is, you made a record and retained in yourself what I saw. For writing is that which makes us remember; and therefore we are accustomed to say, "write this in your memory." HERE SHALL APPEAR YOUR NOBILITY: As if to say that if he can remember all of his contemplation, certainly his memory will be noble.

I began: "Poet who guides me,
  look at my virtue, if it be powerful,
  before you trust me to the deep pass.
You say that the parent of Silvius,
still corruptible, went to the immortal..."

"What the shoulders can bear." <note>A reference to Horace's *Ars Poetica*: "Consider what your shoulders can carry."</note> And he adds that although Aeneas and Paul went, he recognizes that he is not equal to such great men, and should not hope to succeed in what they succeeded in. We have shown above that making this journey is nothing other than arriving at the **knowledge of things**. One arrives there either to remain in that very contemplation and live the **contemplative life**, or to speculate and, through speculating, investigate what the virtues are by which the **active life** is governed. As, for example <note>original: "verbi gratia"</note>, if man is a "civil animal" <note>a social/political being</note> and what a city is and into how many parts it is divided; if the moral virtues are necessary to civil life; and if in general there are more than three: **Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance**; and into how many species these three are divided; and why **Prudence**, one of the intellectual virtues, is added as a guide to the moral virtues; and many other similar things. Therefore, he most wisely demonstrates that two have made this journey: Aeneas and Paul, setting the first for the active life and the second for the contemplative life. For Aeneas was a builder of cities and a just administrator of the republic. And Paul went so high with his speculation that he was caught up even to the **third heaven** and saw those things which it is not lawful for man to speak of. Dante then demonstrates his shrinking back from such an undertaking, for which he judges himself not to be sufficient. And in truth, the human mind can by itself understand things inferior to it, but not those superior. Next, he shows that if Aeneas and Paul went, this was granted to them by special grace from God. It was granted to Aeneas because from his successors the Roman Empire was to be established, and Rome finally was to be the head of the Christian republic and the seat of the Apostolic Church. It was granted to Paul so that he might illuminate the Christian faith. Dante says then to Virgil—that is, the lower reason speaking to the higher—before we begin the journey: "You who understand more, consider if my virtue—that is, human virtue—is powerful enough by itself, before you trust me to the **high pass**," that is, to the high undertaking. And he rightly said "pass," because he who travels takes steps; and here he describes this contemplation of his in the form of a pilgrimage and a journey; and he said "HIGH," or rather deep, as we say "the high sea," meaning the deep sea, out of respect for the descent into Hell. Or better, he said "high" because nothing is a higher thing than such an investigation which reaches even to the Divine Essence. **THE KINSMAN** of Silvius, that is, the father <note>Aeneas</note>, for so the Latins say. And this was Aeneas, whose genealogy is this: Dardanus, son of Jove and of the daughter of Atlas called Electra, came to Troy. Which, according to Eusebius, was in the thirty-fifth year of Moses and the year of the world 3737. He fathered Erichthonius, who was his successor in the kingdom and ruled forty-seven years. He left as son and successor Tros, from whom that region, first called Dardania after Dardanus, was named Troy. Ganymede was born to Tros. And from Ganymede came Ilus, from whom the city of Troy took the name Ilium. Ilus fathered Laomedon, father of Priam. There was also a son of Tros and brother of Ganymede, Assaracus, who fathered Capys, and Capys fathered Anchises, and Anchises fathered Aeneas. This man, while still in Troy, fathered Ascanius by Creusa his wife and daughter of King Priam; and later in Italy, Aeneas having acquired the empire of Latinus, left his son Ascanius as successor. But it is doubted whether it was the one he fathered at Troy by Creusa or the one he acquired in Italy by Lavinia. This man founded Alba and left Silvius as successor. From him was born Aeneas Silvius, from whom all the kings were later called "Silvii." And these were, in order: Latinus, Alba, Atys, Capys, Capetus, and Tiberinus, from whom the river formerly called Albula acquired the name Tiber. Tiberinus was succeeded by Agrippa, from whom was born Romulus Silvius, and from him Aventinus, who gave his name to the Aventine, one of the seven hills of Rome. After him reigned Proca. And from Proca was born Numitor, and from Numitor came Romulus, the author of the Roman people. Therefore, the "kinsman of Silvius," that is Aeneas, according to Virgil, went to the underworld. Virgil uses Aeneas to represent the man who desires to reach the **Supreme Good**. And since happiness is placed in the contemplation of divine things, he makes him come to Italy, setting Italy for the contemplative life. And having arrived in Italy, he makes him, following the Sibyl, descend into the subterranean and infernal places; and in those he finds Tartarus, that is, the place where with eternal punishments and torments the souls of wicked sinners are punished, and other places where lesser sinners stay until they are purged. And finally, he places the Elysian Fields, in which stay the souls of the blessed. And by all this, he allegorically demonstrates that Aeneas, having arrived in Italy—that is, at contemplation—first investigates the nature of vices, then purges himself of them, and being purged, can contemplate the things in which beatitude consists, as I wrote more extensively in our allegories. Therefore, both of these poets, although their fictions...

# INFERNO

be different: Nevertheless, they go toward the same end. **CORRUPTIBLE** also: That is, still living and connected with the body, which is corruptible because it is composed of the four elements <note>Earth, air, fire, and water</note>; once abandoned by the soul, it decays and, dissolving, returns to the four elements. And by allegory, he said "corruptible" because he uses it to represent the **active life**, which is corruptible. **TO THE Immortal world he went**: because Hell, as we shall say later, is eternal. And allegorically we understand that he went to the contemplation of the sciences, which are eternal because they deal with universals. **AND HE WAS there sensibly**: because he went while still in life and with the body, from which the senses proceed. For in truth, even though we are burdened with this mass and weight of the body, we can still go to Hell—that is, to the contemplation of the things already mentioned by us. **THE ADVERSARY of every evil** is God, who is the supreme good. And no one can be contrary to all evil except He who is all and supreme good. And God is so much the supreme and unique good that no other thing is good except by participation in the divine goodness. **HE WAS COURTEOUS**: He was liberal and gracious to Aeneas in letting him descend to Hell. **THINKING of the high effect that should come from him**: because from him issued the founders of the Roman Empire, in which was later established the Papacy and the Empire of the Christians. Therefore, it was a just cause to move God to grant this special grace to Aeneas, since such an end was to come from it. And therefore it did not seem "unworthy"—that is, an unsuitable thing—but it will seem a worthy and just thing to every man who judges with intellect and reason, considering the effect and the end. And through these words, he latently demonstrates what I interpreted above: that allegorically Aeneas represents the active life. And if it seems absurd to anyone that, imitating our poet Virgil, I place Aeneas for the active life when he placed him for the contemplative, I respond that the name gives no weight to the things; and this could easily be demonstrated. Nevertheless, we can also say that he places Aeneas for contemplation written poetically and according to the doctrine of the Gentiles <note>The pagans</note>, and Paul for that which is according to our theology. Hence Dante will be the third who descends to this contemplation composed of both the aforementioned. For he writes in a poetic style and to that adds Christian theology. Therefore, it is a third thing beyond the two already mentioned. And it is perfect, mixing the gravity of divine science with the sweetness and ornament of poetic eloquence, which according to Cassiodorus was proper to the first divine writers, he saying: <note>original: "Omnis splendor eloquentie omnis modus poetice elocutionis a diuinis scriptoribus sumpsit exordium."</note> "All splendor of eloquence, every mode of poetic expression, took its beginning from the divine writers." And certainly the first divine writers taught through figures and metaphors, which is proper to the poet. And this same method is observed by Plato, the most eloquent of all philosophers. Nor should anyone believe that God forbids the doctrine of the ancients. Nor did He intend to imply anything else when, in a figure, He commanded His people to despoil the Egyptians of the vessels of gold and silver borrowed from them, and carrying them away as they fled, except that we should take from the Gentiles their wisdom and the silver of their eloquence. We must, therefore, flee Egypt—that is, depart from the religion of the Gentiles—and return to the Promised Land—that is, to Christian doctrine—but carry with us their gold and silver to adorn the sacred letters. Thus did Paul, who in his epistles took many things from poets; so did Augustine; so did Jerome; so did Ambrose, Lactantius, Leo, and the other early doctors. Would to God that those who followed after had not degenerated from them! For it is much to be grieved that such excellent and admirable doctrine as is in them should be written with such barbarity, and that so beautiful, shapely, and robust a body should be wrapped in such vile garments. Our poet, therefore, deserves divine and immortal praise, who, embracing all Christian theology, illustrates and illuminates it with every poetic ornament. **THAT SHOULD COME from him**: That is, of which he was to be the cause. Some explain "should come from him" because from him was born Iulus Ascanius, from whom the family of the Julii had its origin, from which was born Julius Caesar, the first emperor. But it is perhaps better to take the universal rather than the particular. **THE WHO**: Denotes the substance. **THE WHICH**: Denotes the quality and the power. For when we say "who is he?", we are answered "it is Paul," because we desire to know his essence—that is, if he is a man, or if he is a father, or a citizen, or a foreigner. But when we say "which," we want to understand his quality; hence we are answered "he is learned." This essence, therefore, was to come out of it—that is, the Empire and the Papacy—and this is the "who." Which Empire and Papacy were to be very useful and salutary to the Christian republic, and this is the "which." **THAT**: That is, which Aeneas was elected and predestined by God as father and first author. **OF THE noble <term>Almo</term> Rome**: *Almo* in the Latin language signifies a thing that gives nourishment, increase, and maintenance, because *alere* signifies to nourish. Hence Virgil said *Alma Venus*, because through her all species of animals are maintained and increased. And similarly, he said *Alma luce* <note>Nourishing light</note> because light proceeds from the sun, which generates and nourishes all things. Therefore, he said "noble [almo] Rome" because she created and nourished such an empire and priesthood. **IN THE empyrean heaven**: There are seven first heavens, each of which has in itself only one planet. These are, starting from the lowest: Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. After that is the eighth heaven, which is adorned and filled with a very great number of stars, although astrologers have no knowledge of more than one thousand and sixty. From these are formed seventy-two signs, and it is called the **firmament**. The ninth is called **crystalline** because it is entirely transparent. And the tenth, which is the habitation of God, is called **empyrean** because it is all light, and light is proper to fire; therefore it is called empyrean, as if "on fire," because *pyr* in Greek signifies fire. He was elected in the empyrean heaven—that is, by God, whose providence governs everything. Which God stays in the empyrean heaven, uncircumscribed. **WHICH Rome** and **WHICH Empire** in truth God ordained should rise so that there would be an honored seat for the Apostolic Church, where the shepherd of the Christian flock and successor of the first vicar of God, Peter the Apostle (whom he calls "greater"), should have his residence; for every Pope, in truth, in respect to the dignity he holds, can be called Peter. # CANTO TWO
## b. iiii.

<note>The commentator refers to Augustine's "City of God" here.</note> The book of the City of God says Rome was created as another Babylon; and the daughter of the first Babylon, through whom it pleased God to conquer the whole world and reduce it to a single republic and under the same laws. But returning to Peter: he, both for his sanctity and for having been the first, and for the doctrine received from the Holy Spirit—and especially because he founded our republic with his blood—deserves to be called the "greater." And he <note>Dante</note> rightfully calls it a "holy place" because this seat was established in supreme sanctity and ruled most holily by the first pontiffs. And if their successors have since degenerated, it is not because the place is not holy by its own nature. **WHERE HE SITS**; that is, where he resides. For our ancestors said "U." in the place where we say "where" <note>original: "u." or "ove"</note>; as the Sienese still say in these times. Whence Petrarch says: *Where [U] are the charms, where [u] are the honors.* And through this journey **WHENCE** (that is, through which) **YOU GIVE HIM BOAST**, that is, praise. Aeneas [learned] from Anchises his father, who showed him what was to be, meaning things that were the cause of his victory against Turnus; and from that victory was born the Empire of Rome, and from that the Papacy. Then went the **VESSEL OF ELECTION**; that is, Paul the Apostle, whom Jerome, in the preface to Genesis, writes that God chose as a vessel of the law and a cabinet of the holy scriptures. It seems an absurd thing that Dante says Paul went to Hell, since one reads that he was caught up not to Hell, but to the third heaven. To which it is answered that in that rapture he had knowledge of Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise. He was a "vessel," that is, a receptacle of "election," that is, of the will of God. For he, above all others, understood the true sense of the evangelical doctrine. **TO BRING COMFORT**. For there can be no greater comfort to one who does not have knowledge of a thing but believes it, than the authority and testimony of a man of great reputation. Therefore, Paul, testifying to part of the things he saw when he was caught up to the third heaven, comforted and greatly corroborated our faith. **WHICH**; that is, which is the principle of our salvation. He said "Principle" because no one can be saved without faith; but it is not everything. For faith without works is dead. I would define at present what faith is, but because in a more convenient place it will be necessary for us to define both this and the other two theological virtues, we will defer the definition until that time. **BUT I, WHY COME?**; If I am not powerful enough to endure such difficulty. **OR WHO CONCEDES IT?**: As if to say, why should I deserve this special grace of being fit for such contemplation, being not equal to these men? Whence Horace: *Or whatever Maecenas does, is it right that you, so dissimilar and so much smaller, should strive to do the same?* Also: *It does not happen to every man to go to Corinth.* <note>Latin: "Non cuiuis homini contingit adire corinthum" — a proverb meaning not everyone has the means or luck to reach the highest goals.</note> **I AM NOT AENEAS, I AM NOT PAUL**: There is not in me the vigor that was in these two, nor can such fruit come from my coming. Nor yet, according to my judgment and according to that of others, am I worthy of such grace. And certainly this poet, besides his learning, was also admirable in the adornment of his words. Because having to mention Aeneas and Paul twice, he used an artful variety which removes boredom from the ears of the listener. Therefore, in the first place, he did not put their proper names, but used a rhetorical color called "circumlocution"; which is when that which can be said by a proper name is said by many. As when we want to say Hercules, we say "the unconquered grandson of Alcaeus." And for this, he said "the parent of Silvius" and "the vessel of election." Which brings ornament with it. Now in this second place, putting the proper names, he says: *I am not Aeneas, I am not Paul.* Which two names bring with them gravity and authority. **FOR IF I ABANDON MYSELF TO COMING**. He rightly concludes that not cowardice of soul, but reasonable fear moves him to doubt: that his coming might be "folle," that is, foolish. And certainly it would be a foolish thing to undertake that which was not to succeed: because the judgment of almost everyone is that it is better not to begin than to later leave the undertaking. **YOU ARE WISE AND UNDERSTAND ME BETTER THAN I SPEAK**. According to the Greek Hesiod, there are three generations of men: Of which the best are those who by their own wisdom know what is good and the direct path, and follow it; and these are very rare. The second generation is of those who, knowing that they do not know by themselves, willingly follow the counsel of those who do know, and obey it. These, although they are not perfect, nevertheless deserve no small commendation, because it is no small wisdom to know one's own lack and seek a remedy for it. Because *Virtue is to flee vice, and the first wisdom is to have been without folly.* <note>Latin: "Virtus est uitium fugere et sapientia prima stultitia caruisse."</note> The third generation is of those who neither know by themselves nor want the counsel of others; and these are not useful in any part. Therefore, the poet places himself in the second generation. And in this place he does several things: first, he demonstrates morally that we ought, in great undertakings, to ask counsel of the wiser. He also demonstrates the manner of asking counsel. For when we want to be advised in anything, first we ourselves will examine it with all diligence; and all the doubts that occur to us we will propose together with the thing in which we seek counsel. And finally, by allegory, he demonstrates that the lower reason in universal things ought to submit to the higher. And it follows:

---

> And as one who unwills what he willed,
> and by new thought changes his intent,
> so that from the beginning he wholly withdraws,
> Such I became on that dark slope,
> so that by thinking I consumed the enterprise,
> which had been so quick in the beginning.

Certainly it happens thus that the man who sees himself in ignorance and blindness, and begins to know that man is born to acquire the supreme good, immediately there is born in him no small will to investigate it. Then, disheartened by the greatness and difficulty of the thing and by the labor of the soul, he becomes dismayed and would withdraw from the undertaking if the higher reason did not help him. This [reason], in the forest—that is, in blindness—appears to the lower reason which by itself was directing itself to the good path, but hindered by vices, turns back. Whence the higher...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, specifically focusing on the transition between the poet's hesitation and Virgil's encouragement at the beginning of the journey.</meta>

# INFERNO

<note>Virgil</note> encourages him to take a different journey than the one where the beasts are found. He <note>Dante</note> desires to obey. But becoming terrified by the magnitude of the undertaking, he presents his doubts to his higher reason and almost repents, beginning to "un-will" what he previously willed. Through this new thought—which consisted of considering his own insufficiency on one hand and the difficulty of the task on the other—he changes his purpose and almost decides not to begin, having no hope of being able to finish. This happens to him while he is still on the "dark slope," that is, in ignorance. He consumes and annihilates the undertaking which he had started so quickly. Certainly, once reason has judged a thing to be good, the appetite immediately desires it. But afterwards, the aforementioned difficulties arise which make him change his mind. Therefore, Virgil answers him thus:

---

> "If I have rightly understood your words,"
> replied the shade of that magnanimous one,
> "your soul is harmed by cowardice,
> which many times encumbers a man,
> so that it turns him back from an honorable quest,
> as false seeing does a beast when it starts at a shadow.
> So that you may free yourself from this fear,
> I will tell you why I came and what I heard
> at the first moment I felt pity for you.
> I was among those who are suspended,
> and a lady called to me, so blessed and beautiful
> that I prayed her to command me.
> Her eyes shone brighter than the star,
> and she began to speak to me, sweet and low,
> with an angelic voice in her own tongue."

---

We have shown above that Dante represents himself as sensuality and the lower, practical reason which deals with particulars and can be deceived. Virgil represents the higher reason, enlightened by doctrine—not sacred doctrine, but that of the Gentiles <note>pagan/classical philosophy</note>. This reason is suited to contemplating vices and virtues and showing that vices lead to misery, while virtues lead to the supreme good. It can teach how we may flee vices and acquire virtues, but it cannot give true knowledge of divine things. This knowledge was possessed by Christian philosophers, not through human possibility, but through divine revelation and the light of the Holy Spirit.

Having understood this, it is easy to see that since the lower reason is useless—knowing nothing but particulars and despairing of reaching universals—the higher reason comforts it. It demonstrates that if such contemplation is beyond human strength, he will be made powerful by divine help, just as Aeneas and Paul were. Virgil, then—that is, higher reason—comforting the lower reason and sensuality, shows he can lead the soul to salvation, if not by its own strength, then at least with the help of divine grace, without which such an arduous undertaking would be in vain.

Afterward, he shows, according to true Christian doctrine, the way by which we can arrive at such an exalted place. To understand this better, we must go back a bit further, for the poet feigns that a celestial lady (whom he does not name) <note>likely Mary, representing Prevenient Grace</note> moved Lucia to help Dante. And Lucia moved Beatrice to descend into Limbo to Virgil and persuade him to become Dante's guide.

True theologians affirm that although man possesses free will to do good or evil, nevertheless no one can purge themselves of vices and act according to virtue without divine grace. Whence Solomon says: *Trust in the Lord with all your heart; do not exalt yourself in your own wisdom. In all your ways acknowledge Him, that He may make your paths straight.* <note>original: "Esto confidens in domino intoto corde tuo. In tua autem sapientia ne exalteris. In omnibus uiis tuis cognosce eum ut rectas faciat uias tuas." - Proverbs 3:5-6</note> Therefore, as Jerome says in the third book against the Pelagians: we must not trust in our own wisdom or any other virtue of ours, but in the sole help of God to direct our steps. For this reason it is written: *Make my way straight in your sight.* <note>original: "Rectam fac in conspectu tuo uiam meam" - Psalm 5:8</note> And Solomon: *Commit your works to the Lord, and your thoughts shall be established.* <note>original: "Devolve super dominum opera tua et firmabuntur cogitationes tue." - Proverbs 16:3</note> And Paul the Apostle: *Such confidence we have through Christ toward God; not that we are sufficient to think anything of ourselves as of ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God.* <note>original: "Fiduciam autem talem habemus p christum ad deum non quod sufficientes simus cogitare aliquid ex nobis quasi ex nobis Sed sufficientia nostra ex deo est." - 2 Corinthians 3:4-5</note> And elsewhere: *He who glories, let him glory in the Lord; for it is not he who commends himself who is approved, but he whom God commends.* <note>original: "Qui gloriatur in domino glorietur: Non . n. qui se ipsum commendat ille probatus e/ sed quem deus commendat" - 2 Corinthians 10:17-18</note>

Nor should anyone conclude that if we cannot act by ourselves, then we do not have free will. For free will certainly exists, and as Thomas Aquinas affirms, man is master of all his operations, of willing and not willing, through the deliberation of the reason within him, which can turn to one side or the other. But although he is master of deliberating or not deliberating this way or that, it is nevertheless necessary that this comes from a preceding deliberation. And so as not to proceed into infinity, it is necessary finally to come to this: that our free will is moved by some external principle above the human mind, and this is God.

Therefore Aristotle, in the book *On Good Fortune*, affirms that the human mind does not have dominion over its works in a way that it is not necessary for it to be moved by God. And the Master of the Sentences <note>Peter Lombard</note> writes that the prevenient grace of God prepares our will—not that it creates a will, for that existed before grace arrived, but that it makes it a good and right will. Therefore, it does not follow that there is no free will, but rather that divine grace is joined in us with free will. And such grace was not only infused into man from the beginning in a general sense, but is also ready to succor us in singular and particular operations. Whence David sings: *Unless the Lord builds the house, they labor in vain who build it; and unless the Lord guards the city, he who guards it watches in vain.* <note>original: "Nisi dominus hedificauerit domum in uanum laborauerunt qui hedificant eam Et nisi dominus custodiuerit ciuitate frustra uigilat qui custodit eam." - Psalm 127:1</note>

Wishing to demonstrate this, Dante feigns that Virgil—that is, our reason and intellect—cannot guide us by himself unless he is sent by Beatrice—that is, unless he is instructed in the sacred scriptures, because the author always takes Beatrice to represent Christian theology with perfecting grace. Therefore, such knowledge can in us...

It argues that human reason (Virgil) requires divine grace (Beatrice) to achieve salvation and virtue, citing authorities like Aquinas, Aristotle, and various scriptures.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto II of Dante’s Inferno, focusing on the theological necessity of Divine Grace and the allegorical roles of the three ladies (Mary, Lucia, and Beatrice) before transitioning into a philosophical definition of Fortitude and Magnanimity.</meta>

# CANTO TWO

No one can arrive unless they are sent by divine grace, which is the principle of meritorious work through the virtues. Nor is this grace simple and singular, but threefold. To better understand that we cannot be blessed without these three graces, theologians demonstrate with clear reasoning that to achieve celestial beatitude, it is necessary that we become contemplative of spiritual, incorporeal, and divine things. Nor can one climb to such a high place except by the steps of the virtues. Nor can virtue exist in us without reason, because every virtue proceeds from right reason. Therefore, it is necessary that in a man wishing to become blessed, there be reason; and from that reason, virtue is born, which, by purging us of vices, makes us fit for contemplation. 

And from this, our poet <note>Dante Alighieri</note> forms his three canticles. For with reason, he journeys through the knowledge of vices, which is the **Inferno**. With the virtues acquired through reason, he purges himself of them, which is **Purgatory**. And once purged, he can rise to the contemplation of divine things and become blessed, which is **Paradise**. But because none of these three things can be perfect without divine help, three graces come to us from God. 

The first illuminates reason and makes it capable of forming virtue, which is nothing other than directing the will—found in our free will—to rightly desire the good. This is called **prevenient grace** <note>Grace that "comes before" human action to predispose the soul toward God</note>; and by the poet, it is figured as the first lady <note>The Virgin Mary, though unnamed here to represent the hidden nature of the initial movement of the soul</note>, and she disposes us to will. Because the will is hidden in the soul and unknown before it acts, he places her there without a name. 

The second is **illuminating grace**, through which the good will illuminates and helps us so that we know what we ought to do; and because she offers us the light of knowledge, he deservedly calls her **Lucia** <note>Saint Lucia, whose name derives from "Lux" or light</note> after such light. Regarding this, Augustine says that the first grace makes us will, and the second ensures that such a will is not in vain—that is, that we are able to act. These two graces the Church asks for every day in its prayers, saying:

> We beseech thee, O Lord, that thou mayest forestall our actions with thy inspiration, and then follow them with thy help. <note>Original Latin: "Praeveni, quaesumus, Domine, actiones nostras aspirando, et adiuvando prosequere."</note>

The third is **perfecting** or **consuming grace**, which fulfills our entire desire because it helps us to contemplate and know our supreme good. This he calls **Beatrice**, whom we said above figures as Theology, which gives us knowledge of divine things. And certainly, she is Beatrice <note>The "Bringer of Blessings"</note> because she makes us blessed by making us know God. For by knowing Him, we love Him, and by loving Him, we enjoy Him. 

Nor does it seem right to omit what the poets write of the Graces, because anyone with wit can easily see that they do not differ much from what we have gathered above from true theologians. Hesiod writes in his *Theogony* that the Graces are three, and he does not disagree on the number. They are daughters of Jove <note>Jupiter/God</note>. This signifies nothing else than that every grace proceeds from God alone. Whence Paul says: *By the grace of God I am what I am* <note>1 Corinthians 15:10</note>. And the apostle James:

> Every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights. <note>James 1:17</note>

Jove fathered them by Eurymone; and **Eurymone** in Greek signifies "wide pasture," because nothing is a more abundant pasture for the soul than divine grace. Therefore David says in Psalm 111:

> The merciful and compassionate Lord has made a memorial of his wonders; he has given food to those who fear him. <note>Psalm 111:4-5</note>

Their names are **Aglaia**, **Euphrosyne**, and **Thalia**. *Aglaos* in Greek means "splendid," and certainly only divine grace makes our soul splendid because it illuminates it. *Euphrosyne* means "joy," because only grace makes the soul joyful. *Thalia* means "flowering" and "turning green," because grace makes every virtue flower and turn green again within us. They add that the following two look back at the first, because it depends on her splendor, and from it proceeds the fact that the human soul remains joyful and green.

A man will not hesitate, then, to set out on the path of contemplation, having already disposed his senses to obey reason, and having as a guide the intellect—not only illustrated by all human doctrines but also ennobled by the three divine graces. If I have been too long or too wordy regarding these, let it be imputed to the difficulty of the subject and the utility of knowing it. For once this passage is well understood, many other things will become known to us through it. Now, coming to the text:

**THE SHADE**; that is, the soul. For the ancient Latins often used this name "shade" for the soul. **OF THE magnanimous**: Magnanimity is a species of **Fortitude**. But to better open up this virtue and all its parts, we shall say that Fortitude is excellence, height, and greatness of soul, which desires great and high things and despises the vile and low; and with certain reason, it sets itself to every heavy labor and danger to achieve honored utility. This has seven species within it:

1. **Constancy**: That which informs, hardens, and confirms the soul in honest works, so that it never lets it depart from them.
2. **Confidence**: When the soul has a firm purpose in great and honest things with a firm hope of achieving them.
3. **Magnanimity**: That frankness of soul that pushes us toward illustrious and great things with the expectation of honesty and utility. Its companions are two: **Dignity** and **Liberality**. Dignity gives us honest authority and reputation; Liberality distributes reasonably according to rank.
4. **Perseverance**: When we persist with firm stability in a well-considered undertaking.
5. **Patience**: When for the sake of honesty and utility, we endure difficult and laborious things for a long time without perturbation of soul.
6. **Magnificence**: Height of soul in doing great things from which honor and fame result. Its companions are **Glory**, **Amplitudine** <note>Abundance/Greatness of scope</note>, **Study**, and **Exercise**. Glory gives fame with praise. Amplitudine is an abundance of offices, honors, and riches. Study is the vehement application of the soul. Exercise is the movement of the will that modestly pushes us to act.
7. **Security**: The final part of Fortitude, which ensures the soul has no remorse of conscience in worthy undertakings.

These are the species of Fortitude, among which we have shown Magnanimity to be that which, through the expectation of honor and utility, spurs the soul to great enterprises. Therefore, Virgil is magnanimous if he trusts...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical introduction to the infernal rivers, likely following a discussion on the nature of the soul. The commentator uses Neoplatonic thought to explain Dante’s imagery.</meta>

# INFERNO

> *Then with eyes ashamed and downcast,*
> *fearing that my speaking might be troublesome to him,*
> *I withdrew from talking until we reached the river.*

...taking our beginning from the prince of philosophers, Plato. He holds this view—an opinion largely followed by Origen—that our souls were all created together by God. But afterward, at different times, weighed down by the desire for earthly things, they fall to earth; and "Hell" is the body, into which the soul enters...

...they enter into bodies; and they intend "Hell" to be nothing other than this matter, which, by intoxicating the soul, makes it forget all the things it had knowledge of in heaven. And they call this matter a "river," which they divide into four rivers. The first they call **Lethe**, which in Greek means "oblivion" <note>original: "obliuione"</note>, because the soul, once placed in the body, falls into the aforementioned forgetfulness. From Lethe is born **Acheron**, a name that signifies the "privation of joy" <note>original: "priuatione di gaudio"</note>. This is because the soul, through forgetfulness, loses all that joy it possessed when it was pure and stood fixed in the contemplation of God without the contagion of the body. From Acheron is born the **Stygian** marsh, which signifies "sadness"; for he who is deprived of joy must necessarily live in sadness. And from Styx is born **Cocytus**, which in Greek signifies "wailing and mourning." And because from long-lasting mourning men become inflamed with anger and burning fury, they imagine that from Cocytus is born **Phlegethon**, so named because *phlegetho* means "I burn" <note>original: "ardo"</note>. Plato demonstrates these things at length in the *Phaedrus*. 

But we, who firmly believe that human souls are not created before they are infused into bodies, will say not that the soul, in descending into the body, comes into forgetfulness of the things it saw in heaven, but rather that the contagion of sensuality makes it fall into sin. There it drinks of Lethe—that is, it forgets its Creator—and from Lethe proceed the other rivers as we have said above. To speak more clearly, by Lethe we mean the submerging of reason into sensuality, for then the forgetfulness of all virtue is born. From Lethe is born Acheron, which represents the deliberation to sin. For this reason, Seneca describes it as running swiftly and not without noise; because our intellect, in which there is some remorse of conscience and which possesses within itself <term>synderesis</term> <note>From the Greek *syntéresis*, referring to the innate spark of conscience that inclines us toward good and resists evil.</note>—which we call "conscience"—cannot deliberate upon sin without the noise of a rebelling conscience. 

And because this deliberation is a transition of the will which carries the soul toward sinning, they imagine that **Charon** is here, who crosses the souls in his boat. After this transition into sin, sadness and sorrow follow. Just as a pure conscience always keeps the soul joyful, so he who is conscious of his own crimes and feels himself stained within is always in "perpetual anxiety" <note>original: "perpetua anxietas"</note>, nor does he ever rejoice or have peace within himself. For as Plato says, carnal delights pass in a brief time, leaving nothing behind but repentance. He whose conscience always bears witness to the sin committed never rests. As Juvenal says: *The Pythian prophetess replied to a certain Spartan that he carries a witness in his breast night and day* <note>original: "Noctes atque dies gestare inpectore testem Spartano cuidam respondit Pythia uates"</note>. And Cicero most excellently said: *There is no greater theater than one's conscience* <note>original: "Nullum est maius theatrum conscientia"</note>. 

Therefore, from Acheron is born the Stygian marsh, which signifies "gloom"; from which, because greater mourning and wailing proceed, they say the river Cocytus issues, which in Greek means "wailing." And he who remains for a long time in tears dries out the body and is inflamed with fury. Deservedly, the river that flows from Cocytus is called Phlegethon, or "burning," because *phlegethon* means to burn. You have in brief the meaning of the infernal rivers. This is to be committed to memory, for it will be necessary for the explanation of many other places in this poem. 

Now returning to the text, Dante asks what "custom" <note>original: "costume"</note> makes the souls so ready and eager to want to cross. He wisely used the word "custom." Indeed, every operation of ours is moved either by nature or by custom—that is, by habit. Nature is the best guide for those who follow her. And he who lives according to sincere and uncorrupted nature always arrives at a good end, because she persuades us and draws us toward the true good. But wicked habit often corrupts her. Hence men, following habit, leave virtue and give themselves to vice. Petrarch expressed this, saying: *Our nature, conquered by custom* <note>original: "Nostra natura uinta dal costume"</note>. 

Therefore, Dante, wanting to express that this appetite of the souls to cross the Acheron was not natural but moved by depraved habit, said "custom." Nor did he speak without great learning when he said "it MAKES THEM SEEM" <note>original: "LE FA parere"</note> so ready to cross, using this verb "to seem." For since there is a fixed and innate appetite in man to always follow the good and flee the evil, we must understand, according to the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note>, that there are two kinds of good: namely, the *existing good* and the *apparent good*. The existing good is the true good, which he who follows becomes blessed, because he knows virtue and understands God to be the true good. The apparent good is when our soul, blinded by sensuality, follows pleasures and worldly delights, which are not existing goods but "seem" like goods to the senses. 

Therefore, the soul corrupted by sensuality is ready to cross Acheron—that is, to go toward sin as if to something that "seems" good to it, though it is not. As Petrarch says: *Greedy for such a thing that is sweet to the sense but harmful to salvation.*

**FAINT light** <note>original: "FIOCHO lume"</note>: that is, clouded and obscure. "Fiocho" is properly what the Latins call *raucus* (hoarse). But just as we use a metaphor from light to voice when we say a "clear voice" (meaning well-expressed and without offense), we also use a metaphor from voice to light. Thus, although "fiocho" refers to a voice that is not clear, by the same metaphor we say "faint light" <note>original: "lume fiocho"</note>, meaning not clear. 

It should be noted that the poet makes this entrance to Hell obscure, but not entirely deprived of light, to denote that when a man passes into sin, he has begun to lose the light of reason but is not yet in total darkness. In the beginning, he has not yet formed a habit. A bit of the light of reason remains for him, by which our soul feels remorse, as I explained more extensively regarding Virgil's verse: *Like a path in the woods under the malicious light of an uncertain moon, when Jupiter has hidden the sky in shadow* <note>original: "Quale per incertam lunam sub luce maligna Est iter in siluis ubi celum condidit umbra Iuppiter"</note>. From this it arises that at the beginning we put up some resistance to temptation, although in the end we allow ourselves to be conquered...

<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic and psychological commentary on Dante’s Inferno, specifically Canto III. The previous page established that the infernal rivers represent stages of the soul's descent into matter and forgetfulness. This page focuses on the character of Charon and the moral mechanism of the "free will" in the process of sinning.</meta>

### CANTO THREE

...and it pains us to err. But once the **habit** <note>The term "habito" refers to a settled disposition or character trait formed through repeated actions.</note> is formed, because we remain entirely in darkness, there is no longer any remorse of conscience, and we sin willingly. **AND HE to me: the things shall be made known to you:** An excellent precept where he demonstrates that one ought not to ask about things before we have arrived at their proper place. It is as if he says that every investigation should be carried out in its own time and place, observing the proper method and order. This order would not be observed by the **appetite** <note>The lower, impulsive part of the soul.</note>, which would desire to know everything at once if **reason** did not admonish it. **UPON THE sad shore:** He interprets the name of Acheron by calling it the "Sad Shore," because Acheron signifies sadness <note>original: "tristitia"</note>. **AND I With eyes ashamed and downcast:** This demonstrates how a disciple should behave toward a teacher; he should not only believe him, but also show him such reverence that he feels ashamed of every ill-considered question he asks. In the same way, the appetite should behave toward reason: for every time it moves without reason, once admonished by it, the appetite should grieve and show signs of repentance.

*And behold, coming toward us in a boat,*
*an old man, white with ancient hair,*
*crying out: "Woe to you, wicked souls!*
*Never hope to see the heavens;*
*I come to lead you to the other shore,*
*into eternal darkness, into heat and frost.*
*And you there, who are a living soul,*
*depart from these who are dead."*
*But when he saw that I did not depart,*
*he said: "By other ways, by other ports*
*you shall come to the shore, not here, to pass;*
*a lighter craft must carry you."*
*The guide to him: "Charon, do not vex yourself;*
*it is willed there where what is willed*
*can be done; and ask no more."*
*From then on, the woolly cheeks were quiet*
*of the pilot of the livid marsh,*
*who had wheels of flame around his eyes.*

<column-break/>

**H**e demonstrates that upon arriving at the river, they saw Charon the ferryman, who, having already unloaded his boat on the other bank, was returning to fill it with those who were waiting. He then describes Charon and the boat guided by him through the river Acheron, where many identify Charon as **Death**, which, by separating the sinner's soul from the body, leads it to Hell. Some wish Acheron to be the **disordered appetite**. But it seems to me we should give it the same sense that our written dialogues on Virgil provide. We shall say, therefore, that if Acheron is understood as the movement the soul makes to pass into sin, then Charon is **free will** <note>original: "libero arbitrio"</note>; the boat is the **will**; and the oar is the **choice**. And therefore I conclude that where there is no free will, there can be no choice, nor can the will be used. And that which is not done voluntarily and by choice is not imputed as either vice or virtue. For this reason, violence and non-negligent ignorance excuse a sin. Thus, one does not go to Hell unless the boat—that is, the will—carries them there, steered by Charon—that is, by free will. Charon is named from *charis*, which in Greek signifies **grace** <note>original: "gratia"</note>, because nothing is more free than grace, since it is given without obligation. Furthermore, they say he is the son of Death—that is, of blindness and ignorance. For if

---

there were in us an open and clear knowledge of the truth and the good, unclouded by any darkness of ignorance, our will would of its own accord move toward the good without the choice of free will. Nor do they imagine without reason that Charon is an old man, because nothing is more ancient in the soul than free will. Here Virgil adds that although he is old, nonetheless his old age is green and robust: "Already old, but a god’s old age is raw and green" <note>original: "Iam senior sed cruda deo uiridisque senectus"</note>. This demonstrates that free will is never diminished in us by any length of time. This figure cries out to the souls who are eager to cross that they should never hope to see heaven, because nothing can convince the soul that it deserves Hell except free will; if it were not in us, we could commit neither vice nor virtue. **I COME to lead you to the other shore:** For is it not free will alone that makes the soul, already ready to pass, actually cross? That is, it makes the soul move toward sinning. And Acheron has two shores. The river is moving; the shores are unmoving. But on the first shore, they stay only long enough for Charon to pass them over; but once reached the other shore, they remain there for eternity. The first shore, then, is the **inclination of depraved counsel**, into which the soul, corrupted by the flatteries of sensuality, allows itself to fall; this makes the soul take delight in worldly things, which are a pestilential poison to it. Having arrived at this "counsel"—which is a shore because it is a fixed point, for such a judgment remains fixed in the soul, namely that it is good to proceed to such an action—then there is the river, which is the movement and the acts that lead it toward the **habit**. And after the river is the other shore, where the eternal habitation of sinners begins. This is nothing other than the "habit" <note>A permanent state of sin.</note>. The poet expresses these three things—inclination (or depraved counsel), acts, and habit—in divine verses in the first Psalm. For when it says: "Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly" <note>original: "Beatus uir qui non habit in consilio impiorum"</note>, it demonstrates the depraved counsel; and by adding: "And has not stood in the way of sinners" <note>original: "Et in uia peccatorum non stetit"</note>, it denotes the acts, which are the way that leads to the habit. And finally, by saying: "And has not sat in the seat of pestilence" <note>original: "Et in cathedra pestilentie non sedit"</note>, it places the habit, which is the seat in which the vicious man dies. Next, he calls Dante a **living soul**, not only because he was still alive, but because he was not dead in sin and was not going to Hell like the others—that is, he was not falling into vices. Rather, he was going to contemplate and know the vices; and therefore he did not have to go by the river, which is deprived of joy, nor by the boat that carries sinners, but by a lighter craft. For he who descends into vice goes by the boat weighed down by the concupiscence of vices; but he who goes to speculate <note>To "speculate" here means to engage in deep intellectual and spiritual observation.</note> is carried by a pure will.

It utilizes classical etymology and biblical references (Psalm 1) to explain the mechanics of moral descent.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto III, specifically focusing on the interaction between Virgil and Charon, and the theological significance of Dante's journey as a living man through the underworld.</meta>

### INFERNO

...and light. **MY LEADER:** "Charon, do not vex yourself." Virgil could have offered many reasons to Charon, and Charon could have replied to them. But cutting through every question at once, he says that Dante, still alive, goes to Hell guided by **divine grace** <term>divine grace: the theological concept of God's unmerited favor and assistance given to humans for their salvation</term>. By this, he demonstrates what all theologians—and especially Jerome—affirm: that every man can fall into sin by himself through his own **free will**. But to acquire virtue and live without sin, man cannot do so by free will alone without divine grace. This is why Virgil has Aeneas pass in the same boat as the other souls: because the **gentile** <note>Meaning non-Christian or pagan</note> philosophers believed that free will was sufficient for salvation as well as for damnation. But Dante, as a Christian, does not depart from Christian opinion. Nor without reason did he say, "do not vex yourself." In this, he imitates Virgil, who shows that Charon is angered against Aeneas and the Sibyl. Virgil introduces Charon as unwilling to let Aeneas pass, saying: "It is a sin to carry living bodies in the Stygian boat" <note>original: "Corpora uiua nefas stygia uectare carina"</note>. This denotes that free will, as such, does not want to yield to **reason**; it wants to argue before it comes to action. But Aeneas—that is, **virtue**—has already made the choice and does not wish to remain longer in deliberation and consultation. Instead, he wants to pull the free will toward doing what has already been chosen. Therefore, although the will is always free in potential, in action it is no longer free to do or not do. Because it is pulled by reason, it must do whatever reason dictates. Thus, at first, when Charon sees Aeneas coming armed, he fears his weapons, because force should not be used against free will. But once the Sibyl—that is, the superior reason of the virtuous man—tells him that neither force nor fraud will be used against him, and reveals the **golden bough** <note>In the Aeneid, the golden bough is the key that allows Aeneas to enter the underworld safely</note>—that is, the light of wisdom—he immediately yields. For this same reason, our poet has Charon refuse to let him pass. But Virgil does not appease him as the Sibyl did by showing the golden bough—that is, human wisdom—because, as we have already said, human wisdom is not enough for man's salvation. Instead, he demonstrates that "God wills it so." This is nothing other than saying he comes accompanied by divine grace. **IT IS WILLED** where what is willed can be done, and ask no more. He says two things: first, that Charon must yield to Dante because God wills it so, and He alone can do whatever He wills. Thus, he comes with divine grace, which directs the free will toward the good. Second, he admonishes Charon not to seek to know *why* God wills it so: because it is the height of audacity to search into the secrets of the Divinity, and why this person rather than another follows such grace; for His judgments are incomprehensible, as David says. And elsewhere he writes: "Thy judgments are a great deep" <note>original: "Iudicia tua abissus multa"</note>. And Solomon in the Proverbs: "Just as eating too much honey is not good for a man, so he who is a searcher of Majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory" <note>original: "Sicut qui multum mel comedit non ei bonum: Sic qui scrutator est maiestatis opprimetur a gloria"</note>.

> But those souls, who were weary and naked,
> changed color and gnashed their teeth,
> as soon as they heard those cruel words.
> They blasphemed God and their parents,
> the human race, the place, the time, and the seed
> of their sowing and of their birth.
> Then they all withdrew together,
> weeping loudly, to the evil shore
> that awaits every man who fears not God.
> Charon the demon, with eyes of burning coal,
> beckoning to them, gathers them all;
> he strikes with his oar whoever lingers.

<column-break/>

**THEY WERE WEARY** from pain, and **NAKED**: that is, stripped of their bodies. Or truly naked of divine grace, naked of every defense. And certainly the soul damned to Hell, because it has formed a **habit** in vice, is weary and deprived of all vigor with which it might rise against vice. And it is naked, that is, without weapons with which it might defend itself. For the weapons of the soul against vice are the vibrancy of the light of **reason**, which is entirely extinguished. Thus the soul remains in darkness. Nor can it discern the true good unless divine grace illuminates it anew. For this the prophet prays, saying: "To give light to those who sit in the shadow of death" <note>original: "Illuminare iis qui in umbra mortis sedent"</note>. **THEY CHANGED** color and gnashed their teeth: He attributes to the soul, which is incorporeal, that which belongs to the body, and notes the signs which in the human body demonstrate great fear. For when great consternation arises in the mind, nature—which fears it cannot save

the whole city (that is, the whole body)—strives at least to save the **fortress** <note>original: "roccha"</note> with which it might later regain the whole city. And this is the heart, which is the fortress and principal seat of life. Therefore, it recalls to the heart the blood in which life most greatly consists. Thus, the exterior parts, deprived of blood, lose their color and become pale; and they lose the heat which is in the blood, and remaining cold, they tremble. Thus, by this he denotes the fear that was born from the threats made by Charon. And certainly the sinner never considers his own perdition until he sees himself in Hell. This applies to the dead. But as for the living, the sinner then perceives his ruin when he sees that his free will leads him into the habit of vices. **THEY BLASPHEMED God and their parents.** By these words, the poet denotes a state of total desperation and fury, by which the damned soul would rather lose its existence and be annihilated than stay in perpetual pain. Thus it agrees with the words of Christ against Judas: "It would be better for this man if he had never been born." These words and blasphemies mean, therefore, that they wish they had never been born, or that God and every creature would come to the same damnation. **CHARON the demon with eyes of burning coal.** A description taken from Virgil, who states that his eyes were flames. For the free will has one flame which is the light of the **intellect**, which shows it the good; and another which is the heat of **concupiscence** <term>concupiscence: strong sexual desire or lust; more broadly, any intense longing for worldly pleasures</term> located in the senses, and this invites it to worldly delights. He called him "Charon the demon" because that free will which carries souls to Hell is not the free will guided by the grace of God, but that which is seduced and deceived by diabolic temptation.

<summary>This page provides a theological commentary on Charon’s role in the Inferno, contrasting Virgil’s pagan view of free will with Dante’s Christian emphasis on the necessity of Divine Grace. It also explains the physical and psychological state of the damned souls as they prepare to cross the Acheron.</summary>
