<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto III, following the explanation of Charon’s initial refusal to ferry Dante across the Acheron. It provides a theological and allegorical interpretation of the souls' eagerness to enter Hell and the famous simile of the falling leaves.</meta>

# CANTO THREE

->**As in autumn the leaves lift off**<-
->**one after another until the branch**<-
->**sees all its spoils upon the ground,**<-
->**So the evil seed of Adam**<-
->**throw themselves from that shore one by one**<-
->**at signals, like a bird to its lure.**<-
->**Thus they go over the dark wave,**<-
->**and before they have descended on the other side,**<-
->**a new swarm gathers again on this side.**<-

->**"My son," said the courteous master,**<-
->**"those who die in the wrath of God**<-
->**all gather here from every country;**<-
->**And they are prompt to cross the river,**<-
->**for divine justice spurs them on,**<-
->**so that fear turns into desire.**<-
->**No good soul ever passes this way;**<-
->**and therefore, if Charon complains of you,**<-
->**you can well know now what his speech signifies."**<-

->**This finished, the dark countryside**<-
->**trembled so strongly that from the terror...**<-

<column-break/>

**HE STRIKES** with his oar whoever lingers. i.e., whoever becomes idle and slow. But if the souls are prompt to cross as was said above, why does he say here that any "lingers"—that is, is late and slow? I answer that although sensuality makes the sinner prone to vice, it nevertheless happens that in the beginning, before a habit has been formed, reason and conscience oppose sensuality and delay the act of sinning. But Charon—that is, the **free will** which has already been persuaded by sensuality—pushes them by striking them with the oar: that is, with the **choice** <note>In this context, the "choice" refers to the deliberate act of the will</note> which has already made a habit of sinning. The "oar" with which Charon drives the souls is nothing other than the choice to follow what the appetite has judged to be good.

**A MOST FITTING COMPARISON.** Just as leaves, having lost their natural moisture through the summer heat, fall dry to the ground, so our souls—having the moisture of **reason** that nourished them dried up by the heat of **concupiscence** <term>concupiscence: a theological term for the disordered desire for earthly pleasures rather than spiritual goods</term>—fall into earthly desires. This passage is taken from the text of Virgil: "As many as the leaves that fall in the woods at the first frost of autumn, or as many as the birds that flock toward the land from the deep sea." <note>original Latin: "Quam multa in siluis auctumni frigore primo Lapsa cadunt folia aut ad terrā gurgite ab alto quam multe glomerantur aues"</note> And thus they throw themselves into the river to the demon Charon; i.e., without any reasoned consideration, they go to a depraved free will, just as a bird flies to the **fowler** <note>fowler: a person who catches or hunts wild birds</note> when he shows it the bait. Because of that bait, they do not realize they are losing their liberty and becoming slaves. The fowler shows the bait to the bird, and the bird, seized by greed for such food, flies to him, not noticing it is losing its freedom. So the sinner, when the sensuality of free will shows him worldly delights, immediately throws himself toward them. **THE EVIL SEED OF ADAM.** From Adam proceed both the good and the wicked; but the good are saved, and the wicked are lost in vice. Therefore, he did not say "the seed" in an absolute sense, but "the evil seed." Or, we might say that the body originates from Adam, and the soul from God. Because the body is a great cause of the soul's contagion, he says "the evil seed of Adam." And he prudently says "they throw themselves" (*gittonsi*). For "to throw oneself" signifies going thoughtlessly and without reason. And so does the sinner. Certainly, he who lives according to virtue walks with consideration and measured steps. But he who walks the path of vice throws himself without consideration, now into one extreme, now into another.

**SON:** Because the disciple should be held in both reverence and love in the place of a son to the teacher. And likewise, the teacher should be "courteous" and generous with his doctrine toward the disciple—not like many who, out of greed or envy, do not teach as much as they could. Furthermore, for the reasons stated above regarding the "father" and the "lord," the poet signifies here that in such contemplation, sensuality must be so obedient to the intellect that the intellect can instruct it with paternal clemency, and not with that hardness and rigidity used by a master toward a slave. **THEY DIE IN THE WRATH OF GOD.** Everyone who falls into sin dies, and dies in the wrath of God, and arrives at the river in the manner we have already described. **AND DIVINE JUSTICE SPURS THEM.** Because as they begin to form a habit, they begin to take pleasure in what should cause displeasure. Divine justice allows this because they have made themselves unworthy of all of God's grace, with which they could have defended themselves from vice. Therefore **FEAR**—that is, the dread they should have of vice and which they had before they formed the habit—**TURNS INTO DESIRE**: that is, into longing, because they crave what they should flee. If we wish to understand this passage more clearly, it is necessary to remember the difference we showed above between the **incontinent** and the **intemperate** <note>In Aristotelian ethics, the incontinent person knows what is right but fails to do it, while the intemperate person chooses vice as if it were a good.</note>. **NO GOOD SOUL EVER PASSES THIS WAY.** We showed above that he who falls into vice and allows himself to be conquered by it descends into Hell, as all sinners do. But one also descends who enters to contemplate vices in order to know them and guard against them—as Homer feigns of **Ulysses**, and Virgil of **Aeneas**, and Dante of himself. But the first group enters in the way we have interpreted allegorically above regarding Charon and Acheron: because the "ship"—that is, their own depraved will guided by free will—carries them. The second group is conducted by a will carried by the **Angel**—that is, by the grace of God, which directs the free will toward wanting and choosing the true good.

Various commentators explain this text in various ways. But in my judgment, it demonstrates nothing other than that he who descends into Hell to return—that is, he who enters...

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on Canto III of the Inferno. It interprets the earthquake and Dante’s subsequent fainting not merely as a narrative device, but as an allegorical "sleep of the senses" necessary for the soul to transition from physical awareness to spiritual contemplation.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>INFERNO</header>

> the memory of it even now bathes my mind in sweat:
> The tear-stained earth gave forth a wind
> that flashed a crimson light,
> which overcame my every sense;
> And I fell like a man whom sleep seizes.

<column-break/>

In the contemplation <note>original: *speculatione*, referring to deep philosophical or theological study</note> of vices, in order to guard against them, it is necessary that it happen through an abstraction of the mind: and that the senses remain asleep until they become accustomed to obeying reason without any resistance. For whoever considers the bodily delights which are found in vices—and does not yet have their sensuality <term>Sensuality: in medieval thought, the part of the soul driven by physical urges and instincts rather than logic</term> subject to reason—often finds the snake hidden among the flowers. Wherefore Petrarch says: *This earthly life is like a meadow, where the serpent lies among flowers and grass, and some of its sights please the eyes; and to leave the soul more entangled, it remains trapped and taken by carnal delights, and poisoned by the serpentine bite of sin.*

---

Therefore it is necessary that Dante—representing **sensuality**—be carried into Hell while asleep, so that he does not rise up against reason. And he is carried by the angel—that is, by **divine grace**. Dante then reaches the crossing of the Acheron, which is the entrance to contemplation. And although previously he had given himself entirely to Virgil, showing that one will belonged to both of them, nevertheless, reflecting on how arduous and difficult this undertaking is, he begins to waver: because the task does not seem fit for his shoulders alone. And in truth, human forces by themselves, without divine help, could not pass into Hell and return. He sins, therefore, not through malice (which deserves no mercy), but through fear and weakness <note>original: *imbecillita*, meaning physical or spiritual lack of strength</note>, for which God often has great compassion: because **God saw our frailty and had mercy on us** <note>original Latin: *Vidit deus figmentum nostrum et misertus est nostri*, a paraphrase of Psalm 103:14</note>. Especially for one who implores and asks for His help with tears. Therefore He sends the angel to put him to sleep, and having put him to sleep, he passes. 

This denotes nothing else but that divine grace makes up for our fragility; it separates and draws the mind and the intellect away from the senses, so that it can rise to contemplate the great things for which it was born. It puts sensuality to sleep so that it does not darken or disturb reason. Nor is "philosophizing" anything else, as Plato says—and the Platonist Cicero—than to withdraw the mind from the senses, and to ensure that the soul, while it is in the body, stays as separate from it as possible and "learns to die": that is, to live separated from the body. Having understood this, we will adapt the words of the text to the aforementioned meaning. 

First, the poet says: **THIS FINISHED, the dark countryside trembled.** That is, after the words spoken by Virgil, which showed great difficulty in crossing the "dark countryside"—meaning the sensuality of Dante. This is a "countryside" because it is an open and spacious place, for the desires of the senses are many and extend widely in every direction. And it is "dark" because sensuality is oppressed by the darkness of ignorance. **IT TREMBLED** due to great bewilderment and the fear of not being able to succeed. He grieved at having to abandon the undertaking, sweating from the distress. We have shown that his error proceeds not from the malice of an unwilling heart, but from the desperation of a weak one. 

From this it was born that **THE TEARFUL EARTH gave forth a wind.** That is, the tears of the earth—meaning our sensuality—gave forth a wind, meaning they created a movement: they moved God to mercy. **WHICH** wind **FLASHED a crimson light.** That is, it produced a fiery light with the speed of a lightning bolt. This light is **divine grace**, which God sends suddenly to strengthen the will of those who wish to reach salvation but waver out of fear. This grace is "light" because it illuminates the mind and shows it the true way; and it is "crimson," or fiery, because besides showing the way (which is a **Cherubic** work <note>The Cherubim were the order of angels associated with divine wisdom and light</note>), it ignites the soul with **Seraphic** love <note>The Seraphim were the order of angels associated with fire and the heat of divine love</note>. This is necessary in the contemplation of great things, because if a man did not fall in love with the task, he would not endure such labor. Wherefore Virgil, wishing to guide Aeneas to contemplation, has him follow Venus: that is, the love of divine things. 

This light overcomes every sense in Dante—that is, it lulls and puts sensuality to sleep. This passage is similar to the one in Virgil where Anchises, after Troy was burned, refuses to leave or live any longer. We demonstrated there that Anchises represents sensuality, which refuses to leave bodily pleasures. But Aeneas—higher reason—carries him on his shoulders: because the intellect raises the appetite and does not let it touch the ground—that is, think of earthly things—but guides it to Italy, meaning to contemplation. Nevertheless, before he reaches Italy, he buries him and then finds him again in the Underworld. So here, Dante falls asleep and then wakes up having crossed the river.

<summary>This page provides an allegorical commentary on the conclusion of Canto III, interpreting Dante's faint and the earthquake as the "sleep of the senses" required for divine grace to elevate the human intellect toward spiritual contemplation.</summary>
<keywords>Acheron, Divine Grace, Sensuality vs Reason, Plato, Cicero, Aeneas and Anchises, Cherubim and Seraphim, Contemplation</keywords>

<meta>This page transitions from the end of Canto III, where Dante fainted during the crossing of the Acheron, to the beginning of Canto IV. The commentator, Cristoforo Landino, continues to interpret Dante’s journey as an allegorical progression of the soul from a state of physical overwhelm to intellectual contemplation.</meta>

<header>CANTO FOUR.</header>

### CANTO FOUR OF THE FIRST CANTICLE

A heavy thunder broke the deep sleep in my head,
so that I started,
like a person woken by force;
And I moved my rested eyes around,
standing straight up: and I gazed fixedly
to know the place where I was.
Truly, I found myself on the brink
of the sorrowful valley of the abyss,
which gathers the thunder of infinite woes:
Dark and deep and cloudy,
so much that, though I fixed my sight on the bottom,
I could discern nothing there.

<column-break/>

The poet discusses the first circle of Hell, in which he places those who, although they are not to be punished for great sins, nevertheless do not deserve Heaven because they did not receive baptism. A person cannot move toward the contemplation <note>original: *speculatione*, referring to the philosophical study of a subject</note> of vices if their **sensuality**—which is resistant to reason—is not first quieted. Now, having reached this contemplation, sensuality is awakened by the thunder, and he turns his rested eyes around. This signifies that in the beginning, when a person decides to leave the **active life** and move toward the **contemplative life**, sensuality will not remain obedient to reason. Therefore, it is necessary for it to be made to sleep; and while asleep, it is carried there. But once we have arrived at contemplation, the thunder wakes it: that is, **reason** thundering over it and gravely rebuking it for its laziness, making it vigilant and attentive to obey reason in great matters. Thus, one can turn their "rested eye"—

---

that is, one can use their senses when they are quieted, and no longer inflamed or infuriated by the desire for earthly things. It is a well-known principle in philosophy that only the **intellect** contemplates and observes, because it alone can have knowledge of universal truths. But because it is necessary for principles to be born from particulars, and these particulars are found in the senses, the intellect seeks to make sensuality subject to itself. In the beginning, sensuality is agitated on one side, moved by the charms and flatteries of momentary and temporal things; on the other side, it is repressed by reason and becomes entirely weakened, because it is not yet perfectly obedient to reason. Therefore, it must be put to sleep as previously mentioned. But once we have entered into contemplation without the resistance of the senses—which were asleep then—reason excites and awakens them because they are now entirely obedient. It joins them to itself, because the person has reached such perfection that they discern with the mind and discern with the body. For our corruptible and bodily senses are converted into reason, and reason into intellect, and intellect into **intelligence** <note>In this context, *intelligentia* refers to a higher, more intuitive form of divine understanding above mere logic</note>, and intelligence into God. Nor should one marvel if the soul, made in the likeness of all wisdom, contains within itself the likeness of all things. Hence, Aristotle even called it the "likeness of all things," because it has within itself powers with which it may investigate every thing, and be similar to every thing, even though the soul is one. It is like the **earth** through the senses; like **water** through the imagination; like **air** through reason; like the **firmament** through the intellect; and like the **heaven of heavens** through intelligence.

The poet writes then: *A HEAVY thunder broke the deep sleep in my head*; that is, the very grace of God, which had first quieted the sensuality so it would not impede reason in passing to contemplation, now awakens it so it may be joined with it. And he said *It broke*, to indicate that he did not allow it to wake on its own or finish its sleep. This signifies that sensuality would never wake from its laziness if it were not awakened by divine grace. And he said *deep sleep*, because the sleep and laziness of sensuality are very deep.
> For the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak. <note>original: *Quia spiritus promptus est caro uero infirma*</note>

*IN THE head*: he said this because sleep proceeds from vapors, which, rising from nourishment, go to the brain. There, cooled by the chill of the brain and thus condensed, they block the path of heat and the spirit, which achieves the perfection of the senses in the brain. *SO THAT I started*: it is never without great movement when a person is woken by force. But sensuality, when seized by reason, also causes no small motion in the soul. *AND I MOVED my rested eyes around*: Just as the body has eyes with which it looks and sees, so the soul has power with which it investigates and discerns. The **mind**, therefore, is the eye of the soul; **reason** is its looking; and the **intellect** is its seeing and discerning. Therefore, the soul turns its "rested eye" when it discourses with tranquil reason; and reason is tranquil when the senses and appetite follow it obediently in every part. *STANDING straight up*: to demonstrate that sensuality was rising from low and earthly things to follow the intellect. *AND I GAZED fixedly*: It is necessary, if we wish to contemplate correctly, that the mind—tranquil and void of every perturbation and passion—moves around (that is, turns to all parts) and stays firm and fixed through the gaze of reason. For it is not enough for one who wishes to find the truth to merely discourse through all things; one must turn there with every sharpness of wit and fix it (that is, hold it steady) and not depart from there. Thus, from the eye and its looking, "seeing" is born—which is to say, understanding and knowing the place where we find ourselves. *TRULY, I found myself on the brink*: This is the effect of turning the eye and gazing fixedly; for from this is born "seeing," which is not a doubtful opinion but undoubted and true science. And therefore he says *Truly*, because contemplation of universal things finds the truth, which is the ultimate end of the intellectual virtues, just as "the good" is the end of the moral virtues. *ON THE brink of the abyss*: That is, at the beginning of the depths of Hell. And certainly, nothing is deeper nor further from celestial things than vice. *WHICH* (referring to the valley) *GATHERS THE THUNDER OF INFINITE WOES*: It gathers within itself the sound of infinite sorrows. When a valley, surrounded by very high mountains, is filled with people who cry out in various ways—and various...

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on Canto IV of the Inferno. Having crossed the river Acheron while unconscious, Dante now stands with Virgil at the edge of the first circle of Hell, known as Limbo.</meta>

<header>INFERNO</header>

complaints and shrieks were used. There would arise from the mixture of so many voices, and from the echoing of the valley, a confused sound gathered in the air from all those voices, because the concavity of the place does not let them out. Instead, they swirl and multiply by repercussion, and together they gather and make something like a thunderclap. And this is especially felt by one who is above, as Dante was. But allegorically, he means that in the contemplation of vices, one recognizes that from those many and so diverse vices—contrary among themselves, but all wretched—there results an extreme misery. **IT WAS DARK**: Because whoever wishes to know the nature of vice through contemplation finds everything obscure; that is, he understands that every vice consists in ignorance, which is born from having lost the light of the intellect. **SO MUCH THAT BY** straining my sight to the bottom, I could discern nothing there. He who contemplates vice, which is in the darkness of ignorance, cannot see anything there. For vice is not a thing in itself, but is only a privation <note>In medieval philosophy, "privation" means the absence of a good that should be present, just as darkness is the absence of light.</note>. This is, therefore, the reason why Hell is dark, and why nothing is discerned there. Virgil also expressed this in these verses: *They went darkling through the shadows under the lonely night, through the vacant halls of Pluto and the empty realms.* <note>original: "Ibant obscuri sola sub nocte per umbras Per que domos ditis uacuas et inania regna." — Virgil, Aeneid VI.268–269</note>

Now let us descend down here into the blind world,
began the poet, all pale;
I will be first, and you shall be second.
And I, who had noticed his color,
said: "How shall I come, if you are afraid,
who are usually the comfort to my doubt?"
And he to me: "The anguish of the people
who are down here paints upon my face
that pity which you feel as fear.
Let us go, for the long way urges us on."
Thus he set out, and thus he made me enter
the first circle that girds the abyss.

interprets it as fear, and estimates it to be fear. **I WILL BE** the first, and you shall be second. And rightly so; for in moving toward contemplation, Dante—that is, **sensuality** and the lower reason—must follow Virgil—that is, **superior reason**—as a true guide, because the intellect is that which contemplates and draws the senses after it. But for one who goes to Hell never to return—that is, one who falls into vices—then Dante draws Virgil with him, and Virgil does not guide Dante, because appetite predominates over reason. **AND HE** to me, the anguish of the people. He shows that although the <term>Stoics</term> <note>Ancient philosophers who believed a wise person should be free from all passion.</note> do not wish for the wise man to fall into any passion or disturbance of the mind, nevertheless, according to the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, who believed emotions should be moderated rather than suppressed.</note> and Christian theologians, it is a human thing to have compassion for the misery of men. And for this reason, he feigns that Virgil, entering Hell, became pale out of compassion for the tormented, following <term>Heraclitus of Ephesus</term>. For there were two philosophers of different habits: although both knew the foolishness of men to be infinite, and that almost all their actions proceed from ignorance rather than prudence, nevertheless, one—Heraclitus of Ephesus—always wept whenever he saw such foolishness in anyone. But the other—<term>Democritus of Abdera</term>—on the contrary, laughed, mocking the vanity of men. From which it is concluded that it is not against the constancy of a philosopher, while contemplating the misery in which those in Hell find themselves (that is, those oppressed by vices), to have compassion for them without exceeding moderation, for it is a human thing. And as the character Chremes says in Terence: *I am a man; I consider nothing human alien to me.* <note>original: "Homo sum; Nihil humani a me alienum puto." — Terence, Heauton Timorumenos</note> **LET US GO**, for the long way urges us on. If you consider the site of Hell, it is a long way, because it is from the surface of the earth to the center. But allegorically, the knowledge of vices is a long and difficult path, because they are of many types, and often some are so similar to virtues that it is difficult to discern one from the other. **THUS** he set me. When Dante—that is, sensuality—is placed in Hell by Virgil—that is, by reason—then he knows how detestable vice is and guards himself from it. But when he enters by himself, he lets himself be blinded by it and remains there like a fish on a hook.

Here, as far as could be heard,
there were no plaints, but only sighs,
which made the eternal air tremble.
This arose from grief without torments,
which the crowds had, which were very large,
of infants, and of women, and of men.
The good master to me: "You do not ask..."

<column-break/>

Dante finds himself across the river Acheron, and does not know how he crossed. But then, after he moved his rested eyes around, it seemed right to Virgil to lead him into Hell, and he says: **NOW LET US DESCEND** down here into the blind world: That is, into the contemplation of vices, in which there is nothing but blindness and the privation of the light of reason. And for this, the Psalmist prays for these people, saying: *Give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death.* <note>original: "Illumina re iis qui in tenebris: et umbra mortis sedent." — Luke 1:79 / Psalm 107:10</note> Virgil was pale and bloodless, which signifies a strike to the soul, as much from compassion as from fear. But Dante took this appearance and sign to be fear. This signifies that often our intellect turns toward a good thing, and sensuality interprets it in a worse way, until the intellect makes it learned. And for this reason, Virgil responds that the color changed in his face comes from pity, which Dante feels as fear; that is—

From the gate until the river Acheron, the poet showed there to be a place which, because it was neither entirely in Hell nor entirely out of Hell, he placed those who could be called neither entirely good nor entirely wicked. This was like a precinct and vestibule of the whole place. Now, after the river Acheron, he describes the beginning of Hell, and places the first circle; which, because it girds all the others, is called **Limbo**, by a certain similarity, since the word "limbo" in Latin properly means— <note>The word "limbo" refers to a border, hem, or edge of a garment.</note>

what spirits are these that you see;

<column-break/>

signifies a border: which cinches the entire garment. And in this he intends that just as it is higher than the others; and further from the depths: so lighter sins are punished within it. Here he therefore first places those who, within Christianity, having not had baptism, died in original sin: which deprives them of the eternal vision and glory of God. Also those: who, having lived before Christ, did not properly worship God: because they did not believe in the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—nor in the Christ to come. These, because they lived according to civil virtues <note>The "civil" or "moral" virtues were those attainable by human reason alone, such as justice and temperance, as practiced by the great philosophers of antiquity.</note>, did not deserve torments: But for the reason already stated, they do not deserve glory. But because in this place the poet shows that the souls of little ones: whom baptism has not washed of original sin; which is a debt of punishment, contracted

---

from the fault of the first father. I believe it will be pleasing to the ears of the reader to hear briefly what justice allows that innocent little children: who could not sin either by free will or intent, should be deprived of the divine vision in which our happiness consists. It being written:
> The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father: <note>original: "Quod filius non portabit iniquitatem patris" — Ezekiel 18:20.</note>
And elsewhere.
> The soul that sins, it shall die. <note>original: "Anima que peccauerit ipsa morietur" — Ezekiel 18:4.</note>
But first it is to be understood that original sin is the lack of "original justice": which it was our duty to have. Man was made upright by God. But he, by turning away from his creator, made himself weak: and infirm: and subjected himself to infinite ways of sinning. Adam was therefore created with such uprightness: that in him the lower things were subject to the higher. The formless flesh was subjected to the soul so that nothing could happen to it that would cause it to rise up against the soul. And similarly, the appetite was subject to reason. This was divine justice: because justice requires that the lower things always be under the higher; and it was called "original": because Adam had received it from God at his origin: and by origin he was to transfer it to his descendants: because they were to be as members of Adam. But after Adam rebelled against his superior, God, the order of justice required: that his own lower things should rebel against him: And so the flesh rebelled against the soul: and because of this, contrary dispositions fell upon it. Hence that which could have not died because of sin, by necessity dies. And similarly, the appetite rebelled against reason. Wherefore he who by his uprightness could have not died; and not sinned, fell into the necessity of dying and of sinning. But to avoid being long-winded, we will say as Egidio <note>Egidio Romano (Giles of Rome), a 13th-century theologian and student of Thomas Aquinas.</note> writes: that God having made man perfect and absolute with original justice. Afterwards, by his spontaneous liberality: and by a gracious gift, he granted him beyond his nature that as long as he remained without sin, he could enjoy the divine presence. Wherefore Adam, if he had preserved himself in a state of innocence, could have left us such a gift by the law of inheritance. But not preserving it, he lost it before we were born: and having lost it, he could not leave it to us. This will be better understood by this example. A man-at-arms, for having rallied the battle: and being the cause of victory, received a city from the king as a reward for his virtues. Later, becoming a traitor, for the treason committed, the king took back the city already given. This the knight's children should have had as his heirs if he had remained in the faith. Now, what injustice does the king do to them? if they do not have what was never theirs nor part of their patrimony? For which reason, since the vision of God is not according to our nature, no injustice is done to us if it is not given to us: just as if one by the grace of God had wings and could fly. This would be above human nature. Then his children would complain that they do not have wings like their father. Our soul has no faculty, once it has exited the bodily prisons, to enjoy the divine presence if it is not clean; and pure; because it is not permitted that the impure touch the pure. But was he pure; because in him there is perfect and absolute grace? Therefore the little one could not see God: Nevertheless, he is not deprived of anything of his own: because such a gift had been given to Adam beyond his nature, not for any merit of the receiver; but by the liberality of the giver. He lost it by wishing rather to please his wife than to obey God. But of what can the little child complain if he is not given what is above his nature? From which follows not the "pain of sense": But that of "loss" <note>Medieval theology distinguished between *poena sensus* (physical torment) and *poena damni* (the "pain of loss," or being denied the sight of God).</note>. Therefore the punishment of all these is the deprivation of glory: and of the hope of ever having glory. Therefore **THERE** [QVIVI]—that is, that place according to what could be imagined by hearing—had no weeping, which proceeds from the pain of punishments. He said "by hearing"; because this species of damnation is entirely placed in faith. **BUT FOR** [MA CHE] sighs: That is, if not for sighs: and it is a way of speaking rather Lombard than Florentine: because they say "this is not but for good" [non e/ ma che bene]: that is, "this is nothing if not good." **HAD NO** weeping but for sighs. That is, that place had no other weeping if not of sighs. For true weeping is where there are tears and sad voices: and it signifies grief and pain of sense: But the sigh signifies the pain of loss: and of desire for an absent thing. Whence Juvenal:
> He sighs for the mother not seen for a long time. <note>original: "Suspirat longo non uisam tempore matrem" — Juvenal, Satire XI.152.</note>
A sigh is an anguish of spirit. And he said "the air" [laura]: that is, the eternal air: because Hell, as was said above, lasts eternally: And it shows the greatness of the sighs since they were so great that they moved the air. **THIS HAPPENED** from grief without torture. It was grief of the mind: but not torture: that is, pain of sense. **OF INFANTS.** Infancy is the first age of man: which lasts until seven years. And they are called in this age
> infants, that is, non-speakers <note>original: "infantes. i. non fantes"</note>
that is, not speak—

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the first circle of Hell, Limbo. Having established that the souls here are not punished with physical torment but with the eternal longing for God, Dante now questions Virgil about whether any soul has ever been released from this place to achieve salvation.</meta>

<columns>2</columns>
<header>### INFERNO</header>

> Great grief seized my heart when I heard this,
> because people of great worth
> I knew were suspended in that Limbo.
> "Tell me, my master, tell me, my lord,"
> I began, in order to be certain
> of that faith which conquers every error:
> "Did anyone ever go out from here, either by his own merit
> or by another's, who then was blessed?"
> And he, who understood my hidden speech,

---

> replied: "I was new to this state,
> when I saw a Powerful One come here,
> crowned with a sign of victory.
> He drew out the shade of our first parent <note>Adam.</note>,
> of Abel his son, and that of Noah;
> of Moses the lawgiver, and the obedient
> Abraham the patriarch, and David the king;
> Israel <note>Jacob.</note> with his father and with his children;
> and with Rachel, for whom he did so much;
> and many others, and he made them blessed."

<column-break/>

infants; because either they do not speak, or they do not yet have ready speech. **THE GOOD MASTER**: A teacher is good when he not only teaches when asked, but also invites the student to ask questions. **GO** <note>original: *Andi*</note>: This is a Roman term, not a Florentine one, because in our language we do not use the singular of the present tense for this verb—we do not say *Ando, Andi, Anda*, but instead say *Vo, Vai, Va* <note>Modern English: I go, you go, he goes.</note>. The poet pretends here that Dante does not ask about the damnation of these souls, but that Virgil tells him without being asked. This is because original sin, which damns them, is not known to us through natural science—which begins with the intelligence found in the senses and lower reason—but through theology. Therefore, the physical senses do not aspire to inquire about this, nor does any doubt arise from them about which one might ask. **IT IS NOT ENOUGH BECAUSE THEY HAD NO BAPTISM**: He identifies two types of men who are not saved even though they lived morally: those who lived after Christ but did not receive baptism. For "Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved" <note>original: *Quicunque crediderit et baptizatus fuerit hic ſaluus erit* (Mark 16:16)</note>. And those who lived before the coming of Christ, when baptism was not yet necessary, but **DID NOT WORSHIP** God properly; that is, they did not believe in the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—nor in the Christ to come. Among these, Virgil places himself. **FOR SUCH defects**; that is, for this lack of having true faith. **AND NOT FOR ANY OTHER CRIME**: That is, not for crimes committed; we have no punishment of the senses <note>physical pain</note>, but only of the mind, because we live in desire, namely the desire for the glory of heaven. **WITHOUT HOPE**: Without hope of ever obtaining it. One who is in glory and enjoys God possesses the highest good. One who is outside of glory either has the hope of going there someday, like those in Purgatory, or is without hope. The latter are of two types: some are placed in eternal sensory pains, like those in all the other circles of Hell; others are without sensory pains, like these here. These have no torments of the senses, but of the soul. Their punishment is desire. Desire is nothing other than the longing to have present that thing which is absent, and this absence continuously torments the soul.

He treats two things in these verses. First, he shows great compassion for those men who, having lived morally and being filled with many virtues—having performed many benefits for human generations or at least for their homelands through science or military discipline—are nevertheless damned for not having the Christian or Hebrew faith. In the second place, he wants Virgil to be his witness, making him certain of what he held by faith: that Christ, with his precious blood, redeemed those who, although they practiced the right religion, had died in original sin. **TELL ME, MY MASTER, tell me, my lord**: In the first chapter, we showed why he calls Virgil master, lord, and father; there is no need to repeat it now. **WANTING TO BE certain**: Although every faithful person believes what the Holy Church proposes, every great mind nonetheless willingly seeks knowledge and the confirmation of what it believes. **OF THAT FAITH which conquers every error**: He said this to show that even if he lacked scientific knowledge, he nonetheless held the Christian faith to be most true and without error. **BY HIS OWN MERIT or by another's**: Although no one can escape sin by themselves without the help of divine grace, it is nonetheless necessary that we perform good works as much as our fragility allows. Whence Augustine said: "He who created you without you will not save you without you" <note>original: *Qui fecit te śine te non ſaluabit te ſine te*</note>. Therefore, he wishes to show here that those in Limbo left not only through the merits of Christ’s passion—without which no one is so perfect they can be saved—but also through their own merits, for both are necessary. **MY hidden speech**: Because he did not express clearly what he wanted to say.

Virgil understood that Dante desired to be certain of what he believed: namely, whether Christ drew the souls of the ancient fathers from Limbo as the Holy Church teaches. And therefore he replies: **I WAS NEW IN THIS state**: Because I had arrived here only a short time before. For Virgil died in the twenty-sixth year of the reign of Octavian Augustus, who reigned 56 years. And Christ died in the eighteenth year of the reign of Tiberius, the successor of Augustus. Therefore, Virgil had arrived in Limbo forty-eight years before Christ drew the souls of the ancient fathers from it. **A POWERFUL ONE**: That is, Christ. Note that since Virgil was not a Christian, it did not seem appropriate to Dante that he should name Christ.

->CANTO FOUR<-

> ...and I want you to know that before these,

> We did not stop our walking because he spoke,

Because he was not instructed in Christian doctrine, <note>The commentator is explaining why Virgil, a pagan, refers to Christ only as a "Powerful One" rather than by name.</note> he did not know Christ as Christ, nor as the cause of the liberation of those souls, for he did not know by what means He could do this. But he calls Him powerful because of the effect that he witnessed. Nor does this differ from the words of the prophet: *Lift up your gates, O princes; and be lifted up, eternal gates: and the King of Glory shall enter. Who is this King of Glory? The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle.* <note>original: "Attollite portas principes uestras; et eleuamini porte ethernales: et introibit rex glorie. Quis est iste rex glorie? Deus fortis et potens deus potens in prelio." A quote from Psalm 24, traditionally associated with Christ’s entry into Hell.</note>

<column-break/>

**WITH THE SIGN** of victory. Since He had been powerful in war, He deserved to have the sign of that victory, than which none was greater; for by dying He conquered our death, and by rising He restored our life, which the false Adam had taken from us; and He triumphed over the devil, the prince of this world. **HE DREW FROM US**—that is, He took from here—**THE SHADE**—that is, the soul—**OF THE FIRST** parent. That is, the father; and this was Adam, the first-formed <note>original: "protoplasto," meaning the first created human.</note>; that is, the first creation of God, from whom all men are born. **OF ABEL** his son. Adam in the Hebrew language signifies, according to the interpretations of the Bible, "witnessed" or "testimony." <note>This reflects medieval etymologies rather than modern linguistics.</note> Abel was the second son of Adam, and was a just and very religious man. He was a shepherd, and because God had commanded him and Cain, his brother and Adam’s firstborn, to make a sacrifice, Abel always sacrificed the best animals of his herds and flocks with a prompt will. And for this, he deserved to be prospered by God. Cain, a greedy man with little reverence for God, because he was devoted to agriculture, sacrificed the most barren ears of grain from his fields. And finally, moved by envy, he killed Abel, who was mourned by his parents for a hundred years in a valley that is named the Valley of Tears for this reason. Abel in Hebrew signifies mourning, fear, vanity, and misery. **NOAH** was the beginning of the second age, which lasted until Abraham; from Adam until him lasted the first. This man alone among all the men of that century was found just. And God, angered by the universal wickedness of all men and wishing to kill and extinguish them with a flood of water, commanded him—when he was already eight hundred years old—to make the ark, as the Bible states. It took one hundred years to build, and into it he entered with his three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth, with their wives, and two animals, male and female, of every species. After the flood, Noah and Shem lived in Asia, Ham in Africa, and Japheth in Europe. **MOSES** the lawgiver and the obedient one: from Abraham until Moses lasted the third age. He was born of a father and mother from the tribe of Levi in Egypt, at the time when the King of Egypt had all the males born of the Hebrew people thrown into the river. Therefore, his mother, seeing he was of excellent appearance, kept him hidden for three months. Later, not being able to hide him any longer, she put him in a vessel made of reeds, plastered with bitumen and pitch, and left it on the bank of the river. He came into the hands of Pharaoh’s daughter, and through the work of the boy’s sister, he was raised by his own mother; she adopted him, and because she had found him near the water, she called him Moses. Later, when Moses reached adulthood and saw how much affliction the Hebrew people suffered, having almost become slaves to the Egyptians, one day in vengeance for a Hebrew he killed an Egyptian and hid him in the sand. Later, hearing that the homicide was discovered, he fled in fear from the presence of Pharaoh, who was searching for him, and went to the region of Midian to a priest. By chance, finding his seven daughters, from whom other shepherds had taken the water they had drawn to water their flocks, he defended them and helped them water the animals. For this merit, he had one of these for his wife, named Zipporah. And while pasturing his father-in-law’s herds, he arrived at Mount Horeb, where God appeared to him in the form of a flame; and by Him, he was instructed on the path he must take to liberate the people of Israel from the hands of Pharaoh. It would be very long to recount his innumerable and egregious virtues, for which he deserved to see God face to face, not only on Horeb but also on Sinai. He was a man most admirable in doctrine, military discipline, and holiness of life. Finally, he died on Mount Nebo after God had shown him the Promised Land. He lived one hundred and twenty years, and it was in the times when Cecrops reigned in Athens. **LAWGIVER** and obedient: Lawgiver because God gave the laws to the Hebrew people through his hands. **OBEDIENT**: because he observed the divine precepts so much that no danger or toil ever turned him from them. Let no one complain if I run through these histories very briefly, because one cannot otherwise put many things in a small space. **ABRAHAM** the patriarch. That is, the first of the fathers. He was the first faithful elder to whom God revealed the Trinity. From the year of the flood until Abraham was born was one thousand and seventy-two years. His origin was from Shem, son of Noah. For from Shem was born Arphaxad; from him Cainan; and from Cainan, Shelah; from Shelah, Eber; from Eber, Peleg; from Peleg, Reu; from Reu, Serug; from Serug, Nahor; from Nahor, Terah; from Terah, Abram. He was born in the land of Chaldea at the time when Ninus, son of Belus, reigned. And by God’s command, he came to live in Canaan; and God promised him that He would give 그 region to his seed, which is from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates; and his seed would multiply so much that whoever could count the dust of the earth would count them. He lived, therefore, in the valley of Mamre. In the tenth year after coming to Canaan, seeing that Sarah was sterile, she comforted Abram that he should have seed from her handmaid Hagar, who, seeing herself pregnant, began to grow proud against Sarah; and being afflicted by her, she fled. But through the words of the angel, she returned and bore Ishmael to Abram. Later, when he was already one hundred years old, God told him that he would have a son by Sarah, who was ninety years old. And He commanded him the circumcision of all males, and that he should no longer be called Abram, but Abraham; and similarly his wife Sarah, and not Sarai. Abraham laughed to himself that at one hundred years old he should generate. But later, when the son of Sarah was born, he called him...

# INFERNO

Isaac. Abraham circumcised himself and his son Ishmael when he was ninety-nine years old and his son was thirteen; and likewise all his others. Afterward, when Isaac was born, he circumcised him on the eighth day. This is the one whom he was content to sacrifice to obey God. For this reason, he merited that God should bless his seed. After the death <margin>Note</margin> of Sarah, he took another wife, Keturah, and with her fathered more sons. He lived one hundred and seventy-five years. **Abram** signifies "exalted father"; but **Abraham** means "father seeing the people" or "father of a multitude." **Isaac** means "laughter." **Ishmael** means "man heard by God" or "one who receives the hearing of God." **Sarah** signifies "princess," or "coal," or "veil," or "anguish." **Sarai** means "my princess" or "my coal." **DAVID** signifies "strong of hand" or "desirable of face." This man was the second king of the people of God. He reigned forty years. He was a prophet and a poet, as appears in his Psalms. He reigned at the time when the Athenians, after the death of Codrus, no longer lived under kings. This was in the fifth age <note>The "Fifth Age" of the world, in medieval historiography, spans from the Babylonian Captivity (or sometimes the reign of David) until the birth of Christ.</note> which lasted until Christ. I will not dwell on his history, for it would be too long; but what kind of man he was, God showed by saying He had found a man after His own heart. **ISRAEL** with the father and with his offspring. **Israel** was Jacob, so named because, while going into Mesopotamia, he saw a ladder reaching from earth to heaven, with angels ascending and descending upon it, and God leaning against it. For **Israel** signifies "man seeing God" or "vision of God." Therefore, He drew out Jacob with his father, who was Isaac, the son of Abraham, who lived one hundred and sixty years and died during the reign of Xerxes, the first king of the Assyrians. <note>original: "Xerxe primo re de glassirii" - Medieval chronologies often conflated or synchronized biblical history with legendary accounts of the Assyrian and Persian empires.</note> **AND WITH HIS OFFSPRING**: that is, with his children, who were twelve; and from these descended the twelve tribes of Israel. By Leah, he had Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah. And from the handmaid of Rachel, he fathered Dan and Naphtali. And from Zilpah, the handmaid of Leah, he fathered Gad and Asher. Afterward, Leah conceived by him a fifth son, who was Issachar, and a sixth, Zebulun. And by Rachel, he had Joseph and Benjamin. **AND RACHEL FOR WHOM HE DID SO MUCH.** She was the sister of Laban, the brother of Rebecca, Jacob’s mother, and she lived in Mesopotamia. Jacob went to him, and having been received as a kinsman, he promised to serve him for seven years guarding his flocks if he would give him his younger daughter Rachel as his wife, who was very beautiful. But when the time was finished, Laban deceived him and placed his elder daughter Leah at his side on the first night of the wedding; she was not as beautiful as Rachel and was bleary-eyed. Afterward, in the morning, having discovered the deception, Jacob agreed to serve another seven years, and Laban gave him Rachel. And therefore the poet said **FOR WHOM**: that is, for which Rachel, **HE DID SO MUCH**: that is, he labored so much, serving fourteen years to have her. **THEY DID NOT CEASE** to walk because he spoke: Because he places two types of souls in this Limbo. One type consists of those who, although they were illustrious for many virtues, are nonetheless damned for not having received baptism. The first ones, who have done nothing worthy <note>Likely referring to infants who died before they could perform virtuous or sinful acts.</note>, he wishes to be like a forest. A forest is an uncultivated place, shadowy and without sun; it has thick trees and lacks any sweet fruit; it is inhabited by wild beasts and not by men. Likewise, these souls are not cultivated by any doctrine, because in life they did not have the time or space to comprehend. For this reason, they remain shadowy and obscure, since no doctrine shines within them, nor the sun of any truth. The forest being very thick and full of trees denotes the infinite crowd of such souls.

> Our way was not yet long 
> on this side of the summit, when I saw a fire 
> that conquered a hemisphere of shadows.
> We were still a little distance away,
> but not so far that I could not discern in part
> that honorable people possessed that place.
> "O thou who honorest every science and art,
> who are these who have such great renown
> that it sets them apart from the manner of the others?"

<column-break/>

We have seen that this first circle contains two generations: namely, the little unbaptized children, and those who lived before baptism and who, through doctrine, or deeds of arms, and other civil virtues, acquired great fame in the world. But the first group he places in the first part of the circle in the form of a forest. The second group he places separately in the second part, in a luminous and high place. Of the first, he speaks according to Christian doctrine. Of the second, he invents as a poet, but not without reason. For while it is reasonable that their many great virtues were not enough to save them—since they did not have baptism, nor did they duly worship God—nevertheless, they ought to have

---

some advantage and prerogative over those who lived wickedly; especially since the Truth says that no good deed shall go unrewarded. And for this reason, he attributes to them a pleasant and joyful place, and almost describes the Elysian Fields, striving to imitate Virgil in this, as far as our religion allows. **OUR WAY WAS NOT YET LONG**: that is, we had not moved very far on this side of the summit—that is, from the top from which one descends into the first circle. Some texts say "sleep" (*somno*); then we would say "on this side of the sleep," that is, on this side of the place where I was placed while sleeping, which was the bank of the Acheron. **A HEMISPHERE OF SHADOWS IT CONQUERED.** A round body like a ball is called a sphere. Hence, "hemisphere" signifies half a sphere. And by this, he denotes that the fire illuminated from the middle of the circle upward. **WE WERE STILL A LITTLE DISTANCE AWAY: BUT NOT SO FAR THAT I COULD NOT DISCERN IN PART THAT HONORABLE PEOPLE POSSESSED THAT PLACE.** Although the intellect is what knows doctrines and discerns them, nevertheless, Dante—that is, the lower reason—even if he does not fully discern them yet, still discerns that men of letters are worthy of honor, especially when he sees them honored by others. **O THOU WHO HONOREST EVERY SCIENCE AND ART.** Certainly every doctrine is honored by its own nature; but when it is adorned with poetic eloquence, it is much more honored. It is, therefore, the proper praise of such a poet and such poems.

### CANTO FOUR.

...of which they are most full of every kind of doctrine. And it can rightly be said of him that, just as gold adorns the gem set within it, so he makes more illustrious every science of which he treats. And allegorically, there is no doubt that the human intellect, when it is filled with great and varied doctrine, is not only honored by it, but that doctrine itself, in his mouth and in his writings, becomes more worthy of admiration. **THESE** are those who have such honor <note>original: "chotanth'onoranza"</note>, that is, "honor"; he used a syncope <term>syncope: a grammatical shortening of a word</term> for the sake of the meter. Dante recognized the honor in these men, but he did not know the science from which such honor came to them. Therefore, he asks Virgil about it, because, as I have said, the intellect alone is that which can give true judgment of it.

And he to me: “The honored renown
that sounds of them up in your life
acquires grace in heaven that advances them.”
Meanwhile, a voice was heard by me:
“Honor the highest poet;
his shadow returns, which had departed.”
After the voice had ceased and was quiet,
I saw four great shadows coming to us;
they had an appearance neither sad nor joyful.
The good master began to say:
“Look at him with that sword in hand,
who comes before the three as if he were their lord.
That is Homer, the sovereign poet;
the next is Horace the satirist who comes;
Ovid is the third, and the last is Lucan.”
Because each agrees with me
in the name that the single voice cried,
they do me honor, and in that they do well.
Thus I saw the beautiful school assemble
of those lords of the highest song,
who fly above the others like an eagle.

<column-break/>

It seems a just thing that, having raised themselves from the earth with singular virtues in this life, they should also have a place with some honor and dignity in the other life, even if they are not saved. **GRACE ACQUIRES** in heaven. Virtue pleases God even in those who did not worship Him duly. Thus, as Augustine says, the Gentiles received many benefits from God as a reward for their virtues. For that virtuous life moves God to want them to be in a better state. He then feigns having heard a voice that comforted those spirits to honor Virgil, who a little while before had departed to the rescue of Dante. And he suggests that four poets went to meet him, similar to the honors men pay one another in this life. And he shows the aspect of these poets to have been neither sad nor joyful; truly because their state was not sorrowful, as they were not in physical pain; nor joyful, because they were not in glory; truly because the habit of the wise man always remains in a fitting middle ground <term>mediocrita: the Aristotelian "golden mean," a state of emotional balance</term>, neither easily gladdened nor basely saddened. He places Homer with a sword in hand because he was the first poet among the Greeks who can truly be said to have written of battles. Wherefore Horace says: "What deeds of kings and captains, and what dismal wars / could be written in this meter, Homer showed" <note>original Latin: "Res gestas regumque ducumque : et tristia bella . Quo scribi possent numero monstravit Homerus."</note>. The father of Homer was Maion, and his mother was Ornithone; others affirm that a daughter of Melanopus named

Critheis bore Homer, not knowing who the father was, and gave birth to him in Smyrna near the river Meles; and for this reason, he called him Melesigenes. She raised him in extreme poverty. Later, because of his admirable talent, he was adopted by a master of grammar. Having become an adult and learned, he went searching through most of the cities of Greece, and finally, in Colophon, he became blind; and for this reason, he was called Homer, because the Colophonians call the blind "homeroi." He returned then to Smyrna and there practiced the poetic art, in which he was so excellent that until now no one has surpassed him; nor has he been equaled by anyone except Virgil. He was forced by poverty to go about singing his verses for a price. And in the region of Phocis, he made a pact with a certain Thestorides that, if he would provide him with food and clothing, he would attribute to him all the verses he made. But after some time, Thestorides went to the island of Chios and there recited Homer's verses as his own. Finally, wanting to go from Samos to Athens, a riddle <note>original: "enigma . i. un decto obscuro"</note> was proposed to him which, being unable to solve, he died of grief. The riddle was that, Homer asking, "O men of Arcadia, have we caught anything?" they replied, "Those that we have caught, we leave behind; and those that we have not caught, we bring with us." Homer understood this to mean fish, and therefore did not know how to solve it; but they meant the lice they had on them. But in truth, this death seems unsuitable for such a great man. Therefore, I rather agree with Herodotus, who writes that he died oppressed by extreme old age. Nor is it very clear which was his homeland, for some say Smyrna, others Colophon, others Chios, others Athens. Similarly, there is controversy among writers as to what time he was born: Herodotus wants it to be one hundred and forty years after the destruction of Troy; Eratosthenes says one hundred; Philochorus one hundred and eighty; Apollodorus of Athens two hundred and forty. **HORACE** Flaccus, satiric and lyric poet, was born in Venusia on the eighth day of December in the third year of the 178th Olympiad. His father was a herald and a freedman <note>original: "libertino . i. nato d'huomo gia stato schiavo"</note>, that is, born of a man who had once been a slave. He was cleaner and purer in satire than Lucilius, very free in rebuking, and in lyric verses almost alone among the Latins. **OVID** was born in Sulmona <note>OCR reads "Sermona"</note> in the third year of the 186th Olympiad, a man so suited to every...

> After they had talked together for a while,
> they turned to me with a greeting gesture,
> and my master smiled at this;
> And they did me even greater honor,
> for they made me one of their company,
> so that I was the sixth among such wisdom.
> Thus we went on as far as the light,
> speaking of things which are beautiful to keep silent,
> just as it was beautiful to speak of them there.
> We came to the foot of a noble castle,
> seven times encircled by high walls,
> defended all around by a small stream.

<column-break/>

...genre of poem; and of such genius that if he had not shunned the labor of refining his work, he would have been inferior to no one. He died on the island of Pontus where he had been exiled by Octavian <note>Augustus Caesar</note>. Marcus Annaeus Lucan was the nephew of Seneca the philosopher, born to his son Marcus Annaeus Mela. He was from Cordoba, a city in Spain; he was similar to his grandfather in life and customs, and such a lover of liberty that he became one of the conspirators with Piso against Nero. Having been condemned to death for this, he had his veins cut; he died on the last day of April in the twenty-seventh year of his life, in the third year of the two hundred and tenth Olympiad, and in the sixty-fifth year of Christ. He wrote the *Saturnalia*, ten books of the *Silvae*, *Medea*, *Orpheus*, and the *Pharsalia* <note>An epic poem about the Roman civil wars</note>, where the civil wars between Caesar and Pompey are recorded. The order in which the author places these three Latin poets—giving the first place to Horace, the second to Ovid, and the third to Lucan—can be debated for and against. Various are the judgments. Nor does it please me that some cast these four poets as representing the four moral virtues. **EACH ONE** <note>original: "CIASCHVN"</note> agrees with me in the name. That is, each one is a poet. **THEY DO ME** honor; and in this they do well. This denotes that those who share the same doctrine or art should always honor and favor one another, although envy most often produces the opposite effect. **SCHOOL** <note>original: "SCOLA"</note> in Greek <note>original: "schole"</note> signifies "leisure"; it is used for disputations where, in leisure and having set aside all other business, men exercise their intellect in some liberal doctrine. Likewise, it is used for the place where one exercises. **HIGHEST** song; he calls poetry "highest" because, in the best and most ornate song of verses, it embraces all doctrines, and especially theology. For the first poets were theologians, as appears not only in Orpheus, Musaeus, and Linus, but in David and Job, and in many others, as we wrote more extensively in the preface to this book. **WHO ABOVE** the others flies like an eagle; the eagle has such strength that it gazes at the rays of the sun without being dazzled. Thus, poetic fury transcends even to divinity, as Plato demonstrates when he writes of the four species of divine furies.

The greeting that the poets give to Dante, and the act of making him the sixth among them, signifies nothing other than that he became a poet by being drawn by the beauty and the doctrine of their works, and by having imitated them. Nor is it without reason that they spoke of "things which are beautiful to keep silent," just as it was beautiful to speak of them in that place. For it is reasonable that there was talk among them of things pertaining to their doctrine, which was appropriate there; however, in the present work, it would not be appropriate. Here it should be noted that it is not enough to talk of beautiful things, but they must also be suited to the time, the place, and the subject matter being treated. Furthermore, he shows that they inhabited a "high castle" because they are placed in high fame and renown, which is impregnable; for nothing harms true fame. Therefore, just as high walls defend the castle, so the doctrine and eloquence of poets preserve their immortal fame. Whence Ovid said of himself: "And now I have completed a work which neither the wrath of Jove, nor fire, nor sword, nor consuming age will be able to destroy" <note>original: "Iamque opus exegi quod nec iouis ira nec ignis: Nec poterit ferrum nec edax abolere uetustas"</note>. And a little further on: "I shall be borne up eternally above the high stars, and my name shall be indelible" <note>original: "Super alta perenni astra ferar nomenque erit indelebile nostrum"</note>. And certainly, as the shadow follows the body, so fame follows virtue. Whence Horace: "He will live for a long age, known for the fatherly spirit toward his brothers. Surviving fame will carry him on a wing that fears to be loosened" <note>original: "Viuet extento procu eius euo Notus in fratres animi paterni. Illum aget penna metuente solui fama superstes"</note>. By the walls that defend the castle, understand the virtues and the doctrines, which are those things that defend fame. These are seven: three moral—Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance—which purge the soul of every perturbation and make it fit to receive doctrines; one active, which is Prudence, which directs and regulates the operations of the moral virtues; and three speculative—Intelligence, Science, and Wisdom. Furthermore, he uses the number seven for the perfection of the virtues. For according to the philosophers, this is a perfect number. But it would be too long to report all the arguments with which the Pythagoreans and Platonists prove this. Then they use nature as a witness, which, being most wise, uses the sevenfold number in many things because it is perfect. With this number, they consider the Soul of the World to be generated. Seven are the wandering stars, which we call "planets" with a Greek word, though we say *pianeti*. The moon moves according to the sevenfold number. For in four times seven days, which is twenty-eight, and eight hours, it returns to that same place in the sky from which it departed from the sun. In the seventh month, the child in a woman's womb is mature. Similarly, human life is divided into seven-year periods, as I demonstrated in the first Canto. I leave behind infinite other things worthy of being heard, but they are too lengthy for such a multitude. Some say he placed seven walls for the seven liberal arts, from which all true fame proceeds. For the "small stream," some suggest the abundance of earthly things, without which it is difficult to acquire doctrine. But I believe it is a more learned exposition and better fits to take the small stream as that kind of river which the Latins call a "torrent." Whence Petrarch said: "In this alpine and rapid torrent..."

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's *Inferno*, Canto IV. Following the introduction of the great classical poets, the author now interprets the symbolic "little stream" surrounding the Noble Castle and describes the appearance of the illustrious souls residing within the meadow of Limbo.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>CANTO FOUR.</header>

Every small stream is therefore a torrent: which descends from the mountains and flows into larger rivers; it is called a "torrent" because in the summer it *torret* <note>Latin: "scorches" or dries up</note>, that is, it dries out. But by the rains, it grows and runs with great force. From this abundance and vehemence, the Latins call a forceful style and the abundance of eloquence a "torrent." Thus, Juvenal says: *Sermo promptus et isseo torrentior* <note>original Latin: "A speech ready and more torrential than Isaeus."</note>. Therefore, our poet, not wishing to say "ditch"—which is what it is called in the Florentine language—said "little stream." Furthermore, in Latin, when they wish to demonstrate a great abundance of speech, they often say *Flumen dicendi* <note>original Latin: "A river of speaking."</note>. We shall therefore take the stream to represent the facility and eloquence of writers, who truly defend fame. Indeed, the noble deeds of excellent men would fall into oblivion if the eloquence of writers did not make them eternal, as Sallust demonstrates regarding the Athenians. Petrarch also said: "My Pandolfo, these works are fragile in the long run; but our style is what makes men immortal through fame." And that the river represents eloquence is noted by Petrarch when he speaks of the "admirable thing" of one "who makes a river be born from Helicon" <note>The mountain sacred to the Muses in Greek mythology</note>. We could also take the river to represent the movement of the soul toward learning, which is nothing other than the appetite for it.

**This we passed as if on hard ground**
**through seven gates I entered with these sages;**
**we came to a meadow of fresh greenery:**
**People were there with slow and grave eyes,**
**of great authority in their countenances,**
**they spoke rarely, with sweet voices:**
**We drew aside thus to one of the corners**
**into an open, luminous, and high place**
**so that every one of them could be seen.**
**Right there, upon the green enamel,**
**were shown to me the great spirits,**
**that seeing them exalts me within myself.**

<column-break/>

¶ **THIS we passed as if on hard ground**, that is, without getting wet; it shows that although he equates eloquence to a river, it is nonetheless stable and durable. Or, if you take the river to be "appetite," it shows that appetite to be firm and constant. **THROUGH SEVEN gates**: because there were seven walls. And they entered through the gates in the best way, because in every virtue and every doctrine one must enter through the gate: that is, by its principles and with a certain order. For there are many who pervert the order of learning and wish to learn the final things before the first. From this is born the proverb that he who wants to learn well should "enter through the gate." This signifies that we must begin at the beginning and not at the end. **WE CAME to a meadow of fresh greenery.** He places them in a meadow because such a place, with its various flowers and herbs, is

delightful. And we say that stable fame is "always green." He also imitates Virgil, who says: *Devenere locos letos: et amena vireta* <note>original Latin: "They came to joyful places and pleasant green spaces."</note>. And a little further down: *Pars in gramineis exercet membra palestris* <note>original Latin: "Some exercise their limbs on the grassy wrestling grounds."</note>. The meadow stays always green and produces its fruit without being cultivated. Whence the word "meadow" (*prato*) is said to be almost "prepared" (*parato*). For fields of grain and vineyards are not "prepared" to produce the utility expected from them without some cultivation; but only the meadow produces by itself. Thus fame, which is born from true virtue, always stays green and produces praise by itself. Afterward, he shows that he noticed by their manners and gestures that they were people of authority, noting that it rarely happens that gestures and outward appearance do not show a man's quality. Especially the eyes are like windows through which we see the soul placed inside the body. **SLOW and grave**: He did not mean they were "slow" because their wit was slow (which the Greeks call *brady* <note>original Greek: βραδύς</note> and the Latins *bardus*, meaning dull or stupid). Rather, they were "slow," meaning weighed and deliberate. For just as a foolish lightness and frequent, groundless changeability are easily recognized in the eyes, so, on the contrary, maturity and gravity appear there. Therefore, they were not "slow" like certain dull, stupid, or dreaming people, but like the "grave," deliberate, and steady men we see. Their eyes were slow and grave because in investigation, the eye—that is, the intellect—must not run and judge before it knows. Instead, it is necessary that with the passage of time, one considers minutely and without lightness, and with gravity examines every part, both pro and con, if one wishes to find the truth. **AUTHORITY**: we call that by which reputation and estimation increase in a man, which is the reason why we often believe people even though no reason is shown to us. **COUNTENANCES**: almost like gestures and acts, or more expressly, their outward demonstration. It is a French word, for they say *assembler*, to resemble; and it comes from the word "example." Whence we say someone shows goodness in their "countenances." **SPOKE RARELY**: which signifies maturity and wisdom. For as it is written: *In multiloquio non deest peccatum* <note>original Latin: "In much speaking, sin is not lacking."</note>. **WITH sweet VOICES**: which signifies humanity and affability. He included this so that it would not be believed that their rare speaking proceeded from pride or austerity. Therefore, by rare speaking, he shows gravity and modesty; and by sweet voices, he denotes humanity and pleasantness. Certainly, it is perfect praise in a man when we see in him the highest gravity joined with the highest pleasantness. **WE DREW ASIDE thus to one of the corners**: for so does he who wishes to see better. And he imitates Virgil, who said: *Et tumulum capit unde omnis longo ordine possit Adversos legere: et venientum discere vultus* <note>original Latin: "And he takes a hill from which he can scan the whole long array and recognize the faces of those approaching."</note>. Hidden within this is the meaning that he who wishes to know and speculate draws aside to a "corner," that is, into solitude; for the crowd and frequency of people are enemies to speculation. And then he adds: **IN AN OPEN, luminous, and high PLACE**. For just as he who wishes to see with bodily eyes seeks an open place—that is, one not occupied by trees, mountains, or obstacles that take away the view—and one that is...

**H**e places first in this contemplation of his the men who were excellent in the active and civil life. Afterward, those who were illustrious in the contemplative life. This is not because he prefers the active life; rather, it is because, in considering the nature of man as a human being, action (which deals with particulars) occurs before contemplation (which consists of universals). **ELECTRA** was the daughter of Atlas. Atlas had seven daughters: Electra, Maia, Sterope, Taygete, Alcyone, and Merope <note>The Pleiades of Greek mythology</note>. Electra was the wife of Corythus, a king in Italy, after whom his principal city was named Corythus. Many believe this was the city today called Corneto <note>Modern-day Tarquinia</note>. Electra, therefore, was not 

---

the wife of the husband, but of Jove, and she gave birth to Dardanus. After the death of Corythus, Dardanus came into conflict with Iasius, his brother by the same mother and the son of Corythus. He decided to leave Iasius alone in the kingdom and sailed with part of the people to Samothrace, and later to Phrygia, where Troy was later built; from him, the Trojans had their origin. This was in the thirty-fifth year of Moses, and in the year of the world 3737. **WITH MANY** companions: as if to say, either of the people who followed Dardanus, or rather of many kings who were excellent in the lineage of Dardanus. But because these were less famous, he shows he did not fully recognize them as he did Hector and Aeneas, because these two were most excellent. Hector was the son of Priam and of such virtue that he was almost the sole reason Troy defended itself for ten years. After many most excellent trials, according to Homer and the other writers who follow Homer, he was killed by Achilles. But Dio Chrysostom <note>A Greek philosopher and orator (c. 40–120 AD)</note>, a supreme philosopher and diligent investigator of antiquity, demonstrates—both through Egyptian histories and many signs—that it was not Achilles who killed Hector, but Hector who killed Achilles. And he claims Troy was not destroyed by the Greeks, but that the Greeks were broken and largely consumed by the Trojans. Regarding Aeneas, we spoke above. **CAESAR**: He places Caesar among the Trojans not without merit, because he was of the Julian family, who descended from Iulus Ascanius, the son of Aeneas. He mentions the Trojans and the Romans descended from them because the Roman Empire was founded by such successors, which the poet exalts in many places. Gaius Julius Caesar was the one who waged civil wars against the great Pompey, his son-in-law. Eventually, he obtained victory and became perpetual dictator. He was a man who, without fail, was so admirable for his innumerable virtues that if he had not clouded them with ambition and the desire to rule over mortal peoples, he could have held the highest rank. I do not know who could be placed before him in military discipline. For in ten years, he subjugated innumerable and most warlike peoples of all France, Germany, and England. He conquered Spain, Africa, and a large part of the eastern regions. In fifty judged battles, he was superior, and in his skirmishes, one million one hundred and ninety-two thousand men were killed. Besides his expertise in deeds of arms, he was a man of much and varied learning, and the first among the Latins who, through astronomical reasoning, reduced the year without error to the number of days it has at present. He was adorned with such eloquence that, although he had cursively noted the wars he fought in his commentaries to leave a memory for those who wished to write history, they are nonetheless so adorned and so eloquent that no one ever hoped, even with accurate and diligent leisure, to write a history that could equal them. He was of such fast intellect and such counsel and memory that at one and the same time he would read, dictate, and give audience. He could dictate four letters at once, even if they were of great importance; and if not attending to anything else, he could dictate seven. He was adorned with all civil customs. But most of all, an excellent humanity and affability were known in him. No one was ever more liberal toward friends. No one was more clement in forgiving every injury. For all these things, it is the opinion of many that if he had not been killed so soon, he would have restored liberty to the Republic. Finally, excellent men and lovers of the Republic conspired against Caesar as against a tyrant, and he was killed in the Senate. The leaders of the conspiracy were Brutus and Cassius. **WITH** hawkish eyes <note>original: "occhi grifagni"</note>: that is, bright and sparkling. This signifies a sharp and vehement intellect, and he attributes such eyes to Julius Caesar, just as Virgil gives to Caesar Augustus where he says, *From whose joyful temples a double flame pours forth* <note>original Latin: "Geminas cui tempora flammas leta uomunt"</note>. He said *grifagni* <term>Hawkish; from "griffon"</term> because hawks that have molted in the wild have such eyes. Bird-catchers call hawks *nidiaci* <term>nestlings</term>, *raminghi* <term>branchers</term>, and *grifagni* <term>hagards</term>. *Nidiaci* are those taken in the nest. *Raminghi* are those that, having recently left the nest, do not yet fly much but rest a lot on the branches of trees. *Grifagni* are those that, having already passed a year, have molted in the wild. He therefore said "armed in intellect"
