of military virtue: **He said with eyes like a griffin** <note>original: "occhi gryphagni"</note> as a sign of the vivacity of his intellect and his learning.
**CAMILLA:** We spoke of her above. **AND PENTHESILEA.** Near the river Thermodon <note>A river in modern-day Turkey associated with the Amazons</note> there was a generation of women who lived with such industry, and frankness of spirit and body in military discipline, that they held empire over many regions. They reduced their men under their power and, from childhood, so debilitated their legs and arms that they remained without strength. Because of this, the men performed feminine duties and the women performed masculine ones. To better use the bow, they would burn off the right breast <note>original: "poppa dextra"</note> when they were small so that it would not grow. Hence they were called **Amazons**, which in the Greek language means "without a breast" <note>original: "sanza poppa"</note>. They founded a most noble city at the mouth of the Thermodon, and in the process of time, they extended their empire as far as the Tanais <note>The Don River</note> and on the other side as far as Syria. But finally, defeated by Hercules, they were nearly reduced to total extermination. He took Hippolyta, their queen, and gave her as a wife to Theseus, King of Athens. But after a few years, Penthesilea, having been exiled because she had killed her sister, came to the aid of the Trojans and performed marvelous feats in that war. But finally, she was killed by Achilles. **LATINUS.** Saturn, the most ancient king of Candia (now called Crete), having been driven out by his sons, came to Italy. By Janus, who then reigned in the parts where Rome was later built, the kingdom was shared with him. From Saturn was born Picus; from Picus, Faunus; and from Faunus, Latinus. He was reigning when Aeneas came to Italy and, moved by the oracles of his father and by various omens, he betrothed his daughter Lavinia to Aeneas, whom he had previously promised to Turnus, King of the Rutulians. This was the cause of the wars between Aeneas and Turnus. And he said **HE SAT** <note>original: "SEDEA"</note> to show that his fame arose more from the maturity of his counsel than from the ferocity of arms, as is seen in Virgil. **I SAW THAT** Brutus who drove out Tarquin. The first Tarquin was the fifth king of the Romans, son of Demaratus of Corinth. He was born in Tarquinia, a city of Italy from which he took his name. Later, persuaded by his wife Tanaquil—a woman very skilled in auguries by which she predicted future things—he came to Rome. He held such authority under Ancus, King of the Romans, that upon his death, the king left him as guardian of his children. But through ambition, he used such artifice that he was made king. His son later succeeded not him, but his son-in-law Servius Tullius; and because of his arrogance and cruelty, he was called Tarquin the Proud <note>original: "Tarquino superbo"</note>. In the times when this king was in the field at Ardea, a city of the Rutulians, an altercation arose between Sextus Tarquinius, the king's son, and Collatinus, regarding who had the most virtuous wife. Finally, it was judged that Lucretia, the wife of Collatinus, was the unique example of chastity among Roman women. This was so troublesome to Sextus that he secretly left the camp and came by night to Lucretia; he was liberally received by her as a kinsman. Then, wishing to take her chastity, he threatened her that if she did not consent, he would kill her and one of her servants, and then say he had found her in adultery with him. Lucretia yielded with her body, but not with her mind, to flee everlasting infamy. But the next day she summoned her father, Spurius Lucretius, and her husband. The former brought with him Publius Valerius, and the latter, Lucius Junius Brutus. Lucretia told the whole story. And although she was consoled by them, and they demonstrated to her that where the will had not consented there could be no sin, she nonetheless killed herself with a knife she had hidden under her robe for this purpose. She said first that she did not wish any Roman woman to take a captive example <note>i.e., a bad precedent</note> from her. Lucius Junius was, as we said, present at such a death. Until that time, to escape the cruelty of Tarquin—who either killed or sent into exile anyone of notable prudence—he had feigned being a fool and lived almost like a **brute animal** <note>A pun on his name, Brutus</note>; for this reason, he was called Lucius Junius Brutus. Showing the bloody knife of Lucretia’s death, he summoned the Roman people and, with a long oration demonstrating the cruelty and pride of Tarquin and his sons, persuaded them that they should be sent into exile and deprived of the kingdom. In this way, the monarchy ended in Rome, which had lasted two hundred and forty-four years. Brutus was the son of a sister of Tarquin, a man such a lover of liberty that, having been made consul, he put his own sons to death because, together with their cousins the Aquilii, they had conspired to restore the kingdom to the Tarquins. From him derives the House of Brutus, from which came that other Brutus who, to free his country from the tyrant, killed Caesar. The first killed the last king; the second killed the first tyrant. We have, with the greatest brevity, traversed the history of Tarquin, Brutus, and Lucretia. Now we shall speak of Marcia and Cornelia. Marcia is ennobled both for her chastity and for the excellence of her husband; she was the wife of Cato of Utica <note>Cato the Younger</note> and bore him two sons. Afterward, it appearing to Cato that those children were enough, and seeing that his great friend Hortensius was without children, he divorced her and married her to Hortensius; he himself lived a celibate and chaste life. Nonetheless, when Hortensius died, moved by compassion for her, he took her back. Julia was the daughter of Caesar and wife of Pompey; she loved her husband so much that, when her husband’s robe was brought home stained with blood that had come from his nose, and remembering the civil discords, she felt such grief, fearing he had been killed, that she fainted and suffered a miscarriage; shortly after, she died, not without universal mourning. Because she was of such virtue, there was a constant opinion that if she had lived, she would have been such a bond between Pompey and Caesar that the civil wars would not have followed. **CORNIGLIA**, that is, Cornelia, was the daughter of Scipio Africanus the Elder and wife of Gracchus. She was a woman of prudence and masculine spirit; for this reason, she was so loved by her husband that, when two serpents appeared in their house and the soothsayers replied that it was necessary for one of them to be killed—and if the male were killed, Gracchus would die, and if the female were killed, Cornelia would die—Gracchus willed that the male should be killed, judging that for his family it was more useful...

When she was asked at times by other women to show them her jewels, she would show her sons, adorned with every good character and eloquence, and she would say these were her jewels. After she became a widow, she was sought in marriage by many princes and kings, but she always observed a most chaste widowhood.

**Saladin** was the Sultan of Babylon <note>In the Middle Ages, Cairo was often referred to as "Babylon of Egypt."</note>. He acquired power through wickedness and cruelty by killing the Caliph, his lord; this was in the year of Christ 1163. Later, in 1187, he dealt a great defeat to the Christians and took Jerusalem, which the Christians had held with great glory for eighty-eight years after Godfrey <note>Godfrey of Bouillon, leader of the First Crusade.</note>. Finally, after a long persecution and slaughter of Christians, he died in Damascus in the year 1194, a man excellent in military discipline. Not without reason did Dante say **AND ALONE** <note>original: "ET SOLO"</note> in his own place I saw Saladin: to denote that few of that nation have been so excellent. In the time of Saladin, there was a passage of Christians to recover Jerusalem, which Saladin had occupied. For this reason, he took counsel to observe and spy upon all the states and forces of the Christians. With two of his closest friends and three servants, disguised in the habit of a merchant, he passed into Armenia, and from there into Greece, and then into Sicily, considering everything with diligence. From Sicily he passed to Naples, and from Naples to Rome. Having understood the government of the Church, he passed through Tuscany and Lombardy and crossed the Alps. He traveled through Gaul, through Spain, and Germany. Finally, like a new Ulysses made prudent by having seen many countries and various customs of men, he returned by sea to Alexandria.

<column-break/>

The poet had already recounted some of those who acquired fame in civil and active life. Now he places those who are situated in a more exalted degree, because they are made noble in the intellectual virtues and in the contemplative life, which without doubt is preferred over the active life. This is what he signifies by saying **I RAISED my eyelids a little higher**: because to know who is in a higher place, it is necessary to raise the eyes more. Among these, he gives the first place to **Aristotle**, a man without doubt of marvelous intellect and profound doctrine, and one who holds the palm for having placed all of philosophy in perfect order and for having treated all its parts with excellent distinction. For this reason, the poet places him before Plato, moved not only by this, but perhaps also by his own profession, because he was a **Peripatetic** <term>A follower of Aristotle, so named because Aristotle taught while walking (from the Greek "peripatos").</term>. I would not dare here to give my judgment on two such great men; nor could I if I wished, prohibited by the weakness of my intellect and the defect of learning that is in me. But I see that among the Greeks, Aristotle is held in the highest 

admiration in physical doctrines. And Plato is judged superior in metaphysical and divine matters. Hence they call Aristotle a "demon" <note>In the classical sense of a powerful spirit or genius.</note> and Plato "divine." And certainly all the ancient Latins, who did not separate eloquence from doctrine, hold that the prince of philosophers is Plato. Nor has Aristotle incurred small hatred from these for having condemned Plato in many places; so much so that even a good part of the commentators of Aristotle defend Plato where Aristotle condemns him. Cicero calls him the "Homer of philosophers." And Augustine says he chose the Platonists as those who best understood divinity; and elsewhere he writes, "Let Aristotle be silent, who compared to Plato is always a child." And our Petrarch prefers him, saying: *I turned to my right hand and saw Plato, who in that troop went closest to the mark to which he reaches who is given from heaven. Aristotle then, full of high intellect.* Aristotle was from the city of Stagyra. He was the son of Nicomachus, who originated from Nicomachus the son of Machaon, and grandson of **Asclepius** <note>The Greek god of medicine.</note>, reputed a god in medicine. Apollodorus writes that he was born in the first year of the ninety-ninth Olympiad, and at the age of seventeen, he began to hear Plato and was his auditor for twenty years. He stayed with Philip, King of Macedonia, who gave him his son Alexander to educate for fifteen years. He obtained from Philip the rebuilding of Stagyra, his homeland. He taught philosophy and rhetoric together. He disputed while walking through the school. Hence his followers are called **Peripatetics**, because *peripatin* in Greek means "to walk." He was accused because he performed the same sacrifices for his concubine, whom he loved dearly, that the Athenians performed for Ceres, a great goddess among them. Therefore he fled to Chalcis, and there he died in that same year that Demosthenes died in Calabria. **Socrates** the Athenian, son of Sophroniscus the sculptor, was a helper to Euripides in writing tragedies. He heard Anaxagoras, and after he was condemned, he transferred to Archelaus. He was a sculptor and made the Graces, which were placed in the citadel of Athens. He was vehement and sharp in the oratory art. But the Thirty Tyrants forbade him from teaching it. They write that he was the first who, with Aeschines his disciple, opened and expanded the fields and ornaments of philosophy.

<header>CANTO FOUR</header>

orators. For this reason, he was criticized by the comic poet Aristophanes as a man who could, by the power of eloquence, make an unjust cause appear just. He was the first discoverer of the precepts of **moral philosophy**, for those who lived before him had been vigilant only in <term>physics</term> <note>original: "phyfica," meaning natural philosophy or the study of the physical world</note>. He did not merely dispute this philosophy but lived fully according to it, adorned with every virtue. A scorner of all pleasure, he cheerfully endured poverty and sustained his life through the craft he learned from his father, until Crito, with his liberality, came to his aid and convinced him to leave his craft to become his disciple. He taught in the workshops of artisans without any pomp, but with great utility, proving by the testimony of Homer that moral philosophy is more useful to men than natural philosophy. Finally, because he was judged by the Oracle of Apollo to be the wisest of all men, he attracted such envy that Anytus provoked the poet Aristophanes against him and moved Meletus to accuse him of not worshipping the gods of the fatherland, but of introducing new gods and corrupting the youth. Finally, condemned to death, he drank the poison given to him, for this was the manner in which the Athenians executed those condemned to death.

**Plato**, the prince of the ten sects of philosophers, was an Athenian and the son of Aristo; through his mother’s blood, he was descended from Solon. His proper name was Aristocles, but they called him Plato either due to his excellent physical build or because of his wide-ranging eloquence. Others say it was because of his broad and spacious forehead, for <note>original: "platos" in Greek</note> signifies "broad." He was a student of painting and poetry. Socrates dreamed that a small swan grew in his lap, and once grown, it flew away and sang marvelously; the following day, when Plato’s father gave him to Socrates as a disciple, Socrates said, "This is the swan."

The greatness of his subject matter surpasses any oratorical genius. One cannot, in a short time, traverse either his immortal and varied virtues or the sea of such vast knowledge. Three times he went to Sicily to restore its liberty, and he so offended Dionysius, the tyrant of that land, that the tyrant sold him to Pollis the Spartan. Later, in Aegina, he was ransomed by Anniceris of Cyrene and sent back to Athens. Because of his supreme desire to acquire every doctrine from a great part of the earth, he spent twenty years listening to Socrates; at twenty-seven, he went to Megara to see Euclid the mathematician, then to Cyrene to see Theodorus. He came to Italy to see Philolaus and Eurytus, the Pythagoreans. He sailed with Euripides to Egypt to see the priests, in whom there was supreme learning; then to Babylonia to see the Chaldeans. He wished to go to Persia to see the Magi, but was prevented by the Asian war. Thus, he accumulated such knowledge that after him, it was not necessary for any Greek to seek studies other than those of Greece. He died in the first year of the one hundred and eighth Olympiad while sitting at a wedding feast, in the eighty-first year of his age.

**DEMOCRITUS**, who places the world at chance. Democritus was from the city called Abdera, a man entirely given to the investigation of the secrets of nature. He heard the priests in Egypt and the Magi in Persia. Some say he also went to India to see the <term>Gymnosophists</term> <note>Ancient Indian philosophers who practiced asceticism and went naked.</note>, and in these travels, he spent his entire patrimony, which was one hundred talents. For this reason, it was necessary for his brother to support him. But afterward, he held such authority that his republic honored him with a great sum of money and erected statues to him. He lived always in deep meditation and did not converse with others. He laughed at everything he saw people doing, despising human works as being full of vanity and folly. Because of this, his citizens, thinking he had lost his senses, called the most divine physician Hippocrates to cure him. Hippocrates came and recognized that it was not through folly, but through supreme wisdom, that he appeared foolish. He wrote many things, but because his speech was obscure, he is called by the Greeks <note>original: "scotinos," meaning shadowy or dark</note>. His opinion was that there is an infinite, entirely empty space in which infinite atoms fly—that is, bodies so small they cannot be divided. These, by touching and sticking together by chance, create innumerable worlds throughout this infinite vacuum. Therefore, fortune and chance, and not divine craftsmanship, make them. This is why the poet says he "places the world at chance"—that is, he maintains the world was generated by chance.

**Diogenes**, son of Hicesius, was from the city of Sinope. His father was a money-changer and forged coins. Some say he also forged them. But later, changing his life, he became a **Cynic** philosopher. These held the same opinion as the **Stoics**: that nothing was good except virtue, and nothing was evil except vice. But they dressed in sackcloth and did not refuse any menial labor. They held an austere and hard life. They rebuked vices mordantly; hence they were called "Cynics," which means <note>original: "canini," dog-like</note> in the Greek language. Diogenes then came to Athens and gave himself to the discipline of Antisthenes, the prince of the Cynics. His dwelling was an overturned earthen vessel <note>The famous "tub" of Diogenes.</note>. He begged for his food, and never received more than he needed for that day. He was a man most patient with every hardship. He slept wrapped in his cloak. He ate little with his bread other than herbs. And when Aristippus said to him, "If you knew how to flatter King Dionysius, you would not live in such poverty," he replied, "And if you knew how to live in such poverty, you would not have to be a flatterer to Dionysius." He was in such reputation that Alexander the Great went to visit him and found him under his vessel, facing the sun. Alexander offered him many things, to which Diogenes replied that he wanted nothing else except that Alexander not take the sun away from him. Alexander recognized such greatness of soul and understood that Diogenes was richer than he, for in the philosopher there was no greed, living most content with little; whereas Alexander felt in himself such ambition and desire to rule that, hearing from Democritus that there were multiple worlds, he wept in despair because he could not conquer them all. For this reason, Alexander used to say that if he were not Alexander, he would want to be no one other than Diogenes.

**Anaxagoras** was from the city of Clazomenae. He applied himself to philosophy in Athens under Callias, whose disciple he was for thirty years. He said that the moon contained within itself a great land, with mountains and valleys. Asked why he was born, he replied, "To contemplate the heavens, the sun, and the moon." He said that the poem of Homer was entirely composed of virtue and justice. He was a philosopher—

<meta>This page continues the catalog of great thinkers in Limbo. It transitions from the high philosophy of Plato to the Pre-Socratic philosophers (Anaxagoras, Thales, Empedocles, Heraclitus), the Stoics, legendary figures of music and medicine, and finally the great Roman orators and moralists like Cicero and Seneca.</meta>

<header>INFERNO</header>

natural: and the principle of his work is <note>original: "In principio tutte lechose erono confuse," meaning "In the beginning all things were confused"</note> and mixed together. Then the divine mind ordered and composed them. He said that the mind was the principle of motion. **AND THALES**.
**Thales** was born in Phoenicia of the noble lineage of King Agenor; he came to Miletus, an island, and was there made a citizen. He was one of the seven sages of Greece, and the first to be called a sage. Callimachus writes that he discovered the **Little Bear** <note>the constellation Ursa Minor</note>, by which the Phoenicians navigate. He was the first in Greece to dispute concerning **physics** <term>physics</term> <note>natural philosophy, the study of the physical world</note>. He held that even inanimate things had a soul, drawing this conjecture from the **lodestone** <note>a natural magnet</note> and from amber, because the one draws iron and the other straw. Wishing to demonstrate how easy it would be for him to become rich, and knowing through **astrology** <note>here meaning astronomy and the study of celestial cycles</note> that in that year there would be an abundance of olives, he bought them all before the season and earned a great sum of money. He posited water to be the principle of all things, and the world to be animate and full of spirits. He thanked fortune for three things: that he was a human and not a beast; a male and not a female; a Greek and not a barbarian—although others attribute this saying to Socrates. He said God was the most ancient of all things, most beautiful, unbegotten, and the maker of the whole. **Empedocles** was from Sicily, from the city of Agrigento. He posited six principles for things: namely, the four elements, and **Friendship** and **Discord** <note>also translated as Love and Strife</note>. According to Aristotle in *The Sophist*, he was the first inventor of the art of **oratory**, and in the book of poets he calls him "Homeric Empedocles" because he was an excellent poet. Satyrus writes that he was an excellent physician and the best of orators, and the teacher of Gorgias of Leontini. The latter affirms having been present when Empedocles practiced the **magical arts** and gave potions to drive away diseases and old age, and to make prosperous winds come and adverse ones cease. Heraclides writes that he brought a dead woman back to life. He wrote five thousand verses on Physics and on purifications, and six hundred on medicine. **HERACLITUS**: Heraclitus was of Ephesus, a city in Asia, and through assiduous and most ardent study without a teacher, he became most singular. And just as **Democritus** continually laughed at the folly of men, so on the contrary Heraclitus wept, moved by compassion for human misery; and seeing the captive customs of his fellow citizens, he lived in solitude in the mountains. **ZENO** of Citium established the sect of the **Stoics**. This man, sailing with Phoenician purple dye to Greece, was shipwrecked at sea and lost his merchandise. Thus disconsolate, he came to Athens and, turning to philosophy, heard Crates the **Cynic** philosopher. He became so learned that he was held in the highest veneration, to the extent that the Athenians deposited the keys of the city gates with him. He was also honored by public decree with a golden crown and a bronze statue, and his tomb was made in the Ceramicus. And Antigonus, King of Macedonia, whenever he came to Athens, always listened to him. His opinion was that nothing is good except virtue, and nothing evil except vice. The philosophers of his sect were first called "Zenonians" after his name. Later, because he disputed in the **Pisianactio Portico**—and "portico" in Greek is called <term>stoa</term>—they were named **Stoics** after that porch. **Dioscorides** was an excellent physician and investigator of the qualities and virtues of herbs, trees, and stones. **Orpheus** was of Thrace, and because he was an excellent musician and poet, they say he was the son of Apollo and Calliope. Diodorus Siculus writes that Bacchus <note>Dionysus</note>, due to the snares set for him in Thrace by Lycurgus, would have perished if Tharops, a man of that region, had not first warned him. For this reason, Bacchus gave him the kingdom of Thrace and taught him how to perform his sacrifices. From Tharops was born Oeagrus, and from him Orpheus, who, being adorned with much prudence and learning, refined and greatly adorned the sacrifices taught by Bacchus. And because he wished that on those days in which such sacrifices were made, men should sleep separated from their wives, the women conspired against him and killed him. Other writers say that he went to Egypt and learned the doctrine of the priests, and returning, introduced to Greece the sacrifices of the **Egyptian Bacchus**. They say that with the sound of his lyre he gathered wild beasts to himself, moved mountains, and stopped rivers. This is nothing other than that with his **eloquence** he drew fierce men to civil life, moved stupid and coarse men to virtue, and quieted the impetus of the furious. **TULLY** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note>: It would perhaps be better to say nothing of such a man than to say too little. And certainly, this is not a place where I can—I do not say adorn—but even briefly narrate his many great and divine virtues. For if we consider his governance in the Republic, it seems that nothing could remain for his studies and learning. If, on the other hand, we note the things he wrote, we would judge that he never departed from study. And nevertheless, he served both the one and the other life perfectly. He alone, during the **conspiracy of Catiline**, preserved liberty, at which time Roman liberty was abandoned by all the nobles if he had not come to its aid. For this reason, he deserved to be called **Father of the Fatherland** by the Senate and the Roman people by public decree. And Pompey the Great, returning with his triumph, said that he owed every obligation to Cicero, because if he had not preserved the fatherland, he would have had nowhere to triumph. He was, therefore, the Father of the Fatherland; and no less the father of **Latin eloquence**, which he brought to such sublimity that since then no one has been able—I do not say to raise it higher—but even to maintain it where he placed it. **LINUS** was a Theban, and because of his supreme eloquence, some poets said he was the son of Mercury and Urania. Some say of Apollo. He was the first among the Greeks to find melody and proportion in music, and he was excellent in the poetic art; and the letters which Cadmus brought from Phoenicia to Greece, he adapted into the Greek diction. He had many disciples, but the most excellent were Hercules, Thamyris, and Orpheus. He wrote of the deeds of the first Dionysus. They say that Hercules—because he was of a dull wit in learning to play the lyre, and for this was often beaten by his master with the lyre—killed him with the very lyre with which he was learning. **SENECA**: This was **Annaeus Seneca**, a Spaniard born in Corduba, and later made a Roman citizen. And from him was born the Seneca of whom we now treat, a man...

# CANTO FOUR

<columns>

...most admirable for his great **Stoic** doctrine: no less praiseworthy for his natural wisdom and sanctity of life. Because of these virtues, he was given as a tutor to the Emperor **Nero**, and in the beginning, he was much honored by him. But later, as Nero's cruel tyranny displeased him more each day, and as he often endeavored to oppose Nero's rages, he fell under suspicion. Furthermore, he was often bitten by many detractors in Nero's presence, who claimed that his great wealth—more than that of a private citizen—was something he strove to increase, and that he was winning the favor of the citizens, almost as if he wished to compete with Nero in the magnificence of his villas and the beauty of his gardens. **Seneca**, therefore, under an honorable pretext, wished to free himself from such envy and return all these things to Nero, demonstrating that because of his old age he was no longer fit for the governance of so many things. But Nero, then feigning love for him, did not want them. Later, no longer able to hide his hatred, he determined that Seneca should die. But granting him the choice of how he wished to die, Seneca had his veins cut in a bath of warm water. He was a very close friend of the **Apostle Paul**, as shown by several letters sent from one to the other <note>These letters are now considered apocryphal, but were widely accepted as genuine in the Middle Ages</note>. This persuaded **Jerome** that he might be among the blessed; but **Dante**, since Seneca's baptism does not appear nor is he found in the catalog of saints, places him in Limbo.

**EUCLID** was from the city of Megara, a most studious reader of the books of Parmenides. He became an excellent physicist and mathematician. For this reason, after the death of Socrates, **Plato** and his other disciples fled from Athens to Megara to be with Euclid for fear of the thirty tyrants. This man [Euclid] believed there to be only one "Good," and he called it sometimes God, sometimes Mind, and sometimes Prudence.

**PTOLEMY** was from Egypt—not from the royal lineage of the Alexandrian Ptolemies descended from Lagus, the soldier of Alexander—but was from the city of Pelusium, and lived in the times of the Emperor Trajan. He wrote on the geography of the earth and many things regarding **astrology** <term>astrology</term> <note>At this time, "astrology" and "astronomy" were often used interchangeably to mean the study of celestial bodies</note>.

**HIPPOCRATES** was born on the island of Cos <note>The text says "Chio" (Chios), a common geographical confusion in early manuscripts</note>; he was so excellent in medicine that he was reputed to be a god in that field. He lived in the times of Artaxerxes, King of Persia.

**AVICENNA** was the rival of Averroes and the son of a Spanish king <note>Historical error: Avicenna was a Persian philosopher/physician; the commentator likely confuses his origins with the Andalusian philosophers</note>. He organized the works of Galen. He lived in the times of Antoninus Pius <note>Another chronological error; Avicenna lived in the 11th century AD</note>.

**AVERROES**, a supreme physician and philosopher, and rival of Avicenna, was from the same country. He is the first among those who have commented on **Aristotle**.

> I cannot portray them all in full:
> for the long theme so drives me on
> that many times the word falls short of the fact.
>
> The company of six diminishes by two;
> by another way the wise guide leads me,
> out of the quiet into the air that trembles:
> And I come to a place where nothing shines.

<column-break/>

He excuses himself because the theme—that is, the subject matter—proposed is so long that he cannot dwell distinctly and particularly on every part of it. And in this, he admonishes any writer who has to treat many things in one volume not to expand so much on each one that it becomes too long; as, for example <note>original: "verbi gratia"</note>, **Petrarch** treats only one type of man in each *Triumph*, and for this reason, he can be prolific in describing many of them. But Dante, in this *Inferno*, is not treating only the famous, but also the lustful, the gluttonous, the envious, the greedy, and the proud, and many other vicious people; he must not name many in each of these categories, because he would proceed unto infinity. Thus, it is necessary that the telling—that is, the narration—falls short of the fact; that is, it should not be as much as there are men who have committed deeds and, by their own deeds, are in that place where their life has put them.

**THE SIXTH COMPANY** diminishes by two: because **Homer** and the other three remained behind. And he describes how, just as the air in the castle was tranquil and bright, so outside the castle where the damned were tormented, it trembled and was dark.

**BY ANOTHER WAY**: For just as one proceeds to the contemplation of famous men by the way of virtue, so one goes to the contemplation of the vicious by recognizing vices. Therefore, the wise guide—that is, our intellect enlightened by science—leads us by another way, showing us the virtuous man with one reason and the vicious man with another.

**OUT OF THE QUIET AIR**: Those in the castle were not "blessed" because they did not enjoy God; nevertheless, they were in "quiet air"—that is, immobile and peaceful—because their moral virtue was sufficient to keep them in tranquility. But outside the castle, the air was "trembling," because in vicious men, the soul is always in varied motion and full of perturbations. It moves and boils, agitated by different passions, no less than the sea struck by various winds.

**WHERE NOTHING SHINES**: That is, in which place there is nothing that reflects or makes light. And certainly, in the soul infected by vices—because it is driven by blind appetite—no light of reason appears, but it is entirely in darkness. And these, as the prophet says: *They lie in the shadow of death* <note>original: "In umbra mortis iacent," quoting Psalm 107:10 or Luke 1:79</note>. Furthermore, the poet wished to conform with the Gospel, which shows that in Hell there is outer darkness and "gnashing of teeth"—that is, trembling and cold.

d. v. <note>Printer's signature mark</note>

</columns>

<header>HELL</header>

## CANTO FIVE OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE

Thus I descended from the first circle
down into the second, which cinches less space,
and so much more pain that it goads to wailing.
There stands **Minos** horribly, and he snarls;
he examines the crimes at the entrance,
judges, and sends away according to how he entwines himself.
I say that when the ill-born soul
comes before him, it confesses everything;
and that discerner of sins
sees what place in Hell is for it;
he girds himself with his tail as many times
as the levels he wants it to be put down.
Always before him many of them stand;
they go in turn, each to the judgment;
they speak and hear, and then are turned downward.

<column-break/>

We said above that because the poet has divided Hell into circles, it is necessary according to the dimension of a spherical body—since it departs from the circumference and little by little approaches the depth, which is the center—that the lower circle always be smaller than the upper one. And because the place, the more it approaches the depth and the further it departs from heaven, is more suited to punishment, the order of this descent ensures that the beginning starts from the less grave sins, and then continues descending always to more grave ones. This applies to the physical site of the world and to the essential Hell. Regarding the moral order, it is the same. For only crime is what deprives us of God and of our happiness. Therefore, the less grave the sin, the less it distances man from God; and the more grave it is, the closer it brings him to the depth. For this reason, it is fitting that since the aforementioned spirits are in the first circle, in this second one the less grave sin must be punished: and this is **lust** <note>original: "luxuria"</note>. This is manifest because he said: **WHICH CINCHES LESS** space: that is, surrounds. **AND SO MUCH** more pain that goads to wailing: because beyond the pain of the mind, which those in the first circle also feel, these feel the pain of the senses, which makes them "guaire," that is, lament. **THERE STANDS** Minos. There were in Greece three kings: Minos, Aeacus, and Rhadamanthus, sons of Jove. Because they were very just princes, the poets feign that after their deaths they were made judges of Hell, who had to examine the souls and then punish them according to what their crimes deserved. But regarding Rhadamanthus and Aeacus, we will speak in another place. Minos was the son of Jove and Europa. He reigned in the island of Crete, today called **Candia** <note>A common 15th-century name for Crete</note>. And according to **Diodorus Siculus**, he built several cities there. But the most noble were three: **Knossos** <note>original: "Gnofo"</note> located toward Asia; **Phaistos** located in the southern parts; and **Cydonia** placed to the west. Likewise, he gave laws to the Cretans; and so that they would have greater authority, he feigned to have received them from Jove. And he often entered a certain cave and showed that he had colloquy with him. **Strabo** says that in this he imitated a certain Rhadamanthus—not his brother, but another who lived many centuries before. He was the first, according to **Pliny**, who engaged in naval battles, and he acquired many islands and maritime lands. And many peoples were obedient to him, moved more by his justice than by force. Dante, therefore, imitates the ancient poets, and especially **Virgil**, who writes:
> Minos, the presiding judge, shakes the urn; he calls a council of the silent ones and learns their lives and crimes. <note>original: "Quesitor minos urnam mouet ille silentum Conciliumque uocat uitas : et crimina discit"</note>

Minos is nothing other than the judgment of **conscience**, of which we will speak a little below. This figure is described by Virgil in the form of a man; but Dante configures him as a beast, giving him a tail and a snarl, which is characteristic of a dog. But this is not without reason, for he intends this to represent the conscience of the damned man: that is, one who has already made a habit of vice. For such people are bitten by conscience, which is no longer "man," because such remorse does not turn them back from doing evil. For they have extinguished in themselves the light of reason, through which we are men; instead, it only goads them and makes them become furious. Hence one can say that the conscience in the damned, and in those who have made a habit of vice, is a most cruel beast. Furthermore, he posits that the tail denotes the place where the sinner must be put: the tail is the last part of the beast's body. By this, he signifies that the sin has been committed. And certainly, remorse of conscience never happens except at the end, and when they have committed the sin. And certainly, this is the only judge whom no one can escape. Hence **Juvenal** says:
> This is the first punishment: that no guilty man is acquitted with himself as judge, even if the wicked influence of a deceitful praetor has won over the urn. <note>original: "Prima hec est ultio quod se iudice nemo nocens absoluitur improba quanquam Gratia fallacis pretoris uicerit urnam ."</note>

**THERE STANDS** Minos. Not without merit does he say "stands there": because the conscience is always in our soul, and never departs; but continually this judge makes his residence in us. Nor is it to be wondered at that if Minos is the remorse of conscience, and every sin brings such remorse, why the poet did not place Minos in the first circle where there is some species of sin. For in that circle are the "un-guilty" ones <note>original: "cuilissimi," likely meaning those who lacked faith but not moral virtue</note>, who are punished not for having done evil, but for not having done good; and for this they could not have remorse, not knowing how much of an evil it was not to do good. Or there are the Gentiles, who lived with such virtue that no conscience bit them; and they had no knowledge of baptism. **HORRIBLY** he snarls: There is nothing that snarls and barks and threatens more horribly than the conscience, which day and night goads the one who has committed a crime. The conscience does three things: First, it bites us and gnaws at us for the sin committed. Hence **Isaiah** said:
> Their worm shall not die <note>original: "Vermis eorum non morietur"</note>

And the "worm" he mentions is nothing other than the remorse that never ceases, but gnaws at us like a worm. The second thing is that the conscience always stands against us almost like a witness who...

<meta>Continuity Note: This page continues the commentary on Dante's *Inferno*, specifically the transition into Canto V where Dante encounters Minos, the judge of the underworld. The previous page established the physical and moral structure of the circles of Hell.</meta>

# CANTO FIVE

of reproof. And therefore Juvenal says: <note>original: "Nocte dieque suum gestare in pectore testem Spartano cuidam respondit pythia uates"</note> "The Pythian prophetess answered a certain Spartan that he must carry his own witness in his breast night and day." In the third place, it judges the punishment that the sin deserves. Wherefore, as I said shortly above: <note>original: "Prima est hec ultio quod se iudice nemo nocens absoluitur"</note> "This is the first vengeance: that with himself as judge, no guilty person is acquitted." And for this reason, perhaps, the poets placed three judges in Hell: **Minos**, **Aeacus**, and **Rhadamanthus**. **HE EXAMINES** the faults: Conscience always reflects within itself on the fault committed and judges the penalty. **JUDGES AND SENDS**: He specifies three things that conscience does. First, it examines; then it judges; then it sends to execution that which is judged **ACCORDING** as he entwines: That is, he embraces. This is an ancient Florentine word derived from the Latin word <term>vincire</term> (to bind), because he who embraces, binds. Thus, our peasants still say "A <term>vinghiata</term>," meaning an armful. **I SAY THAT** when the soul is ill-born: That is, when it is polluted by sin. This makes it so miserable that, as Christ said of Judas: <note>original: "Melius fuisset homini isti si nunquam natus fuisset"</note> "It would have been better for that man if he had never been born." Do not understand **ill-born** to mean that at its birth it had such influence from the stars that it was necessitated to sin; for this would destroy <term>free will</term>. This is false not only according to our theologians but also according to the philosophers, who maintain that the stars can incline, but not necessitate. For the soul, created immediately by God without the mediation of the fertile causes (which are the heavens), is not subject to the heavens like the body is. The body, through the senses, can give some inclination to the soul, but not so much that the soul does not remain free and in its own power to do good or evil. Therefore, the learned astrologer said that "the wise man rules the stars." Thus, "ill-born" means born for its own evil, since it was so foolish that from being free, it made itself a slave to sin. **ALL** it confesses: Because nothing can be hidden from our conscience. **AND THAT** knower of sins: And certainly no one knows sins better than the conscience; for this reason Cicero said: <note>original: "Nullum maius theatrum conscientia"</note> "There is no greater theater than conscience." **ALWAYS** before him many of them stand; **THEY GO** in turn: A passage taken from **Virgil**: <note>original: "Quesitor minos urnam mouet ille silentum conciliumque uocat uitasque et crimina discit"</note> "Minos, the investigator, shakes the urn; he summons the council of the silent and learns of their lives and crimes." Virgil says, therefore, that since there is an infinite crowd of souls, their names are all written down and put in a vessel; they are drawn by lot, and the one drawn is examined. **THEY GO IN TURN**: That is, they go according to the turn that falls to them. For <term>vicenda</term> means the turn that falls by lot, and it is derived from the Latin word <term>vice</term>. **THEY SPEAK AND** hear and are turned downward: In a very brief space of time, and almost at once, they speak their sins and hear Minos, who pronounces the penalty; and they are turned downward because the devils turn them toward their torment. And this is certain: for at the same moment, the conscience remembers the sin, reason condemns you, and anxiety afflicts you.

---

> "O you who come to the painful hostelry,"
> Minos cried out to me when he saw me,
> leaving the act of such great office:
> "Look how you enter and in whom you trust;
> let not the breadth of the entrance deceive you!"
> And my leader to him: "Why do you yet cry out?
> Do not hinder his fated journey;
> it is so willed there where what is willed
> can be done; and ask no more."

And he says: **O YOU WHO** come to the painful hostelry of vices. **LOOK** how you enter: Into such contemplation. Do not trust in your own strengths, for they will not be sufficient to draw you out of it. **THE BREADTH** of the entrance: As if to say the entrance is wide, but the exit is narrow; for anyone can enter into vices, but not leave them. A man can enter into vices by himself through his own free will, but he cannot leave them without divine grace. And as I said: <note>original: "Facilis descensus auerni: Sed reuocare gradu: superasque euadere ad auras. Hoc opus hic labor est."</note> "Easy is the descent to Avernus; but to retrace one's steps and escape to the upper air, this is the task, this is the toil." Therefore, sensuality being so dismayed by the recognition of its own fragility, **Virgil** (that is, superior reason, which knows that divine grace does not abandon those who help themselves and set out on a good journey) restrains such conscience and says: **DO NOT HINDER** his fated journey: That is, do not oppose his good purpose, which proceeds from fate—that is, from the disposition ordained by **Divine Providence**. Because Providence can do whatever it wills, it is the height of human foolishness either to wish to oppose it or to wish to know the reason why it wills thus; for <note>original: "incomprensibilia sunt iudicia tua domine"</note> "Your judgments, O Lord, are incomprehensible." Fate is defined variously by various philosophers. Nor can I, in such a crowd of things, treat them all extensively. But because Christians are closer to the truth in these matters, we will speak according to others. Since, as **Augustine** says, he [Plato] approaches the truth more closely in these things, we will speak according to **Plato** regarding what fate is. But first understand that the opinions of philosophers were various as to whether God cares for and provides for things or not. **Leucippus**, **Democritus**, **Protagoras**, **Theodorus**, **Aristippus**, and **Epicurus** maintain that everything happens by chance without any governance. Some believe that God governs everything from the heaven of the moon upwards, but does not care for lower things. Some say he cares for lower things too, but only the great ones. Plato first...

<column-break/>

It is not inappropriate that **Minos** wishes to dismay **Dante**. Indeed, often sensuality (which is aware of its own fragility) discourages itself from entering into Hell—that is, into the contemplation of vices—fearing it might remain trapped by their pleasures. But superior reason opposes such a conscience and demonstrates that divine grace will lead him safely. **Conscience** is nothing other than the awareness a man has of himself, of his merits, and of his strengths within himself. Therefore, this knowledge that sensuality has of its own fragility and small power to defend itself from carnal pleasures cries out to him: That is, at the **painful abode**, which is to say, at the contemplation. **AND IN WHOM** you trust: As if saying, "you trust in yourself." **LET NOT THE BREADTH** deceive you: That is, the width...

<summary>This page analyzes the figure of Minos as an allegory for the human conscience, emphasizing that while man can fall into vice through free will, he requires divine grace and reason to escape. Landino refutes astrological fatalism, asserting that the soul is created directly by God and remains free to choose between good and evil.</summary>

--- Page 98 ---
<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on the nature of divine will and fate, transitioning from the general judgment of Minos into the specific punishment of the lustful in the Second Circle of Hell. It connects the previous discussion of the "ill-born" soul to the mechanism of Providence.</meta>

-># INFERNO<-

[The Prince] of all the philosophers <note>Referring to Plato, whom the commentator often calls the "prince."</note> maintains that divine providence extends through all things, even to the smallest, and governs them all. Empedocles, Hippocrates, Heraclitus, Pythagoras, and the Stoics agree with this sentiment. Aristotle writes in such a way that some interpret him as positing providence, while others argue the contrary. Plato, then, holds that the wisdom of God, knowing His own essence and power—and through that essence, every thing that depends upon it—immediately loves and desires the order of things with His will. This order, which wisdom has judged to be the best, He describes within Himself and establishes in a form that cannot be otherwise. Therefore, this constitution, order, and law of things that must necessarily exist—and yet do not impede **free will**—is called **providence**. This same order, when considered within the things themselves, he calls **fate**. He says that fate is the divine law by which the inevitable thoughts and undertakings of God are fulfilled. For this reason, Augustine does not contend with, nor oppose, those who call fate the connection and continued order of all causes through which whatever happens, happens. But Augustine himself does not wish to call it "fate," because that name was used by the ancients in various senses and could lead men into error. Therefore, Dante spoke of his "fateful journey," meaning his journey which proceeds from the order placed by God in the causes of things. Thus it follows: **IT IS SO WILLED WHERE WHAT IS WILLED CAN BE DONE**. Explain these verses as they were explained above.

Now the doleful notes begin
to make themselves heard; now I am come
to where much wailing strikes me.
I came into a place mute of all light,
which bellows like the sea in a storm,
if it is fought by contrary winds.
The hellish hurricane, which never rests,
sweeps the spirits along with its rapine;
whirling and striking, it molests them.
When they arrive before the ruin,
there the shrieks, the weeping, and the lament;
there they blaspheme the divine virtue.
I understood that to such torment
were damned the carnal sinners,
who subject reason to desire:
And as the starlings carry their wings
in the cold time, in a broad and full flock,
so that breath [carries] the evil spirits:
From here, from there, from up, from down, it leads them;
no hope ever comforts them,
not of rest, but of lesser pain.

<column-break/>

We have already shown that throughout this entire work it is necessary for the text to denote two things: namely, the pains sustained by the damned in the essential Hell, and an allegorical sense which demonstrates the disturbances induced by the vice being discussed. Therefore, since we are here dealing with carnal love—which sin is universally called **lust** (<term>luxuria</term> from the Latin for "excess")—and because our author is both a poet and a Christian theologian, I will strive to satisfy both doctrines. And first, regarding the Hell of the damned: **NOW THE DOLEFUL NOTES BEGIN**: that is, the shrieks and cries, because the sensory pains begin. He places these sinners in a dark place because, having sinned greatly with their eyes—which are the guides in love—and having taken delight in bodily beauties (all of which consist in seeing), it is a fitting punishment that they be deprived of the use of that sense with which they sinned. Furthermore, because it is the custom of lovers to delight in various sounds, songs, and harmonies, it is appropriate that this sense be punished; thus they hear "bellowing" and other troublesome voices. Likewise, because lust induces blindness of mind and lack of consideration, for through it the mind loses the light of superior reason and can no longer contemplate any excellent thing. Similarly with inferior reason: because the soul occupied in impudent love loses all its honor and utility in the civil and active life.

Therefore, the poet places them in darkness. Virgil expressed these two blindnesses—one of superior reason and the other of inferior reason—most excellently. The first in Aeneas, who for Dido's sake left Italy (that is, the seeking and contemplation of heavenly things). The second in Dido, who, hindered by love, neglected everything else. Whence: <note>original: "Non coeptae assurgunt turres"</note> "The towers begun do not rise." Likewise, lust induces inconstancy. For this reason, Love is depicted with wings. Wherefore Propertius, assigning the reason why Love is winged, said: <note>original: "Scilicet alternis quoniam iactamur in undis / Nostraque non ullis permanet aura locis"</note> "Surely because we are tossed on alternating waves, and our breeze remains in no place." Thus the poet said: **THE HELLISH HURRICANE which never rests**. Likewise, in love, counsels are headlong: that is, unconsidered and without reason. And for this reason, he places the **ruin**. <note>The "ruina" in the poem refers to a landslide in Hell, but the commentator links it to the "ruin" of one's plans.</note> And whoever wants to understand exactly the inconstancy of lovers and the ruin of their plans from one extreme to another should read the *Triumph of Love* written by **Francesco Petrarch**, a very useful thing to consider well for anyone seeking to free themselves from such cruel servitude. **NOW the doleful notes begin**: He posits great weeping and lamenting because, of all human disturbances, none makes men more complaining, more tearful, and with greater grief than love. **MUTE OF ALL LIGHT**: that is, deprived; he uses a term belonging to hearing ("mute") to describe sight. The disturbances of the soul are four in genus, but many more in species, as we shall show elsewhere. All these things extinguish in us the light of reason. But above all others, Love makes a man entirely blind. Whence the poets depict him as blind. Likewise, as a child, to show that he lacks all judgment. Hence Propertius: <note>original: "Quicunque ille fuit puerum qui pinxit amorem / Non ne putas miras hunc habuisse ma[nus]"</note> "Whoever he was who painted Love as a boy, do you not think he had marvelous hands?"

It draws on authorities like Plato, Augustine, and Petrarch to define the relationship between Providence, Fate, and human passion.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, moving from the judgment of Minos to the specific punishments of the Second Circle, where the lustful are tormented. The commentator, Cristoforo Landino, provides an allegorical and philological analysis of the "infernal storm" and the famous figures Dante encounters here.</meta>

-># CANTO FIVE<-

<note>original Latin: *...nus Is primum uidit sine sensu uiuere amantes Et leuibus curis magna perire bona.*</note> ...he first saw lovers living without sense, and great goods perishing through light cares. And it is well compared to the sea; which, as we demonstrated in Virgil’s *Aeneid*, optimally represents appetite and sensuality. For just as the sea is calm by itself, but when moved by winds—and especially if they are contrary—it rises into a great tempest, so our appetite, quiet by its own nature, is disturbed by various passions. These are often contrary within the mind, as is shown by Terence’s character Pamphilus <note>A character from the Roman play *Andria*</note>, who on one side is driven by love and compassion for Glycerium, and on the other is held back by reverence for his father. These contrary winds make the sea "bellow"; that is, they move the sensuality of the lover to bellows and wails. **THE INFERNAL STORM**. They use the terms "bufera" <note>storm/hurricane</note> and "busea" properly when, in the mountains, the falling snow is turned and whirled around in ruin by diverse winds. He imagines, then, that those spirits were in the same way whirled and transported through the air. This signifies nothing other than the continuous instability, inconstancy, and sudden mutation found in lovers. For as Terence says, all these things are in love. Therefore, this constant inconstancy and furious mutation snatches the soul away, turning it from purpose to purpose, and striking it—that is, giving it grave pains, molesting and afflicting it. And when they reach "the ruin"—that is, when they fall from the beloved thing and remain deprived of it—there are the shrieks, the weeping, and the laments, and they blaspheme the divine power. This signifies extreme madness, such as is common in lovers. It demonstrates the perversion in love, for they prefer such love to the love of God and the father. **WHO SUBMIT REASON** to talent: That is, to appetite. "Talento" is the inclination of the soul and appetite toward pleasure and sensory delight. Hence, "to talent" <term>talentare: to be pleasing or to consent to desire</term> means to consent. **AND AS THE STARLINGS** are carried by their wings. This is an excellent comparison of birds to souls because of their lightness; and because starlings fly quickly and in great throngs, it expresses the multitude and velocity of the spirits. **HERE, THERE,** up, down, it leads them: The lover never stays in one state; rather, now he rises in the grace of the beloved thing, and now he falls into ruin through enmities and dissensions. **NO HOPE** ever comforts them, not of rest, but even of lesser pain. Regarding the "essential Hell," <note>The actual theological state of the damned</note> this is true of every person damned for any sin. And so the author placed it here in the first place of the punishments, so that it might be understood for all the others. But regarding the allegorical sense, it is specific to the lustful, because such perturbation is insatiable. And the more one exercises it, the more the appetite grows. The poets mean nothing else by Tityos <note>A giant in Greek mythology punished in Tartarus</note>, the son of Earth, who wished to do violence to Latona, mother of Phoebus, except for lust, which is born from the desire for earthly things. Although the vulture gnaws his liver, just as much regrows continuously as the bird devours. Furthermore, a lover is never without pain. For if he is deprived of the beloved thing, he wastes away with the desire to have it; if he possesses it, he is always in jealousy and in suspicion of losing it.

*And as the cranes go singing their lays,*
*making a long line of themselves in the air,*
*so I saw coming, uttering wails,*
*shadows carried by the said strife.*
*Wherefore I said: "Master, who are those*
*people whom the black air so punishes?"*

*The first of those of whom news*
*you wish to know," he then said to me,*
*"was empress of many tongues.*
*To the vice of luxury she was so broken*
*that she made lust lawful in her law,*
*to take away the blame into which she had fallen.*
*She is Semiramis, of whom it is read*
*that she succeeded Ninus and was his spouse;*
*she held the land that the Sultan rules.*

<column-break/>

**J**ust as through the comparison to starlings he expressed the multitude and velocity of the spirits, so through the cranes he signifies their laments. And he well said "they go singing their lays," which means laments. For almost all the verses and all the songs of lovers contain complaints, regrets, and things that move one to commiseration. Hence the Greeks call such verses "Elegies," because *eleos* <note>original Greek: ἔλεος</note> in Greek means mercy and compassion. **MAKING** a long line of themselves in the air. He does not say that the spirits flew making a long line of themselves, because above he showed that they flew in a throng like starlings. But he says they flew singing their lays like cranes do when, flying, they form a long line. **WHO ARE** those people? He does not ask about all the people in that circle, because he already knows what kind of sinners are tormented there. But he asks specifically about those who are near him. And because they are names from ancient history, he asks Virgil. Throughout the poem, he almost always observes this method: he has Virgil speak of ancient histories, while modern histories—those after Virgil’s time—he has spoken by others.

**S**emiramis was the wife of Ninus, king of the Assyrians. Regarding her origin, Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BC</note> records fabulous things. For he writes that she was born in a forest near a lake in the city of Ascalon. Her mother was a goddess who was worshipped there, and her father was a youth who sacrificed to her. Once born, she is said to have been hidden in a cave, and there she was nourished by doves <insert>who brought her milk</insert>. Finally, she was found and given to Simma, the prefect of the King's shepherds. She was then named Semiramis because she had been nourished by doves, for in the Syrian language, *Semiramis* means "dove." Growing up, she became so...

<header>FIFTH INFERNO</header>

> The other is she who killed herself for love:
> and broke faith with the ashes of Sychaeus.
> The other is the lustful Cleopatra.
> I saw Helen, for whom so much evil
> time turned: and I saw the great Achilles
> who at the last fought with love.
> I saw Paris, Tristan: and more than a thousand
> shadows he showed me and named with his finger,
> whom love departed from our life.

<column-break/>

...marvelous beauty: she was the wife of Menon, a man of the King’s council. In this woman, prudence was no less than beauty. Thus, her husband did nothing without her counsel. In these times, Ninus was King of the Assyrians, leading his army against the Bactrians; he was besieging Bactra, the principal city of that region. Seeing that the siege would be long, Menon sent for Semiramis, without whom he lived in nothing but sorrow. The lady came: and by diligently observing the layout of the land, finally, by a difficult and unguarded path—because that part seemed impregnable—she took the citadel of the city. Thus, the Bactrians were forced to surrender. This

---

gave the woman the greatest fame. And the King, moved as much by her beauty as by her virtues, asked her from her husband, promising him in exchange his daughter Sosane; when Menon refused, the King threatened to blind him. Out of grief, Menon hanged himself. In this way, Semiramis became the wife of Ninus, and bore him Ninia. When Ninus died, he left her the kingdom. Desiring to do extraordinary things, she built Babylon upon the Euphrates. Its walls spanned as many <term>stadia</term> <note>An ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 600 feet</note> as there are days in the year; and a stadium is a distant part of a mile. Therefore, 365 stadia are forty-six miles. The walls were made of brick, and they had 250 towers. Upon the raw bricks, she had various forms of wild beasts impressed, each in its own color, so that the circuit formed a hunting scene; and in place of lime, she used bitumen from the Asphaltite marshes. I leave behind many stupendous things regarding this work, for these alone would require a whole volume. She conquered the Medes, where she left admirable works: gardens, aqueducts, and roads. She conquered the Persians, where she leveled many mountains, and on the plains, she made many mountains as tombs for her friends. She conquered the Indians, against whom she led three million men on foot, fifty thousand on horse, and one hundred thousand chariots. She was very lustful, but did not want a permanent husband. She chose from among the youngest and most beautiful men, and afterwards sent them to a place where they were never seen again. This is what Diodorus writes. Justin says that finally, wanting to have relations with her son, she was killed by him. Some say she took him as a husband, and to cover her infamy, she established by law that it was licit for everyone to do the same. **THE OTHER IS** she who killed herself for love—that is, she died for love. Dido follows. She was the daughter of Belus, King of Phoenicia, and wife of Sychaeus. Because Sychaeus had much treasure, he was killed by Pygmalion, Dido’s brother, who hoped to possess his riches. But Dido fled with those riches to Africa, where she built Carthage and lived in great chastity; she never broke faith with her already dead husband. Finally, seeing herself being forced by Iarbas, King of Mauritania, who wanted to marry her, she killed herself with her own hands so as not to break her faith to Sychaeus. But Virgil, to adorn his poem, feigns that when Aeneas arrived at the Carthaginian shores due to a storm and visited her, she fell in love with him; and fleeing the rain during a hunt, they joined together in a cave. Afterward, when Aeneas went to Italy, Dido, overcome by too much love, killed herself. Therefore, Dante, following Virgil in other things, follows him also in this story. **CLEOPATRA** was the daughter of Ptolemy Auletes <note>original: "pythone"</note>, King of Egypt, and sister and wife of Ptolemy Dionysius, who killed Pompey. Civil dissension arose between them; and in the conquest Caesar made of Alexandria, she—with both her beauty and her ornate speech and sweet manners, which were marvelously present in her—allured Caesar into her love, and bore him Caesarion. After the death of Caesar, with the same arts, she so drew Mark Antony to herself that he loved her ardently, and for her, he rejected Octavia, sister of Octavian <note>the future Emperor Augustus</note>. They lived in Alexandria in many delights and great luxury. Finally, after Antony was defeated by Octavian, they fled to Egypt. Antony, seeing he could not otherwise escape Octavian, killed himself. Cleopatra, taken alive and fearing she would be led in a triumph, killed herself with poison. She was a woman of great spirit and very prudent, but no less lascivious; and as Plutarch writes, she was worth more for a certain grace, gestures, and ways full of allurements than for beauty. **HELEN** was the daughter of Leda, wife of Tyndareus, King of Lacedaemonia <note>Sparta</note>. The poets say that Jove, in love with her, transformed himself into a swan—that is, a very white bird—and thus, lying with her, two eggs were born. From one was born Pollux and Helen, who, having reached mature age, married Menelaus. In those same times, Paris, son of King Priam, was reputed a just judge. Therefore, three goddesses—Juno, Minerva, and Venus—contending over which of them surpassed the others in beauty, referred such a dispute to him. Paris accepted the arbitration, but he judged not without corruption. For he favored Venus because she promised to let him have Helen, the most beautiful of all women. Under this hope, he sailed to Greece and abducted Helen. Though some say he did not abduct her, but she followed him of her own will and came to Troy. This injury moved Greece to lead an army to Troy, and after ten years, they won the city, burned it, and sacked it, and Menelaus recovered Helen. Though Herodotus writes that Helen never came to Troy, but that Paris by chance landed in Egypt, and there she was taken from him by a king named Proteus and kept until Menelaus went for her after the Trojan destruction. Dio Chrysostom perverts this whole story. But in such a multitude of things, one cannot treat each one fully. **FOR WHOM SO MUCH EVIL TIME TURNED.** Flourishing...

# CANTO FIVE

**Greece** The riches of the Trojans were incredible before Helen was abducted. But because of her, all of Greece rose up to recover her, and all of Asia rose to defend Troy. From this followed the slaughter of infinite men. Most excellent princes perished. There arose fires, looting, robbery, and the destruction of many cities. Hence, Petrarch said: *And because of it the world was turned upside down.* <note>original: "Et funne el mondo sottosopra uolto"</note>

**ACHILLES** His origin is from Jove <note>Jupiter</note>, because from Jove and Aegina was born Aeacus; from Aeacus came Peleus; and Peleus, with the sea goddess Thetis, fathered Achilles. His mother dipped him entirely into the Stygian marsh <note>the River Styx</note> except for the heel by which she held him. Therefore, they say he could not be wounded except in the heel. He was raised on Mount Pelion by Chiron the centaur; during that time, he never ate cooked food. For this reason, he was named Achilles: because in Greek, *A* signifies "without" and *chilos* means "cooked food." <note>This is a traditional but folk etymology; modern linguistics suggests different origins for the name.</note> He learned astrology, music, and medicine from Chiron. Later, as Thetis did not want him led to the Trojan war, she brought him while asleep to the island of Scyros to King Lycomedes; there he stayed among the king's daughters in female dress, so that he was not recognized as a male. Yet in that time, Deidamia, the daughter of Lycomedes, bore his son Pyrrhus. Eventually, recognized through the cunning of Ulysses, he was forced to go to Troy, where according to Homer he showed incredible strength. The Trojans never won when Achilles was in battle. But while he was angry with Agamemnon—because he had taken Briseis from him—he refused to fight. Patroclus, dressed in Achilles's armor, went against Hector and was killed by him. Then Thetis had Vulcan forge new armor for him, with which he killed Hector and avenged Patroclus. Although Dio Chrysostom narrates the opposite and proves that Hector killed him, following Homer, Achilles killed Hector and Troilus. Later, having fallen in love with Polyxena, the daughter of Priam, he went to speak with her mother Hecuba in the temple of Thymbraean Apollo to obtain her hand; while kneeling to honor Apollo, he was wounded by an arrow in the heel by Paris, who lay in wait for this purpose. And so he died. Hence the poet said: *Who at the last fought with love.*

**TRISTAN** He was the nephew of Mark, King of Cornwall, and he fell in love with Queen Iseult, the wife of King Mark. The King came upon them in the chamber, and with Tristan’s own spear—which Tristan had left outside the door—he wounded him, thrusting the spear through a hole in the door. Tristan died of that wound shortly thereafter. This was the primary of the knights called "errant," whose deeds are more fabulous than true. On this, Francesco Petrarch said: *Behold, the pages fill with the dreams of Lancelot and Tristan and the other errants.*

> After I had heard my teacher name
> the ancient ladies and the knights,
> pity overcame me, and I was as if lost.

> And I began: "Poet, willingly
> would I speak to those two who go together,
> and seem so light upon the wind."
> And he to me: "You shall see when they are
> closer to us; and then you shall entreat them
> by the love that leads them, and they will come."

**more drawn by the wind:** that is, they had greater pain, which they deserved for being related <note>as in-laws</note> and of high status; because these two circumstances aggravate the sin. Morally speaking, those who are relatives and in high standing are more defamed by their actions. Hence Juvenal says: *Every vice of the soul carries a crime so much more conspicuous as the one who sins is held to be greater.* <note>original: "Omne animi uitium tanto conspectius in se crimē habet quanto maior qui peccat habetur."</note>

> As soon as the wind bends them toward us,
> I moved my voice: "O weary souls,
> come speak to us if another does not deny it."

<column-break/>

This demonstrates that Dante—that is, sensuality—is seized with passion by the pains of the lovers. And he is almost "lost" <note>faints</note> because he deviates from reason, which does not wish for us to have compassion for one who is deservedly tormented. Indeed, pity and mercy are commended when we feel compassion for someone placed in misery undeservedly; but toward one who deserves the punishment, we should have no compassion. Hence he says elsewhere: *Here pity lives when it is well dead; who is more wicked than he who feels passion at God's judgment?* <note>original: "Qui regna la pieta quādo e/ ben morta. chi e/ piu scellerato di colui: chal giudicio di dio passion porta."</note> Nevertheless, considering the quality of the vice of lascivious love: it does not proceed like many other sins from cruelty or any inhumanity (which is entirely against human nature), but rather from a nobility of spirit and from humanity, however ill-regulated it may be. For this reason, it is difficult to resist; since even the wisest have fallen low, it is no wonder if our sensuality feels compassion for them. Petrarch confirms this same idea in his first sonnet when he says: *Where there may be one who understands love through experience, I hope to find pity, not just pardon.* <note>original: "Doue fia chi per pruoua intenda amore Spero trouar pieta non che perdono."</note>

He asks advice from Virgil to see if it seems right to speak with these spirits. Allegorically, this signifies that before we speak or write of something that might bring infamy to another, we must seek the counsel of reason. **WHO TOGETHER go:** because those who sin together are punished together. Furthermore, they share in the same infamy. **AND SEEM so light upon the wind.** Lightness is shown by speed. They were faster because they were...

He made a comparison to doves not only because they are swift in flight, but also because the dove is a bird appropriate to lovers. The dove is a very lustful animal and devoted in love...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, Canto V. Having discussed the various figures of lustful antiquity (Helen, Achilles), the text now transitions to the most famous encounter in the poem: the meeting with Francesca da Rimini and Paolo Malatesta.
