# INFERNO

As doves, called by desire,
with wings raised and steady, come to the sweet nest
through the air, carried by their will;
So these came forth from the rank where Dido is,
coming toward us through the malignant air,
so powerful was the affectionate cry.

"O gracious and benign living being <note>original: "animal." In the medieval sense, this refers to a creature possessing an 'anima' or soul.</note>,
who goes visiting through the dark air
us who stained the world blood-red;
If the King of the Universe <note>A circumlocution for God, whom the damned cannot name directly.</note> were a friend,
we would pray to Him for your peace,
since you have pity on our perverse evil.
Of what it pleases you to hear and to speak,
we will hear and we will speak to you,
while the wind, as it does now, falls silent.
The land where I was born sits
upon the coast where the Po descends
to find peace with its followers.
Love, which is quickly kindled in the gentle heart,
seized this man for the fair body
that was taken from me; and the manner still offends me.
Love, which pardons no one loved from loving in return,
seized me with a delight in him so strong
that, as you see, it does not leave me yet.
Love led us to a single death.
Caina <note>The zone of Hell reserved for those who betrayed their kin, named after Cain.</note> awaits him who extinguished our life."
These words were borne from them to us.

<column-break/>

And for this reason the ancients dedicated doves to Venus, just as the eagle was dedicated to Jove <note>Jupiter</note>, the raven to Phoebus <note>Apollo</note>, the crow to Minerva, the woodpecker to Mars, the peacock to Juno; and similarly other birds to other gods. 

**SO THESE came forth from the rank where Dido is.** That is, where Dido was, of whom we spoke above.

It might perhaps seem to some that these spirits should not speak unless they were first questioned; and furthermore, that the man rather than the woman should speak first. To the first point, one responds that since Dante had requested that they speak, it was easy to know that he desired nothing else than to know something of their lives and their characters. Furthermore, lovers take great pleasure in prosperity and great consolation in adversity when recounting what happened to them in love—especially to one who shows compassion for them, as Dante had shown by those words: "O weary souls, come speak to us if another does not forbid it." For this reason, they often narrate even to those who do not ask. To the second point, there is no doubt that the female is more disturbed by love and more plaintive and sorrowful, and less restrained in speaking, and more loquacious.

**O GRACIOUS and benign living being.** He said "animal" because he saw him with both body and soul; for an "animal" is an animated body. **GRACIOUS and benign.** He said this because he understood it from Dante's words when he said "O weary souls, come speak to us." 

**STAINED the world blood-red.** Because we were killed, and we spilled our blood upon the earth.

**WE WILL HEAR and we will speak to you.** <note>original: "uui," a dialectal form of "voi" (you).</note> The author is accustomed to accommodate some vocabulary of the homeland to whichever character he induces to speak. For this reason, he said *uui* not only to make the rhyme, but because this

---

Lady Francesca was from Romagna. 

**WHILE THE wind, as it does now, falls silent.** This seems contrary to what was said earlier about "the hellish hurricane which never rests." But understand that it was paused for the benefit of Dante as far as these two were concerned. Allegorically, this means that although love is in continuous motion, nonetheless, to one who considers it in others from a position outside of love, it has no fury—just as avarice is considered by one who investigates the nature of vices without any personal greed. 

Then he describes the site of Ravenna, her homeland, which is near the mouth of the Po on the sea. This Po runs with its "followers"—that is, the rivers that enter into it—all the way to the sea; and here, like other rivers, it ceases its course. But we shall speak of the Po in a more convenient place.

**FRANCESCA** was the daughter of Guido da Polenta, Lord of Ravenna, a woman of most excellent beauty and manners. She was the wife of Gianciotto, son of Malatesta, Lord of Rimini, a warlike man of great spirit, but ugly of body and lame <note>original: "scianchato."</note>. He had a brother named Paolo, beautiful of body and of sweet manners and habits, more suited to leisure than to arms—almost a Paris in comparison to a Hector. Because he spent time familiarly with Francesca as a brother-in-law, the long practice gave birth between them to a lascivious love. Finally, reading one day the book of the Round Table <note>The Arthurian legends, specifically the story of Lancelot and Guinevere.</note>, the captive example incited them to a captive act. Continuing in this purpose for some time, Gianciotto noticed it; and having ambushed them and caught them in the act, with one and the same blade and blow, he pierced them both. They say that her mother wanted to give her to Paolo, and Gianciotto went to Ravenna to marry her on his behalf; but seeing her so beautiful, he fell in love and asked for her for himself; and because he was a powerful and terrible man, she was given to him more out of fear than love.

**LOVE, WHICH is quickly kindled in the gentle heart.** It is a true sentiment that the generous and elegant soul—that is, one sharp in choosing—easily loves beautiful things. For love is nothing other than a desire for beauty. We call a "gentle" <note>In the sense of 'noble' or 'refined' (Italian: *gentile*).</note> soul one that is humane, affable, clement, benign, gracious, eager to please, and foreign to the opposite; one which delights in beautiful and well-composed things. It holds in horror all cruelty and ferocity—all of which things demonstrate that such a soul is disposed by nature to love, or rather, to have a universal love for all. Thus, it will be easy to love one person in particular. Many...

<header>CANTO FIVE</header>

...things: and those worthy of being understood remain for me regarding love. But because they are divine and proper to true love, they do not fit in this place, where we treat of lascivious love—which so degenerates and strays from true love that it becomes its opposite. Therefore, I shall defer them to another time when we shall treat of that. **LOVE, WHICH is quickly kindled in the gentle heart.** Here is a rhetorical figure called <term>Sententia</term> <note>A brief statement of a general truth or maxim meant to provide moral guidance.</note>, which is a way of speaking drawn from our life, through which is demonstrated what is done or what reasonably ought to be done. And although it is placed in a particular circumstance, it can nevertheless be transferred to the general, as when Petrarch says: *He does poorly who so quickly forgets such faith*; and *A beautiful death honors a whole life*; and *The pain for others is no less than the first*; and similar phrases. Furthermore, in these three <term>tercets</term> <note>Three-line stanzas, the building blocks of Dante’s poem.</note> there is another rhetorical figure called <term>Repetition</term> <note>Also known as anaphora; the repetition of a word at the beginning of successive clauses.</note>. This is when the same word is repeated several times at the start of clauses, as it is here: *Love, which in the gentle heart... Love, which pardons no one loved... Love led us...* Just so Petrarch did in the song *If I ever said it*. **THE MANNER still offends me:** that is, the manner of this love which was disordered. Because the sin committed offends me at present with its punishment; and morally, every crime committed always offends the delinquent afterward through the remorse of conscience. And certainly, the rational soul cannot exist without love, but it requires the proper "manner" or measure. It does not offend her that she loved, but that she loved in a disordered way. **Caina awaits:** that is, it expects the one who killed us. And <term>Caina</term> is a place that will be mentioned below where traitors and murderers are punished, named after Cain, who was the first murderer, as will be treated more fully there.

---

When I heard those troubled souls,
I bowed my head and held it low,
until the poet said to me: "What are you thinking?"
When I replied, I began: "Alas,
how many sweet thoughts, how much desire,
led them to the woeful pass!"
Then I turned to them and spoke,
and I began: "Francesca, your torments
make me weep, sad and full of pity.
But tell me: in the time of sweet sighs,
by what and how did love grant
that you should know your dubious desires?"

torment more than this. **THAT YOU SHOULD know your dubious desires:** that is, you reached the point where one manifested their desires to the other. For the lover does not dare to reveal himself to the beloved while the desires are "dubious"—that is, not yet known. But once the lover understands that the beloved wants the same thing, then he takes courage to reveal himself.

And she to me: "There is no greater sorrow
than to remember happy times
in misery; and this your teacher knows.
But if you have such a great desire
to know the first root of our love,
I will tell it as one who weeps and speaks.
We were reading one day for delight
of Lancelot, how love constrained him;
we were alone and without any suspicion.
Several times that reading urged our eyes
to meet and drained the color from our faces;
but it was just one point that overcame us.
When we read how the longed-for smile
was kissed by such a great lover,
this man, who shall never be divided from me,
kissed my mouth, all trembling!"

<column-break/>

**H**e shows that sensuality, expressed through Dante, is moved to compassion. And the bowing of the face to the earth signifies that sensuality has more care for the bodily pleasures of which these souls are deprived than for the true and immortal pleasure. But higher reason excites it and makes it stand upright. **HOW MANY sweet sighs.** Certainly, bodily pleasure is very sweet to the senses; but if it is followed, it contains a hidden poison within itself, which leads us to extreme ruin. Whence the Tuscan lyric poet <note>Petrarch</note> excellently said: <note>original: "So chome sta tra fiori ascoso sangue." A misquotation or variant of "l'aspe" (the asp/snake) hidden among flowers.</note> *I know how the snake lies hidden among the flowers.* Therefore, we ought to do with pleasure what the Trojan elders said of Helen: "Certainly this woman is beautiful, but yet let her rather go away than that Troy should perish." Pleasure is a very sweet thing and very delightful to the senses; but let it be left behind rather than the soul perish, because it leads us to the "woeful pass," which is not only the essential Hell <note>The physical place of punishment.</note> but also the moral one, because no perturbation

**W**hen the soul departs from the body pure and without any contagion from any sin, it remains simple in its own nature; nor does it think of anything else except its happiness, which is to enjoy God. And to that end, because it is not burdened by any earthly mass, it flies easily and with supreme desire. But that soul which departs filthy and defiled by sins, in which it has placed all its happiness, desires nothing else except to practice those sins. Whence the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation 14:13</note> excellently says: <note>original: "Opera enim illorum sequuntur illos."</note> *For their works follow them.* And Virgil says: <note>original: "Que gratia curru Armorumque fuit uiuis que cura nitentes Pascere equos eadem sequitur tellure repostos." Aeneid VI.653-5. </note> *The same delight in chariots and arms that they had while living, and the same care to pasture their sleek horses, follows them when they are laid in the earth.* And thinking of the pleasures passed in a time when they can no longer practice them is their great passion and no small torment. This, therefore, he demonstrates as a general truth, saying that no sorrow is greater than to remember happy times in misery. And he adds: **AND THIS YOUR teacher KNOWS.** Because Virgil in the sixth book <note>of the Aeneid</note> signifies this very same sentiment in the verses already mentioned. Others say: **THIS**...

# INFERNO

A Gallehaut was the book and he who wrote it:
that day we read in it no further.
While the one spirit said this,
the other wept so that out of pity
I fainted as if I were dying:
And I fell: as a dead body falls.

<column-break/>

**YOUR doctor KNOWS:** Because he <note>Referring to Virgil, Dante's guide.</note> is currently damned in Limbo and deprived of the glory which he once held near Octavian <note>The Roman Emperor Augustus.</note>. But the first interpretation fits better. Then it follows anyway: for notwithstanding that it is painful to remember happy times in misery, nevertheless it is no small consolation to relate it to one who shows compassion for it. These first two <term>tercets</term> <note>Three-line stanzas.</note> serve as the prologue to her speech. And in the first, she captures attention through the gravity of the rhetorical ornament called <term>sententia</term> <note>A brief, authoritative moral saying.</note>, and also gains goodwill through pity. In the second, she makes the listener attentive.

<column-break/>

Then in the third, the narration begins, which the poet makes brief—because he places nothing superfluous there—and clear and open, because he observes proper order and uses plain words. It is also believable, because he shows that all the means that could lead to such an end were present. First, the reading of amorous things and similar cases, which could make even those who do not love fall in love. And everyone understands that an example easily moves one to do the same, especially when it carries the authority of respected persons, such as Lancelot and Guinevere. Then, because they were alone, and finally, without suspicion. These conveniences could lead into sin even one who had not previously been inclined to it; for as the proverb says: *Before an open chest, even the righteous man sins.* <note>Italian: "A archa aperta giusto ui pecca." A warning that opportunity creates the thief—or the sinner.</note> This demonstrates the craft of the writing, but morally it shows that idleness, lascivious readings, and the example of those who have done what we wish to do—especially if they are persons of authority—along with the convenience of place and time, easily induce men to lascivious and forbidden love. **WE READ one day for delight.** To read for delight signifies being in idleness. For he who is occupied does not seek amusement, but seeks to finish his business. Therefore, they were in idleness; and idleness, together with lascivious amusement, generates carnal love. Whence Petrarch says: *And born of idleness and human lasciviousness*; and Ovid: *If you take away idleness, Cupid's bows perish* <note>original Latin: "Otia si tollas periere cupidinis arcus"</note>; and Terence shows Menedemus's son that idleness is what makes men fall into lasciviousness, just as for profit, labor and occupation preserve chastity. On this, Juvenal says: *Humble fortune once kept the Latin women chaste, and did not permit their small homes to be touched by vice: labor, short slumbers, and hands worn and hardened by the Tuscan wool, and Hannibal near the city [kept them so].* <note>original Latin: "Prestabat castas humilis fortuna latinas / Quondam nec uitiis contingi parua sinebat / Tecta labor somnique breues / et uellere tusco / Vexate dureque manus et proximus urbi / Hanibal."</note> **OF LANCELOT, how love constrained him.** In Dante's time, a book called *The Round Table* was highly prized. In it, it is written that Lancelot was in love with Guinevere, the wife of King Mark <note>The commentator likely means King Arthur, though medieval traditions sometimes blurred these details.</note>. And Gallehaut was the go-between so that they could be joined. Therefore, this book and the one who wrote it was a "Gallehaut"—that is, he was a go-between for us, just as Gallehaut was for Lancelot and Guinevere. The book was thus a go-between for us because, under the guise of reading the book, we could discuss other things; and the one who wrote it was also a go-between because his lascivious verses moved us to love. **MANY times that reading drove our eyes together and drained the color from our faces.** That reading pushed our eyes together because, reading of such things in others which we desired for ourselves, each looked at the other before hesitating to begin. **AND DRAINED the color from our faces:** that is, it made us pale, which color is proper to lovers. Whence Ovid: *Let every lover turn pale; this color is fitting for one who loves.* <note>original Latin: "Palleat omnis amans color est hic aptus amanti."</note> Our faces paled from the sudden and great distress that the soul felt. **BUT JUST one point was what overcame us.** For when we arrived in our reading at that passage where it was pleasing to Guinevere to be kissed, both he and I agreed to do the same. And it follows: **THIS ONE:** that is, Paolo. **WHO NEVER shall be divided from me:** referring to the sentence already mentioned above, that after death they strive to practice the same sin. **MY MOUTH he kissed, all trembling.** He expresses by this trembling the great emotion which is in the lover. **A GALLEHAUT was the book.** That is, the book was a go-between, as has already been said. **THAT DAY we read in it no further:** As if to say, we were occupied with other things; and with very honest words he hints at that which cannot be said openly without a blush; as Terence says: *What then? What then, you fool?* <note>original Latin: "Quid tum? Quid tum Fatue."</note> **WHILE THE one spirit:** that is, Francesca. **the other:** that is, Paolo **WEPT:** to show that he was in no less pain. **SO THAT out of pity:** and so forth. Here, through this compassion of his, he demonstrates the very thing we said above regarding sensuality.

# SIXTH CANTO OF THE FIRST CANTICLE OF DANTE

At the return of my mind, which had closed
before the pity for the two kinsmen <note>Referring to Paolo and Francesca from the previous Canto, whose tragic story caused Dante to faint.</note>:
which had utterly confounded me with sadness,
New torments and new tormented souls
I see around me, however I move,
and however I turn, and however I gaze.
I am in the third circle, that of the rain:
eternal, accursed, cold, and heavy;
its rule and quality are never new <note>Meaning the nature of the torment is unchanging and unrelenting.</note>.
Great hail, turgid water, and snow
pour down through the dark air;
the earth stinks that receives this.

<column-break/>

After the sin of lust, he appropriately places that which the Greeks call <term>gastrimargia</term> <note>original: "gastrimargia"; literally "stomach-madness" or gluttony.</note>, and by the Latins is called gluttony. But to better define this sin and the one treated above: nature, wanting animals to endure for the time she prescribes to them, and wanting the species to be immortal through succession, first placed pleasure in eating and drinking. For the animate body being composed of these four qualities—hot, dry, moist, and cold—and the heat continually consuming the moist and dry parts, the animal would perish in a very short space of time if, from hand to hand, matter were not supplied to take the place of that which has perished. Therefore, when the "dry" is diminished in the animal, a desire and appetite is born

<column-break/>

called hunger: through which we crave food, which, once digested and finalized, is converted into the substance of the body and restores the parts we lack. And when the "moist" is diminished, thirst is born, which craves drink to supply the consumed moisture. Eating and drinking being thus necessary, nature placed pleasure in food and drink so that the animal, moved by such pleasure, might be more inclined to maintain its life. Whoever, therefore, for such refreshment and restoration takes food and drink at the proper intervals of time, and in such quantity that it is not too much, and in such quality that it is not harmful, and has respect only for necessity, does not sin—even though such food or drink gives him pleasure. But he who has no respect for necessity, but seeks only pleasure, and to achieve that either exceeds moderation or is more occupied than is required in seeking sweet and exquisite flavors: this man sins and is called a glutton. Similarly, the species would not endure—because every animal comes to death—if while they are alive they did not generate those who would succeed them. Nature, fearing that negligence or the labor involved in nourishing and raising children might hinder such generation, placed pleasure in coitus. Therefore, he who uses this not to seek pleasure but to generate children—and uses it when, how, and with whom is appropriate—does not sin. He who does otherwise, sins. The gluttonous are therefore punished in this third circle. And the poet shows that, returning to himself, he found himself among them. And as for the essential Hell, he assigns a fitting penalty, because every sin must be punished by its opposite <note>The principle of <term>contrapasso</term>, where the punishment either mirrors or contrasts the sin.</note>. Therefore, where the pleasure had been in the finest wines and the sweetest foods and exquisite dishes, the penalty is cold and heavy rain, and foul water in place of wine; and in place of food, there is hail and snow. And as for the moral sense, everyone understands that overindulgence and drunkenness cause various humors and catarrhs to descend from the head, which induce apoplexy, tremors, coldness of the nerves, and a stupor of the soul. And this is denoted by the "dark air," because they induce gloom and oblivion in the soul; which humors, having fallen into the stomach, if they do not create stench, they rot. And all this generates pains of the head, the stomach, the sides, and gout, which make men howl like dogs. And it is a true sentiment and a common proverb: that the throat kills many more than the sword. **RULE AND QUALITY**: because similar effects always arise. Therefore, it is "never new"—that is, it is not unusual—because that rule and quality is always the same.

---

Cerberus, a beast cruel and strange,
with three throats barks like a dog
over the people who are submerged here.
His eyes are red, his beard greasy and black,
his belly large, and his hands clawed;
he scratches the spirits, flays, and quarters them.
The rain makes them howl like dogs;
with one side they make a screen for the other;
often the miserable profanes turn themselves.

<column-break/>

**Cerberus the beast.** Hesiod, the Greek poet, writes that Cerberus was the dog of Pluto with three heads, the son of Typhaon the giant and Echidna the serpent. And from the same parents he says was born Orthus, the dog of Geryon, and the Chimera, which had three heads: one of a lion, one of a dragon, and one of a goat. And we demonstrated in the allegories of Virgil <note>Referring to the commentator's own previous work or the tradition of interpreting Virgil's Aeneid.</note> that Cerberus stands for the necessities of the body: which are food, drink, and sleep, without which three things the animal cannot live. Therefore, Dante has most excellently placed him in this location, because gluttony consists in food and drink when we exceed in them, as has already been said. **CERBERUS, a beast cruel and strange**:

<column-break/>

This serves the fiction; and he is cruel because of the pain he inflicts. **STRANGE** from other beasts, or "strange" because he has different mouths. **CRUEL**, because gluttony consumes everything. Whence Juvenal <note>A Roman satirist known for his critiques of social vices.</note> says: *Who* <note>original: "Quis"; This is the beginning of a quote from Juvenal's Satires (likely Satire I.140: 'Quis ferat istas luxuriae sordes?'), cut off by the end of the page.</note>

<summary>This page introduces Canto VI of the Inferno, where Dante enters the circle of the Gluttonous. The accompanying commentary provides a physiological and moral analysis of gluttony, defining it as an excess of the natural urge for survival, and explains Cerberus as an allegory for bodily needs.</summary>

<columns>2</columns>
<header>INFERNO</header>

...for as your purse fails you and your gluttony grows, there remains an end to your father’s wealth; and with your riches sunk into a belly capable of holding interest payments, heavy silver, flocks, and fields. <note>original: "enim te deficiente crumena... capacem"; This is a quotation from Juvenal’s Satires (XI), describing how a glutton consumes their entire inheritance.</note> **Diverse**: because the glutton is not content with a simple food, but seeks a diversity of them from the earth, the sea, and the air. **BARKS**: "latrare" in the Latin language means to bark. **THE EYES** he has are vermilion: Regarding the fiction, he gives him red eyes to demonstrate the wrath of the beast. For every angry person has red eyes. And regarding the allegory, it shows that such an effect is caused by superfluous food, and especially wine. **THE GREASY BEARD**. Which is characteristic of gluttons. By the greasy beard, he signifies the greed of those who crowd themselves too much in devouring, because not only the mouth, but the whole face becomes oily. The large belly demonstrates the engorging of food. Whence the prophet says: **Whose god is their belly** <note>original: "Quorum deus uenter est"; a reference to Philippians 3:19, describing those who live for physical pleasure.</note>. **CLAWED** hands. This denotes rapacity and greed for food, because he snatches that which he devours. **HE SCRATCHES**, swallows, and flays. He places before the eyes the voracity of the gluttonous; and on the other hand, he demonstrates the torments that men suffer for the vice of the throat, through which they fall into various diseases where it is necessary to both cut and apply fire, and in many ways tear the body. And he adds that they howl, to demonstrate various pains. Whence it happens that stomachs, sides, gout, and fevers give great pain. But they have a proverb: "One morsel, and two woes." **FROM ONE OF THE SIDES** they make a shield for the other: that is, a defense. This shows that from the throat is born the illness which induces turning now on this side and now on that. **WRETCHED** profane ones. Profane in the Latin language means **far from the temple** <note>original: "procul a fano"</note>: that is, far from the temple and from religious things. Whence they call "profane" those who are wicked and contrary to all religion.

When Cerberus, the great worm, noticed us,
he opened his mouths and showed us his fangs;
not a limb of his stayed still.
My leader stretched out his palms:
he took the earth, and with full fists
he threw it into those craving gullets.
As is the dog that, barking, yearns,
and then grows quiet once he bites his food,
for he only intends and struggles to devour it.
Such became those filthy faces
of the demon Cerberus, who so thunders
at the souls that they would wish they were deaf.

<column-break/>

The necessity of the body gives no small impediment to the man who directs himself toward the contemplative life and the investigation of divine things. For without sustenance and without food, life cannot be maintained. And then it happens that upon this natural necessity, depraved and corrupt habit craves many more delicacies and varieties of food than nature requires, which is content with little. Whence Cicero says: **Nature is satisfied with few and very small things** <note>original: "Paucis minimisque natura contenta est"</note>. Therefore, having to think about things for sustenance is a great impediment to the man who wants to go toward contemplation, as food is necessary for life. But the wise man realizes that Cerberus—that is, such necessity—can be satisfied with things of little cost. Returning then to the text: he calls Cerberus a **great worm**, because a worm is born of putrefaction and feeds on earth; and by Cerberus is understood the appetite, which we have already said is for earthly things. **THE MOUTHS** he opened: which are three as we demonstrated; and it demonstrates hunger. And by feigning him in the form of a dog, he does not depart from the canine nature, which, when it craves food or is angry, moves all its limbs. **MY LEADER**: That is, the rational part, to quiet the natural appetite, took the earth in as much abundance as he could. For he stretched his palms over the earth and then gathered it, squeezing it in his fists; where the earth denotes vile foods, and both fists denote the abundance of them, because the body should be fed abundantly, but with vile foods. And certainly nature, if not depraved by custom, is content with little. Whence Lucan: **Learn by how little it is permitted to prolong life, and how much nature requires** <note>original: "Discite quam paruo liceat producere uitam : Et quantum natura petat"</note>. And elsewhere: **The river and grain are enough for the people** <note>original: "Satis est populis fluuiusque ceresque"</note>. **THREW IT** into the craving gullets: And this denotes that food should not be offered to the body unless it is famished. And not without reason did he throw it not into the mouth—where through the palate one tastes the sweetness of food—but into the pipes of the throat, at which place once it has taken the food it grows quiet. This denotes that he who eats for necessity and not for gluttony is not occupied in tasting and savoring, but it is enough for him that the stomach receives the necessary food. **AS IS THE** dog. He equates Cerberus to the dog, which, barking from hunger, grows quiet after it has taken food. And certainly the appetite asks for no more. **DEAFENS** <note>original: "CHENTRONA"; meaning "intronare" (to stun or deafen as if by thunder).</note>. It is called "intronare" from "tonitruo"—that is, from thunder—every time the voice is so great that, besides being heard, it even offends the sense of hearing as if it were thunder. For our senses are in a certain proportion to sensible things; and going out of such proportion, if the sensible thing is lacking, the sense does not do its duty. For a voice too small is not heard. And if it exceeds, it corrupts the sense. Whence they say that those who are where the Nile falls, by the immeasurable noise of that river, become deaf. They have then, besides the other punishments, also this one: that continually Cerberus deafens them. And in life it also happens that gluttons are stunned and excited by this vice; and the more they fill themselves, the more they crave. And allegorically you will understand that he who wants to go toward speculation, as Dante goes, is stunned by Cerberus—that is, he is dismayed by the thought of necessary things—unless he quiets it as we have said. <meta>catchword: Follows</meta>

<summary>This page provides an allegorical and moral commentary on Cerberus in Dante's Inferno, explaining him as a symbol of bodily appetite and the "great worm" of earthly desire. Landino argues that reason (Virgil) must satisfy the body's basic needs with simple things to allow the mind to pursue higher contemplation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, Canto VI. It transitions from the physical description of the gluttons' punishment to the first specific encounter with a Florentine soul, Ciacco. The commentary bridges the gap between the literal scene of the rain-soaked shadows and the allegorical meaning of their physical state.</meta>

# CANTO SIX

We were passing over the shadows that the heavy
rain subdues: and we were placing our feet
upon their emptiness: which seems like people.
They all lie upon the ground, every one of them,
except for one who sat up quickly
as soon as he saw us passing before him.
"O you who are led through this hell,"
he said to me, "recognize me if you can:
you were made before I was unmade."
And I to him: "The anguish you have
perhaps pulls you out of my memory,
so that it does not seem I ever saw you:
But tell me who you are: who are placed in such
a mournful location: and have such a penalty,
that if any other is greater, none is more displeasing."

And he to me: "Your city, which is so full
of envy that the sack already overflows,
held me within it in the serene life.
You citizens called me Ciacco
for the damnable fault of the throat:
as you see, I am broken by the rain:"

<column-break/>

The journey continues, accomplished by him. And although he must deal with souls—which, because they are incorporeal, cannot be perceived by sight, hearing, touch, or any other bodily sense—it is nevertheless necessary to imagine them in such a way that they may be seen and heard. This is easily granted to the poet. Furthermore, many hold that souls can take on an aerial body; which, despite yielding to the touch—like a cloud, for example—is nonetheless seen and forms a voice that is heard. Hence he says that they trod upon the shadows, which were empty things as far as touch was concerned, but to the sight they appeared to be persons. Virgil imagines this same thing when he says: *Three times he attempted to throw his arms around his neck; three times the image, grasped in vain, escaped his hands.* <note>original: "Ter conatus ibi collo dare bracchia circum Ter frustra comprensa manus effugit imago"; Virgil, Aeneid VI, 700-702.</note> **PERSONS**: that is, men; for so we say in our language, although in Latin it has a different meaning. **SUBDUES** <note>term: "ADONA" (from the Italian 'adonare'). The commentator explains this as gathering or huddling together.</note>: which gathers and collects. And he imagines this because heavy rain commonly makes many people gather together, so that one might better defend the other from the elements. He depicts the gluttonous lying on the ground because no vice makes a man more base and more inclined toward earthly things. The lustful man loves a person, even if he loves the basest part of them. The envious man is moved by greater things. The greedy man seeks riches, which are instruments for many things. All these sin and have their minds occupied with base things, but the subject of the glutton is the basest of all, because his highest good is in his belly, and he becomes much more like a sheep than a man. Hence Virgil and Dante—that is, Reason and the Appetite obedient to Reason—tread upon such base men who in appearance seem like men. But they are not, because they retain nothing of the human except the bodily image and appearance. And Reason and Virtue, which alone make us human, are not in them. Thus, in their habits they are beasts, because they are obedient to the belly. This, as Sallust says, is characteristic of beasts. And certainly one can say that a man is vain and entirely empty who has nothing left but that which is common to us and the brute animals. 

Furthermore, Ciacco’s words serve the historical narrative, because in truth he died during the time when Dante was alive, and they had known each other in life. Therefore, *you were made*—that is, created and born—*before I was unmade*—that is, dead. And it is reasonable regarding the essential Hell that such martyrdom changes the form and features of the sinner so that it is not easy to recognize him. Regarding the moral sense, Dante—that is, the lower reason and the appetite following it—existed before Ciacco died: that is, before the sin of gluttony perished. But in the course of time Ciacco dies, and Dante remains alive. Because in a man’s first youth, in which appetite has more power than reason, this sin lives. But once reason is strengthened and the appetite remains subject to it, the vice of gluttony perishes in the man, and the man remains alive; it slips so far into oblivion that he does not recognize it unless he encounters it in his path—that is, in contemplating vices, it does not occur to his mind. And certainly this sin pulls the human soul so far out of its nature that it no longer has the likeness of a rational thing, but appears entirely like a sheep. 

**EXCEPT FOR ONE who sat up quickly**. Because he immediately came to Dante’s mind as he was speculating on this vice; and he did not rise except to a sitting position, because although a base person occurs to our imagination, they do not rise up very high. He chooses Ciacco rather than another noble and rich man because the vice of gluttony is more condemned in the poor and the commoner than in the rich and powerful. Whence Juvenal says: *Atticus is considered exceptionally elegant if he dines sumptuously; if Rutilus does it, he is considered insane.* <note>original: "atticus eximie si cenat lautus habetur Si rutilus demes"; Juvenal, Satire XI. The poet argues that luxury is seen as a virtue in the rich but a madness in the poor.</note> **THAT IF ANY OTHER IS GREATER, none is so displeasing.** There is no doubt that pride and avarice are greater vices, and consequently deserve greater punishment. Nevertheless, this one is more displeasing because in those others there is some excuse and some part of a manly spirit. But the glutton lies in the mud like a pig, and the soul in that body does nothing worthy of a human. It can even be said that to such men the soul is given in place of salt: because it serves no other purpose than to preserve the body so that it does not rot and corrupt. <note>This is a common medieval trope: that a glutton's soul is just a preservative for their meat.</note>

He leads Ciacco to revile envy, which in those times reigned in our republic. Because he tacitly wished to report that his exile did not proceed from his own failings, but from the envy of his adversaries. **THAT THE SACK ALREADY OVERFLOWS in the serene life.** He imitates Virgil, who induces those who are in Hell to always praise the living life, as here: *Those who, deprived of sweet life and snatched from the breast...* <note>original: "Quos dulcis uite exortes et ubere raptos"; Virgil, Aeneid VI, 428.</note>

<meta>This page continues the commentary by Cristoforo Landino on Canto VI of Dante's Inferno. Having introduced the soul of Ciacco, the text now explains his name, his character, and begins the famous political prophecy regarding the fate of Florence.</meta>

# INFERNO

<note>original Latin: "Abstulit atra dies funerique immersit acerbo."</note> "A dark day stole him away and plunged him into a bitter death." And certainly, as human life compared to the heavenly spirits can be called miserable, so by comparing it to the infernal places it shall be deemed happy. Alternatively, he said **IN THE** serene life because in his times Florence was in a very tranquil state, which at present was most disturbed. **YOU CALLED ME** Ciacco. <term>Ciacco</term> in the Florentine tongue signifies "pig"; and because this animal is born only to grow fat and fill its belly, it happened that this man was so named by his fellow citizens. They say he was a man of great eloquence, full of urbanity, witty remarks, and jests, and of the sweetest conversation—not unwise, and in other matters worthy of being loved. But he was such a slave to the <term>gluttony</term><note>The sin of overindulgence in food and drink, punished in this circle of Hell.</note> that in a short time he consumed his substance. Like a <term>mountebank</term> and a parasite, he frequented the houses of the powerful, and with his jests and witticisms he "hunted" for good morsels. Giovanni Boccaccio makes mention of him on the ninth day, in the novella of Lauretta, and demonstrates how dexterously and with wit he took revenge on Biondello. **AND I,** a sad soul, am not alone. Every glutton is commonly ashamed of such a vice, but they excuse themselves by alleging that they have many companions in it.

I began: "Ciacco, your distress
weighs on me so that it invites me to weep;
but tell me, if you know, what they shall come to,
the citizens of the divided city?
If any there is just; and tell me the reason
why such great discord has assailed it?"
And he to me: "After long contention,
they shall come to blood; and the woodland party
shall chase out the other with much offense.
Then it is necessary that this one falls
within three suns, and that the other rises
by the strength of one who currently coasts.
It shall hold its forehead high for a long time,
keeping the other under heavy weights,
however much it may weep or feel shamed by it.
Two are just, but they are not heard there:
pride, envy, and avarice are
the three sparks that have set hearts ablaze."

<column-break/>

To many it seems an absurd thing for the poet to induce a man of such low status to speak of great things and give him the divination of future events. But whoever considers his intellect will see that—as Boccaccio also demonstrates—he was a man of no small prudence, which at first was natural to him, and then increased greatly through long practice and the constant habit and familiarity he had with all the citizens of Florence, both of one faction and the other. Thus, he knew the ambition, the desire, and the passions of each, through which, with the sharpness of his easy intellect, he could conjecture the future. Dante, therefore, questions him not as a parasite and glutton, but as one who is shrewd and, through long experience, learned in the customs, the wills, the honors, and the minds of the governors of the republic—things which were causes that could easily produce the effects he predicts. **I BEGAN:** "Ciacco, your distress..." An excellent opening for an oration, through which he makes Ciacco well-disposed by showing compassion for his pain; and this induces him to respond willingly. Then he briefly poses his request, which contains three parts: The first, that he tell him the future. The second, who in Florence might be just.

---

The third, the cause of the civil discord. **DIVIDED CITY:** The citizenry divided into Whites and Blacks. Nor does it please me that in this place "divided" should be understood as being between Romans and Fiesolans, because the first interpretation is more to the purpose. **IF YOU KNOW:** Because he doubts whether the damned have knowledge of the future. But he will speak more fully of this in the tenth Canto. **AND HE TO ME:** Ciacco responds in order, and first to the first part. For the declaration of these words, it is to be noted that the Florentine Republic in the year 1300 was in the highest reputation, opulence, and serene tranquility. As has happened to many other cities, it occurred that too much prosperity gave birth to most grave discord. The worst seed of this, like many others, came from Pistoia. For the Cancellieri family, then most powerful there, was divided into two factions by internal discord: one called the Blacks, the other the Whites. Having occupied that entire city and the places near it, the discord penetrated as far as Florence. In those times, the Donati and the Cerchi were families and neighbors, and nearly equal in power. The Cerchi were powerful in wealth, which, although they were "new" to the city (having come a short time before from Acone in the Val di Sieve), made them arrogant and won them great favor with the common people. The Donati, as much as they were surpassed in wealth, so much did they surpass in antiquity of blood; they were highly esteemed for the virtue of Messer Corso, the head of that house, whose name was celebrated throughout Italy. But they were somewhat suspect to the common people, as if they directed their minds toward a tyrannical life rather than a civic one. This meant that the Cerchi, being more "of the people," were more loved by the populace. The head of the Whites was thus Messer Vieri de' Cerchi, and of the Blacks, Messer Corso Donati. As a grave calamity prepared itself for the city through such division, Pope Boniface VIII attempted to persuade Messer Vieri to reconcile with Messer Corso. But he—either because the adverse fates of our republic so willed it, or because passion could do more in the knight than reason—was not obedient. Instead, he said he did not wish to make peace because he was not at war. Not long after, as contentions arose between several members of both sides at a dance, the nose of Ricoverino was cut off...

### CANTO SIX
<sig>e.ii.</sig>

...of the Cerchi. Later, seeing himself in such grave danger, Messer Corso <note>Corso Donati, the leader of the "Black" faction in Florence.</note> managed to have Pope Boniface send someone from the house of France to Florence: one who would take the government of the republic away from the Cerchi and from the popular leaders. Because of this, such great indignation was stirred up that he [Corso], along with many of his supporters, was sent into exile. But fortune did not strip Corso of his prudence and assistance. Always helping himself secretly together with Geri degli Spini, they persuaded Boniface to call into Italy Charles "Lackland" <term>sanza terra</term><note>Charles of Valois, brother of King Philip IV of France; he was called "Lackland" because he held many titles but possessed no kingdom of his own.</note>, brother of Philip the Fair, King of France. Not long after, he caused Boniface to die; and he let Charles Lackland pass. This man came under the guise of settling civil discords and afterwards passing against the Sicilians to help Charles II. Having therefore given a favorable answer to the Florentine ambassadors and showing that he came to pacify that republic, he was most honorably received in the city; and with an oath that he would preserve its tranquility, he was granted supreme authority to settle every controversy. But his greedy soul, already corrupted by the money of Messer Musciatto the Frenchman, a Florentine knight (who had brought him to Italy at his own expense), valuing their [money] more than faith, he abandoned the common cause. Wholly turned to the favors of Messer Corso, he brought him back into the city with many of his friends. Whence the Whites were oppressed with great calamity. And although Cardinal Matteo d'Acquasparta came to Florence and reconciled both parties together, nonetheless the Blacks, who were more powerful, did not allow the Whites to have any portion in the government of the city. The Cardinal departed in anger. Therefore, such peace lasted little. Because Simone, son of Messer Corso, killed Messer Niccolò de' Cerchi; although he had first been wounded by him. And finally, some excellent men of the White party, being summoned to judgment and fearing to appear, fled, some to Pisa and some to Arezzo. Two joined the Florentine Ghibellines, who were then rebels; and in this number was our poet, as we showed in his life. And Charles confiscated their goods. I have discussed these few things among many, not to tell a history, but to open the meaning of the text.

Therefore it says **AFTER LONG** tension: that is, long contention. **THEY SHALL COME** to blood: that is, to slaughter as I have said. **AND THE** savage party: that is, the White party, whose heads were the Cerchi, men new to the city, having come a short time before from Acone and from the woods of Valdisieve. Whence in the sixteenth [canto] of *Paradiso* it says: "The Cerchi would be in the rains of Acone." **THAT THIS [ONE] FALLS**: that is, the Whites. **WITHIN** three suns: within three solar years. And although the ancients say <note>original Latin: "Tres soles"</note> "three suns," meaning three days, nonetheless the poet said "three suns" for three solar years. For the ancients posited three types of years: the Lunar, which is from one conjunction of the moon with the sun until the next. And this space is some hours less than thirty days. Because it stays in each sign [of the zodiac] two days, six hours, and two-thirds of an hour. Because in twenty-seven days and eight hours it returns to where it had departed from the sun. But because the sun has moved in that time more than twenty-seven degrees of a sign, it consumes the rest until it catches up and joins with it. The second year is Solar: that is, when the sun has made its revolution through all twelve signs of the zodiac, which is three hundred and sixty-five days, six hours, and the hundredth part of an hour. And of this the poet means; and commonly when saying "year" this is understood, because the solar course makes all the seasons. The third year is called by astrologers the "Great Year"; which is when, all courses being finished, the sun with all the other planets begins the courses again from the same sign. Which space, although opinions have varied, they commonly say is thirty-six thousand years.

**WITH THE FORCE** of such who now coasts. To coast <term>piaggiare</term><note>A nautical metaphor for staying close to the shore, or figuratively, being undecided, playing both sides, or "hedging."</note> is to stay in the middle: because we say "coasting" of one who goes shore to shore, as if between sea and land. Or truly "coasts": that is, he has not yet given his sails to the wind, but stays on the beach and is not moved; and it refers to Charles Lackland, as we have said. **HOLD HIGH its forehead**: You shall live in great state. **LONG TIME**: Especially until the violent death of Messer Corso, which will be told in the twenty-fourth [canto] of *Purgatorio*. **MAY YOU NOT GRIEVE**: <note>original: "nadonti," meaning "ne adonti"</note> that is, do not have shame or spite. **TWO ARE JUST**. Brother Guido del Carmine <note>A Carmelite friar and early commentator on Dante.</note> said in the commentary he made on twenty-seven chapters of this book: that these two were Dante and Messer Guido Cavalcanti. Some understand that the two just are divine and human law, and these are not understood [obeyed] there, as if to say: that divine and human laws are well-ordered in Florence, but they are not understood because they are not observed. **AND THEY ARE NOT** understood there: because faith is not given to their counsels. **PRIDE AND ENVY AND AVARICE**; It did not seem likely that without very great causes a most flourishing state, as was that of our republic in those times—strengthened by the very great riches that were in the city, both public and private, and by no small reputation and authority that it had throughout all Italy—should fall into such calamity. Therefore he posits the causes that are to be, from which then proceeds supreme discord; and as Sallust writes: <note>original Latin: "Concordia parve res crescunt Discordia etiam maxime dilabuntur."</note> "Through harmony small things grow; through discord even the greatest fall apart." He says the causes of the future discord are three vices: Pride, envy, and avarice. Nor is there a vice that more arouses discord in peoples than these three. Discord is born when equality is removed, which happens when citizens want to overreach; and this is born either from wanting more honor than is their due—which is pride and ambition—or from wanting to become rich unjustly and seeking to control the magistrates and judgments, and for this they snatch from the public and the private. This is nothing other than avarice. Or from grieving at the good of others, which does not harm them. Whence envy is born. Therefore he concludes that every time citizens in their republic do not hunger for more honor and more convenience and utility than honesty permits, and will not have envy of those who are deservedly honored, they will always live in supreme harmony. Nor can any...

Here he put an end to the mournful sound;
and I yet want him to teach me,
and to grant me the gift of further speech.
Farinata and Tegghiaio, who were so worthy,
Iacopo Rusticucci, Arrigo, and Mosca,
and the others who set their minds to doing good:
Tell me where they are, and let me recognize them;
for a great desire compels me to know

And he: "They are among the blacker souls;
different sins weigh them down further to the bottom;
if you descend that far, you will be able to see them.
But when you have returned to the world,
I pray that you bring me to the memory of others;

He then turned his straight eyes askance,
looked at me a little, then bowed his head;
he fell with it level with the other blind ones.

<column-break/>

He had already put an end to his sound, that is, his **MOURNFUL** sermon: that is, worthy of tears and compassion, announcing so many calamities for the fatherland. But Dante, having heard about the republic in general, desired to hear in particular about these citizens, who in civil government had been of great spirit and prudence. But as happens in the life of mortals for the most part: that great virtues were accompanied by great vices; so in these men the clear light was obscured by dark shadows. This made the poet uncertain as to which had more power: virtue in elevating them to heaven, or vice in depressing them to hell. And morally he doubted, having examined every work of their lives, which was greater: merit or demerit, praise or blame. As, for example, if we wished to judge Caesar: we would examine in him on one hand supreme clemency, supreme liberality, no mediocre learning, admirable eloquence, an unconquered spirit, and most excellent military discipline. On the other hand, we would see the ambition through which he did violence to his country and forced it to bear the yoke. And in such an examination we would remain doubtful as to which is greater in this man: virtue or vice, praise or blame. And this seems to me the true meaning of the text.

---

Nor do I approve of the opinion of those who claim that the poet speaks ironically, and that in truth he means that in them there were supreme vices without any virtue. This can be refuted not only by the words of the present stanzas, but also by what he will say below. For of Sir Farinata degli Uberti he will make mention in the tenth chapter <note>Canto X, where Farinata appears among the Heretics.</note>; and of Sir Tegghiaio Aldobrandi and Sir Iacopo Rusticucci in the sixteenth <note>Canto XVI, among the Sodomites.</note>. **ARRIGO** was a noble knight of the Fisanti, an ancient and honored family. Of Mosca dei Lamberti he will make mention in chapter twenty-eight <note>Canto XXVIII, among the Sowers of Discord.</note>. And then we will narrate more extensively of their lives and characters. **WHO WERE SO** worthy: As if he almost grieves that, having been so celebrated for their great virtues, nevertheless all who had witnessed them should be made to doubt. **WHO SET THEIR** minds to doing good: As if to say that they turned the sharpness of their natural intellect toward laudable works. He shows a desire to know their end, because naturally every good person desires that men adorned with virtue be led to a happy port, even though they recognize vices in them. **IF HEAVEN** sweetens them: Because beatitude gives sweetness and delight. And hell contains within itself supreme misery, which is such a poison to the soul; for although the soul is immortal, one can still say that it kills it like a toxin by depriving it of the sight of God, who is life. **Poison** <term>Tosco</term> we say in Florentine from what the Latins call <term>Toxicum</term> <note>original Latin: "toxicum"</note>, and they take it for every poison. But *toxicum* properly is that which is made from the yew tree <term>taxo</term> <note>the yew tree, Latin: *taxus*</note>, which we call <term>nasso</term>.

Ciacco responds: that these are further down among the blacker souls, that is, damned in a darker place. And it is an imitation of Virgil, who, wanting to say Daphnis was a celestial soul, said: *The radiant one wonders at the unfamiliar threshold of Olympus* <note>original Latin: "Candidus insuetum miratur limen olimpi"</note>. Therefore, if those of heaven are radiant (white), those of hell are black. Furthermore, white stands for pure and immaculate, and black for the opposite. Whence Juvenal: *Who turn black into white* <note>original Latin: "Qui nigra in candida uertunt"</note>. And Horace: *This man is black; beware of him, Roman* <note>original Latin: "Hic niger est hunc tu romane caueto"</note>. 

To the sweet world: that is, to the place where men live, which he calls sweet because in it they can fulfill their carnal desires, which the soul polluted with vices pulls along with it. Or he said "sweet" in comparison to hell, in which whoever is there would willingly return to the labors they endured in life. Whence Virgil: *How they would wish now to endure both poverty and hard labors in the high air!* <note>original Latin: "Quam uellent ethere in alto nunc et pauperiem et duros perferre labores"</note>. And he prays him to keep him in memory, to show that even those who are in the lowest state and damned for abominable vices desire fame. Furthermore, Ciacco was in a place where he could ask for nothing else. **HIS EYES** [once] straight, [turned] askance: "Askance" <term>bieco</term> by corruption derives from "oblique," which means a thing placed crosswise. Nor does his looking in this way demonstrate anything other than that he thought with pain at the same time of both past pleasures and present pains, and then, moved by despair, he threw himself down to lie [in the mud].

the body is sown in weakness, it shall rise in power <note>original Latin: "corpus in infirmitate surget in uirtute". A reference to 1 Corinthians 15:43.</note>. Therefore, at present, the body cannot satisfy the speed and lightness of the soul: but it will be able to do so then. Hence the Wisdom of Solomon says in the third chapter regarding the just: "They shall run to and fro like sparks among the reeds" <note>original Latin: "Quod tanquam scintille in arundineto discurrent". From Wisdom 3:7.</note>. No deformity shall be in these bodies: and they shall be exempt from things that clash with a state of incorruption while enjoying delights. And just as the blessed soul will participate in the highest divine goodness as much as its nature allows: so the body of such a soul will participate, as much as is possible for it, in the soul's properties through the clarity of the senses, the ordering of bodily appetites, and in every perfection of nature. The aforementioned Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> addressed this question in the same place where he says: "It is sown a natural body, it shall rise a spiritual body" <note>original Latin: "Seminatur corpus animale surget corpus spirituale". From 1 Corinthians 15:44.</note>: not because it is then a spirit, but because it will be subject to the spirit. Therefore, just as the glory to which the human soul is elevated exceeds the natural power of the celestial spirits: so the glory of resurrected bodies exceeds the natural perfection of the heavenly bodies <note>In Renaissance cosmology, "heavenly bodies" refers to the stars and planets, which were thought to be made of a more perfect, unchanging substance than earthly matter.</note>. They will be made more lucid, more impassible <note>meaning they cannot suffer physical decay or pain</note>, more dexterous, and more apt and agile than those. But it is common to both the good and the wicked that their bodies do not age, and they have no need to eat: nevertheless, they are able to do so, as one reads regarding the angels and Christ. They shall rise as male and female with their proper sexes, not because they are to use them, but so that the body may be perfect. They will rise at the age of Christ <note>Tradition suggests the age of 33, considered the "perfect age" of human maturity.</note>: because it is perfect, whereas other ages are either in a state of change or too mature. **THAT WHICH ECHOES THROUGH ETERNITY** <note>original: "QUEL CHINE THERNO"</note> resounds, that is, hearing the judge whose words will echo this phrase for eternity: for he shall say, "Depart, you cursed, into eternal fire." **THROUGH THE FOUL MIXTURE** <note>original: "PER SOSSA"</note> mixture. For it was a foul thing to see those souls rolled in that filthy water like a pig in the mire. And by this, he wishes to express how base a thing it is to consider that the human soul—born for the contemplation and knowledge of great things—should allow itself to be so conquered by the throat <note>The sin of gluttony.</note> that it wallows like a foul pig in the pleasures of corruptible and putrid bodily foods, when its true food is knowledge and doctrine. For just as the body, composed of the four elements, is nourished by foods made of a similar composition, so the incorporeal soul is nourished by incorporeal things. **WITH SLOW STEPS** <note>original: "A PASSI"</note>: which demonstrates deep thought: because one who is pensive walks slowly and often stops. Thus he expressed what Virgil writes of Aeneas and Achates: "With whom faithful Achates goes as companion: and with equal cares plants his footsteps" <note>original Latin: "Cui fidus Achates It comes: et paribus curis uestigia figit". From Virgil's Aeneid VI, 158-159.</note>. **TOUCHING A LITTLE** upon the future life. Reasoning, though with brevity of words, about the life that will be after the last judgment. The reasoning was: Dante asks if the pains of the damned are to be greater, or lesser, or the same after the judgment.

<margin>st</margin>
And he to me: "Return to your science,
which holds that as a thing is more perfect,
the more it feels the good, and so the pain.
Although these people, cursed by God,
into true perfection never go,
they look to be more complete then than now."
We circled all around that road,
speaking much more than I repeat;
we came to the point where the steps go down:
there we found Pluto, the great enemy.

<column-break/>

<margin>H</margin>
Having understood the question, he responds: that if he understands philosophy well, of which he makes profession, he will recognize that every thing feels more of the good and the bad when it is in its perfection than when it is imperfect. As, for example <note>original Latin: "uiui bi gratia" (uerbi gratia)</note>, the sense of sight knows colors better when that sense is perfect than when it has some defect. Therefore, man being composed of soul and body, he will then be naturally perfect when the body is reunited with the soul. He speaks, therefore, of this natural perfection, which even the damned will have after the judgment. And not of another perfection, which is not natural to man, but is granted by divine

clemency—not to all, but only to the saved: who through glorification have four gifts: Agility, Subtlety, Clarity, and Impassibility <note>The four "dotes" or dowries of the glorified body in Scholastic theology.</note>, of which we have spoken above. And therefore he adds: **ALTHOUGH THESE** cursed people never go into true perfection. Because, as I have said, this supernatural perfection belongs only to the saved: and the text is ordered thus: **ALTHOUGH**: that is, even though. **THESE** cursed people: that is, the damned. **NEVER** go into true perfection: that is, into that supernatural state which contains the four aforementioned gifts. Nevertheless, they expect to be more perfect then: that is, after the judgment: because at least they will have that natural perfection <note>Meaning the completeness of being a whole human (soul and body) rather than just a soul.</note>. Then he concludes the chapter, showing that having departed from Ciacco, they followed the road, which was circular and curved. And they circled the whole place where the gluttonous were punished. Which signifies morally: that in this vice, they diligently contemplated the whole from every side. **WE CAME TO THE POINT** where the steps go down: that is, where one descends. For he imagines that one always descends from the wider circle into the narrower. And in truth, the more grave the vice, the further it descends to the bottom, and the further it distances itself from heaven. **THERE**: That is, at the beginning of the next circle. **WE FOUND PLUTO** the great enemy: of whom we shall speak in the following chapter.

<meta>This page transitions from the theological discussion of the Resurrection at the end of Canto VI to the beginning of Canto VII. It introduces the arrival at the Fourth Circle of Hell, where the sins of Greed (Avarice) and Extravagance (Prodigality) are punished.</meta>

. e. iiii.

# CANTO SEVEN OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring classical foliate motifs and a figure's face, beginning the text of the poem.</image-desc>

"Pape Satan, Pape Satan aleppe!" <note>original: "Pape ſatan pape ſatan aleppe". These famous opening words are a nonsensical or demonic invocation; their exact meaning has been debated for centuries, but they serve here to show the irrationality of the demon Pluto.</note>
began Pluto with his clucking voice;
and that noble sage, who knew all things <note>A reference to Virgil, Dante's guide, who represents human reason and wisdom.</note>

<column-break/>

In this seventh chapter, the author describes the fourth circle; and this he divides into two parts. In the first part, he places the punishments of the **avaricious** <note>Those who hoard wealth.</note> and the **prodigal** <note>Those who waste wealth excessively.</note>; and in the second, those of the **wrathful** and the **sullen**. At the entrance of the circle, he imagines Pluto the demon standing as a sort of guardian and lord of this circle. To better interpret this fiction, we should remember how the ancient poets said Pluto was the son of Saturn and Rhea, and the king of hell. There were four children of Saturn, who denote the four elements: Jove is fire; Juno is air; Neptune is water; and Pluto is earth. By "Saturn," they mean **Time**; and they imagine that he ate all his other children except these four, because time consumes everything except the elements themselves.

Since Pluto represents the element of **earth**, they also hold him to be the god of riches; for whatever wealth men seek is either under the earth—such as all kinds of metals and every mine of precious stones—or it is born from the earth, such as grain, fruits, and animals. For the same reason, they make him the god of hell, because the earth is the lowest part of the world; and Pluto—that is, riches—always pulls the human soul toward vile and lowly things. They also say he has his city in hell called **Dis** <note>original: "Dite". The inner city of Hell described later in the poem.</note>, which, according to Virgil, no just man can enter, because no one who is greedy for riches can be truly just. 

It is not unknown to me that Pluto is also taken to have many other meanings, especially for the power that the sun pours into the earth. Through this power, the sun not only brings forth all grasses and trees, but this same virtue creates gold, silver, and all other metals and jewels within the earth. For this reason too, he is the god of riches. Appropriately, then, our poet places him at the head of the place where the avaricious are punished. For **avarice** is nothing other than an immoderate desire for possession. Nor is it without cause that he called him "the great enemy" at the end of the previous canto; for without fail, he excessively infests and molests the human race. 

Avarice incites and stirs up discord between blood relatives, friends, and fellow citizens. Avarice produces injustice, from which riots, seditions, and civil wars are sparked. Avarice is the cause of foreign wars. Avarice fills the sea with pirates and corsairs, and the roads with bandits. Avarice produces within the city thefts, homicides, poisonings, perjuries, false testimonies, and corrupt judges. Finally, it makes the father of the family a cruel enemy to his wife, his children, and even to himself; for out of fear of consuming what he has gathered, he defrauds himself and his whole family of necessary things. He sells the laws and the magistrates. He sells modesty and chastity. Therefore, Pluto is a "great enemy." 

Certainly, there would be great tranquility among men, and we would live in perpetual peace, if everyone remained content with what they have and with what natural need requires—which is little and is acquired without difficulty. Therefore, since Pluto signifies riches, the poet rightfully places him as the lord of the place where the avaricious and the prodigal are punished: which...

--- Page 114 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Fourth Circle of Hell. Having established Pluto as the guardian of wealth, the author now explains the Aristotelian ethics behind the two specific sins punished here—Avarice and Prodigality—and begins a detailed linguistic analysis of Pluto’s famous, nonsensical cry.</meta>

# INFERNO

These two vices have no other subject than wealth. And Pluto is the demon of this place because those who are punished here have sinned through riches: one by holding onto them too tightly, the other by scattering them too much. So that this may be better understood, let us remember that all moral virtues consist not only in right knowledge, but even more in right action. For a person is not "just" simply because they know what justice is, but because they practice justice in the administration of affairs. Furthermore, every virtue is a certain **middle path** <note>original: "mediocrita". Referring to the Aristotelian "Golden Mean," where virtue is the balance between two extremes.</note> placed between two extremes, one of which is "too little" and the other "too much." Just as that middle path is virtue, so the extremes are vice. 

Therefore, in the distribution of our wealth and resources, there is a middle way which follows a certain rule: giving as much as is appropriate, to whom it is appropriate, and for the right reason. This action is a virtue called **liberality** <note>or generosity</note>. One of the extremes of this middle path, which leans toward "less" and fails to reach the middle, involves the defect of not giving as much as is appropriate or to those who deserve it; this vice is **avarice** <note>greed</note>, which we will soon divide into two parts. The other extreme is excess, because it overshoots the middle path and gives more than is appropriate. It considers neither who deserves it nor the right reason for giving; such a vice is called **prodigality** <note>wastefulness</note>. Therefore, although avarice and prodigality are opposites, they nevertheless deserve to be punished in the same place because they share the same subject <note>wealth</note>. 

And whatever is said of the extremes of avarice, understand the same for prodigality. Now, returning to the text, Dante depicts Pluto as being simultaneously marveled and grieved that he <note>Dante</note> descends into his kingdom. There are two ways one descends into these vices: either by actually sinning in them, which happens when the senses rebel against reason (this is how all the avaricious and prodigal descend, and Pluto rejoices at their arrival); or when the senses, accompanied by reason and obedient to it, descend into the consideration of such vices—not to be defiled by them, but to be purged of them. This is what Dante feigns of himself. Pluto grieves at such an arrival, for he desires not the salvation but the damnation of souls. Seeing him approach and doubting his own strength to stop him, he calls to Satan for help, saying: **PAPE SATAN**. 

*Pape* is an interjection of wonder <note>original: "admirantis"</note>; that is, it is a voice that demonstrates marvel. This is why the Supreme Pontiff, as the most marvelous thing among Christians, is called **Papa** <note>the Pope</note>. Thus, saying "Pape Satan" is like saying "Oh, Satan!" and to show greater marvel, he doubles it—that is, he repeats the words, saying twice: *Pape Satan, Pape Satan*—"Oh Satan, Oh Satan!" 

Then, to show his grief, he says **ALEPPE**. In Hebrew, they call *Aleph* what the Greeks call *Alpha* and the Latins call *A*. And because those who grieve use the interjection "Ah!", as seen later in the poem: "Ah, Constantine, of how much ill was mother, not your conversion, but that dowry..." <note>A reference to Inferno XIX, where Dante laments the "Donation of Constantine" which gave the Church temporal wealth.</note> Therefore, in place of the Latin name, he took the Hebrew *Aleph*, and to fit the rhyme, he changed the *h* to a *p* and added an *e*, saying *Aleppe*. Thus, interpreting the whole verse, we shall say: "Oh Satan, Oh Satan, Ah!" Through these interjections and voices, it is shown that he suddenly fell into the greatest wonder and the greatest fear. 

We have stated the cause of his fear. As for the wonder in the narrative fiction, it is that a living man should come to the place of the dead. In the moral sense, it is a marvelous thing that any man should descend into the thought of these temporal goods and subject his appetite to reason, so that he regards them as nothing but something vile, transitory, and momentary. **SATHAN** in Hebrew means "contrary," "adversary," "prevaricator," or "transgressor"; many say this is the name of the prince of demons, whom Pluto calls for help, doubting his own strength. And certainly, Pluto—that is, wealth itself—could not draw a man to such enormous wickedness without a great diabolical stimulus. 

**WITH THE VOICE** clucking <note>original: "chioccia"</note>; that is, with a hoarse voice. This signifies sudden fear, because a sudden consternation of the soul diminishes the voice or loses it entirely. Thus Virgil, wishing to show sudden fear in the souls of the Greeks, said: 
> "Some raised a tiny cry; the shout they began failed them as they gaped." <note>original Latin: "pars tollere uocem Exigua inceptus clamor frustratur hiantes." From the Aeneid, Book VI, describing the Greek ghosts' reaction to seeing Aeneas in the underworld.</note>

**AND THAT SAGE** noble <note>original: "Gentile"</note> who knew all things. This is great praise of Virgil, and worthy of him. For whoever reads his poem attentively sees that it is so full of many and varied things that one easily understands he was universal in all the disciplines of the ancients, as I strove to collect extensively in a preface of mine at the beginning of my lectures on the *Aeneid*. And if one were to say it is false that any man, however learned, can know everything, I respond that the poet here uses a rhetorical figure called **hyperbole**—that is, a surpassing of the truth, used not only by writers but even in daily speech, as when we say "It has been a thousand years since I last saw you." Therefore, he "knew all," meaning he knew much, and as much as almost any man can know. 

But if Virgil is taken allegorically to represent the **intellect** filled with wisdom and accompanied by divine grace, truly it can be said he "knew all." **GENTILE** means noble and generous; it is as if to say that he not only understood through wisdom but also was able to express what he understood through eloquence. For many have been most learned, but because they lacked the eloquence to express what they understood, they remained obscure and ignoble, and achieved no fame. Or, he said **SAGE GENTILE** meaning a sage in the doctrines of the Gentiles <note>Pagans</note>, which we showed above are sufficient for Hell and Purgatory; in that case, we would say he knew everything within those doctrines. For speech must be interpreted according to the subject matter: if, speaking of astrology, we say "this man does everything," it is understood within that science.

<summary>This page explains the moral philosophy of the Fourth Circle, defining Avarice and Prodigality as extremes that stray from the virtuous "middle path" of Liberality. It also provides a linguistic and allegorical breakdown of Pluto's cry and Virgil's role as the symbol of universal human reason.</summary>
