<meta>This page continues the commentary on the entrance to the Fourth Circle of Hell, where Virgil confronts Pluto, the demon of wealth. Having just heard Pluto’s nonsensical cry, Virgil now turns to reassure Dante and rebuke the beast.</meta>

# CANTO SEVEN

To comfort me he said: "Let not your fear
Harm you; for whatever power he may have,
He shall not stop you from descending this rock."

Then he turned to those swollen lips,
And said: "Be silent, cursed wolf!
Consume yourself within with your own rage.
Not without cause is the journey to the abyss.
It is willed on high, there where Michael
Took vengeance for the proud rebellion." <note>original: "strupo". While usually meaning 'rape' or 'violation,' Landino explains it here as the violent arrogance of Lucifer against God.</note>
As sails swollen by the wind
Fall in a heap when the mast snaps:
So fell that cruel beast to the ground.

Thus we descended into the fourth hollow,
Taking in more of the sorrowful slope,
Which bags up all the evil of the universe.
Ah, justice of God! Who else heaps up
New travails and pains? such as I saw...

<column-break/>

He admonishes Dante not to fear Pluto: because such fear would be harmful. Those who fear Pluto are those who lack the courage to despise earthly goods and are so small-minded <note>original: "pusillanimi"</note> that they do not trust they can live without them. This debases them so that they do not dare to descend with a frank spirit into such meditation. But the higher reason, instructed by philosophy, comforts the sensuality <note>the lower, physical part of the soul</note>: showing that Pluto has no power to forbid this descent. For in truth, the appetite for riches is never so great that one who decides to conquer it with reason cannot do so. **TO COMFORT ME**: Sensuality needs the comfort of reason and learning. **LET NOT YOUR FEAR HARM YOU**: As if to say, do not fear, because fear itself would hinder you. **THIS ROCK**: That is, this slope.

Having comforted Dante, he uses a sort of invective against Pluto: that is, against the rich and the avaricious man. He imagines him with **swollen lips** to express his elation and the pride in his appearance and words. This is characteristic of the wealthy, as Aristotle demonstrates in his *Rhetoric*: they are so arrogant that they assume everyone must be inferior and obedient to them. Hence, when the wife of Hiero of Syracuse was asked which was worthier, wisdom or wealth, she replied that she often saw the wise frequenting the houses of the rich, but never the rich at the houses of the wise. This was a completely foolish answer, proceeding from a soul made proud by riches. For if the rich recognized their need for the wise—to become good and virtuous through their counsel—just as the wise recognize their need for the rich to provide for the body’s necessities, we would constantly see the houses of the wise full of the wealthy. **SILENCE, CURSED WOLF**: The author recalls that at the beginning he used the she-wolf to represent avarice. Thus, he perfectly calls the miser a wolf, as an insatiable beast. **CURSED**: No one can praise avarice, because it harms both oneself and one's neighbor. From it proceed infinite evils, for it is a greed more insatiable than all others. Thus, the miser is cursed and hated by friends and relatives as much as by enemies. **CONSUME YOURSELF WITHIN WITH YOUR OWN RAGE**: This is said to show the constant anxiety in the mind of the miser as he thinks of how to accumulate; this worry and thought continually consumes him. Boethius also demonstrates this: "But more cruel than Etna's fires, a burning love for possessing blazes." <note>original: "Sed seuior ignibus ethne Feruens amor ardet habendi"</note> And Jeremiah: "Among my people are wicked men who lie in wait like fowlers." <note>original: "Sunt in populo meo impii insidiantes quasi aucupes"</note> And Horace: "The tireless merchant runs to the furthest Indies across the sea, fleeing poverty through rocks and through fires." <note>original: "Impiger extremos currit mercator ad indos per mare pauperiem fugiens / per saxa / per ignes"</note> **NOT WITHOUT CAUSE IS THE JOURNEY TO THE ABYSS**: As if to say our descent into Hell is not by chance or without counsel (which would make it easier to forbid), but is by divine will, which no power can resist. **IT IS WILLED ON HIGH**: That is, in heaven. Either because God wills that everyone, by acting rightly, purges themselves of every vice—and for this, He gave us reason to comfort us—or he said **IT IS WILLED ON HIGH** to show predestination, which he placed above as so many graces. **THERE WHERE MICHAEL**: As if to say, from where you wicked angels were cast out for your pride. He uses the Archangel Michael to represent all the others who fought and cast out those who were adversaries to God. We will treat this more extensively elsewhere. **REBELLION** <note>original: "strupo"</note>: This signifies any violent intercourse, especially with a virgin. But here he uses it for the proud violence of Lucifer, who wished to violate the incorruptible divine light; he used "strupo" instead of "stupro" <note>violation/rape</note> for the sake of the rhyme. **AS SAILS SWOLLEN BY THE WIND fall to the ground**: An excellent comparison, showing the nature of the angry and proud man who swells up wonderfully. But once defeated, he suddenly becomes base and all his pride falls away. Thus, just as the sails swell from the wind while the mast supports them, but fall when the mast breaks, so the elated and proud man swells while his pride supports him, but when that is dampened, he is debased. **CRUEL BEAST**: Avarice is a wild beast because it is alienated from all humanity, harming both itself and its neighbor; it is truly cruel for this same reason.

**THUS WE DESCENDED**: That is, having first comforted the lower reason and sensuality to endure every difficulty and labor, and having taken great courage and repressed the appetite. For one cannot otherwise descend into the contemplation of vices without remaining entangled in them. **INTO THE...**

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto VII of the Inferno. Having established the setting of the Fourth Circle, Landino now analyzes the specific punishments of the Avaricious (the greedy) and the Prodigal (the wasteful), using the imagery of the clashing waves of Charybdis to explain their eternal conflict.</meta>

->### INFERNO<-

and why our guilt so wastes us.
As the wave does there above Charybdis:
which breaks against that which it meets,
so here must the people dance their round.
Here I saw more people than elsewhere:
and from one side and the other with great howls,
rolling weights by force of chest:
They struck against each other: and then right there
each turned back, rolling the weight away,
crying "Why do you hold?" and "Why do you toss?"
Thus they ran through the dark circle
from every hand to the opposite point:
crying again their shameful meter.
Then each turned back once he had reached
the other jousting-match through his semi-circle;
and I, who had my heart almost pierced.

<column-break/>

**fourth ditch**: that is, the bank: and it is a name derived from *labor laberis* <note>original: "labor laberis". Landino is using a Latin etymology to suggest the "lacca" is a place where one "slips" or "falls."</note>: which in Latin means "to slip": because on very steep places one slips. **TAKING** more of the sorrowful bank. Takes more: because he descends further through it. **WHICH**: that is, the bank which "bags up": and puts inside itself the evil of the universe: that is, all sinners. Understanding this as the bank that contains within itself all the circles of Hell. Or, we shall say, **WHICH**: that is, the fourth ditch: that is, the fourth circle. **BAGS UP** all the evils of the universe: because from avarice—which is punished in this circle—proceed all wickednesses and all evils that happen to men. On which Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, a Roman Stoic philosopher often cited by medieval and Renaissance scholars for his moral teachings.</note> excellently said: "Remove these names *Mine* and *Thine*, and every discord that arises between men will be removed." Then, contemplating the infinite and gravest punishments by which the miser is struck, with both wonder and pity together, he continues saying: **AH JUSTICE** of God: because truly no vice is there which more deserves, according to divine justice, to be punished than this: which harms

---

himself and his neighbor: and is the source and root of all other vices. Avarice according to Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator. Landino draws on classical definitions to categorize the sin.</note> is immoderate desire for having. And Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo. The "literal" commentary on Genesis refers to his work *De Genesi ad litteram*.</note> writing on Genesis "literally" writes: that it is not only immoderate desire to have riches and other things subject to fortune: but also to have dignity and knowledge. But this is avarice understood very broadly. There are two species of avarice. For he is a miser who does not give where and how much he ought: and he who takes from where he ought not. From these, creditors are defrauded; deposits are feigned with perjuries; with false testimonies; with adulterated goods. From here come usury, theft, robbery, ransoms, <term>barratry</term> <note>The sale of church or state offices; corruption.</note>, and assassinations. From here come <term>simony</term> <note>The buying or selling of ecclesiastical privileges or or sacred things.</note> and the improper distribution of sacred things. **WHO HEAPS UP**: *Stipare* in Latin means to stow: that is, to fill by trampling. Whence we say the galley is at the "stowage" <note>original: "stiua"</note>, when wool and similar things are trampled down. Therefore, he who heaps up, who accumulates, and gathers together. As if to say: "You, Justice, unite so many punishments." And the text follows: **AH JUSTICE** of God, who heaps up: that is, who accumulates so many new travails; that is, so many travails and pains not seen elsewhere than here: and so many punishments. And certainly every vice gives travail to man: but none so much as avarice, as we have already shown above. **AND WHY** our guilt so wastes us. That is, so "tears us apart" <note>original: "scerpe"</note>: that is, distracts us: as if to say it torments us. And it is from the Latin word *Scerpo* which means to distract, and to lacerate, and to tear. And the meaning is: why does our guilt lacerate us: that is, why does our sin torment us. **AS DOES** the wave there above Charybdis. In the strait which divides Sicily from Italy called the Faro are two rocks: one on the side of Italy called Scylla, of which we will speak another time. The other on the side of Sicily called Charybdis. The poets feign that she was a most rapacious woman: and because she stole cattle from Hercules, she was struck by Jove's lightning and converted into this monster: where because of the narrowness of the place the sea boils and runs from north to south, and from south to north, where waves constantly break; and from the caverns which are under the rocks, being now swallowed and now spat out, they pull ships into similar danger. Therefore the author says: that just as those two waves, meeting each other, strike together: so two ranks—that of the misers and that of the prodigals—departed from one same place in the circle. But turning their backs, one went to the right and the other to the left, in such a way that without leaving the circle they met in the middle and struck each other. And it is to be noted that the poet used the comparison of Charybdis not only to demonstrate this clash: but it also fits well because poets use Charybdis to represent avarice, as we demonstrated at length in our allegories of Virgil: for just as Charybdis pulls the waves to itself and absorbs and swallows ships and everything, so avarice wants to seize and swallow everything. **SO IT IS NECESSARY** that here the people dance their round <note>original: "riddi"</note>: that is, dance: and go in the manner of a dance around the circle, and he speaks with a certain derision; for in a dance there is joy, and here there is sadness. *Ridda* in our tongue means a dance: and from this name the poet formed a verb which is not in use, and in the present subjunctive said *riddi*, that is, "let them dance." And certainly the poet's genius was admirable in the invention of these punishments. And he expressed that two extremes—avarice and prodigality—come until the middle to meet one another: but they do not stop there. For the middle of these two extremes is liberality. They depart, then, through the circle from a point where liberality is: because everyone leaves it; and they come to the other opposite point where the excesses are. But one goes to the right and the other to the left: because the prodigal departs from the middle by giving more than liberality requires and goes to the extreme, which is excess. The miser departs by not giving as much as is appropriate and goes to the other extreme, which is deficiency. Therefore the middle is where alone virtue consists.

Landino explains the ethical framework of the scene, identifying the two sins as opposite extremes that have abandoned the "middle way" of Liberality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto VII of the Inferno. Following the description of the Fourth Circle's geography, Landino now interprets the symbolic punishment of the Avaricious and the Prodigal, emphasizing the psychological and moral weight of their sins.</meta>

->### SEVENTH CANTO<-

Wherefore Horace says: *There is a measure in things, there are certain fixed limits, beyond and short of which virtue cannot consist.* <note>original: "Est modus in rebus sunt certi denique fines : Quos ultra citraque nequit consistere uirtus." This is a famous quote from Horace’s Satires (1.1.106-107) regarding the "golden mean" of Aristotelian ethics.</note> From this the miser and the spendthrift deviate, and they go to different extremes by different ways. The poet imagines that these push rocks of heavy weight with their chests. In the chest is the heart, and in that are the cares and thoughts, which in the miser are continuously great. His heart never stays quiet, but continuously turns some heavy rock—that is, he turns over in his mind some laborious thought. Wherefore Horace says: *You see what you believe to be the greatest evils—a meager income and a shameful rejection—how much labor of mind and head you endure to avoid them.* <note>original: "Vides que maxima credis esse mala exiguum censum turpemque repulsam Quato deuites animi capitisque labore." From Horace’s Epistles (1.1.42-44).</note> And avarice always goads them, and as Persius writes, it says: *"Rise!" says Avarice. "Come now, rise!" "I won't." "She insists: Rise!"* <note>original: "Surge inquit auaritia Eia surge Negas Instat Surge." From Persius, Satire V, 132-133.</note> Therefore **BY FORCE** of chest—that is, of the breast where the breasts [*poppe*] are; in which chest is the heart, and in it the cares and anxieties. **HERE I SAW** more people than elsewhere; because there is no vice that occupies more men than avarice. **FROM ONE** side and the other; that is, from two extremes. On this side the misers, on this side the spendthrifts, as was said above. **HOWLS**; screams: and it is a name derived from the Latin *ululato* <note>meaning a wail or howl</note>; and because howling is for wolves, it is well-suited to the misers, whom he likens to wolves. **SHOUTING** "Why do you hold?"; and these are the words of the spendthrift who rebukes the miser, who keeps for himself what he ought to give to others. **AND "WHY DO YOU TOSS?"**; that is, *bui/buiare* in the Aretine <note>from Arezzo</note> dialect means "to throw"; and these are the words of the miser, who rebukes the spendthrift for throwing away what he should save. And many ask the reason why Dante, above where he punishes lust and gluttony, does not place all opposites against them as he does here, where in punishing avarice he places prodigality as its opposite. To which I reply: although every vice has its opposite, nonetheless in the two already mentioned they do not appear. For despite lust being an excess in sexual intercourse, the defect—that is, not taking as much pleasure as is required—is found in no one, or in very few, and is without much harm. And we shall say the same of gluttony. The poet says that having reached the point and struck one another, they turned back to repeat the same course anew; and having returned to the point from which they first set out, which is opposite to where they clashed, they began the joust anew. Which signifies that the miser never ceases to strike the spendthrift—that is, to seize and hold—nor the spendthrift to strike the miser—that is, to throw away. But note: rarely is there prodigality without avarice. For in order to be able to give much, they take and seize from others, as Cicero writes of Caesar, who despoiled many Pompeians to give to his own. And they always shout their shameful meter—that is, verse—one: "Why do you hold?" the other: "Why do you toss?" **AND I WHO HAD** my heart almost pierced; that is, I who was much afflicted by compassion for such great pains.

> I said: "My Master, now show me
> what people these are, and if all were clerics
> these tonsured ones on our left."
> And he to me: "All these were squint-eyed
> of mind in their first life,
> such that they made no spending with measure.
> Clearly enough their voice barks it
> when they come to the two points of the circle
> where contrary guilt separates them.
> These were clerics, who have no hairy
> covering on their heads: both Popes and Cardinals,
> in whom avarice exercises its excess."
> "And I, Master, among such as these
> ought surely to recognize someone
> who was filthy with these evils."

<column-break/>

Deservedly Dante always raises doubts and asks questions, and Virgil, in responding, solves them; because to the lower reason, when it investigates, every thing appears doubtful, but the higher reason with its doctrine finds the truth and solves the doubts. He asks if all the tonsured ones—that is, those he saw with the tonsures—were **CLERICS**, that is, priests. **ON OUR LEFT**; by the left he shows greater wickedness in avarice. For just as "right" is used for happy and good, so "left" for the opposite. *Cherici* in our language are what the Latins call *clerici*. It is not, however, a Latin word, but Greek, because in Greek *cleros* <note>original: "cleros" (klēros)</note> means "lot" or "portion." Wherefore *clericus* signifies one chosen by God for his portion. And although God calls us all, nonetheless he strengthens and elects priests as kings to rule with good character; and they shave the circle of hair on the head, shaving the rest in the likeness of a crown. Wherefore the vice is much more ignominious in the priest than in the layman, because he who rules should be an example of all holiness to those who are to be ruled. And when he sins, it is the opposite. Wherefore Juvenal says: *Every vice of the soul carries with it a crime that is all the more conspicuous, the greater the man is held to be who commits it* <note>original: "Omne animi uitium tanto conspectius in se crimen habet ; quanto maior qui peccat habetur" (Juvenal, Satire VIII, 140-141)</note>, as we have said above. The priest is therefore of worse example, because it is more noted in him, and every vice appears more clearly. Therefore the poet deservedly rebukes them more than the others. **AND HE**; that is Virgil, said to me: "Understand, **ALL** were squint-eyed." Dante asked if all those he saw with the tonsure were priests, and Virgil responds that **ALL** were squint-eyed, wanting first to demonstrate their vice than the state in which they were in life. They were therefore squint-eyed—understand this as the eyes of the mind and the intellect—because by not looking straight ahead, they did not know how to discern the truth and see the measure that contains virtue; but looking askance, they took the extremes. **IN THE FIRST LIFE**; that is, while they lived in this world.

<summary>This page analyzes the symbolic punishment of the Avaricious and Prodigal, explaining their eternal conflict as a lack of moral "measure." Landino specifically highlights the presence of corrupt clergy, including Popes and Cardinals, noting that their high status makes their greed even more scandalous.</summary>

--- Page 118 ---
<meta>This page continues Landino’s commentary on Canto VII of the Inferno, moving from the physical description of the Fourth Circle to a scathing moral critique of the souls found there—specifically the clergy. Landino provides an etymological and historical defense of why Dante targets priests for the sins of Avarice and Prodigality.</meta>

# INFERNO

**THAT THEY DID NOT DO**; that is, they did not do so here. **ANY EXPENDITURE**: that is, any distribution of their substance with measure: in which consists the "middle way" <term>mediocrita: the Aristotelian "golden mean" between two extremes</term> and the virtue called liberality. But they sinned either in the "too much"—whereby they became prodigal—or in the "too little"—and were misers. And this is clearly demonstrated by their voices when they come to two points of the circle where they meet: and where they say **"Why do you hold?"** and **"Why do you squander?"** <note>original: "Perche tieni? et perche burli?"</note> And he said **"barks"** <note>original: "abbaia"</note> to liken them to dogs, because they bite one another with words. Or rather, he said "barks" as if to say they speak in vain, because any rebuke given there is worth nothing, as there is no place for penance in Hell. And similarly, in the "moral Hell" <note>Landino distinguishes between the literal Inferno and the state of a soul still living in vice.</note>, there is no redemption for a habit already contracted in vice. **WHERE CONTRARY GUILT**: that is, prodigality and avarice, which are contrary vices. **PARTS THEM**, that is, separates them; because each of the parties returns back through their half-circle until they reach the other point.

Then he responds to Dante's question and affirms that all those whom he sees with the **tonsure** <note>original: "cherica"</note> were clerics. And for two reasons he reproaches the priests in this place: first, because they are more involved in these two vices than all other men, as evidenced by the complaints of our Petrarch regarding the "greedy Babylon" <note>original: "lauara babyllonia." A reference to Petrarch's Sonnet 137, which criticized the papal court at Avignon.</note> and elsewhere: *May fire from heaven rain upon your tresses.* <note>original: "Fiamma dacielo su le tue trecce pioua." From Petrarch’s Sonnet 136.</note> Who has not seen in our times men—or rather monsters of men—without letters, without morals, not even fit to be committed the care of a lowly country chapel? Yet Fortune has elevated them to great dignity, where they have used every extreme of avarice to accumulate infinite treasure through simony <term>simonie: the buying or selling of ecclesiastical privileges</term> and various kinds of theft. Then, they use extreme prodigality to consume it in every form of shameful luxury, such that Sardanapalus and Heliogabalus <note>Two ancient rulers—the last king of Assyria and a Roman Emperor—famed in the Renaissance as the ultimate examples of decadence and excess.</note> could be considered most continent in comparison to them.

While this is very distressing to any well-instituted mind within the Christian name, it hurts even more those prelates who are adorned with every kind of learning and are a most lucid mirror to all others in life and conduct—most prudent in every action and most wise in speculation. Because there is such infamy in their order, it seems impossible that some part of it does not reflect upon them, though undeservedly. For which reason, as much as a most just indignation pushes me against those most luxurious misers, so much am I moved by compassion toward these most innocent ones. But the reverence I bear to such a college makes me keep silent about that which is known to the whole world.

So, this is the first reason that moved Dante to reproach the priests. The second is that vice is more reproachful in them than in the laity. This is because the apostolic—that is, the priestly—church is founded upon chastity and poverty. Whence Petrarch says: *Not nurtured on feathers in the shade / But naked to the wind and barefoot among the thorns / Now you live so that God is disgusted by you.* <note>original: "Gia non sustu nutrita in piume al rezo / Ma nuda al uento : et scalza fra gli stecchi. / Hor uiui si cha dio ne uengha lezo." From Petrarch's Sonnet 138.</note> Furthermore, they are the ones who have the government of the Christian Republic. Therefore they are called **clerics**: that is, the "chosen" and almost "selected" ones and the "magnates," because *cleros* <note>Greek: κλῆρος</note> means "lot" or "fate." And they call us **laity**, that is, "plebeians," because *laos* <note>Greek: λαός</note> means "people." They ought, therefore, as administrators, to give the best example of themselves. Above all, they should signify nothing else by having **shaved their hair** than having cut away every superfluity and pruned every greed. And the circle that is above the shaved hair denotes a **crown**, to show that they are our kings, and it is their office to rule us and direct us onto the right path. The third reason is that there is no cause that should make them greedy to accumulate treasure, having neither wife nor children to support. **IN WHOM**: that is, in those in whom **AVARICE EXERTS ITS EXCESS**. It is as if he says: although all avarice exceeds the proper measure—either by pulling toward oneself or by not giving—nevertheless, in prelates, it uses its "excess," that is, it contains as much excess as can possibly exist within it. **AND I: "MASTER..."** Dante marvels that among so many prelates he does not recognize a single one. To which Virgil responds:

<columns>2</columns>

And he to me: "You gather a vain thought;
the unknowing life that made them foul
now makes them too dark for any recognition.
Unto eternity they will come to the two buttings;
these shall rise again from the sepulcher
with fists clenched, and these with hair shorn.
Ill-giving and ill-keeping have taken the beautiful world
from them, and set them to this scuffle;
what that is like, I will not use fair words to say.
Now you can see, son, the short-lived puff
of the goods that are committed to Fortune,
for which the human race brawls.
For all the gold that is beneath the moon,
or that ever was, for these weary souls,
could not make a single one of them rest."

<column-break/>

The true answer is **THAT THE UNKNOWING LIFE**: that is, the form and the manner of their living, which has been "unknowing," meaning unrecognizable. **MADE THEM FOUL**: that is, infamous. **AND NOW MAKES THEM DARK**: that is, obscure and without fame. And allegorically this demonstrates the stupidity of the miser, who is useful neither to himself nor to others. And for this reason, he can never be in any state of fame. It is certainly a supreme misery to labor in accumulating treasure with which one neither provides for one's own needs nor acquires any fame. They live unknown, without friends, without the familiarity of anyone; they are hardly even known by their neighbors. We can also say "**The unknowing life**" because the life of the miser is so different from the priestly profession that one cannot recognize them as priests through it. Their office is to distribute the fruits and the revenues for the repair of the temple and to assist—according to the degrees of charity—those who are in poverty, keeping for themselves only what is necessary for a sober life.

<summary>In this passage, Landino interprets Dante’s encounter with the Avaricious and Prodigal, focusing heavily on a critique of the corrupt clergy. He explains the etymology of "cleric" and "laic" and argues that the souls are unrecognizable in Hell because their earthly lives were devoid of the light of virtue and fame.</summary>
<keywords>clerical corruption, simony, Petrarch, Avarice, Prodigality, tonsure, Fortune, Sardanapalus, Heliogabalus, etymology of cleric</keywords>

--- Page 119 ---
<meta>This page continues Landino’s commentary on Canto VII. Having identified the sinners as clerics and popes on the previous page, Landino now analyzes the specific physical punishments and symbolic gestures of the avaricious and the prodigal, followed by a philosophical discourse on the nature of Fortune and worldly goods.</meta>

# CANTO SEVEN

...according to their state. This is why, when they are priests, their life causes us to know them; but when they live as was described above, such a life gives no recognition at all that they are priests. **IN ETERNITY** <note>original: "IN ETHERNO"</note> they will come to the two clashes: because each of these two parties, traveling as far as the middle of the circle and then having struck each other, returns backward and they collide at two opposite points of the circle. **THESE**: that is, the avaricious. **WILL RISE** from the grave with a closed fist. This denotes avarice. **AND THESE**: The Prodigal. **WITH CROPPED HAIR** <note>original: "CHOL crin mozi"</note>: which signifies dissipating or wasting. **EVIL GIVING**: that is, prodigality; which gives without regard for to whom, nor how much, nor why, nor when. **AND EVIL HOLDING**: avarice, which holds more than one should. Whereas giving well is liberality; and holding well is parsimony: which are virtues. Therefore, these two vices have taken from them the Beautiful World: that is, the fair world. It is as if he says it has taken from them the happy life; because certainly men would live in supreme happiness if avarice and prodigality did not deprive them of all peace and tranquility. For both the prodigal and the miser are always anxious; and greedy to seize—the latter to keep for himself, the former to squander on others. Or truly, it has taken from them the beautiful world: that is, heaven and the eternal life, in which there is supreme beauty and delight. Some explain: "Giving badly and holding badly the beautiful world": that is, worldly goods, which by their nature are beautiful. "It has taken them from them"; that is, it has taken these people from themselves. Because avarice and prodigality rob a man of himself. Therefore, it has taken them from themselves and placed them in this scuffle. For just as a sold slave is no longer his own, but belongs to the master who bought him, so when a man is made a servant to greed <term>cupidita: an intense desire for worldly things, particularly money</term>, he is no longer in his own liberty. Instead, he is placed by that greed into this scuffle. **TO THIS SCUFFLE**: meaning these two clashes. Or understand "this scuffle" as the dissensions and discords that first arise within the soul of the miser, who is fought by two different wills; one of which comforts him toward quiet, rest, and enjoying the things acquired. The other pushes him toward dangers and labors to acquire more. This battle was clearly expressed by Persius <note>A Roman satirist</note>. For after he shows that avarice pushes him to every danger and labor for gain, and luxury pulls him toward leisure and quiet, he concludes:
> "Look, what are you doing? You are torn in two directions by a double hook. Do you follow this one or that? You must submit to each in turn; in wavering obedience you wander between alternating masters." <note>original Latin: "En quid agis duplici in diuersum scinderis hamo Huncine an hunc sequeris subeas alternus opportet Ancipiti obsequio dominos alternus oberres."</note>

We can also say "to this scuffle" meaning the dissensions and contentions that arise among men through avarice and robbery. This is very manifest. **WHATEVER IT MAY BE**; that is, whether good or bad. **WORDS** I do not "beautify" <note>original: "apulcro," a Latinism from 'pulcher' meaning to make beautiful</note>: I do not embellish with words. It is as if he says: I do not go with an oratorical style—which with highly ornate words censures this scuffle—because the thing is so manifest in itself that there is no need for me to adorn it. **NOW YOU CAN SEE, SON, THE SHORT BUFFA**. Deservedly in this place, Virgil as a father lovingly admonishes Dante; that is, the "Superior Reason" admonishes the "Inferior Reason" and the sensuality not to place hope in the goods of Fortune—that is, not to be greedy for them. Since they are neither durable nor stable, but placed in the recklessness of Fortune, they change in a short time from place to place. Furthermore, it is to be noted that in the two vices already passed <note>Lust and Gluttony</note>, he did not admonish Dante as he admonishes him in this one: because it is more difficult for a man devoted to the investigation of great things to abstain from avarice than from the pleasures of touch or taste, from which arise luxury and gluttony. **THE SHORT BUFFA**; "the brief vanity," said Benvenuto <note>Benvenuto da Imola, an early commentator</note>; and Francesco da Buti explains "buffa" as derision; but strictly **BUFFA** is wind. Thus we say "buffeting" <term>buffectare</term> of one who blows wind from the mouth: and "puffing" <term>sbuffare</term> when someone threatens with the sound of words, or better said, with windy and inflated words. From this we say "to ruffle" <term>rabbuffare</term>, to disturb and move things from their order and disarrange them. And we call it a "rebuff" <term>rabbuffo</term> when we disturb and disarrange the mind of another with words. Hence it follows: "the human race is ruffled" <note>original: "si rabbuffa"</note>, that is, it is disturbed and leaves the true order because it takes dominion away from reason and gives it to the senses. Therefore he used "wind," that is, vanity and a thing unstable and light to move. **OF THE GOODS** that are committed to Fortune. He means to say that it is the height of folly to place your happiness in a thing that is not in your power, but in the judgment of Fortune; who, making a game of men, often takes them from those who deserve them and gives them to those who do not. **WHY THE HUMAN RACE IS RUFFLED**: he speaks with indignation that the human race—that is, that animal which alone on earth was made a participant in reason—might, if it only awakened that reason, know the emptiness of such goods and yet allows itself to be carried away by greed so that for those goods it enters into such contentions. **IS RUFFLED**: We said "buffa" was wind. From which "rabbuffare" [to ruffle/disturb]. **THAT ALL THE GOLD** that is under the moon. Here finally human folly and vanity are demonstrated. For while we ought to labor in those things which can make us blessed, he shows that the goods of Fortune are so far from this that, even if one person had them all, he would nonetheless not have—I will not say a happy—but even one restful hour. Or if we wish to reason according to the "Essential Hell" <note>The literal physical afterlife</note>: no damned person can be saved for all the treasures in the world. Or according to the "Moral Hell": who does not know that the greed of the miser is never extinguished by accumulating? But as Horace says:
> "The dire dropsy grows by indulging itself, nor is thirst banished unless the cause of the disease has first fled from the pale body—the watery languor." <note>original Latin: "Crescit indulgens sibi dirus hydrops Nec sitim pellit nisi causa morbi fugerit prius aquosus albo corpore langor."</note>

Therefore, just as in a person with dropsy <term>ritropico: an old medical term for edema or swelling</term>, thirst is not extinguished by drinking if the cause from which the disease proceeds does not first cease; so greed in the miser does not cease by the accumulation of gold if the mind is not satisfied. Whence Cicero said:
> "It is the soul of a man, and not his money-chest, that should be called rich." <note>original Latin: "Animus hominis: et non arca diues appellandus est."</note>

Nor is he rich who possesses much: but he who is content with what he has. Therefore, he was not rich...

<summary>Landino explains the symbolic punishments of the avaricious and prodigal, emphasizing that their obsession with worldly goods robs them of their reason and peace. He uses classical authorities like Persius, Horace, and Cicero to argue that true wealth resides in the soul, not in the fluctuating "buffa" (vanity) of Fortune.</summary>

--- Page 120 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Fourth Circle of Hell (the Avaricious and the Prodigal). Following the description of the sinners' punishment, the text transitions into a major philosophical discourse on Fortune, using the contrast between Alexander the Great and Diogenes as a starting point before interpreting Virgil’s speech to Dante.</meta>

->INFERNO<-

Alexander: for whom one world was not enough. But Diogenes was rich: who lived content in supreme mediocrity <note>meaning "the golden mean" or a modest, middle state of life</note>.

> "My Master," I said, "now tell me also 
> about this Fortune you mention: 
> what is she, who holds the world’s goods so tightly in her claws?"
> And he to me: "O foolish creatures, 
> how great is the ignorance that harms you! 
> Now I want you to take in my judgment.
> He whose wisdom transcends all,
> made the heavens and gave them those who lead them <note>the angelic intelligences</note>,
> so that every part shines to every other part,
> distributing the light equally. 
> Similarly, for worldly splendors, 
> He ordained a general minister and guide: 
> who should shift the vain goods from time to time, 
> from one people to another, and from one bloodline to another, 
> beyond the defense of human wit. 
> For this reason, one people rules and another languishes, 
> following her judgment, 
> which stays hidden like a snake in the grass. 
> Your wisdom has no contest against her; 
> she foresees, judges, and pursues 
> her reign as the other gods do theirs. 
> Her permutations have no truce; 
> necessity makes her swift; 
> so often comes one who succeeds in turn. 
> This is she who is so often crucified <note>maligned or cursed</note> 
> even by those who should give her praise, 
> giving her blame wrongly and an evil voice. 
> But she is blessed and does not hear this; 
> happy with the other primal creatures <note>the angels</note>, 
> she turns her sphere and, blessed, enjoys herself."

<column-break/>

Since Virgil has made mention of the goods of Fortune, it fit aptly in this place—where avarice and prodigality are treated, the subject of which vices are the goods of Fortune—to briefly define what that thing might be. In order for this to be better known, I judge it useful to report (though with brevity) what Fortune is, circumscribing it in a way that does not diminish our free will. 

And first we must understand that according to the Peripatetic <note>Aristotelian</note> philosophers, there are three generations of goods: those of the soul, of the body, and of fortune. The goods of the soul are those that benefit the soul and preserve it pure in its nature. These are the virtues, whether intellectual—such as Intelligence, Science <note>Knowledge</note>, Wisdom, Prudence, and Art—or moral, such as Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance, of which we must treat in various places. 

The goods of the body are those that benefit the body: such as beauty, strength, dexterity, speed, and the like. Conversely, the evils are disease, ugliness, weakness, slowness, and the like. 

The goods of Fortune are riches, dignity, magistracies <note>political offices</note>, empires, fame, and glory. Their contraries are poverty, infamy, low status, and the like. These goods are called "of Fortune" because they are largely subject to her. 

But it is a long and laborious thing to dispute fully about Fortune and Chance, because it can hardly be explained without the knowledge of Providence and Fate. Therefore, with brevity, we will demonstrate as much as is necessary to express the mind of the poet. 

Divine Providence, according to Boethius <note>original: "Boetio", Roman philosopher and author of The Consolation of Philosophy</note>, is a supreme reason in God, which orders and disposes all things. Fate is a certain disposition in mobile things, through which Providence connects and composes each thing by a certain order. And those things which Providence embraces within the divine mind, Fate disposes in such a way that they proceed in order from time to time. Therefore, Providence is

---

a certain form of future things ordered across various centuries, which is immobile and simple. Fate is a certain mobile connection and temporal order of things that the divine simplicity disposed to be. It follows that whatever is under Fate is also under Providence. Perhaps there is no other difference between these two, except that Providence is when we consider it in the divine mind, while Fate is when we consider it in the temporal order of things. 

Nor does Providence or Fate obstruct or impede our free will, as the Aquinate theologian <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas</note> subtly demonstrates in the book *Against the Gentiles* <note>original: "contra gentiles"</note>. Theologians say Fortune is like a certain lady who turns and changes human affairs extravagantly; and with a purpose different from what was intended, she dispenses them in ways neither thought of nor expected. Whence Boethius calls her a "blind deity" <note>original: "cecum numen"</note>. She inclines as much to the wicked as to the good without any choice. 

And if you investigate what difference there is between Fate and Fortune, the learned respond that Fortune is only in those things which appear fortuitous and happen by chance, and where no manifest causes appear that ought to produce such an effect. Fate has immobile causes imposed by God or by the stars upon things. 

But returning to Fortune, they say it exists only in the animal where there is reason <note>i.e., humans</note>, which directs all its operations toward a certain purpose. For this reason, neither an inanimate thing, nor a brute animal, nor small children can have Fortune. Because they do not operate according to any purpose, nothing can happen to them outside their intention and purpose—which is the specific nature of Fortune. Instead, they have Chance (*caso*). Whence we say that a horse returns home "by chance." It seems to me, if I do not err, that I have in brief words distinguished Providence, Fate, Fortune, and Chance. But I believe the poet in...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto VII. Having introduced the concept of Fortune through the examples of Alexander the Great and Diogenes, the author now distinguishes between Fate, Fortune, and the human soul’s free will, drawing on both Classical philosophy and Renaissance Neoplatonism.</meta>

### CANTO SEVEN

This passage intends to avoid confusing fate and fortune indiscriminately. In one, the causes from which effects proceed are known; in the other—Fortune—they are unknown. Thus, the ignorant man who finds treasure while plowing will say it is "good fortune." But the astrologer, who through the man's birth chart knows the cause that led him to find it, will affirm that it is "fate." Virgil expressed this same sentiment when he said, "Omnipotent Fortune and ineluctable fate" <note>original Latin: "Fortuna omnipotens; et ineluctabile fatum"</note>. We shall conclude, then, that Fortune is nothing other than the varying influence of the heavens hidden from us. Depending on the conjunctions, oppositions, trines, quadratures, sextiles <note>these are various angular relationships between planets in astrology</note>, and other various aspects of the planets in the different houses of the zodiac, Fortune governs all things under the circle of the moon as being inferior to them—except for the souls of men. 

Indeed, our soul cannot be dominated by the stars. Therefore, I confess that the superior powers <note>the celestial bodies</note> are created by God with this privilege: that they always have dominion over inferior things. But the rational soul, although it dwells in an inferior place when placed in the body, is nevertheless created by God without the mediation of the heavens or the stars; thus, it is not inferior to them, but superior. Hence, not only our Sacred Scriptures—which cannot contain error because they derive from the fountain of truth—but all philosophers worthy of any esteem, and all mathematicians who subject the government of earthly things to the will of the heavens, affirm that the soul is free and possesses its own judgment. 

For this reason, the divine Plato demonstrates with most true arguments that no "good" can benefit the soul and no "evil" can harm it unless it is within our own power to either have it or be deprived of it. This is because virtue alone is "good" and vice alone is "evil." Neither can virtue be taken from us, nor vice be given to us, by the influence of the heavens—for as Ptolemy says, "the wise man rules the stars" <note>a famous medieval astrological maxim: *Sapiens dominabitur astris*</note>—nor by the violence of man or any other animal. 

See, then, that if corporal goods are in the hands of the heavens and of other men, those of the soul are in our own liberty; and only these can truly be called "ours." This was truly understood by the Platonist Cicero, whose sentiment in his *Paradoxes* is that nothing can be called "mine" or "yours" or "another’s" if it can be robbed or stolen or lost in any way. The city of Priene had fallen into the hands of enemies under the condition that its citizens were permitted to leave with as much property as they could carry. Bias, one of the Seven Sages of Greece and a citizen of that land, left empty-handed. When asked why he carried nothing, he replied that he was carrying "everything that was his." A true word, and fitting for such a wise man; for he knew that by carrying the virtues of his soul, he was carrying everything he owned. 

I have perhaps strayed too far from the topic, but I have related all this so we may understand that although Fortune is what we have described—and all fleeting and transitory goods are placed within her recklessness and fury—the soul remains free. Without her help, and despite her, the soul can become happy, not only in the next life but in this one. 

But returning to the text. Dante says: "tell me, Virgil, what is this Fortune, who has **IN HER CLAWS**"—that is, in her power—"**WORLDLY GOODS**"—meaning temporal goods, according to the phrase "My kingdom is not of this world" <note>original Latin: "Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo"</note>. **AND HE**—meaning Virgil—**SAID TO ME: "LISTEN"**. **O FOOLISH CREATURES**: meaning stupid. We call a food "foolish" [bland] when it is without salt <note>In Italian, "sale" (salt) also means wit or wisdom</note>. And because we often take "salt" to mean "prudence," we call the imprudent "foolish." **HOW GREAT** is the ignorance that harms your intellects; and he rightly said "harms." For when the intellect gains science and knowledge, it becomes perfect; conversely, it becomes imperfect and "harmed" by ignorance. This ignorance makes us believe that Fortune has power over the soul as it does over the body, and that she is a master rather than a servant. 

**TAKE MY** judgment "in your mouth"—that is, receive it. He uses this word as a metaphor for a dog when it takes the wild beast in its mouth. **HIS WISDOM TRANSCENDS ALL**. That is, God, whose wisdom advances and passes every other and pours itself into everything. **HE MADE** the heavens; whence the Psalmist says: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made, and all their power by the breath of his mouth" <note>original Latin: "Verbo dei celi firmati sunt et spiritu oris eius omnis uirtus eorum"</note>. Similarly, He created all other things, but he names the heavens here because he must show that all Fortune is born from their motion. **AND GAVE THEM THOSE WHO LEAD**, because according to Aristotle, He gave to each heaven an "intelligence" to move it. Our author follows this same sentiment in a song that begins: "You who, through understanding, move the third heaven." 

**SO THAT** every part of their power **TO EVERY PART** of the world capable of receiving it **SHINES**. In shining, it infuses. But regarding splendor and light, we shall speak more conveniently in *Paradiso*: how it exists in God, in the angel, in reason, in the spirit, and in the body. And if you first delight in understanding the whole matter, read in the second book of the *Epistles* by our Marsilio Ficino—the most learned of all the Platonists of our age—and you will be satisfied. 

**DISTRIBUTING** equally. Because God, the giver, infuses equally into all creatures; but they receive more or less according to their capacity. **SIMILARLY** to worldly splendors—meaning riches, dignities, and honors—**HE ORDAINED** a general minister. For Divine Providence, which has disposed these worldly goods temporally by means of Fate, administers everything through Fortune. In this, she is served by the movements of the heavens and the angelic virtue. Thus, these shall be "general ministers," because these motions create Fortune. **WHO SHOULD SHIFT** the vain goods from time to time—meaning the aforementioned worldly splendors, which are not true goods. For that is a true good which makes its possessor good, and this is virtue alone. But worldly goods induce infinite evils. They are, therefore, vain and apparent goods, and not true and existing ones. Fortune changes these according to her judgment. Whence it is written in the first book of Kings: "The Lord makes poor and makes rich; he brings low and lifts up. The pillars of the earth are his, and he has set [the world] upon [them]" <note>original Latin: "Dominus pauperem facit Ditat. humiliat; et sublimat. Ipsius sunt cardines terre; et posuit super"</note>.

It draws on authorities like Plato, Cicero, and Marsilio Ficino to argue that true "goods" are internal virtues, which remain beyond Fortune's reach.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the detailed philosophical and astrological commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto VII. Having previously defined Fortune as a celestial influence, the author now draws upon Classical authorities like Boethius, Ovid, and Seneca to illustrate Fortune’s inescapable and cyclical nature, specifically regarding the "translatio imperii"—the transfer of power between world empires.</meta>

<header>INFERNO</header>

<unclear>the</unclear> orb, that is, the wheel of fortune. And Boethius, speaking in the persona of Fortune, says:
> Riches, honors, and other such things are mine by right. My handmaids recognize me as mistress; this is my law. We play this continuous game. We turn the revolving wheel in a circle; we rejoice to change the lowest with the highest, and the highest with the lowest. <note>original Latin: "Opes honores . ceteraque talium sunt mei iuris Dominam famule cognoscunt hec mea ius est Hunc continuum ludum ludimus . Rota uolubili orbe uersamus infima summis Summeque infimis mutare gaudemus ."</note>

Thus speaks Fortune: and she demonstrates that empires, riches, and powers are under her jurisdiction; and how those who serve her recognize her as their lady. She delights in the continual raising and lowering of men. And Ovid says:
> With wavering steps, revolving Fortune wanders; and she remains firm and tenacious in no place. <note>original Latin: "passibus ambiguis fortuna uolubilis errat: et manet in nullo firma tenaxque loco ."</note>

**FROM NATION to nation:** as we see empires transferred with constant change from one people to another. The Assyrians were the first, of whom it is read that they ruled in the eastern parts through the virtue of Ninus and Semiramis <note>Ninus was the mythical founder of Nineveh; Semiramis was his legendary queen</note>. But from them, the empire was transferred to the Medes, and from the Medes to the Persians, whose first king was Cyrus. Nor can it be recounted without a long narrative how, with constant volatility, empires have continually changed: among the Medes, the Egyptians, and the Scythians—insomuch as at one time, the male sex being conquered, women ruled, as one reads of the Amazons. The Greeks ruled. The Africans ruled. The Romans ruled. Nor is power only shifted from nation to nation, but within the same region from city to city, and within the same city from family to family.

**BEYOND THE defense of human wisdom:** because truly human wisdom can maintain the goods of the soul—which are the virtues—against Fortune, and with those virtues acquire a blessed and eternal life. But human wisdom cannot, without the favor of Fortune, maintain states and other vain goods. Therefore Cato, Cicero, and other excellent citizens were able to maintain their virtues, but they could not, with all their prudence (though it was great), defend their own or the public liberty. Thus Seneca rightly said:
> Every kingdom is under a weightier kingdom. Let no one trust too much in prosperity: Clotho <note>one of the three Fates who spins the thread of life</note> mixes these things with those and forbids Fortune to stand still; all fate rotates; God turns our affairs, stirred by a swift whirlwind. <note>original Latin: "Omne sub regno grauiore regnum . Nemo confidat nimium secundis : Miscet hec illis prohibetque Clotho Stare fortunam rotat omne fatum Res deus nostras celeri citatas turbine uerfat ."</note>

And Boethius says:
> What else does the outcry of tragedies bewail, if not Fortune overturning happy things with an indiscriminate blow? <note>original Latin: "Quid tragediarum clamor aliud deflet/ nisi fortunam indiscreto ictu felicia uertentem ."</note>

The tragic poet tells us, then, that Fortune disturbs happy things without choosing favorites. **FOR ONE** nation commands, and the other languishes. Caesar, raised up by the favor of Fortune, obtained the empire. Pompey, having her as an enemy, lost it.

**LANGUISHES:** that is, lives in languor, meaning misery and grief, fleeing as a conquered man into foreign kingdoms.

**FOLLOWING her judgment:** because no one can appeal the judgment given by Fortune. It is necessary to obey that judgment, which is hidden from us like a **SNAKE:** that is, a serpent which, hidden in the grass, deceives our sight because its color is so similar to its surroundings that it is not seen by the person who steps on it. Similarly, Fortune hides a pestilential poison among felicities and vain hopes that kills us.

**YOUR wisdom has no defense against her:** this is almost the same sentiment as the verse directed against the "defense of human wisdom." **HAS NO defense:** that is, it cannot resist even if it anticipates her blows. Indeed, there have been many who, either through prophecy or some other kind of divination, foresaw their calamity, and yet were unable to resist. Astyages, King of the Medes, saw in a dream that from the genitals of his daughter a vine grew whose branches overshadowed all of Asia. The diviners interpreted this to mean that from her a son would be born who was destined to take his kingdom. Therefore, although Astyages took many precautions against this—first marrying his daughter in Persia to a man of very low status, and later commanding that the newborn son be left in the forest for the wild beasts—nevertheless Fortune willed that the boy, who was Cyrus, should escape every danger and, once grown, take the empire from him and transfer it to the Persians. I could cite infinite examples in confirmation of this sentiment, but the size of this volume does not allow me to dwell too long on such an obvious matter.

**PROVIDES, judges, and pursues:** This shows that Fortune, being an influence proceeding from the movements of the heavens—and the motion of the heavens being guided by the Intelligences <note>angels or celestial beings</note> placed there by God as their movers—everything that arises from it proceeds from reason, and not from chance as it seems to us. Therefore, the first Reason "provides," as if consulting on what is to be done; after the consultation, it "judges"; and then it "pursues," that is, it puts into execution what it has judged to be good. By saying "provides," the author hints at Divine Providence, from which all influences proceed.

**THE OTHER gods:** The other Intelligences. He calls Fortune a "goddess," and likewise all the movers of the heavens according to the poets, who called all the stars "gods." Because they are in continuous movement and course, the Greeks called God *Theos* from the verb *thein*, which means "to run." But even the Sacred Scriptures call men "gods," as in: "You are gods and all sons of the Most High." <note>referencing Psalm 82:6</note> Therefore, in that same way, he calls the movers of the spheres "gods."

**THEIR permutations have no truce:** that is, the changes of earthly goods, which proceed from celestial influences, have no "truce," meaning no rest. **This is a metaphor** taken from soldiers who rest during a truce and do not wage war.

**NECESSITY makes her swift.** Certainly, if Fortune is this mutation of temporal goods, and such mutation arises from the constant and swift movement of the heavens, it is necessary that such mutation be swift. Fate, or rather Fortune, turns with a certain necessity just as the sun and the other planets turn in their courses. Nor is our free will taken away by this. Insofar as we are free, we should not trouble ourselves with earthly goods, which are entirely subject to Fortune; but if we do trouble ourselves with them, it follows that we must submit ourselves to Fortune in those matters. Therefore, such necessity exists in the things that, being subject to Fortune, must necessarily change according to her will—but not in us, who can choose whether to trouble ourselves with them or not. And certainly, if we draw near to God in such a way that we entirely despise earthly things, we are completely free from Fortune. If we give ourselves to divine things and yet still desire temporal goods, we are not entirely free. But if, leaving those thi— <note>the text cuts off mid-sentence</note>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical and astrological commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto VII, focusing on the nature of Fortune and the transition from the Fourth Circle (the Avaricious and Prodigal) to the Fifth Circle (the Wrathful and Sullen).</meta>

<header>CANTO SEVEN</header>

If we devote ourselves entirely to earthly things rather than divine ones, we become servants of Fortune, not out of necessity, but by our own will. A man who is out of the sea can choose whether or not to enter the water; but once he has entered, he is forced to obey the winds and the waves. In the same way, we can choose not to seek the goods of Fortune. But if we do seek them, we submit ourselves to that necessity from which we were previously free. You see, then, that the necessity the poet describes is not against free will. Boethius also posits this, saying:
> The further one departs from the Primal Mind, the more one is entangled in the greater bonds of fate. But a thing is freer from fate the closer it seeks the center of things. But if it clings to the stability of the supernal mind, being free of motion, it also transcends the necessity of fate. <note>original Latin: "Qui longius a prima mente discedit/maioribus fati nexibus implicatur . At tanto a liquid fato liberius est : quanto rerum cardinem uicinus petit . Sed si superne mentis heserit firmitati motu carens fati quoque supergreditur necessitatem."</note>

Now returning to the text, it says that the permutations of Fortune never have a truce, because they happen continually. And this is because there is always someone who follows in succession—that is, someone whose turn it is to succeed you in your happiness, while you fall from it. Thus Claudian says:
> While Croesus <note>the famously wealthy King of Lydia</note> holds the top of the wheel, Codrus <note>a legendary King of Athens who died in poverty to save his city</note> holds the lowest part. Julius ascends; the Great one <note>likely Pompey the Great</note> descends to the depths. Sulla lies down; Marius rises. But as the axis turns, Sulla falls and Marius rises. <note>original Latin: "Summa rote dum cresus habet tenet infima Codrus . Iulius afcendit descendit magnus ad ima Sylla iacet surgit marius Sed cardine uerso. Sylla cadit. Surgit Marius."</note>

**THIS IS SHE who is so reviled:** <note>literally "put on the cross"</note> that is, she is tormented with blasphemies, regrets, and complaints **EVEN BY those who should give her praise.** If we understand this to mean the fortunate and the happy, it is a true sentiment. For men are so ungrateful that if, after a long period of happiness, a brief moment of unhappiness occurs, they complain greatly about the small evil and give no thanks for the long-lasting good. If we understand this to mean those who have received no benefit from Fortune, it is likewise an excellent sentiment. For I might complain about not having wealth or power, when I should instead be praising myself, considering that a life of leisure <note>here meaning "otium," the peaceful pursuit of study and quiet</note> is more tranquil than one of tumult, and it is sweeter to be governed than to govern. Furthermore, no one can complain if Fortune either takes back what she had given or never gives it at all. Since these goods are hers, she can both take them back and withhold them without doing any injury, as Boethius proves at length in his book *The Consolation of Philosophy*. **BUT SHE IS BLESSED and does not hear this.** Because such an influence does not lose its vigor because of our complaints or insults; she "does not hear" them, as if she does not value them because they do not hurt her. And the poet subtly touches upon the truth here: because such an influence is an inanimate thing, even though the author poetically calls her a goddess. **WITH THE OTHER first creatures,** that is, with the heavens, which must exist first because the influence proceeding from them comes after. They are therefore first, if not in time, at least in origin. **SHE TURNS HER SPHERE,** that is, she revolves these worldly goods as if they were her sphere. Or rather, she turns her sphere because Fortune is the influence that proceeds from the revolution of the heavens. And in truth, this wheel turns: for wealth creates pride; pride creates impatience; impatience creates war; war creates poverty; poverty creates humility; humility creates patience; patience creates peace; and peace creates wealth. **AND BLESSED, she enjoys herself,** because she cannot be hindered or offended by our complaints.

---

<margin>
Now let us descend to greater pity;
already every star falls that was rising
when I set out; staying too long is forbidden.
</margin>

Having described the punishments of those who poorly administer money, either through avarice or prodigality, it seems to the author time to descend into the fifth circle, where Wrath and Sloth <note>original Italian: "accidia," a spiritual apathy or "noonday devil"</note> are punished. Here, Virgil admonishes Dante to hurry, showing that the night—in which alone they could be in Hell—was already more than half over. Therefore, since so much of the journey remained and more than half the time was already spent, they had to hasten. **NOW LET US DESCEND:** as if to say, we have stayed long enough. He implies that Dante was slower to leave than was appropriate. This allegorically demonstrates how difficult it is for our sensory nature to leave behind riches and the goods of Fortune. He who cares for and values these too much can never rise to true contemplation. Thus, the Truth says in the Gospel:
> No one can serve two masters: God and Mammon. <note>original Latin: "Nemo potest duobus dominis seruire deo et mamone"</note>
That is, God and money. Because he who is greedy for treasures, which are earthly things, cannot lift his mind to divine things. Regarding the difficulty for a rich man to enter heaven: I believe "rich" refers not to one who possesses things, but to one who is greedy for riches and a lover of them. For riches do not harm those who do not seek them or value them more than they are worth, nor those who do not become their servant. Instead, they are an excellent instrument for many virtues. For this reason, vice does not consist in the riches themselves, but in the excessive greed for them and in their wicked use. **To greater pity:** to greater punishment, for the greater the punishment, the greater the compassion. **ALREADY EVERY star falls that was rising when I set out:** by this description of time, he shows that midnight has passed. For if those stars that were rising at their departure (which was at the beginning of the night, as shown by the phrase "the day was departing") had already passed the quarter of the sky—which is the middle of our hemisphere and the highest part over our heads—and were beginning to set in the west, then midnight had passed. This passage is drawn from Virgil where he says:
> Night rushes on, Aeneas; we spend the hours in weeping. <note>original Latin: "Nox ruit Eneas nos flendo ducimus horas"</note>
**STAYING TOO LONG is forbidden:** because, as we showed above, it was not granted to stay in Hell longer than one night. He creates this fiction because we must not stay in the night and darkness of vices any longer than is necessary to contemplate their ruinous nature once.

<meta>This page continues the transition from the Fourth Circle of the Inferno (the Avaricious and Prodigal) into the Fifth Circle, where the Wrathful and the Sullen are punished in the marsh of the Styx. The commentator, Cristoforo Landino, explores the psychological and moral nature of anger through the lens of Aristotelian and Thomistic philosophy.</meta>

<columns>2</columns>
<header>INFERNO</header>

He describes the place and the site of this fifth circle, and their descent, saying: **WE CUT ACROSS** the circle. To "cut across" usually means to divide, but here he means "we traversed through the middle of the circle" and came to the opposite bank. **OVER A** valley that boils and overflows. This shows that at the summit of the valleys a spring arose; as it rose, it boiled—that is, it sent forth a bubbling spring of water. From this abundance, the river was born, which ran through the valley to its lowest point. There, finding no easy exit, it formed a marsh. **BOILS:** this denotes that anger is nothing other than the re-boiling of the blood. <note>Landino draws on the medieval medical theory of humors, where anger was seen as a literal heating of the blood around the heart.</note> **AND OVERFLOWS:** because this internal boiling in the chest overflows outward, appearing in the face and creating a "river" of action that runs forth. This signifies the fury of the choleric person, which lasts only a short time and is not a supreme vice. Thus Horace says: *Anger is a brief madness.* <note>original Latin: "Ira Furor brevis est"</note> But it becomes a supreme vice when it stagnates and creates a marsh—that is, when it endures,

> We cut across the circle to the other bank
> over a spring that boils and overflows
> through a trench that derives from it.
> The water was much darker than perse; <note>Perse is a dark, purplish-black color, often associated with mourning or gloom in medieval heraldry.</note>
> and we, in the company of the murky waves,
> entered down by a strange and difficult way.
> Into the marsh that is named Styx
> this dismal stream goes when it has descended
> to the foot of the wicked, gray slopes.

<column-break/>

from which hatred is born. It is not without reason that anger is punished neither in the spring nor in the river, but only in the marsh. For the boiling of the spring—which is the first movement of the blood—and the river—which is that headlong and sudden fury born from it—deserve pardon, because "first movements" <note>The concept of "primi moti" refers to initial emotional impulses that occur before the conscious mind can intervene.</note> are not within our power. But the marsh—that is, the perseverance and dwelling in anger from which it becomes hatred—is the vice that deserves punishment. **THE WATER** was dark, meaning obscure, and much more so than "perse." This denotes the obscurity and blindness of the mind in the angry person, because in them every light of reason is extinguished. **AND WE** in the company of the murky waves—meaning not clear—**IN** company, walking along the river. **WE ENTER**

<column-break/>

down: going down the slope, they were accompanied by the river. **BY A** strange way: that is, a difficult one, as this is what the word means in the Florentine dialect; and it appropriately shows that the path leading to anger is difficult. For no one falls into this vice except through those things which seem harsh and difficult to them. One does not become angry over pleasant things, but rather rejoices. This stream, which is born from the aforementioned spring, is "dismal"—meaning deprived of all joy—having already descended the aforementioned slopes, which he describes as **GRAY:** meaning murky, it forms a marsh called Styx. But because the allegorical sense—which we endeavor to give to this poem—is greatly served by the description of the Styx marsh and the other infernal rivers, we will refer to that below where the poet writes of it more distinctly.

> And I, who stood intent on looking,
> saw muddy people in that swamp,
> all naked and with a look of fury.
> These were hitting each other, not just with hands,
> but with the head, the chest, and the feet,
> mangling each other with their teeth, piece by piece.

<column-break/>

He attributes an appropriate place to anger. For since anger is nothing other than the kindling of blood around the heart to take revenge, it is fitting that such an impulse proceeds from the sorrow and sadness taken from the injury received. And we have shown that the Styx marsh signifies sadness and sorrow. <note>Etymologically, medieval scholars often linked "Styx" to the Greek word "stygein," meaning to hate or feel sorrow.</note> Anger is, according to Aristotle, the appetite for giving pain to one's adversary for a perceived slight; as if to say they judge it just to do so. Thus Augustine

<column-break/>

said: that to no angry person does it seem that their anger is unjust. But because anger is permitted when it does not exceed proper limits, and is forbidden when those limits are passed, I will repeat with brevity something of the nature of our souls, so that once the origin and the end of anger are understood, we may know how great a vice it is. Therefore, though our soul is simple, incorporeal, and indivisible, nevertheless, because it has various powers and various forces, we say it is divided into such powers: one we call vegetative; another sensitive; another rational. <note>This is the standard Aristotelian division of the soul: the plant-like (growth), the animal-like (sensation/motion), and the human-unique (reason).</note> And the sensitive power has its senses, partly exterior and partly interior. From the senses proceeds judgment. For the eye seeing that this thing is yellow, and the "common sense" <note>A technical term for the internal faculty that synthesizes different sensory inputs.</note> judging it to be sweet, causes the "cogitative" faculty to conclude it is good. Thus the senses determine what thing is good and what is contrary. After the senses, there is another power in the soul: which, having heard the judgment of the senses, rises up either to want what is already judged to be good, or to flee what is judged to be evil. This power is called "appetite": and that which desires is the **concupiscible**. That which flees is the **irascible**. And just as through the concupiscible we desire what the sense judges to be good, so through the irascible we rise up against that which is evil, or which stands in the way of our good. For just as nature has given fire not only lightness—which leads it to its "good," which is the higher place—but also heat with which it burns and consumes every obstacle that prevents it from rising, so she has given the animal the concupiscible and the irascible. One to pursue the good; the other to remove the impediments to that good. We have seen what "appetite" is. But in man, it must be considered that sometimes it is obedient to reason, and then all its movements are good and produce virtuous operations. Sometimes it does not obey, from which the opposite is born. Therefore, when the irascible appetite...

<summary>Landino provides a philosophical and allegorical commentary on the entrance to the Fifth Circle of the Inferno, explaining the nature of anger as a "boiling of the blood" and distinguishing between temporary fury and the stagnant hatred symbolized by the Styx marsh.</summary>
