<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Fifth Circle of the Inferno. Having established the physical nature of the Styx as a boiling marsh of anger, the commentator now distinguishes between types of wrath and introduces the punishment of the "Accidiosi" (the Sullen or Slothful) who lie beneath the surface.</meta>

<page-num>60</page-num>
<header>CANTO SEVENTH</header>

When it arises according to the dictates of reason, just indignation is born in man, through which we are fired to punish and correct justly. Concerning this, it is written: *Be angry, and sin not.* <note>original Latin: "Irascamini et nolite peccare," a reference to Psalm 4:4 and Ephesians 4:26.</note> But when it boils within us without reason, the capital vice of anger is born, which is defined as a boiling of the blood around the heart for the sake of vengeance, as I have already stated. In its beginning, this is called "excandescence" <term>excandescentia: a sudden flare-up of temper</term>, and by the Greeks, *thymos*. If it persists for a while, it is called "wrath," or in Greek, *menis*. But if it persists and remains for a long time, growing old in the soul, it becomes "hatred," which the Greeks call *kotos*. <note>The transcription reads "coton," likely a corruption of the Greek 'kotos' (grudge/rancor).</note> The seat of anger is in the heart, just as the seat of concupiscence <term>concupiscence: strong desire or lust</term> is in the liver. The poet has signified these three states: first, by the boiling spring; second, by the river; and third, by the marsh. Therefore, this wrathfulness must be suppressed, because, as Horace says: *He who does not moderate his anger will wish that undone which his grief and mind prompted.* <note>original Latin: "Qui non moderabitur ire Infectum esse uolet dolor quod suaserit et mens."</note> Likewise: *Anger is a brief madness; rule your mind, which, unless it obeys, commands; restrain this with bits, this with chains.* <note>original Latin: "Ira furor brevis est animum rege qui nisi paret imperat : hunc frenis hunc tu compesce cathenis."</note> He who does not restrain his anger plunges entirely into the Stygian marsh. For he is submerged in sorrow and sadness, and is **MUDDY**. This denotes being in the swamp of Styx—that is, being in pain. **AND ALL NAKED**. This demonstrates that such a vice is always manifest. Indeed, there is no perturbation that appears more clearly in a man's face than anger, which makes the eyes sparkle and the face burn. For this reason, anger has no cover; rather, the heart is seen in the face, because this agitation cannot be hidden by any modesty or dissimulation. **OFFENDED COUNTENANCE**. This word <note>the Italian "sembiante"</note> is more French than Tuscan, and signifies what the Latins call the *vultus* [expression]. Among the Latins, *facies* [face] signifies the form of the visage, such as saying it is broad or long or similar things. But *vultus* signifies that demonstration which appears on the face from some movement of the soul, whether of pain, joy, fear, or something else. Thus, "with offended countenance" means with a disdainful face. **THESE STRUCK EACH OTHER** not just with hands. This demonstrates the fury of the wrathful person, who behaves in such a way that they strike not only with their hands—which is the mode of battle proper to man—but also like wild beasts they strike with their heads, butting; with their chests, shoving; and with their feet, kicking. Allegorically, we understand that the angry person offends not only with the hands—that is, with deeds—but also with the head, which is the imagination, stirring up inventions (since all the senses are in the head); and with the chest—that is, with agitations and heavy thoughts which are in the heart; and with the feet—that is, with the appetite. For just as the feet carry the body, so the appetite carries the soul. **TEARING THEMSELVES**: Breaking themselves apart. The wrathful person uses all this cruelty not only against others, but against themselves, as we have often seen.

> The good master said: "Son, now see
> the souls of those whom anger overcame;
> and also I want you to believe for certain:
> That under the water there are people who sigh:
> and they make this water bubble at the top
> as your eye tells you wherever it turns:
> Fixed in the slime they say: 'Sullen were we
> in the sweet air that is gladdened by the sun,
> carrying within ourselves a sluggish smoke.
> Now we are sullen in the black mire':
> this hymn they gurgle in their throats,
> for they cannot say it with whole words."

<column-break/>

**HE HAS** spoken of the wrathful. Now he will speak of the slothful <term>accidiosi: those suffering from 'accidia' or spiritual apathy</term>. It is not inappropriate that anger and sloth are punished in the Stygian marsh—that is, in sadness—because both are full of sadness. But the wrathful person not only retains it within himself but, by venting it, inflicts it upon others. For this reason, the poet places them above the water and naked. The slothful person participates so much more in sadness that he is entirely submerged within it; and he does not manifest this sadness to others, and all his acts are hidden. For these two reasons, Dante places the slothful submerged under the Styx, which he makes black because every one of their operations is obscure and black. Nor are they recognized beneath the waves, because their obscure deeds have taken away all their fame in the world. But so that this place may be better understood, the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> posit that the stupidity of men is often displeased by that which ought to please them most because it is good. Therefore, he who rejects what by its nature ought to delight him becomes weary. But if he is more vehement and ardent in rejecting it, he is not merely weary but holds it in horror and abomination. From such weariness and abomination, sadness is born in the soul, which the Greeks call *accidia*. *Accidia* is an "aggravating sadness." Or, according to Augustine, *Accidia* is a "weariness of internal good." Or it is a torpor and laziness of a soul negligent in beginning praiseworthy things. Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great, who codified the Seven Deadly Sins.</note> places "sadness" as a capital sin and places *accidia* as a species of it, because *accidia* is an approach toward rest, while sadness is a departure from the good. Thus, the difference between them is like getting out of a boat and stepping onto land: they are the same thing but have different boundaries, like "doctrine" and "discipline." This vice induces tepidness, softness, idleness, sleepiness, delay, negligence, lack of perseverance, dissolution, and carelessness (which is little different from negligence). It also induces lack of devotion—which is not having the soul entirely turned and fixed on divine precepts—weariness of life (that is, regret at living), and desperation, which is the withdrawal and departure from the good due to having no confidence in being able to achieve it. From such vices procreated by sloth proceed rancors, which are hidden; hatreds; and the wandering of the mind toward illicit things.

<summary>This page analyzes the types of wrath (sudden, persistent, and chronic) and introduces the "Accidiosi" (the Sullen or Slothful), who are punished beneath the mud of the Styx for their internalizing of gloom and spiritual apathy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Fifth Circle of the Inferno. Having discussed the actively wrathful who tear each other apart on the surface of the Styx, the author now addresses the "accidiosi"—those guilty of sloth or spiritual apathy—who are submerged beneath the mud.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>INFERNO</header>

and numbness: and lack of confidence. To counter sloth—which consumes the soul just as rust consumes iron—it is necessary to rouse the soul, to warm it, and to set it on fire. This we can do when we consider that man was not born for sleep and food, but was made in the image and likeness of God to contemplate Him; and, as far as our frailty allows, to know Him, to desire Him, and to enjoy Him. And we should consider that in this alone consists our supreme good. For certainly, it is the height of folly to put ourselves in great danger and undergo various and unbearable labors to acquire honors or treasure—things that are momentary and must soon perish—and yet, to attain the supreme and eternal good without which we must remain in everlasting misery, to be unwilling to endure a brief and light inconvenience. Let us, therefore, exchange perishable things for lasting ones, and the mortal life for the immortal. **THAT BENEATH THE WATER** there are people who sigh. They are beneath the water: that is, submerged in sadness, which continually brings forth sighs. **AND THEY MAKE it bubble**: that is, gurgle. A sigh is wind; and when the wind leaves the bottom and comes to the surface, it causes gurgling and bubbles. **AS YOUR EYE tells you**: that is, demonstrates to you; it is phrased as if he said: **WHEREVER IT TURNS**: that is, wherever it revolves. "V" <note>original: "V", an archaic form of "ove"</note> means "where," and it is an Aretine or Sienese term rather than a Florentine one. **FIXED IN THE SLIME.** "Limo" <note>slime or mud</note> in Latin means silt, and silt is the sediment of murky water. But because the melancholic humor is the sediment and dregs of the blood, we shall understand the slothful person to be "fixed in the slime," that is, in sadness and melancholy. Nor does the poet depart from the Sacred Scriptures by placing the slothful in the slime; for Jeremiah, rebuking Moab, said: *The slothful man, resting on his dregs, has not been poured from vessel to vessel.* <note>original Latin: "Requiescens accidiosus in fecibus suis non est trasfusus de uase in uase." See Jeremiah 48:11.</note> And Solomon in Ecclesiastes: *The sluggard is pelted with a filthy stone*; <note>original Latin: "In lapide luteo lapidatus est piger." This quote is actually from Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 22:1.</note> and David, speaking in the person of the slothful: *I have sunk into the deep mire.* <note>original Latin: "Infusus sum in limo profundi." See Psalm 69:2.</note> **SAYING, "SULLEN WERE WE in the sweet air that is gladdened by the sun."** He says that the sadness—that is, the sloth—which they practiced in this life where the light of the sun is seen, is punished in this place. But allegorically we can understand **THROUGH THE SWEET AIR** to mean the time in which we have not yet made a habit of vice. This time "is gladdened by the sun," that is, illuminated by reason, because we have already shown that the sun represents reason. Thus, he says because in the time when we had not yet made a habit of vice we were "sullen"—that is, we made ourselves sad—it has happened that from those frequent acts we have formed a habit. This refers to Hell, in which there is no redemption for the habit of vice. **CARRYING WITHIN A SLUGGISH smoke.** Excellent, because sloth is a species of sorrow which consumes the soul from within and does not vent itself outwardly like anger. **SMOKE**: smoke is black, and whatever it touches, it likewise makes black. Sloth, born of a black humor <note>referring to black bile, the source of melancholy in medieval medicine</note>, makes a man black. For just as joy clears a man’s face and makes it bright, so sloth clouds it and makes it dark. **NOW WE ARE SULLEN in the black mire**: that is, now we are in the habit of sloth; and you can interpret this with the same meaning as "fixed in the slime." **THIS HYMN**: "hymn" means a verse composed in praise of God or some blessed soul; because *hymnein* in Greek means to praise, especially in sacrifices, and they are commonly sung with joy. But here it is the opposite, because they pronounce with sadness not the praise of a celestial spirit, but the infamy of hellish spirits. But there is no error in the poet: for he speaks through irony <term>irony: using words to mean the opposite of their literal sense</term>, which gives gravity and playfulness to speech, as Virgil does: *Meanwhile, his excellent wife.* <note>original Latin: "Egregia interea coniunx." From Aeneid VI.523, regarding Helen of Troy's betrayal.</note> He will use this irony again below when he says, "Rejoice, Florence, since you are so great." **THEY GURGLED IN THEIR THROATS.** This expresses the voice of one who wants to speak but has his windpipe full; for he does not speak, but gurgles. **THROAT** <note>original: "strossa" / "strozza"</note> is the channel that goes from the lungs to the mouth, through which the breath comes; which, striking the palate, the tongue, and the teeth, is shaped into a distinct and articulate voice. Hence it is called "throttling" when we squeeze the throat in such a way that the breath cannot pass and the animal suffocates. **FOR THEY CANNOT SAY IT with whole words**: because the breath, not having a free exit, cannot form distinct and complete words.

---

<columns>2</columns>
> Thus we circled round the filthy pool
> a great arc between the dry bank and the center,
> with eyes turned toward those who swallow the mud;
> We came to the foot of a tower at last.

<column-break/>

The marsh was, as we have seen, in a circle; and between the edge of the circle and the marsh, there remained some space on dry ground. And through this space Virgil circled with Dante until they arrived at the tower. **FROM THE FILTHY pool.** That marsh was "filthy," that is, defiled, because it was

<columns>1</columns>

muddy. **POOL** <note>original: "poza"</note> properly signifies a small collection of water; but here he uses it for the great marsh of the Styx. In this, he uses a figure of speech very common among Greek and Latin poets called *thapinosis* <term>thapinosis: a rhetorical device where a thing is belittled or understated to emphasize its nature</term>, as if the great thing were lowered by describing it with a term that implies something small. Just as in Virgil when he says, *In the vast abyss*, where he uses "abyss" <note>original Latin: "gurges," literally a whirlpool or pool</note> to mean the sea. **GREAT ARC**: Whoever goes around a whole round makes a circle; but whoever surrounds only a part makes an arc. **BETWEEN THE dry bank**: that is, the bank of the marsh not touched by the water. **AND THE CENTER** <note>original: "mezzo"</note>: that is, that part which was bathed by the water. *Mezzi* in Florentine refers to apples when they are so ripe that they begin to dissolve into putrefaction, which the Latins call *poma mitia* <note>soft or mellow apples</note>. Thus, from this *mitia* comes *mezzo*. And because an overripe apple is soft, we call everything soft *mezzo*. Thus, "between the dry bank and the *mezzo*," that is, the soft place of the marsh. **SWALLOW** <note>original: "ingoza"</note>: they gulp down; because *gozo* <note>throat/maw</note> signifies the gullet. Hence *sgozare* means to cut the gullet.

The commentary concludes with the travelers circling the marsh and arriving at the tower of Dis.</summary>

### EIGHTH CANTO OF THE FIRST CANTICLE OF DANTE.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'I' in blue and gold with red accents, containing scrolling foliage.</image-desc>
I say, continuing, that long before
we reached the foot of the high tower,
our eyes went up toward its summit
Because of two little flames we saw placed there:
and another from afar gave back a signal:
so far off that the eye could barely seize it.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'B' in blue and gold with red accents, containing scrolling foliage.</image-desc>
Although the song changes: nevertheless it still persists in the fifth circle: where the wrathful: and the slothful <note>original: "accidiosi", referring to those guilty of spiritual apathy or gloom</note> are punished. And it demonstrates how, by a signal made from the tower, Phlegyas <note>The mythological king of the Lapiths, here serving as the ferryman of the Styx</note> came and took them aboard: and while sailing they found Filippo Argenti <note>A prominent Florentine politician and rival of Dante</note> in the marsh: and finally they arrived at the city of Dis <note>The inner city of Hell, containing the lower circles of fire and ice</note>. **I SAY, Continuing.** We can simply understand: that the author, wishing to link the beginning of this chapter with the end of the preceding one, uses these words: "I say, continuing in my narration." And note that although he had said above that he had arrived at the tower, he nevertheless turns back somewhat in his speech to narrate: that before they had reached it, they saw the signal made upon the summit. 

But Giovanni Boccaccio <note>The famous author of the Decameron and an early biographer of Dante</note>—a man worthy of faith both for his learning and his character, and for being close to Dante's time—reports having heard from Andrea, son of Leone Poggi <note>Dante's nephew</note>, and from one of Dante's sisters: that after Dante, together with Messer Vieri de' Cerchi, was made an exile from his homeland, his wife named Gemma, before the popular tumult rushed to his house, smuggled his most precious things to a safe place: and among them the writings of Dante. 

Then, after five years or more, she, wishing to recover some of her husband's possessions in the name of her dowry, sent Andrea with a procurator <note>a legal representative</note> to the place where the writings were, to extract certain instruments <note>legal documents or deeds</note> necessary for the case. The procurator, among the writings, found a small notebook in Dante's hand: in which were written these first seven chapters: and being pleased by them, he carried them to Dino, son of Messer Lambertuccio Frescobaldi, a man of letters and experienced in Tuscan verse. Dino, then, having read such a noble beginning not without amazement, and being inflamed with a great desire that the work be finished, sent the notebook to Lunigiana to the Marquis Morello Malaspina. And by his letters, he begged him to see to it that Dante, who in those times was with him, should finish the work. 

It was a most welcome thing to Dante: who, believing these chapters to have perished with many other things that had been the prey of the people, had turned away from his purpose. But then, having recovered them, and being persuaded by the Marquis, he decided to continue: And taking up the material again, he gave this beginning to the eighth canto. **I SAY, Continuing** the work already begun before my exile. This is what Boccaccio said he heard from Andrea. Furthermore, he adds having heard from Ser Dino Perini, who had been very intimate with Dante, that he himself had been the procurator sent by the wife: and that he, and not Andrea, had brought the notebook to Dino. And finally, Boccaccio doubts whether this story is true: because in the fifth chapter <note>actually Canto VI</note> he induces Ciacco to speak of things that occurred three years after Dante's exile.

Here we can place the allegorical sense, understanding by the tower and the flames placed upon the summit the kindling of anger: and by three flames three types of anger, about which we have spoken above. But as for the literal sense, it is this, in imitation of what is done among men when... they look from one land to another, signaling with smoke, and at night—as it was then—with fire.

**AS THE POET** above placed Pluto for the vice of avarice, adapting his fiction to what the ancients write of Pluto. <meta>This page continues the commentary on the entrance to the Fifth Circle of Hell. The previous page discussed the signal towers across the Stygian marsh. Here, the commentator introduces Phlegyas, the boatman of the Styx, explaining his mythological background and the allegorical significance of the sins punished in these waters: Wrath, Pride, Envy, and Sloth.</meta>

# CANTO EIGHT #

This woman <note>Coronis, daughter of Phlegyas</note> was violated by Apollo: and from such a union was born Aesculapius, a man so excellent in medicine that he was called the god of that art. But Phlegyas conceived such anger against Apollo for having violated his daughter that he set fire to and burned his temple. This occurred in the three thousand seven hundred and fifty-second year after the world was created. And the poets feign that Apollo, with his arrows, cast him into hell and decreed such a punishment: that he should have a great rock over his head, which continually kept him in fear of it falling upon him. And of this, Virgil said: <note>original Latin: "Saxum ingens uoluunt alii radiis-que rotarum Districti pendent : sedet eternumque sedebit infelix Theseus Phlegiasque miserrimus omnes Admonet et magna testatur uoce per umbras."</note> "Some roll a huge stone, and others hang stretched on the spokes of wheels; the unhappy Theseus sits and will sit forever, and the most wretched Phlegyas warns everyone and testifies with a loud voice through the shadows." Therefore, the poet, seeing that this man had been so conquered by anger that he became impious and sacrilegious toward the gods, places him in this location for wrath. Not only for wrath, but also for pride: because in this part where the marsh is enclosed between the two towers, pride is also punished. And by the towers, one can denote their haughtiness; and by the flames, the heat of overbearing; and by the ship, the impetus of pride, which swiftly wishes to trample everyone, just as the ship sits atop the water; and he places a single pilot, because the proud man always wishes to be alone and without equal. Nor does the proud man deserve any other punishment, except that, wishing to stand above all, he finds himself beneath the filth and the mud. Whence Jeremiah says: <note>original Latin: "Cadet superbus et non erit qui resuscitet eum : et conculcabitur corona superbie."</note> "The proud one shall fall and there will be no one to raise him up, and the crown of pride shall be trampled." And Job: <note>original Latin: "Si ascenderit in celum superbia et caput eius nubes tetigerit quasi sterquilinium in fine perdetur."</note> "If his pride should climb to heaven and his head touch the clouds, he will be lost in the end like a dunghill." And David: <note>original Latin: "Delebo eos ut puluerē terre. Quasi lutum platearū minuam eos."</note> "I will erase them like the dust of the earth. I will grind them down like the mud of the streets." And for the same reason, Virgil demonstrates that it is the proper office of whoever justly administers the republic <note>original Latin: "Parcere subiectis et debellare superbos."</note> "To spare the humble and to war down the proud." Nor was it without considered judgment that the poet places Wrath, <term>Sloth</term> <note>original: "Accidia," the spiritual apathy or "noonday devil"</note>, Pride, and Envy in almost similar punishment: because there is great kinship between these vices. So that this may be more openly shown, we shall say, following Augustine, that just as virtue is ordered love, so conversely, vice is disordered love. And this disordered love exists in three ways. The first is when it is too great for small goods—that is, temporal ones. From this are born Lust, Gluttony, and Avarice. The second way is when love is too small for great goods—that is, the goods of grace. From this proceeds Sloth, which, because it participates in sadness with the wrathful, deserves to be punished in the Stygian marsh with them. In the third way, disordered love is the love of evil. And this is recognized in pride, envy, and wrath. For the proud man loves another’s ill for his own good; he loves the neighbor's misfortune for his own exaltation. In the envious and the wrathful, there is only the love of another’s ill. But envy has its origin in one's own malice—that is, from pride—because the envious man wants the neighbor's misfortune so that they do not become his equal. Wrath is born from the love of the neighbor's ill through the desire for revenge. Therefore, these four vices are similar. For which reason they are deservedly punished together. And certainly, as soon as pride is born in us, envy is also awakened; because desiring vain reputation and power, we begin to have envy for others, so that they do not equal us. And because of this, we lose gentleness, and in its place succeeds wrath, which saddens us and leads us into sloth. For which reason, without error, we can conclude that these four vices are punished in this swamp. And the two towers serve both for the ascension and elevation of wrath and for the haughtiness of pride, which is double: for we are thus made proud by intrinsic goods, attributing everything to our own wisdom and our own learning, just as we are by extrinsic goods, becoming elated by riches, power, dignity, and honors. We have said this in another place, but here I repeat it: the poet maintains one order in Hell and another in Purgatory regarding the vices. He observes this not only to vary the narration—from which it follows that the reader does not grow weary of hearing the same thing many times in the same way—but also because in the contemplation of vices, we must consider the effects on the soul, which are more numerous than the vices themselves; and in purgation, it is sufficient to recognize the vices themselves that proceed from those effects.

> My guide descended into the boat:
> and then made me enter after him;
> and only when he was inside did it seem laden.
> As soon as the guide and I were in the vessel,
> the ancient prow went on its way,
> cutting more of the water than it usually does with others.

<column-break/>

We said that the wrathful are punished in this marsh, which, according to the "essential" Hell <note>meaning the literal state of the damned in the afterlife</note>, signifies that here are punished the souls who, passing from this life, remained damned by such a vice. But allegorically, we shall say: that those who have made a habit of this vice, and therefore are damned in it, are submerged in the Styx: that is, in perpetual sadness. But those who descend into this place not to be defiled by the vice, but to know it and contemplate it,

<column-break/>

do not fall into the marsh: but are carried across the surface without getting wet, in such a way that remaining dry—that is, pure from the sin—they see those who are plunged beneath. **MY GUIDE** descended into the boat: Virgil enters the boat first. For in proper contemplation, through which we find the truth, superior reason, like a true guide, goes forward; and Dante, who signifies sensuality obedient to that reason, follows him. And Virgil makes him stay near him: that is, he does not let him depart from his obedience. **AND ONLY WHEN** he was inside did it seem laden. As for the fictional narrative, it is an appropriate thing that Dante, having a physical body, should weigh down the boat much more than Virgil. And allegorically, superior reason is so

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s passage across the Styx. The previous text described the boatman Phlegyas and the allegorical nature of the vessel. Here, Landino explains the interaction between the soul’s reason and its lower senses as they traverse the marsh of the wrathful.</meta>

# INFERNO #

...light: and so far from vice: that in contemplation it always stays afloat: and does not drown in it. But sensuality, although it is disposed to follow reason: nevertheless, because of its fragility, cannot help but sink into it somewhat. This same sentiment was expressed by Virgil when he said: *And it took in much water through the leaky marsh* <note>original Latin: "Et multam accepit rimosa palude," from Aeneid VI.414</note>. And as soon as they were in the wood: that is, in the ship: which carried them. Which in this context signifies the will to contemplate. CLEAVING the ancient prow went on: Prow signifies the front of the ship: which is that part which, being pointed, pierces and divides the waters. Wherefore it is placed here for the sharpness of the intellect in the contemplative life, with which we can open up obscure things. IN THE WATER MORE, understand with me, THAN IS accustomed with others. Here apply the same allegory as above. AND ONLY when I was inside did it seem laden. ANCIENT: because such a passage—since the Hell of which he spoke before me—contained no created things except eternal ones. Or, having explained the prow as the sharpness of the intellect in contemplating, we can say Ancient: because only speculation in the first man existed before action.

> While we were running through the dead slime /
> before me appeared one full of mud: /
> and said: "Who are you who come before your hour?" /
> And I to him: "If I come, I do not stay: /
> but you, who are you who have become so ugly?" /
> He replied: "You see that I am one who weeps:" /
> And I to him, with weeping and with mourning /
> accursed spirit, remain: /
> for I know you, even though you are all filthy." /
> Then he stretched out both hands to the boat: /
> wherefore the wary master pushed him back /
> saying: "Away there with the other dogs."

<column-break/>

WHILE we were running through the dead slime. He uses an improper word for the sake of the rhyme. For in Florentine we call a *gora* <term>gora: a man-made canal or mill-race</term> a channel of running water; such as those that turn a mill-wheel: But he corrects this with the opposite adjective that he placed there, calling it "dead." For just as we call "living water" that which runs: so "dead water" is that which does not run. BEFORE ME appeared one full of mud. We said above: because anger: and pride are stuck in the mud: And he asks Dante who he is: and says he comes BEFORE HIS HOUR: that is, before the time. Because souls do not go into hell before they depart from the body. And allegorically, no one is counted among the wrathful who has not first made a habit of it: And Dante not only had not made a habit of it: but had descended to contemplate it so as not to perform any such act. But the damned spirit did not understand that those who direct themselves toward the good descend into hell not to defile themselves with vices: But to know them so that they may guard themselves against them.

AND I TO HIM: he sets up a certain contention between Dante: and the spirit. To denote both the nature of the wrathful in the spirit: and to signify that Dante, that is, sensuality, while he contemplates vices often pursues them with just indignation: But yet, because the contagion of the corporeal mass makes it prone, it would finally be overcome: Which he openly declares by feigning that the spirit, after such contention, stretched out his hands to embrace him and pull him into the mire. This signifies that sensuality was being attacked by the vice: But Virgil: that is, superior reason, defended it by pushing the spirit back into the mire. For when reason sees sensuality being attacked by sin: and yet resisting, then it wakes up: and wakes her: and by showing her the ruin that sin brings with it, drives it entirely from the appetite: But return to the text AND I TO HIM WITH weeping and with mourning accursed spirit remain for I know you: He asked at the beginning who he was: and later he knew him without him saying it. To denote that he who goes speculating often does not understand at the beginning: and asks a teacher for that which in time, without the help of others, he comes to know. Furthermore, he wishes to show that the disturbance of anger is so vehement that it transforms the man into a shape: that in the beginning he is not recognized, so ugly do they become. Wherefore Plato commanded that the angry man should look at himself in a mirror: And therefore he added EVEN THOUGH you are all filthy: And similarly pride transforms a man: and strips him of all humanity: which belongs only to man: and clothes him in cruelty, a vice entirely contrary to man: and proper to wild beasts. Therefore, he who contemplates such a vice recognizes no human likeness in it. WHEREFORE THE MASTER: He calls him master: because superior reason is that which, with its precepts, instructs sensuality. WITH THE other dogs: Because the angry man is very much like a dog.

> My neck then with his arms he encircled: /
> he kissed my face and said: "Disdainful soul, /
> blessed is she who bore you in her womb!" /
> That man was an arrogant person in the world. /
> There is no goodness that graces his memory. /
> Thus is his shade here, full of fury.

<column-break/>

He shows that Virgil, having pushed the spirit back into the water, turned to Dante and embraced his neck: and kissed his face. This signifies that when reason has defended sensuality: which also helped itself; it then embraces it and almost entirely surrounds it to make it better armed against vices: and kisses its face: that is, it applauds it and almost coaxes it toward doing good. AND SAID DISDAINFUL soul:

<meta>This page continues Landino’s commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto VIII. Having just encountered the wrathful in the marsh of the Styx, the text now focuses on the interaction with the shade of Filippo Argenti and the moral distinction between sinful anger and righteous indignation.</meta>

# CANTO EIGHT #

> How many now hold themselves up there as great kings /
> who here will stand like pigs in the mire /
> leaving behind of themselves horrible contempt.

In the Florentine tongue, this properly signifies "reasonable," and thus disdain is found in virtue. Which is excellently illustrated by **BLESSED** <note>original: "BENEDECTA"</note> **is she who was pregnant with you** <note>original: "cholei chen te si cinse"</note>: that is, blessed be your mother, who, when she was pregnant with you, girded herself around her womb where you were; and thus she girded herself in you, that is, over you. Wishing to show literally the congratulation that Virgil used toward Dante, he used the words that are customary when we wish to praise the tree when it produces good fruit. Nor should Dante be reproved for praising himself in this place, because he does not praise himself. But under his own name, he praises sensuality when it takes up a just disdain against vice. And allegorically we can understand that reason always commends the appetite when it is obedient to her. And he shows his mother to be blessed, who is reason herself. Because such an appetite is created by reasonable judgment and not by the senses. **WHO WAS IN THE WORLD an arrogant person.** Arrogant <note>original: "Orgoglioso"</note> signifies arrogant: that is, he who attributes so much to himself that he does not suffer anyone to oppose or contradict any of his opinions, or touch him in any way. And nevertheless, he is worth little. Wherefore it is fitting that of such men no other fame remains except that of their bizarre whims <note>original: "bizarria"</note>: because they have had no goodness or virtue in them for which they might be named. Nor can there be a greater punishment for the arrogant than to acquire infamy instead of fame. And of such vice are princes and lords much stained, who, swollen by their happy fortune, give themselves to understand that they are wiser than others. And certainly, it is difficult not to become proud in happiness, and not to deceive oneself; especially because there are very few who dare to show them their errors: and an infinite crowd they always have around them of flatterers and yes-men, who are prompt to praise even things worthy of the highest vituperation. Therefore, while they are in a good state, everyone praises them: but afterward, everyone blames them. Which, when they realize it, causes them to gnaw and infuriate themselves. And for this reason, he deservedly says **HOW MANY hold themselves up there**, that is, in life and in happiness, **GREAT KINGS**: great princes. As if to say, they hold themselves worthy of that state: and thus everyone proclaims them. They hold themselves to be kings and are not. For he is truly a king who rightly rules himself and others. Therefore, Alexander the Great was not a king when he was conquered by anger or by drunkenness, nor did he judge others rightly, nor did he contain himself within the bounds of temperance. Wherefore the Stoics rightly conclude: that only the wise man is a king; because no one, unless he is wise, rightly rules himself and others. **WHO HERE IN HELL**: that is, either after death, or when they shall be ruined from such a high degree. **WILL STAND LIKE pigs in the mire.** They will be depressed and reviled and placed in infamy: because men will then dare to speak the truth about them. Therefore, in place of the good fame for which they were greedy, they leave behind ignominy.

> And I: "Master, I would be very eager /
> to see him ducked into this slop /
> before we depart from the lake." /
> And he to me: "Before the shore /
> lets itself be seen by you, you shall be satisfied: /
> it is fitting that you enjoy such a desire." /
> After this, I saw a little while later that outrage /
> done to him by the muddy people, /
> that I still praise God for it and thank Him. /
> All were crying out: "At Filippo Argenti!" /
> and the bizarre Florentine spirit /
> turned upon himself with his own teeth. /
> Here we leave him, for I tell no more of him: /
> but into my ears there struck a wailing, /
> wherefore I unbar my eyes, intent, looking forward.

**AFTER THIS, A LITTLE.** A little after Virgil’s words, I saw this man being outraged by the muddy people: that is, by those who were soiled by the same vice. To denote that one proud man punishes another. Nor did compassion for these come to Dante: because no reasonable man feels regret for the punishment of such—

<column-break/>

Understand this as just disdain. And he wishes to show: that just as that anger, which is a vice, was demonstrated in the spirit, so in Dante is demonstrated that irascible part which moves with just disdain against vices; which the Greeks call **Nemesis** <note>original: "Nemesin"</note>. And in the language, "just indignation"; and how pride is a vice Petrarch expressed: "And in a loving woman still / Not proud and stubborn."

The poet proceeds most wisely. For since Dante is in the place of the appetite obedient to reason, and for this reason having been moved to just disdain, he desires that the bizarre man be punished. And Virgil, that is, reason—which ensures that every sin has its punishment following it—promises him that he shall see him outraged. Furthermore, Dante puts this to denote that the arrogant are so hateful to every man that everyone desires to see them punished. And he wants him to be ducked **IN THE SLOP** <note>original: "NELLA BRODA"</note>. We say in Florentine "brodo" [broth] and "broda" [slop]: "Brodo" is that in which some food is cooked and eaten. But "broda" is the wash-water of dirty vessels and any turbid water. And here he uses it for infamy and ignominy. **AND HE TO ME, before the shore lets itself be seen**: that is, before you can see the bank of the marsh to which we are sailing. **YOU SHALL BE SATISFIED**: that is, you will see so much outrage done to him that it will suffice you. **AND IT IS FITTING that you enjoy such a desire**: because he enjoys what he desires who obtains it. **AFTER**—

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto VIII of Dante’s Inferno. Following the encounter with the wrathful souls in the Stygian marsh, the narrative shifts from the punishment of individual anger—specifically that of Filippo Argenti—to the approach of the City of Dis, marking the transition into Lower Hell.</meta>

# INFERNO #

There are some vices for which, although a person is reasonably punished, they nevertheless move our senses to compassion. Thus, it was shown above in the punishment of Francesca and others similar to her that the narrator felt no small pity. On the other hand, there are other vices that move us to indignation rather than compassion, such as this one and all those involving contempt or cruelty. In the punishment of these, we lift our hands to heaven in approval. **EVERYONE** cried out: that is, they said it by shouting. **AT PHILIP:** that is, "get him, Philip." This man, according to what Boccaccio says he heard from Coppo di Borghese Domenichi, was a knight of the noble Cavicciuli family—one of the branches of the Adimari. He was so rich that he used to shoe his horse with silver. He was a man of great stature, muscular, of dark complexion, and of marvelous strength; but he was so overcome by anger that for every small offense he would fly into a rage beyond all measure. **THE FLORENTINE** whimsical <note>original: "bizarro"</note> spirit. **UPON HIMSELF** he turned with his teeth: that is, seeing himself offended and being unable to defend himself, he bit himself out of rage. By these words, the author demonstrates both the bestial nature of the wrathful man and notes that he who gives himself over to anger harms himself more than others. **THERE** we left him, for I tell no more of him: we leave him here because the wrathful man remains in this state, and his end is to turn his anger upon himself in one of two ways: either when he cannot avenge an injury, or when he repents of the error committed, like Alexander the Great <note>The famous Macedonian king and conqueror (356–323 BCE).</note>, who several times wanted to kill himself when, his anger having passed, he recognized how much he had erred. **FOR I TELL** no more of him: that is, one cannot describe a more extreme fury in a wrathful person than this—that he turns his rage upon himself. And when we have narrated this of the wrathful, we can say no more. Or rather, he said "I tell no more" to show that such men are not worthy of being discussed. **BUT UPON** my ears there struck a sound of woe: that is, I heard a sorrowful voice. For we hear when a voice reaches the ear and strikes it. **WHEREFORE** I intently unbar my eyes: that is, having heard the voice, I suddenly and with attention "unbarred," or opened my eyes wide in every direction. **FORWARD:** looking ahead of me. For when we hear a voice, we are accustomed to look diligently to see if we can perceive where it comes from.

The good master said, "Now, son,
The city named Dis approaches,
With its heavy citizens and its great throng."
And I: "Master, already its mosques
There within the valley I discern,
Red, as if they had come out
Of fire." And he told me: "The eternal fire
That burns within them shows them red,
As you see in this low hell."

<column-break/>

Approaching, they were now so near to the city positioned in the middle of the marsh that the larger and taller buildings began to be discerned. Here it is to be understood that the poet in this imitates Virgil as much as our religion allows. For Virgil describes hell and places the lesser sins in the first circles, and those which were mixed with some image of virtue. Then he describes Tartarus surrounded by the Phlegethon, a fiery river. He places doors with diamond columns. He places the tower of iron. He places the infernal fury Tisiphone to guard the gate. Similarly, Dante in the superior circles has placed the lighter sins, which, because they proceed from incontinence <note>The inability to restrain one's physical or emotional impulses.</note>, are worthy of some commiseration. 

And as for the moral aspect, although it is difficult to change any habit once formed, it is nevertheless more difficult to change it in sins that proceed from either violence or fraud. Furthermore, those already mentioned are not entirely stripped of some semblance and image of humanity. But these who are punished in Dis have their origin in supreme savagery and inhumanity. And the more our soul is distanced from humanity by such wickednesses, the more difficult it is to return to it. Therefore, although the first gate—which embraces and encloses within itself all vices—said "Abandon all hope, ye who enter" (showing that there is no redemption for habits formed in any vice), nevertheless, it is found much less so in the more serious ones. And for this reason, he feigns that this city is impregnable. **APPROACHES THE** city named Dis. The author names this city after its lord. For the poets say that Pluto, whom the Latins call Dis, is the lord of the underworld. **WITH HEAVY:** that is, full of gravity and trouble. **WITH THE GREAT THRONG:** To denote that those who go there by sinning are infinite. **AND I, MASTER,** already discern its mosques within: as if to say, I see the largest buildings in it, which he calls mosques. "Mosque" <note>original: "meschite"</note> in the Turkish language signifies their temples where they worship Muhammad. These have tall towers where those who call the people with loud voices ascend, because they do not have bells to gather them. And he deservedly calls the place where sinners are tormented "mosques," because there one can say is the temple where sacrifice is made to the devil. **RED.** As if scorched by fire: because he imagines these buildings to be of fire, and made red-hot by the constant heat. And in this he imitates Virgil: *The Tartarean Phlegethon, a river of fire, surrounds [the walls] with rushing, scorching flames* <note>original: "Que rapidus flammis ambit torrentibus amnis tartareus Phlegeton"</note>. Likewise: *An iron tower stands high in the air* <note>original: "Stat ferrea turris ad auras"</note>. And certainly, much greater and more furious fires burn the souls of such sinners, and there is more hardness in their hearts than there is in those who are outside of Dis.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s *Inferno*, Canto VIII. The previous page concluded the encounter with Filippo Argenti in the Stygian marsh. Now, the travelers approach the formidable fortifications of the City of Dis, marking the entrance to Lower Hell where more serious sins are punished.</meta>

# CANTO EIGHT #

**WE INDEED:** that is, finally. It is as if he says: although the navigation was long, nevertheless we reached **INSIDE THE DEEP DITCHES.** This shows that the land was impregnable. For first, it had very deep ditches which **WALLED IN:** that is, surrounded; and this is a Latin term <note>The commentator notes that "vallare" (to wall in/surround) derives from the Latin *vallum*.</note> **THAT LAND, DISCONSOLATE:** that is, a place where the damned have no consolation. Then it had walls of iron, as we said above. One who descends into the ditches moves away not only from heaven, but from the surface of the earth. Thus, the soul that has formed a habit of wicked vices always sinks deeper and is submerged in earthly things, distancing itself from the celestial. This makes the City of Dis very impregnable because it does not allow a man to escape from sin. And just as a blind man without a guide easily falls into a ditch, so the man who has lost the light of reason—and is thus blind in his appetite—falls into the ditch of vices.

> We indeed arrived inside the deep ditches
> which wall in that disconsolate land;
> the walls seemed to me to be of iron.
> Not without first making a great circuit
> we came to a place where the loud helmsman
> shouted to us: "Out! Here is the entrance."

**NOT WITHOUT** first making a great circuit: If we wish to apply this to one who enters this city through contemplation <note>The term "speculatione" here refers to deep intellectual study or contemplation of the nature of vice.</note>, we will say that it is not without a great circuit—that is, not without a long discourse of reason and a circuit of contemplation—that one comes to the knowledge of these vices. For those who enter to remain there in eternal torment, this is also not without a great circuit, because a habit of vice is not formed such that one cannot leave it unless we have first circled around it many times with many operations and actions; for a habit is formed through repeated actions <note>original: "Habitus fit ex frequentatis actibus"</note>. And so that this helmsman and this gate do not seem superfluous—since another gate was placed above where it is written "Through me one goes..." etc., and another helmsman was at the Acheron—we must understand that up to this point he has described the first precinct, the suburbs of the city, in which he placed those who sin through lack of self-control <note>The term "incontinentia" (incontinence) refers to sins of passion like lust, gluttony, and anger.</note>. Now he presents the second precinct where sins committed through violence are punished. And further inside he will place another helmsman and another precinct where those who have committed fraud are tormented. And although many interpret the rivers for crossing into some form of knowledge, nevertheless it pleases us to interpret them as appetite, which leads the ship of the will and of choice to sin. Above, we have shown what reason moves us to give such an allegory.

> I saw more than a thousand upon the gates
> rained down from heaven, who angrily
> were saying: "Who is this who, without death,
> goes through the kingdom of the dead people?"
> And my wise master made a sign
> of wanting to speak to them secretly.
> Then they shut in a little their great disdain
> and said: "Come you alone, and let him go,
> who so boldly entered through this kingdom.
> Let him return alone by his foolish road;
> let him try if he knows how, for you shall stay here,
> who have escorted him through so dark a country."
> Think, reader, if I lost heart
> at the sound of those cursed words,
> for I did not believe I would ever return here.

**I SAW MORE THAN A THOUSAND:** He uses a specific number for an indeterminate one, like Persius: "A thousand types of men" <note>original: "Mille hominum speties"</note>. Therefore, I saw many. **RAINED DOWN** from heaven: Demons, who, following the side of Lucifer, rained down from heaven as we said above. **ANGRILY:** irascibly. **WHO IS THIS who without death goes through the kingdom of the dead people?** Those in Hell are dead because there is no redemption, and those in the flesh are alive because there is redemption. Allegorically, he who has formed a habit of vice is dead because he cannot detach himself from it. And he is alive who has not formed a habit, nor is entangled in it, but wishes to enter into vice through contemplation, which causes him to guard himself from it thereafter. Therefore the demon, who desires damnation, as willingly as he opens to those who remain there, conversely does not want to open to the living. That is, he does not want one who has not formed the habit to have the knowledge by which he can guard himself. Therefore, they strive to take Virgil away—that is, the rational part—without which Dante could neither enter the city nor return back. For if sensuality and the lower reason were abandoned by the higher reason in the knowledge of vices, they would allow themselves to be lured and caught by them, and would make a habit of them and could not leave Hell, nor enter into the contemplation of vices. Not without reason did he say "more than a thousand," because the temptations that flatter us toward vices are innumerable. **MY WISE MASTER MADE A SIGN of wanting to speak to them secretly.** Virgil wants to speak to the demons in secret from Dante; that is, the higher reason by itself—which has knowledge of universals—wants to placate the guardians of that city so they might open the gates. For every speculative science is of universals and not of particulars, which Dante—that is, the senses and the lower reason—is not occupied with. There cannot be a temptation that overcomes the soul in which ignorance does not fall. Therefore, to overcome temptation, higher reason instructed by science is necessary, which does not err in the senses. **THEN THEY SHUT IN A LITTLE THEIR GREAT DISDAIN.**

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s *Inferno*, Canto VIII, focusing on the moment the fallen angels (demons) at the gates of Dis refuse to let Dante pass. The previous page ended while discussing the "circuit of contemplation" required to understand the nature of vice.</meta>

# INFERNO #

That is, they hid their disdain: and showed themselves to be somewhat calmed. **AND THEY SAID: YOU COME** alone, and let that one go. It is as if they are saying that only higher reason <note>In this commentary, Virgil represents "higher reason" (the intellectual capacity to understand divine principles), while Dante represents "lower reason" (humanity's practical or sensory side).</note> is admitted into this contemplation: nor can the gate be barred to him, because he knows the first principles. And let "Dante" go away, representing the lower reason mentioned just above. **WHO SO BOLDLY ENTERED** this kingdom. And certainly, it is not without temerity for the lower reason to set itself to contemplate [these depths]: for it does not belong to the realm of universal things to be contemplated, but to particular, active things. Nevertheless, the demon could not reasonably reproach Dante for temerity, because he did not set himself to contemplate alone, but followed higher reason. However, the demon often tempts the lower reason in the soul of man to make it feel useless, so that it does not apply itself to knowing; and certainly, if it were not accompanied by the higher, it would grow faint and fall into despair. **ALONE LET HIM** return by the foolish path: That is, let him, being foolish, return alone. This is a poetic way of attribute to a thing what belongs to a man. Likewise Virgil wrote: *Sitting grimly upon savage arms* <note>original: "Seua sedens super arma"</note>. Or truly, he called the path foolish because the road that leads to vice is full of foolishness, since sin is born from ignorance. And he says "let him return alone" as if to say: "which will be impossible for him," because without higher reason, the sensuality <term>sensuality: the part of the soul concerned with physical desires and emotions</term> would neither exit nor disentangle itself from vice. Hence, he demonstrates this a little further down, saying that he never believed he would return there—that is, to emerge from Hell (meaning from vice) and return to life. **LET HIM TRY IF HE KNOWS HOW:** This is a poetic way of expressing our opinion; "let him try if he knows how" is as if saying he will not know how and will not be able to. **FOR YOU SHALL REMAIN HERE;** because in truth our intellect, signified by Virgil, always revolves around things that can be studied; and he is the one who provides light through the darkness: that is, he demonstrates obscure things to the lower part of the soul.

> "O my dear leader, who more than seven
> times has restored my confidence and drawn
> me from other perils that stood against me,
>
> Do not leave me," I said, "so undone;
> and if passing further is denied us,
> let us retrace our steps together quickly."
>
> And that lord who had led me there
> said to me: "Fear not, for our passage
> no one can take from us, by Such a one it is given.
>
> But wait for me here, and comfort
> your weary spirit and feed it with good hope,
> for I will not leave you in the low world."

<column-break/>

He says excellently: **O MY DEAR LEADER:** Because reason is naturally the guide of the sensory part of the soul. But in the man who follows appetite and not reason, such a guide is not "dear"; rather, it is dear to the one who submits his appetite to it, and the appetite follows it not by force—as a bad slave follows a master—but willingly, as a good son follows his father.

->**WHO MORE THAN SEVEN TIMES**<-
->That is, many times: and he uses one number for another:<-

as we showed above. And he named the number seven not without cause: because, as we reported before, it is a perfect number. Hence Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom, was often associated with the number seven in Neoplatonic number theory because it is "virgin" (not produced by multiplication within the first ten numbers).</note>, who is the goddess of wisdom, is referred to by it. Let us therefore understand "seven times" as a perfect number signifying the perfection of the thing; because in truth the senses perish when they are rebellious against reason. But when they follow it, they are perfectly drawn by it from every danger. **YOU HAVE RESTORED CONFIDENCE** and drawn me from danger. He mentions two things which can exist one without the other. For we can be in some danger and, by not knowing it, we do not fear it. In that case, we are "confident"—that is, without fear—and yet we are still in danger. Therefore, he shows that he has not only given him confidence but has also drawn him out of the danger itself. This occurred when you raised me from before the three beasts; when you calmed the wrath of Charon, of Minos, of Cerberus, and of the others who opposed our path. **DO NOT LEAVE ME** undone. And certainly the appetite in the soul of man is "undone" if reason abandons it, because eventually it perishes. **AND IF PASSING** further is denied us... Nothing else feeds the human mind except the knowledge of things; and because the mind must go to that knowledge cleansed of every stain—as we showed above—we must begin with the knowledge of vices. Having made some progress in this, if we cannot proceed further—that is, to know them all—we must turn back: that is, emerge from those vices which we have recognized. And he shows that we must observe three things in turning back. First: "return by the same footprints." This signifies that just as we descended into vice only for the sake of knowing it (and not to praise ourselves for it), so once it is known, we must repent of it by the same path. Second: "return together," because every time the appetite separates from reason, it perishes. Third: we must return "quickly" <note>original: "rapto"</note>. Because once the malignancy of vice is recognized, we must depart from it immediately. We can also give another meaning to this: by which Dante shows that the lower reason, when it finds some difficulty in virtuous operation, willingly withdraws from its purpose. And as Virgil said: *And he left the plows stuck in the middle of the task* <note>original: "Atque opere in medio defixa aratra reliquit"</note>, if the intellect does not restrain and comfort it.

Reason comforts the weary sensuality, which has already fallen into despair. Therefore, he rightly calls him "Lord" in this part. We have shown that reason is a guide to the appetite when the appetite follows it. But because here "Dante"—that is, sensuality—desired to turn back without waiting for the deliberation of reason, reason, as a Lord, [restrains] him...

It explains the demons' attempt to drive away the traveler as a metaphor for how despair and ignorance tempt the human soul to abandon the intellectual study of vice.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto VIII. The previous page discussed the demons’ refusal to let Dante pass through the gates of the City of Dis, and Virgil’s attempt to negotiate with them.</meta>

### CANTO EIGHT ###

he urges him to proceed. **AND THAT LORD WHO HAD LED ME THERE.** As if to say: having led me safely this far, I should hope that he would do the same for the rest of the journey. **DO NOT FEAR:** and he gives the reason: because no one can take this passage from us. **BY SUCH A ONE:** that is, by one so powerful <note>Referring to God, who sanctioned Dante’s journey.</note> **IT IS GIVEN.** Because it was granted to them by God to go through all of Hell. Nor can diabolical temptation harm one who is accompanied by divine grace. **BUT WAIT FOR ME HERE:** here, wait for me. And certainly, when the intellect arrives at some difficulty in contemplation, the appetite <note>The human "appetite" refers to our desires and will, which must sometimes wait for the "intellect" to process difficult truths.</note> must stop and wait until the intellect overcomes that difficulty and understands what it seeks to understand. **AND COMFORT AND FEED THE WEARY SPIRIT.** The sensory and appetitive part—and even the active part—cannot ascend where the intellectual part rises. Instead, it needs some rest and to be comforted by the intellect. **WITH GOOD HOPE:** Not every hope is good, but rather that which the unperturbed soul takes in honest and possible things. **THAT I WILL NOT LEAVE YOU IN THE LOW WORLD:** And certainly, sensuality <term>sensualita: here meaning the lower, bodily senses and desires</term> would remain in the low world, as it is always prone to earthly things unless the intellect raises our soul to divine ones. Therefore, take this hope and trust in this.

> Thus he goes away, and here abandons me
> the sweet father; and I remain in doubt,
> for "no" and "yes" contend within my head.
> 
> I could not hear what he proposed to them;
> but he did not stay there with them long
> before each one rushed back inside.
> 
> Those adversaries of ours closed the gates
> in the face of my lord, who remained outside,
> and he turned back to me with slow steps.
> 
> His eyes were toward the earth, and his brows were shorn
> of all boldness; and he said with sighs:
> "Who has denied me the houses of sorrow?"

<column-break/>

He demonstrates that after the aforementioned words, he departed, going toward the demons, and left Dante behind. **AND HERE HE ABANDONS ME, the sweet father:** He leaves Dante here because sensuality could not reach that height. But he does not abandon him to leave him for good, but to prepare the way through which he can later lead him. **THE SWEET FATHER SPOKE:** To denote that he did not leave him out of hatred or cruelty, but out of paternal love. Just as a father often leaves his children—who cannot follow him—to provide for their needs and return with things prepared, so Virgil left Dante with the intention of returning for him once he has made provision. **AND I REMAIN in doubt:** that is, in uncertainty whether he will return or not. This is better explained by saying: **FOR "NO" AND "YES" contend within my head:** In the head, where the estimative faculty resides, from which judgment is born. "Tenciona" <note>original: "Tenciona"</note> means "battles" or "fights," and it is an old Florentine word; in our times, we rarely use it. But so that the allegory may proceed: Virgil guides Dante, and as long as the way is not denied him—that is, as long as higher reason guides sensuality while the truth can be shown—he moves forward. But when it arrives at a thing that sensuality does not understand, it is necessary for the appetite to stop until the intellect acquires knowledge of that which it currently does not possess. And once acquired, it returns to Dante and moves him to follow the path; that is, it moves the appetite to continue in contemplation. But the appetite, abandoned by reason and not wishing to rashly take a side without its counsel, stops and remains in doubt whether Virgil will return or not—that is, whether the intellect will be able to reach such knowledge or not. **I COULD NOT HEAR what he proposed to them.** Sensuality cannot hear what the intellect says, because speculation belongs only to the intellect. **BUT HE DID NOT STAY THERE with them long:** that is, much. "Guari" <note>original: "guari"</note> is an old Florentine word meaning "a long time," and it is no longer in use in our day. The meaning is that since Virgil could not make them open the gates, he returned to Dante in a short time. For when the intellect cannot understand something by itself quickly, it understands that it *cannot* understand, and returns to sensuality. **THOSE ADVERSARIES OF OURS CLOSED THE GATES.** This verse is pronounced with sorrow and complaint, because it seemed an unworthy thing that the gate should be closed to such a man. And certainly, we marvel when we see a man of great learning arrive at doubts which he does not know how to solve. **IN THE FACE OF my lord, who remained outside.** To denote that thought is in the heart, and the heart is in the chest. Therefore, "our adversaries"—that is, diabolical fraud—prohibit the thought of the learned man from entering inside the gate; that is, he cannot enter into knowledge by the true path. **AND HE TURNED BACK TO me with slow steps.** The intellect returns to sensuality, unable to proceed in knowledge, so that if it cannot guide it further forward, at least it may keep it steady where it is until, with the help of others, it can bring it inside the gates. **WITH SLOW steps:** as every pensive person does, because he goes along thinking and often stops. He who thinks conducts a discourse of the mind, and in that discourse, he often stops where he finds an ambiguous place. And when the soul stops, it makes the body stop or go as slowly as the discourse goes. Virgil expressed this: *With him faithful Achates goes as a companion and fixes his footsteps with equal cares* <note>original Latin: "Cui fidus Achates It comes et paribus curis uestigia figit" from Aeneid VI.158-159</note>. **HIS EYES toward the earth:** and this is also the habit of a man who thinks, to fix his eyes on the ground. The eye, when it turns to various things, distracts the mind from its discourse; and it seems that it pushes the intellect wherever it looks. Therefore, to steady the soul, we also steady the eyes, and especially toward the earth where there is no variety or movement to distract it. **AND HIS BROWS WERE shorn:** As if empty...

<header>INFERNO</header>

And to me he said: "Though I am angry, 
     do not be dismayed, for I shall win the trial, 
     whatever defense is stirred up within.
This arrogance of theirs is not new to me: 
     for they used it already at a less secret gate, 
     which still remains without a bolt.
Above it you saw the dead writing; 
     and already from this side of it, one descends the slope, 
     passing through the circles without an escort, 
such that by him the land shall be opened to us."

<column-break/>

of all boldness; and certainly, in the eyes one recognizes who has boldness—that is, who trusts in themselves—or who has lost it. **AND HE SAID IN SIGHS:** "Who has denied me the sorrowful houses?" Virgil was not speaking to Dante, but was coming along deep in thought, and in his sighs he seemed to say those words. **WHO HAS DENIED ME:** as if to say: he <note>Referring to the demons.</note> who can do nothing against the will of the one who sends me. And truly, although it always grieves one to be defeated, nonetheless it is much more vexing to be defeated by those who are inferior to us.

Virgil does not want Dante to be dismayed just because he is indignant. Because although the intellect cannot apprehend truth by itself, nonetheless it knows that with divine favor it has power. And therefore: **DO NOT BE DISMAYED** that I shall win the trial: if not with my own strength, then with divine help. **WHATEVER DISSENSION:** that is, whatever it may be that stirs within to form a defense so that we do not enter. He used the word "stirs" <note>original: "faggiri" (aggirarsi)</note> either to demonstrate the custom of those who stand in defense of a land, who go around the walls to provide for every part; or truly he said "stirs" meaning to toil in vain. For the Florentine says "he goes stirring about" when one achieves no profit in his labor. And to show that it is not to be wondered at that they are so bold as to set themselves to defend what they cannot defend, he says it is their ancient custom to do this. Therefore **IT IS NOT NEW:** that is, unusual, **THIS ARROGANCE OF THEIRS:** that is, presumption and impudent audacity. Hence below he says "The arrogant breed," meaning bold and reckless. **FOR THEY ALREADY** used it at a less secret gate. He understands this to be the first gate of Hell; between that gate and this one (which is in the sixth circle) are those vices which proceed from incontinence <note>The sins of desire, like lust and gluttony, which are less grave than the sins of malice found inside Dis.</note> and are more easily recognized. Hence Virgil—that is, human intellect—was able to lead Dante by himself. And for this reason it is "less secret," meaning less obscure. And he refers to when the demons tried to resist when Christ despoiled Limbo. Hence the Psalmist said: Lift up your heads, O ye gates, and the King of Glory shall come in <note>original: "Tollite portas principes uestras et introibit rex glorie"</note>. This signifies that all laws and sentences given against the disobedience of the first man were broken. **WHICH STILL WITHOUT** a bolt was found: because since the passion of Christ, it can no longer hold the souls of the righteous who have been baptized. **ABOVE IT** you saw the dead writing: He responds to the phrase "These words of a dark color I saw written at the top of a gate." **AND ALREADY FROM** this side of it, one descends the slope: He says that already the angel sent by God to open the gate has entered the first gate and descends the slope. Every steep place has a slope (rising) and a descent (falling); but it is called a "slope" <term>erta: an upward incline</term> by the one who climbs it, and a "descent" <term>china: a downward incline</term> by the one who goes down it. Thus he used "slope" for the descent, since the angel was descending, just as Virgil puts the end for the beginning: Near the boundary of the Ocean and the setting sun <note>original: "Oceani finem iuxta : solemque cadentem", a quote from Virgil's Aeneid IV.480</note>. Or truly he said "slope" in relation to himself, who being already below, saw it as a slope. **PASSING** through the circles without an escort: because divine power has no need of an escort. **SUCH THAT BY HIM:** that is, by his means, the gate of the land shall be opened to us—that is, of the city. And we shall express this allegory better in the following chapter.

<header>CANTO NINE</header>

# CANTO NINE OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE

<image-desc>A large ornamental initial 'Q' containing floral scrollwork, set within a square frame with red and blue accents, beginning the first verse.</image-desc>

> That color which cowardice <note>The Italian "viltà" here refers to a loss of courage or faint-heartedness born of fear.</note> painted on my face
> seeing my leader turn back in retreat,
> more quickly restrained his own new color within.

IN this ninth chapter he describes the counsel of Virgil regarding the entry into the city and the infernal monsters that are there: and by whose help they entered: and finally he demonstrates with what punishments the heretics are tormented. This is material that is almost new: and where there are horrible sins: which deserve no compassion: because they do not arise from the stimulus of the flesh: such as disordered love, or gluttony, or anger. But from wicked malice of a perverse soul. And although in all vices frequent acts create a habit: nonetheless in those passed previously there is more **incontinence** <note>Lack of self-control over natural desires.</note> than **intemperance** <note>A more hardened, deliberate choice of evil.</note>. But in these one sees a most perverse obstinacy. And because for one who makes a habit of these it is almost impossible to withdraw themselves: he therefore places them inside the city girt with walls of iron. This denotes that it is unassailable; as we said above.

But to return to the text: the meaning of the first tercet is that Dante, being frightened: and for this reason turned pale by the change he had seen in the face of Virgil; and Virgil, perceiving this, repressed his own indignation and perturbation: and cleared his face: and restored it to its natural color: so that Dante, too, might lay down his fear. And certainly every time the **rational part** in man takes fright at not being able to achieve something, the **sensuality** <note>The lower, bodily, and emotional part of the soul.</note> is much afraid. And it secretly admonishes that whoever is placed in government and the rule of others ought often, in dangers, to show a good spirit: so that those who are under his government do not lose heart. Which Virgil attributes to Aeneas when he says: "He feigns hope in his face and suppresses the deep pain in his heart." <note>original: "Spem uultu simulat premit altum corde dolorem" — Virgil, Aeneid I, 209.</note>

And so he orders the text: **THAT COLOR** which **COWARDICE**, that is fear, painted outwardly—understand this as on the face. Because paleness in the face is nothing other than a lack of blood: which out of fear flees to the heart: and leaves the veins of the face empty. **SEEING MY LEADER TURN BACK IN RETREAT**. As if to say without victory and driven back: because we say an army is "put to flight" when, overcome by enemies, it turns its back. **MORE QUICKLY WITHIN HIS OWN NEW RESTRAINED**. The pale color was **new** in Dante. Because fear had made him turn pale. Similarly, the flushed color was **new** in Virgil: because indignation had flushed his face. Because anger being the boiling of blood around the heart, as it boils it runs through all the veins: but it appears more in the face: because there are many subcutaneous veins there; that is, they are in the skin so that they manifest themselves entirely. But Virgil, seeing Dante's fear arise from the mutation of his own face, managed to quickly restrain such color within. Therefore, that color which was in me because of fear born of cowardice, more quickly restrained **his new [color]**: that is, Virgil's. Because Virgil removed from his face the "new color," that is, the non-natural color. But that which had newly appeared out of indignation, seeing that Dante feared because of it: And this he said to denote that the wise man can anticipate and cast out from himself the perturbations of the soul.

---

> Attentively he stood like a man who listens,
> for the eye could not lead him far
> through the black air and through the thick fog.
> "Yet it will behoove us to win the fight,"
> he began, "if not... such a one offered herself to us.
> Oh, how long it seems to me until another arrives here!"

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'A' with interlaced white vine-stem patterns on a dark background, starting the commentary for the second passage.</image-desc>

**ATTENTIVELY HE STOOD**. It happens that when we wait for someone in a dark place; because the eye is of no use, being unable to discern, we use our hearing; so that by the stride or some other noise we perceive when they come. Virgil did the same: But allegorically it is understood that when the **intellect** by itself cannot see the truth, occupied by the shadows of ignorance, it attentively awaits inspiration and divine help. **LIKE A MAN WHO LISTENS** since the anger ceases. **FOR THE EYE COULD NOT LEAD HIM FAR**. He gives the reason: why he used the sense of hearing: because sight did not serve him from a distance **THROUGH THE BLACK AIR**. The more difficult the thing is, the more there is "black air": that is, the greater the obscurity of ignorance. Whence the Psalm asks for this divine favor, saying: "To give light to those who sit in the shadow of death." <note>original: "Illuminare iis qui in umbra mortis sedent" — Luke 1:79 (The Canticle of Zechariah).</note> **YET IT WILL BEHOOVE US TO WIN THE FIGHT**. The human intellect is kindled when it arrives at the contemplation of such high things that it cannot understand them by itself. But then it takes hope: that through divine help it still will. And in comfort to himself and to the lower **reason**, he says **YET**: as if [to say] finally **IT WILL BEHOOVE US** to win the fight: the contest of entering the gate. Which is to enter into **cognition** <note>True knowledge or understanding.</note>. **HE BEGAN**: He began. **IF NOT**: And if we cannot win the fight by ourselves, we shall be helped. **SUCH A ONE OFFERED**: that is, such a one offered herself to us; as a man deep in thought, he speaks with broken words: and does not finish the speech. Which causes Dante to doubt: but we will explain this a little further down. **OH HOW LONG IT SEEMS TO ME**: Oh how much it delays in my opinion. **UNTIL ANOTHER ARRIVES HERE**: that is, the angel whom I expect. Because as **Seneca** says, to one who is in a hurry, every great speed seems like slowness. Allegorically, the intellect awaits the help of God and the additive...

...grace: and especially **prevenient grace** <note>original: "gratia preueniente"; in theology, this is grace that precedes human decision, disposing the soul toward God's will before the person even asks for it</note>: which does not wait to be requested: but often precedes the good will. Because as soon as our free will disposes itself to choose the good / prevenient grace directs it along the right path.
