**V**irgil covered the beginning of his speech; in which he did not give certain hope with the other speech that followed when he said *If such a one were not...* <note>original: "Se non tal ne fosse"</note> which words were cut short. Therefore it is necessary to supply the rest: "if such a one were not for us," that is, one who will make us win, meaning one so powerful (referring to God), "if such a one offered themselves to us." And these were words different from the first: because those showed that he could win [on his own]: these showed that he had need of the help of others. But nonetheless, despite being different, they are not opposite or contrary. Rather, in short, they show more difficulty than he believed at the beginning. And it denotes that the intellect sometimes believes that through continuous discourse it can achieve the knowledge of the thing it investigates; and then realizes it has need of a greater light.

**D**ante perhaps doubted he could enter the city: and having entered, he doubted if Virgil knew how to guide him through the lower circles, as he had guided him through the upper ones. And therefore he asks if anyone from the first circle, in which Virgil stayed for some time, had descended to the bottom. He denotes in this that the "lower reason" (because it does not discern universals) doubts that the "superior reason" can discern them either. And Virgil, noticing his fear, to give him comfort, affirms that he has descended there. And in this place, although our poet [Dante] differs from the poet Virgil [in the *Aeneid*]—inasmuch as Virgil feigns that the Sibyl did not want to lead Aeneas inside this city, but only recounted the punishments seen there—Dante feigns that Virgil *did* lead him in. Nonetheless, they are similar in this: that both show the guide having been there another time (Virgil for the Sibyl, so that Aeneas would trust what she told him; and Dante for Virgil, to remove the fear we showed above). Some suggest that Dante writes this as a fiction by Virgil to show that often wise men feign something, not to deceive, but to introduce [a truth]. And in part, as we have said, he imitates Virgil in a way. And if one asks what reason moved Dante, wanting to imitate Virgil, to be contrary to him here, I respond that it is not as contrary as it seems. Virgil says, when he shows that the Sibyl does not want to conduct Aeneas inside this city: *No holy person is permitted to step upon the threshold of the wicked* <note>original Latin: "Nulli fas casto sceleratum insistere limen"</note>. He means nothing else by saying that no good person is permitted to stay in that place, except that no one can be good who stays there, that is, who makes a habit of vice. But it seemed better to the Sibyl to tell him of the vices and keep him outside—that is, to give him the knowledge of them without him making a habit of them. And Dante feigns that although Virgil conducts him in, nonetheless he does not stay there. Which signifies that same thing: namely, to enter into the knowledge of vice, but not to make a habit of it. And this is more according to the Christian religion, which believes that everyone enters this city—that is, in some way everyone sins. Whence David said: *Every man is a liar* <note>original Latin: "Omnis homo mendax"</note>: and elsewhere: *Seven times a day the righteous man falls* <note>original Latin: "Septies in die cadit iustus"</note>. But it is no small thing not to make a habit of it.

**TO THIS BOTTOM** of the sorrowful basin: In this low part of hell: which he has described in the form of a vessel <note>original: "uaso"</note>: which begins at the top with a wider circle: and as it goes lower, it narrows. **OF THE FIRST DEGREE** / Of the first circle where Limbo is: and where he placed the souls of virtuous men, but without faith: who for punishment (that is, in place of punishment) have **SEVERED** <note>original: "cioncha"</note>: that is, cut off, their hope, as he said above: *that without hope we live in desire.* "Cioncho" is a Lombard word and signifies cut off or diminished: and thus he takes it here. But in the Florentine dialect, *cionchare* means to drink immoderately. **I MADE** this question: that is, this inquiry. For "to seek" in Latin <note>original: "querere"</note> means to search and to ask. **AND HE**: And that Virgil responded, saying **RARELY OCCURS**: It happens rarely; "to encounter" means to happen or to come across. **THAT ANY OF US**: that is, of us. **MAKES THE JOURNEY** by which I go: He says that although rarely...

<summary>In this passage, Dante expresses his fear regarding Virgil's hesitation at the City of Dis, leading Virgil to recount his previous descent to the deepest circle of Hell to reassure Dante of his expertise. The commentary by Landino interprets Virgil’s journey as the intellect's struggle to understand vice without succumbing to it, drawing parallels to Aeneas and the Sibyl.</summary>

# CANTO NINE

...times it happens as it usually happens: and allegorically it demonstrates that few are those who descend into the meditation of vices to purge themselves of them. **IT IS TRUE THAT ANOTHER TIME:** This shows that he had been there shortly after his death, conjured by Erichtho: and Dante feigns that Virgil makes this up to comfort him, as we have said. Erichtho was, according to Lucan <note>Lucan was a Roman poet, author of the *Pharsalia*, where Erichtho appears as a powerful and gruesome necromancer.</note>, a female sorceress in Thessaly: who, at the request of Pompey (the son of Pompey the Great), drew a soul from the underworld back into its body: and made it say what the end of the civil war between Caesar and Pompey would be. Dante therefore imagines that Virgil feigns this about himself for his own comfort: and besides this, it fits an ancient opinion: that Zoroaster <note>Zoroaster was historically considered by Renaissance thinkers to be the inventor of magic and astrology.</note>, the inventor of this art, practiced it to have knowledge of the immortality of the soul and of its nature and power. And we shall speak of the magical art below when that specific sin is treated. But as for the present text, it is to be doubted how Dante posits that the soul of Virgil was conjured and constrained: since our religion forbids it: because theologians do not hold that the magical art has this power. For this reason, Aurelius Augustine writes that the Witch of Endor <note>original: "Phitonissa"; the biblical medium who summoned the spirit of Samuel for King Saul.</note> of whom the first book of Kings recounts—who spoke in the person of the prophet Samuel—was not Samuel: but a demon who feigned being Samuel. But the answer is: that these are not the words of Dante or his own opinion: but those of Virgil, who speaks according to the opinion of the pagan poets, as we see in Homer, in Lucan, and others. Furthermore, happening upon the subject, Dante notes in this place the fourth descent into Hell posited by the ancients. For as we said above, one descends into Hell in the first way: when the soul, departing the body in mortal sin, goes into eternal damnation. In the second way: when still in the body, one descends into the habit of vice. In the third: when we descend into the contemplation of vices to purge ourselves of them. And according to these first three ways, he writes throughout this first canticle. And of the fourth, he touches upon it in this place: not because he approves of it, but so that he does not omit any. **FOR A SHORT TIME** my flesh was naked of me: the flesh was naked, that is, deprived of me, Virgil: and he says "of me" most excellently because, although man consists of soul and body, nonetheless, because man is defined by reason and intellect, the soul is truly that which is the "man": and the body is like a garment to the soul. **INSIDE THAT WALL:** which you see is made of iron, to draw out a soul: which was in the lowest circle: in which Judas is punished: and from him, it is called Giudecca <note>The final zone of the ninth circle of Hell, named after Judas Iscariot.</note>. **THAT IS THE** lowest place. If Hell descends to the center of the earth, and this circle is the lowest, it follows that it is in the center: and because every center is the part furthest from the circumference, it is therefore furthest from the heavens. **WHICH TURNS ALL.** which, turning, contains all within itself <note>This refers to the Primum Mobile, the outermost sphere of the universe that drives the rotation of all other heavens.</note>. **INDEED THE PATH IS LONELY** It happened that Dante feared that Virgil did not know the way because he had not been there: and therefore he concludes that he does know it. And perhaps Dante feigns that Virgil feigned having been there to show that, morally, wise men often say what is not true, not to deceive: but to comfort those who have taken some fright to persevere in good works.

> This swamp which breathes out the great stench
> surrounds the sorrowful city:
> where we cannot enter now without anger.
> And more he said: but I do not have it in mind
> because my eye had drawn me entirely
> toward the high tower with the glowing red top:
> Where in a single moment there suddenly stood upright
> three infernal furies stained with blood/
> who had female limbs and gestures:
> And they were girt with the greenest hydras:
> they had small serpents and horned vipers for hair:
> wherewith their fierce temples were bound.

<column-break/>

**H**e shows that this Stygian swamp "breathes": that is, it exhales the great stench: because from it rise vapors and mists of foul odor. This is natural for any swamp. But also allegorically, from the sadness of the heart, many stenches are born: that is, many vices. **SURROUNDS THE CITY:** of Dis. **SORROWFUL:** because of various and unbearable torments that are there; and certainly, vices leave behind nothing else but repentance and sorrow. Whence Petrarch says most excellently: *Repentance and sorrow follow behind one's shoulders* <note>original: "Penitentia et dolor doppo le spalle"; a quote from Petrarch's *Trionfi* (Triumph of Love).</note>. **WHERE WE CANNOT** where we will not be able to **ENTER** without anger: because the adversaries oppose us. Nor let anyone wonder that he shows anger in the place where anger is punished. For here the poet wants to show that there can be an anger which not only

---

is not a vice: but is a virtue; because it is a just indignation to make the soul bold for every honest undertaking: because as we have said, there is in our soul not only that part which desires the good—that is, the concupiscible—but also that which removes the obstacles that hinder the good: and it is called "irascible." **AND OTHER** he said but I do not have it in mind: he shows himself to have been drawn so suddenly by the wonder of what he saw: that because of the sudden disturbance of the soul, he forgot many things that Virgil had said. And certainly, when a sudden movement arises in the soul, it is so perturbed that it forgets the precepts given to it by reason. And this fiction of forgetting serves two things: first, that which we have said. Second, it happened that Virgil had to instruct him in many things: which, if he had narrated them, would have made the speech too long. Therefore, although he does not narrate them: nonetheless, he hints to the listener what he ought to imagine. **BECAUSE** my eye had drawn me entirely toward the high tower.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's *Inferno*, Canto IX. On the previous page, the commentator discussed Virgil's claim of having descended to the lowest circle of Hell before to reassure Dante of his guidance. Now, the text shifts to the allegorical meaning of Dante being distracted by the sight of the Furies and the philosophical distinction between being guided by reason versus being pulled by passion.</meta>

# INFERNO

I say that a forgetfulness came over me regarding many things that Virgil had told me: because my eye—that is, my sight—**HAD DRAWN ME ALL AWAY**: that is, it had snatched my whole soul. It is one thing to guide; it is another to pull. For we go guided by our own will, but we go pulled by force. Therefore, reason guides us: because by persuading us and showing us that such a path is good, it makes us follow it voluntarily. But when a sudden disturbance arises in us—whether of anger, or of hatred, or of love, or of fear—even though we judge that what such a passion shows us is not good, nevertheless we are pulled by it by force. What does Dante mean then, or shall we say his sensory appetite? Certainly nothing else but that the sight of the Furies pulled him. This denotes that they led him by force, like one who lacks self-control. Mention was made above in the first Canto of the person who lacks self-control and the intemperate person; and similarly of the temperate and self-controlled person. Therefore, you may draw from there what serves this passage. Now, returning to the text, the poet wishes to note in this fiction: that reason was admonishing sensuality; but the disturbance was pulling it in the opposite direction. **HAD DRAWN ME ALL AWAY**: pulled everything, because a great disturbance occupies the whole mind in such a way that reason is not heard there. **TOWARD THE TOWER**: toward the tower of which we spoke above. **RED-HOT**: Flaming, because there is great flame in fury and great burning. **WHERE AT ONE POINT** three Furies suddenly stood upright: who were in the dress and the manner of women. The Furies, according to the poets, were the daughters of Acheron and of Night. Acheron signifies the "deprivation of joy" <note>original: "Acheronte"; the commentator derives this from the Greek *a-cheron*, meaning "without joy."</note>. And from the deprivation of joy, fury is born; and night is dark: and from the blindness and darkness of the mind, fury proceeds. Their names are Alecto, Tisiphone, and Megaera. Alecto signifies "without rest" <note>original: "Alecto"; from the Greek *a-lektos*, meaning "unceasing" or "unresting."</note>, and restlessness is the beginning of fury. Tisiphone in the Greek language sounds like "avenger of slaughter" <note>original: "uendicatrice daccisione"; from *tisis* (vengeance) and *phonos* (murder/slaughter).</note>, and this is the remorse of conscience of which we spoke above. Megaera derives her meaning from "hatred" <note>original: "odio"; from the Greek *megairō*, meaning "to grudge" or "to envy."</note>, from which one arrives at extreme fury. They take the Furies to represent disordered appetite: which, like a fury, sets the human mind on fire, blinds it, and makes it fall headlong without counsel or virtue. For love, anger, hate, ambition, and all other unbridled desires are nothing else but fury: which, like an unbridled horse, carries a man away through ditches and over cliffs until it breaks his neck. Thus, headlong fury without reason carries the soul away. Therefore, not without cause did he say "Where at one point they suddenly stood upright." For just as reason leads the soul with discourse, maturity, and counsel, so, on the contrary, the infuriated appetite pulls us suddenly without any counsel. **THREE FURIES**: as we have said, Alecto, Tisiphone, and Megaera. **INFERNAL**: the Furies inhabit Hell because they are always found in vices. Or he called them "infernal" because there is also found "divine fury": of which we shall speak in a more convenient place; a matter described by Plato and excellently interpreted by our own Platonist, Marsilio Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was a central figure of the Italian Renaissance who translated Plato's works into Latin and sought to reconcile Platonism with Christianity.</note>. **STAINED WITH BLOOD**: because from the Furies are born discords, and from those, wars and killings. **WHO HAD FEMALE MEMBERS AND ACTS**: They had the body and appearance of a woman. This is feigned because a woman is much more easily set aflame in fury than a man. Hence Virgil, when he wanted Alecto to ensure that during Ascanius's hunt the stag of Tyrrheus (the shepherd of Latinus) was killed, made the fury be in the female dogs and not in the male dogs. The reason is that, there being a smaller spirit in the female, she can less resist passions and disturbances. **AND WITH THE GREENEST HYDRAS WERE THEY GIRT**: This shows that in place of belts and hair they had various species of snakes: because there is no more pestiferous poison to our souls and to the lives of mortals than fury. The Hydra is a serpent that lives in the water, named so in Greek because *hydor* signifies water. And the poets say there was in the Lernean swamp of Thessaly a Hydra serpent, daughter of Echidna and Typhon: which Juno nourished against Hercules. And it was such an indomitable monster that when one head was cut off, seven grew back. But Hercules, being unable to kill it with iron, was taught by Minerva to burn it. Cerastes are snakes in Libya which have horns; so called because *ceras* signifies horn. The Furies appeared at the top of the tower because fury cannot remain hidden: nor is it ever without pride and supreme inflammation.

> And he, who well knew the handmaidens
> of the queen of eternal wailing,
> "Look," he said to me, "at the fierce Erinyes.
> This is Megaera on the left side;
> she who wails on the right is Alecto;
> Tisiphone is in the middle"; and then he was silent.

<column-break/>

**AND HE**: that is, Virgil, who **WELL KNEW THE HANDMAIDENS**: the Furies, who truly are handmaidens: that is, miserable ones: because if tranquility of mind brings supreme joy, fury brings the opposite; and if wisdom is the supreme good, insanity is supreme misery. Nor is it without cause that Virgil knows them and Dante does not: because the intellect is that which knows the fury and the cause from which it

proceeds, and not the senses: which, occupied by such insanity, lose all light and do not recognize the fury in which they find themselves. **OF THE QUEEN of eternal wailing**: of Proserpina, queen of Hell. **LOOK, HE SAID TO ME**: It is not enough that the intellect knows what a pestilence these Furies are. But it is necessary that it makes them known to the appetite so that it may flee them. **ERINYES**: the Greeks call the Furies *Eryne* because *eris* signifies contention or strife. **THIS IS Megaera on the left side**: because hatred is worse than

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, Canto IX. The previous page discussed Dante’s fear and Virgil’s reassurance. Here, the focus shifts to the appearance of the three Furies and the deep allegorical meaning behind the myth of Medusa and the hero Theseus.</meta>

# CANTO NINE

restlessness: But the worst is the torment caused by Tisiphone <note>One of the three Furies; her name suggests "avenger of murder."</note>: and therefore he places her in the middle.

> With nails they each tore their own breast
> they beat themselves with their palms and cried so loud:
> that I pressed close to the poet out of fear.
> Let Medusa come and we will turn him to stone
> they all cried looking downward:
> too bad we did not avenge the assault of Theseus.

<column-break/>

He demonstrates the rage of the furious through the scratching of the chest and the beating of the palms. He says that because of their loud cries, he drew close to Virgil to be able to defend himself with his help. And certainly, against the onslaught of fury—which is born from some inner disturbance—lower reason <note>The part of the mind governed by senses and emotions.</note> could not defend itself without the help of higher reason <note>The intellect or spiritual guidance.</note>. **LET MEDUSA COME** so we can turn him to stone. From Phorcys <note>original: "Phorco"</note>, a sea god, and Ceto, daughter of the sea and the earth, were born—according to He—

<column-break/>

—siod <note>Hesiod, an ancient Greek poet.</note>—three daughters: Stheno, Euryale, and Medusa. These were commonly called the Gorgons. The first two were immortal, but Medusa was mortal. They had only one eye between the three of them, and they used it in turn, now one, now the other. Neptune <note>original: "Neptunno"</note> burned with love for Medusa and lay with her in the temple of Pallas <note>Athena, the goddess of wisdom.</note>. Pallas conceived such hatred toward her for this lack of restraint—being the goddess of chastity and wisdom—that as vengeance she turned Medusa’s hair (which, being very beautiful, had greatly moved Neptune to love) into little snakes. And she decreed that whoever looked at her would turn to stone. 

By these Gorgons, the poets mean earthly and momentary goods. If these are desired out of necessity or to practice honest generosity, they are virtues—and this is shown by the two immortal sisters. But if they are desired to satisfy a disordered appetite, it is a supreme vice—and this one is mortal. Neptune loves her, which signifies the sea, and stands for appetite: because an appetite disobedient to reason prefers fleeting and mortal things over celestial ones. He loves her hair most of all—that is, the superfluous—and joins with her in the temple of Minerva <note>Another name for Pallas/Athena.</note>, who is the goddess of chastity and wisdom: because such things are either acquired through worldly prudence or, under the guise of some holiness, deceit and fraud are committed to acquire them. 

Minerva changes the beautiful hair into snakes because wisdom eventually uncovers such frauds and reveals their poison. Medusa turns men to stones because the excessive and disordered greed for false goods makes them seem so beautiful that we become stupefied <note>original: "stupefacti"</note> by them. And to every other thing we are blind, deaf, and as if without sense. 

They say Medusa was killed by Perseus with the sword of Mercury and the shield of Minerva, which, because it was crystalline, allowed him to see Medusa through it without being seen by her. Perseus stands for the wise man, who with the sword of Mercury—that is, with eloquent doctrine—kills Medusa. This is because he knows, and makes others know, that riches, lordships, dignities, powers, and similar things (which the ignorant masses and all fools judge to be the highest good) are fleeting, quickly fail, and always generate scandal, disturbances, and misery in human life. And when he kills her, he hides behind the shield of Minerva: because he places reason and wisdom between himself and these false goods, which defend him so that they cannot harm him or draw him to love them. 

Medusa is rightly placed in the city <note>The City of Dis in Hell.</note> where such atrocious crimes are punished: because if it were not for the immense greed for worldly goods, men would have their minds so elevated that they would reach a true knowledge of God. Desiring Him, they would not become impious against God and would not commit any of those enormous errors that are punished inside the city of Dis. For this reason, the demons call Medusa against us. Indeed, the diabolical temptation cannot conquer us unless it incites us so much to the greed for temporal goods that we become insensible to every virtuous action. 

**TOO BAD WE DID NOT**: that is, let us avenge. *Veggiare* <note>original: "veggiamo"</note> means to avenge in the old Florentine language; it derives from *vendicare* <note>to avenge</note> by syncope and by the changing of the 'd' into 'g'. **THE ASSAULT OF THESEUS**: that is, if they had avenged the injury received from Theseus, this man [Dante] would not have dared to come into our kingdom while still alive. And allegorically, understand that just as in evil, so too in good, example has great power. Therefore, if the Furies, who desire evil, had punished Theseus for coming while alive—that is, for coming to purge himself of vices—Dante would not have followed him. 

Theseus was the son of Aegeus, king of Athens, and many defeated monsters similar to those of Hercules are told of him. The Athenians and Megarians had killed Androgeos, son of Minos of Crete, out of envy. Minos conquered them and, in revenge for his son, imposed a harsh law: that every year seven Athenian youths, chosen by lot, should go to Crete to be devoured by the Minotaur. In the fourth year, the lot fell to Theseus. But with the help of Ariadne, daughter of Minos, he killed the Minotaur and returned free to Athens. He was a man of great counsel and no less spirit. According to Pliny, he was the first to invent confederations and leagues. The poets feign that he went to the underworld with Pirithous to kidnap Proserpina. 

Regarding this fable, Coluccio Salutato <note>A famous Florentine humanist and chancellor.</note>—a most learned man and teacher of Leonardo Aretino <note>Also known as Leonardo Bruni, a key Renaissance historian.</note>—wrote a very subtle allegory. Because the poets feign that Hercules, Aeneas, Theseus, Pirithous, Amphiaraus, and Orpheus descended to the underworld, it demonstrates that various types of desirable things are expressed in them. So that this may be better understood, let us repeat that human life is either active or contemplative. Contemplation is directed toward the Truth. The active life is directed toward the Good. Not that the Truth and the Good are not the same thing: because that which is good is true, and that which is true is good. But Truth is insofar as...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, Canto IX. The previous page introduced the mythological origins of the Gorgons. Here, the commentator uses Renaissance humanist philosophy—referencing figures like Coluccio Salutati—to explain why Dante must shield his eyes from Medusa and why Virgil's "reason" requires divine grace to enter the deeper circles of Hell.</meta>

# INFERNO

and is knowable: and the good insofar as it is desirable. Therefore, the contemplative life tends toward the truth, and the active life toward the good. But the good is of three types: namely, the moral <note>original: "honesto"</note>, the useful, and the pleasurable <note>original: "voluptuoso"</note>. The moral is the true good. Hence, the Stoics placed the highest good in virtue. The pleasurable is that which the Epicureans claimed was the highest good. The useful is the opinion of the common people. Understanding this, our Coluccio <note>Coluccio Salutati (1331–1406), a famous Florentine humanist and scholar.</note> wishes that the speculative good and the knowledge of the truth be expressed in Homer through Hercules, and in Virgil through Aeneas. Similarly, the moral good is represented when the doctrine is certain. But when it is uncertain, as with the Academic skeptics, such a descent is symbolized by Amphiaraus <note>A hero in Greek mythology and one of the Seven against Thebes.</note>; the pleasurable is symbolized by Orpheus; and the useful by Theseus and Pirithous. In this context, he takes Theseus to represent the soul and Pirithous to represent the body; and just as these two were the greatest of friends, so the soul and the body are joined with the greatest friendship. He shows that reason is represented by Theseus and sensuality by Pirithous—things certainly worthy of his teaching and genius. But because they are lengthy and not very relevant to this place, I omit them. Let it suffice that the demons grieve for not having punished Theseus, who dared to descend to Hell while alive—that is, by speculating <note>In the sense of intellectual inquiry or contemplation.</note>—and by whose example Dante has taken the same daring path. For if they did not restrain him who descended to Hell for the knowledge of the "useful"—a thing entirely common and which demonstrates no divinity of reason—they give confidence to Dante that they will not be able to restrain him as he descends for the knowledge of the truth and the moral good, which are heavenly things and always accompanied by divine favor.

<columns>2</columns>
"Turn your back and keep your eyes closed:
for if the Gorgon shows herself and you should see her,
there would be no returning back up."
Thus spoke the master, and he himself
turned me: and did not trust my hands
but with his own he also covered me.

<column-break/>

Most excellently, reason admonishes the senses not to look at such a monster, so that one is not turned into stone by it, as we explained allegorically. But because sensuality, even if admonished, would not be sufficient on its own for defense unless the higher reason corroborated and strengthened it, he feigns that Virgil admonishes him to cover his eyes with his own hands; and not content with this, he

<columns>1</columns>

covers them with his own hands as well. By "hands" we understand "operations" <note>Human actions or works.</note>. Therefore, if the demons were to show the Gorgon to Dante—that is, if they tempted his sensuality by putting before him the delights of earthly goods—he, conquered by them, would never return upward, because he would turn it into a habit. For this reason, it is necessary that first the sensuality and the lower reason cover themselves with their own hands—that is, use every good action possible to them—and submit to the higher reason. Then, the higher reason must cover him with its own; that is, defend him with the virtues it possesses within itself.

<columns>2</columns>
O you who have sound intellects:
gaze upon the teaching that hides itself
beneath the veil of these strange verses.

<column-break/>

Because in this entire comedy of the *Inferno* there is no chapter that has a deeper allegory than this one, the poet captures the attention of his listeners and admonishes them to note the allegory within it. **O YOU WHO HAVE**

<columns>1</columns>

**SOUND INTELLECTS:** that is, the wise. For he who is not of great intellect would look in vain. **GAZE UPON:** Diligently consider. **THE TEACHING that hides itself beneath the veil:** Beneath the fiction. **OF THESE STRANGE VERSES:** i.e., diverse; in which the words sound like one thing, but the meaning <note>original: "sententia"</note> hidden there is another. For he wishes to show that, just as reason resists by itself with "grace freely given" <note>original: "gratia gratis data" - a theological term for spiritual gifts given for the benefit of others.</note> against the vices that proceed from incontinence and lack of restraint—where Virgil was sufficient against Charon, Minos, Cerberus, Pluto, Phlegyas, and Filippo Argenti—so now, in entering the speculation of more serious vices proceeding from malice and brutality, reason and "grace freely given" are not enough. One needs a special grace from God called by theologians "sanctifying grace" <note>original: "gratia gratum faciens" - grace that makes the soul pleasing to God and heals it.</note>. And the entrance is much more difficult because not just one demon, but many are there on guard. This signifies that such sins have many and diverse types and roots, and "a thousand arts of harming" <note>original: "Mille nocendi artes" - a quote from Virgil's Aeneid regarding the fury Allecto.</note>. Therefore, Virgil cannot appease these demons; rather, they have closed the gate in his face. The Furies are the roots of pride and envy, and they have serpents in place of hair, which denotes malice, fraud, and deceit. Hence Virgil writes of Allecto: *A thousand arts of harming*. They hinder Dante. In theological terms, this means the demon does not want a living man—that is, one proceeding with reason—to enter into the knowledge of sin, because by knowing it, he would guard himself against it. But he does want the dead man: that is, he in whom sensuality is superior to reason. Such a man is dead because there are no longer human operations in him, but entirely bestial ones. Dante draws close to Virgil out of fear of the Furies, which are born from the most burning and unbridled desire for illicit things. Seeing that they could not harm him, they called for Medusa—that is, they left him with the flattering delights of worldly things. If we allow ourselves to be taken by these, as we said above, we become stones. Many hold that Medusa signifies oblivion and ignorance, and this makes a man become a stone—that is, hardened and obstinate. And for this reason, reason turns sensuality away.

**D**ante was already armed against the harms of the furies and the gorgons. Now it remains that with the help of the angel they enter the city. He describes, then, his arrival. He describes how Dante was instructed by Virgil to show him reverence. He describes how he opened the gate with his wand. He rebuked the demons for their arrogance: and then he returned: And Virgil and Dante entered, and what they saw. AND NOW THERE WAS COMING through the turbid waves. This shows the coming of the angel, whom we interpreted above as the grace of God. This one came through the waves of Styx. Note that the light received from God in this part was for the knowledge of infernal things.

---

A CRASH OF A SOUND: That is, such a sound as is usual in a crash: and we specifically use "crash" <note>original: "fracasso"</note> for a great sound which proceeds from the ruin and breaking of things: because "to fracture" means to break. FULL OF TERROR: this agrees with the theologians: who say that every vision that proceeds from God scares at first and rassurance in the end. We can also understand that when, through the arrival of divine grace, we enter into the knowledge of the greatest vices: we recognize what a cruel plague and what grave danger they are to our soul. Through such knowledge, terror and no small consternation are born; but rather a feeling full of horror. BECAUSE OF WHICH BOTH SHORES TREMBLED: that is, one and the other bank of the marsh. Limosese <note>A reference to the 14th-century commentator Benvenuto da Imola.</note> interprets that this figure who comes to open the gate is Mercury, the god of eloquence: and he acutely fits the text to this allegory. But whoever diligently regards Dante's purpose easily knows that it cannot be anything other than the divine grace already mentioned above. NOT OTHERWISE than a wind. He excellently equates the angel, who is incorporeal, to the wind: which is such a thin body that it remains invisible: And beyond this, it shows with what speed divine grace descends to a well-disposed will. WHICH STRIKES: which strikes, that is, hits. IMPEVTOUS due to opposing heats: which takes its impetus from the heats different from itself, that is, those contrary to it. Winds are generated from hot and dry vapors: elevated from the earth up to the region where the clouds consist: And there, struck back by the superior heats, they are pushed sideways: and they strike the air: and the part struck strikes the next: and that one the next, hand to hand; because wind is nothing other than struck air: and the more the heats are adverse, the more the wind is impetuous. There are also certain species more impetuous in form that can almost be called thunderbolts: such as the <term>procella</term> <note>A violent storm or gale.</note>, <term>ecnephia</term> <note>A sudden, bursting wind.</note>, <term>typhone</term> <note>A whirlwind or typhoon.</note>, <term>turbine</term>, and <term>prester</term> <note>A scorching whirlwind.</note>. The nature and distinction of these, because it is lengthy, I leave behind.

**H**e has described the impetus of the angel's coming. Now he posits that Virgil, just as before he had closed Dante's eyes so he would not see Medusa, so conversely now he opens them: so that the angel may come. For it is the office of our intellect to rule the appetite in such a way that it has its eyes closed to every disturbance: and thus open to every divine inspiration. Sensuality is very far from divinity: But the intellect is in that middle: and in many things by itself it rules the senses: and in those in which it is not sufficient by itself to rule them, it at least disposes the soul to receive that which, by divine grace, will rule it.

---

HE LOOSENED MY EYES: Removing his hands and mine for the reason already stated above. AND SAID DIRECT THE NERVE of the face: as if to waken the visual power, putting "nerve" for "power." For the bodily forces consist in the nerves. Or truly he said "nerve": because in the cross of the optic nerves <note>The optic chiasm, where the optic nerves intersect in the brain.</note> which come from the brain to the eyes, the visual power consists. UPON THAT ANCIENT foam: If he moved the waters, it was necessary that foam be born from it: And he said "ancient"; not because it was ancient itself, having been born of new movement: But ancient; that is, of the ancient marsh. Some say ancient foam: that is, white: because all foam is white: and as the Latins say <gloss>canas pruinas, that is, gray frosts</gloss> <note>original: "canas pruinas.i. canute brinate"</note>: that is, white: because the hair of the old man is white: Thus Dante said ancient foam as if to say hoary foam: that is, white. <meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, Canto IX. The previous text established that Virgil (Reason) cannot overcome the demons at the gates of Dis alone and must wait for Divine Grace, personified by the Heavenly Messenger.</meta>

# INFERNO

It is very fitting that he calls the Styx an ancient marsh: because sadness is ancient in the human generation, since the first man, Adam, immediately after he fell into sin, fell into sadness and grief. The angel did not come flying over the marsh; rather, he came through the marsh, although he walked across it without wetting the soles of his feet. This denotes that such grace was an aid to the recognition of vices and not of virtues. WHERE THAT SMOKE IS MORE BITTER: more vehement and more obscure. For such grace does not come through luminous places—because the intellect sees those by itself—but through obscure ones, which the intellect cannot see without it. Or rather, he makes it come through an obscure place because such grace comes secretly and its path is not known. LIKE THE FROGS. An excellent comparison from frogs, which are marsh animals, to the souls placed in the mire. And it is a fitting thing to say that the damned souls flee from the grace of God; because all those who have made a habit of vice and take pleasure in it become most inept at receiving divine grace; because <note>original: "In animam malivolam non introibit spiritus sapientie"</note> Wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul. Therefore, making oneself unable to receive the grace of God is to flee from it. Furthermore, just as the saved are confirmed in an optimal will, so the damned can no longer cease to be obstinate in sinning. WATER-SNAKE / A serpent; and this is a figure called onomatopoeia: that is, the invention of a name, because "biscia" <note>the Italian word for a common grass snake or water snake</note> is a name invented to resemble that sound the serpent makes when it goes lashing and hissing with speed. THEY VANISH. To vanish means to disappear, a word derived from the Latin <note>original: "Deliquesco"</note> "to melt away," which means to be dissolved; because whoever vanishes suddenly leaves the sight, like snow when it melts. HUDDLE / They heap themselves up. "Abbiccare" <note>original: "Sabbica"</note> is a heap in the likeness of what the Latins call a <note>original: "meta"</note> "conical pile," which is a round shape that rises and sharpens little by little. And in this shape, the farmer heaps the sheaves of grain. Thus, to "abbicare" is to accumulate. DESTROYED. Damned. For the soul deprived of its "good" <note>In this context, the "Good" refers to God</note> can be said to be undone. FLEEING BEFORE the pass: to the place where the passage was. WITH dry soles: because the grace of God—and whoever contemplates with it—cannot be wetted in the marsh of sadness and hate; that is, he is not contaminated by the vices which he contemplates. And he arranges the text thus: I saw more than a thousand souls fleeing before one who was crossing the Styx with dry soles, just as frogs vanish through the water before their enemy the snake until they all huddle together on the ground.

> From his face he removed that thick air,
> waving his left hand before him often;
> and only from that fatigue did he seem weary.
> Well did I perceive that he was a messenger from heaven:
> and I turned to the master: and he made a sign
> that I should stay still: and bow down immediately.
> Ah, how full of disdain he seemed to me!
> He reached the gate: and with a little wand
> he opened it, for there was no resistance.

<column-break/>

He continues by describing what the angel was doing, and shows that he was driving away the thick air—that is, the mist—with his left hand. This signifies that divine grace performs two operations in the human intellect. First, it removes every mist of ignorance from the face; and understand this as being from the eyes of the mind, preparing us for virtue by purging us of vices. This is the first virtue and the first act of wisdom; because Horace correctly said <note>original: "Virtus est vitium fugere et sapientia prima stultitia caruisse"</note> Virtue is to flee vice, and the first wisdom is to have been free from folly. Then, having removed the mist—that is, the vice and the ignorance—and having thus become pure (as you will see in Purgatory), he easily leads us into the knowledge of God and the truth. Whence Wisdom says in the Evangelist <note>original: "Beati mundo corde: quia ipsi deum videbunt"</note> Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. Those are blessed, then, who have a pure heart, because they will see God; that is, they will be able to rise to the contemplation of divine things. But because this first work is of greater difficulty—that is, to remove ignorance and cleanse the mind—than it is to later induce knowledge, he therefore says: WAVING THE LEFT hand before him often: because it is necessary to perform very frequent virtuous acts before the habit of virtue follows. And he adds: THAT ONLY FROM THAT fatigue did he seem weary: because all our difficulty, exhaustion, and weariness lies in purging ourselves of vices and removing ignorance. For once we have already acquired the habit of virtue, nothing, however difficult it may be, exhausts us or seems laborious. Because he who has made a habit of virtue takes pleasure and delight in exercising it. And the greater the difficulty, the more he enjoys it; as I showed more clearly in our discussions on the fourth book of Virgil: <note>original: "At puer Ascanius mediis in vallibus acri gaudet equo iamque hos cursu iam praeterit illos Spumantemque dari pecora inter inertia votis optat aprum aut fulvum descendere monte leonem."</note> But the boy Ascanius in the midst of the valleys delights in his spirited horse, and now passes these, now those in his course, and prays that a foaming boar might be granted among the helpless herds, or that a tawny lion might descend from the mountain. And we will show this more clearly when it happens that we explain that the moral virtues are of four kinds. Therefore, he seemed weary only from having to remove the mist from before his face—that is, removing the ignorance of the soul. And he says that he did this with his left hand, as if to say with the less noble hand, because of the two acts, that one was still the more ignoble. For having to perform two works: first, to lift the ignorance; second, to open the gate that leads into knowledge with the wand. He ought to reserve the right hand for this second work as the more noble one. Furthermore, to remove ignorance is to remove the vices which are symbolized by the left; and to open the gate is to induce knowledge of the virtues symbolized by the right hand. WELL DID I PERCEIVE THAT he was a messenger from heaven. I perceived that he was sent by God. This denotes that even the lower reason notices when the mind is illuminated.

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on Canto IX of Dante’s Inferno. On the previous page, Landino explained the symbolism of the Angel (Divine Grace) crossing the Stygian marsh to assist Virgil (Reason) and Dante (the human soul) at the gates of the City of Dis.</meta>

# CANTO NINE

->g.ii.<-

...from the divine splendor. But before the Angel arrives, the traveler does not foresee him as Superior Reason <note>Virgil</note> does. And therefore the poet stated above that Virgil was waiting for him. Now, it may seem to many that since the poet showed from the beginning that he is guided by Divine Grace throughout this entire pilgrimage—which, being triple in nature, he represented through three ladies <note>Mary, Lucia, and Beatrice</note>—it would be superfluous to later place Grace in many other locations under various veils. He repeats this pattern in this first part of the poem as he does in the others. To this I respond that although the beginning and the entire journey are aided by Divine Grace, nonetheless, in the face of many difficulties—those grave and varied cases that occur—it is fitting that divine help should appear more expressly. For this reason, acting as an excellent theologian, Dante places Grace in every major difficulty; and as an excellent poet, he always varies the invention and the poetic fiction. This is the highest praise for the "priests of the Muses" <note>a classical term for poets</note>; and in such skill, I see no poet who precedes ours. If I were not a Florentine myself, I would dare to say that in this regard, no one equals or matches him.

But I return to the text. **AND I TURNED TO THE MASTER:** because it is necessary for the traveler to be instructed by the Superior Reason. **AND HE MADE A SIGN:** As if to say, with a silent sign. This denotes that Dante—or let us say the "inferior reason" and sensuality—was so obedient to the superior part that even the slightest sign was enough. And he signaled to me **THAT I SHOULD STAND QUIET.** For it does not belong to the inferior reason to ask questions or engage in disputes concerning the higher forms of knowledge and science, which reside in universal truths, since the inferior reason deals only with particular, earthly things. Furthermore, even Virgil does not speak; for where knowledge comes through revealed grace, the intellect does not need to labor much. **AND BOW DOWN AT ONCE:** that is, in that very moment and without delay. He who bows shows reverence; bowing signifies yielding to a superior and being prompt to submit and obey. This is what the inferior reason must do, as the superior reason demonstrates to it. **AH, HOW HE SEEMED TO ME FULL OF DISDAIN.** The Angel remembers the ancient battle in heaven between the good and the wicked, the pride of Lucifer and his followers, and their stubbornness. This moves him to a most just indignation. Allegorically, when Divine Grace comes to succor our intellect, it must strike with force against ignorance, which is what closes the gate against us. It feels disdain that man, born for the contemplation of divine things, should be forbidden by ignorance from reaching them. Note that he does not say the Angel "was" full of disdain, but that he "seemed" so—not to Virgil, but to Dante’s "sensuality" <note>the lower, feeling part of the soul</note>. No such emotional alteration can exist in divine beings, but it *seems* so to our sensory nature, which believes that the disturbances it feels are also in God—thinking that He does not punish without anger or forgive without mercy. Therefore, as the poet will say elsewhere, the "sacred theologians" attribute human passions to God which do not actually exist in Him, because otherwise our limited senses could not comprehend His works. **HE CAME TO THE GATE AND WITH A LITTLE WAND HE OPENED IT.** Those are not wrong who say the poet used this "little wand" to show how easily the Angel opened the gate. But if I am not mistaken, it should be understood that the poet, intending to imitate Virgil and other ancient poets where Christian theology does not forbid it, here depicts an Angel sent by God—which is consistent with our religion. Yet to adorn the scene with poetic fiction, he gives him the wand of Mercury <note>the Caduceus</note>. In this way, he does not simply place the pagan god Mercury there—as Benvenuto da Imola seemed to think—because that would be idolatry; yet he does not depart entirely from poetic fiction, giving the Angel the wand just like Mercury. Here, the wand signifies the power found in God's grace to rule and teach the human soul. This Grace carries the wand—that is, the scepter—to denote that no one can resist His empire and that every diabolical force must yield. It is Grace that opens the gate for us to the knowledge of inward things.

> "O outcasts from heaven, despised folk,"
> he began upon the horrible threshold,
> "whence does this insolence harbor in you?
> Why do you kick against that will
> whose end can never be cut short,
> and which has many times increased your pain?
> What does it profit to butt against the fates?

> and spoke no word to us, but had the look
> of one whom another care constrains and bites
> than that of him who is before him;
> and we moved our feet toward the city,
> secure after the holy words.

<margin>a</margin>Once the gate is opened, the Angel addresses fitting words to the crowd [of demons], which correspond to the disdain he showed. **O OUTCASTS FROM HEAVEN.** This is an invective; it is written in the "demonstrative genre" of rhetoric, where he utterly censures the actions of the demons from beginning to end. He starts with an exclamation of great gravity and vehemence. He shows that for having tried to oppose the divine will, Lucifer and the others were not only cast out from the sublime heaven but also ruined and cast into the lowest depths. They did not merely lose their preeminence and highest honor, but they remain in extreme shame and vilification; where they were once the first of creatures, they have become the last. Therefore he said: **DESPISED FOLK:** that is, despised by God and all His other rational creatures. **UPON THE HORRIBLE THRESHOLD.** He demonstrates by this that the Angel did not enter inside, and in some par...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto IX of the Inferno. The previous page described the arrival of the Heavenly Messenger (the Angel) at the gates of the City of Dis, where he rebukes the rebellious demons who have blocked Dante and Virgil’s path.</meta>

<header>INFERNO</header>

...conforms to the saying of the Sibyl in the sixth book of Virgil: "It is not permitted for any holy person to tread upon the threshold of the wicked." <note>original: "Nulli fas casto sceleratum insistere limen" from Virgil’s Aeneid, Book VI. The Sibyl explains to Aeneas that the pure cannot enter the place of the damned.</note> **WHENCE THIS.** Meaning, from what reason does **THIS ARROGANCE** <note>Italian: *tracutanza*</note> arise? It is as if he says: from none at all. For it is the height of folly for one who does not excel others to be prideful; and you have fallen from such heights to the lowest depths, both in terms of your location and your condition and dignity. Thus, it is bad for anyone to be proud, but worse for you. **WHY DO YOU KICK AGAINST** that will: He demonstrates their folly first by showing they attempt things that are manifestly impossible. For it is known to all that no one can oppose the divine will. Second, they attempt things that are harmful to themselves. Finally, he proves these two points by inducing the example of Cerberus. **WHY DO YOU KICK** <note>recalcitrate</note>: why do you oppose? This is a metaphor <term>translatione</term> taken from a horse or similar animal which, not wanting to obey its guide, kicks out at him. **AGAINST THAT WILL**: to which the end can never be cut off; that is, a will that cannot be prevented from reaching its proposed goal. **AND WHICH MANY TIMES** has increased your grief: because every time you have opposed it, whether in heaven or in hell, you have been defeated and punished. **WHAT DOES IT PROFIT TO BUTT AGAINST THE FATES.** We spoke above of fate. And according to what we demonstrated there, we shall say of the "fates": that is, divine providence, whose order can neither be changed nor moved. Therefore, what does it profit to butt—that is, to resist—that which divine providence has ordained? **YOUR CERBERUS.** Cerberus is certainly one of the infernal spirits, representing indigestion and the needs of things pertaining to the health of the body. Because of this, he is depicted alongside other diabolical temptations as an impediment to the contemplation of truth. But because the only remedy against this is to provide for necessary things and cast away the superfluous, Virgil feeds him with a bit of "mash" <note>in the Aeneid, Virgil throws a honey-cake to Cerberus</note> and Dante feeds him with earth. But Hercules, whose descent into hell we narrated shortly above, dragged him out of hell with chains. This denotes that heroic virtue—which the poets personify as Hercules—not only makes the body content with necessary things but reduces it entirely to its power and makes it a servant. Hence, Paul said: "I punish my body and bring it into subjection." <note>original: "Castigo corpus: et in seruitutem redigo" from 1 Corinthians 9:27.</note> However, I wrote more extensively about Cerberus in the sixth canto. **NOR DOES HE YET WEAR** his chin and throat hairless: because having been dragged by Hercules by the chains he had around his three necks, it is reasonable that the chain would have stripped the hair from his gullet and chin. Nor was a longer speech or one of a different quality appropriate for the Angel. Thus, he was brief and vehement in rebuking them. He was brief so that it would not seem he esteemed them more than they deserved. He was harsh in speech because such was required by their pride. **THEN HE TURNED BACK**: having said these words, he made his return. **BY THE DIRTY ROAD**: that is, the foul path by which he had come. **AND HE SPOKE NO WORD** to us, but acted with the appearance/likeness and look of a man who is constrained and bitten by a greater care than that which is before him. Through these verses, he denotes that the office of one sent by his superior is to do what is commanded with as much brevity as possible, and then return by the direct path without undertaking any other concern. Allegorically, it demonstrates that divine grace does not stop at a single person but always extends to others. **AND WE MOVED OUR FEET.** Once the door of knowledge is opened to the speculative intellect by divine grace, that grace, guiding the lower part, enters into speculation: because the soul becomes secure and remains full of hope, comforted by divine help.

We said above that the author placed those sins proceeding from incontinence outside the City of Dis, where sensuality allows itself to be ensnared by the pleasures of the body. These do not proceed from malice nor from a savage spirit, but from the fragility of the senses, and thus they merit much less punishment. Now, inside Dis, where more grave punishments are prepared, he places the sins that proceed from an irrational and disordered elevation of the spirit, through which one neither truly recognizes God as superior, nor deigns to submit to human and divine laws, nor to just princes, nor to those who precede them in probity and wisdom. This can generally be called pride, from which all sins proceed. For according to Augustine, every sin is a departure from God and a refusal to submit to Him. Therefore, he places the two towers, which signify Boasting <note>Iactantia</note> and Arrogance <note>Arrogantia</note>; and the Furies, which signify most vehement movements and most burning desires; and Medusa, who signifies the pleasure taken in them. From this is born an indelible habit: and almost...

we passed between the martyrs and the high embankments.

<column-break/>

The same is denoted by the iron walls. And in this city he places the sixth, the seventh, the eighth, and the ninth circles: of which we shall speak particularly in the proper place. Pride, then, is an immoderate desire to advance and stand above others. But so that the sin may be better distinguished, we shall say that this desire to excel is either natural or non-natural. If it is natural, it is either spiritual or personal. If it is spiritual, it is not a sin but a just desire; nor does he deserve rebuke who desires to be more just or stronger than others, and to surpass all in science and wisdom. Similarly, it will not be a vice if it is personal: because a man can justly want to be superior to all the beasts, because the dignity of the human species deserves it. And God, in the precepts given to the first man, said: "Rule over the fish of the sea." <note>original: "Dominamini piscibus maris" from Genesis 1:28</note> But if it is non-natural, it is a sin: and we say it is non-natural when we seek to stand over other men, because nature has produced us to live in fellowship and company, from which republics are born. Nor can such company endure where there is not a universal equality. And God did not command that we should lord over other men. Such a desire to be superior to other men will therefore be vicious, desiring such excellence for itself and for our own respect. But desiring it to help other men, to maintain justice, and to preserve equality among subjects—from which tranquility is born—and not to use it for any [selfish] thing, it will not be a sin, but a merit.

---

Nor is it to be overlooked that pride is either interior or exterior. Interior pride is either in the affect or in the intellect. In the intellect, it exists in four ways. First, when a man presumes that the good he has comes from himself. Second, when it comes from God, but through his own merits. Third, when he judges that to be a virtue which is not. Fourth, when, despising others, he desires to appear to be what he is not. In the affect, it is sometimes presumption, sometimes ambition. Presumption is when we presume that which we ought not, or before the proper time, or beyond our own strength. Ambition consists either in lordship, or in mastery, or in simple excess in any of the graces given by grace, such as riches and the like. Exterior pride is considered either by the cause that produces it or by the thing in which it consists. In the first way, we consider if it is born from a good of nature, a good of fortune, or of grace. Natural goods are either of the body or of the soul. In the body, they are strength, beauty, dexterity, speed, size, and the like. In the soul, they are subtlety of wit, speed, good memory, the power to sustain spiritual exercise, and natural aptitude. Goods of fortune are those which are outside of us and can be taken from us, such as riches, dignity, dominion, glory, and fame. If we consider the subject, we shall see if it is in a private or public man, or in a priest or a layman, and the like. Companions of pride are curiosity, levity, excessive joy, arrogance, defense of sin, simulated humility, and license in sinning. Its daughters are irreverence, heresy, disobedience, vainglory, hypocrisy, boasting, obstinacy, discord, and envy. For all these vices which proceed from a fierce and malignant mind, he places punishments in these four circles located within the walls of Dis; and they are appropriate to the vice. They are in low arches. Note that even in human life, those who exalt themselves too much are depressed and lowered, at least by the sight of the sin. And they are in a heavy and troublesome stench, because the proud man generates nausea, disgust, and a stench to all men and to himself; because, always desiring a higher rank, it seems that where he is, he stinks.

**WE ENTERED WITHIN WITHOUT WAR** / without resistance: having the divine light so illuminated the intellect that every difficulty and obscurity ceased. **AND I** Dante, that is, the appetite, which is what moves the soul to investigation, as we said above. And therefore he says: that he had a desire to look upon the condition, that is, the state and fortune, of that place. **MY EYE** sent around, turned with the eyes. **AND I SEE A GREAT PLAIN:** a great flat land. And by the great space of the place, he demonstrates a great multitude of sinners. **ARLES** <note>original: "Arli"</note> is a city in Provence located at the mouth of the Rhone, not farther than three leagues from Avignon; it is called *Arelate* in Latin. And concerning the abundance of tombs that are around it, they tell such a story: Charlemagne <note>original: "Carlo magno"</note> fought in this place with a great number of pagans and carried away a most bloody victory. Because many Christians were killed there, and Charlemagne desiring to recognize the bodies of his own from those of the enemies to bury them the following morning, he found a great abundance of sepulchers, and all the Christians had their names written on their foreheads. For this reason, they were buried in such tombs. But it is more likely to believe that ancient custom created such sepulchers. **PULA** <note>original: "Pola"</note> is a city at the head of Istria near the gulf in the Adriatic Sea called Carnaro <note>The Kvarner Gulf</note>. This is about forty miles [wide] and is very dangerous because of the South wind, which in that region is likewise called Carnaro. **WHICH CLOSES ITALY:** because here Italy ends, and the shores of the Carnaro are the borders of Italy. I find no history that narrates the origin of such sepulchers. I believe that by long custom they became...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto IX and X of the Inferno, where Dante and Virgil observe the sixth circle of Hell. Having entered the City of Dis, they encounter the "heresiarchs" or leaders of false sects, entombed in fiery sarcophagi. This page provides a detailed theological and historical catalog of various Christian heresies as understood in the late 15th century.</meta>

-># INFERNO<-

multiplied. **THAT IRON** <note>original: "CHE FERRO"</note> no longer requires any craft. The tombs were so fired with heat that no craftsman ever heats iron more when he wishes to manufacture something or harden it into a new shape. Because heresy is punished in this place, we should note that "heresy" is a Greek word <note>original: "heresia," from the Greek "hairesis"</note> and it means **choice** <term>electione; the act of choosing one's own path</term>. This is because the heretic departs from the common opinion or faith and chooses for himself what he wishes to believe. We shall say, therefore, that heresy is the choice of one's own opinion against the determination of the Apostolic Church. Briefly, we shall say that a heretic is anyone who holds an opinion different from the true religion. This cannot happen without the greatest arrogance, for he attributes too much to his own sense who deviates from the common opinion of many most learned men. It is, therefore, one of the daughters of **Pride**. 

There are some who interpret the Furies <note>the mythical Eumenides mentioned in the previous canto</note> in relation to this sin: setting **Alecto** for the evil thought, **Tisiphone** for the evil publication of such a thought, **Megaera** for the evil operation or action, and **Medusa** for when one openly approves of his own falsehood. But this allegory does not seem to me preferable to the one I placed above; nonetheless, let each person approve of the one they judge fits best. **Heresiarchs** <term>the princes or founders of heresies</term> were many. But taking the beginning from where Gratian <note>a 12th-century jurist and author of the Decretum Gratiani</note> takes it, we shall say the first was **Simon Magus**, whom Peter cursed in the Acts of the Apostles because he tried to buy the grace of the Holy Spirit with money. From him, those who sell or buy sacred things are called **Simonists**. Their heresy is the belief that the creature was not made by God, but by a certain supreme power. 

**Menandrians** take their name from Menander the magician, a disciple of Simon; they say the world was not made by God but by angels. **Basilidians** from Basilides, who did not want Jesus Christ to have suffered. **Nicolaites** from Nicolas the deacon—who was appointed by the Apostle Peter along with Stephen—who left his wife to her own judgment to join with whomever she pleased, and he instituted the changing of marriage. **Gnostics** <note>from the Greek "gnosis" meaning knowledge</note> wanted to be so called for their excellence in science; these people say the soul is of the nature of God, and that God is both good and a captive. **Carpocratians** from Carpocrates, who said Christ was only a man, born of a male and a female. **Cerinthians** from Cerinthus; these observe circumcision and say that a thousand years after the resurrection they will live in the pleasure of the flesh. Hence in Greek they are called **Chiliasts** and in Latin **Millennialists** <note>original: "maciliste," likely a variant of "milliarii"</note>. **Nazarenes** confess Christ and yet live according to the law of the Old Testament. 

**Ophites**, named from the serpent which in Greek is called *ophis*, adore the serpent and say that he introduced the knowledge of virtue. **Valentinians** believe that Christ took nothing of his body from Mary, but entered into her as if through a channel or a pipe. **Apellians**, named from Apelles, held that an angel was the god of the law of Israel and affirmed him to be made of fire; he said Christ was not God in truth, but appeared as a man in fantasy. **Archontics** hold that the universe created by God is the work of archangels. **Adamites**, imitating Adam, pray naked and stay together naked, both males and females. **Cainites** adore Cain. **Sethians** said that Seth, the son of Adam, was Christ. **Melchizedekians** say that Melchizedek the priest was not a man but a power of God. 

**Artotyrites** were named from *artos* <note>Greek for bread</note> and *tyros* <note>Greek for cheese</note>, because they offer bread and cheese in their sacrifices, affirming that the first men celebrated sacrifices of the fruits of the earth and the livestock. **Aquarians** put only water into the chalice of the sacrifice. **Severians**, named after Severus, do not drink wine, nor do they believe in the Old Testament or the resurrection. **Alogi**, meaning "without the Word" <note>from the Greek "a" (without) and "logos" (word)</note>, because they do not believe God is the Word, and they do not believe in the Apocalypse <note>the Book of Revelation</note>. **Paulians** from Paul of Samosata, who said Christ had not always existed, but had his beginning from Mary. 

**Manichaeans** from Manes the Persian, who proposed two natures and two substances—one good and one evil—and that our soul derives from God as from a certain fountain; they do not accept the Old Testament, and the New they accept only in part. **Anthropomorphites** believe that God has the form of a man, and from this they have taken their name, because *anthropos* means man and *morphos* means form. **Heraclites** from Heraclius receive only monks; they damn marriages and do not believe that small children have the kingdom of heaven. **Photinians** from Photinus, a bishop in Galatia, said Christ was born of Mary and Joseph through carnal union. **Acacians** say the Son is dissimilar to the Father, and the Spirit to the Son. 

**Origenists** from Origen say that souls sinned at the beginning of the world, and according to their diversity, from heaven down to earth, they have taken different bodies; and for this reason they say the world was made. **Noetians** do not place three persons in God but only one, and say Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are names of office and not a distinction of persons. Hence they are called **Patripassians**, because they hold that the Father also suffered. **Sabellians** are named after Sabellius, a disciple of Noetus, and were in the same error. **Arius**, bishop of Alexandria, distinguished the essence of the Son from the Father, against the word of the Lord who said, "I and the Father are one" <note>original Latin: "Ego et pater unum sumus" from John 10:30</note>. 

**Macedonius** the bishop does not want the Holy Spirit to be God. **Apollinarists** from Apollinaris, who says that Christ took a human body but not a soul. **Priscillianists** say that the substance of human flesh was made by the devil. **Donatus** came from Numidia and subverted all of Africa, saying that the Son is less than the Father, and the Holy Spirit less than the Son. **Bonosus** the bishop, and from him the **Bonosians**, say that Christ was not the proper Son of God but an adopted one. **Circumcellions** kill themselves with their own hands to die as martyrs. **Priscillianists** in Spain made a sect mixed with the errors of the Gnostics. **Paterniani** say that the lower parts of the body were made by the devil. **Arabici** were heretics in Arabia who affirmed the soul dies with the body and...

<meta>This page continues the exhaustive catalog of heretical sects and their specific theological errors begun on the previous page. The author, Cristoforo Landino, provides historical and scriptural context for why Dante depicts heretics in fiery, stone tombs. He moves from early church heresies (like Nestorianism) to medieval groups (like the Patarines) active in Tuscany.</meta>

->### CANTO NINE<-

at the day of judgment, both shall rise again. **Tertullian**, a Carthaginian priest, says the soul is immortal but corporeal, and that sinful souls turn into demons after death. The **Nyctages** <note>A group that supposedly believed the night should be spent in sleep rather than vigils</note> say that anyone who spends the night in vigils acts against God, since God made the night for rest. **Pelagius**, a monk, places free will before divine grace, asserting that the will alone is sufficient to follow the commandments of God. **Nestorius**, Bishop of Constantinople, asserts that Mary was not the Mother of God, but only of the man; for this reason, he claims one person is of the flesh and another of the deity. He sets Christ apart, saying one is the Son of God and another is the son of man. **Eutyches**, an abbot of Constantinople, denies that Christ, after his human assumption, exists in two natures; rather, he maintains that only the divine remains in him. 

The **Acephali** <term>meaning "headless," from the Greek 'a' (without) and 'cephale' (head)</term> were so called because no leader or founder of this sect can be found. They deny the properties of two substances in Christ, but want there to be only one nature in his person. This same error was held by **Theodosius** and **Gaianus**, who were ordained bishops on the same day by the perverse people of Alexandria. They thus make one nature out of two in Christ, like Eutyches and Dioscorus; but the Theodosians consider it corruptible, while the Gaianites consider it incorruptible. From the Theodosians proceed the **Agnoetae**, so called from ignorance, because they assert that the divinity of Christ was ignorant of what was written regarding the day and the final hour; nor do they remember that in the person of Christ, **Isaiah** says: "The day of judgment is in my heart" <note>original: "Dies iudicii in corde meo"</note>. 

The **Tritheists** <note>original: "Tritonite"</note> said there are not three persons in one God, but that there are three gods, contrary to what is written: "Hear, O Israel: The Lord your God is one God" <note>original: "audi israel Dominus deus tuus unus est deus"</note>. There are also some who do not want Christ to have been born of the Father from eternity, but with a beginning in time. Some do not believe that the descent of Christ into Hell freed men. Some believe that our souls after death are converted into demons, or even into every kind of animal. Some posit innumerable worlds, following the opinion of **Democritus**. Some posit water as coeternal with God, like **Thales of Miletus**. Some go barefoot. Some do not eat with other men. Many other sects remain; if I were to narrate them all, I might be condemned for curiosity rather than praised for diligence. But the opinion of the **Fraticelli** <term>the "Little Brethren," a radical splinter group of the Franciscans</term> is very well known, being very close to our own age and perhaps not yet extinguished. 

The **Patarines** <note>A medieval heretical movement often associated with the Cathars</note> are most malignant; besides many other errors they have in common with the **Manichaeans**, they say our souls are evil spirits infused into bodies by the devil. They say that the soul and the body of Christ and of Mary were created in heaven incorruptible, and that they never ate or drank physical food. They say that baptism is not necessary; that the Eucharist is not the body of Christ, but simple bread and wine in memory of the true body. Furthermore, they say that marriage is not a sacrament, nor is anyone in a state of salvation who remains in it. They do not want anyone to confess their sins particularly, but only to confess that they are a sinner, and they believe it suffices for the Patarine to place his hand on the person's head, which they call **"Consolation"** <term>consolamentum; the primary ritual of the Cathar/Patarine faith</term>. They say our bodies are not to rise again. They do not use the sign of the cross, but say it is idolatry to venerate it. They do not want anyone to defend themselves in such a way that the attacker might be harmed. They affirm it is a mortal sin to kill any animal except fish, fleas, and lice. Likewise, they forbid swearing for any reason. They deny it is a sin to practice usury if it is done without fraud. They say that in Tuscany, the true church is the **Florentine church**, which extends from Pisa to Arezzo, Montepulciano, and Grosseto. 

These heresies, although they are discrepant among themselves, nonetheless all conspire against the Apostolic See. All are condemned by the Apostles and other holy men and councils. In short, whoever understands the most Holy Scripture differently than the sense of the Holy Spirit requires—from whom the Scripture proceeds—even if he does not depart from the Church, he may nonetheless be called a heretic. And all heretics ought to be excommunicated according to the saying: "A brother who is rebuked by the church and does not obey, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector" <note>original: "Frater qui corripitur ab ecclesia et non obedit sit tibi sicut ethnicus et publicanus"</note>. 

By the **sepulchres** <note>the tombs Dante sees in the City of Dis</note>, you should understand the mind of the heretic to be buried in obstinacy without redemption. For just as the virtue of faith gives birth to grace in us, which is a faithful guide to salvation, so incredulity extinguishes every divine light in the heart. Whence we remain in the hardest obstinacy; and for this reason, he places the tombs in stone. Nor is it without cause that he places heresy after **Pride**. For Solomon says: "The beginning of all sin is pride" <note>original: "Initium omnis peccati est supbia"</note>. The commentator says that heresy is born from that. And **Jeremiah**: "Your arrogance and the pride of your heart have deceived you" <note>original: "Arrogantia tua et superbia cordis tui decepit te"</note>. Because in truth, heresy is not born from ignorance, but from pride, the man wishing to acquire authority and favor for being the inventor of something new. 

They stay in the sepulchres for the reason already stated, or truly because heretics keep their beliefs hidden, and they hold their congregations and synagogues in occult and hidden places. From here, **Job** says: "By design they departed from God and did not want to understand His ways" <note>original: "De industria recesserunt a deo et uias eius intelligere noluerunt"</note>. That which the **Psalmist** says also fits this figure of the sepulchres: "In it he prepared the vessels of death and made his arrows burning" <note>original: "In eo parauit uasa mortis et sagictas suas ardentes effecit"</note>. Where the gloss says: "The vessels of death are the heretics, who bury their souls." And elsewhere: "Shall any tell of your mercy in the grave?" <note>original: "Nunquid narrabit aliquis in sepulcro misericordiam tuam"</note>. And elsewhere: "Their throat is an open sepulchre" <note>original: "Sepulchrum patens est guttur eorum"</note>. For just as a great stench comes out of an open tomb, so from the mouths of these people come foul opinions, because they are hardened in their views. 

The **fire** denotes the immeasurable love they have had for themselves and for their own opinion. Or truly, a continuous agitation and fluctuation that is in the heretic, and an ignited fury; for although he is hardened in his opinion, nonetheless, seeing himself disagree with the opinion of an innumerable multitude of men who, through their sanctity, were able...
