<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on Dante’s Inferno, moving from a list of specific heretical sects to an explanation of the physical and allegorical layout of the Sixth Circle. It explains why Dante chooses specific vocabulary for the tombs and the symbolic meaning behind Virgil’s movements.</meta>

-># INFERNO<-

having divine revelation of the truth: and through various and much learning, those of great authority can never find peace. Dante asks, then, who are buried in these chests <note>original: "arche," meaning sarcophagi or tombs</note>: that is, the sepulchers: and who he intends to be there: because he hears their sighs, which are born from the highest anguish of the soul. And certainly, those who do not acquiesce to common opinion, searching with the mind for what might seem more true, find their foolish intellect is always in anxiety and anguish. **AND HE TO ME**, Virgil said: understand, **HERE** in these sepulchers are the **HERESIARCHS**: that is, the leaders of the heretical sects, of whom we have briefly narrated above. **AND THEY ARE VERY FULL**: that is, crowded. **THE TOMBS**—the burial places—**MORE THAN YOU BELIEVE**. This is to note that among men there are more heretics than one might believe. Therefore, to avoid always saying the same word, which generates boredom in the reader, he uses this variation, which brings with it ornament and delight, saying now "sepulcher," now "chest," now "tomb," now "vault." **LIKE HERE** like is buried with like: as if to say Manichaeans with Manichaeans, and Priscillians with Priscillian, and so with the others. **AND THEN TO THE RIGHT** he was turned. Here he posits that Virgil turned to the right hand: and then demonstrates that a little later in the journey, he turned to the left. This denotes that the journey began to the right because they went to gain knowledge of sin, not to be defiled by it, but to be purged of it; such an action is virtuous <note>In medieval allegory, the right hand often represents the path of virtue or reason</note>. Then he turned to the left to denote that although the operation is virtuous, nonetheless the matter and the subject are vice. Thus, he wisely takes the leftward journey from the right hand. **MARTYRS**: <term>Martyres</term> in the Greek language are "witnesses." But because those who preferred to suffer pain and death rather than deny the Christian religion were the best witnesses that it was true, they were called martyrs: that is, witnesses of our true faith. This is the proper meaning of the word. But because such testimony was made with grave torments and harsh deaths, for this reason, we often take "martyrdom" to mean pain and torment; and so it is used here. Thus Petrarch used it when he said:

> Brief succor to such long martyrdoms.

**AND THE OTHER** battlements <note>original: "spaldi"</note>. Such a word is not very common nor known to many. Wherefore some say "spaldi" signifies the walls. Others say that "spaldo" in the Romagnol dialect signifies what we call the "space" <note>likely referring to an open area or walkway</note>: and the Latins call it the "pavement" <note>original: "pauimento"</note>.

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on Dante’s Inferno. Having established the nature of the Sixth Circle where the heretics are punished, the text now transitions into the opening of Canto X. The commentary focuses on the specific path Dante takes and the allegorical significance of Virgil as "Supreme Virtue," representing the different levels of human and divine intellect.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>CANTO TEN</header>

### CANTO TEN OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE

Now he goes by a secret path
Between the wall of the land and the martyrs,
My master; and I behind his shoulders.
"O supreme virtue, who through the impious circles
Lead me," I began, "as it pleases you,
Speak to me and satisfy my desires.
The people who lie within the sepulchers,
Could they be seen? For already raised are
All the lids, and no one keeps watch."

And he to me: "They shall all be closed
When from Jehoshaphat <note>The Valley of Jehoshaphat is the biblical site where, according to tradition, the Last Judgment will take place.</note> they return here
With the bodies they have left up above."

<column-break/>

This tenth canto contains much less difficulty than the ninth: because there are few places that receive any allegory other than what has already been stated, and a large part of it is spent on history. It treats the heretics and prepares for the ascent into the seventh circle. He finds Farinata degli Uberti and Cavalcante de' Cavalcanti, Florentine knights; and from Farinata he hears of future things and learns the reason why those placed in Hell can foresee the future. **NOW HE GOES**: He had shown that Virgil was leading him among the martyrs <note>original: "martyri"; here Landino interprets this as the suffering souls or their tombs.</note>. Now, continuing, he posits that the path by which Virgil led Dante was between the wall of the land and the

Martyrs: that is, the tombs where the sufferings were. This denotes that these sepulchers were near the walls, which signifies the hardness and obstinacy of the heretics. We can also understand that just as one who is near the walls of the city is almost outside of it, so the heretic, although he may be a Christian, is nevertheless almost outside the Christian name due to his depraved religion. And similarly, it denotes that such men hold their gatherings in separate and remote places. **PATH** <note>original: "calle"</note> Signifies a path that is not public but narrow, made by the calloused feet of beasts. This denotes that it is a very narrow path that leads correctly through heresies; and certainly, it is difficult to find the truth among so many falsehoods. The text is ordered thus: "My master now goes by a secret path," that is, a way which you understand was between the wall of the land and the martyrs. **AND I BEHIND HIS SHOULDERS**: because sensuality, if it does not wish to err, must always follow its master Virgil, that is, the powers of the intellect. And then he continues: **O SUPREME VIRTUE**. O Virgil, who is of supreme virtue. **WHO LEAD ME**: who turn me as you please **THROUGH THE IMPIOUS CIRCLES**: That is, through impious circles, meaning where the impious and pitiless sinners are. For there can be no greater impiety than to hold a poor opinion of God. Some texts have **AMPLE** <note>original: "ampi"</note>: meaning wide, to note the abundance of sinners. **SPEAK TO ME AND SATISFY ME**: that is, speak to me in a way that satisfies my desires and my will. This is the order of the text. But let us remember that, as has been said at other times, the epithets the author gives to Virgil are always suited to the place where he labors. Therefore, here he calls him "supreme virtue" because Virgil, as the Intellect, has five virtues: **Intelligence** regarding first principles; **Science** <note>original: "Scientia"</note> regarding things that follow from principles; **Wisdom** <note>original: "Sapientia"</note> which, embracing the two already mentioned, is nevertheless not either of them, but a third virtue beyond the two; **Prudence** which is the correct guide in particular actions and civil life; and **Art**, which is a known thing. Of these five, the most excellent is Wisdom, because it is the knowledge not only of human things, but of divine ones. Thus, he could not lead him through heretical falsehoods except with Wisdom, which has true knowledge of divinity as much as the capacity of the human mind allows. And not without reason did he say: "Lead me as it pleases you." Because although in all forms of knowledge it is necessary for the lower reason and the senses to let themselves be turned and guided by the intellect, it is especially necessary in this case. And he makes an excellent preface to this brief speech: because first he gains goodwill by calling him "supreme virtue," and by those same words he shows that what he asks is easy for him, since he possesses supreme virtue; thus, he is able to do it. Then he shows that he *ought* to do it: because equity requires that we satisfy the will of one who gives himself entirely to our judgment. **THE PEOPLE**. Up to here he has shown both that Virgil *can* and that he *ought* to answer him. He now poses the question to which he wants an answer: which is whether he can see those who lie in the sepulchers. This he believes can easily be done, both because the sepulchers are open and because no guard is seen there to forbid looking at them. The reason why they are open we will state a little further below. There is no guard because Holy Church does not keep heretical opinions hidden and does not forbid them from being read and understood; rather, with effective reasons, she refutes them. And then she wants everyone to know both their foolishness and the wisdom of the sacred theologians, so that, understanding what they say is false and having it reproved with true reasons, they may be mocked and scorned rather than imitated and appreciated. And certainly, just as a pit in the road should not be hidden but manifested so that no one falls into it through imprudence, so false opinions must come to light together with their refutation, so that no one falls into such error through ignorance.

Excellent speech of a good teacher: who often not only responds to what the disciple asks, but also adds of his own accord all the other things which he judges...

<summary>This page introduces Canto X of the Inferno, where Dante and Virgil encounter the heretics. Landino explains that Virgil represents "Supreme Virtue" (Wisdom) necessary to navigate theological errors, and notes that heretical tombs are left open as a warning to others.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Dante and Virgil in Canto X. Virgil explains the nature of the heretics' punishment, specifically those who followed Epicurus. The commentary by Landino expands significantly on the theology of the soul, drawing from classical philosophy and Christian doctrine to refute the idea of the soul's mortality.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>INFERNO</header>

Their cemetery on this side they have
With Epicurus and all his followers,
Who make the soul die with the body:
Therefore, to the question that you ask me,
Here within you shall soon be satisfied,
And also to the desire that you keep silent from me.
And I: "Good guide, I do not keep hidden
My heart from you, except to speak little;
And you have not only now disposed me to this."

<column-break/>

...it being useful for him to know. Dante asks if it were possible to see the people of the sepulchers, since they were open. And Virgil not only responds that they can be seen, but also says they will be closed after the universal and final judgment, which will be at the end of the world: when all human generation, having taken up their own bodies again, will gather in the valley called Jehoshaphat <note>A valley in Jerusalem mentioned in the Book of Joel as the site of God's final judgment.</note> near Jerusalem, where Jesus Christ will descend to judge the good to eternal glory and the wicked to eternal pains. Jehoshaphat means "He judges," or "Judgment of the Lord" <note>original: "Ioſaphath ſignifica epſo giudica: Ouero iudicio del ſignore"</note>. At that time, therefore, these summoned souls will return to their own bodies, and after the 

<column-break/>

judgment, they will return with them to these tombs, and then they will be closed. They stay open now, therefore, because the bodies are not there; and this is the reason regarding the essential Hell. But regarding the allegorical sense, we can understand that as long as human generation lasts, they remain open to receive the heretics who arise from time to time. It is as if he says there are and always will be heretics. But once the world is finished, they will cease, because human generation will be lacking. Truly, we shall understand with more subtlety that beneath the universal judgment he shows the particular: and he wishes it understood that the heretic, as soon as he is in such error, has his reason buried. But the sepulcher is not closed until his particular judgment <note>A person's individual judgment by God immediately after death, as opposed to the General Judgment at the end of time.</note>, because he can still return to the true faith. They remain open, therefore, because divine grace can, before the judgment—that is, death—draw them out of the darkness and lead them back to the light. Therefore, one must not kill heretics, but imprison them, admonish them, and lead them back as much as possible. "For he who is wandering ought not to be killed, but brought back to the path" <note>original: "Quis enim errabunda occidi non debet Sed ad cauſam reduci"</note>. This is also shown in the Book of Kings when Absalom, son of David, entered unto his father’s concubines <note>Referencing 2 Samuel 16; Landino uses the concubines as an allegory for heretics who violate the "mother" church.</note>, where by the concubines they understand the heretics. **THEIR CEMETERY:** He ordains thus that all the followers of the philosopher Epicurus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher (341–270 BCE) whose followers were often wrongly accused of seeking only carnal pleasure; here, they are condemned for denying the immortality of the soul.</note> together with him have their cemetery on this side. And he rightly said "cemetery," there being sepulchers. For "cemetery" is where Christians bury the bodies of dead men; and it is a Greek word <note>from koimeterion</note> and means "resting place" <note>original: "giacitorio"</note>, because there the dead bodies lie, named from *kime* <note>Greek: keimai</note>, that is, "I lie down." **WHO MAKE THE SOUL DIE WITH THE BODY.** A most wicked opinion and the greatest ruin to the future life; but no one of sound mind believes this. But they, as the Psalmist says: "They have placed their hope in a lie, and in a lie they have hoped for their work" <note>original: "poſuerunt mendacium ſpem ſuam: et mendacium operi ſperauerunt"; referencing Psalm 26 in the Vulgate.</note>. And Solomon: "They have wandered from the paths of their own cultivation, and they gather fruitless things in their hands" <note>original: "Semitas proprie culture errauerunt Et colligunt in manibus infructuoſa"</note>. The philosopher Epicurus said that the soul dies together with the body. Various are the opinions of the soul according to different philosophers: because many believed it to be a body; many believed it to be a corporeal thing. And it would be tedious to narrate them all. But I, in the first of the three books I wrote in the Latin language *On the Soul* <note>Referring to Landino's own philosophical treatise, *De anima*.</note>, set down the opinion of each person and afterwards refuted them, demonstrating that it is not a body nor a corporeal thing, but incorporeal. I then set down the definition of Aristotle. And because that is common and not specific to the human soul, I took from the Platonic doctrine, in which that great philosopher investigates first why the soul exists, then what it is, whether it was before the body or after the body, and whether it can be divided into several parts. Whether in one and the same man there are several souls—that is, that one soul is the vegetative, another the motive, another the sensitive, and another the rational—or truly it is only one which embraces within itself all these four powers. And finally, I set down its definition: which is that the soul is an incorporeal rational substance which moves itself. After such a definition, I proved why it is a substance and not an accident, and why it is incorporeal and not corporeal. And what Plato means when he says that the soul moves itself, and what thing is active and passive motion, and how wrongly this definition is attacked by the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note>. I said also that souls were not all created together as Plato writes, nor do they enter into bodies because they are weighed down by the desire for earthly things (as pleases the same Plato), or that they wish to flee the harsh commands of the gods and the constant revolutions they must make for the turning of the heavens (as Heraclitus writes), or to endure pain and torment in the bodies for the sins which they committed in heaven (as Empedocles believes, and also Origen). And I added that souls are created from time to time, and in one and the same moment created and put into the body. And they are created by God, not from His own substance (as the Stoics affirmed, and later many Spanish heretics who followed Manichaeus and Priscillian). Nor yet are they created from His breath (as Vincent Victor wishes). But they are created from nothing, rational and immortal, and with free will, through which it follows that in our hand is life and death: that is, the power to save or damn ourselves. Then in the second book, I treated the vegetative power: and how it nourishes the body, and how it grows it, and with what seed it generates more of itself. I treated the motive power. I treated the exterior and interior senses. I treated the appetite and the disturbances that arise from it. I treated all the intellectual and moral virtues. Nor did I only describe all these parts and powers, but I also demonstrated all the instruments of the body which the soul uses in them. In the third, I added the rational: and distinctly I narrated the possible and active intellect, and what is inferior reason and [superior] reason...

<summary>Landino explains the punishment of Epicureans who denied the soul's immortality, using the imagery of open tombs that will close after the Final Judgment. He provides an extensive philosophical defense of the soul as an incorporeal, immortal substance created by God, refuting various ancient heresies and philosophical errors.</summary>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>CANTO TEN</header>
<meta>catchword: SUDDENLY</meta>

...superior: and that intellect and intelligence are distinct. And I confuted the opinion of Averroes <note>Averroes was a medieval Andalusian philosopher who argued for a single, universal human intellect, a view Landino refutes here in favor of individual souls.</note> and many others, demonstrating that there are as many souls as there are men: and that it is false that there is only one universal intellect. And in the final part, I placed many arguments to prove the immortality of the soul. Therefore, through all these things, we understand that the soul did not exist before the body. We understand its essence: and its parts and powers. We understand what it performs in the body, with what instruments, and how it remains after it has departed from the body. I did not cite my own books out of arrogance or to prefer myself to others, but because in them many things are collected which are not found together elsewhere: for I joined the Platonic with the Aristotelian and Stoic disciplines, and subjected them to Christian truth. Narrating them, I have pulled them from the thorny arguments of dialectic and made them clear and open with an oratorical style, so that not only men practiced in philosophy, but even citizens—provided they have some knowledge of letters—may easily understand them. And let this suffice regarding the soul.

I return to Epicurus. He was an Athenian, the son of Neocles. He said that our soul is a body composed of such subtle parts that it penetrates through the entire body. And the matter that makes this soul are atoms, that is, bodies so minute that they are indivisible. And he maintains that such atoms are very round. And because every body is composite, and every composite thing dissolves and consequently perishes, it follows that since the soul is a body, it must perish. Therefore, he maintains that the soul is mortal. This same philosopher placed our happiness in the *voluptas* <note>original: "uolupta"; meaning sensual pleasure or delight.</note> and pleasure of the body, and unhappiness in the pain of the body. This opinion, though it belongs to a beast rather than a man—because we are not born to fill the belly or satisfy lust, but to contemplate divine things—nevertheless, he lived better than he spoke. For he lived with the utmost temperance, both in food and in matters of lust. He bore pains with a great soul. He was most observant of faith. He was most faithful in friendships, for which reason he had many friends. He was very liberal and merciful, and for this, he is much praised in many places by Seneca, the most grave philosopher.

But returning to the text: our poet, seeing that heresies were so many that he could not treat them all, placed this one here, which is more pernicious to the human generation than any other. For whoever considers the soul mortal removes every foundation for just civil living and for true religion.

**WHO MAKE THE SOUL DIE WITH THE** body. They do not "make" it so because it is not in their power to make it mortal or alive, but they "make" it so in their judgment.

**THEREFORE, TO THE QUESTION THAT YOU ASKED** me, whether they can be seen.

**HERE WITHIN** in this space not far away.

**SATISFIED** you shall be soon: because you will see the souls come out of the sepulcher.

**AND ALSO TO THE** desire that you keep silent from me. He had asked if the souls could be seen, but his intention specifically was to see Farinata and Cavalcante, whom he believed were there, knowing they were stained with such a vice.

**O GOOD GUIDE, I DO NOT** keep my heart hidden from you: that is, I did not stay silent to hide my heart from you, meaning my wish.

**BUT TO SPEAK BRIEFLY.** For he who asks in general speaks more briefly than he who searches for particulars. And he adds that he wants to be brief because Virgil, not only now but many times, has admonished him to do this. And Dante subtly demonstrates the difference between the superior intellect and the inferior intellect. For the superior intellect turns to universals and not to particulars; for example <note>original: "uerbi gratia"</note>, it does not investigate whether the homicide committed specifically by Milo against Clodius <note>A famous Roman legal case where Titus Annius Milo killed his rival Clodius Pulcher; Cicero famously defended Milo.</note> or the robbery committed by Verres in Sicily is evil. Rather, it investigates universally whether homicide and robbery are evil. But the inferior intellect considers things as we see them in civil life. But Dante, wishing to arrive at the true science of things, which resides in universals, leaves his own manner and takes up that of Virgil, following universals; because Virgil, wishing to unite him to knowledge, always admonishes him to this. And yet he does not hide his heart from him. For the superior intellect knows this universal: that the inferior intellect seeks the particulars.

> "O Tuscan, who through the city of fire
> Go walking alive, speaking thus modestly,
> May it please you to stay in this place.
> Your speech makes you manifest
> As a native of that noble fatherland
> To which perhaps I was too troublesome."
> Suddenly this sound issued
> From one of the tombs: therefore I drew
> A little closer, fearing, to my guide.

<column-break/>

He sets down the words of the spirit, who was Farinata degli Uberti: which are appropriate for a magnanimous and prudent man of composed manners, as he was.

**O TUSCAN** or "O Man of Tuscany." It is as if he said "O Florentine," as that city is the head of Tuscany.

**THROUGH THE CITY OF FIRE**: through the city of Dis, full of fire.

**ALIVE YOU GO**: and not dead nor as a ghost like us.

**SPEAKING** modestly: because he had heard how he responded to Virgil.

**STAY** / stop yourself.

**YOUR SPEECH**: Shows that he had recognized him by his way of speaking.

**OF THAT NOBLE FATHERLAND**: yours

---

and mine: and he uttered these words not without sorrow. For every fault committed leaves behind repentance, which continually pricks the conscience. Therefore, by saying "of that noble fatherland," he shows he regrets having offended it; because by calling it "noble," it is as if to say it was unworthy of being troubled. And therefore he subjoins:

**TO WHICH** perhaps I was too troublesome. But he said "perhaps" so as not to deprive himself entirely of an excuse: as if to say, "if I was impious toward her, my adversaries gave me cause." **SUDDENLY**

<meta>This page continues the transition from the general discussion of the Epicurean heresy to the specific encounter with the soul of Farinata degli Uberti. Having established that Epicureans believe the soul dies with the body, Landino now moves to the narrative action where Dante is startled by a voice from a tomb.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>HELL</header>

SUDDENLY THIS sound came out: the poet speaks and describes where these words originated, which caused him some dread as they were sudden and unexpected, causing him to draw closer to Virgil. Through this, he denotes that whenever our "sensuality"—that is, our lower reason—is seized by some perturbation, it ought to join itself with the "superior reason." In superior reason resides perfect judgment, which recognizes whether that which causes fear is truly to be fled or not; and if it is not to be feared, it comforts the appetite to go forward and meet it. Therefore, there follows:

"And he said to me: 'Turn around; what are you doing?
Behold Farinata who has risen upright:
from the waist up you will see all of him.'
I had already fixed my gaze on his;
and he rose with his chest and his brow
as if he held Hell in great contempt.
And the spirited hands of the guide, being prompt,
pushed me among the tombs toward him
saying: 'Let your words be clear.'"

<column-break/>

It was no wonder that the words of Farinata perturbed his sensuality. This is because no one can respond to heresy unless they are aided by the intellect. But when one draws near to the intellect, it gives them the courage to respond. **TURN AROUND; WHAT ARE YOU DOING.** As if to say: "Why do you delay?" This denotes that one must rise against heresy quickly and with audacity before any false opinion grows old in the mind. **LET YOUR WORDS BE CLEAR:** that is, prompt and well-considered, so that the adversary has no "hook" or leverage against you. **BEHOLD FARINATA.** He was a Florentine knight of the noble Uberti family. In Florence, he was the leader of the Ghibellines <note>The Ghibellines were a pro-Imperial political faction, often at odds with the pro-Papal Guelfs.</note>. By his counsel, the Ghibellines were victorious in the most unhappy conflict of Montaperti <note>The Battle of Montaperti (1260) was a bloody defeat for the Florentine Guelfs.</note> in the Val d'Arbia. From this followed the flight of the Guelfs, who, abandoning Florence, traveled through much of Italy with a flourishing army; in Bologna, Parma, and Modena, they restored the Guelf cause. Finally, armed in aid of the Pope against Manfred <note>Manfred was the King of Sicily and a patron of the Ghibellines.</note>, they were the primary cause of Manfred’s defeat. 

He was, without fail, a man of great spirit and no less counsel; but he held a wicked and false opinion regarding the human soul, estimating that it perished along with the body. Therefore, he judged it good in this brief life to take every bodily pleasure. Thus, in his victuals and food, he surpassed all modesty. Dante noted this in the tenth canto when he asked Ciacco <note>A Florentine character from Canto VI associated with gluttony.</note> if Farinata was with him. **I HAD ALREADY** [fixed] my face: my sight, that is, my eyes. **FIXED** on his: because I stared at him fixedly to recognize him. **AND HE ROSE WITH** his chest and his brow. Heresy can consist of three parts: feeling it within oneself, speaking of it with others, and making an open profession of it. Therefore, Dante, wishing to show him as a heretic in every part, first gave him speech; now he shows that he rises with his chest, where thought resides, and with his brow, which signifies open and manifest profession. For this reason, it is a laudable institution among Christians—whose religion consists chiefly in the Gospel—that when they hear it, they sign their forehead, their mouth, and their chest. This demonstrates that they believe with the heart, speak with the tongue, and make profession with an open brow. Furthermore, he wishes to show the custom of a haughty man, as he was; for such men, out of pride, walk like "little wolves," displaying their chest and brow. Hence Juvenal says: "Bearing much of the character of the indolent Maecenas" <note>original: "Multum referens de Mecenate supino"</note>. **AS IF HE HELD HELL** in great contempt. It is the nature of the faint-hearted to be afflicted and dismayed in torments; but he who is of great spirit retains a certain pride and haughtiness, and it seems he would sooner despise the torment than grieve over it. And he said *dispicto* instead of *dispecto* [contempt], changing the 'e' to 'i' to make the rhyme. **AND THE SPIRITED HANDS** of the leader, being prompt. It was necessary that the lower reason be corroborated by the excellence and frankness of the superior reason. Therefore, he feigns that the spirited hands of the guide pushed him; nor were they only spirited, but also prompt—that is, cautious and swift. And he commanded that his words be *conte*, meaning clear and open. For whoever wishes to be free of heresy must write and speak without any ambiguity, and should not proceed unless sent by the intellect. It is folly for one whose intellect is not illustrated by true and Christian doctrine to dispute, especially in public, with heretics and infidels; for being defeated by the sharpness of one who affirms a falsehood, they make those who listen waver. Hence, it is prohibited for anyone who is not a declared Master of Sacred Theology to dispute in public.

---

"When I was at the foot of his tomb
he looked at me for a moment, and then, almost disdainfully,
he asked me: 'Who were your ancestors?'
I, who was eager to obey <gloss>m</gloss>,
did not hide it from him, but revealed it all;
at which he raised his eyebrows a little.
Then he said fiercely: 'They were fiercely adverse
to me and to my ancestors and to my party,
so that twice I scattered them.'"

<column-break/>

In the first triplet, he describes the gestures and words of Farinata, through which his haughty nature is demonstrated; for with a certain pride, he asked who his ancestors had been—that is, his ancient kin. **I, WHO WAS** eager to obey: understand this as referring to Virgil, who had told him, "Let your words be clear." **AT WHICH HE RAISED** his eyebrows a little. This is the gesture of a man who hears something he would rather not. And then he said: "These ancestors of yours were fiercely diverse and adversaries to me, and to my ancestors, and to my party," because they were Guelfs.

<meta>This page continues the encounter in the circle of the Heretics. Following the political exchange between Dante and the Ghibelline leader Farinata degli Uberti, Landino provides an allegorical interpretation of the Florentine factions before introducing the next soul, Cavalcante de' Cavalcanti.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>CANTO TEN</header>

## "If they were driven out, they returned from every side,"
## I replied to him, "both the first and the second time;
## but your people never learned that art well."

It remained difficult for them to return. And it can be said that under these names, Guelf and Ghibelline, one should allegorically understand "Catholic" and "Heretic." This is because, in truth, the Guelfs were always the proponents and defenders of the **Apostolic See** <note>The Papacy in Rome</note>; for this reason, he represents them as Catholics. He represents the Ghibellines as Heretics because they rebelled against the Church. And it is true that if the Guelfs were driven out, they always returned. This is because, despite the fact that true religion has often been chased out of many places by **heretical depravity** <note>original: "heretica prauita"</note>, it eventually always returns to its proper state. Conversely, no sect of heretics has ever been extinguished and then later resurrected.

## Then there arose to the uncovered sight
## a shadow alongside this one, visible to the chin;
## I believe it had risen onto its knees.
## It looked all around me as if it had a desire
## to see if someone else were with me;
## and after its suspicion was completely spent,
## Weeping, it said: "If through this blind
## prison you go by height of genius,
## where is my son? and why is he not with you?"
## And I to him: "I do not come by myself;
## he who waits over there leads me through here,
## whom perhaps your Guido held in disdain."
## His words and the manner of his punishment
## had already told me this man's name;
## therefore was my answer so full.
## Suddenly straightening up, he cried: "How
## did you say? 'He held'? Does he not still live?
## Does the sweet light not strike his eyes?"
## When he perceived a certain delay
## that I made before answering,
## he fell back supine, and appeared no more.

<column-break/>

the Guelfs and my Ghibellines. **SO THAT FOR TWO TIMES** I dispersed them. This is because the Guelfs were exiled twice. **BUT YOUR PEOPLE DID NOT LEARN** well that art of returning: for having been driven out once, they never returned again, nor had they hope to.

After Farinata, he places **Cavalcante**, a Florentine knight born of the ancient and most splendid family of the Cavalcanti. In his time, by his virtue and prudence, he was numbered among the leading Guelfs of our republic. However, he incurred infamy solely for holding the <term>Epicurean opinion</term> <note>The belief that the soul dies with the body, meaning there is no afterlife.</note>. But because he spoke of it with more modesty and more secretly than Farinata, the poet does not make him rise as far out of the <term>ark</term> <note>The stone sarcophagus or tomb.</note> as the other. The Cavalcanti family is very ancient in our city and ennobled by many excellent men produced by it, as can easily be seen in the Florentine chronicles.

But to return to where we left off: from Cavalcante was born **Guido**, who was not only excellent in civil life but also practiced in every kind of <term>speculation</term> <note>Philosophical study and contemplation.</note>. He was, above all, a most acute dialectician and an eminent philosopher, and no less practiced in Tuscan verse. These poems still live today, full of gravity and learning. But because he gave himself entirely to philosophy, he did not care much to read the Latin poets, nor to investigate their art and ornaments—at least not with that style and grace which is proper to a poet. Nonetheless, except for Dante, he far surpassed all others who wrote in rhyme up until his age. I have seen a <term>moral song</term> <note>A serious philosophical poem.</note> by Guido, the beginning of which is *A lady asks me, for I wish to speak / Of an accident that is often fierce* <note>original: "Donna mi priegha per chio uoglio dire / Dun accidente che e/ fouente fero"</note>.

---

*And is so haughty that it is called Love.* In this moral poem, which consists of five stanzas, he treats love not according to the divine, as Solomon did, nor according to the gentile poets like Ovid, but according to the philosophers. He demonstrates that love is an <term>accident</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a quality or property that does not exist by itself but only within a "substance" (like a person's soul).</note> and not a substance; just as appetite is in the soul, so are all the passions. He demonstrates that it is a fierce and great accident that has its being in the memory, because the impression of the image of the beloved thing is in the memory, just as light proceeding from a luminous body is held within a **diaphanous body** <note>A transparent medium, like air or glass.</note>. He also demonstrates how love is created and many other things with such great learning that **Giles of Rome** <note>Egidio Romano, a famous medieval theologian.</note>, a most noble physician and metaphysician, and **Dino del Garbo**, a most excellent Florentine doctor, wrote commentaries upon it.

The poet, therefore, wishes to signify all these things. And thus he says: **THEN THERE AROSE to the uncovered sight.** To the open mouth of the sepulcher. **A SHADOW: etc. I BELIEVE IT HAD RISEN onto its knees:** because if it had risen to its feet, it would have shown not just the chin but the chest, like Farinata. **DESIRE:** <note>original: "talento"</note> will. Hence *to please* <note>original: "atalentare"</note> signifies to consent, which is to make the will of another into one's own will. **THAT THE SUSPICION WAS COMPLETELY SPENT.** We use the terms "knowing," "believing," and "suspecting." He who "knows" has true science of the thing. "Believing" is when we are not certain, but we have such firm faith that it is so that we do not doubt it. "Suspecting" is to believe, but with doubt. He said: "If you go through this hell by height of genius, why is my son not with you?" As if to say: he who, like you, is of high genius and great learning. And note that these words—*If through this blind prison you go by height of genius*—serve both the fiction and the allegory. For according to the literal sense, we will say "by height of genius" as if by some miraculous power...

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>INFERNO</header>

...[no]ble art you can go living and without pain through hell. But according to the allegory, understand: if by height of genius and great learning you go through the contemplation of vices, my son is such that he ought to be able to do this same thing. **AND I TO HIM:** Not by myself do I come: As if to say, my own genius would not have given me such an invention. **BUT HE WHO WAITS LEADS ME:** that is, he <note>Virgil, representing Reason</note> awaits her <note>Beatrice, representing Theology/Grace</note>. For the teaching and the example of Virgil, whom I have imitated, **LEADS ME**: He guides me to create such a fiction, because it is not very different from his own. **WHOM PERHAPS YOUR GUIDO HAD IN DISDAIN.** As if to say, because your Guido, having given himself entirely to philosophy, did not value the poets; his philosophy was not enough for him to create a similar poem, which he could have done if he had deigned to read and imitate Virgil. **HIS WORDS:** This shows that through his words—which pointed toward Guido rather than anyone else—and because he was very learned and because he was his closest friend, and because the punishment for heretics was appropriate, he identified the soul as Cavalcante. **SUDDENLY UPRIGHT.** He shows that because Dante said "he held" <note>Italian: *hebbe*</note>, as one usually speaks of those in the past and not of the living, it gave dread and fear to Cavalcante that Guido might be dead. **IT DOES NOT STRIKE / The sweet light does not strike his eyes.** This refers to what happens to the living: for the rays of the sun are what illuminate the air, a diaphanous <note>transparent</note> body, without which two things—or things similar to these—sight cannot exercise its power. **WHEN HE PERCEIVED SOME DELAY.** The first guess he took from that word "held" made him doubt. Now the second delay induces in him a firm opinion that his son was dead. And certainly, when we ask a friend about the life or health of one of our loved ones, and he does not respond quickly, a fear is immediately born in us that things are not as we desire. And it shows in Cavalcante's words how great the love of a father for his son is, since even in hell he loves him so much. Philosophers investigate whether the love for one's kin remains in the soul when it is separated from the body. **HE FELL BACK SUPINE.** This gives to the soul the physical state that usually happens to a man when, through great emotional passion, he falls into a swoon and faints.

But that other noble-hearted man, at whose request

<column-break/>

The first two tercets <note>three-line stanzas</note> have little difficulty and only show you the nature of a man of great and unconquered soul: who makes no gesture nor any act that does not signify his being undefeated. Then he places words that match his gestures; for one of such a spirit does not find torment or death as troublesome as having to yield to the enemy. And similarly, one can note the obstinacy of the damned, who even after death do not set aside the affections and disturbances they held in life. **BUT THE FACE OF THE LADY WHO RULES HERE SHALL NOT BE REKINDLED FIFTY TIMES.** Proserpina, who is the same as the Moon according to the poets, was the daughter of Ceres in Sicily. One day while gathering flowers she was seen by Pluto, god of hell, who, taken by the girl's beauty, snatched her and made her his wife. This great injury much grieved Ceres, nor would she be patient with her daughter remaining with her abductor until Jove settled the dispute. He was the brother of Pluto and father to Proserpina; being elected arbiter by the parties, he judged that she should stay six months with Pluto in hell and six with her mother. She has power in heaven where she is called the Moon; she has it on earth and is called Diana; she has it in hell, and they call her Proserpina. And because of this triple power, Virgil said: <note>original: "Ter geminam hecaten tria uirginis ora Diane"</note> "Triple Hecate, the three faces of the virgin Diana." And because for six months of the year she increases and for six she decreases, the poets feign that she stays six months in hell and six above. They feign the Moon to be the goddess of hell because she especially acts upon inferior bodies, and her greatest power concerns the formation and growth of terrestrial bodies. Poets feign many other things about Proserpina by which they wish to express the nature of the Moon, but they are not for the present purpose. Therefore I return to the poet, who, by saying that the face of the lady who rules in hell—that is, the Moon, who is Proserpina—shall not be lit fifty times, means fifty months shall not pass. Because the moon is a body dark in itself but receives light from the sun, it is said to be "lit" by him. Thus he means that fifty months shall not pass before Dante will be exiled. This, according to Giovanni Boccaccio, happened before two years or a little more had passed. **AND IF YOU EVER [RETURN] To the sweet world:** It is "sweet" in comparison to those who are in hell. Whence Virgil: <note>original: "Quos dulcis uite exortes et ab ubere raptos Abftulit atra dies"</note> "Whom, deprived of sweet life and snatched from the breast, a black day carried off." **RETURN:** that is, go back. And the word is not conditional here—the meaning is not "tell me *if* you ever return"—but it is a prayer, like when we say, "Tell me the truth, so God may help you." As if to say: I pray God helps you if you tell me the truth. **IN EVERY ONE OF ITS LAWS.** Because in truth the Florentines did not use such cruelty toward any Ghibelline family as they did toward the Uberti. It was ordered that no penalty was ever remitted or benefit granted to Ghibellines that the Uberti and Lamberti families were not excluded from, because of the cruelty of the defeat...

<header>CANTO TEN</header>

at Montaperto. This occurred in one thousand two hundred fifty-eight. In this year, as the pride of the Uberti sought to subdue the people, the land rose up in a riot: and in the tumult, Stiattuccio Uberti was killed and Ubertuccio was beheaded. Messer Farinata, along with many Ghibelline nobles, fled to Siena.

<columns>2</columns>

Whereupon I to him: "The slaughter and the great carnage
that dyed the Arbia red
causes such prayer to be made in our temple."
After he had, sighing, shaken his head,
he said: "In 그건 I was not alone, nor certainly
without cause would I have moved with the others:
But I was alone there where it was agreed
by every soul to do away with Florence,
the one who defended her with an open face."

<column-break/>

Farinata had asked for what reason the Florentine people were so cruel toward him and all the Uberti. Dante responds that it is because of the slaughter and the cruel killing which, through his cunning and a conspiracy, was inflicted upon the Guelfs in the defeat at Montaperto: where the Arbia river turned red with blood. **CAUSES SUCH PRAYER TO BE MADE** <note>original: "FA FARE TALE ORATIONE"</note> It makes the people desire and pray to the magistrates that they should make such laws. **IN OUR TEMPLE** <note>original: "NEL NOSTRO TEMPIO"</note> This is a metaphor. Since he had mentioned "prayers" <note>the Italian "oratione" can mean both a prayer and a formal speech or decree</note>, he used "temple" to mean the court and public place where the affairs of the Republic are handled. And the fact is that, as I said above, Messer Farinata

<columns>1</columns>

was in exile: And as a man of great spirit and no less prudence, desiring not only to return but to bring back those of his faction, he went to Siena—a refuge in those times for the Ghibelline party and very much an enemy to the Florentine Guelfs. And there, through secret intermediaries, he plotted with the Ghibellines who remained in Florence regarding what followed. Then he sent certain Friars Minor on behalf of those who ruled in Siena to the elders of Florence, saying that if they approached Siena with their army, they would open a gate for them. For this reason, the Florentine people determined to undertake the enterprise—even though some wise citizens forbade it—and under the pretense of wanting to supply Montalcino, our ally, they came as far as Montaperto in the Valdarbia. There, contrary to all their expectations, the Sienese came out to meet them with German men-at-arms, whom Manfredi <note>King of Sicily and protector of the Ghibellines</note> had sent through Farinata's industrious efforts. And at the beginning of the battle, many in the Florentine army who favored the Ghibellines fled to the enemy's side. Great was the spirit of our people in resisting such force and so many frauds, and they sustained the battle for a long time. Finally, Messer Bocca degli Abati, with supreme treachery, approached Messer Jacopo del Vacca of the ancient Pazzi family, who was carrying the standard, and cut off his hand; whereupon the standard fell to the ground. Four thousand Florentines were killed in this rout, which took place on Saturday, the fourth day of September, in the year of our salvation 1260. **AFTER HE HAD, SIGHING, SHAKEN HIS HEAD.** This depicts the various perturbations in his soul: part indignation at the injury received, part remorse for having acted against his fatherland. And as an excuse he says: **IN THAT I WAS NOT ALONE:** Because many other rebels were with me. **NOR CERTAINLY WITHOUT CAUSE WOULD I HAVE MOVED WITH THE OTHERS.** In short, he shows that coming against his homeland was a common act shared with many; but in defending it, he was alone. Whence follows: **BUT I WAS ALONE THERE WHERE IT WAS AGREED** by every soul to do away with Florence, the one who defended her with an open face. And this was because after the return of the Ghibellines to Florence, the ambassadors and principal men of all the Ghibelline lands of Tuscany gathered to provide for the preservation of the common state of that party. And among many other things, it was advised that the final extermination of the Guelfs would be to destroy Florence, the primary head of that party, and reduce the city to small villages, so that the Guelfs already sent into exile would lose all hope of returning there. At this council—because in truth it was the only salvation for that party—not only the others, but even the Florentine Ghibellines consented. And that day would have given birth to the horrendous destruction of our fatherland had it not been for Messer Farinata, who alone opposed it. This is shown in the history by Leonardo Aretino <note>Leonardo Bruni, a famous humanist historian</note> in a speech which Farinata made in the assembly at Empoli, where he not only contradicted them with words, but like a new Scipio at Cannae, with a naked sword he threatened anyone who persisted in such a sentiment. Wherefore I, in the elegies titled *Xandra* written in my youth, wrote of him this epigram: <note>original Latin: "Guelfa meo fateor superauimus agmina ductu: Sanguine cũ rubris Arbia fluxit aquis. Sed tamen ut priscas teneas florentia sedes Sola farinate mens tibi magna dedit."</note> "I confess that the Guelf ranks were overcome by my leadership, when the Arbia flowed with waters red with blood. But nevertheless, so that you, Florence, might keep your ancient seat, Farinata's great mind alone gave it to you." Farinata thus opposed everyone, demonstrating that while he was an enemy to the Guelfs, he was not an enemy to his fatherland; for the love of his country had more power over him than the enmity of his adversaries. Because of him alone, Florence was defended from perishing.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, Canto X. Having discussed the political conflict between the Guelfs and Ghibellines, the text now turns to the metaphysical question of how the damned perceive time, specifically why they can see the future but are ignorant of the present.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>INFERNO</header>

and in the present you hold a different way:
"We see, like one who has **bad light**,
the things," he said, "that are far from us;
so much still shines on us the Sovereign Guide.
When they approach, or are present, **all is vain**
our intellect; and if another does not bring it to us,
we know nothing of your human state.
Therefore you can understand that all dead
will be our knowledge from 그건 point
that the door of the future will be closed."

<note>This passage explains the "prophetic" vision of the damned. They suffer from a spiritual form of hyperopia (farsightedness): they see distant future events but are blind to the immediate present.</note>

...if they knew the future. **WE SEE LIKE ONE WHO HAS BAD LIGHT.** There are two types of imperfect sight. For some have clear sight, but not much; and these see better from close up. Others have much sight, but it is obscured; thus they see better from a distance: because as the visual rays <note>Medieval science often held the theory of "extramission," where the eyes emit rays to perceive objects.</note> go out in the process, they become clearer and more refined, making them fit for seeing. But to explain why they have visual spirits that are too bright: if they proceed too far through the illuminated air, they are overwhelmed by the light, and therefore they do not see. Thus Farinata says, "We are similar to those who have bad light," that is, they have obscured visual spirits which do not see unless they travel a long distance through the luminous air, which clears them and makes them fit for seeing. But certainly, it seems incredible that these souls, seeing future things, do not also see present ones. Therefore, some understand that the soul, through the memory of past things, makes conjectures about the future; for example <note>original: "verbi gratia"</note>, Farinata, remembering the nature and customs of his citizens and the civil discords, foresees what must follow, and sees it from afar. But because he does not know exactly *when* it will happen, it may already be present, and he does not know it. In this way, they preserve Dante's meaning: that the damned soul sees the future and not the present. But Thomas Aquinas says that the soul stripped of the body no longer has the knowledge of the senses, which concerns particulars. Therefore, it no longer knows this thing or that thing unless it learns it from another soul that has newly arrived or from some spirit. But it knows according to the nature of the intellect, which concerns universals; and in this way, it perceives future things as universals, and not by turning to the imagination as it does when it is in the body. But the saved soul understands past, present, and future things according to Thomas and Gregory, because it sees them in God, in whom nothing is hidden. **WHEN THEY APPROACH OR ARE PRESENT.** When they get close or are happening now. **ALL IS VAIN** our intellect: that is, we understand nothing and know nothing of your human state, nor of anything done among men. Whereupon Augustine said: "It must be admitted that the dead do not know what is happening while it is happening; but afterwards they hear from those who go from here to them by dying; they can also hear something from angels." <note>original: "Fatendũ est nescire mortuos quid agitur dum agitur : sed postea uero audire ab iis qui hinc ad eos moriendo pergunt : Possunt etiam ab angelis audire aliquid."</note> **IF ANOTHER DOES NOT BRING IT TO US** unless another soul or a malignant spirit reports it to us. **THEREFORE YOU CAN UNDERSTAND** that our knowledge will be entirely dead; that is, we will know nothing from that point when the door of the future is closed. This will happen after the Day of Judgment, because the tombs will be locked; and even more so because, there being no more humans to come, there will be no more things to happen.

Then as if stung by my own fault,
I said: "Now you will tell that fallen one
that his son is still joined with the living;
and if I was silent earlier at the answer,
let him know I did so because I was thinking
already in the error that you have solved for me."
And already my master was calling me back;
wherefore I prayed the spirit more quickly
that he would tell me who stayed with him.
He told me: "Here with more than a thousand I lie;
within here is the second Frederick,
the Cardinal; and of the others I am silent."

**MY MASTER WAS CALLING ME BACK.** Dante had been with Farinata and Cavalcante; that is, he had descended into particular things. Now Virgil, that is, the higher mind, calls him back from these particulars to lead him back to universals.

<column-break/>

...to understand for what reason the damned foresee the future and not the present; he cut his words short and added: **MAY YOUR SEED FIND REST** <note>original: "DE SE RIPOSI VOSTRA semẽza"</note>. I prayed to him there; and he arranges it thus: "I prayed to him saying: 'Please untie that knot which has entangled my judgment here, if ever your seed may find rest,'" that is, your descendants who are currently living and those who are to come. And this word "if" is deprecatory <note>meaning used as a wish or a formal plea</note>, as we said above, and not conditional. He takes the "knot" to mean his doubt. For having heard Ciacco earlier, and now Farinata, predict future things, and on the other hand seeing that Cavalcante did not know present things, it seemed incredible to him that not knowing the present...

Once the poet understood the reason why the damned saw the future and not the present, he felt sorrow for not having responded to Cavalcante. For it often happens that the mind, occupied with a greater concern, leaves behind another thing, which it would do willingly once that occupation has passed. Therefore, now grieving for the fault committed in not having answered one who had been his friend, he responds now and prays Farinata to say to that fallen one—that is, to Cavalcante: **THAT HIS SON** his son <note>Guido Cavalcanti, a famous poet and Dante's "first friend."</note> is still joined with the living, and is still alive. **AND IF I WAS** a little while ago silent to the answer, it was not because I did not want to answer him. But because my mind was occupied in thinking about the doubt which you have resolved for me. **AND ALREADY THE MASTER**

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the epicurean heretics in the Tenth Canto of the Inferno. Having established why the damned cannot see the present, the text now identifies the specific historical figures Dante encounters in the tombs, focusing on Emperor Frederick II and "The Cardinal."</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>CANTO TEN</header>

...of which there is true knowledge. But before he departs, understand that here is the second **Frederick**, who was the son of Henry VI, the Emperor, and the grandson of Frederick Barbarossa. Henry took as his wife **Constance**, the daughter of the good King William of Sicily, who had been a nun; but the Pope gave her a dispensation, and she brought as her dowry the Kingdom of Sicily, which had been occupied by Tancred of the house of King Roger, who left it to his son William. This William was then defeated by Henry. Thus the entire kingdom remained to Frederick, the son of Henry and Constance, who is the subject of our current discussion. 

Because he was left an orphan as a child, he was under the guardianship of the Supreme Pontiff and was raised with great care. Having reached manhood, he took possession of the kingdom, and not long after, he was crowned King of the Romans by Pope Honorius in the year 1220. After this coronation, he lived thirty-three years and fell into discord with the Church. This happened because he wished to review the accounts of the administration of the kingdom, and the prelates <note>High-ranking clergy members.</note> did not wish to show them. Afterward, having returned to harmony, he prepared an army against the **Sultan** <note>Al-Kamil, the Ayyubid Sultan of Egypt, with whom Frederick later negotiated a peace treaty.</note> as was required by the peace conditions. This was in 1236. 

While he was already overseas with the army, the Pope, through letters, advised the Sultan on how to defeat and kill him; in the meantime, the Pope caused Sicily and Apulia to rebel against Frederick. To sow discord among the Christians, the Sultan sent these letters to Frederick. From this, a peace was born between them, even though Frederick could have recovered the entire Holy Land. He then returned to Italy and reclaimed his kingdom. Out of spite for the Pope, he sent for many Saracens from Tunis and allowed them to inhabit Lucera (today called Nocera), which is in the plains of Apulia. He waged war against the Pope, used great cruelty against the prelates, and finally greatly afflicted the Roman court and weakened the **Guelfs** of Tuscany, who were supporters of the Church. 

He sent one of his sons, born to a princess of Antioch, against the Florentines with fifteen hundred horsemen; for this reason, he was called **Frederick of Antioch**. The princess of Antioch had not wanted to join with Frederick, hearing that he already had a wife. Therefore, he caused two ships to arrive with black sails, carrying ambassadors who falsely claimed that his wife was dead; with this fraud, he deceived the princess. 

Finally, he died in Apulia. Because he had heard from astrologers that "Florence" would be fatal to him and that he was destined to die there, he never wished to pass through our territories. Eventually, he fell ill in Apulia and was taken to a town called **Firenzuola** <note>Landino refers to Castel Fiorentino. The story highlights the irony of a prophecy fulfilled through a name.</note>. Once he heard the name, he judged himself a dead man. Thus he died excommunicated. Some say that **Manfred**, his natural son and Prince of Taranto, smothered him with a pillow to seize his treasures. He was a man much feared by both Christians and Saracens for his military skill and great spirit. Had he not been provoked by the fraud of the Pope, perhaps he would not have been so cruel toward the Church, which treated him in such a way that he can deservedly be placed among the heretics.

**THE CARDINAL**: All writers agree—especially those closest to Dante's time—that he refers to **Cardinal Ottaviano degli Ubaldini**. He was certainly a man of great governance and invincible spirit, but in his life and habits, he was more like a tyrant than a priest. He was so favorable to the Ghibellines that he did not care if he acted against the Pope's authority to help them. When they later failed to help him in certain needs, he famously said: "If a soul exists, I have lost it for the Ghibellines." These words proved him to be an **Epicurean** <note>In this context, someone who denies the immortality of the soul.</note>. Such was his prudence and authority that he managed the Roman court as he pleased. At one time, he held the court in the mountains of Mugello on the Ubaldini lands, and against the Pope's will, he always favored the Ghibellines. His favor created the first Archbishop from the Visconti family of Milan and led them to the lordship of that city. He was called simply "The Cardinal," and whenever anyone said "The Cardinal says" or "does," it was understood to be him.

**Farinata** finished his words and returned below. Dante returned to **Virgil**, reflecting on the words Farinata had spoken regarding his exile, which seemed hostile and harsh to him. Virgil asked him why he was so lost in thought; having understood it was because of the adverse fortune Farinata had predicted, he gave him excellent advice. This advice is that he should preserve in his memory what he has heard and then seek to understand the entire process of his life from **Beatrice**.

This denotes that when evil is announced to us, we must not allow ourselves to be afflicted with excessive fear, nor should we judge with our senses how unhappy or miserable that thing might be. For the judgment of the senses is poor; it insists that all adversities affecting the body or fortune are great and intolerable, and that men become miserable because of them. This is entirely false. Therefore, reserve this judgment for Beatrice, and she will show you that only he...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Tenth Canto of the Inferno. Having discussed the status of the Epicurean heretics and the Emperor Frederick II, the author now transitions into the moral and philosophical implications of vice and the physical movement of Dante and Virgil toward the lower circles.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>INFERNO</header>

...and in misery: who is divided and separated from God because of the vice committed by him, even though he might have every abundance of wealth and status. And on the contrary, he is most happy who is joined with God through virtue. This sentiment is not only Stoic but Christian: that nothing is an evil except vice, which alone takes the blessed life from us. And because vice cannot be given to us except by ourselves, John Chrysostom <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his eloquent preaching; his "Paradox" refers to the treatise *No One Can Harm the Man Who Does Not Injure Himself*.</note> wrote the paradox through which he proves that no one can be harmed except by himself. Because only vice and sin can harm, and vice and sin come only from our own will and choice. No power can force us into this unless we wish it. 

**AND NOW PAY ATTENTION AND Here I pointed my finger.** He pointed his finger to make him attentive, and to demonstrate with that gesture that what he had to say was a notable thing. For we point our finger when, speaking of any matter, we wish to testify that it is true and of some importance. Or rather, he wanted to demonstrate that it was not enough to attend to the precepts of Beatrice; but it was necessary to put them into practice; and the finger and the hands signify action. Wherefore the Psalmist said: *I lifted up my hands to your commandments, which I loved* <note>original Latin: "Et levavi manus meas ad mandata tua que dilexi."</note>: which means nothing else—lifting the hand to the commandments of God—than to put them into practice. 

**WHEN YOU SHALL BE Before the sweet ray.** For sacred theology <note>Represented here by the character of Beatrice.</note> contains the truth within itself, with which it illuminates the minds of all. And her eye sees everything because she sees the truth. Therefore, in the Inferno, one recognizes the loss that is suffered regarding temporal things. But the remedy against the pain that those things bring with them is shown to us only by Beatrice; and she teaches us the journey of our life: what is the supreme good and what are the vain goods. 

**TO THE LEFT HAND** To depart from the wall and enter through the middle. Which he clarifies by saying **WE LEFT** the wall and went toward the middle **BY A PATH** <note>Dante uses the word *sentiere*.</note>; and it is a French word <note>The commentator notes the term originates from the Old French *sentier*.</note>; which **STRIKES** <note>original: "fiede"</note>: that is, it leads straight to a valley where one descends into the seventh circle. **WHICH EVEN UP THERE**: which valley smelled so strongly that even to the end of that path it **MADE** to spurt out, or reverberate, **ITS FOUL RANKNESS**: that is, its stench. 

Specifically, *rankness* <note>Italian: "lezzo"</note> is a powerful odor that is unpleasant, which does not arise from a corrupted body like the *fetor* and *stink* that a rotten and decaying thing emits. Rather, it is natural to such a thing, and proceeds from sweat and evaporation that a body emits, even if it is not corrupted. Thus, a live billy-goat or she-goat does not "stink" [*pute*], but rather "smells rank" [*lezisce*]. But it stinks when, being already dead, it decays. Nor is rankness found only in the sense of smell, but also in taste. Wherefore we say buffalo meat is rank, and some herbs, when tasting them, we say taste of rankness. And it is specifically, either in taste or in smell, what Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the Roman encyclopedia *Natural History*.</note> in his *Natural History* and other Latin writers call *virus* <note>In Latin, *virus* refers to a potent, often offensive secretion, slime, or sharp odor, rather than a microscopic pathogen.</note>. Although this same word sometimes signifies poison. And he properly said *rankness*, because such a stench is innate to this place, as we will demonstrate more clearly a little further on.

<summary>The commentator explains that moral harm only comes from one's own will and interprets Dante's gestures and movement toward the seventh circle, specifically defining the "rankness" (lezzo) of the infernal abyss.</summary>

<header>CANTO ELEVEN</header>

## ELEVENTH CANTO OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE

At the edge of a high bank
made of great broken rocks in a circle
we came above a more cruel crowding:
And there, because of the horrible excess
of the stench that the deep abyss throws out,
we drew back behind a cover
Of a great tomb where I saw an inscription:
which said, "I hold Pope Anastasius,
whom Photinus drew from the straight path."

"Our descent must be slow:
so that the sense of smell may first become used
to the foul breath: and then we shall not mind it."
Thus the master; and I, "Some compensation,"
said to him, "find for this, so that the time does not pass
lost." And he: "See, I am thinking of that.
My son, within these stones,"
he then began to say, "are three smaller circles
from grade to grade, like those you are leaving.
All are full of cursed spirits:
But so that the sight alone may later suffice you,
understand how and why they are constrained."

<column-break/>

In this eleventh canto, he describes the descent into the seventh circle. But so that we may have full knowledge of what follows, the author places the punishments of the violent and the fraudulent in the 7th, 8th, and 9th circles. And because both these sins proceed from malice <note>The term "malignità" refers to "malice" in the Aristotelian sense—sin committed with deliberate intent to harm.</note>, there is no doubt that their end is injury. And injury is done by violence either to one's neighbor, to oneself, or to God. To one's neighbor, injury is done either to their person—such as hitting, wounding, or killing them—or to their things, such as committing arson, theft, or robbery against them. Similarly, to oneself, injury is done to one's person by killing oneself, and to one's goods by squandering them. In the third place, injury is done to God by blaspheming Him, denying Him, or acting against His things: that is, against nature. Therefore, he distinguishes this seventh circle into three smaller circles or "rounds." In the first and highest, those are punished who have used violence against their neighbor. In the second, against themselves. In the third, against God, against nature, and against art. Afterward, we shall follow to the eighth and ninth circles, where fraud is punished. This is committed either against those who do not trust—and these are punished in the eighth circle—or against those who do trust, for whom the ninth is established because it is more grave. This is because it breaks two levels of love: the natural and universal, and the accidental and particular. **AT THE EDGE** of a high bank. He demonstrates by this into what a precipice such sinners fall: because they ruin themselves from human excellence to bestial depth. No animal is higher than man, because no animal is rational except man; if this reason turns to vice, no animal is more pernicious. **GREAT STONES**: because the ground would not support them. And by the hardness of the stones, understand the firm and immutable habit of these vices, and the great weight of these sinners: that is, how much they are burdened by conscience. **WITH GREATER CROWDING** <note>original: "stipa"</note>: that is, a hedge that surrounds sinners worthy of a more closed prison. Or <term>Stipa</term> <note>Dante uses "stipa" to mean a packed density of people or things, derived from the Latin "stipare" (to cram or pack together).</note> meaning "stowage"; because *stipare* in Latin means to surround and to pack in: and we shall call it "stowage," like a great filling-up of cruelty, as we shall understand better below. He places the stench in this place for the abomination that belongs to these sins, and for the extreme infamy which such sinners incur. For just as Augustine says, "Good fame is a sweet odor," it follows that infamy is a heavy stench. **I SAW AN** inscription that said, "I hold Pope Anastasius." Photinus, a cleric of Thessaly, together with Acacius, were heretics and held that the Holy Spirit did not proceed from the Father, and that the Father was greater than the Son. And they persuaded Pope Anastasius of this heresy. This man was Roman and reigned in the time of the Emperor Theodoric. Making an open profession of such heresy, and being reproved for it by many prelates, he became so obstinate that he wished to maintain it in public consistory. But it happened that while disputing, he was forced by the necessity of his belly to go and set down his weight, where at once all his entrails came out; and thus he perished. And not without reason does he place the inscription on this tomb: because it denotes that heresy in a Supreme Pontiff must be known to all, for the more excellent the sinner, the more noted is the sin. Whence Juvenal <note>A Roman satirist (c. 55–138 AD) known for his critiques of Roman society.</note> said, as has been mentioned many times:

> Every vice of the soul carries a crime so much more conspicuous in itself as he who sins is held to be greater. <note>original Latin: "Omne animi uitium tanto conspectius in se crimen habet quanto maior qui peccat habetur."</note>

They had to descend into the seventh circle; but because the stench was unbearable, Virgil warns Dante that they must pause for a while until they grow accustomed to it. For every hard thing is better supported after a man has become used to it than at the beginning. Whence even Dido, in Virgil's writing:

> I seek a void of time, rest, and space for my frenzy, until my fortune teaches me, being defeated, to grieve. <note>original Latin: "Tempus inane peto requiem spatiumque furori Dum mea me uictam doceant fortuna dolere." Aeneid IV, 433-434. Note that the Italian transcription has "uitam" (life) where the Latin should be "uictam" (conquered/defeated).</note>

And allegorically we shall understand that we should not descend to the meditation of such vices with a sudden impulse of the soul, but maturely and with reason: because otherwise, we might be seized by them. **THUS THE MASTER**. It is the best prudence of men that when they cannot do something without a delay...

<header>INFERNO</header>

Let us spend such an interval of time usefully on something else. **FIND SOME COMPENSATION** <note>Dante asks Virgil to find a way to make their waiting time productive.</note> so that the time does not pass lost. He asks that we do something else that serves as compensation for the time we lose in this [stench]. **FOR I AM THINKING OF THAT.** He was thinking, therefore, before they descended—that is, before arriving at such an inquiry—to provide the division and almost the definition of all these vices. For, as Cicero says: *Every systematic instruction on any subject which is undertaken by reason ought to start from a definition, so that it may be understood what is being discussed.* <note>original: "Omnis que a ratione suscipitur de aliqua re institutio debet a diffinitione profisci ut intelligatur id de quo disputetur." — from Cicero’s *De Officiis* (On Duties) I.7.</note> **MY SON, Within these rocks.** In excellent order. Because Dante—that is, the lower reason, together with the appetite that should be compliant and obedient to it—had to descend into the contemplation of these horrible sins. Therefore, superior reason <note>Represented by Virgil.</note>, as the best guide, wants him first to become accustomed to enduring the stench and to understand what these sins are, and then he will lead him among them. This is because it is first necessary that we accustom ourselves to being able to endure the perturbations of the soul that proceed from those sins. And we should know best what they are and how harmful they are to us, and then finally place ourselves among them; for once we are made cautious and constant, they will not offend us. The text itself is clear.

---

Of every malice that gains hatred in heaven,
injury is the end, and every such end
afflicts others either with force or with fraud:
But because fraud is man's own peculiar evil,
it displeases God more: and therefore lower down
stand the fraudulent, and more pain assails them.
The first circle is entirely for the violent:
but because force is done to three persons,
it is distinct and constructed in three rings.
To God, to oneself, to one's neighbor it is done—
I mean force is done to them and to their things,
as you shall hear with clear reasoning:
Death by force and painful wounds
are given to one's neighbor; and to his property,
ruin, fire, and harmful seizures:
Thus homicides, and everyone who strikes wickedly,
wasters, and plunderers, the first ring torments
all of them in different ranks.

<column-break/>

Let whoever reads this canto be diligent and consider it with the highest attention, because it is the "proposition" <note>An introductory summary or outline.</note> of all the rest of this canticle. Most excellently, therefore, he demonstrates that injury is the end of all malice <note>In this context, "malice" (Latin *malitia*) refers to a deliberate choice to do evil.</note>, which gains hatred in heaven—that is, it is hated by God. And not without reason did he add these words: because there are some malices and cunning acts which are not hated by God, because they do not cause injury. He says, therefore, that injury is the end of the malices displeasing to God, because such malices connect together to cause injury. And understand that injury is every work that man does against reason and justice. Therefore, Cicero rightly said that those things are injuries which either offend the ears with villainy, or the body with beatings, or stain one's reputation with some calumny and reproach. **AND EVERY SUCH END.** Every thing made as an end: that is, every injurious end. **EITHER WITH FORCE OR WITH FRAUD** it afflicts others; that is, it offends either by force or by fraud, as we have shown above. **BUT BECAUSE FRAUD IS Man's own peculiar evil.** Although man has the strength of the body,

---

nevertheless, these strengths cannot be called "proper" to man <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "proper" refers to a trait unique to a species.</note>, because not only are they common to him and other animals, but in those strengths, he is surpassed by many animals. But reason is that which is proper to man, because by it we are named [as humans], and through it—and not through physical strength—are we different from the brutes. Therefore, if reason is the proper good given by God to man, then fraud—which is the abuse of reason—will be man's own peculiar evil, because we do not share it with the brutes. Furthermore, he who deceives offends the one who in some way trusted him or was not on his guard, and thus he breaks faith. But he who uses force often uses it against one who is defending himself. **IT DISPLEASES GOD MORE:** because it is a graver sin to use reason badly—by which we are in a certain way similar to God—than force, by which we are similar to the beasts. And certainly, the more noble a thing is, the greater the sin is to use it badly. And therefore they [the fraudulent] stay lower down, so that they may be further from the highest good; from which it follows that they feel greater pain. For since God is our highest good, the further we are removed from Him, the more miserable we are. **OF THE VIOLENT the first circle is all.** The violent—that is, those who have done injury with force—are punished in the first circle: that is, in the seventh, which is the first of the three that remain. And this is divided into three rings where three generations of violent people are punished, as he clearly demonstrates, and as we have distinctly declared shortly above. **TO GOD, TO ONESELF, TO ONE'S NEIGHBOR:** These are the three persons to whom force can be done. And to each of these three it can be done in two ways: either to themselves or to their things. And note that when he proposes these three persons, he follows the natural order. However, when he distinguishes these sins according to God's judgment, he leaves this order and follows the order of the three rings of the seventh circle. And because the least grave sinners are in the first [ring], he speaks first of those who have used violence against their neighbor, who have the least grave sin. And he lists many types of injuries which are done to one's neighbor: To the person—death and beatings; to their goods—ruin, fire, and seizures (meaning robberies). **IN DIFFERENT**

**GROUPS:** As if to say the homicides are in one group, the plunderers in another, and so on with the others, although they are all within the first ring <note>of the Seventh Circle</note>.

> and upon his own goods; and therefore in the second

> gambles away and squanders his faculty
