they are in grace and in the best of will; likewise, the damned are in perpetual obstinacy. But he says "he repents" because he grieves that he originally formed such a habit in vice.

> Force can be used against the Deity 
> by denying and blaspheming Him in the heart, 
> and by despising Nature and her goodness. 
> And therefore the smallest ring seals 
> with its mark Sodom and Cahors, 
> and he who, despising God, speaks in his heart.

God: such as the Sodomites who commit sin against nature. Or against Art, which is the daughter of nature and the granddaughter of God <note>In medieval philosophy, Nature follows God's plan, and human industry (Art) follows Nature; therefore, to subvert industry—as in usury—is to offend God's "grandchild."</note>, such as the usurers. How these act against Art will be shown in the proper place. Therefore, **SODOM AND CAHORS** <note>Cahors was a city in France famous for its moneylenders.</note> are sealed with its mark. It is as if he says the land places its seal upon such sinners. Sodom and Gomorrah were two cities in Syrian Palestine which, because of the wicked vice against nature, God affirmed to Abraham after his circumcision that He would destroy. He sent two angels to Sodom in the form of youths, who stayed in the house of Lot, an innocent man who had invited them. Before they went to sleep, a crowd of Sodomites came to attack the house, seize the angels, and violate them. Lot begged them to cease such fury and offered them his two beautiful daughters, who were still virgins; but they persevered in their evil purpose until they were struck blind by the angels. Lot, his wife, and two daughters were led by the angels to Zoar so they might be saved. And God rained fire and sulfur upon Sodom and Gomorrah, burning the city and the surrounding region with all inhabitants, animals, and plants. In the Hebrew language, **Sodom** signifies "Burning," "Sterile," and "Blindness," or "Silent Pasture." **Gomorrah** signifies "Blindness," "Sedition," and "Fearful People." Solinus <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, a 3rd-century Roman geographer.</note> writes that in this region, the earth is black and like ash, showing the past fire. He adds that the fruits produced there, when they appear ripe on the outside, are soot within, and if pressed slightly, they turn to ash. This is certainly a divine miracle, so that for all ages there remains an eternal testimony of divine judgment and a severe punishment for a vice so bestial—indeed, worse than bestial, for no animal except man commits it. **Cahors** is a city in Provence that for many centuries was filled with usurers.

> a man can use against one who trusts him, 
> and against one who gathers no confidence. 
> This latter way seems to kill 
> only the bond of love that nature makes; 
> hence in the second circle find their nest 
> Hypocrisy, flattery, and those who use sorcery, 
> falsehood, theft, and simony, 
> pimps, barrators, and similar filth.

taken by infidels, to deceive them in order to escape. **A MAN CAN USE** against one who trusts: that is, the friend who trusts you. **AND AGAINST ONE WHO gathers no confidence**: such as those who are neither friends nor enemies to you; though they have no specific trust in you, they nonetheless do not expect you to want to deceive them. **THIS LATTER WAY**: that is, committing fraud against one who does not specifically trust you...

<column-break/>

**THE** second species is of those who use force against themselves by killing themselves, or against their goods by dissipating them. **OF YOUR WORLD**: that is, of this life. **He repents without profit**: because repentance in Hell is of no value. Morally speaking, although one who has made a habit of vice repents, it is difficult to change. Nor should it be understood that he repents with true penitence; for as we have shown elsewhere, just as the saved are confirmed...

**THIS** is the third species of those who do violence to God. Here you must understand that God cannot be harmed; but they do violence as much as is in them by blaspheming and denying Him. Nor does he say **Speaks in his heart** without reason: for someone might deny God with words out of fear of death or torment, but not in their heart. Or they do violence to His things: that is, to Nature, which is called the daughter of...

**HE** had distinguished the types of violence. Now he divides fraud into two species. One against those who trust you, regarding you as a friend, which we will discuss a bit later. The other is against those who do not trust you; and under this latter category, he places hypocrites, flatterers, and those who use sorcery <note>amalia: enchantment or witchcraft</note>. <meta>This page continues the technical breakdown of Hell's structure. Following the discussion of violence, Virgil now explains the distinction between simple fraud and betrayal (treachery), which leads into Dante's famous question about why some sinners are kept outside the walls of the City of Dis while others are trapped within.</meta>

# INFERNO

Although it is not as atrocious as the first—which breaks two bonds, namely the natural bond and that of a specific friendship—it is nonetheless grave because it breaks the bond of nature. This natural bond binds all men to help one another rather than to harm, and to place trust in one another. And for this reason, such sinners are punished in the eighth circle, which I call the second because it is the second of these final three <note>The three final categories of sin are violence, fraud, and treachery</note>.

> In another way, that love is forgotten
> which nature creates; and that which is later added
> whereby a special trust is born.
> Therefore, in the smallest circle, where the point
> of the universe resides, upon which Dis sits,
> whoever betrays is eternally consumed.

> And I: "Master, your reasoning proceeds
> quite clearly, and distinguishes very well
> this abyss and the people who possess it.
> But tell me: those of the fat marsh
> whom the wind drives, and whom the rain beats,
> and who encounter each other with such harsh tongues,
> Why within the ruddy city
> are they not punished, if God holds them in His anger?
> And if He does not, why are they in such a state?"

> And he to me: "Why does your wit wander
> so far from its usual course?
> Or where else is your mind looking?
> Do you not remember those words
> with which your Ethics treats
> the three dispositions that Heaven wills not:
> Incontinence, malice, and mad bestiality?"

<column-break/>

He presents the second species of fraud, where two bonds are broken. So that this may be better understood: nature has made man a sociable animal, who is joined by a universal bond of nature to love others. This is called **universal love**, through which I love all men; and to this, universal faith <note>meaning social trust</note> bears witness. Then there is another species of love, which is an additional one. This is added upon the natural bond and is directed toward parents and friends; it can be called **special love** because it creates special faith. Therefore, both he who breaks universal faith and he who breaks particular faith commits fraud. But in universal matters, they are called **fraudulent**; in the special, they are called **traitors**. The fraudulent are in the eighth circle, which is divided into ten trenches <term>bolge: ditch-like subdivisions</term> because there are ten types of them. The traitors are in the ninth circle. And because betrayal is committed in four ways, this circle is divided into four parts. Thus, Hell is divided into nine circles: five are outside the City of Dis. The sixth is inside, but near the walls, where heretics are punished. The seventh contains the violent and is divided into three rings. The eighth holds the fraudulent in ten trenches. The ninth encloses the traitors.

Having heard Dante’s distinction of the entire layout of Hell, he raises a doubt to Virgil. It seems to him that if the wicked punished in the five circles outside the city displease God, they should be punished inside the city; and if they do not displease Him, they should not be punished in any place. **AND I SAID**, "O Master, your reasoning proceeds clearly enough in dividing **THIS ABYSS**"—that is, the depth and the vortex. For Hell is nothing other than a vortex from the surface of the earth to the center. **Abyss** <note>original: "baratro"</note> is a dark and deep place, and it is a Greek word. **AND THE PEOPLE** who possess it: that is, the sinners who inhabit it. **BUT TELL ME**, those of the fat marsh: meaning the Stygian marsh which has thick and swampy waters. This refers to those of the fifth circle where the wrathful and the slothful are punished. **WHOM THE WIND DRIVES**: those driven by the wind are the lustful in the second circle. **AND WHOM THE RAIN BEATS**: these are the gluttonous in the third circle. **AND WHO ENCOUNTER EACH OTHER** with such harsh tongues: he means the prodigal and the avaricious, who, placed in the fourth circle, rebuke each other by shouting, "Why do you hoard?" and "Why do you squander?" **WHY WITHIN** the ruddy city are they not punished? He asks why they are not placed inside the City of Dis, which he calls **ruddy** <note>original: "roggia"</note>, meaning red from the fire; the commentator notes this is a French-derived word. Others say "roggia" means "rozza" (harsh). Dante asks this to provide an opportunity to show the logic of why some are punished outside the city and others inside. This question is neither sharp nor prudent, for it does not follow that if sinners are not equal, their punishments should be equal. Nor does the Christian faith hold that all vices are equal—as the Stoic philosophers claimed—but rather that they are greater or lesser according to their nature and circumstances, as will appear shortly. It is a most evident thing, but because sensuality lacks reason, it doubts even manifest truths. Therefore, Virgil responds.

Wishing to resolve the doubt raised by Dante, Virgil silently reproves his logic. Dante's division was: if those outside the city have not sinned, why are they punished? If they have sinned, why are they not inside like the others? This logic is insufficient. It should be: either they have sinned or not; if they have not sinned, they deserve no punishment. If they have sinned, they have...

### CANTO ELEVEN

<margin>h. ii</margin>

> ...bestiality; and how incontinence
> offends God less and gains less blame.
> If you regard this judgment well
> and bring to mind who those are
> who outside endure penance,
> You will see well why from these felons
> they are separated, and why less angered
> divine justice hammers them.

<column-break/>

...sinning gravely: like those who are in [the city of] Dis; and then they would deserve to be punished inside Dis: like those who are there, or who have sinned, but not so gravely. And then they deserve to be punished for the sin committed, but not with as much pain as those within Dis. Therefore, they must be outside of Dis. This is a sufficient division which Dante makes; that is, if the lower reason <note>In medieval philosophy, "lower reason" deals with practical earthly matters and the senses, while "higher reason" deals with divine truths.</note> had seen it through the senses, he would not have fallen into this doubt. Therefore, Virgil, responding to him, openly rebukes him for having fallen into such an error, and says: **WHY DOES YOUR WIT WANDER SO FAR?** <note>original: "PERCHE LONGEGNO TVO TANTO DELIRA?"</note> That is, it leaves the straight path. *Lira* in Latin signifies "furrow." From this, they say that a plow, while plowing, "delirates" when it leaves the straightness of the furrow. But by a certain translation and similarity, we say that an old man "delirates" <note>This is the etymological root of the word "delirium."</note> when he becomes like a child; and likewise, whoever leaves the straight path of reason "delirates." **FROM ITS USUAL COURSE.** It seems that Dante praises himself too much by prompting Virgil to say this sentence: [meaning] "Why do you leave the straight path, from which you are not accustomed to depart when judging vices and moral virtues?" But Dante attributes this to himself not to praise himself, but to show that Dante—that is, the lower reason, which exercises itself in particular matters—is not accustomed to err in moral virtues. **OR ELSE, WHERE IS YOUR MIND LOOKING?** We err in two ways: either when our wit is not sufficient to find the truth, or when, although it is sufficient, it does not understand because it is occupied with other things. **DO YOU NOT REMEMBER:** Do you not recall. **THOSE WORDS;** which **PERFECTLY TREATS;** <note>original: "PER TRACTA"</note> that is, perfectly handles. **HIS ETHICS;** the book of *Ethics*; that is, the book of moral philosophy by Aristotle. And he does not say "yours," meaning written by you, but that which you are very familiar with and understand well. **THE THREE DISPOSITIONS** that Heaven does not want: because they are vicious, and Heaven—that is, the Divine Majesty—does not want vicious things. So that we may better understand this, we shall call to mind that Aristotle, in the seventh book of his *Ethics*, places three species of dispositions which must be fled from in life and in character. There, he says that a good choice cannot exist without true reason and a right appetite <note>The "appetite" here refers to the faculty of desire or the will.</note>. Therefore, when one of these is missing, such a choice must be avoided. Thus, if the perversion proceeds from the appetite, while the reason remains straight, **incontinence** is born. This happens when reason judges rightly, but the perturbed appetite pulls it in the opposite direction, like Medea in Ovid, who correctly judged it to be the ultimate wickedness to betray her father and abandon her homeland; but her appetite for Jason pulled her against reason. Hence she says: **"I see the better and approve of it, but I follow the worse."** <note>original Latin: "Video meliora proboque Deteriora sequor." This is a famous quote from Ovid's Metamorphoses, often used to describe the struggle of the human will.</note> 

But if sometimes the corrupted and perverse appetite rises up so much against reason that it becomes entirely its master, and reason itself is corrupted, then reason follows the appetite, judging that which is proposed to it to be good; it makes a captive choice. Hence it is called a "bad judgment," and such a disposition is **malice**. Therefore, in the first case [incontinence], only the appetite sinned, but the reason still judged correctly, though it was pulled by force by the fury of the appetite. In the second case [malice], both sin, and they agree that what is evil is good. Like Dido, when the poet says of her: **"Dido no longer thinks of a secret love; she calls it marriage."** <note>original Latin: "Nec iam furtiuum Dido meditatur amorem: Coniugiumque uocat." From Virgil's Aeneid, describing how Dido justifies her relationship with Aeneas.</note> 

But sometimes the perversion of the appetite and the reason is so great that they not only agree to sin, but as if forgetting what a human being is, they surpass every boundary of the human species. They adopt the habits and nature of a beast, and such a disposition is called **bestiality**. Against these three vicious dispositions are the best remedies: for to incontinence, **continence** is opposed; to malice, **moral virtue**; and to bestiality, **heroic virtue**—which is more than human. For "heroes," according to the ancients, are more than men and less than gods, such as Hercules and Theseus and the like. But so that we may understand how a man acquires heroic virtue, it should not be unknown to us that the human soul is in the middle between the angels and the brute animals. For it has intellect in common with the former, and senses in common with the latter. Therefore, just as the sensitive part is sometimes depraved in man until he becomes like the beasts—and this is called "bestiality," exceeding human malice—so, on the contrary, the intellectual part is sometimes strengthened and becomes so perfect that it rises above the common mode of human perfection and almost attains the likeness of the angels. This the ancients called heroic virtue, through which they believed men were converted into gods, like Hercules and the like. And just as this virtue is fruitfully rare among men, so bestiality, which is its opposite, is found rarely. It is born either from bestial habits and customs—because they live without any law or doctrine, such as the **anthropophagi** <note>Cannibals.</note>, the Laestrygonians, and the Cyclopes, and others who eat human flesh. Aristotle mentions wild men who lived in the forests not far from the Black Sea who eat human flesh. And Jerome, writing against Jovinian, says there are some barbarians who eat the buttocks of children and the breasts of women. Let us conclude, then, that incontinence is bad, malice is worse, and bestiality is the worst of all. For this reason, the first is punished outside [the walls], while the last two are punished inside Dis.

<summary>This page explains the Aristotelian framework of the "three dispositions"—incontinence, malice, and bestiality—to justify the different levels of punishment in Dante's Hell. It contrasts bestiality with "heroic virtue," citing classical figures like Hercules and Medea to illustrate how the soul fluctuates between the angelic and the animalistic.</summary>

<header>->INFERNO<-</header>

“O sun who heals every troubled sight,
you content me so when you solve [my doubts]
that to doubt pleases me no less than to know.
Turn back a little bit,”
I said, “to where you mentioned usury <note>The OCR reads 'dichiusura' (enclosure), but the context and original Dante text 'd’usura' confirm this refers to usury, the practice of charging interest on loans.</note> offends
the divine goodness, and untie that knot.”

<margin>He asks why usury displeases God</margin>
“Philosophy,” he said to me, “to one who attends to it,
notes, and not in just one place,
how nature takes her course
From the divine intellect and from its art;
and if you note your *Physics* <note>Referring to Aristotle’s 'Physics,' a fundamental text for medieval scholars.</note> well,
you will find, not after many pages,
That your art follows nature, as much as it can,
just as the student follows the master;
so that your art is almost God’s grandchild.
From these two, if you bring to mind
Genesis from its beginning, it is fitting
that people take their life and progress.
But because the usurer takes another way,
he despises nature in itself and in
its follower [art], for he places his hope elsewhere.

But follow me now, for I wish to speak:
the Fish <note>The constellation Pisces.</note> are quivering on the horizon,
and the Wain <note>The Big Dipper or Ursa Major.</note> lies entirely over the Caurus, <note>The Northwest wind.</note>
and the slope is further on to descend.”

<column-break/>

**O SUN**: just as the sun, by illuminating what is in the middle between us and the thing we wish to see, is the reason that we see, so you illuminate the intellect with your doctrine so that it sees what it did not see before. "Sun" is often taken to mean wisdom. And he adds that it is so pleasant to hear his doctrine that he almost desires to doubt just to hear him [explain it]; for he takes no less pleasure in hearing him than in knowing. Then he...

**TO DEMONSTRATE** that usury is a sin, he takes the sentiment which Aristotle puts in the book of *Physics*, and in many other places: that nature takes its course and its process from the divine intellect—because God is the primary cause of all causes—and from his art: that is, his operation and his will. For as God intends, so he wills; and as he wills, so he acts. **YOUR PHYSICS** <term>TVA Physica: Aristotle's "Physics," which Dante studied.</term>: that is, the physics in which you delight. **NOT AFTER MANY PAGES**: For it is not far from the beginning of the book. **THAT OUR ART** follows nature as much as it can. <note>original: "Ars imitatur naturam quo adpotest"</note> Just as **THE STUDENT**: that is, the disciple follows the master. **ALMOST A GRANDCHILD**: by a certain similarity. For if nature proceeds from God as from its principle, it is like a daughter. And if then our art proceeds from nature, being its daughter, it is the grandchild of God; because God has implanted art in the minds of men by means of nature, upon which heaven and nature depend. This nature is imitated by our art as much as is possible. Therefore, since art depends on nature, it is like its daughter, and consequently a grandchild to God. Thus, whoever offends nature offends God immediately; and whoever offends art offends God by means of the offended nature. But the usurer offends nature, because it is not natural that money should give birth to money without its own corruption. Nature wills that the "corruption" (wearing down/use) of one thing should be the generation of another. Likewise, he offends God because he does not exercise the art that God commanded to the first man, when he said, "by the sweat of your brow you shall eat your bread." Likewise, it is not "artificial" [the product of human skill] that money should give birth to money, as the usurer wants, who places "use" in a thing which cannot give use. For if I lend you a garment or a horse, these things are consumed [worn out], but not money. And other arts and trades are subject to the accidents of fortune, but not the usurer. **IF YOU BRING TO MIND GENESIS**: that is, the sentiment written in Genesis, where it treats the creation of the world and the first man and the order of life, which began where it is written: <note>original: "Oportuit ab initio seculi humanum genus summere uitam : et excedere unum alium per naturam et artes."</note> "From the beginning of the world it was necessary for the human race to take up its life, and for one to surpass another through nature and the arts." In the **BEGINNING**: that is, as it appears in its beginning. **PEOPLE MUST TAKE THEIR LIFE**: that is, the mode and order of living. **AND SURPASS** one another in riches and temporal goods; and this is lawful either by one's industry and exercise, or with possessions, or with livestock, which things naturally yield fruit. **AND BECAUSE** the usurer takes another way than that of nature—not keeping his money in livestock—and that of art—because he does not work and does not exercise [a craft]—he despises in himself (as much as is in him) nature and its follower, which is art. He acts against nature, because inanimate things cannot multiply like living ones. Usury is prohibited in the Old Testament. Whence in Leviticus: <note>original: "Pecuniam tuam non dabis fratri tuo ad usuram et frugum super abundantia non exiges."</note> "You shall not give your money to your brother at usury, nor shall you demand an overabundance of crops." And the Psalmist: <note>original: "Quis habitabit in tabernaculo tuo ? Qui pecuniam non dederit ad usuram."</note> "Who shall dwell in your tabernacle? He who has not given his money at usury." And in the New [Testament], Luke writes in the sixth [chapter]: <note>original: "Date mutuum nec in desperantes."</note> "Lend, hoping for nothing in return."

**JUST AS** Virgil had been the cause of their standing still, so now he is the cause of their continuing. And certainly every power of the soul ought to submit itself to the intellect and follow according to its judgment. Virgil says therefore: "it pleases me..."

As the explanation ends, Virgil notes the positions of the stars (Pisces and the Big Dipper) to signal that it is nearly dawn and time to descend further into Hell.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the final lines of Inferno Canto XI. The previous page concluded Virgil’s explanation of usury; now, the commentator explains the astronomical references Virgil uses to indicate that it is roughly 4:00 AM on Holy Saturday morning, signaling that they must move quickly to the next circle of Hell.</meta>

# CANTO ELEVEN

...to follow on the journey: because the Fish <note>The constellation Pisces.</note> are already at our horizon. This shows that the day is now approaching.

We showed above that Dante imagines having this vision on Good Friday before daybreak. And therefore he said that the sun was in Aries; because from the month of March until the eleventh of April it is in that sign. And he intends to have spent that whole day struggling with the beasts and speaking with Virgil. Afterward, he shows that on Friday night he descended into Hell, when he said "the day was departing and the darkened air." Now he adds that a great part of that night had already passed in this exploration of Hell; it was nearly two hours before daybreak. For if the sun rose in our hemisphere with Aries, and Pisces precedes Aries, and each of these signs rises with sixteen degrees—that is, with one hour and one-fifteenth of an hour—it follows that two hours of the night remained, during which they had to search through all of Hell. Therefore he warns Dante that there is no time to lose.

This passage is similar to one in Virgil: <note>original: "Ha vice sermonum roseis aurora quadrigis Iam medio ethereo cursu traiecerat axem . Et fons omne datum traherent per talia tempus Sed comes admonuit breuiterque affata Sybilla est Horruit Eneas nos flendo ducimus horas." These lines are from Virgil's Aeneid, Book VI, where the Sibyl warns Aeneas that time is passing while they talk in the Underworld.</note> *“With such exchange of talk, Aurora in her rose-colored chariot had already crossed the midpoint of her ethereal course. And they might have spent all the allotted time in such things, but his companion, the Sibyl, briefly warned him: 'Night is falling, Aeneas; we waste the hours in weeping.'”*

**THE FISH QUIVER**: He had respect for the nature of the fish, which "quivers"—that is, it moves through the water with great ease. In essence, the constellation was beginning to rise on our horizon.

**ABOVE THE HORIZON**: Upon that circle which divides one hemisphere from the other, which is called the <term>horizon</term> <note>From the Greek for "finisher" or "boundary."</note>; it terminates our sight because, of the whole sky which is round and spherical, we see only half. Thus, that final part which we see all around the sky where our vision ends—because the earth prevents us from seeing further below—is called the horizon. And because the sky makes a full revolution in twenty-four hours, some sign of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>The "circle of animals," the belt of constellations the sun appears to move through.</note> must always be rising at our horizon. At that time, Pisces was rising; which, as I have said, takes an hour and a fifteenth part of an hour to fully emerge from the horizon; after those, Aries would rise with the sun, whose birth creates the day. Therefore, as much of the night remained as it took for the entire sign of Pisces to emerge, as well as all those degrees of Aries that preceded the degree where the sun was located. Pisces is the last sign of the zodiac and is the "house" of Jupiter; we will speak more accurately of this triplicity in the *Purgatorio*.

**THE WAIN LIES ENTIRELY OVER THE CAURUS**: This is the second sign the poet uses to show that day is approaching. For if Pisces was rising then, it was necessary for Leo—the sign opposite to them—to go down. So that you may understand this better: the "Wain" <note>The Big Dipper or Ursa Major.</note> consists of seven stars that revolve around the <term>North Star</term> <note>original: "tramontana"</note>. The first four stand two by two and make the "wain" [the cart], and then three come in a line—though the last one bends slightly—and make the "pole" [the shaft of the cart]. This last one is always pointed toward Leo. Therefore, when Leo is about to set, the pole is pointed to the west, and the four that make the cart are already turned between the west and the north, from where the <term>Caurus</term> <note>original: "choro"; the Northwest wind</note> blows. Thus he spoke correctly: "and the whole Wain lies over the Caurus."

<sig>. b. iii .</sig>

# INFERNO

<margin>MURDERERS</margin>

### CANTO XII OF THE FIRST CANTICLE OF DANTE.

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'E' featuring a blue and red ornamental design with a small portrait or figure inside, beginning the text of Canto XII. Beside it, the commentary column begins with a smaller blue initial 'I'.</image-desc>

The place where we came to descend the bank
was rugged, and because of what was there,
such that every eye would turn away from it.
Like that landslide which, on its flank,
this side of Trent, struck the Adige <note>The Adige is a river in Northern Italy.</note>
either by earthquake or for lack of support:
For from the mountain’s top from which it moved
to the plain, the rock is so shattered
that it would provide a path for one above:
Such was the descent of that ravine;
and on the edge of the broken slope
the infamy of Crete was stretched out:
The one conceived in the false cow:
and when he saw us, he bit himself,
like one whom anger breaks from within.

<column-break/>

In this twelfth canto, the poet describes the descent from the sixth circle into the seventh; and he divides it as we have said above, and places there the punishments of the violent. First, those violent against their neighbors; then against themselves; and lastly against God. He places the monstrous Centaurs as guards of the place, and especially the Minotaur of Crete. He shows that this descent was a precipice of broken and ruined boulders, harsh and steep, much like the landslide of Mount Barco <note>Now known as the Slavini di Marco near Trent.</note> between Treviso and Trent. And on the point of the ruin, where the descent begins, the Minotaur was stretched out. Mount Barco, having its foundations much eroded by the river—either because of this or because of earthquakes—collapsed in large part into the Adige river in such a way that it diverted the river for a good distance. And by this ruin, the rock—that is, the fortress <note>original: "rocca"</note>, the boulders and the bank of the mountain—is so shattered from the summit to the plain that it would provide some path, though not a very easy one, **FOR ONE WHO WAS ABOVE**: that is, for someone at the summit.

---

**SUCH WAS THE DESCENT OF THAT RAVINE** / from that ruin: the Florentines call a deep ditch a "burrato," almost like an abyss. **AND ON THE EDGE** / on the summit **OF THE BROKEN SLOPE** <term>lacca: a slanting side or bank, derived from the Latin "labor," to slide down</term> **WAS STRETCHED OUT**: as if lying there, **THE INFAMY OF CRETE**: that is, the Minotaur. Being born on the island of Crete (today called Candia), he was the disgrace of said island, being not a man but a monstrous thing. **WHICH** Infamy: that is, the monster, **WAS CONCEIVED**: that is, the Minotaur was conceived, **IN THE FALSE COW**. So that this may be more clearly understood, we will briefly narrate the fable. Because Venus, in the adultery she committed with Mars, was discovered by the Sun and accused to her husband Vulcan, she became such an enemy to the Sun that, unable to take revenge on him, she took revenge on his daughters. Therefore, Pasiphae—wife of Minos, King of Crete, and daughter of the Sun—was so inordinately incited to lust by Venus that she was driven to love a bull from her husband’s herds. Some say that Minos, desiring to have an animal suitable for a sacrifice he wished to make to Jove his father, was sent a very beautiful and shapely bull by Jove. But Minos, moved by greed and desire for such a beautiful animal, sent it to his own herds and sacrificed a less beautiful bull to Jove. Wherefore Jove, enraged, induced Pasiphae to love that bull. But whatever the bull was, they add that Pasiphae asked Daedalus <note>The mythical master craftsman.</note> to show her how she could join with the beloved bull. And Daedalus made a wooden image of a cow and enclosed her within it; and thus they joined, for the bull thought it was a cow. From this union was born the Minotaur, a horrendous monster who was half man and half bull. And Minos, to hide the infamy, enclosed him in the Labyrinth, and there he devoured living men. Shortly before those times, Androgeus, son of Minos, had been killed by the Athenians out of envy, because he defeated everyone in the wrestling games. Minos took his revenge and, having conquered them, imposed a law: that every year they should send to Crete fourteen of their children, seven males and seven females. These were chosen by lot, and after some years the lot fell upon Theseus, son of Aegeus, King of Athens. He went; but before he entered the Labyrinth, because of his beauty, he attracted the love of Adriana—or more correctly, Ariadne—daughter of Minos, to whom he promised he would make her his wife. And she decided to free him from such a cruel death. She gave him a ball of thread, balls of pitch <note>original: "pegola"</note>, and an iron club. Theseus tied the end of the thread to the door and pulled the rest with him so that by following it he would know how to return outside. And when the Minotaur opened his mouth to devour him, he threw the balls of pitch, which plastered his mouth so that he could not open it. And then with the club, he struck his head and killed him. You have the fable; now hear the allegory. Some writers of no mediocre learning posit that by Pasiphae—a very beautiful woman and daughter of the Sun—is understood the human soul, created by God, the supreme Sun, and made very beautiful by its innocence. She becomes the wife of Minos, the inventor of laws, because the soul joins with Reason, which directs it on the right path with its laws. Venus, that is, Concupiscence, is her enemy, always opposing Reason. And if the appetite joins with concupiscence, the soul separates from her husband Minos—that is, from Reason—and, pulled by the flatteries of the flesh, loves the bull: that is, the delights of the world, which at first glance appear beautiful. But afterward, by using them poorly, we come to be joined with bestiality. And Pasiphae, enclosed in the wooden cow, joins with the bull because through the artifice of our wit we use natural things not according to the laws of nature...

<summary>This page marks the entrance into the Seventh Circle of Hell, where Dante and Virgil encounter the Minotaur amidst a rugged landscape. The commentary provides the mythological background of the Minotaur and offers a Neo-Platonic allegory regarding the soul's descent into bestiality when it abandons reason.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto XII of the Inferno, specifically focusing on the encounter with the Minotaur at the beginning of the Seventh Circle and the physical descent through the landslide. It transitions from the description of the terrain to the allegorical interpretation of the characters involved.</meta>

<header>CANTO TWELVE</header>

From here is born the Minotaur, who has limbs partly of a man and partly of a bull. This represents the vice of bestiality of which we spoke above. Indeed, those who are defiled by this vice appear human in their aspect, but in their habits they are beasts. The Minotaur is placed in the labyrinth, which signifies that the human heart <note>Original: "pecto humano"</note> is entangled in various frauds. But Theseus, advised by Ariadne—that is, the learned man advised by reason—kills the Minotaur: that is, the vice. Through such an easy allegory you will understand that Dante, with excellent reason, placed such a monster in the place where the cruel and savage sins are punished. **AND WHEN HE SAW US** he bit himself, just as one whom anger shatters within. This shows that violent bestiality, born of pride, is always accompanied by anger, because at the same time it is painful for it not to obtain what it desires, and it gnaws at itself with rage. On the other hand, it grieves that, once fear is removed, no one honors it.

**My sage toward him cried out: perhaps
thou thinkest the Duke of Athens is here,
who in the world above brought thee thy death?
Get gone, beast, for this one does not come
instructed by thy sister,
but goes to see your punishments.
As is that bull that breaks loose at the moment
it has already received the fatal blow,
which cannot walk, but plunges here and there,
I saw the Minotaur do the same;
and he, alert, cried: Run to the passage;
while he is in fury, it is good that you descend.**

<margin>THE DUKE OF ATHENS</margin> Theseus, Duke of Athens, who, as we have said, is understood as the wise man who is the leader of Athens. For just as Athens was a city in Greece—the home and receptacle of all doctrines, without which a man cannot be wise—he brought death to the Minotaur in the world, as we have said. He was able to do this through the instructions of Ariadne: that is, of virtue, who is the sister of bestiality in so far as both are conceived by the soul. When the soul joins with Minos—that is, with reason—it gives birth to virtue; when it joins with the bull—that is, with concupiscence <note>Unregulated desire or lust.</note>—it gives birth to the Minotaur: that is, vice. **BUT GOES TO SEE YOUR PUNISHMENTS.** He does not kill the sin, but contemplates your punishments: that is, the nature of the sin and the evil that comes from it, so that by knowing it, he may guard against it. **AS IS THAT BULL.** It is an excellent and very fitting comparison to liken the Minotaur to the bull. And also, through that movement, he expresses the fury of this monster; and it denotes that the intellect, rising against obstinate bestiality, overcomes it with reason. But that monster, through its obstinacy, becomes enraged rather than yielding. **AND HE, ALERT.** An excellent precept from the intellect to the lower reason: that when the obstinate one rises in fury, one should yield and go through the entrance he abandons: that is, through the reason which puts us into this contemplation.

**Thus we took our way down through the discharge
of those stones, which often moved
under my feet because of the new weight.
I was thinking, and he said: You think
perhaps of this ruin, which is guarded
by that bestial wrath I just now quenched.
Now I want you to know that the other time
that I descended here into deep Hell,
this rock had not yet fallen.
But certainly shortly before, if I discern well,
that He came who took the great prey
from Dis, from the uppermost circle:
on all sides the deep, foul valley
trembled so, that I thought the universe...**

<column-break/>

He shows how Virgil admonishes the Minotaur, who should not fear being killed by Dante, because he is not Theseus, who killed him in Crete. Here it is allegorically shown that the Minotaur could be killed up here in the world, but he cannot be killed in Hell; because, speaking as a Christian, whoever is in life can be brought to penance, and thus kills the vice of bestiality. But he who is in Hell has no space to repent. Morally, in life—that is, where there is not yet an obstinate habit of vice—we can kill it; but in Hell—that is, after we have been reduced to a most obstinate habit—we cannot kill it. **HE CRIED OUT:** To show that the higher reason must rise up vividly and with vehemence. This is expressed through the shouting, and not coldly.

**We were descending through the discharge:** that is, through the ruin which had discharged many stones from the mountain; and many remained half-torn away in such a way that when Dante placed his feet there, they moved. **BECAUSE OF THE NEW:** that is, unaccustomed weight. For no one descended there except souls without bodies, except for Dante. Therefore, Dante went along occasionally stumbling, as the stones moved beneath him. This signifies that while sensuality, along with the lower reason, descends into the contemplation of vices, it cannot be that it does not sometimes go stumbling, because the pleasures that the vices bring with them flatter it. This is because the habit of heroic virtue is not yet formed—or as we might say according to Plato, the habit of the virtues of the soul already purified. But it is enough that he does not fall—that is, does not ruin himself—into the vice. Nor without cause does he show that this ruin leads to where there is...

> ...the universe felt love, whereby some believe
> The world has oft been turned to chaos;
> and at that point this ancient rock
> Here and elsewhere made such a collapse.

The poet expressed these things through the ruin and the stones:
**THINKING:** <note>Original: "SANDO" - a fragment of "pensando"</note> keep the ruin in mind. Because the lower reason always thinks of particular things: And of
**THE RUIN WHICH IS/** <note>Original: "INA CHE E/" - a fragment of "ruina che e"</note> Guarded by that bestial anger. Because the passage where we enter into violence is [built upon]
**WHICH I NOW EXTINGUISHED** because the intellect extinguishes anger with reason. **NOW I WANT YOU TO KNOW:**
motion through the death of Christ: And allegorically it hints that through the death of Christ every violence of the demon against us was broken.
of the holy fathers: who first because of original sin were the prey **OF DIS:** that is, of Pluto, i.e., of Lucifer.
the universe felt love whereby some believe: That is, there are some who believe the world has often returned to chaos. [The poet] places the opinion of Empedocles <note>A Greek philosopher who proposed that the universe is governed by the opposing forces of Love (attraction) and Strife (repulsion).</note> who posited six principles: that is, the four elements and love and discord: and he said that when the elements and motions of the heaven were in concord, everything returned to chaos: and when concord ceased and discord came, the world returned to its former shape. **AND AT THAT POINT** of the sixth hour <note>The hour of Christ's death on the cross.</note>. **THIS ANCIENT ROCK** / this old bank.
**HERE AND ELSEWHERE** as will be said below.

> But fix your eyes below, for the river
> of blood approaches, in which boils
> anyone who by violence harms another.
> O blind greed, o foolish wrath
> that so spurs us in this short life
> and in the eternal one then so ill-steeps us!
> I saw a wide ditch curved in an arch
> like one that embraces the whole plain
> according to what my guide had said:
> And between the foot of the bank and it, in a file
> ran Centaurs armed with arrows,
> as they used to go hunting in the world:
> Seeing us descend, each one stopped;

> with bows and arrows first chosen:
> And one cried from afar: To what torment
> come you who descend the slope?
> Tell us from there, or I draw the bow.
> My master gave the answer:
> We shall make it to Chiron near at hand;
> ill was your will always so hasty.

...and put him in a wineskin full of blood saying: "Blood [you thirsted for, and with blood I fill you]." <note>Referring to the death of Cyrus the Great.</note>
[He places] the violent in the blood: because they are incited by anger, which is the boiling of the blood. And morally, [one must] guard oneself from that. Violence is force used to the harm and evil of others: and it is born from greed: which has its origin
**BETWEEN THE FOOT** of the bank / Among the roots of the mountain. **AND IT** the ditch. **ARMED CENTAURS** ran
in a file: That is, all in a row as if following the track of one another. "Track" <note>Original: "traccia"</note> signifies a footprint and [a path].

<column-break/>

...savage violence is punished. Since the soul cannot descend into such cruelty and violence if the mind does not first fall from the excellence of its nature and does not harden into cruelty: because naturally we are born to love and help and not to hate and harm. Wherefore both these [ruins], which are very hard things. **I NOW THOUGHT** this occurred to superior reason: and therefore he solves the doubt of his thought. **IN THIS RUIN** pride accompanied by anger: by which we forget our humanity and become beasts through cruelty.
He feigns that this, together with many others, collapsed at the sixth hour of Good Friday when the earthquake occurred.
**HE WHO [TOOK] THE GREAT PREY.** i.e., Christ who despoiled Limbo.
**OF THE CIRCLE OF LIMBO:** which is the first circle and the highest. **SO THAT I THOUGHT THE UNIVERSE** [would be turned to chaos].

### The Punishment of the Violent
He demonstrates first that the punishment of these sinners was that they were boiled in the blood. Then he is indignant against unrestrained desires: which drive men with such fury to want to possess in this brief time of life that for which they will later be damned in eternity: and finally he shows the punishers of this [crime] to be the centaurs.
**BUT FIX** your eyes below: that is, downwards. **FOR IT APPROACHES:** that is, because it draws near. **O BLIND** greed: He said "blind" meaning without reason. **O FOOLISH WRATH.** We said above that the force of the irascible appetite is to remove all obstacles that do not let us achieve what we desire. Therefore such appetite is foolish and stupid: which all day long pushes furious souls—those greedy for tyranny—into a thousand dangers and deaths, and into infinite labors. Since water and bread and glass and wood are found much sweeter than gems and gold. It is a fitting punishment for cruel men and tyrants that they be punished in the boiling blood. Since for him who delighted in blood, divine justice promises that he be punished in blood: as happened to Cyrus, king of the Persians: who, after the very heavy defeat given to the Scythians and after the most cruel slaughter of them, was finally conquered by Tomyris <note>Original: "Tamaris"</note> their queen. Her son had been killed by him along with the others; thus Cyrus was killed together with two hundred thousand Persians. And Tomyris, to demonstrate her thirst for human blood, took off his head [and put it in a container of blood], saying: "You thirsted for blood, and I fill you with blood." <note>Original: "sitisti et io disangue tempio" — a version of the Latin "Satiasti te sanguine, satiabor ego te"</note> Furthermore, he who delighted in homicide boils, then he takes such repentance for it: that day and night he is tormented by the memory [of it].
**CURVED IN AN ARCH:** because it went in a circuit, according to the layout that he [the poet] establishes.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, Canto XII. While the previous page discussed the physical ruin of the landslide caused by Christ's descent into Hell, this page transitions to the mythological and moral identity of the Centaurs who guard the river of blood, using them as an allegory for the nature of tyranny and unrestrained ambition.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>CANTO TWELVE</header>

...track <note>Original: "orma"</note> / from which to trace and follow the footprints. The poets say that the Centaurs were monstrous men in Thessaly; they were half horse and half man, the sons of Ixion. He was the son of Phlegyas of Thessaly, and was the first among the Greeks who attempted to seize tyranny by force. For this reason, the poets imagine that he wanted to unite with Juno, the wife of Jove. Jove, mocking him, created an image of mist similar to Juno, and Ixion joined with her, believing her to be the true Juno. From such a union, the Centaurs were born. By Ixion, we understand all men greedy for kingdoms or power, who attempt to acquire princedoms or lordships beyond their strength. And because Juno represents the idea of kingdoms, they imagine that he wanted to join with her. But she mocks and deceives him by showing him that image of mist; for there is no one who can join with Juno as they desire—that is, to acquire as much lordship as they propose in their minds, which is insatiable in the tyrannical life.

For once he has acquired what he first desired, and in which he believed he would find rest, there is born in him a desire for something greater. He never arrives at that quiet life he proposes for himself, which he would quickly reach if he put a bridle on his greed and stayed content with his present state, as the wise Cineas <note>A diplomat and advisor to King Pyrrhus of Epirus, famous for a dialogue where he questioned the King's endless conquests.</note> openly demonstrated to the infuriated Pyrrhus. This makes men always thirsty to increase their empire, where such insanity is manifested that Alexander the Great, hearing the Epicurean philosophers affirm that there was not just one world but many, wept in despair that he could not conquer them all, not having yet conquered even this one. 

Therefore, the thoughts of Alexander were monstrous, because without doubt they were beyond all human strength and contrary to all humanity. Not provoked by any injury, he wished to make slaves of those who were by nature free like him. Thus it clearly follows that the Centaurs—that is, unrestrained and cruel desires—are the children of Ixion, the tyrant. They are fathered by the mist—that is, by a false concept formed in his mind. For just as mist from afar seems a great thing, but upon approaching it is found to be nothing, so such thoughts at the beginning give great hope of success, but then they vanish and return to nothing. Furthermore, just as the Centaur has human upper limbs and the lower parts of a beast, so tyrannical desires have some part of reason at the beginning, but the further they progress, the more they become bestial.

Furthermore, they say that Jove cast him into Hell and there had him bound to wheels that always turn and are full of serpents. This signifies that the mind of the tyrant is always turned by anxious thoughts and continually bitten by poisonous reflections. Certainly, nothing is found more brutal and more contrary to human nature than the life and habits of those who, whether in their republics or their principalities, wish to have more power than the laws and to oppress those whom God and nature made equal to them. Kings and governors of republics were not found to lord over others or cruelly torment them and deprive them of dignity, property, and finally life; nor to convert every comfort and utility to themselves while leaving others with hardships and damages. 

Instead, they were instituted so that the multitude might have a guide and government for honest living, and so that by their prudence and justice they might be an example of every virtue. By means of holy laws, they were to rule their citizens in peace and concord, and instruct the people to exercise themselves in every laudable art. They should perform their duty toward their citizens: offending no one, helping everyone, and loving relatives and friends according to their rank. They should possess such fervent charity toward the fatherland that they are always prepared to give their lives for it if necessary. And finally, they should labor so that others might rest; they should keep watch so that others might sleep securely; and they should put themselves in danger so that others might live safe. For all these things, they should expect no other reward than honor, which is the unique reward of virtue.

These are called *Basylee* <note>Original: "Basylee", referring to the Greek "Basileis" (kings). The author provides a folk etymology linking it to "base."</note> by the Greeks because they are a firm base upon which the entire public weight rests. The Latins call them *Reges* <note>Kings.</note> because they rule and sustain others with their industry and do not let them lapse into any iniquity. Christians call them *pastores* <note>Shepherds.</note> because, just as good shepherds do not seek their own benefit but that of the flock committed to them, so good princes seek the salvation of those committed to their government. They remember the words of Truth: that the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep. 

This, then, is the office and duty of whoever governs and rules. Whoever does the opposite of this is neither king nor governor, but a tyrant. He is not a shepherd but a wolf. He does not guard the sheep but kills them. He does not labor for those who are subject to him, but wishes to live off their labor, to triumph over their spoils, to behave toward them like a devil, and to be adored like a god. He wants his lust to be like a divine precept, his avarice to be just law, and cruelty to befit him. Such men enjoy the torments of the just and rejoice in shedding the blood of the innocent. Therefore, they are not only not kings, but they are not men. Stripped of all humanity and clothed in every brutality, they are the supreme ruin of mankind. Nero and Mezentius <note>Mezentius was a cruel Etruscan king in Virgil's Aeneid.</note> retained the human form; Sulla and Marius retained it; but they entirely set aside the human soul and became tigers and bears. 

These men sin so excessively that they not only harm other men, as we have said, but in as much as they are able, they harm God, because they trample upon the laws, which are the daughters of God. They destroy men, who are creatures of God. They harm themselves, because from the highest and celestial rank where man is placed—similar to the angels or rather to God—they ruin themselves into the deep precipice and abyss of the beasts. Often, wishing to shed the blood of others, they shed their own. Whence Juvenal <note>A Roman satirist.</note> says: 
> To the son-in-law of Ceres <note>Original: "Ad generum cereris..." referring to Pluto, lord of the Underworld and husband of Proserpina.</note> few kings and tyrants descend without slaughter and wounds, or by a bloodless death.

Of these the psalmist <note>Original: "psa", abbreviation for "psalmista".</note> says...

...mixed. <note>original: "mixta"</note> I will not lose my life with the impious: and my soul with men of blood. In whose hands are iniquities and their right hand is filled with gifts <note>original: "Non perdam cum impiis uitam meam : Et cum uiris sanguinum animam meam In quorum manibus iniquitates sunt et dextera eorum repleta est muneribus"</note>; and from the prophet Habakkuk: The devil himself will triumph over kings: and tyrants will be his laughingstock. <note>original: "Ipse diabolus de regibus triumphabit : et tyranni ridiculi eius erunt"</note> And certainly, tyrants lose their lives. Not only the eternal life, but even this transitory one. For, being feared by everyone, it is necessary that they also fear everyone. Therefore, they always live in the highest anxiety and fear, as Cicero openly demonstrates in the fifth *Tusculan Disputation* with the example of the tyrant Dionysius of Syracuse <note>Dionysius I, who was so paranoid he reportedly taught his daughters to shave him with glowing nutshells rather than trust them with a razor.</note>: who was not only forced to guard himself from friends and family and deprive himself of every joyful custom, but he trusted neither his wife nor his daughters. And the better men are, the more he fears them. Because, as Sallust says: To them, another’s virtue is always a source of fear. <note>original: "Semper illis aliena uirtus formidolosa est"</note> But perhaps the just indignation I hold toward such a detestable generation of men has carried me too far from my purpose. But concluding: there is no greater punishment for ambitious men than to generate Centaurs—that is, that their enterprises do not succeed—and therefore he places the Centaurs in this location. Now returning to the text, it follows: **SEEING US DESCEND**: that is, going down to the plain where the trench of blood was—each of those Centaurs stopped. And three departed from the troop, coming toward us with bows and arrows ready to strike us. Dante wanted to descend to the plain: that is, to the contemplation of this vice. But as we have said in several places: the Centaurs—that is, vice—confront concupiscence <note>Strong desire or worldly appetite.</note>, and with their arrows—that is, with their stimuli—they would conquer it if Virgil—that is, the intellect—did not subdue them. Nessus was with these three. And the Centaurs wanted Virgil and Dante to say from a distance to what torment they were coming. It is as if he wants to say that whoever looks at vice from a distance does not know its intrinsic nature. Therefore, he hopes for pleasure and happiness. Wherefore, if he did not watch himself, displeasure and misery would be born in him. **MY MASTER SAID**: we will give the response to Chiron. Chiron the Centaur was not the son of Ixion and the cloud like the other Centaurs, but of Saturn; who, having fallen in love with a nymph named Philyra, joined with her. But when his wife arrived, so as not to be caught in manifest adultery, he turned himself into a horse. For this reason, Philyra gave birth to Chiron from such a union: half man and half horse. He was learned in music, wherefore in this he was the teacher of Achilles. Likewise in that branch of medicine which is called <term>surgery</term> <note>derived from the Greek for "hand-work"; Chiron was the legendary inventor of the craft.</note>: and he taught it to Aesculapius. He was called half-horse because he was a bellicose man. For the horse is an animal suited for war. Therefore Achilles, a bellicose man, is called his disciple. Thus, by this figure we shall understand that soul which, although it is wild in its ambition and greed for lordship, is nonetheless not without some learning and reason, and some justice and civil custom. And therefore Virgil does not want to respond to Nessus, in whom there is nothing but fury. But he says he will respond to Chiron. This signifies that the speculative intellect does not want to proceed with hasty, impetuous, and furious counsel, as Nessus was when—without considering how much injury he was doing to Hercules, a man capable of avenging himself—he violated Deianira. But he wants to proceed with reason, learning, and equity, as was in Chiron. And he will reproach Nessus, because his fury and his swift, unconsidered will finally had to harm him, as he was killed by the arrows of Hercules. And certainly all the unconsidered enterprises of furious tyrants are killed by Hercules: that is, they are overcome by prudent and strong men, as we understand Hercules to be.

Then he nudged me and said: "That is Nessus,
who died for the beautiful Deianira,
and he himself took vengeance for himself.
And the one in the middle, looking at his chest,
is the great Chiron, who nursed Achilles;
the other is Pholus, who was so full of wrath."

<column-break/>

He places these three exiting the troop from the others to demonstrate that violence, as we have said above, is of three types. **THEN HE NUDGED ME** / He touched me to excite him and make him attentive to what he wanted to say to him: because sensuality is lost in these contemplations if the intellect does not excite and admonish it. **THAT IS NESSUS** This Centaur escaped from the war of the Lapiths and fled to Calydon. In 그 time, Hercules...

...having conquered Achelous, was leading away Deianira, whom her father Oeneus, king of Calydon, had given to him as a wife. And having reached the river Evenus, which was greatly swollen by the melting snows, he found Nessus, who offered to carry Deianira across on his back. Hercules thanked him and gave her to him, suspecting no fraud. But after Nessus had carried her to the other bank, he wanted to violate her. Realizing this through the cries of Deianira, Hercules shot him with arrows that were dipped in the poisonous blood of the Hydra. Nessus recognized the mortal blow and immediately thought of revenge; he gave Deianira his shirt, stained with his blood, saying to her: "If your husband is ever occupied by the love of another woman, and you put this shirt on him, he will immediately return to your love." Deianira kept the shirt and the poison of the Hydra. And after some time, Hercules being occupied with the love of Iole, she sent it to him. He put it on, and perished by that poison. And in this way Nessus avenged himself. We have already spoken of Chiron. Pholus was one of the Centaurs who, at the wedding of Pirithous, king of the Lapiths, overcome by wine, fell into such a fury that they wanted to kidnap the bride. From this, a brawl broke out between them and the others who were there, among whom were Hercules, Theseus, and Nestor. And finally they were driven away, and the majority killed. Pholus was a centaur whose drunken behavior at a wedding sparked a legendary battle.</note>

**SWIFT BEASTS** <note>original: "FIERE SNELLE"</note>: that is, fast. *Snello* signifies lithe and lean. Whence we say a "snella" woman: and one who is *snello* is dexterous and rapid.
**CHIRON took an arrow**: He wished to express these verses of Virgil: *She spoke, and from her quiver the Thracian maid drew a gold-winged arrow, and in anger stretched her bow until the curved ends met, and with her hands level, she touched the steel with her left hand and the bowstring with her right breast.* <note>original: "Dixit et auratam uoluerem threiissa sagittam Deprompsit pharetra cornuque infensa tetendit : Et duxit lōge donec curuata coirent Inter se capita : et manibus iam tāgeret equis Leua acie ferri dextra neruoque papillā." Landino is comparing Chiron's archery posture to a scene from Virgil's Aeneid.</note> Therefore, with the notch of the arrow, he pushed his beard back toward his jaws: because by pulling the bowstring toward himself, he caused the notch to come as far as his ears, pulling back the beard so that the mouth remained uncovered. Afterward, he demonstrates that Chiron, like a philosopher, knew that Dante was alive, that is, with his body. For philosophers demonstrate that everything that moves must touch what it moves, and thus it must be a body. And therefore he added: **THE FEET OF THE DEAD ARE NOT ACCUSTOMED** to doing so. Because the soul, being incorporeal, has no touch. Then he says that Virgil was already at the chest of Chiron to demonstrate how quickly the intellect anticipates the fury of vice: and takes away every impulse by striking it down with reason. **AT THE CHEST WHERE TWO NATURES ARE JOINED**. Centaurs are formed with such a figure that the horse members are below, and the human ones are above from the chest up. Therefore, sin is the boundary of the horse and the man: And because thoughts and cogitations reside in the chest, it shows that Virgil approached that: that is, reason traversed the thought, which was part bestial and part human. And he says to Chiron **INDEED HE IS ALIVE**: showing that he has not descended to hell to make a habit of sin, because such people are not truly "alive." Rather, he descends into hell—that is, into the thought of sin—to guard himself against it. For this reason, it is necessary that Virgil—that is, the superior intellect—shows him the dark valley, which is sin. **NECESSITY BRINGS HIM and not pleasure**: because the knowledge of vices brings no delight to the soul, but it is necessary so that one may guard oneself against them. For no one can guard himself from an unknown enemy; however, the knowledge of virtue brings with it the greatest delight. **ONE DEPARTED FROM singing Hallelujah**. He shows that Beatrice (of whom it is spoken in the first Canto) moved Virgil to guide Dante; she came to him from heaven where they sing Hallelujah, which is where all joy resides. For this word, in Hebrew, signifies "praise God" and "joy." **WHO COMMISSIONED ME this new office**: Because regarding the fictional narrative, it is a new thing that a living man is led through hell. And allegorically, it shows that few are those who come to such contemplation. **HE IS NO ROBBER**. He shows he does not come to be punished: because he is no robber, which is to say, one who is violent. For a "robber" <note>original: "ladrone"</note> is one who steals by force, and a "thief" <note>original: "furo"</note> is one who takes by deception. **NOR AM I A THIEVING SOUL**: that is, a thief. And he said this imitating Virgil, who has the Sibyl excuse Aeneas to Charon, demonstrating that he does not come to snatch away from hell either Cerberus or Proserpina or anyone else. Whence he said: *No such treachery is here; be not disturbed. Nor do our weapons bring violence; the huge doorkeeper may bark forever in his cave to terrify the bloodless shadows; chaste Proserpina may keep her uncle's threshold.* <note>original: "Nullē hic insidie tales absiste moueri. Nec uim tela ferunt licet ingens ianitor latrans exāgues terreat umbras Casta licet patrui seruet Proserpina/lymen."</note> Therefore, just as the Sibyl shows that in Aeneas there is neither fraud nor violence, so Virgil shows that in Dante there is no violence (as in robbers) nor in himself fraud (as in thieves).

**BUT BY That power**. He entreats by the divine power to which even the infernal beings yield. **GIVE US ONE OF YOURS**, centaurs. **TO WHOM WE MAY stay near**: that is, who may approve of us, which is as much as to say who may hold us dear and keep us good company. Or truly "to whom we are near" <note>original: "approuo"</note> by way of experience: that is, by whose guidance we find ourselves put to the test. **AND WHO MAY CARRY this man upon his back.**

This page describes the crossing of the river of blood (Phlegethon) and provides a detailed historical and allegorical critique of the tyrants punished there, specifically Alexander the Great and Dionysius of Syracuse.</meta>

and said to Nessus: "Turn and guide them:
and make any other troop that meets them give way."

along the edge of the crimson boiling
where the boiled made loud shrieks.

and the great centaur said: "These are tyrants

Then I turned to the poet: and he said:

<column-break/>

**FOR HE IS NOT A SPIRIT** who can fly through the air. This sentence is clear regarding the literal fiction. But regarding the <term>allegory</term> <note>A story where characters and events represent deeper moral or spiritual meanings.</note> it shows that Virgil, who is without a body, has no need to be carried across the ditch because he can travel through the air. This denotes that the <term>intellect</term> has knowledge of universals, which are not included in any matter, nor in time, nor in place. But the lower reason considers particulars, which are included in matter. Therefore, Virgil will pass through any place. But Dante will be carried by Nessus, because <term>sensuality</term> <note>The faculty of the soul related to physical senses and worldly desires.</note> does not recognize vice in the universal, nor can it consider tyranny abstracted from every subject; rather, it considers it in a particular person, such as in Phalaris, in Nero, and in similar men.

This text is clear in itself, except for the histories. Alexander the Great, king of the Macedonians, deserves without any doubt to be numbered among the tyrants; because in truth, without being provoked by any injury, he occupied the tyranny not only of Greece, but of a great part of Asia. For which reason Petrarch truly said: *Alexander, who gave the world trouble.* <note>original: "Alexandro chal mondo brigha die." From Petrarch's *Triumph of Fame*.</note> He used much cruelty, and many signs demonstrate clearly that he consented to the death of his father, killed by Pausanias. He was of such infamy that he wished to be called and esteemed the son of a god and not of a man. And once he had conquered the Persians, he wished, according to the barbaric custom and to the great indignation of his own people, to be adored as a god. And Callisthenes, an excellent philosopher and his fellow student and a disciple of Aristotle, who tried to pull him back from such infamy, he caused to die most cruelly. Out of anger and drunkenness, he killed Clitus, a man so much his friend that afterward, repenting of it, he wished to kill himself. Nor could one, without a whole volume of history,

---

recount the particular friends he killed, like Clitus in the first place, who was killed because he modestly admonished him not to prefer himself to his father Philip. But one must consider the peoples and the nations which, without having received any injury, he sent to ultimate extermination, and the kings by whom he had never been provoked. Whence Lucan rightly called him the "robber and plunderer of the universe," <note>original: "predone et raptore delluniuerso." Lucan was a Roman poet who depicted Alexander as a destructive force in his epic *Pharsalia*.</note> and desired that his bones, in vengeance for such great ferocity, should be scattered throughout the whole world. And certainly, if we consider his life and customs with diligence, we will say that there were few virtues in him which he did not use poorly. I grant he was most excellent in military deeds. But who does not know that war, by its nature, is entirely opposite to the bond of charity, which naturally embraces the whole human generation? War is approved by God and by wise men only for the defense of oneself, one's people, and the fatherland; to tame monsters; and to reduce ferocious peoples to tranquil peace. But Alexander converted it to the ruin of everyone, to imposing a yoke on those who lived in liberty, and to taking away peace and leisure from those who enjoyed their own goods without injury to others. And it seemed to him that he was worthy for all men to serve him, while he himself was a slave to wine and anger. Nor was he ashamed to make himself the son of Jove and to want to be adored like a god.

Dionysius was a Syracusan of noble lineage. His mother, while pregnant with him, dreamed she gave birth to a little satyr. And the interpreters of dreams predicted he would be most powerful. And Humera, a noble woman in Syracuse, dreamed of being led into heaven and seeing at the feet of Jove a man with red and freckled hair, bound with a thousand chains; and her guide told her that this man was to be the slaughter and destruction of Sicily. Afterward, in the course of time, Dionysius having occupied the lordship, as soon as the woman saw him, she cried out that he was the man whom she had seen in her dream in chains; these words were the reason why Dionysius had her killed. This man became lord of Sicily after the armies of the Carthaginians, which were most powerful on that island, were consumed by pestilence and left the island free. Made king, he crossed into Italy against the Greek cities; and first he conquered Locri. Afterward, he besieged Crotone. But when new armies of Carthaginians came to Sicily, he was constrained to abandon the enterprise and return to the island. He was very cruel, and he oppressed the city of Syracuse, at that time most splendid, in heavy servitude, because by nature he was malicious and unjust. He occupied the tyranny in the twenty-fifth year of his life and held it for thirty-eight years, but with supreme misery. For although he was a noble and literate man, and a poet of some account—and for this reason desirous of the familiarity and conversation of many men—nevertheless, it was necessary for him to guard himself against everyone. Because, as Sallust says, "Tyrants always fear the good more than the wicked," <note>original: "Sempre etyranni temono piu ebuoni che erei." A paraphrase of Sallust’s *Bellum Catilinae*.</note> because the good are greater lovers of liberty. He lived, therefore, with slaves and barbarians; and through the desire for ruling, he kept himself enclosed in narrow...

<summary>This page describes the crossing of the river Phlegethon, where the violent are punished, and provides Landino's extensive historical critique of Alexander the Great and Dionysius of Syracuse as archetypal tyrants. Landino uses classical sources like Lucan and Sallust to argue that military conquest without just cause is mere robbery, contrasting political tyranny with the intellectual search for universal truths.</summary>

<header>CANTO TWELVE</header>

prison: And how great his misery was, he himself demonstrated through Damocles: who, while greatly praising the happy life of the tyrant, was told by Dionysius <note>Dionysius I of Syracuse (c. 432–367 BC), a Greek tyrant known for his cruelty and paranoia.</note> that he should taste it himself. And immediately he had a most noble banquet prepared. He commanded Damocles to sit in a place where, having companions on every side, he could not leave at his own will. And above his head, he had a very sharp sword tied to the ceiling by a single horsehair: which seemed as though it might fall on his head at any moment. The table was adorned with gold and silver vessels. It was filled with many various and most sweet foods. There were young and expert servants: But so great was the fear that the sword might fall on his head that he took no pleasure in the aforementioned things. Thus, Dionysius demonstrated that the life of a tyrant was similar: in which the continuous fear of being either killed or driven out means that no pleasure can be taken from one’s power or treasures. He had two wives: but he never entered the chamber of either without first having it diligently searched to ensure no weapons were hidden there. And because he did not trust his barber, he had himself shaved by his daughters; and when they reached adulthood, he took the razor from them and had his beard singed with glowing walnut shells. He was very impious toward the gods. He plundered the temple of Proserpina: and afterwards, having a good voyage, he added mocking words to the sacrilege, saying, "See what a fine wind the gods give to those who rob them." King Hiero had adorned the statue of Jupiter with a cloth of gold. Dionysius took it and gave him one of wool, asserting that gold was useless in any season: because in winter it was too cold and in summer too heavy. The ancients made statues of Apollo in youthful form, and those of his son Aesculapius <note>The god of medicine.</note> as elderly and with a long beard. Therefore, he removed the beard of Aesculapius, which was made of gold, asserting it was not fitting that while the father was beardless, the son should be bearded.

**AND EZZELINO.** <note>Ezzelino III da Romano (1194–1259).</note> This man was called Ezzelino from the castle of Romano near Treviso. Although Musatto of Padua in one of his tragedies—in which he feigns that he was the son of the devil—calls him Ecerino; and Giovanni Villani in his chronicle states that he was of noble lineage. He was a most powerful tyrant in the March of Treviso during the time of Frederick II. Furthermore, he ruled Padua, Vicenza, Verona, and Brescia: and through his savage cruelty, he killed infinite men and sent many into exile. And after the rebellion of the Paduans, he enclosed twelve thousand men within a palisade in the meadow of Padua and had them all burned. And regarding this cruelty, it is told that having become suspicious of one of his chancellors called Ser Aldobrandino, and determining to put him to death for this reason, he asked if he knew who was enclosed in the palisade. And the chancellor responding that he had noted them all in his notebook, Ezzelino said he had determined to present their souls to the devil for many benefits received from him. Therefore, he wanted the chancellor to go to hell with the notebook along with them: and specifically present them on his behalf. And so, together with the others, he had him burned. This man moved an army against the Milanese and reached the Adda; finding the bridge occupied by the Marquis Pallavicino, his adversary, he set out to ford it. Arriving at the bank at a disadvantage, he was broken by the Marquis, wounded, captured, and led to Cassano, a nearby castle: where, refusing to eat or tend to his wounds, he died of hunger and grief in the year of our salvation 1260. He reigned in Verona for thirty-four years, as we shall say more extensively in the ninth Canto of *Paradiso*.

**AND OBIZZO D’ESTE.** This man was of the family of the Marquises of Ferrara: and having been made Marquis of the March of Ancona by the Apostolic See, he gathered great treasure through robbery and cruelty. Finally, one night he was smothered with a bolster <note>original: "pimaccio," a large pillow or cushion.</note> by his son: whom Dante calls a stepson: because it does not seem credible that he was his true son, having used such cruelty against him. I leave the history of these men of Este, because it is sufficiently celebrated by our scholar from Imola. <note>Refers to Benvenuto da Imola, an early and famous commentator on Dante.</note>

**THEN I MOVED TOWARD THE POET.** It seemed to Dante that Virgil ought to be the guide and not the centaur: and therefore he turned to him. And Virgil, understanding his desire, said: that he wanted the centaur to be the first in that place. And this is understood <term>allegorically</term> <note>The deeper symbolic meaning beyond the literal story.</note> as meaning that Dante—that is, the appetite subjected to reason—in every contemplation and knowledge wants no other judgment than that of Virgil: that is, the intellect. But because the intellect has knowledge of <term>universals</term> <note>General concepts or categories, rather than specific instances.</term>, Virgil can judge what violence and cruelty are in general, and what punishment they deserve. But regarding <term>particulars</term> <note>Specific individual cases or people.</note>—such as saying that Dionysius and Ezzelino are cruel—the senses and the lower reason judge better, especially in a man who has practiced cruelty himself, such as the centaurs. And therefore Virgil did not say, "This one shall be first for you" absolutely: but he said, "This one shall be first for you *now*": that is, in these particulars. And he wishes to be the second in this place: because our soul, having already known the actions of Marius and Sulla to be cruel, abstracts that cruelty from these particulars and considers not the individuals, but in a universal sense what cruelty is; and in this form, Virgil becomes the second guide. The poet is thus of marvelous genius to note, under such fiction, the difference between the intellect and the lower reason.

**BOILING STREAM** <note>original: "BULLICAME"</note> They use this term for any water that rises from the depths with the bubbling of heat. Hence the bath of Viterbo is called *Bullicame* for this reason.

**HE SHOWED US A SHADE.** A soul which he says is alone in that place: because there was no one else who had committed such a crime. And he means Count Guy de Montfort. <note>Guy de Montfort (1244–1288) murdered Henry of Almain in a church in Viterbo during Mass to avenge his father's death; the "heart" was said to be kept in a golden cup over the Thames.</note>
