the heart which on the Thames is still honored.
Then I saw people who out of the river
held their head and even all the chest
and of these I recognized many.
Thus bit by bit it became shallower,
that blood, until it cooked only the feet:
and here was our passage across the ditch.

---

Just as you see on this side
the boiling stream <note>original: "bullicame," a word Dante uses to describe the hot, bubbling source of the river of blood.</note> which always decreases,
the centaur said: I want you to believe:
That on this other side it presses down
its bottom more and more until it joins
where tyranny must groan.
Divine justice on this side pricks
that Attila who was a scourge on earth:
and Pyrrhus: and Sextus: and eternally milks
The tears that the boiling unlocks
from Rinier da Corneto, and Rinier Pazzo,
who made such war upon the roads:
Then he turned and recrossed the ford.

<column-break/>

In order to explain this with brevity: there was a King of England, Henry III <note>Reigned 1216–1272.</note>, who because he was a squanderer and prodigal in consuming the things of the realm, became estranged from his barons. With their favor, Simon de Montfort <note>Simon de Montfort, 6th Earl of Leicester (c. 1208–1265), a leader of the baronial opposition.</note>—an excellent man and fit to rule—imprisoned King Henry, and Richard his brother, and all the sons except Edward <note>The future King Edward I.</note>, who escaped by the speed of his horse. But Simon did not know how to use his good fortune; he became so arrogant that all the barons rebelled. Therefore, Edward took the opportunity to recover the kingdom; he defeated and captured Simon and killed him. He tore him to pieces and had his shameful member <note>A reference to the historical castration and mutilation of Simon de Montfort’s corpse at the Battle of Evesham.</note> put in his mouth. Thus he freed his father, his uncle, and his brothers. 

Times followed where Guy, son of Simon, enjoying the friendship of Charles, Duke of Anjou and brother of Louis, King of France, avenged his father with supreme wickedness in this manner: Charles came to Italy, called by the Pope against Manfred <note>Manfred, King of Sicily, defeated at Benevento in 1266.</note>. Having defeated Manfred and acquired the kingdom of Apulia, he appointed Guy—whose help had been most useful in all the wars—as Vicar of Tuscany. This vicariate had been granted by the Church, which had first had him released by Pope Gregory X from the prisons where he had been placed as an excommunicate. A little later, King Charles returned from Tunis along with King Philip of France and with Henry of Almain <note>Dante refers to him as "Henry of England," the nephew of King Henry III and son of Richard, Earl of Cornwall.</note>, who had been elected King of the Romans <note>Landino notes he was elected Emperor to replace Frederick II.</note>. They came to Viterbo where, the Pope having died, the Cardinals were in disagreement over creating a new pontiff. 

Here Guy, wishing to avenge his father who had been justly killed by Edward, assaulted Henry in the Church of San Silvestro while the priest was showing the body of Christ <note>During the elevation of the Host at Mass.</note>. He killed him, dragged him out of the church by his hair, and fled into the Maremma to the lands of the Red Count, his father-in-law. This was not without infamy for King Charles, who, if he was not complicit as many suspected, ought to have punished him. Henry’s body was carried to London and buried in the chapel of the other kings. Above the tomb was placed a gilded statue which holds a golden cup in its right hand, and within it his embalmed heart; above the heart is a knife as a witness to the murder. In the left hand, it holds a brief <note>A scroll or inscription.</note> whose words are: "I give the heart pierced by the knife to the one who is my kinsman," meaning Edward. From this arose the fact that Edward was never again a friend to Charles nor to the House of France. 

This was therefore a great excess: first, because revenge for his father's death was not justified, as he was killed justly; second, out of respect for the place, because it was in a church and when the body of Christ was being shown; and in the Roman court; and upon the person of a king’s son. For this reason, Dante places him alone <note>Guy de Montfort is set apart from the other souls in the blood.</note>, because he committed a singular excess. **WHO DID THIS** in God’s bosom: in the church, which is the bosom of God. **THE HEART WHICH ON** the Thames still is honored: <note>original: "si cola." Landino provides a specific Latin etymology here.</note> that is, it is honored, because *colere* in the Latin language signifies "to honor." **ON THE** Thames: that is, London, through which the river Thames passes. 

**THEN I SAW PEOPLE**: He shows that as the ditch proceeded further, it had less depth. Thus, the lower the souls were, the more they were out of the blood. He says he recognized many. This demonstrates that the senses, through lower reason, can by themselves recognize such vices in individuals, especially having heard of them from others before. And that the blood is less deep, and that some sinners are further out than others, shows that he who has sinned less is in less pain—contrary to the Stoics, who maintain that all crimes are equal. Dante passed the ditch where the blood became shallowest. By this, he intends nothing else than that he who contemplates vice and is guided by Virgil <note>Representing Reason.</note> passes through it without taking on any stain.

And it is appropriate that just as the ditch on one side decreases and shallows, so on the other side it deepens, so that according to greater and lesser sins there are greater and lesser punishments. And therefore the centaur adds that divine justice pricks and pierces on this side: that is, where the blood is deepest. **THAT** Attila who was a scourge on earth. Attila, King of the Huns, as Paul the Deacon <note>A widely-read 8th-century historian of the Lombards and Romans.</note> writes, in the year 442, being lord of Dacia, Hungary, Macedonia, Moesia, Achaia, and Thrace, was a man most greedy for empire and thirsty for human blood, and cruel above all others. With innumerable troops, he turned his fury toward Italy. With all force and industry, he besieged Aquileia, which was so valiantly defended by its citizens that...

Landino also begins an account of Attila the Hun, explaining that the varying depth of the river of blood represents the proportional nature of divine justice.</summary>

with the heaviest hardships, and after three years he barely conquered it: and cruelly with sword and fire he led it to ultimate ruin. Afterwards, he destroyed Concordia, Altino, and Padua. And he sacked Vicenza, Verona, Brescia, Bergamo, Milan, and Pavia, not without a very great slaughter; and many other lands in Lombardy and Romagna. And finally, having arrived where the Mincio flows into the Po, while he was deliberating whether he should go to Rome, Pope Leo <note>Pope Leo I (the Great), who famously met Attila in 452 AD.</note> arrived; and, not without a divine miracle, he obtained from such a cruel tyrant that he should leave Italy and return to Hungary. Therefore, he returned, having first taken as his wife Honoria, sister of the Emperor Valentinian. And in Hungary, at a banquet, he died from an abundance of blood that came out of his nose; a man greedy for blood drowned in blood. Nor should another miracle be omitted, which gave him the surname by which he was called: Attila, the Scourge of God. Attila had arrived at Modena with his hostile army. And Geminianus, bishop of that city, a man of holy life, trusting in divine help, went out to meet him and asked him who he was. He replied, "I am Attila, the Scourge of God." To whom Geminianus replied, "And I am Geminianus, the servant of God." And after such words, he opened the gates to him. And Attila, moved by divine terror, passed with his men through the middle of the city without harming anyone.

**PYRRHUS.** This was Pyrrhus, the son of Achilles, whom Deidamia, daughter of King Lycomedes, bore. He was called Pyrrhus from the color of his hair, which was red and fiery, because *pyr* in Greek means fire <note>original: "pyringreco significa fuoco"</note>. Likewise, he was called Neoptolemus, which means "new soldier," <note>original: "nuouo soldato"</note> because after the death of his father, while still a youth, he was led into the army at Troy. This man killed with his own hand Polites, the son of Priam; and he sacrificed Polyxena, Priam's daughter, at the tomb of his father; and he killed the aged Priam near the altar where he had fled for refuge. He spared neither old age nor youth, nor the female sex, nor religion. He led into servitude Andromache, the wife of Hector. Afterward, seized by love for Hermione, the daughter of Menelaus, he took her from Orestes. He gave Andromache to Helenus, son of Priam, along with part of the kingdom, because Helenus, with his prophecy, saved him from the perils of the sea. But finally, Orestes, having returned from the Tauric region, killed him in the temple of Apollo. There are some who believe Dante does not name this man, but rather Pyrrhus, King of the Epirotes <note>Pyrrhus of Epirus (318–272 BC), a famous Greek general and opponent of Rome.</note>, born of the lineage of the former, a singular and excellent leader in military discipline. But he was most ambitious, and in order to rule, he provoked many nations from which he had received no injury. He came to Italy, and under the guise of helping the Tarentines, he sought to subjugate the Romans, and for four years he greatly exhausted them. He then passed into Sicily, and having made himself lord of it, he fought many times successfully against the Carthaginians; but in a short time, he lost the island. Therefore, having returned to Epirus, he moved war against Antigonus, King of Macedonia, and drove him most unjustly from the realm. Not content with this, he pursued him to Argos, where he had fled. Having entered the city by force there, he was killed by a roof tile thrown at him by a woman from the windows.

**SEXTUS.** Some understand this to mean Sextus Pompey, son of Pompey the Great, who after the death of his father and brother occupied Sicily, and in those seas became almost a pirate. But all this was to return to his homeland occupied by Augustus. Therefore, I do not see why he deserves to be placed among the tyrants. Rather, we believe that we can more correctly understand this as Sextus Tarquinius, son of Tarquin the Proud <note>The seventh and final legendary King of Rome.</note>, the last king of the Romans; who, pretending to have been beaten and driven out by his father, went to Gabii, a city not far from Rome, to try to take it through treachery since his father had not been able to conquer it with arms; and his fraudulent plan succeeded. For the Gabines, believing that what he feigned was true, received him; and in a short time, as to a man skilled in military discipline, they committed to him the government of the city and the army. Whereupon, he gave it to his father.

**RINIERI DA CORNETO.** Master Rinieri da Corneto, who in his time kept almost the entire Roman coastline in terror with the cruelest acts of banditry, and made the Roman road his prey.

**RINIERI PAZZO.** Master Rinieri de' Pazzi of Valdarno, a man of the same habits, practiced robberies and plundered the roads.

**THEN HE TURNED BACK.** Nessus, having said these words, turned back, recrossing the same ford.

<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>INFERNO</header>

### CANTO XIII OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE .

<image-desc>Illuminated decorative initial 'N' containing a miniature illustration of a landscape with a figure, possibly Dante, entering a dark, dense forest.</image-desc>

Nessus had not yet reached the other side
when we set out through a forest
that was marked by no path.
No green leaves there, but of a dusky color;
no smooth branches, but knotted and twisted;
no fruit was there, but thorns with poison.
Those wild beasts that hold in hatred
the tilled lands between Cecina and Corneto
do not dwell in thickets so harsh or dense.

---

Here begins the second circle, in which those who have used violence against themselves and against their own property are punished. He describes a very thick forest, without any path. I say a forest not of trees, but of thorny bushes. *Nessus had not yet reached the other side.* This shows their speed in walking. For before Nessus <note>The centaur who carried Dante and Virgil across the river of blood in the previous Canto.</note> had recrossed the ditch, they had already entered a wood, that is, a forest; and "bosco" (wood) is a Tuscan word derived from the Greek. For we call a forest a "bosco" because animals graze there; and "to graze" in Greek is called *boskein*. *Marked by no path*: by no way. *Dusky*: black. *Thorns with poison*: thorns, briars, and brambles with poison, because their pricks were as if they were venomous. *Do not dwell*: the Cecina is a river that flows into the sea not far from Vada, where the Maremma <note>A marshy coastal area in Tuscany and Lazio.</note> of Pisa ends; and from this place as far as Corneto, which is a fortified town in the Patrimony, there are many thickets of brambles so dense that they are inhabited by nothing but wild beasts. Some texts do not have "Cecina" but "Cecila," which is a land named Centumcelle <note>Modern-day Civitavecchia.</note> by the ancients; and indeed between this and Corneto they say these thick thickets exist, which he places here for comparison. And this seems more appropriate, because there is a great distance between the Cecina river and Corneto. 

It is a fitting thing that he places the souls of those who have killed themselves to be transformed into bushes. For as there are three powers of the soul within us: the first is called **rational** <term>rational soul: the highest part of the human soul that allows for reason, distinguishing humans from animals</term>, by which we are different from all other animals and similar to the angels and made in the image of God, and through which we contemplate and investigate and acquire sciences and arts, and have prudence in administering ourselves, the family, and the republic. The second is called **sensitive** <term>sensitive soul: the part of the soul responsible for the five senses and basic desires, shared with animals</term>, through which we have external and internal senses and the appetite to either follow what we judge useful or to flee the contrary; and this is common to us and all other animals. The third is named **vegetative** <term>vegetative soul: the basic level of life responsible for growth and nutrition, shared with plants</term>, which nourishes and grows the body and generates another like itself; and this is common not only with other animals but also with plants. 

It appears that he who kills himself has first lost the rational part, which—not only according to theological precepts but also according to **Platonic philosophy** <note>Plato argued in the *Phaedo* that the soul is a soldier at a post and must not abandon it until called by God.</note>—forbids us from casting the soul out of the body, which God has given to it in custody; rather, we should return it when it is requested by the one who created it. Furthermore, he loses the sensitive part, by which not only man but every lowly worm flees death. Therefore, since nothing remains to him but the vegetative part—which is a thing of plants as it is in us—it is a just thing that he be transformed into a plant. And he places here a non-fruiting plant because such a death produces no fruit: neither of fame (like those who for the safety of the fatherland have gone to a voluntary death, like the **Decii** <note>A Roman family (Publius Decius Mus, father and son) famous for sacrificing their lives in battle to ensure victory.</note> and many others), nor of salvation (like the innumerable crowd of martyrs, who, for having voluntarily endured a most cruel death, have acquired eternal life). Nor does it have smooth branches or beautiful leaves; that is, it is not delightful or pleasant, nor of a direct and sincere mind, nor of any good demonstration. But it is black, which signifies gloom and sorrow; and full of twists, meaning many [troubled] thoughts and works; and of thorns, meaning the sharpest stings and remorses of conscience which lead to such desperation. 

And certainly, it is a marvelous fiction in this place, because not only with it does he excellently express the properties of this vice, but he also does not depart from the Sacred Writers. Wherefore Solomon in Ecclesiastes <note>Likely referring to the Book of Sirach/Ecclesiasticus 6:2-3.</note> says: 

> <note>original Latin: "Ne extollas te in cogitatione anime tue sicut thaurus Ne forte elidatur uirtus tua per stultitiam : et relinquaris uelut lignum aridum in heremo ."</note> Do not exalt yourself in the thoughts of your soul like a bull, lest perhaps your strength be shattered through folly, and you be left like a dry tree in the desert. 

Therefore he remains like a dry tree in the desert; nor is it a wonder, because he who falls into despair remains without divine grace. And as Matthew says in the twenty-first chapter: 

> <note>original Latin: "Figura hominis absque gratia est sicut ficus arrida :"</note> The figure of a man without grace is like a withered fig tree. 

And Bernard <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux.</note> says: 

> <note>original Latin: "Homo fine gratia desperans uelut arbor siluestris ferens fructus quibus porci infernales pascuntur :"</note> A man despairing without grace is like a wild tree bearing fruit upon which the hogs of hell feed. 

And certainly, the devil, who is the hog of hell, feeds on the effects of the one who has despaired. And if we look closely at all the fictions the poet makes regarding the punishments and torments of the damned, we will realize that it never happens that they do not somehow arise from sacred Christian doctrine. It is a truly admirable thing that from the opinions of others he makes his own fiction, being at once an excellent poet and an excellent Christian. 

But to return to the first subject: he further describes these bushes as making thick and thorny thickets because such places are the dens and lairs of wild beasts, and no soul can be more savage than that which is an enemy to itself. He places the forest without a path because the despair which induces a man to kill himself arises because he sees no way or path that can lead him where he desires. Furthermore, because through such sins the path of salvation is taken away, and it becomes a **sin against the Holy Spirit** <note>A sin considered unforgivable in Catholic theology because it involves a final rejection of God's mercy.</note>. I know that in this place philosophers and theologians raise the doubt of whether a man can hold himself in hatred, given that the Creator has implanted a singular love for one's own preservation not only in man, but in all created things.

<header>CANTO TWELVE <note>Original: "DVODECIMO". This appears to be a printer's error in the source text, as the commentary and poetry are from Canto XIII.</note></header>

And Paul says to the Ephesians: "No one ever hated his own flesh" <note>Latin: *Nemo unquam carnem suam odio habuit*. From Ephesians 5:29.</note>. How then does any man conceive such hatred against himself that he would kill himself? Especially because, as Thomas Aquinas says, man naturally always desires what is good; and to love is to desire good for the beloved thing, and to hate is to desire evil for the hated thing. To this, one responds that he who kills himself does not do it because he wants to harm himself, but because he believes he is helping himself, and chooses that act in place of a good.

> Here the foul Harpies make their nests,
> who drove the Trojans from the Strophades
> with a grim announcement of future woe.
> They have wide wings, human necks and faces,
> feet with claws, and a great feathered belly;
> they make laments upon the strange, gnarled trees.

The Harpies, according to Hesiod in his *Theogony*, were daughters of Thaumas and Electra, daughter of Ocean; and he names two: Aello and Ocypete. Other poets, and especially the Latins, say they are daughters of Neptune and the Earth, and they hold there to be three, adding Celeno. These Harpies represent avarice <term>avarice: an insatiable greed for riches</term>, which induces men to robbery. Thus they are called "Harpies" because *arpazin* in the Greek language means "to seize" <note>original: "arpazin"</note>. And they are the daughters of Thaumas, that is, of "wonder" <note>Italian: "admiratione"</note>, because the wonder we have for riches—and the opinion of judging them to be very good—induces us to robbery. Others call them daughters of Neptune (the sea) and the Earth, because robberies are committed by sea and by land. Some interpret that three things are found in avarice: First, desiring the things of others. Second, seizing them. Third, hiding them. They similarly interpret the names, saying that Aello is named as if it were *elin allon*, meaning "to choose and want what belongs to another" <note>original: "elin allon"</note>. Ocypete from *ocys* (swift) and *petein* (to fly) <note>original: "ocys... pettin"</note>, because they fly swiftly toward those things. Celeno in Greek signifies "black," and by black they mean obscurity and darkness, as if to hide the things seized. 

WHO DROVE THE TROJANS FROM THE STROPHADES. In the dialogues we wrote concerning the allegorical sense of Virgil, we demonstrated what this signifies. Virgil describes them in this form: "No monster more dismal than these, nor any more cruel pestilence or wrath of the gods ever rose from the Stygian waves. They have the faces of birds like maidens, a most foul discharge from their bellies, hooked hands, and faces always pale with hunger" <note>Latin: "Tristius haud illis monstrum..." quoted from Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book III.</note>. He calls them a "monster" because robbery is entirely contrary to human nature, and he writes that they came from hell because it is not a human thing, but a diabolical one. And because robberies arise from wealth, we showed above how they belong to Pluto <note>The god of the underworld, often conflated with Plutus, the god of wealth.</note>. They are imagined to have maiden faces because the miser, at first meeting, displays extreme modesty, not spending his own money out of parsimony and temperance, and he always preaches this. The rest is a bird of prey with terrible claws to show the rapacity of the miser. They have large wings, which signifies that the miser's greed extends far and flies toward everything. The large belly and the greed for devouring denotes an insatiable appetite. And they defile the tables with filth, because the miser is filthy in everything. 

THEY MAKE LAMENTS UPON THE STRANGE, GNARLED TREES. This denotes that the miser always complains as if he were dying of hunger. And if anyone were to ask why the poet has placed the Harpies in this place, signifying the robbery of the miser: I respond that no one can commit a more injurious robbery than to steal one's own life.

> The good master, before you enter further,
> "Know that you are in the second ring,"
> he began to say to me, "and you shall stay
> until you come to the horrible great sand.
> Therefore look well, and you shall see
> things that would take away belief from my speech."
> I heard wails being drawn from every side,
> and I saw no person who might be making them;
> so that, all bewildered, I stopped.
> I believe that he believed that I believed
> that so many voices issued from among those trunks
> from people who were hidden from us.
> Therefore the master said: "If you break
> any little branch from one of these plants,
> the thoughts you have will all be cut short."

These five stanzas <term>ternarii: three-line stanzas, the building blocks of Dante's poem</term> are quite easy in themselves. Virgil admonishes him that all the forest contains is the second ring, up until the boiling sand where he will enter the third. And because he has to see incredible things here, Virgil does not predict them to him—warning us that when a thing is incredible, it is better not to say it, but to wait until it manifests itself. He shows then that those branches, into which the souls are converted, were lamenting. But since Dante did not see anyone, he did not think the voices issued from them. Virgil, understanding this, told him to break a branch to clarify it. This shows that Virgil reveals this to him not only because the intellect is what creates such fictions, but also because Virgil, in the third book <note>Of the *Aeneid*.</note>, imagines a thing not very different from this: when Aeneas, breaking a shoot growing upon the tomb of Polydorus, saw blood come out and heard a human voice issue forth.

<header>INFERNO</header>

Then I stretched my hand a little forward:
and plucked a tiny branch from a great thorn-bush,
 and its trunk cried out: "Why do you break me?"

After it had become dark with blood,
it began to cry again: "Why do you rip me?
Have you no spirit of pity whatever?
Men we were, and now we are made into brushwood;
truly your hand should have been more merciful,
even if we had been the souls of serpents."
As from a green log that is burning
at one of its ends, and from the other it moans
and hisses because of the wind escaping;
So from that broken splinter came forth together
both words and blood; whereat I let the tip
fall, and I stood like a man who is afraid.

"If he had been able to believe it before,"
responded my sage, "O wounded soul,
what he has seen only through my verse <note>Virgil refers to his own poem, the *Aeneid*, specifically the episode of Polydorus (Book III), where a bush bleeds when its roots are pulled.</note>,
he would not have stretched out his hand against you;
but the incredible thing made me
induce him to a deed that weighs on me myself.
But tell him who you were, so that instead
of some reparation, he may refresh your fame
in the world above, where he is permitted to return."

And the trunk: "You so entice me with sweet speech
that I cannot remain silent; and may it not burden you
if I am lured a little into speaking.
I am he who held both the keys
of Frederick's <note>Emperor Frederick II (1194–1250). The speaker is his chancellor, Pier delle Vigne.</note> heart, and I turned them,
locking and unlocking so softly,
that I excluded almost every man from his secrets;
I bore such faith to the glorious office,
that because of it I lost both sleep and life <note>original: "le uene epolsi" (veins and pulses). This refers to the loss of his health or his very life.</note>.
The harlot <note>This refers to Envy, often personified as a prostitute in the courts of kings.</note> who never from the house [of Caesar]...

<column-break/>

We have already said why the author wants these souls to be converted into brushwood. Now he makes them thorny: because just as thorn-bushes are difficult to handle and harmful to those who touch them, so these people were harmful to themselves. Nor do those who stripped themselves of their human bodies deserve any other body. **AS FROM A LOG.** A *stizo* or *tizone* is what we call a piece of charred wood, and it is an excellent comparison; for just as this, when it burns at one end, the other end hisses and blows. So through that broken end came out wind, which then formed words. **BECAUSE OF THE WIND ESCAPING.** This shows the cause. Every time moisture in a narrow space is oppressed by heat—because it cannot escape all at once—it is converted into spirits and wind, which exit with the force of that confinement. As we see in the cannon <term>bombarda: an early type of cannon or mortar</term>: where the saltpeter—a very humid thing—pushed by the heat which, together with the sulfur, generates such a fury of wind that it pushes any great weight and hurls it from a distance. **WHEREAT I LET THE TIP fall, and stood like a man who is afraid.** This happens to anyone who unexpectedly hears or sees a miraculous thing. Because he stops, and his mind remains so occupied by that wonder that his strength abandons his body; and if he has anything in his hand, it falls. And he takes horror at such a thing, especially if it proceeds from something he himself has done, as here: where, having broken the branch, that break sent out words and blood.

Virgil responds **O WOUNDED SOUL**: that is, offended soul. If Dante had been able to believe, merely by my verse—that is, by my words—what he has now seen, he would not have stretched out his hand against you. **BUT THE INCREDIBLE THING** made me induce him to do the breaking of this branch. **WHICH WEIGHS ON ME MYSELF**: that is, it is troublesome to me that he has offended you. **BUT TELL HIM WHO YOU WERE** in the world, so that instead of some reparation—that is, in exchange for some restoration of the damage he did to you—he may **REFRESH** your fame in the world: that is, renew your reputation. It is as if he said: if he offended you by breaking you, in place of this harm he will restore you by refreshing your fame in the world. **WHERE HE IS PERMITTED**: that is, he is allowed and able to return. It is the duty of the intellect, whenever the senses err, to placate the offended party. Therefore, he first offers an excuse, saying that this is one of those things that lower reason would not have believed without experience. Then he promises to compensate for the injury in the only way he could: which was nothing other than giving him fame. And certainly it is so. For if Dante breaks a branch—that is, defames him for this vice—he gives him fame for many other virtues, as you will see below, where he shows that the highest prudence and the highest faith were in him.

He could not have used a more suitable speech toward one who had died with a false reputation among men than to promise him the refreshing of his fame. Thus the soul responds that it is "baited" by his words. For there can be no greater bait to one who has been wrongly defamed than to give him hope that his reputation will be restored. Nor, certainly, is there a soul so lowly that it is not greedy for glory and fame. Therefore, everyone tries to flee the infamy given to them, especially if it is undeserved. **ENTICE** <note>original: "adeschi"</note> is a metaphor from fowlers <term>giuccellatori: people who catch birds using lures or decoys</term> who put out bait for birds to get them accustomed...

This follows the same metaphor, because when

like the bird-catcher who holds birds with bird-lime

<column-break/>

and false witnesses, were able to persuade the Emperor that Sir Piero had secret dealings with Pope Innocent <note>Pope Innocent IV, a fierce political rival of Frederick II.</note>, then the Emperor's enemy, and that he had revealed important secrets to him. Frederick, being too credulous, had him blinded <note>The original term "abbacinare" refers to a method of blinding where a red-hot metal basin was held before the eyes.</note> in such a way that he remained sightless, and he stripped him of his dignity. After this, Sir Piero went to live in Pisa. There—either because the Pisans did not treat him as he felt he deserved, or because his misfortune tormented him more every day—led into total desperation, he asked his guide one day where in Pisa they were. Upon hearing they were near the church of San Paolo on the banks of the Arno, he had his face turned toward the church wall. Then, moving with the greatest force he could muster, with his head forward like a ram going to butt, he smashed his head against the wall and, his brain being shattered, he died instantly. Others say that after the Emperor had him blinded (who at that time was in San Miniato al Tedesco), he had him placed on a horse and led to Pisa; there, placed before the church of Saint Andrew and asking where he was, the indignation of having been falsely accused and condemned was so great that he struck his head against the wall until he died. Some say he died while imprisoned. Others say that while he was in his palace in Capua and the Emperor was passing by, he threw himself from the windows. Furthermore, in front of the palace in Naples, there was a statue of the Emperor and one of Sir Piero; at the Emperor’s feet were men seeking justice, and a brief inscription on the Emperor’s statue said they should go to Piero delle Vigne, who had all the Emperor's authority in every matter. This demonstrates how great the authority of this secretary was. **WHO HELD BOTH THE KEYS**: of "yes" and "no," of denying and granting, because Frederick neither denied nor granted anything without his counsel. **THAT FROM HIS SECRET almost everyone I excluded.** Because the Emperor trusted almost no one but me. **FAITH I BORE TO the glorious office.** It was a great glory to be his chancellor, and I exercised that office faithfully. **MY VEINS AND PULSES**: that is, life itself, which consists of the blood in the veins and the vital spirits whose movement is called the pulse (since *pulsare* in Latin means to beat). **THE WHORE**: He uses "the whore" as a metaphor for Envy, which is a common vice. For just as a whore approaches a man not for true love but out of greed for his possessions, so Envy looks upon another’s good in order to take it away or diminish it. **FROM CAESAR’S HOUSE**: From the Emperor's court. Every emperor is called "Caesar" because the first to establish that seat in Rome was Gaius Julius Caesar. **LEWD EYES** <note>original: "occhi pucti"</note>: that is, whorish eyes, as if greedy to usurp the goods of others. *Meretrix* (whore) in Latin signifies a woman who sells her modesty for gain. Therefore, even if a woman is immodest or an adulteress, she is not a "meretrix" unless she does it for profit; she is called *meretrix* because *merere* in Latin means to engage in base profit <note>original: "merere in latino significa exercitare uile guadagno"</note>. Thus, he rightly said Envy was a whore: because just as the whore enriches herself to impoverish others, so Envy desires to do. **INFLAMED AGAINST ME**: that is, she kindled the hearts of all the barons with spite and envy, to whom it was bothersome that I was so honored. **AND THE INFLAMED** souls of the barons **INFLAMED AUGUSTUS**: that is, with false testimony they incited the Emperor, who is called "Augustus" for this reason: After Octavian, born of his sister and made his adopted son by his will, succeeded Julius Caesar in the empire, the entire Roman city desired to honor him. Because the city was divided into three orders—Senatorial, Equestrian, and Plebeian—each gave him a name as an ornament. Therefore there were three: Caesar, Quirinus, and Augustus. The name "Caesar" made him like his father. "Quirinus" made him like Romulus, the first founder of Rome, who was called Quirinus, meaning "lord," because *kyrios* <note>original: "ciranos"</note> in Greek means lord. Or perhaps for the spear he used in battle, which the Sabines (neighbors of the Romans) called *Quiris*. "Augustus" means a place to be venerated and consecrated by augury. Therefore, Augustus...

...and as something sacrosanct. From this, it was born that all his successors until these times are called Caesars and Augusti: just as all the kings of Alba were named Silvius after Silvius the first king; and all the kings of Egypt were named Ptolemy after Ptolemy the first king. Therefore, the name of this emperor was Frederick II: but Caesar and Augustus are common names for all emperors. **THAT** Happy honors turned into sad mourning: because he was imprisoned and then blinded. **UNJUST** I made myself against my just self. I was just because I had not erred against Frederick: but I became unjust against myself by taking my life undeservedly. **TO MY** Lord who was so worthy of honor. It seems the author contradicts himself by calling Frederick worthy of honor, whom he previously placed as a heretic and enemy of the Apostolic See. But I respond that it is not the poet speaking now, but Master Piero <note>Pier delle Vigne</note>, who, wishing to persuade that he did not betray him, calls him worthy of honor; so that through this it might seem plausible that he would not have betrayed one so worthy. Or rather, let us say that although he had the vice mentioned above, he was nevertheless excellent in many other things: and especially in military discipline and in lordship. For he was much feared by Christians and Saracens alike. He was Emperor of the Romans, King of the Germans <note>original: "Re deglalamani"</note>, Duke of Swabia, King of Apulia: and held a large part of Syria. He had noble sons, namely Henry the Lame, but of high intellect; the most beautiful Conradin; and the most generous Manfred. He built many castles. He was of medium height with a cheerful appearance, prudent, quite literate, universal in every thing, and skilled in many mechanical arts. He knew the Latin, German, French, Greek, and Turkish languages. Brave in arms, although prone to lust.

the poet said to me: "Do not lose the hour:
but speak and ask him if more pleases you."

He introduces that while Piero is silent, Virgil encourages Dante to ask him if he wants to know anything else: And Dante responds: "Ask those things that you believe will satisfy me." And this is the right order in the soul of man: whose appetite is already made obedient to reason. For Dante—that is, the appetite—does not move to ask if Virgil—that is, the intellect—does not admonish him to ask. And even then he does not ask: because the appetite and the inferior reason do not know how to choose what is good to know if the intellect does not show it to them. Therefore he requests that Virgil ask for him the things which he judges should satisfy him. And Dante says he cannot ask himself because of the compassion he feels for that spirit. But allegorically it shows that the various perturbations, which are in the appetite and the inferior reason, do not allow one to ask and contemplate noble things. Then Virgil asks for what reason the soul is enclosed in that wood, and if it ever comes out.

Virgil had asked two things. First, in what way the soul is bound in these briars. Second, if it is ever released. The spirit responds to the first: that when the savage soul—that is, cruel and brutal toward itself—departs from the body from which it violently uproots itself, it falls into this seventh circle. **FALLS** like a heavy thing by the weight of sin: and like a thing cast down by fury. **AND NO PLACE** is chosen. For among those who kill themselves out of desperation, it does not seem there is a degree where one deserves more punishment than another. **WHERE FORTUNE** slings it: And allegorically it shows that the desperate person strikes where fortune pushes them without any consideration. And where it falls in the forest, there it stops: and begins to put down roots as the grain sown in the earth does. **GRAIN OF SPELT** <note>Spelt is a type of ancient hulled wheat; the commentator uses it here to represent any seed.</note> He put the species for the genus, saying grain, that is, a grain of spelt, for every seed. **RISES INTO A SAPLING.** He describes the natural succession...

# CANTO TWELVE

...they will make a forest of our hanging bodies, each to the thorn of its own molesting shade.

That a savage soul should be converted into a fruit-bearing plant: leaves. They denote the constant memory of the robbery committed <note>The "robbery" refers to the suicide "stealing" their own life from God and nature</note>. They feed on the leaves: that is, such recollection gnaws at the mind. The leaves induce pain. AND THEY MAKE A WINDOW FOR THE PAIN: it sends forth the voice. LIKE THE OTHERS WE SHALL COME: these souls will return for their bodies like the others: But having been cast away as a vile thing, it is not just that they should have them back. That which man has taken from himself.

> We were still intent upon the trunk,
> believing that it wished to say more to us,
> when we were surprised by a noise.
> Similar to him who feels the coming
> of the boar and the hunt to his post,
> who hears the beasts and the branches crashing.

> of himself and a bush he made a huddle <note>original: "groppo"</note>.

> of black bitches, ravenous and running,

> Into him who had crouched they set their teeth,

Toppo: that is, the clashing of lances in battle: and having said these words, lacking breath: that is, a knot in a shrub where the soul was. BEHIND [them] ravenous and running bitches. He imagines these men being persecuted by the conscience of having thrown away their own [possessions]: and hunger: and necessary things: And the infamy and the scorns that follow are so terrible to the human soul. They are black, that is, full [of grief]. RUNNING: because these anxieties with great speed... [seek] to hide in a place where they are not found by those and...

<column-break/>

...and an increase of the plant. Because first it groans to be [broken]: then a tender sprout arises: and finally, growing, it becomes a tree. INTO A WILD PLANT: because it is not fitting and domestic <note>Wild plants represent the "unnatural" state of the suicide's soul</note>. The HARPIES <note>Mythological monsters with bird bodies and human faces</note> feeding then on its [leaves] in its own life and in its own body. These CAUSE PAIN. Because by tearing the [leaves], the spirit sends forth its voice through such a rupture. LIKE THE OTHERS WE SHALL COME: he demonstrates that in the resurrection of the bodies they will not clothe themselves in them: because having [discarded] them... As if to say, it is not just that one should have back that which [they threw away].

HE HAS placed up to this point those who have used violence against their own persons. Now he places the punishments of those who used violence against their own property: and have beastially consumed it. He describes them also as naked because they are stripped of their substances: and scratched: because everyone vituperates them and tears at their reputation: and of their ugly life. They flee: because those who are placed in such misery, being ashamed, flee through the forest: that is, through dark and solitary places and [away from] the sight of men. THEY BREAK THE BRANCHES of the spirits. Because as an excuse for themselves they defame those who have killed themselves, saying even that he did worse than me. Or truly they break the branches <note>original: "roste"</note>: that is, having consumed their own, they take from that of others. He places then two fleeing: and the one in front said "Hurry, death." This was Lano of Siena <note>Lano da Siena was a member of a group of wealthy youths who squandered their fortunes and died at the battle of Pieve del Toppo in 1288</note> who consumed all his goods while in the army of the Sienese sent against the Aretines in favor of the Florentines. And afterward, returning, they were assaulted at the Pieve del Toppo in the territory of Arezzo: and defeated: where Lano, although he could have withdrawn to safety, nevertheless as one desperate threw himself among the enemies: and wished rather to die than to live in such poverty. This is what Iacopo of Padua <note>Iacopo da Santo Andrea, famous for his senseless extravagance, such as throwing money into a river</note> now reproaches him for, saying "your legs were not so nimble at fleeing the jousts," which was between the Sienese and those of Arezzo. That is, the power in running / he entangled himself and made a huddle. BEHIND THEM THE FOREST WAS FULL OF BLACK BITCHES: and by the bitches he means the remorses, the hunger, and the lack of clothing; and of other [necessities]. They see and hear [what people] do. All these things are [colors] of mourning: and of sorrow, ravenous to bite. AND they follow the man wherever he goes: nor can he hide. Torn apart.

MY ESCORT: and correctly because the intellect is our escort which leads the secure appetite. TOOK ME BY THE HAND: as one does who wants to guide someone so they do not err in the path; or not fall. So the superior intellect guards the sensuality so that while it follows it in contemplation, it does not wander: or fall into the sin that is contemplated. <meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, Canto XIII, specifically focusing on the punishment of the squanderers—those who violently destroyed their own earthly possessions—and the soul of a suicide from Florence who has become a bush.</meta>

<columns>2</columns>
<header>INFERNO</header>

...tell [me] who you were, you who through so many wounds produced with blood a sorrowful speech <note>original: "sermo"</note>.

[This follows the] fury of the hounds that had torn Lano apart. 

### GIACOMO DA SANTO ANDREA
This man was a nobleman from Padua, from the chapel of Saint Andrew. He was very wealthy, but he consumed his substance in a most beastly manner. Among his other follies: once, while traveling along the Brenta river toward Venice with other young nobles, and seeing that each of them was busy playing music or singing, he—not wanting to appear idle—began throwing his coins one by one into the river. Another time, when many young men were coming to visit him at his villa, he saw them from a distance and, to honor them with a spectacle, he ordered all the huts and houses of his laborers to be set on fire. 

### WHAT DID IT AVAIL YOU 
To make a screen—that is, a shelter—of me? It is as if the bush says: "You hid yourself within my branches to be sheltered from the hounds, but it availed you nothing." *Schermo* means shelter or protection, from which we get the word *schermire* [to fence or parry], which is nothing other than protecting oneself from blows. Petrarch also says: "I find no other screen <note>original: "schermo"</note> to save me from the clear notice of the people." 

### THROUGH SO MANY wounds: 
Through the many punctures and bites received from the dogs when they tore Giacomo apart while he was hidden inside you. 

### BLOWING YOU MAKE a sorrowful speech: 
That is, a sorrowful way of speaking.

> And he to us: "O souls who have arrived
> to see the shameful slaughter
> of my leaves so severed from me:
> Gather them at the foot of the wretched bush.
> I was of the city that for the Baptist
> changed its first patron: wherefore for this
> He will always make it sorrowful with his art:
> and if it were not that on the passage of the Arno
> there still remains some sight of him:
> Those citizens who later rebuilt it
> upon the ashes that remained from Attila
> would have had it worked in vain:
> I made a gibbet for myself of my own houses."

<column-break/>

**T**he spirit responds, first by praying that they gather his leaves. The poet demonstrates that the spirit asks for his leaves to be collected for no other reason than to show how innate the desire is in every creature to preserve its own being, even when in the depths of misery. Through this supreme desire, he silently suggests how great the regret is for having taken one's first life, since in the second life—though it is most unhappy—the soul still wishes to maintain itself. This concludes that he would willingly return to the first life. This is the sentiment of Virgil where he says:
> The next places are held by the sorrowful who, though innocent, brought death upon themselves with their own hand and, hating the light, threw away their souls. How they would now wish to endure both poverty and hard labors in the air above! Fate stands in the way. <note>original: "Proxima deinde tenent moesti loca qui sibi letum Insonti peperere manu; uitamque perosi proiecere animas quam uellent ethere in alto Nunc et pauperiem et duros perferre labores Fata obstat."</note>

The spirit responds first to this. Then he narrates that he is a Florentine, though without naming the city of Florence. Instead, he uses a circumlocution, saying, "I was of the city," which changed its first patron—who in the time of the pagans was Mars—for the Baptist—that is, Saint John the Baptist. Because Florence was founded by the soldiers of Sulla <note>Roman citizens</note>, they chose Mars as the astrological "ascendant" for its founding, as he was the primary god of the Romans. They built a temple to him which still stands <note>The Baptistery of San Giovanni</note>, and in it was his equestrian statue, honored with solemn sacrifices until the Gospel truth spread through Florence. Once the city became Christian, they dedicated the temple of Mars to the Highest God under the title of Saint John the Baptist, choosing him as patron in place of Mars. 

### WHEREFORE FOR THIS: 
That is, for the reason that the temple once dedicated to himself was rededicated to the Baptist. 

### HE WILL ALWAYS MAKE IT SORROWFUL: 
Meaning the land will be in sadness and tribulation. 

### WITH HIS ART: 
With wars, which are the art of Mars; because the city will always be engaged in wars, either civil or external. Giovanni Villani, the diligent writer of the Florentine chronicle, relates that when the temple of Mars was dedicated to Saint John the Baptist, they removed the statue of Mars, which was an equestrian statue—that is, on horseback—made of stone by a skilled sculptor. Because there were certain ancient prophecies stating that this statue had been made under such a constellation that if it were ever kept in a place less than honorable, or if it suffered any violence, great harm would come to the city, they placed it upon a tower near the Arno. It remained there until Florence was destroyed by Attila <note>Historical accounts often confused Attila the Hun with Totila the Ostrogoth</note>. Attila, King of the Goths, having destroyed many cities in Lombardy and Romagna, passed into Tuscany and besieged Florence. Unable to take it by force, he turned his mind to deception. With many false persuasions, he induced the citizens to receive him inside the city. He was placed in the Capitol. Under the guise of honor, he summoned the principal citizens to him; as they passed from one room to another, he had them killed and thrown into a stream which, diverted from the Arno, passed beneath the Capitol. The people realized the slaughter when they saw the waters of the stream turn bloody. As the people rioted, Attila sent his soldiers through the land and commanded them to kill everyone—males and females, small and great. None escaped except those who fled. Among others, Mauritius, the Florentine bishop of most holy life, was killed. After this slaughter, he destroyed the city with iron and fire. At that time, the statue of Mars fell into the Arno. (And he says this occurred in the year of our Lord 450, on the twenty-eighth day of June, five hundred and twenty years after the city's founding). Those who escaped the slaughter and their descendants often wished to rebuild the city, but they were forbidden by the people of Fiesole and by...

Having discussed the squanderer Giacomo da Santo Andrea, the text now turns to the final lines of the Canto, where an anonymous Florentine suicide speaks about the history and superstitions of his city, specifically the ancient statue of Mars and the city's destruction and rebuilding.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>CANTO XIII</header>
<sig>.L.iiii</sig>

...certain nobles in the surrounding area ceased until the times of Charlemagne. Charlemagne, Emperor of the Romans, and the Roman people themselves—moved by the prayers of the Florentines—provided aid to rebuild it. Many noblemen came from Rome to inhabit it along with those who had remained. It was rebuilt in the year of Christ 802 at the beginning of April. Others say on the 30th of March. At that time, the statue of Mars was found in the Arno, though it was broken; and because of the same opinion they held regarding it, they placed it upon a pillar at the Old Bridge <note>The *Ponte Vecchio*.</note>. And there it stayed until the year of Christ 1333, in which year such a flood occurred that the Arno swept away the Old Bridge and the other two bridges below it; and in this manner, the statue was ruined once again. 

Therefore, in this passage, Dante presents the opinion that our ancestors held regarding this statue—an opinion which many say is heretical. However, these are not Dante's own words, nor his opinion, but the words of the spirit who speaks. Dante prompts him to say this to demonstrate a common opinion held by many. I also believe (always yielding to a truer judgment) that it is not contrary to our religion that, according to astrology, a statue might be fashioned under such a constellation as to possess some momentum and power within itself. 

Thus, Paolo the Florentine, an excellent mathematician of his time, placed the statue of the lion <note>The *Marzocco*, the lion symbol of Florence.</note> upon the railing that encircles the Florentine palace <note>The *Palazzo Vecchio*.</note>, with its head facing toward Milan. Many believe this was of no small help against the power of the Visconti family, who in those times were formidable to our Republic. We also read that Zoroaster the Persian, in Thebes, the hundred-gated city <note>original: "ecatompyle"</note> of Egypt, built the statue of Memnon with a lyre <note>original: "cythara"</note> that would sound. 

Regarding the slaughter and destruction of Florence, I do not dare to speak against the opinion of so great a poet. However, I do not know how Attila could have done this; for Paul the Deacon and others who wrote the history of Attila affirm that he never came into Tuscany, nor did he ever cross the Apennines <note>Historical scholars note that Dante likely confused Attila the Hun with Totila, King of the Ostrogoths, who besieged Florence in the 6th century.</note>. Furthermore, Alcuin <note>original: "Alchindo," referring to Alcuin of York.</note>, who diligently wrote of the deeds of Charlemagne, makes no mention that he restored Florence; he only narrates that he was present in Florence for two Easters. 

**AND HAD IT NOT BEEN AT THE PASSAGE OF THE ARNO...** 
The poet concludes that if the said statue had not been honorably replaced upon the pillar of the Old Bridge, this second rebuilding would have been in vain, because the city would have perished once more. 

**SOME SIGHT:** 
Because the statue was not whole but broken, and what remained was eroded by the injury of time and by its great age. 

**I MADE MYSELF A GIBBET.** 
This spirit concludes that he hanged himself in his own house. *Iubetto* <note>Gibbet.</note> in the city of Paris is the place where the gallows are, and where those condemned to such punishment are hanged. Therefore, "he made a gibbet of his houses"—that is, he turned them into a place for a gallows. 

The poet does not expressly state who this man was. But some wish it to be understood as Messer Rocco de’ Mozzi, who, having consumed his great and varied riches, hanged himself to escape the hardships of poverty. Others understand it to be Messer Lotto degli Agli, who, out of repentance for having given a false judgment, hanged himself with his own golden belt. Messer Giovanni Boccaccio says that in those times many Florentines hanged themselves; and for this reason, Dante leaves it ambiguous as to who this person was.

<header>INFERNO</header>

# CANTO XIV OF THE FIRST CANTICLE OF DANTE

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'P' featuring a blue background with gold leaf and red floral patterns, set within a square frame.</image-desc>

->Since the love of my native place<-
->constrained me, I gathered the scattered leaves<-
->and gave them back to him who was already faint.<-
->Then we came to the stream where the<-
->second ring is separated from the third, and where<-
->a horrible art of justice is seen.<-

...sons of one same homeland. And this is an excellent fiction by Dante. Because if he speaks of Messer Rocco de' Mozzi <note>A Florentine man who hanged himself</note>: since he had used violence against his own person, Dante properly placed him first; and because he was also blameworthy regarding his property, he had him torn by the hounds. And afterward, they came to the boundaries that divide this second ring from the third: where those who have been impious toward God are punished.

->To clearly manifest new things,<-
->I say that we arrived at a plain<-
->which removes every plant from its bed.<-
->The sorrowful wood garlands it<-
->around, just as the dismal trench does to it;<-
->there we halted our steps at the very edge.<-
->The space was a thick and dry sand,<-
->not made in any other fashion than that<-
->which was once trodden by the feet of Cato.<-

...after the death of Pompey in Egypt, he led the remains of the Pompeian armies to join in Africa with Juba of the Numidians, who followed the Pompeian side. He deservedly places this sandy place here, without any plants. For just as sand produces no fruit and is always sterile, so the sin which is against God and against nature—beyond the fact that it kills the soul—is also without any fruit or utility to the body. Fire rains there from heaven because no sin, of any kind, better knows how to make the flaming wrath of God descend from heaven. Furthermore, God, who is the highest thing, is offended. Therefore, the highest element <note>Fire was traditionally considered the "highest" and lightest of the four elements.</note> is the punishment. Furthermore, there can be no greater ignition of a most proud punishment than to use it against God. Nor more burning lust than using it against nature; nor more inflamed greed of avarice than using it against art <note>This refers to usury, which Dante considers violence against industry/art.</note>. It is also appropriate that He punishes them with fire, because we see that God prepared such a punishment for Sodom and Gomorrah. And this sand is surrounded by the forest, the receptacle of wild beasts, because such vice has no kind of humanity in itself but is entirely bestial. And as the forest is dark, so the minds of these people are entirely deprived of the light of reason. In this place, they halted their steps at the edge <note>original: *aranda*, meaning "raasente" or right at the border</note>. This signifies that they did not set foot in the burning sand at all, but they approached as near as they could to it. This denotes that to speculate upon this vice, we must examine it closely; but in no way should we set our feet there—that is, our thoughts. For it is a horrendous and highly abominable thing not only to commit such a sin but even to think of it.

->O vengeance of God, how much you should<-
->be feared by everyone who reads<-
->what was manifest to my eyes.<-
->I saw many flocks of naked souls,<-
->who were all weeping very miserably;<-
->and different laws seemed imposed upon them.<-
->Some people lay supine on the ground;<-
->some sat all huddled up;<-
->and others walked continually.<-
->Those who went around were more numerous.<-

<column-break/>

In this fourteenth canto, the poet treats the punishments of those who have used violence against God. He demonstrates that, constrained by the love of his native place—that is, his homeland—because he was a Florentine, he gathered the leaves scattered by the black hounds as the spirit had begged him, and gave them back to him; who, through many laments, was already faint. And in passing, he shows how strong the bond should be between those who are children of one same homeland.

**W**ishing to manifest the third ring, I say that we arrived at a plain <note>original: *landa*, meaning a sandy flat or moor</note>: that is, a sandy plain—for this is what *landa* and *lama* signify—which removes from itself every plant, because neither grass nor trees grow there. THE SORROWFUL WOOD WHICH GARLANDS: that is, surrounds and circles it. AS THE DISMAL TRENCH: that is, the river Phlegethon <note>original: *phlegetote*</note> surrounds that wood, of which we shall speak below. THE SPACE WAS A SAND: he says that the space of this plain was of such sand as is that of the deserts of sandy Libya, through which Marcus Cato [Cato the Younger], after the defeat of Thessaly and after...

**O** VENGEANCE OF GOD. We say Justice is a virtue which, with constant and perpetual will, attributes to everyone their right as it is fitting. And this is divided into Religion, Innocence, Peace, Concord, Piety, Integrity, and Vengeance. And vengeance or "vendetta," when it is a species of justice, is defined as justice which, with measure and with reason, punishes him who has done injury, or defends him who is injured. Therefore, he did not say "vengeance" to mean a certain satisfaction of anger, as many do who avenge injuries not to observe justice, but to satisfy anger and hatred.

The commentary explains the symbolism of the sterile sand and the nature of divine justice and vengeance.</summary>

and that which lay less [prone] in the torment:
but had its tongue more loosed to its grief.

dilated flakes of fire rained down,
like snow in the Alps when there is no wind.

<margin>Violence against God: and they deserved greater punishment, lying supine. And those who had used [violence] against nature and art, such as the usurers, sat huddled to touch as little of the sand as possible. And nevertheless, they had more pain than those who were walking. And those who had used [violence] against nature were walking. These are the sodomites. It is not without merit that he places these violent ones to be punished by fire for the reasons already stated above.</margin>

As Alexander, in those hot parts
of India, saw above his host
flakes of flames falling even to the ground:
Wherefore he provided for trampling the soil
with his ranks, because the vapor
was extinguished better while it was alone:
Such was the descent of the eternal heat:
whereby the sand caught fire like tinder
under the steel, to double the pain.
Without rest ever was the dance
of the miserable hands, now here, now there,
shaking off from themselves the fresh burning.

<margin>This miraculous thing is not written by Quintus Curtius <note>A Roman historian of Alexander the Great</note>, who diligently narrates his history; nor by Justin, who puts it compendiously. Nor is it in Plutarch in his life [of Alexander]. But they say that Alexander writes this to Aristotle. And Albertus Magnus in his *Meteorologica* says: that that region is under Cancer; where the heat of the sun scorches the watery vapor: and draws up the thick terrestrial vapor: which is driven by the coldness of the earth: and ignites it; and it falls in the form of snow even to the ground. And the remedy that Alexander used was excellent. Because he made the ground be trampled much to extinguish the vapor already ignited before one could join with the other. **OVER HIS HOST**: his army. **WHEREFORE HE PROVIDED FOR TRAMPLING**: to tread upon **THE SOIL**; the earth, which in Latin is called <note>original: "solus"</note>. **WHILE IT WAS ALONE**. Not joined to a thing that could ignite it. **WITHOUT REST EVER WAS THE DANCE**. "Tresca" <note>dance</note> signifies a dance which has in itself swift movement. Wherefore here he says the "dance of the hands"; the swift movement of the hands to shield themselves from the flames.</margin>

I began: "Master, you who overcome
all things, except the stubborn demons
who came out against us at the entrance of the gate.
Who is that great one who does not seem to care
for the fire, and lies scornful and twisted,
so that the rain does not seem to ripen him?"
And that same one, who was so alert

Though Jove weary his blacksmith, from whom

wherewith on my last day I was smitten;
and though he weary the others, turn by turn,

his: But he said "O vengeance," that is, O justice which

who reads of the punishments; with which God avenges

Because those who had used violence...

<margin>India begins from the Median mountains, a very healthy region: and twice a year it has summer: and it makes two harvests of grain. Megasthenes and Dionysius write that it once had five thousand cities and nine thousand peoples. It is so fertile that no people of India ever departs to inhabit elsewhere. It was judged to be the third part of the world. Bacchus was the first who triumphed over India. Afterward, Alexander the Great. The largest rivers of that place are the Ganges, otherwise Gihon <note>original: "Geon"</note>; and the Indus, otherwise Pishon <note>original: "phison"</note>: and from this, it is named India. The poet says, therefore, that such flakes of flames fell upon these sinners as Alexander saw fall in India upon his army.</margin>

He begins to treat the punishments of those violent
against God: And he feigns that the first he saw

Except the stubborn demons. Above, when
we treated the entry into the city of Dis, we explained
allegorically why Virgil had overcome
every other thing which they had found in
Hell: except the demons: who, placed as
guards of the gate of Dis, could not harm.
Therefore, I do not repeat what has already been said
once. **WHO IS THAT GREAT ONE WHO DOES NOT SEEM**
**TO CARE FOR THE FIRE.** He demonstrates excellently the
nature of the impious: because no pride can be
equal to that of him who denies the divine essence.
And he estimates that the world is governed rather by chance
than by the providence of that [essence]; and by adversity
and calamity that might come to him, he does not change his
purpose: And he does not believe that such unhappiness is sent...

->As he did at the battle of Phlegra<-
<note>The Battle of Phlegra was the mythological conflict where the Giants attempted to overthrow the Olympian gods; Jupiter defeated them with his thunderbolts.</note>

<column-break/>

by divine justice through the deserved punishments of his impious wickedness: But he remains obstinate; and rises in **pride**; and in **anger**: both in deeds: and in words. **AND HE DOES NOT SEEM TO CARE FOR THE FIRE.** Because through pride he wishes to show that he does not let

<column-break/>

himself be conquered. **ET GIACE** <note>original: "AND HE LIES"</note>: Not humble and with repentance for the error committed, but **CONTEMPTUOUS AND TWISTED**. This signifies the obstinacy of the soul and its perversity: and a mind not directed [toward God]: and a depraved opinion. **SO THAT THE RAIN** does not seem to ripen him. We call the soul "unripe" or "bitter" <note>Italian: *acerbo*</note> when it remains stubborn and resistant against that which it ought to be obedient to. And conversely, we say a person is "mature" <note>Italian: *maturo*</note> who finally, after many lashes, recognizes his fault: and surrenders: and humbles himself. And this is a metaphor drawn from apples; which while they are unripe are stubborn and adverse to the taste; and when mature are the opposite. **AND THAT SAME ONE.** Dante—that is, the "lower reason"—asks Virgil—who is the "higher reason"—who that great one is: that is, what is the nature of this impiety. But before Virgil can answer him, Capaneus—that is, such a vice—manifests itself. And truly no vice is greater than this. But also, there is none that manifests itself more than this. Nor is Virgil needed; that is, any hidden doctrine or sharpness of intellect to recognize it. **HE SHOUTED: AS I WAS ALIVE, SUCH AM I DEAD.** He shouted, which is a sign of the proud: and he shouted to denote that they show themselves for what they are: and publicly boast of such bestiality. Which proceeds from supreme foolishness. Whence the prophet [said]: <note>original Latin: *Dixit insipiens in corde suo non est deus*</note> *The fool has said in his heart, there is no God.* **AS I WAS ALIVE, SUCH AM I DEAD**: that is, even now, thus damned, I do not repent. In which there can be no greater penalty for him. Because it is an insupportable torment to one who denies and despises the power of another, nonetheless to see himself continually and most bitterly afflicted by that same power. **OR RATHER** "as I was alive": that is, the same pride and impiety: which I had while alive: that is, placed in supreme happiness; such have I dead, that is, afflicted by supreme misery. **THOUGH JOVE WEARY.** Through the words that the author has Capaneus say, he demonstrates and perfectly expresses the nature of this Luciferian pride. Because such men, even when placed in extreme misery—which ought to tame them—become even more proud at every hour: like this man who, struck by lightning into the depths of Hell by Jove, is so obstinate that he says even if Jove were to tire out all the blacksmiths in making thunderbolts: and had spent them all on him, he would not humble himself. **THOUGH JOVE WEARY** his blacksmith: understand this to be Vulcan: whom the poets feign manufactures the bolts for Jove. The ancients posited Jove, Minerva, Vulcan, and Vesta to express the various natures of fire. Because we consider fire in its superior element which is harmless: and for this they call it Jove: because he "helps" <note>A play on the Latin *Iuppiter* / *iuvare* (to help)</note>: because he is an active and generative element: and they call his highest and most subtle part Minerva: who is pure in herself and simple and without any mixture. And for this they say that Jove generated Minerva from his head without joining with a woman: that is, without the mixing of matter. We consider furthermore fire in this middle region when it ignites the vapors raised from the earth: from which ignition are generated the flashes and bolts: and this they call Vulcan. Wherefore the poets feign that he is Jove’s blacksmith: and makes the bolts for him when he wishes to strike something. They feign him to be the son of Jove and Juno: of Jove: because he proceeds from the superior element called Jove. Of Juno: because he is conceived in the air, which is Juno. Since in the air terrestrial vapors are ignited. They also take Vulcan to mean this fire that men use: which burns as long as the matter it feeds upon lasts. You see then what they mean by Minerva, by Jove, and by Vulcan. There remains Vesta, whom they hold to be the fire included within the earth: as we see when it is drawn from stones and wood and other terrestrial things. They attribute three blacksmiths to Vulcan: Brontes, Steropes, and Pyracmon. The first two names denote the qualities of the bolt: because **Brontes** signifies thunder: which is born from the fraction and violent breaking of the cloud: in which the vapor is ignited. **Steropes** signifies lightning, which is nothing other than the flashing of the fire that appears from the broken cloud. The third, who is **Pyracmon**, expresses the smith's tools. Because *pyr* <note>Greek: πῦρ</note> is fire: and *agmon* <note>Greek: ἄκμων</note> is the anvil. Virgil uses these names: *Brontes and Steropes and Pyracmon with bare limbs.* But Hesiod in his *Theogony* does not use Pyracmon. But in that place he puts **Harpes**: to denote the violence of the bolt: which makes a "snatching" or "prey" of everything: and it is said from *harpasin* <note>Greek: ἁρπάζειν</note> which means to snatch. They say these are sons of Heaven and Earth: because the bolt is born, as we have said, from fire (a celestial thing) and from raised vapors (a terrestrial thing). They are called **Cyclopes** in the Greek language: because according to the poets they had a single eye in their forehead. Some also wish that Vulcan is served by those whom the Greeks call **Telchines**. These the fables say are sons of the sea: and they were the first inhabitants of the island of Rhodes. They were inventors of many arts. They sculpted the statues of the gods. Furthermore, they could bring on winds, rains, hail, and snow wherever they wished; and change the forms of things as magicians do. And let this be enough regarding the blacksmiths of Jove. Now because he mentions the celestial bolt which the Latins call *Fulmen* and *fulgure*: it will not be, I believe, unpleasant to the reader to run through: but with brevity, the nature of it. The matter then from which it is made is a vapor very dry and hot: which easily catches fire and inflames: and the place in which this vapor stays as if in its vessel is a vapor, that is, a cloud aqueous and concave.
