<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto XIV. Having described the figure of Capaneus, the text now transitions into a detailed "scientific" explanation of the meteorology behind thunder and lightning, which serves as a physical allegory for the divine fire raining down in this circle of Hell.</meta>

<header>CANTO XIV</header>

These two vapors <note>In medieval meteorology, "vapors" (moist) and "exhalations" (dry) were thought to rise from the earth to create atmospheric phenomena.</note> are drawn up together by the powerful heat of the sun: But the first, through its dryness, gathers itself together and constricts. This second one, through its humidity, spreads around the first: and from every side, it cloaks and covers it. Wherefore the first, being dry, flees this second one which is humid as its contrary: and from every side, it retreats toward the center. But even this one that surrounds it contracts and gathers toward the first because of the coldness of the place: and it beats against it greatly. And the one thus beaten rubs one part against the other, and especially on the outer side: and by such motion, it catches fire. Wherefore the fire, chased by its contrary, unites and increases its strength and breaks through the watery cloud: and in such a rupture, the lightning and the thunder are revealed: and these two occur at the same time. But first, the lightning is seen: because the sense of sight is faster than that of hearing. For this reason, if a tree is being cut from a distance, we first see the axe strike: and afterward, we hear the blow. Nor do I dwell on demonstrating how three species of thunder are generated from such a rupture: or why sometimes the sound is heard without the lightning—certainly a worthy piece of knowledge. But one cannot insist too prolifically on particulars in such a vast and varied abundance of things. Nor do I judge it right to omit the diversity of the cloud that contains the thunder. Nor the diversity of the colors of the fire that is within. Nor the diversity of the falling of the thunderbolt <term>saetta; a bolt of lightning envisioned as a physical projectile</term>. The cloud is sometimes black due to its own coldness: which condenses it in a form that the ray cannot penetrate: and not penetrating it, it cannot whiten it: And this cloud, because it strongly condenses the vapor within itself and ignites it, gives a greater thunder. Sometimes the black is seen to turn reddish: which shows that in the thick cloud, the vapor is already ignited. And this gives a stronger blow than the black one. But the worst is that which mixes green and black with some redness: because it shows that through the blackness it has much vapor: and through the green, it has much water: and through the red, much fire. From this one—because heat combats strongly with cold, and dry with humid—there fall thunderbolts of large stones <note>The author refers to "thunderstones" or ceraunia, which people in the Middle Ages believed were physical stones that fell during storms.</note>: and it throws down every great building: and burns animals. The white cloud is little to be feared because it contains within itself little of one or the other matter. Wherefore its flame is extinguished before it ignites the thing it touches: unless it is very flammable matter like dry wood. Furthermore, we must diligently observe the colors of the lightning: which are roughly three. Bright red. A somewhat ignited white. And red like the color of wine. The first is generated from vapor that is not very dry: and the humidity gives it the red color, like the flame in green wood. In this, because the humidity constricts the matter together, not spreading it out, it catches fire more easily. The white flame is from dry vapor: like the flame in dry wood: And for this reason, it does not spread and does not ignite unless it touches very flammable things. The red, because it is of very dense and terrestrial vapor, ignites. But the thunderbolt falls in four ways: The first is when the red inflamed vapor falls from a green and deep cloud: and this generates stone: because the vaporous mixture of terrestrial vapor catches fire: and touching the green cloud which is already converting into water, it hardens like flour that becomes dough with water: because the great fire does not let it be extinguished by the moisture of the cloud: But it hardens by the vehemence of the heat: and becomes like a fired brick: And because the heat flees the humid, the lower part of such a stone is pointed: because there the vapor begins to distill. The second way is when the vapor is less condensed in a less watery cloud: and then it is not held together but nonetheless comes out ignited with force: and it breaks by the impulse: and catches fire again by the inflammation but it breaks nothing but wood. The third way is of bright red vapor and does not make stone. But the flame does not separate from the vapor. This does not break anything but small and very dense bodies: because if they were of great size, they would resist: This kills men and the smell of scorching is felt in them: and no wound is seen, for by its subtlety it penetrates without breaking. And if it finds gold or silver in a purse, it melts it and does not break the purse: for the leather being porous gives it passage. Sometimes the same vapor, when it is thinner and comes out of a more watery cloud, penetrates without dividing or manifestly igniting: And it greatly harms the grapes, and especially those that are well-covered by vine leaves: And such vaporization not only harms by falling directly. But its ray offends whoever it touches. For which reason it happens that those who look at it often have their faces swell or go blind. The fourth way is when the white vapor comes out of dry flame that is not constricted: and for this reason, it does not spread through the air: But it comes out with great force: because the cloud is very deep in which there is much water. This breaks things and in breaking is extinguished: and leaves the things white so that no sign of combustion appears: And when it has great force it kills: And sometimes by its scattering: and because the vapor is not continuous, it strikes one person and does not touch another who stands near him. But then it strikes another who is further away: And sometimes it reflects from one and does not harm him: and goes to another and harms him. Sometimes it is so weak that it burns the clothes: and in that, it loses its strength: and does not harm the man. The fifth way is when the same vapor comes out of the cloud so weakened that it harms nothing: because as soon as it touches the air it is extinguished: and at once the fire and the violence cease. We have spoken of the smiths and of the bolt. It follows. **AND IF HE WEARIES** <note>original: "ET SEGLI STANCHI"</note> the others, turn by turn: That is, exchanging them crew by crew. Because when there are many at the same exercise: and they do not all work at once: but they exchange, they are said to "make the shift" <note>Italian: *fare la muta*</note>. **IN MONGIBELLO** <note>original: "IN MONGIBELLO"</note>. It is a mountain in Sicily called Etna by the ancients: By the moderns, Mongibello <note>A name derived from the Italian 'Monte' and Arabic 'Jebel', both meaning mountain.</note>: which, because it is cavernous and contains much sulfur, often burns or throws out smoke: And for this reason, the poets feign that here is the forge in which Vulcan fashions the bolts for Jupiter. And he adds that if Jupiter, being angry, urged Vulcan to fashion the bolts with that haste with which he urges him when...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, Canto XIV. Following the physical explanation of lightning as divine fire, the text now focuses on the character of Capaneus—one of the legendary "Seven against Thebes"—who embodies the sin of prideful impiety against God.</meta>

<header>. XIV . INFERNO .</header>
<page-num>LXIX</page-num>

[Capaneus] fought against the giants in the battle of Phlegra <note>A mythical battleground where the Giants fought the Olympian gods.</note> where Jove had need of many arrows to kill them all. Nevertheless, he would not see a joyful vengeance: because he could not make me surrender or yield. According to the poets, the giants were the sons of the Earth: but they possessed such great pride because of their immeasurable stature that they had the audacity to want to drive Jove out of heaven. Therefore, they took three mountains of Thessaly—Pelion, Ossa, and Olympus—and placed one on top of the other to climb into the sky. But Jove killed them with his arrows. And [the author] prudently mentions the giants in the place where the most proud impiety is punished: because by the giants, they mean nothing other than those men who, having become proud through the great power they hold in earthly things, do not remember human fragility. Like a new Lucifer, they rise up against God; they wish to have power over human nature and to hold God in no esteem. Hence, Cicero in his *Cato the Elder* said: *To wage war against the gods in the manner of the giants is nothing other than to rebel against nature* <note>original: "Nihil aliud est more gigantium aduersus deos bellum gerere quam naturę repugnare"</note>. And Macrobius said: *What else do we believe the giants were, if not a certain impious race denying the gods?* <note>original: "Quid aliud credimus gigantes fuisse nisi quandam impiam gentem deos negantem"</note> They are therefore born of the earth because they think of nothing but earthly things. And in such most vile thoughts, they wish to have more power than God. For this reason, they place mountains upon mountains: that is, they accumulate swollen and proud thoughts and enterprises. But the celestial arrow, which is divine wrath, casts them to the ground. But returning to the fable: this battle was in Thessaly; and according to some poets, in that stretch of countryside where Pozzuoli and Cuma are, which is called Phlegra according to Strabo. Nevertheless, Pliny in his *Geography* places Phlegra not far from the mountains mentioned above, which seems more likely.

<columns>2</columns>

Then my guide spoke with such force
that I had never heard him so loud:
"O Capaneus, in that your pride
is not extinguished, you are punished more;
no other torment, save your own rage,
would be a pain sufficient for your fury."
Then he turned to me with a better look,
saying: "That was one of the seven kings
who besieged Thebes; he held, and seems to hold,
God in disdain, and seems to prize him little;
but, as I told him, his own insults
are the most fitting ornaments for his breast."

<column-break/>

Having heard the proud speech of Capaneus, Virgil 
**SPOKE WITH FORCE:** that is, with acrimony
and with vehemence, and with a great shout he rebuked him.
Indeed, Dante affirms that he had never yet 
heard him speak so bitterly. This signifies 
that the intellect is not more disturbed by any 
other vice than by this impiety. **IN THAT YOUR**
**PRIDE IS NOT EXTINGUISHED, YOU ARE PUNISHED MORE.**
It is a most true sentiment that no punishment is 
greater for the proud man than the rage and the anger he feels at 
being defeated and cast down—which grows all the more 
the more he is challenged. **AND NO OTHER PUN-**
**ISHMENT:** that is, no fury or pain that anyone else 
could use against you. **WOULD BE A SUFFICIENT PAIN:** 
meaning a penalty that is enough and sufficient. **THEN HE**
**TURNED TO ME WITH A BETTER LOOK:** with better

<column-break/>

lips: that is, with better words, which are formed in the mouth by the tongue, the teeth, and the lips. And this is the way of the wise: because he rebukes vice with grave acrimony, but in admonishing and instructing a man eager to learn, he uses humane and loving words. **SAYING THAT WAS ONE OF THE SEVEN KINGS WHO BESIEGED:** that is, those who besieged Thebes. Laius, king of the Thebans, had a son named Oedipus, who, according to the oracles, was destined to kill his father. For this reason, he gave him to servants to be killed. Those servants, out of pity, granted him his life; and having pierced his feet with a willow branch, they left him in the forest. Found by shepherds, he was given to Polybus, king of Corinth, and was raised by him as his own. Later, having come to full age, he learned from the oracle of Apollo that in Phocis of Boeotia he would find his true father. He went therefore to Phocis and killed his father, not knowing who he was. At that time in Thebes, there was a monster called the Sphinx, who proposed enigmas—that is, obscure sayings—with this condition: that whoever could not solve them should be killed, and whoever solved them should have Jocasta, queen of Thebes, for his wife (she being then a widow due to the death of Laius). Oedipus solved the enigma, which was this: "What animal is it that first goes on four feet, then with two, and finally with three?" And Oedipus said this was man: who as a small child goes on all fours, then goes on two feet, and finally in old age goes with three feet because he supports himself with a staff. Because he had been able to solve the enigma, he deserved to be given the queen, Jocasta, as his wife. He took her, not knowing she was his mother, and by her had two sons, Eteocles and Polynices. Finally, recognizing his father and mother and the wickedness he had committed, he blinded himself and lived in darkness. After his death, discord arose between his sons because each wanted to rule. Finally, they agreed to rule in turns, each for his own year. It being Eteocles's turn first, Polynices left his homeland to his brother for that year and arrived in Argos; there, Adrastus, king of Argos, gave him his daughter as a wife. When the year ended and Eteocles was unwilling to observe the pact, Adrastus, together with six other kings, went to lay siege to Thebes. The kings were Adrastus, Polynices, Tydeus, Hippomedon, Amphiaraus, Parthenopaeus, and Capaneus. This last one was a despiser of all religion and affirmed that there was no God, and that fear was what had induced men to believe there was a God. He trusted greatly in his own strength because he was very large and robust; and in the battle at Thebes, he climbed the walls by force, and shouting, he boasted that he would conquer the city in spite of the gods, and provoked [them] to battle.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, Canto XIV. Previously, the text discussed the punishment of the giants and Capaneus for their pride. Now, Virgil leads Dante away from the burning sands toward a mysterious red stream, which serves as a transition to the explanation of the "Old Man of Crete" and the origin of the rivers of Hell.</meta>

<header>CANTO XIV</header>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>

Hercules and Bacchus were Theban gods. Later, Jove, feeling ashamed to have to fight against lesser gods, insulted them in battle. And Jove struck him <note>Referring to the proud rebel Capaneus, struck by lightning.</note> with a thunderbolt and killed him.

> "Now follow me, and see that you do not yet
> set your feet upon the scorching sand:
> but always keep your feet close to the woods."
> Silently we came to a place where gushes
> out from the forest a small little stream,
> whose redness still makes my hair stand on end.
> As the brook comes out of the Bullicame <note>A famous hot sulfur spring near Viterbo, Italy, known in the Middle Ages for its reddish water.</note>
> which the sinful women then divide among themselves:
> so did this stream run down across the bank:
> Its bottom and both its sloping sides
> were made of stone, as were the margins on the side:
> wherefore I perceived that the path was there.

<column-break/>

They have now nearly reached the end of the boiling sands, because they were approaching the place where a small stream emerges from the forest, from which all the rivers of Hell originate. For this reason, Virgil warns Dante not to set his feet upon the sand until they reach that river; and he shows that they traveled the remaining distance in silence. This silence signifies the contemplation of the matter. Virgil wants Dante to follow him. In this, "sensuality" and "lower reason" must follow "superior reason." This superior reason warns him not to set foot on the sand—meaning that his appetite should not enter into such a desire for pride. Instead, he must keep his feet in the forest, which is a solitary place suited for contemplation. Therefore, in the investigation of vices, the lower reason

<column-break/>

must follow the superior reason and not enter with desire into the burning and lust of those vices, but rather contemplate their wicked and harmful nature. **WHERE IT GUSHES** (*DOVE SPICCIA*), meaning where it flows out. **A SMALL LITTLE STREAM**: which crossed that circle. **WHOSE REDNESS MAKES MY HAIR STAND ON END** (*EL CVI ROSSORE Miraccapriccia*): that is, it gives me horror. The word *capriccio* <term>capriccio: literally "head-curling" (capo arriccia)</term> properly means when the hair on one's head stands up. This happens from cold, and such cold often comes from fear. He says, therefore, that every time he remembers the boiling of this river, he is struck with horror. **AS THE BULLICAME**: He shows by comparison that this water was as boiling as that which comes out of the Bullicame spring in Viterbo. This water, after a short distance, arrives at the brothel—the place where the prostitutes stay—and, having become lukewarm, is divided among their dwellings for them to wash with. This is a fitting comparison considering how the water passes: for just as the water from the Bullicame flows among the homes of prostitutes, so the water coming from Phlegethon <note>The river of fire/blood in Dante's Hell.</note> flows through the sand where the souls of the sinners of Sodom are punished. **SO DOWN THROUGH THE SAND** it followed the third circle, and stones formed the bottom and the slopes (the banks); and he clarifies further by saying "the margins," meaning the edges. **WERE MADE OF STONE**: This does not entirely deviate from the nature of water, for in some places water generates stone from itself, as we see happen in the river Elsa <note>A river in Tuscany known for its high mineral content that can calcify objects.</note>. **WHEREFORE I PERCEIVED THAT THE PATH WAS THERE**: Because it was easy to pass upon those stones. Allegorically, understand that once we have pulled our desires away from the aforementioned fires through solitude and patience, we reach a firmness and hardness against falling into vice. Not without reason does he add that the water hardened into stone: because by contemplating vice while following Virgil (that is, the intellect and moral doctrine), our burning greed is restrained and hardens like a stone, moving no more. This serves the allegory, and as said above, it does not depart from the physical nature of water. Certainly, if we consider it diligently, the poet has written nothing more notable up to this point. In all the other circles, he described only the vice punished there and the type of punishment. But here, returning to the start of the origins of the human race, he shows its progress and where every sin is born in us. Someone might wonder why he did not include such a description at the beginning of his work or at the entrance to Hell, since both the nature of things and true art require that a writer divide his invention into its principal parts before sending it to the readers, and then describe each in a distinct order. It seems to many that if the poet wanted to express the different states of the human species, the origin of vice, how vice leads us to Hell, the layout of Hell, and the rivers that run there, it would have been more appropriate to place the fiction of this statue <note>The "Old Man of Crete," a massive statue representing the ages of man and the source of Hell's rivers.</note> at the beginning, for under an allegorical veil, it contains the division of the entire work. However, this doubt is easily resolved if we realize that the beginning of Hell (describing the site found by those who descend) is one thing, and the "beginning of sin" (speculating on its origin) is another. Therefore, the poet described the site of Hell immediately from the start. Later, wanting to present the "beginning" not of the location, but of Hell itself—that is, the vice that traps the human species in Hell—he judged it appropriate to delay the statue until the place where the proud rebels against God are punished. For the origin of our sin proceeds from here: nothing else drew the first man from his state of innocence and contaminated him with sin but the pride which chose to overstep the divine command.

<summary>Dante and Virgil approach the red stream of Phlegethon, which provides a safe, stone-lined path across the burning sands. The commentary explains the allegorical significance of the river's heat and the reason Dante chose this specific location to describe the origins of human sin and the rivers of Hell.</summary>

Dentro dalmonte ſta drittun gran ueglio <note>Inside the mountain stands a Great Old Man.</note>
che tienuolte le ſpalle inuer damiata:
et Roma guarda ſi come ſuo ſpeglio <note>He turns his back on Damietta (in Egypt, representing the East/the Past) and looks at Rome as his mirror (representing the West/the Future).</note>
La teſta ſua e/ di finor formata:
et puro argento ſono le braccia elpecto:
poi e/ di rame infino allanforcata <note>His head is fine gold, his chest and arms are silver, then he is brass down to the fork of his legs.</note>
Da indi ingiuſo e/ tucto ferro electo:
ſaluo cheldextro piede e/ terra cotta:
et ſta inſu quel piu che nſu laltro erecto <note>From there down he is iron, except his right foot is terracotta (clay), and he leans more on that fragile foot than the other.</note>
Ciaſchuna parte fuor che loro e/ rotta
duna feſſura che lacrime goccia:
lequali accolte foran queſta grotta <note>Every part except the gold is cracked by a fissure that drips tears; these tears bore through the mountain to form the rivers of Hell.</note>
Lor corſo in queſta ualle ſi diroccia:
fanno Acheronte Stige et phlegethonta
po ſen uan giu per queſta ſtrecta doccia.
Infin doue la piu non ſi diſmonta:
fanno cocito: et qual ſia quello ſtagno
tullo uedrai pero qui nonſi conta. <note>The tears flow down to form the rivers Acheron, Styx, and Phlegethon, eventually pooling at the bottom of Hell to form the frozen lake of Cocytus.</note>

<column-break/>

Virgil captures the highest attention in this place, showing Dante that from the beginning of Hell until now he has seen nothing more notable. **THE THRESHOLD OF WHICH IS DENIED TO NO ONE.** Because, as Virgil says, the gate of Pluto stands open day and night <note>original: "noctes atque dies patet atri ianua Ditis" from the *Aeneid*.</note>. Wherefore it is easy to descend into Hell: because falling into vice is easy for everyone. **WHICH QUENCHES ALL THE FLAMES ABOVE IT.** These words moved Dante, and having become very eager and greedy to know why this was the most notable thing, he begs Virgil to give him the food for which he has given him the desire. This means nothing other than that he should give him the understanding and science of this miraculous thing of which he has made him desirous. And not without merit does he call such science "pasture" and "food." For just as the body is nourished by the four elements of which it is composed, so the soul is nourished by the truth, which is the doctrine and the science of things human and divine.

In these tercets written above, the author describes with his own poetic invention the origin of the infernal rivers. And he imagines that in Mount Ida on Crete there is a cracked statue, which drips tears; and these make a stream that, boring through the mountain, descends into Hell. **IN THE MIDDLE OF THE SEA:** that is, in the Mediterranean Sea, and in that which the Greeks call the Aegean Sea, and which today we call the Archipelago. **SITS:** is located. **A WASTED LAND** called Crete. He said "wasted" because a long time ago many cities there declined; for anciently they said it was *Hecatompolon* <note>original: "Ecatompolon," Greek for "a hundred cities."</note>. But after it lost its sovereignty, it was ruined almost entirely. **CRETE** was in the earliest times called Idea. Later it took its name from Creta, daughter of one of the Curetes and wife of Ammon; today it is called Candia. This island has the Aegean Sea to the north and the African Sea to the south, which reaches the Egyptian Sea. Its length is two thousand three hundred stadia <note>A stadium was an ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 185 meters.</note>, and eight stadia make a mile. The width is proportional to the length. Wherefore its circuit, according to Sophocles, is five thousand stadia, and according to Artemidorus, four thousand one hundred. Others describe it as larger. The highest mountain of this island is Ida, surrounded by three cities in the shape of a garland, and it is located almost in the middle of the island. Its circuit is six hundred stadia. This island was excellently governed by the laws of Rhadamanthus and Minos; and by their laws, it was reduced to a civil and human way of living and adorned with a hundred lands; for this reason, Homer called it *hecatompoli*. **UNDER THE KING** the world was once chaste. Under Saturn, who was king of Olympus and of Crete. **THE WORLD WAS ONCE**

---

**CHASTE:** because the poets imagine it so. The father of Saturn was Caelus (Heaven) and the mother was Vesta, which signifies Earth. But those who write sacred history say he was a most powerful king, and gave the name of his father to the heavens and that of his mother to the earth, whereas before they were called by other names. This name "Saturn" is sometimes understood as this man who, according to the histories, held his realm in great tranquility without homicides, without thefts, without adulteries or other wickednesses. And for this, the poets feigned that in his times there was a "Golden Age"; because just as gold is pure and never rusts, so that age was pure from every vice. Sometimes we take Saturn to be the first of the seven <note>Referring to the seven planets of ancient astronomy.</note>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto XIV. Following the description of the "Old Man of Crete," the commentator explains the symbolic meaning of the statue's materials and its mythological origins, focusing on Saturn, the four elements, and the transition of empires from East to West.</meta>

# CANTO XIV

planets: whose nature we will discuss at length in the *Paradiso*. Sometimes Saturn signifies Time. For this reason, in Greek, he is called *Cronos*: a name which, if the breathing mark is removed, derives from *Chronos*, which means Time. This is why the myths have imagined that he devoured all his children except for Jove <note>Jupiter</note>, Juno, Neptune, and Pluto: because time consumes all things that are born. And <note>original: "omnia orta occidūt: et aucta senescunt" — all things that arise fall, and those that have grown old age</note>, except for the four elements: which, although they undergo constant mutation from one into another, because the finer parts of the denser element always change into the neighboring one. Thus, earth is converted into water, water into air, and air into fire; and likewise, conversely, the denser parts of the finer elements descend into the denser forms, so that fire becomes air, air becomes water, and water becomes earth. Nevertheless, nothing of the four elements ever perishes; rather, one changes into the other, and everything that is generated and composed from them returns to its principle when it perishes. Nor is a body ever consumed after death in such a way that it becomes nothing; but just as it was composed of the four elements, so in dissolving it returns to them. Therefore, time devours everything except for Jove, who is fire; Juno, who is air; Neptune, who is water; and Pluto, who is earth. Let this suffice for Saturn. But let us add an even clearer understanding of this statue, through which the Greek poets have enclosed the ages according to the nature of different metals. They say the first was of gold in the time of Saturn, and by this they mean virtue and innocence. The second was of silver, in which men began to degenerate from virtue just as silver degenerates from gold. There follows the third of copper <note>or bronze</note>, and the fourth of iron.

**THERE IS A MOUNTAIN** that once was joyful. Ida is a mountain in Crete; from its name, there is another mountain in Troy, which was called Ida by Teucer, who went from Crete to live in Troy. But this one in Crete was named thus after the nymph Ida. This mountain was once cultivated, and the forests and springs were maintained there; now it is stripped of everything. **LIKE A FORBIDDEN THING:** that is, old <note>or "worn out"</note>. **RHEA once chose it as a faithful cradle.** Rhea, the wife of Saturn, having given birth to Jove, did not hand him over to Saturn, who wanted to devour him as he had devoured the other children. Instead, she handed him a stone, and hid Jove on Mount Ida. Because she nursed him there, the poet calls it the "cradle" of Jove. *Cuna* means cradle, and it is a common word in the Latin language, but derived from the Greek because *cimi* means to lie down; and this word is used because small children lie there. Thus, he calls Ida the cradle of Jove because he lay and was nursed there. **AND TO HIDE HIM BETTER** when he cried, she caused shouts to be made there: that is, noise and clamor so that his crying would not be heard. The poet wished to describe the various states of the human species and to show that all of them, except for the first, were vicious, and that from those vices proceeds all our misery and damnation. This is our hell. Such a teaching the poet hides under a veiled and allegorical sense, imagining a statue composed of various metals on Mount Ida in Crete, and from that statue the infernal rivers are born. Certainly, Dante showed marvelous genius: because at once, by imitating the statue that appeared in a vision to King Nebuchadnezzar <note>see Daniel 2:31-35</note> and the fiction created by the Greek poets describing the various ages under the figure of various metals, he introduces a third meaning which fits his purpose. 

He places, then, a great statue of an old man on Mount Ida; and this statue turns its back to Damietta, which is a noble city in Egypt located on the Nile, and turns its face toward Rome. By this, he means Time, which began together with the world and will end with the world. Time is nothing other than the motion and the measure of the motion of the heavens and the stars. Therefore, before the creation of the world, there was no time, but only eternity, into which time later came. He imagines this statue as old and large because, among things that have had a beginning and will have an end, almost nothing is older than time, and time is a great thing among mortal matters. But he does not simply place such a statue to represent Time; because along with it, he intends to express the human generation, which is placed in this flux and course of time, and its various states. For this reason, this old man will be Time; he will be the human species; he will be, through the metals of which he is composed, its various states. He places this statue in Crete for two reasons. The first was because Crete is the seat of Saturn, who among the ancient poets—as we said in his myth—signifies Time. The second reason is that, understanding it to represent the human generation which inhabits this globe of the earth divided into three parts—Asia, Africa, and Europe—it is a fitting thing to have placed it in the center, and in that place which borders all three of these parts. And this is shown to be Crete. 

Furthermore, having to describe the various states of human generation—although its beginning was in the first man placed in the paradise of delights, and his first state, which was one of innocence, was nowhere but there—nevertheless, Dante wished to hide this Christian truth under a poetic veil. He said the statue was in Crete because, according to the poets, the Golden Ages of Saturn and the great observance of laws were there, which expresses innocence. Not without reason does he place it on a mountain, because a mountain signifies a mound of earth, denoting that he does not place it for individual men, but for their "mound"—that is, for the whole mass and the human species. The name of this mountain, called Ida, also corresponds to this: because *idos* in Greek means "species" or "form," and not a particular individual. And that he turns his shoulders to Damietta and his face to Rome has a double allegorical meaning. For we can understand that this denotes the course of empires, which had its beginning in the eastern parts—not making such a beginning with the Assyrians, but with the Egyptians, who had Osiris and Bacchus and Hercules, much more ancient than Ninus, king of the...

It expands on the allegory of the "Old Man of Crete" (Veglio di Creta), comparing it to the biblical statue in Nebuchadnezzar’s dream to explain the decline of human history and the origins of the rivers of Hell.</meta>

### XIIII INFERNO

Assyrians; and therefore he placed Damietta <note>An ancient port city in Egypt, representing the East or the old world</note>, a very ancient city of Egypt. And from this beginning, passing through the Assyrians, Persians, Medes, and many other nations, the seat of empire finally settled among the Romans. Therefore, the statue turns its back to Egypt as to an empire already passed, and its face to Rome as to the present empire. This is because things that have passed are behind us, and those we see are present before us. The second meaning is that this denotes that all created things move toward death; as soon as they are produced, they turn their backs to the East—that is, to their birth—and their faces to the West—that is, to their setting and their death.

This statue is made of four metals and one foot of clay. This is not unlike the statue of Nebuchadnezzar. In a dream, Nebuchadnezzar, King of Babylon, saw a very large statue that gazed at him with a terrible aspect. Its head was of fine gold, its chest and arms of silver. The rest, down to the legs, was of copper. The legs were of iron. And the feet were partly iron and partly baked clay. The statue stood before the king until a stone, cut from a mountain without hands, struck its feet and crushed them. Then the clay, the iron, the copper, the silver, and the gold were broken and crushed together, and all were carried away by the wind, and no place was found for them; and the stone that struck the statue became a great mountain.

This statue signified the changing of kingdoms. The head of gold demonstrated the empire of King Nebuchadnezzar, which occupied almost all the Eastern parts and was very rich. Two arms and one chest denote the empire of the Persians and the Medes, because at one time Cyrus reigned over the Persians and Darius over the Medes; in their times, the doctrines signified by silver—which is splendid and resonant—were highly prized. The copper denotes the kingdom of the Macedonians and the Greeks, because in those times eloquence flourished, signified by copper, a very resonant metal. The iron demonstrated the empire of the Romans, who by military virtue occupied all other empires. The clay mixed with iron in the feet of the statue noted the civil discord in the Roman Republic; for just as baked clay never binds well with iron, so in civil discord there is never a true union among citizens. The stone cut from the mountain without hands is Christ, born of Mary (who for her excellence is likened to a mountain) without hands—that is, without human work. This Christ changes all empires.

But I will proceed no further in this interpretation, as it does not belong to the present work. Therefore, I return to our poet <note>Dante</note>, who with supreme genius, joining the statue of this vision with the ages distinguished by poets through different metals, forms a third allegory, reducing the fiction to a true and Christian sense. He says that the gold and the head of this statue were of gold, meaning by the head the beginning of human generation: our first parents, who for the space of time they remained in the garden of delights <note>Eden</note> lived in a state of true innocence. No other time afterward was ever truly innocent. Thus, only the head was gold.

Then, by the chest and arms of silver, he places the second age, which the poets say was under Jove <note>Jupiter</note>. He understands this to be the age that succeeded Adam; although it was not entirely innocent, it began to be clear and shining like silver through the multiplication of generations. There follows then the rest down to the fork of the legs, all of copper; and this is the third age, which by copper (a more resonant metal) signifies nothing other than the fame acquired through the discovery of various sciences and arts. The thighs and legs of iron, a hard and warlike substance, demonstrate the fourth age, in which avarice and ambition multiplied, and various wars were born to usurp the riches and empires of others, as notably began with Ninus among the Assyrians, and then his successors: the Medes, Persians, Greeks, Macedonians, Carthaginians, and Romans.

Then he adds that the right foot of the statue is of baked clay. This signifies the fragility of human things, and how weak is the foundation of empires and other goods subject to fortune and death. He said the "right foot" because the forces of empires, denoted by the right foot, consist entirely of earthly things and are void of every virtue, both moral and intellectual. There are few princes who approve the sentiment of Plato, who affirms that republics cannot be blessed unless they are administered by wise men. But all their confidence is in the strength of the body and in riches, which are earthly things.

The statue was cracked in all parts except for the gold. The rupture signifies vice, which has broken integrity and innocence, and thus has stained all the ages except for the state of innocence, which was without vice. And from this rupture are born the tears that make the infernal rivers—that is, human miseries which generate the pains that afflict us. For just as virtue makes a man blessed, happy, joyful, and glad, so vice makes us miserable, sad, and full of mourning. And these tears pierce the grotto that separates this part where men live from Hell. And certainly, it is true that from our vices is born that sorrow which opens the path leading us to unhappiness. The poet, therefore, wished to place the origin of the infernal rivers in that part where there is tyrannical pride, from which all other vices are born that lead us to Hell. These tears make the four rivers. First is Acheron, which signifies "deprivation of joy," because sin generates repentance in us and deprives us of gladness. From Acheron is born Styx, which is to say "sadness," because after the deprivation of joy comes sadness. And then follows Phlegethon, which is "ardor," because he who is established in sorrow always feels in his mind a fire that boils with various cares. Whence Virgil says: <note>original: "Varioque irarum fluctuat estu" — And he tosses with a varied tide of anger (Aeneid IV.532)</note>. And from Phlegethon the water descends down to the bottom of Hell and forms the pool of Cocytus. For from the deprivation of joy, and from sorrow, and from the burning of cares, is generated Cocytus—that is, "lamentation," which signifies a confirmed...

# CANTO XIV

...mad sorrow. And therefore he wishes that it settles in the final part of Hell: because it is perpetual <gloss>so much of guilt</gloss> mourning <gloss>and placed</gloss> in the depths of the abyss: and there it holds us in eternal misery.

And I to him: "If the present streamlet
derives thus from our world,
why does it only appear at this rim?"

And he to me: "You know that the place is round:
and although you have come a great way,
always descending to the left toward the bottom:

You have not yet turned through the whole circle:
therefore, if a new thing appears to us,
it should not bring wonder to your face."

And I then: "Master, where are
Phlegethon and Lethe found? For of one you are silent
and of the other you say it is formed of this rain."

"In all your questions you certainly please me,"
he replied, "but the boiling of the red water
should surely have solved the one you ask.

Lethe you shall see, but not in this ditch,
there where souls go to wash themselves
when their repented guilt is removed."

Then he said: "Now it is time to depart
from the wood; see that you follow behind me:
the margins provide a path, for they are not scorched,

And above them all vapor is extinguished."

<column-break/>

The meaning in brief is this: that Dante <gloss>so much of guilt</gloss>
wonders if this streamlet—that is, a brook—
which he calls this because *rigo* <note>original: "rigo"</note> in Latin signifies
to soak or wet, DERIVES from our world: because having
already descended so far, he has not seen it elsewhere
except at this rim: that is, at this extremity.
*Viuagno* <term>viuagno: a term for the hem or border of a garment</term> signifies the edge of a cloth. And Virgil
replies to him: YOU KNOW that the place is round,
being divided into circles: And you, in descending, have
always come to the left hand. Therefore, it can
be that there is something on the right hand that you have
not yet seen. But how he has not
yet turned through the whole circle, I demonstrated in the beginning
of the work under the universal illustration of the site of this Hell.

Because above, in no place has Virgil made
mention either of Phlegethon or of
Lethe, Dante therefore asks where these rivers
are. And Virgil replies to him that, although he had
not given a name above to the river that was boiling,
nevertheless, he could understand by such boiling
that it was Phlegethon: because *phlego* <note>original: "plego"</note> in Greek
signifies to burn and set on fire. And he says Lethe
is not in this ditch: that is, in this depth
of Hell, but is after Purgatory <note>Dante places the River Lethe, which brings forgetfulness of sin, in the Earthly Paradise at the summit of Mount Purgatory</note>. For
there he places two rivers: on the left Lethe,
and on the right Eunoe <note>The river of "good memory" which restores the remembrance of good deeds</note>: of which we shall speak in the second
canticle.

<header>INFERNO</header>

# CANTO XV OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.

Now one of the hard margins carries us,
and the smoke of the brook overshadows above,
so that it saves the water and the banks from the fire.
As the Flemings between Wissant and Bruges,
fearing the flood that rushes toward them,
make the bulwark so that the sea may flee;
and as the Paduans along the Brenta,
to defend their villas and their castles
before Chiarentana <note>The Carinthian Alps, where the Brenta river originates.</note> feels the heat;
in such likeness were those [banks] made,
although they were not so high nor so thick,
whoever the master was who made them.

<column-break/>

¶ In this fifteenth canto, together with the sixteenth, the poet treats those who were violent against nature <note>The sodomites.</note>. And in the beginning, he describes what his path was, and the souls he found; and first he makes mention of Ser Brunetto Latini. They went, therefore, upon one of the two margins—that is, of the two banks of the river. **HARD** because they were made of stone. And he demonstrates that the boiling of that stream was so great that such smoke rose from it that it "overshadowed" it; that is, it shaded the air above. And it was so thick that it extinguished the flames that rained down. And this is natural: that smoke extinguishes flame. For by placing a candle over smoke, it is extinguished; and this happens because the smoke drives out the air, without which the flame does not live, because it lacks its exhalation. Therefore, they were able to pass safely, with no flames raining upon the banks. For it will be true according to physical reason that smoke extinguishes flames. But it also serves the allegory. Where we shall remember that always—both in this poet and in Virgil—we have placed "water" for "appetite." Therefore, placing the river in this place for the appetite—not of the sinner, but of the contemplator of the evil nature of sin—it is a fitting thing that from such water a vapor should rise to extinguish the flames. For just as a cold and humid vapor rises from waters, which generates clouds that give us shade against the heat of the sun and make rain that extinguishes fire; so from the appetite of the speculator of vice, because he follows reason, there is born an obstacle against the heats of concupiscence <note>Unbridled desire or lust.</note>, in such a way that the river—that is, the appetite itself—and the hard banks—that is, a firm purpose—are not harmed by such flames. **AS THE FLEMINGS** between Wissant and Bruges. These are two cities in Flanders placed on the shores of the Ocean sea, which is between England and Flanders. And the Ocean in those places moves twice in twenty-four hours from the east toward the west, and just as many times returns back; and in its movement, it leaves its place and enters into the land. Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century German Dominican friar and philosopher.</note> posits in the book *On the Causes of the Properties of the Elements* <note>original: "de cauſis proprietatum elementorum"</note> that although all planets produce their effects in inferior bodies, nonetheless the sun and the moon are most powerful, both for the quantity of light and for the proximity of the moon to the earth. Hence, it rules the humidity of inferior bodies; and through the connaturality of earth and water, it moves all things in which earth and water predominate. And the sun, because it is the source of vivifying heat, makes the humors boil; because humor naturally evaporates toward the heat, rising up. Hence, the Egyptians said that the sun drew the humid for the nourishment of the stars. Nonetheless, the seas have different motions. And some do not move, such as the Pisan and Genoese sea <note>The Mediterranean, which has negligible tides compared to the Atlantic.</note>. Some increase from the new moon until the full moon, and from that until the next new moon they decrease. Some in each day—that is, in the space of twenty-four hours—increase twice and decrease twice: such as the Persian Gulf, the Indian Sea, and all the islands between these. And the sea that is between Constantinople and Venice, and that which is between England and Flanders and Germany, although they are very different in being more intense and more remiss. There are, therefore, four sites in the heavens. One is the eastern horizon when the star is born and rises up into our hemisphere. The other is when it has mounted to the middle of the sky at the zenith of our heads, and it is called the angle of the mid-heaven. The third is when it has arrived at the western horizon and descends into the other hemisphere. The fourth is when it is at the opposite of our zenith, and it is the angle of the middle of the earth and of the night. Therefore, when the moon arrives at the east, the sea rises; when it is at the mid-heaven, it decreases and returns. When it is at the west, it increases and rises again. When it arrives at the angle of the middle of the earth, it decreases. Therefore, the Flemings have made banks that hold back the flood <term>fiotto: a term used by sailors for the tidal surge</term> so that it does not extend further forward. Sailors call such a movement "flood," almost like a "fluctuation." And Albertus Magnus says that with a long span of time, such banks have made the sea move away from Bruges. **THE SCREEN** The rampart. **AND AS** the Paduans along the Brenta. Brenta is a river inside Padua, which is born in the Chiarentana mountain placed in the Alps that divide Italy from Germany—cold and snowy places—and in which the snows do not resolve except when the heat comes. And then the Brenta increases marvelously. And when it arrives at the plain, it would flood many lands if there were not the ramparts of the banks. And this they do **BEFORE CHIAREntana feels the heat**, that is, before the snows of Chiarentana melt from the heat.

<header>CANTO .XV.</header>

Already we were so far removed from the wood
that I would not have seen where it was
even if I had turned myself backward:
When we encountered a troop of souls
who were coming along the bank; and each one
gazed at us as one is wont at evening
To look at another under the new moon;
and toward us they sharpened their brows,
as an old tailor does at the needle's eye.
Thus observed by such a family,
I was recognized by one who took me
by the hem and cried out: "What a marvel!"
And I, when he stretched out his arm toward me,
fixed my eyes upon his scorched aspect,
so that his burnt face did not prevent
His recognition by my intellect;
and lowering my face to his face,
I replied: "Are you here, Ser Brunetto?"
And he: "My son, let it not displease you
if Ser Brunetto Latini turns back a little
with you, and lets the file pass on."

---

I said to him: "With all my power I pray you;
and if you wish that I sit with you,
I will do so, if it pleases this one with whom I go."
"O son," he said, "whoever of this flock
stops for a moment, lies then for a hundred years
without fanning himself when the fire strikes him.
Therefore go onward; I will follow at your skirts,
and then I will rejoin my band,
who go weeping for their eternal woes."
I did not dare descend from the path
to go level with him; but I kept my head
bowed, like a man who walks reverently.

<column-break/>

We were already so far distant from the forest (of which was spoken in the thirteenth canto) that even if I had turned around, I would not have seen it. This denotes that the nature of the vice treated here is different from that which is punished in the forest [suicide], and requires a different consideration. **WHEN we encountered a troop of souls:** by this "encountering" of souls, he denotes the contemplation of this vice. And the "troop" denotes the great number of those who are stained by such beastly wickedness. And each of these souls looked at us as one usually looks at another when it has already become night and the moon is new, because the evening at that time is not entirely without light, but there is a minimal amount of light, such that one cannot discern another unless looking with great diligence. Here he imitates Virgil where he says: *Just as by the uncertain moon under a malicious light is the journey in the woods, where Jupiter has hidden the sky with shadow, and black night has taken the color from things.* <note>original: "Quale per incertam lunam sub luce maligna : Est iter in siluis : ubi caelu condidit umbra Iuppiter : et rebus nox abstulit atra colorem"</note> And always the obscurity and the lack of light in Hell denotes the ignorance and the blindness of the mind from which every vice proceeds. **THEY SHARPENED THEIR BROWS.** One who is old and wishes to look at a small thing, because they have weak sight, sharpens their brows [squints]. When the visual spirits are failing or impeded by thickness or another cause, and they cannot see well, they compel us to sharpen the brows, because thus we restrict the visual power into a smaller space, which, being so united, has more strength. And as Aristotle says in the *Problems* <note>A reference to the *Problemata*, a collection of questions often attributed to Aristotle in the Middle Ages.</note>, crossbowmen do the same when they take aim. **ARE YOU HERE, Ser Brunetto:** The poet does not ask about what he sees, but wonders that he is there. And certainly, it seems no small wonder that a man adorned with so much virtue and learning should let himself fall into such a stain. Furthermore, he shows that it was difficult to recognize these souls because they were so scorched by the fire. This allegorically denotes that the heat of such beastly desire so ruins the face that the man is not recognized; that is, it removes every image of a human and makes them similar to beasts. Ser Brunetto was greatly transfigured, and yet Dante recognized him. He intends to denote nothing else by this than that men adorned with some excellent virtue, as this man was, even though they have some vice in them, nonetheless their fame remains and makes them known; because he is not as Juvenal says: *A monster ransomed from vices by no virtue.* <note>original: "Monstrum nulla uirtute redemptum a uitiis"</note> Ser Brunetto Latini was a Florentine and a man very universal in many liberal arts, especially in physics and metaphysics. He wrote a book which he called the *Tesoretto* <note>A shorter poem in Italian.</note>; and in the profession of notary he surpassed all others. In that art, being accused of falsehood, he chose rather to be condemned than to confess the error. Because of such indignation, he went to live in Paris, and there he wrote another book in the French language which he called the *Trésor* <note>The *Livres dou Trésor*, an influential medieval encyclopedia.</note>. But because he was stained by the vice punished here, the poet feigns finding him here. They say he was an excellent mathematician, and having seen the hour of Dante's birth, he predicted how he would arrive at the highest degree of learning.

---

Ser Brunetto prays that he stop, and Dante gives the reason why he cannot sit. **O SON:** he calls him this because he was his pupil. **WHOEVER of this flock stops.** This is an invention taken from Virgil and translated into another sense. Virgil says that the bodies of those who are not buried stay for a hundred years before Charon crosses them over the river. And the poet feigns that whoever stops in this circle lies then for a hundred years. This can be understood as passing from a lesser sin into a greater one; for since those who are violent against nature are here, by disobeying the divine law in stopping when they must go, they become violent against God. And therefore, it is fitting that he stay still like those others. And allegorically we understand that whoever...

-># INFERNO<-

He began: "What fortune or destiny,
before your final day, leads you down here?
And who is this who shows you the way?"
"Up there above, in the serene life,"
I answered him, "I lost myself in a valley,
before my age was full.
Only yesterday morning I turned my back on it;
this one appeared to me as I was returning to it,
and he leads me home by this path."

---

And he to me: "If you follow your star,
you cannot fail to reach the glorious port,
if I discerned well in the beautiful life.
And if I had not died so prematurely,
seeing heaven so benign toward you,
I would have given you comfort in your work.
But that ungrateful and malignant people
who descended from Fiesole of old,
and still holds to the mountain and the rock,
Will become your enemy for your good deeds;
and it is right, for among the bitter sorbs
it is not fitting for the sweet fig to bear fruit.
Old fame in the world calls them blind,
a greedy, envious, and proud people..."

<column-break/>

**steadfast:** that is, he makes a firmer habit of sin and has no defense against such burning cupidity. <note>original: "ferma"</note> **WHAT FORTUNE OR DESTINY:** regarding fortune and destiny, which we call fate, we have spoken above. And it seems he wishes to say: "What happy celestial influence, or what divine providence?" Since Ser Brunetto was an astrologer and a theologian, he mentions both. For celestial influence does not contradict divine providence, as we shall demonstrate in *Paradiso*. In short, he asks two things: how he arrived in that place, and who did it. And Dante responds how <meta>The word 'NELLA' here is a catchword from the original printer, indicating the first word of the next section.</meta>

**Serene life:** that is, in this life: which in comparison to the heavenly life is miserable and calamitous; but in comparison to the infernal life—where there is never rest from pain nor place for penitence—it is happy and blessed. **I LOST MYSELF in that valley.** Of this valley and the lost path, and of the help of Virgil, we spoke at length in the first canto. **BEFORE MY AGE WAS FULL:** that is, perfected. The ages of human life, as we have already said, are divided by the number seven: and in the first seven years **infancy** ends. In the second seven, reaching fourteen, **childhood** <note>original: "pueritia"</note> ends. The third age, which is **adolescence**, goes until twenty-one. The fourth, which is **youth**, contains two seven-year periods and goes to thirty-five. Two more seven-year periods, reaching forty-nine, make the fifth, which is the **virile age**. And Aristotle wishes this age to be fit for the government of the republic, because it is strong in spirit and body, and is mature, full, and perfect. Therefore the poet was lost before he came to this age—which has reached the perfection that the first four (infancy, childhood, adolescence, and youth) had not yet attained. In that age one remains stable and does not suffer decline, as do the other two that follow: namely, **old age**, which with two seven-year periods reaches sixty-three and begins to diminish the vigor somewhat; and from that time on is **decrepit age**, in which there is a great and manifest lessening of strength. **ONLY YESTERDAY MORNING I turned my back on it.** By this he shows he has been one night in Hell: because he spent the day defending himself from the beasts and in the arrival of Virgil; and "yesterday morning" was the morning of Good Friday. **I TURNED MY BACK ON IT:** when he wished to climb the mountain already illuminated by the sun. But hindered by the three beasts, he was returning into it had Virgil not come to his aid. But this we have shown more extensively in the beginning, in the description of the entire infernal site. And he rightly induced Ser Brunetto to ask such a question, so that through the answer he might better reveal in this place what the first canto had placed very obscurely. **THIS ONE APPEARED TO ME.** This is the answer to the second question. "This one appeared to me," pointing to Virgil. **RETURNING I into that:** When pushed back down by the three beasts, I was returning into the valley from which I had emerged. **AND LEADS ME HOME:** <note>original: "ad cha" / "a casa"</note> that is, to the house. Our house and our fatherland is heaven; because in this world we have no permanent city, but we are on a pilgrimage and a continual journey. And taking the good way, we return to our house where we were created. And taking the captive way, we ruin ourselves down into deep Hell. The true way to return to heaven is the contemplation of vices to flee them, and of virtues to follow them. Therefore he well said that "by this path"—that is, by this way of contemplation—Virgil, which is the intellect illuminated by true doctrine, leads him back to the eternal house and fatherland.

This is the second principal part of this canto, in which Ser Brunetto responds to Dante. First, he praises him and predicts what shall come to him. Then, he uses satire against the Florentine people; and finally, he names those who are with him. **IF YOU FOLLOW YOUR STAR:** As an astrologer, he shows that the stars promise him good if he follows them. And in this he observes excellent moderation: for he wishes to imply that influence comes from the heavens, which inclines but does not necessitate. He informs us that it is in our power to follow or not to follow; and in this way, he reserves their force to the stars but does not take away free will. **YOU CANNOT FAIL to reach the glorious port.** Glory is clear and illustrious fame with praise: just as sailors, if they follow the star well, are led safely to port; so you, if you follow this happy influence, will arrive at the port of honor. <meta>The word 'Impoche' is a catchword for the next page.</meta>

-># CANTO XV<-

From their customs see that you cleanse yourself.
Your fortune reserves such honor for you
that both one party and the other will have a hunger
for you; but let the grass be far from the goat.
Let the Fiesolan beasts make fodder
of their own seed, and not touch the plant—
if any still rises in their dung—
in which the holy seed lives again
of those Romans who remained there when
the nest of so much malice was made.

**People.** Our poet is to be excused if, in reviling his homeland, he exceeds the bounds of that modesty which ought to be in a philosopher and theologian, and forgets the reverence and piety which every citizen ought to have for his republic. For having been most unjustly deprived, a short time before, of his honors, his dignity, his patrimony, and his homeland, and finally relegated to a harsh exile, he could not restrain himself against such a fresh injury. But it would have been more the duty of his wisdom to speak more moderately. Long controversies took place between the Fiesolans and the Florentines, not without damage to both peoples. And finally the Florentines conquered Fiesole and destroyed it; and they joined their republic with the Fiesolans. This occurred during the time of the first Emperor Henry. **WHO DESCENDED** from Fiesole of old. For the soldiers of Sulla <note>Lucius Cornelius Sulla, a Roman general who settled his veterans in colonies like Fiesole.</note>, who were sent into the new colony, inhabited Fiesole. Hating the harshness of that mountain, they stayed on the nearby plain and built Florence; and because of this he said "from of old," that is, from the beginning—as if to say during the first construction. **AND STILL HOLDS** to the mountain and the rock. "Macigno" is a species of stone <term>macigno: a hard, grey sandstone common in the northern Apennines</term> which is quarried from the mountain of Fiesole for all the buildings of Florence. Therefore, it "holds to the mountain," meaning it is wild; and "to the rock," meaning it is hard and harsh like that stone. Some say that by "rock" he means envy, because the stone is livid and dry. **WILL BECOME YOUR** enemy for your good deeds. This proves the hardness of the people. For just as one is soft and flexible who takes compassion even on those who do not deserve it, conversely, one is hard and inhuman who persecutes those who deserve reward. "He will become your enemy for your good deeds." The cause increases the hardness. For if one who becomes an enemy is hard despite being injured, one who has not been injured is even harder. Therefore, one who has not only not been injured but has been benefited is the hardest of all. **AMONG THE BITTER** sorbs <note>original: "lazi" (lazzi). A tart, astringent flavor.</note>. "Lazzo" in the Florentine language signifies a flavor that is very harsh and very restrictive, such as is found especially in the fruit of the sorb tree. Physicians call this "pontic." Therefore, by metaphor, he calls the cruelty of the people "sorb," and the innocence and humanity of the poet the "fig." According to Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire whose theories dominated Western medical science for centuries.</note>, flavors come either from heat or from cold, or from a mixture of these two. From heat, which is of a more subtle substance, like pepper, comes a sharp flavor. From that which has a thicker substance, bitterness is born. But if it is in the middle between these two extremes, it produces saltiness. In a cold thing and of subtle substance, there is the acidic. From the thick, the pontic <term>pontic: an astringent or "puckering" taste</term>. From the mediocre, the styptic flavor, dry and restrictive. But in a tempered thing, if it is subtle, it makes an unctuous flavor; if thick, sweet; if medium, insipid and dull. This is what Galen writes, with whom Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> agrees in the first eight flavors. But the ninth, that is, the insipid, he says is not a flavor. Averroës <note>An Almohad Andalusian philosopher and judge who wrote influential commentaries on Aristotle.</note> maintains that just as white and black proceed now from heat, now from cold, so the bitter...

<column-break/>

From him he receives such teaching and eloquence that if you labor in writing you will acquire immortal fame. **IF I DISCERNED WELL** in the beautiful life. Because it is difficult in Hell to have knowledge of our future things, except through conjecture, astrology, or revelations. But the blessed soul sees the future because he looks into that mirror where every thing is present. Wherefore Saint Gregory says: "What is it that he does not see, who sees Him who sees all things?" <note>original: "Quid est quod non uideat qui uidet uidentem omnia"</note>. Therefore he shows that while he lived, he knew this glory of Dante through his science of astrology. And he adds that if he did not speak of it to him here and did not comfort him in pursuing the work, it was because death overtook him. **BUT THAT** ungrateful pe[ople]...

...and the sweet are easily found in both of these opposites. For we see some apples: although they are hot, they are nonetheless bitter when unripe and sweet when mature. And some are cold by nature, and nonetheless are sweet when mature. But "it is not for us to settle such great disputes among them" <note>original: "non nostrum inter hos tantas componere lites"</note>. Therefore I return to the text that follows. **OLD FAME** in the world calls them blind. Why the Florentines are called blind <note>original: "orbi"</note>, I do not find an authentic account in any scripture, nor is it fitting, because this people is sharp and ingenious. Unless it is this story which Boccaccio also records: the Pisans <note>The OCR reads "epifani", likely a transcription error for "Pisani".</note> once went with a great fleet to conquer the island of Mallorca (formerly called Baleares), so that their city was left almost without guard. Because they were very great friends with the Florentines in those times, they requested that people be sent to guard Pisa until they returned, for they feared the onslaught of the Lucchese, who were preparing an army against them. And it seemed an ignominious thing to leave the enterprise. Therefore, our people guarded it with faith and diligence. The Pisans <note>OCR: "epifani"</note> returned victorious and brought back rich prey from the conquered island, and among it two noble spoils: namely, the doors of a very ornate temple, and two columns of porphyry. Wanting to give one of these two things to the Florentines—and give them the choice—and estimating that they would choose the columns, moved by envy they dulled them with fire <note>original: "abbacinorono"; literally "blinded" the stone to lose its luster</note> and broke them, and then covered them in rose-colored cloth. The Florentines, not suspecting such fraud, took them; nor did they perceive the defect until, having already brought them to Florence, they uncovered them. Thus, the Florentines were called blind for such inadvertence; and the Pisans <note>OCR: "Epifani"</note>, for having deceived the friends who had guarded their city with such faith, were named trai[tors]...

->### CANTO XVI<-

<note>Though the header indicates Canto XVI, the text concludes Canto XV.</note>

...tors. **YOUR FORTUNE**: your happiness. **SO MUCH HONOR**: such great fame for your learning. **THAT ONE PART AND THE OTHER**: both the Whites and the Blacks of Florence <note>The warring political factions in Florence during Dante's time.</note>. It is as if he says: although you have been exiled by these parties, nevertheless both parties desire you. **BUT LET THE GRASS BE FAR FROM THE GOAT**: as if to say that your citizens, who are so wicked toward you, shall not enjoy your learning. **LET THE FIESOLAN BEASTS MAKE FODDER OF THEIR OWN SEED**: this refers to what was said above, that they descended from Fiesole of old. He truly calls the ungrateful citizens "beasts." And to "make fodder of their own seed" means to take the grain and make a bed for the beasts. Since "strame" <term>strame: fodder or bedding for livestock</term> in Latin signifies something beaten down and spread upon the ground, by this metaphor he wants to show that the Florentine people make fodder of their own seed—that is, of those who descend from them. Because the son is the seed of the father, they "make fodder": that is, they despise him and hold him as something as useful as straw thrown under beasts. **AND LET THE PLANT NOT TASTE IT, IF ANY STILL GROWS IN THEIR DUNG**. This is another metaphor but it leads to the same meaning: he calls the vicious people "dung." And because from them some noble and virtuous person is still born, he calls him a "plant" rising from such dung. He shows that such a plant is not tasted by the people, because its virtues are not honored. **IN WHICH LIVES AGAIN THE HOLY SEED OF THOSE ROMANS**: as if to say the Florentine people were born from virtuous and just Roman men. But such seed has degenerated, just as when grain is sown in the Alps and degenerates into rye. **THE NEST WAS MADE**: that is, Florence, which he calls the nest of every vice.

If my prayer were all fulfilled,
I answered him, you would not yet
be banished from human nature;
for in my mind is fixed, and now saddens me,
the dear and good paternal image
of you, when in the world, from hour to hour,
you taught me how man makes himself eternal;
and how much I prize it, while I live,
it is fitting that my tongue should show.
What you narrate of my course, I write,
and keep it to be glossed with another text
by a Lady who will know how, if I reach her.
This much I wish to be manifest to you:
provided my conscience does not chide me,
I am prepared for Fortune as she wills.
Such a pledge is not new to my ears;
therefore, let Fortune turn her wheel
as she pleases, and the peasant his mattock.

<column-break/>

Dante responds that if everything he asks were granted, Ser Brunetto would not be "placed in banishment from human nature"—that is, he would still be alive. For man is the conjunction of soul and body. **PATERNAL IMAGE**: Your death brings passion to my mind when I remember that you loved me with paternal affection. And you showed me the way and the method of how man "eternizes" himself <note>original: "fetherna"</note>—that is, how he becomes eternal and immortal through fame. And how much I value this while I live "will be spread"—that is, will be discerned and known in my speech; as if to say, I will always name you with honor. Then he adds that he "writes"—as if committing to memory—what he has heard from him. But he keeps it to be "glossed"—that is, interpreted and declared—by Beatrice together with "another text." That is, along with what Messer Farinata told him. <note>In Canto X, Farinata degli Uberti prophesied Dante's exile.</note> His words were these: "But the face of the Queen who reigns here shall not be rekindled fifty times before you learn how much that art weighs." In short, he concludes that he keeps both the words of Ser Brunetto and those of Messer Farinata to have them explained by Beatrice. And he does this following the precepts of Virgil, who said to him: "Let your mind preserve what you have heard against yourself," and "Now attend here," and he pointed his finger:

"When you shall be before the sweet radiance
of her whose beautiful eye sees everything,
from her you shall know the journey of your life."
This is in the tenth Canto. And by this we understand that the intellect of the learned man advises us that although astrologers or other diviners predict things to us, nevertheless we should believe only as much as Theology—understood as Beatrice—dictates to us. **IF I REACH HER**. He spoke conditionally so as not to seem arrogant, because it is a great thing to be able to reach the true knowledge of celestial things, which he understands through Beatrice. Our strengths are not sufficient without divine grace. Then he responds that he is ready to yield to Fortune as long as his "conscience does not chide him." Conscience is the knowledge of oneself and can be for good or evil. But when it is for good, it makes the mind content and quiet. Whence the Apostle says: "Our joy is our conscience." <note>original: "Gaudium nostrum est conscientia nostra"; see 2 Corinthians 1:12</note>. And certainly nothing else can be our joy but our conscience; and when it is for evil, it disturbs and afflicts us. Whence Juvenal: "The Pythian prophetess responded to a certain Spartan that night and day he carries his own witness in his breast." <note>original: "Nocte dieque suum gestare in pectore testem / Spartano cuidam respondit pythia uates"</note>. He concludes, therefore, that he is ready to endure any adverse fortune and yield to it in all things, except in those where his conscience would bite him because they were not honest. **SUCH A PLEDGE IS NOT NEW TO MY EARS**. He demonstrates what all noble philosophers concede: that the premeditation of adverse events prepares us to endure them more easily when they come. Whence Petrarch says: "A wound foreseen hurts much less." <note>original: "Piaga antiueduta assai men duole"</note>. "Arra" <term>arra: earnest money or a down payment</term> is a demonstration of a sale; and just as a pledge is a precursor to payment, so the beginnings of adversity can be called a pledge. **THEREFORE LET FORTUNE TURN HER WHEEL AS SHE PLEASES**. As if to say: whether she puts me at the bottom or the top, I will always remain a rigid guardian of fortune. Neither can happy fortune make me elated and proud, nor can adverse fortune make me base; I will not depart from the true rule of living. And certainly the wise man goes through...
