### CANTO .XV .

->l. iii.<-

"The weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left." <note>original: "arma iustitie a dextris et a sinistris" — a reference to 2 Corinthians 6:7.</note> **THE PEASANT** [with] his hoe. It is as if he says: let everyone do their own duty, and I shall persevere in mine.

*Then my master turned back*
*his right cheek and looked at me,*
*then said: "He listens well who notes it."*

They must be put to work when the need arises. And do not act like many who are philosophers in words but not in deeds. For moral philosophy consists in practice, and not in mere doctrine.

*Nonetheless, I went on speaking*
*with Ser Brunetto, and asked who are*
*his most noted and highest companions:*

*And he to me: "To know of some is good,*
*of the others it will be laudable to be silent,*
*for the time would be too short for so much."*

*In short, know that all were clerics*
*and great men of letters and of great fame,*
*soiled in the world by the same sin:*

*Priscian goes with that wretched crowd,*
*and Francesco d’Accorso you may also see there;*
*and if you had a craving for such scurf,*

*You could have seen him who by the Servant of Servants*
*was moved from the Arno to the Bacchiglione,*
*where he left his ill-stretched nerves.*

*I would say more, but my talking and*
*my stay cannot be longer, for I see*
*new smoke rising there from the sand.*

*People are coming with whom I must not be;*
*let my Treasure be recommended to you,*
*in which I still live, and I ask for no more.*

<column-break/>

Virgil turned to the right: that is, [interpreting] the text which always goes to the right, he turned to Dante—to the lower reason—and said **HE LISTENS WELL**: As if to say, he who takes note of it acts well. And by this he means that the best opinions in speech

Dante asks Ser Brunetto who his companions are: and he replies that it is good to know some of them. These men, although they were stained by such a vice, were nonetheless of such learning that they deserve fame. And first he says that all were **CLERICS**: meaning all, or at least the greater part. And there are also **MEN OF LETTERS**. He identifies these two classes of men because they live with high reputations; and because they cannot easily mix with women, they fall into such a vice more than others. Then he names **PRISCIAN**. This man was from Caesarea in Cappadocia, a man highly practiced in philosophy. He came to Rome, and at the request of Julian the Apostate—being himself an apostate—he wrote most elegantly fifteen books on grammar. The first thirteen are called *Priscianus Maior* <note>Priscian Major</note>; they treat all parts of speech. The last two are *Priscianus Minor* <note>Priscian Minor</note>; they treat construction. It is not recorded anywhere else that Priscian was stained by this vice. But I believe that just as the poet placed Cato in Purgatory to represent Liberty, so in this place he placed Priscian to represent every grammarian. And because such men are commonly stained [by this vice] due to having many young students around them, he places him in this location. **FRANCESCO** was a most notable legal expert, the son of that Accorso of Florence who wrote

the glosses <note>explanatory notes</note> to the laws which are used alongside the text. **BY THE SERVANT OF SERVANTS**: meaning by the Pope, a title found by Pope Gregory I out of humility. **WAS MOVED FROM THE ARNO to the Bacchiglione**. Messer Andrea de' Mozzi was Bishop of Florence; and because he was of very little prudence, and lived without any sense, and was a dishonest sodomite, Messer Tommaso, a Florentine knight and his brother, arranged to have him removed. He was transferred by Pope Nicholas III <note>The text mentions "Niccholao orsino," referring to the Orsini Pope, Nicholas III.</note> to the bishopric of Vicenza. Therefore, because the Arno river passes through the middle of Florence, and the Bacchiglione runs along the walls of Vicenza, he uses the rivers to represent the cities. This man, dying in Vicenza, left his body there. **THE ILL-STRETCHED**: that is, extended nerves. This is because he was nearly doubled over by gout. Or truly, he means his obscene member; and he says "ill-stretched" because he exercised it against nature. **PEOPLE WITH WHOM I MUST NOT BE**. Here he denotes that although throughout this circle those who sinned against nature are punished, nonetheless there are various types of this sin: for it can be male with male, and female with female. As Saint Paul demonstrates in the Epistle to the Romans <note>original: "ad Romanos"</note>. Therefore he relates that those he sees are not of his flock. **LET MY TREASURE BE RECOMMENDED**. We said above that Ser Brunetto wrote two works. The first in the Florentine language and in verse, in which he treats the customs of men, the accidents and changes of fortune, and the human state; he titled it the *Tesoretto* <note>The Little Treasure</note>. The other is larger and he calls it the *Thesoro* <note>The Treasure</note>; it is written in the French language and in prose, and divided into three books. The first is like a chronicle of the times and of the things done in the Old and New Testament, the kingdoms of the Gentiles, the prophets, the apostles, the adoption of the Church, and the Roman Empire—transferred to the Greeks, the French, and the Germans. Likewise, it treats the elements, the stars, the regions, and the animals. In the second, he treats moral philosophy. In the third, he gives rhetorical precepts and writes of the administration of cities. The first he called "common money," the second "precious stones," and the third "purest gold." A damned man should not ask for anything pertaining to the body; because, being deprived of corporal life, such things are of no use to him in any part. ### CANTO XVI. OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.

---

<columns>2</columns>

<image-desc>Historiated ornamental initial 'G' containing a landscape illustration with a waterfall cascading between hills, representing the descent of the Phlegethon river into the next circle of Hell.</image-desc>
Already I was in a place where the roar was heard
of the water falling into the next circle,
similar to the hum that beehives make:
When three shadows together departed,
running, from a troop that was passing
under the rain of the harsh torment.
They came toward us, and each one cried out:
"Stop, you who by your dress seem
to be someone from our wicked land."

<term>Properly</term> in Latin, *turma* signifies a squadron of cavalry. And because he mentioned men of arms, he said *turma*. But in our language, it is taken for any multitude. <gloss>Of the fire</gloss> <gloss>UNDER THE RAIN</gloss>

Ah me, what wounds I saw upon their limbs,
recent and old, burned in by the flames!
It pains me still, even to remember it.

<column-break/>

Although the Canto has changed, nonetheless the poet still treats the same matter which he treated in the preceding Canto XV. He relates how, near the end of this circle, he encountered a troop of those violent against nature, who were military men. He had thus arrived at the edge of the circle where the water falls into the next round, making such a noise as a "rumble"—that is, the confused din—made by "hives" <note>original: *arnie*</note>, which are the vessels where bees or wasps live. At that moment, three shadows departed—that is, three souls—**FROM A TROOP**, meaning from a multitude.

He continues by describing their punishments, and adds that he was comforted by Virgil, who [told him] that he should wait for them. This signifies that even Reason dictates that we should have compassion for men damned for [lack of] some virtue, and we ought to honor them.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto XVI. Previously, Dante and Virgil heard the roar of the Phlegethon waterfall. Now, three souls approach them from a troop of sodomites: Guido Guerra, Tegghiaio Aldobrandi, and Jacopo Rusticucci.</meta>

### CANTO. XVI <note>The header in the original incorrectly reads XVII, but the text belongs to Canto XVI.</note>

<columns>
At their cries my lord turned, 
facing toward me, and now he waits; 
he said, “To these one should be courteous. 
And were it not for the fire that shoots 
from the nature of the place, I would say 
that haste would better suit you than them.”

As we stopped, they began 
their ancient cry; and when they reached us, 
all three made a wheel of themselves. 
Just as champions used to do, naked and oiled, 
watching for their grip and their advantage 
before they were struck or pierced; 
thus wheeling, each one directed 
his face toward me, so that his neck 
made a journey contrary to his feet.

“And if the misery of this shifting place 
makes us and our prayers despised,” 
began one, “let our wretched and flayed appearance 
and our fame bend your mind 
to tell us who you are, you who rub 
your living feet so securely through Hell. 
This one, whose tracks you see me tread, 
though he goes naked and flayed, 
was of higher rank than you believe. 
He was the grandson of the good Gualdrada; 
Guido Guerra was his name, and in his life 
he did much with his wisdom and his sword.”

<column-break/>

If on the other hand some excellent virtue shines within them. **AND WERE IT NOT FOR THE FIRE THAT SHOOTS** from the nature of the place: that is, if it were not for the fire which the nature of this place shoots forth, I would judge that haste would better suit you than them. He means to say: if it were not that their burning and unbridled desires could harm you by keeping such close company with them, I would say that you should seek to know them for their virtues rather than they seeking you. And certainly we ought to be eager to know men in whom some virtue shines. But we must not throw ourselves into the flames in which they burn: that is, we must not imitate their burning lusts.

¶ **These reaching us**: those who stopped to wait for them. They said **"Alas!"** <note>Original: *ei*, a cry of pain</note> which is a voice signifying grief. And he said **Their ancient cry**: because they had a long-standing habit of lamenting in this way. And then, because Dante was standing still and they could not stop (as was shown earlier with Brunetto), they circled around. Therefore they were always moving, yet they did not move away. In this way, they simultaneously observed the law of constant movement and yet were able to speak with Dante. **JUST AS champions**: He makes a comparison between these souls and gladiators. Gladiators were men among the ancients who, to provide a spectacle for the people, fought in the theater in various ways and with various weapons; in these battles, the victor killed the defeated unless the surrounding crowd saved him. Therefore, just as gladiators circled in the theater, so these three circled around Dante. **CHAMPIONS** <note>Original: *ecampioni*</note>: this word in the Tuscan language signifies someone great and strong. But perhaps it is better in this context to understand it as referring to the **wrestling-ground** <term>palestra: a public place in ancient Greece or Rome for training in wrestling and athletics</term>. The ancients held many games in the theater, among which was the game of the arms called the *palestra*: in which strong and trained men stripped naked and maneuvered to get a grip on one another so they could throw each other to the ground. They stood naked so they could not be held by clothing, and they oiled themselves so that, once caught by an opponent, they could slip from his hands like an eel. Whence Virgil says: *They practice their ancestral wrestling with glistening oil.* <note>Original Latin: *Exercent patrias oleo nitente palestras* (Aeneid III, 281)</note> These men went around the theater one after another, thinking of how they might embrace their adversary to their advantage; and having embraced, they would struggle and strike and throw each other to the ground; and this is what is meant by **struck or pierced**. **THUS WHEELING**: in a similar way, these three souls circled, moving forward with their steps while their necks were always turned back toward Dante. Thus the neck made a journey contrary to that of the feet. It is a fitting thing that in a man who proceeds in such a vice, the foot—which represents desire—moves forward and pulls toward lust; but the neck twists the head—where reason resides—backward, because reason flees from such wickedness. Some wish to express through this circling the nature of the vice punished here, for just as a circle has no beginning or end, so this vice has no natural beginning or end.

Here he places the speech of **Jacopo Rusticucci**, a Florentine knight, which is full of artifice. It is in the deliberative style, seeking to capture goodwill and attention by showing that, although their current state and the miserable, unhappy place they inhabit—along with their appearance disfigured by fire—might make them seem base and unworthy of being heard, nonetheless the good fame they acquired in the world should move him. **SHIFTING PLACE** <note>Original: *loco sollo*</note>: signifies loose or uncompacted ground. We use the term **loose** <note>Original: *solla*</note> in weaving when the iron has not properly compacted the fabric. This place was "shifting" because it was sandy, and sand does not harden but stays loose. **FLAYED** <note>Original: *brollo*</note>: properly signifies peeled or hairless; hence we say "brollo" for someone who is poor or stripped of possessions.

</columns>

man and stripped of every good. **THIS ONE, WHOSE TRACKS YOU SEE**: the vestiges and footprints of the one you see me treading; because by following him, he placed his foot where the other had left his mark. **ALTHOUGH HE GOES** naked and flayed: that is, although he goes naked because the flames have stripped away his hair and skin. **HE WAS OF HIGHER RANK**: that is, of greater dignity, fortune, and reputation. **OF THE GOOD**: that is, the chaste and wise Gualdrada. 

This was a very beautiful girl and the daughter of Messer Bellincione Berti de’ Ravignani, a very ancient Florentine family and one of the branches of the Adimari. When Otto IV, the Emperor, was in Florence—and in the assembly of women celebrated for the feast of the Baptist—he was amazed by the beauty of the girl and asked who she was. Messer Bellincione was near the Emperor, and before the others, he replied that she was the daughter of a man who would have the heart to let the Emperor kiss her. The girl heard her father’s words, and pricked by honest shame, she stood up and said: "My father, do not be so liberal in promising me; for no one shall ever kiss me who is not my legitimate husband." The Emperor was stunned by the girl's chaste and prudent response; and immediately he called to him one of his barons named Guido, and at that moment had him marry her, and as a dowry gave him the Casentino and part of Romagna, making him a Count. From him originated the family of the Conti Guidi. From Guido and Gualdrada two sons were born, Guglielmo and Ruggieri; and from Guglielmo came Guido Novello, who followed the Ghibelline <term>Ghibelline: a political faction supporting the Holy Roman Emperor</term> party. From Ruggieri came the Guido Guerra mentioned here. He was most excellent in the military arts and of great prudence and counsel. Thus, in the battle fought at Benevento between Charles and Manfred, he was considered the principal cause of Charles’s victory, for he was there as captain of four hundred Florentine Guelf <term>Guelf: a political faction supporting the Pope</term> knights in exile. They returned to Florence after that rout and, with the help of Charles, drove out the Ghibellines. 

**Tegghiaio Aldobrandi**: He was of the Adimari family, much esteemed both at home and in the armies for many marvelous works and counsels. He advised against the campaign against the Sienese, demonstrating that victory could not be had. But his counsel was not accepted, resulting in the most unhappy rout of the Arbia, or rather of Montaperti, and from that, the exile of the Guelfs from Florence. 

**IACOPO RUSTICHUCCI**: He was a Florentine knight, not from a very famous family, but abundant in wealth, of great spirit, and full of liberality. But he had a wife of such perverse habits that it was eventually necessary for him to separate from her; and such a life was the reason that, remaining without a wife, he fell into the abominable vice for which he is punished in this place.

<insert>
9 There is nothing else to note here except that he wishes to demonstrate that a close familiarity should be sought with men adorned with many virtues, even if there is some great vice in them. And if we can be "covered from the fire"—that is, defend ourselves from vicious desires—we should have conversation with them to imitate them in their virtues; and the teacher—that is, Reason—would permit it. But fearing the fire—that is, the contagion of the vice—we shall abstain from it.

He responds that their miserable state has not fixed contempt for them in his heart, but sorrow and compassion. **OF YOUR LAND**: They are of our fatherland. **AND ALWAYS recalled**: As if to say, I wrote and committed to the memory of others. Or "recalled" as in "imitated"; as we say that a painter *retrays* (portrays) Dante: that is, with the painting, he imitates the image of Dante. **AND LISTENED** to those who spoke of you. And by this, he shows he has always held them in the highest veneration. Hence it follows that he cannot hold them in contempt now. **I LEAVE THE GALL And go for the sweet fruits**: In one verse, he manifests the whole journey of one who goes toward beatitude. For he goes through Hell—that is, through the consideration of vices, which are gall—to leave it; and he wishes through purgation to arrive at Paradise, where the sweet fruit and result of the virtues, that is, happiness, is found. **PROMISED TO ME BY THE TRUTHFUL [GUIDE]**

**Leader**. Virgil, that is, the Intellect when we choose him as our leader: and following him promises us happiness, and he does not lie to us. But he gives it to us. Because he is truthful and not a liar. **BUT BEFORE** I reach such fruits <note>Referring to the "sweet fruits" of Paradise mentioned on the previous page.</note>: I must return, almost as if going down to the very center: which place, being the lowest in the world, contains the bottom of Hell: that is, he must go with knowledge down to the lowest of all vices.

"So may your soul long lead
your limbs," he then replied,
"and so may your fame shine after you:

Do courtesy and valor," he said, "dwell
within our city as they used to,
or have they been cast out entirely?

For Guglielmo Borsieri, who grieves
with us and goes there with his companions,
vexes us greatly with his words."

"The new people and sudden gains
have generated pride and excess
in you, Florence, so that you already weep."

Thus I cried out with my face raised;
and the three, who took this as an answer,
looked at one another as one gazes at the truth.

<column-break/>

This shade <note>Jacopo Rusticucci</note> prays to Dante: and to bend him to his will, he wishes two things for him which the damned judge to be the greatest. The first is a long life. The second is perpetual fame after life. Therefore, **SO MAY THE SOUL LEAD**: and as it were, maintain and preserve for a long time **YOUR LIMBS**: your body: which, while the soul is included within it, is preserved whole and incorrupt. Then, once the soul has departed, it immediately dissolves and corrupts. In short: "may you live long," or rather "lead yourself as if held in high esteem." **AND SO MAY** your **fame shine** / be radiant **AFTER YOU**: after your life. **HE SAID** / Jacopo [said] **DWELL**, inhabit our city **COURTESY AND VALOR**, generosity and strength, or rather magnanimity: which two virtues maintain harmony in the republic <gloss>and</gloss> increase the empire. Because the first generates harmony and acquires friends; the second makes men fit for every great undertaking. **GUGLIELMO Borsieri**. Some say "Borsieri" because 

---

at first he made purses <note>original: "borse"</note>. Others assert that Borsieri was a family name of no small nobility. However it may be, he was a courtier-knight and had dealings with all the lords of Italy, a well-bred man of noble manners. It was his office, and that of similar knights, to negotiate peace between great and noble men, to intervene in arranging marriages, and sometimes to refresh the spirits of listeners with witty and pleasant stories. They say that while in Genoa, being asked by Messer Ermino Grimaldi—a man who was simultaneously very rich and very stingy—what he might have painted in the hall of a newly built house, something unknown and never seen before, he replied: "Sir, I will teach you of something you have never known: have 'Generosity' <note>original: "liberalita"</note> painted there." This word so moved the miserly soul of Messer Ermino that he changed his nature and became quite generous. The poet thus imagines that this man, having recently died, has brought fresh news of Florence. **WHO GRIEVES with us**: that is, he endures the same sorrow and punishment we endure, because he is damned for the same vice. **AND GOES THERE with his companions**. He is in that troop from which we have presently emerged. **Vexes** / or torments, i.e., gives us much pain. **THE New people**. Here Dante responds, saying "The new people," meaning the rustic folk who have recently come to live in Florence. **AND THE sudden gains**. As if to say, gains made through illicit contracts and with extreme avarice. **PRIDE and excess**: commonly the latter is born from the former. For when new men become rich and acquire status, they become proud and full of excess, because they are so arrogant that they want more than belongs to them. "Pride" <note>original: "Orgoglio"</note> in the Florentine tongue signifies arrogant haughtiness. Whence Petrarch says: "Wherefore I grieve much when an excessive pride hides many virtues in a beautiful woman." **THUS I cried out with my face raised**. This demonstrates indignation. **AND THESE THREE LOOKED at one another as one gazes at the truth**. When those who hear something look at one another's faces, it seems they approve that what they hear is true.

"If at other times it costs you so little,"
they all replied, "to satisfy others,
happy are you who speak thus at your will.

Therefore, if you escape these dark places
and return to see the beautiful stars,
when it shall please you to say, 'I was there,'

See that you speak of us to the people."
Then they broke their circle; and in fleeing,
their swift legs seemed like wings.

<column-break/>

The meaning is that those three replied to Dante that if every other time it was so easy for him to answer whoever asked him, certainly he is happy since he can speak "at his will": that is, since he can speak at his own discretion, with such ornament and brevity. Then, having gained such goodwill by having praised him so, they pray that when he returns to the world, he brings them back to the memory of men. We can also interpret "if it costs him so little to satisfy others" and "if he speaks at his will." **WHEN It shall please you to say 'I was there.'** That is, when...

An "amen" could not have been said
as quickly as they had vanished:
wherefore it seemed to the master time to depart.

**WHEEL**: The circle that they had formed around us. **AND THEIR SLENDER LEGS**: that is, straight and nimble. **SEEMED LIKE WINGS**: that is, they resembled wings: because they were as fast in running as wings are in flying.

I followed him, and we had gone but a little way
when the sound of the water was so near
that, had we spoken, we should hardly have been heard.
As that river which has its own path
first from Mount Veso <note>Mount Monviso in the Cottian Alps.</note> toward the east,
along the left slope of the Apennines:
Which is called the "Still Water" <note>Acquacheta</note> above,
before it flows down into its low bed,
and at Forlì it is deprived of that name,
It reverberates there above San Benedetto
of the Alp, falling in a single leap
where there should have been room for a thousand:
Thus, down from a steep bank,
we found that dark water resounding
so loudly it would soon have hurt the ear.

<column-break/>

Having emerged from such dangerous places and been brought into such an enclosed space, it will benefit you to narrate past events. For as Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, Roman statesman and philosopher.</note> says: "To remember past danger once we are safe gives us pleasure and delight." <note>original: "Ricordarsi del passato pericolo poiche siamo riducti nel sicuro ci da uolupta et piacere."</note> **I SAW BREAKING THE**

It had already pleased Virgil to depart from those souls: because Reason <note>Virgil represents human reason.</note> dwells upon such vices only as long as is sufficient for the knowledge of them: then it departs, and the appetite and the senses follow it. And they arrived at the end of this circle, where there is the bank that descends into the eighth circle, through which the Phlegethon falls, making such a din to those nearby that they could not hear one another. And he adds that the fall of this river was like that of the Montone. Here it should be noted that Vesulo is a mountain in the Alps above Monferrato, which divides Provence from Italy. From here the Apennines begin, although some say the Apennines begin at Monaco on the Genoese Riviera, and come along coasting toward Pietrapana, leaving on the left Monferrato, Turin, and Vercelli, and on the right Lunigiana and part of the Riviera. There it turns somewhat, and to the left leaves Piacenza, Parma, Reggio, Modena; and to the right Luni, Lucca, Pistoia. Then proceeding, to the left it leaves Bologna, Romagna, and the March; and to the right Florence, Arezzo, Perugia, and the Patrimony <note>The Lands of St. Peter/Papal States.</note> as far as Rome. Then continuing, to the left the Abruzzi, the Land of Bari, Puglia, and the Land of Otranto; to the right Campania, the Land of Labour, Salerno, and part of Calabria; and to the left the other part of Calabria as far as the Lighthouse of Messina. And formerly it continued even into Sicily. For opposite its end in Italy is Mount Peloro in Sicily, which corresponds to it in a way that it seems a coast torn away from the Apennines. And where in Italy the Apennine is cut off by the strait and ends there is Rheggio; which name in Greek demonstrates the "breaking" of this mountain by the sea that divided it. For in that language *Rhegmin* <note>original: "Rhegmin" (ῥήγμην), from the Greek verb meaning to break or shatter.</note> means to break and shatter. Wherefore in Persius <note>Aulus Persius Flaccus, a Roman satirist.</note> one reads: *Thus we withdrew the coast from the long Apennine.* <note>original: "Sic costam longo subduximus apennino."</note> And many writers believe that Sicily was once joined with Italy, and then, either by the force of constant waves or by earthquakes, it was disjoined. And Virgil in the *Aeneid* <note>The text incorrectly cites the "Hecloca" (Eclogues), but this is from Aeneid III, 414-419.</note> says:

> These lands, they say, once ripped apart by a vast upheaval
> (So much can the passage of long ages change things)
> Sprang apart, though both lands were once one;
> The sea came violently between them and with its waves
> Cut the Hesperian side from the Sicilian. <note>original: "qui quodam et uasta conuulsa ruina / Tantum cui longinqua ualet mutare uetustas / Dissiluisse ferunt cum protinus utraque tellus / Vna foret uenit medio ui pontus et undis / Hesperium siculo latus abscidit."</note>

And because we have made mention above of the "right" and the "left": understand the right part to be that which is to the south <note>literally "midday".</note>, and the left that which is northern. For when we turn toward the head of the world, which is the east, the northern site remains to our left, and the meridian to our right. All those rivers, therefore, which are born from the left side of the Apennines enter into the Po before this point—the Po whose origin is at the roots of Vesulo—and they do not go to the sea by their own course. But this river <note>The Montone/Acquacheta.</note> does the opposite. For it does not join the Po but goes by its own course. And the text orders it thus: "As that river which first has its own path," that is, it is the first which has its own path to the sea. **FROM MOUNT VESO** toward the east: Do not understand that it is born in Mount Vesulo, which is more than two hundred miles from the mountain above Forlì where this river is born. But he said "from Mount Veso," meaning from the side of Mount Veso. It is called "Still Water" <note>Acquacheta</note> before it descends the mountain; and "flows down," that is, descends through the valley **DOWN INTO ITS LOW BED**, i.e., into the plain of Romagna. **AND AT FORLÌ** it is deprived of that name: because it is no longer called Acquacheta but the Montone, and it enters the sea near Ravenna. **IT REVERBERATES THERE ABOVE SAN BENEDETTO**: Because here it begins to fall. **AT A FALL**: This is an abbey <note>San Benedetto in Alpe.</note> above that part of the Apennines which divides the Mugello from Romagna. Therefore this mountain takes its name from the abbey. **WHERE THERE SHOULD HAVE BEEN ROOM FOR A THOUSAND**: Giovanni Boccaccio writes that he heard from the abbot of this San Benedetto that the noble lords of that country once discussed building a castle near this waterfall and gathering there many neighboring villages. But the death of the one who desired it more than the others interrupted the design. Thus Dante says: "Where there should have been room," that is, a receptacle and a stay and a habitation for "a thousand," meaning for many. **THUS**: He returns to the subject and says that thus that water reverberated.

water of the Phlegethon through that **RUGGED** valley: that is, precipitous and very steep. **IN A SHORT TIME**: that is, in a brief moment. **IT WOULD HAVE HURT THE EAR**: that is, the sense of hearing, which is overwhelmed by an excess of sound and voice. This is so that one may better understand that although our soul is incorporeal <note>The soul itself has no physical body.</note>: nevertheless, it exercises the power of the senses through bodily instruments. Therefore, it is necessary that as the bodily instrument is finite and limited, so too is the sense finite and limited. Thus, any sensible excess must necessarily offend the sense, because it exceeds its proportion. For this reason, they say that those who live where the Nile falls <note>A reference to the "Catadupa," the great waterfalls of the Nile; ancient writers claimed the inhabitants were deafened by the roar.</note> become deaf from such a great and constant noise.

<column-break/>

This passage contains within it a rather obscure allegory <term>fictione</term>. The poet posits that, by Virgil's command, he untied a cord he had girt around him and handed it, coiled up, to Virgil. Regarding this, some say that Dante in his youth joined the Order of Saint Francis <note>The "Friars Minor," who wear a simple cord as a belt.</note>; and later, having departed from it, he left the habit behind. Because of this, they believe he uses the cord he was girt with to represent hypocrisy. I do not believe this, nor does it seem likely to me. Rather, it is manifest that in what follows, the poet treats ten species of fraud. Thus, it is appropriate that since Virgil wishes to demonstrate to Dante what fraud is, he asks him to untie the cord he was wearing. This denotes that if a man wishes to truly understand fraud—which is a thing more intricate and obscure than any other vice—he cannot see the universal concept with his intellect unless the senses represent some particular example to him. For example, I would not know what "friendship" is in general if I did not first understand a particular friendship, such as the one between me and you, which makes us have the same will in all things. This particular instance, brought from the senses to the intellect, allows the intellect to abstract such a consideration from that

---

particular friendship and reduce it to a general rule. It then understands what friendship is in itself, no longer considering only that which exists between Scipio and Laelius <note>Famous Roman examples of perfect friendship.</note>, or any other; but understands that in general, it is nothing other than a consensus of willing and not willing among several men. Therefore, in this place, Virgil and Dante are like a single man, as we have already demonstrated many times; he who wishes to understand fraud must have the intellect <note>Represented by Virgil.</note> ask the senses <note>Represented by Dante</note> for the cord he has girt. By the cord, he means his own particular fraud, which is born from the senses aided by the "lower reason" <note>The part of the mind dealing with earthly, practical matters rather than divine contemplation.</note>. He "unties" it, which signifies a will to leave it behind, and hands it to the intellect, because he seeks to know its malice through the intellect. But he hands it "knotted," that is, tied and wound up—coiled—because fraud is always full of knots and entanglements. Truly we shall say that the senses and the lower reason offer the cord entangled, because they are not sufficient on their own to explain the nature of such a vice. But the intellect can explain it; and therefore he hands it to him. He rightly uses the cord as a symbol for fraud. The cord is made of hemp, a material suited for entangling and impeding; and the same nature is found in fraud. Furthermore, it is twisted and composed of many strands; similarly, fraud twists and composes many malices together, and nothing in it is simple or open. There is not the same distinction in the Tuscan language between *fune* <note>rope</note> and *corda* <note>string/cord</note> as there is in Latin. For the Latins call *fune* that which is made of hemp or other similar material fit for binding. *Chorda* is a Greek name <note>original: "Chorda e/ nome greco"</note> and signifies the catgut strings with which they play viols, harps, lutes, and similar instruments; and the Latins use it in that same sense. But we take "rope" and "cord" as almost the same thing. Thus, he said "cord," meaning "rope." Nor does the poet distance himself from the Psalmist, who, using the rope to represent fraud, said: *The ropes of sinners have encircled me* <note>original Latin: "Funes peccatorum circumplexi sunt me"; Psalm 119:61.</note>; and Isaiah: *Woe to you who draw iniquity with the cord of vanity* <note>original Latin: "Ve qui tranfitis iniquitate in funiculum uanitatis"; Isaiah 5:18.</note>. **AND WITH IT I THOUGHT ONCE TO CATCH THE LEOPARD.** Having shown that the poet had stripped himself of his own fraud, he now adds two things. First, that such fraud had not been regarding very grave sins, such as using fraud in avarice or proud ambition. Rather, he used it only in lust, having used it to "catch the leopard," that is, in matters of love and lechery; for we showed that the leopard represents lust <note>The "lonza" from Canto I.</note>. It follows that just as the sin of lust is less grave than others, so such fraud is less detestable. The second point is that even in lust, he had thought of it only a few times. Thus he says "once"; therefore, he had not made a habit of it. For this reason, it was easy to untie himself from it <gloss>that is, to put it aside.</gloss> **WHEREUPON HE TURNED** toward the right side. Reason always turns to the righteous right; that is, toward direct and virtuous thoughts: and he threw the cord far from the bank, almost into the middle **INTO THAT HIGH** that is, deep **RAVINE**, or ditch. We call a "borrato" a

The commentator rejects the theory that Dante was a Franciscan friar, arguing instead that the cord represents the specific nature of fraud as a tangle of sensory deception.</summary>

small stream which, because it is in a deep and narrow valley, has high banks on every side. He threw it into the middle to find the center of that very vice: from which center all lines are born. **AND YET IT MUST BE** that novelty responds. Dante, as a prudent man, estimated within himself that Virgil does nothing without the highest consideration. Therefore, from every one of his actions, one should expect something excellent and new. And he admonishes us that we should always place faith in those who are wiser. For as Cicero writes in the second book of *On Duties*: we have faith in those whom we judge to be wiser than ourselves, and whom we believe foresee the future <note>original: "sis fidem habemus quos plus sapere quam nos arbitramur: Et quos futura prospicere credimus."</note>. **THAT THE MASTER** follows with his eye. It is an excellent conjecture that Virgil did not throw the cord by chance, but with consideration, because he follows it with his eye: that is, because he tracks it with his sight. Therefore, he remains attentive to await the end of such a thing. **AH, HOW CAUTIOUS** It is an excellent precept that when we are near wise and learned men—and those we judge to do nothing by chance or without exquisite reason—we must observe and note with the highest attention not only their deeds and words, but every smallest gesture and sign. For these men see not only the deed—that is, what is present—but with the eyes of the mind, they gaze upon the effect that must follow from it. **HE SAID TO ME.** At one and the same time, Virgil was thinking of what was to follow from the thrown cord, and he comforted Dante, for that which he was waiting for—and what Dante was dreaming of—was soon to manifest. And certainly, the intellect perceives the cause and foresees the effect as a certain thing and awaits it. But the senses and the lower reason do not see it, because they more readily know the cause through the effect than the effect through the cause. Thus, before the effect follows, even if one has seen the cause, one does not foresee it. Instead, one goes on imagining various things, similar to one who dreams, and rarely guesses correctly.

<column-break/>

Most excellently and with great art, having to tell an incredible thing, he demonstrates that he understands that one should not narrate incredible things (even if they are true) unless necessity compels us. This is because they wrongly bring us shame; for by telling the truth, we are held to be liars. And because few things are more opposite and contrary to the nature of man than a lie: seeing as speech was given to us—which is not given to any other animal—so that we might express and manifest outwardly what we have conceived in the mind, and yet we use it for the contrary. Therefore, a man should not only not tell a lie, but also not say that which *seems* like a lie unless necessity constrains him. Therefore Dante, to gain faith for that which by its nature seems incredible, demonstrates that he knows what we have said; but he is forced by necessity to tell it, because without it, the matter in this place would remain imperfect.

He tells it, then: and to give it credit, he affirms it with an oath by those things which are most dear to him. He swears in this sentiment: "So may the notes—that is, the words of this comedy that I write—be full of long-lasting grace, as surely as I saw this beast coming." This is an effective oath. Because there is nothing a writer desires so much as that the written work should find favor. And Dante desires this especially, not for vainglory, but because by writing things necessary for the salvation of man, he desires to be read so that his laborious vigils <note>Refers to the long nights spent working by candlelight.</note> may produce the best fruit for many. **THAT I SAW THROUGH** that thick and dark air, a figure come swimming upward. Many have remained deceived, believing that because he says "come swimming," that place is filled with water. And they do not perceive that he is imitating Virgil, who makes a reciprocal translation from the sea to the air. Wherefore Virgil said "sail-flying sea" <note>original: "Mare velivolum," meaning that through which one flies with sails</note>; and flying is only in the air. And likewise from the air to the sea, where in the passage on Mercury he said "oarage of wings" <note>original: "Remigio alarum"</note> although oars belong only to the sea. Similarly, Dante said "come swimming," although the swimmer is properly in the water. And certainly, it is a marvelous fiction and entirely worthy of the divinity of such an intellect. 

He wants to describe fraud: and he says "I saw a figure," but he did not yet see what figure it was. This denotes that fraud is seen, but at first it is not recognized. The Trojans saw Sinon <note>The Greek spy who tricked the Trojans into accepting the Wooden Horse.</note> and heard his words, but they did not know to what end he had come. Furthermore, he saw it through the "thick and dark air." This not only denotes that in Hell—that is, in the habit of vices— there is obscurity (meaning ignorance), but it also wants to show that fraud is always shaded and darkened in such a way that it cannot be discerned. It came swimming through the air to signify that it does not stand in a solid and firm place (that is, in the truth). Instead, it swims: because the fraudulent person always varies and changes things, and when you believe him to be in one place, he is in another. It came "upward" because fraud, from a hidden place, eventually comes to light. And it is marvelous to every "steady heart" because no one is of such an unconquered spirit that he does not fear fraud. For the force which is in...

clearly wounded by some distance, allowing one to provide for defense. Wherefore the **magnanimous** <note>In the Aristotelian sense: a person of great soul and courage.</note> man takes confidence: But fraud strikes us before we can take it. For this reason, the generous man cannot exercise or demonstrate any of his strength to resist such things: and because of this, he greatly fears such assaults. Understand then why Dante saw it through the dark and thick air: because it came swimming: because it came from the bottom to the top: because it was terrifying even to steady men: And finally, he shows that in coming up, it acted like one who has gone to the bottom of the water to unhook an anchor fastened to a reef or to another thing covered by the water: who, returning up, extends the upper parts: that is, the neck: and the arms: and the last parts, which are the legs, he retracts: that is, he curls them up. And truly the fraudulent person always extends the first parts: because he begins with something true: and he wants that to be manifest. Then, at the end, he adds the false: and this he retracts: and wraps it up so that it is hidden: and not understood.

### CANTO. XVII. OF THE FIRST CANTICLE OF DANTE

<columns>2</columns>

"Behold the beast with the pointed tail,
who passes mountains and breaks walls and weapons;
behold she who makes the whole world stink."
So my leader began to speak to me,
and beckoned her to come to the shore,
near the end of the walked-upon marbles.
And that foul image of **fraud** <note>The monster Geryon, who represents the sin of deceit.</note>
came forward and landed its head and chest:
but did not draw its tail onto the bank.
Its face was the face of a **just man**,
so benign was its skin on the outside,
and of a serpent was all the rest of the trunk.
It had two paws, hairy up to the armpits;
the back and the chest and both the sides
were painted with knots and little wheels.

<column-break/>

In this seventeenth canto, the author presents the form of **Geryon**: which he intends to be the figure of fraud: because he must deal with the fraudulent: And first, he shows that it has a tail so sharp that with it, it can pass through mountains; and break walls and weapons: And certainly fraud does not show its harm except in the tail, that is, in the end. For the fraudulent person conceals and hides his thought and counsel: And under the cover of some good, he deceives you. And the end of fraud is always harmful. Nor can you perceive the deception except at the end. Whence is born the proverb that **the poison is in the tail** <note>original: "nella coda sta el ueleno." A common medieval expression meaning the sting or the trick comes at the very end.</note>: And fraud is so powerful that it passes mountains: that is, it overcomes every great power. **AND BREAKS walls and weapons.** This denotes that no protection is effective against it: neither of defense: nor of offense. **THIS IS SHE who stinks up the whole world.** The world is in "good odor": and uncorrupted when men <note>The text breaks off here as the commentary continues on the next page.</note>

and through frauds. **AND BECKONED HER** <note>Referring to Virgil signaling the monster Geryon.</note> to come to the shore. The beast was in the air: because fraud has no stability: nor can it be understood or held: but like air, it slips away from you. But Virgil calls it to the margin: which is made of marble, a hard thing. This is because the intellect considers and contemplates fraud by grounding it in true and stable reasons: and makes it come onto the stone. But that beast places its head and chest there: but not the tail: because, as we have said, the beginnings of the fraudulent are placed upon the truth: and—not to change the example—Sinon, in order to deceive the Trojans, begins his narration with true things, demonstrating the deception of Ulysses in the death of Palamedes. <note>Sinon was the Greek spy who convinced the Trojans to bring the Wooden Horse into their city; Palamede was a Greek hero framed for treason by Ulysses.</note> Then, under this truth, he hides his lie, feigning the hatred that Ulysses bore him: and many other things. Therefore, the first parts of fraud are on the stone: that is, on something solid and true: And the tail remains in the air, a shifting thing. **ITS FACE WAS** the face of a just man. This monster had the face of a man: the rest of the body of a serpent: and the tail of a scorpion. Some say this signifies three types of fraud. One in words: and this is denoted by the human face: because only man uses speech. The second in things: that is, in the arts: and in commerce: And this is denoted by the serpent, which is a cunning animal of various colors: just as such frauds are various and diverse. The third in deed: such as robbers and assassins: who, like the scorpion, give poisonous stings. But I judge the more true allegory to be: that every fraud is composed of these three forms: And if fraud is considered rightly, it has a face: that is, its first appearance is that of a just man: because the fraudulent person at the beginning demonstrates humanity, benevolence: and every part of justice: And as Sallust says: <note>Gaius Sallustius Crispus, a Roman historian.</note> "He has one thing ready on his tongue: and another closed in his breast." <note>original: "Vna chosa ha prompta nella lingua: et unaltra chiusa nel pecto."</note> And from such people David prays to the Lord to defend him when he says: "Deliver my soul from wicked lips and from a deceitful tongue." <note>original: "Libera animam meam a labiis iniquis et a lingua dolosa." (Psalm 120:2)</note> **SO KIND** she had her skin on the outside. To denote that such kindness is not within: that is, in deeds, but in the skin, that is, in appearance. Whence Persius says: "I know you inside and under the skin." <note>original: "Ego te intus et in cute noui." (Persius, Satire 3.30)</note> **AND OF A SERPENT** all the rest of the trunk: that is, all the rest of the body was a serpent. The serpent is a cunning and prudent animal. And because cunning and cleverness can be a virtue when, without fraud and harm to our neighbor, we strive to defend ourselves from the malice of others: and rightly administer our affairs: it can also be a vice when we use such cunning in fraud. Therefore the serpent is sometimes placed in a good sense: as when the Truth <note>Referring to Christ.</note> says in the Gospel: "Be wise as serpents and simple as doves." <note>original: "Estote prudentes sicut serpentes et simplices sicut columbe." (Matthew 10:16)</note> At other times it is in a bad sense; whence in the first part of Genesis the diabolical temptation of the first man is written in the figure of a serpent, which had a human face to denote what we have said. Nor can I, without the greatest amazement, consider the greatness of the genius of this poet: who in the same place mixes the things of the gentiles with those of the Christians: and adds from himself: and from very diverse things makes such a temperament: that he optimally expresses his intention, and while conveying the greatest gravity, adds wonderful delight. Therefore the fraudulent person has a beginning full of humanity and goodness in appearance to allure the minds of men and remove from them any thought of being deceived; then his process is serpentine, cunning, and varied until he arrives at the end to complete the fraud: which is the tail of the scorpion because it harms most greatly. **TWO PAWS.** By these we understand two types of cunning: that is, fraud which is in action: and deceit in words. **HAIRY** as if covered and hidden: because the counsel of the fraudulent is always covered and hidden: And also it is full of cruelty. **TO THE ARMPITS:** Up to the shoulders: which he calls armpits from this Latin word *axilla*. **THE BACK, THE CHEST**, and both the sides. In essence, all the rest of the body was covered with the skin of a serpent which is full of knots and little wheels <note>Referring to the circular patterns on Geryon's skin.</note>. And this allegorically signifies the simulations that are always implicit and involved and colored: and the modes of fraud are various and entangled together: so that from one, one enters another: and they are circular so that one returns to where one began. **WITH MORE colors.** Whoever has seen such cloths understands the comparison to be excellent. **NOR WERE SUCH webs by Arachne laid.** The fables say that in Lydia there was a woman named Arachne, born in a small village and of lowly lineage: But so skilled in the art of embroidery: and in every craft of the needle and the loom that by a long interval she surpassed all others. This made her so arrogant: that not content with surpassing mortals, she wished to compete with the gods: and contend with Pallas, the goddess of wisdom. But Pallas defeated her and broke and cut her web and converted her into a spider. Which animal still does not cease making ingenious webs. By this fable, it is shown that Arachne—that is, human fraud—surpasses all others except for Pallas, who is the goddess of wisdom: because divine wisdom knows the fraud of man. And God is the "searcher of hearts." <note>original: "scrutator cordium."</note> For which reason, let no Arachne believe she can defeat Pallas. Because she will defeat her and break every web: That is, God will know our fraud: And will break all our designs.

Whence Persius says: "I know you inside and under the skin." **AND OF A SERPENT** all the rest of the trunk: that is, all the rest of the body was a serpent. The serpent is a cunning and prudent animal. And because cunning and cleverness can be a virtue when, without fraud and harm to our neighbor, we strive to defend ourselves from the malice of others: and rightly administer our affairs: it can also be a vice when we use such cunning in fraud. Therefore the serpent is sometimes placed in a good sense: as when the Truth says in the Gospel: "Be wise as serpents and simple as doves." At other times it is in a bad sense; whence in the first part of Genesis the diabolical temptation of the first man is written in the figure of a serpent, which had a human face to denote what we have said. Nor can I, without the greatest amazement, consider the greatness of the genius of this poet: who in the same place mixes the things of the gentiles with those of the Christians: and adds from himself: and from very diverse things makes such a temperament: that he optimally expresses his intention, and while conveying the greatest gravity, adds wonderful delight. Therefore the fraudulent person has a beginning full of humanity and goodness in appearance to allure the minds of men and remove from them any thought of being deceived; then his process is serpentine, cunning, and varied until he arrives at the end to complete the fraud: which is the tail of the scorpion because it harms most greatly. **TWO PAWS.** By these we understand two types of cunning: that is, fraud which is in action: and deceit in words. **HAIRY** as if covered and hidden: because the counsel of the fraudulent is always covered and hidden: And also it is full of cruelty. **TO THE ARMPITS:** Up to the shoulders: which he calls armpits from this Latin word *axilla*. **THE BACK, THE CHEST**, and both the sides. In essence, all the rest of the body was covered with the skin of a serpent which is full of knots and little wheels. And this allegorically signifies the simulations that are always implicit and involved and colored: and the modes of fraud are various and entangled together: so that from one, one enters another: and they are circular so that one returns to where one began. **WITH MORE colors.** Whoever has seen such cloths understands the comparison to be excellent. **NOR WERE SUCH webs by Arachne laid.** The fables say that in Lydia there was a woman named Arachne, born in a small village and of lowly lineage: But so skilled in the art of embroidery: and in every craft of the needle and the loom that by a long interval she surpassed all others. This made her so arrogant: that not content with surpassing mortals, she wished to compete with the gods: and contend with Pallas, the goddess of wisdom. But Pallas defeated her and broke and cut her web and converted her into a spider. Which animal still does not cease making ingenious webs. By this fable, it is shown that Arachne—that is, human fraud—surpasses all others except for Pallas, who is the goddess of wisdom: because divine wisdom knows the fraud of man. And God is the "searcher of hearts." For which reason, let no Arachne believe she can defeat Pallas. Because she will defeat her and break every web: That is, God will know our fraud: And will break all our designs.

> As sometimes skiffs lie along the shore,
> that stay part in the water and part on land;

<column-break/>

Thus that beast stayed partly in the air and partly on land, just as skiffs <note>original: "eburchi" or "burchi," referring to small, flat-bottomed boats or barges.</note> stay, or as beavers stay. This animal is called *fibro* <note>Greek: "kastor"</note> by the Greeks. And Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist.</note> says that by natural instinct, knowing that the hunter seeks him to obtain his glands—which are medicinal, especially for paralysis and the "falling sickness" <note>epilepsy</note>—he bites them off himself with his teeth. For this reason, Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville, a medieval scholar.</note> writes that the Latins call him *castore* <note>the castor or beaver</note> because he castrates himself. He has a terrible bite; he cuts trees with his teeth no differently than a man does with iron. And if he bites a man’s limb, he does not let go until he feels he has crushed the bone. He is similar to an otter, and like it, he inhabits both land and water. But he has back feet like a goose, with which he is very dexterous at swimming. He has a broad and scaly tail like a fish, and he always keeps it in the water; this alone is considered precious food, while the other limbs are of an abominable foulness. He builds ingenious houses on rivers with multiple floors, so that even as the water rises and falls, he can keep his tail in the stream and the rest of his body dry. He feeds on fish and the bark of trees. Those who have more strength make slaves of the weaker ones, making them go upside down through the river, and between their back legs and bellies, they load them with wood for the construction of their houses; then by the tail, they pull them to the chosen site. Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century philosopher and scientist.</note> writes that it is false that they castrate themselves, because their glands are attached near the spine or the backbone and cannot be removed without their death. Dioscorides <note>An ancient Greek physician.</note> affirms the same. Useful hats are made from their skins. **AMONG THE gluttonous Germans:** that is, among the greedy and those of great appetite; he says this because the Danube, where beavers are found, runs through those peoples. **TO WAGE HIS WAR** against the fish on which he feeds. **UPON THE EDGE** that binds the sand with stone: This was the bank of the river made of stone which held back the sand, so that it would not be eroded by the river. They appeared clearly out of the water and were upon the stone. Because the beginnings of fraud, as I said, are based on true and solid things; but then the rest wiggles, because they are covered and vain things; and they twist the fork upward because finally the poison appears.

Virgil shows that it was necessary to go right up to the beast, because to have full knowledge of the fraudulent, it was necessary to come to the consideration of cunning <term>lastutia</term><note>astuteness or craftiness used for deception</note>. **IT IS NECESSARY TO twist our path.** He says this because until now they had turned to the left hand, except for sometimes crossing over as they do now. And we have already shown above why he feigns this. **THEREFORE We descended to the right breast:** To denote that the consideration of cunning was for the purpose of guarding against it, and not for using it. **AND TEN STEPS We made upon the outer edge:** Understand this to be upon the rim of the seventh circle. By "ten steps," he means the ten types of cunning <note>the ten "Bolge" or ditches of the Eighth Circle</note> which he will treat successively in the eighth circle. Afterward, Virgil sends Dante to know the people who are there, and he remains to reason with the beast. This signifies that for the knowledge of particular things, lower reason is sufficient; but to consider the whole nature of cunning in general, one needs Virgil—that is, higher reason and the intellect, which persuades the beast to place them upon its strong shoulders and carry them into the eighth circle. For our intellect cannot go to the knowledge of the punishments in that circle if it does not know cunning and its types, and does not know how to distinguish the places according to those types. **PEOPLE Sitting near:** One and the same punishment—namely, flames falling from the sky—punishes the sodomites and the usurers, because each of these does violence to nature. But the sodomites walk and the usurers sit, to show that usury is a greater sin, because it does violence not only to nature but also to art <note>human industry and labor</note>. **HERE THE MASTER:** We have already explained this place above. **THEIR conduct:** <note>original: "mena"</note> their behavior, their actions, and movements; because "to conduct" means to move, whence we say "he conducts [moves] his head." **LET YOUR Reasonings there be brief.** For once it is known that <meta>catchword: hab</meta>

...we must immediately depart from such consideration. While... <note>original: "biamo... While CHE tor." The text here is a fragment of a sentence continued from the previous page's commentary.</note>

Thus still further along the extreme edge
of that seventh circle, all alone
I went to where the sorrowful people sat.
Through their eyes their grief was bursting forth;
on this side and that they protected themselves with their hands,
sometimes from the vapors and sometimes from the hot soil.
Not otherwise do dogs in summer,
now with their snout, now with their paws, when they are bitten
by fleas, or by large flies, or by gadflies.

I fixed my eyes on the faces of several
on whom the painful fire falls:
I did not recognize any of them, but I noticed
that from the neck of each hung a pouch
which had a certain color and a certain sign,
and there it seems their eyes feast.
And as I came among them looking about,
I saw upon a yellow purse something azure:
which had the face and bearing of a lion.
Then, proceeding with the course of my gaze,
I saw another one red as blood,
showing a goose whiter than butter.

And one who had a blue and pregnant sow
marked upon his little white sack,
said to me: "What are you doing in this pit?
Now go away; and because you are still alive,
know that my neighbor Vitaliano
shall sit here at my left side.
Among these Florentines, I am Paduan;
and many times they thunder in my ears,

who will bring the pouch with three goats!'" <note>original: "becchi." In Italian heraldry, this can refer to he-goats or beaks; here it refers to the coat of arms of the Buiamonte family.</note>
Then he twisted his mouth and stuck out
his tongue, like an ox that licks its nose.

...will speak: It has already been declared that only the higher reason understands the universal.

**[Commentary]**
The author shows how he went alone to the usurers.
And he shows how they sit and do not move.
And we have stated the reason above. He makes a 
comparison that just as dogs continually defend
themselves from the bites of insects that harm them:
so these men defend themselves with their hands now from the flames
that rain down, now from the hot soil—that is, from the
burning earth. And because we have arrived at such a sin,
we will speak briefly of usury. Usury is the sale
 of the use of things that have no "use" <note>The commentator is using a technical Aristotelian/Scholastic definition: things like money do not have a separate "use" from their substance.</note>: or of those
which are consumed solely by their use. And it is
to be noted that certain things have "use": others do not.
Those things have use which are useful to human life,
either by necessity or for well-being, such as bread, wine,
and clothing. Those things do not have use without which
we can live comfortably, such as gems: and they have no "multiplication" <note>original: "multiplicatione." This refers to the idea that money is "barren" and cannot naturally produce more of itself; only living things can reproduce.</note>: because gold
does not make gold, nor gems make gems. Furthermore, of the things that have use, some are consumed in that use
alone, such as bread and wine. Others are consumed over time, such as houses: and clothing and the like. Therefore, he who
takes a price for lent money <term>pecunia</term> <gloss>money</gloss> sins: because it has no "use." Similarly, he who takes a price for lent bread or
wine commits usury: because it is consumed in that very use. But lending a house, which is consumed
by time and use, one does not commit usury by taking a price <note>i.e., charging rent</note>: because it worsens through use: and it is
necessary that from time to time it be repaired. But we spoke of usury in the eleventh chapter.

He shows that these souls were so burned by the fire
that they could not be recognized. Meaning 
allegorically that this vice of usury
makes men infamous: and deprives them of every good
name and fame; and among generous souls
and prudent men, they are held in no esteem:
and they do not deign to know them. And certainly,
although ambition is a great vice, nonetheless
it has some generosity of soul. Lust has some
species of benevolence. But avarice is a
sordid, vile, and ignoble thing. For this reason, he feigns that
he knew them by the pouches they had at their necks. This
shows that such men are not known
for any virtue of their own, but only for the heap
of money illicitly gathered: and on these
pouches were painted the arms of these people, because
their dignity consists in nothing else. The blue lion on the yellow field shows him to be of
the house of Gianfigliazzi. **THEN PROCEEDING** with the course of my gaze: almost a passing through.
Because the eye proceeds, continuing from thing to thing, just as the chariot <note>original: "curro" or "carro."</note> proceeds on its journey. And by
the white goose on the red field, he means the Ubbiachi family: which was once very honored in
our republic.

Continuing, he places Messer Rinaldo degli Scrovegni, 
a Paduan knight. This family
had a blue and red sow on a white field.
And in short, he shows that the usurer of himself has
no fame: but only that of money and of 
his family. **THEY THUNDER** in my ears: because
they shout. **LET THE SOVEREIGN KNIGHT COME**:
spoken with irony, as he is vile and avaricious: and he means Messer
Giovanni Buiamonte: whose family carries for their arms
three goats.

# CANTO XVII

One can never travel safely through Hell, and from there exit Purgatory into Heaven, if Dante does not obey Virgil in all his precepts. Therefore, because he had been warned that all stay must be brief, he returns immediately; and he finds Virgil has already climbed upon the beast; because to wish to pass through these circles... <note>The text here is a summary or introduction to the action of the Canto.</note>

And I, fearing that staying longer would anger
him who had warned me to stay only a little,
turned back from those weary souls.
I found my leader who had already climbed
upon the rump of the fierce animal
and said to me: "Now be fierce and bold.
From now on we descend by such stairs;
mount in front, for I wish to be in the middle,
so that the tail cannot harm you."

**NOW UP TO ME:** "Mount up": because sensuality must be exhorted by reason so that it does not allow itself to be corrupted by vice. And Virgil places himself between the tail of the beast and Dante, so that it does not harm him. For when sensuality has recognized craftiness <note>original: "astutia"</note>, it might perhaps slip into following it: and in this way its end would be harmful if reason did not interpose itself.

Like one who approaches the shivering fit
of the quartan fever <note>A form of malaria characterized by paroxysms every third day.</note>, whose nails are already pale,
and trembles all over just looking at the shade:
Such I became at the words he spoke;
but his threats made me feel shame,
which makes a servant strong before a good master.
I settled myself upon those great shoulders;
I wanted to say, but the voice did not come:
"Make sure that you embrace me."

...and having held him in highest reverence, when he commands you, it seems that such precepts are threats. **BEFORE A** good master makes a servant strong. When the servant knows he has a good—that is, just and discreet—master, and feels himself threatened by him, he takes heart: because he knows that he would not command things that he could not do, and that would not be useful to him. **I WANTED TO SAY.** Thus I wanted to say: that is, "make sure you embrace me." But fear hindered me in such a way that the voice did not come out of my mouth: And here he describes the effect of fear, which often hinders speech. Hence Virgil says:
> Some raise their voice, but the shout they begin fails their gaping mouths. <note>Latin: "Pars tollere uocem Exiguum inceptus clamor frustra tur hiantes." A quote from Aeneid VI.492-493.</note>

But he, who at other times had helped me
at high risk, as soon as I mounted,
encircled me with his arms and held me up:
And said: "Geryon, move now;
let the circles be wide and the descent slow;
think of the new weight you carry."
As the little boat leaves its place,
backing away and away, so he withdrew from there;
and when he felt himself fully at play,
He turned his tail to where his chest had been,
and moved it stretched out like an eel,
and with his paws gathered the air to himself.
Greater fear I do not believe there was
when Phaethon let go of the reins...

<column-break/>

...these fraudulent circles, it is necessary that Dante—that is, the lower reason and sensuality—knows the particulars; and Virgil—that is, the higher reason—knows the craftiness in its general nature: and mounts upon it: that is, subjects it to himself: and wishes that Dante also ride it: that is, that the appetite also dominates and subjects it to itself. **I FOUND MY LEADER** Who had already climbed upon the rump. While Dante considers craftiness in this and that particular man, Virgil knows it in its abstract genus from every particular: and having known it, he rides it as we have said: And he was on the rump: that is, he was in the final species of craftiness. **AND HE SAID**

It is not to be wondered at that Dante grew afraid seeing where he had to climb. For although sensuality obeys reason, nevertheless until a firm habit of fortitude is made, it is necessary that the appetite falters in great undertakings. He says then that hearing the words of Virgil he trembled, thinking he had to climb upon that beast: like one who approaches the shivering—that is, the whim <note>original: "capriccio"</note>—of the quartan fever. **THE SHADE** <note>original: "EL REZO"</note> the shadow. **BUT SHAME** made me feel his threats. Virgil did not threaten him. But we understand that every precept has a threat enclosed within it: because when one...

**BUT HE.** He demonstrates that reason by itself succors sensuality. **WITH HIS ARMS** he encircled and sustained me. As if to say that the strength of reason succors the fragility of sensuality. And he said "Geryon": The genius of the poet has been admirable: who with highest art conducts all the monsters described by poets conveniently to his purpose: in a way that, not departing from the Christian religion, he adorns his poem with them. Therefore, because he found Geryon placed among the monsters in Virgil's Hell, where it says:
> Gorgons and Harpies, and the form of the three-bodied shade. <note>Latin: "Gorgones Arpieque: et forma tricorporis umbre." From Aeneid VI.289.</note>
And because besides the fable one reads in history that this man was crafty, he therefore placed him in this location so that, as in the others, so in this circle there would be a monster suitable to express the vice punished here. They say that Geryon was King of Spain: and had three...

> ...because the sky, as it seems, is still shaken.
> Nor when wretched Icarus felt his loins
> losing their feathers because of the heated wax,
> while his father cried to him: "You take an evil way!"—
> was my fear greater than when I saw I was
> in the air on every side, and saw extinguished

<column-break/>

...bodies. This is imagined because he was king of three islands—namely the two Balearics, which are Majorca and Minorca, and Ebusus <note>modern Ibiza; original: "dibuso"</note>—and that Hercules, fighting with him three times, killed him, killing one body each time. This denotes that the virtuous man can extinguish those three species of fraud demonstrated above. **MOVE NOW:** The circles should be wide and the descent should be slight. When we wish to descend or climb a slope with more ease, we usually do not go straight, but make wide circuits so that we descend a little at a time; and especially when we have a heavily burdened beast.

<column-break/>

Therefore the poet says: since you are burdened with Dante, who, having a body, weighs more than the bodiless souls, do not descend steeply. Instead, go circling. Allegorically, this demonstrates that to lead sensuality through the recognition of fraud, it is necessary to proceed with a slower pace; for man does not understand without discourse <note>In philosophy, "discourse" refers to the step-by-step process of reasoning from one thought to another.</note> and does not have that swiftness in comprehension that an incorporeal spirit possesses. **LIKE THE LITTLE BOAT:** An excellent comparison and so clear that it needs no other explanation. **AT PLAY:** We say a bird is "at play" when it is in a place so open that it can turn wherever it wishes; and similarly we say this of a ship when it is out of port and a narrow place and can turn expeditiously. **WHERE THE CHEST WAS:** That is, at the banks of the seventh circle. **HE TURNED HIS TAIL:** He went backward until that point and then turned. **AND THAT NIMBLE:** That is, quickly; and he moved through the air like an eel through the water. **GREATER FEAR:** I do not believe there was. The meaning is: I do not believe that even Phaethon had greater fear when, terrified, he let go of the horses' reins. Nor Icarus when he felt himself deprived of the feathers of his wings. So that this may be better understood, we will briefly narrate both fables. Phaethon was the son of the Sun and Clymene. In those same times lived Epaphus, son of Jove, who, proud of such a father, despised Phaethon and denied that he was born of Phoebus <note>The sun god Apollo</note>. Phaethon complained to his mother, and instructed by her, went to the house of Phoebus and asked him for an unnamed favor. Phoebus swore he would grant whatever he asked. Then the rash youth asked that for one day he be allowed to drive his chariot. Phoebus repented having sworn and tried to dissuade him. But finally, as the boy stood by his rash purpose, he granted him the solar chariot, which poets imagine to be guided by four horses. These are Pyroeis, Eous, Aethon, and Phlegon. Phaethon was already in the middle of the sky when the horses, not fearing such a weak governor, left the fourth heaven in which the sun revolves and descended not only below the third heaven of Venus and the second of Mercury, but below the moon, which is in the first. The earth felt the too-close proximity of the sun, and everything burned. Therefore Jove, moved to pity, struck Phaethon with celestial lightning and threw him into the Po river; and there he died, as an example to all men, warning them not to undertake tasks beyond their own strength. Icarus was the son of Daedalus—of whom it would be too long to narrate every story—but being unable to escape Crete otherwise, because he was of the highest industry and art in many things, he built wings for himself and his son, warning the boy neither to fly too high nor too low; because in the upper parts the heat would melt the wax that held the feathers, and in the lower parts the humidity would weigh them down too much. Both flew safely as long as the son followed behind the father. But after a little while, Icarus, stimulated by too much desire to fly high, became disobedient to the healthy precepts of his father. He rose like an eagle so high that, the wax that held the feathers being melted, he remained without wings and fell into that sea which was afterwards named Icarian after him. Such fear, then, did Dante have seeing himself carried down through the air by Geryon, as Phaethon and Icarus had when they fell to the earth. By these two, the poets mean all those who, moved by too much self-presumption and rashness, dare to undertake tasks above their strength and faculties. Whence it happens that they cannot bring such a task to its proper end and fall along the way under the burden. Thus, then, sensuality, elevated by the contemplation of craftiness <note>original: "astutia"</note>, was terrified of being able to achieve such knowledge. Furthermore, seeing nothing but air signifies the contemplation of craftiness in a general sense, not restricted by place or time; which is entirely incorporeal—that is, stripped not only of matter, but even of the accidents of matter.

<column-break/>

> She goes swimming along, slow, slow;
> she wheels and descends, but I perceive it
> only by the wind blowing upward on my face.
> I already heard the whirlpool on the right hand
> making a horrible roar beneath us;
> because of which I craned my head downward with my eyes.

<column-break/>

**A**s for the text, it shows the ease of the descent. For he who wheels—that is, makes many circuits—goes slowly and descends easily. And as for the allegory, it shows that human knowledge does not descend without the circuit of discourse and reasoning, and not with that speed possessed by the separate substances <note>A Scholastic term for angels or pure spirits who understand truth instantly without logical steps.</note>. **BUT I DO NOT**
