# CANTO XVII

Then I was more fearful at the **cataract** <note>original: "scoscio"; referring to the steep drop where the river Phlegethon falls</note>
because I saw fires and heard wailing;
whereat, trembling, I drew myself completely back.
And I saw then what I did not see before:
the descending and the circling through the great evils
that were approaching from various sides.

...which is born from the falling of the water. For which reason I stretch [my neck]. **THEN I WAS** more fearful than before because I realized the height of the precipice. **AND I SAW THEN THAT** in the air, in a way that one does not see land from any part. But when one begins to see the land, then one realizes—looking toward an island—if the ship is going straight or if it is turning. And then we [turn] to fires and to wails: that is, to the harm to which we are led. **[The realization]** of the descent of the beast: that is, we recognize the rotations.

As the falcon that has been long on its wings,
which, without seeing **lure** <note>a falconry tool made of feathers used to recall the bird</note> or bird,
makes the falconer say: "Ah me, you are falling!"
Descends weary, from where it moved swiftly
through a hundred circles: and sets itself far
from its master, disdainful and wicked;
So Geryon set us at the bottom
at the very foot of the jagged rock:
and having unburdened our persons,
He vanished like the **nocking point** from the string <note>referring to the speed of an arrow leaving a bow</note>.

...the turns lead you to the bottom: and having led you here, **VANISHED**; he disappeared with that velocity that the nock of the string [releases]. For once you perceive the fraud, he has already vanished before you can take [revenge]. Like the girl on the island of Naxos <note>referring to Ariadne</note>. She did not perceive the betrayal [until he was] vanished: and having left her without a ship, with which [she could follow].

<column-break/>

**I REALIZE:** He did not perceive that he was descending, except that in the falling he felt wind on his face, as one would feel who was descending by a rope. And allegorically it demonstrates that fraud conducts itself in a way that a man does not perceive it. **AND HE HEARD ALREADY** from the right hand the **whirlpool** <note>original: "gorgo"</note>. Therefore the beast has gone to the left: and in passing had left the whirlpool—that is, the river—on the right hand. **BELOW US** a horrible **roar** <note>original: "scroscio"</note>: that is, a sound. That is, I put my head out with my eyes downward. **AT THE CATARACT** / at the falling of the water.

**What I did not see before.** One who is in water or in the air does not perceive that the thing carrying him is moving. And if you are at sea, you realize the motion by looking [at land]. Allegorically it demonstrates that when we approach the [evil] to which fraud leads, then we perceive the turning: that is, the deceits and the windings of fraud.

Through this comparison, he shows that Geryon—who had gone for a while circling and sustaining himself on his wings—descended a little later. He dropped like the falcon, which, after being in the air for a while and seeing no bird to strike, drops without being called by a bird or a lure. **DESCENDS WEARY**: that is, tired. **FROM WHERE IT MOVES SWIFTLY**: that is, from that place from which it had departed. **SWIFTLY**: that is, dexterous and fast. **THROUGH A HUNDRED CIRCLES**: that is, through many circles. And he places himself far from the falconer, indignant and angered. And this allegorically is true of the fraudulent person: who keeps the matter suspended for a time in a way that you do not understand what he intends to do: and then he disappears before you and leaves you at the bottom. **VANISHED**: as [the arrow] parts from the string. Because although you may realize [the fraud], you cannot take vengeance. Theseus led **Ariadne** <note>original: "Adriana"</note> to the island of Naxos, and she did not realize the betrayal until, waking, she understood that Theseus had already vanished, so that she could not follow him.

The commentary explains the sensory experience of the descent and links the sudden abandonment to the mythological betrayal of Ariadne by Theseus.</summary>

->INFERNO<-

## CANTO XVIII OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE

In this eighteenth canto, the author begins to treat the eighth circle, where fraud is punished—specifically that committed against those who have no special reason to trust the fraudster. As established in the preceding canto, he described cunning in general through the figure of Geryon, by whom they were transported from the circle of the violent to that of the fraudulent:

> There is a place in Hell called Malebolge,
> made all of stone and of an iron color,
> like the circular wall that surrounds it.
> In the exact center of this malicious field
> there gapes a well, quite wide and deep,
> whose structure I will describe in its proper place.
> That remaining circle is therefore round,
> between the well and the foot of the high, hard bank,
> and its floor is divided into ten sections.

<column-break/>

And here Geryon set them down. This denotes that after the contemplation of fraud in general, they began to consider its specific types and details. And because there are ten species of fraud, this circle is similarly divided into ten *bolge* <note>original: "bolge"; plural of "bolgia," meaning pouches or ditches</note>. But in the present canto, only the first is treated, and the second is begun. He first describes the site of this eighth circle and says that it is A PLACE IN HELL Called, that is named, MALEBOLGE. *Bolgia* signifies a repository, a pocket, a gulf, and a receptacle. Therefore, it is a fitting name for the place of fraud to be called an "evil repository" or receptacle. It is also very appropriate that the fraudulent are punished in valleys and enclosed places, because fraud always stays enclosed and never comes out into the open, but seeks hiding places and darkness.

ALL OF STONE: because the heart of the fraudulent person is hard and void of all charity. AND OF AN IRON COLOR: the color of iron. This is because he is not only void of charity, but is armed with cruelty. It can also be shown through this that fraud is covered in a double hardness: for the violent man only sins by acting against his neighbor, but the fraudulent man adds deceit to the injury. IN THE EXACT CENTER: "Middle" is taken in two ways: improperly, when we call "middle" anything that is between two extremes; and properly, when we call "middle" that part which is equally distant from every extreme. Therefore, he said "in the exact center," meaning the true and proper middle. Thus, IN THE PROPER Middle of the malicious field: Of this level of the eighth circle, truly malicious because nothing is more harmful than fraud. THERE GAPES A well. It is a concave and deep place, "gaping" meaning empty. And this is the ninth circle, which, due to its narrowness and depth compared to the others, appears to be a well. QUITE WIDE: To denote that although he called it a "well," it is nonetheless wide, because it punishes within it three types of traitors. AND DEEP: because it goes down to the center of the earth. AND ITS STRUCTURE <note>original: "lordigno"; referring to the technical arrangement or "engine" of the place</note>: that is, the artificial site of this. He will tell of it in its proper place, meaning when he treats the ninth circle, it will be understood. THAT CIRCLE: points out the eighth circle, which remains encircled on the inner side by the ninth, and on the outer side by the cliff that divides it from the seventh. And this is divided into ten *bolge*. You will understand this site precisely in the "topography" <note>the map or diagram of Hell</note> which we placed at the beginning of the book.

> Just as where, for the guard of the walls,
> many many ditches encircle the castles,
> the ground where they are takes on a form;
> Such an image those ditches made here;
> and as such fortresses have little bridges
> from their thresholds to the outer bank,
> So from the base of the rock, stone ridges
> move across the embankments and ditches
> until the well, which cuts them off and collects them.

Just as many ditches are made around a fortress, and yet from the gate of such a fortress all the way to the outside of all the ditches there are bridges, so all these ditches which were around the ninth circle were crossed by stone ridges which served as bridges. These ditches denote the depth of fraud; and it is a fitting thing that, as fraud always stays in the depths and never shows itself in an open place, so the fraudulent should be punished in a deep place. And the stone ridge that crosses the ditches and forms a bridge over which Virgil and Dante pass signifies the process of contemplation <note>original: "speculatione"; here meaning intellectual investigation or observation</note>, which is conducted on solid and firm ground because it is founded upon the truth. And this stone ridge—which is one continuous path from the bottom of the cliff where Geryon had left them to the well, crossing (that is, traversing) all the ditches and being interrupted in no place—demonstrates that the same will for contemplation carries us in a continuous discourse through the knowledge of all things.

This denotes that after the contemplation of fraud in general, they began to consider the specific details, as we said shortly before. <column-break/>

**ON THE RIGHT HAND**
Because they were circling the place from the left hand, the place where the sinners were remained on the right. **NEW TORMENTS**: because he had not yet found souls who were being whipped, nor demons whipping said souls. **In the bottom were naked sinners** who were being beaten. And he shows that this ditch <note>original: "bolgia"</note> was divided into two parts. Because from the side toward Dante, the sinners were coming toward them. The others who were in the other part were going in the same direction as them, but with larger strides than theirs. Therefore, this ditch was divided like the bridge at Sant’Angelo in the year of the Jubilee, which, divided lengthwise, receives on one side those who go toward the Castel Sant'Angelo and toward Saint Peter’s, and on the other, those who come from Saint Peter’s. **THE YEAR OF THE JUBILEE**. "Jubilee" in the Hebrew language signifies a year of remission and liberation. For the Hebrews, when the seventh septenary of years was finished, which is the fiftieth year, they liberated all servants and remitted and cancelled all debts; and they called such a year the Jubilee. In imitation of this, the Christian Church later ordained that every fiftieth year the Supreme Pontiff should liberate people from their sins, granting plenary indulgence to all those who, confessed and contrite, visited the Roman churches. And because in this year there is an infinite concourse of men in the city of Rome, and

---

a great crowd forms on the bridge at Sant’Angelo by those who go to or come from Saint Peter’s in the Vatican, Pope Boniface [VIII] instituted in the year 1300 that the bridge should be divided by its length, and one part should serve those going to Saint Peter’s, and the other for those returning. Thus, then, is this path of the "evil ditches" <term>Malebolge: the ten circular trenches of the eighth circle of Hell</term> divided: and through one part go those who have corrupted women either with words or with price to provide them to others <note>these are the pimps or procurers</note>; and through the other, those who in the same way have corrupted them to have them for themselves <note>these are the seducers</note>. These people, therefore, are never allowed to rest; but they have demons behind them who beat and drive them with whips. For just as they did not let women live in their peace, but with the "whips" of either flatteries or rewards pushed them to their will, so now the demons drive them. And we can rightly understand the demons to be the remorses of conscience, which always distress those who are stained with such a vice. **FROM HERE, FROM THERE**: That is, both where those who are going are, and where those who are coming are. **UP ALONG THE DARK ROCK**: Black and ugly. I saw demons who, running behind them, beat them cruelly in a way that made them run swiftly. And always at the first lash they would leap away. **LIFT THEIR LEGS**: Their legs. Here it is to be noted that he shows the punishment of the "feducitori" <note>likely "seduttori" or seducers</note>; and seduction is to induce someone by deceit to do what they should not. And although seduction is of many types, nevertheless here he treats the seduction that induces the vice of the flesh. And this is committed in two ways: either by seducing a woman so that she consents to someone else, or truly to oneself. And because the vice of lust is the least grave sin among mortal sins, he therefore places seduction in this vice as less grave than in the others.

by one; and I immediately said:

and my sweet leader paused with me,
and consented that I go back a little.

For such a vice is so abominable, not only among the good but even among the wicked, that no one is so impudent or so brazen that they are not ashamed to be noted for such infamy. There are many vices which, although they are to be fled from, nevertheless have within themselves some shadow of virility. But this

He is noted as most vile even among the most vile. Master Venedico de’ Caccianimici of Bologna was the go-between <note>original: "mezzano"</note> through whom the Marquis Obizzo d’Este, Lord of Ferrara, had his sister, who was called Ghisola the Beautiful. **AND NOT ONLY I weep here as a Bolognese.** This denotes that many Bolognese are stained with this vice, saying that so many tongues are not **TAUGHT** meaning prepared. **TO SAY SIPA.** Between Savena and Reno: As if to say there are not as many tongues in Bologna—where one says *sipa* instead of *si*—as there are here. This Bologna is in the middle of two rivers; one of which is called Savena, about two miles from Bologna toward Romagna on the eastern side. The other is the Reno, of which Pliny makes mention when narrating of the reeds fit for making archery arrows; he writes that no reed is more suited for arrows than that which grows in the Reno of Bologna, because it has much pith and swift weight. This is on the western side of Bologna toward Lombardy. **AND IF OF THIS you want faith or testimony, bring to mind our greedy nature.** He demonstrates that avarice and the desire for money lead men to such vile and abominable vice. Therefore, the saying of the satirist is most welcome to the greedy man: "No one asks where you get it from: but one must have it." <note>original: "Unde habeas quaerit nemo : sed oportet habere"; a quote from Juvenal's Satires.</note> **HERE ARE NO WOMEN**

---

**FOR COIN:** that is, for money which is coined. And he says this because he who wishes to corrupt a woman has no greater means than money. It is well known that avarice is born from vileness and timidity of spirit. Therefore, the old and women, because they are of little spirit—the former due to the accident of age, the latter by nature—are always greedy. And of this, I could report infinite examples; for many have been found similar to Eriphyle <note>A mythological figure who betrayed her husband for a gold necklace.</note>, who, corrupted by gifts, revealed her husband Amphiaraus, who was hiding so as not to be forced to go to the Theban war, in which according to his omens he was to be killed.

**WHERE A CRAG:** An arch of a bridge of those mentioned above. **OF THE BANK:** which shows that it bounds the seventh circle and the first ditch of the eighth. **QUITE EASILY** as far as the literal meaning, it shows the path is not tiring. And allegorically it signifies that having had the knowledge of fraud in general, it was an easy thing to recognize this specific kind.

**TO THE RIGHT HAND:** According to the literal sense, it was necessary to keep to the right hand in order to climb the bridge. And allegorically, one who seeks the knowledge of things always goes to the right hand. **UPON ITS JAGGED RIDGE:** Upon the back of such a crag, which was a fragment sticking out from a bank. Nor could he otherwise see the other crowd of souls, who, coming with them,

turned their backs to them. **FROM THOSE eternal circles:** that is, we distanced ourselves from the outermost circle which embraces all the others, as was shown above. Thus, up to here, Dante had not yet entered the first bridge; but he was still on the edge or bank which encloses all the ditches within itself; and going to the left he encountered Venedico; having departed from him, he now arrives at the first entrance of the first bridge, or rather of the first arch of the bridge.

For being turned toward them, your sight will meet them.

In this second kind of seduction: those who have by flattery drawn women to their will. He sets Jason as an example and entangles many fables together, which we will not narrate in full at present because the space does not allow for such length. Nor will we leave them behind entirely, so that the reader does not remain completely ignorant of them. There were in Thessaly two brothers: Pelias, king of that region, and Aeson. From Aeson was born Jason, who, because he was very beautiful of body, robust, and of a great and excellent spirit, desired to do something worthy of memory. His uncle Pelias also inflamed this desire, not so much to favor his glory, but because he feared—having no male children—that Jason and his father might plot fraud to take the kingdom from him. He hoped that by putting Jason to arduous tasks full of danger, he might easily perish. Therefore, he encouraged him to undertake the capture of the Golden Fleece of the ram of Phrixus, which was in Colchis, a city of Pontus. But let us also briefly mention the Golden Fleece. From Athamas and Nephele were born Phrixus and Helle, who were later driven away by their father due to the deceit of their stepmother Ino. Juno commanded them to mount their ram, which their father had given them, and with it cross the sea. But in this transit Helle, a fearful girl, fell into the sea, and from her that sea is called the **Hellespont** <note>The "Sea of Helle."</note>. Phrixus reached Colchis where Aeetes reigned, and consecrated the skin of the ram to Mars. Jason wanted this. And for this, he built the ship on Mount Pelion, which was called **Argo** <note>The ship of the Argonauts.</note> after the craftsman who composed it, or perhaps from its speed, because *argos* in Greek means swift. With him went the leading men of Greece, among whom were Hercules, Telamon, Orpheus, Castor, and Pollux. And first they arrived in Lemnos, which island was without males. Because they had gone against Thrace and sacrificed first to all the gods except Venus, Venus wanted to take revenge. Because of this, she inflamed those women with such fury that by common counsel they first killed the few who had remained on the island. Later, when the others returned with victory, the women waited for night, and when they had fallen asleep, each one killed her own—except for Hypsipyle <note>original: "Isyphyle o Hisypyle"</note>, who, moved to compassion for her father Thoas the king, secretly sent him out of the island, pretending with honorable funerals that she had already killed him. In Lemnos they stayed one year, mixing with the women. And Jason, to have Hypsipyle who was then queen, promised to take her as his wife and to return there; and he left her pregnant with two sons, Thoas and Euneus. Nor did he ever return to her afterward. He reached Colchis, but he could not have the Golden Fleece unless he first killed the great serpent that guarded it and tamed two fierce bulls which had bronze feet and cast flames from their nostrils. With these, it was then necessary to sow the teeth of the already dead serpent. From such seed were born armed men whom he was required to kill. Human strength could not suffice for such a horrendous war. He therefore used cunning, and with his flatteries drew Medea, daughter of the king, into his love, and promised to make her his wife. She, who was a very great sorceress, and love for Jason being more powerful in her breast than her paternal bond and obligation, with her herbs and incants made Jason the victor; and having snatched the fleece, he went away with her. But Jason

# INFERNO

...having reached Corinth, showing little gratitude for the benefit received—indeed, being most ungrateful—he repudiated Medea and took as his wife the daughter of Creon, King of Corinth, called Glauce according to Lactantius <note>Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius, an early Christian author</note> and Creusa according to Seneca. This ingratitude constrained Medea to serve Jason his two sons as food, whom he had fathered with her; and with enchanted gifts sent to Creusa, she burned both her and her palace. The corruption of these two women, therefore, causes Jason to be punished in this ditch. **THAT THROUGH** heart and wit, through greatness of soul and through prudence. Nor could he have performed such an outstanding feat otherwise, had he not possessed a great soul in such grave dangers and great prudence in conducting himself. For as Sallust says: <note>original: "Prius consulto : et ubi consulueris mature facto opus est."</note> "First one must deliberate; and when you have deliberated, there is need for timely action." Therefore, in great matters, prudence is necessary to show you first if a thing is to be done or not; and if it is to be done, by what way and in what manner. Then one must have strength and boldness of spirit, so that the difficulty and danger do not weaken you. Since it is not plausible that Jason could have accomplished such great things without these two virtues, the poet attributes them to him. Furthermore, Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian</note> writes the same of him; and many of his outstanding deeds were recorded in letters, for which divine honors were attributed to him and temples built, which Alexander the Great—moved, I believe, by envy—caused to be razed to the ground. **THEN HE PASSED** through the island of Lemnos. Lemnos is the island onto which Vulcan fell when Juno, his mother, finding him ugly, threw him from heaven. **OF THE** first valley; of the first ditch, in which are tormented the flatterers of women, who lead them to do the will of others or their own.

He describes the second ditch, and shows that they had already passed the first and arrived at the last support of the first arch, which is founded upon the bank that divides the first ditch from the second; and from that same bank begins the start of the second arch, which goes over the second ditch.

> We were already where the narrow path
> with the second bank crisscrosses,
> and makes of that a shoulder for another arch.
> Thence we heard people who whine
> in the next ditch, who snort with their snouts,
> and beat themselves with their palms.
> The banks were crusted with a mold
> from the breath below that sticks to them,
> which with the eyes and nose joined battle.
> The bottom is so deep that the eye
> cannot see it without mounting to the back
> of the arch, where the rock towers highest.
> Thither we came; and thence down in the ditch
> I saw people plunged in a dung
> that seemed to have moved from human privies.

<column-break/>

**NARROW PATH.** The narrow way: that is, the space of the bridge. **CRISSCROSSES:** they join in a cross, because these arches do not go along the direction of the valleys, but across them, forming the shape of a cross. **AND MAKES** of that bank a shoulder to another circle: that is, to the second. Having described the way that led them over the second ditch, he describes what kind of punishment is contained within it. He shows, then, that this ditch is full of human excrement, and in it the souls are plunged, who in such a form **WHINE**: that is, they lament; and specifically "whining" <term>nichiare: a soft, complaining or querulous lamentation</term> signifies lamenting with a low and complaining voice. **SNORT:** <term>sbuffia: to blow in a way that the breath comes out with force and shocks</term>. Therefore, when an angry person grieves and at the same time reviles and threatens with arrogant words, we say that he "snorts." **THE BANKS WERE** crusted with a mold. This occurs in damp and enclosed places where the vapors rising from such humidity, unable to exhale, remain stuck to the walls and create mold. So in this place

the breath: that is, the exhalation that rose from the bottom, emerged so thick that it stuck to the banks and made such a crust that it "joined battle" with the nose and eyes: that is, it offended the nose with its foul odor and the eyes with its ugliness. And the bottom was so deep that it could not be well seen unless one mounted the back of the rock, which was like the arch of a bridge. From there, one could look straight down. In such a vile and sordid place are punished the flatterers, who in the Florentine tongue are called <term>moinieri: wheedlers or those who use false endearments</term>. Flattery is nothing other than speech containing false praise for the sake of pleasing and acquiring the grace of the one being praised. Such a vice proceeds from a vile and servile soul in which there is no vestige of freedom. And truly they can be called the dregs of men, because in them nothing remains but corruption. And just as in the body of an animal the dregs are nothing but the corrupted part—which nature, in the first digestion made by the stomach, separates from the uncorrupted nourishment and sends down into the lower belly—so from the uncorrupted truth which nourishes the soul and maintains moral life, flattery is separated like something corrupted and harmful to human life. Deservedly, then, it can be said that the flatterer is submerged in dregs, and swallows and rejects them. Because the flatterer is full of lies, he is nothing but corruption; he feeds on nothing else, nor does he feed others anything else. This man shows friendship and benevolence, yet he is the worst enemy. Nor can anyone established in dignity or power find a more pernicious thing than flattery, which, to please, persuades them that what is evil is good and just; and from this proceed many errors that are often the cause of the ruin of princes.

# CANTO XVIII

...and of great men. Because they believe false praise, not only do they not correct their evil deeds, but they are confirmed in their stupidity. Since they are in prosperous fortune, they consider themselves almost like gods, and there is nothing so great that they do not believe it of themselves. Regarding this, Juvenal said: <note>original Latin: "Nihil est quod credere de se non possit cum laudatur diis equa potestas."</note> "There is nothing that a power equal to the gods cannot believe about itself when it is praised." And rightly was Diogenes the Cynic <note>A Greek philosopher known for his blunt honesty</note> asked which beast bit most fiercely; he replied: "Among wild animals, the detractor; and among domestic ones, the flatterer," because with his false praise he leads you to ruin. And he added that words composed not to reveal the truth but to please are a honeyed halter <note>term: "capresto melato" — a sweet-tasting noose that leads one to their death</note>. And Plato demonstrates that there is the same difference between a true friend and a flatterer as there is between a doctor and a cook. For the doctor, in giving food, does not seek to please the taste but to restore health; while the cook attends only to pleasing the taste, and does not care if the food is healthy or harmful. So the true friend only respects telling the truth to his friend to preserve him in virtue and lead him toward it. But the flatterer does not care if others err; it is enough for him to say what pleases in order to achieve his own convenience. Therefore Cicero, in his book *On Duties*, warns us: <note>original Latin: "Atque etiam in fecundissimis rebus maxime utendum est consilio amicorum. iisque maior etiam quam antea tribuenda auctoritas. His denique temporibus cauendum est ne assentatoribus patefaciamus aures ; ne ue adulari nos sinamus : in quo falli facile est. Tales. n. nos putamus. ut iure laudemur : ex quo innu merabilia nascuntur peccata cum homines inflati opinionibus turpiter irridentur : et in maximis uersan tur erroribus."</note> "And even in the most prosperous circumstances, the advice of friends must be most utilized, and even greater authority should be given to them than before. In these times, finally, we must be careful not to open our ears to flatterers, nor allow ourselves to be flattered, in which it is easy to be deceived. For we think ourselves such that we are rightly praised; from which arise innumerable sins when men, inflated by their own opinions, are shamefully mocked and dwell in the greatest errors." We can also say that the poet puts them in such a punishment to penalize their superfluous delicacies and excessive luxuries and splendid foods, which they sought through their flatteries and fawning when they were alive; because a vice is best punished by its opposite.

And while I searched down there with my eyes,
I saw one with his head so soiled with dung
that it did not appear whether he was **layman or cleric**.
He cried to me: "Why are you so greedy
to look more at me than at the other filthy ones?"
And I to him: "Because, if I remember well,
I have seen you before with dry hair;
and you are **Alessio Interminei of Lucca**:
therefore I eye you more than all the others."
And he then, beating his pate, said:
"Down here the flatteries have submerged me,
with which I never had a dry tongue."

<margin>Was he pleasing to Thais? And did she return great thanks to him?</margin>
**Thais** is a prostitute from the plays of Terence; to whom

After this, my leader made me look
a little further forward with my face
so that I could clearly see with my eyes
the face of that filthy, **disheveled slave-girl**,
who scratches herself with dung-stained nails,
now crouching down, and now standing on her feet:
this is **Thais the whore**, who replied
to her lover when he said, "Do I have great thanks 
with you?" — "Nay, marvelous!" <note>original Latin/Italian: "gratie grandi apud te / anzi marauiglose"</note>
And with this, let our sight be satisfied.

<column-break/>

In this place, he puts Master **Alessio Interminei**, a knight of Lucca and a very great flatterer. **LAYMAN OR CLERIC**: These two words are Greek in origin. Here it should be noted that Christians are divided into two types: that is, priests and secular people. The priests are the apostolic church; they are the part "chosen" to rule the seculars and instruct them with the best precepts and an honest life. For this reason they are called *clerici*: that is, *electi* <note>chosen ones</note>; but for ease of speech we say "clerics." The seculars are the Catholic church—that is, the "universal" church—and in spiritual life they must obey the priests. And therefore they are called *laici* <note>laymen</note>, meaning "of the people" or plebeian. This implies that learning should reside in the priests; for which reason it is a great infamy for those who are entirely unlearned to hold such office.

Thraso, a military man, gave a handmaiden or slave-girl as a gift; he then asked Gnatho—the person through whom he had sent the girl—if the gift was well-received with "great thanks." Gnatho, to flatter him, replied not just "great," but "marvelous." Thus, the flatterer was actually Gnatho; but the poet puts **Thais** here instead. He does this because it was by her will that Gnatho used such flattery, and because every prostitute—since they do not love the man but his money—is always full of fawning and flattery. Also, there are two types of flatterers: some are people of name and dignity, though they stain it with such a vile vice; and others are entirely lowly, intent on the smallest gain. Therefore, he used Alessio to represent the first type and Thais for the second. **DISHEVELED SLAVE-GIRL**: The penalty for a lustful person who was once adorned with fine hair is that she should now be disheveled. And the penalty for her stubborn pride toward her lovers is that she should now be a "fante" <note>a servant or slave</note> to her own torment. The nails stained with filth punish the excessively exquisite perfumes she sought in life. That she now "crouches" and now "stands" has its own allegory. But it is better to leave wrapped in its own obscurity that which cannot be decently explained.

XVII.

# CANTO XIX OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.

This is the nineteenth canto: in which he demonstrates that in the third ditch <note>term: "bolgia" — literally a pouch or pocket; Dante uses this to describe the ten circular trenches of the eighth circle of Hell</note> are punished the simonists. And simony is the sale or purchase of sacred and spiritual things for money or for things equivalent to money. Therefore, whoever sells or buys the sacraments of the church, or any spiritual dignity,

<image-desc>A large illuminated initial 'O' depicting a figure (likely a prophet or Simon Magus) in a classical garment, set within a landscape with hills and a blue sky, framed by a gold border with floral motifs.</image-desc>
**O** Simon Magus! O you wretched followers
who the things of God, which of goodness
should be the brides; and you rapacious ones
For gold and for silver you adulterate—
now it is fitting that the trumpet <note>The trumpet was used by town criers to announce the crimes of a condemned person</note> sounds for you
because you reside in the third ditch.
Already we were at the following tomb,
having climbed onto the bridge at that part
which hangs exactly over the middle of the ditch.

<column-break/>

or benefits, or other similar things—the true price of which is not gold nor silver, but holiness of life and of character, and virtue, and doctrine—is a simonist. This name comes from Simon Magus, who was the first to attempt this wickedness in the New Testament. So that this may be more clearly understood, it is written in the Acts of the Apostles that after the death of the first martyr Stephen, Philip preached the word of God <note>original Latin: "verbum dei"</note> in Samaria and converted many through the incredible miracles he performed. There was at that same time in that city Simon, a philosopher and magician, who because of the things he did with his magic arts held great authority and reputation. He, along with the others, believed Philip and was baptized. But the Holy Spirit was not yet in those baptized in Samaria; but later Peter and John arrived and prayed for the baptized, and after the prayer they laid their hands upon them, and they received the Holy Spirit. Because it seemed a great thing to Simon that the Holy Spirit should come through the laying on of hands, he offered money to the apostles so that they might give him such power: that by laying his hand upon a baptized person, the Holy Spirit would come to them. To him, Peter replied: "May your money perish with you. <note>original Latin: "Pecunia tua tecum sit in perditionem"</note> And certainly because you thought that the gift of God could be had for money, you have no part or lot in this matter; and your heart is not right in the sight of God. Keep your money and pray to God if it is possible that this thought may depart from your heart: for I see you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity." From this Simon, therefore, those who trade sacred things for a price were called simonists in the New Testament, just as in the Old Testament they were named after Gehazi, the servant of Elisha the prophet. The prophet Elisha cured Naaman, the commander of the army of the King of Syria, of leprosy by the power of God. He did not wish to receive any reward from him, even though he had brought much treasure. But Gehazi, the servant of Elisha, once Naaman had departed, went after him and caught up to him; he pretended that two sons of the prophets had come to him from Mount Ephraim and asked

for them a talent of silver and two changes of clothes. Naaman gave him the clothes and two talents. When Elisha <note>original: "Heliseo"</note> recognized the fraud and avarice of his servant, he predicted that the leprosy of Naaman would cling to him and remain in his lineage; and immediately he became white with leprosy. These people, therefore, act against the Gospel of Matthew, which in the tenth chapter writes: **What you receive freely from God, give freely.** <note>original Latin: "Quod gratis donante deo accipitis gratis dent"</note> Christ therefore commands through Matthew that those spiritual things which they receive without price from God should likewise be given to those who deserve them without price. O SIMON, first author and prince in the Christian church of such wickedness, and thus the first in this ditch to receive fitting punishment. MAGUS: that is, enchanter. **Magus** in the Persian language means "wise." For this reason, those who among the Greeks were called philosophers were called **Magi** by the Persians. And of this type of philosopher were those three who came to adore Jesus with offerings of gold, incense, and myrrh. But because Zoroaster, one of these Magi, was the first to discover such an art, it is called the "magical art," and those who practice it are called Magi. O WRETCHED followers. O all others who, for the sake of having wealth, followed in his footsteps and now find yourselves in supreme misery. WHO: who **adulterate** or corrupt. THE THINGS of God: the things dedicated to God, as we said shortly before. WHICH: that is, those which ought to be the **brides of goodness**, meaning of virtue, doctrine, and an honest life and habits. An adulterer is he who corrupts and joins himself with a woman who has a husband. A husband is he who joins himself with her who is made his by legitimate marriage. And because spiritual dignities and benefits should deservedly be conferred upon good and learned priests, we—by a certain similarity—call such things the "brides" of such men, and those men the "legitimate husbands" of those things. On the contrary, all those who acquire them not through any virtue but for a price—just as an adulterer joins with an adulteress through corruption—are deservedly called adulterers. Hence, Thomas Aquinas writes that the simonist ensures that the Church, which is the bride of Christ, becomes pregnant by someone other than the groom; and simony causes her, who ought to be impregnated by the Holy Spirit, to be impregnated by an evil spirit. Therefore, it causes God to nourish adulterous children and disinherit the legitimate ones, because the corruptors possess the benefits which they buy with money, and the good and learned men to whom the dignities should be given remain without any benefit. NOW IT IS FITTING THAT for us the **trumpet** sounds: that is, it is necessary that I manifest and publish you in my verses; and it is a metaphor from town criers, who, when they have to publish something, invite the bystanders to hear with the sound of the trumpet. ALREADY WE HAD mounted to the following tomb. We said that "tomb" means a burial place. Therefore, here he deservedly calls this deep place a "tomb," where the souls, because they are damned in eternal death, can be said to be buried. OF THE ROCK: which formed a bridge. EXACTLY OVER the middle of the ditch it falls: that is, it corresponds in a straight line over the middle of the ditch. Masons say "to fall" <note>original: "piombare," referring to a plumb line</note> when they straighten a stone or the corner of a wall with a plumb line so that it rises in a straight line.

By this excellent exclamation, he demonstrates that the supreme God, through His infinite wisdom, knew how to—and through supreme virtue (that is, strength) was able to—create the world, which He administers with admirable justice, distributing to every creature what is due to them in a perfect proportion, whether of reward or punishment. Therefore, He beautifies the angels; on earth, He gives space and convenience to act in a way that we might merit heaven. AND IN THE evil world: that is, in Hell, He punishes sinners with more or less heavy penalties according to the crime. I SAW along the sides: that is, along the banks of the ditch. AND ON THE BOTTOM: that is, down in the depths. THE STONE: That rock full of round holes, no wider than necessary to receive a single man. And to better describe them, he adds that they were in the likeness of those four small pits which, in the temple of John the Baptist <note>The Baptistery of San Giovanni in Florence</note>, are around the font placed in the middle of the temple, made so that the priests who baptize may stand there, so that they may be closer to the water. ONE OF WHICH. It happened that while several children were in the temple of Saint John playing, as is their custom, one fell into one of the pits head-first; and since he could not be extracted in any other way, Dante happened upon it and with a tool <note>original: "disuamano," likely meaning a hatchet or iron tool</note> broke the pit and saved the boy. # CANTO XIX OF THE INFERNO

THIS SHALL BE the seal that disillusion’s everyone. He says this so that no one believes he wished to violate sacred things, or that he had broken that pit out of impiety; rather, it was to save the boy. <note>Dante refers here to an incident at the Baptistery of San Giovanni in Florence where he broke a baptismal font to save a drowning child; he uses this personal defense as a metaphor for his "breaking" of the silence surrounding the Church's corruption.</note> FROM THE MOUTHS of said pits; TO EACH ONE; that is, the pit. SURPASSED; the feet and legs protruded. UP TO THE THICK PART; up to the calf where the leg begins to thicken. And certainly, he assigns a punishment very appropriate to this vice. Inasmuch as man was created to contemplate God and celestial things—and for this reason was produced with his face raised toward heaven, while the beasts look down at the earth—the Simonist, who out of avarice sells divine things to have gold and silver which are born beneath the earth, perverts the office of man by contemplating earthly things instead of celestial ones. Therefore, it is a just thing that he sticks his face in the earth. BOTH <note>original: "intrambe"</note> that is, between one and the other. THEY TWITCHED <note>original: "guisavano"</note>; they moved with quickness. THE JOINTS; the articulations. He shows that since they could not move their legs because they were enclosed in the pit, they moved their feet at the joint which connects them to the legs. Literally, this demonstrates great pain; for we see that those who feel great pain distort their feet. But allegorically, we understand by the feet the cupidity for earthly things; and by the rapid movement of the feet, we understand great cupidity; and by the fire, the heat of such cupidity. AS IS THE CUSTOM <note>original: "qual suole"</note>. An excellent comparison by which he shows that just as a flame follows the oil upon a surface, so these people have followed external gain—that is, worldly goods—and not the internal—that is, heavenly goods. TWISTED <note>original: "ritorte"</note>; twisted twigs for tying bundles. STRAMBE; that is, ropes made of *stramba*, which the Latins call *spartum* <note>esparto grass, used for making sturdy ropes</note>.

Dante asks Virgil who it is that suffers more than the others; and Virgil says he has no knowledge of the specifics, but promises to carry him down to him. This signifies, as we have said many times, that science does not give knowledge of particulars; but it well leads you to them; as, for example <note>original: "verbi gratia"</note>, science does not show

that Boniface shall be a Simonist. <note>Pope Boniface VIII, Dante’s political enemy, whom he places in Hell even though he was still alive at the time the poem is set.</note> But by demonstrating this universal truth—that whoever sells sacred and divine things for money is a Simonist—it leads the senses and the lower reason to recognize that Boniface, who sells sacred and divine things for money, is a Simonist. Therefore, Virgil carries Dante to the bottom where he was: that is, the intellect carries the lower reason into the knowledge of that vice in general, in which Dante then sees Boniface; that is, he knows the particulars. TWITCHING more than his other companions: that is, the others who are placed in the same sort of punishment. A REDDER FLAME; the redder the flame is, the greater vitality and force it shows us. SUCKS; rightly said. Inasmuch as heat draws moisture to itself, it therefore "sucks" it. THAT lies more flat: which is deeper. OF HIMSELF and of his wrongs: that is, of his errors and vices. Inasmuch as every virtue has rectitude, so every vice is "wrong" or "crooked" <note>original: "torto"</note>. AS MUCH AS PLEASES YOU IS GOOD TO ME: that is, it seems as beautiful to me as it is pleasing to you. The meaning 

is that a thing seems as beautiful to me as it pleases you: as if to say that according to how much more or less it pleases you, it seems more or less beautiful to me: that is, desirable. Where the author demonstrates that the lower reason and the senses are entirely submitted to the higher reason. When this occurs, there is never discord in the soul, but it always has right and true judgment. So that this may be better understood, let us take two people: in one, the sensuality is entirely in accord with reason, and in the other, there is discord. We will see that in the latter they will make two different judgments. For reason will judge that one should value divine things more than money, and sensuality will judge that money should be preferred to divine things. In 

the former, sensuality is so obedient to reason that it always approves its judgment. Therefore, only that thing is beautiful and good to Dante (the sensuality) which pleases Virgil (the intellect). YOU ARE LORD. Because the higher reason must command and the sensuality must obey; nor does it ever depart from its will when it is well-disposed. Furthermore, because reason will have knowledge when sensuality is joined with it, it understands not only what it says, but also what it thinks, even though it remains silent. SO GOOD IT IS: that is, lovable and desirable, because love, according to Plato, is nothing other than the desire for beautiful things. YOU ARE Lord and you know I do not part from your will: he declares the same thing more openly. AND YOU KNOW what is left unsaid. Inasmuch as reason can comprehend the thoughts of the soul. Which he also signified above when he said: *Ah, how cautious men must be.*

# CANTO XVIII <note>The heading says XVIII, but the text and commentary clearly discuss Canto XIX, where Dante encounters the Simonists—those who sold church offices for money.</note>

...against those who do not look only at the surface: but look within the thought with wisdom. ON THE FOURTH BANK: which is between the third and the fourth ditch. **B**ecause the recognition of a man consists in his face: therefore Dante could not know this man: who did not show his face: but his feet: because he held them below. THE UPPER PART: that is, the part which should be on top. And certainly the men who stand with their heads fixed downward: that is, all their thoughts and speculations which they should raise to heaven are submerged in the earth through avarice: that is, in the desire for earthly things, they hide their faces in a way that we cannot recognize them. This signifies nothing else than that they transform their character so much that they seem more like cruel beasts than men. Nor can it be known that they are men because they do not live according to reason: which alone makes us men. But according to appetite: which is common to us with all beasts. Nature therefore gave us alone among all animals a face raised to heaven, to demonstrate that our thoughts should be of celestial things: And to the brutes she gave a face bent to the ground: because being without reason they cannot look at anything other than earthly things. For this reason, anyone who, leaving the thought of high things, looks only at the low, turns his head upside down. Ovid clearly demonstrates all this in these verses:
> While other animals look down at the ground, He gave to man a sublime face and commanded him to look at the sky and to lift his upright countenance to the stars. <note>original Latin: "Pronaque cum spectent animantia cetera terram Os homini sublime dedit celumque tueri Iussit et erectos ad sidera tollere uultus."</note>

LIKE A DRIVEN STAKE: that is, fixed in the ground like a pole is driven. I STOOD: An assassin is one who kills a man for money: And it comes from this Latin verb *assideo* <note>meaning to sit by or blockade</note> which means to stop near something. Because such people place themselves in ambush near a place where they estimate the one they want to kill must pass. The punishment for assassins is that they be "propagated" <note>An ancient execution method called *propagazione* where the criminal was buried alive, head-down, in a hole.</note>. Thus it happens that the assassin, after his head is fixed in the pit: because he does not die immediately, often calls back the friar to confess some remaining sin. Whereby it is necessary for the confessor to bend his ear to the ground if he wants to hear the voice which comes out from under the earth: And so it was necessary for Dante to do, wanting to hear that soul. And certainly, he who wants to consider the nature of the Simonist must fix his eyes and ears to the ground: that is, he must recognize in him the thoughts of earthly things. AND HE CRIED. Marvelous genius of the poet who, wanting to damn Pope Boniface for simony: and not being able to find him in hell because he was still alive, makes this soul predict his arrival, showing that his opinion had been deceived in this, that he [Boniface] had died several years earlier than he estimated. This he does because he wants that shade to have believed the truth: But he was deceived by Dante's voice. ARE YOU SO SOON Sated with that wealth. He condemns by these words the foolishness of men: who struggle so much to acquire treasures: with which death in a short time satiates them. Pope Nicholas of the Orsini <note>Pope Nicholas III, reigned 1277–1280.</note> lived as pontiff three years, eight months, and twenty days. This man, to leave his relatives rich, was a great Simonist. And in life he understood through a revelation of prophecy that Boniface was to be a great Simonist and stay in the papacy eight years and nine months. After Nicholas succeeded Martin <note>Pope Martin IV.</note>, a man who, had he not been a glutton, was of laudable life in his other actions: And after Martin succeeded Pope Celestine: of whom we spoke above in the third canto: and after Celestine, Boniface. BY SEVERAL Years the writing lied to me. If you are already there, the prophecy is not verified: because eight years and nine months still lack two years and nine months. For this long Boniface lived after the day that Dante pretends to have descended into hell: which was in the year of our salvation one thousand three hundred: and Boniface died later in one thousand three hundred and three. TAKE BY DECEIT the beautiful lady: Because by fraud he occupied the pontificate of the Christian Church: which he calls the "beautiful lady." So that this may be clearly understood, I say that in the year of Christ one thousand two hundred ninety-four, the cardinals were in Perugia: and were much harassed by the Perugians: because through their discord they had already been without a pontiff for more than two years. Therefore, after many altercations they elected Friar Peter of Sulmona, a man of holy and very harsh life: and who lived in penance on Murrone, which is a mountain not far from Sulmona. This man was Celestine V and in the month of September he created twelve cardinals, almost all from beyond the mountains <note>Meaning they were French, to please the King of Naples.</note> to please Charles II. Afterwards he went with the court to Naples seeking to renounce the pontificate: because he was a very simple man and little suited to governing. There was in the college of cardinals Master Benedetto of Gania <note>Benedetto Caetani, who became Pope Boniface VIII.</note>, a man very...

He was buried in a small church of the friars of his order on the mountain, and placed more than ten cubits deep so that he could not be found. Boniface was more greedy for power than is fitting for a priest: and through his prudence, he increased the state of the church. such a response because it is a universal thing: that when someone thinks you are another, you demonstrate to him that he is far from the truth. **IF KNOWING WHO I AM** concerns you so much. But he will stay less time than I have been thus flattened: because immediately after him, there will come from the western parts a shepherd of even fouler and uglier deeds than his, such that the wretched infamy of myself and Boniface will be covered by his. He made them very rich and lords of many lands. He made seven Roman cardinals almost all related to him. ecclesiastical dignity through Alexander III: because their origin was from "Magna Avena" <note>A legendary German origin for the Orsini family.</note> and they favored Frederick I <note>Frederick Barbarossa.</note> against the Church. He built grand palaces near Saint Peter's. He occupied Bologna and the entire region of Romagna, which the Emperor Rudolph had pledged provided he did not pass into Italy. This was considered an unjust act, as it was manifest to all that it was not for lack of will, but rather great impediments that prevented Rudolph from crossing into Italy. He then appointed Bertoldo Orsini, his nephew, as Count of Romagna. And Latino Brancaleoni, the son of one of his sisters and already a cardinal, he sent as a legate to Bologna.

**FROM THE WEST** a son without law. After Boniface <note>Boniface VIII.</note> came Benedict XI, a man excellent in both letters and character; he died, as many believe, in the ninth month of his papacy and was buried in Perugia. After him, the cardinals remained in contention for eight months because they were divided into two factions. At the head of one was Matteo Orsini and Francesco Caetani, the nephew of Boniface. Of the other, Napoleone Orsini dal Monte and Niccolò da Prato, who, before becoming a cardinal, had been of the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans.</note>, a man highly esteemed for both his learning and his prudence.

This man added cunning to his strength: he secretly persuaded Francesco Caetani to consent to Raymond de Got, the Archbishop of Bordeaux, who was a Gascon and an enemy of the King of France. Afterward, he immediately wrote to the King, who was Philip the Fair in Paris: that if he desired to recover his status with the Church and support the Colonna family, his friends, he should reconcile with Raymond, who had already been elected Pope as his enemy. The King immediately wrote to Raymond, asking him to meet for very important matters. Riding with speed, Raymond reached him on the sixth day. They swore faith to one another upon the altar. First, with appropriate words, the King reconciled him with Charles of Valois, called "Charles Lackland," the King's brother. Then he said it was in his power to make him Pope, and that he would do so if he promised certain things. 

Raymond, most greedy for such dignity, threw himself at the King’s feet and thanked him profoundly for returning good for evil; he promised to always be ready for any request. First, the King asked that he be readmitted to communion along with his followers for the excesses committed against Boniface. Second, that he grant him the tithes of his kingdom for five years to cover the expenses of the war in Flanders. Third, that he extinguish and annul the memory of Boniface. Fourth, that he restore the cardinalates of Giacomo and Pietro Colonna, who had been stripped of them by Boniface. Fifth, that he abolish the Order of the Templars. The sixth grace he reserved in his heart <note>This "secret" favor is often interpreted as the trial of Boniface's memory or further political concessions.</note>. Raymond consented and, like a wicked simoniac, bought the papacy at this price. 

The King wrote back to the Cardinal of Prato to ensure those of his faction consented to Raymond, as did Francesco Caetani and his followers. With this fraud, Raymond was created Pope and called Clement V on the fifth day of June, 1305. The Church had been vacant for six months and ten days. Afterward, on the eleventh day of November, he was crowned at Lyon on the Rhône, and he kept his promises to the King of France. Furthermore, he created twelve cardinals, partly Gascons and partly French, but all the King's men.

**A NEW JASON.** This was a Hebrew man, the brother of Onias the High Priest and a good man. But Jason, being most ambitious and desiring to take the High Priesthood from his brother, went to Antiochus, King of Syria, who held Jerusalem. He promised to give him three hundred and sixty talents of silver and eighty from other revenues, and besides these, another hundred and fifty talents if he would grant him the principality. Having obtained it, he abandoned the ancient sacrifices and the Mosaic laws, and instituted the cult of the Gentiles, along with wrestling arenas and gymnasiums where he made the youth exercise lasciviously; and he kept boys in a brothel. Finally, he had led all the priests to the games of the Gentiles and to every kind of luxury. Nor was he ashamed to send three hundred silver drachmas to Tyre for the five-year games to perform a sacrifice to Hercules. But after three years, he lost the principality, deceived by Menelaus just as he had deceived his brother, and went into exile in the land of the Ammonites. Clement will thus be a "New Jason," because he will acquire the pontificate through simony, just as Jason acquired the High Priesthood.

It seems there is a question of whether an inferior should rebuke a superior. For this reason, the poet offers an excuse: so that without arrogance he may, with the utmost liberty, rebuke the extreme avarice and wicked simony of the unjust shepherds who adulterate the bride of Christ <note>The Church.</note>.

**NOW TELL ME HOW MUCH TREASURE** our Lord wanted. Here he demonstrates that Christ does not sell his vicariate to Peter for gold or silver; he asked nothing of him except that he should follow him. Indeed, the Gospel of Matthew says that Christ, having given the keys to Peter, said only: *Sequere me* <note>original: "Sequere me" — Follow me.</note> and "come after me." This means: follow my doctrine and observe my precepts.

You, Nicholas: as if to say, I do not deem you worthy of anyone having compassion for your just punishments. **AND**

This is a bitter mockery, and one which is deservedly suited to such a wicked simoniac; for by "comforting" him to watch over his unjustly acquired treasure—which he cannot do, because one leaves all earthly goods behind here, and they cannot be used there—it is nothing other than to reproach him for his foolishness: that he wished to prefer transitory things to eternal ones. And this is a rhetorical figure called "concession" <note>An oratorical device where one seemingly grants a point to an opponent to turn it against them.</note>. As when Virgil says: "Go, follow Italy with the winds, seek kingdoms through the waves" <note>original: "I sequere taliam uentis pete regna p undas" — A quote from the Aeneid (IV.381) where Dido mockingly tells Aeneas to leave.</note>. **WHICH MADE YOU** bold against Charles. Nicholas took such heart from his riches that he requested of Charles I <note>Charles of Anjou, King of Sicily and Naples.</note>—who was of the royal blood of France—that he give one of his nieces to Nicholas’s own nephew. But Charles replied that although the Pope had "red feet" <note>A reference to the red shoes worn by the Pope or perhaps the red hats of his cardinal nephews.</note>, he was not worthy to make a family alliance with the blood of France. These words sparked such indignation in the breast of Nicholas that he took the vicariate of Tuscany away from Charles; and in the process of time, he consented to the rebellion of Sicily, for which he received a great sum of money through the hands of Messer Giovanni di Procida, the head and author of the rebellion <note>The "Sicilian Vespers" of 1282, which ended Charles's rule in Sicily.</note>. And in this way Charles lost Sicily, which he had held from the Church, having acquired it not without much blood. **AND IF IT WERE NOT** for. He shows that the reverence for the pontificate, which is equal and eternal, does not allow him to use more bitter words. And he uses a rhetorical figure called "occupation" <note>Also known as paralipsis, where a speaker mentions something by saying they will not mention it.</note>, because he shows he does not wish to say what he is currently saying.

Or rather, the seven virtues: four moral—Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance—and three theological—Faith, Hope, and Charity. This woman "had strength from the ten horns," that is, she had her demonstration and was figured by the ten commandments given to Moses, as long as **VIRTUE** pleased her husband. This signifies as long as virtue pleased the Pontiff, who is the husband of the Church. Because as long as the Pontiffs lived virtuously and without avarice or luxury, it was verified that this woman sat upon the beast of the ten horns. But afterwards, she began to "play the whore with kings," that is, to become the harlot of temporal kings, because for money she sold her dignity and benefices and her liberty, just as a harlot does for money.

sells her body and her chastity. **YOU HAVE MADE** a God of gold and silver: because, having set aside all religion and fear of God, you consider money to be your god. **AND WHAT ELSE.** There is no difference between you and those who worship idols, except that they worship a single idol, and you worship a hundred. He uses "a hundred," a finite number, to represent the infinite, because you worship coins, which are infinite. Of these, the prophet Hosea speaks: *They have reigned, but not by me; they have been princes, and I did not know them. Their gold and their silver they have made into idols for themselves, so that they might perish.* <note>original: "Ipsi regnauerunt et non ex me principes extiterunt et non cognoui. Aurum suum et argentum suum fecerunt sibi idola ne interirent" — Hosea 8:4.</note> And the Psalmist: *The idols of the nations are silver and gold.* <note>original: "Simulacra gentium argentum et aurum" — Psalm 115:4 / 135:15.</note> **AH, CONSTANTINE.** He infers that while the Church was poor and had no property of its own, it lived always in the highest sanctity. But once it began to possess its own goods, wealth brought in every kind of vice. Therefore, with righteous indignation, Petrarch rises up against the apostolic church, saying: *You were not nurtured on feathers in the shade, but naked to the wind and barefoot among the thorns; now you live such that a stench rises to God.* <note>A quote from Petrarch’s "Babylonian Sonnets" (Canzoniere 138), criticizing the corruption of the Papal Court at Avignon.</note> Thus, because Constantine, converted by Pope Sylvester and made a Christian, was the first to endow the Church, the poet laments not his conversion, but the dowry <note>The "Donation of Constantine," a decree then believed to have granted the Pope temporal power over Rome and the Western Empire.</note> that he gave to the Pope, the father of Christians, who became the first wealthy one; for the others had lived in extreme poverty. The poet follows the most common and universal opinion regarding Pope Sylvester and Emperor Constantine. But because there are various opinions concerning his conversion and the dowry of the Church, and each has very weighty authors, I do not wish to be so arrogant as to interject my own judgment. For this reason, we shall leave the dispute unresolved, and the final judgment to the more learned. **WHILE I** sang such notes to him: that is, I spoke such words to him openly. And he said "notes" to stay within the metaphor, since one who sings uses notes. **OR ANGER**: to which Dante's harsh words incited him. **OR CONSCIENCE**: of his own simony. Whichever of these two things it was, **HE KICKED HARD**: that is, he writhed. **WITH BOTH HIS FEET**: that is, soles. To kick <term>springare: a term describing a horse bucking or kicking its hind legs</term> is to move the legs forcefully to strike. Whence we say a horse "kicks" and strikes.

> I believe well that it pleased my leader,
> with such a contented lip he always waited
> for the sound of the true words expressed.
> Therefore, with both his arms he took me,
> and when he had me all upon his breast,
> he remounted by the way where he descended.
> Nor did he tire of holding me close to him,
> until he bore me to the summit of the arch
> which is the passage from the fourth to the fifth bank.
> There softly he set down his burden,
> soft because of the rugged and steep crag,
> which would be a hard passage for goats;
> from there another valley was discovered to me.

<column-break/>

Dante perceived that Virgil was pleased by the rebuke given to the pontiff: because **WITH ATTENTIVE LIP**: that is, with attentive lips he listened, which signifies hearing in silence. Thus it demonstrates that it always greatly pleases the intellect when, in human operations and in the active life, prudence reproves with great liberty and condemns wicked vices. And that he carried him back up the mountain demonstrates that after the lower reason has understood some particular thing, the intellect leads it back to universals by way of a steep path: that is, through difficult speculation. And by carrying him, he held him to his breast where thought resides, to denote that the contemplation of universals is what gives us true knowledge. Nor without reason does he make a comparison to goats. For this animal, in its grazing, always climbs and does not descend. Whence the sign of the winter tropic is called Capricorn <note>The astrological sign associated with the winter solstice.</note>, because the sun there begins to climb. And likewise, whoever proceeds in contemplation must always ascend to higher things and not descend.

### CANTO XX OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.

The poet continues in the description of the ditches <note>The "bolge" or "ditches" are ten circular trenches in the eighth circle of Hell, called Malebolge, where various types of fraud are punished.</note>; and he posits that in the fourth, the diviners of every kind are punished. Certainly, it was a very ancient opinion, confirmed by the consensus of all nations, that among men there is a certain presumption and science of future things, which the Latins call divination and the Greeks call *Mantike* <note>original: "Mantice"</note>. This is either natural or artificial. Natural divination contains within it divine fury and dreams. Thus, many were moved by divine fury, such as the oracles among the Pagans, and the prophets among the Hebrews, to predict future things. The dream is of three types. Sometimes one dreams of what is to be, but it needs interpretation, like the one who dreamed of pressing grapes into a cup, and Joseph interpreted that he would become the king’s cupbearer <note>original: "pincerna"</note> and would serve him the cup at the table. Sometimes one dreams of seeing the thing in the exact way it will happen; and this is called a vision. Sometimes someone appears in the dream who tells you things openly as they will be; and this they call an oracle. But often they are together, as in Virgil’s Aeneas, who saw Hector in a very sad and mournful form and heard the words in which he comforted him to flee. Artificial divination includes Haruspicy, Augury, Astrology, and Lots. Haruspicy includes that divination taken from the shape, site, and color of the entrails of the animal they sacrificed; as on the morning of the day Caesar died, the heart of the ox he sacrificed was not seen. Augury is divination made either from the taste or the chirping of birds. For the augurs sometimes offered bait to chickens, which they kept enclosed for this purpose; and according to how they fed on it, they interpreted the outcome of the matter. Sometimes they watched the flying and the song of birds in the air, and judged according to their type; because the raven gives one augury, the crow another, the woodpecker another, and others different ones; and it is one thing to sing and fly in one way, and another in another. And it is one thing if they come from the right, and another from the left. Nor are birds alone: but also other animals give good and bad auguries, such as wolves, foxes, dogs, and serpents, and the like. Not much different from these are monsters and portents, which occur against nature. Whence, in the army of Xerxes, because a mare gave birth to a hare, the augurs announced the timid flight of that army. Astrology predicts future things according to various courses of the stars, in which there are conjunctions, oppositions, sextiles, trines, quadratures, and other aspects. And of this, they believe Geomancy <note>A method of divination that interprets markings on the ground or patterns formed by tossed handfuls of soil.</note> to be a species, which we will treat in Purgatory; and Lots, found according to the ancients in the city of Praeneste, today called Palestrina. And Pyromancy made with fire. Necromancy with dead bodies to which the soul is recalled. Hydromancy made with water. Chiromancy which is considered in the lines of the hand. All these things would require a long discourse if we wanted to explain them in their order. But time is not enough for one who proposes such long and diverse material.

**OF NEW**
**O**f new punishment I must make verses,
and give matter to the twentieth canto
of the first song, which I submerged.
I was already completely prepared
to look into the uncovered bottom
which was bathed by anguished weeping.

And I saw people through the circular valley
coming silent and weeping at the pace
that litanies <note>Religious processions where prayers are chanted.</note> do in this world.
As my sight descended lower upon them,
each appeared to be wonderfully twisted
between the chin and the start of the chest,
For the face was turned toward the kidneys;
and it was necessary for them to come backward

<column-break/>

**NEW PUNISHMENT:** Almost unusual and unheard of, and greater than the others; and it makes the listener attentive by promising him unusual and no small things. **AND GIVE MATTER** to the twentieth canto: that is, to the twentieth chapter **OF THE FIRST SONG:** that is, of the first canticle. There are three canticles: *Inferno*, *Purgatorio*, and *Paradiso*; and the *Inferno* contains thirty-four cantos, and the other two each contain thirty-three cantos. Therefore, in total, there are one hundred cantos divided into three canticles. **WHICH I SUBMERGED:** <note>original: "CHE IO SOMMERSI"</note> that is, which I plunged into the center of the earth. He does not submerge the canticle, but describes in it the submerged Hell. Some texts have "of the first songs and of the submerged" <note>original: "Delle prime canzone et de sommerfi"</note>: that is, of the damned who are submerged in the center of the earth. And it follows that he was already prepared to see the bottom of the earth uncovered: that is, which he could see from the bridge where he was. **WHICH WAS BATHED BY WEEPING:** by those who were being punished.

**THE PUNISHMENT OF THESE PEOPLE** he posits to be: that they have their faces turned backward; and to want to see where they are going, they must go backward. This is a very appropriate punishment <note>This refers to the concept of *contrapasso*, where the punishment mirrors the sin.</note>, that the contrary should be punished with its contrary. And let him who wanted to see too far ahead see only what is behind; and he who was so rash as to want to see the future—which God has denied to man as something that is not useful to him. Nor is it likely that God, being able to give us true knowledge of things to come—

**Perhaps by the force of paralysis**
**someone was thus completely twisted:**

If these [divinatory powers] had been useful to us, God would have given them to us, because God wills every good, being supreme goodness. PERHAPS BY THE FORCE of paralysis. *Paralysis* in Greek <note>original: "Paralysis in greco"</note> is a disease which, because it loosens the connections of the nerves, induces trembling of the limbs or twists them; in our language it is called "paralytic" <note>original: "parletico"</note>. He concludes, then, that although this disease twists the limbs, nevertheless it never twisted anyone in this form [with the head entirely reversed]. One sees some people with their necks twisted by paralysis, so that they look sideways. But no one is seen so twisted that they look backward. And it is an excellent comparison, because just as the paralytic always trembles, so these who seek future things always tremble—that is, they live in fear and anxiety whether what they predicted will happen or not. They always vacillate and doubt, considering their points and moments, the feathers and songs of birds, changes in the air, from which direction it thunders or lightens, marks on the earth, the movement of fire; and finally, a sneeze often makes them change their purpose.

**S**O MAY GOD LET YOU gather fruit from your reading, whoever learns by reading. Thus, the fruit of this reading is to know the foolishness of those who wish to foresee the future. And not without reason does the poet show great compassion. For since knowledge is the supreme perfection of

our soul, it seems that he deserves compassion who, toiling to know, becomes more ignorant. WHEN I SAW OUR image close by: that is, Dante perceived the human image, for then the image of these people was twisted when he was near them. This denotes that this vice is not recognized unless it is well considered. Because at first glance, wanting to attain this science [of the future] seems to be a virtue and not a vice. But let us understand that foreseeing the future is not of human nature, but is proper to God alone. Whence Isaiah says: "Tell us the former things and the new things, and I will say that you are gods" <note>original: "Isaia Priora et nouissima nuntiate mihi et dicam quod dii estis," referencing Isaiah 41:22-23.</note>. Lucan: "The mortal race is ignorant of the fate of the gods" <note>original: "Lucano Sortisque deorum ignarum mortale genus," from the Pharsalia.</note>. And in the book of Kings: "For man sees only those things that appear, but God looks upon the heart" <note>original: "Non . n. uidet homo nisi ea que apparent . Deus autem intuetur cor," from 1 Samuel 16:7.</note>. Dante wept and Virgil rebuked him. This signifies that the sensitive part [of the soul] induces compassion for every pain, even if it is justly given. But reason forbids a man to be moved to pity by punishments justly inflicted by God; and therefore he says: HERE PIETY LIVES when it is well dead. As if to say: in this place, it is piety to have no pity <note>Dante plays on the word *pietà*, which means both "pity" and "piety" or "religious devotion." Virgil argues that to pity those God has judged is a lack of religious piety.</note>. But it should be noted here that "piety" <term>pietà: the Italian word encompasses both the feeling of compassion and the duty toward God or country.</term> among the Latins is the virtue by which one bears due affection for the fatherland and for those joined by blood. And from this spring compassion and congratulation. Compassion is sorrow at the neighbor's misfortune, and congratulation is joy at the neighbor's good. Therefore, in this place, he used "piety" for compassion for the sinner's pains—feeling sorrow for his misery and that he fell into such error. But although Dante—who represents sensuality—has felt compassion for the sinner in many places, nevertheless he has not been rebuked by Virgil as he is here. This shows us that in those who have sinned through frailty, there is some excuse. But the error of these [diviners] has always been mocked even in life.

**L**ift your head: because, weeping, Dante was standing with his head bowed. And see him for whom the earth opened up. BEFORE THE EYES OF THE THEBANS: that is, in the sight of the Thebans and before their seeing eyes. This was Amphiaraus, who had his origin from Jove. For Aeolus, son of Jove, fathered Erytheius; and from Erytheius came Amythaon, who fathered Bias; and Bias fathered Antiphates; and from Antiphates was born Oicles, the father of Amphiaraus.
