in the same place he found the same serpents. And thinking they had the power to change his sex again, he struck them with the staff and returned from female to male. They also say that there being a dispute between Jupiter and Juno as to which had greater pleasure in sexual union, the male or the female, and not agreeing, they submitted to the judgment of Tiresias, who had experienced both. He pronounced that in females there was greater fury and lust. Nor did he give such a sentence without natural

---

reasons. For although it is established that the male is warmer than the female—because his complexion is more sanguineous, while that of the female is more phlegmatic—nevertheless, in the male there is only a single pleasure in the casting of the seed. But in the woman it is double: both in casting her own and in receiving that of the male into the womb. The womb, being by nature quite cold, once warmed by this seed, takes great pleasure from it, and the heat lasts a long time; for the denser and colder the matter that is heated, the more it maintains the heat, as we see in iron and other similar things. Furthermore, in the female, the instrument is always ready; the opposite is true in the man. Tiresias, pronouncing such a sentence, offended Juno so much that in her anger she took the light from his eyes. And Jupiter, in compensation and restoration for this damage, gave him the light of the mind. For he made him a diviner and gave him knowledge of future things. Because of this, when the Cadmeans <note>The founders/citizens of Thebes</note>, lords of Thebes, were in danger because they were besieged by Alcmaeon, Tiresias predicted to them that their escape lay in fleeing and abandoning the city. Therefore, they retreated to Tilphusa, a region of Boeotia, where Tiresias, dying, was most honorably buried by the Cadmeans. Thebes was taken and sacked, and Daphne, the daughter of Tiresias, was sent to Delphi to the temple of Apollo and dedicated to Apollo. There she was excellent in the art of divining and composed many oracles in verse, many of which Homer placed in his poem; and she was called Sibyl. For in that language, *sibyllenin* <note>A transliteration of a Greek-derived concept</note> means to give the oracle with a living voice. Homer also imagines that in the underworld Tiresias predicted many things to Ulysses. CHANGING EVERY ONE OF HIS LIMBS. Because there is not only a different sex in the female, but also all the limbs have a different quality in the female. AND FIRST AND THEN AGAIN. Understand: first he had to strike the serpents to change from male to female, and then strike them again to return from female to male. THE MASCULINE FEATHERS. He uses "feathers" <note>original: "penne"</note> for hair. As if to say the beard and other hairs which the male has and the female does not.

Thus, Bianor is interpreted as manly strength. His tomb was famous near Mantua. From Eclogue IX, 59-60.</note> Therefore Ochnus built Mantua and gave it the name of Manto, his mother. Although Dante varies the history somewhat, as you will read in the following verses.

it contains all that falls

Numerous streams, springs, and rivers fall from the nearby mountains into Benaco. Garda is on the shore of the lake. Verona. Valmoniaca <note>Now known as Val Camonica.</note> is a valley in the territory of Brescia. The Apennines are a most celebrated mountain range: which begins from the promontory of Monaco, formerly called Meneto, opposite the Ligurian Sea: and divides Italy along its length: on the right is the Tyrrhenian Sea, called the lower <note>original: "infero"</note>: and on the left is the Adriatic, called the upper <note>original: "supero"</note>: and it reaches all the way to Sicily, as we have said elsewhere. **THE PLACE IS** in the middle. The Trentine shepherd. This shows that in the middle of Trento, Brescia, and Verona, the dioceses—that is, the bishoprics—of these cities meet in the middle of the lake and border one another there. Therefore, the shepherd—that is, the bishop—of each of these three cities could "sign"—that is, give a blessing there—as if in his own diocese. This is because by canon law <note>original: "de iure canonico"</note> no bishop can give a blessing except within his own diocese. **COULD SIGN** if he made that journey, meaning passing through that place. **PESCHIERA** is a fortress located at the end of the lake: and it belongs to the diocese of Verona. **GEAR** <note>original: "arnese"</note> signifies an instrument: furnishings and ornament. **TO CONFRONT** to meet, resist, and stand against. **WHERE THE...** properly a "lama" <note>hollow</note> is a concave and humid place. Thus, near rivers, we call certain marshy places covered with trees "lame." But here he calls the lake a "lama": **DESCENDED LOWER:** it is deeper. From here the water flows out: and beginning to run out of the lake, it changes its name and is called Mincio. **ENTERS THE...;** It enters the Po: because "co" in the Lombard language means "head" <note>original: "capo"</note>. The Mincio is born from Benaco and comes all the way to Mantua, where it expands into a swamp around the city: and generates heavy and unhealthy air. **GOVERNOLO** is a castle located where the Mincio enters the Po. **NOT FAR** has it run before it finds a hollow. He describes the place where the Mincio stagnates and creates a marsh: which in the summer, because it nearly dries up, makes the air foul and diseased. **AND OFTEN** in summer it is foul. We call one "gramo" <note>miserable/foul</note> when they are greedy and desiring: and because one who is greedy lacks what they desire. We also call one "gramo" who is needy: and because one who is in need is in misery, we say "gramo" for the miserable and unhappy.

Then passing by, the cruel virgin

without cultivation and bare of inhabitants.
There, to flee all human comfort,

and there she lived, and there she left her empty body.

because of the swamp it had on all sides.
They built the city over those dead remains
and for her who first chose the place,
they called it Mantua without any other lot. <note>Meaning they did not use divination or casting of lots to choose the name.</note>
Formerly its people within were more crowded,
before the madness of Casalodi
was deceived by Pinamonte.
Therefore I charge you, that if you ever hear
my city originated otherwise,
let no falsehood defraud the truth.

<column-break/>

**LAKE BENACO.** This is its ancient name. Whence Virgil [says] *rising with the waves and roar of the sea, O Benaco* <note>original: "fluctibus et fremitu assurgens Benace marino"</note>. But today it is called Lake Garda: because Garda is a town situated on the shore of this lake. Benaco, therefore, is placed between narrow mountain valleys in such a way that the force of the winds generated by such narrowness stirs up fluctuations and storms in this lake similar to those of the sea. Furthermore, they say that its bottom holds gold sand: upon which the carp feed, a most sweet fish: which many say are not found in any other water. **BY A THOUSAND AND MORE.** Into...

It shows how Manto, after searching through many countries, settled in the place surrounded by this swamp as a solitary thing: and suitable for her incantations: through which she fled human comfort: and for this reason, he calls her "cruel." It shows also that after the death of Manto, the surrounding inhabitants built the city where Manto had lived and was afterwards buried: and from her name, they called it Mantua. **SHE LEFT** her empty body: that is, void: because the dead body remains void of the soul. **WITHOUT** any other lot <note>original: "altra sorte"</note>, i.e., without seeking omens or auguries to give a name to the city. For the ancients, once a city was built, they would name it based on some augury: just as Alba was named from the "alba," that is, the white sow found there. **FORMERLY WERE** the people. He touches upon a history that is not very ancient. They say, therefore, that Casalodi was a castle in the territory of Brescia: and it had counts called the Counts of Casalodi: who occupied Mantua and became its lords and tyrants. There were in those same times in Mantua many families of noble men: of whom the lords...

<header>CANTO XX</header>

they had no small suspicion; and they strongly feared the power of those men. Among them, Pinamonte de' Buonacolsi <note>A leader of the Ghibelline faction in Mantua who seized power in 1272.</note>, a man of great spirit and no small prudence, took sagacious counsel to seize the lordship from the Casalodi family. Therefore, seeing that the people were very hostile toward the noblemen, and judging that once these were driven out it would be easy for him to obtain the prize, he simulated great affection toward the lord—who was Count Alberto da Casalodi. He persuaded him to relegate all the nobles to the countryside for a time, demonstrating that this would be so pleasing to the people that, by such a benefit, he would win their favor. Alberto believed the fraudulent counsel. Whereupon Pinamonte, seeing the city empty of noblemen, made himself the head of the people; and with their favor, having driven out the Casalodi, he became the lord.

**A fitting response** from a disciple toward his teacher. For the first quality a student must have is to lend undoubting faith to his teacher's doctrine. And therefore he says, "your reasonings take my faith": that is, they acquire my faith and ensure that my faith is entirely in him. **SO**—that is, in such a way.

And I: "Master, your reasonings
to me are so certain and so take my faith,
that others would be to me as spent coals.
But tell me of the people who precede,
if you see any among them worthy of note;
for my mind resides on that alone."
Then he said to me: "That one who from his cheek
spreads his beard over his brown shoulders,
was an augur when Greece was so empty of males
that they hardly remained for the cradles;
and he gave the moment with Calchas 
in Aulis to cut the first cable.
Eurypilus was his name, and thus my high
tragedy sings of him in a certain place:
you know it well, who know the whole thing."

<column-break/>

**THAT THE OTHERS:** that is, reasonings. **TO ME ARE AS Spent coals:** that is, they give me no light or knowledge. **BUT TELL ME OF THE OTHERS IF ANY BE Worthy of note:** that is, worthy of making a note or mention of them: because my mind and desire **RESIDES**—that is, stops—only on that. **THAT ONE WHO FROM THE cheek spreads his beard upon his shoulders.** Dante had already shown the same meaning in three ways. Now he shows it in a fourth. For the beard cannot fall from the cheeks onto the shoulders unless the face is turned backward. **IT WAS WHEN Greece was empty of males.** That is, in the times when Agamemnon, King of the Greeks, went against the Trojans, and led such a multitude in his armies that he hardly left any but small children behind; this is an hyperbole <note>An intentional exaggeration for emphasis.</note>. **AUGUR:** He was an augur and his name was Eurypilus; who, together with the other augur named Calchas, when all the ships were already full of Greeks in the port of Aulis, declared the hour and the prosperous moment to depart from the port. And therefore he says **TO CUT The first cable:** that is, the rope of the first ship, which is to say the flagship. Because ships in port stay at anchor; and when they are in a hurry to depart, they do not wait to weigh the anchor, but they cut the cable that is tied to the anchor. Hence Virgil says: "And to cut the twisted cables" <note>original: "Tortosque incidere funes"</note>. Aulis is a port in Boeotia, not far from Tanagra: where Agamemnon, King of the Greeks, gathered a thousand ships to go to the siege of Troy. Eurypilus was the one whom Sinon says the Greeks sent to the oracle of Apollo to learn how they could appease the gods so that they would grant a favorable voyage to return to Greece. Hence Virgil says: "We send Eurypilus to consult the oracles of Phoebus, and he brings back from the shrines these grim words" <note>original: "Suspensi Eurypilum scitatum oracula Phebi Mittimus usque aditis hec tristia dicta reportat"</note>. **AND THUS My high tragedy sings of him in a certain place.** He calls it a tragedy both for the excellence of the style—which is found in tragedies—on which account he says in the *Eclogues*: "Only your songs are worthy of the Sophoclean buskin" <note>original: "Sola Sophocleo tua carmina digna coturno." The "buskin" or "coturno" was the high boot worn by tragic actors.</note>—and for the subject matter, which is indeed tragic.

That other who is so thin in the flanks
was Michael Scot, who truly 
knew the game of magical frauds.
See Guido Bonatti; see Asdente,
who now wishes he had attended to his leather 
and his thread, but repents in vain.
See the wretched women who left the needle,
the shuttle, and the spindle, and became diviners;
they made spells with herbs and with images.

Some would have it that this Michael was Spanish, for the custom of those people in those times was to wear very affected clothing and to gird themselves tightly. Therefore, they want this to be why he says: **Who is so thin in the flanks.** Many say that he was from the island of Scotland, and therefore he calls him Michael Scot. But all conclude that he was an excellent astrologer and a great mage. And he often hosted banquets without any preparation of food; and then, at the hour of eating, he would compel spirits to bring dishes from various places; and he would say, "this comes from the kitchen of the King of France," and "this from that of the King of England." He was the astrologer of Frederick II, and wrote a book for him which Benvenuto <note>Benvenuto da Imola, an early commentator on Dante.</note> affirms having read; and in it, he says there is knowledge...

<header>INFERNO</header>

by many signs of nature. He predicted to Frederick <note>Emperor Frederick II (1194–1250), whom Dante places among the Heretics in Canto X.</note> that he would die in Florence. But the equivocation of the name deceived him. For he did not die in our city, but in Apulia in a castle called Firenzuola <note>original: "firenzuola", meaning "little Florence".</note>. He saw that his death would proceed from a small stone <note>original: "faxolino" (sassolino)</note> of a certain weight: and so it happened. For while he was in church with his head uncovered to honor the body of Christ, the rope of the bell caused a small stone to fall on his head; weighing it, he recognized it was the weight he had foreseen and judged himself dead: and so he died. **GUIDO BONATTO** was from Forlì: and how excellent an astrologer he was is shown by a book of astrology which he composed, and which today is much esteemed by astrologers. He was accepted by Count Guido da Montefeltro, who was the lord of Forlì; they say that the Count never moved against his enemies, nor went into battle, except at the hour given to him by this man, and that he always returned as the victor. Furthermore, as Guido Bonatti went with him into battle against the French, he predicted that the Count would be wounded in the thigh; and so it was. He immediately treated him with eggs and tow <note>stoppa: coarse flax or hemp fibers used for bandages.</note> which he had brought for this purpose. Nevertheless, he was bested by a lowly peasant <note>original: "uile uillano"</note>, who affirmed it would rain on a day when Guido said it was impossible for it to rain; asked how he knew this, he replied from his donkey, which had shaken its ears many times when he led it from the stable. **ASDENTE** was from Parma and a shoemaker, a man without letters; nevertheless, he gave himself to the art of divining, and in that—either through the benevolence of the heavens which ordained him to this, or by some other means—he was excellent and predicted many things. Specifically, he predicted that Frederick was to attempt to build the city called Victoria near Parma and would be defeated. **BUT HE REPENTS TOO LATE**: because in hell there is no redemption <note>original: "quia in inferno nulla est redemptio"</note>. **SEE THE WRETCHED WOMEN**: After the specific cases, he comes to generalities, and shows many women to have been sorceresses and enchantresses, who, leaving behind sewing, weaving, and spinning—the feminine arts—gave themselves to sorcery using various herbs and images of wax and earth.

He admonishes Dante that the time to depart is already approaching day, and uses chronography—that is, a description of time. He says then, **COME NOW**: because already the moon, which is in opposition to the sun, touches the western horizon: that is, it is already setting and going below. The heaven is round and therefore

> But come now, for already he holds the confines
> of both hemispheres and touches the wave
> beneath Seville, Cain and the thorns;
> and already last night the moon was round;
> well should you remember, for it did you no harm
> at any time throughout the deep woods.
> Thus he spoke to me, and we went on meanwhile.

<column-break/>

it is called a sphere. But because half is above us and the other half is below, this sphere is divided into two parts: and they are called hemispheres, that is, half-rounds. And we imagine a line that girds all the heaven on every side around, and divides the upper hemisphere from the lower: and it is called the horizon, that is, the "terminator" and, as it were, the divider. Therefore, when a star rises from the hemisphere below to ours and reaches the horizon—which is the boundary between one and the other—it then begins to be seen by us. Likewise, conversely, when it descends

past our entire hemisphere and already touches the western horizon, it then sets and is seen no more. Furthermore, it should be noted that when the moon is "round" <note>Full moon.</note>, it is then in opposition to the sun. And therefore, when the sun rises on the eastern horizon, the moon sets on the western horizon. Thus, when the poet says that the moon touches the boundary of both hemispheres—that is, the western horizon which is below Seville—it shows that day was approaching, because the sun was beginning to come to the eastern horizon. And this is stated excellently according to physics. But when he says "touches the wave," he speaks according to the opinion of the common people. For when a star goes below to the other hemisphere—because the sea is between us and it—it seems to fall into the sea. But since the heaven has a spherical life, and the elements likewise, and since it is the nature of heavy things from every part to descend toward the center, it is necessary that wherever the moon finds itself, it is always equally distant from the water with an equal interval. And in this he imitates the Latin poets, who not through ignorance, but to imitate the fables of the commoners, often describe the sun or another planet either plunging into the sea when it sets, or emerging when it rises. **CAIN AND THE THORNS**: that is, the moon, in which the common people, seeing a certain shadow, believe it is Cain who has a forkful of thorns on his shoulder. But what this shadow actually is will be shown in the third Canticle <note>Paradiso, Canto II, where Beatrice explains the scientific reason for moon spots.</note> and in the description of the heaven of the moon. Cain was the firstborn of Adam and was a farmer, as his brother Abel was a shepherd. He was the first murderer. For seeing that the sacrifice Abel made to God of the firstborn of his flock was more pleasing than the one he made of the first-fruits of his crops, moved by envy, he killed him; and "Cain" signifies "possession" or "lamentation" in the Hebrew language. **BENEATH SEVILLE**. This is a noble city in the westernmost part of Spain. Hence the strait that leaves the ocean sea and divides Spain from Africa is named after it. **AND ALREADY LAST NIGHT**: When you found yourself lost in the woods, it then helped you somewhat that the moon shone in the darkness of the night and the woods. Night signifies blindness and ignorance, in which we go wandering in the woods of vices. Nor can we see the sun, that is, the light of true reason. Nevertheless, Dante not having yet formed a fixed habit in vice, although he did not see the sun which would show him the true path, still the light of the moon—which is nothing other than the reflection of solar rays in some part—showed it to him. But so that I may better express my concept, I say that he who is in vice but has not made it a habit, although he does not have the sun (that is, true reason), nevertheless sees the reflection of it in the moon, which stands for earthly things. For knowing the truth of earthly things is a good beginning to wanting to flee them and seek divine things.

<meta>This page transitions from the end of Canto XX, which dealt with sorcerers and diviners, to the beginning of Canto XXI. The commentary shifts from the history of Mantua and the astrologers Guido Bonatti and Asdente to the introduction of the fifth "bolgia" or ditch of Malebolge.</meta>

.n.iiii

# CANTO XXI OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.

The twenty-first canto follows, in which he places the fifth ditch: and in it, he describes the punishment for the sin of barratry <note>Barratry is the medieval term for what we might call graft or political corruption—the buying and selling of public offices or judicial favors.</note>. He demonstrates, therefore, that in this ditch there is a lake of pitch which continually boils: and into it the barrators are plunged. This penalty is certainly appropriate to the sin. And first, it should be noted that barratry is the selling or buying of that which should be done by virtue of one's office without a price; thus, justice is sold just as much as injustice. For that which we ought to do freely and without charge, we do for a price. And if someone deserves to obtain something because they ask justly, we nonetheless do not grant it to them unless they buy it; and similarly, we absolve those who deserve to be punished. Therefore, they boil in the pitch. Just as pitch is black and dark, so is the reputation of these people blackened and infamous. Thus Solomon here <note>original: "tetigit picem coinquinabitur ab ea"—"He that toucheth pitch shall be defiled with it" (Ecclesiasticus/Sirach 13:1).</note>. Likewise, as pitch is tenacious and sticky, so he who is infected by barratry—which is born of avarice—cannot pull himself away from it. Likewise, as pitch is dark and nothing can be seen within it, so the barrator is covered and hidden; and this vice is committed in secret.

<image-desc>Historiated initial 'C' depicting two figures, Dante and Virgil, standing upon a stone bridge as they observe the dark, boiling pit of the fifth bolgia below.</image-desc>
**C**hus from bridge to bridge, speaking of other things
which my Comedy does not care to sing,
we came; and we were holding the summit when
we stopped to see the other fissure
of Malebolge and the other vain cries:
and I saw it miraculously dark.
As in the Arsenal of the Venetians <note>The Venetian Arsenal was the largest industrial complex in Europe at the time, famous for its efficiency in ship building and repair.</note>
the sticky pitch boils in the winter
to caulk their damaged ships
that cannot sail: and in its place
one builds his ship anew, and another plugs
the ribs of that which made many voyages;
one hammers at the prow, and one at the stern;
others make oars, and some twist the ropes;
some patch the foresail and the mainsail <term>antimone: an archaic term for a specific sail, likely the mizzensail or a staysail.</term>;
so, not by fire, but by divine art,
a thick pitch boiled down there
which glued the bank on every side.

<column-break/>

**THUS** From bridge to bridge: that is, from the bridge of the fourth ditch to that of the fifth. **SPEAKING OF OTHER THINGS** which my comedy does not care to sing. As if to say: we reasoned about many other things pertaining to divination which I have not written in this book. And certainly, beyond the principal types of divination that have some shadow of science, there are many that are so old-womanish and childish—through which simple women believe they can know the future—that they are so ridiculous a learned man is ashamed to write them down. **WE WERE HOLDING THE SUMMIT**: that is, the top of the bridge, which is the midpoint from which one could best see the whole valley of the fifth ditch. **WE STOPPED TO SEE THE OTHER FISSURE**: that is, the other valley, which was like a crack between those rocks. **VAIN CRIES**: because they bear no fruit and are of no help. **AND I SAW IT**: that is, I saw that which was

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the beginning of Canto XXI of the Inferno. The previous page established the setting of the fifth ditch (the boiling pitch) and defined the sin of barratry as political corruption and the sale of justice. This page continues the specific textual analysis of Dante's metaphors, particularly the famous comparison to the Venetian Arsenal.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>INFERNO</header>

**WONDERFULLY DARK:** <note>original: "MIRABILMENTE OBSCVRA"</note> That is, much darker than the others for the reason stated above. For both the judge or official who sells, and similarly the one who buys, strive as much as they can to hide it; and there is nothing done more secretly, because it results in infamy for both parties. And it is certainly a thing entirely opposed to humanity, because from this vice arises the ruin of kingdoms and republics. From it, discord is born in both public and private life. Therefore, with the highest detestation of such a horrendous vice, Virgil cries out: **"This man sold his country for gold and imposed a powerful lord upon it; for a price, he made and unmade laws."** <note>original: "Vendidit hic auro patriam dominumque potentem Imposuit pretioque leges fixit atque refixit." Aeneid VI.621-622.</note> **AS IN THE ARSENAL.** The pitch boiled there no differently than it boils in the Arsenal of Venice when they wish to use it to caulk their ships. **WINTER** When they do not sail, so that the ships may be repaired for the summer when they do sail. **AND ONE MAKES** His new ship in that place: that is, in exchange for the old. **AND OTHERS** Twists the rigging: that is, makes ropes which are made by winding and twisting hemp. **AND WHO PATCHES** The foresail and who the mainsail. There are three sails on a ship: the largest is the mainsail <term>Artimone</term>, the smallest is the foresail <term>Terzeruolo</term>, and one in the middle of the two which is called the mizzen <term>Mezana</term>. **SO, NOT BY FIRE** But by divine art: that is, by divine order. **THAT GUMMED** The bank on every side: The literal meaning is clear. But allegorically, to "gum" the bank on every side signifies that just as one who looks upon offices and judgments is gummed, so too is the buyer stuck—that is, seized by avarice. Therefore, the courts of republics and princes, and especially the Roman court, are an arsenal where in the "winter"—that is, in the fluctuations and tumults of men—the pitch boils. That is, avarice, which gums and ignites souls with the greed for possession; because of this, he who has power over magistrates, ranks, judges, and sentences does not contribute or judge without a foul price. From this it happens that the good are oppressed and the wicked are exalted.

I saw it well, but saw nothing in it
save for the bubbles that the boiling raised,
and saw it all swell up and sink back down.
While I was gazing fixedly down there,
my leader, saying, "Watch out! Watch out!"
pulled me toward him from where I stood.
Then I turned round like one who is delayed
in seeing what he must needs flee from,
and whom a sudden fear unnerves:
So that for all his fleeing he does not delay his departure,
and I saw behind us a black devil
come running up along the crag.
Ah, how fierce he was in his aspect!
And how bitter he seemed to me in his action,
with his wings open and light upon his feet!
His shoulder, which was sharp and high,
was loaded with a sinner by both haunches,
and he held him fast by the tendon of his foot.

<column-break/>

**I saw it:** because pitch is a dense substance, one cannot see the things plunged into it as one can in water. Thus, he did not see into the pitch. **SAVE FOR THE BUBBLES:** that is, nothing other than the bubbles; this is a way of speaking more characteristic of the Lombard dialect than the Tuscan. For we say, "I saw nothing in it except the bubbles," but the Lombard says, "But for the bubbles." And he calls "bubbles" that swelling made by water when it boils. **AND SWELL ALL OVER:** When water boils, because it is a thinner substance, it does not swell equally everywhere. But pitch, because it is a denser substance, swells all over, and then the whole mass falls back, which he calls "sinking back down" <note>original: "rifedere compressa"</note>. This vice is seen because it swells everything up and generates indignation in everyone. But one does not see who is boiling inside for the reason already stated. **WHILE I WAS THERE BELOW** That is, while I was occupied looking down from the bridge, a devil came running to throw someone from the banks where I was standing to watch; and he would have struck me if Virgil had not pulled me to himself, just as often happens when someone would be hit by a running horse if another person who saw it first did not pull him away. And this allegorically signifies that in contemplating a vice, one's sensuality would be struck and pushed into that vice by some impulse born from the pleasure of that vice, which occupies a man before he notices it, unless provident and cautious Reason pulled Sensuality back to itself and defended it. **THEN I TURNED.** He narrates what commonly tends to happen: that when we are frightened by a sudden fear, in our haste to flee, we do not look at what scares us. But in seeking to flee, the fear robs us of our strength.

---

**A DEVIL:** He uses the devil to represent temptation. He makes him black either because temptation is harmful—and in Latin "black" <note>original: "niger"</note> is used for "harmful"—or because temptation is born of ignorance. For he who has perfect knowledge of a thing cannot be deceived by it. Or "black" means "vicious." Whence: **"This man is black [of heart]; of him, O Roman, beware."** <note>original: "Hic niger est hunc tu romane caueto." Horace, Satires I.4.85.</note> He describes this devil as being fierce and bitter because nothing is more cruel or more bitter than temptation. For when an unrestrained greed rises in our soul, its appearance terrifies us in such a way that we do not manage to resist. Furthermore, he makes him extremely fast, both in running and flying, because nothing is faster than the greed born of temptation; for in it there is no mature consideration, nor long consultation, nor well-examined counsel by which we might discern what should or should not be done. Instead, we use inconsiderate and reckless speed, in which there can be no true knowledge.

<summary>This page explains the metaphor of the Venetian Arsenal to describe the sticky, hidden nature of political corruption (barratry). It provides an allegorical interpretation of the "black devil" as a representation of swift, blinding temptation that can only be countered by Reason.</summary>

From our bridge, he called: "O Evil-claws, <note>original: "malebranche"</note>
behold one of the Elders of Saint Zita!
Thrust him beneath, while I return for more
To that city which is so well supplied with them:
every man there is a barrater <term>barrattier: a corrupt official who sells justice or offices for profit</term>, except for Bonturo;
there, for money, 'No' is turned into 'Yes'."
He flung him down: and back over the hard rock
he turned: and never was a mastiff loosed
with such haste to pursue a thief.

That wretch sank down and then rose up again,
but the demons, who were sheltered by the bridge,
cried out: "The Holy Face <note>original: "fancto uolto" — a famous wooden crucifix and relic in Lucca</note> has no place here!
Here one swims differently than in the Serchio <note>a river in Lucca</note>;
therefore, if you do not want our claws,
do not rise above the pitch."
Then they bit him with more than a hundred hooks,
saying: "It is best for you to dance under cover here,
so that, if you can, you may grab your bribes in secret."
Not otherwise do cooks make their scullions
poke the meat into the center of the cauldron
with hooks, so that it does not float.
My good master said to me: "So that it does not appear
that you are here, crouch down
behind a rock that offers some screen.
And whatever offense may be offered to me,
fear not: for I have these matters settled,
and I have been in such a fray before."
Then he passed beyond the head of the bridge,
and when he reached the sixth bank,
he had need of a steady brow.

<column-break/>

This demonstrates the haste of the demon, who did not wish to linger after throwing that soul in. Instead, he called his companions, who are collectively called **Evil-claws** <note>original: "malebranche"</note>; this name is fitting for barraters because they have lion-like claws to snatch money. **ELDERS** <note>original: "Anziani"</note> are the primary magistrates of Lucca, just as the Priors are in Florence. And it is noted in this place that in Lucca, magistracies and honors were sold; thus, those honored there were not the most virtuous, but those who could spend the most.

**OF SAINT ZITA**: Named thus for the saint for whom they have great devotion. She was a woman of holy habits, and in life and death she performed miracles. Francesco da Buti believes that this man, whom the poet does not name, was Martino Bottaio, who died while serving as an Elder. In those times, he was a party leader in Lucca who led half the people, while **BONTURO DATI** led the other half. It is said that when he was an ambassador to Pope Boniface, the Pope, in the middle of speaking, grabbed his arm (as one does to show someone they are being too malicious) and said, laughing: "Ambassador, you are shaking half of Lucca."

**EXCEPT FOR BONTURO**: This is a rhetorical device called irony, where we say one thing but mean the opposite. Just as when one says "Rejoice, Florence, since you are so great." Therefore, the words sound as if everyone in Lucca is a barrater except Bonturo; but he means that Bonturo is the greatest barrater of them all.

He follows by saying that there **FOR MONEY**, "No" is turned into "Yes" <note>original: "fi fa ita"</note>: that is, they ensure that even if one is not worthy of honors and magistracies, they are nonetheless granted for money as if the person were worthy.

**HE FLUNG HIM DOWN**: This shows with what speed the soul was thrown down as the demon returned to Lucca. He uses a very fitting comparison. Princes and great masters often keep mastiffs trained to bite those who arrive and are not familiar with the house; these are kept tied up, so that when they are loosed, they are even more eager to run. Thus, a mastiff loosed by its master does not run as hard after a thief as that demon did.

**N**arrates what happened to the one who was submerged, who, when he rose back up (as one does when going to the bottom), the demons under the bridge mocked him, saying: "Your **HOLY FACE** has no place here." That is, he will not be allowed to stay out of the pitch. At the same time, this alludes to the Lucchese, who venerate the Holy Face and trust in its help when they invoke it. The demons are essentially saying: "The Holy Face in which you trust has no power here." In these words, the poet signifies that in Hell, no saint or prayer can help anyone.

**HERE ONE SWIMS DIFFERENTLY** than in the Serchio. You Lucchese are accustomed to swimming for pleasure in the **SERCHIO** (the river near you), keeping your heads out. But here you must stay beneath. The Serchio is a river near Lucca which the Latins called **Auferis**. Regarding the **HOLY FACE**, Benvenuto da Imola relates having read that Nicodemus, a disciple of Christ, had a life-like portrait of Christ's face made. At his death, he left it to Isaac, who kept it hidden for fear of the Jews. It remained with his descendants until it came into the hands of a very Christian man named Seleucus in Jerusalem. In those times, a holy bishop named Gualfredo went to the Sepulcher, and through a revelation in a dream, he learned where this Holy Face was. With great skill and prayers, he obtained it from Seleucus and carried it to the city of Jaffa. There, by divine grace, a beautifully adorned ship appeared which, without the help of sails or oars, steered itself into the port of Luni...

<summary>This page describes the arrival of a corrupt Lucchese magistrate in the fifth ditch of Hell, where he is mocked by the Malebranche demons and poked with hooks. The commentary identifies the historical figures involved and explains the local Lucchese references to Saint Zita, the river Serchio, and the Holy Face relic.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the fifth ditch of the Eighth Circle, focusing on the arrival of the demons and Virgil’s negotiation with their leader, Malacoda. It interprets the scene both historically (referencing Lucca’s religious relics) and allegorically (Reason vs. Temptation).</meta>

<page-num>XX</page-num>
# INFERNO

Because of this miracle, being amazed, the citizens of Lucca wanted to board the ship: but they could never touch it until the Bishop of Lucca, named Giovanni, arrived. With great veneration, he carried this **Holy Face** <note>original: "uolto" — refers to the *Volto Santo di Lucca*, an ancient cedar-wood crucifix believed to have been carved by Nicodemus</note> into Lucca, and they honorably placed it in the church of San Martino; where, according to the Lucchesi, it has performed many miracles. **SO THAT IF YOU CAN, GRAB YOUR BRIBES IN SECRET** <note>original: "SI CHE SE PVOI Copertamente acciaffi"</note>: that is, to snatch and hook; this denotes that the barrater <term>barrattier: a corrupt official who profits from their office</term> steals the money of others in hiding. 

Later, the poet imagines that Virgil hid him and went to scout if he could pass. This demonstrates that one must contemplate this vice with great caution. It often happens that while someone seeks to understand a vice in order to flee from it, the sweetness of money is such that they fall into it. Therefore, it was not good for Virgil to take Dante with him when approaching these demons: that is, the **appetite** <note>Dante represents the human appetite or the senses</note> should not go together with **reason** <note>Virgil represents human reason</note>. For the traveler would have been overcome by the demons and by temptation. But Virgil, which is higher reason, hid Dante—the sensitive part—and revealed himself. 

When he had bargained with the demons and brought them to his will, he then called Dante to him. This is because reason first considers and recognizes the ugliness and the damnation found in sin. It judges that one must flee from it, and afterwards reveals this to the senses, which, even after the judgment given by reason (and even though the senses agree with it), nevertheless, due to their fragility, doubt that the temptations which yielded to reason might still conquer them. **THE GOOD MASTER**: there is no better master than reason, which does not go to battle unless it first subdues the appetite so that it does not appear to be there. And reason wants the appetite to hide behind a **rock**, which is a hard thing. Certainly, temptation overcomes the appetite easily for no other reason than that the appetite is very effeminate and soft. Therefore, it is necessary that for its screen—that is, for its defense—it takes on hardness. **THAT YOU MAY HAVE SOME SCREEN**: meaning, that you may have some defense. **AND FOR ANY OFFENSE THAT MAY BE DONE TO ME, DO NOT COME FORWARD**: an offense is done to higher reason when it cannot quickly understand the truth. But in this case, he does not want the appetite to help it in any way, because it would have the opposite effect. **FOR I HAVE THESE MATTERS SETTLED, AS I HAVE BEEN IN SUCH A FRAY BEFORE**: that is, in such a battle. Not just once, but often and in various matters, the intellect contends with demons—that is, with temptations. Then, having arrived at the end of the bridge where the demons were, it was necessary for him to have a **steadfast brow**: that is, to show boldness of spirit. For the quality of the soul is shown in the face, whether it is constant or fearful.

<column-break/>

With that fury and with that storm
that dogs rush out upon the poor man
who suddenly begs or stops:
They came out from beneath the little bridge:
and turned all their hooks against him:
but he cried: "Let none of you be savage!
Before your hook seizes me,
let one of you step forward to hear me
and then decide if you should hook me."
They all cried out: "Go, Malacoda!"
so one moved forward and the others stood still
and he came to him saying: "What does it profit you?" <note>original: "che tapproda" — an archaic way of asking "what good does this do you?" or "where does this lead you?"</note>

"Do you believe, Malacoda, that you see me
having come here," my master said,
"already safe from all your screens
without divine will and favorable fate?
Let me pass, for it is willed in heaven
that I show another this wild path."
Then his pride was so fallen...

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap G</image-desc>Having reached the demons, Virgil was met by them with the same fury that dogs show against a poor man who stops at a door to ask for alms. In truth, as soon as our intellect turns to the recognition of vice, various temptations attack it. And because the intellect would be confused if it tried to consider them all at once, it rejects all the others and stops with **Malacoda**; whose name can be interpreted as **"Evil End"** <note>original: "captiuo fine"</note>. 

Therefore, when we turn our will to know if a thing is good or bad—even though the natural order of knowledge goes from the cause to the effect—nevertheless, human genius begins from the end (the effect) and returns to the cause. This, then, is the reason why it is enough for the poet to convince Malacoda: that is, to know the effect of the vice. Furthermore, this agrees with the description made of Geryon <note>the monster of fraud from earlier in the poem</note>, who was said to have a scorpion’s tail, which is the worst part. Thus, Virgil first settles matters with Malacoda. Because the human mind, wishing to consider the vice of barratry, begins to recognize it by the "evil end" (Malacoda) that it produces; once this is known, the others stand still. For once the end is known, other things are easily recognized through it.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap E</image-desc>It is the opinion of holy theologians that although we possess **free will**, and God has placed life and death in our hands, nevertheless, without the favor of God, we cannot extricate ourselves from sin. This we have already shown above. Therefore, what Virgil says to Malacoda is the reasoning that the intellect makes within itself against temptation. And having already overcome temptation in the other vices...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s *Inferno*, Canto XXI. The previous page discussed the "Holy Face" of Lucca and the allegory of the barraters (corrupt officials) being plunged into boiling pitch. It established the symbolic roles of Virgil as "Higher Reason" and Dante as the "Sensitive Appetite." This page focuses on the negotiation between Reason and the demons, and the subsequent fear felt by the Appetite.</meta>

<page-num>.XXI.</page-num>
<header>CANTO .XXI.</header>

...who let his hook fall to his feet: and said to the others, "Now, let him not be struck."

...to quiet that one. Therefore, Malacoda <note>A demon whose name translates to "Evil Tail"</note> would not stop annoying us. But when the divine will is in our favor, then we can conquer every temptation. Therefore, Virgil excellently says: **DO YOU BELIEVE**, Malacoda, that you see me come here? As if to say, do you believe I could have proceeded so far forward through Hell, conquering every sin step by step **SAFE FROM** all your screens: that is, defenses and barriers. As if to say, you have so many barriers to defend yourselves so that we do not conquer your temptations, that I would not have been able to come safely this far **WITHOUT DIVINE WILL**: that is, without divine favor. **AND FAVORABLE FATE**: that is, prosperous predestination. And in this sense, he used the word "fate," of which we spoke more extensively before. **LET ME GO**, for it is willed in heaven: which is like saying, it is necessary to let me pass since it is so willed in heaven. That is, because this is God's will, which cannot be resisted. **THAT I**: Virgil means higher reason and intellect. **SHOW** to another—understand this as lower reason and sensuality—**THIS WILD PATH**: <note>original: "questo camino siluestro"</note> the way of vices which are born from matter, which is the body. The philosophers call this matter *hyle* <note>Greek: *ὕλη*, meaning wood or matter</note>, that is, a "forest," as we discussed at length at the beginning of this comedy. Or rather, he calls everyone's path "wild" because living according to vice is not according to the reason by which we are human, but according to the irrational appetite which belongs to the wild beasts that inhabit the forest. **THEN HIS** pride [failed]—that is, his audacity and haughtiness. For diabolical temptation loses all audacity against divine fury. **WHO LET** his hook fall to his feet. This signifies that he set down every offense. **AND SAID TO THE OTHERS**: the demons. **NOW** let him not be struck. Because once the temptation—which consists of the end of the matter—is conquered, the others are easily overcome.

After Virgil had come to an agreement with the demons and had convinced them, he called Dante to himself. And so it happens that once the intellect has achieved true knowledge and convinced the demons—that is, condemned vice and overcome temptation as a wicked thing—it then calls to itself the hidden appetite:

> My leader said to me, "O you who sit
> crouched low among the rocks of the bridge,
> you may now return to me in safety."
> Wherefore I moved and came to him quickly;
> the demons all stepped forward,
> so that I feared they would not keep their pact.
> Thus I once saw the infantry fear,
> who came out of Caprona under treaty,
> seeing themselves among so many enemies.
> I drew close with my whole person
> alongside my leader, and did not turn my eyes
> from their appearance, which was not good.
> And they lowered their hooks: "Do you want me to touch him?"
> one said to the other, "on the rump?"
> and they answered: "Yes, make sure you nick him."
> But that demon who was holding speech
> with my leader turned all quickly
> and said: "Quiet, quiet, Scarmiglione!"

<column-break/>

...favor, he hopes to still be able to do the same in this. Therefore, once we have recognized the thing to be captive to its end, the allure of sin can still act within us, which would pull us back—that is, it excites the appetite to flee from the thing already judged by itself as evil. And the appetite, which is obedient to reason, moves immediately. But it happens that before it joins with reason, the demons frighten it. For the temptations of the flesh and its softness dismay us, showing us how difficult and laborious the path of virtue is. **CROUCHED LOW**: <note>original: "quatto quatto"</note> that is, hidden. We properly say someone is "squatting" <note>original: "quattarsi"</note> when, to avoid being seen, they bend and lower themselves. **RETURN** to me in safety. Because every time the intellect has known the truth of the matter and judged whether it is good or evil, the appetite can safely follow it. Nevertheless, before we make a habit of virtue, the demons often frighten us, as was said. **THUS** I saw: Caprona <note>A castle near Pisa</note> was once a castle of the Pisans on the banks of the Arno; it was taken from the Pisans by the Lucchesi who, allied with the other Guelphs <term>Guelphs and Ghibellines: opposing political factions in medieval Italy favoring the Pope and Holy Roman Emperor respectively</term> of Tuscany, made war against Pisa, the head of the Ghibellines. Later, being besieged by a large army of Pisans, the Lucchese infantry who were on guard, lacking water, surrendered on the condition of their personal safety. And having come out into the field, they were all bound by Count Guido to a single rope so that they would not separate, for if separated, they would have been killed by the peasants;

---

and having been led to the borders of Lucca, they were released. Nevertheless, because while they were passing through the midst of the enemies, everyone shouted "Hang them, hang them!" they were greatly afraid. **I DREW CLOSE** with my whole person alongside my leader: as one does who, fearing, has trust in another; for he draws close to him and watches the thing he fears. **AND they lowered their hooks**: Those demons lowered their hooks as one does who wants to snag something; and one said, "Do you want me to grab him with the hook on his rump?" and others answered yes. **BUT THAT** demon who was holding speech: that is, the discussion, turned all quickly to the one who wanted to strike, who was named Scarmiglione <note>A demon name suggesting "disheveler" or "troublemaker"</note>; and he commanded him to be still. And this is true. Because...

<page-num>LXX.</page-num>
<header>INFERNO</header>

...because every time the intellect has recognized the malice of the end, it easily despises all other temptations: and this knowledge refutes them.

**N**on-departure of Malacoda from the nature of the fraudulent: which is to start from the truth to gain the trust of those who hear, and then mix the false with the truth to deceive. It was then true, according to Dante's fiction, that the bridge of the sixth ditch <note>bolgia</note> was broken and fallen to the bottom. But it was not true that in this ditch—

<note>Translation of the verse: Then he said to us: "To go further along this ridge will not be possible, because the sixth arch lies all broken at the bottom. And if going forward pleases you more, go up along this cavernous path; nearby is another ridge that provides a way. Yesterday, five hours later than this hour, one thousand two hundred and sixty-six years were completed since the path here was broken. I am sending some of my own that way to see if anyone is airing themselves out; go with them, for they will not be wicked."</note>

<note>Translation of the verse: "Step forward, Alichino and Calcabrina," he began to say, "and you, Cagnazzo; and Barbariccia, lead the ten. Libicocco, come forward, and Draghignazzo, Ciriatto with the tusks, and Graffiacane, and Farfarello, and Rubicante the mad. Search around the boiling pitch; let these [the poets] be safe until the other crag which goes all whole above the dens."</note>

<column-break/>

—there remained any whole cavern that provided a path. Because the poet feigns that during the Passion of Christ all the arches of this ditch, where hypocrisy is punished, were broken, meaning by this that at that time the Synagogue of the Jews was dispersed, and the fraud of the hypocrisy of the priests was broken. Therefore, all the arches of the sixth ditch were broken. But Malacoda confesses what he cannot deny, but about the others, he lies. Hence the author warns us that we must not believe the devil even if we realize he tells the truth in some part, because he never tells it without mixing in falsehood. Furthermore, he expressed here the fallacy of the barrater <note>term: *barattiere*, a corrupt official who sells public offices or favors</note>: who, to entice you to give him a loan quickly, shows paths to conduct his cause which are not in the nature of things <note>original: "non sono in rerum natura"</note>. **YESTERDAY FIVE HOURS LATER THAN THIS HOUR.** Dante wants to show that he found himself in Hell in the year 1300, calculating the years from the Incarnation of Christ. If, then, on the day of the Passion at the sixth hour the arches were broken by the earthquake, and on the day that Dante found himself there, which was the first hour of Holy Saturday, it made 1266 [years since the death of Christ]. It follows that it was in the year 1300. For we must add thirty-three years that Christ had lived, and one year more because he had been for nine months in the womb of his mother. Therefore, adding thirty-four years to 1266, it will be 1300. Dante lived fifty-six years in his life and died in 1321, according to what appears in Ravenna on his tomb. And taking twenty-one from fifty-six, thirty-five remain; and that many he happened to have in 1300, when he feigns having had this vision. And therefore he said, "In the middle of the journey of our life," because the middle of seventy—which is the common life of man—is thirty-five. Although in that place [the beginning of Canto I], we gave it a very appropriate allegorical sense, if I am not much mistaken. And why does he say "yesterday five hours later than this hour"? It shows that just as at the sixth hour of Good Friday the monuments were opened and the veil of the temple was divided, so these circles were broken. And because when he spoke with Malacoda it was the first hour of Holy Saturday, therefore, referring to the sixth hour of Friday, he said: "Yesterday five hours more than this hour," that is, this first hour of Holy Saturday. And he adds that he sends his own to spy if any sinner "airs himself out" <note>original: "si fciorina"</note>: that is, comes out of the pitch. And these he says "will not be wicked": that is, they will be useful to show them the way.

¶ These are the names of the ten demons whom Malacoda sends as an escort. And I believe that through these the poet wants to express various affects, operations, and effects of the barraters. **ALICHINO** is the inclination to such vice, because he inclines others <note>original: "Quia altos inclinat"</note>. After the inclination follows the corruption of the soul when it has already made the purpose to follow the sin, called **Calcabrina**: that is, "trampling the frost" <note>original: "calcante la brinata"</note>, which in sacred letters signifies divine grace. The third is malediction [the curse], into which the sinner runs once he has driven divine grace from himself: and he is called **Cagnazzo**, as if a "captive dog" and "biting." The fourth is the astuteness that hides this vice for the time being, called **Barbariccia**: that is, "curly beard," because according to physiognomy, a frizzy and curly beard demonstrates fraudulence. The fifth is the burning desire to bring barratry to perfection once he has received the reward, and he is called **Libicocco**: as if "burning lust" <note>original: "libidine cocente"</note>, that is, unbridled and burning desire. The sixth is the infection of the vice, which with its worst poison pollutes and stains others, called **Draghignazzo** from the poison of the dragon. The seventh is the offense that is done to one's neighbor, which the barrater lances and tears like a wild boar...

...he lacerates them with his tusk: And therefore he calls him tusked Ciriatto: because *cyro* <note>original: "cyro"</note>—not only in our local rustic language but also in the Greek language—signifies "pig" <note>Landino is likely referencing the Greek *choiros* (pig)</note>. ### CANTO XXII OF THE FIRST POEM BY DANTE

<image-desc>A large decorative drop-cap letter 'I' featuring foliage and possibly a figure inside a square frame.</image-desc>
I have seen horsemen moving camp,
And beginning the skirmish, and making their muster,
And sometimes retreating for their escape;
Scouts I saw across your land,
O Aretines <note>People of Arezzo, frequent enemies of Dante's Florence</note>, and I saw raiding parties go out,
The clashing of tournaments and the running of jousts;
Sometimes with trumpets and sometimes with bells,
With drums and with signals from castles,
And with things of our own and with foreign ones:

<column-break/>

**I**t is the nature of the tempting demon to always frighten the senses in the end: just as, conversely, the angel always comforts in the end. Therefore Dante is frightened by the signals of the demons because they gnash their teeth like dogs greedy to bite: and they threaten by moving their eyebrows. But superior reason <note>representing Virgil</note> comforts him so that he does not fear, asserting that such signals are made for those damned for their vice. BUT FIRST EACH ONE. with their tongue held tight. This passage seems to many to lack any dignity or propriety: but certainly the poet wanted to demonstrate how much these <term>barraters</term> <note>corrupt officials</note>, once they have cheated someone, mock and deride them. To press the tongue between the teeth signifies making such a noise with the mouth as the wind makes when it exits from the posterior parts. This is what impudent buffoons do when they mock someone.

**O**ne and the same <term>bolgia</term> <note>a "ditch" or "pouch" in the eighth circle of Hell</note> is still being discussed, and the same sin is punished. But in the previous chapter he placed those <term>barraters</term> who sold their republic. And in this twenty-second Canto, he places those who, having been placed in a good position by some lord, sold the grace of that lord. Continuing then, he describes the form of the punishment of these souls submerged in the pitch. Then he makes special mention of one: and in the third part he induces him to reveal the others: and in the last he narrates the cunning that such a spirit used in deceiving [the demons].

<summary>This page concludes the commentary on Canto XXI, explaining the names and behaviors of the demons, before transitioning into Canto XXII. Landino justifies Dante's use of vulgar imagery as a reflection of the low character of the barraters.</summary>

<header>.XX. HELL</header>

Nor yet with such a strange wind-instrument <note>original: "cemamella" — a folk instrument, here used euphemistically for the demon's signal</note>
have I seen horsemen move, or infantry,
nor ship by sign of land or of castles.

Through this transition, the poet shows that although we should always flee the comfort and company of the wicked <note>original: "captiui"</note>, nonetheless sometimes either the place, the time, or some other cause leads us to associate with them. Therefore, "in the tavern with gluttons" <note>original: "in tauerna co ghiottoni"</note> should be understood as being there not out of greed, because it is never 

We went along with the ten demons;
ah, fierce company! But in church
with saints, and in the tavern with gluttons.
Still upon the pitch was my attention,
to see every aspect of the trench
and of the people who were burned within.
As dolphins when they make a sign
to sailors with the arching of their backs,
that they might strive to save their vessel,
So at times, to alleviate the pain,
some sinner would show his back
and hide it in less time than lightning flashes.

<column-break/>

all the demons. **I HAVE SEEN.** He shows that he has seen a field of armed men depart. Which requires supreme prudence and caution, because it greatly contributes to safety and victory to well-place and move the camps; a virtue which they say 

permissible to associate with the vicious to commit vice. But one may do so to take necessary food, and thus it is here. For since Dante was in Hell and had need of a guide, it was necessary that he follow the demons. Allegorically, wanting to know the malice and malignity of such vice, it was necessary that he have knowledge of the things compressed under the names of the ten demons; and for this reason, he follows them. **STILL UPON THE PITCH was my attention.** Dante had his "intention," that is, his attention, fixed upon the pitch to see some of the sinners submerged, because the lower reason seeks the knowledge of particulars and not of universals. **AS DOLPHINS.** Just as sometimes dolphins in the sea come so far to the surface that they show their backs, which is a sign that a storm is soon to rise, whereby sailors by 

---

was supreme in Pyrrhus, King of the Epirotes <note>original: "pyrro re de glepyroti"</note>. **AND BEGINNING THE SKIRMISH** <note>original: "stormo"</note>, that is, battle. Properly, a "skirmish" is a multitude of fighting armed people, perhaps named from the Latin word *turma* <note>meaning a troop or squadron</note>. Or truly it is an onomatopoeia, that is, a name taken from the noise and clatter which is heard in fighting. **AND MAKING THEIR MUSTER** and sometimes departing for their escape. The meaning is: I have seen the signal given to soldiers, either when they move the camp, or when they fight, or when they make their show, or when they flee; but not with such a sound. **SCOUTS I Saw.** Here, according to some, he touches upon the expulsion of the Ghibellines from Florence who took Arezzo. But it is difficult, in so many and so frequent changes of those times in the city of Arezzo—through which it was almost desolated—to understand which one he describes at present. **RAIDS** <note>original: "GVALDANE"</note>: Properly the ancients called "raids" the cavalry maneuvers that one city made on the territory of another to lay waste to it and lead away plunder. And these are all things of war and are done in time of war between one enemy and another. But tournaments and jousts are military exercises done for festivals and games, and to give delight to the people. A tournament is when squads go against one another and represent a kind of battle. A joust is when one goes against another man-to-man and represents a singular battle. **With signals from castles** which are made by day with smoke and by night with fire. But I never saw any move **WITH SUCH A STRANGE WIND-INSTRUMENT**, that is, sound, putting the species for the genus. **NOR SHIP BY Sign of land or of castles.** Sailors, when they can see land—that is, some promontory—navigate according to that; and when they cannot see land, they follow the North Star <note>original: "tramontana"</note>.

---

such a sign immediately prepare for escape. Thus those sinners, to alleviate the pain, sometimes drew their backs out of the pitch. But for fear of the demons' hooks, they put them back under in less space than a lightning flash. The dolphin, above all other fish, delights in the sight of man and loves him much, which is known as writers show in many cases, but most clearly in the story of Arion. Arion of Methymna, a city in Lesbos, was a most skilled musician, and by this art was very acceptable to Periander, King of Corinth. But greedy to see the world and to spread his fame (not without profit), he sailed to Sicily and from there to Italy, where with his craft he accumulated great wealth. After some time, desiring to return to Periander, he boarded a ship of certain Corinthians. These men, moved by avarice and foreign to all humanity, agreed to throw Arion into the sea and take his money. Hearing this, the musician first turned to prayers and tried to buy back his life. Then, seeing that he prayed in vain, he asked for time before they threw him in to sing with his lyre <note>original: "cythera"</note>, dressed and adorned in the most precious clothes and jewels he had. It was granted to him; he sang upon the prow, and after the song, he threw himself into the sea. Immediately received by a dolphin, he was carried safely as far as the island of Taenarum <note>original: "Tenaro"</note>. From there he went to Corinth, and Periander summoned those who had wanted to sink him in the sea. They, stupefied by the unexpected presence of Arion, could not deny it. Herodotus affirms that in Taenarum, where the dolphin landed him, there was a bronze statue of him placed upon the dolphin. Pliny also writes that...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto XXII of the *Inferno*. The previous page introduced the comparison between the sinners in the boiling pitch and dolphins surfacing before a storm. This page expands on that natural history with a popular medieval anecdote about dolphins before returning to the analysis of Dante’s verses regarding the "frogs" (the barrators) and their capture by the demons.</meta>

<page-num>XXII</page-num>
<header>CANTO XXII</header>

...a dolphin in the gulf of Baia <note>A Roman resort city on the coast of Campania, famous in antiquity for its thermal springs.</note> became so tame with a boy, who every day offered him bread, that finally at whatever hour the boy called him, he would come and carry him across the narrow gulf from Baia to Pozzuoli. And after several years, the boy having died, the dolphin remained mournful while waiting for him, showing no small signs of grief; and finally, when the boy did not appear, he died of sorrow. It would be very tedious to report many other similar things written by Theophrastus, Aristotle, and other writers. The dolphin is of such speed that it surpasses not only other fish in running, but even birds and the arrow. Nor could any fish escape before it, were it not that the dolphin cannot seize prey except when lying on its back. This is because its mouth is far from its snout and almost in the middle of its belly. And because it breathes like the whale and the "sea-old-man" <note>original: "vecchio marino" — likely referring to a seal or sea calf</note>, it is necessary that it return to the surface with incredible velocity from the depths where it follows its prey. It gives birth to young and not eggs, and nourishes them with milk. It carries its small ones on its back, and accompanies and escorts the youths. They live thirty years. Their voice is similar to a human lament. They love man greatly and delight much in music. If one dies, the others lead it out of the water. I have written these few things out of many, invited rather by the noble nature of the animal than because I judged it necessary in this place. Now I return to the text.

Here no other allegory occurs; but to adorn the passage, he only describes the place of punishment and sets down the simile of the frogs. **I SAW AND ALSO:** that is, "even now." **THE HEART** where the seat of thought is. That is: I saw it then, and even now, my mind passing back over it, it **STRIKES MY HEART WITH HORROR—**

<column-break/>

And as at the edge of a ditch’s water
the frogs stand with their muzzles out
so that they hide their feet and their bulk,
So on every side stood the sinners;
but as Barbariccia <note>The leader of this troop of demons; his name means "Curly-beard."</note> approached,
they ducked back beneath the boiling.
I saw—and even now my heart shudders—
one waiting just as it happens
when one frog stays and the other scurries;
And Graffiacane <note>The demon "Dog-scratcher."</note>, who was most directly opposite,
hooked his pitch-matted hair
and hauled him up, so that he seemed to me an otter.

I already knew the names of every one of them,
for I noted them when they were chosen,
and after they called each other, I listened how.
"O Rubicante <note>The demon "Red-face."</note>, see that you set
your claws upon him so that you flay him!"
the accursed ones all cried out together.
And I: "My Master, see if you can
find out who that unfortunate is,
fallen into the hands of his adversaries."
My leader drew close to his side,
asked him where he was from, and he replied:
"I was born in the Kingdom of Navarre;
My mother placed me as a servant to a lord,
for she had conceived me by a ribald..."

<column-break/>

**STRIKES WITH HORROR:** <note>original: "MENACAPRICCIA"</note> that is, it gives me a fright. *Capriccio* in the Florentine dialect signifies what the Latins call *horror*, which is when the hairs bristle; and this happens due to cold, and because in fear the body remains cold. This is because the blood, in which heat consists, runs to the heart and abandons the other members; therefore *capriccio* is born there. And the word *capriccio* is said as if it were *capo arriccio* <note>Literal translation: "head-bristle."</note> because the hairs on the head bristle. And we say *arricciare* [to bristle] from that animal which we call *riccio* <note>The hedgehog.</note>, that is, spiny; because when it fears, it closes itself up, and in closing, it straightens its spines. **ONE WAITING.** I saw that of all those who held their muzzles out of the pitch, one alone did not flee at the coming of the demons, and all the others fled; just as sometimes happens when someone comes to a ditch where there are frogs with their muzzles out: one stays still and the other **SCURRIES**: that is, flees away. Wherefore Graffiacane hooked him: that is, he took him with the *roncigli*, which are hooks, and pulled him out like a fisherman pulls an otter out of the water, having caught it with a hook or some other thing. The otter is an animal not much smaller than a fox, but long and with black fur; it has a pointed snout and feeds on fish which it catches by going under the water; and it especially goes for those it sees in nets, and it willingly gnaws and tears the nets. In Latin it is called *lutra*.

So that the reader does not wonder how he knows the names of all ten demons, he shows that he noted them when they were chosen, and afterward when they called one another. **MY LEADER DREW CLOSE TO HIS SIDE.** Because the narration of the souls whom the author finds in Hell would bring tedium and disgust if it always kept to one mode, he wonderfully varies and shows them in different ways, as anyone who reads diligently can note. **I WAS BORN IN THE Kingdom of Navarre.** This man was Ciampolo <note>Also known as Zampolo. Historical records of him are scarce outside of Dante's commentary tradition.</note>, or rather Giampolo, the son of a noblewoman. But his father, having consumed his patrimony, left him poor. Therefore his mother placed him with a baron of King Thibault of Navarre <note>Thibault II of Navarre (1239–1270).</note>. And such was his industry that in the course of time he became so accepted by Thibault, a most just king, that the king committed every great business to him. But he did not know how to restrain his greed. And because...

With him frequents Lord Michele Zanche

their tongues never feel weary."

<column-break/>

As Terence says: "We all become worse through license" <note>original: "Omnes sumus deteriores licentia" — a quote from the Roman playwright Terence suggesting that unchecked freedom leads to corruption.</note>; I became a supreme barrator. **CIRRIATTO, FROM WHOSE MOUTH CAME OUT.** These verses are quite clear in themselves: and I judge this passage to be more for the ornament of the poem than for allegory. Nonetheless, it expresses well the nature of these demons in their actions according to the interpretation already given above. **THE LEADER THEN: NOW TELL OF THE OTHER CULPRITS.** Virgil asks the Navarrese if any "Latin" is among these barrators; and he responds that a short while ago he departed from one of whom more will be said below. Then he writes that Libicocco tore an arm with a hook, and carried off a *lacerto*, which is to say a muscle. By the "arm" we understand the power of action. And it was already said above that by Libicocco we understand the occupation of the work; which occurs when the judge, corrupted by money, is hindered from performing justice. Draghignazzo signifies entanglement and the strangling of affection. For every man by his nature is inclined toward doing justice; but barratry often binds such an affection. This one wanted to strike at the legs, because feet and legs signify human affections. And this was said to signify that it often happens that a judge has a good inclination toward justice, and it is not extinguished in him; but avarice makes him err, and it is almost against his own will. **WHEN THEY WERE A LITTLE PACIFIED.** To clarify this text, we note that the island of Sardinia is called *Sandalioti* by Timaeus, because it has the shape of footwear which we call a *pianella* <note>A type of slipper or sandal.</note>. It is near Corsica, about eight miles away. This island, being in the power of the African Saracens, was acquired in the year 1116 by the Pisans; and in the same year it was lost, recovered by Musetto, King of Africa. And the following year, the Pisans <note>The OCR reads 'epifani', likely a transcription error for 'Pisani'.</note>, allied with the Genoese, acquired it again, having agreed between them that every bit of plunder should go to the Genoese, and the lordship would remain with the Pisans. These men divided the island into four parts, and these they called the four "Judicates," because over each they placed a "judge" <term>Giudice: the title for the local rulers of Sardinia during the Middle Ages</term> who would rule it as its lord. The first Judicate was called Logodoro, meaning "Place of Gold," because it was the richest part of the island. Others called it the Judicate of the Towers. The second, Calari, from Cagliari, a noble and ancient city. The third, Gallura, because in the beginning it was given to certain Pisan counts who carried the rooster <note>Italian: "gallo"</note> as their emblem. The fourth, Arborea. The Lord of the Judicate of Gallura was once Nino, a citizen driven out of Pisa, as we shall say more clearly in the eighth

---

chapter of the Purgatorio <note>Referring to Nino Visconti, whom Dante meets in Purgatory.</note>. And Friar Gomita was his enemy, a very cunning man and a supreme barrator, who had so occupied the mind of his lord that the lord would not give credit to those who accused him of his vices. Nonetheless, in the end, because he released certain enemies of Nino who had fallen into his hands in exchange for money, he was hanged by him. He calls him, therefore, Friar Gomita of Gallura, and a "vessel," as if a receptacle of every fraud and every generation of deceit. **WHO HAD THE ENEMIES OF HIS LORD.** Lord, meaning his master. Thus in Sardinia, the master is called *domino*. **AND LET THEM GO SMOOTHLY**, that is, in peace. **WITH HIM FREQUENTS LORD MICHELE ZANCHE.** Frederick II had a natural son named Enzio, to whom he gave the Judicate of Logodoro. This man finally died in prison in Bologna. Whereupon Michele Zanche, his seneschal <note>A senior official or steward in a noble household.</note>, through his frauds and barratry, persuaded Enzio’s mother—who remained the lady of the Judicate—to take him as her 

<meta>Catchword: husband</meta>
