o. i.

...husband. And in this manner, having become lord, he became related to Sir Branca Doria <note>A Genoese nobleman later placed by Dante in the lowest part of Hell for murdering his father-in-law.</note> by giving him his daughter as a wife, or according to others, by taking Doria's sister.

"As you see that other one who gnashes his teeth,
I would say more, but I fear that he
prepares himself to scratch my itch <note>original: "grattarmi la tigna" — a Florentine proverb meaning to beat someone or cause them trouble.</note>."
The great provost <note>original: "proposto" — here referring to Barbariccia, the leader of the ten demons.</note> turned to Farfarello,
who was rolling his eyes to strike,
and said: "Get back there, you wicked bird!"
"If you wish to either see or hear,"
the frightened one then began again,
"Tuscans or Lombards, I will make them come;
But let the Malebranche stay back a little,
so that they do not fear their vengeance;
and I, sitting in this very spot,
for one that I am, will make seven come
when I whistle, as is our custom
to do whenever someone comes out."

...Tuscans if the demons draw back. And therefore he says let the Malebranche <note>The 'Evil-Claws', the name of the demon troop.</note> of the demons stay back a little, that is, at a distance: and I, by whistling, will make them come out: because thus we are accustomed to call one another. Nor is it without reason that the poet feigns this: because he who commits such wickednesses acts more with signs than with open speech. Furthermore, he feigns that some demon touches him, and some do not, because not all parts of this vice fall upon every barrator <term>barrator: a corrupt official who trades government favors for money</term>.

**E** It is the nature of a dog to discover who is hiding by barking. Therefore, deservedly, he [Cagnazzo] with his words discovers the malice of this man: who, under the pretense of wanting to call the others, said that the demons should distance themselves so they could escape their hands and dive back in. And allegorically it demonstrates that when the corrupter and the corrupted speak together, they often reveal their vices.

Cagnazzo at such a word raised his snout,
shaking his head, and said: "Hear the malice
he has thought of to throw himself down!"
Whereupon he [Ciampolo], who had snares <note>original: "lacciuoli" — tricks or deceits.</note> in great abundance,
replied: "I am indeed too malicious
when I procure a greater sorrow for my own."
Alichino did not hold back, and in opposition
to the others said to him: "If you dive down,
I will not come after you at a gallop,
But I will beat my wings above the pitch;
let the hill be left behind, and let the bank be a shield,
to see if you alone are worth more than us."

...so that they might be torn apart, as he knows the demons take pleasure in; and it is irony, as if he said: "If I were malicious I would not do this." ALICHINO: He did not refrain from speaking, for this character, as said above, represents a sudden inclination of the will. Therefore, he performs his office here by inclining the will of his companions with his speech. AND IN OPPOSITION: As if on the opposite side and facing him. I WILL NOT COME AFTER YOU AT A GALLOP: that is, running. Galloping <note>original: "gualoppare"</note> is between trotting and running. BUT I WILL BEAT MY WINGS ABOVE THE PITCH: that is, I will fly to catch you again. LET THE HILL BE LEFT: as if to say, let us throw ourselves down from the hill. AND LET THE BANK BE A SHIELD: As if a shelter and defense. TO SEE IF YOU ALONE ARE WORTH MORE THAN US: and you will see who can do more, you or we.

<column-break/>

**W**HO GNASHES. Gnash <note>original: "digrignare"</note> means to twist the face in such a way that the mouth opens and shows the teeth. This signifies either grieving within oneself or being angry toward others, or sometimes laughing. BUT I FEAR THAT HE. I fear that he. TO SCRATCH MY ITCH. A Florentine proverb: when we want to signify beating someone, we say "I will scratch his itch." THE GREAT PROVOST Barbariccia. Because he was a decurion <term>decurion: an officer in charge of ten men</term>, he calls him provost because he was set over the others. He turned to Farfarello. WHO WAS ROLLING HIS EYES. We say one "rolls their eyes" <note>original: "stralunare"</note> when they turn them with an evil look upon someone, keeping them very wide and fixed. This signifies wrath and threats. WICKED BIRD: because all the demons are imagined as winged. In short, he says that Farfarello would have struck him if their captain had not forbidden it. And it follows that the Navarrese [Ciampolo], though frightened, promises to make Lombard spirits come out of the pitch; and

RAISED HIS SNOUT. We say "mouth" for a human, "beak" for birds, and "snout" <note>original: "muso"</note> for other animals. Therefore, having figured him above as a dog, he deservedly said "snout." He raised his snout: which is what one does when moving and becoming attentive to what they hear. SHAKING HIS HEAD. This is the act of one who notices the malice of others and wants to show that he is not being deceived; and therefore he says: "Hear the malice he has thought of to throw himself down." WHEREUPON HE WHO HAD SNARES: that is, deceits in abundance. It demonstrates the nature of the fraudulent man: who, seeing that others have become aware of his malice, tries to cover it up with other words, and says that if he is malicious, it is in procuring greater sorrow for his companions. As if he said: "I am trying to make them come out..."

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto XXII of the Inferno. <header>INFERNO</header>

O you who read, you shall hear a new sport:
each one turned his eyes to the other side,
he first who was most reluctant to do so.
The Navarrese well seized his moment;
he planted his feet firmly on the ground, and in an instant
he leaped, and freed himself from their purpose.
At this, each one was stung with guilt,
but he most who was the cause of the failure;
therefore he moved and cried out: "You are caught!"
But it availed little, for wings could not outstrip 
his terror; the sinner went under,
and the demon, flying, turned his breast upward:
Not otherwise does the duck suddenly
dive down when the falcon approaches,
and the falcon returns up, angry and defeated.
Enraged by the taunt, Calcabrina 
flew behind him, eager
that the sinner should escape so he might have a scuffle;
And as the barrator disappeared,
so he turned his claws upon his companion,
and was locked with him above the ditch.
But the other was indeed a seasoned hawk
to claw him back well, and both of them
fell into the middle of the boiling pond.
The heat was an immediate mediator;
but nevertheless, there was no way of rising,
so clogged were their wings.
Barbariccia, grieving with the others,
made four of them fly from the other bank
with all their gaffs; and very quickly,
this way and that, they descended to their posts;
they reached their hooks toward those who were caught,
who were already cooked inside their crusts;
And we left them thus embroiled.

<column-break/>

**H**e makes the listener attentive by promising that he will hear a **NEW** sport: that is, mockery and derision: that is, unusual: because he will hear that the demons, who are more malicious, were deceived by the spirit who ought to have been less malicious. **EACH** of the demons turned their eyes to the other side, ceasing to watch the spirit further. **AND HE FIRST WHO** was most reluctant to do so: that is, Cagnazzo: who showed that he could not be deceived. **THE NAVARRESE.** Ciampolo of Navarre. **SEIZED** well his moment: that is, he chose the occasion and the convenience of the time well, seeing the demons' eyes turned elsewhere, he threw himself into the pitch. Wherefore he planted the soles of his feet on the ground to make a swifter step: and in an instant, he leaped. **AND FREED HIMSELF** from their purpose: that is, from their intention, which was to tear him apart. **AT WHICH** each of the demons was stung with guilt: that is, within himself he judged himself guilty for having used negligence in guarding him. **BUT HE MOST** Alichino more than the others: because with his speech he had given assurance to the others. Wherefore Ciampolo had space to flee. Therefore he was the first to fly after him: but it did not help him: because his wings—that is, his flying—could not outstrip—that is, conquer—**HIS TERROR.** The fear of the spirit. In essence, the fear that the spirit had of the demons made him faster than Alichino’s wings. For as Virgil says, *Fear added wings to the feet* <note>original: "Pedibus timor addidit alas"</note>: and the Florentine proverb says, "Need makes the old woman trot." **THAT ONE.** Ciampolo went under; he dove into the pitch. **AND THE OTHER** Alichino. **TURNED** his breast upward while flying: that is, he flew upwards. And it happened as when the falcon follows the duck, which dives into the water before the falcon reaches it; the falcon, angry and defeated—that is, exhausted from where he swooped to have it—rises up, unable to reach it. And here the poet denotes how great is the cunning of the barrator <term>barrattiero: a corrupt official who profits from public office</term>: who, although he often gives cause for suspicion of committing such fraud, is nonetheless so dexterous in diving into the pitch—that is, he covers it up so skillfully—that he is not caught. **ENRAGED CALCABRINA** at the taunt. When Calcabrina, which signifies "deliberation," joins with Alichino—that is, with the "inclination of the will"—it is inevitable that he falls into the pitch: that is, into the fraud of barratry. He was then eager—that is, enamored, greedy, and desirous—that the spirit should escape so as to have a reason for scuffling with Alichino. And for this reason, as soon as Ciampolo had dived, he clawed him: that is, he took him with his talons, both of them being on their wings above the great ditch. And Alichino clawed him like a seasoned hawk <note>original: "sparuer grifagno" — a technical term for a wild hawk caught after its first molt, known for being fiercer than those raised from the nest.</note>: that is, valiant and bold. They call them nestlings <note>original: "nidiace"</note> when they are taken small in the nest when they cannot yet fly. And branchers <note>original: "ramingho"</note> when they begin to fly and stay on the branches. And "grifagno" after they have molted in the wild. And these last, although they are settled with more difficulty, are nonetheless more spirited in hunting. **AND BOTH** two fell. And here it denotes that when some rich man, capable of buying favors, arrives at court, he often finds several barrators: and each would want to pull him to himself. And finally they contend over him and fall into the pitch: because they are discovered and disgraced. **THE HEAT** was an immediate mediator <note>original: "schermidore" — literally a fencer or defender; here used to mean the heat 'separated' the combatants by forcing them to defend themselves from the pitch.</note>: that is, the heat of the pitch which they felt was an immediate defender because it caused each of them to immediately attend to shielding himself from it. But it helped little because their wings were already so coated in pitch that they could not withdraw. **BARBARICCIA** grieving with the others. Barbariccia grieved for the adverse accident of the two who fell, and with the others, he immediately brought aid and pulled them out of the pitch.

### CANTO XXIII OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE

The song changes along with the punishment. For in this sixth ditch <term>bolgia|A "ditch" or "pocket" in the eighth circle of Hell where specific types of fraud are punished.</term> he treats of hypocrisy and the suffering and torment thereof. But in the beginning, he describes their progress toward this ditch, the pursuit they endured from the demons, and how he was saved by Virgil. **SILENT**: which signifies that each was thinking within himself of their sorrow. **ALONE**: each by himself, which signifies the same thing.

<image-desc>Historiated woodcut initial T at the start of the poem, depicting two figures in a landscape walking together.</image-desc>
Silent, alone, and without company
we went, one before and the other after,
as Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans, known for traveling in pairs and observing silence.</note> walk along the way.
My thought was turned toward Aesop’s fable
by the present brawl,
where he spoke of the frog and the mouse;
For "now" and "this moment" <note>original: "mo et issa." Dante compares two synonyms for "now" from different dialects to emphasize how perfectly the fable matches their current situation.</note> are not more alike
than the one case is to the other, if one couples
the beginning and the end with a focused mind.
And as one thought springs from another,
so from that one another was born,
which made my first fear double.
I thought: "These others, because of us,
are mocked, and with such damage and scorn
as I believe must greatly vex them.
If anger is grafted onto their ill will,
they will come after us more cruelly
than a hound after the hare it snaps at."

<column-break/>

For when we wish to diligently think upon any matter, we separate ourselves from others. Hence the character Simon in the works of Terence <note>Publius Terentius Afer, a Roman playwright.</note> said: <note>original: "Venit meditatus ali- cunde ex solo loco."</note> "He comes, having meditated somewhere in a solitary place," meaning without the company of others. **THE ONE** before: that is, Virgil. **THE OTHER AFTER**: that is, Dante. And by this, he wishes to demonstrate that in the contemplation of difficult things, the lower reason (which deals with particulars) cannot be equal to the superior reason (which has knowledge of universals). And therefore the latter goes ahead as the more worthy thing, and the former follows it. **AS FRIARS** Minor walk along the way: This is a fitting comparison both for the manner of walking and for the silence. For those observing the rule on a journey walk one behind the other in silence and deep thought. They were therefore alone in body, but the mind was accompanied by contemplation and investigation, which proceed better then and more easily find the truth, of which the soul can have no better company. It happens, then, to the learned man that the more his body is unaccompanied, the more his soul is accompanied. For this reason, Scipio Africanus <note>A famous Roman general and statesman.</note> used to say that he was never less alone than when he was alone, nor ever less idle than when he was idle. And Leonardo Aretino <note>Leonardo Bruni, a famous humanist and historian of the 15th century.</note>—a man of most ornate eloquence and wit and well-lettered—when a certain citizen of ours (a man not wicked, but without learning) wished to accompany him, saying, "I do not want you to go so alone," replied: "I would be alone if I were with you." And Seneca in an epistle affirms: "The wise man is never alone." **WAS TURNED TOWARD** the fable of Aesop: Aesop the Phrygian was a Greek poet and wrote <term>apologues|Fables or short allegorical stories intended to convey a moral lesson.</term>, that is, fables, which in themselves contain morality and hidden precepts for living well. One of...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto XXIII of the Inferno. Having introduced the comparison between the demons' brawl and Aesop's fables, the commentator Landino now explains the specific fable of the frog and the mouse, the linguistic nuances of Dante's "now," and the psychological nature of fear.</meta>

# INFERNO

these fables tell that as a mouse was walking through a field, he came upon a ditch full of water; and not daring to cross, a frog offered to carry him across. The frog tied the mouse to himself with the intent of pulling him under the water and drowning him. But to the mouse, he pretended to tie him so that he would not fall. At that time, a kite <note>A type of hawk or bird of prey.</note>, seeing the mouse and desiring to feed on it, swooped down and snatched it. In carrying the mouse away, he also carried away the frog because it was tied to the mouse. And so it happened that the fraud which the frog had manufactured to harm the mouse turned into his own death. Dante, therefore, remembered this fable because it was a similar thing; for just as the frog, believing he could trick the mouse, was himself caught, so it happened to the two demons mentioned above. And he secretly demonstrates that similar things often happen among barrators <note>Corrupt officials who trade public office for money; the specific sinners in this circle.</note>: that while one seeks to trick the other, a third party comes and tricks both the trickster and the tricked.

**IN THE PRESENT** brawl of Alichino and Calcabrina <note>The two demons who fell into the pitch while fighting.</note>. And he follows by saying that there is no greater similarity than between **MO AND ISSA**. For both these words in different parts of Lombardy <note>A region in Northern Italy.</note> signify what we call "now" and "just now." This similarity is between Aesop's fable and the brawl of these demons, comparing the beginning—that is, the cause that moved the frog and that which moved the demon, which in each case was to deceive—**AND THE END**: that is, the effect that followed, which was that each remained deceived.

**WITH THE MIND FIXED**: that is, steady. **AND AS** one thought bursts from another: that is, is born; and this is a metaphor from many flowers, which are not born unless the bud in which they are enclosed bursts open. **THUS** there was born from that: from thinking about their brawl. **ANOTHER** thought, which was that they might wish to take revenge upon us, and for this reason, they might pursue us. **THAT THE FIRST FEAR**: which was when he saw he had to go in their company. Wherefore he said: **O MY MASTER**, what is this I see? I said that without an escort we should go alone. Therefore, this thought doubled my fear. And then he posits that, thinking to himself, he said: "Since these ones have received damage and mockery because of us, they certainly must have conceived anger toward us." And if this particular anger toward us **IS GRAFTED**: that is, is linked and joined with their ill will. For by their nature, they willingly harm every man. Nor can they wish for good, being obstinate in evil. **AND THEY WILL COME** after us more cruel than dogs. For if the dog pursues the hare, it is not for a particular injury received from it, but out of a natural and universal hatred; how much more cruel will these ones be, having both a particular and a universal hatred? "Hare" in Latin is called *lepus*, as if it were *levipes*, "light of foot," because it runs swiftly <note>original: "lepus quasi leuipes"</note>. Archelaus <note>An ancient Greek natural philosopher.</note> writes that each hare has in itself both sexes and that they conceive by themselves. And certainly no other animal except the badger performs "concept upon concept" <note>Superfetation: the ability to conceive a second litter while already pregnant.</note>. For at the same time, it suckles the already born young, and meanwhile has one already covered in fur and perfect, and another not yet furred, and another not yet fully formed. Some believe that in the Alps there is a species of hare that stays under the snow in winter and feeds upon it.

The universal saying is that the imagination makes the event come to pass. This is the opinion of all the greatest philosophers and especially of Aristotle: especially when the soul has a fixed imagination. Therefore, by such imagination, the poet was oppressed by great fear, wherefore his hair stood on end. For such imagination causes fear:

Already I felt all my hair bristle
with fear, and I stood intently looking back,
when I said: "Master, see that you hide
yourself and me quickly; I have fear
of the Malebranche <note>The "Evil Claws," the name of the demons guarding this circle.</note>; we have them already behind us;
I imagine them so that I already feel them."
And he: "If I were a leaded mirror <note>A mirror backed with lead to make it reflective.</note>,
I would not draw your outward image to me
more quickly than I receive the inward one.
Just now your thoughts came among mine
with similar action and with similar face,
so that of both I made a single counsel."

<column-break/>

And because fear constricts the heart, the blood runs entirely to its aid, because in the heart is the fountain of life. Because of this, the exterior limbs remain cold, and the cold constricts the pores; and those constricted pores create the shivering that raises the hair that is within. From this arises the "capriccio" <note>A shivering or bristling of the hair due to fear.</note>. **WHEN I SAID** "Master, if you do not hide": that is, conceal **YOURSELF AND ME**. It is not without reason that Dante shows himself to be the one who goes about conjecturing that the demons—both because they are harmful by nature and because of their particular anger—must strive to harm them. And that Virgil responds to him: and that Dante’s imagination has entered into his own as clearly as a physical image enters a mirror. For the lower reason is that which discourses through particulars. And the higher reason, from these particulars, comes to reach

conclusions. For turning itself to the images of particular things which it finds in the senses, it reduces those to universals. Man has within himself five internal senses: Common Sense, Imaginative, Estimative, Phantasy, and Memory. It is the **Common Sense** to which the external senses refer everything they comprehend. And insofar as it is a sense, it receives the images of things without matter, but only while the matter is present. For example, I see you, and my common sense receives the image of your body without the body being there, yet the body must be present. And insofar as the common sense gives perfection to the sensible operation...

<meta>This page continues the psychological and allegorical analysis of Dante’s fear of the demons in Canto XXIII. Landino is explaining how the human mind processes sensory information—moving from external sight to internal judgment—and how Virgil represents the higher intellect confirming these sensory instincts.</meta>

# CANTO XXIII.
o. iii.

Which the external senses do not do. For although the eye sees and the ear hears, neither the eye notices that it sees, nor the ear that it hears. Only the **common sense** <note>In medieval and Renaissance psychology, the "common sense" (*sensus communis*) was the internal faculty that gathered data from the five external senses to create a unified perception.</note> is that through which we understand what we see and hear. And the same occurs with smell, taste, and touch. Furthermore, regarding the external senses: even when things are present, none receives any "sensible" quality other than its own. Sight receives nothing but colors, and hearing nothing but sounds. But the common sense, from the image of one sense, understands that which belongs to another sense. Therefore, if the visual power represents the yellow color of honey to it, even without the sense of taste, it conceives that it is sweet. But let it suffice to have said these few things out of many concerning the common sense.

After this follows the **imaginative power** <note>The *imaginativa*.</note>, which not only receives the image of the present thing but retains and preserves it after the thing has departed. You saw **Marsilio Ficino** <note>A famous Neoplatonic philosopher and friend of the commentator, Landino.</note> yesterday in the temple; today you do not see him. Nevertheless, his image—because it is reserved in this second sense in the same form in which you saw him—not only keeps his face and features and color within you, but also his gestures and expression. And both of these senses are in the front part and in the first ventricle of the brain. After which is the second ventricle; and at the beginning of this is the third sense, called the **estimative** in other animals, but in man, the **cogitative**. At the end is the fourth, called **phantasia**. In the third and last ventricle is the **memory**.

The estimative has this power: turning itself toward the imaginative and finding there the stored images of things now absent, it draws from them something even more incorporeal than the images themselves, which the philosophers call **intention** <note>Original: *intentione*. In this context, it refers to the perceived "meaning" or quality of a thing, such as "dangerous" or "friendly," which isn't a physical color or shape.</note>. For example, the image of Marsilio is stored in my imagination; in which, although he is absent, I see his person: of what stature, what features, what color. Likewise, I see how he walks, with what gestures he speaks, and similar things. Thus, turning to this image, the estimative draws the "intention" from it: such as whether he is a friend or an enemy, whether he is a citizen or a foreigner, whether he is learned or unlearned. And having drawn this intention, it immediately judges whether one should speak to him or not speak to him, whether to love him or not to love him, and similar things which, as I said, are more incorporeal than the image.

In the fourth place is the **phantasia**, whose faculty is to divide and compose all the images found in the imagination and the intentions found in the cogitative. Because of this, my phantasia can take the image of Mount Morello and that of gold and make a "Golden Mount Morello." It can take the horns of a stag and a horse and form an image of a horse with stag's horns. It can make a city that runs or a river that stands still. But because these judgments made by the estimative and phantasia would perish as soon as they were made, they would not remain in our minds. Therefore, even though today I have made the judgment that **Antonio Canigiani** and **Giovanni Cavalcanti** <note>Prominent Florentine figures known to Landino's audience.</note> are most singular friends and deserve to be loved, it would nevertheless be necessary to redo it every hour if there were no memory to preserve what was already done for us.

Repeating, then, what pertains to the present passage: Dante saw the ten demons. This was the duty of the eye and the common sense. And he not only saw them as present, but their images remained fixed in the imagination, whose duty is to preserve them even in the absence of the thing. Therefore, his cogitative power, turning to the imagination, found these images there no differently than if he saw them in a mirror; and from the images, it extracted the intentions. For just as a dog, seeing its master, draws from that image the "intention" which is another more incorporeal image—and this is benevolence—and seeing a wolf, draws from its image the intention of enmity, and judges that it should welcome the former and bite the latter; so Dante's cogitative power drew from the images of the demons the intentions, which were cruelty, perfidy, malevolence, and the like. For this reason, he judged it useful to flee them. And the imagination was so powerful that it seemed to him he felt them coming.

This judgment is proper to the senses, and because of this, it is not only in man but also in other animals. But it is always regarding particular things, because the sense cannot grasp universals. Thus, Dante—that is, the sensitive part—made this particular judgment: that at this time and in this place, these demons should be fled. Toward which judgment **Virgil**—that is, the **intellect**—turns and approves it because it is true. But he leads it from the particular to the universal, and judges that not only at this time and in this place should these demons be fled, but at every time and in every place, all demons similar to these must be fled. It is therefore most true that reason, infusing itself over the sense, receives the judgment given by it no differently than a mirror receives the image of the body toward which it is turned. And if the judgment is well-given, it immediately approves it. You, then, noting with diligence what we have said about the judgment of sense and reason, will easily understand the text to which I return.

->**WE HAVE THEM ALREADY BEHIND.**<-

Not that he saw them; but his imagination was so powerful that it seemed he saw them and felt them. Whence he says:

->**I IMAGINE THEM SO**<-

That is, so strongly,

->**THAT I ALREADY FEEL THEM.**<-

And this we declared just above.

->**AND THAT ONE**<-

Understand Virgil, replied:

->**IF I WERE OF LEADED GLASS.**<-

That is, if I were a mirror. Which is glass covered on the back with a thin plate of lead, which is attached to the glass with certain liquids and juices of herbs, which few know how to do. It happens, then, that when a body is placed before the glass, because the glass is **diaphanous** <note>Transparent.</note>, it receives the image of such a body into itself. But it does not retain it nor multiply it within itself, because the image passes through it. But finding on the other side of the glass the lead, which is an **opaque** and shadowy body, it cannot pass through; and therefore it remains...

<summary>Landino provides a detailed breakdown of Aristotelian psychology to explain Dante's fear, describing how the mind moves from sensory perception to internal judgment. He concludes by explaining the physics of mirrors to clarify Virgil's metaphor of "leaded glass."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto XXIII. Having discussed the internal senses (common sense and imagination) on the previous page, Landino now explains how Virgil—representing Reason—mirrors Dante’s thoughts and provides a way to escape the pursuing demons.</meta>

# INFERNO
.XXIII.

in the glass, and its rays multiply there and become visible. And in this place, Dante has used **periphrasis** <note>A roundabout way of speaking; a circumlocution.</note>, meaning he has said in many words what he could have said in one: he could have said "mirror," but instead said "leaded glass," which is almost the definition of a mirror. **THE IMAGE FROM WITHOUT**: that is, the bodily image, I would not draw to myself any sooner than I **IMPETRO** <note>original: *impetro*; here interpreted as "capture" or "hold fixedly"</note>: that is, I contain it fixedly. **THE IMAGE WITHIN**: that is, that which you imagine and think. **EVEN NOW**: just lately. **YOUR THOUGHTS HAVE ENTERED AMONG MINE**. Because sense and reason both think upon the same thing. **WITH THE SAME ACT**: that is, fearing as you do. **AND THE SAME FACE**: that is, with the same appearance: because the same thing represents itself to me as it does to you. But I, taking your particular judgment, make it universal, and I judge that such things must always be fled. Nor does reason only judge what the senses do. Rather, it transcends with its power and does what the senses could not: because, through the discourse of reason, it consults and investigates whether there is any way to escape, and if there are several ways, which is the most secure; and all the other things we treated at length when we set down the parts of **prudence** <note>In the medieval sense, *prudentia* meant practical wisdom and the ability to choose the right course of action.</note>. This discourse is the office of prudence, and it belongs to reason and not to the senses. Therefore, having led Dante himself to speak as much as the senses can, he then leads Virgil to investigate what is proper to reason. Whence follows:

Virgil sets forth his counsel, which was to descend from the right bank of the other ditch. **HE HAD NOT YET FINISHED**. Virgil had hardly finished these words when the demons were already arriving. And he demonstrates the love and the speed that he used toward Dante through a very fitting comparison, saying:

<columns>2</columns>

"If it be that the right slope so inclines
that we may down to the next ditch descend,
we shall escape the imagined chase."
He had not yet finished giving such counsel
when I saw them coming with wings outspread,
not very far off, seeking to seize us.
My Leader suddenly took hold of me,
just as a mother who is awoken by noise
and sees the kindled flames near her,
Who takes her son and flees, and does not stay,
having more care for him than for herself,
even so much as to put on a single shift;
And down from the ridge of the hard bank,
supine he gave himself to the sloping rock,
which closes one of the sides of the next ditch.

<column-break/>

As the mother, in whom there is the greatest love, when waking she sees the house burning, leaves every other care and takes her son to save him—having more care for him than for herself—so much so that she does not even wait to put on a shirt, and does not mind fleeing naked for his safety. Thus Virgil placed Dante upon his chest, and with his feet forward, almost **supine** <note>Lying on his back.</note>, he let himself slide down to the bottom of the sixth ditch. **TO THE SLOPING ROCK**: that is, to the steep cliff which **closes**: that is, shuts in the sixth ditch from one of its sides. **BUT** so that the allegory of this place is not left behind: Dante and Virgil depart from the **barraters** <note>Corrupt officials who "bartered" their influence for money; the inhabitants of the fifth ditch.</note>: that is, from the contemplation of this vice. And Dante fears that the demons might harm him: that is, he fears the **appetite** <note>The lower, impulsive part of the soul.</note>, lest the knowledge of such a vice should hold him back. And Virgil follows the same line of thought and concludes that it will be useful to descend into the other valley: that is, into the consideration of another vice. But as the demons arrive—that is, the temptation stimulating the appetite sooner than reason (Virgil) estimated—suddenly he took Dante; and he

<column-break/>

placed him upon his chest and slid with his feet forward down all that bank to the bottom of the other ditch. It is to be noted that the departure from a vice already known must be prompt and swift. And certainly a man slides to the bottom **supine** <note>On his back.</note>: because although he descends to the knowledge of another vice, and the "feet"—that is, **cupidity** <note>Desire/greed.</note>—carry us into it, nevertheless, in going supine, the face looks upward; this is so that the knowledge of the vice is for the purpose of rising above it, and not to remain submerged in it. And he presses Dante to his chest, which is the seat of thought. It is to be noted that the appetite must draw close to that which reason thinks and considers; for reason, seeing it in danger with motherly love, leaves all other care and only attends to saving it. Nor can the demons placed in the ditch of the barraters follow Dante into the other ditch: because the temptations of the vice from which he has already departed cannot goad him while he is in the consideration of another vice. And most excellently he demonstrates that reason loves the appetite with motherly love to show an extreme affection, which is even greater in the mother than in the father. Because, as **Aristotle** writes, the mother loves the son more than the father loves him: because she is more certain that he is hers than the father is, and because she has endured more labor. For before the birth he weighs upon her; in the birth he pains her; and after the birth she remains anxious and hardworking for him.

Never ran water so swiftly through a sluice
to turn the wheel of a land-mill,
when it approaches nearest to the paddles,
As did my Master over that border...

<column-break/>

He shows the descent of Virgil to have been swifter than the course of water through a very steep sluice of a **land-mill** <note>A mill built on land using a channeled stream, rather than a floating mill.</note>. For the water that turns a "French mill" has a lesser fall, because such a mill has large wheels...

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto XXIII. Having established the relationship between Virgil (Reason) and Dante (the Senses or Soul), Landino now describes their descent into the sixth ditch (bolgia) of the eighth circle, where they encounter the hypocrites.</meta>

# CANTO XXIII.

carrying me upon his breast
like his son, not as a companion:
Scarcely had his feet reached the bed
of the bottom below, when they reached the hill
above us: but there was no fear:
For the high providence that willed to place
them as ministers of the fifth ditch
takes from them all the power to depart from there.

There below we found a painted people
who went around with very slow steps
weeping and in appearance weary and overcome.
They had cloaks with low hoods
before their eyes, made in that style
which is made for the monks in Cologne.
Outside they are gilded so that it dazzles:
but inside all lead, and so heavy
that Frederick would have called them straw.
Oh, weary mantle for eternity!
we turned again, still to the left hand
together with them, intent on the sad weeping
But because of the weight, those weary people
came so slowly that we were "new"
in company at every movement of the hip.

<column-break/>

and from the side: But the ditch <note>original: *terragno*; referring to the trench or earthy floor of the ditch.</note> is small and narrow. Wherefore it is necessary that the water comes with force: And allegorically it demonstrates an incredible velocity that is in the discourse of the human mind: And the celerity that reason must use to succor the sensuality. <term>THE PADDLES</term> <note>original: *lepale*</note>: In a wheel, these are the parts that the water strikes. <term>APPROACHES</term> <note>original: *approccia*</note>: As if it reaches the shore and descends. <term>THROUGH THAT BORDER</term> <note>original: *viuagno*</note>: A border is properly the edge of a cloth. But here he used "border" for that strip of land which he took in the descent. <term>LIKE A SON and not like a companion</term>: It demonstrates that the affection of reason toward the appetite is paternal: because notwithstanding that sensuality often rebels against reason: Nevertheless [reason] always directs it, corrects it, and raises it up as much as it can.

**IN** this ditch the author finds the hypocrites, the sixth species of fraud. A hypocrite is said to be one who, being wicked, nevertheless in habit, in acts, and in words, strives to counterfeit the good and appear to be what he is not. Christians hold this vice to be of three types. The first is when someone feigns to be full of religion in the sight of men, but in truth does not fear God. The second is when someone does good, not moved by the love of it, but to appear good. The third is when one demonstrates that he is not good so that others might believe he is even better, and that he is not a hypocrite. Hypocrisy is, therefore, a clever and astute cloaking of a hidden vice. These are truly "painted": that is, superficially adorned, because painting adorns only the surface and shows it to be what it is not. Wherefore Virgil says <note>original: *Atque animum pictura pascit inani*</note> "And he feeds his soul on an empty picture." This name "hypocrite" is Greek. Since *Hypocrino* signifies to counterfeit: Wherefore, among the Greeks, actors are called hypocrites. Because just as in festivals and games the actors with masks and various clothes counterfeit themselves and seem to be what they are not, so these counterfeit themselves to appear good. Of these the Evangelist Matthew speaks—or rather our Savior through the mouth of the Evangelist: <note>original: *Attendite a falsis prophetis qui veniunt in vestimentis ovium Intrinsecus vero sunt lupi rapaces*</note> "Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves." This vice is detested in Deuteronomy, where it is written: <note>original: *Ne induatis vestem que ex lino et lana contexta est*</note> "You shall not wear a garment woven of linen and wool mixed together." It forbids, therefore, that they wear a garment which is woven of linen and wool: And by linen they signify hidden and secret proud thoughts, which are characteristic of the hypocrite: And by wool, which is white, they mean the outward demonstration of good which is not there. Because of this, Paul, seeing a priest strike himself in a simulation of zeal, said: <note>original: *Percuriat te deus paries dealbata*</note> "God shall strike you, you whitewashed wall!" And certainly they are like a wall which is whitened on the outside and black within. Nor is there a vice that more harms the human race. Since with such appearance they persuade others that they are such that anything can be believed of them, so that under such faith they can better deceive. These, as Plautus writes, show you bread in one hand to entice you, and in the other hold a hidden stone to strike you when you do not expect it. It is no wonder then if with such impetus and vehemence Juvenal of Aquino thunders against them in his satires, the beginning of which is: <note>original: *Ultra sauromatas fugere hic libet et gracialem occeanum quotiens aliquid de moribus audent Qui curios simulant et bacchanalia vivunt*</note> "I feel like fleeing beyond the Sauromatae and the frozen ocean whenever those who pretend to be Curii <note>The Curii were an ancient Roman family known for their austerity and virtue.</note> but live like Bacchanals dare to speak of morals." And a little below: <note>original: *Frontis nulla fides quis . n . non vicus abundat Tristibus obscenis castigas turpia cum sis Inter socraticos notissima fossa cinedos*</note> "There is no trusting appearances; for what street does not abound in somber-faced debauchees? You rebuke foul deeds while you yourself are a most well-known ditch among Socratic pathics." And certainly he who sins and confesses his error and does not deceive you is worthy of excuse. Wherefore the same poet [Juvenal] says: <note>original: *Verius Ergo Et magis ingenue peribonius Hunc ego fatia imputo qui vultu morbum incessuque fatetur His furor ispe dat veniam Sed peiores qui talia verbis Herculis inuadunt*</note> "More truly and more ingenuously does Peribonius act; I attribute his face to his fate, he who confesses his malady in his look and gait; his very madness grants him pardon. But worse are those who attack such things with the words of Hercules." Of these, Cicero most wisely concludes in his book *On Duties* affirming that the worst generation of men is that of those who, when they wish to deceive, strive to be held as good. This is then the nature of the hypocrite. But returning to the text: the poet feigns that these people were painted, that is, smoothed over. Just as a woman who is naturally ugly, putting on either white or red color to appear beautiful. So these, ugly with some vice, counterfeiting...

<meta>This page continues the commentary by Cristoforo Landino on Canto XXIII of the Inferno. Having described the descent into the sixth ditch, Landino now interprets the appearance and behavior of the hypocrites, specifically their "painted" nature and their heavy leaden cloaks, while providing historical and moral context.</meta>

...so that their outward actions appear beautiful, that is, virtuous in their souls. Truly he says they are **painted**: because just as a painting is an ornament only on the surface, so these people have virtuous customs only on the surface. **WITH SLOW STEPS.** This expresses the nature of the hypocrite, who in all gestures wishes to demonstrate gravity, restraint, and severity. Whence the same satirist <note>Likely referring to the Roman poet Juvenal.</note> says: *Speech is rare among them and they have a great desire for silence* <note>original: "Rarus fermo illis et magna libido tacendi"</note>: and elsewhere: *Bristly limbs indeed and hard bristles along the arms promise a fierce mind* <note>original: "hispida membra quidem et dure per brachia fete promittunt atrocem animum"</note>. They demonstrate, therefore, gravity in their slow steps. These same people, to better deceive their neighbor with false tears, show commiseration and compassion toward him; and they show themselves to be tired and overcome so that they appear removed from all idleness and pleasure, and full of fatigue and hardship, performing heavy penance. This is strictly forbidden by the Author of our salvation <note>Jesus Christ.</note> saying: *Do not be like the hypocrites, sad of face, who disfigure their faces so that they may appear to men to be fasting* <note>original: "Nolite facere sicut hypocrite tristes qui extenuant facies suas ut appareant hominibus ieiunantes"; Matthew 6:16.</note>. **THEY HAD CLOAKS.** Commonly, those who wish to appear holy use vile and poorly made garments, as we see the cloaks of monks; and they pull the hoods down even over their eyes. **MADE IN THAT STYLE:** that is, in the form used in Cologne, a city of Germany <note>original: "Magna"; Landino uses the term for the Germanic lands.</note>, where the monks wear very large and poorly made cloaks in a shape that is more like a sack than a garment. Francesco da Buti <note>An earlier 14th-century commentator on Dante.</note> relates in this place—I do not know if it is history or a fable—and tells of an abbot who was once so insolent and ambitious that he devised a way to obtain from the Pope the right for his monks to wear scarlet cloaks, and belts and spurs of gold, and silver-gilt stirrups for their horses. This petition moved the Pope to just indignation, and he commanded that in the future they should use very poorly made black cloaks, and belts and stirrups made of wood. Cologne is in Lower Germany on the Rhine, so called because it was a colony of the Romans. It was built by Agrippa, the son-in-law of Augustus; for this reason it is called Cologne Agrippina. **OUTSIDE THEY ARE GILDED SO THAT IT DAZZLES / BUT INSIDE ALL LEAD.** By gold, understand virtue; by lead, vice. Therefore, the cloaks are so well gilded on the outside that they dazzle with their splendor. This denotes that their outward actions demonstrate every virtue; and they dazzle well because he who is dazzled thinks he sees what he does not see. Thus, these people show themselves to us to be what they are not. The lead inside signifies the sordid and vicious life. For lead cannot maintain any splendor, but always produces rust that stains it, because it is of a terrestrial and watery nature, and of the nature of Saturn; and therefore it remains dull and dark. The same happens to the vicious soul, polluted in the greed for earthly and low things, and unstable like water. Gold is of the nature of fire, which illuminates, purges, and refines; and it proceeds from the sun, which produces life and every perfect thing. We conclude, therefore, that lead represents the vice that makes the soul of these sinners sordid and obscure, and gold represents the intrinsic splendor of simulated and entirely false virtue; this outward sign deceives us, but does not make them any better. **TO THE SAD WEEPING.** He said "sad" because the nature of the hypocrite is always to show sadness. Whence the Gospel, speaking of these, said: *When you fast, do not be like the hypocrites, sad of face.* <note>original: "Cum ieiunatis nolite fieri sicut hypocrite tristes"</note> And certainly, we see many truly religious people who, although they are diligent in vigils, fasts, and meditations, nevertheless always appear cheerful and with a happy face. This I can testify regarding Bernardino, a friar of the Order of Minors <note>St. Bernardino of Siena (1380–1444), a famous Franciscan preacher.</note>, who was deservedly recorded in the catalog of saints; he was never seen with a troubled face. Conversely, I know some who in their life and habits are a foul sink of enormous vices, and yet always in the sight of others have a tearful and mournful face to hide their dishonest pleasures, which they practice in secret like new Sardanapaluses <note>Sardanapalus was a legendary Assyrian king known for extreme luxury and decadence.</note>. **THAN FREDERICK.** Frederick II, of whom we spoke much above. He was naturally cruel, which he demonstrated in the perpetual imprisonment of his firstborn son and in the blinding of Pier delle Vigne. This man, when he wished to punish someone who had acted against the crown, would have a very thick leaden garment made for them and put them in a vessel over a fire until that lead melted, and thus he would put them to death. Therefore, he says that the cloaks of these sinners were so heavy that, in comparison to these, those of Frederick would seem like straw. **OR FOR ETERNITY.** With admiration, he shows how tiring it was to carry such a weight, and that such pain is eternal. If we understand this as the essential Hell, it is eternal. If we understand it morally, it is true because they are always in constant anguish to hide their vices, and this is a most heavy burden for them. And it follows that they walked with them; but the sinners, because of the weight, went so slowly that at every step the poets left them behind and reached those who were ahead; so that at every movement of the hip, they had new company. And here he clearly expresses what has already been said of their slowness; and it also signifies that there are many modes of hypocrites. Wherefore at every step—that is, at every thought in considering them—they find new modes and new forms of hypocrites.

---

"Therefore to my leader, see that you find
someone who by deed or name is known,
and move your eyes around as we go":
And one who understood the Tuscan word
cried out behind us: "Stay your feet!"

### CANTO XXIII.
<sig>.o.v.</sig>

"You who run so through the dark air, 
Perhaps you will have from me what you ask." 
Whereupon the guide turned and said, "Wait, 
and then proceed according to his pace."

...are easily known either by their name or by some deed they have done. **TOSCAN**: that is, Tuscan, because Dante spoke in the Tuscan language. **DARK**: that is, black.

I stood still and saw two show great haste
in the expression of their faces to be with me,
but the burden and the narrow way delayed them.
When they had arrived, with a very sidelong eye 
they gazed at me without saying a word; 
then they turned to each other and said to themselves:
"This one seems alive by the action of his throat <note>Dante’s breathing proves he is a living man, unlike the fixed, breathless shades of the dead.</note>,
and if they are dead, by what privilege 
do they go uncovered by the heavy cloak?"
Then he said to me: "O Tuscan, who to the college 
of the sad hypocrites has come, 
do not disdain to say who you are."
And I then: "I was born and raised 
over the beautiful river Arno at the great city, 
and I am with the body I have always had. 
But you, who are you, from whom so much distills 
as much sorrow as I see down your cheeks; 
and what pain is it in you that so sparkles?" 
And one replied: "Alas, the orange cloaks 
are of lead, so thick that the weights 
make their scales creak so. 
Jovial Friars we were, from Bologna; 
I, Catalano, and this is Loderingo, 
named and chosen together by your land, 
as a single man is usually taken 
to preserve its peace; and we were such 
that it still appears around the Guardingo." <note>The Guardingo was a district in Florence where the houses of the Ghibelline Uberti family were destroyed while these two friars were in power.</note>

<column-break/>

...who shouted from behind to catch up with them, and then go along with him. This denotes that this vice has so much simulation and dissimulation within itself that such men are not known except by those who have long familiarity with them. **KNOWN BY DEED OR BY NAME.** He said this because men...

**T**hey showed haste in the expression of their faces. This is in the demonstration of the countenance. For it happens that the soul often demonstrates through the face what it feels inside. But they did not show haste in their walking, because they could not quicken their pace. And allegorically, he means that often the hypocrite has a desire in his soul to hurry and bring a thing to a conclusion; but in order not to reveal his malice, he works with a length of time on what he could have done with brevity. **BY THE ACTION of the throat**: that is, in breathing. **STOLA.** He calls the cloak this. For in Latin, a *stola* <note>original: "stola"</note> is a garment reaching down to the feet. **AND I THEN: I WAS BORN AND RAISED.** here he uses circumlocution <note>A roundabout way of speaking.</note>, for he could have said in one word: "Born in Florence," which is situated upon the Arno. And it is a **great villa**: that is, a city, speaking in the French style where the city is called *ville* <note>original: "uilla"</note>. **AND I AM WITH the body that I have always had**: in contrast to the "aerial body" which the soul takes after death, with which it presents itself and speaks and suffers, according to what he [Dante] establishes in the second canticle <note>The Purgatorio.</note>. **DISTILLS** The sorrow down the cheeks: that is, the tears, which proceed from sorrow. **THE CLOAKS Orange**: that is, troublesome; and it is a metaphor <note>original: "translatione"</note> from tastes that are in the sense of taste, to weight which is in the sense of touch. Therefore, this weight was as troublesome to endure as a "rancid" <note>Italian "rancie" means both orange/gilded and rancid/stale.</note> flavor is to the tongue—that is, the flavor of spoiled things. **THAT THE WEIGHTS**: of these cloaks. **MAKE creak**: because of their heaviness. For just as when something hangs, the legs [act as] **scales**: which to better support the pulleys; thus those cloaks made the bones and joints of those who wore them creak. And he called the legs "scales," which to better support...

---

...go balancing and counter-balancing the weight that a man carries to level it and make it more bearable. **JOVIAL FRIARS we were, of Bologna.** There were, in the times of Pope Urban IV, certain noble men of no mediocre status and wealth, especially in Bologna and Modena. In order to live in leisure and be exempt from public duties and burdens, they gathered together. By common counsel, they sent word to the Supreme Pontiff and obtained permission to constitute a new religious order in which they could live in leisure and contemplation. Urban established the order, whose title was "Friars of Saint Mary," and the habit was honorable, but very different from that of the Order of Preachers [the Dominicans]; and they wore a white shield with a red cross. No one could be of this order unless he were a knight, but they could not wear golden spurs or have gilded bridles. They stayed in their own houses with their wives and children, and they made a profession of being ready to fight against infidels and those who violated justice. And although they were named "Friars of Our Lady," nevertheless, because of their splendid and copious life, they were called by the common people **Jovial Friars**; and especially because they were immune from every public tribute and burden. It happened then that after the death of Manfred <note>Manfred, King of Sicily, whose defeat at Benevento in 1266 shifted power in Italy.</note>, the Guelphs in our republic [Florence] began to take heart. Although their leaders had been expelled after the rout of Montaperti <note>The Battle of Montaperti (1260), a major Ghibelline victory over the Guelphs.</note>, they had remained; and the Ghibellines, having lost their patron, began to grow weak, especially because the majority of the common people favored the Guelphs. Therefore, finally, the princes of the Ghibelline party were forced...

<header>INFERNO</header>

...to settle the popular tumult by electing not one, but two <term>Podestà</term> <note>The Podestà was usually a single foreign official brought in to govern a city-state to ensure neutrality.</note>: of whom one was a Guelf and the other a Ghibelline. These two were to have supreme authority and judgment to return the people to whatever state seemed to them most peaceful and tranquil. They therefore chose two Jovial Friars from Bologna: Catalano de’ Catalani as the Guelf, and Loderingo degli Andalò (others say of the Lambertucci family), who appeared to be men full of justice and severity. They resided in the public palace near Saint Apollinare and chose thirty-six men from both factions, with whose counsel they were to limit superfluous expenses and reform all parts of the republic. Afterward, seeing that following the death of Manfred and the victory of Charles <note>Charles of Anjou, who defeated Manfred at the Battle of Benevento.</note> the Guelfs were superior—as Virgil says, <note>original: "Res Agamemnonias victriciaque arma secuti" — "Having followed Agamemnon’s cause and victorious arms."</note>—and also being corrupted by money, they determined, under the guise of the universal good, to favor the Guelfs alone. This so provoked Guido Novello, the vicar in Florence for Manfred, that although he had five hundred German knights and many infantry called from the surrounding cities, he nonetheless fled to Prato on Saint Martin's Day in the year of our salvation 1266. Then, in the following year, upon the arrival of Guy de Montfort sent by King Charles, the Ghibellines fled the city of their own free will; and they never returned thereafter. **THE GUARDINGO.** This was the street where the houses of the noble Ghibelline family, the Uberti, were located. These were burned, and the Palace of the Priors <note>Now known as the Palazzo Vecchio.</note> was built there with the square that surrounds it. **FROM YOUR LAND**—that is, from Florence. **TAKEN**—meaning both elected as Podestà, whereas usually a single man is taken alone. It is as if he said: "We two were elected to the office of power which is usually held by only one; and Florence chose us to preserve its peace, as was said above." **AND WE WERE SUCH**—meaning that the results are still visible around the Guardingo. For we favored the Guelfs so much that the Ghibellines were oppressed, as appears from the ruin of the houses of the Uberti, the heads of the Ghibelline faction.

There is a rhetorical device called "precision" <note>Also known as aposiopesis; a sudden breaking off in speech.</note>. This is when we begin to speak of something and leave the speech cut off and interrupted by some passion or disturbance, as Virgil does: <note>original: "Quos ego . Sed motos prestat componere fluctus" — "Whom I—! But it is better to calm the troubled waves."</note> Therefore, here the poet wished to show that he felt compassion

> but said no more, for to my eyes there ran

for the pains of these men. But afterward, moved by the sight of the crucified soul, he left his speech unfinished as a man seized by a greater concern.

**ONE CRUCIFIED** on the ground with three stakes. Just as Christ was crucified with three nails—because each hand was pierced separately and the feet together—so this man, who had given the counsel that Christ should be killed, deserved similar punishment. But Christ was suspended on high because his death called sinners to heaven; this man was on the ground because his malicious and hypocritical sentence was the cause of his own eternal death and that of many others. This was Caiaphas, whose name signifies "sagacious" or "investigator." Also, "vomiting from the mouth," or "vomit of the mouth."

**WHEN HE SAW ME** he writhed all over, blowing into his beard. These are signs of his grief that Dante should see him. And he grieved because the hypocrite suffers when he sees his hypocrisy and fraud uncovered. He grieved also seeing that the death of Christ, which he advised, gave salvation to the Christian and eternal death to himself.

---

**ADVISED THE PHARISEES**; because they bore envy toward Christ for his miracles and his preaching, and feared that the people, following Christ, would abandon the priests. Nevertheless, they did not dare to speak openly against him. But like a false hypocrite, Caiaphas demonstrated, through the zeal and affection he claimed to bear for the people, that they should seek the death of Christ; and he said it was useful for one to die for the people so that the whole nation should not perish. And therefore the author says: *He advised the Pharisees that it was expedient to put one man to martyrdom for the people.* "Pharisees" in the Hebrew language signifies "divided," or "dividing," or "violent," or "dissipating." But because he places "Pharisees" here, we shall remember that, as Josephus writes in his *Antiquities* and in *The Jewish War*, there were three sects of philosophers among the Hebrews established from the beginning: the Essenes, the Sadducees, and the Pharisees. The Pharisees lived soberly and without any luxury, and in every thing they followed the judgment of reason. They in no way resisted those whom they had to obey; they greatly honored the elders. They believe that everything is governed by fate, yet they do not take away the free will of man. They believe there will be a divine judgment and each will be judged according to their merits. They posit that souls are immortal and that they will have appropriate dwellings in hell according to their virtue and vice. Some will remain in perpetual prison; others will have the power to return to life. And for this reason, they maintain that we should build temples and offer prayers. Therefore, they were held in the highest veneration by the people and had...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto XXIII of the Inferno. Having discussed the Jovial Friars, the text now transitions into a historical and theological digression regarding Jewish sects (Sadducees, Essenes, and Pharisees) to provide context for the figures of Caiaphas and Annas, who are punished among the hypocrites. It then returns to the dialogue between Virgil and the friars regarding their escape from the sixth ditch.</meta>

<page-num>XXIII.</page-num>
<header>CANTO XXIII.</header>

...a great gathering. The **Sadducees** <note>One of the three main Jewish sects of the Second Temple period.</note> posit that the soul is mortal along with the body. They have no other observance than the Law. They consider it the highest glory to contradict the teachers of their own philosophy. But few among them possess true doctrine. The third group they call the **Essenes**; they attribute everything to divine power. They hold the soul to be immortal. They believe that one must fight unto death for the defense of justice. They do not perform any sacrifice together with the people, because they believe they are very different from them in purity and sanctity. For this reason, they sacrifice separately from the multitude. Their customs and habits are full of virtue. With the greatest diligence, they attend to agriculture. And there is something marvelous in them that is not found among the Greeks nor in any other nation: because they all live in community. Nor is there any among them who has private property. It cannot be said that one is richer or poorer than another. None have wives. But they willingly keep servants—actually <note>The original text is slightly ambiguous here; typically Essenes avoided both marriage and slavery.</note>, they believe a wife is a cause of discord, and keeping servants seems an iniquitous thing. Instead, they help one another in all administrations and needs. They have those who diligently keep account of all income, and also those who distribute and divide the fruits of the earth to each according to their needs. They elect as priests those whom they repute to be better than the others. These live on simple food, without a variety of dishes. They have clothing that is not sumptuous, but clean and neat. To these three sects, **Judas** <note>Judas of Gamala, a Jewish leader who led a resistance against the Roman census in 6 AD.</note> added a fourth. These are similar to the Pharisees in other things, but in the defense of liberty, they are entirely immovable and invincible. They will have no other lord but God. They endure every heavy torment and death, and the loss of children, relatives, and friends, so as not to be forced to receive any other master. This was Judas of Gamala; and when the people were settled to acquiesce and consent to the Roman census, he, together with Zadok, moved the people from that purpose, affirming that such a census was manifest slavery. He incited the people to endure every danger to defend their liberty, affirming that God does not help those who do not have such a purpose. **CROSSWISE And naked upon the path.** <note>Dante, Inferno XXIII, 110-111.</note> This demonstrates his punishment, which is very appropriate. For since he was the chief of the hypocrites, it was not enough for him to bear the weight of his own leaden cape; rather, he had to feel the weight of all those who passed over him. And in the same torment was placed his father-in-law, who was **Annas**, and all the other priests who were present at the council in which it was concluded that Christ should die. This council **WAS A BAD SEED** for the Jews. Because it produced the destruction of Jerusalem and the dispersion of that entire nation. Furthermore, the poet feigns that he lay across the path, which is a public and manifest thing. This signifies that the greater the vice that hypocrisy hides, the more it eventually manifests itself. His being naked signifies the same thing.

---

<columns>2</columns>

Then I saw Virgil marveling
over him who was stretched out on a cross
so vilely in the eternal exile.
Then he directed to the friars such words:
"May it not displease you, if it is permitted to tell us,
if on the right hand there lies any opening
where we both might be able to exit
without constraining the black angels
to come down to this depth to retrieve us."

<column-break/>

**Virgil marvels:** that is, the doctrine of the Gentiles <note>Virgil represents human reason or pagan philosophy.</note> marvels at the punishment of those who betrayed Christ. This denotes that through human science, we cannot comprehend the things said of the incarnate God. Nor can it be proved by such science that Christ is true God and true man. **THEN HE DIRECTED.** He asks the friars Catalano and Loderingo to reveal if that ditch has any opening—that is, any exit—on the right hand. Since they had turned to the left when they entered, they had to turn to the right to exit. **IF IT IS PERMITTED:** that is, if you are allowed; for damned souls do not have the will nor the power to know or say everything. **WITHOUT CONSTRAINING** the black angels—that is, the demons. In this, he demonstrates that everything is subject to the power of God.

---

<columns>2</columns>

He answered then: "Nearer than you believe
a rock approaches, which from the great circle
moves and crosses all the foul valleys,
except that this one is broken and does not cover it.
You can climb up over the ruin
which lies against the slope and heaps at the bottom."
The leader stood a while with head bowed,
then said: "He told the matter poorly,
he who hooks the sinners over there."

<column-break/>

**Catalano answered:** "Nearer than you, Virgil, believe, a rock approaches which moves from the [outer] circle that girds all the ten ditches, and cuts through the middle of all of them, forming a bridge over them; except that over this one it is broken," because, as has been said, it broke on the day of Christ's Passion. "But nonetheless you will be able to exit from here by climbing up through its ruins, because it is not entirely a precipice or a sheer drop, but it lies against the slope"—that is, in falling, it left a slope suitable for climbing—"and it heaps at the bottom," meaning it is not ruined all the way to the floor. **THE LEADER STOOD A WHILE** with head bowed, as one does when thinking. Then he said that he who hooks the sinners—that is, **Malacoda** <note>The leader of the Malebranche demons from the previous ditches.</note>, who torments sinners with hooks as was shown above—had told our needs poorly. For he said there was another bridge that made a path, and this is false. But it is the custom of the devil to lie. For when he tempts a sinner to sin, because he cannot entirely take away the intellect...

# INFERNO XXIII.

...knows in any part that it is not bad, he strives to show that there is an excuse and a remedy. And therefore he said above: *There is a rock that makes a path.* <note>Reference to the broken bridge over the sixth ditch of the Inferno, which the demons falsely claimed was intact.</note> For when he comforts the sinner toward hypocrisy, and the sinner resists because he recognizes it as sin, the devil places before him some excuse, and shows that with time he will be able to escape it.

> The friar: “I once heard said in Bologna
> of the devil’s many vices, among which I heard
> that he is a liar and the father of lies.”
> After this the Duke <note>Virgil, representing human reason</note> went on with great strides,
> a little disturbed by anger in his countenance.
> Wherefore I departed from the burdened ones
> following the prints of his beloved feet.

<column-break/>

Friar Catalano shows that he heard it said in Bologna—that is, in that city where the study of all the fine arts flourishes, and especially theology—that the devil is a liar and the father of lies <note>original: *menzogna*</note>: that is, a falsehood; for "menzogna" is so called because it lies. He therefore heard that saying in the schools where one works at holy theology: **The devil is a liar and the father of lies** <note>original Latin: "Diabolus mendax est et pater mendacii"</note>. And certainly the name itself signifies this: for "devil" in Greek means **slanderer** <note>original: "calunniatore"</note>; and slander is nothing other than false infamy and deception. For if you tell me something bad about another falsely, you seek to deceive me, so that I might hold a false opinion of one who is innocent.

Wherefore calumny was excellently painted by **Apelles of Ephesus**, a most noble painter, in this form: On the right hand sits a man, but with ears like a donkey in the manner of **Midas** <note>In Greek mythology, King Midas was given donkey ears by Apollo as a sign of his foolishness and poor judgment.</note>; and he stretches out his hand to...

---

...**Calumny**, who comes toward him. Around this man stand two women, one called **Ignorance**, the other **Suspicion**. Opposite them is Calumny, whose form is magnificent, but she is full of rage and disdain; in her left hand she holds a small torch, and with her right she drags along a youth, who raises his hands to heaven and invokes God as a witness to his innocence. Before her goes **Envy** with a sharp eye but pale, like one who has been oppressed by a long illness. Around Calumny are two who adorn and guide her: these are **Treachery** <note>original: "infidie," meaning ambushes or snares</note> and **Fraud**. But behind her follows **Penance**, dressed in black and torn clothes, full of weeping and confused by shame; and she looks back at **Truth**, who comes to help the youth who was wrongly slandered.

This is therefore the description of Calumny, which I have set down in brief words because, as I said, "devil" in Greek means **slanderer**: that is, one who accuses with lies. And it comes from the verb **to slander** <note>original Greek: "diaballin"</note>. **AFTER THIS THE DUKE WENT ON WITH GREAT STRIDES**: that is, leaving. And certainly our intellect immediately departs from falsehood when it recognizes it, for it is greedy for the truth. And when a man realizes he has been deceived by the devil and by sensuality, he is indignant and becomes angry with himself. But it is an anger that does not sin; rather, it excites our mind against sin and makes it eager to flee from it. Therefore he said, **A LITTLE DISTURBED BY ANGER**. And he added, **IN HIS COUNTENANCE**, which signifies that he shows in his appearance that such a burning is more in his external actions than in his soul.

**WHEREFORE I DEPARTED FROM THE BURDENED ONES**: that is, from those hypocrites who were burdened by the leaden cloaks. **I DEPARTED**. For once we have recognized the vice, we must depart from it and follow the tracks, the steps, and the traces of the **clear footprints** <note>original: "chiare piante"</note> of Virgil—which is to say, the intellect. For once the vice is known, superior reason judges that we must flee from it. Reason, therefore, departs from the fraudulent hypocrites, and Dante—who represents the sensuality obedient to reason—follows him.

<page-num>XXIIII</page-num>
<header>CANTO XXIV</header>

## CANTO XXIV OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE

This twenty-fourth chapter continues from the preceding one. It shows that in this seventh ditch <note>original: "bolgia"</note>, thieves are punished. Because the poet was somewhat dismayed at the end of the last canto upon seeing Virgil disturbed, he demonstrates at the beginning of this canto how he regained his comfort in a short time. He expresses all of this through a comparison: just as it happens that a shepherd, seeing the frost in the morning, fears he cannot lead his sheep to pasture and grieves, but shortly afterward, once the frost is destroyed by the sun, he takes heart again and leads the flock to graze. So too was Dante comforted by the poet Virgil after the dismay he felt at seeing Virgil’s troubled expression.

<image-desc>Decorative initial I containing a portrait of a figure, likely Dante, wearing a red cap and garment, looking right against a blue background, enclosed in a red and gold frame.</image-desc>

In that part of the youthful year
when the sun tempers his locks under Aquarius
and the nights already move toward the half-day <note>meaning the nights are becoming equal to the days as spring approaches</note>,
When the frost mimics upon the ground
the image of her white sister <note>the snow</note>,
but her pen’s temper lasts but a little while,
The poor peasant whose fodder is failing
gets up and looks and sees the countryside
all turned white; whereat he smites his thigh,
Returns indoors and grumbles here and there
like a wretch who knows not what to do;
then he returns and regains hope,
Seeing that the world has changed its face
in so little an hour; and he takes his crook
and chases his little sheep out to pasture.

<column-break/>

**IN THAT part of the youthful year**
He uses a chronography: that is, a description of time. And because he mentions the year, we will, by looking back a bit, demonstrate how many variations and species of years there have been in different nations and different centuries. "Year" <note>original: "Anno"</note> is a Latin name, called *annus* like *anulus* <note>original: "quasi anulus," meaning like a ring</note>, because just as a ring is round and returns into itself, so the year moves circularly; beginning from one sign of the zodiac and passing through all the others, it returns to that same one. For it is the sun that creates it, which, starting from one sign, runs through them all, and when it has returned to the same place from which it departed, the year is finished.

Some say that "year" is derived from a Greek verb *Ananeuste* <note>original: "Ananeuste," likely referring to ananeousthai, to renew</note> which means to renew, because once the year is finished, it renews itself. And although the true year is the completed journey of the sun through all twelve signs of the zodiac—which space is three hundred and sixty-five days and a quarter part (that is, six hours and a hundredth part of a day)—nevertheless, various nations among the ancients reckoned the year differently. For among those of Arcadia, the year was three months. The Acarnanians had a year of six months, and all the rest of Greece had a year of 354 days.

Romulus <note>The legendary founder of Rome</note> willed that the Romans should have a year of ten months, beginning in March. They named this first month after Mars, the father of Romulus. The second after Venus, the mother of Aeneas, from whom the Romans descended. Thus they said *Aphrodite* for April, because in the Greek language Venus is called *Aphrodite* <note>original: "haphrodite"</note>. And because the city was divided into elders and youths—that is, *majores* and *juniores*—May was named by the elders and June by the youths. After these, the following months were named by number: thus the fifth was called *Quintilis*, the sixth *Sextilis*, the seventh *September*, and likewise the eighth *October*, the ninth *November*, and the tenth *December*. In these ten months, there were six months of thirty days and four of thirty-one. Therefore they made a sum of 304 days.

I will not be occupied at present with demonstrating the intercalary days <note>leap days added to align the calendar</note>. We will only say that in the following times, Gaius Julius Caesar the Dictator—of no less genius in learning than in military discipline—corrected every error and ordered the year to be 365 days and a quarter of a day and a hundredth. He willed that every fourth year should be 366 days to account for the four quarters that make one whole in four years, as we have written distinctly in our epistle to Francesco Baldovini regarding intercalation and the bissextile day <note>leap day</note>.

In this, he imitated the Egyptians who, through mathematical learning, knew that the solar year is finished when the sun has completed its circle through all twelve signs. Therefore Caesar added January and February to the year of Romulus. He ordered that the beginning of the year should be January, and for this reason, he named it after Janus, whom the gentiles believed to be the god of every beginning. And he named February from *februa*, which means "purification" <note>original: "februa"</note>, because in this month they performed sacrifices to purify the souls of the dead. For this reason, the Roman Church, following this order, sets the beginning and head of the year there. This moved the poet to say **IN THAT part of the youthful year**, to denote that January is the first age of the year; since it is the beginning, the year is still "youthful."

And this is according to the custom of the Romans and the Church. But according to astrologers, the youth of the year is not in January, but rather its old age. Since the true beginning of the year is the first entry of the sun into Aries (as was shown in the first canto of this canticle), it follows that January would be near the end. Astronomers therefore divide the year into four parts: the first is Spring, which begins with the entry of the sun into Aries. This is the childhood and adolescence of the year. For just as in this age a man grows and keeps his limbs tender and abounds in heat and moisture (which is the nature of blood, and is similar to the element of Air, which is hot and moist), so Spring gives to the earth...
