This serves as a parallel to Dante’s own experience of being dismayed by Virgil’s anger and then comforted by his master’s return to a calm demeanor.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>INFERNO</header>

this complexion <note>In medieval science, "complexion" refers to the balance of the four bodily humors and their qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry).</note> through which all plants germinate, grow, and keep themselves tender. The second season is the summer, which is by nature fiery, hot, and dry, similar to our youth. For once a man has finished his time of growing, he is called a young man: his limbs have already hardened, being hot and dry, and he becomes strong and robust. Likewise, the summer is hot and dry, and it makes plants hard, robust, and strong. The summer begins as soon as the sun reaches the first degree of Cancer. Then, while it passes through Cancer, Leo, and Virgo, the season of summer continues. But when it touches Libra, autumn begins, which is moist and cold like water and gives maturity to the fruits. Therefore, it is similar to the "virile age" <note>Adulthood or middle age.</note>, which, leaving behind games and pastimes, becomes of mature counsel and seeks fruitful and honorable things. Winter is cold and dry, of a melancholic complexion and similar to the earth; it is the old age of the year, and it begins at the first degree of Capricorn. From all these things, it follows that when Dante calls January the "youth of the year," he is not speaking according to the astrologers, but according to the custom of the Romans <note>The Roman calendar began the year in January, whereas many medieval calendars began in March.</note>.

**UNDER AQUARIUS TEMPERS.** This is the fourth house of Saturn, and the sun runs through it in this year, 1481 <note>original: "M. cccc. lxxxi." This dates the commentary to the late 15th century.</note>, from the 10th day of January until the 9th day of February. It is a fixed and masculine sign. By day, Saturn rules it; by night, Mercury; and Jupiter participates with these. It belongs to the air triplicity <note>An astrological grouping of three signs (Gemini, Libra, Aquarius) associated with the element of air.</note>. Its first face belongs to Venus, the second to Mercury, and the third to the Moon. This sign contains eighteen stars. The sign rules over the legs of man down to the ankle joint. It makes a man boastful and of a beautiful, colored face, but with one leg longer than the other; it is the house of friendship. The fables say that Aquarius is Ganymede, snatched up by Jove. It is called Aquarius <note>The Water-Bearer.</note> because it induces rain; and it is the cause, according to Albertus Magnus <note>A famous 13th-century philosopher and scientist.</note>, of a universal flood when the conjunction of the seven planets begins in this sign, specifically in that part called the Hydra, and passes into Pisces. I will not discuss at present why the year begins with the sun's entry into Aries rather than any other sign, because we provided the reason in the first canto of this canticle. I will only add that there are three species of years: this one, which is solar; the second, lunar, which is the space from one conjunction of the moon with the sun to the next; and the third is called the "Great Year," which, according to the opinion of many, contains thirty-six thousand solar years.

**TEMPERS HIS LOCKS.** That is, he tempers his burning rays. For the sun does not heat much while it is in this sign.

**AND ALREADY THE NIGHTS TO THE HALF AND DAYS DEPART.** That is, the nights and days are already moving toward the middle. This means that the nights and days are dividing the time by half. Not because it is already the equinox, but the day has already grown so much and the night diminished that, although they are not yet at the midpoint, they are beginning to move toward it. He did not say "they are," but "they go." Some read "and already the nights to midday depart," meaning the day has begun to grow and the nights to fail. For until the sun goes to Capricorn, the nights have grown and the days failed. Then, having departed from the winter tropic, it comes degree by degree toward the equinoctial line, and the nights begin to diminish until it arrives at the equinoctial, where night is equalized with day, occupying exactly half; this is in the first degree of Aries. Afterward, the nights continue their diminution until the summer solstice in Cancer, so that the days become the longest and the nights the shortest.

**THE FROST.** While the sun is above the earth, it draws humors to itself; those it does not consume fall back down as soon as the sun goes below. In summer, such humor is called dew, because in Latin it is called *ros*; in winter we call it hoarfrost <note>original: "brinata"</note>, because the Latins call it *pruina*, from *perurendo* <note>Latin: "burning through."</note>. For with its cold, it burns the tender plants. Aristotle defines it: frost is dew frozen in the middle region of the air by the frigidity of the place and time when there is no part of heat. Because of the cold, that humor which was previously dew hardens and becomes white, because the cold gathers and constricts it.

**THE IMAGE.** That is, the form of her sister, the snow, which he calls the sister of the frost because of the similarity between them. Thus, in these times, the frost is so great that it resembles snow.

**BUT IT LASTS BUT LITTLE.** Because when the sun warms, it is immediately destroyed.

**AND TEMPERS ITS PAIN.** That is, by melting, the cold diminishes; for when the cold is excessive due to the great frost, it is a "pain" to every thing that has a vegetative soul. Some read *penna* <note>pen</note> instead of *pena* <note>pain</note>, and they want the meaning to be that the frost "tempers the pen"—that is, it lasts as little as the ink's temper lasts for a writer. But it seems more likely to me that the text says *pena* and not *penna*, because such a translation is too harsh.

**THE LITTLE PEASANT TO WHOM STUFF LACKS.** For the poor man lacks "stuff," that is, the fodder to feed the sheep.

**AS A WRETCH.** Miserable, and placed in a low state. For *tapinos* in Greek signifies "dejected" and "low." <note>original: "tapinos in greco"</note>

**THEN HE LAUGHS.** And regains hope because he had lost it.

**SEEING** that the world has changed; that is, changed its face, because it is no longer white from the frost, which has already melted.

Thus did the master make me dismayed
when I saw his brow so troubled,
and thus quickly to the ailment came the plaster.
For as we came to the broken bridge

<column-break/>

In this same way was I dismayed: and so quickly the plaster reached the ailment—that is, the remedy to my dismay. **FOR AS.** He shows the reason why he quickly regained his spirit. For once we reached the bridge...

# CANTO XXIV

->My leader turned with that<-
->sweet look that I saw first at the foot of the mountain;<-
->He opened his arms after some chosen<-
->counsel within himself, looking first<-
->well at the ruin, and took hold of me.<-

The waste <note>original: "guasto"</note>, which as we have said had fallen over the sixth pouch <term>bolgia</term> <note>Malebolge is divided into ten concentric "bolge" or circular trenches.</note>. **My leader turned to me with that look**: that is, with that appearance which he showed me when he first appeared to me at the foot of the mountain from which the three beasts were chasing me, as we saw in the first canto. **HE OPENED HIS ARMS after some counsel**. The arms are interpreted by the Holy Scripture as help, and reason always helps the senses. Therefore, it shows that the intellect and the superior reason succor the inferior one, which by itself was not sufficient. And he helped **after some chosen counsel**. This denotes that the human intellect does not reach true consideration without discourse. And for this reason, before he embraces Dante—which is when he brings the inferior reason and the sensuality back to himself—it is necessary that through such discourse he comes to the knowledge of the truth: and this is to "consider the ruin."

The author describes what the office of the intellect and of the wise man should be: who always, before he undertakes any enterprise, discourses with the mind. And thus he lifts Dante, who is the inferior reason and the **sensuality**. **TOWARD THE SUMMIT**: that is, toward the top, which is speculation and contemplation. **OF A**

<column-break/>

**CRAG** <term>ronchione</term> <note>original: "ronchione," meaning a large, rugged piece of rock or crag.</note>: that is, of a piece of stone from the ruin. **HE NOTICED another splinter** <term>scheggia</term>. Almost another crag. And so it happens because the intellect not only considers the present, but also looks to the future: and it foresees and commands the inferior reason, which acts regarding the particulars of what must be done. And it admonishes her that she should not set out to do anything that is above her strength. And therefore, while Virgil pulls the sensuality toward difficult things before he is at the first considered place, he admonishes him that he should then grapple onto **another higher one**. But before he seats himself there, he wants him to **try if the splinter can support him**. The intellect excites the inferior reason and the sensuality to great

things, and wants it to exit the bottom where the sinners are punished, and rise up to the speculation of truth with his help. But because not every man has such a gift from nature that his wit serves him for great things, every man should have enough intellect to examine his own possibility, and not take it upon himself to do something that is above it. And therefore he says that he should "try first." **IT WAS NO WAY for one clothed in a cloak**. He has placed the hypocrites in this bottom with leaden cloaks; he says therefore that such a steep path was not for men who had such heavy garments. Allegorically, he shows that he who is burdened by the habit of sin cannot exit from it; whereas those who have not made a habit of it free themselves with difficulty. **That We barely—and he being light**: that is, Virgil himself, who is light. **AND I PUSHED**. He says that Virgil was light because the intellect, illustrated by science, is light to fly like an eagle to sublime and heavenly things; **and I pushed**, because sensuality and inferior reason, although heavy by nature, nonetheless when they obey the intellect, they are pushed by it. **THEY COULD MOUNT from ledge to ledge** <note>original: "di chiappa in chiappa"; while "chiappa" can mean "buttock" in modern Italian, here the commentator explains it as "scheggia" (rock-ledge/splinter).</note>: that is, from splinter to splinter. And here he shows that Virgil and he did not fly upward, but with difficulty they went up, climbing from one splinter to another. This can be allegorically referred to moral and intellectual virtue. For if moral virtue is that which distances us from the bottom of vices and pulls us to the summit of the mountain, no one ever made a habit of virtue except little by little and with intervals of time. And if we refer to intellectual virtue, we have already said that the human soul does not know without discourse. Therefore, it goes "from splinter to splinter."

->And if it were not that on that precinct<-
->more than the other the slope was shorter,<-
->I know not of him, but I would have been well defeated;<-
->But because Malebolge toward the entrance<-
->of the lowest well all slopes down,<-
->the site of each valley carries:<-
->That one bank rises and the other descends;<-
->we nevertheless came at last to the point<-
->where the last part breaks away.<-

<column-break/>

The poet shows in this part that if the bank of this precinct of the sixth pouch <term>bolgia</term> had not been **shorter** <note>meaning shorter in height or less steep due to the geography of Hell</note> and for this reason less steep, and a smaller climb, he would have remained defeated by the difficulty of the ascent. **I KNOW NOT Of him, but I would have been well defeated**. This allegorically signifies that the sensuality at least, if not the reason, would have been defeated by such difficulty. And he rightly said **I KNOW NOT Of him**. Because on one hand, considering the excellence of reason, which is fit to overcome every resistance; and on the other, seeing the great difficulty, he remained in doubt as to which would have been defeated. <meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's *Inferno*, Canto XXIV. The previous page concluded with Virgil assisting Dante in climbing the ruins of the collapsed bridge. We now move into the physiological and moral explanation of Dante's exhaustion upon reaching the top of the ridge overlooking the seventh pouch.</meta>

<page-num>CXXIII</page-num>
<header>INFERNO</header>

### The very breath was so spent from my lungs
### when I was up, that I could go no further;
### rather, I sat down at the first arrival.

<column-break/>

He doubted himself: that is, his sensuality: because its frailty cannot resist. **BUT BECAUSE Malebolge** slopes entirely toward the gate of the lowest pit. He assigns the reason why this bank was lower than the one above. Because the site

<column-break/>

of the eighth circle—which he called Malebolge above—slopes entirely toward the ninth: which, because it is the innermost and the lowest circle of the others, he calls a "pit" <term>pozo</term>: because it must be deep, being at the center, and narrow, being the innermost. And it is true that the site of each valley **CARRIES**: that is, it brings with it this: that one bank rises and the other descends. For these ten pouches <term>bolge</term> step down in such a way that the second is lower than the first, and higher than the third; the third is higher than the fourth, and lower than the second. And so on, degree by degree. Therefore, this sixth pouch had a lower bank than the fifth. **THE LAST stone breaks away**. That is, departing from the other bridge, it falls. **THE BREATH** <term>lena</term> **was so spent from my lungs**. The lung embraces the heart, where the fountain of natural heat resides; and because of excessive heat, there is a need for continuous cooling. The lung, like a bellows <note>original: "mantaco"</note>, draws in the exterior air and cools the heart with it. And this is our breathing. But because the heat of the heart increases the more the body moves and labors, it is therefore necessary that the bellows-action of the lungs be more frequent and greater, and draw in more air. Hence it happens that the lung becomes very dried out, to the point that a man reaches such a state of panting that if he is not helped by something cool and moist, he would lose his life; for the lung could no longer breathe. And without such respiration, the heart would perish. Therefore he says rightly **THE BREATH**: that is, the power. **WAS SO SPENT** <note>original: "si munta," literally "milked dry"</note>: So dried out. For just as a teat is dried out by milking, so is the lung by ventilating. **THAT I SAT DOWN**: that is, I placed myself in a seated position and steadied myself at the first arrival. And truly, sensuality labors greatly to escape from sin; so much so that having escaped it, it remains so exhausted that it goes no further. But Reason knows that it is not enough for a man to abstain from one vice if he does not then follow through with the knowledge of another to abstain similarly from that one; and then, having abstained from all, he labors in vain if he does not rise to virtue. For as Horace says: Although **Virtue is to flee vice** <note>original: "Virtus est vitium fugere"</note>, it is nonetheless necessary that, having conquered the difficulty of leaving sin, one must also conquer the difficulty of rising to the virtues. Therefore Virgil, that is, the intellect, comforts and pushes sensuality to such labor. And so what follows:

See what reason the intellect assigns to sensuality to push it toward the arduous things in which moral and intellectual virtue consist. **NOW** it is fitting that you thus—that is, as you are doing at present—**CAST OFF SLOTH**. *Poltro* signifies bed. Whence we call lazy and sleepy men *poltroni* <note>sluggards or cowards</note>. And *spoltre*

### Now it is fitting that you thus cast off sloth,
### said the master; for sitting on down feathers,
### or under a coverlet, one does not come to fame;
### Without which, he who consumes his life
### leaves such a vestige of himself on earth
### as smoke in the air, or foam upon the water.
### And therefore rise up; conquer the exhaustion
### with the spirit that wins every battle,
### if it does not collapse with its heavy body.
### A longer ladder it is fitting that you climb;
### it is not enough to have departed from these people;
### if you understand me, now act so that it profits you.

<column-break/>

*re* <note>original: "spoltre-re," to cast off sloth</note> signifies to get out of bed: that is, to wake oneself and leave sleep and idleness, and give oneself to the virtues, the way of which is fatiguing and steep. And he mentions lying on feathers and staying under a coverlet—which is a bed-covering—to represent the somnolent, lazy, idle, delicate, and voluptuous life, which is the enemy of every virtue and the mother of every vice. Whence Petrarch says: **Gluttony, sleep, and idle feathers have banished every virtue from the world** <note>original: "La gola el sonno et letiose piume Hanno del mondo ogni uirtu sbandita"</note>. The master said then—who is the intellect, the true master of the soul—that he who lives an idle and delicate life does not acquire fame. Here it seems that in admonishing Dante, Virgil should have said "virtue" rather than "fame." For a man ought to direct every action toward virtue, and should rather want virtue with infamy than fame with vice. All the sacred scriptures are full of this sentiment, and every grave philoso-

<column-break/>

-pher affirms that virtues should be sought for themselves, and not to acquire fame. But because fame follows virtue as a shadow follows the body, one should not flee fame if it follows behind virtue, provided that one does not seek virtue just to have fame. To this we will respond that he did not say "fame" without cause. For in this place, Virgil, who is a learned and wise man, admonishes Dante, who acts as one in whom appetite and sense still have more power than true reason. Therefore, having to encourage such a man toward virtue—which is full of difficulty and labor—the wise exhorter must allure him with fame, which is desired by every man. And just as the wise doctor, seeing the child refuse the healthful medicine because he is frightened by its bitterness, mixes honey with it so that the sweetness may trick him into drinking the bitter as well; so the wise teacher, seeing that the appetite is more greedy for fame than for virtue—whence the satirist Juvenal said: **For who embraces virtue itself if you take away the rewards?** <note>original: "Quis enim uirtutem amplectitur ipsam premia si tollas"</note>—proposes fame, for the sweetness of which one also takes the bitterness that is found in virtue at the beginning. <meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on Dante’s *Inferno*, Canto XXIV. The previous page discussed the physical exertion of the climb and the biological function of the lungs. We now move into the moral and allegorical significance of "fame" and the necessity of action over mere knowledge.</meta>

# CANTO XXIV

Indeed, one could also say that the poet used a poetic figure, putting that which follows for that which precedes: and he said "fame," meaning "virtue," which gives birth to fame. Fame is a neutral term <note>original: "nome di mezo"</note>, that is, one that extends to both evil and good. And we say a man has fame when his works are spread abroad and spoken of everywhere; if these works are vicious, they bring "ill fame." Therefore, the description of Fame placed by Virgil in the fourth book <note>Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book IV</note> denotes ill fame—that is, the infamy that Aeneas incurred for having left the straight path of virtue and giving himself to a voluptuous and base life, as I described at length in the fourth book of my *Camaldolese Disputations* where I explained Virgil's allegories. 

But if the works are virtuous, "good fame" follows. It is called "fame" because *fari* in Latin signifies "to speak"; and fame, as stated, is the frequent speaking of someone. And from fame—that is, from the frequent speaking of someone’s works—the "name" is born, because such a man is named everywhere; and from the name, he acquires glory. And glory is a certain splendor which results from good fame and a good name. **WITHOUT WHICH he who consumes his life**. He who lives without fame leaves no other vestige—that is, no other sign that he ever existed—than the smoke leaves in the air or the foam in the water, which, as we see, soon perish and leave no sign after them. A "vestige" <term>vestigio</term> is properly the form that the foot leaves on the ground, which we call a "trace" or "track." Hence we say "to track" and "to trace," or "to investigate" <note>original: "investigare"</note> when we follow someone's tracks to find them. By extension, we say "investigate" to mean searching with diligence. And we call "vestige" any sign which, remaining behind, demonstrates that a thing existed. Therefore, a ruined house, almost destroyed, we call the "vestiges" of a house. 

**AND THEREFORE RISE UP**: that is, rise from sitting, which signifies rising from vices and from the lowest and earthly things. **CONQUER THE BREATHLESSNESS** <term>ambascia</term>. *Ambascia* is an excessive abundance of breath which greatly troubles those who climb steep places. Therefore, just as the body is troubled by breathlessness when going uphill, so our sensuality, setting itself upon the steep path of virtue, is annoyed by that difficulty. But it is necessary to stir up the fortitude and the endurance of the soul, and with that, conquer every difficulty. And certainly, as the spirit is ready but the flesh—that is, the sensuality—is infirm and weak in resisting, it is necessary that the intellect stir up in us fortitude, endurance, patience, and perseverance; which, by conquering every difficulty, pushes the sensuality upward. 

**IF WITH ITS heavy body it does not collapse**. We properly say a thing "collapses" <term>accasciarsi</term> when, unable to support itself because of its weight, it lets itself go to the ground. Therefore, the sensuality and the appetite, being oppressed by the gravity of the body, collapse. But the soul, which by its nature is light, easily rises up to the knowledge of divine things if it does not let itself be weighed down by the contagions of the body. **A LONGER ladder you must climb**: which is not the one you have just climbed. **IT IS NOT ENOUGH to have departed from these**. Allegorically, understand that it is not enough to depart from vice if one does not also ascend to virtue. 

**IF YOU UNDERSTAND, see that it profits you**. Note that it is not enough for a man to understand what is to be done if he does not do it. Nor is he just, or temperate, or strong, who knows what justice, temperance, or fortitude is; but rather he who lives according to such virtues and puts them into practice. Hence Aristotle says: *Virtutis enim laus omnis in actione consistit* <note>original: "All praise of virtue consists in action."</note>. And understand this primarily regarding the moral virtues. Because in the intellectual virtues, a man can be such through knowledge alone, even if he does not put it into practice. Hence we say one is a good physician when he perfectly understands natural principles, even if he does not use them in anything; and similarly an arithmetician, even if he does not perform any calculation; and a geometer, even if he measures nothing, is called such if he knows how to count well and possesses every measure and proportion.

> I rose then, showing myself provided
> with better breath than I felt within me,
> and said: "Go on, for I am strong and bold."
> Up along the ridge we took our way,
> which was craggy, narrow, and difficult,
> and much steeper than the one before.
> I went on speaking so as not to seem faint,
> wherefore a voice came out of the other ditch,
> unsuited for forming words.
> I do not know what it said, although I was already
> upon the back of the arch that crosses there;
> but he who spoke seemed moved to anger.

<column-break/>

He describes the nature of one who is obedient to his teacher <term>preceptore</term>, who, although he does not feel vigorous enough for the labor imposed upon him, nevertheless shows himself to feel so, and says he is. **I ROSE**: because Virgil had said, "And therefore rise up." **AND I SAID: GO ON**. As if to say: "I will follow you." **I AM strong**, made so by the hope of the reward that you proposed to me; because as Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> says: *Honos alit artes omnesque accendimur ad studia gloria* <note>original: "Honor nourishes the arts, and we are all kindled to study by glory."</note>. 

**UP ALONG THE ridge we took our way, which was craggy**. This hurts the feet, which desire to find a delicate and even path. **NARROW**: A steep path, when it is narrow, is more difficult, because you cannot go zig-zagging as you can on a wide one. **AND DIFFICULT**. It follows that being steep, craggy, and narrow, it was difficult. **MUCH MORE than the one before**. The closer they go to the bottom, the heavier the vice found there; and the heavier it is, the more difficulty it gives to those who wish to know it in order to flee from it. Some say that the poet wishes to show the difficulty he had in finding the invention to poetically express this vice. 

**I WENT ON SPEAKING so as not to seem faint**: because the lower reason, already disposed to obey, shows itself more forward to the intellect than it can actually demonstrate of how willingly it obeys. **WHEREFORE A VOICE came out of the other**.

# CANTO XXIII

Scipio. These snakes are produced here by the nature of the place: But the fables say that when Perseus passed through this region with the head of Medusa, such snakes were generated from the drops of blood that fell from it. These are of diverse species and types: among which are the **chelydri**, called so as if they were **chersydri** <note>original: "chersydri"</note>: because they live equally on land and in water: and *chersos* <note>original: "chersos"</note> in Greek signifies land and *idor* <note>original: "idor"</note> signifies water. Furthermore, the **Jaculi** <note>original: "Iaculi"</note> are so called because they throw themselves from trees in the form of a dart <note>original: "jaculum"</note> and pierce the limbs; and the Latins call the dart *jaculum*. **Phareae** <note>original: "Pharee"</note> are snakes that move on their tails and keep the rest of their bodies raised from the ground. **Cenchri** <note>original: "Cencri"</note> are snakes that are spotted with points similar to grains of millet; they are so called because *kenchron* <note>original: "cencron"</note> in Greek signifies millet. They move straight ahead and do not twist like other snakes.

**Amphisbaena** <note>original: "Amphesibene"</note> have two heads, one where it naturally should be, and the other at the tail. Albertus Magnus denies that these have two heads: But he writes that it appears so because of the great mobility of the ribs from every side. It is in the first rank, and its venom kills in three hours.

**NOR SO MANY** pestilences: nor animals so pestiferous. **ETHIOPIA**. *Aithō* <note>original: "Etho"</note> in Greek signifies to burn. Hence Ethiopia is named from the immeasurable heat of the sun, which has the power to produce black men in that region. Ethiopia is full of immeasurable snakes which lie in wait and assault elephants; they put their heads into the nostrils where the elephant cannot reach with its trunk <note>original: "mano"</note> and suck the blood. Many snakes are found in that part of Ethiopia where the people called the Asachaei live. There they are found twenty cubits long. It is said that among the Liri <note>referring to a geographical location or people</note> four or five intertwine together and travel through the sea like ships, carrying their heads high like sails. In India they are as large as Megasthenes writes, swallowing deer and entire bulls. Pliny and many other historians affirm that Marcus Atilius Regulus, consul of the Romans in the first war against the Carthaginians, killed a snake one hundred and twenty feet long in Africa near the Bagrada river using catapults <note>original: "balestra"</note> and similar instruments. There is in Italy a species of snake called **boa** <note>original: "boia"</note>; and in the time of the Emperor Claudius one was found in Rome on the Vatican Hill which had an entire young child in its body.

**THE RED SEA** begins in Egypt and reaches to Palestine. Through this sea Moses passed with the people liberated from the hands of Pharaoh; it is called "red" not because its water is red, but because the earth beneath it is red and shows the water to be red. Others say it is named the Erythraean Sea after King Erythras; but since *erythros* <note>original: "Erithro"</note> in Greek signifies red, they called it red.

**AMIDST THIS** cruel and most sad abundance. Amidst this abundance of cruel snakes, full of sadness and continuous mourning, naked people ran, full of the terror they took from the snakes; and they did not hope to be able to find any hole <note>original: "pertuso"</note> or any opening to hide themselves from the snakes.

**NOR HELIOTROPE**: that is, nor anything that could make them invisible so that the snakes would not see them, as the **heliotrope** <note>original: "helitropia"</note> does. Solinus writes in the book *On the Wonders of the World* <note>original: "de mirabilibus mundi"</note> that the heliotrope is a stone found in Cyprus. But it is more noble in Ethiopia and Africa; it is green in color but clouded and distinguished by purple stars. When placed in a copper cauldron and struck by the sun, it causes the rays reflected from it to become blood-red. There is also a herb similarly called Heliotrope because it always turns toward the sun; *helios* <note>original: "helics"</note> in Greek signifies sun and *trepo* <note>original: "trepo"</note> signifies to turn. The magi write, therefore, that by anointing such a stone with the juice of such a herb, and consecrating it with the proper prayers, the man who carries it becomes invisible. Therefore, these sinners do not hope to be able to find a heliotrope by which they might be made invisible.

**WITH SERPENTS** their hands were tied behind. Because in this ditch <term>bolgia|a "ditch" or "pocket" in Dante's Hell</term> the author places the punishment of the thief <note>original: "furo"</note>, we should note that there are two ways one takes what belongs to others. Either openly and with violence: as do highwaymen, assassins, and road-blockers, and whoever else takes and despoils not by theft but by robbery, often killing to despoil.

Or by theft and in secret with fraud and deceit. The first are called *latrones* <note>robbers</note> by the Latins; the second are *fures* <note>thieves</note>. These second ones are called *fures* from the word *forvum* which in Latin signifies black and obscure, because he who wants to commit a theft seeks night and shadows and obscurity. Therefore, this seventh ditch being one of those where fraud and not violence is punished, it seems that we should treat here of thieves and not of robbers. Nevertheless, because even he who commits robberies with violence first uses fraud—and works with it more than with force, as we see in the highwayman who, before he assaults the traveler, hides in ambush and uses many other frauds—therefore robbery is punished mixed together with theft.

They stand, then, among the snakes, which are animals full of craftiness and cunning, to demonstrate that fraud and deceit are those vices which stain the soul and with which they afflict and perturb the conscience, by which they are always bitten with remorse after the error is committed. Let [the snakes] pass then with the head and the tail through the kidneys to the chest where the heart is, the seat of thought: because such fraud, with the head—that is, from the beginning before the sin is committed—gives great anxiety to the mind, weighing not only upon the sin it prepares to commit, but much more upon the danger of infamy and the harm that can result from it. And then with the tail—that is, after the end—rethinking what he has done, and expecting every hour that such wickedness will be discovered. From which result infamy and punishment. This is the head. This is the tail of the serpent: which, passing through the kidneys to the chest, pierces the heart and knots itself in front: because such thought and such a sting of conscience does not pass away; but remains tied in the mind, and stays forever. Nor can they hide themselves, nor flee such a sting of conscience, nor find any remedy for it: because as Juvenal says:

> This is the first punishment: that no guilty person is acquitted when he himself is the judge. <note>original: "Prima hec est ultio quod se iudice nemo nocens absoluitur"</note>

Therefore, no one who has committed any wickedness is acquitted by himself: because

his conscience always judges that he deserves punishment for the sin committed: and like a witness to such wickedness, it goads him night and day. For this reason, the same poet <note>Likely referring to Juvenal, though the commentator attributes the sentiment broadly to poetic wisdom.</note> said: <margin>Night and day to carry one's own witness in the breast <note>original: "Nocte dieque suum gestare in pectore testem"</note></margin> as the Pythian prophetess replied to a certain Spartan. They bind the hands behind the back because fraud leads to perverse and depraved actions. The hand signifies work: and just as the front parts demonstrate upright and laudable works, so the back parts denote the contrary. **THEY RAN** Naked and terrified. Running demonstrates the discourse of the mind in investigating frauds. They are naked: because most of the time poverty drives them—interpreting poverty as the greed for having: because everyone who does not have as much as they desire is poor. And terrified: because while they think of doing evil, the fear of being punished terrifies them. The serpent is cunning: and so is the thief. The serpent, slithering, enters through every hole. The thief sharpens his wits to enter every place. The serpent is hated by everyone: the thief is the same. The serpent, hidden among the grass, strikes. The thief harms from hiding.

And behold, at one who was near our bank,
a serpent struck him, piercing him
just where the neck and shoulders are knotted.
Neither "o" nor "i" was ever written so quickly
as he caught fire and burned, turning all to ash;
it was necessary that, falling, he vanished.
And after he was so destroyed upon the ground,
the dust gathered itself together by its own power,
and into that same man it returned at once.

Thus by the great sages it is confessed
that the phoenix dies and then is reborn,
when her five-hundredth year approaches.
She eats neither grass nor grain in her life:
but only tears of incense and amomum,
and nard and myrrh are her final swaddling clothes.
And like one who falls and knows not how,

when he rises, and looks around him,

Such was the sinner, once he had risen.
Oh, power of God, how severe it is,
that crashes down such blows in vengeance!

<column-break/>

They do not give the judgment of those who wish the poet to place three species of thieves. The first is of those who have not yet made it a habit. But finding the occasion to steal, they do not abstain: because as the proverb says, "at the open chest, even the just man sins." The second is of those who have already made it a habit and always intend to steal: but nonetheless use such discretion that they do not steal everything, nor in every place, nor from every person. The third is of those who have regard neither for place, nor time, nor person. Therefore, here he treats the first species, demonstrating that although one has not made a habit of stealing, yet happening upon the ability to conveniently take something, his appetite is suddenly Kindled: and he burns in such greed: and burning, he becomes ash: to show that such ardor makes him no longer a man, having lost his reason: and being so blinded by such desire that he feels or hears nothing else. But after he has fulfilled his desire,

reason returns: and he becomes a man again: and judges himself to have erred. But hindered either by shame or by avarice, he does not return the stolen goods. Therefore, the serpent, which is the greed for committing fraud, pierces him and in a moment burns him: and makes ash: that is, it transforms him from a man into a senseless thing: and then, having fallen into sin, he gathers himself together: and returns to being a man. He has expressed, therefore, the first species of thieves.

He affirms that this man's rebirth from his own ashes happens no differently than the phoenix. This is said to be a bird in Arabia as large as an eagle; its neck is the color of gold: the rest of the feathers are purple: except that the tail is azure: but distinct with feathers the color of a rose. They write that it lives five hundred and sixty years. Manilius the senator was the first of the Romans who wrote of the phoenix: and said that no one ever saw it feed; but that in Arabia it is consecrated to the sun. When it is old, it makes a nest of twigs of the cassia tree and of incense: and fills it with odors: and in that, it dies. From its marrow a worm is born: which afterward becomes a phoenix: and suddenly celebrates the funeral rites for its now-dead mother: and it carries the whole nest near the region of Panchaia in Arabia to the City of the Sun: and places it upon the altar. Its death is the revolution of the "Great Year": <note>A cyclical concept where the planets return to their original positions.</note> and that the qualities of the times and of the stars return to their beginning. And this

begins around the middle of that day when the sun enters Aries. Cornelius Valerianus writes: that the phoenix once flew in Egypt, and was brought to Rome in the time when Claudius was emperor and censor: and placed in the <term>Comitium</term> <note>A public meeting space in the Roman Forum.</note> in the eight-hundredth year from the founding of Rome. But no one doubts that this is false. Others write that when death comes, the phoenix turns toward the rays of the sun, and these, reflecting in the splendid feathers, create fire. Whereupon it burns together with the nest: and is reborn first as a worm: and after three days, its wings grow. **GRASS NOR GRAIN** It does not feed on, as other birds feed. But it feeds

# CANTO XXIIII

only TEARS: that is, gums or resins of incense and amomum: which distills like tears from its trunk: and then solidifies as we see in the juniper and in many other trees. Incense in Latin is called *thus* <note>original: "thus"</note>. Amomum, cinnamomum, and cinnamon are the same thing: it grows in Ethiopia in sterile places: it is a small tree that grows no higher than two cubits: they do not harvest it without the permission of Jove: And they obtain this with the internal organs of forty-four oxen, goats, and rams. When they have harvested it, they give half to the sun: and suddenly it catches fire and burns by itself. Vespasian was the first who, in the Capitol and in the Temple of Peace, dedicated a crown made of this wood ornamented with gold. AND NARD AND Myrrh are the final layers: that is, it makes the last nest of nard and myrrh in which it burns. Nard grows in India and produces spikes, whence it is called *spigho* <note>Spikenard; from the Italian "spiga" meaning ear or spike of grain</note>. It also grows in Syria; it grows in Gaul: and this is more well-known to us: and it even grows and is sown in Florence. It also grows in Crete. Myrrh is a tree that grows in Arabia in the same forests as incense. Others claim it grows in more regions of Arabia, whereas incense grows in no more than one called Sheba. This is a thorny tree and grows up to six cubits: the leaves are like those of the olive but wrinkled and sharp. Others describe it as similar to the juniper and of that flavor. AND WHAT is that. An excellent comparison by which he shows that since this man returned from ashes to his first form, he became stunned and dazed and foolish, as happens to one who, by the force of incantations or some <term>obstruction|opilatione: a medical term for a blockage of the humors or "spirits" in the body</term>, has been swooning and recovers. But in that beginning, he is astonished and almost senseless. BY THE FORCE Of a demon: that is, by incantation, as we read of Simon Magus: who by magic art made men swoon in a way that they truly seemed dead: and then, making them recover, he gave the common people to understand that he had the power to resurrect the dead. OR BY ANOTHER Obstruction that binds the man. Such as the <term>falling sickness|morbo comitiale: an old term for epilepsy, so named because an occurrence would suspend the 'comitia' or public assemblies in Rome</term>. It signifies allegorically that just as one who has swooned, either by diabolical incantation or by infirmity, remains stunned and wonders when he returns to himself: because he does not remember from what such a case proceeded. So when the sinner has fallen into theft, either by diabolical temptation or by the personal infirmity of his sensuality, he then wonders within himself how he allowed himself to be overcome by such a sin. O POWER OF GOD. With this exclamation, he admonishes the sinner that although He is full of mercy toward the living, nonetheless after death He uses nothing but severity: which is justice without any mercy. O how severe is the power of God THAT CRASHES DOWN: that is, with vehemence and great impetus He strikes such blows, that is, pains and punishments. Whence we say a "crash" of water when the rain falls with great force. FOR VENGEANCE: that is, for punishment: because vengeance is sometimes taken for legal punishment and is a species of justice.

I RAINED: that is, I fell down here damned: as is said of the demons who rain from heaven. INTO THIS THROAT: that is, into this hell which swallows and devours souls. He truly called this narrow valley a "throat" because the Latins call such places *fauces* <note>Latin for "jaws" or "throat," often used for narrow mountain passes or entrances</note>. ->BEASTLY LIFE<-

The leader then asked who he was,
because he replied, "I rained from Tuscany
a short time ago into this fierce throat.
A beastly life pleased me, and not human,
like the mule that I was; I am Vanni Fucci,
beast; Pistoia was a worthy den for me."
And I to the leader: "Tell him not to slip away,
and ask what fault pushed him down here,
for I saw him once as a man of blood and rages."

<column-break/>

IT Pleased me and not human. Although there are many types of living. For some give themselves to pleasure, wallowing in the mud like pigs. Some to sleep and idleness. Some to cruelty and robbery. Nonetheless, none of these can be called human life: because they are not according to the nature of man, but of beasts: which by their nature follow only appetite. But since man is different from other animals only by reason, that alone can be called human life: which is according to reason, in which other animals do not participate. But it is to be considered that in us there is a double reason. One called by philosophers "higher reason," which

<columns>1</columns>

turns and exercises itself around the knowledge of the truth: and such is found in universals. Wherein consist Intelligence, Science, and Wisdom. The other is "lower reason": and this has knowledge of particulars: and uses prudence, which is the true rule in human operations: and directs them toward right living by means of justice, fortitude, and temperance. Therefore, from the higher reason is born the contemplative life, in which we seek the true knowledge of things human and divine. From the lower reason is born the active life: in which, with the moral virtues, we direct ourselves, our family, and our republic toward right living. We direct ourselves with ethics; the family with economics; the republic with politics. For which reason, as I more openly demonstrated in the first book of the *Camaldolese Disputations*, only these two types of life—namely, the contemplative, represented by Rachel in the Old Testament and by Mary in the New; and the active, represented by Leah and Martha—are proper to man: because they are governed with reason. And every other type of life, where everything depends on unbridled appetite as appears in all the vices, is not human: because it is without reason. But it is beastly because appetite alone rules the beasts. Therefore, having given himself to homicides and robberies and extortions, and to larcenies and thefts, he did not follow the reason that is proper to man, but the appetite according to the...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Vanni Fucci, focusing on his character as a "beast" and the specific earthly crime that led him to this circle of Hell—the theft of the sacristy of San Iacopo—as well as his subsequent prophecy against Dante’s political faction.</meta>

# INFERNO

as beasts live, he lived a beastly life. **JUST AS THE Mule that I was.** It is no wonder that I lived like a beast, being a mule and not a man: and he alludes to this name "mule," which is a beast: because in the common tongue we call bastards "mules": and he was a bastard. **PISTOIA Was a worthy den for me:** as if to say that just as he was beastly, so Pistoia was a worthy habitation for him: because that city was a receptacle for beastly men: and therefore he calls it a den: because "den" <note>original: "tana"</note> signifies a cavern in the forest where wild beasts dwell. **TELL HIM Not to slip away:** that is, let him not flee. **THAT I SAW HIM A man of blood.** A cruel man and a shedder of human blood. **AND OF WRATH:** that is, hot-tempered. Dante marvels, since he had been such a violent, tyrannical man and a murderer: that he was not placed in the higher circles <note>the Seventh Circle, where the violent are punished in the river of blood</note> where such people are punished. Vanni was the son of Messer Fucci de' Lazzari of Pistoia, a noble family, but he was a bastard: yet he was of cruel, tyrannical, and beastly habits. It happened that in those times, many Pistoiese men were dining together one evening: and after dinner, with lutes and other instruments, they went singing through the land: and finally they arrived at the house of Ser Vanni della Nona, a very excellent notary and of good character, who was in their company. And while the others stopped to make merry—because he had a worthy and very beautiful wife—Vanni, with two companions, who was always spurred by diabolical thoughts, went toward the bishop’s palace <note>original: "uescouado"</note> which was near the house of Ser Vanni. Here, some say they accidentally found the door of the church and the sacristy of San Iacopo open, perhaps through the negligence of the priests who, on that night of Carnival <note>original: "carnasciale"</note>, had gone out for their pleasures as is the custom. Others say that with tools and picklocks they opened it: and finally they took from the sacristy all the silver and the jewels of the altar of San Iacopo, which were of great value. They returned to their companions, who, although they greatly rebuked the deed, nevertheless agreed to put the items in the house of Ser Vanni: both because it was the nearest place and because they thought that due to the man's good reputation, such a house would never be searched. The canons noticed the theft the next morning and gave notice to the Podestà <note>The chief magistrate of the city</note>. And he, diligently investigating, examined and tortured everyone he knew to be of bad reputation. Wherefore it happened that many, although they were innocent of this deed, nevertheless out of the pain of torture confessed to other things they had done, and were justly condemned to death. At last, Rampino, son of Messer Francesco Foresi, a noble citizen, was taken: and although he did not confess to the theft because he was truly innocent, nevertheless being of very bad reputation, the Podestà was so incensed against him that he had decided to condemn him. And he had already assigned him a certain term within which he must return the stolen goods. Because of this, Messer Francesco, in utter desperation, had arranged with relatives and friends on the night preceding the final day of the term to run with fire to the palace of the Podestà and take his son by force. But Vanni Fucci, who had retreated to the countryside of Florence, loving Rampino dearly, advised Messer Francesco to have Ser Vanni arrested. This man was taken one morning during Lent while he was in the church of the Friars Minor hearing the divine sermon: and he was led away, not without the indignation of the people, because he was considered to be of the best character. He confessed to having all the stolen goods with him, and said that he had often tried to take them out of the city. But every time he approached the gate, he seemed to see the knight who went looking for him: for this, he was hanged, and Rampino was freed.

The sinner who heard did not feign ignorance,
but directed his soul and his face toward me,
and was colored with sad shame.
Then he said: "It pains me more that you have caught me
in the misery where you see me,
than when I was taken from the other life.
I cannot deny what you ask;
I am put down so far because I was
a thief in the sacristy of the beautiful ornaments,
And falsely it was once attributed to another;
but so that you do not enjoy such a sight,
if ever you shall be out of these dark places,
Open your ears to my announcement and hear:
Pistoia first grows thin of the Blacks,
then Florence renews her people and her ways.
Mars draws a vapor from Val di Magra
which is wrapped in turbid clouds,
and with a storm impetuous and bitter..."

**DAnthe demonstrates** that Vanni was ashamed when he saw him: and affirmed that death had not been more painful to him than being caught in such a place. Which denotes that thieves feel such great sorrow from the infamy of being revealed that they would rather die. Then he narrates the theft committed; and as a man who is not a friend, judging that Dante takes pleasure in seeing him in such misery, to corrupt his pleasure with some pain, he predicts to him what must happen to the Whites <note>the political faction to which Dante belonged</note>. **OPEN YOUR EARS To my announcement and hear.** For the understanding of this text, you will note that in the year 1300, Pistoia was in great prosperity: and in that city, the Cancellieri family held great power, in which there were more than a hundred men of military age. Therefore, it was in great reputation and esteem not only in its own homeland but in all of Italy. This family, through a wicked accident—of which we shall speak below in chapter 32—split with capital hatred into two parties: one called the Whites <note>original: "bianchi"</note> and the other the Blacks <note>original: "neri"</note>. He continues to express the nature of Vanni: and demonstrates how much pride and impiety he used toward God: since, out of contempt, he showed Him the thumb between the smaller fingers. But immediately there followed due punishment after the sin: because a serpent coiled itself around his neck as if it wanted to strangle his throat: so that he could not speak: and another bound his hands behind: and then clinched itself in front: in such a way that he could not move. And by this it is allegorically demonstrated that it is no small punishment to the wicked man who delights in words and in making others sin: that the power of speaking and doing be taken from him. Of speaking, by binding his throat; of doing, by binding his hands. AH PISTOIA Pistoia: He uses an exclamation: which stirs indignation against Pistoia. Furthermore he uses gemination <note>A rhetorical device of repeating a word for emphasis.</note> by doubling the name. Which makes the speech more effective and more grave. WHY DO YOU NOT DECREE: that is, why do you not deliberate. TO TURN YOURSELF TO ASHES.

to burn and become ashes. SINCE IN Evil-doing you surpass and conquer your seed <note>original: "tu auanzi et uinci il tuo seme"</note>: that is, those who founded you, who were the seed from which you were born. And here many explain that the first founders of Pistoia were soldiers who remained after the defeat and death of Catiline <note>Lucius Sergius Catilina, a Roman politician who led a famous conspiracy against the Republic</note>: who, as Sallust writes, were full of wickedness and impious toward their homeland. Above, in the chapter where the tyrannical and violent men are punished, the poet placed the centaurs: and of those we spoke sufficiently there. Now he places Cacus here, who, although he is not the son of Ixion and the cloud as the centaurs are feigned to be, nevertheless he figures him as half-man and half-horse and calls him a centaur: because his habits were savage and beast-like. But he does not place him among the violent: but among the fraudulent: because in his thefts and robberies he mixed fraud with violence. And fraud is a more grievous sin than violence. And he shows that he is not only punished in this place: but also punishes the others. He accompanies him with Vanni Fucci: because they were similar in committing not only thefts: but also sacrilege. Vanni in taking sacred things from a sacred place. Cacus in taking the things of God, since Hercules was one of the gods of the gentiles. Cacus, of whom Virgil said <note>original: "Cacus aventine scelus atque infamia silvae"</note> *Cacus, the crime and infamy of the Aventine woods*. He was the son, according to the fables,
<columns>1</columns>
of Vulcan, the god of fire. They feign this because, being an infamous thief and robber, he laid waste to all the nearby countries with arson and fires. Whence they feign that fire and smoke issued from his mouth. He inhabited the Aventine, one of the seven hills of Rome: and in it he had a terrible cave: and the entrance to it he closed with a very heavy stone: and there he led all his prey. Finally, Hercules returning from Spain and leading the herds of cows which he had taken from Geryon, the king of Spain: Cacus, most greedy for new prey, stole four of them and pulled them by their tails into the cave. This was so that it might appear by the sign of the tracks that they had not gone into the cave, but had returned from it. Hercules searched for them much: and finally, not finding them, he was already departing when, at their lowing, he discovered where they were. He ran to the cave: Cacus defended himself by sending out smoke and flame. But the strength of Hercules was greater, who lifted a stone that covered the cave. He jumped inside and with his club killed Cacus and led away the cows. MAREMMA: Every maritime place where the winter is less cold, and the grass lives for the sustenance of flocks and herds, we call <term>Maremma</term> <note>A marshy coastal area of Tuscany known in Dante's time for being infested with snakes and malaria</note>, almost as if "maritima": and this happens mostly in Tuscany because such maremmas are turned toward the south: And in that of Pisa there is such an abundance of snakes that some places are uninhabitable because of them. UPON HIS back: because he is half horse. UNTO WHERE Our human face begins <note>original: "labbia"</note>: that is, as far as where the belly begins: which he calls "ours" because the centaur from the belly upward has human limbs. He calls the belly "labbia" because in it is the dregs and the filth, which in Latin is called *labes* <note>The commentator is using a creative etymology, linking the Italian word for face/lips ("labbia") to the Latin word for stain or ruin ("labes") to emphasize the impurity of the fraudulent</note>. The snakes or serpents denote frauds: which he places on the centaur upon his back: which limb in him is of a beast: to denote that the frauds were savage and cruel. UPON THE shoulders, behind the nape, with open wings there lay a dragon. He places a dragon for the same reason: and he placed it in the rear parts: to show that he uses cunning in vicious works. A man does not perceive the cunning used against him except from behind, that is, after the deed. WITH OPEN WINGS. Which demonstrates the vehemence and velocity in doing evil. WHICH Sets on fire whoever it encounters: that is, whoever runs into him. For every man who runs into fraud perishes by its fire.

...under the club of Hercules, who perhaps
gave him a hundred blows, yet he did not feel ten.

<note>This refers to the death of Cacus, who was beaten to death by Hercules; the poet suggests Cacus died so quickly from the first ten blows that he didn't even feel the remaining ninety.</note>

...of men: because in that place was the temple of Diana where today stands Santa Sabina: which was common to all the Latin peoples. Or truly because this hill was once surrounded by the river and one went there by boat. **OF BLOOD** He many times made a lake: Because he killed the men who passed through there, flooding the place with their blood. **HE DOES NOT GO** With his brothers: He does not go with the other centaurs: whom the poet calls his brothers, not because he was the son of Ixion like them, but because of the similarity of their limbs and their vices <note>Centaurs are usually punished for violence, but Cacus is here for fraud/theft</note>. And he does not walk the same path: because those others are punished as violent men, and this one is fraudulent: because the cattle of Hercules were stolen with fraud. Hercules, although he gave him a hundred blows with his club, nevertheless he did not feel ten of them: because they were so heavy that he died in the first few strokes.

While he was speaking, he [Cacus] ran past,
and three spirits came beneath us,
of whom neither I nor my leader were aware:
Except when I cried out, “Who are you?”
because our story was then interrupted,
and we then turned our attention only to them.
I did not know them; but it happened,
as usually follows by some chance:
that one had to name the other,
Saying, “Where can Gianfa have stayed?”
Wherefore, so that the leader would be attentive,
I placed my finger from my chin to my nose.

...of his own. But such artifice is easy for the learned to recognize and difficult for the unlearned. **GIANFA** Who remained. This man was of the Donati family, according to what many write <note>Gianfa Donati, a Florentine nobleman known for theft</note>. But no one records what theft he committed. Yet the poet subtly demonstrates here what often happens: that by chance, and without realizing it, one thief exposes another. **WHEREFORE** So that the leader would be attentive. This is a philosophical reason: that Dante perceives these men before Virgil does. Because the science of universals does not come to Virgil (that is, to the intellect) if first Dante (who represents the senses and lower reason) does not know the particular. Many will perhaps marvel that I so often repeat this same thing regarding the difference between superior and inferior reason. But let my excuse be necessity: which constrains me to repeat it as many times as it occurs, for without it, one cannot give the allegorical sense to the text. **I PLACED** My finger from my chin to my nose. This is the gesture by which we show that we want silence: because between the chin and the nose is the mouth, which, when pressed together, makes silence. Whence Juvenal said: *Restrain your lip with a finger* <note>original Latin: "Digito compesce labellum"</note>.

If you are now, reader, slow to believe
that which I shall tell, it will be no marvel:
for I who saw it hardly allow it to myself.
As I held my eyebrows raised toward them,
lo, a serpent with six feet launches itself
in front of one, and fastens itself all over him.
With the middle feet it grasped the belly,
and with the front ones it took the arms;
then it bit both one and the other cheek.
The hindmost feet descended to the thighs,
and it put its tail between them both,
and stretched it up behind over the loins.

<column-break/>

...granted that they should inhabit this mountain, they called it "Aventine" from an "Aventine Hill" which they had in their own countries. Others say it is named Aventine from the "arrival" <note>original: "aduento," meaning coming or arrival</note>, that is, from the arriving...

**AND THREE SPIRITS:** whom he will name from that group. Of whom neither he nor Virgil were yet aware. Which signifies that neither ancient history (which could be known to Virgil) nor modern history (which Dante had read) makes mention of these men. But Dante had heard them named: and therefore he adds that he did not know them. But it happened by chance that one named the other. And it is a marvelous thing in this poet, the variety in his narration to those who pay diligent attention: because he always varies with great artifice, and always with new invention changes the form of the narration. This variety refreshes the mind of the reader and removes the boredom and annoyance that arises from similarity. Nor can anyone hear many things with attention if they are all spoken in the same way. Furthermore, because his narrations are largely placed more in the persons than in the things, he always attributes to each person he brings to speak a speech which is suited to their nature and customs.

...A vivid invention, which through both the fiction and the allegory can not only delight, but lead the mind of the listener into the greatest wonder. At the beginning, he makes the reader attentive by showing he has to say things so new and unusual that he himself, who saw it, can hardly believe it. And therefore he says **IF YOU ARE NOW, reader**, slow to believe. He says, then, that a serpent with six feet threw itself upon one of the three spirits and joined its head and its face with those of the spirit: and joined the front feet and legs with his arms and hands, and with the middle legs embraced the chest and the belly: and those behind he stretched so far that he joined them with the legs of the spirit. This, as far as the hellish essence...

<sig>.p.iii.</sig>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto XXV of the Inferno, specifically focusing on the grotesque physical transformation of the Florentine thief Agnello Brunelleschi as he is attacked and fused with a six-legged serpent (representing the spirit of another thief, Cianfa Donati).</meta>

<page-num>XXV</page-num>
# INFERNO

Ivy was never so rooted
to a tree as that horrible beast
entwined its own limbs around the other's:
Then they stuck together as if they
had been of hot wax: and mixed their color
so that neither one nor the other seemed what he was.
Just as there moves ahead of the flame
across the paper a brown color
which is not yet black, and the white dies away.

The others watched him and each one
cried out: "Alas, Agnello, how you change!
See, you are already neither two nor one."
Already the two heads had become one,
when two figures appeared mixed
in one face where both were lost.
Two arms were made of four strips;
the thighs with the legs, the belly, and the chest
became limbs that were never seen before.
Every former aspect was destroyed;
the perverse image seemed to be both and neither,
and such it went away with slow step.

Just as the lizard, under the great lash
of the dog days, changing hedges,
seems like a lightning bolt if it crosses the path.

<column-break/>

...denotes that after death such a soul joins with the demon that was hidden within. And allegorically it demonstrates that when such a man has made a habit of fraud, he joins with it in such a way that no human intellect appears in him, but a serpentine one, to which he turns all his sharpness to harm with venom. But not entirely serpentine: because in some part he still retains human reason. For this is the second type among those who, although they have made a habit of this vice, nonetheless have some regard for not stealing everything from every man. Therefore, from the serpent and the man a certain thing is made that is neither serpent nor man. **I KEPT** my eyes raised toward them. This signifies that by diligently contemplating the nature of the thief, one recognizes this transformation. **BY THE MIDDLE** of the belly it seized him. The serpent joins head to head because the human senses become serpentine senses. Similarly, the union of the torso where the heart is signifies thoughts and meditations; and by the union of the arms and hands, understand the works; and by that of the legs and feet, the affections and desires. **AND IT PUT** its tail between both. This is the end and the effect which has cunning and the venom of a serpent, aided by the depraved reason of the man. **IVY WAS NEVER** so rooted to a tree. The nature of ivy is to cling to trees and walls, and it is always grasping, putting out certain "beards" and roots everywhere with which it clings. Hence in Latin it is called <term>hedera</term> <note>original Latin: "hedera ab herendo quia hereat", meaning ivy comes from 'clinging' because it clings</note>. **ENTWINED** That is, it stuck as the vine sticks with its tendrils. **THEN THEY STUCK**. As a most sharp writer, the poet demonstrates three stages in this transmutation: first, that being separate, the spirit and the serpent joined tightly, and through all the limbs like ivy, starting from the lower part of the leg, it went clinging up to the top. Nonetheless, although they were thus joined, they were not yet incorporated. Then follows the second stage in which they began to "flesh" together as if two candles of hot wax were stuck together. The third stage is that in which they mixed as if two vessels, one of gold and the other of silver, were melted and mixed together, and from the two metals a third body was made that had the color of neither gold nor silver. And this he demonstrates by comparison to the <term>lucignolo</term> <note>the wick</note> of a candle, which, first being white, when burned becomes black. But before it is burnt, it takes on a brown color between white and black. Whence he says **AS THERE MOVES** ahead of the flame a brown color. Brown is a color which is not fully black, but leans toward black. This the Latins call <term>fusco</term>. **ACROSS THE PAPER**. That is, through the wick which is made of cotton. Although <term>papyro</term> is a species of reed in Egypt, from whose marrow the ancients made many things which we make from cotton.

You might read how many transformations any Greek or Latin poet ever made <note>Landino likely refers here to Ovid's *Metamorphoses* and Lucan's *Pharsalia*</note>. But if I am not mistaken, you will not find any that equals this one in invention. In which he who reads may so greatly delight, marvel, and be amazed by its novelty and its well-hidden allegory. But let us follow the text. With wonder the companions said: **O AGNELLO** <note>Agnello Brunelleschi, a Florentine nobleman of the Ghibelline faction, punished here for theft</note> how you change: how can you convert into a species that is neither you nor the serpent? And he rightly says that two figures were mixed in one face, and in that they were lost: because there was no longer the figure of a serpent nor of a man. **TWO ARMS WERE MADE** of four strips. Because to the two arms were joined the two [front] legs of the serpent. Similarly the thighs and the legs. **EVERY FORMER ASPECT** was destroyed. That is, annulled. Both that of the serpent and that of the spirit. And the perverse image—that is, changed into its opposite—seemed neither one nor two. This allegory we have opened above, and the passage seems to me incomparable.

Here the author begins to treat the third type of theft, in which are those who have not only made a habit of it, but furthermore have no regard in their stealing, nor...

Landino's commentary interprets this transformation as the loss of human reason to serpentine fraud and praises Dante's imaginative superiority over classical poets.</summary>

### CANTO XXV.

So it appeared, coming toward the bellies
of the other two, a small serpent, inflamed,
livid and black as a peppercorn.
And that part where first is taken
our nourishment, he pierced in one of them;
then he fell down before him, stretched out.
The pierced one stared at it but said nothing;
instead, with feet fixed, he yawned,
just as if sleep or fever had assailed him.
He looked at the serpent, and it at him;
one through the wound, the other through the mouth,
smoked violently, and the smoke met.

<column-break/>

...of man, nor of thing, nor of place. He imagines, therefore, that while they were occupied in looking at the three spirits, a small serpent came with such velocity as a lizard crosses the path during the great heats: and it bit the navel of Master Buoso. And finally, the bitten one became a serpent, and the biting serpent took on the human form that it had lost; because previously it was the soul of Master Francesco Cavalcanti, as will appear later. **AS THE** lizard. The comparison is well-known: but some wish that by the various spots the lizard has, one should understand the various cunning and frauds used by the thief. **UNDER THE GREAT LASH.** *Ferza* [lash] we call a whip or scourge with which we beat either man or animal. Whence we say *sferzare* [to lash], to beat with a whip. And by metaphor we call

<column-break/>

the lash of the sun the most burning rays when they scourge us with the most heat. Therefore, "under the great lash" means under the great heat of the dog days. *Canicula* <note>The Dog Star, Sirius</note> among the Greeks is called *Syrios* <note>original: "Syrio"</note> for its brilliance, because it is a star of the first magnitude and shines greatly. Others want *Syrios* to come from *syrin* <note>Greek for drawing or dragging</note> which means to pull and extend: because this image extends for a long interval and occupies with its greatness almost the space of three signs. Furthermore, it is located in the middle center of the sky. When the sun rises to it, such heat is born that human bodies inflame in a way that, as Homer writes, various diseases and fevers plague them, if they are not relieved by the benevolence of another star. It is born, according to Albumasar <note>A famous Persian astrologer</note> in the 29th degree of Cancer: and from this, they are called the "dog days" <note>original: "caniculari"</note>, in which Hippocrates and other noble physicians forbid phlebotomy <note>bloodletting</note> and any purgative medicine. The Greek poets feign that this is the hound that was given together with a serpent to the guard of Europa, daughter of Agenor king of Phoenicia, and beloved by Jove; which later Cephalus the Athenian took to the hunt of Thebes against the fox that was wasting that countryside. And because it was ordained by the fates that neither the hound nor the fox could be killed, Jove transformed the fox into stone and the hound into this image. Some say that Icarius the Athenian was the inventor of wine in that region: and the shepherds who first drank from it, having become drunk, believed they had been poisoned and killed him. Erigone, his daughter, searching for her father's body, was led by her hound named Maera <note>original: "Neera"</note> to the place where he lay dead. Therefore Bacchus prayed Jove that the girl be converted into the sign of the Virgin, and the hound into this Dog Star. And the image of the Dog Star has these stars: one in the head called *Seirios* <note>original: "lius"</note>; one in the tongue, more splendid than all the others and of the first magnitude, and this is specifically called the Dog Star. In the neck, two. In each shoulder, one obscure; in the chest, two obscure. In the left front foot, three; in the right, one clear. In the extremity of the back, three. In the belly, two. In the left thigh, one; in the back left foot, one; in the tip of the tail, one. There are, therefore, twenty. We said a little earlier that the Dog Star in the time of Albumasar was born in the 29th of Cancer. But at present it is born in the 22nd of Leo. **LIGHTNING.** It seems like a flash of lightning because of its great speed. **IF IT CROSSES THE PATH.** Because having left the hedge for the path, it does not stop safely until it enters the other hedge. **TOWARD THE BELLIES.** <note>original: "INVERSO LEPE"</note> Toward the bellies and the guts. *Epa* in Tuscan means that part which is from the stomach to the pubic bone. **A SMALL SERPENT INFLAMED.** This shows that one thief, either by example or by persuasion, makes another a thief: and afterward it often happens that the serpent who has bitten the man—that is, the thief who has induced one who was not a thief to steal—recognizes the ugliness of this vice in the one who has become a thief through his bad example; and having recognized it, he removes himself from the vice. And as Buoso from a man became a serpent (that is, by the example of others he became a thief), so Francesco [became a man]. And this is especially expressed by saying that the smoke of one met the smoke of the other: because he recognized the ruin of such a vice in others and returned to being a man. **HE LOOKED AT IT BUT SAID NOTHING.** Because in looking at the operations of the thief, things happen in the act of stealing that completely alienate him from his mind and he falls to the earth: that is, into the greed for earthly things. **INFLAMED.** By this is shown the flame of greed without which no one would steal. **LIVID**, that is, harmful: because the thief harms his neighbor greatly by taking what is his; or rather livid, that is, envious. For out of envy that others should be richer than we, we set ourselves to stealing. And certainly, we would bear poverty in peace if we did not see the riches of others. Whence Jerome writes that "It is through the eyes that we cannot bear poverty." <note>original: "Oculi sunt per quos paupertatem ferre non possumus"</note> **AND BLACK.** As if to say poisonous and harmful. Whence Horace: "This man is black; you, Roman, beware of him." <note>original: "Hic niger est hunc tu romane caueto"</note> **AND THAT PART WHERE.** Through which our **Nourishment**, that is, sustenance, is first taken. This signifies the navel through which the child in the mother's body receives nourishment before taking it by mouth. He feigns that it bites the navel, from which the first nourishment comes, perhaps to denote that those who are so given to theft are those who...

The commentator provides extensive astronomical and mythological background on the "dog days" and the Dog Star (Sirius) to explain Dante's lizard simile.</summary>
