<meta>This page continues the commentary on the 25th Canto of the Inferno. The previous page discussed the arrival of a small serpent (Francesco de' Cavalcanti) who bites Buoso Donati in the navel, and begins to describe the symbolic significance of these physical actions in the context of the sin of theft.</meta>

<page-num>XXV</page-num>
### XXV CANTO OF THE INFERNO

from the beginning of their creation they have received such influence from the stars. Or truly he bit the navel, that is, he awakened concupiscence <note>A theological term for intense worldly desire or lust, often linked to original sin</note>: because the navel is placed to represent that. **THE PIERCED ONE** stared: but said nothing. Why he did so much from the inflamed serpent: that is, from the greed of stealing, which offered him the bite of the serpent, that is, of theft. **THAT** he said nothing: as if to say he could not argue against such great greed. **INSTEAD WITH FEET FIXED**. The feet are set for affection and for greed: which carries the soul to its operations: just as the feet carry the body. And certainly no power moves the soul to act if not the appetite. For this reason Homer feigns that Achilles could not be wounded except in the soles of his feet. **YAWNED** as if sleep or fever had assailed him. To yawn in Latin is called *oscitare* <note>original: "oscitare"</note>: that is, to open the mouth. The yawn is born from thick and cold vapors generated by the stomach from idleness and sloth: which rise and mount to the mouth by the path of food: and spread through the jaws. Wherefore nature, eager to push them out with an open mouth, aids them. **HE THE SERPENT**. Theft considers fraud in order to take it: and fraud looks at theft because it persuades it. **THE ONE THROUGH THE** wound of the navel and the other through the mouth smoked. Because he who persuades the theft smokes through the mouth: because he uses words: and he to whom it is persuaded smokes through the navel: because it inflames his greed. **THE SMOKE** met: because the words reached the greed: and the greed is set aflame by the words.

Let Lucan now be silent where he touches
upon the wretched Sabellus and Nasidius:
and wait to hear that which is now let fly.
Let Ovid be silent of Cadmus and Arethusa
for if he, in his poetry, converts that one into a serpent
and the other into a fountain, I do not envy him;
For two natures, face to face,
he never transmuted so that both forms
were ready to exchange their matter.

<column-break/>

**H**ere the poet demonstrates that neither Lucan nor Ovid, in feigning fables as poets are accustomed to do, have imagined such a marvelous transformation as I saw in this ditch. For they describe one being transmuted into another thing. But I saw two, where one was transmuted into the other. Therefore **LET LUCAN BE SILENT**: because the transfiguration seen by me surpasses that which he describes of Sabellus and Nasidius: Lucan writes that Sabellus, a soldier of Cato in the sandy Libya, was stung by a serpent called a *seps* <note>A small, highly venomous snake mentioned in ancient texts</note>: and such a sting in a short time consumed the whole body: and broke the skin and the flesh: and finally, like a most burning flame, reduced him to a little ash. And after this, the same poet places the contrary effect of another venom where a serpent called a *prester* <note>Another legendary venomous serpent, associated with swelling</note> stung Nasidius, a soldier of the same army: and such a bite swelled the body in a way that it burst his breastplate: and it grew so large that no member or joint could be discerned:

Nor of such a body did any beast
or bird taste that did not die.
Some say that the *prester* is a species of asp: and always goes with its mouth open and smoking: it causes the body stung by it to swell as mentioned: and after the great tumor, it putrefies. Let Lucan therefore be silent in his transfigurations: because they are not as admirable as these: which have such force in two that one is transformed into the other. And similarly, Ovid does not equal or match his *Metamorphoses*, that is, transmutations of Cadmus and Arethusa, with those I saw. Agenor was the king of Phoenicia. To him, his daughter called Europa was snatched away by Jove transfigured into a bull. For which reason he commanded Cadmus his son to search for her and never return without her: Cadmus, after a long investigation, despairing of finding her, decided to settle in Boeotia, a region of Greece: and there he killed a serpent consecrated to Mars: and with the counsel of Pallas <note>Athena</note> he sowed its teeth: and from such seed were born armed men: who, suddenly coming into battle among themselves, were slain: except for a few who helped him to build Thebes. It would be tedious to narrate the many misfortunes of Cadmus and his family: but finally, afflicted by them, perhaps thinking that changing country would change his fortune, he departed in his old age with his wife and came to Illyria, today called Capodistria: and here, repeating one day with his wife the various cases of fortune, they turned into serpents. Which the poets imagine to demonstrate that men who are of long life: and have experienced various and diverse cases of fortune, become through experience very prudent: and transform themselves into serpents: because the serpent is a most prudent animal. And Ovid adds that such serpents harm no one: indeed, they willingly saw men. Which can signify nothing else but that in them was that prudence which is the virtue that regulates us to live civilly: and to seek concord and tranquility: and to help ourselves and others: and to harm no one. And it was not a certain malice and wicked cunning which induces men to deceive other men: for which reason the Holy Scriptures, wishing to comfort us not toward vicious malice but toward virtuous prudence, said: **Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves.** <note>original: "Estote prudentes sicut serpentes et simplices sicut columbe"</note> As if to say, use the serpentine prudence: but let it be simple without cover or deceit: and just as doves harm no one, so you do not harm: but help, like Cadmus, who did many benefits to men: since he was a builder of cities: and to the Greeks, as Pliny reports, he brought from Phoenicia to Greece sixteen letters of the alphabet; Aristotle says eighteen. To which later, in the Trojan War, Palamedes added four. He was the first who found gold in Greece.

<summary>This page provides a symbolic commentary on the transformations in Inferno XXV, arguing that Dante's depiction of mutual transformation surpasses the classical examples of Lucan and Ovid. It interprets the serpent and the navel as symbols of greed and desire, while viewing the transformation of Cadmus into a serpent as an allegory for the development of prudence through experience.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto XXV. The previous page discussed the symbolic "smoke" rising from the thief and the serpent, representing the exchange of fraud and greed. This page transitions into the physical description of the metamorphosis, comparing Dante’s poetic skill to classical authors like Ovid.</meta>

### CANTO XXV

...and the method of melting it. Arethusa was a nymph, a companion of Diana. Returning from the hunt, she bathed naked in the river Alpheus to refresh herself; this river flows through Arcadia. For this reason, Alpheus, the god of that river, was immediately seized by love for the nymph and wished to defile her. Arethusa, being virginal and chaste, fled; and while running, due to great perspiration, she transformed into a spring. Diana, moved by pity, opened the earth for her. Thus, her water ran beneath the earth and beneath the sea, arriving in Sicily without mixing with the salt water. However, Alpheus did not stop following her because of this: having transformed into a river, he ran after her all the way to Sicily. The poets invent this because, in truth, the river Alpheus—according to most excellent writers—submerges underground in Arcadia and re-emerges in Sicily at the spring called Arethusa. **IF CADMUS**: that is, if Cadmus turned into a serpent <note>In Ovid's *Metamorphoses*, Cadmus is transformed into a snake as a punishment or fate</note>. **AND ARETHUSA**: that is, Arethusa [into a spring]. **I DO NOT envy him.** He says this as if to say: I do not consider these transformations greater than the one I saw; indeed, they are lesser. And so he says, "I do not envy him," meaning I bear him no envy, because we feel envy for things greater than our own, not for lesser ones. He provides the reason that their transformations were lesser: because never did two things ever exist together which transformed one into the other, as I saw Buoso <note>Buoso Donati, one of the five Florentine noblemen punished here for theft</note> turn into a serpent, and the serpent turn into Buoso.

Together they rested under such rules
that the serpent split its tail into a fork,
and the wounded one drew his footsteps together.

The legs with the thighs became so joined
to one another, that in a short time the seam
showed no sign that could be seen.

The split tail took on the shape
that the other was losing, and its skin
became soft, while the other's became hard.

I saw the arms enter through the armpits:
and the two feet of the beast, which were short,
lengthened as much as those [arms] shortened.

Then the hind feet, twisted together,
became the members that man conceals,
and the wretched one had two extended from his.

While the smoke veils both of them
with a new color, it generates hair
on one part, and strips it from the other.

...of the serpent: which, in becoming a man, had to be hairy in those parts. And from the other: the part that was Buoso’s. **STRIPS THE HAIR**: that is, removes the hair, because he was to become a serpent, which has no hair.

One rose up and the other fell down,
yet without turning away their wicked eyes,
beneath which each was changing his face.

The one who was standing drew his [snout] toward the temples:
and from the excess material that came there,
ears came out of the smooth cheeks.

That which did not run back and was retained
made a nose for the face from that excess,
and thickened the lips as much as was needed.

The one lying down thrusts his snout forward,
and pulls back his ears into his head,
just as a snail does with its horns.

And the tongue, which was once united and ready...

<column-break/>

It does not seem to me that any other allegory should be sought in these verses. Rather, one should admire the genius of the poet, who, to make the transformation believable, describes the form and the method with great industry. He says that the serpent’s tail divided into two parts and became two human legs, and Buoso's legs joined together and became a serpent’s tail. And thus the man’s skin became the hard hide of a serpent, and the serpent’s hide became tender human skin. Similarly, Buoso’s arms withdrew inside the armpits—that is, toward the shoulders—and became short like the paws of a serpent, and the front paws lengthened and became human arms. And the hind legs wound themselves together and became **THE MEMBERS** that man conceals and hides—that is, the male organ. **AND THE WRETCHED** Buoso **HAD** "porti" <note>Landino interprets the word "porti" as "distesi" or extended</note>: that is, two feet extended from his male organ. **WHILE** the smoke veils: that is, covers and hides. **BOTH OF THEM**: i.e., the serpent and Buoso. **GENERATES** the hair spread on one part. Arrange it thus: the smoke generates the spread hair. Understand this to be on the pubic area on one side; on the other, it makes him hairy in those parts. **AND FROM THE OTHER** part, because he was to become a serpent, which has no hair.

Up to this point, he has transformed the parts from the shoulders down in such a way that Buoso has become a serpent, and Francesco <note>Francesco de' Cavalcanti, the thief who was the serpent</note> has become a man from a serpent. Now he follows by transforming from there upward. And therefore he says: **ONE ROSE UP**: and this was Francesco, who, having made human legs from the serpentine tail, stood up on his feet. **AND THE OTHER** fell down. And Buoso, because his legs had become a serpent's tail and he could no longer stand upright like a man, fell. **THE ONE WHO** was standing: that is, Francesco, who was already standing upright, began to change his serpent snout into human form. The method was this: since we know that a serpent's snout is not as wide or thick as a man's face, but is long and thin, it was necessary for him, by pulling the snout back, to shorten it to the measure of a face...

I withdraw back toward the temples. **AND OF** that which, by pulling it back, had come toward the temples. **OUT OF THE CHEEKS:** The ears were formed, which protrude out from the cheeks: which in the serpent were absent <note>The original Italian "scempie" suggests they were simple or lacking features</note>: because the serpent has no ears protruding outward like a man. **THAT WHICH did not run back:** All that matter of the muzzle which did not withdraw back into the temples: But the face held it in front of itself as a nose and thickened the lips as we see in a man. **THAT WHICH lay down.** Buoso—having already become a serpent from the shoulders down—begins to change in the face: and as Francesco, by drawing in the muzzle, took on the face of a man: so Buoso, by lengthening the face, took on the muzzle of a serpent. **AND THE ears he withdraws through the head.** He almost makes them return inside: and he draws them in as the **snail** <term>limaccia: a term derived from the Latin "limax"</term> draws in its horns. The Latins call those that carry a house *cocleas* <note>original: "cocleas", meaning snails with shells</note>: and those that have no house *limaces* <note>original: "limaces", meaning slugs</note>. And in Florentine the former are called *chiocciole*: and the latter *lumache*. But the poet, to make the rhyme, said *limaccia* from the Latin word *limace*. **AND THE Tongue which he had**, understand Buoso, **United** that is, whole. **AND READY:** and prompt. **SPLITS:** It divides itself like that of a serpent. They say that the tongue of the serpent is two-forked or three-forked because it appears so due to the great speed that such an animal uses in moving its tongue. Whence Virgil says: <note>original: "Et linguis micat ore trisulcis" - And it flickers with three-pronged tongues in its mouth</note>. **AND THE FORKED:** and that which was forked and divided into two parts. **IN THE OTHER.** Understand in Francesco, who had the tongue of a serpent. This one, then, which was forked, closes and joins together like the tongue of a man. **THE SMOKE STOPS.** This denotes the end of the transfiguration. This is because the spirit of the one had gone entirely into the body of the other. And certainly, when the smoke, through the persuasion of another thief, is entirely stained by such a vice: and then he who has become a thief—he who was not a thief before—recognizes in others the infamy of such a vice: which he did not recognize in himself before: and he amends himself: the one becomes a man from a serpent: and the other becomes a serpent from a man.

He sets down what followed from such a mutation: and narrates that Buoso, having become a serpent, hissed: which means he whistled as serpents do. And he said "soul": because such a transfiguration was in the soul and not just the body. And Francesco, having returned to being a man, spoke and spat. Which is what men do: and

Many, because of this mutual and alternating mutation, wish to interpret that Messer Francesco and Messer Buoso had been companions in stealing: and had taken turns committing thefts. **THUS I saw the seventh ballast:** <term>zauorra: refers to the sand or gravel placed in the bilge of ships to stabilize them</term> that is, the seventh pit <note>bolgia</note>. *Sauorra* is sand and gravel placed in the bilge of ships: so that they do not wobble due to light weight. Therefore, he wisely compares this pit to sterile ground and a dark and fetid place like the bilge where the ballast stays. **CHANGE AND INTERCHANGE:** as has been shown above. **AND HERE let the novelty excuse me.** Certainly, he deserves excuse who has to narrate new and unheard-of things. Then he adds that although his eyes were confused by the novelty of the things: and his mind dismayed: that is, drawn out of its being and almost lost. Nonetheless, he recognized Puccio the Lame: and previously, by hearing them named, he had known Agnolo and Buoso. And these were the three that he saw from the beginning. Then by circumlocution, he declares that he who had returned to a man from a serpent was Messer Francesco "the Squinter" de' Cavalcanti: who was killed by the men of Gaville. This is a village located in the Upper Valdarno or rather in Chianti, fertile with the best wines. **YOU WEEP:** because in vengeance for the Cavalcanti, many peasants of Gaville were killed.

# CANTO XXVI OF DANTE’S FIRST CANTICLE

In this twenty-sixth canto, Dante shows how he arrived at the eighth ditch <note>bolgia</note>. In this place, he establishes that fraudulent counselors are punished within burning flames; and here he hears from Ulysses <note>Ulixe</note> about his end. But in the beginning, with the gravest indignation, he reproaches his homeland for the wicked sin of theft: and

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'G' set within a circular frame, surrounded by a square border with floral and foliate motifs.</image-desc>

**Rejoice**, Florence, since you are so great
that over sea and land you beat your wings:
and through Hell your name is spread.
Among the thieves I found five such
citizens of yours, from which shame comes to me,
and you do not rise to great honor by them.
But if toward the morning one dreams the truth,
you shall feel, a short time from now,
that which Prato <note>A neighboring town often at odds with Florence</note>, if no others, craves for you.
And if it had already happened, it would not be too soon;
would that it were so, since it must come to pass,
for it will weigh on me more as I grow older.

<column-break/>

he especially grieves that she is so impudent: that she is not ashamed of herself: rather, it seems to her that she is great. And there are several rhetorical colors <term>colori rhetorici: stylistic devices used to make speech more persuasive or vivid</term> here: first is **apostrophe**: or **exclamation**: which is when we turn our speech either to a person or an absent thing as if it were present, as we see the poet turns his speech to Florence: and this is done for many respects and especially out of indignation and grave complaint and rebuke. Then there is another "color" called **Irony**: and this is when the words have a contrary meaning to what we intend. Therefore he says **REJOICE**: and he means that she should be supremely saddened. **SINCE YOU ARE so great THAT OVER sea and land you beat your wings.** That is, that your fame is spread over sea and land: and he said "beat your wings" meaning you fly, or rather because Fame is depicted with wings. Wherefore Virgil said: *She flies by night* <note>original: "Nocte volat", a reference to the personification of Fame in the Aeneid</note>. **AND THROUGH Hell your name is spread**

---

**ed.** As if to say your fame is spread everywhere: But much more is she named for vices than for virtues. **AMONG THE Thieves.** Every learned writer, after irony, ought to place words which manifest what the irony made doubtful. Therefore, by saying he has found five noble citizens, he demonstrates that when he said "rejoice," he meant she should be saddened. **FIVE.** Cianfa Donati, Agnello Brunelleschi, Buoso Abati, Puccio Sciancato, Francesco Guercio. **SUCH** ones made so noble. Which is a greater disgrace. Because the greater the authority of the person, the uglier every vice is in them. Just as the more beautiful the garment is, the more a stain is out of place upon it. **BUT IF Toward the morning the truth is dreamed.** He shows that he has foreseen through a dream the calamities and civil dissensions between the White and Black factions <note>The warring political factions of Florence</note> that were to afflict Florence; which in truth had occurred before the poet wrote this work. But he pretends to have written it earlier. Therefore he says "if my dream made toward morning is true," which ought to be true. There are five species of dreaming: Three true. Two false. The Latins call the true ones **Dream**, **Vision**, and **Oracle** <note>original: "Somnium", "Visionem", "Oraculum"</note>. **Dream** is when we dream the truth: But it is obscure and cannot be understood without interpreters, as

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the opening of Canto XXVI, where Dante prophesies the coming woes of Florence. It concludes the discussion on the nature of dreams and moves into the physical and allegorical description of the poets' climb out of the seventh circle.</meta>

<header>INFERNO</header>

when the one who was in prison with Joseph dreamed that he pressed the grapes of three vine-branches into Pharaoh’s cup: and Joseph predicted to him how in three days he would be freed: and afterwards he would become the king's **pincerna** <term>pincerna: a cupbearer or servant who serves wine</term>, that is, his cup-servant. And Polycrates, King of Samos, dreamed that Jove washed him and Phoebus, god of the sun, anointed him: and shortly after, the prefect of Xerxes had him crucified, and he remained on the cross so long that Jove—that is, the air—rained upon him and washed him; and Phoebus—that is, the sun—liquefied and melted the fat of his body. Whence he became "anointed." **Oracle** is when, while sleeping, it seems that someone speaks to us, and what they say turns out to be true. **Vision** is when, while sleeping, we seem to see something, which then appears just as we saw it. Two false types of dreaming are **Insomnium** and **phantasma**. **Insomnium** is when we dream false things: and it proceeds from having taken too much food which, as it sends vapors up to the head, makes us seem to fly or climb. Or, as catarrh descends, we seem to fall. Sometimes it comes from too little food, which makes us seem to be hungry. Sometimes from corrupted humors. Whence choler <note>yellow bile, associated with a fiery temperament</note> makes us see fire and similar things. Phlegm makes us see water. Blood makes us see cheerful things. Melancholy <note>black bile</note> makes us see black and frightening things. It can also be born from the cares and thoughts of the soul. Whence we often dream that either what we thought of while awake is given to us or taken from us. But when we have the soul free from every thought, and the body not weighed down by food or humors, it happens that our soul, through sleep, almost loosens itself from the body and returns to its nature, which is divine: and it can foresee future things. And this happens especially near daybreak: because having digested our food, we remain more unburdened and the body weighs on us less. And for this, the poet said: **BUT IF TOWARD THE MORNING ONE DREAMS THE TRUTH.** Similarly, Ovid says: <note>original: "Namque sub aurora iam dormitante lucina / Somnia quo cerni tempora uera solent."</note> "For near dawn, when the morning light is already fading, is the time when true dreams are usually seen." Nor should it be overlooked that sometimes dreams come through diabolical illusion. Whence Job says in chapter seven: <note>original: "Terrebis me per somnia."</note> "You shall terrify me through dreams." And Gregory says: <note>original: "Ideo sanctos uigilando tentare non ualet grauius per somnia dormiendo tentat."</note> "Therefore, he [the devil] who is unable to tempt the saints while they are awake, tempts them more severely through dreams while they sleep." For which reason the highest teacher, Christ, commanded his disciples to watch, so that they would not enter into temptation. **YOU SHALL FEEL SHORTLY FROM NOW OF THAT:** that is, of those things. **WHICH PRATO CRAVES:** that is, desires for you. **IF NO OTHERS:** that is, no greater or more distant land. As if to say, not only the distant cities, but even a nearby castle. Many believe he says "Prato" out of respect for Cardinal Niccolò da Prato, who was very hostile to our republic. And certainly, shortly after the poet's exile, it happened that during games with great spectacle at the Carraia bridge—which was then made of wood—there was such a gathering of people that the bridge collapsed, and many perished, and even more remained crippled. This filled the city with sudden mourning, not only for those who had lost their kin in that event, but also for those who believed they had lost them. This spectacle represented Hell, with fire and demons who tormented damned souls with various punishments. That event was an omen both of the civil war that was born in the same year between the Whites and the Blacks, and of the fire which consumed over two thousand two hundred houses and burned many precious things. The fire was started by his own wicked work, with which Neri Abati <note>OCR: "de glabati"</note>, prior of San Pietro Scheraggio, set fire to the houses of his own kin. **AND IF IT HAD ALREADY HAPPENED, IT WOULD NOT BE TOO SOON.** The author shows himself desirous of this evil: not for the ruin of his homeland, which was most dear to him, but for the punishment of the wicked citizens who were iniquitously administering it. And therefore he desires it to be soon, so that those who have erred may be punished. And similarly, he shows that the more **IT AGES**—that is, the more it delays and lingers—the more it is troublesome to him. Because he desires that such fortune punish the wicked leaders and free the unhappy people.

We departed, and by the stairs
that the rocky bounds <note>borni</note> had made for our descent before,
my master climbed back up and drew me.
And pursuing the solitary way
among the shards and rocks of the ridge,
the foot without the hand did not make its way.

<column-break/>

This demonstrates the difficulty of the return. Which denotes that falling into the valley of vices is easy: but departing from it is difficult. Whence Virgil says: <note>original: "facilis descensus auerni: / Sed reuocare gradum superasque euadere ad auras / Hoc opus hic labor est."</note> "The descent to Avernus [Hell] is easy: But to retrace one's steps and escape to the upper air, this is the task, this is the labor." And he writes: **UPON THE STAIRS** which, when they had descended by them, had made them **BORNI**: that is, dazzled and of poor sight. For *bornio* in the Bolognese dialect means this. **MY MASTER CLIMBED BACK UP.** Because the intellect is that which, having recognized the ugliness of vice, returns to virtue. **AND DREW ME:** The intellect returns to virtue by itself. But sensuality would not return if it were not pulled back by the intellect. **THE SOLITARY WAY:** that is, the lonely path. To denote that the path by which we contemplate the ugliness of vice is solitary because few go by it. Whence Petrarch says: "Poor and naked you go, Philosophy, says the crowd intent on base gain; you will have few companions on your way." **AMONG THE SHARDS AND ROCKS OF THE RIDGE.** He calls the "ridge" that stone which forms a bridge over the ditches <note>bolge</note>. "Shards" <note>schegge</note> are fissures made along the length of the ridge, and "rocks" <note>rocchi</note> are breaks made across it. **THE FOOT WITHOUT THE HAND DID NOT MAKE ITS WAY.** There was such difficulty in climbing that one could not ascend unless the hands were used for support. And by this, he denotes the difficulty of escaping from sin. For the feet, which signify the "affect" <note>the emotional inclination or will</note>, do not depart from sin—in which we have formed a habit and in which we take pleasure—unless the hands, which are the works...

<meta>This page transitions from the general discussion of dreams and portents into the specific commentary on Canto XXVI of the Inferno. The author, Cristoforo Landino, is moving from the climb out of the previous circle to the moral and philosophical preparation for the Eighth Bolgia, where the Fraudulent Counselors are punished.</meta>

->### CANTO XXVI<-

reason and action do not draw them up, meaning the virtuous actions and operations which pull us out of the habit of vice and place us in the habit of virtue.

These two tercets <note>A poetic unit of three lines, typical of Dante’s terza rima</note> have the force of a preface to the narrative which deals with the vice of fraudulence, which is treated in the eighth bolgia <term>bolgia: literally a "pouch" or "ditch," referring to the ten trenches of the eighth circle of Hell</term>. And by admonishing himself regarding what he feels he must guard against, he makes the listener attentive and gains goodwill by condemning the vice. And so that his meaning may be more

I sorrowed then, and now I sorrow again,
when I direct my mind to what I saw;
and I curb my wit more than I am wont,
lest it run where virtue does not guide it;
so that, if a good star or a better thing
has given me the good, I do not begrudge it to myself.

<column-break/>

aptly understood, we shall say that in treating here the punishment of those who used the sharpness and subtlety of wit—granted to us by God to be used for good—to deceive their neighbor, he wishes by admonishing himself to admonish the listener; that whoever has from nature a subtle wit apt for achieving knowledge in all practical and active things ought to use it for the utility and honor of himself and his neighbor; and in this form, he shall be called **prudent**. For **prudence** is

nothing other than a right discourse of the mind in governing and managing the things that consist in civil life, of which we have spoken. **I SORROWED THEN** when I recognized that those were punished there who had used the subtlety of wit not in prudence, but in fraud and cunning to the harm of their neighbor. **AND NOW I sorrow again.** He demonstrates what is required to want to strip oneself entirely of the habit of vice. For it is not enough, moved by the penalty, to grieve in the moment. Rather, it is necessary to persevere in the purpose and to grieve continually. And this will easily be done by directing the mind: that is, considering continually that which we have seen happen to those who are fraudulent. **AND I CURB my wit more than I am wont.** He sets down the fruit that is born from this assiduous meditation: and this is that, seeing the evil that is born from such vice, we restrain our wit and our sharpness so that it does not run unless virtue guides it. For if we use it for good, it will be prudence; if for evil, it will be fraud. **SO THAT IF a good star or a better thing has given me the good, I do not begrudge it to myself.** This is the reason why he wants the wit not to run without the guidance of virtue. For if I have received this good of having excellent wit, either from a star or from a better thing (that is, from God), I do not want to begrudge it to myself: that is, I do not want to take it away from myself. For by taking away the good, it would seem that I bore envy toward myself. And note why the poet says of this good of the sharpness of wit that either a star or a "better thing" gave it to him. For the human soul—not only according to theologians, but also according to many philosophers, and especially the Platonists—is created by God immediately <note>meaning "directly," without intermediaries</note>. Whence it has a great gift in its creation from God, and especially because He creates it in His image. Whence it is capable of reason and intellect. For this reason, it receives all its virtues and powers from God; and in itself, it is not subject to celestial influences but is superior to them. But because while it is in the body, the soul cannot exercise its forces and powers without the bodily instruments, and these are subject to the stars; and because the stars induce in some bodies excellent and optimally disposed instruments, and in others coarse, inept, and ill-disposed ones, it happens that although souls are created equal, nevertheless some men, through having instruments apt for a benign celestial influence, are ingenious and subtle. Others, having them through an unhappy influence, are by contrast coarse and slow. Whence it can be said that the sharpness and the slowness of wit come to us from the stars: not because they can do anything in the soul, but with respect to the instruments. Therefore, he said **so that a good star**, with respect to the instruments of the body, and **a better thing**, with respect to the soul being created by God immediately.

As many as the peasant who rests on the hill,
in the time when he who lightens the world
keeps his face least hidden from us,
when the fly gives way to the mosquito,
sees fireflies down through the valley,
perhaps there where he harvests and plows:
with as many flames all did shine
the eighth bolgia, as I perceived
as soon as I was where the bottom appeared.

<column-break/>

Having already arrived upon the crag from which the eighth [bolgia] was seen, by an excellent comparison: in that ditch, he saw as many flames as the peasant, who rests on the hill above the valley, is wont to see fireflies in the evening. With so many flames did all the eighth bolgia shine. **AS MANY AS THE peasant.** "As many" you should understand as "fireflies." The peasant: the rustic who rests on the hill. **IN THE TIME when he who lightens the world keeps his face least hidden from us.** He uses here a rhetorical figure called **circumlocution** <note>original: "circunlocutione"</note>. He could have simply

said here "In the time of summer." But to adorn the poem, he used more words, saying "In the time when he who lightens the world," which means in the time of the sun. For the sun is that which lightens—that is, makes clear and luminous—the world. He says, therefore, when the peasant rests in the time the sun stays less [hidden]...

<summary>Landino comments on Dante's self-admonition regarding the use of "ingegno" (wit/intellect), explaining that intellectual gifts must be guided by virtue to be "prudence" rather than "fraud." He also interprets Dante's simile of the fireflies, noting the rhetorical beauty and the philosophical distinction between the soul's divine origin and the stars' influence on the physical body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Eighth Bolgia of the Inferno. The previous page introduced Dante’s self-reflection on his own intellect, warning himself not to misuse the gifts of "wit" as the fraudulent counselors did. Here, Landino begins to describe the visual scene of the flames and the allegorical reasons for this specific punishment.</meta>

LXXVIII
-># INFERNO<-

and in a shorter space, its face is less hidden from us—and this is summer—because its face is hidden from us for a shorter time at night, and in that season the nights are brief. In this manner, he describes that season of the year which we call **summer**. Then he follows and describes the night with the same colorful circumlocution, saying: **AS THE fly yields to the mosquito**. As night comes. For the fly, which comes out during the day, retires when night falls, and **YIELDS**, that is, gives place to the mosquito, which remains hidden during the day and comes out at night. **HE SEES Fireflies down through the valley**: that is, down in the ditch. **PERHAPS THERE Where he harvests the grapes and plows**: meaning in his fields and vineyards. **With so many flames the eighth bolgia <term>bolgia: one of the ten circular trenches in the eighth circle of Hell</term> was all resplendent.** He organizes it thus: The eighth bolgia was resplendent with as many flames as the fireflies the peasant sees down in the valley where he harvests and plows, while he rests on the hillside at the time when the one who lightens the world <note>The Sun</note> keeps his face least hidden from us. And he sees them in the evening when the fly yields to the mosquito. I became aware of this when I arrived upon the bridge from which I could see the bottom of the bolgia. **FIREFLIES**: These are luminous animals known to all; the Greeks name them *lampyrides* <note>original: "lampyrides" from "lampas," meaning light or torch</note>. The poet feigns, not without the highest prudence, that the fraudulent are punished in fire. If we understand this as the essential fire of Hell, it is a fitting punishment that he who has inflamed others with fraud should himself burn similarly. But allegorically, we shall say that such fraud is fire because it has the power to ignite dissension, discord, and wars. Regarding this, the Psalmist says: *The sons of men, whose teeth are weapons and arrows: and sharp with devouring coals* <note>original: "Filii hominum dentes eorum arma et sagitte potentes : et acute cum carbonibus desolatoriis." A reference to Psalms 57:4 and 120:4</note>. Furthermore, it is fire because it is born from a sharp wit, and a sharp wit is born from the heat of the blood. Conversely, cold blood produces a slowness of wit; wishing to express this, Virgil said: *Cold blood stood around the heart* <note>original: "Frigidus extiterit circum precordia sanguis." From Virgil’s Georgics, II.484, reflecting the ancient theory that intelligence depended on the temperature of the blood</note>. One sees the flame but not the sinner, because the speech of the fraudulent person is manifest, but his fraud is hidden and concealed. Dante did not see the bolgia of the thieves <note>the seventh bolgia</note> because that place was dark, as in that sin every action and word is hidden. He sees the bolgia of the fraudulent because their words are manifest, but their counsel is hidden. And this category of people is the worst. The sinners stand separated, each in his own flame, because he who wishes to deceive does not communicate his counsel to others, unless they share the same will. For this reason, he places Ulysses and Diomedes together.

He demonstrated above that the entire valley of the eighth bolgia was full of flames. Now he shows that each of these flames held a sinner hidden within it, so wrapped up in it that he could not be seen. All these flames rose up through the throat of the valley, keeping the sinner hidden within—

<column-break/>

> And as he who was avenged by the bears
> saw the chariot of Elijah at its departure
> when the horses rose erect toward heaven;
> 
> For he could not so follow it with his eyes
> as to see anything but the flame alone,
> like a small cloud ascending upward.
> 
> So each flame moves through the throat
> of the ditch, for none shows the theft,
> and every flame steals away a sinner.

<column-break/>

—Just as perhaps the chariot of Elijah <note>original: "Helya"</note> was when, enveloped in fire, it rose to heaven. And Elisha <note>original: "Heliseo"</note>, looking up, saw the chariot rising, but he did not see Elijah within it because the flame covered him. **AND AS He who was avenged**: that is, he who was avenged **BY THE BEARS**. This was Elisha. For the clarification of this text, let us remember that in the Fourth Book of Kings <note>modern 2 Kings</note> of the Hebrews, which is part of the Old Testament contained in the Bible, one reads that Elijah was the highest and true prophet in the time when Joram reigned. After many miracles, God wished to take him up to heaven. Therefore, he came from Jericho to the river Jordan with Elisha. He took off his cloak and touched the river with it, and immediately

<column-break/>

the waters divided and left a dry path by which the prophets passed. Then, continuing on their way, a chariot of fire suddenly descended from heaven guided by horses of fire, into which Elijah climbed and was snatched on high. Elisha, having gathered the cloak that had fallen during the ascent, returned to the Jordan and divided the water with it and returned to Jericho. From there, going into Bethel, some children came to meet him and, mocking him, said "Come up, you bald head!" <note>original: "vienne caluo"</note> as if reproaching him by saying he lied about Elijah being so snatched away. Elisha cursed them in the name of God. Immediately, two bears came out of the woods and tore forty-two of those children. You see, then, why by saying "he who was avenged by the bears," he means Elisha, who saw the chariot of Elijah snatched to heaven. **BY HORSES ERECT**: that is, upright and raised up. But although he followed it with his eyes, he could discern nothing but the flame, which mounted upward like a cloud from the earth mounts into the air. The text is organized thus: Each flame moves through the throat of the ditch just like the chariot of Elijah, which Elisha saw when the horses rose erect to heaven. And Elisha could not follow the chariot **SO**: that is, in such a way that he saw anything other than the flame alone. **AND EVERY Flame steals away a sinner**: that is, it hides a sinner within itself and does not show the "theft" <note>In this context, the "theft" is the sinner being hidden or "stolen" from view by the flame</note>. In this eighth bolgia are punished those who, under the appearance of giving faithful and prudent counsel to their neighbor, give him harmful counsel through fraud. This counsel can be given not only by speaking or writing, but also with gestures and signs. Sinon deceived the Trojans with words. The followers of such counsel are Simulation, Dissimulation, Lying, Falsehood, and the like; and it gives birth to damage to one's neighbor, either in himself or in his property.

**Eteocles**: But not wishing to yield to his brother Polynices when the year ended, he—with the help of his father-in-law Adrastus, king of Argos, and his brother-in-law Tydeus—led an army of seven kings to Thebes and fought with his brother with such fury that they killed each other. Afterward, with great cunning, they entered Troy at night and took from the temple of Minerva the statue of this goddess, which was called the Palladium, without which the Greeks could not take Troy. And finally, they arranged the horse full of armed men with such fraud that the Trojans brought it into the city; and so that it could enter, they broke down a gate and the tomb of Laomedon which was above that gate. Therefore the poet says: **THE JOINING OF THE HORSE** <note>original: "EL GIVNTO DEL CAVALLO"</note> because with that they "joined"—that is, deceived—the Trojans, who broke the gate. From which Aeneas then went out, from whom the Romans had their origin. Dante shows himself very desirous of speaking with Ulysses and Diomedes if they, enclosed in the sparks—that is, in the flames—can speak. This denotes that the lower reason <note>In Landino's commentary, Dante the character often represents "lower reason" (human appetite and curiosity), while Virgil represents "higher reason" (human wisdom/philosophy)</note> is always greedy and eager to know every particular. **AND HE TO ME: YOUR PRAYER IS WORTHY.** The higher reason approves the will of the lower. But he does not want Dante to be the one who asks. Nor is it without reason. For having to deal with this vice which arises from sharpness of wit and intellect, it is necessary that the higher reason be the one who examines. Therefore he admonishes him to restrain his tongue—that is, keep silence—and adds: **LEAVE Speaking to me. FOR I HAVE Conceived:** that is, conceived and understood, **WHAT YOU WISH** to learn from them. Therefore he could ask them. **FOR THEY WOULD BE SHY** perhaps because they were Greeks, of your speech. The literal meaning is that things written in Greek seem to tolerate the Latin language rather than the Tuscan tongue <note>There was a Renaissance belief that ancient Greeks would only deign to speak to those of equal literary stature or who spoke "noble" Latin rather than the "vulgar" Italian vernacular</note>. But allegorically it is what we said above.

**A**fter he had admonished Dante to be silent, Virgil began to speak; and he prays them by the fame which he gave them in life in his *Aeneid*: that Ulysses narrate to him where, lost for him—that is, as far as he was dead—**HE WENT** <note>original: "GISSI," an archaic form of "andasse"</note> to die. Because, as you will see a little below, Dante does not describe that after many errors he returned home, but that he perished in the ocean. And not without reason did he say: **I wrote the high verses.** For Virgil, besides many small works which he composed in early youth, wrote three volumes: the *Bucolics*, the *Georgics*, and the *Aeneid*. Of these, the first is in the low style. The second in the mediocre. The third in the high and sublime. Therefore, saying "the high verses," he meant the *Aeneid*.

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on Canto XXVI of the *Inferno*. The previous page concluded a summary of the mythological travels of Ulysses (Odysseus), interpreting them as a Neoplatonic allegory for the soul's journey through vice toward virtue. ### CANTO XXVI

Because he has already imagined that Ulysses and Diomedes are within the same flame, and for this reason it has two points—or, if we prefer, two horns—he demonstrates now that the larger horn contained Ulysses, and that one began to speak. He makes Ulysses’s horn larger because in him there was greater cunning and more fraud. Therefore: **THE GREATER HORN**

**The greater horn** of the ancient flame
began to sway, murmuring,
just like a flame that the wind exhausts.
Then, waving its tip here and there,
as if it were a tongue that spoke,
it threw out a voice and said: "When
I departed from Circe, who hid 
me for more than a year there near Gaeta,
before Aeneas had so named it,
neither sweetness for my son, nor the pity
due to an old father, nor the rightful love
that should have made Penelope glad,
could conquer within me the passion
I had to gain experience of the world,
and of human vices and of worth;
but I set out upon the deep, open sea
with but a single ship, and with that small
company by which I was not deserted.
I saw one shore and the other as far as Spain,
as far as Morocco and the island of Sardinia,
and the others that the sea bathes round about.
I and my companions were old and slow
when we came to that narrow strait
where Hercules set up his markers,
so that man should not venture further.
On the right hand I left Seville;
on the other, Ceuta had already left me."

<column-break/>

Where the spirit of Ulysses was. **FROM THE Ancient flame.** He called it "ancient" because of the long time it had been in Hell until Dante’s day. **TO SWAY** Murmuring. An excellent poet: who, while imagining the impossible thing of a flame speaking, strives as much as he can not to depart entirely from the nature of a flame; for while a flame does not speak, it nevertheless murmurs, and such murmuring is born when a certain wind, emerging from the burning matter, strikes it. **TO SWAY.** To move with a murmuring sound. **AS THE ONE WHICH: that which. THE WIND EXHAUSTS** that is, beats and agitates. **THEN THE TIP** the summit. He strives, as far as the nature of the thing allows, to make his narration believable. **IT THREW** A voice out. As if to say: it did not speak entirely like a human, but threw or pushed the voice out without much order. **AND SAID.** And then follows the narration of Ulysses, which begins: **WHEN I DEPARTED** from Circe, as we said above.

Circe, according to some, was the daughter of the Sun and of Colchis; she came to Italy and lived on the island named Circeo after her, which in time became part of the mainland. The poets say that by magic arts she converted men into various beasts, and that she converted Ulysses's companions. But later, Ulysses, with the help of Mercury, frightened her, and she restored his companions to their original form. By Circe, they <note>Landino refers to the allegorical commentators</note> mean bodily pleasures and worldly delights, which, by taking every virtue away from a man, make him a beast. But Ulysses, with the help of Mercury, obtained from Circe that they should return to being men; that is, the wise man, by means of his wisdom and eloquence—which belongs to Mercury—can persuade the voluptuous and lewd man to leave vice and return to virtue.

**WHO Hid me.** Almost as if by flattery in a deceitful way, so that a year passed before I noticed my delay. To better understand the force of the word, and from that the sense of the text: <term>Subtraere</term> <note>original: "Subtraere"</note> in Latin means to pull toward oneself stealthily and in secret. Hence we say "to subtract" someone when, in a cunning way that they do not notice, we lead them to say what they otherwise would not. Therefore, the poet says here: "She subtracted me," almost as if she stole me from myself. **THERE NEAR Gaeta.** The place where Circe lived. Caieta, today called Gaeta, is a maritime land and very noble; and according to Virgil, it took this name from Caieta, the nurse of Aeneas. Others say she was the nurse of Creusa, his wife; others of Ascanius, his son. Others say that because Aeneas's ships accidentally burned in that place, the city took its name from that fire, because <term>chein</term> <note>original: "cein"</note> in Greek means "to burn." **BEFORE Aeneas had so named it.** The meaning is that Ulysses was with Circe on the island of Circeo near Gaeta, but he was there before Gaeta had received this name. For according to Virgil, Ulysses, departing from Troy, navigated these seas before Aeneas. This is understood especially by Aeneas's arrival at the rocks of Polyphemus, for there he finds Polyphemus already blinded by Ulysses.

**NEITHER SWEETNESS** Of a son, nor the pity. To make it believable that Ulysses endured so many hardships and put himself in such dangers to have knowledge of various things, it is necessary to show that there was in him an immeasurable love for understanding and knowing; for only love is what makes one endure every labor and inconvenience. Nor is it against reason; rather, it is entirely natural that a man of excellent intellect should love the knowledge of things more than anything else. For nature constrains not only man, the rational animal, but even the brutes; and not only the brutes, but even inanimate things to love and desire their perfection above all else. And the perfection of the human soul is to know. Therefore, the love of knowledge in an excellent intellect is greater than any other love. And this he demonstrates by comparison to those loves which...

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on Canto XXVI of the *Inferno*. The previous page began the line-by-line analysis of Ulysses’s speech, specifically addressing his departure from Circe. Landino now explores the three types of familial love that Ulysses abandoned in his quest for knowledge.</meta>

->INFERNO<-

men conquer the others: which are three, in the son, in the father, and in the wife. And not without great learning does he distinguish these three species of love with three different epithets, calling the love for the son *sweet*, for the father *pious*, and in marriage *joyful*. For the father sees himself in the son, and in him sees himself extended into perpetuity, which is most sweet to him. From this, Virgil said: **"All the care of the dear parent rests on Ascanius."** <note>original: "Omnis in Ascanio cari stat cura parentis" from the *Aeneid*</note>. The love of the son for the father he calls *pious*, because as we demonstrated above, piety is a species of justice through which we love our fatherland, our father, our mother, and others joined by blood. **OF THE OLD FATHER.** He rightly added "old." For although it is a duty of piety not to abandon one's father, it nonetheless seems a lesser cruelty to abandon them when they are still in their green and robust age than when they are oppressed by extreme old age; for then, languid and without strength, they require from the son what they cannot do for themselves. Therefore, we should take an example from the storks, which, in the same nest where they were nourished and raised by their parents, later nourish those parents in their old age. And finally, he calls the love toward the wife *joyful*, because the preservation of a chaste and obedient wife is the highest joy and pleasantness. And we are constrained by the debt of nature and by divine and human precepts to love the wife in whom such customs exist. And because Penelope is described by writers as most chaste and most obedient, he therefore called it the "rightful love" <note>literally "due love" or "debt of love"</note> which ought to have made Penelope joyful, for she would have been joyful had she had her husband with her. Therefore, the poet demonstrates that all these three equal loves, which are very great, were conquered by the love of knowledge. Penelope was the daughter of Icarius <note>original: "caro" or "Icarioto"</note>, a most chaste woman. When Ulysses did not return from Troy after the war, and it was the opinion that he was dead, she was urged by her father to take a new husband, and many sought her hand. But she, wishing to persevere in her good purpose, feigned that she wanted first to finish the cloth she was weaving; and so that it would never be finished, as much as she wove by day, she unwove by night. Therefore, these three loves could not conquer the ardor that I had to become an expert—that is, learned through experience—of the world. **AND OF HUMAN VICES AND OF WORTH (THAT IS, OF VIRTUE).** Here he expressed what Horace says when interpreting Homer: **"Who saw the customs and cities of many men."** <note>original: "Qui mores hominum multorum uidit et urbes" from Horace's *Ars Poetica*</note>. And certainly, a man cannot be prudent if he has no experience of many and varied things, and if he does not know the nature and customs of different men and nations. And he spoke of "human vices" because, it being given to man by nature to desire the good and flee the evil, as soon as we have known the nature of vices and how harmful they are to the human species, an ardent desire will be kindled in us to flee them and purge ourselves of them. And having reached this level, we will acquire the highest good. **BUT I SET OUT UPON THE DEEP, OPEN SEA.** He means the Ionian Sea, which is ample and spacious. **WITH BUT A SINGLE SHIP.** We can refer here to that same allegorical sense that we placed above in the explanation of the ship. <note>Landino previously interpreted the ship as the human body or the faculties of the soul.</note> **AND WITH THAT SMALL COMPANY.** Homer presents Ulysses sailing as the human soul, which sets itself to investigate the highest good, and finally leads it back to Ithaca and to the fatherland—that is, to happiness—because Homer thought that the highest good could be in this life. But Dante feigns that he perished in his navigation because no port—that is, the highest good—is found in mortal things or in the doctrine of the pagans <note>original: "gentili"</note>. Therefore, the ship perishes before it arrives at Purgatory. Thus, he leads a "small company." For as the soul has four powers in general—which are divided into many species, namely the Vegetative, Sensitive, Motive (from place to place), and Rational—only the rational parts, along with some of the sensitive parts obedient to the rational, are those that follow him. Therefore, they are few. But these few never abandon him, wherefore he said: **BY WHICH I WAS NOT DESERTED.** I was not abandoned. **I SAW ONE SHORE AND THE OTHER AS FAR AS SPAIN.** He sailed through our Mediterranean Sea toward the West. Here it is to be noted that the "day" can easily stand for human life, and the "Western part" for the end of human life. Therefore, Ulysses sailed to the West—that is, he investigated what our end was. And he searched "one shore and the other" because he wanted to have knowledge of virtue and vice. He who sails to the West leaves the North on the right hand and the South on the left. The North is harsh and austere because of the cold, but it is sublime and high; it can be interpreted as virtue, whose path is difficult and arduous but leads on high—that is, to heaven. The South <note>literally "mid-day"</note> is pleasant and sunny and full of delight, but low and deepest. This denotes vice, which brings earthly pleasures and various delights, but finally leads to the depths of Hell. And deservedly, Ulysses had this shore on the left side, which signifies vice, and the other on the right, by which we understand virtue. But it is necessary that he who is kindled by the love of knowing and investigating the end, wishing to have true knowledge of the end, **sees one shore and the other:** vice to flee it, and virtue to follow it. And let this suffice for the allegorical sense. **SPAIN.** This region is called Iberia by the Greeks and Hispania by the Latins. Among the ancients, it was divided into two parts: the "further" and the "nearer." In these centuries, it is divided into many kingdoms. **AS FAR AS MOROCCO.** This region is in Barbary; it is called Maurusia by the Greeks and Mauritania by the Latins; later, by corruption of the word, "Morocco." The island of the Sardinians, **Sardinia**, was called *Sandaleon* by the Greeks because it is in the shape of a human foot, and a "sandal" is a type of footwear; it is eight thousand paces distant from Corsica. **I AND MY COMPANIONS WERE OLD AND SLOW.** Old because they had been at the siege of Troy for ten years and had spent another ten in sailing; <meta>catchword: Slow because they were old</meta> **WHEN WE CAME TO THAT NARROW STRAIT** where Hercules set up his markers.

<summary>Landino interprets Ulysses’s voyage as an allegory for the human soul seeking knowledge, explaining why Ulysses prioritized the "ardor" of discovery over familial duties and defining the geographical boundaries of the journey as symbolic of the choice between virtue and vice.</summary>

# CANTO XXVI
## 140

He describes the strait through which the ocean enters the land, dividing Spain in Europe from Africa, and forming all our Mediterranean seas **WHERE HERCULES MARKED HIS BOUNDARIES.** Here he placed the pillars to demonstrate that one must not navigate further. He placed two pillars in that strait: **Abila** on the African side (that is, in Barbary) and **Calpe** on the Spanish side, which are called the Pillars of Hercules. In truth, however, they are two natural mountains. **ON THE RIGHT HAND I LEFT SEVILLE.** This is a noble city in Spain, fifty miles from the sea. **CEUTA** <note>original: "Setta"</note> is a city in Barbary on the opposite shore; and because it is not as far toward the ocean as Seville, he said that Ceuta had been "left behind."

Ulysses continues in his narration and delivers a brief speech <note>original: "oratione"</note> which he used to comfort his companions to endure hardships and toils and not to be dismayed by dangers. This speech is of the **deliberative genre**; it proposes honest and honorable goals, demonstrating that man was not produced

<columns>2</columns>

"O brothers," I said, "who through a hundred thousand
perils have reached the west,
to this so brief a vigil
of our senses that remains,
do not choose to deny the experience,
following the sun, of the world without people.
Consider your seed:
you were not made to live like brutes,
but to follow virtue and knowledge."
My companions I made so sharp
with this brief speech for the journey,
that I could hardly have held them back.
And having turned our stern toward the morning,
of our oars we made wings for the mad flight,
always gaining ground on the left side.
All the stars of the other pole
the night already saw, and our own was so low
that it did not rise out of the ocean floor.
Five times rekindled, and as many quenched,
was the light beneath the moon
since we had entered the deep passage,
when there appeared to us a dark mountain,
which seemed so high because of the distance,
as I had never seen any other.
We rejoiced, and soon it turned to weeping;
for from the new land a whirlwind rose
and struck the first corner of the ship.
Three times it made her whirl with all the waters;
at the fourth, it lifted the stern aloft
and the prow went down, as pleased Another,
until the sea was closed over us.

<column-break/>

by God in His likeness to live in idleness and give himself over to Bacchus <note>god of wine</note>, Ceres <note>goddess of grain/food</note>, and Venus <note>goddess of lust</note>. Nor should he live according to sensuality, which desires nothing other than earthly, momentary, and corruptible things. Instead, he was made to exercise himself in virtue and to investigate the truth. Therefore, they ought to follow Ulysses, as he comforts them toward that for which they were produced. The beginning <note>term: "exordium" (the opening of a formal speech)</note> of this oration is similar to that which Aeneas uses for his companions after the storm at sea: **"O companions, for we are not unacquainted with previous evils... O you who have suffered worse, God will also give an end to these."** <note>original: "O socii neque enim ignari sumus ante malorum... O passi grauiora dabit deus his quoque finem" from Virgil's Aeneid</note>.

He says, therefore: "O brothers, who have reached the west"—that is, the western ocean—"through a hundred thousand perils." It is as if he said: just as you have been brought to safety through infinite dangers until now, so you ought to have hope for the future; and this is the reward. Then he declares what he wants them to do, saying: **"do not choose to deny the experience to this so brief a vigil of our senses"**—meaning, to this short span of life. For life is a "vigil" and a waking of the senses, which fall asleep in death. **THAT REMAINS:** which is left to us. In short, the meaning is: let us choose to consume this little bit of life that remains to us in the knowledge of great things. And this is to go **"following the sun of the world without people,"** which is nothing other than saying to go from this hemisphere into the other. For once we have reached the west and continue to follow the sun, we follow him where he is no longer in our hemisphere, but in the other, which he calls the "world without people" because it is uninhabited. But we will investigate this location more diligently in the first Canto of *Purgatorio*.

**CONSIDER YOUR SEED:** that is, your origin, and you will understand that you are made in the image of God through the reason He gave you. And because the nourishment of the intellect and its happiness is knowledge, you must not follow "low" things <note>original: "chose di sucto"</note> which satisfy the appetite. Instead, follow **moral virtue**, where the **active life** consists, and **knowledge** <note>original: "conoscentia"</note>, in which the **speculative life** <note>the contemplative life of study and reflection</note> is founded.

**MY COMPANIONS.** Having made the speech, he shows that his companions became so eager for the voyage that he could hardly have restrained them. Through this, he demonstrates **allegorically** that when the internal senses and the appetite are illustrated by the light of the intellect, they are so entirely persuaded that they never abandon the intellect; rather, they are obedient to it like excellent children to a wise father. **AND HAVING TURNED OUR STERN TOWARD THE MORNING.** Whoever sails to the west has the prow turned toward it and the stern toward the morning—that is, the east. **OF OUR OARS WE MADE WINGS.** Because oars are to a ship what wings are to a bird. Thus Virgil said **"oarage of wings"** <note>original: "remigio alarum"</note>, transferring "oars" to "flying"; and elsewhere, he used "flying" for "oars" when speaking of the "wing-sailing sea." **FOR THE MAD FLIGHT.** This uses a metaphor...

Landino provides a moral and allegorical commentary, linking the journey to the "active" and "speculative" lives and comparing Ulysses's rhetoric to Aeneas's in the Aeneid.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on Canto XXVI of the Inferno, specifically focusing on the conclusion of Ulysses's "mad flight" beyond the Pillars of Hercules. The previous page ended with the start of Ulysses’s speech to his crew; this page explains the spiritual and physical nature of their journey toward the Southern Hemisphere and their eventual shipwreck at the base of Mount Purgatory.</meta>

# XXVI INFERNO

Because he had called the oars "wings," he calls the rowing "flying." **MAD.** Foolish, because it is the height of stupidity <note>original: "stultitia"</note> to undertake an enterprise that is beyond one's capability. Nor is this contrary to the allegorical sense given above, where we interpreted Ulysses as a man seeking wisdom. For it does not condemn Ulysses’s purpose in wanting to reach the blessed life; rather, it shows that the "flight"—that is, the path—was mad, or foolish. **ALWAYS** Gaining on the left side. Although they were sailing toward the West, they nevertheless leaned toward the left side, which was toward the South from their perspective. For this reason, they were already so far under the **Antarctic pole** that the pole which is depressed and low for us was elevated above their heads. Consequently, at night they saw the stars of that pole, which we cannot see. And our **Arctic pole**, which is always elevated for us and always above our heads, was depressed for them, and so low that its stars—which always appear to us and never set—did not appear and did not rise for them.

The sky has two points upon which it turns, and these are called **poles**. Of these two, one is always seen by us because it is so far above our heads that even though the heaven revolves, we never lose sight of the stars that are very close to it. This is called the **Arctic pole** by the Greeks <note>original: "arctico"</note> because, according to the myths, Jove transformed Callisto into these nearby stars after she had been loved by him; Juno had previously transformed her into a bear. **Arctos** <note>original: "arctos"</note> in Greek signifies "bear." The Latins name it **Septentrio** <term>The North</term> <note>original: "Septẽtrione," referring to the seven stars of the Big Dipper</note>. This constellation of the Bear, otherwise called **Helice** <note>original: "elice"</note>, has twenty-four stars, among which are the North Star, the Horn, and the Wain <term>the Big Dipper</term>. The myths say that when Juno realized that this nymph of Arcadia, Callisto, had been known by her husband Jove, she changed her into a bear out of jealousy. And Jove, as compensation for such harm, converted her into the aforementioned sign. Juno then entreated Tethys, the goddess of the sea, never to let her bathe in the ocean as the other stars do. The poets feign this because when other stars are in the west and set, they seem to dip into the sea; but this does not appear to happen to the Bear, because it never sets. There is similarly the other bear, called the **Lesser Bear**, and also **Cynosure** <note>original: "cynosura"</note>, by which the Phoenicians used to navigate, just as we navigate by the Greater Bear.

**FIVE TIMES** rekindled and as many extinguished. In the *Paradiso*, we will demonstrate the reason why the moon is rekindled every month, growing and then diminishing until it is extinguished. **WHEN** there appeared to us a mountain, dark due to the distance. After the fifth month of sailing, they finally discover a mountain. **DARK** <note>original: "bruna"</note> Due to the distance, for it was still so distant and far away that it appeared dark and obscure. Many believe this to be the **Mountain of Purgatory** and of the Terrestrial Paradise, which they say is located under the equinoctial region <term>the Equator</term> and is so high that it reaches as far as the sphere of the moon. Wherefore he adds: **AND HIGH** So high as he had never seen any other. We shall speak of this at the beginning of the *Purgatorio*.

**WE** rejoiced: As sailors rejoice when, after a long voyage, they see land where they hope to be able to rest. **AND SOON** it turned to weeping. Because from the place where we hoped for salvation, there came the wind that submerged us. Certainly, he who undertakes a great enterprise beyond his strength often fails just when he hopes to reach perfection. **THAT FROM THE** New land. "New" to us because we had never seen it before. **A whirlwind was born.** That is, a great revolution of wind; and we have shown above what "whirlwind" <note>original: "turbo"</note> means in Latin. **AND STRUCK** the first corner of the vessel. It struck the prow, which is the front part of the ship. **THREE TIMES** It made her whirl with all the waters. Because the waters whirled and created an eddy, and as the waters whirled, the ship whirled; and at the fourth time, it lifted the stern up and the prow down, **as it pleased Another**—that is, God, or Fortune, or Fate—until the sea was closed over us and we remained under the water.

# CANTO XXVII OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE

The poet was forced by the number of verses to change cantos; nevertheless, he continues with the same subject of fraudulent counselors. And just as in the previous canto he brought Ulysses to speak, so in this one speaks Count Guido da Montefeltro.

> **N**ow the flame was upright and quiet,
> having no more to say, and it already moved away from us
> with the leave of the sweet poet [Virgil],
> When another, which came behind it,
> made us turn our eyes toward its tip,
> because of a confused sound that issued from it.
> As the Sicilian bull—which bellowed first
> with the bellowing of him (and this was right)
> who had tempered it with his file—
> Bellowed with the voice of the afflicted one,
> so that although it was made of copper,
> it still seemed transfixed by pain:
> Thus, for having neither path nor opening
> from the beginning, within the fire,
> the sorrowful words were converted into its language.

...in which he <note>The tyrant Phalaris.</note> wanted those who were to be killed to be placed; and fire was made around it; so that when, from the excessive heat, the man placed inside cried out, a voice issued forth that sounded like the horrific bellowing of a bull. Phalaris gave the creator a worthy reward for such a work, for he willed that he should be the first to experience such a torture. And certainly, it is a just thing that the inventor of cruelty should perish by that same cruelty. Ovid expressed this excellently: *There is no law more just than that the architect of death should perish by his own device.* <note>original: "Non est lex equior ulla Quam necis artificem fraude perire sua."</note> This is a clear comparison to Perillus: *And to groan in the bull, O cruel Perillus, which was your own.* <note>original: "Et gemere in tauro seuere perille tuo."</note> And Juvenal says: *Though Phalaris commands you to be false and dictates perjuries with the bull brought near, believe it the greatest crime to prefer life to honor.* <note>original: "Phalaris licet imperet ut sis falsus et admoto dictet periuria tauro Summum crede nephas animam preferre pudori."</note> Thus he [Dante] spoke most excellently: THE SICILIAN BULL. The bull built in Sicily by Perillus, which bellowed first with the cry of him who had tempered it with his file; and this was Perillus, as we have said. IT BELLOWED: Not with its own voice, for it was inanimate, but with the voice of the afflicted one: that is, with the cry of the one who was tormented inside. AND THIS WAS RIGHT. And this was a direct and just thing, because the cruelty of such an inventor deserved such a punishment. So that although this bull was made of copper, it nevertheless seemed to bellow as a living bull does when it is transfixed by pain. THUS FOR NOT HAVING, that soul enclosed in the flame, PATH NOR OPENING: that is, not having any aperture. FROM THE BEGINNING of the fire the SORROWFUL WORDS were converted: that is, the unhappy and miserable words.

> But after they had taken their path
> through the point, giving it that vibration
> which the tongue had given them in their passage,
> We heard it say: "O you to whom I direct
> my voice, and who were just now speaking Lombard,
> saying 'Now go, I do not urge you further,'
> Though I have arrived perhaps a bit late,
> let it not displease you to stay and speak with me;
> see, it does not displease me, though I burn.
> If you have only now into this blind world
> fallen from that sweet Latin land
> from which I bring all my guilt..."

<column-break/>

He joins this canto with the previous one, saying that after the flame where Ulysses and Diomedes were had finished its speech, it straightened its tip, which it had bent toward Dante, and having become quiet, it departed with Virgil's permission. And at the same time, another flame coming toward Dante, because a confused sound came out of it, made them turn their eyes toward its tip. AS THE Sicilian Bull: the comparison is excellent, through which he demonstrates how the bull, made of copper with a man placed inside, when the man cried out, sent out through the mouth of the animal a sound that seemed like its bellowing and not a human voice. Thus this spirit, speaking within the flame, sent out through the tip of the flame a confused sound. But so that you may understand the history: Phalaris was the king of Agrigento, a city in Sicily, who out of extreme cruelty offered a reward to whoever discovered a new torture or torment against men. And in those same times there was Perillus the Athenian, a craftsman of great genius. He fashioned a bull of bronze from very thin plates...

**T**he poet presents how Count Guido, having realized from the words spoken to Ulysses that the poets were Italians, asks them about the state of Romagna, as one eager to hear news of his homeland. Whence he says that after the words—which at first were a confused sound because they found no exit from the flame—took their journey up through the tip of the flame, which gave such a vibration: that is, such a motion as the tongue had given in their passage. "To vibrate" <note>original: "Guizare"</note> is to move quickly. WE HEARD, Virgil and I: "O you, Virgil, to whom I direct my voice." WHO WERE SPEAKING JUST NOW: a little while ago. LOMBARD: referring to Virgil’s homeland <note>Virgil was from Mantua, in Lombardy.</note>, saying *ISSA*: that is, "now" <note>original: "ISSA: cioe adesso"</note>, "GO NOW, I DO NOT URGE YOU FURTHER." "I urge" <note>original: "Adizo"</note> means I provoke or direct you.

signifies to provoke and irritate. **A LITTLE LATE.** Under this veil, he means having arrived late—that is, after the centuries in which Homer and Virgil flourished. It is as if he were saying: "If I had lived in your times, you would have written of me as you wrote of Ulysses." For, having reached the tomb of Achilles, Alexander the Great said: *O fortunate youth, who found such a herald for your praises!* <note>original: “O felicem adolescentem qui talem preconem laudum tuarum adinueneris”</note> And it is undoubtedly the happiness of an eminent man to find a most eloquent writer for his praise. **IF YOU.** He arranges the text: "If you have only just now fallen" **INTO THIS blind world.** He calls Hell the "essential blind world" because it is in the shadows of the center; and "moral" because every vice is blind, arising from ignorance, which is blindness of the mind. **FROM THAT sweet Latin land.** From Italy. **WHENCE I bring all my guilt:** because in that land I committed the error for which I am punished here, as I will demonstrate below. **TELL ME IF the Romagnuols.** He has used an appropriate introduction in this petition: first, making him attentive and praying that it not be burdensome for him to stop, since he is outside the flames and it is not burdensome for the one who burns. Then, he shows the ease of requesting this of him, since he comes newly from Italy. And finally, he makes an honest petition: for it is an honest thing to ask about the state of Romagna, being a Romagnuol himself. **FOR I WAS from the mountains there between Urbino.** He means Montefeltro. His succession has remained there; and today in Ravenna is Dante, a son descended from Dante <note>Landino is likely referring to a grandson or descendant here, as he writes in the 15th century</note>, a very literate and eloquent man worthy of such blood, who should deservedly be recalled to his ancient homeland and our republic. The body of the poet lies honorably in Ravenna. <meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto XXVII of Dante’s Inferno. The previous page discussed Guido da Montefeltro’s request for news about the political state of Romagna.
