### CANTO XXVII

<margin>q.ii.</margin>

...considering the forces of John and his robust army of Frenchmen, he returned to his usual cunning. By a double-dealing plot, he led John to arrive at Forlì with the whole army before dawn on the first day of May. Believing he would be received as a friend, John entered through a gate that Guido had ordered opened with a chosen part of his men, leaving the rest outside in the cool shade of an oak tree. Thus the French entered, and because they are greedy by nature, they immediately gave themselves over to plundering. As John entered, Guido secretly exited through another gate, and in a short time, he crushed those who had remained at the oak. Then, returning to the fortifications, he turned to the slaughter of the enemies who were already scattered through the houses to loot. Consequently, there were few who were able to remount their horses and flee the land; the others were killed in great numbers. This was the beginning of a greater war. For in the following year, Martin <note>Pope Martin IV, who reigned from 1281–1285 and sought to bring Romagna under papal control.</note> sent a new army to John, and with that, he finally took Forlì and drove Guido out.

**THE LAND THAT already made the long proof:** because for a long time it resisted the Pope.

**AND OF THE FRENCH a bloody heap.** <note>original: "Sanguinoso mucchio"</note> That is, a mountain and a pile. "Mucchio" in the Florentine dialect means what *cumulus* <note>Latin for "heap" or "mound."</note> means in Latin: which is a mound made of things gathered together.

**UNDER THE GREEN CLAWS it finds itself.** This refers to the Ordelaffi family; their coat of arms is a green lion from the waist up on a gold field, and from the waist down with three green stripes and three gold. At this time, Sinibaldo Ordelaffi was the lord.

**THE OLD MASTIFF.** The poet uses an artful and very delightful variety in this description, presenting sometimes the coat of arms and sometimes the nicknames of the lords. For the declaration of this text, it is unknown to no one that a "mastiff" signifies a large and biting dog. Therefore, by a fitting similarity, he calls the tyrant a mastiff, who most cruelly mangles and devours his subjects. Here he refers to the two Malatestas, father and son, violent and cruel men who held Rimini. These lords had their origin from a Malatesta who was from Penna de' Billi, a castle located in the territory of Montefeltro. Through many feats of military discipline, he earned the right for the people of Rimini to make him their citizen, honoring him with fine houses and other rewards. From him was born another Malatesta, a man of great spirit and warlike nature, who defeated Count Guido at Monteloro, though he was later defeated by him at the bridge of San Procolo. He held such authority and following that he made himself Lord of Rimini. He fathered "Gianni the Lame" <note>Gianciotto Malatesta, famous for killing his wife Francesca da Rimini and his brother Paolo.</note> and Paolo, whom we mentioned above when we spoke of Francesca and Pandolfo. Also Malatestino, who was blind in one eye and a man of great cunning, succeeded his father. From Malatestino was born Ferrantino, who succeeded his father along with his uncle Pandolfo; these were lords of a large part of the March of Ancona. Therefore, here he means the "Old Mastiff" as the first Malatesta lord, and the "New" as Malatestino.

**OF VERRUCCHIO.** This is a castle that the people of Rimini gave to the first Malatesta. Thus, although their origin was from Penna de' Billi, they were named from here from then on.

**MONTAGNA** was a noble knight of the Parcitati family of Rimini, head of the Ghibelline party <note>The Ghibellines were a political faction that supported the Holy Roman Emperor, opposing the Guelphs, who supported the Pope.</note>. Malatesta, along with other Ghibellines, had him captured and gave him into the custody of Malatestino; later, after Malatestino was asked many times if he was guarding him well, he had him put to death.

**THEY MAKE AN AUGER OF THEIR TEETH.** <note>original: "Fanno succhio di denti"</note> Having called them mastiffs, he stays within the metaphor. Because a mastiff harms with its teeth, he says they make a "succhio"—that is, a drill or an auger—with their teeth, because they pierce their subjects.

**THE CITY OF LAMONE AND SANTERNO.** He means Faenza, by which the river Lamone flows, and Imola, where the Santerno flows. This city was once called *Forum Cornelii* <note>The Roman name for Imola.</note>. Later, because it was fervent in the faith, it was called Imola from the word *immolare*, which means "to sacrifice." This refers to Maghinardo, and the history is this: Maghinardo Pagano was from a castle in the mountains above Imola. No less through luck than through merit, he became Lord of Forlì, Faenza, and Imola, although he did not possess them all at once. In the year 1290, on the twelfth of November, Stefano da Ghinazzano, a Roman and Count of Romagna, was captured in Ravenna by the Polenta family. This gave Maghinardo the opportunity to make himself lord of Faenza, and the Bolognese the opportunity to take Imola. Later, the Pope sent Bandino, Bishop of Arezzo, of the family of the Counts Guidi of Romena, who brought the lands of Romagna back to the obedience of the Apostolic See. But then in the following year, on the twenty-third of December, he took Forlì by stealth at night, and in it Count Aghinolfo of Romena, brother of the aforementioned Bishop. Having taken Forlì, he besieged Cesena, where the Count of Romagna was. And in the year 1296, having made a league with Azzo III d'Este against the Bolognese who were fighting him, having taken Forlì, he took Imola from them, not without damage and ignominy to them. For he fought with them, who were about four thousand, and captured and killed many of them.

**THE LIONCUB of the white nest.** Maghinardo Pagano of Susinana, whose coat of arms was a blue lion—some say vermilion—on a white field.

**WHO CHANGES sides from summer to winter.** This man, as we said above, was of the Pagani house in Romagna, who were Ghibellines. Nevertheless, because he was left as a youth under the guardianship of the Florentines after the death of his father, and was always defended and maintained by them, as a most grateful man he was always in their favor in every enterprise. Thus, in the "winter"—that is, in Romagna, which is a cold northern region to us—he was a Ghibelline. And in the "summer"—that is, in Tuscany, which is a warm southern region compared to Romagna—he was a Guelph. Some explain this passage simply by saying he changed sides often, such that if he was with one side in the summer, he was with the other in the winter.

**AND THAT ONE TO WHICH THE SAVIO:** he means Cesena, by which flows the river called *Sapis* by the Latins and which we call the Savio. In these times, among so many tyrants in Romagna, only...

### INFERNO
### CANTO XXVII

...likewise Cesena was ruled in liberty, although sometimes the leading citizens of that city practiced some tyranny.

Now I pray you to tell us who you are;
do not be more stubborn than others have been,
if you wish your name to hold its head high in the world.
After the fire had roared somewhat
in its own way, it moved the sharp point
to and fro; and then it gave forth this breath:
"If I believed that my answer were
to a person who would ever return to the world,
this flame would stay without further shaking;
But since no one has ever returned alive from this depth,
if what I hear is true,
without fear of infamy I answer you.

I was a man of arms, and then a "cord-wearer" <note>A "cordellero," or a Franciscan friar, named for the knotted cord they wear as a belt.</note>
believing that, so girded, I could make amends;
and certainly my belief was coming true,
if not for the Great Priest—may evil take him!—
who put me back into my earlier sins;
and how and why, I want you to hear from me.
While I was the form of bones and flesh
that my mother gave me, my deeds
were not those of a lion, but of a fox.
The clever tricks and the hidden ways,
I knew them all, and I conducted their art
so well that the sound of it went out to the ends of the earth.
When I saw myself reaching that part
of my life where everyone should
lower the sails and gather in the ropes,
that which had previously pleased me then grieved me,
and repentant and confessed, I surrendered myself;
ah, wretched me! and it would have been enough.</p>

<column-break/>

**H**aving been generous to this soul, our poet now confidently asks him to say his name, adding: IF YOUR NAME in the world should hold its head high <note>original: "sel nome tuo nel mondo tegna fronte"</note>; that is, let it remain in fame. Since we say someone "has no forehead" <note>An idiom meaning someone has no shame or no "face."</note> when they have no respect for honor, we can say the opposite: that he who is honored "has a forehead." To which the soul replies that if he believed he were answering someone who had to return to the world, he would not say a word. And this is because, since a good opinion of him remained due to his having become a friar, he would not want his damnation to be known. But he is content to reveal himself, hoping that the other [Dante] does not have to return to the world, having heard that whoever enters Hell cannot leave it; and the poet writes this to demonstrate how great the desire for fame is in every man, in whatever state he finds himself.

**T**his is the answer that Count Guido makes, through which he shows that his occupation was in deeds of arms; and then toward the end of his life, he became a "cord-wearer." This means a friar of Saint Francis, because they gird themselves with a cord, believing that in this way they can make amends—that is, amend for their sins. And his plan was succeeding; IF THE GREAT PRIEST; that is, the Pope <note>Pope Boniface VIII, whom Dante frequently identifies as his great political and spiritual enemy.</note>, had not persuaded him to return to his former faults and his first errors: the frauds and fraudulent counsels in which he had been practiced in his past life. AND HOW AND WHY; and in what way and for what reason. I WANT YOU TO understand me. WHILE I HAD THE shape of bones and flesh; that is, while I was alive and was both soul and body. For he takes "shape" <note>The commentator uses the Aristotelian concept of "form," where the soul is the "form" that gives life and identity to the "matter" of the body.</note> here to mean the soul, and "flesh and bones" for the body. And certainly, the form is what gives being to a thing. 

As, <term>for example</term> <note>original: "verbi gratia"</note>, we see a bronze statue of Mercury. In that, therefore, it is not the bronze—which is the matter—that makes it Mercury, but the form which is in the matter. Thus, man is not man because he has a body composed of the four elements of which the bodies of all other animals are composed, but because he has a rational soul, without which we would not be men. Therefore, understand the text this way: "While I was the form of bones and flesh." <term>That is</term> <note>original: "i."</note>, of the body, which has bones and meat; that is, while this soul was joined with the body. WHICH MY Mother gave me; which bones and flesh my mother gave to me. For in generation, the father's seed is nothing other than spirits which are the craftsmen for forming the body. But the mother gives her blood from which, as from matter, the father's seed forms the human body; whence she is called *mater* <term>because she provides the matter</term> <note>original: "Quia prebet materiam"</note>. 

MY WORKS were not lion-like. I did not use force openly and without snares or fraud as the lion does: but they were the works of a fox—fox-like works. For my wars and deeds were covered, insidious, and full of cunning and fraud. Regarding which, Cicero in his book *On Duties*: <quote>While an injury can be done in two ways, that is, by force or by fraud; fraud seems like that of the little fox, and force that of the lion. Both are most alien to man, but fraud is worthy of greater hatred. Of all injustice, however, none is more capital [deadly] than those who, even when they deceive most, act so that they appear to be good men.</quote> <note>original Latin: "Cum autem duobus modis... ut boni uiri uideantur."</note> And certainly, the injury done with fraud is much greater than that done with force; and without doubt, human life would be in much greater tranquility if, just as in the island of Crete <note>original: "Candia"</note>—according to Pliny—there are no foxes, so among men there were no fox-like minds. AND THE ARGUMENTS and the hidden ways: He demonstrates what a "fox-like" work is, which has two parts. The first is to sharpen the intellect to find the fraud.

The commentary provides a philosophical explanation of the relationship between soul and body and uses Cicero to condemn fraudulent behavior as "fox-like."</summary>

### CANTO XXVII

Hence he spoke of the arguments. Then finding hidden ways and means: which lead you to fraud before you are discovered. **I KNEW THEM ALL.** To denote that no species of fraud was unknown to him: and this he proves by the effects. Because he used so many and of such kinds that by the most widespread fame he was known everywhere as a supreme architect of fraud: And for this reason he says, **I so conducted their art** <note>original: "Io menai et guidai si l'arte loro"</note>. **THAT THE SOUND**: meaning the fame that derived from it. **AT THE END Of the earth.** Even to the furthest parts of the world. And this was my life until old age. **BUT WHEN I saw myself reaching that part of my age** in which, in old age, **EVERYONE Should lower the sails: and gather in the ropes.** Human life is similar to navigation. Because in it fortune varies so much, giving us now serene happiness: and now cloudy adversity: just as events make the sea now serene and tranquil: and now turbulent and tempestuous. And our living is navigating through this sea: And old age is like a port of this life: and therefore he says, **WHEN I saw myself reaching that part of my age.** And he means when he reached old age. **WHERE EVERYONE** Man **Should lower the sails and gather in the ropes.** This is a metaphor. Because just as sailors reaching port put an end to their navigation: and disarm by lowering the sails and gathering the ropes: So men reaching old age should leave all worldly operations and put an end to them: And so did Guido: who from sin converted himself to spiritual works. And he touches in this place on three things necessary to him who wishes to reconcile with God: The first is contrition: which makes us recognize the sin: and makes it displease us. Hence he says, **THAT WHICH HAD Pleased me then grieved me.** The second is penance which makes us repent of the error committed; and we grieve for it with the intention of not erring for the future: and of making amends for what we are bound to satisfy: Hence he says **AND REPENTED.** The third is confession which makes it so that, once the sin is known, man [reconciles] with God: to whom sin had made him a rebel: and this is **I SURRENDERED MYSELF.** <note>original: "MI RENDEI"</note> Because the sinner seeks peace with God: to whom sin had made him a rebel: and this is the absolution of the priest which is like a form that is impressed in our soul: And the soul is like a matter that must receive such an impression. It is necessary that the matter, that is the soul, prepares itself to be able to receive such a form. Nor can it be prepared without the three aforementioned things. Because if they offend God first by thinking, then by speaking: and finally by acting wickedly, it is necessary that contrition satisfies the bad thought: and confession the bad speech: and penance the bad action: Also because in sin Deliberation, Delight, and Perseverance concur / Contrition restores the bad deliberation. Repentance: because it has sorrow in it, restores the delight. Confession interrupts the perseverance. **AH WRETCHED ME** And it would have been enough. He grieves that having made a good beginning with which he could have saved himself / the pope dragged him away and removed him from it.

> Evil beginning of the new Pharisees <note>A reference to the corrupt clergy of the time, likened to the biblical Pharisees.</note>
> having war near the Lateran:
> and not with Saracens nor with Jews
> For every one of his enemies was Christian
> and none had been to conquer Acre <note>Acre was the last Crusader stronghold to fall in 1291; Dante criticizes the Pope for fighting Christians rather than the Crusades.</note>
> nor a merchant in the land of the Sultan.
> Neither the supreme office nor sacred orders
> did he respect in himself nor in me that cord <note>The "capresto" or cord worn by Franciscan friars.</note>
> that used to make its wearers thinner.
> But as Constantine sought Sylvester
> inside Soracte to cure his leprosy <note>Refers to the legend of Pope Sylvester I curing Emperor Constantine of leprosy, which led to the "Donation of Constantine."</note>
> so this one sought me as a master:
> To cure his proud fever:
> he asked me for counsel: and I was silent
> because his words seemed to me drunken;
> And then he said to me, let your heart not suspect
> from now I absolve you, and you teach me how
> to throw Palestrina to the ground. <note>original: "Prenestrina." This refers to the Colonna stronghold of Palestrina.</note>
> I can lock and unlock heaven
> as you know, for the keys are two
> that my predecessor did not hold dear. <note>A reference to Pope Celestine V, who abdicated the papacy.</note>

<column-break/>

**G**uido had been led to the port of salvation. But the pope induced him to return to his ancient sin of giving fraudulent counsel: which he, not wanting to give at the beginning because he feared the sin, was deceived by the pope who absolved him of that which he could not absolve, as we will say a little below. **THE PRINCE of the new Pharisees.** The Pope is the prince of the prelates whom by metaphor he calls Pharisees: who in the ancient law were in great esteem in the priestly order: But of the Pharisees we spoke a little above. **HAVING War near the Lateran.** The history is this: In 1297, Pope Boniface, having conceived implacable hatred against the Colonna family: whose houses are near Saint John Lateran: because two cardinals of that family, Messere Giacomo and Messere Pietro, had been opposed to his election: And later Sciarra della Colonna had stolen certain sums of his treasures. He deprived this family of all honors: and benefices: and commanded the two aforementioned cardinals that they should put down their hats: and the cardinal's robes. And because they did not obey, he deprived all that family of every honor and dignity: and destroyed their houses in Rome: and took their castles: and part he gave to the Orsini, part he destroyed: and finally besieged Nepi which...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, Canto XXVII. It details the specific act of fraudulent counsel given by Guido da Montefeltro to Pope Boniface VIII regarding the siege of Palestrina, and contrasts the Pope's internal wars with the crusades against non-Christians.</meta>

He trusted him with certain agreements; afterwards, being unable to capture the impregnable city of Palestrina <note>original: "Preneste"</note>, he sent for this Count Guido, who was already a Friar Minor. Being unable to persuade him to become his captain in this war, the Pope asked him for advice. The advice he received was to "promise much and deliver little." For this reason, Boniface—feigning to be moved to mercy—worked through mutual friends so that the Colonna family would humble themselves. The credulous Cardinals came in black robes <note>signifying mourning or humility</note> and threw themselves abjectly at his feet, confessing themselves as sinners and asking for mercy. The Pope promised them the restitution of everything if they gave up Palestrina. After he had it, he razed it to its foundations and had it rebuilt at the foot of the mountain on the plain, calling it "the city of the Pope" <note>This refers to the town of 'Città Papale', later renamed 'Castel San Pietro Romano'</note>. This terrified the two aforementioned Cardinals, who thereafter remained in hiding until finally Boniface, by those same arts with which he had deceived others, was miserably put to death by Sciarra <note>Sciarra Colonna, who participated in the 'Slap of Anagni' against the Pope</note>.

### HAVING WAR Near the Lateran.
He was at war with the Colonna family, who lived in Rome near San Giovanni in Laterano. **AND NOT WITH Saracens nor with Jews.** Therefore, it was an unlawful war. He sets out the circumstances that aggravate the sin. It is foreign to the gentleness of a Pope to wage war; but it is more foreign to wage war against Christians, and most foreign of all against those who are his neighbors. **AND NO ONE Had been at the conquest of Acre.** This removes every excuse: because not only was he making war against those who were Christians, but against those who, being Christians, had never done anything against the religion. They had never denied God, like those who came with the Sultan of Babylon to conquer Acre <note>The Siege of Acre in 1291 marked the end of the Crusades in the Holy Land</note>. Nor had they been merchants who carried merchandise prohibited by the Church to the infidels. To better understand the history, we should remember that after the Christians lost Antioch and Tripoli and every other land in Syria except Acre—which was where ancient Jaffa was located <note>The commentator here incorrectly identifies Acre with Jaffa; Acre was actually the ancient Ptolemais</note>—all the Christian forces positioned against the infidels retreated there. It is on the front of our sea, 70 miles from Jerusalem, in the middle of Syria, and almost in the center of the world; it was a port suited to both Eastern and Western merchants. Because of this, it was a receptacle for every nation and every tongue. Here was the home of the King of Jerusalem and Cyprus, the Prince of Antioch, and the congregation of the Hospital of Saint John. The Pope's legate resided there, as did the lieutenants of the King of France and the King of England, and so many others were in that city. There were 17 courts, each with jurisdiction over capital crimes <note>original: "iuriditione di sangue", literally 'jurisdiction of blood'</note>. This generated great confusion in the administration of the land. Because of this, it happened in the year 1291 that, while there was a truce between them and the Sultan, the truce was broken by the Christians. The aforementioned princes brought about 14,000 soldiers who, being poorly paid, were driven by hunger to rob and kill the Saracens who had come to Acre under the faith of the truce. The Sultan, moved by such injury, sent ambassadors to demand the stolen goods and the robbers; not obtaining them, he came with an army so large that the camps covered twelve miles. At first, our men resisted manfully through the vigilance and great counsel of the Grand Master of the Temple. But after he was wounded in the arm by a poisoned arrow and died within a few days, there was no one left who knew how to govern a crowd gathered from such various nations and languages. They no longer observed orders; they did not obey; and many, abandoning the land out of fear, fled to the sea. This gave the victory to the Sultan. He then took the land, sacked it, and more than sixty thousand men and women were killed. Thus, none of Boniface’s enemies had acted against the religion <note>unlike the Christians who failed to defend Acre</note>. **NEITHER SUPREME Office nor sacred orders did he respect in himself.** He did not consider that, being the Supreme Pontiff and a priest, he should not ask anyone for fraud. Nor did he respect the halter <note>term: <term>capresto</term>; the knotted cord worn by Franciscan friars as a belt</note>; that is, the Order of Saint Francis where the halter takes the place of a belt. **WHICH USED TO Make its belted ones leaner:** In passing, he rebukes the Friars Minor, who did not observe that abstinence they used to observe, for which they were once thin.

### BUT AS.
He says that just as the Emperor Constantine, being a leper, sought out Pope Sylvester—who lived on Mount Soracte—to heal him of his leprosy, so with that same desire Boniface sought me out as a master. **TO CURE The fever of his pride:** He calls his burning pride and his wrath to take revenge against the Colonna "fever" by way of metaphor. For just as a fever is burning and induces thirst, so his wrath burned with a great thirst for revenge. Constantine reigned for 30 years and 10 months. At the end of his era, he was baptized by Eusebius, Bishop of Nicomedia; but he held the Arian heresy. Being infected with leprosy, he was told by his doctors that his health depended on bathing in the pure blood of little children. Although Constantine greatly desired to be freed from such a disease, he nevertheless refused to be so impious as to let so many children die for his sake. Because of this, it pleased the Father of all mercy and the Most High God that the following night, in a vision, the prince apostles Peter and Paul appeared to him. By them, he was warned to seek out Pope Sylvester, who, because of the persecution carried out against Christians and to perform harsh penance, lived in the caves of Soracte. Soracte was called "Syracte" by the ancients; it is a very rugged mountain located in the region of the Hirpini or rather the Falisci.

### HE ASKED ME FOR COUNSEL AND I KEPT SILENT.
Not out of pride, nor for lack of the highest reverence for the Pontiff. **BUT BECAUSE HIS WORDS SEEMED TO ME DRUNK.** That is, his words seemed to me without reason, just as those who are drunk most often speak. And it is to be noted here that although it is a divine precept that we...

# CANTO XXVII
<sig>q. xiii.</sig>

...let us obey our superiors. Nevertheless, one must obey such a precept even in unjust things. **AND THEN HE SAID TO ME: YOUR HEART SHOULD NOT SUSPECT.** Fearing that Guido might suspect the sin <note>The sin of giving fraudulent counsel</note>, the Pope promises to absolve him and demonstrates that he has the authority to do so. **WHICH YOUR PREDECESSOR DID NOT HOLD DEAR.** This was Pope Celestine <note>Celestine V, who famously abdicated the papacy in 1294</note>, who, as we have shown above, renounced the papacy.

---

Then the grave arguments weighed upon me,
where silence seemed to me the worse path,
and I said: "Father, since you wash me
From that sin into which I must now fall:
a long promise with a short fulfillment
will make you triumph on the high seat."

**I would make you triumph:** that is, to achieve victory.

The poet feigns quite appropriately that, since Guido had been of the order of Saint Francis, the Saint had taken up his patronage. And if we want an allegory, we shall say that the conscience of one who has committed fraud at the request of a prelate remains ambiguous after death—that is, after the sin is committed.

**Francis came for me as soon as I was dead**
**for me; but one of the black cherubim**
**said to him: 'Do not take him; do not do me wrong.**
**He must come down here among us wretches**
**because he gave the fraudulent counsel,**
**since which time I have been at his hair.**
**For one cannot be absolved who does not repent,**
**nor can one repent and will a sin at once**
**because of the contradiction which does not allow it.'**
**O miserable me! How I shook myself**
**when he seized me, saying to me: 'Perhaps**
**you did not think I was a logician!'**
**To Minos he carried me; and he twisted**
**his tail eight times around his hardened back,**
**and then out of great rage he bit it.**
**He said: 'This one is for the thieves of the fire';**
**wherefore, where you see, I am lost,**
**and thus clothed, walking, I feel my rancor."**
**When he had thus completed his speech,**
**the flame departed sorrowing,**
**twisting and flapping its sharp horn.**
**We passed onward, I and my leader,**
**up over the crag to the next arch**
**that covers the ditch in which the fee is paid**
**By those who, by severing, acquire a burden.**

**PAYS THE FEE.** That is, the penalty and tribute. It is as if he says: the punishment of those who, by severing with false slanders and dividing those who were joined as friends, "acquire a burden"—they acquire sin, which is a burden and a weight upon the soul.

<column-break/>

The arguments that the Pope had used had power over me. And for this reason **SILENCE SEEMED TO ME THE WORSE [PATH]:** that is, it seemed worse to me because it seemed that by not obeying I might appear to doubt his authority and power, whereby he might proceed against me as a heretic. Therefore I said: "That promising much and delivering little..."

...ambiguous: because on one side Francis—that is, the religious order at whose request the act is done—persuades him that it is not an error; on the other is the devil, who is the sin itself, and condemns him. **ONE OF THE BLACK CHERUBIM.** That is, a devil; and therefore black, who before his damnation was of the order of Cherubim. We shall speak of these more fully in the *Paradiso*. **FOR ONE CANNOT BE ABSOLVED WHO DOES NOT REPENT.** The reason the devil assigns to Saint Francis is that the Count cannot be saved unless he is absolved. Nor can one be absolved who does not repent of the sin committed. Nor can one at the same time wish to commit the sin and repent of it, because "to will" and "not to will" are contraries. **OH MISERABLE WRETCH.** Then, in great distress, he described what had happened to him. **TO MINOS HE CARRIED ME AND HE TWISTED.** Of Minos, enough was said above in the fifth canto, both in recounting history and fables and in demonstrating the allegorical sense. **AND THEN OUT OF GREAT RAGE HE BIT IT.** This is the end of those who are damned by their own conscience: out of desperation, they become furious even against themselves. **THIS ONE IS OF THE GUILTY:** that is, of those damned to enter the flame, which covers and steals away the soul <note>original: "inunola", meaning to wrap or steal away</note> so that it cannot be seen within; and thus he said above: "And every flame steals away a sinner." And thus clothed in this flame, **I FEEL MY RANCOR.** That is, I lament and carry hatred toward myself. For rancor is a hidden hatred. **UP TO THE OTHER ARCH.** Up to the bridge of the ninth ditch <note>The ninth *bolgia* of the eighth circle of Hell</note>. **WHERE THE FEE IS PAID...**

<meta>This page transitions from the punishment of fraudulent counselors in Canto XXVII to the ninth pouch of the eighth circle, where Dante describes the sowers of discord. The commentary by Landino begins here for Canto XXVIII, moving from the advice of Guido da Montefeltro to the physical mutilation of schismatics.</meta>

# CANTO XXVIII OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE

In the two preceding cantos, our author has treated the fraudulent counselors punished in the eighth pouch. Now he places the sowers <note>The original Italian 'efeminatori' is likely a variant or error for 'seminatori' (sowers).</note> of scandals, schisms, and heresies. Because they used fraud to destroy and separate those who previously lived joined in harmony, they are deservedly shown having their own limbs separated, divided, and torn, more or less according to whether they sowed greater or lesser discord. And in this place—

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A decorative square initial 'C' containing a miniature illustration, though the details of the miniature are small and stylized, possibly floral or abstract patterns in red, gold, and blue.</image-desc>
**Who could ever, even with untied words,** <note>The poet uses "parole sciolte" (untied words) to refer to prose, which is not bound by the "ties" of rhyme and meter.</note>
**tell fully of the blood and the wounds**
**that I now saw, even by narrating many times?**
**Every tongue would surely fall short**
**because of our speech and our mind,**
**which have so little capacity to comprehend so much.**

<column-break/>

—the saying of the Psalmist fits: **"The sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows: their tongue a sharp sword."** <note>original: "Filii hominum dentes eorum arma et sagitte: Lingue eorum gladius acutus." Psalm 57:4</note>. **WHO COULD EVER.** As an excellent poet, having to deal with great and tragic matters, he uses a beginning that makes the listener attentive, demonstrating that suitable words cannot be found for the magnitude of these things. Similarly, Virgil says: **"Not if I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths, a voice of iron, could I grasp all the forms of crime or run through all the names of punishments."** <note>original: "Non michi si lingue centusint oraqua centum Ferrea uox omnes scelerum cōprendere formas. Omnia penarum percurrere nomina possem." Virgil, Aeneid, Book VI.</note> Thus he imitates Virgil, and Virgil imitates Homer. Therefore, **Who could ever?** is as if he said, "no one." **TO SPEAK of the blood and the wounds.** The quantity of blood and the cruelty of the wounds. **FULLY**, or sufficiently. **EVEN WITH UNTIED WORDS.** That is, in free speech and in prose; for he who writes in verse uses words bound by certain measures, but he who writes in prose uses words that are free and untied from every measure and rhyme. The meaning is this: No one could sufficiently describe the horrible slaughter even if they wrote in prose, where it is easier to express what we wish than in verse. Alternatively, **BY NARRATING MANY TIMES.** This text can be arranged in two ways: either "who could narrate the wounds I saw, though I saw them with the purpose of narrating them many times," or we shall say, "Who could ever narrate them fully, even if he narrated them many times instead of once?" **EVERY TONGUE would surely fall short** in the telling. And he provides the reason: **BECAUSE OUR SPEECH** is insufficient, **AND THE MIND** is insufficient; **WHICH HAVE**—that is, the speech and mind have—**LITTLE CAPACITY** <term>seno: literally 'breast' or 'fold', used here to mean the intellectual capacity to hold or contain a concept</term>; that is, they are a small receptacle. **TO COMPREHEND SO MUCH:** that is, to understand such a great thing.

<column-break/>

**If one should again assemble all the people**
**who lie upon the fateful land**
**that made its blood sorrowful in Puglia**

<column-break/>

The meaning is that the wounds given in all the battles fought at different times in the countries he mentions would be as nothing compared to the wounds of those who were in this pouch.

The commentary by Landino explains that their physical mutilation is a symbolic punishment for having divided what was meant to be unified in life.</summary>

<header>CANTO XXVIII</header>

**For the Trojans, or for the long war**
**that made of the rings such high spoils,**
**as Livy writes, who does not err;** <note>Reference to the Battle of Cannae (216 BCE), where Hannibal's Carthaginian forces defeated the Romans. So many Roman knights were killed that their gold rings filled several measuring baskets.</note>
**With those who felt the pain of blows**
**for standing against Robert Guiscard;** <note>A Norman adventurer (c. 1015–1085) who conquered Southern Italy and Sicily.</note>
**and the others whose bones are still gathered**
**at Ceperano, where every Apulian**
**was a traitor; and there at Tagliacozzo,**
**where old Alardo won without weapons;** <note>Alardo is Érard de Valéry, who helped Charles of Anjou defeat Conradin in 1268 through a clever tactical ambush rather than direct assault.</note>
**And though one showed his limb pierced and another lopped off,**
**it would be nothing to equal**
**the foul fashion of the ninth pouch.**

**Even a cask, losing its middle-board or side-piece,** <note>original: "mezul" and "lulla". These are technical terms for the parts of a wine barrel.</note>
**does not gape so wide as one I saw,**
**ripped from the chin to the part that breaks wind.**
**Between his legs hung his intestines;**
**the vitals appeared, and the dismal sack**
**that turns into excrement what is swallowed.**
**While I was all intent on looking at him,**
**he watched me and with his hands pulled open his chest,**
**saying: "Now see how I tear myself!**
**See how Mahomet is split!**
**Before me goes Ali, weeping,**
**his face cleft from chin to forelock."**

<column-break/>

**the ninth pouch:** And therefore he says **IF THERE WERE GATHERED**, meaning if all the people were gathered together who were once grieving for their spilled blood upon the fated land of **Puglia** <note>Apulia, in southern Italy</note>: which he calls "fated" because Fortune showed great variety there. And he mentions five wars. The first was between Aeneas and Turnus, which Virgil writes about most elegantly in the last six books [of the *Aeneid*], showing terrible slaughter and killing. **OR FOR THE long war: that made of the rings such high spoils.** He refers to the conflict at Cannae in Puglia, and the massive defeat that Hannibal, captain of the Carthaginians, gave to the Romans through the rashness of the consul Marcus Varro. Varro, against the advice of his colleague Paulus Emilius, insisted on joining battle when he could have avoided it and gradually consumed Hannibal's armies. Hannibal could not recruit new soldiers every day, and he entered battle at that hour of the day when the sun struck the eyes of the Roman soldiers. Similarly, the wind bothered them greatly, carrying dust from dry places against their faces. On that day, eighty senators were killed, along with two quaestors, twenty-one military tribunes, several men who had been consuls, praetors, or ediles, forty thousand infantry, and two thousand seven hundred knights. From so many bodies, Hannibal had a bridge built for his army to pass over. Thus he so weakened the Roman forces that, if he had known how to use such prosperous fortune and had come to Rome immediately before their terrified spirits could recover or provide any defense, he would have taken Rome. But his delay robbed him of victory. Whereupon Maharbal the Carthaginian cried out in indignation: <note>original: "Tu sai uincere Hanibale Ma non sai usar la uictoria."</note> "You know how to conquer, Hannibal, but you do not know how to use the victory." Because of this, Petrarch wisely said: <note>original: "Vinſe hanibal ma non ſeppe uſar poi Ben la uictorioſa ſua uentura."</note> "Hannibal won, but did not know how to use well his victorious fortune afterward." **WITH THOSE who felt the pain of blows.** Richard was an ancient Duke of Normandy, and he had two sons: Richard, who succeeded his father, and Robert Guiscard. In the year of salvation 1070, Robert came to Puglia to Robert the Apulian, who was Duke there at that time, and gave him great help in the wars against the Prince of Salerno. Finally, Robert, having no male children, made him his son-in-law and successor to the Duchy. For this reason, Guiscard, through military virtue, conquered Puglia, Calabria, and the whole realm of Sicily, which Alexios, Emperor of the Greeks, had occupied. Later, he was in favor of Gregory VIII against Henry III. His successors reigned until the time of Henry, father of Frederick II. **AND THE OTHER whose bones are still gathered.** He refers to the war and the defeat that Charles I [of Anjou] gave to Manfred, not without the prompt work of the Florentine Guelphs, as was said elsewhere. **AND THERE AT Tagliacozzo.** This is the other battle that the aforementioned Charles fought against Conradin, nephew of Manfred, on the plain of San Valentino near Tagliacozzo. **Alardo.** This was a Frenchman, a baron of no small authority and already old, who at that time was returning from the Holy Land. Seeing the small forces of Charles against Conradin, he advised him to trust more in counsel than in arms. This carried such authority with Charles that he committed the entire matter to him. Through his prudence, Charles recovered victory most fully when he was almost defeated in the battle. But it was not without great killing on every side. The battle was in the year of salvation 1268, on the twenty-fourth of August. Afterward, as a memory of the event and for the salvation of the souls of the slain, Charles built an excellent abbey called "Victory." <note>The Abbey of Santa Maria della Vittoria.</note>

He sets a fitting punishment: for he is deservedly opened and divided who has divided charity and love—either between man and man, or between God and man—by sowing scandal, discord, and schism. Allegorically, he maintains this in such men because they always have a distracted and divided mind. He feigns, therefore, that these heretics are divided through the middle up to the head, because they have divided the Church of God, which ought to be one body of which Christ is the head. He places first one who is open from the thighs to the chin, and makes a comparison to a **cask** from which either the middle stave (called the **mezule**) or the side stave (which they call the **lulla**, and others **rulla**) has been removed. And he says **CASK**, meaning...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's *Inferno*, Canto XXVIII. Having previously compared the carnage of the ninth pouch to the bloodiest battles in history, the author now focuses on the specific punishments of the "sowers of scandal and schism," specifically Muhammad and Ali, providing a medieval biographical sketch of Muhammad filled with the typical polemics of that era.</meta>

# XXVIII INFERNO

A **cask** <note>original: "botte", which in Latin is called *veges*</note>... **NOT PIERCED**: it is not bored or opened. Just as it would be to lose me, I saw one broken from the chin down to where one **passes wind** <note>original: "trulla"; that is, down to the end of the torso where the exit of the belly's vent is located, from which foul air escapes. When it comes out with sound and noise, some call it *trulla*, though not learnedly.</note>. **THE GUTS**: that is, the intestines. **GULPS**: swallows down. **WHILE I WAS ALL INTENT**: fixedly watching him. **I TEAR MYSELF**: I rip and open myself.

We have said above that the author places here the punishments of the ninth species of fraud, which is called **scandal** or **schism**. These sins are types of envy, because they oppose the love contained within charity; envy is the contrary of charity. These sowers of scandal and schism commit fraud to the harm of their neighbor under the guise of doing good. However, they differ among themselves:

**Infidelity**, **Schism**, and **Heresy**.
**Infidelity** is the opposite of faith; it is not believing what the faith believes in every part and thing.
**Heresy** is departing from the faith in some specific part or making some change within it.
**Schism** is departing entirely from the faith and its union.

Because schism is greater than the first two, the poet imagines it is punished in this lower part. Schism, therefore, is the division and separation of the unity of faith and charity. Furthermore, the division within cities between factions of citizens, and even between man and man, is included under this sin. Therefore, whoever has committed heresy in the faith is divided from the chin downward, because they have divided the body of the Church, of which Christ is the head. Those who have committed scandal between princes, who are the heads of people, have their wounds in the head. Those who have divided relatives have their hands cut off; and those who have divided son from father have had their head cut off and carry it in their hand.

But because the history of **Muhammad** <note>original: "Maumeth"</note> is not to be entirely passed over, we shall note how in the year of our salvation 610, during the papacy of Boniface III and the reign of Emperor Honorius <note>The text likely means Emperor Heraclius, as Honorius ruled much earlier.</note>, Muhammad was in Arabia. He was a magician of the highest cunning and greedy for honor—not human, but divine. In his youth, he saw various lands and nations; in Jerusalem, he learned the **Mosaic law**, and elsewhere the **Christian law**. Thus instructed, and using miracles performed through magical arts, he persuaded the unlearned multitude of Arabia that he was the Messiah come from heaven. He gave new laws, mixing in many voluptuous things, through which he easily drew the crowd to his devotion. With this favor, he acquired lordship, especially by feigning a most holy life and character. With extreme cunning, he had accustomed a white dove to feed in his ears, where he would secretly place millet and similar bait. Consequently, when he was preaching to the people, he would have the dove released, and it would immediately fly to his ears; he would then assert that it was the **Holy Spirit** showing him what was good to do.

To such audacity was added another most pernicious plague. A monk named **Sergius**, falling into the Nestorian heresy <note>A 5th-century doctrine that separated the divine and human natures of Jesus.</note>, was cast out by the other monks. He then went to Arabia and joined Muhammad. Because he was very learned and full of cunning, he provided many shrewd counsels. Muhammad kept him hidden, asserting that he was the **Angel Gabriel** who instructed him in all things useful to the soul. Some say that Sergius was sent from Rome to preach to the Arabs and turn them to our religion, and he was promised that if he behaved manfully, he would receive the **Cardinal’s hat**. When the promise was not kept, he returned to Arabia and **recanted** <note>original: "canto la palinodia"; to sing a different song, or take back what was said before.</note>, preaching the opposite of what he had preached before. He was a great help to Muhammad, so much so that not only in Arabia but in all of Egypt, Muhammad was reputed to be the true Messiah.

He instituted that his people should be called **Sarrains** or **Saracens**, from Sarah, the legitimate wife of Abraham, as if they were the legitimate successors of the divine line. He was of such talent that he even used his ailments to his advantage. Since he was often overcome by the **falling sickness** <note>epilepsy</note>, every time he returned to his senses, he would pretend that the Angel Gabriel had appeared to him and that he had fallen because he could not endure such splendor. He was left fatherless from childhood and poor, raised by his uncle. He died in July in the year of our salvation 621 <note>Historical sources usually cite 632 AD.</note>. Others place it in 632, after which **Caliph** obtained his principality; Caliph was succeeded by **Achaly**, who, being driven from the principality, was replaced by **Ali**. But because Ali was very superstitious, the Egyptians created a new prince, a new Caliph, against him.

**WHAT EXCREMENT IT MAKES**: Although this description is foul, the poet uses it not only to show the natural consequence, but it signifies **allegorically** that whatever enters the mouth of the schismatic becomes dung; that is, whatever he learns of doctrine becomes corruption for other men. Certainly, he was a great corruption among men, which is not only not extinguished, but God, the just judge, permits it to expand its borders to avenge and punish His enemies with His enemies. Wherefore in this year, to the extreme infamy of the Christian name—I do not know what will follow, but the sins of the princes of this age, almost all of whom are infected, and the **Italian discords** fill us with more fear than hope. *Have mercy on us, O God, and let his face shine upon us.*

**ALI**: Some believe he was the uncle of Muhammad and a helper in all his enterprises.

*A devil is back here who carves us*
*so cruelly with the edge of his sword,*
*re-placing each one of this ream.*

<column-break/>

He demonstrates that the damned subjected to such punishment go continuously around that ditch, and a devil, every time they return to him, wounds them anew with the sword. This signifies...

### CANTO XXVIII

When they had turned back on the sorrowful road:
because the wounds are closed up again
before anyone passes before them again.
"But you, who are you who muses on the crag,
perhaps to delay going to the punishment
that was adjudged upon your self-accusations?"
"Neither has death reached him yet, nor does guilt lead him,"
replied my master, "to torment him:
but to give him full experience,
it is necessary for me, who am dead, to lead him
through the Inferno down here, from circle to circle;
and this is as true as the fact that I speak to you."
More than a hundred there were who, when they heard him,
stopped in the ditch to look at me,
forgetting their martyrdom in their wonder.
"Now tell Brother Dolcino then to arm himself,
you who perhaps will see the sun shortly,
if he does not wish to follow me here soon,
with such provisions that, being hemmed in by snow,
he does not grant victory to the Novarese,
which otherwise would not be easy to achieve."
After he had suspended one foot to depart,
Muhammad said these words to me;
then he stretched it out on the ground to leave.

<note>Brother Dolcino was the leader of the Apostolic Brethren, a radical movement in the early 14th century.</note>

...[God] would not allow such grave wickedness to go unpunished. Finally, he was besieged by an army gathered from Lombards, Savoyards, Provencals, and Frenchmen. And finally, because of hunger, his followers surrendered, and he was captured and led to Novara. There, although he was urged by many, he never wished to return to the true law <note>The Catholic Church</note>. For this reason, he was tortured with red-hot pincers throughout the city and cruelly killed. He was a man who, without doubt, would have been worthy of immortal fame had he not fallen into such error; for in so many torments he never changed his expression nor made a lament. Instead, he continually comforted his followers to persevere in his precepts. Nor was Margaret of Trent, his wife, of lesser fortitude of soul: she, being both beautiful and very rich, and finding noble suitors, preferred the same punishments rather than renounce the schism. The siege lasted one year and the schism two.

Another, who had his throat pierced through
and his nose cut off up to his eyebrows,
and had only one ear remaining,
having stayed to look on in wonder
with the others, before the others opened his windpipe,
which on the outside was red in every part;
And he said: "O you whom guilt does not condemn,
and whom I saw above on Italian land,
unless too much resemblance deceives me:
Remember Piero da Medicina,
if ever you return to see the sweet plain
that slopes down from Vercelli to Marcabò.
And make it known to the two best men of Fano,
to Messer Guido and also to Angiolello,
that if the foresight here is not in vain..."

<column-break/>

...that the schismatic always involves himself in the same error; and a devil—that is, his diabolical persistence—keeps him continually divided. **NE MOR TEL GIUNSE ANCHOR** <note>original: "Neither has death reached him yet"</note>. He informs Dolcino to provide himself with victuals before the snows come: because then he could not bring them, being on such a rugged mountain. **CHE NON Cerchi uictoria** <note>original: "That he does not [grant] victory"</note>: that is, that he does not let himself be conquered by the Novarese, his fellow citizens.

Brother Dolcino lived in the time of Pope Boniface VIII and was from Novara in Lombardy. He was raised in Vercelli by a priest named August, from whom, after some time, he fled to Trent after being caught stealing. In the mountains near that city, being eloquent and of great talent, he immediately took the habit of a friar and persuaded those rough and ignorant people to join a new sect, affirming himself to be a true apostle sent by God. He willed that everything should be held in common out of charity, and especially women, except for the mother and the daughter. Hearing this, the Bishop of Trent had Dolcino expelled. Seeing the multitude that followed him grow every day, he believed himself to be impregnable if he retreated into the mountains of Brescia, Bergamo, and Como, not descending to the plain as those places were well fortified by the nature of the terrain and the snows. But finally, being driven from there, he retreated to a very rugged mountain between Novara and Vercelli, where he had with him more than three thousand men capable of bearing arms, both because they could fulfill every pleasure near him and because he delighted every man with his eloquence. But because God...

**DImostra** <note>It demonstrates</note> that Piero da Medicina, having remained like one stupefied at seeing Dante, who was in that place, not only spoke to him but gave him a message. This man was from Medicina, a town in the territory of Bologna. Because of the many scandals and discords he sowed among the noblemen of the territory of Bologna and the Bolognese citizens, and furthermore between the Bolognese and the lords <note>original: "tyrani"</note> of Romagna, he deserved to be punished here. He had his throat cut because he had erred with words, which are formed in the throat; and also his nose cut, which is a great ornament of the head, because he divided the territory, which is the ornament of the city, which is the head. And he had one ear cut for having divided the great citizens, who are the senses of the head. This man admonishes those who live to beware of scandals, not because those in Hell do not want everyone else to go there, but because he had been the origin of so many evils, he feared that the more evil followed, the more [his own punishment would increase]...

# CANTO XXVIII OF THE INFERNO

> They shall be cast out of their vessel
> and weighted down <note>original: "mazerati," referring to a method of execution where the victim is tied in a sack with a stone</note> near Cattolica

> And I to him: "Show me and declare,
> if you want me to carry news of you above,
> who is he of the bitter sight?"

<column-break/>

...so that his pain might increase further. He describes the plain of Lombardy as far as Romagna; Mercabò is on the Po river and at the end of Romagna on the shore opposite Venice, built by the Venetians and later taken by Roberto da Polenta. It was destroyed when the Venetians were defeated at Ferrara in the year thirteen hundred and eight. Therefore, he includes the entire plain of Lombardy and Romagna, which begins at Vercelli and reaches as far as Mercabò. **TO TWO OF THE BEST.** From Fano. Malatestino, Lord of Rimini, under the guise of an invitation, ordered that two principal citizens of Fano should come to dine with him at Cattolica, pretending he wished to discuss great matters with them. As they were coming by sea, by his order, they were drowned by Messer Guido del Cassero and Angiolello da Carignano. **OUT OF THEIR VESSEL.** He says this because their souls will be cast out of the body, which is like a vessel for the soul. **TO WEIGHT DOWN** <note>original: "MASARARE"</note> means to tie a man in a sack and, with a stone attached, throw him into the sea. **BY A CRUEL TYRANT.** This was Messer Malatestino, of whom we spoke above. **BETWEEN THE ISLANDS OF CYPRUS AND MAJORCA.** He shows that in the entire Mediterranean Sea, a more cruel thing was never done. For he places Cyprus as a very eastern island and very distant from Majorca, which is in the west. Cyprus was once joined to Syria, just as Sicily was to Italy and Euboea to Boeotia. This island is located to the east in the <term>Pamphylian Gulf</term> <note>The sea off the southern coast of modern-day Turkey</note>, and to the west, it is opposite Sicily and Syria. It was an island considered very effeminate, where there was an ancient law commanding every woman once in her life to go to the temple of Venus and not leave until she had known a stranger. **MAJORCA.** These are two islands near the shores of Spain, called the <term>Gymnasia</term> by the Greeks because the inhabitants stay almost naked in the summer, and <term>gymnos</term> in Greek signifies "naked." The Latins call them the Balearics because they skillfully use slings <note>from the Greek "ballein," meaning to throw</note>. The larger of these is called Majorca and is as close to Spain as one can sail in a day. Thus, Cyprus being very far east and Majorca far west, by saying "between the islands of Cyprus and Majorca," Dante intends to encompass the entire sea from east to west. **NEPTUNE.** Since he is the god of the sea, he should reasonably have seen everything that was ever done at sea. In the genealogy of the heathens, it is said that Saturn was lord of the sky, the earth, and the sea. Four children remained of him: three sons—Jove, Neptune, and Pluto—and one daughter named Juno. To Jove fell the sky by lot in the division. And Juno, whom he took as his wife, had the air as her dowry. Neptune was content with the sea, and Pluto with hell. The allegory of the fable is that the universe, created by God, is placed in time. Saturn signifies nothing other than time. Hence, in Greek, he is called <term>Kronos</term> from <term>chronos</term>, which is "time." They say he devoured all the children born to him except these four, whose allegory we showed above. In the verse, "Neptune" is written with one 'n' <note>original: "neptuno"</note> rather than two, out of respect for the rhymes that follow. **NOT BY PIRATES.** Meaning sea corsairs. **NOT BY THE ARGIVE RACE.** Greek people, because the Greeks are called <term>Argives</term> from Argos, a principal city of Greece, who for a long time were masters of the seas. Alternatively, he says Argive people to mean seafaring people, calling sailors Argives after the *Argo*, the first ship, of which we shall speak elsewhere. **THAT TRAITOR.** Namely, Malatestino. **WHO SEES ONLY WITH ONE.** That is, he sees with only one eye because he was blind in the other. **AND HOLDS THE LAND.** Understand this as Rimini. **WHICH ONE WHO IS HERE WITH ME.** Who would wish he had never seen it; he refers to Curio. This man was a Roman orator, very eloquent, of whom Cicero writes. He was restless and factious and greatly favored Caesar's faction in the civil war against Pompey. When Caesar was leading the army from Gaul to Rome, he stopped at Rimini because, according to the laws, he could not cross the <term>Rubicon</term> river with an army. Curio came from Rome, who was then a tribune of the plebs, and with his eloquence, he so moved Caesar that where Caesar was still doubtful whether to cross or not, he resolved to cross. Appropriately, therefore, since Curio was a great cause of civil dissension, especially through his eloquence, the poet places him here without a tongue. Thus, he would wish never to have seen Rimini, because in that place he committed the scandal for which he is damned here. **HE WILL MAKE THEM COME TO A PARLEY WITH HIM** and then he will kill them; and because of this, it will not be necessary for them to make vows or prayers to the **WIND OF FOCARA.** Focara is a place in the sea between Pesaro and Cattolica, so dangerous because of the tempest of the winds that all the sailors who pass there make vows and prayers to God for their escape. But these men, being dead, will no longer have to sail through this place to return home.

Dante asks who is the one of the "bitter sight"—that is, who is the one to whom it seems bitter to have seen Rimini, because he had said that he would wish never to have seen it. And Piero...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto XXVIII. # CANTO XXVIII

Then he placed his hand upon the jaw
of one of his companions and forced open his mouth,
crying: "This is he, and he does not speak!
This man, in exile, drowned out the doubt
in Caesar, affirming that he who is prepared
always suffers harm through waiting." <note>This refers to Gaius Scribonius Curio, a Roman tribune who, according to legend, convinced Julius Caesar to cross the Rubicon and start the Roman Civil War.</note>
Oh, how terrified he seemed to me,
with his tongue cut off in his throat—
Curio, who was once so bold in speech!

If Curio, for having done harm with his tongue, had been deprived of his tongue, it was fitting that Mosca should have lost his hands, because with his hands and with force he had done harm. We have placed in the 16th canto of the *Paradiso* the most unhappy wedding of our republic involving Messer Buondelmonte of the noble Buondelmonti family; it is not necessary to repeat it here. <note>In 1215, Buondelmonte de' Buondelmonti broke an engagement to an Amidei girl to marry a Donati, sparking the Guelph and Ghibelline wars in Florence.</note> There lived, then, in those same times, Mosca de' Lamberti, of a noble family and nearly the leader of the Ghibelline faction. This man, more reckless than wise, was present at the consultation held by the Uberti, Lamberti, Amidei, and others of the Ghibelline faction against Messer Buondelmonte, who shortly before had rejected the bride given to him from the Amidei and had married one of the Donati. While some elders prudently advised that they should proceed with maturity and consider the outcome, Mosca, on the contrary, advised that he should be killed immediately, saying: "A thing done has a head" <note>original: "cosa fatta capo ha." A proverb meaning once a deed is done, there is no turning back; it provides its own conclusion.</note>. And after the council, he killed him with men like himself. From this arose infinite discords and the exile now of the Ghibellines, now of the Guelfs. **LIFTING THE STUMPS:** that is, raising his arms without hands. For a "stump" <note>original: "moncherino"</note> is the name for the end of an arm deprived of the hand; and by lifting his arms, the blood that issued from the stumps fouled his face. **WHO SAID:** "Alas, a thing done has a head," as we explained above. **WHICH WAS** an evil seed: because from this advice proceeded infinite discords and wars, not only among our citizens but also throughout all of Tuscany. **AND I:** Dante. **ADDED** to his words **AND DEATH** to your lineage: as if to say, you glory that your words were an evil seed for the Tuscan people, and I add that they were also the destruction of your own stock and progeny. And Dante’s words added grief to the grief of the punishment, such that, confused, **HE WENT AWAY** <note>original: "sengio," an archaic form of "se n'andò"</note>—going off like a sad and vicious man. **AND MAD:** and without prudence. He says this because, in truth, Mosca’s advice was that of a most wicked citizen and a man who entirely abounded in malice and was void of all prudence.

And one who had both one and the other hand cut off,
lifting his stumps through the dark air
so that the blood fouled his face,
Cried: "You shall also remember Mosca,
who said, alas, 'A thing done has a head,'
which was an evil seed for the Tuscan people."
And I added: "And death to your lineage!"
Wherefore he, piling grief upon grief,
went away like a person sad and mad.

But I remained to watch the troop,
and I saw a thing that I would be afraid
to tell of alone without further proof,
Were it not that conscience reassures me—
the good companion that emboldens a man
under the breastplate of feeling itself pure.
I saw surely, and it still seems I see,
a trunk without a head going just as...

<column-break/>

...then with his hand he opened the mouth of Curio, who in that place was his companion, and shows that his tongue had been cut out. This punishment was fitting for him: because having deservedly sinned with the tongue, he ought to be punished in it. **THIS MAN:** Curio. **EXILED:** From Rome by the Pompeians. **DROWNED OUT:** He removed and took away the doubt of Caesar. For when Caesar had reached the end of his province, although the desire for lordship pushed him to cross the river Rubicon and make war on the Pompeians, nevertheless, reverence for the laws restrained him. But Curio incited him to the crossing, affirming that he who is prepared always suffers harm through waiting. This is a verse taken from Lucan. <note>The Roman poet Lucan, author of the Pharsalia.</note> For Lucan depicts Curio persuading Caesar to undertake the enterprise against Pompey the Great, especially since he was instructed and prepared with armies and everything else necessary for war. Wherefore he says: *away with delays; it has always been harmful to those prepared to postpone* <note>original Latin: "tolle moras semper nocuit differre paratis"</note>. Therefore, Curio affirmed to Caesar **THAT THE PREPARED:** he who is ready. **ALWAYS** suffers harm through waiting: that is, through lingering. This signifies that it is always harmful to those who are ready to differ and delay. **OH HOW** terrified Curio seemed to me. A most fitting punishment, that he who had sinned with eloquence and audacity should be punished with their opposites, which are silence and terror.

Curio had his tongue cut out because with it he had sown discord. Mosca had his hands cut off because his advice had been to use hands and force. And for the same reason, he depicts Bertran <note>original: "Beltramo," referring to Bertran de Born, the troubadour lord.</note> having his head separated from the rest of his body; which punishment he imagines to be prepared for those who sow discord between blood relations, because they have divided those who were like members that should have been joined in one body. And morally...

The commentary links Curio's role in the Roman Civil War to Mosca's role in the bloody origins of the Guelph and Ghibelline factions in Florence.</summary>

# INFERNO

> the others of that wretched flock went on.
> **H**e held the severed head by its hair,
> hanging from his hand like a lantern,
> and it looked at us and said, "Woe is me!"
> **O**f himself he made a light for himself,
> and they were two in one and one in two;
> how that can be, He who governs above knows.

...not imprudent: and by showing that he recognizes him, he gains authority and credibility. Thus Ovid says: "Who would believe this of the stones, if antiquity were not for a witness?" <note>original: "Saxa quis hoc credat nisi sit pro teste uetustas." — Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book XIV.</note> **EXCEPT THAT** conscience assures me. A man would fear to say things that would make him be considered a liar because they seem impossible; but being true, the conscience—which is pure—gives him daring. For a good conscience is a guide that makes the soul bold and frank. And just as a man protected by armor, or rather a breastplate, does not fear to put himself among the swords of his enemies, so when a man feels pure and knows he speaks the truth, he takes the security to speak even though the thing may seem impossible. And certainly, conscience gives great boldness not only in speaking, but in every human operation. **I CERTAINLY SAW.** Two things cause lies to be told: first, when for some reason of our own will we say what we know to be false. Second, when although we do not wish to tell a lie, we nevertheless tell it believing it to be true, either through an error made, or through simplicity, or through bad information. Therefore, the poet has shown above that he does not sin out of malice by telling a falsehood. Now he shows that he does not lie out of ignorance either, given that he narrates not what he heard—where he could be deceived—but what he saw. And he saw it so clearly that he still seems to see it. **AND IT STILL SEEMS I SEE.** He shows that what he saw then is so fixed in his memory that it still seems to be before his eyes. And in passing, he shows that the memory retains well those things that have caused wonder or fear, or other great disturbances, because such things make a deeper impression of themselves. **A TORSO:** <term>busto; torso</term> although in Latin *busto* signifies the place where human bodies were burned to then place the ashes in a small tomb, and is also used for the tomb itself; nonetheless, in our language [Italian], we call the "bust" or "torso" the whole human body except for the head. **THE SEVERED HEAD** he held by the hair: he held it by the hair of the head. **HANGING.** i.e., suspended and dangling, as in Latin they say *pensilis*. **IN THE MANNER.** In the likeness and in the form **OF A LANTERN:** thus he carried his head before him to see with its eyes, just as we carry a lantern when we want to see in the darkness. **AND IT:** That head looked at us and said, **"Woe is me."** **OF HIMSELF HE MADE** a light for himself: with his own eyes, although separated from the torso, he made light for himself—that is, for his torso. **AND THEY WERE TWO IN ONE.** Because the head was separated from the torso. **AND ONE IN TWO.** Because one and the same soul was in the torso and in the head. **HOW THAT CAN BE** He who governs above knows. That one and the same soul should be in the head and the torso when joined together is natural and easily understood. But that it should be in one and the other when separated is impossible according to the nature of an animal. For although the soul in the body is entirely in the whole and entirely in every part, nevertheless the origin and the source of the spirits—which are the vehicle that carries the powers of the soul—is in the heart. And the place where from the aforesaid spirits the senses and motion are generated, or at least perfected, and where the motor and sensory nerves originate, is the head. Therefore, since neither the heart by itself nor the head by itself can give perfection to sense or motion, the animal cannot live in any way when the head is separated from the rest of the body, except by supernatural power. Therefore, He who governs above—who is the supreme and only God—brings about how this can be. But man, who cannot understand the soul and the body except according to the nature of it, does not understand how this, being against its nature, can happen.

> When he was directly at the foot of the bridge,
> he raised his arm high with the whole head
> to bring his words closer to us,
> which were: "Now see the distressing punishment,
> you who, breathing, go seeing the dead;
> see if any is as heavy as this one.
> And so that you may carry news of me,
> know that I am Bertran de Born, he
> who gave the Young King evil encouragements;
> I made the father and the son rebels against each other."

<column-break/>

**W**hen the spirit reached the place where Dante was, he brought his head close to Dante so that he might better understand his speech. Then he said he was Bertran de Born. This man was Bertran de Born of England <note>Landino identifies him as English, though he was actually a nobleman from Limousin in France; the confusion likely stems from his involvement with the English royal family.</note>. Others say he was from Gascony, assigned to the guardianship of John <note>This refers to Henry "the Young King," eldest son of Henry II of England. Dante and his commentators often refer to him as "the Young King" or "Re Giovanni" (King John).</note>, whose surname was the Young, son of Henry, King of England. He was raised in the court of the King of France. And it happened that one day the King denied him a favor he had asked for, and the young man who had asked for it departed confused with shame. Whereupon the King turned to those standing around, asking who was more...

<summary>Dante describes the gruesome sight of Bertran de Born carrying his own severed head as a lantern. The commentary explains the physiological impossibility of such a state, attributing it to divine power, and begins the historical account of Bertran's role in the rebellion of the "Young King" against Henry II.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto XXVIII. Previously, the text discussed Mosca de' Lamberti and his role in the Florentine civil strife. We now move to the final and most striking figure of this circle: the headless Bertran de Born.</meta>

# CANTO XXVIII

> Ahithophel did no more for Absalom
> and for David with his wicked proddings.
> Because I divided persons so joined,
> I carry my weary brain parted
> from its source, which is in this trunk.
> Thus is the retribution observed in me.

<column-break/>

...ready to ask a favor or to deny one. John <note>The commentator here refers to John, likely confusing him with Henry the "Young King," the son of Henry II of England, whom the historical Bertran de Born famously incited to rebel.</note> replied that to a generous soul, it was more troublesome to deny it. The king judged this sentence so wise that he conjectured that John would turn out to be most wise and of a great spirit. And in his mature years, he turned out so liberal <note>In the sense of being generous or free-spending.</note> that his father could not sustain such heavy expense. Perhaps the youth would have regulated himself if Bertram <note>Bertran de Born (c. 1140–1215), a soldier and celebrated troubadour.</note> had not encouraged him to such prodigality. Finally, the father was forced to wage war against him, and in battle, the son was mortally wounded. And when the company of the Bardi of Florence <note>A powerful banking family in Florence during Dante's time; the commentator is blending historical periods here.</note> asked him for a hundred thousand florins, he made a will, and in it a legacy in which he left his soul to the devil if his father did not satisfy the Bardi. **YOU WHO GO BREATHING:** that is, you who are alive. To breathe means to draw breath, for no one can live who does not breathe. Therefore, it means: "you who come alive among the dead." **AHITHOPHEL** did no more to Absalom. In the Second Book of Kings <note>original: "Secondo libro de re"; in the Latin Vulgate, the books of Samuel are titled 1 and 2 Kings. This story is found in 2 Samuel 13-18.</note> it is written that Amnon, the firstborn of David, fell in love with Tamar, his sister. On the advice of a trusted friend, he begged David to send Tamar to him to prepare his food. Tamar went, and Amnon took her by force, although the girl constantly resisted. Afterward, it seeming to him that she had been harsh toward him, he cast her out. She revealed the wickedness to her brother Absalom, and later, by his advice, she kept the matter quiet. After two years, Absalom invited his father David and all his brothers to a banquet at one of his villas, and at the end of the banquet, he had Amnon killed and fled to Syria. But after three years, Joab, the prince of David’s militia, reconciled him to his father. Whereupon he returned to Jerusalem, although for two years David did not want him to come into his presence. In the third year, he pardoned him absolutely and spoke to him. But Absalom, with various arts, won over many tribes and made himself an enemy to his father, and they called him king. He drew Ahithophel, David's counselor, into his conspiracy. David ordered that another of his counselors, named Hushai, should pretend to rebel against him just as Ahithophel had, and he arranged things so that Ahithophel's advice was no longer accepted by Absalom. Therefore, Ahithophel hanged himself. And Absalom, believing the fraudulent advice of Hushai, was finally defeated in Ephraim. Afterward, in his flight, passing under an oak, he remained hanging from the branches by his hair, and was killed by Joab, one of David’s captains. **BECAUSE I** divided persons so joined: I divided father and son. **MY BRAIN** is divided from its source, the heart, which is the source of the spirits. **WHICH IS IN THIS TRUNK** in this torso, because the heart is in the breast. **THUS IS OBSERVED IN ME THE RETRIBUTION.** In civil law, the penalty of the talion <term>talione: the law of "an eye for an eye," from the Latin lex talionis</term> is ordained, which is that whoever has done an injury shall be punished in that very same way. As, for example <note>original: "verbi gratia"</note>, for someone who cuts off another’s hand, such a law requires that his hand be similarly cut off. And this person thus punished is called in Latin *contra passus* <note>original: "contra passus" — meaning "suffered in return."</note>, because he has suffered in return that which he had inflicted on others. Therefore, the poet said "the retribution" <term>contrapasso: Dante’s term for the symbolic relationship between a sin and its punishment</term>, that is, "to suffer in return for what I have done is observed in me." For since I divided the son from the father, who are one body—because father and son are considered as the same <note>original: "pater et filius censetur per eadem"</note>—therefore, my body, in return for this, is divided.

<summary>This page concludes the description of Bertran de Born's punishment, explaining his headless state as a "contrapasso" for dividing King Henry II from his son. It provides a lengthy biblical parallel involving the rebellion of Absalom against King David, incited by Ahithophel.</summary>

We now transition into the final "bolgia" or ditch of the eighth circle of Hell, moving from the bloody spectacles of physical division to the diseased state of those who corrupted reality itself through falsification.</meta>
