<columns>2</columns>
<header>INFERNO</header>

### CANTO XXIX. OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE

The many people and the diverse wounds
had made my eyes so intoxicated
that they were longing to stay and weep <note>The OCR reads "piaghe" (wounds) again here, but the context and rhyme scheme of the original Italian poem usually require "vaghe" (longing/desirous). This may be a transcription error in the source or a printer's mistake.</note>
But Virgil said to me: "Why do you still stare?
Why does your vision still linger
down there among the sad and mangled shades?
You did not do so at the other ditches <note>The <term>bolgie</term> or "evil ditches" of the eighth circle.</note>;
consider, if you think to count them,
that the valley winds for twenty-two miles.
And already the moon is beneath our feet;
the time is short that is now granted to us,
and there is more to see than you believe."

"If you had," I then replied,
"attended to the reason why I looked,
perhaps you would have granted me a longer stay."
He was already moving on, and I followed behind,
the leader already fleeing the answer,
and I adding as we went into that hollow:
"Where I was holding my eyes so fixed,
I believe a spirit of my own blood weeps for
the guilt that costs so much down there."
Then the Master said: "Do not let your thoughts be broken..."

<column-break/>

We have finally arrived at the tenth ditch <note>The <term>bolgia</term>, the final sub-division of the eighth circle of Hell.</note>, in which the falsifiers are punished. Falsity is the tenth species of fraud. There can be no falsity unless one thing is shown for another to the harm of one's neighbor: and it is generally defined as denying the truth or pretending that the false is true. And there are two types in words—and this is called a lie—and in deeds—and this is properly called falsity. And although writings and other things are falsified, here he places the falsifiers of metals, who are the alchemists, and the falsifiers of money. And this is done either by falsifying the alloy or by falsifying the coin. He places here at the beginning how he, out of wonder and compassion, willingly stopped to weep. But Virgil admonishes him that he must distribute the time given to him for this journey in a way that he can complete it.

Given that there still remained many and more horrendous things to see. And certainly, Higher Reason <note>Virgil often represents human reason in this allegory.</note>, when it has seen things in general, wishes to pass on to other knowledge: because science is not of particulars. And besides this, it considers the nature of things without any passion. But the lower part and sensuality revolves around particulars: and in those, it does not remain without some passion, whether of love, or of hatred, or of envy, or of compassion. This is why it is necessary for Dante to be admonished by Virgil. **THE MANY PEOPLE.** Not only were there many people, but they also had not similar, but diverse wounds. **HAD** The lights: that is, the eyes. **SO INTOXICATED.** When our eye of the mind is sober—that is, not occupied by any passion—it sees the truth. But when it is intoxicated by the contagion of the body, it willingly follows appetite. But Virgil, who is the Higher Reason, says "why do you still stare?" because **YOUR VISION** lingers: it leans and fixes itself. **THINK IF YOU** believe you can count them, for the valley winds twenty-two miles. Allegorically, Higher Reason admonishes the lower so that it does not waste time in wanting to have knowledge of particulars: because they are innumerable. And to demonstrate this, he affirms that the circuit and circumference of that ditch is twenty-four miles <note>The commentator notes 24 miles here, though the poem states 22 miles; this may reflect varying calculations of Hell's geography by Renaissance scholars.</note>, and it is full of shadows. Therefore, one easily concludes that it is impossible to enumerate them. And he said such a circuit was twenty-two miles to demonstrate that they are already near the center of the earth: because there remained only the tenth ditch and the ninth circle: which in itself holds four circles: and in the fourth is the center. But we, before entering the work, demonstrated in the "Site of Hell" <note>Referring to the introductory section of this commentary where the physical layout of Hell is mapped out.</note> this circuit of 22 miles. **AND ALREADY THE MOON** is under our feet. The time granted was one natural day. Therefore, he reached the center having passed the night and half the day. And the other half of the day became night for him once he passed the center, so that by morning he arrived at Cato <note>Cato the Younger, the guardian of Purgatory.</note>. Therefore, the first night was whole, and the following day was from midday into the night: and when the second night returned to our hemisphere, he had already ascended from the center to the surface of the other hemisphere; and he found the dawn there when it became night here. He demonstrates, therefore, that when they were in this ditch, the day was approaching in our hemisphere. And because the moon was in opposition to the sun, it was already beginning to be in the other hemisphere, which is under the feet of those in ours. After passing the middle of the body of Lucifer, he began to ascend. Therefore, having gone through the part of the day in our hemisphere, and beginning when it is day for us to ascend to the other, he found a new night with which he ascended from the center to the surface of that one; and he arrived at dawn. **AND THERE IS MORE TO SEE.** Because there remained the tenth ditch and the ninth circle, which embraced four sections.

Dante replied: "If you knew the reason why I was looking, you would have granted me," that is, pardoned my staying. **HE MOVED:** in this interval Virgil went on, and Dante following him as he walked, also followed him in the reply already started, and adding, he said: "I believe that a spirit of my blood and of my generation weeps in that hollow where I held my eyes fixed," that is, fastened: and it is a metaphor from one who sets his aim at a target. And Virgil replied: "let not your thought be broken," let not your thought be interrupted over this, that is, do not interrupt the thoughts you have of other things to think about this man; attend to others...

<summary>Dante lingers in the ninth ditch to look for his kinsman, Geri del Bello, but is rebuked by Virgil (Reason) for being distracted by personal grief. The text explains the nature of falsity and the mathematical geography of the final levels of Hell.</summary>

<header>CANTO XXIX</header>

"From this point on, let your thoughts concerning him
turn to something else, and let him remain there;
for I saw him at the foot of the little bridge,
pointing at you and threatening fiercely with his finger,
and I heard him named as Geri del Bello.
You were then so completely preoccupied
with him who once held Hautefort <note>original: "alta forte." This refers to Bertran de Born, the lord of Hautefort, whom Dante saw in the previous canto.</note>
that you did not look that way until he had vanished."

The poet feigns not to have seen this spirit in Hell to denote that he never saw him alive. And that Virgil comforts him so that he does not worry about him signifies that the intellect comforts us: though someone may be joined to us by blood, nevertheless we must not have compassion for the suffering that they reasonably endure. **YOU WERE THEN SO** completely preoccupied with him who held Hautefort. This refers to the aforementioned Bertran, who held the high, strong fortress in England <note>Hautefort is actually in Limousin, France, but was involved in the English dynastic wars.</note>, which he held for King John.

"O my leader, the violent death
which is not yet avenged for him," I said,
"by anyone who shares in his shame,
made him disdainful; wherefore he went on
without speaking to me, as I judge;
and in this, he has made me feel all the more pity."
Thus we spoke until we reached the first place
upon the crag which shows the other valley,
if there were more light, all the way to the bottom.
When we were above the final cloister <note>The <term>chiostra</term> or enclosure of the tenth ditch.</note>
of Malebolge, so that its lay brothers <note>The <term>conversi</term>, here used metaphorically for the suffering sinners.</note>
could appear to our sight,
diverse lamentations pierced me like arrows
which had their shafts barbed with pity;
whereat I covered my ears with my hands.
What pain there would be if the hospitals
of Valdichiana, between July and September,
and of Maremma and Sardinia, and their diseases,
were all together in one ditch;
such was it here, and such a stench came forth
as is wont to come from festered limbs.

They deserve every heavy punishment. **WHAT PAIN THERE WOULD BE.** Such pain was intended in those sinners as is seen in August among the sick, if all those of Valdichiana, Maremma, and Sardinia were in one pit. Here it should be noted that he mentions August because in that month there are many and difficult diseases. Whence Juvenal said: *And poets reciting in the month of August.* <note>original Latin: "Et augusto recitantes mense poetas." Juvenal, Satire 3.9.</note> Because the corruption of the air and water in the great heat and the southern winds generates many diseases, especially in heavy air. And for this reason, he names Valdichiana, Maremma, and Sardinia. Valdichiana is between Arezzo, Cortona, Chiusi, and Montepulciano where the Chiana river is, called by the Latins *Clanis stagna* <note>meaning "the stagnant waters of the Chiana."</note>. It makes the air heavy, especially when the mud that remains dry boils in the summer; from this, various diseases arise. Sardinia, which due to excessive heat, has pestilential air, especially in places closest to the sea.

We descended onto the final bank
of the long crag, still on the left hand;
and then my sight became more vivid.

<column-break/>

things and let him remain. And he adds that he saw this spirit and heard him called Geri del Bello. This man was Geri del Bello, brother of Messer Cione del Bello degli Alighieri, a relative of Dante <note>Geri was Dante’s father's first cousin.</note> who was very prone to causing schisms, and for such a vice was killed by one of the Sacchetti family. No vengeance was taken for this except after thirty years, when a son of Messer Cione killed one of the Sacchetti at the door of his house. And this is a seventh excuse for the poet to be able to name other vicious people, since he does not spare even his own kin. Many say that Dante...

The author assigns the reason for which he thought the spirit had fled, which was mentioned above. **AND IN THIS, HE HAS MADE ME FEEL ALL THE MORE PITY.** As if to say: his indignation has made me more pious toward my kin and less desirous of avenging him. **UNTIL THE FIRST PLACE.** Walking and talking together through this ditch until that crag and bridge from which the other ditch begins to be seen. And from there, one could see everything to the bottom if there were not so little light. **UPON THE FINAL CLOISTER.** Upon the final enclosure. **SO THAT ITS LAY BROTHERS.** This is in the translation: having called that great valley a "cloister" because the sinners are locked in it—just as in the cloisters of monasteries monks and lay brothers are enclosed—he calls those within "lay brothers" of such cloisters. **DIVERSE LAMENTATIONS:** Because they were varied and came from different parts. **PIERCED ME:** They stung my heart with pity. And these laments shot arrows at me which had iron tips made of tears. The iron is what makes the arrow penetrate; therefore the tears were the iron, because they moved me more to compassion. This moved me to such passion that, so as not to hear them, I plugged my ears. Allegorically, it shows that just as Ulysses plugged his ears against the songs of the sirens—that is, he did not want to hear a voluptuous thing—so I did not want to be overcome by any compassion for those who...

He demonstrates that when they had passed the bridge and were on the bank beyond, he began to better see the spirits of that ditch, who were punished in the depths by justice, which they deservedly...

Having moved past the shade of Geri del Bello, the narrator now focuses on the horrific physical suffering of those who corrupted reality through alchemy and forgery.</meta>

<columns>2</columns>
<header># INFERNO</header>

Down toward the bottom, where the minister
of the High Lord, infallible Justice,
punishes the falsifiers <note>Those who corrupted metals (alchemists), persons (impersonators), or money (counterfeiters).</note> recorded here.
I do not believe there was greater sorrow
to be seen in Aegina, with all its people sick,
when the air was so full of malice
that every animal, even to the small worm,
fell dead—and then the ancient peoples,
according to what poets hold as certain,
were restored from the seed of ants—
than it was to see, through that dark valley,
the spirits lying there in various heaps.

One lay on his belly and another on the shoulders
of his neighbor, and another on all fours
was shifting himself along the dismal path.
Step by step we went without speaking,
looking and listening to those sick souls
who could not lift their own persons.
I saw two sitting, leaning against each other
as one props pan against pan <note>original: "teghia a tegghia." A metaphor for how pans are leaned together to dry or keep warm.</note> to heat,
spotted with scabs from head to foot.
And I never saw a curry-comb <note>stregghia: a metal tool for grooming horses.</note> handled
by a stable boy expected by his master,
nor by one who stays awake unwillingly,
as each of these plied the bite
of his nails over himself for the great rage
of the itching which has no other relief.
And thus their nails dragged down the scabs,
just as a knife scrapes the scales
from bream or other fish that has them larger.

<column-break/>

He calls Justice the minister of the High Lord, God. **I DO NOT BELIEVE.** He uses an excellent simile, saying that there was nothing more mournful or horrific than seeing the plague in the island of Aegina, through which every animal perished and the land remained void of inhabitants. Whereupon men were later born from ants—just as it was to see the sick spirits of this <term>bolgia</term> <note>A "bolgia" is a ditch or pocket in the eighth circle of Hell.</note>. Asopus had two daughters, Aegina and Thebes. Jove fell in love with Aegina and knew her in the form of fire; by her he fathered Aeacus, father of Peleus, who sired Achilles, the strongest of all the Greeks according to Homer; and according to this fable, we may call him the grandson or great-grandson of Jove. From this Aegina, the island was named Aegina, which was previously called Enopia. Aeacus reigned in Aegina, and in his time there was such a great and grave pestilence that the island was left desolate. Therefore, Aeacus prayed to his father Jove to either give him death or restore his lost people. And afterward, walking through the island, he saw an infinite number of ants climbing up and down an oak tree, and he desired that his people should be like them. Jove fulfilled his son's desire and converted the ants into men. The fables feign this because, the inhabitants of the island being lost, Aeacus refilled it with rustic folk and new tillers of the soil who were similar to ants: because they were blackened by constant staying in the sun, they were robust and capable of much labor and exercise, and they were very frugal, industriously storing and preserving grain. All of this is seen in the ant. These people were called Myrmidons, because *myrmix* <note>original: "myrmix" (μύρμηξ) is the Greek word for ant.</note> in Greek means ant. These, along with his other people, Achilles, the grandson of Aeacus, led in the Greek armies against the Trojans.

He continues the narrative and describes how the sick spirits lay in "biche"—that is, piled one on top of the other—and some went on all fours. We have shown above that in this ditch and the next, the falsification of metals and money is punished. Now we will show that the punishments placed by the poet are very fitting for such a sin. These are ten-fold: first, they weep and lament, which denotes their infirmity. Furthermore, it rarely happens that a counterfeiter or alchemist is discovered without paying the penalty for the sin, from which grief arises. Second, they lie down to demonstrate their baseness. Commonly, such men are of great intellect; therefore, their lying down notes that such intellect, which they could have used for noble things, they instead applied to vile things and the accumulation of earthly matter. Third, they are naked, which demonstrates that such men are poor, as is seen every day by experience. Fourth, they stink, to denote their abomination and that they are loathed by every man. They are lepers, which signifies their corruption without generation. Alchemists corrupt many things to make a better one from them, and they fail. Therefore, just as leprosy is corruption from which nothing is generated, so this art corrupts metals and other things and does not engender what it desires. They are full of sores, and this signifies the infamy that follows them. They are dropsical <note>Suffering from "idropisia" (edema), an accumulation of fluid.</note>, by which disease avarice is denoted, as we showed above; and as such a disease makes a man sluggish, Virgil uses it for sloth, saying:

> Nor did he suffer his realms
> to grow numb with heavy sloth <note>original: "Nec torpere graui passus sua regna ueterno." From Virgil’s Georgics, 1.124.</note>

And the sluggish remain quite still in one place; likewise, the alchemist never departs from his purpose, though it rarely succeeds for him. The itching demonstrates the great cares and anxieties in hiding their falsehoods and in seeking new ways, new proofs, and new arts. The trembling signifies the fear of being discovered and caught. They bite one another, which denotes the envy that exists among them.

<summary>This page describes the diseased state of the falsifiers in the tenth ditch, comparing their suffering to the mythological plague of Aegina. Landino's commentary provides an allegorical breakdown of why diseases like leprosy and dropsy are appropriate punishments for alchemists and counterfeiters.</summary>

# CANTO XXIX

They lie down, then, because their pursuit—accumulating money—is a vile thing, as we have demonstrated many times. They go on all fours like brute animals. **THEY COULD NOT LIFT** their persons. Men given over to avarice cannot detach themselves from the earth. **I SAW TWO:** whom he will describe below. **SITTING** propped against each other: because they could not stand by themselves. These two were scratching themselves and moving their nails because of the scabies and mange more quickly than a stable boy, hurried **BY HIS MASTER**, moves a curry-comb <note>stregghia: a metal-toothed comb used for grooming horses.</note>: and even more quickly than the curry-comb is moved by one who, being sleepy and desiring to sleep, hurries to finish the grooming. This denotes the constant care and anxiety that is continually present in these alchemists. **FROM THE ITCHING** which has no other relief than scratching in that manner. **THUS THEY DRAGGED** down with their nails the scabies. The crust of that leprosy: just as a knife pulls down the scales of a bream or other fish. This is a fish with many scales.

O you who with your fingers dismail yourself <note>dismagle: a metaphor comparing the scratching of scabs to the unlinking of chainmail armor.</note>
my leader began to one of them,
and who sometimes use them like pincers.
Tell me if any Italian <note>original: "latino." In this period, "Latin" referred to inhabitants of the Italian peninsula.</note> is among those
who are in here, if your nails may suffice
eternally for this work.
We are Italians whom you see so ruined
here, both of us, one replied weeping,
but who are you who asked about us?
And the leader said: I am one who descends
with this living man from ledge to ledge,
and I intend to show him Hell.
Then the common support was broken <note>rinchalzo: the way they were propped up against each other.</note>
and each one turned trembling toward me,
with others who heard him by rebound <note>di rimbalzo: hearing the words indirectly or as an echo.</note>:
The good master gathered me all to himself
saying: "Tell them now whatever you wish."
And I began: "So may your memory
not fade away in the first world of human minds,
but may it live on after many suns,
Tell me who you are and of what people;
let your unsightly and annoying punishment
not frighten you from revealing yourselves to me."

<column-break/>

Having seen the spirits, Virgil asks them who they are, and having turned to one of the two: **O YOU** who dismail yourself: that is, by scratching you skin yourself and remove the crust like one who unfastens a breastplate. **AND SOMETIMES MAKE PINCERS** of your fingers because with them you grip the scabs as pincers grip a drop of metal <note>guto: likely referring to a drop of molten material or a metal stud.</note>. And then, praying that he tell him if he sees any Italians, he entreats him by those things he must value greatly: because, deprived of every other hope, there only remains to him the ability to keep his nails with which he mitigates the itching. The spirit responds and says that he and his companion were Italians, and in turn asks Virgil who he is. And Virgil responded that he is one who leads his living companion through Hell, descending from ledge to ledge. In this place, no allegory occurs that cannot easily be drawn from what has already been said. These words made the two spirits marvel so much—who were leaning one against the other—that they separated from that propping, which was their common support and stay: because by leaning together, one sustained the other. Here is denoted the misery of the alchemists, who, seeing that none of their experiments succeed, often seek help from someone who perhaps knows even less than they do. **AND TREMBLING** from wonder. **WITH THE OTHERS WHO HEARD BY REBOUND.** This is a metaphor from those who play at ball: when one does not hit the ball when it is sent, he hits it after it bounces. Thus, they heard the voice that did not come directly to them. And that Virgil had Dante ask the questions denotes that the Higher Intellect <note>Represented by Virgil.</note> finds universal truths, and then leaves particular things to be found by the Lower Reason <note>Represented by Dante.</note>: as we demonstrated more clearly above.

<column-break/>

I was from Arezzo, and Albero of Siena
he replied, had me put to the fire;
but what I died for does not bring me here.
It is true that I said to him, speaking in jest,
"I would know how to raise myself through the air in flight,"
and he, who had much desire and little sense,
wanted me to show him the art; and only
because I did not make him a Daedalus <note>In Greek mythology, Daedalus fashioned wings of wax and feathers to fly.</note>, he had me
burned by one who held him as a son.

<column-break/>

This man was Master Grifolino of Arezzo, who was a great alchemist. And one day, to gain the favor of one Albero of Siena, son of the Bishop of Siena—who was a foolish and very credulous man—he said that he knew how to make a man fly through magic art. And for a long time he kept Albero occupied with words, sketching such an art for him, and extracted money from him for it. Upon hearing this, the Bishop condemned him as a necromancer and had him burned. Wherefore he says, excusing himself, that he is in Hell not as a magician—because he never practiced such art—but as an alchemist. **PUT TO THE FIRE:** that is, burned. **BUT WHAT...**

# INFERNO

> But to the last pouch of the ten
> for the alchemy I used in the world
> Minos condemned me, who is not allowed to err.

---

> And I said to the poet: "Was there ever
> a people as vain as the Sienese?
> Surely not even the French by so much."
> Whereupon the other leper who heard me
> replied to my words: "Except for Stricca,
> who knew how to make moderate expenditures.
> And Niccolò, who first introduced 
> the rich custom of the clove
> in the garden where such seed takes root;
> And except the company in which Caccia 
> of Asciano squandered the vineyard and the great forest,
> and the Abbagliato displayed his wit."

<column-break/>

**WHY I DIED:** meaning for the magical arts, here in Hell.
**SPEAKING IN JEST:** that is, mocking.
**AND THAT ALBERO WHO HAD A LONGING:** that is, vain desire and little sense, made me burn only because I did not make him **DAEDALUS**: that is, I did not make him fly, as poets imagine of Daedalus, whose fable is narrated elsewhere <note>Daedalus was the mythical Greek craftsman who built wings for himself and his son Icarus.</note>. **TO SUCH A ONE WHO HELD HIM AS A SON:** To the Bishop who considered him his son. It is as if to say that, not being born of legitimate marriage, it could easily be that he was not the Bishop’s; for a woman who couples with one who is not her husband rarely stays faithful to him. And if she gives birth, most often she gives the child to the richest man, so that the son may have a better father. But Minos condemned me to the last pouch for being an alchemist and a falsifier of metals. **TO WHOM IT IS NOT PERMITTED:** It is not permitted to fail in judgment, because conscience never lies to a man. And above, we identified Minos as conscience.

And although the poet rightly damns alchemy—which is the operation of art upon metals in imitation of nature—nonetheless, it should be noted that not every alchemy is entirely illicit. For there are two species: one true and the other sophistical. The true is licit; the sophistical is illicit. And it is reasonable that the true one may be used, for through it the metal is brought to perfection. So that this may be better understood, know according to Aristotle in his *On Minerals* <note>original: "de mineralibus." A medieval scientific text attributed to Aristotle.</note> that all metals, in terms of matter and substantial form, are one and the same thing. For they are all generated from **QUICKSILVER** <term>quicksilver: mercury</term> and sulfur, and are a composite of those. But they differ in accidental form.

And this happens because nature intends from the beginning to produce metal to perfection; and if it succeeds, it generates gold. If it falls short of this perfection, it is outside nature's intention; and then, depending on how much it fails, it produces more or less precious metals. Such imperfection proceeds from the matter, which is not fit to receive the operation of nature. For if the matter is well-disposed—that is, the quicksilver is purified and the sulfur is red and clean—then it can receive the operation of nature to perfection and produce the perfect metal, which is gold. But when the quicksilver is putrefied and the sulfur is white or corrupted red, it makes a viler metal according to the degree of corruption. Therefore, true alchemy, with its art of calcination, distillation, and the juices of herbs with fire, can purify the silver and the sulfur, doing by art what nature does inside the earth. Thus it is clear that whoever knows this art well can reduce metal to its perfection. And such art is licit. But sophistical alchemy introduces falsehood and makes what is not silver or gold appear to be so. This is revealed by the test of fire. For this reason it is forbidden, because it deceives man to his very grave harm, taking for gold that which is not.

Finding an opportunity, the poet censures the vanity and pride of the Sienese, saying: "Was there ever a people more vain": that is, mocked, than the Sienese, even though the French are very boastful. And Capocchia, who was near Griffolino, confirming Dante's sentiment, names some Sienese who he says should be excepted from such vanity. But he speaks with irony, as if to say that these men are the most boastful of all. **EXCEPT FOR STRICCA WHO KNEW HOW TO MAKE MODERATE EXPENDITURES**: And this also he says with irony, wishing to show that through pride and vanity Stricca was so prodigal that he consumed all his substance.

Here it should be noted that in Siena many rich young men formed a company for dinners and lunches; and out of pride they made many luxurious and superfluous expenditures, both in banqueting and in riding and in dressing their servants in livery; and there were those who shod their horses with silver. This was called the **JOYOUS BRIGADE** <note>Brigata godereccia: A famous group of twelve wealthy Sienese youths who spent their entire fortunes on lavish parties.</note>. They put 200,000 florins into a common fund among them all, and in twenty months they consumed all their substance. Among these, Stricca was more prodigal than the others. **AND NICCOLÒ**: He was of the Salimbeni of Siena, who continually studied with every wit to find new and sumptuous foods. Thus many say that he invented *bramangieri* <term>bramangieri: "blancmange," a medieval delicacy usually made of shredded poultry, milk, sugar, and flour.</term> and Ubaldini fritters. And they had a cook who wrote a book of the dishes they invented; and this Niccolò discovered the "rich custom." Some say they cooked roasts over embers made of burning cloves <note>This refers to the legend that they used expensive cloves as fuel for their fires to show off their wealth.</note>. **IN THE GARDEN WHERE SUCH SEED TAKES ROOT**: By a simile he calls Siena a garden, because just as seeds thrown into a garden soon sprout and multiply, so in that city every such custom quickly multiplies. **CACCIA OF SIENA**: He had beautiful and large vineyards at Asciano, a castle in Sienese territory, and consumed them in gluttony. And the great...
<meta>catchword: leaf.</meta>

<summary>Dante and the spirit Capocchia mock the extreme vanity and extravagance of the Sienese "Spendthrift Brigade." The commentary also includes a detailed medieval scientific defense of "true" alchemy versus fraudulent "sophistical" alchemy based on Aristotelian principles.</summary>

<header>CANTO XXIX</header>

...foliage. "Many forests," or rather he means the purse <note>A reference to squandering wealth on the "Spendthrift Club" of Siena</note>. **WHO DISPLAYED HIS** sense clearly and spoke: as if to say, he demonstrated his vanity.

> "But so that you may know who it is who so seconds you
> against the Sienese, sharpen your eye toward me
> so that my face responds well to you;
> And you will see that I am the shade of Capocchio,
> who falsified metals through alchemy;
> and you must remember, if I eye you rightly,
> how I was a good ape of nature."

<column-break/>

Capocchio had pointed out many other Sienese: and now he wishes to say who he himself was. This man was a Sienese, and they say that he studied natural philosophy together with Dante; he became highly learned, and by means of that knowledge, he labored greatly to discover "true" alchemy <note>In the Middle Ages, "true" alchemy was the theoretical science of purifying base metals into gold, while "sophistical" alchemy was the crime of counterfeiting</note>. Being unable to find it, he finally turned to sophistry and subtly falsified metals. Some say that on Good Friday, while lost in meditative abstraction, he drew the entire progression of Christ’s Passion upon his fingernails.

<column-break/>

And Dante, coming upon him, wiped it away with his tongue <note>original: "con la lingua la cancellò". This strange anecdote suggests Dante licked the microscopic drawings off Capocchio's nails, perhaps to snap him out of his trance or out of a sense of religious propriety</note>. This was annoying to Dante because the work seemed more miraculous to him than the feat of the man who wrote Homer’s *Iliad* so minutely that he placed it inside a walnut shell <note>A reference to a famous ancient example of micrography mentioned by Pliny the Elder</note>. He says then: "so that you may know who I am who 'seconds' you"—that is, I follow your lead in speaking against the Sienese. **SHARPEN** your eye / Look at me fixedly: as if to say, you will recognize me, having known me in the world. **WHO FALSIFIED** metals with alchemy: I did not use natural alchemy, which does not falsify metals, but rather works by correcting and purifying matter so that a less precious metal becomes gold. Instead, I used sophistry, which does not create gold but counterfeits and falsifies it so that what is not gold appears to be so. And for this, he was a "good ape of nature": meaning he knew how to counterfeit natural things well, just as an ape mimics human actions.

## CANTO XXX. OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' depicting a figure standing in a landscape with a house or small chapel in the background.</image-desc>

> At the time when Juno was enraged
> against the Theban blood because of Semele,
> as she showed on more than one occasion,
> Athamas became so insane
> that seeing his wife with two sons
> walking burdened on either hand,
> he cried: "Let us spread the nets, so that I may take..."

<column-break/>

The thirtieth Canto follows the twenty-ninth because, just as the poet treated falsifiers in the previous one, so he treats them here. However, because the *species* of falsehood changes, the punishments also change. In the past pouches, we saw leprosy and sluggishness. The present ones are divided into three species. The first are those who falsified their own person <note>Impersonators</note>: and these go about rabidly biting one another. The second are those who falsified...

<header>INFERNO</header>

> the lioness and the little lions at the pass
> and then he stretched out his pitiless claws
> taking the one who was named Learchus
> and whirled him and dashed him against a rock;

<column-break/>

[The second group falsified] money. And the third have falsified their speech <note>These are the three types of falsifiers in Canto XXX: of persons, of coins, and of words (liars)</note>. This is demonstrated in two ancient spirits. In the beginning, then, wishing to demonstrate the rage of the spirits by which they bite and strike one another, he says by way of a comparison that neither was Athamas so Raging toward his son—whom he struck against the rock—nor Hecuba when, out of grief against her enemies, she became a bitch. **IN THE TIME THAT Juno.** Cadmus, of whom we have spoken sufficiently above, had four daughters by his wife Harmonia: Semele, Agave, Autonoe, and Ino. Semele conceived Bacchus by Jove. This was so vexing to Juno that she became an enemy to the entire Theban race, and many times she took revenge against many of them. For she stirred these four sisters to such fury that, while they were making a sacrifice to Bacchus in the woods, and Pentheus, son of Agave, arrived, it seemed to them that he was a boar, and they killed him. Afterward, having already had two sons by her husband 

---

Athamas, she drove Athamas to such fury that, when Ino arrived with the sons, it seemed to him that she was a lioness with two cubs. Therefore he took one, named Learchus, and struck him against a rock. Whereupon Ino, terrified, ran to the sea, carrying the other with her, whose name was Melicerta; and with him she threw herself into the sea. And they were made marine deities; and the Greeks named her Leucothea <note>The "White Goddess"</note> and the Latins [named her] Matuta; and him [the Greeks named] Palaemon and the Latins Portunus <note>God of keys and harbors</note>. Athamas, then, did not show as much fury toward his children as these spirits showed among themselves. **AND WHEN** Fortune turned down the state of the Trojans. We have already shown many times what region Troy is, and what city within it is Ilion. Nor have we omitted the history of the unhappy Priam. It remains, then, that we add to that the misery of Hecuba, who in the Greek siege saw a great part of her children killed. She saw her aged husband cruelly murdered. She saw the city destroyed by iron and fire. And after such calamities, reduced to servitude along with Polyxena, she saw one daughter sacrificed and die at the tomb of the most cruel Achilles. And then, dragged into Thrace, the ghost of her son appeared to her; she had believed he was still living and safe with a good part of the paternal treasures in the care of Polymestor. This caused her long-lasting sadness and heavy mourning to turn into extreme rage; and stirred by such fury, she cursed all the Greeks with every kind of villainy and bit them with the most bitter words. Wherefore the poets feign that she was converted into a raging bitch. **SHE BECAME Aware:** because at first she did not know of the wicked event, which happened in this way. Priam had already sensed the Greek preparations against him; and as a prudent man, he devised a plan so that, whatever might happen, some of his lineage would remain, and not without treasures. Therefore he sent to Polymestor, king of Thrace, his son Polydorus with great treasure, trusting that as this king had always been a friend, he would protect the son and the money. <note>original: "Sed maledictus homo qui confidit in homine"</note> But cursed is the man who trusts in man. For as Plautus writes, <note>original: "lupus eſt homo homini et non homo"</note> man is a wolf to man, and not a man. And every feigned friendship, because it is not true, lasts only as long as it is useful. Therefore Polymestor, seeing Priam and his kingdom fallen, remembered neither his given faith nor friendship. Instead, he turned to the Greeks, where fortune had already turned, and killed Polydorus, and unjustly kept the treasures. When Hecuba, led into servitude by the Greeks, arrived at the shores of Thrace, the ghost of Polydorus—as Euripides writes—came up from the underworld and revealed to her his death and the wickedness of Polymestor. From this followed what we said a little before. **THE HIGHNESS.** He here almost imitates Virgil in his second book: <note>original: "Poſtquam res aſie priamique euertere regnum"</note> "After the power of Asia and Priam’s kingdom were overturned." **WHO DARED EVERYTHING:** This was manifested through Paris, who, trusting in the greatness of his kingdom, dared to snatch Helen, the wife of such a great king, from the midst of Greece, a land most powerful in men-at-arms and wisdom. Until the king was quashed: that is, deprived of life along with the kingdom, because the kingdom also perished according to Homer and many Greek writers; for no one of the lineage of Priam remained who was not either dead or led away as a prisoner. Although Dio Chrysostom proves, both through Egyptian histories and through many likely conjectures, that Homer lied about this destruction, and that Achilles did not kill Hector, but Hector Achilles; and the Greeks did not take Troy, but were driven away by the Trojans. This is made likely by the little reputation with which—as Homer himself shows—they departed from Troy; since many leaders remained dead, few returned to Greece, and those were killed by their own, such as Agamemnon by his wife Clytemnestra, and Pyrrhus by Orestes; and many went into voluntary exile, like Diomedes and Ulysses. **HECUBA SAD / Melancholic. WRETCHED / Unhappy: because from a queen she had become a slave. CAPTIVE / Prisoner. POLYXENA DEAD. Achilles, in love with her, promised great things if Hecuba would give her to him as a wife; and Paris, under the pretense of giving her to him, called him to a meeting in the temple of the Thymbraean Apollo...**

<summary>This page provides a mythological commentary on the opening of Canto XXX, explaining the insanity of Athamas and the grief-stricken rage of Hecuba as parallels for the "falsifiers of persons." It details the fall of Troy and the betrayal of Polydorus by Polymestor, citing classical authorities like Virgil, Homer, and Euripides.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the falsifiers in the Eighth Circle of Hell. While the previous page began the comparison with the madness of Athamas, this page transitions to the grief of Hecuba and introduces the "falsifiers of persons"—those who deceived others by impersonating someone else. # CANTO XXVIII <note>Although the header says Canto XXVIII, the text and commentary describe the events and figures of Canto XXX of the Inferno.</note>

near the walls of Troy. Achilles went there, and while he was kneeling to worship Apollo, he was treacherously struck in the soles of his feet, which were the only places he could be wounded, and so he was killed. For this reason, later, Pyrrhus, the son of Achilles, killed Polyxena at his father's tomb in revenge. The text explains: After Hecuba saw Polyxena dead, and after the grieving Hecuba discovered her son Polydorus on the shore of the sea where she found him buried, she went out of her mind—that is, she lost her reason. **SHE BARKED:** To bark <note>original: *latrare*</note> in Latin means to bark like a dog. This happened to her because such great pain made her mind "twisted," meaning her soul was infuriated. Whenever a passion disturbs the soul so much that it loses reason (which is "straight" because it directs us toward right actions), we can say that our mind is "twisted."

Above, the fury of Athamas of Thebes and Hecuba of Troy was shown. Now, bringing the comparison to the point, the author concludes that neither in the Theban nor the Trojan fury was there anything as great as the fury he saw in two spirits. Although he presents them as falsifiers, they did not falsify metals, but rather

But neither Theban furies nor Trojan
Were ever seen in anyone so cruel,
Not in goading beasts, let alone human limbs,
As I saw two shades, pale and naked,
Who, biting, ran in the same manner
As a pig when it is let out of the pen.
One reached Capocchio, and at the joint
Of the neck he fixed his teeth so that, pulling,
He made him scrape his belly against the hard floor.

<column-break/>

they falsified themselves as others, or others as themselves, and for this, they suffer various punishments. He presents them as furious, naked, and pale, running and biting. They are "furious" because falsifying metals is more like a sickness of the mind, but doing what they did is the height of madness. They are "naked" as a punishment of retribution <term>lex talionis: the law of retaliation, "an eye for an eye"</term>, because through their deceit they stripped others of either their possessions or their honor; and allegorically, because in the end these deceits are revealed, and they remain naked. They are "pale" because such people put themselves in great danger, which cannot be done without constant fear. They bite while running. Their "running" denotes their restlessness and the various worries that distract the soul in different directions. Hence Virgil says:

->And now here, now there, he divides his swift mind, and takes it into various parts, and turns through all things.<- <note>original: *Atque animum celerem nunc huc nunc diuidit illuc In partesque rapit uarias per que omnia uersat*</note>

They "bite" because they gnaw at the goods of others by exchanging or spending false metals for true money and pure goods. **AS A PIG When it is let out of the pen.** The nature of the pig is very cruel, and when irritated, it pardons no one. **ONE Reached Capocchio.** Capocchio in life was a mocker and a censurer beyond measure; and such people commonly find someone to bite them. For this reason, the poet feigns that he was bitten and caught by the neck. This is because those who wrongly criticize others, when they themselves are criticized, have no answer. Therefore, they are caught by the neck, because whoever squeezes the neck and the throat makes one fall silent. **AGAINST THE HARD FLOOR.** He made him strike the hard floor of the ditch. It is as if he said he stretched him on the ground; for whoever strikes others down with infamy will be struck down by others. Nor can one who gives such bites to others stand for long without falling to the bottom and into a low and vile state.

And the Aretine who remained trembling
Said to me: "That goblin is Gianni Schicchi,
And he goes about raging, mangling others so."
"Oh," I said to him, "so may the other not fix
Its teeth into you, may it not be a burden
To tell us who it is before it breaks away from here."
And he to me: "That is the ancient soul
Of wicked Myrrha, who became
A friend to her father beyond rightful love.
She came to sin with her father in this way,
Falsifying herself in the form of another,
Just as the other who goes there undertook,
To gain the lady of the herd,
To falsify himself as Buoso Donati,
Making a will or giving form to a testament."

<column-break/>

Having seen Capocchio bitten, Griffolino of Arezzo, who was in his company, trembled with fear that the same might be done to him. He told Dante that the one who had bitten Capocchio was Gianni Schicchi. Then, entreated by Dante—who was eager to know who the other one running with Gianni was—he said it was Myrrha. Gianni Schicchi de' Cavalcanti was a very clever and versatile <note>original: *eutrapelo*</note> man, capable of counterfeiting whatever he wished. He was a great friend of Simone Donati. When Messer Buoso Donati, a very wealthy man, died without making a will, and having closer relatives than Simone (who would have inherited in the absence of a will <note>original: *ab intestato*</note>), Simone, in order to become the heir, hid the body of Messer Buoso. He had Gianni get into the bed and, impersonating Messer Buoso, Gianni made a will and left Simone as the heir. For this, Simone gave him a mare of great value, which was in the herd and was called "the lady of the herd," as he had promised him. Myrrha was the daughter of Cinyras, king of Paphos, a very lustful island. Hence: Venus, queen of Gnidus and Paphos, spurns beloved Cyprus... <note>original Latin: *Venus regina gnidi paphique sperne dilectam cipro*</note>

# CANTO INFERNO XXX

"And carry the beauty of Cinyras into the temple, as he calls to you with much incense." <note>original: "Et uocantem thure te multa cinare decorem transffer in edem." This is a slightly corrupted Latin quotation, likely referencing the story of Cinyras and Myrrha.</note> Myrrha, in her tender youth, loved her father so passionately that, for a long time, she was torn between the love that inflamed her and the shame that held her back from such wickedness. She wavered miserably, like a ship tossed by opposing winds. Finally, to escape the great pain that her love caused her, she decided to hang herself. Her nurse discovered this plan and prevented her death. After many prayers, having understood the cause that led her to kill herself, the nurse tried to remove such an unholy love from her heart. But unable to persuade her, from a good counselor she became a wicked servant. She went to Cinyras and told him she could bring a most beautiful girl to his bed, but in the dark, because the girl did not want to be recognized. Cinyras consented and slept with his daughter for many nights, believing he was sleeping with someone else. Finally, desiring to know the girl, and against his word, he brought a light into the room and recognized his daughter. He wanted to kill her, but the wicked Myrrha, aided by the darkness of the night, fled. Wandering through many lands, she arrived in Arabia, and there she was transformed into the tree named after her, the **myrrh**. When the ninth month came, she gave birth to Adonis, who was the son and grandson of his father, and the brother and son of his mother.

And after those two rabid ones had passed
upon whom I had kept my eye,
I turned to look at the other ill-born souls.

I saw one shaped like a lute,
if only he had had his groin
cut off from the side where a man is forked.

The heavy dropsy, which so disproportionately
divides the limbs with humor ill-converted,
that the face does not match the belly,

Made him keep his lips open,
as the hectic fever victim does, who from thirst
turns one lip toward the chin and the other upward.

<margin>
He made him keep his lips open as the victim of a hectic fever <note>A "hectic" fever (from the Greek 'hektikos') was a historical term for a persistent, wasting fever often associated with consumption or tuberculosis.</note> does: that is, one who has a wasting fever and, because of thirst, turns one lip up and the other down. *Hydropepsis* (Dropsy) is named from *hydor*, which in Greek means water, because in this disease water multiplies between the layers of the skin.
</margin>

"O you who are without any punishment,"
(and I know not why) "in this wretched world,"
he said to us, "look and attend

To the misery of Master Adam;
in life I had enough of what I wanted,
and now, alas, I crave a drop of water.

The little streams that from the green hills
of the Casentino descend down into the Arno,
making their channels cool and moist,

Always stand before me, and not in vain,
for their image dries me up far more
than the malady that withers my face.

The rigid justice that searches me
takes its reason from the place where I sinned
to put my sighs even more to flight.

There is Romena, where I falsified
the currency sealed with the Baptist,
for which I left my body burnt above.

But if I could see here the wretched soul
of Guido or Alessandro or their brother,
I would not give up the sight for Branda’s fount."

<column-break/>

Removing his eyes from the one over whom the two rabid ones had passed, the poet turned elsewhere and saw one who, because he was **dropsical** (or one might say "water-bloated"), had a belly so swollen that if he had been cut from the groin down—where the thighs are—leaving only the belly and the head, he would have looked like a **lute**. This disease arises when the "humor" <note>In medieval medicine, health was governed by four "humors" or bodily fluids; an imbalance caused disease.</note> which should be converted into true nourishment instead turns into water and wind. It swells the body in such a way that it "disproportions" the limbs, meaning it makes them uneven so that they have no balance. This was the case with this man, whose belly far exceeded the proportion of his head and neck, making him look like a lute, which has a large belly and a thin neck and head. This disease induced a very great thirst in him, and because of it...

The author has described the form and the manner of **Adam**. Now he records his words, who said: "O you, Virgil and Dante, who are without punishment in this wretched world"—"grammo" <note>The commentator notes that *grammo* or *grammeza* is a Lombard dialect term meaning miserable or heavy.</note>—"look at my misery." This **Adam** was from Brescia and was a moneyer <note>A person licensed to mint coins.</note>. In that art, he was a supreme master, but through great avarice and desire for money, he made an agreement with the **Counts of Romena**. There, he secretly falsified the **Florentine florin**, which has the image of John the Baptist (the protector of our republic) on one side and the lily on the other. **IN LIFE I HAD.** His pain is greater because he who finds himself in calamity and lack of things was once rich; because he is not used to poverty, he suffers it more harshly. **AND NOW**, alas, I crave: "I greatly desire a drop of water." He could not demonstrate greater misery than having a vast desire for that which cannot be had. His pain increases when he sees himself deprived of something that no one is so poor as to lack, such as water, yet he cannot have even a single drop. **THE LITTLE STREAMS.** The pain is greatly increased when, in our desire, the image of what we lack is always represented before our eyes...

# CANTO XXX

...image of the desired thing. Therefore, the rigid and inflexible divine justice, which goads and stimulates him, draws the cause of his punishment from the very place where he committed the sin. Because he sinned in the Casentino, the image of the little streams is always turned over in his mind: that is, the brooks and small, even rivers that descend from the ridges of the mountains down into the Casentino. And that image causes me much more thirst than the illness that afflicts me.

**THERE IS ROMENA** The place where I committed the forgery: Because, as we said above, he made an agreement with those Counts. **THE ALLOY** Of the Baptist: The Florentine florin, which has the image of St. John the Baptist stamped upon it as its seal. **BECAUSE I** For which cause I left my body burned. Indeed, he was burned opposite Romena on the road that leads from the village to the hill, where even today a mount of stones can be seen. The peasants who are there at present affirm that their ancestors had heard from their own predecessors that this was so. **BUT IF I** Could see the wretched soul. He desires that these Counts of Romena, who persuaded him to commit such a forgery, be in the same torment—not out of a love for justice, but out of hatred and envy. For the damned soul is never purged of its vices, and all the agitations of the mind remain. Therefore, he would wish to drag every other soul into his torment, as the damned are always malicious. But the soul that is absolved of guilt—though it may not be free from punishment, as we see with those in Purgatory—does not desire nor wish that any other should suffer. Rather, it rejoices in the good of others. This is proper to our nature if it is not corrupted by a habit already formed in vice, as are the spirits punished in Hell. **AND OF THEIR BROTHER** That is, Aghinolfo, the third brother of Guido and Alessandro. **FOR FONTE BRANDA** I would not give up the sight. Although I have an inextinguishable thirst and am entirely deprived of all water, nevertheless, if it were granted to me to choose which of two things I would rather have—either to see these Counts in these pains, or to have the water of Fonte Branda—I would rather see their punishment than have water as clear as that in Fonte Branda. This fountain is in Siena, and it is very abundant and limpid. <note>Fonte Branda is one of Siena's most famous and ancient fountains, known for its cool, plentiful water.</note>

Within, one was already enraged...
shades that go about, they tell the truth
but what does it avail me with my limbs bound?
If I were only still so light
that in a hundred years I could move an inch,
I would have already set out upon the path,
Searching for him among this misshapen folk,
even though it winds for eleven miles,
and is no less than half a mile across.
I am among such a family because of them,
who induced me to strike the florins
that had three carats of dross.
And I to him: "Who are the two wretches
who smoke like wet hands in winter,
lying close to your right boundaries?"
"I found them here, and they haven't turned since,"
he replied, "not since I rained down into this ditch,
and I do not believe they will turn for eternity.
One is the false woman who accused Joseph;
the other is the false Sinon, the Greek from Troy;
from a sharp fever, they cast out such a stench." <note>original: "leppo". This refers to the unpleasant smell of burnt fat or grease, here representing the "smell" of a feverish, diseased body.</note>

<column-break/>

This demonstrates how much heavier is the vengeance that is seen than that which is only heard. One of those Counts was already there. This was a consolation to him, but two things diminished it: first, that he did not see him but only heard him; second, that he heard it from the "enraged spirits," in whom full faith should not be placed. "Even though it winds for eleven miles," as we demonstrated in the layout of Hell. **WHICH HAD** Three carats of dross. The purity and fineness of gold is divided into 24 carats; that which is fine in perfection is 24 carats. Then, when something else is mixed in, it is reduced by that much. Therefore, they struck gold which should have been twenty-four carats, but it was twenty-one. **LIKE** Wet hands in winter. Every breath and vapor that comes out of every living animal carries with it vital heat. But because in summer it finds the air warm, it immediately mixes and dissipates due to their similarity and is not seen. But in cold weather, because it flees from its contrary, it draws together; thus it happens that it maintains itself and condenses more, and therefore it is seen. **HERE I** Found them: because they had died many hundreds of years before him. **THE FALSE WOMAN** Who accused Joseph. From Jacob, the son of Isaac, twelve sons were born, from whom descended the twelve tribes of the Jewish people. But of all of them, Joseph was most dear to Jacob, both because he was of

great talent and because he was born in Jacob's old age. But from the great love the father bore him, envy followed among the brothers, who finally sold him for thirty pence to merchants going into Egypt—a price, without doubt, very small for such a man, but which was to be a figure <note>A "figure" is a theological term for a historical person or event that foreshadows a future one, in this case, the betrayal of Christ.</note> for the sale of Christ, both man and God. The merchants then sold him in Egypt to Potiphar, <note>original: "Sutifar"</note> an official of Pharaoh the King, who was the leader of the army. Joseph, through his virtues, became in a short time so favored by his master that he gave him the administration of his entire house. But on the other hand, the beauty of his body led him into grave danger. For Potiphar’s wife was so vehemently inflamed by the form of the youth that first through flatteries, then by force, she wished to draw him to her perverse will. But Joseph fled, leaving his cloak by which she held him—certainly an outstanding deed. He deserved no less praise than Hippolytus, and he ran into the same danger, for she turned all her love into cruel hatred...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the tenth pit of the eighth circle of Hell, where falsifiers of all kinds are punished. Having discussed Myrrha (a falsifier of person) and Master Adam (a falsifier of money), the text now introduces the "falsifiers of words" (liars), specifically Potiphar’s wife and Sinon of Troy. The preamble provides historical and biblical context for these figures before diving into the poetic dialogue.</meta>

Because as Seneca says, **A woman either loves or hates** <note>original: "Aut amat femina aut odit"</note>: And certainly without any middle ground, she goes from one extreme to the other. And Virgil wisely wrote, **Woman is always a fickle and changeable thing** <note>original: "uarium et mutabile semper femina"</note>. Therefore, the wicked woman accused the innocent <note>The text refers to the biblical story of Joseph and Potiphar’s wife (Genesis 39).</note>: and where she herself had enticed the youth, she claimed that she had been solicited by him. For this reason, Joseph was imprisoned. But after two years, Pharaoh dreamed that he saw seven fat cows being devoured by seven lean ones; and seven full ears of grain likewise being consumed by seven empty ones. There was none among his wise men who knew how to interpret this dream. Joseph interpreted it: and he showed that this signified that the first seven years were to be fertile, but the following seven very sterile. This persuaded the King that the divine spirit was in Joseph; he freed him and made him prefect of all the kingdom. It would be a long story to tell with what diligence and prudence he administered everything: he reserved the grain of the fertile years to sustain the sterile ones. He provided for his father and brothers. He led them into Egypt where he obtained from the King that they be settled in the best region. But it is enough to understand that here <note>in this circle of Hell</note> was punished the wicked wife of the Eunuch <note>Potiphar</note> for the false charge she brought. **THE OTHER IS SINON.** The Greeks had already been at the camp at Troy for ten years: and despairing at last of their strength, they deliberated to attempt cunning and deceit. They therefore built a very large horse of wood; but it was hollow, and in it they shut up many of the leaders of the army. Then came Sinon to the Trojans as a deserter: and he feigned having received many injuries from the Greeks, and finally that they wanted to sacrifice him to the gods, and for this reason he had fled. For this he was accepted as a friend by Priam, and asked with what hope the Greeks lived. Then the fraudulent and most astute Sinon feigned that they had built that horse and consecrated it to Minerva; and made it so high so that the Trojans could not bring it whole into Troy. For the fates decreed that if they damaged it, Troy would have to be taken. But if it were brought inside the city whole, then the Greeks would have to be defeated by the Trojans. These words were the reason that the Trojans cut a gate and brought the horse inside. For which reason, the following night, the armed men came out of the horse and set fire to the land and opened the gates to the army. And in this form Sinon deceived the Trojans, whence Troy was taken. He was the son of Autolycus, the son of Mercury, who was a very great thief; and from him was born the first Sinon, likewise a very great thief. He fathered Sisyphus and Anticlia, who was the mother of Ulysses; and from Sisyphus was born the Sinon of whom the poet <note>Dante</note> presently makes mention. And as you see, he was the cousin of Ulysses.

And one of them, who took offense
perhaps at being named so obscurely,

**IT IS A LIKELY THING** that he who has made a habit of sin will always be accompanied by it, nor will he ever leave it behind, either here or there. For as it is written in the Apocalypse: **For their works follow them** <note>original Latin: "Opera enim illoru sequuntur illos" (Revelation 14:13)</note>. Therefore, one of them, Sinon. **WHO TOOK OFFENSE:** to whom it was annoying. **AT BEING NAMED:** called out. **SO OBSCURELY:** with such infamy. He knew that he named him for the treachery he had done; because good fame generates splendor, and infamy generates obscurity. **WITH HIS FIST** he struck him **ON THE BELLY**; **STIFF** <note>original: "croia"</note>: incrusted, that is, hardened. He depicts these two as enemies and discordant between themselves to show that among the vicious there is always discord, just as among the virtuous there is always concord. **WHEN** you were going to the fire where you were burned: The nature of the vicious is always to reproach one another for their vices. **TRUE WITNESS:** When asked by Priam for the truth, you told a lie. **I AM HERE FOR ONE FAULT:** for a single fraud that I committed at Troy. **YOU ARE HERE FOR MORE THAN ANY OTHER DEMON:** because you have falsified metals infinite times. **REMEMBER** the perjury: Here he increases the vice, showing that it is known throughout the whole world. And the other reproaches him for the disease <term>dropsy|a condition involving an accumulation of fluid in the body's tissues or cavities, causing painful swelling</term> which gives him thirst and swells his body so that it makes a **HEDGE** before his eyes so that he cannot see any further. **A HEDGE:** it interposes itself in front. **THEN** the minter; Adam said: your mouth gapes open, that is, it knows well how to speak ill: and if I have thirst, the moisture **STUFFS ME** <note>original: "rinsarcia"</note>: As if to say, "if I have thirst, the humor of this dropsy refills me." **YOU HAVE** the burning and the head that aches: because fever produces these two things.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the final pit of the eighth circle. Having witnessed the liars and falsifiers, Dante the pilgrim becomes absorbed in a petty, vulgar argument between two of the damned: Sinon the Greek (the liar of Troy) and Master Adam (the counterfeiter). This page captures Virgil's stern reprimand of Dante for his voyeuristic fascination with such "base" behavior and the subsequent philosophical discussion on the nature of shame and the intellect.</meta>

# CANTO XXX.
.r. iiii.

<margin>Ethics</margin> **AND TO LICK THE MIRROR OF NARCISSUS.** <note>original: "ET PER Leccar lo specchio di narcisso"</note> And if he were given a fountain: like the one in which Narcissus mirrored himself, as is shown more extensively elsewhere. <note>In Greek mythology, Narcissus fell in love with his own reflection in a pool. The commentator uses this as a metaphor for the desire to see one's own desires or base interests reflected in others.</note>

**I was completely intent on listening to them**
**when the master said to me: "Go on, look,**
**for it is almost as if I were quarreling with you!"**
**When I heard him speak to me with anger,**
**I turned toward him with such shame**
**that it still circles through my memory.**
**And like one who dreams of his own harm,**
**who, dreaming, desires to be dreaming,**
**so that he longs for what is, as if it were not;**
**So I became, unable to speak,**
**desiring to excuse myself, and excusing**
**myself all the while, and I did not think I was doing it.**
**"Less shame washes away a greater fault**
**than yours has been," said the master,**
**"therefore, unburden yourself of all sadness:**
**And make sure that I am always at your side,**
**if it happens again that fortune catches you**
**where people are in a similar dispute:**
**For wanting to hear such things is a base desire."**

<column-break/>

The author had given himself over to listening to these two. Whereupon Virgil reproves him, saying, **"Go on, look,"** <note>original: "Mira pure"</note> for it often happens that we seem to grant what we actually deny: as when one says, "Go ahead and do evil, and you will be loved." **FOR IT IS ALMOST** <note>original: "CHE POCHO E/"</note> that is, very little is lacking: **as if I were quarreling with you:** <note>original: "non mi concito adira"</note> meaning, I am almost moved to anger. *Aizzare* and *aizare* mean to irritate or incite. Then Dante felt such shame that even now that shame revolves through his memory: that is, he still remembers it. In this, as in many things, is signified the <term>difference between the appetite and reason</term> <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "appetite" refers to our lower, instinctive desires, while "reason" or "intellect" is our higher capacity for logic and morality.</note>: the lower reason allows itself to be conquered by the appetite, while the higher reason resists. The <term>intellect</term>, which always seeks <term>universals</term> <note>General truths or moral principles that apply to everyone, everywhere.</note>, does not wish to occupy its time with <term>particulars</term> <note>Specific, petty, or individual instances, like the squabble Dante was watching.</note>. Furthermore, the rational part does not want <term>sensuality</term> to occupy the time that should be spent on excellent things with such base matters. 

**LESS SHAME WASHES AWAY A GREATER FAULT.** Although the appetite and the lower reason may deviate from the intellect and err, nonetheless, when the intellect turns back toward them and reveals their sin and error—which they could not see before because they were blinded by <term>perturbation</term> <note>A state of emotional agitation or mental confusion.</note>—they realize they have erred and feel shame. In this way, every error is easily washed away; for he who feels shame for a fault repents of it, and by repenting, he ceases to do it and returns to the obedience of the intellect. Therefore, such shame is sufficient for the intellect: for when it sees the appetite being obedient to it, the intellect always stays by its side to admonish and govern it. And the appetite, looking toward the intellect, takes care not to fall into such error again when it happens to find itself where such people are: that is, when it happens to fall into similar thoughts. For when the appetite desires to think on such things, it is a very **base desire.**

<summary>Dante is scolded by Virgil for listening to the vulgar argument between Sinon and Master Adam; the commentary explains this allegorically as the Intellect correcting the lower Appetite.</summary>
<keywords>Dante, Virgil, Narcissus, intellect, appetite, reason, shame, universals vs particulars, repentance, allegory</keywords>

# HELL CANTO XXXI. OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE

<note>This page features the opening of Canto XXXI. The poem is presented in the left column and at the bottom, while the scholarly commentary by Cristoforo Landino wraps around it.</note>

The very same tongue first bit me,
so that it tinged both my cheeks,
and then it offered me the medicine.
Thus I hear that the spear of Achilles
and of his father used to be the cause,
first of a sad and then of a good gift.

<column-break/>

The poet has treated the preceding circle, divided into ten pits <term>bolge: the trenches of the eighth circle of Hell</term>, because in it are punished ten species of fraud; these break only the bond of nature. He had, therefore, already searched the tenth pit of the eighth circle and arrived at its end. Now he places the descent into the ninth circle, where the bond of nature is broken, as well as the bond of faith <note>Dante distinguishes between simple fraud against humanity and "treachery," which violates a specific bond of trust</note>. But first, he narrates what he found on the bank down which he descended. And because he showed above how much shame he felt from Virgil’s reprimand, he now demonstrates through an excellent comparison that the very same tongue of Virgil which had "bitten" him with a rebuke also healed that bite. He shows how much comfort he then received from the words Virgil added after the reprimand. It should be noted here that the anger of a wise man is very useful to one who errs. Thus Seneca says: "The anger of a good man is most welcome." <note>original Latin: "Gratissima est probi hominis iracundia"</note> This tongue, then, was like the spear of Achilles. Telephus, king of Mysia and an ally of the Trojans, wishing to drive the Greeks from his kingdom, was wounded by Achilles. Finding no other remedy to heal the wound, he learned from the oracle that it would heal only if Achilles struck him again in the same place with the same spear; and so it happened. The poets feign this because Achilles had learned that part of medicine called surgery <term>cherufica: from the Greek 'cheirourgia', meaning hand-work or surgery</term> from Chiron; and later he discovered for himself that the best remedy to heal wounds was to treat them with the rust from the point of the spear, whether it was made of iron or bronze. Indeed, Pliny reports that in such cases, Achilles was depicted scraping such rust off with a knife.

---

We turned our backs to the wretched valley,
up along the bank that girds it around,
crossing across without any speech.
Here it was less than night and less than day,
so that my sight sent itself forward little;
but I heard another horn sound,
so loud it would have made any thunder seem faint,
which, following its path against the wind,
directed my eyes all to one place.
After the sorrowful defeat when
Charlemagne lost the holy company,
Orlando did not sound [his horn] so terribly.

<column-break/>

**WE TURNED OUR BACKS.** We turned our shoulders to the valley of the tenth pit. **UP ALONG THE BANK that girds it:** which surrounds it; this was the boundary between the eighth and ninth circles. **CROSSING ACROSS:** They had already circled around to see the damned souls; now they crossed through to exit. **WITHOUT ANY SPEECH.** This shows they were removed from the contemplation of this sin because they had already come to know it. **HERE IT WAS Less than night and less than day.** It was not total darkness, but very little light. For this reason, **MY SIGHT Sent itself forward little:** as if to say, I could see little further than where I stood. **BUT I Heard a sound:** I could not see much, but I could hear; for where light (by which we see) was lacking, sound (by which we hear) abounded. And this sound was so great that thunder would have seemed faint in comparison. This sound, following its path against him—that is, proceeding forward—**DIRECTED** or caused me to direct my eyes to the place from which the sound came. It should be considered why in this place one could not see but could hear. The giants are placed in this spot for their pride, which makes men so reckless that they wish to exceed natural forces and have more power than nature allows them; but we will speak of them shortly below. He depicts obscurity because pride is born from the ignorance of not knowing oneself. But it is heard because the deeds done by the proud are such that many speak of them. **AFTER The sorrowful:** This refers to Roncesvalles in the Pyrenees mountains, which divide Gaul from Spain. There, through the treachery of Ganelon of Mainz <note>Gano di Pontieri/Maganza is the archetypal traitor in Carolingian myth</note>, the paladins were defeated by Marsilio, King of Spain. And Orlando <note>Roland</note> sounded his horn so loudly after the flight of his men that he gathered a hundred of them, and with them made an assault and killed Marsilio. But we shall speak of Orlando in the 18th Canto of *Paradiso*.

---

I had not held my head turned there for long
when I seemed to see many high towers,
whereat I: "Master, what city is this?"
And he to me: "Because you travel
through the darkness from too far away..."

<column-break/>

He follows in his speech, saying: I held my head turned there only a little; that is, after the sound made me turn, I went along looking toward it. **WHEN I Seemed to see:** But they were not. **MANY High towers.** And believing that they were truly towers, although they had not been asked...
