<meta>This page continues the transition into the ninth circle of Hell. Having addressed Virgil’s rebuke in the previous page, the text now focuses on the visual deception Dante experiences as he approaches the central pit, where he mistakes giants for towers.</meta>

.XXXI

# CANTO XXXI

...it happens that later, in your imagination, you go astray.
You will see clearly, if you draw nearer to it,
how much the sense is deceived from a distance;
therefore, spur yourself on a little more.

<note>Dante is being told by Virgil that his eyes are deceiving him because they are still too far away from the objects ahead.</note>

...to fulfill its office if it does not respond according to its power, the distance of the place, the size of the object (that is, what it has to see), and the clarity of the light. Hence it happens that one eye requires one distance and another eye another, because they have different powers; and likewise, the same eye sees differently in greater light than in lesser light.

Then he affectionately took me by the hand
  and said: "Before we go any further,
  so that the reality may seem less strange to you,
know that these are not towers, but giants,
  and they are in the pit, around the bank,
  all of them from the navel downward."
As when a fog dissipates,
  the gaze little by little recognizes
  what the vapor that thickens the air conceals;
so, piercing that thick and dark air,
  drawing closer and closer toward the brink,
  error fled from me, and fear grew within me.
For just as upon its circular wall,
  Monteriggioni crowns itself with towers,
  so the bank that surrounds the pit
was towered over by half their bodies—
  those horrible giants whom Jove
  still threatens from heaven when he thunders.

<column-break/>

That Virgil takes Dante by the hand and kindly shows him that what appeared to be towers are not towers but giants signifies nothing other than when lower reason submits itself to the intellect, the intellect kindly reveals its errors to it. **THEN HE AFFECTIONATELY TOOK ME BY THE HAND.** Understand "with his hand" to signify help; because sensuality cannot rightly provide against pride unless the intellect demonstrates it. **AND SAID: "BEFORE WE GO ANY FURTHER, SO THAT THE REALITY MAY SEEM LESS STRANGE TO YOU."** All things that are foreseen cause less distress than when they happen unexpectedly. Hence Petrarch says: "A foreseen wound hurts much less." <note>original: "Piaga antiueduta assai men duole"</note>. **THEY ARE NOT TOWERS, BUT GIANTS.** Lower reason recognized those things to be taller than others, because the mind of the proud always climbs high; and therefore they appeared as towers to him, because just as towers exceed other buildings in height, so every great purpose in the mind exceeds others. And this high purpose can exist even without pride, and is born from generosity of spirit; or it can exist with pride, and then it proceeds from beastly and reckless audacity. That first kind is the highest virtue; this second kind is the highest vice. But

---

because they share some similarity—inasmuch as both contain within themselves a greatness of spirit—sensuality cannot distinguish between them. It recognizes only that greatness of soul, and not knowing if such greatness is moderated and corrected by true reason (which is Fortitude) or if it is guided by beastly cruelty (which is Pride), it does not realize that such height belongs to giants, by whom pride is signified. **AS WHEN THE FOG DISSIPATES.** It often happens that when we are in a thick fog, though we see something with difficulty, we nevertheless do not discern it. But we discern it once the fog has departed; thus Dante finally discerned the giants. For higher reason was able to help the lower by offering aid in a way that removed the fog—that is, ignorance—and he knew those were giants and not towers; that is, he knew it was not simple haughtiness, but Pride. And this is in imitation of Virgil (though very hidden) where Venus shows Aeneas that he cannot see the gods destroying Troy, but she will remove the fog that takes away his sight, and then he will be able to see them. <note>A reference to Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book II.</note> And certainly among the ancients, the giants are symbols for Pride. According to the fables, the giants were sons of the Earth who, trusting in their own strength, wished to take heaven from Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>. And to do this, they took three mountains in Thessaly—Olympus, Pelion, and Ossa—and placing one on top of the other, they wanted to climb up to heaven. Jove struck them with lightning and caused the mountains to collapse, and cast the giants into Hell. The giants are therefore sons of the Earth because all pride is for the sake of acquiring earthly things—not knowledge of divine things, but riches, dignity, honor, and empire. These are "great" because they wish to rise higher than they deserve; they fight with the gods because, as Cicero says: "Fighting with the gods is nothing other than resisting nature and wishing to conquer it." And for this, they place mountain upon mountain; that is, they make a great display and a great effort, but God scatters and dissipates them. Hence the Psalmist says: "And a giant shall not be saved by the greatness of his strength." <note>original Latin: "Et gygas non saluabitur propter multitudinem uirtutis sue" (Psalm 33:16)</note>. **WHO ARE IN THE PIT:** in the ninth circle, which he calls a pit because it is narrower and lower than the others. **FROM THE NAVEL DOWNWARD:** because they were out of the ice from the navel upward. **AS WHEN.** Just as it happens that when the fog has been very thick, so that it did not let you discern what a thing was, but one thing seemed to be another; when it then clears, it happens that the gaze and the sight little by little recognize what they did not recognize before, because the earthly vapor which fills the air...

<sig>.r.v.</sig>

<summary>Dante and Virgil approach the central pit of Hell, where Dante mistakes massive giants for towers due to the lingering fog and distance. Landino's commentary explains the philosophical nature of sensory error and allegorically links the giants to the vice of Pride.</summary>

The previous page established that Dante’s vision was failing him due to distance and fog; here, the mist clears, and the true nature of the "towers" is revealed.</meta>

<header>INFERNO</header>

...and it condenses the air, that is, it turns into mist. **THAT WHICH IS CONCEALED** hides things: this is what happened to Dante: the closer he approached, the more the mist thinned and the better he could see. Thus, his terror fled little by little—because he realized they were not towers—but his fear grew, because he began to perceive they were giants; and such a sight struck fear into him. At first, Dante did not fear, believing they were towers, but he was mistaken. Now, seeing they were giants, he began to be afraid, because he recognizes that this height of spirit is pride, which is to be feared. No vice is more ruinous to the human race. Let no one wonder why pride is placed here when the subject is fraud: for this type of betrayal under discussion has its beginning and origin in pride. The Bible mentions giants in Genesis: <note>original: "Et gygante erant in diebus illis"</note> "There were giants in those days." And in the Book of Kings, it mentions Goliath the giant. The giants were from the waist up out of the pit, and the rest was inside the pit; for no one was ever so proud that he could lift himself up entirely. Although his beginnings may be high and elevated, God nevertheless strikes him down so that in the end he remains at the bottom, and He binds his arms, taking away his power. **JUST AS** the entire circle was. Thus, all around the bank of the ninth circle, giants were seen like towers, just as the towers rise all around the walls of Monteriggioni, a castle of the Sienese. This is a castle between Staggia and Siena.

*And I already discerned the face of one,*
*the shoulders, the chest, and a great part of the belly,*
*and down along the sides, both arms.*
*Nature certainly, when she abandoned the art*
*of such animals, did very well*
*to take such executioners away from Mars.*
*And if she does not repent of elephants and whales,*
*he who looks subtly*
*holds her to be more just and more discreet;*
*for where the instrument of the mind*
*is added to an evil will and to power,*
*the people can make no defense against it.*

<column-break/>

**A**pproaching, he began to discern the face, the belly, and a large part of the chest: because the arms, which were tied in front, occupied part of it. Hence he says: **AND ALONG THE SIDES BOTH ARMS. NATURE CERTAINLY.** An excellent digression through which he praises Nature for having ceased to produce more giants; for men of such strength were great executioners for Mars—that is, winners of every battle—and through their immeasurable strength, they tyrannized all others. Therefore, Nature is to be commended for no longer producing such men because they have too much power. And if one were to say that she still produces elephants, which surpass other land animals in size, and whales, which are larger than other fish, he responds that although such animals have great strength, nonetheless...

<column-break/>

...men are superior in wit and industry, with which they not only resist them but defeat them. But in the giants, because they were men, wit was joined with strength. **AND WHEN THE INSTRUMENT OF THE MIND**—that is, wit—does not turn toward virtue, but takes on an evil will toward others and has great power, it cannot be resisted. Because he acts through wit, he can succeed through strength, and he desires to do so because he is malicious. But brute animals, though they may desire and have power, nonetheless do not act <note>with the same calculated malice as humans</note>. Nor is it a mythical thing that there were giants, for Hebrew, Greek, and Roman histories write of them, such as Nimrod, Hercules, and Antaeus. There were some in Sicily; there were some in England. And Aurelius Augustine <note>Saint Augustine</note> affirms having seen on the shore of Africa near the city of Utica a molar tooth so large that one hundred of our teeth could be made from it. Furthermore, he writes that shortly before the arrival of the Goths in Italy, there was in Rome a woman of giant-like proportions, to see whom all the people flocked. **FOR WHERE THE INSTRUMENT OF THE MIND IS ADDED TO AN EVIL WILL AND TO POWER.** All brute animals of great strength have an evil will when, incited by anger, fear, hunger, jealousy, or the safety of their offspring, they come against man. But although they desire to harm and have the power to do so, nonetheless, because they lack rational wit and industry, they do not succeed <note>in organized destruction</note>. Thus, man has some defense. But because in the giant the "instrument of the mind"—that is, industry and wit—is added to his evil will and his great power, no defense can be made against him: because he wills, he can, and he acts.

*His face seemed to me as long and large*
*as the pine cone of Saint Peter's in Rome,*
*and his other bones were in proportion to it;*
*so that the bank, which was a <term>perizoma</term> <note>a Greek word for a loincloth or apron</note>*
*from the waist down, showed so much of him*
*above, that to reach his hair,*
*three Frieslanders would have made a poor boast;*
*for I saw thirty large spans of him.*

<column-break/>

**H**e demonstrates by comparison that the face of this being was as large as a bronze pine cone, which they say was once atop the dome of the "Round Saint Mary," called the Pantheon. But having been knocked down by a lightning bolt, in my time it was on the steps of the church outside of Saint Peter's in the Vatican. But of this, it is spoken in the "Topography of Hell." **AND HIS OTHER BONES WERE IN PROPORTION:** Because the other members correspond to the size of the face. **SO THAT THE BANK, WHICH WAS A PERIZOMA...**

<summary>This page explains Dante's encounter with the giants at the edge of the ninth circle, using the clearing fog as a metaphor for the revelation of truth. The commentary justifies the giants' placement here by linking their physical enormity and human intellect to the sin of pride and the dangers of power combined with malice.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, Canto XXXI. On the previous page, the narrator described how the mist cleared to reveal that the "towers" surrounding the central pit were actually giants. Here, the text focuses on the first giant encountered: Nimrod, the biblical figure associated with the Tower of Babel.</meta>

<columns>2</columns>
<header>CANTO XXXI</header>
<page-num>XXXI</page-num>

...from the place downward where the mantle is buckled.
“Raphel mai ameth zabi almi,”
began to cry out the fierce mouth,
for which sweeter psalms were not suited.

And my leader toward him: “Foolish soul,
keep to your horn, and with that vent yourself
when anger or other passion touches you;
Search your neck, and you will find the strap
that holds it tied, O confused soul,
and see it where it drapes across your great chest.”
Then he said to me: “He accuses himself;
this is Nimrod, through whose ill design
a single language is no longer used in the world.
Let us leave him be, and let us not speak in vain;
for every language is the same to him
as his is to others, which is known to no one.”

<column-break/>

The bank covered him from the navel down, where those members are located that are not shown without shame. Therefore, he calls the bank a <term>perizoma</term><note>A Greek word for loincloth or apron, famously used in the Latin Vulgate to describe the fig leaves worn by Adam and Eve.</note>; because it covered the giants from the navel down, **AND IT SHOWED** so much from the navel up that three <term>Frisians</term><note>People from Friesland (modern Netherlands/Germany), known in the Middle Ages for being exceptionally tall.</note> would have boasted in vain of reaching his hair.

<term>Perizoma</term> is a garment that covers the members that are not named or shown without shame. Frisians: tall men such as those in the Frisian part of Germany. **FOR I** saw thirty great spans <note>original: "palmi"</note> starting from the place where the mantle is buckled, which is at the base of the throat, down to the navel that was visible. **RAPHEL** Bay ameth zabi almi. These words mean nothing; and even if they did mean something, no complete meaning could be drawn from them. But the poet induces Nimrod to speak thus to signify the confusion of languages that was born from him.

**FOOLISH SOUL**; without salt: that is, without any prudence. For who can be more foolish than he who wishes to oppose God? **KEEP TO** your horn: as if to say, do not use words since no one understands them; use the horn, a sound suited to your beastliness and brutality. When anger or other passion touches you. To brute animals, articulate voice has not been given by nature, because with that we express the concepts of the mind, which proceed from reason. And because brutes do not have reason, but only the appetite from which passions are born—such as love, anger, fear, and the like—it was enough for them to have a confused and inarticulate voice with which they can express such passions. Therefore, Nimrod, having not used reason but only appetite, is not worthy of using distinct words,

but only the voice of the horn with which hunters call out and make noise. He imagines that he has tied to his neck with a <term>foga</term>, which is a leather strap, this horn which hangs upon his chest. By the horn, he signifies his pride which binds his neck: because such a sin makes him a servant to punishment; and it hangs upon his chest because pride is born from the evil thought that is in the heart. **AND SEE HIM.** See that horn: which <term>togate</term> you: it covers your great chest. It was therefore a great horn since it covered such a great chest, and by this, it denotes his great pride. <term>Toga</term> is a Roman garment, from which he derived the verb "to togate," that is, to clothe. **HE ACCUSES HIMSELF.** Inasmuch as by speaking in a language known to no one, he demonstrates his confusion. Therefore, the words spoken by him cannot be interpreted. **LET US LEAVE** him be and let us not speak in vain, let us not speak fruitlessly. For he would not understand us. And thus every language is to him as his is to others. Nimrod would not understand Virgil because the irrational appetite, guided only by disturbances and the passions of the soul—such as sorrow, fear, anger, and the like—understands neither Dante (representing lower reason) nor Virgil (representing higher reason). **THIS** is Nimrod. Nimrod was the son of Ham, and Ham the son of Noah. This man truly can be said to have been among men what Lucifer had been among the angels. And because he was in abundance of all things and bold and very robust, he persuaded others that their happiness did not come to them from God but from their own virtue. And he encouraged his relatives to seize tyranny, hoping to turn men away from fearing God and to place all hope in himself. And so that God could not punish them with a flood as He had done in the time of Noah, his grandfather, he determined to build a tower so high that the flood could not reach it. He built it, therefore, of bricks instead of stones, and of bitumen instead of mortar. And each day he had twenty thousand men at such work, and all were in total accord in such iniquity. But God, who <note>original: "depofuit potentes de sede et exaltauit humiles"</note> “cast down the mighty from their seat and exalted the humble,” did not wish to extinguish the human generation again as He had done with the flood. Instead, He determined to disunite and confound them. Therefore, He threw the tower to the ground; and where before they used one same language, He generated confusion through the diversity of languages He gave them. Therefore, the tower was called Babylonia, because *Babel* signifies confusion. Of this tower and the confusion of languages, Josephus affirms that the Sibyl writes thus: Men were all of one language, and they all built a very high tower, believing by it to be able to climb to heaven; but the gods with winds destroyed the tower and divided the language, giving to each his own. Therefore, that city was called Babylonia. **THROUGH WHOSE** ill design. Through whose evil desire to want to rebel against God. **A SINGLE LANGUAGE** is no longer used in the world. As was shown above.

<summary>This page explains the encounter with Nimrod, the giant responsible for the Tower of Babel, whose "confused" speech represents the loss of a universal human language. The commentary interprets his horn as a symbol of pride and his nonsensical words as a divine punishment for his attempt to transcend human limits.</summary>

# INFERNO

We then made a longer journey,
turning left, and at the distance of a crossbow shot,
we found another much fiercer and larger.
To bind him, whoever the master might have been,
I cannot say, but he was held bound,
with the left arm in front and the right arm behind,
By a chain that held him wound
from the neck down, so that on his exposed part
it wrapped as far as the fifth coil.
"This proud one wished to test
his power against supreme Jove,"
said my leader, "whereby he has this reward.
Ephialtes is his name, and he performed great deeds
when the giants made the gods afraid;
the arms he once moved, he moves no more."

And I to him: "If it were possible, I would wish
that my eyes might have experience
of the immeasurable Briareus."
To which he replied: "You shall see Antaeus
nearby, who speaks and is unchained,
and who will place us in the bottom of all sin.
The one you wish to see is much further on;
and he is bound and made like this one,
except he appears more ferocious in the face."
Never was an earthquake so violent
that it shook a tower as strongly
as Ephialtes was quick to shake himself.
Then I feared death more than ever,
and there was no need for more than the <term>docta</term> <note>Dante uses the word 'docta' to mean a 'stroke' or 'scare'—here implying the fear alone could have killed him.</note>
if I had not seen the bonds.
We proceeded further along the slope
and came to Antaeus, who, not counting his head,
rose five <term>alle</term> <note>Ells; an old unit of measurement.</note> out of the cavern.

<column-break/>

**S**equencing their journey to the left, and within the distance of a crossbow shot, they found Ephialtes, fiercer and larger than Nimrod. I cannot say who was the master to gird and bind him: But with a chain he had the left arm bound in front, and the right behind. And this chain girded him five times from the neck down to where he began to be covered. This proud Ephialtes wished to be "experienced," that is, to make a test of his power against Jove: and he performed great deeds in the war that the giants waged against Jove. Ephialtes and Otus were the sons of Neptune and Iphimedeia, wife of Aloeus, one of the Titans. They grew nine fingers every month; and according to Homer, they were already nine paces tall. They defeated Mars and for nine months held him in prison. But Juno saw to it that Mercury stealthily drew him out of prison. Later, in the war of the giants, they were killed with arrows by Phoebus [Apollo] while they were still beardless. Allegorically, this demonstrates pride. And they are sons of Neptune because heavy movements and heavy storms stir the proud as Neptune (the sea) stirs them. They defeat Mars because they become victors in battles. But Juno, who is the goddess of kingdoms, takes Mars away from them by means of Mercury, which signifies that the just administration of the kingdom with the help of prudence and wisdom resists tyrants: and often takes from them the victory they had already acquired.

**P**roviding variety in the narration of these giants, so that a single form would not generate boredom, he asks about Briareus; and Virgil answers him that Briareus is much further on; and because he is bound in the same manner as Ephialtes, there is no need to labor in describing him, being made in the same way, except that he is more ferocious in the face. But he says that he will see Antaeus, who speaks and is unchained. And by him they will be placed in the bottom of every "guilty thing": that is, of Hell, where every evil resides. Briareus, Cottus, and Gyges were once sons of Heaven and Earth: and they had a hundred hands and fifty heads. They were strongest and most beautiful above all others. Here the poet follows the opinion of other poets who place Briareus in Hell as an enemy of Jove. But Homer makes him a friend, and tells the fable whose summary is this: Juno, Neptune, and Pallas [Athena] conspired near Nereus, the sea god, to forge a chain with which they would pull Jove out of heaven. Thetis, the sea goddess, revealed this conspiracy to Jove: and Jove called Briareus to his aid, who so terrified the conspirators that they abandoned the enterprise. And this accords with Scripture by placing them bound; for the Psalmist writes: "To bind their kings with chains and their nobles with fetters of iron." <note>original Latin: "Ad alligandos reges eorum in compedibus et nobiles eorum in manicis ferreis."</note> And similarly we will say of the pit; because the same Psalmist [writes]: "But you, O God, shall bring them down into the pit of destruction." <note>original Latin: "Tu uero deus deduces eos in puteum interitus."</note> And elsewhere: "Let not the tempest of water drown me, nor the deep swallow me up, and let not the pit shut her mouth upon me." <note>original Latin: "Non me demergat tempestas aque Neque absorbeat me profundum Neque urgeat super me os putei."</note> NEVER WAS an earthquake: He demonstrates by comparison to an earthquake how strongly Ephialtes shook himself. And certainly nothing creates a greater movement among men and induces greater fear than pride. This caused such fear in the poet that he feared death more than ever; and there was no need for anything to kill him other than a <term>docta</term>: that is, a brief space. For whoever allows himself to be conquered by this vice dies in his sins. <term>Docta</term> in the Florentine tongue means a brief space of time. In essence: in any brief time that I remained in such fear, I would have died. But the "retorts" and bonds that I saw, which were not broken by his shaking, took away my fear. Afterward they went to Antaeus, who, without his head, was five <term>alle</term> higher than the cavern. An <term>alla</term> [ell] is the name of an English measure of two Florentine "arms" [braccia].

<summary>This page describes Dante's encounter with the giants Ephialtes and the mention of Briareus, illustrating their physical restraint as a punishment for their rebellion against the divine. The commentary provides mythological background on the giants' origins and allegorizes their pride as a destructive force that can only be restrained by wisdom and divine law.</summary>

<header>CANTO XXXI</header>

**O** you, who in the fortunate valley
that made Scipio the heir of glory
when Hannibal and his men turned their backs,
once brought a thousand lions as your prey;
and of whom it is still believed
that had you been at the high war
of your brothers, the sons of Earth
would have won—set us down, and do not feel disdain,
where Cocytus is locked in by the cold.
Do not make us go to Tityus nor Typhon;
this man can give what is longed for here;
therefore bend down and do not twist your snout.
He can still restore your fame in the world,
for he is alive and expects a long life yet,
unless grace calls him to itself before his time.

**S**o spoke the master, and he in haste
stretched out those hands and took my leader,
whose great grip Hercules once felt.
Virgil, when he felt himself grasped,
said to me: "Come here, so that I may take you";
then he made it so that he and I were one bundle.
As the Garisenda tower appears to the viewer
under its leaning side when a cloud passes
over it, so that the tower seems to hang—

<column-break/>

**B**ecause he wishes to entreat Antaeus to
set them down, and in order to gain his goodwill,
he says: "O you, Antaeus, who once brought a thousand lions
as prey," because you were of such strength that you easily
could conquer them. IN THE fortunate valley:
Fortunate for Scipio, because it made him the heir of glory.
For Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus the Elder, 
having been made consul against Hannibal, judged
that it was better to conquer the Carthaginians in
Africa than in Italy. Therefore, he went from Pisa to Sicily,
and from Sicily to Carthage, and set up camp in the place
that was first called the kingdom of Antaeus, and later
was called the Cornelian Camp after that same Cornelius Scipio.
FORTUNATE VALLEY for the Cornelian people,
because Scipio Africanus the Elder
reduced Carthage to servitude, and later Africanus the
Younger conquered and destroyed it. AND THAT if you had been
at the high war: he calls it "high" because it was against 
the gods. He says this to gain goodwill. And
he also follows Lucan, who in his fourth book presents
a similar sentiment. Antaeus was the son of the Earth, strong and immeasurable; he fought with Hercules, and every time
Hercules threw him to the ground, the Earth renewed the
strength of her son Antaeus. But finally Hercules
lifted him from the earth and held him to his chest, and
squeezed him so hard that he made him burst. Pomponius Mela
writes that he was the king of the furthest part of Mauritania, and there he built the city of Tingis <note>Modern Tangier</note>, where his ivory shield,
which was very large, remained. Theodontius writes that Hercules with his army took the
kingdom from him many times; but as soon as Hercules departed, he would regain his strength from the nearby places and reclaim the kingdom; but
finally Hercules, feigning flight, led him far away, and then suddenly turning back, conquered
and killed him. This, according to Augustine, was in the time when Danaus reigned in Argos; and according to Eusebius, it was
in the time when Aegeus, father of Theseus, reigned in Athens. SET US DOWN: This is his request.
Where Cocytus is cold: where this river mentioned above freezes. AND DO NOT feel disdain:
Do not be indignant because we are a much lighter weight than is suited to your arms. DO NOT make
us go to Tityus nor Typhon: as if to say, although these two could carry us down, nevertheless carry us
yourself so that the gratitude may be yours. Tityus was the son of Jove and Elara, daughter of Orchomenus; but Jove, fearing
that Juno would find out, hid him under the earth; hence they believed he was a son of the Earth.
He wished to join with Latona, the mother of Apollo. Therefore Apollo pierced him with his arrows and
cast him into Hell. Leontius writes that he was a prince in Boeotia, and trusting in his great strength, he wished
to take Delphi from Apollo; but Apollo conquered him and cast him into Hell—that is, reduced him to a low and private life.
Typhon was one of the Titans who, fighting with his brothers against Jove, was struck by his lightning
and was placed under Mount Etna. THIS MAN can give what is longed for here: as if to say that in a
place of damnation one cannot hope for salvation, but certainly for some fame, and Dante can give it to him. DO NOT
twist your <term>grifo</term> <note>Original: "grifo." In Florentine dialect, this refers to a snout or muzzle, specifically that of a pig.</note>, do not hold us in contempt; because when someone refuses to do something, the Florentines say he "twists his snout,"
as if to say he sharpens his muzzle like a pig.
FOR HE IS ALIVE and expects a long life yet: he can therefore give him fame in the world because he is alive and
hopes to live a long time. UNLESS grace calls him to itself before his time: that is, if by divine grace
he is not called to the celestial life before the natural course of human life. For whoever dies
before the natural course dies before his time. Thus Virgil says of Dido: *But she, wretched, died before her day and by a sudden madness fired.* <note>Original Latin: "Sed misera ante diem subito que accensa furore." From Aeneid, IV, 697.</note>

**T**he meaning of the text is clear. But allegorically
it demonstrates that descending into the
contemplation of pride, not to fall into it, but
to have knowledge of the vice, Antaeus—that is,
such a vice—carries Virgil, who represents reason. Because by
climbing onto the vice, one recognizes it; and Virgil
takes hold of sensuality, which without Virgil would
be conquered by Antaeus. AS THE GARISENDA APPEARS TO THE VIEWER:
The Garisenda is a
tower in Bologna, thick and not very high, but
greatly leaning, named after the Garisendi family.

<header>INFERNO</header>

Such Antaeus appeared to me as I stood watching
to see him bend, and it was such a moment
that I would have wanted to go by another road.
But lightly to the bottom that devours
Lucifer with Judas he placed us;
nor did he remain there bent,
but like a mast in a ship he rose up.

<column-break/>

The Garisenda is a thick tower in Bologna,
and not very tall but very leaning, so named
after the Garisendi family: and it is near the
Asinelli tower. Therefore, whoever stands under this tower from
the side where it leans, and clouds pass quickly through the air
from the opposite side, it seems that the tower leans and
falls. Such, then, did Antaeus appear to him when he
bent down. **AS THE** Garisenda tower **appears to the viewer**
**UNDER THE LEANING** side: under the part where it hangs. **WHEN**
**A cloud goes over it**: and it hangs against
the cloud. Because the eye is deceived and it seems that the clouds do not move but the tower moves, and because it is
leaning from that side it seems that, moving, it falls. **SUCH**
**Antaeus appeared**: and it was such an hour that I would have wanted
to go **BY ANOTHER road** because of the fear I had: and allegorically it shows that sensuality in the recognition
of vice goes at great peril of remaining entangled in it if it is not succored by reason: because it is
always prone to earthly things. **BUT LIGHTLY to the bottom he placed us.** Because he who resists the
flatteries of sin, such knowledge places us lightly at the bottom, <note>i.e.</note> it shows us the baseness and vileness of sin.
**WHICH DEVOURS Lucifer with Judas**: as we will understand below. **AND AS A Mast in a**
**ship he rose up.** Having placed us at the bottom without delay, he rose with that height and gravity with which a mast
in a ship rises.

# CANTO XXXII OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE

<image-desc>A large ornamental drop cap 'S' begins the first verse of Canto XXXII, rendered in gold with intricate vine motifs on a blue square background framed in red.</image-desc>

If I had the rhymes harsh and grating
as would be appropriate for the dismal hole
upon which all the other rocks press,
I would press out the juice of my concept
more fully: but because I do not have them,
not without fear I bring myself to speak;
For it is no enterprise to take in jest
to describe the bottom of the whole universe,
nor for a tongue that calls "mommy" and "daddy" <note>original: "mamma et babbo." Dante argues that describing the center of Hell requires a mature, harsh poetic style, not the simple language of a child.</note>.

<column-break/>

Having narrated of the proud: Now because from pride,
beyond the other infinite vices, proceeds
treachery, he explains in this canto the punishment of
traitors: who are divided into four parts: and the
first is of those who have used treachery
toward relatives: These he places in the ice: because
they are entirely deprived of all warmth of charity; And
as this virtue <note>charity</note>, because it is more acceptable to God
than any other, is placed closer to Him in the highest heaven
in the order of the Seraphim: so this
vice <note>treachery</note> must be in the place most remote and lowest,
being its contrary. And charity is in the highest...

<summary>Dante and Virgil are lowered into the frozen pit of Cocytus by the giant Antaeus. The poet begins Canto XXXII by calling for a harsh poetic style to describe the depth of Hell where traitors are punished in ice.</summary>

<columns>2</columns>
<header>CANTO XXXII</header>

> But may those ladies help my verse
> who helped Amphion to wall in Thebes,
> so that the telling may not differ from the fact.
> O you ill-created rabble, above all others,
> who stay in the place where speaking is hard,
> it would have been better had you been sheep or goats here.

<column-break/>

In the height and in the highest heat <note>God is often associated with light and heat in Dante's cosmology</note>: therefore treachery will be the opposite, in the lowest depths and in the extreme frost. **Where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth** <note>original: "Vbi est fletus et stridor dentium"</note>: the gnashing of teeth denotes the cold, and Cocytus denotes the weeping, because **Cocytos** <note>original: "cocytin"</note> in Greek means "to weep."

Since the author must now begin the narration of the things found in the ninth circle—and because the gravity of the vice makes them difficult and almost unspeakable—he makes an excuse and shows himself to be insufficient for such a subject. These words make the listener attentive. Then he invokes the help of the Muses so that what he cannot do by himself, he may do with their aid. **IF I HAD rhymes**; verses which are in rhyme. **HARSH AND grating** <note>original: "ASPRE Et ghioccie"</note>: the true praise of the poet is that the verse be suited to the subject matter. It is not only his duty to narrate, but he must almost paint with words in a way that makes the thing appear to the eyes of the mind just as things are seen with physical eyes. Hence many have defined poetry as **a painting that speaks**. This is most clearly seen in Virgil.

Therefore, since he has to treat the horrendous, terrible, and harsh things in this last circle, he knows that "harsh and grating" rhymes are required—that is, hoarse sounds that demonstrate misery and sadness. This is appropriate for the **sad hole**; this last circle which is a hole in the center of the earth. **UPON WHICH they lean** <note>original: "SOPRAL Qual pontano"</note>; that is, all the other rocks, stones of the great valley, and circles already mentioned above press down upon it, because all weights of every round body press toward the center as the lowest place. Or truly, if we take "rocks" to mean structures, and structures to mean vice, we could say that all vices lean upon this circle, which is Pride. For pride is the root of all.

**I WOULD squeeze the juice of my concept**; before anyone writes, they always think of what they want to write, and once they have made their invention, they begin to write it. Thus, the mind conceives within itself—as, for example, a grape has conceived its juice. Then, just as it is necessary to squeeze the herb if we want the juice to come out, so when we manifest with words what we have already conceived in the mind, it is like squeezing the juice of what we have conceived. The meaning is: "If I had verses suitable to the subject, I would express my concept more fully."

But because he does not have them, he does not proceed without fear. The reason he does not proceed without fear is that wanting to treat such matter is not an undertaking to be taken as a joke or a game: wanting to write about the **bottom**—that is, the obscure foundation—of the whole universe and all men. And then, because the Florentine language in which he writes is understood with difficulty outside of Italy where one says **daddy or mommy** <note>original: "babbo o mamma"</note>, he adds "or a tongue that calls daddy or mommy," meaning the Italian language. For in all Italy there is but one language, but it is divided into many properties because each region has its own. These properties in Greek are called <term>idioms</term>. The Latins have no idiom because the Latin language, being from the small region of Latium, does not vary in anything. But the Greek language, because it extends through many regions, has many properties, such as the Attic, Aeolic, Doric, and Ionic idioms and the like.

Since he has shown the greatness of the subject through his inability, he now gives hope that although he is not sufficient by himself for such a great thing, he can still do it with the help of the Muses, whom he invokes. We wrote about the Muses and the reason why poets invoke them above in the second Canto. **But those ladies**—namely the Muses—**who helped Amphion to wall in Thebes**; making the walls of Thebes, may they be the ones who help my verse so that

---

my words correspond to the fact and express this fully. Antiope conceived three sons by Jove according to Homer: Amphion, Zethus, and Calais. <note>Landino follows a specific mythological variation here; more commonly Amphion and Zethus are the twin builders of Thebes.</note> Amphion with his sweet music drew the stones to himself and caused them to join together to form the walls of Thebes. This signifies nothing other than that he, with his prudence and most sweet eloquence, was able to lead the men of that region—who lived scattered through the fields and woods—to live civilly in one and the same city.

**O ABOVE ALL**; after the invocation, so that the narration may have appropriate gravity, he begins with an exclamation, which always gives gravity to speech, saying: **O People** <note>original: "Plebe"</note>. For there can be no gentility or nobility among the vicious because, **Virtue is the only and unique nobility** <note>original: "Nobilitas una atque uirtus" from Juvenal, Satire VIII</note>. **O ill-created people**: unhappily created above all other men, even those in the other circles, you who stay in the place of which **speaking is hard**—that is, difficult. **WOULD THAT YOU HAD BEEN sheep or goats** <note>original: "zebe"</note>: sheep or goats or other brute animals, so that the soul would have been mortal, and you would not be in these eternal pains. He calls them **zebe** because that is what our shepherds call them.

---

> When we were down in the dark pit
> beneath the giant’s feet, much lower,
> and I was still looking up at the high wall

Having reached the pit, they found themselves lower than the giant's feet; and Dante, because he was intent on looking up at the height of the walls that girded this ninth circle, did not see that he was...

<header>INFERNO</header>

> We heard it said: "Look how you pass;
> walk so that you do not tread with your soles
> upon the heads of the wretched, weary brothers."
> Whereat I turned and saw before me
> and under my feet a lake that from the frost
> had the appearance of glass and not of water.

> Never did the Danube in Austria <note>original: "Danoia in Obstericchi"</note>
> make for its course so thick a veil in winter,
> nor the Tanais <note>The river Don</note> there under the cold sky,
> As it was here; for if Mount Tabernicchi <note>Mount Javornik in Slovenia</note>
> or Pietra Pana <note>Mount Pania in the Apuan Alps</note> had fallen upon it,
> it would not even have made a "creak" <note>original: "cricchi"</note> at the edge.
> And as the frog sits to croak
> with its muzzle out of the water, when the peasant girl
> often dreams of gleaning,
> Livid, as far as where shame appears <note>The face, where a person blushes from shame</note>,
> were the woeful shades within the ice,
> setting their teeth to the chattering note of the stork.

<column-break/>

frozen lake. But in passing he heard one who said: "watch that you do not tread," that is, do not trample the heads of the wretched brothers: meaning those who are brothers by birth, and are wretched for the pain they suffer in this ice. Now, to understand exactly the poet's invention, this ninth circle is divided into four parts in such a way that the first is the widest and embraces the second, and the second the third, and the third the fourth. In this way, the further inward one goes, the smaller the circuit and the further one descends toward the center, though there is no visible boundary. The first part, which is closest to the wall and is the widest, is called Caina; the reason for this will be known below. The second is Antenora. The third is Ptolomea. The fourth is Judecca.

And if we subtly examine these types of betrayals, we will see that they contain not only pride, but also envy, which the poet has not treated by name here because envy is such that it flows into various other vices. And because this envy comes from pride, the first to be proud and envious was Lucifer. Because fraud committed against one who trusts is called treachery, it stems from pride and envy and is therefore punished here. If it is between blood relatives, it is punished in the first circle, called Caina after Cain, who out of envy killed his brother Abel; this is against the natural bond. If it is against one’s country, where there is a bond of birth, it is worse because it is against many; this is punished in the second part called Antenora. Or if one breaks faith given to a friend, this happens in two ways: either against one whom we have seduced into giving to us through benefits—this is the third degree and is worse than the second, because trust was not just given but earned—and this is punished in the third part called Ptolomea, after Ptolemy, who invited priests to a banquet and killed them there. Or it is committed against a friend who is also a benefactor; this degree is worse than the others, and this is the fourth degree. This fourth degree is the worst because it is ingratitude; it is called Judecca after Judas Iscariot, who betrayed the humanity of Christ. In the center of this pit, as the place furthest removed from heaven, Lucifer is punished, because his crime is above all others.

**I**t was so thick, that ice, that the Danube in Austria <note>original: "Danoia in Obstericchi"</note>, nor the Tanais, ever froze so strongly. Austria is the coldest part of Germany <note>original: "Magna," referring to Alemagna</note> and in Latin is called *Austria*, through which passes the Danube, the largest river in all Europe. It rises in the mountains of Germany, passes through Hungary, and enters the Euxine [Black] Sea with such force that for more than sixty miles into the sea it maintains its fresh water. In winter it freezes so hard that entire armies pass over it with horses and carts; it is commonly called the Danube. The Tanais rises in the north in the Riphean mountains where the cold is immeasurable; it divides Asia from Europe and enters the Euxine Sea near the city of Theodosia.

The ice was so thick that if these very high mountains, Tabernicchi and Pietra Pana, had fallen upon it, not only would the ice not have broken, but it would not even have moved the edge, where, when it moves, it makes this sound: "creak" <note>original: "chricchi"</note>. Tabernicchi is a very high mountain in Slavonia. Pietra Pana is in Tuscany in the Garfagnana region above Lucca; by the Latins it is called the Apuan Stone <note>original: "pietra apuana"</note>. And truly there is a very great coldness in the heart of the proud and the traitor, as we said above. They stood with their heads out of the water like frogs at harvest time, when the peasant girl **OFTEN**: frequently: dreams of gleaning, that is, picking up the fallen ears of grain; he says "dreams" because a person often dreams of doing what they have in their heart to do. **LIVID**: this demonstrates great cold and similarly provides a color suitable for envy. Hence the Latins call envy "lividness" <note>original: "liuore"</note>.

**AS FAR AS WHERE** shame appears: up to the face, which shows signs when one is ashamed. In the same ice he places the traitors of relatives, friends, and country. But those lower down are always in greater cold because they are closer to the center; it is reasonable that he who has committed the greater treachery should be furthest from the fire of charity. Treachery is greater when one breaks the path to one's country, because it is done against more people than against friends, and greatest when against God. They set their teeth to the note of the stork because they were chattering their teeth from trembling, making that noise a stork makes when it strikes the lower part of its beak against the upper. Through this chattering of teeth, great cold is demonstrated, and that which the Gospel calls the **gnashing of teeth** <note>original: "stridor dentium"</note>.

<summary>This page describes the landscape of Cocytus, the frozen lake at the bottom of Hell, and explains the four divisions of the ninth circle—Caina, Antenora, Ptolomea, and Judecca—based on the severity of the betrayal.</summary>

<header>CANTO</header>

Each one held their face turned downward;
the cold is testified by the mouth, and the sad heart by the eyes.
When I had looked around a little,
I turned to my feet and saw two so pressed together
that the hair of their heads was mixed.
"Tell me, you who so clasp your chests,"
I said, "who are you?" and they bent their necks;
and after they had raised their faces toward me,
Their eyes, which before were only wet within,
dripped down over their lips, and the frost froze
the tears between them and locked them up again.
Never did a clamp gird wood to wood
so strongly; wherefore they, like two he-goats,
butted together, such anger overcame them.
And one who had lost both ears
to the cold, still with his face turned down,
said: "Why do you mirror yourself so much in us?
If you want to know who these two are,
the valley where the Bisenzio <note>A river flowing near Prato and Florence</note> descends
belonged to their father Alberto and to them.
They issued from one body; and you may search
all of Caina <note>The zone for traitors to kin</note> and you will not find a shade
more worthy of being fixed in this jelly;
Not him whose chest and shadow were broken
with a single blow by the hand of Arthur <note>original: "Artu"; referring to the death of Mordred</note>;
not Focaccia; not this one who obstructs
My head so that I see no further,
and was named Sassol Mascheroni;
if you are Tuscan, you well know who he was.
And so that you do not put me to more speech,
know that I was Camicion de' Pazzi,
and I wait for Carlino to exonerate me."

<column-break/>

**Each one held their face turned downward.** It is the nature of the traitor never to look anyone in the face. Furthermore, shame compels him because he remembers having always acted against that virtue which is proper to man. And certainly, traitors always turn their faces downward, and consider nothing other than earthly and base things. **WHEN I had looked around a little.** These four tercets are quite well known. But that the tears freeze in such a way that they lock their eyes denotes that the envious person, although he sees misery, lacks understanding. The cold—that is, the lack of <term>charity</term> <note>In the theological sense of 'caritas' or selfless love</note>—does not let him see or be moved to compassion. **AND ONE:** Not responding, those two, another shade answered. **STILL With his face turned down**, as we said above. **THE VALLEY of Bisenzio.** The Bisenzio is a river between Florence and Prato; it joins the Arno six miles from Florence. **ALL The Caina:** we said that he names this first circle after Cain, who was the son of Adam, the first man, and was a farmer. And he had Abel his brother, a shepherd. Abel sacrificed the firstlings of his flock, and such firstlings were accepted by God. Cain offered the firstlings of the fruits of the earth, and they were not accepted by God. Cain was moved to envy, and said to his brother: "let us go outside"; and when they had come to the countryside, Cain killed his brother. And God said to Cain: "where is your brother?" To which Cain replied: "I do not know. Am I my brother's keeper?" And God said: "his blood cries out to me; the earth shall swallow you and will not yield fruit to you, and you shall be cursed upon the earth." **NOT HIM Whose chest and shadow were broken:** that is, the chest and the back; because the shadow of the chest goes to the back. This was Mordred <note>original: "Modrite"</note>, son of King Arthur, King of Britain and head of the Round Table. Mordred rebelled against his father and lay in ambush to kill him. But Arthur, discovering the ambush, struck him with a lance in the chest and passed it through to his back <note>Legend says the wound was so great that light passed through it, breaking his shadow</note>. **Focaccia** was of the Cancellieri of Pistoia and treacherously killed his uncle. In the year 1300, there were three brothers in this family who were knights. And Focaccia, a very bold youth of the worst character, was the son of one of these. It happened that while playing in the snow, Focaccia’s father struck a nephew of his because he had too harshly insulted another child with snow. And he did this as his family, being his uncle. But the child, more reckless and more malicious than his age required, disguised his pain; and after a short time, he pretended to want to speak in his ear. The uncle leaned down and the child gave him a slap. The father was grieved; and the child remained with the uncle so that he might punish him in his own way. But the uncle, thinking no more was needed for the deeds of a child, instead of a beating, kissed his face and sent him back to his father. But the wicked Focaccia, his son, cut off this child's hand; then he ran to the house of the father, who was his uncle, and killed him. From which <term>patricide</term> <note>The killing of a close relative</note> followed such scandal that all of Tuscany was troubled for many years; for from this derived the factions of the Whites and Blacks that first divided Pistoia and then Florence. **NOT This one who obstructs my head** and stands before my eyes so that I cannot see further. This was Sassol Mascheroni of Florence, who similarly killed his uncle.

**AND so that you do not put me to more speech** to ask me who I am. **Camicione**—this was Messer Alberto Camicione de' Pazzi of Valdarno, who treacherously killed Messer Ubertino, who was an uncle of his.

# CANTO XXXII

When another cried out: "What ails you, Bocca?
Is it not enough to chatter with your jaws
unless you bark too? What devil touches you?"
"Now," I said, "I do not want you to speak,
wicked traitor; for to your shame
I will carry true news of you."
"Go away," he replied, "and tell what you wish;
but do not be silent, if you get out from here,
about him who had his tongue so ready just now.
He weeps here for the silver of the French;
'I saw him of Duera,' you can say,
'there where the sinners are kept cool.'
If you should be asked who else was there,
you have at your side him of Beccheria,
whose gorge Florence sawed through.
Gianni de' Soldanieri, I think, is further on
with Ganelon and Tribaldello,
who opened Faenza while it slept."

We had already departed from him
when I saw two frozen in one hole,
so that one head was a hood to the other;
And as bread is devoured for hunger,
so the upper one set his teeth into the other
there where the brain joins the nape.
Not otherwise did Tydeus gnaw
the temples of Menalippus out of disdain
than this one did the skull and the other parts.
"O you who show by such a bestial sign
hatred over him whom you devour,
tell me the reason," I said, "on this condition:
That if you have a rightful complaint against him,
knowing who you are and his sin,
I may yet repay you in the world above,
if that with which I speak does not dry up."

<column-break/>

It does no good for the traitor to wish to cover and keep his crimes hidden, because there is always someone who reveals them; and the poet signifies this through the one who named Bocca, who did not wish to be identified. **CHATTER** <note>original: "SONAR"</note> with the jaws: the clashing of teeth due to the cold. "Unless you bark": *latrare* in Latin is to bark <note>original: "latrare è abbaiare"</note>, and it is proper to dogs. **GO AWAY** he replied: when the wicked have been discovered and can no longer hide, it is their custom to turn to naming others who have committed similar errors; and to excuse themselves, they accuse others. This is Messer Bocca degli Abati of Florence, of whom we spoke above. **AND WEEPS**: this man whom you see there. **WEEPS** for the silver of the French: this was Messer Buoso of the family of Duera from Cremona. He was a Ghibelline and, along with others, was prepared to block the passage of Guy de Montfort, who was leading the army of Charles I from France into the Kingdom of Naples against Manfred. But corrupted by money, he betrayed his friends and acted in a way that allowed the French to pass. **OF BECCHERIA**: This was the Abbot of Vallombrosa; he was from Parma, of the house of Beccheria. Having been sent to Florence by the Church, he plotted through treason to take the state from the Guelphs <note>The pro-papal political faction</note> and give it to the Ghibellines <note>The pro-imperial political faction</note>.

And the Guelphs, discovering this, cut off his head in a popular fury in the Piazza of San Apollinare. For this reason, the city was excommunicated. **Gianni Soldanieri**: In the time when the "Jovial Friars" <note>an order of knights intended to keep the peace</note> were Governors of Florence, as we said above, the Ghibellines attempted an armed uprising to overthrow those who ruled the people, who were Guelphs. Therefore, the people gathered under arms at Santa Trinita. Messer Giovanni Soldanieri, who was a Ghibelline and from a noble and ancient family, became the leader of the people in order to increase his own power; he ultimately won and drove out the Ghibellines, betraying them. **GANELON** <note>original: "GANELLONE"</note>: After Charlemagne had recovered Spain and restored it to the orthodox Christian faith, he sent Ganelon as an ambassador to two Saracen kings who remained there, demanding they be baptized and pay tribute. They promised much, but on the other hand, they corrupted Ganelon with great wealth, and he betrayed his fellow Christians. Ganelon advised that they should secretly occupy the Pyrenees mountains and wait in ambush for Roland, Count of Maine, and Oliver, Count of Geneva, whom Charles kept as a rearguard. The paladins arrived with twenty thousand armed men, and being assaulted by twenty thousand more Saracens, they fought manfully and won. But being exhausted after the victory and assaulted again by thirty thousand, they were finally all killed. But we spoke of the death of Roland above.

He had moved a little further away when he saw two so wretched <note>original: "infierne," likely a variant of "inferni" or "infelici"</note> that one head was a hood to the other, for it touched it; and the sovereign one, that is, the one who was on top, gnawed with his teeth the back of the neck of the other at the point where the brain joins the nape. **NOT OTHERWISE** did Tydeus gnaw. We showed the history of Eteocles and Polynices above. Tydeus, son of King Oeneus of Calydon, arrived in Argos at the same time as Polynices. And although in their first meeting they became great enemies, nonetheless through the mediation of Adrastus, King of Argos, they were reconciled and became most faithful friends and brothers-in-law, for Adrastus made them his sons-in-law. And later in the battles of Thebes, it happened that they fought together: Tydeus on the side of Polynices and Menalippus the Theban on the side of Eteocles. Menalippus wounded Tydeus, and Tydeus killed him. Then, seeing that the wound he had received was mortal, Tydeus had the head of the already dead Menalippus brought to him, and out of rage and anger, he gnawed it with his teeth.

### CANTO XXXIII OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE

The sinner lifted his mouth from the savage meal,
wiping it on the hair of the head
he had wasted from behind.
Then he began: "You wish for me to renew
a desperate grief that presses on my heart
just thinking of it, even before I speak.
But if my words are to be a seed
that bears fruit of infamy for the traitor I gnaw,
you shall see me speak and weep at once.
I do not know who you are, nor by what means
you have come down here, but a Florentine
you seem to me truly when I hear you.
You should know that I was Count Ugolino,
and this is Archbishop Ruggieri;
now I will tell you why I am such a neighbor.
That through the effect of his evil designs,
trusting in him, I was taken
and then killed, there is no need to tell.
But that which you cannot have heard—
that is, how cruel my death was—
you shall hear, and you shall know if he has offended me."

<column-break/>

This thirty-third canto is excellently connected to the previous one because it continues the narrative already begun, and brings one of the two previously found to respond. Therefore, the narration of this second ring <note>Antenora, the zone of the ninth circle where traitors to their country are punished in ice</note> continues, and afterward it will enter the third. This opening is most fitting for capturing attention, both through the cruel act of Count Ugolino and through his words, which promise rare and unusual things.

**HE LIFTED THEREFORE:** that is, the Count raised his mouth **FROM THE SAVAGE MEAL:** from the head upon which he was ferociously feeding; and he wiped that mouth on the hair of that head, which he had already been gnawing from behind at the nape of the neck. And being prepared to tell his story, he shows how much it must pain him if his words are to bring infamy to the Archbishop whom he was gnawing. Afterward, he reveals himself to be Count Ugolino, and the one he gnaws to be Archbishop Ruggieri. He shows he does not wish to tell how, by trusting him, he was betrayed by that man, and through such betrayal captured and killed, because that story was very well known. But he wishes to tell of the cruel manner of his death, which he considers less known. He is silent, therefore, about what would bring him shame to tell, and narrates what would be to the perpetual ignominy of his enemy. 

This Count Ugolino was of the Gherardesca counts, and was a great citizen who governed Pisa. In those times, the Pisans lost the greater part of their territory, which was taken from them by the Florentines and other **Guelphs** <term>Guelphs: the political faction that generally supported the Pope against the authority of the Holy Roman Emperor</term> of Tuscany. It was the opinion that he, although he was a **Ghibelline** <term>Ghibelline: the political faction that supported the Imperial authority of the Holy Roman Emperor</term>, was in league with the Guelphs and wished to weaken the power of the Pisans to make himself their lord. At that time, the Archbishop of Pisa was Master Ruggieri Ubaldini; and it happened that...

### CANTO XXXIII

A nephew of his was killed by a relative of the Count due to jealousy over a woman whom each of them loved; the Archbishop planned to avenge this injury upon the Count. He therefore increased that suspicion and stirred up many enemies against him, especially three principal families: the Gualandi, Sismondi, and Lanfranchi, in such a way that they incited the people against him. He personally, with the cross in hand, led the people to the Count's house. He and four of his sons were captured and imprisoned in the tower which is in the square of the Elders <note>original: "piazza de g’atiani", referring to the Piazza degli Anziani in Pisa</note>. And they threw the keys of the prison into the Arno so that no one could open it. And the prisoners were denied food; hence that tower from that time on was called the Tower of Hunger. The poet, therefore, through the person of the Count, narrates how they all died of hunger, and the circumstances which, in truth, neither the poet nor anyone else could know. But because it was manifest that they had died of hunger, he imagines the circumstances and makes the story plausible; and he brings in the Count who says: "HOWEVER, That which you cannot have heard."

**A small opening within the cage**
**which for me bears the title of hunger,**
**and in which others must yet be shut,**
**Had already shown me through its opening**
**several lights, when I had the evil dream**
**which rent the veil of the future for me.**
**This man appeared to me as master and lord,**
**hunting the wolf and the whelps on the mountain**
**because the Pisans cannot see Lucca.**
**With lean hounds, eager and trained,**
**Gualandi with Sismondi and with Lanfranchi**
**he had placed in front of the line.**
**In a short course, they seemed to me tired,**
**the father and the sons, and with sharp fangs**
**it seemed to me I saw their flanks being rent.**

<column-break/>

**A SMALL** opening. **WITHIN** the cage: they call a "muda" <term>muda: a 'mew' or cage where birds of prey are kept while they 'mute' or shed their feathers</term> a place where they shut up birds of prey so they may "mude," that is, change their feathers. But here, by a fitting metaphor, he calls this prison a "muda." **WHICH** for me bears the title of hunger because, through my death, it is called the Tower of Hunger. **IN WHICH** it is fitting that others should yet be shut: he imagines this because of the frequent political changes that occurred in that city. **HAD SHOWN ME** through its opening: through its hole and small window. This shows that he was still awake when the dawn came, in such a way that the window already let in light; then he fell asleep and dreamed. And as we said above, a dream near daybreak is true. **WHICH OF THE FUTURE RENT**: it broke. **THE VEIL**: the darkness; because through this dream, I understood what was to be. The dream was that it seemed to him he was shown a prelate who was leading a hunt, and he took with him the three families mentioned. **AND HOUNDS** lean and ready. By the prelate, the Archbishop is signified; and by the hounds

---

the people. "I was hunting a wolf with its cubs": which was the Count with his sons. They were running toward Mount Pisano, which is between Pisa and Lucca and takes away the view so that from Pisa one cannot see Lucca. And this signifies that the Count, out of fear, had planned to retreat to Lucca where the Guelphs were gathered. But in a short time, they were exhausted. This denotes that they could not reach Lucca. Wherefore the hounds caught him because the people captured him.

**When I was awake before the morning,**
**I heard my sons, who were with me,**
**weeping in their sleep and asking for bread.**
**You are indeed cruel if you do not grieve already,**
**thinking of what my heart foretold;**
**and if you do not weep, for what do you usually weep?**
**They were already awake, and the hour approached**
**when food used to be brought to us,**
**and each one was fearful because of his own dream.**
**And I heard the locking of the door below**
**of the horrible tower; wherefore I looked**
**into the faces of my sons without saying a word.**

**I did not weep, I so turned to stone within;**
**they were weeping, and my little Anselm**
**said: "You look so, father, what is it?"**
**Therefore I did not cry, nor did I answer.**

<column-break/>

**WHEN** I was awake before the morning: before the morning and the clear day, I heard my sons weeping in their sleep; because they were dreaming, as I had dreamed, of their misery and the hunger to come, and then they asked for bread. And it often happens that those same celestial constellations that bring misery similarly induce dreams that manifest it. And this is what he says a little below: "and each one was fearful because of his own dream."

**I** did not weep: because I turned to stone <note>original: "impetrai"</note>; that is, I hardened inside. That great grief prevents tears is manifest. **THEY WERE WEEPING**: Here the author uses every means that can move one to mercy and compassion: first from the omen of his dream and that of his sons. So says Virgil: "Behold, before my eyes, most sorrowful Hector seemed to be present to me in sleep" <note>original: "In somnis ecce ante oculos mestissimus hee tor Visus adeſſe mihi", from Aeneid II, 270-271</note>. Then from the sons: because it is the greatest grief for a father to see his sons in extreme misery and not be able to help them. **AFTERWARD** When we had become somewhat day-lit. It shows

<meta>This page continues the harrowing conclusion of Count Ugolino’s speech in the Tower of Hunger. Having described his prophetic dream on the previous page, he now recounts the agonizing days of starvation and the death of his children. The subsequent commentary transitions from the narrative to a medieval medical and philosophical analysis of how hunger affects the human body based on the theory of the four humors.</meta>

### XXXIII INFERNO

all that day and the night following,
until another sun came out into the world.
As soon as a little ray had entered
the sorrowful prison, and I discerned
through four faces my own aspect,
I bit both my hands for grief;
and they, thinking I did it for desire
of eating, suddenly rose up
and said: "Father, it would be much less pain
for us if you eat of us; you clothed us in
this miserable flesh, and you strip it off."
I quieted myself then, not to make them more sad;
that day and the other we all stayed silent;
ah, hard earth, why did you not open?
When we had come to the fourth day,
Gaddo threw himself stretched out at my feet,
saying: "My father, why do you not help me?"
There he died; and as you see me,
I saw the three fall one by one
between the fifth day and the sixth; then I gave myself,
already blind, to groping over each,
and for two days I called them after they were dead;
but then, more than grief, hunger had power.

<column-break/>

The poet [narrates] that they all lived without food until the fourth day: and on the fourth day Gaddo, the youngest, died there, overcome by hunger. Then between the fifth and sixth day the three remaining sons died: and he [Ugolino], already blind, survived for two days, that is, all of the sixth and the seventh. Furthermore, he adds that "hunger had more power than grief." Which our Martino Novarese—may God increase his prudence and diminish his arrogance—interprets to mean that "hunger had more power than grief," that is, that the desire for food overcame piety and paternal love and forced him to feed on the flesh of his sons. How absurd <note>original: "absona"</note> this opinion is, I will leave to the judgment of the reader. And I will strive to open up two excellent points unknown to him, with which the author, as both poet and physician, supremely adorned this oration. And first, we will treat physically <note>original: "physice", meaning according to natural philosophy or medicine</note> of the tolerance of fasting. It is unknown to no one that through the constant resolution <note>here meaning "dissipation" or "breaking down"</note> of the natural humor in the living body, it is necessary that—when hunger comes, which is nothing other than the craving and desire for the dry, and thirst for the moist—the animal [living being] continuously generates new chyle <term>chyle: a milky fluid produced during digestion</term> with new food and new drink, which restores the lack; and if it does not take nourishment, in a short space it fails. But because so much resolution of the nutritive humor that kills a man does not happen equally in everyone, it therefore happens that some support lack of food <note>original: "inedia"</note> and fasting less and some more without their ruin. And the physicians, seeking the causes of the variety, attribute it mostly to four things:

---

->Age, Complexions, The substance of the humor, and The pores.<-

Who therefore is either in tender age and not yet consolidated and firm, or in a deficient age <note>meaning old age</note>, supports it less than a man established in a stable age. Hence children and the elderly require more frequent nourishment than a man placed in the perfect age. In the second place, we will note the complexions <note>the balance of the four humors</note> in which the less humor there is or the more resolvable it is, the less hunger can be supported. Therefore, in a very short space the **choleric** <term>choleric: one of the four humors, associated with fire, yellow bile, and a quick temper</term> perishes; the **melancholic** <term>melancholic: associated with earth and black bile</term> supports a little more; the **sanguine** <term>sanguine: associated with air and blood</term> somewhat more; and more than the sanguine, the tempered complexion sustains itself. And finally, the **phlegmatic** <term>phlegmatic: associated with water and phlegm</term> lasts longer than the four already mentioned because he abounds in humor; and that [humor], because it is very viscous, does not easily dissolve; and in dissolving, it easily converts into blood fit to sustain life. Wherefore we see many phlegmatic animals, such as snakes, moles, dormice, and the like, pass the winter and live without food, because the phlegm that abounds in the stomach converts slowly into blood and nourishes. Furthermore, one notes the essence of the humor in any complexion: the thinner it is, the shorter the time it resolves; and it supports hunger less. And conversely, the thicker it is, the more it has the contrary effect. One also notes the porosity: because the more porous body empties sooner. Hence it feels hunger sooner; and in the less porous, understand the opposite. Now, if I am not mistaken, I have with great brevity hinted at rather than narrated the natural causes of the tolerance of fasting. But extrinsic accidents also contribute not a little, such as air, whether thick or thin, or hot or cold; such as foods, whether more or less resolvable; and other similar things. But especially do the various states of the soul [contribute]. Because just as joy, by relaxing and diffusing the soul, also diffuses the humors and makes them more resolvable—whereby hunger is supported less—so grief, by restricting them, makes them less resolvable. Therefore, the greater the grief, the more a man supports fasting and lives longer without food. All these things the poet distinguished: the length of the fasting according to age and according to grief. And because the sons were in the growth of age, he induces them to die first; and among those he puts the first, the one of most tender age; and then the others according as they were more or less advanced in years. And he [Ugolino] is put last, both because he was in the stability of age and also because he was oppressed by greater grief. The first he induces to die on the fourth day; the others from hour to hour until the sixth; he wept for them then for two days, that is, the sixth and the seventh. And on the seventh, although grief—by condensing and constricting the humors—prohibited the resolution which prolonged life, nonetheless the length of the fasting had more power than the prohibition of resolving that proceeded from grief. Nor without natural reason did he take the terms of the fourth and seventh day: because in human life these days are critical due to the movement that nature makes in them. Which proceeds...

<meta>This page continues the transition from the narrative of Count Ugolino’s death to a scholarly commentary.
