### CANTO XXXIII

...from the lunar course. Because the moon in its first quarter moves toward its sextile aspect and in the seventh toward its square: which movements have great power over human life. Nor is the [significance] of the seventh day incredible. Because Ficino <note>original: "Ficino phisico et cerusico"</note>, a physician and surgeon of no small repute and father of our Marsilio Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was one of the most influential humanist philosophers of the Italian Renaissance.</note>, affirms that there was someone in the hospital of Santa Maria Nuova who said he had seen Leonardo Pistolese, a very religious man of such restraint that, by gradually increasing his fasting over time, he brought himself to eating only once a week. We have spoken, I believe, sufficiently regarding fasting. 

But it does not seem right to me to overlook the arrangements and the oratorical force with which the author has shaped this speech of the Count: for it can move even the hardest heart to compassion. To better understand this artistry, I note that rhetoricians call a "pathetic oration" <note>An "oration of pathos," intended to evoke deep emotion.</note> that which moves the souls of the listeners either to anger and hatred or to mercy and compassion: because *pathos* in Greek <note>original: "pathos in greco"</note> signifies passion and disturbance: and such movement is stirred by various means. 

First, the manner and the place stir great commiseration. Therefore, here he shows that such a death occurred in the dark tower. Thus Virgil says: "And they scattered the youth through the wide fields" <note>Latin: *Et latos iuuenem sparfere per agros* (Aeneid).</note>; and elsewhere: "He dragged the trembling man to the very altars" <note>Latin: *Altaria ad ipsa trementem traxit*.</note>. Compassion is also stirred by the manner of death. For it is harsh to kill a man: but much more so to kill him with hunger than with the sword. For this reason, Cicero complained of one who had been killed by the smoke of green wood. And Virgil: "Moreover, he joined dead bodies to the living" <note>Latin: *Mortua quin etiam iungebat corpora uiuis*.</note>. He moves the listener, then, not just because the man is dead, but because he died in prison and died of hunger. 

Furthermore, he includes the dream; thus Virgil: "Behold, in sleep, before my eyes the most mournful hero seemed to be present and to pour forth copious tears" <note>Latin: *In somnis ecce ante oculos moeftiffimus heros Visus adef se largosque effundere fletus*.</note>. Likewise: "But the very image of her unburied husband came in sleep, raising his pale face in wondrous ways" <note>Latin: *Ipsa sed in foinnis inhumati uenit imago Coniugis ora modis attoll lens pallida miris*.</note>. Nor is it told without commiseration when a long-held calamity arrives. Hence, quite rightly, everyone feared because of his dream; Virgil did not overlook this: "I was not unaware how much new glory in arms [can do]" <note>Latin: *Haud ignarus eram quantu noua gloria in armis*.</note>. It is also very disturbing to lose hope: and for this reason, it is a tearful thing when he says: *AND I heard the door below being nailed shut in the horrible tower.* Hence Sinon in Virgil: "Nor is there any hope for me now of seeing my ancient fatherland, nor my sweet children" <note>Latin: *Nec mihi iam patriam antiquam fpes ulla uidendi. Nec dulces natos*.</note>. 

Therefore, if we grieve for one who weeps, how much more shall we grieve for one who, through grief, cannot weep? The weeping of the children was great sorrow to the father. It was great sorrow to the children that the father could not weep. He moves us by the length of time in which they were afflicted by hunger. Virgil often uses this device: "Whence they say he lamented seven whole months in order" <note>Latin: *Vnde septem illum totos perhibent ordine mensis*.</note>; and regarding Palinurus: "Scarcely on the fourth light did I see Italy, raised high from the top of the wave" <note>Latin: *Vix lumine quarto prospexi Italiam summa sublimis ab una*.</note>. He moves us by his weakness. Hence he said: *And I gave myself, already blind, to groping over each one.* Thus Virgil says of Mezentius: "He raises himself on his sick thigh" <note>Latin: *At tollit in egrum se femur*.</note>. Virgil moves us with the youth of the victims: "Unhappy boy, and an unequal match for Achilles" <note>Latin: *Infelix puer atque impar congressus achilli*.</note>. Likewise, by the sight of it: "As youths placed on funeral pyres before the eyes of their parents" <note>Latin: *Ut impositique rogis iuuenes ante ora parentum*.</note>; and because it causes greater pain to see calamity than to hear of it, he said: *AND AS you see me, I saw the three fall.* Thus Virgil: "And those most miserable things which I myself saw" <note>Latin: *Queque ipfe miserrima uidi*.</note>. I could show many other instances in this oration most apt for moving compassion. But with these, we can investigate the supreme artistry of the poet both here and in many other parts of the work.

When he had said this, with his eyes askew,
he seized the wretched skull again with his teeth,
which were strong against the bone like a dog's.
Ah, Pisa, shame of the people
of the beautiful country where "si" <note>Italy is called the land of "si" because of the word for "yes."</note> is spoken,
since your neighbors are slow to punish you.
Let Capraia and Gorgona <note>Two islands near the mouth of the Arno river.</note> move
and make a dam for the Arno at its mouth,
so that it may drown every person in you.
For if Count Ugolino was rumored
to have betrayed you in your castles,
you should not have put his children to such a cross.
Their young age made them innocent—
a new Thebes!—Uguccione and Brigata,
and the other two named in this song.

<column-break/>

**A**s soon as the Count had finished his narration, he returned to biting the skull of his enemy. The poet imagines this because for one who is wronged, and the injury remains before the eyes of the one who did the wrong, his conscience stimulates and gnaws at him day and night. **AH PISA** Shame of the people of the beautiful country where "si" is spoken: that is, the shame of the beautiful country of Italy in which "si" is spoken. For just as the Frenchman says *oy* <note>The Old French word for "yes."</note> and the German *io* <note>Likely referring to the German *ja*.</note> and the Greek *ne* <note>In Greek, *nai* means "yes," but the commentator may be confused with the particle *ne*.</note>, so all of Italy says *si*. And certainly, it is a shame to the Italians not to have punished such cruelty, a vice which is most abominable in the Italian nation, which more than others was always humane and merciful. 

**SINCE** your neighbors are slow to punish you, let Capraia and Gorgona move. These are two small islands located in the sea not far from the mouth of the Arno. He wishes for these to place themselves against the Arno so that, having no exit to the sea, it would swell back into Pisa, through which it passes, and drown it. Count Ugolino, to stabilize his state...

---

...married two daughters, one to Count Guido di Battifolle and the other to Aldobrando, Count of Santa Fiora. To Guido he gave Ripafratta as a dowry, and to Aldobrandino, Suvereto. **FOR IF** Count Ugolino was rumored: that is, had the reputation. He speaks very artfully: first, it was a great cruelty to kill the Count without having certainty of his betrayal; but let us grant that one should have believed **THE RUMOR**: that is, the fame: and for...

### INFERNO

We passed further on where the frost
roughly enwraps another folk,
not turned downward, but all upturned.
The very weeping allows them not to weep,
and the grief which finds a barrier on the eyes
turns inward to make the agony grow;
For the first tears form a knot,
and like a **crystal visor**,
fill the whole socket beneath the eyebrow.

And it happened that, although every sensation
every sensation <note>The repetition of "ciascun sentimento" (every sensation) appears in the original transcription as a likely scribal or typesetting error.</note>
had ceased to have a dwelling in my face;
Already I seemed to feel a certain wind,
wherefore I: "My master, who moves this?
Is not every vapor extinguished down here?"
Whereupon he to me: "Soon you shall be where
of this the eye shall give you the answer,
seeing the cause that rains down the blast."

And one of the wretches of the frozen crust
cried out to us: "O cruel souls,
since the final post has been given to you,
Lift from my face the hard veils,
so that I may vent the grief that impregnates my heart,
but only for a moment before the weeping freezes again."
So I said: "If you wish me to help you,
tell me who you are, and if I do not disentangle you,"

<column-break/>

"this should punish me." Nevertheless, you should not have punished the innocent, especially with such a cross: that is, with such a heavy martyrdom. And he assigns the reason. Because their young and tender age made them innocent: for they were still so young that they neither thought of state affairs themselves, nor were they summoned by their father to any of his councils. **NEW THEBES** <note>original: "NOVELLA THEBE"</note>. A city as cruel as Thebes was: in which the first founders, brothers born from the sown teeth of the serpent, killed each other; and the mother and aunts killed Pentheus. Athamas killed his son Learchus; Oedipus lay with his mother; Eteocles and Polynices, brothers, killed each other out of greed for rule. Then he shows that the age of the sons was still "new" (young), naming those, Uguccione and Brigata, who were the two eldest; and the other two were equal. **THE CANTO ABOVE** <note>original: "EL CANTO SUSO"</note>: This chapter was mentioned above. **NAMES** <note>original: "APPELLA"</note>: Those who were equal were Gaddo and Anselmuccio. And the text is ordered thus: *O New Thebes, the new age of Uguccione and Brigata and of the other two whom the canto names above made them innocent.*

This is the third circle: and it is called **Ptolomea** <term>Ptolomea: The zone of Hell named after Ptolemy, where those who betrayed guests are punished. In this region, the souls lie on their backs (supine), causing their tears to freeze in their eye sockets.</term>. Here the souls stay in the ice upturned; the first tears that come out, because they cannot find vent, freeze in the hollow of the eyes and form like a **crystal visor**. Then those [tears] that follow, finding the exit closed, return inside and make the agony grow. And he feigns this because here those who have betrayed under the guise of benevolence and love are punished. They have therefore shown a sign of charity so that those they wish to betray might be less on guard. And this is expressed by being supine, which is looking up toward heaven. But they do not stay in a way that the tears can exit: because such charity is false. Therefore, the weeping does not allow them to weep, and the agony increases: because that false charity increases the betrayal, wherefore it deserves greater punishment. **VISORS** <note>original: "VISIERE"</note>: like spectacles. **THE WHOLE SOCKET** <note>original: "TUTTO El coppo"</note>: the entire concavity that is beneath the eyebrow, in which the eyes are located.

*And it happened that, although every sensation had thus ceased*: that is, "vacated its dwelling," meaning its place in my face, as from a callus: that is, that my face had no more sensation in it than a callus has, which, because it is dead flesh, does not feel. And this happened to me because of the cold. In essence, although my face was numbed by the cold so that I felt neither cold nor heat any differently than a callus does, I nevertheless seemed to feel a certain wind, which I marveled at. For wind is born from hot and dry vapors raised by certain stars, and especially by the sun; the power of which does not seem able to penetrate down into the center to resolve the vapors into wind. **WHEREUPON HE TO ME: "SOON YOU SHALL BE WHERE"**: because the causes of many things cannot be seen with the eyes, nor felt with any sense. It is necessary that they be demonstrated with natural reason. But where the sense understands it by itself, reason is not needed. Therefore, the sense will demonstrate from where this wind is caused. And this is a very fitting fiction: just as in the highest heaven the Holy Spirit is born from divine power and wisdom, which inflames one toward charity (and for this reason it is compared to fire and to the southern wind), so from Lucifer proceeds the freezing wind of pride, which kills every heat of charity and hardens and freezes all human hearts.

While he was passing among the frozen ones, **Friar Alberigo** <note>Alberigo dei Manfredi, a member of the Jovial Friars, who famously murdered his guests at a banquet after signaling the killers by calling for fruit.</note> begs him to remove the ice from his eyes. And Dante promises to do it with an "execration" of that which he anyway desired to do: and this was to go to the very bottom of hell. **O CRUEL SOULS**, since you were not [contented?] by my pain. **SINCE THE FINAL POST HAS BEEN GIVEN TO YOU**. He believed that Dante and Virgil were also damned for betrayal, and having newly arrived, had not yet been placed...

### CANTO XXXIII

to the bottom of the ice I must go.
He answered then: "I am Friar Alberigo;
I am he of the fruits of the bad garden,
who here receive a date for a fig."
<note>The phrase "a date for a fig" (dactilo per fico) is a proverb meaning to receive something of greater value in return; here, Alberigo notes his punishment is even greater than his crime.</note>

Those who have made a habit of betrayal are not left by any act of pride or hatred. **I AM** Friar Alberigo. This man was of the Manfredi family, lords of Faenza. In his later years, he became a "Jovial Friar" <note>term: *Cavalieri Gaudenti* or Jovial Friars; an order of knights intended to keep the peace but often accused of corruption.</note>; thus he was called Friar Alberigo. He was so cruel that, while in discord with his relatives and desiring to remove them from the earth, he pretended to want to reconcile with them. After peace was made, he invited them to a magnificent banquet, and at the end of the feast, he commanded that "the fruit be brought," which was the signal given to those who were to kill them. Immediately, the assassins jumped inside and killed all those Alberigo wanted dead. Thus, among us, it is still used proverbially when we want to show someone has been struck, saying "he has had the fruits of Friar Alberigo." He said "fruits of the bad garden" because it was a captive garden that gave such fruits. **WHO HERE:** In this hell **RECEIVE:** I get a date in place of a fig: for as much more excellent as the date is than the fig, so much greater is the penalty he receives here than that which he gave his relatives when he murdered them.

> I said to him: "Oh, are you then already dead?"
> And he to me: "How my body stays
> in the world above, I carry no knowledge.
> Such a 'vantage' has this Ptolomea,
> that often the soul falls here
> before Atropos gives it death.
> And so that you may more willingly scrape
> the glassy tears from my face,
> know that as soon as the soul betrays,
> as I did, its body is taken from it
> by a demon, who thereafter governs it
> until its full time has turned.
> The soul falls into such a cistern,
> and perhaps the body still appears above
> of the shade that winters here behind me.

> he is Ser Branca Doria, and many years

And successively there were high priests, and very strong in deeds of arms, and especially Simon, who with the greatest justice and strength defended the liberty of the Hebrew people against many kings and renewed the alliance with the Romans. This man had a son-in-law, Ptolemy son of Abubus, entirely unlike so good a father-in-law, and wicked and impious against him who had honored him so much. Being appointed by Simon as governor in Jericho and trusting in his great treasures, he dared to attempt with extreme wickedness to seize the principality and the high priesthood from his father-in-law. Simon came to Jericho with two sons, and Ptolemy received them most magnificently with a splendid banquet; and at the end of it, he had the old man, his sons, and all the others who had come with them killed. **ATROPOS.** The poets place three [Fates], whom they call the Parcae. Through them, they demonstrate the beginning, the progress or course, and the end of human life. Thus the first, which signifies our birth, is called Clotho, who holds the distaff with the thread. The second is called Lachesis; because *lanchano* in Greek <note>original: "lan chano" from λαγχάνω (lanchano)</note> means to allot and distribute, because to every man who is born she gives his lot—that is, the portion of life that touches him. And so they imagine that she spins the thread that Clotho has, because she produces the course of life. The third denotes the end of the course, which is death. Hence they imagine that she breaks and snaps the threads of Lachesis and call her Atropos; because *a* in Greek signifies "not" and *trepin* <note>original: "trepin" from τρέπειν (trepein)</note> "to turn," because death does not turn nor bend for the instance of anyone and pardons no one. But she is immobile and inflexible. The ancient Latin poets called these three Parcae: Nona, Decima, and Morta. **THE TIME** fully turned: He rightly said "turned," because time is nothing other than the measure of movement and is born from the revolution and cir...

...until staying. Wherefore he says **SO MUCH:** until such time
as the final post is not given / the last verse
where you must always stay. Remove the veil that
veils my eyes so that with tears I may
vent the grief, which, not being vented, impregnates
my heart. This shows that although the damned, and these...

**Such** a 'vantage'. He spoke with irony. Because
besides the other evils, the traitor has this:
that his soul comes to eternal pains before
the time of his death arrives. And he imagines that
a demon enters the body of the traitor and
governs it until the proper death. And by this
he means to signify that the obstinacy of the traitor is
so great that he never repents. This is shown also by
the Evangelist regarding Judas, saying that after the betrayal
the devil entered the body of Judas. He,
despairing, said: "My sin is greater than that I may deserve mercy." <note>original Latin: "Maius est peccatum meum qua ut ueniam merear." This is a reference to Genesis 4:13, often attributed to the despair of Cain and later applied to Judas in medieval theology.</note>
Therefore, notwithstanding that he lives
many years after the act of betrayal, we can
say that the soul is damned, because it is obstinate in
sin; and a devil, in such obstinacy, governs
the body in a way that he seems to be a living man,
but according to his character, he is a devil. **PTOLOMEA:**
Just as the upper circle was called Antenora
from Antenor, so this is Ptolomea from
Ptolemy. So that this may be better understood, we will repeat
with brevity from the book of the Maccabees how the Maccabees,
after the times of Alexander the Great, reigned
in Israel. And there were three brothers adorned with most
excellent virtues: Judas Maccabeus, Jonathan, and Simon.

<header>INFERNO</header>

the circuit of the planets, and especially of the sun, which makes the year through its revolution of the twelve signs. And perhaps his body is the body of the shadow which is in the winter: that is, the cold remains here behind me. **STILL REMAINS ABOVE:** As if to say, he remains alive through a demon that governs him; and you should know: **IF ONLY NOW:** Just now, you have come down here to hell. **HE IS SER BRANCA DORIA.** This Messer Branca was a Genoese of the Doria house, the son-in-law of Messer Zanche, lord of Logodoro in Sardinia, who was mentioned above in the ditch of the pitch <note>original: "bogia della pegola"; referring to the fifth ditch of the eighth circle where barrators are punished in boiling tar</note>. To seize power, he invited his father-in-law to dinner and had him murdered. Therefore, Dante feigns that immediately after the betrayal, his soul was pulled down to hell, and a devil entered his body. In truth, when Dante wrote this, Messer Branca was still alive. He calls him "Ser" and not "Messer" in mockery, because the Genoese call every gentleman "Messer." Naturally, he makes this Romagnolo <note>Friar Alberigo</note> speak this way because it is their nature not to honor anyone with words.

> "I believe," I said to him, "that you deceive me,
> for Branca Doria has not died at all,
> and he eats, and drinks, and sleeps, and wears clothes."
> "In the ditch above," he said, "of the Malebranche,
> there where the tenacious pitch boils,
> Michel Zanche had not yet arrived,
> When this man left a devil in his place
> in his own body; and so did a relative of his,
> who performed the treachery together with him.
> But reach out your hand here now;
> open my eyes." And I did not open them for him;
> and to be a villain toward him was a courtesy.

<column-break/>

In these verses, not much explanation is required. Dante does not believe that Branca Doria is dead, having seen his body performing all the functions of the living. The spirit responds to what was already said above and shows that his relative, who murdered Michel Zanche with him through treachery, is also in this state. **BUT REACH OUT NOW:** This shows that when the spirit asked him for the promise, Dante did not observe it. By this, he means to imply that we should not keep any promise that goes against justice. Here, the highest injustice would have been to impede divine justice. Furthermore, it is not wrong to use cunning to draw the truth from someone, especially while observing an oath. For Dante said to him, "If I do not keep my promise, may I go to the bottom"; and so he shall go <note>Dante is literally traveling to the bottom of Hell, so his oath is technically fulfilled even if he refuses to help the sinner</note>. He concludes that with such men, it is the highest courtesy to be a villain <note>Dante plays on the word "courtesy," suggesting that showing mercy to such a traitor would be a moral failing</note>.

---

> Ah, Genoese! Men estranged
> from every custom and full of every flaw,
> why are you not scattered from the world?
> For with the worst spirit of Romagna
> I found one of yours who, for his deeds,
> even now bathes his soul in Cocytus,
> while in body he still appears alive above.

<column-break/>

This is a worthy and well-placed exclamation against the Genoese people for many reasons. I will not provide an invective here, as it is against my custom <gloss>p<note>abbreviation for "per"</note>: for</gloss>, but they are known to almost everyone. **MEN STRANGED FROM EVERY CUSTOM:** because you are alien and contrary to every good habit. **AND FULL OF EVERY FLAW:** just as a man is not completely good if he merely avoids vice without practicing virtue, so one cannot be called an absolute captive <note>term: "captivo" or "cattivo"; meaning wicked or wretched</note> of evil if he is merely alien to virtue without practicing vice. Thus, wanting to show that the Genoese are completely wicked, he says "full of every flaw."

---

**WHY ARE YOU NOT:** He marvels at how divine justice suffers them and does not extinguish them. But as Valerius writes: "Divine wrath proceeds with a slow step and compensates for the slowness of the punishment with its severity" <note>original Latin: "Lento n. passu divina procedit ira tarditatemque supplicii gravitate compensat." A quote from Valerius Maximus regarding the patience of the gods.</note>. **WITH THE WORST SPIRIT OF ROMAGNA:** This is a great escalation in this comparison. To understand this better: it is a universal reputation that those of Romagna have the worst customs. Thus there is a Tuscan proverb: "A red Lombard, a black Romagnolo, of every hair <note>meaning "of every kind of wickedness"</note>." Therefore, if a Genoese is worse than a Romagnolo, one cannot climb any higher in vice.

<summary>This page discusses the punishment of Branca Doria, whose soul is in Hell while his body remains alive on Earth, inhabited by a demon. Dante concludes the section with a fierce condemnation of the Genoese people for their perceived corruption and treachery.</summary>

### CANTO XXXIV OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'V' containing a miniature illustration of two figures, likely Dante and Virgil, standing in a rocky landscape.</image-desc>
"The banners of the king of hell come forth" <note>original: "Vexilla regis prodeunt inferni"; a parody of the Latin hymn "Vexilla Regis," which honors the Cross of Christ. Here, Virgil uses it to announce the approach of Lucifer.</note>
toward us; therefore, look ahead,
my master said, "if you can discern him."
As when a thick mist exhales,
or when our hemisphere grows dark,
there appears from afar a mill that the wind turns:
Such a structure I seemed to see then;
then because of the wind I shrank back
behind my leader, for there was no other shelter.

<margin>Diabolical temptation does not appear except by hidden ways. **THEN BECAUSE OF THE WIND:** to flee three winds that proceed from the three wings of Lucifer; having no other shelter, he shrank behind Virgil. And certainly Dante, who represents sensuality, would freeze from the wind sent by Pluto <note>The commentator uses "Pluto" interchangeably with Lucifer here</note> if Virgil, who is the intellect and doctrine, did not provide him a defense against such a bitter vice. There are three winds from three wings: Ingratitude, Cruelty, and Hatred. Against these vices, there is no other escape than to have reason as your shield and defense, which opposes those with three virtues: Gratitude, Pity, and Charity.</margin>

I was already—and with fear I put it into verse—
where the shades were all covered
and shone through like straw in glass.
Some are lying down; others stand upright,
this one with the head, and that with the soles;
another, like a bow, bends his face to his feet.

<margin>They equally betray superiors and inferiors; and these stay in the shape of a bow with their heads and feet downward. And all lie supine because they have practiced betrayals brazenly and without shame. Therefore, they stay there in the ice of cruelty and ingratitude. **I WAS ALREADY** And with fear I put it into verse: As if to say that he is terrified even while writing it; he captures attention by showing the magnitude of the thing, which causes horror just to consider.</margin>

When we had been made to go so far forward
that it pleased my master to show me
the creature who once had the beautiful face,
he moved from before me and made me stop,
saying, "Behold Dis, and behold the place
where it is necessary that you arm yourself with fortitude."
How I then became frozen and faint,
do not ask, reader, for I do not write it,
because all speech would be weak.
I did not die, and did not remain alive;
think now for yourself, if you have a grain of wit,
what I became, deprived of both.
The emperor of the sorrowful kingdom
from the mid-chest stood out from the ice;
and I am more comparable to a giant
than giants are to his arms.

<column-break/>

We have, for our salvation, already arrived at the depth of hell and the fourth ring of the ninth circle, which is named Judecca <note>named after Judas Iscariot</note> after the first and greatest of all traitors. Virgil speaks to Dante, saying, *"Vexilla regis inferni prodeunt"*—that is, the banners of the infernal king appear and are already seen. Therefore, look forward if you can discern him. He calls the wings of Lucifer "banners." Then, by comparison, he expresses his appearance. Pluto <note>Lucifer</note> appeared as a windmill turned by the wind appears when seen in a thick mist, or when it becomes night in our hemisphere. He saw Lucifer in the darkness because...

He sets down four types of punishment: one of those who lie flat and overturned; and these are the traitors who have betrayed their equals and benefactors. The second of those who stay with their feet up and heads down; and these have betrayed their superiors, such as lords, masters, and every higher rank. The third of those who, contrary to these, stay with their feet down and heads up, which denotes that they have betrayed their inferiors. The fourth of those who [are bent like a bow]...

When we were so far forward that it pleased Virgil to show me Lucifer, who before he sinned was very beautiful, he placed himself before me—I who had previously been standing straight to flee the wind. **DIS:** He calls the prince of darkness Dis; and we discussed this name when we described Pluto <note>Dis Pater was the Roman god of the underworld; Dante uses 'Dite' for the city of Hell and for Lucifer himself</note>. **BEHOLD** The place where it is necessary that I arm myself with fortitude: because no place is so horrendous to sensuality and to the lower reason as this one is. It is difficult for sensuality to resist any vice, because through the contagion of the body and through temptation, it is easily inclined toward it. But there is none that can be conquered with greater difficulty than pride; because a certain arrogance is innate in man, which wishes to obey no one and seeks to be superior to every man. If this is done according to virtue, it is fortitude; if without reason, it is pride—a vice altogether intolerable, and from which infinite vices proceed. And therefore he says, do not ask how I became...

see today how great that whole must be
which to such a part corresponds.
If he was as beautiful as he is now ugly
and against his Creator lifted up his brows,
well must all sorrow proceed from him.

<column-break/>

...so frozen and faint: because such arrogance deprives us
of every fire of charity: wherefore we remain cold;
and through the cold, faint. Lucifer emerged from the middle
of his chest upwards: And he says, I assure you and I
promise that what was visible was
more than a giant: and he assigns the reason saying
that giants do not <note>original: ".i. non si confanno"</note> compare:
and do not equal the arms of Lucifer. Therefore

consider how much the rest must be to be proportioned with what is seen: But of his greatness we spoke in the topography of hell. **IF HE WAS SO** beautiful: He utters with a condition that which our religion completely affirms. Because he lifted his brows: that is, he rose up in pride against his Creator: Divine justice requires that as much as he was higher than the others, so much should he be placed lower: And as much as he was beautiful, so much should he be ugly. But because the poet makes mention of Lucifer at present, we will say with extreme brevity some things about the nature of demons. And first, let it not be unknown to us that from the beginning, the production and creation of the good angels and those who from heaven rained into hell was the same: because as Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a prominent theologian and teacher of Thomas Aquinas.</note> writes in the compendium of theology, God made all the angels good, yet not supreme: but in the middle between the supreme good and the changeable good, in a form that, by turning to love God—who is a good above them—they could rise to a state of grace. But by turning to the changeable good—which is a good inferior to them—for this reason they had to fall into the evil of guilt and punishment: because there is no ignominy of sin without the loss of the ornament of justice. The ruin of the devil was twofold: because he fell both from his dignity and from the place in which he was created. He fell from dignity: because he fell from the strength of his nature. He fell from the flexibility of free will toward the changeable good. From light into darkness. From knowledge into ignorance. From innocence to guilt. From happiness to punishment. From love to hatred. Because after the ruin, he became impotent and obstinate in evil: and blinded to the truth: and disordered in goodness: and weakened in virtues; and excluded from divine contemplation. Furthermore, his impious will turned to hatred of man and to envy. For which reason, with every effort, he strove to subvert him, and still does with various temptations. And as for his local ruin, he fell from heaven where he was created into hell, or into the misty air which is in the middle, between the part near the earth and the upper part near the fire. Nor did God wish the demons to be in the upper part so that they would not enjoy much light: nor indeed in the lower part so that they would not be too close to harm us. Some say that the demons fell from heaven on the second day. But the opinion of those who write that they fell immediately after their creation is approved. It is believed that the tenth choir of angels fell: not because there were ten choirs, but so many fell from each choir that they could make a choir. There are nine choirs of angels: and each choir has its legions: and each legion has six thousand six hundred and sixty-six <note>original: "semila secen sexansci"</note> angels: And there are as many legions in each choir as there are angels in each legion. I could refer to both Augustine and Damascene <note>St. Augustine and St. John of Damascus.</note> and to other doctors many reasons by which they prove the sin of the devil to be unpardonable: But returning to those, we will say the demons are spirits, enemies of the human species, having a rational mind. Subtle in every iniquity: greedy to harm: puffed up with pride: always intent on fraud: they change the senses: They pollute the affections: They disturb those who are awake: They unsettle the sleeping in dreams: They induce diseases: They stir up storms. They transform themselves into good angels. They always carry their hell with them. In idols, they usurp divine power. Through them, the magical arts are performed. They lay ambushes for the good. They have in themselves a triple sharpness. For they have natural subtlety through evening knowledge <note>A Scholastic term referring to the knowledge angels have of things in their own created nature, as opposed to "morning knowledge" which is seeing things in God.</note>. They have the experience of long time. They have revelation from the superior spirits. And by the first way, they understand natural things present. By the second, the future. By the third, voluntary things. He is named Devil <note>original: "diabolo"</note> which in Greek signifies slanderer. He is named Belial, that is, without a yoke or without a lord: because he always resists him. He is named Demon from his knowledge: because in Greek it signifies to know. He is named Beelzebub <note>original: "Belzabu"</note>, that is, man of flies: that is, of sinful souls: which abandon Christ the true spouse. Likewise, Satan, that is, adversary. Likewise, Behemoth, that is, beast. Likewise, Leviathan, that is, the addition of those who accumulate sin upon sin. Lucifer was of the first order of the supreme hierarchy: and in that held the supreme rank, to whom as a prince many from all the choirs joined themselves: whom he pulled with him into ruin. He was blinded by the consideration of his own beauty. He tempted the first man, that is, Adam, and conquered him. He tempted the second, that is, Christ, and was conquered. The sin of Lucifer was that he loved his private good: And he was presumptuous of the highness received from God: as if he should have his excellence from himself and not from another. He desires the likeness of God, not to imitate Him: but to have power: He wanted to have subjects and not be subject to another. And it is fitting that, the demon being an incorporeal and rational substance, his punishment should be intellectual: And his torment proceeds especially from the place. Because just as the aquatic animal cannot stay without pain on land and out of the water: And the terrestrial animal in water: so the nature of the demon created in heaven, a place connatural to him, cannot inhabit without extreme pain in the center of the earth, the opposite; and

<header>CANTO XXXIV</header>

...contrary to heaven. These are devils obstinate in evil because, since the angel was created with his free will, justice requires that just as God confirmed the good angel in grace—he who chose the good—so He should confirm the wicked one in his evil purpose, he who by his own free will chose evil. Therefore, in that soul, he is obstinate.

Oh, how great a marvel it appeared to me
when I saw three faces on his head!
One was in front, and that one was crimson;
Of the other two, which joined with this one
above the middle of each shoulder,
and they joined at the top of the crest:
The right one seemed between white and yellow;
the left, to look upon, was such as those
who come from where the Nile descends.
Under each there came out two great wings,
of a size befitting such a bird;
sails of the sea I never saw such as these.
They had no feathers, but their fashion was
like a bat’s; and he was beating them
so that three winds moved from him;
By these Cocytus was all frozen.
With six eyes he wept, and over three chins
dripped the tears and bloody foam.

In every mouth he mangled with his teeth
a sinner, in the manner of a hemp-brake,
so that he made three of them thus sorrowful.
To the one in front, the biting was as nothing
compared to the scratching, for at times his back
remained entirely stripped of skin.
"That soul up there who has the greatest punishment,"
said the Master, "is Judas Iscariot,
who has his head inside and kicks his legs outside."

<column-break/>

It is a conclusion reached by all theologians that every vice proceeds from Lucifer. This is why the poet feigns him as being "crested"; and such a crest signifies Pride and her daughter, Envy. The three faces are the other three spiritual sins: Wrath, Avarice, and Sloth. The red face denotes Wrath, which is the "kindling of the blood"; therefore, he deservedly makes it red. The face between white and yellow is "sallow," and it denotes Avarice, because the miser diminishes his food so much that he is always thin and pale; he is also always in great fear of losing his acquired riches, which similarly makes him turn pale. The third face is black, by which Sloth is best understood, as it proceeds from the "melancholic humor," which is black. One who is slothful never rejoices, nor does his face ever brighten; he always remains in darkness. Each face has two eyes, and these represent two "disordered regards." In Wrath, the right eye is too much regard for one's own perceived good, and the left is too much regard for fleeing perceived evil. In Avarice, one eye is too much conservation of what is yours, and the other is too much seeking what belongs to others. Similarly, Sloth regards fleeing labor and taking rest.

The two wings are two "incitements and liftings." For Wrath has disturbance and fury, from which proceeds the wind of cruelty. Avarice has rapacity and tenacity, and from this comes the wind of ingratitude. Sloth has sadness and negligence, and from this is the wind of hate. These three winds—Cruelty, Ingratitude, and Hate—freeze Cocytus <note>The frozen lake at the center of Hell.</note> and extinguish Charity, Piety, and Conscience. The size of the wings signifies the excessive agitations of the mind. Each face has its own mouth because each of these vices devours and torments those who fall into it. The tears on the chin signify repentance at the end, occurring after the deed. **OF THE OTHER TWO which join with this one.** This denotes that the vices are linked and all join together, responding to the "crest"—that is, to Pride. **BETWEEN WHITE AND YELLOW**, meaning pale, for the reasons we gave in the allegory above. **SUCH AS those who come from where the Nile descends.** This means black, like the Ethiopians where the Nile descends into Egypt. **THEY HAD NO Feathers but like a bat.** They did not have the wings of a bird, but were like those of a bat. In Latin, this creature is called a <term>vespertilio</term> <note>original: "vespertello"</note> because it stays hidden during the day and begins to fly when "vesper" <note>evening</note> comes. Lucifer is therefore one of the birds that fly in the night, and "night" stands for ignorance. This denotes that our ignorance is what gives place to diabolical temptations; for this reason, we are warned to walk while we have light, so that darkness does not overtake us. **WITH SIX Eyes he wept**: because all those six excessive agitations repent after the sin is committed. **THROUGH THREE Chins the tears dripped.** By the chin, which is the lowest part of the face, understand the repentance that only comes at the end, after the sin is committed. **AND BLOODY FOAM**: Because in mangling the sinners, it is natural that blood would drip; and allegorically, we say that from pride proceed the most cruel killings.

**He mangled with his teeth a sinner in every mouth. In the manner** <note>original: "A guisa"</note>: in the form. **Of a hemp-brake** <note>original: "Di Maciulla"</note>: A <term>maciulla</term> (also called a <term>gramola</term>) is a wooden tool used to crush flax or hemp so that the outer husk—the part spun for cloth—separates from the hard inner stalk. **JUDAS Iscariot**: He who for thirty pieces of silver betrayed Christ to the Jews. Most ungratefully, this disciple—who had been raised to such a high rank—deceived his excellent Master, who had been most generous toward him. The creature deceived the Creator and led Him to an ignominious death.

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>INFERNO</header>

->Of the other two who have their heads below<-
->that one who hangs from the black snout is Brutus<-
->see how he writhes and says not a word<-
->And the other is Cassius, who seems so large-limbed<-
->but the night rises again, and now<-
->it is time to depart, for he has seen all.<-

<column-break/>

...of the cross, that which he <note>Referring to Christ.</note> desired to raise up to the highest heaven and establish in everlasting glory. He <note>Judas.</note> killed the one who had come to resurrect him and the others dead in sin. The most cruel servant killed his lord, in whom there was so much mercy that he would have even forgiven him if he had been moved to repentance. Therefore, one cannot imagine greater cruelty in the creature, nor greater clemency in the Creator. Of these two—

unheard-of wickedness and ineffable clemency—I do not speak at present, because I could not express as much with words as I conceive in my mind. But let us consider the most just judgment: that Lucifer—most ungrateful for such great privilege received from God—is worthy of the place and the penalty in which the poet places him for his greater punishment. He torments those who deserved no lesser executioner nor lesser henchman, so that the greatest of the sinners of heaven may punish the greatest of the sinners of earth; and so that the High God, through His enemies, may take just vengeance upon His enemies. **BRUTUS**: It was a fitting thing that just as Lucifer tormented Judas, the betrayer of the Divine Emperor, so he should also punish those who had betrayed the human emperor and monarch. Because by the common consensus of the Christian name, it is established that the Roman Emperor is the head of the <term>temporal administration</term> <note>The secular government of the world, as opposed to the spiritual rule of the Church.</note> of the entire Christian republic, just as the Pope is in the spiritual administration. He <note>Dante.</note> sets down Caesar first—not for the sake of Caesar himself, who, not being just, could not have been a just emperor, but for the sake of the Empire. And he does not place Brutus and Cassius there for who they were as individuals, but for those who kill the true monarch. Similarly, in *Purgatorio*, he places Cato—who according to our faith cannot be saved in any way—not for the soul of Cato, but for the sake of Liberty, of which he was the fiercest defender. And certainly, it would have been unheard-of cruelty and entirely foreign to the teaching and equity of such a great poet to place in eternal and so grave a punishment those who, out of most ardent charity, gave themselves to death to free their fatherland from the yoke of servitude. Had they been Christians, they would have acquired a most honored seat in the highest heaven. I do not deny that Caesar was adorned with many varied and most excellent virtues; but as soon as such a wild impiety was born in him that, in the hope of seizing tyranny, he crossed the Rubicon river, from an excellent man he became a most cruel beast. And with this single wickedness, he submerged and extinguished all the benefits for which Rome confessed herself his debtor. Therefore, Brutus and Cassius do not kill that Caesar who, with most laborious and decade-long toils and with horrendous difficulties and gravest dangers, acquired for the Roman people all of Gaul, all of Germany, and Britain (called by us England). They do not kill that Caesar who in ten years and in various battles killed with his victorious armies one million, one hundred and ninety-two thousand men who were enemies to the Roman name. They do not kill that Caesar in whom there was supreme liberality, unheard-of clemency, most ornate eloquence, and much varied learning. Rather, they kill the one who, most ungratefully, turned the forces he had received from his fatherland against it; the one who most wickedly took liberty from the one he ought to have defended. And certainly, what can be a greater virtue than to avenge the injuries of the fatherland, for which every good citizen is bound not to spare his property, nor his children, nor his own life? O excellent men, entirely worthy that Rome should be your fatherland, and of whom eternal memory shall always remain! Let all the laws of any well-instituted republic be read, and we shall find that no greater reward is proposed to anyone than to him who kills the tyrant. But someone might say that I am acting against my purpose by reproaching the poet in this place. I do not reproach him in any way; but I have wished to demonstrate his intended meaning, so that no one, through a false opinion, should think that he wishes to damn Brutus. For it is not difficult for me to believe that—just as Trajan <note>The Roman Emperor Trajan, whom legend says was saved from Hell by the prayers of Pope Gregory the Great.</note> moved Gregory to such compassion by his justice that he, through prayers, brought him back from damnation to supreme happiness—so some other person acceptable to God may have done the same for Brutus. **BUT THE NIGHT RISES AGAIN**: They consumed one night and part of the following day in searching through Hell. And deservedly so, since the night, which signifies ignorance, leads to vice; but he who must exit from it stays there during the day, because with the light of reason and learning, it is necessary to know the nature of vice, which knowledge makes us flee from it. In the beginning of the book, he said: "The day was departing"; and in Canto XX, he shows that the day is being born; and at present, that part of that day has passed. This passage has a similarity to the verses of Virgil: *Night rushes on, Aeneas; we spend the hours in weeping* <note>original: "Nox ruit Eneas nos flendo ducimus horas"</note>. I estimate, rethinking diligently this pilgrimage feigned by the poet, that they had already consumed in Hell the entire night at the beginning of which they made their entry, and part of the following day, for the reason I demonstrated a little above. And having arrived now at Lucifer, who is in the very center, Virgil admonishes Dante that it is well to exit from Hell, which is nothing other than passing the center. Having passed it, immediately that space of the day that remained to them in Hell (which is in our hemisphere) became night in that other hemisphere. And by that way, they went from the center to the surface where they found Cato; and then, as it became night here, the day began there. Because from the beginning of Hell to the beginning of the plain of Purgatory, they consumed one natural day of twenty-four hours. But because the day that came after the night was as much "day" to them as the time they were on this side of the center, and as much "night" as they consumed from the center to Cato, they therefore traveled one night, half a day, and half a night; although elsewhere we have posited two continuous nights without the interposition of day.

# CANTO XXXIV

As it pleased him, I clasped him round the neck,
and he took advantage of the time and place;
and when the wings were opened wide enough,
He laid hold of the shaggy flanks;
from tuft to tuft he then descended down
between the thick hair and the frozen crusts.
When we had reached the point where the thigh
turns exactly upon the thick of the haunches,
The guide, with labor and with great anguish,
Turned his head to where he had his legs,
and grappled the hair like a man who climbs,
so that I thought we were returning into Hell.
“Hold on tight, for by such stairs as these,”
said the master, panting like a weary man,
“must we depart from so much evil.”
Then he came out through the hole of a rock,
and placed me on the edge to sit;
then he turned his wary step toward me.

...rance <note>This appears to be a fragment of the word "ignorance" or perhaps a geographical reference from the previous page.</note>. HE EXITS through Lucifer’s hair: Because the consideration of Lucifer's deformity and the beauty in which he existed before draws our soul out of Hell. HAVING GONE OUT. According to the history, we understand that when Lucifer was cast from heaven and condemned to the center of the earth, it was necessary for him to pierce the rock that stood in the way so that he might pass through to the center. And allegorically, whoever is in Hell—which is the damnation of vices—has formed a habit of vice, such that he can be compared to a stone. HE PLACED ME TO SIT: before the soul entirely exits from Hell, reason must place the soul "to sit," that is, to steady the senses outside of it, and then proceed toward the light.

I raised my eyes and thought I would see
Lucifer as I had left him,
but I saw him with his legs held upward;
And if I then became perplexed,
let the common folk <note>The "gente grossa" refers to those uneducated in the sciences of the time, such as physics and geography.</note> think on it, who do not see
what that point was that I had passed.
“Rise up,” said the master, “on your feet;
the way is long and the road is difficult,
and already the sun returns to middle tierce.” <note>Middle tierce is approximately 7:30 AM.</note>

...so much so that reason shows him: that he must stand up, that is, turn himself toward desiring better things. And this is the recognition of divine things, to which one cannot go unless he first purges himself of the vices he has known. Therefore, the intellect shows him this: and further warns him that the way is long and difficult. Because to form a habit of moral virtue, having left the habit of vice, is very difficult. AND ALREADY THE SUN. Here he notes that in the other hemisphere it was night; this signifies that the sun had gone below. Therefore, it had risen in this other hemisphere and was returning to middle tierce. Thus, the rest of this day—which was night over there—they consumed until reaching Cato <note>Cato the Younger, the guardian of Purgatory.</note>. Nor is it without reason that they made that journey by night. For although we have already exited from vices, nonetheless, until we arrive at the purgatorial virtues, we are always in the darkness of ignorance.

It was no palace hallway <note>The original uses "caminata," a term for a large hall.</note>
there where we were, but a natural dungeon <note>term: natural burella. A "burella" was a narrow, dark passage or prison cell; Dante uses it to describe the rough, natural cavity leading away from the Earth's center.</note>
that had a bad floor and a lack of light.
“Before I pluck myself from the abyss,”
I said, my master, when I had stood up,
“to draw me out of error, speak to me a little:
Where is the ice? And how is this one fixed
so upside down? And how in so few hours
has the sun made its transit from evening to morning?”

<column-break/>

Virgil wanted Dante to cling to his neck and clasp him, that is, encircle him with his arms; and then, having waited for Lucifer to have his wings raised, he descended down his flanks, clinging to his tufts of hair. And so he descended feet-first until the beginning of Lucifer’s thigh. And having reached here, he turned himself, putting his head where he had his feet, to show that from here he had to ascend. Because he had passed the center, and had passed into the other hemisphere where it was necessary to climb by clinging to the hair of Lucifer's thighs and legs. Note that Lucifer, of whose stature we have spoken, is in the lowest part of the world, which is the center of the earth. But because the center is an indivisible point and is not capable of containing such a great body, it happens that his middle is at the center. And from the middle to the head, he remains in our hemisphere. Therefore, it was necessary for the poets, who were descending from the surface of the earth in our hemisphere, to descend through Lucifer's body until the middle, which was at the center. And then, having passed the center and wanting to mount to the other hemisphere, they climbed through the rest of the body to the feet. HOLD ON. It is necessary that the appetite and the lower reason cling to the superior reason. PANTING. This shows that even the superior reason labors and finds it difficult to exit from Hell and from ignorance.

Having exited the point that is the circumference <note>Referring to the center of gravity.</note>, one no longer goes further down but begins to ascend to the other hemisphere. Therefore, Lucifer held his navel at the center, and from the navel up he stood upright in the hemisphere where Hell was; and from the navel down he stood upright in the other hemisphere. Therefore, anyone who did not know the nature of the center and passed through it, departing from Lucifer’s head, would wonder why his legs were turned upward. And thus the common people can consider how much they would wonder. RISE UP on your feet. Since Dante—that is, the senses and the appetite—has exited from the depth of Hell, which is the habit of vice, it is necessary that he sit and rest a while and no longer follow his appetites until reason shows him the way.

Palace hallway. In Lombardy, halls are called "caminate." Therefore, it was no palace hall, because the halls of palaces are usually level and bright, while that way was dark and uneven. It was dark because, from the beginning, the way of virtue is unknown to those who in the past have been in vice; and it is very difficult. But "natural burella": burella signifies a narrow and dark place. Thus, in Florence, a narrow street not far from the Praetor'ary palace <note>The Bargello.</note> is called "Burella." IT HAD A BAD FLOOR: because it was uneven and wandering and treacherous. WHERE IS THE ICE: to Dante it seemed he had returned to our hemisphere from which he had descended, rather than having ascended to the other. And this error was caused...

# INFERNO

...wondering that, having been shortly before in the evening hour, he now found himself in the morning; and having seen Lucifer with his head upward, he now saw him with his legs upward.

And he to me: "You imagine you are still
on the other side of the center, where I grasped
the hair of the wicked worm that pierces the world.
You were on that side as long as I descended;
when I turned myself, you passed the point
to which weights are drawn from every part.
And you are now arrived beneath the hemisphere
which is opposite that which the wide dry land
covers, and beneath whose summit was consumed
The Man who was born and lived without sin.
You have your feet upon a little sphere
that forms the other face of the Giudecca.
Here it is morning when it is evening there;
and he who made us a ladder with his hair
is still fixed just as he was before.
On this side he fell down from heaven;
and the land, which before stood out here,
for fear of him made a veil of the sea,
And came to our hemisphere; and perhaps
to flee from him, that land which appears on this side
left this place empty and rushed back upward."
There is a place below, as far removed from Beelzebub
as his tomb extends,
which is known not by sight, but by the sound
Of a little stream that descends here
through the hollow of a rock which it has worn
with a course that winds about and slopes but little.
The guide and I, by that hidden path,
entered to return to the bright world;
and without caring to have any rest,
We climbed up, he first and I second,
until I saw the beautiful things
that Heaven bears, through a round opening,
And thence we came forth to see again the stars.

<column-break/>

**You imagine you are still on the other side.** He calls "that side" our hemisphere: because he imagines, as you have seen, being in the one that is opposite to us. **OF THE Worm that pierces the world** as we said above <note>Dante refers to Lucifer as a "worm" (vermo) to emphasize his loathsome, soul-devouring nature, contrasting his current state with his former angelic beauty.</note>. **You were on that side** while I descended as far as the thighs. But when I turned myself there and put my head where I had my feet, I passed the center or point which, in a spherical body, is equally distant from every surface and comes to be at the lowest point. And because the nature of heavy things is to go downward, all weights are drawn to that point, and heavy things from every part of the circumference come there. **AND IF you are now arrived beneath the hemisphere.** You are not in the hemisphere that covers the land inhabited by men: **WHERE The man was born without sin** and lived without sin: and he means Christ, who was "consumed," that is, died to redeem us; and tacitly he signifies that He was crucified in our hemisphere and in Jerusalem, and not in the other hemisphere as Origen heretically writes <note>Landino is defending the orthodox geography of the time, placing Jerusalem at the center of the inhabited world and refuting the idea that Christ's sacrifice happened elsewhere.</note>. And he denotes Jerusalem, which is almost the middle of the earth. **YOU HAVE your feet upon a little sphere.** He means that the place where Dante was is the small circle around the center on that hemisphere, corresponding to the circle that in our hemisphere forms the **Giudecca** <note>The Giudecca is the fourth and final zone of the ninth circle of Hell, named after Judas Iscariot, where traitors to their lords and benefactors are punished.</note>. **Here it is morning when it is evening there:** You should not, therefore, marvel if at present you see the sun in the east, whereas a little while ago you saw it in the west: because having passed the center, you are in the opposite hemisphere. For when it is six o'clock under us, it begins to rise in the other hemisphere. **FIXED** in the ice or in the rock as he was before; he has not changed state. But you have changed place: and for having passed the center, you are now "above." **THERE IS A PLACE below:** He shows that from the center where **Beelzebub** (that is, Lucifer) is, to the surface of the other hemisphere, there is as much space as the "tomb" extends. He calls Hell the "tomb" because it is the eternal sepulcher of the damned. Therefore, because Hell is from the surface of our earth down to the center, it remains that the same space exists from the center where Beelzebub is to the surface of the other hemisphere where Cato is <note>Cato the Younger is the guardian of the shores of Purgatory, located in the Southern Hemisphere.</note>. But this place is not known by sight because it is dark, but by sound: because by the echo of the river that falls there, one imagines the distance. **Of a little stream.** This is the one which, in Canto XIV, he imagined comes into the world and goes into Hell. And from this are born Acheron, Styx, and Phlegethon; and then it descends into the center of the earth and enters the bottom of the pit of this place which the author imagines here, and forms Cocytus, which freezes by the wings of Lucifer. This little stream comes up from the world and from the other infernal rivers that it creates, and descends into the pit. **Through the hollow of a rock which is worn.** By the course that is there: that is, it winds around that rock because it descends turning through the circles of Hell, and sometimes crossing through as shown above. But here it turned around the pit somewhat and sloped little: because it fell only slightly from on high. **HIDDEN PATH:** dark because of the shadows. They returned to the bright world without caring to rest. He says this because, without intermission, having recognized our vices, we must go toward the purgatorial virtues. **To see again the stars.** To see the sky again. Because he who departs from Hell (that is, from vices) returns to see the stars (that is, he departs from the bestial life and returns to the human life), which is led to contemplate celestial things. Now, by the grace of God, the author returns from Hell, and here he describes the place from which he exited and the manner of exiting. **THERE IS A PLACE below:** beyond the center. **REMOVED from Beelzebub:** distanced from Lucifer. **AS FAR as the tomb extends.** He calls "tomb" the vacuum he has placed around Lucifer: that is, the ninth circle, already called by him a "pit," which goes to the bottom and the bank of which he made of giants, and inside he put the traitors. Now he shows this pit to be round: and there was just as much in that hemisphere to which they had to climb as in ours, from which they had descended to Lucifer. They went up, therefore, through this tomb to the surface and there they exited through a round hole onto an island surrounded by the ocean; and in that he places a very high mountain, in which, level by level, Purgatory is found; and at the summit is the earthly paradise (*paradisus delitiarum*).

### PROLOGUE OF CRISTOFORO LANDINO, THE FLORENTINE, IN HIS COMMENTARY ON THE DIVINE POET DANTE ALIGHIERI UPON THE PURGATORIO, THE SECOND CANTICLE

<image-desc>The page features a lavishly illuminated left margin border consisting of colorful foliate scrolls, flowers, and gold leaf accents. It delights me, and it delights me exceedingly, O Lord Jesus <note>Original: "I. S. N.", likely abbreviating *Iesu Servatori Nostro* (To Jesus our Savior).</note>, that in this part of the work we have emerged from the outer darkness, where we have seen inconsolable weeping. And through the cold of the northern wind, stirred by the eternal movement of Beelzebub’s wings, we have heard the gnashing of teeth. I hope this has frightened our minds with such terror that we shall never return there. May it please you thus, O omnipotent Jupiter, supreme ruler of Olympus <note>As a Renaissance humanist, Landino frequently uses classical names like 'Jupiter' and 'Olympus' to refer to the Christian God and Heaven.</note>, who—being Three and One with your supreme power, infinite wisdom, and unspeakable love—will provide your light to those traveling through the darkness, so they may be led to where every slave becomes free. And after regaining liberty, recalled from most unhappy exile by the right of return <note>Original: "iure post liminii", a Roman legal term referring to the restoration of rights to a person returning from captivity or exile.</note> and restored to his sweetest homeland, which is the heavenly city of Jerusalem. There we are neither pilgrims nor foreigners, but citizens among the saints, and members of the household, family, and ennobled courtiers of the King whom all Kings serve, and by serving whom they reign. Whose kingdom, just as it was without beginning, so shall it be without end. There we shall rest in the life that is without death; where for all ages of ages we shall be fed with ambrosia and nectar, which is the unique bread and unique wine of all the angelic hierarchies. Grant, I pray you, O supreme giver of all good things, grant to the human generation—which you made in your image and likeness, not for its pain, but so there would be those to succeed to the seats which the angels, once most beautiful and then lost through most foolish pride—grant, I pray, to all men and particularly to the Florentine people, the grace that they may say:

> The Lord looked down from heaven upon the earth. <note>Original Latin: "Dominus de celo in terram aspexit."</note>

From the depths we cry to you, O Lord; Lord, hear our voice. Let your ears be attentive to the voice of our supplication. <note>Original Latin: "Noi de profundis ad te clamamus..." referring to Psalm 130.</note> Extend to us a staff that may sustain our weak and wavering steps, so that we do not ruin ourselves below. Remember what David, moved by your divine fury, sings in the psalm:

> The dead shall not praise you, O Lord, nor all those who go down into hell. But we who live bless you. <note>Original Latin: "Non mortui laudabunt te domine..." referring to Psalm 115.</note>

It is not the damned, Lord—who truly can be called dead—nor those who through such damnation fall into hell, who will praise you. But we who live—either by the true life, being confirmed in the habit of virtue, or at least living because there still remains to us free will to take the path to the right hand—we bless you. Provide light to those who walk through the shadow of death, and direct our feet into the way of peace. And to me, in this interpretation, grant help and form, so that my labor may not be in vain, but may bring praise to your name and some utility to whoever shall read it.

> I am poor and needy. <note>Original Latin: "Pauper et egenus sum ego."</note>

But you, giver of all good things:

> Have mercy on me, O God, and bless me, and shine your countenance upon me, and have mercy on me: <note>Original Latin: "Miserere mei deus et benedic mihi..." combining elements of Psalms 51 and 67.</note>

Under such great hope, I shall begin the interpretation of this second canticle. And because we must treat of Purgatory, we shall say, according to the truest opinion of the theologians, that there are three things we must consider in this place. The first: if there is a Purgatory after this life. The second: who those are who go to Purgatory. The third: if there is any certain place in which souls are purged. To the first, I say that Holy Scripture, many authorities of the saints, and various revelations establish Purgatory. And the Holy Church affirms it, especially with Christ saying through Matthew:

> Whoever speaks a word against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, neither in this world nor in the world to come. <note>Original Latin: "Qui dixerit uerbum contra spiritum sanctum..." (Matthew 12:32). Landino argues that "forgiveness in the world to come" implies a place of purification like Purgatory.</note>

Therefore, Christ demonstrates that in the other life some sins are purged and forgiven. And Gregory demonstrates that in the other life there are certain faults which fire purges. Nor do only Christians establish Purgatory, but also Plato, who holds that the soul, once separated from the body, if it is defiled and stained with most grave and nefarious wickednesses, remains in eternal punishments. But if the sins are less grave, it is purged and then returns to other bodies. And Virgil, in the sixth book [of the *Aeneid*], says in the same vein:

> Until a long day, when the cycle of time is complete, has removed the ingrained stain, and left the ethereal sense pure, and the fire of simple air. <note>Original Latin: "Donec longa dies perfecto temporis orbe..." from Aeneid VI, 745-747.</note>

And let this suffice to demonstrate that Purgatory exists. But wishing to understand where it is located according to the Christian religion: it is the opinion of Richard of Middleton <note>Original: "Riccardo de media uilla", a 13th-century Franciscan theologian.</note> that there are four places beneath the earth. In the lowest part, which is the center of the earth, is where the damned stay in perpetual pain for actual sin. And above this part are those damned for original sin. The first of these two, which is the lowest and near the center, is the true Hell; the second is Limbo. There follows the third place, located above Limbo, called Purgatory, where souls are purged by common law—although some are purged elsewhere for some special reason, which is either to reveal something to help the living or to implore help from them. Then, in the highest part near the surface, which is the fourth from the center and the first from the circumference, there are currently no souls; but before our redemption, accomplished through the passion and death of Christ, the souls of the Holy Fathers stayed there once they had completed their purification in Purgatory. And also those who had departed from their own bodies without a stain that required purging. And this place was named the Bosom of Abraham, because he was the...

Landino defines the physical and spiritual geography of the afterlife, placing Purgatory above Hell and Limbo but beneath the surface of the earth.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s prologue to the Purgatorio. <header>PURGATORIO</header>

the first who separated himself from the infidels and took the distinctive sign of faith. Therefore, the place that was given for the rest of the soul, for faith formed in charity, was for the aforementioned reason called the **Bosom of Abraham** <note>Original: *seno dabraham*. In medieval theology, this was the place where the righteous of the Old Testament rested until the Harrowing of Hell.</note>. Nevertheless, **Hugh of Saint Victor** <note>Hugh of Saint Victor (c. 1096–1141) was a prominent mystic and philosopher; Landino refers to him here as "Vgo dasan uictore."</note> maintains that no common place is assigned to such souls who have to be purged, as it seems more probable to him that each is purged in the place where they committed their crime. But the Doctors <note>The "Doctors" refers to the established authorities of the Church and scholastic theologians.</note> do not approve of this opinion except in special cases by divine dispensation, and not as a common law for everyone.

To **Purgatory** go those who have remained in **venial sins** <term>venial sins: less serious offenses that do not deprive the soul of divine grace but require purification.</term>. A second group are those who did not perform **penance** <term>penance: an act of devotion or self-punishment performed to show sorrow for sin.</term> before death, as happens to those who die without confession and yet are repentant and contrite. A third group are those who did not fulfill the penance imposed upon them by the priest. The penance given to us by the priest is either greater, lesser, or equal [to the sin]. If it is greater than what the man has done in life, the excess redounds and returns to his glory. If it is equal, that alone suffices for full satisfaction. If it is lesser, that which is lacking is fulfilled in Purgatory by divine justice.

See, therefore, what in summary the Christians say of Purgatory. But **Dante**, a man of admirable genius and admirable invention, found a new site which is in no way substantially against Christian opinion. And it serves several purposes, as we demonstrated in the third canto of the *Inferno*. He posits, then, that the earth which **Lucifer** and his followers pushed from our hemisphere rose in the other hemisphere and created a most high mountain reaching up to the element of fire <note>According to the science of the time, the "element of fire" was a literal sphere of flame located between the Earth's atmosphere and the Moon.</note>. And in that place is situated Purgatory, divided into various **circles** <note>Original: *gyroni*. Landino uses this term for the terraces of the mountain.</note>. In the first ones, various types of negligence are purged. After those, in the following ones, each soul purges its own sin. But the lower ones always purge the more serious crimes.

This mountain, then, remains to be climbed—an ascent that is, without fail, harsh and hard, full of labor and sweat. But let us set out on the path with a bold spirit. Nor should we despair of being able to reach the summit, because where our own strength fails, divine grace will copiously supply the rest. And He who sustained us in our descent to the bottom, so that we did not fall to ruin, will now push us upward until we find the summit.
