# PURGATORY, THE SECOND CANTICLE OF THE DIVINE POET DANTE ALIGHIERI: AND THE FIRST CANTO

->**TO RUN**<-
->**THROUGH**<-
->**BETTER**<-
->**WATERS**<-
->**LIFTS**<-
->**ITS SAILS**<-
now the little vessel of my genius,
which leaves behind it a sea so cruel;
And I will sing of that second kingdom
where the human spirit is purged
and becomes worthy of ascending to heaven.

<column-break/>

Our author, well-instructed and learned in the poetic art, divides this second canticle of his—following the imitation of **Virgil** <note>Publius Vergilius Maro (70–19 BCE), Dante’s guide and primary literary model.</note>, **Ovid**, **Statius**, and other heroic Latin poets—into three parts: the **proposition**, the **invocation**, and the **narration**. The first two, the proposition and invocation, serve as the **proem** <term>proem: a formal introduction or preface to a poem.</term>. And because the specific duty of a proem is to make the listener fit and ready to hear, we will easily achieve this if we make the reader **well-disposed**, **attentive**, and **teachable**.

He gains **goodwill** <note>original: *benivolentia*</note> from the subject matter by promising to sing of Purgatory—a thing most excellent for human souls, as it is the only means by which they can reach divine knowledge, in which the highest good consists. He also gains goodwill through his own person, showing that he labors to write what is not only useful but necessary for the mortal generation. Furthermore, he makes the listener **attentive** through the greatness of the matter; for we listen with the greatest attention to things that are either grand or unusual, and especially if they pertain to the world at large, to ourselves in particular, or to our kin and friends. Nor does he move our attention only slightly by his manner of speaking. By using **metaphor** <term>metaphor: Landino uses the term "translatione," the standard Renaissance term for carrying a word's meaning from its literal sense to a figurative one.</term> rather than literal words, he increases the dignity and authority of the subject, as we see in Virgil and many other poets, both Greek and Latin. Nor is it only poets, but orators too who adorn their style with this "color," the power of which we will demonstrate shortly.

He makes the listener **teachable** <note>original: *docile*. In Renaissance rhetoric, this means "ready and able to learn the subject."</note>—that is, ready to understand what must be treated. This happens whenever we propose and explain in brief words what will be discussed in the whole work, as he does here by promising to treat Purgatory. But understand, reader, that although goodwill, attention, and teachability are distinct things, nevertheless one helps to achieve the other. For he who becomes well-disposed makes himself attentive. And he who stands attentive to hear the beginning easily becomes teachable. Often, the writer acquires goodwill, attention, and teachability in a single phrase, as in this verse: **AND I WILL SING of that second kingdom WHERE the human spirit is purged.** Because such a proposition is useful, it creates goodwill; because it is a grand thing, it creates attention; and because it explains what he intends to narrate, it creates teachability.

**TO RUN THROUGH BETTER WATERS** is the sentence that raises up his genius to speak of better subject matter than what he has spoken of until now. But he pronounces this sentiment not through literal words, but through **metaphor** <note>original: *traslatione*</note>. To better demonstrate this rhetorical ornament, let us say that all the words we use are either "proper" or "translated." **Proper words** are those found by use or reason to express the subject underlying such words, as when he says: *In the time when Juno was enraged* <note>Dante quotes his own Inferno, Canto XXX.</note>. For "time," "was," "Juno," and "enraged" are proper words for those things the poet wished to express. But these proper words are sometimes in common use and worn and customary for everyone, as when we say: "I greatly rejoice in your honor," and "often I praise your many and varied virtues." Sometimes they are ancient, almost falling out of all custom, such as *guari* and *fovente* <note>Archaic Italian terms for "much" and "frequently."</note>, both of which are Florentine but no longer in use. Thus our **Giovanni Boccaccio** <note>Famous 14th-century Italian author of the *Decameron*.</note> said "not *guari* far off," meaning "not very far." This was in use then, but today it is not. Sometimes they are new and fabricated by the author himself, as when Dante says: *s’io m’intuassi come tu t’inmii* <note>Dante, Paradiso IX: "If I could 'in-thee' myself as thou 'in-me'st' thyself"—Dante's invented verbs for total spiritual empathy.</note>. For before Dante, no one in the Florentine language said "to in-thee" or "to in-me."

**Translated words** <note>metaphors</note> are when we transfer words from their proper meaning into another meaning not unlike the proper one, as the poet says here: **The little vessel of my genius.** For just as a ship carries a man across the sea to the desired port, so the will carries the genius and our mind to the knowledge of the thing we desire to know. Nor does the learned writer ever use a metaphor without persevering in that metaphor throughout the whole sentence. Therefore, having said "little vessel" in this place, he said "water," because we use the ship in water; he said "sails," because without sails the ship does not go. **Quintilian** <note>A famous Roman rhetorician (c. 35–100 CE).</note> places this "color," which we call translation and the Greeks call **Metaphor**, above all other ornaments. This metaphor is granted to us so much by nature that often unlearned men use it without noticing. We use it either for brevity, as when we say "the flood of the Goths which submerged Italy," or to avoid words that are not decent, as when we say "whose wife delighted in daily..."

<summary>This page marks the beginning of Dante’s Purgatorio, featuring the iconic opening metaphor of the "little vessel of genius." Landino’s commentary provides a masterclass in Renaissance rhetoric, explaining how the proem is designed to capture the reader's interest and defining the nature of metaphorical language.</summary>

<keywords>Dante Alighieri, Purgatory, Canto I, Cristoforo Landino, proem, rhetoric, metaphor, translatione, Boccaccio, Quintilian, poetic structure, Florence, Renaissance education</keywords>

--- Page 342 ---
<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on the opening lines of Purgatorio, Canto I. He moves from the general purpose of the proem to a detailed allegorical analysis of Dante’s metaphors, particularly the "little vessel" and the "cruel sea," before transitioning into a lengthy philosophical digression on the Platonic classification of virtues.</meta>

...nor for marriage: either to increase or to diminish, or to adorn. But returning to the text, we shall say: *The little vessel of my genius now raises its sails to run*, that is, to navigate, *better waters*. He uses "little vessel" to represent the will, as we said in the previous canticle <note>referring to the Inferno</note>; for it is the will that transports the soul. In our allegorical explanation, we treat the will and several other powers and virtues of the human soul as distinct entities.

**BETTER WATERS.** This signifies better subject matter. In terms of allegory, Hell is "good" matter—that is, the contemplation of vices—because the study of them induces hatred toward them and a desire to flee them. But Purgatory is "better" matter because, once vices are known, we begin to purge ourselves of them. I shall strive to explain this more clearly at a more appropriate time; certainly, one cannot, nor is it fitting, to crowd too many things into a single place, as it would result in neither order nor clarity.

**THE SAILS.** We likewise discussed these when the subject matter required an allegorical explanation of navigation.

**A SEA SO CRUEL.** Although the consideration of vice is good, as we have said, vice itself is the most cruel thing there is, because it kills the soul, which nothing else can kill. Nor did he use the word "sea" unlearnedly; for as we said in our commentaries on Virgil <note>Landino published a famous commentary on Virgil in 1488, connecting the Aeneid to Platonic philosophy</note>, every appetite is like a sea. None is more cruel, nor tossed by more contrary winds, than that which leads to vice. For not only is the one who goes to Hell—that is, into the habit of vice—submerged by turbulent storms in such a sea, but even the one who goes there to contemplate the nature of vice is often buffeted by the allurements of various pleasures, and barely escapes the dangerous reefs and hidden shoals of that sea.

**AND I WILL SING:** He makes the listener teachable by briefly describing what he intends to treat throughout the entire work.

**THE SECOND KINGDOM:** Because the first stage is knowing vice; the second is purging oneself of it.

**WHERE THE HUMAN SPIRIT** is purged. He most excellently said "human," because above man there is no spirit that needs purging. Since the angels who did not sin are confirmed in grace and remain pure, there is no need for them to be purged. And below man, there is no animal that possesses an immortal soul. Therefore, when the sensory soul dies along with the body, nothing remains that can be purged.

**AND TO ASCEND TO HEAVEN** becomes worthy. For the soul can finally ascend to the contemplation and knowledge of divine things only when it is purged of vices. Whence: *Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God* <note>original: "Beati mundo corde quoniam ipsi deum videbunt" (Matthew 5:8).</note>. But because there is no stain that can make the soul filthy and ugly except vice, and nothing removes vice except virtue, it is not only useful but necessary for a better understanding to briefly state that the **moral virtues** are divided, according to the Platonists, into four types: **Civil**, **Purgatory**, **Of the Purged Soul**, and **Exemplary**.

**Civil virtues** belong to man because he is an animal born not to be solitary, but to live in congregation and company. From this, cities arise; man uses these virtues to administer the republic. Through **Prudence**, he investigates what is useful; through **Justice**, by distributing honors and duties equally, he preserves union and concord. Through **Fortitude**, he makes his soul bold and unconquered in enduring every labor and danger to defend the fatherland. And through **Temperance**, he desires nothing of which he might later repent, overstepping neither measure nor law. But these virtues are not perfect in the civil and active life, for men who persist in that life alone do not possess true wisdom.

After the civil virtues follow the **Purgatory virtues**. These are not found in civil life but belong to those few men who are capable of divine things. Such virtues speed and liberate the soul of one who is disposed to purge himself from the contagion of the body, giving himself entirely to divine things and fleeing human ones. This is to not labor with **Martha**, but to give oneself entirely to **Mary** <note>A common medieval trope: Martha represents the active life of service, while Mary represents the contemplative life of prayer and study (Luke 10:38–42).</note>; that is, to leave the active life entirely and follow the contemplative life.

Beyond these purgatory virtues are those **Of the Purged Soul**, which has remained without any stain. In this state, the office of **Prudence** is not to prefer divine things to human ones (as the purgatory virtues do), but to choose only the divine as if nothing else existed, and to look at those alone. The office of **Temperance** is not to restrain desires, but to forget them entirely. The office of **Fortitude** is not to overcome the fear of horrific things, but to not even know what fear is. And finally, they use **Justice** to join themselves with the divine mind in such a way that they never depart from it.

The fourth type are the **Exemplary virtues**, which belong to God alone. For since the Platonists place the **Ideas** <term>Ideas: in Platonic thought, the eternal, perfect patterns of all things existing in the divine mind.</term> of all things in the divine mind, the Idea of virtue will be there to a much greater degree. There, then, **Prudence** is nothing other than the divine mind itself. **Temperance** is that mind turning toward itself with perpetual intention. **Fortitude** is that it is always the same and never changes. **Justice** is that it never moves nor swerves from the eternal continuation of its work by eternal law. These are the four generations of moral virtues; although they are all directed against the passions and perturbations of the soul, they are nonetheless different in themselves. For the first type does not entirely remove the passions, but mitigates them; the second removes them; the third forgets them. In the fourth, it is a wicked thing even to name them. I have therefore treated them at length so that the reader, encountering them in many other places, may refer back here.

**DEAD POETRY:** As if to say: "I pray you, holy Muses, that you inspire in me the poetic faculty, which for a long time has been..."

<column-break/>

...dead air. This is because, for many centuries before Dante, Italy had been prey to various generations of barbarians, and afflicted and oppressed by so many wars and tumults that every liberal art had lain dormant. He was among the first who attempted to draw this faculty called poetry out of the darkness. And how much progress he made, we strive to express in his biography. His present poem clearly manifests it: this is therefore the reason that led him to say, **BUT HERE LET DEAD** poetry rise again. Or truly, he wishes that dead poetry should rise as if from the underworld: for until now we have treated the Inferno, where everything is dead. But in what follows, we shall treat Purgatory, through which the soul is resurrected. And certainly, the soul that was dead through vice is resurrected through purgation. **O HOLY MUSES**: we spoke sufficiently of the Muses in the second canto of the Inferno. Therefore, it would be superfluous at present to repeat what we have already written. **SINCE I AM** yours. Because I am a poet, and poets are dedicated to the Muses, being their priests. Whence Virgil says: <note>original: "Me vero in primis placeant ante omnia musae: quarum sacra fero." — "Truly, let the Muses please me first of all, whose sacred symbols I bear." (Georgics 2.475)</note> And he makes his petition honest by saying: because honesty requires that the Muses favor those who are their own. **AND HERE** let Calliope rise somewhat, let her lift herself up: as if to say that since this is higher subject matter, a higher style is fitting. And certainly, for one who provides attentive ears, it is easy to recognize that the style he uses in the Inferno is almost the lowest. For one beginning is **IN THE MIDST** of the journey of our life. Another is *to run through better waters he raises the sails*; and he says "somewhat" because he will rise even higher in the canticle of Paradise. And by name among the Muses he invokes Calliope: because she is the most excellent among them, and her name signifies "good voice." And he who invokes her invokes all the others. Whence Virgil said: <note>original: "Vos o calliope precor aspirate canenti." — "O Calliope, I pray you, breathe upon the singer." (Aeneid 9.525)</note> **FOLLOWING** my song. Because he does not begin his work with Purgatory, but follows after the Inferno. Therefore, let Calliope rise as if to elevate the style and make it more sonorous, following my work. **WITH THAT SOUND**, with that voice by which—from which. **THE WRETCHED MAGPIES**: that is, the wretched daughters of Pierus <note>In Greek mythology, the Pierides challenged the Muses to a singing contest and were transformed into magpies (piche) as punishment for their hubris.</note> were converted into magpies; and this is the "blow" which they felt from the voice of Calliope. These were nine daughters of Pierus from the city of Pella, certainly learned in many arts. But they were so proud of their glory that they esteemed the Muses as nothing. And they presumed to precede them in everything, and especially in song. Nor were they content not to go to Parnassus to find them, near the Pegasean spring, and there with villainous words provoke them to sing. The task was given to Calliope, who won by a long margin, and converted them into magpies. This is a talkative bird and easily learns human speech. *Pica* in Latin means the jay, and also the magpie. But Pliny calls this one in the book of Natural History *pica caudata* because it has a long tail. The meaning is therefore: Let Calliope rise here, following my song with such a voice as that with which she defeated the magpies, which had to be sonorous and excellent. Otherwise, she would not have won. And by this he shows his petition to be easy: by the magpies who provoked the Muses, we shall understand every rash person who presumes to be able to conquer or be equal to the Muses—that is, to divine doctrines.

After the proposition and the invocation, already completed and finished by the poet, the narration begins. And he wishes his beginning to describe the time and the quality of the time in which he emerged from the Inferno into the other hemisphere opposite to ours, where the mountain of Purgatory is. And the meaning is that when he emerged into 그 hemisphere, the sun was not yet born, but it was not very far from its birth. For Venus already appeared in the East, which, because she was in Pisces and the sun was in Aries—neighboring signs with a small interval—rose before the sun. Furthermore, he shows that at that time the air was most pure, and full of serenity and tranquility. Therefore, the color of the air—which was such as that of oriental sapphire—restored delight to my eyes. **SWEET COLOR**, suave and delightful color. And although sweetness is properly in the taste, nonetheless every other thing that delights any other sense is called sweet. Whence Petrarch: "And how sweetly she speaks and sweetly she laughs." And Horace: <note>original: "dulce ridentem lalagen amabo dulce loquentem" — "I will love Lalage who laughs sweetly and speaks sweetly." (Odes 1.22.23)</note> **OF ORIENTAL SAPPHIRE**. Pliny shows that there are Sapphires of purple color and of azure color; of which the poet makes mention in this place, and says that the azure ones are called male Sapphires. **WHICH WAS GATHERED** in the serene aspect. Because if the air were not serene, it would not be azure. And the poet takes great pains to show that the air in that place was pure and clear, and contrary to the cloudy air of the Inferno. For just as vice generates obscurity, so the purgation of vice induces serenity. **OF THE PURE AIR** even to the first circle: even to the first sphere, which is the heaven of the moon, from which downward mutable things begin. Therefore, the serene color of the air restored delight to my eyes: for Dante had such delight before...

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s line-by-line commentary on the first Canto of Purgatorio. Having established the general themes of the poem, he now shifts to the specific astronomical and allegorical conditions of Dante's arrival on the shores of Purgatory, specifically the presence of Venus in the constellation of Pisces and the appearance of the "four stars" near the South Pole.</meta>

# PURGATORY

...he entered into Hell while being in the clear air. Then, entering the infernal shadows, he lost it. Now, having come out of it again, it returns to him. And although he appears to speak of the delight of the physical eyes, nonetheless allegorically he means the spiritual ones. The eyes take delight in bright and beautiful things, and the beauty of a thing is good proportion with suitable color. Therefore, just as the physical eyes take delight in physical beauty and sensible light, so the eyes of the mind greatly delight in its own light, which is **REASON**, and its beauty, which is **VIRTUE**. Whence Plato writes that if we could see the beauty of virtue with the eyes of the mind as we see the beauty of the body with physical eyes, the love that would inflame us for them would be incredible and most ardent.

**THE EYES**: that is, the sense of sight, and **THE BREAST**, the mind. **THE BEAUTIFUL PLANET** that encourages love: The star of Venus. He says, therefore, that it was the morning time and not long before day, because the sun was in Aries: which sign begins to rise after Pisces has completely left the horizon. Therefore, a good part of the sign of Pisces having already risen, Venus was seen, which was in that sign. And we showed in the first canto of the first canticle <note>Inferno</note> that Virgil is imitated in this. And just as that poet posits that Aeneas had Venus—not the earthly but the celestial—as his guide and leader, so both in that place and in this, Dante shows that celestial Venus leads him. Therefore, return to that place, and you will fully understand the allegory that is appropriate here.

Furthermore, know that Pisces is the house of Jupiter, which planet induces chastity, justice, and religion. Thus, Venus in this sign will be celestial and not earthly. Moreover, she will be powerful in inflaming us toward divine things, because she has her exaltation in this sign. According to Isidore <note>St. Isidore of Seville, an influential medieval encyclopedist</note>, it is called the sign of Pisces because when the sun comes to such a sign, through the dissolution that it causes in the moisture by its heat, the fish scatter their seed and generate. Macrobius—who wants the names of all the signs to be reduced to the nature of the sun—writes that they are called "Fishes" to denote that not only terrestrial and aerial animals, but also all those that inhabit the water [are affected].

The poets, according to Nigidius <note>Nigidius Figulus, a Roman scholar</note>, say that in the Euphrates River of Assyria, a very large egg was found, which two fish pushed to the shore. And doves incubated it, and from it was born the Goddess of Syria, whom they call Venus. She is very religious toward the gods and supremely merciful and dutiful toward men. She was the inventor of many arts and other things useful to human life. Hearing this from Mercury, Jupiter allowed her to ask for whatever grace she wished. The goddess asked that he make the two fish immortal, as they had preserved her generation. Jupiter translated them into this last sign of the Zodiac. But one of the fish is northern and the other southern, and they have their tails turned against one another. And between them is a bond that holds them together as far as the feet of Andromeda. The northern fish has twelve stars; the southern one, fifteen. The bond has twelve stars, so that in total there are thirty-nine. Because of this benefit, the Syrians do not eat fish and they worship doves as gods. Thus, even according to this fable, Venus will be well placed in Pisces.

**VEILED** Covered. Because whoever looks up from the earth finds Venus first with their eyes in the third heaven, and then Pisces in the eighth. Whence it is necessary that with her body she takes away some part of the Fishes. Or truly he says "Veiled" to denote that the splendor of this star is so great that it obscures and makes those around it disappear.

> I turned to my right hand and set my mind
> on the other pole: and I saw four stars
> never seen except by the first people:
> The heavens seemed to rejoice in their flames:
> Oh, widowed northern site,
> since you are deprived of looking at those.

<column-break/>

Because in the layout of the world the East is the front part, it happens that whoever turns toward it has the North to the left and the South to the right. And because just as the Arctic pole is in the North and is seen by us, so the Antarctic pole is beyond the South and is seen by those of the other hemisphere, where the poet imagines Purgatory to be. Therefore, turning from the East toward the South, where the Antarctic pole is, he turned to the 

<column-break/>

right hand. **TO THE OTHER** pole: not to ours, but to the one opposite ours. **AND I SAW** four stars never seen except by the first people. **Pole** in Greek <note>original: *polos*</note> signifies the supreme part of heaven upon which the heaven itself turns. For instance, if you took a physical sphere and stuck a rod through the middle, which from one surface of the sphere, arriving at the center in a straight line, passed to the other surface: those two parts that are close to both holes where the rod is placed are called "poles," because the sphere turns upon them. And "to turn" in Greek is *polin*. And in Latin they are called *vertices* [peaks/turning points], because *verto* in Latin is what I call "to turn" <note>original: *volgo*</note> in Tuscan. Whence Virgil, speaking of the Arctic pole, says: "This pole is always high for us, but that one the black Styx and the deep spirits see beneath their feet." <note>original: "Hic uertex nobis semper sublimis at illum: sub pedibus styx atra uidet manesque profundi."</note>

**NEVER SEEN** except by the first people. If these stars are at the [Antarctic] pole, they cannot be seen except by those who are in the other hemisphere. And we do not inhabit that, but according to the poet's fiction, our first parents [Adam and Eve] inhabited it when they were still without sin, because here he places the Earthly Paradise <note>original: *paradiso delle delitie*</note>. And it follows from this that, apart from the first parents, these stars have not been seen by any human being. Thus, he excludes the error of Origen, who maintains that the other hemisphere is inhabited just like this one; because of which it would have been necessary for Christ to have also been crucified in that one for their redemption. These four stars it seems he places for the [cardinal virtues]...

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on the opening of Purgatory. The previous page discussed the allegorical meaning of the stars and the planet Venus as symbols of divine grace and reason. Here, Landino elaborates on the four stars representing the cardinal virtues and introduces the figure of Cato of Utica, the guardian of the shores of Purgatory.</meta>

### CANTO XVII

The four cardinal virtues <note>Justice, Prudence, Temperance, and Fortitude</note> do not exist perfectly in men unless they are in a state of grace. Therefore, they were never seen except by our first parents <note>Adam and Eve</note> when they were in a state of grace. To better understand this, let us recall Plato’s division, which we mentioned above: that these four stars, so splendid, are the four moral virtues in the third category, where they are called "virtues of the soul already purified." And if one asks why he mentions them here in Purgatory—where the "purgatorial virtues" (which we enumerated in the second category) are more appropriate—I answer that on this same mountain is the Earthly Paradise <note>the Garden of Eden</note> where our first parents lived in a state of grace. Thus, by ascending this mountain with the purgatorial virtues, we arrive at the summit where the Earthly Paradise lies, above which these stars appear—that is, the virtues of the soul already purified. **THE HEAVENS SEEMED TO REJOICE in their flames**: that is, in their splendor, because truly the heavens and celestial things rejoice in perfect virtues. **OH WIDOWED NORTHERN SITE.** With an exclamation, he turns to our northern pole; although it is adorned with many stars, their light is nonetheless so inferior to the light of these four that it can be said to be "widowed" and deprived of light. "Widowed" are those souls deprived of the Truth and the Good, to which they should be wedded. And in truth, the men of our pole—that is, the "civil" or worldly men—when compared to the virtuous, are not truly men. And it is not without reason that he places the worldly in the North, a cold place, and the virtuous in the South, a warm region. For every virtue has its motion from charity and the love of the Truth and the Good, and charity is a flame, just as vice is born from a lack of love and the fire of it. This is why the Latins use "cold" to describe something harmful and vicious. Whence Virgil says: *To what place the cold star of Saturn withdraws itself* <note>original: "Frigida Saturni quo se se stella receptet"</note>; and Juvenal: *The listener blushes whose mind is cold* <note>original: "Rubet auditor cui frigida mens est"</note>.

As I had moved my gaze away from them,
turning a little toward the other pole,
from where the Wain <note>The Big Dipper/Ursa Major</note> had already disappeared,
I saw near me an old man alone,
worthy of so much reverence in his look,
that no son owes more to a father.
His beard was long and mixed with white hair,
matching the hair upon his head,
of which a double tress fell to his breast.
The rays of the four holy lights
so adorned his face with light
that I saw him as if the sun were before him.

<column-break/>

**I**t follows that after he had seen the four stars in the Antarctic pole, he turned back toward the Arctic and did not see the "Wain" <note>the Chariot</note> where the Bears are, to denote that just as in this hemisphere we cannot see the stars near the Antarctic pole, so in the other hemisphere one cannot see the stars that form the Bears, which the common people call "the Chariot" and "the Horn" <note>the Little Dipper</note>. **I SAW near me an old man alone**: from the preceding words, it appears that although this old man was at his side—and consequently was in the Antarctic hemisphere—he nonetheless stood facing the Arctic. This character is intended to be <term>Cato of Utica</term> <note>Marcus Porcius Cato, a Roman statesman who chose suicide over living under Caesar's tyranny, becoming a symbol of political and moral liberty</note>. And because it might seem to many that Dante departs from the Christian religion by placing a pagan man who died without baptism in a place of salvation, I answer that he does not 

place Cato here as the literal soul of Cato—which we are compelled to believe is among the damned—but he places him as a symbol for **Liberty**, taking this name because this man, more than any other, was a lover of liberty. And as we shall see below, he preferred liberty to life. Nothing else drives us to wish to purge ourselves and endure every labor to become clean except the love of liberty; for once purged, we become good and wise. And whoever is good and wise is always free. For such a person lives in supreme tranquility, serving no worldly thing because he esteems nothing worldly. He fears no adversity. He knows that neither death, nor infirmity, nor poverty, nor exile, nor any other calamity or blow of fortune can harm him. Only vice can harm him, of which he feels clean. Only by following the virtues does he serve God, whose service not only makes us free but makes us kings. Recognizing this, the Stoic philosophers in their paradoxes write: "All the wise (that is, the good) are free, and all the foolish (that is, the vicious) are slaves." But returning to the text, he places Cato facing the North—that is, facing the vices—because this love of liberty arises in us as soon as we have recognized the misery that exists in the slavery of vices. He does not wish to demonstrate here the "first liberty" that was in the soul before the transgression of our first parents and before sin; for that he would have placed in the South, which denotes virtue. Rather, he shows that liberty which we reacquire when we untangle ourselves from vices, of which we were previously slaves. He imagines him as an old man because nothing is older in the soul than liberty, since it was created and placed in the soul's free will at the same time the soul was made. Whence it is wisely written: *He left her in the hand of her own counsel* <note>original: "Reliquit eam in manu consilii sui"</note>. He is therefore old, and thus he describes him with a beard and long hair, not entirely white but mixed, because he had in mind what Virgil imagines of Charon <note>though here applied to Cato</note>: *Already old, but for a god, old age is raw and green* <note>original: "Iam senior: sed cruda deo uiridisque senectus"</note>. Just as Virgil introduces an old Charon, but an old man who is robust and of good strength, so through this description <term>Dante</term> wishes to show the same in <term>Cato</term>. For although liberty is "old" in the soul, it has not for this reason diminished its strength. He adds **WORTHY OF SO MUCH REVERENCE IN HIS LOOK / That no son owes more to a father**.

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on the opening of Purgatory. Having previously discussed the symbolic meaning of the four stars as the cardinal virtues, Landino now focuses on the character of Cato of Utica, the guardian of Purgatory, and the philosophical nature of true freedom versus the slavery of vice.</meta>

# PURGATORY

Certainly, liberty is what makes our soul worthy of veneration. Consider a man who is a slave to vice; suppose he is a slave to lust or to avarice. You will see him do and say things that make him a laughingstock and an object of scorn to all men. Hercules was so highly esteemed, yet because of unbridled lust, he became the slave of a lowly woman <note>referring to Omphale, the queen for whom Hercules performed domestic tasks in drag</note>; or rather, a slave to his own pressing lust. Alexander the Great wished to conquer the world and make himself lord over innumerable peoples and nations, yet because he could not resist his own anger, he became its slave. He earned much more infamy from that vice than he did true glory from so many victories. Therefore, the paradox of the Stoics is most true, as I mentioned a little while ago: **All wise men are free, and all fools are slaves.** <note>original Latin: "Omnes sapientes liberos esse: et omnes stultos seruos."</note> You see then that by being slaves to vices, we become ridiculous and infamous, and we make a mockery of ourselves. On the other hand, consider one who is free from all cravings, who is not subject to lust, nor avarice, nor ambition, but in whom reason reigns, free from every human passion. Certainly, we will see such gravity, such modesty, and such prudence in him that we will not only offer him the highest reverence, but, if it were permitted, we would adore him like a god. This is why our poet most correctly describes this old man as being worthy of as much reverence as a son should give to his father. He could not have chosen a more fitting comparison, because after God, there is no one we should hold in higher reverence than a father. But the text is ordered thus:

**WORTHY OF SUCH REVERENCE in sight:** that is, in appearance, such that a son should not give more honor or greater reverence to any father. We should not say "to a father" for any son, but "to any father" for a son. And with great reason he said "any father" and not simply "father," because there are certain fathers who, beyond having fathered the child, have done no other good for them. Instead, they have done the opposite and harmed them, setting them on the wrong path and encouraging them toward a life of luxury and pleasure, or toward avarice and unbridled craving for money, or toward ambition. There are some who, with all industry, strive to ensure that from a tender age their children adopt good habits and learn good doctrines. Therefore, there is no doubt that a different kind of reverence is owed to these than to those, even though they are all fathers.

**THE RAYS OF THE FOUR HOLY LIGHTS.** It is appropriate that the rays of the four stars—which we have interpreted as the four virtues—illuminate the face of the old man so brightly that he appeared as if illuminated by the sun. For just as the free will of the soul is clouded by darkness and lost through vice, which drags us into slavery, so from these virtues it receives light, and through them it <unclear>mantiche</unclear> <note>Likely "maintains itself" or "is preserved."</note>

> "Who are you who against the blind stream
> have escaped the eternal prison?"
> he said, moving those honorable plumes.
>
> "Who has guided you, and who was the lamp for you
> as you came forth from the deep night
> that always makes the infernal valley black?
>
> Are the laws of the abyss thus broken?
> Or has a new counsel been changed in heaven,
> that you, though damned, come to my grottoes?"

<column-break/>

In the fourth canto of the first canticle <note>Inferno</note>, mention is made of the rivers that descend from our hemisphere into Hell. And in the final canto, it is described how they enter the center of the earth from the other hemisphere and erode a rock where the center of the universe is located; and by eroding it, they pass through and form Cocytus. And against this stream, as shown in the last canto, Dante came when he exited Hell. **BLIND STREAM.** Because it runs through dark places, as has been shown. And allegorically, this stream is understood to be vice, which runs to the center of Hell and carries there whoever navigates it.

<column-break/>

And it is dark because every vice is born from ignorance and from the blindness of reason. Therefore, whoever goes to Hell follows the stream. But whoever leaves it and goes to purge himself comes against the stream, because he opposes all of them. **HAVE ESCAPED** the eternal prison. Theologically, Hell is the eternal prison of the damned because they never leave it. And morally, if Hell is the habit of vice which keeps our soul in eternal slavery, it is also an eternal prison. For the majority of those who have made a habit of vice remain eternally prisoners to it, and there are very few who can escape it. **PLUMES:** he used this to mean the beard, which a speaker moves by moving the jaw. **WHO HAS GUIDED YOU AND** who was your lamp. Two things are necessary to escape the habit of vice: illuminating grace, which provides light and acts as a lamp, and cooperating grace, which acts as a guide to those who wish to act according to virtue. Who was your lamp to come out of the deep night—that is, from the depth of the long-standing habit of vice. **Are THE LAWS OF THE ABYSS THUS** broken? **OR HAS A NEW COUNSEL BEEN CHANGED IN HEAVEN.** It is as if he says: if divine justice has established Hell as an eternal prison for the damned, and you have come out of it, it must be that you either escaped by force or that God has changed His purpose. But the first is not to be believed, because no force prevails against God; nor the second, because divine wisdom is immutable. **THE LAWS OF THE ABYSS** refers to the laws ordained by God for the abyss—that is, for the depth and lower part of the world, which is called "abyss," a word that in the Greek language signifies "depth" <note>original: "abysso... che in lingua greca significa profondita."</note>. **OR HAS HEAVEN CHANGED:** as if to say the place where there is no mutation, but everything is stable.

<summary>Landino discusses Cato of Utica as the guardian of Purgatory, emphasizing the Stoic theme that true freedom comes from virtue while vice is a form of slavery. He allegorically interprets the "blind stream" of Hell as the darkness of ignorance and explains the roles of illuminating and cooperating grace in escaping the habit of sin.</summary>
<keywords>Cato of Utica, Liberty vs. Slavery, Stoic Paradox, Four Cardinal Virtues, Allegory of Grace, Rivers of Hell, Divine Justice, Cristoforo Landino</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on the first Canto of Purgatory. Following the encounter with Cato, the guardian of the mountain, Virgil (representing Reason) instructs Dante (representing the soul) on the proper attitude of humility and explains the divine mission that has brought them from the depths of Hell to the shores of Purgatory.</meta>

## CANTO ONE

<column-break/>

> My leader then took hold of me,
> and with words, and with hands, and with signs,
> he made my legs and brow reverent.
> Then he answered him: "I did not come by myself;
> a lady descended from heaven, at whose prayers
> I came to aid this man with my company.

---

> But since it is your will that more be unfolded
> of our condition, and how it truly is,
> it cannot be my will that you be denied.
> This man never saw the final evening;
> but through his own folly, he was so near to it
> that there was very little time left to turn.
> So, as I said, I was sent to him
> to rescue him; and there was no other way
> than this one upon which I have set myself.
> I have shown him all the wicked people;
> and now I intend to show him those spirits
> who purge themselves under your authority.
> How I have led him would be a long story to tell;
> from on high descends a virtue that aids me
> in leading him to see you and to hear you."

<column-break/>

**It is a fitting thing** that Virgil admonishes Dante—that is, that Reason admonishes Sensuality <note>Sensuality here refers to the "lower" part of the human soul, governed by instincts and physical desires, which must be tamed by Reason.</note>—to show reverence to Cato. For if the appetite does not bring reverence to the liberation of the soul, it will always be prone to vices. **MY LEADER THEN TOOK HOLD OF ME.** Because one cannot love liberty unless Reason brings the appetite and sensuality back under its power and makes them bow and revere liberty. **And with words** by persuading him; **and with hands** by guiding him; **and with signs** by demonstrating to him. Sensuality is admonished with words, that is, with manifest doctrine; with hands, that is, with excellent works which are an example for us to follow in virtue; and with signs, which are deeper and more obscure meanings. **HE MADE MY LEGS REVERENT** by making me kneel. **AND THE BROW:** by bowing the head. And rightly so: because the knees are attributed to mercy. Hence, when we wish to move someone to mercy, we are accustomed to kneel, and similarly to embrace the knees of the one we wish to appease. **AND THE FOREHEAD:** where the eyebrows are; it is attributed to shame. Sensuality, then, feels shame. This is a sign that it repents of its error, desires to amend itself, and asks for mercy, without which—as we have shown elsewhere—a man cannot be saved. **THEN HE ANSWERED.** Cato had asked who their guide was and what light had led them out of Hell. He had wondered if the laws of the abyss were broken or if the will of God had changed. Therefore, Virgil answers: first, that he has been a guide to Dante, requested by Beatrice. And we showed in the second canto of the *Inferno* how Reason, illustrated by natural and philosophical doctrine (which is Virgil), became a guide to Dante to show him the vices at the prayers of Beatrice, who is **cooperating grace** <term>gratia cooperante: a theological term for grace that works with human will</term>, sent by the light and by another whom he does not name, who are **prevenient grace** <term>gratia preveniente: grace that comes before any human action</term> and **illuminating grace**. And he has satisfied the questions that were asked: **WHO HAS GUIDED YOU** and who serves as your lantern. Then he continues:

Virgil had already satisfied the first two questions of Cato and shown him what guide and what light had led them. Now he answers the third, demonstrating that although they had come out of Hell, the laws were not broken. This is because neither of them was damned in Hell, as you will see in the progression of the text. **BUT SINCE:** but after. **AND YOUR WILL:** that is, you wish. **THAT MORE BE UNFOLDED:** that more be explained, more be shown of our condition. This is a metaphor taken from things that are wrapped up and folded, which cannot be clear to us unless they are unfolded. The meaning, then, is: since it is your will that we manifest more of our condition to you. **AS IT IS TRUE:** that is, just. **IT CANNOT BE MY [WILL]:** my desire. **THAT YOU BE DENIED:** that what you ask be denied to you; and it means: just as your request is just, so it cannot be my will that what you ask be denied. And so that you may understand that the laws of the abyss are not broken, know that I was never damned to Hell, because I am in Limbo. Nor was this man yet damned there, since he is not dead; and no one is damned there except the dead.

There are two Hells, as we have already said above. The **Essential Hell**, in which there are only the souls of those who died in mortal sin. The other is the **Moral Hell**, in which is understood to be anyone who has formed such a habit of vice <note>In the Aristotelian sense, a "habit" is a settled disposition of character that is difficult to change.</note> that they cannot remain free of it. But Dante was alive; and if he was entangled in any vice, he had not yet made it a habit. Therefore, he had not descended into Hell as one damned, because such people are not guided by Virgil (that is, by Reason), but by irrational and beastly appetite. Rather, he had descended to have a true knowledge of vices, so that, having learned how harmful they are, he might have the desire to free himself from them. Whence he says: **THIS MAN NEVER SAW THE FINAL EVENING.** That is, death, which is the final night and darkness of man. This signifies he is not yet dead; that is, he has not made a habit of vice. And therefore, with my guidance, he was able to come out of it. **BUT THROUGH HIS OWN FOLLY:** through his foolishness and ignorance. For through a lack of reason we fall into vice. **HE WAS SO NEAR TO IT:** that very little time was left **TO TURN:** that is, it was about to happen; and he said "turn" because the revolution of the planets, and especially of the sun, creates time...

<summary>In this commentary, Landino interprets Virgil's instructions to Dante as Reason disciplining the lower senses to achieve spiritual humility. He distinguishes between the literal Hell of the dead and the "moral Hell" of living people enslaved by vice, explaining that Dante’s journey is a rational quest for self-correction.</summary>
<keywords>Reason vs Sensuality, Cato of Utica, types of Hell, moral philosophy, cooperating grace, prevenient grace, habit of vice, Dante’s humility</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on the first Canto of Purgatory. Having explained Virgil's initial plea to Cato, Landino now explores the philosophical and literary parallels of the sun as a marker of time and the necessity of witnessing the depths of vice to truly desire the heights of liberty.</meta>

# PURGATORIO

<columns>2</columns>

Wherefore Petrarch, wishing to describe the sun, said: "When the planet that distinguishes the hours"—that is, when the sun, which by its revolution distinguishes the hours and every span of time—imitates Virgil, who said: "As the years roll by" <note>original Latin: "Voluentibus annis"</note>. There remained, then, little time to be able to succor him. This denotes that if he had persevered longer in vices, he would have formed such a habit that he could not afterwards escape it. But Beatrice sent Virgil to him—that is, Divine Grace—and that awakened Reason within him, which made him recognize vice. And he rightly said: "And there was no other way than this one through Hell." For when vice is so precise in its flattery with the pleasures it displays, if Reason does not show their ugliness and punishment—which is to lead us through Hell—we would never desire to free ourselves from them. Therefore, Reason could not lead him to salvation if it did not make the way through Hell. And for this he says he has shown him "all the wicked people"—that is, all the generations of vices. And now I intend to show him Purgatory. For from knowing the malignancy of vices arises the desire for purification. **UNDER YOUR AUTHORITY.** Although everything is under divine power, nonetheless it can be said that Purgatory is under the authority of Cato—that is, of liberty—because no one can enter Purgatory unless they repent of their errors. And no one repents of being a slave to vices unless they become eager and desirous of liberty. **HOW I HAVE LED HIM would be a long story to tell.** It would be long to repeat how many things Reason demonstrates to sensuality before it draws it out of Hell—that is, before it makes it hate vice. **FROM ON HIGH DESCENDS virtue.** Since, as we have said, the human soul is not freed from sin without divine help, and is not led to see and hear Cato—which is to recognize liberty and obey it. And this is against the <term>Pelagians</term> <note>Followers of Pelagius who believed that human free will alone, without divine grace, was sufficient to achieve salvation.</note>, who want only free will to be enough for our salvation.

---

> ->Now may it please you to welcome his coming:<-
> ->he goes seeking liberty, which is so dear,<-
> ->as he knows who for her sake refuses life.<-
> ->You know it, for death was not bitter to you<-
> ->in Utica, where you left<-
> ->the garment that on the great day shall be so bright.<-
> ->The eternal edicts are not broken by us,<-
> ->for this man lives, and Minos does not bind me;<-
> ->but I am of the circle where the chaste eyes<-
> ->of your Marcia are, who in her look still prays you,<-
> ->O holy breast, that you hold her for your own:<-
> ->for her love, then, incline yourself to us.<-
> ->Let us go through your seven kingdoms;<-
> ->I will carry back thanks of you to her,<-
> ->if you deign to be mentioned there below.<-

<column-break/>

**May it please you therefore to welcome:** to hold in favor. For if you hold him in favor, you will not deny him your help. And he induces two reasons for which Cato should be moved by his coming. The first he has already stated by showing that he has not come out of Hell against the eternal laws. Now he adds the second, showing that he goes seeking liberty; as if to say to you: Cato ought therefore to be moved in favor of one who came without violating the eternal edicts and sought liberty, which is the proper gift given by God to the soul. Wherefore he adds: **WHICH IS so dear:** so pleasing, so accepted, so desired. Nor is it necessary that I prove this to you, because you yourself know it. Since you loved it so much that you preferred to leave your life rather than lose it. **AS HE KNOWS WHO FOR her sake refuses life.** Because there have been many who have preferred to die rather than live in servitude. **YOU KNOW IT, FOR death was not bitter to you.** We already narrated this history above: <note>Marcus Porcius Cato (Cato the Younger) committed suicide in 46 BC to avoid living under the tyranny of Julius Caesar.</note> in Utica; this city is in Africa,

---

not far from Carthage. **WHERE YOU LEFT the garment:** the body, which is the garment of the soul. **ON THE GREAT day:** the day on which the Final Judgment shall be, by which the wicked shall be damned to eternal punishments and the elect called to eternal beatitude. And because nothing can be a greater thing for us than such a judgment, he calls it the "Great Day," imitating the Sacred Scriptures which sing: "That day, that great day" <note>original Latin: "Dies ista, dies magna"</note>. **SHALL BE SO BRIGHT:** because we shall all take up our bodies again, and those of the blessed shall be glorified and shall shine more than the sun. And thus he enumerates Cato here among the elect. But understand what we said above regarding liberty, which is signified by Cato. For all those who, by having fled vices, have become free, shall be among the elect. **THE EDICTS ARE NOT.** This we have interpreted above. **THE CHASTE EYES.** Because the eyes greatly demonstrate the affections of the soul. **OF YOUR MARCIA:** who was your wife. **WHO IN HER LOOK.** And of her we spoke in the third canto of the Inferno. **STILL PRAYS YOU.** As if to say that whoever looks her in the face recognizes this affection. And in this place, just as the poet puts Cato for liberty, so he puts Marcia for the civil life and for the administration of the republic; as in our Latin allegories on Virgil we show that Dido is put for this same thing. Therefore Marcia—that is, the civil life—always wants Cato for a husband, because she always desires to be joined with liberty. And while Cato was among civil men—that is, while liberty is exercised and labors in the active and civil life—he loves Marcia and does everything for her; but free will passes to the speculation of heavenly things and does not move except at the request of those. But returning to where we left the text, he says: **O HOLY FATHER.** He almost imitates Sallust, who shows that no holy man ever hesitated to die for liberty. **INCLINE yourself to us. FOR HER love, and let us go THROUGH YOUR SEVEN kingdoms.** Through Purgatory, where the seven mortal sins are punished. Of which below...

<summary>This page analyzes Virgil's appeal to Cato, using Cato’s wife Marcia as an allegory for the "civil life" that seeks liberty. It also emphasizes the necessity of divine grace over the Pelagian belief in pure free will.</summary>
<keywords>Cato the Younger, Marcia, Allegory of Liberty, Pelagianism, Utica, Civil Life vs. Contemplative Life, Divine Grace, Final Judgment</keywords>

--- Page 349 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on the opening of Purgatorio. Having established Cato’s role as the guardian of the mountain, Landino now explains the transition from the "active life" (represented by Cato's wife Marcia) to the "contemplative life" (the path of purification), focusing on the symbolic requirements for Dante to begin his ascent: humility and the washing away of the grime of Hell.</meta>

# CANTO ONE

we will say more things. And it is not without reason that he mentions Virgil praying to him for Marcia and not for Beatrice. This is because Virgil, with his human doctrine, cannot elevate the mind enough to perfectly know Beatrice—that is, the liberty that exists in a mind that is perfect and, according to our theology, purified. But he knows her in the civil life. Wherefore Cato cautiously rebukes him and demonstrates for whose love he condescends to his prayers, saying: "But if a lady from heaven moves and rules you," as you will see a little below.

->Marcia was so pleasing to my eyes / while I was over there, he then said to him / that whatever graces she wanted from me, I performed. / Now that she dwells beyond the evil stream / she can no longer move me, by that law / which was made when I came out from there. / But if a lady from heaven moves and rules you / as you say, there is no need for flattery: / let it be enough that for her sake you ask me. / Go then, and see that you gird this man / with a smooth reed, and that you wash his face / so that every foulness is there extinguished. / For it would not be fitting for the eye, overcome / by any mist, to go before the first / minister, who is one of those of paradise.<-

<column-break/>

While I was with Marcia—that is, in the civil life—she pleased me, and I did everything for her liberty. But since I have passed the evil stream—which denotes the active life <note>The "active life" refers to a life of political and social engagement, which Landino contrasts with the "contemplative life" of spiritual study.</note>, where there are many vices—and I am on this side—that is, in the contemplative life, which is free of every vice—Marcia does not move me, nor can she move me. **BY THAT LAW** which was made when I came out from there. This is divine law instituted by God according to the nature of things: that the love of civil liberty should last as long as that civil life lasts. But once the contemplative life arrives, one must observe its law. Because the contemplative life is eternal. Wherefore in the Gospel:
> <note>original: "Maria autem optimā partem elegit: que non auferetur ab ea."</note> Mary has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her.
And therefore he adds: **BUT IF A LADY** from heaven moves or rules you, as if to say: I am no longer bound to Marcia, but to a celestial lady, if she guides you. **AS YOU SAY** there is no need for flattery; and he most excellently said flattery. Because men

---

are induced to do our will either by reasons alleged by us or by flattery. Reason goes toward the truth and the right. Flattery goes with pleasure, which it shows you, and with fraud it persuades you that something is good which is not. Therefore, to pray for the love of Marcia is flattery, because the active life labors in earthly goods, which with their flattery find us loving them, showing in life and appearance what they are not. But Cato, who has passed the evil stream—that is, appetite—which shows he has abandoned the active life. The life of earthly goods is not moved by the delights and flatteries of those things. But having passed to the contemplation of celestial things by the love of them—where there are no flatteries, but sincere truth—he can be easily persuaded. And being persuaded, he shows Virgil that he must gird Dante with a smooth reed, in which there is no knot, and wash his face. And it is the nature of the reed to be born in low places, and not to grow much, and to have no knot. Wherefore the proverb:
> <note>original: "nodū in scyrpo queris."</note> You are looking for a knot in a reed.
<note>This was a common Latin expression meaning to look for difficulties or moral complications where there are none; the reed is perfectly smooth.</note> When you wish to find in a thing what is not there, we say you seek the knot in the reed. Likewise, it has no leaves, nor ornament of flowers, but only produces seed. By this we understand that he who wishes to be purged must be humble and lowly—that is, be continent, nor let himself fall into concupiscence, like the reed, which by its own nature contains itself, and never bends; let him have no knot—that is, let him not be tied to any earthly desire; nor have leaves. Which signifies that he should not seek worldly honors, nor worldly things, except as much as the necessity of food and clothing requires, which requires few things. Because Cicero says:
> <note>original: "Paucis minimisque natura contenta est."</note> Nature is content with a few and very small things.
Many wish that this <term>ricinghe</term> <note>literally "re-gird" or "gird again"</note> should mean to gird twice: one belt being strength against carnal appetites, and the other patience in penance. And because Saint John distinguishes sins into three species: Pride of life, concupiscence of the flesh, and concupiscence of the eyes. Against two are humility and continence, which are in the reed; and against the third, he washes the eyes with the dew fallen from heaven, and not dried by the heat of the sun—which is illuminating grace, not dried by the splendor of worldly goods. And he adds: that it is not a fitting thing to go with eyes "surprised"—that is, blinded and almost dazzled, which signifies the intellect clouded by ignorance and by the desire for mortal things. *Soppriso*—that is, suppressed—which in our language means "condensed." Wherefore we say milk is <gloss>soppreso</gloss> [curdled] when, with certain herb flowers called rennet or indeed curd, it becomes thick from being thin. Therefore, the eye sees through its clarity, which when it condenses too much, diminishes the vision. **TO THE FIRST MINISTER**, who is the angel, whom he will describe a little further on.

---

->This little island all around / down there where the wave beats upon it / bears reeds upon the soft mud: / No other plant that might produce leaves...<-

<column-break/>

He imagines an island in the ocean in the other hemisphere, placed opposite Jerusalem. And he most excellently wants Purgatory to be on an island. Because whoever sets out to purge himself of vices is struck by various waves of many perturbations and desires.

<summary>This page explores the allegory of Cato's transition from the active to the contemplative life, using the smooth reed as a symbol of humility and the washing of Dante's face as the removal of ignorance. Landino clarifies that while earthly love (Marcia) no longer moves the soul in Purgatory, divine grace (Beatrice) remains the ultimate authority.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the final instructions given by Cato to Virgil and Dante. It explains the allegorical significance of the reed—representing humility and patience—and the transition from the darkness of Hell (ignorance) to the light of Purgatory (reason and purification).</meta>

# PURGATORY

...or hardens itself, can have life:
because it does not yield to the blows.
Afterward, let your return not be this way;
the sun, which is now rising, shows you
where to take the mountain at its easiest ascent.
Thus he vanished; and I raised myself up
without speaking, and drew myself back
to my leader, and fixed my eyes upon him.

<column-break/>

...which would seek to move the soul from its good purpose. But just as the island—though it is surrounded by the sea—nevertheless resists all the blows of the waves, so too one who has entered into the **purgatorial virtues** <note>Landino distinguishes between "civil virtues" (for living in society) and "purgatorial virtues" (which cleanse the soul for God).</note> cannot be conquered by any perturbation in a way that would remove them from their true purpose. These shores, which are struck by the waves, produce nothing but reeds. By **reeds**, we understand tolerance and patience, which are necessary for those who wish to free themselves from vices; for such a person is continually struck by burning desires that would lead them back to pleasure, greed, or ambition. This is especially true when, in giving ourselves to this **contemplative life**, we lose bodily comforts or honors, where we must endure many hardships and many anxieties, and yield to the blows of fortune by bending and not breaking. And he rightly says that the shore produces no plant other than reeds, because no one reigns there except those who possess this patience. For a plant that is not flexible would be broken. And certainly, he who does not bend in adversity and does not bow his shoulders is conquered by it. Nor is it necessary for them to bear leaves—that is, to have desires for vain and fleeting things—which, like leaves, seem beautiful but last only a short time and produce no fruit.

**AFTERWARD, LET YOUR RETURN NOT BE THIS WAY.** Because one who goes toward purgation must not turn back, but proceed forward. Wherefore John also said: *They went and did not return* <note>original: "Ibant et non renertebantur." This is a scriptural reference to the movement of holy beings, emphasizing progress toward God.</note>.

**THE SUN SHOWS YOU THAT IT IS NOW RISING.** He feigned in the other canticle <note>The *Inferno*.</note> that his entry into Hell was at the beginning of the night, because falling into vice comes from ignorance and blindness of mind. In this part, he shows that the ascent to Purgatory was at the birth of the sun. Because exiting vice to return to virtue proceeds from the rising within us of the **light of reason**. And therefore he said: "the sun shows you that it is rising." Because the light of reason, which had previously been submerged, can be regained and show us the way of purging ourselves.

**TAKE THE MOUNTAIN AT ITS EASIEST ASCENT.** Difficult and steep is the way that leads to virtue. Wherefore he admonishes here that we should always take the path that has the least harshness, provided it leads us where we must go. He wants us to climb. But because until we are well-confirmed in our good purpose, we must begin with the easier things so they do not lead us to despair. And later, having become accustomed to such difficulty, the labor will seem less hard to us.

**THUS HE VANISHED.** This is almost to denote that it was not the physical essence of Cato, but an image placed there to signify **liberty**.

**AND I RAISED MYSELF UP WITHOUT SPEAKING.** In this deliberation, reason alone must operate. And the **appetite** <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "appetite" refers to our physical desires and impulses, which must be governed by reason.</note> must listen with reverence and then give itself entirely to reason and look to it, so that it does nothing else except what reason commands or signals.

---

He began: "Son, follow my steps;
let us turn back, for this plain
slopes down this way to its lower boundaries."
The dawn was conquering the morning hour,
which fled before it, so that from afar
I recognized the trembling of the sea.
We went along the solitary plain
like a man who returns to a lost road,
who until he reaches it, seems to walk in vain.

<column-break/>

Virgil calls Dante "son" and "well-deserving." This is because Dante willingly and with love obeyed Virgil, not as a master but as a father. And already several times we have shown that this signifies the appetite being made obedient to **reason**.

**FOLLOW MY STEPS.** Because without reason, the senses would again become entangled in vices.

**LET US TURN BACK.** We cannot enter Purgatory unless we turn back to recognize the vices that are within us. And therefore he wants him to go down—that is, to the recognition of vice—before he begins to climb. Others take this descending to mean **humility**, which is necessary for those who desire to purge themselves; this interpretation does not displease me.

**THE DAWN WAS CONQUERING THE MORNING HOUR.** Dawn is that time in which, although the body of the sun is not yet seen, it is nonetheless so close to our hemisphere that it already illuminates the east and overcomes the morning time, which had already diminished the darkness, but not as much as the dawn. For the dawn makes the air white—and it is so named because *album* in Latin means "white."

**WHICH FLED BEFORE IT.** Just as the dark night flees the morning, so the morning flees the dawn. There was, then, enough light that I discerned the **trembling**—that is, the light rippling—of the sea. There was already so much light that although I could not discern everything, I nonetheless discerned this. This denotes that although he did not yet have so much light of intellect that he could yet speculate on high things, he nonetheless knew it was necessary to purge himself because he had entered the purgatorial virtues. And he saw the trembling of the sea—that is, he already recognized not only the great movements of the appetite (which even "civil virtues" recognize as vices) but even the smallest ones, which the civil life (because it does not have perfect virtues) does not judge as vices, unlike the **purgatorial virtues**.

**WE WENT ALONG THE SOLITARY...**

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the final moments of Purgatorio’s first canto, specifically interpreting the allegorical significance of the dew, the washing of Dante’s face, and the desert shore where the reed of humility grows. It draws heavily on Virgil and Saint Augustine to explain the transition from vice to virtue.</meta>

# CANTO ONE

### THE COMMENTARY OF CRISTOFORO LANDINO

plain. Infinite is the crowd of those who go to Hell—that is, those who fall into vices. But very few are those who leave it to go and purge themselves. Hence Virgil says: <note>original: "Facilis descensus auerni. Sed reuocare gradum superasque euadere ad auras. Hoc opus hic labor est."</note> "Easy is the descent to Hell; but to retrace one's steps and escape to the upper air—this is the task, this is the labor." Therefore, this plain is lonely and solitary because few arrive there. **AS A MAN WHO** returns. A very appropriate comparison. For a man who has left Hell and set out on the "untrue path" to go to Purgatory feels the pain of having to turn back, and it seems to him that he goes in vain until he returns to the true path, just as one does who has left the main road. But yet, as Petrarch says, it is wisdom for one who has lost the way to turn back.

> When we were where the dew
> fights with the sun, which, being in a place
> where there is shade, is little dispersed,
> Both hands upon the grass, outspread,
> Gently my master placed.
> And I, who was aware of his art,
> Offered toward him my tearful cheeks;
> There he made entirely uncovered
> That color which Hell had hidden from me.

<column-break/>

**W**hen we were where the dew fights: that is, battles with the sun, which wants to consume it with heat by thinning and drying it. But the dew, because it is in a place of "orezza"—that is, where there is shade—descends, is little dispersed, and does not dissolve. Virgil bathed his hands in it to wash Dante’s face. Why he takes the dew, and why we said "the sun" a little above, [is explained thus]: Reason, with its hands—that is, with good works—takes the dew, which represents receiving illuminating grace. And it is rightly "with good works," because God does not give it to us unless we help ourselves from our own side. Hence Augustine says: <note>original: "Qui fecit te sine te non salvabit te sine te"</note> "He who created you without you will not save you without you." God has compassion on those who help themselves and sends them such grace. **WHEREFORE I, WHO** was aware. Reason wishes to remove sensuality <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "sensuality" refers to the lower, physical urges of the soul.</note> in order to remove the filth that stains the eyes. And that sensuality, having already been made obedient to reason, does not flee but rather comes forward. And then the dew takes away that color and filth which so occupied his eyes that he could not see Hell. For although Virgil—who is the superior Reason—showed to the sensuality the ugliness and vileness of vice and the detriment it brings to the soul, nevertheless, being occupied by the desire for earthly things, the soul understood it, but not perfectly. Hence he says: **THAT COLOR**, that filth, which hid Hell from me. It did not hide it entirely, but "as if" it hid it. For poets sometimes use this distinction of "as if," which is understood here. Thus Virgil says: <note>original: "Galli per domos aderant arcemque tenebant"</note> "The Gauls were present through the houses and held the citadel"—that is, they *almost* held it. And certainly, the sensuality not yet being purged, he had not absolutely known the ugliness and the mud of vices, which Hell—that is, ignorance—had hidden from him.

> We came then upon the desert shore,
> which never saw its waters navigated
> by any man who was afterwards experienced in returning.
> There he girded me as pleased another;
> Oh marvel! that just as he chose
> the humble plant, such was it reborn
> Immediately there where he plucked it.

[The shore is] deserted and lonely, as was said above of the path. This shore never saw any man navigate its waters who was afterwards "experienced"—that is, who had tried and attempted to turn back. And poetically, he gives feeling to an unfeeling thing, as Virgil does: <note>original: "Iamque ascendebant collem qui plurimis urbi Inminet"</note> "And now they were climbing the hill which hangs over much of the city." **THERE HE GIRDED ME** as pleased another. Because it is in the judgment and will of Reason to impose how much and what kind of humility, patience, and penance it wishes. Other texts have "as [the other] commanded." But that another reed should immediately be reborn where the first was plucked is an imitation of Virgil, who shows that as soon as Aeneas plucked the golden bough in the forest, another was born. Whence he says: <note>original: "Primoque auulso non deficit alter aureus et simili fronde uirga metallo"</note> "When the first is torn away, a second of gold does not fail, a branch of the same metal and leaf." Therefore, as we demonstrated in that place in our Virgilian allegories: the virtues, which are the goods of the soul, do not decrease by being taken. Rather, they grow, because they multiply into more. Thus our poet intends here. Let there be a thousand who clothe themselves in humility; humility will not be lacking for another thousand who wish to clothe themselves in it. Indeed, these latter will clothe themselves more easily by the example of the first. But you will find the opposite in bodily goods: for the more they are taken from the heap, the more it decreases.

**H**aving washed his face, they came to the shore, which never saw any man navigate its sea who afterwards turned back. This, understanding it of the dead, is manifest: for no one goes to Purgatory who afterwards turns back. Rather, he proceeds forward, ascending to heaven. But it is also true of the living. For he who passes from vice to purgation does not then turn back. Rather, he goes from the purgatorial virtues to those of the already purged soul. He says, therefore: We arrived at the desert shore, abando— <note>Catchword for the next page: "abbandonato" (abandoned).</note>

<summary>This page explains the allegorical cleansing of Dante's face with dew, signifying the removal of the "filth of Hell" (ignorance/vice) through divine grace and reason. It also interprets the "desert shore" and the miraculous regrowth of the reed as a symbol of how spiritual virtues like humility are inexhaustible.</summary>

# PURGATORY

### THE SECOND CANTO OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE

<image-desc>Two decorative drop caps: the letter 'G' features a miniature landscape with a figure, and the letter 'F' features a standing figure.</image-desc>

NOW the sun had reached the horizon
whose meridian circle covers
Jerusalem at its highest point;
And the night, which circles opposite him,
was issued forth from the Ganges with the Scales,
which fall from her hand when she prevails;
So that the white and vermillion cheeks
of beautiful Aurora, where I was,
through too much age were becoming orange.
<note>Dante uses "rancie" (orange or rust-colored) to describe how the sky’s colors change as the dawn progresses into full morning.</note>

<column-break/>

**I**t was truly the divine genius of our poet, aided by divine grace, that led him—not without reason—to establish three distinct times of day after he emerged from Hell. First, the Morning, in which the splendor of Venus overcame the darkness. Then, the Dawn. And at present, the birth of the Sun. But we shall speak of these below. To better understand the text, I say that before Dante reaches the gate of Purgatory, he traverses a certain space where those stay for a time who were negligent in coming to penance. There, while waiting, they purge such negligence, and once purged, they enter Purgatory proper to purge the sins they committed.

And because he divides this negligence into six parts, he similarly divides this place into six parts, so that every kind of negligence has its own specific location. 

The first place is the shore leading up to the mountain. In this area, the negligence of those who were occupied by vain and worldly delights and delayed their penance is punished. 

Next follows the second place, which is the first ledge. In this are the negligent who delayed penance because they were in contumacy <note>Contumacy refers to a stubborn refusal to obey the authority of the Church.</note> of excommunication. He writes of these in the third canto. 

In the fourth canto, he places the second ledge and third place, where he puts those who were naturally negligent in all their actions. 

In the fifth canto is the third ledge and fourth place: and in it are the negligent who, because of the occupations of war and arms, delayed their penance. 

In the sixth canto, he places the fifth place and fourth ledge: and in that, those who, because of the occupations of their studies, delayed their penance. 

In the two cantos following this, he places the sixth place: and in that, those who delayed it because of the occupation of lordship or governance. 

All these souls must wait to enter Purgatory for as long as they delayed turning to penance while in the world—except for the excommunicated, who must wait thirty years for every single year [of their excommunication]. Furthermore, any of these negligent souls can walk as far as the gate of Purgatory, but must then return to their assigned place until their time is fulfilled. We will see all these matters more extensively as we proceed. For in this second canto, he only treats the first species of the negligent. 

But first, he describes the time, showing that the sun was already rising in that hemisphere and in our own, the night was beginning. **NOW THE SUN HAD** reached the horizon. The sun had descended to the circle which divides our hemisphere from the other, which in Greek is called the <term>horizon</term>, meaning "terminating." For <term>orizin</term> <note>original: ὁρίζειν (horizein)</note> signifies "to terminate" or "to bound." It is a fitting name because, as I have said, this is the boundary between our hemisphere and the other. Therefore, having arrived there, the sun leaves this one and enters the other, creating sunset for us and sunrise for those on the opposite side. From this it follows that night is made for us, and day for those others. Furthermore, you must understand...
