# CANTO TWO

to extend: because just as the horizon is the circle that divides one hemisphere from the other, so there is another circle that divides each hemisphere into two equal parts: at which, when the sun arrives, it creates midday. This is because it is as distant from the east as it is from the west. For this reason, it is called the meridian circle. Therefore, the sun was at the horizon for us in the west, and at the horizon for the other hemisphere in the east. But the meridian of this horizon in our hemisphere **COVERS**: that is, it stands above Jerusalem with its highest point, which is when the sun is at its greatest height. From this, it follows that Jerusalem is in the center of the world.

**JERUSALEM.** Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), a scholar whose encyclopedias were standard references in the Middle Ages.</note> writes that Shem, the son of Noah, built this city in Syria after the flood and called it Salem. Later, inhabited by the Jebusites, it changed its name and was called Jebus by them. Later, they composed both names, calling it Jebusalem. At another time, it was called Jerusalem; Solomon named it Hierosolyma, and the Romans called it Solyma. Hence Juvenal says: <note>original: "Solimarumque facerdos"</note> "The priest of the Solymians." Finally, the Emperor Aelius Hadrian decreed that it should be called Aelia after himself. 

**AND THE NIGHT** which circles opposite to him. This is because when the sun goes down in the west, the night begins to appear in the east. Therefore, it is opposite to him, and thus opposite, it goes searching through the heaven. **ISSUED FROM THE GANGES:** just as the Ebro is a river of Spain—which, because it runs to the west, is called the western mouth—so the Ganges, a river in India, because it runs to the east, is called the eastern mouth. The Ganges is a river in India named after Ganges, a very ancient King of India. Its origin is not very well known. Many say that it is born in the very high mountains of Scythia and falls to the plain into a lake with a great noise. From there it exits and runs placidly and quietly. Nineteen large and navigable rivers enter into this one. Where it has the least width, it is eight miles wide; where it is widest, one hundred. In no place is it less deep than twenty feet. Many believe it to be that which the Holy Scriptures call the Pishon, <note>One of the four rivers flowing out of the Garden of Eden in Genesis.</note> which signifies "inundation."

**ISSUED FORTH WITH THE SCALES** It was shown above that the sun was in Aries. In this sign, because the sun creates the equinox, it stays as much in our hemisphere as in the one below. It follows that when the sun is in Aries, the Libra (the Scales)—which is the sign opposite to Aries—rises in the east. And therefore he said "with the Scales," that is, with Libra, which **FALL FROM HER HAND WHEN SHE PREVAILS.** This refers to when the night increases. The meaning is this: since there are two equinoxes in which the night is equal to the day, when the sun is in the first point of Aries, it is the vernal equinox. But when it leaves the first degree, the day begins to grow. Hence Petrarch says: <note>original: "Era nella stagione che lequinoctio eldi fa uincitore"</note> "It was the season when the equinox makes the day the victor." And the sun produces the opposite effect at the autumnal equinox, when the sun is in the first point of Libra.

**SO THAT THE WHITE AND VERMILLION CHEEKS.** The poets imagine that Aurora (the Dawn) is a very beautiful goddess who stays in the east. Because this time of day appears in the east a little before the sun. Wanting, therefore, to show that the sun had risen, he says that the cheeks—that is, the white and vermillion faces of Aurora—that is, those two colors which, as we have said, appear in the air before the sun is entirely revealed, had become orange: withered and old; that is, they had disappeared.

We were still alongside the sea,
like people who ponder their journey,
who go in heart and in body stay:
And behold, as just before morning
through the thick vapors Mars reddens
down in the west above the sea floor:
Such appeared to me—may I see it again—
a light coming across the sea so swiftly
that no flight equals its motion:
From which, when I had for a moment
withdrawn my eye to question my leader,
I saw it again, brighter and larger grown:
Then on every side of it appeared
a something—I knew not what—of whiteness,
and little by little another emerged from beneath it.

<column-break/>

**W**e were still on the shore, and we were standing like someone who thinks in order to find the way and the path, and not knowing it yet, does not move with the body; but the soul has set out on the way. And while standing in such thought, Dante saw a light on the sea quite far from himself, which was of that fiery color which is usual in Mars. This happens when Mars is almost opposite to the sun, so that as the dawn comes, he is near the setting. At that time, since this planet is red by its nature, it happens that in the thick vapors exhaling from the sea—already reddening because of the dawn—it appears redder and larger. And he arranges it thus: **WE** were along the shore, etc., and behold, a light appeared to me such—that is, of such a color—as Mars reddens, not only by its nature but also because of the thick vapors. **JUST BEFORE**: at the time near the morning of the dawn. We will speak of Mars in *Paradiso* when we come to its heaven. But following the text, the light came so fast that when I turned my eyes to Virgil, it had already approached, such that it appeared brighter and larger. **THEN ON EVERY SIDE.** This demonstrates what happens in sight, which from afar sees nothing but confusion and without distinction. As it approached, he began to discern the white wings. But first he discerned the color rather than the wings, and therefore he said "a whiteness" and "I knew not what." **AND FROM BENEATH** little by little another emerged. # PURGATORIO

such: because they were more elevated: then, approaching closer: I began to see the white robe. Because, as I have said, such is the nature of the senses <note>Landino is explaining that as objects get closer, our senses perceive their details more clearly—here moving from a generic "white thing" to the recognition of an angel's garment.</note>.

My master still did not say a word
until the first white things appeared as wings;
then, when he well recognized the pilot,
He cried: "Hurry, hurry, bend your knees!
Behold the Angel of God: fold your hands:
from now on you will see such high officials.
See how he scorns human instruments,
so that he wants no oar nor other sail
than his own wings between shores so distant.
See how he holds them straight toward heaven,
beating the air with eternal feathers,
which do not change like mortal hair."

<column-break/>

Virgil said nothing until he first recognized that the one who was coming was the angel. And by this we interpret that the learned man should not affirm knowledge of anything to others unless he first understands it clearly. Or truly it signifies that no knowledge of universals <note>In medieval philosophy, "universals" are general concepts, while "phantasms" are the mental images of specific, physical things.</note> comes to the human intellect except through the **phantasms** of particulars. **SEE HOW HE SCORNS** human arguments <note>original: "argomenti," which Landino interprets here as "instruments" or "means."</note>. Because he who is in the purging virtues begins to leave every human contagion and to direct himself to rise from the earth. But because he places a ship here, and a pilot is necessary—just as in the beginning of the *Inferno* he showed who the pilot was who led souls to eternal damnation—so now he places the one who leads to Purgatory, where there is firm hope of ascending to heaven after purgation. He placed Charon there with the ship and the oar. And Acheron: where we said Acheron signifies the movement that the soul makes when passing into sin; which movement, because it is full of disturbance, is perfectly likened to turbulent and black water. Here he places the sea, which is not in a storm. But has small waves, and is pure water, to demonstrate the movement of the soul toward purgation, which is without any disturbance.

Charon signifies here free will <note>Landino's allegorical reading: Charon represents the choice to sin, while the Angel represents the choice for virtue.</note>. Which, because it is not illuminated by any divine grace, he describes in the form of a bridge demon. Here the Angel of God is placed for free will, because our soul in this place uses free will for virtue and not for vice. And because it is guided by divine grace and illuminated by it, he makes it bright and radiant to denote the light of grace and the heat of the desire to purge oneself. The ship is taken for the **will**, which carries free will, both here and there. But in the *Inferno*, the ship is leaky and weak. And it can take on water. Whence: *And it received much water through the leaky marsh* <note>original Latin: "Et multam accepit rimosa paludem." A quote from Virgil’s Aeneid (VI.414), describing Charon’s decaying boat.</note>. This signifies that there the will allows itself to be filled by disturbances. And in Purgatory it is good, and receives no water. In Hell the pilot guides it with an oar. Purgatory pushes it with a sail, which he makes of his wings. The oar and the sail signify **choice**. But the oar, because it always touches the water, signifies the choice of earthly things; the sails rise above the ship and are wings, which are given to those who inhabit the air, and are wings directed toward heaven. This signifies the choice of celestial things. There are some who want this to be the good angel who is given to guard the soul.

Then as he came more and more toward us,
the bird of God appeared more bright,
so that the eye up close could not sustain it;
But I cast mine down; and he came to the shore
with a vessel so swift and light
that the water swallowed none of it.
At the stern stood the celestial pilot,
such that he seemed blessed by description;
and more than a hundred spirits sat within.
*When Israel came out of Egypt* <note>original Latin: "In exitu Israel de Egypto," the opening of Psalm 114, traditionally sung during funerals and signifying the soul’s liberation from the "Egypt" of sin.</note>
they all sang together with one voice,
with all that is written in that psalm.
Then he made the sign of the holy cross over them,
whereupon they all threw themselves onto the beach,
and he went away as quickly as he had come.

There are some who by this swift vessel—that is, the light boat—understand the **absolution** performed by the priest, which has the power to lead the soul to purgatory. And the angel with the two wings is the cooperating and perfecting grace. And that the water swallowed nothing of the ship signifies that the grace of the Holy Spirit, which is acquired in absolution, makes us so light on the sea of the bitterness of death that we are not submerged in it. This allegory I highly approve of, and it is very fitting. But returning to our allegory, we will say that just as Charon's ship was very pitched and took on much water—whence Virgil said: *And it received much water through the leaky marsh*—which signifies that the will toward vice is always in worldly things, so the angel's little boat comes light upon the water because it rises to celestial things and does not dip into worldly ones. **BECAUSE THE EYE COULD NOT SUSTAIN IT**: because Dante had newly entered into the purging virtues and was not yet...

# CANTO SECOND

something so purified: that it could endure such light: because as we have already said: the impure cannot touch the pure. **HE SEEMED BLESSED** in writing. He appeared as if written—that is, confirmed—to be blessed. This is not false. For whoever goes to Purgatory is already confirmed in grace. **WHEN ISRAEL WENT OUT** of Egypt <note>original Latin: "IN EXITV ISRAELE de egypto." This is the opening of Psalm 114 (113 in the Vulgate).</note>. This psalm was once written in the presence of the Hebrew people when they left Egypt and the slavery of Pharaoh, and were led by Moses into the desert to go to the land of promise. Therefore, these spirits, leaving behind sin and its slavery to come to Purgatory, and from there to the land of promise (which is Paradise), could most excellently sing such a psalm. **THEN HE MADE** the sign of the holy cross over them: By this sign, which is specific to our religion, the poet denotes that such souls have held the Christian faith, without which no merit or virtue of theirs could make them worthy of Purgatory.

The crowd that remained there seemed wild
regarding the place, gazing all around
like one who tastes new things.
On all sides the day was shooting forth
the sun, who with his well-aimed arrows

The souls who became aware of me
by my breathing, that I was still alive,
wondering, they turned pale;

people draw near to hear news,
and none shows himself shy of crowding:
So upon my face those
fortunate souls fixed their gaze, all of them,
almost forgetting to go make themselves beautiful.

<column-break/>

The crowd of those spirits remaining there seemed wild regarding the place, because they stood there like strangers, like someone who is new and not yet confident. And by this, he demonstrates that although we have voluntarily departed from sin and come to purgation, nevertheless at the beginning such a life frightens us somewhat, because we are not yet accustomed to it. And they willingly ask those who are experienced what manner they should maintain. But Virgil and Dante do not yet have such knowledge, being themselves new, to be able to show such a way. **ON ALL SIDES.** The sun was shooting forth the day—that is, it was scattering its rays which make the day. For the day is nothing other than the light of the sun. Therefore, he demonstrates that the sun had already risen so far above our horizon that it was scattering its rays everywhere. And he wishes to show that since the sun was in the first degree of **Aries** <term>Aries: The Ram, the first sign of the zodiac, associated with spring.</term>, it was not only above the horizon with that sign, but the entire sign of Aries was already out. And because every time the first degree of Aries arrives at our horizon in the east, it follows that the sixth sign from it must fall in the western horizon. It is necessary that the third sign from it, which is **Capricorn**, touches the mid-heaven with its first degree. Therefore, when all of Aries is out of the horizon, all of Capricorn will have passed the mid-heaven. For which reason, if the sun (which was in the first degree of Aries) chased all of Capricorn from the mid-heaven, it followed that one sign was already above the earth. We spoke of Capricorn in the *Inferno*, and we showed that the sun makes the winter solstice in that sign. **WITH WELL-AIMED ARROWS**: true and certain. Because the rays of the sun never change their order in striking. **BY ANOTHER** way. He says that they, having come through Hell where they recognized the harsh slavery of vice and the damnation that proceeds from it, the climb—that is, the purging of oneself from it—although it has harshness in itself, nevertheless in comparison to that, it will seem like a game and a light thing.

They noticed that Dante was alive because he breathed—that is, he drew breath. For breathing is characteristic of a living animal. Since neither the body without the soul nor the soul without the body breathes. Breathing is necessary for two things. First: because the heart is the seat of life. If the heart perishes, life perishes. And not being able to endure the heat that is within it unless it is continually refreshed, nature placed the lungs around the heart in the form of **bellows** <note>original: "mantaci." Landino uses a medieval medical analogy where the lungs act as mechanical bellows to cool the heart's "fire."</note>, which, by continually drawing air to themselves, refresh it. The second is so that such air, drawn by the lungs to the heart, may nourish and restore the vital spirit in the heart, as **Albert the Great** <note>original: "Alberto magno." A 13th-century philosopher and scientist.</note> shows in his *Book of Animals*. **LIKE A MESSENGER.** A fitting comparison by which he shows how the spirits crowded around Dante. Just as people run and gather around one who brings news, and especially if he carries an **olive branch**. Because it denotes the bringing of news of either peace or victory. The olive is a tree dedicated to Minerva, goddess of wisdom. And the fables say that being...

<header>PURGATORY</header>

The dispute between this goddess and Neptune <note>Neptune is the Roman god of the sea; Minerva (Athena) is the goddess of wisdom.</note> was over who should give a name to the city that was later called Athens. Jove commanded that each should strike the earth: Minerva with her spear and Neptune with his trident, and the winner of the case would be the one whose strike produced the better thing. Neptune struck, and a horse was born from it. Minerva struck, and an olive tree was born. Because the horse is a warlike animal and the olive a peaceful plant, the victory was awarded to Minerva. Since her name in Greek is Athena, she wished the city to be called Athens. And because, as we have said, it is the tree of peace, all those who went to ask for peace carried the olive branch. Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle, known for his work on botany.</note>, a disciple of Aristotle who lived 440 years after the founding of Rome, asserts that it did not grow further than forty miles from the sea. And Fenestella <note>A Roman historian and encyclopedist.</note>, a writer of no small repute, writes that in the times of Tarquinius Priscus <note>The fifth king of Rome (reigned 616–579 BC).</note>, this tree was not yet in Italy, nor in Africa, nor in Spain. In Athens, all victors were crowned with olive. And the spirits reasonably marveled that a living man was there. For in a living man there is still appetite and sensuality, which are difficult to submit to reason so that it obeys in leaving behind vice and purging oneself of it. **AS IF FORGETTING**: forgetting. **TO MAKE THEMSELVES BEAUTIFUL** <gloss>that is, to be purged of sin</gloss>. And here he notes how great their wonder was, since they delayed their purgation just to see him. And he also notes the negligence in delaying purgation, for which they are punished, as you will see a little further down.

I saw one of them draw forward
to embrace me with such great affection,
that it moved me to do the same.
O empty shadows, except in appearance!
Three times I joined my hands behind it
and as many times returned with them to my breast.
With wonder, I believe, I was painted:
because the shadow smiled and withdrew,
and I, following it, pushed myself further.
Gently it said that I should rest;
then I knew who it was, and I prayed
that he would stop a little to speak with me.
He replied to me: "Just as I loved you
in my mortal body, so I love you freed;
therefore I stay; but you, why do you go?"

**SMILED**. He smiled modestly. And note that the soul could embrace in spirit. And therefore, as a friend, he moved. But then, seeing Dante’s deception <note>In this context, "deception" refers to Dante’s mistaken belief that the soul was a solid body he could touch.</note>, he withdrew so that Dante would not try the impossible again; and having withdrawn, seeing that Dante followed him, he told him to "rest"—that is, that he should not try to embrace him anymore. But he spoke "gently" so that Dante would understand he spoke out of affection and not out of anger. There are some who say Dante contradicts himself in this place. For in the *Inferno* <note>Dante’s first book, *Hell*.</note>, he makes the soul palpable, where he says: *Then I took him by the scruff of the neck and said, "It will be necessary for you to name yourself..."* <note>A reference to Dante’s encounter with the traitor Bocca degli Abati in Inferno 32.</note>. To which some respond that in Hell it is necessary for the soul to be palpable so that it is fit to receive physical punishment. But this does not solve the question. Therefore, we will rather say that in Hell, he poetically attributed to the soul that which it does not naturally have. And here, he physically reveals the truth so that the place does not deceive anyone.

"My Casella, to return another time
to where I am, I make this journey,"
I said, "but to you, how has so much time been taken?"
And he to me: "No outrage has been done to me
if he who takes when and whom he pleases
has many times denied me this passage;
for of a just will his own is made.
Truly for three months he has taken..."

<column-break/>

He demonstrates here that souls are incorporeal <note>Lacking a physical body.</note> and are seen only by having taken an <term>aerial body</term> <note>A philosophical concept that spirits could manifest in a form made of thickened air, appearing visible but remaining untouchable.</note> which, although it is seen like mist or a cloud, nevertheless cannot be touched. Whence Christ said in the Gospel: "For a spirit does not have flesh and bones" <note>original Latin: "Quoniam spiritus carnem et ossa non habet." From Luke 24:39.</note>. And therefore he says: "O empty shadows, except in appearance," and adds that three times he tried to embrace it, and always his hands came back to his chest, finding nothing in his arms. And this is a Virgilian imitation: "Thrice he tried to throw his arms around her neck; thrice the image, grasped in vain, escaped his hands, like light winds and most like a fleeting dream" <note>original Latin: "Ter conatus ibi collo dare bracchia circum. Ter frustra comprensa manus effugit imago. Par leuibus uentis uolucrique simillima somno." From Virgil’s Aeneid, Book II (describing Aeneas trying to hug the ghost of his wife Creusa) and Book VI (his father Anchises).</note>. **WITH WONDER, I believe, I was painted**: because I marveled greatly. I believe that on my face appeared that color which usually appears when one is stupefied by something. Whence we are accustomed to say: "I turned a thousand colors." **BECAUSE THE SHADOW SMILED**: because he noticed the deception I had fallen into, believing him to have a palpable body.

This Casella was our citizen <note>A resident of Florence.</note>, a man of easy nature and happy habits. He was an excellent musician in his time. Our poet, exhausted by long study, would refresh his weary spirits with Casella's singing, imitating the Pythagoreans, Socrates, and many other philosophers who, for the reason already mentioned, delighted in music. Dante demonstrates, then, that he goes to Purgatory to return there another time; by which words he wishes the listener to understand that this fiction of his...

<header>CANTO SECOND</header>

> whoever wished to enter with all peace,
> for which reason I, who am now turned toward the seashore
> where the water of the Tiber becomes salt,
> was kindly gathered up by him
> at that river-mouth where he has set his wing;
> because it is there that they are always gathered
> who do not descend toward Acheron;

Outrage, that is, injury; although he—that is, the angel—who carries them in his boat while passing to Purgatory, when and whom he pleases, may have denied this passage several times. And he gives the reason why no injury has been done to him. For the will of the angel is just, since it is born from the will of God, who is most just. We shall understand this allegorically regarding the living: those who, falling into vices, become dead. And being dead, they are then illuminated by God's mercy through his grace in such a way that they are led to purge themselves of those vices. But not everyone who has fallen into vice is illuminated at the same time; rather, some sooner and some later. Nor can one complain for receiving such grace late. Nor can one know the cause that moves God. For <note>original Latin: "incomprehensibilia sunt iudicia tua domine"</note> *Your judgments are incomprehensible, O Lord*. Therefore, no one should wish to search them out with curiosity. For <note>original Latin: "Scrutator maiestatis deicietur a deo"</note> *The searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory*, as we said in another place. But returning to the poetic fiction: he writes that the souls who are to come to Purgatory are picked up at the mouth of the Tiber by the angel. By this, he means that whoever goes to Purgatory must depart from Rome—that is, come from the obedience of the Church. But from there, some are taken sooner and some later, as it pleases God, except in the year of the Jubilee, in which every soul is taken at its own request. And therefore he says "for three months now he has taken with all peace"—that is, without any contradiction—whoever has wished to enter. And he says "for three months now" because he imagines his descent to have been in the year 1300 in March, and the Jubilee had begun in December for the birth of Christ. Hence, since I was turned toward the seashore where the water of the Tiber <term>un-salts</term> <note>The Italian "sinfala" suggests the mixing of fresh river water with the salt sea.</note>, that is, enters the sea and becomes salt, I was gathered by him at that mouth of the Tiber where the angel has directed his wings, of which he makes a sail, as was said above. And he stays there because from there he goes with his boat to take all the souls who have to go to Purgatory and do not descend toward Acheron, which is the way to Hell. Furthermore, it is manifest that he wished, without departing from his purpose, to imitate Virgil, who feigns that Charon does not transport the souls of those whose bodies are not buried until after a hundred years.

<column-break/>

having gone to Hell and to Purgatory denotes the consideration of vice and then the will to purge oneself of it. This ensures that after death we truly go to Purgatory and not to Hell. Then he turns to Casella, and because he knew that he had already died many years before, he asks him why "so much time," that is, so much time has been taken from him, marveling that from his death until now he had not been transported to Purgatory sooner. And Casella responds that for this reason no injury has been done to him...

> And I: "If a new law does not take from you
> the memory or practice of the amorous song
> that used to quiet all my desires,
> I pray you, please, comfort for a while
> my soul which, coming here with its body,

> he then began so sweetly
> that the sweetness still sounds within me.
> My master and I and those people
> who were with him appeared so content
> as if nothing else touched anyone's mind.

"If a new law": which is imposed from eternity by God in these places. Therefore, it is not new in terms of the law itself, but new to Casella, who was newly subjected to this law. In short, he prays Casella that if the law of that place does not take away the memory of singing (in such a way that he has forgotten it) or the practice (the power to use it), he should sing. Just as in life it used to satisfy him, so now in his death it might console him and give refreshment to his soul, which is weary from having come with the body by such a difficult way. And he, to please Dante, sang a song written by the poet <note>Dante himself composed this poem, which is a philosophical work addressed to Lady Philosophy.</note>, the beginning of which is <note>original: "Amor che nella mente mi ragiona"</note> *Love that discourses in my mind*. This song delighted Dante, Virgil, and the souls who came with Casella so much that it seemed they had no other care in their minds. It is very fitting that just as the entrance to Hell was full of laments and woes, by contrast, the beginning of Purgatory should have sweet songs. For there one goes to manifest damnation, but here to indubitable salvation. He shows that the souls, himself, and Virgil heard the song with great attention. For there is no one whom music does not delight, because our souls, being most perfectly created, cannot exist without supreme proportion, which is nothing other than harmony. Therefore, just as the body composed of elements desires things made of those same elements, so our soul supremely craves harmony. And this moved Aristoxenus <note>A Greek philosopher and pupil of Aristotle who famously argued the soul is a "tuning" or harmony of the body.</note> to say that our soul was harmony. And certainly, it is so natural, as Boethius <note>The 6th-century philosopher whose "De Musica" was the standard textbook on music theory in the Middle Ages.</note> demonstrates in the preface to his *Music*, that every age is delighted by it, and it is so powerful that every man is changed by it. Empedocles <note>A Greek pre-Socratic philosopher.</note> with his music mitigated and extinguished the wrath of a young man who wanted to kill his father's accuser. Pythagoras corrected the one who wanted to burn the house where his girlfriend was with his rival and competitor. Aristotle says in the *Problems* that both he who is grieving and he who...

<header>PURGATORY</header>

and the joyful one uses music. The one to diminish pain; the other to increase joy. There are two kinds of songs, one grave: which the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> and the Romans used, in which Plato wishes the young should exercise. Athanasius forbade that music be used in church: to avoid all lewdness. Ambrose commanded that it be used to excite our minds toward religion. Augustine disputes for and against. Now the author, according to the opinion of Ambrose, denotes through our Casella: that whoever has to support the difficulty and toil of climbing the mountain—that is, purging oneself—should hear that music which invites one to the good, to virtue, and to religion. Nor did Dante introduce, without the highest prudence, that from several love songs written by him, Casella should sing this one: whose beginning is **LOVE that discourses in my mind.** Because as he himself interprets in his *Symposium*, or rather *Convivio* <note>Dante's *Convivio* is a prose work where he provides philosophical commentary on his own poems</note>, he demonstrates in this song that his love is not for a mortal thing: but for philosophy and theology. Whence he said: that love reasons with him—that is, it speaks with ratiocination and the discourse of reason. And it speaks in the mind: that is, in the intellect. Therefore, it is the love of intellectual and celestial things: because lewd love does not "reason"—that is, it does not use reason, as we demonstrated in the first canticle <note>The *Inferno*</note>—but instead excites and moves sensuality: not in the mind, but in the appetite. We shall conclude, therefore, that the poet signifies: that having to endure the laborious difficulty of the climb, we must restore and seek the mind with music, of which nothing is more a friend to the soul. But with that music which contains within itself celestial and divine love: and not earthly love submerged in sensuality.

We all sat fixed and attentive
to his notes: and behold the honest old man <note>Cato of Utica, the guardian of Purgatory</note>
shouting: what is this, slow spirits?
What negligence, what standing-still is this?
Run to the mountain to strip off the slough <note>The "slough" or "skin" refers to the remains of sin that cloud the soul's vision</note>
which does not let God be manifest to you.
As when, gathering grain or tares,
the pigeons gathered at the pasture,
quiet without showing their usual pride,
If something happens that gives them fear,
suddenly they let be the bait,
because they are assaulted by a greater care.
So I saw that fresh troop
leave the song and go toward the slope,
like a man who goes and knows not where he ends up,
Nor was our departure less swift.

<column-break/>

He demonstrates that it often happens: that although we are disposed to purge ourselves of vices: nonetheless some pleasure or delight of earthly and fleeting things attracts us: and makes us leave behind things of importance and stop in those. But after some time Cato—that is, the love of liberty—reproves us and pushes us to purge ourselves. **WE SAT FIXED.** As if to say, we were not only standing still, but standing still with the intent to remain. **WHAT NEGLIGENCE IS THIS.** It is bad in all things we have to do to use negligence. But it is much worse to use it in seeking liberty. **RUN TO THE MOUNTAIN**: to purge yourselves of that stain that so takes away your sight that you do not see God.

However, the souls are rebuked by Cato for lingering, symbolizing how even virtuous distractions can hinder the urgent pursuit of spiritual liberty.</summary>

CANTO THREE
bb ii

### ->.THIRD CANTO OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE.<-

<image-desc>Decorative ornamental initial 'A' at the start of the first verse, featuring a blue letter 'A' on a gold background with red and green floral scrollwork.</image-desc>

Although the sudden flight
scattered them across the plain,
turned toward the mountain where reason probes us,
I drew closer to my faithful companion:
and how would I have run without him?
Who would have led me up the mountain?
He seemed to me remorseful in himself.
O dignified and pure conscience,
how a small fault gives you a bitter bite!

When his feet left behind that haste
which diminishes the dignity of every act,
my mind, which before was restrained,
expanded its focus, as if eager:
and I set my face toward the hill
that rises highest toward the heavens from the sea.
The sun, which behind me was flaming red,
was broken in front of my figure,
for I provided a resting place for its rays.
I turned to my side with fear
of being abandoned, when I saw
the earth darkened only in front of me.

<column-break/>

In this third chapter he places the souls who have been negligent and have deferred their penance and conversion, remaining <term>contumacious<note>Stubbornly disobedient to the authority of the Church</note></term> against the sentence of the Shepherd <note>The Pope</note>, living as excommunicates. Because they did not reconcile themselves out of pride, and because this negligence arises from pride, it is more grave than others. Therefore, it is punished in a lower place. Following the narrative, then, he shows that although the other souls—due to the severe reprimand of Cato—had set off in a scattered run, he nonetheless did not leave, but rather drew closer to Virgil as a faithful companion. For when the desire for liberty spurs a man to leave every delight that might feed the senses in order to purge himself of vices, the lower reason <note>the human faculties</note> ought to wish to hasten to such a work. But nonetheless, one should not move without Virgil: that is, without the higher reason being enlightened, as we have said; because without that, one would err and often leave the enterprise behind due to its difficulty. For the higher reason is that which pulls the lower one toward arduous and laborious things. Whence he said: *Who would have led me up the mountain?*, as if to say: no one, because reason alone pulls one toward the purgatorial virtues. HE SEEMED TO ME REMORSEFUL IN HIMSELF. It is a fitting thing that when the higher reason, adorned with true doctrine, sometimes lets itself grow a bit old through some pleasure—even for a short time, and in a pleasure that is not filthy or ugly, such as this listening to music was—it should feel compunction. Because in such a man there is perfect conscience, every tiny error seems grave to him. Whence he said: *He seemed to me remorseful in himself.* O DIGNIFIED CONSCIENCE. This is an exclamation moved by wonder. Because in truth a dignified and pure conscience is an admirable thing, both for its excellence and because they are rarely found. I do not dislike what is said by many: that the free will in man is the queen of everything, and the intellect and reason are her two assessors and counselors. And discretion and conscience are two officials, and the flesh and the spirit are two messengers. The former <note>the flesh</note> is flattering and a liar. The latter <note>the spirit</note> is harsh and severe. And therefore when the flesh brings forward vicious and mundane things, and the lord <note>the Will</note> contradicts them and agrees with discretion, conscience, reason, and intellect, then this is *conscience*—as if to say <term>with knowledge<note>Original: "con-scientia"</note></term>. But when the lord believes the flesh, the spirit is saddened and the conscience cries out; then it is against conscience. But sometimes, aided by the world and the demon, the flesh imprisons the spirit, the conscience, the reason, and the intellect, and puts in their place as its vicar **obstinacy**, which closes its ears to the lord so that he does not hear the cries of the conscience. Whence he said: *O dignified conscience*, full of dignity and pure, because every small fault bites it greatly.

He shows that Virgil, together with the others, began to run. But it lasted little, because to hasten in taking any side, and not to do things with maturity and consultation but to plunge headlong following one's appetite—even if the thing itself is honorable—is not good. But we must always use maturity, which is the <term>mean<note>The middle path or balance</note></term> between practicing negligence and slowness, and being over-hurried. Whence it happens that sometimes our intellect and reason, moved by an excellent purpose, use too much haste at the beginning, in a way that does not observe gravity and <term>becomingness<note>Original: "condecentia"</note></term>; but soon it realizes and tempers itself so as not to "dismay"—that is, not to disturb the order which requires honesty and appropriateness. This is what the Latins call *decorum* and the Greeks <term>prepon<note>Original Greek: "πρέπον" meaning "that which is appropriate or fitting"</note></term>. And when Virgil—that is, the higher reason—leaves aside

such haste, Dante—who is the lower reason—likewise leaves it, and his intention, which was constrained in that celerity, expands. AND I SET MY FACE TOWARD THE HILL. He did not restrain his haste because he had changed his purpose, but to do that same thing with more order and appropriateness. Therefore, he did not turn his back to the mountain of Purgatory, as one does who wishes to distance himself from it, but he gave it his face because he was going toward it. WHICH TOWARD THE HEAVENS RISES HIGHEST FROM THE SEA <note>Original: "sidiflaga," interpreted here as "dilata" or spreads out</note>. For we say "to flood" [*allagare*] when stagnant water spreads out. THE SUN WHICH BEHIND Dante, in his walking, turned...

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, the text transitions from Dante's realization that he alone casts a shadow into Virgil’s explanation of the nature of spirit-bodies and the limitations of human intellect regarding divine mysteries.</meta>

PURGATORIO

"My comfort, why do you still distrust?"
he began to say to me, turning fully toward me;
"do you not believe I am with you, and that I guide you?
It is already evening <note>original: 'Vesper'</note> there where the body
is buried within which I used to cast a shadow;
Naples possesses it, having been taken from Brindisi.
Now, if no shadow forms in front of me,
do not marvel more than you do at the heavens,
where one ray of light does not block another.
To suffer torments, both heat and frost,
the Divine Virtue disposes such bodies;
how it does so, it does not wish to reveal to us.

Mad is he who hopes that our reason
can traverse the infinite way
held by one substance in three persons.
Be content, human race, with the 'that it is' <note>original: 'quia'. In Scholastic philosophy, a 'demonstration quia' proves that a fact is true without necessarily explaining 'why' it is so.</note>
for if you had been able to see everything,
there would have been no need for Mary to give birth."

<column-break/>

...shoulders to the sun: whereby he saw his shadow before him. And not seeing that of Virgil, he doubted: fearing that Virgil had abandoned him. The sun that was flaming behind him was broken in front of him: it made a shadow before me: which shadow exists because the sun, finding a support—that is, opposition and an obstacle—IN ME, that is, in my body, it is broken and does not penetrate. THE SUN ONLY BEFORE me [darkened] the earth: shadowed. When we begin to ascend toward purgation, the sun—that is, illuminating grace—accompanies us. But its rays penetrate Virgil in such a way that he leaves no shadow of himself. But they do not penetrate Dante, because he has a dense body, with which he holds back the rays and does not let them pass through. Thus it happens that his shadow is seen ahead. Virgil is superior reason, which is entirely penetrable by light; indeed, it is almost light itself. Therefore, no obscurity or ignorance proceeds from it. But Dante—that is, sensuality—has a dense body, not penetrable by rays. Thus he makes a shadow, representing ignorance. Reason is entirely illuminated and has light within itself, like the sun. Sense and appetite are like the moon, which has no light of its own; that which comes from the sun illustrates the surface but does not penetrate. Because on that side which the sun does not strike, it remains obscure. Likewise, appetite and sensuality have no light except what they receive from reason, and that does not penetrate them. Therefore, the other side remains dark. This is, then, the reason why Dante sees the shadow—that is, ignorance—in himself, and not in Virgil.

VIRGIL PERCEIVED that Dante suspected he had been left by him; and therefore, turning fully to him, he said: "Why do you distrust? Do you not believe I am with you? And that I guide you?" And then he adds: "If you do not see my shadow as you see yours, know that this happens because I do not have my body with me, as you have yours. Because that body, at my death, I left in the other hemisphere, where it is already evening—that is, nightfall—because in this place it is morning." NAPLES HAS IT and it was taken from Brindisi: because the poet died in Calabria. But the body was then transferred to Naples, where his epitaph is: "Mantua gave birth to me; Calabria snatched me away. Now Parthenope <note>An ancient name for Naples</note> holds me; I sang of pastures, the countryside, and leaders." <note>original: "Mantua me genuit : calabri rapuere. Tenet nunc parthenope cecini pascua rura duces." This famous epitaph summarizes Virgil's life and his three major works: the Eclogues, Georgics, and Aeneid.</note> And this pertains to the history. But allegorically, the soul that has put down the body—that is, the vices which proceed

from the contagion of the flesh—does not make a shadow, because it remains pure light. And being entirely illuminated, no ignorance remains in it. NOW BEFORE me nothing is shadowed. "If the sun, striking my shoulders, does not make a shadow before me as it does for you, do not marvel, because I do not have a dense body like yours, but a rare one like the celestial bodies. Therefore, do not marvel at these more than at the heavens." For although there are seven planets and the eighth sphere where the fixed stars are, and one is enclosed within the other, nevertheless, because they are of a rare, clear, diaphanous, and transparent body, they give way to their rays, which penetrate down to the earth and to our eyes, so that we see all the way to the fixed stars. And this is because one does not block the ray of the other. TO SUFFER torments, and heats, and frosts. He solves a question that might arise here. For it seems very doubtful: if souls are stripped of bodies (which, being composed of four contrary elements, can suffer pain), how do these souls suffer? To which he responds: that the divine virtue, which every nature serves, wills that they suffer. And it does not want it to be known to us how they can suffer. And therefore he said: "reveal" <note>original: 'si sveli'</note>—that is, be uncovered. This point is much debated by theologians. For all natural reasons seem to conclude that, the soul being incorporeal, it cannot be afflicted by corporeal fire. Therefore, Thomas Aquinas <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas, the preeminent medieval theologian whose work deeply influenced Dante.</note> maintains that they suffer by means of the body: because despite being stripped of their own bodies, God can nonetheless link them to some body in the manner of a "form," just as He linked them to their own bodies to give them life. Or truly, without this, He can link them as necromancers, by the power of demons, link spirits to some image.

IT IS THEREFORE foolish for one to hope that our reason—that is, the human intellect, which is finite—can traverse, can by the discourse of its reason arrive at the end of God's way; and he rightly said "way," because it is that discourse of reason which leads us to the conclusion. WHICH HOLDS ONE substance in three persons. This signifies the Trinity, of which we will narrate some small part in its place...

<summary>Virgil explains why he casts no shadow, contrasting his spiritual state (Reason) with Dante's physical body (Sensuality), and warns against the vanity of trying to comprehend divine mysteries like the Trinity through human reason alone.</summary>

### THIRD CANTO
bb iii
<meta>catchword: / bb iii</meta>

->And you have seen desiring without fruit:<-
->such that their desire would have been quieted,<-
->which is eternally given to them as grief.<-
->I speak of Aristotle, and of Plato,<-
->and of many others: and here he bowed his forehead,<-
->and said no more, and remained troubled.<-

...than one ought to know. BE CONTENT, human race, with the "that it is" <note>original: "quia". In Scholastic philosophy, a "demonstration quia" proves that something is a fact without explaining the underlying "why" or "propter quid."</note>. Aristotle says: In Latin there are two terms: *quare* <note>meaning "why" or "by what means"</note> and *quia* <note>meaning "because" or "that it is"</note>. *Quare* is the "why" that asks a question. *Quia* is that which answers. Therefore, let us imitate the disciples of Pythagoras, to whom they showed such reverence that it was enough, in teaching, to believe: "this is so because it is so." FOR IF YOU HAD BEEN ABLE to see everything—that is, to have knowledge of all divine things—THERE WAS NO NEED for Mary to give birth. Because it was not necessary for God to become incarnate if man had not sinned; nor would he have sinned if he had been able to know everything. AND YOU HAVE SEEN DESIRING without fruit: He proves by the example of the ancient philosophers that the human intellect cannot have perfect knowledge of divine things; since Aristotle and Plato, men of the highest genius, although they supremely satisfied themselves in investigating and supremely desired to find the truth, nevertheless we see that their desiring could not acquire such knowledge. For which reason it was without fruit, and they labored in vain; and the text is arranged thus: You saw desiring without fruit such men as were Aristotle and Plato, and their desire would have been quieted—that is, their desire for knowledge would have been content—had they been able to investigate the truth. But not having been able, such desire is given to them as eternal punishment. For the punishment of such men placed in Limbo, according to Dante, is not being able to have knowledge of that which they have sought. And here he bowed his forehead: which signifies shame and confusion, and he shows himself defeated. AND HE SAID NO MORE: because human reason can say little else of divine things than what it has already said. AND HE REMAINED troubled: considering being deprived of the Supreme Good.

...which will require it more. And certainly he is a fool who believes he has knowledge of divine things. Whence Saint Paul says excellently in the Epistle to the Romans: "O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!" <note>original Latin: "O altitudo divitiarum sapientie et scientie dei: quam incomprehensibilia iudicia eius: et investigabiles vie eius."</note> Therefore, let no one seek how the soul, which is incorporeal and a simple form, can suffer. Since a simple form is <term>impassible</term> <note>incapable of suffering or being affected by external physical action</note>. And let us remember: Do not seek to know more <note>original Latin: "Nolite sapere plus"</note>...

While Virgil was reasoning as has been said, they arrived at the mountain of Purgatory, which is exceedingly high, and at that gate where they had come, it was so steep and sheer that anyone who had a body and had to walk with legs would have been ready and prepared to climb in vain. Because it was impossible. And he made a comparison: that although on the Riviera of Genoa—which to the east toward the Gulf of Spezia has as its furthest limit the castle of the Genoese, <term>Lerice</term>, and to the west has in its furthest part <term>Turbia</term> toward Provence—there are very steep mountains, uninhabitable because of their ruggedness; nevertheless, the most deserted and most lonely [path there] is like a stairway compared to that slope of Purgatory. Therefore, the intellect was attentive—since the way of purgation was so steep and difficult—to find which path might be easier. And certainly it is the office of wisdom for whoever enters into these second types [of life] and virtues to begin from the easiest way before they have formed a <term>habit</term> <note>In Aristotelian ethics, a "habit" is a settled disposition of character acquired through practice.</note>. But little by little, the more we approach the habit, every hour they become easier, as we shall show in the process. But once we have already made a habit of them, not only are they not difficult and laborious, but they are even easy and pleasurable. "Now who knows," as if to say "not I," on which hand the slope falls, either from the right or from the left. HALTING his step: as one does who doubts. SO THAT HE MAY CLIMB who goes without wings: that is, Dante, who has his body with him and does not fly, as the soul does without the body. And allegorically it means that Dante, not being yet purged, does not "fly"—that is, he cannot detach himself from earthly things and elevate himself to divine ones. And he adds that while the mind of Virgil (who stood with his face down) examined the way, Dante looked up around the rock. This signifies that the intellect, with its discourse, examined the way which might lead the soul to purge itself of vices; and he holds his face down, which expresses the gestures of one who is occupied in some research and discourse and in profound cognition. For such a person often stops and keeps his eyes firm and fixed on the ground. Which Virgil expressed elsewhere: "And with equal steps he fixes his tracks" <note>original Latin: "Et paribus auris vestigia figit". A reference to the Aeneid, though the commentator may be paraphrasing.</note>. But Dante, who represents <term>sensuality</term> <note>the part of the soul concerned with the senses and physical experience, rather than pure reason</note>, does not tire himself [with such thought]...

The author wishes to demonstrate how great divine mercy is: and that no one is so great a sinner that up to the extreme point of his life he cannot be saved. And therefore he places Manfred in this spot. Who, although he had been a most cruel enemy to the Holy Church: and to his own kin: as we demonstrated in the 28th Canto of the first canticle: and finally died excommunicated. Nonetheless, he was able to be saved by surrendering to his guilt <note>i.e., repenting</note>. I will not dwell on his history: because we narrated it prolifically above. I will only add this: that Manfred was a very prudent man; and well did he rule his empire. He was beautiful of body. And in his manners pleasant: and cheerful. He delighted in all music: in songs, sounds, and dances. But he was very ambitious and lustful: and of an Epicurean life <note>referring to a life focused on worldly pleasure rather than the soul's immortality</note>: and without religion. <header>PURGATORIO</header>

She <note>Referring to Constance of Sicily (1154–1198).</note> was the daughter of Tancred, King of Sicily, and the wife of Henry VI, the Emperor, and father of Frederick II, who was the father of this Manfred. Therefore, Manfred was the grandson of Constance. He was named after her because the Kingdom of Sicily came to the Emperor Henry through her. **TO MY DAUGHTER:** Who was similarly named Constance; she was the mother <note>original: "genitrice"</note> of Don Frederick, King of Sicily, and of Don James, King of Aragon. **IF SOME SAY.** <note>The OCR "SAL TRINOL" is likely a corruption of "Se alcun dicesse," meaning "If anyone should say."</note> Because it was common rumor that since he died excommunicated, he was surely damned.

> After my body had been broken
> by two mortal stabs, I surrendered myself
> weeping to Him who willingly pardons.
> Horrible were my sins;
> but the infinite goodness has arms so wide
> that it takes all who turn back to it.
> If the Pastor of Cosenza, who was sent
> on the hunt for me by Clement then,
> had well read this page in God,
> the bones of my body would still be
> at the head of the bridge near Benevento,
> under the guard of the heavy cairn;
> now the rain washes them and the wind moves them
> outside the Kingdom, along the Verde,
> where he moved them with lights extinguished.

<column-break/>

This demonstrates how great the divine mercy is, which accepts even a very great sinner who delays conversion until the final moment, like this man; who delayed until after receiving mortal wounds. Nevertheless, whoever surrenders to God by weeping in contrition for their sins can be saved. For we receive the soul from God pure and immaculate, and we must maintain it in such a state until death and so return it to Him. And if we have stained it, confession and contrition wash it clean. **WHO WILLINGLY pardons.** Whereof it is said: *The earth is full of the mercy of God* <note>original Latin: "Misericordia dei plena est terra."</note>. **HORRIBLE were my sins.** God does not pardon one who does not confess as a sinner and does not repent for having sinned; and therefore the author shows that in this man, both were present. The confession: because he says "Horrible were my sins." The repentance: because he says "I surrendered myself weeping." **BUT THE INFINITE goodness has such wide arms.** The arms of God are His mercy toward those who convert, and His justice

---

which rewards every merit. **IF THE PASTOR of Cosenza.** The Cardinal of Cosenza was the legate of Pope Clement IV in the army of Charles of Anjou when King Manfred was killed. After the victory, he had Manfred's body removed from the great tomb which was **AT THE HEAD:** that is, at the head of the bridge of Benevento, treating him as an excommunicated man. Therefore, if this Pastor of Cosenza **HAD READ IN GOD;** that is, in the Holy Scripture, **THIS page:** that is, that passage where this sentence is treated—that divine mercy awaits us until the very last moment of life—he could have surmised that I might be saved and would not have dragged me out from under **THE HEAVY cairn.** At the head of the bridge of Benevento, there was a high tower to guard the passage, and there was a small church there in which Manfred was buried. He calls the tower a *mora* <note>A play on the Italian "dimoranza" (delay/dwelling) or "mola" (mass/tomb).</note> because it causes a delay for those who wish to pass by force; or perhaps he said *mora* to serve the rhyme in place of *mola* <note>meaning a great heap or mass.</note>. For others say that Charles, the victor in this battle, not wishing to bury him in a sacred place due to his excommunication, had him placed in a pit at the head of the bridge, and then had each of the soldiers throw a stone there. Because of this, a massive pile remained over him. Many use this term for any great weight, but especially the great tombs of the ancients were called *moles*. Hence, the Castel Sant'Angelo in Rome, because it was the tomb of the Emperor Hadrian, is called *Moles Adriani* <note>Hadrian's Tomb.</note>. **NOW THE rain washes them:** and the wind moves them, because they have been dug up and left in the open. **OUTSIDE THE kingdom.** Some say that the legate had sworn to drive him out of the kingdom, and not being able to drive him out alive, he drove out the body along the Verde. The Verde is a river <note>Now known as the Liri.</note> that flows into the Tronto, not far from Ascoli. **WITH LIGHT extinguished:** without the honor of candles. He said "with light extinguished" to denote that the Cardinal held him as excommunicated. For when someone is excommunicated, the priest casts down a candle in a way that it is extinguished.

> By their curse, one is not so lost
> that eternal love cannot return,
> as long as hope has a flower of green.
> Truly, he who dies in contumacy
> of Holy Church, even if he repents at the end,
> must stay outside upon this bank
> for thirty times as long as he has been
> in his presumption, unless such a decree
> becomes shorter through good prayers.

<column-break/>

By THEIR curse: by excommunication. **THEIR: the prelates'.** **ONE IS NOT LOST:** one is not lost in such a final manner. **ETERNAL love.** The grace of the eternal God; that this eternal love can indeed return, even though the excommunication had cast him out. **AS LONG AS hope has a flower of green:** As long as we are alive and can return to penitence, hope "has a flower of green," that is, it has life. Anyone who is excommunicated with a "major excommunication" <note>A formal exclusion from the Christian community and sacraments.</note> is cast out from the fellowship of Christians. He does not participate in the orations or prayers made by the Church. He is outside the grace of God and dead...

<header>CANTO THREE</header>
<sig>bb iiii</sig>

See now if you can make me happy:
revealing to my good Constance
how you have seen me and also this prohibition
For here, by those over there, much is gained.

<column-break/>

[...remaining] in such rebellion, he is damned to hell. But returning to obedience before he dies, and being restored to the communion of Catholics, he returns to the grace of God. And if, by the anticipation of death, the time to reconcile with the Church fails him, and nevertheless he repents of his error and dies with true repentance and contrition, the infinite divine clemency forgives his fault; he goes to Purgatory and is saved. 

But Dante here invents <note>The commentator Cristoforo Landino often notes where Dante adds poetic "fictions" to established theology.</note> a rule: that before one can enter Purgatory, he goes wandering around its base for a period thirty times as long as the time he lived in <term>contumacy: willful disobedience to the laws or summons of the Church; here, remaining under excommunication without seeking absolution</term>, so that he may first purge his negligence, as we have said above. However, it is difficult for such contrition to be known to the pastor <note>the Pope or Bishop</note>. And therefore he says: **IT IS TRUE** that whoever dies in contumacy of the Holy Church—understand this regarding the outward demonstration. For he who dies in contumacy regarding the internal act—who does not repent nor humble himself—is damned. **FOR EVERY** time thirty-fold that he has been in his presumption. I believe he sets "thirty" for every number <note>original: "per ogni numero," meaning thirty is used here as a symbolic or representative figure for a long duration</note> and wishes to demonstrate that he who dies excommunicated, even if he returns to penitence, is nonetheless very remote from God; because he delayed his penitence for a long time and received grace late, he multiplied his sins. Whence he is purged late. **UNLESS SUCH A DECREE** becomes shorter through good prayers. 

It is right faith to believe that alms, the sacrifice <note>the Mass</note>, and prayers can induce God to shorten the pains of those who are in Purgatory. Whence Paul the Apostle proves this by the Maccabees <note>Referencing 2 Maccabees 12:43-46, a standard scriptural defense for Purgatory; though the commentary attributes the proof to "Paul," the passage is from the deuterocanonical books</note>, who sent money to the temple to be offered for the souls of the dead. Therefore, our prelates <note>High-ranking church officials</note> ought to bear it in peace if in some place our poet has reproached and reviled their wicked customs, because here he says that which greatly favors them. It demonstrates that he did not have hatred against priests, but against the wicked life of base priests. 

**SEE NOW**: that prayers might be of use to us who are in Purgatory; he says this, in effect, because of the sentence set down above: that you understand how you can make me happy. Revealing to my daughter Constance that I am in a place where she can help me with prayers. **HOW YOU HAVE SEEN ME**. How you have seen me, and also revealing **HOW I STAND [UNDER] PROHIBITION**: that is, forbidden and prohibited from entering Purgatory. And if anyone should say, "What joy does it give you that Dante reveals this?" It is because she will pray for me, and her prayers will cause my time to be shortened. Because here in this place where we purge our negligence, **BY THOSE OVER THERE**—by those who are still in life—much is gained. Much is acquired.

When through delights or perhaps through pains,
that any of our faculties <term>virtu: here meaning a faculty or power of the soul, such as sight or hearing</term> might grasp,
the soul gathers itself so fully to that faculty
That it seems to heed no other power:
and this is against that error which believes
that one soul above another within us is active:
And therefore when something is heard or seen
that keeps the soul strongly turned toward it,
time passes: and the man does not notice it;
For one power is that which listens,
and another is that which keeps the soul entire;
the latter is as if bound, and the former is loose.
Of this I had a true experience,
hearing that spirit and marveling;
for a full fifty degrees the sun had climbed <note>In medieval astronomy, the sun moves 15 degrees every hour. Fifty degrees indicates that over three hours had passed.</note>
And I had not perceived it, when
we came to where those souls, as one,
cried out to us: "Here is what you asked for."

<column-break/>

The same subject matter continues: and he climbs the first ledge; still the place of the excommunicated. Afterwards, in the second, he finds those who purge the negligence caused by sloth <term>accidia: spiritual apathy or sloth, one of the seven deadly sins</term>. But as for these first six tercets: he demonstrates that he had heard Manfredi with such attention that the sun had passed the fourth part of the day, and he had not noticed it. So that no one should marvel at this thing, he demonstrates that when our mind is oppressed by some vehement disturbance, being entirely taken in that form, no other faculty operates.

**WHEN THROUGH** delights or perhaps through pains: he sets down two of the four disturbances: namely, joy (which concerns a present good) and grief or sorrow (which concerns a present evil).

**THAT ANY FACULTY OF OURS MIGHT GRASP**: that is, which delights or pains. **ANY FACULTY OF OURS**: any power of our soul might grasp; for example <note>original: "verbi gratia"</note>; the sensitive faculty has sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Therefore, when the eye sees something that delights it greatly, the whole soul gathers itself so much into that visual power—not ministering its strength to any other power—that it seems to heed nothing else; not only regarding any other sensitive power, but not even the meditative ones, such as the apprehensive, imaginative, and retentive powers. All these powers are species of the soul's capacities, which are vegetative, sensitive, and rational; and each has its own species, which the poet calls "virtues" <term>uirtu: faculties</term>. Thus, the whole soul turns so much to its specific faculty, due to a powerful object of focus, that it abandons the others.

**AND THIS IS AGAINST THAT ERROR WHICH BELIEVES**: against that false opinion of those philosophers who say **THAT ONE SOUL** above another in us is active: that is, that we do not have a single soul, but four. That there are three species of soul is manifest. First is the vegetative soul, which alone, without any other soul, is in plants, such as herbs and trees; through which they grow, nourish themselves, and produce another like themselves. The second is the sensitive soul, and this is in the brute animals; it contains the external senses, such as sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch; and the internal ones: common sense, imagination, thought, fantasy, and memory. The third is the rational soul in man alone. 

Yet there are not three souls in man, but one with three powers. For if there were three souls, in every instance and point of time, each soul would operate its own power. And this is false; as we see here in Dante, who was so occupied in hearing that no other power operated. But if the vegetative and the rational had been distinct souls, the sensitive could well have occupied all its powers, but not those of the others. In man, the vegetative is that which vivifies the body, grows it, and nourishes it; and it begins as soon as the seed is received in the mother's womb. Second is the sensitive; this extends, moves, and feels. Afterwards, when the fetus in the mother's womb has all its members and organs, or rather completed instruments, God creates from nothing the human soul in the body; which takes and unites to itself the vegetative and the sensitive, and gives them that perfection which they would not have on their own. And this union is such that it is the cause of their operation, nor is it ever dissolved; but when it separates from the body, the soul carries them with it, though they have no ability for action. Furthermore, the soul created by God is adorned with three virtues, which it exercises more when separated from the body than when it is in the body. These are memory, intellect, and will. 

There are not, therefore, three or four souls in man, but only the human rational soul; which, finding in the fetus the vegetative power (which we have in common with plants) and the sensitive power (which is common to us with brute animals), does not add itself as a third. Rather, it unites those two to itself, and thus they are together one soul, and not three. For as I said a little above: if they were three distinct ones, it would not follow that when one was entirely occupied in one of its powers, the other two souls would not also be occupied. 

**AND THEREFORE WHEN SOMETHING IS HEARD OR SEEN**: When sight or hearing is much occupied, in a way that it draws the whole soul to itself, time passes away: because that power which would notice this remains dormant. This often happens: when we hear something that delights us for four hours, they seem like one. **FOR ANOTHER POWER**: He assigns the reason why one does not notice [the time]: because the power that sees or hears is not the same as the one that can notice that the...

# CANTO FOUR

...time passes: and because that faculty which sees a delightful thing draws the whole soul to itself, the soul is freed and unhindered. It follows that the part of the soul that should recognize the passage of time remains abandoned and cannot operate. **OF THIS I HAD** true experience: I knew this through experience. This was because while I was hearing and marvelling at that spirit—that is, while I was listening. But listening alone was not enough to make the soul turn entirely toward him, for we often hear something and yet in the meantime we recognize and notice many other things. And so he adds: **AND MARVELLING**: because admiration <note>Landino uses "admiratione" in the sense of profound wonder or being "struck" by something.</note> is what draws the entire soul to itself. **FOR FULLY** fifty degrees the sun had climbed, and through such wonder I had not noticed the journey made, nor that time had passed. This is because each of the two hemispheres is divided by mathematicians into one hundred and eighty degrees. Therefore, five degrees more than the fourth part of the day had passed, because a fourth of one hundred and eighty is forty-five. <note>In medieval timekeeping, 15 degrees equals one hour. 45 degrees is 3 hours; 50 degrees is 3 hours and 20 minutes after sunrise.</note> **WHEN WE CAME WHERE** at that place in which **THOSE SOULS** gather all together **CRIED OUT: "HERE"** showing us the pass. **"IS WHAT YOU ASKED FOR"** which is the place for climbing Purgatory, about which you asked. These negligent souls show the way to Virgil and Dante. This signifies that the errors of others often make us cautious: we see that the voluptuous life of others makes us continent, because such a vice displeases us in them.

> A larger gap is many times hedged up 
> with a little pitchfork-full of thorns
> by the man of the village when the grape darkens <note>Meaning when the grapes ripen and turn purple, requiring protection from thieves or animals.</note>
> Than was the path where he climbed,
> my leader, and I after him alone,
> as that company of souls departed from us.
> One goes to San Leo and descends to Noli,
> one climbs Bismantua and the peak 
> with their very feet, but here a man must fly;
> I mean with the swift wings and with the feathers
> of great desire, following that guide 
> who gave me hope and was my light.

> We were climbing within the broken rock,
> and on every side the edge pressed us close,
> and the ground below required both feet and hands.
> After we were upon the upper rim
> of the high bank, on the open slope,
> "My Master," I said, "what way shall we take?"
> And he to me: "Let not a single step of yours fall back; 
> keep winning your way up the mountain behind me."

<column-break/>

It is no wonder if the way that leads to Purgatory is narrow and steep. For this way represents the "purgatory virtues" <term>uirtu purgatorie: the transitional virtues used to cleanse the soul of vice</term> of which we spoke above; until we have formed a habit in them, they are full of toil and sweat. Hence Hesiod asserts that the gods have placed sweat before virtue. **A LARGER GAP**. First he shows the narrowness of the way, saying that the village man—that is, the peasant—at the time **WHEN THE GRAPE** darkens (begins to turn black because it is ripening) **HEDGES UP** <note>original: "impruna"</note>—mends with thorns—**A LARGER** gap—a larger opening in the hedge—**WITH A LITTLE PITCHFORK OF THORNS**: with as many thorns as can fit on a small fork. **THAN WAS THE PATH**—the narrow way. *Calles* in Latin <note>original: "Calles in latino"</note> properly signifies narrow paths made by the treading of animals. From this we get the word *callaia* (pathway). **ONE GOES TO SAN LEO**. This land is on the summit of Montefeltro; whoever wishes to go there finds a difficult ascent. **NOLI** is a land on the Genoese Riviera, situated in a valley where one descends with great difficulty. **BISMANTUA** is a mountain in the territory of Reggio, very difficult to climb. **THE PEAK** <note>original: "cacume"</note>. Although *cacumen* in Latin means any summit, nonetheless *Cacume* is a very steep mountain in Campania. Some say "on the peak," meaning the summit of the mountain of San Leo. In all these aforementioned places, though they are very steep and rugged, one nonetheless goes there on foot. But the climb of this mountain is almost like a wall, so that wings are needed. He mentions the places above for the height of earthly things—such as riches, power, and lordship—or for the lowliness of a voluptuous life—such as Noli. To these things the feet—that is, human appetite—can reach. But to the purgatory virtues, which have no allurements for the senses, one must fly with the wings of great desire. For he who does not leave behind his feet—which signify sensitive love <term>amore sensitiuo: the soul's physical desires and impulses</term>—and take up wings—that is, the love of incorporeal things—cannot climb there. I am not unaware that some understand the wings to be hope and faith. This is not absurd in this place. And Plato writes that the soul, having come into this low world, cannot return to heaven without two wings, one of which is religion and the other justice; and by religion he understands all the intellectual virtues, and by justice all the moral ones. **FOLLOWING THAT GUIDE**. Following Virgil, my guide, who gave me hope of being able to climb. For the higher reason, adorned with true doctrine, gives hope that a man may ascend. And it shows the way, wherefore he says: **AND WAS MY LIGHT**.

He demonstrates that the way was made by the force of a chisel, breaking the rock, to show that without strength and industry we cannot overcome the difficulty of this ascent, which for the reason stated above is more laborious and troublesome than the rest. This is why the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul</note> said: "A long habit of sinning makes the way of virtue unpleasant and harsh for us." <note>original Latin: "Insuauem et asperam facit nobis uiam uirtutis longa consuetudo peccadi"</note> And Tully <note>Cicero</note>: "The best way of living should be chosen, which habit will then make pleasant." <note>original Latin: "Optima forma uiuendi eligenda e quam iocundam reddet consuetudo"</note> **AND ON EVERY SIDE the edge pressed us close**. The way was...

The text uses rugged Italian geography—San Leo, Noli, and Bismantua—as metaphors for the physical and spiritual effort required.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Purgatorio, Canto IV.
