# PURGATORIO

*...until some wise guide appears /
The summit was so high it defeated the sight /
and the slope much steeper /
than a line from the mid-quadrant to the center /
I was weary when I began /
O sweet father, turn and look /
how I remain alone if you do not stay: /
Son, he said, pull yourself as far as here /
pointing to a ledge a little further up /
that on that side circles the whole hill.*

<column-break/>

very narrow: because virtues consist in the middle, which, compared to the extremes, is extremely narrow. And it is like a line that goes from one part to the other through the center. And every time one leaves this line, one falls into one of the extremes: either in excess or in deficiency. And he adds: that the ground below was so steep that it required feet and hands: that is, it was necessary to go on all fours. Allegorically, this signifies that feet are needed—that is, the appetite—and hands—that is, action and operation. Because it is not enough to have a supreme appetite for climbing, which is to say, for purging oneself, if such desire is not put into action. For as Aristotle says in the *Ethics*: moral virtue consists in operation. <note>original: "lauirtu moral consiste nelloperatione." Referring to the Aristotelian idea that virtue is a habit practiced through action.</note> And in a Christian sense, we can say: that affection is not enough unless one performs satisfaction. **UPON THE BORDER** <note>original: "IN SV LORLO."</note> supreme. They had climbed the highest extremity of the ledge, between which and the other ledge the air was open. For while they were climbing the ledge, they went through that narrow and dark path and did not see. But having reached the edge, they saw the clear slope. **WHAT WAY SHALL WE TAKE?** It is an excellent thing that although the appetite is ignited for the purgation of the soul, nevertheless one must do everything with the counsel of superior reason. And he responds to him: **LET NO STEP OF YOURS FALL.** Do not go toward the slope: that is, never turn back, and do not think of things rejected: both low and earthly. **EVER UP THE MOUNTAIN** straight up the mountain gain ground for me. Follow reason, always ascending toward virtue, until **SOME WISE GUIDE APPEARS TO ME.** For when a man sets out on the journey to climb to the purgatorial virtues, following reason, after some progress God has mercy on his good purpose; and what our fragility cannot do, He supplies with illuminating, cooperating, and perfecting grace: which are wise guides. And of these, we spoke in the first canticle. <note>Referring to the *Inferno*.</note> **THE SUMMIT** the top of the mountain. **WAS SO HIGH THAT:** in such a way that it defeated the sight of my eyes. And in truth, these purgatorial virtues are so lofty and arduous that the eyes of Dante—that is, the contrition of sensuality and inferior reason—cannot reach them. And to demonstrate this difficulty of climbing, he adds: that the slope was "prouder," more steep, than the line <note>original: "lalistra," referring to a geometric line.</note> that goes from the center of the quadrant through its middle up to the circumference. Among the ancient Greeks, the quadrant was called a *Gnomon*. <note>term: <term>Gnomon</term>—the part of a sundial that casts a shadow. Landino uses it here to discuss the measurement of angles.</note> There was no clock of any sort in Rome before this one. And according to Varro and Pliny: Marcus Valerius Messalla was the first who brought the quadrant from Catania, a city in Sicily—which he had conquered during his consulship—in the year 377 after the founding of Rome. And although it was not very accurate, nor did the lines correspond well to the hours, they nevertheless used that one for ninety-nine years. Until Quintus Marcius Philippus—who was censor with Lucius Paulus—placed another more orderly one next to it. This was very pleasing to the people. But because the quadrant is of no use when the sun is covered, Scipio Nasica invented the clock not of dust <note>A sand-glass or hourglass.</note> like ours, but of water: which, dripping very minutely, distinguished the hours. And this was five hundred and ninety-six years after Rome was built; nor do I find that the Romans or other peoples in those times had bells, either for clocks or for anything else. I have said this briefly of the quadrant, which shows the hours. But so that the sense of Dante may be better understood—which is not that the way was straight up like a wall, for it would have been impossible for him to climb it—but that it was slightly less than vertical, we will say that he places the quadrant of the astrologers in this way: Astrologers have three principal instruments. The material sphere, which demonstrates the whole heaven and its circles. The second is the round Astrolabe, <note>term: <term>Astrolabe</term>—an ancient instrument used to calculate the position of celestial bodies.</note> but flattened in the shape of a platter, in which the entire position of the heaven is shown. The third is a quadrant, which is the fourth part of the astrolabe. Therefore, you shall divide a platter from the center by straight lines into four equal parts up to the circumference, and one of those makes the quadrant; and if you take this quadrant and draw a line through the middle from the center to the circumference, and then lay the quadrant down on one of its two sides, then you will see that the line made will not be entirely upright: but nonetheless, it will lack little of it. He concludes, therefore, that the climb was very steep, but not however in the shape of a wall. **I WAS WEARY.** Sensuality and inferior reason are always exhausted in the difficulty of virtuous works. And therefore he asks for comfort. Because the intellect, often going ahead, leaves sensuality behind, which would remain there if one did not turn back and comfort it. <margin>.</margin> And note that Dante calls him "father," and Virgil calls him "son," because he wants to show that already sensuality is so in accord with reason that it obeys, not as a slave to a lord who obeys by force, nor as a disciple to a teacher who wants to understand the reason before he properly obeys, but as a son to a father, who wants his will to be the very same as his father's. When this is in any man, he will not doubt that he can arrive at purgation. These three types of obedience Dante signified in the first canticle when he said: "You father. You teacher. You lord." And there we declared them. **PULL YOURSELF AS FAR AS HERE:** Strive to conduct yourself as far as here.

<summary>Landino explains the extreme physical and allegorical difficulty of the climb up Purgatory, using the geometry of an astronomical quadrant to describe the slope's angle. He emphasizes the transition from human reason to divine grace and the harmonious relationship between Dante (sensuality) and Virgil (reason).</summary>

# CANTO FOUR

For afterwards the way will be less steep: And always in difficult things the beginning is more than half of the whole. <note>original: "el principio e / piu chel mezzo del tutto." A reference to the proverbial idea that "well begun is half done," often attributed to Aristotle.</note> **POINTING TO ME:** Showing me with his finger: which encircled the hill on that side: where Dante was, as we shall see below: because on the other side of the hill there were valleys.

*His words so spurred me on /
that I forced myself to crawl behind him /
until the ledge was beneath my feet. /
There we both sat down /
turned toward the east from which we had climbed: /
for looking back is often a help to one; /
I first directed my eyes to the low shores /
then I raised them to the sun: and I marveled /
that we were struck by it from the left:*

<column-break/>

**T**he higher reason, with its comforts, makes the lower reason do the almost impossible. And it is not without cause that Virgil does not want him to rest until he is on the ledge. Because the slope is a slippery and sliding place: and whoever rests there may slide down. But he who climbs the ledge: because it is not without some level ground: can sit without fear of sliding. Therefore, in very difficult things it is necessary for man to rest. Because otherwise he becomes so weary that he cannot be led to the end. But let him not rest before he is in a place where he does not fall back. They sat down facing where they had come from. <meta>catchword: For</meta>

---

For he who looks back after the climb seems to be comforted by the sight. And allegorically: he who turns his mind back to consider the climb made: that is, the difficulty already passed: comforts and strengthens himself to support what remains. **TURNED TOWARD THE EAST FROM WHICH** they had climbed. Because from there they had begun the ascent. **I FIRST DIRECTED MY EYES** to the low shores. Then I raised them: He takes great comfort who has already set out on the path of virtues, to consider the baseness of earthly things from which he departed. And then the height of the divine things to which he has purposed to climb. And I marveled: that whereas in this hemisphere <note>The Northern Hemisphere, where the readers and Landino reside.</note>, one who stands turned to the east is struck by the sun from the right shoulder—because from there it is midday <note>In the Northern Hemisphere, the sun is to the South at noon.</note>—in that place it struck us from the left. And in this you will note that it is a very great ornament to the poet when, beyond the proper subject of his poem, he illuminates, distinguishes, and embellishes with many other things: as here, deviating somewhat from the main topic, he touches upon some points of astronomy.

---

*The poet clearly perceived that I stood /
dazed by the chariot of light /
where it entered between us and the North. /
Wherefore he said to me: If Castor and Pollux /
were in the company of that mirror /
which leads its light up and down /
You would see the ruddy Zodiac /
rotating even closer to the Bears /
if it did not stray from its ancient path: /
How that may be, if you wish to be able to conceive it /
gathered within yourself, imagine Zion /
standing with this mountain upon the earth /
Such that both have a single horizon /
and different hemispheres; hence the road /
which Phaethon, to his misfortune, knew not how to drive: /
You will see how it must go /
from one side when it goes to the other's flank /
if your intellect observes quite clearly:*

<column-break/>

**V**irgil noticed that I stood dazed: and full of wonder: seeing the chariot of light: that is, the sun <note>original: "carro della luce."</note> being between the north and us. Marvelling then to have it from the north: Since in this hemisphere it would be from the south. The poet wants to show that the other hemisphere, where he pretends to be, is the opposite of this one. Therefore, just as to us the sun always goes from the south and casts shadows toward the north, so to those on the other side the sun comes toward our north. And Virgil and Dante were coming near the side of the equator toward the antarctic pole, which is as far beyond the equator as our arctic is on this side. Nor would Dante have marveled to have the sun from the north if he had considered being in the other hemisphere beyond the torrid zone toward the antarctic. Wherefore Virgil responds that he would see the sun even closer to the north if, as it was in Aries, it had been with Castor and Pollux: that is, in Gemini <note>Castor and Pollux are the two brightest stars in the constellation Gemini.</note>. Where it is to be understood that, starting the Zodiac from Aries, we see that this sign is next to the equator and begins there; after which is Taurus toward the north; and after Taurus are Gemini; and

---

these are so close to the north that the summer tropic ends there. Then is Cancer, which begins on the other side of the north. And after it is Leo, which declines toward the equator. And then is Virgo, which ends at the equator. After these is Libra, which begins below the equator as Aries begins above. The other signs follow, which, moving away from the equator, approach the antarctic pole as far as Sagittarius, where the winter tropic ends. And here begins Capricorn. Then Aquarius, then Pisces, which end at the equator, where Aries begins. Virgil says, therefore, that if the sun were in Gemini, Dante would see it even closer to the north, because that sign is more northerly.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Purgatorio, Canto IV. Landino is explaining the astronomical and mythological context of the Sun’s position in the sky as seen from the Mountain of Purgatory, specifically focusing on the constellation of Gemini and the geography of the spheres.</meta>

-># PURGATORIO<-

He placed Castor and Pollux for Gemini: following, as poets do, the poetic fables which tell that from Jove—who had turned into a swan—and Leda, the wife of Tyndarus, Castor and Pollux were born. Others say that Leda gave birth to two eggs by Jove in the form of a swan: from one was born Pollux and Helen, the wife of Menelaus who was abducted by Paris. And these two were immortal. From the other came Castor and Clytemnestra. Others say there was only one egg, and from it were born Castor, Pollux, and Helen. Some say that Castor was mortal and not the son of Jove, but of Tyndarus. Castor and Pollux, returning with the Argonauts, abducted the daughters of Leucippus, who were betrothed to Lynceus and Idas. Thus Lynceus killed Castor, and Pollux killed Lynceus to avenge his brother. And Idas would have killed Pollux if Jove had not come to his aid. Jove then took them up into heaven and placed them in the third sign of the zodiac called Gemini <note>Latin for "twins"</note>: because it is made of these two brothers, who were twins—that is, born of one birth. And the immortal Pollux shared his immortality with Castor; thus the poets imagine that when one of them descends to the opposite hemisphere, the other rises to ours. Others say they earned their place in heaven because they purged the Greek sea of pirates. Others say because, during the voyage of the Argonauts, they saved the ship *Argo* from many storms. For this reason, they were later invoked in heaven by sailors as "salutary stars"; and when they appeared in the form of lights, the storm would cease, as Pliny writes, and Horace in his Odes: *As soon as their white star has shone for the sailors, the rough water flows down from the rocks, the winds die down, the clouds flee, and the threatening wave—because they willed it so—settles on the deep.* <note>Original: "Quorum simul alba nantis stella refulsit. Concidunt venti levis afflat aura. Et minax quia sic voluere ponto unda recumbit." Horace, Odes 1.12.</note> This is similar to what is said in our times regarding Saint Elmo <note>Saint Elmo’s fire is a luminous electrical discharge seen on ships during storms, traditionally viewed by sailors as a protective omen.</note>. The first, Pollux, has nine stars, of which one in the head and two in the shoulders are very bright. Castor has ten stars. In total, there are nineteen. **WERE THEY IN COMPANY / of that mirror,** the Sun. **WHICH:** who. **SWEATS UP:** in the upper hemisphere and in the lower one, because it illuminates both. Thus Virgil says: *And when the rising Sun has breathed on us with his panting horses, there the red evening sets the lights aglow.* <note>Original: "Nosque ubi primis equis oriens afflavit hanelis. Illic sera rubens accendit lumina vesper." Virgil, Georgics 1.250-251.</note> Others say "up and down" because by its light it illuminates Mars, Jove, and Saturn, the planets located above it, and similarly Venus, Mercury, and the Moon, which are inferior to it. **YOU WOULD SEE THE REDDENING ZODIAC:** You would see that part of the zodiac where Gemini is, which would redden because of the sun if the sun were within it, as it is in Aries. **ROTATE EVEN / closer to the Bears:** because that sign, as we have said, is the closest to the North. **IF IT DID NOT / DEPART FROM the old path.** If it did not take another course than it usually does. **BUT IF YOU WISH / TO COMPREHEND:** why in this place the sun is to our north. **GATHERED WITHIN:** that is, collect your mind within yourself and think of nothing else. **AND IMAGINE Sion:** which is the mountain of Jerusalem. **WITH THIS mountain** of Purgatory. **TO STAND ON THE EARTH:** understand this as being opposite, because Sion is in our hemisphere and this mountain is in the other, one opposite the other; and he explains this saying: **SO THAT BOTH have a single horizon:** that is, the linear circle that divides one hemisphere from the other. But different hemispheres, as has been said. Therefore, just as in our hemisphere the habitable fourth is toward our Arctic pole, so the island of Purgatory is in the other hemisphere toward the Antarctic pole. They say that Jerusalem is at the very center of the earth in our hemisphere, just as Dante imagines that the mountain of Purgatory is in that other hemisphere. **WHERE THE ROAD IS:** the path of the Sun, which never leaves the zodiac. **WHICH PHAETHON knew not how to drive.** Which, to his own misfortune, Phaethon did not know how to hold with his chariot. **KNEW NOT HOW:** to his own harm and ruin he did not know how. Phaethon was the son of the Sun and asked his father to promise him, with an oath, to grant him whatever favor he asked. The Sun promised. Phaethon asked to be allowed to guide his horses through the sky for a single day. The father granted it so as not to be a perjurer. But first, with many reasons, he tried to discourage the rash youth from the undertaking, because he would not be able to manage the ferocity of his horses. But Phaethon did not know how to manage the horses, which, leaving the path of the Sun, came so low that they burned the earth. Thus Jove was forced to strike Phaethon with his celestial lightning bolt. Therefore, he fell dead into the Po River. For this reason Petrarch said, *I hear of Phaethon who fell into the Po and died.* **YOU WILL SEE.** You will understand by these reasons, as is appropriate, that the sun goes to this mountain from the Antarctic pole on one side—that is, the left. **WHEN TO THAT.** of our Arctic pole, goes from our Arctic pole; it goes from the other side—that is, the right. **IF YOUR INTELLECT HEEDS:** that is, pays attention. "To heed" <note>original: "bada"</note> in our language is what in Latin they call "to be vacant for" <note>original: "vacare," meaning to be free from other things to devote oneself to a study or task</note>.

*Certainly, I said, Master, never /
did I see so clearly as I now discern /
where my wit seemed to fail me, /
That the middle circle of the supreme motion, /
which is called the equator in a certain art, /
and which always remains between the sun and winter, /
For the reason that it departs from here /
toward the north, while the Hebrews—*

<column-break/>

Dante demonstrates that he has understood this to denote that sensuality—although by its nature it is not rational—can nonetheless be made a participant in reason. And as a disciple, he tells Virgil what he understands so that he, as a teacher, may correct him where he might fail. **THE MIDDLE circle.** Mathematicians place five parallel circles—that is, equidistant circles—between one pole and the other. The first is near the Arctic pole and is called the Arctic parallel; and this Virgil calls the "cold zone," beneath which

<summary>Cristoforo Landino explains the astronomical orientation of Dante's Purgatory, using the myth of Gemini and Phaethon to illustrate why the Sun appears to the north (left) in the southern hemisphere. He establishes that Purgatory and Jerusalem are antipodal, sharing a horizon but located in opposite hemispheres.</summary>

Following the discussion of the constellation Gemini, the text now moves to Dante’s dialogue with Virgil regarding the arduous climb up the Mountain of Purgatory and the astronomical positioning of the sun relative to Jerusalem and the southern hemisphere.</meta>

# CANTO FOUR

> ...they will see the sun toward the hot part <note>The South</note>.
> But if it pleases you, I would gladly know
> how much further we have to go, for the hill rises
> higher than my eyes can climb.

---

> And he said to me: "This mountain is such
> that it is always difficult at the beginning below,
> and the higher one goes, the less it hurts.
> Therefore, when it shall seem as pleasant to you
> as going downstream in a boat,
> then you will be at the end of this path;
> there, expect to rest your weariness.
> I answer no more; and this I know for certain."
> And when he had spoken his word,
> a voice nearby sounded: "Perhaps
> you will have need to sit down first."

<column-break/>

...is not inhabited because of the extreme cold. And after that, at an equal distance, is another circle called the **Summer Tropic** <note>The Tropic of Cancer</note>. The sun rises to this point in the north. And when it leaves the sign of Gemini, it creates the **summer solstice**, and then it is the longest day of the whole year. All the space between the said circle and the other at the pole is called the **temperate zone**, and it is possible to live there. Afterward comes the third circle, called the **equinoctial**, or rather the **equator**; because when the sun is here, the days are equal to the nights. This occurs at the beginning of the sign of **Aries**, when the sun draws near to us, because until that time the nights were longer. And it occurs at the beginning of **Libra**, when the sun moves far from us, where the days—which were longer—become equal with the nights. From the beginning of Aries until the end of Gemini, the day always grows. Then, from the beginning of **Cancer** until the beginning of Libra, it decreases, because that sign touches the equator circle. On the opposite side from Aries, the day has decreased so much that it equals the night. After that, it continues decreasing through the **meridian signs** <note>southern signs</note> until it reaches Aries: through Libra, Scorpio, and Sagittarius; and at the end of Sagittarius, it makes the longest night of the year. Afterward, at the beginning of **Capricorn**, it makes the tropic and **winter solstice**, and the sun begins to rise toward the north and the days begin to increase, such that at the beginning of Aries they have returned to being equal to the nights.

**THE MIDDLE CIRCLE.** This is the equinoctial circle, which is called the equator because when the sun is in that degree—either of Aries or Libra—which touches this circle, the day and night are equal.

**IN SOME ART:** such as astrology.

**OF THE SUPERNAL MOTION.** The equator circle is in the middle, equidistant from the two poles, the **Arctic** and **Antarctic**, which mathematicians say are fixed and immobile. Within these, the **Primum Mobile** <term>The "First Moved" sphere, which in medieval cosmology was the outermost sphere that imparted motion to all others</term> moves from Aries toward the West, pulling behind it the **eighth sphere** <note>The sphere of the fixed stars</note>, in which is the **zodiac** and the other fixed stars, and all seven planets. Consequently, in twenty-four hours, all these heavens make one entire revolution. Nevertheless, the eighth sphere turns with a contrary motion of one degree every hundred years. Similarly, all the planets turn with contrary movements. This revolution is performed upon two **mobile poles**, which emerge from the two immobile ones mentioned above. And because the space from one pole to the other is 180 degrees, the equator is ninety degrees distant from each pole. Therefore, the equator is the "middle circle" because it is in the middle of the poles and divides the zodiac into two halves.

**AND THAT IT ALWAYS REMAINS** between the sun and the winter. Because if the sun is on this side—that is, in the northern signs—we have summer, and in the other hemisphere beyond the equator, it is winter; and so it is for the opposite. Thus, this circle always remains between the sun (which makes summer) and the winter.

**FOR THE REASON** that it departs from here. The reason is that the sun departs from here—that is, from this hemisphere—which is under the meridian signs: Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces. And it goes toward the north because at that time it was in Aries, which touches the equator from the upper, northern side.

**AS MUCH AS** the Hebrews: that is, as much as the Hebrews <note>meaning the people in Jerusalem</note>. These people are as close to the equator in our hemisphere as Dante was in the other hemisphere. The meaning is this: the sun, going toward the north, is as far from the mountain of Purgatory in that hemisphere as it is far from Jerusalem when going toward the southern signs. And therefore he says "toward the hot part." Nor does it seem to me that any other story is intended here.

**BUT IF IT PLEASES YOU:** Let the poet remember that most true sentence: *The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak* <note>original: "Spiritus promptus est caro vero infirma"</note>. Therefore, although Dante—representing sensuality—is obedient to reason, nevertheless virtuous works seem difficult to him in the beginning. It is no wonder, then, if his eyes do not reach the summit of this mountain; for one who is still at the beginning of the **purgatorial virtues** <note>the process of spiritual purification</note> cannot understand the progress until the end.

Often in the same man a dispute arises between appetite and intellect. Therefore, where there is not yet a true **habit** <term>Habit: An 'habitus' or settled state of character acquired through practice, making virtuous action easy and natural</term> of the virtues, the operation of those virtues is difficult to the senses. But when Reason is asked by the senses when the climb will end, she does not set a determined space; for if one had to always practice virtuous works, the senses would be terrified. Instead, she shows what is true and can greatly comfort the senses, saying: "Climb boldly." For the nature of this steep path is such that the more one climbs, the easier it becomes. Certainly, because frequent and repeated actions little by little induce the "habit," which, once acquired, makes the operations that first seemed difficult become easy. It happens that...

<summary>Dante questions Virgil about the difficulty of the climb, leading to an astronomical explanation of the sun's position and a moral lesson on how the struggle for virtue becomes easier as the soul is purified.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Purgatorio, Canto IV. Following the discussion of the sun's path and the difficult ascent of the mountain, the text now focuses on the transition from effort to "habit"—where virtue becomes easy—and the encounter with the souls of the Late Repentant, specifically the negligent ones who sit in the shade of a large boulder.</meta>

# PURGATORY

The more we approach the habit <note>The term 'habit' (habito) here refers to the Aristotelian concept of a settled disposition where virtuous action becomes second nature.</note> through practice, the less difficult it will be for us. Therefore, when this climb appears pleasant to you, such that mounting it will be as easy as sailing downstream with the current of a river, then you will be at the end of the climb—that is, at the perfection of operations, which is the "habit." For this reason: **THERE, EXPECT TO REST YOUR WEARINESS.** It is as if he says: defer all your rest until that place; and in the meantime, do not stop along the way, because virtuous actions would not lead you to the habit if you did not continue them. **I ANSWER NO MORE**, because this is sufficient for him. Hold it for true, because just as we said a little above regarding Aristotle, so I say: that all philosophers take it as a certain thing, and experience agrees with their authority, that the sign of having formed a habit is to take delight in the actions. But here he especially places the habit of the purgatorial virtues, because they are much more perfect than the civil virtues. This will be easy for you to understand if you return to the place where I have spoken of them in detail. **AND AS he had spoken his word**, **A VOICE nearby sounded**. Who this was, you will understand a little further down. And he says "sounded," as if he wants to show that he spoke clearly and with a certain efficacy, because he spoke from the soul. And since he <note>Referring to the soul of Belacqua.</note> had always fled from labor, this climb seemed much more difficult to him than it appears to one who is used to some virtuous exercise.

> At the sound of it, each of us turned,
> and we saw on the left a great boulder,
> of which neither he nor I had taken notice before.
> We drew near there, and there were people
> who were staying in the shade behind the rock,
> as a man through negligence puts himself to stay.

"In the first, you will have distress"—that is, hardship. These words were meant to discourage Dante. This signifies that whatever notice we have of such men is that, either by example or by words, they discourage us from virtuous undertakings. But since these souls are in Purgatory, it is not to be understood that he used such words to harm Dante. Rather, he could not contain himself; having such horror for the most laborious ascent, he spoke his mind out of compassion rather than envy. The rock that took the heat away from them—that is, the light of the sun—is the stupor and the heaviness of sloth, which takes away the heat of the sun (the love of virtue) and the light (which is the light of reason).

> And one of them who seemed weary to me
> sat and embraced his knees,
> holding his face down low between them.
> "O my sweet lord," I said, "look
> at that one who shows himself more negligent
> than if Sloth were his own sister."
> Then he turned to us and took notice,
> moving his face just up along his thigh,
> and said: "Now go on up, you who are so capable."
> I knew then who he was, and that anguish
> which was still quickening my breath a little
> did not prevent my going to him; and after
> I had reached him, he barely raised his head,
> saying: "Have you well seen how the sun
> drives his chariot from the left shoulder?"
> His lazy actions and his short words
> moved my lips a little to a smile;
> then I began: "Belacqua, I do not grieve
> for you anymore; but tell me, why seated
> right here? Are you waiting for an escort,
> or has your old habit simply taken you back?"

<column-break/>

Virgil and I turned toward where the voice came from. And we saw those souls on the left side, to denote the depraved and slow leisure of negligence. And not without reason does he say that they were not yet aware of them. Because the life of the negligent is like death. He performs no action by which he might come into notice, whether for good or for evil. Therefore, they were passing by without having notice of him, if one of those souls had not spoken.

He could not better express a negligent person than by placing him sitting on the ground with his legs gathered up, in such a way that, wanting to look up, he directs his sight up over his thighs. And although it is uncomfortable to sit in that manner, nevertheless sloth holds him there. Hence Solomon says: <note>original: "Abscondit piger manus suas sub ascellas suas: et laborat si eas ad os convertit."</note> "The sluggard hides his hand in his bosom; it grieves him to bring it again to his mouth." <note>Proverbs 26:15.</note> Furthermore, these words **NOW GO ON UP**, you who are so capable, demonstrate the same thing. For the negligent person is indignant that another is diligent, and mocks him with ironic words. And he does the same a little below, when it says that he barely raised his head and mocked him for wanting to know why the sun cast a shadow to the left; because the lazy always mock those who are diligent in investigating any worthy thing. **THAT ANGUISH**, that toil. **WHICH QUICKENED MY BREATH**, which hurried my breathing or rather my wind. For whoever goes uphill has plenty of breath and it causes him toil. Because the motion and the weight of carrying the body upward excites heat. And the more it heats the heart, the more air and breath the lungs must draw to the heart to cool it. Thus, so much breath causes toil. **A LITTLE TO A SMILE**, because a modest man does not use too much laughter. **I DO NOT GRIEVE** for you, because I see you in a place of safety <note>Belacqua is in Ante-Purgatory, meaning he is eventually destined for Heaven, so Dante no longer fears for his soul's damnation.</note>. He gains goodwill here from his person, showing that...

### CANTO FOUR

it would have been bothersome to have found him in a worse state. And having made him well-disposed, he reproves him to stir him from such great laziness. **WAIT FOR US.** <note>Dante is calling out to Belacqua.</note> You wait. **BELACQUA:** He called him by his proper name, which denotes love and benevolence, as when we speak to equals or inferiors. For this reason, the Virgilian Juno, speaking to Aeolus, names him, saying: "Aeolus, for to you the father of gods and king of men [has given power over the winds]." <note>original: "Eole nanque tibi diuum pater atque hominum rex." A quote from Virgil's Aeneid, Book I.</note>

And he: "O brother, what does it profit to go up?
For God's bird who sits at the gate
would not let me go to the torments.
First it is necessary that heaven circle me
outside of it for as long as it did in life,
because I delayed my good sighs until the end:
Unless a prayer first helps me,
which rises up from a heart that lives in grace;
what good is the other which is not heard in heaven?"

And already the poet was climbing ahead of me
and was saying: "Come now, see that the meridian
is touched by the sun, and from the shore
night already covers Morocco with her foot."

<column-break/>

**O BROTHER.** O brother. **WHAT DOES IT PROFIT:** what use is it **TO GO UP.** As if to say, it is of no use. And the reason is that "God’s bird"—that is, the angel—who sits at the gate of Purgatory (who will be discussed further below) would not let me enter. This is because it is necessary that the sky turn around me for as long a time outside that gate of Purgatory—that is, that as much time passes—as the time that passed during my life. And this is according to the fictional rule established above: because I delayed "good sighs" <note>A poetic term for sighs of repentance and contrition.</note> until the end of my life. That is, the sighs that proceed from true contrition and repentance for errors committed, and from a supreme desire to return to the right path. They are therefore called "good" because they help and make good the one who uses them. And note the author's opinion here: that the prayers of one who is in mortal sin do not help those in Purgatory.

Reason <note>In this commentary, Virgil often represents Human Reason.</note> did not want to delay any longer in laziness, and therefore he admonished Dante to rise. **SEE THAT THE MERIDIAN.** That is, the equatorial circle is touched by the sun. Therefore, if the sun had arrived at this circle, it signifies that it was noon. **AND ALREADY NIGHT COVERS WITH HER MOROCCAN FOOT FROM THE SHORE.** That is, stretching from the sea near Morocco, or Mauritania, which is a region of Africa located in the West. The meaning is this: since it was already midday in the hemisphere where Dante was, night was rising from the shore of Morocco—which is West to us, but was then East for them. And from this, he infers that neither day nor night is equal in all parts of the hemisphere, because it is morning in the East before it is midday, and it is midday before it is evening in the West.

<summary>Belacqua explains that he must wait outside Purgatory proper for a duration equal to his life because he delayed repentance. Virgil then urges Dante forward, noting that it is midday and night is beginning to fall on the opposite side of the globe.</summary>

### CANTO FIVE

...oppressed by some sudden disturbance: it makes the voice hoarse. And "two as if sent by the others asked us" not saying. **MAKE US LEARNED**. <note>original: "FATENE SAGGI"</note> Make us taught and learned. **OF YOUR condition**. Of your state.

"My master: 'You may go your way /
and tell those who sent you back /
that this man's body is true flesh. /
If they stopped to see his shadow, /
as I believe, they have their answer; /
let them do him honor, for it may be dear to them.'" /
Never did I see ignited vapors <note>shooting stars</note> /
at midnight cut through the clear sky /
nor August clouds at sunset: /
That they did not return upward in less time, /
and once there, with the others, turn back to us /
like a troop that runs without a rein. /
"This people pressing toward us is many /
and they come to entreat you," said the poet, /
"so just keep going, and listen as you walk." /

...and corpulent: which do not pass the middle region of the air. But they are congealed by the cold: or truly they dissolve and fall down. But those which are thinner: they rise higher. And of these, less is seen, as they are resolved into wind by the heat. And the more viscous ones, not being able to be resolved: they rise so high that, being near the sphere of fire, they ignite. And if they are of a small quantity: they quickly resolve: and thus ignited they fall in the form of a star. Whence Ovid: <note>original: "Que si non cecidit potuit cecidisse uideri"</note> "Which, if it did not fall, could be seen to have fallen." <note>Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 2.322, describing the fall of Phaethon.</note> And of these the poet speaks at present. But if they are of much material, the fire is hard pressed to resolve them in form: so that sometimes they burn: not only for many days: but even for more months. **AUGUST CLOUDS**. When the sun is in Leo and especially when it is near the dog star <note>Sirius</note>: it happens that the clouds, pushed by the heat, descend quickly. Because heat joined with moisture always generates wind: and the wind pushes the clouds.

"O soul that goes to find joy /
with those members with which you were born," /
they came crying out, "quiet your step a little. /
Look if you have ever seen any of us, /
so that you may carry news of him over there. /
Pray, why do you go? Pray, why do you not stop? /

which, following the steps of such a guide, /
makes me seek it from world to world."

<column-break/>

They wondered that one with a body could climb the mountain. This signifies nothing else: except that it seems impossible that a man still in life can attain the purgatorial virtues. And certainly it is a marvelous thing: that the soul, oppressed by the contagion of the body, submerged in pleasures and corporeal desires, can be freed from them. Whence in Wisdom, not without wonder, it is said:
> <note>original: "Beatus uir qui inuentus e sine macula : et qui post aurum non abiit . Nec sperauit in pecunie thesauris. Quis est hic et laudabimus eum. Fecit enim mirabilia in uita sua ; Qui probatus est in illo ; et perfectus e/."</note> "Blessed is the man who is found without blemish, and who has not gone after gold, nor put his hope in treasures of money. Who is he, and we will praise him? For he has done wonderful things in his life; he who has been tested by it and perfected." <note>Sirach/Ecclesiasticus 31:8-10.</note>

But Virgil, i. the intellect, knows: that although this excellence is in few, nonetheless it exists. Whence he adds: "Let them do him honor": because truly the man who reaches this degree deserves immortal praise. This he expressed by saying: "Who is he, and we will praise him?" **Vapor I never saw**. Aristotle writes in his *Meteorologica*: <note>Landino refers to Aristotle's theories on atmospheric phenomena.</note> that terrestrial vapors drawn on high by the sun are sometimes so thick...

**THEN LIGHT FROM HEAVEN**. The illuminating grace of the Holy Spirit. **REPENTING** and forgiving: one cannot end his life in a form where his guilt is forgiven if he does not repent of the errors committed. And who does not forgive: as it is established in the prayer to God:
> <note>original: "Dimitte nobis debita nostra sicut et nos dimictimus debitoribus nostris."</note> "Forgive us our debts as we also forgive our debtors."

**WHO PIERCES US WITH DESIRE**: With the desire for Himself, God further inflames us and constricts our hearts. Nor should one say that it does not seem just that one who has sinned all his life can be saved at the end by repenting at the end. Because just as the body, while health remains in the heart, can be restored to optimal health although the rest is infirm, so the soul, infirm through sin, is restored to health while **prevenient grace** <term>prevenient grace</term> <note>A theological term for grace that comes before any human action, preparing the soul for salvation.</note> remains in it; which induces and disposes the soul, after which disposition there follows illuminating, cooperating, and perfecting grace. I remember having spoken of divine grace in the second canto of the first canticle <note>Inferno, Canto II</note>: as much as that place required where it treated of virtues lower than the purgatorial ones. Now, because the purgatorial virtues are more excellent, I will add some things about divine grace to those we wrote above, which are very useful to know. And first, that man cannot without divine help...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto V of Dante's Purgatorio, following the interaction with the group of spirits who died by violence but repented at the last moment. The commentator is explaining the theological necessity of grace and the nature of the "peace" Dante seeks.</meta>

<columns>2</columns>
<header>PURGATORIO</header>

and by grace to attain blessedness. For it is clear that man, according to the suitableness of his nature, belongs to the participation of the highest good—which is God—more highly than the inferior creatures. And because he has intellect, he can understand through his own operation that truth which is not understood by the senses. For example: the truth that honey is sweet is understood by the sense of taste, which is common to us and other animals. But that God is our highest good, we do not understand by sense, but by the intellect, in which no other animal but man participates. Nevertheless, the human intellect is not sufficient by itself to reach its highest good—which is placed in a certain divine knowledge that exceeds our natural faculty. If, then, man is ordered toward that end which transcends his strengths, it is necessary that he be helped by divine grace. Nor should anyone say that by the help of divine grace man is forced to act according to virtue. Though Christ says in the Gospel: "No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him" <note>original: "Nemo potest uenire ad me: nisi pater qui misit me traxerit eum." John 6:44</note>. And Paul to the Corinthians: "The love of Christ urges you" <note>original: "Caritas Cristi urget uos." 2 Corinthians 5:14</note>. For divine grace provides for all things according to the proper mode of each, as Thomas Aquinas <term>the Aquinate: a reference to St. Thomas Aquinas, born in Aquino</term> clearly demonstrates in his work *Against the Gentiles*. But it is proper to every rational creature to act voluntarily and to be the master of his own operations. Therefore, he acts according to virtue through the help of divine grace, which corroborates the will but does not constrain it. Because man cannot come to his ultimate happiness without virtue—that being the reward of virtue—and forced operations are not of virtue, since virtue does not exist without choice, nor choice without the voluntary. Whence we do not say that brute animals are happy, except by metaphor and similarity, because they do not act according to virtue. This is demonstrated in the 30th chapter of Deuteronomy, where it says: "Consider that today the Lord has set before your sight life and good, and on the contrary death and evil: that you may love the Lord your God and walk in His ways" <note>original: "Considera quod hodie proposuerit dominus in conspectu tuo uitam et bonum: et e contrario mortem et malum: ut diligas dominum deum tuum: Et ambules in uiis eius."</note>. And in Ecclesiasticus: "Before man is life and death, good and evil. Whatever pleases him shall be given to him" <note>original: "Ante hominem est uita: et mors: bonum: et malum. Quod placuerit ei dabit illi." Sirach 15:17</note>. Nor do I wish to omit in this place that no one by his own merits can attain divine help. Although this is proved with many arguments, this one suffices us: every reward and price that is given and conferred must have proportion to the merit, so that in the retribution just equity is observed, and the reward is not greater than the merit. But the effect of divine help, without any proportion, surpasses and transcends our operations, which we perform according to our own faculty. Therefore, man does not merit divine grace by his own operations. For which reason Paul says to Titus: "Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to His mercy He saved us" <note>original: "Non ex operibus iustitie que fecimus nos. Sed secundum sua misericordiam saluos nos fecit." Titus 3:5</note>. Nor should there be anyone who, because of the words of the prophet saying "Turn to me, and I will turn to you," believes that our operations precede divine grace. Rather, our conversion, with which we turn to God, helps grace subsequently. From this, the error of the Pelagians <term>Pelagians: followers of Pelagius who believed humans could achieve salvation through their own will without divine grace</term> is manifest; they wanted us to receive such help through our merits, and that the beginning of our justification should be in us, and afterwards perfection should come from God. It is, therefore, not a reward for our merits, but grace. Whence Paul to the Romans: "If it is by grace, it is no longer by works. Otherwise grace is no longer grace" <note>original: "Si gratia est iam non ex operibus. Alioquin iam gratia non est gratia." Romans 11:6</note>. Nor is it difficult to understand that through "grace-making-pleasing" <term>gratum facient: a theological term for sanctifying grace which makes the soul pleasing to God</term> man attains the ability to love God, because it is an effect of divine love within us; that is, it makes us love God. And certainly, the first intention of one who loves is that he be loved by the one he loves. And the beloved cannot help but love in return. Therefore, through the same grace, we are loved by God. For which reason Paul to the Romans: "The love of God is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us" <note>original: "Caritas dei diffusa est in cordibus nostris per spiritum sanctum: qui datus est nobis." Romans 5:5</note>. And John: "He who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him" <note>original: "Qui diligit me diligetur a patre meo. Et ego diligam eum. Et manifestabo ei me ipsum." John 14:21</note>. The divine doctors demonstrate that divine grace creates faith in us; it creates the hope of pure beatitude. It shows that man without divine grace cannot persevere in the good, nor can he free himself from sin without it, nor flee from it. But let us return to the text.

**BY THAT PEACE** <note>Dante, *Purgatorio* V, 61</note> as if to say, by the true peace, which is not that which the world gives, but that which our Redeemer left to us as a final testament when ascending back to where he had descended. In which peace is true happiness. For Saint Augustine writes that just as in the City of God the highest good is called eternal life, so too can peace be called the highest good. Whence the Psalm sings: "Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem; praise your God, O Zion. For He has strengthened the bars of your gates; He has blessed your children within you. He who has made peace your borders" <note>original: "Lauda hierusalem dominum: lauda deu tuum fyon. Quoniam confortauit seras portarum tuarum: benedixit filios tuos i te. Qui posuit fines tuos pacem." Psalm 147</note>. The Psalm therefore calls its end—that is, its highest good—peace. And a little further down he defines it: that the peace of the celestial city is a most orderly and most harmonious society and company for enjoying God.

**WHO FOLLOWS THE FEET OF SUCH A GUIDE.** <note>Dante, *Purgatorio* V, 62-63</note> Because, as we have shown: if the appetite does not follow reason, it will never acquire peace. But following reason, reason will lead it from world to world, leading it first through Hell—that is, through the knowledge of the vileness, ugliness, and detriment of vices, which leads to hating and fleeing them. And consequently, we desire to be freed from them. Whence from Hell we pass into Purgatory; that is, we come to the knowledge of those things that purify us. And being purified, we ascend to Heaven.

And one began: "Each of us trusts
in your kindness without you swearing it,
provided that 'I cannot' does not cut off the will"

<column-break/>

**W**ithout swearing it: Without you having said "by that peace." And it is arranged thus: **EACH** trusts in your kindness. Provided that "I cannot"—that is, the lack of power—does not cut off, curtail, or impede the will.

Wherefore I, who speak alone before the others,
pray thee, if ever thou see that country

That thou be courteous to me with thy prayers
in Fano, so that for me it may be well prayed,
that I may purge my heavy offenses:

<gloss>I was from Fano.</gloss> BUT THE DEEP HOLES: The deep and mortal wounds. This man, after the destruction of Troy, sailed to Italy and established Padua, which he called *Patavium* <note>original Latin: "Patavium"</note> according to Servius <note>Servius was a famous 4th-century commentator on Virgil.</note> from that which is *petesthe* <note>original Greek: "petesthe," meaning to fly.</note> i.e., to fly; because he took an omen from the flight of birds; or truly: *quia telo petiuit auem* <note>original Latin: "because he sought a bird with a spear."</note> i.e., he struck a bird with an arrow. WHO HELD ME IN WRATH: who bore me great hatred; MORE THAN WAS right: more than justice and equity permitted. Just as an unjust thing is called "twisted," so justice is called "straight" <note>This explains the Italian word "dritto" (straight/right).</note>. TOWARD LA MIRA: La Mira is a castle in the Paduan territory. WHERE one breathes: where one is alive, where one pants, that is, living. ENTANGLED ME: They enveloped and hindered me.

Then another said: "So may that desire
be fulfilled which draws thee to the high mountain,

I was of Montefeltro, I am Buonconte;
Giovanna and the others have no care for me,
wherefore I go among these with lowered brow."
And I to him: "What force or what fortune
led thee so far astray from Campaldino,
that thy burial place was never known?"

the will. BETWEEN ROMAGNA AND THAT OF
Charles: <gloss>that is, of Puglia;</gloss> of which Charles "Lackland," <note>Charles of Valois was often called "Sans-Terre" (Lackland), though the commentator notes him here as King of Puglia, likely confusing or conflating him with Charles of Anjou.</note> Count of Provence and then King of Puglia, was ruler. And he refers here to the March of Ancona.

The Imolese <note>Benvenuto da Imola, an early and influential commentator on Dante.</note> recites a long history of the war that occurred between Azzo III, Marquis of Ferrara, and the Bolognese and Parmesans; which, because it does not seem necessary to me for this passage, I omit. Let it suffice only that in those times, Azzo, striving to acquire many friends in Bologna out of a desire to make himself lord there, caused such suspicion in that people that they confined many of his friends and killed some. And at this time, Messer Jacopo del Cassero, a citizen of Fano, became the *Podestà* <term>Podestà: a high-ranking city official or chief magistrate in medieval Italian communes</term> of Bologna; he, with crude and reproachful words, disparaged the reputation of the Marquis. And among other things, he said that the Marquis had lain with his stepmother, and that he was descended from a washerwoman. This was so offensive to the Marquis that from that time forward he always had him tracked by hidden assassins. And finally, as Jacopo was going to be the *Podestà* of Milan, he sailed from Fano to Venice, and from there toward Padua. And in the Paduan territory, in the marshes which are near the Oriaco mountain, he was killed by the aforementioned assassins.

Buonconte was the son of Messer Guido, Count of Montefeltro, whom we treated in the 27th Canto of the *Inferno*. This man, fighting against the Guelfs <term>Guelfs: a political faction supporting the Pope, rivals of the Ghibellines</term> in the rout of Casentino, was seen dead there; but his body was never found. Therefore the poet feigns that which he describes here. WHAT FORCE or what fortune: Since either his own strength or good fortune should have pulled him from the hands of the enemies. CAMPALDINO is a plain in Casentino at the foot of the mountain of Poppi toward the village on the hill. In which the Guelfs, in a decided battle, broke the Ghibellines <term>Ghibellines: a political faction supporting the Holy Roman Emperor</term>. Because the army of the Guelfs was already in this place, Guglielmo, Bishop of Arezzo and captain of the Ghibellines, sent Buonconte to scout and spy on the Guelf camps, and how they were governed and arranged. Buonconte, finding everything in excellent order, comforted the Bishop, advising him not to start a fight. But the Bishop, more reckless than skilled, wanted to fight. And he was killed. Likewise, Buonconte was killed, along with about two thousand Aretines. Our people <note>The commentator identifies with the Florentines/Guelfs here.</note> had this victory, especially through the industry and boldness of spirit of Corso Donati, as appears in the Florentine annals.

"Oh," he replied, "at the foot of the Casentino <note>A mountainous valley in the upper Arno region of Tuscany.</note>
a stream crosses named the Archiano,
which rises in the Apennines above the Hermitage. <note>The Hermitage of Camaldoli, a famous monastery.</note>
Where its name becomes void, <note>Meaning where the Archiano flows into the larger river Arno and loses its identity.</note>

fleeing on foot and bloodying the plain.
There I lost my sight and my speech;
I ended with the name of Mary, and there
I fell, and my flesh remained alone.
I tell the truth, and you tell it among the living:
God's angel took me, and he from Hell
cried out: 'O you from Heaven, why do you rob me?
You carry away the eternal part of this man
for one little tear that takes him from me;
but I will deal with the rest in another way.'

You well know how in the air is gathered
that humid vapor which turns back to water
as soon as it rises where the cold catches it.
Joining that evil will which only seeks evil
with the intellect, he moved the smoke and wind
through the power that his nature gave him. <note>Dante suggests that demons, as fallen angels, retain natural powers over the physical elements like weather.</note>
Then the valley, as soon as day was spent,
he covered with mist from Pratomagno to the great ridge,
and made the sky above so heavy
that the pregnant air turned into water;
the rain fell, and to the gullies came

And as it converged into great torrents

My frozen body at its mouth
the raging Archiano found, and swept it
into the Arno, and undid the cross upon my breast
Which I made of myself when pain overcame me;
it rolled me through the banks and through the bottom,
then covered and wrapped me with its prey."

<column-break/>

The Archiano is a river which rises in that
slope of the Apennines which is above the Hermitage of
Camaldoli; it descends into the Casentino and enters the Ar-
no between Poppi and Bibbiena. He arrived, therefore, flee-
ing along the road from Arezzo and along the Arno, until the
point where the Archiano, entering the Arno, loses its name.
And therefore he says: WHERE ITS NAME BECOMES VOID. That is, its name
becomes empty. THERE I ended: I died. IN THE
NAME of Mary: Yielding myself in repentance and invok-
ing Mary for my help. MY FLESH REMAINED:
my body alone without the soul. Our body is
much inferior to the soul because the soul is sim-
ple. The body is composite. The former is incorruptible;
the latter corruptible. The former has eternal life; the latter
has no life except that which it receives from the soul. Therefore,
in the separation, it seems the soul does not remain
alone, because it remains alive and with all its pow-
ers. But the body remains deprived of life, of motion,
of senses, and of all its virtues—therefore, alone.
THE ANGEL of heaven took me because of my conver-
sion and contrition. And he of hell grieved because of my past errors, for he was robbed of the eternal part of me;
that is, my soul, which is eternal and immortal. BUT I WILL DEAL WITH THE OTHER: with the mortal and
corruptible part. ANOTHER way: because you lead the soul to salvation, I will destroy the body. And it follows in what
manner: by moving a sudden rain, he buried it in the mud and sand of the Arno.

The Aristotelian doctrine follows regarding the genera-
tion of rain. For this philosopher
writes in his *Meteorologica* <note>original: "meteora," Aristotle's treatise on natural phenomena.</note> that the humid vapors of the
earth, raised by the sun, rise to the second region
of the air; and there, struck by the cold, they turn back
into water. The Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> divide the air into three
parts: the upper part, being a neighbor
to the sphere of fire, stays always hot. The lower part is simi-
larly hot because the rays of the sun, striking
the surface of the earth, warm it with their reflection.
Therefore, only the middle part—be-
cause it is neither near the fire nor reached by the reflection
already mentioned—remains cold, up to this height,
which many claim to be 40 *stadii* <note>original: "stadii," an ancient unit of distance.</note> i.e., five
miles above the earth. The sun draws humid vapors from the earth
and from the sea. These, condensed there by the cold,
turn into clouds and distill into rain. JOINING THAT evil will. An-
gels were created with free will. And being able
by that to turn their will in whichever direction pleased them
most, the black angels, raised up by pride, turned
it toward evil; just as those obedient to God turned it toward
good. Therefore, being damned, their evil will remains
unchangeable, as the "Aquinante" <note>Thomas Aquinas, referred to by his birthplace, Aquino.</note> demonstrates through many
reasons in the book he wrote *Against the Gentiles* <note>original Latin: "contra gentiles"</note>.
And that demons have power [over the elements] appears both through
Saint Augustine and through Albertus Magnus in a
small book of his titled *On the Power of Demons* <note>original Latin: "de potentia demonum"</note>.

HE MOVED THE SMOKE AND THE WIND. He calls the vapor "smoke"; which, drawn up by the sun, resolves in the humid
and cold part into water, and in the hot and dry part into wind. From this arise sudden and impetuous
rains. THE RAIN fell AND came to the gullies: as much of it as the earth did not sustain. The rain falls and the earth,
sucking it in, suffers and sustains as much water as it can. The rest runs to the gullies, and from the gullies to the rivers, and from the ri-
vers to the sea. Thus the gullies swelled the Archiano; and the Archiano, becoming fierce and impetuous,
found his body at its mouth—that is, where it enters the Arno—and pushed it into the Arno; and the Arno, turning it over...

The Imolese <note>original: "Limolese"; refers to Benvenuto da Imola, a prominent 14th-century commentator on Dante.</note> writes that this Pia was of the Tolomei, a noble family of Siena. And as Messer Nello was very powerful in the Maremma, he often lived there; and one day, while the lady was at the window, he commanded one of his servants to throw her down. The reason that led him to do this was not well known.

# CANTO SIX OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' featuring a stylized floral or landscape scene inside an ornate square frame, colored in blue and gold tones.</image-desc>

When the game of dice <note>original: "zara"; a popular medieval gambling game played with three dice.</note> breaks up,
the one who loses remains behind, grieving,
repeating the throws and sadly learns;
with the winner all the people go;
one goes in front, and one catches him from behind,
and another at his side brings himself to mind.
He does not stop, and listens to this one and that;
the one to whom he reaches out his hand stays no longer,
and thus he defends himself from the crowd.
Such was I in that thick throng,
turning my face to them here and there,
and by promising, I freed myself from it.

<column-break/>

**IN** this canto, at the beginning, he continues his description of those who delayed their conversion and penance until their violent death. And afterward, he begins to treat those who, because of family cares or some worldly teaching, likewise delayed their penance. In the first verses, wishing to show that many were gathering around him—and he, turning now to this one, now to that, and promising as much as they asked, got himself clear of them—he uses the comparison of one who departs as the winner from a game.

**THERE WAS THE ARETINE**: Messer Benincasa of Arezzo, a man most learned in civil law <note>original: "iniure ciuili"</note>, was the deputy of the chief magistrate <note>term: "podestà" (the high official of a medieval Italian city-state)</note> of Siena. He condemned to death Turino da Turrita, a castle in the Sienese territory, who was the brother of Ghino di Tacco, and Taccio, Ghino's uncle, because together with Ghino they had stolen a castle from the Sienese Republic <note>original: "re. p. saneſe"</note> called Radicofani, and were practicing highway robbery in the Maremma. It was nevertheless the custom of Ghino, though he blocked the roads, that he did not wish for any of the captives to be killed. After this time, Messer Benincasa went during the papacy of Boniface <note>Pope Boniface VIII</note> as a judge of the tribunal of Rome—others say he was an Auditor of the Rota <note>term: "auditore di ruota" (a judge in the highest ecclesiastical court of the Catholic Church)</note>. Hearing this, Ghino was so bold that he went to Rome and entered the house, into the hall where Messer Benincasa sat on the bench, and in the presence of many he killed him; and he escaped safely with the head, which he had cut off. They say that Ghino 

was large of stature, big-limbed, and very robust, and very generous. He practiced robbery not out of greed, but to be able to practice generosity. And he always wanted those who fell into his hands to set their own ransom price, and afterwards he would return a good portion of it to them. And if he found studious men, he gave them money and encouraged them in their studies. Boniface, recognizing that he plundered only for the sake of generosity, called him to Rome and made him a Knight of St. John <note>original: "caualier friere"</note> so that he could live honorably. Yet finally he died near Asinalunga. This Ghino is the one about whom Giovanni Boccaccio wrote a novella <note>referring to *The Decameron*, Day X, Novella 2</note>, where he tells how he cured the stomach of the overly pampered Abbot of Cluny <note>original: "abate dumacenſe"</note>. **AND THE OTHER** means the Aretine. This was Ciacco of the Tarlati of Arezzo, who, in the rout of Montaperto <note>a famous battle in 1260</note>, while fleeing, drowned. But I believe more those who say otherwise. The Tarlati were lords of Pietramala in Arezzo, very powerful citizens; and there were also the Bostoli, a most noble family. Tarlato fathered Angelo and Cione. From Angelo was born Guido, Bishop of Arezzo, who ennobled his homeland with walls, roads, castles, and many other things. Cione, the Bishop’s uncle, was a very robust man of great spirit. In those times there was war between the Tarlati and the Bostoli. But the Bostoli, having been driven from Arezzo, had occupied the castle of Rondine, not far from Arezzo. It happened then that in a skirmish, while Cione was pursuing the Bostoli, he was carried by his horse into the Arno, the river near Rondine, and drowned in it. Federigo was the son of Count Guido, of those from Battifolle, and he was killed by one of the Bostoli named Fornajuolo. **THE ONE FROM PISA**. Messer Marzucco of the Scornigiani of Pisa was a knight and a doctor. Riding one day from Suvereto, a serpent of stupendous size crossed his path; he was so terrified by it that he vowed to become a Friar Minor <note>a Franciscan monk</note> if he survived. Having become a friar, his son Farinata was killed. In this calamity he showed such constancy that he celebrated the funeral rites together with the other friars and accompanied him to the grave. Afterwards, turning to his relatives with a long and most fitting speech, he led them to peace. And he kissed the hand of the murderer which had killed his son. He was like another Anaxagoras, who, upon hearing of his son's death, was not at all disturbed, but said to the one who brought the news: "You tell me nothing new, for I knew I had fathered a mortal." And Cato in a similar case said: "My son has satisfied nature, because he was mortal." But so as not to leave behind the case of the serpent: they say it fed on piglets, much to the horror of the locals. They, as a final remedy, gathered all the sows <note>original: "troie"</note> from the surrounding area in the place where the serpent lived. Sows are very ferocious animals toward those who offend them; and gathered together in great harmony and pressed close, they make a simultaneous assault on the enemy. By these, then, the serpent was torn apart and killed. **I SAW COUNT ORSO**. Some believe he was of the Alberti of Florence, killed by his kinsmen. This family has been ennobled in our Republic by many virtues and by great humanity and generosity, and especially by the splendor of two most excellent men. First, Messer Alberto, who for a long time served with great integrity and prudence in the government of the lands subject to the Church, and earned the honor that Pope Eugene IV <note>original: "Eugenio . pp. IIII"</note>, with the great favor of the entire college, made him a Cardinal. The second is Leon Battista <note>referring to Leon Battista Alberti, the famous Renaissance polymath and architect</note>, the delight of our city, a man most eloquent in both the Latin and Tuscan languages, born to investigate the secrets of nature and filled with every kind of science. If I were to enter into his praises now, I would run out of time before running out of material. He was most sharp in every part of philosophy and a supreme mathematician. His book on architecture surpasses all the writers of our century. **SOME**. Which I rather believe, say Pierre de la Broce <note>original: "dalla broccia"</note> was secretary and counselor to Philip the Fair, King of France. Because he had great influence with the King, he was brought into such hatred by the barons of the court through envy that they turned the King’s wife against him; she accused him to her husband of having attempted to corrupt her chastity. Therefore, the overly credulous King had him killed. But he did not entirely follow the example of Otto in...

<columns>2</columns>
<header>CANTO SIX</header>
<sig>cc iiii</sig>

emperor <note>Referring to the King of France, Philip the Bold.</note>: who, having had a knight of great valor killed based on a similar accusation, later learned the truth and had the false accuser, his wife, burned. Let the false queen <note>Mary of Brabant, whom the text accuses of framing Pierre de la Broce.</note> therefore take heed—she who is of the House of Brabant—and perform such penance while she is alive for this false accusation, so that after death she does not remain among the damned.

---

As soon as I was free from all those 
shades who prayed only that others might pray, 
so that their journey to become holy might be hastened, 
I began: "It seems you deny me, 
O my light, expressly in a certain text, <note>Dante is referring to Virgil’s *Aeneid* (Book VI), where the Sibyl tells Palinurus that the decrees of the gods cannot be changed by prayer.</note> 
that the decree of heaven bows to prayer. 
And these people pray for just this: 
would their hope then be in vain, 
or is your word not clearly manifest to me?" 
And he to me: "My writing is plain, 
and the hope of these souls does not fail, 
if one looks well with a healthy mind. 
For the peak of judgment does not stoop <note>term: "non favalla" (does not stoop or lower its standards). This means God's justice remains perfect and intact even when mercy is shown.</note> 
because the fire of love fulfills in a single moment 
that which he who stays here must satisfy. 
And there where I fixed that point, 
it was because prayer was disjointed from God. 
Truly, regarding so deep a doubt, 
do not stop until she tells you— 
she who brings light between the truth and the intellect. 
I do not know if you understand if I say Beatrice; 
you will see her above, upon the summit 
of this mountain, smiling and happy."

<column-break/>

Dante raises a question to Virgil, saying: "These souls have hope that prayers made to God for them will shorten the term of their punishment. And you, in one of your texts, show that God does not bow to prayers." For in the sixth book <note>of the *Aeneid*</note>, when Palinurus prays that Aeneas might carry him across the Acheron, the Sibyl responds: *Cease to hope that the decrees of the gods can be turned by praying.* <note>original: "Desine fata deum flecti sperare precando"</note> And he concludes that he does not doubt Virgil is in error, but whether these souls have a vain hope remains a doubt. And Virgil responds: that his writing (that is, the text mentioned above) is plain, as if to say manifest and open. Therefore Dante understands it well. And on the other hand, the hope of these souls does not fail (that is, it does not deceive them), because prayers move God. And nonetheless, one part does not contradict the other. For he who looks with a healthy mind knows that God is immutable; and nonetheless, through prayer, the punishment of the souls who must be purged is shortened. For God's justice does not fail, even though the time of punishment is shortened. Wherefore he says: **THE PEAK** of judgment—meaning the height of judgment—does not stoop; it does not diminish. **BECAUSE THE FIRE OF LOVE**: because the ardor of charity, which is in the heart of the one who prays for the dead, causes to be completed in a moment **THAT WHICH MUST** be satisfied—the amount one ought to satisfy—**WHO STAYS HERE**: whoever remains here. Or we might say: that God from eternity knows who sins, and how much such a sin deserves to be punished, and also how much the charity of some intercessor can diminish from that time. Therefore He judges the soul to stay in purgatory not as long as the sin deserves, but as much as remains after that which the prayers of others have diminished. As the Holy Scripture says: *Charity covers a multitude of sins.* <note>original: "Caritas operit multitudinem peccatorum" (1 Peter 4:8).</note> And this is according to the Master of the Sentences <note>term: "Maestro delle Sentenze" (Peter Lombard, a 12th-century theologian whose book of *Sentences* was the standard textbook of medieval theology).</note> regarding good works: that the soul in purgatory performed in life those works which earned the merit that such prayers should avail it. But as for those who are still in life, it is manifest: that he who is repentant of sin can recommend himself to God with such fervor, and pray for the remission of his sins, that he satisfies in a moment—through the excessive degree of love—that which he would otherwise not satisfy in many years. **AND THERE WHERE I FIXED THAT POINT.** He shows that Virgil was in Hell when he said that prayers cannot change God, because those who are in Hell are already disjointed by the sentence given from every mercy of God. **AND THERE WHERE I FIXED THAT POINT**, that is, in Hell, where the Sibyl affirmatively says to Palinurus that he must stay a hundred years, as has already been judged. **IT IS NOT AMENDED**, that is, it is not purged, **THE DEFECT**, that is, the sin, by praying. Because God does not hear prayers made for the damned; and therefore he says that in Hell, prayer was disjointed from God. **TRULY**: excellent advice and useful to every Christian: that in similar doubts one should not seek any other determination than that which Holy Theology provides, because one could fall into many heresies. **IF SHE.** Just as visible things are objects of the eye but cannot be understood by it without the medium of light, so the truth is the object of the intellect, and is understood by it through the medium of natural light. But this is not sufficient for the knowledge of every truth. For the knowledge of divine things—which transcend us—the light of illuminating grace is necessary, which is signified by Beatrice. And we see her at the top of the mountain because she surpasses all earthly things. **UPON THE SUMMIT**: upon the peak of this mountain, where Purgatory ends, where the author imagines the Paradise of Delights <note>The Garden of Eden, or Earthly Paradise.</note> to be. He wishes, then, that Beatrice be in such a paradise, smiling and happy, because our first father <note>Adam</note> received such grace in this place, and while he remained in it, he was smiling and happy.

<summary>This page contains Dante's inquiry into whether prayer can alter divine decrees, contrasting Virgil's pagan writings with Christian theology. Virgil explains that while God's justice is immutable, the "fire of love" from the living can satisfy the debt of the souls in Purgatory, though this does not apply to the damned in Hell.</summary>
