# PURGATORY

...certainly that among us mortals one is made worthy of such grace: in short, joy continually feeds on sweetest nectar and ambrosia in the contemplation of divine things.

And I: "Lord, let us go with greater haste,
for I no longer tire as I did before;
and look, the mountain now casts a shadow."
"We shall go forward with this day,"
he answered, "as much as we now can;
but the fact is of a different form than you suppose:
Before you reach the top, you shall see return
him who is already hidden by the slope <note>Referring to the sun, which is setting behind the mountain from Dante's perspective.</note>,
so that you no longer break his rays.
But see there a soul who, placed
all alone, looks toward us;
it will point out to us the quickest way."

We came to it—O Lombard soul,
how you stood there, lofty and disdainful,
and in the movement of your eyes, honest and slow!
It said nothing to us,
but let us pass on, only watching
in the manner of a lion when it rests.
Yet Virgil drew near to it, praying
that it might show us the best ascent;
but that soul did not answer his request,
But of our country and our life
it asked us. And the sweet leader began:
"Mantua..."—and the shade, all withdrawn into itself,
Rose toward him from the place where it first stood,
saying: "O Mantuan, I am Sordello,
of your own land!"—and one embraced the other.

<column-break/>

**It demonstrates:** that once he understood Beatrice was at the summit, his desire to see her was so great that love made him more vigorous and light. And certainly, every time we are certain of where our destination lies and we realize we are on the path, a marvelous desire is created in us to quicken our pace, and every fatigue becomes light. And therefore he says: **I NO LONGER TIRE** as before. **WE SHALL GO** with this day: Virgil responds that we will climb as long as the day lasts, because one cannot climb at night. This is because vices cannot be purged within the darkness of ignorance, but rather by the custom of reason. Hence the divine precept: <note>original: "Ambulate dum lucem habetis: ne tenebre uos comprehendant"</note> "Walk while you have the light, lest the darkness overtake you." And he shows that a single day will not bring him all the way to Beatrice, which signifies that without a long duration of time, one does not form the habit of the purgatorial virtues. **ILL DONE** <note>original: "MAL facto"</note>. But this climb is of another form and manner, and of another logic—as if to say it is much more difficult—**THAN YOU SUPPOSE**—that is, than you establish in your mind, because a long and very steep journey remains for us. And he shows here that in beginning arduous tasks, we are often deceived, because it seems to us immediately at the start that we have acquired much more than we actually have. And he adds: that before we exit, the sun—which now, because it falls to the west, is taken from us by the slope of the mountain—will rise anew from the east. In which fiction he shows that although one goes through Purgatory with the light and glow of reason, nonetheless, because one in this state is not yet in the perfection of virtue but is traveling toward it, the darkness of sensuality can sometimes hide the light of reason from us, and in that time we cannot proceed along the way of salvation. But because reason finally overcomes the senses, the sun returns. We shall say, then, that he who is in Hell never sees the sun, but always walks with darkness. But he who is in Paradise is never overtaken by darkness, but is positioned before the mirror of eternal light, continually seeing everything in it. He who is in Purgatory is sometimes with the sun and sometimes with darkness, but he cannot climb except when he is with the sun for the reason we showed a little while ago. **BUT SEE THERE:** Here he signifies having come to the fifth kind of those who, through family occupations or certain studies, were negligent in their penance. And he places that soul alone because the management of a family and the study of some doctrine is a matter more private than public.

Many read: "we came to it," and then understand that Virgil said: "O Lombard soul." And if anyone should object, asking how Virgil knew this man was a Lombard, they answer: that his clothing, and a certain quality and air—a property, so to speak, of each region—which the Latins call <term>captus</term> <note>Meaning the general appearance, grasp, or "air" a person carries.</note> and which is better understood than expressed, made him recognize him. But it seems to me that Dante, in his narration, says: **WE CAME** to it; and then uses this exclamation in praise of Sordello at the present time of writing, when he already knew it had been Sordello. **LOFTY and disdainful:** in our language we call "lofty and disdainful" one who, through excellence of spirit, does not look at or give thought to base things, nor deems them worthy. So it demonstrates a certain generous refinement and is without vice. For when one despises something not out of greatness of spirit, but out of too much arrogance, he shall be called not lofty, but proud. And likewise, he who through that same arrogance does not yield to anything is called stubborn. Hence **Petrarch** used such words in their proper significance when he said: "Lofty and disdainful..."

<summary>Dante and Virgil encounter the soul of Sordello, a fellow Mantuan, prompting a discussion on the necessity of the light of reason (the sun) for spiritual progress. The commentary explains Sordello's solitary state as a reflection of his private life and scholarly negligence.</summary>

### CANTO SIX

...not proud or shy. **SHE DID NOT SAY A WORD, BUT LET US** pass by, only watching us as a lion does when it lies down. And the author most excellently compares the nobility of Sordello to that beast, which is by its nature very noble. That Sordello did not respond to Virgil, who was asking for the way forward, but instead asked him about their homeland and country, is said to denote that this man had not been a student of philosophical and theological matters, but only of history and <term>geography<note>original: "digrographia." Likely a corruption of "geography" or "chorography," the description of regions.</note></term>—that is, of the form and site of regions and of their cities—for he had written nothing else. Therefore, he could not dispute with those learned in other doctrines. **THE GENTLE GUIDE VIRGIL BEGAN** to respond, intending to say that Mantua was his homeland. But as soon as Sordello heard "Mantua," he interrupted his speech, because he was so devoted to his homeland and loved every citizen of it so much that he immediately revealed himself and embraced him with the greatest affection. Sordello was a Mantuan and a very studious man, an investigator of anyone who at any time had been of excellent learning, talent, or counsel; he wrote a volume which he titled *The Treasure of Treasures* <note>Referring to the "Ensenhamen d'onor" or other works attributed to Sordello in the medieval tradition.</note> regarding such matters.

> Ah, enslaved Italy, hostel of sorrow,
> ship without a pilot in a great storm,
> no mistress of provinces, but a brothel!
> That noble soul was so ready,
> only for the sweet sound of his land,
> to welcome his fellow citizen here;
> while now in you, your living people
> do not stay without war, and one gnaws at the other,
> even those whom one wall and one moat enclose.
> Search, wretched one, around your shores
> and your coastlines, and then look in your heart,
> if any part of you enjoys peace.
> What use is it that Justinian adjusted the bit for you,
> if the saddle is empty?
> Without the rider, the shame would be less.
> Ah, people who should be devoted
> and let Caesar sit in the saddle,
> if you well understand what God marks for you.

<column-break/>

The supreme love that Sordello showed to Virgil for being his compatriot gave Dante the occasion to create an invective against all the cities of Italy, in which—due to the opposing parties of the <term>Guelphs and Ghibellines<note>The two primary rival political factions in medieval Italy, generally supporting the Pope and the Holy Roman Emperor respectively.</note></term>, who were then fellow citizens—all civil charity was extinguished, and they persecuted one another with deadly enmity. **ENSLAVED.** He says this as if to say: while there was unity and virtue within you, you were the empress of other regions. Now, through your discords and vices, you are a slave. But why does he say "slave"? We shall say that one finds "master" and "slave" according to nature, and according to custom and law. But nature, the best mother, makes slave and master according to merit. For just as in a man, reason is naturally the master, and the rule belongs to it and it must be obeyed—because with <term>prudence<note>original: "prudentia"</note></term> it understands what is to be done, and with justice it uses it rightly—and the appetite is the slave and must obey reason, because by nature it is of a robust and vehement impulse to follow what is useful and profitable and to flee the opposite. So, too, in the fellowship of men, those who—either by natural counsel, long experience, or acquired learning—surpass others in prudence and goodness are naturally free and ought to command.

<column-break/>

And others in whom the strengths of the body abound, but who lack industry and wisdom, are slaves and ought to obey their betters. See, then, that "free" and "slave" come from nature. But also a certain consent of men and many civil laws establish "free" and "slave," though in different ways. And free men are of three types: <term>Ingenui<note>Latin for "free-born."</note></term>, <term>Liberti<note>Latin for "freedmen."</note></term>, and <term>Libertini<note>Latin for the children of freedmen.</note></term>. *Ingenui* are those who are born free, and of a father and mother who were always free. By *Liberti*, understand those who at one time were slaves and then, for having served faithfully, were made free. Of these, the ancients chose those who by faith and prudence were fit for domestic government, treating them almost like sons and entrusting them with all family care. *Libertini* were those who, although born free, nevertheless had parents who had been slaves. Although sometimes and in certain periods, as Suetonius shows in the *Life of Claudius*, *libertini* are placed in the same meaning. So much for free men. Slaves are those who, captured by enemies, lose their liberty and remain in the power of those who possess them. There are also slaves by civil law: those who are born to female slaves, and the master of the slave woman could sell them. Later, in Canon Law, it is prohibited to sell or keep in servitude anyone born of a Christian. There was also a law among the ancients by which the <term>praetor<note>A high-ranking Roman magistrate.</note></term> could adjudge a debtor as a slave to his creditor; these were called <term>addicti<note>Latin for "assigned" or "bound."</note></term>. **HOSTEL OF SORROW.** A dwelling of pain. Because your inhabitants, due to factions, are in constant wars, from which infinite calamities and tribulations are born, bringing constant sorrow with them. **SHIP WITHOUT A PILOT** in a great storm. The government of the republic is compared by all writers to seafaring. For in a ship, it is necessary to have someone seated at the helm to direct it on a good path. Thus, every civil government must have a governor. And just as the sea rises in a great storm due to the force of contrary winds, so in cities, through various perturbations of the citizens, many discords, dissensions, furies, and tumults arise. Therefore, Dante judging that of Italy there should be the...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Purgatorio, Canto VI, specifically focusing on the famous invective against Italy ("Ahi serva Italia"). The previous page concluded with the initial description of Sordello's embrace of Virgil upon hearing the word "Mantua."</meta>

# PURGATORIO

the Emperor is the head; and if he is not present, it shows that just as a ship caught in a storm must perish if it is without a pilot, so a city in the midst of discord goes to ruin if it has no excellent guide. **NOT MISTRESS OF PROVINCES.** Not the lady of other regions, as she used to be. **BUT A BROTHEL.** A prostitute; he uses the place to describe those who inhabit it. He says metaphorically that Italy is no longer a "lady"—one who is chaste, uncorrupted, modest, and worthy of reverence, who does not stray from the straight path for any reason and governs her family most honestly with good prudence and equity. Therefore, she is no lady—that is, no just governess. **BUT SHE IS A HARLOT.** This name in Latin <note>original: "meretrix"</note> does not mean every unchaste and lustful woman, but only she who sells her body for a price, who sells her honor and chastity for money. Thus, Italy is a harlot because the spiritual and temporal governors within her do not proceed with justice and restraint, but for the price of <term>barratry<note>The sale of public offices or political favors.</note></term> and <term>simony<note>The buying or selling of ecclesiastical privileges or church offices.</note></term> they turn black into white. Therefore, Italy is a prostitute, because for money she sells honor, honesty, and justice. **THAT SOUL.** These two tercets are clear; they show, to the shame of the living, how sweet a welcome Sordello gave simply by hearing the name of his homeland. **SEARCH, O ITALY,** your coastlines. **AROUND THE SHORES.** Around the extremities. Since Italy is in the middle of two seas: for she has the Tyrrhenian to the south and the Adriatic to the north. It is as if he says: consider all your borders, and then notice if in all that is embraced by these boundaries there is any part that enjoys peace. **WHAT DOES IT AVAIL** that Justinian <note>The Byzantine Emperor (r. 527–565) who codified Roman Law.</note> adjusted the bit for you? He freed Italy from the Goths and reformed it with excellent laws, as we shall say in the sixth canto of *Paradiso*. If **THE SADDLE** is empty, the metaphor continues: for it is not enough to bridle the horse if no one mounts to guide it. Thus, it is not enough for Italy to have the laws of Justinian if the Emperor is not allowed to govern the cities of Italy. And in this, he intends to rebuke the **Guelphs** <note>The political faction supporting the Pope.</note>. They can very well excuse themselves, saying it was not to rise against the Empire, but to defend the liberty of their homeland—which the **Ghibellines** <note>The political faction supporting the Emperor.</note>, with the favor of the Emperors, wished to occupy with tyrannical pride. And to defend the sacred majesty of the Apostolic See, they opposed their unjust arms. **WITHOUT IT, THE SHAME WOULD BE LESS.** For the infamy would be less if Italy had no laws and did not live according to them. And he adds that the Italian people should not take jurisdiction away from Caesar, knowing that God commands it in the Gospel. For when He said: "Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and unto God the things that are God's" <note>original: "Reddite que sunt Cesaris cesari: et que sunt dei deo."</note>, He showed that in temporal matters He wants us to obey temporal lords, and in spiritual matters, spiritual ones. And this same thing is denoted by the symbol when, at His last supper, the apostles said: "Behold, two swords" <note>original: "Ecce duo gladii."</note>, and He replied that they were enough.

-> Look how this beast has become savage <-
-> for not being corrected by the spurs, <-
-> since you laid your hand upon the bridle. <-
-> O German Albert, who abandons <-
-> her who has become wild and untamed, <-
-> and who should have straddled her saddle-bows, <-
-> may a just judgment fall from the stars <-
-> upon your blood, and let it be strange and manifest, <-
-> so that your successor may have fear of it! <-
-> For you and your father, held back <-
-> by greed for those lands yonder, have suffered <-
-> the garden of the Empire to become a desert. <-

<column-break/>

He laments Emperor Albert <note>Albert I of Austria (r. 1298–1308).</note>, who has abandoned Italy, which he calls the "garden of the Empire" as the most beautiful region. Thus, she remains without a legitimate lord and has become rebellious and stubborn, like a horse that is not ridden; this continues the metaphor already begun above. This Albert was the Duke of Austria, the first-born son of Emperor Rudolph. In the year of our salvation 1298, after Adolf <note>Adolf of Nassau.</note>, who had been elected, died in battle, Albert succeeded to the throne. The following year, through his ambassadors, he notified Pope Boniface VIII that he wished, according to custom, to come to Rome for the imperial crown. To these men the Pope replied that Albert was not legitimately elected, nor did he consider him worthy of the Empire, since he had unjustly

moved war against the King his lord and killed him with fraud. At this response, Albert stood armed in the royal seat with the crown on his head. The *predella* is that part of the bridle held in the hand. **MAY IT FALL.** Therefore, let a just judgment fall from heaven, and let it be "strange"—that is, unusual—and "manifest" and "open," so that it causes more terror. This is happening—or rather, had already happened—though the author, following the custom of poets, presents it as a future thing. CC. v

they say to him: that Henry <note>Henry VII of Luxembourg (reigned 1308–1313), whom Dante saw as the potential savior of Italy.</note> his successor wanted, while passing through to Rome, to provide a remedy. But death intervened there. Thence you may know.

Come see the Montecchi and Cappelletti <note>The warring families of Verona, famously known later as the Montagues and Capulets.</note>

those already saddened, and these in dread!

<column-break/>

<margin>These were two families in Verona: who drove out Azzo II, Marquis of Ferrara and governor of Verona. But he, with the favor of the Counts of San Bonifacio, won and returned to Verona. The Monaldi and Filippeschi were two opposing families in Orvieto.</margin> **THE OPPRESSION of your nobles:** the oppression that the lords of Italy practice upon their subjects. **AND CURE their sores.** Correct their failings and vices. **AND YOU SHALL SEE Santa Fiora:** the Counts of Santa Fiora. These are in the Maremma between the territory of Pisa and Siena. **HOW SHE IS CARED FOR:** how she is governed: or truly how "secure" she is: as if to say: that the country is broken and full of robbers and thieves. **WIDOWED AND ALONE:** because the Emperor being the King of the Romans, Rome, deprived of the Emperor, remains widowed and alone. And you shall see hatred and enmities in place of love.

Finally, come to see how much the people love one another; and if you have no pity for Italy, come to be ashamed of your own infamy. And certainly every prince should be ashamed who does not rule with supreme justice and most humane clemency those who are under his protection. Because, as Plato writes—and all philosophers affirm and sacred theologians command—the King and all other princes have not been raised to such dignity for their own profit or leisure, but for the tranquility of all the peoples subject to them. They toil so that the people may rest. They stay awake so that the people may sleep. They do not flee dangers so that the people may live securely. No other reward is proposed to them but honor. Therefore, they must not usurp what belongs to others, but preserve it, and always contemplate the best things. Whence Isaiah: *A prince thinks of things that are worthy of a prince* <note>original: "Princeps que sunt digna principe cogitat"</note>. For this reason they were called "Kings" (*reges*) from "ruling" (*regendo*), because to rule is nothing other than to sustain the people so that they do not fall into ruin, and to direct them toward a tranquil life, in which each holds his own and abstains from that of others. And the Greeks call them *Basileis* because they are the *basis* <note>original: "basis lau. i. fondamento"</note>, that is, the foundation of the people. Because they must be those upon whom the tranquility of all is founded and has its stability. And Homer and all other poets call them *poimenas laon* <note>original: "pimenas laon"</note>, that is, "shepherds of the people," because they must not strip them nor rule them violently, but like a good shepherd, feed and nourish them. But it often happens because of the sins of the people that God permits not a King, but tyrants to govern them. Therefore Augustine said in *The City of God* that God makes the hypocrite reign for the sins of the people. And certainly none is a greater hypocrite than he who, under the guise of a king, becomes a tyrant, who is a wolf in place of a shepherd. No government is better than a single prince, which state is called a Monarchy, about which Dante disputes most acutely in his *Monarchy* <note>Dante's Latin treatise *De Monarchia*.</note>. The opposite of this is the tyrant. Of him Solomon says: *Stay far from the man who has the power to kill* <note>original: "Longe esto ab homine habente potestatem occidendi"</note>. And Virgil: *Alas, flee the cruel land; flee the greedy shore* <note>original: "Heu fuge crudelis terra: fuge litus auarum"</note>. And Solomon in the Proverbs: *A roaring lion and a hungry bear: such is a wicked prince over a poor people* <note>original: "leo rugiens. et ursus exuriens: princeps impius super populum pauperem"</note>. And Cicero writes: that the prince of the city should remain content with glory. And Aristotle: *A prince for whom the reward of honor and glory is not enough becomes a tyrant* <note>original: "Princeps cui non satis e/ premium honoris et glorie tyrannus efficitur"</note>.

Men, inflamed by some perturbation, are sometimes accustomed not to grieve, but to marvel that God suffers great injustices; and then finally, he who has true religion and true prudence corrects himself and concludes that every evil that God permits is for some good end. **IF IT BE LAWFUL for me:** as if to say: I ask you, highest God, if it is lawful for me to ask you if you have turned your just eyes elsewhere—as if to say, if you have removed your love from Italy. **HIGHEST JOVE:** Jove among the gentiles <note>The "Gentiles" or pagans of antiquity.</note> signifies various things, as we said above. But here it signifies the highest God. But because God cannot have a proper name, no word being found that can entirely express the Divinity, it is not inappropriate to call him Jove, which name signifies "help" and "aid" <note>Landino derives *Iove* (Jove) from *giovamento* (benefit/help).</note>. For from Him comes every help, aid, and salvation.

# PURGATORIO

reason. It would be an impious thing to believe that God abandoned—I do not say Italy—but even the least of his creatures; for the belief of the <term>Epicureans</term> <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Epicurus, who in the Middle Ages were often (mis)characterized as believing the soul dies with the body and that God does not intervene in human affairs.</note> that God does not care for human things is false. Therefore, leaving aside such a doubt—which would be impious if stated as a fact—one must turn to what is said with religious devotion: namely, that since God is the highest goodness, he never permits any evil except to the end that it may be a preparation for some greater good. Thus, for the sins of the people, he permits civil discords, robberies, wars, famines, and plagues: partly to punish sins, and partly to punish and amend men, leading them back to a just way of living. But our finite vision cannot understand the infinite depth of divine judgment. Hence the poet said: "or is it a preparation for some future good" which you make in the <term>abyss</term>, <note>original: "nellaby sso"</note> that is, in the depth of your counsel and your providence, with which you govern everything; which is entirely "severed," meaning divided, from our perception. For as I said, our intellect cannot reach such depths.

**AND EVERY PEASANT BECOMES A MARCELLUS.** This shows that every commoner, every man, however base his condition, when he achieves some status in a city, wants to become a "new Marcellus." In this passage, the name is ennobled by many excellent men. But the most excellent was Marcus Marcellus, who in Lombardy at Clastidium <note>original: "achiasteggio", modern Casteggio</note> on the Po, killed Viridomarus, prince of the Gauls. He was the third after Romulus and Cossus to carry the <term>spolia opima</term> <note>The "rich spoils" taken by a Roman general who killed the enemy commander in single combat.</note> into the temple of Jupiter Feretrius. Hence Petrarch wrote: "Who on the banks of the Po near Clastidium / killed with his own hand the great rebel." This man also conquered Syracuse, a most noble city; and having brought the whole island under the power of the Roman people, he returned to Italy and in several battles repulsed Hannibal. However, it seems the poet more likely refers to the M. Marcellus who was consul at the start of the civil war between Pompey and Caesar. He opposed Caesar with all his might in defense of the Senate and Pompey. But after the victory, Caesar mercifully pardoned him, as appears in an oration by Cicero, in which he thanks Caesar on behalf of himself and the Senate for restoring him to his homeland. The poet, then, wishes to show that every base man who acquires status wants to oppose the Emperor, just as Marcellus opposed Caesar. And in this, he secretly condemns the <term>Guelphs</term>. <note>The political faction in Italy that supported the Pope and local autonomy against the Holy Roman Emperor (the Ghibellines).</note>

<column-break/>

Writers use a "digression" when they depart from their main subject for some purpose, just as the poet here has departed from his subject to rebuke the civil discords of Italy, and especially those of our republic. Therefore, through irony—that is, by saying the opposite of the meaning—he says Florence can be "content" because what he has said in this digression does not apply to her; as if to say it applies to her more than to any other. **THANKS TO YOUR PEOPLE:** And this too you should read with irony, because he damns the people, who do not "argue" (strive) to rise against the tyranny of the powerful. "Many have justice in their hearts," but they are slow to "fly," meaning to act, without "counsel"—as if they cannot put it into practice. The meaning is: many would wish to live justly, but they do not want to reveal themselves until they see they can produce results, so that they do not harm themselves while trying to help others; and therefore the arrow flies late. Hence Sallust says:
> To strive in vain, and to achieve nothing by one's weariness but hatred, is the height of madness. <note>original: "Frustra autem niti: nec aliud se fatigando nisi odiū quere extreme dementie est."</note>

**BUT YOUR PEOPLE HAVE IT ON THE TIP OF THEIR TONGUES:** He means they reveal their will before they consider how they might bring that will to perfection. **MANY REFUSE THE COMMON BURDEN.** Many refuse the governance of the republic; but the Florentine people are so prompt that every day one sees new changes. Hence he says with irony: "You rich, you at peace, you so wise." Athens was made noble first by the laws of Draco, and then by the laws of Solon. The laws of Solon were admirable, among which were these: Whoever does not nourish his father and mother shall be treated as infamous. He who lives in idleness may be accused by anyone. The children of those who die in battle shall be nourished by the public. He who gouges out one eye shall have both of his own removed. Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note>...

# CANTO SIX

by the laws imposed by Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta, credited with establishing the rigorous military and social systems of the city-state.</note>: it was reduced to such severity of life and customs that, with their incredible justice and unconquerable strength, they were able to obtain leadership over all Greece and part of Asia. **SIMILAR** to that sick woman. <note>A reference to Dante’s metaphor in Canto VI, comparing Florence to a sick woman who tosses and turns in bed to avoid pain.</note> The nature of the sick person is to desire to change places frequently to find rest. And if she could leave the illness in the place she departs from, it would benefit her. But because she carries it with her, she must suffer wherever she moves. Thus, if the people could leave injustice behind while changing governments, they would live in peace. But because injustice persists in whatever magistrates they create, it happens that such a change does not help them.

## CANTO SEVEN OF THE SECOND CANTICLE OF DANTE.

After the greetings, honest and joyful,
had been repeated three and four times,
Sordello drew back and said, "Who are you?"
"Before the souls worthy of ascending to God
were turned toward this mountain,
my bones were buried by Octavian.
I am Virgil; and for no other sin
did I lose heaven, than for not having faith."
Thus my leader then replied.
As is he who suddenly sees a thing 
before him, which makes him marvel,
who believes and does not, saying: "It is not so,"
Such did that one seem; and then he lowered his brow,
and humbly turned back toward him,
and embraced him where the lesser takes hold. <note>Referring to Sordello embracing Virgil at the knees or feet as a sign of deep respect for a superior.</note>

<column-break/>

**TRULY** the poet presents Sordello as an example of a good citizen: who, being always affectionate toward his fellow citizens, loves and honors them wherever he finds them. And to demonstrate how great his affection was, he shows: that upon hearing that the other was a Mantuan, without seeking anything else, he embraced him with every kind of charity. Now following this, he shows that such greetings were not made just once, but three and four times. And he calls them honest and joyful, to show that in them there was gravity joined with cheerful happiness. He places in this canto those who, through the occupation of kingdoms or other lordships, and through governments and magistracies, have deferred their penitence until the very end. **I AM VIRGIL**: of whom there is nothing to say at present, because in the first Canto of the *Inferno* we set down his life. But we can, in short, agree with the opinion of Macrobius <note>Ambrosius Theodosius Macrobius (5th century AD), a Roman provincial whose works on Virgil and Cicero were highly influential in the Middle Ages.</note>: who affirms that no praise can increase his glory, and no detraction or blame can diminish it.

---

**THREE AND FOUR TIMES.** He imitates Virgil, who said: <note>original: "o ter quaterque beati"</note> "O thrice and four times blessed." And as Macrobius demonstrates, in these two numbers there is the highest perfection. **LOWERED HIS BROW.** First, as a citizen, he performed the aforementioned greetings; now, as a citizen well-deserving of his homeland, and worthy of every veneration for his learning and eloquence, he showed him the highest reverence. And he embraces him "below the arms" <note>Referring to the knees.</note> to show himself as an inferior. Lowering the brow demonstrates reverence, and at the same time compassion: that such a great man should be deprived of beatitude, which is the divine vision.

# PURGATORIO

"O glory of the Latins," he said, "through whom
our language showed all that it could do,
O eternal prize of the place where I was born:
What merit or what grace reveals you to me?
If I am worthy to hear your words,
tell me if you come from Hell, and from which cloister."
He replied to him: "I have come here
through the power of heaven, and with it I come.
Not for doing, but for not doing, have I lost
the sight of the high Sun that you desire,
and which was known too late by me." <note>original: "Non per far ma per non far ho perduto." Virgil explains he is in Limbo not for active sins, but for the "sin of omission"—the lack of Christian faith.</note>

Because when he knew it, he was already in a place where penance and amendment are of no value.

<column-break/>

This is great praise, but in no part is it too much for such a poet. In fact, as I said a little earlier with the authority of Macrobius: <note>Macrobius was a 5th-century Roman philosopher whose commentary on the "Dream of Scipio" was a primary source of Neoplatonism for medieval readers.</note> it is not equal, but much inferior to his eloquence and doctrine. **O ETERNAL PRIZE**: that is, for whom Mantua—the place where I was born—is and will always be in esteem and honor because of you. And he shows he honors him not so much for his doctrine as for the fame he has given to his homeland. **WHAT MERIT**: What have I done to deserve to see you? As if to say "nothing." Therefore, if it is not my merit, **WHAT GRACE**: as if to say, from where do I receive such grace from the Giver of Graces? **NOT FOR DOING**: not for committing errors and sins, from which civil cults can purge us. **BUT FOR NOT DOING**: for not believing and not observing the things commanded by the Christian religion. **WHICH WAS TOO LATE**:

"There is a place down there, not sad with torments

bitten by the teeth of death before

But where, because of the negligence they committed, they must wait, as was said above. And this entire place up to the gate of Purgatory is called by many "Antipurgatory."

<column-break/>

In the *Inferno* <note>Specifically Canto IV.</note> he described this place at length, in which he placed the children who died without baptism; who, if they had been able to do good, would have been exempt and free. **FROM HUMAN GUILT**: that is, from original sin. And this is according to what the Church establishes. **WITH THOSE WHOM THE THREE HOLY**: He shows that besides the little children, he stays with those Gentiles <note>Non-Christians from antiquity.</note> who, through doctrine and civility, were adorned with the moral virtues, which are Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance, of which we spoke above. But because they were not instructed in Christian doctrine, they were not "clothed" in the three holy virtues: Faith, Hope, and Charity, of which we will speak in the third canticle <note>The *Paradiso*.</note>. **TRUE BEGINNING**: the actual start. Because they were not yet where souls are purged of their vices.

He replied: "No fixed place is set for us;
it is permitted for me to go up and around;
as far as I can go, I join you as a guide.
But see now how the day declines,
and to go up by night is not possible;
therefore, it is well to think of a fine resting place.
There are souls to the right, far off here;
if you consent, I will lead you to them,
and not without delight will they be known to you."
"How is that?" was the reply. "If one wished
to climb by night, would he be hindered
by another, or would he simply be unable?"

<column-break/>

As Virgil shows in the sixth book <note>Of the *Aeneid*.</note>, those who live in the Elysian Fields have no fixed place. <note>original: "Vt nulli certa domus lucis habitamus opacis." Translated: "We have no certain home; we dwell in dark groves."</note> Thus Dante, although for another reason, induces Sordello to say the same thing. Because the negligent person cannot have a fixed place in penance, as he has not established any certain order within himself. Furthermore, he shows that when night comes, one cannot move. By "day," one can understand illuminating grace, which illuminates the human intellect just as the sun illuminates the sense of sight. Without this light, one cannot reach liberation from vices. They also equate the sun with the rational part of man, which, as long as it does not lose its light, can proceed forward in purging itself. But I believe it is not discordant to equate the sun with both together:

---

that is, for reason illuminated by divine grace. Therefore, while this prevails in us, we proceed. And let us remember the precept: <note>original: "Ambulate: dum lucem habetis." Translated: "Walk while you have the light" (John 12:35).</note> **SOULS ARE TO THE RIGHT**. Sordello was not fit to lead them upward. Because Sordello's doctrine was history. And that which leads to purgation is philosophy and theology, through which reason has knowledge of the foulness of vice; and through that knowledge, coming to hate it, one comes to the desire to be free of it. And from the same doctrine, one understands how...

# CANTO SEVENTH

...can free oneself from it. Nonetheless, history is not useless: because the particulars and the experience we have gained from histories are of no small help. For from history comes prudence, which persuades us to elevate ourselves to other doctrines. Therefore, Sordello—<gloss>that is, action</gloss>—cannot do this by itself. But he can discern that the souls who are on the right—<gloss>that is, those who have taken a virtuous path</gloss>—even if it is not a theological one, can delight him so much that they hold the day. And certainly, I confess that such studies cannot guide us upward. Nonetheless, until the sun rises, the intellect exercises itself in something that is not useless. And it rouses us from lazy and sleepy idleness.

The good Sordello drew his finger on the ground
saying: "See, you could not even cross
this single line after the sun has set.
Not that anything else would hinder you
except for the nocturnal darkness;
that alone confuses the will with helplessness.
One could indeed go back down with the darkness
and wander about the mountain slope
while the horizon keeps the day closed."

<note>original: "chiudendo gli occhi" — closing the eyes.</note>

Then my lord, as if in wonder,
said: "Lead us then to where you say
one can find delight while dwelling."
We had moved a short distance away
when I perceived that the mountain was hollowed
in the way that valleys hollow them here.
"There," said that shade, "we will go,
where the mountain slope makes a lap of itself,
and there we shall await the new day."

<note>This explains that if we cannot acquire great doctrine in speculations, the soul nonetheless feeds on those things which, as I said shortly before, provide some help.</note> **WHERE THE MOUNTAIN SLOPE MAKES A LAP OF itself**: a ravine, or ditch, or valley in the mountain can be said to be its "lap."

Between the steep and the flat was a crooked path
which led us to the side of the hollow
there where the edge dies away more than halfway.
Gold and fine silver, cochineal and white lead,
Indian wood, bright and clear,
fresh emerald at the moment it is split—
by the herbs and by the flowers within that bosom,
each would be surpassed in color,
as the lesser is surpassed by its greater.

Nature had not only painted there,
but from the sweetness of a thousand odors
she made there an unknown, indistinguishable fragrance.
"Hail, Holy Queen" <note>original: "Salve Regina," a traditional Latin antiphon to the Virgin Mary</note> upon the green and the flowers
I then saw souls sitting and singing,
who because of the valley were not visible from without.

<column-break/>

He declares more openly what was said above, demonstrating that one could not ascend even a single line without the sun. It is as if he says we can make no progress, however small, without the light of the intellect and reason. **ONE COULD INDEED**: Although the appetite alone is what moves the soul to every operation, nonetheless it never leads us upward—that is, toward speculation—unless it is illuminated by reason. But it can indeed lead us downward and wandering around the mountain; that is, toward vicious operations. No crossbowman can hit the target unless he is an excellent craftsman in that art; but any ignorant person can hit elsewhere.

This place serves more for the fiction that Dante creates for this ascent than for the allegory. For Virgil—that is, superior reason, illuminated by all divine graces and human doctrine—should not have wondered that one could not ascend without the day, for he himself should have expected it. Unless we wish to take Virgil here only for inferior reason, unrefined and without any science. Sordello leads him to the shades—that is, to the knowledge of history—which, while the day comes (which is to say, while the time comes that we can give ourselves to speculation), gives us honest delight, empty of every vice.

He uses <term>chorographia</term> <note>a Greek term for the description of a specific region or district</note>; that is, he describes the region where they went, and first the way that led them. He said then that the path, the narrow way—and it is a word derived from <term>semita</term> <note>Latin for a narrow path or lane</note>—was "crooked" or twisted, as is fitting for mountain paths which, to avoid the more difficult passes, twist now here, now there; between steep and flat, because they were neither entirely climbing nor entirely on level ground. **WHICH**: which path led **US TO THE SIDE.** To the extremity, where the descent into the valley begins, of the **HOLLOW** <note>original: "lacca," a term Dante uses for a pit or steep depression</note>; of the descent. The "side" is therefore the rim of the valley, and the "hollow" is the descent that begins from the side and drops toward the bottom. **MORE THAN halfway the edge dies away**: it passes the middle of its concavity. We call the "hem" <note>original: "limbo" or "lembo"</note> the extreme part of a garment, which often makes a "lap" or pocket, and for this reason the poet uses this word for the concavity of the valley. **GOLD AND SILVER**: He shows that place to be clothed in such green herbs and such a variety of flowers, and of living and bright colors...

<summary>Sordello explains that progress up the mountain is impossible without the sun (symbolizing Divine Grace or Reason). He leads Virgil and Dante to a lush, colorful valley where negligent rulers sing the "Salve Regina."</summary>

<page-num>3</page-num>
<header>PURGATORIO</header>

<columns>2</columns>

...that the color of gold, and of silver, and of the stones that he places here, would lose their luster and remain surpassed by it.

All of this denotes Avarice, and the delight and utility that we seek in the **active life**, which especially desires gold. This is the most precious of all metals, and of the most beautiful and good color. It is created in the earth from subtle red sulfur and subtle white quicksilver <note>original: "argento uiuo" — literally 'living silver' or mercury</note>. Thus, its color is most pleasing, because the red in it is much illuminated by the white, and the white receives a pleasing color from the red. Nevertheless, the solidity of the sulfur contributes more to the generation of gold than does the airy, watery quality of the quicksilver. For this reason, it is more solid and heavier than silver. Because of such density, it does not diminish when melted. It is very healthy for the human body. When taken as food, it comforts all the limbs—not because it nourishes them, but because it gnaws away and purges every superfluity in them. For this reason, it preserves one from leprosy. If you mix its filings with borage juice and the heart-bone of a stag, it is very effective against heart disease. No metal stretches into finer threads, nor withstands the hammer better than gold. **Silver** is created from quicksilver and white sulfur. But it participates more in the airy, watery quality of the quicksilver than in the solidity of the sulfur. For this reason, it weighs less than gold. Not only these two aforementioned metals, but all others have their origin in quicksilver. Because of this, some say it is a simple element. **Cochineal** <note>original: "Cocco"</note>, according to Dioscorides, is a branchy herb, and on its twigs, it has berries similar to lentils. **White lead** <note>original: "Biacca"</note> in Latin is called *cerusa*; it is made from perfect vinegar placed in a covered vessel. **Indigo** is a blue color. **Luminous wood**, like ebony, which is a very shining black. Others read "Indian wood," because in India there are wondrous trees. And then they say "serene light," denoting the purity of the air. The **Emerald** has a more joyful aspect than any other gem. And it greatly comforts the sight. The Emperor Nero used to watch the battles of the gladiators through an emerald because it is a very clear mirror and makes the images of things that appear in it from a distance seem large. Pliny states there are twelve species of emeralds. Of no precious gem are larger pieces found. And Theophrastus, a disciple of Aristotle, writes of having read in the Egyptian commentaries that the King of Babylon sent an emerald four cubits long and three high as a gift to their king. And he adds from Plistonicus that in the labyrinth of Egypt there is a colossus of Serapis made of a single emerald nine cubits high. All these things placed inside that "bosom"—that is, the great valley which is the bosom of the mountain—would have their colors surpassed by the flowers and the grass.

**NOT ONLY.** Not only were the colors wondrous, but the scents were also most sweet; from all of them mixed together resulted a most sweet composition, unknown and indistinct, because one could not recognize any certain thing in that mixture. In this place, Francesco da Buti <note>A 14th-century commentator on Dante</note> understands allegorically that Dante, through these seven things, signifies seven virtues: four moral and three theological, in which the lords could be excellent if they were not hindered by sloth. But my opinion is that it rather demonstrates the state and condition of **temporal lordship**. First, he states that the path leading to this place is between steep and flat. For lordships and states are acquired sometimes with virtue and sometimes with vices. And similarly, it is slanting for the same reason. He places them in the valley, whose site is almost submerged under the earth, because it has cliffs on every side that block the view. And certainly, he who hungers for lordship hungers for earthly things, the greed for which takes away our prospect and vision of celestial and divine things. For this reason **Leah**, who in the Old Testament denotes the active life, is described as bleary-eyed <note>original: "lippa et cispa" — referring to Leah's "weak eyes" in Genesis 29:17, interpreted here as being distracted by worldly cares</note>. Nor can the active mind—because it is distracted by various and diverse cares—collect itself in contemplation of great things. Hence, even of **Martha**, who in the New Testament signifies the same thing, the True Wisdom <note>Christ</note> says: *Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things.* <note>original: "Martha Martha sollicita es. Et uerfaris circa plurima." — Luke 10:41</note>. I will not dwell on this, because we treated it fully in the first canticle. It is, therefore, enclosed in the valley: that is, hidden and wrapped in earthly things. Nor is it without cause that such a valley is clothed in very green grass and flowers most beautiful to the sight and sweet to the smell. Because honors, dignities, states, and lordships are like grass and flowers. For just as those things delight the sense but quickly wither and dry up, so such a state brings great delight to men in whom sensuality is more powerful than reason. But it quickly passes. As Petrarch says: *A beautiful mortal thing passes and does not last.*

**HAIL HOLY QUEEN.** <note>original: "SALVE REGINA"</note> After he has denoted the state of the lords, he states that they sang *Salve Regina*, a most excellent prayer ordained in praise of the Queen of Heaven and Virgin Mother, understanding by this prayer the conversion that temporal lords make from earthly cares to true religion.

Before the small sun now seeks its nest,
began the Mantuan who had turned us toward them,
"do not wish for me to lead you among them.
From this ridge, you will better observe
the gestures and faces of every one of them,
than if you were received among them in the hollow below.
He who sits highest and has the appearance
of having neglected what he ought to have done..."

<column-break/>

Sordello advises that it will be better to see the souls in the valley from an elevated place than to go among them. This is so they may more conveniently see a multitude from a separate and high place than by mixing with them. And he imitates Virgil where he says: *And he takes a hillock from where he can see all in a long line and recognize their faces as they come.* <note>original: "Et tumulum capit unde omnes longo ordine poffit. Aduerfos legere et uementum difcere uultus." — Aeneid VI, 753-755</note>. He sets the time at the last hour of the day because such souls deferred their conversion until the night of death. **RUDOLPH the Emperor**: This man...

[Rudolph] was German: and acquired the **duchy of Swabia**: and granted it to **Albert** his son. And having been made emperor he reigned 20 years. He killed in battle the **King of Bohemia** <note>Ottokar II</note>: who did not deign to obey him. This was in the year of salvation **1277**. But afterward he was reconciled with the son: and made him his son-in-law: and restored to him the kingdom of Bohemia. He was a just and religious man: and very powerful in military matters. And if he had come to Italy: he would have reduced it all to his empire. Therefore the poet accuses him of **negligence**: because **Pope Gregory X** had elected him: so that he might reform Italy. And afterward he should have gone to the conquest of the **Holy Land**. But he, greedy for lordship across the mountains <note>meaning in Germany and Austria</note>, did not wish to cross [the Alps]. But he granted to **Pope Nicholas of the Orsini family** Bologna and Romagna. This is what the poet means by saying: *and does not move his mouth to the songs of others*. 

**THE OTHER:** This was his son-in-law, the son of the King of Bohemia: to whom he restored the kingdom. 

**AND THAT SMALL-NOSED ONE:** He means **Philip the Small-Nosed** <note>Philip III of France, "le Hardi"</note>, son of the good **Louis**, King of France: who for his holiness was placed in the catalog of saints <note>King Louis IX, or Saint Louis</note>. This Philip had as his wife the sister of **Don Peter, King of Aragon**: and heard of the rebellion of **Sicily** <note>The Sicilian Vespers of 1282</note>: which Don Peter had taken from **Charles I**, Philip's uncle: he moved war against Don Peter with twenty thousand cavalry: and eighty thousand French, Provençal, and German infantry of the crusade with Charles his son: and with a cardinal legate of the Pope: and with a fleet of one hundred and twenty ships: and joined with **Don James**, the King's brother and his enemy because he had taken from him the island of **Majorca**: He came into Catalonia: and by siege took **Girona** <note>original: "hyronda"</note>. And in a battle Don Peter was <unclear>pressed</unclear> <note>original: "scritto," likely a transcription error for "stretto" meaning hard-pressed or cornered</note>: and his horse taken by the bridle. But he with a bold spirit cut the bridle: and spurring the horse he fled. And shortly after he died. But **Roger de Lauria**, his admiral, broke Philip's fleet: and burned it. Therefore he could not afterward bring provisions to the camp. This thing forced him to leave the enterprise: and sick with grief he died in **Perpignan**. And a great part of the army perished of hunger. To him succeeded **Philip the Fair**, his son. Because of such slaughter of his people, the poet writes: that he "deflowered the lily"—that is, the kingdom of France, which bears three lilies—and states: that he beats his breast. 

**WHO HAS SO BENIGN AN ASPECT.** This was **William, King of Navarre**, father-in-law of the "Evil of France"—that is, of Philip the Fair, the worst of all the kings of France: He says then that these two Kings were the father—that is, Philip the Small-Nosed, father of Philip the Fair—and his father-in-law—that is, William his father-in-law. Of the filthy life, it will be said in Canto XX.

A very true sentiment put forward by our poet, and adorned with a metaphor, placing the father as the tree and the children as the branches. He says, then, that human integrity—that is, virtue—which is in a man, **RARELY RISES**: he does not deny that it happens sometimes, but says it is rare for it to rise through the branches—that is, through the sons—who have their origin from the father, just as branches from a tree. This is not because free will is taken away, but it can be inclined in some part. **AND THIS IS WILLED BY HIM WHO GIVES IT**: and God, who gives it to us, permits this. Because virtue proceeds from the soul, which the father does not generate from the maternal blood as he does the body. But as soon as the mother's womb is quickened, the <unclear>holy</unclear> <note>The OCR "sc̄to" likely represents "sancto" (holy).</note> God in the same instant creates the soul and infuses it into the already living body. And it immediately unites to itself the vegetative, the motive, and the sensitive powers; and there remains one single soul adorned with four powers. If it directs its free will toward the good, it is immediately aided by divine grace and lives according to virtue. But if it turns its free will toward evil, it remains stripped of grace and falls into vice. **ALSO TO THE BIG-NOSED ONE**: that is, to Charles. ->'CANTO EIGHT<-

### CANTO EIGHT OF THE SECOND CANTICLE OF DANTE .

**H**E DESCRIBES the evening very poetically. And he includes a significant allegory in this comparison. The sentiment is true: evening was already coming, which brings longing to sailors, who departed in the morning from the port where they left their relatives and friends; when evening then comes, it causes them, by remembering them, to be overwhelmed by a passion of the soul which the Latins call "desire" <note>original: "desiderio"</note>. And similarly, it in-

<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut initial letter 'E'. Inside the frame, a figure wearing a red hood and robe kneels in prayer, looking up toward a golden celestial radiance in a blue sky. The background of the frame is a deep blue with intricate gold filigree.</image-desc>

**I**t was already the hour that turns back the longing
of those at sea, and melts the heart
on the day they have said goodbye to sweet friends;

And which pierces the new pilgrim with love
if he hears from afar the ringing bell <note>term: "squilla" — a small bell, often referring to the evening curfew or Angelus bell.</note>
that seems to mourn the day as it dies:

When I began to render hearing useless
and to admire one of the souls
who had risen and requested to be heard with a hand.

She joined and lifted both her palms,
fixing her eyes toward the East,
as if saying to God: "I care for nothing else."

"To Thee before the end of light" <note>original: "Te lucis ante [terminum]"; the opening of the hymn sung at Compline, the final prayer service of the day.</note> so devoutly
poured from her mouth with such sweet notes
that it made me step out of my own mind.

And the others then, sweetly and devoutly,
followed her through the entire hymn,
keeping their eyes upon the celestial wheels.

Sharpen your eyes well here, reader, to the truth:
for the veil is now so thin,
certainly, that passing through it is easy.

I saw that noble army <note>original: "exercito gentile"</note>
afterward look upward in silence,
as if waiting, pale and humble.

And I saw coming out from the side and descending
two angels with two flaming swords,
broken and deprived of their points.

<column-break/>

-tervenes for those who begin a journey. And he organizes it thus:
*It was already the hour that turns back the longing*: that is, it was the hour of evening, which turns the longing—that is, the desire—back to thinking of those whom they left in the morning, saying goodbye. *AND WHICH*: that is, which hour pierces the new pilgrim: that is, one who has newly taken up the journey. *WITH LOVE*: for those whom he has left. *IF FROM AFAR HE HEARS the bell*: that is, the bell which seems, with its sound, to mourn the day that moves toward the coming night.
Allegorically, he places this for those who are in the purgatorial virtues: because the soul is not yet purified, if night catches it—that is, if it falls into some perturbation whereby it loses the light of the mind—the past pleasures to which it had said goodbye return to the memory. *SWEET*: Because he who departs from vices to go to Purgatory, although he has made the resolution to strip himself of them, yet because he does not yet have the habit of true virtue, he forces his appetite with reason rather than persuading it; because his sensuality, still entangled in the delights and pleasures of vices, detaches itself unwillingly. This is expressed by Virgil when he says: *I leave the shores of my homeland and the harbor with tears* <note>original: "Litora cum patrie lacrimis portumque relinquo"; from the Aeneid, Book III.</note>. And certainly we ought to imitate those old Trojans whom Homer writes about:

who, seeing Helen coming, greatly praised her beauty and took supreme pleasure in it. But finally they concluded it was much better that Helen should go away, for she was not worth retaining if Troy were to be lost. Thus the wise man, though he be stimulated by the pleasure of the senses, wants Helen—that is, those pleasures—to depart from him, because they are pernicious and lead to vice; he does not want Troy—that is, his soul—to perish. *WHEN I*: I began to render hearing useless because the souls who before were singing "Hail, Holy Queen" <note>original: "salve regina"</note> were now silent. And I began *to admire*: that is, to see. *RISEN*: stood up on her feet, from the Latin verb *surgo*. *WHO REQUESTED to be heard*: asked to be listened to; as if to say she requested silence not with words, but with her *hand*: that is, with signs which she made with her hand. *AND LIFTED*: that is, raised toward heaven both her palms, as one does who adores. *FIXING her eyes*: that is, looking fixedly toward the East. Because our religion has the custom of turning toward the East when adoring. Hence ancient churches have always had their altars turned this way. *AS IF SAYING TO GOD*: she looked so fixedly and devoutly that it seemed she was saying: *I care for nothing ELSE*: that is, I care for nothing else. And she began to sing the hymn that is sung at Compline <note>term: "compieta" — the final church service of the day, before sleep.</note>, the beginning of which is: *To Thee, before the end of light, Creator of all things* <note>original: "Te lucis ante terminum rerum creator"</note>. So sweetly that this sweetness drew all my senses to itself, so that I did not remember myself. And in passing, he demonstrates that in praying we ought to lift the eyes of the mind to heaven, and have the mind entirely turned to God, in such a way that we remember nothing else.

**H**E ADMONISHES the reader to sharpen their intellect to understand the allegorical sense of this fiction; and he demonstrates that the veil of this allegory is not obscure. But it is so transparent that it will be easily seen. Then he presents the fiction, saying that when the hymn was sung, that *army*: that is, that multitude.
But note that *army* <note>original: "exercito"</note> signifies a multitude of men who fight, or who are prepared if there is a need to fight. Therefore such a word fits well in this place, because those who exercise themselves in the purgatorial virtues always stand ready to fight against temptations and those

<column-break/>

to conquer them. **SILENT.** <note>original: "TACITO"</note> This demonstrates the prayer of these spirits: and he said "silent" because God understands the heart; He does not desire prayer of the mouth, although sometimes affection sends forth the words. Wherefore the Psalmist says: *With my voice I prayed to the Lord.* <note>original Latin: "Voce mea addominum deprecatus sum"</note> And elsewhere: *My heart rejoiced: and my tongue exulted.* <note>original Latin: "Letatum est cor meum : et exultauit lingua mea"</note> We say then: that God does not desire words. For this reason, John of Damascus <note>original: "Damasceno"</note> says that prayer is when our intellect directs itself toward God. And for this, Augustine <note>original: "Augustino"</note> asks: *What does the noise of the lips profit if the heart is hardened?* <note>original Latin: "Quid prodest strepitus labiorum : si induratum est cor"</note> And Solomon says: *the prayer of one who humbles himself will penetrate the clouds.* <note>original Latin: "oratio humiliantis se penetrabit nubes"</note> This hymn <note>The hymn "Te lucis ante terminum" mentioned on the previous page.</note> is well-suited because in the Christian church it is sung at the beginning of the night. And the Lord is prayed to: that He guard us from every nocturnal phantom and from every harmful thing, and that He remove from us every temptation. These spirits, then, having finished the hymn, watched the heavens in silence, awaiting help: **PALE** <note>original: "PALLIDO"</note> because of fear of the serpent: and humble, so that the prayer might be more acceptable to God. 

But so that we may understand the allegory of this text: there is no doubt that with the departure of the light and the coming of night—that is, us losing our reason and divine grace through ignorance and sin—we are tempted by the devil and the flesh. Because of this, God's grace is necessary for us, without which our own strengths would not be enough to defend us. Therefore, these souls ask for it in that verse of the hymn. This grace is signified by the angels. And because temptation comes in two ways—either through negligence, by omitting meritorious acts and operations, or through suggestion, which is when the devil tempts us by suggesting and supplying things that lead us to vice—he therefore places two angels. That is, a double grace for ignorance and for the two temptations. One is placed on the right side of the valley to guard us from negligence. The other on the left: and this is against suggestion. The two swords are Justice: which are blunted <note>original: "spuntate"</note> because such justice is mixed with mercy. He places two swords because Paul also said: *by the weapons of justice on the right and on the left.* <note>original Latin: "per arma iustitie adextris et a sinistris"</note> The fire denotes charity. Thus, the immeasurable charity of God sends the angel: that is, the defense: and sends it with justice: because He makes us worthy of it with "prevenient grace," which induces us to ask for "illuminating grace," "cooperating grace," and "preserving grace." <note>These are technical terms in Scholastic theology describing different stages of how God's help interacts with human will.</note> Wherefore the Psalmist says: *May God have mercy on us and shine his face upon us: and have mercy on us.* <note>original Latin: "Mifereatur nostri deus et illuminet uultum fuum super nos : et misereatur nostri"</note> Therefore, prevenient grace makes us turn to God to ask for mercy and light so that we may perform meritorious works. But because our just works are not enough, it is necessary that God's mercy compensates. 

The angels have wings and green garments because the grace of God always remains green <note>Meaning fresh or vigorous.</note> within us; it never dries up, provided we wish it. The garment defends us from heat and frost. The wings lift us above the earth and raise us to heaven. And we can interpret the two wings as Justice and Religion, as you will find according to Plato in the introduction to the third Canticle <note>Referring to the *Paradiso*.</note>.

**T**hey stay above because grace comes from heaven: and they place themselves in the middle: because grace is needed on the right and on the left—that is, in prosperity and in adversity. Their being blonde signifies incorruption. And the splendor was so great that my eye could not endure it without being dazzled. This is because the eye, being a corporeal instrument, cannot support so much light. **FROM THE WOMB OF MARY.** <note>original: "DEL GREMBO DI MARIA"</note> That is, from our Redeemer, who was born from the womb of Mary. He uses the "container" for the "contained" <note>A rhetorical device known as metonymy.</note>. The serpent is the diabolical temptation which assaults us with every cunning to deceive us. **BUT I WHO DID NOT KNOW BY WHICH PATH** <note>original: "MA IO CHE NON SAPEA PER QVAL CAlle"</note> by which he tempts us: it is difficult to understand where it comes from. Therefore we must draw close to Virgil—that is, to reason illuminated by true doctrine—because that makes us cautious so we can foresee what we must provide for. **ALL FROZEN:** for fear of the serpent. **TO THE TRUSTED SHOULDERS:** the shoulders are the limb suited to sustain every weight we carry. And especially all the armor of a man: the helmet and the gorget <note>A piece of armor protecting the throat.</note> rest upon the shoulders; the breastplate hangs from the shoulders; the hand and the arm get their vigor from the shoulders. Therefore he uses the shoulders for the strength that is in the superior reason, suited to defend us from every demonic fraud.

**S**ordello invites him to enter among the shades so that he can speak with them. He descended three steps and was below. Which signifies, according to some, that by descending, not ascending to penance, he made...

Only three steps I believe I descended

the task of contrition of heart: confession of mouth: and satisfaction in deed. But it seems to me: that in the contemplation of the civil life it is not necessary to have the three speculative virtues: Intelligence, Science, and Wisdom. But Prudence suffices: and for this reason, subtly: as he does with all other things: he uses these words: that he descended three steps. **AND I SAW** below: to denote how much the civil life is inferior to the contemplative life. **THE AIR WAS CLEARING**: although even when the sun is out, the air is serene. Nevertheless, we say the sky is "clear" <note>original: "sereno"</note> when the sun is beneath the earth. **JUDGE NINO.** This man was of the house of Visconti of Pisa: a man full of nobility: and very robust of body: the nephew of Master Ubaldo Visconti of Pisa: who with only two companions, Scarpetta degli Ubaldini and the Marquis of Montferrat, challenged one hundred select Germans of the Emperor—who was then at Pisa—and defeated them. Nino asks how long it has been since Dante came across the distant waters: believing he had come across the ocean, led by the angel: according to his fiction. And Dante responds: that he did not come by the ocean sea. But through the sorrowful places of Hell. And "I am in my first life": because I come with my body.

**Sordello**: and Nino fell into the greatest stupor: hearing from Virgil that I was alive. And Nino turned to Currado Malaspina: who was nearby. So that he might see what God by His grace had willed. Because it was a special grace: that against human condition, Dante, still clothed in his mortal body, could make such a pilgrimage. Then Nino turned back to Dante: and said, "I pray you by that singular favor <note>original: "singulare grado"</note>." That is, the singular privilege: for which you are a debtor to God: who hides and conceals His "first why" <note>original: "primo perche"</note>. That is, His first cause: which has no ford <note>original: "guado"</note>, which first cause God keeps so hidden in Himself that it has no ford. That is, that men cannot reach it. And it is a metaphor from a river: which we say has no ford when it is so deep that we cannot cross it. "Tell my Giovanna: that she should call for me." That is, by calling she should intercede for me there where the innocent are answered. That is, where the prayers of the righteous are heard: and this is in the Christian Purgatory. Wherefore the Creator said: *My house shall be called a house of prayer.* <note>original Latin: "Domus mea domus orationis uocabitur"</note> And because it seemed a thing to wonder at: that since his wife Beatrice was still alive, he would rather it be said to Giovanna his daughter than to her: therefore he says: that he does not believe that her mother—that is, Beatrice—loves him anymore: since having left the veils and the state of widowhood: she has remarried Master Galeazzo as I said above: and he announces to her: that a time will yet come when she will long for that state of widowhood which she has now left, because of the way she will be treated by her second husband. **THROUGH** her: by her example: it is easily understood how long the fire of love lasts in a woman. Woman is quite volatile and changeable. Wherefore Virgil says: *Woman is always a fickle and changeable thing.* <note>original Latin: "Varium et mutabile semper femina"</note> And because...

For this reason, such a person loves fervently while receiving pleasure from another, which consists chiefly in sight and touch. And as the pleasure fades, the love is extinguished. The **Viper** <note>The heraldic symbol of the Visconti of Milan, the family of Nino's widow's second husband.</note> of the new husband—who is of the Visconti of Milan—will not provide her as fine a tomb as the **Rooster** would have done—that is, I, the Judge of the district of Gallura, whose coat of arms is a rooster. **FROM THE STAMP OF RIGHT ZEAL.** There was imprinted on his face, and almost sculpted there, the form of the love that set his heart ablaze.

My greedy eyes were still turned to the heavens,
just where the stars are slowest,
as a wheel is closest to its axle.
And my leader: "Son, what are you looking at up there?"
And I to him: "At those three torches
with which the pole on this side is all ablaze."

turning its head from time to time to its back,
licking, like a beast that grooms itself.

how the celestial hawks <note>A metaphor for the two angels guarding the valley.</note> moved,
but I clearly saw both one and the other in motion.
Hearing the air cleft by their green wings,
the serpent fled, and the angels turned back
up to their posts, flying with equal speed.

<column-break/>

**I CONTINUOUSLY GAZED AT THE HEAVENS.** This signifies that the sensory appetite, now fully obedient to reason, had turned its every desire toward celestial things. **PUR LA DOVE LESTELLE SON** [just where the stars are] **slowest.** That is, at the highest part of the heaven, which they call the pole, as we showed above. **WHERE THE STARS ARE SLOWEST.** If we had a wheel full of stars that was turning, there is no doubt that the stars placed further out on the circumference and the edge of the wheel make a larger circle than those closer to the pivot—or let us say the handle of the wheel, which is the center. Nonetheless, they finish their revolution in the same amount of time. Therefore, those closer to the circumference happen to be faster, and those closer to the pivot, slower. Thus, imagining a shaft that starts from the summit of the heaven and goes through the middle of the world-machine to the opposite summit, and the heaven moves around the ends of this shaft: the stars that are closer to these poles, because they make a shorter circuit, are slower in the heavens, like those on a wheel closer to the axle. Dante was therefore looking at the highest part of the heaven—that is, at the Antarctic pole. And he learned from Virgil that the four stars which were in that part of the heaven in the morning had already gone down, and in that same place three had risen, which were so radiant that they illuminated the entire hemisphere of Purgatory. According to the nature of the heavens, this is a likely fiction. But allegorically, according to many, by the first four stars he means the four **moral virtues** <note>Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance.</note>; and by these three he means the three **theological virtues** <note>Faith, Hope, and Charity.</note>. He feigns that the former were in the middle of the sky in the morning because in the first age, and before the coming of Christ, civil men governed themselves according to them. But later, after the coming of Christ, the theological virtues were understood, which set this entire pole ablaze—that is, the other hemisphere where Dante was, and where he imagines Purgatory. For no one seeks to purge themselves unless they have most ardent charity, firm hope, and indubitable faith. Thus, he saw the four in the morning because the moral virtues existed in the first age. He sees these others in the evening because they were not known until this last age, when Christ revealed them. Nor would it perhaps be foreign to take the three as the **intellectual virtues**. For just as the others form the active life, these form the contemplative life, which is not born in a man in his early years, but toward old age. Thus they write that Jacob went out into the fields toward evening, denoting by that the contemplative life.

**THE SNAKE CAME FROM THE LOWER PART OF THE VALLEY.** Because valleys in the mountains are protected and have slopes on all sides, except from below. He rightly places the serpent as temptation. For the serpent is astute, and likewise it is a very earthly animal. And so temptation is full of malice and fraud, and always invites one toward earthly and transitory things. For this same reason, he feigns that the serpent comes from the lower part of this valley and the angels come from above; because preparatory, illuminating, and cooperating grace are divine and celestial things, while the serpent is earthly. **PERHAPS SUCH AS GAVE EVE THE BITTER FOOD.** Many seek to know why he said "perhaps." But one can respond that it is hardly credible that any...

no temptation can be compared to that which was made to the first humans: when the tempter persuaded them that they would be like gods if they tasted of that fruit. **THROUGH THE GRASS AND FLOWERS**. In my judgment, one can interpret the grass and flowers in various ways: that is, as beautiful and virtuous works; they imply that the snake—that is, the diabolical temptation—often comes under the guise of virtue. And certainly, that temptation has little power which is not shaded by some outward honesty. Or, truly, they take the grass and flowers to mean worldly lusts and pleasures, against which men find it difficult to resist. For some are ensnared by bodily pleasures. Some are drawn by money. Many by ambition. Petrarch meant nearly the same thing when he said: *And as the snake lies hidden among flowers* <note>original: "Et chome sta fra fiori ascoso langue"</note>. **THE EVIL STREAK**: the evil snake which goes streaking through the grass. **TURNING ITS HEAD FROM TIME TO TIME TO ITS BACK**. It turned frequently like a cat or a dog or another beast that grooms itself—that is, that smooths its back, licking itself with its tongue. This demonstrates that temptation always adorns itself and shows itself to be pleasant and delicate so that we might accept it. **I DID NOT SEE IT**: This denotes that man does not feel it when the grace of God holds him; but he saw them moved afterward, because he recognizes it later by its effects. **THE CELESTIAL GOSHAWKS**: since the angels have wings and go to strike the serpent, he not undeservedly compares them to goshawks <note>A type of bird of prey used in hunting.</note>. The serpent fled, hearing the air struck by the green wings of the angels. And it fled deservedly. For when divine grace comes into us, every temptation is frightened and flees.

The coming of the serpent did NOT frighten Corrado in any way, so that he never turned his eyes away from Dante. And by this, he demonstrates that one who is accustomed to resisting temptations for a long time does not heed them. **SO MAY THE LANTERN THAT LEADS YOU ON HIGH**. He demonstrates that he has never been in the Lunigiana, where the Malaspina marquises are. But he says that the excellent fame of that family is such that it resounds through all Europe: and it "proclaims"—that is, it highly names the lords—and the "land"—that is, the country—from which it follows that even those who were never there know it. And I, Dante, swear to you: "so may I go on high"—that is, so may I reach the summit of this mountain—as your people "do not strip themselves"—do not lose the adornment of the "purse"—that is, from avarice and the greed for riches—nor of the "sword"—that is, from violence, robbery, and tyranny. "Habit and nature": He demonstrates that in them is true virtue, of which nature gives us certain seeds; these, if they are afterward well cultivated with good and assiduous habit of right action, produce perfect virtue. Therefore, nature gives the best beginnings to your race, and assiduous habit makes it perfect.

**WITH ALL FOUR FEET IT COVERS AND STRADDLES**. Because this is how the constellation is figured. **THAT THIS COURTEOUS OPINION**: That is, the opinion that you hold regarding the Malaspina family. He calls this opinion "courteous," meaning liberal or generous, because Dante had copiously praised this family. **SHALL BE NAILED INTO THE MIDDLE OF YOUR HEAD**: As if to say, it will be confirmed in your brain. He says "in the middle of the head" most aptly, because the *cogitativa* <note>The "cogitative" or thinking faculty, which medieval scholars believed processed sensory information into thought.</note> has its seat distinct from the imagination and the memory, located in the center of the head. **WITH GREATER NAILS THAN ANOTHER'S SPEECH**. The meaning is: you hold this firm opinion because you have heard it said. But the time will come when you will know it for yourself. For when he was sent into exile, he was most liberally received by the Marquis Marcello <note>Historical records usually identify him as Moroello Malaspina.</note> Malaspina, of whom we already spoke in the eighth canto of the first canticle <note>Referring to the Inferno.</note>.
