### CANTO NINE

very talkative. **THE CONCUBINE OF TITHONUS** <note>In mythology, Aurora (the Dawn) was the lover of the mortal Tithonus. Dante uses this to describe the lunar dawn—the light preceding the moonrise.</note> i.e., Aurora: whom they imagine that in the morning she leaves the bed of Tithonus. Whence Virgil says: *Aurora, leaving the saffron bed of Tithonus* <note>original: "Titoni croceum linquens aurora cubile"</note>. **WITH GEMS HER** forehead was shining. This shows that this Aurora rose in that hemisphere along with the Scorpion. This is the eighth sign of the zodiac: and it is called Scorpio: although many maintain that the configuration of this animal occupies the space of two signs: and with its claws it makes the sign of Libra: and with the rest that of Scorpio. The fables say: that because Orion the hunter had sworn not to leave any wild beast alive on earth, the Earth itself created this scorpion to kill Orion. And afterwards, Earth obtained from Jove that he might be transferred into the zodiac. Nigidius <note>Nigidius Figulus, a Roman scholar and occultist.</note> writes: that the earth did not produce it, but Diana formed it on Mount Celypus on the island of Chios so that it might kill Orion, who with supreme insolence put himself before her in hunting. It is configured from nineteen stars and is the domicile of Mars. And this is a new poetic invention: because other poets never place Aurora except for that dawn which appears in the east before the birth of the sun. This cannot be the case here. For since the sun is in Aries, it is necessary that the dawn rises either with the same sign or with the end of Pisces. But by Dante placing her in Scorpio, he shows that he takes "Aurora" here for that light which comes before the moon; which, because it had already moved away from the opposition it had made in Libra (the sun being in Aries), had already entered Scorpio. So that this may be clearly understood, we will remember that as the poet shows in the *Inferno*, on the night he found himself lost in the wood, the moon was in opposition. Then the following day he spent partly in struggling with the beasts and partly in the talk he had with Virgil. On the second night, he descended through all of Hell. And he passed through the center to the other hemisphere. And at the beginning of the second day, according to the precept of Cato, he girded himself with the reed, and spent all that light in climbing the slopes of Ante-Purgatory. Now he has come to the third night, which he will spend in this valley. And on the morning of the third day, while sleeping, he will be carried by Lucy <note>Saint Lucy, representing Illuminating Grace.</note> all the way to the gate of Purgatory. But the night he spent partly reaching the center and partly from the center to the surface of Purgatory was double. Because leaving our hemisphere at the end of the night, where day was already coming, it follows that in the other hemisphere he found a new night. **OF THE COLD ANIMAL**. It seems contrary to Virgil, who said: *Now the burning Scorpion draws in its arms* <note>original: "Iam bracchia contrahit ardens scorpius"</note>. But Virgil was respecting the nature of Mars, the lord of this sign, which is a burning planet. Dante respects the proper nature of the sign, which is cold, fixed, and nocturnal. **WHICH WITH THE tail strikes people**. And rightly so: because astrologers call this sign the house of death, of fear, of toil, of loss, and of contention. And just as the scorpion is an animal that stings with its tail, so the sun, when it is in that sign, is the cause of injury and stinging in the human body: because beginning to decline, it warms the air less. Therefore the air, unbalanced by the cold, soon offends and stings bodies, as Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville, a medieval encyclopedist.</note> writes. **AND THE NIGHT by the steps with which she climbs**. By the "steps" of the night he means the hours. Therefore, it was already two hours of night. **IN THE place where we were**, which was the hemisphere over there. **The Day already leaned down its wings**: understand this as being from the same hemisphere. **OF THAT OF ADAM**, I had the body: as for the body, we all descended from Adam. But the soul is entirely from God.

At the hour when the swallow begins her sad lays
near the morning,
perhaps in memory of her first woes:
And when our mind, a wanderer
further from the flesh and less held by thought,
is in its visions almost divine.
In a dream I seemed to see suspended
an eagle in the sky with golden feathers,
with wings open, and intent on swooping down:
And it seemed to me I was there where
his own were abandoned by Ganymede,
when he was snatched to the supreme consistory:
Within myself I thought: perhaps this one strikes
only here by habit, and perhaps from another place
disdains to carry anyone up in its talons:

<column-break/>

The author, while sleeping, had already passed so much of the night that the day was approaching and the dawn was beginning; at which time the swallow—when it is the season of spring—begins to sing. Then in a vision it appeared to him that he was in the forest of Ida, which is near Troy, where the poets imagine that Jove, in the form of an eagle, snatched Ganymede. And in the sky it seemed to him he saw an eagle with golden feathers, ready to swoop down to take its prey. Wherefore he said to himself: perhaps the habit of this eagle is to stay in this forest, and it does not disdain to carry prey to heaven from anywhere but here. **AT THE Hour when she begins her sad lays, the swallow**: In the time of the morning, when the swallow begins. **AND HER lays**: her laments; and here he touches upon the fable, which is this: Pandion, King of Athens, had two daughters, Procne and Philomela. At the same time there was Tereus, King of Thrace, who, being allied with Pandion, was of no small help to him in a war waged against him. Therefore, after the war, to confirm and establish the friendship, Pandion gave him Procne as a wife. Tereus took her to Thrace; and after some time, urged by his wife who was eager to see her sister, he returned to Pandion and obtained permission to bring Philomela to Procne. But on the journey, overcome by the beauty of the girl, against her will he took her honor. Then, fearing...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Purgatorio, Canto IX. The previous page discussed the astronomical timing of the dream—the lunar dawn—and the mythological figures associated with the stars. This page delves into the first of Dante’s three prophetic dreams on the mountain: the vision of the Golden Eagle.</meta>

PURGATORIO &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; CANTO

doing; so that the poor woman would not reveal such an injury, he cut out her tongue and left her in the woods. But Philomela, deprived of speech, acted with ingenuity: she called upon all her weaving skill <note>The original "abutoria" refers to Philomela's famous tapestry where she wove the story of her rape since she could not speak.</note> and sent the finished work to her sister. Procne, moved not so much by pity toward Philomela as by a doubled hatred toward her adulterous husband, who had broken faith with two sisters, pretended to want to celebrate the sacrifices to Bacchus, which are performed at night and in the woods. She went where her sister was and stealthily brought her into her palace. She killed Itys, the son she had by Tereus, cooked him, and made him a meal for his father. And after he had finished eating, she placed before him the head and feet of his own eaten son. I will not recount how much cruelty the infuriated father prepared to use against her, he who had been made the sepulcher of his own flesh. But the compassion of the gods transformed them all: Tereus became a hoopoe, a stinking bird but with beautiful feathers and a crown, so that it seems he retains his ancient royal attire. Itys became a pheasant; Philomela a nightingale, which lives in the woods and whose tongue is not seen when it sings. Procne became a swallow, and she remains red on her breast from the blood of her son with which she was stained.

**AND THAT OUR MIND, MORE A PILGRIM FROM THE FLESH.** <note>Dante's verse: "E che la mente nostra, peregrina / più da la carne..."</note> At which time the soul is more a "pilgrim," meaning further from the body; as if to say it is more disentangled and free from the contagion of the body. We demonstrated above in the first canticle <note>referring to the *Inferno*</note> through philosophical reasons why at this hour dreams are truer than at others.

**IN A DREAM IT SEEMED TO ME.** The vision is feigned to be this: that it seemed to him he saw an eagle with golden feathers, staying suspended in the sky with open wings, and which seemed continually wanting to swoop down. Allegorically, according to Francesco da Buti <note>A 14th-century commentator on Dante.</note> and several others, by the eagle is understood **Divine Charity**. Because God is charity. And that the eagle stays always ready with open wings to swoop signifies that Divine Charity is always ready to snatch human souls toward God. The golden feathers demonstrate the rays of charity, shining and pure as gold is. Then the author adds that it seemed to him he was in the forest of Ida, where Jove, in the form of an eagle, snatched up Ganymede. And the aforementioned Francesco understands by this that holy men, who perform penance in the forests, are more easily snatched up by Divine Charity. By this, the author means that he was disposed to purge himself like such men. This exposition I do not reject in any way, for it is pious and suited to the Christian religion. Nevertheless, when I consider the depth of the poet’s genius, I judge that he wishes to demonstrate that while sleeping, there came to him that type of dream which the Latins call a *somnium* <term>somnium: a dream that masks a truth under a veil and requires interpretation</term>; which predicts true things, but obscurely and under a veil, in a form that cannot be understood without an interpreter. Thus, Dante dreams with his sensory soul, and then his higher reason interprets the dream. For this reason, we shall say that Dante falls asleep in the valley, exhausted by the "steep journey"—that is, having begun to rise toward **contemplation**. Becoming tired in that effort, human weakness—represented by Sordello (meaning civil doctrines)—is lifted from the climb and led to the **civil life**, in which he falls asleep (becomes lazy). And God, seeing his good will, has compassion for his frailty and sends him **Illuminating Grace**, which in this dream is figured as the eagle. This grace snatches him to the fire, which inflames the heart that is made festive. We should understand nothing else in such a fiction except that Illuminating Grace induces him to rapturous love, from which, being set aflame, he acquires Cherubic intelligence. And it is a wonderful thing with what sharpness of wit and judgment, and how covertly, he imitates Virgil. Which does not seem to me out of place to express here. Both of these poets wished to show that this occurs: that men who give themselves to contemplation, either exhausted by the toil or terrified and dismayed by the difficulty, change their purpose and return to the civil life. And perhaps they would stay there if they were not excited and raised up by divine help. Virgil signifies this in Aeneas: who, afflicted by the storm stirred up by Juno and Aeolus, abandons the undertaking of going to Italy—which, as I showed in our allegories, always represents the **contemplative life**—and decides to go to Carthage, representing the **active life**. And here, having become the husband of Dido, he would have remained if Jove had not sent Mercury to excite him and admonish him not to abandon the first undertaking. That is, if God had not shown him through true doctrine how much Mary is to be preferred to Martha <note>The biblical sisters Mary and Martha are traditional symbols for the contemplative and active lives, respectively.</note>. Similarly, at present, our poet shows that the ascent to the purgatorial virtues is so arduous that, exhausted, he rests and falls asleep in the valley, which we established as the civil life. But Divine Grace excites him and snatches him up, as you will see below.

**IT SEEMED I WAS THERE WHERE WERE.** It seemed to Dante he was in the forest of Ida in Troy, where Ganymede, while hunting, was snatched by Jove in the form of an eagle. He placing it in the forest is excellent: a solitary place to denote the contemplative life, which is solitary and which he desired, although the arduous toil of climbing had made him fall asleep. The eagle perfectly signifies **Illuminating Grace** because just as such grace is full of light, so the eagle more than any other bird fills itself with light, for it can endure the rays of the sun and see itself reflected in them. No other animal can do this. Furthermore, there is no bird that rises higher or lifts itself further from the earth. Similarly, grace itself elevates our intellect.

**ABANDONED HIS OWN BY GANYMEDE.** And he said well that Ganymede "abandoned," and was not abandoned. Because he who goes to the solitary life leaves behind those who remain in the active life.

**WHEN HE WAS SNATCHED.** Snatched to the high consistory: to the council of those who gather in heaven.

**WITHIN MYSELF I THOUGHT:** Seeming to be in the place where Ganymede was snatched, I thought to myself: perhaps this eagle does not strike—that is, does not wound or take prey—except from this place. And certainly, the mind cannot be raised to such contemplation, nor is it snatched by Divine Grace, if it is not in the "forest of Ida"—that is, in the solitary life and separated from all noise and tumult.

...and greed for lowly and earthly things. Let Ganymede therefore be the human mind, which Jove—that is, the highest God—loves. Let his companions be the other powers of the soul, such as the vegetative and sensitive <note>In medieval philosophy, the soul had three levels: the vegetative (responsible for growth), the sensitive (responsible for senses and movement), and the rational (responsible for reason).</note>. Jove therefore intends that the mind be in the woods—that is, removed from mortal things—and with the aforementioned eagle lifts it to heaven. Thus, the mind abandons its companions—the vegetative and sensitive—and becomes abstract, and as Plato says, removed from the body and forgetful of corporeal things, placed entirely in the contemplation of the secrets of heaven. The name of the woods also serves this allegory, because *idin* <note>The author likely refers to the Greek *idein* (ἰδεῖν), meaning "to see."</note> in Greek means to see and to know.

Then it seemed to me that, having wheeled a little more,
terrible as a lightning bolt it descended,
and snatched me up as far as the fire:
There it seemed that it and I burned,
and the imagined fire scorched me so
that it was necessary for my sleep to break.
Not otherwise did Achilles startle,
turning his awakened eyes around

When his mother stole him away from Chiron to Scyros,
carrying him while sleeping in her arms,

So I started, as from my face
sleep fled, and I turned pale,
as a man does when he freezes in fear.

Beside me was my sole comfort,
and the sun was already more than two hours high,

do not tighten, but loosen every strength.
You have now reached Purgatory:

see the entrance where it appears divided.
A while ago, in the dawn that precedes the day,

let me take this one who sleeps;
thus I will make his way easier for him.'

she came up here, and I followed in her footsteps.
Here she placed you, and first her beautiful eyes
showed me that open entrance;
then she and sleep went away together."

<column-break/>

He continues in his fictional vision, narrating how the eagle circled somewhat in the air, then swooped down with no less speed than an arrow falling to earth. It snatched him and carried him as far as the sphere of fire <note>According to the medieval Aristotelian worldview, a layer of fire existed between the Earth's atmosphere and the moon.</note>; and there it seemed he burned together with the eagle; and in that form it seemed he felt the fire so intensely that he woke. As soon as a man is snatched up to the contemplation of purgative virtues, both the eagle and he are set aflame—that is, grace takes fire in him, and he in the love of divine things—so that the fire wakes him from sleep—that is, it rouses him from all sloth.

**NOT OTHERWISE** did Achilles startle. We spoke of Achilles in the first canticle <note>Inferno.</note>. But regarding this text, we will recall that Thetis, his mother, fearing he would be forced to go to the Trojan War, decided to hide him. Therefore she made him fall asleep, and while he was sleeping, she took him from Chiron, his master, and brought him to the island of Scyros to King Lycomedes. There, in female habit and dress, he stayed with the daughters, nor was he known by the King's daughters. And Pyrrhus was born, who...

He calls Virgil his "sole comfort" because the rational part, illustrated by various sciences, is the only one with which we can ascend to purgation and such speculation. Therefore, Sordello did not follow—for history does not record him as a judge—nor did Judge Nino (the knowledge of laws), nor Marquis Conrad (who appropriately represents military discipline), follow Dante in this ascent. Instead, they remained in the valley, because these disciplines are not proper to the civil and active life <note>The commentator argues that legal and military skills belong to the "active life" of the world and cannot aid the soul in the higher "contemplative" climb toward God.</note>. But Virgil—that is, our intellect adorned with learning—is the one who follows Lucia—that is, divine grace—to the purgative virtues. **THE SUN WAS HIGH** more than two hours, because the entire sign of Aries, with which the sun was rising, was above the horizon. Therefore Dante could have ascended, for it was already two hours into the day. **MY FACE WAS TURNED TO THE SEA.** This shows that looking at the sea and not the mountain, he could not perceive that he had been carried up. By the "sea," we understand appetite. **DO NOT TIGHTEN** but loosen. This signifies: do not fear, but hope. Just as our mind contracts and tightens through sorrow or fear, so through joy or hope it diffuses and expands. Lucia, who is illuminating grace (as we showed in the first canticle), carried him to Purgatory. This signifies she illuminated him with those things necessary for his salvation. And Lucia came in the dawn that...

...precedes the day: because such grace leads divine light into the mind in this way, just as the dawn leads the daylight. And when she came: Dante’s soul was sleeping: because before her coming, the soul becomes sluggish in the pleasures of mortal things. "Upon the flowers" <note>original: "Sopra li fiore"</note> in the delight of earthly things: with which the place below is adorned: with which civil life is adorned. **LET ME TAKE THIS ONE:** <note>original: "LASCIATEMI PIGLARE CHOSTUI"</note> as if she <note>Saint Lucy, representing Illuminating Grace.</note> were admonishing Sordello, and Judge Nino, and Conrad the Marquis <note>Nobles Dante encountered in the Valley of the Princes.</note>—that is, the occupations of the active life—that they should yield and leave, so that such grace may lift the mind. **SHE TOOK YOU AWAY:** illuminating grace snatched away the sensuality <note>In this context, "sensuality" refers to the lower, physical part of the soul driven by the senses.</note>, and the intellect followed the tracks of such grace. And this shows the reason for the entrance to Purgatory. **THEN HE [left him] and sleep.** This verse has no allegory: but serves the fiction made of the dream.

Just as a man who, doubting, is reassured
and changes his fear into comfort
once the truth has been discovered,
I changed; and as if without care
my leader saw me, up over the cliff
he moved; and I followed toward the height.
Reader, you see well how I elevate
my subject; and therefore with more art
do not marvel if I reinforce it.

We approached and arrived at a spot
where, at first, it seemed broken to me,
just like a crack that divides a wall;
I saw a gate, and three steps below it
to go up to it, of different colors:
and a gatekeeper who as yet said nothing.
And as I opened my eyes more and more,
I saw him sitting upon the highest step,
such in his face that I could not endure it:
And he had a naked sword in his hand,
which reflected the rays toward us so
that I often directed my eyes in vain.

"Tell from there: what do you want?"
he began to say: "where is your escort?
Take care that coming up does not harm you."
"A Lady of Heaven, aware of these things,"
my master replied to him just now,
"told us: 'Go there, for there is the gate.'"
"And may she advance your steps in good,"
began again the courteous gatekeeper,
"come then forward to our steps."

<column-break/>

The intellect admonishes the sensuality: that it should not fear, being illuminated by divine grace. And as soon as it sees itself out of fear, and void of every care, and full of hope: it guides it where illuminating grace showed him the entrance of Purgatory: and the sensuality follows it. **MY READER, see well.** He excuses himself: so that no one wonders if he adorns his poem more than usual with various fictions in this place: showing that the height of the subject requires it.

From far away it seemed to him he saw a narrow crack; but approaching, he saw that it was a gate. Because when, at the beginning, not yet freed from the love of earthly things, we begin to consider the purgatorial virtues: the way seems very difficult and very narrow. But when afterwards we approach it—that is, we turn our minds more toward it and consider it better—we see that it is a gate and not a crack: because it is an easy and wide way. This gate is climbed by three steps, which are of different colors. And one sits on the top—that is, the superior step. This is the priest who admits one into Purgatory. Therefore, he describes what the priest ought to be. This person he calls the gatekeeper, because to him are left the keys of the kingdom of heaven. **And whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.** <note>original Latin: "Et quodcunque ligauerit in terris: erit ligatum et in celis. Et quodcunque soluerit in terris: erit solutum et in celis." This refers to the "Power of the Keys" granted to the Church in Matthew 16:19.</note> This person remains in silence if someone else does not open themselves to him. For the priest should not absolve one who does not ask for absolution. He sits: because he should always wait for the sinner. **SUCH IN HIS FACE THAT I could not endure it.** This shows that he was so radiant that Dante could not look at him. And in this, it denotes the rays of doctrine and of character that must be in the true priest. **THE NAKED SWORD** signifies righteous deeds: and it shows that the rays from the priest's face strike the sword, and the sword reflected them into the faces of Virgil and Dante. Because the doctrine and good character of the priest shine in his righteous works: and those reflect the rays into the sinners. And they are the best example to them. Wherefore our sensuality cannot look upon such a reflection.

A man must, before approaching the priest, "say it"—that is, he must, before going to confession, deliberate and desire it. Nor should he go without an escort: which is illuminating grace, from which we have the best inspiration, without which confession harms more than it helps. Wherefore Virgil replies that they have the escort with them: because a little while before, Lucy had shown him the way. Hearing which, the gatekeeper replied: "and she"—that is, the same Lucy—"who acted as your escort, may she advance your steps in good"—that is, may she increase your steps in good: because in truth, one cannot make a good acquisition in confession if Lucy, illuminating us, does not... <note>The sentence ends mid-thought at the bottom of the page.</note>

The first step was of white marble, 
so polished and clear
that I mirrored myself in it as I truly appear.
The second was tinted darker than perse <note>A very dark purple or blackish-blue color.</note>, 
of a rough and scorched stone, 
cracked through its length and its breadth.
The third, which rests massive above, 
seemed to me to be porphyry, as flaming red 
as blood that spurts forth from a vein.
Upon this, the Angel of God held both his feet, 
sitting upon the threshold 
which seemed to me to be made of diamond stone.

Up over the three steps, with good will, 
my leader drew me, saying: “Ask 
humbly that he may undo the lock.”
Devoutly I cast myself at the holy feet; 
I asked for mercy and that he might open for me; 
but first, I struck my breast three times.
Seven 'P's <note>Representing the seven "Peccata" or mortal sins: Pride, Envy, Wrath, Sloth, Avarice, Gluttony, and Lust.</note> he inscribed upon my forehead 
with the point of his sword, and said: “Make sure you 
wash these wounds when you are inside.”

<column-break/>

pira. **COME THEN.** <note>original: "VENITE ADVNQVE"</note> The priest must examine whoever comes to confession: to see if they hold divine inspiration. And having recognized this good inspiration, he receives them courteously and with human kindness.

<image-desc>Decorative ornamental initial C in blue</image-desc> With three steps one ascends to purgation. Hence the Psalmist says: "God shall be known through his steps" <note>original Latin: "Deus per gradus eius cognošcetur"</note>. And Job says: "I will proclaim him through each of my steps" <note>original Latin: "per singulos gradus meos pronuntiabo eum"</note>. The first of these is of white marble, and so polished that one can see oneself mirrored in it. This signifies **Confession**: which must be simple, pure, and fitting, without fraud, but from a simple heart. Of this the Psalmist sings: "I will confess to you, Lord, with all my heart" <note>original Latin: "Confitebor tibi domine in toto corde meo"</note>. The second step is of rough, scorched black stone, cracked in every direction. This signifies **Contrition**: repentance and sorrow. Hence the prophet Joel says: "Rend your hearts, and not your garments" <note>original Latin: "Scindite corda ueštra: et non ueštimenta"</note>. This is contrition: the recognition of the sin committed with sorrow and repentance for having committed it, and the resolution not to fall into it again. Indeed, such contrition must have the hardness of stone—that is, it must be a firm and immutable purpose. It must be black, meaning full of sadness and affliction, and rough from the torment that grips the soul. Similarly, it is scorched by the flames that ignite in the conscience. It is cracked in every direction: which signifies how much the mind must be torn apart, in whatever direction it thinks of the sin already committed. The third step was of porphyry. This stone is very hard and red in color. In this, he expresses **Satisfaction**: which must be whole, and from which nothing should be taken away, just as porphyry does not diminish; and it must be done with the fervor of charity. These three steps lead us to purgatory and to the washing away of all our filth. For just as we sin in three ways—with the heart, with the tongue, and with deeds—so in the same ways we must amend ourselves: with contrition of the heart, confession of the tongue, and satisfaction of deeds. The gatekeeper keeps his feet upon the last step to show that confession is not enough if we stop there and do not proceed further; nor is contrition alone enough, but we must not stop until we arrive at satisfaction. The threshold of this gate, upon which the priest sits, is of diamond. This stone cannot be broken or defeated. Thus, the priest must be whole and severe, and not be corrupted. They also say that whoever carries diamond upon them drives away fear; likewise, he who approaches confession does not fear diabolical attacks. Furthermore, they write that the diamond, when placed near a lodestone, does not let it pull iron to itself. Similarly, as long as confession is near the human soul, it does not allow any hardness or obstinacy to be drawn to it.

<image-desc>Decorative ornamental initial V in blue</image-desc> **VIRGIL** drew him up with good will—that is, Reason pulled up Sensuality, which, already inspired by divine grace, followed willingly. And Virgil admonishes him that he should humbly ask the gatekeeper to open. For after the ascent of the three steps—that is, after confession, contrition, and the intent to satisfy—we must humbly ask for absolution. **I ASKED FOR MERCY.** A man cannot, through any deed he performs, merit the remission of guilt; if he merited it, he could demand justice. But because he does not merit it, he asks for mercy. **FIRST I STRUCK MY BREAST THREE TIMES.** Because, as we have said, one sins in three ways, but every sin proceeds from the heart; therefore we strike our breast as if wishing to punish the heart. And the angel wrote seven "P"s on his forehead. This denotes that the good and prudent confessor shows that every sinner at some time sins in all seven mortal sins; and he wrote them with the point of his sword—that is, with the reason of justice. For the prudent priest, when he sees the sinner disposed to purge himself, must show him that he is stained by them all. And therefore he writes them on his forehead and told him that when he was inside—meaning in the place fit for purging—he should wash them all away—that is, he should purge himself of them all.

It also interprets the Angel's diamond threshold as the priest's incorruptibility and the seven 'P's on Dante's forehead as the seven mortal sins.</summary>

# ->PURGATORY<-

This angel, who was given the authority to open the gate, was dressed in a garment that had an ashen color or the color of earth. This denotes the most excellent gift that our Redeemer left to man. For not only did He redeem the human race with His blood, but He also left to that portion of men who are elevated to the priestly order the authority to absolve and to bind. Thus, to show that the angel represented the priest, [the poet] imagines that he wore ashen or earth-colored garments; that is, he had a human body, which is the "garment" of the soul, as is often found in both the works of Plato and in the Holy Scriptures, you will

Ashes, or earth that is dug up dry,
would be of one color with his vestment;
and from beneath it he drew two keys.
One was of gold, and the other was of silver:
**first with the white**, and then with the yellow,
he worked the gate so that I was content.
"Whenever one of these keys fails,
so that it does not turn rightly in the lock,"
he said to us, "this pathway does not open.
One is more precious, but the other requires too much
**art and wit** before it unlocks,
because it is the one that unties the knot.
From Peter I hold them; and he told me to err
rather in opening than in keeping it shut,
provided that the people cast themselves at my feet."

<column-break/>

find. And because this hidden authority resides within man, he imagines that he drew the keys from beneath his garments. The priest possesses this authority, even though he is in human flesh, which seems divine rather than human; this authority was called "keys" by the One who granted it. Hence it says in the Gospel: *And I will give to thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven: and the gates of hell shall not prevail against them.* <note>original: "Et tibi dabo claues regni celorum : Et porte iferi nõ preualebunt aduerfus eas." (Matthew 16:19)</note> Nor is it without reason that there are two keys. For a man cannot absolve unless he has apostolic authority. Nor is this authority enough, if along with it there is not also the sacred knowledge <term>scientia: theological understanding and discernment</term> to recognize vices and distinguish them from virtues, and to differentiate between them. Therefore, he sets the gold key for the authority, of which the priest still makes mention in absolving, saying: *And I, by the authority which I exercise...* <note>original: "Et ego te auctoritate : qua fungor."</note> He sets the white [silver] for the doctrine. And certainly, gold surpasses every metal; it always remains incorrupt and without rust. Nor does it become dirty, even if it were submerged in mud. Similarly, this authority given to the priest is never corrupted. And even if he himself be a sinner, nonetheless it does not pollute or stain such authority. Silver is bright and shining, and of a clear sound. So the evangelical doctrine shines through its truth and integrity. And it makes itself heard everywhere; hence it is written: *Their sound has gone forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world.* <note>original: "In omnem terram exiuit sonus eorum . Et in fines orbis terræ uerba eorum." (Psalm 18:5)</note> **FIRST WITH THE WHITE.** Having heard the confession, the priest must—before he absolves—recognize all the sins together with the sinner; and because many are varied and manifold and tangled together, he must distinguish them and explain them to the sinner, showing which is more or less grave. This he cannot do except through the knowledge of evangelical doctrine, which is signified by the silver key. And after having made such an examination and admonished the sinner, he should absolve him with the authority granted to him by Peter (that is, from the Apostolic See), which is signified by the golden key. Therefore, the poet’s sentence is true: that he opens first with the white (the silver one) and then with the yellow (the gold one), because first, doctrine and prudence are necessary to know sins and their nature, to distinguish them, and to show the person confessing what they entail, and afterward to absolve him. **HE WORKED THE GATE SO THAT I WAS CONTENT** because he opened it as I desired. And he did not speak without prudence, saying: "so that I was content," because he wanted to show how content the sinner remains, and how light and free from all remorse of conscience. **WHENEVER ONE.** Whoever hears the confession of a sinner and lacks either the authority to absolve or the knowledge to recognize sins, such absolution is invalid. And therefore he said: *This pathway does not open* (that is, this narrow entrance). And it is narrow for the reasons we have stated above. **ONE IS MORE PRECIOUS.** Who doubts that the gold one is more precious and more valuable than the silver one? For man can receive no greater gift than this authority, because it is divine and not human. Nor by his own nature does man have the power to forgive injuries done either to God or to one's neighbor. But it is a supernatural privilege given to the creature by the most merciful liberality of the [Lord of the] sinner. **BUT THE OTHER REQUIRES TOO MUCH ART AND WIT.** The authority to absolve can exist, as we often see, in a man without doctrine, without art (that is, prudence), and without wit. But to know how to recognize sins and give a true judgment on them requires prudence and wit. Therefore, the silver key has need of art and wit, because in truth this is the one that *unties the knot* (that is, distinguishes and clarifies). He uses "art" not only for prudence, which concerns particulars, but for science, which concerns universals. For even the Latins—although prudence is one thing and art another—use "art" to mean both prudence and science. **FROM PETER I HOLD THEM.** He shows that no priest can have the authority to absolve except according to the form of the apostolic canons. **AND HE TOLD ME TO ERR RATHER** in opening than in keeping it shut. He notes here that God always mixes mercy with justice. And therefore He wills that the priest should rather err in absolving than in not absolving. For "God does not want the death of a sinner, but that he be converted and live." <note>original: "non uult deus mortem peccatoris . Sed ut conuertatur et uiuat." (Ezekiel 33:11)</note> And Chrysostom says...

It emphasizes that while the authority (gold) is divine and incorruptible, the doctrine (silver) is more difficult to master as it requires careful discernment and knowledge.</summary>

# ->CANTO NINE<-

...God is kind: why the priest should be stern. <note>original: "us benignus: quare sacerdos austerus."</note> Where the father of the family is generous, the steward should not be stingy. **AS LONG AS THE PEOPLE FALL AT MY FEET.** This means as much as humbling oneself: and rendering oneself into guilt: and accusing oneself as a sinner: which can provide the discount for every sin.

**Then he pushed the panel of the sacred gate**
**saying, "Enter; but I make you aware:**
**that whoever looks back returns outside."**
**And when the pivots of that sacred palace,**
**which are made of metal, sounding and strong,**
**were turned in their sockets,**
**Tarpeia did not roar so much, nor show itself so harsh,**
**when the good Metellus was taken from it,**
**whereby it afterwards remained lean.**

**WHEN THE PIVOTS WERE TURNED IN THEIR SOCKETS.** Large doors are not connected to hinges with straps. But instead of straps, they have certain pins. And in place of hinges, they have a concave space into which these pins enter: and upon those the door is balanced in such a way that it opens and shuts. Therefore, he calls those pins "spigoli" <note>edges or pivots</note> which enter into the "cardini," that is, into the concave hinges. **WHICH ARE OF METAL.** He shows the door to be of metal, a most strong and incorruptible material: to denote that it cannot be broken, nor entered by force. Nor should anyone think that by forcing the priest to absolve him, such absolution would be of any value. **SOUNDING AND STRONG.** He imagines that this door makes a great noise when it opens: because it never happens that a man goes from a foul life to laudable life and habits without it being spoken of and discussed everywhere. And he also wished to signify the sentence of the Gospel: that there is more celebration in heaven for one sinner who converts than for ninety-nine righteous people. **IT DID NOT ROAR NOR SHOW ITSELF SO HARSH.** It is very well known, especially through the poet Lucan, that after the most cowardly flight of Pompey and the Senate, Caesar occupied Rome; he wanted all the money from the treasury, that is, the public chamber of the community. And although Metellus, tribune of the plebs, contradicted him and forbade it to be opened, nevertheless Aurelius Cotta, having pushed Metellus aside, had it opened. There are some who adapt this comparison—and almost all others—to Dante's allegorical sense. But to me it seems that it would be a matter too anxious and curious.

**I turned around, attentive to the first thunder,**
**and "We praise Thee, O God" it seemed to me**
**to hear in a voice mixed with the sweet sound.**
**Such an image exactly it gave me,**
**what I heard, as one is used to receiving**
**when one stands to sing with organs:**
**for now the words are understood, and now not.**

...we acknowledge [You] as Lord <note>original: "num confitemur"</note>. And thus afterwards with alternating verses—which the Greeks call "amabaeic" <note>original: "amabei" — responsive singing</note>—they continued to compose the entire hymn. From then on, the custom has always been observed in the Apostolic Church that when a desired thing is brought to its proper end, giving thanks to God, this hymn is sung. For this reason, the poet deservedly imagines that the good spirits sang as Dante entered. Furthermore, he posits that this hymn was sung with one verse by the voice and the other with the organs. Because of this, it happened that in the voice of those spirits the words were understood, but not in the sound of the organs.

<column-break/>

The priest, after he has particularly considered all the sins together with the sinner through a diligent examination and shown him their quality, ought to draw out the keys: that is, come to the absolution. But first he must show him the nature of it and the conditions it must have, and the authority and the science of distinguishing [between sins]. He must show him that if these things are not observed, the absolution is invalid. And after such words, seeing the sinner well-disposed, he should push the door and open it: which is to absolve him. Since the sinner who is absolved can purge himself of his sins afterward, provided that upon entering the purgation he does not turn back: that is, does not return to sinning. Therefore, because the priest should admonish him, saying, "Go and sin no more," <note>original: "Vade et amplius noli peccare"</note> the Author places this precept here, saying: **I MAKE YOU AWARE.** That is, I give you notice: that he who looks back, meaning he who returns to sin, returns and goes out from this gate: that is, he loses his absolution. And it seems that here the angel does not impose any other penance on Dante than what Christ imposed on the woman: "Go and sin no more." **AND**

**I turned around**, not backward, but toward that part where I heard the singing. For if he had turned backward, he would have counteracted the command given to him by the angel. **ATTENTIVE TO THE FIRST thunder.** It is as if he says: I entered into Purgatory with the utmost attention to see and understand what was there. And by this he shows that he who enters into the purgative virtue must be circumspect and use diligent investigation of that which is found therein. Therefore, being attentive, no sooner had the hymn begun than he heard the first thunder. **WE PRAISE THEE, O GOD.** <note>original: "TE DEVM laudamus"</note> This hymn was made in turns by Saint Ambrose and Saint Augustine. For Ambrose, having put great industry into converting Augustine to the Christian faith, after he had converted him through many sermons and disputations, out of the supreme joy of having regained such a man, Ambrose, giving thanks to God, said: "We praise Thee, O God." And Augustine added: "Thee, we acknowledge [to be] Lord." <note>original: "Te dominum [confitemur]"</note>

### . CANTO TEN OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE .

We have already entered inside Purgatory: and because in this place all stains are washed away and all sins are purged, it seemed sufficient to the poet to divide all human faults into the **seven capital sins** <note>Also known as the Seven Deadly Sins.</note>: because no error can be committed that does not fall under one of these seven. And it is to be noted here that the punishments of Hell are of one kind, and those of Purgatory are another. Hell gives punishment <note>original: "supplicio"</note> and does not remove the stain. And this is manifest regarding the dead. But it is also true in life. For whoever has made a habit of vice, even though many punishments may nourish him <note>likely meaning "afflict him"</note>, nonetheless he does not leave the vice. We see the **proud man** incur many difficulties and suffer many dangers, and nonetheless he does not abandon the vice. Among sins, the most grave is **Pride**. Whence the Psalmist says: *and I shall be cleansed of the greatest sin* <note>original Latin: "et mundabor a delicto maximo," referring to Psalm 19:13</note>, that is, from pride; and Solomon says: *Pride is the beginning of all sin* <note>original Latin: "Initium omnis peccati superbia," from the Book of Sirach, traditionally attributed to Solomon</note>. They define Pride as a vicious elevation of the mind which, despising those inferior to itself, strives to lord it over equals and superiors. But the punishments of Purgatory remove the stains and cleanse from every foulness, both

<column-break/>

**ONCE we were inside the threshold of the gate**
**which the bad love of souls makes unused**
**because it makes the crooked path seem straight,**
**I heard it being closed by the sound.**
**And if I had turned my eyes back toward it,**
**what excuse would have been worthy of the fault?**

in the essential Purgatory <note>The physical realm of the afterlife.</note> as in the moral one <note>The internal transformation of the soul.</note>. But so that he may eventually return to the subject: the poet divides this entire place into seven parts, and in each one he places the purgation of a sin. And just as when he descended into Hell, he first found the lighter sins from place to place, and the further he went toward the center, the greater he found them—because reasonably, the greater and more significant the sinners are, the further they must be from heaven—so in the layout of these seven sins, he places the most grave in the first places; because in ascending, the first are always the lowest and furthest from heaven. He places, therefore, in the first place **Pride**, the greatest of all sins, of which we shall speak a little further below.

**ONCE WE WERE INSIDE THE GATE.** **WHICH**: This gate, the "bad love of souls"—that is, the depraved and vicious desire for earthly and mortal things of the soul—**MAKES UNUSED**. That is, it causes it not to be used. And the meaning is that the excessive desire for earthly things which souls have is the reason why this gate is not used: because, entangled and enticed by those things, they do not seek to purge themselves of them. **I HEARD IT BEING CLOSED BY THE SOUND**: Every door of any entrance, being closed, produces different effects in different places. For it neither lets those enter who are outside, nor those exit who are inside. Therefore, just as it was closed before he entered, showing the difficulty of entering into the **purgatorial virtues**, so after he has entered, it shows the difficulty of leaving: because he who has the habit of virtue does not leave it. **AND IF I HAD TURNED MY EYES BACK TO IT**: if I had turned back. Which signifies that, having entered into purgation, if I had returned to vice, I would have found no excuse worthy of the fault. And certainly, for one who is not yet upright on the true path, it seems he deserves more blame...

...passion; for he who is there is ignorant. It is necessary, then, that whoever enters the purgative virtues should not turn back, but should persevere. Whence in the Gospel: *He who endures to the end shall be saved* <note>original Latin: "Non qui inceperit. Sed qui perseveraverit usque in finem salvus erit." From Matthew 24:13.</note>. This is prefigured in Genesis by the wife of Lot. Since the angels told Lot, his wife, and his daughters to flee Sodom and never turn back, and because the wife turned back to see the fire of Sodom, she was immediately turned into a pillar of salt. She is a figure for those who, having departed from the greed of carnal things, return to them. And she becomes a pillar of salt because she is a seasoning and an example to others <note>The commentator suggests that like salt which preserves, she serves as a lasting warning to others.</note>.

**The way** was steep and went through a cleft in the rock. This cleft did not go straight, but swayed like a wave and a fish spine <note>original: "a spina pesce," describing a zigzag or undulating path.</note>, inclining now to the right and now to the left. The reason why the face is steep has already been stated in many places. It shows that this climb is solid rock to demonstrate the hardness and harshness that is greatest at the beginning of the purgative virtues. And the rock is split in such a way that it is necessary to avoid that cleft so as not to fall. And although this cleft runs lengthwise, it nonetheless undulates. By the right, we understand prosperity and a delightful life; by the left, adversity and hardships; and both parts are necessary

Therefore, it is necessary to have a bold spirit and to be unconquered against both one and the other. Therefore, one must use skill, that is, the highest prudence; which according to the philosophers is: *A certain method of things to be done* <note>original Latin: "Certa ratio rerum agendarum," a standard scholastic definition of Prudence.</note>. And in prosperity, one must restrain oneself and not become proud. And in adversity, one must not lose heart and not allow oneself to be overcome. **AND THIS MADE OUR steps scanty.** This difficulty of avoiding the cleft made our steps scanty, that is, brief and rare. And indeed, one cannot make much progress on this path at the beginning, until practice begins to turn into habit. And because we went slowly, the moon—which had already passed its opposition and was waning—had already returned to its bed, that is, it had returned to its setting and had gone down before we had climbed this height. The moon was at its

full on the night Dante found himself lost in the woods. And already the third night had passed. And this was the third day. Therefore, the moon had already approached the sun by more than one sign, because she stays in each for two days, three hours, and two-thirds of an hour. Therefore, on this day when the moon was going down, the sun was at more than the sixth part of the day. Thus, the sixth part of the day had passed before they had begun the purgation; which truly shows that one cannot become fit and capable of purging oneself without the passage of time. Nor do we reach the beginning of the habit of these virtues without frequent actions. **THROUGH that cradle:** through that valley, which has a concavity in the shape of a cradle. And he used this word to denote that these are *incunabula* <note>Latin for "cradle-land" or the very beginnings of a process.</note>, that is, early infancy. **BUT WHEN WE WERE FREE and in the open:** that is, arrived in a spacious and open place where the mountain straightens itself and forms its summit. **I TIRED and both of us uncertain.** We can say that the flesh becomes weary, but not the soul. But more subtly, in investigating, the sense labors and tires. Because it does not operate without corporeal instruments, which become weary and after long exercise become exhausted. But the intellect, which operates on universal things and operates without a corporeal instrument, does not tire, as we demonstrated in our *Dialogue on the Soul* with Platonic and Aristotelian arguments. Thus, only Dante was tired, and not Virgil. But both were uncertain. For not only the senses and practical reason, but even speculative reason would lose the way of the purgative virtues if divine help did not assist it. **WE STOPPED ON A level place.** This is the first terrace of Purgatory, where he places those who purge themselves of Pride. He describes, therefore, that having climbed that divided rock, as has been said, he found a plain at the end of which a new cliff and a new ascent began. And it shows that this plain was lonely, no different than paths in deserts. And the width of the plain from the edge where they had climbed up to the cliff where the ascent begins again was the measure of three human bodies, either from head to foot or by the span of the arms. The lonely road shows that there are few who purge themselves of vices, and especially of pride. And therefore he says:

<column-break/>

We should understand that he imagines that around this mountain there are seven terraces, one above the other with a certain interval between them; and the highest is always of a smaller circumference, because the higher the mountain goes, the more it thins out. And in this first terrace, because it is the lowest and most remote from heaven, the greatest sin is punished, which is Pride. And so following in order, the more serious sins are always punished in the lower parts. Therefore, in the second he purges Envy in Canto XIII. In the third, Sloth in Canto XV. In the fourth, Wrath in Canto XVII. In the fifth, Avarice in Canto XVIII. In the sixth, Gluttony in Canto XXII. <note>The commentator follows a slightly different sequence or canto numbering than modern editions, which usually place Wrath in the third terrace and Sloth in the fourth.</note> And above this, he places the summit of the mountain, and in it the paradise of delights. But returning to the text: he shows this level of the ledge, where pride is purged, to be as wide as a human body can be extended three times. This is to demonstrate that pride in man is spread through cognition, speech, and action; or truly, we use it against our superiors, against our equals, and against our inferiors.

various stories, which serve as examples of humility. The poet places these images of humility in the place where pride is purged, and rightly so. For every contrary is purged by its contrary. Thus we see that hot diseases require cold medicines, and cold ones require hot. Therefore, pride is purged and extinguished with humility. And note that these examples are carved, and not painted. Because a painting is easily removed, but not a carving. And they are carved not in soft material, but in hard. This warns us that if we wish to utterly drive pride from us, it is necessary to have humility sculpted and entirely fixed in our minds. Furthermore, he uses white marble to denote that such humility should be pure and clean, and not spotted with any fiction or simulation. And just as the color white is bright and shining, so should this humility shine. Because:
> nothing is prouder than feigned humility. <note>original Latin: "nichil est ficta humilitate superbius." A common medieval sentiment often attributed to St. Jerome.</note>
Furthermore, he shows that such images are so lifelike that not only Polyclitus or any other excellent sculptor, but Nature herself could not make them so realistic. This signifies nothing other than that such humility must be in its own proper image, in a form that neither the wit of man nor 

---

any natural movement could make more lifelike. Polyclitus was the son of Ageladas and from the city of Sicyon, a sculptor much celebrated among the ancients. He was especially famous for a statue they call the *Diadumenos* <note>A statue of a youth tying a fillet or diadem around his head.</note>, valued at a hundred talents. For this reason, he had a name suited to him, because "Polyclitus" in Greek signifies "a man of much fame." <term>Polyclitus</term> <note>From the Greek 'poly' (much) and 'kleitos' (famed).</note>. BUT NATURE WOULD HAVE: been shamed and remained defeated. Properly speaking, we say someone receives "shame" <note>original: "scorno"</note> when they presume or trust that one thing will happen to them, but then the opposite happens. And "scorno" can be called dishonor. For just as we say a man "puts out his horns" <note>The commentator links "scorno" (shame) to the removal of "corna" (horns).</note> when he exalts himself through victory or for having achieved what he desired, so by opposition we say one is "scorned" [de-horned]. THE ANGEL GABRIEL: who came to earth to announce to Mary, WITH THE DECREE: with the determination made by the omnipotent Three-in-One God, that Mary should conceive the eternal Word by the power of the Holy Spirit, who was to redeem the human race; which incarnation made Jesus our redeemer and mediator between God and man, and reconciled us with God in such a way that we regained peace. This peace for many years had been "wept for"—that is, desired with tears by the saints <note>Refers to the righteous souls in Limbo awaiting the Harrowing of Hell.</note>.

### CANTO X

...fathers. And while they were alive: and after, while suspended in Limbo they awaited being freed by the passion of God: which redemption opened the long prohibition. <note>That is, the sacrifice of Christ opened the way to heaven for the human race, to whom it had been forbidden for so long after the fall of Adam.</note> Because from the sin of Adam until the descent of Christ into Limbo: five thousand two hundred and thirty-two years passed. **APPEARED BEFORE US SO LIFELIKE, AND** [this is] great praise for the sculpture: that although this was before them: where nothing else should have appeared but a mute and inanimate image. Nonetheless, it showed [the angel] speaking with supreme sweetness. And therefore he says: **IT DID NOT SEEM.** <note>That is, it did not resemble.</note> **AN IMAGE:** that is silent. But an image that speaks. And it so happened: because even the image of the angel appeared: as if he were speaking. And nearby was the image of Mary: so that anyone would have sworn: that the angel said "Hail" <note>original: "ave"</note>: just as he said when he made the announcement. **BECAUSE THERE:** because there. **WAS IMAGED THAT ONE:** was the image of Mary. **WHO TO OPEN THE HIGH LOVE turned the keys.** She turned the keys to open the high love of God: which our sin had closed off to us. Because the holiness: and humility of Mary was the key: which opened divine love. And just as the image of the angel was carved so skillfully: that it seemed [real]: so that of Mary appeared: as if she were consenting to the divine command: and through supreme humility said: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord." <note>original: "Ecce ancilla dei." These were Mary's words to Gabriel in the Gospel of Luke.</note> Place here then the image of Mary as a singular: and first example of humility. Of which, as the Carthaginian historian <note>Likely referring to the Roman historian Sallust, who wrote about Carthage; he famously noted that it is better to be silent than to say too little about a great subject.</note> said: it is better to be silent than to say little.

**H**aving set the example of Mary's humility: he sets that of King David: nor is the admirable genius and absolute learning of the poet to be passed over in this place. He knew: that man uses pride in three ways: either toward a superior: or toward a peer and equal: or toward an inferior. Therefore, to these three species of pride, he judged it necessary to oppose three species of humility. Thus, as an example of humility

And the rod of Moses: with which he defeated Pharaoh. And a vessel of the manna: that rained in the desert. <meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto X of the Purgatorio. Having previously described the Annunciation as an example of humility, the author now interprets the next two carved scenes on the marble wall: King David dancing before the Ark of the Covenant and the Emperor Trajan granting justice to a poor widow.</meta>

**FOR WHICH FEAR IS HAD OF AN OFFICE NOT ENTRUSTED:** Because the rashness of Uzzah was punished for touching the ark, which was not entrusted to him. <note>Uzzah was a biblical figure struck dead for touching the Ark of the Covenant to steady it, an act reserved only for priests.</note> And from this it is noted that although the action may be pious and of right will, nevertheless the profane should not touch sacred things. They say, however, that such a death purged Uzzah’s sin, and he, being saved, went to Abraham’s bosom. <note>Abraham's bosom refers to the place where the righteous dead rested before Christ's resurrection.</note> **I STEPPED BEYOND:** I stepped forward past Virgil to see; and it is worth noting that the sense [of sight] cannot perceive if it is not within a certain distance, and it only knows particulars. But the intellect sees universals from any distance. **IT WAS CARVED** there in the marble itself: in the same marble. **THE CART AND OXEN** pulling the holy ark, as we have said. **BEFORE THE ARK** people seemed to be; they were images that looked like living people. And all these were divided into seven choirs. And they were so lifelike that of the two senses—sight and hearing—the eye judged by their gestures that they were singing. But the ear, which heard no voice, judged they were not. **MADE** One, that is the ear, say no—that is, they do not sing because it heard nothing—the other, the eye, say they do sing. In short, they were priests carved with such gestures that they lacked nothing but a voice to say they were singing. **SIMILARLY** The smoke of the incense: just as discord arose between seeing and hearing regarding those who seemed to sing, so—because they were sculpted with censers in such a way that smoke seemed to rise from them—a contention arose between seeing and smelling, because to the eyes it seemed visible, but the nose smelled no odor. **THERE PRECEDED THEM.** The text thus arranges the humble psalmist <gloss>David</gloss> with great humility; and he is called the psalmist because he composed the psalms. <note>In that carved history.</note> **PRECEDED** the blessed vessel: he went before the blessed vessel, before the divine ark, together with the priests, dancing with a high leap <gloss>dancing</gloss> with his lyre; and his clothes were tucked up to be more nimble. **AND MORE AND less than a King:** more than a king because he held the office of the priesthood, and less because out of humility he had set aside his royal robes. **OPPOSITE.** Arrangement: Michal is sculpted <gloss>carved</gloss> opposite <gloss>facing David</gloss>; from a view <gloss>from a window</gloss> of a great palace she admired him like a scornful and sad woman <gloss>who felt contempt that he had stooped to such humility</gloss>. And that in that procession he did not have royal garments. And it rightly says "like a woman" because woman is naturally very boastful. Michal was the daughter of Saul and the wife of David.

I moved my feet from the place where I stood
To examine closely another history,
Which behind Michal gleamed white before me:
Here was storied the high glory
Of the Roman prince whose great worth
Moved Gregory to his great victory; <note>This refers to the legend that Pope Gregory the Great was so moved by Trajan's justice that he prayed for the Emperor's soul, resulting in Trajan being resurrected and converted.</note>
I speak of Trajan the Emperor;
And a poor widow was at his bridle,
Depicted in tears and in grief.

Of knights, and the golden eagles
Above them visibly moved in the wind.
The poor little woman among all these

For my son who is dead, for whom I grieve."
And he seemed to answer her: "Now wait
Until I return"; and she, "My Lord,"
Like a person in whom grief is urgent,
"If you do not return?" And he: "He who shall be
Where I am will do it for you"; and she: "The good of another,
What will it be to you, if you forget your own?"
Wherefore he: "Now be comforted, for it is fitting
That I fulfill my duty before I move;
Justice wills it, and pity holds me back."

<column-break/>

Trajan was an emperor of such excellence that it is difficult to judge whether he was more outstanding in military discipline or in justice and humanity. He greatly increased the Roman Empire, which, by the emperors who came after Augustus and before him, had been more defended than expanded. He was of such humanity that both in Rome and in the provinces everyone wanted him as an equal. He was clement and liberal. And he greatly lightened the people's taxes. He visited friends as a private citizen and not as an emperor. He succeeded Nerva in the one-hundredth year of our salvation; he triumphed over the Dacians and the Scythians. And having removed Decebalus, King of Dacia, he reduced it to a province. <gloss>He had that kingdom governed by Roman magistrates.</gloss> And to him surrendered the Iberians, Sarmatians, Arabs, Bosporans, and Colchians. He occupied Seleucia and Babylonia. And in the Red Sea he prepared a great fleet to go to India. He persecuted the Christians. But being advised by Pliny the Younger—who was in the magistracy—that except for not wanting to make sacrifices in the manner of the pagans, they were of excellent life and customs, he wrote back that such men should not be sought out. But if they happened to fall into his hands, they should be killed. He also reduced Armenia, Assyria, and Mesopotamia to provinces. He died in Selinus <note>Original: Seleutinti; the author likely means Selinus in Cilicia</note>; others write in Seleucia, in the sixty-third year of his life, plus nine months and four days. His ashes, collected in a golden vase, were carried to Rome and placed in the forum under the column. Helinandus the Frenchman and Polycrat the Englishman <note>Referring to the chronicler Helinand of Froidmont and John of Salisbury, author of the Policraticus.</note> write specifically of Trajan that, wanting to go with his army, a widow threw herself at his feet, asking for justice and satisfaction for a son of hers who had been [killed].

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Purgatorio, Canto X. The previous page discussed the carved scene of King David dancing before the Ark of the Covenant. # CANTO X #

-> He who never saw any new thing produced this visible speech, new to us because it is not found here. <-

<margin>I pray for him: for it was revealed to him that he was freed from the pains of hell.</margin>
**HE SAW A NEW THING.** God is everlasting; and from eternity He held in His mind that nothing he saw was ever "new" to Him. **PRODUCED THIS** visible speech. He calls it this because a statue might be sculpted with such skill that its gestures demonstrate what it would say if it spoke; therefore it is "visible speech," because by seeing the gestures and not hearing a voice, they understood. But while it is not new to God—as has already been said—it is new to us mortals, because among us it is not found. <note>original: "non si truoua"</note> This figure here touches upon that which in heaven will appear new to us. For one will see the conception of the other without hearing the sound of the tongue.

Dante was attentive to the examples of humility, for thus it is fitting for the senses to do when they wish to follow reason; and he delighted in looking. This signifies that the senses were so subordinate to reason that they already delighted in virtue, and did not perform the works of virtue with difficulty.

Mentre mi dilectauo di guardare
Imagini di tante humilitadi
er per lo fabbro loro adueder care /

mormoraua il poeta molte genti :
queſte nemeneranno aglalti gradi :

per ueder nouitate onde eſon uaghi
uolgendosi uer loro non furon lenti :
Non uo pero lectore che tu ti ſmaghi
di buon proponimento per udire
chome idio uuol cheldebito ſi paghi :
Non attender la forma delmartire
penſa la ſucceſſion penſa chal peggio
oltra la gran ſententia non puoi gire /

*While I delighted in looking at the images of such great humilities, and for the sake of their maker were dear to see, "Behold, on this side, but they make few steps," the poet murmured, "many people; these will lead us to the high steps." My eyes, which were content to gaze to see novelties for which they are eager, were not slow in turning toward them. I do not wish, however, reader, that you be dismayed from a good resolution by hearing how God wills that the debt be paid. Do not focus on the form of the torment; think of what follows; think that, at the worst, it cannot go beyond the great judgment.*

**HE WHO EXALTS HIMSELF SHALL BE HUMBLED.** <note>original: "Qui se exaltat humiliabitur." A reference to Luke 14:11.</note> And truly divine justice wills it, and men strive for it. With every industry they force themselves to oppress and trample those who are elated and proud. This is done in public, especially where one lives morally. For this reason, the Roman soldiers used the motto: **To spare the subjected and war down the proud.** <note>original: "Parcere subiectis et debellare superbos." From Virgil’s Aeneid VI.853, describing the Roman mission.</note> **THE POET MURMURED.** They write that poets are the punishers of the proud; but they do not speak of them with a clear and loud voice (that is, they do not praise them), but they murmur, which means they blame them. **MANY PEOPLE** to show that the multitude of the proud is very great. He calls them "many people" as if to say a "vile crowd," because the more the proud exalt themselves, the greater indignation we conceive toward them, and the more we strive to debase them and despise them. **THESE** will lead us; these will show us the way. **TO THE HIGH STEPS:** to the ascent of the second terrace. **MY EYES.** There is born in men a great desire to understand new things. And for this reason, the eyes are "eager" (that is, wandering) and often turn in every direction to see. Whence he says, **AND MY EYES** were content to gaze (that is, they took pleasure in looking) to see novelties (that is, new things) for which desire **THEY ARE EAGER:** wandering and fickle. **I DO NOT WISH HOWEVER** reader: this is an admonition, and not only fitting but almost necessary. For in comforting men toward purgation, and fearing that they might be dismayed by such harsh punishments as are shown for the proud—for we often see many have a good will to give themselves to the purgative virtues, but because the way is harsh and difficult, they become dismayed—to comfort them, he makes this digression, saying: "Reader, I do not wish, however, that you be dismayed" (that is, that you be moved and change from your good purpose), though you hear from me how grave is the punishment with which God wills the proud man to pay his debt (that is, to give satisfaction for his error). And for comfort, he says "do not focus" (that is, do not think) on the form and quality of the torments and pains. But in compensation for that, consider two things. First, "the succession" (that is, that which follows):

<column-break/>

the woman had been killed. And in this petition were the words of her and of Trajan, which the poet here recites. **WHOSE GREAT VALOR MOVED** Gregory to his great victory. They say that the virtues of Trajan moved Pope Gregory in such a way that <note>This refers to the legend that Pope Gregory the Great was so moved by the justice of the Emperor Trajan—a pagan—that he prayed for his soul, and Trajan was briefly resurrected to be baptized and saved.</note>

**HE WHO NEVER** [saw any new thing] is God, who is the exemplar of all things. The [visible speech] is so called because it is as if the sculpture itself spoke. And this "visible speech" is new to us, because it is not found on earth. And through it, one understands the thought of the other without hearing the sound of the tongue.

**DANTE WAS ATTENTIVE** to the examples of humility when he looked at them. And he delighted in those images for the love of the maker—that is, the Master who had made them. And this, as far as the history is concerned, signifies that the skill and the authority of the craftsman moved him to watch them, as we see in ourselves. For if we look at a painting and hear that it is by the hand of Giotto, the authority of the man has great power over us. <note>Giotto di Bondone (c. 1267–1337) was the most famous painter of Dante's time, credited with the birth of Renaissance realism.</note> And allegorically, it demonstrates that he watched the examples of humility for love of the Master—that is, for the love of God, who said:
> Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart.
<note>original: "Discite a me: quia mitis sum et humilis corde." Matthew 11:29.</note>

For if a sin is purged by its opposite, it is right that the proud, who walk elated and with heads held high, should be forced to walk depressed and bowed down. And because the nature of the proud is not to want to support any weight or any annoyance, the fitting punishment is that they be oppressed by great weights and humbled. Whence he says...
