<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Purgatorio, Canto X. The previous page concluded with a description of the divine carvings representing humility. This page moves into the encounter with the souls of the Proud, who are punished by carrying massive stones, and provides a theological and moral commentary on the nature of pride versus the "angelic butterfly" of the soul.</meta>

# .X. PURGATORY #

ought to happen: and this is that you will purge yourself; and once purged, you will acquire eternal life. The second: that such pains will not be eternal, like those of Hell. But at the worst they can last no longer than the sentence; that is, until the Day of Judgment.

Because these souls who were coming were so greatly hunched under their heavy weights, they were so transfigured that they could not be recognized. And certainly, pride makes a man so bestial that he no longer appears human, but like a cruel beast. For it is proper to man to be affable, tractable, loving, and gracious toward other men. And therefore this virtue, being proper and—

**I began: "Master, what I see**
**moving toward us does not seem like people to me,**
**and I do not know what they are, my sight falters so much."**
**And he to me: "The heavy condition**
**of their torment doubles them over to the ground,**
**so that my eyes at first had a struggle with it.**
**But look closely there, and disentangle with your eyes**
**what comes beneath those stones;**
**already you can discern how each one beats his breast."**

superior reason could hardly recognize it there. It is the best [method], as Aristotle says: wanting to straighten a crooked piece of wood, one must bend it in the opposite direction. And it is a stony thing <note>The commentator uses "sasso" (stone) as a metaphor for the weight of pride</note> for one who exalts himself too much; because: *He has put down the mighty from their seat and exalted the humble.* <note>original Latin: "Deposuit potentes de sede. et exaltauit humiles."</note> And pride was figured in the stone against Goliath, whom David killed with three stones. Furthermore, the Psalmist speaks of the proud thus: *He shall crush the heads in the land of many.* <note>original Latin: "Conquabit [Conquassabit] capita in terra multorum."</note> And elsewhere: *Because [He shall prepare against] their face.* <note>original Latin: "Quoniam uultum eorum."</note> And Isaiah: *The crown of pride shall be trodden under feet.* <note>original Latin: "Pedibus conculcabitur corona superbie."</note>

He uses a harsh exclamation against proud Christians, who truly are wretched, having lost divine grace through sin. And they are fallen <note>original: "lapsi"</note>, having run and fallen from that grace; because this word *lapsi* in the Latin language carries this meaning. Or we might say not *lapsi* (fallen) but *lassi* (weary); and then it signifies being tired.
**SICK IN VISION AND IN MIND:** Here he means sick in vision, that is, in the sharpness of the intellect.

**O proud Christians, wretched and weary,**
**who, sick in the vision of your minds,**
**put your trust in backward steps!**
**Do you not perceive that we are worms,**
**born to form the angelic butterfly**
**that flies to justice without defense?**
**Why does your mind float so high,**
**since you are like defective insects,**
**like a worm in which formation fails?**

Do you not perceive that we are worms? There are many worms, such as silkworms <note>original: "ebigatti"</note>, that make silk. These are imperfect animals; nonetheless, they conceive within themselves a butterfly, which, by breaking out of the worm, takes flight. Thus man is like a vile worm. Whence the Psalmist says: *But I am a worm and no man; a reproach of men, and despised of the people.* <note>original Latin: "Ego autem sum uermis et non homo obprobrium hominis : et abiectio plebis."</note> But as worms we are fit to form the butterfly. This is the immortal soul within us, which if we guide rightly and direct toward the path of virtue, then once our body is broken—that is, resolved by death—the soul like a butterfly flies up to heaven. But if it is filthy with vices, the weight of those burdens it down and causes it to fall into hell. And he says "butterfly" rather than any other thing that flies, because having used the metaphor of the worm, the butterfly fits that transition.
**BORN TO FORM:** It is not man who forms the soul; but God creates it from nothing and, creating it, infuses it. But because it comes into the body—

<column-break/>

—fitting to human nature, it is called humanity. Therefore, he who strips himself of such virtue and clothes himself in the vice of pride (which is its opposite) no longer appears human. And although he retains the image and form of a man, nonetheless in his character he is a most cruel beast. We can also refer this to the adversity of the proud. For when he falls from a high rank, he can have no patience there. Or truly we shall say: that when the proud man humbles himself, he in no way appears as he did in his pride. It is difficult, therefore, for Dante—that is, for the lower reason—to recognize human nature in such wildness. Since even Virgil—that is, the higher reason—hardly recognized it there. It is an excellent device by which he shows the purgation of the proud: making them stoop just as much in the opposite direction. For as Aristotle writes, to straighten a crooked wood, it is enough to bend it back. But it is a heavy thing that sinks toward the earth. This denotes that God prostrates and casts down whoever exalts himself too much. *He has put down the mighty from their seat and exalted the humble.* <note>Latin: "Deposuit potentes de sede. et exaltauit humiles."</note> And pride was prefigured in Goliath, whom David killed with a stone. Furthermore, the Psalmist speaks of the proud: *He shall crush the heads in the land of many.* <note>Latin: "Conquassabit capita in terra multorum."</note> And elsewhere: *In your remnants you shall prepare their face.* <note>Latin: "In reliquis tuis preparabis vultum eorum."</note> And Isaiah: *The crown of pride shall be trodden under feet.* <note>Latin: "Pedibus conculcabitur corona superbie."</note>

Which [Christians] are truly wretched, having through sin lost divine grace and fallen from it; because this is what "lapsi" signifies in the Latin language. Or we might say not "lapsi" but "lassi"; and then it signifies weary.
The vision is either of the physical eye or the intellect and the subtlety of wit. He says, as if to say: you are of blind intellect, because you do not know the true good; and you are sick in mind, that is, in the will, because you do not desire it. Therefore you are truly wretched, since you neither know the good nor desire it. And from this it arises that you "put your trust in backward steps"—that is, in vicious operations. *Retrofici* in Latin means "backwards." And because he who proceeds in virtuous operations goes forward and approaches God, who is his highest good, it follows that he who performs vicious operations takes backward steps; that is, he moves away from God. What, then, is greater misery and greater blindness of mind than to take trust in those things that separate us from our salvation and from the highest good? **DO YOU NOT PERCEIVE:** and especially the silkworms <note>term: "ebigatti" - an archaic Italian word for silkworms</note> that make silk. These are indeed imperfect animals; nonetheless they conceive in themselves a butterfly, which, by breaking out of the worm, comes forth and flies away. Whence the Psalmist says: *But I am a worm and no man...* <note>Latin: "Ego autem sum uermis..."</note> But as worms we are fit to form the butterfly, which if we rule rightly and direct toward the path of virtue, then once our body is resolved by death, the soul like a butterfly flies up to heaven. But if it is weighed down by vices, the weight of them burdens it and makes it ruin into hell. And he says "butterfly" rather than any other thing that flies, because having called the worm according to Holy Scripture, he stayed with that metaphor. **BORN TO FORM:** it is not man who creates the form, that is, the soul. But God creates it from nothing and, creating it, infuses it. But because it comes into the body—

# CANTO .X. #

### X ###

without knowledge of anything, but capable of learning; thus he says that man is born to shape the soul, because nature produced it so that he might instruct and teach his soul. **ANGELIC:** because our soul, though there is some difference, is nonetheless a rational essence, just like an angel. Whence the Psalmist says: *You have made him a little lower than the angels.* <note>original Latin: "Minuisti eum paullominus ab angelis." From Psalm 8:5.</note> He also calls it "angelic" because it was created by God to fill the seats of the angels who fell from heaven. **WHO FLIES TO JUSTICE WITHOUT shields:** without defenses. For once it has left the body, it goes to judgment without any defense. **WHY DOES OUR SOUL** float on high? In what thing do you exalt yourselves? It is as if he says that man is not such an excellent thing without the grace of God that he should become proud or boastful. Whence Paul says: **YOU ARE LIKE insects in defect.** <note>original Greek/Latin: "entomata in defecto." Dante uses this term to describe the soul as a larval state compared to the "angelic butterfly" it should become.</note> He returns to what he said above and concludes that we are imperfect, like worms, if we are without virtue and without divine grace. For just as the worm is imperfect because it is not formed to completion, so man—who is created to serve God, his highest good—is imperfect if he is deprived of the virtues through which he can be united with God. Whence Saint Augustine says: *You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in You.* <note>original Latin: "Fecisti nos ad te: et inquietum est cor nostrum: donec requiescamus in te." From the Confessions.</note> <term>Entomata</term> <note>original: "Entoma"</note> in Greek and Latin refers to insects; they are all those worms that do not have all their limbs distinct, such as bees, ants, and the like.

**As, to support a ceiling or a roof,**
**for a bracket sometimes a figure**
**is seen to join the knees to the chest;**
**Which makes true distress spring**
**from what is not true, in those who see them;**
**so I saw these ones, when I looked closely.**
**It is true they were more or less contracted**
**according to whether they had more or less on their backs;**
**and the one who had the most patience in his bearing,**
**weeping, seemed to say: "I can do no more."**

<column-break/>

The great weights which these souls carried made them bend and huddle so that the chest touched the knees. Because of this, they appeared just like certain <term>corbels</term> <note>original: "mensole," architectural brackets used to support beams</note> made of wood, which are placed in the wall under the beams of roofs, or ceilings, or indeed floors; these are often carved in the form of a man who supports the beam, and the great weight causes him to bend and huddle, almost resting his chest upon his knees. And although such a figure does not actually suffer labor, because it is wood and not a man, nonetheless it **makes true distress spring from what is not true.** This means: although it is not true that such a weight burdens or annoys the figure, it nevertheless generates true distress—that is, true pity—in those who look at it. **IT IS TRUE THAT THEY WERE MORE** and less contracted: although they were all under heavy weights, one had a less heavy load than another, according to whether they had sinned less or more in the sin of pride.

PURGATORIO

### CANTO ELEVEN OF THE SECOND CANTICLE OF DANTE.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'H' in a blue square with white floral patterns.</image-desc>
In the previous chapter, the poet had already described the place where the proud are purified and demonstrated what form of punishment they suffer. At the end, he added that many were already coming toward him. Now, in this chapter, he describes how they came praying, and their prayer was that which the <term>Word of Truth</term><note>Referring to Jesus Christ.</note> taught to the apostles, saying: *When you pray, it suffices to say: Our Father who art in heaven.* <note>original Latin: "Cum oraueritis; sufficit dicere: Pater noster qui es in celis." From Luke 11:2 and Matthew 6:9.</note> Although this prayer is suitable for everyone, it is nonetheless very appropriate for those who wish to abandon pride. For the head of pride is the failure to recognize any of one's own good as coming from God, instead attributing everything to one's own virtues. Furthermore, the proud person does not esteem his neighbor nor deem him worthy. Therefore, through this

<margin>Our Father</margin>
<image-desc>Large decorative initial 'O' in a blue and gold square with intricate floral motifs.</image-desc>
**O**ur Father, who in the heavens dwell,
not circumscribed, but through the greater love
you have for the first effects up there.
Praised be your name and your valor
by every creature, as it is worthy
to render thanks to your high vapor.
May the peace of your kingdom come to us,
for we cannot reach it by ourselves,
if it comes not with all our wits.
As of their own will your angels
make sacrifice to you, singing Hosanna,
so may men do with theirs.
Give us today our daily manna,
without which, through this harsh desert,
he goes backward who most labors to advance.
And as we forgive the evil we have suffered
to everyone, so do you forgive,
benignly, and look not upon our merit.
Our virtue, which easily surrenders,
do not test with the ancient adversary,
but deliver us from him who so spurs it.

<column-break/>

Lord’s Prayer, the soul confesses its error: first by confessing God's power, then by demonstrating that without His help, it can do nothing. And toward its neighbor, the soul humbles itself by asking God for the remission of its debts, just as it grants remission to those who have offended it. And finally, whereas in its pride the soul hoped to be able to resist the enemy by itself, here in humility it asks God not to lead it into temptation, where it confesses its own imbecility and fragility as insufficient to resist. The poet, therefore, introduces these souls making such a prayer, which he does not provide in Latin; rather, translating it into the Florentine language, he adds some words which neither change, increase, nor diminish the meaning. Instead, they open and clarify it. 

And because in that prayer it says *Our Father, who art in heaven*, some might doubt whether God is in heaven in such a way that, while He is there, He cannot be elsewhere. The poet adds to clarify this doubt: that God is not *circumscribed* in the heavens—that is, contained by the heavens—as, for example, <term>for the sake of the word</term><note>original Latin: "verbi gratia," meaning "for example."</note> when a man or another corporeal thing is in a place, that place circumscribes and surrounds and limits and contains him within itself, in such a way that until he leaves, he cannot be elsewhere nor go beyond those limits. But God is not contained by place, nor surrounded by it. Since God is infinite and the heavens are finite, a thing that has an end and a limit cannot contain that which has neither end

---

nor limit. The finite is incomparably smaller than the infinite, and the smaller thing cannot contain the larger within itself; therefore, God is not contained by the heavens. But He is said to "dwell in the heavens" because He has "greater love" for the heavens, because the heavens and the angels are the *first effects* that He, as the First Cause, produced; and these are then the secondary causes for the lower effects. For every superior is the cause of the movement of its inferior, as we shall declare more expressly elsewhere. 

Up to this point, he has said *Our Father who art in heaven*, which words are the preamble to this prayer. Now he comes to the petitions, which are seven. And the first is *hallowed be thy name* <note>original Latin: "sanctificetur nomen tuum."</note>; hence he says: **PRAISED BE YOUR NAME AND YOUR VALOR.** In the first petition, he asks for the honor of the Father. This signifies love with obedience and veneration toward the Father. And if one were to say it seems superfluous to say "hallowed be thy name," because he who is the Saint of Saints cannot be made more holy, we shall say *sanctificetur*—that is, *firmetur* <note>Latin: "let it be made firm/established."</note>—because "holy" means "firm." **Valor** means virtue. **Vapor** means grace. **BY EVERY CREATURE.** Whatever is produced by God as the First Cause and Creator is called a "creature." But these are divided into six species: 
1. Some have only being, such as stones. 
2. Some have a vegetative soul, through which they nourish themselves, grow, and produce seed to generate their like, such as herbs, trees, and every other plant. 
3. Some, beyond the vegetative, have sensation but lack local movement, such as shellfish <note>literally "calcinegli," small shells or limpets.</note> attached to a rock. 
4. Some have more perfect sensation and local movement, such as all brute animals. 
5. Some, beyond the vegetative, sensitive, and motive powers, have reason, such as man. 
6. But above man is the angel, of whom we shall speak in another place. 

Every creature praises its Creator as much as is in its power—that is, God. In wishing to express the Trinity, the poet used three names: **Name**, as in fame and wisdom, which expresses the Son; **Valor**, that is, power, for the Father; and **Vapor**, that is, heat or grace, for the Holy Spirit. And this is the first request we must make: that every creature recognize its Creator. **MAY THE PEACE COME TOWARD US.**

<meta>This page continues the line-by-verse commentary on the Purgatorial version of the Lord's Prayer. CANTO .XI.

of your kingdom. <note>original Latin: "Adveniat regnum tuum"</note> *Thy kingdom come* is the second petition. Because in saying *thy kingdom come*—that is, may your kingdom come—it is nothing other than asking for the peace of eternal life, which is different from that of this world. And having rightly praised the Father, we ask for the paternal inheritance which he left to us in his final testament when he said: *Peace I leave with you.* <note>original Latin: "pacem meam relinquo uobis," from John 14:27.</note> **FOR WE TOWARD IT** <note>Dante, Purgatorio 11.7</note> **cannot [go] of our own accord.** Such tranquility cannot be acquired by man with all his wit, because by himself he cannot have true knowledge of God, in which the soul finds rest, **UNLESS IT COMES TO US**—that is, if it is not infused in us by divine grace. **AS OF HIS Will.** This is the third petition, which is *thy will be done.* <note>original Latin: "fiat uoluntas tua"</note> Therefore, just as your angels—who, after the ruin of those who rebelled against God, though they remained in their free will, were confirmed in grace—so too the angels perform a sacrifice; that is, they offer to you their good will, meaning they dedicate their entire will to you. And this passage is explained in various ways. Some take "heaven" for the just man and "earth" for the sinner; some by "heaven" understand the spirit, and by "earth" the body. Some take "heaven" to mean Christ and "earth" the militant Church. And these three opinions are posed by Augustine. <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian of Western Christianity.</note> Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), known for translating the Bible into the Vulgate Latin.</note> said: as the angels serve you, O God, in heaven, so may we on earth. This opinion is followed by the <term>Aquinate</term> <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent scholastic philosopher and theologian.</note> and this same path is followed by our poet. **Singing Hosanna:** *Hosanna* in the Hebrew language means *save us* or *give life*, or *save us* or *our salvation*. **GIVE US THIS DAY OUR DAILY manna.** This is the fourth petition. <note>original Latin: "Panis nostru quotidanu da nobis hodie"</note> *Give us this day our daily bread*: by this he understands the grace of God, which is spiritual food upon which the soul nourishes itself. And therefore he said "our," because it is proper to the human as a rational animal and not to the beasts. Bread can also be understood as necessary bodily food. For while we are joined with the body, it is necessary to sustain it; and we say "ours," according to Gregory, <note>Pope Gregory I (the Great), who wrote extensively on the Lord's Prayer.</note> because we receive it from God as his gift. Therefore we say "give" so that it may not be ours by stealth, but by his will. Just as the manna fed the people of God bodily in the desert and held whatever flavor the one tasting it desired, so the spiritual bread fulfills every righteous appetite of our soul. Manna in the eastern regions is nearly the same substance as what we call honey. But there, the sun can more effectively cook the moisture which is drawn upward during the day and falls back to the earth at night. **AND AS TO US the evil we have suffered.** The fifth petition. <note>original Latin: "Et dimitte nobis debita nostra : sicut et nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris"</note> *And forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors.* We ask that he erase our sins, by which we are excluded from paradise, just as we forgive others the injuries received from them. **OUR VIRTUE WHICH willingly surrenders.** <note>Dante, Purgatorio 11.19</note> The last petition: *and lead us not into temptation.* <note>original Latin: "et ne nos inducas in tentationem"</note> *S'addona* means "finishes" or "submits." In this part, we ask for perseverance in the future. To "tempt" means to test and to make experience of a thing and its strength. The virtue of man consists in two things: in doing good and in fleeing from evil. In the first way, God tests man. In the second way, the virtue of man is tempted to lead it to evil by three species of temptation. The first temptation is from the flesh. For as the Apostle <note>Referring to St. James (James 1:14).</note> says: *Each is tempted by his own concupiscence.* The second is of the world with its vanities. The third is of the devil, who tempts us toward those vices to which he sees we are most inclined. No one could resist the diabolical temptation with their own strengths without divine help. Therefore: do not test our virtue, which *surrenders*—meaning it inclines and cannot resist.

> This last prayer, dear Lord,
> is not made for us, for it is not needed,
> but for those who remained behind us:
> Thus for themselves and for us a good journey
> those shades were going, under their weights,
> similar to that which one sometimes dreams,
> Unequally distressed, all in a circle,
> and weary, up along the first terrace,
> purging away the mist of the world:

It happens sometimes that much blood rushes to the heart, and being weighed down in such a way, it seems in sleep that one has an immeasurable weight upon them. **THE MIST:** the sin of pride, which is born from mist—that is, fog and darkness, meaning blindness of mind and ignorance.

> If there [in Purgatory] good is always said for us,
> of that which can be said and done for us
> by those who have a good root in their will,

<column-break/>

This demonstrates the true repentance of these souls: seeing as pride has been cast aside—which does not allow us to have charity or care for our neighbor—they prayed for the salvation of the living. For the soul placed in Purgatory is confirmed by God in that state in such a way that it cannot be tempted. Therefore, that last prayer, *and lead us not into temptation*, they did not say for themselves, because they had no need of it. But charity induced them to do it for those who had remained in life behind them. **GOOD Journey** <note>original Italian: "Ramogna"</note>: prosperous success. *Ramogna* properly means to proceed on a journey. **SIMILAR TO THAT which sometimes is dreamed.** Sleeping upside down <note>A reference to the physical sensation of a nightmare or sleep paralysis, which the commentator links to the physical pressure the souls feel from the stones.</note>

This is an excellent sentiment based in charity: that if there in Purgatory a "good" is said for us who are in life—that is, they pray for us—we ought to help them lift the weights of that which for us is...

<meta>This page transitions from the communal prayer of the proud souls to the personal interaction between Virgil, Dante, and the shade of Omberto Aldobrandeschi. ->.IX. PURGATORIO<-

Truly one ought to help them wash away the stains
that they carried from here: so that, pure and light,
they may go forth from the starry wheels. <note>The "starry wheels" refer to the celestial spheres of heaven. The souls pray for the living, and in turn, the living should pray for them to hasten their purification.</note>

"So may justice and pity soon unburden you,
so that you may be able to move the wing
that lifts you according to your desire:
Show us on which hand the path toward the stairs
is shortest; and if there is more than one passage,
teach us the one that descends less steeply;
For he who comes with me, because of the burden
of Adam's flesh with which he is clothed,
is slow in climbing up, against his will."

Their words, which they returned to these
that had been spoken by him whom I followed,
were not clear as to whom they came from;
But it was said: "To the right hand along the bank
come with us, and you will find the pass
possible for a living person to climb.
And if I were not hindered by the stone
that tames my proud neck,
wherefore I must carry my face low,
I would look at this man, who still lives and is not named,
to see if I know him,
and to make him feel pity for this burden.

I was Italian, and born of a great Tuscan: <note>original: "latino." In Dante's time, this often referred generally to people of the Italian peninsula.</note>
Guglielmo Aldobrandeschi was my father;
I know not if his name was ever with you.
The ancient blood and the gallant deeds
of my ancestors made me so arrogant
that, not thinking of our common mother, <note>The "common mother" is the Earth, implying we all share the same humble origin regardless of noble birth.</note>
I held every man in such great contempt
that I died for it, as the Sienese know,
and every child in Campagnatico knows it too.
I am Omberto; and not only to me has
pride done harm, for all my kinsmen
has she dragged with her into misfortune.
And here I must carry this weight
for her sake until God is satisfied,
since I did not do it among the living, here among the dead."

<column-break/>

[This] can be done through alms and prayers. And this should especially
be done by those who have a "good root"
in their will—that is, those who have confirmed their will
in goodness, and for this reason are in a state of grace.
And their prayers are heard. Other texts have:
*the starry wheels*—that they may, upon leaving Purgatory, ascend to the heavens. **GO FORTH FROM THE STARRY** wheels: [so they]
might exit Purgatory, which—if it is in the other hemisphere—comes to be beneath all the heavens, just as
we are; and when the soul passes from there into eternal life,
it leaves these heavens and goes above them; therefore they
may "go forth from the starry wheels"—that is, from the heavens, which continually rotate and turn.

Virgil prays to the souls with these words:
that they might show him the ascent to the next cliff, especially 
because Dante, who is with him, is "slow" in the ascent—
he is slow in ascending against his will; because if he were 
lazy by his own will, he would not be worthy of receiving 
the purgatorial virtues.

Appropriate words, not for the proud man, but for him who,
through its opposite (which is humility), purges his
pride. First, he shows the way with great humanity;
then he confesses to bearing the rightful penalty for his error,
which a proud man never does. Then he shows a desire 
to know Dante, to move him to compassion.

Omberto, son of Sir Guglielmo Aldobrandeschi,
who are of ancient blood
and Counts of Santafiora in the territory of Siena, was a 
very proud man; and his arrogance and pride 
toward the Sienese incited them in such a way that in 
Campagnatico they had him killed.

<meta>This page continues the encounter on the First Terrace of Purgatory, where the souls of the Proud are purified. Having heard from Omberto Aldobrandeschi, Dante now speaks with Odorisi da Gubbio, a celebrated manuscript illuminator. The text transitions from the general penance of the proud to a specific meditation on the fleeting nature of artistic and literary fame.</meta>

# CANTO XI

*ee i*
Catchword: SE NON

**O**dorisi was from Gubbio. And he was in that time an excellent manuscript illuminator. In Paris, it is called "illuminating" because the minium <note>original: "minio." A red lead pigment used in medieval manuscripts. The commentator explains the etymology of "illumination" as the act of making the text bright and distinct.</note> distinguishes and illuminates the writing.

Listening, I bent my face downward,
and one of them—not the one who was speaking—
twisted himself under the weight that hindered him;
And he saw me, recognized me, and called out,
keeping his eyes fixed with great effort
upon me, who walked all bent over with him.
"Oh," I said to him, "are you not Odorisi,
the honor of Gubbio and the honor of that art
which in Paris is called illuminating?"
"Brother," he said, "the pages smile more
that are painted by Franco of Bologna;
the honor is now all his, and mine only in part.
I would not have been so courteous, indeed,
while I lived, because of the great desire
for excellence upon which my heart was set.
For such pride, the fee is paid here;
and I would not even be here yet, were it not
that, while still able to sin, I turned to God.
O vainglory of human powers!
How little the green lasts upon the summit,
unless it is followed by a crude age. <note>A "crude age" refers to a subsequent generation that lacks talent, thereby allowing the previous generation's fame to linger longer than it naturally would.</note>
Cimabue thought that in painting
he held the field, and now Giotto has the cry,
so that the fame of the former is obscured.
Thus has one Guido taken from the other
the glory of our tongue; and perhaps he is born
who shall drive both one and the other from the nest.
Worldly renown is nothing but a breath
of wind, which comes now from here and now from there,
and changes name because it changes side."

<column-break/>

"BROTHER," HE SAID: as one now repented of his vainglory, he does not place himself before others as he did when he was occupied by such a vice. Instead, he is content to yield to Franco of Bologna as a greater master than himself. And therefore he said: "the pages smile more," as if to say they are better illuminated, "which Franco painted," that is, those which Franco illuminated with his brush. This man was from Bologna and was a better illuminator. "The honor is now all his": as if to say that before he became a good master, I held the first place, nor was there anyone who, in comparison to me, was of any value. But afterward I was defeated by this man, so that the honor is all his. Nevertheless, because after him I was ahead of the others, I have not remained without some share of honor. Nor is it pride when he says "and mine in part," because having placed the Bolognese before himself, he can freely speak the truth of himself. "I WOULD NOT HAVE BEEN SO COURTEOUS." When I was in the sin of vainglory, I would not have been so liberal in praising Franco. And certainly this vice exists in men who have some excellence in themselves: they cannot praise another who possesses the same virtue. And it seems that what they give in praise to another, they take away from themselves. "FOR THE GREAT DESIRE": for the great greed. "FOR EXCELLENCE": for surpassing and defeating others. Wherefore I pay the tribute here, that is, the penalty. "AND I WOULD NOT EVEN BE HERE YET." If he, while he was in life, had always practiced vainglory, it would be necessary that after death he go to damnation; but he shows that he turned to God, that is, to penance, "while still able to sin," that is, while he was alive, during which time one can earn merit and demerit. "O VAINGLORY OF HUMAN POWERS": that which men take from their virtues. Vainglory is called *Cenodoxia* by the Greeks <note>original: "Cenodoxia." From the Greek 'kenos' (empty) and 'doxa' (glory).</note>, which is the same as "vainglory" in Latin. Concerning which Isaiah says: "The flower of the glory of exultation is falling" <note>original: "Flos cadens gloria exultationis." Refers to Isaiah 28:1.</note>; and the Psalmist: "A thousand years before your eyes are like yesterday which has passed" <note>original: "Mille anni ante oculos tuos ficut dies hesterna que periit." Refers to Psalm 90:4.</note>. "With little green upon the summit," that is, how little the green lasts at the top and in its excellence.

---

"Unless it is helped by a crude age." The meaning is: let one be the first in a science, or virtue, or art; nevertheless, being first lasts a short time because someone else more excellent than him follows afterward. "Unless it is helped," that is, aided by "crude ages," meaning that after him follows an age that produces men of dull wit. And he proves it by the example of Cimabue, who obtained the honor and the first place in painting, until Giotto became such a master that he surpassed and defeated Cimabue; thus perhaps in another time, someone will come who will defeat Giotto. Therefore, no one should take vainglory in their own powers. Cimabue: he, seeing that painting was in obscurity, restored it to good fame. Giotto became a greater and more noble master than Cimabue. "TO HOLD THE FIELD": to remain the victor; this is a metaphor from a military army. "THUS HAS ONE GUIDO TAKEN FROM THE OTHER the glory of our tongue": just as Giotto took the glory of painting from Cimabue, so Guido Cavalcanti took it from Guido Guinizzelli of Bologna. "AND PERHAPS HE IS BORN." Many understand that he hints at himself <note>The commentator notes the popular interpretation that Dante is referring to his own future fame as a poet who will surpass both Guido Guinizzelli and Guido Cavalcanti.</note>. But he cannot be reproached for arrogance because it cannot be proven that he speaks of one more than another. And he affirms nothing. "WORLDLY RENOWN IS NOTHING BUT A BREATH": glory, fame, and noise he takes as one and the same thing. Worldly noise is the fame of mortal things. "NOTHING BUT A BREATH": because it flies and in a short time is entirely dispersed. Wherefore Virgil: "Fame, an evil than which no other is swifter. It thrives on movement and gathers strength as it goes" <note>original: "Fama malum quo non aliud uelocius ullum. Mobilitate uiget uiresque acquirit eundo." From the Aeneid, Book IV.</note>.

The commentary explains the nature of vainglory and the specific historical figures Dante encounters on the Terrace of Pride.</summary>

# XI. PURGATORY

Odorisi continues by showing that before a thousand years pass, you will have no more fame if you "shed the old flesh" <note>original: "scindi... la carne uecchia." To strip away or separate the flesh, meaning to die at an advanced age.</note>, that is, if you die old, than if you had died before you left off "pappa" or "dindi" <note>original: "pappa o dindi." Infantile baby talk; the commentator explains these are the first words children use for bread and money.</note>, which is to say, before you passed your earliest years. And if someone should say a thousand years is a great span of time, he demonstrates that a thousand years, compared to eternity, is a shorter space than a blink of an eye compared to the movement of the eighth sphere <note>The Starry Sphere of the heavens, which was believed to move one degree every hundred years.</note>, which is one degree every hundred years. **AND ROTATED** <note>original: "E TORTO." Turned or revolved.</note>:

> What fame will you have more if you shed
> the old flesh, than if you had died
> before you left off "pappa" or "dindi"?
> Before a thousand years pass—which is a shorter
> space to the eternal than the blink of an eye
> to the circle that turns slowest in the heavens.
> He who takes so little of the path
> before me, was known throughout Tuscany,
> and now is hardly whispered of in Siena,
> Where he was lord when the Florentine rage
> was destroyed—which was as proud
> in that time as it is now prostituted.
> Our renown is the color of grass,
> which comes and goes, and is discolored by that
> which makes it spring green from the earth.

He is "whispered of in Siena." **WHERE HE WAS LORD**: of which he was the leader. **WHEN THE FLORENTINE RAGE WAS DESTROYED**: When the Guelphs were defeated at Montaperti <note>The Battle of Montaperti (1260) was a bloody defeat for the Florentine Guelphs at the hands of the Sienese Ghibellines.</note>, a history we treated in the first *cantica*. **WHICH WAS PROUD** at that time and ambitious. **AND NOW IS PROSTITUTED** <note>original: "ET HORA E PVTTA." Literally "is a whore."</note>: as if to say that in those days the citizens were proud, but now they are greedy, and for the sake of greed, they sell the public good. It is similar to that line of Sallust: "O venal city, soon to perish if a buyer can be found!" <note>original: "o urbem uenalem: et cito perituram: si emptore inueneris." A quote from Sallust’s *Jugurthine War* regarding the corruption of Rome.</note> I cannot help but grieve in this place, as in others, that such a great poet of such wonderful genius and learning allowed himself to be carried away by the disturbance of his soul regarding his homeland. But the verse of Homer is true: that God never gave everything to one man alone. **OUR renown is the color of grass**: Our fame is like grass, which stays green for a short time and then withers. The poet stays within the metaphor, for he said above: "How little the green lasts upon the summit." **AND THAT WHICH DISCOLORS IT**: The Sun, which creates time, is that which makes the grass grow and that same thing withers it; thus time produces fame and then consigns it to oblivion.

> And I to him: "Your true words plant
> good humility in my heart and level my great swelling;
> but who is he of whom you spoke just now?"
> "That is," he answered, "Provenzan Salvani;
> and he is here because he was presumptuous
> in seeking to bring all of Siena into his hands.
> He has gone thus and goes without rest
> since he died; such coin he pays
> in satisfaction, who was too daring back there."
> And I: "If that spirit who waits
> until the edge of life is quenched
> remains down there and does not ascend here,
> Unless good prayer aids him,
> until as much time passes as he lived,
> how was his coming here granted to him?"

> "When he lived most gloriously," he said,
> "freely in the marketplace of Siena,"

<column-break/>

**YOUR TRUE WORDS PLANT** <note>original: "VERDIRE." From "veridire," to speak the truth.</note>: they put good humility in my heart. **AND LEVEL**: they flatten my **GREAT SWELLING** <note>original: "gran tumore."</note>, that is, great pride; for *tumor* in Latin signifies a swelling, and the proud are called "tumid" because they are puffed up. **PRESUMPTUOUS** is one who attributes to himself that which is not his and does not belong to him; the same as "arrogant." **TOO DARING**: one who has had too much boldness. **AND I IF THAT**: the text is ordered thus: And I, Dante, replied to Odorisi, raising this doubt: "If that spirit who, before he is quenched <note>returns to penance</note>, waits for the **EDGE** <note>the end</note> of life, remains down there outside of Purgatory proper for as long a time as he lived, and does not **ASCEND** here into Purgatory unless good prayer helps him, how was the arrival here granted to Provenzano?" Because the time since he died is less than the time he spent alive, this seems to contradict what was said above.

by begging for money to rescue his friend from prison, he shortened the time he would have had to stay outside of Purgatory. They say that King Charles <note>Charles I of Anjou, King of Naples and Sicily.</note> had taken a friend of this Provençal <note>Provenzan Salvani, the Sienese leader.</note> captive in the rout <note>The Battle of Tagliacozzo in 1268, where Charles defeated Conradin.</note> that he dealt to Conradin, and set a ransom of 10,000 florins upon him under penalty of death if he did not pay in a short time. ---

greatest state, he freely stationed himself and stood firm in the field of Siena—for so the Sienese call their piazza—setting aside all shame. **HE BROUGHT HIMSELF TO TREMBLE THROUGH EVERY VEIN**: because one who brings himself to calamity to ask for help comes with great trembling, because he fears he will not be heard. And because this sentence is spoken obscurely, he says that in a short time his neighbors—that is, his fellow citizens—will act such that he will be able to interpret it. And in this way he predicts his [Dante's] exile, during which he will understand that he who relies on the mercy of others trembles when he makes a request. **THIS WORK**: of humility. **TOOK AWAY**: took away from Provençal. **THOSE BOUNDARIES**: of having to stay outside Purgatory <note>Those who repented late were normally required to wait outside the gates of Purgatory for a time equal to their lives; Salvani’s act of humility earned him an early entry.</note>.

# TWELFTH CHAPTER OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE

Side by side, like oxen going in a yoke,
I went along with that burdened soul,
as long as the sweet pedagogue permitted it.
But when he said: "Leave him and pass on,
for here it is good for each to urge his boat
with both sail and oars as much as he can,"
I stood as upright as one must to walk.

Having departed from the souls who were purging their past pride, he shows that many histories were sculpted in the ground over which he passed, as an example and admonition to the proud. Virgil, therefore, left him to walk with Oderisi until they reached such sculptures; then he admonished him to pass forward. He walked side by side with Oderisi. And he names Virgil "pedagogue" <note>original: "pedagogo." From the Greek *paidagogos*.</note> not without reason. In Greek, this word signifies the one to whom children are given in custody. He wishes to signify, then, that he—that is, sensuality—is a child, because it is easily overcome by appetite like a child. And the intellect is its guide. **FOR HERE IT IS GOOD... <header>PURGATORIO</header>

...alongside the person, although my thoughts
remained bowed down and diminished:
I had moved myself and was following willingly
the steps of my master, and both of us
already showed how light we had become.
And he said to me: "Turn your eyes downward;
it will be good for you, to soothe the way,
to see the bed beneath the soles of your feet."

<note>original: "consequens purgatomene"</note> Following my purgation, I willingly followed the reasoning of what had happened. But Virgil admonishes him: that as he walks, he should look at everything he sees. These were histories and fables of men, which, although they were sculpted in the earth, they did not deserve <note>to be higher</note>, for neither their nature, their condition, nor their learning allowed it. The "bed" refers to sensuality, so that it does not become more exalted; rather, through the sense of taste <note>the original Italian "gusto" here refers to the spiritual appetite</note>, one should recall such examples to memory. And in his mind, he should consider how the mighty are cast down from their thrones <note>original: "deposuit potentes de fede," likely a corruption of "de sede" from the Magnificat</note>, and in how little esteem their proud height is held, for now they lie in the lowest state. They sought honors; now they are deprived of all human glory. Let him consider this continually. Let him have this fixed in his mind day and night.

He demonstrates that he saw those histories sculpted on the ground—which he will describe shortly—just as one sees images of dead men sculpted upon their tombs. This is done so that such images may bring back the memory of them to our minds. Whence he says: like floor-tombs <note>original: "tombe terragne"</note>, meaning burials placed in the ground over the deceased, carrying the mark of what they were before.

As, so that there may be memory of them,
the floor-tombs over the buried
bear the mark of what they were before /
Whence there, many times, one weeps for them
due to the sting of remembrance,
which only gives spurs to the faithful.
So I saw there, but of better likeness
according to the craftsmanship of the carving,
all that which projects as a path from the mountain.

I saw him who was created noble
more than any other creature, down from heaven
descending like a flash of lightning on one side.
I saw Briareus <note>A giant from Greek mythology who rebelled against Olympus.</note> pierced by the celestial
bolt, lying on the other side,
heavy upon the earth in the chill of death.
I saw Thymbraeus <note>A title for Apollo, derived from his temple at Thymbra.</note>, I saw Pallas <note>Athena</note> and Mars.

<column-break/>

...that we must use speed in our penance, and deservedly so. But he also wishes to signify that there is no vice we should abandon sooner than pride, because it is the greatest of all and the most pernicious of all. **UPRIGHT JUST AS**: because I had been walking bowed down in the company of that soul, I now made myself upright, just as one ought to walk, although my thoughts remained bowed out of compassion for that soul, and also out of the humility with which he was purging his pride. **I HAD MOVED MYSELF** and followed willingly the steps of my leader. Because I had sufficiently contemplated pride through the sculptures that were on the ground. All of these examples had been of great pride. For this reason, it was appropriate to place in another location those who had exalted themselves most, so that they might lie in the lowest place. And he warns here that the path does not require one to look at these sculptures <note>distractedly</note>, but to consider with how much justice God "has cast down the mighty" <note>original: "deposuit [potentes]"</note>. They remained in the memory of men; they sought fame, but now they are in infamy. They sought riches; let the man who wishes to purge himself think on this.

Meaning they carry the likeness of the buried man in the form he had before he was dissolved and returned to ash. And they carve these images so that there may be a memory of them. Whence it happens that over those images, one often weeps. For when friends and relatives pass by, they weep **DUE TO THE STING OF REMEMBRANCE**, because the memory of a dead friend or relative pricks and torments the soul. But such a sting **ONLY GIVES SPURS TO THE FAITHFUL**, meaning it only moves the pious to compassion, for he who is not pious is not moved to pity for the dead. **SO I SAW THERE**: thus I saw that place figured, meaning engraved and sculpted.

**BUT OF BETTER LIKENESS**: of a better image according to the rules of art. "Likeness" signifies a similarity derived from an example. **ALL THAT WHICH PROJECTS AS A PATH FROM THE MOUNTAIN**: He demonstrates that such sculpture was only on the terrace, which projects outward and encircles the mountain, serving as a path. It is fitting that the memory of such men be a "path" for those who purge themselves of that vice, so that they may be set aside. Furthermore, it is a "path" because such memory leads the one who is purging themselves to true humility.

It is a fitting thing that in the place where we purge pride, there should be sculpted on the ground these most proud examples. For nothing makes a vice so displeasing to us as considering it in others. First, therefore, was the history of Lucifer. Most excellently our Petrarch writes in *On the Remedies of Both Kinds of Fortune*: "The remedy against pride is the foundation of true virtue, which is humility. Nor is there any such great brilliance that pride [cannot darken]." <note>original Latin: "Remedium contra superbiam fundamentum uere uirtutis est humilitas. Nec tanta claritas ulla est: quam superbia..."</note>

Scit ille qui clarissimus creatus se ipsum extollens non solum obscurus . Sed princeps fieri meruit tenebrarum ." This refers to Lucifer's fall.</note> Regarding the fictional Briareus:
FROM THE CELESTIAL WEAPON: from the bolt of heaven.

"Weapon" <note>original: "Telum"</note> is a Latin name, but derived from the Greek; it signifies any weapon used for offense, especially lances, darts, arrows, and the like. Because the poets imagine that the bolt from heaven is hurled by Jove, and that with it he punishes those who err, they call it the "weapon of Jove." It is written in poetic fables that the Titans waged war against the gods for ten years. Finally, a great force of gods and goddesses was made, and the Titans were ruined in hell by the bolts of Jove. But as to what this signifies and what allegory it holds, we spoke of it in the fable of the giants: The Titans were children of Heaven and Earth and had the stature and limbs of giants. They had a hundred hands each and fifty heads. There were three: Cottus, Briareus, and Gyges. Homer adds that the gods called him Briareus, but men called him Aegaeon. It is an excellent fiction that the giants follow after Lucifer; let no one reproach the poet for mixing true things about Lucifer with false ones, namely the fables of the Titans. For he does not intend to present the fable itself, but its allegory, which is a most true thing, because it denotes pride, which is currently being mentioned. I know that Homer fables the story of Briareus differently, making him a friend to Jove; but Dante in this place follows other poets, because from Homer's fable one could not draw an allegory suitable to this place. "I saw Thymbraeus." He shows how the gods, who were helping Jove, looked with wonder at the bodies of such monsters, mangled and broken by Jove's bolts; and he uses "Thymbraeus" <note>original: "Tymbreo"</note> for Apollo, who had a temple in Troy, around which grew an abundance of the herb called "thymbra," that is, savory. Thus: "Thymbreus Apollo."

The history of Nimrod we placed in the *Inferno* where he is mentioned in the pit.

Niobe was the daughter of Tantalus and wife of Amphion; she was so proud that she dared to prefer herself to Latona, the mother of Phoebus <note>Apollo</note> and Diana. She wanted the honors and sacrifices attributed to Latona to be given to her, because she had not just two, but fourteen children: seven males and seven females. Therefore, Phoebus killed them all with his bow. Some say Phoebus killed the males and Diana the females. And Niobe was turned into stone. Saul was the first King of Israel, anointed by the hands of the prophet Samuel. He was of great stature, robust, handsome, and strong in battle. He conquered many kings and peoples, occupying lands from Egypt to the Red Sea. But ultimately, because he acted against God’s precept by sparing Agag, King of the Amalekites, <note>original: "Acag Re de malachiti"</note> he was deprived of the vision of future things which God had given him. He was often tormented by a demon. Many times he wished to kill David, a very humble man who had twice saved him from death. Out of necessity, he turned to the witch <note>original: "maga phitonissa"</note> to raise Samuel for him. Finally, hateful to God and men, he fought unhappily against the Philistines and lost his army and his sons. Unable to beg the favor of one of his men to kill him, he killed himself with his own weapons.

The fable of Arachne is very well known. Being most skilled in embroidery, she placed herself above Pallas <note>Athena</note>, by whom she was defeated and turned into a spider. And as she once made excellent webs as a woman, so she does now as an animal. Rehoboam, son of Solomon, succeeded his father in the kingdom. Having come to Shechem where all the people of Israel were gathered, he used such pride that when the people begged him to lighten the heavy yoke Solomon had imposed on them, he—incited by pride—despised the counsel of the elders and followed that of the young men. He replied that his smallest finger was thicker than his father's shoulders. And if his father had beaten them with a rod, he—

But he was defeated and killed with his army by Cyrus. But the Queen, having restored her army, attacked again with an ambush. He was the prince of the militia of Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: "nabuchdonosor"</note>, King of the Assyrians, who became so proud that he wished to be worshipped as a god; he sent Holofernes against the Jews after he had subjugated many other nations. The Jews fortified themselves in the mountains where his path lay into their region. Holofernes besieged Bethulia, located in those parts. And by depriving the Bethulians of water, it was necessary for them to surrender. But through the comforts of Ozias the priest, they decided to wait five days before surrendering. In this time, Judith, a most beautiful woman and widow, pretending to flee the famine, went with one of her handmaids to Holofernes, commending her safety to him and promising to give him the means by which he could conquer the land. Holofernes, moved by the beauty and the promises of the woman, spared her. And she feigned that she had to remain in prayer for four days according to her law. Then, seeing Holofernes sleeping deeply due to great drunkenness, she cut off his head. And she returned to the city. And Ozias went out with the armed people and attacked the army which was already fleeing. And he sent word to the surrounding cities to occupy the passes. Thus that great army suffered a great rout. There were 120,000 foot soldiers and twenty-two thousand horsemen in Holofernes' army. TROY IN ASHES. The destruction of Troy was sculpted there, and the miserable fortune of Priam.

It is a fitting thing that these histories are sculpted on the ground in the path, so that every man who passes may trample them. Because those who, through pride, always wanted to go above others, it is a worthy punishment for them that others should walk over them. Hence, out of indignation, the poet uses this exclamation: **Now be proud, children of Eve**. It is as if he says: mortal men, and of no other origin than the rest. **And do not bow your heads**: as if to say, do not consider your own lowliness and base condition. **SO THAT YOU MIGHT SEE YOUR evil path**: one does not recognize how evil a path is—that is, the wicked way of pride—unless we see by the example of others where it leads us. **MORE OF THE MOUNTAIN HAD ALREADY BEEN**: We had "turned"—that is, we had rotated—walking along the terrace that surrounds the...

so that the lifting of our eyes <note>original: "lecti lo menare in suso"</note> should rise more from the mount than the mount itself: and we had spent more of the path of the sun—that is, of time, which is born from the solar motion—than my mind had thought. I do not know how, but in a fixed contemplation of the mind, time passes, and one does not notice it. **WHEN HE** <note>referring to Virgil</note> who always goes before and waits. A man cannot walk the straight path if appetite precedes reason; but he arrives at the desired end when reason precedes: and not only precedes, but always remains attentive. **HE CRIED OUT:** because reason stimulates appetite with sharp bites, so that when it has considered one thing enough, it may lift its head to the next, and not always remain suspended in a single thought. **SEE THERE AN ANGEL** who approaches: who hastens and prepares himself. This angel is that divine grace of which we have already spoken many times. And although the poet often changes his allegorical fictions, he nevertheless always intends the same thing. See that the sixth handmaiden <note>The handmaidens are the hours of the day.</note> returns from the service of the day: that is, the sixth hour returns because it has already performed its office. The meaning is that the sixth hour was departing from the sun because it was entering the seventh. And by showing that half the day had already passed in contemplating pride, it signifies that much more time is consumed in purging this vice than any other. **WITH REVERENCE** adorn your face and actions: the appetite and reason together must become reverent and obedient to the remitting divine grace, and not lose time when one can go forward with it. Because lost time cannot be recovered. Wherefore the day does not return. And Virgil says: *Each day that is nearest is the first to flee for wretched mortals.* <note>original Latin: "proxima queque dies miseris mortalibus uia: prima fugit" from Virgil's Georgics III, 66-67.</note>

When the appetite, through long habit, is used to obeying the precepts of reason, it understands them easily; and especially when reason warns that time should not be lost, because reason gives this precept continuously, in every age and in every thing. He imagines that the angel is clothed in white and has a splendid face because such grace illuminates us and restores us to the state of innocence and makes us pure. **He opened his arms:** which denotes divine mercy. **EASILY** now one ascends. And indeed, he who lays down pride easily frees himself from other vices: because pride takes God away from us, envy takes our neighbor, and anger takes ourselves.

<margin>l</margin>
The words of the first tercet can belong to both the angel and the poet. He says, therefore, that there are few who come to this invitation—which the angel makes when he says "Come." For there are few who disentangle themselves from pride, and few who ascend to heaven. **O HUMAN RACE:** This is an exclamation. **BORN TO ASCEND:** made by God to climb to heaven. **WHY AT A LITTLE WIND DO YOU FALL:** why do you let yourself be so conquered by worldly honors that you fall into the vice of pride? For just as we say that those who practice virtue "rise up," because it guides us to lift the soul to divine things, so he who commits vice "falls," because all his thought is on low and fleeting things. And he said very well **"come,"** because [they were] above the mountain, which our ancestors called *roccia* and *rocca* <note>terms for a fortress or rock</note>, just as the Latins call them *arces*. And he imagines here that the staircase was cut by the force of a chisel, by which one ascends to the second level. **He beats his wings across Dante's forehead:** to remove one of the seven sins <note>The 'P' for Peccatum/Sin inscribed on Dante's forehead.</note>, he having already been purged of pride, which is one of the seven mortal sins. One of the wings is prevenient and illuminating grace; the other is cooperating and perfecting grace. These cause God to remit our faults; and he places the sins on the forehead because sins must be made manifest. **THEN HE PROMISED ME A SAFE JOURNEY.** The way to purgation is not secure unless pride is extinguished, because pride often deceives us or assaults us even in our good works. **AS ON THE RIGHT HAND.** Such were the...

stairs in this place: such as those we see on the road that leads from the gate up to **Saint Miniato on the Mount** <note>The Basilica of San Miniato al Monte in Florence, accessible via a famous monumental staircase.</note>: which stairs were made for the slope <note>original: ".i. la scondiscesa"</note>: and to speak more plainly, so that the incline was broken <note>original: ".i. non fussi continuata"</note>, but interrupted by level intervals placed between the stairs. **ON THE RIGHT** hand, exiting the gate to go to Saint Miniato, one climbs for a while along a single path: then it divides into two paths: and the one remaining on the right hand for the climber has the stairs that overcome the ascent. The well-guided city of **Florence**: which he called "well-guided" through irony <note>original: ".i. ben condotta: et ben recta"</note>. **ABOVE RUBACONTE** This temple to which one climbs by the aforementioned stairs overlooks—that is, it judges from above and stands over—that part of the city where the **Rubaconte Bridge** <note>Now known as the Ponte alle Grazie in Florence. It was named after Rubaconte da Mandello, the Milanese official (Podestà) who commissioned it in 1237.</note> crosses the Arno. It was named after Messer Rubaconte da Mandello, a Milanese knight who was the governor of Florence when this bridge was built in the year 1237. **THE LEDGER** and the stave: because once a ledger of the communal chamber was falsified—which was made of wood—and a stave was removed from it <note>This refers to a contemporary scandal involving the falsification of public records (the "Quaderno") and the measurement of salt (the "Doga" or stave of a barrel) to defraud the public.</note>. **THUS THE BANK SLACKENS**: just as he previously called the descending bank a "slope" because one crashes down such places with speed, so conversely he calls the bank "slackened" when one climbs. **BUT HERE** and there the other stone grazes. Where the stairs were, the slope was gradual. But then, on every side of the stairs, the path was so narrow that whoever climbs rubs against it: this denotes that the path of virtue is narrow.

We turned our persons there;

Ah, how different are these openings

And I: "Master, what heavy thing

He replied: "When the sins that remain
still on your face—which are fading—

but it will be their delight to be urged upward."

<column-break/>

**The Souls** who were purging themselves of pride showed joy through singing at Dante's ascent. Because here there is no envy of another's good, but charity. And they sang: **"Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven"** <note>original Latin: "beati pauperes spiritu quoniam ipsorum est regnum celorum"</note>. To be "poor in spirit" is nothing other than to be lacking in pride. Therefore, those spirits rejoiced that Dante was already purged of such a vice.

**Dante Shows** that he has become very light. To which Virgil responds in a way that implies this lightness comes to him because one of the seven sins has already been cancelled. But when all of them are cancelled, not only will climbing not be a labor, but it will be a supreme delight. And note that Virgil says the first sin was already entirely extinguished, and the others nearly so. This denotes that once the vice of pride is entirely purged, the other vices remain largely purged as well.

**The Poet** had not realized that one of the seven sins was already completely removed and the others greatly diminished. Therefore, moved by Virgil's words, he felt with his fingers spread <note>original: "sempi .i. semplici"</note> and found only six. This happened to him as it does to one who carries something on his head and does not know it. But seeing those around him laughing, and the eyes being unable to do their office because they cannot see the head, the hands substitute for them. And through this, man realizes that the senses cannot be a true judge if the soul is still purged of some vice. Rather, reason shows it to him. Nor does a man notice the sins he has in his head until after he has been purged of pride—

---

which makes us so tumid and swollen that we seem to ourselves to be virtuous. But once pride is set aside, then we begin to recognize our errors. Virgil smiled because the intellect laughs at the ignorance of the senses, and almost becomes another **Democritus** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher known as the "Laughing Philosopher" because he mocked the follies of mankind.</note>.

### . CANTO . XIII . OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE .

We were at the top of the stairs
where for the second time is cut away
the mountain that un-evils <note>original: "dismala." A verb created by Dante meaning to strip away or purge evil.</note> those who climb:
Here, a terrace binds
the hill around, just like the first one,
except that its arc curves more sharply.
No shade is there, nor any sign to be seen;
the bank appears smooth, and the path as well,
with the livid color of the stone.

"If we wait here to ask people for directions,"
the poet reasoned, "I fear perhaps
that our choice will have too much delay."
Then he fixed his eyes intently upon the sun;
he made his right side a center of movement,
and turned the left part of himself.

<column-break/>

HAVING LEFT the first terrace: where we have seen the punishments of the proud: we enter, having already climbed the stairs, into the second: in which **envy** is purged. Envy is a reciprocal torment of the soul: which wastes away because of the good of others: and such sorrow returns upon itself. And **Augustine** said envy is the sorrow felt at another's happiness. Whence **Horace** [says]: *The envious man is consumed by envy within and without* <note>original: "Inuidus inuidia comburitur intus et extra."</note>. Also: *The envious man grows lean at the fat success of another* <note>original: "Inuidus alterius rebus macrescit opimis."</note>. And **Solomon**, wishing to show how much torment it gives to oneself, said: *He who rejoices in the ruin of another shall not go unpunished* <note>original: "Qui in ruina letatur alterius: non erit impunitus." Landino attributes this to Solomon, likely referencing Proverbs 17:5.</note>. We were, therefore, at the top of the stairs: which lead onto the second terrace: which **un-evils**: that is, it removes the evil and the sin from those who climb it. This terrace girds and surrounds the mountain, creating a level path around it. But its arch curves more sharply: that is, it makes a smaller circuit: because, as we have said above: the more the mountain rises, the more it thins: and for this reason the circle of the terrace becomes smaller. And thus the sins decrease in degree. And the greater sins are always the lower ones. Therefore, the punishments similarly thin out <note>Landino suggests that as the physical space narrows, the gravity of the sins being purged also lessens compared to those below.</note>. **NO SHADE OR SIGN**: no painting is seen there, nor sculpture: as there was in the terrace below. Instead, the path and the bank remain bare and simple. And the stones of which the terrace is made are of a **livid** <note>A leaden, bluish-gray color. In medieval medicine and art, this color was associated with the "cold" humor of envy and the bruising of the spirit.</note> color. He notes by this that there is no painting or sculpture because envy does not manifest or appear except when mixed with another sin. Or truly he said "shade": that is, any soul: because the envious do not walk along the terrace, and were in a distant place. The livid color is appropriate for envy: because it is born from cold, and envy is cold: because it is contrary to charity <note>Charity was traditionally associated with the heat of fire and love; envy, its opposite, was seen as a cold, shriveling emotion.</note>.

Because in this terrace envy is purged: and the punishment of the envious is that they are blind <note>original: "seghino," likely referring to the souls' eyes being sewn shut with iron wire, which Dante describes later in this Canto.</note>; therefore **Virgil** doubts that waiting for someone to show the way would cause too much delay for their choice: that is, their chosen course. And having said these words, he looked toward the sun: and while watching it, he turned to the right side. By the **sun**, we understand our intellect, and also the illuminating grace of God. Since just as the sun shows us...

HE MADE OF THE RIGHT SIDE A CENTER <note>The original Italian "AMVO uer centro" is likely a transcription of "a muover centro," referring to a pivot point.</note>. When we want to make a circle with compasses <note>original: "seſte." A geometric tool.</note>: that point which stays still acts as the center for the circle which guides the one that moves. And similarly when standing upright we wish to turn: one foot stays firm as a center, and the other turns. And if we want to turn to the right: the right foot stays firm.

**B**ECAUSE in this terrace envy is punished: which is extremely cold, and therefore "livid" <note>Envy was traditionally associated with a bluish or leaden color, representing the "coldness" of a heart that lacks the warmth of charity.</note>; not without great reason does the poet bring in spirits whose words demonstrate charity, the flame of which [warms] such cold. We have shown in another place why in the *Inferno* he does not distinctly place the seven mortal sins as he does here, nor does he make special mention of envy and vainglory. THEY HAVE NO WINE <note>original: "VINVM NON HABENT"</note>. These are the words of Mary to Christ at the wedding, where it is expressed that Mary did not dare to be silent—unlike envy which, being by nature starved for glory, cannot look upon another's excellence without malice. But moved by charity, she grieved for the deficiency at the wedding. These examples must always be in the mind of those who purge envy: and in imitation of Mary, one should pray to God to change the water into wine—that is, the cold of envy into the heat of charity—or truly change the waters—that is, the hardships and tribulations—into wine—that is, into joy. The poet then intends that if seeing too much of others' goods...

<column-break/>

...generates this sin: its purgation must be not seeing. And for this reason, a little further on, he will make them blind <note>The envious in Purgatory have their eyelids sewn shut with wire, as they "looked askance" at others' happiness in life.</note>. And similarly, he makes the spirits invisible, who, flying through the air, give "sweet invitations to the table of love"—that is, to charity. Because everything being purged by its contrary, charity is that which entirely extinguishes envy. SPIRITS SPEAKING COURTEOUS INVITATIONS TO THE TABLE OF LOVE: they spoke invitations—that is, by speaking they invited the souls who had to purge themselves of envy to the table of love, which is charity. And he said "table" because the first voice they took was from the Gospel of the wedding, saying: "they have no wine." And certainly, just as envy detracts from and stains the honor and the benefit of one's neighbor, so charity exerts itself and strives to preserve it. The Evangelist <note>Landino attributes the Wedding at Cana to Luke here, though it is found in the Gospel of John.</note> writes: that at the wedding held in Cana of Galilee, the Virgin Mary, moved by charity, seeing the wine was lacking, turned to Jesus and said, "they have no wine": which voice proceeded from supreme charity. He notes that the voice was spoken, and was reiterated—that is, repeated—to denote that charity never tires of feeling compassion for the neighbor's misfortune; and always reminds God of his need, both before it comes, and when it comes, and after it has come. I AM ORESTES. He has set down one kind of charity, which is in those who rejoice in the good of a friend and exert themselves so that it may come. Now he sets down another kind, which is found in few: those who, to save their friend, offer themselves to death, as one reads of Orestes and Pylades. Orestes was the son of **Agamemnon** and **Clytemnestra**. But Clytemnestra, while her husband was occupied in the Trojan War, grew hot with the love of **Aegisthus**: in such a way that, in order not to lose the thing she loved, when her husband returned, she proposed together with Aegisthus to kill him. Thus, after simulated welcomes, she gave him a garment which he put on, not open at the top. And while he was entangled in it, she killed him. Orestes his son, still a child, was secretly taken from his mother's sight by **Strophius** <note>In myth, Strophius was the King of Phocis and Orestes' uncle/foster-father.</note>, because she sought to kill him; so that...

# CANTO XIII

the kingdom remained free for her lover. Later, having reached adulthood, he killed his mother to take revenge for his father <note>Orestes killed his mother Clytemnestra to avenge the murder of his father, King Agamemnon.</note>. And because of such matricide, he became driven by madness. For this reason, having formed a friendship with Pylades, the son of the aforementioned Strophius, he went to the Tauric region, where the temple of Diana Dictynna <note>An epithet for Diana, often associated with hunting nets or Mount Dictynneum in Crete.</note> was located, in which those driven by madness were freed from the Furies. And once he was liberated there, the most cruel King Thoas wished to sacrifice Orestes to the aforementioned goddess. But because he could not distinguish him from Pylades, there arose a miraculous example of friendship. For Pylades, in order to free his friend, claimed to be Orestes. And Orestes, so that his friend would not perish in his place, swore an oath to show he was truly Orestes, and that the king should take him and free Pylades from danger. Because of this, the king, stunned by such wonderful friendship, pardoned both of them. Solinus writes that the bones of Orestes were found by the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> in the city of Tegea; when these were brought back to their place, they formed a body seven cubits long <note>Approximately 10.5 feet or 3.2 meters.</note>. I omit many things in this history, but let it suffice that the poet places Orestes in this spot for that kind of charity through which a man willingly faces death to save his friend. **LOVE THOSE FROM WHOM you have received evil.** It is true charity to rejoice in the good of one's neighbor and to exert oneself so that it may come to pass. But it is greater to submit oneself to manifest dangers for a friend. But what shall we say of those who love those from whom they have received injury? This is the precept of the Savior: "Love your enemies" <note>original Latin: "Diligite inimicos uestros"</note> and "pray for those who persecute you" <note>original Latin: "Et orate pro persequentibus uos"</note>. And the Apostle: "Render to no one evil for evil" <note>original Latin: "Nulli malum pro malo reddetes"</note>. And Luke: "Love those who love you, and those who hate you, and your enemies, and your reward will be great" <note>original Latin: "Diligite eos qui uos diligunt... et erit merces uestra magna"</note>. This is, therefore, the third kind of charity: through which we love our enemies.

Virgil continues the exposition and interpretation of the voices heard. And he demonstrates that because in this circle and terrace Envy is "whipped"—that is, punished and purged—it is necessary that the cords of this whip—that is, such punishment—be drawn from love. And the reason is that the "rein"—which does not let us run headlong into the sin of envy, but draws us back when we have strayed—must be of a contrary nature; and nothing is

> I believe you will hear it, in my judgment,
> before you reach the pass of pardon.
> But fix your eyes through the air very steadily,
> and you will see people sitting before us,
> each one seated along the cliffside."
> Then I opened my eyes wider than before;
> I looked ahead and saw shadows with cloaks
> not different in color from the stone.

<column-break/>

more contrary to envy than charity. Therefore, the voices already mentioned, which draw us away from envy, must proceed from charity. But Virgil will advise him better of this before they arrive at the "pass of pardon"—that is, the stairs which climb to the third terrace and take up the souls purged with the remission of sin. Then he admonishes Dante to look steadily, and he will see the envious and their punishments. Looking steadily signifies nothing else than turning the sharpness of the intellect and fixing it in such consideration. Being admonished, Dante obeyed the command, and looking steadily, he saw all these things. And especially the souls who were purging themselves: they had cloaks of a livid <note>A leaden, bluish-gray color associated with bruising and Envy.</note> color, just as he showed above that the stone of that place was also. Similarly, Ovid wrote: "his mind had infected it, nor was the stone white" <note>original Latin: "nec lapis albus erat sua mens infecerat illa"</note>. And elsewhere: "pallor sits upon the face" <note>original Latin: "pallor in ore sedet"</note>. These sat

<column-break/>

along the cliff, singing the litanies in a way that could move every hard heart to compassion. He saw them dressed in vile <term>hair-shirts</term> <note>original Italian: "ciliccio"; a rough garment made of goat hair worn as a penance.</note>. They were supported by the bank, and one leaned his head upon the shoulder of the other, as blind men do, who stand in a row begging and leaning together to move people to compassion not only with words but also in that manner. He adds later that they could not see anything because their eyes were stitched shut with iron wire, just as they stitch the eyelids of <term>sparrowhawks</term> taken in the woods so that they do not struggle. These new conditions are given by the poet with great ingenuity and learning to the envious soul eager to be purged of such a vice. They remain sitting to purge their haste, not only of the body but more of the soul, which they used to investigate the happiness of others to disturb it, and their misery to take pleasure from it. And Ovid, describing the house of Envy: "The house is in the deepest valleys of a cave, hidden from the sun, not open to any wind. Sad and full of sluggish cold; it always lacks fire and always abounds in darkness" <note>original Latin: "Domus est imis in uallibus antri. Abdita sole carens..."</note>. Their livid cloak demonstrates the "lividity" of envy as has already been said. Whence Ovid says of Aglauros: "Nor was the color white, her mind had infected it." And elsewhere: "pallor sits on the face." **AND THAT IT BE OF VILE HAIR-SHIRT:** this is made of bristles and not of wool; thus it is a cold garment because it is sparsely woven, and it is rough, and it stings and gnaws the flesh of him who wears it. For envy is cold, as it extinguishes charity; and he who clothes himself in envy is always stung and reddened by the happiness he sees in others, and he is consumed by it and loses his flesh. Whence the satirist <note>Juvenal</note> prudently said: "The envious man grows thin at the prosperity of another" <note>original Latin: "Inuidus alterius rebus macrescit opimis"</note>. And Jerome encourages the envious to make a feast of the hair-shirt. They sit leaning against the rock because the envious man is always in coldness and hardness, which two things are found in the rock. We can also refer this to one who purges envy: who, sitting for the reason stated above, leans on a stable and immovable thing. **THEY LEAN THEIR HEADS ONE UPON THE OTHER.** This denotes that one must correct...
