# XIII. PURGATORIO

the other: They sang the litanies in opposition to the habit of speaking ill. They have their eyes sewn shut with iron wire; that is, with the virtue of fortitude: they keep their eyes closed for the reason mentioned above. And certainly, whoever purges themselves of envy must keep their eyes closed to worldly goods, and for this reason the Psalmist said: *Turn away my eyes lest they see vanity* <note>original: "Averte oculos meos ne videam vanitatem"; Psalm 119:37</note>. Or we might say that the envious are blind. Hence Job says: *In the daytime they shall encounter darkness, and grope at midday as if in the night* <note>original: "Per diem incurrent tenebras : et quasi in nocte sic palpabunt in meridie"; Job 5:14</note>. And Gregory says: *The mind of the envious man, when it is afflicted by the good of another, is darkened by the ray of light* <note>original: "Mens invidi cum alieno bono affligitur de radio lucis offuscatur"; Gregory the Great</note>. And in Matthew chapter 20: *The envious grow sick from the health of others, and die from their life* <note>original: "Invidi de sanitate aliorum infirmantur : et de vita moriuntur"</note>. And Socrates used to wish that the envious had eyes and ears in every city, so that they might be tormented even more <note>By seeing more of others' success to be jealous of</note>. And Isaiah says: *Woe to you who call good evil, and evil good* <note>original: "Ve qui dicitis bonum malum : et malum bonum"; Isaiah 5:20</note>. The tears signify true contrition and repentance:

And when we were a little further on,
I heard them praying: "Mary, pray for us,"
then "Michael," and "Peter," and "All the Saints."
I do not believe there walks the earth today
a man so hardened he would not be pierced
by compassion for what I then beheld;
For when I had come close enough to them
that their condition was made clear to me,
heavy grief was milked from my eyes.
They seemed covered in vile hairshirts,
and one supported the other with his shoulder,
and all of them were supported by the bank.
Just so the blind, who lack for basic things,
stand at pardons <note>Religious festivals or church steps where pilgrims gathered</note> to beg for their needs,
and one sinks his head upon the other,
So that pity may be stirred in others quickly,
not only by the sound of their words
but by their appearance, which pleads no less.
And just as the sun does not reach the blind,
so to the shades in the place I speak of now
the light of heaven does not wish to give itself;
For an iron wire pierces all their eyelids
and sews them up, as is done to a wild sparrowhawk <note>A common medieval practice to tame hawks by temporarily sewing their eyes shut</note>
because it will not otherwise stay quiet.
It seemed to me I did an outrage as I walked,
seeing others while not being seen myself,
so I turned to my wise counsel.
He well knew what the mute <note>Dante refers to himself as "the mute" here because he had not yet spoken</note> wished to say,
and therefore did not wait for my request,
but said: "Speak, and be brief and to the point."
Virgil was walking with me on that side
of the cornice from which one might fall,
because it is girded by no outer rim.
On the other side were the devoted
shades, who through that horrible stitching
pressed out tears that bathed their cheeks.
I turned to them and said: "O people certain

<column-break/>

to see the High Light <note>God</note>
which is the only care your desire seeks.
So may grace soon dissolve the scum
of your conscience, so that clearly
the stream of memory may flow down through it,
Tell me—for it would be gracious and dear to me—
if there is any soul among you who is Italian;
perhaps it will be good for them if I learn it."

---

**H**E WELL KNEW WHAT THE MUTE WISHED TO SAY. He means Virgil understood what I wanted to say even though I did not speak. And certainly, Reason understands Appetite <note>The "Appetite" here refers to the soul's natural desires or impulses</note> even if it does not speak. Seeing, then, Dante's desire to speak with those souls, he permitted it, but with a limit, commanding him to be brief and "to the point": brief in words, and "to the point"—that is, cautious in his judgments. Having climbed onto the ledge, they turned to the right. Virgil, being on the outer edge, remained on the right-hand side. Therefore, we note two things here: that Dante has Virgil on his right, and that he has him on the side where there is danger of falling, because the edge of the cornice "is not girded"—that is, it is not surrounded by any parapet. And it is fitting that Reason should be on the right and on the side where there is danger of falling. SO MAY GRACE soon dissolve the scum. "Scum" is the impurity of water, and so here it is used for the stain of the soul, which is washed away as it purges itself, SO THAT CLEARLY through it... The human mind is the origin of the appetite; if it is obedient to reason, it moves and flows toward the things it desires, and it flows "clearly"—that is, without stain. Wherefore, as we have shown in both Virgil and in this poet, the appetite is likened to the movement of water.

# CANTO XIII

"O my brother, each one is a citizen
of one true city; but you mean to say
one who lived in Italy as a pilgrim."
This I seemed to hear for an answer
somewhat further ahead than where I stood,
and so I made myself heard even more.
Among the others I saw a shade that waited
in its look; and if any should ask how:
it raised its chin in the manner of the blind.

Because if I say my body is Florentine, I do not err, for it is composed here. But the soul comes from God and has no other homeland but heaven, as we demonstrated above. This is what all the Platonists and the excellent philosophers sing. Thus also the true theologians. And Ovid: *Every soil is a homeland to the brave, as the sea is to the fish* <note>original: "Omne solum forti patria est ut piscibus equor"; Ovid, Fasti 1.493</note>.
**AMONG THE OTHERS** I saw a shade that waited: because the eyes are those which most greatly show our affects <term>affects: inner emotions or dispositions</term>, and that soul could not open them: Dante presents the gesture by which he understood that it was waiting, and this was that, not being able to look at him, it raised its chin.

"Spirit," I said, "who subdue yourself to climb,
if you are the one who answered me,
make yourself known to me by place or name."
"I was Sienese," it replied, "and with these
others I cleanse here my wicked life,
weeping to Him that He might lend Himself to us.
Wise I was not, although Sapia
I was named, and I was at others' harms
far more glad than at my own good fortune.
And so that you do not think I deceive you,
hear if I was foolish, as I have told you,
already descending the arch of my years.
My fellow citizens were near Colle,
joined in battle with their adversaries,
and I prayed to God for what He willed.
Broken there and turned into the bitter
paths of flight, and seeing the pursuit,
I took a joy beyond all others,
So much that I turned up my bold face,
crying to God: 'Henceforth I fear You no more!'
as the blackbird does for a brief spell of fair weather.
I sought peace with God at the extreme
end of my life; and even then my debt
would not be lessened by penitence,
If it were not that I was kept in memory
by Piero Pectinaro in his holy prayers,
who out of charity felt grief for me.
But who are you, who go asking
about our conditions with your eyes unbound,
as I believe, and speaking as you breathe?"

<column-break/>

Dante was asking if any soul among those was Italian. But this soul that answers—because it was outside the body—could more acceptably consider the true homeland of the soul than Dante, who had his within the body. For this reason, it most modestly corrects Dante's incorrect premise, which was that the homeland of the soul was where the body was generated. But since the soul is created by God from nothing in His image and likeness, and immediately, it can have no other homeland than the celestial one from its Creator—who was neither Florentine nor Roman—nor from the matter of which it is composed.

Sapia was a Sienese noblewoman; but she lived in exile in Colle. And she bore such envy toward the Sienese state that, when the Sienese were defeated not far from Colle, she took such joy in it that, raising her eyes to heaven, she said: "God, do to me from now on the worst You can: for I shall live and die content." **AND I PRAYED TO GOD FOR what He willed.** Because Sapia's prayers were not only unjust but impious; and nonetheless, what she desired followed. It seems unreasonable that God, the highest justice, would grant them; and for this reason Sapia says, *And I prayed to God for what He willed*: as if to say, though I prayed to Him, He did not descend to my unjust prayers, but He did what I desired because He willed it as punishment for the sins of the Sienese. **SO MUCH THAT I TURNED** up my bold face: This is the sin of pride; and from pride, as we showed, envy is born. But we must believe that she was purged of this in the terrace below <note>The first terrace of Purgatory, where pride is punished</note>. **AS THE BLACKBIRD DOES**: It is a common proverb that this bird says when a brief spell of fair weather comes in winter: "I care not for you, Lord, for I have escaped the winter." **I SOUGHT PEACE**: At the end of my life I turned to penitence, which reconciles us in peace with God. And although through penitence I escaped Hell, nonetheless my duty—that is, the debt I had with God for the sins committed—would not yet be lessened through penitence. But the prayers of Piero Pectinaro have twisted back and shortened the time I had to stay in Ante-Purgatory. Piero Pectinaro was a Florentine <note>Historical records typically identify the holy comb-seller Piero Pectinaro as Sienese, though the commentator here labels him Florentine</note>, a very religious man and a hermit. **WITH YOUR EYES UNBOUND**: As if to say, you are not one of ours, who are punished here with sewn-up eyes. **AND SPEAKING AS YOU BREATHE**: You speak while still alive. For souls without bodies do not "breathe," that is, draw breath. **AS I BELIEVE**: Since she could not see, she could not know it for certain. But by conjecture, she believed it. Dante responds and shows...

### PURGATORIO

"My eyes," I said, "will be taken from me here also,
but for a little time, for small is the offense
committed by being turned with envy.
Far greater is the fear which keeps my soul
suspended for the torment below,
for even now the burden from down there weighs upon me."
And she to me: "Who then has led you
up here among us, if you believe you will return below?"
And I: "This man who is with me and says not a word.
And I am alive; and therefore ask of me,
elect spirit, if you wish that I should move
my mortal feet further on your behalf."
"Oh, this is such a new thing to hear,"
she replied, "that it is a great sign that God loves you;
therefore, sometimes assist me with your prayer.
And I ask you by that which you most desire,
if you ever tread the land of Tuscany,
that you restore my reputation among my kinsmen.
You will see them among that vain people
who hope in Talamone, and will lose more hope there
than in finding the Diana;
but the admirals will lose the most."

**WHO SAYS NOT A WORD.** <note>original: "CHE NON FA motto"</note> He remains silent, but having been led to the higher level, he does not seek particulars himself; instead, he admonishes Dante to seek them, because the inferior intellect derives all its strength from the superior. **OH, THIS IS... TO HEAR.** Truly, it is not without manifest signs that someone is loved by God when they receive special graces from Him, which are given to few. **AMONG THAT VAIN PEOPLE.** Vanity is a specific and peculiar vice of the Sienese. **WHO HOPE IN TALAMONE.** They have the hope that, having acquired the port of Talamone <note>A coastal town in Tuscany that Siena purchased in 1303, hoping to become a naval power</note>, they might become great men at sea. Therefore they are "vain," since they hope for what is not to be hoped for. Talamone is a castle and port at the end of the Sienese Maremma. **AND WILL LOSE MORE HOPE THERE THAN IN FINDING THE DIANA.** There was a popular opinion in those times that there was a subterranean river running under Siena. For this reason, with no small expense, they had excavations made in many places hoping to find such water. Thus, the hope they have of being able to build a fleet at sea because they have Talamone will deceive them no less than the hope of finding this water—which they call "Diana"—deceived them. And especially the principal citizens, who also hope to be made admirals <note>original: ".i. capitani dellarmata"</note>, that is, captains of the fleet.

<column-break/>

...shows that he does not have his eyes sewn shut like theirs because he is not yet dead. But when his soul is released from the body to Purgatory, he demonstrates that it too will be punished for envy. But for a short time, because he is little infected by such sin; however, he fears more the pains and torment below—that is, the first terrace where Pride is punished—because he knows he is more entangled in that than in this.

And certainly, in a noble soul, a most sharp intellect, and great judgment, much envy cannot fall; because since envy is between equals, none or very few are his equals. Furthermore, this envy comes from a small soul, and from those who value the goods of the body and of fortune much more than they are worth.

And certainly, whoever considers on one hand the status, riches, and dignities, and on the other the anxieties, the distress, and the unbearable labors involved in acquiring and maintaining them—and the time we consume in this, which we could put into the study of the true sciences which show us the eternal life and the true way that leads us there, or at least in some action by which we might benefit ourselves and our neighbor—without doubt they would deserve not envy, but compassion. 

But the proud man, having obtained the higher position, because he has a noble soul, practices liberality and magnanimity; and it seems to him that he is superior to others in proportion to the greater benefits by which he makes them beholden to him.

And I, Dante, replied to Sapia: **THIS MAN**, that is, Virgil...

<summary>Dante confesses that while he is on the terrace of Envy, he fears the punishment for Pride much more. The commentary discusses the vanity of the Sienese people through their failed civil projects and contrasts the "small-minded" nature of Envy with the "noble" but misplaced nature of Pride.</summary>

# CANTO XIV. OF THE SECOND CANTICLE OF DANTE. XIV.

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'C' at the start of the poem, featuring an illuminated scene of two travelers, likely Dante and Virgil, walking along a winding path in a mountainous landscape.</image-desc>

"Who is this who circles our mountain
before death has given him flight,
and opens his eyes and shuts them at his will?"
"I do not know who he is, but I know he is not alone;
you ask him, since you are closer to him,
and greet him gently so that he may speak to us."
Thus two spirits, leaning toward one another,
were talking of me there on the right hand;
then they turned their faces back to speak to me.
And one said: "O soul that, still fixed
within the body, journey toward heaven,
for charity’s sake console us and tell us:
Whence you come and who you are; for you make us
marvel as much at your grace
as a thing must that never was before."
<margin>from the shores <note>original: "ab oris"</note></margin>
And I: "Through the midst of Tuscany there wanders
a little stream that rises in Falterona,
and a hundred miles of course do not satisfy it.
From above that stream I bring this person;
to tell you who I am would be to speak in vain,
for my name does not yet sound very loud."
"If I grasp your meaning well
with my intellect," then he who spoke first
replied to me, "you speak of the Arno."
And the other said to him: "Why did he hide
the name of that river,
just as a man does with horrible things?"
And the shade who had been asked this
acquitted himself thus: "I do not know; but it is truly
fitting that the name of such a valley should perish;
For from its beginning, where it is so teeming
in the rugged mountain range from which Pelorus was torn,
that in few places does it pass beyond that mark
Until it yields itself up to restore
that which the sky dries from the sea,
whence the rivers have that which flows with them.
Virtue is fled from as an enemy
by all, like a snake, either through some
ill-fortune of the place or through evil habit that goads them;
Wherefore the inhabitants of that wretched valley
have so changed their nature
that it seems Circe had them in her pasture."

<column-break/>

This fourteenth canto continues the purgation of the sin of Envy. Through a conversation between Sir Guido del Duca of Brettinoro and Sir Rinieri da Calvoli of Romagna, it laments the wretched conditions of Italy, and especially of our republic <note>Referring to Florence</note>. It also introduces Virgil speaking about Envy. **WHO IS THIS.** Two spirits, talking together, marvel that Dante has come to Purgatory before his death. **I DO NOT KNOW WHO HE IS:** thus the other spirit responds. **SPEAK TO HIM:** <note>original: "parli a colo"</note> speak to completion. For a "colon" <note>The commentator is making a grammatical pun on the Italian "colui" (him) and "colo" (a colon or period)</note> is a fixed point placed when a sentence is finished. **THAT NEVER WAS BEFORE.** This seems to contradict himself, having affirmed in the second canto of *Inferno* that Aeneas went to the underworld and the Elysian fields; to which you may respond: he speaks hyperbolically, meaning it happens so rarely that one can say "never." **WHENCE YOU COME:** and who you are. This is similar to Virgil’s Venus saying: "But who are you, then? From what shores or [whence] have you come?" <note>original: "Sed uos qui tandem quibus aut uenistis [ab oris]"</note>

The other spirit was Sir Rinieri, who was not speaking to Dante, but said to Guido: as you see, he spoke to him because this man has hidden the name of that river, nor named the Arno, as one does when speaking of horrible things, which out of fear one does not name. And the shade who was asked "acquitted himself" <note>original: "sisdebito"</note>, that is, he responded. For whoever is asked an honest thing is bound to respond. Therefore, when he responds, he "acquits" himself, that is, he pays. And he said the name of this river was never worthy; and therefore it is well that it should perish. And it was never worthy because it has no inhabitants adorned with any virtue. And to demonstrate this, he begins to describe it, placing its birth in Falterona, which is part of the Apennines. He says, therefore, that from the beginning of the Arno, which is born where the rugged mountain—that is, the Apennines—is "so teeming." That is, it is so swollen and high, or truly "teeming" with water, because in a small space it produces both the Arno and the Tiber; in few places does it pass beyond that mark. That is, although the Apennines are very long, nevertheless in few places are they higher than at Falterona. **FROM WHICH PELORUS WAS TORN.** It was the opinion of the ancients that the Apennines, of which we spoke in the *Inferno*, reached not only to Reggio, but also anciently went into Sicily. And its final part was that which later remained as a mountain in Sicily, and is called Pelorus <note>The modern Cape Peloro</note>.

<summary>Dante encounters the spirits of Guido del Duca and Rinieri da Calvoli, who discuss the corruption of the Arno valley and the loss of virtue in Tuscany. The commentary explains the geographical and allegorical significance of the Arno and the Apennine mountains.</summary>

# PURGATORIO

Tra brutti porci piu degni di galle
che daltro cibo facto in human uso
diriza prima el suo pouero calle:
Botoli truoua poi uenendo in giuso
ringhiosi piu che non chiede lor possa :
et alhor disdegnando torce el muso

la maladecta et sventurata fossa/

Chosi uidio l'alt'anima che uolta
staua a udire turbarsi et farsi trista
poichebbe la parola ase raccolta

mise uoglo so di saper lor nome/

Among foul pigs, more worthy of acorns <note>Original: "galle," the bitter oak-galls used for ink, rather than food.</note>
than of any food made for human use,
it first directs its poor path:
It finds curs then, coming downward,
snarling more than their power warrants;
and then, in disdain, it twists its snout away.
It goes on falling; and the more it swells,
the more it finds the dogs becoming wolves,
that accursed and ill-fated ditch.
Descending then through deeper pools,
it finds the foxes so full of fraud
that they fear no trap that might catch them.
I will not stop speaking though another hears me;
and it will be good for him if he still remembers
what a true spirit unfolds to me.
I see your nephew who becomes
a hunter of those wolves on the bank
of the fierce river, and strikes terror into them all.
He sells their flesh while they are still alive;
then he slaughters them like an ancient beast;
he deprives many of life, and himself of honor.
Bloody he emerges from the wretched woods;
he leaves it such that a thousand years from now
it will not return to its primary state.

As at the announcement of coming harms
the face of him who listens is troubled,
from whatever side the danger may snap at him;
So I saw the other soul, who had turned
to listen, become troubled and grow sad,
after he had gathered the words to himself.
The hearing of the one and the look of the other
made me long to know their names;
and I asked them with prayers mixed with tears.
Wherefore the spirit who first spoke to me
began again: "You wish that I should bring myself..."

<column-break/>

Before we explain the words spoken by the soul: understand: that of these two spirits: the one speaking is Sir Guido del Duca of Bertinoro in Romagna. And the other to whom he speaks is Sir Rinieri da Calvoli of Forlì. **PIGS** he calls all of the Casentino as far as Arezzo: and especially the Guidi counts, men of great luxury. **POOR PATH**: because it has little water. **CURS**: these are the Aretines <note>People of Arezzo.</note>: whom he likens to curs, dogs of small body: And he wishes to show that the Aretines have much disdain: and little strength: "in disdain it twists its snout": because after it is near Arezzo: it turns to the right: and leaves Arezzo. **THE MORE IT SWELLS**: because of the tributary rivers: that flow into the Arno. **THE MORE IT FINDS** dogs becoming wolves: the cur snarls and barks. But the wolf is set for labor: and predation: and theft. And by this he means the gentlemen and counts: who were in the Val d'Arno: and partly the Florentines. **DESCENDING THEN** through deeper pools: he places those of the lower Val d'Arno: and finally the Pisans: whom he calls foxes: to denote that they are full of fraud and deceit. **I WILL NOT STOP**: he places three things in this tercet. First, he shows he does not care about being heard. Which signifies that his conscience is already clear: that he speaks not out of envy or hatred: but out of just indignation. Then because he hopes to make it useful to Dante by making him cautious. And in the third place he shows: that having to speak of future things: he will tell the truth: since he heard it from a true spirit. **I SEE** your nephew. This was Sir Fulcieri da Calvoli of Forlì: who predicts: that he will come as *podestà* <term>The chief magistrate or governor of a city-state.</term> to extinguish and thereby kill many. We wrote in the sixth canto of the *Inferno*: that in the year one thousand three hundred and two, enemies were brought into **FLORENCE** by Charles Lackland <note>original: "Carlo senza terra"—Charles of Valois, who arrived in Florence to settle disputes but instead empowered the Black faction.</note>. These men, fearing greatly the power and favor that the Whites had in Florence: corrupted Sir Fulcieri so that he might seize many of the White party: among whom were Sir Betto Gherardini: Masino: and Donato Cavalcanti: Sir Neri Adimari: and Sir Tignoso De’ Macci. And as men who wished to disturb the peaceful state of the city, he had their heads cut off: although Tignoso: because he was very fat: perished on the strappado <term>A form of torture where the victim is suspended by the arms; here, the victim's weight caused his death.</term>. Furthermore, at the instance of Sir Musatto Franzesi, his friend, he wished to seize some of the Abati family. But they, sensing the order given secretly, fled. Whereupon the *podestà* declared all the Abati rebels. Nor after that was such a family in Florence. And let this suffice in this place: because in the canto already mentioned it is narrated more extensively. **LIKE AN ANCIENT BEAST**: like an old animal: as if to say like the ox: which when through old age it can no longer plow: is fattened and sent to the slaughter. Therefore he deprived those of life, and himself of honor and fame. And he came out bloody from Florence: which he calls a woods: because above he called the citizens wolves.

As it happens: that an announcement of some harm: troubles the face of him: who hears of the danger from whatever side. That is, the danger snaps and bites: so I saw the other soul: not Guido who was speaking: but Rinieri: who was listening, become troubled: because such souls are full of charity: and they grieve at the evil of others. And especially is it the duty of these: who purge envy. So that the abundance of charity in Purgatory might entirely extinguish the malice of this life. **THE HEARING OF THE ONE**: the words of Guido: and the troubled face of Rinieri kindled in me the desire to know: who they were: and deservedly: because the words of the one and the gestures of the other made clear conjectures: that they were of honor and worthy of...

# CANTO XIV

in doing for you what you will not do for me.
But since God wills that so much of His grace
shines through in you, I will not be stingy;
therefore, know that I am Guido del Duca.
My blood was so consumed by envy
that if I had seen a man become happy,
you would have seen me pale and spotted with lividity.
From my sowing, I reap such straw as this.
O human race, why do you set your heart
on things that require the exclusion of a partner? <note>Guido refers to material goods: if one person has them, another cannot. This is the root of envy.</note>
This is Rinieri; this is the prize and the honor
of the house of Calboli, where no one since

were known. Rinieri then replied: you want
me to tell you who I am, but you do not want to tell us who
you are. Although it seems unfair that you wish to
know and yet do not wish to teach, nevertheless,
seeing such divine grace in you, I will not be stingy,

could lead me to guess that you were either
proud—deeming us unworthy—or envious—not wishing to

confutes and proves both wrong, because no
special grace comes from God except to men
of merit. **MY BLOOD WAS SO CONSUMED BY**
**ENVY**. And in this, he also practices charity, which
purges envy. By demonstrating his own error
and the punishment he suffers for it, he becomes an example to
others, so they might guard themselves against it. By saying that if he had seen
a man become happy, he shows the express vice of
envy. For the envious person makes no exception
between one man and another. Anyone he sees becoming happy—which can happen even
from a small success—strangely saddens him. **YOU WOULD HAVE SEEN ME** Spotted with lividity. That is: I was suddenly
overwhelmed by so much envy that I showed it in my face,
for I would turn a bruised, leaden color. **FROM MY SOWING** I reap such straw. The actions of men are seeds which produce fruit similar to themselves.
For good and virtuous works produce happiness;
contrary works produce the opposite. And he rightly said "such straw,"
and not fruit, because virtuous action produces not just straw, but also grain, because it builds the habit of
virtue. But vicious action produces vice, which is not a thing in itself, but only a privation. Therefore it can be called
sterile straw. **O HUMAN RACE, WHY DO YOU NOT SET** your heart. He rebukes men who
set their minds, thoughts, and affections on temporal
and transitory goods. These goods have this
condition: that one person cannot have them if another is not deprived. As Boethius says: <note>original: "O angustas et inopes diuitias quas nec pluribus habere totas: simul licet et adquemlibet sine ceterorum paupertate non ueniunt."</note> *“O narrow and impoverished riches, which many cannot possess in full at the same time, and which do not come to anyone without the poverty of others.”* Therefore, the envious person would wish to deprive others to have them all for himself. **WHERE THERE IS EXCLUSION** **OF A PARTNER**. That is: those things which require the exclusion of a companion. This is a metaphor from the magistrates who are distributed in
republics: where, when one "partner" (that is, from the same family) holds a magistrate's office, the others are excluded—they are prohibited from being there while the partner is present. So it happens in the division of the goods of fortune:
the good that Mark possesses, Anthony cannot possess. But the goods of the soul, which are
virtues—because they are incorporeal and indivisible—can likewise be possessed by everyone at once.

<image-desc>A large blue decorative initial N featuring internal white vine patterns.</image-desc>
**N**ot only has the family of these men been made
bare—that is, impoverished of every virtue—but all the men
of Romagna, which he describes by its boundaries.
For Romagna is bounded on the north
by the Po, on the south by the Apennine mountains, and on the
east by the Adriatic sea. The Reno is a small river
which rises in the Apennines near Pistoia; it used to
run between Bologna and Modena, several miles
from Bologna. Later it was diverted to Bologna.
**OF THE GOOD REQUIRED** for truth and for pleasure.
According to the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> there are three kinds of goods:
the honest, the useful, and the delightful. The "honest" is the
true good. Therefore he said "for truth" regarding the goods of the soul,
which is honesty. And "for pleasure" regarding the goods of the body
and of fortune, which are the useful and the delightful. He
concludes, then, that all Romagna has been made bare
and poor of the good required for truth—that is, of the honest good, which is the true good—and of the good
required for pleasure—that is, for joy and delight. This means that it is empty of the virtues that create the honest good, and of the concord and peace that create delight. Then he adds that whatever is inside these boundaries—that is, all Romagna—is filled with poisonous briars; and he says this through a metaphor. For
our souls are likened to the earth. If the earth is not cultivated, it quickly becomes wild and
fills with thorns, burrs, and every wicked weed. But if it is cultivated with diligence, it remains purged of
those, and good trees and every grain produce excellent fruit. So it is with human souls: if they are not...

when stirred into virtue, they become fierce and bestial, performing actions not of a man, but of wild and cruel beasts. This signifies that there are so many more wicked people than good ones that it is impossible to wipe them out, especially because they have formed a firm habit of vice. **OR THE GOOD LIZIO.** This was Messer Lizio da Valbona, an excellent man full of virtue. His daughter Caterina, overcome by love, secretly joined with Riccardo, a noble youth; Messer Lizio, with his prudence, had them marry, as our Boccaccio narrates at length in one of his novellas <note>Lizio da Valbona appears in Boccaccio’s Decameron, Day V, Novel 4, the famous story of the nightingale.</note>. Arrigo Mainardi of Faenza—some say of Bertinoro—was a great friend of the one speaking. Pier Traversaro was the lord of Ravenna, a high-minded and much-reputed man, who married one of his daughters to Stephen, King of Hungary. His power flourished in the times of Frederick II, whom he rebelled against. But after Pier's death, Frederick besieged and conquered Ravenna. Guido di Carpigna was a noble man from Montefeltro, whom none equaled in liberality. **A BLACKSMITH TAKES ROOT**—that is, when a craftsman of lowly condition becomes great, and from a humble origin a lineage and nobility are born, as did Lambertaccio the blacksmith. He rose to such a state that he was almost the lord of Bologna, and from him descended Messer Fabbro de' Lambertacci. **BERNARDIN DI FOSCO.** This was the ancestor of Messer Bernardino, who ruled Faenza; a man of low fortune, but of such excellent wisdom and counsel that he came into great esteem among his fellow citizens.

> Do not wonder, Tuscan, if I weep,

<column-break/>

**Do not wonder**—that is, O Dante the Tuscan—if I weep when I remember—that is, recall—all these virtuous men of great governance. Then he lists them, and places Guido da Prata first. This is a villa between Faenza and Ravenna. Ugolin d’Azzo was of the Ubaldini family. They possessed much land around the Apennine mountains and in Mugello. Federigo Tignoso was of Rimini. The Traversari and Anastagi were two families in Ravenna. **THAT LOVE AND COURTESY ONCE MADE US DESIRE.** Love, benevolence, and courtesy—that is, liberality—made them eager to follow such virtues. For to say "love desires me" means love makes me desirous of it. Therefore, it signifies that they were kindled by these two virtues: namely, benevolence and liberality. And the meaning is: that for love of virtue they were willing to endure hardships; and to practice liberality toward those for whom it was fitting, they sought **ease**—that is, they strove to give comfort to others. **THERE WHERE**, in which place, the hearts which used to be so full of love and gentleness are now full of wickedness. **O BERTINORO.** This is a beautiful castle in the middle of Romagna, placed on a mountain above Forlì.

---

**WHY DO YOU NOT FLEE AWAY?** It is as if he says: why do you not undo yourself, since your family has departed? He refers to the family of this Guido del Duca, in which they say there were at one time many men of such great liberality that a controversy often arose when foreigners arrived there, because everyone wanted them at their own house. For this reason, they erected a column in the square and placed as many rings around it as there were heads of families, each one assigned his own. When a foreigner arrived, he tied his horse to one of the rings, and immediately the one to whom the ring was assigned would lead that foreigner to his house and honor him most liberally.

---

> Bagnacavallo does well to no longer breed,
> and Castracaro does ill, and Conio worse,
> for taking such trouble to breed more counts.
> The Pagani will do well when their "Demon"
> leaves them; but not so well that a pure
> testimony of them shall ever remain.
> O Ugolin de’ Fantolin, you are secure,
> for your name is no longer expected to be
> darkened by those who would stray from it.

<column-break/>

The counts of Bagnacavallo had already diminished—this place is between Imola and Ravenna—and no one new was being born into that family. **AND CASTRACARO DOES ILL.** The counts of Castracaro: these counts were degenerating in the time of the poet. But at present, they have died out. **CONIO.** He grieves that this family continues to breed, since it strays so far from its noble origin. **THE PAGANI WILL DO WELL.** These were noblemen of Faenza descended from Pagano, the father of Mainardo. They ruled over Imola and Faenza, and their domain was called "the power of the Pagani." Of these, Mainardo was the lord of Imola and Faenza; a man distinguished both for the beauty of his body and for his military virtue. And...

> But go your way now, for it delights me
> far more to weep than to speak,

...nevertheless, there will remain no witness to their true praise. He calls him a demon because he was very astute. And in Tuscany, he belonged to the Guelph party, because the Guelphs ruled there; and in Romagna, he favored the Ghibellines, who were powerful in that region. It will be useful, then, for the Pagani <note>A noble family of Romagna; Landino refers here to Mainardo Pagani</note> that Mainardo should die. Nothing more for that which we have said of Mainardo's cunning. But of him it is spoken in the *Inferno*. **O UGOLIN** de' Fantolini: He also was a gentleman of Faenza, full of virtue and good manners. After these words, Guido dismisses Dante and shows that it pains him greatly that virtue is extinguished in Romagna. **SO MUCH HAS YOUR** discourse gripped my mind. It delighted me to weep because your discourse—that is, human reason, which leads every man to charity, which is the proper virtue of man—leads me to compassion.

ALTHOUGH we did not ask the souls for the way, nor did they see if we were keeping to a good path, we nevertheless trusted that since they heard us, they would have corrected us if we were not going well. **AFTER WE** were left alone: we had already passed the souls and remained alone when we heard two voices. And here it is to be noted: that just as above he placed three voices exhorting to charity, so he places two here which, through example, can pull us back from envy.

<columns>2</columns>
> We knew those dear souls
> heard us go, and so by keeping silent
> they made us confident of the path.
> Then we were left alone, proceeding,
> a flash appeared like when the air is cloven
> by a voice that came against us, saying:
> "Whoever finds me shall slay me,"
> and it fled like thunder that dissipates
> if the cloud suddenly breaks apart.

> that it seemed like thunder following quickly.
> "I am Aglauros, who became a stone,"
> and then, to draw closer to the poet,

<column-break/>

But the first three I saw while still among the souls to show that those who enter into the purgatorial virtues benefit from such exhortations. But because he does not need examples to drag him away from envy, he feigns that he heard these last two voices after he had departed from the souls. **"WHOEVER FINDS ME SHALL SLAY ME"**: Abel and Cain were brothers, as we have shown elsewhere. Abel was a shepherd, a just man, and full of religion. And always when he sacrificed to God, he offered the best lambs of the flock. Hence every day he prospered more. Cain, on the contrary, was a wicked man and without religion, and from his farming he always offered the poorest ears of grain from the field; for which impiety he always fell into greater poverty. Wherefore, moved by envy, he killed his brother Abel. God, being angry, cursed him. And he, turning to God, said: "My iniquity is so great that I do not deserve pardon; behold, you shall drive me today from the face of the earth, and I shall be hidden from your face, and I shall be a fugitive in the world. But whoever finds me shall slay me,"

whoever finds me? And God replied that no. Therefore Dante, wishing to recall men from envy, sets down these words. **AND IT FLED** like thunder: because such an example ought to fill every man with terror, so that he guards himself against envy, and such a vice ought to flee from the soul. **IF THE CLOUD SUDDENLY** breaks apart. He demonstrates that thunder is nothing other than the refraction of condensed clouds. **WHEN OUR HEARING** had a truce from it—that is, he heard it no more—behold, the other voice was heard by us with such a great crash—that is, with such a great noise. And he spoke well because "crash" <note>original: "fracasso"</note> signifies that which in Latin is called *fragor* <note>original Latin: "fragor," meaning a breaking or crashing sound</note>, which means a sound made by broken things, like thunder, which seemed to thunder following the flash soon and suddenly; because always the thunder that comes suddenly after the flash is greater. And in truth, the flash and the thunder occur at the same moment. But because the sense of sight is faster than hearing, one first sees the light of the flash before hearing the thunder. And it is to be noted that exhortation to virtue should be gentle, as were the three voices above. But dissuasion from vice should be terrifying. **I AM AGLAUROS** who became a stone. The poets feign that there were three daughters of Cecrops, King of Athens: Herse, Pandrosos, and Aglauros. Mercury saw these during the sacrifices to Minerva and was ensnared in love for Herse, the most beautiful of all three sisters. And wishing to go to Herse's chamber, it was necessary for him to pass through the place where Aglauros was. She wanted to know the reason for Mercury's coming. Mercury revealed his desire to her and with many prayers comforted her so that she would provide him secret help. But the very greedy and envious sister refused to favor him or keep it hidden unless she had received a great sum of money from him. Minerva was offended by Aglauros because shortly before she had dared to uncover the basket under which Erichthonius, born of Vulcan, was hidden. Wherefore, moved to anger, she incited Envy to goad her in such a way that she would envy Mercury's love for her sister and not give way to Mercury. Therefore Mercury, since he could not persuade her either with prayers or promises, converted her into stone. Thus the poet puts this example to frighten men from this vice. Here also fits the description of the house of Envy, which...

# XIIII.
## PURGATORIO

...which Ovid describes with no less learning than eloquence. **AND THEN TO DRAW CLOSER** to the poet. He shows that he was walking ahead of Virgil; but then, out of fear, he pulled back to stay close to him. This demonstrates that the senses often run ahead due to overly burning desire. But when such examples of punishment frighten the sense, it restrains itself and submits to reason.

This which Virgil says now, he had already promised to say when he said: **THE RESTRAINING BIT** <note>original: "lo fren v'uscì"</note> being of the opposite kind: I believe you will hear it by my advice before you reach the pass of pardon. And he said to me: **THAT WAS THE HARD BIT** <note>original: "quel fu duro camo"</note>: that is, the voice of Cain; and that of Aglauros was the hard bit, or the hard bridle. Whence the Psalmist says: *With bit and bridle bind their jaws* <note>original: "In camo et freno maxillas eorum constringe"; Psalm 32:9</note>, because such examples ought to restrain everyone so they do not fall into this vice. For through Cain, death is demonstrated; and through Aglauros, who was turned to stone, obstinacy is shown. Such a bridle must therefore keep a man within his goal <term>meta: the turning post or finish line in a Roman racecourse, representing the limits of human reason</term>, which requires that you love your neighbor as yourself. *Meta* in Latin is the end of the course for horses, which they must not only reach, but having reached it, they must circle it with such art and skill that they neither press so close as to strike it, nor go so wide that other horses enter between them and the post and finish the circuit first.

> The air was already quiet on every side,
> and he said to me: "That was the hard bit
> that should keep a man within his goal.
> But you take the bait, so that the hook
> of the ancient adversary pulls you to him;
> and therefore the bit or the lure avails little.
> The heavens call to you and circle around you,
> showing you their eternal beauties,
> yet your eye looks only at the ground;
> wherefore He who discerns all strikes you."

**BUT YOU TAKE THE BAIT.** In this vice. Just as the fisherman offers bait to the fish on the hook, and thus holds the man as he does the fish. For as the bait deceives, so the devil, our adversary, hunts each one with those worldly pleasures in which vice is hidden; which, like a hook, catches us and pulls us to damnation. He indicates that neither the bit nor the lure—that is, neither comfort nor reprimand—is of any use. **THE HEAVENS CALL TO YOU:** Certainly, God gave man eyes that look upward <note>A reference to Ovid's *Metamorphoses*: "Os homini sublime dedit," meaning "He gave man an uplifted face" to look at the stars</note>, so that he might behold the eternal courses of the heavens and their admirable beauties and ornaments, so that they might desire to ascend to them. And yet we always look at earthly things. **WHEREFORE HE STRIKES YOU.** For which reason God, who discerns all, punishes you; because just anger moves Him, since you are not moved by the beauties He shows you.

<summary>Virgil explains to Dante that the terrifying voices of Cain and Aglauros serve as a "bit" to restrain the vice of envy, warning that mankind too often ignores the beauty of heaven to pursue the devil's earthly bait.</summary>

# CANTO XV OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE.

The poet describes how he ascends from the second circle of Envy to the third, where Wrath is purged. First, he describes the angel who appears to him, purges him of envy, and directs him to the circle of Wrath. Afterward, he explains a statement made in the previous chapter, adds a vision of his own, and finally, Virgil interprets it. **AS MUCH AS**. He describes the evening hour: from which until the

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' containing a seated figure in a landscape, used to begin the first verse of Canto XV.</image-desc>
As much as between the end of the third hour
and the beginning of the day appears of the sphere
that always plays in the manner of a child,
So much appeared now toward the evening
to be remaining of the sun's course;
it was evening there, and here it was midnight.
The rays were striking us full on the nose,
because the mountain had been so circled by us
that we were now walking straight toward the west,
When I felt my forehead weighed down
by the splendor much more than before,
and the things not understood were a marvel to me;
Wherefore I raised my hands toward the top
of my eyebrows, and made for myself a visor <note>original: "solecchio"</note>
which trims away the excess of the visible.

As when from water or from a mirror
the ray leaps to the opposite side,
ascending up in a manner similar
To that which descends, and departs as much
from the falling of a stone in that same distance,
just as experience and art <note>science</note> show;
So it seemed to me by reflected light
to be struck there in front of me,
wherefore my sight was swift to flee.
"What is that, sweet father, which I cannot
shield my eyes from enough to help me?"
I said, "and he seems to be moving toward us."
"Do not marvel if the family of heaven
still dazzles you," he replied to me;
"it is a messenger who comes to invite man to ascend.
Soon it shall be that seeing these things
will not be grave to you, but will be a delight
as much as nature has disposed you to feel."

<column-break/>

setting of the sun: when it goes down, there is as much space of time as there is from the birth of the sun until the third hour <note>The "third hour" refers to 9:00 AM; Dante is saying it is three hours before sunset, or roughly 3:00 PM</note>. Therefore, at the equinox, according to our clocks, it would be the twenty-first hour. **OF THE SPHERE**: that is, of the sun: which in its continuous motion plays like a child. As soon as it is born, it always moves, gaining height until midday. Afterward, it descends. And so does the sun: both in this and in the other hemisphere. **IT WAS EVENING THERE**: in the hemisphere where Purgatory is. And here in Italy, it was midnight. According to the poet, the mountain of Purgatory is positioned exactly opposite to Jerusalem. Therefore, if it had been midnight in Jerusalem at the hour he narrates this, it would have been midday in Purgatory. But because he was in Italy when he was writing this, he says that when it was evening there, it was midnight in Italy; because day and night do not occur equally in every part of the world. **THE RAYS WERE STRIKING** full on the nose: as they walked in a circuit, it followed that they were not always facing one direction. And then it happened that they were turned toward the west. **WEIGHED DOWN THE FOREHEAD**: the splendor of the sun first weighed down his forehead as it struck him from the front. But then, as the splendor of the angel came upon him, it weighed him down much more than before. Wherefore he marveled at the "things not understood," that is, because the appearance of the angel was not yet manifest to him. **WHEREFORE I RAISED**. Seeing myself dazzled by the excessive splendor, I placed my hands above my eyebrows and made a roof for my eyes, so that the rays of the splendor would not strike them. **I MADE FOR MYSELF A VISOR** <term>solecchio: literally "a little sun," a term for shading one's eyes with the hand</term>. That is, I diminished that sun for my eyes. *Solecchio* signifies a "little sun." Hence, when the sun gets in our eyes and we remove those rays from our eyes with some obstacle, we call such a removal *solecchio* because we diminish the sun. **WHICH**: that is, which visor. **TRIMS**: that is, removes and lessens. **OF THE EXCESS** of the visible: of the too-great light.

The meaning is that such reflected light appeared to Dante to strike his face, just like a ray that descends from the sun into water or into a mirror and reflects to the opposite side: because it returns upward in the same way that it descended. For just as the ray of the sun descends without any distance of time <note>instantly</note>, so it makes this reflection without any distance of time. And "departs as much," that is, it is different from the falling of a stone. For a stone falls with a distance of time **IN EQUAL** distance. For if a stone were to descend from the sun in the same time that a ray descends, the stone would arrive much later than the ray. The "falling of the stone," according to Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century philosopher and scientist</note> in the book *On the Properties of the Elements*, is called by a certain translation a line drawn plumb from the center of the sun over our heads, because a falling stone comes down in a plumb line. Therefore, he claims in the same book that the Ethiopians, who live between the summer tropic and the equinoctial line, have two very burning summers because the sun passes the "falling of the stone" over their heads twice. Thus, Dante implies that the rays of the angel came at him in a plumb line <note>directly</note>. **AS EXPERIENCE SHOWS**

And not without reason does he say that the rays of light that struck him were by reflection. This is because he wants to show that the light coming from the angel toward him was a ray which, having struck the angel from the divine light, was reflected from there and struck Dante. We should understand these angels, found at every terrace, to be divine graces: namely, prevenient, illuminating, cooperating, and perfecting grace. Through these, man recognizes the ugliness of sin and the beauty of virtue, and a will is born in him to flee the former and follow the latter; in such a will, he becomes strong, corroborated, and constant. And the fact that Dante shields his eyes with his hands to withstand such splendor signifies that sensuality steps forward with good works, which are represented by the hands. The first works of sensuality are to become obedient to reason and to learn from it how to recognize that which his dazzled eye cannot discern. Reason teaches and instructs him that this is the angel sent by God, who invites him to ascend. For divine grace always exhorts us toward celestial things. **SOON IT WILL**, meaning that when the soul is purged of all [sins], the eye of the mind will be able to endure the divine light—that is, it can come to the knowledge of divine things—though not entirely, but as much as human nature is capable.

**GIVEN BY THE ANGEL**: when they had reached him with a joyful voice, because the more our soul proceeds in its purgation, the more joy it is shown. Or truly, with that voice the angel admonished him as to what he should become in opposition to wrath. This signifies that, having already been purged of two great vices [pride and envy], he remained lighter. **BLESSED ARE THE MERCIFUL** was sung behind them. He says "behind" to show that such a song was in the terrace of Envy, which they were now leaving. This signifies that mercy arrives when envy departs. For mercy grieves for the ill of others, in which envy rejoices. Therefore, this virtue is the opposite of envy. "Blessed are the merciful." In the Gospel of Matthew it is written: "Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy" <note>original Latin: "Beati misericordes quoniam ipsi misericordiam consequentur"</note>. 
**AND REJOICE, YOU WHO OVERCOME**: the sins by purging yourself of them; because in the same Gospel it says: "Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven" <note>original Latin: "Gaudete et exultate: quoniam merces uestra copiosa est in celis"</note>. 
**WE WERE GOING ALONE**. This signifies contemplation, in which the appetite, now joined to reason, desires to learn from it; and he proposes a specific matter to him, asking what Guido del Duca meant when he said: "O human race, why do you set your heart where there is need of excluding partnership?" And from this specific point, Virgil—representing the intellect—enters into the universal.

---

A sentiment certainly appropriate for the intellect wishing to instruct sensuality. For he shows it the origin of envy, so that it may guard itself against it. And he responds that Guido now knows, being in purgatory, the harm that follows from his "greatest flaw"—that is, the sin of envy. And therefore "do not marvel"—do not be surprised. For being at present in a state of charity, he reproves others. And certainly envy always carries its own punishment with it, because other sins have some pleasure. It is sweet to the proud to obtain lordship. It is sweet to the greedy to accumulate gold and silver. The lustful man rejoices in enjoying the thing he loves. But envy always torments its possessor. **BECAUSE YOUR DESIRES ARE FOCUSED**: because our wills are fixed on those things which must necessarily be lessened and diminished when there are more companions sharing the portion. Since temporal goods cannot be possessed by many unless they are divided, a man—seeing that what another has cannot be his—is moved to envy; and envy moves the "bellows of sighs"—that is, it inflames the...

# CANTO XV

ff ii

->...our greed seeks to devour everything. Thus we sigh for it. **BUT IF THE LOVE OF THE SUPREME.** But if the love of celestial things—rather than that of temporal things—ruled us, such fear would not grip your breast. This is because in heaven and regarding celestial goods, the more they are called "ours"—that is, the more people there are who possess them—the more each one possesses. For everyone’s joy increases the more companions there are. And they burn even more intensely in charity. Hence Seneca says: "The possession of no thing is pleasant without a companion." <note>original: "Nullius rei possessio iocunda est sine socio."</note> And Boethius: "Every good brought into common use shines forth more beautifully." <note>original: "Omne bonum in comune deductum pulchrius elucescit."</note> And Augustine in the book *The City of God*: "The possession of goodness is in no way diminished by the arrival of a companion; rather, it is as much wider as the undivided charity of companions possesses it more harmoniously." <note>original: "Nullo modo fit minor accedente consocio possessio bonitatis..."</note> And Gregory: "He who desires to be free from the jaws of envy should seek that possession which the number of possessors does not restrict." <note>original: "Qui faucibus invidie carere desiderat illam possessionem appetat..."</note><-

**I AM MORE FAMISHED** for contentment than if I had been silent. That is: I doubted less before I asked you than I doubt at present. Because I do not understand how it can be that a good distributed among many makes them richer than if it were held by only one or a few. And <term>sensuality: the part of the soul governed by the five senses rather than higher reason</term> rightly doubts this, because by its very nature it cannot understand anything except the things subject to it. And those things being physical, such a doubt follows...

**A FITTING RESPONSE** to the <term>higher reason: the intellect capable of understanding spiritual truths</term>—illustrated by many doctrines—seemed impossible to sensuality and to <term>lower reason: the logic used for worldly, material affairs</term>. It did not seem possible that a good possessed by many could be the whole of it for everyone. And this is what Virgil demonstrates: that sensuality and the lower reason which reflects upon it have no knowledge except of worldly goods, where such conditions exist. Therefore, thinking of nothing but earthly goods, such logic finds error and ignorance instead of the truth, because it considers celestial goods according to the nature of earthly ones. Thus it "plucks darkness"—meaning ignorance—from the light of truth. **THAT INFINITE.** He has shown where the ignorance is born that causes us to have a false opinion of the <term>highest good: "sommo bene," referring to God</term>. Now, by analogy, he demonstrates it to be true that the eternal good, which is in God, is not diminished by being shared by many. And he says God, who is the infinite good (because He has no end, neither in quantity nor in time) **AND INEFFABLE** (meaning unspeakable, because He cannot be described or expressed with words), "runs toward love"—that is, toward whoever loves Him—and shines in them, just as a solar ray shines in bright bodies. The sun has its natural light...

<column-break/>

...and its rays, by striking the stars and other bright bodies, illuminate them. The more bright bodies those rays find, the more they would illuminate. Nor would there be less light for one than for the other because there were more bodies to receive such rays. Rather, the light is greater or lesser according to whether the receiving body is more or less fit. For this reason, a mirror shines more than a plastered wall, even though the sun gives itself equally to each. So God, the only and highest good, shines equally into all souls; and those which are not darkened and clouded by vices, but purged of them, remain bright and are fit to receive such splendor, in proportion to the "heat" and the <term>charity: "carità," the theological virtue of divine love</term> they have within them toward God and their neighbor. And the eternal valor—the eternal goodness and glory—increases in them as their charity is greater. **AND THE MORE PEOPLE.** Glory in the souls in heaven does not decrease because there are more of them; it increases. For just as we see that by placing many mirrors opposite the rays of the sun, each one receives them equally and shines equally (if the defect does not come from the mirror itself), and by positioning them so that the rays of one reflect into the others, the splendor would multiply. So the rays of divine glory come to the blessed souls and make them shine; and then one reflects its own into the others. Because one soul rejoices in the good of another, and thus contentment increases. **AND IF MY REASONING DOES NOT...**

# XV. PURGATORIO

If the reason I show you—that the bliss of souls does not diminish in them because more of them partake in it—does not tire <gloss>original: "non tidiffama"; that is, does not weary you</gloss> and does not satisfy you, it is not because the reason is not true in itself. Rather, it is because Virgil <gloss>that is, human intellect</gloss> with the secular sciences <note>original: "lescientie gentili"; refers to the classical philosophy of the "Gentiles" or non-Christians</note> could not demonstrate it as well as theological doctrine can. You will see Beatrice <gloss>that is, you will read these things in the sacred theologians</gloss>, and they will satisfy you fully. And because we have often shown that the spirit of wisdom cannot enter into a malevolent soul <gloss>that is, in a sinful soul, fouled by vice</gloss>, and cannot have true knowledge of divine things, strive therefore that the five wounds remaining in you are soon extinguished <gloss>that is, the five remaining sins</gloss>, just as the first two—pride and envy—have been extinguished. WHICH <gloss>meaning these wounds; because every vice is a wound of the soul</gloss> ARE CLOSED UP <gloss>they heal</gloss> THROUGH being sorrowful <gloss>through repentance</gloss>.

Dante wanted to respond to Virgil: "You satisfy me." But because he had already reached the third terrace, his wandering eyes <gloss>that is, traveling about in seeing a new place</gloss> pulled him away from such a response. Indeed, having fully understood Virgil’s reasoning, if Dante had had the leisure, he would have responded. But occupied by a sudden sight, he omitted the response. This signifies that unnecessary things—even if they have some value in themselves and would be good to recount in times of leisure—should nevertheless be left behind when a necessary new thing occurs. THERE APPEARED TO ME IN AN ECSTATIC VISION. Ecstasy signifies an elevation of the mind. This occurs when our mind is not alienated by any physical stupor, but is loosened from the body and gathered into itself. It is alienated from the senses not by revelation, but by a powerful imagination which, in its form, captures the mind so entirely that it performs no other operation. It is so bound by a single fixed thought, and so occupied by it, that it understands nothing else, and no other power of the soul functions; the entire mind is fixed on that single thought. In this ecstasy, he seemed to be drawn to a place where many people were. Here he wishes to show that he was entirely absorbed in the thought of when

---

Christ, still a child, went to preach in the temple in the presence of a great crowd of priests, scribes, and Pharisees. His mother and Joseph searched for him for three days without being able to find him. And therefore he says: "and to see in a temple many people." Entering the terrace where wrath is purged, he shows that we must set before our minds examples of patience, such as that of the Virgin Mother, who patiently endured and sweetly rebuked her son, saying: <note>original: "Quid fecisti nobis. Ego et pater tuus dolentes querebamus te."</note> "What have you done to us? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in sorrow." <note>Luke 2:48</note> And because the poet has now ascended into the circle of wrath, the location requires a definition of that sin. We shall say, then, that wrath is a spiritual flame and a boiling of blood around the heart to take vengeance. Hence the Psalmist says: <note>original: "Incenderunt igni sanctuarium tuum in terra"</note> "They have set your sanctuary on fire; they have profaned the dwelling place of your name on earth." <note>Psalm 74:7</note> Likewise, wrath is a fury of the soul which runs from the interior parts to the exterior. And just as smoke arises from natural fire and makes a place dark, so smoke rises from this to the brain and blinds the intellect. Regarding this, Job says: <note>original: "Caligauit ad indignationem oculos meos."</note> "My eye has grown dim with indignation." <note>Job 17:7</note> And Aristotle says: "Two things are against counsel: haste and wrath." And the Psalmist: <note>original: "Ascendit fumus in ira tua. Ignis afacie eius exarsit."</note> "Smoke rose in your wrath; fire broke out from his face." <note>Psalm 18:8</note> Likewise: "Fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun of justice." <note>Psalm 58:8</note> And elsewhere: <note>original: "Turbatus est afurore oculus meus."</note> "My eye is troubled by fury." <note>Psalm 6:7</note> And Paul to the Ephesians: <note>original: "Non occidat sol super iracundiam uestram."</note> "Do not let the sun go down on your anger." <note>Ephesians 4:26</note> Wrath weakens a man. It makes him grow cruel. It corrupts good customs and shortens life.

# CANTO XV

To answer him with a calm face:
“What shall we do to those who wish us ill,
if he who loves us is condemned by us?”

<margin>Marito adira (The husband to the angry wife)</margin> LORD OF THE CITY <note>original: "SIR DELLA Villa"</note>. Here, the word "Sir" signifies lord, and "Villa" signifies city: specifically Athens, which the poet does not name directly but describes as the "city for whose name there was such strife and dissension and controversy among the gods," namely between Minerva and Neptune. Historians write that when Cecrops, the most ancient King of Athens, had restored the city, he pondered what to name it. At that time, two wonders appeared: in one place, a great abundance of water suddenly gushed out, and in the other, an olive tree grew. Because water is sacred to Neptune and the olive to Minerva, the king gathered the people to see which of these gods held more favor. Ultimately, all the women gave their favor to Minerva, and the men to Neptune. Because there was one more woman than there were men, Minerva—whom the Greeks call Athena—prevailed. Thus, the city was named Athens after her. Afterward, to appease Neptune, who in his rage had caused the sea to swell and flood the city, the Athenians issued a public decree that in the future, women would no longer gather to vote, no woman could bear the name Athena, and no daughter could take the name of her mother. Others say that in this contest, Neptune struck the earth with his staff, called a trident, and a horse immediately sprang forth; Minerva struck it with her spear, and an olive tree was born. Because the horse is a warlike animal and heralds war—as Virgil says: "Horses are armed for war; war is threatened by the herds" <note>original: "bello armantur equi: bellum per armenta minantur"; Virgil, Aeneid III.540</note>—and the olive signifies peace, it pleased them to name the city after the goddess who offered peace. The horse produced by Neptune is called by some poets Scythian, by others Syron, and by others Arion. AND WHENCE EVERY SCIENCE RADIATES. Dante had read in Cicero: "The inventors of all the good arts are at Athens" <note>original: "Omnium bonarum artium inuentrices athenis"</note>. Certainly, this city was the common home to all philosophers. Because this is a very well-known fact, I will not labor to prove it. We shall only say this in its praise: that Plato, that great philosopher, thanked God for five things: first, that he was born a human and not a brute; a male and not a female; a Greek and not a barbarian; an Athenian and not a Theban; and that he lived in the time of Socrates.

Then I saw people kindled in a fire of wrath,
with stones killing a youth with force,
shouting to one another: “Kill, kill!”
And I saw him bending down through death,
which already weighed him toward the earth,
but of his eyes he always made gates to heaven,
Praying to the high Lord in such a war,

with 그 look that unlocks pity.

Though he defended himself and affirmed that he saw the heavens open and Jesus standing at the right hand of God, nevertheless, out of envy, they dragged him out of the synagogue and stoned him. Thus, this great man, most unjustly treated, as noted in our prayer above, boldly sustained martyrdom and was the first martyr after the Passion of Christ. KINDLED In a fire of wrath: he rightly said "kindled," because wrath is a kindling of the blood around the heart. AND I SAW HIM Bending: as if weighed down by death. GATES to heaven: the eyes are the gates and windows of the soul.

When my soul returned outward

My leader, who could see me
acting like a man who rouses himself from sleep,

Whoever wishes to purge themselves of wrath should have these thoughts fixed in their mind. THEN THERE APPEARED TO ME another <note>original: "INDE MAPPA Rue unaltra"</note>. This was the wife of Pisistratus <note>The ruler of Athens mentioned in the previous column</note>, speaking with those waters—with those tears—distilled by grief. Then the poet sets down the words the woman used to kindle her husband’s anger.

This is the third example <note>Saint Stephen</note>, which can call one back from wrath and reduce every inflamed heart to a state of peace: considering that Stephen the Protomartyr <note>The "first martyr"</note>, although he was stoned with great injustice—and not only died wrongly, but died cruelly—nevertheless prayed for those who killed him. Stephen, as told in the Acts of the Apostles, was full of grace and strength after the death of Christ and performed signs and miracles in Jerusalem. But when certain men of the synagogue could not resist him in disputation, they brought in false witnesses to accuse him of being against God and Moses. To this accusation, although he responded sharply and with true wisdom, nevertheless, out of envy, they dragged him out and stoned him.

The poet continues by showing that after this ecstasy and fixed imagination, his soul—which had been entirely gathered into itself—returned "outward," that is, it turned back to the things which were real outside of itself. This is nothing other than returning to the consideration of external things. AND I RECOGNIZED my not-false errors. For upon emerging from that fixed imagination, he recognized that his soul had been "erring," that is, wandering through true things. "Error" in Latin signifies the progress of going without a fixed end. MY LEADER. Virgil had seen him walking totteringly and vacillating, that is, reeling and stumbling as one does when oppressed by sleep or drunkenness. And now he lightly...

when my legs were so taken from me.
And he: "If you had a hundred masks
upon your face, your thoughts
would not be closed to me, however small.
What you saw was so that you do not refuse
to open your heart to the waters of peace,
which are poured out from the eternal fountain.
I did not ask 'What is wrong?' for the reason
one asks who looks only with the eye that does not see
when the body lies lifeless;
But I asked to give strength to your feet;
thus must the slow and sluggish be prodded
to use their wakefulness when it returns."

**I asked.** I, Virgil, did not ask you, Dante, for the same reason that one asks who looks only with the physical eye—which cannot see after death when the body lies lifeless, meaning without a soul. The meaning is that he who looks only with the physical eye cannot see the thoughts of the heart. Therefore, such a person asks in order to know. But I did not ask to know; I asked to give strength to your feet—that is, to urge you on. It is proper to prod <note>The Italian "frugare" suggests prodding or poking, like a drover with an ox.</note> those who are slow, just as one prods an ox to make it move. **TO USE THEIR WAKEFULNESS when it returns:** he says this as if to say: "You have been as if asleep in this vision of yours; now, being excited and awake, use your wakefulness"—that is, spend and dispense your time well while you are awake, and do not waste it. In short, because the precept of Sallust is excellent: "For there is need of deliberation before beginning, and when you have deliberated, there is need of timely action." <note>original: "Nam et antea consulto: et ubi consulueris mature: facto opus est." A quote from the Roman historian Sallust's 'The Conspiracy of Catiline'.</note> This shows that since he has received excellent counsel through the vision, he must now fulfill it with speed and put it into execution.

---

**We went toward evening.** That is, toward the west. For just as the eastern parts are called "matutine" (morning) because the dawn appears there—which the Latins call *Matuta*—so the western parts are called "vespro" (evening), because the evening star, the planet Venus, often appears there in the evening. And they walked attentively, looking as far ahead as their eyes could reach against the late rays—that is, the rays of the evening sun. And the further they went...

We were going toward the evening, attentive,
looking as far as our eyes could reach
against the late and shining rays.
And behold, little by little, a smoke arose
toward us, dark as the night;
nor was there any place to escape from it.
This took from us our sight and the pure air.

...he grieves for his sin and seeks to leave it by following reason, just as the poet feigns to have followed Virgil. Certainly, it is no small stimulus to the soul to recognize that one has sinned and abandoned virtue; for the one induces repentance and hatred of vice, while the other induces love and desire for virtue. And this satisfies the requirement of punishment for those who are saved, as it says in the Gospel: "I desire not the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live." <note>original: "Nolo mortem peccatoris: sed ut conuertatur et uiuat." A paraphrase of Ezekiel 18:23, often used in liturgy.</note> Because of this, the proud man humbles himself under the weight. The envious man sews his eyes shut so as not to see. And the wrathful man recognizes his own blindness.

<column-break/>

...seemed as if he were waking up; Virgil asks why he has gone more than half a league in that manner. And Dante prepares to answer him. But Virgil interrupts his words, saying that even if he wanted to hide himself with a hundred masks <note>original: "larue" – masks or ghosts.</note>, he could not hide even one of his smallest thoughts. This is most true, because the senses and the lower reason cannot think of anything that the higher reason does not perceive. Therefore, Virgil does not ask to know, but to have the opportunity to excite and urge him, and to remove all sluggishness from him. **WHAT YOU SAW.** This vision came to you so that you would not refuse to open your heart to the waters of peace—that is, so you would wish to extinguish with the water of peace the fire that wrath has kindled in the heart. For if wrath is fire, then charity, which extinguishes wrath, will be water, which comes from the fountain of God. For God is charity; and he who dwells in charity dwells in God, and God in him. **I DID NOT ASK.**

...the further they went, the closer they came to a mist darker than the night, which occupied that part of the circle so completely that whoever wished to pass through could not avoid it. This mist took from Dante his eyes—that is, the faculty of sight—and took away the pure air, without which one cannot see. The poet therefore posits that in this darkness the souls of the wrathful are purged, because they must recognize that the fury of wrath blinds the mind and removes the light of reason, whereby the mind remains in darkness. Therefore, when a man is in wrath...

<summary>Virgil rouses Dante from his ecstatic visions of patience, explaining that he perceives Dante's thoughts and urges him toward action. As they proceed west, they encounter a thick, blinding smoke that signifies the spiritual darkness caused by the sin of Wrath.</summary>

->PURGATORIO<-
<margin>ff iiii</margin>

### CANTO XVI OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE.

**T**he poet does not change the subject matter in this sixteenth canto. But continuing on, he describes the obscurity of the fog into which he entered, and the souls who were being purged within it. **DARKNESS OF NIGHT**. Dante had been in the infernal shadows during the time of night, and in places where no planet is seen in the sky, but everything is covered by clouds, whereby the sky is as "poor" as it can be. And yet...

<image-desc>A large decorative illuminated initial 'B' at the start of the poetic text, set against a background of blue, red, and gold with leafy green flourishes inside the letter's loops.</image-desc>

**B**lackness of hell and of a night deprived
of every planet under a poor sky,
as much as it can be darkened by clouds,
did not make for my face so thick a veil
as that smoke which covered us there,
nor to the touch a texture so harsh:
that the eye could not endure to stay open;
wherefore my wise and faithful escort
drew near me and offered me his shoulder.
Just as a blind man goes behind his guide
so as not to lose his way and not to bump
into something that might hurt or perhaps kill him,
so I went through that bitter and foul air,
listening to my leader, who was saying:
"Just take care that you are not severed from me."

<column-break/>

...no, such darkness did not create so thick a veil over his eyes as the present smoke. Through these words, he denotes that no sin induces so much blindness of the mind as **Wrath**. This veil and covering of the eyes had two inconveniences: first, because it was thick, it could not be <term>diaphanous</term> <note>Transparent or translucent.</note> and clear in a way that the sight could pass through it, as one might pass through a thin veil. Furthermore, it was of "harsh hairs" <note>The original Italian "aspro pelo" refers to the stinging, abrasive quality of the smoke, likened to a coarse, irritating fabric.</note> which pricked the eyes of anyone who held them open. How then could he see anything, having a thick veil over his eyes and being forced to keep them closed? And certainly, wrath altogether blinds the mind. And the stings that infuriate us therein to take revenge do not allow us to open the eyes of the mind to consider reason. **WHEREFORE MY WISE AND FAITHFUL ESCORT**. Dante cannot exit such smoke unless he follows Virgil, because the <term>senses and appetite</term> <note>In medieval philosophy, "appetite" refers to our emotional desires and impulses.</note> cannot emerge from the blindness of wrath unless they take **Reason** as their guide. **WISE AND FAITHFUL**. These two things are sought in whoever gives us counsel: first, learning and prudence, through which he "knows" (is wise); then, faith, through which he desires to rule us well. **DREW NEAR ME**: when reason draws near to the appetite, the appetite cannot err. **AND OFFERED ME HIS SHOULDER**: he gave me his shoulder so that, by leaning on him who could see, I would not strike anything. By "shoulder," understand **Fortitude**. Because just as the shoulders and the back sustain every weight, so fortitude defends us so that wrath does not overcome us. And certainly, reason corroborates and strengthens the appetite to resist wrath. **WATCH THAT YOU ARE NOT SEVERED FROM ME**. The appetite is admonished by reason to take care not to be "severed"—that is, separated—from reason. For whenever one's desire becomes separated from reason, it becomes infinite and bestial.

<summary>Dante enters the third terrace of Purgatory, where a thick, stinging smoke blinds those purging the sin of Wrath. The commentary explains that Virgil represents Reason, whose "shoulder" of Fortitude must guide the human impulse to prevent it from falling into bestial error.</summary>
