PURGATORIO

The souls are a sink of filth: those who were purging wrath were praying for peace and for mercy, which are the opposites of wrath—a sin that always seeks war and vengeance. And they said:
> Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, have mercy on us <note>original: "Agnus dei: qui tollis peccata mundi miserere nobis"</note>; and thus they prayed for mercy. And "Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, grant us peace" <note>original: "dona nobis pacem"</note>; praying in this manner for peace.

->**ONE WORD WAS IN ALL AND ONE MELODY**<-

I heard voices, and each one seemed
to pray for peace and for mercy
to the Lamb of God who takes away sins.
"Lamb of God" <note>original: "Agnus dei"</note> was their opening;
one word was in all and one melody,
so that there seemed to be total harmony among them.
"What spirits are these, Master, that I hear?"
I said; and he to me: "You perceive the truth;
they go about loosening the knot of wrath."
"Now, who are you that pierces our smoke,
and speaks of us just as if you still
divided time by <term>calends</term>?" <note>The first day of the Roman month; here it implies being alive and subject to time.</note>
Thus it was said by a single voice;
wherefore my master said: "Respond,
and ask if one goes upward from here."
And I: "O creature, who cleanses yourself
to return beautiful to Him who made you,
you shall hear a marvel if you follow me."

<column-break/>

They all said the same words and in the same melody, which demonstrates that there is supreme harmony among them; and with this, they loosen the "knot of wrath," which is entirely discord. **DIVIDED TIME BY CALENDS**. That is, as if you were still alive. For the souls stripped of the body, because they are immortal, do not feel the passage of time. But we, who are living, divide time into years, months, days, hours, and minutes. And <term>calends</term> are what the first days of the month are called in Latin. And because it seems to me a thing not useless, and quite pleasant to understand precisely the days of the month noted by the ancients, we will repeat from a bit further back with what order and number of days the ancients marked their years. Among all men, therefore, the Egyptians had, in the earliest times, the perfect and absolute year. Because they were skilled in astronomy, they saw that after 365 days and a quarter of a day have passed, the sun has traveled through the entire circle of the zodiac and returns to the first degree of Aries, from where it first departed. For this reason, they had their year of twelve months. In this distribution of 360 days, they gave thirty to each month. Then they placed the five remaining days between August and September;

---

and every four years they counted 366 days in one year to consume that fourth part of a day that remained every year. After them, the Greeks had various customs. Those of Arcadia made years of three months. The Arcananians made them of six. Others made them of 354 days. Romulus, among the Romans, ordered ten months, beginning the month on the first day that the new moon was seen. And he instituted that the <term>minor pontiff</term> <note>A lesser priest in the Roman college of pontiffs.</note>, having seen the new moon, should announce it to another priest called the <term>sacrificial king</term> <note>Latin: "rex sacrificulus"; a high-ranking priest.</note>, and both of these would convoke the people on the Capitoline Hill and announce how many days remained until the <term>Nones</term> <note>The 5th or 7th day of the Roman month.</note>. Therefore, they called this first day of the month the "calends" from that invocation of the people, because *calare* means "to call" and "to convoke." And because it happens for certain reasons that the moon is not always seen at the same time, it occurred that in the first year, some months were of thirty days, and some were of thirty-one. This order they later observed in the following years: there were six months of 30 days—April, June, August, September, November, and December. The other four were of 31. The beginning of the year was March, named thus after Mars, whom Romulus claimed was his father. And in this month, the <term>Vestal Virgins</term> <note>Priestesses of the goddess Vesta who tended the sacred fire.</note> renewed the fire on the altar of Vesta. Salaries were paid. Taxes were allocated. And the matrons held banquets for the servants to have them more prompt as servants for the rest of the year. The second month they called April from Venus <note>original: "da Venere"</note>, who was the mother of Aeneas, from whom the Romans had their origin. Because in Greek *aphrodite* means Venus. Others say that Romulus, having named the first month after Mars, the killer of men (because it is the planet signifying wars, and called *Andriphonte*—that is, "homicide"—by Homer), wished the second to have its name from Venus, a benevolent planet apt for procreating and for mitigating the malignancy of Mars. Whence we see that nature has ordained that even in the twelve signs of the zodiac, after Aries (the domicile of Mars), follows Taurus (the domicile of Venus). And similarly, before the Scorpio of Mars is the Libra of Venus, so that with the domiciles of the benign Venus, the Martial fury might be tempered. Others say that the month is not called *Haprile* from Venus, but *Aprile* without the "h," because in that month the earth, previously frozen and restricted by the cold, "opens" <note>Italian: "sapre" / Latin: "aperire"</note> to produce new flowers and leaves. Whence the Athenians call it *Anthesterion*, as if "powerful in flowers," because then everything flourishes. Then Romulus, having divided the people into two parts—the *maiores* (that is, the elders) and the *iuniores* (that is, the youth)—the third month was called May <note>Maggio</note> after the elders. And the fourth was called June <note>Giugno</note> after the youth. The other months were named by number; after June, the fourth month, follows Quintile (fifth), Sextile (sixth), September, October, November, and December. But later, Gaius Julius Caesar wished that Quintile be called July <note>Iulio</note> after himself; and Augustus instituted that Sextile be named August. This, then, was the first year composed of ten months and 304 days. This number did not agree with either the solar or the lunar course. Whence often summer came in the...

# CANTO XVI

ff v

...winter, or winter in the summer. Because Numa Pompilius, the second King and successor of Romulus—either through his own natural prudence or by following Greek learning—added fifty days to the number already established. He made the year consist of three hundred and sixty-four days and added two equal months of twenty-nine days each, taking those fifty added days and six days from six other months that were previously thirty days long. The first of these two months he called January after Janus, who is the god of the beginnings of things, and he willed that it should be the start of the year. The second he called February after Februus, the god of <term>purgations</term> <note>original: "purgationi"</note>; hence *februa* signifies purgation. Afterward, understanding that odd numbers are more perfect than even ones, he added one day to January. From this, two things resulted: first, that the year had an entirely odd number of days, namely three hundred and fifty-five. Second, that all the days of the months were in odd numbers—there being four months of thirty-one days and seven of twenty-nine. He left February with an even number, smaller than the others, because it was consecrated to the infernal gods; since purgative sacrifices were made in that month for the souls of the dead, he judged it should have both a smaller and an even number, which is less perfect.

Once Numa had reduced the year to this form, though it was not yet perfect because it did not align with the solar course (which is three hundred and sixty-five days and six hours), he followed the custom of the Greeks. Since they had eleven extra days each year, they <term>intercalated</term> <note>To insert days into a calendar to keep it aligned with the seasons.</note> ninety days every eighth year. However, an error arose because of that extra day added by Numa. Therefore, it was instituted that every twenty-fourth year—which was the third intercalation—one should interpose not ninety, but sixty-six days. In this way, the Roman year moved in step with the Greek. Nevertheless, it is uncertain who first discovered this method of intercalating days in Rome. Marcus Licinius attributes it to Romulus; Valerius Antias to Numa; Junius to King Servius Tullius; and Tuditanus to the ten men of the Law of the Twelve Tables. But in the process of time, it happened that this intercalation was sometimes omitted due to some religious reason, or sometimes performed ahead of time. Furthermore, no account was taken of the six hours that were left over each year; thus, in three intercalations, six days were lost. 

But Gaius Julius Caesar, in his third consulate, deliberating to correct these errors, first consumed all the lost days and made that year four hundred and forty-three days long. Afterward, he ordered that the year should be three hundred and sixty-six days <note>Landino likely means 365, with the leap year being 366.</note> and a quarter of a day. He reduced the months to the number they are at present, and every four years he intercalated one day to consume the four sets of six hours that remain each year. He placed that day in the month of February after the twenty-third day, and ordained that the twenty-fourth day should be counted twice. Because that day in Latin is called the <term>calends</term>, and they say "twice" <note>original: "bis"</note> for the "sixth" <note>original: "sexto"</note>, they call it <term>bissextile</term> <note>original: "bis fexto"</note>. Furthermore, of all the days of the month, only three had specific names. The first name they called <term>calends</term>, which is the first day. The second they called <term>nones</term>; in four months (March, May, July, and October) it was the seventh day of the month, and in the others, the fifth. Then, eight days after the nones were the <term>ides</term>. Thus, in those four months, they were on the fifteenth, and in the others, on the thirteenth day of the month. Let this be sufficient for the explanation of this passage. **YOU SHALL HEAR A MARVEL.** Because it will make you marvel to hear that I am alive. **IF YOU FOLLOW ME**: if you follow behind me.

"I will follow you as far as I am permitted,"
he replied; "and if the smoke does not let us see,
hearing shall keep us joined in its stead."
Then I began: "With that bandage
which death dissolves I go upward,
and I came here through the anguish of hell.
And if God has so enclosed me in His grace,
that He wills that I should see His court
in a manner entirely outside modern use,
do not conceal from me who you were before death,
but tell me, and tell me if I am on the right path to the pass;
and let your words be our guides."
"I was a Lombard, and I was called Marco;
I knew the world, and I practiced 그at worth
at which everyone has now unbent their bow.
To mount upward, you are going the right way,"
he thus replied; and added, "I pray you
that you pray for me when you are above."

<column-break/>

The soul responds: *I will follow you as far as I am permitted* <note>original: "quanto mi lece"</note>, that is, as is allowed to me. For he was not allowed to follow him except as far as the smoke reached, which he could not leave until he was purged. And if the smoke does not let us see one another, and because of this we might lose our way as we walk, *hearing*—by speaking together—will serve to keep us from getting lost. **IN ITS STEAD**: in that exchange. **THEN I BEGAN** to speak and said: I am going upward toward heaven with that *bandage* that death dissolves and corrupts. This is the body, which is corrupted by death and is the "bandage" of the soul because it binds the soul within itself. Thus the Greeks call the body *demas* <note>original: "demas"</note>, as if it were the bond of the soul, because *deo* <note>original: "deo"</note> signifies "to bind." **AND IF GOD HAS ENCLOSED ME IN HIS GRACE.** He shows that since God has so enclosed him within His grace that He has granted him—outside of modern and customary usage—to go to heaven with his body, the spirit should not hide who he was or what he is named. The grace that the poet feigns to have received—to ascend to heaven while alive—is allegorically the ability to conquer the flatteries and enticements of vices, to enter into the purgatorial virtues, and with those to finally reach the virtues of the soul already purged, where one is to enjoy the divine sight. **I WAS A LOMBARD:**

<header>PURGATORIO</header>

...and I was called Marco. Marco was a Venetian gentleman, well-practiced in military discipline, liberal, and an enemy of idleness and the life of sluggards. But he was prone to anger, and especially to that indignation which usually dwells in a noble soul. Limofese relates of him that while he was in prison and burdened by a <term>ransom</term> <note>original: "taglia", the price set for a prisoner's release</note> that was impossible for him to pay, he wrote a letter to Riccardo da Camino, the Lord of Treviso and his old friend, begging him not to let him rot in jail. Sir Riccardo arranged with many lords of Lombardy that each should contribute whatever portion of the ransom they pleased. Marco heard of this and, moved by indignation, wrote back to Riccardo saying he would rather die than remain obligated to so many people. Riccardo was ashamed by this and paid the entire ransom out of his own money. This Marco also prophesied to Count Ugolino, the tyrant of Pisa, the wrath that God was conceiving toward him. He kept company with many lords, and studied nothing more than how to reconcile and restore friendships. **I KNEW THE WORLD**: I was expert in civil and active matters, which are called "worldly" because they are momentary and transitory—not because they cannot or should not be governed virtuously through moral virtues. Great merit is acquired before God and men by those who exert themselves and labor to establish peace and tranquility, which is an office of charity—a virtue required above all others. **AND THAT WORTH I USED**: those moral virtues and that liberality, from which worth every man now departs and uses no longer.

---

And I to him: "By my faith I bind myself
To do what you ask of me; but I am bursting
Within a doubt, if I do not explain it.
First it was simple, and now it is made double
By your statement, which makes certain for me,
Here and elsewhere, that with which I couple it.
The world is indeed thus, entirely a desert
Of every virtue, as you sound to me,
And pregnant and covered with malice.
But I pray that you point out the cause to me,
So that I may see it and show it to others;
For one places it in the heavens, and one here below."

<column-break/>

**P**romises him his faith to pray for him, and then begs him to resolve a doubt in which he says he is **bursting** <note>original: "scoppiare", meaning to crack or explode</note>. And truly, one who is entangled in a doubt and cannot unravel himself, the more he searches, the more he becomes entangled; he is like one who is so constricted that he cannot endure without bursting. **IF I DO NOT EXPLAIN IT**: if I do not unfold myself, that is, if I do not disentangle myself. **FIRST it was simple and now it is made DOUBLE**: he had heard this same sentiment above from Guido del Duca when he spoke of the inhabitants near the Arno, where the doubt was single. Now, hearing it from Marco, it becomes double. **BUT I PRAY THAT YOU POINT IT OUT TO ME**: that is, show me clearly, like one who points with a finger. The **world**, meaning all the humans inhabiting the world, is not only a desert and destitute of every virtue, but is also filled with every malice. **FOR ONE PLACES IT IN THE HEAVENS AND ONE HERE BELOW**: because some wish the cause of our movements to be from the influence of the heavens, and some place it down here—that is, in us and in our **free will** <note>original: "libero arbitrio"</note>.

**M**arco, being full of charity and averse to the state of the human generation, is moved to compassion—like a second Heraclitus <note>Heraclitus was a Greek philosopher known for weeping over the folly and ignorance of mankind.</note>—over the blindness and ignorance found in many men who persuade themselves that the influence of the stars and the heavens has such power over us that we are necessitated to do everything toward which we incline, and that we can do nothing without their movements. This opinion is not only heretical and rejected by Christians with the truest and most manifest reasons, but it is also contrary to the judgment of all philosophers who are authors and approvers of moral virtues and of political and civil life. These philosophers maintain that both good and evil are in our power, and no work is virtuous or vicious if it is not voluntary and by our own choice. Plato affirms that since the human soul was created immediately by God without intermediary causes, it is above the heavens. And because a superior thing cannot be under an inferior one, it follows that no celestial influence can constrain the soul either to vice or to virtue, as we have demonstrated more extensively above. But while the soul is in the body and uses the instruments of the body—over which the heavens do have dominion—the soul can be inclined by this accident, but not necessitated or forced. Marco, grieving, therefore sighed and, sighing, said **Alas!** <note>original: "hui", a Latinate exclamation of grief</note>, which is a word signifying sorrow. **THE WORLD**...

<sig>v ii</sig>
<meta>catchword: THE WORLD</meta>

---

A deep sigh, which grief wrung into "Alas!"
He sent forth first, and then began: "Brother,
The world is blind, and you indeed come from it.
You who are living refer every reason
Only up to the heavens, as if they
Moved everything with them by necessity.
If it were so, <term>Free Will</term> would be destroyed
Within you, and it would not be justice
To have joy for good, and mourning for evil.
The heavens initiate your movements;
I do not say all, but suppose I did say it,
Light is given to you for both good and evil,
And a free will, which, if it fatigues itself
In its first battles with the heavens, endures..."

<column-break/>

...heretical, and refuted with the truest and most manifest reasons by Christians. But it is also contrary to the opinion of all philosophers, authors, and approvers of the moral virtues and of political and civic life, who maintain that both good and evil are in our power, and no act is virtuous or vicious if it is not voluntary and by our own choice. Plato affirms that because the human soul was created immediately by God without intermediary causes, it is above the heavens. And because the superior thing cannot be under the inferior, it follows that no celestial influence can constrain the soul toward either vice or virtue, as we have demonstrated more extensively above. But while the soul is in the body and uses the instruments of the body (over which the heavens have dominion), the soul can be inclined by this circumstance, but not necessitated or forced. Marco, grieving therefore, sighed, and sighing said "Alas!" <note>original: "hui"</note>, which is a voice signifying sorrow. **THE WORLD**...

<summary>In this passage, Dante speaks with Marco Lombardo about the corruption of the world and the source of evil. Marco refutes the idea of astrological determinism, arguing instead for the existence of Free Will and human responsibility.</summary>

This page transitions into the core philosophical debate of the Canto: whether human actions are determined by the stars (astrology) or by free will.</meta>

<header>CANTO XVI</header>

then it conquers everything, if it is well-nourished
**To a greater force and a greater nature**
you lie free; and that creates
the mind which the heavens do not have in their care.
Therefore, if the present world goes astray,
in you is the cause, in you it is sought,
and I will now be a true scout for you.

**It comes from the hand of Him who cherishes it**
before it exists, in the likeness of a little girl
who, weeping and laughing, plays like a child:
The simple little soul, which knows nothing
except that, moved by a joyful Maker,
it willingly turns to what amuses it.
Of a small good, it first tastes the flavor;
there it is deceived, and runs after it,
if a guide or curb does not turn its love.
Therefore it was necessary to set law as a curb;
it was necessary to have a king who could discern
at least the tower of the true city.

<column-break/>

The world is blind: because it falls into the greatest darkness of ignorance when it believes that secondary causes—which are the celestial influences—can rule over our soul. **AND YOU COME RIGHTLY FROM HIM**: since you hold that same opinion: **YOU WHO LIVE**. This is the reason that shows men to be blind: since they attribute every cause to the heavens; that is, they attribute every cause of our operations to celestial influence, as if the heavens by necessity pushed us to act or not act, and to do either evil or good according to the nature of such an influence, and we could not defend ourselves against it. If this were so, **free will** would be extinguished in us. This is something not only theologians posit, but all the most excellent philosophers confess. Nor would there be **virtue**—which is an <term>elective habit</term> <note>a disposition to choose the good</note>—if it were not in our power to be able to choose between good and evil.

**THE HEAVENS INITIATE YOUR MOVEMENTS**. According to theologians, philosophers, and astrologers, the celestial bodies have no influence that necessitates the rational soul in its intellect, nor the will, nor free will; as Ptolemy demonstrates in the *Centiloquium* <note>a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms</note>, and Aristotle in the first book of *On Interpretation* <note>original: "iherminias"</note>. And the <term>Aquinate</term> <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> in his work *Against the Gentiles* affirms, with the authority of Aristotle in the third book of *On the Soul*, that the heavens are not the cause of our wills and choices directly. But they can make an impression on the "first movements" of the soul, which we can resist with reason and with free will—through which, if we choose well, we deserve merit, and if poorly, we deserve blame. This merit is not found in the first movements, because they are not in our power. But the stars influence bodily movements, which can incline the soul, but not necessitate it.

Mars inflames <term>choler</term> <note>the humor associated with anger</note> toward wrath, and this moves the soul. But the soul, through its free will, can resist. Similarly, the sun, along with human seed, generates a human being, but it cannot infuse the rational soul, which comes solely from God without intermediary; for the soul is more noble than the entire sensible world, and the stars are merely physical. Therefore, the heavens do not necessitate the soul. If they did, free will would perish. In short, first there is **appetite** in us, and then the **rational will**. Appetite has its first movement and inclination from the external constellation. The will has its internal movement and inclination from reason. And this comes to pass by means of free will. And this second will is what makes us deserve merit or blame.

**BUT SUPPOSE I SHOULD SAY**: even if all our inclinations and movements of the soul proceeded from the heavens, nonetheless, one thing is given to you: that is, **reason** and **intellect** are given to you, with which you know good and virtue, and evil and vice. And certainly free will is in you, and it is in your power to choose what you wish. Therefore, if one exerts effort to resist those first movements that the heavens begin, and if it **endures**—that is, if it resists in those first battles between the inclination given by the heavens and reason (which, knowing that thing to be evil, desires to flee it)—**THEN IT CONQUERS EVERYTHING**. For if it resists the first impulse, it becomes temperate and conquers.

**TO A GREATER FORCE** and to a greater nature: the human soul is subject not only to God—who is a greater force and a greater nature than the secondary causes—but even though it is created, it remains free from God. **AND THAT** greater force **CREATES** the human mind, which the heavens do not have in their care. For God does not create the soul through secondary causes, but creates it immediately. Therefore, he concludes that **IF THE PRESENT WORLD**—that is, the false opinions and the depraved and corrupt appetites you have toward virtue because of the contagion the body gives the soul—**MISLEADS YOU**, leading you away from the right path and from reason, **THE CAUSE IS IN YOU**, since you have free will. **IN YOU IT IS SOUGHT** <note>original: "scheggia"</note>: let it be searched for and found within yourselves.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial L, approximately six lines high, featuring classical architectural motifs and leafy scrolls.</image-desc>

The human soul, of which we have spoken, **COMES FROM THE HAND**. It is produced by the power **OF HIM**: that is, God, which God **CHERISHES**: He considers it with pleasure, because as He says in Genesis:
-> <note>original: "Viditque deus omnia que fecerat: et erant ualde bona"</note> <-
-> "And God saw everything that He had made, and they were very good." <-

For God, in His eternity, sees whatever He must subsequently produce in time. I say, therefore, that the human soul comes from the hand of God; that is, it is created by Him. And not without cause did he say it "comes forth," because it departs having been created, not bound in a form so that it cannot go where it wishes, but with free will to be able to return or not return. **IN THE LIKENESS**: in the similarity of a little girl who **PLAYS LIKE A CHILD**: that is, she demonstrates her small and tender age, now crying and now laughing. For just as the tiny little girl...

It emphasizes that the moral failings of the world stem from human choices rather than divine or astrological necessity.</summary>

# PURGATORIO CANTO XVI

...without prudence, moved by appetite and not by reason, for a small thing it cries and laughs. And it almost shows that our soul is naturally disposed to passions and disturbances. **THE SIMPLE LITTLE SOUL**; which knows nothing; According to the opinion of Aristotle <note>The Greek philosopher Aristotle (384–322 BC) was the primary authority on science and logic in Dante's time.</note>, who argues that it is like a blank tablet <note>This refers to the concept of the *tabula rasa*, the idea that the mind is born as a blank slate without innate ideas.</note> ready to receive whatever is impressed upon it. **EXCEPT THAT, MOVED BY A JOYFUL** Maker, it willingly turns to what amuses it. It is innate in every created thing to have the greatest desire to return to its principle, which is its creator, the supreme good. Therefore our soul, created by God—in whom, because He is the supreme good, there is supreme joy—naturally desires to be joined with God himself. But greedy and desirous of this supreme good, it often deceives itself; because having newly arrived in the body, it cannot yet exercise reason, which could know the true good and discern it from the false. It therefore uses only the senses and the appetite, with which it cannot taste the flavor of the supreme good, which is God; but it tastes the flavor of a small good, that is, of temporal goods, and in those it deceives itself. For the senses, enticed by the pleasures and displeasures of earthly things, judge that to be supreme which is either not a good at all or a very small good. Aristotle writes most correctly in the third book *On the Soul*: *The good of the intellect is the ultimate happiness* <note>original: "Bonum intellectus est ultima beatitudo"</note>. And if the good of the intellect is the ultimate happiness, it follows that it is God. Therefore our intellect seeks this, if it is not deceived in its choosing by sense and appetite. I know that to explain this passage it would be useful to refer to many things which I recounted in the second book of our *Camaldolese Disputations* <note>Landino refers here to his own philosophical work, the *Disputationes Camaldulenses* (c. 1472), where he discusses the active versus the contemplative life.</note>, but such a great volume does not permit me to be too prolix in every detail. **OF A SMALL** good: reason not yet being awakened, it follows the senses, which falsely judge that earthly goods, where there is some amusement, are the supreme good. **IF A GUIDE**; if our intellect awakens; if the doctrine or precepts of a more learned man admonish us; if the grace of God illuminates us. **OR A CURB**, either divine or human law. **DOES NOT TURN** its love; it does not turn back the love that it has placed in earthly and fleeting things toward the celestial and supreme good. **WHENCE IT WAS NECESSARY** to set law as a curb: it was a necessity that men, letting themselves be carried away by appetite and not governing themselves according to reason, should have their pride, ambition, avarice, and lust restrained by laws, so that those who did not abstain from evil deeds for the love of virtue would abstain out of fear of punishment. *For the wicked hate to sin for fear of punishment* <note>original: "Nam oderunt peccare mali formidine pene" — a quote from Horace's *Epistles*.</note>, as Horace learnedly writes. **IT WAS NECESSARY** to have a king. It is not enough to have laws if there is no King, or prince, or magistrate to defend them and make them observed. And this person must be of such a life, doctrine, and prudence that, if he does not know the true city of eternal life, at least he discerns the tower—that is, the guardianship of it—which is justice.

Certainly there are laws. But there is no one who puts their hand to them. For natural law is innate in our minds, but concupiscence <term>concupiscence: strong sensory desire, often specifically referring to lust or greed that overwhelms reason</term> conquers reason. Nor was there ever a nation or religion that had divine and human laws as perfect as the Christian. The Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> had Lycurgus; the Athenians had Draco and Solon; the Cretans had Minos—whose laws were much regulated toward justice, as much as human prudence could allow. 

<margin>
But Christian laws have their origin in divine truth. But what does it profit if the administrators of such laws are the first to break them? **THEREFORE WHO PUTS THEIR HAND** to them: who rules them? No one. For neither do the Popes put their hand to ecclesiastical laws, nor do princes and lay magistrates defend temporal ones. **PUT THEIR HAND**: i.e., they act according to the laws. For no one can correct others if he does not first correct himself. **THE SHEPHERD**: he rightly calls every prince a shepherd, according to what we have said in another place. **CAN RUMINATE** but does not have cloven hooves. One reads in Leviticus that God commanded Moses that they should eat the meat of every animal that had cloven hooves and ruminated.
</margin>

> Laws there are, but who puts their hand to them? /
> None, because the shepherd who goes before /
> can ruminate, but has not cloven hooves. /
> Because the people, who see their guide /
> strike only at that good for which they are greedy, /
> feed on that and ask for nothing more. /
> Well can you see that bad leadership /
> is the cause that the world is made wicked, /
> and not nature that is corrupt in you.

...of every animal that had cloven hooves and ruminated. Therefore one of the two is not enough. And for this reason, the meat of the pig and the camel was not permitted, because they do not ruminate, although they have cloven hooves. These two things are necessary for whoever governs. And by ruminating we mean to diligently examine and consult in whatever thing they have to do, in the likeness of the ox and the sheep, which swallow grass without chewing it, and then, searching for it with diligence, return it to the mouth and chew it part by part, "ruminating." Whence it is a Florentine proverb: "He has ruminated well on this thing," meaning well-considered and thought out. Therefore, first, it is necessary that every governor, whether cleric or layman, consider well and understand what he has to do. Then he places cloven hooves for "discretion" <note>In this context, discretion means the ability to distinguish and separate different things.</note>, which distinguishes temporal things from spiritual things. And the prince must not confuse them together. But the prelate should care for the spiritual, and the prince for the temporal. These two principles, as is written in the decrees, are from Christ, as the mediator between God and man. Because Christ did certain things as emperor...

It is a marvel how much the example of princes—both good and bad—can influence those who must obey them. Therefore the poet concludes that seeing the people and the shepherds (who ought to guide them toward a righteous end) direct themselves toward worldly things, they too give themselves over to those things, because the appetite sees... Thus, the people being prone to such things and finding a guide [who leads them there], it is inevitable that they fall into a precipice. **YOU WELL WISH** to see. He concludes that bad conduct—that is, bad leadership—is the cause that the world (meaning mankind) is made wicked, and not nature.

He praises the time in which the Christian republic was ruled by the Pope in spiritual matters and by the Emperor in temporal matters, because each one cared for the part committed to him; and attending to only one thing, he could perform it with greater diligence. **ROME WAS ACCUSTOMED**: the Christian republic, of which Rome is the head.

*Because, being joined, the one does not fear the other;*
*if you do not believe me, look at the ear of grain,*

two suns: two principles: the Pope, Bishop of Rome, and the Emperor, King of the Romans. And one and the other road they made visible: just as the sun shows all the ways and regions of the world, so these princes showed one and the other road. That is, the Emperor made the road of the world visible; the Pontiff, that of God. **THE ONE THE OTHER** has extinguished. Because of the Emperor’s desire to occupy spiritual jurisdictions and the Pope’s to occupy temporal ones—as appears in many histories of both past and present centuries—both dignities have fallen into decline. And the sword is joined with the shepherd's crook. And being together, the one extinguishes the other; not because they are naturally contrary to one another, but because it is necessary that one fears the other. For the Emperor ought to punish with bodily penalty those who disturb the Christian republic, and the Pope with spiritual censures. Whence King David submitted himself to Nathan the prophet. **LOOK AT THE ear of grain**; as if to say, look at the fruit and the effect that is born from it. Because just as every plant of every grain is known by its seed, so every action is known by its fruit. Whence the Divine Truth says: *by their fruits you shall know them* <note>original: *a fructibus eorū cognoscetis eos*; Matthew 7:16.</note>.

# PURGATORIO

Parma: which was defended by the allies of the Church and besieged by Frederick <note>Frederick II (1194–1250), Holy Roman Emperor.</note>. The people of Parma, having reached a state of utter desperation and seeing that the Emperor held them in little regard, waited for him to go out hawking; they then assaulted and captured the great bastion he had built in the form of a city and named Victoria <note>Original: *Victoria*. Frederick intended this fortified camp to replace Parma after its fall.</note>. They seized all his baggage, including his jewels and his crown. He fled to Cremona, not without danger. The defeat occurred on the first day of February, 1248. The following year, his son Henry <note>Enzo of Sardinia, often called Arrigo in historical texts.</note> was captured by the Bolognese in the territory of Modena. Three years later, Frederick died. **NOW ONE MAY SAFELY** pass there. If there were anyone who felt ashamed to speak with such people—as happens to the wretched, who therefore flee inhabited places—he need not flee these lands, for there are no such people there. Or perhaps it is better to draw another meaning from this text: since he mentioned liberality <note>The medieval virtue of generosity and noble conduct.</note>, and the liberal invite passing strangers to their homes and almost pull them in by force. Often it happens that one traveling in a foreign land feels ashamed to go to the house of someone they do not know well, and they pass by with caution and almost in secret. Therefore, we shall say: now that there is no longer anyone courtly there, one can pass through safely without fearing anyone would shame them by speaking to them or offering hospitality. **THREE OLD MEN:** certainly there are three. That is, in all these lands, which used to abound with many high-minded and liberal men, there are now only three of such character. **IN WHOM:** in which three old men the ancient age **REBUKES:** reproaches the new. The meaning is that those three old men are an example by which one sees how much better the ancients were than the moderns. **AND IT SEEMS TO THEM LATE:** it seems to them that God delays too long in restoring them to a better life—that is, to eternal life. The meaning is that they desire to die. For just as the wicked fear death for fear of punishment, the good desire it because they hope to go to a better life and wish to be removed from the contagion of the wicked. **CURRADO DI PALAZZO.** He was a gentleman of Brescia; the chronicler from Imola <note>Benvenuto da Imola, a famous 14th-century commentator on Dante.</note> writes of hearing that while Currado held the standard of his people in battle, his hands were cut off, yet he embraced the standard with his arms and did not let go until he lost his life. Gherardo da Treviso of the Da Camino family, which often held the lordship in Treviso. This man, for his excellent counsel and virtue, was called the "Good Gherardo." Guido da Castello was from Reggio in Lombardy, of the noble family called "da Castello"; he was prudent, good, and a lover of the liberty in which Reggio flourished at that time, and he was a contemporary of Dante. **WHO IS NAMED FOR ME** in the French manner. The French call all Italians "Lombards." And such was the fame of his integrity and his life—clean of all fraud and entirely simple—that everywhere he was called "the simple Lombard." **FROM NOW ON** That the Church of Rome. He concludes that because the Shepherd <note>The Pope.</note> wishes to confound and mix within himself two regimes—the temporal and the spiritual—it is the cause of all evils.

> "O my Marco," I said, "you reason well;
> and now I discern why the sons of Levi
> were exempted from the inheritance.
> But who is that Gherardo who you say
> remains as a sample of the extinct folk,
> in reproach of this savage age?"
> "Either your speech deceives or tests me,"
> he answered me; "for speaking to me in Tuscan,
> it seems you know nothing of the good Gherardo.
> By no other surname do I know him,

> already whitening; and I must depart—
> the Angel is there—before he appears."
> Thus he turned back and would hear me no more.

<column-break/>

He approves of Marco’s judgment: that priests should not meddle in temporal matters. He produces as evidence the example of the Bible, where by the laws of Moses, the sons of Levi <note>The Levites, the priestly tribe of Israel.</note> (one of the sons of Jacob), because they were ordained for the priesthood and the administration of sacred and divine things, were deprived of temporal goods <note>Inheritance of land.</note> so that they would have no care other than for sacred things, living instead off the tithes. **EITHER YOUR** speech: as if to say, since you are Tuscan, it cannot be that you do not know the fame of such a man. Therefore, by denying you know him, either you deceive me by telling a lie, or you are testing me. But because it often happens that we do not know a man by his proper name, but rather by some surname or nickname, I do not know by what more famous thing I can name him for you than to say he was the father of Gaia. She, for being both very beautiful and very virtuous, was renowned throughout all Italy. **MAY GOD BE WITH YOU.** He takes his leave because they had traveled together so long that they had reached the place where the thick smoke ended, and the light of dawn was already

---

beginning to be seen. And he could not emerge from the darkness. He arranges the text: **SEE THE DAWN** which rays—that is, shines and casts its beams—already turning white. And I must depart before it "appears"—that is, before the light is fully seen. **THE ANGEL IS THERE:** as if to say, do not fear losing your way, for the Angel is there at the end of the smoke, and he will show it to you. The allegory of the Angel is already known, and the interpretation does not change: it denotes that at any entrance to a new stage of purgation, divine grace shows us the true way.

## CANTO XVII OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE.

In this seventeenth canto, our author emerges from the circle of wrath and ascends to the fourth ledge, where <term>sloth</term> <note>Original: *laccidia*. In medieval theology, sloth or *acedia* was a spiritual apathy or "tepid" love for the good.</note> is punished. But first, he imagines certain visions appearing to him; after these depart, he finds the angel who leads him to the stairway of the fourth ledge. **REMEMBER, READER:** if ever in the mountains—in any very high mountain. **Alps** is the proper name for the mountains that divide Italy from France; however, in the Tuscan language, though not in Latin, all other high mountains are called "Alps." **A FOG CAUGHT YOU:** a very thick fog reached you, which is usually thicker in the mountains because it is drawn upward by the sun; not rising above five miles, it condenses there.

> Remember, reader, if ever in the Alps
> a fog caught you, through which you saw
> no differently than moles see through their skin.
> How and when the moist and thick vapors
> begin to thin, so that the harsh sphere
> of the sun enters through them weakly;
> And let your imagination be nimble
> to reach the point of seeing how I saw again
> the sun, which was already on the verge of setting.
> Thus, matching my steps with the faithful steps
> of my master, I emerged from such a cloud
> to rays already dead upon the low shores.

<column-break/>

**THROUGH THE SKIN OF MOLES:** because the mole always lives underground. It certainly has eyes, but they are covered by a thin skin, wherefore it sees very little. But that it sees something is manifest; first, because nature would have made its eyes in vain, and she does nothing in vain. Furthermore, because as soon as it leaves the earth and sees the air, it dies. Of this creature, Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), a Roman author and naturalist.</note> says that it is condemned by nature in many ways and lives buried in perpetual darkness. **HOW AND WHEN:** He first admonishes the reader to remember the thick fog of the Alps. Then he wants them to imagine the vapors which, because they were previously condensed by moisture, could not be penetrated by the sun's rays. But then, as the sun dissolves the moisture that made them dense, it thins them, and the rays begin to penetrate, but weakly. By imagining these two things, the reader understands first what the darkness of the smoke was like, and how afterward, as the end of the smoke approached, he began to see some glimmer of light. **AND LET YOUR IMAGINATION BE NIMBLE:** let your fantasy be quick to understand this. Let this power be nimble, meaning easy in joining and connecting these images. **I SAW THE SUN AGAIN FIRST:** that is <note>Original: *i.*, a common Latin abbreviation for *id est*.</note>, before I was entirely out of the fog. **DEAD:** because the sun was already setting, and the rays were beginning to fade on the low shores. **MATCHING:** Thus matching my steps with the faithful steps of Virgil.

<summary>This page describes Dante's exit from the blinding smoke of the Terrace of Wrath. The commentator explains Dante's metaphor of the mole's limited vision and the thinning of mountain fog to describe the transition back into the light of the setting sun.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Purgatorio, specifically Canto XVII. It transitions from the physical description of the fog on the Third Terrace (Wrath) to a philosophical and psychological analysis of how the mind perceives internal visions when the external senses are suspended.</meta>

->PURGATORIO<-

**O IMAGINATION** that steals us away: he wishes to describe an imagination and a vision that appeared to him. And he raises this doubt: the internal senses—which are <term>common sense</term> <note>The internal faculty that synthesizes data from the five senses.</note>, **imagination**, **fantasy**, the **cogitative power**, and **memory**—are moved by the external senses, which are sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Other philosophers propose three internal senses. In the first part of the head, they place a power which they call the apprehensive, or fantasy, or common sense. In the second, they place the imaginative, or the cogitative, or the <term>estimative faculty</term> <note>The ability to perceive the "intentions" of objects, such as a sheep perceiving a wolf as dangerous.</note>. The third is memory. And in this place, the poet uses "imagination" to mean the "estimative faculty," whose duty—aided by reason—is to consider the things that common sense, receiving them from the exterior, has placed in the imagination (which is the second sense), and to judge whether they are true or false, good or evil. And such judgment is then placed in the memory, as I demonstrated more extensively in my third book *On the Soul* <note>original: "libro dell’anima"</note>. The poet demonstrates, therefore, that although the imagination (that is, the estimative faculty) receives from the external senses, nonetheless it sometimes gathers the entire soul into itself in such a way that the senses "fall asleep," nor can they offer it any information. And afterward, either by celestial influence or, more likely, by a light sent from God, it considers and judges that which the divine light offers it without the help of any sense. And this appears manifest because we see people so deeply immersed in their imaginations that, even though they are in the presence of various people and where many sounds and noises are heard,

<margin>
O imagination, that sometimes 
steals us from outside so much 
that a man does not notice, 
though a thousand trumpets sound around him; 
Who moves you, if the sense offers you nothing? 
A light moves you that is formed in heaven, 
by itself, or by the will that guides it down. 
Of her impiety, who changed her form 
into the bird that most delights in singing, 
the trace appeared in my imagination. 
And here my mind was so enclosed 
within itself, that from outside there came 
nothing that was then received by it.
</margin>

nonetheless they see or hear nothing for the reason already stated, and especially when aided by fantasy, whose duty is to compose and divide. **WHO MOVES YOU** if the sense offers you nothing? If the order in the senses is this: that first the thing reaches the exterior—as, for example <note>original: "uerbi gratia"</note>, the eye sees the enemy and offers such a vision to the common sense, and that faculty stores it in the imagination, and afterward the cogitative faculty (which he here calls imagination), turning to the imagination as if to a mirror, sees and judges that it is useful to flee from it—after which judgment is given, the appetite is immediately awakened and moves one to flee. Therefore, the poet asks: if the external senses offer nothing to the cogitative faculty because they are dormant, who offers it to her? And he responds as we have already said. **AND A LIGHT MOVES YOU**: understand this as the <term>active intellect</term> <note>The power of the mind that processes sensory data into abstract thought.</note> **WHICH** in heaven **is formed**, that is, takes its being from the celestial influences which minister activity and operation down to such a light, or from the divine will without a medium, or from the will of the angels who are free and confirmed in grace. **WHICH**: that is, the divine power or the angel. **GUIDES IT DOWN**, that is, guides the activity of said light. Although the human intellect is passive in accordance with what the external senses minister to it, it is nonetheless active insofar as it operates upon the thing presented to it by the senses. And sometimes it operates without the senses on things influenced only by God without any medium, or by God through the medium of second causes, which are the angels. In short, I find the cogitative faculty within the imagination, which is a mirror to it, where it sees the things presented by the senses. But the form of the bird was influenced by God immediately or through the medium of angels. This is the nightingale, which is so eager to sing that it sings day and night. Now, returning to the poet’s fiction: just as he previously presented examples exhorting temperance (which is the best brake to contain anger), so at present he presents examples that draw one back from anger, considering through them into what cruelty one falls if we let ourselves run away into wrath. And therefore he feigns that he was in a fixed imagination of the fable of **Procne and Philomela** <note>In Greek myth, Procne kills her son to avenge her husband Tereus's rape of her sister Philomela; they are transformed into birds.</note>, who, for not having withdrawn from anger, used unheard-of cruelty. We narrated this fable at length above. **OF HER IMPIETY**: The order is: it appeared in my image, that is, in my imaginative form—namely, the vestige and the form of the impiety, that is, of the impetuous anger of her—namely, of that woman who changed her form into the bird; that is, from a woman she became that bird which delights in singing more than other birds. And although many here understand this as Philomela, nonetheless, because this cruelty proceeding from anger was greater in Procne, we can also understand it as her. Especially because the swallow also sings very willingly.

<margin>
Then there rained down into the high fantasy 
one crucified, disdainful and fierce 
in his appearance, and such he died. 
Around him was the great Ahasuerus, 
Esther his wife, and the just Mordecai, 
who was so whole in speech and deed.
</margin>

**ONE CRUCIFIED**. This was **Haman** <note>original: "Aman"</note>, the prefect of the military of King Ahasuerus. Ahasuerus, king of the Persians, repudiated his wife because she would not come to him at his banquet. Afterward, from among all the most beautiful, he chose **Esther**, daughter of **Mordecai**, a Hebrew man. At that time, Haman was the prefect of the military; he became so enraged against Mordecai because he would not worship him as the others did, that he persuaded the king that he wished to kill...

<summary>This page explains the psychological process of imagination and divine inspiration in Dante’s Purgatorio, using the examples of Procne’s wrath and Haman’s pride to illustrate the dangers of uncontrolled anger.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Purgatorio, Canto XVII. The previous page discussed the psychological nature of the "imaginative faculty" and how the mind receives visions from a divine source when the external senses are suspended. Here, the author provides specific examples of the sin of Wrath through the stories of Haman and Queen Amata, before transitioning to Dante's encounter with the Angel of Peace.</meta>

# CANTO XVII

### XVII

> And as this image broke
> of its own accord, like a bubble
> for which the water fails beneath it, so it happened.
> There rose in my vision a young girl
> weeping loudly, and she said: "O queen,
> why through anger have you wished to be nothing?
> You have killed yourself not to lose Lavinia;
> now you have lost me; I am she who mourns,
> mother, for your ruin more than for another's."

<note>Dante is describing a series of "ecstatic visions" illustrating the consequences of Wrath. The "young girl" is Lavinia, mourning her mother, Queen Amata.</note>

...to kill all the Jews who were in his kingdom, as a defiant nation that did not render him the due honors. The King believed him and gave him his ring so that he would be believed by others. He ordered by his letters that throughout the entire kingdom of the Persians, all Jews should be killed on a determined day. Then Esther, having heard this, put herself in the way of death to obey her father <note>original: "padre"—referring here to her guardian/cousin Mordecai</note>. She went without being called to the King, which was a capital offense. She entreated the King to call Haman and Mordecai to a banquet. And Haman, seeing again that Mordecai did not honor him, had a beam erected fifty cubits high to crucify him. But after the banquet, the queen told the King the whole story and obtained the liberation of the Hebrew people. Whereupon Haman was crucified where he had wished to crucify Mordecai. And Mordecai was placed in the dignity that Haman previously held. And Haman's ten sons were hanged, and the Jews killed a great multitude of those whom Haman had ordered to kill them. See, therefore, to what end Haman’s headlong anger led him. **AND AS THIS IMAGE BROKE** of itself—that is, it broke itself like a bubble made in the water by the rain, which bursts of its own accord. These bubbles or "bells" are born in the water when raindrops fall upon it. He thus compares the imagination, which falls into our <term>cogitative power</term> <note>The faculty of the mind that connects and compares individual thoughts.</note> from the celestial influence, to the drop that falls into the water and makes a bubble, which in a short time breaks. And so such an imagination or form is extinguished in the cogitative power, and another comes. **A YOUNG GIRL**. This was Lavinia, daughter of Latinus. When Aeneas came to Italy, Latinus gave her to him as a wife. This was so grievous to Amata, his wife and the mother of the girl, that she hanged herself out of the anger she took from this, especially because she wanted to give her to Turnus, her kinsman. From this followed the battles between the Trojans and the Latins described so excellently by Virgil.

---

> Just as sleep is broken when suddenly
> a new light strikes the closed face,
> which, broken, quivers before it dies entirely,
> so my imagining fell down
> as soon as a light struck my face,
> far greater than that which is in our common use.
> I turned myself to see where I was,
> when a voice said, "Here one ascends,"
> which removed me from every other intent,
> and made my will so ready
> to look upon who it was that spoke,
> that it never rests unless it meets him.
> But as the sun which weighs upon our sight
> and veils its own form through excess [of light],
> so my power here was failing me.

Through a most fitting comparison, he shows himself exiting his imaginations (which had put every other thing to sleep) just as one exits sleep and wakes when, while sleeping, he is struck in the face by a sudden splendor. Therefore, as it **BREAKS**—that is, sleep is broken. **WHEN**—at the moment. **SUDDENLY**—all at once. **A NEW LIGHT** <note>The OCR text glosses "NVOVA LEGGE" (new law), but the verse and context clearly indicate "nuova luce" (new light).</note> strikes the closed face, the closed eye. **WHICH**—which sleep. **BROKEN**—ruptured, because it begins to go away. **QUIVERS**—makes the man quiver and move. **BEFORE IT DIES ENTIRELY**—before sleep departs completely; thus **SUDDENLY** <note>original: "dibotto"</note>. This signifies "at once." **QUIVERS**: that thing which moves often and with speed, just as we say a fish quivers in the water. **FAR GREATER**. The splendor proceeding from the angel was much greater than that of the sun which is in our sight. **WHEN A VOICE**—of the angel, which was so powerful in me that it removed me from every other intent—that is, from every other thought that could hold my mind attentive. And this voice made my will so ready—that is, so solicitous and desirous to see who was speaking—that it could not rest if it did not **MEET** him—that is, if it did not encounter him. But gazing at the angel who spoke, his light dazzled me, just as the excessive light of the sun dazzles. The voice of the angel is the <term>speculative theological doctrine</term> <note>Abstract philosophical or religious teaching that leads the mind toward God.</note>, which is so sweet that, having heard it, we cannot rest or be quiet unless we see where it comes from, which is the Eternal Truth. But we cannot see it perfectly because the human mind is not capable; but we can well hear the voice when it says, "Here one ascends"—that is, when it demonstrates the way to climb to heaven.

---

> This is a divine spirit who in the
> way of going up directs us without prayer,
> and with his own light conceals himself.

He shows that this is that angel who leads us upward without prayer—that is, without being asked—and **CONCEALS**—that is, hides himself with his own light. **HE ACTS WITH US** as a man acts with himself. Thus the angel acts with us.

The commentary explains the mechanics of the imagination through the metaphor of bubbles in water and interprets the Angel's voice as theological truth.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the transition from the Third Terrace (Wrath) to the Fourth Terrace (Sloth) in Dante’s Purgatorio, Canto XVII. Following the visions of wrath, Dante encounters the Angel of Peace and begins to feel his physical strength fail as evening approaches, leading to Virgil’s explanation of the sins purged in this new circle.</meta>

# PURGATORIO

He acts toward us as a man acts toward himself;
for he who waits for a prayer when he sees the need
maliciously sets himself already to the denial.
Now let us tune our feet to such an invitation;
let us strive to ascend before it grows dark,
for later one could not until the day returns.
So said my leader, and I with him
turned our steps toward a stairway;
and as soon as I was on the first step:
I felt near me as it were the moving of a wing
and a fanning in my face and heard said: "Blessed 
are the peacemakers, who are without evil wrath!"

Already were the last rays, which the night follows,
lifted so high above us 
that the stars appeared on many sides.
"O my virtue, why do you melt away?"
I said within myself, for I felt 
the power of my legs placed in a truce.
We were where the stairs ascended no more,
and we were halted
just as a ship that arrives at the shore.
And I waited a little to see if I heard
anything in the new circle;
then I turned to my master and said:
"My sweet father, for what offense
is one purged here in the circle where we are?
If our feet are still, let not your speech be still."

And he to me: "The love of the good, falling short
of its duty, is here restored;
here the ill-delayed oar is struck again.
But so that you may understand more clearly yet..."

<column-break/>

...moves toward us without being asked. **AS MAN**, that is, as human people act toward themselves <note>original: "sifa sego: fa seco"</note>. That is, how one man should act with another, because we ought to help one another without waiting to be asked. **FOR HE WHO**: a man who sees the "uopo," <term>uopo</term> <note>an archaic Italian term for "need" or "necessity"</note> the need of another man, and waits for a prayer, already maliciously prepares to deny him. **NOW Let us tune** our feet to such an invitation, that is, let us go where he invites us to climb. And because the "foot" signifies the affection <note>the soul’s desire or inclination</note>, which moves the soul just as the physical foot moves the body, Virgil’s foot represents the **will**, and Dante’s represents **appetite**. It demonstrates that one cannot climb except by day. Wherefore it is said: "Walk while you have the light" <note>original Latin: "ambulate dum lucem habetis"—a reference to John 12:35</note>. But we have declared this above. Having reached the stairs that left the present circle, Dante felt his forehead fanned by the wing, because the Angel erased

with his wing the third sin <note>The third "P" for Peccatum (sin) carved on Dante's forehead, representing Wrath</note>. This wind stirred by the Angel's wing signifies the inspiration that the Holy Spirit works within a good will, belonging to one who is eager to purge sin, which, by inspiring, removes the vice. **BLESSED ARE THE PEACEMAKERS**: the words of Saint Matthew: "Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God" <note>original: "beati pacifici: quoniam filii dei uocabuntur"—Matthew 5:9</note>. **WITHOUT evil wrath.** Because peace is the opposite of evil wrath; and he did not say "evil" without reason. For a just and reasonable anger can be stirred in us by a zeal for justice against a sinner. In such anger, the "sun does not set" <note>original: "non occidit sol"—alluding to Ephesians 4:26</note>, that is, the light of reason is not extinguished. And this is a good wrath.

It shows that they have ascended into the fourth circle when the sun was already going down in that hemisphere; and when the sun goes down, its rays do not spread across the earth but rather rise higher, because the last rays (followed by night) were so elevated because the sun was setting that the stars were already visible. **O MY VIRTUE**: he says that the power to climb fails him because the sun, without which one cannot ascend, was going down. It is not necessary to provide the allegorical sense here, having already placed it in the <unclear>verticolo</unclear>. The good Sordello <note>A 13th-century poet Dante met in the lower parts of Purgatory</note> marked the ground with his finger and said only that "this line you would not cross after the sun has departed." And certainly without the sun—that is, without the light of Divine Grace—one cannot ascend to the heights. I said to myself: "O virtue, O my power, you melt away," that is, you vanish. **PLACED IN A TRUCE**: to rest, a metaphor from war, in which men on all sides rest when a truce is made.

### FOR WHAT OFFENSE is one purged here:
He seems to investigate this because Dante asks what vice is purged here, not having asked about the others in the other circles. To which I feel I should answer: that this poet, having always been in constant meditation on great things and very practiced in the active life, had never fallen into the vice of **Sloth** <note>original: "accidia"</note>, which is treated here, in a way that he could well recognize it.

Virgil wants to demonstrate that in this circle the vice of Sloth is purged, which is nothing other than failing to love God and virtue with the appropriate fervor; and therefore he says: **LOVE OF the good falling short**, that is, of the good diminished from its duty. **HERE THE ILL-DELAYED OAR IS STRUCK.** Here, through diligence, negligence is restored; and he uses a metaphor of a galley crew which, because it rowed sluggishly, is punished by the boatswain and forced to **strike the oar**, that is, to row so fast that it makes up for past negligence. **NEITHER CREATOR** nor creature is ever without love: This is true, because neither God (who alone is the Creator) is without love, as we shall demonstrate in Paradise, **NOR CREATURE**...

<summary>Dante ascends to the Fourth Terrace of Purgatory, where the sin of Sloth is purged. The commentary explains the Angel of Peace’s blessing and Virgil’s teaching that Sloth is a deficiency of love for the Divine.</summary>
<keywords>Sloth, Accidia, Virgil, Angel of Peace, Divine Grace, galley metaphor, righteous anger, Purgatorio Canto XVII, Cristoforo Landino</keywords>

--- Page 455 ---
<meta>This page continues Virgil’s discourse in the Fourth Terrace (Sloth). Having halted for the night, Virgil uses the pause to explain the moral structure of Purgatory, grounded in the concept that all human action—both virtuous and sinful—springs from love.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>CANTO XVII</header>

Turn your mind toward me, and you shall gather
some good fruit from our stay here.
"Neither Creator nor creature ever,"
he began, "my son, was without love,
either natural or of the mind, as you know.
The natural is always without error,
but the other can err through an evil object,
or through too little or too much vigor.

While it is directed toward the first goods,
and in the second ones it measures itself,
it cannot be the cause of ill delight.
But when it turns toward evil, or with more care
or with less than it should it runs toward the good,
against the Creator the creature works.
Hence you can understand that it must be
love is the seed in us of every virtue,
and of every action that deserves punishment."

<column-break/>

This can be understood generally of every creature: not only the rational, but the irrational; and not only the animate, but the inanimate; because all creatures have love: that is, an inclination toward the preservation of themselves. Nevertheless, here it is narrowed to man, who through the acts of **free will** <term>libero arbitrio: the capacity to choose between different possible courses of action unimpeded</term> merits or loses merit. **OR NATURAL OR OF THE MIND**. Love, as far as this place is concerned, is either natural or of the mind. Natural love is that which exists between us and God, and between the soul and the body, or between the will and the good, which is the object of the will; the love of the mind <note>original: "danimo"</note> is that which desires within him. And this is also subdivided. For some love is simply good, such as the love of friendship. Some is not simply good but guilty because of its object. Because just as virtue is ordered love, so vice is disordered love. And this occurs if it is either the love of evil, or the love of good which is either too little or too much, according to two species of good. For some good is small, such as temporal and physical goods. Some is great, such as the goods of grace and glory. Therefore, the love of the great good is disordered if it is **too little**. And such is the root of **sloth** <term>accidia: spiritual apathy or a failure to love God with sufficient intensity</term>. The love of the small good is disordered if it is **too much**. And this is the root of gluttony, lust, and avarice; although the miser loves such goods to possess them, while the glutton and the lustful do so to take pleasure. The disordered love of nature is the love of another’s evil or one’s own. But no one loves their own evil insofar as it is evil; rather, they judge it to be good. The love of another's evil is the root of **pride, envy, and wrath**. Because pride is the love of one’s own good joined with the evil of one’s neighbor, loving one’s own exaltation by the depressing of others. Envy and wrath are the love of another’s evil, but they differ: the love of wrath is born from another’s evil because he who is angry against me wishes me ill because he receives evil from me. Envy is born from one's own malice, i.e., from pride, and loves the neighbor's evil even when it does not benefit oneself, simply so that the neighbor is not one's equal. Thus, in its subject matter, it shares with wrath, but its end proceeds from pride. But repeating briefly what suffices for the present division: there are two species of love and desire. One is **natural**, which is infused in all creatures, by which they desire that good by which they preserve their being. **THE OTHER IS ANIMATED** <note>original: "ANIMALE": referring to the "anima" or soul, involving conscious choice</note>, and this proceeds from the will, in which there is choice and free will. The natural never errs. The animated can err in three ways: either by **object**, which is when the appetite, uncorrected by the light of reason, loves that which is evil instead of good. **OR BY LITTLE VIGOR**, which is when that which deserves to be loved supremely and above all other things is loved little and coldly, such as God, the supreme good, and virtue, which contains all the virtues. Whence in the precepts given by Moses, or rather by God through Moses: > "Love the Lord your God." < <note>original: "Dilige dominum deum tuum"</note> **OR BY TOO MUCH**, when temporal goods—which either should not be considered goods or are truly the lowliest of goods—are loved by us more than the eternal good. From this, the aforementioned vices are born.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'Q' depicting a figure in a landscape, framed by a decorative square border.</image-desc>
This is the conclusion, and it says: Therefore, while this animated love **IS STRAIGHT** toward the first good, i.e., it rightly loves God because it loves Him as much as is fitting and as the Creator; and while it **measures itself** in the second good, i.e., it loves created things moderately, which as works of God should be loved because they are good— > "For God saw everything he had made, and they were very good." < <note>original: "Quia uidit deus omnia que fecit : et erant ualde bona."</note>—and this second love is divided into two types: the useful and the pleasant. **IT CANNOT BE**: this love, when so ordered, cannot be the cause of dishonorable delight. But when love **turns to evil**—because evil is not loved directly for the sake of being evil, but indirectly, either to flee discomfort or to achieve convenience—he has already established one way of sinning. Then he adds the second, saying: **or runs toward the good with more care** than it should, i.e., it loves the secondary good more than it ought. **OR WITH LESS CARE**, and this is the third way of sinning: when we do not love the first good as much as is fitting. **AGAINST THE MAKER**: when one sins in these ways, man **WORKS**, i.e., he uses his own manufacture against the Maker. That is, he employs himself—who is the manufacture of God his Maker—against His precepts, because God wills that we love Him first above all things, and then created things according to their degrees. **HENCE YOU CAN UNDERSTAND** by the reasons already shown, you can know that love is the seed and cause of virtues when it is ordered, and of the actions that **deserve punishment**, i.e., vices, when it is disordered.

<summary>This page contains Virgil’s pivotal speech explaining that love is the root of all human behavior. It distinguishes between natural instinct and the conscious love of the soul, classifying all seven deadly sins as distortions of this love.</summary>
<keywords>Dante Alighieri, Purgatorio, Canto XVII, nature of love, natural love, spiritual love, free will, Seven Deadly Sins, Sloth, Pride, Envy, Wrath, Gluttony, Lust, Avarice, theology of love, Virgil's discourse</keywords>

--- Page 456 ---
<meta>This page continues Virgil’s explanation of the moral geography of Purgatory. Following the previous page, where Virgil established that love is the root of all human action, he now explains why certain forms of love result in sin—specifically the sins of Pride, Envy, and Wrath—and begins to define Sloth.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>PURGATORY</header>

And because love can never turn its sight
from the well-being of its own subject,
all things are safe from hating themselves.
And because no being can be understood
as separate and standing by itself from the First <note>The "First" refers to God, the First Cause of all existence.</note>,
every affection is cut off from hating Him.
It follows, if I divide well in my judgment,
that the evil one loves is in one's neighbor;
and this love is born in three ways in your clay <note>original: "limo." This refers to the "slime" or "clay" of the earth from which humanity was formed, symbolizing our physical, mortal nature.</note>.

There is he who, through his neighbor’s suppression,
hopes for excellence, and only for this reason longs
that his neighbor’s greatness be brought low.
And there is he who fears to lose power,
honor, grace, and fame because another rises,
wherefore he becomes so saddened that he loves the opposite.
And there is he who, due to injury, seems so shamed
that he becomes greedy for revenge,
and such a man must seek to harm another.

This threefold love is lamented here below;
now I wish for you to understand the other,
which runs toward the good in a corrupted order.
Everyone confusedly apprehends a good
in which the soul may rest, and desires it;
therefore, everyone strives to reach it.
If a lukewarm love draws you to see it
or to acquire it, this terrace
punishes you after a just repentance.

<column-break/>

**It demonstrates:** that because love cannot turn its face—that is, it cannot depart from its subject, namely itself—it cannot fail to always love itself. It follows: that every thing is "all"—that is, secure—from hating itself. Therefore, no one hates himself, because to hate is to wish ill upon the thing hated. **AND BECAUSE NO BEING CAN BE UNDERSTOOD AS DIVIDED.** The meaning is that any thing which has being does not have it except insofar as God, who is the First Being, preserves it. It cannot be understood that any being is divided from the First Being, nor can any being be understood as "standing by itself"—that is, it cannot be understood that any being exists through its own power alone. Therefore, naturally, every thing loves its own being, and likewise loves God. For this reason, every affection is "cut off"—that is, divided—from hating that God. **IT FOLLOWS THEREFORE:** If man cannot love evil for himself or for God, it follows that every evil we do, we do to our neighbor. **IF I DIVIDE WELL** in my judgment: that is, if I make a good division, which is this: if the "good" that is done is toward God, or ourselves, or our neighbor, then evil is similarly tripartite <note>tripartite: divided into three parts</note>. But it has already been shown that we cannot love evil in God, nor in ourselves; it follows that we love it in our neighbor. **IT IS BORN IN THREE WAYS:** it moves through three causes, as we shall say below. **IN YOUR CLAY:** in your "mud," so to speak, not through reason (which is the divine part of the soul), but through sensuality, which proceeds from the contagion of the body, an earthly thing.

He had already shown that man does not love evil unless it is toward his neighbor. Now he shows that evil toward the neighbor is done in three ways for three ends. For no one loves evil for its own sake, but loves it for the sake of some good he expects will be born from that evil, because "good" is that which is loved. Therefore, one loves evil in his neighbor because he hopes to become great through his neighbor's oppression <note>This defines the sin of Pride (Superbia).</note>. Another desires that others do not rise to a higher degree because he fears that they might take away his power—that is, his strength—or his honor, grace, and fame; he loves these things more than is proper, and for this reason, he loves that the other should not rise <note>This defines the sin of Envy (Inuidia).</note>. Another, having received an injury, desires revenge, and for this reason, he loves the other’s harm <note>This defines the sin of Wrath (Ira).</note>. And so he shows that the love of evil is the cause of pride, envy, and wrath. Through all these things, one recognizes that the will cannot simply love evil, but rather loves the neighbor's evil for the sake of one's own perceived good.

Since he has treated the love that twists toward the neighbor’s evil—which was divided into three parts: pride, envy, and wrath—he now places the love that goes toward the good with less vigor than it should. The first type, which is tripartite, is punished in the three terraces already mentioned. This second type, because it lacks fervor, creates **sloth** <term>laccidia: spiritual apathy or laziness in practicing virtue</term> and is purged in this fourth terrace. **THIS THREEFOLD [LOVE] IS LAMENTED BELOW:** below in the four terraces already passed. **THE OTHER RUNS TOWARD THE GOOD WITH CORRUPTED ORDER:** the higher tripartite love twists toward evil; the other—that is, this one—does not twist toward evil. Rather, it runs toward the Supreme Good, which is God, and toward the virtues, but with "corrupted order," because it does not love Him as much as is proper, and places utility and pleasure before that love. **EVERYONE CONFUSEDLY APPREHENDS A GOOD.** In the mind of every man, there is an innate desire to know the Supreme Good, in which the ultimate end is found; in that good, the soul is satisfied and contented, so that it seeks nothing further. Therefore, every mind **STRIVES**—that is, forces itself—to join with that. **IF A LUKEWARM LOVE DRAWS YOU** to see or acquire Him: if love lacks its proper fervor, from which sloth is born, **THIS TERRACE**: this level [of Purgatory] punishes you after just repentance.

<summary>In this passage, Virgil explains to Dante that all sins of malice (Pride, Envy, and Wrath) arise from a perverted love for one's neighbor, as humans naturally love themselves and God. He then introduces the sin of Sloth as a "lukewarm" or insufficient love for the True Good.</summary>
<keywords>Purgatory, Dante Alighieri, Virgil, commentary, Cristoforo Landino, Pride (Superbia), Envy (Inuidia), Wrath (Ira), Sloth (Accidia), Threefold Love, Moral Philosophy</keywords>

Another good exists that does not make man happy;
it is not true happiness, it is not the good
essence of every good, both fruit and root.
The love that abandons itself too much to this <note>original: "Lamor cha esso troppo fabbandona." This refers to the excessive love for secondary, earthly goods like wealth, food, or pleasure.</note>
is lamented above us through three circles;
but how it is reasoned to be tripartite,
