### CANTO XVIII OF THE SECOND CANTICLE OF DANTE.

<image-desc>Large decorated initial 'P' containing a miniature of a figure, likely Virgil or Dante, standing at a lectern or writing desk with a book.</image-desc>
The high doctor <note>referring to Virgil</note> had put an end to his reasoning
and was looking attentively
at my face to see if I appeared content:
And I, whom a new thirst still urged,
remained silent outwardly, but within I said, "Perhaps
the excessive questioning I do burdens him."
But that true father, who perceived
the timid will that did not open itself,
by speaking, gave me the courage to speak.

<column-break/>

How a lack of love toward the highest good causes sloth <note>original: "accidia."</note>. Likewise, too much love toward worldly goods causes greed, lust, and gluttony: which three sins are purged in the higher circles. **ANOTHER GOOD** exists that does not make man happy. This refers to all created things: which are good. But they are imperfect goods: and not the "good essence": because that is God: who is the fruit of every good. For the fruit and the reward of our good works is to enjoy God himself: and He is the root of every good. The love that abandons itself to it <note>the worldly good</note>. That is, it runs into it abandonedly—namely, without the bridle and measure of reason: for this reason it is "excessive" and exceeds the proper limit. **THROUGH THREE** circles. Because in the first—which is the fifth in the sequence—greed <note>original: "auaritia."</note> is purged: which is the disordered love for the goods of fortune. In the second—which is the sixth—gluttony is purged. In the third—which is the seventh—lust is purged. **I KEEP SILENT** so that you may seek it for yourself. Virgil has demonstrated the highest and perfect good: which resides only in the intellect. Now, regarding the "sensible good" <term>sensible good<gloss>things perceived by the senses rather than the mind alone</gloss></term>, Dante can proceed by himself: and therefore Virgil leaves such inquiry to him.

**IT FOLLOWS** in this chapter to clarify the nature of love: and then it demonstrates how sloth is purged. **BUT THAT FATHER**: demonstrates what the teacher should be toward the disciple. And likewise the intellect toward the senses <note>original: "sensualita."</note>. But of this we have already spoken many times. Not without reason does he call him "high doctor." Then "father." And finally "master." He calls him "high doctor" to show that he can explain every great matter. "Master" because he is accustomed to showing it. "Father" because Dante is, in a sense, his son. **OF THE TIMID** speaking that would not open: because fearing that I might be troublesome in speaking, I did not open my will, and he with his words gave me the courage to speak. **MY** sight was so quickened in your light: by this, he shows that the sensitive part and the "lower reason" gain strength and become intelligent through the light of the intellect. And he incites Virgil to teach...

<meta>This page continues Virgil’s explanation of the nature of love, moving from the classification of sins to a deeper philosophical and psychological definition of how the human soul is moved by desire.</meta>

# XVIII PURGATORIO

Wherefore, Master, my will is so enlivened
in your light that I clearly discern
as far as your reason carries or describes.
Therefore, I pray you, sweet dear father,
that you show me love, to which you reduce
every good deed and its contrary <note>Dante asks Virgil to explain how both virtue and vice can stem from the same root: love.</note>.

"Direct toward me," he said, "the sharp lights
of the intellect: and the error of the blind
who make themselves leaders will be manifest to you <note>Virgil warns against the false philosophy that all love is inherently good because it feels natural.</note>.
The soul, which is created ready to love,
is mobile toward everything that pleases,
as soon as it is awakened into action by pleasure.
Your apprehensive faculty <note>term: "apprensiva" - the cognitive power of the mind to take in an external image and form a mental representation.</note> draws an image from a real being
and unfolds it within you,
so that it makes the soul turn toward it.
And if, having turned, the soul leans toward it,
that leaning is love; that is nature,
which is bound in you anew by pleasure.
Then, just as fire moves upward
because of its form, which is born to ascend
to where it lasts longest in its own element <note>In medieval science, fire was believed to seek its "natural place" in a sphere above the air.</note>:
So the soul, captured, enters into desire,
which is a spiritual motion that never rests
until the beloved thing makes it rejoice.
Now it can appear to you how hidden
the truth is from the people who maintain
that every love is in itself a laudable thing:
Because perhaps its matter <note>original: "matera" - the raw capacity or potential for love.</note> always appears
to be good, but not every seal
is good, even if the wax is good <note>Dante uses the metaphor of a seal and wax: the capacity to love (wax) is a gift from God and good, but the specific form it takes (the seal's impression) can be wicked if directed at the wrong object.</note>."

<column-break/>

...for the more easily the disciple learns, the more willingly the liberal teacher shows him. **CARRIES** [PORTI]: in knowing things previously unknown. **AND DESCRIBES** [DISCRIVA]: in defining and dividing. For this reason, I pray you show me what thing love is, from which you wish for virtue and vice to proceed. Wherefore he thus narrates:

**Show**: what thing love is: and reprove those philosophers who wish for every love to be laudable. **DIRECT THE SHARP LIGHTS OF THE INTELLECT**: because such science requires sharpness of wit and diligence. **THE ERROR of the blind who make themselves leaders**: The error of those who do not see the truth and do not know, and yet wish to give doctrine. Thus they guide the disciple no differently than a blind man guides one who follows him. These people say that every love is laudable. Which is false. **THE SOUL WHICH IS CREATED ready to love**: Because the human soul is created by God with a concupiscible power <note>term: "concupiscibile" - the faculty of the soul that desires perceived goods.</note>, which power it can quickly bring into action. Because when either that sense called the "cogitative," or reason, or the intellect has judged something to be good, immediately after such judgment is given, the concupiscible power awakes and desires it; as, for example <note>original: "verbi gratia"</note>: the eye sees a horse, and the common sense receives this form from the sight, and once received, places it in the imaginative faculty. And the cogitative faculty considers it in the imaginative. And judges that thing to be good and beautiful. Which judgment, once made, suddenly excites this power of the soul, which we call the appetite, to love it and desire it. **YOUR APPREHENSIVE FACULTY FROM A REAL BEING draws an image**: this apprehensive faculty which judges what one should choose. **DRAWS** the image: it pulls the appetite toward it from what is truly good. And that is loved as a good thing. And if it is not good, and yet it is loved, it is because one remains deceived. Nor

---

does one love it except because they believe it to be good. **AND UNFOLDS**: opens and demonstrates this intention to the soul (i.e., to the will) in a way that the soul turns toward it; and if, in turning, it begins to lean and incline toward it, such inclination toward the thing that pleases it is love and nature (i.e., natural love). Therefore, we shall say that love is an inclination of the soul toward the thing that pleases it after it is offered. **WHICH by pleasure is bound in you anew**: Because such an inclination, newly made by the soul toward the thing that pleases it, is a binding of the soul with the thing that pleases it; and from this is born concupiscence and desire. **That leaning** (i.e., that inclination) **IS LOVE, that is nature** (i.e., natural love). **THEN AS FIRE**: Every created thing was produced by its creator with an innate inclination for that which is its supreme good. Nor does it ever rest until it follows it. But such an innate inclination in the creature is either from nature, or from sense, or from reason. From nature, it is even in inanimate things, as we say of fire. From sense, we see it not only in men but also in brutes. For seeing the bait, the bird moves to feed on it. The inclination from reason is in man alone, as when we see Cato seeking dangers to liberate his fatherland <note>Marcus Porcius Cato the Younger, who chose death over life under Caesar's tyranny, cited here as an example of rational, virtuous love for the common good.</note>. Therefore, just as fire has from its specific form (i.e., from its being distinct from other things) the tendency to mount upward, as a light thing, nor does it ever rest (unless hindered) until it returns to its region, which is above the element of air. **WHERE IT LASTS LONGER IN ITS element**: So our soul, captured by what it judges to be good and beautiful, **ENTERS into desire**: into the desire to obtain it. **WHICH IS A SPIRITUAL MOTION**: which desire is a spiritual motion and not a bodily one. Because desire moves the spirit and not the body. Nor does such a motion of the soul ever rest **UNTIL THE BELOVED THING makes it rejoice** (i.e., until with joy...)

<summary>This page contains the opening of Purgatorio Canto XVIII, where Virgil provides a foundational lecture on the psychology of love, explaining it as a natural inclination of the soul toward perceived beauty and goodness. The commentary expands on this by explaining the Scholastic process of perception—how the mind receives an image, judges it, and moves the will toward desire.</summary>

--- Page 459 ---
<meta>This page continues Virgil’s discourse on the nature of love, specifically addressing Dante’s concern that if love is an external impulse, the soul cannot be held responsible for its actions. Virgil begins to explain the interplay between natural instinct and the "virtue that counsels"—free will.</meta>

# CANTO XVIII
->gg ii<-

God does not obtain the beloved thing. **NOW IT CAN:** Conclude: that by what has been said above: it is seen: that those who affirm that every love is laudable are in error. And the error arises because they argue in this fixed way: The apprehensive part <note>The cognitive faculty that perceives and forms mental images of external things.</note> does not place anything before the will except what it judges to be good; and the soul and will do not incline themselves except toward what the apprehension has already judged to be good. But this argument would follow of necessity if that power of the soul which judges did not err. But because it does err and offers as good that which is wicked, the appetite is deceived and falls in love with that thing as if it were good; which, although it might be good in itself (since every thing created by God is good), was nonetheless judged to be better than it is. Thus, the love was greater than it ought to have been.

"Your words and my following wit,"
I replied to him, "have revealed love to me;
but this has made me more pregnant with doubt;
for if love is offered to us from the outside,
and the soul walks with no other foot,
whether she goes straight or crooked is not her merit."
And he to me: "As far as reason sees here,
I can tell you; from there onward, wait
only for Beatrice, for it is a work of faith <note>Virgil, representing human reason, can explain moral philosophy, but the deeper mysteries of the soul's origin and grace belong to Beatrice, representing Theology.</note>."

Through sensible things, theology teaches spiritual things; therefore he said that Beatrice was the work of faith.

Every substantial form <note>term: "substantial form" - in Aristotelian philosophy, this is the essence that makes a thing what it is; for humans, this is the rational soul.</note> that is distinct
from matter and yet is united with it,
has a specific virtue collected within itself,
Which is not perceived except through operation,
nor does it show itself except by its effect,
as life in a plant is shown by green leaves.
Therefore, from where the understanding
of the first cognitions <note>original: "prime notitie" - innate primary concepts or self-evident truths.</note> comes to man, no one knows;
nor the affection for the first objects of desire <note>original: "primo appetibile" - the natural, instinctive pull toward the Good (God).</note>.
Which are in us just as the instinct in the bee
to make honey; and this first will
is not capable of the merit of praise or blame.
And so that every other will may gather to this one,
there is innate in you the virtue that counsels <note>original: "la virtù che consiglia" - the faculty of Reason and Free Will.</note>,
which ought to hold the threshold of assent.
This is the principle from which is gathered
the reason for deserving in us, according to how
it gathers and winnows good and wicked loves.

<column-break/>

"I have understood what love may be," Dante responds. But from this arises a doubt: because if love arises from a thing that is extrinsic <note>Coming from the outside.</note>, placed before the soul, and the soul walks with no other foot because nothing moves except the appetite, it follows that since this movement arises from an external thing, the soul deserves neither a reward for good nor a penalty for evil. And to this, Virgil responds that he will solve such a doubt as far as he can understand. But because this is not enough, he [Dante] must wait for Beatrice, who signifies theology. For that which human reason does not comprehend—which comprehends only sensible and intellectual things—must be learned through faith and not through reason; and

**Form** is that which gives being to a thing. Therefore, the form in man is the rational soul, because only through reason are we different from other animals. And the body is the matter. Therefore he says that every substantial form—which is the soul—which is **DISTINCT**: which is separated, that is, divided from matter, that is, it has its own being after it is separated from its matter, which is the body. And it is also united with matter. In short, every soul has its being both in the body and when it shall be separated from the body. This is not so in the souls of brutes <note>Animals without reason.</note>, because once separated from their bodies, they have no being. Thus, the human soul is pure form, because it is divided from matter. And through this, it has in itself a power different from all other species, which constitutes its essence. This power is not seen nor known except through its effect, just as in a plant it is not known to be alive except by the green leaves. And because of this, man does not know where the intellect of the **first cognitions** comes from; that is, how the first notions are in a small child, such as knowing his father and other similar things, and other general things in grown men. Nor does he know from where the **affection** proceeds; that is, the love of the **first object of desire**; that is, of the Supreme Good, which is God, whom every man

desires. But he does not know why it is naturally in the soul, just as the desire to make honey is in the bee. This first desire is not attributed to us for either praise or blame because, as Aristotle says, the first movements are not in our power. But afterward, in the second and third movements, and in all others, there is reason itself. For despite the fact that every other will that follows gathers to this first will—that is, although subsequent desires are directed by these first movements—they nonetheless have merit and demerit. This the first ones did not have, because [humans] have innate in them the **virtue that counsels**, that is, reason, which is given to us by God so that it may **hold the threshold of assent**; that is, be the master of consenting or not consenting. And from this reason—which can consent or resist as it pleases—is the principle from which our merit is born: if it consents to the good and does not consent to the evil. And thus demerit is judged to the contrary.

<summary>In this commentary on Purgatorio Canto XVIII, Virgil explains that while the soul has an innate, blameless instinct for the Good, humans possess the faculty of Reason ("the virtue that counsels") to judge and control these impulses, thereby establishing moral responsibility and the basis for divine justice.</summary>
<keywords>Dante Alighieri, Purgatorio, Virgil, Beatrice, Cristoforo Landino, commentary, free will, love, appetite, first cognitions, intellect, substantial form</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Virgil’s explanation of how human reason relates to divine grace. Virgil has just explained that while the impulse of love is natural, the soul possesses a "counseling virtue" that must judge which loves to follow. Here, he connects this philosophy to the origin of moral law and the concept of free will, which Beatrice (Theology) will later expand upon.</meta>

# PURGATORIO

->Those who, by reasoning, went to the very bottom,<-
->perceived this innate liberty;<-
->therefore they left moral philosophy to the world.<-
->Wherefore, let us suppose that of necessity<-
->every love that kindles within you arises;<-
->the power to restrain it is within you.<-
->The noble virtue is what Beatrice understands<-
->as free will, and therefore see<-
->that you have it in mind, if she takes up the subject with you.<-

->The moon, delayed nearly to the middle of the night,<-
->made the stars appear more sparse to us,<-
->shaped like a bucket that is all ablaze;<-
<note>The poet describes the moon as "secchione" (a large bucket), referring to its gibbous, waning shape as it rises late at night.</note>
->And it ran against the sky along those paths<-
->which the sun inflames when those in Rome<-
->see it falling between Sardinia and Corsica.<-
->And that gentle shade for whom Pietola is named,<-
->more famous than any Mantuan village,<-
->had laid down the burden of my loading.<-
<note>The "gentle shade" is Virgil. Pietola (anciently called Andes) was his birthplace near Mantua.</note>

->Because I, who had harvested his reason,<-
->so open and plain, upon my questions,<-
->stood like a man who wanders, drowsy;<-
->But this sleepiness was taken from me<-
->suddenly by people who, behind<-
->our backs, had already turned toward us.<-

<column-break/>

Virgil follows here by demonstrating the reason that moved the philosophers to believe that virtuous operations in us deserve a reward, and vicious ones a penalty. Therefore, those same ones by reasoning <note>original: "raciocinando"</note> **WENT to the bottom**, that is, they found the truth, which is this: that notwithstanding that love—namely, the appetite—arises in us by necessity. Because a man cannot, when the senses offer him a pleasurable thing, prevent the appetite from directing itself there. Nevertheless, we have in us **free will**, with which we can follow that which reason dictates, and restrain and contain the appetite. **THEY PERCEIVED**, these philosophers, **this innate liberty**, that is, free will. **THEREFORE THEY LEFT MORAL PHILOSOPHY to the world**: so that men might live honestly according to the moral virtues; and they wrote such precepts to help those who were to follow them. **THE NOBLE VIRTUE BEATRICE UNDERSTANDS**. Dante here admonishes that when Beatrice—namely, sacred Theology—names the "noble virtue," she means by that free will. Wherefore in the fifth canto of the *Paradiso*: "The greatest gift that God [in his bounty made]..."

It demonstrates, according to the order of astrology, that the third part of the night had already passed. In order that this may be better understood: the moon, when it is full, being in opposition to the sun, rises when the sun goes down. And afterwards, when the fifteenth day has passed, because it wanes, it rises every evening later. Therefore, having been in opposition on the night the poet found himself lost in the woods, and this being the fourth night, it is reasonable that it did not rise until the third part of the night. **MORE SPARSE**: because the light of the moon prevails so much that it overcomes that of the lesser stars. Wherefore none appear to it except the greatest, because a greater light always obscures a lesser one. **SHAPED LIKE A BUCKET**: because it is already diminished. Other texts have "scheggione" <note>meaning a large splinter or crag</note>. **AGAINST the sky**: all the planets go against the sky, because they move from west to east. Nevertheless, the velocity of the spheres pulls them, as we have shown in another place. **WHEN THAT FROM ROME**: the moon had left Libra, where it had been in opposition, and was now in Scorpio, a very southern sign. And when the sun is in this sign toward the west, those who are in Rome see it by looking between the islands of Sardinia and Corsica, because that part is to the west of Rome. **FOR WHOM Pietola is named**. He means Virgil, who, because he was born in a village of the Mantuan territory called Pietola in our times, it happens that this village is more famous than any other. Among the ancients this was called Andes. <note>original: "Apud antiquos haec appellabatur Andes"</note> **HAD LAID DOWN THE BURDEN of my loading**. When someone is asked a particularly difficult thing, it seems that such a question sits upon them almost like a burden. And similarly, when he has satisfied the question asked of him with an answer, he seems to be unloaded and to have set down such a burden.

Because Dante had already understood the reasons, open and plain, with which Virgil had resolved his question, he remained idle, and almost like a drowsy man, he wandered about full of sleep. It is as if he says he remained empty of every noble thought. And for this reason, he confesses to **sloth** <term>Accidia: spiritual apathy or laziness, the sin being purged on this terrace</term>, of which he had to be purged in this circle. Which, nonetheless, he shows was not present except after he had understood the reasons, and then only for a short time. This matches what we said above regarding the poet's sloth, which, because of his profound and diligent thought and contemplation in the deep sciences, was small and rare. **BUT THIS SLEEPINESS was taken from me**: he sets down the form of the purging and the penalty that the slothful bore, which is most appropriate, because every contrary is cured by its contrary. Therefore, negligence and laziness are purged [by rapid movement].

<summary>Virgil concludes his discourse on free will as the basis of morality before they are interrupted by the souls of the slothful. Dante also provides an astronomical description of the waning moon rising late over the terrace of Purgatory.</summary>

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on free will and the nature of love. Dante and Virgil are now on the Fourth Terrace of Purgatory, where the sin of Sloth (accidia) is purged. The previous page ended with Virgil explaining that humans have the power to restrain improper desires. This page transitions into the physical manifestation of the cure for sloth: frenetic, purposeful movement.</meta>

# CANTO XVIII

> And just as Ismenus and Asopus once saw
> along their banks at night a fury and a crowd,
> provided the Thebans had need of Bacchus,
> So along that circle, their pace quickens,
> from what I saw of those coming toward us,
> whom good will and righteous love bestride.

<column-break/>

...with speed. And it shows that he [Dante] was also excited and awakened; because in truth, not only him, but any lazy man, seeing speed in others, begins to do the same. **AND JUST AS ISMENUS**. These people went with no less speed than the Thebans went along the Ismenus and Asopus—rivers of Boeotia, where Thebes is located—when they sacrificed to Bacchus. Bacchus, as the poets feign, was the son of Jove and of Semele, the daughter of Cadmus, King 

---

of Thebes. And this union was so annoying to Juno that, having changed herself into an old woman under the guise of charity, she said to Semele: "Many men deceive women by pretending to be a god when they are not. And perhaps this same thing is happening to you. I advise you, therefore, that when Jove returns, you ask him to grant you whatever you request. And then ask him to join with you in the same manner that he is accustomed to doing with Juno." The young girl believed Juno’s fraud. And she asked Jove to be content to please her with whatever she asked. Jove swore to do so. But once he understood her demand, he repented having sworn. But since it was not permitted to break the oath, he went to heaven and returned adorned with lightning and thunderbolts, though he chose the smaller ones. The mortal woman could not endure such tumult and heat, but was burned to ashes. Bacchus was still in his mother’s womb, and the time for birth had not yet come. But Jove tied the infant to his own thigh until the ninth month arrived. And because he was delivered twice—first from his mother and then from his father—he was called <term>dityrambos</term> <note>original: "dityrambos". A Greek term for a choral hymn to Bacchus, interpreted here by the commentator as "twice-born" (from *dis* "twice" and *thyra* "door/gate").</note>. The Thebans adored him because he was the inventor of wine. In these sacrifices, the women were filled with a frenzy. Instead of staying in temples, they ran along the rivers Asopus and Ismenus with lit torches and staves wrapped in vine leaves, invoking the many names of Bacchus with loud voices. Therefore, these souls—who were purging their sloth with speed because they had previously lived in total laziness—now ran, and despite the silence of the mountain, they spoke loudly. **HAD NEED**: they had need of his help. **QUICKENS HIS STEP**: <note>original: "suo passo falca"</note> bends his step. This is because they did not leave the circle, but by circling continuously, they constantly bent and curved their path. *Falcare* means to bend, a word derived from *falce* (sickle), which is bent and curved. **WHOM GOOD WILL**. i.e., those whom righteous love bestrides through a good will; as if to say they are carried along by righteous love.

The poet introduces these examples with great prudence: first, those in front to encourage speed, and then those behind to demonstrate how much harm is caused by delay. The first examples cause a man to leave his sloth and return to study and fervor. And the righteous examples keep us there, so that we 

> Soon they were upon us, because running
> came that whole great crowd,
> and two in front cried out in tears:
> "Mary ran with haste to the mountain,"
> and "Caesar, to subjugate Ilerda,
> pricked Marseilles and then ran into Spain."
> "Haste, haste, let time not be lost
> through little love," cried the others following,
> "so that zeal for doing well may renew grace."

<column-break/>

do not fall again into sleepiness, tedium, and sloth. Therefore, weeping—which signifies repentance for past sloth and slowness in acting virtuously—they cried out. This signifies a spurring of the mind. For whoever wishes to return to true fervor, or lead others to it, reproves and awakens them by recalling all the examples that can spur us on. **MARY RAN** with haste to the mountain. When Herod, in order to kill Christ—whom he had learned from the Magi was born—commanded that all those born from two years old and under should be killed. Wherefore Mary, advised by the angel to flee to Egypt, carried her son Jesus with the utmost speed 

---

upon an ass, running toward the mountains and passing them quickly. <note>The commentator here blends the "Visitation" to Elizabeth (the biblical source for Mary "running to the mountain") with the "Flight into Egypt."</note> **AND CAESAR** departed from Rome with extreme speed. Caesar did this to crush Pompey’s armies in Spain, whom he had already broken in Thessaly and turned to flight toward Egypt. And although Marseilles, a city of Provence, tried to delay him, he was not overcome. He left Brutus there to besiege it and ran into Spain, where he defeated Afranius, Petreius, and a son of Pompey. Ilerda is a city in Spain <note>Modern-day Lérida.</note>. **HASTE, HASTE**: This shows how much efficacy a good example has. Because of the words of the first two, all the others cry out "haste, haste, let time not be lost." Our life is short; therefore, it is necessary to compensate for its brevity with our own speed. **FOR LITTLE LOVE**: because of the slowness of sloth, which is nothing other than a deficiency of love, as was shown above. **THAT ZEAL** in doing well. i.e., the diligence and velocity of doing good "renews" in us—that is, it makes the grace of God be born again and return, which had dried up in us because of sin. And certainly, the more a man forces himself to do good, the more God is inclined to help him.

**FOR TEPIDITY:** for sloth: which is nothing other than a lack of ardent charity. **I DO NOT LIE TO YOU:** I do not tell you a falsehood. **AS LONG AS THE SUN SHINES:** because as we have shown, without the sun <note>In the Divine Comedy, the sun often represents Divine Grace or the light of Reason</note> one can turn back and wander in the same place, but one cannot move upward.

<column-break/>

"O people in whom sharp fervor now 
perhaps redeems your negligence and delay 
shown by your tepidity in doing good, 
This one who lives—and I certainly do not lie to you— 
wishes to go up, as long as the sun shines; 
so tell us where the opening is near." 
These were the words of my leader; 
and one of those spirits said: "Come 
behind us, and you will find the gap. 
We are so filled with the desire to move 
that we cannot stop; therefore, forgive us 
if you take our justice for rudeness. 
I was the Abbot of San Zeno in Verona 
under the empire of the good Barbarossa, 
of whom Milan still speaks with sorrow. 
And there is one who already has one foot in the grave 
who will soon weep for that monastery, 
and will be sad for having had power there; 
Because his son—deformed in his whole body, 
and worse in his mind, and born base— 
he has put in the place of its true shepherd." 
I do not know if he said more or then fell silent, 
for he had already raced so far beyond us; 
but this I heard, and it pleased me to remember it.

<column-break/>

**I WAS THE ABBOT**: This man was a contemporary of Dante named Alberto, a man of good character but very remiss. <note>The speaker is likely Gherardo II, Abbot of San Zeno from 1163 to 1187.</note> Zeno was the eighth bishop in Verona: a man of holy life, excellent character, and profound theology, as clearly appears in several volumes written by him. **BARBAROSSA**: Frederick I of Swabia, called Barbarossa <note>Barbarossa means "Redbeard" in Italian.</note> from his color, held the Empire for thirty-seven years. At first a friend to the Church, he later became an enemy to Alexander III, a native of Siena, and was excommunicated by him. He waged terrible wars in Italy against the Lombards who favored the Pope. He destroyed Spoleto; he moved Lodi; he built Crema. He took Milan by siege in the year of salvation 1162. He burned it all and destroyed it; he plowed it and sowed salt there. And they say that eighty-two thousand men of this city went into exile. He committed a very great slaughter of the Romans, which is why the Pope fled terrified to Venice. And the Doge, in favor of the Church, raised a great fleet against Henry, the son of Frederick, captured him, and brought him to Venice. Seeing his fortune changed, and seeing the favor that Alexander had from Louis, King of France, and from Henry, King of England, and from William, the excellent King of Sicily, and from the Venetians and the Lombards, Frederick determined to humble himself to the Pontiff and ask for peace. He came to the feet of the Pope, who, pressing his throat with his feet, said the verses of the Psalmist: "I shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and I shall trample the lion and the dragon." <note>original: "Super aspidem et basylicum ambulabo: et conculcabo leonem: et draconem." (Psalm 91:13)</note> To which words Frederick responded: "Not to you, but to Peter." The Pope said: "To both me and Peter." <note>original: "Non tibi: sed Petro" ... "et mihi et petro." This famous anecdote illustrates the power struggle between the Papacy and the Holy Roman Empire.</note> After this reconciliation, Frederick, as satisfaction for the injuries done to the Church, 

---

crossed with his armies into Syria against the infidels. But being in Antioch, while bathing in the river during the great heat, he drowned. Milan remained destroyed for five years. **AND THERE IS ONE WHO ALREADY HAS**: This proverb is used for those who are already close to death. He refers to Master Alberto dalla Scala, Lord of Verona, who more by force than by righteous means made one of his sons—who was crippled and of wicked character—the abbot of the aforementioned monastery. Thus he says "deformed in body and worse in mind." **AND BORN BASE**: because he was born of adultery. **HE HAS PUT IN THE PLACE** of its true shepherd. For the abbot ought to be the true shepherd of the monastery. But this man, greedy and rapacious, was not its true shepherd, but a wolf. **I DO NOT KNOW IF** he said more. This is meant to show the great speed with which the Abbot hurried away. For in this brief time in which he spoke what we have seen, he was already so far from Dante that Dante could not hear if he spoke more or if he was silent.

---

<column-break/>

Just as two preceded the crowd with examples to urge them to speed, so these two came behind with other examples, drawing them away from laziness. **AND THAT WHICH HAD HELPED ME** in every need—that is, in every necessity. For reason is that which helps man.

> And he who had been my help in every need 
> said: "Turn this way and see two 
> coming, giving a bite to sloth." 
> Behind all of them, they said: "First were 
> dead the people for whom the sea opened, 
> before the Jordan saw their heirs."

<column-break/>

**COMING** giving a bite to sloth—that is, they were rebuking it. For sloth is the mother of idleness, the nurse of lust, and the delayer of every good work. An enemy of labor, it weighs down the soul and binds the limbs. It rots in the bosom of laziness and without any study. **FIRST WERE** dead the people for whom the sea opened. The meaning is that the people of Israel, for whom the Red Sea opened as they fled Egypt, died <note>The Israelites who complained in the desert were not permitted to enter the Promised Land (the land across the Jordan), a classic biblical example of spiritual sloth and lack of faith.</note>

There was no people who sinned more in sloth <term>Accidia: spiritual apathy or laziness, considered a capital sin</term> or was more ungrateful toward their benefactor, God. He had liberated them from the harsh servitude of Pharaoh with most manifest miracles, which he showed through Moses. They were fed with manna in the desert for forty years, and they received many other benefits. And nonetheless, they were so wicked that often, to flee hardships and toil, and out of extreme laziness, they wanted to turn back; and many times they wanted to kill their leader Moses. **THE PEOPLE** who were more than six hundred thousand males: for whom the sea opened, and they passed through on dry land; and then, as Pharaoh followed them through that opening with his army, it closed again and drowned them all. **AND SHE WHO** did not endure the hardship: the meaning is, those people who, coming with the son of Anchises—who was Aeneas—did not endure the hardship of the journey all the way to Italy; and for this reason, they offered themselves to a life without glory. During the funeral rites that Aeneas celebrated for his father in Sicily, Juno—the enemy of the Trojans—transformed herself into an old woman named Beroe, who was a woman of authority. She lamented with the other women the unhappiness of those people who had already been wandering for seven years through so many seas and still could not reach Italy. And with a long speech, she persuaded them that, being in Sicily where Acestes their compatriot was, they should burn the ships. This was so that their husbands, unable to repair the new vessels, would establish their seats on that island and finally find rest. The women obeyed and set the ships on fire. Aeneas and the others came to help, but they could not arrive in time before four ships had burned. Aeneas decided to leave part of his people with Acestes. Therefore, those stayed behind who were more slothful and those who cared less for glory.

Having parted from the souls he was thinking of, the poet entered into new thoughts. And from these first ones, many others and different ones were born. He says this because, having investigated the purgation of four

already stated sins, he was now investigating that of the others. And because our investigation proceeds with reasoning—that is, with the discourse of reason—he demonstrates such discourse moving from thought to thought. **AND I WANDERED SO MUCH** from one to another. It was still night; and because we have said that without the sun one cannot ascend—which is to acquire some new knowledge—he says that he wandered—that is <note>original: "i." (id est)</note>, he roamed with his mind from thought to thought. And nonetheless, all were vain because he did not find the truth; and for this reason, he fell asleep out of "wandering desire"—that is, because of that wandering discourse. 

<column-break/>

Because whenever, after much discourse, we do not find the truth, the fatigue and boredom generate sleep. And the thoughts that were in us while waking are converted into a dream. All of which things, if we note them well, are not foreign to sloth, of which we are presently speaking.

### CANTO XIX OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE

**H**e has treated until now four spiritual and diabolical vices: which proceed from malice. These are Pride, Envy, Vainglory <note>The commentator includes Vainglory here, though in Dante's structure, the fourth vice is Sloth; he likely views Vainglory as a branch of the spiritual sins</note>, and Sloth. Now three follow: which are born more from the senses than from reason: and they are corporeal and voluptuous. But in this nineteenth canto the poet presents a vision: which appeared to him in a dream: and afterward he arrives at the stairs: which lead to the fifth circle: in which Avarice is purged. But first he describes the time, saying: **AT THE HOUR THAT THE DIURNAL HEAT** can no longer warm the light of the moon: where it is to be noted: that the reflection

of the rays of the sun: which, striking the earth, reverberate upwards: warming the air. Then, once night has come, the air begins to grow cold due to the departure of the sun: and by the rays of the moon: which are cold because the moon has no light of its own: but receives it from the sun: and it reflects the rays received from the sun downwards: and every reflection directed downwards produces cold: just as that which is directed upwards produces heat. Nevertheless, until midnight the air retains some of the day's heat: but afterward the rays of the moon overcome the heat in such a way: that the further the night goes, the more the cold increases: because the diurnal heat has no more power: and the moon is helped by the earth: which is cold and dry. And sometimes it is helped by Saturn. Because when Saturn gives its vigor to the moon: because it is a cold and dry planet: it greatly increases the lunar cold. Wherefore Alan the astrologer <note>Alanus de Insulis (Alan of Lille), a 12th-century scholar and poet</note> writes of Saturn:
> Here with its chill it steals the joys of spring, / and steals the beauty from the meadows and the stars from the flowers. <note>original: "Hic algore suo furatur gaudia ueris. Furaturque decus pratis et sidera florum."</note>
He describes therefore the morning time: which is near to the day: in which, as we showed in the first canticle, dreams are true. **WHEN THE GEOMANCERS.** He describes the same time in another way. Because geomancers practice their art in the morning time: when the dawn comes: because at that time the human soul and body are more obedient to celestial inclinations. # CANTO XIX

free will. Second, from the will moved by some passion: such as from too much fullness or emptiness of the stomach, or from too much dissolution of the humors, or a deficiency of the vital spirits. Third, from natural inclination: which is caused by the movements of the heavens. And this last one alone possesses the power of divination. Therefore, the geomancer <note>A practitioner of geomancy, a method of divination using patterns of points</note>, wishing to exclude the first two in favor of the third, requires that the points be made without counting them or thinking about them, so that they are not chosen by our own will, but according to celestial inclination. And to counter the second cause, he chooses the morning time, in which the soul and body are more sober: neither too full nor too empty. Geomancy is a type of divination which the Easterners practiced especially around the dawn upon the shores; sixteen rows are made, not of lines, but of random points, not numbered by the one who makes them. Then they are divided into four parts, so that each part has four rows; and they pair the points of the row in such a way that in the last row there remains either an even number or a single point. And from every set of four, they take the final parts and create a figure. The names of the figures are: *Joy, Sadness, Greater Fortune, Lesser Fortune, Gain, Loss, White, Red, Conjunction, Prison, People, Way, Boy, Girl, Head, Tail*.

### GREATER FORTUNE
This figure mentioned above is similar to a constellation of stars found at the end of Aquarius and the beginning of Pisces. Therefore, if the sun was then rising with Aries, it follows that the figure of "Greater Fortune"—which is at the beginning of Pisces and rises about an hour before Aries—would appear in the East at dawn, which is about an hour before the sun. **THERE CAME TO ME IN A DREAM** a stuttering woman. Because the three vices that follow are due to excessive and immoderate love of temporary goods—which are not truly good but false—the poet intends to demonstrate through this vision the false happiness that results from them. To do this, he imagines a woman with five defects: she speaks distortedly because she stutters and babbles; she sees distortedly because she is cross-eyed; she walks with a limp; and similarly, she performs manual tasks imperfectly because she is maimed; and finally, she is of an ugly color. False happiness consists of these five things: Riches, Dominions, Honors, Fame, and Corporeal Pleasure. Thus, she is "stuttering," meaning she babbles and does not speak clearly, because the fame of such things is imperfect, or rather, it is infamy. Being cross-eyed signifies the imperfection of honors; hence it is contrary to that Virgilian verse: *and breathed upon his eyes the joyful light of honor* <note>original: "et laetos oculis afflarat honores"</note>. And she is "crippled" to show that men who sustain and support themselves with riches are like those who support their bodies on a lame foot. And because temporal dominions have imperfect and vicious operations, she is "maimed," for we have said that the hands signify operations. The sallow and pale color demonstrates carnal pleasures, which consist mostly of colors and beauties. He treats, therefore, of immoderate love toward false goods, in which there is either only the desire (and then comes Avarice), or both desire and action (which belongs to the sense of taste, giving rise to Gluttony, or to the sense of touch, giving rise to Lust). **I LOOKED AT HER.** The meaning is that while he was looking at this woman, it happened that—just as the rays of the sun comfort and straighten the limbs of animals and plants which the night cold had withered—so Dante's gaze straightened the limbs of that woman and restored her color in such a way that she remained a beautiful woman. This signifies that Dante (representing sensuality), looking at these worldly goods, judges them to be beautiful with his false judgment. Thus, our false opinion makes them beautiful. **AS LOVE WILLS.** Because the inordinate love we place in these goods makes them appear as what they are not, and as we would wish them to be. And this proceeds because, despising divine things, we place all our care in earthly things. Hence the Psalmist says: *My soul clings to the dust* <note>original: "adhesit pauimento anima mea"</note>; and John in the Apocalypse: *Woe to those who dwell on the earth* <note>original: "ue habitantibus in terra"</note>; and Luke in the Gospel, when he describes the infirmity of the woman who could not look upward.

Once the woman was free from every distortion, and especially once her tongue was loosened, she began to sing in such a way that her song so delighted Dante that he could hardly have turned his *intento*—that is, his intention and affection—away from her. This signifies that once temporal goods, which

This woman, singing, claimed to be a Siren. In order that this be clearly understood: the poets imagine that the Sirens were three daughters of the river Achelous and of Calliope, named so from a Greek verb that means "to bind" and "to retain," and not "to pull" as many say; for the poets use them to represent corporeal pleasures and the delights of worldly things, which entangle and bind our senses in such a way that we do not know how to leave them. And although there is much variety in their number and names, nevertheless the most learned identify three sirens: Parthenope, Leucosia...

<column-break/>

and Ligeia <note>original: "Ligia," one of the Sirens of Greek mythology</note>: they say they inhabited certain rocks in Sicily near Mount Pelorus. They sang so sweetly that they drew sailors to them with the sweetness of their song, and then they devoured them in such a way that nothing remained but bones. Homer adds that Ulysses, sailing through those seas and fearing the song would draw him to go to them, had himself bound to the mast of the ship; and so as not to hear, he plugged his ears with wax. And certainly, it is true: the false delights of worldly and transitory things draw us to love them with their sweet flatteries, and then they devour us. For such pleasures take from us the strength of the body, the goods of fortune, and the wisdom of the soul. Because of this, men <unclear>remain</unclear> unhealthy, poor, infamous, without reputation, and without learning.

But Ulysses—that is, the wise man—so that the flatteries of these pleasures do not draw him in, has himself bound to the mast of the ship, which signifies the temperance of the soul. This temperance holds him back so that he does not fall into pleasures. The wax with which he plugs his ears is the fortitude that arms him against the furious impulses of sensuality. Thus, he passes near the Sirens but is not captured by them, because the wise man, having already made a habit of virtue, cannot be defiled by vices. 

See then why Dante calls this a Siren, and why, although she is ugly, she becomes beautiful when Dante (representing <term>Sensuality</term> <note>In this context, "Sensuality" refers to the lower, physical appetites and perceptions of the human soul</note>) looks at her. **THAT SAILORS** in the midst of the sea go astray: we previously established the sea as appetite. Therefore, the sailors are those who let themselves be carried away by appetite, and these are the ones whom worldly pleasures flatter and attract. **I TURNED ULYSSES**. Perhaps he was moved because our first impulses are not in our power, and even the wise struggle at times when they see something voluptuous. Hence Solomon said: *Wine and women make even the wise man fall away* <note>original: "Vinum et mulier apoſtatat ſapientem," a reference to Ecclesiasticus 19:2</note>. 

But I believe the poet induces the Siren to speak falsely because it is the nature of voluptuous and intemperate men, when they wish to corrupt others, to bring up examples of great and famous men. They say that Solomon, David, Hercules, and many others allowed themselves to be conquered by a woman, and Alexander the Great by wine. **AND WHOEVER ABIDES WITH ME**: <gloss>he who frequents me</gloss>. That is, those who make a habit of the pleasures of earthly goods rarely depart or extricate themselves from them. **UNTIL ENTIRELY** satisfied: <gloss>all his desire is filled</gloss>, in such a way that he no longer thinks of great and celestial things. This is the ultimate misery. For whoever is with the Sirens and is nonetheless not content with their songs, there is hope that eventually he will depart and seek truer goods—indeed, the truest goods—and leave these false ones behind.

**NOT YET WAS** her mouth closed. False happiness was still drawing sensuality to itself when another lady—who is Philosophy—came to the aid of the first to refute the vain pleasures, and with fierce words says to Virgil: "Who is this?" It is as if she reproaches Virgil for not driving her away from Dante, because it is the office of <term>Reason</term> <note>Represented by Virgil</note> to remove every desire for non-virtuous things from the senses. And Virgil (Reason) looked upon Philosophy and tore the clothes of the other woman [the Siren]. Pleasures are like an ugly body that appears beautiful because it is adorned with very beautiful garments. Therefore, Reason, by tearing the clothes of this pleasure, reveals her ugliness; and by opening her belly, makes her stench appear. For truly, whoever searches the interior of these vices and every pleasure finds nothing but ugliness and corruption.

<br/>

**AT LEAST THREE VOICES**. We can understand that Reason awakens the senses by exciting the memory, so that it remembers. Likewise with the intellect, so that it understands that it is a man and not a beast; and with the will, to do what it understands. **SO I ROSE** shows that the senses, excited by the intellect, become obedient to it and can rise; and especially they could do so now that the sun had risen, which illuminated all the circles of the mountain. **AND WE WENT** with the new sun: as if with new speculation, because they recognized that these three following vices proceed from a different origin than the four already passed. **AND FOLLOWING HIM**, that is, Virgil, I carried my brow near the back of Virgil. This signifies that he bowed his head almost onto Virgil’s back, as one does who bears a heavy load of thoughts. In this form, it shows that the senses are sustained by Reason. **WHEN I** heard. Having reached the stairs from which one climbed somewhat...

The passage concludes with Dante and Virgil ascending the mountain as the sun rises, representing new intellectual clarity.</summary>

# CANTO XIX <note>The original header incorrectly labels this as Canto XVIII, but the text and commentary clearly describe the events of Canto XIX.</note>

> He moved his wings and fanned us,
> affirming that "those who mourn" are blessed, <note>original: "qui lugent," referring to the Beatitude "Beati qui lugent" (Blessed are those who mourn), as they will be comforted. This represents the purging of Sloth.</note>
> for their souls shall be masters of consolation.

The comfort of those who were purging themselves. The Angel and the two wings. They walked between two walls—that is, walls of solid rock <note>original: "matigno," a type of hard, grey Tuscan sandstone</note>—because it was in the middle; that is, on the path of virtue, having a wall on every side.

Dante walked with his head bowed toward the ground. This denotes that his sensuality <term>sensualità: the part of the soul driven by physical senses and desires</term> was enticed by the song of worldly pleasures. Although Virgil had shown him the Siren's stinking belly and pulled him away from it, he was nonetheless still weighed down by the greed for such goods, and so he looked at the earth; that is, his thoughts were on earthly pleasures. Therefore, he confessed to Virgil, his guide who was reproaching him, that this new vision—which appeared as false happiness—still bent his thoughts toward it.

> "What ails you, that you seem to gaze toward the earth?"
> my guide began to say to me,
> shortly after both had climbed above the angel.
> And I: "With such suspicion I am made to go
> by a new vision that bends me to itself,
> so that I cannot leave the thought of it."
> "You saw," he said, "that ancient witch
> who alone is now the cause of weeping above us;
> you saw how man unties himself from her.
> Let it suffice you, and strike your heels upon the ground;
> turn your eyes to the lure that is spun
> by the eternal King with the great wheels."

First, Virgil says "strike your heels upon the ground"—that is, proceed in virtuous action or, truly, trample upon worldly desires. Then he gives the second command, saying: "TURN YOUR EYES." Turn your thoughts and reflections to the "recall" <note>The poet uses a metaphor from falconry: the lure.</note> that God makes to us, inspiring us with His grace. This is a metaphor from falconers, who, by spinning a lure <term>logoro: a tool made of feathers used to call back a falcon</term>, call the hawk. Turn your eyes, therefore, to the lure which the eternal God spins with the "great wheels" of the heavens, which, by their turning, show us eternal beauties.

First he used the falconer’s metaphor, and now he uses a comparison: he says that just as the falcon, when it feels the cry of the falconer showing it the lure, first looks down at its feet and then stretches itself toward the lure because it believes there is food there which it desires; so did I at the words of Virgil.

> As the falcon, which first looks at its feet,
> then turns to the cry and stretches forward
> through desire for the food that draws it there,
> So I became; and so, as far as the rock is split
> to provide a path for those who go up,
> I went until I reached the start of the circling.
> When I was set free in the fifth circle,
> I saw people within it who were weeping,
> lying on the ground, all turned face down.
> "My soul cleaves to the dust," <note>original: "Adhesit pavimento anima mea," from Psalm 119:25.</note>
> I heard them say with such deep sighs
> that the word could hardly be understood.

My soul—which should have raised itself to the love of celestial things—has remained stuck to the love of earthly goods.

<column-break/>

circle: they found the Angel who, with the sweetest words, said: "Come, here is the pass," and with his wings he fanned Dante's forehead, absolving him of Sloth. And he said "Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted" <note>original: "beati qui lugēt quoniam ipfi confolabuntur"</note> as it is written in Matthew; and this was to signify what we said above: now the senses are so strengthened that, by going through the obstacle of not falling into any extremes, the appearance of happiness bends the soul toward itself. And he rightly says "bends" <note>original: "piega"</note>: because just as virtue guides us straight, so conversely this vision bends us and makes us twist away, so that we cannot detach our thoughts from it.

"YOU SAW THAT ancient witch": the common folk say that "witches" <note>original: "streghe"</note> are old women who transform into various animal forms and then suck the blood of children. Thus, he calls this false happiness a "witch" because it sucks out our spirits and senses. And he comforts Dante to climb, because he has passed the four major vices, and only this one remains for him, which contains Avarice, Gluttony, and Lust.

"YOU SAW HOW MAN unties himself from her": that is, how he frees himself. And Virgil has already demonstrated this to him when he tore her clothing. "LET IT SUFFICE YOU": it should be enough for us to flee this witch now that reason has shown us how we can untie ourselves from her. "AND STRIKE": Two precepts given by reason: as far as the rock is split—that is, as much as the cliff opens to make a staircase for those who wish to climb to the fifth circle; and I went until the end and the summit of that staircase where the "circling" begins—that is, where the terrace starts, which forms a circle.

"AND AS I WAS set free in the fifth circle": that is, as soon as I exited the stairs and entered the terrace, I SAW people in it who were weeping, repenting with contrition for their sins, and they lay prostrate on the ground—that is, with their faces turned downward. By this, he denotes the punishment of the avaricious: because of their greed for earthly things, they are deprived of the sight and vision of heavenly things, which are the true good. These people, weeping, recognized their error and said: "My soul cleaves to the dust." This is a verse [from the Psalms] and it means my soul remains stuck to the pavement and the soil of the earth—that is, the soul...

**A**nd he to me: "Why our backs are turned toward heaven you shall know; but first, <note>original: "scias quod ego sum successor petri"</note> know that I am a successor of Peter. But when I was made the Roman Shepherd, then I discovered the lying life. I saw that there the heart found no rest, nor could one climb higher in that life; wherefore the love of this one was kindled in me. Until 그 moment, I was a wretched soul, parted from God, wholly avaricious; now, as you see, I am punished here."

<column-break/>

grace bears the penalty in peace: which is given to him justly, and through that, he hopes—once purged—that he will become blessed. IF YOU COME SECURE FROM LYING DOWN. One of the souls responds: if you come free from lying down, as we lie, and you wish to climb further ahead: let your right hands always be ON THE OUTSIDE. That is, on the exterior. The meaning is: turn yourselves to your right hand, and thus the mountain will always remain to your left, and the right will remain on the outside. Thus then Virgil asked, and thus the soul responded. Wherefore I noticed—that is, I understood—the "other" was hidden from him: namely, that I was alive. Or truly, I noticed that the "other" was hidden from him which I desired to know: namely, who he was, and why they are purged here. AND I TURNED my eyes to the eyes. The meaning is that Virgil perceived, by looking at me, what I desired.

**A**FTER I COULD act according to my own mind. According to true reason, the appetite is subject to the intellect, nor can it extend itself further toward anything without the judgment of the latter. Whence it follows that one cannot act in one's own way, except when the intellect concedes it. IN WHOM weeping matures: in which weeping matures—that is, hastens it—namely, penance and purgation, without which one cannot—that is, it is impossible to—return to God.

**W**HY OUR BACKS and our rears: and our kidneys. KNOW THAT I AM: know that I am. SUCCESSOR OF PETER: successor of Peter—that is, the Pope. This was Master Ottobuono da Fiesco, a gentleman of Genoa; and those of Fiesco <note>The Fieschi family</note> were Counts of Lavagna, so named from a river which runs in the Riviera of Genoa between Sestri and Chiavari. He was made Pope Adrian IV <note>The text says Adrian IV, but the historical figure was Adrian V, who reigned briefly in 1276.</note> in the year of our salvation 1276. And he lived in the Apostolic See for one month and nine days. ONE MONTH AND A LITTLE more I proved how the great mantle weighs: that is, the pontifical dignity. ON HIM WHO KEEPS IT FROM THE MUD: that is, on him who maintains it without vice. And not without reason does he bring these words to Adrian. Because he used to say: that the See of Peter was full of thorns, and his mantle weighed so much that it broke even the sturdiest shoulder. And certainly, the pontificate is—to him who rules it well—the highest honor; a most heavy weight; a wretched servitude; extreme labor. And to him who rules it badly: it is the highest danger to the soul, and the highest infamy. SO THAT ALL OTHER BURDENS SEEM: that all other burdens seem and represent themselves as lesser.

**BUT ONCE I WAS MADE** the Roman shepherd, I discovered how life is a lie. Before I was Pope, I hoped that if I ever reached such a rank, I would be content and satisfied with riches. Afterward, desiring even more and being unable to climb any higher, I realized this life of ours is a lie; because it gives hope to the greedy man that he might at some point be satisfied, and yet he never is. And for this reason, having abandoned the greed for earthly goods, I turned toward the heavenly ones.

What avarice does is here declared
in the purging of converted souls,
and the mountain has no more bitter pain.
Just as our eyes were not opened
upward, fixed instead on earthly things,
so justice here has submerged them in the earth.
As avarice extinguished all good within
our love, whereby our works were lost,
so justice here holds us bound.
In feet and in hands tied and taken,
and as long as it shall please the Just King,
so shall we stay, motionless and outstretched.

<column-break/>

**HE DEMONSTRATES** the punishment that the greedy endure. Nor is it an absurd statement to say that the Mountain of Purgatory has no more bitter pain. **JUST AS**, so the text ordains. Just as our eyes, fixed on earthly things, did not open toward the heights, so justice submerged them—that is, sank them—here to the earth. As avarice extinguished our love—that is, every fervor that the soul has for doing good. **WHEREBY OUR WORKS WERE LOST**—that is, whereby every good deed is lost and extinguished—so justice holds us tightly here with hands and feet bound. I do not expand here on the denunciation of avarice, because I have written many things about it in various places in the *Inferno*.

**FOR THIS** sole purpose he wrote the four triplets placed above: so that everyone might understand that at death every human dignity ceases. It is of no more value to have been Pope than a hired laborer in terms of rank. **FELLOW SERVANT** I am. Take these words from the Book of Revelation <note>original: "apolalypse"</note>. Where it is written that when John the Evangelist knelt at the feet of the Angel, the Angel refused such honor, saying: "See that you do not do it: I am your fellow servant and of your brothers who have the testimony of Jesus" <note>original: "Vide ne feceris: coferuus tuus sum et fratrum tuorum habentium testimonium Hieſu"</note>. **THEY NEITHER MARRY** <note>original: "NEQVE NVBENT"</note> you gave heed to. He proves by another example that in the other life every human dignity ceases, as Matthew the Evangelist notes in the twenty-second chapter: when the disciples asked about the woman who had several husbands, whose she would be in the next life. Christ replied: "You err, knowing neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels in heaven" <note>original: "erratis neſcientes ſcripturas nec uirtutem dei. In reſurrectione enim neque nubent: neque nubentur. Sed erunt ſicunt angeli in celo"</note>. And by this he meant that in the future life we shall all be equal.

### . CANTO XX . OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE .

**HE** continues to treat the subject of avarice; and in the beginning, he shows that although he was eager to hear more things, he nonetheless departed from the spirit who had dismissed him: **AGAINST A BETTER** <note>original: "CONTRO AMIGLOR"</note> **will, the will fights poorly.** When there are two differing wills, the one that is less good fights poorly—that is, it fights badly and resists against the better one. And therefore he, whose desire was to learn from the spirit that which was not of great importance, chose to yield to the spirit's will, which was better because the spirit desired to purge himself of the vice of avarice. He follows this precept accordingly: whenever we choose to be overcome by better reason, we will always align our own will with the will of others. **I DREW FROM THE WATER THE SPONGE NOT SATED**: an excellent metaphor to show that a man may depart while still thirsty for that which he desires to know. **I MOVED**: departing from the spirit. **MY LEADER**: who was waiting for me and was ahead of me. **MOVED**: preceding me. **THROUGH THE CLEARED PLACES**: that is, those not occupied by the souls who were lying down. **ALONG THE ROCK**: along the narrow stone, right against the mass, just as one walks narrowly along the battlements <note>term: "merli" - the notched parapets atop a castle wall</note> if walking atop a wall. They did this because the people who were weeping for the sin of avarice—which occupies the whole world—were approaching too closely on the other side. **ACCURSED BE YOU, ancient wolf.** Avarice began in the world as far back as Cain; according to the Master of Histories <note>Referring to Petrus Comestor, author of the *Historia Scholastica*, a popular medieval biblical commentary</note>, he was the one who discovered weights and measures. He was more intent on gain than was required, and his avarice was revealed in the first-fruits he offered to God. Therefore, it is the most ancient

It is a most fitting thing that those who desire to purge themselves of the vice of avarice—which is nothing other than the greed for treasures—should hold in their minds the examples of those who were content with little. Therefore, he first shows that the spirits of this place all at once invoked the name of Mary, as a woman does who is about to give birth. And they remembered how cheerfully she endured poverty, saying: "You were so poor, as is shown by the hostelry in which you gave birth to our Salvation." **O GOOD FABRICIUS.** <note>Gaius Fabricius Luscinus, a Roman consul famous for his austerity and for refusing bribes from the Samnites.</note> In all the purgings of these sins, he places examples that are not only Christian but also Gentile <note>non-Christian/Pagan</note>, because morality is common both to our religion and to theirs. Furthermore, a sinner might excuse themselves by claiming impossibility, because not everyone is lifted up to the grace to which Mary and many holy men were lifted. Such an excuse cannot be produced regarding the example of the Gentiles. Fabricius was in extreme poverty. Nor did he ever seek riches. But when the Samnite people—who were very hostile to the Romans—presented him with most ample gifts and begged him to receive them for his needs, he replied that as long as he could use his own limbs, he had no need for anything.

I, Dante, said: "O soul that speaks," that is, who speaks so well, "and renews," that is, brings back to memory these worthy praises, because you praise Mary and Fabricius and Nicholas worthily. **TELL ME WHO YOU WERE**, and if you tell me, your words "shall not be without reward," that is, without a prize. For I shall give you fame if I return to finish the "short journey," that is, to end the mortal life, which is brief and flies to its end. **AND HE**: understand that this Hugh responded. **I WILL TELL**: that which you ask, **NOT FOR COMFORT** that I expect from there: because those who are in the purging virtues do not care for mortal fame; **BUT BECAUSE GRACE** shines in you before you are dead. As if to say: "But because the grace that I see shining in you makes me deem you worthy of an answer." **I WAS THE ROOT OF THE EVIL PLANT**: I was the beginning of the new lineage of the kings of France, which he calls an "evil plant" because he wants to show that in that stock there were many wicked Kings. **THAT OVERSHADOWS ALL THE CHRISTIAN LAND.** "Uggia" is a shadow that is harmful. **BUT IF DOUAI, GHENT, LILLE, OR BRUGES.** These are lands in Flanders oppressed by the King of France. **JUDGES**: <note>original: "GIUGGIA"</note> He judges. **HUGH CAPET.** In France, according to some chronicles—which I neither approve nor condemn—the successors of the illustrious Charlemagne (who was called "the Great" for many outstanding deeds) reigned for many centuries. And the last...

Louis, who later became a saint <note>Saint Louis IX</note>, and his brother Charles <note>Charles I of Anjou</note>, to whom the Kingdom of Sicily fell, both took as wives two daughters of Raymond Berengar of Toulouse. Under the name of a dowry, they occupied all of Provence, as we shall say more clearly in the sixth canto of *Paradiso*. Therefore, the great Provencal dowry ensured that this House of Hugh was no longer considered to be of lowly lineage. **AND BY WAY OF REPARATION**

...worthy of the highest abomination of all ages. He speaks of Thomas Aquinas, a man inferior to none in life and optimal character. He was a treasure of every kind of doctrine, for which two things he could justly be called more than a man. Therefore, as much as he raised himself above human nature, so much did Charles submerge himself in a feral and bestial life through this wickedness. This vessel of innocence and wisdom was traveling to the general council in Lyon, France, without any suspicion. But the suspicious King, conscious of his own vices and fearing that Thomas, being good and free of speech, might manifest his failings, arranged for a physician close to Thomas to poison him. Thus died the ornament of our religion at the Abbey of Fossanova, truly a martyr, because he was killed for the truth, having intended not to keep silent about the impious government of Charles. But the Supreme Judge did not leave this unjust death without vengeance; for He willed that the King, puffed up by many victories, should see the rebellion of Sicily <note>The Sicilian Vespers of 1282</note> and the capture of his son. Whereupon he died of grief.

Some say it was Louis <note>Louis V, the last Carolingian king</note> who left a son of young age under the guardianship of Hugh Capet, who was born of a butcher in Paris, but was a Great Seneschal. Hugh, blinded by the desire to reign, plotted to remove the boy and made his own son King. Others say that Louis V died without a successor, and for this reason many wanted to transfer the kingdom to Charles, Duke of Lorraine, his uncle. Hugh occupied the kingdom with the favor of fortune and his friends.

He speaks ironically, because he makes "reparations" poorly who afterwards does worse than before. The aforementioned Charles made a victim of Conradin. Conradin was defeated by Charles and, on the advice of Alardo, fled to the Roman shore to go to Sicily. But captured by Giovanni Frangipani, a Roman, he was led to Naples; and there Charles had his head cut off in the square, and did the same to the Duke of Austria and many barons, and forbade them from being buried in a sacred place. And it is to be noted that although the poet later places this Charles in Purgatory as a defender of the Church, he nevertheless does not wish to overlook his vices, which were many. **PUSHED THOMAS back to heaven.** A supreme wickedness, and...

But of him we spoke in the sixth canto of the *Inferno*. Afterward, with Robert, son of Charles II, he prepared a great fleet against Sicily, and in a short time returned from there with an ignominious peace. ...and a despiser of riches. BUT WHEN

And some are enticed to this purgation by

Regarding this, Petrarch says: *And I saw Cyrus more greedy for blood / Than Crassus was for gold, and each had the other / So much that in the end each seemed bitter.* <note>original: "Et uidi cyrrho disangue piu auaro: Che craffo doro et l'un laltro nhebbe. striving to purge themselves of avarice begin to hold it

# CANTO XX

...as much as was permitted to my power.
When I felt the mountain tremble
like a thing that falls: whence a chill seized me
such as seizes him who goes to his death.
Surely Delos <note>The Greek island where Apollo and Diana were born; mythologically, it was a floating island until fixed in place.</note> was not shaken so strongly
before Latona made her nest in it
to give birth to the two eyes of heaven <note>The sun (Apollo) and the moon (Diana).</note>.
Then a cry began from every side,
such that the Master turned toward me
saying: "Do not doubt while I lead you."
"Glory to God in the highest" <note>original: "Gloria in excelsis deo"</note> they all
were saying, from what I understood nearby,
from where the cry could be heard.

Where the sun turned as its homeland: so that it moved no more. And he bound it with Gyaros and Mykonos, neighboring islands. The truth they wish it to be is that this island was often shaken by earthquakes. Wherefore the inhabitants went to the oracle of Apollo to ask for a remedy. And he commanded that certain sacrifices be made: and for the future, the dead should not be buried there. Therefore Apollo made it immobile: and that he bound it to Gyaros and Mykonos signifies that the men of those islands inhabited it. It was called first Asteria: afterwards Delos. Which in Greek signifies "clear" and "manifest": because returning to the surface it became manifest: or rather because Apollo gave manifest answers there. **SUCH THAT THE MASTER** turned toward me. **THEN BEGAN** from all sides a cry: Dante felt the mountain shake: and after such shaking he heard that all the spirits of that place with one voice sang: "Glory to God in the highest" <note>original: "Gloria in excelsis deo"</note>: which song the Church uses when with joy and gladness we return thanks to God. This hymn was sung by the angels at the birth of the Savior.

We remained immobile and in suspense
like the shepherds who first heard that song
until the trembling ceased and it was finished.
Then we resumed our holy path,
watching the shadows that lay upon the ground,
returned already to their accustomed weeping.
No ignorance ever with such great war
made me desirous of knowing,
if my memory does not err in this,
as it seemed to me then, thinking upon it;
nor because of the haste was I daring to ask,
nor could I see anything by myself.
Thus I went on, timid and pensive.

...to understand. **THERE.** i.e., in that place. It is easy for anyone in whom there is at least mediocre talent to notice how much this place requires that many and various things be said in detestation of avarice. Because if we could free human minds from such a pernicious disease, the life of mortals would be too happy: and all domestic and civil dissension would cease, as would every foreign war. Nor would we take up many laborious cares, all useless to us, which strip us of honor and peace, and deprive us of that leisure <note>term: "ocio" - referring here to the classical ideal of productive, contemplative rest.</note> which we could spend on things pertaining to our salvation. But if we collect what has been said in various places of this volume, perhaps the listener will feel partly satisfied.

<column-break/>

...they strove to overcome, i.e., to conquer the road, i.e., to pass it. When Dante felt such trembling in the mountain as usually happens with a thing that is about to fall, which first trembles and then drops. And he uses this comparison: that Delos did not shake so strongly when it was moved by earthquakes, before Latona—mother of Apollo and Diana, i.e., of the sun and the moon—gave birth there to the two eyes of heaven. Because the moon and the sun are like two eyes of heaven. Delos is one of the Cyclades islands, of which there is such a fable: Jove loved Asteria; she fled him, and obtained from the gods to be transformed into a quail. But Jove, wanting her to cross the sea, changed her into stone: whence she fell into the water and went to the bottom, where she stayed for a long time. Afterwards Jove, at the prayers of Latona his sister <note>In classical mythology, Latona (Leto) was a lover of Jupiter, not his sister.</note>, who conceived Phoebus and Diana by him, brought her back to the surface and made her an island, but a mobile one. In this island Latona gave birth to the sun and the moon.

<image-desc>A decorative blue drop-cap 'N' featuring white scrollwork and floral motifs.</image-desc> **We remained immobile:** we stayed without going any further. **AND IN SUSPENSE:** doubtful in mind. **LIKE THE SHEPHERDS** who first heard: thus we were stupefied; as were the shepherds to whom the angels, singing this canticle, announced that Christ was born. Whence they, descending from the mountains, heard him in the manger between the ox and the ass. **UNTIL THE TREMBLING CEASED:** until the shaking of the mountain stopped. **AND THAT finished:** and until that whole song was completed. Then we resumed our way, and the souls returned to their accustomed weeping. **NO IGNORANCE** ever [put] so much war: because naturally every man desires to know; it happens that ignorance of a thing, i.e., not knowing it, makes war on man: because it goads him and fights him to seek to know it. I did not dare ask Virgil, nor by myself could I...

<summary>This page depicts a sudden, terrifying earthquake on the mountain of Purgatory followed by the souls singing the "Gloria," which Dante compares to the shepherds at the Nativity. Landino’s commentary explains the earthquake through the Greek myth of Delos and provides a moral reflection on how greed destroys social peace.</summary>
