<meta>This page follows the dramatic earthquake and the collective singing of the "Gloria" by the souls on the terrace of Avarice. We now transition from the physical manifestation of the mountain’s joy to the arrival of a new companion, the poet Statius, who will explain these phenomena.</meta>

# CANTO XXI OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE.

### THE NOBLE SUBJECT MATTER: and nobly treated in this twenty-first canto. In which he sets forth: how as they follow their path they were joined by a soul, from whom they learned the cause of the shaking of the mountain and of the song of the souls. And finally they recognized this man to have been a poet; nor without the greatest pleasure did Virgil recognize him.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A large historiated initial 'L' containing a scene with two figures in a landscape, representing the meeting of Dante and Virgil with the spirit of Statius. The initial is framed in a square border with decorative elements.</image-desc>

The natural thirst that is never satisfied
except with the water for which the young 
Samaritan woman <note>A reference to the woman at the well in John 4:1-42, who asks Jesus for "living water."</note> asked for grace
troubled me, and the haste pricked me
along the obstructed way behind my leader,
and I grieved for the just vengeance <note>The punishment of the souls on the terrace of Avarice.</note>.
And behold, just as Luke describes to us:
that Christ appeared to two who along the way
had already gone out from the sepulchral tomb,
a shade appeared to us, and it came behind us,
looking from its feet at the crowd that lies there;
nor were we aware of it until it spoke first,
saying: "My brothers, may God give you peace."
We turned suddenly, and Virgil
returned to him the sign that is appropriate for that.

<column-break/>

**THE NATURAL THIRST.** He shows us that there can be an innate thirst and desire in man to know. And because the knowledge of divine things is that through which we are blessed, we cannot have this perfectly through our own industry nor by natural ways unless we are illuminated by the Holy Spirit. Which Christ indicated in the Gospel of Saint John, Chapter IV, when asking for a drink from the Samaritan woman at the well of Jacob; and she denying it to him, alleging that the Jews do not associate with Samaritans. He added: "if you knew who it is who asks you for a drink, you would have asked him, and he would have given you to drink from a water of a fountain that springs up into eternal life." <note>original: "fons aquae salientis in vitam aeternam"</note> The young woman, then, after many words, asked for the grace, and Christ filled her with the Holy Spirit. Therefore, most wisely, the poet shows at present that the natural thirst—that is, the natural desire for knowing and understanding—is never satisfied except with the water. Wherefore the young Samaritan woman asked for grace—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit. **IT TROUBLED ME.** <note>original: "mitravagliava"</note> This is a metaphor <term>translation: a figurative use of a word</term> from grain already threshed, which, so that it remains purged and clean, is "travailed"—that is, they make it pass from sieve to sieve <note>The commentator connects the word "travailed" (troubled) with "vagliare" (to sieve or winnow), suggesting a process of refinement.</note>; thus our soul, wishing to find the truth, goes on purging itself from time to time. **AND THE HASTE PRICKED ME** shows that at the same time the soul was eager to investigate the cause of the shaking of the mountain and the song of the souls, and the body had to hurry in following its journey. But Statius, arriving, explains that which neither Dante—that is, sensuality—nor Virgil—that is, human intellect, although illuminated by much learning—could understand by themselves. But Statius, who because of being accustomed to such things, explains them. And he puts Statius for the human intellect, which extends to comprehending that which cannot be understood by way of reason. And by comparison he shows, according to what Luke writes in the twenty-third chapter <note>The commentator likely means Luke 24, which describes Christ appearing to two disciples on the road to Emmaus.</note>.

<meta>This page continues the encounter with the spirit of Statius. Having just offered a greeting of peace, Statius now questions Virgil and Dante's presence, leading Virgil to explain Dante's mortal state and the purpose of their journey through the realms of the afterlife.</meta>

Just as Christ, recently resurrected and already "stolen"—meaning lifted out of the sepulchral pit or tomb—appearing on the road to two disciples who were walking toward Emmaus in the form of a pilgrim, declared many things from the sacred scripture: so Statius demonstrated to Dante the causes of the accidents already mentioned. **MAY GOD GIVE YOU PEACE** <note>original: "DIO VIDIA pace"</note>. The most excellent salutation: because nothing better can be requested than peace, in which our highest good consists. Whence also Christ said: "My peace I leave with you" <note>original: "pacem meam relinquo uobis" - John 14:27</note>.

Then he began in the blessed council:
"May the truthful court place you in peace,
which relegates me to eternal exile."
"How," he said, "and why do you travel so fast,
if you are not shades that God deigns to have above?
Who has escorted you so far up his stairs?"
My teacher said: "If you look at the signs
that this man carries, which the angel marked,
you will see well that he must reign with the good.
But because she who spins day and night
had not yet drawn all the wool from the distaff
that Clotho imposes on each and compiles,
his soul, which is your sister and mine,
coming up, could not come alone,
because it does not see in our manner.
Therefore I was drawn out of the impious throat
of Hell to show him, and I will show him
as far as my school can lead him."

He confirmed the grace and I give it <note>The translator or commentator acknowledges the text here</note>. And he is still in doubt. **COMING UP, IT COULD NOT COME ALONE**; regarding the literal sense, it is true that the soul still situated in the body does not travel through a country unknown to it. And regarding the allegory, the soul still wrapped in the body cannot contemplate incorporeal things like a soul that is already separated from the body. And therefore he says because "it does not see" or look, and does not **WATCH IN OUR MANNER** <note>original: "GVATA ALNOSTRO modo"</note>, that is, like those who are separated from the body. **WHEREFORE I WAS DRAWN OUT OF THE IMPIOUS THROAT** of Hell, which he finished describing above. And understand this allegorically: mortal doctrine, which treats virtue and vice, was drawn from the Gentiles <note>Referring to Classical/Pagan philosophy</note> **AS FAR AS MY SCHOOL CAN LEAD HIM**. For the philosophy of the Gentiles can lead through Hell and Purgatory; that is, it can give knowledge of vices and their damnation. And it can also demonstrate in what way a man can purge himself of them. But it does not lead to Heaven; that is, it does not lead to that true knowledge of divine and celestial things which comes from Christian theology. Therefore, because to achieve the highest good one must first purge the soul of every impurity, and then, with the soul thus purged and pure, go to the speculation of divine things, Gentile philosophy performs the first task, but cannot perform the second to perfection.

"But tell us, if you know, why such tremors
just now shook the mountain, and why all together
everyone seemed to shout down to its soft feet?"
So he asked me, threading the needle
of my desire, so that just with the hope,
my thirst became less fasted.
He began: "There is nothing here without
order within the religion
of the mountain, or that is outside of custom.
It is free here from every alteration;
only what heaven receives from itself into itself
can be a cause here, and no other.
Because neither rain, nor hail, nor snow..."

<column-break/>

In the **BLESSED COUNCIL**, in the blessed congregation of the saved. **THE TRUTHFUL COURT** <note>original: "LA VERACE Corte"</note>, the celestial court which is truthful because that is the true kingdom **WHICH**—referring to the court—**RELEGATES** or confines me because I was not a Christian. **HOW, HE SAID**, Statius asked: "If you are not shades **THAT GOD DOES NOT DEIGN ABOVE**," meaning those He does not consider worthy to stay in heaven. **WHO GOES SO** escorted, meaning so securely conducted. Statius should not have wondered that shades relegated to Hell could rise to salvation; furthermore, morally, he who has made a habit of vice can only with great difficulty come to the purgatorial virtues. **IF YOU LOOK AT** these signs, which are the seven "P"s <note>Representing the seven Peccata, or sins</note> which the angel had carved into his forehead. **BUT BECAUSE SHE WHO SPINS DAY AND NIGHT**, meaning life, whose course passes continuously day and night and never stops; and he means Lachesis. In the first Canticle we established three Fates: Clotho, who holds the distaff and signifies the beginning of life; Lachesis, who spins and denotes the time one lives; and Atropos, who breaks the spun threads, and this is death. You will find the other details in the place already mentioned. "His soul, which is your sister and mine," because they are of the same species, although you are still with [a body]...

Virgil asked why Statius had said the mountain had trembled down to its "soft feet," meaning down to its roots which, because they emerge from the sea, are soft. And by asking this, he touched exactly upon what Dante desired to know. And therefore, through a metaphor, he says he "threaded the eye of the needle" <note>original: "die pla cruna"</note> of his desire. **WHICH JUST WITH THE HOPE**: It happens to a man that when he has a very great desire to understand something, if a firm hope of being able to fulfill it is born in him, such thirst and longing is in great part mitigated; and therefore he says that his "thirst became less fasted." **HE BEGAN**; Statius replied, saying: "There is nothing here that the 'religion of the mountain'—that is, this mountain full of holiness—does without order or that is outside of custom." This demonstrates the principle that alterations and various movements, such as those caused by vapors lifted by the sun...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Virgil, Dante, and the spirit of Statius. Having explained Dante’s presence as a living man, the focus shifts to the physical and spiritual laws of Mount Purgatory. # PURGATORIO
## XXI

<margin>XXI</margin>

Neither thick nor thin clouds appear here,
nor flashes of lightning, nor the daughter of Thaumas <note>Iris, the rainbow</note>,
who often changes her place in the world below.
Dry vapor <note>The "dry vapor" mentioned here refers to the classical scientific belief that wind was caused by dry gases rising from the earth.</note> does not rise further up
than the top of the three steps I spoke of,
where the vicar of Peter <note>The angel at the gate of Purgatory</note> sets his feet.

and that no cloud of sorrow reaches that place, nor hail of fury, nor flash of anger. But, confirmed in grace, they only wait to purge the old stains. Rain, which comes from cold and humid vapors gathered in a cloud. **HAIL** <note>original: "GRANDINE"</note> is a drop of rain frozen in the air by the force of cold and wind. It is made of cold and humid vapor rubbed together in the interior parts of the cloud. Snow is an impression generated by moderate cold and humidity; such cold is less than that which generates rain and hail, and it has some warmth within it. Dew is an impression in the air generated by cold and humidity that has not yet solidified. And according to Aristotle <note>Referring to the Greek philosopher's work *Meteorology*</note>, dew is not made except when the south wind blows. Frost is air frozen in the middle of the air. **THE DAUGHTER OF THAUMAS** <note>original: "LAFIGLIA DITAVMANTE"</note> refers to the celestial arch called Iris; whom the poets imagine to be the daughter of Thaumas and the beloved daughter of the Ocean. **DRY** vapor, that is, wind, which is generated from dry and hot vapor.

It shakes perhaps further down, a little or a lot;
but because of wind that hides in the earth,
I know not how, it never moves up here.
It shakes here when some soul feels pure,
so that it rises or moves itself
to climb upward; and such a cry follows it.
The will alone gives proof of the purity,
which, being completely free to change its company,
takes hold of the soul and helps it in its desire.
It wants to do well before, but the inclination does not allow it,
which Divine Justice, against the will,
sets toward the torment, just as it once was toward the sin.
And I, who have lain in this suffering
five hundred years and more, only just now felt
a free will for a better threshold.
Therefore you felt the earthquake and heard the pious
spirits throughout the mountain give praise
to that Lord—may He soon send them upward."
Thus he spoke to us; and because one enjoys
drinking as much as the thirst is great,
I cannot say how much he did me good.

<column-break/>

These things [weather events] are generated only as far as that mountain's entrance to Purgatory and no higher. **DANTE WANTS, THEREFORE, THAT** <note>original: "VUOLE ADVNQVE . DANTHECHEL"</note> motion does not pass further up than where the three steps are. And according to the literal sense, we understand that the part of the mountain where the three steps are is so elevated that it exceeds five miles in altitude. But allegorically we say that the soul that arrives there is outside of every human passion and disturbance.

He assigns the cause of the mountain’s shaking and the singing of the souls. And he says that perhaps the mountain shakes sometimes, a little or a lot, from the three steps downward, **BUT BY WIND THAT IS HIDDEN IN THE EARTH**, that is, by an earthquake: which is born from wind trapped under the earth that has no exit. **BUT I KNOW NOT HOW**: I do not know if it is strong or soft. **IT NEVER SHAKES UP HERE**: Understand this refers to subterranean wind. **BUT IT SHAKES HERE WHEN SOME SOUL IS PURE**, that is, purged of its sins. Therefore, it shakes here when some soul feels itself so pure: **THAT IT RISES** toward heaven; or moves from one circle where it has purged one sin to another where it has to purge another sin. And such a cry follows: and such a song as we have described. It seconds, that is, it follows the shaking of the mountain. And not without supreme wisdom does the poet imagine this shaking. For just as when dry vapor, drawn up by the force of the sun, is converted into wind and moves the earth to escape and rise high, so the soul, drawn by the supernal sun—that is, by divine love—separating itself from sin and earthly things and mounting to God, makes the air and earth show a sign. Virgil also imagines this when he brings the Sibyl to perform a sacrifice for Aeneas’s descent:

> "But look, beneath the first lights of the rising sun and its dawn, the ground began to bellow underfoot and the ridges began to move." <note>original: "Ecce autem primi sublumina solis et ortuf . Subpedibuf mugire solum et iuga cepta moueri." - Aeneid VI, 255-256</note>

**OF THE PURITY**. He says that the soul realizes it is pure when the will to depart is born within it. But because someone could say that in our minds there is always the will to flee evil, misery, and pain, and to achieve good and happiness—nor is there anyone who desires evil except under the appearance of good—therefore, the soul that is in the pains of Purgatory should always have the will to leave. But we must understand that in us there is a double will: one is absolute and simple, and this always wills, for example, as one who is tormented by thirst always wills to drink. This will always desires the highest good and cannot not desire it. The other will is relative <note>term: relative (uolonta respectiua): In Scholastic philosophy, this refers to a will that considers circumstances, such as accepting a deserved punishment before seeking a reward.</note> and does not want it except in a just manner. Therefore, this relative will gives proof of purity when it no longer resists the natural will. This is why the text says: **THE ONLY** wanting, that is, the relative will alone, which is not simple but relative, which is entirely free to change with the wind because it is not hindered by any respect that forbids it for not being a just way of willing. **GIVES PROOF OF PURITY**. Because when the soul is not pure, although it has a natural will to rise to heaven, nevertheless the relative will does not consent because it is not [ready]...

<summary>Statius explains that Mount Purgatory is free from physical weather and earthquakes above the gate, revealing that the mountain only shakes when a soul is purified and ready to ascend. He clarifies the theological distinction between the absolute desire for God and the relative will that accepts purgation as a just necessity.</summary>

# CANTO XXI

just: so that the thing not yet pure does not go to pure things. But when it is pure, this will alone takes hold and occupies the whole soul: because there is no remaining regard <note>The "regard" or "respect" refers to a soul's lingering attachment to its penance as a form of divine justice.</note> that resists it. Thus it enjoys its willing. As on the contrary it happens: that although sometimes we desire something, nevertheless because the conscience is not just, it feels remorse in a way that we do not "will to will." **FIRST IT WILLS** well. The simple will desires the good. But it does not let the "talent" <note>In this context, "talento" or talent refers to the "relative will"—the soul's inclination to fulfill its punishment out of respect for God's justice.</note> go. That is, the simple will desires the good, but the "talent"—the relative will—does not allow the willing, and assigns the reason. For just as divine justice, when the simple will desires vice, sets against it the relative will; so when it desires to exit Purgatory before its time, it opposes it with that same will. **AND I** who have lain here. This shows that he <note>Statius, the spirit speaking to Virgil and Dante.</note>, who had been there more than five hundred years, now being purged, felt his will liberated: that is, the will no longer hindered by any regard, because it was now just. **BECAUSE** one enjoys drinking as much as the thirst is great. Just as the pleasure of drinking is as great as the thirst, so great was the will to understand this as had been the desire.

The NET THAT catches us here. For just as a net holds a bird so it cannot fly away, so this relative will retains the soul, which does not wish to leave until it has paid the penalty for the sin. **SCALAPPIA** <note>original: "SCALAPPIA"</note>: unbinds and frees itself. A "calappio" is a wicker vessel or trap in which they place bait; if a bird enters, it is shut inside because the opening, which was first open, is tempered. Thus, "scappiare" is to exit

> The wise leader said: "Now I see the net

> I speak of the *Aeneid*, which was a mother

from the place where one was locked. **WHY** the mountain trembles. **REJOICE TOGETHER** <note>original: "CONGAVDETE"</note>: singing "Glory to God in the highest." **IN THE TIME** that the good Titus: This shows he was in the time when Titus, son of Vespasian, destroyed Jerusalem, **WITH THE AID** of the High King: of the High God. And he wishes to conclude that although the war made by the Romans against the Jews appeared to have another origin, nevertheless God permitted it because of the sin of the killing of His Son. Therefore he "avenged the wounds" <note>the wounds of Christ</note> from which issued the precious blood, which Judas traded for money. **WITH THE NAME** that lasts longest and honors most: with the name of "Poet," which lasts longer than any other writer and honors more those truly distinguished by such a title. Hence Lucan wrote: *O sacred and great labor of the poets, you snatch all fates away and grant immortality to mortal peoples.* <note>original: "O sacer et magnus uatum labor omnia fata. Eripis et donas populis mortalibus euu."</note> and Virgil: *As for me, may the Muses, whose sacred objects I carry, struck by a great love, first receive me before all things.* <note>original: "Me uero primum capiant ante omnia muſe. Quarum ſacra fero ingenti perculſus amore."</note> **I WAS** there: in our world. **FAMOUS** for my poetic name. **BUT NOT** with Christian faith. **SO SWEET WAS** my vocal spirit: so sweet was my verse and my delivery. Hence Juvenal wrote: *People run to the pleasant voice and the song of a friend when Statius has made the city happy with his Thebaid: he promised the day and affects their minds, captured with such sweetness, and is heard with such great desire by the common crowd.* <note>original: "Curritur ad uocem iocunda et carmen amice. Thebaidos letam cum fecit ſtatius urbem: Promiſitque diem tanta dulcedine captos. afficit ille animos tantaque libidine uulgi: Auditur."</note> **THAT OF TOULOUSE** <note>original: "TOLOSANO"</note>: because I was from Toulouse, which city is on the borders of Gascony towards Brittany; and through his learning and eloquence, he became a Roman citizen. **OF MYRTLE** <note>original: "DIMYRTO"</note>: with which poets were crowned. Hence Petrarch: *What longing for laurel or what for myrtle.* <note>original: "Qual uagheza dilauro o qual dimyrto."</note> **STATIUS**: it is no wonder if this poet, so occupied in such excellent, varied, diverse, and numerous things, followed the opinion that occupied all the men

of his time, and did not investigate the homeland of Statius; which served him nothing in this place, because such a great genius did not esteem minor details. And he could well defend himself with the authority of Lactantius, commentator on his *Thebaid*, a man of much eloquence. But Statius writes in his *Silvae* that his father was Neapolitan <note>The commentator notes that while the common belief was that Statius came from Toulouse, he actually came from Naples.</note>. **I SANG** of Thebes: where he describes the discord born over the kingdom between Eteocles and Polynices, which I mentioned in the *Inferno*. And the war that Adrastus, King of Argos and father-in-law of Polynices, moved against Thebes. **GREAT ACHILLES**: Of whom you will seek the history in the second canto.

# PURGATORIO

of hell. **BUT I FELL ON THE WAY** with the second burden. That is, I did not bring perfection <note>In this context, "perfection" means completion or finishing a work.</note> to the second book, which was the *Achilleid*, because I was prevented by death. Here, Francesco da Buti <note>An early and influential commentator on Dante's Divine Comedy (1324–1406).</note> errs greatly: he takes issue with Dante for saying that such a work was imperfect and insists it was perfect. But if he had carefully noted the beginning, he would have clearly understood that the poem was only started and not finished. Furthermore, some say that he did not fall with the second burden, but with the third: because he had finished not only the *Thebaid*, but also the *Silvae*. To this we respond: the *Silvae* are not a laborious work, but rather written to relax the mind exhausted from the laborious vigils of the *Thebaid*. Therefore, the *Silvae* did not deserve to be called a "burden" <note>original: "soma"</note> like the *Achilleid*, the undertaking of which was no less difficult than the *Thebaid*.

**TO MY ARDOR THE sparks WERE** seed. He shows that the beginning of his learning and fame was Virgil’s *Aeneid*, which by imitating, he was able to become an excellent poet. Thus, arrange the text: "The sparks of your genius, which warmed me with the divine flame of poetry, were the seed of my passion." That is, they were the cause of my excitement. **WHENCE**. From which sparks more than a thousand are enlightened, because Virgil has been the norm and example for all poets. **AND FOR HAVING lived** there, that is, in our world. And he says "I would content myself with one sun," that is, one solar course, which is 375 days <note>The text specifies 375 days and six hours, though a standard solar year is 365 days; this may reflect a specific astronomical calculation used by the commentator.</note> and six hours, for having lived with Virgil. And the meaning is: I would agree to stay one more year in exile—that is, out of the pains of Purgatory to which I was condemned—if I could have lived at the same time as Virgil. But there are some to whom it seems that Statius shows little desire, offering no more than one year. But if we remember the words of Gregory <note>Saint Gregory the Great, who wrote extensively on the severity of the soul's purification.</note> regarding the pains of Purgatory, we will understand that one year in that suffering is a very great thing.

**VIRGIL TURNED**. That is, these words made Virgil turn to me with such a face that, by being silent, he signaled to me that I should keep silent. **BUT THE power that wills**. That is, that power called the "will" cannot do everything: because it often happens that a man, not wanting to weep, weeps; and not wanting to laugh, laughs. Because every passion of the soul—such as joy, sadness, and the like—has certain acts and gestures that follow said passions, even if the man does not wish it. Therefore, laughter follows joy even if we do not want it, and weeping follows sadness. **THAT THEY FOLLOW LESS**. That they follow less. **WILL**: the will, nor the most truthful in those who can least feign. **I JUST** smiled. Although by Virgil’s signs I did not want Statius to recognize Virgil yet, and for this reason I wanted to restrain the laugh, nevertheless, for the reason stated above, I could not restrain it. **LIKE THE MAN who winks**. Like one who makes a sign. **AND LOOKING AT ME in the eyes**: he looked at my eyes seeing me laugh. **WHERE THE expression is most fixed**: where the image and likeness of the soul is most expressed and carved; because the eyes are like windows through

---

which the soul is seen. **MAY YOU BRING so much labor to a good end**. That is, if you lead to a good end as much labor as it is to ascend to Paradise. "Because your face showed me just now a flash of a smile." **NOW AM I**. He was in difficulty on every side: because Virgil signaled that he should not speak, and Statius prayed that he should speak. **WHEREFORE I sigh**: because of such anguish; and by such a sigh I was understood by Virgil. But Virgil, seeing me in this ambiguity, gave me permission to speak.

<meta>This page continues the transition from the fifth terrace of Purgatory, where the sin of avarice is purged, to the sixth terrace. Virgil and the Roman poet Statius are conversing as they ascend, with Dante following closely behind, now physically lighter after having another "P" (representing a sin) removed from his forehead by the Angel of Justice.</meta>

# CANTO XXII OF THE SECOND CANTICLE OF DANTE

<margin>summary</margin>The poet is already ascending from the fifth circle to the sixth: where the souls are purged from the vice of gluttony <note>In Dante's Purgatory, the sixth terrace is dedicated to those who must overcome the craving for food and drink.</note>. It treats the conversion of Statius with great praise of Virgil. Starting, then, he says: that they had already left the angel behind, who had shown them the sixth circle.

<margin>verse</margin>The angel had already stayed behind us,
the angel who had turned us to the sixth circle,
having erased a stroke from my face;
And those who have their desire for justice
had been called blessed by him, and his words,
with "I thirst" <note>original: "sitio"</note> and nothing more, completed it.
And I, lighter than through the other passes,
went on so that without any labor
I followed the swift spirits upward.
When Virgil began: "Love,
kindled by virtue, always kindled another,
provided that its flame appeared outward;
Whence, from the hour that Juvenal descended
among us in the limbo of hell,
he who made your affection manifest,
my benevolence toward you was such
as ever bound one to a person never seen,
so that these stairs will now seem short to me.
But tell me, and as a friend forgive me,
if too much liberty slackens my rein,
and as a friend now speak with me..."

<column-break/>

...erased from my face: because he had erased the fifth sin: so that there remained only the sixth and the seventh. **AND THOSE WHO HAVE**. He shows that the souls who were purging themselves in the fifth circle, seeing Dante ascend purged of avarice, sang out of joy and congratulation: *Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered* <note>original Latin: "Beati quorum remisse sunt iniquitates / et quorum tecta sunt peccata." This is a quote from Psalm 32:1, used here to celebrate the soul's progress.</note>; and at the end, turning to Dante as he ascended, they said: *sitio* <note>Latin: "I thirst."</note>, that is, I have a thirst for eternal salvation. **AND I LIGHTER**: he was lighter than in the circles below because he was purged of more vices. And through such lightness he could ascend alongside Virgil and Statius, who were swift spirits. **LOVE KINDLED BY VIRTUE ALWAYS kindled another**. If one loves another for the virtue they see in them, it follows that the beloved must love the lover. **PROVIDED THAT THE FLAME**: that is, that such love is known to the one who is loved. But this does not happen in carnal love, because often someone is loved carnally who does not love the lover in return. **WHENCE**: for which reason it happened that when Juvenal <note>Decimus Junius Juvenalis, the Roman satirist who lived in the 1st/2nd century AD.</note> descended into Limbo and told me of your great love toward me, I was moved to feel such benevolence toward you as was never felt toward a person "never seen," that is, not personally known. And he says this because virtue has the power in itself to make us love those whom we never saw, and even more so if we hear that they love us. **SO THAT THESE STAIRS WILL NOW SEEM SHORT**.

<sig>bb iii</sig>

<summary>Virgil expresses his deep affection for Statius, explaining how the poet Juvenal brought news of Statius's admiration to Limbo. The passage also describes Dante's physical lightening as he is purged of the sin of avarice and moves toward the terrace of gluttony.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the conversation between the Roman poets Virgil and Statius as they ascend the mountain of Purgatory. Virgil has just asked Statius how a man of such great wisdom could have fallen into the vice of greed (avarice), as he found him in the circle where that sin is purged.</meta>

### PURGATORIO

> "How could avarice find a place
> within your breast, amidst such wisdom
> as you were filled with through your care?"

These words made Statius move
a little toward a smile; then he replied:
"Every word of yours is a dear sign of love to me.
Truly, many times things appear
that give false matter for doubt,
because of slight causes that are hidden.
Your question makes me certain of your belief
that I was avaricious in the other life,
perhaps because of that circle where I was.
Now know that avarice was parted
too far from me, and this excess <note>The sin of "prodigality" or wasteful spending, which is the opposite extreme of avarice.</note>
thousands of lunar cycles have punished.
And were it not that I corrected my concern
when I heard where you cry out—
almost angry at human nature—
'Why do you not govern, O sacred hunger <note>original: "sacra fame". This refers to the famous line from Virgil’s Aeneid: "Auri sacra fames," which can mean "holy hunger" or "accursed greed."</note>
for gold, the appetite of mortals?'
I would feel the dismal jousts <note>In Dante's Inferno, the avaricious and the prodigal are forced to crash heavy weights against one another in a "joust."</note> while rolling weights.
Then I perceived that hands could open their wings
too wide in spending, and I repented
of that as of other evils.
How many will rise again with shorn hair <note>A symbol of those who were wasteful (prodigal) in life.</note>
through ignorance, which takes away repentance
for this sin while living or at the end!
And know that the fault which rebuts
any sin through direct opposition,
dries up its greenness here together with it.
Therefore, if I have been among those people
who weep for avarice to purge myself,
it happened to me because of its opposite."

<column-break/>

...scarce. Because it is true: that being with a friend makes every difficulty bearable; and especially where there is eloquence. Whence the ancient poet said: *A pleasant companion on the road is as good as a carriage* <note>original: "Comes facundus pro uehiculo est in uia."</note>. **BUT TELL ME** And as a friend forgive me. Virgil, finding Statius where avarice was being purged, believed that he had been stained by that vice. And it appearing to him that such a vice was very alien to a wise man, he asked how it could be that he, with so much wisdom, had fallen into the vice of avarice. **BUT TELL ME** and as a friend forgive me. Because such a question does not seem to be without some blame toward Statius, Virgil excuses himself: that he seeks this as a friend who grieves, and not as a detractor. **THROUGH YOUR CARE** you were filled. Because wisdom is in those who exercise their talent and intellect.

Statius saw the error that Virgil was making and understood that his words did not come from a malicious spirit, but from a friend; and therefore he smiled. Then he showed that often men are deceived by false conjectures and signs: like Virgil then, who, understanding Statius to have been so long in the circle of the avaricious, estimated that he was there to purge avarice. But he demonstrates to him: that not in avarice, but in its opposite vice, which is prodigality, had he sinned. And therefore he says: **AND THIS EXCESS**. Because prodigality—as we distinctly showed in the *Inferno*—is punished along with avarice. And the reason both there and here is manifest. **WHEN I UNDERSTOOD** where you call out. When I understood where you make an exclamation in your third book <note>Virgil's Aeneid, Book III.</note> saying: *To what do you not drive mortal hearts, O sacred hunger for gold?* <note>original: "Quid non mortalia pectora cogis. Auri sacra fames."</note> **ALMOST ANGRY** at human nature. That is, angry at all men. Who, having a nature that can stay content with few and minimal things, are nevertheless insatiable. **WHY DO YOU NOT** govern, O sacred hunger. He imitates Virgil, as we said. And with the highest indignation, he flares up in exclamation. **I WOULD FEEL THE JOUSTS** dismal. That is, sorrowful ones. And this is what he imagines in the seventh canto of the *Inferno*. **THEN I PERCEIVED**: then I saw that I could sin thus [in spending], and I brought myself to penance. **HOW MANY** will rise again with shorn hair: in the same chapter of the *Inferno*, he imagined that the prodigal will rise with cut hair and the avaricious with closed fists; and in that place, we set down the allegory. So how many will those be, who, because ignorance of this sin takes away repentance—that is, by not recognizing prodigality—they do not repent, and will be damned for it. And indeed, because avarice is entirely opposite to liberality, it is easy to recognize. But the opposite is true of prodigality, because it is so similar to liberality that few can distinguish it. **KNOW THAT THE FAULT**. He says that in the same place where one sin is purged, the other sin is punished which is contrary to it by opposition. And the text ordains: Know that the fault—that is, the sin—that rebuts any sin—that is, that beats back through direct opposition. "Rebutting" <note>original: "rimbeccare"</note> is properly when we strike back the ball that comes toward us.

<summary>Statius explains to Virgil that he was not in the fifth terrace for avarice, but for its opposite sin, prodigality (excessive spending). He credits Virgil's own poetry with opening his eyes to this vice, leading to his eventual repentance.</summary>

# CANTO XXII

Now, when you sang of the cruel arms
of the double sorrow of Jocasta, <note>Jocasta was the mother of Eteocles and Polynices, who killed each other in a struggle for the throne of Thebes; this "double sorrow" is the subject of Statius's epic poem, the *Thebaid*.</note>
said the singer of bucolic songs, <note>Virgil, known for his *Eclogues* or "bucolic" (pastoral) poems.</note>
by that which Clio <note>The Muse of History, whom Statius invoked in his poetry.</note> probes there with you,
it does not seem that faith had yet made you
a believer, the faith without which doing good is not enough.
If this is so, then what sun or what candles
cleared your darkness so that you thereafter
set your sails behind the fisherman? <note>Saint Peter, the "fisherman," representing the Christian Church.</note>

And he to him: You first sent me
toward Parnassus <note>A mountain sacred to the Muses and poetry.</note> to drink in its grottoes,
and you first enlightened me near to God.
You did as one who walks by night,
who carries the light behind him and does not help himself,
but makes the people behind him wise,
when you said: "The age renews itself;
justice returns and the first human time,
and a new progeny descends from heaven." <note>Statius is quoting Virgil’s *Fourth Eclogue*, which many medieval Christians believed was a prophecy of the birth of Christ.</note>
Through you I was a poet, through you a Christian;
but so that you may better see what I sketch,
I will stretch out my hand to color it.
Already the whole world was pregnant
with the true belief, sown
by the messengers of the eternal kingdom;
and your word mentioned above
was so in harmony with the new preachers,
that I took up the habit of visiting them.
They then began to seem so holy to me
that when Domitian <note>The Roman Emperor who persecuted Christians in the late 1st century AD.</note> persecuted them,
their cries were not without my tears.
And while I remained in that world,
I helped them, and their upright customs
made me despise all other sects.
And before I led the Greeks to the rivers
of Thebes <note>Meaning, before he reached that point in writing his poem, the *Thebaid*.</note> in my poetry, I received baptism;
but out of fear I was a secret Christian,
for a long time pretending to be a pagan.

<column-break/>

Here Virgil responds and arranges his thoughts. **THE SINGER of bucolic songs**, that is, Virgil, who among the other books he wrote, composed the *Bucolics* [the *Eclogues*]. **SAID: when YOU SANG of the cruel arms**, that is, the cruel battles. **OF THE double sorrow of Jocasta**: which battle was between Eteocles and Polynices, the two sons of Jocasta, who, by killing one another, brought a doubled sorrow to their mother. This is the subject matter that Statius sang of in his *Thebaid*, a history we narrated in the twenty-sixth canto of the *Inferno*. **BY THAT WHICH Clio probes there with you**: by what I understand in your subject matter, for Clio—who is one of the nine Muses—is invoked by you. **PROBES**: searches and tests; as if to say: the subject matter you place in that work and your manner of treating it do not demonstrate that you had come to the Christian faith, without which doing well is not enough. **IF THIS IS SO**: as if asking how it happened. **WHAT sun**: what grace illuminating your intellect. **WHAT candles**: what human doctrine. **CLEARED your darkness**: took away the shadows of ignorance. **SET your sails**: that is, proposed your voyage, which is to live. **BEHIND the fisherman**: behind Saint Peter, that is, according to the Christian religion.

**And he to him.** He shows that Virgil was the cause for him both in making him a poet and making him a Christian. Because in reading his poems, he was moved to imitate him, and therefore he says: **You sent me toward Parnassus**, of which we spoke above in the first canto. **IN ITS grottoes.** Because on its slopes were the Pargasean springs consecrated to the Muses. Statius read these verses of the Sibyl translated by Virgil, in which it is said that the ages are renewed and the Virgin returns. And he says: "a new progeny descends." And then, hearing the Christian teachers relate this to the incarnation of Christ, and being moved by the authority of Virgil, he became a Christian. The verses are:
> "The final age of the Cumaean song has come; <note>original Latin: "Ultima cumei uenit iam temporis etas."</note>
> The great order of the ages is born anew. <note>original Latin: "Magnus abintegro ſeclorum naſcitur ordo."</note>
> Now the Virgin returns, and the Saturnian realms return; <note>original Latin: "Iam redit: et uirgo redeunt ſaturnia regna;"</note>
> Now a new progeny is sent down from high heaven." <note>original Latin: "Iam noua progenies celo demittitur alto."</note>

And therefore he says: **You did like one who, walking at night, carries the light behind him**, which does not provide light for himself, but for those behind him. Similarly, you composed these verses; but not interpreting them correctly, you applied them to the honor of Octavian [Augustus]. But I, helped by Christian interpreters, understood them according to their true sense. Already the world was pregnant with the true belief of the Christians, and those who preached exhorted us to the Christian religion. **THEY THEN BEGAN TO SEEM**: The works of the Christians seemed so holy to me that when they were persecuted by Domitian, it grieved me greatly. I helped them secretly, and I despised every other sect and religion. **DOMITIAN.** This man was the twelfth emperor; he reigned for fifteen years and five months. He succeeded Titus, his brother, who was as pious and just as Domitian was impious and unjust. He took the empire in the eighty-second year from the incarnation of Christ. He most cruelly afflicted the Christians and wished to be called "our Lord and God." Nevertheless, despite many vices, he was severe in suppressing adultery and favored the learned. **AND BEFORE I led the Greeks to the rivers of Thebes**: that is, before I had reached the place in my *Thebaid* where I describe the...

-># PURGATORY<-

and this lukewarmness made me seek the fourth circle for more than four hundred [years] <note>The "fourth circle" refers to the terrace of Sloth; Statius explains he spent over 400 years there because he was "tepid" or slow to openly profess his Christian faith.</note> first. And for being so lukewarm, I fell into that sin [of the] fourth circle: and there I stayed for more than four hundred [years], that is, having been in the fifth [circle]: and some time in the first and second [circles]: [having been] purged in the year 1300. And having been Statius in the times of Domitian, <note>Roman Emperor from 81 to 96 AD.</note> who reigned until the year ninety-eight, the time is quite clearly shown.

"You, therefore, who have lifted the lid for me / that was hiding the great good I speak of, / while we have a surplus of climbing, / tell me where our friend Terence is, / Caecilius, Plautus, and Varro, if you know; / tell me if they are damned and in what ward." <note>Statius asks Virgil about the fate of other famous Roman comic and lyric poets.</note>
My leader replied: "They are with that Greek <note>Homer, the author of the *Iliad* and *Odyssey*.</note> / whom the Muses suckled more than any other ever; / in the first circle of the blind prison, <note>Limbo, the first circle of Hell, where virtuous pagans reside.</note> / we often speak of the mountain / that our nurses always have with them. <note>Mount Parnassus, the home of the Muses, who "nursed" the poets' inspiration.</note>
Euripides is there with us, and Anacreon, / Simonides, Agathon, and many other / Greeks who once adorned their brows with laurel.
There, your own people are seen: / Antigone, Deiphyle, and Argia, / and Ismene, as sorrowful as she ever was.
She who showed the Langia is seen there; <note>Hypsipyle, who saved her father and later showed the fountain of Langia to the thirsty Seven against Thebes.</note> / there is the daughter of Tiresias, and Thetis, / and Deidamia with her sisters."

<column-break/>

When the army of Adrastus arrived at the rivers of Thebes with the other Kings, which are Ismenus and Asopus: I became a Christian. But I lived as a hidden Christian, and I was not fervent in the faith in a way that I dared to discover it <note>Meaning he did not dare to openly reveal his faith.</note> because of my slowness in doing good, which is punished in the fourth [terrace]. He spent four hundred years there; and he was there more than five hundred years and [also in the] third [terrace]. Therefore, Dante finding him in the year 1300, and he having lived in the time of Domitian—who reigned until the year 98—the time is quite well demonstrated.

Statius continues his speech and says: "You, Virgil, who have lifted the lid for me," that is, you have removed my ignorance through the verses already mentioned above, which ignorance hid from me the great good I speak of—which is God and Christian doctrine. "Tell me while we have a surplus of climbing," that is, while there is still climbing to be done: "where is TERENCE our friend?" Terence was Carthaginian; taken in war, he became a slave, and in Rome, he served Terence Lucanus, a senator. Because of his excellent intellect, he was raised as a free man and became learned and wrote six comedies. He was a friend to Scipio and Laelius. He calls Terence his friend and Virgil’s because the poets who came after Terence were more familiar with him than the other ancients. He also imitates Cicero, who for this same reason calls Terence his "familiar."

CAECILIUS: Statius Caecilius was a comic poet. Others say he was from that part of Gaul where the Insubres are; others say he was Milanese. He was a close friend of Ennius and died the year following Ennius's death in the 150th Olympiad. He was buried on Mount Janiculum.

PLAUTUS: He was from Umbria, from the city of Sarsina, and was so poor that he turned a millstone for a price. He lived during the 145th Olympiad.

VARRO: Marcus Terentius Varro was born in the 166th Olympiad. He was the most learned of all Romans, an outstanding poet and philosopher. Many learned men did not hesitate to equate him with Aristotle. He wrote forty-one books on antiquity, which he divided into human and divine things. There was another Varro, a contemporary of Virgil, of whom Virgil writes honorably in the *Bucolics*: "But I do not yet seem to say things worthy of Varro or of Cinna, but to cackle like a goose among tuneful swans." <note>original Latin: "Sed neque adhuc Varo uideor neque dicere cyna Digna : ſed argutos interſtrepere anſer olores."</note> To him, along with Tucca, Octavian [Augustus] gave the task of amending the *Aeneid* after Virgil's death, which Virgil, prevented by death, left imperfect. For this reason, Virgil left instructions in his will that it should be burned. But Octavian would not allow the honor of the Latin language to be extinguished.

THESE MEN: My leader Virgil replied: "Those of whom you ask, and Persius and I, are with that Greek who was suckled by the Muses more than any other poet," and he means Homer, of whom we spoke in the *Inferno*. Nor does he place Homer above Virgil by these words; but by having him speak this way, he makes him modest.

PERSIUS: He was from Volterra; the genius shown in his satires, though they are few, is clearly evident.

IN THE FIRST circle: As was shown in the first canticle [the *Inferno*]; and there we often reason together about the mountain. WHICH, that is, the one which has our nurses, that is, the Muses; in short, they talk about the Muses by whom poets are nourished.

EURIPIDES: An excellent poet and writer of tragedies; he was a disciple of Anaxagoras and a fellow disciple of Socrates. He was very skilled at writing tragic things with compassion.

ANACREON: An elegiac poet born on the island of Teos.

SIMONIDES: A poet from the island of Ceos. He was the inventor of the methods and images belonging to artificial memory. He had written hymns in honor of Scopas, a very powerful and rich man in Thessaly, in which he had interposed much praise for Pollux and Castor, the sons of Jove called the Dioscuri. He recited them at a banquet to which Scopas had invited many. After the verses were recited, Scopas told Simonides that he would give him half the prize the verses deserved, and for the other half, he should ask the Dioscuri, whom he had praised equally. Simonides agreed, and a little later two young men dressed in white arrived. For a matter of importance, they had Simonides called out of the house. As soon as he had exited, the house collapsed, and the young men vanished. This...

# CANTO XXII

it was judged: that those had been the Dioscuri <note>original: "edioscuri"; refers to the twin deities Castor and Pollux.</note> who had come to save him from ruin. OF YOUR PEOPLE: not "yours" because they are related by blood—since you are a Tolosan <note>A common medieval error; Statius was actually from Naples, but Dante followed the tradition that he was from Toulouse.</note> and they are Greeks—but "yours" because in your most ornate heroic verses you touched upon them and treated them in your poem. Antigone was the sister of Eteocles and Polynices. Deiphyle and Argia were daughters of Adrastus. Deiphyle married Polynices, and Argia married Tydeus. Ismene is a river in Boeotia. SHE IS SEEN who showed the Langia: she showed the fountain of Langia to the army of Adrastus, and in that moment Archemorus died, bitten by a serpent. This was Hypsipyle, daughter of Thoas, whom we spoke of in the first Canticle <note>Referencing the *Inferno*.</note>. THE DAUGHTER OF TIRESIAS: this was Manto. And she is mentioned again in the account of the founding of Mantua. Similarly, we included the fabulous history of Thetis, mother of Achilles, and how she hid her son on the island of Scyros with the daughters of Lycomedes. And Deidamia, who bore him Pyrrhus.

---

The two poets were silent now,
attentive once more to looking around,
free from the climbing and from walls.
And already four handmaidens of the day <note>The "handmaidens" represent the hours; it is now roughly between 10:00 and 11:00 AM.</note>
had stayed behind, and the fifth was at the tiller,
directing upward its burning horn,
When my leader said: "I believe that at the end,
we must turn our right shoulders
circling the mountain as we are accustomed to do."
Thus, custom was our guide there,
and we took the path with less doubt
because of the assent of that worthy soul.
They went ahead and I was alone
behind, and I listened to their speech,
which gave me understanding of poetry.

<column-break/>

The author imagines the poets to be attentive once more because new subject matter will be treated. FREE from the climbing: because such matter does not require greater <term>speculation</term> <note>In a theological sense, "speculation" refers to the deep contemplation of divine truths.</note>. AND FROM WALLS: because whoever climbs the stairs has a wall on every side that blocks the view. But here there was no impediment to speculation. AND ALREADY the four handmaidens. Since the sun takes a certain amount of time to make one revolution—that is, from leaving the east until it returns—it is divided into twenty-four hours. And for this reason, poets imagine that the hours are the handmaidens of the sun. And they divide them into twenty-four parts, stationing them as if at posts, so that each one guides the tiller of the solar chariot for its allotted time. Thus, when the fourth hour has led the chariot through its span, she stops, and the fifth succeeds her, and then the others in order. The poet wishes to show in this place that four hours had already passed, and the fifth had come; and for this reason, he says: that already the four handmaidens were left behind, and the fifth was

---

at the tiller. DIRECTING upward the burning horn: because until midday the sun always rises, and he calls the "horn" the point of the tiller. I BELIEVE that at the end: because in all the other terraces he had seen that turning to the right side kept them on the right path. I estimate the same here. And therefore he says: THUS CUSTOM was our guide: demonstrating that habit and experience generate doctrine. BY THE ASSENT of that worthy soul. He means the soul of Statius, which, being purged of sins, was truly worthy and must have had greater knowledge of such a journey. THEY WENT ahead: because the intellect and reason must precede. I LISTENED to their speech. And certainly, the senses and appetite must follow the intellect when it is adorned and illustrated by true doctrine, nor should they deviate from it. OF POETRY they gave me understanding. Allegorically, this denotes that by imitating these poets, he became a poet.

---

But soon the sweet talk was broken
by a tree we found in the middle of the road,
with fruits sweet and good to smell.
And as a fir tree tapers upward
from branch to branch, so did that one downward,
I believe so that no person might go up it.
On the side where our path was closed,
there fell from the high rock a clear liquid
that spread itself over the leaves above.
The two poets approached the tree,
and a voice from within the foliage
cried out: "Of this food you shall have a lack." <note>original: "harete caro"; in this context, it implies a scarcity or that the food is forbidden to them.</note>

<column-break/>

The author imagines that in the sixth circle, where the vice of <term>gluttony</term> <note>The sin of overindulgence in food or drink.</note> is punished, there are two trees: one almost at the entrance of the circle, and the other at the end, near the ascent to the seventh. These have their roots toward heaven and their tops toward the earth <note>The trees are "upside down" to prevent the gluttons from reaching the fruit.</note>, and he imagines they are full of fruits that give off an excellent and most sweet scent. Furthermore, he posits that from the cliff of the mountain, two streams emerge, which descend from the terrestrial paradise to the grotto of the sixth circle; and from there, one climbs up one tree and the other up the other. One is called Eunoe, which awakens the memory of good; the other is Lethe, and this takes away the memory of evil. The streams climb up each through its tree, refreshing its leaves, and at the end, they return to where they came from. He also shows that along the side of the mountain

---

the path is closed: nor is there any other passage except on the outer side of the tree toward the edge, which has no barrier. The shape of the tree was like a fir, but with the tip turned downward. He imagines the firs...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto XXII of the Purgatorio. Having left the terrace of Sloth, Dante, Virgil, and Statius have encountered a mysterious tree that tapers downward, unlike natural trees, and are now hearing voices from within its branches citing examples of temperance.</meta>

# PURGATORIO

...deriving this allegory from the tree from which our first parents ate. They, contrary to the divine command, tasted the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, from which issued the bait for all sins. And because by tasting the fruit they fell into the sin of gluttony, he places them here. These trees have their roots turned upward <note>In Dante’s *Purgatorio*, the trees on the terrace of Gluttony are shaped like upside-down cones to prevent the souls from climbing them to reach the fruit.</note>, because the root of knowing good and evil comes from God; and we are the low-hanging branches—that is, its appearance and its pomp. But its vitality is directed toward heaven, because all knowledge comes from God. Its fruits are fragrant, for giving praise to abstinence and cursing vice generates the delights of the eternal life, which cannot be possessed in this world. The streams that descend from paradise through the grotto, and then return upward through the branches of the trees, signify divine grace. This grace is poured into men who are established and firm in the habit of virtue, and then, through the green leaves—which represent living deeds—it returns to God. For the good refer back to God every grace received from Him. We can also relate this to the fable of Tantalus <note>A figure from Greek mythology punished in the underworld by being placed in a pool of water beneath a fruit tree, both of which receded whenever he tried to eat or drink.</note>, whom the poets place in hell, hungry and thirsty, with water up to his chin and various fruits hanging above his nose. If he rises, the fruits rise; if he stoops, the water recedes. Thus, in the midst of great plenty, he always finds himself in scarcity. This punishment is very fitting for the gluttonous. **I BELIEVE SO THAT** no person may go up, so that no one can reach to take the fruits. **ON THE SIDE** where our path was closed: because we could not pass between the tree and the grotto, but had to go between the tree and the slope. **A CLEAR LIQUID**: because nothing is clearer than the grace of God, especially that which illuminates. **THE TWO POETS** approach the tree. This is fitting, for the intellect raised to contemplation approaches divine grace, being capable of receiving it. **AND A VOICE CRIED OUT**: This is the authority through which the intellect understands that it must be grateful to receive it.

->Then it said: Mary thought more<-
->of how the wedding should be honorable and complete<-
->than of her own mouth, which now responds for you.<-
->And the ancient Roman women were content<-
->with water for their drink; and Daniel<-
->despised food and acquired knowledge.<-
->The first age was as beautiful as gold:<-
->hunger made acorns savory,<-
->and thirst made every stream nectar.<-
->Honey and locusts were the foods<-
->that nourished the Baptist in the desert,<-
->which is why he is glorious and so great,<-
->as is revealed to you by the Gospel.<-

<column-break/>

**THEN IT SAID**: the voice continued its words, providing historical examples that invite sobriety and abstinence, all of which are opposed to gluttony. And first, that Mary, at the wedding of John the Evangelist <note>A common medieval legend held that the Wedding at Cana was for the marriage of John the Evangelist.</note>, did not think of her own mouth—that is, of satisfying her taste—when she heard it said: "they have no wine" <note>original: "uinum non habet"; Mary’s concern was for the hospitality of the hosts, not her own thirst.</note>, but thought of making the wedding honorable and complete. **WHICH FOR YOU RESPONDS**: this mouth is always an advocate for you in heaven. **AND THE ROMAN WOMEN**: The use of wine was unknown among ancient Roman women. It is said that for this reason, they were kissed in greetings, so that relatives might notice by the smell of wine if they had been drinking. Nevertheless, a woman becomes intoxicated less easily than a man, because her body is very moist—as shown by the delicacy and the radiance of her flesh. Therefore, wine pouring into so much moisture becomes very watery and loses the power

to evaporate into the brain. **DANIEL**: Nebuchadnezzar, King of Babylon, conquered Jerusalem and carried away great treasures and many noble youths, among whom was the prophet Daniel. He ordered that many should eat of the precious foods from his table. But Daniel, who had determined not to defile his mind with gluttony and wine, obtained permission from his guardian to be fed on legumes and water. And thus he and his companions became more beautiful, as they had promised the guard. But we shall speak of Daniel at length in the twenty-fourth canto <note>The text says "fourth," likely a scribal error for the 24th or 29th of *Paradiso*.</note> of the *Paradiso*. **THE FIRST AGE WAS AS BEAUTIFUL AS GOLD**: In many places, the poets state that in the first century, men fed themselves on acorns and drank water. **HONEY AND LOCUSTS WERE THE FOODS**: This is a very well-known fact regarding the life of John the Baptist.

<page-num>XXIII</page-num>
->CANTO XXIII<-

# CANTO XXIII OF THE SECOND CANTICLE OF DANTE.

While I was fixing my eyes through the green foliage,
just as he is accustomed to do
who loses his life following the little birds:
The one who was more than a father said to me: "Son,
come now, for the time that is allotted to us
must be more usefully partitioned."
I turned my face and my step no less quickly
toward the sages, who were speaking in such a way
that they made the walking cost me nothing.
And behold, weeping and singing was heard:
"Lord, open my lips" <note>original: "labia mea domine"; from Psalm 51:15, "O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall declare your praise."</note> in such a way
that it gave birth to both delight and grief.
"O sweet father, what is that which I hear?"
I began; and he: "Shadows that go,
perhaps loosening the knot of their debt."

**I turned my face.** To attend to that which I was warned of. **MY STEP:** To put into execution what he commanded: which was that I should follow him. **WHO WERE SPEAKING in such a way:** Because, as I said before, "a pleasant companion is as good as a carriage on a journey." <note>original: "facundus comes pro uehiculo est in uia"</note> Therefore, the walking was of no cost. **AND BEHOLD** weeping and singing: they wept out of contrition and true repentance for the sin committed, and they sang for the hope of being able to purge it, and once purged, to go to salvation. **LORD open my lips.** It is in the prophetic psalm, "Lord, you will open my lips, and my mouth shall declare your praise." <note>original: "domine labia mea aperies : et os meum annuntiabit laudem tuam"</note> This prayer is appropriate for the gluttonous. So that the mouth—which in the past they held open for superfluous food—may in the future be used to sing divine praises. **IN SUCH A WAY** delight: because I saw that those souls were to be saved. **AND GRIEF** to see them in their present pain. **PERHAPS** their debt... that is, they go "loosening the knot," meaning they are releasing the obligation of their duty; that is, the debt of punishment they still owe to God, which they must pay.

Just as pensive pilgrims do,
reaching people unknown to them on the road,
who turn toward them and do not stop,
So, behind us, moving more rapidly,
coming and passing by, there marveled at us
a crowd of souls, silent and devout.
In the eyes, each one was dark and hollow,
pale in the face, and so wasted
that the skin took its shape from the bones.
I do not believe that Erysichthon <note>A mythical King of Thessaly punished with insatiable hunger for violating a grove sacred to Ceres.</note>
became so withered to the very bone
by starving, even when he feared it most.

...who held in contempt Ceres, the goddess of grain, and prohibited sacrifices from being made to her. For this reason, an angry Ceres sent an unheard-of hunger upon him, through which in a short time he consumed all his substance. And finally, he sold his daughter multiple times; and after this, he ate his own limbs. Under such a fable, Ovid expresses the nature of the glutton.

I said to myself in thought: "Behold
the people who lost Jerusalem,
when Mary set her beak into her son!" <note>A reference to the Roman siege of Jerusalem (70 AD) recorded by Josephus, where a starving mother named Mary committed cannibalism upon her infant.</note>
The eye-sockets appeared like rings without gems.

<column-break/>

HE DEMONSTRATES in this 23rd chapter the punishment through which the gluttonous are purged in the sixth circle; and he recognizes a certain soul there, specifically Forese, with whom he speaks. **WHILE** the eyes: an excellent comparison: for just as I fixed my eyes through the green foliage of the tree, so do those who consume all their time following birds; and as they lose time, so was I losing it. **MORE THAN** a father: if there can be any greater affection than the paternal. **SAID TO ME** son: <note>original: "filiole"; a diminutive of the Latin *filius*, meaning "little son."</note>. **COME** now: as a true father, Reason admonishes Sensuality <note>The commentator frames Virgil as Reason and Dante as Sensuality/the physical self.</note> to follow it; and it demonstrates that nothing is more harmful than consuming time in useless things, which we ought to spend usefully. **PARTITION.** There is not just one thing required in human life, but many. Therefore, it is necessary that we allocate to each as much time as is required. **I turned...**

CONTINUING on the journey, he shows that a crowd of souls was coming behind them. Because they were "moving more rapidly"—that is, they moved faster—they caught up to them, stared at them, and passed ahead, just as pilgrims do, who travel not without suspicion and, reaching unknown people, stare and pass by. **PILGRIM** <note>original: "peregrino"</note> is a Latin name and signifies anyone who makes a journey outside of his own country. **IN THE EYES:** Wishing to demonstrate that those souls were greatly thinned by long and great abstinence, he sets down the signs we see in thin bodies. The first is that the eyes are sunken inward. The second, that the color has left them. The third, that the skin is right on the bone—that is, that between the skin and the bone there is no flesh. **ERYSI**-chthon: This man was an impious man in Thessaly.

I THOUGHT, seeing such great thinness, that these were those Jews whom Titus besieged in Jerusalem, of whom many thousands perished of hunger. **MARY** Josephus <note>original: "Iosapho"</note> in the book of *The Jewish War* places among other extreme things that the Hebrew people did while constrained...

<summary>Dante enters the terrace of Gluttony, where he sees souls wasted by starvation singing psalms of praise. He compares their emaciated appearance to the mythical Erysichthon and the historical Mary of Jerusalem, who was driven to cannibalism during the Roman siege.</summary>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>PURGATORIO</header>

Whoever reads the word "man" <note>original: "homo"</note> in the faces of men
would have easily recognized the "m" here.
Who would believe that the scent of an apple,
governing them by creating such a craving,
and that of water, not knowing how,
I was already wondering what so afflicted them,
for the cause of their leanness and their
sad, scaly skin was not yet apparent.
And behold, from the depths of the skull,
a shade turned his eyes toward me and looked fixedly;
then he cried out loudly: "What grace is this to me?"
I would never have recognized him by his face,
but in his voice that became clear to me
which his appearance had consumed within itself.
That speech rekindled all my knowledge
of those altered features,
and I recognized the face of Forese.

<margin>XXV. THEIR SAD SCALY SKIN.</margin> **SCALY** <note>original: "squama"</note> is proper to fish, which we call scales. But here he calls "scale" the crust that is on the face of one who is squalid and almost perished by hunger. **FORESE** was the brother of Accursio <note>The commentator likely means Corso Donati, Forese's brother and a famous political leader, or is referencing a specific jurist</note>, the legal consultant, and of Piccarda, a most beautiful and honorable woman. Therefore, these three have been divided among the three realms: to Accursio was given Hell, to Forese Purgatory, and Piccarda will be found in Paradise.

"Pray, do not look at the dry leprosy
that discolors my skin," he begged,
"nor at any lack of flesh that I may have;
But tell me the truth about yourself, and who those
two souls are who act as your escort;
do not remain there without speaking to me!"
"Your face, which I once wept for when dead,
gives me now no less grief for weeping,"
I replied to him, "seeing it so twisted.
Therefore tell me, for God's sake, what strips you so;
do not make me speak while I am marvelling,
for he can ill speak who is full of another desire."
And he to me: "From the eternal counsel,
virtue falls into the water and into the plant
left behind, whereby I become so thin.
All these people who singing weep
for following their appetite beyond measure,
here make themselves holy again in hunger and thirst.
The scent that comes from the fruit and from the spray
that spreads over the greenery
kindles in us a longing to eat and drink.
And not just once as we circle this space
is our pain refreshed—
I say pain, but I should say solace;
For that desire leads us to the tree
that led Christ joyfully to say 'Eli' <note>original: "hely"; Hebrew for "My God," referencing Christ's words on the cross: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"</note>
when he delivered us with his blood."

<column-break/>

...from hunger: when Jerusalem was besieged by Titus, a certain Mary, daughter of Eleazar, having come to the ultimate desperation through hunger, killed her own son whom she had at her breast; she roasted half of him and ate him. Certain robbers ran there at the smell and coerced the woman to give them a share of that food. She, enraged and more desirous of death than life, offered the other half of the child and affirmed he was her son. But they, overcome by nature, fled such wickedness. **THEIR EYE-SOCKETS SEEMED** rings without gems: the circles of the eyes appeared like round rings without a setting where the gem enters. They say that in a man's face, the eyes and the nose form an "M" in this shape: **M**, and the eyes are in the middle as two "O"s in this shape: <image-desc>A circular diagram representing the human face where the eyes form 'O's and the features form an 'M', creating the word 'OMO' (man, in Italian).</image-desc> and thus they say "man" <note>original: "omo"</note>. Therefore, the poet wants to show that their thinness made this word appear more expressly. **WHO WOULD BELIEVE:** as if to say: no one, not knowing how, would believe that the scent of that tree and that water would generate such craving, that is, the will to eat. But he shows the cause in the canto.

**IT SHOWS:** that he is moved no less to weep at the face of Forese at present, seeing it so "twisted"—that is, so removed from its accustomed form—than he was when he saw him dead. And through these words, he shows that one should weep more for vice in a man than for death. **DO NOT MAKE ME SPEAK:** while I am in admiration of what I see; **FOR HE CAN ILL SPEAK:** he can poorly narrate to others who desires that things be narrated to him. **FROM THE ETERNAL COUNSEL:** which is divine providence, "virtue falls." For if this is the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, divine providence has infused into our souls the desire to know it. It seems necessary to me in this place to provide a double sense: First, as to the punishment, it is a just thing that divine providence has instituted for the vice of gluttony, that the tree induces incredible hunger in the gluttonous. Then we shall follow the allegory placed here. **IN HUNGER AND THIRST:** so that gluttony may be punished by its contrary; and he said excellently **MAKES THEMSELVES HOLY AGAIN**, that is, returns to the first form which sin had undone. For the soul is created pure by God, but sin stains and fouls it. **FOR THAT DESIRE:** someone might doubt why the souls go so much around this tree if the smell of the fruit increases their hunger and the sight of the water kindles their thirst; to which he responds that "desire" leads them—not the simple will, which is to flee every pain, but the "respective will" <note>the will directed toward a specific higher goal</note> which we discussed above. This desire leads them to the pain, not to suffer pain for its own sake, but to be able to purge themselves by suffering such pain, and once purged, to go to beatitude. Therefore, just as Christ...

<summary>Dante encounters his friend Forese Donati among the gluttonous, whose extreme emaciation makes their faces resemble the word "OMO." Forese explains that their suffering is a voluntary process of purification, comparing their thirst for penance to Christ's sacrifice.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the conversation between Dante and Forese Donati. The translation maintains the distinction between the poetic verses (left column) and the extensive commentary (right column) which explores the theological implications of Forese's rapid ascent through Purgatory and a sharp social critique of Florentine women.</meta>

-># CANTO XXIII<-

...to say "Hely" <note>original: "hely"; Hebrew/Aramaic for "My God"</note> of his own will. Understand this as "relative." That is, he went to the torment and the death of the cross, upon which he said "Hely" to redeem us. So the soul goes to this punishment to ascend to heaven. He said "Hely" to serve the verse instead of saying "Eloi" <note>original: "Eloi"; also meaning "My God"</note>, which in Hebrew signifies "my God" or "my deity," just as "Eloi" means "God" or "deity" to them. **BY HIS OWN VEIN.** That is, by his blood, which flowed from his veins.

And I to him: "Forese, from that day
in which you changed the world for a better life,
five years have not yet passed until now.
If the power to sin was ended in you
before the hour of the good sorrow arrived,
which remarries us to God,
how have you come here already?
I thought to find you down below
where time is restored by time."

<gloss>Sorrow remarries us to God. That is, it reconnects the soul with God. **DOWN BELOW**: in the Ante-purgatory where time is restored for time; because as it is said, the soul is held there before it can enter Purgatory for as many years as it lived in sin before it repented.</gloss>

And he to me: "She led me so quickly
to drink the sweet wormwood of the martyrs,
my little Nella with her overflowing tears.
With her devout prayers and with sighs
she has drawn me from the shore where one waits
and delivered me from the other circles.
So much more dear to God and more beloved
is my little widow, whom I loved so much,
as she is more alone in her good deeds.
For the Barbagia of Sardinia
is much more modest in its women
than the Barbagia where I left her."

<gloss>On the island of Sardinia there are very rugged mountains, and among those people of barbaric customs, the women are very lewd; and the region is called Barbagia <note>A mountainous region in Sardinia traditionally considered uncivilized by outsiders</note>, as if 'barbaric.' He says, then, that the women of that Barbagia are more honest than the Florentine women.</gloss>

"O sweet brother, what do you want me to say?
A future time is already in my sight,
to which this hour will not be very old,
In which it will be forbidden from the pulpit
to the brazen Florentine women
to go about showing their breasts with their nipples.
What barbarian women were ever there, or what Saracens,
who needed, to make them go covered,
either spiritual or other disciplines?
But if the shameless ones were certain
of what the swift heaven prepares for them,
they would already have their mouths open to howl.
For if foresight here does not deceive me,
they will be sad before cheeks grow hair
on him who is now consoled with a lullaby."

<column-break/>

**M**oveth a doubt saying: that since five years have not yet passed after his death, and having been negligent for a long time in thinking of such sin—because the power to commit the vice of gluttony was taken from him by the illness from which he died before he repented—it seems a marvel that he is not further down in the Ante-purgatory, where the soul stays as many years before it can go to purge itself as the years it delayed repenting in life. **IF THE POWER WAS FIRST ENDED IN HIM.** By the illness. **THAT THE HOUR OF GOOD SORROW SHOULD ARRIVE.** That is, penitence and contrition, which gives "good sorrow." And this

**C**onfirms what has already been said so many times: that devout prayers shorten the pains of Purgatory; and he commends the honesty and the sanctity of the wife, who was called Nella. And certainly nothing is more excellent in a woman than chastity, because such virtue makes her loved by her elders, because she does not corrupt their blood; she is loved by her children, because they do not have to be ashamed of their mother, and they do not have doubts about their father. Chastity makes her who is poor commended; it makes the rich woman exalted; it makes the ugliness of the one who is not beautiful covered. **WITH HER PRAYERS**, because prayers without devotion and sighs have no efficacy. **SO MUCH MORE DEAR.** Chastity is always pleasing to a husband and to others, but more so where it is little practiced. **FOR THE BARBAGIA OF SARDINIA**

**R**ebukes the Florentine women, who in those times, as still in ours, went with their necks and chests uncovered. A style of dress without fail more worthy of a prostitute than a matron. But just as shortly after they changed, so much so that they wore collars up to the chin covering all the neck and throat, so I hope they will change again—not so much for honesty as for levity, because in no act of theirs are they stable. **BEFORE CHEEKS GROW HAIR.** That is, before the beard grows on him who now—that is, who at present—is consoled with a lullaby <note>original: "nanna"</note>, meaning a small child. For in the first age, babies are amused and put to sleep by the nurses saying "nanna nanna." Therefore, "nanna" is the voice with which nurses invite the baby to sleep. He responds to Forese and shows that Virgil had taken and removed him from that vicious life with which he had lived with Forese a few days before, when the moon was round; and he means here...

<summary>Dante expresses surprise that his friend Forese Donati has reached the upper terraces of Purgatory so quickly, to which Forese credits the devoted prayers of his widow, Nella. This leads into a harsh critique of the immodesty of Florentine women compared to the inhabitants of the barbaric Sardinian Barbagia.</summary>
