<header>PURGATORY</header>

"Now, brother, see that you hide yourself no longer from me;
see that not only I, but all these people
gaze toward where you veil the sun."
Then I to him: "If you bring back to mind
what you were with me and what I was with you,
the present memory will still be heavy.
From that life, this man who walks before me
turned me back the other day, when the sister
of him <note>The Moon, sister of the Sun (Apollo)</note> showed herself round to you.
I showed him <note>Virgil</note> this man through the deep
night, led through the truly dead,
with this true flesh that follows him.
From there his encouragements have drawn me up,
climbing and circling the mountain
that straightens us whom the world made crooked."

<column-break/>

"He says he will be my companion
until I shall be where Beatrice is;
there it is fitting that I remain without him.
Virgil is he who says this to me,"
and I pointed to him; "and this other is that shadow
for whom every slope of your kingdom
shook just now, as it clears itself of him."

<gloss>On Good Friday: which was in the year 1300, when he made this journey; and when Virgil appeared to him. And therefore he says: 'the other day when the sister of this one showed herself round'—that is, the sister of the sun <note>the moon</note>; and when he said 'of this one' he showed the sun. **THROUGH THE DEEP NIGHT.** Through Hell: where there are deep shadows and the truly dead; because the separation of the soul from the body is not true death unless the soul remains damned. Rather, it is going to a better life. But if the soul goes to Hell: **THE MOUNTAIN: THAT STRAIGHTENS US WHOM THE WORLD MADE CROOKED**: this is the mountain of Purgatory, which, by cleansing us of the sins that we committed in the world, makes our crooked ways straight.</gloss>

### CANTO XXIII OF THE SECOND CANTICLE OF DANTE.

<image-desc>Ornamental initial 'E' with a blue background and gold highlights, containing leafy decorations.</image-desc>
Neither the talking nor the walking made him slower,
but talking, we went along strongly,
like a ship driven by a good wind.
And the shadows, who appeared like twice-dead things,
drew admiration for me through the pits
of their eyes, perceiving that I was alive.
And I, continuing my discourse,
said: "Perhaps he <note>Statius</note> goes up more slowly
than he would for another's sake.
But tell me, if you know, where Piccarda is;
tell me if I see any person of note
among this crowd that gazes so at me."
"My sister, who between beautiful and good,
I know not which she was more, triumphs joyful..."

<column-break/>

"...in high Olympus already with her crown."
So he said first; and then: "Here it is not forbidden
to name each one, since our appearance
is so milked away by the diet.
This one," and he pointed with his finger, "is Bonagiunta,
Bonagiunta from Lucca; and that face
beyond him, more punctured than the others,
Held the Holy Church in his arms;
he was from Tours, and purges through fasting
the eels of Bolsena and the Vernaccia wine."
Many others he named to me one by one,
and at their naming many seemed content,
so that I did not see a single dark gesture.
I saw, using their teeth on the void..."

---

<image-desc>A large blue initial 'N'.</image-desc>
The author does **NOT** change the subject matter because he changes the title. But continuing, he demonstrates that they did not go slower for the sake of talking together, nor did they talk less for the sake of going fast. Therefore, talking, they went strongly: like a ship driven by a good wind. **AND I CONTINUING**: continuing the speech which he had begun about Statius, he said: **SHE**: that is, the soul of Statius itself perhaps goes more slowly up to Paradise than it would otherwise: **FOR ANOTHER'S SAKE**: to be longer with Virgil. He [Forese] replied first regarding his sister <note>Piccarda Donati</note>: who was so beautiful and so good that he did not know which she was more. **TRIUMPHS WITH HER CROWN**: for the battle she won against the flesh; because as Juvenal says: "Rare is the harmony of beauty and modesty" <note>original: "Rara est concordia forme: atque pudicitie"</note>. **OLYMPUS**: heaven, like *ololampòs* <note>original: "ololamp os"; Greek for "all-shining"</note>, that is, all-shining. **AND THEN**: He shows that it is not troublesome to any soul to be named and known, since their appearance is so **MILKED**—that is, it is so thinned out by the diet—that we are not recognized. **BONAGIUNTA**: was of the Orbicciani family from Lucca; and he was an excellent composer of sonnets and songs, and a friend to Dante. **HELD THE HOLY CHURCH**: this was Pope Martin IV from Tours in France; he sat for three years and one month and twenty-seven days. He used to kill the eels of Bolsena in Vernaccia wine, and then cook them with various spices. Finally, through too much devotion to his throat, he died of fatness. **A DARK GESTURE**: that is, an angry act.

<header>CANTO XXIV</header>

I saw Master Marchese, who once had the opportunity
to drink at Forlì with less dryness <note>meaning he was less thirsty then than he is now in Purgatory</note>,
and yet he was such that he never felt satisfied.
But as one does who looks and then prizes
one more than another, I did to the one from Lucca,
who seemed to want more knowledge of me.
He was murmuring, and I heard something like "Gentucca"
there where he felt the wound
of justice that so plucks them <note>the "plucking" refers to the extreme thinness of the gluttonous souls</note>.

<gloss>never satisfied. I HEARD SOMETHING LIKE GENTUCCA. He shows in this place a prediction of future things. Dante in his exile stayed for some time in Lucca, and fell in love with a noblewoman of refined manners named Lady Gentucca. But this was after the year 1300, which is the time he pretends to write these things; and therefore he pretends that the spirit, divining the future, murmured this name "Gentucca." But the poet did not understand it then because it had not yet happened. The people of Lucca use many diminutives and shortened words, like "tucco" or "bo tuccolo," or "Boiuto" for "Bonaiuto."</gloss>

"O soul," I said, "who seems so eager
to speak with me, act so that I may understand you,
and satisfy both yourself and me with your speech."
"A woman is born, and does not yet wear the veil," <note>literally "the headband," indicating she is not yet married or a widow</note>
he began, "who will make
my city pleasing to you, however men may blame it.
You shall go hence with this foresight;
if in my murmuring you took error,
the real things will yet make it clear to you.
But tell me if I see here him who brought
forth the new rhymes, beginning:
*Ladies who have intelligence of love*?"
And I to him: "I am one who, when
Love inspires me, takes note, and in that manner
which he dictates within, I go signifying."
"O brother, now I see," said he, "the knot
that held the Notary, and Guittone, and me
short of the sweet new style that I hear.
I see well how your pens
follow close behind the dictator <note>referring to Love as the one who dictates the poetry</note>,
which certainly did not happen with ours.
And he who sets himself to look further
sees no more difference between one style and the other";
and as if satisfied, he fell silent.

<gloss>to his mind. Or we wish to understand Virgil, whom he imitates greatly, although the language is different. AND THIS NOT: because we cannot express our concepts with the pen as you do. AND HE WHO FURTHER: and whoever sets himself to look and consider your style and ours sees no more between one and the other; as if to say: that Dante advances so far that one cannot see the whole space that is between him and those who remain behind. This is the opinion of Cicero, who says that Crassus was first and Antonius was second, but second by a great interval. And from this Virgil in the fifth book <note>of the Aeneid</note>: <note>original: "Proximus at longo proximus intervallo."</note> Next, but next by a long interval.</gloss>

As the birds that winter along the Nile
sometimes form themselves into a flock,
then fly faster and go in a line—

<column-break/>

**FROM THE PILA:** is the place from which one part of this house was named. **BONIFACE** was a Frenchman and Archbishop of Ravenna, who was very gluttonous. **MARCHESE** was a knight of Forlì of the Rigogliosi family, a very great drinker, especially of their *ribolla* wine. To him, when the cellarer said that everyone was saying he did nothing but drink, he responded laughing: "Why don't they say instead that I am always thirsty?" **WITH LESS DRYNESS:** meaning it was not the thirst he had in Purgatory; and he was such that he never felt satisfied. The meaning is that although the dryness of the thirst he had in Purgatory was greater than what he had in the world, [he was never sated].

He turns his speech to **BONAGIUNTA**, and prays him to judge openly that which he had said confusedly; and he responds that in Lucca a woman is already born, for whom his city will please him. **DOES NOT YET WEAR THE VEIL:** denotes her tender age, in which young girls do not yet wear the headband. **YOU SHALL GO HENCE:** with this announcement which I give you, and the real things—that is, the effects that you will see—will declare to you if you took error in my murmuring. **BUT TELL ME IF I SEE:** In essence, Bonagiunta says: tell me if I see Dante here; as if to say: tell me if you are Dante, though he does not use his name, but uses a circumlocution, praising him as the finder of new rhymes. And he quotes the beginning of a song by Dante, which is *Ladies who have intelligence of love*. Dante wrote this and many other songs in which, under the name of Beatrice, he allegorically praises theology and the moral and theological virtues. **O BROTHER.** **ISSA:** "at present," a Lucchese word; *hora*, *teste*, *adesso*, *mo*, *aual*, *cetto*, *sauia*, *hiecotu* <note>various dialect terms for "now"</note> according to different idioms mean the same thing. **THE KNOT:** the difficulty which held back the Notary, **JACOPO DA LENTINI**, who for his excellence in that art was called "The Notary." **GUITTONE:** this is Fra Guittone d'Arezzo. **SWEET STYLE:** suave. **NEW:** never heard before. **I SEE WELL:** that is, the style of you, Dante, goes closely behind the dictator—that is, they approach the mind of the dictator, which is to say nothing else than that Dante can optimally express the affection [of his mind].

**AS THE BIRDS:** Cranes are migratory birds; in the summer they inhabit cold places, but in the winter they retreat to warm places. And therefore there is a great abundance of them in Egypt along the Nile. Of the cranes we say...

<header>PURGATORIO</header>

So all the people who were there,
turning their faces, quickened their step,
both through thinness and through will, light-footed.
And as a man who is tired of walking
lets his companions go on and walks slowly
until the panting of his chest is eased,
So Forese let the holy flock pass by
and came along behind with me,
saying: "When will it be that I see you again?"
"I do not know," I replied to him, "how long I shall live;
but my return will not be so soon
that I will not be at the shore <note>the shore of Purgatory where souls arrive after death</note> first with my desire;
Because the place where I was set to live <note>Florence</note>
is being stripped of its good from day to day,
and seems destined for a sad ruin."
"Now go," he said, "for him who is most to blame <note>Corso Donati, leader of the Black Guelphs</note>
I see dragged at the tail of a beast
toward the valley where one is never absolved <note>Hell</note>.
The beast at every step goes faster,
increasing always until it strikes him,
and leaves the body vilely undone.
Those wheels <note>the celestial spheres that measure time</note> have not much to turn—"
and he raised his eyes to heaven "—until that shall be clear to you
which my speech cannot further explain.
Remain you now, for time is precious
in this realm, so that I lose too much
coming with you thus side by side."

As sometimes a knight gallops out
from a troop of horsemen,
going to win honor in the first encounter,
So he departed from us with greater strides;
and I remained on the path with those two <note>Virgil and Statius</note>,
who were such great marshals <term>mariscalchi: military commanders or high-ranking court officials</term> of the world.
And when he had gone so far ahead of us
that my eyes became followers of him,
as my mind was of his words,
There appeared to me branches heavy and lively
with another apple tree, and not very far off,
because I had only just then turned that way.
I saw people under it raising their hands...

<column-break/>

...sufficiency in the first canticle <note>referring to the *Inferno*</note>. **UNTIL** the panting of the lungs and the excessive gasping and huffing from the fast journey **is eased** [sif foga]. **To pant** [affollare] specifically in our language means to gasp and huff; it is derived from the word **bellows** [folle], which in Latin signifies a pair of bellows <note>original: "mantaco"</note>, because it arises from the great motion of the lungs, which like bellows draw in the breath and send it out. **THE return will not be**: here in Purgatory. **TO THE shore**: of the mountain of Purgatory. In short, he says: that his return to Purgatory after death will not be so soon that his will does not go there before him. And allegorically, every well-disposed mind desires to be purged. **BECAUSE the place**: this is Florence. **STRIPPED OF FLESH** [sispolpa]: deprived of, and it is a metaphor used when the meat is removed from a chicken. **NOW GO, said he**: Here Forese predicts the violent death of Messer Corso Donati, whom he says bears more blame for the ruin of Florence than any other citizen. Messer Corso, leader of the Black party, had returned to Florence with the favor of Charles of Valois <note>original: "Carlo sanza terra," Charles Lackland</note>, and had taken power from the Whites. He remained a leader so powerful that he became suspicious to the people, as it seemed he exceeded what was proper in a free republic. Finally, suspicion grew greatly when he became the son-in-law of Uguccione della Faggiuola, the lord of Pisa. This caused him to be summoned and condemned during a sudden popular riot. The people ran to his house with the banner of justice. At first, because he was of great spirit and quick not only of tongue but of hand, he joined his friends in defense; later, insulted by the day and abandoned by many, he took to flight. Being pursued by certain Catalan soldiers—whom he could neither appease with prayers nor promises—

he either threw himself or fell from his horse; his foot caught in the stirrup and the horse dragged him so far that, when he was overtaken, he was killed. He was buried by the monks of San Salvi without any funeral rites. And his houses were destroyed by popular fury. **I SEE HIM AT THE TAIL**: This serves the historical account, and allegorically it also means that he is dragged by the devil into many vices. **THE BEAST at every step goes faster**: In the beginning, the devil does not have much force in pulling the sinner into vice. But the more a man perseveres in sin, the worse he becomes; and if he becomes worse, the more power the devil has over him. **AND LEAVES THE BODY**: Shows that the death of tyrannical and unjust men leaves the body vilely undone, because nothing remains of them but infamy. **THEY HAVE NOT**: not much time must pass. **UNTIL TO YOU**: as if to say, I speak to you so obscurely that at present you do not understand of whom I speak, but in a short time the outcome of the matter will show it to you. **FOR THE time is precious**: Especially to us, who desire purification.

**AS WITH speed sometimes a man**: a man-at-arms galloping ahead of the troop to be the first to engage with his lance. Thus Forese went swiftly to rejoin his companions. **MARSHALS**: these are the governors of courts and armies. Therefore, by simile, he calls the two poets marshals because they held the first rank among poets. **THE EYES followers**: thus I followed his steps with my eyes as I had previously followed his words with my mind. **THERE APPEARED to me branches**: he begins to see the second tree, whose branches were heavy and full of apples, and **lively**: vigorous and very green. **RAISING the hands**: the hands signify actions. **HOLDS HIGH their desire**: It shows the thing they desire but does not let them take it.

<meta>This page continues the transition in Canto XXIV. Dante has just parted from Forese Donati and is now moving with Virgil and Statius toward the end of the Terrace of Gluttony. They encounter a second mysterious tree and hear voices warning against the vice of overindulgence.</meta>

<header>CANTO XXIV</header>

and I heard a cry, I know not what, beneath the leaves,
like greedy and foolish little children
who beg, and the one they beg does not respond,
but to make their longing more acute,
holds their desire high and does not hide it.
Then the crowd departed as if **convinced**;
and we came to the great tree immediately,
which refuses so many prayers and tears.
"Pass on further without drawing near;
the wood is higher up that was bitten by Eve,
and this plant was raised from it."
So said someone among the branches, I know not who;
wherefore Virgil and Statius and I, drawn close together,
went on further along the side that rises.
"Remember," one said, "those cursed ones
formed of clouds <note>The Centaurs, who were born from Ixion and a cloud shaped like Hera.</note> who, when they were drunk,
fought Theseus with their double breasts;
And the Hebrews who showed themselves soft at the drinking,
wherefore Gideon did not want them as companions
when he descended the hills toward Midian."
Thus, staying close to one of the two edges,
we passed, hearing of the faults of gluttony,
already followed by miserable gains.

**Drunkenness**: remembering that at the wedding of Pirithous, those conquered by wine attempted to kidnap the bride <note>The battle between the Centaurs and the Lapiths at the wedding of Hippodamia and Pirithous.</note>. And certainly through drunkenness men become most beastly, and grow fierce in every vice, especially in lust, and they seize the wives of others. For as Terence says: *Without food and wine, love grows cold* <note>original: "Sine cerere et libero friget uenus."</note>. But Theseus and Hercules—that is, reason and the intellect—tame such bestiality in man. **AND OF THE HEBREWS**. God permitted sins so that the people of Israel were long vexed by the Midianites with hunger and war. But converting with tears and prayers, the angel came to Gideon, telling him to move against the enemies. Gideon gathered thirty thousand Hebrews; which number seemed small compared to the Midianites who, because of their innumerable multitude, covered the earth like locusts. Then the angel commanded that he dismiss the fearful, wherefore twenty thousand left. He came a third time and commanded that in the burning sun he should lead the remaining ten thousand to the river. And all those who drank by putting their mouths to the water he should send away; and he should keep those who drank by drawing water with the hollow of their hands, who were no more than three hundred. And with these, by the power of God, he conquered the enemies and killed one hundred and twenty thousand. Wherefore the Jews lived afterward in tranquil peace for forty years, which was as long as Gideon lived. **Edges** <term>vivagni: literally the hems or borders of a cloth</term>: the extremities and borders; this is a metaphor from cloth. **From miserable gains**: illicit gains are the cause of the sins of gluttony.

Then, spread out along the lonely road,
a full thousand paces and more carried us onward,
each of us contemplating without a word.
"What go you three thinking so deep in thought?"
suddenly a voice said, whereat I startled
as frightened and sluggish beasts do.
I raised my head to see who it was;
and never were seen in a furnace
glass or metals so glowing and red
as one I saw, who said: "If it please you
to mount up, here you must make the turn;
this way he goes who wishes to go for peace."

-> Beginning of the seventh terrace, in which Lust is purged. <-

<column-break/>

Then that aforementioned people departed. **CONVINCED** <note>original: "ricreduta"</note>: like one who believes anew that they are not yet purified. **TO THE GREAT TREE**: Nothing is greater than knowledge, which, as we have said, is signified by the tree that refuses so many prayers and tears as those souls offer it. And certainly everyone desires knowledge; but she does not listen, except to a very few, and these are the lovers of virtue. Whence he himself [Dante] says in one of his songs, the beginning of which is *Three women around my heart*, he says: "Song, let no man lay a hand upon your clothes to see what a beautiful woman hides; let the naked parts suffice; she denies the sweet apple to all people, for which everyone reaches out a hand." <note>A reference to Dante's canzone "Tre donne intorno al cor mi son venute."</note> **PASS ON BEYOND**: because it is not yet time for you to touch these apples. **The wood is higher up**: This is in the earthly paradise, and it is the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Therefore he feigns that these trees in this place were born from that one, because from that one the sin of gluttony properly began when Eve tasted the fruit, and all others followed. **AMONG THE BRANCHES**: just as in the previous tree he did not see who spoke, so also in this one; because to one who is not purified, the truth cannot be known. **ALONG THE SIDE THAT RISES**: from the part of the mountain which ascends, and by this he signifies virtue. **THOSE CURSED ONES FORMED OF CLOUDS**: He means the Centaurs, of whom we have spoken fully elsewhere; he places them in this spot because of their drunkenness.

**You three alone**: you three only, Virgil, Statius, and Dante. **I STARTLED**: not the other two, but I. For neither the intellect nor reason fears, but sensuality does. **FRIGHTENED AND SLUGGISH BEASTS**: The beast shakes itself from a sudden fright because it fears either when it leaves the stable where it has been idle—for then it wakes up and drives away all laziness; and therefore he says: **SLUGGISH** <note>original: "poltre"</note> as if to say "lazy" [poltrone]. Some say *poltre* means "fillies" [puledre], from which we say *poltruccio* [colt]. And even in this way the text proceeds well, because colts are more fearful than domesticated beasts. **GLOWING AND RED**: He gives such a color to the Angel because through the light he demonstrates doctrine, and through the red color, charity. With these two things one knows the truth. **HERE YOU MUST MAKE THE TURN**: showing the stairway.

<meta>This page continues from the end of Cante XXIV, where Dante, Virgil, and Statius have just heard voices from the second tree on the Terrace of Gluttony. Having been warned by the examples of the Centaurs and the Hebrews against overindulgence, they are now approached by the Angel of Temperance, who will lead them toward the next circle.</meta>

<header>PURGATORIO</header>

His appearance had taken away my sight,
wherefore I turned back toward my teachers,
like a man who goes according to what he hears.
And like the messenger of the dawns,
the breeze of May moves and smells sweet,
all impregnated by the grass and flowers,
So I felt a wind strike the middle
of my forehead, and clearly felt the feathers move,
which made me sense the fragrance of ambrosia.
And I heard it said: "Blessed are they whom so much
grace illumines that the love of taste
does not smoke too much desire in their breast:
Hungering always for what is just."

# .CANTO. XXV. OF THE SECOND CANTICLE OF DANTE.

<image-desc>Decorative initial O containing a miniature illustration of two figures, likely Dante and Virgil, walking on a rocky mountain path.</image-desc>
Now was the hour when climbing allowed no delay:
for the sun had left the meridian circle
to the Taurus and the Night to the Scorpio.
Because as a man does who does not stop,
but goes on his way, whatever appears to him,
if the sting of necessity pricks him,
Thus we entered through the gap,
one before the other taking the stairs,
which, by its narrowness, separates the climbers.
And like the little stork that lifts its wing
for the desire to fly, and yet does not dare
to abandon the nest, and lets it drop back down,
Such was I, with desire lit and extinguished
to ask, coming even to the act
that he makes who prepares himself to speak.
My sweet father did not stop because our pace was swift,
but said: "Shoot the bow
of speech that you have drawn to the iron."
Then I confidently opened my mouth.

<column-break/>

Sensuality is dazzled by the excessive splendor: and is blinded in such a way that by itself it could not proceed forward: and for this reason it turns to the intellect and reason, and goes according to what they say: and therefore he says: *goes according to what he hears*.

**AND LIKE** the messenger of the dawns. He shows that as the angel struck his wings, he moved a little breeze full of the finest scent: and he felt such an odor and such a breeze as is a gentle and small wind that rises in May before the dawn. Which is a sign that soon the dawns of the day will be seen. This little breeze, rising, smells sweet <note>original: "oleza"</note>, that is, it gives off the best odor, because it moves the new grasses and flowers.

**WHICH** makes one feel the fragrance <note>original: "loreza"</note>, that is, the scent of ambrosia. Taken from the first book of Virgil when he feigns that Venus, in departing from Aeneas, scattered a great scent. Wherefore he says: "And her ambrosial hair breathed a divine fragrance from her head." <note>original: "Ambrosieque come diuinum uertice odorem Spiratuere."</note>.

**AND** heard it said "Blessed": These words are from Matthew the Evangelist where he says: "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for justice, for they shall be satisfied." <note>original: "Beati qui exuriunt et sitiunt iustitiam: quoniam ipsi saturabuntur."</note>. This voice was therefore: "Blessed are those whom [it] **ILLUMINES** with so much grace," that is, they have so much light of God's grace that the love and greed for taste and gluttony **DOES NOT SMOKE**: does not evaporate and does not **GIVE** too much desire—superfluous desire and appetite of the throat—**HUNGERING** <note>original: "exuriendo"</note>, that is, having as much desire to eat as is just and reasonable, and no more.

He describes in the present canto how they climbed to the seventh terrace where lust is purged in the fire. He describes the time. He shows he has a desire to have a doubt clarified. Virgil encourages him to ask: and having heard the doubt, he solves part of it: part he leaves to be solved by Statius, who demonstrates the creation of the fetus in the mother's womb and likewise the infusion of the soul.

**NOW WAS** the hour. He describes the time and shows that midday had passed. Because since the sun was in Aries, and had already declined with that sign toward the west, Taurus, which follows it, had now risen to the meridian. Therefore it was necessary that, with Taurus being at the middle of the hemisphere on the side of day, Scorpio would be on this side at the middle of our hemisphere at night, because these two signs are opposite.

**BECAUSE** as a man does who does not stop <note>original: "non s'affigge"</note>, that is, he does not stay still. But goes on his way, **WHATEVER APPEARS TO HIM**, that is, for whatever thing may appear to him.

**THUS** we entered through the gap <note>original: "callaia"</note>, that is, through the entrance of the stairs. **ONE BEFORE THE OTHER**: we did not all three go together, but one by one. And this because the **NARROWNESS** <note>original: "arteza"</note> of the stairs separates the climbers. The meaning is that the stairs were so narrow <note>original: "arcta"</note> that he who climbs cannot go side-by-side. And certainly, in such high contemplation, sensuality cannot go side-by-side with the intellect. But it is enough if it follows it and goes after it.

**AND LIKE** the little stork. A fitting comparison which expresses this: I had a great desire to ask Virgil about the doubt mentioned below, and it brought me right up to speaking, and then shame did not let me send out the word. He acted therefore like the little stork, which, having the desire to leave the nest, begins to beat its wings. But then for fear of falling, it does not dare to fly. **WITH** desire lit and extinguished: the desire to ask was lit and inflamed, but shame extinguished it.

Prudence and learning make a man almost divine. Therefore Virgil, by certain gestures in Dante, perceived that he was in doubt. And remembering the thinness of the souls, he understood his doubt through conjecture. And to take away his shame...

<summary>This page marks the transition from the Terrace of Gluttony to the Terrace of Lust, beginning with an angelic encounter and an astrological determination of the time (around 2:00 PM). Dante expresses his internal struggle to ask Virgil a difficult question about how shades can become thin from hunger if they do not require physical food.</summary>
<keywords>Angel of Temperance, May breeze, ambrosia, Matthew 5:6, Taurus, Scorpio, Aries, stork metaphor, intellect vs. sensuality, Cristoforo Landino commentary</keywords>

--- Page 495 ---
<meta>This page continues Dante’s ascent through the Circle of Gluttony. Dante is puzzled by how the spirits of the gluttonous can appear physically emaciated since they no longer possess mortal bodies that require food. Virgil begins to answer by using mythological and physical analogies before deferring to the Christian poet Statius for a deeper theological explanation.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>CANTO XXV</header>

...and I began: "How can one become thin
there where the need for nourishment does not touch?"
"If you remembered how Meleager
was consumed at the consuming of a fire-brand,"
he said, "this would not be so bitter to you;
And if you thought how at your every twitch
your image twitches within the mirror,
what seems hard to you would seem easy.
But so that your desire may rest easy,
here is Statius <note>A 1st-century Roman poet whom Dante portrays as a secret convert to Christianity; he acts as a bridge between Virgil's pagan wisdom and Christian theology.</note>; and him I call and pray
that he now be the healer of your wounds."

"If I explain the eternal vengeance
to him where you are present,"
Statius replied, "let it excuse me that I cannot deny you."
Then he began: "If my words,
my son, your mind heeds and receives,
they will be a light to you on the 'how' that you ask.
Perfect blood, which is never drunk
by the thirsty veins and remains behind,
like food that one removes from the table,
Takes from the heart power for all human limbs:
the formative virtue, like that blood
which flows through the veins to become the limbs.
Once more refined, it descends to where it is more beautiful..."

<column-break/>

...shame: <note>Referring to Dante’s hesitation to speak.</note> which did not let him speak: he urged him to ask, saying to him "draw the bow of speech," which you have pulled even to the iron head: And here is an excellent metaphor <note>original: "optima translatione"</note> comparing arrows to words. Then he safely opened his mouth. Encouraged by Virgil, Dante spoke with confidence. And he opened his doubt: which was how it could happen that souls grow thin in Purgatory. For thinness is born from a lack of nourishment: Wherefore when a man fasts and is deprived of food, his body grows thin. But souls, which are incorporeal, have no need for food. And therefore he says: how can one grow thin in Purgatory, there where it "does not touch": and the "need for nourishment" does not occur, that is <note>original: ".i." for "id est"</note>, the need to be fed. IF YOU REMEMBERED how

Meleager <note>A hero of Greek mythology whose life was tied to a piece of wood.</note>. Meleager was the son of Oeneus, King of Calydon. And his mother Althaea, when he was born, saw that the Fates placed a piece of wood on the fire. And they said: that Meleager would live as long as that wood lasted. His mother took it from the fire so it would not burn. Meleager grew up, and having become a young man, it happened that a terrible boar wasted the whole region of Calydon; therefore he summoned many nobles of Greece to the hunt: Theseus, Pirithous, Castor and Pollux, Jason, Telamon, Nestor, Peleus the father of Achilles, Speusippus, and Toxeus the brothers of his mother, and Atalanta, a most beautiful woman. She was the first who struck the boar's ear with an arrow. But Meleager killed it, and inflamed with love for the girl, he gave her the head of the beast, which is usually the prize for the one who kills it. This was offensive to the mother’s brothers. And they took it from the girl; which thing was so annoying to Meleager that he killed both of them. And Althaea, in vengeance for her brothers, put the fire-brand back on the fire: and at the same time it burned, and Meleager was consumed. Through this fable it seems that Virgil wishes to imply as a poet that Dante can thus imagine the thinness of souls, even though they cannot naturally grow thin, just as other poets imagine this story of Meleager; or truly we say that just as in truth Meleager was consumed by the repentance he felt for the fault committed and by the pain he took from it, so these souls, through their painful repentance, suffer in themselves a similar condition: desiring with extreme restraint to compensate for the luxury of the throat <note>Gluttony.</note> which the body suffered by abstaining. AND IF YOU THOUGHT HOW: He places the second example of the mirror, in which we see our image make the same twitches—that is, movements—that the one whose image it is makes. The reason for this is that the mirror is suited to represent every gesture that is before it. Therefore our image and our gestures are imprinted in the luminous air, and such air strikes the mirror with the same impression, and the mirror catching them shows them. So therefore he wishes it to happen in the aerial bodies <note>The "shadow bodies" souls wear in the afterlife to experience physical sensations.</note> which our souls take up after death and clothe themselves in. In these, because they are like mirrors, all the passions of the soul are represented. And this is what shows the souls as thin. But that the soul takes an aerial body is not human reason <note>Meaning it is not found in pagan philosophy.</note>, but from some theologians. And for this reason, he has Statius, as a Christian, speak of it more extensively. BUT SO THAT YOUR DESIRE MAY REST EASY, that is, your will may be content. HERE IS STATIUS. Having to treat things belonging to Christian theology, Virgil, not being a Christian, quite rightly has them explained by Statius, a Christian.

"If I explain the eternal vengeance": if divine justice, which avenges and corrects every crime, ordains the text. Statius replied: if I "explain"—that is, manifest—to Dante himself "the eternal vengeance"—that is, what eternal justice disposes. "There where you are" <note>original: "LA doue tu fie"</note>: in the place where you are: as if to say: it seems like presumption that where you are, full of all doctrine, I should dare to speak. But even if I do so, it does not spring from arrogance, but from obedience, because I cannot deny you what you ask of me, whence he says: "EXCUSE ME"—that is, forgive me—for not being able to "deny you"—that is, to refuse you anything. Because a soul set on the path of charity cannot deny a just thing. "THEY WILL BE A LIGHT TO YOU": they will give you knowledge. "HOW THAT YOU ASK": regarding your doubt, where you ask how it is possible that...

<summary>In this passage, Dante asks how spirits can appear emaciated without physical bodies. Virgil uses the myth of Meleager and the analogy of a mirror to explain before deferring to Statius for a theological explanation of the 'aerial body.'</summary>

<meta>This page continues the speech of Statius in Canto XXV of the Purgatorio. Having been asked by Dante how spirits can grow thin without physical bodies, Statius provides a detailed lecture on medieval embryology and the formation of the soul, explaining how "perfect blood" becomes the formative power of the human body.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>PURGATORIO</header>

...to be silent than to speak, and from there it distills
down upon the blood of another in the natural vessel.
There it gathers the one and the other together:
the one disposed to be passive, the other to act
because of the perfect place from which it is pressed.
And having arrived there, it begins to operate,
coagulating first, and then it gives life
to that which it had made to stay for its material.
The active virtue, having become a soul,
is like that of a plant, but so different in this:
that the plant is at the end of its journey, while this is still on its way.
It works so much then that it moves and feels,
like a sea-sponge <note>original: "fungo marino." In medieval science, sponges were seen as an intermediate stage between plants and animals because they seemed to possess sensation but not movement.</note>; and from there it begins
to organize the powers of which it is capable.
Now it bends, my son, now it extends,
the virtue that comes from the generator's heart,
where nature intends for all the limbs.

<column-break/>

...the souls grow thin. Then, to clarify his doubt and demonstrate to him how the soul clothes itself in an aerial body after the death of the physical body: he repeats from the beginning the creation of the vegetative, motive, and sensitive soul: which nature produces from the potential of matter, which we have in common with the lower animals. And then he demonstrates: that as soon as the sensitive soul is produced in the human body through the virtue of the acting male seed and the passive matter of the female—which is the blood—God infuses the rational soul into it. This rational soul is unique to man and is created by God out of nothing. And this soul, thus infused, draws to itself the sensitive soul which it finds in the body with all its powers, and it informs and unites that soul to itself, so that they are not two souls, but one. And this single soul, when it departs from the body, clothes itself anew in an aerial body.

**PERFECT BLOOD WHICH THEN IS NOT**
drunk by the thirsty veins. All the food and drink that we take is cooked and digested four times before it is perfect. First in the stomach, where the part that is to be for the health of the animal is divided from the putrefied and harmful dregs, and it is called chyle. And these dregs fall into the belly and the intestines and are sent out. And the chyle from the stomach goes through a vein called the "great gate" <note>The portal vein.</note> to the liver, and there it is cooked a second time. And the superfluous humor is separated—the "false" one called urine—and it distills through the kidneys into the bladder, and is pushed out through its neck. The chyle, having been sufficiently purged and cooked by the liver, takes on the color of the liver and becomes red. Then, in the third digestion—which happens either in the heart or in the liver with the virtue of the heart—it removes from itself the superfluous choler, which the Latins call **bile**, and it is the foam of the blood and is sent to the gall bladder; and the melancholy humor, which is the dross of the blood, which the Latins call **black bile** <note>original: "atra bile."</note>, and it is sent to the spleen. After the third digestion, the blood spreads through all the veins, and in them it is cooked a fourth time. And all the superfluous and harmful humor that remained in it is pushed out by nature through sweat, or else it is converted into fur, hair, and nails. Of this entirely purified blood, the veins suck up as much as is enough to nourish and maintain the body. And that which remains runs to the veins called the "seminal vessels," because it is intended to be the seed to generate another human. This, through a process that cannot be decently named, descends to the two witnesses of generation. And just as the blood that is to nourish the infant, having entered the "sponge" of the breast, changes color and is converted into milk, so this—by the virtue of that member—becomes white and takes on the generative virtue. And infused into the vessel of the woman, there with her blood, which is virtuous <note>Meaning "full of potential/power."</note>, it forms a new creature. Nor should anyone believe that this seed becomes the body of the infant. Rather, its subtle parts are all "spirits," which, nourished by the coarse parts, like an excellent craftsman, form the body from the mother's blood and give it life and the sensitive soul—which later the rational and immortal soul unites to itself, as I have said. I will not narrate at present why it generates a male rather than a female, why one or many, why it resembles the father or the mother or others of the kin, or why hermaphrodites are born; these are various things, certainly worthy of being understood. But I have collected all the effective arguments of Galen, Avicenna, Aristotle, and Albertus Magnus and many other doctors and philosophers at length; and if I do not deceive myself, I narrated them very clearly in my second book **On the Soul** <note>original: "de anima." Landino is referencing his own philosophical dialogue.</note>, written as a dialogue in the Latin language. Now I return to the text. **WHICH IS NOT DRUNK**: because it remains over, just as we see food remain for one who has eaten sufficiently. **TAKES FROM THE HEART**: according to many philosophers, every virtue of the animal has its origin in the heart. But then it takes its perfection in different members: because the nutritive virtue takes it in the liver, the sensitive in the brain, and the generative where I said above. **THERE IT GATHERS**: i.e., in the vessel of the female, which is the womb. **THE ONE AND the other**: i.e., the seed of the male, which is active and formative, and the blood of the female which is passive, which is the matter from which the creature is made and which receives the form into itself. **THROUGH THE PERFECT place**: because it proceeds from a human, who is perfect and active. **THE active VIRTUE** having become a vegetative soul, such as is in plants. But in plants this virtue is perfect, because it does not wait for the sensitive soul. But in man it is imperfect, because it must still have the motive and sensitive souls. And therefore he adds: "It works so much then that it moves and feels." **SEA-SPONGE** <note>original: "FVNGO MARINO."</note> is a coagulation of sea foam, which becomes alive, and moves and feels, but does not have formed limbs. So is the fetus...

<meta>This page continues the explanation of Canto XXV of Purgatorio, where Statius (speaking for Dante) describes the biological and spiritual transition from a developing fetus to a human being endowed with an immortal soul. It specifically addresses the theological point where the "vegetative" and "sensitive" soul (shared with plants and animals) is joined by the "rational" soul created directly by God.</meta>

# CANTO XXV

...in the mother’s womb. But then this power begins to form various members: which the soul uses to exercise its powers. For example <note>original: "verbi gratia"</note>, it forms the ear to use the power of hearing, and the eye to be able to use the power of sight. **IT UNFOLDS.** That is, the power—which is united in itself—divides into different parts: it extends itself by making the limbs grow. **THE ACTIVE VIRTUE** which came into the seed from the power of the heart of the parent.

---

<columns>2</columns>

**P**ecause he has shown until now how the human body is generated, and how it takes on the vegetative and sensitive soul—which two powers are held in common with other animals and come from the potential of matter—he continues by demonstrating how, once the creature is formed and made alive and sensible, the supreme creator infuses the rational soul created by Him from nothing; and it is created and infused at one and the same time.

> But how from animal it becomes a speaker <note>original: "fante." Dante uses this term to denote a human capable of speech and reason.</note>
> you do not yet see; this is the point
> that once led a wiser man than you astray,
> So that by his teaching, the possible intellect
> was separated from the soul,
> because he saw no organ assumed by it.
> Open your heart to the truth that comes,
> and know that as soon as the articulation
> of the brain is perfected in the fetus,
> The First Mover <note>A medieval term for God, the source of all motion in the universe.</note> turns to it, joyful
> over such an art of nature, and breathes
> a new spirit, full of power,
> Which draws into its own substance
> whatever it finds active there, and becomes a single soul,
> which lives, and feels, and revolves upon itself.
> And so that you admire the word less,
> look at the sun's heat which becomes wine
> when joined to the juice that flows from the vine.

<column-break/>

**BUT HOW FROM ANIMAL** it becomes a speaker: Until this point, the soul within the fetus has no more power than the soul of brute animals. Afterward, it becomes a "fante"—that is, speaking—meaning a rational soul. For speaking is granted only to humans, so that they may express the reason they have within themselves. And this is the point where **Averroës** <note>original: "Auerois." A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose "monopsychism" theory suggested all humans share one single intellect. This was a major theological controversy in Dante's time.</note> erred, for he claimed that there is no individual intellect in man such that one could say: "this was the intellect of Plato, and that was of Cicero." Instead, he argued there is one universal intellect infused through all men, as the sun shines through the whole world. If this were so, it would be false to say that God infuses the rational soul into us; and after this life, our soul would remain dead along with the body. For this reason, this opinion has been most sharply refuted by many sharp and learned philosophers. Their arguments we have diligently collected in our third book on the soul. Therefore, Averroës by his teaching divided reason and the intellect from our soul. He was moved perhaps because he did not see a physical organ for the intellect in the human body, as he saw those that serve the vegetative and sensitive functions. **OPEN TO THE TRUTH.** But you, Dante, open yourself

<columns>1</columns>

to the truth that you shall hear from me. And he says: that as soon as the brain is articulated—that is, it has its passages distinct and perfected—meaning that within it, the location of common sense, the location of imagination, of fantasy, of thought, and of memory are perfected. Furthermore, all the things that belong to the external senses are ready. Therefore, when all the organs that serve motion and sense are perfected, then God infuses the rational soul, as was said, which Dante calls the "new spirit," because it is not of the same kind as the spirits found in the body. Rather, it is a new thing. And it has the perfection of power, having reason and intellect. This new spirit draws to itself and makes of its own nature whatever it finds active in the soul that was there before; and there remains a single vegetative, sensitive, and rational soul. And it is entirely in the whole body, and entirely in every part of it.

---

<columns>2</columns>

> And when Lachesis <note>One of the three Fates in Greek mythology; she is the one who spins the thread of life and determines its length.</note> has no more flax,
> it is released from the flesh, and in its power
> it carries both the human and the divine away:
> The other powers are all nearly mute;
> memory, intelligence, and will
> are in action much more acute than before.
> Without stopping, it falls of its own accord,
> marvelously, to one of the shores;
> there it first learns its paths.

<column-break/>

**H**e demonstrates that afterward, when the soul leaves its body, it carries with it all its powers. **THE HUMAN.** That is, the powers that come from the potential of matter, such as the vegetative and sensitive. And **the divine**: such as reason. But only reason stays awake in the soul, which consists of will, intelligence, and memory. And the vegetative and the senses remain dormant until the soul arrives where it is meant to be. And there, the formative power forms an aerial body for the soul, and the soul lives within that, just as it lived before in its own body. And into this aerial body, it imprints all the internal and external senses.

<meta>This page continues the explanation of Canto XXV of Purgatorio. Having previously described how the rational soul is infused into the body by God, the text now explains what happens to the soul after death: how it forms a "shade-body" from the air to maintain its sensory functions and appearance until the Resurrection.</meta>

### PURGATORIO CXXV

As soon as the place there circumscribes it,
the formative power radiates around,
in the same way and measure as in the living limbs.
And as the air, when it is most heavy with rain,
through another’s ray that is reflected in it,
becomes adorned with diverse colors,
So the nearby air here sets itself
into that form which the soul, that stayed there,
seals upon it through its power.
And then, similar to the little flame
that follows the fire wherever it shifts,
the spirit follows its new form.
Because from this its outward appearance 
is then called a "shade," and from this it then organizes
every sense, even including sight.
From this we speak, and from this we laugh;
from this we produce the tears and the sighs
that you may have heard throughout the mountain.
According as the desires and the other 
affections affect us, the shade takes its figure;
and this is the reason for what you marvel at.
And already we had come to the final turn <note>original: "tortura." This refers to the final bend or "turn" of the mountain, but also implies the "torment" of the souls found there.</note>
and had turned to the right hand,
and we were intent on another care.
Here the bank flashes forth flames,
and the cornice breathes a blast upward
that reflects them back and keeps them away from the edge.
Thus it was necessary for us to go by the open side,
one by one; and I feared the fire
on this side, and on that side I feared falling down.
My Leader said: "Through this place,
one must keep a tight rein on the eyes,
because one could easily go astray."

<column-break/>

...through these organs, the soul exercises the senses and can fall into passions. It is no wonder that God joins souls to these bodies. For even necromancers, with diabolic power, bind spirits to images. **TO ONE OF** the shores. That is, either to the shore of the Acheron river, because the soul is damned to Hell; or to the shore of Ostia at the Tiber. From there, the author imagines that the angel takes the souls who are to be purged and carries them by sea to the mountain of Purgatory, from which—once made pure—they finally fly to heaven. In this way, therefore, souls can suffer not only spiritual pains, but physical ones. Nor were those philosophers ignoble who claim that the entirely incorporeal soul rejoins the dense body composed of the four elements by means of an extremely thin body <note>This refers to the "spiritus," a medium believed to connect the physical and spiritual realms.</note>. This is so that it may be, as it were, common to both the corporeal and incorporeal nature; and through such communion, it may be fit to join two extremes. For truly, in natural things, one does not go from one extreme to another without a middle ground. As, for example <note>original: "verbi gratia"</note>, from heat one does not become cold unless one first becomes lukewarm. Nor does light become darkness without a certain twilight which, being neither one nor the other, nonetheless participates in both; as we see between the departure of the sun and the obscurity of the night.

**AT THE LAST** turn: at the last torment. Because this is the seventh and final circle of Purgatory, in which lust <note>original: "luxuria"</note> is purged with fire, which is a very appropriate punishment. For earthly goods are those which, with leisure and delicate foods, inflame us to lust. And the wind that blows from the cornice—which forms the boundary between this circle and the sixth, where gluttony is punished—pushes the flame back and separates it <note>original: "sequestra," meaning to divide or set apart.</note> from the path. This signifies that the wind pushes the flame back from the edge of the terrace so much that a space and a path remain for those who pass through. It is not without the highest reason that the intellect admonishes the senses to restrain the eyes; for the eyes are the window through which love enters. Love is nothing other than the desire for beauty. Nor can beauty be judged by any other 

---

sense than the eye. Hence Propertius says: *If you know it not, the eyes are the leaders in love.* <note>original: "Si nescis oculi sunt in amore duces."</note> And our Florentine elegant and lyric poet <note>Referring to Petrarch.</note> marvelously declares this sentiment in this sonnet: *Weep, eyes, accompany the heart, which through your failing suffers death.* And certainly this desire does not strike the heart before the eyes have judged the beloved thing to be beautiful. Therefore, we must always restrain our eyes if we do not wish to fall into this perturbation, which overcomes every kind of madness and often leads the lover to voluntary death. It makes us blind in judgment and children in greed. And for this reason, the aforementioned Propertius said: *Whoever he was, that boy who painted Love, do you not think he had marvelous hands? He first realized that a lover lives without sense, and that great goods perish through light-hearted cares.* <note>A translation of the Latin quote from Propertius's Elegies.</note> It would be very tedious to relate how harmful, how grave, how dangerous, and how pestilential the perturbations of love are. And similarly how light, how mobile, how varied, how childish, and how similar to madness they are—all of which have been not only expressed but painted by all the elegiac and lyric poets, both Greek and Latin. But our Petrarch, in his *Triumph of Love*, gathers them all into a heap that cannot be read without the greatest amazement. And Virgil, with worthy exclamation in very brief words, embraced it all when he said: *O cruel Love, to what do you not compel human hearts?* <note>original: "Improbe amor quid non mortalia pectora cogis" from the Aeneid.</note> And I, in the elegies which I wrote in my youth under the title of *Xandra*, moved more by...

The commentary emphasizes the danger of the eyes as the gateway to desire, citing classical and contemporary poets.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto XXV of Purgatorio. Having established the physical state of the "shade-bodies" in the previous page, the text now transitions to the specific punishment of the lustful on the final terrace of Purgatory. It explores the relationship between divine fire and the fire of passion.</meta>

# CANTO XXV

...impetus: which comes from art: wanting to demonstrate the most grave punishments and insupportable torments that oppress men in such a disturbance, I placed these verses: *Why, Jupiter, do you strike the savage hearts of the giants with rapid lightning? A greater penalty must be prepared for the wicked. Whoever strives to climb the star-bearing heaven also attempts to wage war against the gods above. Here let him be suddenly inflamed by the torches of harsh love, and let him hold his neck under the yoke of his mistress. Then he will know that these burdens surpass eternal labors, and he would rather choose to endure the Pellaean rocks.* <note>original: "Fulmine quid rapido..." This Latin poem, likely written by the commentator Landino himself, argues that the torment of lust is more painful than the divine lightning that struck down the rebellious Giants of myth. "Pellaean rocks" likely refers to the heavy burdens or the tomb of Alexander the Great in Pella.</note> But returning to the text, it follows:

->God of supreme clemency,<-
within the heart of the great heat
I then saw [spirits] singing,
which made me no less eager to turn [and look].
And I saw spirits walking through the flame;
for which reason I watched them and my steps,
dividing my sight from time to time.
After the end of this hymn, 
they cried aloud: "I know not man," <note>original: "virum non cognosco." These are the words of the Virgin Mary to the Archangel Gabriel (Luke 1:34), used here as an example of perfect chastity.</note>
then they began the hymn again in low voices.
When this was finished, they cried: "To the woods
ran Diana, and drove out Helice, 
who had felt the poison of Venus."

<column-break/>

HE had no less "calere" <note>An archaic Italian term for "care" or "concern."</note>, that is, no less care to turn and see the spirits who were in the flame, than to watch his own feet. And [Dante] feigns that these spirits, who were being purged from the sin of luxury <term>lust</term>, sang the hymn which the Holy Church sings, the beginning of which is *Summe deus clementie* <note>original: "God of supreme clemency." This is a traditional hymn for the Saturday Matins service, traditionally sung to pray for the quenching of the fires of lust through the fire of the Holy Spirit.</note>. And in it, one prays to God to inflame the hearts with the Holy Spirit. Which produces an effect entirely contrary to the heat of concupiscence <term>unnatural or excessive desire</term>. The former restores us to health by urging us to place our love in God and celestial things; then it demonstrates with what order, from grade to grade, we ought to love created beings. The latter, perverting all order, makes us prefer the creature to the Creator; the false good to the true and supreme good; and corruptible and mortal things to the incorruptible and immortal.

### FOR WHICH REASON I WATCHED THEM AND MY STEPS DIVIDING MY SIGHT FROM TIME TO
time. That is, I divided my sight from moment to moment, looking now at them and now at my feet. Nor is it without cause that in this place he shows such diligence in looking at his feet: He watched them, that is, he contemplated such concupiscence; and he watched his feet, so that they would not slip into the flames; and he remained attentive, so that his appetite in this contemplation would not fall into the heat of the flesh. And then, as he has observed in all the other circles, he introduces the souls proposing examples of supreme chastity. And first, of her who truly, in this and in every other virtue, is first among mortals...
**I KNOW NOT MAN** <note>original: "VIRVM NON cognosco."</note>. Luke writes in the Gospel that when the Angel announced [the birth] to Mary and predicted the future conception to her, she replied: "How can this be? That is, that I should become pregnant, since I do not know man," that is, I have no intention of ever knowing one. Next, he introduces Diana, who drove away the nymph already defiled by Jove. She was Callisto, daughter of Lycaon, King of Arcadia, and one of the number of virgins consecrated to Diana. And until those times she lived chaste and pure. Then, violated by Jove, she conceived Arcas. Seeing this one day when she was naked to wash herself, Diana held her in supreme abomination, and drove her from her choir, and she fled into the forest. The rest of the fable we have narrated elsewhere. Dante does not call her Callisto here, but **Helice** <note>original: "Elice."</note>, because the poets thus name that celestial sign <note>The constellation Ursa Major.</note> into which she was transformed. He shows, therefore, the chastity of Diana, who not only never corrupted herself, but fled from those who had been violated as if from a supreme pestilence. The poets feigned that this same goddess was the Moon in heaven, Diana on earth, and Proserpina in hell. And they maintain that she has a hundred powers; for which reason Virgil in the fourth book of the *Aeneid* said: *Triple Hecate, the three faces of the virgin Diana.* <note>original: "Ter geminam hecaten tria uirginis ora Diane."</note> And shortly after: *He thunders with his voice the three hundred gods.* <note>original: "ter centum tonat ore deos."</note> The ancients posit two Dianas: the first was the daughter of the first Jove and Proserpina; the second daughter of Jove and Latona, born of the same birth with Apollo on Mount Cynthus on the island of Delos. For this reason she is called Delia and Cynthia. This goddess observed perpetual virginity, and was always a huntress, accompanied by a choir of nymphs. She converted Actaeon the Theban into a stag and had him torn apart by his own dogs because he saw her bathing naked in a cool fountain. All roads are consecrated to Diana to denote virginity, which produces no fruit, just as roads are also unfruitful.

Then they returned to singing once more;
they cried out of husbands who were chaste,
as virtue and marriage impose.
And this way, I believe, suffices them
for all the time that the fire burns them:
with such care it is necessary, and with such food,
that the wound [of sin] be sewn back up.

<column-break/>

Just as the spirits of the women mentioned above sang "I know not man," praising virginity, so now they praise the chastity both of themselves and of other husbands who, following the commandments of marriage and the precepts of virtue, observe chastity. And certainly there is no other way by which we more quickly flee from luxury <term>lust</term> than the way of chastity. **And this way, I believe, suffices them**: [it] lasts for them. <meta>The catchword "CON tal" indicates the start of the next page.</meta>

<summary>This page explains the punishment of the lustful on the final terrace of Purgatory, where souls are purified by fire while singing hymns of chastity and citing examples like the Virgin Mary and the goddess Diana. The commentary emphasizes that both celibate virginity and chaste marriage are remedies for the "heat" of disordered desire.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the final terrace of Purgatory, where the sin of lust is purged through fire. The previous page introduced the spirits singing hymns of chastity. Here, the commentator Cristoforo Landino explains the metaphors used for the soul's healing and the nature of lust compared to other sins.</meta>

# XXV PURGATORIO

...with such contrition. **FOODS**: the nourishment and sustenance of virtue. For purgation is a **food** that nourishes virtue and extinguishes vice. Just as, on the contrary, voluptuousness extinguishes virtue and nourishes vice, which kills the soul. **THE LAST WOUND** <note>original: "PIAGA DASESO." The word "dasezo" or "da sezzo" means "at the end" or "last."</note>: the wound that lust has made in the soul, which is "at the end" because it is the last [of the seven capital sins]; for at the end of life, the soul departs the body with this wound, and cannot commit any further vice afterward. **STITCH UP**: To heal or mend. For just as the body remains torn by a blow dealt to it, so the soul receives a **wound** when vice strikes it. And it is not only in this case, but in many other things that we apply to the soul, through metaphor, those things which belong to the body. Hence Virgil says:
> But the queen, long since wounded by heavy care, feeds the wound in her veins and is consumed by hidden fire. <note>original: "At regina graui iam dudum saucia cura. Vulnus alit uenis et ceco rapitur igni." This refers to Queen Dido of Carthage falling in love with Aeneas in Book IV of the *Aeneid*.</note>
Here he portrays Dido's soul as being wounded and burning, things which belong to the body and not the soul. But they are used as similes. Lust is certainly the last in the order of capital sins <note>The "capital sins" are the seven deadly sins; in Purgatory, they are arranged from the heaviest (pride) to the lightest (lust).</note>. But it becomes very abominable because it removes the man who submerges himself in it from all manly nobility. And it makes him like the beasts. Nevertheless, because there are various types of lust, there is no doubt that while some seem worthy of some slight excuse, there are others so far from all reason and so contrary to nature that whoever practices them strips himself not only of human nature, but even of the nature of beasts, who do not fall into such errors. Instead, he becomes a more horrendous monster than a **centaur** <note>A mythological creature, half-man and half-horse.</note> or a **chimera** <note>A fire-breathing monster composed of parts from multiple animals.</note>. And he creates a riddle <note>original: "enygma"</note> that the Theban **Sphinx** <note>The "spinge" or Sphinx, who famously posed a riddle to Oedipus in Thebes.</note> could hardly solve. Therefore, let everyone flee from these. But let this [unnatural lust] be forgotten entirely. So that if, perhaps through frailty, or bad habit, or some natural inclination we are overcome and led to something not permitted, we may say with some compassion for those who say this:
> God saw our fragile makeup, and had mercy on us. <note>original: "Vidit deus figmentum nostrum. Et misertus est nostri." A paraphrase of Psalm 103:14: "For he knows our frame [figmentum]; he remembers that we are dust."</note>

<summary>Landino explains the metaphor of vice as a physical wound and lust as the final "food" of purgation, distinguishing between human frailty and "monstrous" unnatural acts.</summary>
<keywords>purgation, virtue, vice, lust, metaphor, Virgil, Dido, capital sins, Sphinx, monsters, divine mercy</keywords>

Having established that lust is the final sin to be purged before reaching the Earthly Paradise, the text now moves into Canto XXVI, where Dante encounters the spirits of the lustful—both those who followed natural appetite and those who committed "sin against nature"—purifying themselves within a wall of flames.</meta>

# CANTO XXVI OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'M' showing a human figure in a landscape with a building in the background.</image-desc>

While along the edge, one before the other,
we went, and often the good master
said: "Look out; let my warning benefit you." <note>original: "chio tiscaltro." Landino explains this as making one "shrewd" or "experienced."</note>
The sun was striking me on my right shoulder,
which, already beaming, was changing the whole west
from its azure aspect into white.
And I, with my shadow, made the flame
appear more ruddy; and even at such a slight sign
I saw many shades, as they walked, take notice:
This was the cause that gave them the start
to speak of me, and they began to say:
"That one does not seem to have a fictitious body."

**SHREWD:** a man is shrewd when he is practical and experienced. **ON MY RIGHT SHOULDER:** they had turned to the right, and the sun, which was toward the west, cast shadows toward the mountain; therefore, it struck his right side. **BEAMING:** striking with rays. **CHANGING INTO WHITE** the azure aspect: it caused the western part of the sky—which is naturally azure—to become white due to the abundance of solar rays. And certainly, that part of the sky where the solar body is always changes from azure to white. **MADE** the flame appear more ruddy with the shadow: A flame exposed to the sun loses much of its red color—which the Latins call *candente* <note>meaning glowing or white-hot</note>—and turns pale, becoming almost invisible. But if it is covered by a shadow so that the sun does not touch it, it becomes more vivid. This, then, was the reason that Dante’s shadow made the fire appear more ruddy. Whence the souls perceived that such a shadow came from a solid body like a human one, and not from the souls, who have an aerial and "fictitious" body, as we showed just above.

Then toward me, as far as they could come,
certain ones made themselves, always with care
not to come out where they would not be burned.
"O you who go—not for being more slow,
but perhaps out of reverence for the others behind—
answer me, who burn in thirst and in fire.
Nor to me alone is your answer needed,
for all these have a greater thirst for it
than for cold water the Indian or the Ethiopian.
Tell us how it is that you make yourself a wall
to the sun, as if you had not yet
entered inside the net of death."

being troublesome while being out of pain. **NOR TO ME ALONE:** He shows that such an answer will be pleasing not only to himself but to many. **THAN FOR COLD WATER** the Indian or Ethiopian: These peoples, because they are very close to the Torrid Zone <note>The equatorial region, thought in the Middle Ages to be uninhabitably hot.</note>, endure unbearable heat. **TELL ME HOW** it is: Tell me how it happens that you make yourself a "wall" (that is, a barrier) to the sun, as if you were not yet dead and stripped of your body, but still possessed a human body.

He was speaking to me, when already I would have
made myself manifest, were I not intent
on another novelty that appeared then;
For through the middle of the burning path,
people came with their faces opposite to these,
which made me gaze in suspended wonder.
There I see them on every side making haste,

<column-break/>

In this 26th Canto, he demonstrates the manner of his progress and that of the souls; who, walking through the flame and encountering one another, kissed each other on the mouth and spoke words in abomination of lust. And here he speaks with Master Guido <note>Guido Guinizelli (c. 1230–1276), an influential Italian poet whom Dante considered his literary "father."</note>, who shows him many others and explains the words they say. **ALONG THE EDGE:** along the extremity of the terrace so that they would not be harmed by the flame. **ONE BEFORE THE OTHER:** Because reason should precede and appetite follow after; and reason always admonishes appetite, saying **WATCH** (that is, go with care and circumspection) **ALONG THE WAY** (as if to say, "go quickly"). He gives, therefore, two precepts: that in walking one should be cautious and one should be swift. **I WILL MAKE YOU SHREWD:** I discern you and show you the way and make you experienced. Whence we say:

**AS FAR AS THEY COULD COME:** Because they could not leave the flame, but they came right to its edge; and therefore he says "with care not to come out of the place" so they would not cease to be burned. And one of them said: "O you who go after the others, not because you are more tardy or slow than they, but perhaps because you are more reverent" (that is, to show them reverence you go behind). And he demonstrates that appetite most often precedes reason, except in well-mannered men, who may have a swift appetite but nonetheless, out of the reverence they bear for reason, they follow it and do not precede it. **ANSWER ME WHO** burn in thirst and in fire: No one can be in a great fire without being in great thirst. It is as if he says: "If for me, who am in such a burning, it is not troublesome to speak, it should not be so for you."

Dante would have responded to the soul who was asking him where he was from, but a new thing appeared that turned his mind to itself. And this was that another troop of souls, coming toward this one, met them; and as they met one another, each one of them kissed one of the others. They did not stop for this, but continued their journey, content with a very brief greeting; and in passing one another, those who were coming shouted: "Sodom and Gomorrah!" <note>The souls are divided into two groups: those who sinned through natural lust and those who committed "unnatural" acts (Sodomites). They exchange a brief, chaste kiss—a "holy kiss"—to replace the disordered lust of their earthly lives.</note>

<summary>Dante enters the 26th Canto of Purgatorio, where he encounters souls being purified by fire for the sin of lust. The poet Guido Guinizelli questions Dante about his physical presence, while the commentator Landino explains the symbolism of reason, appetite, and the nature of the spirits' aerial bodies.</summary>
<keywords>Canto XXVI, Purgatorio, lust, fire, Guido Guinizelli, reason and appetite, shadow, aerial body, Sodom and Gomorrah, Cristoforo Landino</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the transition from the end of Canto XXV into Canto XXVI. The previous commentary established the physical and spiritual state of the lustful on the final terrace of Purgatory. Here, Dante observes the two groups of souls—those who sinned according to nature and those who committed "sins against nature"—and begins his dialogue with them.</meta>

<header>CANTO XXVI.</header>

each shade and kissing one with another
without staying, content with a brief greeting;
just so within their dark battalion
one ant muzzles another,
perhaps to spy their way and their fortune.
As soon as they end the friendly welcome,
before the first step carries them past,
each one strives to shout louder:
"The new people: Sodom and Gomorrah!"
and the other: "Pasiphae enters the cow
so that the bull might run to her lust."

Then, like cranes that to the Rhipaean mountains
should fly in part, and part toward the sands,
these shy of the ice, those of the sun,
one group departs, the other comes on,
and they return weeping to their first chants
and to the cry that best befits them.
And they drew near to me as before,
the same ones who had entreated me,
attentive to listen in their appearance.
I, who twice had seen their desire,
began: "O souls certain
of having, whenever it may be, a state of peace,
my limbs have not remained unripe nor mature
over there, but are here with me
with their blood and their joints.
I go up from here to no longer be blind;
there is a lady above who gains this grace,
so that I carry my mortal part through your world.
But—so may your greater desire be satisfied
soon, so that the heaven may house you
which is full of love and spreads most wide—
tell me, so that I may yet mark the pages,
who are you, and who is that crowd
that goes away behind your backs?"

Not otherwise is the mountain-man stunned,
and looking around he grows mute,
when, rough and rustic, he enters the city, <term>inurba</term> <note>Dante’s invented verb "inurbarsi" means to enter or become part of a city (from the Latin "urbs").</note>
than each shade was in its appearance

<column-break/>

and those who were with Dante. **Pasiphae entered the cow:** <note>Pasiphae was a mythological queen of Crete who, cursed with passion for a bull, hid inside a wooden cow to satisfy her lust.</note> that Sodom and Gomorrah represent the deepest depths of the detestable sin against nature, as we demonstrated above in the fifteenth Canto of the *Inferno*. The souls then shouted this in reproach of their committed sin; and through such cries they condemned their past life and came into greater contrition. And similarly, those who had practiced lust in a bestial form shouted in their confusion of how Pasiphae was used by the bull—a fable we narrated above in the twelfth Canto of the *Inferno*. **The kissing on the mouth** came from charity and modest affection. And this they did as penance for their former immodest and lustful kisses. **SO WITHIN HIS DARK BATTALION.** He makes a comparison to the ants who, carrying grain to their caverns, muzzle one another when they meet. We have spoken of ants in another place. **PERHAPS TO SPY:** he rightly said "perhaps," because it is difficult to know the internal feeling of an animal that does not express itself with words.

After the greetings were made, one part went down and the other up, as cranes would do when part of them come toward the north—where the **Rhipaean mountains** are <note>Legendary mountains in the far north of Eurasia</note>—and part toward the south in an opposite line where sandy Libya is. Those flying to the south would flee the cold, and the others flying to the north would flee the heat. **TWO TIMES:** once before the new people arrived, and the second time at the present. **THEIR DESIRE:** <note>original: "loro grato"</note> that is, that which was pleasing to them. **HAVE NOT REMAINED** my limbs neither **UNRIPE** <note>original: "acerbe"</note>—which is said of those who die young of a "bitter" death—nor **MATURE**, as is said of those who die old and in a mature age. In short, he says he is not yet dead, but has come with soul and body. **FROM HERE I GO UP TO NO LONGER BE BLIND.** Understand this as the eyes of the mind. I go, then, to remove the shadows of ignorance and illuminate myself with the light of truth. **A LADY IS ABOVE:** Understand Beatrice, of whom we have already spoken many times, who acquires such grace for him that he can bring his mortal part, that is, the body. **BUT SO MAY YOUR GREATER DESIRE:** which was to ascend to heaven, a desire greater than that which they had to speak to Dante. **THE HEAVEN:** <note>original: "EL CIELD"</note> which is full of love because God is there; and this is the Empyrean heaven. Whence he says **SPREADS MOST WIDE** <note>original: "piu ampio si spatia"</note>, meaning it is larger, because it embraces the other nine heavens inferior to it, as we will say more clearly in its proper place. **DITE MI [TELL ME]** who you are so that I may **MARK THE PAGES:** that is, so I may write it. For he who writes "marks" or "rules" the pages with the black lines of letters. **AND WHO IS THAT CROWD** and multitude which goes away behind your **BACKS** <note>original: "terghi"</note>, since in Latin *tergum* signifies the back.

Just as the mountain-man and rustic, who has never seen a city, marvels greatly when, entering any city, he sees things never seen before. **ENTERS THE CITY:** <note>original: "SINNVRBA"</note> he enters the city; because the Latins call the city *urbem*. Whence the poet has said "inurba"...

<summary>This page describes the encounter between Dante and two groups of souls purging the sin of lust, who greet each other briefly like ants before shouting examples of their sins (Sodom and Pasiphae). Landino's commentary explains the poetic similes of ants and cranes and clarifies Dante's assertion that he travels in his physical body through the grace of Beatrice.</summary>
