<meta>This page continues the transition from Canto XXV to Canto XXVI of the Purgatorio. Having previously described the mountain-dweller’s wonder upon entering a city, the text now transitions into the direct dialogue between Dante and the spirits of the lustful, specifically the poet Guido Guinizzelli.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>PURGATORIO</header>

But once they were emptied of their wonder,
which in noble hearts soon subsides,
"Blessed are you, who from our borders,"
began the one who had first questioned me,
"to die better, embark with experience.
The people who do not come with us offended
in that for which Caesar, once in his triumph,
heard himself called 'Queen' against him;
Therefore they depart shouting 'Sodom,'
reproaching themselves as you have heard,
and they aid the burning through their shame.
Our sin was hermaphrodite;
but because we did not observe human law,
following our appetite like beasts,
to our own disgrace it is read by us,
when we part, the name of her
who made herself a beast in the beast-shaped wooden frame." <note>This refers to Pasiphae, who hid inside a wooden cow to satisfy her lust for a bull.</note>

Now you know our acts and of what we were guilty;
if perhaps you wish to know us by name,
there is no time to tell, and I would not know how.
I will indeed satisfy your desire regarding me:
I am Guido Guinizzelli, and already I purge myself,
for having truly grieved before reaching the end."

<column-break/>

**To enter the city** <note>original: "inurba . i : entrare in turbe"</note>: to enter the crowds that make up the city. **EMPTIED of wonder**: discharged of that marvel which had seized them upon seeing me. **IN NOBLE hearts soon subsides**: Because one who possesses great intellect and a great soul quickly sets aside any shock or wonder. **BLESSED are you**: Dante, who for a better death—that is, by a greater grace of God—embarks with experience, or carries experience away: experience of our borders, of our lands. **THE PEOPLE who do not come**: This shows that the souls who do not go with these, but who pass by in the opposite direction, purge the vice of sodomy. Because this is against nature, the poet imagines that they go in the opposite direction to those who sinned according to nature but did not observe the proper measure. And so that you understand they were sodomites, the soul says they "offended in that" sin. **BECAUSE**: For which Caesar, while triumphing, heard himself called "Queen." It was a custom of free speech among the soldiers when their lord triumphed that they could reproach him for any vice. And because Caesar, in his youth, serving under the quaestor Thermus in Asia, was sent by him to Nicomedes, King of Bithynia, it was rumored that the King had used Caesar as a wife. Therefore, when he triumphed over Gaul, the soldiers around the triumphal chariot shouted: "Caesar has subdued Gaul, and Nicomedes subdued Caesar." **THEREFORE THEY DEPART** from us shouting "Sodom," and by this they reproach themselves for such a vice so that they may feel more shame, and through such shame merit more, and thus they "aid the burning." For the fire that causes the burning is extinguished by this penance. **OUR sin was hermaphrodite**. I believe that in this place he means by "hermaphrodites" those who, in intercourse, although they do not sin against nature, exercise it in such dishonest ways that as much as is in them, one and the other behave now as male and now as female, in such a way that they can be called hermaphrodites. But so that the meaning is better understood, first we will tell the fable, then we will add the natural reason. From Mercury and Venus was born a son who was called Hermaphroditus from the names of his father and mother, because *Hermes* in Greek signifies Mercury and *Aphrodite* signifies Venus. This boy, having reached the years of youth and arriving in Caria at a fountain, found the nymph Salmacis. She, seized by love for him, ran to him as he was already bathing in the fountain. And the youth wishing to flee her, she embraced him, praying to the gods that they should make it so he could never be separated from her. Her prayers were heard, and they were transformed in such a way that out of two they became one. But this one retained both sexes, and thus remained both male and female; and let this suffice for the fable. Physicians hold that in the womb of a woman there are thirteen cells <note>This reflects a variation of medieval anatomical theories (more commonly citing seven cells) which attempted to explain biological variety through the "compartments" of the uterus.</note>: the six on the right conceive a male, and the six on the left a female; the one in the middle they say conceives the sex with one and the other. Others say that a hermaphrodite is born when in the conception the man himself and the blood of the woman are of equal force, whereby in the same fetus each produces his own sex. Therefore, when this creature reaches full age, it can use both. Such men are called by the Greeks **Androgynes** <note>original: "Androgyni"</note>, that is, male-females: because in their language they call the male *andra* and the female *gynen*. And it is a rule in law that each may choose which of the two sexes they wish to use, and they use them alternately, now one, now the other. And Aristotle adds that these have the right breast of a male and the left of a female. **BUT BECAUSE WE DID NOT observe human law**: which always requires that the male use the form of a male as the natural law of man invites, and the female always suffers as a female. **FOLLOWING APPETITE LIKE BEASTS**, which man must not do; rather, it is his duty always to follow reason. **OUR ACTS**, which were lustful. **AND OF WHAT sin WE WERE GUILTY**: let them be accused. "Guilty" is the one accused, just as the "actor" is the one who accuses others. **THERE IS NO TIME**, because it is late; **and I would not know**, because they are many and unknown to me. **I WILL indeed DIMINISH your desire**: I will make it so that your will to know me will be satisfied, because I will tell you. **I AM GUIDO Guinizzelli**.

<summary>Guido Guinizzelli explains the two groups of the lustful: those who sinned against nature (shouting 'Sodom') and those who followed their appetites like beasts. The commentary provides a detailed mythological and medieval biological explanation of the term 'hermaphrodite' and the scandal of Julius Caesar and Nicomedes.</summary>
<keywords>Guido Guinizzelli, Sodom and Gomorrah, Julius Caesar, Nicomedes, Hermaphroditus, Androgynes, medieval embryology, lust, Purgatorio Canto XXVI</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto XXVI of the Purgatorio. Having just identified himself as the poet Guido Guinizzelli, Guido now explains why he is already in Purgatory proper rather than waiting in the Ante-Purgatory. Dante reacts with great emotion to meeting the "father" of his poetic style.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>

<header>CANTO XXVI.</header>

**Left Column:**

As in the sorrow of Lycurgus <note>Lycurgus was the King of Nemea who intended to kill Hypsipyle; her sons' sudden arrival saved her.</note>
two sons became, seeing their mother again,
such I became, but I do not rise so far,
When I hear naming himself the father
of me and of others, my betters, who ever
used sweet and graceful rhymes of love;
And without hearing or speaking, pensive I went
a long time, gazing at him,
nor for the fire did I draw any closer.

When I was fed with looking upon him,
I offered myself promptly to his service
with the affirmation that makes another believe.
And he to me: "You leave such a trace
by what I hear in me, and so clear,
that Lethe cannot take it away or make it dim.
But if your words just now swore the truth,
tell me what is the cause that you demonstrate,
in speech and in look, that you hold me dear?"
And I to him: "Your sweet sayings,
which, as long as modern usage shall last,
will still make your ink-stained pages dear."

->of the rhythm and the style of the rhymes<-

"O brother," he said, "this one I distinguish for you
with my finger"—and he pointed to one ahead—
"was a better craftsman of the mother tongue.
Verses of love and prose of romances
he surpassed them all; and let the fools talk
who believe the one from Limoges <note>Refers to the troubadour Giraut de Bornelh.</note> excels.
To voice more than truth they turn their faces,
and thus they fix their opinion
before any reason or art is heard by them."

<column-break/>

**Right Column:**

This man was our citizen and a knight, and in his
time he surpassed all others in Tuscan rhymes: **AND
ALREADY** I purge myself <note>original: "ET GIA mipurgo"</note>; he says this as if to say, although it has been a little time
since I died, nevertheless I am already in Purgatory;
and I have not had to wait in the Ante-Purgatory;
and this is because I was not very negligent
in converting myself: But I grieved well <gloss>that is: with good contrition</gloss> before the end <gloss>that is: I did not wait until the very last moment to grieve, but grieved before</gloss>.
**AS IN THE** sorrow of Lycurgus: **SO** became
the two sons: In *Inferno* we told the fable of Hypsipyle
and Jason; now we will add that when in Lemnos
it was known she had spared her father’s life and sent
him to the island of Chios, she fled the feminine fury, and sent her children to Thoas, their father. But she, captured
by pirates, was sold to Lycurgus, King of Nemea, and the care of his little son, named Archemorus—and after death, Opheltes—was committed to her. In those times, Adrastus and the other seven kings were passing through with their army, and being plagued by great thirst, Hypsipyle showed them the fountain called Langia; and in that interval, Opheltes, left by her asleep in a meadow, was killed by a serpent. Lycurgus ran to the scene and wanted to kill Hypsipyle; but her two sons, who had recently come to Lycurgus seeking their mother, hearing her lamenting her misfortune and naming Lemnos and Thoas, recognized her and, embracing her, saved her. **SUCH I BECAME**: I was filled with such great joy **BUT DO NOT** rise so far: I do not exalt and extend myself as far as the sons of Hypsipyle extended themselves; for they ran to embrace their mother. But I did not go to embrace Guido because he was in the fire. And this joy took hold of me when **I HEAR THE FATHER** naming himself <gloss>that is: when I heard Guido name himself</gloss>; whom he calls his father because he was his teacher and the praiser of many others in rhyme; and of others better than him **WHO**: who **EVER**: for any time used graceful, sweet rhymes of love. **PENSIVE I WENT**: He wants to show that he was thinking how such a learned man had fallen into such vice, and he felt compassion for human fragility.

I offered myself to Guido **WITH THE AFFIRMATION**
that makes one believe: with an oath. And he
replied to me: "O Dante, you leave such a trace and signs
of benevolence in me, that is, toward me, **BY THAT**
which I hear from you at present, that Lethe—the river
which induces oblivion—cannot take it away; it cannot
make me forget it, **NOR MAKE** it dim <note>original: "bigio"</note>, nor obscure it. We will speak of Lethe in its proper place. **TELL ME** what the cause is; tell me what is the reason that you demonstrate in speaking to me and in looking at me that you **HOLD ME** dear: that you love me. **AND I**, Dante, replied to him: **YOUR** sweet sayings, your sweet style in rhyme, is the reason that I love you. **WHICH**: which sayings **WILL MAKE** dear: pleasing. **AND THEIR** inks: the books written in such a style. **AS LONG AS** modern usage lasts: As long as the language we currently use shall last.

"I distinguish" <note>original: "Cerno"</note> means "I point out." **CRAFTSMAN**: composer.
This was **Arnaut of Provence** <note>Arnaut Daniel, a famous Occitan troubadour.</note>, much praised
and approved in the rhymes of that language, who, being
oppressed by poverty in his old age, wrote
a moral work with which he obtained much money from the Kings of France and England. Petrarch claims to have imitated this man in many places. As for "the one from Limoges," he does not give the name, but names him by his homeland, which is in France. **THUS** many ancients did regarding **Guittone**: This was Friar Guittone d'Arezzo, of whom we have already made mention.

# .XXVI. PURGATORIO

<column-break/>

So did many of the ancients with Guittone <note>Guittone d’Arezzo (c. 1235–1294), a poet whose complex and often obscure style Dante rejected in favor of the "Sweet New Style."</note>,
from cry to cry giving him the prize,
until the truth conquered him through many people.
Now, if you have so broad a privilege
that it is permitted for you to go to the cloister
in which Christ is abbot of the college <note>A metaphor for Heaven, envisioned as a monastic community where Christ is the head.</note>,
say for me there a "Our Father" <note>original: "Pater noster"</note>
as much as is needed for us of this world
where the power to sin is no longer ours.
Then perhaps to give place to another following,
who was near, he disappeared through the fire,
as a fish goes to the bottom through the water.
I drew forward a little toward the one shown
and said that for his name my desire
was preparing a gracious place.
He began freely to say:
> "Your courteous request so pleases me <note>original: "tant mabelis uotre cortois doman"</note>
> that I cannot nor wish to hide myself from you.
> I am Arnaut, who weeps and goes singing;
> with grief I see my past folly,
> and joyful I see before me the day I hope for.
> Now I pray you, by that power
> which guides you to the summit of the stairway,
> be mindful in due time of my pain."
Then he hid himself in the fire that refines them <note>The fire of Purgatory, which purifies the soul of the lustful.</note>.

<column-break/>

**SO BROAD** a privilege: it is certainly a great privilege to be able to go before death to the "cloister," meaning Heaven, **IN WHICH** Christ is abbot of the college. This is an excellent comparison: because Christ always holds the highest priestly dignity. **SAY FOR ME** a "Our Father": see that Christ hears a "Our Father" <note>original: "paternoſtro"</note> for me—that is, for my salvation. And he says to recite only "as much as is needed," for those in Purgatory, because they can no longer sin, do not need to say "and lead us not into temptation" <note>original: "et nenos inducas intentationem"</note>. The remaining verses close the chapter; they do not require any further explanation. The poet wrote these verses partly in the French language and partly in Catalan <note>The commentator identifies the language as French and Catalan; however, modern scholars recognize this as Old Occitan, the language of the troubadours.</note> because Arnaut was learned in both languages. But they are interpreted in this way: Your courteous request so pleases me that I cannot nor wish to hide myself from you. I am Arnaut, who weeps and goes singing in this red passage <note>A reference to the wall of fire.</note> the past folly; and I see before me the day that I hope for. Now I pray you by that power which guides you to the summit of this heat, that you remember in time my sorrow.

<header>CANTO XXVI.</header>

### CANTO XXVII OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE

As when he vibrates his first rays
at the place where his Maker shed His blood <note>Jerusalem, where Christ was crucified. Dante uses Jerusalem as the longitudinal reference point for the world.</note>,
with the Ebro falling under the high Scales <note>original: "hibero... libra". The Ebro river represents Spain. The "Scales" refers to the constellation Libra. This astronomical description indicates it is sunrise in Jerusalem and sunset in Purgatory.</note>,
and the waves in the Ganges newly scorched by noon,
so stood the sun; thus the day was departing,
when God’s glad angel appeared to us.
He stood on the bank outside the flame
and sang **"Blessed are the pure in heart"** <note>original: "beati mundo corde". Matthew 5:8. This beatitude is sung to those who have completed their purification from lust.</note>
in a voice much more alive than ours.
Then: "Go no further, holy souls, if the fire
does not first bite you; enter into it,
and be not deaf to the singing on the other side,"
he said to us when we were near him;
wherefore I became, when I heard him,
like one who is put into the grave.
I stretched forward over my clasped hands,
watching the fire and strongly imagining
human bodies I had once seen burned <note>Dante likely refers to the public execution by burning of heretics or criminals common in his era.</note>.

Having been led at last to the end of the purgation: **BLESSED are the pure in heart**: because truly, this being the last terrace, whoever leaves it is purged of every thing. **IN A VOICE much more alive than ours**: that is, in a voice far more living than yours. And certainly the voice of grace is more alive and has more efficacy than the human voice. **THEN: go no further**: These are the words the angel used, saying: "O holy souls, after this one goes no further unless the fire first bites you; therefore enter into it." **WHEREFORE I became such**: He says that no other color was in him than what is in a dead man when he is buried. This shows Dante's fear of entering these flames, even though he never feared the other terraces; this silently denotes that he had almost no other penalty to receive but this one, which was against the sin of the flesh <note>Lust, the sin being purged in this final circle.</note>. **OVER MY CLASPED hands I stretched forward**: I made such a gesture as one does who is in great pain, clasping the hands by interlacing the fingers, and I stretched out, almost recoiling, imagining within myself what happens to a human body placed in the fire.

The good guides turned toward me,
and Virgil said to me: "My son,
here there may be torment, but not death.
Remember, remember! If I
guided you safely even upon Geryon <note>The monster of fraud in Inferno Canto XVII, who carried the poets down the Great Barrier on his back.</note>,
what shall I do now that I am closer to God?
Believe for certain that if you stayed within the belly
of this flame for a full thousand years,
it could not make you bald of a single hair.
And if you think perhaps that I deceive you,
go toward it and satisfy yourself
with your own hands on the hem of your clothes.
Put down now, put down all fear;
turn this way and come with me in safety."
And I stood still, against my conscience.

<column-break/>

In this 27th canto, the author passes through the wall of fire and arrives at the Paradise of Delights <note>The Earthly Paradise (Eden) at the summit of Mount Purgatory.</note>. This canticle is structured so that the first eight chapters contain the Ante-Purgatory where the negligent wait. Then, up to this 27th canto, he has described the seven terraces of Purgatory and the penalties for the seven mortal sins. Now, in the remainder of the canticle, he proposes to describe the Post-Purgatory in which he places the paradise of delights. **AS WHEN** the first rays vibrate: He shows that in the upper hemisphere day was beginning in the sign of Aries, and in the other, night was falling in the sign of Libra. **WHERE his Maker**: By this, he points to our hemisphere where Jerusalem is, where Christ suffered. **THUS THE DAY was departing**: Understand this from the hemisphere where Dante was; for as the sun rose in our hemisphere, it followed that it was leaving the other. **WHEN THE ANGEL OF GOD**: In these seven terraces of Purgatory, the angel is always understood as a manifestation of the same Divine Grace. **GLAD**: Although divine grace brings joy everywhere, nonetheless such joy appears greatly here as the souls reach their end.

**THE GOOD GUIDES TURNED TOWARD ME**: There is no better guide to lead a man safely so that he does not perish in vice than reason and the knowledge of theology. **AND VIRGIL**: That is, Reason admonishes him, saying **HERE there may be torment**: because where sins are purged there is no damnation; rather, there is the torment that removes stains and restores one to a happy life. **REMEMBER, remember**: He uses repetition to gain greater trust. **UPON GERYON**: Which we explained in the 17th canto of the *Inferno*. **WHAT SHALL I DO** now closer to God: One who has sinned through fragility—such as the sin of the flesh—is much less remote from God than was Geryon, who represents the sin of malice. If, therefore, I could free you from the greater danger among the damned, much more easily will I free you from the lesser danger among the saved. **WITHIN THE BELLY**: That is, inside the center of that flame, because its nature is to purge and not to consume. **AND...**

<summary>This page marks the transition to the final stage of Purgatory, where Dante must pass through a wall of fire to reach the Earthly Paradise. Virgil uses the memory of their past trials to encourage a terrified Dante, emphasizing that the fire purifies the soul without destroying the body.</summary>

<header>XXVII PURGATORIO</header>
<sig>ll. iiii</sig>

**IF YOU BELIEVE perhaps that I deceive you**: It often happens that although reason demonstrates true things to the senses, the senses are nonetheless not persuaded. Therefore, experience must intervene <note>original: "experientia". Here, Landino emphasizes that intellectual reasoning is sometimes insufficient without physical proof.</note>. Virgil thus wanted him to take the hem of his clothes and put it in the flame; it would then be clear that such a flame does not consume. Allegorically, this shows that whenever someone is in a state of great perturbation, and on the other hand reason persuades them that what causes the perturbation is false, they must always test what reason dictates before departing from it. **AND I STILL FIRM**, persevering in my resolution not to go **AGAINST CONSCIENCE**, because my conscience stung me for not obeying Virgil and for not believing him, even though he had always led me safely.

---

When he saw me stand still and stubborn,
a little troubled, he said: "Now see, my son,
between Beatrice and you is this wall."
As at the name of Thisbe, Pyramus opened his eyes
at the point of death, and looked at her,
when the mulberry tree turned vermilion;
so, my stubbornness being softened,
I turned to my wise leader, hearing the name
that always springs up in my mind.

Whereat he shook his head and said: "How?
Do we wish to stay on this side?" then he smiled
as one does to a child won over by an apple.
Then he placed himself into the fire ahead of me,
praying Statius that he should come behind,
who for a long stretch of road had previously divided us.

When I was inside, I would have thrown myself
into boiling glass to cool myself,
so measureless was the burning there.

<column-break/>

**WHEN HE SAW ME**: This establishes what the duty of the learned teacher should be toward a disciple who is disobedient—not out of spite, but out of fear. Indeed, the teacher must truly remember the goal already proposed in the mind and demonstrate that, to arrive there, there is no other way. **A LITTLE TROUBLED**: The teacher should be slightly troubled when he sees the disciple is disobedient, because through that perturbation he ignites the student’s will; but such trouble should not be excessive, as it might confirm the student in their defiance through despair. **SON**: By this name, he shows that everything he wishes to lead him toward arises from the affection he bears him. **BETWEEN BEATRICE AND YOU**: This demonstrates that since his goal is to reach Beatrice, it is impossible to arrive unless he passes through the flame that divides him from her. And certainly, as Dante was most eager to see Beatrice—who we said from the beginning represents Theology and the knowledge of divine things—he could not grasp her if he did not first purge himself of the vice of **lust** <note>original: "luxuria". Lust is the final sin purged on the seventh terrace of Purgatory.</note>, just as he had already purged the other vices. **AS AT THE NAME of Thisbe**: Pyramus and Thisbe were from Babylon, most beautiful and joined by an immeasurable love. But since Pyramus could not have the girl openly, they agreed to steal out of the city at night and meet at the tomb of Ninus. It happened that Thisbe, more driven by love <note>original: "perchossa dalla morte", likely a typo for "perchossa dall'amore" or referring to her impending doom.</note>, arrived first at the location. But seeing a lioness coming to drink at a nearby spring, she fled in fear of the beast and hid, dropping a veil she wore on her head. The lioness found it, tore it, and stained it with blood because she had recently fed on prey and her muzzle was foul with gore. Pyramus arrived shortly after the lioness left, and recognizing the veil, was convinced Thisbe had been devoured. He took such grief and fell into such despair that he struck himself with his own knife with a mortal wound. Thisbe returned, and seeing him in such a state, cried out, saying, "Answer your Thisbe!" Her name had such power over the lover that, although he was oppressed by death, he yet opened his eyes to see the thing he loved so much. Thisbe, with the same knife, put an end to her life and her sorrow. And they add to the fable that a mulberry tree <term>gelso</term>, under which Pyramus killed himself, having previously had white berries, took its color from the blood; and thereafter always produced black berries. Thus, Dante rejoiced in his great distress at the name of Beatrice, just as Pyramus did at the name of Thisbe. **Stubbornness being SOFTENED** <note>original: "solla". Landino glosses this as soft or rarefied rather than stretched tight.</note>. We have provided the explanation of this word elsewhere. **HEARING the name**, that is, of Beatrice, **WHICH always springs up**, that is, always rises, as they say water "springs up" when it rises from the earth. **WHEREAT he shook his head**, not threatening but reassuring him. **AND SAID, "How? Do we wish to stay on this side?"** as if to say: have we endured so much labor both in descending into Hell and ascending Purgatory only to remain on this side of the place that contains Beatrice? **THEN he smiled** modestly. The wise man smiles when he sees he has moved a man who lacks prudence. **AS IS DONE to a child won over by an apple**: It often happens that a child refuses to come or obey to avoid effort, but if shown an apple, a pear, or other fruit, he goes and obeys. **THEN INTO THE FIRE**: This shows that Virgil entered the fire before Dante, because reason adorned with moral philosophy is sufficient to guide man to purgation and repentance of sins. But nonetheless, it is necessary that Statius stay in a position so that he does not allow him to turn back; rather, he purges him further forward. This is especially the office of the intellect illuminated by the Christian religion.

**WHEN I WAS INSIDE**, that is, in the flame, I felt such heat that I would have thrown myself into the glass that boils in the furnace, because I would have believed that place to be cool in comparison to the flame—

# CANTO XXVI. <note>Note: Though the header says XXVI, the text and commentary belong to Canto XXVII.</note>

->My sweet father, to comfort me,<-
->went on speaking only of Beatrice,<-
->saying, "I seem already to see her eyes."<-
->A voice that was singing guided us<-
->from beyond; and we, paying attention only to it,<-
->came as far as where the ascent began.<-
->"Come, you blessed of my Father,"<- <note>original: "Venite benedicti patris mei"</note>
->sounded from within a light that was there,<-
->such that it overcame me and I could not look at it.<-
->"The sun goes," it added, "and evening comes;<-
->do not stop, but quicken your pace<-
->while the west does not yet darken."<-

->Straight up the path rose through the rock,<-
->toward such a direction that I blocked the rays<-
->of the sun, which was already low, in front of me.<-
->And after a few steps, we perceived<- <note>original: "leuamo efaggi," likely a transcription of "levammo i saggi" or "passi" (we took our steps/tests).</note>
->that the sun had set, by the shadow that vanished,<-
->behind me and my wise companions.<-
->And before the horizon, in all its immense parts,<-
->had become of a single aspect<-
->and night had all its distributions spread out,<-
->Each of us made a bed of a step;<-
->for the nature of the mountain broke in us<-
->the power to climb more than the desire.<-

<column-break/>

**BUT:** Therefore he wishes to imply that it was an immeasurable burning, and thus he says "fire without meter," that is, without measure; because in Greek *metron* <term>metron: Greek for "measure"</term> signifies measure. **THE SWEET FATHER:** Shows that wishing to comfort the burning sensuality in the fire of lust, he speaks to him of Beatrice; because there is nothing that more extinguishes the heat of carnal desires than speaking of Beatrice, that is, of the reasons with which sacred theology demonstrates every carnal pleasure to be harmful to our souls, which must only feed on the contemplation of divine things, from which results the highest joy. **SAYING HER EYES:** The eyes of theology are the most acute speculations investigated by the most acute wits of the most learned theologians, which things attract our souls, just as the eyes of a beautiful woman allure and attract the mind of the one who loves her. **A VOICE GUIDED US** that was singing from beyond, that is, from within the flame; because there being no path nor light, we acted like one who goes by night who, not seeing the way, follows either a voice or a sound that he hears. Paying attention, we came from the flame to the end of the circle where the stairs mounted up. And here was an angel so splendid that, looking at it, it overcame me and dazzled my sight so that I could not look at it. From this angel came the words that Matthew the Evangelist writes that Christ will say at the last judgment, turning to the elect, saying: *Come, you blessed of my Father.* <note>original: "Venite benedicti patris mei"</note> Allegorically, in emerging from the final purgation and remaining absolutely unblemished, one cannot proceed by way of intellectual discourse nor any trace of human reason; but one solely follows grace; and it alone draws one out of these final flames. **THE SUN GOES**, it added, and evening comes: the day departs and the night arrives. In this world, the "day" signifies the time of grace in which we can earn merit; the "night" is the time after death in which our works are for satisfaction but not for merit; for in Purgatory we satisfy for sins committed, but we do not acquire or merit anew; rather, the works done in life help them. Therefore, he feigns that in Purgatory one cannot climb except by day. He posits, furthermore, that he spent four days and three nights searching Purgatory. The first he describes in the second canto: *Already the sun had reached the horizon.* The second in the ninth canto: *The concubine of ancient Tithonus.* <note>A mythological reference to the dawn.</note> The third in the eighteenth canto: *The moon, delayed almost until midnight.* The fourth in the twenty-seventh canto: *And already through the brightness before dawn.* And this fourth day sufficed to search the Earthly Paradise. He makes no mention of the night that followed this day. Therefore, in this place, as the third night approaches—which preceded the fourth day—the angel hurries them.

He demonstrates that the path ascended straight and toward the east. Because the sun was in the west, the shadow of the one climbing appeared before his eyes. And therefore he says: *toward such a direction that I blocked the rays of the sun, which was already low, in front of me.* He knew the sun had gone down when he no longer saw his shadow. He feigns, therefore, that the ascent from this seventh terrace to the Earthly Paradise was through a cliff of rock, and in that cliff was a staircase made by the chisel which ascended through a valley. He who rises to the state of innocence rises toward the east; he who rises to truth and he who rises to happiness. The ascent was straight: which always signifies virtue, just as the crooked signifies vice. It was steep because the end of man is placed on high, nor does one go there without climbing, because we elevate ourselves from earthly things to celestial ones. It has steps because one does not go without a distinction of degrees of virtue, which we have already shown in many places. And the steps are there by force of the chisel because such an ascent is not acquired without difficulty. And the steps are in the solid rock: because the purged soul is already confirmed and established in that virtue, and has made such a foundation that it can no longer collapse downward. **AND AFTER A FEW STEPS** we perceived <note>original: "experientia," meaning by experience/observation</note>: i.e., they had mounted a few steps when he felt the sun setting, not because he saw it, being behind his back, but because he saw his shadow vanish and fail. We can repeat in this place the allegory already stated regarding day and night in Purgatory. **AND BEFORE** all its parts—before the horizon was made all of one aspect—i.e., it had become dark in all its immense [parts]...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Purgatorio, Canto XXVII. Dante, Virgil, and the poet Statius have just passed through the wall of fire and are resting on the stairs as night falls, as it is impossible to climb the mountain of Purgatory after sunset.</meta>

# PURGATORY

...that is, an immeasurable part, and it is the first sentence, that the day had entirely departed. **EACH OF US** <note>original: "CIASCHVN di noi"</note> **made a bed of a step.** That is, each one placed himself to lie down on the step where he found himself: because the nature of the mountain—which is such that one cannot climb by night—**BROKE US.** <note>original: "CIAFFRANSE"</note> That is, it broke our power, strength, and delight. It is as if he said: we were able to climb and took delight in it, but the night took both from us. Notwithstanding that they were purged of every stain, nevertheless, every shadow of ignorance was not yet entirely removed. Therefore, until the night passed, it was necessary to rest. But he says "on the rock," a firm and stable thing, and "on the step of the ladder." This signifies that if, after purgation, some ignorance still remains in us, it cannot, however, turn us from our purpose in which we are established. And although it does not let us mount—that is, proceed forward—and it is necessary to stop, nonetheless, it does not remove us from the true way, as happened when Sordello led them into the valley. Therefore, the night here caused us not only to stop but also to turn aside from the path; here it only stops us but does not twist us from the straight way.

> As the goats stay quiet while chewing the cud,
> having been swift and bold
> upon the peaks before they fed,
> Silent in the shade while the sun seethes,
> watched by the shepherd who upon his staff
> leans and serves as their rest;
> And as the herdsman who stays outside,
> throughout the night beside his quiet flock,
> watching lest a wild beast scatter them;
> Such were we all three then:
> I as the goat and they as shepherds,
> hemmed in on this side and that by the rock.
> Little could appear of the sky outside,
> but through that little I saw the stars,
> brighter and larger than was their wont.

> While admiring and re-admiring those,
> sleep took me, and the dream that often
> tells the news before the event occurs.
> In the hour, I believe, when from the east
> Cytherea <note>A name for the goddess Venus, often associated with the planet that rises before the sun.</note> first beamed upon the mountain,
> she who seems always burning with the fire of love,
> Young and beautiful in a dream she seemed to me,
> to see a lady walking through a meadow,
> gathering flowers, and singing she said:
> Know, whoever asks my name,
> that I am Leah, and I go moving around
> my beautiful hands to make myself a garland.
> Here to please me I adorn myself at the mirror;
> but my sister Rachel never turns away
> from her looking-glass, and sits all day long.
> She is as eager to look with her beautiful eyes...

<column-break/>

As the goats, which at first were voracious and without any restraint in grazing, when they have eaten and midday arrives, they retreat to the shade and there, "manse"—that is, gentle—they stay **RUMINATING** <note>original: "RVMINANDO"</note>: chewing the cud; and the shepherd, leaning on his staff, watches them. Or truly, like the herdsman—that is, the shepherd of the herd—**STAYS THE NIGHT** <note>original: "PERNOCTA"</note>: that is, shelters for the night beside the herd, guarding it from wild beasts so they do not scatter it. Such were we three: I the goat, because I was being guarded; they the shepherds, because they were guarding me. This demonstrates that sensuality, placed between these two poets <note>Virgil (Reason) and Statius (Moral Philosophy)</note>, is always safe from the encounter of every wild beast—that is, from vice. **LITTLE COULD** appear of the sky outside: the meaning is this, that they were in such a depth of the passage that they could not see any other part of the sky except what was directly above their heads; but nonetheless in that part they saw the stars, both larger and brighter than their wont—that is, more than they were usually seen in lower places, because celestial things appear so much larger the more we are joined to them.

The author feigns in this place that while he was looking at the stars with wonder, at the same time he was taken by sleep and by a dream which announced to him what he was to see the following day. **WHICH OFTEN** <note>original: "CHE SOVENTE"</note> which dream many times **HAS THE NEWS** <note>original: "SA LEN OVELLE"</note>: it has the announcement. Then he describes the time in which he had such a vision, saying it was in the first hour that Cytherea beamed—that is, shone in the east—that is, at the time when Venus rises in the east shortly before the sun. The reason why Venus is either preceding or following the sun by a short interval is already written. Then he shows that the vision was: that it seemed to him a young and beautiful woman went through a "landa"—through a meadow—who said "I am Leah, who goes moving my hands around and exercising them to make myself a garland, and I adorn myself at the mirror." Because in the first canticle <note>Inferno</note> when it occurred, we showed how by Leah is understood the active life and by Rachel the contemplative life, I will not repeat at present what has already been said. But in this place, I judge he places Leah to denote that the man already purged of vices exercises himself in the earthly paradise—that is, in the mortal life—in the active life according to the civil virtues and according to the Christian religion. In such a way that, having been a good citizen in this Jerusalem, the earthly city, we may ascend to Jerusalem, the supernal city, where Leah is not, but Rachel—that is, the contemplative life—through which, with fixed and eagle-like eyes, we will be able in the first...

This section concludes the transition from the final terrace of Purgatory into the Earthly Paradise (Eden), focusing on the allegorical figures of Leah and Rachel and Virgil’s final address to Dante.</meta>

<page-num>XXVII.</page-num>
## CANTO XXVI.

->...I take pleasure in adorning myself with my hands,<-
->but she finds joy in seeing her own reflection.<-
<note>This refers to Leah’s speech in Dante's dream, where she represents the active life, while her sister Rachel represents the contemplative life.</note>

The "source and mirror" represent seeing, knowing, and understanding the ultimate Truth, and in understanding it, enjoying it. He introduces **Leah**, who exercises her hands—that is, she occupies herself in works—because the active virtue consists in these actions, and its end is justice. **Rachel** exercises her eyes because she is entirely focused on contemplation. Nor should we overlook that he places this Paradise in the state of innocence, because it cannot be found except after Purgatory. Furthermore, this does not disagree with many theologians who place it on a mountain, as shown in Genesis: <note>original: "Plantauerat autem dominus paradisum uoluptatis in principio in quo posuit hominem quem formauerat"</note> "And the Lord God had planted a paradise of pleasure from the beginning, in which he placed the man whom he had formed." <note>original: "Produxitque dominus deus de humo omnem lignum pulchrū uisu et ad uescendū suauelignum etiam uite in medio paradisi: lignumque scientie boni et mali"</note> "And the Lord God brought forth from the ground every tree beautiful to the sight and sweet to eat, also the tree of life in the midst of paradise, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil." And he rightly places the active life in this paradise, because a little further down it says: <note>original: "Tulit ergo dominus deus hominem et posuit eum in paradiso uoluptatis ut operaretur: Et custodiret illum"</note> "The Lord God therefore took the man and placed him in the paradise of pleasure so that he might work and keep it." God thus placed man there so that he might work and exercise himself in its care, which is the proper office of the active life. For this reason, Leah deservedly moves her hands through this meadow and adorns herself with flowers, which are beautiful and produce fruit. These flowers are the virtues, than which nothing is more beautiful, nor produces better fruit. Some commentators of Genesis claim that the mountain of Purgatory rose as high as the circle of the moon. **Hugh of Saint Victor** writes that holy men believe this paradise is in the eastern parts, and in a place so high that the waters of the Flood could not reach it. **The Aquinas** <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> writes that paradise is in the right part of the East, since Aristotle in the book *On the Heavens and the Earth* posits that the right is always more noble than the left. And he adds that it is separated from us by certain impediments, either mountains or seas or uninhabitable regions due to the heat. Genesis places a river there which waters it, and this then divides into four: The first is **Phison** which circles the whole region called Havilah where gold is born, and there is found bdellium and the onyx stone. The second is **Gihon** which circles Ethiopia. The third is **Tigris** which goes to the Assyrians. The fourth is **Euphrates**.

**And now, through the splendors before dawn**
which rise more welcome to pilgrims
the less distant they lodge upon their return,
**The darkness fled from every side,**
and my sleep with it; wherefore I rose,
seeing the great masters already standing.
**"That sweet apple which, through so many branches,**
the care of mortals goes seeking,
today shall lay your hungers to rest."
**Virgil toward me used such**
words; and never were there gifts
that were equal to these in pleasure.
**So much desire upon desire came over me**
to be above, that at every step thereafter
I felt my feathers growing for the flight.

**When the whole stairway beneath us**
had been run, and we were on the highest step,
Virgil fixed his eyes upon me,
**And said: "The temporal fire and the eternal...**

<column-break/>

**D**ante describes the arrival of day, saying that through the splendors before dawn—that is, through the radiance that appears before the light of the sun removes the night that makes darkness—the dark was fleeing from every part of the sky. And at once the night departed, and my sleep with it. **SEEING** <note>original: "VEDENDO"</note> the great masters already standing: This is to note that just as in voluptuous and earthly things the senses wake before reason, so on the contrary in virtuous things, reason precedes. **THAT SWEET APPLE** <note>original: "QUEL DOLCE POMO"</note>: He introduces Virgil predicting his happiness and the supreme good, and by metaphor calls it "sweet apple." For just as the cultivator of trees directs all his work, toil, and industry toward the final goal, which is the fruit of the tree, so men toil for nothing else but to arrive at the supreme good. Hence, human and civil life "has duties and ends" <note>original: "habet officia et fines"</note>. He calls it "sweet" because nothing is more pleasant than achieving the goal we set for ourselves, to acquire which we endure much bitterness. This is not, then, that apple which Eve tasted, which was sweet to the taste but bitter to salvation. But it is a sweetness after which no bitterness is ever born. **THROUGH SO MANY BRANCHES** <note>original: "PER TANTI RAMI"</note>: that is, through so many paths, which are as many as there are many mansions in the kingdom of the ethereal Father. **SHALL LAY TO REST** <note>original: "PORRA in pace"</note> your hungers: that is, it will satisfy them. And this difference exists between human happiness and the eternal: human happiness, because it is finite, cannot satisfy the soul which is infinite; but God, the infinite good, satisfies it. **AND NEVER** <note>original: "ET MAI"</note> were there gifts <note>original: "strenne"</note>: that is, presents. "Strenne" in the Lombard language signifies tips or small gifts. He means to imply that no news or announcement ever gave anyone as much pleasure as these words gave him. Because of this, his initial desire to climb became so great that at every step he felt his feathers growing—that is, his virtues.

**T**hey climbed the stairs which mount from the seventh circle to the Earthly Paradise. And in this way we have seen Dante descending to Hell—that is, the knowledge of vices—and ascending Purgatory—that is, purging himself of them—and arriving at the Earthly Paradise.

It interprets the allegorical figures of Leah and Rachel as the active and contemplative lives and provides a theological-geographical context for the location of Eden.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Purgatorio, Canto XXVII. Following the poets' ascent of the final staircase, we reach the summit of the mountain. Here, Virgil delivers his final speech to Dante, signaling that human reason has reached its limit and Dante is now fit to enter the Earthly Paradise (Eden).</meta>

# PURGATORIO

Son, you have seen and have come to a part
where I, by myself, discern no further.
I have brought you here with wit and with art;
take your own pleasure henceforth as your guide;
you are out of the steep ways, out of the narrow.
**See the sun that shines upon your brow;**
see the little grass, the flowers, and the shrubs
that the earth here produces of itself.
**While those beautiful eyes come in joy,**
which, weeping, made me come to you in Hell,
you can sit and you can go among them.
**Expect no further word or sign from me;**
free, upright, and healthy is your will,
and it would be a mistake not to act according to its judgment;
**Therefore, over yourself, I crown and miter you.**

<column-break/>

...terrestrial, by which we understand the state of innocence. Now returning to the text: as the staircase that rises from the seventh terrace to the Earthly Paradise was run beneath us, we climbed it and were on the highest step. Then Virgil fixed his eyes upon me, that is, he looked at me intently. This signifies that Reason <note>Virgil represents human reason throughout the poem.</note> stopped at the senses and illustrated and illuminated them with its light; informing us that henceforth it is not necessary for Virgil to guide Dante—that is, that the appetite <note>The term "appetite" here refers to human desire or the "will."</note> should wait to be guided by reason. For, being united with reason, it can go by itself and cannot stray from the path, because the light of reason which shines within him reveals to him both good and evil. Therefore we can say that the appetite in man exists in various modes: for sometimes it is entirely repugnant to reason, and sometimes it obeys as if forced; sometimes it obeys willingly, yet often declines and wavers. But when, after the habit

---

of virtue has been formed, it is entirely united with the intellect and illuminated by it and by divine grace: and as if confirmed in grace, it has no other guide than its own free will, and that leads it most excellently. Now returning to the exposition of the present text, the author masterfully imagines Virgil saying he has shown him the temporary fire of Purgatory where punishments are for a time, and the eternal fire—which is in Hell where sufferings are eternal. He says these two things because the knowledge of vices, in which those who make a habit of them remain in eternal misery, and the purgation that can cleanse us from them, can be known by man through natural reason and philosophical science, signified by Virgil. But Virgil cannot show him further because what follows—concerning the Earthly Paradise, blessedness, and divinity—natural doctrine is not enough; rather, holy Theology <note>Beatrice represents Theology or Divine Revelation, who will take over as guide.</note> guides us more by faith than by natural reason. Thus Virgil rightly says, **AND YOU** have come to a part where I, by myself, discern no further: as if to say that although natural reason is necessary for such knowledge, nonetheless, by itself it cannot proceed without Theology. **I HAVE BROUGHT YOU HERE**: He rightly said "drawn" <note>original: "tracto"</note>, that is, pulled; because for the contemplation of great things, the appetite does not come by itself unless it is drawn by reason with wit and art. Whatever a man understands is either by natural wit (whereby we say we "know") or by art (that is, doctrine, whereby we say we "learn"). **YOUR** pleasure henceforth take as your guide: Before purgation, our pleasures and lusts come from the love of earthly things; whoever follows these goes to ultimate misery. But after the soul is purged, because no pleasure remains except for those things that are truly good—because they are eternal and divine—whoever follows those is truly blessed. **OUT OF THE STEEP** ways, out of the narrow: that is, out of the constricted ways, because he has entered the third kind of virtues of the already-purged soul. In this state, it is not only not difficult to live according to virtue, but it is the highest pleasure. **SEE THE SUN** that shines on your brow: for the sun had already risen, and as he looked toward the East, its rays struck his forehead. Allegorically, being already clean from sins, divine grace and the truth of things began to shine in him, reflecting on his forehead because he had already illuminated all his internal senses. **SEE THE GRASS**, the flowers, and the shrubs: He describes the landscape and the Earthly Paradise producing of itself, and by power placed by God in that land, every herb and tree without any seed or cultivation. And truly, when the soul is brought back to the state of innocence, it produces of itself the greenness of grass—that is, the highest hope of beatitude; and flowers—that is, the beauties of honesty; and shrubs—that is, the excellent fruits of its works. **WHILE** they come in joy: The meaning is: you have the will to sit or walk among the flowers while Beatrice comes, who came to Hell with weeping eyes, fearing that, being lost, you might lose yourself. But at present, caring for your salvation, she will have joyful eyes. And certainly, all theological scriptures that speak against sinners announce evil to them, and conversely demonstrate the highest joy to purged souls. **EXPECT NO FURTHER WORD FROM ME**: when the appetite is not yet joined with reason, it must wait for reason's precepts; but when it is joined and operates rightly by itself in everything, **YOUR** will is free. Although free will exists in everyone, nonetheless where the senses are repugnant to reason, such freedom is greatly obscured and the appetite almost becomes a tyrant. But in the soul that is purged and clean of sins, the will is true liberty because it is "upright"—that is, it does not twist away from the true path—and it is "healthy" because it is not oppressed by any dishonest desire. Therefore, such a soul has no need of one to govern it. **AND IT WOULD BE A MISTAKE** not to act according to its judgment: certainly, when the appetite is joined with reason, it would be an error if it did not do what it desires. **THEREFORE I** crown you over yourself: that is, I make you king of yourself; and miter you: I place on you the miter of the pastor; <note>The "crown and miter" signify that Dante has achieved both temporal and spiritual self-governance, becoming his own king and his own priest.</note> because you shall rule yourself and you shall watch over yourself.

<summary>This page contains Virgil's famous final address to Dante, declaring his will to be free, upright, and healthy. The commentary explains the transition from natural reason to divine theology as Dante enters the Earthly Paradise.</summary>

# PURGATORIO

### CANTO XXVIII OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE

**Eager** already to search within and around the divine forest, thick and living, which tempered the new day for my eyes, without waiting any longer, I left the bank, taking the plain slowly, slowly, over the ground that was fragrant on every side. A sweet breeze, unchanging within itself, struck my forehead with no more force than a gentle wind, through which the leaves, trembling readily, all bent toward the side where the holy mountain casts its first shadow <note>The shadows fall toward the west in the morning.</note>; yet not so far were they swayed from their upright state that the little birds among the treetops should cease to practice their every art, but with full joy, they welcomed the early hours, singing among the leaves, which kept the bass-note <note>term: "bordone" – the underlying drone or accompaniment in music.</note> for their rhymes, just as from branch to branch the sound gathers through the pine grove on the shore of Classe <note>original: "Chiaſſi" – the historic pine forest near Ravenna.</note> when Aeolus releases the Sirocco wind <note>Aeolus is the king of the winds in mythology; the Sirocco is the warm wind blowing from the southeast.</note>.

<column-break/>

**Dante** had already arrived from the final circle of Purgatory to the Earthly Paradise, which theologians call "Paradise of Pleasure" <note>original: "delitiam .i. de dilecti" – a place of delights.</note>. As we have said, he places this as the state of innocence and finds Leah there, who is interpreted as the Active Life <note>In medieval allegory, the biblical sisters Leah and Rachel represented the Active and Contemplative lives respectively.</note>. This demonstrates that once a man is purified, he must exercise the active moral virtues according to Christian precepts, from which follows that happiness which can exist in the active life. This is done so that, having been practiced in such a life as a citizen of this "lower Jerusalem" <note>A metaphor for the Church on Earth or the state of grace in this life.</note>, he may ascend to contemplate the "celestial Jerusalem" <note>The city of God in Heaven.</note>, which will be the subject of the third canticle [Paradiso]. 

For this reason, in the following cantos, he will set down the beginning of the New Church founded on the Evangelical law, which was signified first in the ancient Mosaic law and in the synagogue of the Jews. He first describes the greenery of the flowers, the pleasant wind, and the sweetest melody of the birds. He demonstrates through the grass and the flowers the certain hope that, after that state of innocence, they will lead to the true Paradise. By the light wind without change, he signifies the tranquil and orderly movement in holy operations, in which no disturbance can arise. And he walked with slow steps because every thought of ours should be considered with good maturity, and not be thoughtless or precipitated with too much speed. He walked, therefore, because we must never cease from good works; but he walked with slow steps—that is, with mature consideration. After this, he describes Matilda <note>Matilda is the mysterious lady Dante meets in Eden who represents the state of original innocence.</note>, of whom we will speak in her place...

<summary>Dante enters the Earthly Paradise, described as a fragrant, musical forest. The commentary explains that this garden represents the state of human innocence and the "Active Life," serving as a bridge between earthly purification and heavenly contemplation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto XXVIII of the Purgatorio. On the previous page, the commentator introduced the Earthly Paradise (Eden) as the "Paradise of Pleasure" and began explaining Dante's entry into this state of regained innocence. This page focuses on the sensory details of the forest—the light, the breeze, and the birdsong—interpreting them as symbols of the "Active Life" before introducing the river Lethe.</meta>

# PURGATORIO

### CANTO XXVIII

[The poet] asks what cause produces the wind and the river in that place. **EAGER ALREADY TO EXPLORE** within and around: He was thus desirous to explore the divine forest, that is, the true active life <note>The "Active Life" refers to the virtuous practice of earthly duties, which prepares the soul for the "Contemplative Life" of heaven.</note>; "within" as if to say its own essence, and "around," which denotes the circumstances. He wanted, therefore, to explore Paradise through the middle and in a circle, that is, through its extremities. We showed at the beginning of the first canticle <note>The *Inferno*.</note> that Dante finding himself in the dark forest signified nothing other than the troublesome prison of the body, in which the soul, enclosed by its contagion, contracts various faults and is stained by various sins. Therefore, he placed that forest as dark and full of beasts that hindered him from going toward the sun. Now, because he posits that after the knowledge of sins he has ascended through all the levels of Purgatory—that is, he is purged of every vice, and now his senses and appetite (which by the contagion of the body were previously rebellious to reason) are so united with reason that they have almost become the same thing—it follows that the forest, which was previously thorny, dark, and full of beasts, has become pleasant and delightful, full of light and full of flowers. This denotes the virtues from which the best fruits emerge; for a flower at the beginning has the sweetness of beauty and scent, and finally produces the best fruit. **THE DIVINE FOREST**, that is, the divine wood made for the habitation of humans, with every beauty contrary to that described in Hell. **THICK** with trees and grass, and alive with light **WHICH TO THE EYES** tempered the new day: the greenery of the trees and the herbs so tempered the splendor of the sun already risen (for it was now the fourth day) that my eyes could endure it. This signifies nothing else but that the virtues of a person established in a state of innocence in the active life make their intellect capable of receiving the divine light. **WITHOUT WAITING LONGER** for time or a guide, **I LEFT THE BANK**, that is, the edge, and began to enter the middle, as one can do who is sufficient unto themselves. **TAKING** the plain: as if it were a wide and spacious contemplation. **SLOWLY, SLOWLY**: to show that whoever wishes to take up any doctrine must proceed at a slow pace. **OVER THE GROUND**, that is, over the earth **WHICH**, that is, which **BREATHED FRAGRANCE** through its herbs and flowers. And certainly, the operations of the already purged soul cast the finest fragrance everywhere. **A SWEET BREEZE** was born from the eastern parts; **BREEZE**, that is, a soft and temperate wind. This is the good will inspired by God; this was like a temperate wind because the will that moves toward good works is always temperate and not impetuous, as are unbridled desires. Therefore, the right will toward good comes from the east—that is, from God—and such a wind bends the leaves toward the west—that is, toward worldly things. For the active life consists in the prudent, just, bold, and temperate administration of fleeting goods. Nor is this active life sufficient except for as long as this mortal life lasts; but the contemplative life is eternal because it deals with eternal and celestial things. Therefore, the Truth <note>Referring to Jesus Christ.</note> in the Gospel said: "Mary has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her" <note>original: "Maria autem optimam partem elegit que non auferetur abea" — Luke 10:42.</note>. **NOT HOWEVER** turned from their upright state or position: they do not bend from their uprightness so much that the birds in the treetops would leave off their singing. This denotes that although the operations of the active life bend toward the administration of the body, nonetheless they do not depart from those "birds that sing"—that is, a person does not cease for this reason to continually give thanks to God. But they sang their "prime" <note>A reference to the canonical hour of morning prayer.</note>, that is, the verses they sing in the morning among the leaves. For nothing forbids us from praising God among the "leaves"—that is, among civil lectures and operations. **WHICH KEPT UP** the burden, that is, the tenor: so sweet was the murmur of the breeze as it struck the leaves that it provided a tenor <note>term: "tenore" – the steady sustaining part in music that anchors the melody.</note> to the song of the birds. Because the movements of the soul already purged are without perturbation and help in the singing of divine praises. **JUST AS**: such was that sweet murmur in that forest as is in the pine grove of Ravenna, where Classe <note>original: "chiaffi" — the ancient port and pine forest near Ravenna.</note> is, a land near Ravenna on the shore where the Emperor Justinian built the church of Saint Apollinaris, which land was later destroyed by Leopardo while he was besieging Ravenna.

<column-break/>

Already my slow steps had carried me
so far within the ancient wood that I
could no longer see where I had entered;
And behold, a stream stopped my further
progress, which to the left, with its little waves,
bent the grass that sprouted on its bank.
All the waters that are purest here
would seem to have some mixture in them
compared to that one, which hides nothing,
Although it moves dark, dark,
under the perpetual shadow that never
lets sun or moon shine there.

<column-break/>

**A**lthough his steps had been slow, they had nonetheless transported him so far into the ancient forest that he could no longer see where he had entered. And he rightly called it "ancient," because the Earthly Paradise was created by God at the beginning of the world; furthermore, taking it as the state of innocence, no state is more ancient in souls because in that state the soul was created by God. **I COULD NOT SEE AGAIN** where I entered. Man entered the state of innocence as soon as he was created, and we cannot remember this entry, because no one remembers the entry the soul makes into the body; hence in the first canticle he said: "I cannot well repeat how I entered there." **AND BEHOLD FURTHER** progress was taken from me by a river: Just as Holy Scripture posits that from the Earthly Paradise there flow from a single source the Euphrates and the Tigris, so the poet feigns that from the eastern part of this paradise, and from a single source, two rivers emerge: Lethe and Eunoe. Lethe, of which he makes mention at present, flows to the left hand. This name <meta>catchword: This name (Questo nome)</meta>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Purgatorio, Canto XXVIII, where the poet explores the Earthly Paradise. The previous page established that the "divine forest" represents the "Active Life"—the practice of earthly virtue—which has become delightful and clear now that Dante is purged of sin. # CANTO XXVIII.

<columns>
**Lethe** means oblivion <note>From the Greek *lethe*, meaning forgetfulness.</note>. And whoever rises from Purgatory to the state of innocence drinks of this water, and by drinking it, forgets all sins. This is because he enters the third kind of virtue, which belongs to the soul already purged; through these virtues, he no longer fights against vices as he did during the "purgatory virtues." Instead, he makes such a habit of virtue that he forgets vice altogether, as Juvenal said: "let him not know how to be angry, let him desire nothing" <note>original Latin: "nesciat irasci cupiat nihil"</note>. For this reason, the poet feigns that the river runs to the left—which signifies something vicious—carrying away the memory of evil. The other river he calls **Eunoe**, which means "good mind" <note>From the Greek *eu* (good) and *noos* (mind).</note>, because nothing comes to the memory except good and virtue. This is the reason why one rises from the state of innocence to the contemplation of divine things. **ALL THE WATERS**: the meaning of this tercet is that the water of Lethe is clearer than any water found in this world here below. This signifies that the soul which, in the state of innocence, is so accustomed to virtue that it does not merely conquer vice but forgets it, is most pure. **ALTHOUGH IT MOVES DARK**: The water of Lethe is most clear; but because it runs under the constant shade of the trees of Paradise, which do not let the rays of the sun or moon pass through, it appears dark. We can say that such oblivion removes the disturbances that make us proud or elated in prosperous worldly matters. Nor do miseries hinder us from doing good. This was also expressed by the Psalmist, saying: "the sun shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night" <note>original Latin: "per diem sol non uret te: neque luna per noctem"</note>, where he takes the sun of the day for burning desire in prosperous fortune, and the moon of the night for the passions that burn our minds in adversity.

**Having reached the river, I stayed my feet.** He did not cross the river because he was drawn by the variety of fresh May-boughs. Indeed, with greatest wonder, he gazed at the varied abundance of trees that were there, and these he calls "mai" <note>In the Tuscan dialect of the time, *mai* referred to the green flowering branches hung at windows to celebrate the first of May.</note>. Allegorically, he stopped upon reaching the river because he could not pass to the active life and virtuous operations unless he first

With feet stayed and with eyes I passed
beyond the streamlet to admire
the great variation of fresh May-boughs
And there appeared to me, as there appears
suddenly something that drives away
through wonder every other thought
A lady all alone, who went
singing and choosing flower from flower
with which all her path was painted.

<column-break/>

had drunk of Lethe; that is, he was not yet so confirmed in virtuous acts that he not only conquered every vice but also forgot it. Nevertheless, although he could not yet pass—that is, operate in virtuous works for the reason stated—his eyes passed with their sight, because he could begin to consider what those works might be. And not without reason did he see a variety of fresh May-boughs, for the active life has various and diverse actions which distract the soul in many directions. Whence the Gospel, which Matthew <note>The commentator likely means Luke 10:41, though he attributes the sentiment to Matthew's context of the active life.</note> sets down for this active life, says: "Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things" <note>original Latin: "Martha Martha solicita es et turbaris erga plurima"</note>. **AND THERE**, he says, across the

river there appeared to me a woman in that form in which some thing usually appears suddenly; which brings such wonder that it drives every other thought from our mind. This woman went along alone, singing, through a path full of flowers, and she chose flower from flower. By this woman, he means the **Active Life**; and he calls her **Mathelda**. This is from the Countess Matilda <note>Matilda of Canossa (c. 1046–1115), a powerful medieval margravine and supporter of the Papacy.</note>, a woman of supreme nobility and the greatest virtues in administration. She was the daughter of Beatrice. This Beatrice was the daughter of the Emperor of Constantinople; taken by the love of an Italian lord of the house of Canossa, she followed him to Italy secretly from her father. But finally, the Emperor endowed her with many lands in Italy, and especially the "Patrimony." From these two was born Matilda, a woman of most honest character and great spirit and prudence in administering her lordship, and of supreme piety. Because of this, she gave great aid to the Pope against the Emperor. She endowed many churches, and especially the Cathedral of Pisa, near which she was buried in the year 1060 <note>The commentator's date is historically inaccurate; Matilda died in 1115.</note> in the tomb of Beatrice, her mother. She built many churches, and finally, her lordship, which today they call the "Patrimony," she offered to the Church of Saint Peter in Rome. Therefore, just as at the beginning of Purgatory our poet places Cato as a man most loving of liberty, so in this beginning of the Paradise of Delights, in which he establishes the active life, he feigns finding Matilda. In her, the union of civil life with true Christian religion occurs. He places her "alone" because the active life should be in solitude <note>Possibly suggesting a focus on God even amidst worldly work.</note>. But to show that even in this there is need for constant meditation, she "sings," which demonstrates the eloquence with which the good are sweetly persuaded to good works and the wicked are dissuaded from their governing. **AND CHOOSES** flower from flower: among many works that come in the active life, she chooses those which possess more virtue.

O beautiful lady, who in the rays of love
dost warm thyself, if I am to believe appearances
which are wont to be witnesses of the heart
May it please thee to draw forward

<column-break/>

**O BEAUTIFUL LADY**: These are the words that Dante used toward the woman to persuade her to approach the stream so that he could understand what she was singing. Having thus captured her goodwill by using this word "O"; and he who calls...

The poet recalls for us the abduction of Proserpina, who, while in a meadow in Sicily, was abducted by Pluto and taken to Hell, so that the meadow where Mathelda was is similar to that one.
**AS SHE TURNS**: He shows that the woman moves with her feet close to the ground and together: because she hardly lifts them when she dances. **RED AND YELLOW**: He notes that those who are virtuous in the active life must be full of fire—that is, charity—and pure from every vicious stain. This is denoted by the yellow, which is the color of gold. **AND SHE CAUSED** my prayers to be satisfied: because she approached me so closely that I could discern the meaning of her words.

**As soon as she was there where the grasses are**

**The river kept us three steps apart;**

Venus’s own mother was accidentally grazed by an arrow from Cupid's quiver; she immediately burned with love for the son of Cinyras and Myrrha <note>Adonis</note>, who was a most beautiful youth and was later killed by a boar and turned into a flower. **ENTIRELY**

The Hellespont is a narrow sea which divides Asia from Europe.

<margin>1.</margin>
The beautiful lady: and certainly civil actions performed with virtue are beautiful. And he adds **WHO**, being easy for the rays of love to reach. Nor can it be otherwise; for the active life takes on many tasks for the homeland, for relatives, for friends, and finally for all men. And no one would want to exert themselves for others if they were not warmed by the fire and rays of love and charity. "Charity does not seek its own" <note>original Latin: *Caritas non quaerit quae sua sunt* (1 Corinthians 13:5).</note>. **IF I SHOULD BELIEVE** her appearance: Dante could not know if this woman was inflamed by the flames of love, having just seen her; but he judged her by her appearance—that is, by certain acts and gestures which had in them the sign and likeness of love. And these gestures are most often certain and indubitable signs of the soul. **COME TO ME:** He poses his request, which is that she approach so close to the river bank that he can understand what she sings. **YOU MAKE ME** remember where Proserpina was before. It has already been described as most pleasant and highly adorned with herbs and flowers. Her mother lost her, and she lost the flowers: This shows where Ovid describes the abduction of Proserpina. With dexterity she turned toward him, just as a lady who dances is accustomed to turn her feet on the ground and hardly moves from her place. The colors of the red flowers denote that the acts of those in the active life must be full of the fire of charity (denoted by the color red) and pure from every stain (denoted by the yellow color of pure gold). **AND SHE CAUSED** me to be satisfied, so that I not only heard the sound of the words but perceived their meaning.

She came as far as the river with her eyes lowered, not looking at Dante. But having reached the bank, she looked up at him. He imagines this because the doctrine <term>doctrine: the spiritual teaching or wisdom</term> of which we have already spoken does not shine in our soul until it is around the river Lethe—that is, in the virtues of a soul already purged. For as is already manifest: "The spirit of wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul" <note>original Latin: *In animam malevolam non introibit spiritus sapientiae* (Wisdom of Solomon 1:4).</note>. And this river is three steps wide because three things are necessary to enter into these virtues: first, to recognize the vice; second, having recognized it, to hate it; third, having hated it, to forget it. Mathelda sings and laughs because this third stage makes us not only abstain from vices without difficulty, but we exercise such virtues with the highest pleasure. The great splendor of her eyes demonstrates the purity and open, clear truth of this doctrine. Wishing to demonstrate the great splendor, he makes a comparison between her and Venus, specifically when she was inflamed with love for Adonis. It is in the fables that while Cupid was embracing Venus, he accidentally wounded her in the breast; because of this wound, she fell in love with Adonis, a most beautiful youth. This was "contrary to his custom" because the wound was accidental. It has already been said that the operations of the active life are many, but those of the earthly paradise are the highest. **BUT THE HELLESPONT** where Xerxes passed: The Hellespont was not as much an object of hatred to Leander, who swam from Abydos to Sestos to reach Hero, as this river was to Dante. The Hellespont is a narrow stretch of sea between Asia and Europe. Sestos is on the European side, and Abydos was on the Asian side.

These two things, he says, clash and combat the faith that he had recently placed in Statius, when he heard from him something contrary to what he presently feels: namely, that no alteration rose above the aforementioned three steps. To resolve the doubt that Dante has, she first demonstrates that Statius told him the truth: that no alteration of those that arise from the vapors of the earth, drawn up by the sun into the third region [of the air], can reach here. And the reason shown is that God, creating the Paradise of Delights so that man might live without any discomfort, raised this mountain so high above the earth that Purgatory and Paradise surpass the third region, which such vapors cannot cross. Therefore, there can be no winds, nor rains, nor snow, nor hail, nor lightning. And allegorically she shows that whoever is in the purgatorial virtues and in those of the already purified soul feels no perturbation of the soul. **THE HIGHEST GOOD:** which is God, **WHO ONLY** pleases Himself: God alone, for His own sake and not for any other extrinsic thing, is pleasing to Himself. The intention of the author is that man, in the virtues of the already purified soul, exercises himself in the active life according to our religion.

The Earthly Paradise [is] A PLEDGE OF ETERNAL peace.** <note>original: "arra d'eterna pace"</note> God willed that man in a state of innocence should inhabit this place as long as it pleased God: and afterward, He wished to lead him to heaven. Therefore, it was a pledge of eternal peace, that is, of heaven where the highest beatitude resides. **THROUGH HIS OWN fault:** <note>original: "difalta"</note> through his own defect, a word derived from "undoing" <note>original: "diffare"</note>: Because he who sins does not *do*, and sin is nothing other than the privation of good. Therefore, he undoes and does not do. **HERE HE DWELT but a short while:** They say that the first man was created in Damascus and from there translated to the paradise of delights at the hour of the third <note>approximately 9:00 AM</note>. Afterward, He put him to sleep: and formed the woman from his rib: and afterward the serpent came and tempted Eve: and after the hour of the ninth <note>approximately 3:00 PM</note> they ate the forbidden apple. From which it is gathered that he did not stay three hours in paradise. **BECAUSE THE [air] disturbing.** <note>Dante, Purgatorio XXVIII, 101: "Perché 'l turbar..."</note> He showed how the first man was put in paradise: Now he shows why such a place was more eminent above the earth than others. And he says that this mountain rose, that is, elevated and raised itself toward heaven so much that it is free from exhalations **FROM THERE UPWARD** where it is locked, that is, from the gate of Purgatory. And this was done so that the disturbed air—which terrestrial exhalations and vapors raised by the heat of the sun cause—would not make any war upon man, such as inducing winds: rain, hail, snow, and the like. But allegorically it shows that he who is elevated from the earth, that is, from the thoughts of earthly things, and has pulled up his sensuality and made it obedient to reason and united with it in a form so that the flesh does not fight against the spirit, has a tranquil mind: and is outside the winds of appetite and the waters of sadness and every other perturbation.

the air revolves with the first revolution,
unless the circle is broken at some point,
At this height, which is all disconnected

and makes the forest sound because it is thick;

And the other land, according to its worth
