<column-break/>

He has shown that Statius did not lie to Dante when he told him that this mountain was free from the alterations already mentioned. Now he shows that, notwithstanding this, there is nonetheless a wind here that moves the branches: which is born because the first revolution—that is, the Primum Mobile <note>The outermost moving sphere in the medieval geocentric model</note>—which in twenty-eight <note>likely a scribal error for 24</note> hours turns from East to West and from there returns to the East: moves the air through the same circuit, and from this motion a wind is born: which can move the branches; and he calls it "living air," that which is above the third region [of the atmosphere]. **AND THE STRUCK plant. i.** the tree struck by such a wind impregnates the air with its virtue: and the air, revolving, shakes it from itself: whence that [virtue] falls into the other land: that is, into this land of our hemisphere; and such land into which such virtue falls conceives according to what it—either through its fertility or through the virtue of the heavens and the stars to which it is subject—can do, and generates such a plant as the virtue wills. Therefore, we should not marvel if some plant is born here without visible seed: that is, without us seeing it or sowing it: because it is born through the aforementioned virtue. And concluding, he describes the countryside of the paradise of delights, which he calls "countryside" because it is flat. And it is holy because it signifies innocence. It is full of every seed: which is why it produces every fruit that is found here [on earth], and even those which are not plucked here: that is, are not gathered: because there is the Tree of Life, and whoever eats of that fruit does not die.

As he has shown that the wind which strikes the leaves is not born from hot and dry vapors as it is here: so now he shows that the water of the two rivers of paradise is not born from cold and moist vapors as our rivers are born from vapors that the sky converts into water: **BUT IT IS BORN from a fountain:** He feigns that one and the same fountain exists in the paradise of delights: which grows—

### CANTO XXVIII.

it never diminishes: but always remains as one being and is toward the east and has two mouths: one to the left from which **Lethe** <note>In Greek mythology, the river of forgetfulness; here, it signifies the forgetting of past sins.</note> is born, the other to the right from which **Eunoe** <note>A name coined by Dante from Greek roots meaning "good memory"; it restores the memory of good deeds.</note> is born. And through this, he wishes to express the habit of the virtues of a soul already purified. For this reason, he says this fountain is steady and certain: steady because it does not fail, for such a habit <note>In the philosophical sense of a permanent disposition of character.</note> cannot be removed or taken from the soul; and certain because it neither grows nor diminishes but always remains of one quality. This is true because the operations that proceed from such a soul are continuous; they neither increase nor decrease as they do in the **civil virtues** <note>term: civil virtues (virtù civili). These are the practical, social virtues (like justice or temperance) practiced by citizens in worldly life, which can fluctuate.</note>. This fountain is, therefore, what we have said: that which proceeds from perfecting and confirming grace, which does not allow the source to fail. **Lethe** on the left is the oblivion of vices, which signifies perfection because it makes us—I do not say resist vices as in other virtues—but actually forget them, because every irrational appetite is submerged and entirely extinguished. From the right of this fountain is born the river **Eunoe**, which signifies a "good mind": and this is the most burning fervor of charity and an intense will in virtuous operations. **AND IT DOES NOT WORK:** this fountain does not truly benefit unless it is tasted here and there, that is, if we do not taste both Lethe and Eunoe together: because the soul cannot be perfect if it has not forgotten every disturbance and is not entirely inflamed with the love of virtue. **TO ALL OTHER SAVORS:** it surpasses them, just as the sense of taste is in supreme happiness when it has food that exceeds the flavor of all others; so the soul, through these two rivers—understood according to the allegory already established—lives in perfect happiness. **AND ALTHOUGH:** that is, although your thirst—the desire to understand the conditions of this place—might be satisfied, **NONETHELESS I SHALL REVEAL:** <note>original: "perchio non ti scuopra"</note> I will tell you even more as a favor, as if to say by my own liberality, a **corollary**: properly, they call a corollary a conclusion that embraces all others. It follows from the things already said rather than proceeding by its own order. For example: when we have demonstrated by many arguments that the soul is immortal, we will conclude that it is necessary to keep it pure from vices so that, separated from the body, it may return to its highest good.

> Those who in ancient times sang in verse
> of the Golden Age and its happy state,
> perhaps on Parnassus dreamed of this place.
> Here the human root was innocent;
> here it is always spring and every fruit;
> this is the nectar of which each one spoke.
> I turned then entirely back
> to my poets, and saw that with a smile
> they had heard the final statement;
> then to the beautiful lady I turned my face.

<column-break/>

I believe the meaning of the first tercet is that the poets who anciently divided the ages according to metals and said that the first was golden and called it the **Golden Age** <note>original: "secolo delloro"</note>: because men in that age lived most innocently and cleansed of every stain of vice, like gold in the furnace, most pure—they saw this state of innocence as if under a cloud and almost as if through a dream. And therefore he says, "perhaps on **Parnassus** <note>The mountain sacred to the Muses and Apollo, representing poetic inspiration.</note> they dreamed of this place," that is, in their poetic art and in their **furor** <note>term: furor (furore poetico). This refers to the concept of "divine madness" or inspiration that allows a poet to perceive truths beyond ordinary reason.</note> by which, elevating the mind, they were able to describe high and admirable meanings. Placing Parnassus, the mountain dedicated to the Muses, for art and poetic frenzy, they saw it as if dreaming and not perfectly.

this innocence. **HERE THE HUMAN ROOT WAS INNOCENT:** As if to say in no other place and in no other time was there a first age which was golden except here, where the human root—the first humans—were innocent. **HERE IS ALWAYS SPRING:** As if the year had a perpetual spring, it would always be temperate: and there would be neither excessive heat nor excessive cold. So the state of innocence, because it is in a perpetual spring, is not molested by the heat of excessive cupidity and desires, nor by the cold of excessive sorrow and fear. **I TURNED BACK TO MY POETS:** This signifies that with his mind he returned to poetic doctrine; he easily confesses it to be laughable in this part <note>That is, the ancient myths are mere shadows compared to the theological reality.</note> if they did not understand this same truth through their fiction. Then, having seen how insufficient poetic doctrine is for this, he returns his face to **Mathelda**, that is, to theological doctrine: which describes the happiness of the **active life**, just as **Beatrice** contains the doctrine of the **contemplative life**.

### CANTO XXVIII OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE

Singing like a woman in love
she continued to the end of her words:
*Blessed are those whose sins are covered* <note>original Latin: "beati quorum tecta sunt peccata." This is a quote from Psalm 32, referring to the forgiveness of sins which Lethe will soon facilitate.</note>
And like nymphs who used to wander alone
through the wild shadows, one desiring
to see the sun and another to flee it,
She then moved, walking along the bank
against the stream, and I kept pace with her,
following her small steps with my own.
There were not a hundred steps between hers and mine
when the banks both made a turn in such a way
that I was facing back toward the East.

<margin>In this beginning of Paradise, things will be hidden from him because he will forget them.</margin> **AND LIKE NYMPHS:** A fitting comparison between the nymphs who inhabit the forests, meadows, and waters, and the woman placed in such a pleasant and delightful greenery and garden. **SHE THEN MOVED:** This shows that the lady was walking along the riverbank, going against the current toward the source of the river; and Dante followed her, taking small steps just as she did. He does not include any of these details without reason. For she was leading the poet to the ford of the river which he had to cross, and she did not stray from it; and she went toward the East, which signifies the most perfect direction; and against the water, because we must not let ourselves be led away by its waves, but rather resist them and cross when it is the proper time and place. **THERE WERE NOT A HUNDRED** steps between hers and mine: they had not even gone a hundred steps together—which was a distance of fifty paces—when we reached the bend in the river, which, in turning, caused me to face the East. Through this, he demonstrates that one proceeds only a short time in the investigation of this doctrine and in the operations of these virtues of the soul already purified before we are illuminated by the power of divine grace.

Nor had our path yet gone much further
when the lady turned completely toward me,
saying, "My brother, look and listen."
And behold, a sudden brightness flashed
from all sides through the great forest,
such that it made me wonder if it were lightning.
But because lightning stops as quickly as it comes,
and this, enduring, shone more and more,
within my thoughts I said: "What thing is this?"
And a sweet melody ran
through the luminous air, wherefore a good zeal
made me reproach the boldness of Eve,
That there, where earth and heaven were obedient,
a lone woman, and but recently formed,
could not endure to stay under any veil;
Under which, if she had remained devoted,
I would have tasted those ineffable delights
sooner, and for a much longer time.

<column-break/>

**She sang excellently like a woman in love:** <note>original: "Optime cantatua chome donna innamorata"</note> because the interpreters and teachers of our theology, openly and with the greatest zeal toward their neighbor, continually instruct us by preaching or by admonishing and teaching in other ways. Therefore, singing like a woman in love, she continues to the end of her words. That is, once she had finished explaining to Dante what we have already said, she began without pause to sing the Psalm whose beginning is: *Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered* <note>original: "Beati quorum remisse sunt iniquitates et quorum tecta sunt peccata." This is the full opening of Psalm 32.</note>. A song suited to the subject matter: for Dante was soon to drink from the water of **Lethe** <note>The river of forgetfulness.</note>, through which he was to forget his sins. Therefore, through Purgatory, his sins had been forgiven; and—

Having now turned toward the East and become attentive, he began to see most excellent things through Mathelda. **LOOK AND LISTEN:** We can come to knowledge in two ways: either by investigating with our own wit and searching with the discourse of reason—and this we call "seeing" by analogy to the physical eyes—or truly, when we cannot find the truth by ourselves, we learn from others. Thus, Dante is admonished by Mathelda, saying "look" so that he may investigate for himself, and saying "listen" so that in what he cannot see for himself, he may hear from one who teaches him. **A BRIGHTNESS:** <note>term: lustro. A sudden, intense radiance.</note> a splendor which at first he doubted might be lightning. But then, considering that lightning passes quickly and extinguishes itself, and seeing that this endured and grew, he did not understand what it might be; and through the air shining with such splendor, he heard a marvelous melody. This represents the arrival of the **Holy Spirit**, in which he places the splendor and the song as the first two singular graces which the Holy Spirit gives to the human mind. The first is light, which drives away the shadows of ignorance and brings knowledge of the truth; the second is the song, through which—

it demonstrates the sweetness that is instilled through the knowledge of divine things. And such light, coming into the soul already purified, lasts forever and is not extinguished. **WHEREFORE GOOD ZEAL:** Because of this, he took such zeal in knowing divine things that "I took on the boldness of Eve." That is, I had that same daring that Eve had, who was not yet [firmly] formed in mind; although she had a commandment from God not to taste of the apple, which gave knowledge...

<summary>This page describes Dante following Mathelda along the river Lethe toward the East, where a sudden, enduring divine light and a sweet melody signal the arrival of the Holy Spirit. The commentary explains the symbolic importance of the East, the nature of divine revelation through "looking and listening," and reproaches Eve's original disobedience which delayed humanity's access to these heavenly delights.</summary>

<page-num>XXVIIII</page-num>

# CANTO XXIX

While I was walking among so many first-fruits
of the eternal pleasure, entirely suspended
and still desiring even greater joys,
In front of us, just like a fire ignited,
the air became beneath the green branches,
and the sweet sound was already understood as a song.
O holy, sacred virgins, if hunger,
cold, or vigils I ever suffered for you,
the cause spurs me to claim my reward.
Now it is necessary that Helicon pour for me,
and Urania help me with her choir,
to put into verse things difficult to conceive.

A little further on, seven trees of gold
falsely appeared due to the long distance
of the space that was still between us and them.
But when I had come so near to them
that the common object <note>The "common object" (obiecto comune) refers to an Aristotelian concept where distance blurs specific details, leaving only general shapes like size or color.</note>, which deceives the senses,
lost no detail because of the distance,
The faculty that prepares discourse for reason
perceived them as they were: candelabra,
and in the voices of the singing: "Hosanna."
From above, the beautiful arrangement flamed,
much clearer than the moon in a clear sky
at midnight in her middle month.
I turned back, full of wonder,
to the good Virgil, and he replied to me
with a look no less laden with amazement.
Then I turned my gaze back to the other things
that were moving toward us so slowly...

<column-break/>

of good and evil: Nevertheless, she <note>Refers to Eve.</note> did not endure staying under any veil or obscurity of ignorance:
Rather, too readily against the divine precept, she tasted the apple which gave her knowledge of good and evil: And therefore he says that Eve, in that restless place—that is, in the paradise of delights in which the earth obeys the heaven, performing what the heaven imprints upon it and not discordant with its influences—she alone, without help from others, and a woman, whose sex ought to have been more timid, and having just been formed: because a few hours before she had been created from Adam's rib, which novelty similarly should have made her timid. **UNDER WHICH**—that is, under which ignorance—had she been devout and obedient, I would have felt those ineffable—that is, inexpressible—delights sooner and for a longer time: In short, I would have been born in this paradise and lived there for a longer time and remained in a state of innocence; nor would I have contracted original sin.

Proceeding forward, the poet approaches closer to the splendor and hears the song better. **AMONG** so many first-fruits: because these were the first things he began to see and hear in contemplation **OF ETERNAL PLEASURE**—that is, of the supreme good which consists in contemplation. **AND DESIRING** because our soul is not content until it arrives at the summit: **JUST LIKE** an ignited fire the air became: He always places love before intelligence: of which I have warned the reader many times: And in the place that most requires it, I will strive to explain the cause. **THE SOUND** as a song: We understand that the sound first heard was singing. **O HOLY** sacred: Justly, having to treat most difficult and divine things, he distrusts human intellect unless he has help from the Muses. Therefore necessity spurs him to invoke them: and the vigils and labors that he has endured for them give him hope of being heard by them: for which reason he ordains thus: **O HOLY SACRED** virgins, the cause: which proceeds from necessity **SPURS ME**—that is, pushes me—**THAT I** call upon you—that is, that I ask you for **GRACE IF I** ever suffered: as if to say, which grace I hope for because I have suffered for you hunger, cold, and vigils. **NOW IT IS NECESSARY** that Helicon pour for me. To "pour" denotes the supreme abundance and flow of the favor of the Muses which he needs; and he used Helicon, the mountain, for the fountain that is consecrated to the Muses in it: and the fountain for their favor. **URANIA**: Wishing to treat celestial things, he appropriately invokes that Muse who is named after the heavens: as we showed in the first canticle. **A DIFFICULT THING** to think and put into verse: He makes the listener attentive by demonstrating the greatness of the matter: which cannot be expressed in verse without difficulty, and at the same time shows that he does not invoke Urania without need.

He shows that by approaching the place, he gained clarity of that which the great distance between him and the candelabra and the voices had falsified: because the golden candelabra appeared to him as trees. And here briefly, as a supreme philosopher, he declares what thing deceives the visual power and how the deception can be escaped: And allegorically he shows that even the sight of the mind is often deceived at the beginning of an investigation when it is still so far from a conclusion that it seems to be what it is not. Then, having seen Virgil, I turned my gaze back to the other things: that is, I turned my eyes to the candelabra: whose significance will soon appear: which were coming more slowly than new brides walk. Mathelda—that is, Christian doctrine—demonstrates the order and the process of human salvation from the creation of man until the advent of Christ. Therefore the sun, which sees first, represents the sun of the Holy Spirit, which illuminated the paradise of delights and Adam and Eve.

<summary>Dante experiences a divine vision of seven golden candelabra in the Earthly Paradise, signaling the start of a celestial procession. Landino’s commentary links this sensory experience to the soul’s pursuit of divine truth and the role of the Holy Spirit in human history.</summary>

# PURGATORIO CANTO XXIX

## ...that they would have outshone new-wed brides.
## The lady scolded me: "Why do you only gaze
## so ardently upon the living lights,
## and do not look at what comes behind them?"
## Then I saw people, as if following their leaders,
## coming close behind, dressed in white;
## and such whiteness was never seen here.
## The water shone on my left side,
## and reflected back to me my left rib,
## if I looked into it, just like a mirror.

Which things demonstrate that whoever wishes to pass to the state of innocence and forget all vices must exercise themselves in the study of the aforementioned things, all of which the Bible contains. But returning to the text above, we say **THE FACULTY PERCEIVED THE CANDELABRA:** <note>original: "LA VIRTV APERESE ECANDELABRI"</note> that is, he could discern that those were not trees but candelabra; and similarly, he described how the voices, which were at first confused due to distance, were saying **HOSANNA.** <note>original: "OSANNA"</note> In Hebrew, this signifies "save," or truly "give life," or truly "make us safe," or "our salvation." **FROM ABOVE** the beautiful arrangement flamed: he uses "beautiful arrangement" for the candelabra. **FLAMED FROM ABOVE:** it threw out flames from its highest part **MUCH CLEARER:** the meaning is that the splendor of the candelabra was greater than that which the moon spreads when it is in a clear sky, in its mid-month phase and at midnight. **I TURNED BACK** full of wonder: this shows that great wonder seized him at such light, and he turned to Virgil to ask him about the nature of the thing. But Virgil did not answer him with words but showed by his look that he too was full of wonder. This signifies that human science <note>Represented by Virgil.</note> is rather stunned by such great things than able to understand them. Then follows **THEN I RETURNED:** that is, from the sight of Virgil, to whom I had turned my gaze <note>original: "aspecto"</note>, and I returned to look at the other things, and especially the candelabra of which we have already spoken. **THE LADY:** that is, Mathelda answered me saying: that it is not enough solely to burn with affection for the first lights, that is, in the love and desire of these seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; but one must also consider the effects that follow from this guide of the Holy Spirit, which is the true leader and guide of every virtuous operation. **I THEN SAW PEOPLE:** he means, as I said a little before, these holy men, patriarchs and prophets and others mentioned who believed in the Christ to come; to whom white clothing is due because faith must be pure. Hence the ancient Gentiles, when they sacrificed to Faith, held their hands wrapped in white cloth; and he adds that they were of such whiteness as was never seen in this world here. And allegorically, he means that our current age does not have that pure faith which those people had. **THE WATER:** of the river already mentioned **SHONE:** by the light of the candelabra. This river is the meditation and consideration of innocence, which makes one forget vices and is illuminated by the Holy Spirit, which reflects back to whoever looks into it their left rib; that is, it frees the heart of whoever considers it from all sensuality by which they were previously held. And this is as far as the allegory goes; but according to the literal sense it is also true.

## When I had reached such a position on my bank
## that only the river kept me distant,
## to see better, I brought my steps to a halt.
## And I saw the little flames moving forward,
## leaving the air behind them painted,
## which had the appearance of brushstrokes;
## So that the air above remained marked
## by seven streaks, all in those colors
## of which the sun makes its bow and Delia her girdle.
## These banners stretched back further
## than my sight could reach; and as I judged,
## the outermost were ten paces apart.

<column-break/>

our first parents. Afterward, the seven candelabra were the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which before the incarnation of the Divine Word came slowly to men and to few, because the time of grace had not yet arrived. Afterward, by those whom he places dressed in white, he signifies those who believed in the Christ to come. And by the twenty-four elders <note>original: "xxiiii seniori"</note> he means the twenty-four books of the Bible. <note>In the medieval tradition, the Old Testament was often counted as 24 books.</note> It signifies also the four Evangelists; the three theological virtues and the four cardinal virtues; the eight apostles; and the epistles written by Saint Luke and Saint Paul; and the four disciples who wrote the other epistles; likewise the Apocalypse of Saint John.

He continues by narrating that when the lights were already so near that there was no other distance or interval between them and the poet except for the river, he brought his steps to a halt; that is, he paused. But the flames of the candelabra continued proceeding forward, and behind them they left the air painted with seven streaks and lines of the brush, just as a painter does when he wants to make a line. And they were of the colors that the sun makes in the celestial bow <note>The rainbow.</note> or the moon when she is among white clouds <note>Delia's girdle refers to a lunar halo.</note>; the colors of the bow are blood-red, green, and white. These banners—that is, these streaks—were greater than his sight because he could not see the end. But according to his judgment, they were not raised from the flowers—that is, from the ground—which was flowering, by more than ten paces. But allegorically, understand that between the candelabra and Dante there was no other interval but the river. Because he, being purged of vices, nothing else stood in the way of being able to join with the gifts of the Holy Spirit except to cross the river and wash himself; that is, to extinguish every thought that could ignite sensuality.

# CANTO XXIX

...in a way that I would entirely forget them. The seven strips of colors mentioned before, preceding from the seven candelabra, signify the seven sacraments of the Church, which are sacred signs of sacred things. Therefore, they are signs of the **seven gifts of the Holy Spirit**, and so he imagines them as being figured by these: and that the candelabra and the strips are **ten paces** high from the ground because, from outside the meadow—which signifies the first exemplary virtuous life—one ascends to these seven gifts by means of the **Ten Commandments**. This is because the primitive church, called the Synagogue, was earthly and full of figures, signs, and creation, and is therefore signified by flowers, which are not fruit but signify the future fruit. Therefore, through the passion of Christ, we can ascend with the ladder of the Ten Commandments to the seven graces of the Holy Spirit, which are **Fear, Piety, Fortitude, Knowledge, Counsel, Wisdom, and Understanding**. As a sign of these, the New Church holds the seven sacraments, which are **Confirmation, Baptism, Holy Orders, Eucharist, Penance, Extreme Unction, and Marriage**.

The author imagines **Confirmation** <note>original: "Cresima"</note> to be red, which is a sign of **fear** <note>The "fear of the Lord," one of the seven gifts</note> that is rooted in the charity man has toward God. From this arises humility, which is against pride. **Baptism** is vermilion, which signifies **piety**, founded on the charity man has toward his neighbor—which is lesser than that toward God—and is figured as blood-colored or vermilion; from this arises love, which is against envy. **Holy Orders** is green, signifying **fortitude**, and is rooted in the hope we have in God. From this arises religion, which is against wrath. The **Eucharist** is white, signifying **knowledge** founded on faith, which man has in the body of Christ that comes upon the altar. From this arises virtuous action against sloth. **Penance** is green, a sign of **counsel**, rooted in hope in God. From this arises moderation against avarice. **Extreme Unction** is red, a sign of **wisdom** rooted in charity toward one's neighbor; from this arises abstinence against gluttony. **Marriage** is blood-colored or vermilion, a sign of **understanding**, rooted in charity toward one's neighbor. From this arises chastity against lust.

> Under so fair a sky as I have described,
> twenty-four elders, two by two,
> came crowned with lilies.
>
> All were singing: "Blessed art thou
> among the daughters of Adam; and blessed
> be your beauties forever."
>
> After the flowers and other fresh grasses
> across from me on the other bank
> were cleared of those chosen people,
>
> Just as light follows light in the heavens,
> there came after them four animals,
> each crowned with green leaves.
>
> Each was plumed with six wings,
> the feathers full of eyes; and the eyes of Argus,
> if they were alive, would be such as these.

<column-break/>

After the seven candelabra and the crowd dressed in white came **twenty-four elders**, by whom are denoted the twenty-four books of the Bible <note>The Old Testament was historically counted as 24 books in the Hebrew tradition</note>, which contain all Christian doctrine. These are divided thus: they come **two by two** to show that the two Testaments are joined, because in the Old are contained the mysteries and the figures, and in the New are the things prefigured in the mysteries of the Old. **For example** <note>original: "Verbi gratia"</note>: In the Old, Jonah is swallowed by the fish; in the New, Christ is placed in the tomb. They were **dressed in white**, which expresses the pure truth of this doctrine, clean of all falsehood, and faith. They were **crowned with lilies**, which denotes faith. And these are the twenty-four elders whom John wrote about in the Apocalypse. **Under so fair a sky**: fair air. This is because the Latins use the word "sky" for "air"; <gloss>hence Virgil says: "sea and lands and the deep sky"</gloss> <note>Original Latin: "mare ac terras celumque profudum"</note>. He calls it fair air because it was adorned with the seven strips.

**DESCRIBED:** <note>original: "diviso"</note> I have distinguished and described. **ELDERS:** <note>original: "SENIORI"</note> old men; it is a Latin word. <gloss>*Senes* means old men, hence *seniores*.</gloss> **All singing, "Blessed art thou":** All singing, they praised the Virgin; for the Old Testament contains nothing other than mysteries and prophecies that denote the incarnation of the Word in the Virgin, who was greeted by the angel Gabriel as "blessed among all women," all of whom are daughters of Adam. **YOUR BEAUTIES:** your virtues. This is because the beauties of the soul are, without any comparison, more excellent than the beauties of the body; and nothing is beautiful in the soul that is not virtue, and nothing is virtue that is not beautiful. **After the flowers:** the meaning is: after all these people had passed that part of the meadow which was across from me on the other bank of the river. For a place remains free when he who treads upon it has passed and left it empty; and thus, by their passage, he shows that the Old Testament had already passed, in which men were still servants of sin. Whereupon followed the New, in which came our redemption and liberation. **Just as light:** He excellently expresses the progress of all these people and the splendor of all, saying that just as in the turning of the heavens the sky is never seen empty of lights, but always after one star comes another, so after the lights of those who had already passed came the **four animals** with similar splendor. **JUST AS light:** that is, a star. **FOLLOWS:** <note>original: "SECONDA"</note> follows. **LIGHT:** the star that goes before it. And allegorically we can say that the mind of one who studies sacred theology is illuminated from time to time with splendor and knowledge; because one thing already understood opens the intellect to understand the next that follows. Furthermore, it demonstrates the perfect order because first was...

<meta>This page continues the allegorical commentary on Canto XXIX of the Purgatorio. Having previously discussed the seven candelabra and the sacraments they represent, the commentator now moves to the procession's next figures: the four living creatures (the Evangelists) and the triumphal chariot representing the Church, led by a Griffin.</meta>

<header>CANTO XXIX OF PURGATORIO</header>
<sig>m m .ii</sig>

The celestial spheres have passed, and the prophecies now follow the things prefigured. **Four animals:** Here are prefigured the four Evangelists: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Matthew takes a human form because, more than the others, he describes the humanity of Christ. Mark is in the form of a lion because, just as the lion restores his cubs to life with his roar after the third day <note>A common medieval belief found in bestiaries was that lion cubs were born dead and brought to life by the father's roar on the third day, symbolizing the Resurrection.</note>, so Mark, more clearly than the others, spoke of the resurrection of Christ. Luke is in the form of an ox because, just as the ox makes a great lowing, so Luke writes more clearly than the others of the preaching of Christ. John is in the form of an eagle because, just as the eagle flies above all other birds and keeps its eyes fixed on the light, so John, above all others, extended his intellect to the divinity of Christ and was better able to behold its splendor. **CROWNED** each with green leaves: This denotes that the evangelical doctrine, because it is true, will always remain green. I believe he means green leaves of the laurel, the triumphal tree, because this doctrine—which alone is true—has conquered all others that are false and triumphs over them. **EACH** was feathered with six wings: Here the poet follows the Apocalypse of John, who likewise describes them with six wings, of which two were raised at the head to denote their beginning; two were lowered to the feet to denote their progress until the end; and two were on the arms and hands, which signify their works. And because the height of Christ's divinity was little understood by them through natural reason, Ezekiel feigns that with the feathers that went to the head and those that went to the feet they covered the body—that is, the height of Christ and the divinity which was little revealed to them—and the depth, which signifies the coming of Christ, the time of which they did not know. And although John places six and Ezekiel four, they nevertheless come to the same meaning: for the Evangelist understood the reason and the intellect, while the prophet understood only the intellect. But the length, which was the bodily life of Christ, and the bliss, which was the doctrine, was known to them. **THE FEATHERS** full of eyes: By the eyes which John says the wings had inside and out, he signifies the circumspection <note>The quality of being wary and taking in all perspectives.</note> that God granted to the Evangelists to see the divinity veiled beneath humanity on the inside, and humanity joined with divinity on the outside. So these two natures made one individual. Furthermore, according to John, they had eyes in front and behind; this signifies that they considered the prophecies and mysteries of the Old Testament from the beginning of the world until the sixth age (in which Christ came) and from Him began the seventh, and from the seventh until the end of the world, which will be when Christ comes to judge. **AND THE EYES OF ARGUS:** Argus had a hundred eyes and was placed by Juno to guard Io, who had been changed into a cow, so that Jove could not return her to human form. Because of this, Mercury, sent by Jove, killed him; and Juno adorned the feathers of her peacocks with those eyes.

To describe their form I scatter no more 
rhymes, reader, for other expenses so constrain me
that in this I cannot be lavish: 
But read Ezekiel who depicts them
as he saw them coming from the cold region
with wind, with cloud, and with fire;
And such as you will find them in his pages,
such were they here: except that for the wings
John is with me and departs from him.

<column-break/>

The poet excuses his brevity, saying that he cannot be lavish and liberal in scattering more rhymes to describe the Evangelists because "other expenses constrain him"—as if to say that it is necessary for him to describe other things. **BUT READ** Ezekiel: He was one of the prophets who, with Joachim the king of Jerusalem, was led as a slave to Babylon. At one time he prophesied in Chaldea to his fellow Hebrew slaves there, while Jeremiah prophesied in Judea. **AND SUCH** as they were there: Such they appeared to me in that procession as Ezekiel describes them. **EXCEPT THAT** regarding the wings, John is with me: He is in my favor and defense of my opinion and departs from Ezekiel; for John imagines them with six wings and Ezekiel with four, of which two covered their bodies and two of one joined with the feathers of the other.

<column-break/>

The space within the four of them contained 
a triumphal chariot on two wheels
which came drawn at the neck of a Griffin;
And he held both wings stretched upward
between the middle and the three and three strips,
so that by cleaving none, he did no harm.
They rose so high they were not seen;
the limbs were of gold as far as he was a bird,
and the others were white mixed with vermilion.
Not even Rome with a chariot so beautiful
gladdened Africanus or Augustus...

<column-break/>

Between the four animals described above was a golden triumphal chariot with two wheels, pulled by a Griffin bird. The Griffin stretched its wings between the middle strip and the other three and three <note>Refers to the seven colored trails left by the candelabra mentioned in the previous section.</note> without touching any of them; and these wings rose so high they could not be seen. And the limbs of the Griffin that were bird-like were of gold; the others were white mixed with vermilion. This chariot is the New Church; and the two wheels are the Old and New Testaments. And it is truly a triumphal chariot because no other synagogue or congregation triumphs over the devil and remains the victor of its battles except for the Church founded in Christ. And it is of gold because it is the best, most beautiful, and most incorruptible. It is...

<meta>This page continues the allegorical commentary on Canto XXIX of Purgatorio. It explains the symbolism of the Griffin (representing Christ's dual nature) and the triumphal chariot (the Church), followed by the introduction of the three Theological Virtues.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>CANTO XXVIII</header>

...but that of the sun would seem poor beside it,
That of the sun which, straying, was consumed
by the prayer of the devout Earth,
when Jove was mysteriously just. <note>These verses refer to the myth of Phaethon, who lost control of the sun chariot and was struck down by Jove's thunderbolt to save the Earth from burning.</note>

and human. Therefore, the part of the bird represents divinity: and that of the lion, humanity. Christ thus built the Church: and He draws it to the will and obedience of the Father. The wings of the Griffin are two; the right shows divine justice: and the left, mercy: which, while He was on earth, were always extended toward heaven and joined with the Father and with the Holy Spirit. These wings extend between the seven lists, which are the seven sacraments—signs of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. They are arranged so that they place in the center the one in the middle, which is the Eucharist, that is, the most holy body of Christ, which is truly in the middle between justice and mercy. Because Christ instituted this sacrament as a sign of justice, through which we might offer to the Father such a sacrifice as we are bound to give / because no other was fitting for the divine excellence. He instituted it also as a sign of mercy: because by God preserving us in these three graces, we can justly please God and merit eternal life. On the left are Penance, Extreme Unction, and Matrimony: and these are from the wing of mercy / and are signs of the other three gifts of the Holy Spirit: Counsel, Wisdom, and Understanding. The Eucharist, which is a sign of Knowledge <term>scientia</term>, stands between the two wings for the reasons already stated above. Nor should anyone say because of this that the poet divides justice from mercy, one by the right and the other by the left wing. Rather, he intends that in those on the right, justice precedes: and in those on the left, mercy precedes. And therefore he says that the wings, in ascending, did no harm to any list. Now returning to the exposition of the text. **TRIUMPHAL CHARIOT:** as a prize of honor, it was established among the ancients that the leader of an army who had brought a full victory over enemies—and had killed at least five thousand of them in one battle: and broken and put the rest to flight—could not triumph among the Romans unless he had been a dictator, consul, or praetor in the army. The triumphing leader went upon an ornate chariot pulled by four white horses. And the Senate walked before him all the way to the Capitol: and there he sacrificed bulls. But the Spartans <note>original: "lacedemoni"</note> had the custom that if the triumphing leader had conquered the enemies with his cunning, he should sacrifice an ox: if through battle, he should sacrifice a rooster; they valued things done with prudence more, which is proper to man, than those done by force. They say that Bacchus was the first who discovered the triumph after conquering the eastern regions: and his chariot was pulled by elephants. Sesostris, King of Egypt <note>A legendary king of Egypt said to have conquered the world.</note>, out of extreme pride, placed four kings subject to him at his yoke. The triumphing leader sat in the chariot in a golden chair with a palm-patterned garment <note>The "toga palmata," worn by victorious generals.</note>. His face was painted red in imitation of the element of fire: from his neck hung a gold chain to which was attached a golden <term>bulla</term> <note>A locket or amulet worn by Roman triumphators and children.</note>: he had a crown of laurel: and an ivory scepter. **THEY WERE NOT** seen: because they ascend all the way to God, whom no one can comprehend: and justice goes to the Father and mercy to the Holy Spirit. **THE MEMBERS** of gold: these denote divinity. **AND WHITE** the others mixed with vermilion: these two colors, which are of flesh and blood, denote the humanity of Christ: white represents His innocence, and red His charity. **NOT EVEN ROME**: the meaning is that not even the triumphal chariots used by Rome and many others—most notably those of Africanus and Augustus—could be compared to this one. **AFRICANUS:** he means either the Elder, who defeated Hannibal, or the Younger, who destroyed Carthage. **Augustus:** We wrote of him in the first canto of the first canticle. **THAT OF THE SUN** which, straying, was consumed: This touches on the fable of Phaethon, which we have narrated elsewhere.

Three women in a circle by the right wheel
came dancing, one so red
that she would hardly be noticed inside a fire;
The other was as if her flesh and bones
had been made of emerald;
the third appeared like freshly fallen snow;
And now they seemed led by the white one,
now by the red; and to the song of this one,
the others took their pace, slow or rapid.
On the left, four made a celebration,
dressed in purple, and following the lead

He places at the right wheel, which signifies the New Testament, three women: who come dancing in a circle, by whom he means the three theological virtues: because these were less known in the Old Testament than in the New. **THE ONE** so red: this is Charity, which is the fervent love of God and neighbor: and therefore he places her in the color of fire: and adds that if she had been inside a fire, she would not have been distinguished from it: to denote that the fervor of charity is not less than that of fire. **THE OTHER** was as if she had flesh and bones of emerald: that is, she was green like an emerald: and this is Hope, which must always remain green: nor ever fail, which theologians define...

<header>XXVIIII PURGATORIO</header>

...being a certain expectation of future glory produced by the grace of God and preceding merit; THE THIRD part moves in their heads; this is faith which, for the reasons already stated above, must be pure and white. And faith is the substance of things to be hoped for and the evidence <note>original: "substantia rerum sperandarum et argumentum non apparentium"</note> of things not seen. We will treat these theological virtues in the twenty-fourth canto of Paradiso. And now she seemed drawn by the white, now by the red. He writes this because sometimes it is faith that generates charity and hope in us: and sometimes charity generates faith and hope. But hope never goes before faith and charity. And from the song of this charity, the others take their pace, slow or swift: which signifies nothing other than that faith and hope go only as far as charity moves them. And the chariot, that is, the Church Militant, is in the midst of the seven virtues: because with the three theological ones which she has on her right hand, she governs spiritual matters as more noble; and with the four cardinal ones, she governs temporal matters which, being less noble, are on the left: Wherefore Solomon says: *In her left hand are riches and glory.* <note>Proverbs 3:16: "In sinistra illius divitiae et gloria"</note>. On the left: he places by that wheel which represents the Old Testament the four cardinal virtues with which even those of the Old Testament were filled. He introduces these dressed in purple to denote charity and the fervor of love, without which no one can have these virtues. Behind them, in the manner of one of them who had three eyes in her head. These virtues are four and each has its office, which is not perfect if Prudence does not guide it; for example, Justice and Fortitude do not mean refusing laborious anguish and horrible dangers to preserve with honesty the homeland, parents, and friends. But it does not achieve the manner or the way it should hold to accomplish this if Prudence does not teach it. Similarly, Prudence demonstrates to Justice how much it should attribute to each, and to Temperance which pleasures it should flee. Now, since the poet places these four virtues here, I judge that the place requires us to briefly state their origin and distinction. There are, therefore, in our minds four principles and sources impressed by nature from which proceed four virtues. And first, everyone knows they have in themselves a supreme desire <term>cupidità</term> to understand and know everything. Wherefore it is troublesome to us when we err or when we are deceived by others. This desire induces in us Prudence. Furthermore, we have a certain generosity given to our mind by the same nature: which does not want us to submit to others except to reason and honesty, from which generosity Fortitude is born. There also arises in us a sense of shame <term>pudore</term> and an obstacle which holds us back from doing or saying things that are not fitting, and that would make us fall into shameful pleasures. And this is the progenitor of Temperance. In the fourth place is Justice, which nature produces in us: because man, being desirous of living in comfort and in the company of other men, knows that this cannot last if he does not faithfully give to each what is due to him. These are four—I do not say virtues—but principles and seeds of virtue through which we can achieve the perfect virtues. Prudence is that through which we have certain knowledge of things that should be sought or fled: which the poet depicts with three eyes because, as Seneca writes, the prudent man should grasp the future, dispense the present, and remember the past. And Justice is a habit of the soul which, preserving the common utility, attributes to each what is due to him according to his dignity. Fortitude is that which, with certain reason, pushes us against dangers and to support every laborious difficulty. Temperance is that through which we abstain from every dishonest pleasure. These virtues and the types of each you will find explained in various places in the first canticle.

Behold, therefore, that the clothing was different, because Luke showed the clothing of a physician who maintains life. <header>### CANTO XXVIIII</header>

...born. **THE OTHER SHOWED** <note>Referring to St. Luke, mentioned on the previous page as the companion to St. Paul.</note> a contrary concern: and this is Paul, who, holding a sword, does not have the habit of healing, but of killing. **BRIGHT AND SHARP:** the sword is attributed to Paul because of his supreme sharpness, vehemence, and endurance of spirit.

---

Then I saw four in humble appearance,
and behind them all a lone old man
coming as if asleep, with a keen face.
And these seven were dressed like
the first group, but of lilies
they did not make a wreath around their heads;
Rather, of roses and other vermilion flowers;
a viewer from a short distance away
would have sworn they were all aflame above their brows.

And when the chariot was directly across from me,
a thunderclap was heard; and those worthy people
seemed to have their progress forbidden,
stopping there along with the first standards.

<column-break/>

These four in humble appearance are the four apostles who wrote the letters called "canonical," <note>These are the General or Catholic Epistles of the New Testament.</note> which are placed in the Bible after the Acts of the Apostles. They are James, the brother of Christ; Peter; John; and Jude, the brother of James. These men wrote mystical epistles, both short and long: short in words, but long in their meanings. **IN HUMBLE** appearance: because of their humility of spirit and their poor and lowly status. **A LONE OLD MAN:** he means John, referring to the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>, which is the final book of the New Testament. **SLEEPING:** This denotes that Saint John had the visions he describes in the Apocalypse when he fell asleep upon the breast of Christ at the Last Supper; he described them later in his old age on the island of Patmos. **WITH** a keen face: subtle in appearance, which he says because he was of high and profound intellect. **AND THESE SEVEN:** that is, the first two elders, Paul and Luke; and the four of humble appearance, James, Peter, John, and Jude for their epistles; and John for the Apocalypse. **THEY WERE** dressed like the first group because they were similarly in white robes, but they did not have garlands of lilies like the others. **THEY DID NOT MAKE** a wreath <note>original: "brolo"</note> of lilies—"brolo" means greenery in the Lombard language. In short, the twenty-four books of the Old Testament have crowns of lilies, because to those who study them without faith, they are worth nothing. The Evangelists have green, signifying hope, because the beginning of the Gospel is the vigor of hope; it would be in vain to study them if we did not hope for what they promise. And these seven have vermilion flowers, because their principle is charity.

**WHEN** the chariot, which was proceeding forward, arrived at that spot directly across from me, a thunderclap was heard which seemed to forbid those worthy people from going further. Therefore they stopped, and also the first standards, which were the seven candelabra, stopped. Thus the Griffin, which is Christ, through his passion and death, has pulled the chariot—that is, the Synagogue transformed into the Holy Church—until it is across from Dante, which means in the sight of every man, manifesting it to all. Certainly, whoever studies the sacred letters and proceeds in this order described by the poet sees and understands his salvation. This is the path that leads us to the contemplation of eternal life and divine things, where our happiness consists after we have drunk from the river Lethe <note>The river of forgetfulness of sins.</note> and washed ourselves in it—that is, after we act in the virtues of a soul already purged, in which we entirely forget not only all sins but everything that could inflame us toward them. And then from the river Eunoe, through which the love of the virtues of the Supreme Good is sparked within us—which is inestimable—so that while on earth we are like angels. **A THUNDERCLAP WAS HEARD:** literally, it is necessary that such thunder in this place, which is above the third region where no vapor can rise, must be supernatural and made by God as a sign for the chariot to stop. But allegorically, according to Francesco da Buti, <note>A prominent 14th-century commentator on Dante.</note> we understand that from the tree of knowledge of good and evil, from which the disobedience of our first parents was born, until the wood of the cross, human generation always went toward the "west"—because the wicked went to Hell and the good to Limbo. But after Christ pulled the chariot to the river Jordan and created baptism, then the thunder was heard—that is, the voice of God the Father toward Christ at his baptism, which was: "This is my beloved son in whom I am well pleased." <note>original Latin: "Hic est filius meus dilectus in quo mihi bene complacui." See Matthew 3:17.</note> Therefore, after this time, human generation left the law of servitude and entered that of grace, and stopped going further "west." The law of Moses and circumcision ended, and the evangelical law and baptism began; and here God willed that through obedience we should return to the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Wherefore below, the poet will show this group turning around. **SEEMED** to have their progress forbidden: it seemed to those people that the thunder forbade and prohibited them from going any further; understand this as the Law of Moses. Stopping there in the evangelical law. **WITH THE** first standards: with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and with the seven gifts of the Holy Church, and with all the other things already narrated.

# CANTO XXX OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'Q' containing a miniature illustration of a figure (possibly an angel or a personification of a virtue) in a green and red robe, holding a staff or palm branch against a blue background.</image-desc>

When the "septentrion" <note>The seven stars of the Great Bear (Ursa Major), used here as a metaphor for the Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit.</note> of the highest heaven,
which never knew setting or rising,
nor the veil of any cloud but that of sin:
And which made everyone there as aware
of their duty as the lower [constellation] makes
whoever turns the rudder to reach port,
Had stopped firmly, the truthful people
who had come first between the griffin and [the chariot]
turned to the chariot as to their peace;
And one of them, as if sent from heaven,
singing "Come, bride from Lebanon" <note>original: "Veni sponsa de libano," a quote from the Song of Solomon 4:8.</note>
shouted three times, and all the others followed.
Just as the blessed at the final summons
will rise quickly, each from his tomb,
singing with their regained flesh,
So, upon the divine chariot,
a hundred rose up at the voice of such an elder,
ministers and messengers of eternal life.
> They all were saying: "Blessed are you who come" <note>original: "benedictus qui venis." This phrase, used to welcome Christ into Jerusalem, is here applied to the arrival of Beatrice.</note>
while throwing flowers above and around,
> "Oh, give lilies with full hands." <note>original: "manibus o date lilia plenis." Dante poignantly quotes Virgil's Aeneid (6.883), though Virgil is about to vanish from the narrative.</note>

<column-break/>

This thirtieth canto of Purgatory contains the form in which Beatrice appears to the poet; how she rebukes him; and finally, how Virgil abandons him. **WHEN THE SEPTENTRION:** The meaning is: when the aforementioned chariot was fixed and still, the people who had come before the griffin, and the griffin itself, turned toward the chariot. But by way of a simile, he calls this chariot the "septentrion of the first heaven"—that is, of the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest, non-physical heaven in medieval cosmology, where God and the blessed reside.</note> where the seats of the blessed are. This is because just as the septentrion of the eighth sphere <note>The sphere of the fixed stars in the Ptolemaic system.</note> has seven stars that form a "horn" in front of the chariot... **OF THE FIRST HEAVEN:** to distinguish it from the septentrion we see in the eighth sphere. **WHICH NEVER FEELS SETTING OR RISING:** Because just as our septentrion is so elevated above us and so close to our pole that it is always visible and does not behave like other stars that now rise and now go under, so the **seven gifts of the Holy Spirit** do not experience setting <term>ideft</term> <note>Latin "id est": that is</note> sinking, nor rising <term>ideft</term> <note>Latin "id est": that is</note> birth; because being eternal, they have no beginning. **NOR HAVE ANY OTHER VEIL BUT THAT OF SIN:** For it is not like our septentrion, which is often taken from our sight by darkness and by clouds that occupy the air. But this one cannot be hidden from us or covered by any veil other than that of guilt and sin. Because sin alone is that which hides the gifts of the Holy Spirit from man. **AND WHICH MADE [EVERYONE] THERE:** he follows the simile already made of this septentrion to our own in the eighth sphere: and says that just as our septentrion, where the North Star is, makes the pilot aware of how to steer his rudder if he wishes to come safely to port, so this one did there in Paradise—that is, in the state of innocence. Because whoever wishes to come to blessedness must steer his ship; and to

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto XXX of Purgatorio. It moves from the symbolic movement of the divine procession to the specific interpretation of the figures present, focusing on the biblical authorities and the heralded arrival of Beatrice.</meta>

Direct it according to the guidance of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. And organize the text thus: When the "septentrion" <note>The seven stars of the Great Bear, here symbolizing the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.</note> of the first heaven became fixed—which never knew setting nor rising, that is, it never felt descent nor ascent; and it never knew a "veil," meaning it never had any covering except for the sin that might take it from us; and which made everyone there in the earthly paradise aware and instructed, just as our lower septentrion <note>The physical constellation Ursa Major used by sailors.</note> **MAKES** <note>original: "FACE"</note>—that is, makes one aware and instructed to take a good voyage; **WHICH**: that is, whoever turns the rudder to come to port: When, therefore, this septentrion—that is, the seven candelabra—stopped: **THE TRUTHFUL PEOPLE**: that is, those who followed, whom we showed above to be the holy men of the Old Testament, who truly predicted the coming of Christ and believed in him; **AND THE GRIFFIN ITSELF**: that is, Christ: **THEY TURNED** to the chariot: that is, to the Holy Church: as to their peace, that is, as to their end. For everything contained in the Old Testament is for the purpose of establishing the Holy Church. **AND ONE OF THEM**: He means Solomon, who, prophesying as if the message were sent from heaven and seeking the future Church founded upon Christ—and how much Christ was to love her—said in his song <note>The Song of Solomon.</note> in the person of Christ: "Come, bride from Lebanon," <note>original: "Veni sposa delibano"</note> inviting the Synagogue of the Jews, which was to be transformed into the Church, to be the bride of Christ. Solomon thus predicted how Christ, with his preaching and doctrine, was to call the Synagogue to the new Church. **AND ALL THE OTHERS AFTERWARD**. This signifies that just as Solomon predicted the coming Church, so did all the other prophets predict it. **AS THE BLESSED**. He makes an excellent comparison: that just as on the day of the Great Judgment all the blessed will suddenly emerge from their caves at the sound of the angelic trumpets, reclothed in their own flesh, so at the voice of Solomon a hundred rose up; and all were saying: "Blessed are you who come." <note>original: "Benedictus qui venis"</note> **AT THE FINAL SUMMONS**: at the last request. A "summons" <note>original: "bando"</note> is everything publicly manifested preceding the sound of the trumpet. **BASTERNA**: The ancients called certain vehicles "basternas," or small carts, in which Roman priests and the Vestal Virgins carried their sacred objects as if in a procession; but by way of a likeness, he uses "basterna" for the aforementioned chariot. **MINISTERS** and messengers of eternal life. Many understand these to be angels; but perhaps it is better to understand them as the other prophets, who were messengers of eternal life because they predicted the future things ordained by God, and especially the incarnation of the Word and the new Church, the bride of Christ. **BLESSED ARE YOU WHO COME** <note>original: "BENEDICTVS qui uenis"</note>: As the people of Jerusalem shouted on Palm Sunday when Christ entered the city upon the donkey. **GIVE LILIES WITH FULL HANDS** <note>original: "MANIBVS date lilia plenis"</note>: This is a sentence taken from Virgil, who, deploring the death of Marcellus, encourages such funeral rites to be adorned with lilies and flowers. Wherefore he says in the text: "Give lilies with full hands; I shall scatter purple flowers and heap these gifts, at least, upon the soul of my descendant." <note>original: "Manibus date lilia plenis Purpureos spargam flores animamque nepotis His saltem accumulem donis"</note> And in such a way, in passing, he admonishes us to honor the passion of Christ.

> I saw once, at the beginning of the day,
> the eastern part all rosy,
> and the rest of heaven adorned with a beautiful serenity;
> And the face of the sun rising shaded,
> so that through the tempering of vapors,
> the eye could sustain it for a long time;
> So, within a cloud of flowers
> that rose from angelic hands
> and fell back down, inside and out,
> Upon a white veil, encircled by olive,
> a woman appeared to me under a green mantle,
> dressed in the color of living flame;
> And my spirit, which for so long a
> time had been in her presence,
> was no longer broken, trembling with awe.

<column-break/>

He demonstrates that Beatrice appears in a cloud of flowers in the same way that the sun sometimes appears in the morning, shaded by certain vapors which take away enough of its light that a person can endure looking at it. And the cloud of flowers rose toward heaven from the hands of the angels and fell back down. And Beatrice had a white veil on her head which encircled a garland of olive; and she had a crimson dress beneath and a green mantle on top. He demonstrates that just as it happens that we can see the body of the sun if some thin cloud partially dampens the splendor of its rays, so Dante would not have been able to endure the splendor of Beatrice's face if the flowers raining down around her had not stood in the way in the form of a cloud. This signifies that we could not understand divine and incorporeal things—which theologians treat when discussing God—if they did not make them palpable through some likeness to corporeal things. Beatrice’s head was covered with a white veil and crowned with olive. Some interpret the veil as practice <note>Active life or practical application.</note> and the olive as wisdom, because it is a tree consecrated to Minerva. To me, it seems that Theology should have the white veil for **Faith**—as he has placed it elsewhere in this very work—and the crown of olive denotes **Peace**, according to what all the other poets suggest; because Theology, founded on Faith, gives peace and tranquility to whoever follows it. The green and red clothing represents **Hope** and **Charity**; these three virtues belong solely to Theology, and for this reason, they are called the "theological virtues." **AND MY SPIRIT**: In the *Life of the Poet* <note>Referring to Dante's 'Vita Nuova'.</note> we showed who Beatrice was: the daughter of Folco Portinari. And afterward, in many parts of this poem, it has been manifest that the chaste love he bore for this lady caused him to reduce the history to a poetic fantasy and fiction, and to place her as the representative of the **contemplative life** according to the Christian religion. In this, he was greatly aided by her name <note>The name Beatrice means "bringer of blessings" or "she who makes blessed."</note>.

### PURGATORIO
->m m v<-

...because Beatrice means "full of beatitude." And nothing abounds in beatitude except the knowledge of God and of celestial things.

Without having more knowledge through my eyes,
by a hidden virtue that moved from her,
of ancient love I felt the great power.
As soon as the high virtue struck my sight,
which already had transfixed me
before I was out of my boyhood,
I turned to the left with the respect
with which a child runs to his mother
when he is afraid or when he is distressed,
To say to Virgil: "Less than a drop <note>original: "dragma" — a dram, a very small weight or measurement</note>
of blood is left in me that does not tremble;
I recognize the signs of the ancient flame."
But Virgil had left us bereft
of himself, Virgil, sweetest father,
Virgil, to whom for my salvation I gave myself.

<column-break/>

**WITHOUT THROUGH THE EYES**: The meaning is that although my eyes did not recognize her, nonetheless a hidden virtue moving from her made me feel the great power of the ancient love. He suggests that he had been in love with Beatrice since childhood; and now, it was not because he recognized her face, but through a hidden inspiration proceeding from her that he felt the ancient love again. This denotes that from tender years man begins to love Beatrice—that is, the <term>Supreme Good</term> <note>The ultimate source of happiness, identified with God.</note>—which makes us blessed. But at that time we recognize it with difficulty. Later, sensuality and appetite—which twist us toward the path of pleasures and the goods of fortune—have such power that we follow them as the Supreme Good. And in this way we are disjoined from Beatrice in such a form that our eyes, guided by appetite, no longer recognize her; for not seeing anything but pleasure, they do not believe there is any other good but that. But after we are purged of vices and have come to the state of innocence, <term>prevenient grace</term> <note>In theology, grace that "comes before" human action, pre-disposing the soul toward God.</note> breathes in us, which he calls "hidden virtue"; and this makes us recognize Beatrice, whom we loved from the beginning. And this grace inflames us with her love, she being the Supreme Good.

**SOON**. Suddenly, through this glory, the "high virtue"—that is, the celestial love which already in childhood had transfixed me—struck me at present. And certainly, the love of the true good is innate in men; but false good deceives us. Therefore we are divided from it until reason begins to have more power in us than appetite. I turned to the left toward Virgil just as a little child turns to his mother when he is afraid or when he has some injury. But turning, I perceived that Virgil had already departed from me and had left me and Statius bereft; because the Virgilian number was diminished <note>The company of three (Dante, Virgil, Statius) was reduced to two.</note>. I say "sweetest father," to whom I had given myself for my salvation; and I wanted to say to him, "not a drop of blood remains in me that does not tremble for love," and I know it proceeds from love because "I recognize the signs of the ancient flame." This sentence he took from Virgil, where he said: "I recognize the traces of the ancient flame" <note>original: "Agnosco ueteris uestigia flammae" — Dido’s words from Virgil's Aeneid, Book IV, line 23.</note>. He turned to Virgil, which denotes that, struck by love, he recurred to reason—which is in man to know such love and the cause of it. But Virgil had abandoned him; that is, human reason could not recognize it by itself without divine grace. But Statius remained—that is, the intellect enlightened by Christian theology. Dante recognized her through prevenient grace.

Nor did all that the ancient mother lost <note>A reference to the Garden of Eden lost by Eve.</note>
avail my cheeks, though cleansed with dew,
that weeping they should not turn dark again.
"Dante, though Virgil goes away,
do not weep yet, do not weep yet;
for you must weep by another sword."
Like an admiral who at stern and at bow
comes to see the people who serve
upon the other ships, and encourages them to do well;
Upon the left side of the chariot,
when I turned at the sound of my name,
which of necessity is recorded here,
I saw the lady who first appeared to me,
veiled beneath the angelic celebration,
direct her eyes toward me from across the stream.
All that veil which descended from her...

<column-break/>

**THE LOSS OF VIRGIL** had such power in me that although I was in the paradise of delights—which the **ancient mother** (that is, Eve, the first woman) lost through her disobedience—and although I had my cheeks cleansed of dew <note>In Canto I of Purgatorio, Virgil used the morning dew to wash the stains of Hell from Dante's face.</note>, nonetheless they became dark and mournful and weeping. **DARK** <note>original: "ADRE" — a variant of "atre," meaning black or gloomy.</note>: that is, "atro" in Latin signifies black, and consequently mournful and sad. **DANTE BECAUSE**: Seeing Dante's grief for Virgil's departure, Beatrice turned to him with these words: "Dante, do not weep because Virgil goes away; for you must yet weep by a **greater sword**"—that is, for a greater sorrow, as we shall see a little further below. **LIKE AN ADMIRAL**: An excellent comparison in which he likens **Theology** to the admiral of a fleet. For just as the admiral, without leaving his own ship, but moving now to the stern and now to the bow, comforts those who are on the other ships and ignites them to do well; so...

The commentary explains this transition as the soul moving from the guidance of reason to the influence of divine grace.</summary>

# CANTO XXX

...encircled with the leaves of Minerva <note>The olive branch, sacred to Minerva (Athena), symbol of wisdom and peace.</note> did not allow her to appear clearly. Beatrice, on the left side, was urging Dante to do what you will hear below. Thus, Theology does not leave the chariot—which signifies the body of all Holy Scripture. From the left side—which signifies the Old Testament, where the prohibitive and punitive doctrine of the Church is found—because in the Old Testament, God made manifest and swift vengeance. And here, Beatrice threatens Dante. Therefore, she was not on the right side, which signifies the New Testament, where the Church is exhortative and the promiser of eternal life; for she does not yet promise him anything, but rather reproaches him. And he turns at the sound of his own name to denote that these words were directed against sensuality, which is signified by Dante. And therefore he says that "of necessity" it is recorded here. **I SAW THE LADY.** Turning to the sound of the voice, I saw that the one speaking was the lady who had first appeared to me. **VEILED BENEATH THE angelic feast:** Surrounded by the angels, whom we said above were singing *Blessed is he who comes* <note>original: "Benedictus qui venis"</note>. And she directed her eyes at me from across the stream. **ALTHOUGH THE VEIL:** We have shown above what the veil and the garland signify. But here he adds that he recognized her despite the veil not letting her be seen clearly, to demonstrate that faith does not possess full knowledge <note>original: "scientia" — certain, demonstrated knowledge as opposed to belief</note>.

> Royally, in her gesture still haughty,
> she continued like one who speaks
> and keeps the hottest speech for the end:
> "Look at me well; I am, I am indeed Beatrice!
> How did you deign to approach the mountain?
> Did you not know that here man is happy?"
> My eyes fell down into the clear fountain,
> but seeing myself in it, I withdrew to the grass,
> such great shame weighed upon my brow.
> So does the mother seem stern to the child
> as she appeared to me; for the taste 
> of bitter pity feels sharp.
> She fell silent, and the angels sang
> suddenly: "In you, O Lord, have I hoped" <note>original: "In te domine speravi" — Psalm 31</note>
> but they did not pass beyond "my feet" <note>original: "pedes meos" — they sang only the first eight verses of the Psalm</note>.

<column-break/>

**R**oyally: that is, loftily and imperiously without regard, just as kings are accustomed to do. **IN HER GESTURE:** In her outward appearance. **STILL:** Here he says that although she was about to be appeased, she was "still" haughty—that is, proud. **LIKE ONE Who speaks and keeps the hottest speech for the end:** It is a <term>precept</term> <note>A rule or principle of an art or science.</note> of the art of rhetoric that one who must rebuke and accuse should first demonstrate and prove the error sharply rather than harshly; and then, in the conclusion, with great impetus and gravity of words and sentences, strike like a thunderbolt and bitterly rebuke him. But naturally, anyone who rebukes does the same. **LOOK AT ME WELL:** Words full of asperity and vehement reproach. **I AM, I AM INDEED Beatrice:** As if to say: "That woman whom you began to love and then abandoned." **HOW Did you deign to approach the mountain?** Some want Beatrice to rebuke him with a question, and they interpret it thus: "How did you? That is, how did you judge yourself to be worthy to approach—meaning to come to the mountain?"

As if she were saying: "not being worthy to climb the mountain, upon whose summit is paradise." **DID YOU NOT KNOW** that here man is happy? You should not have been so bold, not deserving to climb to this happiness. But in my judgment, another explanation fits better. For she speaks to Dante as one often speaks who is indignant toward someone who has left them, and for a long time, as if out of pride, does not visit; then, upon returning, we are accustomed to say: "How did you deign to come here?" Meaning: "You seemed so proud to me that I did not believe you would deign to visit any longer." And while we say such words, we use irony—as if saying "you should have deigned to visit us." Therefore: "You who had become so proud, how did you deign to climb the mountain?" As if to say: "I have seen you so puffed up with pride that I did not believe you would deign." **THE MOUNTAIN:** Allegorically, this means contemplation. Up to now, she has rebuked his pride; now she rebukes the folly and the ignorance that for a long time prevented him from realizing that man cannot be happy in any other place. This was the reason he delayed so long in coming. **DID YOU NOT KNOW** that here man is happy? This sentence is not joined to the previous one, because one who speaks haughtily uses broken speech. Therefore, having said with irony "How did you deign to come to the mountain," she then adds with great gravity: "Did you not know that here man is happy?" As if to say: "O fool, why have you delayed so long, since nowhere else but here is man happy?" And if we still want to join one sentence with the other, we would say: "How did you deign to come to the mountain, which for so long you have despised? Did you not know that here man is happy?" As if saying: "Perhaps you want to make me believe that you did not know it; but I know that you did know it. Therefore, this delay of yours has no excuse." But so that we may better understand this entire passage, Beatrice's complaints against Dante are that, having loved her in his first age, he then—in the second age, in which she changed her life and rose from flesh to spirit and was more beautiful—left her for another. This is what Dante feigns. But we understand Beatrice to be Theology, which is of two types: positive and speculative. Positive theology is that which consists in living according to the morality of the active life. Speculation is that which deals with God and separate substances <note>Angels or pure intellects without physical bodies.</note>. He feigns, then, that in his youth he fell in love with Beatrice when she was still in the flesh—that is, he followed the studies of that theology which dealt with moral living. But then, when he began to deal with...
