<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Purgatorio, Canto XXX. The previous page discussed Beatrice's appearance on the chariot and the allegorical significance of her stern demeanor, representing the prohibitive doctrine of the Old Testament. This page transitions into Dante’s internal reaction—his shame, his "thawing" through the angels' compassion, and the beginning of his spiritual renewal.</meta>

# PURGATORIO.

leaving behind speculative matters: **MY EYES** fell: an excellent sign that, having heard the rebuke, one feels shame for the error and lowers the eyes. And lowering his eyes, he saw his image in the fountain, that is, in the stream. This denotes that shame induces you to examine your conscience, and in it, you see yourself as you truly are; whereby your shame increases further. For this reason, you lift your eyes from such a mirror and return them to the grass and the green: that is, to hope. For after the recognition of sin and the shame that comes from it—which causes you to repent—despair must not follow. Rather, we must trust in the infinite mercy of God and take up good hope. **SO THE** mother appears proud to the son: Just as it seemed to the son that when his mother rebukes him, she is proud toward him, so it seemed to me that Beatrice was bitter toward me; yet she was being merciful. **SHE FELL SILENT and the angels sang.** Once we have recognized our error as demonstrated to us by sacred doctrine, the angels sing; that is, holy inspirations invite us to hope. And therefore he imagines that they sing the psalm suited to hope. This is the thirtieth <note>Psalm 31 in modern numbering, but 30 in the Vulgate used by Dante and Landino.</note>: *In you, O Lord, I have hoped, let me never be confounded* <note>original: "In te domine speraui non confundar ineternum"</note>. In this, David, demonstrating the hope he has in God, exhorts every man who repents for a committed fault to do the same. **BUT BEYOND** *My feet* **they did not pass:** They did not pass the verse of this psalm: *Nor have you shut me up in the hands of the enemy; you have set my feet in a spacious place* <note>original: "Nec conclusisti me in manibus meis Stauisti in loco pedes meos"</note>; because the rest of the psalm contains other matter.

---

->Just as the snow among the living beams<-
->along the back of Italy congeals<-
->blown and packed by the Slavic winds<-
->Then, liquefied, it trickles through itself<-
->provided only that the land that loses shadow breathes<-
->just as the candle melts before the fire<-
->So was I without tears and sighs<-
->before the song of those who always sing<-
->following the notes of the eternal gyres<-
->But after I heard in the sweet melodies<-
->their compassion for me more than if they had said<-
->“Lady, why do you so distress him?”<-
->The ice that was tight around my heart<-
->became spirit and water, and with anguish<-
->through mouth and eyes issued from my breast<-

<column-break/>

The meaning is that just as snow, first frozen by northern winds, liquefies by southern winds; and as wax hardened in a candle liquefies by fire; so he, first frozen within by fear, was without tears and sighs before the song of the angels. Afterward, having heard the song which comforted him, the frost liquefied into tears and sighs. **JUST AS** snow among the living beams: "Beams" <note>original: "traui"</note> properly refers to trees that have been cut and prepared; but he uses "beams" to mean trees, and therefore says "living." For trees have a vegetative life through which they nourish themselves on the moisture of the earth, sucking it up with their roots. **ALONG THE** back of Italy: he means the Apennine mountains, which, as we said above, rise through the middle of Italy just as the back and spine extend through the middle of animals. **BY THE** Slavic winds: referring to the northern winds, which he calls "Slavic" because Slavonia <note>The region of the Balkans/Croatia.</note> is to the north of us. **THEN** liquefied: **IT TRICKLES:** It distills. "To trickle" <note>original: "trapelare"</note> is when, from 

---

a thing not well sealed, the liquor within drips out. **PROVIDED THAT** the land that loses shadow: that is, provided that the southern region, in which the sun creates little shadow, **BREATHES:** creates wind. For just as the winds from the north create ice and cold, so those from the south create sweetness and dissolve it. **SO WAS I** without tears and sighs: because fear had chilled me, and the cold had so closed the pores that neither tears could exit, nor sighs. **WHO ALWAYS SING following the notes of the eternal gyres:** Just as a good musician follows the notes written in a book while singing, so the angels, watching the influences and effects that proceed from the perpetual movements of the heavens, sing what they see marked in the fatal order of divine providence—about which we have spoken and shall speak. **BUT AFTER** I heard in the sweet melodies: that is, in the sweet song, which is tempered with various voices. **THEIR** compassion: that is, the compassion they had for me, which I understood more in the singing of that psalm than if they had said to Beatrice, "Why do you distress him so?" And certainly, it is the office of Theology to rebuke sins with acrimony. But the divine intelligences <note>The angels.</note> have compassion for the contrite and humbled heart, which God will not despise. **THE ICE that was tight around my heart:** fear, because being bloodless, it retreats to the heart and induces frost; and dread condenses the cold. Afterward, the power of warmth at the heart thins the frozen thing and liquefies it; whence it distills into tears through the eyes and into sighs through the mouth. And this is what he means by **Spirit and water it became:** that is, it became sighs (which are nothing but wind) and water (that is, tears). In short, he demonstrates that after penance and purgation, remembering how much the sacred scriptures threaten those who, having begun to follow them, leave them—and because of this, having almost fallen into despair—the angels (that is, divine grace) comforted him and led him back to hope.

---

->She, still standing firm upon the right side<-
->of the chariot, addressing the pious substances<-
->then directed her words thus:<-

<column-break/>

**SHE STILL** standing firm: To show that she still persevered in the rebuke. **DIRECTED** her words to the substances: that is, to the angels; **PIOUS** because in their song they had shown compassion.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Purgatorio, Canto XXX. The previous page described Dante’s shame and the angels’ singing of a psalm of hope. Here, Beatrice addresses the angels to explain why she must remain stern toward Dante, transitioning into a discussion of Dante’s natural potential and his subsequent straying from the right path.</meta>

# CANTO XXX.

### .XXX.

You keep watch in the eternal day <note>The "eternal day" refers to the state of the angels and blessed souls who see God directly, where there is no passage of time or ignorance.</note>
so that neither death nor sleep steals from you
a single step the world takes on its paths;
Wherefore my answer is with greater care
directed to him who weeps on the other side,
so that the guilt and the grief may be of one measure. <note>Beatrice explains that her harsh words are for Dante’s benefit, to ensure his repentance matches the scale of his sins.</note>

Not only through the work of the great wheels <note>The "great wheels" are the celestial spheres whose movements were believed to influence human character and earthly events.</note>
which direct every seed to some certain end
according to which stars are its companions,
But through the bounties of divine graces,
which have such high vapors for their rain
that our sights do not even come near them;
This man was such in his *new life* <note>original: "uita noua". This refers both to Dante's youth and his earlier literary work of the same name.</note>
virtually, with every favorable disposition,
that every miraculous proof would have been fulfilled in him.
But the more vigorous and wild
the ground becomes with bad seed and left unplowed,
the more it possesses of good earthly strength.
For some time I sustained him with my countenance;
showing my youthful eyes to him,
I led him with me, turned toward the right path.

<column-break/>

[This section] addresses Dante. And the poet uses a wonderful artifice <note>A term for poetic skill or structural design.</note>. Because the angels had sung that psalm <note>Psalm 31, "In te, Domine, speravi."</note> demonstrating that mercy should be shown toward Dante, it seemed reasonable that Beatrice should respond and assign a reason why she persevered in her severity. This was not to harm him, but to help him by inducing a contrition that would be equal to his sin. On the other hand, it seemed superfluous to explain such reasons to the angels, since they already knew this and all other things. Therefore, the poet chose a middle way to satisfy both: that is, it did not seem as if he wanted to teach the angels, but rather he responded to the psalm they sang, so that Dante would understand what it was necessary for him to do. **YOU WATCH in the eternal day:** This is nothing other than contemplating all things as they are understood in God, as if in a purest mirror and in the clearest light without any obscurity. Because God is the true light that illuminates the whole world, and is light without end; therefore it can truly be called "eternal day." **SO THAT neither night nor sleep steals from you:** because you always contemplate that light in which all things are seen; therefore, neither night (meaning ignorance) nor sleep (meaning sloth or bodily desire) takes away or "steals" any step which the world (meaning time) takes. **THROUGH its ways:** meaning through its extensions and progress. Because in the angels there falls no ignorance or earthly desire as there does in us, burdened by sin and sensuality; but always contemplating God, they see all things in Him. "Age" <note>original: *secolo*</note> among the Latins is most often placed for the space of a hundred years. Whence they spoke of the "secular games" of Apollo because they were celebrated once in a hundred years. But in Holy Scripture, it signifies time; and time is born from the eternity of God, and it is said to go "step by step" because it proceeds from instant to instant. **WHEREFORE My answer is with greater care:** as if she said, "Insofar as you do not need an answer, I have turned my words toward you in respect to the psalm you sang. But I do so so that through my careful answer, [Dante] may understand in what danger he finds himself if he does not understand and learn that the grief and contrition of the sinner must be so great that it equals the fault committed."

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'N' at the start of the following commentary block.</image-desc>

**NOT ONLY through the work:** The poet concedes that although all human souls are by their nature similar and equal, nevertheless the influences of the heavens—which can do much in the bodies with which the souls are joined—can do much in the talents through the instruments they use. But beyond the celestial influences, the grace freely given <note>original: "gratia gratis data"</note> by divine clemency is of great value. He concludes that Dante had favor both from the stars and from divine grace, in such a way that he could have achieved a "miraculous proof" if he had followed the love of Beatrice (meaning the study of sacred letters). But just as bad seed becomes much more malignant in fertile ground than in sterile ground, so vice becomes greater in a sharp mind than in a dull one. **NOT ONLY THROUGH the work of the great wheels:** meaning through the revolutions of the heavens and the planets. The first mobile <note>The *Primum Mobile*, the outermost moving sphere in the Ptolemaic universe.</note> finishes its circuit in twenty-four hours and draws with it all the heavens contained within it. But it would be tedious at present to report on the celestial movements; and in many places of this work, we have, if not clearly demonstrated, at least not entirely obscurely hinted at a good part of them. And it is certainly supreme wisdom observed here, as elsewhere, that the poet allows for celestial influences as far as they do not forbid our redemption and as far as the truth allows. And nevertheless, he does not remove, but rather affirms, the freedom of our will <note>term: "libero arbitrio" - the capacity of humans to make choices regardless of celestial influence.</note> and the help of divine grace. Beatrice concludes that none of these things were lacking in Dante, but his own straying will distracted him for some time from the true way, through which he had proceeded from the beginning until a certain point. **WHICH Direct every seed to some certain end:** those wheels and revolutions make every seed that has generative power come to some effect, which is the end of the thing, **according to which the stars are companions:** meaning according to various conjunctions of various planets; because the conjunction of Mars and Venus produces one effect, and that of Venus and Jupiter another. **BUT THROUGH the bounties of divine graces:** She shows that although the celestial influences can do much, nevertheless the graces...

<summary>Beatrice explains to the angels that her severity toward Dante is a necessary tool for his salvation, intended to make his remorse equal to his sins. The text then discusses how Dante's great natural potential—granted by both the stars and divine grace—made his eventual spiritual wandering even more tragic, comparing his sharp mind to fertile soil that produces worse weeds if neglected.</summary>

--- Page 533 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on Beatrice’s speech in Purgatorio XXX. After establishing that Dante had immense natural potential in his youth ("New Life"), Beatrice now explains how he strayed from the path of virtue following her death, necessitating his journey through the afterlife for his salvation.</meta>

# PURGATORIO.

divine things can, beyond comparison, do much more. THAT SUCH HIGH Vapors have then rain. The author uses an excellent simile <note>A common medieval literary device comparing spiritual truths to natural phenomena.</note>, and the meaning is that just as copious rain descends when cold and humid vapors in the appropriate region are converted into water, so does divine grace rain down abundantly. THAT our sights do not come near them: because human sight and intellect cannot approach the knowledge needed to understand the greatness of divine graces. These things [concern] Dante. IN HIS *New Life* <note>original: "uita noua"</note>: in his first age. Virtually, potentially <note>original: "ideft"</note>; that is, he had a natural disposition and aptitude of such a kind that if he had formed a "right habit"—meaning a virtuous one in the speculative virtues—such a habit would have produced miraculous fruit. BUT SO MUCH MORE: in this simile, he uses the "ground" to represent the aptitude mentioned before, and the "bad seed" for a vicious habit. He says that just as bad seed, if not gathered before it falls to earth, multiplies more in fertile ground than in sterile ground, so the seed of vice multiplies more in a great and sharp intellect than in a lowly, small, or dull one. FOR SOME TIME I sustained [him] with my face: showing him my beautiful face and lovely eyes, which signifies that he, being in love with the "courteous surface" of theology <note>The "surface" refers to the literal or initial attraction to study, before reaching deeper spiritual truths.</note> without yet tasting the "marrow," followed for some time those studies which led him on the right path: that is, toward the virtues.

<column-break/>

> **A**s soon as I was on the threshold
> of my second age and changed my life,
> this man took himself from me and gave himself to others.
> When from flesh to spirit I had ascended,
> and beauty and virtue had increased in me,
> I was to him less dear and less pleasing;
> And he turned his steps along a way not true,
> following false images of good,
> which render no promise whole.
> Nor did it avail me to obtain inspirations,
> with which both in dream and otherwise
> I called him back, so little did he care for it.
> So far he fell that all arguments
> for his salvation were already short,
> except to show him the lost people. <note>The "lost people" refers to the damned souls in Hell.</note>
> For this I visited the gate of the dead,
> and to him who has conducted him up here,
> my prayers were offered with weeping.

<column-break/>

**A**S SOON AS I was on the threshold of my second age. There are two theological ages: the youthful and the mature. We consider these in two ways: according to the "letter" and the "morality," which pertains to the active and civil life <note>The "active life" involves worldly duties and moral actions in society.</note>. This is the "new" or youthful age; and it is said that Beatrice—meaning Theology—is "in the flesh" when we interpret sacred letters literally. Or, truly, we interpret sacred letters allegorically and anagogically <note><term>Anagogical</term>: the highest level of scriptural interpretation, dealing with eternal glory and the soul's journey to God.</note>. This serves the contemplative life, and it is the "second" or mature age of Beatrice, in which she is "without flesh" because she deals with incorporeal and eternal things. That is, she treats of God himself, who is entirely unknown to human sense and comprehensible to the intellect only in the smallest part. Therefore: AS SOON AS I was on the threshold of my second age: we have explained this above. This man took himself from me: because he left the study of theology. AND GAVE HIMSELF TO OTHERS: he followed other studies. WHEN I had ascended to spirit from flesh: I had changed from carnal to spiritual. AND beauty and virtue [increased]: because the allegorical sense is more beautiful and contains more virtue of the intellect within it. And he turned his steps: he turned his affections. ALONG A WAY not true: along the "left-hand" path of vices. FOLLOWING false images of good: he did not follow the virtues of the soul, which are the true good, but sought riches, dignity, high offices, and power. These are called "goods of fortune," and they are not true goods; BUT they appear so because they have an image, albeit a false one, of the true good. They do not render any promise "whole" because they promise true peace of the soul but then do not provide it.

<column-break/>

NOR DID IT AVAIL me to obtain inspirations. An inspiration is a sudden and burning desire for virtue moved by God in the heart of man, which often comes to one who reads sacred scripture. Therefore, the poet feigns that Beatrice often obtained from God the sending of some inspiration to direct him toward the true path. BUT IT DID NOT AVAIL him: that is, it did not help him. NOR DREAM: because such aspirations also appear in dreams and intuitions. SO LITTLE did he care for me: "Non mi cale di te" in the Florentine language <note>The translator notes that Dante is using a local Tuscan idiom.</note> means "I do not care about you." SO FAR he fell: that is, he ruined himself so deeply in vice. THAT ALL arguments: that is, all the efforts and aids that can be made. WERE SHORT: they were not sufficient. EXCEPT showing him the lost people. A man already ensnared and captured by the allurements and false flatteries of bodily pleasures cannot be brought back to true virtue unless we show him how much perdition, how much calamity, how much damage, and how much manifest ruin and eternal death comes to us from vices. This is so that, if he is not moved by reason and the love of celestial good, at least the fear of eternal evil might move him. For this is the difference between the good and the wicked: the good flee evil for the love they bear for virtue, and the wicked flee it for fear of punishment. FOR this I visited the gate of the dead: the soul is called "dead" when it is buried in Hell, because it is eternally deprived of the Highest Good <note>God.</note>, without which, even though the soul is immortal, it cannot be called "alive." And certainly, theology would not treat of vices and the damned if it were not out of respect for the living, who by such examples can be withdrawn from vice. And to him who has conducted him up here: Virgil, about whom it is not necessary to say more, as we have already said so much.

<summary>Beatrice explains to the angels how Dante strayed into vice and worldly pursuits after her death, ignoring spiritual inspirations. She concludes that the only way to save him was to show him the punishments of Hell, leading her to seek Virgil’s help.</summary>
<keywords>Beatrice, Dante, Theology, Second Age, active life, contemplative life, false images of good, Hell, Virgil, divine grace, repentance</keywords>

<meta>This page transitions from Beatrice’s speech to the angels regarding Dante’s failures to her direct confrontation of the Poet. It concludes the commentary on Canto XXX and begins the analysis of Canto XXXI, focusing on the necessity of confession and the metaphor of the sword’s point versus its edge.</meta>

->CANTO<-
->.XXX.<-

God’s high fate would be broken
if Lethe were passed and such food
were tasted without some toll
of repentance that pours forth tears.

<column-break/>

Beatrice concludes that the high order imposed by divine providence would be broken if Dante, having committed such error, passed the river Lethe <note>In Greek mythology and Dante’s Purgatory, Lethe is the river of forgetfulness that washes away the memory of sin.</note> without such repentance as is appropriate for the sin committed. And as far as it pertains to the knowledge of fate, you shall return to the first canticle <note>original: "cantica," referring here to the *Inferno*</note> where these matters are harmonized with the sacred letters. Therefore, the divine order would be broken **IF** such food—which is the tasting of the water of this river that induces oblivion of sin and extinguishes every spark <note>original: "fomite," a technical theological term for the "tinder" or inclination toward sin</note> of it—were tasted without a toll, that is, without payment. This is a metaphor taken from one who takes food at an inn. **OF repentance** that pours forth tears: of such penance and contrition that it causes tears to be shed.

### CANTO XXXI OF THE SECOND CANTICLE OF DANTE

<image-desc>Decorative illuminated initial 'O' depicting a figure or scene within a blue and red frame.</image-desc>

"O you who are on the other side of the sacred river,"
turning the point of her speech toward me,
which even by its edge had seemed sharp to me,
**she began again**, continuing without delay:
"Say, say if this is true; to such an accusation
your confession must be joined."
My power was so confused
that my voice moved and yet was silenced
before it could be released from its organs.
**She waited little**, then said: "What are you thinking?
Answer me, for the sad memories
in you are not yet hindered by the waters."

<column-break/>

This thirty-first canto contains how the poet was asked by Beatrice if her accusation was true. Then follows the poet’s confession with the highest contrition, through which he earned the merit to be able to pass the river and taste of it; and finally, he was led into the presence of Beatrice. **O YOU WHO ARE.** Until this point, Beatrice, speaking of Dante, had directed her words to the angels for the reason already stated. Now, wishing to compel him to confess the things of which she had accused him, she turns her speech to him. **O YOU**, Dante: who are still on the other side of the river; nor do you deserve to cross it if you do not first confess your error and repent of it. **BY THE point:** He who strikes with the point [of a sword] deals a more dangerous wound than he who strikes with the edge. Therefore, the poet, through a certain metaphor, demonstrates that even

---

though the speech Beatrice made about him to the angels stung him greatly, the words she directed specifically at him caused him even greater confusion. **WITHOUT delay:** Without hesitation; because <term>cunctari</term> in the Latin language means to delay or hesitate. He infers that, having finished speaking with the angels, she turned to him without any intermission of time to denote with what speed theological scripture <note>The commentator identifies Beatrice here with Theology or Divine Revelation.</note> desires to make us safe. Until now, she has spoken to the angels.

<summary>Beatrice demands that Dante confesses his sins before crossing the River Lethe, using the metaphor of a sword's point to describe the sharpness of her direct rebuke. The commentary explains the necessity of repentance as a 'toll' for divine forgiveness.</summary>

# PURGATORY

<columns>
...to them: So that they may be witnesses that what she narrates is true. And certainly, although the Sacred Scriptures are founded on faith, they are nevertheless very full of many reasons, various examples, and very weighty authorities—all of which excite and move the sinner. And for this reason, she turns to him and shows him that simple confession and total contrition is the penalty through which guilt can be remitted. Hence she adds: **TO SO GREAT** an accusation, his confession must be joined. **MY POWER WAS** so confused. Such was the shame and contrition for the error committed that he could not speak. For great perturbation of the soul so hinders the tongue and the other members with which we form the voice and words that they cannot perform their office. Therefore, his natural power was so confused and perturbed that the voice could not detach itself from the tongue that forms it **BEFORE** it was released—that is, sent out from its organs, from those members which are instruments to form it. For *organon* in the Greek language <note>original: "organon"</note> means any kind of instrument. **THAT THE** memories in you are not yet harmed by the water. She says this as if to say: "If you do not answer, it is not because you have forgotten your errors, having not yet tasted of the river Lethe." <note>In the Divine Comedy, the river Lethe erases the memory of sin; Beatrice is pointing out that Dante still carries the full, painful weight of his transgressions.</note> **THE SAD** memories: because remembering a committed sin induces sadness and pain in us.

Confusion and fear mixed together
pushed such a "yes" out of my mouth
that to understand it, sight was necessary.
As a crossbow breaks when it shoots,
its cord and the bow being too strained,
and the bolt touches the mark with less force;
So I burst under that heavy burden,
pouring forth tears and sighs,
and my voice faltered in its passage.
Then she said to me: "Within my desires,
which led you to love the good
beyond which there is nothing to aspire to,
What trenches across the path, or what chains
did you find, that you should have
thus stripped yourself of hope?
And what attractions or what advantages
did the faces of others show you,
that you should have paraded before them?"

After the drawing of a bitter sigh,
I hardly had the voice that answered,
for my lips formed it with great effort.
Weeping, I said: "The present things,
with their false pleasure, turned my steps
as soon as your face was hidden from us."
And she: "If you were silent or if you denied
that which you confess, your guilt would not be
less known; by such a Judge it is known.
But when the accusation of sin bursts
from one's own cheek in our court,
the grindstone turns itself against the edge."
<note>This metaphor suggests that while divine justice is sharp like a sword, the act of self-accusation (confession) acts as a grindstone that blunts the blade's edge, tempering justice with mercy.</note>

<column-break/>

**THE** confusion and shame of the error committed, and the fear of punishment, pushed such a "yes" out of my mouth; that is, they forced me to confess. But his power was so weakened that the sound could not be understood. But it was known by looking at my face. **AS A CROSSBOW** As it often happens that by pulling the crossbow too much, the string and the bow break, the bolt <note>original: "ghiera," the iron tip of the bolt</note> comes out with less force, and thus its hit is almost in vain. So the poet burst under such great perturbation of soul. Hence, in the pouring out of tears and sighs, the voice faltered. **THEN SHE TO ME.** Continuing, Beatrice asks Dante: "What trenches were placed across your path, or what chains did you find?" In my desires: that is, while you loved me, which desires led you to love the Highest Good <note>The "Sommo Bene" refers to God, the ultimate object of all righteous desire.</note>. In short: since you were directed toward the Highest Good by loving me, what thing hindered you so that you did not pass forward, and instead had to abandon all hope? **ON THIS SIDE OF WHICH THERE IS NO** [stepping beyond]: to God; and our ultimate end, for the attainment of which we do all other things; and beyond Him there is nothing to which one can aspire, because after Him there is nothing. **AND WHAT attractions.** The meaning is: what induced you to leave me? Tell me if they were obstacles that you found on the path along which I was leading you, or indeed attractions and gains that others—whom you loved, leaving me—showed you "in the face," that is, at first sight, for which you should have paraded before them—that is, proceeded forward and not departed from them. And she wants to conclude that everything else he loved could not have shown him anything truly useful or honorable, but it appeared so to his
* appetite.

**THE** first tercet is easily understood with the expositions made above. **WEEPING** I said the aforementioned things. He responds to Beatrice’s question saying that the reason that led him to love others was that as soon as her face was hidden from him, "present things" <note>Worldly, transitory pleasures.</note> turned him toward them by showing him false pleasures. This is true: for just as we cast into oblivion the Sacred Scriptures and their moral precepts, which direct us toward honor, immediately the appetite turns to worldly things; and intoxicated by the pleasures of those things, it esteems nothing else to be good. **AND SHE: IF YOU WERE SILENT or if you denied.** The author demonstrates in this place that in divine judgment the confession of the sinner is not required so that the judge may be better informed of the truth, for the Judge already knows all.

Having established that he cannot hide his sins from God, she now explains the purpose of her public rebuke: to instill a healthy sense of shame that will fortify him against future temptations. # CANTO XXXI

...because nothing is hidden from him: because whether you deny or stay silent, every thing is known to God. But it is so that the sinner may humble himself and repent for the error. When he does so, it mitigates God's anger: just as the wheel which thins the iron if it turns against the cutting edge, but thickens it if turned the other way. <note>This metaphor suggests that the "grindstone" of divine justice can either sharpen a soul through repentance or blunt it through resistance.</note>

->**for your error, and so that another time,**<-

<column-break/>

**NEVERTHELESS** <note>original: "TVCTAVIA"</note>: sometimes means "always," and sometimes "nonetheless." **SO THAT YOU CARRY SHAME**: so that you may better bear the shame, that is, so you may more willingly be ashamed: and so that another time you may be stronger against the **SIRENS** when you hear them: that is, against worldly pleasures, which are allegorically described as sirens, of which we have written extensively in this same canticle. **PUT DOWN THE SEED OF WEEPING**: put down the tears which weeping produces, just as every herb produces its seed; and he remembered the psalm: *He who sows in tears* <note>original: "Qui seminat in lachrimis" - Psalm 126:5. The full verse implies they shall reap in joy.</note>. **AND YOU SHALL HEAR**: and you will understand how my **BURIED FLESH** should have moved you in the opposite direction: as if she said, "I will show you that my death should not have been a reason for you to follow others. But rather, it should have moved you to the contrary, that is, to follow me." **NEVER DID NATURE OR ART PRESENT**: He assigns the reason, saying there was never any thing produced by nature or art that gave you as much pleasure as my limbs gave you: which after my death are scattered in the earth. But if this pleasure that you took from my limbs failed you—because it was lost to you through my death—no mortal thing should have then drawn you into its desire (that is, to its love). For you should have considered that it would have to fail, being mortal, just as my flesh failed you. You should not, therefore, have esteemed that anything which fails could be your happiness and highest good. 

Because the highest good is that which is eternal and is not found except in God. Therefore, if I in the flesh—that is, if Theology in the active life, <note>Beatrice is often interpreted as an allegory for Divine Theology.</note> which admonishes us concerning the government of the body and for this reason finally fails—could not make you blessed, no other mortal thing will be able to do so. Because in this life, in no way is true happiness found: and if any rest is found here, it is placed in the moral life and according to our religion. Therefore, if in this world true peace is not found even in the virtuous life, much less will it be found in any other kind of life. **YOU SHOULD INDEED, AT THE FIRST ARROW**: *Strale* <note>arrow/bolt</note> means a metal tip or arrow or bolt: and it is derived from this Latin verb *sterno* <note>to prostrate or strike down</note>, because it strikes a man down when it wounds him. But in this place, he uses the rhetorical figure of intellection <note>synecdoche/metonymy</note>, putting the weapon that wounds for the wound itself. And because whoever places hope in something and then loses it is said to have received a blow from fortune whose goods are fallacious. And therefore she says: "O Dante, you should have risen up (that is, to divine and immortal things) at the first arrow: that is, at the first blow that fortune gave you when it took my body; and you should not have placed more hope in mortal things, seeing that they can be lost." 

Regarding this, Cicero said: *Nothing should be called mine or yours which can be taken away, snatched, or lost* <note>original: "Nihil meum neque tuum appellandum est quod auferri quod eripi quod admitti potest"</note>. And Petrarch: *Wretched is he who places [hope] in mortal things.* You should, therefore, have risen up after me, Beatrice (that is, Theology), who was no longer such (that is, I was no longer in the flesh, but was a bodiless spirit). For whoever follows Beatrice already stripped of flesh (that is, follows speculative theology) because he has knowledge of celestial things and of God himself, finds true happiness there. **YOUR WINGS SHOULD NOT HAVE BEEN WEIGHTED DOWNWARD, O YOUNG GIRL**: *Pargoletta* <note>literally "little girl"</note> refers to a girl of small age. Therefore, O Dante, neither a *pargoletta* (that is, a young maiden, meaning another girl) nor any other **VANITY** (that is, any other temporal good) should have weighted your wings downward. Our soul is naturally born to fly to heaven; but when sensuality leads it to worldly pleasures, it remains oppressed by them. **THE YOUNG BIRD WAITS FOR TWO OR THREE**: He stays within the metaphor and shows that the fledgling bird, which still has its down feathers, waits for more blows; but if a net is spread or a bow is drawn against one that is already feathered, it flees immediately and does not wait. And by this, he signifies that Dante deserves compassion if, in his early age—which, not having the use and experience of things, is easily lured by worldly pleasures—he was deceived.

<summary>Beatrice explains that her death should have taught Dante the futility of mortal desires, using the metaphor of a fledgling bird to describe his youthful susceptibility to "vanities." The commentary links these verses to theological concepts of the "Active" versus "Speculative" life and cites Cicero and Petrarch on the transience of earthly possessions.</summary>

# PURGATORIO. CANTO XXXI

**As children, ashamed and silent,**
**stand listening with eyes upon the ground,**
**recognizing themselves and repentant,**
**So I stood; and she said: "Since**
**you are grieving from hearing, lift up your beard,**
**and you shall feel more grief by looking."**
**With less resistance is uprooted**
**the sturdy oak, whether by our north wind**
**or by that from the land of Iarbas,** <note>Iarbas was a legendary king of Numidia (modern-day North Africa); the "wind from his land" refers to the hot south wind or sirocco.</note>
**Than I lifted my chin at her command;**
**and when by "the beard" she asked for my face,**
**I well knew the poison of her point.** <note>By saying "beard" instead of "face," Beatrice mocks Dante, implying he is an old man who should have known better, rather than an innocent youth.</note>

The land of Iarbas: the southern wind which comes from Africa where Iarbas reigned; he was the king of Numidia. **AND WHEN BY THE BEARD SHE ASKED FOR MY FACE:** that is, when she, wanting me to lift my face, said "lift your beard." **I KNEW THE POISON OF HER POINT:** I knew that she was arguing subtly and with hidden but piercing reasons, like a poison that reaches the heart before it is felt. Thus I understood that by saying "lift your beard," she did not only mean "lift your face," but wanted to show that I was no longer a child; and it was no longer time to delay, lest I fall into such habits or vices from which I could not later untangle myself. And here she almost interprets Juvenal where he says: "Some crimes are cut away with the first beard." <note>original: "Quedam cum prima resecentur crimina barba." From Juvenal's Satires, suggesting that youthful errors should end when one reaches manhood.</note>

**AND AS.** that is, as soon as my face was lifted, my eye understood those **FIRST CREATURES** — that is, the angels — **RESTING** or stopping **FROM THEIR APPEARANCE:** that is, from hearing Beatrice further. This was a sign that she was to speak no more. **AND MY EYES:** until now Beatrice has been acting

**And as my face was spread open,**
**those first creatures rested;**
**from their appearance, my eye understood.**
**And my eyes, still a little unsure,**
**saw Beatrice turned toward the beast,** <note>The "beast" is the Gryphon, representing Christ.</note>
**which is only one person in two natures.**
**Under her veil and beyond the river,**
**she seemed to surpass her former self in beauty,**
**more than she surpassed all others when she was here.**
**The nettle of repentance stung me there,**
**so that of all other things, those which most**
**turned me to their love, now became most my enemy.**
**Such recognition bit my heart**
**that I fell overcome; and what I then became,**
**she knows who provided the cause.**

<column-break/>

Thus I remained mute and confused and with eyes cast down due to Beatrice's rebuke; like children listening to their error, recognizing it, and repenting of it. **AND SHE SAID, SINCE BY HEARING YOU ARE SORROWFUL:** because the more grief and contrition one takes from sin, the sooner pardon follows. Therefore, Beatrice wanted Dante, having heard her, to now look at her; for if hearing gave him pain, seeing her should give him greater pain. For the sense of sight has more power to move us than that of hearing. And allegorically, it shows that more grief is felt when we consider the beauty of that which we have abandoned than from hearing its rebukes. **OUR WIND:** the northern wind, because we are further north than any other part. **FROM THE**

as the rebuker of Dante's error, and now she appears as the object of contemplation. **STILL A LITTLE UNSURE** because I was still ashamed and afraid. **SAW BEATRICE.** This signifies that, now purged of vices, I began to be able to see Beatrice not in the flesh but in the spirit — that is, I began to be able to contemplate. **TURNED TOWARD THE BEAST:** this is said to denote that her contemplation of God and heavenly things was not like that of the pagan philosophers, but was according to our religion which is founded in Christ. And therefore he says that Beatrice was turned toward the **GRYPHON**; the allegory of which we set forth above, showing him to be Christ. And so he says such a beast is **ONE PERSON IN TWO NATURES**: because it represents Christ who is one of the three Persons and is in two natures, because in Him divinity was joined with humanity. **UNDER HER VEIL AND BEYOND THE RIVER.** We have already spoken of the veil; but she was beyond the river because she always stays in the place of innocence, which is across the river that extinguishes every carnal desire and forgets evil. **SHE SEEMED TO SURPASS.** The meaning is that Beatrice in that second state — which he calls "former" — surpassed herself in beauty more than she had surpassed all other women when she was in her first life on earth. And the text is ordered: it seemed to me that the "former" Beatrice (at present, meaning in her eternal state) surpassed herself (meaning when she was in her first life) more than she seemed to surpass others when she was alive. **THE NETTLE OF REPENTANCE STUNG ME THERE:** when the nettle stings, it excites a great itch, which is nothing other than a supreme desire to scratch. Therefore, in this place, he takes the nettle to mean a supreme desire. **THE NETTLE:** the highest will. **TO REPENT:** for having left Beatrice and followed others. **STUNG ME:** incited me. **THERE:** where I saw her beauties. **THAT WHICH:** that is, whichever of all the other things most turned me before to its love (to loving it), now became most my enemy (it became most hated by me). And certainly, although it profits a man much to be rebuked for his vices, and to be shown the ugliness of them and how fleeting and earthly goods are, and although all these things can draw us back from the path of vice and set us on the path...

straight. Nevertheless, seeing the beauties of Beatrice and considering how they surpass every other thing makes us repent exceedingly for our errors and hold them in the highest hatred. And therefore he shows that such recognition bit his heart—that is, the recognition of your errors and the vanity and fallacy of worldly goods—and the excellence and ineffable beauty of **CELESTIAL THINGS** caused me to fall defeated. Dante, who represents sensuality, fell defeated because he submits to reason. **AND WHAT I THEN BECAME AND HOW I WAS**, I cannot express to you. But she who gave me the cause for it knows. When a man arrives at the point of entering into the virtues of a soul already purified, he becomes like many others whom the sacred letters do not describe.

**A**fter the great perturbation in which every animal and vital virtue was drawn back to the heart—the blood and spirits following it—they returned from the heart to the external limbs. **THE LADY WHOM I HAD FOUND ALONE**: Mathelda, of whom we spoke above. **HOLD ME**: cling to me, so that while I carry you, you do not fall. **DRAWN ME INTO THE RIVER**: It is necessary that Mathelda—that is, the <term>active life</term> <note>Mathelda symbolizes the "active life" of the soul, which prepares a person for contemplation through good works and moral discipline.</note> illuminated by the moral virtues—pulls us into the river Lethe, which in its nature washes us from every sin, so that no vestige of an old stain remains, and we forget it entirely. And then, thus purified, she presents us to Beatrice, who is now out of the flesh and remains a pure spirit—that is, to <term>contemplative theology</term> <note>Beatrice symbolizes divine wisdom or theology, which can only be approached after the soul is cleansed.</note> wherein our highest good consists, and which would not accept us unless we were washed and cleansed.

And we demonstrated at the beginning of the first canticle, according to both the Christians and the Platonists, that although physics—in which we chiefly understand theology—makes us blessed, nonetheless we must begin from morality. For if we are not purged, we cannot, being filthy, aspire to this. **UP TO THE THROAT**: And pulling me thus submerged and dipped up to the throat, she went straight over the water without sinking. This is because the purgatorial virtues always go straight and never sink into Lethe, for they have no need to forget evil, as they never knew it. **LIKE A SHUTTLE**: This is that instrument which, thrown through the warp, places the weft; it is so light that it runs over the threads, neither breaking nor entangling them. Thus she went over the water without breaking it or dipping into it. **TO THE BLESSED SHORE** of the river, which is the side where the blessed are. **PURGE ME**: They sing this verse in the Church when they sprinkle consecrated water, which has the power to drive away impure spirits. And because the river Lethe induces the forgetting of sins and drives them away, he has the angels sing it. **THE BEAUTIFUL LADY**: Mathelda, who had first pulled him through the water up to his throat, now embraced his head and dipped him entirely so that it was necessary to swallow the water. It was necessary that, having to forget, the part of the body where memory is located <note>In medieval physiology, memory was believed to be located in the back of the brain.</note> should be submerged.

**T**HEN: From that river. **SHE TOOK ME OUT BATHED**: Made innocent by Mathelda—that is, by priestly doctrine and authority—having forgotten every fuel for vice. **THE FOUR** beautiful moral virtues of which we spoke above. **AND EACH ONE COVERED ME WITH HER ARM**: That is, with her power and her help. For the arm of Justice defends against injustice; Prudence against folly; Fortitude against fear; and Temperance against lust. **WE ARE HERE**: That is, in this world where men are still in the flesh. **NYMPHS**: Meaning helpers to men, because the paradise of delights is on earth. **AND IN HEAVEN**: Where man cannot err. **WE ARE STARS**: As if to say, as an ornament. Some say the poet wants to show by this that the virtues are here in "act" and there in "habit." For the nymphs, who are wandering, easily denote the act; and the stars, because...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto XXXI of Purgatorio. In the previous section, the four cardinal virtues (represented as nymphs) led Dante to Beatrice, who stands by the Gryphon. This page transitions from the four virtues to the three theological virtues (Faith, Hope, and Charity) and focuses on Dante’s intense gaze upon Beatrice’s eyes, where the mystery of Christ—the Gryphon—is reflected.</meta>

## IX PURGATORIO.

A thousand desires hotter than flame
pressed my eyes to those shining eyes
that remained fixed upon the gryphon.
Just as the sun in a mirror, no differently,
the double beast radiated within them,
now with one, now with another aspect. <note>original: "reggimenti"; refers to the different modes or behaviors through which the gryphon's nature is revealed.</note>
Think, reader, if I wondered,
when I saw the thing itself remain still,
and yet it transformed in its image. <note>original: "idol"; from the Greek "eidolon," meaning image or representation.</note>

While my soul, full of wonder and joy,
tasted of that food
which, while satiating, creates a thirst for itself,
Showing themselves to be of a higher tribe, <note>original: "tribo"; referring to the three theological virtues being superior to the four cardinal virtues.</note>
the other three appeared before us,
dancing to their angelic rhythm.
"Turn, Beatrice, turn your holy eyes,"
was their song, "to your faithful one,
who has moved so many steps to see you!
By grace, do us the grace to unveil
your mouth to him, so that he may discern
the second beauty that you hide." <note>The "second beauty" is Beatrice’s smile, while the first beauty was found in her eyes.</note>

<column-break/>

**they are firm** they demonstrate their disposition. **BEATRICE DESCENDED** to the world: Beatrice descended to the world when the studies of theology began through divine inspiration. **AS HER handmaids**, that is, as her ministers: because no one can be a true theologian—that is, live according to the precepts of theology—without these virtues. And they were **first** because the virtues, though not perfect, appeared in men before they had the knowledge of theology. **WE WILL LEAD** you: because as I said, the moral virtues, by purging us, make us fit to rise to the contemplative life. But since we are the other three women who are on the right side of the chariot, they **sharpen** your eyes to be able to see her profound light. And certainly, if we take the three to be the theological virtues, there is no doubt that they refine the mind to contemplate divine things. For God willingly opens His secrets to those who have sincere faith, firm hope, and burning charity. And if we take them as the intellectual virtues, it is similarly well known that such knowledge is acquired through intelligence, science, and wisdom. **THEY WILL LEAD me to the breast** of the gryphon, that is, to Christian theology where Beatrice was standing. We, because we do not look upon this doctrine, could not arrive at the gryphon: that is, at the knowledge of the mysteries of Christ. **SEE THAT you do not spare your sight**: that is, use all your visual power to admire Beatrice. It is as if they say: we have conducted you into her presence, but it is not in our power to make you truly see her. But you, with the help of the three, will gaze upon the **emeralds**, that is, her eyes shining like emeralds, from which eyes Love once drew his weapons—that is, shot his arrows—against you.

**A thousand desires.** As if to say infinite desires and cravings, more burning than fire. **PRESSED MY eyes.** They fixed my eyes upon the eyes of Beatrice, which remained steady upon the gryphon. And he says this because she is reflected in theology, which always regards the Word of God made man. **AS THE sun in a mirror.** Just as it happens that the sun’s ray strikes a mirror and is reflected elsewhere, so the image of the **double beast**—that is, the gryphon—strikes the eyes of Beatrice and is reflected in me. And he says this so that whoever reads Christian theology may recognize Christ within it. And the text continues: **The double beast**, that is, the gryphon, which is part bird (signifying divinity) and part lion (which signifies the humanity in Christ). <note>original: "leone che significa la diuinita in christo"; the commentator likely meant "humanity," as the eagle/bird typically represents divinity and the lion represents humanity in Christology.</note> **RADIATED WITHIN ME**, that is, it shone and showed its image **INSIDE the eyes** of Beatrice, just as the sun radiates in a mirror. But although Beatrice's eyes continually represented the image of the gryphon to me, nonetheless they represented it now with one, and now with another argument, representation, and figure. For Sacred Scripture figures God sometimes as a man, sometimes a lamb, and sometimes a lion. **WHEN I saw the thing** stay quiet in itself: I wondered at the thing—that is, the gryphon—remaining quiet within itself, because it did not change in its substance; but it changed in its "idol," that is, in its image. For as we have said, the sacred letters always present Christ as one and the same thing, but change Him into various figures. **Idol** in Greek signifies "figure" or "image." Hence we speak of "adoring idols," those who adore statues, of which the Psalmist sings: "They have eyes and will not see." <note>original Latin: "Oculos habent et non uidebunt"; from Psalm 115:5.</note>

While my soul joyfully tasted of such **food** which satiates, but in satiating increases the desire for itself: the other three virtues, which are theological, came forward dancing. **MY SOUL** full of wonder at the greatness and beauty of the things, **AND JOYFUL**: to show that such wonder gave him neither suspicion nor fear, but supreme joy. And certainly, the knowledge of divine things is the only thing that makes us wonder, because every other thing is "vanity of vanities." <note>original Latin: "uanitas uanitatum"; from Ecclesiastes 1:2.</note> And it makes us joyful because in that consists the supreme good. **Of that food which, WHILE SATIATING**, while it satiates, **THE SOUL ITSELF THIRSTS**, it increases the thirst—the desire—**FOR IT**, the said food. In short, he writes that his soul tasted a food which truly—

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Purgatorio, Canto XXXI. It explores the transition from the four cardinal virtues to the three theological virtues (Faith, Hope, and Charity) and the profound intellectual pleasure Dante experiences as Beatrice finally unveils her "second beauty"—her smile—which represents the deeper spiritual truths of theology.</meta>

->### CANTO XXXI.<-

...it weary him: But although it was a labor, the desire to taste did not lessen, but rather increased. From this we should understand that there are two types of **pleasure** <term>voluptà: derived from the Latin "voluptas," meaning pleasure or delight</term>. One is that which our senses take from corporeal and carnal things, and this is called **imperfect pleasure**, because it always brings with it satiety and regret, and in a short time becomes offensive. This is what **Juvenal** meant when he said: <note>original Latin: "Facere non possis quinque diebus continuis: quia talis quoque tedia uite." Translation: "You could not do this for five continuous days; for such is the weariness of life."</note> The other is that which our intellect takes from incorporeal and celestial things, and this is called **perfect pleasure**, because it never brings boredom or regret afterward. Thus the poet rightly says of this that it "wearies," because we remain content in it; and yet we always desire it, and it never becomes tedious. **THE OTHER THREE** stood so fiercely in front: These are **Faith, Hope, and Charity**, or we might say **Intelligence, Science, and Wisdom**, of which we spoke above. **SHOWING** themselves to be of a more noble **tribe**: Of a more excellent lineage. **NEGLECTED** in their ways and gestures. **TRIBE**: that is, of a more noble family, because the moral virtues are of a mortal lineage, being in the **active life**, while these are of an immortal lineage, being in the **speculative life**. **DANCING** to their **angelic rhythm** <term>garibo: an archaic word for grace, manner, or rhythmic movement</term>: that is, to their divine movement. "Garibo" comes from *garbo*, and *garbo* signifies mode and form. And their song was this: **"Obediently turn, turn your holy eyes to your faithful Dante,"** who has moved so many steps for you. For step by step, he first descended into Hell, considering every kind of vice, and afterward he ascended through Purgatory, purging himself of them **BY** **prevenient grace** <note>Prevenient grace is a theological concept referring to divine grace that precedes human decision or action.</note>. **DO FOR HIM** **illuminating, cooperating, and consuming grace** <note>These represent the stages of spiritual enlightenment: the grace that reveals truth, the grace that works with the human will, and the grace that perfects the soul.</note>: **THAT** it may **unveil**, that it may discover **YOUR MOUTH**: your literal and moral meaning. **UNTIL** he **discerns**: that is, knows the **SECOND BEAUTY**: The spiritual intellect, **WHICH** **you hide** **under** the literal and moral sense. For beneath the **veil of faith**, where the moral sense is located, the **allegorical** and **anagogical** <term>anagogical: the highest level of scriptural interpretation, dealing with the soul's journey toward eternal glory</term> intellect is hidden.

**O splendor of living eternal light,**
**who has grown so pale under the shade**
**of Parnassus, or drunk at its cistern,**
**that they would not seem to have a clouded mind,**
**attempting to render you as you appeared**
**there where the heaven harmonizing overshadows you,**
**when in the open air you revealed yourself?**

<column-break/>

**O SPLENDOR of living eternal light.** We must understand that after the words of the angels—that is, after the graces entered the soul already purified—Beatrice lifted the veil and showed the splendors of the divine eternal light. For with the graces mentioned above, a person in that state can know the secrets of **theology** and the divine light, which the human tongue cannot express. And so, with wonder, he said: **O SPLENDORS**; and this diction "O" is a sign of one marveling. And he adds that no one—neither by growing pale under the laurels of **Parnassus** <note>A mountain in Greece sacred to the Muses; Dante uses it to represent the highest achievement in secular poetry.</note>, nor by drinking from the fountain of the Muses—was ever so inspired by divine fury that they could express what the light of Beatrice was like when she was uncovered. **WHO** **became pale**: because those who give themselves much to poetic study grow pale. Thus **Juvenal** says: <note>original Latin: "Fuit utile multis pallere et uinum toto nescire decembri." Translation: "It was useful to many to grow pale and to know no wine for the whole of December."</note> **IN ITS** **Cistern**: that is, in the fountain of Parnassus. **THAT WOULD NOT** **seem to have a clouded mind**: that would not seem an unlearned and insufficient poet. For one who has a mind occupied and clouded by other things cannot be a good poet, as Juvenal clearly demonstrates. **ATTEMPTING TO** **render you**: that is, attempting to express in verse you, such and so bright as you appeared there where the **heaven overshadows you**: that is, where you remained uncovered, having no other covering than the sky. And thus he demonstrates that no poet could describe the beauties of theology; here he imitates **Plato**, who expressed the same sentiment by showing that the place where God is was never seen by man, nor described by any poet.

<summary>This page explains the transition from moral virtues to theological ones, interpreting Beatrice's "second beauty" (her smile) as the deep spiritual meaning of Theology that surpasses human language and poetic skill. The commentator draws on Juvenal and Plato to emphasize that divine truth is an intellectual pleasure far superior to any earthly delight.</summary>

### CANTO XXXII OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE

So fixed and attentive were my eyes
To satisfy their ten-year thirst <note>The "ten-year thirst" refers to the decade between Beatrice's death in 1290 and Dante's vision in 1300, symbolizing a period where he felt separated from divine wisdom.</note>
That my other senses were all extinguished;
And they had walls on this side and that,
Indifferent to all else; thus did the holy smile
Draw them to itself with the ancient net;
When by force my face was turned
Toward my left by those goddesses,
For I heard from them a "Too fixedly!"

And the condition that exists in the sight
Of eyes just struck by the sun,
Left me for a while without my vision;
But after my sight restored itself to the "little"—
I say "little" in respect to the "much"
Sensibility from which I was forced away—
I saw the glorious army had moved
Upon its right flank and was returning,
Turning with the sun and the seven flames.
As a troop turns under their shields to save themselves,
And wheels around with the banner
Before the whole line can shift its ground,
That militia of the celestial kingdom
Which preceded us, all passed by
Before the chariot's pole had turned.
Then the ladies returned to the wheels.

<column-break/>

This joins the thirty-second chapter to the preceding one; because having shown at the end of that the splendor of Beatrice's face already uncovered, he continues by adding how great was his attention in looking at her until he was admonished by the virtues. This chapter contains the movement of the Gryphon <note>A mythical creature with the body of a lion and the head and wings of an eagle, representing Christ’s dual nature as both human and divine.</note> to the Tree of Knowledge: and it represents the whole early Church: and it sets out how the Gryphon led back the chariot with all those who followed it, and how the plant turned green again with leaves, and how he, falling asleep, had a vision: and having awakened, he asks Matelda about Beatrice: and she points her out to him: and from there he is...

...attentive to see the things that will come. TO SATISFY THE LONGING: <gloss>to remove the craving, that is, the desire</gloss>. Longing is a great desire for something. Hence, to long for is to desire supremely. TEN-YEAR thirst: a desire lasting ten years. He means to imply that after he had knowledge of the literal and moral sense of the sacred letters, after which he abandoned such studies until he returned to have the allegorical and spiritual understanding, ten years passed in between. And therefore he feigns that he was ten years without Beatrice. THAT the other senses were extinguished: I was so attentive to see her that my other senses were extinguished and lulled to sleep. This signifies that he was so given to these studies that his mind was turned to nothing else; and it naturally happens, as this same poet showed above, that when we are completely turned toward one thing, all the other powers of the soul except the one we are exercising cease to function. AND they had walls on this side and that: his eyes, straight and fixed on Beatrice, had a WALL <gloss>that is, a wall and obstacle</gloss> on this side, meaning from the right and the left side. And thus he demonstrates his constancy and perseverance in contemplation was such that neither prosperity (signified by the right hand) nor adversity (signified by the left) could remove him; because on the right he placed Temperance, and on the left, Fortitude. INDIFFERENT: <gloss>not to care</gloss>. This is a Tuscan verb and is only used impersonally, as in "I do not care about you." THUS did the holy smile: he assigns the reason and says the eyes cared for nothing else. THUS, that is, in such a manner, they were fixed on Beatrice. WITH THE ancient net: with the ancient love, which catches the mind just as a net catches birds. When by force my face was twisted away by those goddesses <gloss>that is, by the four cardinal virtues, who are described as goddesses in this classical-style commentary</gloss> toward my left; and they twisted it with words I saw them say, which were "a too-fixed looking at yours." He turned toward the left where the moral virtues were. These goddesses made him turn his eyes from Beatrice to another part because he was looking too fixedly; because the moral virtues—and especially Temperance, advised by Prudence—show us that we must do everything with manner and measure. Hence the proverb of the learned: "Nothing in excess" <note>original Latin: "Ne quid nimis"</note>. And **Juvenal** said: "The wise man imposes a limit even on honorable things" <note>original Latin: "Imponitque modum sapiens et rebus honestis"</note>.

It shows that the procession seen first by him coming from the East toward the West would then, after he was turned toward his left, turn back upon its right arm toward the East. But first he narrates that when he turned his eyes from Beatrice, he remained blinded like one who has looked at the sun: and he describes the condition that the sight has in eyes just struck by the sun. This induces a glare: it made me be for a while without sight. And in passing, he shows how the physical eye is not capable of the sun's light: just as our intellect is not capable of Theology. BUT AFTER the sight restored itself to the "little": his face—that is, Dante's sight—was blinded by the excessive splendor of Beatrice. But after he turned back to the sun and the candlesticks, although that was great splendor, nonetheless in comparison to that of Beatrice, it was small. And then his face was reformed, that is, it returned to its proper form with the little sensory splendor <gloss>the splendor of the candlesticks</gloss>. I SAY LITTLE in respect to the much sensory [splendor]. As if he were to say, it explains...

It also details the symbolic movement of the Gryphon and the celestial procession as they turn back toward the East and the Tree of Knowledge.</summary>

### CANTO XXXII

The Gryphon moved the blessed chariot
In such a way that not a single feather shook.
<br/>
having departed from the wood of obedience. This signifies the transgression of the commandment of our first fathers. Now he brings him back to demonstrate the coming of Christ, who through his obedience—for he was obedient unto death, even death on a cross <note>original Latin: "Nam fuit obediens usque ad mortem mortem autem crucis"</note>—led us back to obedience and reconciled us with God. He made human nature turn from the west, which signifies perdition, to the east, which signifies salvation. By the right side, he shows the way of virtue: WITH THE SUN: that is, with divine help. WITH THE seven flames: i.e., the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit with which anyone who follows evangelical virtue is directed. AS if under shields: because all those we mentioned above were walking in front of the chariot, it was necessary that when the troop turned back, they should wheel around and re-enter in front of the chariot. This demonstrates that they acted skillfully, observing the order just as a troop does when it wishes to turn while fighting, and in turning, shields itself from the enemy's blows. Thus, they all passed in front before the chariot turned its first wood, that is, the pole. Then the ladies returned to the wheels: the three on the right and the four on the left, because without the governance of these virtues, the chariot—i.e., the Church of Christ—would go poorly toward obedience. THE GRYPHON moved the blessed chariot: we are informed that although he moved it, he did not shake any of his feathers or his wings; this denotes that the holy justice and mercy of our highest and most supreme God are invariable.

> The beautiful lady who drew me to the crossing
> and Statius and I were following the wheel
> that made its orbit with a smaller arc.
> So walking through the high, empty forest—
> the fault of her who believed the serpent—
> an angelic note tempered our steps.
> Perhaps in three flights an arrow, once released,
> would have covered as much space as we had
> moved when Beatrice descended.
> I heard "Adam" murmured by everyone;
> then they circled a plant stripped
> of leaves and other foliage on every branch.
> Its crown, which spreads out so much wider
> the higher it goes, would be marveled at for its height
> even by the Indians in their own forests.

the one who believed the serpent: the fault of Eve. PERHAPS in three flights: perhaps as far as an arrow travels in three flights—that is, in three stretches. He says "flights" because of the speed of the arrow and also because it has feathers. RELEASED: as if let go from the string which acts as its brake; the meaning is that they had already traveled three arrow-shots when Beatrice descended. He uses "three flights" because this number, as the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the ancient Greek philosopher Pythagoras, who believed numbers were the essence of all things; three was considered the first "perfect" number representing beginning, middle, and end.</note> demonstrate, is perfect. And Christian doctrine demonstrates the excellence of the Trinity in one God. ADAM: they lamented the disobedience of Adam, through which the human generation was deprived of such a pleasant and joyful place. A plant: this is the tree of knowledge. It also stands for obedience; by not observing it, Adam contracted original sin, which took this paradise from us. ITS CROWN Which Spreads out so much: This demonstrates that the shape of this tree was such that the higher the branches were, the more they spread out. This is the opposite of other trees. Besides this, the tree was extremely tall: he notes that even if it had been in the forests of India where trees are tallest, its height would be a marvelous thing. It is reasonable that the tree of science <note>In this context, "science" refers to "scientia" or organized knowledge/wisdom.</note> should be very tall, because it proceeds step by step until the cognition of God. And the higher it rises, the more its branches spread and dilate: because the more we understand, the more remains for us to see. This same tree also figures as holy obedience, which is founded in humility; it rises toward God and extends through infinite virtues.

> Blessed are you, Gryphon, who does not tear
> with your beak from this wood sweet to the taste,
> since the belly is ill-twisted thereafter.

the splendor of the candelabra and the sun was very great.
But in comparison to the splendor of the eyes of

sweet to sensuality but not to reason. Similar to that of Petrarch: *and greedy for such things as are sweet to the taste but harmful to health* <note>original: "et di tal choſe ingordo chal guſto e dolce alla ſalute e rea"</note>, and reason assigns this. AFTERWARDS from there, i.e., from this tree. THE BELLY twists toward evil: and does not direct itself toward good. THUS around it all the others sang as much as is <unclear>proper</unclear>. But the Gryphon: YES, that is, understand it thus: by not tasting of this wood, THE SEED of every just person IS PRESERVED. The obedience from which every virtue that makes a man just is born, as if from an excellent seed, is preserved. AND TURNING to the pole that he had pulled: the meaning is that he tied the pole of the chariot—which had been made from the wood of this tree—to the tree itself. He feigns that the pole was made of the wood of obedience, because obedience is what guides and conducts the Church, and it is joined with obedience. Therefore, the Gryphon pulled the pole to the foot of the widowed branch: a branch deprived of leaves, and widowed because it was abandoned by the first man who was disobedient to God.

As our plants, when the great light
falls down mixed with that
which radiates behind the celestial fish,
become turgid, and then each is renewed
with its own color, before the sun
joins his coursers under another star;
less than roses and more than violets,
opening its color, the plant was renewed,
which before had its branches so desolate.
I did not understand it, and here one does not sing
the hymn that those people then sang,
nor did I endure the melody in its entirety.

<column-break/>

Which is to say, as happens when the sun has entered into Aries—in which springtime begins—the trees that had been stripped of leaves in the winter begin to swell their buds and then put forth new flowers; so the tree turned green and blossomed again after the chariot was tied to it. And the color of the flowers was less bright than that of roses and more than that of violets. Therefore, it was blood-red: and by this, he denotes the Passion of Christ, because his blood restored the human race to its ancient obedience. WHEN it falls: when it is shed from heaven to earth. THE great light: that is, the sun. MIXED WITH that which radiates behind the celestial fish <note>original: "la celeſte laſca"</note>: mixed with the light of the stars of Aries, which rises in our hemisphere after Pisces, which he calls the "roach" <note>A "lasca" is a freshwater fish; here Dante uses it to refer to the constellation Pisces</note>, putting the species for the genus. And in this way, he describes the spring, which begins at the entry of the sun into the first degree of Aries. TURGID: swollen and enlarged. Because at that time every tree begins to swell its buds, which we call <term>brochire</term> <note>an archaic Tuscan term for budding or sprouting</note>. BEFORE THE sun joins his coursers—which we showed to be four—UNDER another star: under another sign of the zodiac. I DID NOT understand it: I did not understand the hymn which those people sang who were around the chariot, who signify the ancient fathers, both of the Old Testament and of the primitive Church. And here in this world and in this age, it is not sung. NOR DID I ENDURE THE MELODY IN ITS ENTIRETY: that is, I did not sustain the whole song without falling asleep.

If I could portray how the pitiless
eyes fell asleep, hearing of Syrinx—
the eyes whose constant watching cost so dear—
as a painter who paints from a model,
I would design how I fell asleep;
but let him be who can well feign slumber.
Therefore I pass over it, and when I awoke,
I say that a splendor tore the veil
of my sleep, and a call: "Rise, what are you doing?"
As, to see the blossoms of the apple tree
which make the angels greedy for its fruit
and which makes perpetual marriage in heaven,
Peter and John and James, being led
and overcome, returned at the word
by which greater sleeps are broken,
and saw their school diminished
both of Moses and Elias,
and their Master's raiment changed;
so I returned, and saw that pious woman...

<column-break/>

The poet narrates that he cannot in any way describe the sweetness of the song that caused his sleep—that is, which induced sleep and made him slumber. But if he could express how the eyes of Argus fell asleep at the song of Mercury, he would do as the painter who, not knowing how to paint from his own imagination, paints things already painted by another painter; as if to say, I would say I had been put to sleep by the song of such a hymn as Argus was by the sound of Mercury's pipe. You have already heard this fable above. HOW they slumbered: they fell asleep. THE EYES of Argus, PITILESS: cruel in watching too closely. HEARING of Syrinx: while he heard Mercury singing of the nymph Syrinx. She was loved by Pan, the god of shepherds, and she fled from him; he followed her until they reached the river Ladon. Not being able to cross it, the nymph asked for help from the gods to escape from Pan's hands. The gods, moved to pity, transformed her into marsh reeds. And Pan, not being able to have her otherwise, formed the pipe from those reeds, which he called "Syrinx" from the name of the beloved nymph; although this word in Greek...
