<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Purgatorio, Canto XXXII. Having witnessed the Gryphon (representing Christ) tether the chariot (the Church) to the Tree of Knowledge, the poet falls into a deep sleep and now describes his awakening and the scene left behind.</meta>

-># PURGATORIO CANTO XXXII<-

standing over me, she who was the 
guide of my steps along the river before. <note>Matilda, who led Dante through the Earthly Paradise.</note>

And all in doubt I said: "Where is Beatrice?"
And she: "See her sitting under the new 
foliage, upon its root.
See the company that surrounds her;
the others, following the Gryphon, go up
with a sweeter and more profound song."
And if her speech was more diffuse,
I know not, for already she was in my eyes,
she who had closed me off from understanding anything else.

Sitting alone upon the true earth,
like a guard left there for the chariot
which I saw the biform beast <note>The Gryphon, half-eagle and half-lion.</note> tie.
In a circle, the seven nymphs made a cloister
for her with those lights in their hands
that are safe from the North and South winds. <note>The seven virtues holding the candles of the Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are never extinguished by worldly winds.</note>

<column-break/>

I pass over it: because I cannot express it. AND When I woke up: so that you may understand what it was.
**Shaken**: it shows that a very great splendor came and the voice of Matilda calling him, saying:
*Rise* <note>original: "SURGE"</note>, that is, "get up," I woke him. And certainly, a great light can often wake one who sleeps because it penetrates the eyes which, in sleep, desire darkness. But light awakens more; by **splendor** he means the knowledge which we acquire by ourselves; by **voice** is meant the precepts of others. **AS TO see the blossoms of the apple tree**: It shows that he became such when he woke as Peter, John, and James became, the apostles of Christ, after the Transfiguration of the Savior on Mount Tabor: About which Mark the Evangelist writes in the ninth chapter thus: *Jesus took Peter, James, and John and led them up a high mountain, and he was transfigured in their sight. And he shone like the sun. And there appeared Moses and Elijah. And Peter said: "It is good to be here; let us make three tabernacles, one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah." And they were defended from the sun by a white cloud, and behold a voice from heaven saying: "This is my beloved son in whom I am well pleased."* Then the disciples fell, and Christ called them; and looking at him, they saw him alone. And the text is ordered thus: I, Dante, became such—that is, I woke up in such a way as they returned after the Transfiguration: Peter, James, and John led by Christ to see the **BLOSSOMS of the apple tree**. That is, the apple tree, which is Christ, makes the angels greedy for his fruit and makes perpetual weddings in heaven. And note that he calls the Transfiguration of Christ "blossoms" and calls him the "apple tree," because such a Transfiguration was not his full glory, but a demonstration, just as the flower is not the fruit but a demonstration of it. And he calls Christ the apple tree, which tree produces sweet fruit, because the blessed in heaven feed upon the contemplation of God, just as on earth bodies feed on physical food. Thus, it makes the angels "greedy," meaning desirous, and he says "perpetual weddings" because blessedness in heaven is perpetual. **AND Overcome, they returned at the word**: that is, being stunned, they recovered at the word of God. **Elijah**: the history of this man and his chariot has already been set down. **Changed stole**: changed garment. **That pious one**: Matilda; she will teach him of Beatrice, because the doctrine of the active life shows us theology.

**AND all in doubt**: because so remains one who is 
suddenly awakened, and especially not seeing 
Beatrice. This falling asleep signifies that 
in wanting to understand the things that follow—both in 
this end of Purgatory and in Paradise—Dante 
(who signifies sensuality and the lower reason) 
fails at so many things. But he was awakened by the 
splendor, which is the higher reason and the intellect, 
and by the voice, which is cooperating grace. And thus 
awakened, Matilda (that is, doctrine) showed him Beatrice 
(that is, opened for him the knowledge of sacred things). 
Beatrice sits under the tree of good and evil, and 

of obedience, newly green—that is, renewed by the passion of Christ. And she sits upon the root, which signifies humility, just as the plant signifies obedience. For whoever truly desires to know divine things as much as human talent allows must become so humble that he has entirely captivated his talent and placed it under the yoke of faith. And for this reason, Theology sits upon the root. **SEE The company**, which are the seven virtues. **THE OTHERS**: those of the Old and New Testament. **THEY GO UP**: they ascend to heaven after the Gryphon, because the first to ascend to heaven was Christ. **WITH A Sweeter and more profound song**: to show that what we understand and taste of celestial things in the pilgrimage of this mortal life, though sweet, is not as sweet as what is tasted later in the eternal homeland. **AND IF HER speech was more diffuse**: It shows that although active doctrine shows us various things, nevertheless, one who has arrived at the state of innocence opens his ears to nothing else but theological things. **IN MY EYES she was**: understand, in the eyes of the intellect.

**It is not** inconsistent with what was said 
above—that Beatrice sat upon the root of 
the tree—and here [it says] upon the earth, because the 
root is underground. She was left as the 
guard of the chariot, because the true and only 
guardian of the Church Militant is Theology. 
Christ ascended with the others into heaven, 
but Beatrice remained on earth, because without 
the theological rule, the Church would perish.

He now witnesses a series of allegorical attacks upon the chariot representing the Church.</meta>

### PURGATORIO.

"Here you shall be a forest-dweller for a short time, <note>Dante uses the word 'sylvano' (from *silva*, forest) to refer to the earthly life, which he previously described as a 'dark wood.'</note>
and you shall be with me forever a citizen
of that Rome where Christ is Roman. <note>This refers to the Heavenly City, the celestial Rome of the afterlife.</note>
Thus Beatrice; and I, who was wholly devoted 
to her commands at her feet,
gave my mind and my eyes to where she willed.

Never did fire descend from a dense cloud 
with such swift motion, when it rains 
from that boundary which is most remote, <note>A reference to lightning falling from the highest reaches of the atmosphere.</note>
as I saw the bird of Jove descend <note>The eagle, the symbol of the Roman Empire.</note>
down through the tree, breaking the bark,
not to mention the flowers and the new leaves;
And it struck the chariot with all its strength,
overcome like a ship by the waves, now to starboard, now to port.
Then I saw a fox leap into the cradle
of the triumphal vehicle, a fox
who seemed fasted of every good meal. <note>The fox represents heresy, which 'starves' for lack of true spiritual nourishment.</note>
But rebuking her for her foul faults,
my lady put her to such flight
as much as her fleshless bones would allow.

<column-break/>

the Christian religion. And the seven virtues already described above formed a circle around her because Theology, left to guard the Church Militant, cannot exist without these virtues. This is not difficult to understand: for we see in our own century that Simon Magus <note>A biblical figure who tried to buy spiritual power; his name is the root of the word <term>simony</term>, the practice of buying or selling church offices.</note> is worth more there than Paul and John. Ambition, avarice, and luxury have more power there than apostolic poverty, humility, virginity, and chastity, to which state things have now been led. And because of this, the Church falls headlong into manifest ruin. May God provide a lamp to those who walk in darkness.

> And may He cause His face to shine 
> upon them, lest the blind and the leaders of the blind fall into the pit: And have mercy on us. <note>original: "Et illuminet uultum suū super eos ne ceci et cecorum duces in foueam cadant: Et misereatur nostri." A paraphrasing of Psalm 67 and Matthew 15:14.</note>

**WITH THOSE** lights in hand: we have already shown that the seven lights are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. Justice holds the Fear of God which drives out pride; Prudence with Piety drives out envy; Fortitude drives out anger; Temperance with Counsel drives out avarice; Faith with the light of Knowledge drives out sloth; Hope with the light of Wisdom drives out gluttony; and finally, Charity with the light of Understanding drives out lust. **IN HAND**: to show that such gifts must be put into action and into works. **FROM THE NORTH** and from the south: <note>original: "DA AQVILONE et da austro"</note> These seven virtues with their seven gifts are not extinguished in man either by prosperous things (signified by the North Wind) or by adverse things (signified by the South Wind). For the North wind brings serenity and comes from the highest part of the world, denoting prosperity. And the South wind blows from the lower meridian part, signifying adversity. We can also take the North wind for pride and the South wind for cowardice. **HERE YOU SHALL BE** a forest-dweller for a short time: This demonstrates the brevity of human life, in which the soul—the observer of celestial things—remains for only a short time. But once it has left the body, guided by Beatrice herself, it ascends to heaven where it is no longer a pilgrim or a stranger, but an eternal citizen with Beatrice. **Of that Rome where Christ is Roman**: of that true city, the head of the eternal empire, just as Rome is the head of the earthly empire; and just as the ancients called the celestial and eternal fatherland the "Upper Jerusalem," so the poet gives the same meaning to Rome. And not without reason did he say "forest-dweller" (*sylvano*): because in this brief life we walk through the forest—an uncultivated place abandoned by men and full of wild beasts. It is not cultivated by virtue; it is not inhabited by those who have humanity and charity, but by those filled with savage customs. **THEREFORE** for the benefit of the world: The poet had already described what the ancient Church was like and with how many virtues it was adorned. Now, considering how it had already begun to be defiled by every vice and to degenerate and stray from the true Christian Church, he describes its vices and predicts its miseries with highly appropriate fictions. **THEREFORE** for the benefit—the utility—of the world. **WHICH LIVES ILL**: because it is of the greatest utility to sinners to show them the disgrace and misery of their vices. **KEEP YOUR EYES ON THE CHARIOT**: consider what will happen to the Church. And then he continues the description.

With the fury of an arrow coming from heaven, an eagle came, which, streaking down through the tree, not only scattered the flowers and leaves but broke the bark. There were two persecutions that the Church suffered: one from the emperors and the other from the heretics. He therefore uses the eagle for the emperors, because their ensign is the eagle; and the fox for the heretics, who with foxy fraud strive to stain the true religion. The persecutions of the eagle were foreseen by Ezekiel where he says:

> A great eagle with great wings, long-limbed, 
> full of feathers and variety, came to Lebanon 
> and took the marrow of the cedar and tore off 
> the top of the mountains. <note>original: "Aquila grandis Ales magnus lōgo mēbrorū ductu plena plumis et uarietate uenit ad libanum et tulit medullam cedri et summitatem moncium auulsit" (Ezekiel 17:3-4).</note>

The persecutions of the emperors were ten, as Augustine states in the book *The City of God*: the first universal persecution in the Church was made by Nero; the second by Domitian and Trajan; the third and fourth by Antoninus and Severus; the fifth and sixth by Maximinus <note>OCR reads "marcelliano," likely a transcription error for Maximinus.</note> and Decius; the seventh and eighth by Valerian and Aurelian; the ninth and tenth by Diocletian and Maximian. The eleventh, which has not yet happened, will be by the Antichrist, who is figured under the likeness of a dragon. And the fox signifies Muhammad, of whom we spoke in the twenty-eighth canto of the first canticle <note>*Inferno* Canto XXVIII, where Muhammad is placed among the sowers of discord.</note> and referred to the seven heretics. **THE BIRD OF JOVE**: The eagle was the ensign of Jove [Jupiter] and remained with his successors, the kings of Crete. And it was transported by Teucer to Troy, and from Troy by Aeneas...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Purgatorio, Canto XXXII. The previous column concluded the discussion of the "fox" representing heresy and the Ghibelline influence within the Church. Here, the commentator Cristoforo Landino explains the second descent of the eagle (the Donation of Constantine), the emergence of the dragon (Muhammad), and the resulting corruption and transformation of the Church into a many-headed monster.</meta>

.XXXII
# CANTO

was brought to the Roman Empire: by ornaments you should understand the dignities: by the bark, salvation. <note>The "bark" or "scorza" refers to the protective outer layer of the tree, symbolizing the protection of the Church.</note> WHENCE IT SWERVED: because the state of the Church often wavers. FROM THE PORT: this is the rope that ties the end of the right yardarm. <note>A nautical term used here to describe the Church as a ship.</note> BEAR: <note>original: "ORSA"</note> The rope that ties the other end on the left. IN THE CRADLE: that is, inside the chariot: because the Ghibellines <note>Pro-imperial political faction often at odds with the Papacy.</note> were in the heart of the Church, pretending to be insiders and true Christians. TRIUMPHANT: because in the end, the Church overcame every adversary. OF EVERY GOOD MEAL: Referring to the soul, which the Ghibellines feed with false opinions where there is no Catholic truth. BUT REBUKING: Against the Ghibellines, the theologians sufficed, who refuted them in form during the councils, so that they were condemned to the fire. IN SUCH A FLIGHT: in such a refutation. BONES WITHOUT FLESH: because one who is burned remains with bones without meat.

---

*Then from the place where it had come before,*
*I saw the eagle descend into the chest*
*of the chariot, and leave it feathered with its plumage.*
*And as a voice comes from a heart that grieves,*
*such a voice came from heaven, and thus it said:*
*"O my little bark, how ill-laden you are!"*
*Then it seemed to me that the earth opened*
*between the two wheels, and I saw a dragon emerge*
*who fixed his tail through the chariot.*
*And like a wasp that pulls back its sting,*
*drawing back his malignant tail,*
*he tore out part of the floor and went wandering off.*
*That which remained, like grass on fertile soil,*
*from the first offering—perhaps with*
*a healthy and kind intention—*
*Covered itself again, and was covered,*
*both one and the other wheel and the pole, in such a time*
*as a sigh keeps the mouth open.*

voluptuous. And he fixed his tail, that is, fraud, dividing the wheels. Because Muhammad <note>original: "Maumetto"</note> withdrew the Saracens from the Church, who had newly come from the Old Testament and circumcision and the synagogue to the Christian Church, the New Testament, and baptism. AND WENT WANDERING: because his religion has no certain foundation, but goes wandering and straying. THAT WHICH REMAINED: The rest of the Christian Church which was not seduced and persuaded by Muhammad, but remained in the true faith, covered itself with the feathers of the eagle, as the earth is covered with weeds. <note>original: "gramigna"</note> That is, it became rich with goods received from the Empire. PERHAPS WITH A HEALTHY AND KIND INTENTION: As if to say, although wealth has filled the priestly order and especially the Apostolic See with every vice, nonetheless, he who first accepted it did so for a good purpose. And both wheels were covered. That is, both the Antiochene Church—which was ordained by those who first held the Old Testament—and the Roman Church—which had newly come to the Christian faith. IN SUCH A TIME: that is, as quickly as a sigh holds the mouth open.

*Thus transformed, the sacred edifice*
*put forth heads from its various parts:*
*three on the pole and one in each corner.*
*The first were horned like oxen,*
*but the four had a single horn on the forehead;*
*such a monster was never seen before.*
*Secure as a fortress on a high mountain,*
*seated upon it appeared to me a loose harlot,*
*with her eyes darting all around.*

<column-break/>

He has narrated above the persecution of the Emperors against the Church and the various sects of heresies. Now he places the Donation of Constantine <note>The historical event, believed in the Middle Ages to be a legal gift, where Emperor Constantine gave temporal power and wealth to the Pope.</note> and the complaint that Saint Peter made about it. And after this, he places the schism made by Muhammad. He figures the gift of Constantine by the feathers which the eagle, descending from where it had come before (that is, from the Empire), left in the chest of the chariot (that is, in the innermost part, which is the Apostolic Church) of its temporal goods. AND AS COMES FROM A HEART THAT GRIEVES: Thus a miserable voice came from heaven, like that which comes from a grieving and mourning heart, and said: "O my little bark, how ill-laden you are," that is, loaded with evil and harmful things. He suggests that Saint Peter, the first Pope, foresaw that the temporal goods donated to the Church (which in the past had maintained itself holy and in every virtue through poverty) would corrupt it with so many delicacies. THEN IT SEEMED TO ME THAT THE EARTH OPENED: He describes a dragon emerging from beneath the earth between one wheel and the other of the chariot, and it put its tail through the chariot and pierced the floor, like a wasp that, pulling out its sting, pierces and then pulls it back to itself. The dragon emerged from the earth is Muhammad, who was an earthly man, and

We spoke sufficiently in the 18th Canto of the *Inferno*: how in the Christian Church the seven heads signify the seven sacraments corresponding to the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, and how by the ten horns they understand the ten commandments of the law. And in this place, he puts three heads on the pole for the three sacraments which the prelates administer, who are at the helm <note>original: "temone," referring to the steering pole of the chariot.</note> (that is, the government of the Church): which are Confirmation <note>original: "cresma"</note>, Baptism, and Penance. And the other four he places each in one of the four corners of the chariot. Return then to the place already mentioned

<header>PURGATORY.</header>

*And just as if to ensure she would not be taken from him,*
*I saw a giant standing upright beside her,*
*and they kissed each other from time to time.*
*But because she turned her greedy and wandering eye*
*toward me, that fierce paramour* <note>original: "drudo" - a lover, often used here in a derogatory sense to imply an illicit or sinful relationship.</note>
*scourged her from her head to the soles of her feet.*
*Then, full of spite and cruel with anger,*
*he untied the monster and dragged it through the wood,*
*so far that the wood alone shielded me*
*from the harlot and the new beast.*

<column-break/>

of hell: and you will have the full allegory of this chariot thus transformed. Now, add the harlot and the giant who is her paramour: where by the harlot he understands the Church and the Supreme Pontiff Boniface VIII <note>Pope Boniface VIII (reigned 1294–1303), often criticized by Dante for his political ambitions and worldliness.</note>; and by the giant, the King of France <note>Philip IV, known as Philip the Fair, who came into violent conflict with Boniface VIII.</note>. For the Church—which with the utmost chastity ought to love its spouse, Christ, and never depart from spiritual things—became a prostitute; and in the hope of temporal goods, she loved the King of France, whom he calls a giant. Two things are in the giant: first, he is of great stature; second, "giant" signifies one generated from the earth. Similarly, the King of France was of the greatest power and lordship, and he was a product of the earth, despising spiritual goods and loving only earthly goods such as empires and riches. There sat, therefore, upon the chariot—that is, in the Apostolic Seat—a **harlot**, that is, Pope Boniface, who like a prostitute corrupted by money and to acquire treasure, having left her spouse, had given herself to the adulterer. **UNTIED:** free and without any restraint. **WITH HER EYES CAST ROUND:** Just as the harlot draws the lover to herself with quick and wandering eyes, so Boniface lured the King with various promises. The giant was near her, fearing she might be taken from him: that is, the King continually maintained the Pope in his friendship through legates and orators, so that he would not turn elsewhere. **AND THEY KISSED** each other from time to time: By kisses, understand the loving offers and presents and gifts they made to one another. But because this harlot turned her eyes toward me, the giant became jealous. In truth, Boniface—a vehement, eloquent man, and most greedy for honor—held dealings with various lords. Therefore, the King did not cease until he led the court to Provence, beyond the Alps <note>A reference to the "Babylonian Captivity" or the Avignon Papacy, where the papal seat was moved to France in 1309.</note>. And so he says that the giant untied the chariot, which is the Church, and dragged it so far through the wood that the great distance made the "wood" alone—that is, the terrain of the forest—a shield between me and her; that is, it was an obstacle so that I could no longer see her. And he puts himself in place of the other powers of which the King was jealous, fearing they might take the Pope from him. **TO THE HARLOT**, that is, to the Pope. **AND TO THE NEW BEAST**, that is, to the Church having become a new wild animal.

### CANTO XXXIII OF THE SECOND CANTICLE OF DANTE

*“O God, the nations have come,”* <note>original: "Deus venerunt gentes" - the opening of Psalm 79, lamenting the destruction of Jerusalem, here applied to the corruption of the Church.</note> *alternating*
*now three, now four, in sweet psalmody,*
*the women began, weeping.*
*And Beatrice, sighing and compassionate,*
*listened to them, so changed that little*
*more did Mary change at the cross.*

<column-break/>

This is the thirty-third and final canto, in which the poet, wishing now to bring an end to the *Purgatorio*, follows the description already begun. He demonstrates how, through the persecutions and transformations of the chariot and the pole—that is, of the Church and the prelates—the virtues were scattered. And Beatrice exhorted him to follow her and to ask her...

<header>CANTO XXXIII</header>
<page-num>.XXXIII</page-num>

But after the other virgins gave way
to her to speak, she stood up on her feet
and responded, colored like fire:
"A little while and you will no longer see me" <note>original: "Modicum et iam non uidebitis me" - Jesus's words from John 16:16. Beatrice uses this liturgical language to signal a transition in Dante's journey.</note>
"and again, my beloved sisters,
a little while and you shall see me."
Then she placed all seven in front of her,
and after her, with only a nod, she moved
me, the lady, and the sage who remained.

...to commit cruelty against her. And Beatrice, with tears and a piteous face, listened to her, changed in her appearance almost as Mary was at the cross. For the true theologian always grieves for things done in dishonor of God and to the harm of one's neighbor. **BUT AFTER THE OTHER VIRGINS:** After the lamentations of the virtues, Beatrice stood up on her feet, which demonstrates the vigilance of holy theologians. **AND COLORED LIKE FIRE** signifies fervor and charity; because they, with vigilance and with fervent charity, always offer comfort. **A little while and you will no longer see me: and again a little while and you will see me.** **THEN SHE PLACED ALL SEVEN IN FRONT OF HER:** because there is nothing in Christian theology that does not always follow these seven virtues <note>The three theological virtues (Faith, Hope, Charity) and the four cardinal virtues (Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, Temperance).</note>. **And after her, with only a nod, she moved me:** because one who is already in that state has no need of much exhortation. **And the lady:** Matilda. **And the sage who remained:** Statius.

Thus she went on, and I do not believe
her tenth step was placed upon the ground,
when with her eyes she struck my eyes,
and with a tranquil look she said, "Come more quickly,"
so much so that if I speak with you,
you are well-disposed to listen to me.
As soon as I was with her as I ought to be,
she said to me: "Brother, why do you not attempt
to ask me questions, now as you come with me?"
Like those who are too reverent
speaking before their superiors,
who do not bring a clear voice through their teeth,
it happened to me that without a complete sound
I began: "My lady, my need
you know, and that which is good for it."

...to give it, as if to say that whoever follows the studies of theology should not be discouraged because the subjects are most high. Rather, one must ask of her—that is, by reading frequently and sharpening the intellect and investigating—and by asking others, strive to understand every doubt within it. And she calls him "brother" to denote that he is a man just as the writers of theology were. And through this, by using assiduous and long-lasting diligence, he can understand it just as many have understood it. **AS THOSE WHO:** he says it happened to me as happens to those who, when they speak with their lords, are so hindered by the reverence they bear them that they do not bring a clear voice through their teeth: because the voice dies before it leaves the mouth. And in this she admonishes us that although we must dare to set ourselves to understand every obscure passage, nonetheless we should do so with modesty and with supreme reverence toward theology, and without presumption. And finally, she teaches what our questions ought to be.

And she to me: "From fear and from shame
I wish you now to disentangle yourself,
so that you no longer speak like a man who dreams.
Know that the vessel which the serpent broke
was, and is not; but let him who is at fault believe
that God's vengeance fears no sops." <note>original: "uendecta da dio non teme ſuppe" - Referring to an old folk belief that a murderer could escape vengeance by eating a piece of bread (a "sop") dipped in wine over the victim's grave for nine days. Dante warns that the corrupt cannot use rituals to escape divine justice.</note>

<column-break/>

Concerning the doubts he had, and she resolves them, demonstrating that whoever harms the Church shall be punished, and soon. He raises Dante's doubts and excuses his low intellect. This excuse Beatrice demonstrates to be sufficient. Now beginning, it shows that because of the disturbance of the chariot, the three theological and the four cardinal virtues grieved, and with sweet psalmody—that is, sweet song and almost an incitement to mercy—they said: "O God, the nations have come into your inheritance" <note>original: "Deus uenerunt gentes ihereditatē tuam" - Psalm 79:1. In the medieval context, this was often sung as a lament for the loss of the Holy Land or the corruption of the Church.</note>. In this psalm David laments the destruction that was to come to the temple of God. This demonstrated that the enemies of the church had...

It demonstrates that Beatrice had not gone ten steps when she struck his eyes with her own. This signifies that there are not ten clauses from where John in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>, in the first part of the seventeenth chapter, places the harlot who commits fornication with the kings of the earth, to where he says: "The beast which you saw was, and is not" <note>original: "beſtia quam uidiſti fuit et non eſt" - Revelation 17:8.</note>. The eyes of Beatrice are the intellect of that text which struck the intellect of Dante. Furthermore, "with a tranquil look": this denotes that it is necessary for the soul of one who wishes to attain this doctrine to be tranquil; or truly it signifies that theological doctrine purges the soul of every perturbation and makes it tranquil and quiet. She admonishes Dante to walk so close that he can understand what she speaks. Because whoever does not separate himself from other cares and does not approach such doctrine with all his mind will never be fit to understand it. Then she asks Dante why, being with her, he does not attempt—that is, does not dare—to ask...

Rightly she posits that "the vessel is not." Because being broken, it is no longer a vessel. Therefore, the Church is no longer as it used to be because it is divided, and in great part, from being spiritual and virtuous, it has become carnal and vicious. And he imitates in this place John in the seventeenth chapter of the Apocalypse where he says: "The beast which you saw was, and is not."

<summary>This page covers the opening of Purgatorio Canto XXXIII, where Beatrice comforts the weeping virtues and encourages Dante to overcome his hesitation and ask questions about the vision he has witnessed. The commentary explains the symbolic meaning of Beatrice's movements and her prophecy regarding the corrupted Church, linking it to the Book of Revelation.</summary>

It transitions from the poetic text of Canto XXXIII to Cristoforo Landino’s detailed commentary on the "DXV" prophecy and the mythological references to Themis and the Sphinx.</meta>

<header>->PURGATORY.<-</header>

The eagle that left its feathers in the chariot,
whereby it became a monster and then a prey,
shall not be without an heir for all time;
For I see certainly, and therefore I tell it,
stars already near to us, to bring a time
secure from every obstacle and every barrier,
In which a five hundred, ten, and five, <note>Beatrice refers to the famous "DXV" prophecy. In Roman numerals, D=500, X=10, V=5. Rearranged, they spell "DVX," the Latin word for "Leader."</note>
sent by God, shall slay the thievish woman
along with that giant who sins with her.

And perhaps my narration is dark,
like that of Themis and the Sphinx, and fails to persuade,
because in their fashion it clouds the intellect;
But soon the facts shall be the Naiads <note>Landino follows a common medieval reading of Ovid's *Metamorphoses*. Modern editions suggest the word was "Laiades" (referring to Oedipus, son of Laius), but Dante's sources read "Naiades" as the solvers of riddles.</note>
that will solve this difficult enigma
without damage to flocks or to grain:
Take note; and even as these words are borne
from me, so teach them to those who live
the life that is a race unto death.
And bear in mind when you write them down
not to hide what you have seen of the plant
which has now been twice plundered here.

<column-break/>

**BUT WHO IS TO BLAME:** Who has been the cause of such ruin and the adultery of the church? **BELIEVE** that God's vengeance does not fear soups. <note>original: "vendecta di dio non teme zuppe." This refers to an old Florentine superstition that if a murderer ate a piece of bread soaked in wine (a "soup") over the grave of their victim within nine days, they would be safe from the family's revenge. Landino explains that God's justice cannot be thwarted by such superstitions.</note> That is, believe that God will take vengeance. This can be understood as referring to Boniface, <note>Pope Boniface VIII, a primary antagonist in Dante's work.</note> who by divine justice lost the papacy through a raging death. It can also refer to Philip, King of France, <note>Philip IV, known as Philip the Fair.</note> who made ignominious agreements with a demented Pope against the high honor of the Church. **DOES NOT FEAR soups:** That is, the vain defenses of men. The commentator from Imola <note>Benvenuto da Imola, an early and influential commentator on Dante.</note> relates that in Florence there was an opinion that if someone committed a murder and ate a soup over the body of the deceased, he could not afterwards be killed in revenge. And the son of Dante, <note>Pietro Alighieri.</note> who commented on this Comedy, affirms that in those times when any of the great citizens was killed in our city, the relatives guarded the grave for up to nine days so that no one would eat a soup upon it. Because it belongs to the eagle to direct and correct the errors of the Church, he adds that the eagle will not always be without an heir, meaning without an emperor. For everyone who is made emperor becomes the heir of the eagle. And he shows that at that time the eagle was without an heir because, despite there being emperors, they served the Pope and did not dare to correct things through councils. **THAT LEFT its feathers to the chariot:** That is, left its treasures to the Church. **BECAUSE it became a monster and then a prey:** It became a monster because through riches it abandoned virtue and gave itself to vice, which was the cause of its becoming prey. **I SEE already stars near:** All the stars in the sky were there from the beginning; therefore, he means "favorable stars." **SECURE FROM every obstacle:** From every opposition. **AND FROM EVERY barrier:** And from every resistance. **IN WHICH a five hundred, ten, and five:** He does not use this number for the count of years, but because five hundred is noted with the letter **D**, five with **V**, and ten with **X**, which makes **DUX** [Leader]. He says there will be a Duke, that is, a leader of an army sent by God, who will kill the thief and the adultery of the harlot—meaning the Pope and the Roman court, corrupted in every vice. **WITH that giant:** By which he means the temporal lord who sins, that is, commits vice, with her.

Because until this point Beatrice has spoken with obscurity, she therefore adds, saying: perhaps my narration is dark and such as **WHICH Necte:** That is, joins and binds and persuades, like **THEMIS and the Sphinx**, who gave their responses so obscurely that a most sharp interpreter was necessary to understand them. And my narration is so obscure because it is "sharp": that is, it thins itself out and makes the intellect thin itself in their manner—meaning the manner of Themis and the Sphinx. The meaning is that I speak as obscurely as Themis and the Sphinx. Themis was a goddess of the heathens who gave oracles on Mount Parnassus, but many were obscure, such as the one she gave to Deucalion and Pyrrha after the flood. When they asked how they could restore the human race, she responded that they should throw behind their backs the bones of their mother. <note>The "mother" was the Earth, and her "bones" were stones.</note>

Deucalion interpreted this oracle to mean that the mother is the Earth, and the bones in the Earth are the stones. The Sphinx was a monster near Thebes who, according to Hesiod, was the child of Chimera and Orthrus, the dog of Geryon. This creature stayed on a mountain near Thebes and proposed a riddle—which the Greeks call an *enigma*—to anyone passing by, with the condition that if they did not know how to explain it, they would be killed by the monster. It proposed to Oedipus, the father of Eteocles and Polynices: what is the animal that at the beginning goes on four feet, then on two, and finally on three? This enigma was sharply explained by Oedipus, saying it was Man: who in the beginning goes on all fours with hands and feet; then goes upright on two feet; and in the end of his life goes with three because he leans on a staff. **BUT SOON SHALL BE the facts the Naiads:** But soon the events I announce will follow, and the facts will then declare what I meant to say, just as the Naiads declared the obscure words of Themis. <note>As noted above, this is based on a scribal error in Ovid's text.</note> **WHICH:** Which facts. **SHALL SOLVE:** Shall declare. **THIS Enigma:** This obscure saying. *Enigma* is a Greek word, as was said. Aristotle defines it in his book on poets <note>The *Poetics*.</note> as a speech that is either impossible or difficult to reduce to a certain understanding. And Averroes <note>The Andalusian philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to medieval thought.</note> writes that this often occurs in Arabic poets. **WITHOUT damage to sheep or to grain:** That is, without having to seek the interpretation through the augurs, who sacrificed some beast and, according to the disposition they found in the liver or other entrails, predicted what was to be; or through the *pullarii* [chicken-diviners], who brought out chickens for this purpose...

### CANTO XXXIII

...they held the army and gave them grain: and according to the way in which the chickens pecked, they predicted what the chickens divined. **TAKE NOTE:** that is, attend with diligence and teach it to those living. **THE LIVING:** <note>original: "AVIVI"</note> concerning the living, whose life is a race toward death. Those in heaven are truly living because they have life without death; but we are not truly living since our life is a brief course that leads us to death. **TWO TIMES:** the first when the eagle descended, the second when the giant untied the chariot and led it away. For after the griffin tied the chariot to the tree, the chariot and the tree became one and the same thing.

---

Whoever robs that plant or breaks it
with blasphemy in deed offends God,
who created it holy only for His own use.
For biting that, in pain and longing,
the first soul <note>Adam.</note> for five thousand years or more
craved Him who punished the bite in Himself.
Your wit sleeps if it does not judge it
to be so tall and so wide at the top
for a singular reason.
And if your vain thoughts had not been
the waters of the Elsa <note>The Elsa is a river in Tuscany known for its high mineral content that "petrifies" or encrusts objects left in its waters.</note> around your mind,
and their pleasure a Pyramus at the mulberry, <note>In the myth of Pyramus and Thisbe, the white berries of the mulberry tree were stained red by the lovers' blood. Dante suggests his vain thoughts have "stained" his mind.</note>
By so many circumstances alone,
you would recognize God’s justice
in the prohibition of the tree, morally speaking.

But because I see you in your intellect
made of stone and stained in sin,
so that the light of my word dazzles you,
I also wish—and if not written, at least depicted—
that you carry it within you for that reason
that the pilgrim’s staff is brought back wreathed with palm. <note>Pilgrims returning from the Holy Land wreathed their staves in palm fronds as proof of their journey.</note>
And I: "Just as wax under the seal,
which does not change the figure impressed,
so my brain is now stamped by you."

<column-break/>

It is no wonder that whoever harms the Church bears the penalty: because he offends God, who created the said plant of obedience and the said chariot which is the Church. He created it holy because He blessed it and sanctified it; and He created it for His own use so that it might return worship and honor to Him, through which we might merit eternal life. **WHOEVER ROBS IT:** as the giant robbed it, **OR BREAKS IT:** as the eagle broke it, offends God with blasphemy in deed. In Latin, it is called *blasphemia*; this is a Greek distinction <note>original: "greca distinction"</note> and comes from the verb *blatin* <note>original: "blatin" (likely a corruption of the Greek *bláptein*)</note> which means to harm or bring detriment. Therefore, blasphemy is the detriment and harming of honor. There is blasphemy of word and blasphemy of deed. Of word, when with words alone we fail in God’s honor; of deed, when we fail in our actions. **FOR BITING THAT:** He demonstrates by example how much God punishes whoever breaks or robs it; for the soul of Adam, our first parent, for biting it—that is, for tasting its fruit—remained:

in the pain he had in life, in the labor of body and mind, living nine hundred and thirty years; and in the longing he had in Limbo, which was five thousand two hundred and thirty-one years from the beginning of the world until the eighteenth year of the empire of Tiberius, in which Christ suffered. Therefore he says "more than five thousand years" he craved the coming of Christ, who punished in Himself the bite of Adam. For as a restoration for Adam’s disobedience, Christ—God made man—became obedient against that disobedience and sustained the penalty on the cross, which, as we said above, was made from that plant. **YOUR WIT SLEEPS:** If you do not judge it [the tree] to be excellent for a singular reason. **AND IF THEY HAD NOT BEEN THE WATERS OF THE ELSA:** that is, if your vain thoughts and thoughts of carnal things had not hardened your mind like the water of the Elsa, which, as we said above, hardens the things that enter it and turns them to stone. The inhabitants near this river use these stones in their buildings. The Sarno river in Puglia does the same thing. And Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and philosopher.</note> writes in his *Book of Minerals* <note>original: "libro de metalli"</note> that there is a spring in Boeotia which changes into stone whatever is placed in it. The Emperor Frederick II <note>Frederick II (1194–1250), Holy Roman Emperor.</note> proved this: he dipped his glove in it halfway; the dipped part became stone, and the other part remained leather as it was before. But let us return to the text where it follows. **AND IF THE PLEASURES:** if the pleasures you had from such thoughts had not been a Pyramus at the mulberry—that is, had you not stained your mind as Pyramus stained the mulberry, which he turned from white to black; we narrated the fable in the twenty-seventh canto of the first canticle. <note>The *Inferno*.</note> **BY SO MANY CIRCUMSTANCES:** Beatrice says that if you had held your thoughts firm in God, and they had not been hardened toward worldly things, you would recognize that God, by His justice, forbade man from touching that fruit according to morality. This thing was demonstrated by the circumstances of the tree: the first being that the tree was created by God and blessed so that man would return proper worship to God, which is justice. The second is the long deprivation of Adam for his transgression. The third is the satisfaction made through the passion of Christ.

She then wants that, as he currently cannot understand it for the reasons stated above, he at least carry her sentence in his heart, so that after he is well-purged of all vices, he may understand it by repeating it in his mind. Therefore she says, since you have made your intellect like stone—that is, you have made a habit of vice—and stained it in sin, because your mind is infected such that the eye of the infirm intellect is dazzled in the splendor of my words, at least carry them with you. If not written, at least depicted; although writing expresses it more and better than a picture. **FOR THAT REASON THAT:**

<summary>In this passage, Beatrice explains that the plundering of the mystical tree represents an offense against God's justice. Landino's commentary provides historical and mythological context, including the length of Adam's time in Limbo and natural wonders like petrifying rivers to explain Dante's clouded intellect.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Beatrice and Dante in the Earthly Paradise. Beatrice has just finished explaining that Dante’s human intellect has been "petrified" and "stained" by his worldly preoccupations, making it difficult for him to grasp her divine revelations.</meta>

# PURGATORY
### PAGE XXXIII

->**The staff is carried wreathed in palm.**<- The meaning is: although you do not understand my words exactly, at least carry away the gist of them. Let this be a sign, just as the pilgrim’s staff wreathed in palm is a sign that the traveler comes from the Holy Sepulcher <note>Palm leaves were traditional tokens brought back by pilgrims who reached Jerusalem.</note>, where palms are abundant. For this reason, she gives the precept that even though our minds are infected in such a way that we cannot understand sacred things while studying them—because **Wisdom’s spirit will not enter a malevolent soul** <note>original Latin: "In animam maliuolam non introibit spiritus sapientie." This is a quote from the Book of Wisdom 1:4.</note>—nonetheless, we must read sacred things and understand the words. Later, by purging ourselves, we will understand the allegorical sense. **IN MY BRAIN:** in the memory, which is the final cell of the ventricle of the brain <note>In medieval physiology, the brain was thought to be divided into "cells" or ventricles, with memory located in the rear.</note>.

"But why does your word fly so far
above my sight," I said, "that the more
it strives, the more it loses the way?"
"So that you may know," she said, "that school
which you have followed, and see its doctrine,
and how it can follow my word;
And see that your way from the divine
is as distant as the earth is removed
from the highest heaven that speeds above."

Philosophy can be suited to understand theology insofar as the philosopher seeks the reason in every thing. However, theology cannot be grasped by human reason alone. In this way, Dante can see how our way and philosophical doctrine are distant—that is, as different and distant from divine doctrine (theology) as the heaven that speeds most high <note>The *Primum Mobile*, the fastest and highest of the physical heavens.</note> is distant from the earth.

To which I answered her: "I do not remember
that I ever estranged myself from you,
nor have I a conscience that gnaws at me."
"And if you cannot remember it,"
she replied, smiling, "now recall
how you have drunk of Lethe even today;
And if from smoke we argue there is fire,
this forgetfulness clearly concludes
there was fault in your will, intent elsewhere.
Truly, from now on, my words
shall be as naked as is fitting
to reveal them to your coarse sight."

And more radiant, and with slower steps,
the sun held the circle of midday <note>The sun appears to move more slowly when it is at its zenith (noon).</note>
which shifts here and there as the place requires,
When the seven ladies halted, just as
he who goes before a group as a guide
stops if he finds something new in his path.
At the edge of a dim shadow, such as
the mountains cast over cold streams
beneath green leaves and dark branches.
In front of them, Euphrates and Tigris
I seemed to see issuing from a single fountain,
and like friends, parting from one another.

<column-break/>

Dante asks Beatrice why her words, which he so desires, fly so far above his sight—that is, above his intellect—so that the more his intellect strives to understand them, the more it loses them. In truth, the high meanings of theologians, which are reached through faith alone, distance themselves from our cognition the more we try to understand them by human reason. Hence, Gregory says: **Faith has no merit where human reason provides proof.** <note>original Latin: "fides non habet meritum ubi humana ratio prebet experimentum." A famous maxim by St. Gregory the Great.</note> Because of this, Beatrice replies that she has spoken in this form so that he may recognize the school of natural philosophers he has followed, and see how their doctrine...

Dante demonstrates that he does not remember being estranged or departed from Beatrice. She replies that such forgetfulness occurs because he has drunk from the river Lethe. Since Lethe only makes one forget the memory of evil, this forgetfulness is proof that leaving theology for philosophy (or other sciences) was indeed a "bad" or sinful act. Then she promises that in the future she will speak to him openly, as is appropriate for his "coarse wit," because he has not yet drunk from the river Eunoe, which he will drink from shortly hereafter.

**IT WAS MIDDAY:** The sun at midday is at its highest, appears to move more slowly, and is more radiant or "coruscant." It held the meridian circle, which is not the same in every part of the world; as the sphere of the earth turns, noon comes earlier or later in different places. **WHEN THEY HALTED:** When the seven ladies <note>Representing the four Cardinal and three Theological virtues.</note> stopped, just as a guide stops when encountering something new. **EUPHRATES AND TIGRIS:** The Bible places these rivers in Paradise. However, the poet, to serve his allegory, calls them Lethe (which he mentioned above) and Eunoe. They emerge from one fountain because each gives a great grace: Lethe makes us forget vice and all its triggers and incentives; and Eunoe—which in Greek signifies **"a good mind"** <note>original: "buonamente"</note>—leads us to remember virtue and inflames us with love.

<summary>Beatrice explains that human philosophy is insufficient to grasp divine mysteries, using the river Lethe to explain Dante's forgetfulness of his past errors. The scene concludes with the party arriving at the source of two mystical rivers, Lethe and Eunoe.</summary>
<keywords>Theology vs Philosophy, Lethe, Eunoe, St. Gregory the Great, memory, pilgrim's staff, seven virtues, Euphrates and Tigris</keywords>

# CANTO XXXIII

"O light, O glory of the human race,
what water is this that unfolds here
from one beginning and flows away from itself?"

At such a prayer, it was said to me: "Ask
Matilda to tell you"; and here responded
the beautiful lady, as one does who frees herself from blame:

"These and other things
were told to him by me; and I am sure
that the water of Lethe did not hide them from him."

And Beatrice: "Perhaps a greater care,
which often deprives the memory,
has made his mind dark in his eyes.

But see Eunoe, which flows down there;
lead him to it, and as is your custom,
revive his fainting strength."

**Oftentimes memory has made his mind dark in his eyes**, that is, in his intellect. And by this it is denoted that the active theologian <note>A reference to the "active life" of the soul, represented here by Matilda, which focuses on works and teaching.</note> must not warn, correct, and instruct only once, but often, because men occupied in civil actions do not have a mind so free that they can, in a short time, make a habit of such virtues. **BUT SEE EUNOE**, of which was spoken above. **LEAD HIM TO IT, AS IS YOUR CUSTOM**: because as we have said, this belongs to practical theology. **REVIVE HIS FAINTING STRENGTH**: There was in man naturally a strength with its internal spark. But sin extinguished it, and the spark hid itself like an ember under the fire. But coming to the state of innocence, the grace of the most benign God rekindles it.

As a gentle soul that makes no excuse,
but makes its will the will of another
as soon as that will is disclosed by a sign;

So, after I was taken by her,
the beautiful lady moved on, and to Statius
she said with grace: "Come with him."

If I had, Reader, a much longer space
to write, I would sing at least in part
of the sweet drink that would never have sated me;

But because all the pages are full,
ordained for this second canticle,
the restraint of art lets me go no further.

I returned from that most holy wave,
remade, just like new plants
renewed with new leaves,

Pure and prepared to climb to the stars.

...are very fresh and very green. Whence David said: **Your children are like olive shoots** <note>original Latin: "Filii tui sicut novellae olivarum" (Psalm 128:3). The commentator compares the soul's renewal to new plant growth.</note>. And truly, just as the old tree is renewed by the new plants that rise from the roots, so the soul, purged of the sin which had made it old, is renewed by returning to the state of innocence, and made pure and apt and willing to climb to the stars—that is, to the contemplation of divine things. To which may He who created us—and then, when we had fallen into the death of sin, created us anew by His established mercy—lead us.

<column-break/>

Dante asks Beatrice what water it is that makes two rivers from one source: namely, Lethe, which flows to the left, and Eunoe, which flows to the right. **O LIGHT**: Truly light, because theology illuminates the human mind to know God. **O GLORY**: The glory of man is to have a mind enlightened by divine things. **AT SUCH A PRAYER**, it was said to me by Beatrice: "Ask Matilda." This is because he uses Matilda to represent practical theology, whose office is to preach, teach, baptize, and similar things. Therefore, he imagines that Beatrice commits to Matilda the task of bathing him in the river Eunoe. **AND HERE**, that is, then, the beautiful lady Matilda responded, as one does who **frees herself**: as if she unties and defends herself from blame. For he who knows and does not teach is at fault. Thus, Matilda shows that she has already instructed Dante about these rivers and other things, as appears above. And Beatrice responded that although you have already shown him these things, nonetheless perhaps some greater care and occupation which takes away...

**AS A GENTLE SOUL** that makes no excuse: There is no greater nobility in the soul than humanity and charity; and he who has this does not seek excuses, but accords his will with the will of the one who asks, provided it is in honest matters. **AS SOON AS**, that is, immediately after the will of another is spoken. **DISCLOSED**, that is, appearing through a sign or through words in a way that the gentle soul understands it. And in passing, the poet shows that active theology has no will separate from the will of speculative theology <note>Speculative theology, represented by Beatrice, focuses on the contemplation of God; active theology, represented by Matilda, focuses on putting that knowledge into practice.</note>. For it purges the minds of men so that they may be able to rise to contemplation. **SO, AFTER I WAS TAKEN BY HER**, Matilda took him and told Statius to go with him, to denote that the learning of the Gentiles <note>Statius, a Roman poet, represents classical learning/philosophy which, when it serves sacred scripture, is useful to the soul.</note>, when it is in obedience to sacred letters and does not deviate from them, is useful. **IF I HAD, READER, A LONGER SPACE**, the poet excuses himself for not writing of the sweetness of this water, because this second canticle has its fixed number of verses. But truly, he reserves it for the following canticle <note>Paradise.</note>. **I RETURNED REMADE AS NEW PLANTS**, which...

PARADISO

### PROLOGUE BY CRISTOFORO LANDINO OF FLORENCE IN THE COMMENTARY ON THE DIVINE
### POET DANTE ALIGHIERI UPON THE PARADISO, THE THIRD CANTICLE

<image-desc>A magnificent illuminated border decorates the left margin, featuring vibrant floral motifs, scrolling leaves, and jewels. At the center of the border is a circular medallion containing a red cross on a blue shield. A large historiated initial "T" in gold on a blue background, decorated with delicate white patterns, initiates the main body of the text.</image-desc>

**WE PRAISE YOU, O GOD; WE ACKNOWLEDGE YOU TO BE THE LORD** <note>original: "Te DEVM LAVDAMVS TE DOMINVM CONFITEMVR," the opening of a famous Christian hymn of praise.</note>
If Cicero, a great philosopher and orator, when proposing in his old age to write about *Old Age* <term>De Senectute: Cicero’s famous essay on aging</term> to Atticus—who was also an old man—took his beginning from the poet Ennius who had written in that same stage of life, it seems similarly fitting for me, having been drawn through Hell and Purgatory, to move toward Paradise with the same hymn in which the most excellent doctors <note>The "Doctors of the Church," influential early Christian theologians.</note> sang their due thanks for both life and doctrine. This occurred when the divine **Augustine** <note>Landino uses "Aurelio," referring to Aurelius Augustine of Hippo.</note>, with the help of **Ambrose**, was liberated from diabolical snares and led to the port of salvation. Therefore, we praise you, most high God, and we confess you as the true Lord. 

By your grace, you drew those enlightened by **civil virtues** <term>Virtues related to one’s duty as a citizen and social conduct</term> from the low and shadowy depths of Hell. And then, lighting a splendid lamp at our feet with the **purgatorial virtues**, you lightened us, your servants—still heavy with earthly mud—so that we overcame every difficulty of the arduous and steep ascent of the mountain of Purgatory. Now, with your holy hyssop <note>A plant used in biblical rituals for ritual purification.</note>, you will make us clean; and by washing us, we shall remain whiter than any snow and so pure that your Paradise—spiritually infused into us more by your grace than by our merit—will adorn us with the third kind of virtue: that of the already purified soul. 

These will acquire for us two wings: **Justice** and **Religion**. With these, we shall fly even unto the Empyrean heaven to see ourselves reflected in the divine fountain. No other way remains, nor any other faculty for miserable mortals to elevate themselves to such height, except for Justice—which the divine **Plato** places as the sum of all moral virtues—and Religion, which contains within itself all the intellectual virtues. 

This is what the "Platonic" **Virgil** <note>Landino views the Roman poet Virgil through a Neoplatonic lens, common in the Renaissance.</note> signified in his sixth book: "To escape to the upper air, this is the task, this is the toil; only the few whom impartial Jupiter has loved, or whom glowing virtue has carried up to heaven, born of gods, were able to do so" <note>original: "Superas euadere ad auras hoc opus hic labor est pauci quos equus amauit Iuppiter aut ardens euexit ad ethera uirtus Diis geniti potuere" from Aeneid VI.</note>, as we interpreted extensively in that place. There is no other way to lead us; let no man be so far from reason that he wishes to imitate the rash stupidity of the **Giants**, who hoped to build a ladder to the stars by placing Mount Pelion atop high Mount Ossa, and Olympus atop Pelion. For the supreme Jove, with celestial lightning, turns mountains to ruin and submerges the Giants beneath them. According to the poets, the Giants were "sons of the earth," which denotes men given over to earthly things. These men believe they can climb to heaven like mountains—that is, by accumulating riches, power, and lordships to become happy. But the lightning of Jove—that is, the just divine indignation—dissipates these false goods and submerges their possessors. 

For this reason, the Psalmist rightly says: "For the Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the ungodly shall perish. Then he shall speak to them in his wrath, and vex them in his sore displeasure" <note>original: "Quoniam nouit dominus uiam iustorum..." Psalm 1.</note>. And elsewhere: "The Lord brings the counsel of the nations to nothing; he frustrates the thoughts of the people, and rejects the counsels of princes" <note>original: "Dominus dissipat consilia gentium..." Psalm 33.</note>. From this comes the most true sentiment of the "Aquiline" Evangelist <note>St. John the Evangelist, traditionally symbolized by an eagle.</note>: "No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven" <note>original: "Nemo ascendit in celum nisi qui decelo descendit," John 3:13.</note>. And certainly, no one rises to true beatitude unless they proceed from celestial things. 

Let us, therefore, fit ourselves with these wings—not with the stupidity of **Icarus**, but with **Daedalian prudence**—and fly to heaven. Let us not be so rash as to hope that we can fly to heaven by ourselves through our own aforementioned virtues. But when we strive to fit these two wings to ourselves, may the most powerful God be moved to compassion by our weakness, and with most liberal grace, he will supply that which we cannot do for ourselves; he alone raises us to himself and snatches us up to heaven. 

Thus, the **Apostle Paul** does not write of himself that he climbed to the third heaven, but affirms that he was "caught up" there by God. Therefore, that great Apostle does not glory in having climbed there, but says all glory is in God, the King of Glory. And certainly, as our Platonic **Marsilio Ficino** <note>A famous Florentine philosopher and contemporary of Landino; the reference is to Ficino's work *On the Rapture of Paul*.</note> most learnedly writes in his book *On the Rapture of Paul*: the heavy elements of the world cannot rise on high unless they are elevated by the Most High; and he who inhabits the earth does not rise by celestial steps if the celestial Father does not pull him. 

To you, therefore, we turn, O supreme Jove <note>A common Renaissance poetic substitution of the Roman name Jove/Jupiter for the Christian God.</note>, with warm sighs and with all our hearts we humbly pray that you extend the right hand of your help and raise us up, so that following the tracks of our poet, we may mount from heaven to heaven until we reach your presence. This presence enriches all poverty, satiates all hunger, heals all infirmity, strengthens all weakness, and finally fills us with that happiness which is neither diminished by any defect nor circumscribed by time.

## PARADISO: THE THIRD CANTICLE OF THE DIVINE POET DANTE ALIGHIERI

Because, as we have shown in the first canticle <note>The *Inferno*</note>, all heroic poets divide their work into three parts: the Proposition, the Invocation, and the Narrative. These four tercets <note>three-line stanzas</note> contain the **Proposition**, in which the matter of the entire work is briefly handled. This matter is the treatment of the celestial kingdom—not according to its true nature, because that transcends our intellect, but as much as the mind can grasp and, having grasped it, commit to memory. And because the proposition and invocation serve as a **proem** <note>a formal introduction or preface</note>, the poet observes here what is proper to a proem. We demonstrated the office of the proem quite clearly at the beginning of the *Inferno*, so I will not tire myself by describing its parts again. Instead, I will explain how the poet observes them here. He **captures attention** by showing that he has to speak of a matter so high that all others are far inferior to it, for there is no comparison between the infinite and the finite—that is, from God to his creatures. He **captures benevolence** through his own person, demonstrating that his labor in writing will be very useful to others. He **captures docility** <note>the reader's readiness to be taught</note> because he briefly demonstrates what the entire canticle will treat: namely, the eternal kingdom.

> THE GLORY OF HIM WHO MOVES ALL THINGS
> penetrates through the universe and glows
> in one part more, and in another less.
> In the heaven that receives most of His light
> was I, and I saw things that to recount
> he neither knows nor can who descends from there;
> Because as it approaches its desire,
> our intellect sinks so deep
> that memory cannot follow behind.
> Truly, as much of the holy kingdom
> as I could treasure within my mind
> shall now be the matter of my song.

**THE GLORY** Although fame and glory seem to many to be almost the same thing, fame is merely the common notice of a thing. **Glory** is clear notice of a thing accompanied by praise. Therefore, there can be fame for a thing that brings neither splendor nor praise, but glory cannot exist without them. Thus, it is defined by Cicero in the *Tusculan Disputations*: **Glory is the consistent praise of the good, the uncorrupted voice of those judging well concerning excellent virtue.** <note>original: "Gloria est consentiens laus bonorum incorrupta uox bene iudicantium de excellente uirtute."</note> From this, it follows that all glory is fame, but not all fame is glory. **THE GLORY** refers to the glorious work, which is God’s work, the universe. **OF HIM** who moves everything—that is, God. This is a rhetorical device called **circumlocution** <note>original: "circuituone"</note>, which is when what can be said in one word is said in many. **Moves all things.** Thus Boethius says: **Remaining stable Yourself, You grant all things to be moved.** <note>original: "Stabilisque mouens das cuncta moueri."</note> Therefore, He alone is stable. This is proven by Thomas Aquinas: every thing that is moved must be moved by another, such as the sun, the moon, and the others. To avoid proceeding into infinity, it is necessary to establish one **unmoved mover** <note>Aristotle’s concept of God as the primary cause of motion</note>. God, therefore, being immobile, moves all. And "He who moves all" means God. Because He is stable and immobile, He is the first mover. He moves the angels, the angels move the heavens, and the heavens with their revolutions bring about various effects down in the world. Therefore, God is the first mover and the primary cause of all causes. For this reason, we say the glory of God **penetrates** through the universe—that is, it passes through all creatures. He was able to produce the most perfect creature through His power; He knew how through His wisdom; and He willed it through His supreme goodness and love. By saying **universe**, we mean the whole, which is composed of different species. For some things have only "being," like a stone. Some have being and life, like herbs and trees. Some add to the first two "feeling," such as certain small shellfish. Some have being, life, feeling, and imagination, such as the brute animals. To these four powers, some add the discourse of reason, such as men. But the most noble creature is that which has "formal being" and intellect, such as the angel. In brief, according to the philosophers, we can divide this universe into three species: for whatever exists is either **pure form**, such as God, Angels, and the human soul (though God is the "Form of forms"); or **pure matter**, such as the indistinct production of the elements called **chaos**; or **matter with form**, such as "elemented" things—that is, things composed of elements. In these elemented things, there are six grades: being, living, feeling, imagining, reasoning (using the discourse of reason), and understanding. In these, the superior always encompasses the inferior. **AND GLOWS** because God is the true light, through which every thing shines. His splendor appears, therefore, in every thing: but more so in those that are pure form. Just as, for example, the same form appears in a mirror, in polished metal, in water, and in a wall. It is therefore the same light that shows itself to all...

<summary>This page introduces the Paradiso, featuring Dante's opening verses on the divine light and Cristoforo Landino's commentary on the nature of God as the Unmoved Mover and the hierarchy of existence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary by Cristoforo Landino on the first Canto of Dante’s *Paradiso*. The text begins mid-sentence, completing the thought from the previous page regarding how divine light is received differently by different beings.</meta>

->PARADISO<-

shows equally. But it is not received equally. Instead, each receives as much as their nature allows. Therefore, a mirror receives it more clearly than metal; and among metals, silver more than tin, and tin more than lead. Thus, in an excellent mirror, you will see the truest image. Then it degenerates: elsewhere it will be larger, elsewhere smaller, elsewhere distorted. Silver will show fewer lines, tin even fewer. Lead will show them confused. A wall will not show any lines at all, but rather a shadow, and that will be distorted, larger, or smaller. Nevertheless, all these images come from one and the same source. 

It is therefore no wonder that God, who is unique, is not seen as the same in all things, because not every subject can receive Him as the nature of God Himself—which is perfect—but rather according to the subject's own nature, and according to whether it is capable of more or less. God is in heaven for greater glory; as David says, "The heavens declare the glory of God" <note>original: "Celi enarrant gloriam dei"</note>. But He is virtually in every place. As Augustine says: "God is whole in heaven; whole on earth; and whole in both" <note>original: "Deus in celo totus est: In terra totus: et in utroque totus"</note>. And the <term>Master of the Sentences</term> <note>Peter Lombard, a primary medieval theologian</note> says: "Angels are limited by location; God is uncircumscribed" <note>original: "Angeli circunscripti localiter: Deus in circunscriptus est"</note>. But He shines more in heaven. And because of this, the prophet Isaiah says: "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool" <note>original: "Celum mihi sedes est: Terra autem scabellum pedum meorum"</note>. **IN THE HEAVEN THAT TAKES MOST OF HIS LIGHT**: this is the <term>Empyrean heaven</term> <note>the highest, most spiritual part of heaven in medieval cosmology</note>, which is made of pure light, and therefore receives more of it than the others that are made of light. But we shall say more about light in a more convenient place. **I WAS THERE**: according to the fiction, Dante ascended to heaven with his body; according to the allegory, he ascended with his intellect, because through theological doctrine he reached as far into the knowledge of divine things as is permitted to man. **AND I SAW** things that he neither knows how to nor can retell. This is similar to that of Saint Paul: "And I saw things which it is not permitted for man to speak" <note>original: "Et uidi ea que non licet homini loqui"</note>. 

**WHO DESCENDS FROM THERE**. While we are in heaven—that is, in the contemplation of celestial things—we can understand something. But when we descend to earth, we cannot retell anything—that is, returning to earthly things, we cannot demonstrate the divine within them. Furthermore, while the intellect contemplates God and divine things, the memory fails and cannot retain them. And for this reason, Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, an early Church Father</note> says in his commentary on Paul's epistle to the Hebrews: "Just as we understand many things about God that we cannot speak, so we speak many things that we cannot understand" <note>original: "Sicut multa de deo intelligimus que loqui non ualemus . Ita multa loquimur que intelligere non possimus"</note>. And certainly, we say many things about God which we both understand and do not understand; for example, although we understand that God is infinite, and consequently uncircumscribed and in every place, nevertheless our intellect cannot be capable of that infinity. Wherefore it can be concluded that we hear it rather than understand it, though in some way we do understand it, but not sufficiently. **BECAUSE I REACH**. He assigns the reason why he cannot retell it: because the memory does not retain what the intellect, deepening itself in Him, knew. The intellect, elevated to God, sees; but the memory does not retain it. Therefore, once the intellect is departed from God, we cannot retell what we saw. **TRULY, WHATEVER I [COULD TREASURE] OF THE HOLY KINGDOM**: A "Kingdom" because there is a true King there. "Holy" because it is consecrated to God, and because it is firm, stable, and immobile, and lasts forever. "Holy" means a thing consecrated to God, and also a thing firm and stable. **WHATEVER**: he does not promise to say absolutely everything, because human [memory] alone cannot comprehend everything; and nevertheless it conceives much more than it can express. **BUT AS MUCH AS HE COULD TREASURE**: that is, to express as much as he committed to memory. They call "Treasure" the place where we store our riches. And for this reason, Cicero and many other Latin writers call the memory "treasure," because it is that power of the soul which preserves for us what we have understood or learned.

O good Apollo, for this last labor,
make me such a vessel of your value
as you require for the gift of the beloved laurel.
Up to here, one peak of Parnassus
has been enough for me; but now with both
I must enter the remaining arena.
Enter into my breast and breathe yourself,
just as when you drew Marsyas
from the sheath of his limbs.
O divine virtue, if you lend yourself to me
so much that the shadow of the blessed kingdom
marked in my head I may make manifest,
You will see me come to the foot of your beloved tree
and crown myself with those leaves
of which the subject matter and you will make me worthy.
So rarely, Father, are they gathered
to triumph over Caesar or a poet—
the fault and shame of human wills.

<column-break/>

He has, until now, written the **Proposition**, in which he has briefly shown what he intends to treat. Now follows the **Invocation**, in which he invokes Apollo to inspire in him his <term>divine fury</term> <note>a state of inspired madness or creative ecstasy</note> through which men become poets. Therefore, I would judge it useful and pleasant in this place to briefly run through—according to Plato—what divine fury is, and how it breathes in the poet. But let it suffice to have treated this at the beginning of this work, where, as much as the strength of our genius allowed, we praised the poetic faculty. 

**Apollo** is a Greek name, but common also among the Latins. This is the god of the sun according to the gentiles; and the name comes from a Greek verb meaning "to kill" and "to undo," because the solar rays are as suited to corruption through excessive heat as they are to generation through temperate heat. For this reason, Homer introduces him as the giver of pestilence, and the ancients attribute to him the bow and the lyre: the former to demonstrate that he is harmful, the latter to signify his harmony, temperance, proportion, and suitableness, from which everything is generated. Whence Horace, in his odes, prays that [Apollo] might come...
