### CANTO ONE
<sig>A. iii</sig>

That the Penean branch <note>original: "fronda peneia" — the laurel tree, named for the nymph Daphne, daughter of the river-god Peneus</note> should bring forth joy to the joyful Delphic deity <note>Apollo</note> when someone thirsts for it. A tiny spark facilitates a great fire; perhaps after me, with better voices, prayers will be offered so that Cyrrha <note>one of the peaks of Mount Parnassus</note> might respond.

<column-break/>

...soften, without your arrows and with your lyre. Hide your weapon and be mild; graciously hear the boys who pray, Apollo. <note>original: "Condito mitis placidusque telo. Suplices audi pueros apollo." — a reference to Horace’s Secular Hymn</note>. They say he is the god of poets because, since no one can be a true poet without the knowledge of all disciplines, the physicists and especially the <term>Platonists</term> <note>philosophers following the tradition of Plato, who believed in the soul's journey through the celestial spheres</note> say that our soul, descending into the body, receives from the Sun a virtue through which it acquires knowledge and opinion. And so as not to leave the others behind, it similarly takes certain powers from every other planet.

<column-break/>

For Saturn gives it reasoning; Jupiter gives it practice and action; Mars gives it ardor and courage; Venus gives it the movement of desire; Mercury gives it speech; the Moon grants it the power to plant, generate, and increase physical bodies. This is therefore the natural reason why poets are under the protection of the Sun <note>represented by Apollo</note>. Poets are crowned with laurel because this tree is dedicated to Apollo. The myth is that Apollo, burning with love for Daphne—a nymph and daughter of the river Peneus—chased her swiftly. But the girl did not flee him slowly; finally exhausted, and being unable to otherwise escape the strength of her eager lover, she was transformed by the mercy of the gods into a tree of the same name. For the Greeks call it *daphne*, the Latins call it *lauro*, and we call it *alloro* <note>Laurel</note>. Therefore, as he loved the nymph, so he loves the tree. With laurel they used to crown conquerors in triumphs, and with laurel they crown poets. They say that a bolt from heaven <note>lightning</note> never touches it; for this reason, the Emperor Tiberius always wore a laurel crown during thunderstorms because he greatly feared lightning. Some write that whoever keeps it under their head while sleeping has true dreams. **TO THE FINAL labor:** to this, my final effort and work, because this is the third and last <term>cantica</term> <note>the third major division of the Divine Comedy</note>. And here he makes his request easier to grant, because he almost promises not to labor any further; and he also silently suggests that having helped with the first two parts, Apollo should not withdraw his favor now, leaving the work—begun in two parts—incomplete in the third. **MAKE ME such a vessel** of your worth: make me such a vessel and fill me with your power, that is, with the divine inspiration mentioned before. **AS IT demands** to be given the beloved laurel: as the laurel demands, meaning it requires that you grant this, since it is loved by me. In short: make me such a vessel for your divine fury as is deserved by the love I bear for the laurel—that is, for the poetic faculty. And this is the best way to ask; for if one wishes a petition to be just, one must show that they deserve what they ask for. And if he showed he deserved it through his own wisdom and learning, or through some service rendered, it would be a most arrogant request. But by pleading through the love he bears for the laurel, he makes his prayers humble and yet full of efficacy. **UNTIL NOW one peak** of Parnassus: Parnassus is a mountain in Boeotia, or rather in Phocis, which is very high and has two peaks: one dedicated to Apollo, the other to Bacchus, whom the ancients likewise considered a god of poets. For this reason, they also crowned themselves with ivy, which is dedicated to Bacchus. And so Virgil says:
> Allow this ivy also to creep around your temples among the conqueror's laurels. <note>original: "Hanc quoque sine tempora circum Inter victrices hederam tibi serpere lauros."</note>

And Propertius:
> Offer me leaves from your ivy, Bacchus. <note>original: "Mi folia ex edera porrige bacche tua."</note>

Servius <note>an ancient commentator on Virgil</note> affirms these two peaks are named Helicon and Cithaeron. Parnassus is consecrated to the Muses, and they live there around the Pegasean spring. Of Parnassus, Ovid writes:
> There a mountain seeks the stars with two steep peaks, named Parnassus and Perseo. <note>original: "Mons ibi uerticibus petit arduus astra duobus: Nomine parnafus: et Perfro:"</note>

"Nor do I remember having dreamed on two-peaked Parnassus," <note>original: "Nec in bicipiti fommiaffe parnafe memini me" — Persius</note> and Lucan:
> Parnassus, which sent forth deserted peaks... <note>original: "Parnafus que iugo mifit desertus:"</note>

And it seems he considers the peak of Cithaeron, consecrated to Bacchus, to represent the lower sciences—which are all the other parts of philosophy except "First Philosophy"—and Metaphysics and Theology. For in worldly matters, those lower sciences are sufficient for everything; but he places Helicon for Theology, which alone has knowledge of celestial things. Therefore, by comparison, he calls the peak an "arena." **I NEED:** <note>original: "ME uo pot" — a contraction of "me è uopo"</note> it is necessary for me, as in Latin one says *mihi est opus*. **ENTER MY breast:** into my mind, and breathe into me such a song as you used when you defeated Marsyas. It is written in the myths that Minerva, playing the <term>tibia</term> <note>a reed pipe or flute</note> over the water of the Tritonian marsh, saw her cheeks swelling. This seemed so ugly to her that she threw the pipe away and would play it no more. Marsyas the satyr found it and, by persevering in playing it, became a learned musician; but he grew so insolent and rash that he set himself above Apollo, the god of the musical art, and challenged him to a singing contest. Minerva and Midas, King of Lydia, sat as judges. Apollo won according to the true judgment of Minerva, but Midas, being ignorant, favored Marsyas. Because of this, Apollo gave Midas the ears of a donkey and flayed Marsyas. **FROM THE sheath:** from the skin, which is like the scabbard of the body. **O DIVINE virtue:** o divine fury of Apollo; and in passing he shows that although he says "Apollo," he means the divine grace that illuminates, cooperates, and perfects—and finally, the Holy Spirit itself. **THE SHADOW traced** in my head: the image impressed upon my memory, which is located in the last of the three ventricles of the head. And he said "shadow" to show that he did not have the exact image of heaven expressed in his memory, but rather a shadowed version. **WILL SEE ME at the foot:** your grace will not be placed in me in vain, for I will use it in such a way that I will deserve to be crowned with laurel as an excellent poet. And so that he does not seem arrogant in attributing so much praise to himself, he says that not he, nor his own talent, will make him worthy of such a crown, but rather divine grace and the subject matter he treats. **SO RARELY** father, are they gathered: as if to say, so great is the laziness and negligence of men that they rarely give themselves either to poetry or to military discipline in a way that makes them worthy of being crowned with laurel.

<header>PARADISO</header>

The rarer they are, the more one ought to favor those who seek to crown themselves; and he used "Caesar" to represent every triumphant man. **GUILT** and shame of human desires: it is the fault of human desires because our desires and appetites, having become rebels against reason, follow sensuality; they are infinite in searching for corporeal things, and because of their care for these, they desire nothing that is truly excellent. It is, therefore, a fault and a shame because it brings great ignominy to human life. **THAT BROUGHT FORTH JOY** <note>original: "CHE partori letitia"</note>: this refers to the sentence regarding the Penean leaf—that is, the laurel, which originated from Daphne, daughter of the river-god Peneus—which should bring joy to the Delphic deity, namely Apollo. He is called "Delphic" because he delivers oracles in his temple in the city of Delphi in Phocis, not far from Parnassus, whenever someone is crowned with it. **A LITTLE SPARK FOSTERS A GREAT FIRE.** This shows that, speaking modestly of himself, he deserves Apollo’s favor. For although he himself may not achieve excellent things, nonetheless those who come after him, moved by his example, will increase the poetic faculty over time; just as we see that from a small spark a great flame often arises. **WITH BETTER VOICES**, with more elegant style, and with more poetic art: **SO THAT CYRRHA MAY RESPOND**, meaning so that he may be heard by Apollo, to whom Cyrrha is dedicated. Hence Juvenal said: *The darts of the Cyrrhean prophet.* <note>original: "Cyrrhe i ſpicula uatis" — Juvenal, Satire 7.64</note> Cyrrha is a city in Phocis near Crissa and not far from Mount Parnassus.

The lamp of the world rises for mortals
From different outlets; but from that one
Which joins four circles with three crosses,
With a better course and with a better star,
It comes out joined, and the worldly wax
It tempers and seals more in its own way.
It had made morning there and evening here,
Almost through such an outlet, and all was white
In that hemisphere, and the other part was black,
When Beatrice upon her left side
I saw turned and gazing into the sun:
Never did an eagle so fix its gaze upon it.

<column-break/>

<margin>After the invocation, his narration begins, describing his ascent to the first heaven, which is that of the Moon.</margin> Furthermore, he describes that he began to ascend in the morning when the sun was rising in that hemisphere where he was, making it morning there. And the sun was at the beginning of <term>Aries</term> <note>the zodiac sign of the Ram</note>, in which sign this planet has its **exaltation** <note>an astrological term for the sign where a planet’s power is most potent</note>. For this reason, it produces more worthy effects. And it was at the equinoctial circle where, as appears in the **material sphere** <note>an armillary sphere, a physical model of the heavens used by students in Landino's time</note>, four circles join: the horizon, the zodiac, the <term>colure</term> <note>one of the two principal circles that intersect at the celestial poles</note>, and the equinoctial line. And in this conjunction, three crosses are made—that is, three intersections. He imagines, then, that the sun was in Aries, as we have said, because just as the physical sun operates most excellently upon inferior things when it is there, so the celestial Sun, which is God Himself, pours 

---

most excellent grace into the human soul when He draws it to contemplate His divinity. There are many who allegorically interpret the **four circles** as the four moral virtues <note>Justice, Prudence, Temperance, and Fortitude</note> and the **three crosses** as the three theological virtues <note>Faith, Hope, and Charity</note>. And the text follows: **The lamp of the world**, that is, the sun which illuminates the world, rises and is born for us mortals from different **outlets** <note>original: "foci" — refers to the points on the horizon where the sun rises at different times of the year</note>. For when it rises with Aries, it appears in the true East. But from day to day, it rises toward the North until it reaches Cancer. And from there, likewise descending step by step into Libra, it is in the same place it was in Aries. And then, departing from there, it goes descending through the southern signs until Capricorn; and from there, through Aquarius and Pisces, it rises again to the equator. Therefore, although the sun always rises from the East, it does not always rise from the same part of the East. For this reason, astrologers divide the East into three parts: equinoctial, northern, and southern. It rises, then, from different parts of the East, but **with a better course**—that is, with a happier influence—it rises from the vernal equinox where the aforementioned circles and crosses are. And **with a better star**: and he calls the sign of Aries a "star," using one star to represent all the others that make up that sign; and he says "better" because, as we have said, Aries is the exaltation of the sun; or rather, he meant **Venus**, which at the beginning of the second canticle <note>the *Purgatorio*</note> he placed in Pisces near the sun. **And the worldly wax**: he says, then, that when the sun rises with Aries and has Venus joined with it, it can better dispose the earth and animals to produce fruit with its influence. Therefore it **tempers**—that is, disposes—and **seals**. **The worldly wax**: thus it disposes and imprints its virtue, just as wax becomes fit to receive the figure imprinted by a seal when it is well-disposed; and this is true because in that season, heat and moisture arise in a balanced way, from which balance the best generation is born. **It had made**: "there," in that hemisphere where I was then, it was morning. **And here**: in our hemisphere, it was evening. And allegorically, "here" represents death because there are vices and ignorance; and "there" represents day because there are those who are purged of vices and illuminated by divine grace. **Upon her left side**: from where the sun casts its rays in that hemisphere to one turned toward the East. That Beatrice could look at the sun signifies that only **theology** can look upon the divinity, which is the true Sun. **Never did an eagle so fix its gaze**: the eagle has such powerful eyes that, beyond the ability of any other animal, it fixes its eyes on the sun without being dazzled. For this reason, Beatrice is like the eagle because, alone among all doctrines, Christian theology can endure the rays of the divine Sun and look into God, the First Light, and know Him without being dazzled. This same reason causes John the Evangelist to be depicted in the form of an eagle, because he discerns the divinity above all others.

<summary>This page contains Landino's commentary on the astronomical and allegorical timing of Dante's ascent into Paradise, explaining the significance of the sun's position in Aries. It highlights the comparison between Beatrice's theological vision and the eagle's ability to stare directly into the sun.</summary>

On the previous page, the author discussed the invocation of Apollo and the symbolic value of the laurel crown. Here, the focus shifts to the physical and spiritual ascent of Dante as he gazes into the sun alongside Beatrice, transitioning from human limits to a divine state.</meta>

<header>CANTO ONE</header>

And it issued as a second ray of the sun
issues from the first and reflects upward,
just like a pilgrim who wishes to return;
So, from her action, infused through the eyes
into my imagination, my own was made,
and I fixed my eyes on the sun beyond our custom.
Much is permitted there that is not permitted here
to our powers, thanks to the place
made specifically for the human race.
I did not endure it for long, yet not so briefly
that I did not see it sparking all around,
like iron coming white-hot out of the fire.
And suddenly it seemed to me that day was added
to day, as if He who is able
had adorned the heaven with another sun.

...his blessedness. For this reason, since by means of the purgative virtues we have returned to the state of innocence, it is no wonder if in that place—that is, in such a state—it is permitted for us to look into the sun, which is not permitted to us here—that is, in the state of sin. **I DID NOT ENDURE IT FOR LONG, YET NOT SO BRIEFLY.** The poet’s meaning is that once the sun rose, he began to lift himself toward heaven—that is, to contemplate. For: "Contemplation is the free, clear-sightedness of the mind in the speculation of wisdom, suspended with admiration." <note>original: "Contemplatio eft libera mentis perfpicatia in fapientie fpiculatione cum admiratione fufpenfa"</note> And to look into the sun: this is nothing other than being illuminated by divine grace so as to be able to look into the sun—that is, to rise to the speculation of the divinity. Nevertheless, he did not endure it for long: because if the eyes—that is, the edge of the intellect—had endured the light for a longer time, he would have been able to discern the entire solar body—that is, he would have had true knowledge of the divine essence. But he did not have such a powerful eye. Nevertheless, for that little bit he endured, he saw the sparks and flashes that were born from the solar body, in the same way they are born from a red-hot iron. The allegorical sense is that the purified soul can contemplate God, but not in a way that it knows His essence; rather, it has knowledge of the sparks that come from the sun—that is, the effects that proceed from God. For we know the cause through its effects, and not the effects through the cause. And that the sun had given greater light, as if it were doubled, signifies that theological contemplation illuminates the intellect much more than philosophy does, because it is not without the infusion of the Holy Spirit, as you will see a little further down.

Beatrice stood with her eyes fixed entirely
upon the eternal spheres, and I on her,
my eyes withdrawn from those lights above.
In her aspect I became such within
as Glaucus became upon tasting the herb
which made him a companion in the sea to the other gods.
To "transhumanize" cannot be signified
by words; therefore, let the example suffice
for those to whom grace reserves the experience.

<column-break/>

As a ray of the sun, reflecting, returns upward to where it came from—resembling a pilgrim who returns home—so the fixed act of Beatrice looking intently into the sun entered into my "image"—that is, my imagination—and disposed me to look similarly into the sun. Because when the rays of the divine sun strike theological doctrine—which alone can withstand their sight—it illuminates us; it strengthens and corroborates our eyes in such a way that we too can look at the sun. Thus, Augustine correctly wrote: "The good of God is known through theology, which perfects the intellect and directs the affection." <note>original: "Bonum dei cognofcitur per theologiam que perficit itellectum: et dirigit affectum."</note> And so that we do not marvel that he could look so fixedly into the sun beyond our custom, he adds that the power of that place makes it so that we can do many things there that we cannot do here; because that place was made specifically for the human species. And the Earthly Paradise was created by God so that man might dwell there for a time in a state of innocence; and then, when it pleased Him, he would have been taken up to...

He wishes to express nothing else by showing that Beatrice kept her eyes fixed on heaven, and he his on the eyes of Beatrice, except that sacred theology contemplates nothing other than divine things; and whoever wishes to understand them must place their entire mind into theology and into its doctors. And it follows that in looking at her, he was transformed within—that is, in his soul—just as Glaucus was transformed, who by eating the herb became a god. Thus he shows that his soul was "deified." And certainly, through the contemplation of divinity, we become divine and gods, as Boethius extensively demonstrates. Glaucus, son of Anthedon, was a fisherman. <note>The text refers to the myth of Glaucus of Anthedon from Ovid's Metamorphoses.</note> Having placed the fish he caught on the meadow so that the nets might dry, it happened that some of them, tasting a certain herb, regained their strength and jumped back into the water. Glaucus was amazed by the event and likewise tasted the same herb; seized by a sudden fury, he threw himself into the sea, and there from a man he became a sea god. <term>TRASHVMANARE</term> means to transcend from human nature to divine nature.

If I was only that part of me which you created
most recently, O Love who governs the heavens,
you know it, you who lifted me with your light.
When the sphere that you make eternal
by being desired, made me intent upon you...

The poet shows that he was rapt by the Holy Spirit, and by the sweetness of the song that he heard, and by the great light that shone upon him. Therefore, he was filled with ineffable joy in his sight and his taste. Wherefore, turning to the Holy Spirit, he speaks as a man now returned to the world. O Holy Spirit...

<header>->PARADISO<-</header>

with the harmony that you temper and distinguish
It seemed to me then that so much of the heaven was kindled
by the flame of the sun, that neither rain nor river
ever made a lake so wide-spread.
The novelty of the sound and the great light
kindled in me a desire for their cause,
never before felt with such sharp edge.

Whereupon she, who saw me as I see myself,
to quiet my troubled mind,
opened her mouth before I could ask,
And began: "You make yourself dull
with false imagining, so that you do not see
what you would see if you had shaken it off.
You are not on earth, as you believe;
but lightning, fleeing its own home,
never ran as fast as you, who return to yours."

If I was stripped of my first doubt
by these brief, smiling words,
I was more entangled within a new one.
And I said: "Already I rested content,
satisfied of my great wonder; but now I wonder
how I can transcend these light bodies."

<column-break/>

...that if love, which governs the heavens: only when I was in such meditation, I was that sun which you created in me anew when you transformed me, you do it. Because you raised me with your light, <term>i.</term> <note>original: "i."; abbreviation for the Latin *id est*, meaning "that is"</note> you made me elevated to such contemplation with the light that you infused into my mind. And he shows here that what the sacred letters affirm was in him: that without the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, one does not come to such high speculations. **WHEN THE WHEEL** <note>original: "QUANDO Larota"</note>: because not only the heavens but all things created by God turn around with the desire they have to see Him. Therefore, when the wheel—that is, the revolution of the heavens which you, Holy Spirit, desired: because every creature desires, as much as its nature allows, to enjoy God—**ETERNAL** <note>original: "sempiterni"</note>. That is, you cause them to turn eternally; "turned toward you," that is, I became attentive to that revolution of the heavens which you make. And this was because of the harmony that I heard from them. And the Platonists especially approved of such harmony. All the heavens revolve from the **First Mobile** <term>Primum Mobile; the outermost moving sphere in the geocentric model which moves all the others</term> downward. These are nine: seven spheres of the seven planets, the eighth sphere <note>the sphere of the fixed stars</note>, and the First Mobile. And through their movement, each generates its own sound. But they are varied according to whether they are higher or lower; and from all of them results a most sweet melody and an excellent proportion of voices which the Greeks call **harmony**. **WITH THE HARMONY WHICH YOU TEMPER AND DISTINGUISH** <note>original: "CON lharmonia che tu tempri et discerni"</note>: he spoke correctly, because a sweet melody cannot result from many voices unless they are tempered with due proportion; nor can they have proportion if they are not distinct with variety. **IT SEEMED TO ME THEN THAT SO MUCH OF THE HEAVEN WAS KINDLED** <note>original: "PARVIMI tanto allhor del cielo acceso"</note>: He proceeds in great order: because first the Holy Spirit was infused into him; then, having been "transhumanized" <note>elevated beyond human limits</note> by that, he was elevated to heaven, and in that elevation he heard the harmony. Through this, looking attentively, he began to see the moon, the first planet—not as small as it is seen down here, but as large as it is in its own measure. And he concludes that the flame of the sun kindles so much space in the heaven of the moon that no river on earth ever made so great a lake. **THE NOVELTY OF THE SOUND** <note>original: "LANOUITA del sono"</note>: that is, the harmony newly heard; and the greatness of that light **GAVE ME DESIRE** <note>original: "MI dectono disio"</note>: that is, the desire to know the cause of the harmony and the light. **WITH SUCH SHARP EDGE** <note>original: "DITANTO acume"</note>: that is, with such piercing and stimulus.

I was kindled with fervent desire to understand the cause of the light and the song. **WHEREUPON SHE** <note>original: "ONDE ella"</note>: that is, Beatrice herself, **WHO SAW ME** <note>original: "LAQVAL uedea me"</note>: she knew my will, although I did not manifest it to her. **AS I SEE MYSELF** <note>original: "SI chomio"</note>: no differently than I do myself. **OPENED HER MOUTH** <note>original: "APRIO laboccha"</note>: she opened her mouth and began to speak to quiet my mind, which was moved by the aforementioned desire. **BEFORE I COULD ASK** <note>original: "CHE adimandare"</note>: the meaning is that, although it seemed appropriate that I should first ask what I desired to understand, and then she should explain it to me so that my mind might remain quiet, nevertheless, because she knew my will no differently than I did, she anticipated me. **AND BEGAN: YOU MAKE YOURSELF DULL** <note>original: "ET comincio tu stessi ti fai grosso"</note>: your imagination of being on earth when you are in heaven. **YOU MAKE YOURSELF DULL** <note>original: "TI fai grosso"</note>: that is, of slow wit in understanding the cause of the light you see and the sound you hear. Because if you realized you were in heaven and had shaken such an imagination from your mind, you would easily understand the cause yourself. **YOU ARE NOT ON EARTH AS YOU BELIEVE** <note>original: "TV non se interra si come tu credi"</note>: He demonstrates his false imagining. **BUT LIGHTNING** <note>original: "MAI folgore"</note>: He shows that Dante has climbed to the first heaven with more speed than lightning descends to earth from its first site where it is created, which is the second region of the air. **THAT YOU NOW RETURN** <note>original: "CHE adesso riedi"</note>: that you now return; and not without reason did he not say "approach," but "return." This is so Dante does not intend to show that he climbed to heaven with his body, even though he feigns it so, but with the mind, whose site is heaven. Nor should it be unknown to us that every created thing has its own place granted to it by nature. Therefore, since the proper site of the soul is heaven, it can elevate itself to God in an instant.

**DANTE HAVING UNDERSTOOD BEATRICE** <note>original: "HAVERE inteso Danthea Beatrice"</note>: that he had already ascended to the first heaven, it made the first doubt clear to him. But from that, a second doubt was born: how he, a heavy body, could have mounted through the light bodies—that is, through the air and through the element of fire. He says, therefore: **IF I WAS STRIPPED** <note>original: "SIO fui disuestito"</note>: that is, despoiled. **OF THE FIRST DOUBT** <note>original: "DEL Primo dubio"</note>: which was from where such great light and such sweet sound arose, by the brief words of Beatrice...

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on Dante's Paradiso, Canto I. Beatrice has just corrected Dante’s misconception that he is still on earth, explaining that he is actually ascending through the spheres of air and fire toward the heavens. This page focuses on the philosophical "Order of the Universe" and the natural instincts that guide all creatures toward their proper "port" or destination.</meta>

<columns>2</columns>
<header>->CANTO ONE<-</header>

Whereupon she, after a pious sigh,
directed her eyes toward me with the look
that a mother gives her delirious son,
And began: "All things whatever
have an order among themselves, and this is the form
that makes the universe like unto God.
Here the higher creatures see the footprint
of the eternal power, which is the end
for which the aforementioned rule was made.

In the order of which I speak, all natures
are inclined, through diverse fates,
more or less near to their origin;
Wherefore they move to different ports
across the great sea of being, and each one
with an instinct given to it that carries it.
This carries fire toward the moon;
this is the mover in mortal hearts;
this binds and unites the earth in itself.
Nor does this bow shoot only creatures
devoid of intelligence,
but those who have intellect and love.
The Providence that settles so much
with its light makes the heaven forever quiet
in which that sphere turns which has the greatest haste."

<column-break/>

...you when she said "you are not on earth." **SHE SMILED**, meaning she said this smiling. **I WAS ENTANGLED**, <term>i.</term> <note>original: "i."; abbreviation for the Latin *id est*, meaning "that is"</note> caught and wrapped up: like a bird in a net. **AND I SAID** to Beatrice: **I RESTED**, <term>i.</term> <note>original: "Requieui"</note> I became quiet and remained satisfied regarding my **GREAT WONDER**, which caused my first doubt. **BUT NOW AGAIN I WONDER**, <term>i.</term> I marvel how I transcend: how I, a heavy body, can ascend and pass through these light and airy bodies of air and fire. **WHEREUPON AFTERWARD**: first Beatrice sighs out of the pity she felt for Dante's error and ignorance; and she looked at him as a mother looks at her son. **DELIRIOUS**, <term>i.</term> <note>original: "deliro"</note> he who is off the true path. *Lira* in Latin is the "furrow"; hence we say the plowman is *delirious* <note>the word "delirious" historically comes from *de-lira*, meaning to "deviate from the furrow" while plowing</note> when he goes out of the furrow while plowing. And then, by similarity, we call an old person *delirious* when through age they wander from the true path. And in short, we sometimes simply call any foolish person *delirious*. **THE DELIRIOUS SON**: the son who has lost his reason. **AND BEGAN** to speak, saying **ALL THINGS WHATEVER HAVE ORDER**: She shows that no one marvels except at things for which the reason is unknown to them. Therefore, Dante marvelling at his ascent shows that the reason for natural things is unknown to him—things in which there is the highest reason and order, which, if Dante knew it, he would not marvel. Because of this, his wondering reveals his ignorance; this moved Beatrice to look at him like a mother looks at a delirious son. **ALL THINGS**: created by God, have order among themselves. **ORDER** is the arrangement of many things, equal and unequal, which places each one according to its being, and according to its dignity or merit. God, therefore, has placed this order in his creatures. **AND THIS IS THE FORM**: **FORM** is that which gives "being" to a thing. For example: an image of Caesar has within it the matter and the form. The matter is the marble from which it is made, and the form is that which the sculptor introduced, which is like Caesar. Therefore, it is not the marble that makes it like Caesar, but the form, without which it would not be an image of Caesar. We also say that reason is the "form" of man, because one cannot be a man if reason is not in him. **THAT MAKES THE UNIVERSE LIKE UNTO GOD**: God created every creature in his likeness. Regarding this, Boethius says: *You lead all things from the heavenly pattern, yourself most beautiful, bearing the beautiful world in your mind, and fashioning it in a like image, you command the perfect parts to complete a perfect whole.* <note>original Latin: "Tu cuncta superno ducis ab exemplo pulchrum pulcherrimus ipse mundum mente gerens similique imagine formas perfectas que iubes perfectas absoluere partes." From *The Consolation of Philosophy*.</note> **HERE** in this order **THE HIGHER CREATURES**, which are the angels and men of high intellect, see **THE FOOTPRINT**: the vestige of the eternal power <term>i.</term> of God, who was able, knew how, and willed to produce every creature with such order that his vestige appears in each one. **WHICH IS THE END**: God is the end of every thing, because just as every thing has its beginning from him, so to him every thing refers. The order placed in things is that by which things produced by the highest principle might return to it as their end. This order connects the creature to the Creator. **IN THE ORDER OF WHICH I SPEAK**: In this order, God has placed all creatures, and to them he has given a natural state to return to their Creator as their end. They are inclined to this. This inclination was established by divine wisdom, which Plato calls **PROVIDENCE**. And he placed it in the creatures. Therefore, when Plato considers such inclination in the divine mind, he calls it Providence; but when he considers it in the creature, he calls it **FATE**. Nevertheless, it is necessary that in such an order some creatures are closer to God, <term>i.</term> more capable of divinity, such as first the angels, then men. Some are further away; for the tree is further than the brute animal, and the stone further than the tree. Therefore, **BEING** (since it subsists in all creatures) is like a **SPACIOUS SEA**. And because in this "being" there is one nature for the angel, another for man (in whom there is reason), another in the brute (in whom there is sense), another in the tree (in whom there is no sense but only vegetative life), and another in the stone (which lacks reason, sense, and vegetative life), it follows that as their natures are diverse, so too are their inclinations toward diverse ends. Therefore, from this "sea of being," not all sail to one port, <term>i.</term> to one end, but to diverse ones, because there are diverse ends and diverse ends have diverse ways, which Dante calls "fates" <note>original: "forti"</note>...

<summary>Beatrice explains the divine order of the universe to Dante, using the metaphor of a "sea of being" where every creature is guided by instinct toward its proper destination. Landino provides a scholastic commentary on "form," "order," and the etymology of "delirious," while citing Boethius to support the idea of God as the architect of the world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on the first canto of Dante’s Paradiso. Beatrice is explaining the "Order of the Universe," a central concept in medieval philosophy where every object and soul has a natural place it seeks to return to. She is addressing Dante's confusion about how his physical body can ascend through the spheres of air and fire.</meta>

# CANTO PARADISO

...calling it fate according to Plato. Therefore, they move toward diverse ports and ends: and every creature is gathered with the instinct given to it by God, which moves it to its end. Therefore, the human mind, whose end and highest good is to know, love, and enjoy God, has a natural instinct to return to God; for which reason Dante should not have wondered if he had ascended to the contemplation of God, because our natural instinct carries our mind toward God in this way. Just as the natural instinct of fire carries it upward toward the moon—because there is the resting place of light things—this same instinct moves our hearts toward God for the reason already stated; and likewise, it moves the earth to compress itself in the center of the world, because being heavy, it desires the lowest position. Nor is only this bow made: by comparison, he uses the "bow" to represent the aforementioned inclination, and the "arrow" for the thing moved by that inclination, like an arrow from a bow. Therefore, the meaning is that this inclination is not only in irrational creatures, but also in rational ones, such as man who has intelligence and love. The Providence that so much adjusts—<term>that is <note>original: "i."; abbreviation for the Latin id est</note></term> prepares and opportunely disposes—always makes the heaven quiet: the Empyrean heaven where His celestial court is, by His light, because such a heaven is filled with seraphic flames. Whence it is called Empyrean, meaning as if ignited or on fire. And for this reason, the Greeks call it Olympus, as if <term>all-shining <note>original: "ololampos"</note></term>, which signifies completely splendid. Within which revolves that which has the greatest haste—<term>that is <note>original: "i."</note></term> the First Mobile <note>The Primum Mobile, the outermost moving sphere in the medieval cosmos which moves the fastest to distribute motion to the lower spheres</note>, which moves with more velocity than the others.

> And now there, as to a decreed site,
> the power of that string carries us,
> which directs whatever it shoots to a happy mark.
> It is true that, as a form often does not accord
> with the intention of the art,
> because the material is deaf to responding,
> So from this course the creature
> sometimes departs, having the power
> to swerve, though thus impelled, in another direction;
> And just as fire may be seen to fall
> from a cloud, if the first impulse
> is twisted toward the earth by false pleasure.
> You should not wonder more, if I judge rightly,
> at your climbing, any more than at a stream
> if it descends from a high mountain to the base.
> It would be a wonder in you if, deprived
> of impediment, you had remained seated below,
> like living fire remaining quiet on the earth."
> With this, she turned her face back toward heaven.

<column-break/>

**AND NOW THERE AS TO A DECREED SITE.** The power of that string carries us. The power of that string—<term>that is <note>original: "i."</note></term> of that inclination: which inclination **DIRECTS TO A HAPPY MARK**: <term>that is <note>original: "idest"</note></term> to the right end where our highest good is. **WHATEVER SHOOTS**: whatever proceeds. **CARRIES**: it conducts us. **THERE**: <term>that is <note>original: "idest"</note></term> to that Empyrean heaven where God, our highest good, is. **AS TO A DECREED SITE**: <term>that is <note>original: "idest"</note></term> as to the place determined for our rest. **IT IS TRUE THAT AS**: He removes a doubt: because someone could infer: "If in our soul there is a natural instinct to return to God, why are there many who go the opposite way?" To which he responds that the creature who has power—<term>that is <note>original: "i."</note></term> has free will in themselves to choose good and evil—sometimes, overcome by sensuality, which pushes them in the opposite direction, distances themselves from God. Just as we see fire, which although by its nature is impelled upward, nevertheless if in the air it creates a thick vapor <note>A reference to the medieval scientific explanation for lightning, which was thought to be fire trapped in moist clouds and forced downward</note> desirous of that element, it follows it even to the earth; so the rational soul, which has as its natural instinct the following of its own good, often, deceived by sensuality, follows a false good. **YOU SHOULD NOT WONDER MORE**: He concludes, for the reasons already stated, that Dante should no longer marvel if his mind ascends to God;

because natural instinct draws it toward its good, just as one would marvel if a river located in the mountains descended to the bottom where its nature pulls it. But one should marvel if his soul, placed on earth—<term>that is <note>original: "idest"</note></term> in the body—remained at the bottom, just as if "living fire"—<term>that is <note>original: "idest"</note></term> a flame—lay at the bottom and did not rise up. **THERE SHE TURNED**: Having said these words, Beatrice turned back toward heaven. This signifies that Theology sometimes descends into lower things for our salvation, but only to turn us afterward, through those things, toward celestial matters.

<summary>This page explains the metaphysical "gravity" of the universe, where the soul's natural instinct is to rise toward God just as fire rises toward the heavens. It addresses the existence of sin as a deviation caused by free will and the "deafness" of material things to the divine artist's intention.</summary>
<keywords>natural instinct, Empyrean, free will, sensuality, Beatrice, Christoforo Landino, allegory of fire, Primum Mobile, divine order</keywords>

# SECOND CANTO OF THE THIRD CANTICLE OF DANTE

<image-desc>The manuscript page features two illuminated initial letters at the top. On the left, a large decorative 'O' initiates the poetic text, containing a circular miniature portrait of a figure in blue robes, possibly a poet or scholar, against a dark blue background. On the right, a large decorative 'E' initiates the commentary, filled with vibrant red and green floral and foliate motifs on a gold leaf background.</image-desc>

O you who are in a little boat,
eager to listen, following
behind my ship that singing sails,
Turn back to see your own shores;
do not trust yourselves to the open sea, for perhaps,
losing me, you would remain lost.
The water I take was never cruised before;
Minerva breathes and Apollo leads me,
and nine Muses show me the Bears. <note>The "Bears" refers to the constellations Ursa Major and Ursa Minor, which sailors used for navigation toward the North Star.</note>
You other few who lifted your necks
betimes for the bread of angels, on which
one lives here but never comes away sated,
You may well commit to the salt deep
your vessel, keeping to my furrow
before the water that returns level.
Those glorious ones who crossed to Colchis <note>A reference to the Argonauts, the first sailors in Greek mythology who sought the Golden Fleece.</note>
did not marvel as much as you shall do,
when they saw Jason turned plowman.

<column-break/>

The poet has already ascended to the first sphere. Wherefore this, his second canto, describes how he entered the lunar body; and having asked Beatrice the cause of the darkness and shadow which appears in the moon, she speaks her opinion. But Beatrice refutes it and then demonstrates the truth to him. Now, as for this beginning, he admonishes the vulgar crowd: those who are learned only in the minor doctrines, and not learned in sacred things; who have been able to follow him until now: that they should not hold on any further: because not being capable of such high matter, they might become lost. Especially because he treats that which has never been treated by any other. And on the other hand, he comforts the learned in sacred theology—who are few—to follow him, promising them that they will marvel more than the companions of Jason marveled in Colchis. **O YOU** who are in a little boat. It is a metaphor used by many poets to set the sea for the subject matter, and the ship for the intellect or the doctrine. Therefore: **O you who in a little boat**: <term>that is <note>original: "cioe"</note></term> with little doctrine or talent. Eager to listen to my poem. **FOLLOW** behind my ship: come behind my style and my doctrine. **WHICH** sails singing: because every poet is said to sing. Whence in the first canticle: *I was a poet and I sang of that just one.* <note>Dante quotes Virgil’s introduction from Inferno, Canto I.</note> **TURN** back to see your shores: from which you departed, <term>as if to say <note>original: "quasi dicat"</note></term>: stay in low matter suitable to your weak talents. **DO NOT** put yourselves to the open sea, <term>that is <note>original: "i."</note></term> in such profound and difficult matter: that perhaps **LOSING** me you will remain lost: like one who, not knowing the route, follows the guide; if he loses the guide, he becomes lost. Thus, he who follows an author writing high and difficult things can understand something at the beginning; but when he arrives where he does not understand, it can be said that he has lost him and remains lost. **LOSING** me: losing my way, which is not well-trodden among other poets. **THE** water I run was never cruised before: through an abundance of eloquence, he says now "sea," now "deep," and now "water" for the same thing; and he stays within the metaphor. The meaning is that the sea he sails was never sailed: meaning by other poets or other writers. He does not deny that many have written most learnedly of the things he writes; but no one ever wrote poetically and in an allegorical sense, adorned with poetic faculty, such matter. **MINERVA** breathes: the poet could seem presumptuous affirming that no poet ever wrote of such high matter. Wherefore he demonstrates that not by his own talent, but by the help of Minerva, of Apollo, and of the Muses has he been able to; <term>as if to say <note>original: "quasi dica"</note></term> not by himself, but by grace infused by the Holy Spirit. He intends Minerva as the giver of wisdom; and through Apollo and through the Muses proceeds the style and the poetic song. Because the Holy Spirit, infusing itself into the human mind, makes the unlearned learned and the coarse eloquent, as we see in the prophets and in the apostles. Therefore, he does not say he runs water never run before out of simple arrogance, but says he has run it by means of divine favor. **MINERVA** breathes: three things are necessary to one who desires prosperous navigation: first, the wind that pushes you to the port. Therefore Minerva, who is wisdom, directs the ship to a good port. And Apollo, who is harmony, disposes and orders the body with due proportion. The Muses show the Bears, <term>that is <note>original: "idest"</note></term> the north star, without which every ship is lost. By the Muses, understand the poetic faculty, without which the poet does not see what style he has to follow. **YOU** other few: having admonished the unlearned that they should not follow him through this sea, now he comforts the learned to follow him because they will be able to understand him; and he says "few" because in every century there has been a small number of the learned and of elevated talents. Whence Aristotle: <note>original: "Ingeniu rude et non subtilissimus intellectus ita se habet ad diuina sicut uisus noctue ad solem."</note> *A crude mind and a not very subtle intellect is related to divine things as the sight of an owl is to the sun.* And Thomas Aquinas: <note>original: "Cognitio diuinorum paucis hominibus inest"</note> *Knowledge of divine things exists in few men.* And certainly there is great difficulty in this knowledge, because all the other parts of philosophy were found so they might be a ladder by which we can climb to this height. **WHO** lifted your necks: who raised the head, which cannot be raised if the neck is not straightened. And by the raising of the head, he means that they lifted their minds and their talent to celestial things, and he covertly touches upon the sentiment of Ovid: <note>original: "Pronaque cum spectent animalia cetera terras. Os homini sublime dedit celumque tueri. Iussit et erectos ad sydera tollere uultus."</note> *And while other animals look downwards at the earth, He gave to man an uplifted face and ordered him to gaze at the sky and raise his countenance erect toward the stars.* **BETIMES**: <term>as if to say <note>original: "quasi dica"</note></term> from your youth...

Landino’s commentary explains the nautical metaphors of the ship and the sea as symbols for the intellect and the divine subject matter.</summary>

# PARADISO

### Page 2

...youth <note>original: "adolescentia"</note>: signifying by this the difficulty of divine doctrine, which we cannot well acquire if from our earliest years we do not give ourselves to the study of the liberal arts. **To the bread of angels**: just as the body feeds and lives on corporeal food, so the intellect is nourished by divine fruition and cognition, which he calls the "bread of angels" because they enjoy this, and in this alone they find life. **Of which river**: that is <note>original: "idest"</note>, among us mortals, because the soul, while it is in the body, sustains itself with this doctrine. **But one does not come away sated**: because we cannot have so much cognition that it satisfies us and is enough for us on earth. But it is so in heaven. **You may well commit to the salt deep**: that is, to the high sea; meaning, you can follow me into this profound matter. **Keeping to my furrow**: He wants them to follow him so closely that the furrow made by his ship does not close up for them; when the water returns to being level, the distinction made in the water is lost. He warns those who follow him not to wait until such a distinction disappears, because when they no longer recognize the distinction between the allegorical and literal senses, and from the fictional thing to the truth, they will not be able to understand him.

**THOSE GLORIOUS ONES**: An excellent comparison through which he demonstrates that the Greek Argonauts did not marvel so much when in Colchis they saw Jason sowing the dragon's teeth—from which armed men were born—as you will marvel at what I shall say, and not without merit. For if that was against nature, this is so hidden in the secrets of nature that it does not seem natural. **Glorious**: greedy for glory, or truly glorious because they were held in great fame among the Greeks. **In Colchis**: a city in Pontus where the Golden Fleece was kept. **Plowman** <note>original: "Bifolco"</note>: a plowman, which in Latin is called *bubulcus*. I do not narrate this fable at present because we have narrated it elsewhere.

The concreated and perpetual thirst
for the deiform kingdom carried us away,
swift almost as you see the heavens move.
Beatrice looked upward, and I at her;
and perhaps in such time as a bolt <note>a "quadrel" is a square-headed arrow used in crossbows</note> strikes,
and flies, and is released from the notch,
I saw myself arrived where a marvelous thing
turned my sight to itself; and therefore she,
from whom my work could not be hidden,
turned toward me, as glad as she was beautiful,
and said: "Direct your mind to God in gratitude,
who has joined us with the first star."

It seemed to me that a cloud covered us,
lucid, thick, solid, and polished,
like a diamond struck by the sun.
Within itself the eternal pearl
received us, just as water receives
a ray of light, remaining united.
If I was a body—and here it is not conceived
how one dimension could suffer another,
which must be if one body enters another—
the desire should further inflame us...

<column-break/>

**The Thirst**: that is, the great desire. **Concreated**: created together. For God created, together with our soul, a supreme desire within it to go to the Highest Good, which is God Himself. And He not only created this desire in us, but created it so that it lives forever in our soul, perpetual. Therefore he says they were carried by the concreated and perpetual thirst they possessed. **Of the deiform kingdom**: that is, of blessedness and the Highest Good, of which God is the form; nor is the Highest Good anything other than God Himself. **Beatrice upward**: this sentence was explained above. **And perhaps as much**: he demonstrates that the interval of time was no longer than placing a bolt or arrow on a loaded crossbow and "un-notching," that is, releasing the crossbow and the arrow flying to the mark. And it is from the earth to the heaven of the Moon, ascending in a straight line, one hundred forty-eight thousand and five hundred forty miles. **I saw myself arrived**: he saw himself arrived in a marvelous place; and Beatrice, who knew his wondering and that he did not understand what place that was—because nothing that was in Dante could be hidden from her, since Theology knows what our already-purified soul desires—said: "Direct your mind in gratitude to God because He has joined us with the first star," that is, with the Moon, which is the first star and planet above the elements. Nor for any other reason did Beatrice admonish him to direct his mind in gratitude to God for having arrived at the first star, except to demonstrate that every good work of ours, and every cognition and intelligence, comes from divine help. **Because** we must not glory in ourselves but give glory to Him, and be grateful for the gift received. **Furthermore**, he said "as glad as she was beautiful": Theology is always beautiful because she always tells true things, which are always beautiful. But when she narrates punishments and threats to the sinner, she does not show herself glad. But when she gives us cognition of celestial things, she always appears beautiful to us and gives us joy.

**He describes** the nature of the lunar body, which is lucid, dense, solid, and polished. The Moon is seven times larger than the Earth. **A thick, lucid cloud** appeared to be the body of the Moon. And note here that some bodies are naturally luminous, like the sun. Some reflect like a mirror. Some are transparent like glass and water. **Like a diamond**. Because the lunar body, dark by its own nature, shines when the sun strikes it, just as a diamond does. **Within itself the eternal pearl**: he calls the Moon a pearl <note>original: "margherita"</note>, and explains the same thing: that the lunar body...

it has no light of its own: But is lucid <gloss>that is, receptive of light</gloss> like a diamond and the pearl, which, if they had their own light, would shine at night. **R**egarding the thanks to God: he thanks God as he was admonished by Beatrice for such an immense benefit, having already been elevated to the first heaven and separated from the mortal world. This was the opinion of Albumasar <note>A famous Persian astronomer known in the Middle Ages as Abu Ma'shar</note>, that such darkness in the moon is from its specific nature, just as we say the magnet <note>original: "calamita"</note> pulls iron to itself; nor can we give any other reason for it, except that it is by its specific nature. Others say it comes from the shadow of the earth. With her arguments, she will show him that this is false.

**A**rguing against the author, Beatrice says that if Dante's opinion were true, an inconsistency would follow, which we shall see shortly below. But first she puts forward a proposition that is true: that the eighth heaven has many stars of different splendor and different size. For example, the star called the Dog Star <note>Sirius</note> shines more and is larger than many others. This is why astronomers divide them into first and [second magnitudes]...

<column-break/>

In the previous argument, Beatrice had demonstrated that Dante's opinion was generally false regarding all celestial bodies. Now, through this, she demonstrates it specifically regarding the body of the moon. The argument is this: If "rarity" is the reason for the moon’s shadows, I ask you if that rarity passes through the lunar body from one surface to the other, or if it does not pass through entirely. But it is false that it passes through entirely. Because if the moon were perforated from one side to the other, when a lunar eclipse occurs, the sun's rays would pass through that hole. If you say that such a hole does not pass to the other side, but after some distance is closed off by the "dense," the shadow could still not appear, as experience shows in the section that follows. **OR OTHERWISE**: i.e., throughout the whole body; in essence, if where the shadow is there were rarity, like the body of an animal that first has fat... **PAGES**: This is a metaphor from a book where one face is white. **BY SHINING THROUGH**: i.e., by the ray of the sun which passes through.

She has demonstrated that the shadow cannot proceed from rarity if such rarity passed all the way through. Now she demonstrates that if the rarity does not pass to the other side, it similarly cannot be the cause of the shadow. Therefore, if the rarity passes for a certain distance and then the "dense"—its contrary—follows, it is necessary that the solar rays pass through all the "rare" and then, finding the "dense," they are reflected back as in a mirror where the color is reflected and returns through the glass itself. And in this way, rarity will not be the cause of the shadow, since the rays reflect from the dense as we have shown. **NOW YOU WILL SAY**: But you might say that although the reflection still illuminates in that rarity, nevertheless, because it originates deeper within the lunar body where the rarity is than it does in the rest where it originates on the surface [it appears darker]. Beatrice responds that Dante can free himself from...

She proves that although the reflection comes from different distances, the one further away does not reflect less for that reason; and she proves it thus: Take three mirrors and place them before your sight, but in a way that one of the mirrors is further from you and the other two are closer. And above your head let there be a light that strikes all three mirrors: there is no doubt that although in the closer ones the light appears larger, nevertheless it does not shine more brightly in the closer ones than in the distant one.

The sight further away you will see
how it is necessary that it reflects equally
Now, as by the strikes of the warm rays
the underlying subject of the snow remains naked,
both of its color and its former cold
So, you, having remained thus in your intellect,
I wish to form with a light so true
that it will quiver in your sight.

<column-break/>

**in the distance**. And if you said that the light is smaller there, there should be less splendor and not equal: I respond that the splendor is not in the *quánto* <note>original: "quánto," meaning "how much" or quantity.</note>—that is, in the quantity—but in the quality. Therefore, the ray that reflects from further away will not shine less as it enters [the mirror], as long as the ray lasts until it reaches the dense part, than those rays which reflect off the surface where they find the dense material. **AND RETURNS To** thee, reflected from all. That is, the light is such that it strikes all the lights; and you are in a place where such a reflection returns to your eyes: because otherwise you would not see it. **NOW as by the strikes.** <note>D. f. p. likely stands for the opening of the verse: "della fredda parte" or similar shorthand.</note> Just as the **subject of the snow**—that is, the place upon which the snow sits—remains naked and deprived of the color and the cold of the snow by the warm rays of the sun, so you, having remained naked of your [false] opinion, I will inform you with **light so true**—that is, with such open truth—that it will shine and be resplendent in your breast.

<column-break/>

Within the heaven of divine peace
there turns a body in whose virtue
the being of all that it contains rests.
The following heaven, which has so many sights,
distributes that being through diverse essences
distinguished by it and contained by it.

<column-break/>

Because he brings Beatrice to speak—whom we have said is **Theology**—he makes her speak not as a **physicist** but as a **theologian**. For the common opinion of philosophers is that the shadow on the moon, divided into roughly three parts, is the shadow of the Earth. We divide the Earth into three parts: **Asia** in the eastern part, which is alone as large as the other two together with the Mediterranean Sea; **Africa** in the southern part; and **Europe** in the north. But of this we shall speak more extensively in Canto XXII. However, Beatrice, speaking as a theologian, proposes this argument: All celestial bodies induce diverse effects in lower things according to their power and the virtue of the **Intelligences** <note>Angelic beings responsible for moving the celestial spheres.</note> infused in them. This is proven by the influences that the lower bodies receive from them. He says, therefore: **WITHIN THE heaven of divine peace**: This is the **Empyrean heaven**, which, because it is immobile and does not turn, he calls the heaven of divine peace, wherein lies the celestial kingdom where souls enjoy eternal peace. **There turns a body**: this is the **Primum Mobile** <term>Primum Mobile: The "First Mover," the ninth and outermost moving sphere in the Ptolemaic universe which drives the motion of all other spheres.</term>, the ninth heaven; and it is called the **Crystalline heaven**, contained within the immobile Empyrean heaven. **IN whose virtue**: In the virtue of that Crystalline heaven, which is both the motive [moving] and effective power. **THE BEING of all that it contains**: the conservation of existence, and the motive and effective virtue of all its contents. This ninth heaven, which is the "First Mover"—that is, the first that is moved by the Empyrean—embraces all the other heavens, which are the eighth sphere and the seven planets. The heavens of the **seven planets** are not made of compact and dense matter, and for this reason they are transparent and do not prevent our sight from passing through to the eighth, where the **Zodiac** and the other fixed stars are. But if the eighth were not so, we would see the ninth in the tenth. All move with the Primum Mobile and make one revolution in twenty-four hours from East to West, and then back to the East. And through that natural and uniform motion, each takes an effective virtue according to its power to preserve itself in being and to preserve other lower things; and nonetheless, each turns with its own proper movement in the opposite direction from West to East. Because of this, the eighth heaven moves one degree every hundred years. Therefore, in the virtue of the ninth heaven (the Primum Mobile) which is inside the Empyrean heaven (the heaven of divine peace), lies the being of all that it contains—that is, all things contained by it—because it, with its effective virtue, moves them, which is the cause of the conservation of the others and of their movement. Just as the **moving angels** are the cause of the conservation of being and movement. **SO MANY Sights**: so many stars, which are all seen. **THAT being**: that essential effective and motive virtue which preserves the existence that is in the virtue of the ninth heaven and which is received from it. **DISTRIBUTES**: divides and distributes through diverse essences and substances that the eighth heaven has within itself, distinct from it, such as the stars; which are of a different matter than it, and have different effects, yet they are contained by it. The other seven heavens of the planets turn the distinction they have within themselves—that is, the seven planets distinguished by various differences: because the planets are very different in position, in course, and in nature, as has already been said; and it will be said more distinctly of each one. **AND THEY DISPOSE their seeds**: that is, their causative virtues are the cause of the lower effects and dispose them to their proper end. Just as the seed of grain produces the effect (the grain), which afterward is the seed for another grain, so the celestial bodies which are the cause of lower effects are also the effect of causes superior to them. Therefore, the Primum Mobile has virtue infused by God and by its movers, which must preserve its own being and that of all the heavens and elements it contains. This is the motive and effective virtue that moves all the other heavens and...

-># PARADISO<-

elements and cause in their various effects according to their various powers. And so the superior virtue always pours into all the inferior ones, and causes, as has been said, diverse effects according to how the inferior bodies are diverse. But it acts more effectively in the most immediate inferior body, and changes according to how one is different from the other. Thus, the ninth heaven <note>The Primum Mobile, the outermost physical sphere of the universe in the Ptolemaic system.</note> more effectively pours its essential, motive, and conservative virtue into the eighth heaven than into the others; and that virtue, changed within it, pours more into the seventh than into the others, and so on. Furthermore, every planet has its own virtue infused into it by external movers, moving according to its own non-uniform motion. **THESE organs of the world**, that is, these heavens. For just as in man the inferior organs correspond to the superior—the sensory to the brain, the vital to the heart, the nutritive to the liver—and then these two principal ones, the brain and the liver, correspond to the heart, which is the fountain of life and the principal member; so all celestial bodies have their being from God as the first cause of the whole, who has placed in them diverse virtues, just as they are of diverse bodies and movers. And although every heaven has multiple movers that move it to produce its effects, it is nonetheless called one intelligence; just as one soul gives life to the body with multiple powers which move it to produce its effects. Therefore, the first order of angels, which are the **Seraphim**, move the first heaven. The **Cherubim**, the second order, move the eighth heaven. The **Thrones** move Saturn. The **Dominations**, Jupiter. The **Virtues**, Mars. The **Powers**, the Sun. The **Principalities**, Venus. The **Archangels**, Mercury. The **Angels**, the Moon. All these intelligences are moved by God, who is immobile. God moves as the understood and the loved, just as the thing understood and loved moves the one who understands and loves. For this reason, the intelligences, which are all love, turn around God, who is understood and loved by them. These, by moving and turning around Him, always understanding and loving Him, move the things committed to them by God with the virtue that God has placed in them. **From grade to grade**: because the superior always influences the inferior, and each is an effect in relation to the superior, and a cause in relation to the inferior; and therefore he says: **WHICH from above they take** as effects, **and from below they act** as causes. But the ninth heaven has only one movement; however, the others contained by it—that is, the eighth sphere and the seven planets—have two movements. One is from East to West, caused by the first mover and its movers, and is called uniform motion, which occurs in twenty-four hours; and according to this motion, all heavens have effective virtue infused by the first mover, each according to its power to preserve the being of the inferiors; and according to their diverse powers, they have diverse effective virtue. The other motion is erratic and non-uniform, and is produced by the power of the specific movers of each heaven, and goes from West to East; and some complete it more quickly and some more slowly. And always, as has been said, the superior pours its virtue into the one below, and that virtue is diversified according to the power of the one that receives it. And they agree in helping one another, and by counteracting each other, they temper one another. Perhaps the poet also calls them **organs** to touch upon the Platonic opinion that all the heavens make a most sweet sound. <note>A reference to the 'Music of the Spheres,' the ancient theory that the movement of celestial bodies produces a divine harmony.</note>

The motion and the virtue of the holy gyres,
as from the smith the art of the hammer,
from the blessed movers must breathe.
The heaven which so many lights make beautiful,
from the profound mind that turns it,
takes the image and becomes its seal.
And as the soul within our dust,
through different members and adapted
to diverse powers, resolves itself,
So the intelligence its goodness,
multiplied through the stars, unfolds,
turning itself upon its own unity.

<column-break/>

Through the things already said, what the poet presently posits is nearly manifest. Therefore, the **motion of the holy gyres**, that is, of the heavens, must breathe and proceed from the **blessed movers** of whom we have spoken, just as the **art of the hammer proceeds from the smith**. For the hammer, striking in various ways, induces form into the iron, and makes of it either a sickle for the farmer or a sword for the warrior; nevertheless, such motion is from the smith. **The heaven which**: that is, the eighth heaven, where the fixed stars are. And he says that this heaven, from the **profound virtue**—that is, the infinite divine virtue which turns it by means of its Cherubim—takes the **image**, that is, the virtue imprinted in it as the image of a seal is imprinted in wax, both in regard to its non-uniform motion and its natural and uniform motion through the medium of the first heaven. **AND becomes its seal**: because it then imprints, according to its power, that virtue first imprinted in it into the inferior things.

**PROFOUNDLY**: this is the divine virtue, which is infinite. Whence Boethius: *He circles the profound mind and turns the heaven with a similar image.* <note>original Latin: "Mentemque profundam circuit et simili conuertit imagine celum." From Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, Book III, meter 9.</note> Then, to better declare it, he says that just as the soul of man, which is one, extending itself into various members, demonstrates various powers according to the nature of the member—for in the heart it gives life, in the liver it nourishes, in the brain it senses—so the **intelligence**, which is one in the eighth heaven, extending itself into all the stars, gives various influences, acting according to the various powers of those stars. It infuses itself into Saturn, which is cold and dry, and gives it the influence according to the nature of Saturn; and so in the others.

Diverse virtue makes a diverse alloy
with the precious body that it quickens.

<column-break/>

**DIVERSE Virtue**: this is the conclusion of the things mentioned above; and by those, one understands this place of—

<header>CANTO TWO</header>

> wherein life binds itself within it,
> through the joyful nature from which it derives,
> the mixed virtue shines through the body,
> as joy does through a living pupil.
> From this comes what appears different from light to light,
> not from dense and rare;
> this is the formal principle that produces,
> according to its goodness, the dark and the bright.

<column-break/>

diverse connection and mixture: just as we say silver is made of different alloys. **WITH THE PRECIOUS body**: These are celestial bodies, but made of more precious matter than other bodies. **TO THE DIVINE**: Because it knows how to live and operate its effects. The Platonists hold that all stars are animate. And Augustine, in his *Retractations* <note>Augustine’s late-life revisions of his earlier works.</note>, writes that he has not found in Holy Scripture how he might prove or refute whether the world is animate. But if it has a soul, he asserts that the soul is not God, but made by God. **IN WHICH**: Life binds itself within the body just as vegetative life binds itself within the human body. And such a connection causes the diversity of effects according to the diversity of the celestial bodies. **THROUGH the joyful nature**: Which is God, simple in form and immutable, by whom the angels are created. And from this joyful nature—that is, from God, the highest good—derive the angels, who are a **mixed virtue** because they are of an immutable nature insofar as they are confirmed in grace, and of a mutable nature insofar as they perform their operations successively. It is, therefore, a mixed, life-giving nature. Whence Boethius says: <note>original: "Tu triplicis medium nature cuncta mouentem. Conuertens animam per consona membra resoluis. Que conserta duos motus glomerauit in orbem. In semet reditura meat mentemque profundam. Circuit et simili conuertit imagine celum."</note> "You, distributing the soul through harmonious members, move the middle of the triple nature that moves all things; which, being joined together, gathers two motions into a circle, and returning into itself, circles the deep mind and turns the heaven in a similar image." Or rather, let us understand the virtue as being mixed with the body and infused by the movers. **SHINES**: It resplends through the divine nature. **AS joy through a living pupil**: Just as through an eye of flashing and gleaming light we understand the joy of the heart. Therefore, from the divine light proceeds every difference that exists from light to light—that is, from star to star—and not from "rare and dense" <note>The physical theory Beatrice has just spent the canto debunking.</note> as you believed.

That sun which first warmed my breast with love,

Not because [they are only in this] first heaven. This is the argument of [these] grouped tercets: that Beatrice, whom he calls the sun, had [shown him the truth]. The meaning and order of the text is: I saw in that place many faces [ready] to speak, which were **SUCH**: <note>original: "TALI"</note> that is, made in such a way as those [images] that return to us from glass or clear water. So faintly expressed and so little evident that a pearl, which [on a white forehead] is hardly discerned, does not come less strongly—that is, it comes more strongly [than these faces]. In short, those spirits did not appear so clearly as to be [fully] recognized. But how are they seen? **OR IN THE WATER**: [when] the bottoms are lost, that is, black, or in well-polished glass; and like a pearl [on the forehead of a] woman, such that I do not discern that face. Therefore, I took [the opposite error to that which] kindled love between the man—that is, Narcissus—and the fountain in which [he saw himself]. For his error was that he believed his image, which he saw in the fountain, [was a real man]; but I, seeing these true spirits, did not believe they were spirits but images [reflected]. Thus, my error was the contrary of Narcissus's, whose fable we told in the [thirtieth canto of the first part]. **CLEAR WATERS**: The water cannot hold the image well unless it is clear, still, and shallow. Therefore, [what was said] above could be better explained. **AND BLACK BOTTOMS**: <note>original: "EFONDI PERSI"; "persi" refers to a dark, purplish-black color common in Dante's vocabulary.</note> [where the] water's [depths] are not discerned.

<column-break/>

...of which he will treat in the thirtieth canto: nevertheless, he feigns that they represent themselves to him in that heaven which figures the degree they hold in eternal life and in the Empyrean heaven. <note>The Empyrean is the highest heaven, the actual dwelling place of God and the saints, beyond the physical spheres.</note> And under such a fiction, he wishes not only to express the souls separated from bodies and placed in the sight of God, but also those who are still in their bodies but are in the third kind of virtue, called the virtues of the already purified soul. Dante passes through all the heavens, and in each, he finds those souls we have mentioned; and afterward, he finds those same souls in the Empyrean heaven, in the sight of God. Nor is it inconvenient that, being lifted by Beatrice from heaven to heaven up to the Empyrean—that is, being enraptured by theological doctrine—[the truth] presents to the mind those who are blessed through the influence of those virtues. Therefore, let it not be understood that the blessed souls are all in the lowest [heaven]; he finds many blessed souls there, and Beatrice tells him [the truth]. He asks about a doubt, and she responds not only to that [one], but to the whole canto. But the meaning of the six [tercets] has already shown the truth. And he: I was raised to confess. **SUN**: Beatrice, who is the sun because, like the sun [illuminates the world, she illuminates the] mind. **THAT FIRST**: [kindled me] with love... [she] revealed to me the aspect of truth; and he says "sweet" because beauty is so proper to truth that nothing can be beautiful if it is not true. **PROVING**: [the truth] by demonstrative <term>syllogism</term> <note>A logical argument where a conclusion is reached from two linked premises.</term>. And I, to confess myself corrected—that is, [having raised] my head. **MORE UPRIGHT**: more erect, that is, high. [So that] one does not lower the head—that is, does not feel shame. [This denotes a] liberal [mind] and one eager to find the truth; and he who [denies it is] eager for contention. **SUCH**: those ready faces, that is, eager and prepared to [speak]. **OUR OUTLINES**: <note>original: "postille"</note> that is, our images within [the reflection]. And these faces appeared to me so faint, that is, [like a pearl] because it is white; placing it on a white thing, it is more [clearly] discerned when placed on a white forehead. [Like] an image in a mirror which is [seen]. But [the water] is not deep or dark, that is, [the image] is better discerned on a white forehead than in a [dark pool]. I fell into error, but the contrary to that error which [kindled Narcissus]. For the error of Narcissus was [to believe that what he saw] was not an image but a man; and I, seeing [them], believed they were images [and not] spirits. And so it appears that his error [is explained] in the thirtieth canto of the first canticle <note>Referencing the end of the *Inferno* or the logic of reflections in the *Commedia*.</note>. **CLEAR WATERS**: It is clear, still, and with little depth. Therefore... that is, lost and equal through the depth of the [water].

He demonstrates that, having fallen into error, he turned back to see the bodies of which he believed those were images; and he saw nothing. Therefore, he turned his eyes back to Beatrice, and in her eyes [he saw the light] shining. This signifies that the sense and the lower reason, which cannot apprehend anything except particular and corporeal things, judged the universal things to be false. Therefore, he returned to Beatrice—that is, he turned with the higher reason to the Holy Scripture; she was smiling, because the error of the simple always moves the learned to laughter; and she was glowing in her eyes, that is, very [brightly].
