### CANTO THREE

> But you turn back, as is the custom, into the void;
> what you see are **real substances**
> relegated here for a lack of devotion.
> Therefore speak with them, and listen and believe,
> for the truthful light that satisfies them
> does not allow them to turn their feet away from it.

> And I, to the shade that seemed most eager
> to speak, directed myself and began,
> like a man whom too much desire weakens:

> "O well-created spirit, who in the rays
> of eternal life feel that sweetness
> which, if not tasted, is never understood,
> it would be gracious to me if you would satisfy me
> with your name and your lot."
> Whereupon she, prompt and with laughing eyes:
> "Our charity does not lock its doors
> to a just prayer, no more than that Charity
> which wills that all its court be like itself.

> "I was a virgin sister in the world;
> and if your mind searches itself well,
> my being more beautiful will not hide me from you,
> but you will recognize that I am **Piccarda**,
> who, placed here with these other blessed ones,
> am blessed in the slowest sphere.
> Our affections, which are inflamed
> only in the pleasure of the Holy Spirit,
> find joy in being formed by His order.
> And this lot, which seems so low,
> is given to us because our vows were neglected,"

<column-break/>

shines. Hence she was fit to infuse light <note>original: "idest"</note>, that is, truth. And Beatrice said: "Do not marvel that I smile at your **childish judgment**" <note>original: "puerile quoto"</note>. *Quotus* in the Latin language signifies "how much" in order; and to place a thing in its proper order is to judge. It is no wonder, then, if I laugh at your low judgment, which does not yet trust its foot upon the truth—that is, it does not yet proceed according to the truth—and you do not understand that these are souls joined

to the lunar globe. To be "joined with a planet" is nothing other than to act according to its influence. And the influence of the Moon is to give a mutation of temporal goods to eternal ones, and from eternal to temporal. Therefore, these spirits had used that influence well, preferring heavenly goods to earthly ones, and using eternal things well, though not as the ultimate good, but according to what necessity requires. For insofar as it pertains to **food and clothing** <note>original: "uicto et uestito"</note> and the provision for our relatives and friends, these things ought to be sought, but no further. And if we have an abundance, we ought to convert it into honorable liberality. The Moon is cold and moist and a feminine planet; it induces virginity and chastity in women and inclines them toward it. For this reason, the poets feign that **Diana**—who signifies the Moon—was always a virgin and accompanied by virgin nymphs. Therefore, the poet feigns to find in that sphere the souls of virgin and chaste women. **REAL SUBSTANCES** <note>original: "VERE SVBstantie"</note>: these are they, and not images. **RELEGATED HERE**: as if far from God and the first heaven. **FOR LACK OF DEVOTION**: for a deficiency in devotion; and here he takes "vow" to mean profession and promise, because every Christian makes a vow and profession to observe the divine precepts—as if to say that although good works brought them here, because they were not sufficiently abundant, they merit only this lowest degree. **THEREFORE SPEAK**: because, being substances, they will hear you. **AND LISTEN**: because they will answer you. **AND BELIEVE**: because they will tell you the truth. And this is because the divine light—that is, God, who is Truth itself—**SATISFIES THEM**: it contents them in such a way that it does not let them turn their feet from Him—that is, they are confirmed in grace. They have no other desire nor any other longing than to acquiesce to the divine will. And this is what ensures that, although there is more glory in one than in another, they are nonetheless equally blessed, because beatitude consists in having the highest contentment, and they desire nothing else but to please God.

The Author, inflamed by a great desire to know, asks a spirit near to him for her name and the state of the souls who are in that place; and the spirit shows that she will answer him willingly, because the charity within them does not deny anything that is justly asked, for it is like divine charity, which wills that all its **court**—that is, all the blessed souls—be like itself in charity.

The spirit responds in the order in which the questions were asked: first she gives her name, then she shows what the state of those spirits is. She shows, then, that she was a **virgin sister**—that is, of the nuns of **Saint Clare**—named Piccarda, of whom we spoke in the twenty-fourth chapter of the second canticle <note>Purgatorio Canto 24</note> where it says: "My sister, who was between beautiful and good." **IN THE SLOWEST SPHERE**: The sphere of the Moon is the slowest because, although in its non-uniform motion it completes its course faster than any other planet, nevertheless, considering how much smaller this sphere is than the others, one sees that it is the slowest; and allegorically it means that the further they are removed from the first heaven, the less ardent they are in charity. **AND OUR AFFECTIONS**: she responds to the second part, that their state is in beatitude. For their affections and desires are inflamed and burning in the pleasure of the Holy Spirit, nor do they desire anything else, because from the Holy Spirit proceeds charity. And so that one does not doubt that their affections might seek a higher degree...

# PARADISO

...our vows and vows in any part <note>original: "canto"</note> desired. The poet imagines that all these spirits of religious life—who remained for some time constrained against their will, yet always kept the religious life in their hearts—merit blessedness, even if they did not observe the vow of virginal chastity promised to God, provided they observed the matrimonial chastity promised to their husbands. And because the vow made was nonetheless broken in some way and not observed, they do not merit a higher degree than this. Therefore he adds: "therefore this lot <note>that is, degree</note> is given to us, which is so low that it is the last," because our vows, which we made in the profession of religion (which was to observe an honest life in the cloister and virginal chastity, and obedience to the superior), were neglected and shattered; and they were "vows" <note>that is, empty or void</note> "in some part" <note>in some aspect</note>. According to the Master of Sentences <note>Peter Lombard, a famous medieval theologian</note>, a **Vow** is: "A certain testimony of a spontaneous promise which ought to be made concerning God and those things which belong to God" <note>original: "Est testificatio quedam promissionis spontanee que de deo et de his que sunt deo fieri debet."</note>.

> Whereupon I to her: "In your wondrous
> faces there shines I know not what divine
> that transforms you from my first concepts.
> Therefore I was not quick to remember,
> but now what you tell me helps me,
> so that re-imaging is clearer <note>original: "piu latino"</note> to me.
> But tell me, you who are happy here,
> do you desire a higher place
> to see more and to make yourselves more friends?"
> With those other shades she smiled a little first,
> then she answered me so joyfully
> that she seemed to burn with love in the first fire.

**BUT TELL ME**: because our soul has a continuous and natural desire—further increased by reason—to approach God as much as it can, Dante asks if those spirits desire to climb higher, either to see more or to make themselves closer friends of God. **WITH THOSE OTHER** shades: The blessed and benign spirit always smiles at human folly because, having true knowledge, it recognizes our errors. But moved by charity, it willingly demonstrates the truth. Therefore he says that it seemed Piccarda burned because of the great charity within her to remove Dante's ignorance. **IN THE FIRST fire**: in the Moon, which is the first splendor and the first planet to us.

> "Brother, the power of charity quiets
> our will, making us wish
> only for what we have, and we thirst for nothing else.
> If we desired to be more lofty,
> our desires would be discordant
> with the will of Him who sorts us here—
> which you will see cannot happen in these circles,
> if to be in charity is here necessary,
> and if you consider its nature well.
> Rather, it is essential <note>original: "formale"</note> to this blessed existence
> to hold oneself within the divine will,
> so that our very wills are made one.
> So that how we are from rank to rank <note>original: "di foglia in foglia," literally 'from leaf to leaf'</note>
> throughout this kingdom, pleases the whole kingdom,
> as it does the King who binds our will to His.
> And His will is our peace:
> it is that sea to which everything moves,
> that which it creates or which nature makes."

<column-break/>

...demonstrates that those souls are formed in that order <note>that is, they are born into that degree</note>; and no thing more... they were women who, having made a public vow... relatives [forced them] to leave it and marry. But because it was with...

The author excuses himself for not having recognized Piccarda due to a divine splendor which shines so much in them that it "transforms them from first concepts" <note>that is, from the first images that the <term>imagination <note>original: "phantasia"</note></term> had conceived of Piccarda's physical form</note>. This splendor denotes that the beatified soul never appears in our mind as we saw it before, but much more perfect, in a form that seems different and more excellent to us. **THEREFORE I WAS NOT QUICK** <note>original: "festino," i.e., fast</note> to remember and recall. **MORE CLEAR** <note>original: "piu latino," literally 'more Latin'</note>: more easy. In Florentine, we say "latino" for "lato" <note>wide/broad</note>. Therefore "piu latino" means "more broad"; and because in a broad space there is more ease to explain and dispatch what we want, "latino" is taken to mean "easy." And it is not "latino" derived from "Latium" as we say of the language...

This proves that the souls of that place do not desire to go further forward in this manner. It is necessary that the blessed soul be in perfect charity, because where there is charity, there is God, and where there is God, there is charity. And whoever is in perfect charity cannot disagree with the will of God, because whoever is in charity is united with God's will. Therefore, two wills become one. **IF WE DESIRED**: <note>original: "dissiaffimo"</note>. **TO BE more lofty**: higher. **OUR desires**: our wishes. **WOULD BE**: <note>original: "foran"</note> discordant from the will of Him who is God, who **SORTS US** <note>original: "ne cerne," meaning He judges us or truly chooses us for this place</note>. **WHICH**: which God **YOU WILL SEE cannot happen in these circles**: in these heavens. **RATHER IT IS THE ESSENTIAL FORM** <note>original: "formale"</note> of this blessed existence. <term>Form</term> is that which gives being to a thing, and no one is blessed except by being united with God. Therefore, the "form" of this beatitude is union with God, and their will becomes God's will. **SO THAT AS WE ARE**: He concludes that because the blessed are united with God's will, it pleases everyone to be in that heaven where God has placed them, because it so pleases God who "en-wills" us <note>original: "nenuogla," meaning He puts His own will into our wills</note>. So that the vow is nothing else...

<summary>In this passage, Piccarda Donati explains to Dante that the souls in the Sphere of the Moon do not envy those in higher heavens because their wills are perfectly aligned with God's will, which is the source of their peace. The commentary explains the theological concept of broken vows and clarifies the linguistic use of "latino" to mean clarity or ease.</summary>

# CANTO THREE

...better than our own: and his will is our supreme good. Our mind has peace only insofar as it desires nothing but the good, and God desires nothing but the good. **IT IS** that sea: the will of God is a depth that cannot be understood. Whence the Apostle says: "The will of God is a great abyss" <note>original: "Voluntas dei abyssus multa"; likely a reference to Psalm 36:6</note>, toward which will everything moves. Just as all waters move to go to the sea, so all things move from the divine will to return to it. **WHATEVER** he creates: to create is to make something out of nothing, and this God does without any intermediary. Afterwards, God placed virtue in the things created by him, which do not make things from nothing but from some material, making something similar—as, for example, a man with his seed makes another man. This is called **natured nature** <term>Latin: *natura naturata*; the world as it exists through natural processes rather than direct creation from nothing</term>; and they define nature as a virtue placed in things by God, generating similar things from similar things. Therefore, God creates without intermediary and without matter, and nature *makes*—that is, the virtue placed in things by God makes something out of matter. Thus we conclude, as Augustine says, that the will of God is the first and supreme cause of all movements, both bodily and spiritual.

> It was clear to me then how everywhere
> in heaven is paradise, though the grace
> of the Supreme Good does not rain there in one way.
> But just as it happens when one food satisfies
> and for another the appetite remains,
> so that the one is asked for and the other thanked;
> So did I do, with gesture and with word,
> to learn from her what was the web
> through which she had not drawn the shuttle to the end.

<gloss>Where one asks for that which is not yet had, and gives thanks for that which is had. This second doubt of which he wanted to be cleared was to understand what her life was like when she began in religion but did not finish it there. He speaks through a metaphor, calling her life a "web" <note>original: "tela"</note> through which she did not draw the "shuttle" <note>original: "spola"</note> to the end—that is, to the head or the finish. For the shuttle is what carries the thread of the weave back and forth until the cloth is filled.</gloss>

> "A perfect life and high merit enheaven
> a lady higher up," she said to me, "by whose rule
> in your world below they clothe and veil themselves,
> So that until death they may watch or sleep
> with that Spouse who accepts every vow
> that charity conforms to his pleasure.
> From the world, to follow her, as a young girl
> I fled, and in her habit I enclosed myself,
> and promised the path of her order.
> Men then, used more to evil than to good,
> snatched me forth from the sweet cloister;
> God knows what my life then became."

<gloss>FROM THE WORLD: I, Piccarda, in my earliest youth, fled from the world—that is, from earthly things—to follow her. AND ENCLOSED MYSELF: that is, I entered the enclosure in her habit. AND PROMISED THE PATH: that is, I made profession of the rule. OF HER ORDER: of her religious order. MEN then, used more to evil than to good: This shows that the beatified soul is free from all carnal affection; family ties do not prevent her from condemning their wicked behavior. WHAT LIFE my life was: she does not want to praise herself and openly speak of her honest life, but she wants God to be her witness; or truly "what life," as if to say with how much distress she lived, and against her will, outside of the monastery.</gloss>

> "And this other splendor that shows itself to you
> on my right side, and who is kindled
> with all the light of our sphere,
> What I say of myself, she understands of herself."

<column-break/>

He concludes that through Piccarda's words it was made manifest to him that "everywhere"—that is, every place—in heaven is paradise. That is: in every heaven, whether superior or inferior, there is beatitude. **AND YET** <note>original: "E SI"</note> although the **GRACE** of the Supreme Good (God) does not "rain in one way" <note>does not fall equally</note>, because the higher heavens have greater and better influence, nevertheless, it has already been said above that all wills are filled, even though the glory is not identical in everyone. **BUT** just as it happens: having been cleared of one doubt, there remained "hunger"—that is, the desire to be cleared of another. Just as it happens that one food satisfies and for another the "throat" remains—that is, the desire for what has not been had.

Piccarda declares in what way her vows were lacking and describes Saint Clare, and how she entered her religion, and how she was taken from it by force. The text is ordered thus: Piccarda said to me, **PERFECT** life (virtuous and conducted to the end) **AND HIGH** merit (as if excellent) **ENHEAVENS** further up (that is, places her in a higher heaven than this one of the Moon). **LADY**: this is Saint Clare, the sister of Saint Francis. **BY WHOSE RULE**: by the rule and according to the rule by which they "clothe and veil" themselves. For her rule is that these sisters wear grey cloth and stay veiled. This order was so that until death her sisters, whether "watching or sleeping," should be with Christ, who is the Spouse of every good virgin, and who accepts every vow which charity conforms to his pleasure.

Having told of herself, Piccarda tells of the spirit who was near her. And she declares her to be Constance of the House of Bavaria <note>The commentator Landino erroneously identifies Constance of Sicily as being from the "House of Bavaria"</note>, who is of older blood than any other in Germany. She was snatched by her relatives from the monastery where she had become a nun...

# PARADISO

she was a sister, and thus from her head was taken
the shadow of the sacred veils;

This is the light of the great Constance
who from the second wind of Swabia
generated the third and final power.

<note>Dante is referring to Constance of Sicily (1154–1198). Legend claimed she was taken from a convent against her will to marry Emperor Henry VI.</note>

Henry was crowned emperor by Celestine: and from Constance he had Frederick II: who was the third and last emperor of this family. WIND: that is, worldly glory, which Saint Jerome, because of its brevity and mutability, calls wind. <note>The "second wind" refers to Henry VI, the second Hohenstaufen emperor; the "third power" is his son, Frederick II.</note>

Thus she spoke to me, and then began singing 
*Ave Maria*, and singing she vanished
as a heavy thing does through deep water.
My sight, which followed her as much 
as was possible, after it lost her,
turned to the target of greater desire,
And back to Beatrice it wholly reverted;
but she flashed so brightly in my gaze
that at first my sight could not endure it;
And this made me slower to ask.

<column-break/>

and married. But in marriage she was most well-mannered and full of all the virtues that the Moon influences; and therefore he says that she shines and glows with all the light of that sphere. This Constance was the daughter of Roger, King of Sicily. When Roger died without an heir, Tancred, one of the barons, occupied the kingdom. But because he did not obey the Church, the Bishop of Palermo had Constance taken from the monastery of Palermo where she had made her profession <note>The "profession" refers to her formal vows as a nun.</note> and gave her as a wife to Henry, son of the first Emperor Frederick of the Swabian family.

After the words already spoken, Piccarda departed singing *Ave Maria* <note>original: "Ave Maria"; the angelic salutation to the Virgin Mary</note> because it is a fitting thing that those who, as far as was in their power, have preserved their virginity, should give continual praise to the Virgin of virgins. **AND SINGING** she vanished: *in vanum* <note>original Latin: "in vanum" meaning "into the void" or "vanishing"</note> that is, she disappeared, though not all at once. But as it happens when a heavy thing is cast into water whose bottom cannot be seen: the further it sinks, the less it is seen, until it is entirely lost from sight; thus she, drawing further away, disappeared. And by this he demonstrates that, in truth, the souls do not stay in the moon: but as has been said, considering the nature of the planet, the chaste souls come into our contemplation. **AFTER SHE HAD TAKEN**: After the 

---

just soul was lost to sight. **TURNED TO THE SIGN**: that is, to Beatrice, who was my sign and target where eyes are always directed. For just as our intellect goes astray in any of its contemplations, it must immediately return to theology. **SO THAT AT FIRST THE** face could not endure it. The higher we rise in contemplation with theology, the greater the splendor of divine things appears in it; in such a way that at first the human intellect is dazzled just as the eye is by the rays of the sun. <note>Beatrice represents Theology here; the "dazzling" effect symbolizes the human mind's struggle to grasp divine truths directly without preparation.</note>

CANTO FOUR <sig>Biiii</sig>

# CANTO FOUR OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE

<image-desc>Historiated drop cap 'I' featuring a figure in a landscape, set within a blue and red ornamental frame.</image-desc>
Between two foods, equidistant and tempting
In the same way, a man would die of hunger
Before a free man would bring one to his teeth;
So would a lamb stand between two cravings
Of fierce wolves, fearing both equally;
So would a hound stand between two does.
Therefore, if I was silent, I do not blame myself,
Urged equally by my own doubts,
Since it was necessary; nor do I commend myself.
I was silent, but my desire was painted
Upon my face, and my questioning with it,
Much clearer than if spoken in distinct words.

was one than the other. THAT FREE MAN: that is, one who was at liberty to choose and take whichever he pleased. SO WOULD HE STAND: that is, in this way and similarly he would stand. He has placed the simile in the act of desiring; now he places it in the act of fleeing and says: that a lamb, that is a little sheep, which in the midst of two wolves fears one as much as the other, would stand between two cravings of fierce wolves: that is, between two ravenous and fierce wolves. *Bramare* in the Florentine language means to desire supremely <note>To "crave."</note>. BETWEEN TWO <term>does</term>: *Dama* in Latin <note>original: "Dama"</note> is a beast not much unlike a roebuck, and we call them fallow deer. THEREFORE: he arranges it thus: Therefore, i.e., for the reasons said above: I do not blame myself because, as a man moved by his senses, I deserve some excuse. NOR DO I COMMEND MYSELF: because although my appetite was equally urged by my doubts and moved me equally, nonetheless reason should have considered which was of greater importance and preferred that one. SINCE IT WAS NECESSARY: lacking the free will to choose <note>This refers to the "Buridan's Ass" paradox, where a creature placed between two identical options cannot choose and thus starves.</note>. I WAS SILENT: but my desire, that is my will, and the questioning together were painted on my face: in a man’s face various signs appear according to various affections of the mind.

Beatrice did what Daniel did
When he lifted Nebuchadnezzar from the rage
That had made him unjustly wicked.
And she said: "I see well how one and another
Desire draws you, so that your concern
Binds itself so tight it cannot breathe outward.
You argue: 'If the good will endures,
By what reason does the violence of others
Decrease the measure of my merit?'
Furthermore, it gives you cause to doubt
That souls seem to return to the stars,
According to the opinion of Plato.
These are the questions that within your will
Press equally; and therefore first
I will treat the one that has more gall."

is: if a nun like Piccarda was always of good will to remain in religious life, nor ever changed as much as she could against the violence done to her by others—when she was forcefully taken from the cloister—how could her merits be diminished and make it so she did not deserve as much as she would have deserved staying in the cloister? FURTHERMORE TO DOUBT: The second doubt is that Dante, having seen these spirits in the lunar sphere, was almost inclined to the opinion that the souls of men, leaving their bodies, returned to the stars <note>Referring to Plato's *Timaeus*, which suggests souls are assigned to stars and return to them after death.</note> assigned to them, according to the opinion of Plato.

<column-break/>

Two doubts were born in the poet’s mind:
And these doubts were so equal that he did not
know where to begin. But Beatrice, who perceived
them without him speaking, came to his aid. And
therefore in this beginning he uses suitable com-
parisons, saying that if a man’s appetite were equal
toward two different foods, and he had the liberty to
take whichever he pleased, he would never move
toward one more than the other. Similarly, a lamb
placed between two wolves and fearing them
equally would not move more here than there. And
similarly, if a dog were in the middle of two does
and desired them equally, he would not follow this
one more than that. BETWEEN TWO foods distant:
that is, far away. AND MOVING: the appetite.
IN ONE way: that is, equally, meaning that one
was no closer...

Beatrice, seeing Dante’s desires, quieted them
by solving his doubts, just as the prophet Daniel
solved the doubts of King Nebuchadnezzar, who
became wicked against the wise men of Babylon.
The history is long, but in brief: King Nebuchad-
nezzar saw a horrific dream which fled from his
mind. Whereupon, having summoned all the wise
men of Babylon, he commanded that they tell him
the dream and its interpretation. The wise men
were ready to interpret the dream but excused
themselves for not knowing it. The king flew into
a rage and commanded Arioch, the captain of the

his companions. And having prayed for the safety of
the wise men, Daniel had a vision revealing the
dream and its interpretation. And immediately he
told it to the king, whence followed the liberation
of them all. I do not narrate the dream because we
narrated it in the *Inferno* <note>Dante discusses the "Old Man of Crete" statue from Nebuchadnezzar's dream in Canto XIV of the *Inferno*.</note>, where Dante describes the statue made of diverse metals with feet of terracotta. YOU ARGUE: Your first doubt...

**Of** the Seraphim, he who most in-Gods himself, <note>original: "s'india." A neologism created by Dante meaning to enter into or be transformed by God.</note>

you choose to take—I say, not even Mary—
Have their seats in no other heaven
than those spirits who just appeared to you,
nor do they have more or fewer years to their being;
But all make the first circle beautiful,
and possess sweet life in different ways,
by feeling more or less of the sweet breath.
They showed themselves here, not because this sphere
is allotted to them, but to provide a sign
of the celestial rank that is less exalted.

Where the poet narrates part of those who were drawn from Limbo; he means Moses. But he means all the patriarchs. SAMUEL and that John whichever you want to take: as if to say, either the Baptist or the Evangelist. NOT MARY: because she is not only above all human spirits, but also above all angels. All these who hold the supreme place in eternal life do not inhabit any other heaven than these spirits who appeared to you in the lunar sphere. NOR DO THEY HAVE more or fewer years to their being: because all are eternal. ALL MAKE the first circle beautiful: all inhabit the first heaven which, because it is spherical, he calls a "circle" <note>original: "giro"</note>. Therefore, there is no difference in the place nor in their eternity, but in their beatitude. Of which, although each is as full as they can hold, and thus each has a sweet life. Nor can they desire more because they find themselves full; nevertheless, he who has more merit has greater capacity: and God breathes into the blessed. The souls are like vessels of various sizes, but all are full. A cup and a large jug, when they are full—although the jug holds more—nevertheless, the cup being full is without lack just like the jug. Thus, every soul being full of glory, the one that holds less is no less full than the one that holds more. Rightly, therefore, Thomas Aquinas <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas, a key theological influence on Dante.</note> noted this. And the poet had a marvelous intellect in this. Because, to adorn his poem and to demonstrate the influences of the heavens, he feigns that the ranks of the blessed in eternal life are distinct across various spheres of the heavens. But because this is not according to the Christian religion, he declares in this place that he speaks figuratively so that the human intellect can better understand divine things. Which, so it does not seem inappropriate, follows saying:

**Therefore** the poet does not deserve reprimand if, under the fiction that souls inhabit different heavens, he intends otherwise; because it is necessary for the human intellect to use more material and corporeal things to give understanding of incorporeal things. Because our intellect does not learn except from the senses. Aristotle says: *Nothing is in the intellect unless it was first in the sense* <note>original: "Nihil est in intellectu nisi prius fuerit in sensu"</note>. Therefore, from the senses—which are particulars distinguished by "here" and "now" <note>original: "hic: et nunc"</note>—the intellect learns and makes them universals. From the friendship that Cicero's sense-perception knows in Atticus, the intellect takes a universal thing in which everyone who participates is a friend. Therefore, he placed these spirits in the first heaven so that we would understand they were in the lowest degree of beatitude. FOR THIS reason Holy Scripture condescends: Here it leaves divine and lofty speech and takes the material and corporeal to adapt itself to our faculty; and it attributes feet and hands. Which is not in God because He has no body, but it intends something else. Because

<header>CANTO FOURTH</header>

**Of** the tribe of Naphtali, there was a just man in Nineveh: and for the love of God he was very generous toward the poor. And sleeping one day, swallow droppings fell from the nest into his eyes, which blinded him. Whereupon, his inheritance being spent, it was necessary for his wife Anna to nourish him by weaving. As is the nature of women, she reproached him every day, saying he had been too generous to the needy. Therefore God, who does not abandon the good, put it into his heart to send his son—who was also named Tobias—to Rages, a city of Media, to a relative named Gabel. This man owed him a certain sum of money. Tobias did not know how to get there, but went into the square to see if anyone was making that journey to go with him. For this, Raphael assumed a human body and offered himself as a companion, pretending he had business in the same place. They set out on the road and, having arrived at the river Tigris, a fish came at Tobias while he was washing his feet. He caught it by command of the angel and gutted it, saving the heart and the gall, and salted the rest to have food for the journey. They came to Rages where Raguel, the father’s cousin, lived. Raguel had a daughter named Sarah. She had already had seven husbands, but a demon named Asmodeus strangled them all on the first night before they could consummate the marriage. Tobias took her as his wife, and with the heart of the fish burned upon the coals, he drove away the demon. He received half of Raguel’s wealth as a dowry, recovered the money from Gabel, and returned with his wife to his father; and with the gall of the fish, he freed his father from blindness. **THAT WHICH** Timaeus: In the first book of our dialogues *On the Soul*, we have placed the descent of the soul into the body according to the Platonists, who believed that all souls were created at one time, and then from time to time they descend into bodies with the knowledge of all things, but immersed in the dark matter of the body, they forget them.

*And perhaps his opinion is of another sort*
  *than the words sound, and it may be*
  *with an intention not to be mocked.*
*If he intends that the honor of their influence*
  *and the blame returns to these wheels,*
  *perhaps his bow hits upon some truth.*
*This principle, being misunderstood, once twisted*
  *the whole world, so that it went astray naming*
  *Jupiter, Mercury, and Mars.*

**His** intention is directed toward some truth. **THIS** principle: which Plato posits, that every soul returns to the star from which it departed. **MISUNDERSTOOD**: because they understood according to the words and not according to the sense which we have stated above. **TWISTED**: removed from the true way of worshiping one God. **ALMOST** the whole world: because, except for the people of God, all nations through idolatry worshiped the stars, or Jupiter, or Mercury, or Mars, or other stars.

*The other doubt that moves you*
  *has less poison, because its malice*
  *could not lead you away from me elsewhere.*
*That our justice appears unjust*
  *in the eyes of mortals is an argument*
  *of faith, and not of heretical wickedness.*
*But because your understanding is able*
  *to penetrate well into this truth,*
  *as you desire, I will make you content.*

**Poison**: because it does not make you a heretic, which is a poison that kills the soul and removes it from the faith held by holy theology. But this is not a doubt that can remove you from Beatrice—that is, from our faith. Because by doubting whether that which our faith holds is a just thing, he affirms the faith to be true. Therefore, this doubt is an "argument," that is, a demonstration of faith.

*If violence is when he who suffers*
  *contributes nothing to him who compels,*
  *these souls were not excused by it.*
*For the will, if it does not want to, is not quenched.*

**Dante** does not affirm this: but he says it could be that Plato's opinion is not exactly as the words sound. Rather, he does not mean that the soul returns to the stars, but denotes that the influence which inclines one toward virtue or vice—from which comes honor or blame—is attributed to the stars. Nevertheless, one can resist such inclination both through our free will and through divine grace, which is given to those who duly ask for it. <term>Because the wise man shall rule the stars. <note>original Latin: "Quia sapiens dominabitur astris." **THIS** was the first doubt of Dante, which Beatrice, for the reason already stated in responding, made last. The doubt was: if the good will lasts, can the force used by others diminish its merit? Since it is our will that earns merit or demerit. But Piccarda and Constance remained in the good will to stay in the cloister. Therefore, the violence of those who took them out by force should not have diminished their merits, for which, if they had not left the cloister, they would have ascended to a higher heaven. Whereupon it follows: **THE OTHER** doubt that concerns you. **LESS** [poison].

once it has found the good, it always desires it: For example <note>original: "Verbi gratia"</note>, Lawrence the martyr wished to stand firm in the Christian faith. The other kind of will is called **relative** <term>relative will: a choice made under pressure where one chooses the lesser of two evils</term>; and this wishes either for the greater good or the lesser evil. Therefore, if violence occurs when the one who suffers—that is, endures—and is forced contributes nothing—that is, does not incline the will in any part toward that which forces it. Because of this, Piccarda and Constance are not entirely excused, because there was no such violence that could have prohibited them from returning. And they could have, after they were taken out, returned there. Nor could they be forced into marriage against their will: And the will is not halved—that is, it is not extinguished—unless it wishes to be. Nor is there any punishment so harsh that it can constrain us to will if we do not wish to will. But as the nature of fire in the fire itself does not twist of its own accord: And if it is twisted by force: as soon as the violence ceases, it returns upward. Because if it bends much or little, it follows the force. Every time the will bends to violence, much or little, it follows the violence: and it cannot be said absolutely that it is against its will: and thus these women acted. **IF THEIR WILL HAD BEEN**: although they of their own spontaneous will would have rather chosen religion than marriage: nonetheless, the force of their relatives partially turned them away: and they did not stay in a firm purpose like Saint Lawrence or Mucius; had they been so, their merit would not have diminished, but they would have rather chosen death than consented to marriage. **Lawrence**, in the year two hundred fifty-five, was martyred under Emperor Decius: who wanted him to reveal the money of Sixtus the High Pontiff: and he preferred to die with a joyful and very great soul, enduring many martyrdoms, than to reveal the treasures. **MUCIUS**. In the time when Porsena, King of Chiusi, had besieged Rome, C. Mucius, a noble youth, obtained permission from the senate and went into the enemy camp with the firm purpose of either dying or killing the king: But fortune was envious of such a high undertaking. The magnanimous youth found the king together with his secretary in similar clothing and dress: and he killed the secretary, believing he was killing the king. Once captured, he confessed both his error and his purpose. Then, turning to his right hand, he determined to punish it for the error: and upon the fire prepared there for sacrifice, he burned it. Porsena was amazed by such excellence of soul and pardoned him. But Mucius, to further daunt him, told him that three hundred youths had conspired to come one by one to kill him. This man was later called **Scaevola**—that is, "without a hand" <note>original: "sine uola"</note>—because he had burned the palm of his hand in the fire. If, therefore, they had remained with a firm will after they were snatched from the monastery: every time they had the opportunity, they would have fled from their relatives and returned to the monastery. **BUT SUCH FIRM WILL IS FAR TOO RARE**: As if to say that God had compassion, considering our fragility: Because choosing the good of one's own will and following it until violence is seen is an angelic thing and rare among men: But to yield to violence in things which, although they do not have as much merit, are nonetheless permitted by the church, is a human thing.

Beatrice had shown Dante that a blessed soul cannot lie. ...tion, she would have returned to the monastery. IF SHE HAD BEEN: he has placed the doubt; now before he resolves it, he puts forth a sentence by which he affirms that often to flee that which we do not want, we do...

**H**e resolves the doubt by posing such a distinction: There are two species of will, absolute and respective [relative]. The absolute cannot want evil. The respective wants the lesser evil to flee the greater. But often man is deceived in discerning and judging, thinking that which is a greater evil to be the lesser. For which reason Piccarda, with absolute will, wanted and chose the virginal life; but it seeming to her a greater evil to die than to leave such a life, with respective will she chose marriage. Therefore when Constance affirms having wanted the monastic life rather than marriage, she means the absolute will. But when Beatrice says she did not want it, she means the respective will. Similarly, when we say that Alcmaeon wanted to kill Eriphyle, we mean the respective will, falsely [believing] it to be a lesser evil to kill her than not to avenge Amphiaraus; and his will was in the wrong...

**H**e renders thanks to Beatrice, who—being sacred Theology—is also Divine Wisdom. Wherefore he most optimally calls her "lover of the first lover," that is, of God, who is First Love, as we shall demonstrate in a more proper place. O DIVINE: o goddess, because divinity is power, wisdom, and love; and she is divine because she makes us divine. NEAR WHOM whose speech cleanses me: that is, her speech cleanses me near God. For only wisdom is that which takes from us ignorance, which is the root of every vice. AND warms: that is, it enflames me and makes me live in Seraphic love. MY AFFECTION IS NOT: he excuses himself that his affection toward her cannot be so deep that it can correspond to her grace toward him: that is, love for love. BUT HE WHO SEES and can respond to this: And this is God, who because He sees—that is, knows what wisdom is—loves it; and because He can do as much as He wills, He loves it as much as He can...

satisfy the body. Therefore, the intellect is not satisfied unless it is illustrated—<term>that is, illuminated</term>—by that truth outside of which no truth wanders. And this is God, who as He Himself says, is the way, the truth, and the life; and He is Truth in such a way that outside of Him no truth wanders or extends. **IT RESTS WITHIN IT LIKE A WILD BEAST** in its lair: *Lustrum* in the Latin language signifies the den of wild beasts. <note>original: "Lustrum". And as <term>the Aquinas</term> <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary philosopher-theologian of the Middle Ages.</note> says in his book *Against the Gentiles*: The ultimate and supreme happiness of man consists in contemplating God. <note>original: "contra gentiles". <header>CANTO FIVE</header>

# CANTO FIVE OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE

"If I flame upon you in the heat of love
beyond the world that is seen on earth,
so that it overcomes the power of your eyes,
Do not wonder, for this proceeds
from perfect vision: which as it learns,
so it moves its foot toward the goodness found.
I see well how there already shines
within your intellect the eternal light
which, once seen, alone and always kindles love;
And if another thing seduces your love,
it is nothing but some vestige of that light,
poorly recognized, which shines through there.
You wish to know if, by some other service,
for a failed vow, so much can be paid
that the soul is secured from litigation."
So Beatrice began this canto,
and like one who does not break their speech,
she continued thus her holy discourse.

<column-break/>

This fifth canto contains the response made by Beatrice: whether a failed vow can be restored by other good works; and it concludes as you will see. Then it narrates how they ascended from the first heaven of the Moon to the second, of Mercury. In these first verses Beatrice speaks, saying: do not wonder if I flame upon you, <term>that is, if I am more radiant</term> in the heat of love beyond the world that is seen on earth—that is, more than I flamed upon you in the world, meaning that part of the world which is on earth. "World" in the Latin language signifies the entire universe, <term>that is, the heavens with all the elements</term>. This the Greeks call *cosmos*. <note>original: "cosmos". The commentator notes that while the word often means "earth," in a philosophical context it encompasses the entire physical and celestial universe.</note> The meaning is: do not wonder if I inflame you more now that you are in heaven—<term>that is, elevated to the contemplation of divine things</term> as a celestial man and with the virtues of a soul already purged—than I did when you were on earth: <term>that is, when you followed more the literal sense</term>; and you could not yet reach the true allegorical senses, which can inflame you much more than those others. For since love is nothing other than a desire for beauty, as much as the allegorical senses are more beautiful than the moral ones, so much more do they move and delight us with greater love.

---

Do not wonder, therefore, if I seem more luminous to you: because this occurs because you see better than before. And indeed, our intellect, the further it removes itself from the contemplation of earthly things, the more it becomes lucid and understands celestial things; and the more it learns, the more it moves "the foot"—<term>that is, the affection or will</term>—to attain it. Whence Augustine said: <note>original: "Accedendo enim ad deum illuminatur ignorantia et corroboratur infirmitas data sibi intelligentia qua uident et caritate qua feruiunt."</note> "For by approaching God, ignorance is illuminated and weakness is strengthened, as intelligence is given by which they see and charity by which they serve." **I SEE WELL**: This demonstrates why she spoke the sentence above: it is because she sees him already so elevated that the divine light shines in him more than usual. For just as a metal, the more it is polished and wiped clean, the more it reflects the rays of the sun, so our intellect, the higher it can be elevated by being more cleansed of the contagion of earthly things, the more the divine light shines within it. And as this light increases in us, it kindles a greater love to attain it, because our love extends to nothing but the good and the true. And if we love something that is neither good nor true, it is because it deceives us and appears true and good, though it is not. Whence follows: **AND IF ANOTHER THING** seduces your love: No other thing is loved by man except the true and the good. And if sometimes we love that which is neither true nor good, it is because that thing "seduces" us—<term>that is, deceives us</term>—and shows itself as good and true, yet it is captive and false. Therefore we love it believing it to be good, because we see shining through it some "vestige" and sign of a good poorly recognized by us, because we believe in that which is not. **YOU WISH TO KNOW**: as if she said, your doubt is whether a man, having made a vow and then not observed it, can—with some other service, and another good, such as fasting, or prayers, or almsgiving—render so much in exchange for the failed vow that the act frees the soul from "litigation," <term>that is, from the judgment of God where we must plead our case.</term> **VOW** is an obligation of our free will, made with a promise to God concerning some thing belonging to God. It is asked, therefore, if such an obligation can be annulled once it is made: and the response is no; because this is a sacrifice rendered to God and is already accepted by God. Therefore it cannot be broken, nor satisfied with another thing, since nothing is of such great dignity as the free choice of our will. But for a true vow, it is necessary that the person making the vow can obligate themselves. Thus a woman or a servant <note>In the medieval legal and social context, those under the authority of another were limited in their ability to make binding spiritual contracts.</note> [cannot], because they are in the power of others. Furthermore, because a vow is an obligation of some good made to God with deliberation, Isidore <note>St. Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), an influential scholar and archbishop.</note> says: <note>original: "In malis promissis scinde fide et in turpi uoto muta decretum et quod incaute nouisti non facias: Et impia est promissio que scelere adimpletur."</note> "In evil promises, break your faith; in a shameful vow, change your decree; and do not do what you have unwisely acknowledged. For a promise is impious that is fulfilled by a crime." And <term>the Aquinas</term> <note>St. Thomas Aquinas. The OCR "laqui ate" is a transcription of "l'Aquinate."</note> divides this, saying that some things always turn out well, such as virtuous works. Some are the opposite, such as contrary things; and these do not fall under a vow. Some are good by their nature, but sometimes have a wretched end; and such vows so made ought not to be observed.

---

"The greatest gift that God in His bounty
made in creating, and to His own goodness..."

<column-break/>

...most conformed to Him, and which He most prizes,
Was the freedom of the will;
With which the intelligent creatures,
All of them and they alone, are and were endowed.
Now it will appear to you, if you argue from here,
The high value of the vow, if it is so made
That God consents when you consent;
For in closing the pact between God and man,
A victim is made of this treasure,
Such as I say, and it is done by its own act.
Therefore, what can be rendered in return?
If you think to use well what you have offered,
You wish to do a good work from ill-gotten gains.

...now made in the image and likeness of God <note>original: "imagine et similitudine didio"</note>. And it also presupposes memory, because without that, no work could be done: neither reason, nor will, nor judgment. These three things God has given to you alone—to the angel and to man—and through these we draw closer to God than other creatures. Therefore, they are the greatest; and all three are within the freedom of choice, which is radically and causally in the reason, and formally and essentially in the will. **IT IS CONFORMED** to goodness: because through it we can save ourselves. He prizes this most because it is the greatest thing man can do. **NOW IT WILL APPEAR TO YOU** if you argue from here: The high value: She concludes thus: now having shown the great gift that is free will, if you argue from here—that is, from this reasoning—it will appear to you—that is, it will be revealed—the high value of the vow. For if the greatest gift God has given to man is the free will, and man in the vow binds it to God, it follows that he binds the greatest thing he has; provided that the vow is of such quality that God accepts it when you make it; for God does not accept a vow made incorrectly. And it follows that in closing the pact between God and man—that is, in making the vow—you make a victim <term>that is, a sacrifice</term> of this treasure, which is as great as I have said: because you offer to God your free will, for it is that which binds itself with the promise. **THEREFORE:** She concludes that he who breaks the vow cannot give sufficient restoration. And certainly, if the free will is the greatest gift we can give to God, having taken that away, we cannot give Him an equivalent thing in exchange. And she adds that in no way should you believe you can use well <term>that is, justly convert to your own use</term> that which you have already offered to God. For this is as if you believed you were doing a good work <term>meaning a good deed</term> from ill-gotten gains <term>that is, from something wrongly acquired</term>.

You are now certain of the major point;
But because Holy Church gives dispensation in this,
Which seems contrary to the truth I have disclosed to you,
You must still sit a while at the table,
Because the tough food you have taken
Still requires help for its digestion.
Open your mind to what I reveal to you
And fix it within; for there is no knowledge
Without retaining what has been understood.

<gloss>knowledge is to have understood a thing without retaining it: as for example if I had understood what the philosophers say in moral philosophy and I had not retained it, I would not have that knowledge.</gloss>

Two things come together for the essence
Of this sacrifice: one is that
Of which it is made; the other is the covenant.
This last one is never canceled
Except by being kept; and concerning it
So precisely was spoken above.

<column-break/>

things, and it was the most conformed to His goodness. And there is nothing He prizes more. **OF WHICH** all intelligent creatures: God gave free will not to all creatures, but to the intelligent ones, which are the angel and man. And from the beginning it was given equally; now it is unequal because in the angel it is confirmed and he can no longer sin; for all those who remained innocent after the fall of Lucifer have been confirmed in grace. She says three things about free will: first, that it is the greatest gift God has given; second, that it is most conformed to His goodness; third, that He prizes it most. The first is shown because free will presupposes reason and will. For it belongs to reason to judge and to discourse on what should be willed or not. To the will belongs the act of willing, and therefore it is called free. And through these two things it shall be...

She had declared that for a broken vow one cannot give suitable restoration. Now, seeing that the Church often grants dispensations for vows, someone might believe that what Beatrice has said is false, or rather that such a dispensation is made against duty. Therefore she admonishes the poet to wait for this clarification and speaks through a metaphor, calling this reasoning which she has stated above "food," for the mind feeds on doctrine just as the body feeds on physical food. And she calls it "tough," like food hard to digest, and therefore it needs help. And she admonishes him to open and turn his mind to that which she will say, and fix it within—that is, retain it—because one does not possess...

Because we see that the Church grants dispensations for vows, Beatrice wants to demonstrate in what way they can be dispensed. Therefore she shows that two things are in a vow: the matter that is promised—such as fasting, money, real estate, and the like—and this is the matter of the vow. The other is the covenant <term>that is, the convention and the pact</term> that you...

<summary>Beatrice explains that free will is God's greatest gift to humanity and that a vow is the sacrifice of this gift. She then addresses the apparent contradiction of Church dispensations, distinguishing between the "matter" of a vow and the "covenant" itself.</summary>
<keywords>free will, vows, sacrifice, Church dispensation, reason and will, Beatrice, Dante, covenant, moral philosophy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discourse on the nature of vows. Beatrice is explaining the distinction between the "matter" of a vow (the specific thing promised) and its "form" (the solemn pact with God). She now addresses the strict conditions under which a vow's matter may be changed and provides historical and mythological examples of "foolish" vows that should never have been kept.</meta>

<columns>2</columns>
<header>CANTO FIVE</header>

Therefore it was necessary for the Hebrews
still to offer, though some offerings
were permuted, as you must know.
The other [part], which is revealed to you as the matter,
can well be such that no error is made
if it is converted into another matter.

But let no one shift the burden on his shoulder
by his own judgment, without the turning
of both the white and the yellow key.
And believe every permutation foolish
if the thing set aside is not included in the thing taken up
as four is in six.
Therefore, whatever thing weighs so much
by its own value that it tips every scale
cannot be satisfied with any other expenditure.
Let mortals not take a vow lightly;
be faithful, and in doing so, do not be cross-eyed
as Jephthah was at his first offering;
To whom it would have been more fitting to say "I did ill"
than, by keeping it, to do worse; and as foolish
you can find the great leader of the Greeks
Whence Iphigenia wept for her fair face
and made both the foolish and the wise weep
who heard tell of such a ritual.

<column-break/>

...you make with God: and this is the form that gives being to the thing: Of these two, the latter, that is, the form <note>original Latin: "id est la forma"</note>, cannot be dispensed. Nor is he ever absolved who makes the vow if he does not observe it: and therefore she says it is not canceled: because he who makes a vow makes himself a debtor and binds the will which was free: and the debtor is not canceled unless he pays: and of this form Beatrice spoke above so precisely without any exception that it could not be dispensed. **THEREFORE NECESSITY**

it was for the Hebrews: she proves by example that the form cannot be changed. Because the Hebrews, having made a vow to sacrifice: it was necessary that they always sacrificed: But they could well change the matter of the sacrifice: and because of this, at one time they sacrificed animals: at another grain, at another money. **THE OTHER**: as she has shown that the form cannot be changed: so now she shows that the matter can be changed as the example of the Hebrews declares. And therefore she says that the matter can be such that there is no fault: if it is converted and permuted with another matter: as if we had promised to give to God the first-born of our herds: the Pope can dispense so that we give the equivalent in money. But if we have promised chastity and obedience in the cloister <note>Meaning monastic life</note>, what could be given as an equivalent to this?

She has shown that the Pope can permute vows regarding the matter: now she warns first that no one should presume by himself to make a permutation of vows without the will of the white and yellow keys: that is, without the license of a priest who can absolve. Of the keys we spoke in the ninth canto of the second canticle <note>Referencing Purgatorio, where the keys represent authority and discernment</note>. **AND EVERY PERMUTATION:** every permutation of a vow is foolish if the vow made is not less than that which is permuted: Whence she says if the thing set aside—that is, the left vow—is not gathered—that is, contained—in the thing taken up—in that which is taken in place of the vow—as four is in six <note>The new offering must exceed the value of the old one by half</note>. **AS WAS JEPHTHAH.** He was the son of Gilead, but born of adultery: And by the legitimate sons of Gilead he was cast out of the house: and he went to the land of Tob. He was a very strong man: and for this reason, the people of Israel being greatly oppressed by the sons of Ammon, his fellow citizens made him prince in that war: And he made a vow that if he returned victorious, he would offer to God as a burnt offering <term>holocaust: a sacrifice where the victim is entirely consumed by fire</term> the first person who came out of his house to meet him. He conquered the enemies: and occupied twenty cities of Ammon. And he returned to Mizpah <note>original: "Maspha"</note>, his home: his only daughter came out to meet him with the tambourine and with the chorus. The father was greatly grieved by such a miserable encounter: and the daughter, understanding the father's vow: comforted her father that he should observe to God what he had promised: But that he should grant her a space of two months before he sacrificed her: So that she might wander through the mountains with her companions to bewail her virginity: And in this way, the two months having passed, the wretched maiden returned to her father and was sacrificed. From this arose a custom among the people of Israel that each year the virgins gather together: and for four days they weep for the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite. He was therefore foolish: and it was less evil not to have observed the vow than to have killed his daughter. Nor is the case of Agamemnon very different, the first leader among the Greeks: who with a thousand armed ships was in the port of Aulis: and they awaited nothing else but the prosperous wind that would lead them to Troy which they wished to besiege to recover Helen, stolen by Paris. Agamemnon, then, eager to sail, hearing from the oracle that he would have a prosperous wind if Diana—angry because in a hunt Agamemnon had killed a doe consecrated to her—were appeased with the blood of Iphigenia his daughter: he consented that she be sacrificed: But Diana, moved to great compassion for the innocent girl, had her snatched away and carried to the Tauric region: and there guarded until Orestes her brother brought her back to her homeland. These vows, therefore, should not be made: Nor, if made, observed: Since God, because He is the father of mercy and clemency, hates all cruelty. **OF SUCH A RITUAL** <note>original: "di si facto colto"</note>: of such a cruel sacrifice: because the Latins say "worship of God" <note>original Latin: "cultum dei"</note> for every honor and sacrifice made to God.

<summary>This page explores the conditions for changing the "matter" of a religious vow, emphasizing that only the Church (the "keys") can grant such changes and only if the new offering is significantly more valuable. It uses the tragic stories of Jephthah and Agamemnon to warn against making or keeping rash, cruel vows that offend God's mercy.</summary>

# PARADISO

->PARADISO<-

Be Christians, and move with more gravity;
be not like feathers tossed by every wind,
and do not believe that every water washes you.
You have the Old and the New Testaments,
and the shepherd of the Church who guides you;
let this suffice for your salvation.
If evil greed cries out something else to you,
be men, and not witless sheep,
so that the Jew among you does not laugh at you.
Do not act like the lamb that leaves the milk
of its mother, simple and wanton,
and fights against itself for its own pleasure.

Follow, therefore, the precepts of the shepherd and of the holy Church: in such a way that the Jew—that is, all the Jews who live among us—do not laugh at our foolishness. Do not act like the lambs: who, out of a desire to play and be wanton, leave the milk. So the fools, for temporal and momentary pleasures, leave their own salvation.

Thus Beatrice [spoke] to me as I write;
then she turned away, all longing,
toward that part where the world is most alive.
Her silence and her changing appearance
put to rest my greedy mind,
which already had new questions before it.
And as an arrow that strikes the target
before the bowstring is even quiet,
so we ran into the second realm.
There I saw my lady so joyful
as she entered the light of that heaven
that the planet itself became more glowing.
And if the star changed and laughed,
what did I become, who by my very nature
am transmutable in every way!

<column-break/>

**S**he admonishes us not to be so light in making vows or in believing it is easy to be absolved of them. And if someone should say they do not know how to rule themselves, she demonstrates that we have the doctrine of the New and Old Testaments, and the shepherd—that is, the priestly order <term>sacerdotal order: the hierarchy of the Church authorized to interpret scripture</term> which explains this doctrine to us. And this is enough for our salvation. And if someone says greed—that is, appetite and sensuality—cries out something else—that is, pulls us to follow worldly pleasures and leave virtuous works—he responds that we are men and not sheep. That is <note>original Latin: "i." for "id est"</note>, we have not only senses as the sheep do, but we also possess reason and intellect, which are not given to any other animal; and with this, we can overcome appetite and sensuality. Therefore, he who lets himself be overcome by appetite has no excuse.

**THUS BEATRICE:** Because the poet describes the ascent to the second heaven—in which Mercury resides—let it not be unknown to us that this planet has two homes in the zodiac: Gemini and Virgo. It is a temperate and nocturnal planet; sometimes masculine and sometimes feminine. It easily converts to the nature of the planet with which it joins: with the good it becomes good, with the evil, evil, and with the mediocre, it becomes mediocre. Such a nature in the upper part of its circle mixes its qualities with Venus, and in the lower with the sun. According to Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer</note>, it produces studious and eloquent men. For this reason, it is called by poets the god of wisdom and eloquence. The Greeks call him Hermes, and among them *hermeneuin* means to interpret <note>original Greek: "hermeneuin"</note>, because eloquence is the interpreter of the concepts of our minds. They hold that he is the messenger of the gods for two reasons: first, because it is an extremely fast planet (whence he is depicted with winged sandals); second, because just as a messenger reports nothing of himself but explains only what has been committed to him by others, so Mercury produces effects not according to his own influence but according to that of the planet to which he is joined. Most especially, he disposes and enables men for arithmetic and the calculation of numbers. For this reason, he is called the god of merchants. Finally, when well-placed, he brings forth open oracles and manifest divination. He induces supreme eloquence, which has such power in persuading and dissuading, in moving and quieting our minds, that it leads man to whatever he pleases. Because of this, they give him the staff in hand, but entwined with two serpents, to signify that the ornament of words is not sufficient for true eloquence if supreme prudence is not added, which is signified by the serpent. Whence: "Be wise as serpents" <note>original Latin: "Estote prudentes sicut serpentes"</note>. He induces, therefore, eloquence and sweetness of pronunciation. He induces doctrine, the memory of histories, astrology, sharpness of mind, credulity, beauty, and the desire for empire, as well as the speculation on obscure things. But if he is in a bad place, he induces thefts, fraud, lies, false testimony, cunning, and craftiness. He is rarely outside the rays of the sun, and for this reason, he is rarely seen; and being accustomed to it, he does not fear "combustion" <term>combustion: an astrological state where a planet is so close to the sun its influence is obscured</term> as much as the other planets do. And for this, they imagine that he wears a hat on his head. Nor does he ever move away from the sun more than thirty degrees, which is the space of one sign. He completes his course in 338 days and does not stay in one sign more than twenty-eight days and six hours. According to what Alfraganus <note>Al-Farghani, a 9th-century Persian astronomer</note> reports, the lowest part of the sphere of Mercury is closer to the earth by 208,542 miles, and the highest part by 542,750 miles. Now, because Mercury gives great influence to the active life, in this heaven the poet shows that illustrious princes are represented, those who in their governments demonstrated excellent virtue. BEATRICE said to me thus as I write; then she turned herself completely...

# CANTO FIVE

->CANTO FIVE<-

...desiring, <note>original: "distante," likely a transcription variant for "disiante" (desiring)</note> that is, full of desire. It means that once she had spoken these words, Beatrice turned toward the East with the highest desire to ascend to the second heaven of Mercury. And by this he suggests that the contemplation of divine things, through which we climb from heaven to heaven, must be done with the greatest desire and fervor. He calls the East the part where the world is "most alive," either because every light is born from there, as is every revolution [of the spheres], or because celestial influences are most potent in the eastern parts. **AND AS AN ARROW**—It follows that once the desire to ascend to the second heaven was born in Beatrice, they rose there as quickly as an arrow runs, which reaches the mark before the bowstring that propelled it is even still. The "string" is the **will**, which pushes the **intellect** and makes it ascend. And the "arrow" is **ingenuity** <note>or wit/talent</note>, which reaches the goal before the will is at rest. And having reached that heaven, Beatrice was so joyful in that light that the planet itself became more glowing. The poet imagines that the higher Beatrice ascends, the more joyful she becomes, because the soul, filled with doctrine, takes greater joy the higher the things it contemplates. **AND MORE** glowing the planet became: Mercury influences <term>doctrine and eloquence</term>, and the more such influence makes men learned, the more the planet shines—that is, the more its nature is made manifest. Or we might say that Beatrice—that is, Christian Theology—makes Mercury shine, because in no other religion does its influence appear more than in ours. And according to the astrologers, it plays a great part in the Christian religion. For at the birth of our Redeemer—the unbreakable and immovable stone upon which the Christian Church is built—Mercury was found in Gemini, its own domicile, and in the ninth house, which is the house of religion and faith. Through its influence, our Doctors <note>learned teachers of the Church</note> have surpassed all writers of every other religion in both depth of wisdom and the ornament of eloquence. And Mercury is especially powerful in that place regarding "profound science" given through metaphor. And if anyone should say it is impious folly to attribute influence to the birth of Christ, I respond that I do not doubt for a moment that the Creator of the universe does not wait for help from His creatures; and I am certain that all the planets and stars and heavens depend on Him, and from Him they have whatever power is in them. But I believe it pleased Him who can do all things—and by whose power everything can do what it does—that His true religion should have favor from Him not only directly, but also in some part through the medium of His "secondary causes" <note>the stars/nature</note>. I do not wish this opinion to extend further than the Catholic faith allows, to which I always submit myself. This reason, then, was perhaps what induced the poet to write that Beatrice made the heaven of Mercury shine. **AND IF THE** star changed and laughed: if the star, which is immutable and incorruptible, changed and laughed and shone—for we say a thing "laughs" when it shines and glows—how much more ought I to change, I who am a man and am by nature transmutable in every way, that is, in every mode? For not only is the body mutable, but also the soul, through various disturbances.

> As in a fish-pond that is still and clear,
> the fish draw near to what comes from outside
> in such a way they think it is their food,
> so I saw more than a thousand splendors
> drawing toward us, and in each was heard:
> "Behold one who shall increase our loves!"
> And as each one came toward us,
> the shade was seen to be filled with joy
> within the bright glow that issued from it.
> Think, reader, if what begins here
> did not proceed, how you would feel
> an agonizing craving to know more;
> and by yourself you will see how I
> felt a great desire to hear of their condition
> as soon as they were manifest to my eyes.
> "O well-born one, to whom grace is granted
> to see the thrones of the eternal triumph
> before your warfare is abandoned, <note>meaning before death</note>
> by the light that spreads through all of heaven
> we are kindled; and so, if you desire
> to be enlightened by us, sate yourself at will."
> Thus by one of those pious spirits...

<column-break/>

This is an excellent comparison and very appropriate, but it is so clear that it does not need further explanation. If you, reader, wish to understand how much I desired to hear from those spirits about their state, consider if I did not follow up immediately with what "begins here"—that is, what is starting now—how great your desire would be for me to speak; and thus you will understand mine. **O WELL BORN**: these are the words of one of these souls. He says, therefore, "O you, Dante, well-born"—that is, born at a happy moment—to whom God grants the grace to see the **eternal triumph**, which is the state of bliss that men can acquire after Jesus Christ, through His passion, triumphed over our adversary <note>the Devil</note>. **BEFORE THE warfare is abandoned**: A man in this life is in the <term>Church Militant</term>, in which one who fights boldly against the flesh and the devil wins; then, in the other life, he triumphs in that victory, and it is called the <term>Church Triumphant</term>. But Dante feigns having this grace above all others who still live: that while still in the "militant" life, he could see the eternal glory which is seen only by those who, after death, are in the "triumphant" life. **BY THE LIGHT THAT**: He demonstrates how much charity is in the blessed souls, who live by the light of God, which is the highest charity. This is evident because, without even being asked by the poet, they offer to tell him whatever he wishes to know, so that he may understand that they...

# PARADISO

->PARADISO<-

...said to me, and by Beatrice: "Speak, speak surely, and believe as if they were gods." This spirit demonstrates what they do because they are illuminated by the light that expands—that is, extends—throughout all of heaven, and this is the light of God. Thus the spirit offered itself so generously. And Beatrice, turning to Dante, said: "Speak surely," meaning ask without suspicion. By this the poet intends that Holy Theology <note>represented by Beatrice</note> comforts us so that we strive to learn, not from malignant spirits—in whom there is fraud, snares, malice, and deception—but from the good, who desire to speak the truth out of charity and because they are enlightened. And therefore he adds: "believe them as gods."

> "I see well how you nestle yourself
> in the first light that flows from your eyes,
> because they sparkle as you smile;
> But I do not know who you are, nor why you hold,
> worthy soul, the rank of this sphere
> which is veiled to mortals by another's rays."
> This I said, directed toward the light
> that had first spoken to me; whereat it became
> far more radiant than it was before.

The spirit had generously promised Dante his assistance, and Beatrice comforted him, urging him to ask. For this reason, Dante now speaks and says: "I see well how you nestle yourself" <note>original: "tannidi," meaning to make a nest or settle comfortably</note>, that is, how you place and fix yourself in the **First Light**, which is God. It is as if he said: "I know that you can tell me, because by always mirroring yourself in the light of God, you can see all things therein." "And I see also that you draw it [the light] from your eyes," as if to say the eyes receive the light of God and illuminate you—and you should understand "eyes" to mean the **intellect**. "But, O worthy soul, I do not know who you are, nor why you have been assigned the rank of the sphere of Mercury," which is veiled and covered from the sight of mortals by the rays of the sun. And why it is veiled, we have shown above. **THIS I SAID**: Dante, directed toward the light—that is, turned toward the light of that spirit.

---

> Just as the sun, which hides itself
> through too much light when the heat has gnawed away
> the tempering of the thick vapors,
> So, through greater joy, the holy figure
> hid itself from me within its own radiance;
> and thus, closely enclosed, it answered me
> in the manner that the following canto sings.

A most appropriate comparison between the light of Justinian and that of the sun. It often happens that as the sun rises in our hemisphere, it excites and draws upward many vapors which shade and dim it, and in a way strip it of its splendor so that the human eye can endure it. But once the sun has "gnawed" and consumed such vapors, and no obstacle remains between its rays and our sight, the eye can no longer withstand such great light. So it was that the great joy appearing in the face of Justinian meant that Dante could no longer look at him. 

**Justinian**, the son of the sister of Emperor Justin, succeeded Justin in the year of our Lord 522 <note>original: "d xxii"</note>, and in the year of the world 5,622. A just man, he organized all the ancient Roman laws, which were scattered through many volumes, with marvelous order and reduced them to brevity <note>referring to the *Corpus Juris Civilis*</note>. He reigned for thirty-eight years. Through **Belisarius**, a man most excellent in military discipline, he extinguished the Vandals in Africa; he conquered the Goths in Dalmatia and took Salona. He sent Belisarius to liberate Italy, who took Naples; and at Ravenna, he captured Witiges, King of the Goths, along with his wife and many barons. Furthermore, in the following year, Florence—which was besieged by the Goths—was defended by Justinian’s generals. Justinian also sent John, his prefect, to Africa and defeated the Moors. Finally, he sent **Narses** to Italy, who first defeated Totila and then Teia, kings of the Goths, capturing and killing them. Finally, in the final years of his life, he lost his intellect and became dull and senseless, and at last he died.
