CANTO SIX SIX

### CANTO SIX OF THE THIRD CANTICLE OF DANTE

After Constantine turned the Eagle
against the course of heaven, which it followed
behind that ancient one who took Lavinia,
for a hundred and a hundred years and more the bird of God <note>original: "luccel didio," referring to the Roman Eagle as a divine symbol</note>
stayed at the edge of Europe,
near the mountains from which it first came forth;
and under the shadow of its sacred wings
it governed the world from hand to hand,
and so by changing, it came into my hands.

I was Caesar and I am Justinian,
who, by the will of the first love which I feel,
cleared the laws of the excess and the vain. <note>Justinian refers to his reorganization of Roman law into the *Corpus Juris Civilis*</note>
And before I was focused on that work,
one nature in Christ, and no more,
I believed, and with such faith I was content;
but the blessed Agapetus, who was
supreme shepherd of the sincere faith,
directed me with his words.
I believed him; and what was in his faith
I now see clearly, just as you see
that every contradiction is both false and true.

As soon as I moved my feet with the Church,
it pleased God by His grace to inspire me

<column-break/>

The poet uses a wonderful artifice here: knowing that the subject matter is difficult and subtle—and that the reader’s mind might grow weary—he varies this sixth canto by interspersing almost all of Roman history. He does this in a way that does not seem to depart from the proposed subject. He had already spoken with the Emperor Justinian, although he did not yet know him, and asked who he was and what the condition of the spirits of that heaven was. Now Justinian answers him; and before telling how he was Emperor, he describes the "translation" <term>translation: the historical term for the relocation of the seat of the Empire</term> of the Empire made by Constantine from Rome to Constantinople. "After Constantine turned the Eagle"—that is, the Roman Empire, whose ensign is the eagle—"AGAINST THE COURSE OF THE HEAVEN": because the heavens move from east to west, and Constantine, going from Italy to Thrace, went from west to east. Therefore, he went against the course of heaven, which previously had "followed behind the ancient one who took Lavinia": this means that when Aeneas <note>original: "enea," the Trojan hero</note> came from Troy to Italy with the eagle, because he came from the east to the west, the course of heaven followed him. We can also say that the eagle that came from Troy to Italy came according to the course of heaven because it came with great fortune and established the Roman Empire. But when it went from Italy to Thrace, it went against the course of heaven because the Empire declined from then on. We have spoken of the Eagle and Constantine. We have likewise spoken of Aeneas. "A HUNDRED AND A HUNDRED YEARS AND MORE THE BIRD OF GOD": The reign of Constantine began in the year of our salvation 309. And the reign of Justinian began in the year 523. Thus, there were 214 years between them. The eagle, because it is consecrated to Jove <note>Jupiter</note>, is called the "bird of God," and it remained at the edge of Europe, namely in Constantinople, where Constantine moved the Empire; this city is in the furthest part of Europe, which is divided from Asia by the river Don <note>original: "tanai"</note>. "NEAR THE MOUNTAINS" of Troy from which Aeneas led it to Italy. For Troy is not further from Constantinople than 138 miles as the crow flies. But according to the charts of our times, it is 150 miles away. Therefore, with the Empire in Constantinople, the Roman eagles were near the mountains from which they had departed when following Aeneas to Italy. And he said "mountains" and not the "city of Ilium" <note>Troy</note> to allude to the nature of eagles, which inhabit mountains.

To show who he was, it was necessary to present both his public and private person. First, the public one, which was no longer in him then, but was while he lived; and therefore he said "I was Caesar," meaning Emperor, a dignity that ends in death. "And I am Justinian," because death separates the soul from the body, but nonetheless that same soul remains, which is the true man. Justinian was the son of the sister of Emperor Justin and succeeded him. "AND BEFORE I WAS FOCUSED ON THE WORK. One nature": In those times, Theodatus <note>Theodahad</note>, King of the Goths, was in the Roman kingdom, and hearing that Justinian was his enemy, he sent Pope Agapetus to appease him. Agapetus understood that Justinian was in the heresy of those who estimated that Christ had been a pure man and not God <note>The commentator here describes the Monophysite heresy, which Justinian historically renounced</note>. For this reason, Agapetus disputed very sharply against him and finally brought him back to the true Catholic faith. And shortly after, Agapetus died, and Vigilius succeeded him. "WHAT WAS IN HIS FAITH": It is most true that faith, being such an excellent virtue, does not inhabit heaven; for as soon as the spirit enters heaven, he is certain of that which he previously held through faith. "EVERY contradiction is false and true": It is certain that in every contradiction, one part is true and one is false. Thus, if I say: "The Arno passes through Florence" and "The Arno does not pass through Florence," this is a contradiction; and one is true (that the Arno passes through Florence) and the other is false (that the Arno does not pass through Florence).

It did not seem credible that such a great work as the composition of the volumes of the laws <note>The *Digest* and *Code* of Justinian</note> could have been done by Justinian without divine help.

# PARADISO

<columns>2</columns>

That high labor <note>Justinian refers to the *Corpus Juris Civilis*, his massive reorganization of Roman law.</note> and I gave myself entirely to it,

to whom the right hand of heaven was so joined

Now here to the first question is pointed
my answer; but the condition
constrains me to follow with some addition,
so that you may see with how much reason
one moves against the sacrosanct sign,
and who appropriates it and who opposes it.

...and military [affairs] so that he could with more leisure devote himself to the correction of the laws. **NOW HERE TO THE QUESTION**: The sentence and my response to your first question and inquiry: it comes to a point here, that is, it makes a point here and does not follow [further] because the condition of the things I have said, especially regarding the eagle, constrains me to write somewhat on the subject: and to follow something that is joined to your question, that is, something beyond what you asked. And in short, the poet wants to put here in brevity what he treats extensively in his *Monarchia* <note>Dante’s Latin treatise on secular power</note>: In which he tries to prove that by reason we all must obey the empire in temporal things. And therefore he says "so that you see and understand with how much reason"—using irony, that is, "with how much injustice"—one moves against the sacrosanct sign of the eagle, that is, against the sacrosanct empire. **AND WHO APPROPRIATES IT**: he who appropriates the said sign for himself, that is, wants to usurp some part of the empire; **and who opposes it**: and he who does not obey, he goes against it: he acts against God.

See how much virtue has made it worthy
of reverence; and it began from the hour
when Pallas died to give it a kingdom. <note>In the *Aeneid*, Pallas was the son of Evander who died fighting for Aeneas.</note>
You know it made its home in Alba
for three hundred years and more until the end,
when three fought for it still. <note>The three Horatii and three Curiatii who fought to decide the supremacy of Rome over Alba Longa.</note>
You know what it did from the harm to the Sabine women
to the grief of Lucretia, in seven kings,
conquering the neighboring peoples around.

<column-break/>

Nor did he ever deserve, being either pagan or heretic, to have such help. Therefore he says well that it pleased God to dispose me to such labor, that is <note>original: "idest"</note>, to pour into me the will to take up such a task; and it pleased Him immediately that I moved my feet with the Church, that is <note>original: "idest"</note>, having become a true Christian I followed the Catholic faith: and I gave myself entirely to Him, that is, to the said labor of correcting the laws; that is <note>original: "idest"</note>, setting aside every other care, I devoted myself to this work. And because the empire cannot be defended without military discipline, I commanded and committed such care to one who was not only practiced in it but also had joined with him the "right hand," that is <note>original: ". i ."</note>, the favor of heaven. And this seemed to be a sign that God willed that I should rest from active cares.

Wishing to prove that obedience is unjustly taken away from this sign, he uses this argument: That sign is worthy of obedience which for many centuries, with many and various virtues, has acquired a great empire. But the eagle has done this; therefore it deserves reverence and obedience. And that it has done so is proved by the histories which he briefly sets down. And having narrated how it came from Troy, carried by Aeneas, he follows to demonstrate the greatest victory that Aeneas had in Italy against Latinus and Turnus when Pallas was killed. After the destruction of Troy, Aeneas came to Italy...

<columns>1</columns>

...and first he allied himself with King Latinus, who betrothed to him his daughter Lavinia. This was very distressing to Amata, the girl's mother, who desired that she be the wife of Turnus, king of the Rutuli. And she acted in such a way that Latinus was forced, together with Turnus, to stir up war, in which Aeneas had favor from the Tuscans and from Evander, king of Pallanteum—the city where Rome was later. This war had various outcomes; and in the first battle Aeneas fought after returning from Tuscany, Pallas, the son of Evander, was killed by Turnus. But finally, Turnus being killed by Aeneas, the victory went to the Trojans, and the rule of the Latins came to Aeneas. He drowned in the river Numicus and was counted among the number of the gods. He was succeeded by Ascanius, whom he had fathered in Troy by Creusa. Ascanius, leaving the kingdom to Lavinia, his stepmother, founded a new city which he called Alba Longa: "Alba" from the omen of the white [alba] sow and the thirty white [albi] piglets; and "Longa" from the city, that is, from the shape of the city which stretched in length along the ridge of the mountain. In this city reigned fourteen kings: Ascanius, Silvius, Aeneas, Latinus, Alba, Atys, Capys, Capetus, Tiberinus, Agrippa, Romulus [Silvius], Aventinus, Proca, and Amulius. This man, to remain alone in the kingdom, drove out Numitor his brother, who had an only daughter; and Amulius made her a Vestal Virgin so that no seed might remain from his brother. But pregnant by Mars, she gave birth to Romulus and Remus. These drove Amulius from the kingdom and restored Numitor, their maternal grandfather, and afterward they founded Rome, for which the empire of a good part of the world was reserved. Rome was built in the year of the world 4454, in the eighth Olympiad. And Alba was built by Ascanius in the year of the world 4030 or thereabouts, and was destroyed by Tullus Hostilius, the third king of the Romans, who succeeded Numa Pompilius in the year of the world 4536. In the same war, the Roman people agreed with the Alban people that they should choose three from each army, and that the people whose champions were defeated should submit to the other people whose three remained victors. There were in those times among the Romans three Horatii, young brothers born at one birth; and among the Albans similarly three Curiatii. To these, therefore, lot gave the task of fighting for all the others. And in the course of the battle, two Horatii were killed, and three Curiatii remained wounded. There was...

### SIXTH CANTO

And Horatius was left deprived of every other help, but without any wound. Therefore, he decided to compensate for his solitude by the separation of the three Curiatii <note>The Horatii were three Roman brothers and the Curiatii were three brothers from the rival city of Alba Longa; they fought to decide the war between their cities.</note>, and he feigned flight. The Curiatii followed him, but with unequal speed because they were wounded differently; the most robust was ahead of those who, due to more serious wounds, were less able to run. When Horatius saw them separated by a wide interval, he turned back to the first one and killed him before the second could arrive. He finally killed the second before the third could offer him help. Nor was there much resistance in the last one, because the mortal wounds received earlier had taken away all his strength. In this way, the Albans were wounded; in this way, Horatius returned honored with victory. But deprived of his brothers, he did not find his fortune yet appeased in Rome. He had a sister who was already betrothed to one of the Curiatii; when she saw among her brother’s spoils the bloody garment of her husband <note>Technically her fiancé, but often referred to as her husband in these accounts.</note>, which she herself had woven, she could not contain her tears at her husband's death. Horatius was enraged by this, as it did not seem to him appropriate that she should put private grief before public joy, and in his anger, he killed her. For such a sister-slaying <note>original: "fororicidio," likely a scribal error for "sororicidio."</note>, he was condemned by the king. But it was granted that he could appeal to the people, and by the people, he was acquitted. **AND YOU KNOW WHAT IT DID** regarding the wrong of the Sabines. Romulus had already not only built Rome, but had made it well-populated through the gathering of many youths. But because all the neighboring peoples disdained to intermarry with such men—because for the most part they had been exiled from their own homelands for various crimes—and there were no women in Rome, the king decided to pursue through deception what he could not obtain by favor. He ordered sacrifices and games with very grand and ornate preparation. The Sabines, neighbors to Rome, gathered for such a celebration; they came willingly and without suspicion with their wives and children. But when Romulus saw the whole crowd paying close attention to the games, he gave the ordered signal to his men, who with a sudden and unforeseen tumult snatched so many of the Sabine virgins that each man had his own. The Sabines could not endure such a contemptuous injury. They returned home and, having organized a robust army, they came with such force that they entered Rome. The battle was most atrocious, and many perished on every side. But in the women there appeared a prudence and boldness of spirit more than womanly, and a piety worthy of eternal memory. For the abducted Sabine women, by common counsel and without fear of death, threw themselves into the middle of the two combatant ranks with many tears and torn hair; turning now to their fathers and now to their husbands, they said: "We, we are the cause of so much evil; turn all your discord and fury upon us." This miserable act of the girls and the supreme piety they showed everywhere were so powerful that they made the battle cease. Having put aside all hatred, they not only became friends, but of two cities they became one. For the Sabines, leaving their city of Cures, inhabited Rome on this condition: that Rome should not change its name, but all citizens, both Romans and Sabines, should be called Quirites <note>A formal name for Roman citizens, traditionally derived from the Sabine town of Cures.</note> after Cures.

**ON THE GRIEF of Lucretia**: We tell of her in the first canto of the first canticle <note>Referencing Inferno IV, where Lucretia is seen in Limbo.</note>. **SEVEN KINGS** gave the best foundation for expressing the Roman Empire. For Romulus, a very warlike man, made the people intrepid against every danger. Numa Pompilius, the second king, introduced peace and religion. Tullus Hostilius, the third king, a man of great spirit and no less intellect, was almost the first author of every military discipline and order. Ancus Marcius, the fourth king and born of a sister of Numa, encircled the city with walls. Nor was Tarquinius Priscus a small ornament. And Servius Tullius, who first organized the census and the taxes so that the soldiers might have public pay. Tarquinius the Proud gave the cause for the city to be reduced to liberty <note>His tyranny led to the Roman revolt and the establishment of the Republic.</note>. Thus the Roman people were: under Romulus, bold; under Numa, religious; under Hostilius, armed; under Ancus, secure; under Priscus, adorned; under Servius, rewarded; under the Proud, liberated. The kings reigned in Rome for 243 years.

It is not necessary, says Justinian, that I tell you the illustrious things of this sign <note>The Eagle</note> because you know what it did; he says this as if to say: how many victories it brought, carried by the illustrious Romans. **AGAINST BRENNUS**: This man was the leader of the Senonian Gauls who, having passed into Italy, occupied everything between the Alps and the Po. Then they came into Tuscany and besieged Chiusi—today almost desolate and under Sienese jurisdiction. But in those times, one of the heads of Tuscany. There, offended by the Romans, they turned all their fury against them. They broke them at the river Allia and took Rome, except for the Capitol, which they besieged for six months. And finally, the Romans, oppressed by hunger, agreed to pay a thousand pounds of gold so that the Gauls would depart. But Camillus, of whom it would be a long history to tell, was made dictator although absent and in exile.

But he was greedy for empire, and for this reason too restless. And in military discipline...

After discussing the early Roman Republic and the war against the Albans, the narrative now moves to the expansion of the Roman Empire, focusing on the wars against Pyrrhus and the rise of Julius Caesar.</meta>

# PARADISO

...no less a commander than Alexander the Great. He was awarded the palm of victory for his skill in <term>castrametation|the art of designing and laying out military camps</term>. He came to Italy to fight against the Romans under the guise of defending the Tarentines, and he was the first to bring elephants into Italy. He fought many times against the Romans with varying fortune—sometimes the victor and sometimes the vanquished—largely due to the efforts of <note>Manius Curius Dentatus and Fabricius Luscinus were Roman consuls famous for their incorruptibility and simple lifestyle.</note> Curius and Fabricius, who triumphed over him. He wished to make peace with the Romans on fair terms, but the authority of **Appius Claudius the Blind** <note>Appius Claudius Caecus was an aging statesman who gave a famous speech in the Senate, arguing that Rome should never negotiate while enemy troops remained on Italian soil.</note> was so great that the Senate never consented to grant him peace until his army first returned home. The war lasted four years, but it was fought without treachery or cruelty; they sought to conquer as much through magnanimity as through arms. The Romans wished to ransom a great number of prisoners he had taken in battle, and Pyrrhus returned them without payment, asserting that he had not come to make a "merchandise of men," but rather to test to whom Fortune wished to grant the empire. Nor were the Romans outdone in this benefit: when an offer was made to them by Pyrrhus’s physician to poison the king, the Romans immediately revealed the fraud and its author, demonstrating how alien such deceit was to the Roman people. Thus, Pyrrhus gave the prisoners to the Romans, and the Romans gave life back to Pyrrhus. He finally departed from Italy, and not long after, having entered the city of Argos by force, he was killed in the heat of battle by a woman who threw a roof-tile <note>original: "ebrice," from the Latin imbrex</note> from a window onto his head.

**AND AGAINST THE OTHER** princes and allies—that is, against various nations and peoples—of whom I judge it better to remain silent than to say too little. Considering that we could scarcely recount in a dedicated volume the innumerable triumphs that various Roman leaders brought back from diverse parts of the world and in different times with illustrious victories.

**WHEREFORE TORQUATUS** The family of the **Manlii** <note>The Manlii were a distinguished patrician family in Rome.</note> was most excellent, adorned with many victories won for their fatherland. But a distinguished example is that of **Titus Manlius**, who, although his father treated him very harshly and kept him in the countryside, forbidding him from the city, nevertheless freed his father from the danger of the <term>tribune of the plebs|an elected official tasked with protecting the common people</term>. The tribune was attempting, using the testimony of the younger Manlius (whom he judged to be his father's enemy), to strip the father of his reputation and his country. This same Titus was the first in this family to be named **Torquatus**. This name came from an action during a battle against the Gauls—men who are always fierce in their first assault. One Gaul of great size and no small courage continually insulted the Romans, considering them timid and base, and challenged anyone to single combat. Manlius did not suffer such an insult; he went out to meet the Gaul and, with strength and skill, conquered and killed him. He stripped from him a neck-chain which the Latins call a <term>torques|a twisted metal neck-ring worn by Gallic warriors</term>, and he adorned himself with that sign of victory. Because of this *torque*, he was thereafter named Torquatus. Just as he was pious toward his father, he was equally severe toward his own son; because the son had fought dangerously against his orders in the Latin War, Titus called him before his tribunal. In the sight of the army, he commanded the <term>lictor|an officer attending a magistrate</term> to first beat him with rods and then strike off his head with an axe.

**AND AS MUCH AS BY THE CYRRHO.** The fifth was named **Cincinnatus**. In our language, we might say "ruffled-hooked," and *pyrrhe* in Latin means short hair. This is sometimes considered an ornament when the hair is composed with great art using iron or other instruments to make it ringed and curly. Hence Persius says: <note>original: "Ten cyrrhotorum centum durata fuisse" (Persius, Satire 1.29), meaning "That you should have been the hardiness of a hundred curly-headed ones."</note> and Juvenal: <note>original: "Altior hic quare cincinnus" (Juvenal, Satire 6.502), meaning "Why is this curl higher?"</note>. At other times, the hair on the head is twisted when it is not combed, and so it remains tangled. In that case, the curl <note>original: "cinninno"</note> or the *cyrrho* is not an ornament but the opposite. For this reason, **Quinctius** <note>The OCR reads "curiatio," likely a transcription error for "Quinctius" (Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus).</note>, a man of hard life, was called Cincinnatus because he kept his hair neglected, wild, and without a comb. Hence Petrarch wrote: "And Cincinnatus with the uncultivated locks." He was poor and cultivated his own small possessions with his own hands. Created Dictator to face the Aequi—who had trapped the consul Minucius and his army—he broke the enemy, freed the consul, and triumphed; on the sixteenth day, he resigned the dictatorship. Of the Fabii and the Decii, it is spoken of elsewhere.

This sign performed all the things already mentioned up until the advent of Christ the Savior. And then, when His Incarnation approached—which occurred under the empire of **Augustus Caesar**—it did miraculous things with this sign. Because these are narrated in the fourth canto of the first canticle <note>A reference to the *Inferno*, though the specific deeds of the Eagle are primarily the subject of this current canto, *Paradiso* VI.</note>, we will omit them for now. Here the author demonstrates that God gave such favor to Julius Caesar because He willed that, at the time the Word became flesh, the whole world should be under one monarch who would rule the world in peace. This was Augustus, who took up the monarchy already established by Julius—chiefly so that Christ, through His passion and death, might liberate the human race from the slavery of the devil. And so he says He willed to "bring the world to its serene state."

# CANTO SIX

### Then it descended like a lightning bolt upon Juba
### then it turned back toward your west
### where it heard the Pompeian trumpet

<margin>Gaul. Where it also acquired Germany and Britain, today called England.</margin> And what it did. **FROM THE VAR:** This is the river which divides Cisalpine Gaul <note>The part of Gaul on the Italian side of the Alps.</note> from Transalpine Gaul. The Rhine rises in the Alps where the people called the Lepontii dwell. After a short course, it forms two lakes: one called Veneto, the other Acronius <note>Modern Lake Constance.</note>. It then flows through the lands of the Helvetians, the Sequani, the Treveri, and other peoples. As it nears the ocean, it divides into several parts and forms a number of islands. The first to build a bridge over this river was Julius Caesar, with admirable skill, as he describes in his *Commentaries*. The Isère is a river of Gaul that flows into the Rhône. The Arar <note>The modern Saône.</note> is a river of Germany that rises in the Vosges mountains. It flows through the lands of the Aedui and the Sequani so gently that one can hardly discern in which direction it moves. It flows into the Rhône.

**SEINE.** In Latin *Sequana*, a river of Gaul abundant in fish, which separates the Belgians from the Celts. It passes through Paris and creates in that region the island called Lutetia. The Rhône river rises in the Alps, not far from the sources of the Danube and the Rhine. It took its name from the city of Rhodanus, built by the Rhodians, which it passes. It enters the Tyrrhenian Sea through three mouths. **THAT WHICH** after it left Ravenna: And it came to the Rubicon river, the boundary of the province committed to him, beyond which, according to Roman laws, he could not lead his army unless the Senate permitted it. But he found an excuse in the malice of his adversaries, who, by denying him just things, gave him the courage to undertake an unjust enterprise. Incited by this, and also by Curio, Mark Antony, and other friends, he crossed in a brief time and came to Rome, which, having been abandoned by the Senate and Pompey, he easily brought under his power. This was the exalted beginning of his tyranny, which I do not see how one can praise in any way. **AND LEAPED** the Rubicon: This is a small river between Rimini and Ravenna, and in those times, it was the boundary of Cisalpine Gaul. **TOWARD** Spain: After settling matters in Italy, he went to Spain against Petreius and Afranius, the legates <term>legates|military commanders or deputies</term> of Pompey, and defeated and killed them near Ilerda, a city of Aragon. In forty days, he subjugated all of Spain. When he went there, he said he was going to an army without a leader, and afterward, he would return to a leader without an army, as appeared in Thessaly, where Pompey had many soldiers but of little value. **TOWARD DURAZZO** The volume would grow too large if I related in order how Caesar, as the victor of Spain, returned to Rome; how from Rome he went to Brindisi and from there sailed to Durazzo <note>Also known as Dyrrachium.</note> where he was besieged by Pompey. Finally, by force of arms, he made his way through the midst of the enemies, and many of his men were killed by the Pompeians. It was the opinion that on that day Pompey did not know how to win, because he recalled his men from the battle, either because he did not hope for victory or because he hoped he could defeat them without a battle. Caesar fled to Thessaly, and finally at Pharsalia, a place in Thessaly, with a universal gathering of both armies, a most atrocious battle took place. Finally, Caesar, with a much smaller army but of veteran and highly trained soldiers, long accustomed to his command, defeated Pompey. Of the Roman citizens who fought in the legions, fifteen thousand men perished, and an innumerable multitude of other peoples who had come from almost all parts of the world to aid Pompey. Never had the Roman people gathered such great forces, for both sides together numbered three hundred thousand. But of Roman legions, Caesar had eleven and Pompey eighteen. Pompey fled to Egypt, and Ptolemy sent Achillas and Photinus to meet him, who killed him. Ptolemy presented the head to Caesar. But shortly after, Ptolemy rebelled against Caesar. Not without danger did Caesar escape his treacheries; at last, he defeated him and occupied Alexandria and Egypt. **SO THAT THE NILE** Felt the pain: he places the Nile, which flows through Egypt; and calls it "hot" as it comes from the eastern regions. **ANTANDROS:** This shows when Caesar went to Egypt; he crossed the Hellespont and went to Phrygia where Troy is, from whence Aeneas brought the Eagle into Latium and to the Albans, and from the Albans it came to the Romans. Antandros is an island near Troy. **SIMOIS** is a river which rises in Mount Ida and flows near Troy. It forms a marsh near the Sigean promontory joined to the Xanthus and enters the sea. **HECTOR** is buried there: where Hector, the son of Priam, is buried; Lucan writes that Caesar visited his tomb.

**BY PTOLEMY:** Because he was dispatched by him <note>Meaning Pompey was killed by Ptolemy's orders.</note>. **THEN IT DESCENDED** lightning-like upon Juba: After the unhappy slaughter of Pharsalia, Cato gathered the remains of the Pompeian army and led them through the sandy Libya into Africa. He joined with Scipio and with Juba, the King of Mauritania, where Petreius had also fled from Spain. Caesar, having arrived in Sicily from Egypt and hearing of the great preparations, led his army into Africa. After several battles near Thapsus, he defeated the enemies. After the rout, Juba and Petreius, seeing no remedy, killed each other with their own hands after a bountiful banquet. The same was done by Cato, who had fled to Utica, not out of fear, but out of greatness of soul, which could not endure to see the face of the tyrant. Scipio was fleeing by sea to Spain, but when Caesar's men overtook him, he likewise killed himself. After this war, there remained the one in Spain, where two sons of Pompey were with a very powerful army. The battle was near Munda. Never was there a fight with greater fury, nor was Caesar ever in greater danger; it is said he even considered killing himself. Finally, he dismounted from his horse and, with supreme fury, placed himself in front of the infantry; he made the veterans, who were already fleeing, feel ashamed. Out of shame, they turned back against the enemy and achieved victory. Labienus was killed, as was Gnaeus, one of the sons of Pompey. This was the end of the civil war, which had lasted four years.

It chronicles the defeat of Pompey and his supporters, marking the transition from the Roman Republic to the era of the Caesars.</summary>

->PARADISE<-

**O**f what it <note>The Roman Eagle, the symbol of divine authority.</note> did with the following bearer <note>original: "baiulo"; referring to Augustus, who followed Julius Caesar.</note>
Brutus and Cassius howl in Hell,
and Modena and Perugia were mournful.
Sad Cleopatra still weeps for it,
who, fleeing before it from the asp,
took a sudden and black death.
With him it ran as far as the Red Sea;
with him it placed the world in such peace
that the temple of Janus was locked up.

The fatherland's distinguished and equal men were content to lay down their lives to extinguish the tyrant. But let us say that he <note>Dante</note> does not place Brutus here for the sake of the individual Brutus <note>Brutus the Elder, who founded the Republic</note>, but for those who betray their lord and especially the Emperor, whose name the poet wished to honor greatly. **MODENA AND PERUGIA**: In Modena, Augustus—still a young man—was praetor; with the veteran soldiers of Julius Caesar and the encouragement of Cicero, he defeated Mark Antony, who had been declared a rebel by the Senate after Caesar’s death. Later, he changed his counsel, and overcome by ambition, he preferred unjust tyranny over holy liberty. Along with Mark Antony and Marcus Lepidus, they divided the empire among themselves and made their fatherland a slave; shortly after, at Philippi, they killed Brutus and Cassius. Later, Octavian returned to Italy and went against Lucius Antony, brother of Mark Antony, who had become an enemy; he besieged him in Perugia, and through famine defeated him and sacked the city. **CLEOPATRA**: We spoke of her in the fifth canto of the first canticle <note>Inferno, Canto V, among the lustful.</note>. **FROM THE ASP** <note>original: "dal colubro"</note>: By the snake, as we narrated in that place; she killed herself so as not to be led alive in Octavian's triumph. **TO THE RED SEA** <note>original: "al lito rubro"</note>: To the Red Sea because after the death of Mark Antony, who killed himself with his own hands, he occupied all of Egypt as far as the Red Sea. **TO JANUS HIS TEMPLE**: Janus was a very ancient king in Italy who initially reigned with great harmony alongside Cameses. From Janus, the hill that is in Rome near the Vatican across the Tiber was named the Janiculum. From Cameses, that region was named Camesena. After the death of Cameses, Janus took Saturn as a partner in the kingdom. Because of his prudence, he was depicted with two faces, one looking forward and the other backward. For the prudent man, through the memory of past things, makes conjectures about future ones. Zeno wrote that he was the first to institute temples and sacrifices to the gods in Italy. For this, he also merited divine honors, and in all sacrifices, his name was mentioned at the beginning. The first month of the year was called January after Janus. His temple was closed during times of peace. This happened twice before Octavian: the first time under Numa, the second king of the Romans, in whose reign there was never war in Rome; the second time after the First Punic War. Then the third time was under Emperor Octavian. And this was a long-lasting and universal peace. For this reason, the poet says that he closed the temple <note>original: "Delubro"</note> of Janus.

**B**ut what the sign that makes me speak
had done before and was yet to do
throughout the mortal realm that is subject to it,
becomes in appearance somewhat obscure,
if in the hand of the third Caesar <note>Tiberius</note> it is looked upon
with clear eye and pure heart.
For the living justice that inspires me
granted it, in the hand of him I mention,
the glory of wreaking vengeance for its [God's] wrath.
Now marvel here at what I repeat to you:
later it ran with Titus to take vengeance
for the vengeance of the ancient sin.
And when the Lombard tooth bit
the Holy Church, under its wings
Charlemagne, conquering, came to her aid.

...because it seems he speaks obscurely by saying that Titus set out to take vengeance for the vengeance of the ancient sin. Titus thus took vengeance for the death of Christ, which was the vengeance for the sin of the first father [Adam], since His passion and death were for the satisfaction of the guilt committed by Adam and passed down into...

<column-break/>

**A**fter Julius Caesar succeeded Caesar Augustus, who, to avenge the death of Julius, made war against Brutus and Cassius as we showed at the end of the first canticle. Therefore he says **Brutus with Cassius**. **Howls** <note>original: "latra"</note>, that is, barks, as we said in Hell; that this greatest sign [the Eagle] did this with the **following bearer**, that is, with him who carried it after Caesar, who was Augustus. To "bear" <note>original: "baiulare"</note> in the Latin language means to carry; hence a *baiulus* is one who carries. If, as we said another time, the poet were to place Brutus and Cassius as traitors, there would be no excuse for the poet, because they were not traitors, but liberators of...

**BUT WHAT THE SIGN**. The meaning is that this eagle never did—neither before nor after—a greater thing than during the empire of the third Caesar, who was Tiberius; for in his reign occurred the redemption of the human generation. **HAD DONE**: Before, through the Roman fathers, the consuls, and dictators, and finally through Julius Caesar and then Augustus. **AND WAS YET TO DO**: Through the emperors who followed. **FOR THE LIVING JUSTICE**: That is, the Divine Majesty, which inspires me, Justinian, to say this thing, granted to Tiberius the glory of taking vengeance for His wrath—that is, to punish the Jews who, through the death of Christ, had stirred God to anger. Thus, Tiberius was able to take vengeance for Christ, as later Vespasian and Titus did, of which we spoke in Purgatory. Orosius says that Tiberius wanted the Senate to enroll Christ among the number of their gods, and not obtaining it, he turned to every fury. **NOW MARVEL HERE**: He continues by demonstrating what the eagle did in the empire of Titus, and he makes the listener attentive...

The text interprets these events as divine "vengeance" for original sin and concludes with Charlemagne's defense of the Church against the Lombards.</summary>

<header>CANTO SIXTH</header>
<sig>C. iiii.</sig>

us. **AND WHEN THE LOMBARD TOOTH** bit <note>original: "el dente longobardo morse"; a metaphor for the Lombard invasion and harassment of the Papacy.</note>: The Lombards, in great numbers with their wives, children, and other barbarian nations, held Italy under their leader Alboin in the year of Christ 567. These people were called from Pannonia into Italy by Narses. He had been a eunuch of Sophia, wife of the Emperor Justinian; having risen to such great esteem through his virtue, Justinian sent him with a most powerful army for the defense of Italy, where he performed excellent deeds. But later, having been recalled in disgrace to servile duties by Sophia, and having been very ungratefully removed from the administration of Italy by Justinian, Narses—incited by such injury—did not cease for three continuous years to urge the Lombards to cross into Italy. In the beginning, they took Cisalpine Gaul, though for many years they were occupied with the siege of Pavia, which they took in the year 570; and from them, this part of Gaul was renamed Lombardy. In process of time, they occupied all of Italy except Rome. The Lombards reigned in Italy for two hundred and four years. The head of the kingdom was Pavia; but beyond this place, they established principalities throughout all Italy where they held captains of their people: especially in Friuli at the entrance of Italy; likewise at Spoleto, almost in the middle of Italy; and the third at Benevento. Finally, Charles, King of the Franks—who for his egregious deeds was named the Great <note>Charlemagne</note>—called into Italy by Pope Hadrian, came with a powerful army and defeated the Lombards. He captured Desiderius with his wife and children and sent them to France in the year of salvation 774. His father was Pepin, King of the Franks; because in his time the Empire was continually failing in the East and the Emperor was persecuting Christians, Pope Stephen transferred the title and imperial dignity to Pepin and his successors in the kingdom who were of his lineage. Boniface, Bishop of Mainz and apostolic legate, consecrated and anointed him in this ceremony. Pepin was succeeded by Charlemagne, a prince most excellent in military discipline and many virtues, who defeated Himoldus, King of Aquitaine, and having driven him out, occupied the kingdom. He waged war against the Saxons with the greatest success for thirty-three years; in that time, partly by going in person and partly by sending his sons or dukes, he conquered the Spanish and the English. And he came into Italy and defeated Desiderius, as we said. In Spain, he conquered Pamplona and the most noble city of Augusta because they would not come to the faith of Christ. He returned to Italy and defeated Arechis, Duke of Benevento. In this year, which was 783, Constantine, son of Leo, held the empire in Constantinople with his mother Irene. And a golden plate was found in Constantinople on which were carved letters saying: "Christ shall be born of the Virgin Mary and I believe in him. And you, O Sun, under Constantine and Irene, shall see me again." But I return to Charles, who for eight years fought in Pannonia against the Huns and destroyed them. He made his army rich with infinite spoils which the Huns had gathered from various provinces. He returned again to Italy and restored to the pontifical seat Pope Leo III, whom the Romans had unjustly driven out. For this reason, he was called Augustus by Leo and was the first to reign in Rome after Augustulus. He restored Florence, which was largely abandoned, and brought back all the noble families scattered through the surrounding lands. He composed some new laws. Finally, he defeated the Saxons and brought them to the Christian faith. He died in the 72nd year of his age and was succeeded by Louis. This man left three sons: Lothair, Charles, and Louis. These, after a long discord, agreed that Lothair should be Emperor, Charles should have the kingdom of France, and Louis that of Germany. Lothair the Emperor was crowned by Pope Sergius; in his old age, he became a monk and left the Empire to his son Louis, the fourth emperor. The fifth was Charles II, called "the Bald"; the sixth was Charles the Fat, who after several wars became so weak in mind and body that it was necessary for Arnulf, the son of one of his brothers, to govern him. Arnulf became the seventh emperor. He died while making war against the Normans in the year of salvation 907. And thus the Empire ceased in the lineage of Charlemagne, not without the grief of all Italy that it was transferred to Germany <note>original: "magna"; referring to Alemagna or Germany.</note>. Because of this, neither the Romans nor the Pope ever wished to crown or honor any German with the imperial title until Otto I. Thus the empire of Pepin began in the year of Christ 750 and ended with Arnulf in the year 907.

*Now you can judge those*
*whom I accused above, and their faults,*
*which are the cause of all your evils.*
*One opposes the yellow lilies* <note>The symbol of the French monarchy and the Guelph faction.</note>
*to the public sign, and the other appropriates it for a faction,*
*so that it is hard to see which fails more.*
*Let the Ghibellines practice their art*
*under another sign, for he follows it ill*
*whoever separates justice and it;*
*And let this new Charles* <note>Charles II of Anjou.</note> *not strike it down*
*with his Guelphs, but let him fear the talons...*

<column-break/>

Although Dante was a Guelph, nevertheless after his exile he inclined his mind toward the Imperial party. For this reason, in all his work, he honors that seat as much as he can and demonstrates that all Christian peoples and nations should obey the Emperor in temporal matters, just as they obey the Pope in spiritual matters. But because he is not moved by passion but by a zeal for justice, he reproves the Ghibellines as much as the Guelphs. Since the Emperor, as a monarch, ought to be common to both parties, Dante shows that the Guelphs should not have opposed their superior by defending themselves with the authority of the blood of France, nor should the Ghibellines have used the defense of the Empire as a partisan tool.

<meta>This page continues the discourse of the Emperor Justinian in the Sphere of Mercury. Having concluded the history of the Roman Eagle and its transition to the Holy Roman Empire, Justinian now critiques the political factions of Dante’s time—the Guelphs and Ghibellines—before identifying the souls who inhabit this planet.</meta>

*Which have stripped the pelt from greater lions;*
*Oftentimes already have the children wept*
*for the father's fault; and let it not be believed*
*that God will change His emblems for his lilies.* <note>original: "gigli"; the fleur-de-lis, symbol of the French monarchy and the Guelph faction, which Justinian warns is no substitute for the Imperial Eagle.</note>

the whole and not a part. Therefore, they followed the Ghibellines <note>original: "bellini"; likely an abbreviation or transcription error for "Ghibellini."</note> poorly: because they separate the eagle from justice; for as much as it makes itself a partisan of the Ghibellines, it departs from justice.

**This** little star equips itself
with good spirits who have been active
so that honor and fame might follow them.
And when desires climb toward this,
deviating thus, it is inevitable that the rays
of true love mount upward with less life.
But in the measuring of our rewards <note>original: "gaggi"; literally "wages" or "pay," here referring to the level of heavenly bliss.</note>
with merit is part of our joy,
because we see them neither less nor greater.
Hereby the living justice sweetens
the affection in us, so that it can
never be twisted toward any iniquity.
Diverse voices make sweet notes;
so diverse ranks in our court
render sweet harmony among these wheels.

*And within the present pearl* <note>original: "margherita"; an archaic term for a pearl, used here to describe the planet Mercury.</note>
*shines the light of Romeo, whose work*
*was great and beautiful, and poorly received.*
*But the Provençals who acted against him*
*do not have the last laugh, and thus walk a bad path.*

<column-break/>

Because these two parties—one with the favor of the French who have for their arms the golden lilies, the other with the Empire—have ruined Italy through their divisions and civil wars. And therefore it follows that if the Ghibellines wish to be seditious and partisan, they should not practice such arts under the sign of the eagle, which should be a universal sign; that is, they do not rightly follow the eagle whenever the eagle, which should be common to all...

**This** is the answer to the second question of the poet: for he had asked Justinian what was the reason that he inhabited the second sphere, which is that of Mercury. It demonstrates, then, that here are those who have virtuously exercised themselves in the active life. And therefore it says: this star of Mercury equips itself, that is <note>original: "ideſt"</note>, adorns and furnishes itself. Hence we say "to equip the ships" <note>original: "corredare le nati" [navi]</note> with good active spirits, that is <note>original: "ideſt"</note>, spirits who have exercised the political virtues so that honor and fame result from them. Here there appears to be a doubt: whether one deserves to come to heaven who exercises virtue to acquire fame: since he is truly good who loves virtue for itself, and not for the honor or fame that follows; rather, he would prefer to acquire infamy living according to virtue than honor living by the opposite. Therefore I answer that Dante, as a poet, placed the consequence for the antecedent and said "They have been active," that is <note>original: "ideſt"</note>, they exercised themselves in the active life to acquire virtue, from which fame and honor are born.

**LITTLE** star: which is smaller than the other planets, and is rarely seen because it is almost always under the rays of the sun. And of Mercury, we have spoken above. AND WHEN THE desires climb here, that is <note>original: "ideſt"</note>, when our appetites focus on seeking mortal fame and honors: it is fitting and necessary that the rays of true love, of true charity which seeks God—who is the sovereign good—climb upward "less lively," that is, with less vitality. And by this he warns us that in seeking the virtues, we should not base ourselves upon worldly glory, but seek that glory to attain celestial things. BUT IN THE measuring of our rewards: Someone might be persuaded that these spirits were not entirely content. Because they know they have merited less, and by having merited less, they have less beatitude. Therefore they desire more. But to this Justinian answers: since the blessed spirit loves justice, it is content with that state because it sees it receives as much glory as there was merit, which is a work of justice. And therefore he says measuring our rewards, that is, joys, with our merits is part of our joy: because we see justice within them, since those are equal to the merits, and are not "lesser nor greater" <note>original: "maggi"; archaic form of "maggiori."</note>. HEREBY: from this measure that balances glory with merit, living justice "sweetens," that is, increases the affection in us to want what justice itself wants. And it ensures that such affection cannot be twisted from the true path to any "iniquity," that is <note>original: "ideſt"</note>, to any unjust desire. Just as if in a republic the governors were perfectly just, they would always divide the dignities among themselves according to merits; and he who deserved a lower rank would stay content with that, because he desires nothing with more fervor than justice, so he would remain absolutely content. And as the diversity of voices makes sweet harmony, so in our courts, that is <note>original: "ideſt"</note>, in eternal life, "diverse ranks," that is, different seats that denote different grades in the blessed life, render sweet harmony. And thus he concludes two things. First, that this diversity does not cause any spirit to remain less content for being in a lower grade. The second, that as sweet harmony results from various voices, so from various grades of blessed spirits, ornament and beauty are born for the kingdom of heaven.

**After** he had shown which were the spirits of this sphere, he shows him one whom he calls Romeo, whose history is this: There was Raymond Berengar, Count of Provence, a man full of humanity and eloquent in rhymed verses, and so liberal that he always had his revenues in pawn. And in this...

It explains how different degrees of heavenly merit create a harmonious "sweet music" of justice and introduces the tragic figure of Romeo of Villeneuve.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the Emperor Justinian within the Sphere of Mercury. After describing the history of the Roman Empire, Justinian introduces the soul of Romeo of Villanova, a humble minister to Count Raymond Berengar IV of Provence. The text transitions from the poetic verses of Dante into the detailed historical and linguistic commentary by Cristoforo Landino.</meta>

### CANTO SIX

->...who walks a bad path<-
->who makes a harm of doing good to others.<-
Four daughters had he, and each one a queen,
Raymond Berengar; and this was done for him
by Romeo, a person humble and a pilgrim.
And then the crooked words moved the Count
to demand an account from this just man,
who assigned him seven and five for ten.
Thence he departed, poor and old;
and if the world knew the heart he had,
begging for his life bit by bit,
much it praises him, and more it would praise him.

<column-break/>

In those times a pilgrim, who from the extreme West <note>referring to the region of Galicia in Spain</note> was visiting the church of Saint James, arrived in Toulouse. Because in his appearance and speech he showed nobility of soul and great prudence, he was invited to the court. Hearing of the income and the governance of the Count, he promised that if the care of it were given to him, he would shortly rescue the Count from usury <note>excessive debt to moneylenders</note> and, with suitable generosity, would increase his revenues. But he never wished to reveal his homeland or his name. For this reason, he was called Romeo, <gloss>that is, a man who goes on a pilgrimage</gloss>. Nevertheless, having been given the care and governance, he did much more than he had promised.

Finally, as Raymond had four daughters without a male heir, Romeo through his industry saw to it that Raymond married them to four kings: the first to Louis, King of France (who was later Saint Louis); the second to Edward, King of England, a most excellent man; the third to Richard, his brother, who was later King of the Romans; the fourth to Charles, Duke of Anjou, who was the brother of Saint Louis and later King of Sicily. After so many benefits, envy—that most wicked vice common to all courts—prevailed so much that Raymond became suspicious. He demanded an account of Romeo's administration, which moved Romeo to such indignation that he took up his old clothes and his staff and departed, saying: "Poor I came, and poor I depart." Raymond later regretted his excessive credulity, but despite many prayers, he could not make him stay. Not much time passed before Raymond suffered the penalty of his ingratitude. For the King of France shortly thereafter took half of Provence from him, and after his death, occupied the rest based on his wife's claims.

**THE LIGHT LIGHTS:** it shines. **WITHIN THE** present pearl: *Margharita* in the Greek language means "pearl," <note>original: "margharita"; Landino explains the etymology of the name for the planet Mercury used by Dante.</note> but here he uses it for the light of this soul. **THE WORK WAS** great, as you saw above, marrying four daughters of a count to four kings; **AND BEAUTIFUL:** because it was just and upright. **POORLY RECEIVED:** because of the ingratitude of Raymond. **WALKS A BAD** path: he goes by a twisted and vicious way who considers it a loss to himself to do good for others. **PERSON HUMBLE:** unknown or of low birth, for this is what the word signifies in Latin. <note>original: "humilis"; Landino is clarifying that in a courtly context, this refers to social rank rather than just a modest personality.</note> **PILGRIM:** a foreigner. **AND THEN** after this work, **THEY MOVED**—they moved the Count. **WORDS CROOKED:** twisted and false things said by the Provençals. **TO DEMAND AN ACCOUNT FROM THIS JUST MAN:** to ask that this Romeo, who had administered so justly, give him a reckoning—which he should not have had to do. But he assigned him **SEVEN AND FIVE**, that is twelve, **FOR TEN**: in essence, he showed him a great profit. This was testimony to his prudence and innocence. **THENCE HE DEPARTED POOR AND OLD:** as if to say he consumed his age near an ungrateful lord without reward; this moves one to compassion for his age. For as Diogenes used to say: "Nothing is more miserable than a man who is old and poor." **AND IF THE WORLD KNEW THE HEART:** which was continent, just, a despiser of riches, and of a frank and unconquered soul while he went about begging for necessary food. **BIT BY BIT:** *frustum* in Latin signifies a piece or scrap. <note>original: "afrusto afrusto"; from the Latin 'frustum'.</note> Thus it denotes that he begged where a whole loaf of bread is not given, but only in pieces. **MANY PRAISE HIM:** as if to say for his manifest virtues many praise him, but if they knew his hidden virtues—which were more marvelous—they would praise him much more.

### CANTO SEVEN OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE

<image-desc>A large historiated drop cap 'O' depicting two figures, likely Dante and Beatrice. Dante stands on the left in a contemplative pose, while Beatrice stands facing him on the right in a simple landscape.</image-desc>

Hosanna, holy God of hosts <note>original: "Osanna sanctus deus sabaoth"</note>,
shining from above with your brightness
upon the happy fires of these kingdoms <note>original: "horum malachoth"</note>.
Thus, turning to his own wheeling rhythm,
I saw that substance <note>The soul of the Emperor Justinian</note> singing,

And this is the seventh canto in which Beatrice

AND HE AND THE OTHERS MOVED TO THEIR DANCE: this shows

---

that the souls of those spheres turn just as the heavens do with much circling; and that by such motion they distanced themselves from Dante. And he describes these spirits in the form of sparks which "veiled themselves," <gloss>that is, they covered themselves from him</gloss> by sudden distance. And the meaning is that they suddenly moved so far away that he could no longer see them. I WAS IN DOUBT: A doubt was born in me which persuaded me that I should say to Beatrice: that she might "slake my thirst," <gloss>that is, remove the thirst with her sweet drops</gloss>, meaning the droplets of truth; and he means that he desired Beatrice, <gloss>that is, Holy Theology</gloss>, to show him what he desired to know. But the reverence that I bear her is no other reverence than having regard not to fail in the honor that is duly owed. WHICH MASTERS <note>original: "CHE SINDONNA"</note>: which signifies the office of "all of me," that is, which can do more in me than any other thing; "even for the 'Be' and for the 'ice'": <gloss>that is, even for Beatrice</gloss>, placing the first and the last syllables. IT BOWED ME DOWN: it took away my daring to lift my eyes and look at her; "like a man who is falling asleep": <gloss>that is, who grows drowsy</gloss>, who lowers his head and does not raise it. The meaning is that my will was to search for the truth in the Sacred Scriptures; but the reverence for them, which says, "Do not seek to know more than it is appropriate to know" <note>original Latin: "Nolite sapere plusquam oportet sapere," from Romans 12:3</note>, restrained me so that I did not ask. And the reverence I bear her was only for Beatrice, <gloss>that is, for herself</gloss>, to denote that the love and reverence one bears for sacred letters must not be to acquire honor or treasure, but for the sake of knowledge, as has been said.

<columns>2</columns>

<image-desc>A decorative drop cap 'P' with ornate foliate details.</image-desc>

Beatrice remained thus for only a short while,
and she began, radiating a smile upon me
such as would make a man happy even in the fire:
"According to my infallible advice,
how a just vengeance was justly
punished, has set you thinking.
But I will soon release your mind;
and you, listen, for my words
will present you with a great doctrine."

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A decorative drop cap 'F' featuring intricate vine and architectural motifs.</image-desc>

The poet feigns that Beatrice knew his thought
although he did not manifest it. And for this
reason, she did not let him "remain thus," <gloss>that is, she did not let him stay</gloss> 
so pensive. Rather, she deliberated to clear up his doubt. 
And he feigns this because no doubt can arise in 
the human mind that cannot be found 
resolved and declared in the Sacred Scriptures. 
Nor is it without reason that he shows she 
spoke to him with a smile, which 
could make one happy even if he were in fire: 
because there is nothing that gives greater joy and 
pleasure to the mind than the knowledge of divine things, 
which content and satisfy our soul so much 
that even in every adversity they make us live

---

joyfully. ACCORDING TO MY INFALLIBLE ADVICE: <gloss>according to my opinion which can never be deceived</gloss>, because this alone is true doctrine. YOU HAVE SET YOURSELF IN THOUGHT: <gloss>that is, you think and go about investigating</gloss> how a "just vengeance was justly punished." That is, how the guilt of our first parents was justly punished in Christ, and if it was punished justly, how the Jews could be justly punished for that which had been justly done. The doubt does not seem small: for if the death of Christ was just for the sin of the first parents, then the vengeance taken against the Jews <note>The destruction of Jerusalem in 70 AD, interpreted by medieval theologians as punishment for the Crucifixion</note> was unjust. And if the vengeance taken against the Jews was just, then the death of Christ was unjust.

The commentary by Landino provides linguistic analysis of Hebrew terms and frames Beatrice as a personification of Holy Theology.</summary>

<header>CANTO SEVEN</header>

By not enduring a restraint upon the power of the will <note>referring to the faculty of free will</note>
for his own benefit, that man who was never born <note>Adam, who was created directly by God</note>
by damning himself, damned all his offspring;
whereby the human species lay sick
down through many centuries in great errors,
until it pleased the Word of God to descend.
There, the nature which from its Creator
had distanced itself, He joined to Himself in His person
by the sole act of His eternal love.
Now direct your sight to what is now reasoned:
this nature, united to its Creator—
as it was when first created, it was sincere and good;
but by its own self it was exiled
from paradise, because it turned away
from the way of truth and from its life.

<column-break/>

**W**ishing to resolve the doubt: first he demonstrates the sin of the first parent Adam, saying: "The man who was not born," that is: Adam, who was not born from the womb of a mother, nor was he generated by paternal seed, but was shaped from the clay of the earth by God. Adam, therefore, damning himself by not enduring a restraint. "On the power of the will" <note>original: "ALLA Virtu che uole freno"</note>: that is, on concupiscence <term>concupiscence: the inclination toward base or worldly desires</term> which requires restraint. "For all his benefit" <note>original: "TVCTA ad sua prode"</note>: that is, for his own utility. "His offspring" <note>original: "SVE prole"</note>: that is, his lineage, namely all those who descended from him. "Whereby" <note>original: "ONde"</note>: for which reason, the human species lay sick. "Down": in the world, or rather in sin. "Through many centuries." He did not wish the Word to become incarnate except at the end and in the fullness of many centuries, following the law of nature and of signs <note>the biblical eras before Christ</note>. Wherefore Paul says: "The fullness of time has come" <note>original Latin: "Venit plenitudo temporis"</note>. "In great error": in great ignorance; and certainly the disease is dangerous in one who does not recognize it. "Through many centuries": because the incarnation came after five thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine years. "Where" <note>original: "V doue"</note>: and it is notable...

---

...to the Word and the Holy Spirit. It pleased Him to descend: God, who is in every place, but invisible, wished to descend in a form that was visible. And he explains how He joined human nature to Himself—that is, He took such a nature by assuming a human body and soul, not through carnal union, but by the act of His eternal love—that is, through the power of the Holy Spirit, which is love. Therefore, He was incarnated by the Holy Spirit, and He united humanity with divinity. Here it seems to me notable that it was not fitting for the Father to be sent, because He does not proceed from the Son. Nor was it fitting for the Holy Spirit, so that there would not be two sons in the Trinity: one in the divinity and the other in the humanity. Therefore, the person of the Son was incarnated, so that the same one would be the Son in divinity and in humanity. Furthermore, it was a fitting thing that, just as God made the world through His wisdom, He should redeem it through that same wisdom. And because in man both the soul and the body were corrupted, He therefore took a human soul and body so that He might redeem both. Nevertheless, as Augustine says in the book *On Faith* <note>original Latin: "de fide"</note>: the eternal Word did not take the *person* of a man, but the *nature* of a man. Therefore, we conclude that in Christ there are two natures, divine and human; and three substances: body, soul, and Word; and only one person, and that one is divine. "Now direct" <note>original: "HOR drizza"</note>: he makes the listener attentive because of the greatness and difficulty of the matter. And he demonstrates that the Passion was necessary for our redemption. And it is here to be considered that although the human nature in the person of Christ was pure and immaculate, nevertheless, insofar as it was human, it was deprived of beatitude <note>bliss/divine happiness</note>; because His flesh, taken from the blood of Mary, had descended from Adam in terms of corporeal matter, although in Christ it was free from Adam's sin, just as Adam's was before he sinned. For Christ took from Adam only the matter of the pure blood of the Virgin. But the Holy Spirit made that human nature active. Christ took, therefore, the corporal passions, such as hunger, thirst, heat, cold, fatigue, and pains. He also took those of the soul, such as joy, sadness, fear, and the like. Nevertheless, He did not take all the corporal ones—He did not suffer from many diseases—nor all the spiritual ones, because there was no ignorance in Him, nor any rebellion of the flesh against the spirit. "Into life... His Creator": that is, God in the person of the Son, "through whom all things were made" <note>original Latin: "per quem omnia facta sunt"</note>. "Was good": and how it was created, you must understand, in Adam. "From the way of truth and from its life": that is, it rebelled against God. Of whom it is written: "I am the way, the truth, and the life" <note>original Latin: "Ego sum uia ueritas et uita"</note>.

---

The penalty, therefore, which the cross provided,
if measured by the nature assumed,
nothing ever bit so justly;
and likewise, nothing was of such great injury,
looking to the Person who suffered it,
in whom that nature was bound.
Therefore, from one thing came diverse results:
for the same death pleased both God and the Jews;
at it, the earth trembled and the heavens opened.
It should no longer seem a difficult thing to you
when it is said that a just vengeance
was afterwards avenged by a just court.

<column-break/>

**T**his was Dante’s doubt: if the death of Christ was just, how could the Jews have been justly punished? Therefore he responds that if we look at the nature that Christ assumed—which was human nature—such a death was just, because human nature had sinned. But if we look at the person of Christ—who is the Son of God and true God—they could not have committed a more horrendous sin, nor one of such great injury. Therefore, from the same act and from the same death issued diverse things: that is, supreme justice insofar as the humanity suffered, because it had sinned; and supreme injustice toward the divine Person, in whom there is supreme innocence, in which that nature was bound—that is, the human—because in the incarnate Word of God there were...

the divinity and humanity were united: so that two natures made one subject; and it was the humanity that suffered. But it was not enough for a person who was simply human to satisfy the debt of the fault. **TO GOD** and to the Jews, one death was pleasing. But it pleased God through justice, and the Jews through envy. **BY IT**: through this death. **TREMBLED** the earth. Wherefore Matthew said in the Gospel: <note>original: "Velum templi scissum est in duas partes asummo usque deorsum et terra mota est."</note> "The veil of the temple was torn in two parts from the top even to the bottom and the earth shook."
**THE HEAVENS** opened: because through the death of Christ, man was reconciled with God and became able to ascend to heaven. You must not, therefore, marvel, having understood from me that a just vengeance <note>the Crucifixion as punishment for Adam's sin</note> was afterwards **AVENGED**: that is, vindicated. **BY A JUST COURT**: that is, by a just judge <note>referring to the Roman destruction of Jerusalem, seen by medieval theologians as divine punishment for the execution of Christ</note>.

> But I see your mind is narrowed
> from thought to thought within a knot,
> from which it waits with great desire to be loosed.
> You say: "I discern well what I hear,
> but why God willed for our redemption
> specifically this mode, is hidden from me."
> This decree, brother, lies buried
> from the eyes of everyone whose intellect
> has not matured within the flame of love.
> Truly, however, because this mark
> is much stared at and little discerned,
> I will tell why such a mode was most worthy.
> The Divine Goodness, which from itself spurns
> all envy, burning within itself, sparkles
> so that it unfolds its eternal beauties.
> Whatever distills from it without a medium
> has no end thereafter, because its imprint
> does not move when it sets its seal.
> Whatever rains down from it without a medium
> is entirely free, because it is not subject
> to the power of the new things. <note>The "new things" refer to the celestial spheres and secondary causes created in time, rather than from eternity.</note>
> It is more conformed to Him, and therefore pleases Him more;
> for the Holy Ardor, which radiates through everything,
> is most living in that which is most like Himself.

<column-break/>

Beatrice continues in her speech and says: I see that you enter from one doubt into another, for once the first is resolved, you wonder why God chose this mode of buying us back <note>redemption</note> rather than another. And I tell you that this decree—that is, this determination of His—lies buried, meaning hidden, from those whose intellect is not "adult," that is, grown in the flame of love. Therefore I will resolve this doubt, considering that much is "stared at"—as if to say everyone thinks on it—and "little is discerned," meaning it is not understood by those whose intellect is not nourished and grown in the flame of love, that is, in charity <term>Charity: in a theological sense, the highest form of love between God and man</term> without which no one can understand the Holy Scriptures, as we have already said many times. Before Beatrice comes to the declaration of the doubt she has proposed, she presupposes seven things disputed and concluded in theology. First, that God has created every thing moved by His goodness and burning love, in which there is no "envy" <note>original: "liuore"</note>; and for this reason, He has communicated His goodness to His creatures. And He "sparkles" so much in love that He "unfolds"—that is, manifestly demonstrates—His eternal beauties in many creatures; and she said "eternal" because they have existed exemplarily in His mind from eternity. **WHATEVER** from her: Here she posits two things: first, that of the things created by Divine Goodness, some were created by means of "secondary causes" <note>natural processes or the influence of the stars</note> such as all brute animals, human bodies, and every other thing produced by the earth. Others were produced immediately and by Himself, without any secondary cause, such as the angels and human souls.

---

The second point is that the things created immediately are eternal. And therefore she says "whatever distills" and proceeds from her—that is, from that Divine Goodness—without a medium "has no end thereafter," meaning it is eternal. And she gives the reason, saying: because "its imprint"—that is, its impression—"does not move," meaning it does not change, "when it seals," meaning when it imprints. And these are the angels and human souls, in which He, like a seal, imprints His image, which is reason and intellect. Wherefore the Psalmist says: <note>original: "Signatum est super nos lumen uultus tui domine"</note> "The light of your countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us."
And certainly, the things created by God without a medium degenerate and stray less than those created with a medium. Therefore, because God is immobile and immutable, the things created by Him immediately are immutable and eternal. **WHATEVER FROM HER**: This is the fourth conclusion: that the things which are created without a medium are free, because they are not subject to the power and influence of the heavens, which she calls "new things," because they were not created from eternity like God, but were created in time. **IT IS MORE** Conformed: she posits that eternal and free things are more conformed to God. Therefore, in those things, He shines more brightly. Consequently, they please Him more.

---

> In all these things the human creature 
> possesses an advantage; and if one fails, 
> it must fall from its nobility.
> Sin alone is that which disenfranchises it
> and makes it dissimilar to the Supreme Good.

<column-break/>

Having reviewed the conclusions already stated, which are very fitting to clarify the doubt, she demonstrates that our soul, created by God immediately, is eternal, free, and splendid—that is, capable of the grace of the Holy Spirit—made in His likeness and image, and consequently pleases Him more. She argues in this form: nothing pleases God except

<header>SEVENTH CANTO</header>

because it is little whitened by His light,
And to its dignity it never returns
unless it fills where fault has emptied,
against evil pleasure with just pains.
Your nature, when it sinned in its entirety
in its seed, from these dignities
was removed, as if from paradise;
Nor could it recover them, if you look
very subtly, by any path
without passing through one of these steps:
either that God alone by His courtesy
had dismissed it, or that man by himself
had satisfied for his folly.
Now fix your eye within the abyss
of the eternal counsel, as much as you can,
fixed closely upon my speech.
Man could not, within his limits,
ever satisfy, for not being able to go down
with humility, obeying then,
as much as by disobeying he intended to ascend;
and this is the reason why man was
shut out from being able to satisfy by himself.
Therefore it was necessary for God, by His own ways,
to restore man to his whole life:
I mean by one, or indeed by both.
But because the work is so much more pleasing
to the doer, the more it represents
the goodness of the heart from which it issued,
the Divine Goodness, which stamps the world,
was content to proceed by all its ways
to raise you up again.

<column-break/>

and no perfection in which it was created, and the human soul fell from perfection through sin. Therefore it was necessary to return to its perfection in some way so that it might please God. In all these things [man] has the advantage, that is, he excels other animals and other creatures; and if one [dignity] is missing, it must fall from its nobility, that is, it does not hold that rank of nobility it held before; and the soul loses its liberty, because through sin it became a servant of the devil. Therefore it has fallen from its nobility. Wherefore it follows: "only sin is that which disenfranchises" <note>original: "difrancha"</note>, that is, takes away its liberty; "francho" means free, and "franchare" to free, and "difrancare" to take away liberty; and makes it unlike the Supreme Good, that is, to God, in whose image and likeness it had been created. And the reason is: because God Himself "whitens it little," that is, little illumines it with His greatest light, that is, with His grace. **AND TO ITS** dignity it never returns: Man had fallen from his dignity, which was liberty, through the sin of disobedience. Now he says that he cannot return and come back to his pristine dignity. Because sin is nothing other than the privation of good; therefore, if we wish to return to liberty, it is necessary to fill with restoration the privation of good, where the fault proceeding from sin has emptied. Furthermore, because the sin was committed with pleasure, it was necessary therefore to labor against such evil pleasure with the pain of punishment. Therefore it was necessary to fill that which had been emptied by sin, and to fill it with pains against the evil pleasure.

<image-desc>Large decorative initial 'A' featuring scrolling vine and floral motifs.</image-desc>
**A**t this point Beatrice adds the minor premise and the conclusion to the major premise stated above; and this is the meaning: if human nature through the sin of the first parents became entirely unlike God and displeasing, and was removed from the dignities mentioned above and from the earthly paradise, it was necessary that in some way it should return to its perfection to be reconciled. **And if you attend** <note>original: "badi"</note>, that is, look diligently, these dignities could not be recovered, that is, recuperated and reacquired, without passing through one of these steps: either that God by His most liberal clemency had dismissed and canceled such sin; or that man by himself had satisfied for such folly, that is, for such sin. The first is **mercy**; the second is **justice**. **BUT** fix your eyes, that is, look fixedly into the **abyss**, that is, into the depth of the eternal counsel. As if she says: consider in my speech how ineffable the divine counsel was. **MAN could not**: she shows that of the two ways mentioned above, one was impossible and the other was not according to justice. It was impossible, then, that man by himself should satisfy within his limits, that is, not going outside the limits of human nature, and not being more than man as Christ was. And the reason why he could not satisfy as a man is that, having sinned through pride by wanting to equal himself to God—because wanting to know good and evil <note>an allusion to the Tree of Knowledge</note> was an attempt to equal himself to God—he could not, by obeying, descend into such lowliness that it would be equal to the height of God, to which by disobeying he had wished to ascend. Because the height of God is infinite, but no lowliness is found that is not finite. If, therefore, man could not by himself satisfy for the fault, it was necessary that God should be the one to satisfy and recover man to his whole life by one of the two ways, or rather by both: that is, with mercy and with justice. For if God had created a man so excellent that he could have satisfied, it would have been justice alone. And if He had freed us from sin by absolute power, it would have been mercy alone. But in the incarnation of the Word, as to the divinity He used mercy; as to the humanity, justice. But because the meaning is this: But the divine goodness which stamps <note>original: "imprempta"</note>, that is, prompts and impresses all the world; all nature was content to proceed by all its ways to raise you, you men, fall...

<meta>catchword: fall</meta>

<summary>Beatrice explains that humanity lost its divine dignity and freedom through Adam's prideful sin, creating a debt that man alone could not repay. She concludes that God, in His goodness, chose to use both Mercy and Justice through the Incarnation to restore humanity.</summary>
