fallen into sin: because from the doer a work is so much more pleasing—that is, grateful and acceptable <note>original: "idest grata et accepta"</note>—the more it represents the goodness of the heart from which it issued.

Neither between the last night and the first day
has so high and so magnificent a process
either by the one or by the other been or will be
For God was more generous to give Himself
to make man capable of rising again
than if He had only by Himself dismissed the debt
And all the other ways were insufficient
for justice, if the Son of God
had not been humbled to become incarnate

Now to fill every desire of yours
I return to declare a certain point
so that you may see these things as I do
You say: "I see the air and I see the fire
the water and the earth and all their mixtures
come to corruption and last but a little while"
And these things were yet creatures;
therefore, if what has been said was true,
they should be secure from corruption.
The angels, brother, and the pure country
in which you are, can be said to be created
just as they are in their entire being.
But the elements that you have named
and those things that are made from them
are shaped by a created power.
Created was the matter they contain;
created was the informing power
in these stars that circle around them.
The soul of every brute and of the plants,
drawn from a material composition <term>complexion potentiata: the specific mixture of physical elements that allows for life</term>
by the ray and motion of the holy lights.
But your life breathes without intermediary
the supreme goodness, and He makes it fall in love
with Himself, so that it always desires Him thereafter.

<column-break/>

**H**aving demonstrated the incarnation: she demonstrates that from the beginning of the world, which was the first day on which God said: "Let there be light, and there was light" <note>original: "fiat lux et facta est lux"</note>, to the last night which will occur when the world shall perish by fire—because afterwards the heavens and the earth will remain most pure and splendid, the celestial motions will cease, and the sun, standing still, will give continuous light—there has not been, nor shall be, a process so high or so magnificent by "one or the other." That is, neither through divinity nor humanity was anything so high as to humanity (which was drawn up to God) or so magnificent as to the generosity of God. For it was a greater generosity to give Himself to make man—that is, the humanity that was in Christ—sufficient to be able to raise himself up, than it would have been if He had, by His absolute power, simply forgiven the fault. **AND ALL THE OTHER** ways were insufficient: Not only was it a high and magnificent process, but also a necessary one; for God by Himself could not and should not suffer according to justice because He had no sin, and a pure man was not sufficient, as was said above.

**B**eatrice continues her speech and says: because I affirmed above that our souls are immortal because they were created by God, you might doubt why the elements and the bodies made of them are not immortal, given that the elements were also created by God. To which I respond thus: **THE ANGELS, BROTHER, AND THE PURE COUNTRY.** She provides the resolution to the doubt by saying that although everything is created by God, nevertheless the angels and the "pure country"—that is, the heavens <note>original: "idest e cieli"</note>, which are of pure matter and in which heavens you are at present—can be said to be created in their "entire being." This is because God created both their matter and their form at once, and He created them by Himself without the mediation of secondary causes. But the elements and the bodies composed of them were formed by a "created power" <note>the influence of the stars</note> which God placed into the elements when He created their matter from nothing. Thus, their form is from God by means of that created power. Therefore, their natural form, although it emerged into being from the potential of matter (and thus can be said to be "made" from something), is not like the light which is said to be the principle before every form and matter. Thus, they cannot be perpetual or free, because the form the elements currently have was not created by God immediately <note>without an intermediary</note>, but through the created power that God placed in the "first matter" in that formlessness in which it was created. Matter was created by God without an intermediary and is therefore perpetual and free, subject only to God. The informing power was created to bring elementary things into being, and this power is in the stars which revolve around the elements. **THE SOUL** of every brute: the sensitive soul in animals and the vegetative soul of plants is not perpetual because it is of a "potentialized complexion," meaning a material composition. This is made from the simple formal quality of the elements, purified by the influence of the heavens, and is therefore temporary and subject to celestial influence. It is derived from the influence of the stars, infused with their rays and motion; thus she says "the ray and the motion of the holy lights." But your life—the human soul—**BREATHES**, that is, it lives without an intermediary. For once the body is organized, God immediately creates our soul without an intermediary, and in creating it, He infuses it into the body. Therefore, the "supreme benevolence"—that is, goodness <note>original: "idest bonta"</note>—creates the soul and enamors it of Himself...

<header>CANTO SEVEN</header>

...that one innate desire to attain the supreme good, which is God Himself.

And from this you can further argue
for our resurrection, if you reflect
how human flesh was then made
when the first parents were both formed.
<column-break/>
The author presents a corollary conclusion <term>corolaria: a logical consequence of a proven proposition</term> to the reasoning already stated: it proves that we must be resurrected with our own physical flesh. Because God created the body of the first man without any intermediary <note>meaning God shaped Adam directly from the earth, rather than through natural reproduction</note>, and for this reason, it will be perpetual; and from that body, He made the first woman. Therefore, it must be perpetual; and so too must our bodies be, as they descend from them. Therefore, the death of said bodies must be temporary. However, concerning the resurrection of the body, we have spoken sufficiently in another place.

---

### CANTO EIGHT OF THE THIRD CANTICLE OF DANTE

---

The world used to believe, to its peril,
that the beautiful Cyprian <note>Venus, so called because she was traditionally said to have risen from the sea near Cyprus</note> radiated mad love,
revolving in the third epicycle <term>epiciclo: a small circle in which a planet moves, while the center of that circle moves around a larger circle</term>;
Wherefore not only to her did they do honor
with sacrifice and votive cries,
the ancient peoples in their ancient error;
But they honored Dione and Cupid,
the former as her mother, the latter as her son,
and said that he sat in Dido’s lap;
And from her, from whom I take my beginning,
they took the name of the star
which the sun gazes upon, now from the neck, now from the brow. <note>Venus appears as both the morning star (at the sun's "brow") and the evening star (at the sun's "neck").</note>
<column-break/>
The author has finished treating what was necessary regarding the second heaven, Mercury. Now, in this eighth canto, he shows he has arrived at the third, which is of Venus, where he finds many spirits. But first, he speaks at length with Charles Martel <note>The young prince and titular King of Hungary who had met Dante in Florence</note>, and later with King Robert. And in the first verses, he demonstrates the erroneous opinion the ancients had of Venus, which, although expressed in brief words, I think is useful to review. 

Among the ancients, there was not just one Venus, but three. The first is the daughter of Heaven and of the Day. This "Day" was fathered by Jove, or according to others, by Bacchus. From her were born Cupid, the god of love, and the Graces; and they give her the *cestus* <note>original: "cesto"</note>, which is a belt worn at legitimate weddings. The second was generated when Saturn cut the virile member of Caelus, his father, and threw it into the sea. Because it was struck by the waves, it made foam; and from that, Venus was born; or rather, she was born from the blood of that member and was nourished by the foam, from which she is named by the Greeks Aphrodite: because *aphros* <note>original: "aphros"</note> in Greek means foam. Of her alone, without a male, the poet Simonides claims Cupid was born. The third was the daughter of Jove and Dione, and she bore Aeneas to Anchises. These fables in part express many natural things, and in part contain history...

<summary>This page concludes the theological argument for the resurrection of the human body and begins Canto VIII, transitioning to the sphere of Venus and explaining the ancient mythological origins and errors surrounding the goddess of love.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the transition into the Third Heaven (Venus) in Dante's Paradiso, following the introduction of Canto VIII. It expands on the philosophical and mythological distinctions between divine and earthly love.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>PARADISO</header>

...ries. But forgive the long work if I omit them in this place. Plato, not as a poet but as a philosopher and excellent investigator of the secrets of nature, writes in the *Symposium* <note>original: "symposio"</note> that there are two Venuses and two Loves: one is celestial, the other vulgar and earthly. Because our soul, detaching itself from the contagion of the body, rises toward heaven and immediately kindles within itself an extremely burning desire for divine and incorporeal things; and from this is born celestial love, which despises everything earthly and goes seeking true beauty, which is only found in incorporeal, divine, and eternal things. This love is called a "great god" by Phaedrus in Plato's *Symposium*; and they say this Venus is the daughter of Heaven and had no mother. She was born from Heaven because she seeks nothing other than celestial things, and she was born without a mother because she does not proceed from corporeal things. 

But if our soul, forgetting its origin, turns its eye downward and looks only at the earth, it conceives within itself the earthly Venus from which libidinous love is born. This love seeks nothing but corporeal delights and carnal pleasures. It does not love the beauty of the soul, which is its own proper substance, but seeks the beauty of the body. This is expressed in the fable of Narcissus, whom the poets pretend fell in love with his own image seeing it in the fountain. They present Narcissus as the soul of an unlearned and reckless man who does not contemplate his own face—that is, he does not consider his own essence and virtue, nor the beauty in which he was created by God—but is intent on gazing at the image of it in the water. This is nothing other than following corporeal beauty, which has no substance, but is a vain shadow of true beauty. He sees this in the water—that is, in the body—which is fluid and runs like water and never stops; thus the body, which he alone loves, continually runs toward death and its own corruption. Therefore, such a soul is wretched because, as Petrarch says:

> Wretched is he who places hope in mortal things <note>original: "Miser chi speme in chosa mortal pone"</note>

and leaves true beauty to love the shadow. Certainly wretched, and more than wretched, are those men who, because they know nothing in themselves but the body, firmly believe themselves to be nothing other than body. For all these reasons, and for many others which I omit for the sake of brevity, the divine Plato demonstrates that there are two Venuses: the celestial one, following whom Aeneas became happy in Italy; and the earthly one, by whose allurements Paris was enticed, leading both himself and his homeland to ultimate extermination. 

Such influences proceed in large part from the star of the third heaven called Venus. Having already been led to this heaven by Beatrice, our poet is now required to report some astrological matters concerning it. Venus is a benevolent planet and a bringer of friendships; she is feminine and nocturnal, and in her quality, she is warm and humid, being very temperate. She is also very healthful, as Ptolemy shows in the *Book of Harmony* <note>original: "libro dellharmonia"</note>. From her influence proceeds all music—and not only that which consists in the harmony of voices, but also the composition of verses. She induces love, and according to the aspects of different planets, this love is sometimes modest and chaste, and sometimes lustful and impure. She makes her course in three hundred and forty-eight days. She never moves further from the sun than forty-six degrees. When she precedes it, she appears in the east in the morning before the sun and is called Lucifer <note>Light-bringer</note>, and by common folk, Diana. When she is behind it, she is seen in the evening in the west and is called Hesperus. Pythagoras was the first among the Greeks to realize that Lucifer and Hesperus were the same star. Her dwellings in the zodiac are Taurus and Libra; she reigns in Pisces, and her reign fails in Virgo. She is a generative star. Venus alone of all the planets moves two degrees out of the zodiac. Her splendor is so great that it casts a shadow. Among the ancients, she had many names: she was called Juno, she was called Isis, she was called Cybele, who is the mother of the gods. Therefore, he [Dante] places in this heaven those spirits who lived in pleasure, joy, and love, yet without departing from true honesty—or if they sometimes exceeded the limit, they immediately returned to it.

### THE WORLD:
As if to say universally all men.

### TO ITS peril:
That is, because believing such things is against true religion and cannot be believed without danger of damnation.

### CYPRian:
Venus is called thus from Cyprus, where she was most honored. Hence Horace says:

> Queen Venus of Cnidus and Paphos, spurn your beloved Cyprus, and transfer yourself into the beautiful temple of Glycera who calls you with much incense. <note>original: "Venus regina gnidi paphique sperne dilecta cypron: et uocantis thure te multo glycere decoram transffer in ede."</note>

And certainly, Cyprus was always a very lustful island. Thus it was once a custom there for girls to go to the port and mingle with foreigners to earn their dowry in that way. And there was a law that once in her life, every woman should go to the temple of Venus and not leave until she had had relations with some man. Therefore, the foolish believed that no other love proceeded from Venus than that which is impure and lustful.

### MAD love:
Foolish love. Love is the desire for a beautiful thing; true beauty consists in divine and immortal things. Just as desiring these is a prudent love because it chooses true beauty, so too is that love foolish which is born of leisure and human lust, desiring corporeal beauty libidinously. Therefore, he correctly said "mad love" so that we might understand the distinction between libidinous and chaste love.

### IN THE third epicycle:
In the third heaven where the planet Venus is. An epicycle <term>epicycle: a small circle described by the planet with the movement of its body</term> is a small circle, and the planet moves along its circumference. In the upper part, it moves from east to west, and in the lower part, the opposite. In this epicycle, they make their direct, stationary, and retrograde movements.

### DIONE:
As we have said, she was the mother of Venus. Hence Virgil says: 

> Behold, the star of Dionean Caesar has proceeded. <note>original: "Ecce dionei processit cesaris astrum."</note>

### AND FROM her:
From this Venus, from whom I take the beginning of this chapter, they took the name of the star and called it Venus—the star which the sun woos: now from the stern <note>original: "da poppa"</note>, that is, behind itself (because on a ship the stern is the last part), and now from the brow <note>original: "da ciglio"</note>, that is, in front of itself, as we showed a little above. When she rises before the sun, she brings with her such splendor that it makes it seem like day before the sun has arrived.

<meta>This page continues the transition into the Third Heaven (Venus). <header>CANTO</header>

When it appears behind the sun in the evening in the west: and performs its own office for the moon: that is, giving light to the night as the moon does.

I did not perceive my ascent into it,
but of being within it, my lady gave me
full proof, whom I saw become more beautiful.
And as a spark is seen within a flame,
and as one voice is discerned within another
when one is steady and the other goes and returns,
I saw within that light other lamps
moving in a circle, more and less swift,
in the manner, I believe, of their eternal visions.
From a cold cloud no winds ever descended,
whether visible or not, so rapidly
that they would not seem hindered or slow
to anyone who had seen those divine lights
coming toward us, leaving the circling
begun first among the high seraphim;
and behind those who appeared furthest forward
sounded "Hosanna" so sweetly that never since
was I without the desire to hear it again.

**Their visions. ETERNAL:** that is, according to what each one demonstrates based on how much more or less virtuously they had acted according to such divine influence. **FROM A COLD cloud:** Aristotle shows in his *Meteorology* <note>original: "meteora"</note> that warm and dry vapors, rising to the furthest part of the third region of the air and struck by cold mists, reflect downward and stir the air; that movement creates wind. **Winds did NOT descend:** because they are struck back by their opposite. **OR VISIBLE:** when they are in the turbulent air and move the clouds, or truly when they are ignited as often happens. **OR NOT:** when they are in the clear sky or are not ignited and therefore are not seen. And he says, coming toward us, they left the circle first begun among the **high seraphim**: he calls them "high" because they are in the first and highest heaven. He says this because he imagines elsewhere seeing God as a point above everything: and in the middle and around that point, in a lower place, the orders of angels revolve, though not with equal speed, as we shall demonstrate in its proper place. **AND BEHIND THOSE:** he says that behind those spirits coming toward him were spirits singing Hosanna so sweetly that **never since** <note>original: "unque poi dest non mai poi"</note> was I **without the desire** <note>original: ".i. sanza desiderio"</note> to **hear it again** <note>original: ".i. dudir dinuouo"</note>. **Hosanna** means "God save" <note>original: "idio fa saluo"</note>: but in the Hebrew language it denotes a joy that can hardly be expressed in Greek or Latin.

Then one of them drew closer to us
and alone began: "We are all ready
for your pleasure, so that you may joy in us.
We revolve with the celestial Principalities
in one circle, one circling, and one thirst,
to whom you once said in the world below:
*You who by understanding move the third heaven*;
and they shall be so full of love that, to please you,
a little quiet will not be less sweet."
After my eyes were offered
to my lady with reverence, and she
had made them content and certain of herself,
They turned back to the light that
had promised so much, and "Who are you?" was
my voice, impressed with great affection.

<column-break/>

Above we have shown why the author feigns not to perceive the ascent from heaven to heaven: and why Beatrice always becomes more beautiful as they ascend. **AND AS A SPARK IS SEEN WITHIN A FLAME:** because it seems difficult that the lights of those souls placed in the body of this third planet could be seen within its own light, he uses two very fitting comparisons. Thus he says: I saw in the light of the star of Venus other lamps—other particular lights—which were the blessed spirits placed in that sphere; just as within a rising flame one sees an ignited spark rise. This can be discerned because the spark has a more vivid color than the flame; and so also the lights of the spirits, because they were more radiant than the light of Venus, could be perceived. **AND AS ONE VOICE IS DISCERNED WITHIN ANOTHER:** another very fitting comparison: because we see in music the **tenor** proceed steadily and the **soprano** go and return. **MOVING in a circle and more or less swift:** They move with the motion of the star, and at the same time they finished their revolution; but as much as any was closer to the center of the star, so much was its motion slower, and so conversely; and therefore he says in the manner of...

Afterward, one spirit more than the others offered on behalf of himself and the others that they were all ready to please him, in a way that he could rejoice in them. Nor is it contrary to the nature of the heaven of love to find such liberal, benign, and loving spirits within it. Because love always wishes to gratify the beloved thing. **WITH PRINCIPALITIES:** because over every heaven a specific order of blessed spirits is placed. Over the second heaven (Mercury) are the Archangels. Over the third (Venus) are the **Principalities**. **TO WHOM you spoke down in the world:** Because Dante wrote a moral song <note>A reference to the first canzone of Dante’s *Convivio*</note> in which he treats love—not lascivious but celestial—and therefore it begins: "You Principalities who, by understanding"—that is, learning with your intellect God and His will. For which reason the angels are called **Intelligences**. **MOVE the third heaven**, making it revolve by your power given by God, and making its effects flow down into the world...

The commentary explains Dante's use of meteorological and musical metaphors to describe the visual and auditory experience of the divine.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Dante’s entry into the Heaven of Venus. # PARADISO

And they shall be more full of love and of the charity of God and neighbor, which proceeds from the influence of this planet, to which the human soul entrusts itself when the grace of God inspires the will to cling to it; and in this application lies our merit. **BECAUSE** <note>original: "CHE"</note> to please you, a little rest shall be no less sweet to us than circling. And certainly, charity toward one's neighbor causes us at times to interrupt our contemplation <term>speculare: the act of intellectual or spiritual looking/theorizing</term> to offer pleasure to others. **AFTER** <note>original: "POSCIA"</note> those eyes: This shows that before he asked anything of the spirit, he wished to see if Beatrice would permit it. And by this, he admonishes us that in the investigation of celestial things, we must not attempt anything that is not permitted to us by theology <note>Beatrice represents Theology in the allegory of the Divine Comedy</note>. Therefore, I offered my eyes to Beatrice, that is, I looked at her, and she looked back at me in a way that showed me she was content. For which reason I turned to the light—that is, to that spirit who had offered himself so very grandly—and then I, Dante, asked who that spirit was.

*And how much and of what sort did I see her become,*
*through new joy that was added*
*unto her beauties when I spoke!*
*Thus transformed, it said to me: The world held me*
*below but little time; and had it been longer,*
*much evil shall befall that would not have been.*
*My gladness keeps me hidden from you,*
*which radiates around me and conceals me*
*like a creature swathed in its own silk.*

<margin>
...of Hungary. Robert occupied all these lordships.
</margin>

*That left bank which is washed*
*by the Rhone after it has joined with the Sorgue,*
*awaited me as its lord in due time;*
*And that horn of Ausonia <note>Ausonia is a poetic name for Italy</note> which is walled*
*by Bari, Gaeta, and Catona,*
*from where the Tronto and the Verde empty into the sea.*
*Already the crown of that land which the Danube*
*waters after it leaves the German banks*
*flashed upon my brow.*
*And beautiful Trinacria <note>The ancient name for Sicily, meaning "three-pointed"</note>, which is darkened*
*between Pachynus and Pelorus, over the gulf*
*that receives the greatest stress from the East Wind,*
*Not because of Typhon <note>A mythological giant buried under Mount Etna</note>, but by nascent sulfur,*
*would have still awaited its kings,*
*born through me from Charles and Rudolf,*
*If bad lordship, which always embitters*
*the subject people, had not*
*moved Palermo to cry out: "Die! Die!"* <note>original: "mora mora" — a reference to the bloody uprising known as the Sicilian Vespers in 1282</note>

<column-break/>

The aforementioned spirit reveals himself: and says he is Charles Martel, Prince of Taranto, son of King Charles the Lame, who had seven children. Of these, three held titles of lordship: Louis, the eldest, who was captured in Sicily and later became a Friar Minor <note>a Franciscan monk</note>; Charles Martel, Prince of Taranto; and Robert, Prince of Durazzo. But because the aforementioned Louis became a friar, Martel succeeded to the Kingdom of Sicily and Apulia, and also the County of Provence. He succeeded to these provinces as the second-born following the first-born's renunciation; but he was also crowned King of Hungary.

He describes the countries of which he would have been lord. And he describes these poetically, naming them either by rivers, cities, or mountains. And first, by the Rhone, he denotes Provence. We have spoken of the Rhone in another place. This river divides Provence, of which the right side belongs to the King of France and the left to the King of Apulia. **SORGUE** <note>original: "SORGA"</note> is a river that rises at the start of Provence and flows into the Rhone. **AS ITS LORD**: because it belongs to the realm of Apulia of which I was to be lord, had I not been King of Hungary. **THAT HORN OF AUSONIA**: that point of Italy. **WHICH IS WALLED**: which is clothed by the cities written below. **OF BARI**: This is by the Adriatic Sea. **CATONA**: <note>OCR: "CROTONA"</note> today called Catona, where the sea, which naturally shows a green color, separates Sicily from Italy. **FLASHED UPON MY HEAD THE CROWN**: already the crown of Hungary shone on my head, through which the Danube runs after it leaves Germany <note>original: "Magna," referring to Almagna</note>. **AND BEAUTIFUL TRINACRIA**: And the kingdom of Sicily belonged to me, which was called Trinacria by the ancients because it has three promontories: Pachynus, Pelorus, and Lilybaeum. But Pachynus and Pelorus correspond to the Gulf of Venice, which is struck more by the East Wind <note>original: "euro"</note> than by any other wind. **WHICH IS DARKENED**: that is, in which mist and smoke appear. Not because Typhon, of whom it was spoken above, breathes out flame and smoke as the fables feign, but because Mount Etna is cavernous; from which it generates wind, which by its motion ignites the caverns that hold sulfur. For this reason, it sends out much smoke and sometimes flames. **FROM CHARLES**: the first Count of Provence, my grandfather. **FROM RUDOLF**: who was Duke of Austria <note>original: "Sterlich," a corruption of Oesterreich</note>, whose daughter I had as my wife. **IF BAD LORDSHIP**: He says this because Sicily rebelled against Charles due to the greed and injustice of the officials he kept there; and it gave itself to Lord Peter of Aragon, as we have described at length in another place. **ALWAYS EMBITTERS**: that is, it makes the subject peoples fierce and strong by driving them to desperation.

<summary>Charles Martel, a soul in the Heaven of Venus, explains his identity and the vast territories he was meant to rule across Europe, while reflecting on how poor governance led to the loss of Sicily during the Sicilian Vespers.</summary>

### CANTO EIGHT

And if my brother had foreseen this,
the greedy poverty of Catalonia
would already flee so as not to offend him;
For truly it is necessary to provide,
either by him or by another, so that his bark,
already loaded, is not burdened with more weight.
His nature, which from a generous one
descended to a stingy one, would have need of such ministers
who did not care only for filling their chests.
"Because I believe that the high joy
which your speech pours into me, my lord,
there where every good ends and is finished,
Is seen by you just as I see it;
this makes it more pleasing to me, and I also hold it dear
because you discern it by gazing into God.
You have made me glad; and now make me clear,
since by speaking you have moved me to doubt
how from sweet seed bitter fruit can emerge."
This I said to him; and he to me: "If I can
show you a truth to the question you ask,
you will hold your face where you now hold your back.

The Good that turns and satisfies all the realm
through which you climb, makes its providence
become a power within these great celestial bodies.
And not only are the natures provided for
within the mind that is perfect in itself,
but they are provided together with their well-being.
Because whatever this bow shoots
falls disposed toward a foreseen end,
just like a thing directed to its target.
If this were not so, the heavens you walk through
would produce their effects in such a way
that they would not be works of art, but ruins.
And this cannot be, unless the intellects
that move these stars are flawed,
and flawed too is the First, who did not make them perfect.
Do you wish for this truth to be made even whiter to you?"
And I: "No, indeed, for I see it is impossible
that nature should weary in what is necessary."

<column-break/>

He narrates that if King Robert <note>Robert of Anjou, brother of Charles Martel</note> had foreseen how great a vice greed is in a prince, and how apt it is to the ruin of states, he would not have attended—neither by himself nor through his officials—to the accumulation of treasure. The poet responds to the spirit and says: **THE JOY** <note>original: "LA LETITIA"</note> that I take in seeing you in this beatitude is more pleasing to me because I believe that it is seen and understood by you no differently than I, who have it within me, see it. And if anyone were to ask how the spirit can see his heart, the author adds that he sees it in God, where every good ends and is finished <note>original: "finitia"</note>—that is, in God. Inasmuch as the blessed souls, looking into God as into a mirror that represents the images of all things, they know every truth and cannot be deceived.
The text then proceeds: **O MY LORD** <note>original: "O SIGNOR mio"</note>—that is, **O Charles**, whom I had as a lord while you were living. Because I believe that you see, as I see, the joy that your speech pours into me, because through that I understand your beatitude in God, where every good is finished and ends; therefore, this joy of mine is more pleasing to me than if you did not see it. **AND ALSO THIS I hold dear:** and similarly, I hold dear what you have spoken because you discern it—that is, you see and understand it—by gazing upon God, in which mirror every thing is seen. It is as if he said: "it is pleasing to me to have heard you because I know what you speak is true." But because your most pleasing speech has generated a doubt in my mind, make me clear on this, just as you have made me glad.
**The doubt is how from sweet seed** <note>original: "dolcie seme"</note>—that is, from a good father—can be born **bitter seed**—that is, a bad son. For since you, Charles, condemn Robert as greedy while praising the generosity <term>liberalità: the virtue of being noble and generous with wealth</term> of his ancestors, it seems that this contradiction we have mentioned follows. **This I said to him.** And he—that is, Charles—answered me saying: "if I can show you a truth"—that is, a certainty, because truth is always one and cannot be more. **YOU WILL HOLD YOUR FACE WHERE YOU HOLD YOUR BACK:** that is, you will see that which you do not now see. For having your back turned to the temple, you do not see it; but if you then turn toward where your back was before, you see it.

To explain the doubt, he concludes that every thing that happens is provided by God according to what is best, if not for the individual, then for the universe. Whence he says: **THE GOOD:** God, who is the supreme good, who **TURNS:** because He is the first cause of the revolution of the heavens; and **satisfies**, because He preserves them in their being. **ALL THE REALM** that you climb—all the heavens that you ascend. And further, God makes His providence be a "virtue" <term>uirtu: here meaning a directed power or influence</term> in these great bodies—that is, that the power He has placed in the government of the planets and the heavens (which are "great bodies" as shown above) should be according to His providence. And he adds that in the mind of God, there are not only the natures and things that He has foreseen, but they are there together with their "salvation" <note>meaning their well-being or perfection</note>. **The meaning is that God, not only with divine providence** produces things into being, but also provides that they should be for the best—if not for the individual part, at least for the whole universe. And whatever this bow shoots, the thing shot falls and arrives at the foreseen end: that is, every thing that God provides and ordains arrives at the end designated by God Himself, just as the well-aimed arrow arrives at its mark and its target. And if it were not that every...

He uses the metaphor of an arrow hitting a target to describe how nature unerringly fulfills God's plan for the universal good.</summary>

--- Page 606 ---
<meta>This page continues the discourse between Dante and the spirit of Charles Martel in the Heaven of Venus, following the discussion on how divine providence governs the celestial spheres to ensure earthly order. The commentary here addresses why children often differ so drastically in character from their parents.</meta>

<header>PARADISO</header>

an ordered thing should arrive at its ordered end. The heaven through which you walk <note>that is, all these heavens and the stars and the planets through which you ascend</note> would produce their effects so poorly that they would not be "acts" <note>that is, well-ordered and perfect</note>, as we see things made with art to be. Instead, they would be ruins because they would be without order. But this cannot be if the intellects <note>that is, the angelic Intelligences which God has placed in charge of the movement and governance of the stars and heavens</note> are not "lacking" <note>that is, imperfect and defective</note>. And if the First <note>that is, God himself, who is the First Mover</note> is not lacking <note>that is, imperfect</note>, which cannot be. **DO YOU WISH**: after Beatrice <note>The commentator attributes these words to Beatrice, though in the poem they are spoken by the spirit of Charles Martel</note> had said this to him, she prepared to demonstrate it more clearly; and therefore she said: "O Dante, do you wish for this truth to be 'whitened' <note>made more manifest</note>?" For just as we call "obscure" those things which are difficult to understand, so we can call "white" those things which are manifest. And Dante replied: "Not I, for I know it is impossible that nature—that is, God—should tire <note>that is, fail</note> in what is necessary <note>that is, in that which is needed</note>."

And he said again: "Now tell me, would it be worse
for man on earth if he were not a citizen?"
"Yes," I replied, "and here I ask for the reason."
"And can he be so, if one does not live below
differently, through different offices?
No, if your master <note>Aristotle</note> writes well for you."
Thus he came deducing down to here;
then he concluded: "Therefore, it is necessary
for the roots of your effects to be diverse:
For one is born an Absalom <note>or Solon, depending on the manuscript</note>, and another a Xerxes,
another a Melchizedek, and another he
who, flying through the air, lost his son."

The circular nature, which is a seal
to the mortal wax, performs its art well,
but does not distinguish one dwelling from another.
Hence it happens that Esau is separated
by seed from Jacob, and Quirinus comes
from so vile a father that he is attributed to Mars.
A generated nature would always make its path
similar to its progenitors,
if divine providence did not prevail.
Now that which was behind you is before you.

<column-break/>

The spirit adds the argument, which is this: because man is an animal desiring company, it is better that he be a "citizen" on earth <note>that is, that he live in company and not in a solitary life</note>. And this cannot be unless one lives differently with different offices. Because, as Aristotle describes <note>whom he calls "our master"</note>, human life has need of various arts and offices. It is necessary that there be counselors in the republic; soldiers to defend it; doctors and jurists; artisans; farmers; and priests; and many others. Therefore, it was necessary that, having to be different effects in men, such effects proceed from various roots <note>that is, from various causes</note>. Well, then, the spirit deduced part by part until here where I have said; and then he concluded. BECAUSE one is born an Absalom: Nature provided optimally so that various influences of the heavens would produce men apt for various exercises, because the city has need of various exercises. And therefore one influence produced Absalom; another Xerxes; and another someone else. Absalom was the son of David, of whom we have spoken above; and here he places him as a military man apt to defend the republic. <note>original: "Abſalone"</note> Other texts have not Absalom, but Solon, who was an Athenian and one of the seven sages of Greece, and he devised the laws for his republic; and we shall place him as an excellent founder of laws. Xerxes was the son of Darius, King of the Persians, who with an incredible multitude of soldiers came against the Greeks. And he made a bridge over the Hellespont sea <note>original: "helleſponto"</note> through which he entered from Asia into Greece. And Mount Athos, which was previously mainland, he made into an island by digging a great trench and bringing the sea around it. Finally, through the industry of Themistocles <note>original: "Themiſtode"</note>, the Athenian, he was ignominiously broken in a naval battle; and with great cowardice he fled. This was demonstrated by a portent born shortly before in his armies: for a mare—which is a very warlike animal—gave birth to a hare, a vile and fleeting animal. And he places Xerxes here for every king. Melchizedek was the first priest and king, and he went to meet Abraham, who was bringing back an ample victory from three conquered kings. And he was the first who sacrificed bread and wine to God. In him was prefigured Christ, who was king and priest, and who in heaven was without a mother and on earth without a father. Melchizedek means in Hebrew <term>Just King</term> and <term>Peaceful King</term>. Of Daedalus and his son Icarus, and of their flight, we wrote in another more suitable place.

He concludes whence the diversity among progeny proceeds. Wherefore he says "the circular nature"—that is, the nature of the heavens which exerts influence and is therefore a "seal to the mortal wax," because it imprints its influences in us just as the seal imprints its mark in the wax. And he rightly said "mortal," because elemental bodies are corruptible. Therefore, this celestial power performs its art well and pours out its influences. But it does not distinguish one "dwelling" from another. For from Cicero, a most excellent man, was born his son Cicero, who was most intemperate; and from Africanus <note>Scipio Africanus</note>, a man most apt for military discipline, was born Scipio, who was entirely foreign to such exercise. And this is because the influence of the fathers was from certain stars, and from others that...

<summary>This page explains how divine providence uses celestial influences to ensure humans are born with diverse talents and dispositions, which is necessary for a functioning society. It uses historical and biblical figures like Solon, Xerxes, and Melchizedek to illustrate how different roles—legislators, kings, and priests—are populated regardless of their parentage.</summary>

but so that you know I take joy in you,

Nature always, if it finds fortune

by following it, its people would be good.

# CANTO NINE OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE

After your Charles, beautiful Clemence <note>Clemence of Hungary, daughter of Charles Martel</note>,
had clarified things for me, he told of the deceits
that his offspring were to receive.
But he said: "Be silent, and let the years roll on,"
so that I can say nothing except that a just lament
shall follow after your wrongs.

<column-break/>

of sons. **FROM THIS** it follows: because the same family has different influences: it happens that in the son compared to the father, or brother to brother, they are dissimilar: As is noted in Esau, who was born of Jacob; nonetheless Esau was warlike and Jacob peaceful. Quirinus—that is, Romulus—who was born of a most base and unknown father, because of the influence of Mars was warlike and was called the son of Mars. **NOW THAT WHICH SHALL FOLLOW**: that is, what you did not see before you, now you see.

**JUST AS IT HAPPENS**: that every seed turns out poorly if it is placed in soil not suited to its nature: so it happens that if a man is put to a task opposite to his nature, he never becomes excellent in it. Therefore, if the world—that is, living men—considered the foundation that nature lays—that is, that aptitude and principle, or almost a "seed" that the influence of the heavens puts into the man—and if that were followed, as for example <note>original: "verbigratia"</note> if he who has an aptitude for arms gave himself to arms, and he who has an aptitude for learning gave himself to learning, and the same were done in other inclinations, certainly men would become good, because everyone would have more diligence for that to which nature invites him. But often the opposite is done: And one becomes a man of religion <note>original: "religioso," referring here to a monk or priest</note> who is inclined toward military service, and sometimes one becomes a king who is suited for sermons—that is, for preaching and academic learning. **WHENCE THE TRACK**: that is, the vestige and also the footprint <note>meaning that human society has strayed from the correct path</note>.

**ALTHOUGH** the poet enters the ninth canto, nevertheless he does not yet leave the third sphere <note>the Heaven of Venus</note>. But having finished the discourse held with Charles, he speaks first to Cunizza da Romano. Afterwards with Folco of Marseille. But in these first verses, he turns his speech to Clemence, daughter of Charles, and recounts to her how, after he had clarified the doubt for him, he predicted the deceits that his descendants were to receive.

But he commanded him to be silent: and let the years move—that is, the passage of time, which is nothing other than the revolution of the planets. Then the author makes an apostrophe <note>A rhetorical device where the writer breaks off to address a person or thing</note>—that is, he turns...

He brings Cunizza da Romano to speak. This woman was the sister of Ezzelino <note>original: "accerino"</note> da Romano: a woman of noble manners, full of humanity and piety: kind and gracious. But she was very prone to love, as we showed in the sixth chapter of the *Purgatorio*. Nor should anyone wonder that the poet places among the blessed one whose life had this stain: because he wishes to show that everyone, by amending themselves, can be saved: especially if they have mixed many virtues with the vice that oppresses them, as we see in her. Describing then the country where she was born—that is, the Trevisan March <note>original: "marcha triuigiana"</note>—he says: "in that part of the Italian land"—that is, of Italy—and he says "wicked" <note>original: "praua"</note> not because he disparages Italy, so praised by Virgil, but he says "wicked" because in his times it was governed by wicked—that is, captive—men. But I well believe that if the poet were alive in our times, he would say the same or perhaps worse. Because our own situation is very harsh. Therefore, in that part of Italy that "sits"—that is, is placed—between Rialto (the city of Venice where Rialto is) and the springs of Brenta and Piave. These are two rivers that run through the Trevisan region.

**A HILL**: upon which is a land called Romano, from which came Ezzelino; otherwise Azzolino, of whom we have sufficiently narrated elsewhere. **FROM ONE ROOT BORN**: we descended from one father. **I SHINE**: I sparkle because the light of the star overcame me—that is, because the influence of this star <note>Referring to the planet Venus, associated with love</note> had great power in me. "But gladly within myself I indulge"—that is, with joy I take pleasure. The reason for my fate; the meaning is: I am very...

After Cunizza had spoken what is said above, she turned and showed Dante the spirit of Folquet of Marseille <note>original: "Folcho damarsilia"</note>, saying: "Great fame has remained in the world of this spirit who is a precious and brilliant jewel"—that is, full of light and splendor. And this year, which is the hundredth since he left the world, shall yet **BE QUINTUPLED**—that is, this hundredth year will return five times: meaning five hundred years will pass before this fame of his...

<column-break/>

**fame.** SEE if doing—one might say—consider by this how much a man should strive to make himself excellent before he dies, since the fame of virtue lasts so long after death. *So that the first may leave another life:* <note>original: "Sichal tra uita la prima relinqua"</note> that is, so that his first life, in which he lived, may leave after death another life, which is this life of fame. And so he stated that the fame of Folco <note>Folco of Marseille, a famous troubadour who became a monk and then a bishop.</note> would last five hundred years. Folco was from Marseille, the son of Alfonzo, a wealthy merchant. He was a man of handsome body, honorable and liberal, a lover, and a good poet in the rhymes of his own language. For this reason, he was most welcome to Richard, King of England, to Raymond, Count of Toulouse, and to the Lord of Marseille. He loved Adalagia, the wife of the Lord; and to hide the fact, he feigned to love her two sisters. He was in great mourning at her death; and finally, he dedicated himself, his wife, and two sons to the Cistercian monastery. Later he was Abbot of Toronet, and finally Bishop of Marseille, from where he drove out the heretics.

**AND HE DOES NOT think.** He reproaches his fellow countrymen, namely the common rabble of the March of Treviso, which is situated between the Tagliamento and Adige rivers, for these two rivers enclose it. He shows, therefore, that these people do not think of any glory or fame because they live in vice. Nor do they repent, though God has beaten them with many tribulations. And he predicts that the Paduans will be defeated by the Vicentines, and so many will be killed that the water running near Vicenza will change color with blood. And this will happen because they are cruel against reason.

**And where Sile and Cagnano accompany each other:** that is, where these two rivers join. And by this, he indicates Treviso, where these rivers mix. **ONE SUCH:** This is Lord Riccardo da Cammino, who was the lord of Treviso; and he walks with his head held high, which demonstrates his pride. **THE SPIDER’S WEB is being spun:** the net is being woven; that is, deceptions are being prepared to "snatch" him, to capture him. This man, while playing chess, was treacherously killed by a most wicked scoundrel.

He follows his discourse and divines, predicting that Feltre—a city on the borders of the March—will weep for the "transgression," that is, the wickedness of Alessandro, its bishop. Transgression <note>original: "diffalta"</note> signifies a misdeed, a wicked sin, which was such that no equal to it was ever punished in **Malta.** They say Malta is a river that runs into Lake Bolsena, where there is a tower in which the Pope kept in perpetual prison those clerics who had committed unpardonable sins. This bishop was of the Piacentine nation, and in Monte Feltre he was a spiritual and temporal lord. In those times, noblemen from the Ferrara families fled because they had acted against the state; they believed they would be safe in Feltre, a free land. But Lord Pino della Tosa, a Florentine knight who was lieutenant in Ferrara for King Robert (who held the lordship for the Church after the death of Azzo III, Marquess of Ferrara), persuaded the bishop to let him take them from his land. The bishop consented against all justice. Because of this, they were brought back to Ferrara, and many were beheaded, among whom were Lancilotto, Chiaruccio, and Antonello.

**ABOVE ARE Mirrors, you call them <term>Thrones</term>.** This is the third order of angels, through whom God sends all his judgments into execution. Therefore, because the judgments of the great and mighty God shine in them as in mirrors, we, by looking at them, see those judgments. But of the orders of the Archangels and the angelic hierarchies, we shall speak in a more appropriate place.

After Cunizza, Folco came forward, who was already known to him through the words spoken by Cunizza. He shone like a **balas ruby** struck by the sun; and this is because the blessed spirits shine more brightly the more joyful they are, because joy there generates splendor just as [laughter does here].

<image-desc>Decorative initial V</image-desc> Wishing to reveal himself, Folco describes the land where he was born, that is, Marseille; and shows that it is on the Mediterranean Sea, which comes out of the Ocean between Spain and Africa through a narrow place called the Strait of Seville <note>The Strait of Gibraltar.</note> near the mountain of Gibraltar. And he says the Mediterranean Sea, which reaches to Jerusalem, makes the meridian circle, as we have shown elsewhere. Therefore, since it makes a longer progression here, the author says that this is a "greater valley" than the others through which it enters here, and he arranges the text. "Then," that is, when I had spoken, his words began thus: "the greatest valley in which water spreads, which comes out from the ocean sea which 'garlands'—that is, surrounds—the earth; it goes so far—that is, it extends so far against the sun, that is, toward the east—between discordant shores because it divides Spain from Africa; and the shores are inhabited by discordant men and enemies to each other, because on the African side are the Barbarians and from Spain the Christians; which makes a meridian where it previously made the horizon."

<columns>1</columns>

**horizon:** We have said enough about the meridian circle and the horizon. But here I understand that the sea entering from the west, which makes the horizon because it divides one hemisphere from the other, extends so far from the west that it reaches the meridian circle toward Jerusalem. **I WAS A SHORE-DWELLER:** because Marseille is on the shore. This city was built by Greeks. **BETWEEN EBRO:** Not the great river of Thrace, but another not far from Marseille. **MACRA:** a river that divides Tuscany from Liguria, or rather the Genoese Riviera. **BOUGIE:** <note>original: "Buggea." A city in modern-day Algeria.</note> This city is on the African shore opposite Marseille. And these two places are equally distant from the east and the west, and almost have the same meridian. **WHICH MADE THE HARBOR WARM WITH ITS OWN BLOOD:** This refers covertly to the siege of Marseille when Caesar, going to Spain and not being able to bring Marseille to his devotion, left Brutus in the field, who finally conquered it, not without much blood from both sides. Folco was the son of Alfonso, a wealthy merchant. Because he remained wealthy, he followed the courts and great men. He gave himself to composing verses and to many refinements. He was very well-received by Richard, King of England, and by Raymond, Count of Toulouse, and by the lords of Marseille. He was very much taken with love for his wife Adalagia—though he covered it by pretending to love her two sisters—and when she died, he felt the greatest grief. Therefore, he dedicated himself, his wife, and his two children to religious life. He became the Abbot of Thoronet <note>original: "Torinello"</note> and finally the Bishop of Marseille, and he drove out many heretics. He was a handsome, pleasant, and generous man.

You wish to know who is within this light
that sparkles here beside me,
like a ray of sun in clear water.
Know then, that within it Rahab finds her peace;
she is joined to our order,
and our highest rank is sealed by her.

<column-break/>

**THE DAUGHTER OF BELUS.** Her name was Elissa, but for her manly spirit she was named Dido. According to historical records, she was an entirely chaste woman. But Virgil feigns that she fell in love with Aeneas, and because of that love, she killed herself when he left her; and the poet [Dante] follows this fiction. **WRONGING SYCHAEUS AND CREUSA:** because in this union Aeneas did not keep faith with Creusa, his wife, nor Dido with Sychaeus, her husband. But such a fable has already been told many times. **AS LONG AS IT SUITED MY HAIR:** that is, in that age when his hair was not yet gray. For when old age arrives, loving is no longer fitting.

**RHODOPEA:** that is, Phyllis, the Queen of Thrace, whom the poet Ovid calls "Rhodopean" from Mount Rhodope in Thrace. She welcomed Demophon, the son of Theseus, King of Athens, who was returning from the Trojan War and had been shipwrecked. Phyllis fell most passionately in love with him and gave him her kingdom. After some time, Demophon returned to his kingdom in Athens and promised her he would return shortly. But a lover is impatient of any delay; despairing of his return because of her great love, she hanged herself near the port upon an almond tree. Later, when Demophon returned, the almond tree, which had appeared withered, put forth its leaves again. Thus, from this Phyllis, the Greeks called the leaves of trees *phylla*, <note>original: "philla"; the Greek word is *phylla*.</note> which they previously called *petala*. **ALCIDES:** that is, Hercules, so named because in Greek *alce* means "strength." <note>original: "alce in greco significa gagliardia."</note> Alternatively, he was named Alcides after Alceus, his maternal grandfather. Hercules defeated Eurytus, King of Oechalia, and became so enamored with Iole, the king's daughter, that she could do with him as she pleased. She made him dress like a woman and made him spin wool and perform other feminine tasks. **YET HERE ONE DOES NOT REPENT, BUT RATHER SMILES:** one might ask, "Since you remember your lustful love, should you not still repent and be saddened by it? And shouldn't such sadness diminish your bliss?" To this he responds: here the fault does not return to the mind because it has already been purged and extinguished, so there is no cause for sorrow. Therefore, one does not repent of the fault, but smiles at the Power—that is, God—who ordered and provided in this star. **Here we gaze upon the art that adorns with such great effect:** that is, we spirits, contemplating the heavens, see the "art," which is the power of nature placed there by God with great effect; for from such natural power, most marvelous effects proceed. **And we discern the good:** that is, in those effects produced by the heavens, we recognize God through them; because through "the world below"—the effects produced down here in the elements and in men—the soul returns to the "world above," which is the First Cause. **THE WORLD BELOW TURNS:** that is, the lower world which is mortal by nature turns (becomes) like the world above—immortal—through the influence of Venus, which is the cause of generation. In this way, the human species becomes immortal through succession.

Proceeding in his speech, Folco shows that the most splendid spirit in that star was Rahab. She was the first among the Gentile people to believe in the religion of the Old Testament. In the Book of Joshua, <note>original: "Iesu naue."</note> it is written that when he entered the Promised Land, he fought against Jericho because they had refused to receive him. To conquer the city more quickly, he sent spies to learn the layout and the movements of the men. After a few days, they were discovered; being chased by the people who wanted to capture them, they took refuge in the house of Rahab, a woman much inflamed by the fires of Venus [a prostitute]. Moved by love for God and her neighbor, she hid them. Later, because her house was joined to the city walls, she lowered them down and saved them. She herself was saved because she made a pact with them: when Joshua sacked the land, she would place a scarlet cloth in her windows, and seeing this, they would preserve her house. And because God wills that in every order of the blessed there are distinct ranks according to whether their merits are greater or lesser, the poet feigns that she "sparkled"—that is, flashed and shone—more than the others because she had greater merit.

<summary>Folco of Marseille compares his youthful passions to those of Dido, Phyllis, and Hercules, explaining that in Heaven, memories of past sins bring joy in God's providence rather than regret. He then introduces the spirit of Rahab, the harlot of Jericho, as the most luminous soul in the sphere of Venus.</summary>
<keywords>Dido, Phyllis and Demophon, Hercules and Iole, Rahab, Jericho, repentance in Heaven, divine providence, Venus (sphere), crystalline art, Joshua</keywords>

# PARADISO

<meta>catchword: conduffe</meta>

Of this heaven where the tip of the shadow
cast by your world comes to a point, before any other soul
of Christ’s triumph was assumed,
It well befitted her to be left as a palm <note>A "palm" here signifies a trophy or symbol of victory.</note>
in some heaven of the high victory
which was won with one and the other palm. <note>original: "l'una & l'altra palma." A wordplay on the palm of victory and the palms of Christ’s hands nailed to the cross.</note>
Because she favored the first glory
of Joshua in the Holy Land,
of which the Pope has but a short memory.
Your city, which was planted by him <note>Lucifer.</note>
who first turned his back on his Maker,
and from whom all envy springs,
Produces and spreads the cursed flower <note>The florin, the gold coin of Florence, which featured a lily (the flower).</note>
which has led the sheep and lambs astray,
for it has made a wolf of the shepherd.
For this the Gospel and the great Doctors <note>The Church Fathers and theologians.</note>
are abandoned, and only the Decretals <note>Books of papal decrees regarding Canon Law, studied for legal profit rather than spiritual growth.</note>
are studied, as is shown by their margins.
To this the Pope and Cardinals attend;
their thoughts do not go to Nazareth,
to where Gabriel opened his wings.
But the Vatican and the other chosen parts
of Rome, which have been a cemetery
for the soldiers who followed Peter,
will soon be free from the adulterer.

<column-break/>

The story of Rahab follows, and it says that from the triumph Christ brought back from the demon when he despoiled Limbo, she was assumed before any other soul from this heaven of Venus—the heaven where the shadow cast by your world comes to a point. That is, the shadow made by the earth where you men live. He says this because the cone—that is, the tip—of the shadow of the earth reaches as far as the heaven of Venus. **IT WELL BEFITTED:** It was very appropriate, considering the merits of this woman, that God should leave her in this heaven as a palm, which is to say a sign of the high victory which Christ achieved against the demon with one palm and the other—that is, with both hands, which were fixed upon the cross. And the reason why this is appropriate is because she, as we have said, quickly favored Joshua by believing his commands and saving his men during his first glory: that is, in the conquest of Jericho, which was the first city Joshua took after crossing the River Jordan. The memory of this Holy Land, where Jerusalem is, little touches the Pope; for he does not care to recover the Holy Land, being given over to simony <term>Simony: the act of selling church offices and roles for money</term> to acquire wealth. And here he blames Florence. **YOUR CITY:** He continues by shaming the prelates of the Church who, moved by avarice, leave the care of the Holy Land in the hands of the Saracens. This city has produced the florins, and he calls it the plant of Lucifer. Therefore he says "your city," O Dante, which is the plant of him who was the first to turn his back on God—that is, who disobeyed Him—and from whom all envy comes. For he, through envy, wished to equal God, and through envy of our well-being, he led

con-
-ducted <note>The text breaks mid-word "conduffe" (conducted) to match the original layout.</note> the first man to sin. It "produces" because the city mints it, and "spreads" because it spends the cursed flower—that is, the florin, which has the lily on one side and Saint John the Baptist on the other. And in truth, the Florentine merchants have always kept the court of Rome abundant with florins, whereby avarice was kindled in the prelates. And so the sheep and the lambs—that is, the great and the small—have been led away from the true path, because they have made a wolf of the shepherd. For this avarice has caused the Pope, who ought to be a true shepherd, to become a predatory wolf. And for this reason, they have abandoned the study of sacred letters, which are the Gospels and the great Doctors who interpret them. They only study the Decretals and canon laws so they can sell them to litigants and make a profit, in such a way that it "appears on their margins"—that is, on their garments, the superfluity and pomp of which he shames more extensively in another place. "Margin" specifically refers to the hem of the cloth, but here he uses the part to represent the whole. **TO THIS:** To this avarice and the accumulation of wealth through simony the Pope attends. He says this specifically regarding Boniface [VIII], whom he mentioned in the *Inferno*. Their thoughts do not go to Nazareth, which is to say the things of God; he mentions this city because it was there that the Mother of the Lord received the Annunciation. Therefore he adds: **THERE WHERE GABRIEL OPENED HIS WINGS**, meaning he flew to announce to the Virgin, who alone among women remained a virgin after childbirth. **BUT THE VATICAN:** He predicts that Boniface will soon suffer punishment for his sins and will be dead. Thus the Vatican and the other places of Rome—which are sacred for having been the cemetery of martyrs who, fighting for the faith and following Peter, the first Vicar of Christ, were killed—will be free from the adulterer through the death of Boniface. He calls him an "adulterer" because the true spouse of the Church and the true Pope was Celestine; or truly an "adulterer" because, abandoning the true spouse (the Church), he is faithful to simony.

<summary>This page contains Dante’s fierce denunciation of Church corruption, specifically targeting Pope Boniface VIII and the city of Florence for their role in spreading avarice through the florin. The commentary explains the astronomical positioning of the Heaven of Venus and interprets the "adulterer" as a reference to the illegitimate or corrupt papacy.</summary>

# CANTO TEN

D.iii.

### CANTO TEN OF THE THIRD CANTICLE OF DANTE

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'G' with blue, red, and gold patterns.</image-desc>
Gazing into His Son with the Love
which the one and the other eternally breathe forth,
the first and ineffable Power <note>original: "l’oprimo & ineffabile valore." This refers to God the Father, acting in concert with the Son (Wisdom) and the Holy Spirit (Love).</note>
Created all that revolves through mind and eye
with such order that he who looks upon it
cannot be without a taste of Him.
Lift up your sight then, reader, with me
to the high wheels, directed to that part
where the one motion strikes against the other; <note>The intersection of the celestial equator and the zodiac (the ecliptic), forming an 'X' shape—a symbol of the Cross in the cosmos.</note>
And there begin to gaze with love upon the art
of that Master who so loves it within Himself
that His eye never departs from it.
See how the oblique circle <note>The zodiac.</note> branches out from there,
which carries the planets
to satisfy the world that calls upon them.
And if their path were not slanted,
much power in the heavens would be in vain,
and almost every potency here below would be dead.
And if it were more or less distant
from the straight path, much would be lacking
in the order of the world, both above and below.
Now remain, reader, upon your bench,
thinking back on what has been sampled,
if you wish to be joyful long before you are weary.
I have set the food before you; now feed yourself,
for that matter of which I have been made the scribe
now turns all my care toward itself.

<column-break/>

The author finds himself already ascended from the third planet to the fourth; and in this tenth chapter he describes the order of the heaven and its motion. Then he relates how he entered and the excellence of the souls who are in that sphere; and he brings forth a modern soul to speak. Having ascended, then, not without wonder, considering the uniform motion of the heavens and the erratic motion of the planets, he begins to demonstrate that the Divine Essence, distinct in three persons, created the universe with miraculous order and says: The First Power <note>original: "el primo valore."</note>, that is the Father to whom is attributed power, which is ineffable, that is to say, <gloss>unspeakable</gloss>, gazing, that is, intending, into His Son to whom is attributed wisdom, because the Son is the wisdom of the Father. With Love: <gloss>that is, with the Holy Spirit</gloss>. WHICH: <gloss>that is, which love</gloss> the one and the other, that is the Father and the Son, eternally breathe forth, because the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. Therefore the Father with His power: and with the wisdom of the Son: and with the love of the Holy Spirit made all that revolves: and considers and understands: either through the mind, as are invisible things, or through the eye, as are visible things, with such order that whoever gazes upon this cannot be without tasting of Him, that is, without knowledge of God. But to avoid error in the things said above, we must hold for certain that God is one and alone in essence. But this one essence which is one God is distinct in the three aforementioned persons. He concludes, therefore, that the universe, both visible and invisible, is established with such order that no smallest particle of it can decline or depart from such order. Nor could there be such order if it did not proceed from a prince and mover who composed and linked together so many things, so diverse and contrary. Nor can anyone have knowledge of these things who does not taste what a thing God is. LIFT UP THEN: he invites the reader to consider the motions of the heavens, especially in that part where one motion strikes against the other. It is known through astronomy that the motion of the firmament proceeds from East to West; and the planets make a motion contrary to this from West to East, always under the zodiac which divides the equinoctial circle <note>The celestial equator.</note> and is similarly divided by it into two equal parts; and one rises to the North; the other declines to the South, as we demonstrated at length in the second cantica. THE ONE MOTION TO THE OTHER: because they are contrary. TO GAZE WITH LOVE: <gloss>that is, to look upon with pleasure and delight</gloss>. IN THE ART: <gloss>that is, in the admirable mastery</gloss> which is the nature of things skillfully established by God. Whence Petrarch says: "He who showed infinite providence and art / In his miraculous mastery / And created this and the other hemisphere / And Jupiter more gentle than Mars."

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'V' in blue with white patterns on a red background.</image-desc>
See then how from there: <gloss>that is, from the equator</gloss> it branches out: <gloss>that is, it departs like a branch from a tree</gloss>. Thus it turns from the first part of Aries, ascending over our northern hemisphere: and it goes through Aries, Taurus, and Gemini until the summer tropic <note>The Tropic of Cancer.</note> which is between the end of Gemini and the beginning of Cancer; and then follows Cancer, Leo, and Virgo until the first point of Libra. And these six signs are northern. And from Libra through Scorpio and Sagittarius it arrives at Capricorn, at the beginning of which is the winter tropic <note>The Tropic of Capricorn.</note>. And from there through Aquarius and Pisces it returns to Aries; and these six are southern signs. TO SATISFY THE WORLD THAT CALLS IT: <gloss>that is, to preserve through this motion this lower world</gloss>, which is governed by the oblique motion of the planets. AND IF THE PATH WERE NOT SLANTED: if the zodiac, which is the path of the planets, were not slanted and oblique, much power in the heaven—that is, much formative power that the heaven has, which flows into the planets and the planets into the elements and into things made of elements—would be in vain because it would not flow into the lower bodies as in...

<summary>Dante ascends to the Heaven of the Sun and marvels at the perfect astronomical order created by the Trinity. The commentary explains the complex movements of the zodiac and the necessity of its tilt for supporting life on Earth.</summary>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>PARADISO</header>

...to have flowed: because there would be no one to prepare it to act. Just as the planets are, they would not dispose the things subjected to them—and only a small part would be subject—if they did not move away from the circle of the equator. Almost every potential—that is, every virtue <note>In this context, 'virtue' refers to an inherent power or medicinal/life-giving property.</note> that is fit to receive the influences that create life, whether vegetative, sensitive, or motive—would be without this life. And similarly, the elements fit to receive generation and corruption <note>A philosophical term for the cycle of birth and decay.</note>—which is the life within them—would not receive it through that motion. It was therefore necessary for the zodiac to distance itself from the equator and the meridian circle (which is straight and not slanted) by twenty-four degrees <note>The axial tilt is actually about 23.5 degrees, but was often rounded to 24 in medieval astronomy.</note> in each hemisphere, as we see in our northern summer tropic, which is at the beginning of Cancer, being twenty-four degrees distant from the beginning of Aries, which is on the equator in the east. And similarly, from the beginning of Libra, which is on the equator in the west, to the beginning of Capricorn, which is the winter tropic, there are twenty-four degrees. And as Aristotle says in the book *On Generation and Corruption*, if the sun and the other planets did not move further from and closer to us, there would be no generation and corruption, because from this comes the distinction of seasons, of which some are fit for generation and some for corruption: in one, one sows; in another, the grass grows; in another, it ripens. But if this departure from the meridian circle were more or less, much would be lacking in the order that God placed in the world, both in the heavens and down in the elements: because they would not make the proper distinction of seasons as they do. **NOW stay, reader:** as if to say, I have sampled and briefly touched upon certain things regarding the celestial motions as they pertain to my purpose; but you, reader, remaining at your bench—that is, in your study—will follow this doctrine until the end. Although it is difficult and very tiring, it nonetheless gives such contentment and pleasure to the soul that the fatigue is borne; and first, man is happy to have perfect knowledge so that he is not weary in his study. I have set the matter before you, and you, by following, will feed upon it. For the food of the soul is understanding. And I shall go no further [with this explanation], because this is not my main purpose.

**The greatest minister of nature**
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**who imprints the world with the power of heaven**
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**and with his light measures time,**
**being joined with that part mentioned above,** <note>Referring to the intersection of the celestial equator and the ecliptic (the zodiac).</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**was revolving through the spirals**
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**in which he presents himself earlier every hour.**
**And I was with him; but of the ascent**
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**I was no more aware than a man is aware**
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**of his first thought before it comes.**

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' containing a floral/foliage design.</image-desc>
Dante demonstrates that he had already ascended into the fourth heaven, the sphere of the sun, without having noticed it; and he calls the sun the "greatest minister." In truth, it is greater in body, because it is larger than all other celestial bodies. And while the earth is one million, three hundred thirty-three thousand, and six hundred miles <note>Medieval measurements for the earth's size varied greatly from modern ones.</note>, the sun is one hundred sixty-six times the size of the earth. And as you see it is greater in body, so understand that it is even greater in virtue: because it is the cause of the tempering of the elements and of natures, and of the composition of individual things made of elements through the participation of the other planets. The sun, as

we see, is placed in the fourth heaven, although the Egyptians placed it in the second. This is called by Cicero the "leader of the other stars," because by the majesty of its light, it precedes all other lights. Furthermore, he calls it "prince" for its excellence. He calls it "moderator and temperer" of the other planets: because it rules the course and the progress and regress of all the other planets. For there is a certain distance at which, when the planet arrives toward the sun, it must move away, and similarly having moved away to another determined distance, it then returns. It is also called by physicians the "mind of the world" and "heart of heaven": because heat, cold, and temperance, and every other thing generated in the air, come from the sun, just as in an animal every motion comes from the heart. It makes its course in three hundred sixty-five and a quarter days. Therefore, every four years a day is "intercalated"—that is, placed in between—as we said in another place when showing the "bissextile" <note>A leap year.</note>; and such a year has three hundred sixty-six days. Furthermore, there remains a hundredth part of a day. But we also speak of this in that verse: "But before January is entirely un-wintered." <note>original: "Ma innanzi che giennaio tutto si fuerni." This refers to the slight error in the Julian calendar that caused the dates of the seasons to drift.</note> This planet creates the year by finishing the whole zodiac; it creates the month by finishing one sign of the zodiac; it creates the day, which is the span of twenty-four hours. It makes day when it is in our hemisphere above the earth. It makes night when it is below the earth. When it comes to the east, it makes morning; when at the midpoint of the day, it makes midday. When it declines to the west, it makes evening. When it enters Aries, which is the first point of the equator, it makes spring. When it reaches Cancer, it makes summer. When at Libra, autumn. When at Capricorn, winter. Therefore, for these four seasons of the year, the poets imagine him in a chariot pulled by four horses. The names of the horses, according to Ovid, are: *Pyroeis*, *Eous*, *Aethon*, and *Phlegon*. *Pyroeis* is named from *pyr*, which signifies "fire" <note>original: "decto da pyr che significa fuotho [fuoco]."</note>. *Eous* from *eos*, which signifies "the dawn." *Aethon* and *Phlegon* from *aithein* and *phlegein*, both of which signify "to burn." They have their names, then, from the heat of the sun. But Hyginus and many others name the first horse *Erythraeus*: that is, "red," from the red color the sun has in the morning. The second, *Acteon*, because toward the third hour it extends its rays, which the Greeks call *actin*. The third, *Lampros*, meaning "splendid," because at midday it shines greatly. The fourth, *Philogeus*, that is, "lover of the earth," because toward evening it sinks toward the earth. It is called *Sol* [Sun] because it is the "sole" [only] one that shines; and with its light, it illuminates the things above and below, and every star takes its light from it. It is a fortunate planet: masculine, diurnal, hot, and dry. It gives life to all things. Whence Aristotle writes that...
