### CANTO TEN

#### D iiii

<meta>The transcription notes a ghosting of the word "PARADISO" from the reverse page and slight foxing on the original paper.</meta>

The sun and man generate man <note>original: "elſole et lhuomo genera lhuomo"; a common medieval Aristotelian principle that life requires both a biological parent and the heat/influence of the sun</note>: And in the book of the elements, it is affirmed that the sun has its own light, while the other planets receive it from it. It is greater than all the other planets in quantity, in dignity, and in power. And with its orderly motion, without any confusion, it orders and gives perfection to all things. The sun is the eye of the world, the joy of the day, the beauty of heaven, the measure of time, the virtue and vigor of all things being born, the lord of the planets, the perfection of the stars, and the king of nature. Plato writes in the *Timaeus* that God made the sun so that with its splendor it might illuminate the heavens and all inferior things. It is most simple and not composed of contrary parts; from such simplicity, it follows that it is most light. For gravity <note>meaning weight or heaviness</note> is born from the connection of material parts, and from lightness is born agility and the speed of motion; and from this, it follows that it is very active. Thus, it is productive and generative: it opens the pores of the earth and excites the other <gloss>humor</gloss> <note>liquid or moisture</note> that is in the roots, and it renews all plants and nourishes them by resolving the humor in the earth and converting it into nourishment. It heals and preserves. For the elements, through their contrarieties, would destroy one another if they were not reconciled by the influence of celestial virtue. In the sun is the life-giving virtue. Therefore, nothing lives where the power of the sun does not penetrate. The sun influences in man the nature of knowing and imagining. This fact moved the poet to indicate that within the body of this planet are men excellent in doctrine. **MINISTER:** of natures, whether we mean "naturing nature" <note>original: "natura naturante"; referring to God as the creative source</note>, whom it obeys, or "natured nature" <note>original: "natura naturata"; the created world</note>, because it causes its effects there. **OF THE VALUE OF HEAVEN:** of the informative virtue <note>the power that gives "form" or essence to matter</note> that the heaven infuses. It imprints <note>original: "imprempta idest imprompta"; it stamps or seals</note> and seals the things of the world upon the world, because into them it transfuses the virtue of heaven and disposes them to receive it. **AND WITH its light it measures time:** because its course creates morning, day, evening, night, weeks, months, years; it creates spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Whence Petrarch, speaking of the sun, wrote: *When the planet that distinguishes the hours.* We shall say, then, that the minister of heaven is joined with that part of the zodiac which was mentioned—that is, which I mentioned at the beginning of the book: Aries. **IT WAS CIRCLING.** **THROUGH THE SPIRALS:** through its circulations, because every twenty-four hours it circles the entire sky. The Latins call a "circle" that which returns into itself like a ring; and they call a "spiral" <note>original: "spira"</note> that which, although it goes around, does not return into itself, as we see many rounds in a rope. Therefore, because the sun moves one degree every day and never returns to that same point, it creates spirals and not circles. **IN WHICH:** in which Aries. **EVERY HOUR it presents itself sooner:** because at the equinox, the hours of the night are equal to those of the day. And he adds that he did not perceive himself having ascended to the heaven of the sun, otherwise than a man perceives his first thought before it arrives—before it comes—of which he never perceives or realizes that it must come, because it came suddenly, inspired by the heavens, or by God, or persuaded by the devil.

**T**he poet feigns that in the sun itself, Beatrice was more shining than the sun. And similarly, the other spirits who are in that sphere, he says, are more shining than the sun. And this is because in it he places the souls of those who were illustrated by the highest science. And he orders the text: "Oh, how much it was fitting for her to be shining of herself..."

-> for above the sun there was no eye that could go <-

<column-break/>

**OF HERSELF:** that is, how much it was necessary that she shine through her own self, for that which was inside the sun—that is, Beatrice—had to be more shining than the light of the sun; because otherwise, she would not have been seen within the sun. **THAT WHICH** was Beatrice. **SHE WHO is perceived from good to better:** because the more she ascends, the more she shines, and she shines so suddenly that her action is not presented to us through time—that is, with the succession of time. And by this, he declares that man can apprehend natural things and the science of them with his own genius, using reasoning and discourse where the succession of time appears. But of celestial and divine things, our genius is not capable of itself. Whence we do not acquire such knowledge with the succession of time or through our discourse, but by divine inspiration and in an instant. **NOT BY COLOR:** not by corporeal light such as colors are. **BUT BY LIGHT APPEARING:** that is, appearing <note>original: "paruente"</note>, as if to say so excessive that it appeared as the sun in its splendor. He adds that although he used all genius, art, and practice, it would not be so eloquent that it could be said. **SO:** that is, in such a way that it could never be imagined by those who read, for he who learns of the splendor never saw anything more shining than the sun. Therefore, let us not wonder that our fantasy—which cannot learn except for those things that the senses provide—does not reach such a height. Nonetheless, man, although he cannot imagine such splendor, can believe it and desire <note>original: "brama idest diderare"</note> to see it.

# PARADISO

Tale era here the fourth family
by the high Father who always satisfies them,
showing how He breathes and how He generates.
And Beatrice began: "Give thanks,
give thanks to the Sun of the Angels, who by His grace
has raised you to this visible sun."
No mortal heart was ever so disposed
to devotion and to give itself to God
with all its will so readily,
As I became at those words;
and so much did I place all my love in Him
that Beatrice was eclipsed in oblivion.
This did not displease her, but she smiled at it,
so that the splendor of her laughing eyes
divided my united mind into many things.

I saw many living and shining splendors
make us a center and themselves a crown,
sweeter in voice than glowing in appearance.
Thus we sometimes see the daughter of Latona <note>Diana, the Moon</note>
girded, when the air is so heavy
that it retains the thread that makes her zone <note>The lunar halo</note>.
In the court of heaven, from which I return,
are found many jewels so precious and beautiful
that they cannot be taken out of the kingdom;
And the song of those lights was among them;
he who does not take wing to fly up there
must wait for news from those who are mute.

Then, singing thus, those burning suns
circled around us three times

<column-break/>

He follows by showing that the **fourth family**, that is, the spirits of this fourth heaven, was such—that is, so shining—as was said of Beatrice. **BY THE HIGH FATHER**: He is the true Father because He creates, generates, governs, and nourishes. **WHO ALWAYS SATISFIES THEM** with Himself, just as a father satisfies his family with his substance. **SHOWING HOW HE BREATHES AND HOW HE GENERATES**: He satisfies them with Himself by showing a single essence in the divinity and also the Trinity in the Persons; and therefore he says *how He breathes* the Son, the eternal love <note>original: "ideſt lo ſpirito ſancto"; that is, the Holy Spirit</note>, and *how He generates* as the Father generates the Son from eternity <note>original: "abeterno"</note>. Therefore, He demonstrates to the blessed His unique essence and the Trinity of Persons because they remain in Him as in a mirror and understand everything. Some do not refer this to God but to the sun; however, how much this goes against its nature, as we said a little before, will be easily understood. **BEATRICE** began to tell me: thank the **Sun of the Angels**, the supreme God who illuminates the angels and, by illuminating them, gives them knowledge; and thank Him because He has lifted and raised you up to this **sensible sun** <note>The physical sun visible to the senses</note>. And certainly, this planet in the fourth heaven is the sensible sun because it is perceived by the senses, especially the eye. And God is the "insensible" <note>intellectual or spiritual</note> sun, where **Petrarch** said: "Crowned with stars to the highest Sun," <note>original: "Coronata di ſtelle al ſonmo ſole"</note> that is, to the highest God from whose light all other light proceeds. **MORTAL HEART**: Great was the efficacy of Beatrice’s comforts and precepts, since she so suddenly placed such devotion in his heart and made him place all his love in God. **THAT BEATRICE ECLIPSED**, that is, darkened. The meaning is this: when the poet was entirely elevated to God, God inspired such grace in him and joined him so closely to Himself that he turned all his love toward Him. Thus, as a greater light obscures a smaller one—just as we see the stars that shine at night disappear when the sun, which is a greater light, arrives—so the love toward God obscured the love he had toward Beatrice. This warns us that we should carry the greatest love toward the **Sacred Scripture** <note>represented by Beatrice</note>. But our end must not be to remain in that, loving it only for its own sake, but rather through it to be able to join ourselves with all our love to God. Nor was it bothersome to Beatrice that the poet forgot her for God’s sake. For all the precepts of Sacred Scripture agree—indeed, they command—that we prefer divine love to every other love. **MY UNITED MIND DIVIDED INTO MANY THINGS**: His mind was united and fixed in prayer and in giving thanks to God; and the splendor of Beatrice's eyes distracted him toward contemplating various spirits.

Those souls, who were shining splendors, had formed a circle around us, and we were in the middle as the center is in the middle of its circumference. **SWEETER IN VOICE THAN GLOWING IN APPEARANCE**: The sweetness of the song surpassed the splendor of the light. This denotes that the sweetness of the **doctrine** <term>doctrina</term> <note>teaching or theological wisdom</note> is greater in itself than the fame that is born from it. And the great artifice of the poet appears here: wanting to show the excellence of the sweetness of the song, he first showed the greatness of the light and then stated that such melody surpassed that splendor. And we were so surrounded by the circle of those souls as we see the **daughter of Latona**—that is, the **Moon**—when the air is pregnant with vapors; because then the surrounding parts take the color of the moon and make a circle for it. **IN THE COURT OF HEAVEN**: A most excellent comparison: just as it happens on earth that if there are excellent jewels in some realm, it is forbidden to take them out; so such a song was so precious a joy that it cannot be taken from that heaven—that is, human wit cannot comprehend it unless one is in heaven. **FROM THOSE WHO ARE MUTE**: "the news"; as if to say, do not expect to hear such things from others unless you go to heaven.

He calls these spirits **burning suns** because of the splendor of their doctrine; they circled three times around Dante.

Bishop of Paris around the year 1172. THE FIFTH light. This is Solomon, son of David, born of Bathsheba, wife of Uriah: whose wisdom is most manifest. ## CANTO XI OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE

<image-desc>Two large historiated initials open the columns. The 'O' on the left contains a miniature of a man in a red robe gesturing within a landscape. The 'C' on the right contains the face of a figure.</image-desc>

O senseless care of mortals!
How defective are those syllogisms <note>original: "esilogismi"; logical arguments used in Scholastic philosophy to derive a conclusion from two premises.</note>
that make you beat your wings in a downward flight!
One went after the law <note>original: "iura"; referring to the study of civil or canon law for profit.</note> and another after aphorisms <note>original: "anphorismi"; a reference to the Aphorisms of Hippocrates, representing the study of medicine.</note>,
one following the priesthood,
and another seeking to rule by force and by sophisms <note>original: "sophismi"; deceptive or fallacious arguments used to maintain power.</note>,
One in theft and another in civic business,
one entangled in the pleasures of the flesh
was wearing himself out, and another gave himself to idleness;
When, released from all these things,
I was high in heaven with Beatrice,
so gloriously received.

<column-break/>

The summary of this eleventh canto contains the praises of two religious orders: Saint Francis and Saint Dominic. It asserts they were raised up in an opportune time by Divine Providence. But first, Saint Thomas resumes his speech and resolves a doubt.
**O SENSELESS CARE:** He rebukes human folly which either gives itself to things that do not lead to the proper end, or rots in idleness and laziness. And therefore, it is "care," meaning concern and senseless desire without true feeling: because it is not only vain and useless, but also harmful to the Highest Good.
**HOW** defective are the syllogisms: that is, how imperfect are their arguments and reasons, because they do not conclude with the truth. A <term>syllogism</term> <note>original: "Silocifmo"</note> is the argument that provides proof for a doubtful thing.

---

But it must not be defective: rather, the major and the minor <note>The two starting premises of a logical argument.</note> must be true, and the conclusion must follow from the premises. **ONE AFTER THE LAWS:** the meaning is this: Granting that the Highest Good consists in the contemplation of divine things to which I and Beatrice were attentive, the majority of men err because some place the Highest Good in riches. Thus they give themselves either to civil law or to aphorisms (that is, to medicine), or to the priesthood, or to civic business (that is, the government of the Republic). All these things, although by their nature they are honest and good, nevertheless, he who does them solely for the purpose of gain is neither a good man nor can he be happy. And much less so if he openly seizes what is not his. Some place happiness in lordships and honors and rule by force tyrannically, or by sophisms (that is, by fraud). A sophism is an argument that appears true and is false. But here he uses it for fraud. Some place happiness in idleness and laziness. Some in luxury; and all err because true happiness cannot be found there.

---

After each had returned to the 
point of the circle where he was before, 
he stopped, as a candle in a candlestick.

<column-break/>

Solomon: *no second arose*. Here then it is necessary <note>original: "fa mestieri"</note> that a clear distinction be made.

Because the difficulty of these verses lies in the ordering of the text: proceed thus. Divine providence, which governs the visible and invisible world with that counsel in which *every created aspect*—that is, every created intellect, both angelic and human—is defeated before it reaches the bottom. *I shall speak*: It will be sufficient to speak of one of the two. Insofar as by praising Francis one also praises Dominic, because their lives and religious devotion were equal in both. Not without the highest artistry does the Aquinate <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas</note> be led to praise Francis and not Dominic; for, Thomas being of the Order of Dominic, he has more credibility in praising Francis. And for the same reason, he is led to rebuke the friars of the Order of Saint Dominic.

The most holy circle stopped, smiling at the ignorance of Dante, and began to speak: and the light became more *mera*, that is, more pure. And he said: as I look into God, from whose rays I shine—as in a mirror in which every truth is seen—I learn and understand your thoughts, which are the reason I speak. Your thoughts are that you *dubii*, that is, you doubt, and in doubting you have the desire and will that my speech be *ricerna*, that is, again distinguished and opened in such plain discourse that your **SENSING**, that is, your intellect, **DISCERNS**, that is, distinguishes and knows two doubts. For the Church is the bride of Christ, who on the cross with loud cries espoused her with His blessed blood, which He shed for our redemption; and she went secure in herself through the guidance of the two aforementioned princes, and *more faithful in Him*, that is, with more faith toward Him. And these two were Francis and Dominic. And the one, namely Francis, was all seraphic in ardor, that is, all burning in charity, because charity is attributed to the Seraphim, who are the highest angels. The other, namely Dominic, was through wisdom a splendor of cherubic light, because wisdom is attributed to the Cherubim. **OF THE ONE**

Topino is the river to the west of Assisi. **THE HILL** chosen: this is to the east; and on this the blessed Ubaldo of Gubbio performed penance; and from this is born the river called Chiuscio. **PORTA** Sole: is a gate of Perugia that goes toward Assisi, as is known to many. **FERTILE** slope: is placed at Assisi on a slope which is very fertile. **UBALDO**: This man was first a hermit on this mountain, then was bishop of Gubbio. **FROM THIS SLOPE**: Shows Francis to have been born in Assisi, who truly was a sun, because through the sanctity of his life and...

### CANTO XI

Therefore, let him who speaks of that place
not say "I ascended" <note>original: "ascesi"; a pun on the town of Assisi and the word for "I rose."</note>, for that would be too little,
but "Orient" <note>original: "oriente"; the East, where the sun rises.</note>, if he wishes to speak properly.

He was not yet very far from his rising
when he began to make the earth feel
some comfort from his great virtue.
For such a lady, even as a youth, he ran into war
against his father, to whom—as to death—
no one unlocks the gate of pleasure.
And before his spiritual court,
and *in the presence of his father* <note>Latin: "coram patre".</note>, he was joined to her;
thereafter, from day to day, he loved her more strongly.
She, deprived of her first husband <note>Jesus Christ.</note>,
for eleven hundred years and more, despised and obscure,
remained without an invitation until his coming.
Nor did it avail her to hear that he <note>Julius Caesar.</note> found her secure
with Amyclas <note>A poor fisherman mentioned in Lucan’s epic poem, *Pharsalia*.</note> at the sound of his voice—
he who made the whole world afraid.
Nor did it avail her to be constant and fierce,
so much so that where Mary remained below,
she climbed upon the Cross with Christ.
But lest I proceed too cryptically,
take Francis and Poverty for these lovers
henceforth in my diffusive speech.

Their harmony and their joyful countenances,
their love, wonder, and sweet gaze,
became the cause of holy thoughts;
So much so that the venerable Bernard
first unbooted himself <note>The act of removing shoes symbolizes the vow of poverty and the following of the apostolic path.</note>, and toward such peace
he ran, and running, it seemed to him he was too slow.
O unknown riches! O fertile good!
Giles unboots himself, Sylvester unboots himself,
following the bridegroom, so much does the bride please them.

<column-break/>

...by excellent examples, he removed all heretical darkness, which in those times greatly occupied human minds. At the same time, Francis was a guide and guardian of the Order of Friars Minor <term>Order of Friars Minor: The Franciscans, characterized by their commitment to poverty.</term>, and Dominic, born in Caleruega, a place in Spain, with whom he instituted the Order of Preachers <term>Order of Preachers: The Dominican Order, founded to combat heresy through education and preaching.</term>. They flourished after the year 1210 of our salvation.

**IT WAS NOT YET VERY FAR** from his birth, because he was of a young age when the earth and men began to know his virtue and take comfort. **FOR SUCH A LADY**: because he ran into war with his father, who was Bernardone, a citizen of Assisi, and his nature <note>OCR error "lanatuolo"; likely "la amò" (he loved her).</note> for such a lady, that is, for Poverty. **TO WHOM**: to which Poverty no one unlocks <note>original: "disserra"; meaning opens.</note> the gate of pleasure, just as they do not for death. **AND IN HIS SPIRITUAL COURT**: because with the counsel of his spiritual father <note>The Bishop of Assisi.</note> he made a profession of poverty, and then he adds **AND IN THE PRESENCE OF HIS FATHER**. **THEREAFTER FROM DAY TO DAY HE LOVED HER MORE STRONGLY**: because his love always grew. **SHE, DEPRIVED** of Christ when He returned to heaven, who was her first husband, remained without an invitation—that is, without being sought—for more than eleven hundred years until this man of whom I speak, who is Francis. And he said "more than eleven hundred" because, as we showed above, twelve hundred years passed from Christ to Francis. **NOR DID IT AVAIL** this Poverty that her great frankness of soul was known everywhere, which was so great that she did not fear the invincible Emperor Caesar when she stayed with Amyclas. Lucan writes that while both the armies of Caesar and Pompey were in Epirus, such that every man was in great trembling, only Amyclas, a very poor fisherman, having nothing to lose—or because death was to be desired by him—lived most securely in his little hut where, after fishing, he retired under cover. Caesar wanted, against the force of the winds, to return to Italy to bring the rest of his army to Epirus; and finally, rebuffed by the tempest, he withdrew to the hut of Amyclas. **NOR DID IT AVAIL HER** also to have such constancy with her spouse and such ferocity that she did not abandon him even in death; and not only did she accompany Him with Mary to the cross, but while Mary remained on the ground, she ascended with Christ onto the cross. Men do not consider how much wealth is in voluntary poverty, and what tranquility of mind. Therefore, the infallible Truth truly said: *Blessed are the poor in spirit* <note>Latin: "Beati pauperes spiritu".</note>, that is, the humble of heart. Because nothing is lacking to him who desires nothing; and certainly Diogenes the Cynic was rich, living joyfully and desiring nothing, and Alexander the Great was poor, for whom nothing was enough, and the more he acquired, the more he desired. Caesar always lived in anxiety and fear, but he found the aforementioned Amyclas very cheerful, of whom Lucan said: ->O safe state of the poor man's life! O narrow homes and gifts of the gods not yet understood! To which temples has it happened to tremble at no tumult, though the hand of Caesar knocks? <note>Latin: "O uita tuta facultas pauperis..." from Lucan's Pharsalia.</note><- And Juvenal: ->But more are strangled by the care of too much heaped-up money. Even if you carry but a few small vessels of pure silver, you will fear the sword and the pole in the night's entry, and at night you will tremble at the shadow of a reed in the moonlight. The empty-handed traveler sings in the face of the thief. <note>Latin: "Sed plures nimia congesta pechunia cura..." from Juvenal's Satires.</note><-

**THEIR HARMONY** and their joyful countenances: If every discord is born from nature and from the greed of possessing treasure, voluntary poverty will always create a harmonious form. And if riches are full of fear, poverty will be full of joy. **LOVE**: that is, the supreme charity with which one kindles the other. **WONDER**: because one was a mirror of probity and sanctity to the other; they became the cause of holy thoughts. For harmony and love and being content with one's present state always direct a man to virtuous works. **BERNARDO**: This was the first companion that Saint...

# PARADISO

O UNKNOWN wealth! Truly this wealth and this good are not recognized; they are "above us," that is, fertile and abundant.

> Then that father and that master moved on
> with his lady and with his family,
> who already bound the humble cord <note>The "capresto" or hempen rope worn by Franciscans instead of a belt.</note>.
> No baseness of heart weighed down his brow
> for being the son of Pietro Bernardone,
> nor for appearing wonderfully despised.
> But regally, his stern intent
> he revealed to Innocent <note>Pope Innocent III.</note> and from him received
> the first seal <note>Official papal approval.</note> for his religious order.

> After the poor people grew in number
> behind him, whose marvelous life
> would be better sung in the glory of heaven,
> the holy will of this archimandrite <note>A title for a head of a monastery or order; from the Greek for "head of the fold."</note>
> was crowned with a second wreath
> by Honorius <note>Pope Honorius III.</note> through the Eternal Spirit.
> And after, through thirst for martyrdom,
> in the proud presence of the Sultan,
> he preached Christ and the others who followed Him;
> and finding the people too unripe
> for conversion, and not wishing to stay in vain,
> he returned to the fruit of the Italian fields.
> On the harsh rock between the Tiber and the Arno <note>Mount La Verna.</note>
> he received from Christ the final seal,
> which his limbs bore for two years <note>The Stigmata, the wounds of Christ's crucifixion.</note>.
> When it pleased Him who destined him for such good
> to draw him up to the reward
> he merited in making himself little <note>A reference to the "Friars Minor" (Little Brothers).</note>,
> to his brothers, as to his rightful heirs,
> he recommended his most dear lady
> and commanded them to love her with faith.
> And from her lap, his illustrious soul
> chose to depart, returning to its kingdom,
> and for his body he wished no other bier <note>Francis requested to be laid on the bare earth at his death.</note>.
> Think now what sort of man he was, who was
> a worthy colleague to maintain the bark
> of Peter <note>The Church.</note> on the high sea in the right direction;
> and this was our patriarch.

<column-break/>

Francis, who girded himself with the cord and went barefoot as Saint Francis had done, and ran toward such great peace.

**That father** because of the care and solicitude he had for the family already begun; and **master** for the precepts he gave. **WITH his lady**: with poverty and baseness of heart—meaning to debase and humble oneself by one's own will. **It did not weigh down his brow**: it did not make him ashamed; he said "brow" because shame shows on the forehead. Or truly, he said "baseness of heart" <note>Latin: "id est"; that is.</note> meaning humility, which is born from a great spirit. He was not ashamed, then, for being the son of Pietro Bernardone—that is, of not very great lineage—nor because he was wonderfully despised for his vile garment and his poverty. But regally, with a royal and unconquered spirit, he revealed to Pope Innocent III his **stern intent**, which was to observe: Obedience, Chastity, and Poverty. These things are very hard and difficult, because obedience is contrary to the freedom of the will (of the evil that arises from turning away from religion); chastity is against the itching of the flesh; and poverty is against the excess of earthly goods. Innocent III, in the twelve hundreds, had a vision that the church of Saint John Lateran was falling, but two men in vile dress held it up. Later, when Saint Francis came so that the Pope might confirm his order, the Pope recognized him as the one he had seen in his dream. Therefore, with a papal bull, he confirmed it for him.

Once the order of Saint Francis had grown, he received from Pope Honorius the power to administer sacraments and hold priestly dignities.
**ARCHIMANDRITE**: Arch-shepherd. Afterward, desiring martyrdom, he went to preach the Christian faith in the land of the Sultan. But producing no fruit, he returned to Italy. Having returned to Italy, he withdrew to the rugged mountain of La Verna, which is between the Tiber and the Arno. There, performing the greatest penance, he received the stigmata from Christ, which the poet calls a "seal." They are called stigmata because *stigma* <note>original: "stign" [stigma]; Greek: στίγμα.</note> in Greek means to strike, and by striking, to leave a mark. And then, when it pleased God to draw him to heaven where he would receive the reward and prize for his merits—which were great because he made himself **little** (that is, small and humble)—he recommended to his brothers his most dear lady. This is Poverty. Here it is to be considered that Poverty was dearer to him than Chastity and Obedience, because Poverty is the cause of Chastity; for as chastity is lost through too much luxury and abundance of things, so it is acquired through poverty. Similarly, he who despises riches can easily remain in obedience. **He wished no other bier**: than that Poverty—that is, he desired no other funeral rites or other honors. Having narrated the story of Saint Francis, he continues and says: **Think** what sort of man he was who was a worthy colleague—that is, a companion to Saint Francis—to support the **bark of Peter**, that is, the Church of God. And this was our patriarch, namely Saint Dominic. He says "our" because Saint Thomas is the one speaking, and he was of the Order of Saint Dominic, as are those who follow him as he commands—that is, those who follow his constitutions. For Saint Dominic did not make a new rule, but took that of Saint Augustine.

that is, if they did not attend for themselves to the

# PARADISE

...before another of a circle enclosed it,
and motion to motion and song to song it matched;
A song that so far surpasses our Muses,
our Sirens, in those sweet pipes,
as the first splendor surpasses that which is reflected.

As through a thin cloud there turn
two parallel and matching-colored arches <note>The poet is describing a double rainbow.</note>
when Juno commands her handmaid <note>Juno’s handmaid is Iris, the goddess of the rainbow.</note>,
The outer one being born from the inner,
in the manner of the speech of that wandering one <note>This refers to the nymph Echo, who could only repeat the words of others.</note>
whom love consumed as the sun evaporates the mist;
And they make people here become prophetic
because of the covenant that God placed with Noah
regarding the world, that it shall never again be flooded;
So of those everlasting roses
the two garlands turned around us,
and so the outer one responded to the inner.

After the dance and the other great celebration,
both of the singing and of the flaming
light with light, gracious and mild,
Stilled themselves together at the same point and will,
just as the eyes, by the pleasure that moves them,
must together close and lift themselves;
From the heart of one of the new lights <note>This "new light" is Saint Bonaventure, a Franciscan.</note>
there moved a voice which made me seem like the needle to the star <note>The poet is drawn to the voice like a compass needle to the North Star.</note>
as I turned toward its source;
And it began: "The love that makes me beautiful
draws me to speak of the other leader..."

<column-break/>

one of these commends the life of Saint Dominic.
And after this, he reproaches the Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans.</note>; and finally, the said soul reveals himself and the others of that
crown. As soon as the blessed flame—that is,
Saint Thomas—took the last word to speak it,
the circle in which he was began to turn. Nor
did it finish turning before another circle appeared there,
which enclosed this one: which denotes that the first circle
rotated closer to the center of the sun, and this one
girding it further away denotes that the souls already mentioned
were of greater beatitude and greater doctrine
than those of whom he will speak. Furthermore, it shows
that the song and the motion of this second circle,
mentioned above, accorded with the song and motion of the
first, to signify that in the Holy Scripture there is no
discord at all. This song surpasses all our Muses
and Sirens—that is, all human melodies—
as much as the first ray surpasses that which reverberates from it.
As, for example, the rays of the sun striking
the water: it reverberates, that is, it shines on a wall;
but the reverberation is not as clear as the
primary ray from which it proceeds.

**A**s through a thin cloud two parallel,
equidistant, and matching-colored arches turn—that is, of
the same colors—of which the first is the one that is
closer to the sun and more apparent, and from that by

first souls was born that of these second ones; and
from the speech of Thomas was born that of Bonaventure.
"WHEN Juno commands"—that is, orders

...the color of the arch from that within, that is, from the cloud and the vapors from which the cloud is generated: just as an echo
is born from the preceding cloud <note>Echo was often associated with mountain air and clouds in medieval physics.</note>: because it is its reflection. "IN THE MANNER": in the likeness of the speech of that
wandering one—that is, the wandering Echo, whose words were born from the voice of others. I will not repeat the fable here, which
we explained at length elsewhere. "AND THEY MAKE PEOPLE HERE become prophetic"—that is, diviners by

**A**FTER THE DANCE <term>tripudio: a rhythmic, joyful dance of celebration</term>—that is, the dance and the
other great celebration that was among the souls of those
two circles; and it was a celebration both of singing, because they
accorded together, AND OF flaming,
because they corresponded in the splendor that signifies
a reciprocal charity. "STILLED THEMSELVES"—that is,

which is God, who is the point of every motion;

# CANTO XII

...through whom my Siger speaks so well.
It is fitting that where one is, the other should shine;
so that as they worked toward a single goal,
so their glory should shine together.

The army of Christ, which cost so dear
to re-arm, moved behind the banner,
slow, suspicious, and few in number,
When the Emperor who reigns forever
provided for his soldiers who were in peril,
by grace alone, and not because they were worthy;
And as was said, He came to the aid of His bride <note>The "bride" refers to the Church.</note>
with two champions, by whose deeds and words
the straying people were gathered back.

In that region where the sweet West Wind <note>The poet refers to Zephyr, the wind of Spring.</note>
rises to open the new leaves
with which Europe sees herself reclothed—
Not far from the beating of the waves
behind which, because of his long flight,
the sun sometimes hides from every man—
Sits the fortunate Calaruega,
under the protection of the great shield
on which the lion is both subject and sovereign. <note>This refers to the coat of arms of the Kingdom of Castile, which featured alternating lions and castles.</note>
Therein was born the amorous lover
of the Christian faith, the great athlete,
kind to his own and cruel to his enemies;
And from its creation, his soul was so filled
with divine virtue
that it made his mother a prophet while he was in her womb.

<column-break/>

A voice moved from the heart and the mind of one in those new lights <note>original: "nuoue luce"</note>—that is, those who were of the circle that had newly arrived—which made me turn toward it like the needle to the star: that is, like the needle in a compass when it points to the North Star. And this soul began to say: "The love that makes me beautiful" <note>original: "LAMOre che mi fa bella"</note>, because the splendor of these souls signifies their charity. This charity leads me—since Saint Francis has been praised by Saint Thomas of the Order of Saint Dominic—that I, Bonaventure of the Order of Saint Francis, should praise Saint Dominic. This is especially appropriate because, having fought as soldiers together, it is a worthy thing that they should be praised together.

Wishing to praise these two champions, the poet not only presents their great virtues but also demonstrates that they appeared at a necessary time, and concerning matters without which eternal damnation follows for the soul. For they were defenders of the faith, without which no one can be saved. They appeared at a time when the Christian people moved behind the banner of God's path in a slow and lazy manner, suspicious because of the many doubts that arose every day due to the sects of the heretics. They were "few" <note>original: "rare"</note> because there were so few faithful left. They were therefore few, and those few were lazy and full of doubts. Therefore, the "army of Christ" <note>original: "L exercito dichristo"</note>—that is, the Christian people who are the Church Militant—which cost so much to "re-arm." This signifies that God created man "armed"—that is, with such virtue that he could defend himself from the Adversary <note>The Devil</note>—if he had not transgressed the commandments. Afterward, sin "disarmed" him so that he could no longer defend or save himself. But Christ the Redeemer re-armed him, ransoming him with His precious blood; this redemption brought us back into divine grace. And these were the weapons with which we can defend ourselves from temptations and from sin. When God, whose empire is eternal, provided for our army by re-arming the Church Militant as was said, "WHO WAS IN PERIL" <note>original: "che era inforse"</note>: that is, in doubt and in danger. And He provided through His superabundant grace, and not because our army deserved it; for the Christian people did not merit being helped by God. And as was said, the provision was that He sent these two champions to act with deeds and speak with teachings: the people who had strayed because of the errors of the heretics were thus gathered back into the Christian army.

Bonaventure, having to narrate the life of Dominic, first describes his homeland, which was Calaruega, a city in Spain located in the West: in that part of the world where the sweet "Zephyr" <note>The West Wind</note> blows. It is a temperate and very delightful wind because when it begins, it brings Spring and gives power to the earth so that everything conceives, clothing the land in grass and flowers, and making the trees grow leaves. This is why he says "with which Europe sees herself reclothed." "NOT FAR from the beating of the waves" <note>original: "Non molto lungi alpercuoter dellonde"</note>: that is, not far from the Western Atlantic Ocean, behind whose waves the sun sets for us. There sits and is located Calaruega, which he calls "fortunate" because it produced such a great man. This city is under the King of Castile, who has a "quartered" shield for his coat of arms: in one part is painted a castle with a lion beneath it, and in another part a lion with a castle beneath it. Therefore he says the lion is "subject" to the castle where it is below, and "sovereign" over the castle where it is above. And within it was born Dominic, the "lover" <note>original: "drudo," meaning a devoted servant or lover</note>—that is, the supreme lover of the Christian faith—and "Athlete" <note>original: "athleta"</note>, that is, a fighter for the faith against the heretics. *Athlete* is a Greek word <note>original: "uocabolo greco"</note> and signifies a fighter, and *athlon* is the prize of the fighter. "KIND TO HIS OWN" Christians, and "cruel to his enemies," that is, the heretics. As soon as his soul was created and infused into his mother's womb, he was a prophet; and through his virtue, his mother also prophesied. For she had dreamed that she gave birth to a black and white dog who carried a small lit torch in its mouth, which predicted that he would be...

<summary>Saint Bonaventure begins his praise of Saint Dominic, describing the saint's birth in Spain (Calaruega) and his role as a "champion" and "athlete" of the faith sent by God to rescue the struggling Church Militant from heresy.</summary>

After describing Dominic's birth in Spain, the text now moves to his baptism and his early dedication to a life of poverty and theological study, contrasting his spiritual mission with the worldly pursuits of legal and medical scholars.</meta>

world and would be sharp against heretics. And he would be of the most burning charity, and certainly he sold everything and gave it for God. And she who held him at the baptismal font dreamed that he had a star on his forehead that illuminated the whole world.

> After the betrothal was completed
> at the sacred font between him and the faith,
> where they dowered each other with mutual salvation,
> the lady who gave the consent for him <note>The "lady" refers to Dominic's godmother.</note>
> saw in a dream the wondrous fruit
> that was to come from him and from his heirs.
> And so that he might be in name what he was in essence,
> a spirit moved from here to name him
> from the possessive of Him to whom he belonged entirely. <note>The poet explains that the name "Dominic" comes from "Dominus" (Lord).</note>
> Dominic was he named; and I speak of him
> as of the tiller of the field whom Christ
> chose for His garden to assist Him.
> Well did he seem a messenger and familiar of Christ,
> for the first love that was manifest in him

> Many times he was found silent and awake

> as if to say: "I have come for this."
> O father of his, truly Felice! <note>A play on his father’s name, Felix, which means "happy."</note>

> in a short time he became a great teacher,
> such that he began to go about the vineyard
> which quickly turns white if the vine-dresser is at fault.
> And from the See that was once kind <note>The "See" refers to the Papacy.</note>
> to the righteous poor—not because of itself
> but because of him who sits there and goes astray—
> he did not ask to dispense two or three for six, <note>He did not ask for permission to keep a portion of wealth for himself.</note>
> nor the fortune of the first vacant spot,
> nor the tithes which belong to God's poor; <note>original: "decimas que sunt pauperum dei"</note>
> but against the errant world
> he asked for leave to fight for the seed
> from which these twenty-four plants have sprung.

<column-break/>

He calls the "betrothal" the baptism, in which the one who holds the child at the font promises that the baptized will renounce the pomps of the devil and other things. *Where they dowered each other with mutual salvation*: because he was a savior to the faith and defended it, and the faith saved him. *The lady who gave consent for him*—that is, she who made the promises for him—saw in her sleep that which we narrated above. And because he was to belong entirely to his Lord God, and the world was to have no part of him, it was by divine inspiration that they named him Dominic. *Dominus* in Latin means "Lord," and from this name *Dominus* derives *Dominicus*, which means "a thing belonging to his Lord." <note>original: "Dominus... dominichus"</note> And therefore I speak of Dominic as a tiller of the field chosen by Christ to cultivate His garden—that is, the Christian people. He appeared to be sent by God, since in his first public act he followed the first counsel that Christ spoke, where He says: *If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have and give to the poor, and follow me.* <note>original: "Si uis perfectus esse Vade et uende omnia que habes et da pauperibus: et sequere me"</note> For while he was still a young student, he sold his books and everything he had and distributed them to the poor during a great famine. Because of this, notice of him reached the Bishop, who made him a canon regular, from which point he gave himself entirely to the study of theology. **O FATHER OF HIS:** He calls the father Felice and the mother Joanna. Regarding this, Bonaventure says with admiration that those names were fulfilled in both: for he was truly "Felice" (Happy), and she was truly "Joanna," because this name in Hebrew means "full of grace." And Dominic was not "silent and awake" for the world—that is, for worldly and temporal things for which many now weary themselves following the Ostian and Thaddeus. The Ostian <note>Henry of Susa, known as Ostiensis.</note> wrote on the Decretals; Thaddeus was a Florentine physician who, for his great learning, was called more than a mere commentator. Dominic, then, was not intent on profit, but followed the true manna of the soul's real food, which is theological doctrine.

Having reached his mature years, although he was already of great authority because of his learning, he did not ask the Supreme Pontiff for dignities from which he might draw profit or honor, nor to be excused from "returning two or three for six"—which is a third or a half—nor did he ask for the first vacant benefice. Instead, he asked for license to battle and preach against the errant world—that is, against the heretics. **FOR THE SEED:** For the faith, which is the seed whose fruit is eternal beatitude, from which "twenty-four plants" are made—that is, the twenty-four books of the Bible, which all speak of the Christian faith. Some understand these twenty-four plants to be the souls in these two circles, which he states are twenty-four in number; and they say "of which they make you, Dante," meaning they surround you as twenty-four plants.

# CANTO XII

Then with doctrine and will together
he moved with the apostolic office,
like a torrent pressed by a deep vein;
And he struck the heretical brambles
his impetus most vigorously there
where the resistance was strongest.
From him then flowed several streams
by which the Catholic garden is irrigated,
so that its bushes stand more lively.
If such was one wheel of the chariot <note>The "chariot" represents the Church; the two wheels are Saint Dominic and Saint Francis.</note>
in which the Holy Church defended herself
and won her civil strife in the field,
The excellence of the other should indeed
be quite plain to you, of whom Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, who spoke in the previous Canto.</note>
was so courteous before my arrival.
But the track that the highest part
of its circumference made is abandoned,
so that there is mold where the crust used to be. <note>original: "muffa douera lagromma." This wine metaphor suggests that where there was once the "crust" or "tartar" of good aged wine (representing the founders' virtues), there is now only mold (decay).</note>
His family, which once moved straight
with feet in his footprints, has turned so far
that the one in front throws back at the one behind. <note>This suggests the friars are now moving in the opposite direction of Saint Francis.</note>
But soon the harvest of the bad cultivation
will be seen, when the tares <note>original: "gioglio." Biblical reference to weeds among wheat.</note>
will complain that the granary is taken from them.
I say indeed, whoever searched our volume leaf by leaf
would still find a page
where he would read: "I am what I used to be."
But it will not be from Casale nor from Acquasparta,
from whence come such men to the scripture
that one flees it and the other restricts it.

<gloss>I am what I used to be: that is, one who would observe the accustomed rule of Francis.</gloss> <gloss>Casale: This was Brother Ubertino da Casale who, being Minister General, loosened the rule too much. He wrote a book which he called the *Penteloquio* on the power of the Pope. Casale is a land in Piedmont. Therefore, he "flees the scripture" by loosening the precepts.</gloss> <gloss>Acquasparta: Brother Matteo da Acquasparta, which is a town in the territory of Todi; he restricted it too much. He wrote on the *Sentences*.</gloss>
<sig>bi ob</sig>

I am Bonaventure of Bagnoregio,
who in the great offices
always put the "left-hand care" last. <note>The "left-hand care" refers to worldly or temporal concerns, as opposed to spiritual contemplation.</note>
Illuminato and Augustine are here,
who were among the first barefoot poor ones
who in the cord <note>The rope belt worn by Franciscans.</note> became friends to God.
Hugh of Saint Victor is here with them,
and Peter the Eater, and Peter of Spain,
who down there shines in twelve booklets.
Nathan the prophet and the metropolitan
Chrysostom, and Anselm, and that Donatus
who deigned to lay his hand to the first art. <note>Aelius Donatus, author of the standard medieval Latin grammar (the "first art" of the Trivium).</note>

<column-break/>

Then he moved against the heretics with three necessary things: with doctrine, by which he might know; with will, so that there would be desire; and with the apostolic office, which is the Inquisition, so that he could overcome the heretics and punish them. FROM HIM THEN FLOWED several streams: from him, as from a fountain, many streams were born to irrigate the Catholic garden, so that its bushes would be green. Having praised Saint Dominic—whom he places as one of the two wheels of the chariot that defended the Church from heretics—he rightly said "civil strife," because the heretics were Christians, and all Christians are citizens of one and the same city, that is, of the Church Militant. Now he turns to Saint Francis and affirms what Thomas had said of him. Then he shows that the majority of his friars have deviated from his precepts and constitutions; and staying with the metaphor he made of the chariot, he says that the track—that is, the path left by this wheel, which are the excellent precepts of his holy works—has been deserted and abandoned by the circumference—that is, by the ministers and prelates of that religion. Thus, where there used to be the crust that gives the best scent to the wine in the vessel, now there is mold that gives a foul odor. HIS FAMILY: his friars, who from the beginning moved behind the footprints of Saint Francis, following his precepts and examples, have turned so far that they place their toes where he placed his heel; that is, they go the opposite way in life and customs. But they will realize their error at the harvest, because they will not find anyone to put their tares into the granaries; that is, God will not want their souls in His kingdom, for they will have produced captive fruit. For it is written in Saint Matthew: <note>original: "Collige primum zizania et alligate ea infafciculos adcomburendum tristicum autem congregate inorreum meum." Translation: "Gather first the weeds and bind them in bundles to be burned, but gather the wheat into my barn." (Matthew 13:30)</note>. Nevertheless, whoever searched our volume—that is, our Order—leaf by leaf, friar by friar, would still find a page—that is, some friar—WHERE he would read: "I [am what I used to be]."

After the praises bestowed upon Saint Dominic, and the complaints and accusations against the friars of Saint Francis, Bonaventure names himself and the souls who are in his circle. There was, then, Bonaventure of Bagnoregio, a land in the Marche; he was most learned in sacred letters, and although he was General of the Order and later a Cardinal, nevertheless in these great offices he always put the "left-hand care" last, that is, the active life, and followed the contemplative. Illuminato was a Friar Minor. Augustine was a Friar Minor. These two were among the first companions of Saint Francis. And although in this circle are placed the souls of those who, shining like the sun with supreme doctrine, were able to illuminate others, he nonetheless places these two who, though they did not shine through doctrine, yet illuminated others through examples of most holy life. HUGH was of Pavia and a monk of the monastery of Saint [Victor]...

The meaning is that the inflamed love of Thomas toward Saint Francis moved me to emulate him and do the same toward Saint Dominic.

Let him imagine, who desires to understand well
what I now saw, and let him hold the image
while I speak, like a firm rock:
Fifteen stars that in different regions
enliven the sky with such serenity
that it surpasses every density of the air; <note>original: "compage."</note>
Let him imagine that chariot for which the axle <note>The Big Dipper, or Charles's Wain.</note>

> Those stars for which our sky suffices both night and day
> so that they never set even as the poles turn;
> Imagine the mouth of that horn <note>The constellation Ursa Minor, often visualized as a horn.</note>
> which begins at the point of the axle
> around which the first wheel revolves;
> To have made of themselves two signs in the sky,
> such as the daughter of Minos <note>Ariadne, whose crown became the constellation Corona Borealis.</note> once made,
> with her rays reflected toward one another;
> and both revolving in such a way
> that one moved first and the other after;
> and you will have almost the shadow of the true
> constellation and the double dance
> that circled the point where I was.

<column-break/>

just as one moves against the other: And to create these two crowns, let him imagine being able to gather together fifteen stars of the first magnitude <note>The brightest category of stars in ancient and Renaissance astronomy.</note> which are scattered in different parts of the sky. Then those seven that make up the Wain <note>The Big Dipper (Ursa Major).</note> in our northern pole. And then two which are at the beginning of the Little Bear <note>Ursa Minor.</note>. And from the twelve brightest among the fifteen, let him make the inner crown closer to the center, and from the rest make the outer crown, and you would have made something similar to the two crowns of the twenty-four souls mentioned above. And the text continues: HE WHO DESIRES <note>original: "CHI CUPE"</note>: that is, whoever wishes to understand well what I saw: let him imagine it in his mind and hold the image firm as a rock <note>original: "rupe," meaning a cliff or mountain stone</note>. Because it would not be enough to imagine it if he did not hold the image in his memory. Imagine then fifteen stars which assist the heavens with their splendor because they are the brightest and the largest: And they emerge from every gathering <note>original: "compage," meaning a structural joining or aggregation</note> of the air. IN DIFFERENT regions <note>original: "plage"</note>: in different parts of the sky. And further imagine the Wain where there are seven stars of the second magnitude; for this wagon, the reach <note>original: "seno," literally 'bosom' or 'gulf'</note> of our sky suffices, that is, our pole: because they revolve so close to our pole that they never set: but are always above our heads. THE DAUGHTER of Minos: Theseus defeated the Minotaur in Crete; and returning from there he took Phaedra and Ariadne (called Adriana), daughters of Minos. And because when they reached the island of Chios, or rather Naxos, Ariadne fell into a deep sleep due to too much wine, she was left on the island by Theseus. But Bacchus took her as his friend and gave her a most precious crown made by Vulcan of gold and gems, which the poets imagine was later translated into a celestial sign. This constellation has eight stars, three of which are very brilliant. THAT ONE moved: First, that is, it rotated against the first. AND the other after: it rotated against the second. THE POINT: that is, with equidistant space they revolved around me, who was in the middle like a center to the circumference.

---

> Since it is as far beyond our custom
> as the movement of the Chiana <note>A river in Tuscany known in Dante's time for its stagnant, slow-moving waters.</note>
> is surpassed by the heaven that outspeeds all others.
> There they sang not of Bacchus nor of Paean <note>A hymn to Apollo.</note>
> but of three persons in a divine nature,
> and in one person, both that and the human.
> The singer completed the turning of his measure,
> and those holy lights turned their attention to us,
> finding joy as they passed from task to task.
> The silence among the harmonious deities was broken
> by the light in which the wondrous life
> of God's poor man <note>Saint Francis of Assisi.</note> had been narrated to me.

<column-break/>

**H**e places the end of the song of these crowns so that Thomas may resolve the second doubt, and he organizes it thus: SINCE they: that is, in that crown, it was so far beyond our custom, meaning much more excellently than is usual among us men, as the heaven that surpasses and overcomes all other heavens moves faster. BEYOND the movement of the Chiana: that is, it moves more than a "chiana," which is dead water. THEY SANG NOT OF BACCHUS NOR Paean: that is, neither Bacchus nor Apollo. For the ancients sang hymns in honor of various gods, and especially of Bacchus and Apollo. And he used the word "Paean" here for Apollo because many believe the Greeks called the hymns made in honor of Apollo "Paeans," although any praise of God is called a Paean. BUT they sang of three persons in a divine nature: that is, they sang of the Trinity, which is one essence in three persons; and they sang of that nature and the human in one person. Because in the person of the Son, there is both divinity and humanity. Therefore, after they sang what was described: THE SONG completed: that is, it finished its circular turn. ITS Measure: that is, the time that was needed for the song. AND TURNED TO US: that is, they stopped and faced us. Those holy lights: those shining souls. FINDING JOY: making themselves happy. FROM TASK to task: from love to love because they were full of perfect charity. BROKE: he organizes it thus: afterwards, that is, after the light in which the wondrous life of God's poor man, that is Saint Francis, was narrated to me—which light, as we saw above, was Thomas Aquinas—he broke the silence, that is, he began to speak; because silence is broken by speaking. As Virgil says: "Why do you force me to break the deep silence?" <note>original: "Quid me alta silentia cogis rumpere."</note> AMONG THE HARMONIOUS deities <note>original: "numi"</note>: that is, among the harmonious souls who had become deities through their blessedness. DEITIES <note>original: "NVMINI"</note>: that is, gods.

> and its seed is already stored away..."

<column-break/>

<meta>Following the visualization of the twenty-four spirits as two concentric crowns of stars, Saint Thomas Aquinas continues his discourse. Having previously praised Solomon as having "no second" in wisdom, Thomas now addresses Dante’s internal confusion: how could Solomon be the wisest if Adam and Christ—both created directly by God—were perfect in human nature? This page begins the philosophical and theological reconciliation of these two truths.</meta>

# PARADISO

To strike down the other doubt, sweet love invites me <note>original: "abbatter laltra dolce amor minuita" — The poet describes the divine love of Saint Thomas Aquinas prompting him to clear Dante's confusion.</note>.
You believe that in the breast from which the rib
was drawn to form the beautiful cheek <note>A poetic reference to Eve, created from Adam's rib.</note>
whose palate cost all the world so much;
And in that breast which, pierced by the lance,
both after and before, offered such satisfaction
that it outweighs the scale of every guilt;
Whatever light is permitted to human nature
was all infused by that Valor <note>God, the Creator.</note>
who made the one and the other.
And therefore you marvel at what I said before,
when I recounted that he had no second <note>He had no equal.</note>
the good that is enclosed in the fifth light <note>The soul of King Solomon, the fifth light in the first circle of spirits.</note>.

<column-break/>

The first straw is threshed, and the seed that came from it is stored away: <note>A metaphor for completing the first part of the explanation.</note> the love and charity which move me to make known to others that which does not diminish me to share. That is to say, since we have explained the first doubt, I will now explain the second. And here it is to be noted before the translation, which is very fitting: that just as one cannot pull the seed from the straw (that is, from the ear of grain) if it is not well-threshed, so too the hidden truth cannot be drawn from among many falsehoods if it is not beaten and shaken with the greatest diligence. **YOU BELIEVE**: The meaning is, you believe that whatever light, intellect, and wisdom can exist in human nature was infused into the breast of Adam and into that of Christ by that divine Valor—that is, by the divine power which is the Father, who made the one and the other (Adam and Christ). And therefore you wonder why I said above that the good which is enclosed in the **fifth light** (that is, in the soul of Solomon) had no equal in wisdom, since Adam and Christ were more perfect men. This is the meaning, though he does not name them by their proper names, but by circumlocution <note>A roundabout way of speaking.</note>. And therefore he mentions the breast of Adam, from whose right side the rib was drawn to form the **beautiful cheek**, meaning the beautiful body of Eve. He uses a part to represent the whole. **Whose palate**: that is, the taste of Eve who, by savoring the forbidden apple, **cost all the world**—meaning all men—because we lost our state of perpetual happiness and the power to never die. He said "palate" because the sense of taste is largely located there. **And that breast** of Christ, which was **pierced by the lance** of Longinus, satisfied so much for the sin of the first parents. **Before and after**: as if to say, with His entire Passion. **Outweighs the scale of every guilt**: as if to say, if one were to put all the sins committed on one side of a scale, and the great merits of Christ's Passion on the other, the side with the merits of our Savior Christ would outweigh the side containing all the sins of men.

---

Now open your eyes to what I shall answer you,
and you will see your belief and my speech
meet in the truth like the center in a circle.
That which does not die and that which can die
are nothing but the splendor of that Idea <term>Idea: The eternal forms or blueprints of all things existing in the Mind of God.</term>
which our Lord, in loving, brings forth;
For that living light which flows out <note>original: "simmea" — A word Dante invented to describe light centering itself or flowing from its source.</note>
from its radiant source, which does not disunite
from Him, nor from the Love which is in-three'd <note>original: "sintrea" — Refers to the Trinity: Father (Radiance), Son (Living Light), and Holy Spirit (Love).</note> with them,
Through its goodness, it gathers its rays,
as if mirrored in nine substances <note>The nine celestial spheres or the nine hierarchies of angels.</note>,
while eternally remaining one.
From there it descends to the lowest powers,
down from act to act, becoming such
that it produces only brief contingencies;
And these contingencies I mean to be
the generated things produced by the moving heavens
with seed and without seed.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A'</image-desc>The author admonishes the reader to open the eyes of the intellect to what he will say, because it is a matter that deserves attention for its greatness and difficulty. You will see that which you believe of Christ and Adam, and that which I say of Solomon (that he had no equal), become the truth like the **center in a circle**—that is, your belief and my words will agree and reside in the truth as perfectly as the center sits within a circle. **THAT WHICH**: All things, visible and invisible, corporeal and incorporeal, are produced by God in the likeness of the **Idea** which God has held in His mind from eternity. "Idea" is a name brought forth by Plato and challenged by Aristotle, though not with true arguments (since no truth contradicts another truth), but with sophisticated quibbling. Cicero, Seneca, Eustratius, Augustine, Boethius, Altividus, Calcidius, and many others agree with Plato. There is, therefore, an example and form in the divine mind, in whose likeness the highest wisdom produces all things visible and invisible. Plato and Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom and alchemy.</note> write that God knows all things from eternity. Therefore, they place the cognition of all things within the divine mind and wisdom, and Plato calls these "Ideas." But I will not expand upon this matter, for it is much more difficult than is appropriate for this place. **That which does not die**: such as the angels, the heavens, primary matter, and human souls. **And that which can die**: such as things made of elements and matter. These are the **splendor**—that is, the effect, seal, impression, and act—of that Idea we mentioned, which our Lord God brings forth and produces **lovingly**, that is, through His own goodness. Therefore, he rightly called the Idea "God," because whatever is in God is God, and the Idea is in God. **For**: because that **living light** (meaning the Wisdom which is the true light and the Word and the Son of God, of whom Saint John says: *He was the true light which illuminates every man coming into this world* <note>original Latin: "Erat lux uera que lluminat omnem hominem uenientem in hunc mundum."</note>). Therefore, this living light, which **flows out** <gloss>that is, centers itself</gloss>...

<summary>This page explains that while Adam and Christ were created perfect by God, Solomon's unique wisdom must be understood through the lens of divine creation. It introduces the Platonic concept of the "Idea" to explain how God's eternal light descends through the heavens to create both immortal beings and temporary, mortal things.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the speech of Saint Thomas Aquinas in the Sphere of the Sun. Having established that Adam and Christ were created directly by God and were thus perfect, Thomas now explains why other created things vary in quality and why Solomon’s "kingly" wisdom remains a distinct type of perfection.</meta>

# CANTO XIII

The wax of these things and that which shapes it
do not always act in the same way, and therefore
under the ideal seal, the light shines through more or less:
From this it follows that the same kind of tree
produces better or worse fruit according to its species,
and you are born with diverse dispositions.
If the wax were perfectly prepared,
and if the heavens were at the height of their power,
the light of the seal would appear in its fullness.
But nature always provides it in a diminished state,
working much like the artist
who has the skill of his craft but a hand that trembles.

But if the warm Love disposes and imprints
the clear vision of the First Power,
then all perfection is acquired there.
Thus was the earth once made worthy
of the full perfection of a living being;
thus was the Virgin made pregnant.
So that I commend your opinion:
that human nature never was,
nor shall be, what it was in those two persons. <note>The "two persons" are Adam (created from "the earth") and Christ (born of the Virgin).</note>

<column-break/>

**proceeds:** because *meare* in Latin signifies to proceed or pass through. <note>original: "meare ilatino"</note> **Thus:** in such a way from its shining source, from its Father, that it does not "un-unite"—that is, it does not depart from the unity of the Father’s substance—nor from the Love: that is, from the Holy Spirit, who **In-threes himself:** <note>original: "Sintrea"</note> that is, He is the third person within them, in the Father who is the first person and the Son who is the second. And the substance of all three persons is one: one nature and one divinity. **By His Goodness:** by His own benevolence and for no other cause. Hence Boethius says:
> Whom no external causes impelled to fashion the work of flowing matter, but the innate form of the highest good, lacking in envy. <note>original: "Quem non externe pepulentur fingere cauſe. Materie fluitantis opus uerum inſita ſumi forma boni liuore carens." — From Boethius's *Consolation of Philosophy*.</note>

**AS ONE:** it congregates. **His radiance:** his operation of the **informative power**; <note>term: "informative power" — in Scholastic philosophy, the capacity of a higher cause to give "form" or essence to matter.</note> because God is the form of forms and the cause of causes. **Which, mirrored in nine subsisting names:** <note>original: "noue chori dangioli"</note> that is, in the nine choirs of angels. The comparison is that just as the sun striking mirrors reflects in them, so the divine value reflects in all things created by Him. **From there:** from the nine heavens and from their movers, the informative power descends into the heavens—which are form and incorruptible matter—and from there into things that are corruptible form and matter. And first, the informative power descends by means of the mover of the first order into the **Primum Mobile**; <note>term: "Primum Mobile" — the "First Moved" sphere, the outermost of the physical heavens in the Ptolemaic system.</note> and into the second heaven by means of the second mover, and so on through the others. But the Primum Mobile also infuses its united power into the second heaven, and the latter divides it among all its stars through the power infused by its mover. And each star of the eighth heaven infuses its power into the planets and into things disposed by the power given to the planets by their movers. Thus one infuses into the other, until it descends into things lower than the heaven of the moon—that is, the elements. And this is what is meant by **to the final powers.** **FROM ACT TO ACT:** from heaven to heaven, because each is active and operates its power infused from above; and the informative power descends from body to body until it produces nothing more than **brief contingencies:** that is, things that last but a short time. And these "contingencies" are generated things: either with seed, like animals born of mating, or without mating, like those born of decay. **THE HEAVENS MOVING:** that is, by the motion of the heavens. The heavens receive from above and infuse into what is below; and if they did not move, they would not spread their influence except in one fixed place.

The argument of Saint Thomas is to demonstrate where the diversity in produced things arises. The principles and formal causes—that is, the informative ones—produce the form which, coming from the **Idea**, <note>term: "Idea" — the eternal blueprints in the mind of God.</note> shines in them according to how the "patient" (the receiver) is disposed to receive it, and how the heavens are disposed to influence it. But they themselves are not always disposed in the same way to influence, nor is matter always disposed to receive. And therefore, diversity occurs among individuals. **The wax of these things:** the matter of individuals which are disposed to receive the impression of the heavens, which is the form infused by the ideal form. **AND WHO LEADS IT:** that is, the heavens themselves. And therefore **under the ideal seal:** that is, the influence that proceeds from the Idea. **MORE AND LESS shines through:** From which it happens that in one and the same species of tree, one is better than the other; and similarly in the human species, one man comes forth more perfect than another. But if the matter that is to receive and the heaven that is to influence were without imperfection, that which is born would be perfect. Just as when the wax and the seal are both well-disposed, the imprint comes out perfect. For example, if Jupiter, who is to give the power, were in Pisces or in its exaltation, and were in a good aspect with good planets and free from "captives," <note>original: "libero da captiui" — an astrological term referring to planets not being hindered by unfavorable positions.</note> then the thing would be excellent and the power of Jupiter would appear perfect in it. But **nature**, which is the power of the heavens, **gives it diminished:** that is, with lack and lessening, and not as it is received from the movers. Just like the craftsman who has the **habit of art**—that is, he possesses it perfectly—but the instruments with which he works are imperfect.

He concludes from the things already said: that if God works on matter immediately, without the mediation of any other secondary cause, the generated thing comes forth perfect. **THEREFORE:** that is, for which reason. **IF THE WARM LOVE:** that is, if the divine goodness disposes and imprints—because first it disposes nature to receive, and then imprints the form upon it. **THE CLEAR VISION of the first power:** that is, the clear light of God. **THERE:** in that thing thus generated, as were Adam and Christ, **all perfection is acquired.** And thus the other [the earth] from which God fashioned Adam was made worthy of all...

It concludes that only direct divine intervention, as seen in Adam and Christ, results in absolute perfection.</summary>
