# PARADISO

...the perfection that can occur in a living being. And **THUS WAS** the Virgin made pregnant: that is, the incarnation of the Word. <note>The "Word" refers to Christ, the Logos.</note> And for this reason, I commend your opinion as true: that human nature never was, nor shall be, as perfect as in those two. <note>Referring to Adam and Christ, as established on the previous page.</note>

---

Now if I did not proceed any further,
"how then was this man without a peer?"
your words would surely demand.
But so that what is hidden may appear,
consider who he was and the cause that moved him,
when it was said to him: "Ask," to make his request. <note>This refers to 1 Kings 3:5, where God tells the young King Solomon, "Ask what I shall give thee."</note>
I have not spoken so that you could not
clearly see that he was a king who asked for wisdom,
so that he might be a sufficient king.
It was not to know the number of
the celestial motors up here, or if a necessary premise
with a contingent one ever produced a necessary conclusion. <note>These are technical questions of medieval physics (the number of angels moving the spheres) and Aristotelian logic (the rules of the syllogism).</note>
Not if it must be granted that a first motion exists, <note>original: "Non si est dare primum motum esse"</note>
or if in a semicircle one can make
a triangle that does not have a right angle. <note>A reference to Thales's Theorem in geometry; a triangle inscribed in a semicircle must have a right angle.</note>

->Whether in a semicircle a triangle can be made that does not have a right angle. Which cannot be done.<-

---

Wherefore, if you note what I said and this:
"kingly prudence" is that peerless vision
at which the arrow of my intention strikes.
And if you turn your clear eyes to the word "was,"
you will see it has respect only
to kings, who are many, while the good ones are rare.
With this distinction, take my word;
and thus it can stand with what you believe
of the first father and of our Beloved. <note>The "first father" is Adam, and the "Beloved" is Christ.</note>
And let this always be as lead upon your feet,
to make you move slowly, like a weary man,
toward both the "yes" and the "no" that you do not see.
For he is very low among the fools
who affirms or denies without distinction,
in one case as in the other.
Because it happens that many times
current opinion leans toward the false side,
and then passion binds the intellect.
Far more than in vain does one leave the shore,
since he does not return the same as he set out,
who fishes for the truth without the necessary art.
And of this there are open proofs in the world:
Parmenides, Melissus, Bryson, and many others,
who went along and did not know where.
So were Sabellius and Arius and those fools
who were like swords unto the Scriptures
in rendering straight faces distorted. <note>Refers to heretics who twisted the meaning of the Bible.</note>

<column-break/>

**IF** I DID NOT proceed further, your words would be convincing in saying "how then was this man without a peer?" But so that what is hidden may appear: consider who this man was and the cause that moved him to ask for prudence when he was told by God, "Ask." And by your own words, I have shown you that it was Solomon, who in a dream asked God for wisdom so that he might rightly govern the people. Therefore, the cause that moved him to ask for wisdom was for the public utility, and not for the vainglory of knowing; unlike those who seek to know how many are the separate substances that move the heavens—which Aristotle says are not as many as the heavens—or if a necessary premise with a contingent one makes a necessary conclusion, as is sought in logic <note>original: "dialectica"</note>: that is, whether the major premise is necessary and the minor is contingent. **NOT** if it must be granted that a first motion exists: <note>original: "Non si est dare primum motum esse"</note> that is, whether the first motion is or is not. Aristotle posited that motion is eternal. Christian theologians, however, posit a beginning to motion and the world. Nor did he ask for wisdom to know if in a semicircle one can make a triangle that does not have a right angle. Which cannot be done.

**In these** verses, he declares how one can reconcile the belief of Dante and the saying of Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>. For while it is most true that the extreme perfection of human nature was in Christ and in Adam, nonetheless, when it is said that Solomon had no peer, it is not meant absolutely among all men, but among kings who governed peoples, among whom are neither Christ nor Adam. And therefore, he comforts the poet not to affirm or deny without the proper distinction. Thus, it is true that no man was equal to Christ and to Adam; and it is also true that no king was similar to Solomon. I would place here the words that Solomon wrote of himself, if I did not fear being too prolix. **BECAUSE** it happens. He shows the reason why he is a fool who affirms or denies without distinction, saying that because most of the time it happens that "current opinion"—because it does not stop for distinction—leans toward the false side; and then passion—for as Democritus says, the love we place in a false judgment binds and occupies the intellect in such a way that it cannot see the truth. **FAR MORE** than in vain: the meaning is this—we can say that a person is "at the shore" when they have not yet thought whether a thing is true or not. But when they begin to investigate, then they "leave the shore" and enter the river. Therefore, just as the fisherman, if he leaves the shore and does not have the art of fishing nor the proper tools, leaves in vain because he catches nothing: so he who sets out to investigate the truth without logic <note>original: "dialectica"</note> and philosophy and without the sciences that can show it to him, toils in vain. But it is even worse, because besides losing his labor, he enters into error where he was not before. Thus, he is worse off than the fisherman, because by not catching anything, he...

<summary>Thomas Aquinas clarifies that Solomon's "peerless" wisdom refers specifically to "kingly prudence" for governance, rather than absolute human perfection or abstract academic knowledge. He warns Dante against making hasty judgments without logical distinctions, citing failed philosophers and heretics as cautionary examples.</summary>

### CANTO XIII

...not such as it set out. But this man returns in a worse state because he holds a false opinion which he did not have before. Of this, manifest proof appears in the ancient philosophers who, struggling without finding the truth, held false opinions, such as Melissus. <note>Melissus of Samos (5th century BCE) was a philosopher who argued that the universe was infinite and unchangeable.</note> He was from the island of Samos and took on the familiarity of Heraclitus the Ephesian, <note>Heraclitus was a pre-Socratic philosopher known for his doctrine of change being central to the universe.</note> and highly commended him to his citizens, who did not recognize his virtue. He held the opinion that this universe was infinite, immutable, and immobile, and that motion did not exist, but only appeared to. He said that we should not define anything concerning God, because we have no certain knowledge of Him. Parmenides <note>Parmenides of Elea was another influential pre-Socratic philosopher who argued that reality is a single, unchanging substance.</note> was a disciple of Xenophanes, and according to Theophrastus, a disciple of Anaximander. He was the first who proposed that the earth is round and placed in the center, and that the elements are two: Fire and Earth; and that one was the craftsman <note>The "artificer" or active principle.</note> and the other the matter. He wrote that the generation of humans had its beginning from the sun, and that the sun is both hot and cold, and from it all things come. Plato, in his book of ideas, named a character Parmenides after him. Sabellius <note>Sabellius (3rd century CE) was a priest and theologian who taught "Sabellianism," the heretical view that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not distinct persons but merely different "modes" of one God.</note>—just as those philosophers erred regarding the first principles, so many theologians held false opinions in Christian theology and were heretics. **THESE** were like swords to the scriptures: A most excellent comparison. For true and well-learned theologians are like mirrors, because they open the scriptures in such a way that in their books one sees the straight and true sense of them, just as in a mirror one sees the true and straight face. But heretics are like swords, because just as one who looks at himself in a sword sees his face distorted, so he who looks into the books of heretics sees the sense of the scriptures distorted.

> Let not people be yet too certain
> in judging, like the one who values
> the grain in the field before it is ripe;
> For I have seen, all the winter through,
> the briar appear rigid and fierce,
> then later carry the rose upon its tip.
> And I once saw a ship, straight and swift,
> run across the sea for its entire journey,
> and perish at last at the entrance of the harbor.
> Let not Lady Bertha and Master Martin believe, <note>Dante uses "Donna Berta and Ser Martino" as generic names for common folk who presume to know the secrets of divine judgment.</note>
> seeing one steal and the other make an offering,
> that they see them within the divine counsel;
> For one can rise, and the other can fall.

<column-break/>

**A** golden precept is given in this place by Saint Thomas: that one should not rush to judgment, because human judgment is often deceived. And he gives three examples. First, of the grain, which, being beautiful while still green, causes those who are not slow in judging to judge that it will produce much fruit, and often the opposite occurs. Similarly, winter shows the briar to be rough, yet in the spring the rose is born there. And a ship sometimes runs its course with the wind at its back and then breaks at the port. And therefore he concludes that Lady Bertha and Master Martin—that is, simple people—want to judge men by their exterior acts; let them not judge that he who makes an offering is saved and he who steals is damned, because he who steals can correct himself and rise from sin, and he who makes an offering can fall into sin.

### CANTO XIV OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE

From the center to the rim and from the rim to the center
the water moves in a round vessel,
depending on whether it is struck from without or within.
Into my mind there fell suddenly
this thought of which I speak, as soon as
the glorious life of **Thomas** became silent,
Because of the similarity that arose
between his speech and that of **Beatrice**,
whom it pleased to begin after him:
"This man has a need, though he does not tell you,
neither with his voice nor yet in his thoughts,
to go to the root of another truth."

As those who are overcome and drawn by greater joy,
at times, those who dance in a circle
raise their voices and gladden their gestures;
So, at that prompt and devoted prayer,
the holy circles showed new joy
in their turning and in their wondrous melody.
Whoever laments that we must die here
to live up there, has not seen in that place
the refreshment of the eternal rain.
That One and Two and Three who ever lives,
and ever reigns in Three and Two and One,
uncircumscribed, circumscribing all,
Was sung three times by each of them.

<column-break/>

In this fourteenth canto, a doubt is raised which is then clarified by the author: he finds himself ascended to the fifth heaven, which is **Mars**. Therefore, first Beatrice raises the doubt. Then it is resolved. In the third part, he describes the ascent to the star of Mars. In the fourth, he describes which spirits are in that place. But regarding the beginning of the chapter, Beatrice raises a doubt on behalf of the author, which was not yet in his thoughts. In short, she wishes that through the alternating and reciprocal speeches—made now by Beatrice and now by the spirits—his mind should move from the center where Beatrice was to the circumference where the two circles <note>The "crowns" or circles of wise spirits.</note> were, and again from that circumference return to the center. Just as in a round vessel, the water moves from the circle—that is, from the circumference—when the vessel is struck from the outside, and such motion goes toward the center; and if the water is struck from within, the motion is born from the center—that is, from the middle—and goes toward the circumference. Water is a continuous liquid body, so when one part of it is moved, that motion moves the adjacent part, and that the next, until the final part. "This thought of which I speak" fell suddenly; that is, it occurred suddenly in my mind as soon as the life of Thomas—that is, Thomas who is in the true life—became silent, because of the similarity that arose from his speaking and that of Beatrice. For while Thomas spoke, my mind moved from the circle to the center, and now as Beatrice speaks, it moves from the center to the circle. Nor is it without cause that Beatrice, rather than Dante, raises this doubt. For many doubts arise in the minds of teachers while reading the holy scriptures, which they resolve by the power of the Holy Spirit or through other passages of scripture. Nor could the poet have had this doubt if he had not first read in the Holy Scripture about the splendor in which the glorified bodies must be wrapped, through which they shall rise brighter than the sun. Therefore, Beatrice—that is, **Sacred Scripture**—is the one who introduces the doubt of how the physical eye will be able to endure such splendor without being dazzled, so that if one is present, the other cannot be known. And it is fitting that this doubt concerning excessive light be raised in this heaven, where he has found more excessive light than elsewhere. "This man has a need": that is, a necessity. "And does not tell you": because he does not yet recognize it. Tell him, therefore, first if the light that **enfleurs** <note>Original: *infiora*, meaning to bloom or adorn with flowers; here used to mean "to illuminate" or "clothe in beauty."</note>—that is, illustrates and illuminates—**your substance**—your soul, which is the substance of that splendor—**will remain in you** when you have reassumed your bodies and become visible. Will the splendor remain in you just as it is at present? And if it remains, tell him how it can be that such splendor does not harm you or prevent you from seeing one another.

To demonstrate the joy of those spirits at the words of Beatrice, he says that just as those who "dance in a circle"—that is, perform a round dance—are always happy, nevertheless "at times"—that is, occasionally—by raising their voice and gladdening their gestures, they show greater joy; so the souls of the two circles, always joyful, at the words of Beatrice show more joy in their "turning"—that is, in moving in a circle—and in the marvelous melody of their song. And certainly, those who grieve over physical death in this world, after which they go to heaven, do so because they have not seen the "refreshment of the eternal rain"—that is, the refreshment of the abundant grace of God—which "is able" there—that is, is widely scattered. Then follows that the two circles sang this hymn three times so sweetly that such a song would be a "just reward"—that is, a fair compensation—to...

<summary>Dante ascends to the Heaven of Mars, where Beatrice asks the spirits to resolve a doubt: how will their resurrected bodies endure the intense divine light? The text uses the metaphor of ripples in a water basin to describe the flow of thought between the center and the surrounding circles of souls.</summary>

# CANTO XIV

...of these spirits with such melody
that to every merit it would be a just reward. <note>original: "munio," meaning a gift or remuneration</note>

And I heard in the most divine <note>original: "dia," a poetic contraction of "divina"</note> voice
of the inner circle a modest voice,
perhaps such as was the angel’s to Mary,
Answering: "As long as the feast
of paradise shall last, so long our love
shall radiate around us such a garment.
Its brightness shall follow the heat,
the heat the vision, and that [vision] as much
as it has of grace above its own worth.
When the glorious and holy flesh
is clothed again, our person
shall be more pleasing by being whole,
Because that which the Supreme Father gives us
of his gratuitous light will increase—
the light that enables us to see him.

Thus the vision must increase,
the heat must increase which is kindled by it,
the radiance must increase which comes from it.
But just as a coal that gives off flame
and through its living white-heat surpasses it,
so that its own appearance is maintained,
So this splendor which already encircles us
shall be overcome in appearance by the flesh
which the earth covers even now;
Nor will such light be able to tire us,
for the organs of the body will be strong
for all that can delight us."
So sudden and alert seemed to me
both one and the other choir to say "Amen!"
that they clearly showed desire for their dead bodies—
Perhaps not only for themselves, but for their mothers,
for their fathers, and for the others who were dear
before they became eternal flames.

<column-break/>

...every merit that man could acquire in this
world; this was a hymn in praise of the Trinity.
This one God who is one in essence and two because
He has in Himself the divine and human nature <note>Referring to the Incarnation of Christ within the Godhead</note> and three—i.e.,
Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—who are one God in essence, but three persons. Who always lives and
does not "live" <note>An interpretive note on the nature of eternal existence versus mortal life</note> because He is one God and no more. And the poet uses the present tense because eternity has no distinction either
of the past or of the future, but is always present: **NOT CIRCUMSCRIBED**, i.e., not contained because
He is infinite and is not included in anything. **AND CIRCUMSCRIBES ALL**: because every created thing
He contains within Himself.

After the hymn, the poet heard a voice more divine,
that is, godly: which came from a spirit of the
inner circle where the most excellent doctors were,
and therefore he feigns that it was more divine: which was as
modest as perhaps was the voice of Gabriel when
he announced to Mary: The poet feigns that this voice
was from the Master of the Sentences <note>Peter Lombard, a 12th-century theologian, though most modern commentators identify this speaker as Solomon</note>: because in truth here
he solves this doubt in the form that the Master of the
Sentences solves it in his fourth book. Therefore he
leads him to say thus: As long as the feast,
that is, the glory of paradise, which shall always last, so much
our love, which is the cause of the splendor,
**SHALL RADIATE**, that is, shall shine around such a garment, i.e.,
around our body. Therefore it will always radiate;
its brightness shall follow the heat. Inasmuch as our splendor
shall be as great as our charity. And the
heat shall follow the vision. Inasmuch as we know
God, so much shall we love: and as much as we love,
so much shall we shine. And the vision of God: that is, to
know God, shall be as much as the soul shall have of grace from
God above its own worth. And it follows that when after the judgment the blessed souls shall have taken back the body which
shall be glorified, their person will be more pleasing for being whole: And being then we more perfect
by being the soul united with the body, we shall see more perfectly: Therefore shall increase in us that which the
Supreme Good, i.e., God, **GIVES US, OF GRATUITOUS LIGHT**, i.e., of intellect which He gives us through His most
benign grace. And this light **CONDITIONS US**, i.e., it conditions us, that is, it makes us apt to see:
i.e., to know Him.

He concludes through the things already said that it is necessary
that the vision increase, i.e., the light of the intellect;
and the vision increasing, the heat shall increase, i.e., the
charity which is kindled by the vision: and similarly
the radiance shall increase, i.e., the splendor, because it is born from the
heat of charity. **BUT JUST AS A COAL**:
An excellent comparison which shows that just as
we see coals in the fire so vividly kindled that although they are surrounded by the flame,
nevertheless their white-heat advances so much beyond that of the
flame that they do not lose their appearance, i.e., they appear and
are seen. So your bodies which after death
are covered by the earth, but after the great judgment
must return to us because they will be glorified,
will have more of a splendor than this which at
present encloses these spirits. Wherefore the evangelist
Matthew [says]: <note>original: "Fulgebunt iusti ut sol in regno patris eorum"</note> "The righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their father."
And Augustine says that the splendor of the glorified body
is according to the natural color of the human body.
And just as the colored body receives splendor in
different ways from the illumination of the sun, according
to the manner of its color, so it is in the power of the
glorified man that his body may be seen and not be seen.

E.iiii

<summary>In this passage, a spirit (identified here as Peter Lombard, but traditionally Solomon) explains how the souls in Heaven will regain their physical bodies at the Resurrection. He uses the metaphor of a glowing coal to explain how the physical body will remain visible even within the intense light of the soul's glory.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Paradiso, Canto XIV. Following the discussion of the "Amen" sung by the spirits, the text now explores the theological implications of the resurrection and the transition from the Sun (the fourth heaven) to Mars (the fifth heaven).</meta>

# XIV PARADISO

<margin>nn.3</margin>
<meta>catchword: And to the [Et al]</meta>

And in this way Christ appeared after the resurrection. Therefore, their flesh shall rise again at the age of thirty years. Whence Solomon: *Thy youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s.* <note>original: "Renouabitur ut aquila iuuentus tua"</note> **NOR WILL IT BE ABLE**: He resolves the doubt raised above and demonstrates that although the human sight by its nature cannot endure such splendor because of the weakness of the organ, nevertheless, in the beatified body the sense of sight will be so strengthened that it will be able to endure any great light without being exhausted by it. **SO MUCH it seemed to me**: The Master of Sentences <note>Peter Lombard, a 12th-century theologian whose "Sentences" was the standard textbook of divinity</note> had already concluded how great the splendor of the beatified bodies would be and how much the power of vision in them would become stronger and more robust. For this reason, all the spirits of the two crowns were so swift to say to me "Amen," which means "so be it," that they clearly demonstrated a very great desire and longing to take back their dead bodies—that is, the same bodies they had left on earth after death. And they did not only desire to take back their bodies for their own glory, but because they are full of charity, they desired it for the glory of their mothers and fathers and other relatives and friends whom they loved in life. And before they rose to this fourth heaven where they are eternal flames: the desire to take back the flesh is innate in us because, man being produced as a composition of soul and body, he has in himself a natural desire to preserve both. Furthermore, it is noted here that the blessed souls retain love and honest friendship even after the separation from the body.

And behold, around us, a glow of equal brightness
was born, above what was already there,
like a horizon that is clearing.
And just as at the fall of early evening,
new appearances begin throughout the sky,
so that the sight seems and does not seem real,
It seemed to me that new substances
began to be seen, forming a circle
outside the other two circumferences.
O true sparkling of the Holy Spirit!
How sudden and glowing it became
before my eyes, which, overcome, could not endure it.

But Beatrice showed herself to me
so beautiful and smiling, that it must be left
among those sights that do not follow the memory.
From this, my eyes regained the strength
to raise themselves again, and I saw myself translated,
alone with my lady, into a higher salvation.
I well perceived that I was raised higher
by the fiery smile of the star,
which seemed to me redder than usual.
With all my heart, and with that speech
which is one in all, I made a holocaust to God,
such as was fitting for this new grace.

<column-break/>

**H**e demonstrates that beyond the two circles of the aforementioned spirits, there came a third circle which was equal in clarity to the splendor that was there before from the other two, like the likeness of a horizon that clears. The souls of this third circle were not very well known to the poet, which he feigns to demonstrate that they were not as excellent as those of the first two circles. And therefore he says that: just as in the time between day and night the stars begin to appear—but they are still seen so little that they seem and do not seem to be there—so these souls appeared to me, which made a circle outside the two circles already mentioned. **O TRUE SPARKLING**: This is an exclamation that shows he marvels at such splendor. Therefore, "O true sparkling of the Holy Spirit" <note>original: "sancto spiro: idest del sancto spirito"</note>; how it became suddenly "glowing" <note>original: "candente"</note>, that is, resplendent, informs you that my eyes, because they were corporeal, could not endure such great splendor. And he feigns this either to demonstrate that these were doctors who wrote subtly and with obscurity, or because they were not known to him.

**H**e begins to describe his ascent to the fifth heaven, which is Mars. He recognized this by seeing Beatrice more shining than usual. And the beauty and joy increased so much in Beatrice that the poet cannot express it; and for this reason, he leaves it among those sights that do not follow the mind—that is, they do not follow but rather abandon the mind when it wants to describe them. "From this": that is, from that splendor of Beatrice, my eyes took strength and vigor so that I raised them up, and having raised them, I perceived that I had risen alone with my lady—that is, I alone with Beatrice—because the spirits of the three circles had remained in the fourth heaven. And it is certain that his eyes, that is, his intellect, took strength from Beatrice—that is, from theological doctrine—to rise to the fifth heaven. **TO A HIGHER SALVATION**: because every heaven is salvation and glory for the spirits, he calls the heaven of Mars a "higher salvation" because it is higher than the others he has spoken of; or truly "higher salvation" because it is closer to God, who is our salvation. For it cannot be said that Mars is a greater "salvation" than the Sun. And he says that he perceived he was raised higher than when he was in the Sun, because he recognized he was in Mars by its fiery color. And he wants to demonstrate the elevation of this planet because its lowest distance, which is the highest of the Sun, is 3,965,000 miles. <note>original: "tremila uolte mille et nouecento sexantacinque migliaia di miglia"</note> And the highest is 28,847,000 miles. <note>original: "uentocto uolte mille mille et ottocento quaranta septe migliaia di miglia"</note> The diameter of the body of Mars is as large as the diameter of the Earth plus a sixth part more. Mars, for its fiery color, is called *Pyroi* <note>original: "pyroi"</note> by the Greeks because *pyr* <note>original: "pyr"</note> means fire. But the proper name in that language is *Ares*. <note>original: "ares"</note> And to the...

<summary>This page describes the appearance of a third circle of spirits in the Heaven of the Sun and Dante's subsequent ascent to the Heaven of Mars, marked by Beatrice's increasing beauty and the planet's distinct red color. The commentary explains the physical resurrection of the body at the "perfect age" of thirty and provides medieval astronomical measurements for the distance of Mars.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Paradiso, Canto XIV (mislabeled as Canto XIII in the original header). Having discussed the transition to the fifth heaven, the text now details the nature of the planet Mars and the vision of the Cross formed by blessed spirits.</meta>

# CANTO XIII 
<note>Although the header reads Canto XIII, the content continues the commentary on Canto XIV of the Paradiso.</note>

Some called this star Hercules. The pagans worshipped Mars as the god of wars because it is a hot and dry planet, masculine and nocturnal. It induces anger and fire. It induces animosity, audacity, and a desire for vengeance. For this reason, it has a greater power to heat than any other planet. It makes men long and thin of body due to its heat and dryness; but in old age, because the heat consumes and the dryness shrivels, it makes them curved and bent. It makes minds mobile, light, and prone to anger. Its houses are Aries and Scorpio. It reigns in Capricorn. When it is well-disposed at a man’s birth, it influences him with excellent virtue in military discipline. This fact led the poet to represent in this heaven the spirits of those who, through honest and virtuous battles, merited beatitude. **WITH ALL THE HEART**: He demonstrates here that he could not rise to this contemplation through his own power of wit, but through the grace of God, which is acquired through prayer made in the "common tongue" to all—that is, made with the mind. And this prayer is the sacrifice called a <term>holocaust</term><note>A "whole-burnt offering." From the Greek "holos" (whole) and "kaustos" (burnt).</note>. A holocaust was that sacrifice which the ancients burned entirely in honor of God; so named because in Greek *olon* <note>original: "olon"</note> means "whole" and *causton* <note>original: "causton"</note> means "burnt." It denotes, therefore, through this, that he became a flame entirely of most ardent charity; and this sacrifice was appropriate for this new grace.

---

And the heat of the sacrifice was not yet
exhausted from my breast when I knew
the solitary state was accepted and auspicious
For with such brightness and such redness
splendors appeared to me within two rays
that I said, "O Helios, who so adorns them!"
As, distinct with lesser and greater
lights, the Milky Way whitens between 
the world's poles, so that it makes even the wise doubt,
So constellation-like, those rays made
the venerable sign in the deep Mars
that the joining of quadrants makes in a circle.

<column-break/>

**Not yet exhausted**: that is, emptied from my breast (that is, from my mind) was the heat of the sacrifice (that is, the ardent fervor) which issued in my mental prayer, when I recognized the "solitary state"—that is, the spirits of those holy fathers who in solitude and in the deserts had continually fought against the devil, such as Paul the First Hermit, Anthony, and the like. This state was accepted by God and was "fausto" (that is, happy) then. Because the author places in this sphere all those who have fought for the faith, he divides this entire sphere with two lines which make a cross and four quarters. **WHICH WITH such brightness**: He posits that in the body of Mars there were two most lucid rays (that is, two strips) which made a cross that divided the whole body of the planet into four squares. These strips were full of splendors so "robbi" (that is, so red) that they were blessed spirits, so that I, out of wonder, said: "O Helios" (that is, O God), as if wanting to say, "how great is your goodness." **WHO SO adorns them** (that is, who so beautifies them). *Helios* in Hebrew means "exalted" and is one of the names of God <note>Landino likely conflates the Greek "Helios" (Sun) with the Hebrew "Eli" or "Elyon" (Most High).</note>. "Addobbare" in the French language means to adorn. **AS distinct**: like the "milky circle" which by the Greeks is called the <term>Galaxy</term><note>From the Greek "gala," meaning milk.</note>, which begins from the parallel of the Arctic pole and reaches the parallel of the Antarctic pole; it is distinct and adorned with many stars, large and small. So those two strips in the depth of the body of Mars—"constellated" (that is, distinct with stars that were blessed souls)—made that venerable sign of the cross which "makes the joining of quadrants in a circle," because placing a cross in a circle creates four squares.

---

Because in this planet he places, as has been said, those who have fought for the salvation of souls, he describes how in that cross appeared the Passion of Christ, which defeated the adversary of human nature. This appeared to him such a marvelous thing that although he remembered it later when he was writing, nonetheless his wit was not sufficient to find an example with which to express what he had in his memory...

---

Here my memory defeats my wit,
for in that cross Christ was flashing,
so that I cannot find a worthy example;
But he who takes up his cross and follows Christ
will yet excuse me for what I leave out,
seeing Christ lightning in that dawn.
From horn to horn and from the top to the base,
lights moved, sparkling intensely
as they joined together and as they passed by.

<column-break/>

...of the flashing of the Passion of Christ; and therefore "memory defeats wit." Some texts have: "Here my memory conquers my wit," and this is easy to understand. **BUT HE WHO takes his cross**: I cannot express what I saw of the victory that Christ achieved against our adversary on the cross. But he who "takes up his cross"—that is, he who applies himself to such a battle as much as his strength allows—and "follows Christ" (that is, imitates the footsteps of Christ as much as he can), this person, because after death he will arrive in this planet and will see that it is impossible with human tongue to express such a victory, will excuse me for not having written it, considering that in such a dawn Christ "flashes" (that is, the divinity of Christ shone), which no mortal can imitate. **FROM HORN to horn**: the lights (that is, the spirits) ran from one "horn" of the cross to the other (that is, from right to left) and from the head to the feet. And because when they joined together or passed each other they "sparkled," this encounter revealed their mutual charity.

<sig>E.ij</sig>

<summary>In this commentary on Canto XIV, Landino explains the astrological nature of Mars and Dante's vision of the cross of light formed by the souls of holy warriors, noting that the divine spectacle surpasses the capacity of human language and memory.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Paradiso, Canto XIV. The previous page discussed the nature of the planet Mars and the initial vision of the Cross of light. Here, the text compares the movement of the spirits within that Cross to dust motes in a sunbeam and explains the divine melody Dante hears.</meta>

# PARADISO
<column-break/>

Thus are seen here, straight and crooked,
fast and slow, renewing their appearance,
the particles of bodies, long and short,
Moving through the ray of light that streaks
at times the shadow which, for their protection,
people acquire with wit and art.
And as the viol <note>original: "giga" — a medieval stringed instrument, often called a rebec or fiddle.</note> and harp, with strings stretched in tune,
make a sweet tinkling from many chords
to one by whom the melody is not understood,
So from the lights that appeared there,
there gathered through the cross a melody
which enraptured me without my understanding the hymn.
Well did I perceive that it was of high praise,
because there came to me "Rise" and "Conquer"
as to one who hears but does not understand.
I fell so much in love from that point
that until then there was nothing
that bound me with such sweet bonds.
Perhaps my word seems too daring,
placing second the pleasure of the beautiful eyes <note>A reference to Beatrice's eyes, which represent divine revelation.</note>
in which, gazing, my desire finds rest.
But he who perceives that those living seals
of every beauty become more powerful higher up,
and that I had not yet turned back to them,
Can excuse me for that of which I accuse myself
to excuse me and see that I speak the truth:
for the holy pleasure is not excluded here,
Because it becomes purer as one ascends.

<column-break/>

Those lights move along the streaks of the cross just as we see here in this world the <term>particles</term> <note>original: "minutie"</note> — that is, the smallest parts of bodies which are almost like atoms <note>original: "atomi" — used here in the classical sense of indivisible physical units.</note> (indivisible bodies) — moving in a ray of the sun which makes a streak in the shadow. This occurs in a building that creates shade, which people acquire or build through human wit and art.

The meaning is that the lights moved across the cross just as we see infinite tiny bodies move in a shaft of sunlight entering through a window into a house, among which some move fast, some slow, some straight, and some crooked; and they often "renew their appearance" — that is, their look — because the fast becomes slow and the crooked becomes straight.

And I heard through the cross a sweet melody that enraptured me — that is, it drew me to itself — without my understanding the hymn, because I did not understand the words. And that melody was gathered from the various voices of the spirits, just as we see that either a viol or a harp (which are musical instruments) make a sweet **TINKLING** — that is, a sweet sound of many strings when they are stretched in tune.

And he adds that although he had not understood the words of the hymn, he nevertheless perceived that such a melody contained the highest praise, because among many words he understood only: **RISE** <note>original: "SVRGE"</note> and **Conquer** <note>original: "uinci"</note>. These two words are spoken in Holy Scripture to Christ: "Rise from death and conquer the devil." The author feigns that of the entire hymn the souls sang to Christ, he understood only "Rise" and "Conquer" to demonstrate that it is easy for everyone to understand that the passion and death of Christ was the victory that liberated us from the servitude of the devil. But many other marvelous things appropriate to that place are not understood except by the most learned men.

He demonstrates that although he asserts that in all this mental pilgrimage he has found nothing until this place that binds him with more love, he nevertheless does not contradict what he has already said so many times about Beatrice; nor for this does he place her second in his love.

**AND SEE ME SPEAK THE TRUTH** — that is, one can see that I spoke the truth in saying that no other thing had bound me so much as this melody, because the pleasure of Beatrice is included in that. And through Beatrice <note>original: "p. B."</note> this is understood; and the pleasure I take in Beatrice becomes more sincere and more pure the higher I ascend, because her eyes show me all these things.

<summary>This page describes the spirits in the Heaven of Mars moving like dust motes in a sunbeam and singing a hymn of "Rise and Conquer" to Christ. Dante explains that while this divine melody is the most beautiful thing he has yet experienced, it does not diminish his love for Beatrice, as her beauty only increases as they ascend.</summary>
<keywords>Paradiso, Canto XIV, Mars, Cross of Light, atoms, music, Christ, Rise and Conquer, Beatrice, Landino commentary</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the transition from the general description of the Sphere of Mars to the specific encounter with Dante's ancestor. The previous page concluded with a description of the divine melody and the movement of the spirits within the celestial cross.</meta>

CANTO XV

# CANTO XV OF THE THIRD CANTICLE OF DANTE

Benign will, in which is always
distilled the love that breathes rightly,
as greed does in the iniquitous will,
Placed silence upon that sweet lyre,
and quieted the holy strings
which the right hand of heaven loosens and pulls.
How shall those beings be deaf
to righteous prayers, who, to give me the desire
to pray to them, were in agreement to be silent?
It is well that he should grieve without end
who, for the love of a thing that does not last,
strips himself eternally of that love.

<gloss>The poet describes it like a lyre, and the spirits were like the strings of that lyre; strings which the right hand of heaven loosens and pulls—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit tempers them, pulling the strings that are too loose and loosening those too tight as it pleases Him. Then the poet, seeing that those substances (that is, those spirits) had finished singing only to give him the desire and courage to pray and ask for what he wished to hear, and were in agreement (concordant) to be silent, he asks: "How will they be deaf to righteous prayers?" as if to say, they will never be deaf. And he adds that it is a very just thing that one should grieve without end (that is, eternally) who deprives himself of that perfect love for the love of a thing that does not last (that is, for a temporal thing).</gloss>

<margin>From the infinite spirits that moved through the cross—which the poet calls light and stars—one ran from the right arm of the cross, like certain flames which are often seen moving across the sky when it is clear and pure, appearing like stars moving from place to place. But reason proves they are not stars.</margin>

Just as through the tranquil and pure evenings
a sudden fire flashes from time to time,
moving the eyes that were resting securely,
And seems to be a star changing place,
except that from the part where it is kindled
nothing is lost, and it lasts but a while;
So from the arm that extends to the right,
to the foot of that cross, ran a star
from the constellation that shines there.
Nor did the gem move from its ribbon,
but ran along the radial strip,
appearing like fire behind alabaster.

<gloss>White and bright, named after Alabastron, a place in Egypt not far from Egyptian Thebes, from which the ancients once made vases for ointments because they are best preserved in them. It is clear, diaphanous, and transparent. And I saw in Rome, in the time of Pope Eugenius IV, an alabaster vase in which a candle shone more than in the thinnest lantern. Dante does not enter the cross to speak to Cacciaguida, but Cacciaguida descends to him, which denotes that the poet was not yet of the rank to be at that level.</gloss>

So piteous did the shade of Anchises <note>The father of Aeneas in Virgil's Aeneid.</note> reach out,
if our greatest Muse <note>Virgil, whom Dante considers the greatest poet.</note> merits belief,
when in Elysium he perceived his son.
"O blood of mine! O grace of God
poured from above! Just as to you, to whom..."
<note>original: "O sanguis meus o super infusa gratia dei sicut tibi cui"</note>

<column-break/>

Because in the previous chapter the author demonstrated which spirits are represented in the sphere of Mars, in this fifteenth Canto he introduces Master Cacciaguida, the father of Alighiero and his own great-great-grandfather, who tells him of his genealogy and how justly Florence was ruled in his time, with the finest customs. And in these first verses he tells that the benign will which those spirits had toward the poet—in which will "IS DISTILLED" (that is, manifested) true and honest love, just as in the iniquitous will is manifested greed (that is, dishonest love)—"PLACED SILENCE upon that sweet lyre" (that is, the hymn they were singing). This song had the sweetness of a lyre, meaning a <term>viola</term> <note>original: "uiuola" — Landino uses the term for a bowed string instrument to explain the classical "lyra".</note>. And because he called that song a lyre, he now calls the voices of the spirits "strings." For the entire congregation of those spirits is...

...it is certain that in that part of the sky from which it departs, "nothing is lost," meaning no star is missing there, and that flame lasts only a short time; if it were a star, it would never be extinguished. But they are vapors, of which we have spoken sufficiently above. Therefore a "star" (that is, the spirit of Master Cacciaguida) ran as described, departing from the "constellation" (that is, a configuration of stars which were spirits) "THAT SHINES there" (that is, glows in that place). "NOR DID the gem MOVE FROM its ribbon" (that is, although it moved, it did not leave the border of the cross, which he calls a ribbon). But it ran along the "radial strip" (that is, the path full of rays of the cross). Some understand this to mean he did not leave the right arm where he was, but seemed to descend because a ray came down from him in a straight line to where the poet was; and in its movement, it seemed like a flame enclosed in a vase of alabaster. Alabaster is a species of very white marble...

He describes how the welcome Master Cacciaguida gave to Dante was as piteous as that which Anchises gave to Aeneas in the Elysian Fields. "IF our GREATER MUSE" (that is, if Virgil, who writes this and is the "greater muse," meaning the greatest poet among the Latins) "merits belief." It is as if he says, do not affirm...

<summary>A spirit (Dante's ancestor Cacciaguida) descends from the celestial cross in Mars to greet Dante, moving like a shooting star. The commentary compares this meeting to the classical reunion of Aeneas and Anchises and explains the scientific and musical metaphors used by the poet.</summary>
<keywords>Cacciaguida, Mars, Alabaster, Anchises, Virgil, Divine Love, Shooting Star, Florence, Genealogy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the encounter between Dante and the spirit of his ancestor, Cacciaguida, in the Heaven of Mars. The previous page described the spirit moving toward Dante like a shooting star across the celestial cross.</meta>

# CANTO XV

->"twice, I say, the gate of heaven opened"<-
<note>original: "bis inquam celi ianua reclusa"</note>
Thus that light to which I gave heed;
then I turned my face back to my lady,
and on either side I was struck with wonder;
For within her eyes such a smile was burning
that I thought with mine I had touched the bottom
of my grace and of my paradise.

<columns>2</columns>
"To whom, I say" <note>original: "CVI EIS inquam"</note> the gate of heaven is opened: At present with your body and <insert>twice</insert> this he said of himself: because it harmonizes with what he said: **THUS THAT light**. That is, thus spoke that spirit. I turned to Beatrice and was stupefied—that is, full of the highest admiration. **On either side**. That is, from Cacciaguida because of the words he spoke to me, and from Beatrice because in her eyes a smile burned and shone, in such a way that I thought my eyes **touched the bottom of my grace**. That is, I thought my eyes had arrived at the ultimate end of what we could see of grace and of my paradise—that is, of my glory. The meaning is that the poet, having heard the spirit—who here stands for the words of Holy Scripture—turned to Beatrice, that is, to the exposition of those words. And because until this place he had not yet contemplated any higher thing, he says that Beatrice burned with a greater smile.

<column-break/>

the things fashioned by Virgil: neither that Anchises saw Aeneas in the Elysian Fields, as this poet fashions in the sixth book of the *Aeneid*. But to show that Cacciaguida took as much joy in the arrival of Dante as Virgil describes the joy of Anchises to have been for the arrival of Aeneas. **O MY BLOOD** <note>original: "OSANGUIS meus"</note>: These are the words that Sir Cacciaguida used toward Dante: "O my blood, why have you descended from my seed?" **O GRACE OF GOD POURED FROM ABOVE** <note>original: "O SUP iſuſa gratia dei"</note>: with admiration he says "I say the grace of God poured from above," as if given by extraordinary means. And **the gate of heaven opened** <note>original: "celi ianua recluſa"</note>, to whom certainly twice after death: nor is it arrogance that the poet pronounces above, from where one does not descend without returning. Because I gave heed—that is, I stood attentive to him: and then I <unclear>turned</unclear> that she was still burning.

---

Then, joyful to hear and to see,
the spirit added things to his beginning
which I did not understand, he spoke so deep:
Nor by choice did he hide himself from me,
but by necessity, for his concept
was set above the mark of mortals.
And when the bow of his burning affection
was so vented that his speech descended
toward the mark of our intellect,
The first thing that was understood by me:
"Blessed be Thou, Three and One,
who toward my seed art so courteous!"

<columns>2</columns>
the elements and things composed of them: But those which God created without a medium <note>meaning: created directly by God, rather than through natural processes</note> he cannot understand. He does not understand what God is, nor what light is (which was the first matter), nor what the soul is, nor what the **predestination** of God is; of which no one can give a true account because we are not capable of divine intelligence. And therefore it seems to us that predestination contradicts **free will** <term>libero arbitrio: the theological concept that humans choose their actions despite God's foreknowledge</term>. **NOR BY CHOICE did he hide**: because Cacciaguida did not want Dante to not understand; but the defect of human nature did not let him understand. But **when the bow of burning affection**—that is, when his speech, from which words of burning charity toward God come forth, was vented, praising the divine intelligence in predestination. His speech descended from such high matter **toward the mark**—that is, toward the limit to which our intellect can reach. The first thing I understood was: **BLESSED be thou, Three and One**. That is, you, God, who are one in three persons. It is not understood except by those to whom the highest God reveals the reason of predestination. But any mediocre mind understands that it is a just and reasonable thing that we thank God for the benefits received.

<column-break/>

He follows by saying that the spirit of Cacciaguida added to the beginning—that is, to the things he had said with a beginning **joyful to hear**: and "to hear things that I did not understand, he spoke so deep." In which place, if we consider that the beginning was "O grace of God poured from above," the subsequent part must have been about **predestination**. For having Dante received the grace to be able to ascend with his body from heaven to heaven, someone might doubt: why more to Dante than to another? And it was necessary to dispute regarding predestination and to show that it does not take away free will. And those things are so hidden and deep that our intellect cannot comprehend them; and therefore he fashions that he did not understand it. And certainly the human intellect can comprehend things created by God by means of **secondary causes** <note>Natural laws or physical processes through which God acts in the world</note>, such as...

---

And he followed: "A grateful and long fast,
derived from reading the Greater Volume
where white or brown is never changed,
You have satisfied, my son, within this light
in which I speak to you, thanks to her
who for the high flight clothed you with feathers.
You believe that your thought flows to me..."

<columns>2</columns>
<column-break/>
The meaning is that Cacciaguida followed—that is, continued in his speech saying: "You, O son, you have satisfied"—that is, broken—"a grateful and long fast." To break a fast means to eat. Therefore: "You have fulfilled a long desire of mine that I had to see you, which desire I have drawn from the **Greater Volume** <note>A metaphor for the Mind of God, which contains all events</note> by reading—that is, by looking into God, in whom the blessed, by contemplating, see all things, just as by reading we understand what is in a book; and therefore he calls it contemplation...

<summary>Dante meets his ancestor Cacciaguida, who greets him in Latin and praises God for the grace shown to his descendant. The commentary explains the difficulty of understanding divine mysteries like predestination and the joy of the ancestor seeing Dante's journey reflected in the "Greater Volume" of God's mind.</summary>

# CANTO XV

# XV

from that which is first, as that which radiates
from the one, if one knows the five
And therefore why I behave or why I seem
more joyful to you, you do not ask me
more than any other in this happy crowd.
You believe the truth: that the lesser and the great
of this life gaze into the mirror
in which, before you think, you display your thought.
But so that the sacred love in which I watch
with perpetual vision, and which affects me
with sweet desire, may be better fulfilled,
let your voice, secure, bold, and glad,
sound your will, sound your desire,
to which my answer is already decreed.

thoughts: because I see them in God: you do not ask me who I am, nor why I show more happiness at your coming than the others: And you believe the truth, that I know your thought and your will. Because in this blessed and eternal life all spirits, both of higher and lower rank, gaze into the mirror—that is, the mirror of divinity—in which you "display" <note>original: "pandi"</note>, that is, you manifest your thought before you even think it. But so that the sacred love and most ardent charity, in which I "watch" <note>original: "ueglio"</note>—that is, I stay awake, which means I live; because just as sleeping is like dying, so watching is like living—**AND WHICH AFFECTS ME** <note>original: "ET CHE Ma seta"</note>, that is, increases my thirst and desire for "sweet desire" <note>original: "dolce distare"</note>, meaning charity which always burns in the blessed. **MAY BE BETTER FULFILLED** <note>original: "SADEMPIA MEGLIO"</note>: that is, may it increase more. I wish for your voice, with security, boldness, and joy, **TO SOUND**: that is, let it speak your will and your desire, to which my answer is already "decreed" <note>original: "decreta"</note>, that is, decided.

I turned to Beatrice and she heard
before I spoke, and granted me a sign
that made the wings of my flight grow.
Then I began thus: affection and intellect,
as soon as the first equality appeared to you,
became of one weight for each of you,
Because the Sun that warmed and burned you
with heat and with light is so equal
that all comparisons are meager.
But will and argument in mortals,
for the reason that is manifest to you,
are differently feathered in their wings.
Wherefore I, who am mortal, feel myself in this
inequality, and therefore I give thanks
only with my heart for this paternal welcome.
I do indeed supplicate you, new topaz,
who engems this precious jewel,
to make me satisfied with your name.
"O my leaf, in whom I took delight
while only waiting, I was your root,"
such a beginning he made in answering me.
Then he said to me: "He from whom is called
your kinship, and who for a hundred years and more
has circled the mountain on the first terrace..."

<column-break/>

to read God as the volume: and call it "greater" because in God everything is read, that is, seen. Therefore, my son, you who have satisfied my wish to see you, which was within this light—that is, in my mind—who are in this splendor, which wish proceeded from my having seen in God that you were destined to arrive here almost by **Grace** <note>original: "Merce"</note>—that is, by the favor and benefit of her **WHO clothed your feathers for the high flight** <note>original: "ti uesti le piume allalto uolto"</note>: meaning, by the grace of Beatrice, from whom you received the wings to be able to fly so high. And certainly Theology is that which lends us the wings with which we lift ourselves from this low world to the flight of heaven. **YOU BELIEVE THAT** your thought descends to me from that which flows: *Meare* in Latin means to flow or pass through—from that, meaning from God, who is the principle of every thing, in whom shines every thing made or yet to be made; and all our thoughts, before they exist, shine forth just as the numbers five and six and every number shine from the one, which is the principle of every number. Because five is five times one. And because you believe this—that is, that I know your every thought...

After the words of Cacciaguida, the author turns to Beatrice to understand if she wished him to respond. But she, who already knew his will without him speaking, nodded her head: so that his will became faster. This signifies that in no such contemplation should one proceed except according to Theology, which responds without being asked. But here, let it be granted that the poet imagines Cacciaguida to be in this glory because he died fighting for the faith. **O MY LEAF** <note>original: "OFRONDA Mia"</note>: Cacciaguida calls the poet his leaf, not only because he is descended from him, but also because he is an ornament to that family, like the leaf to the tree. **In whom I took delight while only waiting**: that is, from whom I have taken the highest pleasure <note>original: "uoluptate"</note> merely by expecting you. As if to say, before your birth, I gloried in heaven that you were to be born of my blood, and I awaited you with delight. **THEN** <note>original: "POSCIA"</note>: after these words he said to me: he from whom your kinship is named—that is, after whom your family is called—who had the name **Alighieri** <note>original: "aleghieri"</note>; and thus this family was called, from which we say **Dante Alighieri**. He was my son and your **great-grandfather** <note>original: "bifauo"</note>—that is, the father of the father of your father, who in Latin is called *proauo*. He has circled for more than a hundred years the first terrace of the mountain of Purgatory, in which place, as shown in the ninth canto of the second canticle, pride is purged. **IT IS WELL SUITED**: As if to say, it is very much your duty that you shorten and abbreviate the long labor and suffering he endures in purging himself, with your works—that is, with prayers, alms, and similar things.

<summary>Cacciaguida explains how spirits in Heaven see human thoughts through God, the "Mirror of Divinity," and identifies himself as the "root" to Dante's "leaf." He reveals that Dante's great-grandfather, the first Alighiero, has been suffering in the Terrace of Pride in Purgatory for over a century and needs Dante's prayers.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Canto XV of the Paradiso. In the preceding verses, Cacciaguida—Dante’s great-great-grandfather—revealed his identity and the lineage of the Alighieri family. He now begins a nostalgic contrast between the virtuous, modest Florence of his own time (the 12th century) and the decadent, extravagant city of Dante’s time (the early 14th century).</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>PARADISO</header>

"He was my son and was your great-grandfather;
it is truly fitting that you should shorten
his long labor with your own good works.
Florence, within the ancient circle of her walls,
from which she still takes both her Third and Nones,
abided then in peace, sober and modest.
She had no small chains, no crowns,
no embroidered gowns, no girdles
that were more to be looked at than the person.
The birth of a daughter did not yet strike
fear into a father, for the time and the dowry
did not yet flee the measure on either side.
She had no houses emptied of families;
Sardanapalus had not yet arrived
to show what can be done within a chamber.
Monte Malo had not yet been surpassed
by your Uccellatoio, which, as it has surpassed it
in its rising, so shall it in its fall."

<column-break/>

And here he demonstrates how much we are bound to help our relatives: not only the living, but also the dead. Our poet, because in the *Inferno* and in the *Purgatorio* he has many times reproached our citizens, wishes now to show us that such vices have been more a product of the times than of the nature of our republic. Anyone who considers this rightly, without the passion of love or hate, will find that our republic is inferior to no other Italian republic in terms of the excellence of its minds, its best institutions, or its good customs. Therefore, having so often reproached his own times, he praises the ancient way of living in Florence. **FLORENCE** <note>original: "FIRENZE"</note> within the ancient circle: It seems very difficult to me to be able to report on the many and various opinions regarding not only the first building of the city but also its restoration. But one can clearly see how small a space the first circle of walls contained, not only because the remains of the first walls still appear in many places, but also because the San Piero gate, the Red gate, and the Santa Maria gate <note>These are names of original city gates: Porta San Piero, Porta Rossa, and Porta Santa Maria.</note> bear witness that what remains of the city outside of those was added later. **SHE HAD NO** <note>original: "NON HAuea"</note> small chain: There was not yet such luxury and superfluity in clothing and in the adornment of women as in the times of the

---

poet, in which they wore around their necks and sleeves small chains of gilded silver buttons strung together. And crowns, and garlands made of gilded silver foliage, and adorned with precious stones and pearls. **ADORNED FOOTWEAR** <term>contigie: a type of decorative footwear or buskins</term>: they called these "soled stockings" covered with perforated leather. Nor did they marry at such a young age, or with such a large dowry <note>A "dote" or dowry was the wealth a bride brought to a marriage.</note> that the father had fear of being able to marry them off. And nevertheless, in the times of Dante (in which he complains of the large dowries), the largest were four hundred or up to five hundred florins <note>The gold florin was the currency of Florence.</note>, which number at present is not enough for the shoemaker or the blacksmith. **SHE HAD NO** <note>original: "NON HAuea"</note> houses emptied of families: because there were no civil dissensions, through which one party drives out the other and the houses remain empty. Sardanapalus had not yet reached Florence—that is, an extreme luxury did not yet reign there, which would seek to understand "what can be done in a chamber." Sardanapalus was the thirtieth and also the last king of the Assyrians <note>A legendary figure representing extreme decadence and effeminacy.</note>, a man most dedicated to every kind of unbridled pleasure. He stayed shut up among his concubines, dressed and adorned like a woman, and like a woman, he wore makeup; nor would he let himself be seen by anyone. This so delightful and idle life gave hope to Arbaces, captain of the Persians and Medes who served in the king's guard, that he could take the kingdom from him. And he conspired with Belesys, who was also a captain of the Babylonians in that service. And because Belesys was learned in astrology, he willingly undertook the enterprise, because the stars promised him certain victory, though not without laborious hardships and bloody battles. They were thus twice broken by the king's armies, but finally they besieged him. Therefore, despairing of his safety, Sardanapalus ordered a very great fire, and in it he burned himself, his dearest friends, all his concubines, and his most precious things. He made an epitaph for his tomb to this effect: "Only that has been mine which I have eaten and drunk and consumed in love." **NOT YET WAS** <note>original: "NON ERA"</note> Monte Malo surpassed: He who goes to Rome by the road from Viterbo does not see it until he arrives at Monte Malo <note>Now known as Monte Mario.</note> near the city; but having reached this mountain, he sees all the Roman buildings. And similarly, he who comes to Florence by the Bolognese road does not see it until he first arrives at the Uccellatoio <note>A hill north of Florence.</note>, which mountain is five miles from Florence on the way to Bologna. But having arrived there, he sees not only the buildings of the city but also those of the villas near the city. And because the poet wishes to rebuke the superfluous building done by the Florentine people in his times, and to praise the ancient parsimony, he says that the Uccellatoio—from where one sees the Florentine buildings—had not yet surpassed Monte Malo, from where one sees the Roman buildings. This in short signifies that in the time of Cacciaguida, there was not the luxury in building that there was in the time of Dante. And then, wishing to predict the ruin of the republic, he adds: that just as the Uccellatoio in its rising (that is, in Florentine prosperity) surpassed Monte Malo because the Uccellatoio can show more Florentine buildings than that one can show Roman ones, so it will surpass it in the "fall" (that is, in the ruin). From the Uccellatoio, a greater ruin of Florence will be seen than was seen of Rome from Monte Malo. Many in this place believe the author predicts the ruin of the city of Florence that was to be born from pride and ambition, and from the factions and partiality of the Guelfs and Ghibellines <note>The two main opposing political factions in medieval Italy.</note>.

<summary>Cacciaguida describes the modest and peaceful Florence of the 12th century, contrasting its simple clothing and social stability with the excessive luxury, high dowries, and political instability of Dante's era.</summary>
<keywords>Cacciaguida, Florence walls, modesty, women's dress, Sardanapalus, Monte Malo, Uccellatoio, Guelfs and Ghibellines, urban luxury</keywords>

<header>CANTO XV</header>

I saw Bellincion Berti go girt
with leather and bone, and his lady
come from her mirror without a painted face.
And I saw those of Nerli and those of Vecchio
be content with uncovered skin,
and their ladies at the spindle and the spool.
O fortunate women! each one was certain
of her burial place, and as yet none
was deserted in her bed because of France.
One kept watch tending the cradle,
and to comfort her child used the language
that first delights fathers and mothers.
The other, drawing the thread from the distaff,
would tell stories to her family
of the Trojans, of Fiesole, and of Rome.

A Cianghella or a Lapo Salterello
would have been held as great a marvel then
as Cincinnatus and Cornelia would be now.
To such a restful, to such a beautiful
life of citizens, to such a faithful
citizenry, in such a sweet dwelling:
Mary gave me, called upon with loud cries,
and in your ancient Baptistery
I became at once a Christian and Cacciaguida.
Moronto was my father, and Eliseo;
my wife came to me from the Po Valley,
and from there your surname was derived.

<column-break/>

Truly in those times there was supreme temperance, parsimony, and sobriety among our people. Consider that Bellincion Berti was a rich <term>knight</term> <note>original: "caualiere"</note> born of the noble lineage of the Ravignani, yet he wore no other belt than one of leather with a bone buckle. And his lady used no cosmetics or dyes. The houses of these knights were located at the gate of San Piero. But through the inheritance of Gualdrada, his daughter, who was the wife of the first Count Guido, they passed to the Counts Guidi. **THOSE OF THE VECCHIO** <note>original: "QUE DEL VECCHIO"</note>: We shall speak of these in the following chapter. **WITH UNCOVERED SKIN** <note>original: "Alla pelle scoperta"</note>: This is because they wore garments of tanned leather without fur, such as chamois and the like. And **the women at the spindle and the spool**: this refers to their dedication to feminine labor. **O FORTUNATE** <note>original: "O FORTUNATE"</note>: O happy women! This passage is drawn from Juvenal: <note>original: "Prestabant castas humilis fortuna latinas Quondam nec uitiis cotigi parua sinebat tecta labor somnique breues et uellere tusco uexate dureque manus: Et proximus urbi Hanibal." — "In the old days, humble fortune kept Latin women chaste, and their small homes were kept from vice by labor, short sleep, and hands hardened by Tuscan wool, even when Hannibal was near the city."</note>. **And each was certain of her burial place**: because there were no civil wars to make them fear dying in exile. **And as yet none was deserted in her bed**: meaning abandoned by a husband traveling to France. The greed for wealth had not yet grown so great that Florentine merchants would leave for France or other regions to seek profit. **ONE WATCHED** <note>original: "LVNA VEGGHIAVA"</note> **tending the cradle**: that is, caring for her small child; and to comfort that child she used the **language**—the "baby talk" used to soothe a crying infant—which is the first thing that brings joy to fathers and mothers. For the first pleasure a parent takes in a child who cannot yet speak is this. **THE OTHER** <note>original: "LALTRA"</note> **drawing from the distaff**: intent on spinning, she told old stories so that the family would stay awake and focused on their work.

In such modesty and sobriety, and among such excellent customs, it seemed no less a marvel to see a man or woman of wicked habits then, than it would seem in these current wicked times to see someone of excellent virtue, such as Cincinnatus or Cornelia. **Cianghella**, according to a disciple of Giovanni Boccaccio, belonged to the Tosa family, a very noble house. She married into the Alidosi family of Imola. She was a very lewd, proud, and hot-tempered woman; once, when she attended a sermon and no one rose to honor her, she began pulling the hair of the other women, causing such a laugh and a riot that the preaching had to stop. As a young widow, she returned to Florence and lived a life of shamelessness with many lovers. **Lapo Salterello** was a very litigious and slanderous lawyer, and a great enemy of our poet. **Cincinnatus** was discussed previously in the sixth chapter of this book. **CORNELIA** <note>original: "CORNIGla"</note>: her proper name is Cornelia, but the rhyme forced the poet to write "Corniglia." She was the daughter of Scipio Africanus and wife of Tiberius Gracchus, a woman of supreme honesty and masculine spirit. It is told that when two snakes were found in her house, the omens said that if the male was killed, the husband would die, and if the female was killed, the wife would die. Her husband Tiberius, valuing her life more than his own for the sake of the family, ordered the male snake killed. She was highly educated and trained her sons, Gaius and Tiberius, to be great orators. She remained a widow for many years, so famous for her virtue that kings sought her hand. Thus, Cacciaguida was born in the time of such a well-ordered republic. He says that the Virgin **Mary**, called upon for help by his mother during the pains of labor (as is the custom of Christian women), gave him life. He was born into the restful and beautiful life of the Florentine citizens, in a **faithful citizenry**—faithful because it was not yet split by discord—and in a **sweet dwelling**, meaning his fatherland. "Dwelling" <note>original: "hostello"</note> is properly...

<summary>Cacciaguida describes the virtuous, hardworking domestic life of 12th-century Florence, contrasting it with the scandalous behavior of contemporary figures like Cianghella. He then recounts his own birth and the origins of the Alighieri surname.</summary>

<header>XV PARADISO</header>

...signifies hostelry. And because we do not have a permanent city in this life, but are on a journey, I therefore call our homeland a "hostel." **AND IN** your ancient baptistery: in the temple of Saint John: which was built from the beginning with the city and dedicated to Mars <note>Ancient Florentine tradition held that the Baptistery was originally a Roman temple dedicated to the god of war.</note>: later in the time of the Christians it was dedicated to John the Baptist, <note>original: ". i . baptezatore"</note> that is, the baptizer; and in it the baptistery was made, <note>original: ". i . el fonte del baptiſmo"</note> that is, the baptismal font in which he was baptized and at once became a Christian through baptism; and he was named Cacciaguida because such a name was given to him at his baptism. My brothers were Moronto and Eliseo: but of his progeny we spoke in the life of the poet. My lady came to me from the Po Valley <note>original: "ualdipado"</note>. They say that his wife was of the Alighieri of Ferrara: and from her this family, which was first called Elisei, was named Alighieri.

*Then I followed the Emperor Conrad*
*and he girded me with his knighthood,*
*so much by good deeds did I please him.*
*Behind him I went against the wickedness*
*of that people whose folk usurp*
*our justice, through the fault of the shepherds.*
*There was I by that foul people*
*disentangled from the deceitful world,*
*the love of which defiles many souls;*
*and I came from martyrdom to this peace.*

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'Q' in blue ink with intricate white scrolling and geometric patterns inside.</image-desc>
**THESE** things concern Conrad, under whom Cacciaguida served as a soldier: this was Conrad I <note>The commentator identifies him as Conrad I (r. 1024–1039), though modern scholars believe Dante referred to Conrad III (r. 1138–1152).</note> in the year of the Lord one thousand and fifteen. This fits well because the poet writes this in the year one thousand three hundred. And it is likely that from his great-great-grandfather to this time two hundred and eighty-five years had passed. Nor is it against the art of poetry for the poet to have Cacciaguida praise himself: because it is not out of arrogance, or any kind of pride or vainglory—which vices cannot exist in those who are already confirmed in grace—but rather to simply narrate the truth, which is an excellent example to all men: that they should not refuse

<column-break/>

death for the defense of the Christian faith: understanding that he, immediately after such a death, remained so purified that without any stay in Purgatory he ascended to heaven. For which reason let our people stand ready: and especially in these times let them have an unconquered soul, ready for every grave danger against the <term>Agarenissimi</term> <note>A term for Muslims, referring to the biblical Hagar; here specifically referencing the Ottoman Turks.</note> Turks, who—<note>original: "quod nunquam ueriti ſumus"</note> which we never feared—are now in Italy; for in such a brief space of time one can acquire the celestial and holy kingdom. **TO THIS** peace: <note>original: "ideſt al ſommo bene"</note> that is, to the highest good: which, as we demonstrated above, is located in celestial peace. But regarding the highest good and the various opinions of the ancients, we treated this distinctly in the second book of our *Camaldolese Disputations and Allegories* <note>The commentator is Cristoforo Landino, referencing his own philosophical work, the "Disputationes Camaldulenses" (c. 1472).</note>. This place does not require that we treat it at present, because it requires more exquisite diligence.

The commentator emphasizes that Cacciaguida's self-praise is a virtuous example of martyrdom and calls for contemporary Christians to defend Italy against the Turks.</summary>
