<page-num>320</page-num>
<header>CANTO XVI</header>

# CANTO XVI OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE

**W**isely at the beginning of this sixteenth chapter: the poet rebukes those who take vainglory in the antiquity of blood as if it were great nobility. Then he leads Cacciaguida to describe the entire origin of his house. And after such a description, he narrates the state that existed in that age in our republic <note>Referring to the Republic of Florence.</note>. And at the end, he names many Florentine families.

**O** our small nobility of blood,
if you make the people glory in you
down here where our affection languishes,
it will never be a marvelous thing to me;
for there, where appetite does not warp,
I mean in Heaven, I myself gloried in it.
Truly you are a cloak that soon shortens,
so that if one does not add to it day by day,
time goes around it with its shears.

After that "You" <note>original: "uoi"</note> which Rome first suffered,
in which her family least persevered,
my words began again;
And Beatrice, who stood a little apart,
smiling, appeared like she who coughed
at the first fault written of Guinevere.
I began: "You are my father;
you give me such boldness to speak;
you lift me up so that I am more than myself."
By so many streams is my mind filled
with gladness, that it makes a joy of itself,
because it can endure it without bursting.
Tell me then, my dear origin,
who were your ancestors, and what were the years
that were marked in your boyhood;
tell me of the sheepfold of Saint John <note>A poetic name for Florence, referring to its patron saint, John the Baptist.</note>,
how large it was then, and who were the people
within it worthy of the highest seats.

<column-break/>

**O OUR SMALL NOBILITY OF BLOOD:** The poet uses a fitting exclamation, demonstrating that the nobility which consists in the antiquity of blood is truly "small." But nonetheless, it is no wonder if here among mortals, where our affection "languishes" and is infirm—that is, where disturbances and appetite, being discordant with reason, are infirm and not upright—the people glory in it, since he himself, being in Heaven where appetite does not warp (because it is direct and does not depart from reason), gloried in it. True nobility is the virtue of the soul. But civil nobility, according to Aristotle <note>Landino references Aristotle’s *Politics*, where nobility is often defined as "ancient wealth and virtue."</note>, is antiquity of blood. And it seems he wishes to express that even men placed in the highest contemplation cannot help but take vainglory in the antiquity of blood. **SMALL:** Because it rarely happens that a family maintains itself for a long time in name without virtue, or can acquire honors or dignity and riches without it; thus it happens that such a family is esteemed noble. But because in truth virtue alone is that which makes a man noble, and it often happens that men through wicked and vicious ways acquire riches, dignity, and lordships, it follows that they cannot be called noble for this reason; hence he said "small." Nonetheless, when such things have been acquired through virtue, it is to be tolerated if someone, though wise, glories in such antiquity. **TRULY YOU ARE A CLOAK:** An excellent comparison. For the glory of the virtues of the first ancestor, although it extends to his descendants, nonetheless, if they do not continually maintain it with their own virtues, time consumes it, just as a garment is consumed bit by bit when trimmed with shears. As, for example <note>original: "uerbi gratia"</note>, it is reasonable that from some of the men who were once in great fame, descendants remain; but because virtue was not maintained in such succession, they are not recognized. And in brief, their fame passes away.

**A**fter the exclamation made about nobility, the poet turns his words to Cacciaguida to ask him more fully about his family and other noble Florentine families. And he says that his words "began again." That is, he began again with his words using "You" <note>Dante uses the formal/plural *Voi* to address his ancestor as a sign of extreme respect, rather than the singular *Tu* used for most other souls.</note>; for at the beginning of his speech, he said, "You are my father." Therefore, he began to say "You" to him, whereas previously he had said "Thou" to him, as appears above when he said: "I truly pray to you, living topaz, who gems this precious jewel, that you make me satisfied with your name." And because the incorrect speech of saying "You" to a single person as if they were more than one—he says that the beginning of saying "You" to one was suffered and permitted by Rome when Caesar was made perpetual dictator. Because having included all other magistrates under his power, when a man spoke to him, it seemed he spoke to many. And therefore one did not say, "I pray to you [singular], Caesar," but "I pray to you [plural], Caesar." And therefore the poet says "from that 'You' which was said to one, which you, Rome, were the first to suffer," using such flatteries to Caesar, and in which "You" her family—that is, the Roman citizens—least persevered. For from that time until now, almost all nations and peoples say "You" to one, except for the Romans who say "Thou" to every man. This seems to be the meaning of the poet. And thus the commentators explain it, and they bring into testimony these verses from the fifth book of Lucan: "For all those titles by which for so long a time we lie to our masters, this age first discovered." <note>original: "Nanque omnes uoces per quas iam tempore tanto Mentimur dominis haec primu repperit etas" — Lucan, *Pharsalia*, V.385-6. Landino uses this to explain the historical origin of the formal plural 'you'.</note>

<summary>Dante reflects on the vanity of ancestral nobility, comparing it to a cloak that shrinks over time if not renewed by virtue. He addresses Cacciaguida with the formal 'Voi,' prompting a historical digression on the Roman origins of this respectful address.</summary>

<header>PARADISO CANTO XVI</header>

Returning then to the text, I begin by saying: You, Cacciaguida, and Beatrice—though she was somewhat obscured <note>i.e., standing slightly apart</note>—separated by her laughter, she gave him a sign that she saw and heard, and as if comforting him in his speaking. "To sever" <note>original: "Sceuerare"</note> is a word derived from "to discern" <note>original: "secernerre"</note>. And the author places Beatrice here, separated from them, to show that this dialogue was not about theological matters; nevertheless, these matters were not forbidden by theology but permitted, because they were moral matters which theology accepts and approves. And he uses a simile that her smile was the same sign given to Guinevere during her first fault—the cough when she came to the kiss by means of Galeotto <note>Galeotto was the intermediary between Lancelot and Queen Guinevere in the Arthurian romances; a reference to the same story told by Francesca in Inferno V.</note>. And her companion, who saw them although she was not seen, coughed to show she had noticed them, as is written at length in the fabled and not very elegant book of the Round Table. **YOU** are my father: because not only he who generates us is our father, but every superior from whom we are descended. **YOU** give me such boldness in speaking: because, being of your seed, I take such confidence. **I AM MORE THAN MYSELF**: because you give me more than human strength. And the joy comes into me from you through so many streams—that is, from so many parts—that my mind makes a gladness of itself because it is like a fountain of joy. And because this mind makes a gladness of itself, it can resist so that it does not burst. **TELL ME THEN**: he asks to know three things: who were his ancestors; in what time he was born; how large Florence was then; and which were the most worthy families. And he calls Florence the "sheepfold of Saint John" <note>original: "ouile di sancto Iohanni"</note>. Since Saint John is the patron of the Florentine people, Florence is his sheepfold.

As a coal kindles by the blowing of winds
into flame, so I saw that light
shine at my blandishments;
And as it became more beautiful to my eyes,
so with a voice more sweet and soft,
but not with this modern speech,
He said to me: "From that day when 'Ave' was said
to the birth in which my mother, who is now a saint,
was lightened of me, with whom she had been heavy,
To the burning Lion, five hundred, fifty,
and thirty times did this fire come
to re-kindle itself beneath its paw.
My ancestors and I were born in the place
where the last ward is first found
by him who runs in your annual games.
Suffice it to say this of my elders:
who they were and from whence they came there,
it is more honest to be silent than to speak."

<column-break/>

**H**e became more radiant: and with a softer voice Cacciaguida replied: that from the day of the Incarnation of Christ until his birth, Mars—in which planet they found themselves—had returned to the Lion, where it was when he was born, five hundred and eighty times. The Lion is the domicile of the Sun, and the Sun enters it on the fourteenth of July. And because Mars does not return to any sign in less than two years, it follows that one thousand, one hundred and sixty years had passed <note>Cacciaguida calculates his birth year (c. 1091 AD) by the orbits of the planet Mars.</note>. This demonstrates three things: the years of Christ in which he was born, in which sign Mars was, and that his mother is saved <note>meaning she is in Heaven</note>. And it follows by saying that he was born in the place where those who run the "yearly yoke"—which is the horse race <note>original: "palio"</note> of Saint John—find the last ward <note>original: "sexto," referring to the six administrative divisions or 'sesti' of Florence.</note>. And because those who run come from the western part of the city toward the east, the last ward they find is the ward of Porta San Piero, which is to the east. This ward began at Porta San Piero, which was where the Canto de' Pazzi is at present, and it came into the Old Market <note>original: "mercato uecchio"</note>; and it joined with the ward of San Brancazio <note>San Pancrazio</note> which is to the west, and with the ward of the Duomo or rather San Lorenzo which is to the north. From the Old Market to the Arno toward the south, two wards remain: San Piero, which radiates from the east, and Porta Santa Maria from the west. And the last ward was Oltrarno. Therefore, as Cacciaguida’s ancestors were born in that place in Florence where the race of Saint John first finds the last ward of those through which it runs, we understand this to be in the Old Market and on the borders of the ward of Porta San Piero. **IT SUFFICES** of my relatives: either our poet did not know a more ancient origin for his family than Cacciaguida, or he knew it was ignoble and lowly, and therefore he has the spirit say that "this suffices."

---

**H**e continues in the narration and shows that the men Florence produced to bear arms were a fifth part of what they are now, in the times when Florence was "between Mars and the Baptist"—that is, she had begun to leave the pagan faith, in which they had the temple of Mars, and take up the Christian faith, in which they consecrated said temple to

All those who at that time were there
fit to bear arms, between Mars and the Baptist,
were one-fifth of those who are living;
But the citizenry, which is now mixed
with Campi, with Certaldo, and with Figline,
was seen pure down to the lowliest artisan.
Oh, how much better it would be to be neighbors...

<column-break/>

Saint John the Baptist—compared to those who were in the time of the poet. Then he laments that from Campi (a castle near Prato), from Figline (a castle in the upper Valdarno), and from Certaldo (a castle in the Val d'Elsa), peasants have come and become citizens; so that the citizenry, which was previously pure down to the lowliest artisan—because all were Florentines down to the last craftsman—is now mixed. This has been a great ruin to the city; it would have been better if the aforementioned lands had not been made part of the territory of Florence, because this is...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Paradiso, Canto XVI. Having established the nobility of his lineage through Cacciaguida, Dante now hears a lament for the "pure" Florence of old. Cacciaguida contrasts the ancient, smaller city with the modern city of Dante's time, which has been corrupted by the influx of families from the surrounding countryside (the "contado") and the decline of imperial authority.</meta>

<columns>2</columns>
<header>CANTO XVI</header>

**Column 1**

> That those people whom I mention, and at Galluzzo
> and at Trespiano, had your borders
> than to have them inside, enduring the stench
> of the peasant of Aguglione, and of him from Signa,
> who already has a sharp eye for fraud.

<gloss>Sharp eye for fraud <note>original: "Barattare ha locchio aguzo"</note>—that is, to commit acts of barratry <term>barratry: the buying or selling of office or legal favors</term>.</gloss>

> If the people who most degenerate in the world
> had not been a stepmother to Caesar,
> but like a mother, kind to her son:
> many a one who became a Florentine, and trades and deals,
> would have turned back to Semifonte,
> where his grandfather went about begging.
> Montemurlo would still belong to the Counts;
> the Cerchi would still be in the parish of Acone;
> and perhaps the Buondelmonti would still be in Valdigrieve.
> Always the mixing of people
> was the beginning of the city's ills,
> as added food is to your body.
> and a blind bull falls more headlong
> than a blind lamb; and many times one sword
> cuts more and better than five.

...sects in the republics, and especially in ours: which, emptying itself through the exile of many, has made such a man a citizen and merchant who would otherwise have turned back to Semifonte <note>a fortified village in the Val d'Elsa</note>: which castle, captured with great effort by the Florentines, was destroyed in 1202. **MONTEMURLO WOULD BE**: this castle is not far from Prato, and belonged to the Counts Guidi. This would still belong to the Counts because the Emperor would have forbidden injuries between the Florentines and the Counts, and everyone would have stayed within their own limits. And the Cerchi—of whom we spoke in the *Inferno*—if there had been no wars, they would have remained in the parish of Acone, which is above the bridge at Sieve. The Buondelmonti were noblemen in Valdigrieve; they possessed Montebuoni and other castles which, after a long siege, they gave to the Florentines on the condition that they become Florentine citizens. **ALWAYS THE CONFUSION**: He demonstrates that mixing diverse men into a republic—because they are of different natures and customs—generates confusion, just as different foods do in the stomach. For someone might say that through such mixing the Florentine people became more robust; he responds that this is the cause of its ruin, and demonstrates it by the comparison of the bull and the lamb. For the bull, by its fury, does not know how to stop itself, and spinning around, it falls. But the lamb, which is peaceful and mild, lies down, and therefore does not fall. Thus great cities, because of their great power, grow proud, and through great pride they trouble others, whereby they often fall into ruin. But small ones, because they do not fight others, last longer. And understand the same regarding the swords.

> If you look at Luni and Urbisaglia,
> how they have gone, and how they are going
> after them, Chiusi and Sinigaglia,
> to hear how families undo themselves
> will not seem a new or strange thing to you,
> since even cities have an end.
> All your things have their death,
> even if you hide it in some
> that last a long time, for your lives are short.
> And as the turning of the lunar heaven
> covers and uncovers the shores without rest,
> so Fortune does to Florence.
> Therefore it should not seem a wonderful thing,
> what I shall say of the great Florentines
> whose fame is hidden by time.

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

...the reason they were able to become citizens. But rather, the countryside should not have extended further than Galluzzo and Trespiano. If that had been the case, the peasant of Aguglione—who was Messer Baldo d'Aguglione—and the one from Signa—who was Messer Bonifacio da Signa—would not have become citizens; these men committed much barratry, selling favors and benefits; and therefore he says that already [they have a sharp eye].

**D**eferring to the great discord that existed between the Church and the Emperor, from which sects of Guelphs and Ghibellines were born in Italy: this was the reason that as cities were emptied by the exile of the banished, they were filled with peasants. And such a mixture of men—part ancient, part new—because they are of diverse wills and customs, generates disturbance in the city, just as a variety of foods does in the stomach. **IF THE PEOPLE OF THE WORLD**: that is, if the Apostolic Church, which has most degenerated <note>original: "tralignata"</note> and fallen away from its first authors, **HAD NOT BEEN A STEPMOTHER**: that is, a stepmother to Caesar <note>original: "Cesare"</note>—that is, to the Emperor. The meaning is: if the Church, whose head is the Pope—which Church ought to be a pious mother to all—had not become a stepmother instead of a mother: that is, unjust and cruel as stepmothers are toward stepchildren, to Caesar, the Emperor. But if she had been kind as a mother, the discords between the Church and the Empire would not have been born. And if those had not been born, [the factions] would not have been born.

**B**ecause the poet had asked which were the noble families in his time, and Cacciaguida had to narrate many that by Dante's time had almost vanished: therefore he shows that it is not to be wondered at if families fail with time, since even cities fail. He proves this by **LUNI**, a city at the end of Tuscany beside the mouth of the Magra. **URBISAGLIA**: This city was in the March of Ancona, not far from Macerata. **CHIUSI**, a city between Siena and Perugia: where King Porsena once reigned, made noble by the admirable labyrinth which Pliny <note>original: "Plinio"</note> describes in the book of *Natural History*. **SINIGAGLIA** is between Ancona and Fano on the shore of the Adriatic Sea: which in our [days is diminished].

<summary>Cacciaguida laments the expansion of Florence's borders and the influx of corrupt rural families, blaming the conflict between the Papacy and the Empire for the city's decline. He illustrates the inevitable decay of all human things by pointing to the ruins of once-great cities like Luni and Urbisaglia.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary by Cristoforo Landino on Canto XVI of Dante’s Paradiso. Having discussed the decline of noble families, the text now transitions into a philosophical reflection on the transience of human works, the influence of celestial bodies (specifically the moon) on earthly affairs, and a detailed historical reconstruction of the ancient walls and gates of Florence.</meta>

<header>PARADISO</header>

Sigismondo Malatesta <note>Sigismondo Pandolfo Malatesta (1417–1468), Lord of Rimini, a famous condottiero and patron of the arts</note> attempted to restore [the work]: but the war waged against him by the holy supreme pontiff <note>Pope Pius II, who excommunicated Sigismondo</note> interrupted the labor. Your things—that is, the things of mortals—all possess death, because they are all born and composed of the four elements <note>Earth, air, fire, and water</note>, and every born thing dies if it comes through the means of secondary causes; and every composed thing dissolves. But because some things endure for a long time, such as certain cities, they appear immortal to many: because the life of a man is so brief that he cannot see their end. Therefore, returning to the subject, just as we see the sea in many places covering and uncovering the shores according to the motion of the moon: so does the fortune of Florence. For in this republic, the state does not remain fixed in those same people: but fortune pushes it now to this family, now withdraws it to itself and sends it to another. 

But since the motion of the moon is mentioned, it is not useless to know that although every planet induces its effects on lower things, nevertheless the sun and the moon lead more effectively for three reasons. Of these, the first is the quantity of light, which is greater in these than in the others. The second is the place where they are positioned. For the sun is in the middle of the planets, like the heart in the middle of an animal, and it supplies strength to every part. The moon, because it is closer to lower things and for this reason is more similar to their nature, influences them more effectively. This governs the moisture of bodies, whereby it nourishes metals, plants, and the limbs of animals. The third is that the moon, because it is contrary to the earth and water, moves all things in which earth and water predominate. 

But it should be noted that the seas have different motions. For some never swell, such as the Pisan and Genoese sea <note>The Tyrrhenian and Ligurian seas</note>. Some swell from the new moon until the fifteenth day, and for the rest, they decrease. Some increase twice every day and decrease twice, such as the Persian Gulf, the Indian Sea, and all the islands between them; and that which is between Constantinople and Venice; and between England, Flanders, and Germany. They increase, therefore, when the moon rises from the east until the middle of the sky, and it returns until it descends from the middle of the sky to the west; and from the west it increases again until it reaches the middle of the sky below; and again it decreases until it reaches our east. And each of these intervals is six hours. The cause of these motions are two equal circles that make four arcs. For the circle of the horizon makes the first arc in the east and the second in the west. And the meridian circle makes the first arc in the middle of the sky, which is our zenith, and the second in the opposite part under the earth. Therefore, when the moon touches the arcs of the horizon, it moves the sea to increase; when it touches the arcs of the meridian, it makes it decrease. 

Having spoken of the moon, now because the poet mentions both the first circuit of Florence and also many ancient families, it will not be useless, nor will it be unpleasing to the listener, to relate in brief words the ancient boundaries of both the first and second circles <note>The successive sets of defensive walls built as Florence grew</note>, and similarly the ancient families. And although the matter is very old, nevertheless so many vestiges still remain that for one who searches with great diligence, it is not very difficult to find the truth. And in this part, we easily agree with Ricordano Malispini <note>Landino writes "Perdano," likely a transcription error for Ricordano Malispini, a 13th-century chronicler</note>, a writer of a chronicle, a man who, if not learned and eloquent, was at least very faithful and diligent, and who in all things strives to provide evidence. He lived in the year 1200 of our salvation. 

The first walls, then, were where the remains of Capaccio still stand—as if <gloss>head of waters <note>original: "caput aquarum"</note></gloss>—because there the waters of the aqueducts fell; and from there they came to where Vacchereccia was later, as far as the houses of the Ormanni, today called Foraboschi. And from there toward San Martino, encircling the houses of the Uberti and the Ormanni; and from San Martino as far as where the tower of Santa Reparata is; and from there passing near the place where the Loggia degli Adimari was later, it reached the tavern of Frascato; and then it turned toward the corner of Ferravecchi, encircling part of the space where the Arrigucci and Santa Maria in Campidoglio were later; and from that corner where San Piero Buonconsiglio is, it returned to Capaccio through the piazza of San Miniato among the towers. 

Within this city were sixty-two towers inhabited by noblemen, who, as many affirm, were largely Romans. One gate was in Capaccio, one at the Ormanni, the third was at San Martino, the fourth at Ferravecchi. These were the four principal gates. Besides these, four postern gates <term>postern: a secondary door or gate, usually in a fortification</term>. The Malispini lived at the piazza of Santa Cecilia, then called the piazza of the Malispini. I will not dispute in this place whether Florence, as we have described it, was destroyed by Totila <note>Totila (died 552), King of the Ostrogoths; Landino spells it "Totile"</note> or not, because I will leave such inquiry to those who have more accurately researched the chronicles of those times. 

But I certainly affirm that Florence was, a long time afterward, rebuilt or restored larger than before by Charlemagne <note>original: "Carlo magno"</note>, whether it had been destroyed before or, if it had not been destroyed, it was expanded with the second circle. I truly believe, based on many conjectures and various chronicles I have read, not that Florence was destroyed by Totila, but that through continuous wars both with the people of Fiesole and various barbarian nations, it was largely desolated, because the most powerful citizens had retreated into the surrounding castles and fortresses where they lived more securely. 

But then coming to the year 802, Charlemagne, returning from Rome to France having already been elected Emperor, stopped at Florence and enlarged it. And he brought the nobles of the city back within the walls, who had previously been scattered in various places. And the circuit of the walls, beginning from the eastern part, was then where the houses of Messer Bellincion Berti Ravignati were; and there was the San Piero gate, and a suburb as far as San Pier Maggiore. Then the walls followed toward San Giovanni and the Bishopric; and there was the second gate called the Cathedral Gate <note>original: "porta di duomo"</note>; and going out from this, one found the San Lorenzo suburb. The walls then proceeded as far as Santa Maria Maggiore and as far as San Pancrazio, where the third gate was, named after the saint, although it remained outside the walls. Then going toward the Arno, similarly leaving Santa Trinita outside, and not far from that temple was a postern called the Red Gate <note>original: "porta rossa"</note>, by which the street is still named today...

It details the boundaries of the "first" and "second" circles of the city's defensive walls, citing the chronicler Ricordano Malispini and the interventions of Charlemagne.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the historical and genealogical commentary on Florence as mentioned in Canto XVI of Dante’s Paradiso. The previous page concluded with a discussion of the moon’s influence on the ebb and flow of fortune and the beginnings of the city’s ancient gates.</meta>

# CANTO XVI

...finished. The fourth was the St. Mary’s Gate. But returning to the first circle <note>the original inner walls of Florence</note>: in which among the first families we find the Alberighi, the Philippi, and the Infangati—three families. But all of them had their origin from a sixth man <note>referring to a shared ancestor or administrative division</note> who was highly regarded in those times. And from Arriguccio came the Arrigucci, patrons and defenders of the Bishopric of Fiesole because they came from there. Constant enmities lasted between the Florentines and the people of Fiesole for about five hundred years. Finally, the Florentines entered Fiesole by stealth; they destroyed it and dismantled everything except the Bishopric. And they brought all the noble families to Florence, among whom were the Pazzi and the Canigiani; hence both families have the moon <note>a crescent symbol</note> in their coats of arms. Furthermore, they unified the insignia of the republics. The coat of arms of the Florentines was a red shield with a lily that was then white; and the coat of arms of Fiesole was a white shield with a blue moon. Therefore, they made a single shield divided lengthwise, white and red, and this remained the insignia of the Florentine people made of two peoples; and such was the standard carried in military service, called the *Carroccio* <note>a ceremonial war wagon used as a rallying point in battle</note>, which today can be seen hanging from the top of our Baptistery. The first magistrates were two consuls who, with a senate of one hundred men, administered the republic. In its second circle of walls, Florence had one hundred and fifty towers, each more than one hundred cubits <note>approx. 150-180 feet</note> high. 

Knights were made by Charlemagne, Conrad, and Otto: Giovanni, Anselmo Figineldi, Arnaldo Fisanti, Schiatta Uberti, Moscardo Lamberti, Ormanno Ormanni, and Tano dell’Arca. These seven families were therefore most noble. Furthermore, he also made knights from these other families, which were: the Galigai, the Alepri, the Della Pressa, and the Buonguisi. But these last three were born from the Galigai, from whom also come the Giugni. The Giuberti were where the Piazza de' Priori <note>now Piazza della Signoria</note> is today. The Ormanni, or rather the Foraboschi, were near Saint Cecilia; and near them were the Malespini; and on the other side toward the Oratory of Saint Michael were the Tebalducci and later the Compiobbesi. And toward Calimala were the Chiaramontesi, the Guadagnuoli, the Malpigli, and the Romaldeghi. Then came the Cavalcanti. There were also the Abati and the Macci; they were neighbors of the Garbo <note>a neighborhood known for wool manufacturing</note> toward Saint Martin. The Galigai, the Giugni, the Buonguisi, those of the Pressa, and the Alepri were all born of the Galigai. Then at the end of the Garbo were the Facchetti. And along the street today called Anguillara were the Schelmi, and in the other street were the Greci, from whom it was later named; but these were first located in the Terme. The Magalotti were not far from the Facchetti; they were toward the Arno, along with the Belculacci and those of the Asino. Behind the Ormanni settled the Manieri and those of the Pera—which families Dante affirms were extinct in his time. Toward Saint Romeo settled the Guidalotti, the Bagnesi, those of the Migliaccio, and those from Cuona, neighbors of those from Volognano and Castiglionchio. The Infangati, or "Eaters of Troughs" <note>a literal translation of 'mangiatroi'</note>, were between the New Market and Saint Cecilia. In Vacchereccia settled the Baroncelli, descended from Baroncello; and having been reduced to a small number, they made a "Casaccia"—that is, they added commoners <note>this refers to 'rifarsi di gente plebea', or diluting noble blood to maintain family numbers</note>. Toward St. Mary’s Gate were the Sifanti, the Galli, the Cappiardi, and the Philippi. Then came the Scolari and the Buondelmonti, who were of one blood; they were lords of Monte Buoni and there they collected tolls. These were in the street that goes into the Terme as far as the Borough of the Holy Apostle. In the Terme were the Giudi and the Importuni. And on the corner of St. Mary’s Gate were the Gualterotti. At Saint Trinita were the Palermini and the Scali; and further toward Santa Maria Maggiore were the Barucci. But all three of these families were of one blood. 

Then came to Saint Apostle the Altoviti, whose origin was Bernardo di Pagolo Altoviti, a man of much industry and natural eloquence, but reported to be descended from Thebalduolo the Lombard, who campaigned under Alboin, King of the Lombards. And after the death of the king, he established his home at Poggio Imperiale. From him are descended the Altoviti, the Corbizi, and the Squarcialupi. The Altoviti spread through the Val d'Arno and were possessors of almost all of it. Later, twelve families were called by the Florentine people and even granted citizenship, among which were the Medici—who many times have held the summit of government in the Florentine republic—and the Altoviti, the Ricci, the Albizzi, the Guasconi, and the Strozzi. But the Medici, the Rucellai, and the Altoviti conspired against the Duke of Athens <note>Walter VI of Brienne, an unpopular ruler expelled in 1343</note>, and at the palace gate, they killed some of his barons and his primary secretary. Then came the Bonciani, descended from Guido the Frenchman, a baron of Charlemagne; and when Charlemagne departed, he remained in Florence. And I have clear evidence of the antiquity of this house: because Neri di Guido Bonciani, a well-learned man of excellent character, has shown me a marriage contracted in that family without a papal dispensation <note>indicating they were exempt or pre-dated certain canonical restrictions</note> between Lottiera and Bartolo, both of the Bonciani, as far back as the year of Christ 1368. In Porta Rossa were the 
<margin>*</margin> Conforti of the Adimari, who built Saint Mary Nipotecosa next to the Lily. Near the Barucci were the Counts of Gangalandi, named so from a man named "Conte" <note>Count</note> who was the founder of such a family, and not because they were actual counts. Near these were the Ciuffagni. Near Saint Trinita were the Soldanieri. Around Saint Miniato among the Towers were the Pigli and the Erri, born of one blood. Among the Old Sawyers are the Manfredi, the Vecchietti, the Miglioreguidi, and the Ughi—from which family the name Montughi was taken. Near the Vecchietti were the Benvenuti. At the end of the street settled the Tornaquinci, who later split into the Tornabuoni, the Giachinotti, and the Popoleschi. Around Saint Peter of Good Counsel were the Cipriani, the Toschi, and the Amieri. Around Saint Mary in Capitolio were the Alfieri, the Arrigucci, the Corbizi, the Brunelleschi, those of the Becchuto, the Agli, and toward the Old Market, the Galluzi. And in the Old Market were the Nerli. But their houses were later occupied by the Amieri. Opposite the Nerli were those of the Tosa, of the lineage of the Visdomini. The Giubaldini were between Saint Thomas and the Bishopric; and near the church of Saint Thomas were the Agolanti. Later the Minerbetti lived opposite Saint Miniato among the Towers where the pawnshop of the Borghese is currently located. And for a long time they held private enmities with the Amieri, a Ghibelline family. And when the Guelphs were exiled, the Amieri burned their houses. Later, the Guelphs having returned with the favor of the Royals of France and the people of Lucca, the Guelph party restored their ruined houses; and on the exterior walls of those houses, as a perpetual memory, they painted the coats of arms of the Party, of France, and of the Minerbetti, which still remain there today.

# XVI PARADISO

Tomaso d’Andrea Minerbetti, a man distinguished in letters and very dutiful, once showed me certain writings. At the Cathedral gate <note>the Porta del Duomo</note> lived the Figiovanni, the Firidolfi, the Figibineldi, the Cattani da Barberino from Mugello, and the Ferrantini. The Visdomini are located toward San Benedetto and the San Piero Gate. Furthermore, the Tebaldini, the Donati, the Ravignani, and the Alberighi. And from Santa Maria, the Giochi and the Stoldi. Toward San Martino were the Bonitii and the Erazzanti, who came from Fiesole. Not far away are the Adimari and the Belisei—the family to which our poet belonged—and the Malefesti. In the Old Market <note>Mercato Vecchio</note> were the ancient Caponsacchi from Fiesole, and from San Andrea, the Catellini, likewise from Fiesole. The Lamberti were at Santa Maria sopra Porto, and the Tebaldi lived in the "Iron Alley" <note>Chiaffo di Ferro</note>, named for their protection. In the New Market <note>Mercato Nuovo</note> were the Giandonati, the Bostichi, and those of the Zannella. Likewise, the Uccellini, allies of the Donati, and those of the Arca, and the Pesci. The Girolami were at the Saint Mary Gate; Saint Zenobius, Bishop of Florence, belonged to their family. Neighboring these were the Amidei and the Gherardini, who considered themselves allies. Then the Pulci; and toward the Abbey <note>the Badia Fiorentina</note>, the Ardinghi and the Ubriachi; and at the Red Gate <note>Porta Rossa</note>, those of the Forese and the Monaldi. The Pazzi of Florence were near Santa Maria in Campo. Later, the Medici lived near the Old Market.

**Greci.** These people, in their decline, went to Bologna and, being extinguished in Florence, lived there. **The stock from which the Calfucci were born:** These were the Donati, from whom descended another family called the Calfucci. **Column of Miniver:** These are the Pitti family, whose coat of arms is a red shield containing a column of miniver <note>vair, a type of heraldic fur</note>. **Blush for the bushel:** These were the Chiaramontesi, one of whom, being in charge of the public grain and especially the wheat, removed a stave from the bushel measure to make it smaller. When the fraud was discovered, he was punished with the death penalty; afterwards, the bushel was remade in iron so that it could no longer be tampered with. **The stock:** He means the Donati, from whom the Calfucci descended. **To the curule:** <term>curule seats</term> <note>original: "alle crudele" / "sella curule"</note> meaning the first and most worthy magistrates; this is drawn from the custom of the Romans, among whom consuls, dictators, praetors, and ediles sat in a curule chair, which is a seat placed upon a chariot. **Those who are undone:** He refers to the Abati family—men who were certainly wise and respected in government, but too proud, according to what is read of them. **So did the fathers of those:** These first ones are the Visdomini, the Tosinghi, and the Cortigiani, all of whom are allies and descended from the same blood and origin. They were the patrons and founders of the Bishopric (then) and later the Archbishopric of Florence. Therefore, every time the seat is vacant, they are the stewards and dispensers; they gather there to guard the place, and they eat and sleep there until the new bishop takes possession. **The arrogant:** meaning discord in appetite. In Latin, *quotus* signifies "how much" in order; therefore, "arrogant" <note>original: "tracotato"</note> is one who oversteps the order within which he should contain himself. These are the Cavicciuli and the Adimari, whom the poet condemns as cruel but useful and greedy. Thus, they "act like a dragon" <note>original: "sindraca"</note>: they pursue those who flee, but to those who show their teeth—those who offer resistance—or their purse, they are placated, as if to say that for money they will set aside any injury. This proceeds not from magnanimity but from greed. The poet was angry with this family because Boccaccio Adimari occupied Dante's property after he was sent into exile and was always his bitterest adversary, preventing him from being recalled to his homeland. **But from such humble folk:** This was the origin of this most base family, such that when Messer Bellincione married one daughter to Ubertino Donato, Ubertino was later very annoyed that Messer Bellincione gave his other daughter to...

# CANTO XVI

In the small circle <note>the ancient inner walls of Florence</note>, one entered through a gate
named after those of the Pera.
Everyone who carries the beautiful insignia
of the great baron <note>Count Ugo of Brandenburg</note>, whose sign and whose merit
the feast of Thomas restores,
received from him knighthood and privilege;
although he who rings it with a fringe <note>Giano della Bella</note>
gathers today with the common people.
Already there were the Gualterotti and Importuni;
and the Borgo <note>the Borgo Santi Apostoli district</note> would still be quieter
if they were fasting from new neighbors.

The house from which our weeping was born <note>the Amidei family</note>
because of the just resentment that has killed you
and put an end to your joyful living,
was honored, it and its consorts.
O Buondelmonte, how ill you fled
its nuptials through the advice of others!
Many would be happy who now are sad
if God had conceded you to the Ema <note>the river Ema, which Buondelmonte crossed to enter the city</note>
the first time you came to the city.
But it was fitting for that broken stone <note>the ancient, weathered statue of Mars at the head of the Ponte Vecchio</note>
that guards the bridge that Florence should make
a victim upon her final peace.

<column-break/>

...one of the Adimari and made him his brother-in-law. Caponsacco was a man of Fiesole and came to live in Florence in the district of the San Piero Gate in the Old Market, and was the beginning of the Caponsacchi family. These men and the Giudigiunfangati were exiled as Ghibellines <note>the political faction supporting the Holy Roman Emperor</note>. I will say a true thing, but it is incredible to anyone who sees Florence expanded at present. **In the small circle** <note>original: "In piccol cerchio"</note>: that is, in Florence when it was within the small circle of walls, one entered through a gate called the Peruzza Gate. These people of the Pera, according to Perdana Malespini, are now extinct. **EVERYONE who carries the beautiful insignia**: Count Ugo of Luxembourg <note>Landino identifies him as Luxembourg, though historically he was the Margrave of Brandenburg, known as the "Great Baron" for his reforms</note> was the Imperial Vicar in Tuscany under Emperor Otto. He was a man of excellent governance and most religious in the Christian faith. He founded seven abbeys; the first was this one in Florence <note>the Badia Fiorentina</note>, and the last was that of Settimo. At that time, he became a very close friend to the Pulci family, who, being lords of nearby castles, honored him greatly. Furthermore, he befriended four other noble Florentine families: the Nerli, the Counts of Gangalandi, the Giandonati, and those of the Della Bella. To all four of these families, he gave his coat of arms and many privileges. But although his arms are red and white stripes, nevertheless only the Pulci keep the Count's own version, in the manner seen in the Abbey. All the others have varied it. And Giano della Bella, when he joined the side of the common people and renounced his status as a nobleman, encircled the said arms with a gold fringe. The Count died in December on the day of Saint Thomas. For this reason, every year on that day, the monks of the Abbey celebrate his funeral rites. Therefore, by the "great baron," he means Count Ugo. And he says well that the feast of Saint Thomas comforts his name and his merit—that is, his fame—because through the annual funeral rites held on that day, his memory is refreshed. His bones are in the Abbey in an iron chest. But at present, the monks of that place, grateful for the ancient benefit, are having him carved in a well-decorated marble sepulcher. The Gualterotti and Importuni lived in the district of Borgo, which he says would be quieter if it had not had new neighbors. Some say that the Bardi were sent to live in Borgo Santo Apostolo so that they might repress the impetus of these two great Ghibelline families. Others understand this as referring to the Buondelmonti family.

This is the house of the Amidei, which was the beginning of the weeping <note>original: "fleto," meaning sorrow or lamentation</note>, that is, the crying of our republic. There was, therefore, Messer Buondelmonte de' Buondelmonti, a young knight of twenty-four years, whose marriage, repudiation, and the resulting killings and discords we narrated at length in the first canticle <note>referring to Landino's commentary on the *Inferno*</note>. This killing, therefore, although it seemed that the resentment was just, nevertheless possessed more pride and cruelty than is fitting in a free republic; and it was the cause of the division of the city. The principal Guelfs <note>the political faction supporting the Pope</note> who were in Florence at that time were in the district across the Arno: the Nerli, although they first lived in the Old Market. Then the Giacoppi, later called the Rossi; the Frescobaldi; the Bardi; and the Mozzi; the Canigiani—of whom at present two are worthy of account, Antonio and Matteo, and Bernardo; the Frescobaldi; the Magli; the Machianegli; the Belfredegli; the Rinucci; the Barbadori; the Soderini; the Malduri; and the Ammirati. The Ghibellines were the Counts of Gangalandi, the Ubriachi, and the Mannelli. In the district of San Pier Scheraggio, the Guelfs were the Pulci, the Gherardini, the Foraboschi (formerly called the Ormanni), the Bagnesi, the Guidalotti, the Sacchetti, and the Manieri. Those from Quona, allies of those from Volognano; the Lucardesi; the Chiaramontesi; the Compiobbesi; and the Cavalcanti, who are famous because of Guido Cavalcanti, whom we spoke of in the *Inferno*. And at present, I hold in high regard Giovanni Cavalcanti, a man of both natural prudence and learning, worthy of the highest praise. The Ghibellines: the Uberti, Fifanti, Infangati, and Amidei. Those from Volognano; the Malispini, although later, due to an injury received from the Uberti, they became Guelfs. In the district of Borgo, the Guelfs were: the Buondelmonti, the Giandonati, the Gianfigliazzi, the Scali, the Gualterotti, and the Importuni. The Ghibellines are the Scolari, who are of the Buondelmonti; the Giudi, the Galli, and the Cappiardi. In the district of San Pancrazio, the Guelfs were: the Bostichi, Tornaquinci, Vecchietti, Minerbetti, Scali, Spini, and the Balduinetti; the Ghibellines: the Lamberti, Soldanieri, Cipriani, Toschi, Amieri, Palmerini, Miglioregli, and Pigli; but of this party, they later became Guelfs. In the district of the Duomo, the Guelfs were the Tosinghi, Arrigucci, Agli, and Sisti. The Ghibellines were the Barucci, the Cattani da Castiglione, those from Certaldo, and the Agolanti.

# PARADISO

**Brunelleschi**: But part of them became Guelfs <note>The Guelfs supported the Pope, while the Ghibellines supported the Holy Roman Emperor</note>. In the district of the San Piero Gate, the Guelfs were: the **Adimari**, **Visdomini**, **Donati**, **Pazzi**, the **House of della Bella**, **Ardinghi**, and the **Tebaldi** called those of the Vitella; and the **Cerchi** were already beginning to rise, even though they were quite new as merchants. And the Ghibellines were: the **Caponsacchi**, **Elisei**, **Abbati**, **Tebaldi**, **Giuochi**, and **Galigai**; although in all these houses many changes occurred due to various grievances. This ruined the republic and put an end to joyful living.

*If God had conceded you to the Ema*: This refers not to this man who was born in Florence, but to the first of his ancestors who came to Florence; and he says "to the Ema" because those who come to Florence from Monte Buono cross this river <note>referring to the Buondelmonti family's origin</note>. *But it was fitting for that broken stone*: that is, that base which was at the foot of the Ponte Vecchio <note>the "Old Bridge"</note>, which was "broken" because the statue of Mars had been removed from it. And at the foot of this base, Messer Buondelmonte was killed. This seemed a terrible omen for the future civil wars, since the base near which he was killed was dedicated to Mars, the god of wars. Therefore, it was fitting for this stone that Florence should make a *victim*, that is, a sacrifice, upon her *final peace*, meaning at the very end of her peace that was failing.

With these families and others with them,
   I saw Florence in such a state of rest
   that she had no reason for which to weep.
With these families I saw her people so glorious
   and just, that the lily
   was never placed backward upon the staff,
   nor made crimson by division.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A large blue ornamental initial 'E' with white filigree patterns, marking the start of the commentary.</image-desc>
The lily, the Florentine emblem, was anciently white on a red field. And Cacciaguida affirms here that in the civil concord which existed at that time, they lived with such justice and the republic was administered with such prudence that the *lily*—that is, the banner where the lily was—was never *placed backward upon the staff*. This means the Florentines were never defeated in battle nor were their banners captured; when banners are taken by enemies, they are placed upside down on the staff. And they say that the Roman people gave their own coat of arms to all their colonies, which was red without the letters **S. P. Q. R.** <note>original: "Senatus Populusque Romanus," meaning the Senate and the People of Rome</note>. Afterward, the colonies placed in that red field whatever emblem they pleased. For this reason, the Florentines placed the white lily there, which is still seen in some very ancient places. But after the civil division, the Guelfs changed it, setting a white shield and a crimson lily.

   of what he had heard against himself,
   he who still makes fathers stingy toward their sons;
   such was I, and such was I felt to be.

<meta>Continuity: This page begins the commentary and text for Canto XVII of the Paradiso. In the previous Canto, Dante spoke with his ancestor Cacciaguida about the ancient families of Florence. Now, Dante seeks to understand the prophecies of his own future exile that he heard during his journey through Hell and Purgatory.</meta>

# CANTO XVII

from Beatrice and from the holy lamp <note>The "holy lamp" refers to Cacciaguida, who appears as a brilliant light within the constellation of the Cross in the Heaven of Mars.</note>
that had previously changed its place for me:
"Because my lady sends forth the flame
of your desire," she said, "so that it may come out
marked well by the internal stamp;
Not so that our knowledge may increase
through your speaking, but so that you may accustom yourself
to tell your thirst, so that one may pour for you."

"O my dear root, who are so uplifted <note>Dante addresses his ancestor as "piota" (root or sole of the foot), the foundation of his lineage.</note>
that just as earthly minds see
that two obtuse angles cannot fit in a triangle,
So you see contingent things <note>Contingent things are events that may or may not happen, as opposed to necessary truths like those in geometry.</note>
before they exist, by gazing at the point <note>The "point" is God, in whom all time and space are eternally present.</note>
to which all times are present.
While I was joined with Virgil
up along the mountain that heals souls <note>Mount Purgatory.</note>
and descending into the world of the dead,
Words were spoken to me of my future life,
heavy words, although I feel myself
well-squared <note>Original: "tetragono," a four-square or cubic figure that stands firm no matter how it is thrown.</note> against the blows of fortune.
Because my will would be content
to understand what fortune approaches me."
Thus I spoke to that same light
that had previously spoken to me; and as she willed,
Beatrice, so my will confesses.

<column-break/>

of certain prognostications that he received, part in Hell and part in Purgatory. Then the spirit interprets them for him. In the third place, he shows him the refuge from his misfortunes; and in the last, he is assured of the perfection and publication of this work. But as for the beginning, it says that after the spirit’s words, he became such as **Phaethon** became when he went to his mother **Clymene** to be certain of what he had heard from **Epaphus** against himself. Phaethon was the son of the Sun; however, Epaphus said he was not the Sun's son. But after he was sent by his mother to **Phoebus** <note>Apollo, the Sun god</note> and understood from him that he was truly his son, all his sorrow was cast aside and he was filled with joy. This fable I will omit for now, as we have told it elsewhere. Therefore, the order is this: I, Dante, was such—and by that, understand Phaethon, who still makes fathers "scarce" to their sons; that is, his example is the reason why fathers do not make promises to sons as Phoebus promised Phaethon the governing of the chariot for a day, whereby he perished. And I was perceived so by Beatrice; that is, Beatrice noticed that I was such. And by the *holy lamp*, meaning the holy splendor of the spirit which, to be with me, had changed its place in the cross. **BECAUSE**: for which reason my lady, meaning Beatrice, said to me: "send out the flame of your desire," that is, the burning of your wish; as if to say, if you desire to know more, speak. But see that the words come out marked by the *eternal stamp*, which is our immobile mind: the charity of the Holy Spirit. Beatrice does not want the poet to ask the spirit so that the spirit may know his will (because without asking, he sees it in the divine mirror as was said), but so that Dante may accustom himself to asking for what he needs. And this is fashioned because, although God knows our needs, He wants us to ask Him, both to humble ourselves in prayer and to recognize that we are nothing without His grace. Hence in the Gospel: **"Ask and you shall receive"** <note>Original Latin: "Petite et accipietis"</note>. The spirit wants Dante to humble himself in asking. Thus Dante knows by means of Beatrice, that is, through sacred Theology.

**THIS** is the oration that the poet makes to Cacciaguida, in which, because he wants to ask him about what was said to him, which is a *contingent future*, he uses an opening to gain goodwill. He shows that it is easy for the spirit, demonstrating that he "infuses" or raises himself up toward God in such a way that he sees contingent things before they happen, just as we humans, without any proof, see that a triangle <note>Original Latin: "trigono"</note> cannot contain two obtuse angles. Every triangle, whether right-angled, acute, or obtuse, cannot have more than one obtuse angle. **O DEAR root**: this is in the translation, because above he called him a "living topaz." *Contingent things* are those that can be or not be. For things are either necessary, impossible, or contingent. *Necessary* things are those that cannot *not* be. Thus, it was necessary that Dante should die, because all things born must die. It was *contingent* that he lived longer at one time than another. And he adds that the spirit can see future contingent things, not by his own power, but by looking into God, in whom—as in a living mirror—every thing is seen. And he calls God a *point*, which we shall declare in the twenty-seventh chapter. **TO WHICH ALL things**

are present: because with one gaze He sees the past, the present, and the future. For eternity is the total, simultaneous, and perfect possession of a unity that has no end. **WHILE I WAS joined with Virgil**: things were told to me descending into the world of the dead, that is, in Hell, by Messer Farinata: "But the face of the lady who reigns here shall not be rekindled fifty times before you shall know how much that art weighs" <note>A prophecy of Dante's exile within 50 lunar months.</note>. And afterward, *up along the mountain that heals souls*, that is, on the mountain of Purgatory, I was told: "I will say no more, and I know I speak obscurely; but little time will pass before your neighbors will act so that you can explain it." I was with Virgil, although I feel myself *four-square* against the blows of fortune; that is, strong to resist. For a strong man is the same in every kind of fortune, like the *tetragonal* (four-sided) figure, which, however it falls, always shows a flat face. **THAT AN ARROW foreseen comes more slowly**: Because he who has time to think about the adverse things that are to come can, in some part, provide for them, if not to flee them...

<meta>catchword: End</meta>

<summary>Dante asks his ancestor Cacciaguida to clarify the dark prophecies of exile he received in Hell and Purgatory, comparing his anxiety to that of Phaethon. The commentary explains the nature of divine vision, where God sees all future "contingent" events as clearly as humans see geometric truths.</summary>

# CANTO XVII

if at least to mitigate them: furthermore, adverse things which are not in our power are evils of fortune: such as infamy, poverty, exile, deprivation of children, diseases, and similar things: which, if we have the space to consider them before they arrive, it is not very difficult to recognize that they are not as great as they appear: because we consider that they harm only the body and the present life, which is momentary and transitory, and not the soul and the future life, which is eternal and in which true happiness consists: which meditation makes us a new Job <note>The biblical Job is the archetype of patience and faith in the face of sudden worldly misfortune.</note> to support every calamity in peace: And it finds us armed with true reasons.

Not through ambiguities in which the foolish folk
were once entangled before the Lamb of God
who takes away sins was slain,
But with clear words and with precise
speech she replied: that fatherly love,
enclosed and appearing in his clear smile:
The contingency <term>contingency: events that are possible but not certain to happen; the opposite of necessity</term> that does not extend
beyond the notebook of your material world
is all depicted in the eternal sight;
Yet it does not take necessity from there,
any more than a ship descending a downstream current
takes it from the eye in which it is mirrored.
From there, just as a sweet harmony of an organ
comes to the ear, so to my sight
comes the time that is being prepared for you.

<column-break/>

**D**ante had made his request: and that fatherly love: that is, Cacciaguida, replied to him with clear words and with precise Latin <note>original: "latino." In this period, "Latin" was often used to mean "clear or refined speech" generally, not just the language of ancient Rome.</note>: that is, with determined and clear speaking. AND not through ambiguities <note>original: "ambage"</note>: that is, through circumlocutions of words that make the meaning obscure and ambiguous: such as were the responses of Apollo and of the other oracles which entangled and trapped human minds, demonstrating they said the opposite of what they actually spoke: And so that one example among many might suffice for this. Pyrrhus, king of the Epiroti, asked the oracle of Apollo if he was to defeat the Romans: and the response was: "I tell you, descendant of Aeacus, the Romans you can defeat" <note>original: "Aio te aeacidem romanos uincere posse." This Latin phrase is famous for its grammatical ambiguity; it can mean either "you can defeat the Romans" or "the Romans can defeat you."</note>. Which was so ambiguous that it could be understood either that the Romans will defeat you, or that you will defeat the Romans. Before the Lamb of God was slain: that is, Christ Jesus who with his passion and death freed us from sin. And this fatherly love was enclosed in splendor and was appearing: that is, it appeared and showed itself in its joy. And

---

he places his response, which is this. The contingency—that is, the occurrence of future things that are not necessary but which can either be or not be: which contingency does not extend outside the notebook <note>Dante uses the metaphor of a "quaderno" (notebook) to describe the physical, material world of time and space.</note> of your material world. Because things that are simple form are always necessary—it is all painted in the eternal sight. Because whatever is to be is in God: But His seeing them does not make them necessary, just as although we see a ship driven by a rapid river go to strike a rock: nevertheless our seeing it is not the reason that it goes there. FROM THERE: the meaning is that just as that harmony comes to my ears from the organ that plays. SO From there: that is, from the divine mind, the time that is prepared for you comes to my sight: because I see that in my mind just as in a mirror.

As Hippolytus departed from Athens
because of his pitiless and treacherous stepmother,
so it is necessary for you to depart from Florence.
This is willed, and this is already sought,
and will soon be done by him who thinks of it
there where Christ is traded all day long.
The blame will follow the offended party
in public outcry, as is usual; but the vengeance
will be a witness to the truth that dispenses it.
You shall leave behind everything beloved
most dearly; and this is that arrow
which the bow of exile shoots first.
You shall prove how salty is the taste
of another’s bread; and how hard a path it is
to go down and up another’s stairs.

<column-break/>

**C**acciaguida predicts his exile to the poet: which he shows to be unjust because just as Hippolytus <note>Hippolytus was the son of Theseus, falsely accused of rape by his stepmother Phaedra after he rejected her advances. He was exiled and killed as a result of the lie.</note>, for not wishing to consent to the fury of his stepmother, was driven from Athens: so Dante, for not wishing to consent to the unjust wills of those who were administering the republic, was driven from Florence. But we treated Hippolytus sufficiently in the twelfth canto of the Inferno. We endeavor to express the origin of the poet's exile in his biography. THERE WHERE CHRIST IS TRADED: that is, where a market is made of spiritual things and those pertaining to the Christian religion: and they are sold and bartered with simony <term>simony: the sin of buying or selling sacred things or church offices</term>. THE BLAME will follow the offended party: because all those who are driven out will be those who are judged to have erred: and thus the cry—that is, the fame—will go as is usual: and it is customary in every matter that he who fares poorly is held to be in the wrong. BUT the vengeance that God will take upon those who drive you out will be a witness of the truth, which is their injustice and your innocence. WHICH dispenses it: that is, which

---

truth dispenses and contributes that vengeance: Because God makes the truth, he prepares the vengeance upon those who have erred according to that truth: and this is as far as the vengeance that is to follow: but nevertheless you, in your exile, will be struck by the first arrow that exile draws: and this is that it will be necessary for you to leave the things to you

**And what shall most weigh upon your shoulders**

<column-break/>

<margin>a</margin> To the miseries already mentioned, he adds the company of citizens with whom you shall be driven out: and you shall fall into this valley, that is, into this lowliness which I predict to you: because this wicked and foolish company—that is, divided—will turn against you: but a short time later it, and not you, will receive shame and harm. And here he predicts the cruel death of Messer Corso Donati. The conduct of their government will provide proof of their bestiality: in such a way that it will be noble and honorable for you to depart from them. This refers to the Cerchi family. For Messer Vieri de' Cerchi was very obstinate in the enmities he had with Messer Corso. Nor could Pope Boniface ever appease him and bring him to concord with his adversaries. Wherefore, not three years passed before the Cerchi fell into great calamity. Therefore, it will be wise counsel for Dante to leave them and live far from every faction.

<margin>b</margin> Having told of the exile, the spirit now identifies his refuge: Which was the court of Bartolomeo della Scala of Verona, whose coat of arms is a red shield with a vermillion ladder, and upon it a black eagle, which he calls "the holy bird" because it is the sign of the Empire. This man will be so liberal toward your virtues that in doing and asking, the order will be reversed from what is common among other men; for it usually happens that no one performs a favor unless they are first asked. But this man will grant favors to you before you ask for them. And he adds that he will see with him Messer Cane della Scala <note>Commonly known as Cangrande della Scala, Dante's most famous patron.</note>, who at his birth received such an impression from the star of Mars, which is "strong," that is, it induces strength and magnanimity: so that his works in military discipline shall be admirable. But people have not yet noticed this because he is of a new and tender age; since this star [Mars] has not revolved around him more than nine times since he was born. Therefore, Cangrande was in his eighteenth year of age. This is because Mars makes its circuit and course through the zodiac in two years: and thus one "year" of Mars—that is, one of its revolutions—is two solar years. He is, therefore, not well-known at present. But the sparks and splendor of his virtues shall appear and be visible before the Gascon—<term>ideſt</term> <note>Latin: "that is"</note> Pope Clement, who was from Gascony—deceives the noble Henry—that is, the excellent Henry of Luxembourg, who was Emperor. And these sparks, that is, the splendor and heat of his virtues, shall appear in two virtues: in temperance, because neither avarice nor greed for money can prevail in him; and in

---

strength: because he will be of supreme tolerance and patience in supporting every labor and hardship. Regarding the deception that Pope Clement plotted against Emperor Henry, we shall speak in the thirtieth Canto. **AND YOU SHALL CARRY IT WRITTEN IN YOUR MIND.** This is the excellent counsel of a poet: for having introduced Cacciaguida up to this point to divine and predict things which had truly already happened, he now comes to Messer Cane [Cangrande], who was then young. Although he showed signs of being destined for great things, he had yet done little, and the poet could not know the future; he feigns that Cacciaguida predicted it to him, but commanded him not to tell others. This man was indeed excellent in military discipline: and after the death of Henry, in the year of our Lord 1314, he defeated the Paduans at Vicenza, who had already taken the suburbs. Afterward, he besieged Cremona, and held it so tightly that it could not have resisted had they not been aided by the Bolognese. And after this he went...

<margin>a</margin>Cacciaguida has therefore interpreted <note>original: *chosato*</note> what had been obscurely said to the poet in the *Inferno* and in the *Purgatorio*: and what was soon to happen to him. And he adds that because he is in exile, he should not envy his neighbors: because his life is destined to last into the future much longer than the punishment for their treachery will be delayed. **WHEN BY BEING silent that holy soul showed it had finished**: having said these things, the spirit fell silent: and this was a sign that he was finished putting the "woof" to the "web" that I had held out "warped." i.e. <note>original: *i.*, an abbreviation for the Latin *id est*, meaning "that is"</note> that he had finished the explanation of what I had asked him. I began like one who, in doubtful cases, longs and desires to have counsel from a person: **who sees**, i.e. who understands, and **wills**: because it is not enough to see what is better if one does not wish to speak it; **and loves rightly**, i.e. is a true friend.

The poet continues his speech. **I see that time runs to give me the blow** of exile, which is always heavier to those who abandon themselves and allow themselves to be struck down by grief. And for this reason, it is useful that I arm myself with foresight: and take care that, while losing my homeland, my **songs**—that is, my verses in which I vituperate many—do not cause me to lose other places [of refuge]. For while I have gone **down through the world whose bitterness is without end** (and this is Hell), and afterwards climbed the **mountain of Purgatory**, from the peak and summit of which Beatrice, appearing to me, carried me up with her eyes to heaven, and guides me from heaven to heaven: I have understood and heard many things about many men: which, if I tell them again (i.e. if I write them in my verses), will have for them a **taste of strong bitterness**. And if I am an **intimate friend to the truth** (i.e. if I keep this truth within me and do not write it), I fear not to live among those who will live so long after us that they will call this time "ancient" in fame. <note>Dante is articulating the poet's dilemma: if he tells the truth about the powerful people he saw in Hell, they will persecute him now; if he stays silent to stay safe, his poem will not be remembered by future generations.</note>

<margin>b</margin>The poet had proposed his doubt, to which, before it responded, the **light in which his treasure laughed** (i.e. the spirit of Cacciaguida) became **coruscating**, that is, splendid and shining, like a golden mirror becomes in a ray of the sun. And the poet feigns this because, by writing the things found in this his journey, the fame of Cacciaguida remained more shining. And through this splendor, which was joy within him, he demonstrates that the discourse the poet had made pleased him. And then he responded to the doubt proposed to him in this form: "You, Dante, shall write what you have seen, so that the **dimmed** (that is, black) **conscience**—that is, so that men who do not have a pure conscience, but one stained either by their own shame (that is, by their sins)..."

<summary>Dante asks Cacciaguida for advice on whether he should publish the harsh truths he learned in the afterlife, fearing both the revenge of his contemporaries and the loss of his future legacy. Cacciaguida encourages him to be bold and tell the full truth, regardless of the offense it may cause to the "dimmed consciences" of the wicked.</summary>

-># PARADISO<-

foretold: and the honor was sweet that I was to receive from such a magnanimous lord; and yet my life had to extend itself. And Beatrice admonished me that I should change my thought: that is, that I should return to the contemplation of celestial things; and think that she, already judging me, was preparing me for God; and she added that every wrong is lightened—as if to say, let not the injury of exile give you distress, for God holds the vengeance; because He says: **Vengeance is mine, and I will repay.** <note>original: "Mihi uindictam et ego retribuam" — a quote from Romans 12:19</note> And this saying fits excellently in this place because they were preparing for the planet of Jupiter, the governor of justice. I turned back to the loving sound: that is, to the words of Beatrice, with whom I was in love—that is, I returned to thinking about the doctrine of theology, which is true comfort. Because, in truth, the words of Cacciaguida had been about the active life <note>The "active life" refers to a life of external action and social duty, as opposed to the internal "contemplative life" of prayer and study.</note>. Therefore Beatrice—that is, Theology—allows that in the appropriate time and place we may use some digression from the contemplative life and provide what is necessary for the active life: but let it be brief and only as much as is needed, and then immediately let us return to contemplation. AND I DO NOT write what love I saw then in those holy eyes, not only because words fail me, but also because the mind cannot retell and rethink and return so far above itself—that is, to consider that which was so far above its power that it cannot comprehend it again: unless another, which is the grace of God, guides it.

> I can say only this much about that moment:
> that as I gazed again at Beatrice, I remained free
> free I was from every other desire,
> Until the eternal pleasure that directly
> radiated into Beatrice from her beautiful face
> contented me with its serene aspect,
> Vanquishing me with the light of a smile.

> to which I turned, I recognized the will

to which the whole soul would be drawn.

> He began: "In this fifth leaf
> of the tree that lives from the top,
> and always bears fruit and never loses a leaf,
> Are blessed spirits who, down below, before
> they came to heaven, were of such great fame
> that every Muse would be enriched by them.
> Therefore, look upon the horns of the cross;
> the one I name will perform the movement
> that lightning makes in its cloud."
> I saw a light drawn across the cross
> at the naming of Joshua, as it was done;
> nor was the word known to me before the act.
> And at the name of the high Maccabeus
> I saw another move spinning,
> and joy was the cord of the top. <note>original: "paleo" — a wooden toy top spun with a cord.</note>
> Thus for Charlemagne and for Roland
> my attentive gaze followed two of them.

<column-break/>

I cannot say anything else of that moment except that, gazing again at Beatrice, I remained free from every other desire. And certainly the studies of theology content the whole soul, so that nothing else is desired: because they give the knowledge of God and of the supreme good. Therefore, although the soul may be entangled and caught by the care of active and earthly things, nevertheless, when we turn ourselves to Beatrice—that is, to speculation <note>In this context, "speculation" refers to the deep intellectual contemplation of divine truths.</note>—she ravishes us into her form so that we forget every other thing. **NOT ONLY IN MY EYES IS PARADISE.** This signifies that beatitude is not found solely in the doctrines and speculations of the most learned theologians. Therefore, the poet turning again to the spirit in the flaming of his holy lightning and greatest splendor, he recognized that he <note>Cacciaguida</note> had a longing—that is, a desire—to speak a little more. And thus he recognized this in his light: as sometimes here in the world, looking at a face, one knows the affection if it is intense.

This is the beginning of the speech of Cacciaguida, who shows that in that **fifth leaf**—that is, in the fifth heaven—is the tree that lives from the top. And this top is Christ, from whose passion all the pains of the martyrs take their value, and not only those, but the merit of all Christians. The fruit is the beatitude which is eternal; and the leaves are the virtues which adorn the soul eternally, just as leaves are the ornament of the tree. Therefore, in this fifth heaven of Mars, where the tree of the cross is, there are blessed spirits who, before they departed from human life, were of great fame for their excellent deeds: in such a way that they are material to enrich every great poem—that is, to make every great poem remain abundant and full of them. And because of this, "look upon the horns of the cross": and you will see that the one I name will perform there—that is, in those horns—the act that swift fire makes in its cloud: that is, they will cast out ignited splendor just as we see ignited vapors in a cloud rushing like little torches. And this fits warlike men who are of a choleric nature similar to Mars and of burning virtue. I look...

# CANTO XVII <note>Although the header says Canto XVII, the text here covers the conclusion of Canto XVIII and the transition to the next sphere.</note>

> As the eye follows its falcon as it flies,
> so did Duke Godfrey, and Robert Guiscard,
> and William and Renouard draw my sight;
> then, moved and mingled among the other lights,
> the soul that had spoken to me showed me
> how he was an artist among the singers of heaven.

<column-break/>

Therefore the poet saw a light move suddenly through the cross, which Cacciaguida named as Joshua. This happened just as he said it—that is, the illumination was made suddenly. Nor was the word known to me before the act—that is, at the same moment that Cacciaguida named Joshua, the flame appeared. Joshua was the son of Nun <note>original: "figliuolo di naue" — "Nave" is the Latin form of the Hebrew "Nun"</note>; and he was a "type" <note>original: "typo" — a biblical person or event that foreshadows something in the future, especially Christ</note>—that is, a figure of Christ, not only in name, but also in his deeds. Because, succeeding the deceased Moses, he crossed the Jordan river, destroyed the realms of his enemies,

<column-break/>

and acquired the Promised Land and divided it among the victorious people of Israel. This man was called by the Hebrews Joshua ben Nun <note>original: "Iosue ben nun" — Hebrew for "Joshua son of Nun"</note>, which means Joshua, son of Nun. Judas Maccabeus: he would be next, and it would be too long a thing to recount the most strong and religious deeds of the Maccabees, as it is written in the Bible in the Book of Maccabees. In the times of King Antiochus, there was an impious transgression among the Hebrew people; and a great part of them, leaving the divine worship, gave themselves to King Antiochus and adored idols. Because of this, Antiochus conquered Egypt and afterwards took Jerusalem and despoiled the temple. And in those times, Mattathias with five sons—who would not obey the king nor adore idols—did many things in defense of the Law. Afterwards, he died in the 146th year of his life and left his son Judas Maccabeus as the leader of the militia. This man, with the help of his brothers, did miraculous things against the transgressors of the law of God, and expanded the power of those who observed it; he was of such strength that on the day he died in battle, he killed a thousand men. This soul moved spinning like a top <note>original: "palco"</note> revolves when children strike it with a whip; and joy was the force of the top—that is, he was moved by joy just as the top is moved by the whip. **CHARLEMAGNE**: we narrated the life and lineage of this man above in the sixth canto of this canticle; and similarly of Orlando <note>The hero of the "Song of Roland"</note> we spoke in his place. William was the Count of Orange, son of the Count of Narbonne. Richard <note>Dante's text refers to Renouard, a companion of William in the Old French epics, though the commentator here writes "Riccardo."</note> was a very strong fighter against the infidels and a relative of William. **GODFREY**: In the year of Christian salvation 1096, Peter the Hermit, a man of France previously unknown, raised many Christian princes to take up the enterprise against the Saracens. The leader of the army was Duke Godfrey of Bouillon, most excellent in military discipline. Departing from France, he passed through Germany and Hungary to Constantinople; and through the Hellespont he passed into Asia and captured Nicaea and Antioch and many other cities; and in the third year he took Jerusalem. And when the Christians wished to crown him king of this realm, he refused it, affirming that he did not wish to wear a crown of gold in that city where Christ wore a crown of thorns. He was nonetheless made Duke, and when he died, his brother Baldwin succeeded him and reigned eighteen years; and three times he defeated the Egyptians and killed King Caliphalo. Robert Guiscard, Duke of Normandy: of whom we treated in the first canticle <note>The Inferno</note>. And finally, that blessed soul of Cacciaguida himself, who had shown me what an artist he was among the singers of heaven.
