> I turned to my right side
> to see in Beatrice my duty,
> signaled either by words or by gesture;
> and I saw her eyes so clear,
> so joyful, that her appearance
> surpassed her other and her latest habits.
> And as, by feeling more delight
> in doing well, a man from day to day
> becomes aware that his virtue advances,
> so I became aware that my circling round
> together with the heaven had increased its arc,
> seeing that miracle so adorned.
> As is the change, in a brief passage
> of time, in a pale woman when her face
> sheds the burden of its bashfulness,
> such was it to my eyes when I turned
> because of the whiteness of the temperate
> sixth star, which had received me within itself.

<column-break/>

The poet had already described the heaven of Mars; and now wishing to describe that of Jupiter, not departing from Christian theology, he feigns that he turned to Beatrice to see in her his duty—that is, how much it was his debt to discern; and he expected to understand such duty from her either by words or by sign. Therefore, the poet, as in the other parts of his volume, so in this one, did not wish to depart from the Christian religion but proceeded according to theology, which is the mistress of truth: either by words—that is, by suitable sentences—or by sign—that is, by hidden things. AND I SAW HER EYES. In short, her eyes were so lucid and cheerful—more so than other times, and even more lucid than the last time he saw her in the heaven of Mars. Through these words he denotes the splendor of the star of Jupiter and its benign and joyful influence, of which we will narrate a little further down; then by comparison he shows that just as a man, by always doing well from day to day, perceives that his virtue grows, so "I perceived that my circling around the heaven had increased its arc"—that is, its circumference—seeing that

# CANTO XVIII OF PARADISO

...so adorned with a miracle: as if to say, "I realized I had ascended to the next heaven" by seeing Beatrice appear more adorned than ever. He calls her a "miracle" because her beauty seemed an incredible thing. He describes the arc of his ascent as being "greater," for he found the heaven to have a larger circumference. *As the transformation in a small passage*: This is an excellent and most fitting comparison through which he demonstrates how, just as it happens in a short time that a woman whose face was red with shame turns white if the shame that burdened her is removed, so he, in a brief space, found himself ascended from the red and fiery star of Mars to the white star of Jove <note>Jupiter</note>, which is in the sixth heaven. He calls this planet "temperate" because, being situated between the hot planet Mars and the cold planet Saturn, it remains balanced. Furthermore, he did not assign the colors of the planets without reason, for they are different in each. Saturn is of a fiery color. Jove is of a silvery and white color. Mars is like a glowing coal. Venus surpasses the others in splendor. Mercury is called "good" because it radiates. But because he is currently treating the star of Jove, the astrologers write—calling it "Phaethon" <note>An ancient name for Jupiter, often associated with brilliance</note>—that it stays in each zodiac sign for one year, and in twelve years it completes its course through the entire zodiac. It is a benevolent planet, hot and moist, diurnal, masculine, and temperate in its qualities. Its color is silvery: a clear, pleasing white. The philosophers placed the cause of happiness in the orbit of Jove. This circle is joined to the circle of Saturn, and with its goodness, it represses the malice of Saturn when the lower part of its circle is joined to Saturn's. For this reason, the poets feign that Saturn is his father and that Jove drove him from his kingdom. When joined with good planets, it imparts good and useful influences. It makes a man handsome and honorable, with a white and ruddy complexion; it creates beautiful eyes, teeth, and hair, and a round beard, as the astronomer Ptolemy writes. It has great power over the air and the blood. Its houses are Sagittarius and Pisces; it reigns in Cancer. From Jove come justice, laws, and kingdoms. This is why Homer often says: <term>Kings nourished by Jove</term> <note>original Greek: "Basyleas diotropheas"</note>. Under Jove are contained honors, riches, and festive garments. He is truthful, and when he appears in the ascendant, he induces reverence, honesty, faith, and discipline. Jove comforts and strengthens the goodness of every sign of the zodiac. He signifies good in whichever sign he is found, except in the twelfth house, where he signifies servitude and poverty, loss of livestock, and illness in the family.

> I saw within that jovial torch
> the sparkling of the love that was there
> signaling to my eyes our speech.
> And like birds risen from a riverbank,
> as if congratulating one another on their food,
> they form themselves now into a round, now into another flock;
> So within the lights, holy creatures
> flying were singing, and made of themselves
> now a D, now an I, now an L in their figures.
> First, singing, they moved to their own rhythm;
> then, becoming one of these signs,
> they would stop a little and fall silent.

> O divine Muse of Pegasus, who the wits of men
> make glorious and render long-lived,
> as they do with you for cities and kingdoms,
> Illumine me with yourself, so that I may set down
> their figures just as I have conceived them:
> let your power appear in these brief verses.
> They showed themselves then in five times seven...

<column-break/>

Having arrived in the body of Jove, he saw within it the "sparkling of love"—that is, he saw the blessed spirits full of charity. These are those who, having had government and lordship over men, lived with the highest justice, and therefore they are in the body of the planet whose influence produces kings, princes, justice, and laws, as was said before. He says, therefore, that they signaled "our speech" to his eyes: meaning that through the shapes of letters, they spoke as literate people do. For just as birds that depart from high places to go to pasture fly while singing, as if wishing to "congratulate"—that is, to show celebration and joy for the pastures where they arrive—and in flying they form an O, or indeed another figure (as we see cranes, storks, and similar birds do), so these souls, flying and singing, made of themselves these letters: D, I, and L. This was their speech, because through these letters they signified what their song was: *Love justice, laws* <note>original: "Diligite iustitiam leges"</note>, or rather, *Love the justice of laws* <note>original: "Diligite iustitiam legum"</note>, for it is written in the Book of Solomon: *Love justice, you who judge the earth* <note>original Latin: "Diligite iustitiam qui iudicatis terram," the opening line of the Book of Wisdom</note>. He adds that they moved to "their own rhythm," which means they made an equal circular motion, proper to the perfected soul. For just as such a motion begins from a point and returns to itself, so the good soul, proceeding from God with its virtues, returns to God. Then, becoming one of these signs—which are D, I, and L—they would stop and fall silent so that there would be a little interval, a small space between one figure and another, so it could be understood that each of these letters signified a word.

It is the custom of Greek and Latin poets not only to invoke the help of the Muses at the beginning of a book, but also later when, in writing, they arrive at a great matter, as we see especially in Homer and Virgil. They renew the invocation both to have divine favor and to make the listener attentive, who, hearing the invocation, expects great things. *O DIVA*: O Goddess Muse. And although he uses the singular, he intends to invoke them all, imitating...

# CANTO XVIII

...vowels and consonants, and I noted
the parts just as they appeared to be spoken to me.
"Love justice" <note>original: *Diligite iustitiam*</note> were the first 
verb and noun of all that was depicted;
"you who judge the earth" <note>original: *qui iudicatis terram*</note> were the last.

Then, in the 'M' of the fifth word
they remained arranged, so that Jove <note>Jupiter</note>
seemed there to be silver patterned with gold.
And I saw other lights descend to where
the peak of the 'M' was, and there they settled,
singing, I believe, the Good that draws them to Itself.

Then, as when burning logs are struck,
innumerable sparks fly up,
from which the foolish are accustomed to draw omens,
more than a thousand lights seemed to rise from there
and ascend, some much and some a little,
just as the Sun that ignites them ordained.

And once each had settled in its place,
I saw the head and neck of an eagle
represented by that patterned fire.

He who paints there has no one to guide Him,
but He guides, and from Him is recognized
that power <term>Virtù: in this context, the divine creative power or instinct that guides nature</term> which gives form to nests.
The other blessed souls, who seemed
content at first to form a lily on the 'M',
...O sweet star, what and how many gems...

<column-break/>

Virgil, who said: "O Calliope, I pray, breathe upon me as I sing" <note>original: *Vos o caliope precor aspira te canenti*</note>. *Pegasea*: She who dwells near the Pegasean fount <note>The Muses, specifically associated with the fountain of Hippocrene created by Pegasus; Dante invokes their inspiration to help him record the complex visual signs he saw</note>. In my judgment, one cannot understand this as an invocation of Minerva, as Francesco da Buti explains. *That you know glorious wits*: Certainly, no wit is to be equated with a poet, who is not only instructed by human art but, moved by divine fury <note>The Platonic concept of 'poetic madness' or divine inspiration</note>, transcends his own nature and becomes more than a man; from which follows true glory and a long-lived, vibrant life—that is, of great age through the fame he leaves behind. And he does not only give birth to a very long life for himself, but also, with your help, for cities and kingdoms. This is because, through poems in which they are praised, they remain in perpetual fame. *ENLIGHTEN ME with yourself*: Pour your inspiration into me, which may enlighten and illuminate in such a way that I may reveal their figures. Since the spirits make letters of themselves, and each one highlights a word, the poet could not interpret the divine signs without divine favor. *Let your power appear*: Let it be shown how much you can do in these brief verses of mine. *To show themselves*: Therefore, these spirits transformed from figure to figure until they made five times seven—that is, thirty-five letters, including vowels and consonants—which are the number of letters in these words: "Love justice, you who judge the earth" <note>original: *Diligite iustitiam qui iudicatis terram*, the opening of the Book of Wisdom</note>. Therefore, in all that depiction—that is, in that whole configuration of those letters—the first part had "Love justice," where the verb "Love" <note>*diligite*</note> is, and the last part had "you who judge the earth."

After all these figures, they stopped at the
last letter, which is the 'M' of the word *terram* <note>earth</note>,
to denote that these were those who had
the manner dictated by this letter 'M'. And he has taken
the 'M' of this word *terram* because their government
was not in the universal world (for the
world contains within itself all the heavens and the elements
enclosed within); it was not, therefore, in the universal world,
but in this part of the world which is the earth
inhabited by men. These spirits who moved themselves
into the 'M' are good men without sovereign power,
who, whether in office or out of office, had always
observed justice; and therefore he places them lower down.
He has other spirits descend from the Empyrean heaven
above the peak of the 'M' to form a crown; and these
are kings and princes who sing of the Good that moves them—
that is, they sing of God, who is the supreme Good
and who moves men toward Himself, because He inclines
the well-disposed will to His path. From those who
formed the figure of a crown, many spirits rose up,
lifting themselves and flying up, some more and some less, according
to whether they had merited more or less. And therefore
he says: "just as the Sun that ignites them ordained"—that is, just as God,
who is the Sun of Justice, has placed them. And to
express it better, he shows that those spirits who flew
upward, some more and some less, were like the
sparks that come out of two lit logs that are rubbed together—
which sparks the foolish take for omens <note>A reference to the folk practice of divination by watching sparks</note>. And after
these spirits, ascending, stopped in their place, either higher
or lower, they remained fixed
in the figure of the head and neck of an eagle. By this,
he means the Emperors, whose ensign is the eagle.
Thus, there will be three generations of men: citizens in the 'M',
lords and kings above the 'M', and the emperors above these.

The main fiction follows, saying that
He who paints there—that is, He who moves
the spirits there to make such a configuration—has
no one to guide Him—that is, God, the first immobile mover.
But He guides all other things, and pours power into the
heavens, and then the heavens influence it in us. And therefore,
from Him is recognized and acknowledged the power <term>Virtù: here, justice as a divinely-instilled quality</term> which is justice; He forms it "for the nests"—that is, for the
birds—calling "birds" the spirits who in this...

# PARADISO

...demonstrated to me that our justice
is the effect of the heaven that you engem. <note>original: *ingemme*; Dante addresses the planet Jupiter, which is "gemmed" or adorned by the souls of the just.</note>
> Therefore I pray the Mind in which is initiated
> your motion and your power, that it look
> to where the smoke comes from that taints your ray,
> So that once again it may be angered
> by the buying and selling within the temple
> which was walled with blood and martyrs.

<column-break/>

The planets make such figures. **The other beatitude**, that is, that second order of spirits who at first seemed content to stay atop the peak of the 'M' and **to lily themselves**—that is, to form a crown shaped like lilies, which are holy and golden <note>likely "noble" or "yellow"</note> princes—afterward, with little movement, that is, rising upward, they followed the imprint: that is, the figure of the eagle. The meaning is that by moving they made the rest of the figure of the eagle, of which the spirits had already made the head and neck. This denotes that divine providence disposed, through the influence of this star <note>Jupiter</note>, for princes to consent to the **monarchy** of one alone who was Emperor.

---

Or rather, it implies that the influence of Jove <note>Jupiter</note> would produce monarchy in a way that the government would be most perfect in justice if men were willing to receive it. And perhaps he interprets here "the Greyhound" <note>The *Veltro*, a mysterious savior figure Dante prophesied in *Inferno* Canto I</note> of whom we spoke in the first canticle. **Those gems** then, that is, those spirits whom I saw in you, Jove, sweet star, demonstrated to me that human justice proceeds from your heaven, which you **engem**, that is, you "gem" or adorn like a precious jewel, and that you are the cause of such an effect.

But because I see that the wickedness of men corrupts your justice, that is, your influence—and especially the leaders of the Christian Church—I pray the divine Mind in which your motion and your power and influence **is initiated**, that it look to where the smoke is born—that is, the vice which originates and corrupts the ray of justice, which Scripture calls the sun, just as smoke and fog obscure the light of the sun. Whence: "the sun of justice has arisen" <note>original: *exortus est sol iustitiae*</note>. And I pray that the divine Mind looks upon this wickedness, so that just as another time, in the humanity of Christ, it was angered against those who sold and bought in the temple and drove them out, so may it be angered against the shepherds and prelates who sell sacred things through **simony** <term>Simony: the sin of buying or selling ecclesiastical offices or spiritual things</term> in the church of God. This church was **walled with blood and martyrs** because it is founded upon the passion of Christ and the martyrs. That Christ Jesus drove out the sellers and buyers of the temple appears in the Holy Gospel.

Seeing that the poet knows the shepherd of the Christian flock and the other prelates—who should be an example of sanctity to us, guiding us to good works—are so involved in avarice and in all other kinds of injustice that they give us nothing but captive examples with which they pull us from the right path, he turns his speech to the militia of heaven.

> O militia of heaven whom I contemplate,
> pray for those who are on earth,
> all gone astray following bad example.
> Once it was customary to make war with swords,
> but now it is done by taking, now here, now there,
> the bread that the pious Father denies to no one.
> But you who write only to erase,
> think that Peter and Paul, who died
> for the vineyard that you lay waste, are still alive.
> Well can you say: "I have fixed my desire
> so much on him who willed to live alone
> and who for leaps was led to martyrdom,
> that I know neither the Fisherman nor Paul."

<column-break/>

...to the **militia of heaven**, that is, to the blessed souls of heaven, whom he contemplates and prays that they may pray for us who, having gone astray, follow the wicked example of the prelates. And here he demonstrates how gravely he sins who is placed in a position to be an example to others. **ONCE IT WAS CUSTOMARY**: here he shows that in ancient times, men who were greedy and covetous of others' treasure moved to war and took it by force. While this was unjust, it nonetheless had some shadow of frankness of soul. But now it is taken with greater injustice, because under the guise of religion they excommunicate and interdict in order to then sell absolution and the sacraments. These are the **spiritual bread** with which we lead ourselves to eternal life, and for this reason it is called **viaticum** <term>Viaticum: literally "provisions for a journey," referring to the Eucharist given to a person near death</term>, which the pious Father—that is, God full of mercy—does not lock away or forbid to anyone, but wants to be given to everyone who returns to penance.

**But you**, shepherd, **who write in order to erase** <note>This refers to the Pope issuing decrees of excommunication only to "erase" them when paid a fee</note>: that is, you make censures not to punish sinners but to make them buy them back. Remember that Peter and Paul, the first apostles who died for the **vineyard**—that is, the Church which you lay waste with simony—are still alive; it is as if to say, they will be able to punish you. **WELL CAN YOU SAY**: with more ambiguous speech, he reproves the shepherd. You, shepherd, can say: "Do not reprove me, because I have fixed my desire on following him who willed to live alone," that is, to dwell in the desert. This was the precursor of Christ, **John the Baptist**, who through **leaps**—that is, through the balls and dances of the daughter of Herod—was led to martyrdom because he was beheaded. Therefore, you will say: "I have fixed my desire so firmly on Saint John the Baptist that I do not know the Fisherman <note>Saint Peter</note> nor Paul." And this is true, not because you follow the life of the Baptist, but because you follow the **Florin** <note>The gold coin of Florence, which bore the image of St. John the Baptist</note> on which is his image. And for this, you despise the sin.

<header>PARADISO</header>

# CANTO XIX OF DANTE’S THIRD CANTICLE

Because he has already narrated the nature of Jove <note>The planet Jupiter, associated with Justice</note> and which spirits represent themselves in this star, now in this nineteenth chapter, having shaped the sign of the eagle, he brings the eagle forward to speak. First, he demonstrates an unheard-of way in which the eagle speaks. Then, he raises the question of whether a person living justly can be saved without the Christian faith. In the third part, he resolves it. And

<columns>2</columns>

> Before me, with wings outspread, appeared
> the beautiful image that those souls, joined
> in sweet enjoyment, made joyful.
> Each appeared like a small ruby in which
> a ray of sun burned so brightly
> that it reflected back into my eyes.
> And what I must now describe
> no voice ever carried, nor did ink ever write,
> nor was it ever grasped by the imagination,
> For I saw, and even heard, the beak speak,
> and sound in its voice both "I" and "my"
> when in its thought it was "we" and "our."

<column-break/>

in the final part, he rebukes the Christian princes: because by living and ruling unjustly, they stray from those spirits who form the sign of the eagle. Thus, *the beautiful image* appears before me with wings outspread—that is, the image of the eagle, which is beautiful because it signifies justice. And this eagle was made by the *joined souls*—that is, connected and united to one another—and they were joyful in *sweet enjoyment*, meaning they were happy in the divine bliss they possessed by enjoying God. The outspread wings signify two acts of justice: rewarding and punishing. And each soul shone like a ruby struck by a ray of sun. By the ruby, he denotes charity <note>love or divine grace</note>, without which there can be no true justice. Then the poet follows by saying that, having to describe and report the eagle's speech, he must say something that *no voice ever carried*—that is, it was never spoken. *Nor did ink write it*—meaning it was never written. Nor was it ever grasped by 

<column-break/>

imagination. For no one ever imagined that an eagle could speak. He makes the listener attentive by promising to report unusual and new things. *I saw*: he states what this thing is and demonstrates that he saw and heard the *beak*—the mouth of the eagle—speak. And in speaking, it said "I" and "my," as if it were a single being, though in its concept <note>its collective mind</note> it was "we" and "our." The meaning is that all those spirits who formed the body of the eagle—each of whom, because they were all together, should have spoken for themselves—all spoke at once through the beak of the eagle. They say "I" and "my" in the singular, despite the fact that the thought, which came from the minds of many spirits, should have said "we" and "our." And certainly, it was never understood by the imagination that a body made of many minds, as that one was, could speak as if it were one and not many. From this appears the wondrous genius of the poet and the wondrous transformation in such a great mind.

<summary>This page introduces Canto XIX of Paradiso, focusing on the miraculous singular voice of the Imperial Eagle, which is composed of countless just souls. The commentary explains how the eagle's speech represents the perfect unity of Divine Justice, transcending human imagination.</summary>
<keywords>Dante, Paradiso, Eagle of Justice, Jupiter, Charity, Salvation of the Just, Collective Voice, Monarchy, Rubies</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discourse in the Sphere of Jupiter. Having witnessed the formation of the celestial eagle from the souls of the just, the narrator now hears the eagle speak with a single voice, though it is composed of thousands of spirits. The commentary by Cristoforo Landino explains the theological implications of this collective voice and sets the stage for Dante's central question about divine justice.</meta>

<columns>2</columns>
<header>PARADISO</header>

> And I began: "Because I was just and pious,
> I am here exalted to that glory
> which does not allow itself to be surpassed by desire;
> And on earth I left my memory
> fashioned in such a way that the wicked people
> commend it, but do not follow its story."
> Just as one single heat from many coals
> makes itself felt, so from many loves
> there issued only one sound from this image.
> Wherefore I said then: "O perpetual flowers
> of eternal joy, you who make all
> your odors seem but one to me,
> Solve for me, by your breathing, the great fast
> which has long held me in hunger,
> finding no food for it on earth."

<column-break/>

He sets down the words of the eagle's beak; which, although they come from one place, nonetheless belong to all those spirits who formed the eagle. He says, therefore: *I am exalted to that glory which does not allow itself to be surpassed by desire*—that is, a glory so great that our desire cannot be greater, because we cannot desire anything greater. And this is *for being just and pious*—that is, for having practiced justice mixed with mercy. For considering human fragility, a total and unbending justice would be almost like cruelty. And therefore it is said: "God saw our frailty and had mercy on us" <note>original Latin: "Vidit deus figmentum nostrum et misertus est nostri," a paraphrase of Psalm 103:14</note>. And elsewhere: "Justice is impious which does not know how to forgive human frailty" <note>original Latin: "Impia est iustitia que humane fragilitati non nouit ignoscere"</note>. 

*AND ON EARTH I left my memory*: The poet demonstrates what an excellent thing justice is, since it not only guides us to eternal life but also makes us live here through fame, by which not only the good praise us, but even the wicked are constrained to praise us, although they do not follow 

---

the *story*—that is, they do not act according to how they hear we have acted. And certainly, the force of virtue is so great that even the vicious cannot help but love it. *JUST AS one single heat from many coals*: just as it happens that from many coals (that is, many pieces of charcoal lit together) a single heat results, so from many loves—that is, the spirits who shaped the eagle—there issued a single sound and a single voice. Through this fiction, it is demonstrated that in the active life—which princes administer and rule—there is nothing that so maintains love and concord, and preserves human society (to which nature produces us), as much as justice does. Therefore, it is no wonder if those who have ruled with supreme justice are now so united in this heaven. 

Understanding this union, the poet did not turn to the eagle as to one, but as to many spirits, whom he calls "flowers" because they are the ornaments of that heaven where they have eternal joy. And he says that although there are many flowers, nonetheless not many odors, but only one comes from them. Then he requests that by breathing into him the truth, they *solve*—that is, dissolve and take away—the *great fast* which has long held him in hunger. For he who remains fasting feels hunger. And this is a Latin way of speaking, because <term>soluere ieiunium</term> <note>to break a fast</note> means to end a period of hunger. This is a metaphor because he intends to express that he has been fasting for a long time—that is, empty of that truth for which he has great hunger (meaning a great desire to know). And the reason why he has been fasting is because on earth he has found no food that could take away such hunger—that is, he has found no food among earthly and human sciences (meaning doctrine) that could satisfy him in demonstrating this truth for which he hungers (meaning his desire).

---

> Well do I know that if in heaven’s high realm
> divine justice makes its mirror,
> yours does not perceive it through a veil.
> You know how attentively I prepare myself
> to listen; you know what that doubt is
> which has been so old a fast for me.
> Like a falcon, which, emerging from its hood,
> moves its head and flaps its wings,
> showing its will and making itself beautiful,
> So I saw that sign become, which was woven
> with praises of divine grace,
> with songs such as are known to those who rejoice up there.

<column-break/>

The author had prayed to the spirits to satisfy his long hunger—that is, his long desire to understand the truth. But he had not yet shown what thing he wished to understand as truth. Nor does he say it even now. But he certainly affirms that they, looking into the divine mirror, can understand it for themselves. Therefore, the spirits act while the author stands attentive to the response; and they know what that doubt is: which was whether, without the Christian faith, justice can lead to eternal life. And this doubt is for him a very old "fast." After these words were spoken by the poet, he sees the sign of the eagle become like a falcon which, when its hood is removed, moves its head around watching, and *flaps its wings*—that is, it shows joy, displaying a will to fly and making itself beautiful by smoothing 

---

its feathers upon itself. Thus, then, appeared the eagle that was *woven*—that is, composed—of praises of divine grace (meaning the spirits who were giving praise to divine grace with such songs as mortal tongues cannot express). And for this reason, they are not made on earth. But they are made by those who are in heaven in eternal beatitude; because the human intellect cannot understand celestial things unless it rises to heaven—that is, if first purged of every vice, it does not rise to such high speculation.

<summary>Dante asks the collective spirits of the Eagle to resolve a long-standing theological doubt regarding the salvation of the "virtuous pagan." The Eagle responds with joyful movement, compared to a falcon, signaling its readiness to explain the mysteries of Divine Justice.</summary>
<keywords>Divine Justice, the Eagle of Jupiter, Cristoforo Landino, salvation of non-Christians, virtuous pagans, falcon simile, allegory of justice, breaking the fast of ignorance</keywords>

# CANTO XVIII
<note>While the header reads Canto XVIII, the text corresponds to the beginning of Canto XIX of the Paradiso.</note>

Then began he who turns the compasses
at the edge of the world, and within it
mapped out so much, both hidden and manifest,
His power could not be so impressed
upon the whole universe that His Word
would not remain in infinite excess.
And this makes it certain that the first proud one,
who was the summit of every creature,
by not waiting for light, fell unripe;
And hence it appears that every lesser nature
is a short receptacle for that Good
which has no end and measures itself with itself.

<note>original: "volge el sesto" — The OCR reads "dextro," but the context and Landino's commentary confirm "sesto," referring to the compasses used by God as the Architect of the Universe (Proverbs 8:27).</note>

...so outside the universe in infinite excess. The meaning is that His wisdom infinitely exceeds every creature. And it is not improper for the author to say that God cannot put all His power into any single creature; because this would be to make a creature equal to Himself. Wherefore His power would be lacking, because the creature could then create itself and thus would not be a creature but a creator; and thus there would be multiple first principles, which is impossible. Therefore, God could not put all His power into one creature, such that it would not be infinitely less than Him. God cannot make something greater than or equal to Himself; He cannot do evil. Nor does this "inability" of God arise from any impotence within Him, but from the infinite excellence of His power. Therefore, God’s inability to pour His entire power into a creature demonstrates that He is omnipotent.

And this makes it certain—that is, it proves what has been said in this form: If Lucifer, who was the most excellent creature God made, and was the first who became proud against his creator, did not wait <margin>for the light of grace</margin> for the causes of God’s providence, the other less excellent creatures will not be able to see them either. But he did not see them. This is seen because he did not wait for the light of confirming grace; rather, he considered himself equal to the divine Word and therefore fell "unripe" <note>Dante uses "acerbo" (unripe) to describe Lucifer's fall, suggesting he fell before his creation was fully "ripened" or perfected by the grace he refused to wait for.</note>. Thus, it is manifest that the creature cannot see everything in the Creator.

And hence it appears that every "lesser nature"—understand this as "natured nature," <term>natura naturata</term> <note>A scholastic term referring to created things, as opposed to "natura naturans," the creative power of God.</note> that is, every creature—because it is smaller than the Creator, is a "short" and insufficient receptacle for that Good. That is, it is not capable enough to contain within itself that Good which has no end—meaning the infinite Good, which is God. And because He is infinite, He "measures himself with himself," because the infinite cannot be measured by anything finite. And no mind is infinite except God’s. If, therefore, the creature is a "smaller receptacle," it may receive some part of God’s power, but not all of it.

<column-break/>

**T**he Eagle responds and sets forth the reasons why the poet cannot find the solution to his question, which cannot be solved except through faith. For no one is capable <note>of fully grasping</note> divine justice. And for this reason, he first establishes the infinite and incomprehensible power of God, saying: "He who is the highest God and turns the compasses"—that is, He who turns Jove, which is the sixth planet according to some. Others say the "sixth" refers to the roundness of the heavens which turns near the extremes. And he says "the sixth" <note>original: "el sesto"</note> because we call "the compasses" <term>le seste</term> that instrument with which we make a round circle. He could not "so impress His power"—that is, God could not imprint so much of His value and power into the universe that His Word—that is, His wisdom, which is called the Word and the Son—would not remain <note>that is, exceed the creation</note>.
<meta>catchword: non reſtaſ</meta>

**H**e concludes that since our understanding and knowledge come from some "ray of the divine Mind" which is diffused into all things—because all created things have their form and being from it—and this ray is the divine power that is infused into each thing as much as suffices for its being: the human intelligence cannot be so powerful by its nature that it could discern and know its source (that is, God) except "far beyond that which is apparent to it"—that is, beyond the limit that it sees. And although one sees more than another, nevertheless no one sees the whole. "THEREFORE": for which reason; and he arranges the text in this way: "THE SIGHT that your world receives"—that is, the knowledge which is in man still dwelling on earth—"enters into the eternal justice"—that is, into knowing divine justice—no differently than the eye and physical sight "enters into the sea." For the human eye sees the bottom of the sea at the shore where the water is shallow. But in the deep ocean <note>original: "pelago"</note>, that is, where the water is high, it does not see the bottom; not because the bottom is not there, but because of the depth, which the visual power cannot reach through such a great distance.

Therefore your vision, which must
be one of the rays of the Mind
with which all things are filled,
Cannot by its nature be so powerful
that it does not discern its source
far beyond that which is apparent to it.
Therefore, into the eternal justice,
the sight that your world receives
enters as the eye into the sea;
Which, though from the shore it sees the bottom,
in the deep ocean it does not see it, and nonetheless
it is there, but the deepness hides it.
There is no light unless it comes from the Serene
that is never clouded; otherwise it is darkness,
either the shadow of the flesh or its poison.

<meta>catchword: alla</meta>

<summary>This page explains the theological limit of human reason in understanding divine justice, using the metaphor of a compass to describe God's creation and the ocean to describe the depth of His judgment. Landino's commentary emphasizes that because God is infinite, no finite creature—not even Lucifer—can fully contain or comprehend the Divine Word.</summary>
<keywords>Divine Justice, human intellect, Lucifer's fall, compasses of God, infinite power, divine grace, Cristoforo Landino, Paradiso Canto XIX</keywords>

# PARADISO

Now the hiding place is fully opened to you
that was hiding the living justice from you,
about which you made such frequent questioning;
For you said: "A man is born on the bank
of the Nile, and there is no one there who speaks
of Christ, nor any who reads or writes of Him;
And all his desires and his good deeds
are as far as human reason can discern,
without sin in his life or in his speech;
He dies unbaptized and without faith:
where is this justice that condemns him?
Where is his fault, if he does not believe?"

->WHENCE THIS JUSTICE THAT CONDEMNS him: as if to say, it cannot be justice to condemn<-
->just ignorance.<-

He rebukes the presumptuous ignorance of those men who have the audacity—with a dull intellect incapable of God’s secrets—to place themselves on the judge's bench to judge what is a thousand miles away with a sight as short as a span. Therefore, as it would be the height of folly for a man who was—

<margin>If I said "short sight" that could not see further than a span, and yet wanted to judge what was distant a thousand miles: so it is the height of rashness for the human spirit</margin>

Now, who are you who wants to sit on the bench
to judge from a thousand miles away
with a sight as short as a span?
Certainly, for him who would scrutinize with me,
if the Scripture were not set above us,
there would be cause for marvelous doubt.
O earthly animals! O dull minds!
The First Will, which is good in itself,
never moved from itself, which is the Supreme Good.
So much is just as is consistent with It;
no created good draws It to itself,
but It, by radiating, causes that good.

CERTAINLY To him: In this place, the Eagle—so that no one may excuse themselves through ignorance—removes all ignorance by saying: Certainly there would be much to doubt and it would be a "marvel" <note>meaning: a cause for wonder or confusion</note> to anyone who "scrutinizes with me" <note>meaning: strives with every subtlety to investigate the divine justice that shines in me, the Eagle</note> if the Scripture were not "above us," which teaches us that the will of God is just, and that we must not investigate the reason why He does this rather than that. O EARTHLY Animals: The Eagle shows a righteous indignation that man—an earthly animal and consequently of a dull mind—wishes to understand divine matters, considering that not even the celestial creatures can perfectly know the divine wisdom, power, and goodness. THE FIRST will: He has rebuked those who go seeking the reasons for divine justice; since it ought to be enough for them to understand that God cannot err. For it is known that the First Will is good not because of anything else; if God shared His will with another, He would not be God, as He could sometimes lose it and not be good. But because that will is good in itself and not from another, it never departs from itself, which is the Supreme Good. And if the divine will never departs from the good, whatever is consistent with it and pleases it must be good, and every good is just. Therefore, no one can justly complain, even though it may seem to them at times that they suffer unjustly. And the reason why one cannot complain is that no "created good" draws God to itself: for God is the creditor of all and a debtor to no one; rather, everyone is beholden to Him for every gift received. Instead, that divine will "causes" the good where it is, being the reason why the good created by Him has its being. In this, He is like the potter who makes some vessels to hold precious things and others to hold unclean things. <note>This refers to a famous biblical metaphor from the Book of Romans, suggesting God has the right to shape human destiny as a potter shapes clay.</note>

<column-break/>

By what I have told you, O Dante, the "hiding place"—that is, the darkness—is opened to you, which was hiding the living justice; that is, it made it so that you could not understand the divine justice about which you made such "frequent questioning" <note>meaning: so often searched for within yourself.</note> For you said: one shall be born in Egypt near the Nile where there are none but infidels, and there is no one who preaches of Christ, nor any who read or write of Him; and nonetheless, he lives according to virtue in thought and in deed, and without sin in word or action, as far as human reason can understand. But finally, because he dies without baptism and without the Christian faith, he is damned. Therefore, where is the divine justice here, which requires of this man more than he was able to do?

...human [intellect] with little knowledge which, because it is finite, cannot comprehend God who is infinite, or presume to understand the secrets of God. Nor does he remember the saying: <note>original: "Incomprehensibilia sunt iudicia tua domine"</note> "Incomprehensible are your judgments, O Lord." And Saint Paul forbids it, saying: <note>original: "Scrutator maiestatis reicietur adeo"</note> "He who is a searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by its glory" <note>This warns against trying to understand the full nature of God's power.</note>; and elsewhere: <note>original: "Nolite sapere plusquam oportet sapere: Sed sapere ad sobrietatem"</note> "Do not seek to know more than it is proper to know: but to know with sobriety." And in Matthew: <note>original: "Dico aute uobis quod multi ab oriente uenient et recumbent cum habraam in regno celorum, filii regni reicietur in tenebras"</note> "I tell you that many will come from the east and will recline with Abraham in the kingdom of heaven, while the children of the kingdom will be cast out into the darkness." We must therefore believe that whatever is done by the Supreme Good is good, and that He sees what man cannot see. Especially as Mark says: <note>original: "De die aut illa et hora nemo scit: non angelus celi: non filius nisi pater"</note> "But of that day and hour no one knows: not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father." Therefore, man will know it even less.

<summary>This page addresses Dante's profound doubt regarding the salvation of "virtuous pagans"—those born in lands like Egypt where Christ is unknown. The Eagle (representing Divine Justice) rebukes human arrogance, explaining that God's will is the absolute standard of what is just, far beyond the "short span" of human comprehension.</summary>
<keywords>divine justice, virtuous pagans, Nile, baptism, human reason, God's will, arrogance, salvation, predestination</keywords>

# CANTO XVIII

As the stork circles over her nest
after she has fed her young,
and as the one who has been fed looks up at her;
So did the blessed image act,
moving its wings, which were driven
by so many spirits <note>Original: "consigli"—referring to the individual souls making up the Eagle's form.</note>.
Wheeling, it sang and said: "As
my notes are to you, who do not understand them,
such is the eternal judgment to you mortals."
Then those glowing fires of the Holy Spirit
grew quiet, still formed in the sign
that made the Romans revered by the world.

<margin>They were revered for their innumerable victories</margin>

The Eagle began again, saying that no one ever ascended to the celestial kingdom who did not believe in Christ. And this belief was held either by those who lived before the coming of Christ—and these believed in Christ to come, as those whom He drew out of Limbo—or by those who lived after His passion; and these—

It began again: "To this kingdom
no one ever rose who did not believe in Christ,
either before or after He was nailed to the tree.
But look, many cry 'Christ, Christ!'
who at the Judgment shall be far less near
to Him than those who never knew Christ.
And the Ethiopian shall condemn such Christians
when the two companies shall be separated,
the one eternally rich, and the other poor.
What can the Persians say to your kings
when they see that volume opened
in which all their shames are written?"

—believed that He had already come and redeemed the world with His blood. "But look"—meaning, understand that many cry "Christ, Christ!" and these are false Christians who show belief with words but do not believe in their hearts; hence it is written: <note>original: "populus iste labiis me honorat : cor autem eorum longe a me est"</note> "This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." And these, at the Great Judgment, will be "less near" to Him than those who did not know Christ. For he who has had no knowledge of Christ has some excuse, while the wicked Christian sins much more, having no excuse. And therefore he says that when the final sentence is given, and the "two companies"—that is, the two congregations of souls—are separated, the good shall rise to heaven to eternal riches, which is the happiness where there is an infinite abundance of every good; and the wicked shall descend to hell, and shall be "poor"—that is, deprived of every happiness. At that time, some "Ethiopian"—meaning someone from Ethiopia where there is no knowledge of the Christian religion—shall condemn and blame the wicked Christian and reproach him for his filthy life. What can the "Persians"—those who have had no light of faith—say to our Christian kings, if not to blame them when they see that "opened volume" at the Judgment? That is, they will see Christ the Judge, in whom, as in a book, all merits and demerits will be read; and these demerits are "shames" to Christ. For he who sins acts against the Gospel doctrine, and therefore despises it.

There shall be seen among the deeds of Albert
that one which will soon move the pen,
so that the kingdom of Prague <note>Original: "plaga," referring to Bohemia.</note> shall be made a desert.
There shall be seen the woe that, upon the Seine,
he brings by falsifying the coinage,
he who shall die from the blow of a hide <note>Dante refers to Philip the Fair of France, who died in a hunting accident involving a wild boar.</note>.
There shall be seen the pride that parches,
which makes the Scot and the Englishman mad,
so that neither can stay within his own borders.

<margin>The woe upon the Seine... In Paris, through which the river Seine runs, was caused by the Flemings.</margin>

<column-break/>

By a simile it shows that just as the
stork, having brought food to its young,
circles over the nest, and they, having been fed,
look up at her: so the Eagle did
above me after it had fed me
with its speech; and I looked up at said Eagle.
Then the blessed image lifted its brow—
that is, the image of the Eagle which moved
its wings driven by so many spirits—
that is, by as many spirits as were in those wings.
THEN THOSE GLOWING FIRES FOLLOWED. The meaning
is that those glowing splendors, which were
enkindled in charity, continued speaking
in the sign of the Eagle; that is, that a single voice
issued from them all through the beak of the Eagle,
which made the Romans revered.
For the said sign of the Eagle was
on the battle standards of the Romans, who for their—

—innumerable victories were revered.

It continues by rebuking Christian kings,
and especially kings, and traverses all the realms
that are among Christians. And it begins from the
northern part where there are four realms: Prague,
France, Scotland, and England. It says, therefore,
that it will be seen in that book, among the unjust
deeds of Albert, that deed which, because it is most
unjust, will soon move the pen to write his vices.
Albert <note>Albert I of Austria, King of the Romans.</note> was the Emperor crowned by Pope Boniface
in the year of our salvation 1298.
He was the Duke of Austria, and fought
with Adolf, called Andulph, King of the Romans,
and defeated him and killed him. There shall be
seen the woe of the defeat—

<summary>The Eagle (representing Divine Justice) explains that virtuous non-Christians may be closer to God than hypocritical Christian rulers. It begins a scathing critique of European monarchs, including Albert of Austria and Philip the Fair, whose sins are recorded in the "book" of God's judgment.</summary>

# PARADISO

### CANTO XIX

->There shall be seen the lust and soft living<-
->of him of Spain and him of Bohemia,<-
->who never knew nor wished for valor.<-
->There shall be seen the Cripple of Jerusalem,<-
->his goodness marked with a single I,<-
->while the contrary will be marked with an M.<-
->There shall be seen the greed and the cowardice<-
->of him who guards the Island of Fire,<-
->where Anchises ended his long life;<-
->And to let it be known how little he is,<-
->his record shall be in abbreviated letters,<-
->which will note much in a small space.<-

->And to everyone shall appear the foul deeds<-
->of his uncle and his brother, who have disgraced<-
->so noble a lineage and two crowns.<-
->And he of Portugal and of Norway<-
->shall be known there, and he of Rascia<-
->who has seen the coinage of Venice to his ill.<-
->O happy Hungary, if she lets herself<-
->be mistreated no more! And happy Navarre,<-
->if she would arm herself with the mountains that encircle her!<-
->And everyone should believe that already, as an earnest<-
->of this, Nicosia and Famagusta<-
->lament and bark because of their beast,<-
->who does not step away from the side of the others.<-

<column-break/>

...the money was falsified. This man was Philip, called "the Fair," King of France. In the year 1300, having been defeated by the Flemings, he raised a large new army. To obtain the necessary funds, he had his coins falsified in such a way that they were reduced to a third of their value, causing extreme harm to merchants and others. He died while hunting, killed by a wild boar; and so the poet says he died "by a blow to the hide," because the Florentines call the skin of a pig the *cotenna*. There one could see the pride that parches the heart, the arrogance a man has when he believes he deserves more than others. From this pride comes the thirsty desire to rule. For this vice, the poet reproaches the King of England and the King of Scotland, who are so proud that they cannot endure staying within their own <term>meta<note>boundary or limit</note></term>. We have provided the explanation of this word *meta* in another place. This was King Edward of England, a man very thirsty for dominion.

He condemns the lust and the idle living of Alfonso, King of Spain, and of Ladislaus, King of Bohemia. Alfonso, in the year 1260, was elected Emperor, but due to cowardice and softness, he did not pursue the enterprise. Mention was made of Ladislaus in the seventh chapter of *Purgatorio*. The "Cripple of Jerusalem" was Charles II, son of Charles I, King of Apulia; he was <term>ciotto<note>lame or crippled</note></term>. He was a very lustful man and a corrupter of virgins, for which he excused himself by saying he did so because otherwise he would have become a leper. The poet says his goodness will be marked in the book of Christ with a single **I**, representing the number one, because he had no other goodness except being generous; but the contrary, his vice, will be marked with an **M**, representing a thousand, because he had infinite vices. **THERE SHALL BE SEEN** the

greed and the cowardice. And certainly, greed proceeds from cowardice of the soul; thus women and the elderly are often more greedy. "Of him who guards the Island of Fire," that is, Sicily, where Mount Etna is. In this island, Anchises, the father of Aeneas, died as an old man in the city of Trapani, called *Drepanum*. This ruler was Frederick, King of Sicily, son of King Peter of Aragon, a most noble prince. And so that one may understand how small his record is—that is, the writing that contains his vices—it shall be in "abbreviated letters"; that is, there will be only a portion of a letter for each part, and in this way, they will take up little space while noting many vices.

The "Uncle" of Don Frederick was Don James, King of Majorca, Menorca, and Ibiza. In the Lombard language, *barba* means "uncle." **AND OF HIS BROTHER**: this was Don James II, King of Aragon. **WHO SO NOBLE A LINEAGE**: so noble a family. **AND TWO CROWNS**: that of Aragon and that of Majorca, they have **disgraced** <note>original: "boze"—interpreted here as making someone a cuckold or shaming them</note>. It is as if he said they were disgraced. **PORTUGAL**: in ancient times called Lusitania, it is part of Spain, which is divided into four kingdoms. **NORWAY**: this region is in the far North, where during the summer solstice the days are very long and the nights very short. **RASCIA**: this is a kingdom in <term>Slavonia<note>modern-day Serbia/Balkans</note></term> whose king used to counterfeit Venetian ducats. **NAVARRE**: a kingdom in Spain which at that time was under the French; therefore, he warns it to defend itself with the mountains <note>the Pyrenees</note> that divide it from France. **NICOSIA AND FAMAGUSTA**

are cities in Cyprus which are already beginning to lament. This is an "earnest" or a sign of future vices: "Because of their beast," that is, their beastly king. Truly a holy poet, to whom the human race is much indebted, since he so strictly reproaches princes; for their sins do not harm only one or a few, like the errors of private citizens, but they harm the entire country they govern, and often a single man is the cause of the ruin of many regions.

## CANTO XX OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE

Just as in the preceding chapter the eagle demonstrated the incomprehensible justice of God and rebuked the kings, so in this one it shows the author some of the spirits who formed its shape. This twentieth chapter contains four parts. In the first, it describes the disposition of the eagle. In the second, the eagle names five <note>Dante identifies six spirits in total: David as the pupil of the eye, and five others forming the eyebrow. In the third, it resolves a doubt born of having seen two of those souls <note>The "doubt" refers to how the pagans Trajan and Rhipeus could be in Heaven.</note>. In the fourth, it describes the depth of <term>predestination</term> <note>The theological concept that God has already ordained who will be saved.</note>. 

In the written verses, he uses a simile, saying that the place where the eagle was appeared to him just as the sky appears when the sun descends to the other hemisphere. For when the light of the sun is missing, the sky adorns itself with various stars, and thus all those spirits kindled with charity appeared like stars in that eagle. 

After the lucid <term>pebbles</term>—that is, the shining spirits whom he calls "lapilli" (meaning precious stones) with which Jove, the sixth planet, was engemmed—had ended their songs, the eagle resumed its speech. And he describes by comparison the flow of the voice from the neck of the eagle, showing that it rose through the channel of the neck with that sound of copious water descending from stone to stone. And just as the sound of the *cetra* (that is, the lyre) takes its form in the neck of said instrument because there the fingers of the player touch the strings; and as through the <term>openings</term> <note>original: "pertugi"; the finger-holes of the instrument</note> of the bagpipe or whistle or pipe, the wind—that is, the breath put in by the player—takes its form as a voice by penetrating (that is, passing through) the said holes; so through the neck of the eagle rose that murmur, and at the beak the voice became firm and spoke those things that my heart desired. And...

**Now he knows much:** It seems impossible to us in the world that a non-Christian spirit could be saved. But it is seen in God as in a mirror: because divine providence has willed this, despite the fact that even in heaven the blessed soul cannot see into the depths. The poet implies here that divine grace extends even to the unfaithful and gives them faith, so that they can be saved. But we cannot understand His judgment. And this is the answer to the doubt proposed above concerning the man who is just and good but unfaithful. LIKE A LARK: It is the nature of the lark to rise from the earth, and ascending little by little, to climb while singing, and then it takes pleasure in wandering through the air which is silent. Therefore, the eagle was similar to this bird, which he calls the im—

Although my doubt appeared in me to those spirits like color through glass, and because of this they knew what I desired to hear, nonetheless the most ardent desire to hear did not let me remain silent and wait for the solution. BUT I SAID, "What things are these?" marvelling that if no one can be saved who does not have true faith in Christ, in what way could a Trojan, not having been a Christian, have ascended to heaven? **The kingdom of heaven:** <note>original: "Regnum Celorum"</note> the answer in essence is this: although the divine will does not allow those who are not Christians to ascend to heaven, nonetheless an most ardent charity and undoubting faith conquers and forces such a will—in such a way that it allows the pagan to be saved. Not, however, that the divine will is conquered as one man conquers another by force, but it is conquered because it *wills* to be; and thus, being conquered, it conquers with its own benevolence, that is, with its kindness. Just as it happens when we defeat a friend in a dispute: nonetheless, out of humanity and so that he is not shamed, we yield and let him win.

<column-break/>

The Eagle continues speaking to resolve the doubt that was in the poet's mind: how could it be that without the Christian faith, Emperor **Trajan** and **Ripheus** the Trojan were saved, whom he saw depicted and adorning the most holy region of the angels (that is, heaven). It says, therefore, that they did not die as Gentile pagans, but as Christians. This is because divine grace, moved by the justice of Ripheus, enlightened him such that before he died, he believed in the Christ to come—even though he lived more than a thousand years before the advent of Christ. And therefore it says "in the feet of God to suffer," using the feet to represent the whole body of Christ who was to be born and suffer.

And Emperor Trajan, who lived after the Passion of Christ, believed in the "feet already suffered," which had already endured the pain. However, having died and already gone to Hell—where those who are obstinate cannot repent of their evil—the hope he had in God while he was alive (that God would enlighten him in the true belief) was his "reward" (meaning his merit). Because of this, that hope was the reason that the prayers of **Gregory** <note>Pope Gregory the Great, who according to legend prayed for Trajan's soul because of the Emperor's legendary justice.</note> had the power before God to return him to life. This was so that his will—which in Hell cannot change—might change toward the good while back in the body. Thus, having returned to the body where he stayed but a short time, he was immediately converted to God and believed in Him who could help him. And he was kindled with such charity of true love that, having departed the body (which was his second death), he merited ascending to this heaven.

The other, who is the soul of Ripheus, because he observed justice on earth, God infused him with the gift of understanding that the Son of God was to take flesh and suffer to redeem us. This is that Ripheus of whom **Virgil** wrote: <note>original: "Cadit et rihpheus iustissimus omni qui fuit in teucriis: Et seruatissimus equi"</note> "Ripheus falls, the most just among the Trojans, and the most observant of right."

**THOSE THREE LADIES**: These three virtues—Faith, Hope, and Charity—which we have already seen previously in the earthly paradise at the right of the **Gryphon**, <note>A mythical beast, half-eagle and half-lion, representing Christ's dual nature (divine and human).</note> were to him in the place of baptism.

**MORE THAN A MILLENNIUM**: Because from the ruin of Troy until the beginning of Rome was 414 years. And from the founding of Rome to the birth of Christ was 752 years.

**O PREDESTINATION, how remote**: An excellent and appropriate exclamation to show how unknown to man is the first root and the depth of divine predestination, from which it arises that Ripheus, rather than another, could mount to such grace. And this arises because we cannot see the whole First Cause (that is, we cannot know the abyss of the divine mind, which is the First Cause, nor its counsels). For this reason, men must not overstep or judge; even though the blessed spirits see things in God as in a mirror, nonetheless they do not see everything there. Nor can they penetrate...

# CANTO XX

So while I spoke, if I recall,
I saw those two blessed lights,
just as eyes blink in unison,
move their little flames along with the words.

<column-break/>

...until the end. In knowing all the chosen <note>original: "electi"</note>—that is, the entire number of the predestined. Nor are these souls in lesser glory; for as it is the highest pleasure of the righteous to conform to the divine will, they enjoy not knowing everything, seeing that it pleases God. Thus, such a lack—that is, such a reduction in knowledge—refines <note>original: "glassina," likely a typo for "affina" (refines) or a variant of "glossa" (explains)</note> them and makes them perfectly blessed. 

I recognize that this passage not only hints at but openly requires a detailed discussion of predestination. This is a very difficult thing for someone who is not highly learned to describe in a way that does not take away free will. Nor can this be conveniently debated if one does not also understand foreknowledge, <note>original: "prescientia"</note> rejection, <note>original: "reprobatione," the theological concept of being left out of the elect</note> and finally the divine will. But we will not expand upon this at length because the size of the book forbids it. Nor will we skip it entirely, because without it, the poet’s mind remains obscured.

Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian of the Western Church.</note> posed four definitions for predestination: 
1. Predestination is the foreknowledge of God’s benefits.
2. Predestination is the predestining of someone to glory.
3. It is the purpose of having mercy.
4. It is the preparation of grace in the present and of glory in the future.

In the first definition, God’s knowledge is noted. In the second, the selection <note>original: "elettione"</note>. In the third, the will. In the fourth, the direction toward the final goal. Augustine thus establishes: Calling, Justification, Predestination, and Glorification <note>original: "magnificatione"</note>. Calling <note>original: "vocatione"</note> pulls us away from evil. Justification regards the good that grace begins. Predestination regards the final good of grace. Glorification regards the good of future glory. Or we might say: Predestination prepares glory through grace; Calling offers us grace; Justification gives it to us; but Glorification multiplies glory through grace.

Predestination does not impose necessity <note>The idea that an event *must* happen, removing human choice.</note> upon things. If it did, many problems would arise: rewards would be offered in vain to the good and punishments to the guilty, and the former would be unjustly rewarded while the latter were punished. Furthermore, God would be the author of evil, and free will would be lost. Nonetheless, it is necessary that whatever God foresees is "necessary"—not simply, but by consequence. 

For example: Scipio sees that Hannibal <note>Scipio Africanus and Hannibal were the two greatest rival generals of the Punic Wars.</note> is arranging his battle lines. It is not necessary for Hannibal to arrange them just because Scipio sees it. But because Scipio sees Hannibal arranging them, it follows by necessity that he *is* arranging them; nevertheless, Scipio’s seeing is not the cause of the arrangement of the troops. Similarly, although God sees the evil works of man, He is not the cause of them.

Theologians make a distinction between predestination and foreknowledge <note>original: "prescientia"</note>. For predestination is the knowledge of good things and contains within itself the cause of them. But foreknowledge perceives evil things and is *not* the cause of them. And certainly, if God permits free will, He uses no injustice if He punishes one who has erred and could have guarded against that error. But if He provides grace beforehand, He does no injury to anyone. Therefore, when He damns the guilty, as He did Judas, He observes justice. When He predestines someone, as He did Paul, He uses grace and great mercy, which does not exclude justice. 

Thus, the primary will of God first wants everyone to be saved insofar as they are human. But the second will wants some humans to be damned insofar as they are worthy of it. Therefore, the "antecedent" will regards the order of nature as it was instituted by Him. But the "consequent" will—which comes after the error of the sinner—regards the order of the person acting by their free will. But I return to the text.

**AND LIKE** a good singer: The meaning is that the two spirits—Trajan and Ripheus—accorded with the words of the Eagle to demonstrate joy, just as a good lute player <note>original: "cytharista"</note> accords the voice with the sound. And so between them, they agreed to move their little flames—that is, their splendors—just as eyes agree to blink.

# PARADISO

### CANTO XXI OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE

In the previous chapter, the author showed the illustrious spirits of the sphere of Jupiter: those who, through the practical virtues of the active life and with justice, had ruled and rightly administered the magistracies and empires committed to them. Already my eyes were fixed again upon the face
of my lady, and my soul with them
from every other intent was withdrawn.
And she did not smile; but, "If I were to smile,"
she began to me, "you would become such
as was Semele when she turned to ashes;
For my beauty, which along the stairs
of the eternal palace is kindled more,
as you have seen, the higher we ascend,
If it were not tempered, it shines so brightly
that your mortal power at its radiance
would be like a branch that a thunderbolt shatters.
We have been raised to the seventh splendor,
which beneath the breast of the burning Lion
now radiates downward, mixed with its power.
Fix your mind straight behind your eyes,
and make of them mirrors for the figure
that in this mirror shall appear to you."

<column-break/>

and from him he receives the solution to that doubt. In the third part, he moves a question which arises from the solution of the first doubt. In the fifth, the spirit reveals himself to the author and rebukes the popes of those times. Now, regarding the beginning of the chapter, it shows that once the words of the Eagle were finished, he turned his eyes and his soul toward Beatrice; which denotes that having been attracted by new subject matter, he did not wish to begin until he first turned his whole intellect and mind to Holy Scripture; and therefore he was "withdrawn from every other intent" and thought, because he wished to follow only that. And thus, in passing, it shows that whoever wishes to be in the true contemplation of divine things must necessarily leave every other thing and fix themselves in that. And this is demonstrated in the Gospel where Martha, who represents the active life, busies herself about the house and turns to various ministries, while Mary—that is, the contemplative life <note>original: "contemplatiua"</note>—does not help her, but sits and does not move from the feet of the Lord. **AND SHE DID NOT SMILE**: Beatrice does not smile here to denote that the contemplative life is more grave and severe than the active one; furthermore, it denotes the nature of the planet, which is grave and slow, as we shall soon demonstrate. It can also be interpreted according to Beatrice’s own words: that when a man transcends to the supreme degree of divine speculation, if Beatrice smiled—that is, if she showed all her splendor—the human intellect (which is to that splendor as the eye of the owl <note>original: "noctua .i. cuetta"</note> is to the rays of the sun) would be so dazzled that, in wanting to see everything, it would see nothing. **WAS SEMELE**: "When she turned to ashes." Just as Semele was the daughter of Cadmus of Thebes, and how she bore Bacchus to Jove, and how Juno, changed into an old woman, persuaded her to ask Jove to lie with her in the same form that he lay with Juno; and how Jove, to keep his promise, came to her armed with celestial lightning because he lay thus with Juno; and how finally Semele, unable to suffer the heat, was burned by it, as we described in detail in the *Inferno*. **WE HAVE BEEN** raised to the seventh splendor: we have ascended into the seventh planet, which is Saturn, which the poet feigns was in the sign of Leo at the time of this vision—that is, in the year 1300 <note>original: "M.ccc"</note>. They say, therefore, that Saturn was in the seventh degree of Leo, Jupiter in the twenty-fourth of Aries, the Sun at the beginning of Aries, Venus was in Pisces, and the Moon in Libra. **RADIATES**: it radiates at present mixed with its power. It is as if he implies that although Saturn is very cold, nevertheless the heat of Leo tempers it. **FIX**: "Straight behind your eyes your mind"—that is, consider well what you will see, which is the ladder of which he will speak shortly. "And make of those eyes of yours mirrors for the figure"—that is, for the said ladder, which will appear to you in this mirror, meaning in this planet. He had already ascended to the seventh heaven, which is that of Saturn; which planet, when it is well-disposed at a man's birth, makes him an investigator of ancient and hidden things, and influences sharp reasoning and discourse of reason. And also, according to Macrobius <note>Ambrosius Theodosius Macrobius, a 5th-century Roman philosopher whose work on Cicero's "Dream of Scipio" was a primary source for medieval cosmology.</note>, that virtue of the mind which the Greeks call *theoriticon* <note>original: "theoriti con," meaning the power of contemplation and speculation</note> is associated with it. This causes the poet to represent the speculative souls in this sphere. To treat more fully the nature of Saturn: this planet is diurnal, masculine, cold, and dry; melancholic, timid, old, lazy, sterile, and malignant. And although it is more remote from the earth than the others, it is nonetheless more harmful. It is the signifier of the ancients, and the ancestor of burials and the dead, and of the earth and all cultivation of it, of buildings, of every metal mine, and of hidden treasures. It signifies large beasts, long infirmities, quartan fevers, and leprosy <note>original: "morphea"</note>. It makes a man have foul breath and be a lover of foul and filthy things. It makes him lazy, slow, pale in color, with a curved, thin, and veiny body, thick lips, and thin legs; he always looks at the ground, speaks little, and has little lust, desiring the male more than the female. When it is well-disposed...

<summary>This page introduces Canto XXI of Paradiso, marking the transition from the Heaven of Jupiter to the Heaven of Saturn, the realm of the contemplative life. The commentary explains the symbolism of Beatrice's lack of a smile and the astrological qualities of Saturn as a cold, slow planet associated with deep thought and ancient things.</summary>

<meta>The text continues the transition into the Seventh Heaven (Saturn), moving from a general description of the planet's astrological qualities to Dante's specific vision of the Golden Ladder and the spirits of the contemplative life.</meta>

# CANTO XX <note>Though the header says Canto XX, the text and commentary describe Canto XXI of the *Paradiso*.</note>

It makes a man sharp, hot, and of deep and diverse opinions. He does not rejoice; he draws out anger and is implacable; he loves little and easily leaves love behind. It produces priests, and especially those religious orders that wear black and the color of the earth. Also, those who are apostates, simoniacs, and heretics and schismatics; and those who fight body-to-body; it produces <term>surgeons</term> <note>original: "cerusici"</note>. In conception, it rules the first month; for this reason, with its coldness and dryness, it shrivels and binds the matter from which the creature is to be made. It produces <term>harmonious ones</term> <note>original: "harmoniaci"</note>, enchanters, and every species of diviner. In honors, it rules over melancholy. In sects, it is the signifier of the Jewish sect and of the Sabbath day. In metals, it signifies lead and rusty iron. It has no light in itself but receives it from the other planets, and especially from the sun. And because the sun makes it bright and warms it, the sun is its enemy; because the house of the sun, which is Leo, is opposite to the house of Saturn, which is Capricorn; and its darkness and coldness are contrary to the light and heat of the sun. The ancients figure him with the scythe because, just as the scythe does more harm returning than proceeding, so Saturn does more harm <term>retrograde</term> <note>appearing to move backward in the sky</note> than direct. This planet shines in Gemini, in Cancer, and in Leo—that is, it is more powerful there. And because the poet places the sun in Leo, it then diminishes its light in Virgo, in Libra, and in Scorpio. It becomes dark in Sagittarius, Capricorn, and Aquarius. It diminishes its darkness in Pisces, in Aries, and in Taurus. It has the color of lead; but when it enters the circle of Jupiter, because of its warmth, it becomes white and clear.

If one knew what the feeding
of my sight was in that blessed aspect,
when I transformed myself from the other care,
they would recognize how pleasing it was to me
to obey my celestial guide,
balancing one side with the other.
Within the crystal that bears the name,
circling the world, of its bright leader,
under whom every malice lay dead,
Of the color of gold in which a ray shines through,
I saw a ladder erected upward,
so far that my sight did not follow it.
I saw also descending down the steps
so much splendor that I thought every light
that appears in heaven was diffused from there.

<column-break/>

**T**he meaning of the first verses is this: that if one knew what the "pasture" of my face was in that blessed aspect—that is, how sweetly my eyes fed upon the face of Beatrice—when I transformed myself from that other care (that is, when I departed from the matter already discussed and turned myself to that which follows), they would know how much pleasure I took in obeying Beatrice, who was my guide. In short, he means that it was a supreme pleasure to gaze upon Beatrice; nevertheless, it was so pleasing to obey her when she commanded that he turn toward the ladder, that he balanced the pleasure of obeying her with the pleasure of gazing at her. WITHIN the crystal: he posits that he saw in the body of Saturn a ladder of gold in which the rays of the sun shone. He calls it "crystal" because it is a transparent body. And certainly, just as one climbs by a ladder from bottom to top, step by step, so through the <term>contemplative virtue</term> one mounts from heaven to heaven up to God. This ladder is of gold. This is because, just as gold is more excellent than any other metal, so the

---

contemplative life surpasses every other life; and the ray of grace of the eternal sun shines within it. "Which bears the name of its leader": because it is called Saturn after the ruler Saturn. UNDER whom every malice lay dead: this refers to the history, or rather the fable, of the Golden Age. But of this age and of Saturn, we have spoken in many places in such a way that nothing remains to be told. OF THE COLOR of gold in which a ray shines through, I saw a ladder: we have spoken of this above. But he says the ladder was so direct and high that his "light"—that is, his sight—did not follow it, to denote that the knowledge of divine things is so high that the human intellect cannot reach it. And it also denotes the great interval that exists from the heaven of Saturn to the Empyrean heaven. And just as gold is most pure without any mixture, so is the contemplation of divine things. And down that ladder descended innumerable splendors, which are spirits.

And as by natural custom,
the <term>daws</term> <note>original: "pole," referring to jackdaws or similar crows</note> together at the start of day
move to warm their cold feathers;
Then some go away without return,
others turn back to where they started,
and others, wheeling, make a stay;
Such a fashion seemed to me to be there
in that sparkling that came together
as soon as it struck a certain step.
And he who stayed near us...

<column-break/>

Here is a fitting comparison by which he demonstrates that just as it happens that certain birds called "pole" <note>jackdaws</note> in the morning, upon departing, move all at once; then some fly far away, some fly back and place themselves where they had risen, and some circle around; so it happened that those spirits, encountering one another, seemed to sparkle, and some went away while others remained. I SEE well the love that you signal to me: because that splendor demonstrated the ardor of charity and the affection to speak to him.
