# PARADISO

->He fixed himself so clearly that I said in thought,<-
->“I see well the love that you kindle for me.”<-
But she <note>Beatrice, representing Divine Revelation</note> from whom I await the how and the when
of speaking and of silence, stands still; wherefore I,
against my desire, do well if I do not ask.
Because she, who saw my silence
within the sight of Him who sees all,
said to me: “Release <note>original: "solui," from the Latin *solve*, meaning to set free or fulfill</note> your hot desire.”
And I began: “My own merit
does not make me worthy of your answer,
but for her sake who grants me leave to ask,
O blessed life who remains hidden
within your own joy, make known to me
the cause that has brought you so near to me;
And tell me why, within this wheel,
the sweet symphony of Paradise is silent,
which below, through the others, sounds so devoutly.”

“You have mortal hearing as you have mortal sight,”
he answered me, “therefore here there is no singing
for the same reason that Beatrice has not smiled.
Down through the steps of the holy ladder
I descended so far only to give you welcome
with my speech and with the light that cloaks me.
Nor did greater love make me more ready,
for as much and more love fervently burns up there,
as the flaming makes manifest to you;
But the high charity, which makes us ready servants
to the Counsel that governs the world,
apportions here even as you observe.”

<margin>IV</margin>
“I see well,” I said, “O sacred lamp,
how free love in this court
suffices to follow the eternal Providence;
But this is what seems hard for me to discern:
why you alone were predestined
to this office among your companions.”
I had not come to the last word
before the light made a center of its middle,
spinning like a swift millstone.

<sig>D</sig>

<column-break/>

Dante desired to question the spirit.
But Beatrice, from whom he expected the “how”
and the “when”—meaning the manner and the time to speak and
to be silent—stood still. Wherefore he said within himself,
against his desire: “I do well if I do not
ask.” But Beatrice, seeing my silence—meaning
the reason why I was silent—said to me: “Release”—meaning
solve and fulfill your hot desire—meaning your ar-
dent will. And I turned to the spirit, saying:
“Not my own merit or worth makes me worthy that
you should answer me; but answer me for the love of Be-
atrice, who allows me to ask you two
things: first, why you have come closer to me
than the others. Second, why in this heaven one does not
sing the sweet symphony of Paradise which
is sung in the other heavens.”

The blessed soul answers Dante’s doubts;
and first the second one, in which he was
asked why there was no singing in this planet as
in the others. He says, then, that in that planet,
laughter and song are mental; and because he,
being in the body, cannot use spiritual sight or
hearing, but only corporal; therefore he did not see Bea-
trice laugh, nor did he hear those spirits sing. The
poet feigns this because the contemplative virtues are
mental, and cannot in any way be
understood by the bodily senses. **THROUGH THE STEPS:**
Peter Damian <note>St. Peter Damian (c. 1007–1072), a monk and theologian known for his asceticism.</note> answers the first question:
why he, rather than the other spirits, came
to Dante; and he says: “I descended to give you welcome and
congratulate you with words and with the light that
cloaks us”—that is, dresses us. **NOR DID GREATER LOVE:** meaning
nor did a greater love—meaning I did not come sooner than
others because I was driven more by charity than the others.
For up here, there fervently burns—meaning boils and glows—more and
as much love in every spirit; that is, there are spir-
its who surpass me in charity and spirits who are my
equals, as the flaming of all can manifest to you, because here the quality of the splendor demonstrates
love. But nonetheless, this is not the cause. But it is the will of God, whom it pleased that I should come. Be-
cause charity—meaning God Himself—which makes us ready servants to obey the Counsel that governs the world—meaning
Divine Providence, which governs the universe—apportions—meaning assigns to each what He wants them to do,
as you observe—meaning as you see. Therefore, the poet always remains in the first position: that the abyss of
Divine Counsel is hidden even from the blessed spirits.

<margin>P</margin>
The author responds that he knows well that free
love is sufficient to follow Divine Providence;
for here you obey freely and not servile-
ly. “But for me it is difficult to discern”—meaning to know—
“for what reason you were predestined more than
the others to this office.”

<page-num>XXI</page-num>

# CANTO XXI

> Then the love that was within answered:
> “Divine light is focused upon me,
> penetrating through this light wherein I dwell,
> Whose virtue, joined with my own vision,
> lifts me so far above myself that I see
> the Supreme Essence from which it is drawn. <note>original: "munta," literally "milked," suggesting the light is drawn directly from the source of God's being.</note>
> From this comes the joy with which I flame;
> for as my vision becomes clear,
> I match the clarity of my flame to it.”

<column-break/>

Dante had made his request and the light had spun around. Now, following this, the poet shows how the love that was within that light—that is, that blessed soul full of love—responded, saying: “Divine light”—meaning divine grace—“is focused upon me,” meaning it descends upon me through its rays, the point of which reaches me, penetrating and passing through this light in which I am wrapped and within which I dwell. The meaning is that although the blessed spirit does not discern the full depth of the divine counsel, nevertheless, divine grace sometimes descends...

<column-break/>

...into a spirit through which it understands what God wills. This grace, breathed into me by God, joins with my own will; and thus joined, it lifts me above myself—that is, it makes me intelligent beyond my natural state, so much so that I can see, or rather, I can know the Divine Essence from which my light is drawn. FROM THIS comes the joy: The meaning is that as much as he sees, so much he shines and rejoices, such that the amount of splendor corresponds to the depth of his vision. AS MUCH AS IT IS CLEAR: My vision and knowledge are as clear as the clarity of my light and splendor. This shows that the flame and clarity grow within him the more he sees the Divine Essence; for at that moment, I am more inflamed to want what that Essence wants. This demonstrates that his will is free, and of its own accord, he wills what God wills—statutes <note>rules or decrees of God</note> that make His will known to me. Therefore, when these spirits sparkle, it happens through a new grace that comes into them, which at that moment had entered this spirit, and he had newly understood it to be God's will that he should descend to Dante. And he willed it, because God willed it.

> “But even that soul in heaven who is most clear,
> that Seraph <note>The Seraphim are the highest order of angels, characterized by their proximity to God and their fiery love.</note> who has his eye most fixed on God,
> would not satisfy your request;
> For that which you ask is hidden so deep
> within the abyss of the eternal statute
> that it is cut off from every created sight.
> And when you return to the mortal world,
> report this, so that humanity does not presume
> to move its feet toward such a goal.
> The mind that shines here is smoke on earth;
> consider then how it can do down there
> what it cannot do even when heaven takes it up.”
> His words so restricted me
> that I left the question and withdrew,
> humbly asking him who he was.

<column-break/>

The spirit has shown that he came rather than someone else because it so pleased God. Now, because Dante wants to know why it pleased God this way rather than another, the spirit responds that although the blessed spirits see many secrets in God, they nevertheless cannot see the reason why He wills one thing over another. And therefore he says that even the soul that is "most clear" in heaven—meaning the one who receives the most rays of divine grace and thus sees God most clearly (which applies especially to the Seraphim, because they contemplate God more than the other angels, as we shall say elsewhere)—would not "satisfy," meaning he could not provide a sufficient answer to Dante’s question. This is because this question goes so far—it enters so deep into the "abyss," meaning the depth of the "eternal statute" or divine providence—that it is "cut off," meaning severed from every "created sight," or every created intelligence. AND TO THE WORLD: Therefore, when you return to the world, to mortal men whose intellect is submerged by...

<column-break/>

...the contagion of the flesh, you shall say that since even the angels cannot see this (though they can see many things that men cannot), humans should not presume to move their feet—that is, their desires—toward such a goal. The human mind, which "shines" here in heaven because it is illuminated by the rays of divine grace, "smokes" while ON EARTH—that is, while it is still in the body, it is obscure like smoke. These words "restricted" me—they enclosed me within a limit I was not to cross—so that I withdrew from that line of questioning and asked him who he was. And he answered me thus:

> “Between two shores of Italy rise rocks,
> and not far distant from your homeland,
> so high that the thunders sound much lower;
> And they form a hump called Catria,
> beneath which a hermitage is consecrated,
> which used to be devoted to worship <term>latria: the highest form of worship, reserved for God alone, as opposed to the honor given to saints.</term> alone.”

<column-break/>

Between two shores: that is, between the Tyrrhenian Sea to the south and the Adriatic Sea to the north, lies the Apennines, which divides Italy down the middle. In that part of the mountain range where the Apennines are higher than anywhere else—this mountain is between Abruzzi and the March of Ancona—they say that Peter Damian <note>A 11th-century Benedictine monk and reformer known for his asceticism.</note> built two monasteries in the Apennines. The text is arranged thus: Peter Damian...

<meta>This page continues the conversation in the Seventh Heaven (the Sphere of Saturn). The spirit of Saint Peter Damian has just explained that he cannot reveal the secret of predestination, as it is hidden even from the highest angels. He now shifts to describing his earthly life and the corruption of the contemporary Church.</meta>

<header>PARADISO</header>

Thus he began his third speech to me,
and then continuing, he said: "In that place,
in the service of God, I became so firm
That with only foods seasoned with olive oil
I lightly passed through heats and frosts,
content in my contemplative thoughts.
That cloister used to yield to these heavens
a fertile harvest, but now it has become so vain
that its emptiness must soon be revealed."

<term>Latria</term> <note>original: "LATRIA"</note> signifies a deserted place. It also refers to the service which we owe solely to God; hence "idolatry" is the greatest sin, because we give to others that which we owe only to God. **HERE** <note>original: "QUIUI"</note>—that is, in this place—I remained in such a way that, using only foods seasoned with oil, I gave myself to serving God in contemplation, enduring both heat and frost. **USED TO YIELD**: He grieves that this monastery used to produce men who were saints, and who ascended to this heaven through contemplation; but now it has become vain and empty of good men. And for this reason, it must be **revealed**—that is, it must be made manifest that it is no longer what it used to be.

"In that place I was Peter Damian,
and Peter the Sinner was in the house
of Our Lady on the Adriatic shore.
Little of mortal life was left to me
when I was called and dragged to that hat
which is poured only from bad to worse.
Cephas came, and the great vessel
of the Holy Spirit came, lean and barefoot,
taking their food from whatever inn they found.
Now the modern pastors want someone to prop them up
on either side, and someone to lead them—
so heavy are they!—and someone to lift their trains.
They cover their palfreys with their mantles,
so that two beasts go under one skin.
Oh Patience, that you endure so much!"

This refers to the fact that Peter and Paul were lean because of their continent and austere lives, and barefoot because of their extreme poverty; they took food from every inn—as if to say they begged for their bread. **NOW** they are so great <note>meaning "so worldly/pompous"</note>. Not without reason does this spirit feel such grief, for he wrote two works—one of letters and one of sermons—which record these things without any shame. Certainly, the sentiment of Saint Bernard is true: all other states of life involve more labor than pleasure, but the priestly order has found a way to flee everything that might be troublesome and follow every kind of pleasure. **CEPHAS CAME**: because Peter is interpreted as **Cephas** <note>original: "cephas . i . caput"</note>, meaning "head," because he is the head of the Apostles and the first Pope. **THE GREAT VESSEL**: that is, Paul, who, as we showed in the second canto of the *Inferno*, is called the "vessel of election" <note>original: "vas electionis"</note>.

At this voice, I saw many little flames
descending from step to step and spinning,
and every turn made them more beautiful.
They came and stopped around this one,
and let out a cry of such a high sound
that nothing here could be compared to it;
Nor did I understand it, so did the thunder overcome me.

These are spirits. It is easy to draw the allegory if you remember what we said above regarding contemplation.

<column-break/>

He began his third speech because he had previously said two things: first, "you have a mortal hearing," and second, when he spoke of "divine light." And now he tells how between two shores of Italy rocks rise—that is, the Apennine mountains rise to such an altitude that the thunders generated in the air are lower than the heights of the rocks. This place is not far from your homeland—that is, from Tuscany—for it is between Gubbio and Pergola. These rocks rising up form a **hump** <note>original: "gibbo," meaning a hunch or protuberance</note> called Catria, beneath which a hermitage is consecrated. A "hermitage" <note>original: "hermo"</note> is a forest; "heremos" in Greek <note>original: "heremo in greco"</note> signifies a deserted place. **HERE**—that is, in this place—I remained in such a way that, using only foods seasoned with oil, I gave myself to serving God in contemplation, enduring both heat and frost.

**IN THAT PLACE**: That is, in the hermitage of Catria, I was Peter Damian; and he gives his proper name. And Peter the Sinner was in the house of Our Lady on the Adriatic shore: The meaning is: "I was a hermit in Catria where I was not called 'the sinner,' because, having already been purged of vices, I was devoted to contemplation. But before that, I had been a monk in Saint Mary’s of Ravenna on the Adriatic shore, and there I was called 'the sinner' because I was not yet purged of my vices." **LITTLE MORTAL LIFE**: We say a man lives while the soul is joined to the body; but such a life is mortal because it fades quickly. Therefore, he was already old when he was not only called, but dragged by force to the **hat**—that is, the Cardinalate. **WHICH IS POURED FROM BAD TO WORSE**: This dignity goes from bad to worse every day because those who succeed to it are always worse. **CEPHAS CAME**: He wants to show how much the modern pastors have degenerated and strayed from the first march of Christ.

At the exclamation of Peter Damian, more spirits descended toward him from the steps of the ladder, whom he calls "little flames." Their great circling signifies the reflection of the soul upon God, which makes us rejoice more; and as the joy is greater, so too is the splendor. And they cried out so loudly that in this world there is nothing to which it could be compared, for everything else would be lesser. Therefore, having no sound to equal it to, he calls it "thunder," which overcame him in such a way that he did not understand what the spirits said.

The page concludes with a celestial display of spirits descending the ladder of contemplation with a deafening, incomprehensible cry.</summary>

<header>CANTO XXII OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE</header>

<image-desc>An illuminated initial 'A' featuring a pink letter on a blue ground with gold leaf, surrounded by ornate floral and leafy scrollwork in green, blue, and red that extends into the left margin.</image-desc>
Overcome with stupor, to my guide
I turned, like a little child who runs back
always to where he trusts the most;
And she, like a mother who aids
her pale and breathless son at once
with her voice that is used to comforting,
Said to me: "Do you not know you are in heaven?
And do you not know that heaven is all holy,
and that what is done here comes from good zeal?
How the singing would have transformed you,
and my smile too—now you can imagine it <note>Dante implies that if the shout alone terrified him, the beauty of the song and Beatrice’s smile in this higher sphere would have been more than his mortal senses could bear.</note>
since that cry has moved you so much.
In which, had you understood its prayers,
the vengeance would already be known to you,
which you shall see before you die. <note>A prophecy concerning the divine punishment of corrupt church leaders.</note>
The sword from up here does not strike in haste
nor slow, except in the eyes of him
who awaits it with desire or with fear.
But turn yourself now toward others;
for many illustrious spirits you shall see,
if you direct your gaze as I say."

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A large blue initial 'S' set within a square gold-leaf frame.</image-desc>
We have arrived at the twenty-second chapter, which contains five parts. In the first, it contains the matter placed in the previous canto. In the second, it introduces the spirit of Benedict <note>Saint Benedict of Nursia (c. 480–547), the founder of Western monasticism.</note>, who reveals himself and his other companions. In the third, the author raises a doubt to Saint Benedict. In the fourth, he describes his ascent to the firmament <note>The Eighth Heaven, or the Starry Sphere.</note>. In the last, he places his reflection upon all the lower spheres.

Dismayed, then, by the great sound, he ran back to Beatrice like a son to his mother, and she, comforting him, showed him that because he is in heaven—which, because it is holy, nothing harmful is done there—he must not fear, because everything there is done with good zeal. And Beatrice adds: think how the singing of these spirits would have transformed and disturbed you if human ears could have heard it, since this cry has so moved you. And the author interposed these words, smiling, and said: "Now you can imagine it," as if to say: "from this you can think how much the song would have moved me." In that cry, if you had understood its prayers—that is, if you had understood what Peter Damian was praying for—you would know the vengeance that God has ordained against the [corrupt] prelates. And here he predicts the capture of Pope Boniface <note>Refers to the Outrage of Anagni in 1303, where Pope Boniface VIII was seized by French forces and Italian rivals.</note>, of whom mention was made in Purgatory. But he does not want to show that he has heard it, because he would be making a profession of prophecy; rather, he pretends that Beatrice shows it to him. <gloss>i.e., he shows that he believes this will happen according to theological judgments.</gloss>

**THE SWORD FROM ABOVE** <gloss>i.e., the punitive justice of God</gloss> **DOES NOT CUT**: does not punish in haste nor late...

<summary>Dante is terrified by a thunderous shout from the spirits calling for divine justice, but Beatrice reassures him of heaven's goodness. The commentary identifies this as the opening of Canto XXII, outlining its structure and explaining the prophecy of divine vengeance against corrupt clergy.</summary>

...because in everything He observes the appropriate time. But "to the view"—that is, if not to the view of him who expects it, either despairing because it seems to others that He strikes in haste, or fearing because it seems to others that He comes before His time. But turn yourself now toward others, that is, toward these other spirits, and you will see many illustrious ones: if you direct, that is, direct your gaze—your sight—as I say.

As it pleased her, I directed my eyes
and saw a hundred small spheres that together
were beautifying each other with mutual rays.
I stood as one who represses within himself
the point of desire, and does not venture
to ask, fearing too much.
And the greatest and most luminous
of those pearls came forward
to make my desire content with itself.
Then from within it I heard: "If you could see,
as I do, the charity that burns among us,
your thoughts would be expressed.
But so that you do not delay by waiting
for your high goal, I will give you an answer
even to the thought of which you are so wary.
That mountain on whose slope Cassino lies
was once frequented upon its summit
by the people deceived and ill-disposed. <note>Monte Cassino was a site of pagan worship before Saint Benedict arrived.</note>
And I am he who first carried up there
the name of Him who brought to earth
the truth that so uplifts us. <note>Saint Benedict refers to Christ, who brought the Gospel to humanity.</note>
And so much grace shines upon me
that I drew the surrounding towns
away from the impious cult that seduced the world.
These other fires were all contemplative
men, kindled by that heat
which brings forth holy flowers and fruits.
Here is Macarius, here is Romuald, <note>Saint Macarius of Egypt and Saint Romuald, founder of the Camaldolese Order.</note>
here are my brothers who, within the cloisters,
stayed their feet and kept their hearts firm."
And I to him: "The affection you show
by speaking with me, and the good appearance
that I see and note in all your ardors,
has so dilated my confidence,
just as the sun does to the rose when opened,
it becomes as great as it has the power to be.
Therefore I pray you, and you, father, assure me
if I can receive such grace that I
may see you with your face revealed." <note>Dante asks to see the saint's actual human form, which is currently hidden inside a sphere of light.</note>
Whereupon he: "Brother, your high desire
shall be fulfilled in the final sphere,
where all the others and my own are fulfilled."

<column-break/>

I turned to the spirits as it pleased Beatrice, but I did not dare to say what I desired to understand. But the greatest flame, who was Saint Benedict, said: "If you knew the charity that burns among us, you would express your every thought, because you would not fear being a nuisance in asking."

Cassino is a mountain in Campania. On this mountain was the temple of Apollo, and afterwards Saint Benedict worked so much that, having brought the surrounding people to the true religion, he destroyed the temple of Apollo and dedicated there the Church of Saint Martin; and the altar of Apollo he dedicated to John the Baptist. And he established his monastery there. And therefore he says he carried there the name of Him who introduced the truth—that is, the name of Christ, who is the truth and the life <note>original: "veritas et vita"</note>. This is that truth that so uplifts us—that is, lifts us so much from the earth, because it leads us to heaven. And divine grace shone so much in Saint Benedict that he brought all the surrounding lands to the Christian religion. Benedict was from Norcia, a monk and then an abbot; and he established the rule of the "white monks" <note>The Benedictine Order.</note>. He built many monasteries, but especially that of Monte Cassino. For having, by divine miracle, caused the temple of Apollo to fall into ruin before a great crowd, he was able to lead the people to the Christian religion. He lived in the times of Emperor Justinian, in the year of our salvation 525, during the pontificate of Boniface I. KINDLED BY THAT HEAT: that is, by the love of God, from which every good flower and fruit is born.

The words that the spirit had spoken gave the author the boldness to ask, and he asked if he could have such grace as to see his face revealed and not wrapped in 그 light. And it is reasonable that the poet, being already in the sphere of the contemplatives, should reach such a high thought as to desire to know the essence of the human soul. To this, the spirit responds and demonstrates that this desire of his—and likewise that of the other elevated spirits—cannot be fulfilled except in the final sphere, that is, in the Empyrean heaven where God is: who alone gives perfection to human and angelic nature. And therefore in that sphere is perfection, and in it every part is where it always was because it does not move. But it is the first mover and is always quiet. Therefore it does not happen that a part of it which is now in one place is afterwards in another, as happens in the other spheres which are in constant movement because it is not "in a place"—that is, it is not located and contained like the other nine spheres. And it does not rotate—that is, it does not stop upon poles like the others, for the ninth sphere has two poles: the arctic and the antarctic.

<summary>Dante encounters Saint Benedict in the Seventh Heaven, who recounts his mission to convert Monte Cassino from paganism to Christianity and introduces other contemplative spirits. Dante asks to see Benedict's true form, but is told such a vision is only possible in the Empyrean, the final, unmoving heaven.</summary>

<header>CANTO XXII</header>

In it, every desire is perfect,
mature, and whole; in that one alone,
and every part is where it always was.
Because it is not in space and has no poles,
and our ladder reaches all the way to it,
which is why it vanishes from your sight.
The patriarch Jacob saw it reaching
that far up, stretching its upper part,
when it appeared to him so laden with angels.

<margin>One evening on his journey he lay down to sleep in the open air, and for a pillow he took a stone; and that night he saw in a vision a ladder that rose from the earth to heaven, and many angels ascended and descended upon it.</margin>

But to climb it now, no one lifts
their feet from the earth, and my Rule
remains below to the detriment of the parchment.
The walls that used to be an abbey
have become dens, and the cowls
are sacks full of foul flour.
But even heavy usury is not taken
so much against God’s pleasure as that fruit
which makes the hearts of monks so foolish.
For whatever the Church guards belongs
entirely to the people who ask in God’s name,
not to relatives or other uglier things.
The flesh of mortals is so soft
that a good beginning does not suffice below
from the sprouting of the oak to the making of the acorn.

<margin>And everything that the Church guards—that is, preserves because it is leftover from the clerics who serve it—belongs to the poor; and not to the relatives of priests nor to other "ugly" things, meaning their mistresses.</margin>

Peter began without gold and without silver,
and I with prayers and with fasting,
and Francis humbly began his convent.
And if you look at the beginning of each,
then look again at where they have strayed,
you will see the white turned to brown.
Truly, the Jordan turned backward,
and the sea's flight when God willed it,
were more marvelous to see than help would be here.
Thus he spoke to me, and then he withdrew
to his college; the college drew together,
then like a whirlwind it all gathered itself upward.

<margin>The people of Israel passed through, and so it was. Therefore, it was more miraculous to see the sea flee than it will be to see the rescue of the Church here, which is in ruins.</margin>

The sweet lady then pushed me behind them
with a single sign up that ladder

<column-break/>

and so then it leaps; and "our ladder reaches" and passes up to there. Because the contemplatives reach that point through their contemplation, and passing through all the heavens, they reach God. But "it vanishes from Dante's sight"—that is, from his vision—because the soul within the body cannot contemplate so high. "The patriarch saw it up there." It is written in Genesis that when Jacob <note>Original text says "isach" (Isaac), but refers to Jacob's flight</note> fled the wrath of his brother whom he had defrauded of the blessing and paternal inheritance, and his father had commanded him to go to Mesopotamia and take a wife from the daughters of Laban and not of Canaan, it happened that...

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter D in blue ink.</image-desc>
He says that none of his monks lift their feet from the earth—meaning, they do not lift their affections out of earthly things—to climb this ladder—meaning, to devote themselves to contemplation. "And my Rule"—the institutions which I have left written so that the monks observing them might be saved—remains down in the world "to the detriment of the parchment." Because, not being observed, it is of no use to the monks, and the parchment was wasted in writing it. "The walls that used to be an abbey have become dens," because the monks are worse than thieves, as they attend to nothing but stealing the fruits of the monasteries. "And the cowls"—that is, the garments of the monks—are sacks for flour. An excellent metaphor to demonstrate the degenerate life of his monks. But usury is not so heavy a sin against God’s pleasure as that "fruit" <note>Referring to the misuse of ecclesiastical tithes or income</note> which they take more than they should, beyond an honest life, which makes their hearts and wills so foolish that they wander in secular things.

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter E in blue ink.</image-desc>
And without fail, it is a matter of the highest amazement to consider the beginning of our religion founded in poverty and charity, and then to see how much the succession has degenerated. And some understand "Peter" here to be Peter Damian, who began the Order of the Dove. "Truly the Jordan turned backward." This river, turning back, left a dry space for the people of Israel when they came to the Promised Land. The Jordan, according to Jerome, is named from two springs from which it is born: one is called *Jor* and the other *Dan*. "The sea's flight was more..." the meaning is that it should not seem a marvelous thing to anyone that God punishes the vices of the prelates, since it was a more marvelous thing that the Red Sea fled and gave a dry place when through that...

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter N in blue ink.</image-desc>
Man would not understand by himself that the "Supreme Good" was found in contemplation if the study of theology did not push him toward it.

# PARADISO
## XXII

if its power ever overcame my nature.
Never here below, where one ascends and descends
naturally, was there a motion so rapid
that it could be compared to my wing.
O Reader, as I may yet return to that devout
triumph for which I often weep for
my sins and beat my breast,
you would not have pulled out and thrust
your finger into the fire as quickly as I saw the sign
that follows the Bull and was within it.

**O** glorious stars, O light pregnant
with great virtue, from which I acknowledge
all my genius, whatever it may be!
With you was born and with you was hidden
he who is the father of every mortal life <note>The Sun, which gives life to the physical world.</note>
when I first felt the Tuscan air.
And then, when grace was bestowed upon me
to enter the high wheel that turns you,
your region was allotted to me.
To you my soul now devoutly sighs
to acquire strength for the difficult passage
that draws me to itself.

"You are so near to the ultimate salvation,"
Beatrice began, "that you must
have your eyes clear and sharp.
And therefore, before you enter further into it,
look down and see how much of the world
I have already set beneath your feet;
so that your heart, as joyful as can be,
may present itself to the triumphant throng
that moves gladly through this round ether."
With my sight I returned through all
the seven spheres and saw this globe
such that I smiled at its humble appearance;
and I truly approve of that counsel
which holds it for least, and he who thinks on other things
can truly be called upright.

"So much did he fill [the heavens], and having contemplated the wandering stars and the fixed stars of the poles, he saw how much of our day lay under night; and he laughed at the mockery of his own [headless] corpse." <note>original Latin: "tanto impleuit stellasque uagas mitatus et astra fixa polis uidit quanta sub nocte iaceret nostra dies : risitque sui ludibria trunci". This is a reference to Lucan's Pharsalia, describing the soul of Pompey the Great looking back at Earth.</note> AND WHAT COUNSEL: He concludes that the best counsel is that of the person who has called the earth "least"—that is, who esteems earthly and fleeting things less than all others. And he who thinks of things other than earthly matters can truly be called upright, meaning good.

I saw the daughter of Latona <note>The Moon</note> aflame,
without that shadow which was once the reason
why I believed it to be rare and dense.
The aspect of your son, Hyperion <note>The Sun</note>

<column-break/>

The swift motion signifies the passage of the mind, than which nothing swifter can be found. YOU WOULD NOT HAVE: Here the author uses an effective comparison, because we use great speed in things that can harm us. With this speed, he entered from the seventh heaven into the eighth sphere where all the stars are, except for the seven planets; and he entered it through that sign of the zodiac that comes after the Bull [Taurus], and this is Gemini.

**E**ntered into Gemini, he congratulates the stars of this sign which grant the influence of great virtue, and says that from them, as a secondary cause, he acknowledges the powers of his intellect, whether small or great. For in the hour when he came forth from his mother's womb and began to breathe this Tuscan air where he was born, Gemini was ascending and the sun was within them. And he calls the sun the father of every mortal life because it is the generator of all sensitive life, though not of the rational soul. And similarly, "when I entered the eighth heaven, I entered through the part occupied by you."
<margin>Dante affirms that at his birth he had Gemini as his ascendant, and the sun within them, a nature which influences supreme knowledge. Because Gemini is the house of Mercury; and if Mercury is fortunate, it disposes a person toward supreme knowledge. And according to Misabel <note>Mashallah ibn Athari (c. 740–815 AD), a Persian Jewish astronomer and astrologer whose works were widely used in the Middle Ages.</note>, it is an aerial, masculine, and diurnal sign. But we have spoken of them elsewhere.</margin>

<insert>o</insert> The first precept of Beatrice—that is, of Sacred Scripture—is that when a person has made such progress in contemplation that they have already ascended with the mind to the contemplation of God, and already have their light clear—that is, the mind is empty of every perturbation—and it is sharp—meaning the intellect is subtle—which is nothing other than knowing the good and confirming oneself in it so that no appetite can move one to evil: then she wishes that one should turn back and consider the lowliness and vileness of fleeting and mortal things. Once these things are considered, he will take greater joy in the spheres, having reached such a degree. Therefore, returning through all seven spheres down to the earth—that is, through all secondary causes down to matter and to fleeting and mortal things—he smiled at its humble appearance. This passage is taken from Cicero’s text in the *Republic* <note>Specifically "The Dream of Scipio."</note>, in which he depicts Scipio, having ascended to this heaven, doing the same. And Lucan also writes similarly of Pompey having ascended to heaven. "After [he filled himself] with light..."

**I** saw the daughter of Latona—that is, the moon, daughter of Latona, whose fable was told by us elsewhere. Aflame: that is, lit up; and he wishes to show that it was illuminated by the sun from the upper side, which he could see being in the eighth sphere.

<summary>Dante enters the Heaven of the Fixed Stars through the constellation of Gemini, his birth sign, and looks back across the seven planetary spheres to see the smallness and vanity of the Earth. The commentary links this celestial perspective to classical sources like Cicero and Lucan, emphasizing the superiority of spiritual contemplation over earthly concerns.</summary>

There I endured and saw how Maia and Dione
move near and around him <note>The sun.</note>;
From there appeared to me the tempering of Jove

**And near to him**: <gloss>Maia was one of the seven daughters of Atlas and bore Mercury to Jove. And Mercury, in his course, never moves far from the sun. Dione, as we have shown, is the mother of Venus. And he says that these two planets, Venus and Mercury, move near and around the sun.</gloss> **The tempering of Jove between his father [Saturn] and his son [Mars]**: <gloss>because Jove, being situated between the cold Saturn and the hot Mars, becomes temperate.</gloss> **Became clear to me**: <gloss>that is, it was made manifest to me.</gloss> **The variation they make**: <gloss>because he had already ascended so far in contemplation that all these things were known to him.</gloss>

as I revolved with the twins,
appeared all to me, from its hills to its river mouths.
Then I turned my eyes back to the beautiful eyes.

**Makes us so fierce**: <gloss>He marvels at human folly, which takes such insolence for a thing so small as the earth.</gloss> **From hills to river mouths**: <gloss>that is, from the mountains to the seas.</gloss> **Then I turned my eyes back to the beautiful eyes of Beatrice**: <gloss>as if to say, "I returned to theology."</gloss>

### CANTO XXIII

As the bird among the beloved leaves,
having rested on the nest of her sweet brood
throughout the night that hides things from us,
who, to see the aspects she longs for
and to find the food wherewith to feed them—
in which her heavy labors are a delight—
anticipates the time upon the open spray,
and with ardent affection awaits the sun,
gazing fixedly for the dawn to break;
so my lady was standing erect
and attentive, turned toward the region
beneath which the sun shows less haste. <note>The meridian or mid-day sky, where the sun appears to move more slowly at its zenith.</note>

So that, seeing her suspended and longing,
I became as one who, desiring,
would wish for something else, and is stilled by hope.
But there was little time between one moment and the other—
I mean of my waiting and of my seeing
the heavens becoming more and more bright.
And Beatrice said: "Behold the hosts
of the triumph of Christ, and all the fruit
harvested from the turning of these spheres!" <note>The "fruit" refers to the souls who have been saved through the celestial influences of the planets.</note>
It seemed to me her face was all aflame,
and her eyes were so full of joy
that I must pass it by without description.

As in the full moons and in the clear skies,
Trivia <note>An epithet for Diana, the moon goddess</note> smiles among the eternal nymphs <note>The stars</note>
who paint the sky through all its depths,
I saw, above thousands of lamps,
a Sun that kindled every one of them,
as our sun does for the sights above; <note>In medieval cosmology, it was believed the stars reflected the light of the physical sun; here, Christ kindles the "stars" of the blessed souls.</note>
and through that living light shone through
the glowing substance, so bright
that my vision could not endure it.
O Beatrice, sweet guide and dear!
She said to me: "That which overcomes you
is a power against which nothing can defend itself.
Here is the wisdom and the power
that opened the roads between heaven and earth,
for which there was once so long a longing."

As fire from a cloud is unlocked,
expanding so that it cannot be contained,
and against its own nature falls to earth,
so my mind, among those feasts
becoming greater than itself, issued forth...

<column-break/>

the Church Triumphant. In the second part, he describes the
leader of this army. In the third, the soldiers
who follow him. In the fourth, he describes the ninth
sphere. Thus, as the bird among the beloved
branches—because she has placed her children there
near the nest and waits through the night for the day
to come, both to see them and to provide the food
with which she feeds them, in which every heavy labor
and fatigue is a comfort to her—she anticipates and looks ahead,
rising before the day and, turned toward the east, awaits the dawn. So Beatrice, to feed Dante with celestial
food, stood erect and attentive toward that region where the sun shows less haste, that is, toward the
meridian part. For when the sun is in the middle of the sky, it seems to move more slowly than when it is in the east
or the west; and he imagines that just as when the sun is at midday it is over our heads and illuminates
everything, so Christ, who led this army, illuminates them all.

Seeing the poet Beatrice suspended in
anticipation and longing, he knew that she
awaited something beautiful; he became a man who
desires something other than what he has, and hoped
to have it, and therefore was appeased and contented by
that hope. But there was little space between the one and the other—that is,
between the waiting and the seeing—before the sky, painted at that
point, became brighter. And Beatrice said: "Behold the
hosts of the triumph of Christ," that is, of the blessed
recovered by Christ, who by dying destroyed
our death and triumphed over the enemy; "and all
the fruit harvested from the turning of these spheres," that is,
the gain that the movements of the heavens have made
by sending their influences into our souls. And he
rightly gathers the fruit of all the spheres in the eighth
sphere. For all the others receive influence
from this one; and this one from the First Mover; and the
First Mover from the Intelligence that God has
placed there, and that from God as the first cause.
**SO FULL OF JOY**: to denote that
contemplation takes great joy when it approaches its
end.

In this eighth sphere, Christ appeared
with the souls of all the blessed, as if from
that place from which the influences come to all
the other heavens below him. He posits then that
Christ in this army was such as Trivia is—
that is, the moon—among the eternal nymphs—that is, among the
stars which paint the sky—that is, adorn the sky—
through all its depths, which is to say its parts. And thus Christ
illuminated and kindled those souls
as the sun illuminates the sights above, that is, the stars
which receive their light from him. And through the living
light of Christ, the glowing substance shone through, that is,
the humanity of Christ, which was so bright that
Dante's mortal eyes were dazzled by it. **O
BEATRICE**: he does not merely call her, but it is an exclamation. "That
which overcomes you," that is, conquers you, is divine power
against which nothing can defend itself because it conquers everything.
Here in Christ was the wisdom which is attributed
to the Son, and the power which, although it is
attributed to the Father, nevertheless all three
persons in the divinity are omnipotent.

<summary>Dante witnesses the "Triumph of Christ" in the Eighth Heaven, where Christ appears as a sun illuminating thousands of souls (the "eternal nymphs"), symbolizing the culmination of celestial influence and the opening of the way to heaven.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Canto XXIII of Paradiso. Dante has just witnessed the blinding light of Christ’s triumph. Beatrice now encourages him to look at her again, as his sight has been strengthened by the divine vision, though he finds himself unable to fully recall or describe the experience.</meta>

<page-num>340</page-num>
<header>CANTO XXII</header> <note>Though the header indicates Canto XXII, the text continues Canto XXIII of the *Paradiso*.</note>

...and what it did to remember, it does not know.
"Open your eyes and look at what I am;
you have seen things that have made you
powerful enough to sustain my smile."
I was like one who finds himself
waking from a forgotten vision, and who strives
in vain to bring it back to mind.

**Dapes** in Latin means food, whether royal or divine; and we reasonably call them food because just as the body feeds on elemental nourishment, so the human mind feeds on contemplation. And therefore it follows: **Made** (*Facta*) greater: and understand this as being through divine nourishment. **AND THAT** it did to remember, it does not know. Note that he himself could not remember in what manner he had arrived at this height. **OPEN YOUR EYES.** Beatrice concludes that since Dante has seen Christ and his army, he has become capable of sustaining her smile.

If all those tongues were to sound now
which Polyhymnia <note>The Muse of sacred poetry and hymns.</note> and her sisters made
most rich with their sweetest milk,

to help me, not a thousandth of the truth
would be reached in singing of the holy smile,
and how it made the holy countenance clear.

And so, in depicting Paradise,
 the sacred poem must leap over,
like one who finds his path cut off.

But whoever considers the weighty theme
and the mortal shoulder that is burdened by it,
would not blame it if it trembles underneath.

It is no voyage for a little boat,
this water that my daring prow goes cleaving,
nor for a pilot who would spare himself.

"Why does my face so enamor you
that you do not turn to the beautiful garden
which flowers beneath the rays of Christ?

There is the Rose <note>The Virgin Mary.</note> in which the Divine Word
became flesh; there are the Lilies <note>The Apostles and Saints.</note>
by whose odor the good way was found."

So said Beatrice; and I, ready for her
counsels, gave myself once again
to the struggle of my feeble eyes.

As, under a ray of sun which streams
through a broken cloud, my eyes—even while covered in shadow—
once saw a meadow of flowers,

so I saw many crowds of splendors,
flashed upon from above by burning rays,
without seeing the source of the glows.

O sovereign virtue who so imprints them,
you uplifted yourself to grant me space
for my eyes, which were not powerful enough.

<column-break/>

The poet shows wonderful genius in describing how his mind was strengthened so much beyond its nature and above human possibility that it became capable of the vision of God. He makes a comparison to a cloud made of dry vapors in which fire is kindled; and because it cannot be contained, it expands and breaks out, running downward against its nature, given that the nature of fire is always to go upward. Thus my mind, among those **dapes**, that is, among those divine foods.

The meaning of the verses already written is that if all the poets nourished by the milk of the Muses <note>The "sisters" of Polyhymnia mentioned in the poem.</note> wished to undertake the description of the present matter, in no way would their verses be equal to the subject. Nor by singing could they reach the "holy smile," nor even the thousandth part of it. And certainly that part of theology which treats of the Divine Essence is neither comprehensible nor speakable to any human intellect. Plato feels this same way when he writes. <note>The commentator likely refers to Plato's views on the ineffability of the Supreme Good or the One.</note>

He begins to describe the celestial militia. And he feigns that Beatrice urges him to look at it; she says, "O Dante, why does my face enamor you so much that you do not turn?" as if to say: although I have been made so beautiful—because in this place the incomprehensible matter of Christ is handled through me—nevertheless, consider also his family, which truly is a "garden" that flowers, that is, which produces flowers under the rays of Christ. For just as the rays of the sun illuminate all earthly things and generate them by their virtue, so Christ, the true Sun, illuminates these spirits. **THERE IS THE ROSE**: Mary the Virgin, who is deservedly likened to the rose, which, for its utility in various ailments, for its beauty, and for its scent, holds the princedom among flowers. **LILIES**: the apostles, doctors, and martyrs, in whom there is the highest brightness of purity. **I GAVE MYSELF** to the struggle: he denotes that although the eye of the human mind is dazzled by the light of the knowledge of such ineffable things, nonetheless we must contemplate as much as sacred theology commands us. **AS** (*Chome*): the text arranges it thus: "I saw many crowds of splendors," that is, of shining spirits, "flashed upon," that is, many illuminated by burning rays "from above," that is, from the upper part; just as my eyes once saw a meadow of flowers covered in shadow under the rays of the sun, which "just now" (*pur hora*), that is, recently, "passed through" (*mei*); because *meare* in Latin <note>original: 'meare'</note> means "to pass through." **THROUGH A BROKEN CLOUD**, that is, through a shattered cloud. Therefore, the spirits shone, struck by the rays of light that came to them from Christ, just as flowers in a meadow shine.

<summary>Dante describes his inability to fully recall or articulate the divine vision of Christ's triumph, using metaphors of a "weighty theme" and a "little boat." Beatrice directs his attention away from her own beauty toward the "garden" of the blessed, specifically identifying the Virgin Mary as the Rose and the Apostles as the Lilies.</summary>

...as when a meadow, being in shadow, is suddenly struck by rays of sunlight that come through broken clouds.

**T**he name of the beautiful flower <note>The "beautiful flower" is a common poetic title for the Virgin Mary.</note> which I always invoke
both morning and evening, completely drew
my soul to contemplate the greatest fire <note>The "greatest fire" refers to the supreme brightness of Mary among the created spirits.</note>:
And as my two eyes were painted by
the quality and the quantity of the living star
which conquers up there as it conquered down here,
from within the sky a small torch descended,
formed in a circle in the manner of a crown,
and it encircled her and revolved around her.
Whatever melody sounds sweetest
down here and draws the soul most to itself,
would seem like a cloud that thunders when torn,
compared to the sounding of that lyre
with which was crowned the beautiful sapphire <note>The sapphire represents Mary, whose beauty gives the heaven its blue hue.</note>
by which the brightest heaven is "ensapphired."
"I am angelic love, who circles
the high joy that breathes from the womb
which was the host of our desire;
And I shall circle, Lady of Heaven, while
you follow your son, and make the supreme sphere
more divine because you enter it."
Thus the circling melody
sealed itself, and all the other lights
made the name of Mary resound.
The royal mantle of all the volumes <note>The "royal mantle" refers to the Primum Mobile, the ninth and outermost physical sphere of the universe, which encloses all the others.</note>
of the world, which most burns and is most quickened
in the breath of God and in His ways,
had its inner shore <note>The "shore" or "rim" of this sphere.</note> above us
at so great a distance that its appearance
did not yet appear to me where I was.
Therefore my eyes did not have the power
to follow the crowned flame
which rose up after her seed <note>Mary’s "seed" refers to her son, Jesus Christ, who has already ascended.</note>.
And like a little child who toward his mother
stretches his arms after he has taken the milk,
because of the soul which even outwardly catches fire,
each of those splendors stretched upward
with its flame, so that the deep affection
they had for Mary was made plain to me.

<gloss>He knows her gestures, stretching them toward the mother to touch her, because the affection of the soul catches fire in a way that it comes to the exterior parts; likewise those flames of the blessed spirits stretched themselves toward Mary, demonstrating their affection toward her.</gloss>

Then they remained there in my sight,
singing *Regina Coeli* <note>Latin: "Queen of Heaven," an ancient Latin Marian antiphon.</note> so sweetly
that the delight of it has never left me.

<column-break/>

**T**he name of Mary drew me so much to her with
all my soul that I watched for where the greatest
fire was—that is, the greatest splendor—because
I knew that she must be there. **AND AS BOTH
eyes were painted for me** by the quality and the quantity: he continues
demonstrating what he saw in the greatest fire—that is, in
Mary, who surpasses all others in the light of grace:
the "how much"—that is, the quality and the quantity
of her splendor. **Of the living star**: Of Mary,
the true morning star <note>original: "lucifero"</note> and close to the eternal sun,
of whom the Apocalypse writes:

> A woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars. <note>Latin: "Mulier amicta sole : et luna sub pedibus eius . Et in capite eius corona stellarum duodecim." (Revelation 12:1).</note>

He saw also the
angel Gabriel who came from on high to raise her up; and
he describes him as a circular crown entirely of fire.
**WHATEVER melody**: an excellent comparison
to denote how much sweetness was in the song of
the angel: since our music, in comparison
to that, would not seem sweet, but would seem
disturbing like the sound of thunder. **BECAUSE you
enter it**: that is, because you enter; and certainly no
soul ever entered into heaven with more glory. **THE ROYAL
mantle of all the volumes.** He places the return of Mary
at the ninth sphere; and how the other blessed ones remained
there; and the distance above him where
Mary passed; and he returns to the text: **THE ROYAL MANTLE**
is the Primum Mobile <note>The First Moved sphere.</note> which covers all the other
spheres, which "most burns"—that is, most heats itself—and is most
quickened—that is, shines more and is more active and effective
than the other volumes—that is, the other heavens.
**In the manner of God and in His ways**: because this
sphere is closer to God than the others, and therefore receives
His virtue more directly. This is the principle of motion
and of life, and has a universal power that shapes
worldly particulars. And from this all
the others receive, according to the natural order, a preserving
and shaping power, just as from God comes
natural being. Therefore it is quickened in the manner of God
because it receives from Him the life-giving power. **HAD
ABOVE US**: above me and Beatrice. **THE INNER
SHORE**: the lower part of the circumference. But
it was so distant that it could not be seen from the place
where I was. And because of this my eyes could not
follow the crowned flame—that is, MARY
encircled by the angel in the form of a crown. And truly
the human intellect cannot elevate itself so much that
it sees the end of the ascent of Mary, who
rose up after her seed—that is, after Christ.
And as the child, sucking the milk, takes
such pleasure that it cannot be contained; and therefore with his hands...

**T**he author imagines that in the eighth sphere he saw all
the blessed ones, as if in the place from which by
influence the grace of God proceeded...

<header>CANTO</header>

Oh, how great is the abundance that is stored up
in those richest coffers <note>The "coffers" or "chests" (arche) represent the minds of the blessed spirits.</note> which were
good sowers <note>term: "bubulce" (plowmen/sowers). This refers to those who "sowed" good works on earth to reap heavenly rewards.</note> here below.
Here they live and enjoy the treasure
that was acquired by weeping in the exile
of Babylon, where the gold was left behind.
Here triumphs, under the high Son
of God and Mary, in his victory,
and with the ancient and the new council <note>The "ancient and new council" refers to the saints of the Old and New Testaments.</note>,
he who holds the keys of such glory <note>St. Peter, traditionally depicted with the keys to the Kingdom of Heaven.</note>.

<column-break/>

...precedes first in all virtuous acts. And it demonstrates that he first meditated on the ascension of Christ, and then on Mary: **QUEEN of heaven**: This antiphon or hymn is sung by the Church during the season of the Resurrection: *Queen of heaven, rejoice, alleluia. For He whom you were worthy to bear, alleluia. Has risen, as He said, alleluia. Pray for us to God, alleluia.* <note>original: "Regina celi letare..."</note> **OH HOW GREAT is the abundance**: oh how great is the plenty and the abundance of blessedness that is stored up, rests, and dwells in those richest coffers—that is, in the minds of the blessed which were very capable of receiving divine grace and which were "good sowers"—that is, excellent tillers. *Bubulcus* in Latin signifies the plowman, whom we call a *bidonfolco* <note>An archaic term for an ox-driver or farm laborer.</note>. Hence the Psalmist says: *He who sows sparingly shall reap sparingly. And he who sows in blessings shall also reap of blessings.* <note>original: "Qui parce seminat..."</note> **Here they live and enjoy the treasure**. Because in the world they acquired through tears and mourning that glory in which they now rejoice: **here triumphs he**, meaning the apostle Peter in his victory: because he conquered the devil, the world, and the flesh. **And he triumphs under the Son of God**, because if He had not redeemed us, we would have remained in the miserable servitude of the devil. And it says that he holds the keys of such glory to align with the words of Christ saying: *And I will give to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. And whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven: And whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.* <note>original: "Et dabo tibi claues..."</note>

## CANTO XXIII <note>Though the original heading says XXIII, the text that follows is actually the beginning of Canto XXIV.</note> OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut drop cap 'S' featuring foliate and floral motifs within a square border.</image-desc>
**O** fellowship elect to the great supper
of the blessed Lamb, who feeds you
so that your desire is always full,
if by the grace of God this man tastes
of that which falls from your table
before death prescribes his time,
pay heed to his immense affection
and bedew him <note>The imagery suggests "sprinkling" or "refreshing" Dante with the water of divine truth.</note> with as much as you drink;
you drink always from the fountain from which comes his thought.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Small decorative initial 'I' with simple geometric or floral patterns.</image-desc>
**H**e introduces in this twenty-fourth canto the apostle Peter. And because there are three principal steps that lead us to this celestial kingdom—Faith, Hope, and Charity—it follows that Peter examines him on Faith. Therefore, first is the prayer of Beatrice to the blessed spirits. After that, Peter, through the prayers of Beatrice, examines the author on Faith. In the third part, he treats certain doubts of Faith. In the last part, he questions Dante about his belief. Beatrice’s prayer has this beginning: **O FELLOWSHIP elect to the great supper**.

<summary>This page concludes Canto XXIII with a reflection on the heavenly rewards of the saints and the triumph of St. Peter, then opens Canto XXIV with Beatrice's appeal to the saints to examine Dante's faith.</summary>

<page-num>XXIIII</page-num>
<header>PARADISO CANTO</header>

Thus Beatrice and those joyful souls
made themselves spheres upon fixed poles,
flaming strongly in the manner of comets.
And as wheels in the works of clocks
turn so that the first, to one who watches,
seems quiet, and the last seems to fly,
so those dancing circles, differently
dancing according to their wealth,
made me judge them swift and slow.

From the one I noted for greatest beauty,
I saw emerge a fire so happy
that none it left behind excelled its clarity;
And three times around Beatrice
it swept with a song so divine
that my fantasy does not repeat it to me.
Therefore my pen leaps and I do not write it;
for our imagination, much less our speech,
is too vivid a color for such folds. <note>Dante uses a painting metaphor: just as bright colors cannot depict the subtle shadows of folds in fabric, human language cannot capture the divine song.</note>
"O my holy sister, who so prays to us
devoutly by your ardent affection,
that you release me from that beautiful sphere."
After the blessed fire had come to a stop,
it directed its breath toward my lady,
which spoke just as I have said.

<note>Commentary on the verses above:</note>
**Theology is the sister of Peter.** **WHO SO PRAYS TO US**: that is, you inform me by praying to me through your ardent affection toward Dante, that you might release me <note>term: "disfleghe" (to unfold/release). In this context, it refers to the soul of St. Peter detaching itself from the circling group to speak.</note> and take me and make me depart from the sphere and the dance where I was. **AFTER the blessed fire had come to a stop.** The meaning is that after this fire, which is the soul of Peter, had spun three times, he stopped and directed his breath—that is, his speech—toward Beatrice, which Peter spoke using the words already mentioned above.

And she: "O eternal light of the great man
to whom our Lord left the keys
that he brought down of this wondrous joy,
test this man on points both light and grave
as it pleases you, concerning the faith
by which you once walked upon the sea."

<column-break/>

[Continuation from the previous page's commentary] ...ion: **O company elect** to the blessedness upon which the blessed spirits feed; and the food of this supper is the Lamb, which food ensures that whoever feeds upon it is always satisfied. **Fellowship** [Sodalitio]: consortium. Because in Latin *sodalis* signifies a companion. **IF THIS MAN**: if these habits. That is, Dante tastes beforehand that which falls from our table: meaning he tastes ahead of time the celestial glory which the souls already assumed into the supernal heaven enjoy, and into which he will come in due time through the grace of God, without which no good work can exist in man. **BEFORE death prescribes his time**: that is, before death occupies and takes away his time of living. **GIVE HEED to the immense affection.** It is as if she says: it is a just thing that you grant him such grace, since he desires it so much. **DEW from heaven** [Rora celo]: that is, bathe him lightly. *Ros* in Latin signifies "dew." Whence they say: *Rorate caeli* <note>original: "Rorate caeli desuper" (Drop down dew, ye heavens, from above). A traditional liturgical opening during Advent.</note>; and this is easy for you to do because you drink always from the fountain from which every desire comes. **THUS as circles** that rotate upon their blessedness as wheels turn upon poles, that is, the pivots. The meaning is that those souls performed many circular dances. **FLAMING**: that is, shining and flaming. **IN THE MANNER**: in the likeness of comets, which throw their rays far out. We have spoken of the comet before. **AND AS WHEELS**: Just as in a clock there are many wheels where one turns quickly, another less so, and another even less; and thus they decrease in such a way that the last one hardly moves, so did those *carole* <note>term: "carola" (a circular dance accompanied by singing). Landino explains that the speed of the dance corresponds to the degree of the soul's beatitude.</note>—that is, souls—that were turning. Specifically *carola*, which signifies a circular dance, dancing differently. And by this difference, he demonstrates greater or lesser beatitude; and therefore they made me judge them "swift and slow" according to their "wealth."

**From that dancing circle**, that is, the circular dance that is more beautiful than the others because it was where the apostles were, there came out a fire so splendid that none remained there more clear. And this was the soul of Peter, who is among the first happy ones, such that none is more happy; and it turned three times around Beatrice to denote that the doctrine and examples of Peter give true knowledge of the Trinity and of the three theological virtues; and it composes the three principal parts of our soul: that is, the rational, the concupiscible, and the irascible. **With a song so divine**: that is, celestial, that my fantasy does not repeat it—as if to say: I do not remember it, nor with my imagination can I find it again. Therefore I do not write it, because imagination does not serve me. **Too vivid a color for such folds**: This is a metaphor from painting, where to make the distinction of the folds of a garment, it is necessary to use dark colors; and the meaning is that for such distinctions I find no way. **O HOLY sister**: and certainly...

These are the words of Beatrice to the soul of Peter, whom she deservedly calls a **great man**, that is, a man because he was left as Christ’s vicar on earth. And He left him the keys of eternal life which He brought down from heaven to earth. Therefore Beatrice prays to Peter that he might test and examine Dante on faith, on every point, both light and easy as well as grave and difficult; for by which faith you [Peter]...

<summary>In this opening to Canto XXIV, Beatrice calls upon the soul of Saint Peter to examine Dante's faith. Peter emerges from a choir of dancing, flaming spirits described through a complex clockwork metaphor.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the examination of Dante by Saint Peter in the Heaven of the Fixed Stars. Having been introduced by Beatrice, Dante now prepares to define the theological virtue of Faith, drawing on the definitions provided by Saint Paul.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>CANTO XXIV</header>
<sig>H i</sig>

"If he loves well, hopes well, and believes well,
it is not hidden from you, for you have your sight there
where everything is seen depicted. <note>In the "mirror" of God's mind, the blessed see all truths.</note>
But because this kingdom has made citizens
through the true faith, to glorify it,
it is good that he should speak of it."

Just as the bachelor <note>term: "baccellier" (bachelor). In medieval universities, a student who has reached the stage where they can defend a thesis but has not yet become a master.</note> arms himself and does not speak
until the master proposes the question,
to support it and not to define it,
so I was arming myself with every reason
while she was speaking, so as to be ready
for such a questioner and such a profession.
"Speak, good Christian, and make manifest:
what is faith?" At which I raised my brow
toward that light from which this was breathed.
Then I turned to Beatrice, and she promptly
made a sign to me that I should pour
the water out from my inner fountain.
"May the grace that allows me to confess myself,"
I began, "to the high first centurion, <note>term: "primipilo" (primipilus). The highest-ranking centurion in a Roman legion. Dante uses this military term to describe St. Peter's leadership in the Church.</note>
make my thoughts be clearly expressed."
And I followed: "As the true pen
wrote of it, the father of your dear brother, <note>Referring to St. Paul, who with Peter founded the Church in Rome. Dante calls him the "father" of the pen/scripture.</note>
who with you set Rome on the good path: <note>original: "buon filo" (good thread/path).</note>
Faith is the substance of things hoped for,
and the evidence of things not seen;
and this seems to me its quiddity." <note>term: "quiditate" (quiddity). The essential nature or "what-ness" of a thing.</note>
Then I heard: "Rightly you perceive,
if you understand well why he placed it
among the substances and then among the evidences."

Therefore, hope stays in faith like an accident within its subject; and for this reason, faith is **SUBSTANCE**. **AND IT IS EVIDENCE** of things not seen, that is, it is the proof of things that do not appear and are not seen by us. For with faith, we demonstrate what eternal life is and all the other things that do not appear. Evidence is that which makes one believe doubtful things. **AND THIS SEEMS TO ME ITS QUIDDITY**, that is, the true definition according to its essential elements. For this word "quiddity" is the essence or rather the substance of the thing; it is not an ancient Latin word, but was found by Christian philosophers, derived from the word "what" <note>original: "quid".</note>. For when one asks "What is man?" <note>original: "quid est homo?"</note> we are asking about his substance; and the answer is "a rational, mortal animal." Just as asking "What quality is he?" <note>original: "qualis est"</note> we ask about the accident; and the answer is "he is good," or "he is bad," and similar things.

And I followed: "The profound things
which grant me here their appearance
are so hidden from the eyes below..."

<column-break/>

...went out upon the sea. For it is written in the Gospel <note>Matthew 14:28-31.</note> that Peter, being in the boat, said to Christ who was on the shore: "Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you." <note>original: "Si dominus es iube me uenire ad te".</note> and Christ commanded him to come to Him; wherefore he descended from the boat into the sea and walked upon the waves without wetting his feet as long as his faith lasted. Then, as it began to fail him, he began to sink; for which Christ took him and pulled him to Himself, saying: "O man of little faith, why did you doubt?" <note>original: "modice fidei quid dubitasti".</note> **IF HE**: Dante loves well, that is, he has true charity; and hopes well, that is, he has true hope; and believes well, that is, he has true faith, which are the three theological virtues. It is not hidden from you, Peter, because by looking into God, in whom—as in a mirror—everything is seen, you can see this also. And because Peter could say in response that there is no need to ask since he knows that Dante knows it, Beatrice adds: saying it is good that you reach him (Dante) to speak of faith, because through it one acquires the heavenly kingdom.

He turned to Beatrice and she signaled him to respond. This signifies that no one should presume to dispute concerning the faith if Beatrice does not grant it to him—that is, if he cannot defend it with **THEOLOGY**. Then follows Dante's prayer, in which he prays that that same grace which allows him to confess himself to Saint Peter might also grant him the power to express the concepts of his mind. And he calls Peter **FIRST CENTURION** <note>original: "primipilo".</note> because he was the first to carry the banner of Christ. The "primipilus," as Livy <note>Titus Livius, Roman historian.</note> shows, was the first rank of soldiers in the Roman army. And Peter was the first in the Church Militant. And then, having invoked the grace of God, he adds the definition of faith, which he sets down just as the "true pen" of Peter's "dear brother" wrote it—that is, as the Apostle Paul wrote in the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter eleven. This Paul, together with Peter, by preaching the evangelical doctrine, "set Rome on the good path," that is, in the right order and true way, bringing many to the Christian faith with their preaching and miracles. **FAITH IS THE SUBSTANCE OF THINGS HOPED FOR.** This is the definition of faith; and the definition is the rational account of a thing which demonstrates its being according to its substantial properties. Therefore, faith is the substance of things hoped for; that is, faith is that in which hope stays and is founded. For if we did not believe that God exists, and that He is just in a way that He prepares a reward for the good and punishment for the wicked, we would not believe that by doing good we go to the blessed life...

Like an excellent dialectician <note>One skilled in the art of logical argument.</note> knowing what "substance" means among the ten categories <note>The "predicaments" or categories of Aristotle.</note>, he demonstrates the reason why it is placed in the definition of faith, saying that those things which...

[Those things] are manifest in heaven, they are so hidden among men that we cannot know them: But we believe what we do not see as firmly as if we saw it. And upon this we found our hope, hoping through good works to reach the vision of the things we believe. Which is ac...

Peter asks Dante whence faith came to him and where was the beginning, and he responds that it came from the generous rain, i.e. rain, i.e. from the supreme abundance of the Holy Spirit which, infusing itself into many holy men and illuminating them with the truth, they wrote it in the new and the old <term>parchments</term> <note>original: "chuota," a variant of "cuoia" (skins).</note>, i.e. papers: As if to say, in the books of both the New and Old Testament I have drawn this, that through the prophets of the Old Testament the incarnation and the death and resurrection of Christ were announced: and then in the New Testament, i.e. through the gospels and epistles and acts of the apostles, it was shown that what the prophecies said had come to pass. The syllogism can be formed artificially. Wherefore this reason is so manifest that every other reason and probation [is nothing compared] to this. After this Peter asks [why he holds] the testaments to be divine speech, i.e. procee[ding from God].

Dante responds that he believes the words of the Old and New Testament are of God: And the proof that discloses to me, i.e. that opens the truth to me: are the subsequent works, i.e. miracles performed by Christ and by the apostles and by martyrs: which are above nature: And therefore he says that nature does not heat iron and does not strike anvil. After this response, Peter asks him, saying: tell me who assures you, who makes you certain that those works and miracles occurred as they say: As if to say, perhaps it is not to be believed that these miracles were as they say: Therefore who makes you certain of it? Since you are not certain even of these miracles with which you wish to prove the faith to be true. To this Dante responded: if the miracles were not true, this [the conversion of the world] would [be the greatest miracle of all].

Of the profound divine condition
that I touch upon, my mind is sealed
many times by the evangelical doctrine..."

<column-break/>

...[it is] a miracle that the world turned to the faith of Christ without miracles; this is the greatest of all miracles, such that the others are not even a hundredth of it. For it is a great miracle that such a crowd of men was converted by the words of a poor fisherman and the other apostles, who were ignoble, poor, and without reputation or authority. And therefore he says: you entered [the world] poor and fasting, and for this reason you could not draw men to you with wealth or any gifts, nor with lusts and pleasures, as you preached poverty and abstinence. Into the field, in the way to sow the plant: that is, to build the holy Church, which was once a vine (that is, fruitful) and now has become a briar: that is, sterile.

Deservedly the spheres: that is, the circular dances of those souls thanked God for the poet's true faith, singing: *We praise thee, O God* <note>original: "te deum laudamus"</note> with celestial melody. And Peter the baron who, by questioning him on faith from branch to branch: as if to say from grade to grade: had led him near to the final leaves: that is, to the top of the tree that signifies faith. For first he asked what faith is; then the explanation of the definition; then if he had it in his soul and where it came from; and if he held that holy scripture was the word of God. To this he added the proof and the final miracle. Therefore now Peter concludes that the grace of God which "holds court"—that is, dominates and rules in him—opened his mouth and made him speak correctly. And for this reason he approves what the author "emerged"—that is, what came out of his mouth. But now he wishes to understand two things: first, what he believes (that is, the articles of faith); and second, from where his belief proceeded.

The author speaks to Peter, and having to confess what he believes, he shows that what he believes now, Peter believed while down in the world. But now Peter does not "believe" [by faith] because he has true knowledge [through direct vision]: and for this reason it is said that faith does not enter heaven. SO THAT you surpassed toward the tomb even younger feet. He did not surpass the youthful feet of John because, hearing of the resurrection of Christ from the women, he reached the tomb before John did; but he preceded him because he believed in such a resurrection before John reached the tomb to see if he had risen. IN ONE God alone: there is one God and no more. (But we will treat of God in another part above). ETERNAL: without beginning and without end. To whom nothing is past or future, but everything is present to Him. WHO moves all the heaven, unmoved: for He, stable and firm, moves the movers of the heavens. Whence Boethius: *Remaining stable, You grant all things to move.* <note>original Latin: "Stabilisque manens das cuncta moueri."</note> WITH Love and with desire: He moves with love, that is, of His own spontaneous will; with desire: because He is loved and desired. AND For such belief: there are physical and metaphysical reasons which prove there is one God. BUT FROM ME: that is, the truth that rains from here—that is, from heaven—gives it to me.

For the grace of the Holy Spirit poured into the minds of holy men—such as Moses, the prophets, David, the Gospels, and the Acts of the Apostles—has shown them that there is one God. Through Moses, who said in Genesis: *In the beginning God created heaven and earth.* <note>original Latin: "Imprincipio creauit deus celum et terram."</note> Through the prophets like Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel, and others. Through you, Peter, Paul, and James, whose epistles appear in the Bible. And I believe in three eternal persons: and these I believe to be one essence.

He concludes that what he touches upon at present, being in heaven, touches upon the profound divinity; many times it is sealed and imprinted in the [mind]...

It is as if he implies that whoever departs from evangelical doctrine cannot proceed correctly. **LIKE THE lord:** after Peter had heard Dante’s words, he encircled him three times: that is, he embraced him as a lord embraces a servant after hearing good news from him. He said "three times" for the reasons we have mentioned many times regarding the number three: or truly because he has expressed the Trinity in one essence, or to demonstrate [how they are] connected together so that they cannot be separated.
