### CANTO XXV OF THE THIRD CANTICLE OF DANTE

---

In the preceding chapter, our poet treated of Faith. And at present, in this twenty-fifth [canto], he treats of the second theological virtue, which is Hope. Therefore, he first places his hope in returning to his homeland <note>Florence, from which Dante was exiled in 1302 under threat of death.</note> and being crowned there. After this, he brings in the apostle James to examine

It is useful to demonstrate the innocence and gentleness of the people, who were poorly governed by the leading citizens, who were like wolves to the sheep. Then Beatrice, truly his lady, full of joy—because every demonstration that Theology makes gives our soul supreme joy—said: **look and behold, for here is the baron. FOR WHOM** below on earth, people visit **Galicia**; because many make a vow to go visit his church which is in Galicia <note>The shrine of St. James at Santiago de Compostela</note>. **JUST AS**: an excellent comparison by which he shows that just as it happens in the mating of doves, when one places itself near the other, circling and murmuring, it shows the affection it bears for it; so, and with that affection, one apostle welcomed the other, praising God who is the food of blessed souls.

Holy Scripture maintains that the three disciples, Peter, James, and John—whom Christ took up to Mount Tabor when he was transfigured—are the forms of the three theological virtues <term>theological virtues: Faith, Hope, and Charity</term>. And Peter, which means "stone" and "firmness," stands for the firmness of **Faith**. James, which means "supplanter," stands for **Hope**, because hope makes us trample and put under our feet <note>the literal meaning of supplanting</note> every adversity and toil. And John means "full of grace" and stands for **Charity**. Therefore, just as Peter examined the poet on Faith, so James examines him on Hope; and Beatrice turns to him, calling him **illustrious life**—that is, glorious soul—by whom was written the **bounty of our basilica**, that is, of the triumphant Church of eternal life. And certainly, in his epistle, he demonstrates how great is the liberality...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's *Paradiso*, moving into Canto XXV. The previous page concluded the examination on Faith by Saint Peter. Here, the focus shifts to the second theological virtue, Hope, as represented by Saint James the Greater.</meta>

<header>PARADISO</header>

...and Saint John and you: and these three <note>Peter, James, and John</note> had as much knowledge of these virtues as the others had greater knowledge of the divinity of Christ at his Transfiguration. And after Beatrice had spoken these words to James: James turned to Dante and admonished him to lift up his face and reassure himself to look into their light, since the souls who come from earth to heaven must "ripen"—that is, become able to withstand the divine light. And certainly, the intellect that rises to the contemplation of God becomes capable through hope, because it is strengthened and comforted. This comfort of the fire came to me from the "second" <note>Saint James, the second of the three apostles to examine Dante</note>. James, who was the second after Peter to greet me, gave me this comfort. Whence I "lifted up"—that is, I raised—my eyes to the mountains, meaning toward the Apostles, who are in a high place like mountains. Similarly, the Psalmist uses mountains to represent the comfort and stability that hope brings; whence he said: *I lifted up my eyes to the hills: from whence comes my help* <note>original: "Leuaui oculos meos in montes : unde uenit auxilium mihi"; Psalm 121:1</note>. These were the same mountains that previously made him bow under too great a weight.

---

**Since by grace He wills that you face**
**our Emperor before your death**
**in the most secret hall of his counts,**
**So that, having seen the truth of this court,**
**the hope that truly enamors those below**
**may be strengthened in you and in others by this.**
**Tell what it is, and how it blossoms**
**in your mind, and from whence it came to you.**
**Thus the second light continued further.**

<column-break/>

James speaks and says that since our Emperor, God, wills by His grace and not through any merit <note>original: "debito," meaning a debt or something owed</note> that you should face and meet Him before death—which does not usually happen, that anyone goes in the flesh to heaven in the "most secret hall," that is, in the most excellent part of the divine palace. So that, having seen the truth of this celestial court and known true beatitude, you may be comforted by it: by the beatitude of hope—that is, the expectation within you and in others—which "enamors well" down in the world, because love proceeds from hope. Say, therefore, what hope is and how your

---

mind "blossoms" with it—that is, how it is adorned. And not without reason did he name flowers in relation to hope: because just as the flower is not the fruit, but gives a sign that the fruit will be born from it, so hope shows us our future beatitude. And "from whence it came to you"—that is, tell me what it is to hope. "Thus the second light continued further"—meaning, just as Peter, the first light, asked what faith is and how it came to him, so James, the second light, similarly asked him.

---

**And that compassionate one who guided the feathers**
**of my wings to such a high flight**
**prevented my answer by speaking thus:**
**"The Church Militant has no child**
**with more hope, as it is written**
**in the Sun that radiates through all our host.**
**Therefore it is granted to him to come**
**from Egypt to Jerusalem to see,**
**before his term of soldiering is prescribed.**
**The other two points—which are not asked**
**for the sake of knowing, but so that he may report**
**how much this virtue is pleasing to you—**
**I leave to him, for they will not be hard for him**
**nor an occasion for boasting; let him answer them,**
**and may the grace of God permit him this."**

<column-break/>

James had asked what hope is, whether he possessed this virtue, and from whence it had come to him. Now, as Dante was about to respond, Beatrice anticipated the second part <note>the question of whether Dante possesses hope</note> and answered on the author's behalf, affirming that he possesses as much hope as any other Christian in the "Church Militant"—that is, the church of the living—as can be seen in God, in whom every thing is seen as in a mirror. And because of this hope that he has, it is granted to him by divine grace to come "from Egypt to Jerusalem"—that is, from the world to heaven. For "Egypt" is interpreted as "darkness" or "tribulation" <note>a common medieval etymology for Egypt</note>. From that height of supreme soldiering, the people of God were led back to the land of promise and happiness. "Jerusalem" is interpreted as "vision of peace" <note>the traditional etymological meaning of Jerusalem</note>, the flower of our happiness. Whence the Psalmist: *Praise becomes you in Zion, and to you shall the vow be performed in Jerusalem* <note>original: "Te decet hymnus insion et tibi reddetur uotum in hierusalem"; Psalm 65:1</note>. "Before his soldiering is prescribed"—meaning before his temporal life is taken from him, in which we "militate"—that is, we fight continually with the world, the flesh, and the devil. And if we win, we are called to heaven where we triumph over the conquered adversary. "The other two points": of the three questions, Beatrice has answered this one; for if the author had answered it himself, it might have seemed like "vainglory" <note>boasting</note>. Now she continues her speech and says that the other two points James asked were not for the sake of knowing, but so that Dante might report down in the world how much this virtue pleases God. She leaves these to him because they will not be "hard"—that is, difficult—nor will they be an occasion for "boasting"—that is, vainglory. Therefore he responds, and may the grace of God "permit" it—that is, be pleasing to him.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Paradiso, Canto XXV. # CANTO XXV
## H.iiii

**Left Column:**
"Hope," I said, "is a certain expectation
of future glory, which is produced
by divine grace and preceding merit.
From many stars this light comes to me;
but he distilled it into my heart first
who was the supreme singer of the supreme Leader. <note>David, the author of the Psalms, singing of God</note>
'Let them hope in You' in your song of God, <note>original: "Sperent in te nella tua theodia"; Psalm 9:11. Dante uses the term "theodia" to mean divine song or theodicy.</note>
he says, to those who know Your name;
and who does not know it, if he has my faith?
You distilled it into me with his distilling
afterward in your Epistle, so that I am full,
and rain back your rain upon others." <note>Dante suggests he is overflowing with the teachings of David and James, sharing them with the world.</note>

While I spoke, within the living heart
of that fire, a flash trembled
suddenly and often, in the manner of lightning.
Then breathed the love with which I burn
still for the virtue that followed me
even to the palm and the exit from the field, <note>James refers to his martyrdom ("the palm") and his departure from the earthly life ("the field").</note>
He willed that I breathe to you, who delight
in her; and it is pleasing to me that you tell
what it is that hope promises you.

And I: "The new and the ancient scriptures
set down the sign, and it points it out to me,
of the souls whom God has made His friends.
Isaiah says that each one, clothed
in his own land, shall have a double garment;
and their land is this sweet life. <note>Isaiah 61:7; the "double garment" refers to the glorified soul and the resurrected body.</note>
And your brother, much more clearly,
there where he treats of the white robes,
makes this revelation manifest to us." <note>Refers to Saint John the Evangelist and the Book of Revelation.</note>

<column-break/>

Responding to the first point, I said that hope is nothing other than certain expectation—that is, to wait with certainty—for future glory. The definition of the Master of the Sentences <note>Peter Lombard, a 12th-century theologian whose "Sentences" was the standard textbook of divinity</note> is: 
> Hope is the certain expectation of future blessedness, coming from the grace of God and preceding merits. <note>original: "Spes est certa expectatio future beatitudinis ueniens ex dei gratia precedentibus meritis."</note> 
Then he responds to the second point and says that such hope is granted to us by divine grace preceding any merit of ours.
Then, having shown the first cause, he shows the second cause, which is the influence of the stars: from which, as written above, the influx of various virtues is born. But although an influx is born from the stars that disposes us to various virtues and consequently to the hope through which we will acquire eternal life, nonetheless it is necessary that such a disposition be aided by doctrine. Therefore he adds that he who was the supreme singer of the supreme Leader—that is, David, the supreme prophet of the supreme God—first distilled this hope into his heart. David is the supreme singer because he is the greatest prophet in the Old Law. **LET THEM HOPE in you**: he uses the words of David, which are: 
> Let all those who have known your name hope in you: for you have not forsaken those who seek you. <note>original: "Sperent inte omnes qui nouerunt nomen tuu: quoniam non dereliquisti querentes te"; Psalm 9:10-11</note> 
Let all those who know your name hope in you. And in your **theodia**: that is, deity <note>or divine song</note>: because *theos* in Greek signifies God. And then the poet adds, saying: "and who does not know the name of God if he has my faith?"—that is, he has the Christian faith as I do; it is as if he says every Christian knows it. Therefore, David first distilled it into me, and then you, James, distilled it with his distilling in your canonical Epistle. For that which you wrote there you had from him; so that I am so full of this distilling that I "rain back"—that is, I demonstrate to others—our rain. **YOU distilled into me**: in the canonical epistle of James it says: 
> Blessed is the man who suffers temptation: for when he has been proved, he shall receive the crown of life which God has promised to those who love him. <note>original: "Beatus uir qui suffert temtationem: Quia cum probatus fuerit accipiet coronam uite quam promisit deus diligentibus se"; James 1:12</note> 
And at the end of the same: 
> Be patient and strengthen your hearts: for the coming of the Lord draws near. <note>original: "Patientes confirmate corda uestra: Quoniam aduentus domini appropinquabit"; James 5:8</note>

<image-desc>Blue decorative initial M</image-desc>While the author spoke, he saw the light of James always trembling like a flash of lightning. Then James spoke and said: the love of the virtue of hope, which followed me even to the palm—that is, even to victory—and to the exit from the field <note>death</note>, wants me to ask you what that hope promises you: that is, what you hope for. And note that hope followed him to the palm—that is, to victory—which we cannot say we have while we are in this mortal life, because we always fight against the flesh and the devil. But when we "exit the field"—that is, the place where one fights, which is this world—and we exit victorious because we have conquered every vice, the hope of reaching blessedness accompanies us always even unto that blessedness. But it does not enter into it, because a present good is not hoped for, but enjoyed. And he used the palm for victory, because the palm is given to whoever obtains victory. And the reason for this we have made manifest more extensively elsewhere.

<image-desc>Red decorative initial R</image-desc>James requesting that the poet reveal what hope promises him, he responds that it promises a happy and everlasting life to both soul and body. And this he proves with the testimony of the scriptures of the New Testament. He says, therefore, the new and ancient scriptures set the "sign" for the souls whom God has made His friends—as if to say the goal toward which they must direct their hope—and that sign points it out to me: that is, shows it to me. And through the ancient scriptures, he shows and alleges Isaiah, who says in the sixty-first chapter... <note>The text says "sixth chapter," but refers to Isaiah 61:7 regarding the double portion/garment.</note>

# PARADISO
## H.iiii

> And first, near the end of these words,
> "Let them hope in You" <note>original: "sperent in te"; Psalm 9:11</note> was heard from above us;
> to which all the carols <note>original: "carole"; circular dances accompanied by singing</note> responded.

<br/>
<br/>
<br/>

> Then among them a light brightened
> such that if the constellation Cancer had such a crystal,
> winter would have a month of a single day. <note>In winter, Cancer is visible all night. If it had a star as bright as this spirit, the night would be as light as day.</note>
> And as a happy virgin rises and goes
> and enters the dance, only to do honor
> to the new bride and not for any failing,
> So did I see the brightened splendor
> come to the two who were turning in a wheel,
> as was fitting for their burning love.
> He joined himself there in the song and the note,
> and my lady <note>Beatrice</note> kept her gaze upon them,
> just like a bride, silent and unmoved.

> of our Pelican, <note>A traditional symbol for Christ, who nourishes his children with his own blood.</note> and this was he
> chosen from upon the cross for the great office." <note>Referring to Christ entrusting the Virgin Mary to John's care.</note>
> My lady spoke no more than this;
> nor did she move her sight from being attentive
> after these words more than she had before.

<br/>
<br/>

> As is he who gazes and exerts himself
> to see the sun eclipsed a little,
> who by seeing becomes unseeing,
> So did I become at that last fire
> while it was said: "Why do you dazzle yourself

<column-break/>

"In their land they shall possess double" <note>original Latin: "In terra tua duplicia possidebunt"; Isaiah 61:7</note>: And Solomon in the Proverbs: "All her household are clothed in double garments." <note>original Latin: "Omnes domestici eius uestiti sunt duplicibus"; Proverbs 31:21</note>. Our homeland is heaven, because as Paul says: "We have here no lasting city, but we seek the one to come." <note>original Latin: "Non habemus hic ciuitatē manentem sed futuram inquirimus"; Hebrews 13:14</note>. Wherefore the poet says: "and their land is this sweet life." By this "double good" the learned understand: the happiness of the soul and of the body, which the blessed will feel in the celestial life after the resurrection of the bodies. "YOUR BROTHER": refers to the testimony of John the Evangelist, brother of James; he in the Apocalypse describes a great multitude in white robes who followed Christ wherever He went, which denotes that "the pure in heart shall see God" <note>original Latin: "quod mundi corde deum uidebunt"; Matthew 5:8</note>, and in the divine vision our supreme beatitude is located. Therefore "more digested," that is, better ordered, John sets down in this revelation what hope promises to the good. At the end of these words, the sphere of the apostles sang "Let them hope in You, all those who know Your name" <note>original Latin: "Sperent in te omnes qui nouerunt nomen tuum"</note>: and all the other carols responded to the song. Nor could there be a psalm more fitting for Hope.

After the words of James, another light showed a great brightness: And this was John the Evangelist. And this splendor came to Peter and to James with that gravity and modesty and honesty that is seen in a virgin when she rises from sitting and goes to the dance and enters it. Not without reason does he compare him to the virgin: because he persevered in perpetual virginity. Furthermore, it shows that his splendor was so great that if in the sign of Cancer there were a star of such brightness, it would happen that while the sun is in Capricorn, a month would have no night but only day because it would never be dark. Cancer is the sign opposite to Capricorn: and when the sun enters Capricorn, which is in the month of December, while it is under the earth, Cancer is always above the earth. Therefore, if in that constellation there were a star that shone as much as the Evangelist shone, it would happen that in that month when the sun is in Capricorn, there would never be night, because the day is lit by the sun and the night would be lit by that star. Because of this splendor, this apostle—due to the admirable wisdom and doctrine that was in him—joined himself there, that is, with the two apostles, in the song and the note they were singing, as if to say in agreement with them in singing "Let them hope in the Lord" <note>original: "Sperent i domino"</note>: which denotes that these virtues <note>Faith, Hope, and Charity</note> make a single harmony. And Beatrice watched these three with silence and immobility, because in truth sacred theology never departs from the intuition and sight of these three virtues. "THIS IS HE" are the words of Beatrice, who, wishing to show that this is John the Evangelist, uses this circumlocution: that he is the one who at the [Last] Supper lay upon the breast of Christ; and while sleeping he saw the things of divinity as he writes in his Gospel. And she calls Christ a "pelican." This is a bird in Egypt which with its own blood revives its dead children. They say that the children of the pelican, after the father has nourished them, rise up against him, and he, defending himself, kills them. And afterward, moved by pity, he wounds himself with his beak and, spreading his blood over them, revives them. Thus man, by sinning, rises against his Maker, and the divine Majesty kills him because He condemns him to death for sin. Afterward, moved by pity with the passion of His own blood, by freeing us from sin, He revives us. "FROM UPON THE CROSS chosen for the great office": Christ on the cross told his mother to have John in place of a son, and John to have her in place of a mother. Therefore he was chosen for the great office. And these words Beatrice said; and afterward she remained no less attentive toward those aforementioned apostles than before.

The author <note>Dante</note> gazed fixedly at the Evangelist to see if he had a body; and in looking, it happened to him as it does to one who stares at the sun to see an eclipse and is dazzled in such a way that he then sees nothing. And from John it was said to him: "Why do you dazzle yourself

...dazzle yourself in trying to see a thing that has no place here, that is, which is not here." <note>John explains that his body is not yet in heaven; only Christ and Mary have their bodies there before the general resurrection.</note>

[The Saint says:] "Why do you seek to see my body, which is not here? But it is earth down on earth, and it will be there for a long time <note>The OCR "lĩ . t." likely abbreviates "lungo tempo" (long time)</note> as earth until our number—that is, the number of the blessed—equals and matches the eternal purpose, that is, what God has ordained. This is to say, until the end of the world; because the world must last until the number of the blessed fills the vacant seats <note>Medieval theology suggested humans were created to fill the seats in heaven left empty by the fallen angels.</note>. Therefore, assign these two sayings to John: The first, that he died and left his body on earth; because in his Gospel he wrote: <term>Exiit</term> <note>original Latin: "it went out," referring to the rumor of his immortality</note> and Jesus did not say "he does not die," but "if I wish him [to remain] until I come." [The second,] that the world shall last until the blessed fill the vacancies. It is said to them that they should rest for a little while yet <note>original Latin: "est illis quod requiescent tempus adhuc modicum"</note> [until the number of those] who are to be killed is complete, just as they were. And he returns to the text: With [their two robes], that is, with Christ and his mother Mary.

<image-desc>Ornamental initial letter F begins the commentary section.</image-desc>

**F**inished were the words of John, and the flaming circle, that is, the sphere of the three apostles, became quiet from its turning. And this was their song, which was a mixture—that is, a mingling—that was made of the sound and the voices of the triple breath, meaning the three apostles <note>Peter, James, and John, representing Faith, Hope, and Charity.</note>. And this circle stopped all at once; just as in a galley those who row, hearing the whistle—which is blown either so the crew may rest or to flee danger—stop at such a signal. Then I was much moved in my mind because of being unable to see Beatrice, even though I turned toward her and she was near me and we were in heaven. He could not see Beatrice because he had already ascended to the contemplation of such high things that, through their overly great light, dazzle every keen intellect.

<header>PARADISO</header>

# CANTO XXVI OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE

<margin>i</margin>
In this twenty-sixth chapter, John the Evangelist is introduced to treat Charity, the third theological virtue <note>The three theological virtues are Faith, Hope, and Charity (Love). Dante has already been examined on the first two by St. Peter and St. James.</note>. First, the author is examined by him on this virtue. Then, he asks another petition regarding the same virtue. In the third part, Adam appears, to whom the author poses certain doubts; and in the final part, Adam responds to those doubts. Returning then to the beginning, the author writes that while he was "doubting"—that is, standing in uncertainty because of his "quenched sight," meaning his visual power which was extinguished by the brilliant

<columns>2</columns>
**While** I was in doubt because of my quenched sight
by the glowing flame that had extinguished it,
a breath came forth that made me attentive,
Saying: "Until you regain the sense
of the sight you have consumed in me,
it is well that you compensate for it by speaking.
Begin then, and say where your soul 
aims; and be assured that
your sight is bewildered in you, but not dead;
Because the lady who through this divine 
region conducts you, has in her look 
the power that the hand of Ananias held."

by the glowing flame that had extinguished it,

<column-break/>

flame of the Evangelist, there came forth a "breath"—that is, a speech—and it said: "While you regain your sense of sight—meaning, you reacquire the living sense that you have 'consumed' in me (that is, while you were looking at me)—it is good that you compensate and restore it by speaking. Therefore, where does your soul 'aim'?—meaning, toward what end does your spirit extend itself as its final point. And be assured that your sight is 'bewildered' for a time, but not 'dead'—meaning, not deceased and lost entirely. Because Beatrice, who conducts you through this 'divine'—that is, godly—region of the heavens, has in her look—meaning in her vision—the power of the hand of Ananias, who, by baptizing the Apostle Paul, made his sight return." This refers to Ananias and Paul. It is written in the Acts of the Apostles <note>original: "actis degappostoli"</note> that Saul (afterwards Paul) was a most bitter persecutor of Christians. And with letters from the prince of priests, while coming

<columns>1</columns>

from Jerusalem to Damascus to lead away as prisoners those who confessed Christ, he was suddenly surrounded by a great light and fell to the ground and heard a voice saying: "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" And he, responding, said: "Who are you, Lord?" He heard: "I am Jesus whom you persecute; and it is hard for you to kick against the goad." Then he, full of wonder and trembling, replied: "Lord, what do you want me to do?" To him the Lord said: "Go into the city, and there it will be told to you." He went then, guided by his companions because he had become blind; and for three days he stayed without food in the house of Judas. And Jesus appeared to one of his disciples, namely to Ananias, and commanded him to go to Saul as a "vessel of election" <note>original: "uaso delectione"; from the Latin 'vas electionis,' meaning a chosen instrument</note> who was to carry his name before the people, and kings, and the children of Israel. Ananias went then and placed his hands upon him; and immediately there fell from Paul's eyes something like scales and he received back his sight. Therefore, just as the hand of Ananias restored sight to Paul, so Beatrice restored sight to Dante, who was dazzled by the excessive light. And certainly, Sacred Scripture is that which comforts the eye of the intellect in such a way that it can perceive the light of divinity, which previously confounded it.

<columns>2</columns>

I said: "At her pleasure, soon or late,
let remedy come to the eyes that were the gates
when she entered with the fire with which I always burn.
The Good that makes this court content
is Alpha and Omega <note>original: "alpha et o"</note> of all the scripture
that Love reads to me, both low and loud."
That same voice which had taken away 
the fear of the sudden dazzling
made me care to speak again,
And said: "Truly, through a narrower sieve
you must clarify; it behooves you to say 
who directed your bow to such a target."

<column-break/>

**These words** are from the poet, by which he first responds to the comfort given to him by John, and then to his question. First, John having comforted him that Beatrice would refill his sight, lost through the excessive light, he responds that he submits to Beatrice's judgment for such a remedy, whether late or soon, however she wishes to send it to his dazzled eyes—which he says were "gates" to her when she entered into him with the fire of love for which he always burns. Beatrice is Sacred Scripture and the grace of God, which raises us so high in contemplation—not a little of the divine light which, without Beatrice, would dazzle us and would not let us discern. The poet is dazzled in the light of John—meaning he is confounded by John in the Gospel, and in the Epistles, and in the

<columns>1</columns>

Book of Revelation <note>original: "appocalypse"</note>. But Theology opens and declares it, and makes man capable of it. "THE GOOD THAT..." responds to John's question, and demonstrates that the Good which satisfies all the court of Paradise—meaning all the blessed—is "Alpha" (meaning the beginning) and "Omega" (meaning the end) of all the scripture that "Love reads to me"—meaning that which Charity demonstrates to me, "lowly or loudly" (meaning easily or with difficulty). For all of Scripture says that God must principally be loved for Himself, and then creatures for the love of Him. "That same voice..." The poet continues and shows that the same voice—meaning the same spirit with his voice, which was John...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto XXVI of Paradiso. Dante is being examined by Saint John the Evangelist on the nature of Charity (Divine Love). Having lost his physical sight temporarily to the saint's brilliance, Dante must rely on his intellectual "vision" to answer.</meta>

...who had taken away from me the fear of the sudden dazzle: because he had told me that Beatrice would free me from the sudden blindness that had come upon me. I applied myself with care and diligence to reason further, and he said: "It is necessary that you clear your sight through a narrower sieve" <note>The Italian 'vaglio' means a sieve or winnowing fan. The commentator explains this as a transition from coarse to fine purification of the soul's understanding.</note>, that is, more constricted: and this is a metaphor taken from grain, which they begin to purge and clean first with wide sieves, and afterwards with denser ones until they are perfectly purified. He says: "It is necessary for you to say who directed your bow," that is, your will, to such a target: that is, to such a mark. For a target [berzaglio] is that mark at which crossbowmen shoot, which in Greek is called *skopos* <note>original: 'scopon'</note>. Therefore, who was it that directed your mind to this end, so that you would love the eternal God for Himself, and all other things for the love of Him?

**And I: "Through philosophical arguments**
**and through authority that descends from here,**
**such love must be imprinted in me;**
**For the good, in as much as it is understood as good,**
**so enkindles love, and so much the more**
**as it contains more goodness within itself.**
**Therefore, toward the Essence where there is such advantage**
**that every good found outside of it**
**is nothing but a light of its own ray,**
**the mind of everyone who discerns the truth**
**upon which this proof is founded**
**must move, more than toward any other, in loving.**
**Such truth is discerned by my intellect**
**by him who demonstrates to me the first love**
**of all the eternal substances.**
**It is discerned in the voice of the truthful Author**
**who says to Moses, speaking of Himself:**
**'I will make you feel every worth.'** <note>original: 'io ti faro sentire ogni valore', a translation of Exodus 33:19.</note>
**You also discern it for me, beginning**
**the high proclamation that cries the secret**
**down here from above every other herald's cry."**

<column-break/>

The poet demonstrates that two things especially lead him to the love of the supreme good: philosophical arguments, which not only show there to be a unique Creator toward whom every creature turns as its ultimate end and supreme good. Indeed, the Platonists wrote many things very much in harmony with the Word and the Holy Spirit, as Augustine shows in his *City of God*. The second is from the Apostles, the Evangelists, the martyrs, and the doctors, which carries much more weight in the Holy Scriptures than in the natural sciences because they come from divine infusion and from revelation made to holy men. **FOR THE GOOD**: He argues philosophically according to Aristotle and the Platonists, according to whom, as soon as the good is known by us, it draws us to love it; and the greater the good, the greater the love. Therefore, since God is the supreme good—and a supreme good such that no other thing is good except in as much as it participates in Him—it follows (as the poet says) that every good found outside of God is nothing other than the light of His rays. It follows that we are naturally inclined most greatly and with most ardent charity toward His love. And this is the "first love"; afterwards, it extends with a certain order: to the homeland, to the father, to the children, and consequently to others according to their rank. **THAT TRUTH TO MY INTELLECT DISCERNS**: that is, it demonstrates this truth:

that God should be loved above all things. **HIM**: that is, Aristotle, who proved this in many places. **THE VOICE DISCERNS**: Because when God spoke to Moses, He said: "I will show you all good" <note>original Latin: 'Ostendam tibi omne bonum'</note>, and certainly He showed him all good by showing him Himself. **DISCERN IT FOR ME**: that is, show it to me, you, John, beginning the "high proclamation": and he means his Gospel proclamation in which he made manifest on earth the "secret," that is, the secrets of the food <note>likely referring to the Bread of Life or spiritual sustenance</note> and especially the incarnation of the Divine Word.

**And I heard: "Through human intellect**
**and through authorities concordant with it,**
**keep the highest of your loves for God.**
**But tell me still if you feel other cords**
**drawing you toward Him, so that you may declare**
**with how many teeth this love bites you."**
**The holy intention of the**
**eagle of Christ was not hidden; rather, I perceived**
**where he wished to lead my profession.**

<column-break/>

John gathers this conclusion from Dante's words: that he, both through human intellect—that is, through philosophical reasons which the human intellect learns—and through the authority of sacred letters, keeps and preserves the sovereign and first and greatest love for God. But he wants to know if, beyond these two things, he feels "other cords": that is, other incitements that draw him toward Him, to His love. Therefore, he wants him to "sound"—that is, speak—with "how many teeth" the love of God bites him: that is, with how many movements God awakens him and incites him to love Him. And after John had said these words to Dante,

"it was not hidden"—that is, it was not concealed—the intention of John himself; rather, he [Dante] perceived and understood where he wished to lead his "profession": that is, of what thing he wished to make him make a profession. And he says "**eagle**": because as we demonstrated elsewhere, this Evangelist is represented in the form of an eagle, because just as this bird flies higher than others and can look into the rays of the sun without being dazzled, so John, in describing the divinity...

<summary>In this passage, Dante explains to Saint John that both reason (philosophy) and revelation (Scripture) identify God as the Supreme Good and the primary object of love. The commentary emphasizes the harmony between Platonic/Aristotelian thought and Christian theology regarding the soul's natural inclination toward the Divine.</summary>

His own existence, in which one considers the immortal soul, which is unhappy if it does not join with God. Therefore we must seek Him with supreme charity. **THE DEATH** that He endured: because he would be most ungrateful who does not love the giver of so many benefits. **AND that which every believer hopes for as I do:** because once the reward that awaits him is considered, he must fix all his affection on Him. All these things, with the

And they have placed me on the shore of right love, because just as worldly love always strikes us in a tempestuous sea with various perturbations that torment the mind day and night, so divine love leads us into this port of eternal tranquility. **THE LEAVES** wherewith all the garden is enleafed. Having shown the reasons that make him love God, he shows the reason why he loves the blessed spirits of God: saying that he loves them because he knows they are loved by God. # CANTO XXVI

<column-break/>

Just as the branch that bends its tip
at the passing of the wind and then raises itself
by its own power which uplifts it,
So did I do while she <note>Beatrice</note> was speaking,
in wonder, and then I was made secure again
by a desire to speak of which I burned.

And I began: "O fruit that alone
was produced mature, O ancient father
to whom every bride is daughter and daughter-in-law,
Devoutly as I can I pray to you
that you speak to me; you see my wish,
and to hear you sooner, I do not speak it."
Sometimes an animal covered [with a cloth] stirs
so that its feeling must be shown
by the movement its desire makes within it;
And similarly the first-made soul
made his joy shine through his covering
as he came to please me.
Then he breathed: "Without you expressing it,
I discern your wish better
than you [discern] whatever thing is most certain to you;
Because I see it in the blessed mirror <note>God</note>
which makes itself a reflection of all other things,
while nothing makes itself a reflection of Him.
You wish to hear how long it has been since God placed me
in the high garden where she <note>Beatrice</note>
prepared you for so high a ladder,
And how long the delight lasted for my eyes,
and the true cause of the great anger,
and the language that I used and that I fashioned."

"Now, my son, it was not the tasting of the wood <note>the tree of knowledge</note>
that was in itself the cause of such exile,
but only the passing of the mark <note>original: "trapassar del segno" — the act of disobedience</note>.
In the place from which your lady moved Virgil <note>Limbo</note>,
for four thousand three hundred and two cycles
of the sun I longed for this assembly;
And I saw him return to all the lights..."

<column-break/>

...the first soul <note>Adam</note> told me that the first power <note>God</note> ever created: that is, God, gazes upon His creator within those rays: that is, within that fourth light that you see. **Just as the branch** <note>original: "CHome la fronde"</note>; the meaning is this: I was wondering for as long as Beatrice spoke the words already mentioned, and I acted like the branch. That is, the leafy branch which, struck by the wind, bows its tip at its passing, and then, the wind having ceased, it rises and returns upright as it was before by the natural power that keeps it straight. The meaning is that while Beatrice spoke to me, out of the wonder of her being the soul of Adam, I bowed like a rod bows in the wind; afterward, the desire I had to speak to him raised me up again.

**AND I began** <note>original: "ET cominciai"</note>: Dante in this form, wishing to speak to Adam. **O fruit that was produced mature** <note>original: "Opomo che fusti producto maturo"</note>: because other men are born imperfect, both in size and in many powers of the soul; but Adam was formed from the earth at the age of thirty years and in perfect stature and with perfect senses. **O ancient father**: who was the first, and every bride to you is a daughter because she is descended from you, and a daughter-in-law <note>original: "nuro"</note> because she is married to one who is descended from you. **SOMETIMES an animal**: just as an animal covered by its skin shows by its "brogliare" <note>stirring or moving</note>—that is, by its movement—the affection of its soul, so Adam, by the trembling of the light which covered him, showed the eagerness he had to speak to the poet. **THEN he breathed**: Adam shows that he fulfills the author's wish without him speaking it, because he sees it in God, who makes Himself a "pareglo" <note>original: "pareglo," here meaning a mirror or receptacle</note> of Himself for all things. But nothing makes itself a reflection of Him: because God sees and contains all things in Himself, but not vice-versa <note>the other way around</note>, because no one sees God perfectly and no one contains Him. Not without reason does he have Adam call him by name: because, being the first father of men, it is fitting for him to show that he knows all his good children. And that the superior calls the inferior by name signifies familiarity and human kindness <note>original: "humana dementia," likely meaning clemency or gentleness</note>. Then he shows what Dante wants to know, which he has seen in God: And first he wants to know how long ago God placed him in the high garden: that is, in the Paradise of Delights <note>Eden</note>, in which you arrived when she: that is, Holy Theology <note>Beatrice</note>, prepared you and made you capable of such a high ladder of the celestial paradise; for once man has come to the purgative virtues, he can pass to contemplation through the virtues of a soul already purified. **AND HOW MUCH DELIGHT WAS IN MY EYES**: And you wish to know how long my delight lasted in the terrestrial paradise; and the true cause of the anger that God took against man, which was great both toward God (who is the greatest of all things) and toward the human generation.

**He responds** to the questions asked; and as for the first, it was not the tasting of the wood: that is, of the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, that was the cause of the exile of the human generation; but the **passing of the mark**. God commanded Adam that he should not touch the fruit of the aforementioned tree as a creature created with free will, so that through obedience he might acquire eternal life; and that he should have not only grace and mercy...

<summary>Dante encounters the soul of Adam, who explains that the Fall of Man was caused by the sin of disobedience ("passing the mark") rather than the mere act of eating the fruit. The commentary provides theological context on Adam's creation as a "mature fruit" and the nature of God as a universal mirror.</summary>

the sun, but also of His justice, and thus he was abundant in all virtues; and having tasted all the goodness of God’s virtues, he was yet not obedient: but he overstepped the mark set for him. And he has answered the part that asked about the cause of the great anger. Now he responds to the question: "How long ago did God place you there?" and "Where did your Lady move Virgil?"—that is, in Limbo, where Beatrice moved Virgil, I stayed for four thousand three hundred and two revolutions of the sun, which is four thousand three hundred and two years; because every revolution of the sun is one year. And I saw it—the sun—return to all the lights of its path: that is, return nine hundred and thirty times through the zodiac, which is the way through which it continuously passes, which has twelve signs and each has many stars. Therefore,

---

he said he was on earth: that is, he lived nine hundred and thirty years. **The language I spoke**: the meaning is that the language that he and those descended from him used faded away before Nimrod began the Tower of Babel, which was an "unfinishable work," meaning it could not be completed. And in that work was born the division of language, so that there were many and diverse tongues. Mention of Nimrod and the confusion of various languages was made in the first canticle <note>The *Inferno*</note>. And it is not without reason that language changed: because no effect produced by human reason was ever durable, following the heavens. The meaning is that since men change their purpose according to various influences of the heavens—which renew our pleasures—they also change and vary things and arts. And here we must understand that in all brute animals there is no movement other than the natural one. But in man there is the natural and the rational. The natural does not change. Therefore, the brutes, who are deprived of reason and guided by nature, have unchanging works. Thus, they never change their food nor the way of seeking it; nor is one lion different from another, nor horse from horse, in producing offspring, in feeding them, or in other things pertaining to the preservation of life. All swallows feed in one way. But man is not drawn by natural instinct more than he wills. Rather, he is the master of his own operations. From which it follows that not all men speak in one way, nor do they build or dress in one way. From all these things we conclude that speaking in man is a natural work. For nature, having given reason to man, found it necessary to give him speech to express rational concepts. But whether we speak this way or that—that is, more in one language than in another—is not a natural work; but proceeds from our reason and will; and therefore nature leaves this to us according to what "pleases us" <note>original: "ci abella"</note>: that is, what we like.

---

Before I descended to the infernal anguish,
the Supreme Good <note>God</note> was called *I* <note>The letter 'I', representing 'One' or the first letter of a name for God</note> on earth,
from whom comes the joy that wraps me;
*Eli* He was called afterward, and that is fitting,
for the usage of mortals is like a leaf
on a branch, which goes away while another comes.
On the mountain that rises highest from the waves,
I lived with a life pure and then dishonorable,
from the first hour to that which follows
when the sun changes its quadrant at the sixth hour.

<column-break/>

He had said that speaking in man is a 
natural thing; but using one language more than
another comes from custom, which changes.
Wherefore Horace says: <note>original: "Multa renascentur que iam cecidere. cadentque que nunc sunt in honore uocabula si uolet usus."</note> *Many words shall be reborn that have now fallen, and those now in honor shall fall, if usage so wills.*
And this he proves by demonstrating 
that before he descended to the infernal anguish, 
God was called *I*. And it was fitting that the name 
should change: since, just as on a branch the leaves 
change because every year they fall and are reborn, 
so the usage of mortals continually changes.
**On the mountain**: He responds to the fourth question, 
which was how long he stayed in the earthly paradise, 
which the poet imagines to be in the other hemisphere on a 

---

mountain which is very high and rises out of the sea, as we demonstrated above. **With life pure and dishonorable**: understand "pure life" before the sin, and "dishonorable" when, after the sin, he knew himself to be naked and was ashamed. **As the sun changes its quadrant**: the sun’s clock, which is called a quadrant; in the first quadrant it contains six hours; then the seventh follows <note>Adam explains he was only in Eden for about seven hours</note>.

# CANTO XXVII OF THE THIRD CANTICLE OF DANTE

->To the Father, to the Son, to the Holy Spirit,<-
all of Paradise began "Glory,"
so that the sweet song intoxicated me.
What I heard seemed to me a smile
of the universe; for my intoxication
entered through my hearing and my sight.
O joy! O ineffable gladness!
O life entire of love and of peace!
O secure wealth without longing!
Before my eyes the four torches
stood lit: and the one that came first <note>St. Peter</note>
began to become more vivid:
And he became such in his appearance
as Jupiter would become if he and Mars
were birds and had swapped their feathers.

Calling this blessedness "joy," and the "smile of the universe" because here were gathered all the effects of all the spheres and all the planets; and "ineffable gladness," meaning unspeakable. In contrast to the joy of our world, which is brief and mixed with bitterness, the heavenly life is "entire of love and of peace": entire because it lacks nothing. **O SECURE wealth without longing.** Two things without which no wealth is perfect: first, that it be without longing, meaning nothing more is desired; second, that it be secure, meaning without any fear of losing it or it diminishing. **BEFORE my eyes**: having made his exclamation, the author returns to his narration and shows that he still had before his eyes the four lights, which were the three apostles and Adam. But that light which had come first, namely Peter, began to become more alive and bright. And he was such as Jupiter would be if he took on the color of Mars <note>Jupiter was associated with a white/silvery light, while Mars was associated with a fiery red</note>. Peter adopts this appearance according to the influence of Jupiter because he was the best shepherd and teacher and a most just administrator; and he is given the color of Mars for two reasons: first, because having been a martyr for Christ, he reasonably takes the color of that planet where the martyrs of Christ are placed; second, because since he wished to rebuke his successors, it was appropriate that he should take on vehemence, ardor, and just wrath in his scolding, which comes from Mars.

The providence which here assigns
turn and office in the blessed choir
had imposed silence on every side,
When I heard: "If I change color,
do not marvel, for as I speak,
you shall see all these others change color too.
He who usurps on earth my place,
my place, my place, which stands vacant
in the presence of the Son of God,
Has made of my cemetery a sewer
of blood and of stench, wherewith the Perverse One <note>Lucifer/Satan</note>
who fell from up here, is appeased down there."

Our poet had, in the chapters just written, introduced three apostles who examined him on the three <term>theological virtues</term> <note>Faith, Hope, and Charity</note>. Now, in this twenty-seventh canto, the Apostle Peter bitterly rebukes his successors. Furthermore, it shows how he was snatched from the eighth sphere to the <term>Primum Mobile</term> <note>the "First Mover," the ninth and outermost physical sphere of the universe</note>. He places first, then, Peter's invective against the prelates; next, he describes the ascent of the whole triumphant army to the Empyrean heaven and the reflection of himself back toward Earth; in the third part, he places his entry with Beatrice into the ninth sphere; in the fourth, he places a most vehement exclamation against the blind greed for earthly things. But returning to the beginning, the author narrates that after the resolution of the doubts already written, all the blessed sang, "Glory be to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit" <note>original: "Gloria patri et filio et spiritui sancto"</note> so sweetly that the song intoxicated him—that is, he fell into an ecstasy. And it seemed to him that this was the joy of the universe and of every creature. Nor can he help but use an exclamation in the midst of such great joy.

It shows that divine providence, which extends from the highest to the smallest things, distributes within the divine choir **TURN**—that is, vicissitude—and **OFFICE**, because it commits to each their own duty, changing in turn. It had placed silence upon the song, and then Peter began with these words: "Do not marvel if I change color"—that is, change my color from my silver to the fiery red of Mars—"because when I change color, all these others will do the same." We noted this joy above. <column-break/>

God, why has he perverted his office? And consequently, Christ rejects him as an apostate. He does not hold the position among men by right, even if his decree is technically valid; but as far as God is concerned, he does not hold such a rank of reason, but usurps it. **He has made a sewer <note>original: *cloaca*</note> of my cemetery.** "Sewer" signifies a drain that receives stenches and filth and corruptions. "Cemetery" <note>original: *cymiterio*</note> in Greek means "sleeping place" <note>original: *giacitorio*</note>, a place where dead bodies are laid. Therefore, he means that the place which was a sanctuary for the holy martyrs full of every virtue and other good men, now receives practitioners of simony <note>the buying or selling of church offices</note>, the greedy, robbers, and the lustful, who are well-matched to the blood—that is, to cruelty and stench. And just as God was pleased by the virtues of holy men, so His adversary and the enemy of human nature—who, having rebelled against God, fell from here in heaven down to earth—satisfies his evil desire with the vices of these men.

The air becomes red either in the evening or in the morning due to the sun being opposite the cloud. And with such a color all the spirits were inflamed with the love of justice against the captive shepherds. **AND LIKE a woman**: thus Beatrice blushed, pure and chaste, for the failing of such shepherds; just as a chaste woman blushes, who, although she is sure of herself because she knows she is beyond any fault, nevertheless feels shame and stands timid upon hearing something dishonest said of another. And he adds that all the lights in heaven darkened for the abomination of the shepherds' crimes, in a way that he believes was no different from how the sun eclipsed <note>original: *eclipsassi*</note> at the death of Christ. After this, Peter followed in speaking with a voice as much changed from his usual voice as his color was changed. The literal sense is manifest, and the allegory can be easily drawn from it.

Without doubt, it is a wicked abuse to use the bride of Christ—that is, the Apostolic See—for avarice, she who was nurtured by Peter, Linus, and Cletus with such generosity that they were content to shed their blood to increase her. Therefore, what pain, what punishment, what death is fitting for that pontiff who uses the Apostolic dignity for the acquisition of riches? **Linus**, the first pope after Peter, held the seat for eleven years. **Cletus**, the second pope, held it for twelve years. **Pius** was the ninth pope and held it for twelve years. **Sixtus** was the sixth pope and reigned for ten years. **Calixtus** was the fifteenth pope in the time of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus; he held it for five years. He was succeeded by **Urban**, the sixteenth pope, who held it for nine years. It was not our intention that part of the Christian people should sit on the right and part on the left of the pontiffs, our successors—meaning that some should be in their favor and others in their disgrace. Nor that the **keys** granted to me should be a sign on a banner <note>original: *gonfalone*</note> to fight against those who are baptized. It is certainly a horrendous and monstrous thing that the shepherd becomes a wolf. Nor was it our intention that I should be the **image on seals**. On the leaden papal bulls, the heads of Saint Peter and Saint Paul are on one side of the lead. It was not, therefore, my intention that for a price and through simony, privileges for unjust and false things should be made, stamped with our sign. And certainly, if we consider the reverence of that seal on one hand, and what is contained in many bulls on the other, one could say: **Now griffins shall be joined with horses** <note>original Latin: *Iungentur iam gryphes equis*. A quote from Virgil’s Eclogues signifying a monstrous or impossible union.</note>.

These verses are easily understood: **Caorsini and Gascons.** Note in this place the poet mentions two most rapacious French pontiffs: John XXII and Clement IV <note>likely a reference to Clement V, the Gascon pope, though the text says "quarto" (IV)</note>. John was...

<summary>St. Peter delivers a fierce rebuke of the corrupt Papacy, lamenting that the Church, founded on the blood of martyrs, has become a "sewer" of greed and political partisanship. The commentary explains the historical popes Peter mentions and the symbolic significance of the celestial colors changing to red with shame.</summary>

"Of our blood, Cahorsines <note>People from Cahors; a reference to Pope John XXII</note> and Gascons <note>A reference to Pope Clement V, who moved the Papacy to Avignon</note>
make ready to drink; O good beginning,
to what a vile end must you fall!
But the high Providence, which with Scipio
defended the glory of the world for Rome,
will soon bring help, as I conceive it.
And you, my son, who for your mortal weight
shall yet return below, open your mouth,
and do not hide what I do not hide."
Just as our air flakes downward with frozen vapors
when the horn of the Goat of heaven <note>The constellation Capricorn</note>
is touched by the sun,
so I saw the ether on high become adorned,
flaking upward with triumphant vapors
who had made their dwelling-place here with us.
My sight followed their countenances,
and followed until the medium, through its vastness,
took from it the power of passing further ahead.
Whereupon the Lady, who saw me released
from looking upward, said to me: "Cast down
your gaze, and see how far you have turned."

<gloss>to stretch and look upward. Because [the poet], being no longer able to discern them, does not look, she said to me: "Cast down your gaze," i.e., lower your eyes and turn them down and see how you are positioned.</gloss>

Since the hour I had looked before,
I saw myself moved through the entire arch
that the first climate <note>A geographical term for a specific latitudinal zone of the Earth</note> makes from the middle to the end.
So that I saw, beyond Cadiz, the mad
track of Ulysses, and on this side near the shore
where Europa made herself a sweet burden <note>Referring to the myth of Jupiter, in the form of a bull, carrying Europa across the sea</note>.
And more of the site of this little threshing-floor <note>A famous Dantean metaphor for the smallness of Earth compared to the heavens</note>
would have been discovered to me, but the sun preceded
under my feet a sign and more away.
The enamored mind, which dotes
upon my lady always, burned more than ever
to bring back my eyes to her.
And if nature or art ever made lures
to catch the eyes in order to possess the mind,
in human flesh or in its paintings,
all joined together would seem as nothing
compared to the divine pleasure that shone upon me
when I turned to her smiling face.

<column-break/>

of Cahors, a city always abundant in usurers: and
Clement was from Gascony: And the Gascons are
reputed by other Frenchmen to be most rapacious: Whence is the
proverb that the English have the tail of a serpent:
the Gascons have the tail of a wolf. Of this Urban

**BUT THE HIGH [PROVIDENCE]** prays that divine providence
as it once defended the Roman Empire through Scipio
from the barbarian and cruel Hannibal: So also through

pontiffs. After the words of Peter, all the triumph
of the blessed rose up, ascending to the ninth sphere: and
they were so many and so dense and thick and so white that
they seemed in their ascent like snow
in the air when it falls downward in flakes. Snow
is generated from humid and cold vapors. And for
this reason he said **"of frozen vapors"**: **"When
the horn of the Goat of heaven is touched by the sun,"** i.e.,
when the sun is in Capricorn: Of the nature and

Since the poet, being no longer able to see the

he saw that from the hour he had first looked

until this hour, he had moved as much as Gemini moves

a quarter of the circle that the zodiac makes around

the arch"** which the **"first climate"**, which is toward the
summer tropic, makes from its middle where the beginning

Because of which he could not see all the habitable earth
as when he was at the meridian. Therefore
he saw less than half: that is, from this side of
Jerusalem until further beyond the west and
further beyond the other quarter. Because at the middle
of the two quarters one sees everything from east to west.
And then the other colure, which is a quarter, sees the
middle of the whole. Therefore he sees beyond Cadiz. i.e.

beyond the western hemisphere. **Gades** <note>Cadiz</note> is in furthest Spain, far from Calpe, one of the columns of Hercules,
about a hundred miles. Near the mouth of the **Betis** <note>The Guadalquivir river</note>. The **"mad passage of Ulysses"** of which we spoke in the twenty-sixth
of the first canticle <note>Inferno XXVI</note>. Near the shore that ends Asia and is in the Sidonian region which is
in Syria. Whereon **Europa**, riding Jove transformed into a bull, was a sweet burden to Jove who loved her: And of this elsewhere [the poet] narrates fully.

<meta>This page continues from the previous section where Dante, positioned in the Heaven of the Fixed Stars within the constellation of Gemini, was instructed by Beatrice to look down at the Earth to see how far he had ascended. <header>PARADISO</header>

...now the story. Then he adds that he would have seen the entire site of this "threshing floor": that is, of this small courtyard and square. He calls it a **threshing floor** <note>original: "aiuola"; a term Dante uses to emphasize the insignificance and smallness of the Earth compared to the vastness of the heavens</note> to denote how small the habitable earth is. For all of the fourth part <note>referring to the known world of the 14th century</note> is not inhabited, because that which is under the northern cold zone is uninhabitable, as is that which is under the torrid zone, which would extend to the equator of the fourth part in the middle of the torrid zone. But the sun, which was beneath his feet because it is in the fourth heaven and Dante was in the eighth, was preceding him: that is, it was going ahead by one sign and more. For as the poet was in Gemini, the sun was ahead of the entire sign of Taurus and part of Aries. **THE MIND** in love: my mind, enamored with Beatrice. Who **dallies** with Beatrice who follows. Beatrice, as his lady, burned more than ever to lead his eyes back to her. And certainly, although sacred doctrine is always worthy of being loved, nonetheless it deserves a much greater love when it treats of supreme things. **And if nature or art**: Many bodies, whether natural or made by art—such as those sculpted or painted—capture the eyes of others by their beauty and lead them away with pleasure, so that such pleasure enters through the eyes into the soul. Whence Petrarch says:
*Eyes, weep; accompany the heart: which through your failing suffers death*
And elsewhere:
*Love found me entirely disarmed, and the way open through the eyes to the heart*
And the Latin elegiac poet:
> If you know it not, the eyes are the leaders in love <note>original: "Si nescis oculi sunt in amore duces"</note>

And Solomon:
> But the woman captures the precious soul of the man <note>original: "Mulier autē uiri pretiosam animam capit"</note>

Therefore, if all the beautiful things which, by feeding the eyes, capture the mind were gathered together, they would seem as nothing in comparison to the divine pleasure that reflected—that is, shone—into my eyes when I turned to the smiling face of Beatrice.

*And the power that her gaze bestowed on me*
*from the beautiful nest of Leda plucked me*
*and into the swiftest heaven impelled me.*
*Its parts, most living and sublime,*
*are so uniform that I cannot say*
*which place Beatrice chose for me.*
*But she, who saw my desire,*
*began, smiling so happily*
*that God seemed to rejoice in her face:*
*"The nature of motion, which keeps quiet*
*the center and moves all the rest around it,*
*begins here as if from its goal.*
*And this heaven has no other 'where'*
*than the divine mind, in which is kindled*
*the love that turns it and the power it rains down."*

<column-break/>

They moved from the eighth sphere to the ninth, which is the **First Mover** <term>Primum Mobile: the swiftest, outermost sphere of the physical universe that originates all motion</term>, through the power that Beatrice's gaze bestowed on him: that is, gave to him with love. The meaning is that such was the power that came out of Beatrice's gaze that it plucked him from the **nest of Leda**: that is, from the sign of Gemini, and impelled him: that is, pushed him into the swiftest heaven, which is the ninth sphere. And he calls Gemini the "nest of Leda" because Jove, loving Leda, transformed himself into a swan and knew her; from that union were born two eggs, and from one came Pollux and Helen, and from the other Castor and Clytemnestra. Pollux and Castor were called the Dioscuri: that is, sons of Jove, and were transformed in heaven into the sign of Gemini. **Its parts, most living and sublime**: he calls this heaven "most living" because of its supreme velocity and greatest power, and "sublime" because it is the highest heaven. Its faces are **so uniform**, all in one way, and are not distinguished by various stars as they are in the eighth sphere. And all the power of all the inferior spheres is united in this 

ninth one. And because it is uniform, I cannot say in which place Beatrice chose for me. But she, seeing that I desired to know it, began to speak with such happiness that God seemed to rejoice in her face. Then he sets down the words of Beatrice, which were these: **The nature of motion**: that is, the "natured nature" <note>original: "natura naturata"; a philosophical term referring to the created world as an expression of God's will</note> that God has placed in this sphere, which nature keeps the center quiet—that is, the Earth, which is its center and is immobile, while all the other spheres, both of the elements and of the heavens, are mobile. Therefore, nature keeps the center quiet and moves all the others. And for this reason, Aristotle says that nature is the principle of motion and of rest. **Begins here**: that is, from this ninth sphere as from its goal: that is, from its beginning. **AND this heaven has no other 'where'**: that is, it has no other place where it stops than the divine mind. For its motion revolves around the divine mind. Whence Boethius:
> It circles the deep mind and turns the heaven in a similar image <note>original: "Mentemque profundam circuit et simili conuertit imagine celum"</note>

**In which**: that is, in which divine mind is kindled the love that turns it: that is, the Intelligence <note>the angelic being assigned to move the sphere</note> that turns it. For this Intelligence has love for its Creator and, burning with love for Him, returns to Him. **And the power** of this ninth heaven which **rains down**: that is, pours into the other inferior spheres. Therefore, this power is kindled in the divine mind and is poured into the First Mover equally through all its parts; and from there it is poured into the other spheres and celestial bodies. And thus one pours into another, and thus it becomes diversified, even though it is one power and comes from one principle.

*Light and love in one circle encompass it,*
*just as this heaven does the others; and that belt*
*only He who girds it understands.*
*Its motion is not by another's distinguished,*
*but the others are measured by this one...*

<column-break/>

He demonstrates that this ninth heaven is encompassed by the Empyrean heaven <term>Empyrean: the highest heaven, which is non-physical and consists of pure light and love</term>, which is nothing but light and love, just as this ninth heaven encompasses the others. Therefore, this light and love pours into the ninth sphere, which is the First Mover, and encompasses it. And we conclude that the elements and the things...

<header>CANTO XXVII</header>

...just as ten is [measured] by its half and its fifth;
And how time keeps its roots in such a vessel
and its leaves in the others,
can now be manifest to you.

**The Empyrean heaven encircles it** <note>The commentator explains that the Primum Mobile is "encircled" by the Empyrean</note>—by this he means the Empyrean heaven and no other: God alone understands the Empyrean, and it [the Empyrean] understands the ninth heaven, and that the eighth, and so on; the superior heaven always encompasses the inferior. **ITS MOTION IS NOT MARKED BY ANOTHER**: that is, the motion of the Primum Mobile is not measured by any other motion. Instead, the other heavens are measured by this one: because this Primum Mobile completes its revolution in twenty-four hours, which hours are taken from the variation of its parts. **AND HOW IT KEEPS [TIME] IN SUCH A VESSEL**: The meaning is that the motion of the ninth sphere is the measure of all other motions; as has been said, it is the "root" of time, since time is nothing other than the measure of motion in changeable things. And if the root is in this [the ninth sphere], its parts [the leaves] extend through the motions of the other heavens. Therefore, this aforementioned Primum Mobile completes its revolution in twenty-four hours. Whence it is the root of days, and the root of months and years, which are distinguished by the sun.

O greed, who drowns mortals
so far beneath you that no one has the power
to pull their eyes out of your waves!
The will blossoms well in men,
but the continuous rain converts
the true plums into blighted, shriveled fruit.
Faith and innocence are found
only in little children; then both
flee before the cheeks are covered [with a beard].
One, still stammering, keeps the fasts,
who later devours with an open mouth
any food through any moon <note>meaning: at any time, regardless of religious fasting periods</note>.
And another, while stammering, loves and listens to
his mother, who, once he has full speech,
then desires to see her buried.
Thus the white skin turns black
at the first sight of the beautiful daughter
of him who brings morning and leaves evening.

...and changes these virtues into vices in such a way that before the cheeks—that is, the jowls—are covered by a beard, they have become vicious. **And some stammering**: that is, in early childhood when the child cannot yet pronounce every word. For "to stammer" <note>original: "balbutire"</note> means to be tongue-tied. **He fasts and then, having become an adult, he devours**: strictly speaking, "to devour" <note>original: "devorare"</note> in Latin means to swallow without chewing, which is an act of gluttony and greed at any time. **And another at that same age loves and reveres** his mother, but then with "full speech"—that is, as a grown adult—he desires her death. **THUS THE WHITE SKIN TURNS BLACK**: the meaning is that the white skin, which is on the tender face, turns black. **At the first sight**: almost in the first stage of life. **Of the beautiful daughter**: that is, of human nature, which is the daughter of the sun; because the sun is the universal father of all living things. **Who brings morning**: that is, produces the light when it rises. **And leaves evening**: when it goes to the west. It turns from white to black because from being pure, it becomes infected with vices. And allegorically we understand the sun to be God himself, of whom the human soul is the daughter.

You, so that you do not marvel at this,
know that on earth there is no one to govern;
wherefore the human family goes astray.
But before January is entirely un-wintered
by that hundredth [of a day] which is neglected down there...

<column-break/>

...composed by those [heavens] moved by planets and epicycles <note>term: epicycles; small circles centered on the circumference of a larger circle, used in Ptolemaic astronomy to explain planetary motion</note> from the eighth sphere; and the eighth by the ninth; and the ninth by God, either with or without a medium. But the Empyrean heaven is immediate from God and is immobile. Whence the poet's sentence is true, that only He who encircles that perimeter understands it: that is, God, who...

**O** First exclamation, by which Peter condemns the insatiable greed for earthly things, which sinks and submerges the human mind into the sea of affection for momentary and fleeting goods, so that they cannot raise their eyes to this wondrous region of heaven arranged with ineffable order. Therefore, he cries out with just indignation: **O greed**: that is, O unrestrained desire. **Which drowns**: that is, submerges in its sea so deeply that no man has the power to pull his eyes out of its waves: that is, out of its perturbations and affections. **The will blossoms well in men**: there is innate in men a will for the Supreme Good, and it blossoms in them. But then, just as constant rain prevents plum trees from producing true fruit, but converts them into "bozacchi" <note>term: "bozacchi"; blighted, swollen, or worm-eaten plums that never ripen</note> which are full of water and worms, so the rain of greed for earthly things corrupts the sincere will. Similar to this is Ovid: <note>original: "Cepisti melius quã desinis ultima primis . Cedunt dissimiles hic uir et ille senex"</note> *You began better than you end; the last parts yield to the first; this man and that old man are unlike.* And Isaiah: <note>original: "Expectauit ut faceret uuas fecit autem labruscas"</note> *He expected it to make grapes, but it made wild grapes.* And that this is so, we see that men in childhood have honest innocence, shame, and purity. Afterward comes the more adult age...

**He concludes** that no one should marvel if men, who are the "family" governed by the shepherd, go astray: that is, exit the straight path and reason, because there is no one who governs. For the "shepherds" <note>referring to the corrupt leaders of the Church</note> have become wolves. **BUT before January is entirely un-wintered**, that is, before... <note>Dante refers to the error in the Julian calendar which was slowly shifting the seasons; he predicts a great change will come before the error adds up to an entire month.</note>

<summary>In this passage, Dante explains the astronomical nature of the Primum Mobile as the source of time and the measurement for all other heavens, followed by a fierce condemnation of human greed and the corruption of the Church leaders.</summary>

<header>PARADISO</header>

### these heavenly circles shall roar
### That the fortune so long awaited
### will turn the sterns to where the bows are
### so that the fleet will run straight
### And true fruit will come after the flower

<column-break/>

January, which at present is in the winter, begins from the entry of the sun into Capricorn: and finishes when it leaves Pisces: because of the hundredth part <note>Dante refers to the slight error in the Julian calendar—about 1/100th of a day—which caused the calendar year to slowly drift away from the solar year</note> which is down there—that is, on the neglected earth <note>original: "neglecta idest sprezzata"</note>. We demonstrated in the first canticle <note>Referring to Landino's commentary on the *Inferno*</note> that the solar course contains three hundred sixty-five days and a quarter part of a day, and beyond that quarter, a hundredth part. 

But the quarter is accounted for every four years because in the leap year <term>bixesto (leap year)</term> the year is made of three hundred sixty-six days. But the hundredth part is not accounted for: and because of this, the entry of the sun into Capricorn—which gives a beginning to the winter—has moved nearly fifteen days closer to January; and continuing so in the course of time, it will move through January and then through February: and then January will remain in the autumn and outside of the winter. **THESE HEAVENLY CIRCLES**: these heavens. **They shall roar**. The heaven does not make a different sound at one time than another. But by "roaring" he wants to denote a cruel influence. For roaring is for lions, just as lowing is for oxen. Therefore, such an influence shall come from the stars that Fortune will turn the sterns to where the bows are <note>A nautical metaphor meaning the ship of the Church or the State will be completely turned around or set on a new course</note>—that is, the order instituted by Divine Providence will turn the government to a good path, which at present goes poorly. **SO THAT THE FLEET WILL RUN STRAIGHT**: that is, all the ships that are in this fleet together will take a good voyage. *Classe* <note>original: "Classe"</note> in Latin <term>classis</term> signifies not one ship, but the entire fleet or armada. **AND TRUE FRUIT shall come after the flower**: that is, such government will produce true fruit that will bring about eternal salvation.

<summary>This page contains Landino's commentary on Beatrice’s prophecy at the end of Canto XXVII, explaining the astronomical shift of the calendar and the metaphorical "roaring" of the heavens that will bring a divine correction to human corruption.</summary>
