<page-num>XXVIII</page-num>
<header>CANTO XXVIII</header>
<sig>.i.1</sig>

# CANTO XXVIII OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE

After she who "enparadises" <note>Dante’s invented verb *imparadisa* suggests being placed in or filled with Paradise</note> my mind
opened up the truth against the present life
of wretched mortals,
Like one who sees in a mirror the flame
of a torch <note>original: "doppiero," a large wax candle or torch</note> behind him
before he has it in sight or in thought,
And turns around to see if the glass
tells him the truth, and sees that it matches
with the truth, as a melody does with its rhythm,
So my memory remembers
that I did, looking into the beautiful eyes
from which Love made the cord to capture me.

<margin>A lit torch behind oneself: not seeing it directly, one looks into a mirror placed in front and sees the image of the torch and the flame; turning around, one sees that the mirror represented the truth. Not without reason does the poet relate that he saw the ray of deity in Beatrice’s eyes—that is, in the contemplation of theology. For as Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great</note> writes: "Just as we cannot look at the sun in its own body, but look at it in every other place; so too we cannot discern God in His primary being, but we can look at Him in theological scripture as if through a certain reflection."</margin>

And as I turned, and my own eyes were touched
by what appears in that volume <note>Dante often uses the metaphor of a "volume" or book to describe the divine mind or the totality of the universe</note>
whenever one looks closely into its circling,
I saw a point that radiated light
so sharp that the sight it inflames
must close because of the intense keenness;
And whichever star seems smallest from here
would seem a moon if placed beside it,
as star is placed with star.

<margin>That is, the eyes—which face that light inflames and burns. Nor is it a marvel, for if the physical eye cannot endure the light of the sun, how much more shall the eye of the intellect be unable to endure the light of the eternal Sun that made this perceptible sun and moon. He describes God, therefore, under the form and figure of a fixed and immobile point; and further describes the orders of the angels in the form of ignited circles—that is, circles of fire.</margin>

Perhaps as close as a halo appears
around the light that paints it
when the vapor that carries it is most thick,
Distant around the point, a circle of fire <note>original: "digne," a poetic contraction for "di igne" (of fire)</note>
revolved so fast it would have surpassed
the motion that most quickly girds the world;
And this was surrounded by another,
and that by the third, and the third by the fourth,
the fourth by the fifth, and the fifth by the sixth.
Above followed the seventh, so spread out
that the messenger of Juno <note>Iris, the rainbow</note>
entire would be too narrow to contain it.

<column-break/>

Because in the previous chapter the author described the ninth sphere, it is fitting that in this twenty-eighth he describes the orders of angels that are within it. Beatrice shows him the point of divinity and the hierarchies of angels that are around it; then she clarifies certain doubts for him in a way that remains clear. **AFTER SHE**: since she who "enparadises"—that is, puts into paradise—my mind, opened and manifested the truth against the present life, full of the vices of wretched mortals. **LIKE IN A MIRROR**: The meaning is that the author, looking into the eyes of Beatrice—from which Love made the cord to capture him—saw the most ardent light of the divinity, which he could not see directly because he had his back to it. This is like having a lit torch behind oneself; not seeing it, one looks in a mirror in front and sees the image of the torch and the flame; turning around, he sees that the mirror has represented the truth to him.

He describes the true thing whose image he had already seen in Beatrice’s eyes. Therefore, as he was turned back toward where the light was—the image of which he had seen in Beatrice’s eyes—his own eyes were "touched" by what appears in that "volume": that is, by what is seen in that deity which is infinite. **WHENEVER**: that is, every time one "looks closely" <note>original: "fadocchi," literally "makes eyes at"</note>: that is, looks diligently. For if one does not look very well, it is not seen. Having turned, therefore, he saw a point which radiated—that is, it cast out a light so sharp and penetrating that it is necessary to close one’s sight.

The author had already described the first principle under the appearance of an immobile and fixed point; now he describes the orders of the angels under the form of circles of fire. And beginning from the first, he says that it revolves most swiftly, as close to the point as the circle generated around the moon by thick and dense vapors is close to the moon. It is certainly an arduous and difficult matter, and situated above human possibility, to fully express the angelic nature; but from many things written first by Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-century theologian whose work *The Celestial Hierarchy* is the primary source for Dante’s angelology</note> and afterward by many other theologians, we will run through a few of them with brevity. And first we will say that although "angel" is the proper name of the incorporeal spirits of the last and ninth choir, nevertheless all the other spirits...

The commentary by Landino explains the metaphor of Beatrice's eyes as a mirror for divine truth and introduces the theological study of angels.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Paradiso, Canto XXVIII. Having seen the point of light representing the Divine Essence, Dante now observes the concentric circles of fire surrounding it, which are the nine angelic hierarchies. This page provides a theological definition of angels and explains the specific roles and characteristics of each order according to medieval scholasticism and mystical theology.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>

<header>PARADISO</header>

### Thus far the ninth [circle], and each one
### moved more slowly according as it was
### in number distant from the One <note>The "One" refers to the central point of light, representing God, around which the angelic circles revolve.</note>
### And that one had the clearest flame
### to which the pure spark was least distant
### I believe, however, because it "in-truths" itself more with her <note>original: "sinvera." This is a verb created by Dante, meaning to align oneself with or be filled by the truth.</note>

<column-break/>

All, from whatever choir or hierarchy, are called "angels" by a universal name. An Angel, according to Damascus <note>John of Damascus (c. 675–749), a Syrian monk and theologian</note> and Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and teacher of Thomas Aquinas</note> and all other theologians, is an incorporeal intellectual substance: always mobile, with free will <note>original: "libera dalbitrio," literally free of judgment/choice</note>, serving God, and immortal not by nature but by grace. And Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century Christian Neoplatonist whose "The Celestial Hierarchy" is the primary source for angelic lore in the Middle Ages</note> in the book *On Divine Names* <note>original: "de diuinis nominibus"</note> writes that the angel is the image of God: a manifestation of hidden light, a most splendid, pure, and immaculate mirror: the

<column-break/>

which receives in itself, if it is permissible to say, the beauty of well-formed deiformity <note>The quality of being like God in form or nature</note>: and purely declares within itself, as far as possible, the hidden goodness. The angel differs from our soul in four ways. First, the soul can be united to a body, but the angel cannot. The soul is rational, while the angel is intellectual; for the soul acquires knowledge by investigating and comparing, whereas the angel acquires it simply by beholding. The angel does not suffer except in respect to his superiors, while the soul suffers in respect to inferiors, because it can be changed by sensory things. The soul can turn from good to evil and from evil to good; but the angel cannot, because he remains firm in that toward which he once turned. Angels are all similar in that they are immortal, invisible, indissoluble, simple, distinct in person, and incommunicable in their nature. But they are dissimilar in their gifts of grace and nature. Dionysius adds that in every created spiritual nature, the essence is one thing, the power another, and the operation another.

The celestial hierarchies are three, and each has three orders. The superior hierarchy has: **Cherubim**, **Seraphim**, and **Thrones**. The Cherubim consider the goodness of God; the Seraphim, the virtue; and the Thrones, the equity. Furthermore, in the first, God loves as charity; in the second, He knows as truth; in the third, He sits as equity. It is the nature of the Seraphim to burn in the love of God, and to draw others to such fire and order them in God. These are immediately joined with God and see God most purely; nor do they turn away, even when they are "outside" of God <note>This likely refers to their focus remaining on God even when performing tasks in the created world</note>. In the Cherubim, first and primarily, the ray of divine light shines continually, because they are joined most closely to the divine truth. These move man toward divine knowledge; they shine more than the others and pour down upon those below the fullness of light which they receive. They are called "Thrones" because the Lord sits upon them, and through them He determines His judgments; and these also pour truth into the lower orders.

The second hierarchy has **Dominations**, **Principalities**, and **Powers**. The Dominations rule the offices of the angels. The Principalities are presidents over the heads of peoples. The Powers restrain the powers of the demons. In the Dominations, God rules as majesty; in the Principalities, He governs as sovereignty; in the Powers, He defends as salvation.

The third hierarchy has **Virtues**, **Archangels**, and **Angels**. To the first belongs the operation of miracles. To the second, the announcement of the greatest things. To the third, the care of human guardianship. In the first, God works as power; in the second, He reveals as light; in the third, He sends as a spirit of inspiration. This is the order given by Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great</note> and Bernard <note>Bernard of Clairvaux</note>; but Dionysius places the Virtues in the second order of the second hierarchy, and the Principalities in the first order of the third.

In the angels, there is dignity of creation, grace of confirmation, love of the Creator, and vision of the divinity. They have substance of essence, perspicacity of intelligence, and speed of motion. The higher angels are without pride; the lower ones obey without indignation; and all are without any lack. Those who are more excellent by nature precede the others in grace and glory. The superiors participate in every truth of the inferiors, but not the opposite.

But because it is a thing worthy of knowledge, we will demonstrate according to the doctrine of Dionysius why the choirs or orders of angels are nine. Although, as Damascus writes, only God who created them knows the species and the limit of angelic substances, taking this principle we shall say that love is the supreme of all things, and it is that which first receives the influences from God and unites the mind with God. Therefore, this is the most excellent way, without which nothing else is of use.
<margin>•</margin> And because the soul void of the nature of love is malevolent, and into a malevolent soul true wisdom does not enter, it follows that through love we can receive the true doctrine which never puffs up. Then, from love and from the mind comes knowledge <note>original: "scientia"</note>, and from no other source; it is necessary that there proceed from it a just and perfectly complete judgment. Thus we already see three choirs: **Seraphim** in love, **Cherubim** in knowledge, and **Thrones** in judgment. After judgment follows command <note>original: "imperio"</note>, so that what ought to be done is done; and after command, a certain virtue which is the executor of the command. Nor is such execution enough unless a certain resistance and power is added against the opposing power which always strives to hinder good commands. Therefore, in this second hierarchy are: **Dominations**, **Virtues**, and **Powers**. 

And now we have seen six reasons. Now follows the doctrine which must be given to those who do not know. And this is of two kinds: for the ignorant are erudite and taught either with words or with works. And doctrine through works is more effective than words, whether they be spoken or inspired; and especially it is so with the doctrine of operations when those are unusual, rare, and supernatural. Therefore, the supreme of operations for those who do not know is that of miracles; the second is the operation of contemplation and apprehension of the easiest things and those most belonging to our salvation; the third is the doctrine of active, civil, and minor things. These, then, are nine operations which follow the order already shown. Thus, the first, the loving power, are called **Seraphim**, which name in Hebrew <note>original: "seraphim"</note> means "incendiary" or "burning" or "those who heat." This is the power of fire and its...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Paradiso, Canto XXVIII. Having previously defined the general nature of angels as incorporeal intellectual substances, the text now moves into a specific breakdown of the nine angelic orders, their etymologies, and their cosmic functions based on scholastic theology. It then transitions back to the narrative of Dante and Beatrice observing the divine point and the revolving circles of light.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<page-num>XXVIII</page-num>
<header>CANTO XXVIII</header>

the spiritual is nothing other than love. And this is the fire that God came to place on the earth: which, entering into the bones of the prophet Jeremiah <note>original: "gierũdi" (Geremia)</note>, and according to their act of absolute and perfect knowledge, the second order are named **Cherubim**; which in Hebrew means "multitude of knowledge" or truly "infusion of wisdom." The third are **Thrones**, named thus from the judicial power in their act of judging: because *thronos* in Greek signifies an exalted and elevated seat where one who judges sits. These three acts are much more spiritualized than the others. Whence Paul writes of this last one: *He who judges all things and is judged by no one* <note>original: "Qui omnia iudicat et anemine iudicatur" — 1 Corinthians 2:15</note>. The fourth order are the **Dominations**, because they have an imperative act which most greatly accords with lordship. The fifth order are the **Virtues**, because they intrepidly and without any diminution carry into execution that which God has imperated—that is, commanded. The sixth are the **Powers**, because they resist the powers of the demons. And these second three orders of angels are less quiet and more active than the first three. The seventh are the **Principalities**, operating in a powerful and principal way of doctrine, performing supernatural things and miracles for the instruction of the ignorant. The eighth are **Archangels**, named thus because they announce more principal and greater things: because *arche* in Greek signifies "principality" or "beginning." And this order, being in the middle between the Principalities and the Angels, has taken the name of the superiors and the inferiors: because, reformed by the Principalities, it reforms and vivifies the Angels in simple unity. The order among the blessed spirits is that the superior infuses doctrine into the inferior, as a master to a disciple. But such doctrine is clearer in the first than in the second, and in the second than in the third, and so on successively down to the first. For this reason, the prophet Zechariah, when the Lord wished to free the people from the Babylonian captivity, saw one of these angels who appeared from God; and then he taught it to the inferior; and finally, the inferior taught it to the prophets. The order of **Angels**, because it is the last and closest to us, announces future things to us. The Archangels announce to us through the medium of the Angels, and perhaps sometimes without a medium. Just as Gabriel the Archangel brought the news to Mary—though in the Gospel he is always called "Angel." But whether this annunciation was made through an angel or by him without a medium is not to be judged without the greatest consideration. The inferior orders begin from the virtue of the superiors, but always less so, degree by degree. Therefore, observed in proportion, they participate in the wisdom that is in the Cherubim. Many seek the vast number of the angels; and among many, it is manifest that the three hierarchies are nine choirs. But how many angels there may be is not manifest. The prophet Daniel, according to the seventy interpreters <note>Referring to the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note>, says: "A thousand thousands and ten thousand times ten thousand," where he places the thousands and the myriads, which two numbers are very large. And because he recirculates them into themselves—for he says: *mille millenariis et myrias myriadas*, that is, *ten thousand ten thousands*—he silently demonstrates that they are infinite. Because a circle beginning in itself and ending in itself seems to demonstrate an infinite number. Furthermore, the other translation has another number: that is, *thousands of thousands and ten thousand times a hundred thousand*. But **Albert the Great** <note>original: "Alberto magno"</note> in his *Compendium of Theology* writes that each choir has within it six thousand, six hundred, and sixty-six legions; and each legion has as many angels as there are legions: that is, six thousand, six hundred, and sixty-six. Therefore, each choir has within itself forty-four million, four hundred thirty-five thousand, and five hundred fifty-six angels. Which number multiplied by nine choirs makes the sum of three hundred ninety-nine million, ninety-two thousand, and four angels. From which, if one removes the number of one choir—because that many fell—there will remain in the nine choirs three hundred fifty-five million, four hundred eighty-four thousand, and four hundred forty-eight angels. And let this suffice for the present regarding the angels, for we treated of the wicked angels, and how very brief their stay was from their creation, and many other things, in the last canto of the first canticle <note>Referring to the end of the *Inferno*</note>.

->fearing and suspended, said: From that point<-
->depends the heaven and all of nature.<-

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'V' with complex floral and foliate motifs surrounding the letter.</image-desc>
**B**eatrice sees the author suspended and anxious for not understanding. Therefore, she showed him how upon the point already mentioned depends all created nature—that is, the whole universe. But then a doubt arises in Dante: how can it be that these circles closer to the point make a faster motion than those further away? For in the sensible world—that is, in the world and in the elements—the opposite is seen: because as the turns <gloss>that is, the revolutions</gloss> made by the heavens are more remote from the center, they are so much more divine and burning with divine love, and consequently swifter. For the ninth sphere <note>the Primum Mobile</note> moves faster than the eighth. Therefore, he concludes that if his desire is to reach its end—that is, if it must find rest in this temple where the angels dwell, which is not included in any sphere but has for its boundary love and light (that is, the **Empyrean heaven**, made of love and light)—these equals, being without end, also make...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Paradiso, Canto XXVIII. The previous page concluded the description of the nine angelic orders. This page addresses Dante’s confusion regarding why the physical heavens (the "example") and the angelic circles (the "exemplar") appear to operate in reverse—where the smallest, fastest angelic circle corresponds to the largest, most distant physical sphere.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>PARADISO CANTO XXVIII</header>

I must yet hear how the example
and the exemplar do not go in one way,
for by myself I contemplate this in vain.
If your fingers are not for such a knot
sufficient, it is no wonder,
so much by not being tried has it become hard.
Thus my Lady said: "Take
what I shall tell you, if you wish to be satisfied,
and sharpen your wits around it.
The physical circles are wide or narrow
according to the more or less of the virtue
that spreads through all their parts.
Greater goodness wishes to work greater health;
greater health is contained in a greater body,
if it has its parts equally complete.
Therefore, this one that sweeps along
all the rest of the universe, corresponds
to the circle that loves most and knows most.
For if you draw your measure around
the virtue, and not the appearance
of the substances that appear round to you,
You will see a marvelous consistency
of the greater to the more and the smaller to the less,
of each heaven to its intelligence."

---

As the hemisphere of the air
remains splendid and serene when
Boreas blows from that cheek which is more mild,
Because the murk is purged and resolved
which before troubled it, so that the sky smiles
with the beauties of every district;
So did I, after my Lady provided me
with her clear response,
and like a star in heaven the truth was seen.

<column-break/>

the infinite temple <note>The "infinite temple" refers to the divine or intelligible realm.</note> must be understood because the example—that is, the inferior and sensible world, such as the elements and the heavens, which is made in the likeness of the intelligible—and the exemplar—that is, the intelligible world—do not go in one way, as has been said. **IF your fingers**: Beatrice responds that it is no wonder if his fingers are not sufficient to untie such a knot, because it has become harder by being less attempted. And by this, it signifies that doubts and difficulties in any science, the less they are attempted to be understood, the more difficult they become to understand. Then she solves the doubt in this form, demonstrating that as the circles of the intelligible world have more virtue <note>term: "virtue" (virtù) here refers to spiritual power or divine influence rather than moral character.</note>, so the first sphere of the sensible world, because it is closest to God, has more virtue. And in this way, the nine orders of angels proportionally correspond to the nine heavens, always the most worthy to the most worthy. **The physical circles**, that is, the heavens that have a body, are wide—that is, broad and large—and narrow—that is, small and tight—according to whether they have more or less virtue. For the ninth sphere is as much greater than that of the moon as it has more virtue. And **greater goodness wishes to work greater health**—that is, that which has greater virtue produces a more salutary effect. And **greater health is contained**—that is, a larger body contains in itself greater virtue if it has its parts equally complete and perfect. Therefore, this ninth sphere, which is larger than all the others and sweeps with it all the other spheres (for in turning in twenty-four hours it pulls with it in the same time all the other spheres), as the most perfect sphere, corresponds to the first circle of angels, which is most perfect in love and in knowledge. **FOR**: she demonstrates that the similarity should be understood according to virtue, and not according to physical quantity. Whence she says: if you draw your measure—that is, place the measure you make of the circles of angels, which are incorporeal, upon their virtue and not upon the appearance—that is, the physical quantity—that is, upon the intensive virtue <note>term: "intensive virtue" (uirtu itersiua) is a scholastic concept where power is measured by its "intensity" or quality rather than its physical size or "extension."</note> which is spiritual and does not appear, and not upon the intensity <note>original: "intensitia"</note> which is physical and appears. You will see a marvelous consistency and agreement of the greater to the more—that is, of the larger body to the more virtue, and of the smaller body to the less virtue of each heaven, of which there are nine, to its intelligence—that is, to its circle of angels. Therefore, the ninth sphere corresponds to the Seraphim; the eighth to the Cherubim; Saturn to the Thrones; Jupiter to the Dominations; Mars to the Virtues; the Sun to the Powers; Venus to the Principalities; Mercury to the Archangels; and the Moon to the Angels.

---

**The comparison** is that just as the air remains serene when the north wind blows, so the truth remained clear in me after Beatrice's response. And he says **when Boreas**—that is, the northern wind—**blows from that cheek**—that is, part (because winds are depicted with a mouth)—**WHENCE it is more mild**—that is, toward the west, from whence comes the northwest wind <note>original: "choro"</note>, which wind, although it is northern, nevertheless, because it comes from that part of the north which is closer to the west, inclines toward the sweet nature of Zephyrus <note>The west wind.</note>. **Murk** <note>original: "roffia"</note> is the condensation of humid and condensed vapors. **THE SKY smiles**: it remains serene. And it is a shared metaphor; for just as we say a man's face is serene when he smiles, so we say the sky smiles when it is serene. **OF EVERY DISTRICT** <note>original: "parroffia"</note>: of every part. And he said *paroffia* in place of *parochia* <note>parish</note>. And a parish in a city is that group of men who are under one same church.

<summary>Dante struggles to understand why the smallest divine circles correspond to the largest physical heavens; Beatrice explains that spiritual "virtue" is the true measure, not physical size. The text concludes with a metaphor of the north wind clearing the sky, representing Dante's newfound clarity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Paradiso, Canto XXVIII. Having explained why the angelic circles appear to move faster when they are closer to the center (God), Beatrice now identifies the specific orders of angels that compose these circles and explains the nature of their beatitude, which is rooted in vision rather than love.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>CANTO XXVIII</header>
<sig>I. iii</sig>

And after her words ceased,
no differently does iron throw off sparks
when it boils, than did the circles sparkle.
Every spark followed their fire,
and they were so many that in their number
they multiplied more than the doubling of the chess squares. <note>Refers to the legend where a grain of wheat is doubled on each of the 64 squares of a chessboard, resulting in a number in the quintillions.</note>
I heard "Hosanna" sung from choir to choir
to the fixed point that holds them to their "where" <note>original: "ubi", a Latin philosophical term for location.</note>
and will always hold them where they have always been.

<gloss>In the 4th square: 8; in the 5th: 16; and so on until a massive number. These angels sang Hosanna, that is, they praised God from choir to choir, one choir responding to the next; and [He] orders [them] to the fixed point, that is, to God, who holds them to their "where," that is, their own firm and proper place, because they were confirmed in grace; and He will always keep them there, meaning from the moment He created them.</gloss>

And she who felt the doubtful thoughts
within my mind said: "The first circles
have shown you Seraphim and Cherubim.
They follow their bonds <note>original: "vimi", literally willow-withes used for binding.</note> so swiftly
to liken themselves to the point as much as they can,
and they can as much as they are exalted to see.
Those other loves that go around them
are called Thrones of the divine aspect,
because they concluded the first triad. <note>original: "ternaro".</note>
And you should know that all have delight
in proportion to how deep their vision sinks
into the Truth in which every intellect is stilled.
From this it can be seen how the state
of being blessed is founded on the act that sees:
not on that of love, which follows after.
And of this seeing, merit is the measure,
which grace brings forth and good will;
thus they proceed from rank to rank.
The other triad that thus blossoms
in this eternal springtime
which the nightly Aries does not despoil, <note>In autumn, the sign of Aries is in the night sky; Dante uses this to contrast earthly seasons with the unchanging heaven.</note>
here perpetually sings "Hosanna" with an "un-wintering" song <note>original: "suerna", to sing like a bird at the end of winter.</note>
with three melodies that sound in three
orders of joy with which it is tripled.
In this hierarchy are the three goddesses:
first Dominations, and then Virtues;
the third order is Powers.
Then in the two penultimate dances,
Principalities and Archangels appear;
the last is composed entirely of Angelic sports.
These orders all gaze upward,
and downward they prevail so that toward God
all are drawn, and they all draw."

<column-break/>

**W**hen her words finished, the nine angelic hosts sparkled as boiling iron sparks. The meaning is that just as many sparks fly out from boiling iron, so from those circles appeared many angels flying like sparks. But although they were flying, they did not leave their order. Instead, they all followed their fire, that is, the order of their circle. And they were so many that the number multiplied into many thousands, more than the doubling of the chess squares. There are sixty-four squares on a chessboard; if they were doubled, so that in the first square there was one, in the second two, [the third four, etc.]

**B**eatrice shows Dante the orders of the angels to remove the doubts she saw him holding in his mind. She does this so he may understand that the blessedness of the saints is caused by vision. For seeing and understanding are the cause of blessedness, because the mind feeds on this alone; this is its nectar and its ambrosia. **SERAPHIM** and Cherubim: of whom we have already spoken. **AND THEIR BONDS:** their ties and links, which is God; for the desire to know Him ensures they do not distance themselves from Him; and they are able to know Him more as they are closer to Him and rise higher to see Him. **THRONES OF THE DIVINE** aspect: because, as has been said, God ordains His judgments through them. **SINKS DEEP** into the truth, that is, into God, who is the supreme truth. **FROM THIS IT CAN** be seen: From here it is understood that the state of being blessed consists in seeing, that is, in knowing. And not in loving. Because love proceeds from cognition, and not cognition from love. And the creature loves the Creator more as it knows Him more, and receives merit and grace according to the measure of knowing. Therefore, from rank to rank, the more it sees, the more grace and good will it has—that is, the will to want what God wants. There follows the second triad: which is Dominations, Virtues, and Powers; which buds and puts forth leaves in blessedness, which he calls eternal spring, which the nightly Aries, that is, autumn, does not despoil. Our spring blossoms, but autumn then makes the leaves fall. But the spring of heaven always stays green. And he used "nightly Aries" for autumn because autumn begins when the sun enters Libra; and then Libra in our hemisphere is only seen by day. From which it follows that Aries, the opposite sign, is only seen at night. Here they "un-winter," that is, they continually sing Hosanna with three melodies. Because three songs proceed from three choirs; and he places here the three orders of the second hierarchy. **THEN IN THE TWO** penultimate dances: that is, in the two penultimate dances which belong to the third hierarchy: Principalities and Archangels; and the last, which are Angels. These new orders all gaze upward. Because the inferior always has in...

### CANTO XXVIII OF THE THIRD CANTICLE OF DANTE <note>Although the heading says Canto XXVIII, the following verses actually mark the beginning of Canto XXIX in modern editions.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'Q' featuring a man in a landscape observing two celestial bodies, likely the sun and moon, positioned opposite each other above the horizon.</image-desc>
When both the children of Latona, <note>Apollo (the Sun) and Diana (the Moon).</note>
covered by the Ram and by the Scales, <note>The zodiac signs of Aries and Libra, signifying the spring and autumn equinoxes.</note>
make of the horizon together a zone
as much as from the point that the zenith balances
until one and the other from that belt,
changing the hemisphere, unbalances itself;
just so long, with her face painted with a smile,
Beatrice stayed silent, looking
fixedly at the point that had overcome me.
Then she began: I say, and I do not ask,
what you wish to hear, for I have seen it
where every "where" and every "when" is fixed. <note>original: "ubi et ogni quando". In God, all space and time are present simultaneously.</note>

<column-break/>

It demonstrates that the number: the order: the distinctions: and the names of these angels were held by Dionysius, who [wrote] in the book *On the Divine Names* <note>original: "denominibus"</note> and *On the Celestial Hierarchy* <note>original: "de angelica hierarchia"</note>. Later, Gregory disagreed with him. Because Dionysius placed the Principalities in the third hierarchy: and in the first order: and Gregory placed them in the second order of the second hierarchy: where Dionysius placed the Virtues. But after death, coming to this heaven, he saw his error: and laughed at himself. And Beatrice concludes: that the poet should not marvel: that a mortal truth—that is, the truth of a mortal man—should proffer and manifest such a secret. Because he who had seen it up here in heaven: who was Paul the Apostle: when he was raptured to these circles: that is, to these heavens.

BECAUSE the poet has already treated the distinction of the nine orders of angels: it remains in this 28th chapter to treat: where: and when: and in what way the angelic nature was created: and what an angel is: and the number of them. He treats therefore first two questions. Then he describes the ruin of the wicked angels: and touches upon some doubts of the intellect: memory: and will of the angels. In the third place, he rebukes those who postpone and pervert the Scripture. And finally, he returns to the principal matter of the angels. In the beginning of the chapter, he demonstrates: that Beatrice, turned toward God, stayed silent long enough that she saw the doubts of the poet: but she stayed thus for a brief time. And this brevity and moment he declares by an excellent comparison, saying: that as

<page-num>XXVIII</page-num>
<header>CANTO</header>

[Beatrice] intervenes: that when the sun is in Aries <term>the Ram</term>: and the moon is in Libra <term>the Scales</term>, the opposite sign, in such a way that the sun is in the east: and the moon is in the west: they suddenly change place: because one rises to our hemisphere: and the other descends. WHEN both of them broaden; that is, the sun and the moon: as we have already said: one moving from the Ram: and the other from the Scales: they make a *zona*, that is, a belt of the horizon: because both are on the horizon. But one is for rising: and the other for descending. Therefore, when the moon and the sun stay in this form: Beatrice was silent for as long as the moon and the sun stay in the circle of the hemisphere where they are aligned. That is, where it is marked: as in a point, every *ubi* <term>where/place</term>: and every *quando* <term>when/time</term>: just as in the First Cause. From which places and times proceed: although God is not in a place: because He is infinite: nor in time because He is eternal. Nevertheless, from Him both one and the other proceed.

---

Not for gaining any good for himself,
which cannot be, but so that his splendor
shining back could say "**I subsist.**"
In his eternity beyond time,
outside of every other comprehension as it pleased him,
**the eternal Love opened himself into new loves.**
Nor did he lie before as if sluggish,
for neither "before" nor "after" proceeded
**the moving of God over these waters.**

<column-break/>

**R**egarding Beatrice in the divinity, she recognized three doubts that were in Dante: First, if time preceded the creation of the universe: Second, where such creation was made: Third, how it was made, whether in an instant or successively. Therefore, she first demonstrates the cause that moved God to create the universe: it was not to increase His own beatitude: because nothing can be added to the most perfect. Therefore, it was not to gain a benefit for Himself: because that cannot be. But so that His splendor, that is, His goodness, might be shown in creatures: and could subsist in created nature: and appear within it, and be the substantial form of every creature: because every created thing is good. Whence in Genesis: <note>original: "Et uidit deus cuncta que fecerat: et erant ualde bona"</note> *And God saw all the things that he had made: and they were very good.* And Boethius: <note>original: "Quem non externe pepulerunt fingere cause materie fluctuanti opus Verum insita summe forma boni liuore carens"</note> *Whom no external causes compelled to fashion a work from fluctuating matter, but the innate form of the highest good, free from envy.* God wanted to communicate His being and goodness with the things created by Him: and to demonstrate His perfection He distinguished them into three degrees. In the first are purely intellectual creatures: which are the angels placed above the heavens. In the second, purely corporal ones placed around the center of the world at the bottom: which are the elements. In the third, corporal and intellectual joined together, which are men and the heavens.

---

And in each degree there are greater, middle, and lesser. In the intellectual ones, we have said there are three hierarchies: higher, middle, and lower: and the orders: higher, middle, and lower. In the purely corporal ones, the higher order consists of the brutes <term>animals</term>: the middle, the vegetative ones, that is, trees and plants: and the lower, the elements: which have only being. The creatures joined of soul and body are in two degrees: because some have incorruptible bodies: and these are the movers: who move the heavens. Some are corruptible and these are men: And in the heavens, some are not "organized" <term>organato: meaning having distinct organs or limbs</term>: that is, they do not have distinct limbs: but have all their parts similar in nature and effect. And therefore the whole shines: and has in every part similar virtue. And this is the ninth sphere <term>the Primum Mobile</term>. But the eighth heaven does not shine entirely: and has different virtues in its parts: because it has different stars. Some have a single organ, that is, a star: and in that is its virtue: as we see in the seven planets. Furthermore, there is diversity in their movements. For the ninth sphere has a single motion upon its poles. Some have three motions: one upon the poles of the ninth sphere: the other upon their own poles: the third by the excess and decrease of ten degrees. And this is the eighth heaven. For all these motions it is necessary to come to a first immobile mover: which is God: who causes such motions. But men do not have diversity of degrees in their essence: because they are similar: and from a similar form receive their being. But they have degrees according to their ranks: which proceed from their temperaments <term>complexionii: the physical and humoral makeup of a person</term> and according to their will: which proceeds from free will. For some are suited to speculation and science: such as those who have soft flesh. But those of hard flesh are suited to sensitive delights: and pass into bestiality. Some are in the middle of these two degrees: and those reasonably bring things into action: and these are suited to civil life. But the more one's reason governs the sensuality: the greater is the praise. **THE ETERNAL LOVE OPENED HIMSELF INTO NEW LOVES**: God, who is eternal love, opened and manifested Himself in new loves, that is, in creatures: which, being newly created, all have an inclination, though varied, toward God. For God said: <note>original: "Fiat lux et facta est lux"</note> *Let there be light, and there was light:* for by this light is understood the angelic nature: and afterward He made the other creatures. And this was in His eternity: that is, in His being. **NOR BEFORE**. Many could doubt whether God created the world already six thousand six hundred and seventy-nine years ago <note>A medieval calculation of the age of the world from creation to the time of writing.</note>: because before such creation: and after that: He remained idle. To which Beatrice responds that divine love did not lie there lazy or idle. **BEFORE**, that is, before this creation: because the "running through" of God is the discourse of creation. **OVER THESE WATERS**: that is, over these creatures. Whence it says in Genesis: <note>original: "Et spiritus domini ferebatur super aquas"</note> *And the spirit of the Lord was moved over the waters.* Nor did it proceed "before" or "after": that is, before creation: nor after. And not without reason did he say it "did not proceed" because "proceeding" demonstrates time: And similarly, "before" and "after" denote time. Whence time is defined as the measure of motion according to before and after: as Aristotle says in the *Physics*. And similarly, rest denotes time. And therefore He did not lie in laziness: because as it is said, God is not in time: but in eternity He made the world.

<summary>This page provides a philosophical and theological commentary on the beginning of Canto XXIX, explaining God's motivation for creation and the hierarchy of intellectual and corporal beings. It refutes the idea of a "before" or "after" in God's eternity, defining time as a measure of motion that only began with creation.</summary>

<header>CANTO XXIX.</header>

all things. Wherefore from eternity he had in his mind the exemplary world: which afterward he produced into act and freely created time. Because if time is the measure of motion: and motion cannot be without a body/ time could not exist before the body was created.

Form and matter, joined and pure
came into being that had no flaw
like three arrows from a three-stringed bow
And as in glass, in amber, and in crystal
a ray shines so that from its arrival
to its being complete there is no interval
So the triform effect from its Lord
into its being rayed all together
without distinction in its beginning
Order was created and constructed
for the substances, and those were the summit
in the world in which pure act was produced
Pure potency held the lowest part
in the middle tied potency with act
such a bond <note>original: "vime", literally a willow-withe or binding-tie</note> that it is never unloosed

Jerome wrote a long stretch
of centuries of angels created
before the other world was made
But this truth is written in many places
by the writers of the Holy Spirit
and you will see it if you look well
And even reason sees it somewhat
which would not grant that the movers
without their perfection could be so long
Now you know where and when these loves
were created and how, so that extinguished
in your desire are now the three burnings
Nor would you reach twenty by counting
as quickly as part of the angels
disturbed the subject of your elements
The other part remained and began this art
which you discern with such delight
that it never departs from its circling

<column-break/>

It demonstrates that the creation was made in an instant without succession of time. It then sets out the three grades of creatures already mentioned: namely those that are incorporeal and simple form above the heavens: and those that are simple matter and are around the center: and those joined of matter and form. These three grades came into being by the will of God, which had no flaw, that is, to be <term>perfectos</term> <note>Latin: perfect</note>: because they were created from nothing by God. And they came into being as three arrows come at once from a bow that has three strings: And as the solar ray penetrates through glass or amber or crystal at once without succession: and in that same instant it is at the end as it is at the beginning: and so there is no interval from the coming, that is, from the beginning, and the being complete, that is, at perfection: so the <term>triform effect</term> <note>The simultaneous creation of pure spirit (angels), pure matter, and the combination of the two (the physical heavens).</note> of which we have spoken rayed from its Sire, that is, the Lord who is God, entirely in its being, that is, in its perfection. Therefore, just as the rays of the sun penetrate through those three bodies at once without succession of time or place: so the rays of the eternal sun, God, penetrate into these three grades of creatures without distinction in their <term>exordire</term> <note>Latin/Italian: beginning or commencement</note>, that is, in an instant, so that the beginning cannot be distinguished from the perfection. And finally, it concludes by saying that God <term>concreated</term> <note>Created multiple things simultaneously in a single act.</note> order, that is, in one and the same instant he produced the creatures we call substances: and the order of these three grades which was that those in which there is <term>pure act</term> <note>Aristotelian/Thomistic term for entities that are fully realized and unchanging, like angels.</note>, that is, only action because they are simple intellect, should hold the summit, that is, the top of the world: they were above the heavens: and these are the three hierarchies of the angels. And those in which there is <term>pure potency</term> <note>Matter that has the potential to become something but has no form of its own.</note> and not act: because they are only matter, should hold the lowest part: and low around the center as they are more ignoble. And those that are joined of act and potency, God bound in the middle with such a bond, that is, with such a tie that is never unloosed, that is, does not dissolve. For the heavens will always stay joined with their movers <note>The angels who guide the celestial spheres.</note>: and our souls, even if they depart from the body: nonetheless they will be reunited and will stay joined in eternity.

Jerome writes to Titus: <note>original Latin: "Sex millium non dum nostri temporis completur annorum numerus: Et quanta tempora a seculorum origine fluxisse arbitrandum est: In quibus angeli throni et dominationes ceterique ordines deo servierunt"</note> "The number of six thousand years of our time is not yet completed: And how many ages must we think have flowed from the origin of the centuries: In which angels, thrones, and dominations and the other orders served God." For which reason Jerome wants a long order of centuries to have passed from the creation of the angels to the creation of the rest of the world. But Saint Thomas Aquinas excuses him by saying that he speaks according to the opinion of the Greeks. But he and all the other doctors maintain: that in one instant the angels and the other creatures were created: And therefore he says that this truth is written in many places by the writers of the Holy Spirit. Furthermore, it can be demonstrated by natural reason which is formed thus: The angels were created by God to move the heavens: And if they had been created many centuries before the heavens, the angelic nature would have been in vain: Since the movers would have been without perfection: because they would have had nothing to move, the heavens not yet existing. NOW YOU KNOW: He concludes, having already extinguished the three burnings, that is, having solved the three doubts for Dante. Wherefore he understands where these loves and three grades of creatures were created, that is, in the eternity of God, and when it pleased God outside...

<summary>This page explains the simultaneous creation of the universe's three components—pure spirit (angels), pure matter, and the physical heavens—using the metaphor of three arrows from a single bow. It specifically refutes Saint Jerome's view that angels existed long before the physical world, arguing that "movers" require something to move.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the theological discourse on the creation and nature of angels from Canto XXIX. # CANTO XXVIII <note>Although the header says XXVIII, the text on this page actually contains the verses and commentary for Canto XXIX, lines 49–81.</note>

The beginning of the fall was the accursed
pride of that one <note>Lucifer</note> whom you saw
constrained by all the weights of the world.
Those whom you see here were modest
in recognizing themselves as coming from the goodness
that had made them so ready for such understanding;
Therefore their visions were exalted
with illuminating grace and with their merit,
so that they have a firm and full will.
And I do not want you to doubt, but be certain,
that receiving grace is meritorious
according to how much the affection is open to it.
By now, concerning this consistory,
you can contemplate much, if my words
have been gathered up without further help.

But because on earth, through your schools,
it is taught that the angelic nature
is such that it understands, remembers, and wills,
I will speak further so that you may see the pure
truth that down there is confused,
equivocating in such readings.
These substances, since they were made joyful
by the face of God, have never turned their sight
from Him, from whom nothing is hidden;
Therefore they do not have their vision interrupted
by a new object, and thus there is no need
to remember through a divided concept.

<column-break/>

beyond every comprehension of time: and as and why in an instant. NOR WOULD YOU REACH TWENTY COUNTING: Since he has shown where and when and how the world was made, he demonstrates that suddenly—and with less interval than one would reach in counting to twenty—part of the angels rebelled against God and fell, changing the subject of the elements. For by their malice, they caused the earth and the air, which were first pure, to become infected. The other part of the angels, already confirmed in grace, remained; and they began this art of circling God and contemplating all things in Him, nor do they ever cease from this circling.

**Beatrice declares the cause of the ruin of the rebel angels and the confirmation of the good ones.**
The origin of the fall, then, was the pride of Lucifer, whom the poet had seen at the center of the earth, which, as the lowest place, is where all heavy things fall. This one, most ungrateful for the benefits received from his creator and most proud, said: *Disponam sedem meam ab aquilone: et ero similis altissimo* <note>original Latin: "I will place my throne in the north: and I will be like the Most High." A reference to Isaiah 14:13–14, traditionally associated with Lucifer's fall.</note>. For this reason, both he and those infected by him fell. THOSE WHOM YOU SEE here around God were modest and not proud in recognizing themselves as originating from divine goodness; that is, they knew themselves to be creatures of God and created by Him, not for their own merits but by His goodness. This modesty was their merit. And because of this, their visions were exalted with illuminating grace; and it was also a merit that they accepted the illuminating grace and followed it. From this then comes the cooperating, confirming, and consuming grace. And these graces make their will full and perfect, because they want as much as is necessary. And it is firm because it cannot be changed. And finally, she concludes that it is a meritorious thing to receive grace, according to how the affection—that is, the will—is open to God. The meaning is that illuminating grace generates in you a will for good. Therefore, if you do not resist but accept it, you merit. Because of this, you can easily contemplate this consistory; that is, you can know for yourself for what reason these angels have merited, if you understand my words without other interpretation. A **consistory** is a gathering of cardinals around the Supreme Pontiff. And by this likeness, he calls the angels gathered around God a consistory.

**Beatrice's intention is to demonstrate that although we say there is intellect, memory, and will in the angel, it is nonetheless a different thing.** But in the schools of the philosophers, they are called such by **equivocation** <note>In medieval logic, "equivocation" means using the same word for two fundamentally different things.</note>. For in the angel there is no <term>agent or possible intellect</term> <note>Scholastic terms for the parts of the human mind that process sensory data into abstract thoughts.</note>, which are in the human soul, in which understanding is sometimes in potential and sometimes in act. Thus, one cannot speak of intellect in the angel except by equivocation and by likeness. As soon as the angels were joyful—that is, blessed by the face of God (the vision of God)—they never turned their sight from it; that is, their <gloss>in</gloss>telligence never ceased. Nor is the "sight" of the angel anything other than its understanding; nor is God seen in any other way than by understanding. And nothing is hidden from the face of God, that is, from His intelligence. And for this reason, the angels do not have "interrupted seeing"—that is, understanding interrupted by anything. Man, in his reasoning, often trips over something new and not well understood, which interrupts his discourse. But the angel, seeing all things in God, nothing can be new to him. And therefore he does not need to remember through a "divided concept." The angel does not understand through "species" <note>mental images or representations</note> which he abstracts from things, nor by composing and dividing, nor by discourse as man does; but he understands through <term>innate species</term> <note>knowledge implanted directly by God rather than learned through experience.</note>. Furthermore, there is not in the angel that will which is in man, although each is called "will." For man wills the good through the discourse of reason, and the angel in an instant. Therefore, as he understands more excellently than man, he has a more excellent will. **Memory**, similarly, cannot be spoken of in the angel except equivocally. For memory in us is founded in a bodily organ, and the angel has no body. Likewise, it is of things past...

<meta>catchword: past</meta>

<summary>This page explains the fall of Lucifer and the rebel angels due to pride, contrasting them with the 'modest' angels who accepted God's grace. It also provides a technical theological explanation of how angelic intellect differs from human reasoning, noting that angels perceive all things instantly in God without the need for memory or linear thought.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the critique of the pride and distractions of the angelic nature and shifts into a sharp rebuke of human vanity, specifically targeting theologians and preachers who abandon the Gospel for philosophical novelties and folk tales. # PARADISO

<note>original: "terite: et l'angelo uede in dio ogni chosa presente."</note> ...and the angel sees every present thing in God.

> So that down there, people dream while awake,
> believing and not believing they speak the truth;
> but in the latter there is more guilt and more shame.
> You do not walk a single path down there
> when philosophizing; so far does the love
> of appearances and the thought of it carry you away.
> And even this is tolerated up here
> with less disdain than when Divine Scripture
> is set aside or when it is twisted.
> People do not think how much blood it costs
> to sow it in the world, and how much he pleases
> who humbly draws near to it.

every thought of yours and every opinion. Although this is a great error: nevertheless, up here in heaven it is tolerated with less disdain than it is tolerated that you Christian theologians set aside Christian Scripture: and being ashamed to cite **Mark, Luke, John, and Matthew**, you always insist upon **Aristotle and Plato**. Truly, you twist it into various senses alien to the doctors who received it from the Holy Spirit. And you do not think how much blood—first of Christ and then of the holy martyrs—was shed to establish this religion: and how much it pleases God when we humbly, without seeking pomp, approach this Christian doctrine.

> To show off, everyone strives and makes up
> their own inventions; and these are debated
> by preachers, while the Gospel is silent.
> One says that the moon turned back
> during the Passion of Christ and interposed itself,
> so that the light of the sun did not reach below.
> and others say that the light hid
> itself, so that for the Spaniards and the Indians
> such an eclipse occurred as for the Jews.
> Florence does not have as many **Lapi** or **Bindi** <note>Lapo and Bindo were extremely common nicknames in 14th-century Florence, like "Tom, Dick, or Harry."</note>
> as the fables of this kind that are shouted
> from the pulpit every year, here and there.
> So that the little sheep, who do not know,
> return from the pasture fed on wind,
> and not seeing their own harm does not excuse them.

As for the Jews, who are in the center of the earth. This naturally cannot be: because a solar eclipse is caused by the interposition of the moon between us and the sun. Nor can it ever be interposed in such a way that it takes the sun away from all parts of the world at the same time. And in conclusion, he demonstrates that Florence does not have as many **Lapi** and **Bindi**—which names were very frequent in our Republic in the poet's time, and many citizens were called by these two names—as there are fables and useless things told by preachers, leaving behind useful things. Wherefore **the little sheep**: that is, the men who are like sheep; and the doctors who ought to instruct them are like shepherds. **Who do not know**: and for this reason they seek to be instructed in the Christian religion. **They return from the pasture**: that is, from the preaching, which is food that nourishes the soul, **fed on wind**: that is, on vain doctrine. **And not knowing their own harm does not excuse them**: because such ignorance is "crass" <note>In legal/theological terms, "crass ignorance" is a failure to know what one can and should know, and therefore is not an excuse for error.</note> and not excusable.

> Christ did not say to his first assembly:
> "Go and preach nonsense to the world,"
> but gave them a truthful foundation.

<column-break/>

He rebukes the modern philosophers and theologians who dream while awake. Because, just as one who dreams seems to see what is not there, so it happens to those who wish to distance themselves from the ancients. But their error is of two kinds. For some believe their own opinions to be the truth, even though they are not, and they sin through ignorance. Others realize they are not telling the truth, and yet, to appear more learned than others, they strive to defend what is false. And these, because they sin through malice, commit a greater sin, and their shame is greater. Wherefore he adds: you do not walk through the world philosophizing on a single path, because through malice you strive to pervert the sciences, because in you there is no true love for knowing the truth. But...

Beatrice greatly rebukes the preachers who, while they ought to explain the Gospel and demonstrate what brings salvation and what brings damnation to man, and exhort him to virtue and discourage him from vice, instead abandon such doctrine. To appear learned, they make up useless inventions, such as, <term>verbi gratia</term> <note>for example</note>: narrating from the Gospel that the sun darkened during the Passion of Christ. This is against nature, since the sun never loses its light; rather, it is hidden from us when the moon is interposed between us and it. And this can only happen during a conjunction <note>a new moon</note>, which was not the case then <note>The Passion occurred during the Passover, which is always at a full moon.</note>. Therefore, the preachers, to appear as astronomers, narrate all these difficulties. And then they "solve" them: some saying that the moon suddenly left its opposition and ran through six signs of the zodiac to join the ecliptic line. Others say that God willed the light in the sun to hide itself, so that such a defect of light was a common thing for the **Indians** (the eastern parts) and the **Spaniards** (the western parts).

Christ, after his resurrection, did not say: "Preach nonsense." But giving them a true foundation, which was the doctrine that the Holy Spirit infused into them, He said to his first assembly...

<summary>In this passage from Canto XXIX, Beatrice and the commentator condemn preachers and theologians who prioritize personal fame and philosophical jargon over the simple truth of the Gospel. The text specifically refutes pseudo-scientific explanations for the eclipse during Christ's crucifixion, emphasizing that vanity leads the "flock" to spiritual starvation.</summary>
<keywords>vanity of preachers, Canto XXIX, solar eclipse, Passion of Christ, scholasticism vs. scripture, Florence, Lapi and Bindi, theological error, Gospel, Holy Spirit</keywords>

--- Page 719 ---
<meta>This page continues the critique of vanity in preaching, moving from the distortion of scripture to the specific corruption of selling false indulgences. It then returns to the primary subject: the nature and infinite number of the angelic hierarchies as explained by Beatrice to Dante.</meta>

<header>CANTO XXVIII</header>

<margin>That is, to the apostles: "Go and preach the Gospel to every creature." Which sound [the Gospel] existed only in the cheeks—that is, in the mouth—of Christ, so that the apostles made of the Gospel a shield and a spear. That is, with it, as with a solid shield, they defended the faith; and with the same, as with a strong spear, they attacked the false religion of the gentiles. But at present, having abandoned the way of preaching of the apostles, they focus on telling jokes: that is—</margin>

> Which sounded so much in his cheeks,
> that to fight to kindle the faith,
> they made shields and spears of the Gospel.
> Now one goes with jests and with buffooneries
> to preach, and as long as there is a good laugh,
> the hood inflates, and nothing more is asked.

—playful words and buffoonery. And when with jests and buffoonery they have made the audience laugh, their hood inflates—that is, their head swells—because of the vainglory they take in it. **And nothing more is asked**—that is, they seek nothing else but to please the people.

---

> But such a bird nests in the tip of the hood,
> that if the common folk could see it, they would see
> the pardon in which they trust;
> Through which so much foolishness grew on earth,
> that without proof of any testimony,
> they would run to every promise.
> On this, Saint Anthony’s pig grows fat,
> and many others who are worse than pigs,
> paying with uncoined money.
> But because we have wandered enough in digression,
> turn your eyes now toward the straight path,
> so that the way may be shortened with time.

It follows that since such people preach not out of zeal for God but out of vanity—from which their hood inflates—it happens that in the tip of the hood <note>The "bird" refers to the devil, often depicted as a winged creature lurking in the shadows of deceitful men.</note> such a bird nests: he means the devil, who is depicted with wings; so that if the common people who hear the sermon could see him, they would see the "pardon"—that is, the indulgence—that the preachers promise them. The meaning is: because of the confidence the common folk have in every preacher, so much foolishness has grown on earth among men that they run to every promise of indulgence they make, although they have neither privileges nor papal bulls to testify to such an indulgence. And from this false promising of indulgences, which they cannot give, **Saint Anthony**—that is, the friars of Saint Anthony <note>The Order of St. Anthony was known for raising pigs; Dante uses them here as a symbol of greed and corruption.</note>—fatten the pig with the things they get from credulous and simple men. And others who are worse than pigs, such as harlots and the like, pay those from whom they receive alms with **uncoined money**—that is, false indulgences that are worth nothing, just as uncoined metal is not worth money. But because we have made a digression: while Beatrice shows Dante the angelic nature, it happened to go off-topic to condemn those who do not proceed correctly by failing to give true doctrine. Now wanting to return to the subject, she admonishes him to turn his eyes toward the straight path and return to the primary contemplation.

---

> This nature scales so high
> in number, that there never was speech
> nor mortal concept that could reach so far.
> And if you look at what is revealed
> through Daniel, you will see that in his thousands
> a determinate number is hidden.
> The first light that radiates through it all
> is received in it in as many ways
> as there are splendors to which it is paired.
> Wherefore, following the act of conceiving,
> follows the affection of loving the sweetness,
> which burns and cools differently within it.
> See now the height and the breadth
> of the eternal value, since it has made for itself
> so many mirrors in which it is broken,
> remaining One in itself as before.

Beatrice returns to where she had begun her digression and continues on the angelic nature, showing that it **scales in number**—that is, it descends in such vast numbers that there was never a man who could express it in words or conceive it in his mind. Wherefore the prophet Daniel, in the eighth chapter <note>The text cites the eighth chapter, but the quote is actually from Daniel 7:10: "Thousands upon thousands ministered to him and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him." Original: "Mille millia ministrabant ei et decies centena milia assistebant ei."</note> writes: "A thousand thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him." Here it is clearly seen that he uses a finite number to represent an infinite one. But of this we have spoken more extensively. **The first light**, which is God himself, which radiates—that is, shines into and illuminates all this angelic nature—is received in as many ways in that nature as there are **splendors**—that is, the angels. This is because as much light is given to each as he is able to receive. Wherefore the sweetness of love—that is, the love of God—which is received, **burns and cools**—that is, it boils or is lukewarm. This is because, as I have said, He infuses Himself equally, but is not received equally; rather, each one receives the divine vision more or less according to his capacity, and as much as he receives, so much he loves. **SEE the height**—that is, the infinite altitude; **AND the breadth**—that is, the latitude. He concludes with the immense magnitude of God and of His goodness, since He has so many angels in whom, as in mirrors, He is reflected. **REMAINING ONE in itself as before**—that is, remaining the same as He was before He created the world.

<summary>A scathing critique of corrupt preachers who trade in jokes and false indulgences for profit, followed by Beatrice's return to the sublime topic of the infinite number and diverse capacities of angels.</summary>
<keywords>Beatrice, Daniel, indulgences, Saint Anthony, angelic nature, corruption in preaching, divine light, mirror imagery</keywords>

<page-num>CLXXX</page-num>
<header>PARADISE</header>

### CANTO XXX OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE

**P**erhaps six thousand miles away from us
the sixth hour <note>Noon</note> glows, and this world
already inclines its shadow almost to a level bed:
When the mid-sky, deep above us,
begins to change such that some stars
lose their appearance down to this depth;
And as the brightest handmaid of the sun <note>The Dawn (Aurora)</note>
comes further on, so the sky closes itself,
vision by vision, even to the most beautiful.
Not otherwise the triumph that plays
forever around the point that overcame me,
seeming enclosed by that which it encloses:
Little by little my vision faded,
so that seeing nothing and love constrained me
to return with my eyes to Beatrice.

**I**f all that has been said of her until now
were all concluded in a single praise,
it would be too little to serve this turn.
The beauty I saw transcends measure,
not only beyond our reach, but certainly I believe
that only her Maker <note>God</note> enjoys it all.
By this passage I concede myself defeated,
more than ever by a point of his theme
was overcome a comic or tragic poet.
For as the sun does to the eyes that tremble most,
so the memory of that sweet smile
robs my mind of its very self.

<column-break/>

**B**ecause the poet’s sight becomes more refined with every hour, he becomes more capable of perceiving incorporeal things; and having already traversed the <term>angelic nature</term> <note>The hierarchies of angels described in the previous cantos.</note>, order requires that in this 30th Canto he express the essence and effect of the Empyrean heaven. Similarly, he shows how he was transformed, and once transformed, was able to see the supreme glory of Paradise. He first describes the appearance of the angels and the supreme excellence of Beatrice’s beauty. Then he demonstrates his ascent to the Empyrean, or the highest heaven. In the third place, he describes it in its proper form. Finally, he places an empty seat <note>This refers to the seat reserved for Emperor Henry VII.</note>. But returning to the beginning and to the verses already written: just as he willed that souls be represented in all the spheres—who are blessed according to the influence of that heaven—so in this ninth sphere the angels have been represented. And now, departing from that sphere, the sight of the angels gradually vanished from him, just as the stars vanish from us when the sun arrives in the east and the dawn brightens. But he describes this

time of dawn with mathematical reasoning, which manifests as follows: The globe of the earth, according to them <note>Medieval astronomers</note>, has a circumference of twenty-four thousand miles. And the sun circles it in twenty-four hours. For this reason, it happens that the sun passes through a thousand miles of it in each hour. Therefore, when it is the sixth hour <note>noon</note> in the east, which is when the sun is over our heads in the mid-sky, it is six thousand miles away from us. And then this world—that is, this hemisphere—inclines its shadow <note>original: "allecto piano"</note>, as if to say it strikes it down; because when the sun is in the east, the night (which is nothing other than the shadow of the earth) gradually descends so much that it levels with the earth and becomes nothing. And then the "deep mid-sky," that is, the high sky—that part of the sky in our hemisphere which is above us—begins to change due to the coming of the dawn, so that "some stars lose their appearance"—that is, they are not seen "down to this depth," meaning down here on earth. "And as the brightest handmaid comes": the poets feign that Aurora is the handmaid of the sun, and that she goes before him to prepare the journey. Therefore, the further the brightness of the dawn proceeds, the more the sky "closes." Not because the sky actually closes and covers the stars, but it *appears* to close because the light of the sun, being greater, obscures the light of the stars, which is lesser. And for this reason, it appears that the sky closes and hides its stars "from part to part even to the most beautiful," because the largest stars are always those that vanish last. "Not otherwise the triumph of the angels," which plays and circles always around the Point which is God, "which overcame me"—that is, it overcame my sight. For he seemed enclosed and encircled by the <term>hierarchies</term> <note>The nine orders of angels.</note>, yet He encloses them within Himself by His power, wisdom, and goodness. "Distinguished"—that is, He divided and separated my seeing and my sight little by little as I moved further away. Wherefore, both because I could see no more and because of the love I bore for Beatrice, I was made to turn my eyes to her. And deservedly, having to treat the divinity, it was necessary that I return to Beatrice—that is, to the <term>Scriptures</term> <note>The commentator Landino often interprets Beatrice as "Sacred Scripture" or "Theology."</note>, in which alone we have as much knowledge as human nature can receive.

**T**he poet has shown until now that the
more Beatrice has ascended from heaven to heaven, the
more beautiful she has always become, to denote that the higher one
climbs in the matter of theology, the more beautiful
things are found. But when he arrives at the summit
of his speculation where the source of
power, wisdom, and goodness lies—where the
divine essence is described in Trinity and Unity, in Divinity and
Humanity—so great is her beauty that if
all that has been said of her in various places were concluded
in one, it would do little to satisfy this turn.
And this is because the beauty of Beatrice in this state
"transmotes"—that is, it not only
exceeds the mode and measure of human intellect,
but he certainly believes it exceeds the intellect of the highest
angels, in such a way that no creature can
comprehend it all, but only God Himself.

<summary>This page marks the beginning of Canto XXX of Paradiso, where Dante transitions from the physical heavens to the Empyrean. The commentary explains the mathematical calculation of dawn to symbolize the fading of angelic visions as Dante's focus shifts entirely to Beatrice, representing Theology and the overwhelming beauty of Divine Revelation.</summary>
