<meta>The previous page introduced the transition into Canto XXX of the Paradiso, where Dante begins to describe the Empyrean—the highest heaven of pure light. The poet has just admitted that his powers of description are failing in the face of Beatrice’s transcendent beauty.</meta>

# CANTO XXX

Therefore he concludes that he is more defeated by this step of being able to describe, or with the mind to comprehend, the beauty of **Theology** <note>represented by Beatrice</note> than any poet, comic or tragic, was ever surpassed and defeated by any part of his theme. And for this reason, the mere memory of her smile diminishes my mind—that is, my memory's power—just as the sun diminishes the sight by its excessive light, which trembles all the more because it cannot endure it.

From the first day that I saw her face
in this life until this present sight,
my song has never been cut off from following her;
But now it is necessary that my pursuit desist
from following her beauty further in my poetry,
as every artist must at his ultimate limit.
Such as I leave her to a greater proclamation
than that of my trumpet, which leads
its difficult material to its conclusion.
With the action and voice of a ready leader,
she began again: "We have gone forth
from the largest body to the heaven of pure light:
Intellectual light full of love;
love of the true good, full of joy;
joy that transcends every sweetness.
Here you shall see both of the militias
of Paradise, and one in those aspects
that you shall see at the Last Judgment."

Like a sudden flash of lightning that scatters
the visual spirits, so that it deprives
the eye of the action of even stronger objects,
So did a living light shine around me,
leaving me wrapped in such a veil
of its brightness that nothing appeared to me.
Always the love that quiets this heaven
welcomes into itself such a greeting,
to make the candle ready for its flame.

No sooner had these brief words
come to me than I understood
myself to rise above my own power.

<column-break/>

From the first day that the poet saw Beatrice until now, although she has grown in beauty every day, he has nevertheless been able to follow her beauties with his style. But now she has become so admirable and so inexpressible that it is entirely cut off and severed for him to follow them further. Therefore, it is necessary that he desist from narrating them, just as it is necessary that every craftsman desist and stop in his art when he reaches as far as he can go. He does not express her beauty, then, because he cannot. But he leaves it to a "greater proclamation" than that of his "trumpet" <note>his poetic voice</note> which leads his difficult subject to the end; for he now wishes to ascend to the **Empyrean** heaven <note>the highest, non-physical heaven in medieval cosmology</note>, which is the end of his journey. **WITH THE ACTION** and voice of a ready leader: He cannot narrate what Beatrice was like, but he narrates what she said. For with the action and voice of a ready leader she said: "We have gone forth from the largest body," meaning the Ninth Heaven, which is the **Primum Mobile** <note>the "First Mover" that drives the motion of all other celestial spheres</note>. It is corporeal and the largest because it embraces all the others. We have come to the Empyrean heaven, which is pure light, because it is the formal light of all other lights. And he says it is **intellectual light**, as distinct from corporeal light, and full of true love—love of the true and supreme Good. This Good brings supreme joy that surpasses all sweetness. This light is nothing other than God himself. Hence John the Evangelist said: *He was the true light, which lighteth every man that cometh into this world* <note>original Latin: "Erat lux uera que illuminat omnem hominem uenientem in hunc mundum"</note>. And in this place, you will see both of the **militias** <note>armies or hosts</note> of Paradise: that is, the angelic and the human natures. Thus, the militia of angels and that of the blessed souls. The angels fought in heaven against the wicked angels, just as the blessed souls fought on earth against the flesh and the adversary; and now they triumph in the eternal and blessed life. But "the one"—that is, the human host—will be in those "aspects," as if to say in those splendors and beauties which you shall see at the **Last Judgment** <note>original: "ultima iustitia"</note>. There is no doubt that the angels are in their perfection, for all those who did not consent to Lucifer were immediately confirmed in grace and have their perfect beatitude. But because man in heaven does not have his completed body, he does not have his full perfection; but he will have it after the Great Judgment, because they will have resumed their glorified bodies. **ULTIMATE JUSTICE**: understand this as the corrective judgment, for both the rewards of the good and the punishments of the wicked will be made eternal.

The meaning of these verses is that just as it happens that a sudden splendor scatters—that is, breaks apart—the visual power, so that it deprives the eye of seeing, so the living light of that heaven dazzled and obscured him with its brilliance, so that he saw nothing else. And this was because the love that quiets and contents that heaven—that is, the Supreme God who makes the blessed souls content—welcomes him. Alternatively, "quiets this heaven" means it makes it so that it feels no motion, as all the others do. It draws man to itself with such a "greeting" (as it has done for the author) to make the "candle" ready for its "flame"—that is, to prepare him to be able to conceive the splendor of that glory.

A marvelous fiction and worthy of the poet's genius. In this, he first demonstrates that after the brief words spoken by Beatrice, he perceived himself to have risen so far above his human power and...

<sig>L. i.</sig>

<vocab>Dante Alighieri, Paradiso, Beatrice, Empyrean Heaven, Commentary of Cristoforo Landino, militia, Last Judgment, intellectual light</vocab>

<summary>Dante and Beatrice ascend into the Empyrean, the heaven of pure light, where the poet finds himself blinded by the divine splendor and unable to describe Beatrice's beauty. Landino explains the nature of this "intellectual light" and introduces the two "militias" (angels and humans) that Dante will encounter there.</summary>

<header>PARADISO</header>

And with new vision I was rekindled
such that no light is so pure
that my eyes would not have withstood it.
And I saw light in the form of a river,
tawny with brightness, between two banks
painted with a miraculous springtime.
From such a stream came out living sparks,
and from every side they settled in the flowers,
like rubies that gold encompasses.
Then, as if inebriated by the scents,
they plunged themselves again into the wondrous depth,
and as one entered, another came out.

And they entered the flowers. This river is the **illuminating grace**: which comes immediately from God: and therefore he places it here as the influence of this heaven. It is never-failing like a river: And it seems he intends for this river to be the one of which the canticle speaks: *Bless the Lord, all you waters that are above the heavens* <note>Original Latin: "Benedicite aque que super celos sunt domino." This refers to the Song of the Three Children from the Book of Daniel.</note>. Just as the river comes from the mountain and descends into the valley: so grace from God descends into man. By the banks, understand those of the **Old and the New Testament**: because both are irrigated and bathed by such grace. The grasses are virtuous works. The flowers are the blessed souls. The sparks are the angels.

"The high desire which now inflames and urges you
to have knowledge of that which you see,
pleases me the more, the more it swells;
But of this water you must drink
before such thirst in you is satisfied";
so said the sun of my eyes to me.
She added further: "The river and the topazes
that enter and exit, and the smiling of the grasses,
are of their truth the shadowy prefaces.
Not that these things are bitter in themselves,
but the defect is on your part,
that you do not yet have such exalted vision."

Still the vision, meaning the eyes. **Exalted**, meaning so noble. Not without reason does he call Beatrice the "sun of his eyes": because **Theology** is that which truly illuminates the intellect. Furthermore, he mentioned **topazes** to signify the whole and uncorrupted life of the blessed souls: because the topaz signifies chastity.

No infant rushes so suddenly
with his face toward the milk, if he awakes
much later than is his custom,
As I did, to make better mirrors
yet of my eyes, bending down to the wave
which flows so that one may find improvement there.
And as soon as the eaves of my eyelids
drank of it, so it seemed to me
to have changed from its length into a circle.
Then, like people who have been under masks,
who seem other than before if they strip away
the appearance not their own in which they disappeared.

<column-break/>

To have such new visual power that, although light is more blinding and takes away the sight the more pure and clear it is, nonetheless, no light could be so pure that his eyes could not have endured it. And then he saw a light in the form of a river: that is, a stream: which was **fulvid**, meaning shining with brightness, that is, with splendors. Between two banks painted with a miraculous springtime: meaning adorned with such grasses and flowers as are common in a wonderful spring. From that river issued continuously sparks: and on both banks they entered the flowers in a way that they appeared like rubies set in gold. Then, as if intoxicated by the scent of those flowers, they plunged themselves back: meaning they dived again: into the **wondrous depth**: meaning into the marvelous river. And as those entered the river, many others continuously came out.

Beatrice, as in other things, so in this one knows the poet's mind and will by herself. And therefore she tells him that the desire pleases her more: that is, the longing which inflames him and **urges**: meaning compels him to have knowledge of what he sees: meaning the river and the sparks, the more it **swells**: meaning expands and grows. And she adds that he must first drink of that river to be made joyful: and fulfill his wish to understand what this river is. Furthermore, she says that the river and the **topazes**: meaning the sparks that come out of it: and the smiling of the grasses are not yet for him the true spring: that is, blessedness. But they are **shadowy prefaces**: meaning announcements of the shadow: of the said springtime. And this is not because there is no perfect blessedness in heaven, but the defect comes from the poet who does not yet have <note>his sight fully prepared</note>.

The poet had understood from Beatrice how much it would help him to drink of the water of that river. Wherefore he bent down more suddenly toward the river than an infant does toward the nurse's breasts when he is awakened later than usual: from which comes having a greater hunger. And this he did to make **better mirrors**: meaning mirrors of his eyes. Already, as was said, he had achieved better sight: but now he had to make it perfect. Therefore he bent to the river: meaning he humbly asked for the grace which flows from God into his creatures: so that he may **improve himself**: that is, become better in it. And as soon as the **eaves of the eyelids**: meaning the edge of the rim of the eyelids, drank of this water: the river which before seemed long to me appeared round. By this he demonstrates that men...

<summary>Dante encounters a symbolic river of light populated by angelic sparks and soulful flowers, representing divine grace. Beatrice explains that these sights are mere "shadowy prefaces" of the ultimate reality, which Dante begins to see as he symbolically "drinks" the light with his eyes.</summary>

<header>CANTO XXX</header>
<sig>.L.ii.</sig>

Thus they changed for me into greater festivities,
both the flowers and the sparks, so that I saw
both the courts of heaven made manifest.

The circle is easy to understand as the return to God. **THEN AS PEOPLE.** After they had drunk of the water of his games, he saw the flowers and the grasses and the sparks in their true form, and they appeared to him as things far more marvelous. And it happened as it does with people who have been in "masks" <note>Original: "larue," meaning masks or specters.</note>—that is, in masks that are not beautiful—who, once the masks are removed, remain in their own form. Thus, the flowers showed themselves to be human souls, and the sparks to be angels. And because of this, he saw both the two courts of heaven. For in heaven, near to God, there are none but angels and human souls.

O splendor of God, through which I saw
the high triumph of the true world,
give me the power to tell how I saw it!
There is a light up there that makes visible
the Creator to that creature
who only in seeing Him has its peace.
And it spreads out in a circular shape,
so far that its circumference
would be a belt too wide for the sun.
All its presence is made of a ray
reflected on the summit of the First Mover <note>The "mobile primo" or Primum Mobile is the outermost moving sphere of the universe in medieval cosmology.</note>
which draws from it life and power.

This light makes the Creator visible. For just as the material sun, by reflecting its rays upon the earth, makes the things of this world visible to us, so this light makes God visible—not to every creature, but to that one who has its peace—that is, its highest good—placed only in God. Nor does it think of anything else, because its soul is pure from every contagion. This light spreads out in a circular and spherical shape, and creates such a great circumference that it would be too large to gird the sun. It is nothing other than a ray that comes from the highest light, which is God, and reflects off the summit of the Mover—that is, the highest part of the ninth heaven, which is the First Mover. This ninth heaven receives from that reflection "Life"—that is, motion, which is a sign of life—and "Power"—that is, the virtue to give its influence to all the other heavens.

And as a hillside mirrors itself in water at its base,
as if to see itself adorned
when it is rich in greenery and little flowers,
So, standing above the light, all around,
I saw mirrored in more than a thousand ranks
all of us who have made the return up there.
And if the lowest step gathers within itself
so great a light, how vast is the width
of this rose in its furthest petals!
My vision, in that breadth and height,
did not lose its way, but took it all in:
the quantity and the quality of that joy.
Being near or far there neither adds nor subtracts,
for where God governs without a medium,
natural law has no relevance.
In the yellow of the eternal rose,
which expands and rises in steps and breathes out
an odor of praise to the sun that is always spring,

<column-break/>

He rightly invokes the Splendor, by whose grace he saw the triumphant court of heaven, wishing to express what he beheld. Therefore, **O Splendor of God**, or Holy Spirit, through whom I saw, and without whom I could not see: for without illuminating grace, the human soul cannot transcend to these contemplations. **THE HIGH TRIUMPH** of the Church Triumphant. It is certainly easy to know the Church Militant <note>The "Church Militant" refers to Christians currently living on earth, struggling against sin.</note>, because its works are largely placed in active operations and moral virtues. But to comprehend the **Triumphant** <note>The "Church Triumphant" refers to the souls of the blessed in heaven.</note> with the mind is very difficult, because it is situated in contemplation, which is an incorporeal thing. **Of the true kingdom**: because this is the true kingdom, and whoever serves in this one, reigns. And all other kingdoms are servitude. **Light** of the Holy Spirit.

Just as it would happen if a mountain were in the middle of the waters, it would be seen from top to bottom—that is, from the upper part down to the lower. Thus the blessed souls, standing above the light all around, were mirrored all around in the said light. He imagines these souls were in more than a thousand seats—that is, in infinite seats. And he says: **All of us who have made the return up there**—that is, all those souls who, having come from God through creation, have returned to God for blessedness through their merits. **MY VISION in that breadth and height.** The poet's sight had become so noble that it did not lose its way and did not fail, neither in the breadth (the latitude) nor in the height, although each was immense. Instead, he understood and discerned the whole, and within it, the quantity and the quality. Human sight can discern all these things within a certain distance, but beyond that, the vision becomes confused. But in heaven, neither being near nor far adds or subtracts—that is, it does not make the thing grow or diminish. Being near does not make one see better, nor far see worse; but it appears exactly as it is. **FOR WHERE God governs without a medium.** Someone might say...

<summary>Dante describes the Empyrean where divine light forms a vast circular sea, reflecting off the Primum Mobile to create the "Celestial Rose" of blessed souls. He explains that in this realm, the laws of nature are suspended, allowing his vision to perceive the entire heavenly court regardless of distance.</summary>

<header>PARADISE</header>

> Like one who holds his peace and yet wishes to speak,
> Beatrice drew me forward and said: "Behold
> how great is the assembly of the white robes!"

The natural law of the earth does not apply to what was said above. But in the Empyrean heaven, in which God works directly and without the secondary causes <note>Medieval science believed God moved the outer heavens, which then moved the lower ones; in the Empyrean, His influence is direct.</note>, natural law can do nothing. Then it follows that Beatrice drew him like one who, out of a desire for knowledge, wants to speak but is silenced by wonder. And she drew him into the "yellow of the rose"—that is, into the center of that sphere, just as the yellow is in the center of a rose. This rose expands because the circumference of this heaven is vast and it "steps down"—that is, it is distinguished by its tiers. And it "breathes forth a scent"—that is, it casts a scent of praise to the "sun"—that is, to the eternal God who illuminates that heaven. This sun "always brings spring"—that is, it makes it forever springtime there. And she said: "Behold how great is the assembly and the number of blessed souls who, as John places them in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation 7:9 describes the redeemed in white robes.</note>, are in white robes." A "stole" is a long garment reaching down to the feet.

> "See our city, how wide its circle;
> see our thrones so filled
> that few people are further desired there.
> And on that great seat where you hold your eyes
> because of the crown that was already placed there,
> before you join these wedding feasts,
> shall sit the soul—who on earth shall be 'August'—
> of the great Henry, who to set Italy straight
> shall come before she is ready."

...those rebels. Others say there must be as many souls as there were angels who remained in heaven, so that our number is equal to that of the angels. Or truly, we say according to Aquinas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the dominant theologian of the era.</note> that God alone determines the number of the angels.

> "The blind greed that bewitches you
> makes you like the little child
> who dies of hunger and drives away his nurse.
> And there shall be a prefect in the divine forum
> at that time, such that openly or in secret
> he will not walk the same path as him.
> But God shall not long endure him
> in the holy office; he shall be thrust down
> where Simon Magus is for his merits,
> and he shall make him of Anagni go deeper."

...where he places the Simoniacs <note>Those who bought or sold church offices, named after Simon Magus from the Bible.</note> in certain narrow pits with their heads downward and their legs outside until another condemned person arrives at the same pit; and then the one who was there first falls to the bottom, and the newcomer remains with his legs outside. Thus, Clement shall come to the pit in Hell where his predecessor, Boniface of Anagni <note>Pope Boniface VIII, Dante's political enemy, who was born in Anagni.</note>, was shown to be.

<column-break/>

...it is likely that one who is far away sees as much as one who is near; and one who is high as much as one who is low. To which he responds that in things created by God, but through the means of secondary causes—such as the heavens and the elements and all things—

Beatrice concludes that the celestial seats which were vacant to be filled by blessed souls are nearly full. Then she points out a vacant seat adorned with a crown, and says it is prepared for Henry of Luxembourg, the fourth emperor <note>Henry VII, whom Dante hoped would restore order to Italy.</note>. And he shall sit in it before Dante "dines at these weddings"—that is, before Dante reaches that state of bliss. This man reigned during the poet's time while the "Gascon" Clement <note>Pope Clement V, originally from Gascony, France.</note> was sitting [in the Papal chair]. And she silently notes that we are in the final age and near the end. And it is the opinion of some that there must be as many blessed souls as there were—

She damns the blind greed of the Italians who, through avarice and ambition, drove away Henry, who wished to bring them back to the right path and to liberty. She makes them like the little child who, although hungry, drives away his nurse out of a tantrum. And she adds that at that time, there shall be a High Pontiff such that neither openly nor secretly will he walk the path of the Emperor. For he will seek to corrupt Italy and keep her in discord. This is Clement. But God will suffer him only a short time in the "Holy Office" of the papacy; for he will die and be pushed down to Hell where Simon Magus and his followers are punished. This place is described in the nineteenth chapter of the *Inferno*.

<meta>This page continues the description of the Empyrean, moving from the general vision of the light to the specific structure of the "White Rose" and the angels that inhabit it. It marks the transition to Canto XXXI, where Saint Bernard will soon replace Beatrice as Dante's guide.</meta>

### CANTO XXXI OF THE THIRD CANTICLE OF DANTE

In the form, then, of a white rose
the holy host <note>original: "militia sancta"; referring to the assembly of the blessed souls</note> displayed itself to me,
which Christ, with his own blood, made his spouse.

But the other <note>The angels</note>, which flying sees and sings
the glory of Him who enamors it,
and the goodness that made it so great,

Just like a swarm of bees that enflowers itself
one moment and the next returns
to where its labor is turned to sweetness,

Into the great flower it descended, which is adorned
with so many petals, and from there it rose again
to where its love forever dwells.

<term>Host</term>—that is, the angelic host which sees and understands the glory of God that enamors it, and His goodness which made these angels so many—that is, so great and so noble—and seeing this, it sings—that is, it praises Him. These angels descended into the great flower, namely the rose that he calls the seats of the blessed; this flower is adorned with as many petals as there are seats. And from these petals, it rose again to God, in whom their love always dwells. They act like bees, which leave their hives to enter flowers and then return to the hives where their labor—that is, their toil—turns to sweetness <note>original: "sinsapora"</note> because it produces honey. And certainly, this is an excellent comparison between the angels and the bees: because just as bees are prompt and ready in their duty toward the king, so are the angels in their service to God. Bees delight in the scent of flowers and conceive honey; so the angels delight in the scent of the good works of holy men and carry that sweetness to God. And just as bees drive the lazy and useless ones from the hives, so the angels drive from heaven the lazy who have not practiced good works.

Their faces were all of living flame,
and their wings of gold, and the rest so white
that no snow ever reaches that limit.

When they descended into the flower, from tier to tier <note>original: "di bianco in bianco"; literally 'from white to white'</note>,
they offered of the peace and of the ardor
that they acquired by fanning their sides.

Nor did the interposing of such a flying multitude
between what was above and the flower
impede the vision or the splendor;

For the divine light is penetrating
through the universe according to its worth,
so that nothing can be an obstacle to it.

Standing between the poet and the blessed souls, it seemed reasonable that they should have taken away his sight of the souls, and also created a shadow so that he would not receive the light. But neither was the case, because the light of God penetrates throughout the entire universe in one same way as far as God is concerned, but not as far as the one who receives it. For the divine light penetrates more or less into different creatures according to whether they are more or less capable of receiving it.

This secure and joyful kingdom,
crowded with people both ancient and new,
had its sight and love all fixed on one mark.

O triple light, which in a single star
sparkling, so satisfies their sight...

<column-break/>

Our poet, having already treated the celestial court in general, in this thirty-first chapter describes it distinctly and in detail. Thus, in the beginning, he describes the actions and the appearance of the blessed souls and the angels. Afterward, he invokes the Trinity and sets down his most happy contemplation. In the third place, he describes Saint Bernard and Beatrice returning to her seat. Finally, Bernard shows him the blessed souls, and especially the Virgin Mary. But in these first verses, summarizing what was said in the preceding chapter, he says that the holy host—that is, the souls of the blessed, who having campaigned in the world <note>Using the metaphor of "militia" or military service for a spiritual life</note>, triumphed in heaven. They were in the form of a white rose, which host Christ redeemed with His death and united to Himself; thus it was His spouse. The other...

The faces of the angels were red in the form of flame to denote their most ardent charity. The wings with which they flew were of gold because their work is most precious and shines like fine gold. The other white parts demonstrate supreme purity and cleanliness, or truly, perfect wisdom. We can also take them to represent the incorruptible nature of the angels, which, being confirmed in grace, can no longer sin. The white denotes the supreme purity of the angel because he never sinned. When the angels descended "in white"—that is, from seat to seat—they offered to the souls in those seats the peace which is beatitude and the charity which they acquire from God by fanning their sides—that is, by beating their wings. This signifies their operations. It was, then, a marvelous multitude of flying angels which, interposed...

This kingdom is "secure" from every danger and "joyful"—that is, full of joy. These two properties are not found in mortal kingdoms, where there are always dangers and joy is often lacking. "Crowded with people both ancient and new"—that is, which is filled with people of old, starting from...

<summary>Dante describes the Empyrean as a White Rose composed of the souls of the redeemed, tended by angels who resemble a swarm of bees moving between the souls and God. The commentary explains the symbolism of the angels' colors—red for charity, gold for precious works, and white for purity.</summary>

-> # PARADISO <-

...look down here upon our storm. <note>original: "procella"; Dante refers to the turbulent and sinful state of the mortal world compared to the peace of heaven.</note>
If the barbarians, coming from such a region
that is covered every day by Helice <note>Helice refers to the nymph Callisto, who was transformed into the constellation Ursa Major (the Great Bear).</note>
wheeling with her son whom she gazes upon, <note>Her son is Arcas, the constellation Ursa Minor (the Little Bear).</note>
Seeing Rome and her towering works
were struck dumb with wonder, when the Lateran <note>The Lateran Palace in Rome, which in Dante's time represented the height of earthly architectural and ecclesiastical grandeur.</note>
rose above all mortal things;
I, who to the divine from the human,
to the eternal from time had come,
and from Florence to a people just and sane,
With what great amazement must I have been filled!
Truly, between this and my joy, I was content
not to hear anything and to remain mute.

**BARBARIANS.** This is an excellent simile to demonstrate how great his wonder was in contemplating the kingdom of the blessed: and it is a comparison from the lesser to the greater in this way. If the barbarian and foreign peoples who come from the northern parts—which Helice, that is, the Great Bear, called the North Star <note>original: "tramontana"</note>, covers every day with her son, that is, with the Little Bear—on arriving in Rome were stunned seeing the miraculous things of that city: when the Lateran (that is, Rome itself, using the part to represent the whole) rose above mortal things—that is, surpassed in magnificence and power all other cities—how much more greatly ought I to have been amazed, who had come from the human and mortal world to the divine and immortal heaven. I had come from time, which is an extensive succession of life that can end, to eternity, which is the perfect and simultaneous possession of life without end. **AND FROM FLORENCE** To a people just and sane—that is, from men who in this life often wander into error, to the heavenly Jerusalem, whose citizens, confirmed in grace, cannot sin. Whence he concludes that between this wonder and his joy, he found pleasure not in speaking, but in remaining silent.

And like a pilgrim who finds refreshment
in the temple of his vow, looking around,
and already hopes to tell again how it stands,
Walking up through the living light,
I led my eyes through the ranks, <note>original: "gradi"; the tiered seating of the blessed in the celestial amphitheater.</note>
now up, now down, and now circling back.
I saw faces persuasive of charity, <note>original: "visi di carita suadi"</note>
adorned by the light of another and by their own smile,
and gestures graced with every dignity.
The general form of Paradise
my gaze had already taken in as a whole,
without my eyes having yet fixed on any one part.
And I turned with rekindled desire
to ask my Lady about things
concerning which my mind was in suspense.

The poet had reached the ultimate goal and that beatitude for which he had made so long a journey. Therefore, nothing remained for him but to contemplate the great temple of God, in which all the souls of the blessed, finding rest, enjoy the supreme joy. Thus, he went searching with his eyes, now up, now down, and now in a circuit, refreshing himself there like a pilgrim who has reached the temple—whether of Rome, or the Holy Sepulcher <note>In Jerusalem</note>, or Saint James <note>Santiago de Compostela in Spain</note>—where he had come by a vow, and finds refreshment in looking at the form and the decorations and the things that are within; and he already hopes for his return, and once returned, to be able to tell his people how that temple stands. Here the poet saw the faces of those persuasive of charity: in whom they were so inflamed with love that they persuaded those who saw them to feel that same love. And they were decorated and adorned by the light of another—that is, by the light of the divine radiance—and by their own smile, that is, by their own inner joy, and by gestures full of all dignity—that is, of all the virtues. And he has already understood the whole form of Paradise in general, but not yet in particular, because he had not fixed his gaze more on one place than another. Afterward, he turned to ask Beatrice about many doubts that held his mind in suspense.

I intended one thing, and another answered me;
I thought to see Beatrice, and I saw an elder, <note>original: "sene"; refers to Saint Bernard of Clairvaux.</note>
clothed like the glorious folk.
Diffuse was he through his eyes and his cheeks
with a kindly joy, in a pious gesture...

<column-break/>

...Adam and the others, whom Christ drew out of Limbo, and afterward the apostles and the other faithful of the primitive Church, and then the other virtuous and faithful ones up to this day. All these blessed ones, both ancient and new, had their faces and their love—that is, their contemplating faces and their wills burning with charity—turned toward a single mark—that is, toward God Himself, whom the blessed understand and love. He invokes God, then, that as He cares for heaven, so He might deign to look upon this low and mortal world, and says: **O TRIPLE LIGHT:** O Trinity who are the light from which every thing receives illumination. And although you are in three persons, you are nonetheless one single star, because you are one substance. And from this star sparkle the sparks that satisfy and content the souls in heaven. **LOOK DOWN** here upon our storm—that is, the tempest—for human life is continually in greater perturbation than a ship in a stormy sea. <meta>The catchword "SE" matches the "Se" at the beginning of the stanzas above, indicating a reference back to the barbarian simile.</meta>

When Dante turned to ask Beatrice about his doubts, she had already returned to her seat. Whence he rightly says that he intended one thing—that is, to speak with Beatrice—and another answered him: because Saint Bernard had already come, whom he portrays as an elder, that is, an old man, kind, joyful, and pious, as he is known...

Upon turning to consult Beatrice, he finds she has been replaced by Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, who will serve as his final guide.</summary>

<header>CANTO .XXXI.</header>
<page-num>.XXXI.</page-num>

...as is fitting for a tender father.
And "Where is she?" I suddenly asked,
wherefore he: "To fulfill your desire
Beatrice moved me from my place;
And if you look up at the third circle
of the highest tier, you will see her again
upon the throne that her merits earned for her."

Without answering, I raised my eyes,
and I saw her as she made herself a crown,
reflecting from herself the eternal rays.
From that region which thunders highest up
no mortal eye is so distant,
no matter how deep in the sea one abandons oneself:
As my sight was from Beatrice;
but it mattered nothing to me, for her image
did not descend to me blurred by any medium.

...she reflects onto others and teaches and illuminates. And Beatrice was as much higher than the poet as someone at the bottom of the sea would be distant from the region where thunder is born. <note>The region where thunder is "born" refers to the middle region of the air, where meteorological phenomena were thought to originate in medieval science.</note> Nevertheless, this distance was no impediment: because the image of Beatrice did not descend to him mixed through any medium. It was not, therefore, like among us mortals where our eyes see through a transparent medium—that is, "diaphanous"—such as air and glass and similar things. For this reason, our sight cannot extend beyond the proportion of the sense, or the object, or the medium which is the air. But in heaven it is otherwise.

O Lady in whom my hope flourishes,
and who suffered for my salvation
to leave your footprints in Hell, <note>A reference to Beatrice descending into Limbo to ask Virgil to guide Dante, as told in Inferno II.</note>
Of so many things as I have seen,
from your power and from your goodness
I recognize the grace and the virtue:
You have drawn me from a slave to freedom
through all those ways and all those modes
that had the power to do so.
Preserve your magnificence within me,
so that my soul, which you have made whole,
may unknot itself from the body pleasing to you.
Thus I prayed; and she, so far away
as she appeared, smiled and looked at me;
then she turned back to the eternal fountain.

...to him such magnificence of hers: and how she has made him free through knowledge and virtue. Wherefore the soul, first sick through vices and ignorance, is made whole as was said. Thus may she preserve it in this state until it unknots and releases from the body. After this prayer, Beatrice, as far away as she appeared, smiled. This was a sign that she had heard him: And not without reason did he say "as far away as she appeared," and not "as she was." Because although the divine greatness is most remote from the human condition, nonetheless His grace through His mercy draws near to us. Whence it is written: "God is near to those who call upon Him" <note>original: "Deus prope est inuocantibus se"; from Psalm 145.</note>. And she looked at him: as if to confirm and establish him in that true way. THEN SHE TURNED BACK TO THE ETERNAL FOUNTAIN. Which denotes that such grace comes from God and returns to God: as to an inexhaustible fountain.

<column-break/>

...comes to be like a tender father desirous of the salvation of his son: and he describes him as such as he was in the government of his monks. <note>Saint Bernard was the Cistercian abbot of Clairvaux, known for his fatherly care of his monastic community.</note> Here Dante said, "Where is she?" Which signifies that he sought in sacred theology to understand that which he will say shortly after. And Bernard answered him because the doctrine of this old man opened this place to him. Therefore Bernard replied that she had returned to her seat: which he says is in the third circle starting from the point: and that she had commissioned him to come to Dante to finish and fulfill his desire.

**H**e was so greedy for Beatrice, the author, that he did not answer Bernard: but suddenly raised his eyes searching for her. Furthermore, it denotes the habit of contemplating: which always raises the eyes of the intellect to superior and celestial things. Whence in the Psalm:
> I lifted up my eyes to the mountain. <note>original: "Leuaui oculos meos in montem"; Psalm 121:1.</note>

And Isaiah: <note>The commentator attributes this to Isaiah, but it is actually from Lamentations 3:28.</note>
> He shall sit solitary and keep silence, because he has lifted himself above himself. <note>original: "Sedebit solitarius et tacebit quia leuauit se supra se"</note>

Rays of eternal light descended upon the head of Beatrice: and she reflected them from every side: and thus she made a crown of them for herself. This signifies that the ray of the Holy Spirit descends upon the theologian and illuminates him: and he has the doctrine, a grace received.

**H**E OFFERS a prayer to Beatrice: through which he says that his firm hope flourishes—that is, lasts and is preserved. Because theology, accompanied by cooperating and consummate grace, brings man to such perfection that he always hopes for true beatitude: considering especially that she descended into Hell for his salvation when she comforted Virgil so that he might help him in the forest where he was lost: and finally she has made him free from being a slave, infusing him with knowledge and virtue. Whence:
> Virtues and knowledge have liberated the soul from the captivity of nature. <note>original: "Virtutes et scientie liberauerunt animam a captiuitate nature"</note>

THROUGH ALL those ways and through all those modes. As if he were to say, with fear of punishments and with exhortation of rewards that had the power to do that: that is, to withdraw from the slavery of vices to the freedom of virtues. With these words, then, the poet had thanked Beatrice for the benefits received. Afterward, he prays her that, as she has used clemency and supreme liberality toward him until now by granting him such great gifts, so may it please her for the future to guard and preserve in...

Saint Bernard explains her new position, and the commentary clarifies that in heaven, divine grace allows the soul to see clearly regardless of distance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Dante's encounter with Saint Bernard of Clairvaux in the Empyrean. Bernard has just revealed himself as Dante's new guide, sent by Beatrice to lead him through the final stages of his vision to the presence of God.</meta>

<page-num>CCCCXXX.</page-num>
->### PARADISO<-

The holy elder, so that you might perfectly
complete your journey, said:
"To which end prayer and holy love sent me;
Fly with your eyes through this garden,
for seeing it will prepare your gaze
to mount further through the divine radiance.
And the Queen of Heaven, for whom I burn
all with love, will grant us every grace,
because I am her faithful Bernard."

...principles, it is fitting that beginning from the lowest and most remote things and ascending grade by grade to those near to the divinity, the more one rises, the more one is diligent and apt to contemplate it. <note>original: "cipia" likely completing "principia." This refers to the Aristotelian method of moving from effects back to first causes.</note>

Like one who perhaps from Croatia
comes to see our Veronica,
who by her ancient fame is not satisfied;
But says in his thought as long as she is shown:
"My Lord Jesus Christ, true God,
now was your likeness truly made thus?"
Such was I, gazing upon the living
charity of him who, in this world,
by contemplating, tasted of that peace.

...He was also very devoted to Mary. For which reason it is fitting that through her intercession the poet can persuade Mary to intercede for him before the supreme God.

"Son of grace, this joyful being,"
he began, "will not be known to you
by keeping your eyes only down here at the bottom;
But look at the circles even to the most remote,
until you see the Queen sitting,
to whom this kingdom is subject and devoted."
I raised my eyes; and as at morning
the oriental part of the horizon
surpasses that where the sun declines,
So, as if going from a valley to a mountain,
with my eyes I saw a part at the outer edge
conquer with light all the rest of the front.
And as in that place where the pole is expected
which Phaethon guided poorly, it most inflames,
and here and there the light grows dim;
So that peaceful oriflame <note>The "oriflame" (Italian: *oriafiamma*) was originally the royal banner of France, used here by Dante to describe the intense, golden brilliance surrounding the Virgin Mary.</note>
was quickened in the center, and on every side
in equal measure the flame slackened.
And in that center, with wings spread,
I saw more than a thousand festive angels,
each distinct in brightness and in art.
I saw there, at their games and at their songs,
a beauty smiling, which was joy...

<column-break/>

Here Bernard comforts the poet so that he might "complete" (assommi), that is, lead to the summit and to the end, his journey; which will then be finished when he has arrived at the supreme God. **THAT YOU FLY** with your eyes through **THIS GARDEN**: i.e., run with your sight through the entire council of blessed souls. And he said **GARDEN**, interpreting the Greek word. Because <term>Paradise</term> <note>original: "paradiso"</note> in Greek signifies a garden. And he adds that by looking at this garden, he will "prepare" and make apt and suitable his face to be able to mount through the divine ray. Because, granted that the progress of knowing in man does not start from principles but moves toward principles <note>original: "Non sit a pricipiis sed ad prin..." This refers to the theological idea that humans learn about God by looking at His creations (effects) rather than knowing His essence directly.</note>.

With no less longing does one look upon the **VERONICA** <note>The "Veronica" refers to a famous relic in St. Peter's Basilica in Rome, believed to be the veil used to wipe Christ's face, which retained his image. It was a major destination for medieval pilgrims.</note>: which is the effigy of Christ. One who, to see it, comes to Rome all the way from Croatia, a northern and very distant part. And while it is shown, he says, stupefied: "O Lord Jesus Christ, was your image truly made like this?" In this way the poet became stupefied seeing the image of Saint Bernard, desiring to know if in this world he was truly like that. Because it appears impossible to human frailty to be able to comprehend the divinity without the intercession of Mary; therefore he brings in that Beatrice sent him Bernard, both because he was a very contemplative theologian and also very devoted to Mary.

**SON OF GRACE**: And rightly so, because we are not regenerated from the death of sin by our own merits, but by divine grace. Therefore we are children of grace. **THIS JOYFUL BEING**: This supreme celestial good will not be known to you by keeping your eyes at the bottom. As if to say: if you do not pull yourself away from the earthly mud and fly like an eagle toward the divine sun. **I RAISED MY EYES**: What this signifies has already been explained above. **AND AS AT MORNING**: He demonstrates by comparison that just as in the morning the eastern part is brighter than the western because the sun begins to illuminate it, so that most supreme part of Paradise was more lucid than the other parts. **WHERE THE POLE IS EXPECTED**: i.e., the chariot of the sun; putting the "pole," which is part of the chariot, for the whole chariot. And the fable of **PHAETHON** was narrated in Canto XVII of the first canticle. <note>Phaethon was the son of Helios who tried to drive the sun's chariot but lost control, nearly burning the earth.</note> **IT MOST INFLAMES**: i.e., it flames more; because the brightness always appears greater in that place where the sun is soon to appear. **SO THAT PEACEFUL ORIFLAME**: i.e., peaceful flame: because the most burning charity of Mary was the mediatrix to reconcile man to God. **AND IN THAT CENTER WITH WINGS SPREAD**: The spread wings of the angels signify the grace and the cognition that is dilated through all souls. But those were distinct because according to merits they are more or less illuminated. Their faces are of **BRIGHTNESS** (fulgore): that is, of splendor, which signifies charity. **AND IN ART**...

The text compares Dante's awe to that of a pilgrim viewing the Veronica veil and explains the symbolic light of the Empyrean.</summary>

->### CANTO XXXI<-

...was in the eyes of all the other saints.
And if I had such wealth in speaking
as I have in imagining, I would not dare
to attempt the least of her delight.
Bernard, when he saw my eyes
fixed and attentive upon his own warm heat,
turned his own toward her with such affection:
that he made mine more attentive in gazing back.

<column-break/>

...that is, of practice: because as I said, they have distinct <term>functions and offices</term> according to the diversity of grace and of glory. **A BEAUTY:** This was the Virgin Mary, who smiled at the games and songs of the angels; and this created joy in the eyes of all the saints. **AND IF I HAD such wealth in speaking.** A man can imagine much more and much better than he can express; nonetheless, the poet shows that even if he had as much wealth—that is, as much faculty in speaking—as he has in imagining, he would not dare to attempt the smallest part of her glory. **AND WHEN BERNARD saw my eyes attentive in his warm heat.** He turned his own to her, that is, to Mary, with such affection that he made mine more burning to gaze back. He concludes that the fervor <note>The "heat" or "furore" refers to Bernard’s famous mystical devotion to the Virgin Mary.</note> with which Bernard wrote his contemplations of Mary made the poet more fervent in contemplating her.

### CANTO XXXII OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE

Devoted to his pleasure, that contemplative <note>Saint Bernard</note>
assumed the free office of a teacher
and began these holy words:
"The wound that Mary closed and anointed—
she who is so beautiful at her feet
is the one who opened it and pierced it.
In the order that the third seats form,
Rachel sits below her
with Beatrice, just as you see.
Sarah, Rebecca, Judith, and her <note>Ruth</note>
who was the great-grandmother of the singer <note>King David</note> who in the sorrow
of his sin said: Have mercy on me." <note>original Latin: "miserere mei," the opening of Psalm 51.</note>

<column-break/>

Having already described Paradise in general, the author wishes in this thirty-second chapter to describe it in particular. Therefore, in the first part he describes the order of the ranks of the blessed of the Old and New Testaments. In the second, he removes a doubt regarding small children. In the third, he narrates the blessedness of our Lady and shows the angel Gabriel. In the last, he shows the principal "patricians" <note>The "patritii" are the high-ranking citizens or noble elders of the heavenly court.</note> of this court. Now returning to the first verses, he arranges the text thus: **That contemplative**, that is, Bernard; **Devoted**, that is, made affectionate, or filled with affection. **Assumed** and took up the **free office of a teacher**: because of his own free will he becomes my teacher and shows me all the ranks of Paradise. And he began thus: **She who is so beautiful**: that is, Eve, the first woman, at the feet of...

<sig>.L.Y.</sig>

<summary>In this passage, Saint Bernard directs Dante's gaze toward the Virgin Mary and begins to explain the hierarchical seating of the "Celestial Rose," beginning with Eve and other matriarchs of the Old Testament seated below Mary.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto XXXII of Paradiso. Saint Bernard is describing the structure of the Empyrean, specifically the "Celestial Rose" where the souls of the blessed reside. He is identifying the holy women who form a vertical line descending from the Virgin Mary.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>PARADISO</header>

You can see thus from leaf to leaf
descending down as I, with their proper names,
go through the rose down from leaf to leaf.

Of which Eve was the inductive cause: and therefore she pierced and opened this wound. And Mary, through her obedience and purity, was the inductive cause for God the Father to send His son to take flesh from her: and to redeem man from the slavery of sin. Hence the scripture says: **A woman damned us, a woman saved us** <note>original: "Mulier damnavit quae sanavit." This is a traditional theological contrast between Eve and Mary.</note>. Through the intervention of the wicked angel in the form of a serpent, Eve struck the human generation; and through the intervention of the blessed angel, Mary healed it. From the most proud Eve was born the disease; and from the most humble Mary was born the medicine. Thus he said that Mary closed and anointed—that is, mitigated and healed—this wound. In the third rank he places Rachel and Beatrice. Rachel was the wife of Jacob and represents the contemplative life, as we have already shown in various places. Sarah was the wife of Abraham, who in her old age gave birth to Isaac. Rebecca was the wife of Isaac, who gave birth to Jacob and Esau. These three are held in great esteem in the Old Testament: Rachel for her husband’s love, Rebecca for her prudence, and Sarah for her faithfulness. Judith, a most holy woman, through her greatness of soul, freed the Bethulians <note>The citizens of Bethulia, whom Judith saved by beheading the general Holofernes.</note> from Holofernes; we told her story above. The great-grandmother of the singer—that is, of David, who, moved by the fervor of the Holy Spirit, sang the psalms. He, having fallen in love with Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah his knight, had her husband killed in order to have her. Thus he committed adultery, homicide, and treason. Later, repenting for his error, he sang the psalm **Have mercy on me, O God** <note>original: "Miserere mei deus," the opening of Psalm 51.</note>. The great-grandmother of David was Ruth, the wife of Boaz; and Boaz fathered Obed; and he was the father of Jesse, from whom David was born. These are the seven seats: the first of Mary, Queen of Heaven; the second of Eve; the third of Rachel, and Beatrice is the fourth; the fifth of Rebecca; the sixth of Judith; the seventh of Ruth. Therefore, in the second seat are those who lived according to natural law, more in contemplation.

And from the seventh rank down, just as
until now, Hebrew women follow
dividing all the tresses of the flower;
Because according to the look that faith
bestowed on Christ, these are the wall
at which the sacred stairs are parted.
On this side where the flower is mature
with all its leaves, those have ascended
who believed in Christ yet to come.
On the other side, where the semicircles
are broken by gaps, those stand
who held their sight on Christ already come.

Imagine the rose divided down the middle lengthwise: and let that part over which Mary sits have its semicircles all full. In the middle of the upper part of these semicircles are the Hebrew women, and from there downwards, the little children who died before they had knowledge of good and evil. Similarly, to the left of Mary the Queen, imagine Adam; and next to him Moses and the others who earned that rank. In the following ranks, seven by seven, are the males who believed in Christ yet to come; and from the middle downwards are the little ones, as was said. And then, on the right hand, is Peter and John and the other apostles. Under Saint Peter, kept in the same order, are those who believed in Christ when He was present. Under Moses, who is on the left, is Anna; and under her, following the ranks, are the women who were saved in Christ when He was present; and then the little ones. All these seats are full. Opposite our Lady is John the Baptist, under whom in the second rank are Francis, Benedict, and Augustine; and each under himself in descending ranks, dividing as those above, are their brothers and monks and others according to their merits. From the middle downwards are the little ones saved by baptism according to the merits of their fathers. Therefore, in the middle between the men of the Old Testament who believed in Christ yet to come, and the men of the New who believed in Christ already come, are the women who believed in Christ when He was present, acting as a wall that divides them. And between the women who believed in Christ yet to come and those who believed in Him after He came, are the men who believed in the present Christ. Thus, to show that every blessed soul is saved through faith, he divides the souls of the saved first into three types: those who believed in Christ to come, those who believed in Christ present, and those who believed in Him having come. Each is divided into males and females, making six differences. Each has adults and children, making twelve. But the six categories of adults are from the middle of the rose upwards, and the children from the middle downwards.

<column-break/>

Mary: because she is in the second seat. After Mary is the one who opened and pierced the wound that Mary closed and anointed. This is the wound of human nature caused by Adam’s sin, which made all men incapable of being able to have eternal life.

AND from the seventh where Ruth sits downwards—that is, descending to the base of the flower of the rose—just as until now—that is, just as from the first seat of our Lady down to the seventh of Ruth—Hebrew women follow, dividing—that is, splitting—all the tresses—that is, all the leaves of the flower. In short, understand that beneath our Lady down to the base of the rose are souls of the Old Testament, always dividing by seven ranks as those first described were divided. Therefore, he who has merited more is in the rank that befits him in the first group of seven; and he who has merited less is in the rank that contains him in the second group of seven, down to the middle of the rose’s length. And from there down are the little ones saved in the faith of their fathers, similarly divided into seven ranks. Imagine, therefore, being at the bottom of a rose and seeing...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the final cantos of Dante's Paradiso. After describing the holy women descending from the Virgin Mary, Saint Bernard now describes the opposite side of the Celestial Rose, headed by Saint John the Baptist, and addresses Dante’s confusion regarding the ranking of children in Heaven.</meta>

# CANTO XXXII

Following that part of the rose divided lengthwise where our Queen <note>The Virgin Mary</note> sits, all the seats are full: because there are those who believed in the Christ to come, or in the Christ of the present; and therefore the flower is mature. But those who believed in the Christ already come are not yet full. However, day by day, all those who are saved go there.

And just as on this side the glorious seat
of the Lady of Heaven and the other seats
below her make such a division,
So, opposite, is the seat of Saint John,
who, ever holy, endured the desert and martyrdom,
and suffered in Hell <note>This refers to Limbo, where the holy figures of the Old Testament waited for Christ's descent after the Crucifixion.</note> for two years;
And beneath him, such a division was chosen by
Francis, Benedict, and Augustine,
and others down to here, circling round and round.
Now admire the high divine providence:
for both aspects of the faith <note>Belief in Christ "to come" (Old Testament) and "already come" (New Testament).</note>
will equally fill this garden.
And know that from the step that sits
halfway down these two divisions,
they sit through no merit of their own,
But by the merit of others, under certain conditions;
for all these are spirits released
before they had the power of true choice.
You can surely perceive this by their faces
and also by their youthful voices,
if you look well and if you listen to them.
Now you doubt, and in doubting you are silent;
but I will untie the strong bond for you
in which your subtle thoughts grip you.
Within the vastness of this realm,
a point of chance can have no place,
any more than sadness, thirst, or hunger;
For by eternal law it is established,
so that whatever you see corresponds exactly,
just as the ring fits the finger.
And therefore these people, hurried
to the true life, have not without cause
entered here with more or less excellence.
The King through whom this kingdom rests
in so much love and in such delight
that no will dares to ask for more,
Creating all minds in His joyful sight,
endows them with grace at His pleasure
in diverse ways; and here, let the effect suffice.
And this is expressly and clearly noted for you
in Holy Scripture regarding those twins <note>Jacob and Esau.</note>
whose anger was stirred within their mother.
Therefore, according to the color of their hair...

<column-break/>

**This** order and distinction we have shown just above: we have shown who is beneath the seat of the great Queen, and who is beneath that of Saint John. He was sanctified in his mother's womb, lived in the desert, and was a martyred, beheaded by Herod. And because he died two years before Christ, he stayed that time in Limbo. Both aspects of the faith: <gloss>that is</gloss> the faith of those who believed in Christ to come, and of those who believed in Christ already come. And know that from the step that sits: <gloss>that is</gloss> it divides the two "discretions" <gloss>that is</gloss> distinctions and divisions. In all the ranks from the middle downward, there are saved children, not by their own merit, but through baptism and through the faith of their parents.

**NOW YOU DOUBT.** Bernard recognized that Dante doubted whether these seats were given to the blessed little ones by chance or not; and therefore he promises to clarify it. And first he shows that in the vastness—<gloss>that is</gloss> in the greatness—of the celestial kingdom, nothing can happen by chance, just as there can be no sadness, hunger, or thirst. These cannot be there because sadness is a lack of joy; hunger and thirst are a lack of food and drink. But in Heaven there is perfect joy and nothing is lacking. Chance cannot exist because everything you see is established by divine law: and it responds justly like the ring to the finger: <gloss>that is</gloss> from the place to the one placed. <gloss>That is</gloss> they are placed in a location suitable to them, just as the ring is made to suit the finger. Therefore, these people hurried to the true life—<gloss>that is</gloss> these little ones who were hurried—<gloss>that is</gloss> hastened to the true life—it is not without cause that they are more or less excellent among themselves—<gloss>that is</gloss> between each other.

**THE KING THROUGH WHOM.** This kingdom rests—<gloss>that is</gloss> God the King, through whom the celestial realm rests; <gloss>that is</gloss> it reposes in such charity and joy that no will of any blessed soul is "daring"—<gloss>that is</gloss> has the audacity to want more. <gloss>That is</gloss> they have as much delight as they desire. He endows human minds with as much grace as pleases Him, and endows them diversely, giving more to some and less to others. And one must not ask why more to this one than that one, because the reason cannot be understood; but it is enough to know the effect. This is proven in Holy Scripture by two brothers born of one birth: Esau and Jacob. Of whom God said before they were born: <note>original Latin: "Esau odio habui Iacob autem dilexi." Translation: "I hated Esau, but I loved Jacob."</note>. These were the sons of Isaac and Rebecca, who, as soon as they were conceived in their mother's womb, created movement and disturbance between them. And God revealed to the father that from these two, two nations were to descend: and that the people descended from the elder would serve the people descended from the younger. Afterward, at the time of birth, Esau came out first, red in color; and after him, Jacob, small and dark, who held Esau's foot with his hand as if to say, "You shall not leave..."

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Paradiso, Canto XXXII. It follows the explanation that the souls of children in the Celestial Rose are ranked not by their own merits—as they died before they could exercise free will—but by the varying degrees of divine grace bestowed upon them at creation.</meta>

->PARADISO<-

Of such grace, it is fitting that the highest light
dignifies them with a crown. <note>original: "sincappelli" — literally "to be capped" or "to be hatted," here meaning to be crowned with glory.</note>
Thus, without merit of their own conduct,
they are placed in different ranks,
differing only in their primary keenness <note>The "acume" or keenness refers to the soul's capacity to perceive God, which determines its level of beatitude.</note>.

king and red hair: and Jacob black <note>The commentator is referencing the biblical twins Esau and Jacob to explain predestination.</note>: Thus it pleased Him to give more grace to Jacob than to Esau. Although Isaac loved Esau more, and Rebecca loved Jacob more, it was God’s will that Rebecca should be able to deceive Isaac. Therefore, the highest light of Paradise, which blesses the souls, must worthily crown them according to the "color of their hair" <note>This is a metaphor for the specific "shade" or measure of grace assigned by God.</note>: And finally, it concludes that the blessed little children, without the reward or merit of their own conduct—that is, of their virtue—are placed in different ranks where they have more or less beatitude; and this occurs because they are different in their "primary light," meaning they received grace differently when God created them. Just as when He created the angels, He gave more grace to one than to another, and for that reason, that angel held a higher rank; and through their subsequent obedience, each was confirmed in his rank in such grace. Similarly, when He creates souls, He gives more or less grace to one or the other. Afterwards, our good works are the reason why we do not lose the grace through which we merit beatitude; and as greater merit responds to greater grace, so does greater beatitude. Therefore, it is concluded that the cause of the difference does not lie in one's own works, but in the grace granted by God.

In recent centuries, it was enough
to have salvation through innocence
and only the faith of the parents.
Once those first ages were complete,
it became necessary for males to acquire virtue
with innocent wings through circumcision.
But once the time of grace arrived,
without the perfect baptism of Christ,
such innocence was held back down there <note>Refers to Limbo.</note>.

Look now upon the face that most
resembles Christ, for its brightness
alone can prepare you to see Christ.
I saw such great joy rain down upon her,
carried by the holy minds <note>The angels.</note>
created to fly through those heights,
That whatever I had seen before
did not hold me in such great admiration,
nor showed me such a likeness of God.
And that Love which first descended there,
singing "Hail Mary, full of grace," <note>original Latin: "Ave Maria gratia plena"</note>
spread his wings before her.
The blessed court responded
to the divine song from all sides,
so that every gaze became more serene.

<column-break/>

without me. One cannot, therefore, give a reason why God endowed Jacob with more grace than Esau, except because it so pleased Him. But this much is known: he who has more grace acts better, and he who acts better merits more, and through this acquires more glory. Therefore, according to the "color of the hair"—that is, as it pleased God that Esau should have that color...

Having shown the place of the children and how they are saved without their own merit, the text concludes that in the "recent"—that is, the fresh and earliest—centuries, the faith of their fathers together with innocence was enough to save them. The faith of the first age was a firm hope that, by living purely, God would have mercy on them and would send someone who would liberate them. And these two ages were the first, from Adam to Noah, and the second, from Noah to Abraham. After these came the third, from Abraham to David, in which the iniquity of men, idolatry, and concupiscence had grown; God commanded Abraham to be circumcised with his followers as a sign of the faith they had in God. At that time, they were saved through the faith of their parents and through circumcision. But once Christ came, which was the "time of grace," innocence, circumcision, or the faith of the fathers was no longer enough. Because without baptism, the innocent children were held back down there in Limbo and did not come out.

The text comforts Dante, urging him to look upon the face of Mary, who, because she resembles Christ more than any other, can through her brightness prepare him to see Christ. And looking, he saw infinite joy raining down upon her, carried by the "holy minds" of the angels, whom God created to fly through that height of heaven and to be messengers of His will. Whence they are called "angels," because in Greek *angelos* <note>original: "angelos"</note> means "messenger." AND THAT LOVE: That is, that angel full of charity <note>The Archangel Gabriel.</note>, who was the first to arrive in that place, spread his wings before Mary, SINGING "HAIL MARY, FULL OF GRACE" <note>original Latin: "AVE MARIA GRATIA PLENA"</note>: And this is the angel Gabriel, who descended to Mary when he brought her the message of the incarnation of the Word. AND TO THE SONG: That is, to the words that Gabriel sang, THE BLESSED COURT RESPONDED: That is, all the other angels. And through this, every sight became more serene and more radiant.

It concludes with the appearance of the Archangel Gabriel before the Virgin Mary in the Celestial Rose.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Paradiso, Canto XXXII. Having established that the seating of the innocent children is determined by God's diverse distribution of grace, St. Bernard now identifies the great biblical figures who occupy the highest tiers of the Celestial Rose, surrounding the Virgin Mary.</meta>

### CANTO XXXII

"O holy father, who for my sake endures
being down here, leaving the sweet place
in which you sit by eternal lot,
Who is that angel who with such joy
looks into the eyes of our Queen,
so enamored that he seems like fire?"
Thus I turned once more to the teaching
of him who drew beauty from Mary,
as the morning star does from the sun.
And he to me: "Such confidence and grace
as can be found in an angel or a soul,
is all in him; and so we wish it to be,
Because he is the one who carried the palm
down to Mary, when the Son of God
willed to load Himself with our burden <note>The "burden" refers to the human body and the weight of human sin assumed by Christ during the Incarnation.</note>.
But come now with your eyes, as I
shall go on speaking; and note the great patricians
of this most just and pious empire.
Those two who sit up there most happy,
for being nearest to the Empress <note>original: "Augusta" — a title for the Virgin Mary, identifying her as the Empress of Heaven.</note>,
are like two roots of this rose.
The one who on the left is placed near her
is the father through whose bold taste
the human race tastes such bitterness <note>A reference to Adam and the eating of the forbidden fruit in Eden.</note>.
On the right, see that ancient father
of Holy Church to whom Christ the keys
entrusted of this lovely flower.
And he who saw all the heavy times <note>Referring to St. John the Evangelist and his visions of the tribulations of the Church in the Book of Revelation.</note>,
before he died, of the beautiful bride
who was won with the spear and the nails.
Beside him sits, and beside the other rests,
that leader under whom lived on manna
the ungrateful, fickle, and stubborn people.
Opposite Peter, see Anna sitting,
so content to gaze upon her daughter
that she does not move her eyes while singing Hosanna.
And opposite the greatest father of the family <note>The "greatest father" is Adam.</note>
sits Lucia, who moved your lady <note>Beatrice.</note>
when you were lowering your brows to your ruin."
But because the time that puts you to sleep is fleeing,
here we shall stop, like a good tailor
who makes the gown according to the cloth he has <note>A metaphor for the poet's need to limit his description based on the remaining time and space.</note>,
And we shall direct our eyes to the First Love,
so that, looking toward Him, you may penetrate
as far as possible through His brilliance.
Truly, lest you perhaps fall back,
moving your wings believing to move forward,
it is necessary that grace be obtained through prayer.

<column-break/>

The Author prays to Bernard, who had descended from the seat granted to him in eternity to show him the celestial court: that he tell him which angel it is that seems more enamored than the others. And he responds that it is Gabriel, who made the announcement to Mary when the Son of God willed to become incarnate. **BUT COME NOW** with your eyes as I. "Come with your eyes as I shall go on speaking," that is: look at what I show you with my words. **To the Empress.** Namely, to Mary. **Is placed near her.** That is, he approaches her; because in Latin *iuxta* <note>original Latin: "iuxta" — meaning near, beside, or according to.</note> means "nearby." **The father.** Namely, Adam. **Through whose bold taste.** That is, by his daring taste; because it was great audacity to taste the forbidden apple. **The human race tastes such bitterness.** Because it tastes death and labor. **AND HE WHO Saw all the heavy times.** He who, before he died, saw—that is, foresaw—all the heavy and adverse times that were to happen to the Church, which is the bride: which Christ acquired when he was given the conflict on the cross and his side was pierced with the spear. This is John the Evangelist, who wrote the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> in which he predicted all the evils that were to happen to the Church, and the persecutions of princes and the simonies <note>The buying or selling of ecclesiastical privileges.</note>. **SITS Beside him.** That is, near Peter. **AND Beside the other.** That is, near the other who is Adam, sits Moses, who in the desert fed with manna the Jewish people, who were ungrateful, fickle, and stubborn. Ungrateful: because despite receiving innumerable benefits from God every day, they always rebelled against divine worship. Fickle: because at every hour they changed their purpose. And stubborn: because they were always angry with their leader Moses, nor were they content with anything. **OPPOSITE to Peter see Anna sitting.** His description is that on one side, between Mary and John the Evangelist, sits Peter, and beneath him follows, degree by degree, the men who believed in Christ as present <note>Those who lived during the time of Christ's earthly life.</note>; and these were in the middle between the Hebrew women who believed in the Christ to come and the Christian women who believed in the Christ who had come. And on the side of Moses, he places Anna, mother of Mary, opposite Peter; and beneath her the Hebrew and Gentile women who believed in Christ as present. And these are in the middle between the Hebrew men who believed in the Christ to come, who were beneath Adam and Moses, and the Christians who are beneath the Baptist. Anna, therefore, was so intent on looking at her daughter that although she sang Hosanna—which means "God save us" <note>original Hebrew: "Hosanna" — a liturgical cry of praise or entreaty.</note>—nevertheless, for that reason she did not move her eyes from Mary. **AND OPPOSITE the greatest father of the family**, who is Adam, sat Lucia, which means "illuminating grace," of whom we spoke in the second chapter of the first comedy <note>Referring to Inferno, Canto II, where Lucia acts as an intermediary of grace.</note>. Therefore, he places her among the Christian women. She moved Beatrice when Dante was lowering his brows to ruin. **BUT BECAUSE THE Time that puts you to sleep is fleeing.** The poet intends to make a final point in the contemplation of the blessedness of souls, not because there does not remain much to say, but because the time that puts him to sleep is fleeing: because after so long and...
