<header>CANTO</header>

Lady, you are so great and so powerful
that whoever desires grace and does not turn to you,
their desire seeks to fly without wings.
Your kindness not only succors
him who asks, but many times
it freely precedes the asking.
In you is mercy, in you is pity,
in you is magnificence, in you is gathered
whatever goodness exists in a creature.

Now he who from the lowest pit
of the universe up to here has seen
the spiritual lives one by one
Supplicates you by grace for such strength
that he may lift his eyes
higher toward the ultimate salvation.
And I, who never for my own vision burned
more than I do for his, offer you all my prayers
and pray they be not insufficient:
So that you may dissolve every cloud...

<column-break/>

nature of any animal that one can be both mother and virgin at the same time: because these are contrary things. Nor daughter of her son: But it happened in Mary through divine grace. Therefore, these things are not said without the wonder of those who hear them. From this results attention: nor are they said without the highest praise for her of whom they are spoken, which produces goodwill toward her. To this is added the third prerogative: that a mortal woman be made mother of the immortal God. To this is added the fourth: that she be more humble and more exalted than any other creature. To this is added the fifth: that she is the fixed limit of eternal counsel. Therefore, by narrating these things, one can acquire goodwill from Mary and the highest attention from the listener. And let this suffice for the preamble. Furthermore, because this <term>oration</term><note>A formal speech or prayer</note> is in the <term>deliberative genre</term><note>A style of rhetoric intended to persuade someone to take a specific action</note>, in which he wishes to persuade the supreme queen to obtain grace from God that makes him capable of His light beyond what a man still dwelling in the body can achieve. And since such a petition seems impossible, he demonstrates through this preamble that it is not only not impossible for Mary, but it is easy. For if the Most High granted her that she should be mother and virgin beyond human nature—Mother of God, daughter of the Son, Humble and high—He will very easily grant her that she make Dante capable of the divine light. Therefore, he shows his petition to be easy for her. Since Mary can do all these things which are above nature, she will therefore be able to show the supreme God to Dante while he is still in the flesh, though it be above human nature.

**VIRGIN MOTHER.** An unheard-of prerogative and supernatural privilege that a virgin should be a mother, and that a woman should be the mother of God. If, therefore, she was able to give birth to the Son of God, she will certainly be able to lead Dante into His presence. **DAUGHTER** Of your son: because she was the daughter of the almighty Father, who regarding his divinity is one and the same thing as the Son whom she bore. **HUMBLE:** In character and in words, she who said: *Behold the handmaid of the Lord* <note>original: "Ecce ancilla domini"</note> and in the psalm: *He has regarded the humility of his handmaid. For behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed* <note>original: "Respexit humilitatem ancille sue... beata me dicent omnes generationes"</note>. **HIGH:** *Because the mother of God, queen of heaven, is exalted above all saints* <note>original: "Quia mater dei regina celi exaltata super omnes sanctos"</note>. **LIMIT** Fixed by eternal counsel. She was not chosen without premeditation, but by counsel that is not human and mutable (which can have defects), but divine and eternal (which cannot be deceived). You so ennobled human nature with your infinite virtues that its Maker—that is, God, the maker of that human nature—did not disdain to become its own creation <note>original: "factura di te"</note> regarding the flesh. In your womb love was rekindled. God loved man, His creation, as long as he was without sin. Afterward, the sin of Adam extinguished that love. And finally, the incarnation of Christ, accomplished in the womb of the Virgin, rekindled it. And this advocate of ours was able to join divinity to humanity, and to ennoble our lowly nature, and to bring us back from exile, and to fill the empty heaven. From this, this flower has germinated: that is, the rose mentioned above. **IN ETERNAL PEACE:** because from here apostles, martyrs, and confessors were born, and prophets and patriarchs were reborn. Here you are among us: Here in heaven, you are a *midday torch* <note>original: "face meridiana"</note>—that is, such splendor as is in the sun at midday. So great a queen performs two miraculous effects: for in the pilgrimage on earth, she inspires sinners in their souls with the virtue of hope to reach heaven; and in heaven, she preserves the blessed with the virtue of charity. And truly among mortals, she is a living fountain of hope. These words are very fitting for Bernard, because he says:

> O man, you have a safe recourse to God where the mother stands before the son, and the son before the father. The mother shows the son her breast and paps; the son shows the father his side and wounds. <note>original Latin: "Securum habes recursum ad deum o homo ubi mater ante filium et filius ante patrem Mater ostendit filio pectus et ubera Filius ostendit patri latus et vulnera."</note> Therefore, no refusal can be given to you where so many signs of charity meet.

**YOUR** kindness not only succors. As Aristotle, the greatest sign of liberality, mentions in many places, it is to provide a benefit before it is requested.

Up to this point, Bernard has shown, in the form of a preamble, that the Queen of Heaven is able and knows how to help Dante's needs. Now he places his petition: which is that she favor the author so much that he may lift himself up to God. This he demonstrates to be honorable, since he has helped himself and continues to help himself as much as he can; because he has raised himself from the *lowest pit* <note>original: "infima lacuna"</note>—that is, from the low bottom of the universe, which is the center where Hell is—and has seen the spiritual lives one by one. And certainly, he who in contemplation has begun from Hell to know vice, and afterward has ascended to Purgatory to be purged of it, has made himself as capable as human nature allows...

<header>XXXIII PARADISO</header>

...of his mortality with your prayers,
so that the supreme pleasure may be revealed to him.
Again I pray you, Queen, who can
do whatever you will, that you preserve healthy
his affections after so great a vision.
May your protection conquer human impulses;
see Beatrice with how many of the blessed
clasping their hands to you for my prayers.

The eyes beloved and venerated by God,
fixed upon the speaker, showed me
how much devout prayers are pleasing to her.
Then they were directed to the eternal light,
into which one cannot believe that
a creature's eye could penetrate so clearly.
And I, who to the end of all desires
was approaching, just as I ought,
ended the heat of desire within me.
Bernard signaled to me and smiled
that I should look upward; but I was
already, of my own accord, as he wished me to be.
For my vision, becoming pure,
more and more entered through the ray
of the high light which in itself is true.

From then on, my vision was greater
than speech can show, which yields to such a sight,
and memory yields to such excess.
As he who sees while dreaming,
for after the dream the passion impressed
remains, and nothing else returns to the mind...

<column-break/>

...weakness <note>original: "imbecillita"</note> in receiving such grace as Bernard seeks for him. He therefore supplicates—that is, he humbly asks—that through your grace, and not by his own merits, he may obtain enough grace to lift his eyes—that is, his intellect—to the ultimate salvation. And Bernard wonderfully adds that he "never burned more"—that is, he never desired more ardently for his own vision or understanding than he does for that of Dante—to show how great the charity of the blessed is, who are no less eager for the salvation of their neighbor than for their own. He prays, therefore, to Mary that with her

prayers she may reveal and dissolve every cloud—that is, every ignorance—from Dante, which proceeds from his mortality, so that the supreme pleasure—that is, God, who is the supreme good—may be revealed to him. Nor is it enough that she intercede for the grace for him to see God; it is also necessary that God preserve his affections healthy after this cognition—that is, confirm him in grace and grant him such a habit in this third kind of <term>purgated soul's virtue</term><note>A state where the soul is not only free from sin but has no inclination toward it</note> that he not only has no inclination toward vice, but forgets it entirely. Let there be in him what the Aquinian Juvenal <note>Landino refers to the Roman poet Juvenal, who was from the same town (Aquino) as St. Thomas Aquinas</note> judges one should ask of God: "One should pray for a sound mind in a sound body. Ask for a brave soul that lacks the fear of death, which places the end of life among nature's gifts, which can bear any labors, knows not anger, and desires nothing." <note>original: "Orandum est ut sit mens sana in corpore sano. Forte posce animum mortis terrore carentem Qui spatiu uite extrema inter munera ponat nature qui ferre queat quoscunque labores Nesciat irasci cupiat nihil."</note> But the same sentiment is almost in Solomon: "Guard your foot when entering the house of God, and approach to listen." <note>original: "Custodi pedem tuum ingrediendo domum dei: et appropinqua ut audias."</note> He meant nothing else by "guarding the foot" than containing one's desires. For this reason he said, "May your protection conquer human impulses"—that is, grant me grace that the movements and affections of my soul do not decline into any sensuality. "See Beatrice with how many blessed ones clasping their hands"—that is, praying to you. For he who prays joins his hands together. He denotes in this place what he has denoted in many others: that the charity in the blessed spirits is most ardent. And just as the damned desire the damnation of all, so the saved desire their salvation. And if we look at the <term>oratory art</term><note>The structure and persuasive power of the speech</note>, it is an excellent way to persuade when we show that the benefit conferred upon us will be pleasing not only to the one who receives it, but to many other good people. Nor could Bernard ask for anything more perfect for Dante—that is, for a man still on his pilgrimage—than to show him his supreme good and then preserve his soul so pure from every perturbation that he would not depart from the good he had known.

The eyes of Mary, turned kindly toward Bernard the orator, showed how much devout prayers are pleasing to her. This is an excellent comfort to those who read, and a sentiment approved by every theologian. Then the eyes of Mary were directed to the eternal light—that is, to the supreme God, toward whom no creature can send a clearer eye. For Mary being <term>superexalted</term> above every other soul, it is fitting that she be more capable of the divinity than any other. Then the poet ended the heat of his desire, because he had already arrived at the goal and the ultimate limit of all his desires. It is not without reason that, point by point, his light became more pure, because the human mind in every cognition proceeds with the succession of time.

It followed, through the grace infused in me by the intercession of Mary, that my seeing was much more than my speech can show, for speech yields and confesses itself defeated by such a sight. And similarly, memory yields to such "excess"—that is, such an overwhelming force. And he shows himself to have become like one who has dreamed some great thing that has given him the highest joy or the highest wonder; afterward he is awake and the impression of that joy remains, but the things dreamed do not return to his mind. Therefore, the poet remains in a state of forgetting...

### CANTO XXXIII

Such is the sleep that almost entirely ceases
my vision, and yet still there drips
within my heart the sweetness born from it.
Thus the snow is unsealed by the sun;
thus on the wind, upon the light leaves,
the oracle of the Sibyl was lost.

<gloss>The words that the Sibyl writes on the leaves are lost: and she placed her answers on palm leaves crosswise; and then the cave would open, and the wind disturbed the leaves in such a way that it was difficult to return them to their original order to be able to read them.</gloss>

O supreme light that so far uplifts yourself
from mortal concepts, to my mind
lend back a little of how you appeared,
and make my tongue so powerful
that a single spark of your glory
it may leave to future people;
for by returning somewhat to my memory
and by sounding a little in these verses,
more will be conceived of your victory.
I believe, because of the keenness I endured
of the living ray, that I would have been lost
if my eyes had been turned away from it.
And I remember that I was more emboldened
for this reason to sustain so much that I joined
my gaze with the infinite goodness.

<gloss>Let more be conceived of your victory: because your glory will be more manifested among men, which conquers all other things.</gloss> <note>original: "Si concepa di tua uictoria"</note> **I BELIEVE because of the keenness I endured.** This demonstrates how his prayers were heard: because the power to sustain the keenness of the divine rays was strengthened in him. And it shows that if he had not kept his eyes fixed on those rays, but had turned them elsewhere, he would have been lost. But the boldness to sustain and endure the rays of that light was the reason that he joined his vision with God. Whereby one may know what a contrary effect the ray of divine light produces upon the eyes of the intellect compared to what the sun does to physical eyes. For the light of the sun, when it surpasses the physical eye, corrupts the sensory power of the sun <note>Landino likely means the "sight" or "organ of the eye"</note>. But the divine light, the more it grows in our soul, the more the intellect grows there; and the more we become capable of contemplating God.

O abundant grace, whereby I presumed
to fix my gaze through the eternal light
so much that I consumed my sight therein!
In its depth I saw that there is internalized,
bound with love in a single volume,
that which is scattered through the universe:
**Substances** and **accidents** and their habit,
all fused together in such a way
that what I speak of is a simple light.
The universal form of this knot
I believe I saw, because in saying this,
I feel myself rejoice more spaciously.

<column-break/>

...nor almost of all that he then saw: but still
the sweetness that proceeds from the
vision remains in his heart; and this remains in the fiction which he proposed in the

had this entire pilgrimage in a dream. But
the vision is as removed from his mind as
the snow is "unsealed"—that is, the form of the snow is lost
by the heat of the sun. And as by the blowing of the wind,
as we showed above, the Cumaean Sibyl wrote
her answers on palm leaves crosswise; and then the cave would open and the wind disturbed [them].

Concluding that the poet's memory
was not sufficient to retain that
which he had seen of God, he turns with prayers to Him:
that He might bring back to his mind a small particle of what
he saw. Because, as He is the supreme light, He can easily
illuminate him. He says then: **O supreme
light that so far uplifts yourself from mortal concepts**—that is, you who
so far surpass the human intellect. **LEND BACK
to my mind a little of how you appeared.** Give back
to my memory a part of that glory
that appeared to me of you in heaven. And because it is not enough
to want to retell part of what he saw, even if God showed it
to him again, but there was a necessity for such eloquence
that with it he could express that
which he had already conceived in his mind, he invokes Him
to make his tongue powerful to express a
spark of that light. And this is to give glory to
Him, and to be useful to men. For it
will not be without use to the men who will come to hear
some part of the divine glory. **THAT MORE**

**Abundant is the divine grace** to those who ask for it,

see the whole of the eternal light. And I saw in the
depth of the divinity, which "internalizes" itself <note>original: "finterna"</note>—that is, it makes a Trinity
of three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
I saw, then, in the depth of the Trinity,
bound in one volume that which is scattered through
the universe. **SO MUCH that I consumed my sight
therein:** I consumed as much of the intellect as is in me:
Because our intellect is not sufficient for even a tiny part
of such speculation. And well did I consume it,
because that is the ultimate of human desires.
Wherefore Augustine says: *Lord, you made us for yourself, and [our heart is restless until it rests in you].* <note>original: "Domine fecisti nos ad te : et in..."</note>

<meta>This page continues the commentary by Cristoforo Landino on the final Canto of Dante's Paradiso. The previous page discussed Dante’s prayer to God for the ability to record his vision. Here, Dante describes the overwhelming nature of the divine light and the immediate "forgetfulness" or "lethargy" that follows such an intense experience, comparing it to the ancient voyage of the Argo.</meta>

### CANTO XXXIII

A single moment brings me more oblivion
than twenty-five centuries have brought to that enterprise
which made Neptune wonder at the shadow of the Argo:
Thus my mind, all suspended,
gazed fixed, immobile, and attentive,
and ever more became inflamed by its gazing.

<column-break/>

> Our heart is restless until it rests in you. <note>original: "quietum est cor nostrum donec requiescat in te," a famous quote from St. Augustine’s *Confessions*.</note>

And the <term>Master of the Sentences</term> <note>Peter Lombard (c. 1096–1160), a hugely influential medieval theologian whose "Sentences" was the standard textbook for theology students.</note> writes that with the utmost modesty and fear we must treat of God, and listen with attentive and devout ears because there we seek the Unity and the Trinity: because in no other thing do we err with greater danger, nor is anything sought with greater difficulty, nor found with greater utility. In short, the poet saw in God, as if in a little mirror, the idea of all things created—corporeal and incorporeal, temporal and eternal—because God is the first cause of everything. In Him, in a single instant, are the past, the present, and the future, because all things that spread throughout the world proceed from that Principle and in that Principle are fused together, and to it, in some way, they return.

**SUBSTANCES** And accidents and their behaviors: created things have <term>substance</term> <note>In medieval philosophy, "substance" refers to the core essence of a thing that exists by itself.</note>, which is their own essence, such as, for example <note>original: "uerbi gratia"</note>, "man" is a substance. **Accident** is everything that does not stand by itself, but exists within some substance, **Such as Virtue, Vice, Humanity, Cruelty**, and similar things, which are in man like accidents in their subject. But in God there is no accident; rather, whatever is in God is God Himself. **BEHAVIORS**—that is, operations. **HE IS** a simple light, because in God no composition <note>the combination of different parts or qualities</note> can fall. **THE FORM** I believe I saw the universal form of this knot: as if one were to say the "idea" of the universe, which is in the breast of God, from whom all things proceed, bound together as if by a single knot. And not without reason did he say "I believe," because such knowledge is not perfectly given to man.

**BECAUSE MORE** By saying this, I feel myself rejoicing more widely. Because I feel that I rejoice more "at large"—that is, I take a broader joy in saying and manifesting this little bit. Or we might say, and perhaps better: because by describing this more broadly—that is, speaking more at length and not strictly where I might err—I rejoice, because I believe I am less likely to err.

**A SINGLE MOMENT** brings me more oblivion <note>original: "letargo"</note>. This demonstrates how great the joy of remembering that vision is. Even a single moment in which he does not remember such a vision brings him a greater <term>lethargy</term> <note>In Landino’s time, "lethargy" (letargo) was a medical term for a pathological state of forgetfulness or deep sleep.</note>—that is, that vision burdens him more in a single moment of time, and he is more troubled than Neptune would be if he were to wait twenty-five centuries (which would be two thousand five hundred years) and still not remember, through lethargy, the ship called the *Argo*. According to <term>Galen and Avicenna</term> <note>Classical and Islamic physicians whose works were the foundation of medieval medicine.</note> and other doctors, lethargy is an oppression of the brain involving forgetfulness and continuous sleep. But here he uses it to mean forgetfulness. As Petrarch also does when he writes, *Perhaps I scatter my words in the air. But I announce to you that you are afflicted by a heavy and pestilential lethargy.* 

But to clarify this passage, we will say that the first to find the ship was Danaus, son of Belus, with which he sailed from Egypt to Greece; before that, <term>rafts</term> <note>original: "rati"</note> were in use—that is, several beams bound together. This was an invention derived from the Red Sea, called the Erythraean, by him. But the principle of building those which they call "long ships," according to Pliny with the testimony of Philostephanus, came from Jason, whose navigation in Colchis we described above. He was the first, and to his ship he gave the name *Argo*. Because it was the first and very beautiful and excellent, it is likely that Neptune, god of the sea, felt supreme wonder and delight at it. Conclude, then, that the lethargy—that is, the forgetting—of a single moment of his vision was more troublesome to him than it was for Neptune to suffer the oblivion of seeing the *Argo* for twenty-five centuries.

---

At that light one becomes such
that to turn from it for any other sight
is impossible ever to consent to;
Because the good, which is the object of the will,
is all gathered in it, and outside of it
that which is perfect there is defective.
Now my speech will be shorter,
even regarding what I remember, than that of an infant
who still bathes his tongue at the breast.
Not because more than a single appearance
was in the living light that I gazed upon,
for that is always what it was before;
But because of the sight that gained strength
in me as I looked, a single appearance,
as I changed, was transformed before me.

<column-break/>

<note>Decorative initial C at start of commentary block</note>
It is a most true sentence that the soul which attentively regards the divine light becomes such that it is impossible that it should ever want to turn from it for any other sight—that is, to see any other thing. The human mind cannot help but want the supreme good, nor can anything be offered to it that would pull it away from that. And since "good" is the object of the will, and in that light every good is gathered in form—for outside of that light no good is perfect—it follows that the will, knowing God, is satisfied by Him alone. 

**NOW** my speech will be shorter. He excuses his own inability with respect to the infinite thing of which he must speak. He says, therefore, that his speaking will be shorter and more insufficient than that of a baby who still sucks milk—not only in narrating what he saw, but in narrating what he remembers, which is much less. And this happens because of God's infinite greatness, and not because He is varied or composed of parts. For in Him there are no varied appearances; rather, He is pure act and simple in...

<summary>This page analyzes Dante's overwhelming vision of the Divine, comparing the poet's immediate loss of memory (lethargy) to the ancient history of the ship Argo. Landino provides a theological and philosophical breakdown of substances, accidents, and the nature of the supreme good.</summary>

...intellect: it is unity and simplicity; and there is in Him a single and simple appearance; and He is always as He was before there was <term>substance</term> <note>The essential nature of a thing.</note> and <term>accident</term> <note>A property or quality of a thing that is not essential to its nature (e.g., color or size).</note>, or any thing created by Him. But this single appearance changed within me. Because the more I looked, the more, by divine grace, my understanding grew. Thus, by changing me, He worked upon me; but not upon Himself.

### CANTO XXXIII

In the deep and clear subsistence,
of the high light, there appeared to me three circles
of three colors and of one dimension;
And one by the other as rainbow by rainbow
seemed reflected, and the third seemed fire
breathing equally from here and there.
Oh, how short is speech, and how faint
to my concept! and this, compared to what I saw,
is so much that it does not suffice to say "little."
O supreme light, that dwellest in thyself alone,
alone understandest thyself, and, understood by thyself
and understanding, smilest upon thyself!
This circling, which appeared to be conceived
in thee as a reflected light,
when surveyed by my eyes for a while,
within itself, of its own very color,
seemed painted with our image;
wherefore my sight was wholly set upon it.

<column-break/>

Already our poet has arrived at the summit of his contemplation, who, as a finite thing within the infinite, as a creature within the creator, contains all that is lacking. Nevertheless, as much as the human intellect is able, he describes the divine essence regarding the Trinity within the Unity, and regarding the humanity within the divinity. And first, he strives to express the Trinity in Unity in a spherical form, positing three circles of three colors—not because in God, who is simple and incorporeal, colors and figures actually occur, but because it is difficult for the human mind to comprehend invisible things without the likeness of visible ones. Therefore, not only Dante, but many philosophers describe the divinity under such figures. The poet thus expresses one essence in three persons under a circular figure. And many centuries before, <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term> <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a syncretism of the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth, credited with ancient mystical writings.</note> had defined God as a circular sphere. Because the knowledge of God is the knowledge of Himself, He is from Himself within Himself, like a circle without beginning and without end. **IN THE DEEP Subsistence:** that is, in the divine essence. **OF THE HIGH Light:** that is, of God. **THERE APPEARED TO ME Three circles:** by which he denotes the three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and **one dimension**, because they are equally eternal, immense, and omnipotent, for they are one. **AND ONE By the other as rainbow by rainbow:** Through this comparison, he describes the union of the persons and their production within the divine substance, demonstrating that just as in a rainbow (the celestial arc) there are multiple circles of different equal colors that seem to reflect one from another, and yet it is a single arc; so in that divine sphere there were three circles distinct in color and reflected, yet they were one sphere, and not three, but one divinity. **AND THE ONE:** that is, the Son, seemed reflected from the other, that is, from the Father, because only the Father is the generator, and the Son is begotten but not made. **THE THIRD** which is the Holy Spirit **SEEMED FIRE:** because it is the love which proceeds eternally **FROM HERE:** that is, from the Father, **AND FROM THERE:** that is, from the Son. And this is the true faith, although some heretics <note>A reference to the theological dispute regarding the "Filioque" clause, which contributed to the split between the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches.</note> falsely affirm that He proceeds only from the Father. **OH, HOW:** Deservedly he exclaims, grieving that his speech is not sufficient to express the Trinity; and **how faint:** as if to show that just as faint words are not understood, so he cannot express what he feels and what he conceives. Because, as Augustine says: <note>original: "Deus uerius cogitatur quam exprimitur: Et uerius est quam cogitetur."</note> "God is more truly thought than expressed, and He is more truly than He is thought." And certainly, it is true that we can think and conceive more of God in our souls than we can express. And nevertheless, God is still a much greater thing than we can conceive or think. And therefore he adds that it is not a "little" thing if, before we can know what He is, we at least know what He is not. **AND THIS:** which I have conceived is **so much:** that is, of such a measure in respect to what I saw, that it is not enough to say it is "little," but one must say it is a most minute thing. **O SUPREME LIGHT:** from which every other light is born. **THAT DWELLEST In thyself alone:** That you rest in yourself alone, because you cannot be contained except by yourself, nor understood except by yourself. **AND UNDERSTANDING THYSELF:** which no one can do but you, because no one understands God except God. **SMILEST UPON ME:** as if to say, you show yourself to me joyfully. For man understands of God only as much as God manifests Himself to him. **This circling thus conceived**, as we have said above, appeared in you **AS REFLECTED LIGHT:** because one circle reflected its light into the other. **WHEN SURVEYED** by my eyes **FOR A WHILE:** as if to say, seen by me, but in a very small part. **WITHIN ITSELF:** He arranges it thus: this circling appeared within itself **painted:** that is, figured with its own brilliance, because it receives nothing from outside of itself. **With our image:** that is, the human figure; because here is the humanity of Christ joined with the divinity. And this I saw because **my sight:** that is, all my visual power, was placed within it. Which signifies that he had put all the strength of his intellect into contemplating that.

<summary>Dante describes his vision of the Holy Trinity as three concentric circles of different colors but equal size, and the mystery of the Incarnation where a human face appears within the divine light. Landino's commentary explains these metaphors through the lenses of Thomistic theology, Augustinian philosophy, and Hermetic traditions.</summary>
<keywords>Holy Trinity, Incarnation of Christ, Divine Light, Hermes Trismegistus, St. Augustine, religious metaphor, human intellect, Filioque controversy</keywords>

### CANTO XXXIII

Like the geometer who applies himself entirely
to measure the circle and does not find,
by thinking, that principle which he lacks <note>original: "indige"; the starting point or mathematical principle needed to square the circle.</note>.
Such was I at that new sight;
I wished to know how the image <note>The human form of Christ perceived within the divine circles of the Trinity.</note>
conformed to the circle and how it finds its place there;
but my own feathers were not for this <note>The poet's own intellectual abilities or "wings" were insufficient for such a height.</note>,
except that my mind was struck
by a flash in which its will was fulfilled.
Here power failed the high fantasy;
but already my desire and will were turned,
like a wheel that is moved evenly,
by the Love that moves the sun and the other stars.

<column-break/>

He desires to know how humanity was joined with divinity. And he demonstrates that he was as fixed in this inquiry as the geometer who wishes to measure the circle and does not find that principle which he lacks—that is, of which he has need. Therefore, such was Dante at that new sight—that is, in that image which he had newly seen in the circles of divinity. And he desired to know how it is fitting, and how the image—that is, the image of humanity—is adapted to the circle <note>Representing the divine nature.</note> of divinity, and how such a union was made. But his own feathers—that is, my powers, my virtues, my doctrines—were not for this—that is, they were not sufficient for this. Except that the mind was struck by a flash and splendor of new divine grace that illuminated me. And in this came its will—that is, the will of said mind—that is, the will of his mind was fulfilled

<column-break/>

the will of his mind: And the poet wished to write what he had understood. But the fantasy was not so powerful that it could grasp in form what the poet could write. But the divine love and the Holy Spirit, which moves the sun and the stars—because the mover of all already turned my desire and my will—that is, my desire and my volition—like a wheel that is moved evenly. In essence, he expresses that the human mind, moved by God, moves equally toward all things, accordinging its will with the will of God. And for this reason, God not giving him more power, he accords his will with the divine will. Therefore, we shall say that, power failing me, the love—that is, the Holy Spirit, which moves the sun and the other stars—that is, all creatures—to love their creator, turned to will what I was able to do. And it is certainly a most excellent end to such a work, because in one sentence it concludes many things. First, it demonstrates that although the human mind is most greedy to know everything, nevertheless each one should be content with as much light as divine grace provides. Furthermore, it warns the reader that they should not recognize the excellence of God from his words; because he who is finite cannot, in the smallest part, comprehend the infinite. And from those same words it is drawn that the small part he has expressed, he has been able to express not by his own wit, but by divine grace. For which thing, I, similarly imitating the footsteps of such a poet, ingenuously confess not to have known how to interpret and open with perfection the highest senses which lie hidden in this Comedy under poetic veils. And that small part which I have been able to do, I do not arrogantly attribute to myself, but humbly recognize as from divine grace; because as Paul said, so I affirm of myself: **By the grace of God I am what I am** <note>original: "Gratia dei id sum quod sum"; quoting 1 Corinthians 15:10.</note>. Wherefore, if there is any thing of truth here, let the praise be to that Truth, the giver of all truth. And let all errors be attributed to my weak wit. And if any place should be found in this our commentary that is either entirely contrary or in any part discordant from our orthodox religion, let it be immediately corrected, condemning in that not my will—which I affirm to be pure and sincere—but the little doctrine which I wish were not as deficient in me as I know it to be.
